## Volume Front Matter

### Series Title Page

**The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, and Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the Apostolic Age down to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reissue of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived through the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, collated with one another and with certain manuscript codices, corrected with the greatest diligence; continually illustrated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each author of any importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject treated; augmented with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and also with works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever any Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it is readily apparent to the reader which Fathers have commented on the individual books of Scripture, and in which places in their works. An extremely accurate edition, easily preferable to all others if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the very convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the whole work, the low price, and above all this collection—one, methodical, and chronological—of six hundred fragments and short works previously scattered here and there, but now gathered for the first time in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.**

**First Series**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers of the Latin Church, from Tertullian to Gregory the Great. Edited by J. P. Migne, publisher of the Complete Courses in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning.

## Volume LII of Patrology

**The Complete Works of Saint Peter Chrysologus, Archbishop of Ravenna**

Reprinted according to the most carefully corrected recension of Sebastian Pauli, who supplied a preface and added notes containing collations of manuscript codices, selected observations of Domenico Mita, the various readings of Latinius, and the corrections of Meursius. This edition, more complete than all previous ones, is enriched with sermons taken both from Saint Augustine and from Luca d’Acherio, together with three Lives of Saint Chrysologus and the dissertation of Joseph Amadesius on the metropolitan Church of Ravenna.

There follow the complete writings of Saints Valerian and Nicetas, bishops of Cemelia and Aquileia, expressed and corrected with the greatest accuracy according to the labors of Jacques Sirmond, Braida, and the Most Eminent Cardinal Mai.

**Single volume. One volume. Price: 7 francs.**

Available from the publisher, Paris, on the street called d’Amboise, near the Barrière d’Enfer, or Petit-Montrouge. 1846.

# Saint Peter Chrysologus

[Col. 0009]

## Sebastian Pauli’s Preface to This New Edition of Saint Peter Chrysologus

I think no one is unaware that the sermons of Saint Peter, Archbishop of Ravenna—whose eloquence in speaking earned him the name Chrysologus—were regarded during the last two centuries by ecclesiastical writers and preachers of the word of God as a source of delight. Their frequent editions attest this: editions appeared at intervals of scarcely a year in Mainz, Cologne, Paris, Venice, and elsewhere, so that the principal concern of the printers of those times seems to have been, in publishing Chrysologus’s sermons, to snatch the work from one another’s hands and forestall an opportunity for profit.

In our own age, when good things are despised and better things are nevertheless accepted only with difficulty, they have begun to be held in lower esteem. Some complain that his eloquence is weak; that the force of his speech is loose; that his discourse is sprinkled to excess with somewhat cold maxims and, though brief, is nevertheless diffuse; that in it one misses not indeed a lively, but a solid intellect; that his style is too compressed, from which obscurity sometimes arises; and that one searches in vain more than once for natural ease and unaffected purity.

I admit that none of these criticisms is advanced falsely or unfairly. Yet a more equitable judgment of Chrysologus would have treated him more gently and would have attributed some of these alleged faults to the character of the people of Ravenna and of the Greeks living among them. Their bodily and intellectual vigor had been weakened, and they disdained stronger eloquence, being attracted instead by such embellishments of language.

The chief duty of a wise and sacred orator, however, is to adapt himself to the ears of the common people, so that the people may hear the truth, caring nothing whether it is served to them in golden vessels or in vessels of clay and earthenware. Gregory of Nyssa rightly praises this care and diligence in Saint Basil at the beginning of his explanation of the Hexaemeron, addressed to his brother Peter. It is especially conspicuous above all in Saint John Chrysostom, who considered the ears of his hearers to be the measure of his discourse; thus, as Ferrarius says in *On Preaching*, book XI, p. 244, he adapted himself to their understanding and benefit.

Indeed, if many of them, departing from purer and more elegant speech, sometimes used a humbler style, they should not therefore be judged wholly devoid of literary refinement and elegance. They often preferred ordinary speech to more polished language by a kind of deliberate choice, arranging their sermons according to the understanding of those whom they wished to instruct in the precepts of the Christian religion. They should not therefore be rejected at once if they appear marked by some stain of negligence, especially when they contain something useful for strengthening the teachings of our purpose and religion or for forming moral character. Their chief concern was to please those whom they had undertaken to help.

To return to Chrysologus, I confidently say that the faults censured in him are not of such a kind as to make a work appear distasteful to our more delicate palate merely because of its style. Far weightier qualities may be commended in him. Among these must rightly be counted his frequent use of Sacred Scripture. He does not wrench the words of the divine mouth by violent interpretations to make them serve whatever he wishes; rather, he adapts them as though they flowed spontaneously.

There is also a continuous elegance of speech, soothing and attracting the minds of his hearers by the sweet sound of falling words and the graceful flowers of his diction. His discourse is likewise pleasing, expressed through certain brief clauses and powerful emotions, at times in tragic language. Finally, it was the brightness of his style and the abundance of his speech that at that time earned our author the name Chrysologus. In that age such qualities were especially valued, and the taste of the hearers was attached to them, as those who wear out in their hands the writers contemporary with Chrysologus know very well.

The sermons we publish are, for the most part, concerned with Sacred Scripture. It is difficult to say whether he explained its meaning with greater grace and charm than purity. First he presents the literal sense, then the allegorical; this is often followed by some moral consideration or precept of sacred ethics. The sermons are not burdened by tedious length, but, in keeping with the practice of the times, are confined to less than—or scarcely—an entire hour. To prevent them from becoming wearisome to his hearers, he sometimes divided them into several parts, as happened with the sermons on the Creed. He announced this either at the end of one sermon or at the beginning of another, as at the end of Sermon 22: “Let us postpone it today”—a phrase that may also be read elsewhere.

It is uncertain whether he delivered them on the same day or on different days. Although it may seem sufficient to have called the people together for preaching once a day, he appears in Sermons 22 and 23 to indicate that he did so on the same day, since the latter begins, “You have heard today,” and this expression occurs more than once.

There is also frequent mention in these sermons of fasting, prayer, almsgiving, and the Creed. At times he undertakes to celebrate the feasts of the saints and other solemnities of the Church. Heresies are repeatedly touched upon with a brief but firm and vigorous hand, and the ringleaders of the heretics are challenged: those who loudly proclaimed that Christ had come by appearance alone, or merely in semblance, or in phantom form—*δοκήσει*, “by appearance”; those who denied the resurrection of our flesh; those who denied that the Blessed Virgin could be called *Θεοτόκος*, “God-bearer,” or *Deipara*, “Mother of God,” contrary to the decrees of the Council of Ephesus; those who removed from the Church of God the authority to remit sins again; and finally those who defended other such clauses of falsehood and lies. [Col. 0011]

He also attacked the Circumcellions, or Agonistici—whom one may call Montenses in Roman usage because they lived in the mountains—a fierce and bold class of men. Above all, he did not miss any opportunity to attack the heresy of Eutyches with a war of annihilation, since it had only recently crept into the Church and had begun to spread its fresh poison.

Against this heresy he proclaims in the clearest terms that the natures in Christ are unmixed, while confessing the same person to be true God and man, performing divine and human works. In Sermon 84, when he says, “Let the heretics come now,” he addresses him together with Nestorius. This removes the charge of Sabellianism that some falsely fasten upon Chrysologus, as though, when speaking of the prodigal son in Sermon 1, he had confused the persons of the Father and the Son.

The learned bishop, however, by the word “Father” in that passage understands Christ, not the eternal Father, but Christ himself, that is, God incarnate. He is speaking of a man who had two sons: if he has sons, then he is a father. The sons possessed by God incarnate, or Christ, are humanity and divinity—distinct natures, just as the two sons are distinct—yet intermingled—that is, united—in the same suppositum. This is opposed to Eutychianism.

Chrysologus was also heard denouncing the corrupt customs of his time, which had fallen into evil: whether those of depraved men who observed the horoscope, or those who devoted themselves to spells, magic, and medicated potions, or those who on the Kalends of January stained themselves with filth and the obscene performances of mountebanks until they were hoarse.

Nor did he leave uncorrected the pride of the powerful, the display of clothing, the preparation of tables, the throngs of parasites, the immense retinue of household attendants, and other things of this kind. He attacks all these with vigorous eloquence and apostolic zeal.

More thoughtful men therefore lamented that these sermons, as though born under an unlucky star, had always emerged from the printers’ presses corrupted and horribly disfigured by countless errors, despite the splendid claims made in many editions concerning their correction. Until then, no one had labored to cleanse them and restore them to their former purity—except two men, Martin Castillo and Domenico Mita. The latter, with the help of the Caesenate and Urbinate manuscripts, contributed no small or insignificant assistance.

Yet, I do not know by what fate it happened that these editions too abounded in innumerable errors and required the physician’s hand in more than one place. Castillo was not able to revise all the sermons of Chrysologus and illustrate them with the lengthy commentaries with which he had begun to burden them. For when he had reached the twenty-fourth sermon and had assembled a volume of no moderate size, a sudden and troublesome inflammation of the eyes forced him to withdraw his hand from the work.

I have now undertaken, as best I could, to dress this task. Although unwilling, I allowed myself to be summoned to these sacred labors, moved by certain reasons which it would neither interest the reader to recount nor be worth the effort to describe.

My chief concern was to restore the text, since its corruption sometimes created considerable obscurity for readers. To accomplish this as far as I was able, I consulted several manuscripts of this holy Father. First was the Caesenate manuscript in the library of the Fathers of Saint Francis, which the founder of that library, Prince Novello Malatesta, had transcribed around the year 1450. It is uncertain what sort of exemplar the copy was taken from; certainly it was neither better nor more corrected.

The Vallicellian manuscript at Rome, praised by Baronius, presents an older form; but it too was carelessly written and gapped in many places. It is preceded by a Life of Saint Peter Chrysologus written by Agnellus, and published from the same author’s *Pontifical Book*, with the help of the Este codex, by the distinguished Benedictine, Don Benedict Bacchini.

The Vallicellian manuscript is not divided into chapters with a summary of each chapter added, as it is in Bacchini; instead, Roman numerals are placed along the margins of the pages. These perhaps indicate that nine Matins lessons were once formed from this Life.

I find it difficult to agree with that most learned man who, in his dissertation on the Patena of Forum Cornelii, inferred from the words “dearest ones” that this writing was nothing more than a sermon delivered by Agnellus, a certain Ravenna priest, in honor of Chrysologus. The solemn formula with which sermons are customarily concluded seems to support this view: “Who, with the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns,” and so forth.

Another manuscript, found in the Vatican Library under number 4952 and approximately four hundred years old, was first at Ravenna in the monastery of Saint Mary of Porto; from there it passed into the library of Cardinal Sirlet and from that library into the Vatican. Whenever I doubted the editors’ reliability, I consulted it repeatedly through the distinguished Don Teoli. The result would have been entirely successful and beyond my hopes, given his courtesy, had the codex itself not been corrupted and thus frustrated the hope it sometimes inspired.

Nor may I pass over without praise the Very Reverend Father Don Aloysius Mignanelli. At my request he was solicited from the Reverend Don Francisco Maria Mancurti, canon of the Church of Imola and a man highly deserving in letters and friendship. It is difficult to say whether he reviewed the six sermons of Chrysologus preserved in the Spanish College at Bologna with greater courtesy or diligence.

In one or another of these sermons, interrupted and interpolated wording occurs. Thus, in Sermon 71, after the words “and the other Mary to see the tomb,” the copyist jumps to line 19 of Sermon 75, according to Mita’s edition, where the same words occur. In Sermon 75, line 29, after “might restore her to eternal life,” the same copyist returns to Sermon 74; and after the words in line 6, “there had been a fall and ruin,” he adds: “Mary Magdalene came to see the tomb; and the sight of the tomb restored the one whom the sight of the forbidden tree had deceived.”

After this I left nothing undone to discover, through the kindness of friends, whether anything lay hidden in other libraries by whose aid I might present the work sound and complete and irrigate my little plot with a more abundant rain. But my efforts fell fruitlessly, and I still lament that I have been left with my mouth open in expectation.

I was able to collate only some of the more carefully corrected editions, if indeed there are any. While struggling against the printers’ errors—a task incredibly wearisome—I labored relentlessly to make considerable progress in restoring and cleansing the text, unless I flatter myself with excessive vanity.

If I have brought anything from my own storehouse, or if anything has been altered according to my judgment—which happened very rarely—it was done only after careful investigation and prolonged consideration. I wished to inform the reader of this, so that I would not pass off my own words as another’s.

I restored to their proper places the passages of Sacred Scripture cited by the author, which had been corruptly marked in the editions. In transcribing them, Chrysologus appears to have used the version translated into Latin from the Greek of the Seventy Translators, which Augustine calls the Italic and generally preferred above countless others. Augustine gives the same advice in chapters XIV and XLIX of Isaiah: “Among the translations themselves, let the Italic be preferred, for it is more faithful to the words while preserving the clarity of the meaning.”

Its author and date, however, are unknown. It is certain only that, after the Hieronymian Vulgate began to appear, this version began to be called the Ancient, by which name it is known in Gregory’s preface to the Book of Job, and in Cassian, Eucherius, and others. See what has been noted in the notes to Sermon 20.

I also ventured to explain certain passages of Sacred Scripture on the authority of better interpreters, but only in those matters where the clarification of the passage also shed light on what Chrysologus wrote.

I further decided to add notes—not extensive ones that might cause readers boredom and annoyance, but brief notes that would rather indicate matters worthy of observation than envelop them in long convolutions of words and quotations from many places, thereby enlarging the little book into a more substantial form.

Since these notes were written at different times and as occasion presented itself, it happened that some matters requiring annotation in the earlier sermons were deferred to the later ones, and conversely. I was more expansive in praising authors, so that I might serve readers as a kind of index, guiding them to the writers named above, whom they could then consult.

I also thought that I might do something for preachers by indicating other passages of the holy Fathers in which they either illuminated the same words of Sacred Scripture as Chrysologus or rose against similarly corrupt and depraved human customs.

In all the editions one finds various inscriptions for the sermons—or, to use the legal term, various titles—as though they had been delivered on different feasts of the saints and of the Blessed Virgin. Domenico Mita rejected these as spurious and adulterine, having entered the printed editions from the side, and substituted others in their place.

Following the authority of the manuscripts, I judged that both sets should be erased.

> **Note:** Although the distinguished Sebastian Pauli, following the authority of the manuscript codices, rejected the inscriptions prefixed by Domenico Mita to the individual sermons, the booksellers, considering the convenience of readers and preachers, judged that they should again be attached to this latest edition.

Moreover, these sermons of the holy bishop were first brought out from the shelves of a private library by Felix, himself the fortieth bishop of Ravenna. He held that see at the beginning of the eighth century, from about the year 707 until 717. Agnellus gives his Life in Bacchini’s *Pontifical Book*.

They were first published for the public at Bologna in 1534 through the art of printing, under the care of Don Agapitus of Vicenza, a canon of the Lateran order. It is therefore clear how wrongly some advertise the Paris edition of 1544 as the first.

I would not swear that all these works are genuine offspring of Chrysologus. Some are obscure, involved in expression, and unworthy of our author. Moreover, when I observed that the style was not everywhere equal or consistent with itself, and that the same subjects were repeated not once but several times on the same festivals, I very readily fell into the suspicion that this work had been assembled from various compositions of holy bishops who perhaps taught in the Church of Ravenna after Chrysologus, and that some learned man had gathered them into such a collection to serve as an example for his successors.

I did not dare, however, to remove what I suspected to be of doubtful authenticity. I merely indicated it, believing that it is religiously dangerous to diminish ancient sacred codices by private judgment and to lay rash hands upon them.

Lest I seem to belong among the most ungrateful, before bringing the first part of this preface to an end I will not allow the distinguished and learned Father Don James Maria Paitonus of the Congregation of the Somaschi to go without praise. He was a man born to help his friends, and especially worthy of my remembrance; he spared no diligence or skill to ensure that this edition should appear more elegant and more carefully corrected.

[Col. 0013]

# Life of Saint Peter Chrysologus, Archbishop of Ravenna

From the *Pontifical Book* of Agnellus, also called Andreas, published by the distinguished Bacchini, vol. I, p. 321. Various readings of the Vallicellian manuscript have now been added.

[Col. 0013]

## Chapter One

[Col. 0013A] Peter XXI was handsome in appearance and pleasing in form. Before him no pontiff had been like him in wisdom [Vallicellian Codex: “among the pontiffs”], nor did any arise after him. He composed many books and volumes, and divine wisdom flowed into him daily like a well-watered spring. Thus, because of his eloquence, they called him Chrysologus [Vallicellian: “they called him”], that is, “golden speaker” [Vallicellian: “a golden speaker.”

He was born in the territory of Cornelii Forum. He was nourished and taught by Cornelius, the bishop of that see; and because of his affection for his foster father, this blessed Peter—who until then had called the aforesaid territory Imola—began from that time to call it Cornelii Forum. Others, however, say that it was called Cornelii Forum because it had been the forum of Cornelius.

He governed the cathedra of the Church of Ravenna under the most holy Pope Leo I.

In those days the most savage presbyter Eutyches was stirred up by an evil spirit and began, through his wicked thoughts, to raise up a malignant heresy concerning the holy and indivisible Catholic faith. Saint Leo admonished him through a letter in the presence of many holy bishops of God [Vallicellian: “admonished him”]. He was never able to recall his superstitious belief to a sound purpose [Vallicellian: “And he was never able …”].

Saint Leo therefore quickly communicated the facts to blessed Peter, bishop of this city of Ravenna [Vallicellian omits “of this city,” and so forth]. Peter wrote a letter to the heretic himself and sent it to him, through which he did not consent at the Council of Chalcedon [Vallicellian: “not consenting”]; he was cast down.

But the most holy Leo sent many times, by his letters, to the city of Constantinople—not only to Galla Placidia but also to Valentinian and Honorius [Vallicellian adds: “the emperors”] and to all the other defenders of the faith. He also sent separate letters to the blessed Gratian [Vallicellian: “Martian should be restored here”] and Eudoxia against the aforesaid presbyter Eutyches. The matter, as we have said, was prolonged for so long, down to the time of the Emperor Martian.

Thus, as we have said, after much dispute concerning the holy, undefiled Catholic faith had continued for many days, it happened that, when the aforesaid heretic had been brought before all the priests by the counsel of the bishops, Bishop Theodore began to contend with him. He displayed individual volumes of the holy Scriptures and various testimonies showing that the holy and undivided Trinity—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—is one equal God, remaining in two natures [Vallicellian: “These words should properly be understood of Christ the Lord”], divine [Col. 0015D] and human.

Eutyches did not consent. Then, when apostolic authority had been demonstrated, he did not repent. The letter of Blessed Peter Chrysologus was then displayed, containing in part the following:

“Human laws within thirty years put an end among us to all contentious disputes; and you presume, after about five hundred years, to heap insults upon Christ in your speech? Truly, you ought to humble yourself before the holy Roman pontiff, carefully observe his commands, and fear nothing other than that the blessed Apostle Peter is alive and, in the flesh, holds the primacy of the apostolic cathedra of the Roman see.”

After this the most savage Eutyches fell in that very council [Vallicellian: “counsel”]. When the assembly of priests had been dismissed, all went away together with the whole Christian people, giving immense thanks to God and the greatest praises to the emperor who observed the Catholic and certain faith [Vallicellian: “offering the greatest praises to those observing the Catholic and true faith,” and so forth], bidding one another farewell.

[Col. 0016]

## Chapter Two. The Ordination of Peter Chrysologus Commanded from Heaven

Therefore, dearest ones, let us bring forward what remains of Chrysologus’s life and inquire how, or in what manner, in such an orthodox see the citizens of Ravenna ordained as their bishop a man not from their own flock but from the subordinate Church of Cornelii Forum [Vallicellian: “the Ravennates”].

At that time, after the blessed bishop John, mentioned above, had died [Vallicellian omits “mentioned above,” [Col. 0016B]], the entire assembly of the people gathered together with the priests, as is customary in the rite of the Church, and chose a shepherd for themselves. They then hastened with him to Rome [Vallicellian: “when all had come with him”] to the holy pope of the apostolic see, so that he might ordain their chosen man and such a Church might not remain without a bishop for so many days.

On the following day they were all prepared to present to the holy apostolic presence the man whom they had chosen [Vallicellian omits “holy”]. That same night the blessed Apostle Peter, the key-bearer of Christ, appeared in a vision to Saint Sixtus, bishop of the city of Rome [Vallicellian: “to Saint Sixtus, bishop …”], together with his disciple Apollinaris; and between them stood Blessed Peter Chrysologus.

The blessed Apostle Peter planted his foot slightly forward and said to Saint Pope Sixtus:

“Look at this man, whom we have chosen, who stands in the midst of our number [omitted in the Vallicellian manuscript]; consecrate him, and no other.”

Therefore, when the pope awoke, he ordered the whole people and the man who was to be ordained to be brought in at dawn. Saint Sixtus looked at him for a very long time and said:

“Go, take him away from among you. I do not recognize this man. Unless you bring me the one who was shown to me, I will ordain no other.”

They began to inquire among themselves what this matter could mean, and, having put everyone out, they were saddened.

The next day he ordered the people, together with all the chosen men—great, middling, and small [Vallicellian: “clerics”]—to be brought before him. When he did not see the appearance of the man who had been shown to him, he said:

“Search among yourselves. Perhaps not all of you have come, and there are more of you than this” [Vallicellian: “whether there are more”].

They answered:

“You will find no one from among us, lord pope” [Vallicellian: “from the newcomers”].

He said:

“Go out. I still do not see the chosen man.”

On the third day [Vallicellian: “night”] the prince of the Apostles again appeared to the same pope, neither fully awake nor fully asleep [Vallicellian: “to the same pope, while he was neither fully awake nor fully asleep”], with his disciple as before, and with the most holy Peter Chrysologus whom they held between them. They said to him:

“We have already told you not to lay hands upon any other man except this one, because in those days the Church of Ravenna will become so enriched and illuminated by his teaching that it will be like the richness of oil illuminating a lamp when it is brought near the fire” [Vallicellian: “when it has been brought near the fire”].

The next day everyone was brought in, but the man was not found.

Then the holy pope of the Roman see [“of the Roman see” is absent from the manuscript] said to the bishop of Cornelii Forum, who at that time had gone to Rome with the citizens of Ravenna:

“Bring in all your priests and clerics. Perhaps there I shall find the man who was shown to me.”

He answered him humbly:

“I have no such man, except one deacon who presides over all my affairs, upon whose hands I, your servant, rely. If you command that he come into the midst, let him be brought.”

The blessed pope said to him:

“Let him come—not he alone, but all the others as well. If I see the man I desire, I shall gladly receive him.”

When they had all entered, as soon as the holy pope saw the man who had been shown to him in the vision, he recognized him as a shining gem. By the Spirit he perceived on either side of him the faces of the blessed Apostle Peter and Bishop Apollinaris, holding Peter Chrysologus by his right and left hands [the manuscript omits “Peter”].

When the holy pope saw all this, he immediately rose from his seat and went to meet him, almost across the middle of the atrium. They greeted one another willingly, down to the knees. When Peter Chrysologus wished to withdraw from the pope, the blessed pope did not permit him [Vallicellian: “permitted him”].

At once the people began to murmur among themselves, raising a great cry to heaven. Some said:

“We do not accept a novice. He was not from our flock, but suddenly he invades the episcopal cathedra like a thief. Take him away, take him away from among us! We do not accept him, because it is not permitted to transfer someone from a subordinate Church to a greater one.” [Col. 0017C]

Others replied:

“This is a just man; you are speaking wrongly. Let us receive him, so that it may be well with our city, because he is exceedingly prudent, most chaste, a good teacher, and worthy of every honor. He is of our own kindred; we perceive no evil in him. He is full of the fear of the Lord. You wish to destroy him without cause.”

When Saint Sixtus III [“III” is absent from the manuscript] saw the people divided in such a dispute, he publicly recounted to everyone the vision, as we have described above, explaining how he was obliged by apostolic admonition to consecrate him.

“And if you do not want this man as your father, depart from me and let all of you be separated from the holy Catholic Church” [Vallicellian: “from the Roman Church”].

Then, as though with one voice, they began to cry:

“Let him be ordained! Let him be ordained!”

They quickly drew up a decree. Through the laying on of hands he received the Holy Spirit, was ordained bishop with glory, and returned to Ravenna [Vallicellian: “to the Ravenna see”]. From that day onward everyone began to venerate him as an angel of God.

[Col. 0017]

## Chapter Three. Buildings Constructed Under Peter’s Care; The Synchronology of Peter and Projectus of Cornelii Forum; The Burial of Saint Barbatian

This most blessed man built a fountain in the city near the church called Petriana, which Bishop Peter founded. The fountain was of extraordinary size, constructed with double walls and high ramparts according to the art of arithmetic [Vallicellian: “architecture”].

He also built a house within the episcopal residence [Vallicellian: “a house in the archbishop’s residence”] of the see of Ravenna [Vallicellian: “of Ravenna”], called Tricolis because it contained three sections. These buildings [the manuscript reads thus; Bacchini thinks “aedes,” “buildings,” should be read] were constructed below with great ingenuity.

Not far from that house he built a monastery of the Apostle Saint Andrew. His image was painted in mosaic above the doors of the same monastery, below [Vallicellian: “and he had his image painted …”]. He decorated all the walls with well-fitted marble [Vallicellian: “carefully fitted marbles”]. On the outer entrance, above the threshold, he caused the following verses to be inscribed [Vallicellian: “caused the following to be inscribed”]:

> Either light was born here, or, captured here, it reigns free.  
>   
> Light has come before: from heaven comes the world’s adornment.  
>   
> Or private walls have brought forth the day, shining brightly,  
>   
> And enclosed radiance gleams, with Olympus shut away.  
>   
> See the marble blooming with rays beneath the serene heavens;  
>   
> And all the stones struck with a starry purple sheen.  
>   
> Through the cost of the Author, Peter’s gifts shine brightly.  
>   
> To him honor, to him merit, for thus adorning small things,  
>   
> So that, though confined, they may surpass a spacious expanse.  
>   
> Nothing is small for Christ. He rightly possesses narrow dwellings,  
>   
> Whose temples stand in the human breast.  
>   
> Peter is the foundation; Peter is founder and hall.  
>   
> What the house is, the Lord is; what is made, the Maker is also—  
>   
> The same in character and in work. Christ is held to be its possessor,  
>   
> Who, joining the two, as mediator makes them one [Vallicellian: “made them one”].  
>   
> Coming here, he establishes tears that will bring forth joys,  
>   
> Strengthening the contrite mind in the stricken breast.  
>   
> So that it may not lie prostrate, let it cast itself upon the ground and disclose  
>   
> Hidden illnesses before the feet of the Physician, as care hastens to help.

Often the fear of death becomes the cause of blessed life. He composed many volumes and was exceedingly wise. This man, together with Projectus, was consecrated by Blessed Cornelius as a deacon of the church of Imola at the same hour. Later, by divine providence, both held episcopal sees. Peter received the church of Ravenna, while Projectus was assigned the Imolese church [Vallic.: Peter received the Ravennate church, Projectus the Imolese]. After he had been ordained bishop, this other man was subsequently consecrated by him as bishop of the Cornelian church, in the time of Galla Placidia Augusta, as we find written [Vallic.: as it is written]. The same Peter Chrysologus and the aforesaid Augusta embalmed the body of Blessed Barbatian with spices and buried it with great honor, not far away at Posterula [Vallic.: Pusterula] of Ovilio; and he consecrated the church of Saint John the Baptist, which Baduarius [Vallic.: Baudarius] built.

[Col. 0018]

## CHAPTER IV. Peter Foresees and Announces His Death. He Goes to Forum Cornelii and Dies There. The Place of His Tomb.

After these events, the most blessed Peter learned through the Spirit the end of his life. He went to the Cornelian church and, entering beneath the basilica of Blessed Cassian, offered gifts: namely, one golden bowl, another silver dish, and large golden diadems adorned with very precious gems. He consecrated all these to the body of Saint Cassian, placed them upon the altar of that church, and, standing on the step beside the altar with his hands extended, blessed the entire populace, the priests, and the people. Then he prayed, saying:

“You gave, O God, a soul to this body; mercifully receive it again, because I am your creature. Let the most wicked devil not confront me [Vallic.: confront him], but let your holy angel [Vallic.: your is absent] receive it [Vallic.: receive it], and command that it be placed in the bosoms of the patriarchs, where light remains and immeasurable joy abides.

“And now, Lord, I confess you with my lips and heart [Vallic.: with lips and heart]. You who created all things from nothing, who alone know the past, the present, and the future, give this people an teachable heart, so that they may fear you and acknowledge that you are God in heaven above and on earth below. Through your holy Son you restored the salvation of the whole human race; in him we believe as God and Lord of the angels. Blessed are you forever and ever.

“Send them, Lord, [Col. 0019B] a true shepherd who will gather your sheep, not scattering them, but recalling them to the folds of the church. Let him not sleep as a hireling; let him not be the guardian of another’s sheep [Vallic.: an alien guardian], but a true shepherd who will present the sheep entrusted to him, together with their lambs, immaculate before your sight [Vallic.: the sheep entrusted to him]. Let that fierce and most savage wolf, who seeks to snatch away his prey from you, not rouse the shepherd’s heart; let swift desire be driven away; let him not tear apart the fleeces of the faithful sheep, lest the holy Church groan with bleating voices.

“Grant this people a good shepherd [Vallic.: You, good shepherd, grant a shepherd]; send them a gentle shepherd [Vallic.: a mild shepherd], not one who strikes but one who nourishes; not one who batters but one who defends; not one who despises but one who recalls; not a robber but a giver. Let him not [Col. 0019C] … [Vallic.: tear apart], but restrain; not greedy but a payer of dues; not arrogant but humble; not savage but gentle. Guard them: they are your people and the work of your hands. Blessed are you forever.

“To the grieving people he said: ‘Dearest sons, listen to me. I am going away and entering upon the way of all flesh, where the house of every living person has been established. Now, my sons, take courage and be prudent men. The Lord God will give you a shepherd and ruler, as it is written: “The Lord will not reject his people forever, nor abandon his inheritance.” He will teach you. He will lead you through pleasant pastures; he will refresh you with the nourishment of his word. Listen to him; do not be disturbed.

“And you, my inmost beloved, do not rise up against him in the swelling of your hearts; do not choose a shepherd amid tumult and quarrelling. Let not the father of this country obtain this seat for money [Vallic.: for whom], but love the one whom the Lord will choose [Vallic.: this man]. Be perfect sons. Guard yourselves from every heresy. Beware of the Arian doctrine. Hold fast the holy, undefiled Catholic faith [the manuscript lacks *catholicam*]. Preserve your bodies without pollution, because they are living temples of God. Guard and practice these things, so that you may merit, together with your shepherd, to prepare a way amid all things pleasing for the heavenly Lord [Vallic.: amid the holy, pleasing sheep].

“Carefully keep his commands; obey him, so that he may pray for you. For almighty God does not seek a cheerful person, but receives a contrite heart and a humbled spirit. May the blessing of the Lord God almighty be upon you and upon your children, from generation to generation, now and always, forever and ever.’”

When everyone had answered “Amen,” he turned toward the altar of Blessed Cassian and said:

“I beseech you, blessed Cassian: intercede for me. I was like a servant of your household, nourished by Cornelius of this see within the bosom of the church [Vallic.: nourished by Cornelius in the bosom of this church]. Returning to you once more, I now entrust my soul to almighty God, but I commend my body to you.”

As he said these and similar things, as though belching forth, exulting, and rejoicing, while all who were present were weeping, he gave up the spirit on the third day before the Nones of December. The masons promptly prepared a tomb behind the seat of that church, in the place where he had ordered it; and there the holy body was received and remains to this day. He sat for … years, … months, … days … [Instead of “He sat…” and the following lacuna, the manuscript has: “But our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.”]

[Col. 0019]

## OBSERVATIONS OF THE ABBOT DOM BENEDICT BACCHINI, etc., on the Life of Saint Peter Chrysologus from Agnellus’s *Pontifical*, vol. I, p. 335

The length of Peter’s life. The account of his election, said to have been made by divine impulse, is defended against Dupin. Agnellus acknowledges that the Ravennate Church was subject to the Roman Church. Peter’s letter to Eutyches. Whether he wrote another. Whether he wrote the final sections of that letter. Whether the house called Tricoli was built by Chrysologus. The Petriana church. Whether the chapel of Saint Andrew was built by Chrysologus. Gifts presented to the Cornelian church.

[Col. 0019D] **1.** In our preceding dissertation we indicated the age of the divine Peter Chrysologus, insofar as this could suffice to remove the confusion of dates. Now it must be determined explicitly, as far as possible. As for the beginning of his episcopate, I persist in the view that he was ordained either in the year 440, the last year of Sixtus III’s pontificate, or in the preceding year, 439. The year of his death can be placed neither before 448 nor later than 451. The truth of the latter assertion is clear from the fact that the cities of Emilia suffered disaster and plunder while Attila was raging widely in the year 452; and, when he was hastening toward Ravenna, John was bishop there. Perhaps that was not the first year of his see, but he had begun in the preceding year, 451.

The former assertion, however, is established by the Acts of Saint Germanus of Auxerre, faithfully and accurately written by Constantius. From these the most eminent Cardinal Norisius drew the certain conclusion that Germanus died at Ravenna in that same year, 448, on July 31 (*History of Pelagius*, book II, chapter 12). It is established, moreover, that Peter Chrysologus arranged that holy man’s funeral.

The same most eminent and learned cardinal writes the following concerning the year of Peter Chrysologus’s death: “That he died in that year (450), or perhaps the preceding one, on December 2, the day on which his memory is celebrated, is evident from Leo’s thirty-fifth letter to Leo of Ravenna, dated October 24, under the consulship of Marcian, that is, in the year 451. For in the year 448 Chrysologus sent a letter to Eutyches, already in bad repute because of heresy; but in that very year Eutyches was held in good standing among the Catholics of Italy until the Kalends of June, as appears from Leo’s letter to him dated on that same day, in which he praises Eutyches’s zeal in fighting against the Nestorians. That is the sixth letter.”

I thought these matters should be inserted in order to correct those who write that Peter Chrysologus died around the year 440, which was the opinion of Jerome Rossi and the common view of the Ravennate writers. If that were true, Germanus of Auxerre would have died at Ravenna before the year 440, while Chrysologus was bishop. Rossi, however, records the death of Peter Chrysologus not in 440 but in 450, in *History of Ravenna*, book II; thus he is refuted without justification.

Furthermore, since Eutyches was in good standing in Italy until the Kalends of June in the year 448, the extant letter could not have been written to him by Peter in 440. When it was written, Eutyches was in bad repute in Italy, as is clear from the tenor of that letter. Therefore Chrysologus’s letter could not have been written before the year [Col. 0021B] 449.

The letter of Saint Leo said to have been written to Leo—or Neon—is, from the arguments given above in the dissertation, no proof of the point, even though, with Pagi against Quesnel, it is assigned to the year 451. Because of the conjecture I offered in the dissertation concerning the name Ravennius, which may lie hidden in a corruption of the inscription, I thought it worth adding that it may perhaps have been written to John, whose name was changed into Leo through the error of copyists.

Yet even if this is admitted, it helps the argument nothing, since Quesnel’s arguments compel us to transfer the same letter to the year 458. In the first place, there is the question of those returning from barbarian captivity, which cannot refer to the exiles who were forced to change their place of residence solely because of Genseric’s persecution, since they were not returning from the barbarians, as the question itself presupposes.

What proves that John was bishop before the year 452 is Attila’s invasion, which occurred in that same year and which John himself confronted, as Our Author relates. When all these matters are considered, it follows that Peter Chrysologus died in 450 or 451, that John was appointed in his place in the same year, and that there is no room here for Neon, who must have occupied the see for several years because of the many notable deeds narrated in his Life.

**2.** To preserve the order of time, which Agnellus neglected, we must observe Peter’s election to the episcopate, accomplished by the will of God and through the apparition of Saints Peter and Apollinaris. Ferretus was the first to bring the matter to light from Our Author; then Rossi narrated it explicitly, as he usually does in his *History*, followed by Baronius and the others.

But just as the waters of rivers acquire different flavors from the nature of the soil from which they flow, so that they are eventually no longer what they were when they sprang from the source, anyone who has tasted Agnellus’s sources will easily recognize that this account has undergone the same process, although the substance of the event has been preserved.

It is astonishing, however, that many people are so disposed as to believe everything too readily, while others, by contrast, throw everything into doubt. Dupin, in his *Bibliotheca of Ecclesiastical Writers*, gives the following concerning this story, translated from French into Latin: “But no credence can be given to a narrative of this kind, for no trustworthy author presents it.” Agnellus, now brought to light, I do not know whether he will be a trustworthy authority for Dupin. This much I affirm: from this account it can be recognized that the antiquity of the tradition of this story, as Agnellus narrates it, is exceptionally well attested.

**3.** The privileges granted by Valentinian to the Ravennate Church deserve notice, if indeed there were any, and if John, Peter’s immediate predecessor, obtained them, as Agnellus himself testifies. Although elsewhere impatient of Roman primacy, Agnellus nevertheless in no way exempted the bishops themselves from the authority of the Roman pontiff.

For if those privileges had ever been able to produce such an exemption, it ought to have occurred when Valentinian himself was emperor. Since the death of the man to whom the privilege had been granted made it necessary for a new bishop to be ordained, Agnellus tells us that the people and priests—by whom I also think the provincial bishops are to be understood—after issuing a decree concerning the election of a certain man, hastened with him to Rome, to Sixtus, the holy pope of the apostolic see, so that he might ordain their chosen candidate.

In what follows, Agnellus adds that, when the Ravennate populace dissented and caused an uproar, Sixtus said, after the vision had been related: “And if you do not want this man as father, depart from me, and let all of you be alienated from the holy Catholic Church.” Therefore all cried out with one voice: “Let him be ordained.” A decree was quickly written, and through the laying on of hands Peter received the Holy Spirit and was ordained pontiff.

This clearly shows that Valentinian granted a privilege, if he ever granted one at all. He could have granted us something unknown that in no way violated the rights of the Holy See; nor did it thereby follow that the bishops of Ravenna were in some sense autonomous.

These and similar passages, which we shall examine in their proper places as occasion requires, are narrated by Agnellus. They make it impossible for me not to wonder greatly how it happened that the same man who, in one place while writing his *Pontifical*, shows himself properly and correctly disposed toward the primacy of the Roman see, elsewhere—and here, after prefacing his account with a rotten fabrication—reveals himself as a partisan of the schismatic faction. But the condition of lies and a bad cause is such that it destroys itself with its own sword.

**4.** We must now return to what Agnellus relates earlier about Saint Peter, although these events occurred in his final years and concern the heresy of Eutyches, abbot of Constantinople. Our Author has infected the account with such a great rasping harshness of expression and confusion of facts that one must guess what he had in mind.

In the case of Eutyches, the sequence of events must be considered so that the truth may be restored to its proper dates, if anything can be extracted from Agnellus’s history. This will also shed light on what we said in the first section concerning the final years of Chrysologus.

After Nestorius’s heresy had been condemned at the general Council of Ephesus, partisan zeal caused those who wished to depart from it as far as possible to fall into the opposite and impious error. Eutyches sinned more absurdly than all the rest: he obstinately denied the distinction of natures in Christ and accused those who held the opposite view of Nestorianism. He sent letters to Leo, the supreme pontiff, to which Leo himself replied on July 1, 448.

In the same year, at a council held at Constantinople in November under Flavian, bishop of that city, Eutyches was repeatedly summoned and finally appeared. After arrogantly asserting his heresy, he was condemned. Immediately afterward he wrote again to Leo, lamenting that he had been condemned unlawfully, and he petitioned the emperor that a general council be convened.

Meanwhile, at a gathering of thirty bishops held at Constantinople on April 1, 449, he entangled the matter in still greater complications. On February 18 Leo had written to Flavian and to Theodosius, inquiring into the reasons for which Eutyches had been condemned. After learning these from Flavian, he praised Flavian’s zeal and piety in a letter dated May 21 of that same year.

Before that date Chrysologus could not have written a letter to Eutyches in which he explicitly reproved the heresy; otherwise he would have known what the supreme pontiff did not know. A new synod was then convened at Ephesus. Leo himself sent legates of the Holy See and furnished them with letters.

Among these letters, praised by everyone and with the common consent of the Church, is the one numbered 24 in Quesnel’s edition, dated June 13. In it the mystery of the Incarnation is explained with such elegance, purity, and clarity that it would be difficult to find in all antiquity a more illustrious monument for strengthening the orthodox doctrine.

The synod at Ephesus began on August 8 of that same year, 449. Because of the predatory deeds unlawfully carried out there, it was afterward called the “Robber” Council, and it placed the Catholic faith in the greatest danger: Eutyches was acquitted and Flavian condemned. Shortly afterward, afflicted by hardships and injuries, Flavian died while being led into exile.

For these reasons Pope Leo repeatedly petitioned Theodosius that the Catholic cause be restored by a general council. Two letters to the emperor survive, dated October 13 and 15, together with others to different recipients. He also dealt with the matter with Valentinian, Placidia, and Eudoxia, and sent legates to Constantinople. Yet he obtained nothing from Theodosius in this most serious affair.

After Theodosius died and Marcian was appointed in his place, with Marcian’s wife Pulcheria taking the initiative, a council was first held at Constantinople under Anatolius. The legates of the apostolic see attended. Leo’s letter to Flavian was read there and confirmed by the subscriptions of the bishops; Nestorius and Eutyches were both condemned.

Then, at the council that began on the eighth day of that same year, the same letter of Leo the Great served as the standard, and the doctrine of the two natures in Christ was confirmed against the heresy of Eutyches. The council subscribed to it after it had been read during the second and fourth sessions.

**5.** Having briefly reviewed the history of the Eutychian heresy, let us return to Agnellus’s complications. First he says that Eutyches did not repent when admonished by the most holy Leo through a letter; he says that the letter was read in an assembly of many bishops.

No letter of Leo addressed to Eutyches was read at any council. Indeed, at none of the preceding councils—including the council at Constantinople under Anatolius—was the famous letter to Flavian read, the one discussed above. Thus this is the letter about which Agnellus must be speaking. But Eutyches was not present at that council, nor was the matter still open.

Agnellus then adds an exceedingly confused paragraph: “Therefore Saint Leo quickly made known the matters to blessed Peter, pontiff of this city of Ravenna. Peter wrote a letter and sent it to the heretic himself; through it he did not consent at the Council of Chalcedon and was overwhelmed.”

From this, as I think, some have believed they possessed an argument for saying that Blessed Chrysologus’s letter was read at the Council of Chalcedon. Yet this conflicts with the acts of that council, which say nothing about the matter. Nor could it have happened that the letter of a bishop of Ravenna was read there as the rule of faith, when the bishops first held that one must adhere solely to the creeds of the Councils of Nicaea, Constantinople, and Ephesus.

They admitted Cyril’s second letter to Nestorius and another letter of Cyril to John of Antioch. For the same reason they received Saint Leo’s letter to Flavian, since it did not depart from the sense of those documents and clearly explained what was to be believed concerning the heresy of Eutyches.

Dominicus Mita thinks the matter can be resolved in this way, in his *Responses to the Objections against the Life of Chrysologus* written by him, sections 5, 6, 7, and 8: once Saint Leo had learned from Flavian about the heresy of Eutyches and its circumstances, he summoned Peter to Rome, and Peter, at the pontiff’s command, composed that most famous letter in the pontiff’s own name to Flavian. It was read first at the Constantinopolitan council under Anatolius and then at the general Council of Chalcedon as the rule of what was to be believed, against Nestorius as well as Eutyches.

To avoid the objection that might be raised from the difference in style between this letter and Peter’s other writings, Mita limits his conjecture by supposing that Leo recast the letter composed by Peter in his own style and added certain things on his own initiative.

He tries to confirm the entire hypothesis from Chrysologus’s Sermon 75, where Chrysologus says that he had returned to Ravenna from a journey during Lent and was therefore extremely tired. Mita might perhaps have believed that he had reached the truth if he had read Our Author, since the passage cited seems to assert that Peter, summoned by Leo, wrote the letter that suppressed the heresy of Eutyches at the Council of Chalcedon.

But the subsequent context shows that Agnellus was speaking of a letter written with everyone in agreement. For he says that the letter of Blessed Peter Chrysologus was displayed and even gives part of it, which we shall discuss immediately. Mita’s conjecture therefore cannot be supported by this passage in any way; from other considerations it splits apart and collapses.

The letter of Leo under discussion was written after Lent in the year 449, namely on June 13, since the preceding letter to the same Flavian was also written after Lent, specifically on May 21. But who could doubt the matter, when the style and the very words clearly sound like Leo?

**6.** Agnellus next discusses other letters of Leo, written to obtain the help of the emperors, so that the Catholic cause, badly treated at the pseudo-synod of Nicaea, might be restored through a new general council.

He makes a gross error, unless the names of the emperors and empresses were changed through the fault of copyists, when he mentions Honorius and Gratian, who had died long before the time of the Eutychian heresy. In place of Honorius I wondered whether Honoria might be substituted. But since no letter of Leo to her survives—and since she was burdened with an especially bad reputation because of her sexual misconduct—I recognize that such an emendation cannot be maintained.

I also suspected that Gratian had been inserted through an easy error in place of Marcian. But this is contradicted by the fact that Agnellus says in the same period that the matter was carried forward as far as Marcian.

He also mentions Theodore, who, he says, contended with Eutyches at the holy council and, after producing volumes of Sacred Scripture and testimonies of the holy Fathers, established the Catholic faith concerning the two natures. Yet the entire sequence of the ancient acts of the council convened by Flavian—at which only Eutyches was heard, with Eusebius of Dorylaeum accusing him and Flavian himself pressing the charge against the heretic—knows nothing of Theodore. Thus everything here in Our Author departs from the truth.

**7.** No one will deny that it is relevant to the integrity of the letter discussed above. From Agnellus’s passage we have abundant proof against those who contend that the final words, concerning the supreme authority of the supreme pontiff in matters of the doctrines of faith, do not belong to Chrysologus but were added later by someone devoted to and attached to the Roman see.

These men rely on the authority of Gerardus Vossius, who published Chrysologus’s letter in Greek and Latin together with several others, appended to printed works of Gregory Thaumaturgus at Mainz in 1604. Vossius noted that those final words were absent from two Vatican manuscripts.

The much-praised Dupin consequently says the following in his *Bibliotheca*, which I give in Latin: “Furthermore, the letter seems to end before those words; what follows was added to commend the authority of the Holy See.”

But, as we have noted and as is clear from his own passages, Agnellus was not well disposed toward the Holy See; nevertheless he reports the words from the letter, or their meaning. No serious textual critic will resist this conclusion.

It is clear that, down to Agnellus’s time, the complete letter of Chrysologus existed in the codices of the Ravennate Church, although that church had long been afflicted by schism. Later it was shortened by those who attacked the authority of the Holy See in defining matters of faith. This must be attributed especially to those who, out of Greek religious conviction, translated the Latin letter into Greek from a Greek standpoint.

Here I thought it worthwhile to transcribe the standard Latin version found in Baronius and others, together with the corresponding text as I found it in the Estense manuscript, adding in their proper places the sections reported by Agnellus, so that the reader may judge what should be thought about the matter.

[Col. 0024]

## LATIN LETTER OF DOM PETER CHRYSOLOGUS

[Note: [Col. 0024] The two versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0024]

### STANDARD VERSION

To the most beloved and deservedly honorable son, the presbyter Eutyches: Peter, bishop of Ravenna.

I read your sorrowful letter with sorrow, and I went through your mournful writings with the grief they deserved. For just as the peace of the churches, the harmony of priests, and the tranquility of the people cause us to rejoice with heavenly joy, so fraternal dissension afflicts and casts us down—especially when it arises from such causes.

[Note: [Col. 0023D] Agnellus’s paraphrase: “Human laws within thirty years extinguish all contentious disputes among us; and you presume, after about five hundred years, to heap such insults upon Christ in your speech?”]

For human laws settle human disputes within thirty years, while the birth of Christ, which is written of in divine law and is ineffable, is subjected after so many centuries to rash disputation. You are not unaware of what Origen, investigator of first principles, encountered, or how Nestorius fell when disputing about the natures.

The Magi confess God in the manger through mystical gifts, while priests investigate with mournful questioning who he is who was born through a virginal birth from the Holy Spirit. When Jesus uttered a cry in the cradle, the heavenly host proclaimed, “Glory to God in the highest”; and now, when every knee of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth bows at the name of Jesus, the question of his origin is stirred up?

We, dearest brother, say together with the Apostle: “Even if we have known Jesus according to the flesh, now we no longer know him in that way.” Nor can we scrutinize with curiosity the one whom we are commanded to honor, to render fear, and to await—not to investigate—the one whom we confess as judge.

I have briefly replied to your letter. I would have written more in reply if our brother and fellow bishop Flavian had sent me some written account concerning this matter. For if you are displeased by what you write, having chosen judgment for yourself, how shall we be able to judge matters concerning people whom we have not seen because of their absence, and whose understanding we do not know because of their silence?

A mediator is not just if he hears one party in such a way that he reserves nothing for the other party.

[Note: [Col. 0025D] Agnellus’s paraphrase: “Truly you ought to humble yourself before the holy Roman pontiff and carefully keep his commands. Do not regard him otherwise than as though Blessed Peter the Apostle himself were alive and held in the flesh the primacy of the apostolic chair of the Roman see.”]

In all things, however, we exhort you, honorable brother, to attend obediently to what has been written to you by the most blessed pope of the Roman city. For Blessed Peter, who lives and presides in his own see, grants the truth of faith to those who seek it. For the sake of peace and faith, we cannot hear cases outside the consent of the bishop of the Roman city.

May the Lord deign to preserve your affection in safety for a very long time, dearest and most honored son.

[Col. 0024]

### FROM THE ESTENSE MANUSCRIPT

To the most beloved and deservedly honorable son, the presbyter Eutyches: Peter, bishop.

I read your sorrowful letters with sorrow, and I went through writings filled with mournful grief and lamentation. For just as the peace of priests and the tranquility of the people cause us to rejoice with heavenly joy, so fraternal dissension afflicts and casts us down, especially when it arises from such causes.

For human laws settle human disputes within thirty years, while the birth of Christ, which is written of in divine law and is ineffable, is subjected after so many centuries to rash disputation. What Origen, investigator of first principles, encountered, and how Nestorius fell when disputing about the natures, is not hidden from your prudence.

The Magi confess Jesus as God in the manger through mystical gifts, while priests run about in mournful questioning as to what he is who was born through a virginal birth from the Holy Spirit. When Jesus uttered a cry in the cradle, the heavenly host proclaims, “Glory to God in the highest”; and now, when every knee of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth bows at the name of Jesus, the question of his origin is stirred up?

We, brothers, say with Paul: “Even if we have known Jesus according to the flesh, now we no longer know him in that way.” Nor can we examine him curiously, since we are commanded to give honor, render fear, and await—not investigate—the one whom we confess as judge.

I have replied to all these matters, brother, in my letter to you. The rest is missing.

**8.** Since the same meanings are expressed in very different words in the standard versions and in the passages that Agnellus chose to report, the evidence shows that he took the sense from Chrysologus’s letter, not its words. Everyone can see that even the Agnellian version has been corrupted by Agnellus’s rasping style.

As for the earlier passages, where an argument against Eutyches is drawn from the thirty-year prescription established by human law, they were either spoken by the same Chrysologus in both places or taken from Sermon 145:

“Human laws within thirty years extinguish all contentious disputes, while Christ, after about five hundred years from his birth, presents the causes of his birth, suffers disputes about his origin, and endures questions concerning his status? Heretic, cease judging your judge, and adore in heaven the God whom … adored on earth.”

Although Chrysologus may have delivered that sermon after the law enacted by Valentinian during the consulship of Arturus and Protogenes, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July, concerning the thirty-year prescription, and although he may have delivered it around the feast of the Lord’s Advent in the year 449, attentive readers will nevertheless see that it principally attacks the heresy of Nestorius and those who attempted, amid the Greek turmoil, to cloud the purity of the Latin language by removing the terms *anthropotokos* (ἀνθρωποτόκον, “man-bearer”) and *Christotokos* (Χριστοτόκον, “Christ-bearer”) in order blasphemously to eliminate *Theotokos* (Θεοτόκον, “God-bearer”).

From this a by no means slight argument can be drawn that Chrysologus lived beyond the year mentioned above and that the letter was written later than is generally thought.

**9.** In second place among the buildings erected through Chrysologus’s munificent expenditure is listed the house within the episcopal complex of the Ravennate church called Tricoli. Our Author says that it was so called because it contained three *cola*, since it was divided into three notable members; the Greeks called these τὰ κῶλα (*ta kōla*).

Those therefore deserve no credence who wish the building to have been called Tricoli because it approached the appearance of three hills.

That Agnellus attributed to Peter Chrysologus what ought to be attributed to Peter III of that name is clearly recognized from the verses that Agnellus himself says were read in the Tricoli building, completed by Bishop Maximian. These verses set out the succession of Ravennate pontiffs who contributed to constructing Tricoli, and they call Peter, surnamed the Younger, its founder, in order to distinguish him from the Elder and from Chrysologus. It is useful to transfer some of them here from their original location:

> Here Peter the Younger, following Christ’s conception,  
> As he taught, set forth what he had conceived in holy conduct;  
> He also founded this stronghold with wondrous masses,  
> He himself gave these monuments of his own name.  
>   
> After his death Aurelian held the honors;  
> After him Ecclesius became bishop.

The Peter who laid the foundations of Tricoli was therefore the man who preceded Aurelian, not Chrysologus, whom another John succeeded. Thus Agnellus corrects Agnellus: perhaps he found here the occasion for his error and for placing Peter surnamed Chrysologus immediately before Aurelian, although Peter Chrysologus preceded Aurelian by nearly half a century.

[Col. 0026C]

**10.** In the first place, however, the baptismal font is rightly attributed to Chrysologus among the other buildings. It was of extraordinary size and enclosed by double, lofty walls.

Since Agnellus explicitly states that this font was built beside the church called Petriana, which Bishop Peter founded, and since Rossi could have obtained knowledge of this work nowhere else than from this passage of Agnellus, it is surprising that he attributed the construction of the font to Chrysologus on page 103, while, after deleting the earlier Peter from the Ravennate diptychs, he assigned the Petriana basilica to the Peter who flourished in the time of Pope Symmachus and preceded Aurelian in the Ravennate see.

It is therefore plainly established from this passage that another Peter held the see before Peter Chrysologus. For we are compelled to acknowledge that the font attributed to Chrysologus was added to the Petriana basilica, to which a font had originally been attached together with a small chapel of Saint James, still surviving in Agnellus’s time. In that chapel the body of a bishop Peter was found, and Agnellus judged that it belonged to the Elder.

[Col. 0026D] Another building attributed to Chrysologus is the monastery, or chapel, of the apostle Saint Andrew, not far from the Tricoli house. Agnellus asserts that an image of Saint Peter and verses were inscribed there.

I am somewhat doubtful, however, whether it should be attributed to Chrysologus or to Peter the Younger. It appears to have been built for the convenience of the Tricoli house, and the verses themselves do not seem to bear the style or the age of Chrysologus, but rather to have a more recent sound.

The final word of the second verse, *modernum* (“modern”), suggests the age of Cassiodorus, and the phrase itself is by no means unlike Cassiodorus’s phrasing. In the passage cited above, Rossi calls this chapel elegant, but says that it was supported by wooden columns.

The inscribed verses establish nothing of the kind. Rather, they describe a small chapel, scarcely accessible to the daylight because of its narrow windows, but splendid with precious marbles adorned with purple stone. External light was excluded, yet the chapel shone with its own light, as the earlier verses say:

> Either light was born here, or, captured here, it reigns free,

together with the remaining verses that follow.

The final verses show that sins were expiated through a private confession, as Rossi rightly noted. Since these verses were written after the time of Nectarius, patriarch of Constantinople, it is evident that they have nothing to do with the famous and controversial deed attributed to that patriarch in the histories, by which some suppose that auricular confession was abolished. On the contrary, it is clearly established from this evidence that the practice continued even after Nectarius.

The image also, which Agnellus believed to have been Chrysologus’s and which was rendered in tesserae above the doors, should, in my opinion, be attributed to Peter the Younger, as should the chapel itself.

11. What follows concerning Saint Projectus of Cornelium is clear, as is also the material concerning the church of Saint John, which Saint Barbatianus, dear to Placidia, held and which Baduarius had built; these accounts derive their light from the Acts of Saint Barbatianus. What Our Author reports concerning the death of Saint Peter Chrysologus is also clear and contains nothing to delay the reader. It seems worth adding that, among the gifts Chrysologus presented upon entering the church, a silver paten is preserved with the greatest reverence. Dominicus Mita reproduced an engraved bronze copy of it before his edition of the Sermons of Saint Peter; around its rim are engraved verses of a more recent style, which I think should be transcribed. They are as follows: They are as follows:

> The lamb of the people, whom this dear multitude fixed upon the altar of the cross,  
> Becomes the sacrifice of the race, for the sin of the first parent.

The same Mita prefixed to his book what he believed to be a true likeness of Peter Chrysologus, and said that it existed, executed in mosaic, in the apse of the choir of the metropolitan church at Ravenna. Yet that image could have been made only after the eleventh century from Christ’s birth; that part of the church was likewise restored after that period, and the form of the pallium is also more recent. I hear that a learned work on the aforementioned paten is expected from the learned gentleman, the Reverend Abbot Pastrizio. Perhaps I shall be able to read it before this work of mine is published. But these matters are sufficient for the life of Chrysologus.

[Col. 0027]

# LIFE OF SAINT PETER CHRYSOLOGUS, ARCHBISHOP OF RAVENNA, BY CASTILLO

[Col. 0027C]

## § I. His homeland, birth, and the name Chrysologus are presented.

### 1.

In Italy, that most renowned region of Europe, there is a certain part—one of its sixteen provinces—no less famous, exceedingly pleasant, beautiful, and prosperous, formerly called Aemilia, but now Flaminia or Romandiola. It is so fertile and productive because it is watered on every side by the river Vatrenus. After the Greeks had driven the Trojans from Ilium, Troy, with a flaming sword, these fugitives flew to Italy and founded a town in a very beautiful part of Aemilia, giving it the name Ilium also.

When, after the passage of many years, Lucius Cornelius Sulla, a Roman of noble Cornelian lineage, quaestor and later dictator, had banished Marius the Elder, the Roman consul for the seventh time, and had brought all Asia under his rule, he assigned Aemilia as a colony to his Roman Cornelians, designating Ilium as the forum where justice would be administered and the nine-day markets held. Hence the inhabitants of Ilium and of all Aemilia—which from that time began to be called Imola—called that town, in honor of their Lucius Cornelius, the Forum of Sulla, but more commonly the Forum of Cornelius. Pliny, however, in Book III of his *Natural History*, chapter 16, after the middle, calls the territory around Imola the Forocornelian territory.

This province of Flaminia, then; this region of Romandiola; this part of Italian territory belonging to Aemilia, or Imola, was the common homeland of our bishop Chrysologus. His particular native soil, however, was Forum Cornelii, made all the happier by the birth of so holy a man, and thereby most fortunate.

> **Note [Col. 0027D].** The material reported about his Trojan origin must be regarded as rubbish. The city was not otherwise ancient, and although renowned and sufficiently distinguished for the elegance of its buildings, the healthfulness of its air, the fertility of its soil, the multitude of its inhabitants, and its production of famous men, it has no need of these fictitious and subtle inventions in order to be praised above many others. Scipio Claromontanus writes in *History of Cesena*, Book V, p. 93, that it was called Imola after Cleophis, successor of Alboin, restored Forum Cornelii, which had been destroyed by Narses. Others say that its name arose either from a corruption of the word Aemilia or from a fortress built there by Antiochus, Narses’ commander.

Thus Apollinaris, a disciple of Saint Peter the Apostle and the first bishop of Ravenna, strengthened Forum Cornelii in faith through his most holy example and preaching. But the city, stained by the most abominable morals of the nations and fallen into idolatry, again needed the assistance of Cassian, bishop of Sabiona in Germany, who spiritually restored, strengthened, and established Forum Cornelii in the faith through his teaching and holiness; indeed, in the year of the Lord 362, on the Ides of August, under the rule of Julian the Apostate, he consecrated it through martyrdom and his sacred blood.

> **Note [Col. 0028D].** Ericus, or Ercius, a monk who was writing in Gaul toward the end of the ninth century, testifies in the *Life of Saint Germanus, Bishop of Auxerre*, that Chrysologus was born of an ancient and noble bloodline:
>
> *Peter, deserving by rank and name to shine as a prince of the Church,*  
> *In the city preserved the apostolic teachings;*  
> *Perhaps he guarded the flock, conspicuous for the lofty splendor*  
> *Of his ancestral lineage, and radiant with great integrity.*

The same man’s life, recovered from an ancient manuscript, was reported by Surius; from him, Peter in the *Catalog*, Book VI, chapter 128; Saint Gregory in the *Register*, Book V, chapter 33; Bede, Usuard, the Roman Martyrology, and others. Under Vespasian, in the year preceding his death—namely, in the year 78 of the common era—he completed an illustrious life by a particularly distinguished martyrdom. See what we discussed about him in the notes to Sermon 128 of Chrysologus.

> **Note [Col. 0028D].** Ughellus reproduces a fragment of his life in the section on the bishops of Imola, p. 620 of the recent edition, from an ancient chronicle. The genuine acts of his martyrdom, from Prudentius’ book *On Crowns*, are found in Ruinart, p. 532. The other accounts in circulation are of doubtful reliability; nor are those of better quality which Baronius professed to have found at Rome in connection with the Martyrology, in which Cassian is said to have held the see of Brescia. Perhaps, however, through a scribal error, *Brixina* was read as *Brixia* in Baronius, as Ferrarius observes in his *Annotations*, p. 508. Brixina was the city to which the episcopal see was transferred after Sabiona was destroyed. Our Florentinius, in the Martyrology under 11 August, p. 747, incorrectly reports that he was bishop of Forum Cornelii. Ferrarius and Mita, in the *Life of Chrysologus*, say that he was ordained bishop of Sabiona by Fortunatus of Aquileia; yet we know that Fortunatus lived in the time of the Emperor Constantius and was infected with the Arian taint. But the short Roman Martyrology; the Reichenau Martyrology under 11 August; the Augsburg Martyrology under 13 August; the Ottobonian Martyrology, on that same day, of the Queen of Sweden; the Auxerre Martyrology published by Martène in volume VI of the *Anecdota Collecta*; the Stavelot Martyrology of Ado, as edited by Florentinius under 11 August; Prudentius in Hymn IX; and Bede’s little book—while all remember him only as a martyr—never mention him as a bishop. Consult the Bollandists under 13 August.

> An anonymous writer of Imola, in the chronicle preserved by Ughellus, volume II, p. 619, writes that he lived at Brescia, or Brixina, formerly called Sales, in Germany, in the province of Tyrol, whose bishopric is subject to the metropolitan of Salzburg; he says that he was distinguished for Christian integrity and that, expelled by enemies, he came from there to Imola. But concerning his episcopate there is not even the faintest trace. The year in which he suffered is uncertain. Pastrizio, in his work on the paten of Saint Peter Chrysologus, assigns his martyrdom to the year 362. Julian, under whom Cassian is said to have suffered, obtained the empire in the year 361, on 3 October; he held it through the following year and died on 26 June 363, struck by lightning, according to the *Fasti* of Hydatius. John Malalas notes that Julian died at the fifth hour of the night on 27 June—that is, during the night preceding that day. Since that intermediate night may be assigned to either day, some writers consequently place the day of his death on 26 June. There are very different opinions concerning the manner of his death, as Gothofredus shows in his dissertation on Book VII, chapter 15, of Philostorgius. But this is beside the point.
