I will add only that Pastrizio did not derive from an obscure source the report that Cassian died after being struck by lightning. It is established that, pierced by the point of a spear, he ended his impious days by a most impious death as divine vengeance.

### 2.

The city, shaken by wars and at times occupied by heretics, at times by pagans, lost the faith over the course of time. But God repeatedly brought it back into his bosom, preserving it as a garden planted with so many roses of virgins, lilies of confessors—among which the white lily of Chrysologus excelled—and violets of martyrs.

Forty-three years after the martyrdom of Saint Cassian, Cornelius obtained the see of the restored Church of Forum Cornelii. A Roman by nationality, distinguished in life and most excellent in conduct, he deserved after his death to be praised in a sermon by Chrysologus, Sermon 165. Cornelius had occupied the episcopal chair of the Church of Forum Cornelii in the year of the Lord 405 or 406. By then, from the noble lineage of the men of Forum Cornelii, a new light seemed to have arisen in Chrysologus, as though for that Church a firmest support of the new rock upon the rock had been born.

> **Note [Col. 0029D].** You will not find even one of the writers of Chrysologus’ life who, with the slightest hesitation, doubts that this Cornelius was bishop of Imola. All assert it with complete consistency; and Ughellus places him first and says that he was consecrated by Pope Celestine in the year 400. It is surprising, however, that when Chrysologus, in his praise of Bishop Projectus in Sermon 165, digresses somewhat in his eulogy, he did not seize the opportunity that naturally presented itself to speak of this dignity. He merely says that Cornelius loved the city which had received its name from Cornelius, by whom Chrysologus himself had been initiated into the sacred rites. Hence Tillemont, volume V, p. 865 of the Venetian edition, thought that the Cornelius mentioned by Chrysologus had held the episcopate of some other city.

At the sacred baptismal font, in the new washing of regeneration, our man was given the name Peter, to foreshadow the accumulation of future virtues in so great a bishop.

> **Note [Col. 0030C].** Castillo inferred from Mita’s observations on this sermon that the bishop Adelphus mentioned in Sermon 107 among the sermons of Chrysologus was bishop of Metz. Mita was guided by Baronius, who writes the following in his notes to the Martyrology under 29 August: “Bishop Adelphus is placed here tenth in succession in the list of the bishops of Metz according to Demochus, *On the Sacrifice of the Mass*. Nolanus discusses the translation of the same man on this day in his additions to Usuard. There is a Sermon of Saint Peter Chrysologus, number 136, on the feast of Saint Adelphus; whether he is the man under discussion, I dare not affirm.”

> Mita thinks that Paul the Deacon caused Baronius to hesitate by writing in his *History of the Bishops of the Church of Metz*, in volume VIII of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*: “Adelphus was tenth in succession,” without indicating in what year he held the see. This is all the more significant because, from the reckoning of the years in the table of episcopal names appended to the *History*, it can be inferred that this Adelphus had ceased to live during Chrysologus’ lifetime. To strengthen Baronius’ opinion and remove his uncertainty, however, Mita attempts to weaken the reliability of this table with empty arguments.

> In the Sermon cited above, number 136, Chrysologus calls him “first in place.” Before Ravenna was endowed with metropolitan rights, it acknowledged no superior except the Roman pontiff and the bishop of Milan, or perhaps of Aquileia. At that time there was no Adelphus in any of these sees. We must therefore follow Tillemont, volume V, p. 189: this Adelphus, a bishop of uncertain see, preceded Chrysologus only in age. The same point will have to be repeated elsewhere. See Sermon 136, note 3.

Concerning our Chrysologus, Saint Adelphus, bishop of Metz, says in Sermon 107:

> “For the name Peter in others is merely the designation of a name; in this man—that is, Peter Chrysologus—it is the prerogative of virtues.”

Our own Chrysologus likewise says in Sermon 154:

> “The very names of the saints often indicate their merits. Thus Peter received his name from the rock, because he first deserved to establish the Church through the firmness of faith.”

For from childhood Peter surpassed the other boys in excellence of intellect, and as an adult he surpassed his elders and other teachers in Latin and Greek eloquence. The Greeks who came from Byzantium to Ravenna at the emperor’s favor gave him the surname *Chrysologos*, or *Chrysologus*: from *chrysos*, “gold,” and *logos*, “word”—as though “golden speech,” or “one who speaks golden words.”

Similarly, the Byzantine Greeks themselves, not many years before Chrysologus’ birth, had called their own bishop John, most eloquent in Attic learning, *Chrysostom*, namely “golden mouth.” Thus among all people, both in his own time and in ours, Peter deserved to retain continually the name Chrysologus, so that even his homilies, or sermons, are commonly called “golden” by learned men.

## § II. Chrysologus’ education, his election to the bishopric of Ravenna, and his consecration are recounted.

### 3.

From his earliest childhood Chrysologus devoted himself wholly, first to prayer and then to the study of good and sacred literature. He frequented sacred buildings and visited the metropolitan church, where he would prostrate himself before the altars of Cassian, the patron martyr of his homeland, and spend an entire day together with a considerable part of the night.

This extraordinary piety and devotion of our Peter so seized the mind of Saint Cornelius, then bishop of the aforementioned town of Forum Cornelii, and so attracted his affection that he summoned Peter to himself, received him into his pastoral care, and raised him. The aforementioned bishop thoroughly instructed him in the service of God.

I call Chrysologus himself as witness in Sermon 165, where he says:

> “For Cornelius, illustrious in life and of most blessed memory, everywhere resplendent with every title of virtue, known to all for the greatness of his works, was a father to me. He begot me through the Gospel; he tenderly, most tenderly, nourished me; he, holy himself, instructed me in holy service.”

When Peter had reached adulthood, Saint Cornelius made him his deacon. Recognizing that he was burning with the most ardent love for the poor, Cornelius chose him as his steward and sacred treasurer, entrusting to him—as Pope Sixtus once entrusted Laurentiu­s—the resources and wealth of the Church, so that through his most faithful distribution he might draw assistance from the sacred storehouse for the needy and come to the aid of the wretched. Cornelius was no less inflamed by Chrysologus’ pointed eloquence, philosophy, theology, and mastery of sacred literature, in all of which he shone brilliantly, like a burning lamp in the temple of God.

### 4.

After several years, at Ravenna—which is a city of the Sabines in the eighth region of Italy, founded and situated on the shore of the Adriatic, between two not particularly wealthy rivers called the Sabio and the Roneus, one of which washes its walls, and which faces Imola, Faenza, Cesena, and Forlì—we find a city so ancient that it saw its own foundations laid after the confusion of languages.

Cassiodorus the senator, blessed Apollinaris, its first bishop, Saint Vitalis, Gervasius and Protasius, and Peter of Ravenna, bishop of Forum Cornelii, about whom more will be said below, originated there. This is not the Ravenna of Faustina in the territory of Tarracina, twenty miles from Rome. For our Ravenna, see Pliny, Book III, sections 4–13, and Martial, Book III, epigram 56.

Its bishop John, the first of that name but nevertheless the twentieth bishop of Ravenna, fell asleep in the Lord. Because of his holiness, purity, and innocence, the Greeks called him *Angeloptos*.

> **Note [Col. 0031C].** Ferrarius attributes this to his continuous, or at least frequent, association with angels, on pp. 721–722, and assigns his feast to 21 November. Some believe him to have been the first archbishop of Ravenna, relying on an old document which Baronius, in the year 432, very deservedly brands as false. Whether he was Chrysologus’ immediate predecessor, see Tillemont, p. 181, and note 5, p. 866; and Ughellus, volume XI, p. 351.

In accordance with the customary practice, the suffragan bishops came to Ravenna to elect the new bishop: the bishops of Rimini, Cesena, Forlì, Faenza, Brindisi, Bologna, Modena, Reggio, Parma, Piacenza, and Forum Cornelii, which at that time was called Saint Cornelius. Cornelius came together with his deacon Chrysologus.

> **Note [Col. 0031C].** Ravenna had been, at least from the year 408, the metropolis of the province of Flaminia, to which it is assigned. But this dignity concerned only civil jurisdiction. Its bishop, together with the other bishops of Flaminia, was subject to the metropolitan of Milan. Flaminia was bounded by the territory of Cisalpine Gaul, which is now called the vicariate of Italy.

> It is hitherto unknown why, as the years passed, Ravenna deserved to be honored with metropolitan jurisdiction. I would be mistaken unless this were attributable to the presence of imperial dignity, with which it had been adorned from the year 402, when the Emperor Honorius, having departed from Milan and stayed at Ravenna for several months, established his residence there in that same year, and Valentinian III did so from 426 onward. Hence a certain prerogative flowed to the city, so that it might deserve to be declared a metropolis by decree of pope and emperor—a decree which some, perhaps including the bishop of Milan whose rights were being diminished, tried to oppose.

> In much the same way, the cause of the vicars of Italy, who lived at Milan, began to distinguish the bishop of that city, upon whom rested the responsibility of ordaining bishops and convening the synod throughout Italy, in the narrower sense in which the term was used.

> Some, however, think that the Church of Ravenna was enlarged with metropolitan honor only toward the end of the time of John Angeloptos, through the efforts of the younger Valentinian and the most devout Augusta Galla Placidia; and that Peter Chrysologus exercised such a function only because of the disturbances and complications that arose, when he ordained the bishop of Vicohaventinum.

> Henschenius, volume XI of the *Acta Sanctorum* for May, p. 154, seems nevertheless inclined to believe that Chrysologus himself was honored with this dignity under Saint Leo the Great and Valentinian, around the year 450, having previously received from Sixtus III, Leo’s predecessor, only the title and authority of a bishop. Consult what I published from Pastrizio in the notes to the sermons.

> As I write this, I hear that there are highly learned men at Ravenna who, after ransacking the drawers of the archives, have—under favorable auspices—come upon certain more ancient documents, hitherto known to no one. With their help, the metropolitan dignity of Ravenna may be asserted as exceedingly ancient, so that all doubt about the matter may be removed and disputes settled. I regret that, although I addressed the distinguished learned man Father Paciaudi, Cleric Regular, by letters and services, he sent me no reply. Thus, as a stranger, I can do nothing but report what more accurate writers have transmitted. Perhaps a later day will bring forth better evidence.

Thus Cornelius came with his deacon Chrysologus to assist in the election of his metropolitan, the archbishop of Ravenna; at that time the citizens also participated by marks, or votes. When the bishops disagreed in the assembly, after various debates had taken place during the election, one of the citizens of Ravenna was selected for the episcopate. Ravenna sent its citizens as envoys to Rome, so that they might obtain from Sixtus III, the supreme Vicar of Christ, the blessing of their elected bishop.

> **Note [Col. 0034D].** The daughter of the Emperor Theodosius and sister of the Emperors Arcadius and Honorius, Galla Placidia reluctantly married Ataulf, king of the Goths, in 411. Later restored to freedom—for she had been a captive of the Goths—and after Ataulf had been killed by them, she entered a second marriage with Caesar Constantius by the authority of her brother Honorius. At Ravenna she bore him Valentinian III.

> **Note [Col. 0032D].** Mita, Castillo, and other writers of submissive intellect maintain that what they report about Chrysologus’ ordination from Agnellus’ *Pontifical* must be relegated to the realm of fables. Yet Bacchinius remarks in his *Observations on Agnellus*, above, p. 11, no. 2: “It is astonishing,” he says, “that some men are so constituted that they readily believe everything, while others, on the contrary, question everything.”

> Tillemont also detected the mark of falsehood upon these little narratives, chiefly because the ordination of the bishops of Ravenna belonged to the rights of the metropolitan of Milan, not to those of the Roman pontiff. The custom of bishops summoning the Roman pontiff so that they might receive consecration from him was already said to be ancient from the time of Pope Leo. “In his time,” Anastasius says in his account of Leo VI, “the Church of Ravenna was restored under the authority of the apostolic see, so that when an archbishop had died, the man who had been elected came to the city of Rome to be ordained, according to the ancient custom.” Perhaps this was imposed as punishment for an earlier attempt at autocephaly. But because this practice had come into use in later times, recent writers too readily believed that it suited the age of Chrysologus.

At that time, it is said, Bishop Cornelius came to Rome with his deacon Chrysologus, either to confirm the aforementioned election of the bishop of Ravenna or to conduct the affairs of his own Church of Forum Cornelii. The supreme pontiff, Sixtus III, then saw in a dream a vision descending from heaven: namely, Peter, prince of the apostles, and Saint Apollinaris, the disciple of the same Saint Peter and the first bishop of Ravenna. They presented Chrysologus’ appearance to Sixtus, indicating that he—not the other man whom the people of Ravenna had proposed and whom they had rejected—ought to be elected bishop, and that it would be more pleasing to God Almighty for him to be made bishop of Ravenna.

The people of Ravenna approached the pontifical tribunal and presented to Sixtus the citizen whom they themselves had elected as bishop, kneeling and begging him to confirm the election by an authoritative declaration. But the Head of the Church, already sufficiently enlightened from above, carried out the heavenly business: he rejected the man presented and ordered the other Ravennans to appear. Bishop Cornelius of Forum Cornelii arrived, and Sixtus commanded him to bring his companions and associates into the consistory. Obeying so great a command, Cornelius brought the deacon Chrysologus together with his attendants and ministers.

### 5.

When Sixtus saw him, he immediately recognized that he was the man shown to him from heaven and already designated by the supreme divinity as bishop of Ravenna. Accordingly, before the countless people standing by and listening, both from Forum Cornelii and from Ravenna, he proclaimed in a solemn declaration:

> “We appoint no other than this man as archbishop and place him over the Church of Ravenna.”

When the Ravennans understood this, they were all seized with grief and lamented the outcome as though it were an omen against them, because contrary to ancestral custom a citizen had not been elected and made bishop, but an outsider from Forum Cornelii had been chosen for the office.

The supreme ruler, who understood this well, sought to calm the troubled minds of the citizens of Ravenna. Chrysologus was refusing to accept the archiepiscopal insignia, lest he and the citizens resist the divine will. The ruler therefore explained to him the revelation that had been made to him from heaven with such eloquence, spiritual power, and force of expression that he not only overcame the Ravennans but also compelled Chrysologus to accept the dignity he had renounced.

After kissing the feet of the pope and visiting the sacred thresholds of the apostles, the new bishop of Ravenna, Chrysologus, returned to his homeland, Forum Cornelii, with his protector Cornelius and a considerable retinue of citizens of Ravenna. He did so not only to accompany with pious courtesy Cornelius, bishop of Forum Cornelii, but also to greet the altars of Saint Cassian the martyr.

There, clinging to the sarcophagus of the holy martyr, he earnestly sought with a great abundance of tears the protection of the shepherding of his sheep. He distributed to the poor the temporal possessions of his entire household. After bidding farewell to his beloved homeland, Forum Cornelii, he proceeded with his household retinue and returned to Ravenna.

### 6.

It is believed that Cornelius arrived at Ravenna together with Chrysologus. The Emperor Valentinian III and his mother Galla Placidia received these most holy men at the entrance of the gate with a festive procession and joyful applause. They then held the reins of the empire and maintained their residence at Ravenna, in that city which at that time claimed the first place in Italy after Rome.

It remains to recount the gathering and reception of the people of Ravenna.

In the year of the Lord 433, on a solemn day before the consecration, Chrysologus received the priesthood from the hand of Saint Cornelius, scarcely able to restrain his tears. The Sunday was therefore appointed for the sacred rite of consecration and publicly announced, lest the humble man should lose among his own people the exaltation promised him by God before God and men.

The other provincial bishops assembled, and in the great basilica of Ravenna, in the presence of the Christian rulers—the emperor and his mother—and of the nobles of the people, Chrysologus was consecrated bishop by Saint Cornelius according to the ancient custom.

Thus Chrysologus himself says in Sermon 165, speaking of Cornelius:

> “The bishop himself presented me to the sacred altars and consecrated me; therefore the name of Cornelius is dear and worthy of veneration to me.”

Once made bishop, Chrysologus delivered to the people a very brief but most celebrated sermon, in which, with lofty spiritual power, he outlined the obligations and duties of a good bishop. He gave thanks for the office and the festive procession, and praised the presence and Christian piety of the emperor and his mother Galla Placidia. The whole matter is clear from Sermon 130 of Chrysologus. See it there.

The entire province of Aemilia, or Imola, in which Ravenna was the greatest city and the imperial seat of the West, rejoiced in its new bishop, father, and teacher. Earlier, around the year 390, God had granted Ambrose to Milan. Likewise, shortly before our own time, around the year 430, he had given Augustine to the Church of Hippo. Now, not forgetting Aemilia, the Lord gave Chrysologus to it in the year 433, so that by his holiness he might strengthen the faith of the Ravennans and by his eloquence and marvelous teaching eradicate all the heresies of Aemilia.

> **Note [Col. 0034D].** See what has been noted in the notes to Sermon 130.

## § III. Various deeds and virtues of Chrysologus, archbishop of Ravenna, are reviewed.

### 7.

Our Peter Chrysologus was not that Peter of Ravenna who was born at Ravenna and was its twenty-fourth bishop, who was also bishop of Forum Cornelii, attended the Roman council under Symmachus, and lived long after our Chrysologus, around the year 502.

> **Note [Col. 0034D].** This Peter was famous in the time of King Theoderic and played a significant role in the councils held concerning Pope Symmachus in the years 500 and 504. They write that he occupied the see of Ravenna for approximately sixty years. But from a letter of Saint Leo to Neon, bishop of Ravenna, dated either 451 or 458, and from another letter of Pope Simplicius to John, bishop of that same see, it is correctly inferred that this Peter, who was alive around 448 or 449, had already died. See Saint Leo, Epistle 135, p. 716, and volume IV of the Councils, pp. 1068–1069. According to Ughellus, John II succeeded him in 494, or, more accurately according to Bacchinius, in 496. From where Castillo learned that this Peter occupied the see of Forum Cornelii is still unknown to me.

Whether this Peter of Ravenna, so called from his homeland and episcopal see, was surnamed Altinas, the man whom King Theoderic the Goth sent to Rome because of his outstanding theology, on which he wrote much, or not, matters little. For although many people and the ordinary Gloss call our man “Peter of Ravenna,” this is not because he was born at Ravenna—for he recognized no homeland except Forum Cornelii—but because he was Ravenna’s most celebrated bishop and teacher.

### 8.

Scarcely had our Chrysologus obtained the archiepiscopate at Ravenna when he immediately devoted himself entirely to the welfare of his people, separating the grain from the chaff and uprooting pagan and superstitious rites. He either banished or converted to good and orthodox customs those who observed the kalends of January with excessive superstition in honor of the new annual cycle, as may be gathered from the author’s Sermon 155.

He likewise restrained the corrupt and excessively altered fasts of the Ravennans. For the citizens sometimes observed the Lenten weeks with excessive rigor, while at other times they preferred them too indulgent and lax. See the whole of Sermon 166 on this subject.

He also recalled and completely corrected the catechumens who were postponing the sacred washing for a long time, as is evident from Sermons 10 and 59. He baptized countless pagans who came from various regions to the Emperor Valentinian on business, washing them in the sacred water of baptism. After filling them with the nourishment of sacred doctrine, and even satisfying them with material food, he sent them away, as appears from Sermon 62.

He instructed the catechumens not through assistants or ministers but personally in the faith of the Lord’s Prayer and the Apostles’ Creed. This may properly be drawn from Sermons 40 and 56 through 62 inclusive, and from Sermons 67 through 72 inclusive.

But in order to raise young men from the death of vanities, like another Elisha in conduct, he adapted himself to the young so as to restrain their most subtle intellects. He checked their harmful cleverness and led the lofty but vain thoughts of their philosophy back to the true path of orthodox truth.

This quality shone forth in Chrysologus. Saint Adelphus, bishop of Metz, had traveled from Gaul to Ravenna to visit the emperor. In a certain sermon, which is number 107 in the author’s collection, he touched upon Chrysologus’ sacred conduct and publicly declared:

> “He himself is also most blessed and apostolic, a hunter who touches the souls of young men in flight with the pen of divine speech.”

For the young men, philosophizing vainly, used to say—not merely with their lips but by their conduct—and feared the words of Plautus in *The Braggart Soldier*:

> “Look around, lest someone become a bird-catcher of our speech.”

But an apostolic bird-catcher, Chrysologus, was given to them from heaven. He seized them like wicked birds flying through the air and placed them in the cage of the Church.

### 9.

Chrysologus is not accidentally called by Adelphus a most blessed and apostolic man. He loved the apostolic life so deeply that he appeared to be another apostle. Hence he introduced into his clergy a common and apostolic form of life, teaching them to serve continually in regular ministries, as Adelphus suggests in the same sermon when he says:

> “Thus, having been imbued with monastic disciplines, he practices the rule of holiness,”

and so forth.

Chrysologus himself also clearly indicates this throughout Sermon 39, where he mentions the canonical hours recited at dawn.

But so that the holy bishop might acquire all this more conveniently, according to Ursinus he erected at Ravenna a large marble building, which his fellow citizens thereafter called the *Tricolum*, because it had been skillfully constructed in the form of three hills.

> **Note [Col. 0036D].** Nonsense. “Tricolum,” says Agnellus, because it contained three *cola*, since it was divided into three notable sections—what the Greeks called *ta kōla* (τὰ κῶλα). But it may be observed from the above-mentioned Bacchinius, whom I ask you to consult concerning the other buildings attributed to our Chrysologus, that this structure should be attributed to Peter III of that name, not to Peter Chrysologus.

The sacred building of this structure was commonly called Chrysologus’ Canonica. For the clergy who lived and served in the metropolitan church devoted themselves there to the regular discipline of the canonica and, living together in community as in a convent, freely served God and dwelt there.

Before Chrysologus, my own Saint Martin had done something similar around the year 370. The Roman Breviary, under 11 November, reports of him:

> “Having been made bishop of Tours, he built a monastery where he lived for some time in the greatest holiness with eighty monks.”

Aurelius Augustine likewise did this at Hippo before the year of the Lord 340, as his historians report.

Chrysologus also dedicated a sacred church to the holy apostle Andrew, which he built from its foundations near the aforementioned Ursinian building. On the front of its vault there could be seen an image of Chrysologus, as the Ravennese annalist Rubeus testifies in Book II of his *History*, under the year 449.

Our Chrysologus, overtaken by death, did not put the final hand to the basilica of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, which he had begun with deep affection and already dedicated to him in spirit and intention. He contributed significantly, both in assistance and in expense, to the construction of the church of the Holy Cross, as well as to the chapel of Saints Nazarius and Celsus, where the emperor’s parent and empress Augusta had erected a mausoleum and sarcophagus for herself.

10. For he who opened the baptismal pool so widely to the gentiles, who so diligently and anxiously offered the water of the sacred font to unbelievers, also took care, as a good shepherd, not only to water his flock with the streams of doctrine [Col. 0037A], but also to open a material spring for his sheep. For, having investigated a spring of very sweet water in a small town near Ravenna, Chrysologus built a fountain and fortified it with a double wall or tower, so that it might serve not only the people of Ravenna but also be available, more securely, to the flocks at the very place where it welled up. The divine oracle commends this as worthy of praise in the case of Uzziah, 2 Chronicles 26:10, where, while he was still seeking the Lord, it says: “He built towers in the wilderness and dug many cisterns, because he possessed much livestock.”

Similarly, among the most celebrated works by which the most holy pontiff Innocent X has adorned the City in recent years is the fountain called Innocent’s Fountain. He also decorated it with a double tower and various onyx statues. We omit [Col. 0037B] the many and varied alms by which he relieved the distress of the poor and needy with open hand and redeemed their misery; this can be inferred with reasonable clarity from the Author’s hundred-and-third sermon. In fasting, prayers, and hair shirts he was so penitential and austere that, while he was still alive, he deserved to hear those epithets from the mouth of the preaching bishop Adelphus: “holy and most blessed,” as is clear from sermon 107.

Other praises of Chrysologus may be drawn from Natalis, Trithemius, Baronius, volume V of the *Annals*, under the year 435, and from Saint Felix, archbishop of Ravenna, in the preface to Chrysologus’s *Homilies*, as well as from Mita and others. As regards episcopal matters, Chrysologus consecrated two bishops [Note: [Col. 0037D] Add what we discussed in the notes to sermons 165 and 175]: namely, Projectus, bishop of Forum Cornelii and successor of Saint Cornelius of Rome, as is established from sermon 165, and [Col. 0037C] Marcellinus, bishop of Vicohaventia, whom Chrysologus consecrated at Ravenna on the Nativity of the Lord in the year 449 or at the beginning of 450. For Vicohaventia, from which Marcellinus came, was a city of Aemilia subject to Ravenna’s jurisdiction and archbishopric; it now exists as a village within the territory of Ferrara.

§ IV. On the precious death of Chrysologus and his glorious tomb

11. Chrysologus had already completed eighteen successful years in his episcopal office when, around the year 450 of the Lord, foreseeing his death, he sought Forum Cornelii, his native land. There he desired to be released from this life and to be with Christ—there where he had first seen the light of the world and where he had first learned, in the office of the diaconate, to serve the sacred altars.

When the bishop of Ravenna, Chrysologus, entered the city, his fellow citizens of Forum Cornelii, together with their bishop Projectus, received him with great joy and cheerful applause. Everyone congratulated Chrysologus for having honored his homeland by his authority and presence. After the sons had been kindly received by their father, Chrysologus went the next day to the church of Saint Cassian the martyr, so that he might publicly offer the Eucharistic sacrifice there. He greeted his patron Cassian with devotion and earnestly entreated him before God at the hour of death, since he already knew that the end of his life was approaching.

At the altar of the holy martyr Cassian he asked the bishop and clergy for a burial place, offering the sacred martyr, prostrate upon the ground, his mitre—a gold-worked cap variegated with gems—together with a golden cup and a silver dish, which he himself had often used in sacred rites. Among the other words he addressed aloud to his patron Cassian, he added:

“I beseech you, blessed martyr Cassian, intercede for me. I was almost a servant of your household, nourished in this temple by Cornelius, bishop of this see. Returning to you once more, I now render my soul to almighty God; but I commend my body to you.”

After concluding these and similar words, he gave the people an episcopal blessing in the sign of the cross and quietly, indeed exceedingly peacefully, fell asleep in the Lord there beside the altar, around midday on the second day of December, in the year of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0037D] Bacchinius explicitly confirms that Chrysologus’s year of death cannot be placed before 448 or deferred beyond 451. Pastritius de Patena and others think that Chrysologus went to Rome in 449 and returned to Ravenna at Easter in 450. From a letter of Saint Leo the pope to Neon of Ravenna, written in 451, it is likewise inferred that Chrysologus had already departed to the blessed in 450.] 440, under Leo I, supreme pontiff, in the consulship of Marcian Augustus, while Valentinian III ruled in the West and Theodosius the Younger in the East, in the forty-fourth year of his age. This is gathered [Col. 0038C] from letter 37 of Pope Leo I, written in the consulship of the aforesaid Marcian Augustus and addressed to Neon, bishop of Ravenna and Chrysologus’s successor.

Among Chrysologus’s clothing were found a hooded garment and the hair shirt [Note: [Col. 0037D] When the Armo—[the text appears corrupt]—had already defected from Valentinian for the second time in 448 in order to assert their liberty, Aetius, who at that time governed the Western Empire in the emperor’s place, sent against them Eocaricus, or whatever his name may have been, a leading man barbarous in religion and morals and equipped with very powerful forces. To avert this scourge that threatened his beloved peoples, Saint Germanus of Auxerre, bishop, was entreated by their envoys; he set out on the road and reached Ravenna to ask the emperor for pardon. On entering the city, he was entertained as a guest by Chrysologus. There, enriched with gifts by the empress Placidia and treated with great honor, he performed several miracles, until he was overcome by illness and died on the seventh day after taking to his bed, on the thirty-first day of July in the year 448. On that date his feast passed into the Parisian calendar from many calendars of the provinces of Gaul. He is mentioned by the Martyrology of Ado, edited by the illustrious Georgius, p. 366; by the Hieronymian, Gellonense, and Rabanus, and by Notker, who copied Rabanus. At the beginning of the old Gallican Missal printed by Thomasius there is a Mass of Saint Germanus, but nothing about the day on which his feast was celebrated. From several martyrologies it appears that his translation was solemnly observed on the Kalends of October. Certainly in ninth-century Gaul the Kalends of October were sacred to Remigius and Germanus.] of Saint Germanus, bishop of Auxerre. When Germanus exchanged the death he had foreseen at Ravenna for heavenly life, his corpse was buried by Chrysologus and sent to Gaul; and the saintly heir of that most holy man had put on his hooded garment and hair shirt. This was fully revealed after Chrysologus’s death.

12. On the third day before the Nones of December, when the whole people had assembled in the afternoon, the funeral of Chrysologus was celebrated by Projectus, bishop of Forum Cornelii, and Saint Donatus, deacon of that same city and Church, together with [Col. 0039A] all the clergy and the assistance of the city’s praetor. The body of the holy man was placed in an urn and buried beside the altar of Saint Cassian, the place he himself had selected.

Not many days later, after the matter had been carefully considered, the entire people assembled with Bishop Projectus in the church and, by acclamation and the common vote of all, with the authority of Bishop Projectus, enrolled Chrysologus among the saints. In former times, the canonization of God’s servants by particular canonization—for a single province, nation, or kingdom—with the consent of the people belonged to bishops, as is sufficiently clear from the words of Saint Cyprian, martyr and bishop of Carthage. In book III, letter 6, toward the middle, speaking of martyrs, he says:

“Finally, mark down also the days on which they depart, so that we may be able to celebrate their commemorations among the memorials of the martyrs.” [Col. 0039B]

But the supreme pastors of the Church, in order to address certain difficulties arising from the aforementioned customary practice, decreed that this matter of canonization should belong solely to the Church’s supreme head. The same is found in Alexander III, chapter *Audivimus*, and Innocent III, chapter *Cum ex eo*, concerning relics and the veneration of saints. Thus Felix Contelorius, *On the Canonization of Saints*, no. 17; Troilus Malvetius, doubt 2, beginning with no. 1; Augustine Triumphus, *On the Power of the Church*, question 14, no. 2; and others commonly hold.

[Note: [Col. 0039D] The devastation of Italy by Attila began in 452, and while he was advancing, John was bishop at Ravenna. From this a weightier argument is drawn that Chrysologus’s death cannot be pushed beyond the year 451.]

At that time Attila was ravaging Italy with extreme ferocity when Chrysologus departed to heaven. For this reason the costly elevation or placement of his body was postponed until the year of the Lord 455. In that year Chrysologus’s glorious tomb was gloriously and expensively adorned at the cost of the church of Forum Cornelii, and the jasper urn containing his body was raised aloft and decorated with great veneration.

Chrysologus was succeeded in the episcopate of Ravenna by Neon, a most modest and learned man [Note: [Col. 0039D] Bacchinius thoroughly removes the conjecture from which authors derived the claim that Neon was Chrysologus’s successor.] under the same Pope Leo I. The pontiff himself wrote him a letter, which occupies the thirty-seventh place among Leo’s letters.

13. The arm of Saint Peter Chrysologus, adorned with gold and gems, appears whole and unharmed to this day and is venerated in the Ursine church at Ravenna. His silver dish is likewise kept there [Note: [Col. 0040D] Abbot Joannes Pastritius prepared a dissertation on this object and published it at Rome from the press of Antonius de Rubeis in 1706. I too have written something about it in a work published at Naples in 1746.]. It is so beneficial to all, both the sick and those in poor health, that water poured through it and drunk by the faithful both protects against pestilences and heals the bite of a rabid dog, besides treating various other diseases [Col. 0039D]. Hence all who are afflicted with the fevers mentioned above hasten to Chrysologus’s tomb and immediately regain their health.

The body of Saint Chrysologus is said to have been found incorrupt and unharmed by the bishop and clergy of the church of Forum Cornelii after 1,042 years. Later, namely in the year of the Lord 1497, on August 29, under Pope Alexander VI, we read that the body of Saint Chrysologus was again placed in its resting place by Simon, bishop of Ravenna, and Matthaeus a Phaello, provost of the cathedral church of Imola [Col. 0040A].

We said “after 1,042 years” because when Phaellus says in his letter, “I profess in faith that I have touched with my own hands the body of our fellow citizen Chrysologus, honorably buried from the year 455, and so forth,” he does not mean that only 455 years had elapsed from Chrysologus’s burial to his own time. For from the year 450, when Chrysologus died, until Phaellus’s time, 1,042 years had passed. Rather, he wishes the year 455 to be remembered, when, after Attila’s scourge, the body of Saint Chrysologus was buried and raised aloft, as we said above, § 4, no. 12.

§ V. On the writings of Saint Peter Chrysologus

14. The sermons of Saint Peter Chrysologus that now circulate under his name and are continually cited in pulpits number 176. They begin with the sermon on the Prodigal Son, in these words: “Today the Lord for us …,” and end with the sermon on the Blind Man, in these words: “He will rise in glory.”

Of these 176 homilies or sermons, however, six do not belong to Saint Chrysologus, according to the more probable opinion of experts. Sermon 53, for example, is believed to have been written by Saint Barbatius, adviser to the empress Placidia. Sermon 107 is the work of Saint Adelphus, bishop of Metz; and sermon 129 was both written and preached by another priest of that period. Saint Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, composed sermon 138; and Saint Severianus, bishop of Gabala, dictated sermon 149 [Col. 0040C].

Conversely, sermon 152 is attributed to that same Severianus, although it truly belongs to Chrysologus, as both its style and its teaching sufficiently prove. Some attribute sermons 50 and 127 to Saint John Chrysostom, although they were truly preached by Chrysologus. See, concerning these matters, volume V of the *Library of the Ancient Fathers*, fourth edition, at the beginning. There you will find certain sermons falsely attributed to Chrysologus that are not his, while others that do belong to Chrysologus are assigned sometimes to Saint Jerome and sometimes to Saint Chrysostom.

15. Besides the sermons mentioned above, Chrysologus wrote many other works, which perished through the passage of time. He wrote certain commentaries and several letters against the Arians, which, together with sermon 171, had been preserved at Imola and carefully prepared by the nobleman Balthasar, of Chrysologus’s lineage [Col. 0040D]. But when this man was imprisoned during a siege and the persecution of the tyrant Theodoric, king of the Ostrogoths, because of his defense of the faith, and died there of starvation, all Chrysologus’s works kept by him perished in the fire during that conflagration by which the savage tyrant brutally devastated Ravenna and Forum Cornelii around the year of the Lord 524.

Because other original manuscripts—perhaps the copies from which that Balthasar had drawn his exemplars—had been hidden somewhere during Theodoric’s invasion and were found unharmed, Chrysologus’s works later suffered fire once again, when, in the year of the Lord 700, during the time of Damian, thirty-ninth bishop of Ravenna, the entire archiepiscopal library was accidentally consumed by flames. In that year 176 sermons of Chrysologus, those that now survive, were found in the house of a certain most learned priest, together with the *Letter to Eutyches*.

16. Thus in the time of our Chrysologus it happened that Eutyches, a Byzantine abbot, supported by the protection of certain people and strengthened by the assistance of evildoers, under the pretext of faith, confidently claiming and promising that he would write against Nestorius—who taught that there were two persons in Christ—spread a heretical and false doctrine throughout the entire empire [Col. 0041B]. He taught that Christ’s divine nature and human nature had been reduced to one and the same thing.

Flavianus, bishop of Byzantium, condemned this heresy in a synod convened against Eutyches and ordered that the acts be sent to Leo, the first pontiff of that name. Therefore the holy pontiff Leo, well aware of Saint Chrysologus’s eloquence, subtlety, and learning, summoned him to himself. After various doubts had been resolved, he ordered Chrysologus to dictate and write an encyclical letter—that is, a circular letter, because it had been written to several people in the same words. Leo himself, deeming it worthy of so great a name, sent it under his own name to Flavianus, bishop of Constantinople.

The letter begins, “Having read the letter of your Charity,” and ends, after being divided into six chapters, “In the consulship of the most illustrious men Asterius and Protogenes.” Era 486. It is letter 10 in the order of the decretals of Saint Pope Leo and was received at the Council of Chalcedon by 630 Fathers. It is found in the Council of Chalcedon, session IV, act 2, and Pope Gelasius ordered it to be venerated and observed under penalty of anathema.

But the wicked abbot Eutyches, sensing the effectiveness and piercing words of Chrysologus’s letter under Leo’s name, seized his pen in a frenzy and wrote another letter against Flavianus and to the bishops of the West, so that, like a deadly basilisk with his breath, he might draw them into his error. Chrysologus, however, inflamed with love of the faith and unable to tolerate Eutyches’s insolence, replied to Eutyches in another letter under his own name. It begins, “Sadly I read your sad letter,” and ends, “most honored son” [Col. 0042A]. This letter is found in the Vatican manuscripts 2574 and 2580 and in volume II of the Councils, in the preambles to the Council of Chalcedon, at the beginning, from the Cologne printing of 1644. Dominicus Mita Ficchius also cites it at the beginning of the *Sermons of Saint Peter Chrysologus*, drawing his citation from Rodulphus’s *Life of Chrysologus* and from the archive of the senate of Imola.

17. After Damian, bishop of Ravenna, his successor, Blessed Felix, the fortieth archbishop of Ravenna, around the year of the Lord 715, recollected Chrysologus’s sermons and wrote them out in a selected series. These manuscripts now exist in the library of our Seraphic convent at Cesena.

They were first published afterward, through the work and labor of Agapitus Vicentinus, rector of the Lateran canons, in 1534. Later many corrections were made to them by F. Petrus Rodulphus, bishop of Senigallia, in 1594. But this work no longer exists today and cannot be found. Finally, the distinguished Dominicus Mita Ficchius a Ceronio, a priest of Imola and parish priest of Saint Agnes, once again emended and corrected Chrysologus’s sermons in 1642 and enlarged them with scholia and notes, though very brief ones, and with extensive indexes. They were published at Bologna in 1643, together with a copy of Saint Chrysologus’s silver dish, mentioned above in § 4, no. 11, and with an image of Saint Chrysologus showing half his body, according to the model painted on the choir screen of the metropolitan church of Ravenna.

A note concerning Chrysologus’s writings: bear in mind what we placed above as a preface. For you will often find entire sentences, indeed even sermons, of Chrysologus word for word in Saint [Col. 0042C] Jerome, Chrysostom, and even Augustine. In such cases, however, the sermons are either falsely attributed to Chrysologus or wrongly attributed to the aforementioned Fathers, as I noted in the passage cited above.

You will find entire sentences of Chrysologus concerning Saint Matthew’s Gospel—for example, in the sermons on the Centurion, on Peter’s Mother-in-law, on the Expulsion of Demons, on the Calming of the Storm, and so forth—in Paschasius Radbertus, abbot of Corbie, in the books on Matthew, volume IX, ninth century, of the *Library of the Ancient Fathers*. But our Chrysologus was earlier than Radbertus. The latter lived around the year 900 of the Lord, in the time of the emperor Louis the Pious and Charles the Bald, king of the Franks; Chrysologus, however, lived in the year 450 of the Lord, in the fifth century. Let this suffice concerning the life of Chrysologus.

[THE LIFE OF SAINT PETER CHRYSOLOGUS BY DOMINICUS MITA]

[Col. 0041]

PREFACE OF DOMINICUS MITA, APPENDED TO HIS EDITIONS, WHICH IT SEEMED NOT INAPPROPRIATE TO REPRINT HERE

[Col. 0041D]

The *Golden Sermons of Blessed Peter Chrysologus*, produced through the work of the Reverend Lord Agapitus Vicentinus, rector of the canons of the Lateran order, and drawn out of the darkness of manuscript exemplars, were first released to the public from the Bologna press of Joannes Baptista Phaellus in the year of the Lord 1534.

They were subsequently reprinted at Cologne in 1541 and 1618; at Paris in 1575, 1585, 1614, and 1631; at Antwerp in 1577; at Venice in 1588 and 1636; at Mainz in 1607 and 1613; at Lyon in 1622, 1623, 1627, 1634, and 1636; and again at Bologna in that same year, 1636. Yet all the copies contain a very large number of errors [Col. 0042D], since they descend from Phaellus’s first edition, which, as Agapitus claimed, had not been fully corrected, and they were further disfigured by the peculiar mistakes of each original and subsequent printer.

Nevertheless, marvelous claims are read about the corrections supposedly made in their exemplars. But after collating them individually, I discovered that the typographers and booksellers had asserted this rashly, more from their own profit than from truth. The same was confirmed by experience concerning the indexes of Sacred Scripture and notable subjects, most recently added for the use of preachers, which must be regarded as worthless [Col. 0043A].

For this reason, after complaining more than once to learned and reputable men, I amicably urged them to let me try, according to my ability and strength, whether I could remedy this disease. Yet, conscious of my innate weakness, I did not sufficiently grasp what I could accomplish in so difficult a work, where at times the alteration of a single letter or punctuation mark can overturn the author’s entire meaning, while the rector of so great an order is known to have failed in many matters.

Meanwhile I was delighted to hear that the most learned and universally acclaimed bishop Petrus Rodulphus Tussignanensis, formerly bishop of Senigallia, had corrected these sermons from certain manuscripts found at Rome and, having illustrated them with scholia composed on his own initiative, had sent them to our senate for publication. Yet neither the edition nor the labor and effort of so great a man appeared anywhere in the world, despite every diligent search [Col. 0043B]. Perhaps it is concealed by the envious cunning of certain people, so that it may serve only private purposes.

Nevertheless, since the human mind is drawn toward what is forbidden and desires what is denied, by continuing my search I learned that four manuscript copies of this work still survive: two at Rome, differing little from the printed editions; one at Urbino in the Roverian Library; and another at Cesena in the Franciscan Library. These agree with one another in almost everything, yet differ from the published versions in very many places.

Therefore, once access to the manuscripts had scarcely been opened, I examined them partly through friends and partly myself. With the assistance of a colleague, I collated them once and again from beginning to end with the copy first printed at Bologna, and corrected with my pen whatever errors I could. I also entered various and useful readings in the margin [Col. 0043C], rejecting the errors with which the manuscripts abound. If anything in them could not be corrected in every respect, I tried to supply it through reflection; yet this was done rarely, since such a method is obstructed by great difficulties and is slippery and deceptive.

Accordingly, with Blessed Peter as my guide, I believe that I have restored the genuine reading to the work so adequately that henceforth, among the materials that could be found, little more should be desired. After the corrections had been completed, there remained the most accurate interpretation of obscure passages and an account of the restored correction. But could a table be furnished with rich dishes from my own storehouse, if I am a man who did not touch sacred letters until, in legal studies and forensic business, I had already passed half my life?

Nevertheless, trusting in the patronage of the blessed bishop whose cause was at stake, I was pleased to append these scholia, whatever their quality, to my labors [Col. 0043D]. At least they may benefit the unlearned to some extent, or stimulate the minds of the educated to investigate superior things. For once the text has been purged and its gold freed from dross, more learned men, with more vigilant minds, will easily unfold and explain more fully and clearly the hidden meanings of this great theologian and golden preacher.

Moreover, so that these sermons might be useful to you, I added an index arranged alphabetically and adapted to the subjects chiefly treated in each sermon. I then extracted into another index the words of Scripture, arranged according to the literary order of the books, so that they might be easier for me to find. Finally, I appended a very rich catalogue of all notable matters, arranged sometimes by letter and sometimes by meaning [Col. 0044A]. It would have been even fuller had I not been restrained by that saying used by Saint Chrysologus himself: “Excess made bitter what measure could have seasoned” (sermon 123).

For the profundity of this man’s judgments and the distinctiveness of his words called for concordances more suitably than for a catalogue. And so that you might easily find the references, I assigned numbers in the margins of the sermons, so that once the sermon had been found, the particular part where the sentence is precisely noted could immediately be located.

Tautology is not usually considered a defect in indexes, since readers’ abilities vary, the same word does not always occur to everyone, and each person searches the indexes for sentences according to his own wishes. They therefore think that the same item should be placed in several locations [Col. 0044B], so that each reader may find what he needs more quickly.

Do not look for an index arranged according to the order of the Gospels, as they are read at the appropriate times in the sacred liturgy and used by modern preachers, since it would be superfluous in this work. From the indexes already compiled, the preacher will be able, through his own investigation, to prepare whatever he wishes more conveniently.

You will nevertheless find a very full account of the life of this most holy man, written in a modest style that expresses its judgments with the greatest clarity. It shows that a purer truth than that previously explained by certain writers has been set forth, and makes clear through it what kind of man and how great our Saint Peter was.

The completed work prompted me to give it the title: *Sermons Illustrated for the Most Part*, because their text and the index of the Life, drawn out of darkness and freed from impurities, have been made more fully clear and intelligible to readers than before. In polish [Col. 0044C] and splendor, moreover, this edition surpasses all the exemplars by far.

He himself knows what expenses, labors, and dangers I underwent in producing it; how often I lay prostrate with failing health; and what adversaries and deserters I endured at home and abroad—he who at last protected me from heaven, Saint Chrysologus. Many learned and reputable Fathers know it as well. They marvel that, while living far from the company of the wise, even among the forests and devoted to the care of souls, deprived of books and good health, I overcame nearly every adversity and finally completed at least part of the proposed work. It would still lie hidden in darkness had I not been compelled by their sincere judgment to publish it now.

In composing it, following Seneca’s advice (*Letters* 116), I sought more what I should write than how I should write it. For that reason the style, composed of many writers and drawn from many sources, is not always uniform: when reporting the judgments of others, I thought they should be transcribed in my own words, so that they might shine with their own authority [Col. 0044D].

It is nevertheless easy for many things to have slipped out, either carelessly or less appropriately placed, both in composition and transcription. But consider that this happened by God’s permission, so that “the nations may know that they are but human beings” (Psalm 9). Let these remarks about my work suffice for you, friendly reader.

But why did I call it mine? Indeed, it is rightly not mine, since, apart from the errors and anything written more ineptly or with blunt judgment, I can acknowledge nothing here as my own. The sermons belong to the holy Chrysologus; the indexes were drawn from them; the corrections, observations, and scholia were suggested under his patronage [Col. 0045A]; and his Life was collected with his assistance.

Therefore, if anything in it is pleasing to God and the saint, or useful to the Church, all praise and glory belong to the Most High, while veneration and honor belong to Blessed Peter Chrysologus. As for me, I ask nothing else, most humane reader, except that in your piety you seek from the Father of mercies forgiveness for my errors. Farewell.

Written from the sacred church of the parish of Saint Agnes of Ugutionellus, on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, 1643.

[Col. 0045A]

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1642. THE LIFE OF SAINT PETER CHRYSOLOGUS, ARCHBISHOP OF RAVENNA,

Carefully sought out from his own Homilies and from various monuments of writers, both printed and manuscript, diligently collected, and arranged here in order, by DOMINICUS MITA, PRIEST AND PARISH PRIEST.

“The memory of the just is with praises.” Proverbs 10:7.

1. I am about to write the life of a man illustrious equally for holiness and learning, Peter, archbishop of the Church of Ravenna, who later received the surname Chrysologus from his eloquence. Before I begin this undertaking, the subject itself seems to urge me to repeat above a few things about Forum Cornelii, his homeland, so that everything to be said may be more illustrious and more clearly visible.

After Ilium had been captured by the Greeks and destroyed by sword and flame, many nobles of Trojan origin—as our writers believe [Note: [Col. 0045D] The Imola Annals, manuscript of Joannes Baptista Florius, also called Florentinus, held by the noble family de Quanis; or rather, fragments of the *Annals*. The Imola Chronicle circulated under the name of Philippus Saxus, manuscript of Jacobus. Philippus of Bergamo, *Supplement to the Chronicle*.]—who had come to Italy as exiles under the leadership of Antenor, eventually reached Aemilia, a distinguished region of Italy. Settling beside the river Vatrennus and along the Flaminian Way, they were captivated by the beauty of the place and the fertility of the soil. There they founded and occupied a town called Ilium [Col. 0045C].

Later, after Lucius Sulla, descended from the Cornelian family—the wealthiest and most patrician of all the families that had existed at Rome—had triumphed over Africa and Asia after conquering and subduing them, and, having defeated Marius, had attained the summit of power, he granted this town—as I have learned from many sources [Note: [Col. 0045D] The Imola Annals, which comment on the poet Prudentius’s hymn to Saint Cassian; Sigonius, *On the Ancient Law of Italy*, book II; Joannes Andreas Palatius, in his *Oration on Forum Cornelii*, published at Bologna in 1573. Others hold that the name Forum Cornelii was spontaneously adopted by the inhabitants themselves in order to win the dictator’s favor.]—to his discharged soldiers and its inhabitants for settlement. There he established a forum where justice could be administered and markets held.

They say that, so that later generations would know of this Roman colony and who had founded it, he ordered the town thereafter to be called Forum Cornelii, after the family name of its founder. After these soldiers gradually mingled with our people through intermarriage, they made Forum Cornelii [Col. 0046B] so famous for its buildings and population that it soon grew into a large and heavily fortified city. It was capable not only of receiving and holding the strong armies of Octavian Caesar [Note: [Col. 0045D] Cicero, book XII, *Letters to Gaius Cassius*, letter 5.], but also, several centuries later, of pleasing Athawulf, the great king of the Goths, descended from the most famous family of the Balthi [Note: [Col. 0046D] Hieronymus Rubeus, second edition of the *History of Ravenna*, book II, under the year 412 of the Lord; the *Chorus* of the Peutinger map; Volateranus, book II of the *Geography*; Baronius, *Ecclesiastical Annals*, volume V, under the year 411; Jordanes of Ravenna, *Chronicle of the Goths*; Florius and Saxus, who comment on the matter above in manuscript.], so that he chose this one city from among all others in which to celebrate with great ceremony his marriage to Galla Placidia, illustrious through her father and brothers, the Augusti, and to remain there for more than a year with his nobles and a very large army.

2. At first, as the neighboring gentile cities had always worshiped idols, it is said that this city eventually accepted the evangelical faith preached throughout Aemilia by Saint Apollinaris, the first bishop of Ravenna [Note: [Col. 0046D] The Imola Annals mentioned above, which my most illustrious lord, Lord Ferdinand Millinus, recorded in the catalogue of the bishops of the Church of Imola in the first diocesan synod; Rubeus, book I of the *History*, and book V, under the year 1040 of the Lord.], and that a few years later it was provided with a bishop [Col. 0046C].

But as the years passed, since it had often suffered hostile attacks and had been inhabited indiscriminately with our people by barbarian nations that sacrificed to the gods of the gentiles, while one person lived according to one custom and another according to another, and since the gentiles’ strength prevailed, it was easy both for the city to be deprived of a shepherd of souls and for the name of Christ, through the passage of time, to remain almost obliterated among our people. This was always the grave opinion of our ancestors.

But when almighty God took pity on the people of Forum Cornelii, he sent from those regions to our city Cassianus, a man illustrious for learning and holiness [Note: [Col. 0046D] Florius, Saxus, and the other writers of the Life of Saint Cassianus, both printed and manuscript.], who had been bishop at Sabiona in Germany, as a new apostle. By teaching and preaching, he instructed the inhabitants in the Christian faith for a long time [Col. 0047A] and finally strengthened it by his own martyrdom [Note: [Col. 0047D] In the year of the Lord 362, on the Ides of August, Saint Cassian the martyr received the crown of martyrdom. See our notes to the Author’s sermon 165.]. All the people of Forum Cornelii embraced the evangelical faith with their whole heart, and, so that they might preserve it perpetually, they were supported by the most blessed vicar of Christ on earth, the firmest shepherd of souls.

3. Among the other bishops whose memory has not been carried down to us because of the injuries of time, one stood out: Cornelius, a Roman by nationality [Note: [Col. 0047D] Saint Chrysologus, in the sermon cited; Petrus Rodulphus Tussignanensis, in the manuscript Life of Saint Chrysologus in my possession and in the archive of the senate of Imola, at the end of the senate’s commentary codex for the year 1595.], conspicuous for the holiness of his life and everywhere radiant with every title of virtue.

During his episcopate, before Blessed John Chrysostom, bishop of Byzantium, departed to God, in the four hundred and sixth year from the Virgin Birth, a child was born into an honorable family of the people of Forum Cornelii, religious in the Christian name [Note: [Col. 0047D] The Imola Annals, Baronius, Natalis, Rodulphus, and all the manuscripts; Bishop Adelphus, sermon 107 among the Author’s sermons; and our observations concerning him.]. His parents ordered that, in the sacred bath of regeneration, he be given the name Peter in honor of the chief of the apostles, as though already foreseeing the boy’s future merits and, by divine judgment, proclaiming to all that being called Peter in him would mean not merely a name but also a prerogative of virtue [Col. 0047B].

4. Since this boy, handsome in appearance and pleasing in form, seemed to display a marvelous natural inclination toward virtue [Note: [Col. 0047D] Florius and Rodulphus, cited above.], as soon as his age allowed, his parents enrolled him in school. There he progressed so well in the first elements of letters, in Christian conduct, and in the fear of God that he far surpassed his peers. Carrying a manly spirit in a boy’s body, he despised everything trivial and weak.

For this reason he spent even the times of recreation very frequently at the altar of Saint Cassian the martyr and patron, in humble prayer to God [Note: [Col. 0047D] Rodulphus, manuscripts, many of which I have seen.]. He piously gloried in being, and in being freely called by others, the little servant of Blessed Cassian, with a particular and remarkable devotion [Col. 0047C].

### 5.

Since it had frequently happened that the venerable holy shepherd Cornelius looked upon this with admiration, the blessed bishop, discerning future things from present indications, perceived that the humble young man would one day become great in the Church of God if he were more diligently instructed and consecrated to divine worship. At length, since the youth himself greatly desired this, he enrolled him among the members of his household clergy. [Note: [Col. 0047D] Chrysologus, Sermon 865, on Saint Projectus, Bishop of Cornelianus; and our author notes this there.] From that time he taught him human and divine letters so thoroughly that, owing to the teachability of his intellect and the swiftness of his speech, he was quickly imbued with every distinguished branch of learning. He attained such holiness of life that the most prudent bishop duly initiated him into the sacred order of levites and appointed him deacon of the Cornelian Church, as another Stephen of the Jerusalem Church or Lawrence, the chief deacon of the Roman Church. [Col. 0047D]

### 6.

At that time the duty of deacons was to serve at table—that is, to stand beside the priest when he was celebrating the sacred rites; when the priest was prevented from doing so, to recite the homilies of the holy Fathers to the people; to distribute among the poor the goods of the churches entrusted to their keeping; [Note: [Col. 0048D] Baronius, vol. V, year 402, alludes to this in Chrysologus, Sermon 135.] and, after visiting everyone, to report to the bishop whatever was necessary, so that he might strengthen those who stood firm, support those who were collapsing, and raise up the fallen. [Col. 0048A] This office was performed only by men distinguished in probity and learning. [Note: Acts 6:2; Council of Vaison II, canon 2; Baronius, *Ecclesiastical Annals*, vol. I, year 34.] They were called, as it were, the bishops’ eyes [Note: [Col. 0048D] *Decretum*, distinction 93, chapter “Deacons, as it were, the eyes”] and messengers, indeed more truly angels [Note: [Col. 0048D] Clement, *Apostolic Constitutions*, book II, chapter 30] and prophets.

### 7.

Thus Peter, appointed to this number of levites, being an ideal of the virtues and a supreme theologian, excelled in prudence, chastity, and outstanding charity toward God and neighbor. He demonstrated to citizens and foreigners alike that he was a true follower—indeed, a son—who in no respect fell short of his holy teacher. [Col. 0048B] [Note: [Col. 0048D] Rodulphus, in the place cited above, and Chrysologus himself, Sermon 165.]

Nevertheless, since it had been divinely ordained that this splendid light of virtue should shine not only upon his native city but upon the whole world—though at that time it was thought to be hidden beneath a bushel—it was destined to be raised from an obscure hiding place to the eminent summit of ecclesiastical dignity, like the radiance of the Church shining in the house of God, so that by its brightness it might drive away the darkness of error far and wide and remove and eradicate the vices of savage men that had made those times gloomy and wretched.

### 8.

Accordingly, when John, the first of that name, whom they called in Greek Ἀγγελὸπτην (*Angelopectes*, “angel-seer”), had been taken up to the Creator, [Note: [Col. 0048D] Rubeus, cited above, book II, year 433; Rodulphus, Florius, and others. Although Baronius, vol. V, under the same year 433, says that Saint Cornelius happened to be in Rome with Saint Peter Chrysologus, he nevertheless refers the reader back to Rubeus.] and when the twentieth of those who had governed the Church of Ravenna, distinguished for the holiness of his life, had likewise died, the provincial bishops came to Ravenna according to the customary practice of those times for the election of a metropolitan bishop. [Col. 0048C] Among them was Saint Cornelius with his deacon Peter. After various and frequent disagreements among the people and clergy during the election, one of the Ravennates was finally chosen. He hastened to the City with the Ravennate legates and Saint Cornelius the bishop, while, by divine inspiration, Saint Peter the levite accompanied him on the journey, in order to obtain the canonical confirmation of the supreme pontiff.

### 9.

At that time Saint Sixtus III held the helm of the ecclesiastical ship. In a dream the Apostle Peter and the martyr Apollinaris appeared to him with the venerable young man between them, and instructed the pontiff to make him archbishop of Ravenna, setting everything else aside. [Col. 0048D] [Note: Peter de Natalibus, in the *Life of Chrysologus*; Rodulphus; the Imolese Annals; and the Breviary of Saint Peter Chrysologus, discussed below in the observations on the *Life of Chrysologus*, no. 9; and Baronius, under the year of the Lord 433.]

Warned by the divine revelation, Sixtus saw the Ravennates enter the papal palace on the following day to seek confirmation. [Col. 0049A] He first rejected the man whom they had elected and then ordered all who were there to come before him. Since he had not yet seen among the Ravennates the appearance of the young man shown to him, he ordered Bishop Cornelius also to bring his own people into his presence. When this had been done, scarcely had the supreme pontiff looked upon Peter, Cornelius’s deacon, when he recognized him as the very man who had been shown to him from heaven. With joyful spirit, and in the hearing of all, he said:

> “By divine providence we appoint this man, who has indeed been chosen, to preside as archbishop over the Church of Ravenna, and no other.”

### 10.

The unexpected decision of the pontiff deeply disturbed the minds of the Ravennates, because, contrary to ancestral custom, a foreigner was being chosen after one of their own citizens had been rejected. [Col. 0049B] It also shook Peter’s mind with a heavy burden and troubled his inmost being, since he saw that an office fearful even for angelic shoulders was being imposed upon him by supreme authority. Therefore, taking the complaints of the Ravennates as an opportunity for making an excuse—for otherwise, out of reverence and humility, he would not have had the right to offer strong opposition—he threw himself at the feet of the supreme pontiff and humbly begged him to avert from him this great office, so entirely alien to his mind and condition.

### 11.

Accordingly, the most blessed Sixtus, in order to calm the minds of the Ravennates and strengthen the resources of humble Peter, explained with sufficient clarity the entire matter that had been revealed from heaven. [Col. 0049C] By powerful arguments he persuaded both parties to submit to the divine will. The pontiff’s authority and sacred eloquence were so effective that Peter, although unwilling and trembling, did not dare any longer to reject the office of pontiff of the Church of Ravenna, conferred upon him by the indication of the divine will and by apostolic appointment. Thus, submitting his shoulders to the burden, lest he be said to have refused an office assigned by God, he immediately consecrated himself wholly to the divine will.

The Ravennates, meanwhile, reverently received Peter as their new bishop. Although he had not been foretold by the Dove, as had many of the bishops who preceded him, he had nevertheless been indicated from heaven in a marvelous manner and had been set over their Church through the work of all those elect of God. They hailed him and continually held him in the highest honor, as an angel of God.

[Note: [Col. 0049D] The last of these was Saint Severus, twelfth in the order of the archbishops of Ravenna. Rubeus, book I of the *History*.]

### 12.

Peter was therefore designated the twenty-first archbishop of the Church of Ravenna in the year 433 after the Lord’s Nativity. [Col. 0049D] [Note: Rubeus; Rodulphus; Baronius.] After he had been ordained priest, he visited the thresholds of the apostles according to the ancient rite and devoutly and humbly traversed the other places of the City, filled with the greatest religious devotion. [Note: [Col. 0049D] Rubeus, cited above.] He entreated the Most High through the intercession of the saints to grant him, just as he had once done for Moses, the strength needed to bear suitably the burden of so great an office.

At length, as he was setting out with Saint Cornelius and the Ravennates for Ravenna, when he reached Forum Cornelii, he entered with singular devotion the beloved church of the holy martyr Cassian. [Col. 0050A] With poured-out tears and humble prayer, he repeatedly begged the holy patron not to abandon him in such great need, but rather to favor him through divine illumination, so that, through God, he might be able to serve worthily the office of the pontificate.

After he had piously arranged his household affairs, he was escorted to Ravenna by the men mentioned above. There he was first received by the Emperor Valentinian and his mother Galla Placidia, the Augusti, [Note: [Col. 0049D] Rubeus; the aforementioned Breviary; the Imolese Annals; Rodulphus; and others.] and then by all the Ravennates with the greatest eagerness and joy. He told them that he asked only this of them: since he had not refused to undertake so great a burden for their salvation, they too should strive to obey his admonitions and not resist the divine commands. [Col. 0050B]

### 13.

Finally, on the following Sunday, in the presence of the Christian princes and the entire people, with incredible magnificence and indescribable rejoicing, he was consecrated archbishop by Saint Cornelius, as we believe, and the other co-bishops, according to ancient custom, in the principal church. [Note: [Col. 0050D] The same is stated by Chrysologus, Sermon 130; Rodulphus; Rubeus under the year 449; and numerous ancient manuscripts describing his life.]

The Church of Ravenna was then regarded as second in Italy after the Roman Church. [Note: [Col. 0050D] Liutprand, Deacon of the Church of Pavia, book V, year 923; the same is stated by Chrysologus, Sermon 130.] Peter himself attests this in part in a golden speech delivered soon afterward, saying:

> “Today a son has been born to the Church of Ravenna in place of a father: one who will not bend her down by his weight, frighten her by his authority, trouble her by agitation, or disturb her by harshness, but will support her with faithful service; by vigilant care will make her secure; by kindly instruction will order her household; will go out to meet her guests; will serve her parents; will obey kings; will cooperate with authorities; will offer reverence to God’s elders, grace to children, love to brothers, and affection to little ones; and will show all people, through Christ, a free servitude.” [Col. 0050C]

Events proved most clearly that he observed all these things, and even greater ones, exactly as he had promised.

### 14.

Just as, shortly before, in Liguria, the sweet eloquence of Saint Ambrose had come to the aid of the afflictions of the Church of Milan, and in Africa the learned eloquence of Saint Augustine had come to the needs of the Church of Hippo, so that the sickness of the Church of Ravenna, the firstborn of the Roman Church in Aemilia—where the imperial seat of the Western Empire then properly shone in its majesty—might be splendidly driven away, the Almighty bestowed upon our blessed Chrysologus golden eloquence and supreme teaching, so that he might teach by tongue and hand what was necessary for salvation to the princes and people of that empire entrusted to him from heaven. [Col. 0050D]

Therefore Peter the bishop, an immovable foundation of salvation, fearless in danger and indefatigable in labor, who had set before himself only the salvation of the flock entrusted to him, never seemed for even an hour to have been absent either in word or deed from his pastoral duty of driving away vices and implanting virtues.

### 15.

This was especially clear when, on the Kalends of January, he saw not only men enveloped in pagan superstition but Christians themselves clinging to pagan practices. In accordance with a gentile custom, they fashioned themselves into likenesses of idols [Col. 0051A] and, throughout the imperial city, reproduced the vices and crimes that they were said once to have committed. [Note: [Col. 0051D] Rubeus; Rodulphus; the Sur manuscript; and others. The same is found in Chrysologus, Sermon 155.] Thus they displayed shameful spectacles to everyone, making themselves and their neighbors miserable slaves of sin, and did not hesitate to proclaim that these things were merely the vows of jesting, the joy of novelty, and the beginning of the year.

Unable to tolerate this in his pastoral office, blessed Peter ascended the pulpit with more-than-human courage. As soon as he began to condemn the devil’s portents and, with remarkable skill, to calm the hostile and alienated people, he demonstrated with such vehement persuasion that sacrilege must be avoided that, after the excuses had been presented, the people came to their senses and thereafter willingly refrained from such things for God’s sake. [Col. 0051B]

### 16.

He also restrained and abolished the novel practices that had been introduced superstitiously by some concerning the Lenten fast, contrary to the divine command. [Note: [Col. 0051D] Read the author’s Sermon 166, together with the note.] Some weeks of the sacred abstinence were excessively strict and others too lax; people appointed separate fasts for warm foods as distinct from cold, and for salted foods as distinct from unsalted, according to practices of their own devising, while neglecting the Creator of their whole life. He prescribed and secured the observance of an equal fast, as it had been handed down by God and by the Church, for the discipline of body and soul.

### 17.

He frequently warned against a custom, introduced at that time among many, that was especially pernicious, hateful to God, and altogether intolerable: catechumens were accustomed to postpone the sacred washing of regeneration for a long time, even while life was declining, and meanwhile to heap sin upon sin in the hope of pardon. [Col. 0051D] [Note: Sermon 10 throughout, and Sermon 59.]

He earnestly urged that this practice be avoided. By God he entreated the faithful of Christ to bring those who were to be baptized to Christ himself; and those whom voluntary reluctance or necessity prevented from coming, whom age hindered, ignorance delayed, vices held back, expectation deceived, or poverty misled through shame, they were to attract and bring by careful invitation at the proper time—on Holy Saturday and at Easter, when this divine sacrament was conferred by the hands of bishops.

He said that, since human beings are always uncertain of life, care should be taken lest servants, children, spouses, or parents who had not yet been baptized, overtaken by death, should be deprived both of the present life and of the possibility of attaining the future one. [Col. 0051C] Rather, laboring diligently in the Lord’s vineyard, they should deserve to receive both the reward of life and the highest crown of glory.

By what teaching and charity our Peter, who shone no less with the ornaments of wisdom than with the dignity of his pontificate, corrected the lost and depraved morals of nobles, heroes, and courtiers, no one knows well except one who has studied his golden sermons with the closest attention. [Col. 0051D] [Note: Read the author’s Sermons 20, 21, and 127.]

### 18.

But we are still lingering over only a few matters. Greater were the things our bishop accomplished during those times, when, as he himself says, the sea of the world was swelling with pomp, raised into a whirlpool, billowing with divisions, fluctuating through ignorance, clamorous with disputes, raging with anger, savage through treachery, shipwrecked by sins, and submerged in impiety. [Col. 0052A] [Note: [Col. 0051D] Sermon 46.] Thus the Lord’s ship was continually shaken from without by the waves of the nations and from within by the swollen surges of heretics. [Note: [Col. 0052D] Sermon 21.]

But Peter, skilled in navigation and holding the second helm, was seen to keep watch for salvation with far greater vigilance than the entire host of hell for the destruction of souls. [Col. 0052B] Therefore, guarding the ship lest it be sunk by raging storms, he deserved the privilege both of Christ’s sailor and of the apostolic fisherman, just as, when an infant, he had received the name itself.
