And as he gently drew toward himself with the hook of holiness the crowds submerged in the waves of error, he enclosed a great multitude of people in the nets of his teaching for the Christian faith.

### 19.

For it pleased God that countless people—both Ravennates themselves and inhabitants of various cities of Italy, but still more people from barbarian nations spread by then through almost the whole world—who lived at Ravenna, whether by force or voluntarily, whether they had fled there to Valentinian III, then Emperor of the West, or had been captured in war and were serving there, or were staying among the Ravennates under any other title, should be cleansed by the water of sacred baptism and called from the filth of barbarism and pagan unbelief to faith and Christian life through evangelical teaching by Peter, the guardian of the faith. [Col. 0052C]

He carried this out with such devotion of spirit that he seemed to “not square his sermons to slaves and simple children, but to liquefy them,” [Note: [Col. 0052D] Sermon 62.] and pour them into tender throats like milk. He professed that he occupied himself wholly with forming the minds of little ones, having meanwhile obtained the pardon of the wise.

### 20.

Therefore, drawing from the teaching of Christ himself and from the Lord’s Prayer what catechumens ought to believe and hope, how they ought to live, and how they might think themselves capable of being received into eternal life through faith in grace that works through love, this doorkeeper of heaven taught them with such abundance of the divine Spirit and eloquence that, after hearing him in profound silence, they would request purification by baptism even before the catechism had been completed. [Note: [Col. 0052D] Read Sermon 40 and all the sermons on the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer.]

They obtained this most rightly and speedily, even over the course of several days, when he had set aside his preaching office during the Lenten abstinence because of that instruction and was burdened with the greatest labors. [Col. 0052D] He called those people his life, his salvation, and his glory whom he did not allow to remain ignorant of what God had granted him to know. [Note: [Col. 0052D] Sermon 147.]

For what he had received from God he freely distributed in God’s grace, so that he might enlighten with the light of truth people who were captives of death, slaves of demons, household servants of idols, and fettered by crimes; and, having liberated them from wicked masters, washed them in the sacred water, and recalled them to the service of the Most High, he might gain them for Christ, the King of the ages. [Col. 0053A]

### 21.

So great was the exceptional beauty of intellect in this holy bishop, so rare the eloquence that illumined his mind, and so great his wisdom in every matter, that he could refute through the most learned interpretation any people of exceptionally acute mind and outstanding education—whether pagans, Jews, or faithful Christians—who had then come to the imperial city of Ravenna from every part of the world and had at times engaged in the most subtle discussions of the divine Scriptures.

With the same Spirit by whom the most blessed apostles once acted in the primitive Church, he drew all learned people toward faith in Christ and a conversion of morals, unless they were held by extreme obstinacy, captivating their understanding. Thus Saint Adelphus truly said that our most blessed Chrysologus was an apostolic fowler, who attracted toward himself with the pen of his sweet eloquence the minds of young men flying through the air of subtle speculations, and compelled them by his teaching to cling to solid truth as to birdlime. [Col. 0053B] [Note: [Col. 0053D] Read the whole of Sermon 107.]

### 22.

Since our bishop was an especially vigorous cultivator of the Lord Sabaoth’s field, he once found in it a parabolic fig tree—that is, people entrusted to his diligence—who bore no fruit. Yet, skilled in his art, he always desired to dig around the tree and apply every effort so that it might bear fruit. If he could not immediately restore someone to good productivity, he very often entreated the Lord meanwhile to wait patiently for another year and not allow the tree to be cut down, thereby making his labor fruitless. [Col. 0053C]

He appealed to the Lord not to severity of justice but rather to kindness and patience, and assigned the blame for the fruitless tree to himself rather than to the tree itself, promising that thereafter he would cultivate it more diligently. Repeatedly pouring out abundant streams of tears from the innermost affection of his heart through the channels of his eyes, he labored with the greatest zeal both to wipe away the filth of the fig tree and to obtain from heaven an abundance of fruits for its roots. [Note: [Col. 0053D] Sermon 107, cited above.]

### 23.

Nevertheless, in the Lord’s field there flourished not only a tree that produced no fruit at all, but also—horrible and supreme disaster!—one that infected the others with a deadly shadow and, through harmful roots, caused harmful shoots to sprout among them. Thus, most unhappily, as many pernicious heresies arose in the Lord’s field as there were doctrines professed by the divine law. [Col. 0053D] [Note: [Col. 0053D] Sermon 21.]

Our Peter, whom God had given as the foundational rock of the Catholic Church and not so much a propagator as a true defender of the faith, was never anything but a perpetual sword against heretics, to remove such men from the midst. He continually struck the Arians, Manichaeans, Novatians, Pelagians, Donatists, Nestorians, and other ministers of Tartarus—not so much trees as ministers, and most hostile to the Catholic faith—with spoken and written word, as with a sickle laid to the root. [Col. 0054A] [Note: [Col. 0053D] Read the author’s index of notes, under “Heretic.”] He demonstrated by the manifest light of Scripture that they were faithless and deranged.

Vigorously defending the true orthodox faith and religion, he openly proclaimed the most wretched destruction of those who thought wrongly about God and contrary to the unanimous judgment of the Catholic Church. He very often strove to persuade them through heavenly instruction, both by tongue and by pen. [Note: [Col. 0053D] Sermon 44.]

### 24.

Nevertheless, the Lord did not allow Peter Chrysologus to remain free from the attacks of heretics, so that his firm faith might appear all the more clearly in the sight of men.

When Eutyches, a Byzantine abbot already weighed down by old age and sitting in the chair of pestilence, attempted, under the appearance of faith and with honeyed speech, to tear apart and divide the unity of the faith, he did not blush to assert, as though he were firmly opposing Nestorius, who taught that there were two persons in Christ, that in the Incarnation of the divine Word the divine nature had fallen together into one with the human, as though one could be mixed with the other and a third thing, composed—or rather confused—from the two mixed natures could arise. [Col. 0054B] With the help of factious secular persons he had attracted many to this most impious dogma, as well as ecclesiastical leaders. [Note: [Col. 0053D] Rubeus; Rodulphus; Baronius, vol. VI, under the year 448; and all who have written about Chrysologus.]

Therefore Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, attempting to destroy the poison of this deadly doctrine, summoned a synod and condemned the heresy together with its author. [Note: [Col. 0053D] This synod was held in the year of the Lord 448; Baronius, cited above.] At the same time he arranged for the acts to be sent by trustworthy messengers to the most blessed Leo I, supreme pontiff. [Note: [Col. 0053D] Flavian was crowned with martyrdom for this cause; Baronius, year 449.] [Col. 0054D]

The pontiff, recognizing the golden abundance of intellect and eloquence in Peter, archbishop of Ravenna, consulted him according to custom and ancestral practice concerning the truth of the faith that the heretics had called into dispute. At length, aided by the teaching and letters of the great Peter, the great Leo gave Bishop Flavian an encyclical letter—one that, as I reasonably judge from many indications, was dictated by Chrysologus but written in Leo’s own name. [Col. 0054C] It most clearly refuted the heresy by the doctrines and arguments of Eutyches and contained a complete exposition of the Catholic faith. [Note: [Col. 0054D] Council of Chalcedon, acts 4 and 6, held in the year of Christ 451, in December; Roman Council concerning authentic books, chapter “The Holy Roman Church”; Baronius, vol. VI, under the year 449.]

The letter was made common to all; afterward it was approved at the Council of Chalcedon by six hundred and thirty Fathers. Finally, Pope Gelasius declared that anyone who did not accept it down to a single iota was under anathema.

The utterly depraved Eutyches, distressed by this letter of the supreme pontiff, attempted another deception. In letters written against Flavian and sent to bishops of great name in the West, [Col. 0054D] he tried to incite them against Flavian and gradually draw them into his own heresy. Among them our Peter was foremost, since Eutyches knew of the service he had rendered to Saint Leo. But the faithful bishop not only refused to listen to Eutyches; he also wrote back in his own name a golden letter, urging him with remarkable charity to obey the supreme pontiff’s letters. [Col. 0055A] [Note: [Col. 0054D] The letter of Chrysologus begins, “I read sad things, sad things”; it is reported in Baronius’s *Annals* under the year 449.] He urged him so angelically to recover from his blind and rash disputation and contradiction that, had the deluded old man not been steeped in diabolical obstinacy, he could easily have been corrected and brought back to the Catholic faith.

### 25.

Amid such confusion of events and times, he instructed Christian princes and peoples through frequent sermons concerning how they ought to defend and retain the Catholic faith amid the greatest storms of nations and heretics; amid slaughter by the sword; amid the shipwreck of bodies and souls; amid tyrannical powers invading kingdoms; amid the varied pestilence of living creatures raging everywhere among the nations; amid the sterility of the earth; and amid the other scourges of God. [Col. 0055B] [Note: [Col. 0055D] Sermons 20, 21, and 45.]

He reminded them to approach God with him, to trust in the true God, to remain strong in faith, and day and night to entreat the Most High with tears and repentance for peace. And when he offered himself for the sins of the people as an acceptable sacrifice to God, so as to turn away the divine anger and obtain pardon and grace for sinners, who could say how pleasing a fragrance of spices he exhaled in the sight of heaven? [Note: [Col. 0055D] Rodulphus, cited above.]

### 26.

Scarcely had the blessed bishop been placed in charge of the Church of Ravenna when he turned his attention to establishing or restoring an apostolic manner of life among its clergy. He planned to instruct and retain those chosen for God’s portion in regular ministries and a common life.

Accordingly, beside the Ursian Church, he laid the foundations, on a grand scale, of a building called the Tricollis because it had been constructed in the likeness of three hills—what we commonly call the Canonica—for the safe and continual residence of the priests and of the entire clergy who were to serve the Almighty in that metropolitan church. [Col. 0055C] [Note: [Col. 0055D] Rubeus, under the year 458; Chrysologus, Sermons 39 and 107.]

That the building was completed by his successors with remarkable care is also attested by the very ancient verses reported by Rubeus, in these words: [Note: [Col. 0055D] Rubeus, book III of the aforementioned *History*, p. 162.]

> Here Peter, the younger, following Christ’s commands,  
> As was fitting, excelled in sacred ways.  
> Here too he founded, with wondrous masses, a citadel;  
> He himself gave these monuments of his name.  
> After his death Aurelian held the honors;  
> After him Ecclesius became bishop.  
> Then came Ursicinus; Victor followed in order;  
> In his time the younger Maximianus appeared. [Col. 0055D]

Since, through the injuries of time, such a building no longer exists today, its place is nevertheless represented by the gardens that are seen around the same Ursian Church.

After he had written down this monastic rule of life together with the others, blessed Peter had first chosen a stricter rule for himself. Although, because he had assumed the office of bishop, he was deeply engaged in active life, he nevertheless remained constantly devoted to the divine choir with consecrated men. [Col. 0056A] There he prayed to God Almighty during the nightly vigils and hours; [Note: [Col. 0055D] Sermons 39 and 107, cited above.] and with hymns and songs he celebrated the divine praises.

Thus he had daily attained such great love for God that, on one occasion when he was about to explain the most sacred Passion of the Lord to the people, he was unable to utter the words because of the tenderness of his love for God. Tears and groans bursting from his inmost heart restrained his speech. Therefore, himself giving the reason for his silence in his Easter rejoicings, he acknowledges that he said: [Note: [Col. 0056D] Sermon 77.]

> Then our inmost parts died;  
> our understanding died together with them;  
> our speech was buried with its Author,  
> so that it might be raised entirely for his glory.  
> This was the cause of my silence;  
> this was the devout delay of my duty,  
> since our speech, with the whole service of its affection,  
> followed its Giver even to the underworld. [Col. 0056B]

### 27.

Anyone can easily persuade himself of the affection of charity that he had for the poor if he reads the miserable histories of those times and recognizes that, through the frequent devastations of enemies, there was throughout almost every land a very great—indeed, I might say innumerable—multitude of poor and captives.

To ensure that Christian piety would feed and redeem them, Peter very often persuaded the people suitably through his sermons [Note: [Col. 0056D] Sermon 103, no. 12. Read the index of the author’s sermons, under “Almsgiving” and “Poor.”] and encouraged his hearers by his own example. He was accustomed to expend everything except what was necessary for his own poor sustenance and for that of his ministers on giving alms, redeeming captives, and carrying out the other works of mercy and piety. [Note: [Col. 0056D] Rodulphus and the manuscripts that describe his life say that he looked only toward heaven.]

### 28.

Advancing still farther along the way of the Lord, the blessed bishop despised the flesh and the earth. [Col. 0056C] [Note: [Col. 0056D] Sermon 107; Rodulphus and numerous manuscripts.] Through frequent fasts, nightly vigils, the harshest hair shirt, continual scourging, and tears poured out in abundance, he had so reduced his body to the service of his soul that his face grew pale and his once large and vigorous body, without exceeding a proper stature, had been attenuated by emaciation.

Therefore, while he was still alive and present, and almost at the beginning of his pontificate, Saint Adelphus—who, I believe, was bishop of Metz—called him holy and most blessed in a sermon. [Note: [Col. 0056D] Sermon 107, cited above.]

The fame of Peter’s holiness and learning, as archbishop of Ravenna, had filled the entire world so completely that crowds of people rushed to him from different regions, eager to see him. Those who lived in inaccessible solitudes or the blind recesses of the wilderness went to behold the remarkable Peter rather than the world. [Col. 0056D] He was gloriously wrestling with this world and arraying a kind of battle line of holiness against the organized forces of sinners, because in that man—crucified to the world and to himself—Christ lived, reigned, and commanded. [Note: [Col. 0056D] Sermon 116.]

### 29.

The most holy shepherd, who was building living temples of God, did not neglect inanimate temples either, in which, as we believe, God dwells in a special manner. [Col. 0057A] Indeed, beside the aforementioned Ursian Church at Ravenna, he built from the foundations a church for the holy apostle Andrew. [Note: [Col. 0057D] Rubeus, book II, year 433 and following; Rodulphus and others.]

In the vaulted ceiling of that church there could be seen an image of blessed Peter himself, woven in mosaic work and painted in tesserae, with a most devout epigram said to have been composed by him. It clearly demonstrated that our Peter had been the founder of the same basilica. Its text is as follows: [Note: [Col. 0057D] These verses are read in Rubeus under the year 449 and in Rodulphus’s *Life of the Lord Chrysologus*. The church still exists, but the image and verses are no longer visible. Rubeus, Rodulphus, and Florius assert that they did not see all of these in their own time. The church has now been restored and whitewashed in a later style; for that reason the things mentioned above no longer survive.]

> Either light was born here, or, captured here, it reigns free:  
> It is the light from which the glory of heaven has now come before us;  
> Or private buildings have brought forth a shining day,  
> And the enclosed radiance gleams with the secluded heavens.  
>   
> Behold the marbles blooming with serene rays,  
> And all the stones struck by a heavenly [uncertain: *munice*] light.  
> The gifts of the author, Peter, shine forth.  
> To him honor is due; to his merit he has granted  
> That these small things, confined within narrow spaces,  
> Might nevertheless surpass what is vast.  
>   
> Nothing is small for Christ: he possesses narrow dwellings well,  
> He whose temple stands in the human breast.  
> Peter is the foundation; Peter the founder; and the sanctuary;  
> What the house is, the Lord is; what is made, the Maker likewise.  
> In character and in work Christ is held to be its possessor,  
> Who, joining two things together, the Mediator makes one.  
>   
Let the one who comes here pour forth tears destined to bring forth joys,
> Strengthening the contrite mind in the stricken breast.  
> Let him not lie inert; let him cast himself upon the ground,  
> And uncover hidden diseases before the physician’s feet,  
> While care hastens to attend them.  
> Often the fear of death becomes the cause of blessed life.

Nor was he content with this. He began another basilica in honor of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, whose name he too had obtained from heaven. [Note: [Col. 0057D] Rubeus, under the year 438.] Prevented by death, he could not complete it. He also devoted much labor and diligence to the construction of the church of the Holy Cross and of the chapel of the holy Nazarius and Celsus, where the Empress Augusta Placidia had chosen a tomb for herself. [Col. 0057C]

### 30.

Since the aforementioned Placidia, in fulfillment of a vow that she had made during a great storm at sea, had built at Ravenna a most magnificent temple to Saint John the Evangelist, she was deeply anxious and troubled because she could not obtain its dedication from our holy bishop according to the rite then observed in the Catholic Church, since there were no relics of so great a man of God with which the dedication could be celebrated canonically. [Note: [Col. 0058D] Rubeus, under the year 433.]

She therefore decided to consult the priest Saint Barbatianus, who served her as chaplain and was famous for miracles during his life, asking what means he would recommend for remedying the matter. They report that the man of God immediately advised that they should hold sacred vigils together in the church itself and pray sincerely that God might be propitious to them in this matter. [Col. 0057D]

When the two of them were standing before the Most High in the church on the third night of the vigils, Barbatianus suddenly saw a venerable man clothed in pontifical garments walking about and filling the basilica with incense. Thinking him to be Saint John the Evangelist, he immediately awakened Placidia, who was overcome by sleep, and urged her also to look. She rose at once, and as she approached the Evangelist’s sacred feet and attempted to embrace and kiss them, the figure vanished from sight, and a sandal from the Evangelist’s foot was left in the empress’s hands. [Col. 0058A]

She received it joyfully, piously and reverently kissed it, and displayed it with great exultation to her son, the Emperor Valentinian, and to the entire people. Thus she deserved to obtain the dedication of the temple, with the heavenly relic, according to solemn rite and with swift ceremony.

After Augusta herself had arranged for the church to be adorned with sacred images in royal splendor, she also wished an image of our Peter to be placed there, in the form of a holy bishop celebrating the sacred rites and astonished by the presence of the heavenly beings, who could be seen receiving prayers from his mouth. [Col. 0058B]

31. In the same manner the blessed bishop consecrated the church of St. John the Baptist [Note: Rub., under the year 438; Rod. and others; there is a sermon of St. Peter Damian on the Nativity of St. Barbatianus, on the last day of December. See Baronius’s note in the Roman Martyrology for this day.], where the aforementioned Barbatianus, the true servant of God, was dwelling. Peter, foreseeing— as it is right to believe, through divine inspiration—that he would die from a slight but stubborn illness, warned Placidia, who was then staying at Ariminum. She immediately hastened to Ravenna and visited Barbatianus before he breathed his last. Chrysologus himself buried Barbatianus’s body in the aforesaid church, after it had been washed and anointed with precious ointments.

32. Likewise, when the holy bishop Germanus of Auxerre [Note: Rub. and Bar. on his feast day, vol. V, under the years 431 and 435; Antoninus II, *Historia*, part 2, title 11, chapter 17, § 6. The presbyter Constantius, *Life of St. Germanus*; Rodulphus and Rabanus both in the life of St. Chrysologus and in the *Life of St. Germanus*, July 31.]—called the apostle of Britain—was summoned to the Creator at Ravenna in the year of Christ 435, Peter entrusted his body, smeared with ointments compounded with Arabian fragrance, to a wooden coffin so that it might be transported to Gaul, as Germanus himself had requested while dying. Peter claimed the bishop’s hood, together with the hair shirt worn beneath it, as his inheritance; and Antonius, the second heir of Paul, prince of the hermits, who himself survived for fifteen years, held it in the highest veneration.

33. Since the blessed Chrysologus’s efforts were directed not so much toward his own churches as toward those of others, he therefore consecrated Projectus, bishop of Forocornelium [Note: Sermon 165, with its note.], as successor to St. Cornelius the Roman in the Church of Cornelium. He likewise ordained Marcellinus [Note: Sermon 175, with its note.], formerly a fisherman, as bishop of the Church of Vicohaventina, consecrating him in the same manner around the year of the Lord 449. The appendix to Usuard’s Martyrology asserts that he was enrolled in the catalogue of the saints [Col. 0058D].

34. So that he might omit no duty which he believed could proceed from him toward the people of Ravenna entrusted to him from heaven, he constructed and maintained at Classe, a town adjoining Ravenna and lacking potable water, a cistern—which others call a fountain—of extraordinary size, with two high walls, for the use of the entire population [Col. 0059A].

35. Nor, amid such great cares and the changing circumstances of the times, did he omit the preaching of the divine word [Note: Rodulphus, under the year 449.], whether from the steps or pulpit, from the episcopal seat, or from the sacred apse, especially on the Lord’s days and other feast days. [Note: Rodulphus and many manuscripts. See sermons 118 and 137.]

In broad daylight he unlocked the mystical questions of the sacred books and brought the precepts of justice before the people. He did not cease to teach, according to the capacity of his hearers, the things belonging to divine power, through the golden eloquence of his preaching and the holiness of his life. He entreated and implored God [Note: In sermon 107 Ambrose acted in this way, as Augustine attests, *Confessions* V.13, at the end.] to deign mysteriously to pour the whole fullness of doctrine into the minds of his listeners. Sometimes the fervor of his preaching was so intense [Col. 0059B] that he seemed carried away by a kind of divine madness [Note: Sermons 43, no. 1, and 126 and 159, 1; Rub., book II, under the year 451]. By this he drew everyone’s faces and minds toward himself, and his words so gladdened the people that, even in the height of great heat, the listeners restrained themselves [Note: Sermon 51]. He was so beloved that, when his voice was once lost during a sermon [Note: Sermons 35 and 86], everyone, moved with compassion and tears, commended him to God in an outpouring of prayer.

36. At that time among the Italians the common Latin language and its ordinary pronunciation still flourished. Yet, since Roman eloquence had steadily declined from the days of Cicero until its destruction, in Chrysologus’s time it lay so prostrate under the confusion and intermingling of the barbarian peoples with the Italians that it might almost be called dead. Nevertheless, lest Roman eloquence should be entirely exiled from the Church of God [Col. 0059C], it was granted from heaven that it should often flourish among consecrated men. We see that this was also bestowed upon our bishop, by a singular privilege for the benefit of souls. Through his elegant and eloquent command of Latin speech—and sometimes of Greek as well—through the sharpness and gravity of his intellect, and through his abundance of every kind of learning, we find that Chrysologus acquired his distinguished name.

For many Greeks, according to the judgment of certain people who only a few years earlier had given their own John the surname Chrysostom—“Golden-Mouthed”—because of his Attic eloquence, had come from Byzantium to Ravenna to the emperor. Since most of the emperor’s court was Greek by nation, they heard Peter preaching his golden stream of speech. At the same time, they admired in him the great maturity of his intellect and the purest, most limpid abundance and sweetness of his sound doctrine [Col. 0059D]. Wishing to proclaim in their own language that he was a golden speaker, or that the speech of Peter, archbishop of Ravenna, was golden, they called him Chrysologus. From then on he deserved to retain this name as a perpetual possession among all peoples [Col. 0060A]. [Note: P. Christophorus Verucchinus, in the manuscript work entitled *The Golden Gate Opened to Sacred Theology*, preserved in the archive of the Capuchin Fathers at Bologna, where he discusses St. Peter Chrysologus; he often confirmed this aloud in my hearing.]

His sermons, which he delivered orally, are also proclaimed by learned people everywhere to be golden when written in a book, as though cast from the purest gold, and composed with exceptional vigor. Yet Chrysologus himself, out of humility [Note: Natalis, Rub., Rod., and all who have written about him.], acknowledged that he was poor in spirit, of limited ability, and only moderate in eloquence. He professed that whatever understanding of sacred Scripture he possessed had flowed to him from the all-good and all-great God for the salvation of souls, as we repeatedly read that he testified in many sermons [Note: See sermon 136.].

So great was this man of God’s contempt for all human glory that, abandoning his ancestral family names, he called and signed himself only “Peter, bishop of Ravenna.” With the name of his parents erased [Note: Sermons 5, 39, 94, 95, 109, and 136 throughout.] [Col. 0060B], he took great pleasure in being called the evangelical son of St. Cornelius, bishop of Forocornelium, by whom, as we mentioned above, he had been offered at the sacred altars.

Finally, this man of God was endowed with such holiness and learning that, had the injuries of the times and the fires of war not most miserably taken from us what he wrote and accomplished, it would plainly be evident to everyone that in both respects he had been a great marvel. But who knows whether the Almighty, in the counsel of his supreme wisdom, permitted only these few things to be known so that from them each person might, according to his devotion, contemplate far greater things, and thus worship and praise God himself in his saints?

37. Peter Chrysologus, therefore, the resplendent glory of the Church of Ravenna, renowned in life for miracles and holiness [Col. 0060C], a theologian of the greatest learning and eloquence [Note: Natalis; Trithemius; Baronius, vol. I, under the year 435; and Blessed Felix, archbishop of Ravenna, in the preface reproduced below the sermons of Chrysologus; Florus and others.], and also the most faithful interpreter of sacred Scripture, was called “Great” by Cardinal Baronius in his *Ecclesiastical Annals*. After many labors undertaken for the Church of God with immense benefit to souls, and after he had most holily discharged for eighteen years every part of his office and pontifical ministry, he was filled with merits and with the Holy Spirit. Foreknowing by divine indication the day of the crown laid up for him, and about to surrender his spirit where he had received it from the Most High through creation, and to adorn his native land [Note: Natalis, Rub., Baronius, Rodulphus, Florus, and the Breviary mentioned above and the manuscript.] and the Church of Cornelium—as I shall call it—with sacred relics and the laying down of his body, he hastened back to his native soil.

When the blessed bishop Projectus, the consecrated clergy, and all the citizens had joyfully gone out to meet him, he was received into his homeland with the greatest honor, gratitude, and devotion. On the following day, at the proper hour, he most reverently offered to God at the altar of St. Cassian, before the altar of that blessed martyr, the holy sacrifice of the Mass for the living and [Col. 0061A] the dead. [Note: Natalis, Rodulphus, Florus, F. James of Genoa in the legend of St. Cassian the martyr, in the year of the Lord 1582. Perennial tradition and the most ancient images in the church of St. Cassian at Imola.]

Then he addressed the large assembly that had gathered and chose to warn them of the hour of his approaching death. Selecting a tomb for himself beside the altar of St. Cassian, he left to the altar of Blessed Cassian, by the hereditary right of his evangelical poverty, the sacred mitre decorated with gold and the most precious gems, the golden chalice, and the silver paten engraved with mystical figures and characters, which he had used in the sacred rites. [Note: Rodulphus and Rub., under the year 450.]

The people of Ravenna who had followed him in order to remain vigilant in choosing the best shepherd; the citizens, so that they might honor St. Cassian with the highest solemnities; and the whole people, so that they might preserve the Catholic faith against whatever legions of the Tartars might rise up, never depart from the divine commandments [Col. 0061B], love true peace, honor their shepherds, willingly hear the words of God from their mouths, and diligently keep every saving admonition—he exhorted with almost divine eloquence and from the depths of his heart. [Note: The Acts of the Vallicella and Rodulphus, in which many words and prayers spoken by that most holy man are recorded.]

38. But while everyone was already weeping, who could fully recount how fatherly he consoled them all in the Lord? How he tried to lift the sorrow of their hearts through holy admonitions and divine conversations? Finally, after having obtained from heaven, according to the rite of the pontificate, the blessing of almighty God upon them and their children throughout every generation and descent for all ages, and after pouring it over all with the sign of the holy cross, he turned immediately to the altar of Blessed Cassian. Removing the mitre from his head, he placed it upon the altar at the feet of the Lamb of God, offered for us on the altar of the cross [Col. 0061C], and, kneeling, most devoutly prayed to God and his holy patron that they might receive his departing soul into heaven. They report that he offered, among others, these prayers: [Note: The Acts of the Vallicella, Rodulphus, and many manuscripts.]

“I beseech you, blessed martyr Cassian: intercede for me. I was a member of your household, as it were, and was raised in this very church by Cornelius, the bishop of this see. Now, returning to you once again, I surrender my soul to almighty God, but I commend my body to you.”

While he prayed at length in this manner and with similar words, he put off his humanity and surrendered his spirit to God with a peaceful and serene countenance. He was to receive in glory the eternal mitre prepared for him here, on the fourth day before the Nones of December, while Leo I was supreme pontiff [Note: The Breviary mentioned above states that he died in the more probable year 450; the original of the *Annals* of our Florus agrees, as does Baronius, who gives either 449 or 450. Rubeus likewise gives this date.], and Valentinian III and Theodosius the Younger were Augustan emperors in the West and East, respectively [Col. 0061D], in the year of the Lord 450, at approximately forty-four years of age.

His sacred body was buried on the following day in a venerable tomb near the body and altar of St. Cassian, according to his own choice, with incredible grief and the greatest devotion by St. Projectus, as they say, bishop of his own Forocornelium, together with the provincial co-bishops and St. Donatus, chief deacon of Cornelium [Col. 0062A]. By unanimous consent, annual honors were decreed for him on the day of his burial, since he had been numbered among the saints, as testimony to the life he had led piously and holily. After five years, once Athilam’s fury—which had long ravaged Italy—had by God’s grace been extinguished, his tomb was more splendidly adorned in the same place.

59. The silver paten left by him to the chalice is truly endowed with marvelous power. Water poured through it and piously tasted by the faithful has very often been found to cure the bite of a rabid dog [Note: Natalis, Rodulphus, and *Experimentum*.] and to remove pestilential fevers. [Note: Pliny, book XXV, chapter 5.] Since no natural remedy is known to suffice for such evils [Col. 0062B], many people wounded by the bite of a mad or rabid dog come from every direction to the tomb of Blessed Peter Chrysologus, reverently approach his bones, and drink or carry away water.

Of all the saint’s many external relics, entrusted with paternal affection, this paten alone among the more precious relics mentioned is preserved there with veneration; the others either perished in the fires of war or were carried off in hostile plundering.

40. Yet far more marvelous are the monuments of his writings that remain. In them not only Greeks but all learned people admire and marvel at the true sharpness of his intellect, the holiness of his doctrine, the gravity and sincerity of his words and thoughts, the elegance of his structure, and the almost divine power of his speech [Note: Sixtus of Siena, book IV of the *Holy Library*; St. Antoninus, cited above, § 7; D. Agapitus of Vicenza in the preface to the sermons of Chrysologus reproduced below.].

Just as gold is ordinarily more precious and more pleasing than every other kind of metal [Note: Sermon 29], so they acknowledge that Chrysologus’s writings, though few, contain an exceedingly large amount of learning and elegance, and are the most weighty and delightful of all. They express even greater admiration because they do not judge this from everything he wrote and from the manner in which he wrote it—for he published commentaries, letters, and other volumes displaying his splendid intellect and learning [Note: Rub., Trithemius, Rodulphus, and all the manuscripts that record his life.]—but from the few fragments of his homilies that survived the injuries of the times, the fires of war, and plundering, like a few relics left after a funeral pyre.

Many of these fragments have been altered, mutilated, and corrupted. Yet from the writings of Peter Chrysologus that remain, they proclaim him to have been a library of divine and human sciences, a cherubic interpreter of sacred Scripture, and a consummate orator—vigorous and concise. Consequently, among Catholic preachers no polished discourse is found in which Chrysologus’s radiant eloquence does not often shine.

If we had been worthy to see everything he wrote with laconic brevity and refinement, our age and every human age would plainly recognize that he possessed an intellect more divine than human and devoted his supreme power to the glory of God and the salvation of souls. But perhaps God, marvelous in his saints, willed that the lion should thus be known from his claw.

41. For, alas, the copies he himself wrote perished either at Ravenna or at Forocornelium. In both places this happened through the treachery of Theodoric, king of the Ostrogoths, who occupied Ravenna [Note: Rub. gives this account of Theodoric around the year of the Lord 524. Baronius confirms it in his *Annals*; Dolionus in his *Historical Compendium*; and many others.]. Internally touched by the stain of Arianism and externally wrapped in it, he raged against the Catholics and threatened to destroy them, all their churches, and their entire territory by sword and fire. Finally, because Boethius and Symmachus were opposed to the Arians, he killed them, those brightest lights of Italy [Col. 0063B].

Indeed, he forced John himself, the first supreme pontiff of that name, distinguished for the holiness of his life—what sacrilege!—to end his life after being confined in the prison at Ravenna and consumed by filth, squalor, and starvation. He likewise dealt a similar kind of death to Balthasar, a member of the household of St. Peter Chrysologus [Note: The *Annals of Imola* by Florus Saxi and other manuscripts.], a man wise in every branch of sacred learning, merely because in those times he had visited the city of Ravenna.

It is therefore not an insignificant conjecture that the treacherous king diligently sought out all of Chrysologus’s writings at Ravenna, at Forocornelium, and from Balthasar himself, who was reasonably believed to possess them, and consigned all of them to fire and destruction together with the acts, the proceedings concerning the sanctity, and the miracles of St. Peter Chrysologus. He did this so that no one could use Chrysologus’s doctrine, sermons, and commentaries against the Arians, whom he had always opposed with tongue and pen. This second Herod, fearing Chrysologus’s holiness, authority, and doctrine as a threat to his own treachery and heresy, followed Diocletian [Note: Eusebius, book VIII, chapters 2 and 3.], who ordered all the books of the Christian religion to be burned, or Julian the Apostate [Note: All historians in the life of Julian.], who wickedly attempted to deprive Christian youth of the study of the liberal arts by removing pagan and Christian teachers.

For tyrants who ravage territories or religions have no more effective device than to strip them of their books, as of their strongest defenses [Note: John Gerson, *On the Praise of Writers*, chapter 9]. But, with God as avenger, this impious man soon perished, and as punishment for his crime he deservedly suffered eternal torments in the fire of Gehenna together with Herod, the slayer of John the Baptist [Col. 0063D].

42. Or perhaps this occurred earlier at Forocornelium, around the year of the Lord 554 [Note: Raphael of Volterra, book IV of the *Geography*; Tarcagnota, book VII of the *History of the World*; Dolionus, *Historical Compendium*; the manuscript *Annals of Imola*.], when Narses the eunuch, prefect of the Emperor Justinian and eventually an unfaithful servant of his master, destroyed the remnants of the Ostrogoths who had fled to Forocornelium and fortified themselves there with the necessities of life [Col. 0064C]. After a long siege he captured Forocornelium itself, a very flourishing and extensive city, plundered it with terrible devastation, and rashly and cruelly dared to overthrow it completely by fire and sword.

Later, when the emperor, angered by this, summoned the Lombards from Pannonia to rule Italy [Note: The *Annals of Imola*; Blondus of Forlì, book VIII of his *History*; Rub., book III, under the year 577; and other historians.], their most cruel king Cleph, after an interval of sixteen years, rebuilt a city with great speed beside the remaining traces of ancient Forocornelium, although on a site shifted many paces away and kept within considerably narrower bounds. It contained the river Vatrenus within it and was rebuilt on both sides of the waters with a very strong bridge.

On the opposite bank of the river, toward the south, on the adjoining hill, he built a circular fortress surrounded by walls and supported by an extremely strong and immense citadel [Note: Rub., Tarcagnota, Dolionus, Blondus, and many others.], so that it might stand as a perpetual goad against the people of Ravenna and the neighboring cities. Because of its hardness and strength, he ordered it to be called in Latin *Castrum Immolle*—that is, “hard and almost iron fortress”—and its citadel, although built beside gentle waters and surrounded by them on every side, resisted the enemy by nature and situation.

Soon the city itself acquired in common usage the name of the citadel and fortress. Strengthened by continuous possession, it was eventually accustomed by more recent inhabitants to be called and written Imola, as though by syncope, if not by a corrupted form of the word.

Yet it is not sufficiently known in our time whether the church dedicated to St. Cassian, constructed in the western part of the ancient city of Cornelium, where the body of Blessed Chrysologus rested, escaped the destruction and fire. We do know with certainty that after the city’s destruction a town called St. Cassian was built there, where both the cathedral church and the episcopal residence remained [Note: These matters are recorded at greater length in the acts of the Most Reverend Canons, preserved in the archive of the cathedral church of Imola].

Eventually, however, after the Aemilians and Bolognese had long pressed one another in war, the Bolognese burned that town and utterly destroyed it, and demolished the aforementioned citadel, or fortress of Immolle, from its foundations forever [Col. 0065B]. Consequently, the church dedicated to St. Cassian [Note: It was then called the Church of Cornelium, as I read at greater length in the acts; this is also reported above by Glossator and Archdeacon in canon 12, distinction 63.], the episcopal see, and the bodies of many saints buried there were transferred to the renewed city of Imola and placed in the lacuna. Among them was the body of Blessed Peter Chrysologus, placed at the right hand of the tomb of St. Cassian, beneath its own altar, in the year of the Lord 1200 [Col. 0066A]. [Note: Florus and Rodulphus in the life of Chrysologus, at the end.]

Previously, the body had been discovered by Troilus Nordilius, then the leading citizen of Imola, and had been buried with greater honor in the same church where Chrysologus had died, around the year of Christ 946. At that time Troilus arranged for the church itself, which had been most shamefully defiled by barbarians, to be restored, and for these services deserved to receive several gifts from Agapetus II, supreme pontiff.

44. In the new and presently existing church of St. Cassian within the city itself [Note: The testimony of Phaellus, which I reproduce below; Florus in the manuscript *Annals of Imola*.], Matthew Phaellus, provost of that cathedral, by order of the Most Reverend Lord Simon, bishop, in the year of Christ 1497, searched for and found the same body of Blessed Chrysologus beneath its own altar. He touched and identified it and faithfully placed it in a marble sarcophagus above the same altar, which is likewise on the right of the altar of St. Cassian, on the day before the Kalends of September.

On the left, the bones of Blessed Projectus, citizen and bishop of Cornelium, likewise rest in a stone coffin above an altar [Col. 0066B]. Here, in veneration of this triad of saints, God is continually worshiped and their protection is invoked by the citizens; and outsiders, too, are drawn there—not without immense Christian benefit and spiritual joy—to praise the Most High and venerate his blessed saints.

[Col. 0065B]

## Reply to the Oppositions

Although what we have sincerely written about the life and acts of Blessed Peter Chrysologus appears sufficiently supported by the authorities cited in the margin, nevertheless, since some of those authorities seem to oppose it, we have decided to answer the contrary arguments as best we can, so that the truth we have reported may shine forth more clearly and the reader’s mind may rest peacefully in it.

1. First, Blondus of Forlì and his transcriber, Jacobus Philippus Bergomensis, the Hermit, together with a very few other followers of these men, assert that Peter Chrysologus was by birth a Ravennate and bishop of the Church of Cornelium [Col. 0065C]. [Note: Blondus, *Italy Illustrated*, region 6, where he discusses Bergamo, in the supplement to book VI of the *Chronicle*, where he discusses Ravenna.]

But unless Blondus is found to have been badly transcribed through the usual carelessness of scribes, the testimonies of others indicate that he was completely mistaken. They report that our Peter was elected archbishop of Ravenna from his homeland of Cornelium. Peter himself, a witness to his own case beyond all objection, consistently affirms that he was raised, religiously instructed, and initiated into sacred orders at Forocornelium by St. Cornelius, bishop of that see [Note: Sermon 165]. Out of his special love for his evangelical father, he consecrated St. Projectus bishop of that same Forocornelium with particular affection.

He certainly could not have done this if Chrysologus himself had been bishop of the Church of Cornelium, as will be perfectly clear to anyone who does not disdain to read his sermon 165 together with our observations on it [Col. 0065D].

2. Surius, Rabanus, and others state in the life of Chrysologus that he was consecrated bishop in the year of the Lord 430 and departed this life after ten years. But these writers deserve pardon, since, when reading this in the first edition of Hieronymus Rubeus’s *History of Ravenna*, they mistook the words of their master.

Rubeus himself, correcting the errors in the second edition of the same history, is read to have more cautiously pursued the truth and asserted that Chrysologus was elected in 433 and died in 450.

3. Before Rubeus published his *History*, many people did not hesitate to extend the life of Blessed Peter Chrysologus into the time of Pope Symmachus. They had examined the signature of Peter, bishop of Ravenna, in two councils held under that pontiff [Note: Notatus, in canon “Councils of Priests,” distinction 17, and distinction 96, canon “Bene,” § “when it had been read.”], and this signature had also been mistakenly attributed to our Peter.

Nevertheless, after reading much and many sources, as he asserted, Rubeus found the truth. He demonstrated that the Chrysologus who signed those conciliar acts was not our Chrysologus, but another Peter. In tracing the succession of the bishops of Ravenna, he states that when Chrysologus died in the year of Christ 450, Neon succeeded him until 453; John succeeded Neon until 493; and Peter II succeeded John, a Ravennate by birth, who was the twenty-fourth archbishop of that Church and who took part in and signed those councils [Note: Not Peter of Altinum, as some assert, although he too took part in the council.]

This is also established by Baronius’s interpretation of the letter numbered 37 among the letters of Pope St. Leo, sent in the year of the Lord 451 to Neon, bishop of Ravenna. If Chrysologus had then been alive, Neon would certainly not have been bishop. Rubeus proves from several other substantial reasons and numerous conjectures that what we have reported concerning the date of Blessed Chrysologus’s death is true. Baronius agrees with him; it is enough to refer readers to them.

4. Yet what we have said seems at first sight to conflict too sharply with Chrysologus’s own words. In sermon 145 he says:

> “Christ, around five hundred years after his birth, brings forward the causes of his nativity; he suffers disputes concerning his origin.”

The person who first published the sermon noted in the margin that this concerned the age of Chrysologus. For if, when he spoke these words, nearly five hundred years had passed since the virginal birth, who could deny that Blessed Chrysologus had lived to that time?

Nevertheless, if a prudent reader observes that our author uttered these words against Eutyches and his heresy, he will acknowledge that this was done at no more suitable time than when that deadly poison began to spread through the churches of God. But it was shown above that this heresy arose in the year of Christ 448, was condemned by the general Council of Chalcedon, consisting of six hundred and thirty Fathers, in the year of Christ 451, and that the Catholic faith was thereby strengthened. Thus, in 449, Blessed Peter replied to Eutyches by letter and at the same time instructed the people in his sermons. [Note: Sermons 145 and 175.]

He would certainly not have postponed doing this until forty years or more after the Council of Chalcedon. He rightly said “around five hundred years,” appearing to speak of the fifth century as having begun and reached its midpoint, although it was not yet complete. When replying to Eutyches, he seems to have used a similar phrase [Col. 0067C], saying:

> “The generation of Christ, after so many ages, is being debated in a rash dispute.”

Thus, in order to refute Eutyches, he employed the very long span of a hundred-year reckoning, enlarging the point in the manner of an excellent orator. No one can fail to see this.

5. Manuscripts and printed documents of many kinds testify that, at the command of Pope St. Leo, St. Chrysologus wrote to the Council of Chalcedon against the heresy of Eutyches, in addition to the reply written below. Many also assert that the letter itself survives and is found transcribed before the acts of that council.

After carefully investigating the truth of the matter, however, I was able to find only Chrysologus’s reply to Eutyches, of which all the historians also make mention, beginning, “I read with sadness your sad letter,” and so forth [Col. 0067D].

Yet I have always thought that so many otherwise truthful writers did not all err together in this matter, but spoke truly, though in an obscure or confused way. Therefore, prudent reader, I ask you to attend to what I have often read and considered.

6. It is universally agreed that Eutyches, abbot of Constantinople, disseminated his heresy around the year of the Lord 448. At that time Flavian, bishop of that imperial city, convened a synod of many Fathers to oppose the deadly fire with all his strength [Col. 0068A]. Against the treacherous and obstinate abbot and his heresy, a canonical judgment was issued.

Eutyches bore this condemnation most bitterly. With the help of the eunuch Chrysaphius, prefect of the imperial bedchamber, who was hostile to Flavian out of personal hatred, Eutyches fabricated charges and complained about Flavian in letters to Pope St. Leo. He obtained from the supreme pontiff a letter rebuking Flavian.

Soon, however, the pontiff received letters from Flavian and examined the lawful proceedings of the entire case. He learned that the abbot had written falsely and that he had rightly been declared and condemned as a heretic.

Nevertheless, because a matter of the greatest importance concerning the faith was at stake, and the faithful awaited the decisive reply of the most holy vicar of Christ on earth, Blessed Leo—who deferred to learned Fathers in accordance with the practice of the Catholic Church, so that he might hear their views—either summoned Peter Chrysologus to Rome, which is more credible [Note: See sermon 75, with its note.], or at least sent him the proceedings and acts, as the most holy and most learned of all the Latin Fathers of that time and an expert in the Greek language.

He did this so that Peter, after examining the proceedings and investigating the whole truth of the question, might write what seemed appropriate to him for confirmation of the faith. No rational person will deny that Peter, that outstanding teacher of Catholic truth, most willingly did this for the Church of God.

7. Yet the diligent reader may object that nowhere in the Council of Chalcedon does a letter of Chrysologus appear, but only one of Pope St. Leo is recorded as having been read. I would readily subscribe to the view that the letter of Pope St. Leo, numbered 10 and beginning “After reading the letter of your affection,” and so forth [Col. 0068C], was itself composed in substance by Chrysologus and presented to the holy Leo.

To ensure that not a bishop of a particular church but the universal pastor, who held on earth the see of Blessed Peter the Apostle, might suitably declare the truth to those seeking the faith and rebuke the person straying from the path of truth, it was written under the name of St. Leo himself and sent to Bishop Flavian, while in fact belonging to all Catholics.

Perhaps for this reason some denied that it was composed by St. Leo himself [Note: Marcellinus Comes, in his *Chronicle*, says that these letters were dictated by St. Prosper to Pope St. Leo. Gennadius thought the same, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 84.], especially since in style and doctrine it appears to differ greatly from his other letters.

Yet, failing to recognize in it the sharpness of intellect, the learning of its thoughts, and its eloquence, they did not hesitate, without any sound reason, to attribute that letter not to our Chrysologus but to others [Col. 0068D].

## 8.

Nevertheless, I do not deny that the blessed Leo, a most learned and elegant teacher, transcribed the letter received from the blessed Peter of Ravenna in his own style and added certain things on his own initiative. Nevertheless, the divine genius and acumen of Chrysologus could not be wholly concealed in it. This is that circular letter addressed to Flavian, decisive for the whole question debated by the Council of Chalcedon in 630, and received with great reverence by the Fathers. The authors report that Peter Chrysologus wrote it, [Note: It appears in the Council of Chalcedon, act 2, p. 204, in the Roman edition of 1609. Baronius reproduced it in Greek and Latin in volume VI of his *Annals*, under the year 449, and we have transcribed it in full below.] although they do not explain themselves well, or their writings have reached our own times in a corrupted form. If this long observation of my own intellect has not yet attained sound truth, it may perhaps provide some with an incentive to investigate the matter with sounder judgment.

## 9.

From what has been said concerning the age of the blessed Peter, it is sufficiently clear that some people in our own time have not represented his likeness truthfully, since we see it portraying not a man of forty, but a very old man. Yet the painters, deceived by the same error as the writers—who committed to writing that the blessed Peter died when he was almost a hundred—could be excused to some extent if they said that they had painted a man not yet certainly fifty years old, but so weakened by fasts, prayer, vigils, study, scourging, hair shirts, labors, and tears that he appeared rather to bear the image of a seventy-year-old.

A true and authenticated image of Chrysologus, executed in mosaic, may therefore be seen at Ravenna in the apse of the choir of the metropolitan church. It appears to represent a venerable man of at most forty-four years, with a lively face, somewhat reddish beard, and a book held before him as a sign of his singular learning.

## 10.

It would be surprising if even the day of death of this most holy man had not been disputed. Some—for example, Peter de Natalibus and Baronius in the Roman Martyrology and in his *Ecclesiastical Annals*—have declared that he died on the fourth day before the Nones of December; others, such as Rubeus and many manuscripts, have written that he died on the third day before the Nones of the same month.

But if we proceed by distinguishing the circumstances, the reader will find no contradiction whatsoever. The blessed Peter Chrysologus died, according to our records, on the fourth day before the Nones of December, near midday, before the altar of Saint Cassian in the church. His sacred body, however, was not committed to burial until the evening of the following day. Since the ancient custom of our church has always been to celebrate annually the day of his deposition, and since the Church of Ravenna likewise continued, as is clear, to observe this practice with us down to the time of Rubeus, the writers who stated that he died on the fourth day before the Nones could easily have been misled when they saw the annual honors paid to our blessed Peter by those churches on the same day.

Moreover, the Ravennate historians Ferrettus and Carrarius, as well as our Florius and the very ancient office of the same Saint Peter belonging to the Church of Imola, demonstrate that the day of death was the fourth day before the Nones, but the day of deposition the third, as we have said. Hence our people celebrate the annual sacred feast of this pontiff on the third day before the Nones of December, while others observe it on the fourth.

## 11.

We have otherwise learned that certain shallow scholars have not fully approved the laconic brevity of our most holy teacher. In distinguishing kinds of brevity, we say that one kind is to be approved and the other rejected. The first is that which corresponds proportionately to the subject matter, [Note: Aristotle, *On Rhetoric*, book III.] in which there are as many words as are necessary to express the meaning under discussion. We deny that this kind produces any obscurity among the learned. [Note: Cicero, book II, *To Quintus Frater*.]

The second kind is unequal and deficient in what is required for expressing the subject matter; [Note: Horace, *To the Pisones*, *The Art of Poetry*.] and we do not hesitate to say that this alone contains darkness. Of it Saint Augustine says in treatise 67 on John: “Brevity itself is another kind of obscurity.” But who does not see that the brevity employed by Chrysologus in his sermons—where the text has not been altered or corrupted—is not only proportionate to the matters treated, [Note: Florius, in his *Annals*, where he discusses Chrysologus.] but also lucid, adorned with acumen, and so suitable to learned minds that every wise person may judge it foolish, if not impious, to condemn it?

I believe that he aptly employed this grandiloquent manner of speaking, with its breadth of thought and majesty of expression, because, in the words of Nazianzen, [Note: Nazianzen, Oration 16, *On the Love of the Poor*; Seneca, letter 76.] “Whatever is easily understood is also easily held in contempt; and whatever eludes our desire exercises our longing.” Or perhaps because this style surpasses the others in excellence, as the statements written by Plutarch in his *Political Works* concerning the brevity of Phocion are well suited to show. He says: [Note: In Granat, *Collection of Moral Philosophy*, volume II, “Eloquence”:] “Everyone admired the brevity of Phocion’s speech, for Polyeuctus used to say that Demosthenes was the most expansive of orators, but Phocion the most weighty in persuasion: his very brief diction contained the richest thoughts.” For this reason Demosthenes, who did not greatly esteem the others, is said to have been accustomed to say, whenever he saw Phocion rise: “The sword of my words is rising.”

If those shallow scholars had previously considered these few points with an unprejudiced gaze, they might perhaps have been more cautious in passing judgment and would not have been blameworthy in their criticism.

## 12.

Sixtus of Siena, [Note: Book IV, *Sacred Bibliotheca*.] and Bellarmine, his copyist in this matter, [Note: *Description of the Ecclesiastical Writers*, where he discusses Peter Chrysologus.] reported that the sermons of the blessed Chrysologus numbered one hundred and twenty-two. If this was not an error in transcription, the codex of Siena must necessarily have been altogether incomplete, since one hundred and seventy-six appear in the printed copies and in many manuscripts. [The text says “five,” but then lists six sermons:] among these, however, are sermons 53, 107, 128, 129, 138, and 149, which we conjecture were not delivered by our Chrysologus, as our observations also demonstrate concerning them.

[Col. 0070D]

## 13.

And these few points, candid reader, are what I—an investigator of truth rather than a rash assertor, and not one endowed with lynx-like vision—have been scarcely able to discover through long and arduous inquiry amid the obscurity of such ancient times and such differing writers, with the divine Spirit breathing upon me. As you see, when simply brought together, they await with equanimity, for the glory of the Almighty, the veneration of the blessed Chrysologus, and the spiritual joy of our fellow citizens, any hosts of opponents who may arise, so that through multiplied investigation the supreme truth may become increasingly known. May I, together with men endowed with distinguished and devout learning, cling to it forever, and for that reason render continual thanks throughout the eternal ages to the everlasting and immeasurable Truth.

# TESTIMONIES

For fuller confirmation of certain matters that we have mentioned above in the Life of the Author, receive, candid reader, the letter of the blessed Chrysologus to Eutyches; the letter of Saint Leo the pope; the attestation of Master Matthaeus Phaellus; certain praises of the blessed Peter by writers; the preface of the blessed Felix to some sermons of Chrysologus; and the letter of the Reverend Father Peter Rodulphus, bishop of Senigallia, to the senators of Imola, as follows.

## I. Letter of Saint Peter Chrysologus to Eutyches the Heretic

**Peter, bishop of Ravenna, to his most beloved and deservedly honored son, the presbyter Eutyches.**

I read your sorrowful letter with sorrow, and with the grief it deserved I read through your mournful writing. For just as the peace of the churches, the harmony of the priests, and the tranquility of the people make us rejoice with heavenly joy, so fraternal dissension afflicts and casts us down—especially when it arises from such causes.

Human laws settle human questions within thirty years; yet the generation of Christ, which is written in the divine law to be ineffable, is being rashly debated after so many centuries? You are not unaware what Origen, an investigator of beginnings, encountered, or how Nestorius fell when disputing about natures. The Magi confess Jesus to be God in the manger through mystical gifts, while priests investigate with a sorrowful question who he is who was born of the Virgin’s womb from the Holy Spirit. When Jesus cried in the cradle, the heavenly host proclaimed, “Glory to God in the highest”; and now, when every knee bows at the name of Jesus—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—is the question of his origin being stirred up?

We, dearest brother, say together with the Apostle: “Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him no longer in that way” (2 Cor. 5:16). Nor can we inquisitively scrutinize him whom we are commanded to honor, to render fear, and to await, not to examine, whom we confess to be the judge.

I have answered you briefly, brother, and would have written more in reply to your letter if our brother and fellow bishop Flavian had sent me some written account concerning this matter. For if you are displeased—as you indeed write—with the judgment chosen for you, how can we judge concerning those whom we have not seen because of their absence, and whose understanding we do not know because of their silence? A judge is not just if he hears one party in such a way that he reserves nothing for the other.

In all things, however, we exhort you, honorable brother, to attend obediently to what has been written by the most blessed pope of the city of Rome, since the blessed Peter, who lives and presides in his own see, grants the truth of the faith to those who seek it. For, out of zeal for peace and faith, we cannot hear cases without the agreement of the bishop of the city of Rome.

May the Lord deign to preserve your affection safe for a very long time, dearest and most honored son.

This letter appears at the end of the sermons of the blessed Peter Chrysologus in the fourth edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, volume V, part II, with notes and variant readings by Gerhard Vossius. It also appears before the acts of the Council of Chalcedon, written in Greek and Latin; in volume VI of Baronius’s *Annals*; and in the Life of Chrysologus written by Peter Rodulphus and recorded in the archive of the senate of Imola.

## II. Letter of Saint Leo the First, Pope, to Flavian, Bishop of Constantinople, against the Treachery and Heresy of Eutyches

**Leo, bishop, to his beloved brother Flavian, bishop of Constantinople.**

### 1.

After reading the letter of your affection—which we marvel was so long delayed—and reviewing the order of the episcopal proceedings, we finally learned what scandal had occurred among you and what had arisen against the integrity of the faith. Matters that had previously seemed hidden have now been disclosed to us.

In these proceedings Eutyches, who appeared honorable because of the title of presbyter, is shown to be extremely imprudent and exceedingly unlearned, so that what the Prophet said of him may also be applied: “He refused to understand, that he might do good; he meditated iniquity in his bed” (Ps. 35:3 [Vulgate 35:4]). For what is more wicked than to entertain impious opinions and not believe those who are wiser and more learned?

But those who, when obstructed by some obscurity in their effort to know the truth, turn not to prophetic utterances, not to the apostolic writings, not to the authority of the Gospels, but to themselves, fall into this folly. They become teachers of error because they have not been disciples of truth.

What learning from the pages of the Old and New Testament did he acquire who has not even grasped the beginning of the Creed itself? What is proclaimed throughout the whole world by the voice of all the regenerate is still not contained in the heart of this old man.

### 2.

Since he did not know what he ought to think concerning the incarnation of the Word of God, and was unwilling to labor through the breadth of the sacred Scriptures in order to obtain the light of understanding, he should at least have received with attentive hearing that common and undifferentiated confession by which the whole company of the faithful professes that it believes in God the almighty Father, and in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord, who was born from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary.

These three statements overthrow the contrivances of nearly all heretics. When the Father is believed to be God, almighty, and eternal, the Son is shown to be co-eternal with him and in no respect different from the Father: God from God, almighty from almighty, born eternal from the eternal. He is not later in time, inferior in power, unlike in glory, or divided in essence. The only-begotten and eternal Son of the everlasting Begetter was born from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary.

That temporal birth neither diminished nor added anything to his divine and eternal birth; rather, it wholly devoted itself to restoring the human being who had been deceived, so that he might conquer death and by his power destroy the devil, who possessed dominion over death. We could not overcome the author of sin and death unless he assumed our nature and made it his own—a nature that neither sin could contaminate nor death retain.

He was conceived from the Holy Spirit within the womb of his virgin mother, who gave birth to him while preserving her virginity, just as she had conceived him while preserving her virginity.

But if he could not draw this sound understanding from the purest source of Christian faith, because he had darkened for himself the brightness of manifest truth by his own blindness, he should have submitted himself to evangelical teaching. Matthew says: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham” (Matt. 1:1).

He should also have sought the instrument of apostolic preaching and, reading in the Epistle to the Romans, “Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle, set apart for the Gospel of God, which he had promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Rom. 1:1–3), he should likewise have directed devout attention to the prophetic pages and found God’s promise to Abraham: “In your seed all the nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18).

And so that he might not doubt the particular identity of this seed, he should have followed the Apostle, who says: “The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. He does not say, ‘and to seeds,’ as though referring to many, but as though referring to one: ‘and to your seed,’ which is Christ” (Gal. 3:16).

He should also have grasped inwardly the preaching of Isaiah, who says: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and shall bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel,” which is interpreted, “God with us” (Isa. 7:14).

He should likewise have read faithfully the words of the same prophet: “A child is born to us, a son is given to us, whose authority is upon his shoulder; and his name shall be called the Angel of Great Counsel, Wonderful, Counselor, God, Mighty, Prince of Peace, Father of the Age to Come” (Isa. 9:6).

Speaking falsely, would he then say that the Word became flesh in such a way that Christ, born from the Virgin’s womb, had the form of a human being but did not possess the reality of his mother’s body?

Or did he perhaps think that our Lord Jesus Christ was not of our nature because, when the angel was sent to the blessed Mary, ever-virgin, he said: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore also the holy one who will be born from you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35)? Did he therefore suppose that, because the Virgin’s conception was a work of divine power, the flesh conceived did not come from the nature of the one conceiving?

But that uniquely marvelous and marvelously unique birth must not be understood in such a way that the novelty of creation removes the particularity of the human race. The Holy Spirit gave fertility to the virgin Mary; but the reality of the body was taken from a body. And while Wisdom was building a house for herself (Prov. 9:1), “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14)—that is, in the flesh which he assumed from a human being and which the spirit of rational life animated.

### 3.

Thus, with the particularity of both natures preserved and joined in one person, humility was assumed by majesty, weakness by power, and mortality by eternity. To cancel the debt of our condition, an inviolable nature was united to a passible nature, so that one and the same mediator between God and human beings, the human being Jesus Christ, could die by virtue of one nature and could not die by virtue of the other.

Accordingly, in the complete and perfect nature of a true human being, God is wholly present both in what belongs to him and in what belongs to us. By “ours” we mean what the Creator established in us from the beginning and what he assumed in order to restore. Those things that the deceiver introduced and the deceived human being admitted left no trace in the Savior. Nor, because he shared in the weaknesses of human beings, did he therefore share in our sins.

He assumed the form of a servant without the stain of sin, increasing what was human without diminishing what was divine. For that emptying by which he who was invisible made himself visible, and by which the Creator and Lord of all things willed to become one of mortal beings, was an inclination of mercy, not a failure of power.

Therefore the one who, remaining in the form of God, made the human being was himself made human in the form of a servant. Each nature retains its own particularity without defect. And just as the form of a servant does not remove the form of God, so the form of God does not diminish the form of a servant.

For the devil gloried that the human being, deceived by his fraud, had been deprived of divine gifts and, stripped of the endowment of immortality, had undergone the harsh sentence of death. He took a certain consolation in his own evils from sharing in the transgression and supposed that, in accordance with the demands of justice, God had also changed his own sentence concerning the human being whom he had created in such great honor.

It was therefore necessary that, through the dispensation of a hidden plan, the unchangeable God—whose will cannot be deprived of its goodness—should complete by a more hidden mystery the first dispensation of his mercy toward us, so that the human being, driven into guilt by the devil’s wicked cunning, might not perish contrary to God’s purpose.

### 4.

The Son of God therefore enters the lowliness of this world, descending from his heavenly seat, yet not departing from the Father’s glory; he is generated in a new order and by a new birth.

In a new order, because he who was invisible in what belonged to him became visible in what belonged to us, and he who was incomprehensible willed to be comprehended. While existing before the ages, he began to exist in time. The Lord of the universe assumed the form of a servant, the immensity of his majesty being veiled.

God impassible did not disdain to become a passible human being, nor did the immortal disdain to submit to the laws of death.

He was generated by a new birth because inviolate virginity, knowing nothing of carnal desire, supplied the material of the flesh. The nature, not the guilt, was taken from the Lord’s mother. Nor, because the birth of the Lord Jesus Christ from the Virgin’s womb was marvelous, is it therefore unlike our nature.

For he who is true God is likewise true human being, and there is no falsehood in this unity, since in it are both the lowliness of humanity and the exaltation of divinity. Just as God is not changed by mercy, so the human being is not consumed by dignity.

Each form acts, in communion with the other, according to what is proper to it: the Word doing what belongs to the Word, and the flesh carrying out what belongs to the flesh. One of these shines with miracles; the other submits to insults. And just as the Word did not depart from equality with the Father’s glory, so the flesh did not abandon the nature of our race.

For one and the same person—and this must often be said—is truly the Son of God and truly the son of a human being: God by virtue of the words, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God”; human by virtue of the words, “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” God by virtue of the words, “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made”; human by virtue of the words, “He was made from a woman, made under the law.”

The birth of the flesh is the manifestation of human nature; the Virgin’s delivery is a sign of divine power. The infancy of the child is shown by the lowliness of the cradle. The greatness of the Most High is declared by the voices of angels. He whom the impious Herod plots to kill is like the beginnings of human life; yet he is the Lord of all, whom the Magi rejoice humbly to adore.

When he came to the baptism of his forerunner John, lest it remain hidden that he was concealed beneath the veil of flesh, the Father’s voice thundered from heaven: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17).

Thus the devil’s cunning tempts him as a human being, while the ministry of angels serves him as God. To hunger, thirst, grow weary, and sleep is plainly human; but to satisfy five thousand people with five loaves, to grant the Samaritan woman living water whose drinking prevents further thirst, to walk upon the back of the sea without sinking feet, and to calm the rising waves by rebuking the storm is unmistakably divine.

Therefore, to pass over much else, it is not of the same nature to weep out of compassionate affection over a dead friend and, removing the barrier of a four-day burial, to raise that same friend alive at a command; or to hang upon a tree and, when daylight is turned into night, make all the elements tremble; or to be pierced with nails and open the gates of paradise to the faith of a robber.

Likewise, it is not of the same nature to say, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), and to say, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28). For although there is one person in the Lord Jesus Christ, God and human being, one thing is the source of the shared dishonor of both, and another the source of their shared glory. From us comes his humanity, which is less than the Father; from the Father comes his divinity, which is equal with the Father.

### 5.

Because of this unity of person, which must be understood in both natures, the Son of Man is read to have descended from heaven, since the Son of God assumed flesh from that Virgin from whom he was born.

Again, the Son of God is said to have been crucified and buried, although he endured these things not in the divinity itself—in which he is the only-begotten, co-eternal, and consubstantial Son with the Father—but in the weakness of human nature.

Accordingly, in the Creed also we all confess that the only-begotten Son of God was crucified and buried, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement: “If they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8).

When our Lord and Savior was teaching the faith of his disciples through his questions, he said: “Who do people say that the Son of Man is?” (Matt. 16:13). After they had recounted the various opinions of others, he said: “But who do you say that I am?” That is: I, who am the Son of Man, whom you see in the form of a servant and in the reality of flesh—who do you say that I am?
