Then the blessed Peter, inspired by God and destined through his confession to benefit all the nations, said: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” It was not without reason that the Lord pronounced him blessed, and that he drew both solidity of virtue and of name from the principal rock, since by the Father’s revelation he confessed him to be both the Son of God and the Christ.

For accepting one of these without the other did not benefit salvation; rather, it was equally dangerous to believe the Lord Jesus Christ to be either God alone without a human being or a human being alone without God.

After the Lord’s resurrection—which was certainly the resurrection of a true human being, since no one other than the one who had been crucified and had died was raised—what else was accomplished during the delay of forty days except that the integrity of our faith might be cleansed of every obscurity?

He spoke with his disciples, lived with them, ate with them, and allowed himself to be handled by those whom doubt had touched, with careful and inquisitive contact. For this reason he entered to the disciples through closed doors, gave them the Holy Spirit with his breath, and, granting them the light of understanding, revealed the hidden things of the sacred Scriptures.

Again, he displayed the wound in his side, the marks of the nails, and all the freshest signs of his passion, saying: “See my hands and feet, for I am he myself. Touch and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have” (Luke 24:39).

This was so that it might be recognized that the particularity of the divine and human nature remained indivisible in him, and so that we might know that the Word is not the same as the flesh, while confessing one Son of God and one Word, together with the flesh.

Eutyches must therefore be judged exceedingly empty of this mystery of faith, since he recognized our nature in the Only-Begotten Son of God neither through the humility of mortality nor through the glory of the resurrection.

Nor did he heed the judgment of the blessed apostle and evangelist John, who says: “Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God; and every spirit that dissolves Jesus is not from God, and this is the Antichrist” (1 John 4:2–3).

For what does it mean to dissolve Jesus except to separate the human nature from him and to empty, by the most shameless fictions, the mystery of the faith through which we have been saved?

Since he is blind concerning the nature of Christ’s body, he must also be deceived by the same blindness concerning his passion. For if he does not think the Lord’s cross false, and does not doubt that the punishment endured for the salvation of the world was real, let him acknowledge whose death he believes in and whose flesh he recognizes.

Let him not deny the human being of our body whom he acknowledges to have been capable of suffering, since denial of true flesh is also denial of bodily suffering.

If he has embraced the Christian faith and has not turned his hearing away from the preaching of the Gospel, let him see what nature was clearly pierced and hung upon the wood of the cross. When he sees the side of the crucified man opened by the soldier’s lance, let him understand from where the blood and water flowed, so that the Church of God might be watered both by the bath and by the cup.

Let him not read casually the words of the same Apostle: “Knowing that you were redeemed, not with perishable silver and gold from your empty way of life inherited from your fathers, but with the precious blood, as of a spotless and undefiled Lamb, Jesus Christ” (1 Pet. 1:18–19).

Nor should he resist the testimony of the blessed Apostle John, who says: “The blood of Jesus Christ cleanses us from every sin” (1 John 1:7).

And again: “This is the victory that conquers the world, our faith. And who is the one who conquers the world except the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God? This is the one who came through water and blood, Jesus Christ—not in water only, but in water and blood. And the Spirit is the one who testifies, because the Spirit is truth. For there are three that testify: the Spirit, the water, and the blood; and these three are one” (1 John 5:4–8).

The Spirit, certainly, is the Spirit of sanctification; the blood, of redemption; and the water, of baptism. These three are one and remain indivisible, and none of them is separated from its connection with the others, because the Catholic Church lives and advances by this faith: that in Christ Jesus humanity is not believed to exist without true divinity, nor divinity without true humanity.

### 6.

When, in response to your examination, Eutyches answered: “I confess that our Lord existed from two natures before the union; but after the union I confess one nature,” I marvel that so absurd and perverse a profession was not rebuked by any condemning judgment of yours, and that a speech so foolish and so blasphemous was passed over as though nothing offensive had been heard.

For it is as impious to say that the only-begotten Son of God existed from two natures before the incarnation as it is wicked to assert that, after the Word became flesh, there is in him a single nature.

To prevent Eutyches from judging that this statement was therefore correct or tolerable simply because it was not refuted by any sentence of yours, we urge your diligent concern, dearest brother, that if, through the inspiration of God’s mercy, the case is brought to a satisfactory conclusion, the imprudence of this unlearned man may also be cleansed by you of this stain upon his understanding.

As the order of the proceedings made clear, he had almost begun to withdraw from his persuasion when, compelled by your judgment, he professed that he was saying what he had not said before and assenting to the faith from which he had previously been alien. But because he refused to give his consent by anathematizing the impious doctrine, your fraternity understood that he remained in his own perfidy and was deserving of a sentence of condemnation.

If he grieves over this faithfully and beneficially, and recognizes, even if late, how rightly episcopal authority was moved—or if, for the fullness of satisfaction, he condemns aloud and by a present subscription everything that he has thought wrongly—then no degree of mercy toward one who has corrected himself will be blameworthy.

For our Lord, the true and good Shepherd, who laid down his life for his sheep (John 10:11) and who came to save human lives, not to destroy them (Luke 9:56), wishes us to imitate his mercy, so that justice may restrain sinners but mercy may not reject those who have turned back.

True faith is defended most fruitfully when false opinion is condemned even by its own followers.

To carry out the entire case piously and faithfully, we have sent in our place our brothers Julian, bishop, and Renatus, presbyter of the title of Saint Clement, together with my son Hilary, deacon. We have associated with them our notary Dulcitius, whose faithfulness has often been tested by us, trusting in the future help of the Divinity, so that the one who had gone astray may be saved after condemning the perversity of his own understanding.

May God keep you safe, dearest brother.

Given on the Ides of June, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Asterius and Protogenes, in the year 486 of the era.

## III. Letter of Matthaeus Phaellus, Provost of the Cathedral Church of Imola, Transcribed from a Tablet in His Own Hand, in Which He Testifies That He Touched the Body of the Blessed Peter Chrysologus

**Matthaeus Phaellus, provost, sends greetings to the city of Cornelia.**

I congratulate you, and I rejoice for myself, Cornelia, my mother, that by digging here I have discovered so great a pledge—namely, the body of our fellow citizen Chrysologus—which you, perhaps doubting, once hesitated to believe lay hidden here.

Therefore I, Matthaeus Phaellus, provost, though unworthy, of this church, fully and faithfully confess that I touched with my own hands the body, honorably buried in the four hundred and fifty-fifth year [etc.], and that I faithfully placed it in this sarcophagus beside the Reverend Father and Lord, Master Simon, bishop of Imola, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1497, on the twenty-ninth day of August, or Sextilis, while the most merciful Father, Lord Alexander VI, supreme pontiff, was seated, and the most illustrious Lady Caterina Sforza and her distinguished firstborn, Lord Octavian Visconti de Riario, were governing Imola and Forlì as vicars of the Holy Roman Church.

Let us therefore pray, people of Cornelia, with the greatest devotion to that supreme, mighty, and all-powerful God, that the true Shepherd may not abandon his flock of Imola, but, through the merits of all the saints whom the people of our city humbly venerate, may protect us from the storm of wars, preserve us from raging famine, and deign to keep us unharmed from dreadful plague—he who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

Therefore I pray, O bishop, as I now lay your shrine to rest:

Be gracious to me, and gracious to your people.

## IV. Eulogy of the Life of the Distinguished Teacher Peter Chrysologus, from John Trithemius, a Most Religious Man and Abbot of Sponheim, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*

Peter, archbishop of Ravenna, was an educated and most holy man, distinguished in life by many miracles. In delivering homilies to the people, he possessed outstanding talent, and he converted many to the path of truth both by word and by example.

He wrote many works for the edification of the faithful, among which are said to be:

- *Sermons and Many Homilies*, book I;
- *Letter to Eutyches*, beginning: “I read your sorrowful letter with sorrow.”

He also wrote other letters. He flourished under Emperor Marcian.

## V. Dedicatory Letter of the Reverend Father Agapitus of Vicenza, Canon of the Lateran Order and Rector, to His Eminence Cardinal Hercules Gonzaga, Printed before the Sermons of Chrysologus, First Published through His Efforts at Bologna in the Year of Our Lord 1534
Upon receiving a very large number of sermons by the most holy and equally eloquent man Peter Chrysologus, archbishop of Ravenna—sermons certainly far more precious than every kind of gold and the most precious gems—I should rightly be judged guilty of avarice if I either allowed such illustrious works to remain shrouded in darkness any longer, or calmly tolerated our people being deprived and bereft, not without great inconvenience and loss to them, of monuments of such outstanding genius. This is especially so since, as a certain wise man says, hidden wisdom brings no more benefit to the human race than buried gems or an unwillingly hidden and buried treasure.

Therefore, so far as lies within my power, I have now decided to publish these sermons of Chrysologus, so that I may benefit not only myself but others as well; for in them one encounters nothing that is not learned, excellent, and complete. Such is this man’s knowledge of all divine and human matters, and so extraordinary—almost divine—is the power of his speech, together with such abundance, that I think no one could admire him sufficiently when he sees him pouring forth that golden river of eloquence.

For whether he attempts to explain the hidden and obscure meanings of the divine oracles, who is more subtle than this man? Whether he wishes to give an account of heavenly and saving doctrine, who is more learned than he? Or whether he desires to exhort to virtue, who is more ardent? Or strives to recall people from vices, who is more forceful? Finally, whether he seeks to raise illustrious men to heaven with his praises, who is more dignified? Or attacks the wicked, who is more vehement?

Hence Chrysologus was not without reason both regarded and called “Chrysologus” by our people. Yet it is incredible to say how much labor I undertook in thoroughly purifying, or rather restoring, these sermons. The manuscript that we first obtained had been so defaced by a kind of rust produced by the ignorance of later centuries, and was so mutilated, that scarcely any part of it could be found whole and uncorrupted.

Nevertheless, insofar as we were able to achieve anything by comparing ancient copies, we endeavored to provide assistance and support. Thus, unless my judgment deceives me, it has come about that the writings of this most eloquent man have now been restored to a reasonably good measure of their former brilliance, apart from certain exceptions.

The remaining material is omitted, since it is irrelevant to the matter at hand.

## VI. Preface of Blessed Felix, the forty-first archbishop of Ravenna, to several sermons of Saint Peter Chrysologus

From manuscript copies of Chrysologus’s sermons at Vallicella, Cesena, and elsewhere.

When the divine gifts of grace, brought forth from the heavenly treasury, have abundantly filled religious hearts with the rich mysteries of virtues, they distribute the sweetness of the Holy Spirit through fragrant discourse, so that these gifts may both be displayed in manifest praises and serve as adornments of salvation, in accordance with the Lord’s utterance resounding in the sacred pages of the Gospel: “Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John 7:38). And again: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Psalm 80). Solomon likewise says: “The Spirit will give wisdom to those who seek him”; and, “He made the tongues of teachers eloquent” (Proverbs 2; Wisdom 11).

For this reason, the venerable and blessed bishop Peter, the radiant glory of the Church of Ravenna and the foremost teacher of catholic truth, inflamed by the warmth of heavenly love and watered by the irrigation of unfailing grace, filled everyone’s ears and hearts with delightful sweetness. With fitting eloquence, he composed in polished language little works of flourishing discourses on the individual parables of the Gospels.

Therefore, beloved ones, let us read with attentive and anxious minds the writings of so great a shepherd, and embrace them with ardent desire in our spiritual arms, so that, storing the fruit of his labor in the granary of our minds, we may together with him enjoy the glory of magnificent praise and receive the rewards of an eternal gift.

This humble bishop Felix has offered this gift to his readers in a brief discourse from the poor little storehouse of his heart. The end.

## VII. Letter of R. P. F. Peter Rodulphus of Tussignano to the senators of Imola

Recorded in the commentaries of that Senate in the year of the Lord 1595.

To the illustrious and noble men, the lords Gonfalonier, Conservators, and Senate of Imola: Brother Peter Rodulphus of Tussignano, bishop and count of Senigallia, sends greetings and wishes for happiness.

I have heard that you are now considering a truly pious and salutary undertaking, and one entirely worthy of your persons: to restore to the light the illustrious monuments of the genius of the most blessed Peter Chrysologus, formerly our fellow citizen. This proposal is not merely highly agreeable to me, since I see you thereby repaying, according to your ability, a fitting debt of gratitude both to a citizen who has deserved well of his native city—or rather of the whole Christian commonwealth—and to all students of sacred literature; it also prompts me all the more strongly to encourage you to press forward and complete your holy undertaking quickly.

For it is universally acknowledged that, whether through the negligence of unlearned people and the passage of time, through the injury inflicted by copyists, or perhaps through the envy of certain persons, his most learned and holy writings have in part been obscured and in part lost. Those that remain have been so corrupted and defiled, as though after a shipwreck, that they can scarcely be read; some are so confused and entangled that they can scarcely be understood.

Moreover, in order to repay, as it were, the debt of gratitude that I owe to our common homeland and to your beneficence, and to perform a pleasing service for Chrysologus himself, I thought I should not be acting improperly if I assisted your plan by some labor and industry of my own.

I have found that no greater assistance could be offered by me than to correct and emend this author’s homilies insofar as possible, so that they may be rescued from all the injury they have hitherto suffered amid dirt and moths. Thus no one will henceforth shrink from reading them—readings in which, because of the author’s golden eloquence, from which he received his surname, outstanding and eminent men formerly took the greatest delight.

I have also written a life of this most holy man with as much brevity and care as I could. For this purpose I examined ancient and very old archives, insofar as I was able to obtain materials from the Vatican Library and the most extensive Serletan Library. By comparing the most faithful and ancient manuscripts, I worked as diligently as possible to correct and heal this book of the sermons of Blessed Peter Chrysologus and nearly restore it to its original purity.

Finally, omitting no kind of duty or piety, I did not rest until I had added certain scholia and many observations by which both the reasoning behind our emendations is supplied and the more difficult passages are explained with the greatest ease.

Accept, then, with cheerful countenance this entire labor—gladly dedicated to you, most illustrious men, and consecrated as an expression of gratitude. If it meets with your approval, publish it; and farewell, remembering me.

Senigallia, the day before the Ides of March, 1594.

## Schoenemann’s account indicating the place, time, and form of all editions of Saint Peter Chrysologus

After so much has already been said about the life and works of Blessed Peter Chrysologus, the following account of editions of the writings of the holy Father will perhaps not be unwelcome to the reader; the name and age of the author promise that it will be both exceptional and comprehensive. **Editor.**

It has been stated that the collection of Peter Chrysologus’s sermons that we have just described is the oldest of all, since it was compiled and provided with a prologue by Felix of Ravenna, himself the forty-first bishop, at the beginning of the eighth century. He held the episcopal see from approximately 707 to 717. This prologue is found prefixed not only to the sermons in manuscript copies, but was also copied from there and added to the Life of Peter written by Dominicus Mita.

[Note: Casimir Oudinus likewise included it in his Commentaries, volume I, p. 1251.]

After more than eight hundred years, Agapitus Vicentinus was the first to rescue this collection from neglect and had it printed at Bologna by Joannes Baptista Phaellus from a single manuscript. It was subsequently reprinted at Cologne in 1541 and 1618; at Paris in 1574, 1585, 1612, 1614, 1618, 1631, and 1633; at Antwerp in 1577; at Venice in 1588 and 1636; at Mainz in 1607 and 1613; and at Lyon in 1622, 1623, 1627, 1634, and 1636. Yet it contracted many stains and faults from the negligence of printing houses everywhere.

Peter Rodulphus of Tussignano, formerly bishop of Senigallia, had prepared a new recension based on certain manuscripts found at Rome, and in 1594 had offered it to the Senate of Imola for publication, furnished with his own scholia. His letter was indeed entered in the Senate’s records, but what became of this manuscript is unknown.

[Note: Dominicus Mita presents this letter in the appendix of documents to the Life of Peter Chrysologus. Rodulphus indicates that he had heard that the Senate of Imola had resolved to restore to the light the splendid monuments of the genius of its fellow citizen. He says that he wished to assist this undertaking through his own labor and industry as far as he could. “I have found,” he says, “that no greater assistance can be offered by me than to correct and emend this author’s homilies insofar as possible, so that they may be rescued from all the injury they have hitherto suffered amid dirt and moths; thus no one will henceforth shrink from reading them . . . I have also written a life of this most holy man with as much brevity and care as I could. For this purpose I examined ancient and very old archives, insofar as I was able to obtain materials from the Vatican Library or the most extensive Serletan Library. By applying the most faithful comparison of ancient manuscripts, I worked as diligently as possible to correct and heal this book of Peter Chrysologus’s sermons and nearly restore it to its original purity. Finally, omitting no kind of duty or piety, I did not rest until I had added certain scholia by which both the reasoning behind our emendations is supplied and the more difficult passages are explained with the greatest ease. Accept this entire labor, gladly dedicated to you and consecrated as an expression of gratitude, with cheerful countenance; and, if it meets with your approval, publish it, and farewell, remembering me.”]

Nevertheless, Dominicus Mita completed the plan for a new edition and published at Bologna in 1643, in quarto, a text revised against ancient manuscripts and elucidated by his own, not especially learned, scholia. But the benefit of this edition did not reach the French and Germans, who continued to copy older exemplars repeatedly, although there were some who desired better ones. For there were people who took pleasure in Chrysologus’s diction and admired in him a certain sharpness of thought.

It is also reported that a learned Swede, Zacharias Lundius, composed commentaries on variant readings and observations concerning Chrysologus. They were never published, but in the time of Joannes Albertus Fabricius they were preserved in manuscript at Copenhagen in the collection of Rostgaard.

[Note: Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Mediae et Infimae Latinitatis*.]

In Italy itself, however, Mita’s edition was not reprinted from Venetian types until almost a full century later, in 1740. Sebastian Pauli, a priest of the Congregation of the Mother of God of Lucca, then undertook the preparation of a new edition. His varied learning led people to expect no ordinary results from him. The work appeared at Venice in 1750, highly praised by Mansi, whom no one will deny ought to be regarded as a fair judge in this matter, although in certain matters reported by him concerning the edition one may regret the absence of proper editorial diligence.

It is commonly said that there are two editions of the letter to Eutyches: one in the earlier Quesnellian editions of the works of Saint Leo the Great, in which the whole of the second chapter after the words “I have briefly replied, brother, to your letters” is missing; and another complete edition, first published by Gerard Vossius in 1604. In this matter, Quesnellus seems all the more deserving of confidence because he adds that the former was copied from a manuscript of the Thuane Library. The Ballerini brothers likewise followed him in good faith.

Nevertheless, these statements are false. There is no edition of Leo the Great before Quesnellus in which this letter occurs. Experience has taught us this, and the indexes representing the order of the letters in the earlier editions, as well as in the Quesnellian edition and that of the Ballerini brothers, prevent us from believing that we ourselves have been deceived.

[Note: No one should suppose that Quesnellus confused editions of Leo’s works with editions in which the works of Peter Chrysologus were published together with those of Leo the Great. We note that even in the latter editions, wherever the letter is represented, a complete copy of it is not lacking.]

Nor is the other statement made by Quesnellus any more accurate: namely, that the complete letter first appeared only in Gerard Vossius’s edition. It had in fact been read in complete Latin form long before that in the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon, which Vossius himself cites.

It should rather be said that in certain manuscript copies, whose sources the Ballerini brothers identified, this letter is found in a form half as long and lacking the second chapter from the words quoted above; but the more reliable text of the editors derives from the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon.

## Sixteenth century

### 1534

Bologna, from the printing house of Joannes Baptista Phaellus; quarto.

*The Sermons of Saint Peter Chrysologus* . . . .

The editor, Father Agapitus Vicentinus, rector of the Lateran Canons Regular, dedicated these sermons to Cardinal Hercules Gonzaga, and prefaced his editorial work as follows:

“Upon receiving a very large number of sermons by the most holy and equally eloquent man Peter Chrysologus, bishop of Ravenna—sermons certainly more precious than every kind of gold and gems—I should rightly be judged guilty of avarice if I either allowed such illustrious works to remain shrouded in darkness any longer, or calmly tolerated our people being deprived and bereft, not without great inconvenience and loss to them, of monuments of such outstanding genius . . . Yet it is incredible to say how much labor I undertook in thoroughly purifying, or rather restoring, these sermons. The manuscript that we first obtained had been so defaced by a kind of rust produced by the ignorance of later centuries, and was so mutilated, that scarcely any part of it could be found whole and uncorrupted. Nevertheless, insofar as we were able to achieve anything by comparing ancient copies, we endeavored to provide assistance and support. Thus, unless my judgment deceives me, it has come about that the writings of this most eloquent man have now been restored to a reasonably good measure of their former brilliance, apart from certain exceptions.”

This edition is noted as exceedingly rare in the catalogues of the Barberiniana and Pinelliana Libraries.

### 1538

Cologne, at the house of Peter Quentel; folio.

The complete letter of Peter, bishop of Ravenna, to Eutyches the abbot, in the preliminary materials to the Council of Chalcedon, in Peter Crabbe’s edition of the Councils, volume I, folio 394.

### 1541

Cologne; folio.

*The Sermons of Saint Peter Chrysologus* . . . .

Dominicus Mita also mentions this edition, as does Joannes Albertus Fabricius after him in his *Bibliotheca Mediae et Infimae Latinitatis*, where he supplied the format of the volume.

It is recorded in the catalogue of the Bodleian Library without indication of the volume’s format.

### 1544

Paris; octavo.

*The Sermons of Saint Peter Chrysologus* . . . .

Fabricius mentions this description in his work and adds that in the *Rudolphine Autographs*, volume I, p. 467, it is improperly marketed as the first edition. In the Bodleian Library catalogue there is, however, an edition printed at Paris in 1545, octavo; whether it is the same or a different one, I do not know.

### 1574

Paris, at the house of Hieronymus de Marnef; octavo.

*The Sermons of Saint Peter Chrysologus.*

Latinus Latinius wrote his emendations into this edition. Fabricius reports that it was printed in octavo. Dominicus Mita praises a Parisian edition of 1575.

### 1577

Antwerp . . . .

*The Sermons of Peter Chrysologus.*

Mita praises it in his preface.

### 1579

Cologne, at the house of Joannes Carolus Munnich; quarto.

An edition of the sermons of Peter Chrysologus and Maximus of Turin which bears this year on its title page because of a printer’s error must be assigned to the following century.

### 1585

Paris, at the house of Hieronymus de Marnef; octavo.

*The Work of Homilies of the Lord Peter Chrysologus, Archbishop of Ravenna, Now Published for the First Time* (so the title reads).

### 1588

Venice.

*The Sermons of Peter Chrysologus.*

According to Mita.

## Seventeenth century

### 1604

Mainz, at the house of Balthasar Lippius, at the expense of Antonius Hierat; quarto.

*The Letter of Peter of Ravenna, or Chrysologus, against Eutyches, in Greek and Latin, with the Notes of Gerard Vossius, Doctor and Provost of Tongeren*, in *Miscellanies of Several Previously Unpublished Greek and Latin Holy Fathers*, with the works of Gregory Thaumaturgus added, pp. 205–208.

The Greek text was published from the manuscript of Cardinal Sirleto; the Latin text from Vatican manuscripts numbered 2574, 2576, and 2580. In the first two of these, only the first part of the letter was present.

### 1606

Cologne, at the expense of Joannes Gymnicus and Antonius Hierat; folio.

The Latin letter of Peter of Ravenna to Eutyches, in Severinus Binius’s *Councils*, volume II, from the beginning, among the preliminary letters to the ecumenical Council of Chalcedon.

### 1607

Mainz; octavo.

*The Sermons of Saint Peter Chrysologus.*

Christian Daumius praises this edition, known to him through personal use.

### 1609

Rome, from the Vatican printing house; folio.

The letter of Peter of Ravenna to Eutyches, Greek and Latin, in *The General Councils of the Catholic Church*, volume II, p. 22.

Catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris. The copy in the Royal Library has throughout been supplied with emendations from a manuscript through the efforts of T. Mantellus.

### 1643

Bologna, through Nicolaus du Solié; quarto.

*The Sacred Homilies, or Golden Sermons, of the Lord Peter Chrysologus of Forocornelius, Archbishop of Ravenna, Revised, Corrected, and for the Most Part Illustrated [by Various Readings, Scholia, and Observations], through the Work and Study of Dominicus Mita.*

Catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris.

We have at hand a Venetian copy that seems to have been reproduced from the Bolognese edition with considerable accuracy. From it we learn that Dominicus Mita, a priest and parish rector of Ugutionellus, formerly occupied with the study of law and forensic affairs, was a moderately learned man who had long been troubled by the desire for a more accurate text of Chrysologus. At length, after obtaining access to several manuscript copies, he was moved to devote his services to purifying and illustrating it.

“By investigating further,” he says, “I learned that four manuscript copies of this work still existed: two at Rome, differing little from the printed copies; one at Urbino in the Roveriana Library; and another at Cesena in the Franciscan Library. The latter two agree with one another in almost everything, but differ from the commonly printed copies in very many places.

“Thus, as soon as access to the manuscripts was scarcely opened to me, I went through them, partly through friends and partly in person. With the assistance of a companion, I compared them once, from beginning to end, with the copy first printed at Bologna, and corrected in ink every error I could. I also wrote various and useful readings in the margin, rejecting the corrupt readings with which the manuscripts abound. If anything in them could not be completely corrected, I tried to supply it by reflection; although this was rarely done, since this method, obstructed by the greatest difficulties, is slippery and deceptive.”

He added scholia that would at least benefit the unlearned or stimulate the minds of the learned to investigate more excellent matters. Some are moral; others explain the sense more fully than was generally necessary. He rarely descends to dogmas or historical matters, and when he does, he usually labels the material “Scholia and Notes,” or “Observations.” He very rarely discusses the variation or correction of readings.

He also prepared two indexes: one alphabetical index of the sermons, in which, however, the individual sermons themselves are not so much listed as the principal subjects treated in each sermon; the other of notable things and words. He omitted as superfluous the list of the Gospels read in the sacred services according to the season, which was generally added in earlier editions for the use of preachers.

Finally, he added a Life of Peter Chrysologus, carefully sought out from his homilies and from various monuments of writers, both printed and manuscript, diligently collected and arranged in order. For further testimony, as he says, to certain matters mentioned in it, he appended the following documents:

1. The letter of Saint Peter Chrysologus to the heretic Eutyches.
2. The letter of Pope Leo I to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, against the perfidy and heresy of Eutyches.
3. The letter of Matthew, provost of the cathedral church of Imola, transcribed from a tablet in his own hand, in which he testifies that he had touched the body of Blessed Peter Chrysologus.
4. The eulogy from Trithemius.
5. The preface of Agapitus Vicentinus to the Bolognese edition.
6. The preface of Blessed Felix, the forty-first archbishop of Ravenna, to several sermons of Saint Peter Chrysologus, from manuscript copies at Vallicella, Cesena, and elsewhere.
7. The letter of Brother Peter Rodulphus of Tussignano, bishop of Senigallia, to the senators of Imola, in which he offered them the sermons of Peter Chrysologus that he had revised, taken from the records of that Senate in 1595.

“This work,” he says, “thus prepared, induced me to give it the title *Sermons Illustrated for the Most Part*, since their text, and the index to the Life, having been brought out of darkness and freed from filth, have been made more clearly accessible and intelligible to readers than before. Moreover, in brilliance and splendor it surpasses by far all copies through this labor.

“In accomplishing this, what expenses, labors, and dangers I underwent; how often I lay prostrate, overcome by very poor health; and what adversaries and deserters I endured at home and abroad—the holy Chrysologus himself knows, since he at last protected me from heaven. Many learned and approved Fathers know this as well: they marvel that, even while I was living among the forests, far from the company of the wise, concerned with the care of souls, deprived of books and good health, I overcame almost every adversity and finally completed part of the work I had undertaken. It would still lie hidden in darkness if I had not been compelled by their sincere judgment to publish it.”

Finally, he adds a necessary and genuinely witty defense of his style. He says that, following Seneca’s advice, in composing this work he had sought above all to determine what he should write; and because, when reporting the opinions of others, he had considered it necessary to transcribe them in his own words, it had inevitably followed that a style composed of many styles and drawn from many authors could not always remain uniform.

“If, nevertheless, many things have slipped in, whether in composition or transcription, that have been placed carelessly or less appropriately, readers should regard this as having happened by God’s permission, so that at last ‘the nations may know that they are but human’” (according to Psalm 9).

He dedicated his edition to Ferdinand Millinus, bishop of the Imolan Church and count of Bagni. It was dated from the sacred building of the parish church of Saint Agnes at Ugutionellus, five days before the Kalends of April of the present year.

### 1644

Paris, from the Royal Printing House; folio.

The letter of Peter of Ravenna to Eutyches, Greek and Latin, in the Royal Collection of Councils, volume VIII, p. 41.

### 1661

Paris, at the house of Simeon Piget; folio.

*The Works of Saint Peter Chrysologus* . . . , in Theophilus Raynaudus’s *Heptad*, reprinted in the same year and place.

### 1662

Paris, at the expense of Antonius Bertier; folio.

*Various Sermons of Saint Peter Chrysologus Arranged According to the Gospels, Sundays, and Feasts of the Entire Year*, in François Combefis’s *Preaching Library of the Fathers*.

Combefis follows Dominicus Mita and in most matters also agrees with him concerning Peter’s life. He does not, however, reject the opinion that not all the sermons in this collection belong to one and the same author, although he infers this not so much from arguments drawn from the individual sermons as from the fact that the same practice is customary in the case of other writers of homilies, such as Chrysostom, Bernard, and others.

### 1666

Paris, at the house of Charles Savreux; quarto.

Five sermons of Saint Peter Chrysologus on the Lord’s Prayer, under the title *Saint Peter Damian, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church*, in volume VII of Luke d’Achery’s *Old Spicilegium of Several Writers Who Had Remained Hidden Especially in the Benedictine Libraries of France*, pp. 120–137.

What often happens to the authors of such collections, including the highly learned Baluze, also happened to D’Achery in the case of these sermons: while undertaking the great labor of publishing the works of a single author, they sometimes failed either in memory or diligence and presented works long published as though they were unpublished. These sermons, which are found in the Felician collection under numbers 67, 68, 70, 71, and 72—and indeed in more accurate form than they are represented here from a Corbie manuscript—were treated in this way by D’Achery.

When he was informed of the matter, he wrote the following after the table of contents in volume VII:

“To my assigning five sermons on the Lord’s Prayer to Peter Damian in volume VII of the *Spicilegium*, I was persuaded by a manuscript written four hundred years ago which clearly bore the name of Peter Damian. But after that volume had appeared, our most learned theologian Stephen de Marcés informed me by letter that these sermons are genuinely those of Peter of Ravenna, or Chrysologus, for various and by no means contemptible reasons. I gladly add my own judgment to his. I leave the decision, however, to the learned.”

So far D’Achery. He did not set out the reasons that the learned theologian had supplied, although none could have been more decisive than the fact that these sermons had long existed in the very ancient collection of Chrysologus’s sermons—certainly older than Peter Damian—and had been printed with it. Perhaps D’Achery was embarrassed to admit this.

Nevertheless, in the general index appended to volume XIII of the *Spicilegium*, he identified them as belonging to Peter Chrysologus. Their heading also bears Chrysologus’s name in the second edition of the work, although its editor, Louis-François-Joseph de la Barre, was completely unaware on what grounds the later attribution ought to be preferred to the earlier one.

Rather, de la Barre reproached D’Achery for not publishing the reasons that had led him to place less confidence in his manuscript, and added that if anyone argued that D’Achery had set a bad example, he would not oppose the claim.

If he had examined any published edition of Chrysologus’s sermons, he would not only have easily discovered those reasons for himself, but would also have spared himself many of the emendations he presented there—emendations by no means foolish, but less necessary, since for the most part they are all already clearly found in the older editions of Chrysologus.

[Note: “These homilies,” says de la Barre in the first note to Sermon II, “are filled with as many errors as even the most perceptive person could not remove by conjecture alone. Accordingly, I would not have the reader expect anything here unless it has been entirely corrected. We have restored quite a few passages that were badly corrupt, but we did not even consider restoring every one of them, since some cannot be corrected without the aid of a manuscript. Yet sometimes his corrections in the most corrupt passages agree so closely with the printed copies of Chrysologus that one might wonder whether a human being could have attained so much by conjecture alone. Indeed, he detected the true reading not merely once, but almost everywhere.”]

The example of D’Achery and de la Barre misled others, such as Fabricius and Mansi, and even the latest editor, to such an extent that he arranged for these five sermons to be added to the others.

### 1670

Zwickau, printed and published at the expense of Samuel Ebel; octavo.

Sermons CXLI and CXLIX of the Lord Peter Chrysologus on the Incarnation of Christ, and Sermons CLII and CLIII on the Massacre of the Infants, in *Homilies of the Holy Fathers Published for the Feast of the Nativity of Jesus Christ* by Christian Daumius, pp. 81–91.

They were reproduced from the Mainz edition of 1607, the Lyon edition of 1623, and the copy contained in the Cologne *Bibliotheca Patrum*. Yet Mita’s edition seems not to have been known to Daumius, since in his preface he wrote that those editions required a new recension and the same demand for variant readings that can be observed from what Thomas of Ireland, and after him the Collector of Allegories, transferred into their collections.

In the same place he also reports Caspar Barth’s praises of Chrysologus.

### 1671

Paris, at the expense of the Typographical Society; folio.

The letter of Peter of Ravenna to Eutyches, Greek and Latin, in the Councils of Labbe and Cossart, volume IV, p. 35.

### 1671

Paris, at the expense of Peter Variquet; folio.

*The 176 Sermons of Peter Chrysologus*, together with the collected works of Leo the Great and others, edited by Raynaudus.

### 1672

Paris, at the house of the widow of Charles Savreux; quarto.

Peter Chrysologus’s sermon on the Nativity of the Lord against Nestorius, published by Luke D’Achery from an ancient manuscript as the work of an uncertain author, in volume XI, pp. 279–281.

He had received it from Chifflet. In the commonly printed editions it exists in a fuller and more accurate form as Sermon CXLV. Paul Colomesius was the first to point this out, in *Paralipomena on the Holy Churches*, p. 263, and in *Sacred Observations*, p. 133. Compare Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Mediae et Infimae Latinitatis*. The latest editor therefore certainly ought not to have overlooked it.

### 1675

Paris, at the expense of Joannes Baptista Coignard; quarto.

The letter of Peter Chrysologus, bishop of Ravenna, to the presbyter Eutyches, in Latin with the notes of Paschasius Quesnellus; together with the works of Leo the Great, after Letter 22, volume I, p. 477. The notes appear in volume II, pp. 839–841; in the Lyon edition of 1700, folio, volume I, pp. 241–242, and volume II, pp. 456–458.

“Regarding this letter,” says Quesnellus, “I find three editions: one contained in the later editions of Saint Leo, where the letter is read as having been copied from a manuscript of the Thuane Library; another procured by Gerard Vossius, Doctor of the Catholic Church, from the Vatican manuscripts numbered 2574 and 2580 and from those of Cardinal Sirleto; and finally a third, which is found in the first part of the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon together with the Greek version.

“The first edition contains only the first chapter and lacks the entire second; the other two contain both chapters.

[Note: Consequently, there ought to have been counted not three editions but only two, as Fabricius and the Ballerini brothers more correctly did.]

“I cannot confidently assert where this difference originated. Nevertheless, it is plausible either that the editor encountered a mutilated manuscript or that the manuscript itself was mutilated by the editor.”

He then investigates what the causes of this mutilation might have been, and whether the complete form can also be regarded as the genuine work of the bishop of Ravenna. He affirms that it can, and continues:

“Accordingly, I cannot determine how it came about that the letter is found shortened in the commonly printed editions of Saint Leo. They mention a Thuan manuscript from which it was taken by the editor. Whether this is so, I do not know.

“What I do know is that I found in the catalogue of the Thuan manuscripts a single manuscript containing the letter of Saint Peter Chrysologus, together with several others relating to the Council of Chalcedon; in this manuscript the letter is complete.

“If you add to it the Vatican manuscripts, the manuscripts of Cardinal Sirleto, and the ancient and recent editions of Baronius and the Councils, scarcely any room for doubt remains that the abbreviation of the letter must be attributed either to the bad faith—or at least the carelessness—of that editor, or to a defect in the manuscript.”

Would that Quesnellus had chosen to identify the folio or page of the editions of Leo the Great in which Peter’s letter appears, which he so explicitly indicates that he himself had read.

### 1676

Lyon, at the expense of the Brothers Anisson and Joan Poysnel; folio. *The Golden Sermons of the divine Peter Chrysologus, archbishop of Ravenna, corrected according to the exemplar of the Seraphic Library of Cesena, enriched with scholia and commentaries of the greatest abundance and variety of moral concepts. Now newly issued for the benefit of preachers of the divine word, with the Life of the Most Holy Doctor added, as well as his Epistle to Eutyches, likewise elucidated with notes, through the work and labor of the Reverend Father Brother MARTIN DEL CASTILLO of Burgos, Franciscan Friar of the Observance, emeritus lecturer in the Mexican Province of the Holy Gospel, Master of Theology decorated by a rescript of Alexander VII, formerly Provincial Minister in the same Province, and Rector and Regent of Studies in the great College of St. Bonaventure.* To these was added a fourfold index: I, of the Sermons; II, of passages of Sacred Scripture; III, of the Gospels for the sermons throughout the year; IV, finally, of notable matters.

This attractive craftsman filled nine and somewhat more alphabets with his commentaries on twenty-two sermons of Chrysologus and on the Epistle to Eutyches. He has this in common with the preceding editor, Dominicus Mita: although he trails behind his name a huge train of titles, he nevertheless complains of the injustice of Fortune and found the goddess Eloquence no more favorable. “I resolved in my heart,” he says, “to illustrate all 176 Sermons of St. Peter Chrysologus with my commentaries. For this reason, after completing in brief a marginal scholium on all of them, I applied myself to drawing out and examining his most subtle meaning. I began, in more expansive language—for, as the younger Pliny used to say, there is no danger that what ought to be very great will be too great—and I have completed and present twenty-two sermons together with his epistle to the heretic Eutyches. But alas! Ophthalmia tormented my eyes at excessive length; and, what is more, for nine and more years Fortune looked upon me, bleary-eyed, with narrowed eyes, withdrawing enviously from labor the man who desired to labor at his appointed task. Many times I repeated with Diogenes the Cynic: ‘Well done, Fortune, that you have treated me manfully!’ God, the Great and Good, made me—a sinner, a criminal—happy through scourges; he always kept me as my own copyist, with no amanuensis anywhere, deprived of a library and almost an exile from my cell.”

He also testifies that he sought more what he should write than how he should write it; that he did not concern himself with an elaborate, polished, and refined style, but wished to speak more loosely, so that he might speak more securely. The one work which you may judge not wholly inept is the *Life of Peter Chrysologus*, in which he also touches upon his writings and editions. The epistle is dedicated to Pietro, Prince of Portocarero Folch de Arragon y Corduba, etc., and shines with all the lights of its author’s intellect.

### 1677

Rome, at the expense of Pontius Bernardon; folio. *Various Readings and Observations on Peter Chrysologus by Latinius Latinius of Viterbo*, in his *Sacred and Profane Library*, vol. I, pp. 98–103.

These observations, which require no other recommendation than the author’s name, belong to the preceding century. Latinius died in 1593. He used the Paris edition of 1574.

[Col. 0088C] 1677. Lyon, at the Anisson press; folio. *The 176 Sermons of St. Peter Chrysologus and the Epistle to Eutyches, with notes by Gerard Vossius*, in the *Maxima Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. VII, pp. 803–979.

### 1679

Cologne, at the press of Johann Carolus Munich and Petrus Ketteler; quarto. *The distinguished Sermons on the Gospels for Sundays and certain more solemn feasts of the whole year, by the most learned and holy man Peter Chrysologus, archbishop of Ravenna, published with a triple index of the Gospels and Epistles, passages of Sacred Scripture, and subjects and words.* (The Sermons of Maximus of Turin were also added.) First edition in Germany (so it says).

Through the printer’s carelessness, the year printed in the title is MDLXXIX [1579]. Although both the type and the whole description sufficiently betrayed the century, I nevertheless did not dare decide the matter on my own authority before it was established for me from another source. But I am now certain, and I wish readers to be warned, that they should transfer the edition of Maximus of Turin dated 1579 to the following century. In the *Catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris*, this edition is listed as belonging to the year 1678.

### 1684

Paris, at the press of François Muguet; folio. Two sermons of Peter Chrysologus: one on peace, on the words of Matthew 5, “Blessed are the peacemakers,” etc. (LIII); the other on the Nativity of John the Baptist; among the Augustinian sermons which the Benedictines separated into the Appendix of volume V, class 1, no. 61, and class 3, no. CXCIX.

The former was once numbered CLXIX among the *Sermons on Time*, and afterward Appendix LVII; the latter was numbered XXII among the *Sermons on the Saints*, and afterward Appendix LXXVII. But the former has everywhere been interpolated and enlarged by many sentences, which the Maurists accordingly marked with little brackets; the latter has been abridged from the beginning. There was therefore a reason why the most recent editor should add both to his edition, as we learn from Mansius. Two others also occur among the Augustinian sermons: namely, no. CXXI, *On the Nativity of the Lord V*, which they note as bearing the name of Peter of Ravenna in certain manuscripts; and Sermon XCVII, *On the Words of the Gospel of John 14, “My peace I give you,”* etc., which the same scholars point out as agreeing in style with Sermon LXI of Chrysologus.

## EIGHTEENTH CENTURY

### 1714

Paris, from the Royal Press; folio. *The Epistle of Peter of Ravenna to Eutyches*, in Hardouin’s *Councils*, vol. II, p. 22.

### 1723

Paris, at the press of Montalant; folio. *Peter Chrysologus’s Sermon on the Nativity of the Lord and Five Sermons on the Lord’s Prayer*, in the new edition of Luc d’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, edited by Louis-François-Joseph de La Barre, vol. I, pp. 41, 215–221.

See what was said in connection with the first editions of 1666 and 1672.

### 1742

Venice, at the press of Augustinus Savioli; folio. *The Complete Works of St. Peter Chrysologus of Forum Cornelii, Archbishop of Ravenna, with the Observations and Most Complete Index of Subjects by Dominicus Mita.* In addition, this edition of ours included all the extant homilies of St. Valerian, bishop of Cemele.

The edition of the Bolognese bookseller of 1643 was accurately reprinted and furnished not merely with respectable, but even magnificent, embellishment.

### 1750

Venice …; folio. *The Complete Works of St. Peter Chrysologus, revised from manuscript codices by Father Sebastian Pauli, cleric of the Congregation of the Mother of God of Lucca.*

This edition is known only from what the distinguished Mansius reported in volume V, p. 253, of his *Fabrician Library of Middle and Low Latin Literature*, in order to supplement the information about Chrysologus:

“There is no reason for me to pass over here the edition published in its own year of death by the distinguished Father Sebastian Pauli of the Congregation of the Mother of God of Lucca, my beloved colleague and, while he lived, especially dear friend. It appeared in Venetian type in 1750, volume I—which I take to mean a single volume—in folio. Besides what had become known in the preceding editions, he added seven sermons on the Lord’s Prayer, taken from volume VII, p. 120, of the old edition of D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*; he also added two others from the appendix of the Maurist edition of the Sermons of St. Augustine. He revised the entire work from ancient manuscript codices; he retained the notes formerly prepared by Dominicus Mita, to which he added his own—neither few nor, to speak honestly, unlearned. Although I approve this labor of the outstanding man, I nevertheless believe that the edition of Chrysologus’s Works is still far from being regarded as complete in every respect.

“The distinguished man warns that some of these discourses are attributed to a certain Severian in ancient codices. Instructed by this warning, and having found in an old homiliary codex discovered in the library of the canons of the Major Church of Lucca—one which, in my judgment, is not later than the twelfth century—certain homilies prefixed with the name of Severian, I undertook to compare one of them with the homily of Chrysologus numbered CII among the published works. I found the two to agree; at the same time, however, I recognized that there were certain gaps in the printed text which were admirably supplied by that codex.”

He gives there several examples of variant readings. But that warning—that some homilies are attributed to Severian in ancient codices—was not peculiar to this editor; it had long before been observed by Agapitus in the first Bolognese edition. Nor does the editor’s diligence receive much commendation from the fact that he had the same Five Sermons on the Lord’s Prayer copied out twice.

### 1753

Venice, at the press of Simon Occhi; folio. *The Epistle of Peter Chrysologus, bishop of Ravenna, to Eutyches the presbyter*, Greek and Latin, with a preface and notes by the Ballerini brothers; in the *Works of Leo the Great*, vol. I, epistle XXV, pp. 775–778.

The Ballerini brothers teach that the abridged epistle, of which Quesnellus first gave notice, derives from the Spanish Collection of Canons, and from it flowed into the Isidorian Collection and thence into the remaining collections. At the same time, they show that the fuller version has the stronger claim in both antiquity and authority, since it is found in the collection of letters concerning the case of Eutyches, which is customarily prefixed to the acts of the Council of Chalcedon and was compiled in Latin before the middle of the sixth century. They suspect, however, that the earlier part of the epistle, which the Spanish collection also transmits, is original, while the latter part was derived from the Greek.

### 1761

Florence, at the expense of Antonio Zatta of Venice; folio. *The Epistle of Peter of Ravenna to Eutyches*, Greek and Latin, with the preface and notes of the Ballerini brothers; in the *Most Complete Collection of the Councils*, vol. V, pp. 1347–1350.

# Dissertation of Joseph A. Amadesi on the Ecclesiastical Metropolis of Ravenna, addressed to the distinguished man Paul Paciaudi

## The Venetian Printer to the Reader

This edition had reached its final stage when this dissertation, sent from Ravenna to Venice through the diligence and care of the distinguished man Paul Maria Paciaudi, a Cleric Regular, came into my hands. I judged that adding it here as the crown of these prolegomena would be neither unwelcome to the editor nor disagreeable to readers. Farewell.

## Preface

When I was considering consigning to darkness and oblivion what I had discussed in previous days concerning the dignity of the Church of Ravenna, your convictions, excellent Paciaudi, recalled me from that decision. And although I long and greatly hesitated over whether it would be more expedient to resist your wishes or to obey them—for the former course was suggested by the danger of obedience, the latter by my respect and affection for you—nevertheless I preferred to entrust myself wholly to this danger, whatever it might be, so as to obey my respect and affection, rather than violate even in the slightest these duties by which I am bound to you in order to avoid the danger.

I repeatedly set before you the weakness of my intellect, my inexperience in writing on a critical subject, the difficulty of the matter itself under discussion, the authority of the most celebrated men who hold opinions against us, and the extreme scarcity of documents, arguments, and writings to which we are subject—all of which deterred me from this manner of writing. But since, setting these objections aside, you persisted in your purpose and drove me, wavering, with sails and oars into this sea, your wishes must be obeyed completely, and some specimen of our little works, whatever their ultimate quality, must be submitted to public judgment.

Thus, in our literary circle, we treated three questions concerning this Church of Ravenna. First, we asked whether it had been subordinate to the bishop of Milan during the first four centuries of the Christian era. Next, we defended against the charge of falsity the letters of Clement II, Roman pontiff, by which the prerogative of sitting in councils before the bishop of Milan was restored to the bishop of Ravenna. Then, after weighing the opinions of the sounder authorities, we investigated what should be thought concerning the origin of metropolitan dignity in the Church of Ravenna. We now judge that all those arguments which we had written with a fuller pen and in the vernacular, in several dissertations, should be reduced to three chapters and set forth in briefer language.

# CHAPTER I  
## Whether the Church of Ravenna was subject to the Church of Milan during the first four centuries of the Christian era

### § I. The arguments of authors affirming this are set forth

**1.** Eustachius of St. Ubaldo, an Augustinian Discalced friar, inserted toward the end of the previous century a sufficiently lengthy dissertation on the metropolitan Church of Milan. In it he attempted, by every kind of argument and monument—if Heaven so willed—to demonstrate that among the more illustrious Churches subject to the bishop of Milan as suffragans were also the Churches of Ravenna and Aquileia.

In establishing this opinion, however, our Augustinian had only one concern: to rely solely upon the traces and authority of Sirmond, Schelstratius, Norisius, and several others. For although he admitted that no ancient, positive, and unalterable document concerning the subjection of these Churches remained for him, and although he thought that the decrees of the Councils of Nicaea and Antioch strongly opposed the claim, the authority of such great men—experts in ecclesiastical antiquities—satisfied him in place of every ancient monument.

And rightly so, if our age valued the great names of authors rather than the arguments and foundations upon which their opinions rest.

**2.** Moreover, these equally celebrated critics, no less than their Milanese fellow-thinker, entirely lacked all the ancient, positive, and unalterable documents by which they could establish with certainty the subjection of the Churches of Ravenna and Aquileia. For neither councils of the first centuries, nor episcopal consecrations, nor visitations of Churches, nor sanctions, appeals, or consultations—which ordinarily serve as indications either of suffragan status, if I may so speak, in lesser Churches or of pre-eminence in the principal Churches—much less the testimonies of historians or Fathers, supplied them with any such document.

All therefore proceeded by the path of conjectures and arguments for the negative, a path certainly rough and full of difficulties. They devised this route for establishing the ecclesiastical hierarchy from the hierarchy of the empire. They readily attribute to the earliest times of the Churches just mentioned a metropolitan bishop for almost every province into which the empire was divided far and wide throughout Asia, Africa, and Europe: namely, those bishops who, established in the chief city of each province, would govern all the others in the lesser cities of the same province. Yet they deny this hierarchical order to Italy alone. Although, as they say, Italy was divided into seventeen provinces, they wish only two metropolitan bishops to have been assigned to it in those times: the Roman and the Milanese, while extending the beginnings of the Church of Aquileia to the fourth century and those of Ravenna to the fifth.

**3.** But if you ask these same authors how it happened that in the other provinces of the Roman world metropolitan bishops were ordained according to apostolic institution, whereas in Italy—where Paul preached, where Peter established Churches, and where the apostolic see existed in the earliest times of the Church—that institution did not immediately take effect, just as Emanuel Schelstratius had asked himself (vol. I, dissertation, chapter 5), their authors first do not approve the answer of those who attribute the cause and reason for so great a difference to the will of the apostles or of their successors who established the arrangement.

Second, they themselves answer that the apostles or their successors also organized the ecclesiastical government of Italy according to the pattern of the secular government. Since the whole region was administered by two vicars, the prefects of the praetorium—one Roman, under whom ten provinces were subject, and one Milanese, under whom there were seven—the same method required two ecclesiastical metropolitans to be established in Italy, so that, there as elsewhere, the order of the ecclesiastical hierarchy might correspond to that of the secular hierarchy.

Accordingly, the supreme pontiff himself presided immediately as metropolitan over the bishops of the ten suburban provinces; but in the other seven, which were distinguished by the name of Italy, the bishop of Milan exercised metropolitan authority. Hence arose the distinction between the bishops of the Roman province and those whom they called the bishops of the province of Italy; and hence originated, among these same authors, the conjecture concerning the subjection of the Churches of Ravenna and Aquileia. For Ravenna was the first city of Aemilia, and Aquileia of Venetia—provinces included in the Vicariate of Italy—and therefore their bishops, it was said, ought to have rendered obedience to the metropolitan of Italy.

**4.** No one denies that Ravenna and Aquileia were cities of the Italian vicariate. The subscriptions of the Council of Sardica also testify that their bishops were called “from Italy”: Fortunatianus, from Italy, of Aquileia; Severus, from Italy, of Ravenna; Protasius, from Italy, of Milan. Finally, Athanasius asserts in his letter to the Solitaries that Milan was the metropolis of Italy.

Among those he lists are men of the clearest confession, religious men and good bishops: Paulinus of Trier, which is the metropolis of Gaul; Lucifer, metropolitan bishop of Sardinia; Eusebius of Vercelli, a city of Italy; and Dionysius of Milan, which itself is the metropolis of Italy.

The testimony of St. Ambrose also supports this. Writing both to the people of Vercelli and to the bishop of Vicohabentia, he confirms that Venetia and Aemilia belonged to him, as Sirmond interprets it (book I). In his letter to the Vercellians, the holy Doctor complains that their Church still lay desolate, deprived of a pastor, while the Churches of the neighboring cities rejoiced in such consolation:

“I am overwhelmed with grief because the Church of the Lord which is among you still has no priest, and now alone among all the regions of Liguria, Aemilia, Venetia, and the other neighboring parts of Italy lacks this service.” (Ambrose, epistle 82.)

In another letter to the bishop of Vicohabentia, he earnestly commends the Church of Imola to his care until a new bishop might be appointed there:

“I commend to you, my son, the Church which is at Forum Cornelii, so that you may visit it frequently in the near future, until a bishop is ordained for it. Occupied as I am during the approaching days of Lent, I cannot travel so far.” (Ambrose, epistle 2.)

Forum Cornelii, or Imola, is a city of the province of Aemilia—or of Flaminia, whose capital was Ravenna. Vicohabentia likewise lay in Aemilia; it is now Ferrara.

From the words of Ambrose just cited, therefore, it is clear that Forum Cornelii was under his care, visitation, and ordination; and that Vicohabentia likewise belonged to him. This follows both because he entrusts the visitation of another Church to its bishop, whom he calls “son” in the language of subjection, and because, from homily 175 of St. Peter Chrysologus, which we shall cite below, our critics believe that this subjection of Vicohabentia can be inferred.

The ecclesiastical province of Milan therefore contained Venetia and Aemilia, and consequently Ravenna and Aquileia.

**5.** Schelstratius, however, in order to raise the authority of the Church of Milan over these provinces still further, borrows another argument from the synodal letter which Eusebius, its bishop, wrote to Leo the Great in approval of that most celebrated pontiff’s letter to Flavian.

When Schelstratius observed the subscriptions of certain bishops of Aemilia, Raetia, and the Cottian Alps at the end of Eusebius’s letter, he supposed that this bishop had extended his jurisdiction over almost all Italy and beyond its boundaries. Here are Schelstratius’s words:

“How widely the Church of Milan possessed metropolitan jurisdiction throughout Italy before the metropolitan sees of the Churches of Ravenna and Aquileia were established may be gathered from the letter of Eusebius of Milan which was sent to Leo the Great concerning the faith that he had directed to the East. For not only did the bishops of Liguria subscribe it—Crispinus of Ticinum, Cyriacus of Lodi, Abundantius of Como, and the rest—but also Faventius of Reggio, Majoranus of Piacenza, and Cyprianus of Brescello from the province of Aemilia; Abundantius of Como on behalf of Agimo of Chur; Gradus on behalf of Eustasius of Augusta in Raetia; Maximus of Turin and Quintus of Durnum from the Cottian Alps. It is consequently clear that these belonged to Eusebius’s synod.

“If you add to these the bishops of Flaminia, whose bishop of Forum Cornelii St. Ambrose indicates to have belonged to his obedience, you will have almost all the regions that constituted the ecclesiastical province of Italy: namely, Liguria, Aemilia, Flaminia, the Cottian Alps, and Raetia. Only the provinces of Istria and Venetia are recognized as missing. With these exceptions, the bishop of Milan possessed jurisdiction over the remaining regions of Italy as metropolitan of Italy.”

**6.** To these arguments, based entirely upon conjecture, some add the force of a negative argument. It is this: the ancient writers and the surviving monuments of antiquity speak only of the Roman pontiff as metropolitan of the ten suburban provinces and of the bishop of Milan as metropolitan of the seven provinces of Italy; concerning all other metropolitans there is profound silence among everyone.

**7.** All these claims, however, which nearly all critics repeat on almost every page when treating the ecclesiastical hierarchy, and which they enlarge with virtually limitless learning until the reader is sated, can, I believe, easily be dissolved and exposed as frivolous by anyone who has read the very learned dissertation of Abbot Bacchinius on the origin of the ecclesiastical hierarchy.

For there the celebrated Cassinese scholar devotes himself entirely to undermining the foundation of the conjectures and arguments just cited, and completely demolishes it with an excellent and unshakable learning. Since, therefore, the force of all the proofs concerning the subjection of the Churches of Ravenna and Aquileia flows from the civil system of government in Italy—a system which these authors themselves wish the ecclesiastical hierarchy of Italy to have followed—we shall demonstrate with Bacchinius that this system is fictitious, and from there proceed with firmer step to weaken the remaining arguments of the Milanese.

Although in passing we may have occasion to mix in some discussion of the patriarchate of Aquileia, we nevertheless declare that we shall make no judgment whatsoever concerning its prerogatives—especially if all have not equally approved what Father Bernard Rubeus wrote in his most learned work and what the distinguished Joseph Motta most recently wrote in his dissertation on metropolitan jurisdiction, no. 31 and following, concerning the origin, extent, and jurisdiction of the Church of Aquileia.

We seek only the Milanese, and turn to them. Yet we do not intend thereby to detract in any way from the excellence and extent of the Church of Milan. We shall be more than satisfied if we vindicate the Church of Ravenna from its domination and reject as merely fictitious the arguments by which Ravenna is attacked.

We are not unaware that nothing is gained from vanity by candid Milanese writers, to use the words of Ripamonti, who aptly speaks against excessive magnifiers of their native Church (vol. I of the *History of the Church of Milan*, book I):

“Nor are we of such a disposition,” he says, “that, by mingling falsehoods with truths and thereby making the beginnings of our affairs narrower, we should wish to deserve reproaches and cavils, and to go down through all future ages with that reputation and estimation of character—as though our concern had been to gratify and advertise the name of our homeland with things attractive in speech.”

With these words, taken from book IV of the first decade of Livy, Ripamonti ridicules the simplicity of his fellow citizen Galvaneus Flamma, who had gathered into his chronicle every little tale picked up here and there, especially where he had incompetently assigned a vast number of provinces to the authority of the city of Milan, as in these verses:

> Second city after Rome, crowned with the highest laurels,  
> Seat of empire and of Jupiter, engraved with wondrous structures,  
> First metropolis, ruling the cities of Liguria,  
> Both Raetias, Bavaria, Churia, Cumae,  
> Corsica, Sardinia, Ravenna, Genoa, Pisa,  
> Grado, Aquileia, Ticinum, Piacenza, Siena—  
> Angusta with Secundia are subject; you, Subria, are Rome’s.

These things might perhaps be understood of civil rather than ecclesiastical jurisdiction, unless elsewhere—namely, in his Chronicles—this good author equated ecclesiastical authority with the temporal domination of the Milanese in these words:

“The Churches of Aquileia and Ravenna, Genoa, Grado, Cumae, Augusta, Cologne, Basel, Chur, Pavia, Piacenza, and all the other bishops of Italy were suffragan bishops of the bishop of Milan.”

But setting these matters aside, let us now approach more closely the arguments of the critics whom we have already praised, with observations and replies.

### § II. The arguments of authors denying this are set forth

**8.** Several very distinguished authors adopted the negative opinion, among whom, on the Catholic side, were Peter de Marca, Benedict Bacchinius, and Hieronymus Rubeus, and among the heterodox, Salmasius—although not all were led by the same reasons or, as they say, by the same spirit.

Some freed the Church of Ravenna from the Milanese yoke because they believed it to have been metropolitan from the time of its foundation. Others, although they deferred the beginnings of this dignity until as late as the fifth century, nevertheless denied that it could in any way be proved that the Ravennates had ever obeyed the Church of Milan; indeed, they seem scarcely and reluctantly to grant even to the Church of Milan itself the beginnings of its metropolitan jurisdiction in the fourth Christian century.

We shall defer examination of both opinions concerning the origin of this prerogative in the Church of Ravenna to the third chapter, while leaving the question of the origin of the illustrious Ambrosian metropolitan see intact to more learned critics. For now, it is enough for us to bring forward the replies of the authors who deny the claim, by which they refute the arguments advanced in the preceding section against the liberty of our Church.

**9.** Their first argument, therefore, which is the origin and foundation of the others, is drawn from the form of government in Italy, to which they maintain that the form of ecclesiastical government must correspond.

Since all Italy was divided into two vicariates, the Roman and the Italian, they say that there must likewise have been only two metropolitans in that region: the supreme pontiff, as bishop of Rome, and the bishop of Milan, as bishop of the city that was the capital of the Italian vicariate. Just as the bishops of the ten suburban provinces obeyed the pope as their metropolitan, so the bishops of the seven Italian provinces obeyed the bishop of Milan, among whom Ravenna was undoubtedly numbered.

**10.** “Those who argue in this way,” says Bacchinius, “must either admit that the ecclesiastical hierarchy of Italy in the fourth and fifth centuries was very different from that which the apostles had established there, or acknowledge that it was not adapted to the system of the civil empire” (*Dissertation on the Origin of the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, part II), if they regard the apostles as its authors.

For in the time of the apostles—and indeed not even during the whole of the first three centuries—the government of Italy had assumed the form of two vicariates, upon which writers otherwise most learned have built their entire structure.

Augustus had divided Italy from Sicily to the Cottian Alps, as Pliny (book III, chapter 5) and Tacitus (*Annals*, book V, chapter 11) testify, into eleven regions under a single prefect. Pancirolus believed, however, that he had assigned a praetor to each, apart from the decurions, who represented the Roman Senate in the Italian cities, and the duumviri, who represented the consuls (*Commentary on the Notice of the Empire of the West*, chapter 49).

This form of government in Italy was altered by the emperor Hadrian into four prefectures, each of them assigned to individual consular governors. Aurelian, according to Pancirolus, introduced yet another system of administration into Italy (*ibid.*); Pancirolus thought that it could be inferred from Spartianus that the whole region was then brought under one corrector. From Vopiscus (*On Tacitus*, cited by Bacchinius in the work mentioned above), Bacchinius infers that indications of four consular provinces appeared with some clarity under the emperor Tacitus.

Since all these forms of government differ very greatly from the form of the Roman and Italian vicariates, and since they occupied three complete centuries and more from the age of the apostles, it is permissible to conclude either that the apostles did not shape the ecclesiastical hierarchy in Italy according to the imperial model, or that the hierarchy prevailing in the fourth and fifth centuries differed utterly from the apostolic institution.

Since, therefore, the principal foundation of the opinion concerning the suffragan status of the Church of Ravenna is shaken, the opinion itself must collapse, for it is supported by no other genuinely solid reason.

**11.** Only at the beginning of the fourth century did Constantine the Great divide the whole empire among four prefects of the praetorium. The prefect of the praetorium of Italy governed Africa, Sardinia, Corsica, and Sicily with the neighboring islands, in addition to Italy itself, which he ruled through the aforementioned vicars—one residing at Rome, the other at Milan—with the division of the Italian provinces that we indicated above (Zosimus, *History*, book II, cited by Bacchinius).

But how many changes did this very division of Constantine the Great’s Roman dominion suffer under the emperors who succeeded him! How many alterations, combinations, and varied distributions of the provinces of Italy occurred! Anyone who wants more on this subject should consult Bacchinius (in the work cited above) and the many ancient and recent authors who have written about it at greater length.

It is therefore not even permissible to suspect that in the fourth century the hierarchical order of the Churches of Italy had been adapted to the imperial system amid so many upheavals in human affairs.

To this were added the times of the Arian heresy, during which—and especially under Constantius, the son of Constantine—almost all the Italian Churches were disturbed, confused, and overturned. Thus, in my opinion, anyone would be mistaken who asserted that in so turbulent an age the supreme pontiffs had assigned to the bishop of Milan the Churches of the seven provinces of Italy in the strict sense, especially since, while the heresy was still raging in Italy during that very century, the bishop of Aquileia already shone with the metropolitan insignia, as everyone knows.

What conjecture, then, what argument remains in favor of the subjection of the Church of Ravenna?

**12.** The subscriptions of the Council of Sardica may indeed suggest in some way that the distinction of the Italian provinces had already been introduced and established at the time when that council was held—that is, around the middle of the fourth century—and several years after Constantine had distinguished the Urban Vicariate from the Italian. For this reason, the bishops of the seven provinces who attended the council may perhaps have added *τὸ ab Italia* (“from Italy”) to indicate that distinction.

But the most learned men have vainly extracted from this addition an indication—or a pretext—for constructing the claim that the Church of Milan was the metropolitan of all the Churches of the Italian vicariate, not merely in the fourth century itself but also, and even more so, in the preceding centuries.

First, we could rightly call into question whether *ab Italia* was added to designate the provinces of the Milanese vicariate. For that designation had been in use since the age of Augustus, so that throughout the world the whole region was known as Italy which, as we noted above, is bounded on one side by the Cottian Alps and on the other by the Sicilian Sea. Before Augustus, the territory extending from the Alps to the river Rubicon was everywhere called Cisalpine Gaul, whereas the territory stretching from the Rubicon to Sicily was called Italy (Strabo, Polybius, Cluverius, cited by Bacchinius in the work mentioned above).

Second, the Council of Sardica itself made sufficiently clear what it understood by the name “Italy”: not merely the Milanese vicariate, but Italy as a whole, and especially the suburban provinces. For in its letter to Julius, the Roman pontiff, it exhorts him as follows:

“Your excellent prudence ought to arrange that, through your letters, our brothers who are in Sicily, who are in Sardinia, and who are in Italy may learn what has been done and what has been decreed.” (*Among the fragments of Hilary.*)

For if at that time the council had directed its attention only to the brothers who were in Italy—that is, only to the bishops of the Milanese vicariate—it would have excluded from knowledge of its proceedings and decrees all the others who resided in Campania, Bruttium, Umbria, and the other provinces of the Roman vicariate.
