Indeed, it would have mentioned to the pontiff only those who had attended the synod with the imaginary metropolitan of Italy, while remaining silent about those who had been absent from the provinces of the Roman vicariate, of whom we find scarcely one or two among the Fathers of Sardica.

### 13

Third, because neither Athanasius nor, more importantly for the present question, Constantine the Great always observed this narrower designation of Italy, by which only the vicariate of Milan was intended. The former, in his book *On the Synods*, nevertheless calls Picenum Annonarium—which certainly belonged among the provinces of the Roman vicariate—by the name of Italy, when he says: “Ariminum, a city of Italy.” Cardinal Norisius has attempted with every effort to prove that this city was situated in Picenum and that, for this reason, its bishop belonged to the metropolitan of the Roman province, not to that of Ravenna (*Dissertation on the Fifth Synod*).

Constantine Augustus, writing in Eusebius concerning the celebration of Easter, says: “Therefore all judged that to be fair and right, and I promised that it would also please you: namely, that what is observed by common agreement in the city of Rome and throughout all Italy, Africa, Egypt, and so forth, your prudence should likewise embrace with willing minds.” From these words it is clearer than daylight that the expression “throughout all Italy” must, in Constantine’s sense, be extended both to the seven provinces of the Milanese vicariate and to the ten provinces of the Roman vicariate, just as, by heaven, everyone extends it.

### 14

Fourth and finally, long after the administrative office of the two vicars of Italy had been established, the term “Italy” continued to be used for the whole region comprised by both vicariates. Thus, in title 13 of the Theodosian Code, concerning accusations, and in title 2, concerning restoration to full rights, we read of all Italy taken together and distinguished from the other regions of the Empire. In title 1, concerning deserters, and title 9, concerning extraordinary matters, the entire tract from the Alps to the Sicilian sea is designated by the name of Italy.

Likewise, Campania, Tuscia, Picenum, Samnium, Apulia, Lucania, Bruttium, and Calabria are called provinces of Italy in title 7, concerning the remission of debts; indeed, they are called the provinces of urban and suburban Italy, in titles 9 and 13. Their judges, consular governors, correctors, and vicars are indiscriminately called judges within Italy. Therefore, since the designation “Italy” was wholly—or at least ambiguously—used both under Constantine and after Constantine, or rather was understood to mean the entire region of Italy, the most learned critics sought support from such a designation in vain, whether to establish a distinction in the government and distribution of the provinces, or, still less, to reduce the form of ecclesiastical government before and after Constantine to two metropolitans of Italy.

### 15

“But,” they say, “the dispute is settled by Athanasius’s letter to the Solitaries, which both designates the provinces of the Milanese vicariate by the name of Italy and calls Milan itself the metropolis of Italy.”

Granted. But what does this imply concerning that bishop’s ecclesiastical jurisdiction over seven provinces, especially during the three earlier centuries of our era? Certainly, anyone who examines Athanasius’s words more carefully will find that they convey one of two meanings. Either the holy doctor does not in any way understand the bishop of Milan there as a metropolitan, or he does not consider him to preside over all the provinces of the vicariate.

In fact, Athanasius does not say, “Dionysius, metropolitan of Milan and of Italy,” as he says of Lucifer of Cagliari, “Lucifer, metropolitan bishop of Sardinia.” Rather, immediately after mentioning Lucifer, when he names Dionysius, he calls him simply a bishop, while he calls Milan the metropolis of Italy: “Dionysius, bishop of Milan, which itself is the metropolis of Italy.”

Athanasius may have added this so that, just as he had called Trier the metropolis of Gaul, Milan might likewise be recognized by his Solitaries as the metropolis of Italy, since by the time at which he was writing to them Italy had already been divided between two vicars of the praetorian prefect, and the narrower designation “Italy,” with reference to the provinces of the Milanese vicariate, had become current among many.

But if you wish Athanasius to be speaking there of ecclesiastical metropolises, it must be determined whether the phrase “which itself is the metropolis of Italy” is to be understood of all the provinces of Italy taken strictly, or only of some part of it. For the words “which itself is the metropolis of Italy” can be interpreted equally in the first or the second sense.

Under the first interpretation, as we have said, they would include the seven provinces of the Italian vicariate. Under the second, they would mean that Milan was one of the ecclesiastical metropolises of Italy. On that interpretation Athanasius would not exclude other metropolises; indeed, he would rather admit their existence within the Milanese vicariate.

That the words cited—“which itself is the metropolis of Italy”—should perhaps more correctly be understood in this second sense is evident from Athanasius’s comparison of Milan with Trier. Paulinus had said, “Trier is the metropolis of the Treveri and of Gaul”; Athanasius then says, “Dionysius, bishop of Milan, which itself is the metropolis of Italy.”

Just as Trier was therefore not at that time the sole ecclesiastical metropolis of Gaul—for even in the earliest centuries of Christianity there were the metropolises of Arles, Lyon, and Vienne—so Milan was neither the sole ecclesiastical metropolis of Italy nor understood by Athanasius as such. The writers just mentioned therefore gain little by abusing the testimony of so great a Father: first, because his words in no way prove that during the three earlier centuries the bishop of Milan was metropolitan of the seven provinces, which above all they had to demonstrate according to their position; and second, because Athanasius’s own words either cannot be interpreted of Milan as an ecclesiastical metropolis, or must be understood of Milan not as the metropolis of all Italy, but as one of Italy’s metropolises.

### 16

The arguments next drawn from the letters of Saint Ambrose to subject the Church of Ravenna to the bishop of Milan are no more substantial; indeed, we are greatly surprised that men of such refined judgment should have placed excessive trust in documents of this kind.

As for Ambrose’s letter to the people of Vercelli, the words are these:

> “I am overwhelmed with grief because the Church of the Lord which is among you still has no priest, and now, alone among all the regions of Liguria, Aemilia, Venetia, and the other neighboring parts of Italy, it is in need of such an office.”

Sirmondus, with triumphant confidence, had adapted these words to his own opinion concerning a metropolitan of Milan over all Italy. “Does he not,” he says, “confirm abundantly that all the Churches of Liguria, Aemilia, Venetia, and the other neighboring parts of Italy belonged to the care of the Church of Milan?” (*Book I of the Propositions*, chapter 8).

Cardinal Norisius nevertheless perceived the futility of Sirmondus’s interpretation. Correctly understanding Ambrose’s words, he says: “In his letter to the people of Vercelli, Ambrose mentions those provinces, not because they were all subject to him, but because, as they were nearer and better known to him, he could more readily adduce them as examples” (*Dissertation on the Fifth Synod*, chapter 10).

### 17

With this single reply from the most learned cardinal, we may dispose of the letter to the people of Vercelli and proceed to the other, addressed to the bishop of Vicohabentia.

“I commend to you, my son,” says the holy doctor, “the Church situated at Forum Cornelii, so that, since it is nearby, you may visit it more frequently until a bishop is ordained for it. Since I am occupied by the approaching days of Lent, I cannot travel so far.”

Here, they say, is the Church of Imola, beyond doubt a suffragan of Milan, since its bishop’s ordination depended upon Ambrose and it was subject to his visitation. Even the Church of Vicohabentia itself, they add, was subject to him: first, because Ambrose addresses its bishop by the title “son,” which is a title of subjection; and second, because nearly fifty years later Saint Peter Chrysologus, at the consecration of Marcellinus of Vicohabentia, confessed that, despite the opposition of the bishop of Milan—as they interpret his words—he had exercised that first act of metropolitan jurisdiction.

Since the Churches of Forum Cornelii and Vicohabentia were situated in the provinces of Aemilia and Flaminia, it follows, they conclude, that these provinces, and therefore Ravenna also, their capital, acknowledged the jurisdiction of the bishop of Milan.

### 18

If we consulted the opinion of Ludovico Antonio Muratori concerning this letter of Ambrose, the celebrated author might perhaps regard it as of doubtful authenticity and, as they say, apocryphal. He would be led to this conclusion by the fact that Ambrose calls the bishop of Vicohabentia “son.” Muratori censures this title in a diploma of Saint Gregory the Great addressed to Marinianus, archbishop of Ravenna, whom that holy pontiff calls “brother and most beloved son” (*Italian Historical Matters*, vol. II, p. 13). For this reason he also consigned the diploma to the apocrypha and accused Hieronymus Rubeus and Ferdinand Ughellus of frivolity for having inserted such a document into their histories.

What Muratori thinks Gregory the Great, supreme pontiff, was not permitted to say to Marinianus—whom Gregory himself had instructed, cultivated, and loved while Marinianus was living within the monastic cloister—we shall say Ambrose was permitted to say to Constantius, toward whom, so far as we know, he had no paternal relationship, unless perhaps it was that of a metropolitan, if we believe his opponents (*John the Deacon, Life of Saint Gregory*, book III, chapter 7; *Saint Gregory*, book IV, letter 5).

But where do we read that a metropolitan called the bishops of his province “sons”? Yet let us set these matters aside, since they seem in no way relevant to our question. Elsewhere, as we believe, we have adequately answered these and similar objections raised by the distinguished Muratori against the letters of Saint Gregory.

### 19

I believe, however, that our critics’ argument may be answered as follows. Even if it were admitted that the Churches of Imola and Vicohabentia were at some time subject to Milan, it could nevertheless be denied that Ravenna’s subjection follows from this.

According to Bacchinius, it is a weak and futile argument to infer the form and ecclesiastical government of particular provinces from their civil form and government. It would take too long to present all the evidence by which we have observed the most well-established opinion of so great a man to be confirmed. Its substance, however, is this.

First, it is wholly improbable that the most holy and apostolic hierarchy of the Church was confined within the boundaries of civil provinces—boundaries that were sometimes contracted and sometimes extended—and that it followed the forms of their government, which certainly changed a thousand times. We read both that two provinces were united into one and that one was divided into two; sometimes one province, which had possessed its own governor, obeyed the governor of another; at other times provinces were subject to other and frequent alterations.

Second, since the apostles measured the Church’s hierarchy not by the division of the provinces of the Empire but by the conversion of peoples and the foundation of Churches—as Bacchinius himself has demonstrated at greater length with remarkable learning (*Parts I and II*, cited above), and as we shall briefly indicate in chapter 3—it follows that the subordination of one Church to a metropolitan cannot and should not be inferred from the boundaries, government, or physical extent of the provinces, and therefore not from the city of one civil province or another.

This is especially true of the earliest periods of our era, when not all cities immediately embraced the faith of Christ, and not all those converted to Christ obtained a bishopric. The apostles and their disciples measured Christian provinces not by entire civil provinces, but by the many peoples won to Christ in the surrounding regions and by the Churches founded among them.

### 20

But it is more appropriate to answer directly the interpretation of Saint Ambrose’s words that has been advanced against the people of Ravenna.

First, it must be said that Ambrose’s words contain no indication whatsoever—whether certain or probable—that the ordination or consecration of the bishop of Imola depended upon the bishop of Milan. The holy doctor does not say, “until a bishop is ordained or approved by me,” but simply commends that Church to the bishop of Vicohabentia “until a bishop is ordained for it.” Such a commendation, proceeding from charity, could belong to any bishop, as we shall immediately observe.

Second, as for the office of visitation which Ambrose seems in those words to claim for himself in the Church of Imola—“Since I am occupied by the approaching days of Lent, I cannot travel so far”—it will readily be apparent to anyone who considers Ambrose’s circumstances that this visitation was not a sign of metropolitan jurisdiction, but an act and indication of apostolic preaching and legation.

Here we must remember what we touched upon briefly above concerning the disasters caused by the Arian heresy: the faith of Italy had been corrupted, discipline thoroughly disturbed, many Churches deprived of Catholic bishops, and invaded by Arian wolves. Some believe that, through the usurpation of Auxentius of Milan, the ecclesiastical province of Milan was then first consolidated, when not a few Italian bishops from the surrounding regions came over to that heretic’s party and attended his assemblies, in order to escape the threats of Auxentius and of the supporters of his heresy and to avoid exile and death (Bacchinius, cited above).

This miserable condition of Italy was maintained for many years after the death of the emperor Constantius: during the still more disastrous times of Julian the Apostate, under the prevailing tyranny of the Arians, and through the favor shown by the Arian empress Justina, while Pope Damasus, with the second synod held by him at Rome, hurled the thunderbolts of anathema and deposition against Auxentius to no effect.

### 21

After the belated death of Auxentius, when Ambrose had been established as bishop of Milan, all Italy was converted to the orthodox faith, as Saint Jerome testifies (*Chronicle*, under the eleventh year of Gratian). Ambrose himself says:

> “The storm of all dissensions has subsided. All the fires and heats of secular desire by which the people of Italy had formerly been scorched in the conflagrations of Jewish and Arian frivolity are now tempered by the breath of a tranquil atmosphere.”

(*Ambrose, Commentary on Luke*, book IX, chapter 20.)

When Ambrose assumed, together with the episcopal insignia, the apostolate and the legation of the holy see, he traveled through the Churches of the Italian provinces that had been corrupted. By preaching, disputation, teaching, labor, and every kind of struggle, he restored the Catholic faith; he repaired the Churches; he drove out the Arian wolves in some places, converted them into legitimate pastors in others, and appointed new bishops elsewhere.

From this, some have inferred that the metropolitan jurisdiction which had unlawfully intruded under the usurper Auxentius was sanctified and confirmed under the true apostle and father, over the Churches of the various provinces which Ambrose had restored to the faith. We neither oppose nor endorse this opinion.

### 22

We, however, follow Ambrose in his apostolate and attribute his actions in the Church of Imola, and, if one wishes, also in that of Vicohabentia, to his pontifical legation, which he exercised, rather than to metropolitan dignity.

No one with even a modest knowledge of ecclesiastical history will be surprised that Ambrose exercised the offices of preaching, visitation, and ordination in foreign provinces and foreign Churches. History supplies a hundred examples of bishops who carried deep in their hearts the care of peoples and Churches not entrusted to their own jurisdiction and who therefore, whether exercising an apostolic legation or under some other legitimate title, visited them, held synods there, ordained bishops, and commended them to neighboring or principal bishops.

Who does not know the journeys and labors through the East of Eusebius of Vercelli, Hosius of Corduba, Hilary of Poitiers, and Lucifer of Cagliari, as well as the synods they held and the bishops they consecrated? Who is unaware of Cyprian’s letters on behalf of the Churches of Gaul, or of Theodoret’s on behalf of those of Africa?

We read that Athanasius seemed to reproach Pope Damasus because, after Auxentius had been expelled, he did not take counsel for the Church of Milan. He wrote to the beloved Damasus, bishop of great Rome, against Auxentius, the invader of the Church of Milan:

> “We marvel that he has not yet been deposed and expelled from the Church.”

(Athanasius, *Synodal Letter to the Africans*.)

We likewise hear Cyril of Alexandria, although the condemnation of Nestorius had made all the Easterners, and even the younger Theodosius himself, hostile to him, protesting a hundred times that he had to care for all the Churches, not merely his own.

Perhaps he had drawn this apostolic zeal from Cyprian. Writing to Stephen, the Roman pontiff, concerning the Church of Arles, which Martianus, a bishop of the Novatian sect, was infecting, Cyprian did not hesitate to assert:

> “It is our responsibility to provide counsel and assistance in this matter, dearest brother, since we consider the divine clemency and hold the balance of governing the Church,” and so forth.

The most holy bishop judged that the welfare of the Church of Arles was also his concern, out of zeal and charity; but he judged that it was Stephen’s responsibility by reason of the power and authority of supreme jurisdiction over the universal Church.

### 23

Ambrose, therefore, acting as an apostle and pontifical legate, could easily have enriched the Churches of Imola and Vicohabentia with these benefits, among the many Churches which he had either restored to the faith or supplied with bishops. These Churches may previously have been infected with the stain of Arianism or deprived of their bishops through the power of the Arians, even though they in no way belonged to the rights of his own jurisdiction.

Any doubt is removed by the assertion of certain writers concerning Ambrose’s pontifical legation. As the representative of the supreme pontiffs Damasus and Siricius, Ambrose could lawfully and validly accomplish in these Churches everything that otherwise he could not have done.

There can be no reasonable doubt about this legation if we examine the discipline of the Churches of the earliest centuries and the sacred canons. Nor can those authors reasonably doubt it who—among them Bacchinius, Thomassinus, and others—have obstinately maintained and taught that there was no metropolitan in Italy apart from the Roman bishop, and that he presided over all the Churches of this region not merely as primate but also as their immediate archbishop, during the first three or four centuries.

For the opinion of all prudent critics is that whenever we read of a bishop presiding over a synod of another province, ordaining new bishops for another Church, or performing any other act of jurisdiction, we must believe that it was done by pontifical authority or through an apostolic legation.

Accordingly, when Lucifer of Cagliari bestowed the blessing of consecration upon Paulinus, bishop of Antioch, Christianus Lupus asserted that Lucifer had been equipped with a Roman legation. Eusebius of Vercelli and Hilary of Poitiers are likewise believed to have been invested with this ministry.

### 24

Franciscus Ballarinus explicitly asserts this of Saint Ambrose on the basis of an ancient Patriarchal Breviary that remained in use in the Church of Como until the time of Clement VIII:

> “In the time of Pope Damasus and the emperor Theodosius, blessed Ambrose governed the Church of Milan, exercising an apostolic legation. He also presided over the Christians of the neighboring regions of Liguria, Aemilia, Venetia, Rhaetia, and the Cottian Alps, since through the calamities of earlier times they had been deprived of bishops.”

Benedict Jovius and the recently cited Christianus Lupus held the same view.

This assertion is greatly strengthened by the affair at Sirmium, reported by Baronius under the year 330 and much earlier by Paulinus in his *Life of Ambrose*. After the bishop of Sirmium had died, a dispute arose between Catholics and Arians over the election of a new pastor. The Catholics demanded a Catholic, while the Arians demanded an Arian; the heretical empress Justina supported the latter.

When the matter was referred to Ambrose, the holy doctor hastened there, arranged for a Catholic bishop to be elected, and consecrated the elected Anemius.

Sirmium was beyond doubt the chief city of Illyricum and also an ecclesiastical metropolis. The bishops of Milan therefore had acquired no right over that Church. Consequently, the acts concerning the election and ordination of Anemius must be attributed solely to the apostolic legation whose powers Ambrose was exercising.

It must therefore be concluded from the holy doctor’s letter to the bishop of Vicohabentia that neither the ordination nor the approval of the bishop of Imola can be falsely derived from it, nor the subjection of that Church or of Vicohabentia, and still less the subjection of Ravenna.

### 25

A few points remain to be considered concerning Schelstratius’s inflated argument, by which he attempts to enlarge the jurisdiction of Milan on the basis of the synod and synodal letter of Eusebius to Leo the Great.

Once we observe that Schelstratius boasts of this synod and of these letters in order to show the extent of the metropolitan jurisdiction of Milan before metropolitans were established for the Churches of Ravenna and Aquileia, his celebrated argument will immediately collapse altogether.

First, scarcely one, and perhaps not even one, of all the bishops of the province of Aquileia attended that synod. From their presence, therefore, no conclusion concerning the suffragan status of that province could be drawn.

More remarkably, Schelstratius himself noted and admitted this in the place cited, in these words:

> “Only the provinces of Histria and Venetia are recognized as absent; except for these, the bishop of Milan possessed rights in the remaining regions of Italy as metropolitan of Italy.”

How, then, can the Eusebian synod provide an argument for the vaunted extent of Milan’s jurisdiction before the metropolitan of Aquileia had been established?

Moreover, this synod of Milan was held in the middle of the fifth century, namely in the year 451, as may be seen in Baronius, Binius, and other writers. But, according to Schelstratius himself, the Church of Aquileia is believed to have been raised to metropolitan dignity under Pope Damasus. On this opinion one should consult Bernardus Rubeus, who recently attempted to vindicate the rights of the Church of Aquileia in a learned work. This occurred almost an entire century before the Eusebian synod was held.

The Church of Ravenna had already enjoyed the same prerogative for at least twenty years, namely from the year 431, according to Tillemont, and perhaps much earlier, as others believe. It certainly possessed it under Peter Chrysologus, while he governed that Church, as everyone agrees.

When the holy doctor departed to heaven in the year 451, he had already consecrated the bishop of Vicohabentia on the preceding Nativity of Our Lord Jesus Christ; indeed, in the year 446 he had also consecrated Saint Projectus as bishop of Imola. We shall discuss all these matters more fully in chapter 3. It is therefore evident that he had already assumed metropolitan status before the Milanese synod was held.

Where, then, is the extent of jurisdiction boasted by Schelstratius, if it is derived from such a synod held before the metropolitans of Aquileia and Ravenna had been established?

### 26

It must therefore be admitted that neither the Eusebian synod nor its synodal letter proves anything against the liberty of the people of Ravenna.

If someone objects that the letter was signed by the bishops of Piacenza, Brescello, and Reggio, and from this renews the argument that the province of Aemilia—whose cities were Piacenza, Brescello, and Reggio—obeyed the bishop of Milan, and that Ravenna, the chief city of Aemilia, consequently suffered the same mark of subjection, at least before it received the archiepiscopal pallium, there are several answers of equally great weight.

### 27

First, some have doubted whether this synod of Eusebius was provincial—that is, whether it was a synod solely of the province of Milan.

Baronius, Ughellus, and others considered it provincial and thought that all the suffragan bishops had assembled for it and signed the letters in their own names. “There survives,” says Baronius, “a synodal letter concerning these matters, authenticated by the subscriptions of all the bishops of the province.”

The writers of Pavia nevertheless deny this. They wish their native Church to have been endowed with a special privilege of liberty from the earliest centuries. They deny, I say, that Crispinus, bishop of Pavia, whose subscription appears at the end of the letter, took part in the council as a suffragan of Milan, and they bring forward many arguments, which we leave for critics to examine.

The historians of the Church of Como and the champions of the patriarchate of Aquileia hold the same view. They were convinced that the bishop of Como, one of those present at the Eusebian synod, had never recognized the bishop of Milan as his archbishop, but had always recognized the bishop of Aquileia as such.

The people of Ravenna join this negative position, asserting that the bishops of Brescello, Reggio, and Piacenza in Aemilia could in no way have attended the Milanese synod as suffragans. For either all Aemilia had been subject to the bishop of Ravenna from the beginnings of the Christian religion, or this metropolitan dignity in Aemilia arose only in the fifth century.

It is evident that those three bishops could never be counted among the suffragans of Milan, since none of the authors of either position concerning the origin of this dignity can or does admit that Aemilia was divided in such a way that some of its Churches were assigned to Milan and others to Ravenna. Such an arrangement would contradict the universal hypothesis of all these writers: namely, that the ecclesiastical hierarchy was everywhere fitted to the civil hierarchy.

The abbot Bacchinius, along with most critics, thinks that this adaptation began to occur especially in the fourth and fifth centuries in the particular provinces of Italy.

If, therefore, those bishops of Aemilia attended the Eusebian synod and signed the letter to Leo the Great, they should not for that reason be considered bishops of the province of Milan. Consequently, that synod should not be regarded as merely provincial.

### 28

Second, there is an observation of no slight weight.

If we say that all the provincial bishops assembled at this synod and that no bishops of another ecclesiastical province attended, we must necessarily admit a considerable absurdity in the order of ecclesiastical government: several provinces of Italy would have been mutilated, and the hierarchy—which was otherwise so beautifully ordered—would have been thrown into the greatest confusion.

The ecclesiastical province of Milan in the earliest centuries would have to be said to consist of the three bishops of Aemilia, two of Rhaetia, two of the Cottian Alps, and one of Venetia, besides the bishops of Liguria. According to the recently stated view of the ecclesiastical hierarchy held by all critics, this would be utterly absurd.

### 29

Third, it must be noted that Leo the Great sent Abundantius and Senator as legates to this very synod of Eusebius.

Insofar as this apostolic legation was genuine, the convocation to Eusebius’s assembly of several bishops from another province can appropriately be attributed to it. Numerous examples show that this was neither new nor unusual.

Eustachius a Sancto Ubaldo, defending against the distinguished Muratori the diploma of Atto, bishop of Vercelli, which was read at the synod held at Milan in the year 945 under Archbishop Ulricus, supplied us with an observation of this kind. In answering Muratori’s objection that certain bishops who did not belong to the province of Milan were present at that synod, Eustachius says:

> “I wish it to be observed that a pontifical legate presided over the council of which we are speaking. From this it may be understood that bishops not included within metropolitan jurisdiction could have been summoned to it by that legate.”

We also judge it necessary to observe that, for this same reason—namely, the condemnation of the Eutychian heresy and the approval of the letter of the great Leo to Flavian—other synods were convened in the West, especially in Gaul, Spain, and Illyricum. All these were not provincial synods but national synods of several provinces, and synodal letters similar to this one of Eusebius were written from them to the holy pontiff.

Nothing, therefore, prevents us from calling the Eusebian synod non-provincial but national. Indeed, reason suggests that bishops from some of the other provinces of Italy were summoned to it, perhaps by the legates of Leo the Great.

Natalis Alexander appears in fact to support this opinion when he says that Eusebius convened an assembly of the diocese of Italy—something he certainly did by the mandate of Leo and the authority of the apostolic envoys.

### 30

Nor should Eustachius a Sancto Ubaldo’s empty interpretation of the term “co-bishops” trouble us. Under this designation he claims that only suffragan bishops are meant, and therefore, since Eusebius calls those whom we see subscribed to the synodal letter “co-bishops,” he argues that all of them were Eusebius’s suffragans.

When someone advances such an argument in broad daylight, we think he is simply blind. The ancient records of the Fathers are full of the term *co-bishop*, used when speaking of a bishop of another province, of an equal, of an inferior, or of a superior.

For an example applicable to all cases, consult Saint Cyprian, who, in his letter to Stephen, the Roman pontiff, explicitly calls the Gallic bishops “our co-bishops.”

But it is burdensome to dwell longer on a matter so evident. We therefore conclude the argument: since the council of Eusebius cannot be shown to have been provincial, the presence of the bishops of Aemilia provides no basis for inferring their suffragan status.

### 31

There are still two matters to consider concerning this very presence.

The first is that during the earliest centuries of the Church, and perhaps even during some later ones, the presence of bishops at a synod was not a certain indication of subjection. The second is that, even if those three bishops of Aemilia had truly been suffragans of Eusebius at that time, it would not therefore follow that the Church of Ravenna was likewise subject to him before it acquired archiepiscopal dignity.

As for the first point, we need only turn our attention to the councils of the earlier and also of the later period to become more certain of the truth of our proposition.

At the first Council of Arles against the Donatists, convened through the care of Constantine the Great, it is well known how many bishops attended from the various provinces of the entire West. No one would say with certainty that they were suffragans of Arles.

Under Pope Liberius another council was held in the same city, yet not all the pastors of the Churches who had gathered there—including Paulinus of Trier—regarded Saturninus, the metropolitan of Arles, as their metropolitan.

We know that Hosius of Corduba, Eusebius of Vercelli, and Hilary of Poitiers attended councils in Egypt and the East. Were they therefore to be called fellow-provincials of the bishops of Alexandria or Antioch?

Finally, at the synod of Aquileia concerning Palladius under Bishop Valerian, Italian, African, and Gallic prelates took part, although they were completely exempt from the jurisdiction of Aquileia. Otherwise Ambrose himself, the bishop of Milan, who was also present, would have to be considered subject to Valerian.

32. Nor should you object, with Baronius (under the year 381), that Ambrose presided over the Council of Aquileia and that, although Valerian sat first and subscribed first, this was conceded to the precedence of age and ordination, as had been the custom of the early councils. For even if we readily grant this custom—although it was not always and everywhere observed—we nevertheless just as readily deny that it applied to metropolitans in whose provinces [Col. 0109A] synods were held, or to the presidents of those synods. Thus, in agreement with Leone Allatius, Peter de Marca demonstrates, citing Apostolic Canon 35, Antiochene Canon 9, and Bracarense Canon 24, that whenever bishops sat and subscribed in disordered sequence at councils, the earlier order of seating and subscription was nevertheless preserved for metropolitans within their provinces and for council presidents. For the Bracarense canon says:

“While preserving the primacy of the metropolitan bishop, let each of the other bishops, according to the time of his ordination, show the others the honor of taking his seat.”

Let the Milanese take care lest, while they stubbornly maintain that Ambrose presided over the Synod of Aquileia—although he both sat and subscribed second after Valerian—they themselves call into question the fact that Eusebius was president of the Synod of Milan [Col. 0109B] of which we are now speaking, even though he signed the letter to Leo the Great before him; and lest they thereby provide us with weapons against the session at councils which they claim was granted to the bishop of Milan above the bishop of Ravenna. As examples from councils held after that period, the Synod of Pavia, celebrated in the year 876 and later confirmed by another synod at Pontigon in the same year, will suffice for all (vol. XI of the Councils, p. 279). Among many others, the bishops of Modena, Piacenza, and Florence subscribed to that Synod of Pavia—bishops who most certainly at that time did not belong to the province of Milan.

We pass over the synod of Ulric mentioned above, held in 945, where Boso of Piacenza, Sigifrid of Parma, Guido of Modena, and other bishops of foreign [Col. 0109C] provinces were present and subscribed. We pass over another synod which Anspert, archbishop of Milan, held at Pavia in 876, where, with no president and no papal legate present, there attended bishops of Modena, Como, and Arezzo, who were most certainly not subject to the metropolitan of Liguria. Nor do we adduce the other Synod of Pavia, convened in 966 by Walpert, archbishop of Milan, which the bishops of Parma, Piacenza, and Novara confirmed by their presence and subscription. For what has been said makes it sufficiently and abundantly clear that the subscriptions and presence of bishops at a synod do not always prove their subjection to it.

As the final point of this observation, it may be added that among the ancients it was customary for archbishops, or metropolitans, to summon even bishops of another province to their own synods in more serious [Col. 0109D] cases. This is inferred from the Antiochene canons and from the notes of Zonaras and Balsamon by the distinguished Joseph Motta in his excellent dissertation *On Metropolitan Law*, nos. 112 and following.

33. The second point that we had proposed to ourselves remains to be noted in conclusion: even if we were to concede to the Milanese that those bishops of Emilia whom we find listed in the synodal letter of Eusebius were their suffragans, no conclusion would thereby follow proving that Emilia itself, as well as Flaminia, and with them the city of Ravenna, had rendered obedience to the metropolitan of Liguria before the time of Eusebius. This would be so if we reconsider what we conjectured above with Bacchinius concerning the Churches of Forum Cornelii and Vicohabentia [Col. 0110A], in no. 19 and following: first, because in earlier centuries the government of ecclesiastical provinces could not always have been confined within the boundaries of the civil provinces, so that their civil boundaries were identical with their ecclesiastical boundaries; and second, because the Arian schism disturbed the ecclesiastical order of Italy, and those cities could easily have defected from subjection to the bishop of Ravenna and followed Auxentius of Milan amid that general upheaval of all things. Later, after Ambrose restored them to the orthodox faith, they continued to favor the Church of Milan under Eusebius, although their own metropolitan had already been restored by papal decree and imperial sanction.

[Col. 0110B] 34. Having thus examined the conjectures of the critics, which they derived from the form of Italian ecclesiastical government, from the letters of Athanasius and Ambrose, and from the synodal letter of Eusebius of Milan, we now undertake to examine those supplied by the negative argument. “The ancient records,” they say, “mention no other metropolitan of Italy except the Roman and the Milanese in the earliest periods of the Christian era. Therefore all the Churches of Italy must necessarily have been subject to one or the other.”

The very ancient description of the suburbicarian provinces is well known. They obeyed the Roman pontiff as metropolitan, and he consecrated their bishops. Yet that list of suburbicarian provinces includes neither Emilia, nor Flaminia, nor Venetia. Therefore, since we find that neither Aquileia nor Ravenna had yet become metropolises in those times, they must certainly be counted among the suffragans of the archbishopric of Milan.

35. Against this sort of negative argument—which excludes all metropolises except Rome and Milan in the first centuries of the Church—we shall argue deliberately in chapter 3. For the present, we answer briefly with Bacchinius that the same negative argument can be turned against the Milanese, since they too cannot produce any indisputable document from those very early times establishing their metropolitan jurisdiction.

“No one,” says Bacchinius, “can assert by certain documents that there was a metropolitan in Italy before Ambrose.” He subjects to the most rigorous scrutiny, explains, and rejects everything brought forward from earlier times that appears to support the metropolitan status of Milan [Col. 0110D]. Above all, he does not hesitate to consign to the number of the apocryphal certain stories about Saint Barnabas the Apostle, whom they portray as the first founder of the Milanese Church and as metropolitan of Italy.

We, however, shall not introduce our own opinion into that question, nor do we begrudge the most distinguished Ambrosian Church its rights, prerogatives, and honors—especially after the distinguished Joseph Antonius Saxius has adorned with most learned defenses the tradition of his native Church concerning Saint Barnabas’s arrival in Milan. We are defending only the liberty of the equally illustrious and equally celebrated Church of Ravenna. For the present, it is more than sufficient [Col. 0111A] for us that no ancient, positive, and unalterable document whatever—indeed, as they themselves admit, not even the slightest one—nor any testimony of an ancient writer, nor any probable indication, as we have already shown, remains for the Milanese by which they might boast even to the smallest degree of a Ravenna Church subject to them.

36. We therefore omit weighing what they magnify concerning the consecration of certain bishops of Emilia and concerning several other acts of jurisdiction. Nor do we think it necessary to examine on which authorities they rely or how they interpret certain ancient words, for our discourse would be extended farther than we had intended.

There is one point on which we insist: absolutely no, not even the slightest, kind of proof operates against the bishop of Ravenna in favor of Milan [Col. 0111B]. On the contrary, we could certainly produce several positive indications of our exemption from the alleged yoke of servitude. Among these the principal would be that the bishops of Ravenna were accustomed to be consecrated by the Roman pontiff—something which the metropolitans of Milan would not have tolerated if they had possessed metropolitan jurisdiction over the Church of Ravenna, in accordance with the Church’s most ancient and unshaken discipline.

This is proved by the acts of Saint Severus, who was consecrated before Ambrose; and by the acts of Saint Peter Chrysologus, who was consecrated almost fifty years after Ambrose: both were consecrated by Roman pontiffs. I speak of Peter Chrysologus, provided that the commonly held opinion concerning the beginning of metropolitan dignity by this holy bishop is not erroneous—a matter to be discussed below.

A second positive indication of this [Col. 0111C] exemption is furnished by the subscriptions which will be discussed in the following chapter: those of the First Roman Council under Julius I and of the Council of Sardica. Among them, the subscription of the bishop of Ravenna appears before that of the bishop of Milan. This could in no way have happened if the bishop of Ravenna had then been the suffragan of the bishop of Milan. Schelstratius argues in the same way from the subscription of Valerian before Saint Ambrose at the previously described Synod of Aquileia, in order to vindicate the freedom of that Church in those times from the yoke of Milan (Schelst., vol. II, *Ecclesiastical Antiquities*, Dissertation 4, chap. 5, no. 8 and following).

## CHAPTER II. On the Letters of Clement II, Supreme Pontiff of Rome, Assert­ing the Precedence of the Bishop of Ravenna over the Bishop of Milan [Col. 0111D] in Councils

A significant indication of the freedom we have defended is the precedence of seating which Clement II, supreme pontiff, confirmed for the archbishop of Ravenna over the archbishops of Milan and Aquileia at a synod held at Rome in 1047, with the entire synod supporting the ancient right of the people of Ravenna. For if our Church had ever been subject to the yoke of Milan, the Milanese archbishops would have proclaimed it loudly during the heat of the controversy, which, they say, was repeatedly raised at Rome. Yet, by God’s favor, we have never read that this happened; nor would the supreme pontiffs have placed our bishops before the most celebrated successor of Ambrose if they had been marked by such a sign of subjection.

Accordingly, Clement II confirmed for the archbishop of Ravenna the place at the pontiff’s right hand [Col. 0112A] in conciliar session when the emperor was absent, and at his left hand when the emperor was present; and he prohibited the Milanese and Aquileian archbishops from raising any further dispute over such precedence. Ughellus reported Clement’s diploma in his account of the archbishops of Ravenna, where he speaks of Archbishop Humfridus.

This matter so provoked the Milanese that they did not hesitate to brand the synod as a fabrication and Clement’s judgment as false, thereby staining the letters of that pontiff with the mark of forgery. Puricellius stands out among these detractors in the *Life* he wrote of Laurentius Litta. Eustachius a Saint Ubaldo, whom we have mentioned from the beginning, followed in his footsteps (section 4, chapter 11, no. 389).

As for the Aquileians, relying on the strength of the Milanese [Col. 0112B] arguments, they accepted them entirely and pursued the matter no further, as may be seen in P. Bernard Rubeus (chapter 56). They made no effort to vindicate the precedence of their patriarchs. The distinguished Muratorius did indeed report the testimony of a certain Patriarch Dominic (vol. VI, under the year 1047), who wrote that he possessed the right to sit at the pope’s right; the aforementioned Motta repeats the same testimony in his dissertation on metropolitan law, no. 31.

But apart from the fact that this Dominic does not say even a word about whether he enjoyed that prerogative when the archbishop of Ravenna was present, I find no mention whatever of this Dominic in Rubeus, nor is he found in any of the catalogues of the patriarchs of Aquileia listed at the end of his work [Col. 0112C]. Therefore, since the arguments and testimonies of Milanese writers—whatever their authority may be—have, as far as I know, never been examined by the people of Ravenna, perhaps because of their superficiality, I resolved to collect and review them here in summary form.

### § I. Arguments Against the Authenticity of Clement II’s Diploma

37. Puricellius and Eustachius a Saint Ubaldo therefore say that Clement’s letters were composed by some impostor for the benefit of the archbishop of Ravenna and were subsequently deposited both at Ravenna in the library of Saint Vitalis and at Rome in the Vatican archive, from which Ughellus obtained them. Baronius says nothing by which he indicates that he approves them; Norisius likewise says nothing when he mentions them.

Hieronymus [Col. 0112D] Rubeus, the historian of Ravenna who was the first to report the wording of these letters, is a suspect authority for documents of this kind, since under the year 426 he produced another document in favor of the bishop of Ravenna, supposedly issued by the emperor Valentinian III. Against that document, almost all writers after Baronius have raged as against something entirely fabricated.

38. Several considerations weaken the authenticity of Clement’s confirmation. First, its improbability is demonstrated by a contrary decree issued only a few years before Clement II’s Roman synod, at a similar council.

At the coronation of Conrad the Salian, celebrated in 1027 by Pope John XIX at the Vatican, Heribert, archbishop of Ravenna, presumed to take the emperor by the right hand and present him to the pontiff, who was seated at the altar [Col. 0113A]. When the Milanese protested and a tumult arose, Conrad himself publicly declared that the duty of presenting the king belonged equally and fairly to the archbishop of Milan, since he had initiated the consecration and coronation of that king when he entered Italy.

The pontiff, obeying this declaration, adjudicated to the archbishop of Milan the prerogative of presenting the king, and, with a synod convened on the eighth day before the Ides of April of that same year, confirmed it by a law decreeing that henceforth the archbishop of Ravenna should not dare to place himself before the archbishop of Milan in pontifical affairs.

Our authors derived this account from Arnulphus, a Milanese writer whose work was then in manuscript but was later printed, first through the labors of the learned Leibniz and afterward [Col. 0113B] through those of Muratorius, with notes added, in volume IV of the *Scriptores of Italy*.

Thus the council resolved the dispute not in favor of Ravenna but in favor of Milan. The same is written by Galvaneus Flamma, who cites Henry Barbamigra; by Tristanus Calchus; by Sigonius; and by Albericus de Rosate.

The possession of the right to present new emperors makes this law of the council more credible, for that right certainly stood on the side of Milan. For, according to Sigonius himself, this same archbishop accompanied Otto the Great to Rome after first consecrating him in the church of Saint Ambrose and crowning him with the iron crown, and presented him to the pontiff to be anointed and crowned.

They also say that the archbishop of Milan himself performed the same service in 972, on the testimony likewise of Sigonius, who writes of Otto II: “After the assembly had been completed, he proceeded to Rome to receive the third crown of the Roman [Col. 0113C] Empire, with the archbishop himself leading him.””

How, then, could it have been decreed otherwise under Clement II in 1047, and precedence granted to Ravenna, when twenty years earlier the matter had been decided in favor of Milan, and Milan had thereby been deprived of a right it had acquired? This certainly diminishes the credibility of Clement’s letters.

39. Moreover, the aforementioned Arnulphus—whom they regard as an eyewitness author of the previously related history of Clement II’s election, and indeed of the pontificate of Leo IX, Clement’s successor—wrote nothing at all about Clement’s letters. He would have done so if they had been genuine, for that writer did not spare even the Milanese archbishops themselves.

This deserves even greater notice because Arnulphus himself relates that Pope Nicholas II [Col. 0113D] later granted Wido, archbishop of Milan, the privilege of sitting first at his right hand in the Roman council. It is also significant that the same author states that the dispute raised at the inauguration of Conrad the Salian was settled in such a way that the whole controversy thereafter came to rest.

It therefore cannot be true that this dispute broke out again after Conrad’s inauguration and continued until the time of Arnulphus.

40. Since Clement’s diploma also records certain letters of Pope John, successor of Symmachus, by which precedence in councils was granted to the bishop of Ravenna, the Milanese press their argument:

“If, then, those letters of John are genuine, and if Clement II’s diploma itself is genuine [Col. 0114A], how did Wido, archbishop of Milan, sit at the right hand of Nicholas II in 1059, and Ulric, archbishop of Milan, at the right hand of Calixtus II in 1122?”

Add Gratian, who, speaking in distinction 17 of the synods celebrated by Pope Symmachus, says:

“This also ought to be noted: in this council, and in another synod of Pope Symmachus, the bishop of Milan is said to have subscribed and replied before the bishop of Ravenna; from this it is inferred that he also possessed precedence of rank before him.”

Gratian, who, according to Trithemius, composed his *Decree* from 1127 to 1151, was thoroughly informed about the manner in which the two archbishops then took their seats at synods. Therefore, by speaking of the present—“to have,” rather than “to have had”—he sufficiently indicates that during his lifetime the Milanese preceded the Ravennate, and that no account was taken of [Col. 0114B] Clement’s bull. Had it existed, it would not have escaped Gratian.

To sit in a higher place at synods and to speak first, as we find written of the Milanese in the councils of Symmachus, bears the character of an indication of precedence in dignity. This they attempt to prove from Gratian himself, the Gloss, Tiraquellus, Barbosa, and others.

41. We see, however, that in the three synods of Symmachus held in the years 501, 502, and 503, Laurentius of Milan was distinguished by that twofold honor of precedence over Peter, bishop of Ravenna. Indeed, those very synods, Ennodius in his defense of them, King Theodoric in writing to them, and Baronius and Sigonius in their accounts of those synods, whenever they mention both prelates, name Laurentius first and Peter [Col. 0114C] afterward.

At the council held at Rome under Agatho in 680, Mansuetus of Milan subscribed first, then the bishop of Aquileia, and third Theodore of Ravenna. Cardinal Norisius praises this as the true order of subscription in his dissertation *On the Fifth Synod*, chapter 10.

Then, at another assembly held at Rome in 963 under the presidency of John XII and in the presence of Otto I, Walpert of Milan sat and subscribed before the bishop of Ravenna, according to the accounts of Liutprand and Binius.

As stated above, Arnulphus, Galvaneus Flamma, and Ughellus affirm that Wido sat at the right hand of Nicholas II and subscribed first in 1059.

Likewise, at the Lateran Council under Calixtus II, Ulric of Milan occupied the right-hand place of the apostolic pontiff, as is shown by Landulphus of Saint [Col. 0114D] Paul, a writer of that period. He says the same concerning Grosulanus in 1103 and Jordan in 1116, both archbishops of Milan; and from him Puricellius does likewise in the *Life of Laurentius Litta*, chapter 23, no. 42.

But because it does not appear that the archbishop of Ravenna was present with the archbishop of Milan at the synod of Nicholas II, nor can it be established with precision from Landulphus’s account that the Ravennate was present at the assembly of Calixtus when Ulric is said to have sat at the pope’s right, Eustachius a Saint Ubaldo anticipates the difficulty. He believes that at those councils the archbishop of Ravenna must also have been present, because 113 fathers attended the first, more than 300 the second, and perhaps as many as 426; and therefore that he sat beneath the archbishop of Milan, who was first at the pope’s right.

[Col. 0115A] 42. The Milanese themselves supply another argument for suspecting the authenticity of Clement’s letters: the wording of the letters. They do not approve of the address, “Clement, bishop, to all the sons of the Holy Church,” nor of the conclusion, “farewell.”

They say that the controversy did not concern an article of faith whose explanation would affect all the sons of the Church to whom this bull was addressed; and, if the formula of the conclusion is properly considered, “farewell” was inappropriate.

The Clementine letters also reveal that Peter of Ravenna yielded the first place to Laurentius of Milan in the synods of Pope Symmachus not by any right, but out of humility. Yet it is certain that the more holy prelates were, the more firmly they stood for the rights of their Churches; and that it belongs to virtue not to yield the place due to oneself [Col. 0115B].

But let us grant that he yielded out of humility. Must humility also be attributed to Ennodius, King Theodoric, and the other authors who named Laurentius before Peter? What purpose would such humility have served in those synods? And what sort of title to humility would this be, if the first place before Peter of Ravenna was due to Laurentius both because of his earlier consecration and because of the precedence of his own dignity?

Let at least some document be produced by which it may be proved that before the episcopate of Laurentius the first place had been assigned to Ravenna.

43. Furthermore, in the spurious bull Clement II says that Peter of Ravenna yielded to Laurentius in the synods of Symmachus only in that particular case. But why in that case and not in others as an act of humility?

Here is a contradiction [Col. 0115C]: the Milanese did not subscribe and sit before Peter of Ravenna in only one instance but at three different times—namely, in the third, fourth, and fifth synods of Symmachus.

Likewise, if the dispute over seating at synods had been repeatedly debated by our pontifical predecessors, or had scarcely, or never, been brought to an end, as these Clementine letters say, why is it nowhere recorded that there had been a quarrel between these archbishops over the right of precedence?

Indeed, no indication of such a quarrel appears except in the reported account of the coronation of Conrad the Salian, where the decision was pronounced in favor of the Milanese. Therefore, since from the age of Symmachus to the year 1027 no memory of the alleged dispute emerges, it must be said that the Milanese continued in possession of precedence, and that the Clementine letters [Col. 0115D]—which claim that the matter had been disputed repeatedly—do not deserve credence on this point either.

44. The diploma also limps on two further grounds. It says that when a controversy arose in the council of Clement II over precedence in seating between the two archbishops, the Milanese brought forward their own rights and documents. Immediately afterward, however, it presents a certain catalogue of the names of those archbishops who had attended the synod of Pope Symmachus, in which the archbishop of Milan was listed first, without any other right or privilege being alleged.

This seems altogether implausible. Where is the antiquity of the metropolitan see? Where is the ancient subjection of Ravenna? Where is the right to elect and crown the kings of Italy? Why were the examples of precedence obtained in later councils omitted [Col. 0116A]—examples not in doubt, under Agatho in 680 and under John XII in 963? Why is the seating of Laurentius in the synods of Symmachus alone brought forward as an example in a matter of such importance? Certainly no appearance of credibility can be found in such an omission.

Moreover, the letters of John I, which testify that Peter of Ravenna yielded his place in the synods of Symmachus out of humility, are called a privilege in the same diploma of Clement II. For when the Milanese boasted of that example, the Ravennates immediately opposed to them the aforementioned letters of John I, supreme pontiff:

“Against this was shown the privilege of the Church of Ravenna: namely, that the list of names had occurred not by any right but rather by an act of humility [Col. 0116B]; and again, that Pope John, the successor of Symmachus, approved that the privilege itself should be granted.”

But since these letters contain only a testimony, they are entirely inconsistent with the idea of a privilege.

Finally, how can the concluding words of Clement’s bull be verified?

“For we command that the seat of the archbishop of Ravenna shall always be at our right hand and at that of our successors, in accordance with the authority of an ancient constitution.”

What, then, is this ancient constitution in favor of Ravenna? Even if it existed beforehand, with what face could the pontiff shortly before have said the following?

“For when someone claimed for himself the place at our right hand, and to whom it was due by right, this was uncertain to us.”

If the ancient constitution in favor of Ravenna was known to Clement, how could it have been uncertain to him to whom his right hand was owed? Conversely [Col. 0116C], if this was uncertain to him, how could that ancient constitution have been known?

Puricellius and Eustachius therefore conclude:

“No other arguments are needed for rejecting these letters.”

They were consequently fabricated by some amplifier of the privileges of Ravenna after the year 1027, when the question had been raised at the coronation of Conrad and decided in favor of the Milanese.

45. Since the Ravennates could readily object that their bishop was named before the bishop of Milan both at the First Roman Council under Julius I and in several writings—namely, in the distribution of Charlemagne’s gifts as reported by Einhard and preserved by Baluze; in Otto of Freising’s *Deeds of the Emperor Frederick*; and in the *Deeds of the Emperor Otto I* compiled by [Col. 0116D] Liutprand, who calls the archbishop of Ravenna second after the pope—the Milanese respond as follows.

In the year 337, when Julius I held the council, the bishop of Ravenna was not yet a metropolitan. Therefore, his being named before an archbishop under the designation of a simple bishop cannot prove the precedence of Ravenna. The question is which archbishop, after the pope, was first.

Moreover, in those early councils the order of precedence was not observed, as can be seen at Arles, where bishops of other provinces are subscribed before the pope’s legates; and at the aforementioned First Roman Council, where the bishop of Aquileia is placed before Rufus of Carthage, primate of Africa. At Sardica, an alphabetical order is thought to have been used in [Col. 0117A] naming the bishops, according to Binius (vol. I, p. 439, col. 1).

46. As for the distribution of Charlemagne’s gifts, it is not certain whether the Church of Ravenna was named by Charlemagne himself or by the writer of his life. If it was named by Charlemagne himself, this may perhaps be attributed to a special benevolence.

Otto of Freising, who lived beyond the Alps, named first the one he thought closer to himself—namely, the bishop of Aquileia—then the bishop of Ravenna, and third the bishop of Milan.

Liutprand did not say that the bishop of Ravenna had always been the second archbishop after the Roman pontiff, but only that he was so at that particular time—namely, when John X, bishop of Ravenna, had risen to the papal throne through the factions of the powerful woman Theodora. Once this is observed, it is not surprising [Col. 0117B] that at that time the bishop of Ravenna, for this reason, carried greater weight than was proper with certain people, and even at the Apostolic See, above the other metropolitans.

I omit the right to crown the kings of Italy, which has been vaunted a hundred times—indeed, even the right to elect them—which our authors also wish to have supported the prerogative of the bishop of Milan to precede others in ecclesiastical functions. I omit it lest I give readers occasion to repeat the words of Pope Gelasius concerning Acacius of Constantinople:

“We laughed at the claim that they wish to compare the prerogative to that of Milan, because he was the bishop of a royal city.”

(*Letter to the bishops of Dardania*)

### § II. A Response to the Milanese Objections to the Letters of Clement II

47. We have compressed these objections into the preceding [Col. 0117C] paragraph, and set them out in almost the same words and with the same meaning as Father Eustachius, so that anyone may immediately perceive their futility at a glance and without excessive effort.

As for the first objection, if the learned cardinals Baronius and Norisius did not expressly call Clement’s bull apocryphal, but rejected its credibility because of Hieronymus Rubeus, the historian of Ravenna, is this not clear evidence that those eminent men found nothing in the bull that raised any doubt about its authenticity? Were they not men who knew how to distinguish the apocryphal from the authentic, openly reject the apocryphal, and openly establish the authentic?

Although Rubeus may perhaps have shown too little discernment in reporting certain ancient documents, as in the diploma of Valentinian III—which all critics regard as worthless and which we shall discuss in the following [Col. 0117D] chapter 3—he nevertheless enjoys an excellent reputation among everyone for the hundreds and thousands of other matters that he narrates and produces.

Indeed, when Rubeus is so openly reproved on account of Valentinian’s diploma, but is in no way discredited by the learned men who customarily scrutinized such ancient wares with hooked noses and extremely sharp eyes on account of Clement II’s letters, must we not say that they regarded those letters as possessing rather unquestionable authority?

The distinguished Muratorius actually judges them to be such. Speaking of them, he says:

“The bull of Clement II mentioned by Rossi and published by Ughellus truly has every appearance of not being fabricated.”

(Muratori, vol. IV, *Italian Annals*, under the year 1047.)

[Col. 0118A] 48. Yet perhaps the marks which Baronius, Norisius, Muratorius, and other discerning men were unable to detect were detected by Puricellius and Eustachius a Saint Ubaldo. We are surprised that the distinguished Joseph Antonius Saxius also supported them in his notes on Arnulphus, chapter 35, and in his notes on Sigonius.

According to these authors, then, the history of the coronation of Conrad the Salian, which took place in 1027, supplies a second mark of forgery in the Clementine bull. For it was then indicated that the prerogative belonged to the archbishop of Milan rather than to the archbishop of Ravenna: the Milanese was to take the king by the right hand and present him to the supreme pontiff’s [Col. 0118B] right for coronation.

Good heavens! What sort of argument is this? Was the question whether the prerogative of presenting kings belonged to one or the other? Or rather, was it who had the right to sit at the pontiff’s right hand in councils?

It may perhaps have been equitable to grant the former to the Milanese archbishops, who crowned the king with the iron crown when he first entered Italy. But no conclusion followed from that question to the other question concerning seating in councils.

On that occasion the decision was made in favor of Milan, and the right to present Conrad was granted to the Milanese. That right was permanently acquired by him through the pontiff’s decree. But nothing was done, nothing was decreed, concerning seating in synods, which was precisely what had to be proved.

The Muratorius mentioned above also distinguishes one question from the other. After recounting under the year 1027, from Arnulphus, the quarrel that arose over Conrad’s inauguration and the decision of the subsequent synod, he later records under the year 1047 a second dispute concerning seating in councils and calls it a new [Col. 0118C] controversy over precedence:

“A new dispute over precedence arose between the archbishops of Ravenna and Milan and the patriarch of Aquileia, and judgment was given in favor of the Ravennate.”

(Muratori, vol. IV, *Italian Annals*.)

49. “Nevertheless,” reply the Milanese, “the synod convened by John XIX for that very reason on the eighth day before the Ides of April of the same year 1027 decreed that in all pontifical affairs the archbishop of Ravenna should in no way and for all eternity place himself before the archbishop of Milan.”

A papal decree! They were quarrelling over the presentation of the king, yet the synod’s sentence defines precedence of every kind. What a novel order of judicial proceedings!

But let us grant that the whole matter happened in this way; perhaps, as a punishment for the disturbance of the solemnity, the judges who had come to Rome with the emperor and with Eribert of Milan, and who consequently favored Eribert, issued [Col. 0118D] a decree destined to stand forever against every right of the people of Ravenna.

Let it be so, I say. Does it follow, then, that the later reconsideration of this matter in Clement II’s synod is false? Or that Clement’s letters are apocryphal because they claim to revoke the earlier judgment?

Puricellius and Father Eustachius are indeed trifling with this kind of argument. Who does not know that, apart from matters of faith, the very same questions—even when confirmed by conciliar judgments—can and often do return for examination a second and a third time? Who would deny that councils themselves are corrected by councils, and that later decisions are always preferred to earlier ones? Certainly no one who wishes to appear [Col. 0119A] sane would deny it.

How often do we read that the celebrated question between the metropolitan sees of Arles and Vienne was reconsidered, although it had so often been strengthened by papal and conciliar decrees—sometimes in favor of Arles, sometimes in favor of Vienne? But let us omit examples of a matter so evident.

Therefore Clement II’s letters cannot be apocryphal merely because they are later than the synod of John XIX. Rather, they ought to be regarded as possessing greater authority, since they emerged after the controversy had been discussed again and after a papal and synodal judgment had been issued in its favor.

For, as Cicero certainly says, “the most recent things have been corrected, and corrected most thoroughly” (Cicero, *Academic Questions*, book I).

50. Thus far we have proceeded as though the things that Arnulphus was the first of all to write about the controversy over the coronation of Conrad the Salian and about the synod held afterward [Col. 0119B] were true, certain, and beyond doubt.

Yet Arnulphus’s testimony is not so authoritative that no room for doubt remains. He alone—if we believe Pagius, eighty years later, or Muratorius, sixty years later—carefully embellished that little Milanese history.

Rudolphus Glaber, Volpherus, and, to say nothing of others, Wippo, contemporary writers—and among them Wippo, an eyewitness, courtier, and chaplain of Conrad the Salian, who collected all his deeds, especially the coronation of Conrad and his wife at Rome by John XIX—do not utter even a single word about the great scandal allegedly raised by the archbishop of Ravenna, about the king’s much-vaunted judgment, about the struggle between the Milanese and Ravennates which Arnulphus adds took place for that reason, or finally about the synod subsequently held concerning that controversy [Col. 0119C].

Again, would the most meticulous collectors of all the councils—who very frequently publish even the bare titles of synods when their acts are lacking—have ignored this one, which, although concerned only with a controversy over precedence, was nevertheless to be regarded as a matter of no slight importance, as we shall indicate below?

### 51

[Cols. 0119D–0121A]

Sigonius, writing in the fifth century after Arnulf’s inventions, repeats in Book VIII of *The Kingdom of Italy* the story of Conrad’s attempted presentation by the archbishop of Ravenna, and of its assignment to the Milanese by decree of the pontiff. Nevertheless, Sigonius’s account differs considerably from Arnulf’s, as will readily be evident to anyone who reads both. He does not say that a synod was held, nor that precedence was decreed for the Milanese over the Ravennate in all pontifical matters. Thus, to the most exact and learned historian, Arnulf’s account has the odor of a little tale. Sigonius’s narrative is as follows:

> “When all the leading men of Italy had gathered at Rome, as was customary at the coronation of a new emperor, the bishop of Ravenna also arrived. On the day of the Resurrection, when Conrad was to receive the imperial insignia in the Vatican basilica, he was present at the ceremony. While the Milanese bishop happened to be absent, the Ravennate took Conrad by the hand in order to present him to the pontiff standing before the altar. When the Milanese legates noticed this, they loudly proclaimed that this was the office of their bishop, who possessed the right to elect and crown the king of Italy. When a tumult consequently arose among the assembled princes and bishops, Conrad then said, in the hearing of all:

> “‘There is no doubt, reverend fathers, that just as the anointing of the emperor belongs to the Roman pontiff, so the consecration of the king of Italy belongs entirely to the Milanese bishop. Therefore it is proper that, if he is present, the Milanese bishop—by whose hand the future emperor is joined to the kingship of Italy—should present to the pontiff the king whom the pontiff is to advance to the empire, so that by his authority he may rule who by that same pontiff’s ordination has learned and begun to reign.’

> “With the pontiff’s assent, the Milanese was summoned to perform this office. But when it was said that he was absent for a legitimate reason, the pontiff ordered Arderic, bishop of Vercelli, to discharge the duties reserved for his metropolitan. Thus Conrad, presented by Arderic, received the golden crown.”

This is Sigonius’s narrative. Anyone who compares it with Arnulf’s account will easily perceive the fraud of the schismatic author. We omit, for the moment, the observation that in this sequence of events Conrad, or the Milanese legates, claimed no superiority of the Milanese Church over the Ravennate, no metropolitan right, no prior metropolitan standing, and—what is most important—no prerogative of precedence in session from earlier councils, but only the office of crowning the king of Italy.

We likewise omit drawing from the tumult that arose on this occasion among the princes and assembled bishops a significant argument for the greatness of the Ravennate Church, which was regarded as either superior to, or at least not inferior to, the Milanese Church.

But, to return to Arnulf’s fables, he is finally refuted as a liar by Landulf the Elder, a man of the same homeland, intellectual disposition, sect, and general character. Landulf wrote fourteen lengthy paragraphs, or chapters, about Heribert himself, the archbishop of Milan. In them there is not even a syllable about the tumult that arose at the inauguration of the emperor Conrad, nor even a syllable about the synod of John XIX. Indeed, what further diminishes Arnulf’s authority and at the same time makes Landulf’s own account appear highly suspect is that Landulf attributes the quarrel between the archbishops at Rome not, as Arnulf does, to the time of Heribert, but to the time of Archbishop Guido; and he assigns it not to the presentation of the king, but to precedence in the synod of Pope Stephen. There is an error in the pope’s name itself: it was not Stephen but Nicholas II.

Arnulf connects the battle between the two peoples at Rome, caused by the disagreement between their bishops, with Conrad’s coronation under John XIX. Landulf, however, connects it with the synod of Stephen—or rather Nicholas II—because of the dispute over precedence. Does not this contradiction between contemporary authors of the same homeland and sect greatly detract from their trustworthiness and authority, and show that all the things they report concerning this question are pure, rotten inventions? We shall demonstrate this more fully below.

Meanwhile, it will not be out of place to warn the reader that this Landulf the Elder sold almost as many fables as Arnulf, virtually without end. His annotators should be consulted concerning them, especially the distinguished Saxius, who in his *Vindications concerning the Arrival of Saint Barnabas at Milan* also accuses Landulf of fabricating the story that Saint Ambrose had granted the Milanese clergy permission to marry wives. This one fable alone entirely reveals the man’s character.

### 52

[Cols. 0121A–0121C]

The Milanese have attempted to diminish the authority of Hieronymus Rubeus, a distinguished benefactor of letters and famous for the many works he wrote and published, because of the widely circulated diploma of Clement II. Whether Arnulf should be compared with that author may be judged by the learned.

Certainly, as regards Arnulf, this much is evident, and his modern commentators admit it here and there in their notes: his little work is filled with anachronisms, falsehoods, and fables. We say nothing of the donation of Nonantula made by the king of the Burgundians to the Ambrosian Church in expiation for eighty men who had been killed; of Otto II’s liberation from the hands of the Greeks and Saracens; of Conrad Salic’s election, coronation, and arrival in Italy; or of a hundred other matters noted by his commentators.

But does not the entire account of the Milanese schism—or rather heresy—teem with the most disgusting falsehoods? Nearly every word contains a calumny, blasphemy, or attack upon the doctrine of the faith and the Apostolic See. He deceitfully mixes and confuses everything with falsehoods and inventions.

More directly relevant to our subject is the fact that he appears to bear impatiently the summoning and calling of the archbishop of Milan before the Roman pontiff to the Roman synod; he growls and rages. He repeatedly proclaims, to the point of nausea, that Milan is equal to the Roman See.

Can such a writer—one who impiously denies subjection to Christ’s vicar and adulterates all statements, actions, and writings in favor of the Milanese Church—be rashly and thoughtlessly believed concerning his fable about the tumult at Conrad Salic’s coronation and the decree of John XIX’s synod, while every contemporary author without exception, including eyewitnesses, remains silent?

### 53

[Cols. 0121C–0122A]

For this reason the distinguished Muratori himself, when he inserted the history of Conrad’s coronation into his *Annals of Italy*, openly expressed his suspicion in these words: “*Se vogliamo credere ad Arnolfo istorico Milanese*”—“If we are to believe Arnulf, the Milanese historian.”

Regarding our diploma of Clement II, however, he pronounced most emphatically: “*La bolla di Clemente II veramente ha tutta l’apparenza di non esser finta*”—“The bull of Clement II truly has every appearance of not being forged.”

Pagius himself, who evidently had read Arnulf, as appears from the catalogue of authors prefixed to Volume II of his *Breviary*, nevertheless entirely passes over his fable about Conrad’s coronation being disrupted by the Ravennate and about a synod held by John XIX, although later, by contrast, he reports and accepts Clement II’s bull in favor of Ravenna.

Therefore, since Arnulf wrote sixty or eighty years after the letters of Clement II had been issued, one may rightly and reasonably suspect that he composed his invention in order to evade the force of those very letters. We may accordingly turn back against Arnulf, with stronger justification, the words which Puricellus rashly poured out against our Ravennates as though they had forged this bull. After the year 1047, when this question—namely, precedence in council—had again arisen between the archbishops of Milan and Ravenna, that little history was composed by a man who wished thereby to establish firmly for the future the pre-eminence which Milan claimed over Ravenna. Since he believed that nothing could more obstruct the Ravennate cause than a synod held under Pope Clement II, he therefore devised that fiction concerning the year 1027, so that, by means of that fabricated little story, [lacuna] and by assigning it to the aforesaid year 1027, Clement II’s synodal decree might silently be buried and weakened on every occasion, although it had been issued in the year 1047.

### 54

[Cols. 0122A–0122B]

Nor is Arnulf’s fable made more credible by the possession which the Milanese archbishops supposedly had in the year 1027 of presenting the new emperor to the supreme pontiff, as they attempt to prove by citing examples from Sigonius under the years 962 and 972. For such examples do not touch the question of the prerogative of sitting at the pope’s right hand in council—the sole privilege which Clement’s letter insists must be preserved intact for the Ravennates.

The Milanese had to prove their possession of that privilege before the synod, not of the other privilege, which we do not contest and which the archbishop of Ravenna either did not violate at all during Conrad’s coronation or, if he really took the king by the hand in order to claim that honor for himself, perhaps did so in the Milanese’s absence, as Sigonius reports.

### 55

[Cols. 0122B–0123A]

Arnulf’s silence concerning the Ravennate bull of Clement II, although he writes about Clement’s election, is an argument not that the bull is false, but either of his ignorance or, rather, of the malice of this schismatic.
