Since he likewise does not mention the synod held by Clement against the simoniacs, will everything that Saint Peter Damian and other men of the greatest authority committed to memory concerning that synod therefore be false?

That Arnulf either did not know the events conducted under Clement or deliberately falsified them is clear from his own account of that pontiff’s election, the only account he gives of him, if it is compared with the truth of the histories. Arnulf says:

> “When a general assembly of bishops had been held at Rome, it seemed to the king”—that was Henry III—“and to all the bishops that the pope was unjustly occupying the chair. After immediately casting him out, the king put in his place one of the bishops from Germany, whom, after changing his name, he called Clement; from him he also received the crown.”

How many falsehoods in a few lines! The assembly of bishops was held not at Rome but at Sutri, in the presence of King Henry. Pope Gregory VI was not cast out. Rather, recognizing that he could not justly administer the honor of so great a priesthood, he leapt from the papal chair, stripped himself of the pontifical vestments, and, having sought pardon, laid down the dignity of the supreme priesthood.

See the indisputable and almost eyewitness testimony of Pope Victor III in Book III of his *Dialogues*, where he continues the account as follows:

> “After this, he [Henry] entered the City, and, having gathered in the church of the blessed Apostle Peter the clergy and people together with the bishops who had assembled at the aforesaid synod [that of Sutri], by common agreement they elected Clement, bishop of Bamberg.”

Henry, therefore, did not immediately cast out Gregory and substitute one of the German bishops in his place. Rather, Clement’s election took place after the synod of Sutri, where Gregory voluntarily abdicated, and it took place at Rome—not through Henry, but through the Roman clergy and people, together with the bishops of the Synod of Sutri, by common agreement and according to canonical rule.

Arnulf displays no less ignorance in reporting the deeds of Leo IX. For what does he mean when he says, “He [Leo] held two synods in Italy, namely at Pavia and Mantua”? Did he not know of a third at Vercelli and three Roman synods? A man who either neglected or did not know so many matters of the greatest importance and so close to his own times is introduced as a negative witness against Clement’s bull?

### 56

[Cols. 0123A–0124A]

Arnulf indeed relates that Guido, the bishop of Milan, was graciously received at Rome by Nicholas II and sat in council at the pontiff’s right hand. This is likewise confirmed by Landulf the Elder, mentioned above, though he says that the event occurred at the council of Stephen IX, with the archbishop of Ravenna resisting in vain.

Good heavens, whom should we believe? Certainly neither of them. Stephen IX, during his brief pontificate of a few months, held no synod at Rome or anywhere else. Nicholas II did indeed hold a synod in the year 1059, but neither the archbishop of Ravenna nor the archbishop of Milan attended it.

As for Guido of Milan, he was then infected with the stain of simony. He had broken the oath and penance promised into the hands of Saint Peter Damian, had relapsed into heresy, and, together with his concubinary clergy, had become more hardened than before. Far from having gone to Rome and reclined at the pontiff’s right hand in synod, he could not have done so.

Indeed, in the very notes to Arnulf’s history, learned commentators rightly argue that the assertion of both Arnulf and Landulf concerning Guido’s presence at Nicholas’s synod is entirely false. Not only, they say, can Guido’s having gone to Rome and attended the synod be denied on the basis of the silence of all authors; it can also be denied from the acts of the synod itself, in which Guido’s subscription does not appear, and even from Guido’s condemnation by that same synod, as reported by Sigonius.

As for the Ravennate, who at that time was Henry, all authors, as well as the records we possess concerning him, are silent about his attendance at this Roman synod. Ughellus himself is silent, although he introduces Guido of Milan as present at that synod, relying—I do not know on what acts—which he claims to have read; for this reason he is rightly chastised by the authors of the annotations which we find attached to that council.

Nor was the archbishop of Ravenna alone absent from Nicholas’s synod. All his suffragans without exception were absent as well. Perhaps Henry was not in good favor with Nicholas II at that time, or perhaps some disagreements had arisen between them.

This much is certain: although Henry had been accustomed to insert pontifical dating formulas into his charters—as Hieronymus Rubeus reports for the time of Pope Victor, “with the universal pope seated in the apostolic and most sacred church of the blessed Apostle Peter, in the second year”; under Nicholas, and especially in the year 1059, he omitted the pontifical formulas and adopted royal dating instead:

> “In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1059, while Henry, the honorable boy, son of the late Emperor Henry, was reigning in his fourth year, on the twenty-ninth day of December, in the thirteenth indiction, at Ravenna.”

He was still using the same formulas in the following year, 1060.

### 57

[Cols. 0124A–0124D]

Landulf the Younger writes that in the year 1122 Ulric of Milan held the right hand of Calixtus II at the Roman council, in the same manner as the Milanese archbishops had likewise done before him: Grosulanus in 1103 and Jordan in 1116.

Indeed, Landulf boasts that he was an eyewitness to what occurred at the council of Calixtus between Ulric of Milan and Gualterius, the archbishop of Ravenna, and that his own bishop had the precedence.

Ah, what an eyewitness! Gualterius was most certainly not at Rome in 1122, especially in March, or, if one prefers, even in April, the months in which our Milanese writers believe the First General Lateran Council was convened.

This is proved by the indisputable parchments of our archive:

> “In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1122, in the time of our lord Pope Calixtus and the Emperor Henry, on the fifteenth day of March, in the fifteenth indiction, at Ravenna. Gualterius, servant of the servants of God, by divine grace archbishop of the sacred Church of Ravenna, to Lauterius the priest and prior of the church of Saint James situated on the island of Volana, etc.”

Gualterius was therefore at Ravenna on 15 March 1122. He was residing at Cervia on 10 April of the same year:

> “In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1122, on the tenth day of April, in the fifteenth indiction, at Ficocle. With the lord Gualterius, archbishop of the sacred Church of Ravenna, residing in the church of Saint John in the place of Ficocle in order to administer justice, etc.”

But if Pagius is to be trusted—and he cites not a few contemporary authors—that council was convened in the following year and began on 19 March. Gualterius certainly attended it and was one of the judges to whom Calixtus entrusted the task of settling the dispute between the bishops of Pisa and Genoa.

Yet in the duplicate acts of that synod, which are reproduced in the collection of councils, there is no indication whatsoever of a dispute or quarrel between Gualterius and Ulric. Landulf the Younger’s narrative was indeed added in the latest edition of the collection, but its credibility was left to the author.

### 58

[Cols. 0124D–0125B]

This very narrative, to which the distinguished Joseph Antonius Saxius adds his own opinion concerning the primacy of the Church of his homeland over Ravenna and praises Puricellus, who had defended that position most vigorously against Rubeus, either contains a contradiction, favors us, or favors neither side.

Landulf says that he himself was personally present at that synod:

> “I entered the synod and felt great sorrow because I saw the Ravennate contend with the Milanese for the pontiff’s right hand.”

Then he continues:

> “Nevertheless, on Monday, on which the synod began and was held, Ulric himself, the Milanese, did not appear, although the place was vacant, either in the palace or in the synod.”

I ask: how can a quarrel in the synod over precedence in session be reconciled with absence from both the synod and the palace? If Ulric was absent, how did he quarrel? Landulf saw the contenders, yet Ulric was far away? Here, then, is a contradiction.

Why, while the Ravennate Gualterius was contending, was the Milanese absent from the first session of the synod, unless certainly because Gualterius had prevailed? Here, then, Landulf’s narrative favors us.

But when Landulf adds that Ulric sat in the desired place at the second session, why does he not also state that the Ravennate was present at the synod and that he received the second, third, or fourth seat after the Milanese? Why is this omitted? Could not the Ravennate archbishop have been absent from the second session just as the Milanese was absent from the first?

Thus, in the end, this sort of narrative favors no one.

We still remain uncertain about the truth of the narrative itself. Although the distinguished men who recently published this author have attempted to portray him as different from Landulf the Elder and Arnulf, we nevertheless do not place excessive trust in his zeal for enlarging the privileges of his native Church. Our hesitation is certainly increased by the silence of the acts of the synod and of Abbot Suggerius, who was present at the synod itself.

### 59

[Cols. 0125B–0125D]

The examples of the archbishops Grosulanus and Jordan, which Puricellus wishes to have occurred in the years 1103 and 1116, do not bear upon the matter.

First, Landulf alone records them, especially the episode concerning Grosulanus, during whose time Landulf himself was still living in Gaul. Second, in those years no council was held at which the Milanese archbishops participated while sitting at the pontiff’s right hand. Third, even if councils had been held, no bishop of Ravenna could have attended them.

The Roman synod under Paschal II was held not in 1103 or 1105, as the distinguished Saxius attempts to prove against Puricellus, but in 1104, as Pagius says. Apart from the deposition of Bruno, archbishop of Trier, on the authority of a certain anonymous author, no other memory of that synod has survived.

This is certain: the archbishop of Ravenna did not attend that synod, for at that time there was no archbishop there, at least no legitimate one. After the death of the antipope Wibert, the Emperor Henry, hostile to Paschal II, had intruded a certain Otto into the archbishopric of Ravenna. Because he was attached to Henry’s party, Otto refused obedience to the supreme pontiff.

Moreover, the documents issued in his name as “Otto elect,” dated only according to the years of Henry, suggest clearly enough that he never received episcopal consecration:

> “In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1103, in the twentieth year of Henry’s reign, on the thirteenth day of August, in the eleventh indiction. Otto elect, servant of the servants of God, etc.”

What was true in 1103 was also true in the following year, 1104:

> “In the year 1104, in the twenty-second year of Henry, son of the late Emperor Henry, on the twentieth day of the month [lacuna] twelfth. John, by the grace of God of Firminiana, a petitioner indeed, because I petitioned you, Otto elect archbishop, etc.”

### 60

[Cols. 0125D–0126C]

As for the year 1116, it is indeed recorded, as Pagius notes from Puricellus, that the case of Grosulanus was argued with Jordan, then archbishop of Milan, in the Lateran Council under Paschal II.

But that Jordan was present and sat at the pope’s right hand while it was still uncertain whether he was the legitimate archbishop is taught neither by the acts nor by anyone who asserts it—except Landulf the Younger, who certainly was not present.

Nevertheless, whether Jordan sat close to the pontiff or not is of no concern to us. We know with certainty that this occurred in the absence of the archbishop of Ravenna; nor do we concern ourselves anxiously with this Milanese prerogative when our own bishops are not present at the council.

In 1116 no legitimate pastor yet presided over our Church. Rather, there was a certain Jeremiah, substituted by the schismatic Emperor Henry after Otto’s death. He too was merely elect in that same year 1116 and perhaps was never subsequently consecrated bishop. We infer this from the records of our archiepiscopal archive, especially the following:

> “In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1116, in the time of our lord Emperor Henry, on the twenty-eighth day of June, in the ninth indiction, at Ravenna. To the sacred and most blessed lord, and Apostolic Father, lord Jeremiah, elect archbishop of the holy Church of Ravenna, Andreas of Calcinaria, or his sons, your nephews, etc.”

The evidence which Ughellus extracted from some ancient page of Countess Matilda, as though this Jeremiah had been a legitimate bishop, does not contradict our assertion. The distinguished annotator of Ughellus has exposed and explained his delusion sufficiently and more than sufficiently.

Since, therefore, neither intruder could go to Rome or attend Roman synods, it follows that the sitting of the Milanese archbishops Grosulanus and Jordan in the councils of 1104 and 1116—assuming Landulf the Younger is to be trusted—caused no prejudice to the rights of Ravenna.

This is all the more true because our Church had been stripped of nearly all its principal honors by Paschal II himself, then seated in the Apostolic See, at the council held at Guastalla in 1106, especially its metropolitan jurisdiction over the province of Emilia, as reported by Cencius Camerarius, who later became Pope Honorius III. The Church did not return to its former dignity and greatness until Gualterius, the successor of Jeremiah in the archbishopric, was reconciled after rendering obedience to Gelasius II, the Vicar of Christ, and renouncing the schism.

### 61

[Cols. 0126C–0127B]

Let us now gather these little bundles together for a moment.

If discrepancy and dissimilarity among contemporary authors in their accounts of one and the same matter—especially when they belong to the same homeland—are generally regarded by everyone as evidence that the reported event is false, what should we think of the alleged quarrel between the archbishops in the synods?

Arnulf writes that in the year 1027 it occurred between Heribert of Milan and the archbishop of Ravenna of the same name. He asserts that, once a decision favorable to Milan had been issued in the synod of John XIX, the entire controversy thereafter subsided, as Eustachius of Saint Ubaldo, Puricellus’s fellow member, explicitly notes for his own purposes.

Since Arnulf was scribbling his little tales around the year 1085, he consequently testifies that from 1027 until that year, 1085, no such quarrel between the archbishops had again been stirred up.

Nevertheless, despite Arnulf’s clear assertion, his contemporary Landulf the Elder, as we noted above, gives a lengthy account of the same Heribert of Milan without mentioning anything of the controversy, tumult, synod, decision, or battle between the two peoples reported by Arnulf. Instead, he transfers all these events to the time of Guido, archbishop of Milan, more than thirty years after Heribert. He introduces Guido as quarreling with and prevailing over the Ravennate at the council of Nicholas II—whom he calls Stephen—and describes the courtiers and retainers of the two bishops fighting with one another, the Ravennates being defeated, precisely as Arnulf had reported the matter under the year 1027 at Conrad’s coronation.

I am therefore compelled to marvel at so enormous a contradiction between two authors of the same age, homeland, and sect.

### 62

[Cols. 0127B–0127C]

A third author, Landulf the Younger, also enters the discussion; his editors and commentators regard him as more trustworthy than the other two.

When he describes Ulric of Milan defending his own rights in the Lateran synod against Gualterius of Ravenna, he too is silent about the famous decree—if Arnulf is to be believed—of the council held under John XIX, in which the whole matter would have been decided in Ulric’s favor. He is silent about Guido’s precedence over Henry of Ravenna at the council of Stephen IX, if we believe Landulf the Elder. He mentions only the examples of Grosulanus and Jordan, which do not bear upon the matter.

On the basis of these examples, and many other considerations that were not then in mind, Lord Ulric, archbishop of Milan, did not hesitate to obtain that place. These are Landulf’s words. Yet he admits that Ulric did not obtain the desired place at the first session.

Meanwhile, who would not marvel that Ulric did not hesitate to obtain the place on the basis of examples and many other considerations that were not then in mind? A truly novel kind of proof! If Ulric did not then have many other reasons or examples in mind, how could he hope to secure victory for his case through them? But let us pass over these entanglements.

### 63

[Cols. 0127C–0128A]

Thus one of our authors contradicts another; each diminishes the credibility of the other; each casts the other’s histories into doubt and suspicion of falsehood.

Yet all of them agree remarkably on one point: it is impossible that Puricellus, Father Eustachius, and all those who have written about the Milanese Church could have failed to notice that neither Arnulf nor either of the two Landulfs ever, anywhere—and still less on the occasion of such great quarrels—boasted of, or even hinted at, the subjection of the Ravennate Church and the obedience rendered during the first four centuries of our era to the metropolitan of Milan to whom it was subject.

That would have been the greatest, most irresistible, and most legitimate argument and foundation for the desired precedence in the synods—not the rights of crowning and presenting the king, nor the ill-timed and useless examples of earlier archbishops.

What have the Milanese to say to this?

Nevertheless, we have no reason to be offended by this kind of proof and exaggeration. We know how love of one’s homeland carries away the minds of citizens, while each city, deceived by falsehood, draws to itself the fame of its deeds and honors. (*Livy, Book VIII.*)

### 64

[Cols. 0128A–0128D]

Up to this point we have demonstrated that Clement II’s bull is free from the falsity which Puricellus and Father Eustachius attributed to it on the authority of Milanese writers and later synods.

It is now worthwhile to turn back to earlier times and discuss those councils that preceded the age of Clement himself, in which they claim that the Milanese was placed before the Ravennate bishop in session and subscription.

Reserving the synods of Pope Symmachus for final examination, we begin in reverse order with the Roman synod which, they say, was held under John XII in the year 963 before the Emperor Otto I, and at which Walpertus of Milan sat and subscribed before the archbishop of Ravenna, as reported by Liudprand and Binius.

But which synod was it? Was it that impious assembly, detested by all Catholics, which the powerful Augustus convened not while John XII presided, but while he was absent; which dared to issue a sacrilegious judgment against the legitimate pontiff and, after violently deposing him, created Leo VIII as antipope?

Did the Milanese take precedence in that synod? Let it be so; we do not begrudge him the honor. In that disorderly assembly, where the patriarch of Aquileia is named before Walpertus, indeed even Rodulf the deacon, his procurator—whom, if one is to accept the Milanese opinion, who would not say ought to receive the prerogative of the see?—where the pontiff was not present but the emperor presided, and therefore there was no place for the question of whom the pope’s right or left hand should belong to—in such an assembly, I say, Puricellus and Father Eustachius seek precedence.

We do not care about that kind of honor.

As for whether Liudprand and Binius are cited here incorrectly, let us consult what Binius says in his notes to this little council and in his notes to another assembly of the same sort against Benedict V, Roman pontiff. There he protests against the most disgusting impostor who, under Liudprand’s name, inserted these inventions into his history.

Let us therefore examine instead what occurred in the legitimate synod under Agatho in the year 680. For we are pressed too strongly by the authority of Cardinal Noris, who approves the order of the subscriptions of this synod: first Mansuetus of Milan, then the patriarch of Aquileia, and third Theodore of Ravenna.

Theodore, therefore, would be third in the precedence of sees, after the Milanese archbishop.

### 65

[Cols. 0128D–0129A]

In the year 680, or 679, as Pagius believes, Constantine Pogonatus, emperor of the Greeks, wrote to Agatho, Roman pontiff, concerning the convocation of a general synod against the Monothelites.

For this purpose Agatho convened a council of bishops at Rome and ordered another to assemble at Milan, as well as others in Gaul and other regions, so that a solemn delegation might be sent to the general council at Constantinople in the name of all the bishops of the West.

Accordingly, legates from the Gallican, northern, and Milanese synods gathered at Rome for the aforementioned council of Agatho. Among them, according to Pagius, were Mansuetus of Milan and Anastasius of Pavia, representing the bishops of the Milanese province.

It is also certain that Theodore, bishop of Ravenna, was present. He had not yet renounced the schism by which the Church of Ravenna had defected from the Apostolic See sixty years earlier, under the instigation of the archbishop Maurus. On the occasion of this synod, however, when Theodore returned to unity, that schism was extinguished.

### 66

[Cols. 0129A–0129C]

Almost none of the acts of Agatho’s council have survived, except two letters which are known to have been read in the fourth general council: one from Agatho to the Emperor Constantine, and the other a synodal letter subscribed by the bishops of the West.

It is therefore futile to investigate who sat first after the pope or who first gave his name in the conciliar acts. The Milanese have certainly dreamed that Mansuetus preceded Theodore.

They manufacture their argument for precedence solely from the subscriptions which we have just read appended to the synodal letter. Although the question concerns sitting at the pope’s right hand, they nevertheless beg support even from the subscriptions. They do not remember that little or no reliance should be placed on the order of subscriptions, as they themselves proclaim and as we shall repeat below.

Anyone who merely runs over the subscriptions under discussion will very easily recognize the frivolity of these authors, for no order whatsoever was observed among the bishops.

After Pope Agatho, therefore, it is not Mansuetus of Milan who subscribes, but most of the bishops of Apulia, Calabria, and Bruttium. Then follow the Sicilians, led by their metropolitan, the bishop of Syracuse. The legates of Gaul come next; they are followed by Mansuetus, bishop of Milan, with his suffragans, although I do not know whether some bishops of another province are interspersed among them.

After these come the bishops of Lucca and Pisa, together with not a few from Tuscany. Then come again the suburbicarian bishops: those of Tusculum, Anagni, Alatri, and others. They are followed by Agatho of Aquileia with his suffragans. Next come the bishops of the Pentapolis, namely the bishop of Pesaro, the bishop of Ancona, and the others. Then comes the bishop of Perugia, after which the list returns to the bishops of Etruria.

The last of all to subscribe was Theodore, archbishop of Ravenna, together with his suffragans.

67. When, therefore, the Milanese wish to infer an order of precedence from the order of the subscriptions, they will be forced to contradict themselves, [Col. 0129D] since they seek for their own bishop a place immediately after the pope. For, according to the sequence of the subscriptions, they yielded at the Synod of Agatho not only to the suburbicarian bishops—as they are called, whom in almost all other councils we see listed after the prelates of the greater sees—but also to the archbishop of Syracuse and his suffragans, and even to the legates of the Gauls. Yet no sane person would adapt the order of precedence to so confused a series of subscriptions.

I myself suspect that the synodical letter of the Westerners was either subscribed by the bishops present also in the names of those who were absent, or, more likely, that after the synod had concluded it was sent through the various provinces of Italy to be subscribed by bishops who had not [Col. 0130A] attended. Let no one, I ask, condemn me for rashness in explaining this suspicion. I know that everyone repeats that Agatho’s synod consisted of 225 Fathers, and that the synodical letter was signed by the same number. This seems to be clearly confirmed by Eddius’s account in the *Life of Saint Wilfrid, Bishop of York*, who himself subscribed that synod in the name of the northern Churches.

But if what Pagius reports is probable—namely, that from the Milanese council only two bishops were delegated to Rome, Mansuetus the archbishop and Anastasius, bishop of Ticinum—I shall be compelled to doubt whether the authors who wrote about the number of Fathers present at Agatho’s synod may have taken that number solely from the subscriptions to that synodical letter, which was read and inserted into the acts of the ecumenical [Col. 0130B] council, rather than from reliable knowledge of the acts of Agatho’s synod.

How can the delegation of only two bishops from the province of Milan to the Roman synod be reconciled with the subscription of all the bishops of that same province? They cannot be reconciled at all, unless we say either that the bishops who attended the synod added the names of their fellow bishops, or that after the synod had been completed the letter was circulated through the various provinces of Italy so that it might be subscribed even by those who had been absent.

68. Our suspicion is most opportunely strengthened by the very confusion of the subscriptions, as will readily be apparent to anyone who considers it with a calm mind. This is neither novel nor surprising to one who recalls what Mabillon asserts and proves concerning this [Col. 0130C] introduced practice of subscribing, with numerous arguments and examples—too lengthy to repeat here.

The most learned Joseph Garampi made excellent use of this point in a recent dissertation on the silver coin of Benedict III, Supreme Pontiff, in order to prove that Lothair Augustus was by no means present at the synod held at Rome in 853, although the synodal acts were authenticated by his subscription after the name of Pope Leo.

From this very suspicion of ours another may arise: either Theodore of Ravenna and his associates did not attend Agatho’s council, although they later signed the synodical letter brought to them; or, if he did attend, he subscribed it after his departure from Rome. Unless we prefer to say that, because his reconciliation with the Apostolic See was postponed until the end of the council, the last place in the synodical [Col. 0130D] subscription remained for him.

Whatever the truth may be, Agatho’s council supports neither Puricellus nor Father Eustachius; rather, it harms the magnitude and breadth of the Milanese prerogatives, by which they elevate their own bishop above all the bishops of Italy without exception, indeed above all metropolitans.

From this it is clear what judgment should be formed concerning the testimony of Norisius cited by those authors. The eminent scholar does not seem to have noticed the confusion of the subscriptions of the synodical letter, nor that the archbishop of Syracuse was signed before three others, and especially before the bishop of Milan. A man otherwise praised in every kind of learning would certainly not have approved such a disordered series of subscriptions. [Col. 0131A]

What could be devised more effectively to overturn completely the objection concerning Theodore’s subscription than the response of Father Eustachius himself of Saint Ubaldo? Let us at last append his very words.

That learned barefoot Augustinian had produced against the Church of Ticinum, which was seeking to free itself from the Milanese yoke, a certain diploma of Anselm IV, archbishop of Milan, signed, among others, by William, bishop of Pavia. The distinguished Muratori, however, doubted this document and attached several indications of suspicion to it, including the fact that the subscription of the bishop of Pavia occurred not only after the other bishops but also after a long series of priests and abbots.

Our Eustachius therefore tries to dispel this indication [Col. 0131B] of suspicion with a response particularly apt to our purpose:

> “After others of lower rank, namely abbots and priests, the subscription of the bishop of Ticinum is certainly seen. For that reason, without doubt, the place appropriate to him was after the archbishop. But what if, for some reasonable cause, this order was not observed? Sometimes bishops subscribed in councils in a place otherwise not owed to them, either because at the time of subscribing they were occupied with other matters, or because the order of the parties was observed, so that after those who sat on one side had subscribed, those who were more distinguished but sat on the other side subscribed afterward. Concerning this practice, see Hallier, *De Ecclesiastica Hierarchia*, book IV, section 4, chapter 2, article 4, §75, and Cantelius, *Historia Metropolitanae Urbis*, volume I, part I, dissertation 6, chapter 2. Or it happened because sometimes the subscriptions were made tumultuously, with no order observed, [Col. 0131C] but according to the convenience of each person; or finally because, just as a subscription was not necessary in that circumstance, so neither was careful order among those subscribing. . . . Therefore the irregular subscription of the bishop of Ticinum is not of such importance that, since it could have had a reasonable explanation—even if, after five centuries, its precise cause cannot be assigned—and since it is not without precedent, it could cast suspicion of falsity upon this document.”

69. It remains, then, to speak of the councils of Pope Symmachus, where Laurentius of Milan appears to have subscribed before Peter, archbishop of Ravenna. The Milanese have conceived three degrees of precedence acquired by their metropolitan in these synods: precedence in speaking, in session, and in subscription.

They add that the synods themselves—when they name both prelates—prefer the Milanese to the Ravennate, as do King Theodoric, Ennodius [Col. 0131D] the deacon, and others. Gratian, because the Milanese spoke and subscribed first, is said to assert the prerogative of that see. Let us discuss each point briefly.

70. Since, then, in the councils of Symmachus the Milanese speaks before the Ravennate, is he to be considered the more dignified? We read that Laurentius spoke only once in these synods, namely at the third, which Pagius proves to have been the Palmary Synod. But there it was not Laurentius who spoke first: Cresconius, bishop of the Church of Todi, spoke first; Maximus, bishop of the Church of Blera, second; Stephen, bishop of the Church of Venusia, third; and Laurentius of Milan fourth.

Woe [Col. 0132A] to us, then, if we consult the priority of speakers in councils as a means of establishing their superiority! Saint Jerome, speaking of the profession of faith of the Fathers of the Council of Ariminum, adds (*Dialogue against the Luciferians*):

> “On another day, in the church near Ariminum, with crowds of bishops and laypeople gathering together, Bishop Musonius of the province of Byzantium, to whom, on account of his age, the first place was accorded by everyone, spoke in this way,” and so forth.

Is this Musonius therefore to be called a man of greater prerogative and of a more honorable see than the other bishops of the Council of Ariminum?

As for the session which, in the councils of Symmachus, they confidently assign to Laurentius as the more elevated place, with due respect to the Milanese writers we deny it with equal confidence, until the truth is made clear to us by certain arguments or documents, not by a bare subscription, [Col. 0132B] on which we can place no reliance. For what do we have in the synodal acts that even remotely indicates the prerogative of this session?

Our letters of Clement II, however, record that Peter of Ravenna was granted the superior place over Laurentius of Milan in the subscription, not in the session.

71. Finally, as regards the subscription, we would not admit it so readily unless the Clementine letter just mentioned made it credible. For in the notes to one of those synods—namely, the one celebrated in 501—we read that Baluzius asserts:

> “The subscriptions, however, are very different from those published in the ancient copies, and they are arranged in a different order in the book of canons of the Roman Church.”

Regarding the other synod, which [Col. 0132C] some call the Palmary Synod, Pagius repeats Baluzius’s observation concerning the order of the subscriptions. In the last synod we observed this annotation:

> “The subscriptions are the same in the Paris manuscript, but not in the same order.”

Indeed, Binius doubts whether these same subscriptions belong to this synod. Here are his words:

> “In the subscription many Orientals are named who attended the Council of Chalcedon fifty-two years earlier, and of whom, ten years after the time of that council, no mention is found. Hence it appears probable that this subscription belongs not to a Roman synod but to some other synod celebrated long before these times.”

We would therefore certainly not know what weight ought to be assigned to subscriptions of this kind. The doubt would be even stronger [Col. 0132D] if attention were to be paid to the heading of the Palmary Synod:

> “With the venerable man Pope Symmachus presiding, together with the venerable men Laurentius, Maximus, Peter, Laurentius, Aemilianus, and others.”

For which of these two Laurentiuses is to be believed to be the Milanese? And who is that intermediate Maximus? Is he Maximus, bishop of Blera, as in the subscriptions? Or Marcellinus of Aquileia? Yet Marcellinus nowhere subscribes the acts of the synods, although it is certain from the letter of King Theodoric and from the decree of the Senate that he attended at least the second synod. In Marcellinus’s own document, the name of the bishop of Aquileia alone is expressed first, with no consideration given to the bishop of Milan.

What weight, then, I ask, should be assigned to the vaunted subscriptions by which they strive with all their might to prove the precedence of Milan? [Col. 0133A]

The frequently mentioned letter of Clement II, however, leaves no room for doubting it. For it clearly declares that, through the voluntary concession of Peter of Ravenna, and only on that occasion and out of humility alone, Laurentius of Milan was permitted to subscribe first. A diploma was also issued concerning this matter by John, Supreme Pontiff and successor of Symmachus, as a perpetual safeguard and preservation of the Ravennate prerogative; it was read and approved at Clement II’s council by the suffrage of all the Fathers.

What advantage, then, do the Milanese claim for themselves from Laurentius’s subscription in support of an undue preeminence?

72. “The declaration of John, Roman Pontiff and successor of Symmachus, [Col. 0133B] is not to be believed,” they reply, “nor are the Clementine letters, for they are false.”

Very well. Either these letters are genuine or they are false, as they insist. If the first is the case, it must be conceded to us that the subscription over which we are arguing benefits the Milanese nothing. If the second is the case, we shall refer the Milanese to all the observations by which, as we explained above, the foundation of these subscriptions can easily be destroyed. For when their authenticity totters, the subscriptions themselves totter and are brought into doubt.

Add that the Milanese themselves, who, following Baronius, assert that Saint Ambrose presided over the Council of Aquileia, although he sat and subscribed second after Valerian, bishop of Aquileia, provide us with weapons to turn against themselves—even if our Clementine letters were to be rejected [Col. 0133C] as apocryphal.

For the Milanese respond to the objection drawn from Saint Ambrose’s session and subscription:

> “It is not proved that precedence was granted to Valerian by right, but rather by propriety and on account of the greater antiquity of his ordination.”

In the same Council of Aquileia, Norisius observes that Nymenius, bishop of Vercelli, was placed before Anemius, metropolitan of Sirmium; and the same occurred in other councils. For the bishops of the more distinguished sees did not always subscribe first. In the Council of Sardica, Lucilius, bishop of Verona, is read as having subscribed before Protasius of Milan, although, as the Milanese claim, at that time he was subject to Protasius.

Baronius had held the same opinion. He notes that the bishop of Genoa is sometimes placed before the bishop of Brescia and sometimes after him; he says the same of the bishop of Vercelli and of several others. Indeed, a point especially [Col. 0133D] worthy of note is that in the Roman council under Pope Hilary he indicates that Maximus, bishop of Turin, was placed first after the Roman Pontiff, although more distinguished metropolitans were present there, including the bishop of Milan himself.

Hallier, Albertus Picolus—who observes that this was the practice in the subscriptions of metropolitans—Peter de Marca, and Baluzius produce countless other examples.

Therefore, even at the Council of Aquileia, the Fathers of the synod may indeed have deferred to Valerian’s precedence and, in consideration of it, granted him the precedence mentioned above, while always preserving the right of superiority with respect to Saint Ambrose, whom Baronius wished to have presided.

They add that the bishops of Aquileia did not acquire [Col. 0134A] a greater degree of honor than the Milanese from being named before them at the Councils of Arles and Rome. As for Arles, this was because even the legates of the Supreme Pontiff were placed after lesser bishops, and the bishop of Syracuse himself was preferred to the bishop of Aquileia.

As for the Roman council, Rufus of Carthage was placed after the bishop of Aquileia, although, as primate of Africa, he ought to have been placed before him. And so, since no order was observed in the naming of these men, it is not surprising if Theodorus of Dalmatia at Arles, and Benedict of Aquileia at Rome, are named before the province of Italy and the bishop of Milan.

Therefore, just as no greater excellence or preeminence is inferred for the bishops placed first over the Roman Church, the papal legates, or the primate of Africa from those bishops and legates [Col. 0134B] and the bishop of Carthage having been named out of their proper places, so neither should the bishop of Aquileia be considered preeminent over the bishop of Milan because the former was named before the latter in the councils cited.

73. We pass over the other documents of the Milanese intended to strengthen this observation, content with what we have so far produced, in order to dissolve, by their own weapons, the argument for prerogative drawn from the subscription of Laurentius before our Peter.

Even if the letters of Clement II must be considered apocryphal, it nevertheless cannot be proved that the Milanese enjoyed a greater prerogative because the Ravennate was found to have subscribed first in the councils of Symmachus.

Indeed, let us also append whatever conjectures we may have, [Col. 0134C] on the supposition that the Clementine letters are false, and concede to the Milanese that the order of synodal subscriptions is authentic and genuine.

Whatever may be said, then, about those synods of Symmachus which the pontiff himself convened and at which he subscribed first, it is nevertheless certain that one of them was held without Symmachus presiding. The archbishops of Ravenna and Milan presided there, and they also subscribed first of all.

Everyone knows that this synod was compelled by King Theodoric and that the bishops were summoned by him, although he pretended that he possessed Symmachus’s consent, which he had extorted by force.

Why, then, should Theodoric himself not have designated the presidents of the synod, on his own authority, as the Milanese and Ravennate, one before the other? Why should the Ravennate [Col. 0134D] not have unwillingly yielded to the violent king?

Or if they deny that this can be imagined of Theodoric, and wish everything to have been arranged with Symmachus’s consent, cannot it be supposed that both archbishops presided over that council by authority conferred upon them by Symmachus, and that in that circumstance the precedence of the Milanese derived from the pontiff’s will?

The Milanese may perhaps say that Symmachus then had regard to the dignity of the Churches. I do not think so. Otherwise it would have to be said that the Roman Pontiffs, when choosing legates for general and other councils, considered the excellence of rank in those chosen, and not prudence or expertise in the matters to be handled.

In such a case, however, no greater dignity was added to the Milanese Church over the Ravennate, because Laurentius [Col. 0135A] presided over the council first by Symmachus’s will, spoke first, and subscribed first.

When, in that synod, the Ravennate was preceded by the Milanese at the command either of the king or of the pope, what difference did it make to the Ravennate if he subscribed second in other synods in which the Supreme Pontiff himself presided, and in which neither the earlier nor the later subscription established a prerogative?

74. I had added these points in support of the supposition that the Clementine diploma was false. But whether that diploma is genuine or not, the Milanese vainly seek more substantial rights of prerogative from these Symmachian subscriptions.

It is easy to answer Gratian, who constructs from them an argument for the excellence of the archbishop of Milan, as well as all the more recent writers cited by Eustachius: they wrongly measure the ancient practice of councils [Col. 0135B] by the custom introduced in their own time.

The evidence which the Milanese themselves frankly supplied above, the teaching of many authors concerning this discipline, and especially what we have observed in the councils of Symmachus, prove that in antiquity no account was taken of the prerogatives of sees in the subscriptions of councils.

In later centuries, indeed, the earlier discipline began to cool. The prelates of the Churches forgot the command of Christ the Lord, “Let the greater among you become as the younger, and the leader as one who serves” (Luke 22:26), and instead assumed the weakness of the disciples who had not yet been confirmed: “Which of them should be regarded as the greatest?” (ibid., 24). Ambition put on the appearance of necessity for defending the rights of one’s own Church.

Gratian had regard to this, and so did his [Col. 0135C] followers in the cases cited, but not to the simplicity of the earliest centuries.

75. Nevertheless, because of the authority of Gratian cited above, Eustachius of Saint Ubaldo is somewhat irritated with Felice Antonio Guarnieri, who attributed the earlier subscription of the Milanese in the councils of Symmachus not to superiority of dignity but to the earlier date of his ordination as bishop.

Since Guarnieri’s reasoning agreed perfectly with the arguments of the Milanese, by which they try to defend the preeminence of their own bishop against the bishops of Aquileia, and since it also accorded with the opinion of the sounder critics, our Augustinian sets Gratian against Guarnieri. Gratian says that, since Laurentius subscribed before Peter of Ravenna, he “has the prerogative of the See” before him.

Eustachius observes that Gratian does not [Col. 0135D] say “the prerogative of rank” (*Ordinis*), but “the prerogative of the See” (*Sedis*); nor does he say “had,” but “has”—that is, at the time when Gratian was writing. He would not have said this, Eustachius notes, if the letters of Clement II had been authentic, since he would have known of them.

I, however, had thought that Guarnieri’s opinion should have been weakened not by Gratian’s authority—which does not greatly influence our age—but by stronger arguments. Or one should investigate whether Laurentius entered the episcopate before Peter, or not. For if the Ravennate had perhaps become a bishop first, that would have been by far the strongest argument against Guarnieri.

For the rest, unless Gratian’s assertion rests on a firmer foundation than the Symmachian subscriptions, we gladly leave it among [Col. 0136A] the countless other statements of this author that everyone rejects. Nor are we astonished that an otherwise distinguished compiler of decretals failed to remember the Clementine diploma, since among so many other matters, perhaps of greater importance and requiring deeper investigation, he either remained silent, omitted them, was ignorant of them, or misunderstood them.

76. As for the synods of Symmachus, and King Theodoric, and Ennodius, and a hundred others, if one wishes, who, when naming both metropolitans, place the Milanese first—it is truly ridiculous to turn this into an argument for superiority.

Saint Paul writes to the Galatians: “When they recognized the grace that had been given to me, James and Cephas” (Galatians 2:9). Did Paul therefore consider Cephas, the prince of the apostles, inferior?

Athanasius, praising the synodical [Col. 0136B] letter of the Council of Sardica and listing the bishops who subscribed it, says (*Apology 2*):

> “These are the names of those who subscribed in the synod, and of the other men: Hosius from Spain; Julius of Rome through Archidamus and Philoxenus, his priests; Protogenes of Sardica,” and so forth.

Is Julius, the Roman Pontiff, therefore to be placed after Hosius of Córdoba?

But what becomes of the Milanese preeminence over the bishops of Vercelli if we abuse the authority of Athanasius himself, who says in his letter to the Solitaries:

> “The men of most illustrious confession, religious men and good bishops, are Paulinus of Trier, Lucifer, bishop of Sardinia, Eusebius of Vercelli, Dionysius of Milan.”

Again, because the fifth Council of Constantinople, in condemning the Three Chapters, says, “We condemn and anathematize [Col. 0136C] what Theodoret wrote impiously against the true faith, against the Twelve Chapters of Saint Cyril, and against the First Synod of Ephesus,” and so forth, is that universal Council of Ephesus to be considered inferior to Saint Cyril and his chapters?

Because Saint Augustine, whose authority ought to carry more weight [Col. 0136D] than Theodoric’s, says that, having received the volume of that same council—the Pseudo-Sardican Council—and considering its decrees, he read that Athanasius of Alexandria, a Catholic bishop, and Julius, the bishop of the Roman Church, likewise a Catholic, had been rejected by that Council of Sardica (*Against Cresconius*, book IV; letters 44 and 163), are we therefore to suppose that Augustine wished to place Athanasius before the Supreme Pontiff Julius in the prerogative of the see?

77. But why say more? In the Roman council under Julius I, is not the bishop of Ravenna named before the bishop of Milan? In the Council of Sardica, do we not read the two prelates subscribed three times in that same order?

And apart from the hundred, apart from the thousand authors who chose to praise the Ravennate before the Milanese, did not Sigonius himself—whom Eustachius tries to draw over to his side—assign Milan only the fourth place among the leading Churches of Italy, placing Ravenna before it?

We, however, do not rely so heavily on arguments of this kind that we would derive the prerogatives of our Church from them. It is enough for us to oppose examples to examples, to show that some are false, and to explain others according to sound reasoning, custom, and discipline, so that we may expose the weakness of the arguments which the Milanese [Col. 0137A] employ against the diploma of Clement II.

78. Yet they still do not cease attacking that diploma. Examining its meaning and wording to the very core, they draw new indications of falsity both from the opening formula, “Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the sons of the Church,” and from the salutation, “Farewell in good health.”

“It was not a matter,” they say, “of some article of faith, so that the letter should be addressed to all the sons of the Church. Moreover, the salutation ‘Farewell in good health’ is by no means appropriate to all the sons of the Church.”

Nonsense! It was indeed not a matter of an article of faith; but it was a question whose settlement ought not to be unknown to all the sons of the Church, since the good order of councils and the unanimity and concord of the Fathers are an edification to all Christians, whereas the altercations, ambitions, and dissensions [Col. 0137B] of the Fathers are a scandal and a source of ridicule to everyone.

The question also concerned those metropolitans of Italy who, because of the extent of their sees and dignity, stood before the eyes of the entire Christian world—namely, the Milanese and Ravennate.

Furthermore, such a controversy could have arisen in any synods, even general ones, which represent the universal Church. It was therefore expedient to establish a rule and publish it solemnly, so that it would become known everywhere and bind everyone.

For the rest, we read letters of Pope Urban II addressed “to all the sons of the Church” on behalf of the Church of Saint Martin of Tours, although they concerned neither a matter of faith nor a matter of discipline pertaining to the universal Church.

The same should be said of thousands [Col. 0137C] of other diplomas of the Supreme Pontiffs that bear this address.

As for the salutation “Farewell in good health,” if it is less suitable for all the faithful of Christ, let the Milanese teach us a more appropriate form of salutation. Meanwhile, we remind them that medieval diplomas are full of similar salutations—“Farewell in good health”—even when they are addressed to all the sons of the Church.

79. The Milanese add that this document of the Ravennates is apocryphal because it reports that Peter of Ravenna yielded to Laurentius of Milan in the Symmachian councils, not by any right but out of humility, although the proper duties of virtue and office would have required his Church to defend its rights rather than yield them.

Let the Milanese Arnulphus answer this very slight objection, together with his archbishop Heribertus. When the Ravennate [Col. 0137D] prelate—also called Heribertus—was disputing with the Milanese over the right to present the king for coronation in 1027, “Lord Heribertus, archbishop of the holy Milanese Church, a vigorous and modest man, indeed exceedingly patient, lest a tumult arise among the people, opposed to his [the Ravennate archbishop’s] dreadful madness a holy restraint; he humbly withdrew from the storm of so great a sedition and urged his fellow bishops and all his own people, who condemned this rashness and wished to resist him openly, by gentle persuasion to avoid scandal by humbling themselves.”

Why, then, did the archbishop of Milan at that time withdraw from the tumult out of humility, leave the church, and restrain his fellow bishops? Do not the Milanese [Col. 0138A] teach that the holier prelates stood more firmly for the rights of their Churches? Would virtue not have consisted in yielding no place but maintaining what was owed to them?

These are the words and moral lesson of Father Eustachius. If, therefore, the Clementine letters are to be regarded as apocryphal because they assert that Peter yielded to Laurentius out of humility in the Symmachian synods, then Arnulphus’s narrative must also bear the same mark, since it plainly explains that Heribertus of Milan withdrew from the church and did not resist the Ravennate out of humility.

80. But Father Eustachius presses the point:

> “For what purpose, from what necessity, or for what good was humility then to be exercised by Peter of Ravenna in the Symmachian synods with regard to the place?”

Let him therefore ask his own Arnulphus for what purpose, from what necessity, or for what good Heribertus of Milan withdrew from the tumult at Conrad’s [Col. 0138B] coronation, left the church, and reproved his fellow bishops.

“Lest,” that writing replies—the writing from which Arnulphus is said to have drawn his narrative, as Beroldus testifies, and whose authority we refrain from discussing again since its value will easily appear to readers—“lest, I say, a tumult arise among the people . . . so that they might avoid scandal by humbling themselves, and so that a violent sedition might not grow among the great multitude, lest the devil, the author of every error, should snatch the good of peace from the bishops’ purpose—a good which by custom ought to be present among laymen.”

These words of the cited writing can teach Father Eustachius the purpose, necessity, and good for which humility was to be exercised by Peter of Ravenna in the councils of Symmachus with respect to the subscription—or, [Col. 0138C] if he prefers, with respect to the place of session.

81. Yet there was no place for humility, Father Eustachius insists again, both because no document can be produced proving that before the synods of Symmachus the Ravennate bishop had ever preceded the Milanese in councils, so that one might say that the preeminence of place had been renounced under Symmachus out of humility, and also because, as a result of his more ancient consecration, precedence was still owed to Laurentius of Milan, whose preeminence of proper dignity had otherwise been cut off. From what source, then, did Peter yield his place to him out of humility?

The documents of our precedence before the time of Symmachus are supplied [Col. 0138D] by the Roman council under Julius I and by the Council of Sardica, in which we read that the Ravennate was placed before the Milanese.

Another document consists in the fact that nowhere in councils before Symmachus is the Milanese bishop found placed before the Ravennate. What our authors object against the former documents we shall indicate below; but what they object against the latter negative evidence we entirely fail to understand.

It could therefore rightly be said that Peter yielded to Laurentius in the councils of Symmachus out of humility.

As for the claim that precedence was owed to Laurentius because he had been consecrated bishop first, we pass over the question of what the preeminence of his proper dignity was, by which the Milanese could elevate himself above the archbishop of Ravenna—especially in the time of Symmachus.

It may be difficult for these authors to prove this preeminence of dignity if we compare and weigh the two cities, [Col. 0139A] the two Churches, their origins, their extent, their prerogatives, and their prelates in the light of purely historical truth, with legends excluded.

For the rest, let the most learned Milanese take care lest, while trying to construct a new argument from the earlier date of the ordination against the Clementine letters, they advance our cause, though unwillingly and unknowingly. For if, despite Laurentius’s earlier consecration, Peter out of humility granted him the first place, we have another argument readily available by which to prove the excellence of the Ravennate archbishops over those of Milan.

82. It is better not to dwell longer on these points, so that we may hear the final indications of falsity which Puricellus and Eustachius of Saint Ubaldo think they find in the Clementine diploma.

They consider one of them to be the statement [Col. 0139B] in that diploma that Peter of Ravenna yielded to the Milanese “on that occasion alone.” “The matter is inconsistent,” they say. “For in three Symmachian synods Peter of Ravenna sat and subscribed second after the Milanese, whereas here he is said to have granted this concession only on that occasion.”

How well they reason! As though *illo casu* (“on that occasion”) necessarily meant “for one occurrence,” and could in no way be interpreted as referring to those synods which were held in the circumstances of Symmachus; or as though, because the two men acted as presidents at only one of them, precedence granted to the Milanese out of Peter’s humility could not be understood as applying to that synod alone.

Even if the Clementine words were to be explained as referring to that one occasion, why should we understand them as referring to one synod only? What novice in grammar [Col. 0139C] would ever interpret them in that way?

These synods were repeated over several successive years, and perhaps the Fathers never departed from Rome for that reason, since the tumult did not subside even after the councils had been repeated and decrees had been issued against the supporters of the antipope. Indeed, some consider these councils to have been one single council continuing over all those years.

Therefore John I, successor of Symmachus, could rightly include all those assemblies in the declaration issued on behalf of the Ravennate, to which the Clementine letters refer, and could indicate by the words “on that occasion alone,” or even “on that one occasion alone,” the whole series.

Once Puricellus’s opinion is admitted—that Laurentius preceded Peter three times—the words of the Clementine diploma by no means produce a contradiction.

There is nothing surprising if, after precedence had been granted out of [Col. 0139D] humility at the first synod, the same humility persuaded Peter to grant it at the subsequent synods, lest repeated controversy should provoke scandal, and lest those who had come to Rome to settle the most detestable schism should be said to renew another dispute over empty titles of precedence.

83. It is shameful to linger any longer over such intricacies, all the more because the authors mentioned persist in vaunting other indications of the same kind.

The second is that Clement II allegedly said in his letters: “What had often been debated by our predecessors the pontiffs had scarcely, or not at all, been brought to an end”—namely, the quarrel over precedence in the synods among those three contenders.

“Where,” they ask, [Col. 0140A] “are the indications that this quarrel was repeated?”

We read of it being raised only at the coronation of Conrad the Salian in 1027, when Heribertus, the archbishop of Ravenna, had arrogated to himself the office belonging to the archbishop of Milan.

Indeed, we add, even at that emperor’s inauguration the dispute was not over the right of precedence in councils.

But what follows from that? Could this contention therefore not have arisen in any other councils before 1027? Could it not have arisen in the Symmachian synods, though it was quieted by the humility of the Ravennate? Does the subsequent declaration of John I not indicate this with sufficient clarity?

Could this question not have been debated in so many other synods in which we see the Ravennate sometimes and the Milanese sometimes subscribed after the Roman Pontiff?

Are we therefore to conclude that, because these quarrels were unknown to Puricellus and Father Eustachius, they were also unknown to the [Col. 0140B] Fathers who, eight centuries earlier, had gathered in Clement’s synod?

84. Why, then, they exclaim, is the following said to be the sole evidence in this synod on behalf of all the rights of the Church of Milan: “a certain list of the names of those archbishops who attended the synod of Pope Symmachus, in which the Milanese archbishop had been written before them”? Why were a thousand other, more important rights of the Milanese omitted? Where is the seniority of the metropolitan see? Where is the ancient subjection of the Ravennate Church? Why were the examples of the precedence so often acquired over Ravenna—under Agatho in 680 and under John XII in 963, discussed above—passed over? With these matters of such importance omitted, is only Laurence’s sitting under Symmachus—say rather, his being written before him—remembered?

Please, Milanese friends, use more moderate language. Why will you boast of the seniority of your metropolitan see when the question is still before the court whether the Milanese see arose before the Ravennate? The arguments that the Ravennates will bring forward in the following chapter 3 are certainly not so weak as to permit so easy a reply. As for the ancient subjection of our Church, it would be better for you now to moderate your opinion. Granted that the most illustrious metropolitan of Insubria arose at the end of the fourth century, whereas ours came into existence only at the beginning of the fifth: it nevertheless remains utterly false that the Ravennates rendered obedience even for a single day to the bishop of Milan, as I believe has already been demonstrated in the preceding chapter. What right did the power of electing and crowning the kings of Italy—which you repeat here as well—add to the Milanese bishop’s authority in ecclesiastical affairs? What right did the power of crowning the supreme pontiffs ever acquire for the bishop of Ostia over the bishops of Ravenna, Aquileia, or Milan?

85. We have already seen above, in numbers 44, 45, and 46, that the precedence mentioned under Agatho and John XII is, in the one case, in no way proved, and in the other, entirely false. What if the Ravennates produce more certain documents proving that they obtained precedence over Milan in councils held after the synods of Symmachus, before the coronation of Conrad the Salian, and before the diploma of Clement II?

The first document—and indeed a very clear one—was supplied to us by the distinguished Joseph Garampi. It was further brought forward in his dissertation on the silver coin of Benedict III. May we here reproduce the words of that most learned man:

> “I infer that the emperor Louis was present at this council, held in the Church of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, at Rome in the year 850, from a certain synodal decree issued in the case of Peter, bishop of Arezzo, and Cantius, bishop of the Church of Siena. It was first published by the distinguished Muratori, p. 389 of volume IV of *Italian Antiquities of the Middle Ages*, and again by the distinguished Giovanni Domenico Mansi, p. 936 of volume I of the *Supplement to the Councils of Veneto-Labbe*. Twelve bishops subscribe to it, among them John, archbishop of Ravenna; Angelbert, archbishop of Milan; Ambrose, bishop of Lucca; Oschisius, bishop of Pistoia; Donatus of Fiesole; Gerard of Florence; John of Pisa; Andrew of Volterra; Taceprand of Chiusi; Otto of Roselle; and John of Tuscania.
>
> “Since this document bears no certain chronological indication, it seemed highly probable to the distinguished Muratori that it should be referred to the council convened in the Vatican Basilica on 8 December 853. Yet the emperor Louis was not present at that council—although he had taken part in the aforesaid synodal judgment, as we observed above in number 7 of this chapter—nor were those bishops whom we have named and who signed the document present there. For, although they subscribe the document and were present, as Muratori states on p. 391 at the cited place, they were certainly not present at the council of 853, since their names appear nowhere among its subscriptions, published by Holstenius in *Roman Collection*, part II, p. 114, and in volume IX of the Venetian edition of the *Councils*, p. 1137.
>
> “Indeed, John himself, archbishop of Ravenna, signed the document and was present, as appears on p. 391 of the same work; yet he was absent from the council of 853 and subscribed through his legate. For there we read: ‘Paul the deacon, acting in the place of John, archbishop of Ravenna . . .’
>
> “I, however, according to my own judgment, believe that the document was issued at the council convened at Rome on 16 December, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 850, concerning Anastasius. Leo IV had ordered the history of that council to be painted in the Vatican Basilica, with an inscription in which, among other things, the following was recorded: ‘After the Roman pontiff, the archbishop of Ravenna and the archbishop of Milan, together with the others mentioned in number 75, concurred in this excommunication’—as reported by Holstenius in *Roman Collection*, part II, p. 109, and in the cited volume of the *Councils*, p. 1145.
>
> “Since, therefore, the same men—John, archbishop of Ravenna, and Angelbert, archbishop of Milan—were present and subscribed both the aforesaid synodal decree and the council of 16 December 850, it seems to me exceedingly probable that the aforementioned decree was produced and enacted at this council. Accordingly, I would not hesitate to affirm that the emperor Louis was present at the Roman council of 850, and so forth.”

86. A second document is furnished by the Ravennate council held in the presence of John XIII, Roman pontiff, and the emperor Otto I in 967. There Walpert, archbishop of Milan, subscribed after Peter of Ravenna to the condemnation of the bishop of Salisbury.

Since this council was restored in the following year, 968, on account of certain affairs of the Church of Magdeburg, and since at that same synod at Ravenna some exchange—I know not what—was arranged between the bishops of Magdeburg and Halberstadt, the *Magdeburg Chronicle* reports that Peter, archbishop of Ravenna, and very many bishops of Italy and Germany also subscribed to this exchange in the year 968 from the Lord’s Incarnation, in the twelfth indiction. Walpert of Milan was probably confused among the many Italian bishops.

We omit other examples of this kind. The few already cited, which we believe to be open to no objection, sufficiently and more than sufficiently prove the preeminence of our archbishops in councils held before the coronation of the Salian emperor and before Clement II’s letters.

Let the most learned defenders of the Milanese metropolitan see cease opposing to us the precedence allegedly obtained in the earliest councils, the right of electing kings, and the primordial suffragan status of our bishops. Let them learn—I beg them—from their own highly praised authorities, Arnulf and both Landulfs, who, in their annals, uttered not a word about the earlier origin of the metropolitan see, not a word about the ancient subjection of the Ravennates, and not a word about precedence in the synods of Agatho and John XII when recounting the disputes between their bishops and ours. Let them learn, I say, not to turn such prerogatives into an argument for the falsity of the Clementine diploma.

87. But behold another quibble from our Augustinian opponents. That privilege of John I, the successor of Symmachus, which is reported in Clement’s bull, casts suspicion upon the bull itself. Here our opponent seems to himself to have perceived something quite acute. Let us continue listening:

> “At most,” he says, “the matter concerned a simple testimony given by John I himself: namely, that Peter of Ravenna had yielded his place to Laurence out of humility and only on that particular occasion. But a simple testimony cannot be called a privilege. Moreover, Clement II established that the Ravennate see should be on the pope’s right when the emperor was absent, but on his left when the emperor was present, in accordance with the authority of an ancient constitution. And what was this ancient constitution in favor of Ravenna? And if it existed, how could Clement II have said shortly before: ‘For whoever claimed for himself the place on our right, and to whom it was due by right, was unknown to us’? For if the ancient constitution in favor of Ravenna was known to Clement II, how could it not likewise have been certain to him to whom the place on the pontiff’s right was legally due? And if it was uncertain to him, what was this constitution, and whose authority did it possess? No further arguments are needed to reject those letters.”

What a fine argument indeed! What a magnificent conclusion!

88. John I’s testimony could be called a privilege even if it presented nothing more than a bare attestation: either because the testimony concerned a privilege of the Ravennate Church, and the testimony of the supreme pontiff concerning a privilege is itself a privilege; or because the testimony itself decreed that the prerogative of the Ravennate Church would not be impaired by Peter’s voluntary yielding of his place on that one occasion at the Synod of Symmachus; or because, in the same testimony, John I also confirmed the Ravennate prerogative of sitting before the Milanese.

In any case, John I’s testimony, as reported by Clement II, could both constitute and be called a decree and a privilege. Moreover, this very testimony could have been that ancient constitution by whose authority the Roman synod, together with Clement II, pronounced judgment in favor of Ravenna—unless someone should produce the privileges of still earlier pontiffs, granted to the Ravennate Church, the firstborn of the apostolic see, which are mentioned by Saint Gregory the Great.

89. But, good God, what shall we answer to that dilemma by which we feel ourselves entangled and constricted: If the ancient constitution in favor of Ravenna was known to Clement II, how could it not have been certain to him to whom the place on the pontiff’s right was legally due? And if it was uncertain to him, what was this constitution, and whose authority did it possess?

Woe to us because of such dilemmas! When the question of precedence in seating arose between the archbishops, the pontiff—a German and perhaps inexperienced in Italian affairs—did not know to whom it was due, because this ancient constitution, which had been hidden from him, had not yet been read in the synod. Once the ancient constitution had been read and approved in the synod, behold, it became known to Clement; behold, in accordance with it, he pronounced in favor of Ravenna. While the constitution remained uncertain, it possessed no authority; but once it became certain through its reading and the examination conducted concerning it in the synod, it acquired full authority with Clement and all the Fathers.

What an easy escape from the labyrinth! It was enough to attend to the sequence of Clement’s letters, which our authors had energetically distorted. Let them say, then: Are further arguments needed to cast out those letters?

90. Yet the defenders of the Milanese metropolitan see were not unaware that many things could be brought forward in favor of the Ravennate Church which would greatly weaken, indeed completely overturn, their badly stitched-together hypothesis. Accordingly, they raised some of these objections against themselves and attempted to dissolve them, but without success.

Thus, when the bishop of Ravenna is named before the bishop of Milan in the list of bishops at the Roman council under Julius I, they say that this has no significance for establishing the precedence of the Ravennate bishop, because at that time he was not yet a metropolitan but merely a bishop. The designation of a simple bishop before an archbishop, they say, does not prove his precedence, since the question is which archbishop was first after the pope.

Eustachius might also have added the Council of Sardica, where the Ravennate is written before the Milanese three times, and by the same very easy escape diminished the force of those subscriptions.

As for whether it is the greatest error in reasoning to establish something uncertain by means of something equally uncertain—or, worse, to disprove something certain by means of another matter that is doubtful and itself under dispute—I shall appeal to students of logic, and I shall challenge our Milanese friends before them.

For they assume that at the time of the Roman and Sardican councils the Milanese bishop was already a metropolitan, although the most learned authorities have shown this to be far removed from the truth, deriving the beginning of this dignity only from the time of Ambrose, after the Sardican council and the Roman synod under Julius; or else they assume that at the time of the Roman and Sardican councils the bishop of Ravenna had not yet been raised to that honor, although there are celebrated writers and weighty arguments that indicate and almost demonstrate the contrary.

Even if we granted that the Milanese bishop was then marked by metropolitan honor while the Ravennate was merely a bishop, did they not also wish the latter to have obeyed the former at that same time as a suffragan? Who, however, would say that among the more distinguished prelates of the principal Churches, the lesser bishop was in those days placed before his metropolitan, as in the Roman council cited here?

“While the venerable men were seated and hearing together with him”—that is, with Julius, the Roman pontiff—“Benedict, bishop of Aquileia; Rufus, bishop of Carthage; Agapitus, bishop of the Ravennate Church; Julius, bishop of Milan; Lucian, bishop of Mauriana; and the remaining 116 bishops with them.”

We do not speak of the Council of Sardica, because when the Milanese are pressed by the subscription even of the bishop of Aquileia, they reply that the subscriptions of this council were arranged in alphabetical order, and they cite Binius. Yet, when the matter is carefully considered, it is childish to believe that in so august and numerous an assembly the bishops were called to subscribe alphabetically, rather than according to the dignity of their Churches, or according to the antiquity of their consecration, or perhaps occasionally because of the reputation, holiness, learning, or skill in administering ecclesiastical affairs possessed by some bishop.

For our part, in accordance with what was said more fully in the preceding paragraphs, we disdain to derive arguments for a certain prerogative from so turbid a source as the subscriptions of councils.

91. Since Einhard, in distributing the largesses of Charlemagne, places the Ravennate Church before the Milanese, our authors wish to inquire whether Charlemagne himself did this out of some special benevolence, or whether Einhard, the historian of his life, did it on his own initiative. For Otto of Freising, in the last place among the principal Churches of Italy, mentions Milan.

They say that, being a man who lived beyond the Alps, he began his account with the metropolitan sees nearest to him—Aquileia and Ravenna—and ended with the more distant one, Milan. Whether in this matter our authors measured the regions according to the true lines of geography, and whether Freising, a city of Bavaria whose bishop Otto was, or rather the Cistercian monastery of Morimond in France, in the diocese of Langres, where he had long resided before his episcopate and many years before his death, which occurred there, is nearer to Ravenna than to Milan, let others decide.

Let them likewise decide to whose fault it should be attributed that Gelasius I, that most learned pontiff, praised Ravenna before Milan when he wrote against Acacius of Constantinople to the bishops of Dardania, saying:

> “Did an emperor not reside for many years at Ravenna, at Milan, at Sirmium, and at Trier? Did the priests of these cities ever usurp for their dignities anything beyond the measure assigned to them from ancient times?”

Let them likewise decide to whose fault it should be attributed that Cardinal Bona excluded the bishop of Milan from the use of the pallium for many centuries and granted it in Italy only to the bishop of Ravenna:

> “Moreover,” he says, “no one versed in ancient history is unaware that this honor was not granted to all archbishops, but only to those who were preeminent among them. For in Gaul it was sent to no one except the bishop of Arles, concerning which there are letters of Vigilius to Auxanius, of Pelagius I to Sapaudus, and of Gregory the Great to Childebert, king of the Franks, book IV, letter 53. In Spain, only to the bishop of Seville; in Dalmatia, to the bishop of Salona; in Italy, to the bishop of Ravenna; in Sicily, to the bishop of Syracuse; in Sardinia, to the bishop of Cagliari, as is clear from Gregory’s letters, and so forth.” (*Bona, Liturgy*, book I, chapter 24, number 16.)

Let them also decide to whose fault it should be attributed that Sigonius, the most accurate describer of Italy, assigned the first place to Ravenna and the last to Milan—something that Puricellus either did not see or pretended not to see.

Likewise, because Liutprand called the archbishop of Ravenna the second bishop in Italy after the Roman one, the Milanese claim that Liutprand was speaking only of his own time, when John X of Ravenna exercised great power in Italy through the factions of the powerful Theodora. They will easily be refuted in this interpretation if some minor grammarian reads Liutprand’s words more carefully:

> “At that time Peter held the pontificate of the Ravennate see, which was regarded as the second archiepiscopate after the Roman Archpriest.”

For no one fails to see that *per idem tempus* (“at that time”) does not refer to the status of the archiepiscopate as second, but to Peter, who at that time held the pontificate at Ravenna; and Peter had absolutely nothing to do with that most shameless Roman woman.

If we should also bring forward the testimonies of the supreme pontiffs, who call the Ravennate Church the Firstborn among the daughters of the Roman Church; if we should bring forward the emperors, who call it the greatest Church after the Roman Church—what disturbances, good God, would the Milanese raise against such documents?

But we shall not dwell on these matters. It is enough to have defended Clement’s letters against the charge of falsity; it is enough perhaps to have proved with evident clarity that in the Roman synod the Ravennate bishop was placed before the Milanese by the supreme pontiff.

## CHAPTER III. What may be thought concerning the origin of metropolitan dignity in the Ravennate Church

[Col. 0145D] Thus far we have fought face-to-face with the Milanese in defense of the freedom of the Ravennate Church and the prerogative of its seating. Now, however, as we are about to discuss the beginnings, or origin, of its metropolitan dignity, we lay aside partisan zeal. We are dealing with a matter so uncertain and with such a scarcity of documents that amid so many dense clouds it is impossible to discern anything certain, anything bearing the appearance of unquestionable credibility.
