We shall therefore be content merely to report and explain the various opinions of the authors and their arguments. We shall follow none of them, leaving it to the judgment of wiser men to declare which possesses greater force.

No one is unaware that there are two opinions concerning this origin. The first, which we acknowledge to be more common, traces the origin back to the fifth century; the second, held by fewer authors—though by authors of a name not to be despised—places these beginnings in the first century of the Christian era. Let us examine the former opinion.

### § I. The opinion that this dignity originated in the fifth century

92. Emmanuel Schelstratius, Sebastian Tillemont, Jacques Sirmond, Norisius, Bacchinius, and a hundred others who rank among the foremost critics defend this opinion with every effort and zeal.

The argument common to all of them is that no indication whatsoever of this honor is found in the Ravennate Church before the fifth century, and that the first of the Ravennate bishops to shine with the metropolitan mitre and exercise the rights of that dignity was Saint Peter Chrysologus, around the middle of that century.

They do not all agree, however, in understanding Chrysologus in the same way. For Bacchinius—followed by a certain Pastrizius, author of a dissertation on the silver paten of Saint Chrysologus—departing from the more common view, attributes to this doctor of our Church the first exercise of metropolitan rights, but denies that he was the first metropolitan, distinguishing the beginnings of the dignity from the exercise of it. Bacchinius holds that the first to rise to that rank was John, surnamed Angeloptes, Chrysologus’s immediate predecessor in the Ravennate see.

93. The foundation of the more common opinion, which recognizes in Peter Chrysologus the beginning both of the dignity and of its exercise, is drawn entirely from his Homily 175, which he delivered to the Ravennate people at the consecration of Marcellinus, bishop of Vicohabentia—now Ferrara.

The supporters of that opinion say that the words of the celebrated homily indicate clearly, unambiguously, and most explicitly that Marcellinus was the first to receive from the Ravennate Church the office of consecration by decree of the apostolic see, with the emperor’s intervention.

And, so that no alternative interpretation might remain possible, they say that Peter Chrysologus compares this first consecration conferred by the Ravennate Church with the most sacred birth of Mary, whose solemn feast the consecration had fittingly coincided with. Just as, after the edict of the pagan Caesar, Mary gave birth to her firstborn Son, so, because of the decree of Saint Peter and the decree of the Christian emperor, the Ravennate Church was giving birth in Marcellinus to its first son. And just as Mary first had to overcome the doubts of her most holy spouse, then, far from her native home amid the rigors of winter and every kind of hardship, bring the divine child into the light, so likewise the new mother, amid the opposition attributed to the bishop of Milan, then metropolitan of Vicohabentia, produced the first acts of her new jurisdiction—namely, the first consecration of a suffragan bishop.

With something like this explanation, the learned critics interpret these words of Chrysologus:

> “All beginnings of things are indeed difficult, but the beginnings of one who gives birth are more difficult. The holy Church of Ravenna, in order to give birth for the first time, made a way, endured anguish, felt pains, and accomplished this, brothers, so that it might preserve the order of the divine birth along the entire path of truth . . . . . The Lord, about to obey the edict of the pagan Caesar, came forth, and by the decree of Blessed Peter, the decree of the Christian prince, some servant still resists.” (*Sermon* 175.)

94. As for Bacchinius’s view that this dignity did not begin with John Angeloptes, the authors who supported Chrysologus—before Agnellus’s *Pontifical* was published—would, I think, have been sufficiently able to assert that this could not be proved by any genuine document. The document first reported by Jerome Rubeus and then by Ughellus, they would have said, was a pure invention, in accordance with the judgment of Baronius and everyone who wrote about it after Baronius.

We are speaking of the diploma of Valentinian III Augustus, by which metropolitan dignity over fourteen cities of Emilia and Flaminia, together with the use of the archiepiscopal pallium, was conferred upon John Angeloptes.

“Good heavens!” they say. “It is not within imperial power to grant archiepiscopal jurisdiction, much less the sacred pallium, which signifies the fullness of that jurisdiction. This diploma, therefore, is the fabrication of some schismatic.”

Once it is rejected, no other monument remains by which the beginning of metropolitan dignity could be assigned to John Angeloptes. We must therefore stand by Chrysologus’s homily, which seems to assert with excessive clarity both the beginning of the exercise and the beginning of the dignity in this holy doctor.

95. On the other hand, Bacchinius did adopt the more common view insofar as he admits from Chrysologus’s homily the first act of metropolitan authority in the Ravennate Church—namely, the consecration of Marcellinus. Indeed, he too detests that diploma of Valentinian, and is angry with Agnellus, its first proponent, as well as with Jerome Rubeus and Ughellus, whom he regards as Agnellus’s associates.

Nevertheless, he does not abandon his preconceived opinion concerning John Angeloptes. The learned Cassinese knew very well that the beginnings of this honor could in no way be placed in Chrysologus, since before that bishop the Ravennate Church already displayed such clear indications of an acquired dignity that no sane person could any longer doubt them.

Nor would Schelstratius, Tillemont, and all the others probably have judged otherwise if, while they were writing, the most ancient Agnellus had already emerged from the Este library.

These authors did not believe Rubeus when he recounted what had happened at Chrysologus’s election, especially Tillemont, with his customary freedom to affirm and deny everything indiscriminately. They may nevertheless be excused: Rubeus had not cited Agnellus for that account, although, since he often declared that he had drawn from Agnellus many details which he had inserted most opportunely here and there into the history of Ravenna, he deserved to be treated less harshly and less arrogantly.

Baronius had given him complete credence; the elder Pagi, Baronius’s annotator, had not disparaged him; and the younger Pagi had admitted Rubeus’s narrative into the *Brief History of the Roman Pontiffs*.

96. When Bacchinius made Agnellus publicly available and provided him with most learned notes, he carefully observed, on the one hand, the circumstances in which this author recounts the election of the successor after John Angeloptes’s death. He saw that the bishops of Emilia had assembled for this election together with the clergy and people of Ravenna.

He noted that the man elected proceeded to Rome with the representatives of the Ravennates, among whom was Cornelius, bishop of Imola, in order to receive, as was customary, approval and consecration from the supreme pontiff, Sixtus III.

He saw that when this elected man was not accepted, Peter Chrysologus—whom the pontiff preferred—was rejected by the Ravennates because he was a deacon of a suffragan Church, namely Imola; that he was then accepted and consecrated by Sixtus; and that from these facts there followed the undeniable conclusion that, before Chrysologus, the Ravennate Church already possessed the beginnings of metropolitan dignity.

On the other hand, since Bacchinius finds no similar arguments in the election of any of Chrysologus’s predecessors, and since none of them is recorded as having issued an act of this power, while he knows that Agnellus asserts that Valentinian conferred this dignity upon John Angeloptes, he holds that, although Agnellus’s assertion must be rejected, there nevertheless remains room for a probable conjecture. One may rightly conclude, Bacchinius says, that with Valentinian’s intervention and the consent of the apostolic see, Angeloptes was the very first to be marked with archiepiscopal dignity.

But since someone might have objected to our Bacchinius that it was exceedingly difficult to understand how, during the seven or eight years which Bacchinius assigns to Angeloptes’s episcopate, not even a single occasion arose for the exercise of the new jurisdiction—especially because, according to Bacchinius’s chronology, several new suffragan bishops would have had to be consecrated or at least approved during Angeloptes’s time, certainly including the bishop of Foropopili, Gratian’s successor, who died in 434—the Cassinese scholar was forced to devise the explanation that the archiepiscopal pallium had been conferred upon John Angeloptes only in the final days of his life, so that he did not have even a moment of life remaining in which to perform the least act of the new jurisdiction.

For he was intent on preserving Chrysologus’s status as the agent of that first act, in the consecration of the bishop of Vicohabentia, as though the whole of metropolitan jurisdiction consisted in such an act alone.

### § II. Objections that can be made both to the opinion concerning Peter Chrysologus and to that concerning John Angeloptes

97. Although the arguments of these distinguished men at first sight seem to possess considerable weight for establishing the beginnings of the archiepiscopate either in John Angeloptes or in Chrysologus, neither opinion is free from difficulties which, in my judgment, are extremely hard to resolve if examined more closely.

Before postponing the examination of the negative argument common to all these authors to the following paragraphs, it must first be stated that the writers do not agree in fixing the chronology of the periods of John Angeloptes and Peter Chrysologus.

Our Rubeus, followed by Baronius and Pagi, assigns Chrysologus’s remarkable election to the year 433 of the Lord, and Angeloptes’s to approximately 418. Bacchinius, however, moves both of them forward by several years, assigning Angeloptes to 432 and Chrysologus to 438.

We shall not involve ourselves in this question, which would doubtless weary our readers. The author of the *Meditations on the Life of Saint Geminianus*, bishop of Modena, has written something highly learned on this chronology; anyone who wishes may readily consult him.

98. Once this necessary information concerning both chronologies has been stated, the opinions presented concerning the first metropolitan of Ravenna seem to conflict with one another, and each to destroy the other.

Indeed, if what Agnellus recounts concerning Chrysologus’s election is to be believed, as Bacchinius insists it must be, Tillemont and the critics who follow him will certainly be unable to avoid placing the beginnings of our dignity before Chrysologus.

But if Bacchinius’s chronology is adopted, our Cassinese scholar will be compelled to move those beginnings back even before Angeloptes, whom he believes to have begun his archiepiscopate in 432. For Tillemont proves quite clearly that as early as 431 the Ravennate bishop was regarded as a metropolitan, on the basis of a letter written in that year by the Easterners to the bishops of Milan, Aquileia, and Ravenna against the anathemas of Saint Cyril.

Accordingly, on Bacchinius’s chronology we would have to go back at least to the time of Saint Exuperantius, who immediately preceded Angeloptes.

99. Nor will Rubeus’s chronology help Tillemont and the others. For even if we grant, with Rubeus—and perhaps more truly—that Chrysologus was elected in 433, nevertheless this letter of the Easterners, written in 431, will persuade Tillemont and the others to abandon their preconceived opinion concerning this first metropolitan.

If they appeal to Chrysologus’s Homily 175 and borrow from it an argument in defense of their own opinion, Bacchinius will easily reply that the words of the homily indicate the first use of metropolitan power in the consecration of Marcellinus, bishop of Vicohabentia, by Chrysologus, but do not indicate that Chrysologus was the first metropolitan.

Therefore, whether they wish it or not, the beginnings of this dignity must be placed in one of Chrysologus’s predecessors.

100. Furthermore, we do not believe that Rubeus’s chronology—which Bacchinius otherwise attempts to refute—can stand in Bacchinius’s favor. That is, even if we say with Rubeus that Angeloptes was elected in 418 and Chrysologus in 433, it will be possible to infer from this the establishment of the beginnings of metropolitan authority in Angeloptes and its exercise in Chrysologus.

For, apart from the fact that Bacchinius’s hypothesis would thereby be destroyed—namely, that Angeloptes acquired that honor only in the final days of his life and therefore could not perform even a single act of the new power—once the letter of the Easterners is admitted, Angeloptes was already a metropolitan at least by 431, nearly three years before Chrysologus, and was recognized as a metropolitan by the Easterners.

During that interval of years, who, I ask, would believe that Angeloptes neither consecrated nor approved a single suffragan, convened no provincial council against the recent canons of the general councils, and displayed not even one sign of jurisdiction in so extensive a province?

Apart from the fact, I repeat, that Bacchinius’s hypothesis would be destroyed, on what probable foundation, by what reasoning, shall we say that this dignity arose in Angeloptes’s time?

First, it cannot be said that it arose because it was granted to him through Valentinian’s intervention and by decree of the Roman see. That is merely Bacchinius’s invention, since, if we consult Chrysologus’s homily, the favor of both rulers seems rather to have assisted this holy doctor when he was about to ordain Marcellinus.

Second, it cannot be said that it arose because, by the diploma of Valentinian III reported by Rubeus and Ughellus, the metropolitan rank was conferred upon John rather than Peter. Bacchinius, together with the entire body of learned men, detests that diploma and consigns it to every curse. Once it is rejected, no probable conjecture in favor of Angeloptes can be drawn from it.

Third, it cannot be said that, because this bishop’s death found such a prerogative in the Ravennate Church, the dignity began with Angeloptes. Such reasoning would either be exceedingly unhappy or smack of divination: because the Ravennate Church was metropolitan when Angeloptes departed this life, therefore he was the first metropolitan.

101. Bacchinius himself may perhaps take refuge in Chrysologus’s Homily 175, which, in the words already cited, assigns the first act of metropolitan jurisdiction in the Ravennate Church to the consecration of Marcellinus. It would therefore be necessary that this power was then most recent, having been conferred upon John Angeloptes only a few days before his death, so that he could in no way have exercised it. Nor can anything else be conjectured if we wish to preserve both the words of the homily and the existence of this dignity before Chrysologus’s election.

But these considerations overturn Bacchinius’s refuge.

First, the consecration of a bishop is not the only act of metropolitan jurisdiction. Therefore, even if the consecration of the bishop of Vicohabentia had been the first consecration of a suffragan bishop performed by the Ravennate Church, it would not follow that Chrysologus’s words must be interpreted as referring to the first exercise of that jurisdiction.

John Angeloptes, or Exuperantius, Ursus, Liberius, and Angeloptes’s other predecessors could convene provincial synods, visit the suffragan dioceses, judge the cases of bishops, and even confirm their elections without themselves consecrating those bishops. These acts, and a hundred others of the same kind, would not have deprived Chrysologus’s consecration of the quality of being the first consecration, nor would they have detracted from the truth of the words of Saint Chrysologus.

### 102

Secondly, because it is exceedingly difficult to believe that, during the seventeen-year interval in which Chrysologus occupied the see of Ravenna—if we follow the chronology of the historians of Ravenna—or at least twelve years, if we follow Bacchinius’s chronology, the very first exercise of metropolitan authority was Marcellinus’s consecration [Col. 0151A]. For if it is true, as we shall say shortly, that this sacred blessing was conferred upon the bishop of Vicohabentia on the Nativity of Our Lord Jesus Christ in the year 450, or rather 449, only a few months before Chrysologus’s death, can it plausibly be said that during so many years he exercised no other function belonging to his dignity in the province?

While he was seated there, the Church of Placentia became vacant, and Florianus was elected in 439. Bologna became vacant, and Adrian was called to the episcopate—or, if someone else succeeded Saint Petronius, around the year 450. The Church of Foropopilia likewise became vacant, as did that of Ariminum (for there are some who wish this church also to have been anciently numbered among Ravenna’s suffragans); finally, the see of Imola became vacant twice. When, therefore, we attend to the discipline of those centuries [Col. 0151B], it would have belonged to Chrysologus both to approve the elected bishops and, if he wished, to consecrate them as well.

Moreover, apart from the approval and ordination of bishops, could Chrysologus—not to say should he—not have celebrated some provincial council during so many years? That outstanding doctor of the Church could neither have been unaware of nor neglected the holy canons composed by the Spirit of God concerning such synods, which were to be convened once and even twice each year. Finally, if throughout Italy and all the regions of the West, by order of Leo the Great, provincial and national councils were assembled so that all the bishops and Churches might approve and subscribe the letter of so great a pontiff to Flavian—a letter that became the standard by which the Fathers of the Council of Chalcedon defined the faith—it is surely incredible that Leo’s commands did not reach Chrysologus, a man [Col. 0151C] highly esteemed throughout the universal Church for his wisdom and holiness, or that he did not gather the Fathers of Emilia and Flaminia for so celebrated a cause.

### 103

Thirdly, even if, by an untenable hypothesis, the consecration of a bishop were admitted to be the sole act of metropolitan power, Marcellinus would still not have been the first bishop consecrated by Chrysologus. Let us, please, consult the authors who speak of that prelate of Vicohabentia: they all think that he was consecrated at the end of the year 450, on the Nativity of the Lord. Ughellus even extends the date to the year 451, though this cannot be established unless the beginning of the year 451 is reckoned from the Lord’s birthday, according to the practice of certain authors. For there can be no doubt that Chrysologus had departed to heaven long before the end of the year 451, and that Neon had already succeeded him in the episcopate, if we accept Saint Leo’s letter addressed to this bishop in the year 451—a letter which Bacchinius, as it seems to me, doubted without reasonable grounds [Col. 0151D].

In any event, if what the authors of Imola and others establish has any weight, this holy doctor died at the beginning of December in the year 450. Consequently, Marcellinus’s consecration must be assigned to the Nativity of the Lord in the year 449, as the authors cited above believe.

On the other hand, if what has been written about Saint Projectus, bishop of Imola, deserves credence, we are compelled to assert that he preceded Marcellinus’s ordination by a considerable interval and was therefore consecrated earlier by Chrysologus. We do not agree with Baronius’s opinion, together with Tillemont: Baronius, I say, thought that this Projectus of Imola was the very man whom we read had presided over the Council of Ephesus as legate of the Apostolic See. For at the time of that council, namely in the year 431, Chrysologus—who certainly ordained Projectus of Imola—had not yet been appointed bishop of Ravenna. Nevertheless, nothing prevents us from following the historians of the Church of Imola, who affirm that Projectus was consecrated in the year 446, four years before Chrysologus died [Col. 0152A].

### 104

How, then, Bacchinius might perhaps object, did this holy doctor call Saint Marcellinus the first son and firstborn of the Church of Ravenna? How did our Church preserve, along the entire path of truth, the order of the divine birth [Col. 0152B], if Marcellinus was not the first to receive a blessing from the metropolitan of Ravenna by decree of blessed Peter and by decree of the Christian emperor, despite the futile resistance of some servant whom they interpret as the bishop of Milan? And how will the words be verified that “the beginnings of things are difficult, but the beginnings of the one giving birth are more difficult”?

If, therefore, these words of Chrysologus cannot be understood in any other way than as referring to the very first episcopal consecration performed by the bishops of Ravenna after they had obtained the pallium, then it would rather have to be said that the writers were mistaken: either those who postponed Marcellinus’s ordination until the Nativity of the year 450 or 449, that is, until after Projectus, or those who say that Projectus was consecrated in 446. We frankly admit that Bacchinius’s argument is not insignificant. It rests upon the interpretation of almost all critics, who wish Chrysologus’s [Col. 0152C] words to be explained as referring to the very first consecration of a bishop.

### 105

Nevertheless, setting aside the response that, even if this interpretation were granted, the points we noted above in no. 100 and following would still remain unshaken, perhaps the words quoted from Chrysologus will not appear, if we weigh his style, his figurative expressions, and the meanings he ordinarily employs, to require interpretation in the strictest possible sense.

The first sons and firstborn of the Church are the bishops whom the mother Church bears before all others; through them, in turn, all the rest have the status of sons of so great a mother. Augustine explained those words of Psalm 44 in this sense: “In place of your fathers, sons are born to you; you shall appoint them princes over all the earth.”

Scripture itself does not always understand the name “firstborn” in its strictest sense [Col. 0152D]: “And you shall say to him [Pharaoh]: Israel is my firstborn son. I said to you, Let my son go, that he may serve me, and you refused to let him go; behold, I shall kill your firstborn son.” In these words God not only calls Israel by the name of “firstborn son”; to show that Israel is treated as a firstborn, he threatens Pharaoh, who would not release Israel, with the destruction of his firstborn son—as a punishment of retaliation, firstborn for firstborn.

But who would say that Israel was God’s true firstborn? This quality is properly attributed to Jesus Christ alone, both insofar as he is the Father’s Word and insofar as he is man, as we learn from Paul: when he says to the Hebrews, “And when he again brings the firstborn into the world, he says: And let all the angels of God adore him” (Heb. 1:6); and when he says to the Romans, “The firstborn among many brothers,” and “the firstborn of every creature” (Rom. 8:9). Therefore the name “firstborn,” when applied to Israel, cannot and should not be understood in its proper and natural sense.

Nor did Saint John Chrysostom use the term in that way when he said: “And departing from this Church, he came to that which is the Church of the firstborn enrolled in heaven.”

### 106

The same should be said of the term “only-begotten,” which is ordinarily applied to an only son, yet is used by God in addressing Abraham: “Take your only-begotten son, whom you love, Isaac . . . and you did not spare your only-begotten son for my sake” (Gen. 22:2, 12) [Col. 0153A]. This is said to Abraham at a time when he had not only Isaac but also Ishmael, his older son, although by another wife, so that, in relation to Abraham, Isaac was not truly and naturally an only-begotten son.

Accordingly, in the passages cited from Holy Scripture, the terms “firstborn” refer to some greater dignity and excellence by which Israel stood out among the other nations in the knowledge and worship of God, or to the greater love and kindness with which God loved and guarded Israel above the others, as a firstborn.

Chrysologus, therefore, could also have called Marcellinus the first and firstborn son of the Church of Ravenna in a figurative sense: in comparison with the lesser priests and the rest of the people, not as though the Church of Ravenna had borne a son for the first time in that bishop, but as though in him it had borne one of its first, or greater and firstborn, sons [Col. 0153C].

### 107

Nor does the comparison between Marcellinus’s consecration and Mary’s childbirth cause us difficulty, insofar as, just as Mary bore her first son, so the Church of Ravenna consecrated its first bishop. For we say that all comparisons, and especially this one made by the holy doctor, should not be understood so strictly that the things compared must agree in absolutely every circumstance, and that every circumstance of Mary’s divine childbirth must correspond to every circumstance of Marcellinus’s consecration.

It is sufficient that these two births—one natural, the other spiritual—agree in time: Marcellinus received his consecration on the day on which Christ the Lord was born. Let them also agree in the mothers’ travail, insofar as they bore sons. Just as Mary left her homeland and her own dwelling, undertook a journey in the intensifying winter, and was about to give birth in the manger at Bethlehem amid the greatest poverty [Col. 0153D], so the Church of Ravenna, because of Marcellinus’s consecration, was subjected to contradictions like the pangs of childbirth; it was forced to make a journey, namely to the Roman See, and to seek refuge in imperial protection.

Thirdly, it is sufficient that the two births agree in the edict of supreme rulers. For Mary obeyed the edict of Augustus and bore Jesus at Bethlehem; and by the decree of the Roman pontiff and the Caesar, the Church of Ravenna, after overcoming the opposition, consecrated Marcellinus.

Finally, it is sufficient that they agree in some way in the character of the birth. For just as Mary bore her firstborn son, so the archbishop of Ravenna also anointed a bishop, namely a son firstborn in dignity to the Church [Col. 0154A].

But why can it not be believed that the contradictions of which Chrysologus speaks concerned not consecration in the abstract, but Marcellinus’s person, so that it was necessary to seek refuge with the pontiff and the Caesar in order that episcopal blessing might be conferred upon that elected man? May we not suspect or conjecture that those contradictions, whatever their nature, arose from Marcellinus’s humble condition? The words of Chrysologus seem to indicate that he was nothing more than a fisherman and perhaps married, and consequently despised by the clergy and the people of Vicohabentia.

### 108

But if Bacchinius pressed us to compare one birth with the other in the strictest manner and in every circumstance [Col. 0154B], perhaps we could turn that comparison, to some extent, against his own opinion.

For if the Church of Ravenna had to preserve, along the entire path of truth, the order of the divine birth, Bacchinius should take care lest he provide Hieronymus Rubeus and his supporters with a way, through that comparison, to restore the beginnings of the dignity under attack to apostolic times.

Indeed, just as the decree of the pagan Caesar did not grant Mary the ability to give birth to the firstborn whom her most pure womb had already carried for nine months, and whose mother she had been chosen to be from all eternity, so neither did the decree of blessed Peter or the decree of the Christian ruler grant the Church of Ravenna the ability, for the first time, to consecrate a suffragan bishop in the person of Marcellinus; for it possessed that power from the earliest times of the Church.

Indeed, just as the decree of the pagan Augustus could not influence Mary’s childbirth except that Jesus should be born in the cave at Bethlehem, in fulfillment of the prophecies that had foretold so many centuries earlier that Jesus would be born there [Col. 0154C], so the decree of the Christian pope and emperor influenced Marcellinus’s consecration only by removing the difficulties that opposed its taking place—not by causing the Church of Ravenna then for the first time to begin using metropolitan authority, which perhaps the most holy Apollinaris had conferred upon it four centuries earlier by the will of blessed Peter.

### 109

Thus Rubeus could argue against Bacchinius, himself also making use of the comparison cited above.

But what else were those “more difficult beginnings of the one giving birth” that Chrysologus mentions, except the difficulties and contradictions encountered when discussion began concerning Marcellinus’s consecration, difficulties that may have been greater in proportion to the greater birth it was to bring forth—namely, a son firstborn among the Church’s children in dignity and order [Col. 0154D]?

Certainly, the beginnings of all great things usually bring with them a comparable difficulty. Yet they cannot for that reason be said to have been undertaken then for the first time, simply because they are undertaken amid labor. The same work, when repeated, can always—or almost always—bring the same labor when it begins to be repeated; therefore its beginnings are always rightly called difficult.

Accordingly, from what has been said up to this point, it seems that the words of Chrysologus indicate not the first acts of metropolitan jurisdiction—since the Church of Ravenna was already metropolitan before Chrysologus and could exercise a hundred similar acts even without consecrating any bishop [Col. 0155A]—nor even the first episcopal consecration. For the emphatic words of the homily can be rendered in a more accommodating sense, and the fact itself urges this interpretation, namely, that the consecration of Saint Projectus, bishop of Imola, had already been performed by Chrysologus—not to mention others.

### 110

If anyone were to maintain that Marcellinus was the first bishop of Vicohabentia because he had been anointed by the bishop of Ravenna, and that Chrysologus’s words should therefore suitably be explained not as referring to the first consecration in general, but specifically to the first consecration of a bishop of Vicohabentia, some might perhaps concede the point. For then Marcellinus could aptly be called the firstborn of the Church of Ravenna in relation to Vicohabentia, while the interpretation of such distinguished men concerning the obstacles that they believe were opposed to that first consecration by the bishop of Milan would likewise remain intact.

Indeed, if consideration were given to what we proposed in chapter 1 concerning the Churches of Imola and Vicohabentia themselves, such a conjecture would not appear altogether improbable. We have not hesitated to suspect that those Churches were led astray by the Arians and carried, by force or fear, into the party of Auxentius, the pseudo-bishop of Milan; and that, when the storm had subsided, Saint Ambrose reconciled them and provided them with a Catholic pastor.

For this reason, it would perhaps not be incredible that the bishops of Milan were regarded for a number of years as fathers and benefactors by those Churches, and that the Churches of Imola and Vicohabentia obeyed them. If these circumstances are granted, it is not surprising that, when they were finally recalled to the province of Ravenna by imperial and papal decree, the bishop of Milan should have opposed the measure [Col. 0155C].

### 111

Whatever the truth of such conjectures may be, it is evident that the assertion of Tillemont and his followers, as well as Bacchinius’s opinion concerning the beginnings of our dignity—whether they are to be established in Angeloptes or in Chrysologus—is entangled in so many inextricable difficulties that it is perilous to embrace either position, while the mind still recoils from both.

This is especially so because, against these theories burdened with so many difficulties, we can bring forward another kind of argument [Col. 0155D], one that may perhaps carry some weight with sensible men experienced in the ecclesiastical discipline of those times, and especially with Bacchinius’s followers. For he himself turns this argument most sharply against Agnellus and Rubeus when he presses them concerning Valentinian’s unfortunate diploma.

### 112

We derive this argument from the understanding of the universal Church, and especially from that of the Roman pontiffs of the same century, as well as from the laws directed against changes and disturbances in the ecclesiastical hierarchy.

In fact, nothing was then more hated by the Church, and nothing did the Roman pontiffs oppose more vigorously, than the creation of new metropolises and new archbishops to the detriment of the hierarchy established by the apostles. The Church and the pontiffs resisted these innovations so firmly that they did not fear imperial power and even nullified the canons of general councils.

I omit the more ancient sixth canon of the Council of Nicaea, by which those most holy Fathers sought to settle the dissensions of the Eastern Church. Those dissensions had arisen from no other source than the ambition of bishops who, after the imperial hierarchy had been altered and new civil metropolises established, presumed to adapt the hierarchy and the new ecclesiastical metropolises to them. I omit that canon, I say, and come to examples closer to the times of John Angeloptes and Peter Chrysologus [Col. 0156A].

### 113

The bishop of Antioch had consulted Innocent I, the Roman pontiff, about whether the government of the Churches ought to be adapted to changes in the civil provinces, so that, if the imperial provinces and their chief cities were multiplied or diminished, the ecclesiastical provinces and metropolises should likewise be multiplied or diminished.

In response, Innocent wrote:

> “As to what you ask—whether, when provinces are divided by imperial decision so that two metropolises are created, two metropolitan bishops ought likewise to be appointed—it has not truly seemed right that the Church of God should be altered according to the mutability of worldly necessities, or that it should endure honors or divisions which the emperor has judged should be made for his own reasons.”

If we believe Thomasinus, the consultation of the bishop of Antioch concerned the controversy that had already arisen in the fourth century between Basil the Great of Caesarea and Antimus, bishop of Tyana, over Cappadocia, which the emperor Valens had divided into two provinces out of hostility toward Basil [Col. 0156B]. Perhaps that controversy had not yet ceased among the successors of those prelates. Whatever the truth of this matter, Innocent’s position against new metropolises is entirely clear.

Innocent occupied the Apostolic See from the year 401 to 417. Juvenal, bishop of Jerusalem, with the support of Theodosius the Younger, Augustus, had arrogated to himself jurisdiction over the three Palestines, both Phoenicias, and Arabia. His ambitious efforts were first rejected by Celestine, the supreme pontiff, and by the general Council of Ephesus, and then by Leo the Great and the Council of Chalcedon. At the latter council Juvenal was finally recalled to his office and was forced to restore Arabia and the Phoenicias to the patriarchate of Antioch, while scarcely retaining Palestine.

Celestine presided over the universal Church from 422 to 432, and Leo the Great from 440 until 461. In the time and by the decree of that same Theodosius, had not Phoenicia been divided into two provinces? The bishop of Tyre retained the administration of one, while the bishop of Berytus sought the administration of the other. Their disputes were settled at that same Council of Chalcedon, where judgment was issued in favor of the ancient metropolitan, the bishop of Tyre, and the bishop of Berytus was reduced to order [Col. 0156D].

Was not the ill-advised ambition of the bishop of Nicaea likewise suppressed at that time? He had arranged for Nicaea to be made a metropolis by the Augusti and had raised himself to metropolitan rank.

### 114

Besides these examples, the twelfth canon of the Council of Chalcedon itself demonstrates most clearly the universal Church’s profound opposition to such changes in her hierarchy [Col. 0157A]. By that canon, the license of the Augusti in erecting ecclesiastical metropolises was restrained, and a curb was placed upon the ambition of bishops; they were forbidden, under penalty of deposition, to obtain such dignities from the Augusti for themselves.

Indeed, this was the constant mind of the Church and of the supreme pontiffs, both in earlier and in later centuries: they resisted with every effort and denied that the ecclesiastical hierarchy depended upon civil principalities or should be adapted to the civil administration.

The legates of Hadrian II, the Roman pontiff, protested this against the Greeks in the famous controversy concerning the kingdom of Bulgaria. The Greeks had seized the ordinations of the Bulgarians on the pretext that the province of the Bulgarians was a member of the Greek Empire. The legates said:

> “When we say that the ordination of Bulgaria belongs to us in a different manner, we do not speak falsely; likewise, we never deny that Bulgaria was part of the Greek kingdom. But you ought to understand that the laws of sees ordain one thing, while divisions of kingdoms permit another. We are not dealing with the division of kingdoms, but with the division of sees” [Col. 0157B].

### 115

However, since some think that Leo the Great was the founder of our metropolis, although it was already a metropolis long before that pontiff, even while Celestine occupied the See—as the arguments set forth above most certainly prove—it is nevertheless worthwhile to explain the mind of so great a pontiff concerning such disturbances of the hierarchy.

For this reason, let us repeat here the famous deed of Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, who dared to arrogate to himself the second rank after the Roman pontiff in the government of the Church. He was supported both by the emperors of the East and by the Fathers of the Council of Chalcedon. So long as they shared the mind of the most holy Leo and followed him as their leader, they enacted laws filled with the Spirit of God; but as soon as they departed from his discipline, they yielded to Anatolius’s ambition and to the insinuations of the Augusti, opening the way to a most dreadful schism [Col. 0157C].

The great-hearted Leo roared against them. He reproached Anatolius, the Augusti, and the council for violating the Nicene canons, disturbing the peace of the Church, and disrupting apostolic hierarchy and discipline; and by papal authority he annulled the synodal decree.

Permit me to quote here some words excerpted from the most holy pontiff’s reply to the emperor Marcian:

> “Let the city of Constantinople possess, as we desire, its glory, and, under the protecting right hand of God, enjoy for a long time the benefit of your clemency. Yet the order of secular affairs is one thing, and that of divine affairs another; and apart from that rock which the Lord wondrously established as a foundation, no structure will be stable. But he loses what is his own who covets what is not his due. Let it be enough for the aforementioned man [Anatolius] that, through the help of your piety and with the consent of my favor, he obtained the episcopate of so great a city. Let him not disdain the royal city, which he cannot make an apostolic see; nor let him hope in any way that it can be enlarged through the offenses of others” [Col. 0157D].

From these words of Saint Leo we learn that the Church’s intention was never to shape the ecclesiastical hierarchy according to the system of civil government: the order of secular affairs is one thing, and that of divine affairs another.

Likewise, when he says that no structure will be stable apart from that rock which the Lord established as its foundation, and commands Anatolius not to disdain the royal city, which he could not make an apostolic see, he plainly indicates that the order and hierarchical structure of the Church was shown and commanded by Christ the Lord, and constructed by the apostles. This applies especially to the patriarchal sees, which were truly apostolic, so that it would be impious to tear that structure apart by erecting new metropolises and diminishing or altering the authority and jurisdiction of other Churches [Col. 0158A].

### 116

Leo himself reproached the same conduct even more forcefully in Letter 55, saying:

> “It is exceedingly arrogant and immoderate to extend oneself beyond one’s own boundaries, and, trampling upon antiquity, to seek to seize another’s right, and, so that the dignity of one may increase, to attack the three primacies of metropolitan bishops.”

It is also well known how severely that same Leo proceeded against Saint Hilary of Arles because of jurisdiction usurped in another province. As the most vigorous defender of the sacred canons and of ecclesiastical discipline, he could not tolerate the beautiful order of the hierarchy established by the apostles throughout the world being disturbed in any way [Col. 0158B].

### 117

Such, then, was the mind, spirit, and steadfastness of the Church. Such were the courageous pontiffs who presided over her and clung tenaciously to this apostolic hierarchy, at the very time when almost all authors wish this new metropolis of Ravenna to have emerged, whether under Angeloptes or under Chrysologus [Col. 0158C].

But can we really regard this as credible? Is there any appearance of probability in it?

While Celestine and Leo, while the councils, while the Church itself protested, resisted, and thundered in the East against new metropolises that diminished the excellence, jurisdiction, and majesty of other Churches, were the complaints of the Milanese in the West being heard at that same time and under those same pontiffs because jurisdiction had been taken from them and a new metropolis had been built upon the losses of the Ambrosian Church?

At the time when Celestine resisted Theodosius the Younger and Leo the Great resisted Marcian because the order of the Church had been disturbed, would the bishop of Milan at that same time resist Celestine and Leo themselves because that same ecclesiastical order had been disturbed?

Could not the Easterners, the Egyptians, and the bishops of Constantinople have hurled back against Celestine and Leo the same shafts of reproach that those pontiffs had directed against them in such vigorous language, if they had established new metropolises in Italy contrary to the hierarchy introduced by the apostles, while those very controversies were still raging in the East [Col. 0158D]?

### 118

Considerable weight may also be added to this reasoning by the holiness of both prelates, namely John Angeloptes and Peter Chrysologus.

For they say that the former possessed such holiness that heavenly beings were accustomed to visit him familiarly; and even to this day John, who saw an angel, is called by that name. The universal Church, and the surviving monuments of so great a doctor, proclaim the holiness, zeal, learning, and eloquence of the other.

Would such men have committed an outrageous act of ambition that was detested by the Church in those times, condemned by councils and supreme pontiffs, attacked with curses throughout the whole East, and devoted to every form of execration? Would Angeloptes and Chrysologus have disturbed the Church’s most beautiful order, harmony, and apostolic rules; confused and occupied rights belonging to others; seized jurisdiction; and divided and usurped Churches?

I can scarcely believe that anyone suspected such things of them.

Gelasius, the first Roman pontiff of that name, seems clearly to absolve these most holy prelates from such a charge when he says:

> “Did an emperor not reside for many years at Ravenna, at Milan, at Sirmium, and at Trier? Did the priests of these cities ever usurp anything in their dignities beyond the measure anciently assigned to them?”

## § III. The opinion that the beginnings of this metropolitan dignity are to be traced back to the apostolic age is explained

### 119

The historian of Ravenna, Hieronymus Rubeus, had followed this opinion in the sixteenth century. Peter de Marca, Salmasius, and others whom Bacchinius cites agreed with him.

In my judgment, their entire argument is derived both from the universal order of the ecclesiastical hierarchy and from Ravenna’s prominence in the apostolic age.

As for the first point, it is certainly established that the same hierarchy of government had been constituted throughout the whole Church: namely, that each province should have its own metropolitan, to whom the bishops of the cities within the province should be subject. The apostles instituted this form of order as common to the universal Church.

The apostles also wished that the metropolitan should be one of the bishops who held his see in the principal city of the whole province—either because the civil president or governor resided there and issued laws to the cities subject to it; or because the city was more distinguished by the frequency of its population, its size, its wealth, its arms, or its commerce; or because there the priests or chief priests of idolatrous superstition presided over divine worship.

This kind of hierarchy therefore flourished even in the earliest centuries of the Church, including apostolic times. Many traces still survive of ecclesiastical provinces and of the first bishops of each province—not only in Asia and Africa but also in Europe—if the accounts circulated concerning the ecclesiastical metropolises of Gaul, Spain, and Illyricum in the earlier centuries deserve any credence [Col. 0159D].

### 120

Since, then, the rule of this most distinguished order and hierarchy ought to have been universal in the Church of God, so that every province possessed its own first bishop or metropolitan, what prevents us from admitting that this same rule was observed in the provinces of Italy also during those earliest centuries?

No argument, reason, law, or canon has yet been found that would prevent Italy from possessing the very hierarchy that was common to all the other regions of the Church. Not one of the countless critics who defend the contrary position has yet offered even a single reason that would persuade us that the apostles and their successors, the supreme pontiffs, disregarded the system of the universal Church and devised and established an entirely different arrangement for Italy alone, that vast region [Col. 0160A].

Indeed, this consideration appeared to the distinguished Emmanuel Schelstrate to be of no small importance, and he proposes to examine and resolve it. “The very question,” he says, “is by what reasoning it happened that in the other provinces of the Christian world metropolitans were ordained according to apostolic institution, whereas in Italy, where Paul preached, where Peter founded Churches, and where the Apostolic See existed in the earliest times of the Church, that institution did not immediately prevail.”

### 121

Schelstrate did attempt to weaken the force of this argument by appealing to Italy’s division into two vicariates of the praetorian prefect, which we discussed in chapter 1 [Col. 0160B]. Assuming that division, and positing two metropolitans corresponding to those vicariates—namely, the bishops of Rome and Milan, to whom the others in the Italian provinces would be subject—the distinguished author believed that he had also found and demonstrated in Italy the observance, during the earlier centuries, of that apostolic hierarchy which prevailed throughout the rest of the Christian world.

But his attempt was unsuccessful. First, it is beyond dispute that before Constantine the Great Italy was not subject to the division just mentioned. At one time a single corrector or prefect governed it; at another, four consular officials were in charge of its administration. Therefore, if Schelstrate’s system were valid, the Italian Church ought at one time to have counted only one metropolitan and at another time four, but never two, throughout the first three centuries of our era [Col. 0160C].

### 122

Secondly, even if Schelstrate and all the authors who share his opinion were granted that Italy was divided in those centuries into two vicariates, the argument for establishing a universal hierarchy in that region would still remain.

For even if those vicariates had existed, they would not have excluded the division into the civil provinces of which the vicariates themselves consisted. Nor would they have excluded the particular prefecture, magistracy, assembly, principal city, and—even if we wish—the chief center of pagan priesthood belonging to each province.

The other praetorian prefectures of the Roman Empire provide an example. Although they were composed of very extensive and numerous provinces [Col. 0160D], each province was subject to its own prefect—whether consular official, governor, or rector—held its own assemblies, and possessed its own metropolis, to which the cities of the province were attached. This was the situation in temporal affairs.

If we examine spiritual government, although the East, Egypt, Africa, Gaul, and Illyricum were divided among ecclesiastical primates and exarchs who presided over those vast Christian regions, who would nevertheless deny that almost every individual province of those regions had its own metropolitan, subject to the patriarch, primate, or exarch, but superior to all the lesser bishops of his own province?

I omit the patriarchates of Alexandria and Antioch, about which no one has any doubt, and appeal to the nearer example of Africa. Did not the whole African Church obey the primate of Carthage? Yet each province of Africa was immediately subject to its own metropolitan, who was called the first bishop [Col. 0161A].

### 123

Even if those two vicars had governed Italy during the first three centuries, and even if only two ecclesiastical primates had corresponded to them, it would not for that reason follow that the individual provinces of Italy lacked first bishops, or metropolitans, who held their sees in the principal city and corresponded to the provincial magistrate—and also, as some think, to the chief pagan priesthood of the entire province.

In such a case, these metropolitans would certainly have taken nothing away from the legal primacy of Rome or Milan, if such a primacy ever existed in reality. They would have done so in roughly the same way that the metropolitans of the patriarchates of Antioch, Alexandria, and Africa caused no prejudice to the rights of their primates; indeed, they seemed rather to increase their splendor and dignity [Col. 0161B].

We have proposed these points, however, in order to close every avenue of escape to Schelstrate and those who agree with him, so that they cannot evade the argument that the hierarchy of the whole Church must also be admitted in the provinces of Italy.

Moreover, since the division of Italy into vicariates during the first three centuries of our era was entirely false, the division into those two metropolitans, the Roman and the Milanese, is likewise false. Therefore, in view of the universal rule of ecclesiastical hierarchy, it remains for us, justly and prudently, to conjecture that throughout Italy also the same order of hierarchy was distributed by the apostles as existed throughout the whole of the rest of the Church [Col. 0161C].

124. There are also those who concede that in those centuries there was no division in Italy into civil vicariates or metropolitan districts. They deny, however, that any metropolitan presided there other than the Roman bishop. Since the ancient records are silent about any other metropolitan, they say that the Roman pontiff alone is recorded as having consecrated bishops and performed in the Italian Churches all those acts that belonged to immediate metropolitans; and they produce a hundred examples, which may be consulted in their authors.

Yet this kind of argument proves nothing, because, as dialecticians say, it proves too much. The patriarchs of Alexandria and Antioch likewise claimed for themselves all those rights in the provinces subject to them, [Col. 0161D] especially the ordination of bishops throughout the Churches of the East and Egypt. Nevertheless, the authors just mentioned will not therefore reply that no metropolitans then existed throughout the Eastern and Egyptian dioceses, but that those acts of jurisdiction belonged cumulatively to the patriarchs—as jurists would say—together with the subordinate metropolitans, by reason of their primacy and of the custom that had been introduced.

This answer is especially pertinent to our case, since those distinguished men ought to have observed that the patriarchates of Alexandria and Antioch were constituted according to the model of the Roman, or Western, patriarchate, if the sixth canon of the Council of Nicaea is understood in its more obvious sense. Thus, whatever the Roman pontiff could do in the West by reason of his patriarchate, the Alexandrian could do in Egypt, and the bishop of Antioch [Col. 0162A] in the East. What, then, was permitted to these lesser patriarchs in the provinces of their respective patriarchates, although those provinces had their own metropolitans, could it not have been permitted to the greatest of all patriarchs, the Roman bishop, in the provinces of Italy, even where they were subject to some immediate metropolitan?

Moreover, Roman pontiffs truly exercised this kind of jurisdiction in those regions of their patriarchate about which there can be no doubt among writers that proper metropolitans had long since been appointed. There they ordained indiscriminately not only the metropolitans themselves but also the lesser bishops. Natalis Alexander proved this by citing the third letter of Pope Symmachus; the first letter of Nicholas I to Michael, emperor of the Greeks; the thirty-fourth letter of Book IV and the thirteenth of Book V of St. Gregory the Great; the third letter of Celestine I to the bishops of Calabria and Sicily; and the testimony of John the Deacon in the *Life of Gregory the Great*.

Therefore, from the fact that Roman pontiffs are read to have exercised metropolitan jurisdiction in particular provinces of Italy and in particular Churches, no argument can be drawn that the pope was the sole and immediate metropolitan of the eleven—or seventeen—provinces of Italy.

125. Nor are there lacking those who wish to maintain that, through the avarice and ambition of the Roman pontiffs, the hierarchy of the rest of the world was excluded from Italy in the beginnings of the Church; or, if there were metropolitans, that the use even of immediate jurisdiction was taken away from them by the pontiffs themselves, and that they consequently remained unnamed.

These accusations refute themselves sufficiently, if anyone of sound mind and judgment recalls Peter and Paul as the first founders of the Italian Churches, and recalls their most holy successors, the pontiffs of the earlier centuries, as men exceptionally steadfast in ecclesiastical discipline, apostolic traditions, and the most blameless habits of life. Rather, the opposite conjecture and a diametrically contrary argument emerge from this. For if Peter and Paul were the founders of the Italian Churches, and if their most holy successors were so tenacious of the apostolic traditions and of the unimpaired form and discipline of the Churches received from them, then, just as there is no reason to deny that the apostles conformed the Italian hierarchy to the order of the whole Church, so their successors must be judged to have preserved and extended that same order everywhere with almost every effort and care in the earlier centuries.

126. The universal discipline of the Church can generally suggest this in support of the opinion of Rubeus and those who follow him. Something more particular must now be discussed in support of the same opinion, and an argument must be drawn from the eminence of the city of Ravenna.

Let us therefore either embrace the view of those who hold that, in establishing metropolitan Churches, the apostles took account of the cities that were the metropolises of the provinces—namely, those to which, as Peter de Marca says, the provinces of the empire were attached, where the magistrate judged the cases of the subject peoples, and to which the population consequently gathered, since the cities depended upon the mother-city by a certain special right—or let us follow the assertion of others, who think that the apostles looked not only to the cities that were the civil capitals of the provinces, but also to those that were more distinguished and celebrated, stronger in arms and wealth, and more suitable for propagating the faith by their situation, commerce, and the presence of foreign nations.

Or finally, let us adhere to those who believe that, in establishing the Christian order, the apostles kept the form of the pagan hierarchy before their eyes: namely, that they placed lesser bishops where paganism had its flamines, and established greater bishops, that is, metropolitans, where it had its chief flamines. Whichever of these opinions, I say, we choose to follow, we shall find that Ravenna most certainly possessed the qualifications required of a metropolitan see.

[Col. 0163B] 127. From the time of the Roman Republic, Ravenna was regarded as the metropolis of Cisalpine Gaul. There Gaius Caesar, having distributed the army into winter quarters, remained and held assemblies, administering justice to all the Gauls. Augustus and Tiberius likewise customarily resided there for long periods.

When Augustus divided all Italy into eleven provinces, the eighth was Emilia, subdivided into two provinces. One extended from Piacenza to Bologna, the other from Bologna as far as Rimini. Yet Ravenna was the capital of both: there were the provincial praetor, the capitol, the senate, and the patrician order, which was granted only to the more important cities among the metropolises.

Who does not know how flourishing the affairs of the Ravennates were in those days? Its position was suitable for commerce; its proximity to the sea gave it a vast and exceptionally safe harbor; it was the station of the Roman fleet prepared to defend the shores of the empire; and, finally, it was a celebrated emporium of the world, frequented by foreign nations, powerful and preeminent above all in wealth and arms. Thus it was called the city second only to Rome when Apollinaris, the disciple of Peter, first sowed in it the seeds of the Gospel, as Martin of Poland, cited by Rubeus, had acknowledged.

Finally, it was not lesser flamines or chief flamines, but a college of pagan pontiffs, that held the seat and the “pestilential chair” there. This clearly demonstrates the preeminence of the city, as a kind of second Rome.

[Col. 0163D] 128. Therefore, if it must not be said that the apostles neglected in Italy the rule of the universal hierarchy—or at least if no positive and probable reason remains for us to think so—what could be inferred, indeed asserted, more fittingly, more consonantly with right reason, and more suitable both to the universal ecclesiastical discipline and to the needs of particular Churches, than that the apostles chose such a city?

It was the metropolis of a flourishing province, the most powerful of the Italian cities, and the center of pagan superstition. Through it, because so many nations converged there, the broadest access was opened for communicating the faith. Such a city, I say, the apostles most probably chose as the place where the see of a bishop would be established—one who would carry and extend the Gospel to the surrounding cities and peoples, establish Churches, [Col. 0164A] and ordain bishops; one whom the converted people and the new Church would regard and honor as their teacher, father, and leader.

What the apostles are said to have granted to so many illustrious metropolises of Europe—namely, that they should be established as the capitals of ecclesiastical provinces, as we read was done throughout Spain, Gaul, and Illyricum—must therefore, with the greatest probability, be judged to have been granted also to Ravenna, the most noble metropolis of Italy, in accordance with the rule of the universal hierarchy and in view of the eminence of so great a city.

## § IV. Objections against the opinion of Rubeus and others are set forth

129. We have already presented some of the points that seem to tell against Jerome Rubeus and his followers, and have refuted them in the words of the Ravennates. These include the fiction of the vicariates of Italy and of the two metropolitans, once all the other arguments have been rejected, as well as the words of Homily 175 of St. Peter Chrysologus, which, according to the interpretation of his adversaries, assert that this most holy prelate first exercised metropolitan jurisdiction.

There are, however, other objections, perhaps no less weighty, that seem to weaken Rubeus’s position. First, nearly all the great authorities, highly expert in ecclesiastical history, joined together in establishing this contrary contention, and nearly the entire body of critics, historians, and geographers followed them. This ordinarily lends great force to their opinion.

Their position is that the metropolitan see of Ravenna arose only at the beginning of the fifth century, while either John Angeloptes or Peter Chrysologus governed that Church. In addition to the positive arguments mentioned above that they have amassed, all these authors and writers never cease to brandish one other truly “Achillean” and insuperable argument: and rightly so, they say—namely, the silence of the ancients and the absence of records from which at least one indication might be drawn that Ravenna exercised metropolitan jurisdiction over the Churches during the first four centuries.

Now, just as the Ravennates claim liberty for their own Church from the yoke of the Milanese chiefly because no act whatsoever—even the smallest—of such jurisdiction over the Church of Ravenna can be produced on behalf of Milan—no episcopal ordination or approval, no synod, no visitation, no letter, decree, canon, or testimony of any writer—so, by the same rule, if the bishops of Ravenna are found to have performed none of these acts before Angeloptes or Chrysologus, and to have possessed no testimony of this kind, it must plainly be said that the opinion deriving this dignity from the age of the apostles has no firmness.

130. Peter Chrysologus himself, in so many learned homilies that have been published, did not utter a single word about this dignity as outstanding in his predecessors, nor did he do so when speaking of Apollinaris, the first bishop of Ravenna.

Agnellus himself, although otherwise an unsophisticated historian of the ninth century, did not whisper even a syllable about this kind of prerogative, though he sometimes devoted excessive effort to magnifying the power of the Ravennate bishops and showed great reluctance to acknowledge the divine primacy of the Roman Church.

What more is there to say? Agnellus placed the beginnings of the metropolitan dignity in John Angeloptes, although he impiously invented Valentinian III Augustus as the conferrer of that rank and pallium.

What patron of their opinion, then, and what argument will Rubeus, de Marca, Salmasius, and any other advocates of the same view offer us?

131. Moreover, their principal foundation totters—the foundation based on the universal order of the Church’s hierarchy and on the rule spread throughout the entire world, namely, that the apostles gave almost every province of the empire its own metropolitan, residing in its chief city, and adapted the government of the Churches to the government of the civil provinces.

For whether we attend to the general system of the entire empire or to that of particular provinces at the time when the order of the Church began to be established by the apostles, we are compelled to acknowledge that both systems were entirely unsuitable as the model to which the apostles conformed the ecclesiastical hierarchy.

The learned Cassinese abbot Bacchini is the author of this most serious proposition. He published a dissertation on the origin of the ecclesiastical hierarchy that is complete in every respect, rich in sacred and secular learning, and supported by strong arguments.

After considering the structure of the Roman Empire, the distribution of its governments and magistracies, the distinction and division of its provinces, and which cities were the more important and the metropolises of the provinces, and after comparing all these matters, following an extensive examination, with the government of the Church and the division of its hierarchy in the first century, the learned Cassinese concludes that the apostles could not have taken the form of the civil hierarchy into account when distributing and arranging the order of the Churches. As he himself says, the distribution of the ecclesiastical provinces emerged as almost everywhere different from the imperial distribution.

Anyone may read the arguments by which the learned author established this conclusion in the first chapters of the first part of the dissertation mentioned above.

132. Bacchini also strengthens his argument against the presumed correspondence of the sacred hierarchy with the civil magistracies from the system of the particular provinces. If a metropolitan is believed to have been assigned to each province so that the other bishops of the same province would obey him because, in every province and in the chief city of each province, a governor, president, or consular stood above the magistrates of the other cities of the province, this cannot stand if one consults the truth.

We read that the administration of the individual provinces was so disordered and so varied: sometimes the same province was governed by its own governor, sometimes by the president of another province; sometimes several provinces obeyed one official, sometimes several consulars. This was especially true of our Emilia, which at one time had its own consular together with Flaminia, and at another time was subject, together with Liguria, to a single president.

It is therefore wholly impossible that the apostles and their successors built the hierarchy of the ecclesiastical provinces upon such an unstable foundation.

133. Bacchini proceeds from the system of the empire in apostolic times to examine the system of the Synagogue. He describes the form that the Israelite community then possessed throughout the provinces of Judea and outside the boundaries of Judea; namely, what kinds of synedria, or councils, presided over the sacred and civil government in the various cities of Judea, some lesser and some greater, all deriving their authority and jurisdiction from the supreme general synedrium of Jerusalem.

Outside Judea there was indeed only one synedrium for each province, or for some large expanse of a region. Yet in every city of that region there were schools or synagogues, which depended upon and were governed by the synedrium of the region or province, as by a provincial council.

He shows that the synedria at Antioch and Alexandria, and those of other cities in various regions, possessed the greatest authority throughout the East and Egypt.

Bacchini then compares the order of the developing Christian Church with this system of the Synagogue and draws a second conclusion from the comparison: namely, that the apostles, and especially Peter, in founding the principal Churches, did not look primarily to the form of the Roman Empire, but rather adapted themselves to the polity of the Jews, taking account of the density of their population and of their prerogatives according to the diversity of times and places, and also of the Gentiles when they were admitted to the grace of baptism.

Our Cassinese author frankly admits that this opinion had been approved by other writers before him, including Grotius, who had said that the entire government of the Churches of Christ was conformed to the model of the synagogues, and Father Thomasinus in *The Old and New Discipline of the Church*. More recently Joseph Motta has added his support in the cited dissertation *On Metropolitan Law*, no. 8 and following.

134. Yet, because innumerable provinces remained in the empire—and indeed throughout the whole world—in which either no Jews or very few Jews were found, so that it seemed impossible, at least there, for the ecclesiastical hierarchy to be adapted to the pattern of the Synagogue, the learned Bacchini distinguishes three different periods in the apostles’ preaching and likewise three different constitutions of the Churches.

The first period concerns the time of the apostolic preaching that, by the command of Christ the Lord, was given only to the Jews within the provinces of Judea. The second concerns the interval during which the apostles brought the faith to Gentiles mixed with Jews, throughout regions lying far and wide outside Judea. Finally, the third period designates the time when the Gospel was spread through regions inhabited entirely by idolaters, with no Jews or almost none.

135. In the first period of preaching, it was more appropriate for the apostles to imitate the form of the synedria in ordering the Church. Thus, to the general and supreme synedrium of Jerusalem, presided over by the high priest of the Synagogue, there corresponded the college of the apostles and disciples of Christ, with Peter presiding.

In the individual cities, lesser Churches were founded where there had been lesser synedria, and greater Churches where there had been greater synedria. Just as in each of the Jewish provinces—Samaria, Galilee, and Judea—the lesser synedria depended upon the supreme synedrium of each province, and all depended upon that of Jerusalem, so it came about that the lesser Christian Churches depended upon the greater Church of each province, while all depended upon the Church of Jerusalem.

In the second period, the apostles went out beyond the borders of Judea and traveled through those regions in which Jews were mixed with Gentiles. They had synagogues in the individual cities, but a synedrium in each province, or in certain districts of a region.

Because, through the ineffable providence of God, it had been arranged that the Synagogue itself should prepare the way for the conversion of the nations, and that the Jews should introduce Christ’s disciples to the knowledge and friendship of the Gentiles, so that through this natural means they might come to know the supernatural faith to which God’s mercy called them, we learn that during this period the apostles founded so many Churches in Asia, Africa, and Europe, united from Jews and Gentiles, and established Christian metropolises there where the synedria of the provinces had been: Ephesus, Sardica, and—to pass over others—Antioch and Alexandria.

136. According to the conjectures of the most learned Bacchini, the final period of the apostolic preaching brought the faith to the Churches of the Gentiles, among whom the Jews had neither synedria nor perhaps even synagogues.

Peter, the chief of the apostles, founded the first of all these Churches—the Roman Church—in the city that was the metropolis of the whole world. Since Jew and Gentile alike were subject to it, it was fitting that there the greatest of the Churches should be raised and founded, a Church that had to be formed and composed from both peoples.

From this principal Church, therefore, which Peter and Paul built and established with their own blood, messengers were sent in every direction to proclaim Christ to the Gentiles and to gather Christian Churches everywhere. From this source streams of faith, baptism, and tradition flowed happily into Italy, Gaul, Spain, Illyricum, and Africa.

Thus Innocent I rightly wrote to the bishop of Gubbio: “Let them read whether in those provinces another of the apostles is found or is read to have taught. If they do not read this, because it is found nowhere, they ought to follow what the Roman Church observes, from which it is beyond doubt that they received their beginning.”

We therefore think that those who maintain that the rights of the Roman patriarchate extended over the whole of the West are not far from the truth.

137. It must be observed here in what way the foundations of the Churches of the first and second periods differed from the foundations of the Churches of the third period.

In the case of the first Churches, bishops were not ordained until the Churches themselves had been formed in some fashion, whether from Jews alone or from Jews together with Gentiles who had already converted. In the case of the others, however, bishops were ordained and sent before the people were converted or the Churches formed in any way.

They were either designated for a particular province or city, so that there they might form their own Church by preaching the Gospel and establish a see; or they were not designated for any specific province or city, but were sent so that wherever chance—or rather divine Providence—opened a way for them to spread the faith, they might settle there and organize a Church from the converted people.

Thus, in either manner, these disciples and bishops sent to the Gentiles, once they had founded a distinguished Church in some city, proclaimed Christ from there to the neighboring cities and peoples, sanctifying new Churches throughout the surrounding area and sometimes, if it seemed expedient, consecrating bishops for them as well.

138. From this most wise economy of evangelical preaching it is understood not only how the apostles founded so many Churches and established so many bishoprics in pagan regions, but also by what method the first ecclesiastical metropolises were constituted.

A city acquired this dignity wherever the disciples of the apostles, sent to preach, established a see. From it they traveled about teaching the neighboring peoples and cities, imposing the laws of the Gospel upon the converts, forming Churches, and giving them bishops.

The converted peoples began to regard and venerate those disciples and missionaries as fathers, teachers, and superiors in spiritual matters. They acknowledged that their own faith, Churches, and bishoprics had received their beginning from those sees from which the first rudiments of the faith had been transmitted to them, and they treated those sees as a mother.

From that mother they received traditions, counsel in doubtful matters, and rules of discipline, rites, and morals; from her they obtained either the consecration or the approval of their bishops, especially after the apostles’ death. They attributed this ecclesiastical form of government to the prudent institution of the apostles.

139. This will appear probable, indeed wholly undeniable, if one observes, first, that the apostles proposed for themselves a form of government that would be perpetual and better suited to unite all peoples everywhere in one body and one flock, and to govern and instruct them more easily.

Second, they could not themselves, with only a few disciples, complete so great a work. Those few seeds had to be scattered throughout the vast field of the whole world, and those few workers had to labor in the great harvest of the Gospel.

It was therefore necessary to establish principal Churches in several provinces of the world and to place in them the sees of apostles or disciples, as so many metropolitan sees, together with the deposit of the faith and tradition. From those principal Churches, as time passed, other Churches would both arise and be governed through preaching.

These more important Churches, erected by the apostles or by the disciples of the apostles, were called apostolic Churches. Bacchinius reports their most beautiful distinction from Tertullian.

140. We therefore frankly admit that, more than any other, we find this opinion of the learned Cassinese concerning the origin of the ecclesiastical metropolises attractive. We know that it has been approved by men of the greatest authority, whatever others—especially the French—may have foolishly uttered against it.

For it accords with the idea that every clear-minded person ought to form concerning the propagation of the Gospel, a work completed throughout the whole world in a manner incomprehensible, no less powerful than gentle.

Nevertheless, we do not know whether this opinion of Bacchinius harms or rather favors the position of the Ravennates concerning the apostolic origin of their metropolitan dignity.

## § V. The Ravennates’ responses

141. So that we may not seem to neglect the responses of the Ravennates, whatever they may be, to difficulties capable of diminishing the force of the arguments brought forward, we shall set them out here very briefly.

First, they are not at all troubled by the fact that the opposing opinion is the more common, indeed almost universally held—an opinion followed and defended by nearly all the more celebrated writers, highly expert in ecclesiastical history, discipline, and morals.

The truth of such opinions is discerned not by their multitude or by the fame of their authors, but by the solidity of their foundations. Almost innumerable opinions have prevailed in individual ages because they enjoyed universal agreement; yet now they are all known to have been false.

To avoid looking for examples farther afield, was not the opinion concerning the Milanese metropolitan, founded upon the division of Italy into two vicariates, until now almost universally held, and applauded by nearly all critics? Yet once that false foundation was destroyed and so many inventions, regarded as unquestionable records, were relegated to the realm of fable, that opinion withdrew from the field and vanished.

142. Second, the Ravennates attach little importance to the negative argument of their adversaries. Woe to us if such reasoning were to be feared: “It is not found written; therefore it did not exist!”

The result would be the destruction of many things now regarded as entirely certain, both sacred and secular. The antiquity of so many Churches would be destroyed; they would either be said not to have existed in the earlier centuries or to have had no bishops, if we were to rely upon the silence of authors and the scarcity of records.
