Because, therefore, a memory or notice of the bishop of some Church first emerged only in the fourth or fifth century, must it be believed that no one preceded that bishop in governing the Church? Because writers spoke of some Church only later, shall we conclude that it began to exist only then?

Where, I ask, do our critics derive their argument for proving that the metropolises of Aquileia and Milan arose in the fourth century? “From the silence of the older records,” they will answer, “and because it is only in that century that we begin to read of some act of metropolitan jurisdiction exercised by those bishops.”

What an unfortunate argument! Because the beginning is not found, it must therefore be said to depend upon human conjecture and opinion.

Yet in our case our authors wish this very kind of reasoning to prevail. Since the beginnings of this dignity cannot be detected either in Chrysologus or in Angeloptes, nevertheless it must have begun with one of those two, they say, because it was only under one or the other of them that certain acts of metropolitan authority began to be read.

Is it possible that the minds of so many learned men have been satisfied with such reasoning?

143. The weakness of this negative argument becomes all the more apparent in proportion as the opinion of those who assert that the rule of the ecclesiastical hierarchy must have been universal throughout the entire Christian world becomes more probable.

No reason has been offered, nor can any be offered, why the hierarchy of the Italian provinces should have differed from that of the rest of the Church. Would the apostles and the first most holy Roman pontiffs, who were exceptionally devoted to discipline, traditions, and apostolic rules, have neglected them in Italy alone?

Would they have altered only in Italy laws so necessary for the foundation of ecclesiastical order and for the preservation of the holy faith and Christian morals—in Italy, I say, the head of the entire world and the standard of discipline, morals, and faith?

What if significant evidence for other metropolises of Italy, and indeed for those of the earliest centuries, is not lacking? What if it is no longer reasonable to doubt Syracuse, Palermo, Capua, and perhaps Rhegium?

It is certain that in our own age extremely learned dissertations on these matters have appeared, leaving scarcely any room for doubt. They greatly diminish the force of the loudly proclaimed denial by which it was wickedly asserted that, after all metropolitans had been excluded from Italy, only the Roman pontiffs exercised metropolitan rights in that region throughout the first four centuries.

144. But what should be said about Ravenna? If the arguments against opinions that trace its beginnings either to the time of John Angeloptes or to Peter Chrysologus display some degree of probability, neither opinion seems capable of being maintained, and the beginnings of our dignity should not be assigned to either of those holy prelates.

When we find with certainty that they were metropolitans, but do not find that they were the first to attain that dignity, it follows necessarily that, before them, the bishops of Ravenna had been metropolitans. We must therefore return to apostolic times, in accordance with the rule of the universal hierarchy, since no beginning of this dignity can be found in any of Angeloptes’ or Chrysologus’s predecessors.

As we said above, because Chrysologus is recorded to have consecrated the bishop of Vicohabentia only at the end of his life, it cannot absolutely be denied—indeed, in the case of so great a teacher it must be asserted as certain, given the circumstances of those ecclesiastical times—that before the ordination of the bishop of Vicohabentia he had performed many acts of this kind of authority over the course of eighteen years, even though no one, not even Chrysologus himself, wrote about them.

145. The Ravennates also think that the silence of this holy bishop does not work against them, both because not all his works have survived to our age—he was the author of many books and volumes, and, as a richly flowing spring, divine wisdom poured into him daily, as Agnellus testifies—and because many works perished, not only those of Chrysologus but also those of his predecessors, whom earlier historians report to have written not a few works of the greatest importance.

These works were lost either through the incursions of the barbarians, through fires in the archive and library of our Church of Ravenna, through the hatred of later centuries for literary culture, or through the negligence or malice of earlier bishops, especially schismatics.

Moreover, in the homilies of Chrysologus—the only works to survive the ravages of time, apart from his letters to Eutyches the heresiarch and to the Fathers of the Council of Chalcedon—there was neither place nor occasion to mention this subject.

Further, Chrysologus is silent about the fact that the Church of Ravenna had already been adorned with this prerogative before he himself took up its government, although this can no longer be called into question.

Again, the holy doctor mentions one or another act of metropolitan jurisdiction performed by himself, namely the consecrations of Projectus of Imola and Marcellinus, bishop of Vicohabentia. Is it credible, then, that during an interval of eighteen years he enhanced so great a dignity by no other acts?

146. Agnellus, however, was a schismatic who indulged the emperors more than was right in ecclesiastical matters. Being impatient of Roman subjection, he impiously defended the Ravennate *anacephaleosis*—the claim of independent ecclesiastical authority—several times. It is therefore probable that, deliberately, he remained silent about this dignity in Angeloptes’ predecessors, lest he be forced to admit that it derived from the Apostolic See.

The matters omitted by Agnellus concerning our archbishops, but made known from other sources, are almost innumerable. Among them the remarkable election of eleven successors of St. Apollinaris by means of a visible dove is especially notable. For although Agnellus wrote about each of them, he seemed to have forgotten or been unaware of this ineffable prodigy; yet he finally provided splendid indications of it in the case of St. Severus, the last of them.

Should it then be surprising if he failed to report matters that would have condemned his error?

When, to quiet certain disturbances, the emperor Valentinian III, as Chrysologus says in the words cited from Homily 175, strengthened the decrees of the Roman pontiff by an imperial sanction, so that the bishops of Ravenna might preserve their dignity inviolate, Agnellus probably seized the opportunity to attribute to Valentinian the grant both of that dignity and of the sacred pallium—privileges that could be granted only by the Apostolic See.

If this was Agnellus’s intention, and if his words convey it, his account perhaps cannot prove that he meant the dignity of our metropolitan see to have been created entirely for the first time then. Rather, he may have meant that the ecclesiastical province of Emilia and Flaminia had then for the first time been circumscribed within definite boundaries.

147. We have never ceased to wonder why so many most learned men, highly expert in ancient discipline, rage so violently against this assertion of our Agnellus and against Jerome Rubeus, and condemn Valentinian’s diploma with every possible imprecation.

They chiefly note and condemn two things in it, without any charitable interpretation: first, that the establishment of our metropolitan see is attributed to Valentinian; and second, that the grant of the archiepiscopal pallium is attributed to him. Yet we cannot see what novelty or monstrosity these distinguished men find so horrifying in them.

Was not that century, were not the very times of Valentinian, teeming with examples of this kind? Was Valentinian the first, or the only one, to lay his hand upon ecclesiastical rights?

Who had divided the jurisdiction of Phoenicia between the bishops of Tyre and Berytus? Who had granted the Jerusalemite the primacy over Arabia, Phoenicia, and Palestine? Who had elevated Nicaea and Chalcedon to metropolitan rank? Were they not emperors of that very age?

What did Canon 12 of the Council of Chalcedon concern, with its terrible threat of deposition against bishops, unless they ceased seeking from the Augusti the establishment of such new metropolises?

From this point of view, then, Valentinian’s diploma would have been neither new nor monstrous, nor would Agnellus deserve to be condemned as though he had attributed the creation of a new metropolitan see of Ravenna to that emperor.

### 148

As for the granting of the pallium, here too the prudent economy of the ancient Church eluded these most distinguished men. Whether that pallium was an imperial insignia, a gift of the emperors for indicating and honoring the royal priesthood of bishops, or merely an ecclesiastical kind of garment signifying the fullness of authority in metropolitans, there is no doubt that, for several centuries after Constantine the Great, the supreme pontiffs awaited either the requests or the consent of emperors and kings before granting metropolitan bishops the use of the pallium. [Col. 0172C] The clearest witnesses to this truth are so many letters of the Roman pontiffs, especially those of Gregory the Great to Caesarius of Arles.

On this subject one may consult the learned Thomasinus, who explains this custom of the Church at greater length, especially in these words:

> It is certain that, for at least several centuries, in the East the pallium was not granted without the will of the emperor, just as it was in the West. For since this kind of garment had originally been royal, and since the emperors—such was their remarkable and singular piety—wished by it to honor Christ’s royal priesthood, the Church in turn repaid them for several centuries with this piety and gratitude: no one was to wear it without their approval.

### 149

[Col. 0172D] What novelty, then, what portent was there in the concession of the Emperor Valentinian, when, according to the practice of those centuries, it could so conveniently be understood as the consent granted by that Augustus both for the establishment of our metropolitan church and for the use of the pallium?

That Valentinian III issued some decree, concession, or confirmation of the privileges of our Church seems to be indicated by the mosaic work of Sant’Apollinare in Classe, in which the image of that Augustus holds a scroll in its hands, and on it we read: “The privileges of the Church of Ravenna.” But let others investigate these matters.

The remaining marks of falsity which the authors mentioned above examined with excessive curiosity, and which they claim to have found in Valentinian’s letter, are certainly not sufficient grounds for their making such an outcry against that diploma. [Col. 0173A] One of them may be the title “archbishop,” which was not yet used by the bishop of Ravenna in the fifth century; the other is the title “the Greater,” which Valentinian gives himself. Agnellus did not write these little words; they probably slipped into copies of the diploma through the fault of scribes.

We, however, think that Valentinian’s authentic letter—for the words of Saint Chrysologus’s Homily 175, quoted above, do not permit us to doubt that some letters were indeed issued by the Augustus himself—was either destroyed in the fire of the archiepiscopal archive, consumed by the malice of the schismatics, or lost during the captivity of Archbishop George, who had carried the more venerable monuments of our Church into Germany to display its greatness. We think, I say, that it was subsequently renewed through the work and ingenuity of some petty pedant, [Col. 0173B] perhaps in the ninth or tenth century, when the bishops of Ravenna commonly used the title “archbishop” and when *the Greater* (*τὸ major*) had likewise become customary among titles, examples of which would have been available, if necessary, in the parchments of the Ravenna archive.

We willingly leave this conjecture, however, to the judgment of more prudent men.

### 150

We have no certain knowledge of the occasion on which Valentinian’s letter was genuinely issued, or whether it was obtained by Angeloptes or by Chrysologus. If we may disclose whatever conjectures we have, we believe that the letter was not issued by the Augustus for the creation of a new metropolitan church of Ravenna. The very serious arguments which we explained above against Bacchinius stand in the way of such a belief. Rather, it was issued so that Chrysologus [Col. 0173C] or Angeloptes might recover, with its support, the churches which, as we have said, had perhaps been taken away by the Arians and later, through the preaching of Ambrose, received under the protection of the bishops of Milan, remaining under them for nearly fifty years. For that reason it was necessary to invoke both apostolic and imperial authority against those who sought to prevent their restoration.

It is also probable that, when—as Bacchinius says—the boundaries of ecclesiastical hierarchy in Italy began in the fifth century to be adjusted to the boundaries of the civil provinces, the decrees of the apostolic see and the favor of the emperors converged, [Col. 0173D] in the time either of Angeloptes or of Chrysologus, to restrain the complaints of those who opposed them. Their purpose would have been either to contract or to extend the metropolitan jurisdiction of Ravenna within the boundaries of Emilia and Flaminia.

Whatever the reason for which Valentinian’s letter appeared, it does not prejudice the opinion of the people of Ravenna concerning the contested origin of their dignity.

### 151

The people of Ravenna believe that this origin can be defended not only by the reasons already given against the force of the negative argument, but also by a positive document. They do not hesitate to derive such evidence from the letter of Gelasius I, Roman pontiff, to the bishops of Dardania, quoted above. In it Gelasius attacks Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, who was trying to extend his fringes in every direction and raise himself to the rank of patriarch of the East because he was bishop of an imperial city.

Gelasius proves, however, that the hierarchy of the Church was formed not from the imperial system, not [Col. 0174A] from the eminence of civil magistrates, not from the eminence of civil magistrates, and not from the residence of kings, but from apostolic institution. He presses Acacius with the examples of bishops who, although they presided over imperial cities, nevertheless kept themselves within the ancient limits of their jurisdiction:

> “We laughed,” he says, “at the attempt to compare a prerogative with Acacius because he was bishop of a royal city. Was an emperor not resident for many years at Ravenna, Milan, Sirmium, and Trier? Did the bishops of those cities ever usurp anything for their dignities beyond the measure anciently assigned to them?”

The people of Ravenna therefore argue: although emperors resided at Ravenna for many years, the bishops of that city nevertheless added nothing to their dignity and usurped no greater right, according to Gelasius’s testimony. [Col. 0174B] They remained within the measure of dignity and jurisdiction which they had possessed before the emperors and from ancient times.

Yet it is beyond doubt, and is confirmed by all historians, that the bishops of Ravenna possessed metropolitan dignity while emperors resided in that city. They therefore did not obtain that dignity through the authority or intercession of the emperors while the emperors were resident there; rather, they retained the dignity in the measure anciently assigned to them, adding nothing further to it. When Ravenna became an imperial city, it was already, from ancient times, the seat of an ecclesiastical metropolitan.

### 152

Bacchinius had perceived the force of Gelasius’s words and of this argument. He says that he was the first of all defenders of the metropolitan jurisdiction of Ravenna to detect it—[Col. 0174C]although, when Eustachius of Saint Ubald spoke of the metropolitan Church of Sirmium, he may perhaps have indicated the force of Gelasius’s authority even before Bacchinius.

It is remarkable, however, how this type of argument twisted Bacchinius’s mind and at times drove him almost completely off course, and in what sense he attempted to explain Gelasius’s otherwise very clear words. For if they were taken in their obvious sense, that most learned man saw that his own opinion and that of the others concerning the origin of the metropolitan church of Ravenna collapsed entirely of themselves.

It is therefore preferable to set out Bacchinius’s interpretation in his own words, lest we appear to have diminished its force.

### 153

> “Since it can in no way be called into doubt,” he says, “that, while the supreme pontiff Gelasius was seated at Rome, [Col. 0174D] the bishop of Ravenna was a metropolitan, it seems to follow that, according to the testimony of that same Gelasius, metropolitan jurisdiction did not then begin in the Church of Ravenna, when that city became the royal seat of the Augusti, but remained at the level at which it had previously stood, and that the bishop usurped nothing for his dignities beyond the measure anciently assigned to him.
>
> “Certainly Gelasius’s testimony is beyond all exception, both because he flourished shortly after the period when we have said that metropolitan jurisdiction was conferred upon the Church of Ravenna, and because it must be presumed that such a matter was well understood by so learned a Roman pontiff, so thoroughly versed in ecclesiastical rights.
>
> “Nevertheless, there are so many and such clear proofs that metropolitan jurisdiction was introduced into Italy later than in the rest of the West, [Col. 0175A] and so many indications that this jurisdiction was conferred upon the Church of Ravenna only later, that it is evident that the matter cannot be understood in the obvious sense preferred by Gelasius’s words. It is established that certain churches, such as Forocornelian, obeyed the bishop of Milan while Ambrose was alive, and that, at the time of Peter Chrysologus—or rather at the time of his election—they were counted among the churches subject to Ravenna.
>
> “After seriously considering the matter, I therefore believe that Gelasius intended only what the argument required: namely, that no jurisdiction was added by which bishops might rule over others merely because emperors had sometimes resided in their cities, but that ecclesiastical rights depend upon the authority of the Church.
>
> “For this reason he denies that any ecclesiastical jurisdiction was added to the bishops of Ravenna, Milan, Sirmium, or Trier [Col. 0175B] merely because emperors had dwelt for a long time in those cities. He says that, because of the emperors’ residence, the bishops of those cities usurped nothing for their dignities beyond the measure anciently assigned to them. He does not deny that their jurisdiction could have been enlarged from another source—namely, through the legitimate power of the Church—even with regard to the fact that the imperial seats had been located there.
>
> “Gelasius’s words therefore convey what was expressed by the sounder and more common interpretation of the Fathers and councils: ecclesiastical rights do not in any way depend upon secular power, nor should the dignity of the chief churches be attributed to the splendor of the chief cities. Rather, everything is effected and ordered by the prescriptions of the canons and by the supreme judgment of Peter, as circumstances of events and times are recognized to require. [Col. 0175C]
>
> “It follows that if anything was added to the measure anciently assigned to the bishops of Ravenna, Milan, Sirmium, Trier, and all the others, they did not usurp it because emperors had sometimes resided there, but possessed it legitimately by the authority of Peter, without prejudice to the prescriptions of the canons.
>
> “This, I think, is how Gelasius’s words must be understood. They consequently show that the account written by that eminent man concerning the beginnings of metropolitan jurisdiction at Ravenna was insufficiently considered and inconsistent with what preceded it—namely, that this jurisdiction was acquired in precisely the way in which the see of Constantinople usurped and ultimately peacefully retained patriarchal rights because of the imperial throne.
>
> “For the pontiff says the opposite, and testifies that, because of the imperial throne, the bishops of Ravenna usurped nothing beyond the ancient measure of their dignity.”

[Col. 0175D]

### 154

This is Bacchinius’s interpretation of Gelasius’s words, which he himself admits departs from their obvious meaning. The considerations that compel Bacchinius to force Gelasius’s sense in this way are the arguments proving that metropolitan jurisdiction was introduced into Italy later than in the rest of the West, that in that region only the Roman pontiff possessed metropolitan jurisdiction for the fourth century and beyond, and especially that this jurisdiction was conferred upon the Church of Ravenna only later, while certain churches, such as Forocornelian, are known to have obeyed the bishop of Milan while Ambrose was alive and to have been counted among the churches subject to Ravenna at the time of Chrysologus’s election.

But we have already examined all these considerations of Bacchinius: those which he derives from the negative argument, [Col. 0176A] and from the opinion that only the Roman pontiff was metropolitan in Italy, as well as those which he advances concerning John Angeloptes, Chrysologus, and his Homily 175.

As for the churches which, while Ambrose was alive, he says obeyed the bishop of Milan, such as Forocornelian, we have likewise answered sufficiently and more than sufficiently in chapter 1. Thus these considerations of the learned Cassinese appear altogether doubtful, uncertain, and almost improbable.

They therefore ought not to count for so much with a reasonable man that, on their account, the meaning of Gelasius’s words—clear, plain, and obvious in themselves—should be violently dragged into a distorted interpretation. Rather, a doubtful and uncertain matter, such as they wish the origin of the dignity of Ravenna to be, ought to be explained by the words of so learned a pontiff, words so open, so clear, and so obvious. This is especially true because the opinion favorable to Ravenna [Col. 0176B] is supported by so many other arguments already presented, whereas the contrary opinion, although extremely common, is entangled in so many evasions and difficulties.

### 155

Indeed, with all due respect to the learned Bacchinius, his interpretation seems excessively twisted and Gelasius’s meaning excessively disordered. Gelasius insults Acacius because, although he is bishop of a royal city, he attempts to enlarge his jurisdiction and raise himself above the patriarchs of the East. He therefore sets against him the example of four bishops of the West who, although they too were bishops of imperial cities, claimed no jurisdiction beyond what they had possessed from ancient times.

What Bacchinius says is true: in those words Gelasius did not deny that the jurisdiction of those churches could have been increased through the legitimate authority of the Church, even on the grounds that the imperial seats had been located there. [Col. 0176C] But since Gelasius says nothing about such an increase of jurisdiction actually having taken place through a concession of the Church during the emperors’ time, this is a clear indication that it did not take place.

For Gelasius’s argument against Acacius would have been stronger against the Constantinopolitan bishop if he had added that, if those four bishops had acquired any jurisdiction beyond the ancient measure because of the emperors, they had acquired it only through the indulgence of the Roman pontiffs. Moreover, since Gelasius is silent about such a thing, another highly significant conjecture arises from that silence: it most certainly did not happen.

If, because they were bishops of royal cities, those four bishops had received greater dignity from the apostolic see, the Acacian party would have seized the most opportune occasion to reproach Gelasius and the Roman Church. They would have said that Acacius was being denied what had not been denied to those other four bishops—even though emperors had intervened and even though two ecumenical councils, the First Council of Constantinople and the Council of Chalcedon, had granted their concessions. [Col. 0176D] They would have accused Rome of disturbing the ecclesiastical hierarchy and adding new jurisdiction, although those bishops had been supported by no canon or consent of a council.

Finally, Gelasius could not have insulted Acacius so freely if the Roman Church itself could have been accused of having disturbed the apostolic hierarchy of the churches in the West for the sake of the emperors, at the very time when it was defending that hierarchy with such determination in the East against the bishops of Constantinople, [Col. 0177A] against two general councils, and against the emperors themselves.

This conjecture may acquire still greater force from what we noted above concerning the resistance of the Church, and especially of the supreme pontiffs, to the establishment of new metropolitan churches of this kind.

### 156

By these arguments the people of Ravenna believe that they can free themselves from Bacchinius’s interpretation of Gelasius’s words. They maintain that, according to the obvious and natural meaning of those words, it is proved that the bishops of Ravenna did not obtain metropolitan rank from the time of the emperors, but had already possessed that honor before the emperors and from ancient times. Since no definite period can be established for the beginning of that honor, [Col. 0177B] its origin must therefore be referred to apostolic times and to the primitive institution of the ecclesiastical hierarchy.

We should also note in passing that the Milanese likewise employ Gelasius’s words according to their obvious meaning to prove that the illustrious Church of Milan had already risen to metropolitan dignity before Saint Ambrose, and not because of the residence of emperors. This observation will not be irrelevant.

The people of Ravenna also do not hesitate to think that the conclusion just reported and their understanding of Gelasius’s words can be strengthened by the authority of Saint Gregory VII, likewise a Roman pontiff, equally learned and equally zealous in defending ecclesiastical rights. For, writing to the people of Ravenna, Gregory conveys the following about their Church:

> “We believe that your knowledge is not unaware that the Church of Ravenna was accustomed to cling more closely than others to the apostolic see, and that it was specially loved by that see; [Col. 0177C] whatever dignity and honor it anciently possessed through blessed Apollinaris, it received as a gift from the aforementioned see.”

The holy pontiff calls the Church of Ravenna especially beloved by the apostolic see, since it ought to regard as received from that see whatever dignity and honor it had possessed from ancient times through blessed Apollinaris.

But if, in ancient times and through its first apostle and bishop, the Church of Ravenna had obtained nothing other than the chair of a simple bishop together with the Christian faith, Gregory would have vaunted in vain its special love for the apostolic see, its closer attachment to it, and the honors and dignities obtained from that see.

The pontiff was therefore speaking of those honors and dignities by which the Church of Ravenna was distinguished in his own age, and which he affirms had been conferred upon it from ancient times by the apostolic see [Col. 0177D] through blessed Apollinaris, the first bishop of Ravenna and a disciple of the apostle Peter. If the matter is properly considered, no other dignity and no other honors can be understood here than metropolitan dignity and honors.

The author of the *History of the Miracles of Saint Apollinaris* in the territory of Dijon agrees with Gregory VII. This author is believed to have flourished in the tenth century, and therefore before Gregory. He says:

> “As the recorded acts of his passion testify, this martyr, consecrated by Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, was sent as the first archbishop to Ravenna, the noblest of the metropolitan cities of Italy.”

### 157

By this series of positive testimonies, and by others which, in the interests of brevity, we shall not seek out—[Col. 0178A] especially those of Saint Peter Damian—the people of Ravenna believe that they destroy the contrary negative argument.

Turning their attention from this point to the learned observations of Bacchinius, they do not refuse to surrender to them, as it were, with hands willingly raised in defeat. They will gladly concede that the hierarchy of the churches was in no way formed by the apostles according to the pattern of civil magistracies.

They will also concede that the truth of Bacchinius’s opinion can very probably be deduced from the general system of the empire as it existed in apostolic times and from the particular government of each province, although they suspect that the learned material which the Cassinese abbot assembled concerning the instability of the government of every particular province is irrelevant to the matter.

For, first, this instability of provincial government may not have existed at the time [Col. 0178B] when the apostles were spreading the Gospel. It arose in the course of time, when the Christian faith had already been widely diffused and the order and system of the ecclesiastical hierarchy had already been established, especially in Italy.

Augustus had divided Italy into eleven regions, assigning to each its own governor, decurions, and duumvirs. This form of magistracy and government continued for nearly two centuries, until it was altered by the Emperor Hadrian. The Church therefore had ample time and opportunity to establish the hierarchical order in this region according to the civil hierarchy constituted by Augustus, insofar as it conformed itself to that hierarchy.

Once the hierarchy had been established by the apostles and their successors, however, it could remain subject to no changes, [Col. 0178C] whatever disturbances subsequently affected the civil administration of the provinces under Hadrian, Aurelian, and other emperors.

Even if it had been true that, in apostolic times, one province had obeyed several governors or several provinces one governor, this would provide a reasonable explanation for why, in the ecclesiastical hierarchy, one metropolitan did not everywhere preside over one province only, but several provinces could be subject to one metropolitan; and why a province that had once been single could become two provinces, as happened with our Emilia, which was divided into two regions, one called Flaminia and the other Emilia.

Second, even if the instability of the administration of particular provinces had existed in apostolic times and had presented an obstacle to the establishment of the ecclesiastical hierarchy in certain regions, this perhaps cannot be shown of Emilia itself, either then [Col. 0178D] or for a long period afterward. For after the division into Emilia and Flaminia mentioned above, Ravenna remained immutably the capital and metropolitan city of both, even after Constantine divided Italy into two vicariates.

### 158

Nevertheless, despite these considerations, and despite granting all these points freely to the learned Bacchinius, the people of Ravenna still congratulate themselves that the opinion of so great a man concerning the origin of ecclesiastical metropolitan churches not only fails to destroy their position but increasingly confirms the view of those who attribute the beginnings of this dignity in the Church of Ravenna to apostolic times and institution.

For if it is highly probable—indeed, I would almost call it certain—that the disciples of the apostles, [Col. 0179A] scattered throughout the world in every direction, founded churches among the peoples whom they had converted; that, after establishing their own seats there, they spread the faith from those seats to neighboring regions, cities, and peoples; and that they established new churches and ordained new bishops there; then, by apostolic ordinance, these disciples would have presided over the converted regions, the new churches, and their bishops as their first fathers and teachers.

The people of the new churches would have looked to their cathedra as the mother of their own faith. From it they would have sought and accepted traditions, the rules of apostolic discipline, counsel in doubtful matters, refuge in disagreements and afflictions, and consent in ordinations. This was undoubtedly then both the beginning and foundation of metropolitan jurisdiction and the prerogative of metropolitan dignity.

If, I say, Bacchinius considers this highly probable, [Col. 0179B] then the case of Ravenna is most opportune. The people of Ravenna are firmly convinced that Apollinaris, a disciple of Peter sent by the apostle to Ravenna—the most distinguished of the cities of Italy—established and secured an episcopal chair there, preached the Gospel of Christ from that place throughout Emilia, and formed flourishing churches from the converted peoples in its cities.

This is testified not only by the enduring and celebrated tradition of the Church of Ravenna, but also by the traditions of the churches of Emilia themselves, which recognize and confess Ravenna as their teacher in the faith through Apollinaris.

Benedict XIV, who now occupies Peter’s chair, an incomparable pontiff in learning, doctrine, and wisdom, clearly asserted this about our Bologna in the elegant address [Col. 0179C] which he recently delivered at Rome for the dedication of the magnificent new basilica consecrated to Saint Apollinaris.

The learned pontiff was preceded by Sigonius, cited by Ughelli, who says that Bologna received the Christian rites from Apollinaris, the apostle of Emilia, whom Peter, prince of the apostles, is said to have sent there. Although Apollinaris established his seat at Ravenna, he nevertheless filled all Emilia with the Gospel of Christ.

We omit, so as not to make this too long, what the historians of the other churches of Emilia assert concerning the churches formed by that same Apollinaris.

### 159

[Col. 0179D]

It would also be excessively long to append here the testimonies of the acts of Saint Apollinaris, of sacred writers, and of the many churches throughout the world which provide abundant evidence of his mission and apostolate throughout Emilia. Anyone may consult Peter Chrysologus, Peter Damian, a hundred historians, and especially the learned Bollandists.

There have indeed been authors who, arrogantly rejecting the very ancient acts of Apollinaris, cast them among the apocrypha. There have also been others, such as the abbot Fleury, who did not deign to insert even a word in his *Ecclesiastical History* about this most celebrated disciple of Peter, although he is frequently mentioned by the holy doctors, in so many letters and monuments [Col. 0180A] of the Roman pontiffs, and in so many historical records, while the excellence of the churches founded by him at Ravenna is celebrated by all authors.

A recent author of the *Observations on that same History* rightly reproached Fleury for this arrogant omission, among the many other blemishes with which the abbot’s *Ecclesiastical History* abounds.

As for the most ancient acts of Saint Apollinaris, celebrated authors have defended them. Among these, the aforementioned Bollandists clearly show that they cannot rightly be doubted, noting only that they were corrupted and interpolated in certain places.

### 160

Yet not one among all these writers—whether those who accept such acts or those who reject them—has sharpened his critical rigor to the point of denying Apollinaris’s apostolate in Emilia, the conversion [Col. 0180B] of the cities of that province, or the foundation of its churches. They rely on the testimony of the Fathers and historians and on the immemorial tradition of so many churches.

Therefore, if a law was established by the apostles, and if it was the custom of the universal Church throughout the East—as Bacchinius argues invincibly—that churches founded from another church, which an apostle had established through his disciples, should recognize that mother church as their teacher, mother, and head, and if this was the origin of metropolitan jurisdiction and dignity; if the assertions of the supreme pontiffs Gelasius I and Gregory VII are to be understood in their obvious and natural sense; if the same rule of hierarchy had to prevail everywhere throughout the Church; and if the opinion of those authors who placed the origin of Ravenna’s metropolitan [Col. 0180C] dignity either in John Angeloptes or in Peter Chrysologus can scarcely any longer be defended, then, say the people of Ravenna, the view of Hieronymus Rubeus, Peter de Marca, and the other writers—that this origin should be traced back to apostolic times and to Saint Apollinaris, the first bishop of Ravenna—must appear far more probable and superior to every other opinion on this subject.

This is the position of the people of Ravenna.

Although we fully recognize the force of their reasoning—indeed, now more than ever—we do not claim that it is insuperable. We willingly leave our entire judgment to the wiser and more experienced critics with whom our own age is abundantly supplied.

These, then, learned Paciaude, were the exercises with which, according to our modest ability, we occupied our leisure hours in the literary contests of the people of Ravenna. At that time, from the metropolitan [Col. 0180D] pulpit, you were stirring and filling this illustrious city with admiration for yourself, and the hearts of all with the riches of your doctrine, eloquence, and learning, as an evangelical herald.

I therefore wish—and hope—that after you have calmly read these pages of ours and examined them with that penetrating eye of yours, you will judge them less unworthy of emerging from our hiding places and of exposing and testifying to the literary world the author’s ignorance.

Farewell.

## SERMONS OF SAINT PETER CHRYSOLOGUS

[Col. 0179D]

### Censure of the Sermons

**Sermon XII.** From beginning to end this sermon is attributed to Saint Augustine, and it is found among the *Eulogies* of Augustine’s *Milleloquium*, first compiled by Bartholomew, Bishop of Urbino, and afterward printed by John Collier in Paris in 1649, column 1, letter D. In the same place Saint Augustine’s Sermon 13 *On Lent* is cited.

Since the death of this most holy doctor occurred seventeen years before the death of Chrysologus, [Col. 0181] one might suspect that this sermon was borrowed from Saint Augustine by some compiler. Yet it is found nowhere in Augustine’s works. Only Sermon 172 *On the Season* resembles it at the beginning, and not at all in its continuation; nor does that sermon contain even a word about the temptations of Christ.

**Sermon L.** Some attribute this sermon to Chrysostom, others to Jerome: the former to the foremost doctor of the Greek Church, the latter to the foremost doctor of the Latin Church. It would be extraordinary indeed if two writers of different languages could pronounce the same sermon in the same words.

The Roman Church reads it in the Breviary at the second Nocturn for the Eighteenth Sunday after Pentecost and attributes it to Chrysologus. Saint Thomas cites such a sermon in the *Catena* under the name of John the bishop; in older *Catenae*, Chrysostom is frequently cited by this formula of expression.

The more expansive style of the discourse, which is not broken up in the manner customary for Chrysologus, might persuade someone to attribute it to Chrysostom rather than to him or to Jerome. The manuscripts of Cesena and Urbino claim it for our author.

**Sermon LIII.** It is found in the appendix to the sermons of Saint Augustine under number 61, volume V, page 75, formerly *On the Season* 169. It has, however, been interpolated throughout, or expanded by many sentences, which are enclosed between brackets on both sides.

Alcuin transcribes some passages from it in chapter 6 of *On Virtues and Vices*. It is more correctly attributed to the priest Barbatius, concerning whom Saint Peter Damian speaks in volume XI, page 306 of the Lyon edition, Sermon LXV, delivered on his feast day.

Barbatius lived at Ravenna during the reign of the Empress Placidia, around the year 449; see Surius, 31 December; Peter de Natalibus, book XI, chapter 21, page 183; and Rubeus, *History of Ravenna*, under the year 433.

Perhaps moved by Chrysologus’s exhortations, he rebuked the people of Ravenna for their mutual dissensions and encouraged them to peace with one another and to humble obedience to their pastor. Whatever the truth may be, the difference in style excludes this sermon from the works of our author.

**Sermon LXXIV.** Brother Antonius Ghislandus, in his book entitled *The Golden Work on the Gospels*, in the sections on the Gospel of Holy Saturday, doubts 17 and 23, and elsewhere, attributes this sermon to Saint Severianus or Severinus, as he does also Sermon LXXVI below. He may perhaps have taken this from Saint Thomas’s *Commentary*, as Maldonatus seems to suggest in his discussion of Matthew 28, number 9.

The style, however, is not dissimilar; the accumulation of different phrases repeating the same ideas, the agreement of learned men, and the authority of all the manuscripts that exist claim it for Chrysologus.

Franciscus Combefisius, in his work *Authors Reviewed*, and so forth, Paris 1662, page 135, wondered whether, in Saint Thomas’s *Catena*, where this sermon and the following sermons on Christ’s Resurrection are cited, the abbreviated name “Sever.” should be read as Severus of Malaca. The chronology would fit, as would the error which the author attacks: the denial of the resurrection of true flesh.

Yet no sermons are attributed to any Severus of Malaca, and Chrysologus may have been referring to the older error of Origen.

**Sermon XCI.** The same sermon, though considerably shortened at its beginning, is found among Saint Augustine’s sermons *On the Saints*, formerly numbered 22 and now in the appendix to volume V, page 135, number 199. Nevertheless, Mita rightly believes from its very opening that it belongs to Chrysologus.

**Sermon CVII.** Although distinguished in style and doctrine, says Mita, this sermon is very far removed from the sermons of Chrysologus. Fabricius, in volume I, book III, page 1055 of his *Bibliotheca mediae Latinae*, and Tillemont, volume V, page 485 of the Venetian edition, rightly take it away from Chrysologus.

In a manuscript it is entitled *On Saint Peter the Bishop*. The title “Saint,” however, betrays a later age. Moreover, the diction here is much more polished than is usual for our author; it is neither burdened by circumlocutions nor elevated by unusual expressions.

One must nevertheless admit that it speaks of a Peter who was bishop of some place. Nor was it unusual among the ancients to include among an author’s works writings which were either addressed to him or had been delivered in his honor. I therefore gladly yield to those who think that this sermon was pronounced at Ravenna in praise of our Peter Chrysologus.

**Sermon CXXVII.** Franciscus Garcia de Valle, in book I, discourse 25, number 38 of his *Evangelical Preacher*, argues with all his strength that this sermon belongs to John Chrysostom, Homily 16 from various passages in Matthew.

Indeed, it appears among the Chrysostomian works in the Paris edition printed by Sebastian Nivellus at the Ciconiae press in 1581, volume II, page 1074, but with a mark in the margin of the book by which the editor himself warns readers that it should be relegated among the spurious works.

One would have to be a stone or a tree-stump not to perceive that Chrysostom’s gravity is absent from it, and that it has, on the contrary, the pure and unmistakable character of Chrysologus’s diction.

**Sermon CXXIX.** “This sermon,” says Latinius, “contains nothing of Chrysologus.” Mita agrees, observing that the word *Charissimi*—“most beloved”—is never found in Chrysologus, for whom another form is familiar, namely *Fratres*, “brothers.”

Tillemont likewise considers it spurious, volume V, page 866. Above all, this is suggested by the purity of the style and the easy flow of the words.

**Sermon CXXXV.** Concerning this sermon, which has the same clause-structure as the preceding one, Tillemont and Latinius make similar observations. Ruinart, in the *Acts of the Martyrs*, page 188, accepts it as a genuine offspring of our author and calls it an excellent sermon.

**Sermon CXXXVI.** This is a fragment of a sermon by an author different from Chrysologus, in which a certain Bishop Adelphus figures.

**Sermon CXXXVIII.** Mita considers it the work of Saint Germanus of Auxerre. While this holy bishop was staying as a guest with Chrysologus at Ravenna, it is not unlikely that he delivered these few remarks about peace.

At the beginning he calls Chrysologus “Father and Teacher,” on account of his pontifical dignity in that city and his overflowing learning; he describes himself as a foreigner and a rustic, as though he had come from barbarous regions.

Although these statements are put forward in the manner of conjecture, it is certain that the sermon is not by Chrysologus. Saint Germanus will be discussed elsewhere.

### Sermon CXLIII

Some things in it occur in Jerome’s sermon on the Annunciation, in the final volume, p. 101 of the Paris edition published by Nivellius in 1579, addressed to Paula and Eustochium—especially those passages cited by D. Thomas in the *Catena*, vol. V of his works, p. 14 of the recent Venetian edition. Possevinus observes in the *Apparatus*, vol. II, p. 44, and Nicolaus, following him, in the notes to the aforementioned *Catena*, that a sermon of this sort should be relegated among Jerome’s spurious works and attributed rather to a Greek than to a Latin author, since in it one can see a Greek author speaking Latin. Not a few writers of no inferior standing, as they like to say, believe it to be the work of Sophronius, the friend of St. Jerome—namely, the man who rendered Jerome’s *Catalogue of Writers* into Greek—as though this were completely certain.

### Sermon CXLIX

Without a doubt it must be attributed to Saint Severianus, bishop of Gabala. It appears under his name among the works of Saint John Chrysostom, vol. III, p. 140 of the recent Paris edition, edited by Dom de Montfaucon, who gives the following preface:

> “Severianus, bishop of Gabala, who was then residing in Constantinople and had won the friendship of the holy bishop through feigned acts of service, frequently preached to the people. Taking advantage of Chrysostom’s absence, when he had gone to Asia, he strove to bind the people to himself and, as is thought, to divert their allegiance from Chrysostom. When Serapion informed Chrysostom of this, Chrysostom returned from Asia and, seeing the people rejoicing and full of gladness at his return, seems not to have paid much attention to the matter. But when Severianus, angered at Serapion, uttered words full of impiety, and the people were in tumult and stirred to anger, he was driven from Constantinople. Later, through the intervention of the Empress Eudoxia and the emperor himself, he was recalled and, though reluctantly, admitted by Chrysostom. But since the anger of the people could be calmed only by the exhortations of their shepherd, Chrysostom, in this brief address [it appears there on p. 412], soothed their embittered minds and persuaded them to admit Severianus.”

Thus writes the most learned editor in his notes of admonition to the aforementioned homily. On the following day Severianus himself delivered a brief address to the people, in which he rejoiced over the restored peace. He commends this peace, achieved through the care of their common Father, with the highest praise. This address of Severianus, however, slipped among the sermons of Chrysologus and became number 149 in the sequence.

I have no doubt that the expression “common Father” refers to Chrysostom, who was present, as is observed in other homilies and especially in one delivered by a certain Antiochene presbyter before Flavian, bishop of that city, among the spurious works of Chrysostom, vol. VI, p. 555 of the recently cited edition.

As for the claim that Baronius removed this Severianus from the Roman Martyrology as Chrysostom’s most bitter enemy, this is falsely asserted. I would add that the distinguished Georgius, in his notes to Ado’s *Martyrology*, vol. I, p. 63, has wiped away this unjust stigma which Rosweidus placed upon him.

In some editions a title is prefixed to this sermon which certain people think belonged to Severianus, but wrongly. Nevertheless, Latinius observes that its inclusion was not entirely arbitrary, for, he says, it contains nothing of Chrysologus.

### Sermon CLII

This sermon is read in Latin among other homilies of the Fathers collected by Alcuin; nor are there lacking those who think it should be added to the sermons of Saint Severianus. Mita, however, is indignant in his notes. He compares the envy, as he calls it, of those who tried to take this sermon away from Chrysologus with Herod’s envy toward the lives of the Innocents, and he expresses his aversion toward them. He adds that Chrysologus’ surname was never more aptly justified than on account of a sermon of this kind:

> “For in this sermon he truly poured forth a golden stream of eloquence and displayed the highest learning. In style and doctrine it does not differ from his more eminent homilies, and no prudent person would say that this is a composition of Saint Severianus, since in its entire phrasing and doctrine it differs from the sermon of his reported above as number 149. Moreover, Severianus was Greek by birth and wrote in Greek. But the sermon in question is Latin throughout in its origin and nowhere bears the scent of Greek expression; nor has any person skilled in languages yet judged it to have been translated from a Greek original into Latin.”

So writes Mita, expanding at much greater length in praise of this sermon. In truth, it agrees so closely with Chrysologus’ phrasing that one could not say that an egg is more like another egg.

Finally, I have added an appendix to this edition, including in it several sermons of Chrysologus that had hitherto circulated under another name. First place is occupied by five sermons on the Lord’s Prayer, which I borrowed from Dacher’s *Spicilegium*, vol. VII, p. 120. He had formerly published them, on the authority of the Corbie manuscript, as works of Peter Damian; later, after Stephen de Marces had drawn his attention to the matter, he discovered that they were Chrysologus’ sermons.

Sermons 73 and 97, printed in the appendix to Augustine, vol. V, pp. 92 and 120—sermons concerning which the Louvain scholars rightly expressed doubt—have been assigned to our author by the highly learned Benedictine editors of Saint-Maur. Supported by the testimony of such men, I have done the same.

There are some who, relying on the authority of certain manuscripts, also assert that sermon 120 of the appendix is a genuine work of Chrysologus. But the style does not permit this assertion: the sermon is almost inflated, rather than brief and pointed in the manner customary to our author, and seemed excessively ornate to Petavius in book XVI of his work *On the Incarnation*.

P. Labbe, in the *Bibliotheca*, p. 783, cites another sermon under Chrysologus’ name, on the nativity of the Blessed Virgin. But, as has been observed elsewhere, the titles of the sermons have been corrupted; nor do we know that such a feast was yet celebrated in Chrysologus’ time.

Those who arrange sermons LXVII, LXVIII, LXX, and LXXI in sequence and attribute them to Peter Damian are striking the air and building castles in the clouds. For these sermons are present in the first collection of Saint Felix, bishop of Ravenna, which we know to have been produced near the beginning of the eighth century, whereas Damian lived much later. It is therefore already clear how empty are the supports upon which their opinion rests.

The more polished and effortless diction of sermon CXXIX, on Saint Cyprian, and sermon CXXXV, on Saint Lawrence, has likewise deceived some people and provided them with grounds for suspicion.

[Col. 0183]

## Sermons of Saint Peter Chrysologus, Archbishop of Ravenna (C, G)*

[Col. 0183A]

## Sermon I

### On the two sons, the prodigal and the dutiful; first, on the prodigal’s departure from his father

Today the Lord has summoned and brought before us a father with his two sons, so that through a figure he might disclose the immense evidence of his mercy, the savage envy of the Jewish people, and the humble return of the Christian people.

> “A certain man had two sons, and the younger of them said to his father: ‘Father, give me the portion of the property that falls to me.’ And he divided the property between them” (Luke 15).

How loving the father, so impatient the heir! He is wearied by his father’s continuing life; and because he cannot take away his father’s time, he tries to take away his property. He deserved not to retain the very privilege of being a son, since he refused to possess what belonged to his father together with his father.

But let us ask what carried the son away to such an undertaking, what confidence emboldened him to make so great a request. What was it? Clearly, the fact that he knew the heavenly Father could be confined by no limit, enclosed by no period of time, or released by any power of death. And therefore he wishes to enjoy the freedom of living, since he did not wish to become rich through the resources of one who was dying.

Finally, the father’s generosity confirms that his request was an offense:

> “And he divided the property between them.”

At the request of one, he immediately divided the entire property between both, so that the sons might know that what their father had previously held back was withheld not out of greed but out of love; not from ill will, but from prudence. The father was concerned to preserve the property for his sons, not to deny it to them, and wished these pledges to remain for them rather than perish.

Blessed are the sons whose entire wealth consists in their father’s love! Blessed are those for whom possession remains wholly in obedience to their father and in their father’s worship!

But material resources divide unity, separate brotherhood, scatter kinship, destroy and violate the affection of parents, as the following words make clear:

> “Father, give me the portion of the property that falls to me.”  
> “And he divided the property between them.”

> “And not many days later, the younger son gathered everything together and departed into a distant region, and there he squandered his property by living dissolutely. After he had consumed everything, a severe famine occurred in that region, and he began to be in need. He went and attached himself to one of the citizens of that region, and he sent him into his fields to feed pigs. And he longed to fill his belly with the pods that the pigs were eating, and no one gave him any.”

See what desire for wealth does when it rushes headlong! See how, without his father, wealth stripped the son naked rather than enriched him: wealth carried the son from his father’s embrace, expelled him from his house, removed him from his homeland, robbed him of his reputation, and stripped him of chastity. Of his life, his character, his piety, his freedom, and his glory, it left nothing.

Finally, it changed a citizen into a foreigner, a son into a hired servant, a wealthy man into a pauper, and a free man into a slave. It joined him to pigs, away from the most devoted father whom he had abandoned, so that he might serve a filthy herd—he who had scorned obedience to holy devotion.

> “When he had gathered everything together, the younger son…”

This younger son was plainly younger not in age but in understanding. He gathered his father’s goods and went away, far more distant in mind than in place, so that, having given rather than received a price, he might miserably sell himself into slavery.

Thus he became a merchant who had entered into such a bargain: he did not know how to repay what he owed his parents, or to return an equivalent to the one who had begotten him.

With one’s father there is a sweet condition: free servitude, unrestrained protection, joyful fear, gentle correction, wealthy poverty, and secure possession. For the labor falls upon the father, while the fruits overflow to the sons.

> “He squandered his property.”

What had been gathered under the father’s direction was scattered by the son’s prodigality, so that, even if only late, he might understand that the father had been a guardian of the property, not one who merely hoarded it.

> “By living dissolutely.”

That life is mortal, because it dies with respect to the virtues. Whoever lives by vices is buried as far as reputation is concerned and perishes in glory. Whoever remains in disgrace grows in infamy.

> “After he had consumed everything, a severe famine occurred in that region.”

To luxury, the belly, and gluttony, famine is imposed as a torturer, so that avenging punishment may rage where punishable guilt had burned.

A severe famine occurred. Such an end is always sought by greediness; such a limit is reached by the outpouring of pleasure that ought to be avoided.

> “And he himself began to be in need.”

The property he had been given made the son needy; if it had been withheld, it would have preserved him rich. Thus, by possessing, he failed within himself—he who, by not possessing, had abounded in his father’s house.

> “And he attached himself to one of the citizens of that region, and he sent him into his fields to feed pigs.”

Thus one who denies his father and entrusts himself to a stranger finds a master, so that he may experience the severity of the judge after fleeing from the most indulgent provider.

A deserter of affection, a fugitive from devotion, he is assigned to pigs, handed over to pigs, and delivered into the slavery of pigs. He traverses the muddy pasture of pigs; he is trampled by the rush of the restless herd and stained by it, so that he may learn how wretched it is—and how bitter—to have lost the blessedness of his father’s repose.

> “And he longed to fill his belly with the pods that the pigs were eating, and no one gave him any.”

What a cruel service! He could not even share a meal with the pigs, although he lived among pigs. Wretched man, who, while tending filthy beasts, languished and hungered for their food! Wretched man, who desired the filthy animals’ food but could not obtain even its quality!

Instructed and warned by these examples, let us remain in our father’s house; let us endure in the bosom of our mother; let us be bound together in the embraces of our relatives; let our father’s heart hold us fast, lest the pitiable freedom of youth drag us into the evils mentioned above.

Let reverence for our father surround us; let our mother’s affection shape us; let us be guarded by the love of our relatives. Among the watchful eyes of our kindred, sins cannot move about. As many eyes as our relatives possess, so many lamps are there. The mother’s gaze is day; the father’s face shines like the sun.

Therefore, while one lives among so many lights of virtue, the darkness of crimes cannot approach. But our father’s table nourishes us with the food of virtue, the feast of salvation, and the delights of honor and glory.

And because the extended sequence of the reading compels us to speak at greater length about this parable, in the following sermon we shall examine who the father is—generous in giving, more generous in receiving; who the brother is—most sorrowful over his brother’s salvation; and who the younger son is—foolish in departing, but wisest in returning.

We shall investigate these matters in our common prayers.

Editorial notes to Sermon I:

- “Immense evidence of his mercy”: this is the theme of infinite mercy; see the author below in Sermon 49 (Mita). The expression is familiar to Chrysologus; some editions read “judgment.”
- The two sons prefigure the two peoples, Jewish and Gentile; so also Dionysius the Areopagite, Epistle 8; Irenaeus, *Against Heresies* IV.70; Jerome, Epistle 46 to Damasus; Augustine, *Questions on the Gospels* II.33; and others.
- “He is wearied by his father’s continuing life”: he can scarcely bear that his father lives.
- The printed manuscripts formerly corruptly read *audire*. Latinius read: “Because he cannot take away his father’s time or day, he tries to take away his property.” Compare Ambrose, *On Naboth* I.4, p. 308, col. 1, Paris edition: “The idle heir watches; the fastidious heir complains that you die too late”; and Augustine, *Questions on the Gospels* II.29: “The avaricious man would wish no other person to exist, so that he alone might possess everything.”
- Other editions read *valuerat*; so too the Vallicellian manuscript and the Cologne and Bologna editions. The sense is: he who had not wished to be enriched by the resources of his dying father.
- The “offense” is the shameless conduct employed by the son in making this request (Mita).
- Some think Christ refers to a custom, if not among the Jews, at least among neighboring peoples, by which sons on reaching puberty could claim a share of their paternal estate in order to trade. Others, including our author, hold that the father gave his sons the inheritance for free use, though bound by no law or custom.
- Chrysologus disagrees with those who think that the Prodigal asked not for his father’s property but for a share of his mother’s inheritance. See Du Hamel here.
- “Pledges” (*pignora*) is regularly used for children by better-era writers. Compare also Tertullian, *On Idolatry* 12, and Cyprian, *On the Death of Job’s Children*: “After the funerals of his pledges.”
- On “resources”: all human possessions that serve the necessities of life are so called, notes Caspar Barthius on this passage in Chrysologus, *Adversaria* XI.3, col. 517. There he cites Gaudentius to Germinius and Venantius Fortunatus XI. See also Lactantius, *On Justice* V.19. Read Chrysologus below, Sermon 162, and its note.
- The Greek has ἀποσκευὴν (*aposkeuēn*), where the Latin translator rendered “property” (*substantiam*), which our writers sometimes render “estate” (*censum*): Augustine, *Questions on Exodus* 47.
- Compare Columella VII.10: “No breed delights more than swine in wallowing in streams and a muddy pool.”
- The younger son is plainly younger not in age but in understanding. Euthymius, notes on the Catena on Luke 15, ch. 57: “not younger in time, but deficient in understanding.” Some editions wrongly read “not in age, but in estate.”
- On “a distant region”: because the author interprets this region mystically, it was thought fitting to add that the distant region is forgetfulness of God, as Augustine teaches, *Questions on the Gospels* II.33. See Ambrose aptly here: “The distant region is the shadow of death, that is, sin” (Mita). See Chrysostom, homily *On the Father and the Two Sons*, II, p. 1166, Paris edition, 1581.
- “To return an equivalent”: a Chrysologan expression for repaying one benefit with another. Plautus, *Menaechmi*: “Safe and sound I return to you the purse which you gave me.”
- Compare Quintilian X: “He brooded over them as though over locked treasures.”
- We restore “if it had been withheld, it would have preserved him rich” from the Caesena manuscript. Other editions read: “When withheld, it satisfied [him].”
- Other copies have, in Castillo, “the true judge within himself.”
- No service was baser among Jews and Egyptians, who excluded such persons from access to temples as profane. No one even of the lower populace wished to enter into familiarity and intercourse with them. See Herodotus II.47.
- Corrupt editions read “splendid pastures”; on the basis of Meursius’s corrections, ch. 11, p. 130, the error has been removed.
- He could not be a table-companion of the pigs which he labored to feed.
- We restore “who, while tending the filthy herd, languishes and hungers for their fodder” from the Bologna edition, Mita, and Castillo. Other editions read: “who lacks the pigs.”
- “Pods” translates Greek ἀπὸ τῶν κερατίων (*apo tōn keratiōn*). This is fodder more suited to beasts than men, taken from trees called pod-bearing. Others understand by *siliquae* certain trees called by Greeks καῤῥουβα (*karrhouba*), and likewise by French, Spaniards, and Italians. Strictly, a *siliqua* is the sheath or covering in which legumes grow. *Ceratia* appear to be wild pods, very abundant in Judaea and Syria. The Syrians also had a kind of pod from which, according to Pliny, *On Artificial Wines* IV, they extracted wine. On why the Prodigal lacked the pods on which the pigs fed, see Maldonatus on Luke 15.16.
- By “mother” Chrysologus plainly figures the Catholic Church.
- Some editions read “thresholds”; the Caesena manuscript, “lights.” It is an easy scribal slip.
- All manuscript and printed copies read “guides.” Although boldly made, Castillo’s correction, “lights,” pleased me: after lights, lamps, day, and sun, why should “guides,” rather than “lights,” follow? Further, darkness is opposed not to a guide but to light. It is remarkable how earnestly Chrysologus connects opposites with opposites.
- Barthius, *Adversaria* VI.18, p. 287, explains “common prayers” as shared prayers and cites this passage. In VIII.21 he observes that the words contain a spondaic hexameter, which he says occurs frequently also in Chrysostom, Hyginus, Hilary, and others. But I do not know to what use the learned man puts this observation. Paulinus of Nola uses *vota* for prayers: “Now it delights us to utter words with the mouth and to discharge songs in prayers.”

## Sermon II

### On the same subject, concerning the son’s return to his father

We have briefly discussed in the preceding sermon, as far as we were able, the prodigal son—the deserter of his most devoted father—and the evils that struck him so severely that, emaciated by hunger, he surrendered himself to the slavery of pigs.

Now, with a better hope and happier words, let us pursue his return and his repentance.

> “Coming to himself, he said: ‘How many hired servants of my father have an abundance of bread’” (Luke 15:17), and so forth.

Chrysologus agrees here with Ambrose and Bede in following the Greeks, who do not have the words “in the house.”

He came back to himself; indeed, he first returns to himself, so that he might return to his father—he who had first departed from himself when he departed from his father. He migrated from himself and passed entirely from being human into being a beast, forgetful of his father’s devotion and oblivious to his parent’s grace.

> “How many hired servants of my father have an abundance of bread, while I perish here from hunger!”

Hunger recalls the one whom fullness had exiled. Hunger taught him to recognize his father, whereas abundance had prevented him from sensing his parent. And if involuntary hunger accomplished so much, consider what voluntary fasting can achieve.

A burdened belly lays the heart down beneath vices; it weighs upon the mind, preventing it from perceiving heavenly devotion.

> “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” (Wisdom 9:5).

Hence the Lord also says:

> “Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down with gluttony and drunkenness” (Luke 21:34).

The belly must therefore be emptied through the moderation of fasting, so that the unburdened spirit may strive toward higher things, ascend toward the virtues, and, wholly winged, fly toward the very author of devotion.

Elijah proves this: purified by the continuation of the Lord’s fast and freed from the burden of the flesh, he flew forth victorious over death toward heaven (3 Kings 19:8; 4 Kings 2:11).

> “I will arise and go to my father.”

He was lying there who said, “I will arise.” He understood his fall; he perceived his ruin; he recognized that he lay on the slippery ground of disgraceful luxury. Therefore he cried out:

> “I will arise and go to my father.”

With what hope? With what confidence? With what assurance? With the hope that comes from the fact that he has a father.

I lost what belonged to a son; he did not lose what belongs to a father. With the father, no stranger intervenes: within the father’s breast is affection itself, which intervenes and pleads.

The father’s heart is stirred to beget his son again through forgiveness. I shall go to my father as one guilty; but as soon as the father sees his son, he immediately covers his guilt. He suppresses the judge because he prefers to fulfill the role of father; he quickly turns the sentence into forgiveness, because he desires his son’s return, not his destruction.

> “I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him: ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you.’”

Confession reveals the father; repentance speaks of the parent.

> “I have sinned against heaven and before you.”

“Against heaven” is understood as “against God” more than once in Sacred Scripture—as though he were saying: “I have sinned against God,” against that power which shines forth most clearly in heaven, as in Daniel 4:28; 1 Maccabees 3:18; Matthew 21:25; and Luke 20:4. Clear examples of this meaning also appear in the apocryphal books of the Old Testament.

But, as Castillo rightly notes, from the words quoted it is perfectly clear that Chrysologus does not understand the evangelist to mean God by “heaven,” but either God’s throne and seat, or the assembly and unity of the just. Hilary agrees most clearly in his exposition of Psalm 118. The passage is too long for the limits of this note. See also Chrysostom’s homily *On the Father and the Two Sons*, if it is a genuine work, vol. II, p. 1167 of the Paris edition of 1581.

The one against whom sin is committed in heaven is not an earthly father but also a heavenly one; therefore he added:

> “Before you.”

For him before whose eyes are all things that occur in heaven and on earth, the penitent says:

> “I have sinned against heaven and before you, and I am no longer worthy to be called your son.”

This man went away and fled into a distant region, but he did not flee from his accusers, his witnesses, or the eyes of the divine Father.

David makes this clearer when he says:

> “Where shall I go from your spirit? And where shall I flee from your face? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into the underworld, you are present. If I take my wings at dawn and dwell at the farthest end of the sea, even there your hand will lead me, and your right hand will hold me” (Psalm 138:7–10).

The son sees that his sins stand exposed throughout the whole world before God’s eyes. Neither heaven, nor earth, nor the seas, nor the abyss, nor night itself can conceal sins from God. He realizes how great a crime it is, how great an evil, to sin in God’s sight, and therefore cries:

> “Against you alone have I sinned, and I have done evil before you” (Psalm 50:6).

Hence the younger son likewise cries out:

> “I have sinned against heaven and before you, and I am no longer worthy to be called your son.”

He does not say, “I am not worthy to be your son,” but “I am not worthy to be called your son,” because “to be called” pertains to grace, whereas “to be” pertains to nature.

Hear the Apostle saying:

> “By him who called you into his grace” (Galatians 1).

Thus the younger son, because he had lost what belonged to nature, judged himself unworthy of what belongs to grace.

> “Make me like one of your hired servants.”

See to what the son of his own authority has descended! What has the pleasure of luxury, what has the freedom of youth, advanced the son into? “Make me like one of your hired servants.”

Let servitude be renewed through annual hiring; let the condition of an employee be worn away by continual labor; let him sigh all day in his work for the miserable wage of a servant; let him always be the seller of himself and never be able to deny his own slavery.

He asks this because, having experienced liberty as a slave under a stranger, he believes that with his father he will have a free servitude.

Now, brothers, I would like to disclose the mystery of this reading, if the purpose of its usefulness did not call me back, because I see that you are not listening to these things as our own matters, with the sorrow they deserve, but are hastening to pass over them in your understanding as though they were foreign.

Our own matters—our own matters, and matters always profitable to us—is what Christ speaks. And to correct us, the Lord repeatedly employs mystical examples: he who wished to be the father of his servants; who wished rather to be loved than feared; who gave himself as the bread of life; who poured out his blood as a cup of salvation.

Through examples from the past he corrects both the present and the future, lest, abandoning the good father and devoted parent, we hasten toward the distant and exceedingly foreign regions of the world, and there, by living dissolutely, squander the entire substance of salvation and life; and, after consuming everything, endure the most grievous hunger for hope; and thus finally be handed over to the ruler of that region—that is, to the devil, the author of despair.

Let him send us into his field—that is, into the alluring valleys of this age. Let him send us to feed pigs, namely those who always live bent toward the earth, devoted to the belly, and who temper the heat of the flesh in the mud of the wallow, suppress it in the mire, and cool it in the whirlpool of vices.

But when he sends his hired servants to pigs, this is the work of insatiable cruelty, which is not satisfied that people become guilty unless it also makes them leaders and teachers of vices and crimes. Once he has made them such, he does not allow them to be satisfied even with the food and nourishment of pigs, so that, remaining hungry, they may sin more; for the luxurious cannot be satisfied by satiety, and pleasure does not know how to be fulfilled.

Therefore, since we are with the good father, let us remain with our devoted parent, so that we may both avoid the snares of the devil and continually enjoy the father’s blessings.

We shall search out the deeper matters later, because we owe more to the communion and conduct of our reciprocal unity as believers.

Editorial notes to Sermon II:

- “Emaciated by hunger”: the particle *se* is supplied from the Vallicellian manuscript and Latinius; it is absent from the printed editions.
- Chrysologus agrees with Ambrose and Bede in following the Greek manuscripts, which do not read “in the house.”
- “Coming to himself” is also read by Montanus as *cum rediisset*, “when he had returned.” Latin too speaks of one’s returning to oneself when one returns to a better course. The Greek is εἰς ἑαυτὸν ἐλθών (*eis heauton elthōn*), “having come to himself.” See Euthymius and Theophylact here on Luke 15.
- Meursius, *Exercitationes* ch. 2, p. 130, proposes *expulerat*, “had expelled,” for “had exiled,” but doubts whether the active meaning existed in that barbarous age. Isidore’s glosses show that it did.
- The Caesena and Urbino manuscripts, and the Cologne and first Bologna editions, read: “Hunger made him understand his father,” instead of the other editions’ “A share made him understand.” Compare the Greek saying Πολλῶν δ᾽ ὁ λιμὸς γίνεται διδάσκαλος, “hunger is wont to teach mortals many things.”
- Ambrose, *On Elijah and Fasting*, pp. 31, 312: “Fasting, he was carried up to heaven in a chariot; by this step Elijah ascended.”
- The Vallicellian manuscript and Cologne edition read “with what confidence?” Mita reads “with what conscience?” and the Caesena manuscript “with what steadfastness?”
- Paschasius Radbertus, books III and V on Matthew: “If I sinned and am not worthy to be called a son, you have never ceased to be a father.”
- “Heaven” is more than once understood as God in sacred Scripture, as though he said: “I have sinned against God,” namely the power that shines most clearly in heaven; see Daniel 4.28, 1 Maccabees 3.18, Matthew 21.25, Luke 20.4, and clear examples in Old Testament apocrypha. See Vorstius, *Philologia Sacra* ch. 3, pp. 72–73, and Selden, *Syntagma on the Syrian Gods* II.18. Yet, as Castillo rightly notes, the quoted words make it entirely clear that Chrysologus does not understand “heaven” in the evangelist to mean God, but either God’s throne and seat or the assembly and unity of the just. Hilary agrees most clearly in his exposition of Psalm 118; the passage would exceed the limits of this note. See also Chrysostom, homily *On the Father and the Two Sons*, if it is genuine, II, p. 1167, Paris edition, 1581.
- Hilary, I, p. 628, recent edition: “He is not far away who, by the power of his nature, is himself everywhere and always, and is always wholly and everywhere present.”
- Prudentius, morning hymn: “The Watcher stands above, who sees us through all our days and beholds our deeds from first light to evening. He is witness, he is judge; he looks upon all that is; no one deceives this judge concerning what the human mind conceives.”
- The evangelist says “before you”: “with you as witness, with you as judge,” explains Brugensis.
- If, in Augustine’s view, no vice is so great that it can erase the last traces of nature, why is it so here? Because he had lost what belonged to him from the very nature of sonship, whether the honor or glory of offspring. See below, Sermon 5 (Mita).
- Augustine II, Epistle 120, ch. 2; and Psalm 99, at the beginning: “With the Lord there is free servitude: free servitude where not necessity but love serves.”
- Christians formerly called one another “brothers.” Lactantius V.16: “We bestow the name of brothers on one another for no other reason than because we believe ourselves equals.” Jerome, *Against Helvidius* 8: “All Christians are called brothers because all human beings are born from one father and are joined among themselves by equal kinship.” See Justin, *Apology to Antoninus*, p. 161; Asterius, bishop of Amasea, in Photius, codex 271; Athenagoras, *Apology*; Tertullian, *Apology* 39 and Herold’s notes there; and Minucius Felix, *Octavius*, p. 336.
- In the rich man to whom the Prodigal attached himself, Augustine, *Questions on the Gospels* II.33, Bonaventure on Luke 15, and many others, together with Chrysologus, recognize the devil.
- That is, to our reciprocal unity and fellowship as believers.

## Sermon III

### On the same subject, concerning the father’s meeting with his son.
