We have thus far traversed, in a repeated discourse, the departure, return, guilt, and repentance of the prodigal son; let us now pursue the father’s meeting with him, the father’s goodness, and the father’s ineffable mercy.

“Rising, he came to his father. But while he was still far away, his father saw him, was moved with compassion, ran to him, fell upon his neck, and kissed him” (Luke 15:20).

“Rising, he came to his father.” He rose from the ruin of mind and body; he rose from the depths of hell, touching the heights of heaven. In the presence of the heavenly Father, the son rises to more forgiveness than he had fallen into guilt.

[Note: Because, in restoration through repentance, grace is accustomed to rise more abundantly. See Bernard, Sermon 16 on the Song of Songs; Leo the Great, Sermon 12 on the Lord’s Passion, citing the Apostle in Romans 5: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded still more,” and drawing the conclusion that “the gift of liberty was made stronger than the debt of servitude.” For this reason he gives them the first robe—that is, one more precious than the robe he had worn before committing the crime—as Maldonatus suggests here, no. 22, following Mita. See Guarric, Sermon 2 for Lent, on the Prodigal Son; Leo the Great, Sermon 12 on the Passion, near the beginning; Tertullian, On the Resurrection, chap. 37.]

“Rising, he came to his father.” He came not by the movement of his feet but by the progress of his mind. He did not need a long earthly journey, because he found the shortcuts of the way of salvation. Whoever seeks the divine Father by faith soon discovers that he is already present.

“Rising, he came to his father; but while he was still far away.” How can one who has come still be far away? Because he has not yet arrived.

[Note: Lucas of Bruges here: “He was far from the father because he had not yet completed in action the repentance he had conceived in his mind.”]

This man who comes has come to repentance, but has not yet arrived at grace. He has come to the father’s house, but has not yet arrived at the glory of his former condition, status, or honor.

“But while he was still far away, his father saw him.” That Father saw him who dwells on high and looks upon the lowly, and who recognizes the lofty from afar (Psalm 112:5–6). His father saw him. The father saw him so that he too might be able to turn his attention toward the father. The father’s gaze illumined the sight of the approaching son, so that all the darkness which guilt had spread around him might be driven away.

The darkness of night is not like the darkness that comes from the confusion of sins. Hear the prophet say: “My iniquities have overtaken me, and I was unable to see” (Psalm 39:13). And elsewhere: “My iniquities have weighed upon me” (Psalm 37:5). And afterward: “The light of my eyes is not with me” (ibid., 11). Night buries yesterday’s light; sins confuse the understanding; they confound the mind and its members. Therefore, unless the heavenly Father had shone upon the returning son’s face and removed all the darkness of confusion by the light of his regard, this son would never have seen the brightness of the divine countenance.

“He saw him from afar and was moved with compassion.” He is moved with compassion who cannot be moved from his place. He runs—not by bodily movement but by the affection of his loving kindness.

“He fell upon his neck”—not by the collapse of his entrails, but by compassion.

[Note: Ambrose here: “As though overcome by a certain affection of the father’s love, he falls upon his neck in order to raise up the one lying there.”]

He fell upon his neck in order that, by the weight of love, he might lift away the burden of sins.

[Note: Sin is a heavy burden, as in Psalm 38:5; but when the heavenly Father falls upon such a burden in love, he lifts it from the son’s neck and places upon that neck the gentle yoke—which, in Ambrose’s understanding, is the yoke of the Gospel, or, in Chrysostom’s understanding, the love of God himself and the observance of his commandments. By this burden the son is not weighed down but helped. Mita.]

“Come to me,” he says, “all you who labor and are burdened. Take my burden upon yourselves, because it is light” (Matthew 11:28–30). You see that the son is helped by this father’s burden, not weighed down.

“He fell upon his neck and kissed him.” Thus the father judges; thus he corrects; thus he gives kisses to the sinful son, not blows. The force of love does not see the offenses, and therefore the father redeemed the son’s sins with a kiss.

[Note: That is, he concealed them. At times, as Castillo observes, *claudere* also means “to drive away” or “to repel.” Nonius, book 10:

“Behold, the great sea has shut us in with its barrier.”]

He concealed them in an embrace, lest the father expose the son’s crimes and lest the father defile the son. The father tends the son’s wounds in such a way that he leaves neither a scar on the son nor a blemish upon him.

“Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered” (Psalm 31:1).

If this young man’s conduct displeases us, if his departure horrifies us, let us never depart from such a father. The father’s gaze drives away crimes; it expels guilt; it repels every wickedness and every temptation.

[Note: That is, the devil’s devices. Gregory, Book 4 on Book 1 of Kings, chap. 9: “It is exceedingly difficult to overcome all temptations.”]

[Note: Ephrem the Syrian has similar words in volume 1, Lamentation, or Prayer 5, addressed to the negligent soul. Remarkably apt and devout!]

Certainly, if we have departed; if by living luxuriously we have squandered the father’s entire substance; if we have committed whatever crime or offense anywhere; if we have come altogether to the precipice of impiety and to complete ruin—let us rise at last and, invited by such an example, return to such a father.

“When he saw him, he was moved with compassion, ran to him, fell upon his neck, and kissed him.” I ask: what place is left here for despair? What opportunity for excuse? What feigned fear is there? Unless perhaps the meeting is feared: the kiss terrifies; the embrace causes alarm; and the father is believed to seize him for vengeance rather than receive him for forgiveness, when he draws the son with his hands, encloses him in his bosom, and binds him with his arms.

[Note: Alternatively, “delivers him into his hands.”]

But the thought destructive of life and hostile to salvation is utterly defeated and removed by what follows:

“But the father said to his servants, ‘Quickly bring out the first robe and clothe him; put a gold ring on his hand and shoes on his feet; bring the fattened calf, kill it, and let us eat and celebrate, because this son of mine was dead and has come to life again; he was lost and has been found.’”

After hearing this, do we still delay? Do we still not return to the father?

“Quickly bring out the first robe and clothe him.”

[Note: We have restored the passage, corrupted in other editions, from the Bologna edition. Nakedness produces shame, but God does not tolerate the shame of a sinner returning to him. Or nakedness signifies the lack of virtues, which God does not tolerate in the penitent; or it signifies the shame before human beings arising from sins committed—a shame which the sinner will not suffer on the last day if he discloses his sins to a priest. From Mita.]

He endured the son’s crimes, but did not endure his nakedness. For this reason he wished the son to be clothed by the servants before he was seen: so that his nakedness might be known only to the father, since the father alone could not bear to see the son’s nakedness.

“Quickly bring out the first robe.” This father did not allow the sinner to remain among the second-ranked, and he wishes him to possess joy more from forgiveness than from justice.

[Note: Mita explains: Either because God wishes the sinner who has turned back to him to be numbered among the first of his friends, or because he does not allow him to remain among the second sinners, who are condemned to eternal death. Choose whichever interpretation you prefer. I would interpret it, in the spirit of Chrysologus, as follows: “He did not allow the sinner to remain among the second”—that is, in inferior garments, which, by the familiar usage of contrasting terms, he calls “second”—but wished him to be clothed in the first robe. He may also have had in mind the Latin expression “to be among one’s foremost friends,” as Mita perhaps thought.]

“Quickly bring out the first robe.” He did not say: “Where have you come from? Where were you? Where are the things you took? Why did you exchange such glory for such shame?” Rather: “Quickly bring out the first robe and clothe him.” You see that the force of love does not see the offenses. The father does not know delayed mercy. Whoever scrutinizes offenses exposes them.

“And put a ring on his hand.” Paternal compassion is not content merely to restore innocence unless it also restores his former honor.

[Note: The author asserts that the Prodigal is restored to honor through the giving of the ring. Among the Hebrews and Romans it was a mark of freedom and free birth. James 2:2: “If a man wearing a gold ring and splendid clothing enters your assembly,” and so forth. The use of rings among the Hebrews is very ancient, whether as a sign of trust, authority, or gratitude. Genesis 28:18; 41:42; Numbers 31:50. Mystically, here it is the pledge and guarantee of God dwelling in the soul through grace.]

“And put shoes on his feet.” How poor he returned, although he had departed enriched, when from all his substance he brings back no shoes for his feet.

“Put shoes on his feet.” Let not even deformity remain in the foot as a trace of nakedness; certainly, let him return shod to the course of his former life.

[Note: A shoe, says Lucas of Bruges here, is the clothing and ornament proper to a well-born and nobly educated person. Perhaps for this reason Christ forbade the apostles the use of shoes in Matthew 10:10, though not sandals or soles. Suicer discusses the question in *Thesaurus*, volume 2, page 1387. Vossius, *On the Vices of Language*, book 7, notes *calciari* and *calciare* in Pliny the Younger and Suetonius. Some editions read *calciamenta*.]

“And bring the fattened calf.” An ordinary calf is not enough unless it is fat, unless it has been fattened.

[Note: Calves and oxen were raised for solemn banquets and sacrifices. The Greeks counted them among the most expensive foods, *πολυτελεστάτους* (*polytele­statous*).]

The fat calf testifies to the richness of paternal love.

“And bring the fattened calf, kill it, and let us eat and celebrate, because this son of mine was dead and has come to life again; he was lost and has been found.”

[Note: Here Chrysologus calls the evangelical parable a “history.” For “history” means any explanation and exposition of events.]

We are still speaking historically, yet already we are considering the unveiling of the secret mystery.

[Note: Philo said that the impious, even while living to extreme old age, are dead. In connection with this, Drusius cites the Hebrew proverb: “While the wicked live, they are dead.”]

The dead son is raised from death by the calf, and one calf alone is poured out for the nourishment of the whole household.

[Note: No one doubts that by these words the most holy body of Jesus Christ, offered to the faithful in the Eucharist, is signified. See Euthymius, chap. 57 on Luke.]

But this must be deferred, so that we may pursue the elder brother’s longstanding grief and his still more ancient envy.

## SERMON IV. On the Same Subject: Concerning the Envy of the Elder Son toward the Returning Prodigal

While rejoicing over the younger son’s return and salvation, we sorrowfully unfold and lament the envy of the elder son, who lost the supreme good of self-restraint through the ultimate evil of zeal and jealousy.

[Note: Chrysostom, volume 2, Homily 16, page 1074 of the Paris edition: “Frugality is the opposite of luxury.”]

“He had,” he says, “an elder son in the field. When he came and drew near to the house, he heard music and dancing. He called one of the servants and asked what these things meant. The servant replied, ‘Your brother has come, and your father has killed the fattened calf because he has received him back safe and sound.’ But he became angry and refused to enter.”

“He had,” he says, “an elder son in the field.” He was in the field, cultivating the earth and abandoning himself, loosening the hardness of the turf while keeping his heart’s disposition hardened; he uproots thorns and weeds, but does not uproot the goads of envy. Thus, in the crop of desire, he gathers the harvest of jealousy and spite.

“When he came,” he says, “and drew near to the house, he heard music and dancing.” The music of compassion drives away the envious man; the chorus of charity excludes him. Reason of nature calls him to come to his brother and draw near to the house, but jealousy does not allow him to arrive, nor envy permit him to enter.

[Note: Virgil, *Aeneid* 2:

“Here was the first stain of my ruin.”

The envious man, says Basil, volume 2, Homily on Envy, page 92 of the recent edition, where he gathers many further examples, “holds within him a disease that consumes and gnaws his entrails.” Consult Chrysostom, Homily 40 on Matthew, page 269; Homily 37 on John, page 751; and many other places. Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 28, page 466 of the Paris edition of 1630. Gregory of Nyssa, volume 1, page 242 of the Paris edition of 1622.]

Envy is an ancient evil, the first stain, an old poison, the venom of the ages, the cause of death. At the beginning it cast out the angel himself and cast him down from heaven.

[Note: Others likewise attribute the devil’s fall to envy. See Rufinus of Palestine in Sirmond, volume 1, page 169, no. 22: “Hence he whom Sacred Scripture customarily calls the devil, and likewise those who are called his angels, when they envied the first human beings—Adam, I mean, and Eve—they deprived themselves of the blessed life which they had first possessed.” Cyprian agrees remarkably in *On Jealousy and Envy*: “Hence the devil, at the very beginning of the world, both perished first and caused the ruin of another. Once supported by angelic majesty, once pleasing and dear to God, after he saw the human being made in God’s image, he burst into malicious jealousy through envy. He did not first cast down another through the impulse of jealousy before he himself had first been cast down; captive before becoming a captor; ruined before becoming a destroyer, while, provoked by envy, he snatched away the grace of the immortality that had been given, and he too”—thus Sirmond reads it, rejecting Pamelius’s emendation—“lost what he had previously been.” Augustine, volume 9, Tractate 5 on the First Epistle of John; Nazianzen, Oration 27; and Bernard, Sermon 17 on the Song of Songs, most eloquently.]

It was envy that excluded from paradise the founder of our race, the human being. It was envy that shut this elder brother out of his father’s house. It was envy that armed the offspring of Abraham, the people of holiness, against the slaughter of their author and the death of their Savior.

Envy is an internal enemy. It does not shake the walls of the flesh or batter down the barriers of the limbs; rather, it assaults the very citadel of the heart. Before the entrails perceive it, the robber captures the soul, mistress of the body itself, and leads her away enclosed.

If, therefore, we wish to merit heavenly glory, to possess the blessedness of paradise, to dwell in the house of the eternal Father, and not to be held guilty of the murder of a heavenly reality, let us drive away envy’s dark forces with watchful faith and the light of the spirit, exclude its ambushes, and suppress envy with the full strength of our heavenly weapons, lest we be held guilty of heavenly parricide.

[Note: Corrupt editions read “the lands of envy.” Meursius removed the error in chapter 2, page 130.]

For just as charity joins us to God, so envy separates us from God.

[Note: Hence Cyril of Alexandria calls charity *θεοσύνακος* (*theosynakos*), “that which unites to God”; Suicer says that the lexicons lack this word, volume 1, page 1386. Cyril’s words, *Oration on the Mystical Supper*: “Let us desire the descent that produces exalted charity, which joins us to God.”]

“Therefore his father went out and began to entreat him.”

The father’s anxious heart is constricted by the various movements of his sons. Amid the differing circumstances of his children, the father’s loving compassion runs about in bewilderment: he sees that one brother is immediately driven away by the return of the other, and that the salvation of one instantly causes the other to perish; he sees a long sorrow disturbed by the jealousy of envy, although it has been balanced by a brief joy.

O swelling jealousy! Does a spacious house not contain two brothers? And what is surprising, brothers? Envy caused the whole world to be too narrow for two brothers.

[Note: Zeno of Verona, Sermon on Patience, page 238, concerning envious Cain and righteous Abel: “The empty world marvels that it is too narrow for two.”]

For envy itself incited Cain to the death of his younger brother (Genesis 4), so that jealous envy might make him alone whom the law of nature had first made a brother.

[Note: Basil also brings forward the example of Cain in the passage cited above, calling him the devil’s first disciple, taught by the devil both envy and murder. Zeno of Verona calls him by the same name in the passage cited above, page 303.]

[Note: Similar statements occur in Nazianzen, Oration 27; Cyprian, volume 2, *On Jealousy*; and Gregory the Pope, part 3 of the *Pastoral Rule*, chap. 2.]

“But he answered and said to his father, ‘Father, behold, for so many years I have served you.’” This is how one speaks who dares to judge the father’s kindness.

[Note: This means “to condemn kindness,” as ancient Latin writers use the verb.]

“Behold, for so many years I have served you.” There the son presents to his father the benefits of his birth and tries to compensate for them by his service. “I have never transgressed your command.” This was given to you not by your own innocence but by your father’s forgiveness, because in great love he preferred to cover his son’s offenses rather than expose them.

“And you have never given me a kid, so that I might celebrate with my friends.” A mind envious of its brother cannot be grateful to its father. Whoever is forgetful of brotherly love is not mindful of paternal generosity. He denies that a kid was given to him, although at the time of the division he received the whole share of the substance.

For when the younger brother asked that a portion of the substance be given to him, the father immediately divided everything between both brothers, as the evangelist says: “And he divided his substance between them.” But the envious man always pretends; the envious man always lies.

“And you have never given me a kid, so that I might celebrate with my friends.” He does not count his father’s servants as his friends. He regards as strangers those whom he has seen being loved by the father and accepted into the father’s favor.

“But after this son of yours came, who devoured his substance with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf.” He grieves that his brother has returned; he does not grieve that the substance has perished. The cause of the loss is not investigated, but only the cause of his jealousy. The returning brother should have been adorned from what belonged to him; he should not have been so disgraced because of what had been lost.

The father’s entire substance is in the son, and therefore the father lost nothing when he received his son back. The brother considered it a loss when he saw his co-heir return.

And when is an envious man not greedy? When does he not count whatever another possesses as something he himself has lost?

[Note: Ambrose, volume 1, *On Naboth*, chap. 12: “He considers himself poorer because he thinks that whatever is possessed by others is lacking to him.”]

But he said to him, “Son, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours. But it was necessary to celebrate and rejoice, because this brother of yours was dead and has come to life again; he was lost and has been found.”

O what the force of love accomplishes! Although the son is evil, the father does not know how not to be a father; he cannot cease to be one. He sees that his son has degenerated in mind; he sees that he possesses nothing of paternal kindness or paternal lineage, yet he calls him “son.” He urges him toward the reality—or at least the hope—of that relationship by saying: “You are always with me, and everything I have is yours.”

This is to say: “Allow the son to have returned to his father; permit the father to have received his son. Nor did he seek anything other than his father, since, when he came, he wished to be placed not as a son but as a hired servant, saying: ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you, and I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Make me like one of your hired servants.’”

Let everything be yours; the father is enough for him. And lest you think that anything has been diminished for you from what is present or from what formerly belonged to you, I shall seek new and future things for him. Certainly, if you follow your father’s counsel and command, share the present with your brother, so that the future may be common to you both with him.

Rejoice, then, and rejoice that he has been found, so that he may rejoice that you have not perished.

But let us now conclude the historical discourse, so that afterward, with Christ revealing them, we may unfold the mystical and profound matters.

## SERMON V. On the Same Subject, Representing the Jew and the Gentile

It is characteristic of a shrewd and shameless debtor often not to fulfill his agreements and to postpone an extremely patient creditor through prolonged and artful quibbling.

[Note: Cassiodorus, *Variae*, book 5, letter 34, page 84 of the recent edition, depicts a shrewd debtor and calls him *Frontosus*, a testimony to his name. For *Frontosus* is Greek ἐυμετωπος (*eumetōpos*), that is, “easily changeable,” as Castillo says here.]

This is our fifth sermon on the departure and return of the luxurious son. As we promised, we shall attempt to raise the historical meaning to a mystical and singular understanding of the Godhead.

[Note: Paul, Colossians 4:3: “Pray at the same time for us also, that God may open for us a door for the word, to speak the mystery of Christ.”]

Pray for us, so that although, in so great a debt, I am an inadequate debtor in myself, through God I may prove to you an adequate payer.

“A certain man,” he says, “had two sons.”

After Christ took upon himself the burden of our flesh and God clothed himself in human garb, God truly calls himself man. The Lord truly names himself the father of two sons, because divinity mingled with humanity, and loving kindness joined to divinity, united man and God and made the Lord into a father.

[Note: “Mingling” is used here improperly and in a broader sense for the union of the two natures in Christ. Nevertheless, Irenaeus, cited by Castillo, uses the same word: “The Son of God became the son of man, man mingled with the Word of God.” The Council of Chalcedon, 451, act 5: “We confess that in these last days the only-begotten Son of God is to be acknowledged in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, and without separation; the distinction of the natures having in no way been removed because of the union.”]

This man, this father, therefore had two sons.

[Note: We have rendered the text according to the Lyon edition. We acknowledge, however, that almost all other editions, as well as the Vallicellian manuscript, retain *conditoris pontificio*. The author uses this word in the sense of “benefit” below, Sermon 113.]

He had two sons by the beneficence of the Creator, not by the necessity of generation. He had two sons whom he did not earn the right to have but commanded into being, because Christ was man in our eyes while God always remained within the mystery of his majesty.

He had two sons—namely, two peoples, the Jewish and the Gentile. He made the Jewish people older through the wisdom of the Law, while the folly of paganism made the Gentile people younger. For just as wisdom gives gray hairs, so folly removes whatever belongs to manhood.

Customs, therefore, made the latter younger, not age.

[Note: From the Caesena manuscript. Printed editions read “ages.”]

Time did not make the former older; understanding did.

“And the younger of them,” he says, “said to his father, ‘Father, give me the portion of the substance that falls to me.’”

He asks the knower of the heart not with his voice but with his desire, because in us the will itself brings back from God either good or evil.

[Note: This is the reading of the first Bologna edition and of all the others. Mita, on the authority of the manuscripts, restored *prima voluntas*, “the first will,” explaining it as the will that exists first in us before action. The clearer and more obvious sense seemed preferable.]

Thus, while he was a possessor with his father of the entire inheritance,

[Note: That is, of possessions and inheritance. Isaiah 17:6: “In the portions of the torrent is your portion,” that is, your lot.]

he came by his own will to a share of the whole inheritance, saying: “Give me the portion of the substance that falls to me.”

And what is this portion? What is it? Habit, speech, knowledge, reason, and judgment—those things which, in an earthly dwelling, fall to the human being above the other living creatures. This is, according to the Apostle, the law of nature.

Therefore he divided the substance between them, giving the younger the five natural benefits just mentioned, and inscribing for the elder the five books of the Law by divine authority. Through these, although the substance differed in merit, it was equal in number: the one preserved the human order, the other endured by divine institution.

[Note: Understand “natural” and “written.” Mita.]

Yet both laws would lead both sons to knowledge of the Father and keep them in reverence for their Creator.

[Note: Ambrose, Book 3 above, chapter 5 on Romans: “The first part of the natural law is that the Creator, once known, should be honored.”]

“And not many days later,” he says, “the younger son gathered everything together and departed into a distant country; and there he squandered his substance by living luxuriously.”

We have said that customs, not time, made the younger son younger; therefore he says, “Not many days later.”

For, from the very beginning of the world, paganism hastened toward the homeland of idols. It journeyed in mind, not in place, to the distant region of the devil.

[Note: The commoner opinion of the Fathers is that in this evangelical parable the younger son signifies the Gentiles, as Chrysologus says, along with Jerome in his Letter to Damasus 146 and Dionysius the Areopagite in his Letter to the Monk Demophilus. The objection is that the Gentiles were never sons of God and consequently never departed from the Father. I wish you would read Irenaeus, Book 4 *Against the Nations*, chap. 24, page 260; and Tertullian, *On Modesty*, chap. 8, page 1200 of the Paris edition of 1684.]

It wandered through the elements in vain thoughts.

[Note: Some editions have the thoroughly corrupt reading *per clementiam*. The reference is to the Gentiles’ fashioning deities from the elements. Theophylact here: “The younger son, that is, the Gentile, saw heaven and made heaven into a god; he saw earth and worshiped it.” See the Book of Wisdom, chap. 13.]

It was not tossed about over the earth by bodily movements. For it was without the Father while standing before the Father; and while it existed within itself, it was not with itself.

[Note: Some editions corruptly add the particle *nec*.]

Hence the luxurious son, through his desire for secular eloquence,

[Note: That is, profane and worldly eloquence.]

through the brothels of the schools,

[Note: He calls the schools “brothels” because of the immoderate and luxurious appetite for philosophical knowledge. Saint Augustine sharply criticizes its excessively curious investigation in volume 1, *On True Religion*, chapters 4 and 5. Mita. Jerome, volume 4, page 829 of the Paris edition of 1678, on Ezekiel 16:31: “He who misuses the testimonies of Scripture for the perversion of doctrine builds his brothel at every beginning of the roads.”]

and through the crossroads of the sects, squandered the substance of God the Father by senseless disputation.

When he had exhausted in conjectures whatever there was of speech, knowledge, reason, and judgment, the wretched man endured extreme poverty and a great hunger for the knowledge of truth. For philosophy imposed the labor of seeking divinity but yielded no fruit of finding the truth.

Hence he clung to the leading man of that region, who sent him into this world—that is, into one farm among many superstitions—to feed swine, namely demons, who say to the Lord: “If you cast us out, send us into the swine” (Matthew 8:31).

He fed demons with incense, sacrifices, blood, and the payment for false prophetic answers, receiving such a reward for his labor.

Cattle were slaughtered so that what had known nothing while alive might prophesy once dead, and that the dead animal might speak from its entrails what it had never uttered with its mouth.

[Note: Here too he touches upon haruspicy and the Gentiles’ method of divination.]

But when the Gentile found nothing divine in such practices, nothing that could benefit or save him, he despaired of God, providence, judgment, and the future. He descended from the school to the belly and gluttony,

[Note: The Vallicellian manuscript reads *ingluvium*, “gullet” or “gluttony.”]

desiring to be filled with the pods that the pigs were eating.

[Note: Euthymius also uses “pods” allegorically for pleasures and the allurements of the world, chap. 57 on Luke 15.]

This is known to the Epicureans, who, when they had passed through the schools of Plato and Aristotle and found there no discipline either of divinity or of knowledge,

[Note: I believe Epicurus was called the author of despair for no other reason than that, by making the gods idle and unconcerned with us, he removed every hope of fleeing to their protection. The ancient poet says:

“For I have learned that the gods pass their age in tranquil ease;

Nor, if nature performs some marvel, do the gods

Send it down, grimly, from the lofty roof of heaven.”

Some have attempted to defend Epicurus, as though under the name of “blessed nature” he acknowledged God as the first Creator. See Nicolaus Bandellus in his book written in French, *On the Life and Character of Epicurus*, Paris 1679, and in the expanded Latin edition of 1693. But the consensus of the ancients stands against this: with one voice they testify that Epicurus imagined idle gods and regarded all religion with complete indifference. See Minucius Felix, page 179 of the Lyon edition; Cicero, Book 2 *On Divination* and Book 1 *On the Nature of the Gods*, page 202; Theodoret, *Oration against the Greeks*, page 57; and Plutarch, *On the Opinions of the Philosophers*, page 877. Nor should I say that Gassendi attempted to turn this charge away from him, for while he praises Epicurus in many respects and denies that God cares for human beings, he attacks him vigorously. See Augustine, *The City of God*, in various passages.]

They give themselves over to Epicurus, the ultimate author of despair and pleasure. And they eat husks—that is, they eagerly pursue the falsely sweet pleasures of the body [Col. 0199B] and feed demons, who are always fattened on the vices and filth of bodies. For just as “whoever is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (I Cor. VI, 17), so whoever is joined to the devil is one demon.

[Note: Cyril explains this very elegantly; Castillo praises him in his commentary on John, chapter VI, concerning the words “one of you is a devil.” For just as one who adheres to the Lord becomes one spirit with the Lord, so one who adheres to the devil becomes one spirit with the devil, and is himself a devil.]

But although this younger son desired them, he was not filled with these husks. Why? Because no one gave him any. The devil indeed wished, through hunger for knowledge and through the difficulty of pleasures, to make the Gentile more eager to seek forbidden things and commit crimes. But God the Father permitted the Gentile to hunger for this reason:

[Note: From Castillo’s edition and the Vallicellian manuscript. Other editions corruptly read, “to come to the Gentile.”]

that the opportunity for error might become the occasion of salvation.

[Note: Other editions, including those of Cologne and Bologna, read *Mitae*: “For he thus left the devil so that he might destroy.” We have restored the reading from Castillo’s recension.]

For he left the Jew in such a condition lest he perish, and allowed the Gentile to suffer hunger so that he might return. He returns, then, to his father and cries: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before [Col. 0199C] you.” That the younger son has returned to his father’s house and cries to God the Father is attested by the Church’s daily voice, which says: “Our Father, who are in heaven” (Matt. VI, 9).

“I have sinned against heaven and before you.” He sinned against heaven when, in heaven, he blasphemed the sun, moon, and stars, [Col. 0200A] calling them gods, and then profaned these same things by worshiping them.

[Note: Many writers report that the sun, moon, and stars—which seemed to be beneficent toward human beings—gave the Gentiles the beginnings of idolatry. We refrain from naming them. See Budaeus, vol. I, p. 135; Levit. XVIII, 23; Deut. IV, 19.]

“And I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me like one of your hired servants.” This means: I no longer deserve the glory of sonship; at least let me obtain, in return for the labor of a hired servant, my wages.

“And for one who has lost the honor of a son, let the substance of daily bread, at least, remain as a means of life.”

But the father runs to him, and runs from far away. “While we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Rom. V, 8, 9). The father runs; he runs in the Son, when through him he descended from heaven and reached the earth. “The Father,” he says, “who sent me is with me” (John VIII, 19).

“He fell upon his neck.” He fell upon it when, through Christ, the whole divinity reclines upon and adheres to our flesh. [Col. 0200B]

[Note: *Decumbit*, that is, “rests in our flesh”; *incumbit*, that is, “adheres hypostatically.” Mita.]

“And he kissed him.” When? When “mercy and truth met one another; righteousness and peace kissed one another” (Ps. LXXXIV, 11).

“He gave him the first robe.”

[Note: Tertullian, *On Modesty*, chapter 9, p. 1201, speaking of the Prodigal: “He received back his former garment—that is, the condition which Adam had lost when he transgressed.”]

The robe which Adam lost: the everlasting glory of immortality.

“He put a ring on his hand.” A ring of honor,[Note: Slaves who were released from slavery were given a ring.] a title of liberty, the distinctive pledge of the Spirit, the seal of faith, the earnest of the heavenly marriage. Hear the Apostle: “I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ” (II Cor. XI, 2).

“And shoes on his feet.” So that his feet might be shod for the preaching of the Gospel, so that “beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace” (Rom. X, 15).

[Note: That is, his temporal affections were covered, says Mita. When penitents are restored to grace, God also grants them this, so that they may themselves be fit to teach others.]

“And he killed the fatted calf for him.” That calf of which David sang: “Then he will be pleased with God more than with a young bull that grows horns and hoofs” (Ps. LXVIII, 32). The father orders that the calf be killed, [Col. 0200C] because Christ, God the Son of God, could not be killed without the Father’s will. Hear the Apostle: “He did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all” (Rom. VIII, 31).

[Note: Ennodius, *Poems*, book II, no. 9, among other names attributed by the ancients to Jesus Christ, also lists “Calf”:

> Fountain, Way, Right Hand, Stone, Calf, Lion, Day-Star, Lamb. [Col. 0201C]

Mita notes that Christ is called the fatted Calf “because he was fattened by virtues chosen from among thousands; or because he was fattened by reproaches and patience.” To this may be added the prophet’s statement, “He will be filled with reproaches”; or, as Anastasius of Sinai says in *Hexameron*, book I, “because he was about to bear the yoke of the cross.” See Cotelerius, vol. I, p. 25, in the notes.]

This is the calf that is sacrificed daily and continually for our banquet. [Col. 0201A]

But the elder brother—the elder son, namely the Jew—coming in from the field, the legal people, for “the harvest is plentiful but the laborers are few” (Luke X, 2), hears in the father’s house a symphony and hears choruses, but does not wish to enter (Luke X). We see this every day with our own eyes.

For the Jew comes to the father’s house, that is, to the Church. He stands outside through envy; he hears David’s harp resounding; he hears, from the prophetic harmony, a symphony.

[Note: Montanus renders *symphonia*, as it appears in the Gospel, by *concentus* (“concert” or “harmony”). The Syriac calls it “the song of many.” Chrysologus agrees with both.]

[Note: That laypeople and the people used to sing Davidic psalms in the ancient Church is inferred from Caesarius of Arles, in Mabillon, preface to the first Benedictine century, no. 110. Fortunatus also testifies that this was provided for by Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, *Poems*, book II, no. 10:

> At the bishop’s command, clergy, people, and child sing psalms.]

He hears choruses arising from the varied assembly of the peoples, yet refuses to enter, standing outside through envy. While he judges and recoils from his Gentile brother because of his former conduct, he himself withdraws from his father’s goods and excludes himself from his father’s joys.

But what he said—“Behold, I have served you for so many years, and I have never transgressed your commandment, and you have never given me a kid” [Col. 0201B]—we have already said ought rather to be silenced than spoken, because it is the Jew who speaks. These are not the words of one who acts, but of one who swells with pride.

The father goes out and says to his son: “Son, you are always with me.” How? Through Abel, through Enoch, through Shem, through Noah, through Abraham, through Isaac, through Jacob, through Moses, through all the saints through whom the Jewish descent is traced in the Gospel, when it says: “Abraham begot Isaac, Isaac begot Jacob” (Matt. I, 2).

“And all that is mine is yours.” How so? Because the law is yours, the prophecy is yours, the temple is yours, the priesthood is yours, the sacrifices are yours, the kingdom is yours, the gifts are yours—and, what is above all, Christ was born for you. But because you wish, through envy, to destroy your brother, [Col. 0201C] you are unworthy to possess the father’s banquets and the father’s joys.

[Note: Some printed editions read *Augusto* (“narrow”) instead of *angusto*.]

In a narrow discourse we have not been able to unfold such extensive matters as we wished; yet what appears narrow in our speech is broad for your knowledge and understanding. Let this simple and hidden gathering not be displeasing, since it compelled us not to narrate or declaim mystical and exalted matters, but to open and explain them.

[Col. 0202A]

[Note: This sermon is entitled “On Psalm XCIX,” which Genebrard also calls “A prophetic psalm concerning the conversion of the nations.” Lorinus writes concerning it: “Chrysologus devotes his sixth sermon to the present psalm, to teach how great is the joy over the conversion of the prodigal son, who was a type of all the nations.”]

## Sermon VI. On the joy arising from the bringing of the nations to faith and grace

On Psalm XCIX.

Since, when the younger son returned, the whole household formed choruses and sang a heavenly symphony, it is fitting that we too today should take up the psalm, strike the drum,

[Note: Mabillon asserts that drums and organs were first introduced into the Gallican Church, preface to the third Benedictine century. Marianus Scotus writes that in the year of the Lord 757 the first organ came to France, sent from Greece to King Pepin by the emperor Constantine. Bale, likewise, an English bishop, relates that Vitalianus, a native of Signia or Campania and a distinguished musician, introduced singing and organs into churches around the year of the Lord 609. Chrysologus, however, earlier than these, declares that such instruments were already in the Church of Ravenna. Indeed, they were still earlier, as is clear from Prudentius, who flourished around the year of the Lord 380. He mentions an organ of such great size that some suspected a man might hide inside it. Aldhelm, an Englishman, has similar material in his book *On Virginity*. He flourished in the year 709.]

set up the organ,

[Note: On the lyre of the ancients, see Isidore, *Etymologies*, book III, chapter 21.]

touch the harp, and make David’s melody resound for the great joy of God the Father.

“Shout joyfully to God,” he says, “all the earth” (Ps. XCIX, 1). What is this understanding of exultation that he seeks? What is it that, after so many commands concerning the deity—so terrifying and so wondrous—the earth is now summoned and invited to joyful shouting? “Shout joyfully to God,” he says, “all the earth.”

[Note: Castillo corrected an error found in all the copies known to us, using a manuscript from Cesena.]

What else can this mean except that, after the terrifying God chose the office of the most gentle shepherd, he assumed the shepherd’s role in order that the merciful shepherd might gather wandering peoples, straying populations, and nations scattered far and wide, like wandering sheep, into one flock? Indeed, it means that he might bring savage nations—prey to death, for whom flesh was food and blood drink, and who thirsted for the fury of beasts—back and restore them to the use of milk, the food of grass, and the entire gentleness of sheep.

He imposes and commands a pastoral discipline upon all the earth, saying: “All the earth, shout joyfully to God.” Just as a terrifying trumpet brings a soldier forth to war, so the sweetness of joyful shouting invites sheep to pasture.

[Note: In the printed editions, through a not insignificant typographical error, *turba* (“crowd”) is read instead of *tuba* (“trumpet”).]

It is therefore fitting to soften the roar of warfare with pastoral gentleness, so that such a mild grace might save the nations whom their natural savagery had long destroyed.

When Christ came to earth, he himself proclaimed today what a good shepherd’s return would be: “I am the good shepherd; the good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep” (John X, 11).

For this reason the Teacher himself seeks helpers and companions in the care of the whole world, saying: “All the earth, shout joyfully to God.” For this reason, as he was about to return to heaven, he entrusted his sheep to Peter in his place, so that Peter might feed them. “Peter,” he says, “do you love me? Feed my sheep.” And so that he would not compel their tender beginnings by power but would carry them by devotion, he repeats: “Peter, do you love me? Feed my sheep.” He entrusts the sheep and entrusts the offspring of the sheep, because the shepherd, who knew the future, already understood the fruitfulness of his flock. “Peter, do you love me? Feed my sheep” (John XXI, 16, 17).

To these sheep Paul, Peter’s fellow shepherd, presented, through devoted nourishment, breasts full of milk, saying: “I gave you milk to drink, not food” (I Cor. III).

The blessed King understood this, and therefore, instead of bleating, he cries: “The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing. In a green place he has settled me; beside the water of refreshment he has brought me up” (Ps. XXII, 1, 2).

[Note: In his exposition of this psalm, Lorinus praises Chrysologus, who reads “in a green place,” looking to the Hebrew source. Apollinaris likewise translated the passage in this manner, as Castillo reports: “Indeed, he settled me in a green place.”]

After the continuous groans of wars, after the sad life of blood, the verse that follows now announces joy to the servant returning to the pastures of evangelical peace.

Humanity was the slave of sin, captive to death, the chattel of demons, [Col. 0203B] a home-born slave of idols, a scourge of vices, shackled by crimes.

[Note: This is a familiar expression of Chrysologus for describing a slave under domination. See Pignorius, *On Slaves*, p. 55, Amsterdam edition, 1674. Slaves themselves seem to have flattered themselves with this designation. An inscription in the same author reads:

> FUSCUS, A SERVANT OF OUR AUGUST LORDS.]

Thus a human being rendered a wretched and evil service to such and so many bad masters. When is a person not sorrowful under sin? When not mourning under death? When not pale under demons? When not trembling under idols? When not suspected under vices? When not despairing under crimes? And therefore a person uttered the deepest sighs while continually enduring such cruel masters.

[Note: Most printed editions omit *jugiter* (“continually”); we have added the word from the Vallicellian manuscript.]

The prophet, therefore, seeing that we have been freed from such masters and recalled to the service of the Creator, to the Father’s grace, and to the free service of the one good Lord, rightly exclaims: “Serve the Lord with gladness; enter,” he says, “into his presence with exultation.” Enter not by place but by the heart. “Enter into his presence with exultation.” Whoever enters his presence with exultation is free from guilt and will obtain the reward.

Yet what is he urging? What is this prophet trying to persuade us to do? “Enter into his presence with exultation.” Who is free in God’s presence? Who lies in the divine eyes? Who exults before the terror of the heavenly majesty? Archangels tremble, angels are afraid, powers are terrified, elders fall upon their faces before heaven; the elements flee, rocks dissolve, mountains flow down, the earth trembles. How fearlessly, then, will a human being of earth enter? How can he still stand there exulting? Why does the prophet presume that we ought to do this? Why?

Because of what follows: “Know,” he says, “that the Lord himself is God.” For the Lord who is God is the one who was small in our flesh. This is why the Lord who is God is the one who was contained in our cradles, sweet in the lap, gentle in appearance, and affectionate in our companionship. And therefore: “Enter into his presence with exultation.”

For he hid all the terror of divinity and all the fear of the judge in our appearance, placing it within a provident manifestation,

[Note: Another reading is *dedit* (“he gave”).]

so that the one who enters might not fear the punishments of the judge but might confidently claim the embrace of the parent. And how could one not exult who has found a begetter whom he had feared as a judge?

“Enter into his presence with exultation; know that the Lord himself is God. He himself made us, and not we ourselves.” The labor of father and mother is empty unless the work and authority of the Creator are present in the offspring. “Your hands,” he says, “made me and fashioned me” (Ps. CXVIII, 37). And elsewhere: “You formed me and placed your hand upon me” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 5). Therefore, that we are born and that we exist is not owed to ourselves, because we owe everything to the Author.

“But we are his people and the sheep of his pasture.” It has been proved very often in the Proverbs that the shepherd came from heaven—the shepherd who, through heavenly jubilation, would recall wandering sheep, wounded by deadly grass, to life-giving pastures.

“Enter,” he says, “his gates with confession.” Confession alone makes us enter through the door of faith. “His courts with hymns: confess to him, praise his name.” We have said that, once we have been placed within the father’s house, we ought to take up the spiritual symphony of heavenly songs, so that at our entrance there may be confession, in the courts hymns, and in the inner chambers praise, where the whole fullness of divinity dwells.

[Note: One who desires baptism first professes the faith of Christ with his own mouth. Then, having been catechized in the courts of the Church, he joyfully sings a hymn to God; finally, cleansed by baptism, he offers God a sacrifice of praise in the inner sanctuaries of the Church, concerning which see Psalm XLIX. The subject is treated sufficiently by Ludovicus de Angelis, *Life and Praise of Saint Augustine*, book III, no. 16. Mita.]

“Confess to him, praise his name.” Confess to him because he is God; praise his name. Through him we have been saved; in him every creature—heavenly, earthly, and infernal—bows the knee and loves the Lord God.

“For the Lord is gracious.”

[Note: Not, however, *vere* (“truly”), as in the printed editions.]

Why? Because “his mercy is everlasting.” He is truly gracious through mercy, through which alone he has deigned to remove the bitterest sentence from the whole world. “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world.”

[Note: Suicerus discusses at length why Christ is called the Lamb in *Thesaurus*, vol. I, col. 23, under the word ἄγνος. I touched on the matter in my dissertation on the silver paten of Forum Cornelii.]

“And his truth endures forever and ever.” For God [Col. 0205A] has mercy while preserving truth: he grants forgiveness of sins in such a way that he preserves justice in that very act and order of mercy. He is blessed forever and ever.

[Note: On Christ’s part, he assumed upon himself the sentence of the debt owed by us; on our part, forgiveness of crimes is given by God if we sincerely grieve over them because of God, whom we love above all. This is Augustine’s view in his commentary on Psalm L, 8: “God forgives the one who confesses, but punishes himself.” Thus mercy is preserved because the human being is freed, and truth because sin is punished. See, if desired, John of Damascus, *On the Orthodox Faith*, book III, chapter 3. Mita.]

Amen.

[Note: It was customary in ancient times in the Church for the people, after the sacred prayers of the bishop, to respond with one voice, “Amen.” Paulinus, *Poem* 19, *Natale* 11, concerning Saint Felix:

> And when the devout crowd had said “Amen” to the shepherds’ sacred prayers.

See Bona, *On Liturgical Matters*, book II, chapter 5; Calvorius, *Ritual*, title “On the Voice Amen.” The prelates themselves, after prayers offered to God, also responded “Amen” to themselves, as many examples clearly show.]

## Sermon VII. On hypocrisy and almsgiving

On the words of Matthew VI: “When you fast, do not become like the hypocrites, who are sad.”

[Note: The phrase is absent in some copies.]

When God changed the title “Lord” into “Father,” he wished to reign more by love than by power and preferred to be loved rather than feared.

[Note: From the Cesena manuscript. In other editions *unde* (“therefore”) is absent.]

Therefore, in paternal affection, he warned that none of the just labor performed by us should be lost.

The Evangelist says: “When you fast, do not become like the hypocrites, who are sad; for they disfigure their faces so that they may appear to people to be fasting. Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matt. VI, 16).

Hypocrisy is a subtle evil, a hidden poison, a concealed venom, the counterfeit of virtues, the moth of holiness.

[Note: Cyprian called it “a most subtle” evil in his sermon *On Fasting and the Temptation of Christ*. Gregory the Great likewise uses the following word, *virus* (“poison”), in his commentary on I Kings VIII, book IV, chapter 2. See Augustine, exposition of Psalm CXXXIX, verse 3.]

All other adversaries rely on their own strength and fight with their own weapons; they attack openly, and so they are avoided as easily as they are seen. Hypocrisy confidently pretends, deceives amid prosperity, lies with eager curiosity, and by a cruel art cuts down virtues with the sword of virtues. It kills fasting through fasting, empties prayer through prayer, and overthrows mercy through an act of mercy.

Hypocrisy, a fever of the same family,

[Note: So Mita and the Bologna edition. Castillo and others read a related fever.]

serves heat in a cold drink. What dropsy is to bodies, hypocrisy is to souls: dropsy thirsts while drinking, and hypocrisy, once intoxicated, thirsts.

“For they disfigure their faces so that they may appear to people to be fasting.” Hypocrisy, while wishing to capture the eyes, becomes itself captive to the eyes. “For they disfigure their faces.” And if they disfigure their faces, what bodily adornment will remain?

Truly, as the Lord said: “If the light that is in you is darkness, how great will the darkness itself be?” (Matt. VI, 5).

[Note: Christ is not speaking here about the emaciation and pallor that naturally follow fasting, but about a certain fabricated sadness and gestures such as those of the people described by Isaiah, chapter LVIII, 5.]

Hypocrite, even if your face is unkempt, your skin neglected, your expression sad, and your appearance disfigured; even if you have found no praise among people, you have lost the fruit of fasting with God. Hypocrite, you have labored through fasts so that the labor of fasting might not benefit you. Hypocrite, you entered the waves of abstinence, climbed the billows of self-control, and swam across the sea of fasting—and in the very harbor of fasting you suffered shipwreck. For you gained no profit but traded in vanity.

[Note: That is, you turned the virtues entrusted to your faith into a human business: you wished to be praised by people. But this is not to acquire profit; it is to trade in vanity. Therefore you will render an account to God for fraud and interest. Mita.]

You who made a human business from God’s deposit will therefore have to render an account to God, since you received from people the interest of wretched praise.

[Note: Thus Castillo and Mita. Other editions read *stipendium* (“wage” or “payment”).]

Brothers, we must flee this poison; we must beware this pestilence, which creates diseases from remedies, produces sickness from medicine, turns holiness into crime, makes appeasement into guilt, and generates danger from reconciliation. Whoever flees hypocrisy conquers it; whoever falls into it is defeated.

Let us flee hypocrisy, brothers, let us flee it. Let our fasting arise from simplicity; let it be holy through innocence, pure through purity, sincere through sincerity; let it be hidden from people, unknown to the devil, and known to God.

Whoever does not hide a treasure betrays it; virtues that are betrayed will not remain. Just as virtues abandon those who betray them, so they strive to guard those who guard them.

Therefore, since fasting is our first virtue against vices,

[Note: Either by origin, since it was given to Adam when he had recently been created, so that it might preserve him free from sin; or by power, since rightly and properly observed it protects from vices. Mita—perhaps *prima* should be read for *principali eximiaque* (“principal and eminent”).]

let it be placed in the citadel of the heart. For when it presides within, vices will not be able to shake us outwardly.

Christ urges us to possess this virtue as Christians when he says: “But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face, so that you may not appear to people to be fasting, but to your Father who is in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.”

When he says, “Anoint your head and wash your face,”

[Note: Jerome observes that Christ is speaking here according to the custom of the province of Palestine, where it was customary to anoint the head on feast days. Jews abstained from this anointing during fasting, as may be inferred from II Kings XII, 20, compared with verse 16, and elsewhere.]

the serious Master does not command that the hair of the head flow luxuriantly with alluring ointment, nor does he wish the face to shine through an ordinary washing.

[Note: In truth, Christ does not command that the head be anointed for pleasure and elegance of appearance; rather, he wishes the face to appear cheerful instead of mournful, as Chrysologus himself says shortly afterward. Chrysostom, on Psalm XLVII: “He does not say this by commanding anointing, for none of us does this; rather, he wishes us to show gladness and cheerfulness of mind, and therefore to fast joyfully, not displaying sadness.”]

Rather, he wishes the Christian’s fasting to be concealed beneath the appearance of one who has eaten, because he does not wish Christian fasting to be claimed through artificial sorrow.

But let us return to what we began. “Anoint your head and wash your face, so that you may not appear to people to be fasting, but to your Father who is in secret.” Thus he does not encourage pleasure-seeking appearances but excludes faces that are falsely assumed. A face cast down with sorrow invites reputation; it does not proclaim voluntary fasting.

If he wishes it, why are you sad? If he does not wish it, why are you fasting? He deservedly lives under such punishment who makes vice from virtue, falsehood from truth, loss from reward,

[Note: So Castillo and Mita. Other editions read *stipendium* (“payment”).]

and sin from forgiveness.

If a farmer does not drive in the plow, if he does not cut a furrow deeply, if he does not cut out the thorns, if he does not pull up the grasses, if he does not place the seed in safety, he deceives himself, not the earth. He does not harm the earth; he merely fails to produce fruit for himself. Thus the one who deceives the earth with a treacherous hand empties, cheats, and attacks himself.

What will he do? What will he possess? What will he find who lies to God while his flesh hungers and his hypocrisy luxuriates?

Since we have mentioned the farmer, let him know that he labors in vain and will possess nothing if, while pressing the plow of fasting, cutting away the grasses of the throat, and rooting out the thorns of luxury, he has sown no seeds of mercy.

[Note: Ambrose provides a fitting parallel in vol. V, sermon 40, which is the Tuesday of the second week of Lent: “The earth is cut by plows so that it may be suitable for worldly crops; my earth is plowed by fasts so that it may be suitable for heavenly seeds.”]

The Lord wished to make this clear. When teaching about fasting, he immediately added: “Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth, where rust and moth destroy, and where thieves break in and steal. But store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys, and where thieves do not break in or steal.”

What could be more paternal? What could proceed so completely from love? What advice could be more provident in its charity? He who wishes your possessions to be stored in heavenly treasures wishes nothing of yours to perish.

How securely does the one sleep who has deserved to have God as guardian of his possessions!

[Note: Cyprian, sermon 1, *On Almsgiving*: “An inheritance is placed in safety when it is preserved with God as its guardian.”]

How free from cares, how free from anxieties, how untroubled, how free from the arrogance of servants

[Note: Latinius thinks that one might perhaps read *servorum caret actu* (“is free from the conduct of servants”).]

is the person who entrusts his possessions to his father to preserve!

How does paternal affection preserve what servile fear cannot preserve in the same way? A father, when he gives his possessions to his children, does not diminish what has been entrusted to the children.

The one who does not trust his father does not know what a father is; he does not know that he is a son.

Locks do not exclude moths; they shut them in. They generate them rather than repel them. What is stored away nourishes rust rather than avoiding it, because what arises from a thing cannot be avoided.

[Note: That is, things and metals kept shut away nourish rust. Perhaps the author added “rust,” although it is not found in the sacred text, because he noticed that the Greek word βρῶσις (*brōsis*, “eating” or “corrosion”) could signify not only the moth but also rust, at least rust that adheres to crops.]

Where there is need, thieves cannot be absent. Therefore, whoever places his possessions among moths, rust, and thieves exposes what is his rather than storing it.

Just as moths arise from clothing, rust from metal, and thieves from necessity, so avarice arises from riches, greed from profit, and the passion for possessing arises from possession.

Therefore, whoever wishes to conquer avarice should distribute riches, not store them.

[Note: That is, let him display or give them. The word is characteristically Chrysologian.]

Let us send our treasures ahead to heaven, brothers. Let the poor be the carriers who can transport what is ours upward in their bosom.

[Note: Augustine, vol. X, sermon 50, *On Time*, chapter 8: “Who are the poor to whom we give, except our carriers? You give to your carrier, and he carries what you give to heaven.”]

Let no one doubt the honesty of the bearers. This is your transport: through it, with God as guarantor, our possessions are carried to God.

[Note: Leo, sermon 6, *On the Fast of the Tenth Month*, calls God “the trustworthy guarantor of the poor.”]

To him belong all honor and glory, power and dominion, and thanksgiving forever and ever. Amen.

[Note: See, in vol. I of the *Bibliotheca Veterum Patrum*, Lyon edition, 1644, the commentary of Saint Julian, bishop of Toledo, on the prophet Nahum, so that you may know how much that author transferred from this sermon into his own work.]

## Sermon VIII. On fasting and almsgiving

[Col. 0208B]

A prudent helmsman, when he casts off from the shore with his ship, when he enters the waves to cross the sea: household, homeland, wife, and children,

[Note: *Pignora* is used of children; we have noted this elsewhere. Paulinus, *Poem* 9, p. 349, verse 48:

> And together he will dash his children against the solid rock.

This corresponds to the Psalm: “He will dash his little ones against the rock.”]

Having laid aside the cares of children, he devotes himself wholly in mind, body, and feeling to the labors of the sea, so that he can both overcome the dangers of the waves and, victorious over peril, enter the haven of profitable gain. [Note: In some copies, “if the harbor is profitable.” Meursius corrected the text.]

So let us, brothers, as we enter upon the journey of abstinence—the sea of fasting, the road of the forty days—launch the vessel [Note: On the Lenten fast, Cyril, *On Leviticus*, book X, fol. 731, translated by Trapezuntius: “We have the days of Lent consecrated to fasts. We abstain from other things; for the ancient books are full of the fasts of Christians.”] of our body from the worldly shore; let us renounce the cares of our secular homeland; let us stretch all the sails of our mind upon the tree of the cross; and with the ropes of the virtues, the oars of wisdom, and the rudders of discipline, let us fortify the progress of our voyage. Once withdrawn from the earth, let us contemplate heaven, so that, guided by the heavenly signs, we may keep to an unhindered course through the liquid pathways of the hidden route; and, with Christ as our helmsman and the Holy Spirit breathing upon us, having overcome the foam of pleasures, mastered the waves of vices, passed through the storms of crimes, crossed the reefs of sins, and avoided the shipwrecks of all offenses, let us enter the harbor of Easter, the profit of life, and the joys of the resurrection. [Note: Augustine, on Psalm 103, sermon 4: “Christ is the helmsman; there the ships will travel.”]

But since we are to make our journey across barren fields, through false whirlpools, and across uncertain deserts [Note: Elsewhere, “cares.”], we must carry with us a full supply of food and drink. Let us place abundant mercy in our provision-bag. [Note: *Sitarchia*, a Greek word, here means the military grain allowance, or food and nourishment; in other writers it denotes a small provision-bag, as below in Sermon 39. MITA.—Among the Greeks, the army’s provisions are called *sitērēsia* (σιτηρέσια). Suidas uses the word *sitērēsion* (σιτηρέσιον): “What is given to some for the sake of nourishment.” Philostorgius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, chapter 4, page 90, says that Julian gave “the provisions of the churches” (τὰ σιτηρέσια τῶν ἐκκλησιῶν) to the ministers of demons. Sozomen likewise relates this in *History*, book V, chapter 5, page 63, where they are similarly called provisions, σιτηρέσια. Properly, *sitarcia* is a small provision-bag or pouch for carrying food, 1 Kings 9:7: “Saul said to his servant, ‘Our bread has failed in our provision-bags.’”]

Brothers, fasting hungers; fasting thirsts when it is not nourished with the food of compassion and watered with the drink of mercy. Fasting grows cold; fasting wastes away when it is not covered by the fleece of almsgiving and clothed with the garment of pity.

Brothers, what spring is on earth, we know mercy to be for fasting. Just as the breath of spring causes all the shoots of the fields to flower, so mercy brings all the seeds of fasting into bloom and makes the entire virtue of fasting bear fruit in a heavenly harvest. [Note: Cardinal Hugh, in his commentary on Isaiah 34, either fell upon this passage or composed something similar: “Fasting without almsgiving is like a lamp without oil.”]

What oil is for a lamp, compassion is for fasting. As the fatness of oil kindles the lamp’s light and, by measured feeding, makes it shine for the comfort of the whole night, so compassion makes fasting shine and radiate the full brightness of self-restraint.

What the sun is to the day, almsgiving is recognized to be for fasting. As the sun’s radiance makes the day brighter and scatters all the darkness of the clouds, so almsgiving sanctifies the sanctity of fasting and drives away the entire night of desire with the light of compassion. [Note: Thus we have restored the text from the Bologna edition. Other copies read “death,” less appropriately.]

And, not to linger over many things [Note: A phrase familiar to Quintilian], what the soul is to the body, generosity is to fasting. For just as the body dies when the soul departs from the body, so the death of fasting is the departure of generosity. Fasting is the death of vices and the life of virtues. Fasting is peace for the body, the adornment of the limbs, and the ornament of life. Fasting is strength for minds. [Note: Basil has nearly similar words in Homily 2 on Fasting: “Fasting guards children, makes the young man temperate, and makes the old man venerable. For gray hair adorned with fasting is more venerable. Fasting is the most fitting adornment for women; for those strong and vigorous in age it serves as a bridle. It guards marriage and nourishes virginity.” Chrysostom likewise agrees in Homily 122, volume VI of the old edition; Gregory of Nyssa also, Homily on the Beginning of the Fast, volume II, page 248; Cyril of Alexandria, Paschal Oration 1, page 8.]

Fasting is the wall of chastity, the fortress of modesty, the city of holiness. Fasting is the school of merits, the mastery of instruction, the discipline of disciplines. Fasting is the saving provision for the ecclesiastical way of life. [Note: From Castelli’s edition and the manuscript of Cesena. Other copies read “of ecclesiastical life,” less aptly.]

Fasting is the unconquered command of Christian warfare. [Note: Pope Leo, Sermon 7, calls fasts “the defenses of the Christian army.”] But fasting flourishes, conquers, and triumphs in these virtues when it fights under the leadership of mercy.

Mercy and compassion are the wings of fasting, by which it is lifted up and carried to heaven; without them it lies and rolls about on the earth. [Note: Chrysostom, Homily 99, volume VI: “If fasting does not have its sister, almsgiving, joined to it, it does not ascend to heaven; for almsgiving is its equal—not merely its equal, but also its vehicle.” Severian, in Suicer’s *Thesaurus Ecclesiasticus*, volume II, page 409, no. 4, comes closer to Chrysologus: “Fasting has two wings, prayer and almsgiving, without which it cannot run.”]

Fasting without mercy is an image of hunger, not an image of holiness. Without compassion, fasting is an opportunity for greed, not a commitment to moderation; for to the extent that this moderation dries out the body, it swells the purse. Fasting without mercy is not reality but appearance; where mercy is, there too is truth, as the prophet testifies when he says: “Mercy and truth have met one another” (Psalm 84:11).

Fasting without mercy is not virtue but hypocrisy, as the Lord says: “But when you fast, do not become like the hypocrites, who are sorrowful; for they disfigure their faces so that they may appear to people to be fasting” (Matthew 6:16). [Note: That is, the person who fasts does not care that the food he abstains from be distributed for the nourishment of the poor.]

Whoever does not fast for the poor pretends before God; whoever, while fasting, does not distribute his midday meal but stores it up is shown to be fasting for greed, not for Christ. Therefore, brothers, while fasting, let us place our midday meal in the hand of the poor, so that the poor man’s hand may preserve for us what our stomach would have lost.

The hand of the poor is Abraham’s bosom; whatever the poor person receives, he immediately stores there. The hand of the poor is heaven’s treasury: what it receives, so that it may not perish on earth, it stores in heaven. “Store up for yourselves treasures in heaven” (Matthew 6:20). The hand of the poor is Christ’s treasury, because whatever the poor person receives, Christ accepts. [Note: Ambrose, Sermon 26, toward the end: “The hand of the poor is Christ’s treasury.” In ancient temples there was a place called the treasury, in which alms intended for distribution to the poor were stored. The Fathers frequently mention it. Chrysostom, Homily 22 on Almsgiving and the Collection for the Saints, says: “In this way, then, let each person’s house become a church, preserving sacred wealth within itself.” It should be observed here, as a digression, that Chrysostom is not addressing the people of Constantinople here, as Ferrarius thinks in book II, chapter 10 of *On the Antiquity of Ecclesiastical Epistles* and book I, chapter 26 of *On the Rite of Sacred Councils*, but the people of Antioch; Rossweidus argues in his notes on Paulinus’s Sermon 34 that the homily was delivered at Antioch. See also Augustine on Psalm 63 and Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, chapter 24, concerning the treasury in the church; and the Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 93.]

Give earth to the poor, human being, so that you may receive heaven. Give a coin, so that you may receive a kingdom. Give a crumb, so that you may receive the whole. Give to the poor, so that you may give to yourself; for whatever you give to the poor, you will have, while what you do not give to the poor another will have.

God cries out: “I desire mercy” (Hosea 6:6). Whoever denies to God what God desires wants what he himself desires to be denied him by God.

“I desire mercy.” Human being, God asks—but for you, not for himself. [Note: Latinius attempts to help this passage, perhaps corrupted through scribal error, and thinks it should read, “This God seeks.” Nothing is easier than for the little word *Hoc* (“this”) to have been contracted and mistaken for *homo* (“human being”). Yet the author’s meaning may also be: “O human being, God seeks it, but for you, not for himself”; how familiar this form of expression is to Chrysologus is abundantly clear. See Sermon 9, at the end.]

“I desire mercy.” He seeks human mercy in order to bestow divine mercy. There is mercy in heaven, and one reaches it through earthly acts of mercy. “Lord, your mercy is in heaven” (Psalm 53:6).

When you are about to plead your case in God’s judgment, take mercy as your advocate, through which you may be set free. Whoever is confident of mercy’s advocacy may be secure of pardon and have no doubt of acquittal. Mercy not only goes before the case and anticipates the judge; it also recalls the sentence and acquits those condemned.

The Ninevites prove this (Jonah 3): though already subjected to sentence, handed over to punishment, standing ready for sacrifice, and given over to death, mercy snatched them away, held them fast, and anticipated their doom, so that God preferred the sentence to be withdrawn rather than deny anything to mercy. [Note: That is, destined for sacrifice and already marked out for divine vengeance.] [Note: That is, the sentence of death pronounced against them was recalled or removed. MITA.—Latinius reads “the sentence to be imposed.” But *deducere* in the sense of “change” is a Ciceronian expression.]

At that time fasting also stood on behalf of their cause: they sprinkled ashes, spread sackcloth, uttered groans, and shed tears. What they could not excuse in words, they moderated through mourning; but they could not change the sentence unless mercy had come to their aid in pleading.

Mercy both frees sinners and restores saints. For unless mercy had been present, David too, when he committed adultery, would have lost his prophetic office (2 Samuel 11); and Peter, when he denied Christ, had lost the primacy of the apostolic order (Matthew 26). [Note: He means that by sinning Peter somehow lost his claim to primacy, just as David had made himself unworthy to prophesy through adultery. Jerome likewise asserts, in chapter 16 of Mark, volume VI, page 198, Paris 1589, that Peter judged himself unworthy of discipleship because he had denied his master three times; and, according to Gregory, Homily 21, Christ allowed Peter to sin by denying him three times so that he who was to become the shepherd of the Church might learn through his own fault how he ought to show mercy to others.]

And Paul, when he blasphemed, would have remained a persecutor. Paul acknowledges this when he says: “I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man; but I obtained mercy” (1 Timothy 1:13).

Brothers, through the mercies shown to the poor, let us acquire mercy, so that we may be free from punishment and secure of salvation. [Note: From Castelli’s edition. Other copies read, “Let us prepare mercy.”] “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matthew 5:7). Whoever has not shown mercy here hopes in vain to receive mercy there. Whoever shows mercy runs toward reward; whoever does not show mercy runs toward punishment.

## SERMON IX. On the Same Matters. On the Saying of Matthew: “Take heed that you do not perform your righteousness before people.”

God deals with us—he acts in this world—so that nothing of ours may perish in the future, as is evident from the very beginning of the reading: “Take heed,” he says, “that you do not perform your righteousness before people, in order to be seen by them; otherwise you have no reward with your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 6:1).

And how can something done by people before people not be done before people? The meaning of an evident righteousness lies hidden; what is secret in a public work? Whoever can conceal the rays of the sun of righteousness will be able to hide its radiance. The righteousness of one’s purposes is not veiled by obscure devices. Justice, the light of things, is not veiled by obscure counsels. When righteousness shines through its own deed, it illuminates everyone by its example.

What, then, does the Lord mean by not wanting it performed before people, when human affairs are ordered through it? And what of the saying: “Let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16)? How does he wish to conceal the righteousness whose works he wishes to shine forth in this way? [Note: The Fathers resolve the apparent contradiction arising from the sacred words in this way, especially Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, Part III, admonition 36; Isidore of Pelusium, *Letters*, book IV, letter 159; and Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, *Letters*, book II, letter 19 to Galla.]

Brothers, this heavenly command wishes to remove boastfulness, take away display, eliminate vanity, and drive off empty glory: in this way it wishes righteousness to be concealed. [Note: Ambrose, *On Duties*, book I: “Justice is twofold: particular justice, which gives each person what is his and claims nothing belonging to another, and is one of the cardinal virtues; and general and universal justice, which is a useful virtue and perfection, containing no injustice or sin.” Hence Saint Jerome, *To Demetrias*: “All kinds of virtues are contained under the one name of justice.” Here justice is understood as every good work that can be ordered toward grace or reward. MITA.]

Righteousness, which by itself abounds for glory, does not seek the spectacle of the crowd, the praise of the common people, the favor of human beings, or the glory of the world. Born from God, it looks toward heaven; it acts before divine eyes; mingled always with heavenly virtues, it awaits glory from God alone.

But that righteousness which is hypocrisy is not righteousness. It lies to the eyes, deceives the sight, mocks those who see, tricks those who hear, misleads the crowds, draws the people, sells reputation, purchases applause, conforms itself to the world but not to God, seizes a present reward, seeks no prize in the future, blinds the eyes, and, though itself blind and seeing nothing, wishes to be seen. Because of this blindness Christ begins the present command as follows: “Take heed”—that is, do not desire to be noticed.

“Do not perform your righteousness before people.” Why? “So that you may not be seen by them.” And if you are seen, what then? “You have no reward with your Father who is in heaven.”

Brothers, here the Lord does not judge but explains; he lays bare the deceits of thoughts and exposes the secrets of minds. To those who handle righteousness unjustly, he prescribes the measure of just recompense. Righteousness that displays itself to human eyes cannot expect a reward from the divine Father. It wanted to be seen, and it was seen; it wanted to please people, and it pleased them. It has the reward it wanted; the prize it did not want, it will not have.

Let us hear from what follows why these things were stated beforehand. “When you give alms, do not sound a trumpet before you, as the hypocrites do.” The trumpet is apt, because such almsgiving is hostile, not civic; devoted not to mercy but to noise; a minion of sedition, not a nursling of compassion; a marketplace sale of ostentation, not a transaction of charity.
