[Note: Commentators debate whether the Pharisees really had pipers sound before them so that people might gather in the synagogues for their distributions. Rupert, Lyra, Cajetan, Jansenius, and perhaps Chrysologus support the affirmative; Chrysostom, Theophylact, Abulensis, and others take the opposite view.] Whoever displays almsgiving insults the recipient.

“But you,” he says, “when you give alms, do not sound a trumpet before you, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, so that they may be glorified by people. Truly I tell you, they have received their reward.”

You have heard how he marks out almsgiving in assemblies, in public squares, and at crossroads—not as an expenditure intended to relieve the poor, but as something put before people to win favor, so that they may be shown to sell mercy rather than give it.

Hypocrisy must be avoided—avoided, brothers—the hypocrisy that, captive to glory, does not relieve the poor person’s shame. [Note: All editions read “reveals,” which is extremely inept.] [Note: Cyril of Alexandria, *On Adoration*, pages 245–246: “What, or what kind of, life do hypocrites have? Is it not that they appear kind before people and seem to be so, while in reality they are not kind?” There he says much, and indeed much that is excellent, about hypocrisy. Theophylact on Matthew 6: “Hypocrites are those who are one thing but appear to be another.” Hence Hesychius: simulation, deception, fraud. Chrysologus says much the same a little below.] Rather, it exhausts the poor; it seeks the pomp of its own glorification from the poor person’s groaning; it magnifies its own praise through the poor person’s pain; and from the misery of the petitioner it spreads the reputation of its own display.

But someone may say: “Then is mercy to be denied in assemblies, in public squares, and at crossroads? Is food not to be provided?” Certainly not: mercy must be practiced in every place and at every time, food must be provided, and nakedness must be covered. But it must be done as the author of mercy taught: so that mercy is known not to earth but to heaven, not commended to people but to God.

In public squares and at crossroads, compassion has its secret. On the other hand, it is a public square and a crossroads when a hypocrite acts secretly while nothing remains secret.

Brothers, by his warning God condemns not the places but the purposes; not the acts but the meaning; not the work but the giver. He rebukes the person who gives for his own reputation, not for the poor person’s hunger. He judges not where or when you act, but how you act, because God measures deeds by hearts, not hands, and determines their quality from their meaning, not from the locations of the deeds. [Note: That is, from the mind’s meaning and the intention of the heart.]

He wishes mercy to be performed before himself alone, since he alone is both the rewarder and the witness of mercy; and he says: “I was hungry, and you gave me food” (Matthew 25:35). He wishes it to be given to himself in the poor person. And whoever wishes it to be given to himself wishes what has been given to be owed to him; and whoever wishes himself to be owed what has been given wishes nothing to be lost by those who give.

God asks for little, intending to return great things. Therefore, human being, if you lend to God in the poor person, do not seek human witnesses. Faith does not require assessors. The person who gives nothing without intermediaries disputes the faith of the recipient; he who publicizes what was entrusted to him burns the debtor with shame.

Therefore, human being, when you are about to give to God, give secretly, so that what you have given may be not a burden but an honor. For this reason your Enricher comes to you in the poor person: so that you may not hesitate to regard as repayment what he has received, since he freely gave you the ability to possess what you could give.

How shamefully poverty in the poor person seeks the secrecy of your generosity, he himself reveals when he says: “But when you give alms, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing.”

Do you suppose that he wishes one part of you not to know what the other is doing, when he wishes even you yourself—the person who gives—not to know through some part of yourself what you are doing? “Do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing.”

Just as virtues are on our right side, so the part of vices is on our left. [Note: Proverbs 5:27: “For the Lord knows the ways that are on the right.” Secular writers have much on this subject.] [Note: In the *Apophthegmata* preserved by Plutarch: good things are on the right, evil things on the left. See Chrysostom, *Imperfect Work*, Homily 54 on Matthew. Gaudentius, bishop of Brescia, says nearly the same in Sermon 18, page 212: “For the devil attempts to corrupt our faith and our works from the perfect number one hundred, established on the right, toward the deceitful gains of the left side.” Macarius calls demons “left-hand angels” in Homily 22. Among Latin authors, *sinister* often means evil. Hence Ovid’s “ill omen” and Pliny the Younger’s “evil speeches.”]

Therefore, what a silent giver does belongs to the right hand; what a talkative giver does is the hypocrisy of the left. Hypocrisy, deceit, pretense, fraud, falsehood, arrogance, swelling pride, and boasting stand against us and threaten us from the left.

Whenever, then, we are concerned with goodness, compassion, and mercy, let the left hand not know it. The left hand is what always declares war against our souls and works to prevent virtues from coming into effect. It acts impiously so that there may be no compassion; greed fights so that almsgiving may not prevail; avarice rages so that mercy may not grow strong; and hypocrisy alone struggles so that innocence, purity, simplicity, and holiness may not reign. Christ excludes this hypocrisy from us through the following proclamation: “But when you give alms, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing.”

Brothers, in this world let us flee what belongs to the left, if in the future we desire to stand at the right and hear: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:34).

Human being, give the poor person on earth what you wish to remain yours in heaven. Human being, fight here as a fellow soldier beside the poor person, if you wish to reign there with our Lord Jesus Christ himself, who is blessed forever and ever. Amen. [Note: That is, you too should be a soldier of Christ: together with the poor person, a poor person in the Church militant, needy in the weapons of patience—which you ought to use against internal and external enemies—and rich in love for the poor. In this way you will be fellow soldiers. MITA.—See Saint Leo, Sermon 8 on Fasting, at the end, and Sermon 4 on the Fast of the Seventh Month.]

## SERMON X. On Bringing Unbelievers to Baptism. On Psalm 28.

All who lift up the burdens of their work and ease their hardships prove that song has been given to us naturally as a consolation for labor. [Note: Ovid composed verses full of graceful charm relevant to this subject in book IV of the *Tristia*. For there is a great kinship between our soul and rhythms; hence it is easily moved and lifted up by fitting and harmonious melody. Dissonance produces toil and weariness. See Gassendi, *Manuductio*.]

Hence sailors overcome the dangers of the sea with song; hence they draw immense weights along with the relief of singing; hence a ringing voice enables travelers to cross steep hills; hence song, going before the warriors themselves, urges them to undertake the bitter struggles of war. [Note: Paulinus, *On the Return of Nicetas*:

> Joyful sailors sing their customary hauling-song,  
> Joining measured melodies into hymns;  
> And with devout voices they lead their companions  
> Across the sea and through the winds.

Asterius, bishop of Amasea, in his discourse on the martyr Phocas, says that sailors and rowers everywhere sing the customary hauling-songs by which they console the weariness of those at sea, and transfers them to the common praise of the martyr.]

And, not to dwell on many examples, every kind of harsh work and labor is overcome and made bearable by sweet singing.

So let us, brothers, join divine songs to the fast of Lent, so that heavenly harmony may temper and lighten the burden of abstinence, urging us to these things through blessed David [Note: Athanasius says the same concerning David’s singing. Only Davidic psalms were permitted to be publicly recited or sung, according to canon 59 of the Council of Laodicea, where Zonaras observes that there are also others called those of Solomon and of others; Balsamon observes the same there. Eusebius relates that it was the custom of the ancient Christians to compose psalms and hymns in God’s honor, *Ecclesiastical History*, book II, page 16, Paris, 1554, and book V, chapter 38.], who, while soothing and delighting his beloved flock in the pastures with his pipe, learned through song to overcome the hardships of war; through song he was able to summon nations, restore the Jews [Note: This refers to Saul, who, tormented by an evil spirit, was comforted by David’s playing of the lyre.], drive away the demon, and call the children of God to the service of the heavenly Father, as he sang his melody beautifully. [Note: It is agreed by all that the psalms were metrical and set to music, though the kind of metre in which they were written is uncertain. Gomarus published a *Davidic Lyre*, in which he imagined that he had scanned the psalms in Horatian or similar metres and discovered the true character of this poetry. Ludovicus Cappellus, however, attempted to strike through Gomarus’s entire work in his *Animadversions*, so that, as Mivetus adds, the reader may learn that scarcely any agreement on the matter is possible among scholars. Blasius Cariophylus should be consulted in his Italian dissertation on Hebrew poetry, where he investigates most learnedly both metre and similar word-endings in Hebrew songs. The psalms are to be divided in two ways: some are called *ode psalms*, such as 30 and 65, because voices led and instruments followed; others *psalms ode*, such as 48 and 66, because instruments led and voices followed. On this distinction see Athenaeus, book XIV; for more, Lamy, *On the Temple*, book VII, sections 5–6.] [Note: There can be no doubt that Chrysologus is speaking of the shepherd’s pipe. Its form was not uniform but varied, although it was generally taken to mean a set of small pipes, the French *musette*. Among the instruments of the Hebrews, a pipe was called *masacrokita*, from whistling.]

“Bring to the Lord,” he says, “you sons of God” (Psalm 28:1). Do you think that he calls heavenly powers by this name? [Note: In Scripture “sons of God” sometimes means angels: Job 1:6 and 2:1; Psalm 88:7.] Or does he adapt human beings as God’s sons and raise earthly flesh to a heavenly nature? “Bring to the Lord, you sons of God.”

Here the prophet calls human beings “sons of God,” whom elsewhere he celebrates as God’s children: “I said, ‘You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High’” (Psalm 81:6).

We have heard, brothers, to what height divine favor has lifted us, to what elevation heavenly fatherhood has raised us. Let us believe that we are God’s sons; let us answer to our lineage; let us live for heaven; let us reflect the Father in our likeness, lest through vices we lose what we have obtained through grace.

“Bring to the Lord, you sons of God.” You see that the heavenly Father feels love through gifts, receives affection through things bestowed, and proves charity by presents. [Note: Other copies, including the Vallicellian manuscript, read “effect.”] Indeed, brothers, the person who does not know himself to be a son, who lacks filial feeling, denies his nature, and is ungrateful to his father is the one who does not please the author of his life through obedience, does not win him over through worship, and does not honor him with gifts.

“Bring to the Lord, you sons of God.” Let us see what this prophet here reminds us and urges us to bring to such a great Father: “Bring to the Lord, you sons of God; bring to the Lord the sons of rams.”

This is all that he seeks and requires: the offspring of sheep, the humble germ of earthly livestock, young animals laid along the road in birth. [Note: “The offspring of sheep,” as in Ovid, book III of the *Fasti*, verse 10: ]

That you might give great seeds to this city. ] He is admonished to scatter seeds through the fields for the divine Father, so that a divine offspring may make an offering. Or perhaps God, the Creator of all, now demands Jewish victims, bloody sacrifices, bleating offerings beneath the knives? And where is what he says:

“I will not accept calves from your house, nor goats from your flocks, because all the wild animals of the forests are mine, the beasts on the mountains, and the cattle. I know all [Col. 0216B] the birds of heaven, and the produce of the field is with me. If I were hungry, I would not tell you: the world and its fullness are mine” (Psalm LX, 9–12).

And if he rejected these things, whose sons of rams does he demand to be brought to him? He speaks to Abraham:

“Take your beloved son, and you shall offer him to me as a burnt offering” (Genesis 22).

[Note: [Col. 0216D] On account of the strength of his virtue.]

Abraham was a mature ram in innocence, [Note: [Col. 0216D] On Abraham’s faith, from which his obedience and patience flowed, see Clement of Alexandria, *The Tutor*, book III, p. 221; Theodoret, *Oration on Charity*, vol. IV, p. 691; Basil in the *Ascetic Works*, chapter 22, vol. II, p. 716, and vol. I, p. 672; Chrysostom, Letter 2 to Olympias and Letter 237, vol. IV of the Paris edition, pp. 946–947, and Homily 10, vol. V, p. 45; Gregory of Nyssa, *Oration on God the Son and the Holy Spirit*, vol. III, pp. 473–476. It is enough to have indicated these.]

advanced in age, perfected in faith, prepared for sacrifice, ready for a burnt offering. He was bringing his son, the son of a ram; indeed, he was sacrificing himself in his son, sanctifying his mind and gladdening his faith, so that he might be both victim and priest, both priest and sacrifice. The father’s whole suffering was present there, where the son was being sacrificed; the son was stationed unaware, [Note: [Col. 0216D] Some printed editions, through a scribal error: “the sluggish son.”] the son, ignorant of what was happening, [Note: [Col. 0216D] Printed editions: “the bound son was fitted.” Meursius emended it and observed that Chrysologus used *aptare* in its proper frequentative sense, from the unused *apio*, “to bind,” as Festus explains under “Apex.” And indeed our author is fond of using ancient and obsolete words.] was being fitted with bonds, so that he might take martyrdom from the father’s suffering, [Col. 0217A] reward from the father’s punishment, and snatch the crown from the father’s struggle. [Note: [Col. 0217B] Latinius thinks this should be read in this way. Mita and Castillo read “might recover.” The first reading seemed preferable.]

Finally, the father’s hand was stayed, and the father’s sword was removed, because the son’s death was not being sought, but the father’s love was being tested. Nor was the son’s blood demanded, since the whole sacrifice consisted in the father’s love, as Scripture says:

“Now I know that you love God, because you did not spare your only-begotten son for me” (Genesis 22:12).

We called Abraham a ram, so that we might prove Isaac to be the son of a ram; and thus it becomes clear whom the Prophet wishes us to offer to the Lord as sons of rams:

“Offer to the Lord the sons of rams.”

[Note: [Col. 0217B] Rupertus, on Ecclesiasticus 24: “Here we understand the Lord’s sheepfold by the name *Elim*, that is, ‘rams.’ For rams are the leaders of the flock and the chiefs of the sheepfold; concerning them the Psalmist says: ‘Offer,’ he says, ‘the sons of rams.’ Interpreters believe that this refers to prophets and patriarchs, apostles, and others, in Isaiah 60:7: ‘The rams of Nebaioth will minister to him.’]

The sons of fathers, patriarchs, prophets, apostles, martyrs, and confessors: the Christian is now admonished to offer them, when the Lord’s flock is released to pasture in faith, when the heavenly Shepherd wishes his lambs to be brought to the Lord’s sheepfold, lest, scattered through the uncultivated regions of the nations, they be devoured by the attacks of wolves.

But let us now speak more plainly about what the divine voice commands:

“Offer to the Lord the sons of rams.”

[Note: [Col. 0217C] There are many complaints by the holy Fathers against those who procrastinate over baptism. See Gregory of Nazianzus, *Oration on the Holy Lights*, and especially Oration 40, which is on holy baptism; likewise Chrysostom, Homily on Acts, p. 615 of the 1612 edition; Justellus in his notes on the canon of the Council of Neo-Caesarea; and Vossius, *Disputation on Baptism*. They advanced as the reason for delay that they wished to be baptized and die at the same time, lest, after receiving baptism, they should sin again, having been misled by a misunderstood passage of the Apostle in Hebrews 6:4. From this the Novatians concluded that no hope remained after baptism for those who sinned. From this sermon of Chrysologus, however, it is clear that the holy man exerted all his strength to bring people to baptism, because Easter was approaching, which according to the discipline of that period was the second solemnity after Pentecost appointed for the faithful to be washed in the sacred font. Although some hear this unwillingly, the testimonies of the holy Fathers, which fill both sides of the question, whether they wish it or not establish the same point: Tertullian, *On Baptism*, chapter 19; Jerome, *To Pammachius*; Fortunatus, book III of the poems, poem 7, and book V, poem 4; Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, book IV, chapter 22; and from Socrates, Nicephorus, book XII, chapter 34; Basil, *Exhortation to Baptism*; Siricius, *Letter to the Decretals*, no. 2, p. 190; *Library of Canon Law*, Paris, 1661; Pope Leo’s decree in Gratian, Distinction 4, “Two Times”; Gelasius, *On Consecration*, Distinction 4, “Those to Be Baptized”; the *Capitularies of the Frankish Kings*, edited by Baluze, vol. II of the *Councils*; the Council of Gerunda, 517, canon 4; the Council of Tribur, 895, canon 12; the Council of Mainz, 813, canon 4; and innumerable others. On the days of Easter and Pentecost the Greeks added Epiphany; this, however, is condemned by the decree of Pope Leo, [Col. 0218C] *Library of Canon Law*, VII, p. 224, and by Peter of Blois at the beginning of Sermon 13. The Gauls added Christmas Day and the feast of Saint John the Baptist. See Avitus of Vienne, Letter to Clovis, and Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 69. This custom of baptism, namely at Easter and Pentecost, continued until the end of the eleventh century, according to Theophylact, *Commentary on Luke* 10. What has been said must nevertheless be understood with the exception of cases of necessity.]

Offer to the Lord those who are to be baptized; offer those whom faith, not flesh, conceives; offer those whom the grace of God, not worldly nature, generates; offer those whom innocence makes lambs, not the dullness of cattle. Offer, offer those whom their own will prevents from coming, or necessity, or age obstructs, or ignorance delays, or vices hold back, or sins hinder, or expectation deceives, or poverty, through shame, misleads. Bring those who are willing, [Note: [Col. 0218C] Either the elderly, or rather infants, because even at that time baptism was administered to infants. Everyone knows what the African synod of sixty-six bishops under Cyprian decreed against the bishop Fidus. For, as Cyprian reports in his letter to him, which is Letter 65, Fidus maintained that infants ought not to be baptized before their second or third year. See Augustine, Letter to Jerome 28.]

[Note: [Col. 0218C–D] Augustine teaches how this is done in Tractate 26 on John 6 and Sermon 2, *On the Words of the Apostle*; so too Maldonado on John 6:44, whose words he explains most learnedly against Calvin, Luther, and Pelagius. He likewise teaches how Augustine’s words in the Sermon 2 just cited, which say that the compulsion by which we are said to be drawn is applied to the heart, not the flesh, are to be understood. The author gives three examples: Jacob, Lot, and Peter, who freely desired to do what God commanded, yet were nevertheless held back by certain obstacles and needed another’s assistance in order freely to accomplish what was present in their first intention. On this matter, almost parallel to our case, see St Augustine’s final letter, vol. II. See St Gregory of Nyssa, *Treatise on Those Who Delay Baptism*. MITA.]

draw along those who are unwilling; make a reward for yourselves from another’s necessity. If a master has a slave who is a catechumen, let him bring him, so that he may now have him as a believer. Let a father offer his son, not delay him, so that the one to whom he has granted present life he may also give future life. Let a husband lead his wife to faith, lest what is one in flesh be divided in spirit. Let a friend draw his friend toward salvation, so that he may prove human love through divine grace. Let a citizen bring a stranger, a landowner his guest, to God’s table, so that, without expense to himself, he may show humanity from divine riches.

Draw along those who are unwilling. Let no one say, “He does not want to,” because Abraham also bound his son in order to offer him (Genesis 22:9); and the angels, in order to rescue Lot from the flames, lifted him out by the hands after dragging him away (Genesis 19:16); and the Lord, in order to lead Peter to the martyrdom he did not want, girded him with the power of his aid, saying: “Another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish to go” (John 21:18). The heavenly Father not only receives those who are willing, but also draws along those who are unwilling, as the Son says:

“No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me has drawn him” (John 6:44).

[Note: [Col. 0218D] The Gospel reads “unless he draws him.” Ambrose, along with our author, reads the Greek *ἐλκῦσαι*, “to draw.”]

How can he believe himself a Christian who does not bring the old and aged to Christ? Or how can he judge his house to be God’s sheepfold when God’s flock does not bring forth its pasture-born offspring with bleating?

I beseech and implore you, dearest brothers, by our Lord, to remain all of you watchful in this matter, so that during these days no one may be left deprived of God’s grace, no one [Note: [Col. 0218D] Thus according to the Vallicellian manuscript and Latinius. The printed editions, following Mita, read “from generation.”] deprived of divine regeneration; so that what God is about to bestow on others through his grace may increase and overflow into your joy.

We are human beings living amid uncertainty, and we do not know what the coming day will bring forth (Proverbs 27). Let us act, therefore, beloved, lest slaves, sons, wives, [Col. 0219A] or parents, overtaken by death, lose both the present life and the opportunity to reach the future one.

## SERMON XI. On Fasting and Christ’s Temptations

What human curiosity, what the labor of the ancients, what worldly wisdom, searching and searching for a long time, could not discover, the divine law has easily enabled us both to know and not to know. From where evil comes, from where guilt, from where the power of vices, from where the fury of crimes, from where the wars of bodies, from where the soul’s conflict, from where so great a storm of life, from where death’s so cruel shipwreck—man would not know, unless God’s law had exposed the devil. [Note: [Col. 0219C] Compare Romans 7:7: “I did not know sin except through the law; for I would not have known covetousness unless the law had said, ‘You shall not covet.’”]

The devil is the author of evil, the origin of wickedness, the enemy of all things, the perpetual enemy of the second man. [Note: [Col. 0219C] Latinius wonders whether this is to be read thus. Perhaps it is in the sense of Chrysostom on Psalm 4, “the common enemy of the world,” and of Justin Martyr in the *Exhortation to the Greeks*, “the enemy of the human race.” Other similar expressions are collected in Ignatius, *Letter to the Philippians*, p. 43.] He stretches snares, prepares falls, digs pits, arranges ruin, goads bodies, pricks souls, suggests thoughts, injects anger, makes virtues hateful, [Note: [Col. 0219C] The printed editions read “gives love.” Meursius emended it.] gives vices to love, sows errors, nourishes discord, disturbs peace, scatters affections, tears unity apart. He understands evil well enough, goodness not at all; he violates divine things, attacks human things.

Hence the reckless tempter is reported to have stretched his assault even to Christ:

“And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, afterward he was hungry. And the tempter approached and said to him: ‘If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves of bread’” (Matthew 4:2–3).

When we hear these things, let them not turn us against God, [Note: [Col. 0219C] See Augustine, vol. I of the *Retractions*, chapter 11; book I of *On the Morals of the Manichaeans*; book II of *On Faith to Peter the Deacon*, chapter 20; and book VII of the *Confessions*, chapter 13; and Leo the Great, Sermon 4 *On Lent*, p. 38, column 1 of the Lyon edition. He also condemns the Manichaeans in words that sufficiently clarify Chrysologus’s meaning: “But woe to the doctrine of those men”—namely, the Manichaeans, whom he had shortly before called servants of the devil—“among whom one sins even by fasting. For they condemn the nature of creatures, to the injury of the Creator, and assert that those things become polluted when eaten whose creator they define to be not God but the devil, although absolutely no substance is evil and there is no nature belonging to evil itself. For the good Author established all things good,” and so forth. These points should also be observed against the Saturninians, who, together with the Manichaeans, taught that sin is present in human beings by nature and not by guilt.]

let them not insult the Creator, accuse the flesh, question the soul, or attack the times; let them not blame the stars, [Note: [Col. 0219D] More than one of the ancients foolishly persuaded himself that the influence and aspects of the stars greatly contributed to the things we do. Gregory the Great says in Homily 10 on the Gospel that the Priscillianists adhered to this view—namely, that every human being is born under the power of the stars—and from their movements they inferred that many things destined to happen to us were foretold. See Rufinus of Aquileia, in Sirmond, vol. I, p. 167, on Origen, who raved exceptionally about the stars. This was also the opinion of the pagans, but not of all of them—only of the foolish and deranged, as Theodoret notes in Question 15.] and let them cease defaming the innocence of creation. [Col. 0220A] Let them understand that evil is accidental, not created, and that God is the Creator of good while the devil is the discoverer of evil. Thus let them ascribe evils to the devil and good things to God; let them avoid evil and do good, having God as their helper in good things, who gives the ability to do what he commands and himself accomplishes what he orders. For just as the devil [Note: [Col. 0220C] Latinius and Mita. Others read, “drives toward evil.”] drives toward evil, so God leads toward good.

[Note: [Col. 0220C] Augustine, *On Faith to Peter the Deacon*, chapter 20: “There is no evil nature, because every nature, insofar as it is nature, is good; but because good can be increased and diminished in it, it is called evil insofar as its good is diminished. For evil is nothing other than the privation of good,” and so forth. —Mita. Jerome, Homily 5 on Ecclesiastes, p. 417: “Vice does not subsist in itself, but consists in the privation of good.” See Basil, Homily 2 on the *Hexaemeron*, p. 22.]

Therefore let no one, as though vices had been created together with him, obey them, or suppose that what is a crime belongs to nature. Rather, let him take up with Christ the weapons of fasting, repel the assaults of crimes, overthrow the camps of vices, and [Note: [Col. 0220C] Namely, from the discoverer of evil mentioned above, who provokes and leads us toward evil. In this sense Cyril, *Paschal Homily* 6, p. 68: “The demon is the author of evil, the father of sin.”] while Christ fights, win victory over the author of evil. Once the devil has been defeated, the vices will have no power; for when the tyrant has been extinguished, the tyrant’s battle-lines are dissolved.

Hear the Apostle saying:

“Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 6:12).

[Note: [Col. 0220C] Several Fathers, together with Chrysologus, cite this passage of the Apostle in this same sense: Leo I, Sermon 4 *On Lent*, chapter 4; Paschasius, book III on Matthew; William of Évreux, Sermon 1 on the First Sunday of Lent; and others.]

“Then,” he says, “Jesus was led by the Spirit into the desert.”

[Note: [Col. 0220C] To indicate that Christ was led by the Spirit—not a human spirit but the divine Spirit—and withdrew voluntarily. Severus, from the Greek word *ἀνῆθαι*, translates it as “was withdrawn,” as though he had been separated from the crowd.]

Not by the devil, so that the course might be divine rather than a human assault; so that there might be the Spirit’s foreknowledge and no human ignorance; so that it might be God’s power and not the enemy’s power.

The devil always strikes at the beginnings of good, tests the first stages of virtue, and hastens to extinguish holy things at their very birth, knowing that he cannot overthrow what has been firmly founded. Christ, who did not ignore this, patiently allowed the devil, who was seeking him, to proceed, so that the enemy might be caught in his own snare and captured at the very point from which he thought he could capture Christ, and thus, defeated by Christ, might yield to Christians.

[Note: [Col. 0220D] Lest anyone suppose that Christ was tempted by necessity rather than willingly; for, as Hilary says here, the tempter would have had no opportunity to tempt him unless it had been granted.]

“And when he had fasted,” he says, “forty days and forty nights.”

You see, brothers, that the fact that we fast for Lent is not [Note: [Col. 0220D] That the Lenten fast passed into the Church from the Savior’s abstinence in the desert, despite whatever the heterodox may object, is attested by Ignatius, Letter to the Philippians, p. 45 of the Geneva edition of 1623; the compiler of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, chapter 12, whose passages they attempt in vain to undermine; likewise Ambrose, Sermon 34; Jerome on Isaiah 58; Augustine, Letter 119, chapter 15; Theodoret, *History*, chapter 26; and Basil, *Oration on Fasting*.]

a human invention but has divine authority; it is mystical, not presumptuous; it does not arise from earthly custom but from heavenly mysteries.

Lent contains four decades, a square pattern of the discipline of faith, because perfection is always square. [Note: [Col. 0221C] That is, perfect, explains Mita.] Since the number four and the number ten contain mysteries [Note: [Col. 0221C] The mystical mysteries of the number four are explained by Ambrose in Sermon 4, which is for the Tuesday after the Second Sunday of Lent; Theophylact, Patriarch of Antioch, book IV of the *Allegories of the Gospel*; Gregory the Great, Homily 16 on the Gospel; Hilary; Maximus; Basil; and, above all, Paschasius, book III on Matthew.] both in heaven and on earth, and since there is not now enough time to unfold them, let us explain the Lord’s fast as it began:

“And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights.”

Man, [Note: [Col. 0221C] “In your humanity, and for you,” that is, for your benefit, explains Mita.] God fasts in you; in you he is hungry. Indeed, he fasts for you and is hungry for you, who, just as he does not know how to eat for himself, so cannot be hungry for himself.

Therefore, when Christ fasts for your sake, he hungers for you.

“And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, afterward he was hungry.”

This is not a sign of weakness but a mark of virtue, because when it says “afterward he was hungry,” it proves that during the forty days and forty nights there had been no hunger in him. To feel hunger and overcome it is a human labor; [Note: [Col. 0221C] Here the Cerinthians, Ebionites, and their followers—Paul of Samosata and Photinus—may be condemned, for they asserted that there was nothing in Christ beyond the human. The Theodotians may likewise be condemned; for Theodore, having lapsed during the persecution and wishing not to seem to have denied God, called Christ a mere human being. Certainly, when the word “virtue” is used of Christ, it should almost always be understood by the holy Fathers, especially Hilary, as referring to his divine nature.]

but it is divine virtue not to have hunger.

Therefore Christ does not grow weary from fasting, nor does he hunger from starvation; rather, [Note: [Col. 0221D] Hilary, vol. I, p. 677: “For the devil was not from God but was to be conquered by the flesh. He would certainly not have dared to tempt him unless, through the weakness of hunger, he had recognized in him the things that belong to a human being.” Augustine—or whoever is the author of the work under his name—*On the Wonders of Holy Scripture*, vol. III, book III, chapter 6: “Our Redeemer endures hunger and labor after completing so great a number of days, both to give the tempter an opportunity and to make known how truly he regarded the substance of human flesh.”] Christ became hungry so that the devil might find an opportunity to tempt him, because [Note: [Col. 0222C] He approached Jesus only after the forty days had been completed. Origen—or some other author—in Homily 29 thinks that he was tempted throughout the forty days.] he did not dare approach him while he was fasting, because, seeing him fasting in this way, he perceived him to be God, not a human being.

Then he perceived him as human; then he believed him mortal; then he thought he could be tempted, when the clever investigator saw that he was hungry.

“And the tempter approached and said.”

He approached with the deceit of one tempting, not with the affection of one obeying. He approached more shamelessly than he withdrew; but let us hear what he offered the hungry man:

“Command that these stones become loaves of bread.”

He offers stones to a hungry man. Such is always the enemy’s kindness; thus the author of death feeds; thus [Note: [Col. 0222C] From the Vatican manuscript. Another reading: “unwillingly.”] the one who envies life:

“Command that these stones become loaves of bread.”

Devil, your plan deceives you. He who can change stones into bread can turn hunger into satiety. What use is your counsel to one whose own power is sufficient?

“Command that these stones become loaves of bread.”

Devil, [Note: [Col. 0222C] I restored the passage, corrupted in many editions, from the Bologna edition and the Vallicellian manuscript.] you have betrayed yourself, and you have not feared your own Lord.

“Command that these stones become loaves of bread.”

Wretched creature! You want to be evil, but you cannot; you desire to tempt, but you do not know how. You should have offered something tender to the hungry, not something hard; you should have touched hunger with pleasant things, not harsh ones; you should have pressed upon his fasting with things suited to appetite, not with horrors. With these things you could not ensnare not only the Son of God but even the son of man.

Understand, tempter, that at Christ’s presence your arts are doomed to perish.

“Command that these stones become loaves of bread.”

He can make bread from stones who changed water into wine. But signs must be offered for faith, not for deceit; they must be given to one who believes, not to one who tempts; and they must be performed for the salvation of the one who asks, not for the injury of the one who performs them.

Devil, why should signs be given to you, for whom they contribute nothing to salvation, for whom everything remains for punishment, and for whom even signs advance your ruin?

But receive the answer, so that you may understand yourself and be subjected to the Creator:

“Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.”

Hear the Father’s Word hungering for the words of our salvation, not for bread, and acting so that man may always live by the heavenly word, not always by earthly bread. [Note: [Col. 0222D] Interpreters explain the Gospel phrase “by every word” in this way: since a human being consists of soul and body, the soul is nourished by the word of God and the body by bread. This is a Hebraism, says Calmet: “word” is understood as any thing whatsoever; nothing becomes unsuitable as food when God commands it.]

Thus let him live for God, unaware of his own labor, because that life is truly life which knows no sweat, suffers no pain, and has no end.

## SERMON XII. On the Same Subject

Since [Note: [Col. 0222D] The author followed Chrysostom, *Sermon on Fasting and Genesis*: “The days of fasting are joyful, the spiritual springtime of souls.” *Vernum* is used for *ver*. See Barthius, *Adversarial Notes*, book X, chapter 12, who praises Chrysologus. Ennodius, poem 4:

> In the world, captive Venus, nurturing goddess, with gifts poured forth,  
> playing amid the pleasant flowers,  
> while she makes the springtime’s splendor and that of the glittering—
The springtime of the stars’ beauty. The same author, in the preface to the *Carmen Epiph.*: “In him there still smiled both the springtime of childhood and the springtime of worldly license.”] We see that the springtime of fasting and the season of spiritual warfare have arrived. Therefore, as soldiers of Christ, having laid aside the sluggishness of body and soul, let us advance onto the field of virtues, so that our limbs, softened by winter’s leisure, may be strengthened through the exercise of heavenly arms. We have given the body a year; let us give the soul some days. We have spent seasons on ourselves; let us assign a season to our Creator. Let us live for God a little while, who have lived wholly for the world. Let us set aside household cares and remain in the camp of the Church. Let us keep watch in Christ’s battle line; let us not seek the sleep of our beds. Let us join the brave; let us separate ourselves from soft embraces. Let the love of triumphs possess us; let the blandishments of little children not draw us away. Let the divine voice resound in our ears; let familiar noise not confuse our hearing.

[Note: [Col. 0223C] This means that we should live sparingly on the fruits that nature itself produces, not on what the hands of cooks prepare. Augustine, vol. X, Sermon 56 *de tempore*: “It is of no benefit to have prolonged one’s fast throughout the day if afterward the soul is overwhelmed by the delicacy or excess of foods. Immediately, when the mind is filled, it grows sluggish, and when the soil of our body is watered, it will sprout the thorns of lust.” MITA.—“From the heavenly grain,” that is, from divine Providence, which supplies us with what is necessary for our nourishment. Judith V, 14: “They obtained grain from heaven.”]

Let scanty food be taken from the heavenly grain; let the abundance of earthly luxury not be sought. Let sobriety remain steadfast in our cups; let drunkenness not weaken our strength.

[Note: [Col. 0223C] St Leo, Sermon 8, *On Fasting*: “Daily experience proves that the mind’s keenness is dulled by satiety in drinking and the heart’s vigor blunted by excess in food, so that the pleasure of eating is even harmful to the health of the body unless the discipline of temperance resists the enticement, and what is destined to become a burden is withdrawn from pleasure.” See Sermon 8 of the seventh month, near the end. A soldier is removed from military service because of drunkenness. *Digest*, title *De re militari*, law *Omne*, section *Per vinum*. MITA.]

Of whatever exceeds the military allowance, let the poor fellow-soldier take his share.

[Note: [Col. 0224C] “Fellow” and “fellow messmate” occur frequently in writers. Paulinus of Nola, Letter 25, p. 162: “My fellow messmate.”]

Let no ruinous dissipation squander anything.

[Note: [Col. 0224C] It is called “pestilential waste” because whatever is squandered in sins is poured out to the soul’s destruction.]

In battle you will have as an auxiliary the hungry companion whom you feed.

[Note: [Col. 0224C] Other editions, and some manuscripts, read “the hungry wounded man” or “the wounded man through hunger.” “The hungry companion,” that is, a poor man; if you feed him when he is starving, he will become your companion in battle, if not by his hands, at least by his prayer before God.]

Thus fortified, brothers—thus equipped—let us declare war on sins; let us establish battle against crimes; let us announce conflict to vices, confident of victory. For earthly enemies will not be able to overcome those who are armed with heavenly weapons, nor will worldly forces be able to resist the divine King.

Nor will hostile overthrow prevail against us, established in the battle line of faith.

[Note: [Col. 0224C] The Catholic Church is called the *procinctus fidei*, that is, an impregnable wall. Likewise, fasting is a battle line against enemies, as below. Catholics are said to stand in the battle line of faith because they are continually prepared to fight for the faith itself, even to the shedding of blood, as martyrs do. MITA.—*Procinctus* is the same as a military expedition. [Col. 0224D] Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXIX, p. 579: “Aquileia was besieged by the Marcomanni, Opitergium destroyed, and many bloody events were carried out with swift military action.” Paulinus of Nola, Letter 7, p. 37: “From the *bucellatum*—a kind of twice-baked military bread—of the Christian expedition, in whose battle line we daily serve for the grain of frugality.”]

Nor will the devil be able to disturb the cautious, watchful, and sober through his sudden attacks. Certainly he will not dare challenge us, armed in this fashion, in open battle; he will not presume to assail us by deceit. Let the soul remain in the heavenly mirror; let it crush and avoid the devil’s deceitful and hidden snares.

The devil is indeed evil in himself, yet when provoked he becomes still worse. Hear the Apostle say: “The devil, like a roaring lion, prowls about, seeking someone to devour” (1 Peter V, 8). While we fast, the devil hungers—he who is always filled by our sins. He turns our food into gluttony and pours our drink into drunkenness, so that he may make the mind senseless, make the flesh muddy, and turn the body—the dwelling of the soul, the vessel of the soul, the wall of the spirit, the school of virtues, the temple of God—into a stage for crimes and a spectacle of vices; he turns pleasure into a theater.

He obtains satiety and experiences pleasure; he is filled with feasts when luxury loosens us, lust goads us, display carries us away, ambition drives us on, anger presses us, fury fills us, envy inflames us, greed sets us ablaze, cares trouble us, quarrels torment us, profits seize us, usury binds us, bonds tie us, purses weigh us down, and gold strikes us down.

When virtues die, vices live; pleasure flows out, honor perishes, mercy fails, greed abounds, confusion reigns, order collapses, and discipline is overthrown. These things wage war against the soldier of Christ. These are Satan’s cohorts; these are the devil’s legions. These are the forces that have besieged the world with tombs, conquered peoples, laid nations waste, and led the whole world captive.

[Note: [Col. 0224D] That is, they filled the world with tombs because of the countless wars that followed from them. MITA.]

These are things that no mortal could resist by himself.

[Note: [Col. 0224D] The Catholic doctrine is lightly touched upon here against the Pelagians: no human being, without God’s habitual grace, can avoid all sins by the powers of nature alone.]

Therefore God himself came to conquer them; the King of heaven himself descended; the one victorious champion himself arrived, establishing the fast of Lent as a battle line, so that by a fourfold decade of fasting he might fortify the whole compass of the world with an impregnable wall.

[Note: [Col. 0224D] Namely, the East, West, North, and South; or Asia, Africa, Europe, and America, which perhaps were then known. MITA.]

Fasting, brothers, is, as we know, God’s stronghold,

[Note: [Col. 0225C] Ambrose, vol. V, Sermon 36, near the beginning: “For our fasts are our military camp.”]

Christ’s camp, the wall of the spirit, the banner of faith, the sign of chastity, and the trophy of holiness.

If Adam had preserved this in paradise, he would not have been driven from it by gluttony (Genesis III).

[Note: [Col. 0225C] From Mita. Other editions read *servavit* (“preserved”).]

This fasting Noah preserved in the ark (Genesis VII), when drunkenness submerged the world.

[Note: [Col. 0225C] Isidore of Pelusium says the same in the passage cited. St Eligius, bishop of Noviomagus, aptly says in his sermon on the first Sunday of Lent: “Noah, a sober man, was preserved amid the waves of the flood while the world perished.”]

Through this Lot extinguished the fire of Sodom, though through drunkenness he was burned in the fire of incest (Genesis XIX).

This made Moses shine with the light of divine fervor

[Note: [Col. 0225C] From the Vallicellian manuscript. Some printed editions incorrectly read *perducere* (“to bring”).]

when feasting and drunkenness plunged the Israelite people into the darkness of errors concerning idols (Exodus XXXII).

This carried Elijah up to heaven when drunkenness cast the impious Ahab down to hell (4 Kings II).

[Note: [Col. 0225C] Some read *perduxit* (“brought”). The Fathers were not of one opinion concerning Elijah’s ascent. Some think that he did not ascend into heaven but as if into heaven. Theodoret, on Psalm XXIV, p. 486: “The great Elijah was indeed taken up, but not into heaven, rather as though into heaven.” Athanasius, *Oration on the Assumption of Christ*, vol. II, p. 4: “Elijah was taken up as though into heaven.” See also—since we are sparing paper—Theophylact on Luke XXIV, p. 546; Chrysostom, Homily 87, which concerns the Ascension, vol. V, p. 600; and Oecumenius on Acts I. Suicer attributes the reason why these and others were deceived to their reading of the Septuagint in 2 Kings II, 11. Others, with Scripture—and our author agrees with them—teach that Elijah was taken up into heaven itself. The same is taught by Chrysostom, Homily 121, vol. VI, p. 792, and Homily 2 to the people of Antioch, vol. I, p. 37, Paris edition; Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 34, p. 549; and Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, book V, chapter 12, p. 795.]

This made John greater than those born of women, when Herod’s drunkenness made the ruler a murderer at the command of women (Mark VI).

[Note: [Col. 0226C] Chrysostom, vol. VI, Homily 84, calls John “without food” (*ἄσιτος*), suffering from abstinence. Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 29, p. 633, calls him “unfed” (*ἄτροφος*).]

The fast of Lent, brothers, exposed and revealed the devil’s ancient snares.

[Note: [Col. 0226C] At the beginning of the world he also persuaded Eve to break her fast. From Mita. This is rather far-fetched. I would suppose that *vetustas* (“antiquity”) should be read here for *fraudulentas* (“fraudulent”), as below, “the devil’s fraudulent wiles.” Thus Claudian, speaking of Rufinus, calls a very crafty man “an old fox.”]

For the devil, who had despised Christ when he was eating and had regarded him as a man when he was drinking, suspected him to be God and confessed him to be the Son of God when he saw him fasting. “If you are the Son of God,” he said, “command that these stones become loaves” (Matthew IV).

By saying this, the devil wants to show that he is dealing with a man, not God. He does not want to provide food; he wants to break the fast. “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves.” After the fast, it is not divine power but human weakness that seeks bread. Yet God does not grow so weary from hunger that he would renounce his power to provide food for himself.

[Note: [Col. 0226C] The printed editions incorrectly read *lacessit* (“provokes”).]

[Note: [Col. 0226C] Thus Latinius emends what all lexicons have as *addicat* (“assigns”).]

From what follows, then, the devil reveals what he is attempting: “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down.”

[Note: [Col. 0226C] Chrysologus follows the order of the temptations according to Matthew. That order is shown to be genuine by the fact that in certain ancient manuscripts, which Faber testifies to having seen in Jansenius’s *Concordia*, the order is the same in Luke, as Stapulensis notes. The word “depart” (*ὕπαγε*) is also better connected in this sequence than with the exceedingly shameless temptation of worship, which is third in Mark and second in Luke. But whether this or that occurred first makes no difference, provided it is clear that all occurred, says Augustine, *On the Harmony of the Gospels*, book II, chapter 16.]

He wants to prove that he is dealing with a man for whom he has not provided ascent but a fall; the human condition is found to be difficult for ascent and easy for falling. “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down.”

You are mistaken, devil; you do not even know how to tempt. God cannot fall.

Then he showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory and said to him: “All these things I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me.”

O the devil’s audacity! He says to God, “Worship me.” But he soon perceived in the one he sought to entice that he was God in his powers, judge in his punishments, and generous in his rewards. For at the name of Christ—the name of the fasting one—he began to be driven from possessed bodies, and, trembling, to give glory to him whom in his pride and cunning he had insulted. Christ conquered by fasts, so that he might bestow on us the strength and the pattern for conquering in the same way. “This kind,” he said, “is expelled only by fasting and prayer.”

Let us therefore fast, brothers, if we wish to imitate Christ; if we wish to overcome the devil’s fraudulent wiles.

## SERMON XIII. On the Same Subject

Behold the time when the soldier advances onto the field; the Christian returns to God’s fasts.

Behold the time when the leisure of the flesh, the sluggishness of the mind, the care of the belly, and all the torpor of familiar service must be laid aside.

Behold the time when the powers of soul and body must be exercised in meditation upon heavenly arms.

Behold the time when, with Christ seated and angels standing by,

[Note: [Col. 0226D] I do not know of anything similar to this except St Asterius, bishop of Amasea, Homily 8, “At the Beginning of the Fast”: “Know, O man, that the house of the one who fasts has angels as its guardians and, as it were, our constant guards.”]

our strength must be exercised in combat.

Now is the time when gluttony fights with fasting, abstinence with excess, chastity with luxury, faith with treachery, piety with impiety, patience with fury, generosity with greed, mercy with avarice, humility with pride, and holiness with guilt, while Christ rewards us.

If anyone, while God looks on, the heavenly trumpet already resounding, and the angelic host standing near, neglects to come to the exercise of virtue because he is entangled in the allurements of his bedroom, weakened by softness,

[Note: [Col. 0226D] Other editions read “the army of virtue.”]

and entirely undone by marital blandishments, he loses the prize of the struggle, the glory of virtue, the palm of combat, and the crown of justice; moreover, he will eventually be punished for the crime of desertion.

[Note: [Col. 0226D] The punishment of deserters and defectors varied among different peoples. *Digest*, book III, title *De re militari*, law *Desertor*; *Code*, title *De desertoribus*, book XII. See Alexander ab Alexandro, book XII, chapter 13.]

Today, brothers, Christ our King has addressed his fellow soldiers from the evangelical tribunal. He has declared war against the enemies, promised rewards to those who fight, disclosed the causes of the wars and the enemy’s deceits and designs, and marked out for us, by a triumphant decree, where, when, and how we must fight.

And although he alone can obtain the victory, for our sake and because of our fear he has commanded all the forces from above to be present.

[Note: [Col. 0227B] Hilary, *Commentary on Matthew III*, p. 679, section 5: “After this flight of the devil, angels minister to Christ, showing that, once the devil’s head has been conquered and crushed by us, both the ministry of angels and the services of heavenly powers toward us will not be lacking.”]

Therefore, if anyone refused to hear these things, if he despised knowing such and such great decrees of our King, judge whether he has not himself stripped off the military oath of our service, made himself an exile from the heavenly mess, and rendered himself an outcast.

But you, brothers, who wish to follow in this Lenten fast the pattern of the Lord’s fast, prove yourselves—as we said earlier—destined to triumph over the troops of vices, the battle lines of crimes, the shapeless forms of desires, and all the aerial, dispersed, and innumerable legions of demons,

[Note: [Col. 0227C] Jerome, vol. VI, on Ephesians VI, p. 432: “This is the opinion of all teachers: that the air, which divides heaven and earth in the middle and is called the void, is full of opposing powers, that is, demons.” Gregory, *Moralia*, book XIII, chapter 17, and Bernard, vol. II, Sermon 63, *On the State of Purgatory*, article 1, chapter 3, aptly address the matter. I do not know, nor would I dare affirm or deny, whether Chrysologus followed the opinion of those who believed that demons were created from an aerial and subtler material, not subject to death. Augustine seems not far removed from this view in book III of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 10, vol. III, p. 113, column E, Antwerp edition, 1700: “And if demons are aerial animals, since they thrive by the nature of aerial bodies and therefore are not dissolved by death, because the element that is more suited to acting than to suffering prevails in them.” Nevertheless, in his letter to Paulinus, Letter 95, he argues about the matter in a somewhat similar way, but finally asks him to inform him if he has thought of or received from others anything further. Tatian the Assyrian, *Oration to the Greeks*, p. 154: “All demons consist not of flesh but of a spiritual compound, such as fire and air.”]

through the temptations that follow the Lord’s fast.

For when the Lord undertook the fast of Lent as an unwearied demonstration of his virtue, the devil immediately confronted him, ready to fight by deceit, because he was unable to resist the one who fasted by force.

For however much he dominates those devoted to gluttony and the drunken, he fears those who pray; he flees those who fast just as much.

[Note: [Col. 0227D] See Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, book II, chapter 1, and *Paedagogue*, book II, chapter 1, p. 148, column D, where he says that a demon presides over drunkards and gluttons, whom he does not hesitate to call *κοιλιοδαίμων*, “belly-demon,” the most wicked and destructive of all demons.]

The Lord says: “This kind is expelled only by fasting and prayer” (Matthew XVII).

But let us hear by what deception the devil dared to tempt him:

“If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves.”

You have heard what he himself thinks and judges concerning fasts—and the enemy himself is the judge.

“If you are the Son of God.” You see that he now believes in not merely a man but the Son of God,

[Note: [Col. 0227D] Certainly the devil had recognized Christ as the Son of God not only from the prophets and from what had happened at Christ’s birth, and from John’s testimony, but also from Christ’s blameless life. He did, however, suspect that he might be an adopted son. See Augustine, vol. VII, book IX, p. 179, *City of God*, chapter 21, and all commentators on James II, 19: “The demons believe and tremble.”]

whom he had seen freed from the service of the belly. The devil perceived—indeed, he perceived—that fasting is placed before all virtues.

He had seen John exchange the delights of the cities for the habitation of a barren wilderness,

[Note: [Col. 0228B] Virgil, *Georgics* I: “The fields bristle, their farmers having been taken away.”]

trample the softness of the flesh beneath the harshness of clothing, restrain all the world’s luxury with rustic food, and—something that belongs solely to the distinction of divinity—release sins to human beings.

[Note: [Col. 0228B] Because he gave the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins—not because John’s baptism itself granted remission of sins, but because it aroused people to obtain it through repentance. See Sermon 137 below. MITA.—The following material is from Latinius: He asserts the contrary below in Sermon 50. The passage should be noted, but the opinion seems wholly to be rejected. For the power to forgive sins belongs to God alone, and we never read that Christ granted his apostles the power to forgive sins before the Resurrection. Then, when grace was granted to the sacraments of the new law and the power to remit sins was bestowed upon the apostles through the Holy Spirit breathed into them, that power was given. John himself openly confessed this and, pointing out Jesus as the true Lamb of God, confirmed that remission of sins was to be given to the world by him. Basil likewise asserts this in Sermon 2, *On Baptism*. This is Latinius’s view. Nevertheless, some of the Fathers held that sins were remitted through John’s baptism, though only dispositionally, by preparing people for repentance through which we obtain grace. Hence Justin Martyr called John’s baptism the “prelude” (*προοίμιον*) of evangelical grace. Basil himself, whom Latinius cites, vol. II, book I, *On Baptism*, chapter 2, p. 632, although he everywhere proclaims that evangelical baptism is superior to John’s baptism, says: “As soon as someone approached the grace of God and of his Christ, whatever sins and however many he had confessed, and was baptized in the river Jordan, he immediately obtained the grace of sins.”]

And yet the devil did not say to him, “If you are the Son of God.” But when he saw the Lord continually fasting, he cried out, “If you are the Son of God” (Matthew III).

The devil is mistaken when he hurls against the Lord the wicked devices and arguments of his cunning.

“If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves.” Why, when Christ was fasting, did he seek all the signs of divinity solely in the promise of bread? Why does he, who perceives from the continual sign of fasting that Jesus is the Son of God, desire to prove that he is the Son of God by providing bread and caring for his belly?

“If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves.” Why did he not say, “If you are the Son of God, command that human beings, or angels, or something else come into being”? Why did he say, “Command that these stones become loaves”?

He asks for the sign of bread because he fears the sign of fasting. He asks for the sign of bread so that he may escape the sign of fasting, which is dreadful to him.

The evil counselor offers bread in order to change virtue and violate the fasting person’s resolve.

[Note: [Col. 0228D] From the Vatican manuscript. Other editions read, not incorrectly, “the consoler.” Below, however, the phrase “let him change virtue” means “let him remove or overturn it”; the verb is often used in this sense by Plautus.]

But let us see what the Bread who descended from heaven answered concerning bread:

“Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.”

How truly he lives in the word of God—the Word of God. How truly bread has no need of bread. How divinely he turns stones into human beings, who raises up the children of Abraham from stones as a sign of his majesty.

[Note: [Col. 0229B] Augustine, vol. III, on Psalm XLVI: “Who were the stones, if not the nations that worshiped stones?” Chrysologus therefore understands God to have raised up from stones—that is, from Gentiles—children of Abraham, that is, believers. Ignatius says the same in his Letter to the Magnesians, p. 59, and Clement of Alexandria in the *Protrepticus to the Greeks*, p. 3. [Col. 0229C] Chrysostom draws out another allusion in Homily 11 on Matthew, vol. II, p. 961, as though it could not seem incredible for God to make children for Abraham from stones, since Isaac himself was born from Abraham when Abraham’s body was already exhausted. Abraham’s exhausted body is compared with a stone in Isaiah LII. Theophylact defends this view in his commentary on Matthew III, p. 19. Photius, Letter 77, pp. 25, 126, after recounting these interpretations, commends the view of those who refer the passage to the conversion of the Jews, who, when they saw rocks split at the time of the Lord’s Passion, embraced Christ in true faith. Our author introduces the passage very aptly, since he was speaking at Ravenna, where many Gentiles had gathered from Rome in order to be present in large numbers at Caesar’s court.]

And because the shameless enemy does not know how to be defeated once and for all, to multiply the triumph of the victor he set the Lord upon the pinnacle of the Temple and said: “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down” (Matthew III, 12).

[Note: [Col. 0229C] There was formerly a question whether Christ had actually been placed bodily upon the pinnacles of the Temple. Among others, an ancient author of *On the Work* preserved by Cardinal, cited by Cyprian in *On Fasting and Temptation*, p. 425, denies it. That opinion should not be followed. For who, being lifted on high solely by a thought of the mind, could calm himself by falling headlong? Christ therefore had to be truly lifted from the earth so that there might be a place for the temptation. But what the pinnacle was on which Jesus had been placed I would investigate in vain, unless the learned Lamy should provide a torch in his work *On the Temple*, p. 798. The ambiguity in the Latin word *templi* is removed by the Greek source. It says, “the wing of the sanctuary” (*τὸ πτερύγιον τοῦ ἱεροῦ*), and the term *ἱερόν* must be distinguished from *ναός*, which properly denotes the sacred building. Thus those who thought that Jesus was brought by the devil to the summit of the sacred building have hitherto been mistaken. For the text does not read *τοῦ ναοῦ* but *τοῦ ἱεροῦ*. Grotius thinks that the term *πτερύγιον*, which occurs in Matthew and Luke, is not Greek but a Hellenism, which Greeks or Jews fashioned from the Hebrew *kānāf*, meaning “edge,” “border,” or “summit.” All the buildings surrounding the Temple courts had “wings” (*τὰ πτερύγια*), the upper edges with which the walls were crowned, both to prevent anyone from falling from them and to enable defenders more safely to repel enemies attempting to climb the walls. See Josephus, *Jewish War*, book V, chapter 9, and *Antiquities*, book XIII, chapter 9. We therefore believe that in this Gospel passage, which is under discussion, the reference is to the pinnacle of the porticoes surrounding the Court of the Gentiles. Their southern part overlooked deep valleys which, Josephus says, could not be looked down upon without dizziness, the sight failing because of their excessive depth. No place could be more suitable for a leap. The highest ridge of the sacred building, however, bristled with spikes intended to drive away birds and was not a suitable place for the devil to set Jesus.]

O what a sign! “Throw yourself down.” More appropriately he should have said, “If you are the Son of God, ascend to heaven,” since it is characteristic of a human being to fall toward the depths, while it belongs to God to ascend to the heights.

“If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down.” This is how he always counsels his own and provides for his own; he raises his followers so high that he may hurl them more forcefully into ruin.

“If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down.” The devil betrays himself by his own counsels: “Throw yourself down.”

He seeks a fall; he commands a plunge. By such counsel he makes martyrs throughout Africa, without a shout, saying: “If you wish to be a martyr, throw yourself down.”

[Note: [Col. 0230C] Maximus of Turin, Homily 1, *On Fasting*, has something very similar, almost like one egg resembles another.]

Thus he drives them from a height to death, rather than lifting them from a low place and raising them to a crown.

And just as the devil betrays himself by his counsels, so the Lord reveals himself by his answer when he says: “You shall not tempt the Lord your God” (Deuteronomy VI).

By saying this, he clearly wished himself to be understood as Lord and God—he who not only gave himself from the pinnacle of the Temple to the earth but hurled himself from the heavens all the way to the underworld, so that he might be not the pattern of those who fall but the resurrection of the dead.

Pay attention, brothers, whether the enemy, though often defeated, can yield more savagely to a human being who hears and recognizes the Lord God, yet still does not cease to tempt him.

He placed him upon a high mountain and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory, and said to him, “All these things I will give you if, falling down, you will worship me.”

[Note: [Col. 0230D] In the ancient text of Matthew, Ambrose in his sermon on the first Sunday of Lent, Chrysostom in Homily 13 on Matthew, and Maximus in Homilies 1 and 2 *On Fasting and Temptation*, together with our author, read “falling down” rather than “falling.”]

He says this not because he is able to give, but in order to deceive; not to confer what he promises, but by his promises to take away the very things that are possessed.

“All these things I will give you.” He offers God’s things to God; he promises the Creator what belongs to the Creator. He urges the one who is to be worshiped by all to worship him, and, blinded by his own audacity, confesses before the judgment how he might deceive the simple.

The Lord answers him not so much by the testimony of the Law as by the authority of his divinity: “You shall worship the Lord your God” (Deuteronomy VI)—you, O devil, shall worship that Lord God before whom all things bend the knee, not only heavenly and earthly things but also those beneath the earth (Philippians II).

You shall therefore worship in hell, hissing and wailing, the one whom you, rash deserter, now invite to worship you.

Thus, beaten by the Lord so many times and in so many ways, the devil now runs about us, his servants, with every fury. As Christ addresses and arms his soldiers, so he addresses and arms his own ministers.

The devil therefore says: “At present the time of fasting is severely defeating us through its observance. We cannot attack human beings through gluttony, excess, drunkenness, or luxury. Arm quarrels; sow discord; stir up hatred; incite anger; inspire lies; extort perjuries; suggest blasphemies; spread empty talk; pour in deceit; kindle greed; arrange disgraceful profits, so that what the belly now does not expend on luxury, the purse may at least close up and store for punishment.

“Above all, take care that mercy, almsgiving, and humaneness do not erase our past labors, remove our present gains, or take away those of the future.”

But we, brothers, recognizing the commands of our King and hearing what the devil has ordered his own, should carry out our fasts without quarrel, without clamor, without anger, without deceit, and without pretense, with complete mercy, charity, and piety.

Thus may the Lord Christ, who rejected the bloody sacrifices of animals and sought the sacrifice of a contrite and broken heart, accept with the silence of peace the offerings of our fast, appeased and propitiated.

## SERMON XIV. On the Fruits of Almsgiving, on Psalm XL
To those experienced in warfare, the military trumpet sounds the call to discipline; to the inexperienced it gives only a terrifying cry. As the teacher of battles, it gives strength to its own troops and fear to the enemy. Whoever fights without a trumpet is not a soldier: he is driven by fury, not by battle; he acts not with courage but with recklessness; he seeks to perish, not to conquer.

We have said this so that the soldier of Christ may understand why a song has been provided from heaven. Set in the field of the world, we sustain battle with the devil and with vices. Therefore, whenever the prophetic trumpet sounds for us, it makes us each time cautious in peace, strong in the line of battle, and unconquered in combat.

For today the blessed Psalmist summons us to heavenly understanding with a cry:

> Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and the poor (Ps. XL, 2).

And what is understanding, where is it, when poverty is openly professed? The power of understanding lies in searching out the inward parts, in detecting what is hidden, in uncovering what is concealed. But what is placed before the eyes, displayed in public, and thrust upon the senses does not require understanding, but merely seeing.

**[Note: [Col. 0231D]** Since David is commonly heard from the Fathers as the Psalmist, it is clear that Chrysologus considered him the author of this psalm, against those who incorrectly attributed it to Hezekiah.**]**

A person chilled by nakedness, weakened by hunger, parched by thirst, trembling from exhaustion, and pallid from deprivation—what effort is required to understand that he is needy?

**[Note: [Col. 0232D]** The editions of Castillo of Cologne, no. 1, and the manuscript of Cesena read: “who is suffering?”**]**

And if understanding requires no effort, whence comes the fruit of understanding? Let us pray, brothers, that he himself grant us understanding of what must be understood—he who so demonstrates that he is to be understood in the poor.

**[Note: [Col. 0231D]** This means “open and manifest.” Mita. “He understands”: The author says that we ought to investigate the need of others and assist hidden misery, not merely what is openly visible to everyone. On Chrysologus’ near-contemporary, Peter Damian, see *Opusc.* 9, *De eleemosyna*, chap. 3, p. 474, Lyons edition, 1623.**]**

How can it fail to be a great thing to understand that he who covers heaven is naked in the poor; that the fullness of all things hungers in the hungry; that the fountain of fountains thirsts in the thirsty? How can it fail to be blessed to understand that he possesses an abundant poverty for whom heaven is narrow; that he who enriches the world is needy in the needy; that the giver of all things seeks a piece of bread and a cup of water; that God so humbles himself for love of the poor that he is not merely present with the poor, but is himself poor?

Whoever God has enabled to see this truly sees. But let him himself now tell us how he has poured the poor man into himself, or himself into the poor man:

> I was hungry, he says, and you gave me food.

He did not say, “The poor man was hungry, and you gave him food,” but, “I was hungry, and you gave me food” (Matt. XXV, 35). He proclaims that what the poor man received was given to him; he says that he eats what the poor man has eaten, and testifies that what the poor man drinks is poured into himself.

**[Note: [Col. 0232D]** Castillo reads “he considers it given.”**]**

O what love of the poor accomplishes! God glories in heaven in what causes the poor man to blush on earth, and he counts as an honor to himself what is reckoned an insult to the poor man. It would have been enough to say, “You gave me food; you gave me drink.” But he first says, “I was hungry; I was thirsty,” because the love of the poor would have been small if he had merely received the poor man and had not also received the poor man’s sufferings. Certainly true love is proved only by sufferings.

True love consists in making the distresses of the afflicted one’s own.

**[Note: [Col. 0232D]** Elsewhere: “the distresses that cause anguish.”**]**

It is extraordinary that the food of the poor should be pleasing to God, who does not hunger for the goods of the whole creation; that he should proclaim himself fed by the poor man’s food in the kingdom of heaven, before all the angels and in the assembly of the risen.

God is silent about Abel’s suffering (Gen. IV), Noah’s preservation of the world (Gen. VI), Abraham’s acceptance of faith (Gen. XV), Moses’ reception of the law (Ex. XX), and Peter’s ascent, lying back upon the cross; but he proclaims only this: that the poor man ate.

In heaven the first matter is the hungry man’s food; the poor man’s support is the first thing considered; the poor man’s gift is entered first in the divine records.

**[Note: [Col. 0232D]** That is, the first matter examined in heaven is the food given to the poor and the support distributed to him. For this is recorded at the head of the divine books, so that it is immediately apparent to the reader. Mita.**]**

Indeed, whatever was done day by day was recorded in the *diurna*.

**[Note: [Col. 0232D]** In the *diurna*, whatever was done each day was recorded. “Daily tablets” occur in book II of the Theodosian Code, *On the Distribution of Military Rations*. In Greek, ἐφημερίς (*ephemeris*), “daily record.” See Pignorius, *De Servis*, p. 315. An old inscription cited by the same author reads:

> PROC. AB EPHEMERIDE PROC. A MANDATIS PROC. AD PRAEDIA, etc.
>
> “Procurator of the daily record; procurator of mandates; procurator of estates,” etc.

“From the *ephemeris*” and “from the daily record” mean the same thing. The *diurnarii*, whom Valentinian and Valens mention in book VIII of the Theodosian Code, *On the Imperial Guard*, do not belong here, but were of the same class as the *scribendarii*, *tabularii*, and others of that kind.**]**

Blessed is the person whose name is read before God as often as the account of the poor is recited in heaven.

But let us also hear the fruit of this blessedness:

> On the evil day the Lord will deliver him.

Whoever knows that he is passing his life amid the evils of the world should always carry with him the aid of almsgiving; he should summon companies of the poor to his protection; he should abound as a generous provider in feeding the poor; he should frequent the poor man’s gift and not tremble at distributing it. The frugal recipient to whom he extends his hand does not know how to lack; that treasury cannot be exhausted from which a single coin is sufficient:

> On the evil day the Lord will deliver him.

On the evil day God will stand beside him as deliverer—the one who delivered the poor man from evils. In his distress God will hear him crying—the one who heard the poor man when he cried. He will not see an evil day who made the poor man possess good days.

He will see an evil day who enters the day of judgment without the advocacy of poverty.

**[Note: [Col. 0233D]** In Ovid, *Fasti*, book V: “to enter their minds.”**]**

Sins accuse in vain the person whom the poor man excuses. He cannot be excused whom the hunger of the poor man has accused.

The Lord, he says, will preserve him and give him life. He did not say, “He preserves and gives life,” but, “May he preserve and give life.” He said this not so that it would be the voice of one announcing, but of one entreating.

He who heard the needy man when I prayed has now heard throughout the whole world the Church praying on his behalf:

> May the Lord preserve him and give him life.

May he preserve him, so that he may not be seized for punishment; may he give him life, so that he may rise from the dead and receive life.

And he will not hand him over to the power of his enemy.

**[Note: [Col. 0233D]** Arnobius and Cassiodorus read this way.**]**

Whose enemy? The devil, of course. He is the prince of enmities. He who has trampled underfoot the author of enmities despises enemies.

But the Lord will help him upon his bed of pain. The prophet works through all the sufferings of human frailty:

> The Lord will help him upon his bed of pain.

What is the bed of our pain except our body?

**[Note: [Col. 0233D]** Ambrose, vol. III, book V, *On Luke*, p. 463, L, Paris edition, 1551: “The bed of pain, on which our soul lay sick, afflicted by the grievous torment of conscience.”**]**

In it the soul lies; and it lies in pain; and it grieves because, desiring to return to heaven, it is weighed down by the earth of the body.

> You have transformed his entire bed in his sickness.

The Lord does not transform the bed for the just man, nor for the unjust man; rather, the Lord transforms the bed for the sick person.

**[Note: [Col. 0233D]** This passage is buried under astonishing obscurity in some editions, and even caused difficulty for Latinius.**]**

It is therefore the flesh that is transformed and that transforms. It is the flesh that is rolled about in adversity and that transforms things in prosperity. The Lord, therefore, transforms our bed when he turns adversities into prosperity.

**[Note: [Col. 0233D]** See Augustine, *Enarrationes on this psalm*.**]**

And because, on the bed of pain—that is, on the bed of the body—the sick mind was being rolled about, the one who was being rolled about cries out:

> I said, Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, because I have sinned against you.

Because through the consent of the flesh he feels that he has contracted sickness of mind, he implores healing for his soul. He asks for mercy with confidence, because he has shown mercy to the poor.

Blessed is the person who, by lending to the poor, has made the judge himself his debtor.

**[Note: [Col. 0233D]** Gregory Nazianzen, in the *Tetrastics*:

> And having made God debtor beyond all,  
> He repays him with a fragment of bread, the heavenly scepters—  
> Feeding and sheltering the poor, who are God.

**]**

## SERMON XV. On the Centurion

Today, brothers, you will hear how the centurion of a Roman cohort

**[Note: [Col. 0234C]** At that time the Jews were subject to the Romans; and the Romans maintained military garrisons not only in Judaea but also in the principal cities of other parts of their empire, in order to keep the peoples to their duty. These garrisons were smaller at Caesarea, Capernaum, and so forth, than at Jerusalem. The Syriac retains the Roman word *centurio* as though it were very familiar. See Grotius here; and, on the centurion’s office, consult Vegetius, book II, chap. 14. I add only that Roman centurions were once called *vites*, because commanders gave them a vine-rod for punishing soldiers. Sceva in Lucan, VI, 145:

> [lacuna]
> There, advanced through much bloodshed, he bears the broad vine-rod in a long rank.
