See Salmasius in his notes on Spartianus; Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, chap. 15, p. 341 of the recent edition, where Valesius disentangles the difficult passage in his notes.**]**

became commander of the Christian soldiery—and deservedly so, because he began to teach before he began to believe.

> Jesus came to Capernaum, and a centurion approached him, asking and saying: “Lord, my servant lies paralyzed in the house and is suffering terribly.” And Jesus said to him: “I will come and heal him.” The centurion replied: “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof, but only say the word, and my servant will be healed. For I too am a man placed under authority, having soldiers under me; and I say to this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it” (Matt. VIII, 5).

You see that, before undertaking the office of discipleship, the centurion had already obtained the place of a teacher. He provides a model for asking; he gives a rule for believing; he lays open the grounds of faith; he commends examples of virtue, although he has not yet entered the discipline of the Christian school.

> A centurion approached him, asking him.

This is to act wisely, not merely to ask.

**[Note: [Col. 0234D]** Latinius reads “to seize,” and perhaps more correctly. Nevertheless, I have retained the reading of the manuscripts, as it agrees better with what precedes.**]**

> My servant lies in the house.

He pleads the servant’s cause as a teacher: truly a centurion, who exchanged an earthly military stipend for the hundredfold fruit of heaven and raised the servitude of worldly soldiery to divine dignity.

> Lord, my servant lies in the house.

The person who calls him Lord faithfully acknowledges his own servitude.

**[Note: [Col. 0234D]** Similar remarks are found in Hugh, cardinal, on 1 Kings VIII: “Tribune” and “centurion” are names of dignities; they are also counted among burdens, exactions, and servitudes.**]**

And how did this centurion, who so acknowledges the Lord, dare to call him his own servant?

**[Note: [Col. 0235C]** That is, whom he professes to be his own. “Servant” signifies a slave, as appears from comparison with Luke VII, 3. The Hebrews speak in this way in 1 Kings XX, 14, and Esther II, 2, as do the gentiles. In Aristophanes, Terence, Horace, and Cicero, *puer* denotes a slave. “It was the custom of the ancients,” says Grotius, “to express harsh things gently.” See Servius on Virgil’s “Now close the channels, boys”; and Pliny in his *Letters*, from which servants are still called “members of the household” to remove the insult of servitude. Macrobius, book I, chap. 2, p. 210, Paris edition, notes this practice as ancient: “For our ancestors, removing all resentment from masters and insult from slaves, called the master the father of the household and the slaves members of the household.”**]**

Was he unaware that the slave’s property belongs to the Lord? Or does he not understand common matters who teaches such secret and profound things?

> My servant.

I call him “mine” because he lies. If he were yours, Lord, he would not lie there. The prophet proves this when he says:

> Behold now, bless the Lord, all servants of the Lord, who stand in the house of the Lord (Ps. CXXXIII, 1).

“Who stand,” he says, “not who lie.” Your servants stand; the servants of men lie.

> My servant, who lies there:

Let him rise, so that he may be yours. Mine, because he is paralyzed: let him now be healed, so that he may be yours. Mine, because he is suffering terribly: let him now no longer be in punishment, so that he may be yours.

Lord, it is not fitting for your servants to be subject to evils. The punishment of your servants is an injury to you. The power of evils ought not to possess your servants. Even if your servants suffer evils, they do not undergo them as punishment but encounter them for crowns. Adversities are not causes of necessity for them, but causes of victory.

It is the servants of men who suffer evils unwillingly, because, when their master despairs, they are unable to help them. But you, Lord, whom virtues serve, to whom healings obey, and to whom health submits—how will you count as your servant one whom you see to be the servant of so many diseases?

Your goodness toward the wicked is well known; even the impious confess your mercy; outsiders cry out for your compassion. Would I call this man yours, whom your kindness does not seek while he lies there?

> He lies in the house and is suffering terribly.

This is why the magnitude of his punishment prevents him from bringing him and presenting him to you, lest his family illness be publicly exposed and become both a source of grief and a cause of shame.

**[Note: [Col. 0236C]** That is, confined thus far within the household and not known to everyone. Or “a family illness,” that is, an illness of one member of my household. Seneca, *Letter* 47: “Our ancestors called slaves members of the household.”**]**

**[Note: [Col. 0236C]** In nearly all editions, to the great detriment of this passage, the word “exposed” is missing.**]**

The centurion moved the judge by pleading such great things, and moved him so that he brought the Lord of heaven himself to resolve to go to his servant.

> I will come, says Christ, and heal him.

Brothers, the centurion did not draw the author of compassion toward compassion; nor did he compel Christ to go for the purpose for which Christ had come. Rather, the centurion was taught to understand why Christ, as he came in the servant, had come to the servant; why God, as he came in man, had come to man.

**[Note: [Col. 0236C]** The centurion had learned through contact with the Hebrews that Christ the Redeemer had been promised to the Jews. Chrysologus’ view is shared by Lucas of Bruges. Although some of the Fathers thought that this centurion was a Jew, the more common opinion makes him a gentile. Some, like Chrysologus, hold him to have been a Roman; Eusebius agrees in his homily on the centurion’s servant, as does Theophylact on Luke VII. More recent interpreters assert that he was a Spaniard.**]**

He came, of course, to raise those who were lying down, lift up those who had been struck down, release those in chains, and himself, as the most merciful bearer of his work, carry those whom no one could any longer bring or present.

But let us now hear what the centurion replied:

> Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof.

**[Note: [Col. 0236D]** Ambrose here writes: “The Lord proceeds; the centurion excuses himself, and, laying aside military arrogance, assumes reverence.”**]**

He gave the required answer of humility and marked by extraordinary fear that he recognized him as Lord, since he feared to lead him into the house of his soul, into the secret place of his heart, under the roof of his conscience, into the inner chamber of his mind, where the disorderly and confused household of thoughts moves about. He does not allow the palace of the human breast to remain in the silence of purity without the noise of vices.

Thus he answered with the fear proper to a teacher:

> Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof.

This is why Peter, when he recognized Christ as the author of all things, cried out:

> Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man (Luke V).

Peter asks him to depart from him in the same way that the centurion begs him not to come to him.

**[Note: [Col. 0236D]** The word “for” is absent from the printed editions.**]**

Each is acting so that the unworthiness of the lodging may not remain an injury to the guest.

**[Note: [Col. 0236D]** Castillo notes that some, such as Laurentius a Ponte, vol. II, on Matthew, chap. 8, no. 23, and Sylveira, vol. III, *On the Gospel*, book V, chap. 11, question 12, no. 79, read: “may the injury remain.” But the manuscript of Cesena has *manet injuriam*, “the injury remains,” from *mano*, “to remain,” not *maneo*.**]**

> I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof.

This would have been blessed before God entered the lodging of our flesh. But now what prevents the centurion from allowing Christ to enter his roof, when he sees him already dwelling wholly within the roof of his body?

Brothers, the centurion already saw in Christ the form of his body, but he did not see in him the sufferings of his body. Christ was born in the flesh, but he was born of the Holy Spirit. He took the lodging of flesh, but in the Virgin’s palace, so that the truth of a human body might be present in him and he might possess nothing from the pollution of a human body.

**[Note: [Col. 0236D]** Not a few among the heretics impiously denied that Christ’s flesh was real and that he was truly human. Cerdo, Marcion, and Mani said that Christ had appeared as a man while possessing nothing human. Theodoret, book V, chapter on Marcion, p. 375, vol. II, Cologne edition, 1573; Epiphanius, *Heresies* 22 or 42, vol. I, part I, p. 302, Cologne edition, 1682; Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, book I, chap. 22, p. 185; Photius, final letter, p. 381. The Gnostics must also be included here. According to the same Epiphanius, *Heresy* 26, p. 91, C, they babbled that Christ was not born from Mary but was manifested through Mary. All these, and other people of the same kind, are called by Theophylact Φαντασιοδοκῆται (*Phantasiodokētai*), “those who hold that Christ’s appearance was merely imaginary.” Some asserted that Christ’s flesh was astral and airy. Tertullian calls these people Apellitians in *On the Flesh of Christ*, chap. 8, and Augustine calls them Apellites in *On Heresies addressed to Quodvultdeus*, chap. 23. Epiphanius, *Heresy* 44, p. 381, calls them Ἀπελλῖανοι (*Apelleianoi*), Apelleians. This was indeed the teaching of the impious Apelles. His followers, insulting Catholics, called them “Anthropolaters,” because they said that Christ was truly human. Gregory Nazianzen recalls this sharp insult in vol. I, Oration 11, p. 742, Paris edition, demonstrating to the Apollinarians that they deserved the name “Sarcolaters” much more: for if Christ did not possess a human soul, they must be judged to worship only flesh.**]**

The centurion therefore rightly judged his roof unworthy of Christ, because Christ dwelt beneath the singular roof of our body:

> I kept vigil, and I became like a solitary sparrow on the roof (Ps. CI, 8).

**[Note: [Col. 0237C]** Many genuinely think that this passage of the psalm applies to Christ. The interlinear gloss reads: “Christ, the solitary and unique sparrow.”**]**

But say only a word, and my servant will be healed.

This centurion, although he was without the law, did nothing without the law.

**[Note: [Col. 0237D]** The centurion represented the gentiles, who came nearer to Christ while he was absent than the Jews did while he was present. Another meaning, however, may be given to these words. Although the centurion was not versed in the books and law of the Jews, he nevertheless spoke according to what is written in the law: “He spoke, and they came to be.” Therefore he too said: “Say only a word.” It should be observed that among the holy Fathers gentiles are called ἄνομοι (*anomoi*), “without law,” because the Mosaic law had not been given to them concerning ritual matters. Theodoret, on 1 Corinthians IX, 21, calls them “without law”; Paul calls those “without law” who lived without the law; and Theophylact says that those without the law are those who did not possess the Mosaic law, namely, those from the gentiles, as Cornelius was. Hesychius seems to have had the same meaning in view when he interprets ἄνομον as “not subject to the law.”**]**

> Say only a word.

For it was said:

> He spoke, and they came to be (Ps. XLVIII, 5).

And if all things were perfected by speech, how could the illness of one person fail to be cured by speech alone?

> Say only a word.

And what is said without the word that is spoken? But this man asks for a word not in the ordinary sense of speaking, but for a word possessing the power to act—the word of which it was said:

> He sent his word and healed them (Ps. CVI, 20).

> Say only a word.

For he believed that all powers reside in the Word. Your word, Lord, is health; your word is life. Wherever your word comes, pain immediately flees and illness at once departs. It is the word by which Peter, when he let down the nets, caught a multitude of fish; without it, though he endured the night of ignorance, the watchful fisherman found no fruit.

> Lord, he says, we have labored all night and caught nothing; but at your word I will let down the nets (Luke V).

And as though it were not enough that he had spoken about the Word, he establishes and commends by an example that what he requests can be accomplished by a word:

> For I too am a man placed under authority, having soldiers under me; and I say to this one, “Go,” and he goes; and to another, “Come,” and he comes; and to my servant, “Do this,” and he does it.

> For I too am a man.

This means: “You are God.”

> Placed under authority.

This means: “You are the very power of powers.”

> Having soldiers under me.

This means: “You have the powers.”

> I say to this one, “Go,” and he goes.

This means: “Say to the illness, ‘Go,’ and it goes.”

> To another, “Come,” and he comes.

This means: “Say to health, ‘Come,’ and it comes.”

> And to my servant, “Do this,” and he does it.

That boy will be both my servant and your servant when he has recovered his health.

Let him hear—and what should he hear?

> You have been made well; now do not sin anymore (John V).

Let him practice righteousness, so that he may be freed from the paralysis of all sins and may sing with the prophet:

> Return, my soul, to your rest, because the Lord has dealt generously with you; for he has rescued my soul from death, my eyes from tears, and my feet from falling. I will please the Lord in the land of the living (Ps. CXIV, 7–9).

Brothers, let us imitate the centurion, who desires to reach the hundredfold fruit.

**[Note: [Col. 0237D]** The interest of one percent per month, also called *usura assis*, was the greatest of all lawful rates; each month it returned one denarius from one hundred. See Sidonius Apollinaris, *Letters*, book IV, letter 24, and Sirmond’s notes there, vol. I, p. 553; Chrysostom, vol. VII, homily on Matthew 56, alternatively 58, p. 573, recent edition, G. L., in the notes; and the inscription in Gruter, no. CLXXV, 4, which reads:

> DONUM DATUM  
> UT EX CENTESIMIS EJUS QUANTITATIS QUAE EFFECIT ANNOS X DE DIE VIII. KALEND. OCTOB. NATALI DIVI AUGUSTI EROGARENTUR EX ARKA, etc.
>
> “A gift given, so that distributions might be made from the treasury out of the one-percent interest on that capital, which yielded [interest] for ten years from the eighth day before the Kalends of October, the birthday of the deified Augustus,” etc.

Interest rates greater than one percent per month are condemned in the *Lex L* “On Loaned Property” and the final law “On Interest.” See Paulus, *Sentences*, II, 15, 2; Schoock, *Sacred Exercises* XIX, in support of Salmasius against Gronovius; Gronovius himself, *On Interest at One Percent*; and Chrysostom, vol. IV, preface, § 5.**]**

Therefore, so that we may not pass lightly over this centurion’s wisdom, let what has been said about him suffice for today, because it is a very great mystery in which a gentile is made into a figure.

**[Note: [Col. 0238C]** The Paris, Cologne, Mainz, Lyons, and Venetian editions, and almost all the others, read “Jew.” I have restored “gentile” from the manuscripts of Cesena and Vallicella and from Castillo’s edition.**]**

**[Note: [Col. 0238C]** Paschasius Radbertus borrowed much from this sermon; he lived approximately four hundred years after Chrysologus.**]**

## SERMON XVI. On the Two Demoniacs
Christus [Note: [Col. 0238C] Mark calls the one lake a sea, as does the Gospel. Matthew says that Jesus came into the region of the Gerasenes; Luke, of the Gadarenes. But that Gadara and Gerasa were not one and the same city—a view that had gained currency among some people in Jerome’s time—but different cities, Josephus demonstrates most clearly in *The Jewish War*, book II, chapter 19, and Jerome in *On Hebrew Place Names*. Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 66, says that Gergesa, Gadara, and Gergesa were places of three districts situated in the middle. Yet it does not seem sufficient reason for attributing to one region a miracle performed in another merely because they were neighboring territories. Therefore I think one should follow the observation of Abbé Pezron, to which Du Hamel willingly subscribes: namely, that the region of the Gerasenes was at that time subject to the Gadarenes, a city which Pompey had ordered to be restored for the benefit of his freedman Demetrius. By that name the city was known as one of the principal cities of the Decapolis. I shall add, from Josephus, *The Jewish War*, book V, chapter 3, p. 888, that Gadara may perhaps have been the metropolis of the Gergesenes. Concerning the name Gerasa, see Origen, *Commentary on John*, Huet’s edition, vol. II, p. 130.] who crosses seas, who travels through regions, is not acting from human desire but for the sake of human salvation. Christ walks, not in order to see places, but in order to find people who had perished through various misfortunes. What new thing could the one who had made the places see in them? Or what was lacking to him who was everywhere? He appeared as a human being in particular places, but as God he saw everywhere; indeed, he saw the desperate, to whom he was going to bestow divine remedies. He went to care for those whose human care had already failed, as today’s reading has demonstrated.

“When Jesus had crossed the sea and come into the region of the Gerasenes,” it says, “two men possessed by demons met him, coming out of the tombs, exceedingly fierce, so that no one could pass along that road” (Matthew 8).

[Note: [Col. 0239C] In the printed editions this passage is affected by a considerable error: *lubet* is found where *lucet* is intended.]

It is pleasant to know and to see that the Lord understood what evil and what danger existed in those places, and therefore went there so that he might assist those who were so desperate, afflicted, and miserable. Two men possessed by demons met him, coming out of the tombs.

[Note: [Col. 0239C] The Hebrews built tombs in the countryside, not in the cities, so that they would not be polluted. There is an excellent passage in Josephus concerning Herod the tetrarch as builder of Tiberias, book XVIII, chapter 3, which it will be worthwhile to consult. Since the Jews’ tombs were high and covered with vaults, resembling bedrooms, according to Menochius, or wine-cellars, according to Maldonatus, someone could easily dwell in them. See further in the learned Nicolaus, *On Tombs*.]

They had made their dwelling in the tombs,

[Note: [Col. 0239C] It is indeed reported by Clement of Alexandria in the *Protrepticus*, Lactantius, book II, chapter 11, and Theophylact in his commentary on Matthew 10, that demons haunt tombs. Theophylact thinks that the doctrine was then prevalent that the souls of the dead became demons. See Tatian the Assyrian, *Address to the Greeks*, p. 154: “Moreover, the demons who rule human beings are not human souls”; and Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, book VI, p. 311. This was the opinion of the Platonists, from which Tertullian was not far removed, as Augustine testifies in *The City of God*, book IX, chapter 11; nor was Josephus, book VII of *The Jewish War*, chapter 25, p. 981. Chrysostom, however, in vol. V, homily 36, whose title is “That the souls of those who die a violent death do not become demons,” says that the following was believed only about those who had died violently and whom they call *biothanatoi*. See Baronius, under the year of Christ 138, §45. It seems more likely to others that many, deceived by empty philosophy, then believed that the souls of the dead lingered around the tombs.]

the authors of death. Consider what savagery, what madness, what frenzy the demons display toward the human race. Although they cannot endure even a brief span of human life, it is not enough for them that human beings die: they eagerly desire to bury human beings alive. They consign themselves to tombs so that they may drag human beings back into tombs:

[Note: [Col. 0239D] I have emended the text on the basis of the Vallicellian and Vatican manuscripts. The editions read *redigant*. Maldonatus thinks that the demons did this in order to torment the possessed more severely with the foulness of the place. I could readily adopt the view of those who think that these men were not only possessed but also lycanthropic—*loups-garous* to the French, *lupi manari* to the Italians—and suffered from severe melancholy. Luke 8:27 says: “A certain man who had a demon met him, and for a long time had worn no clothing, and did not remain in a house but in the tombs.” He should be compared with the physician Paulus of Aegina, book III, chapter 16: “For by night those afflicted with lycanthropy go out imitating wolves, and until daylight they wander around the tombs of the dead.”]

they feed on corpses, are fattened on decay, delight in stench, and take their entire pleasure in human beings’ destruction. But let us understand what they contrive by their deceptions and what they plot through their evils, whose cruelty has no limit when it is openly displayed.

What do these beings do when they parade riches,

[Note: [Col. 0240C] In several printed editions *nisi* is missing. It is nevertheless found in the Cologne edition and in Castillo.]

if not to sow greed? To implant pride, they display pomp. They advertise exclusiveness, so as to exclude what belongs to the community,

[Note: [Col. 0240C] That is, what is common and ordinary to everyone.]

what is communal. To nourish anger, they disguise its causes. To violate piety, they give grievances to the passions.

[Note: [Col. 0240C] See what Augustine writes on this subject in book XIII of *On the Trinity*, chapter 19.]

They fabricate philosophy in order to make people know nothing by seeking more. They fashion many gods so that the one true God may remain unknown.

“Two men possessed by demons met him.” Why, when many demons possessed two men, does the account signify that an entire legion had gathered around one?

[Note: [Col. 0240C] In Mark: “Legion is my name, for we are many.” Lactantius says, book II, chapter 15, that demons not only confess that they are demons but also disclose their names. *Legion* comes from the Hebrew word meaning “multitude.” Hence “a legion of olives” in *Beref. Rabb.*: “It is easier to raise a legion of olives.” The number of soldiers in a Roman legion was not always the same; it was often altered. See Livy, book VIII, first decade.]

He does this in order to teach that demons should be avoided, not feared; and at the same time he shows how singular Christ’s power is, since the entire multitude of demons is driven away by Christ’s name alone.

“Two men possessed by demons met him.” They came when brought forward, not willingly; at the command of the one who ruled them, not on their own initiative. They were dragged there against their will, not running of their own accord. Finally, at Christ’s presence, the men come out of the tombs, and, in a reversal of roles,

[Note: [Col. 0240D] For the demons, compelled to come at Christ’s presence, were no more masters of themselves then than the possessed men had previously been.]

they carry away as captives those by whom they had been held captive. They stand before the punishments by which they had been tormented; they submit to the sentence of those by whom they had already been consigned to the tombs.

“Two men possessed by demons met him, exceedingly fierce, so that no one could pass along that road.” You see that the demons had barred the way for those coming to Christ and denied them passage. For this is the demons’ concern: that people should be unable to find a return to God. They cannot possess people in any other way than by withdrawing them from the fellowship of their creator.

“So that no one could pass along that road.” This is why

[Note: [Col. 0240D] On why Christ is called “the way,” and in what sense he is so called, see Hammonius in the *Catena* on John 14:6; Clement of Alexandria, *Protrepticus*, p. 63; Gregory of Nyssa, *Oration 10 against Eunomius*; Chrysostom, vol. V, homilies 193 and 18 of the Paris edition; Gregory of Nazianzus, oration 36; Epiphanius, heresy 69, more fully in the *Ancoratus*; Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechetical Lecture* 10; Cyril of Alexandria, book IX on John 14:4; Theodoret on this passage, and there Theophylact.]

Christ became the way. “So that no one could pass along that road.” That road, not this one. “I am the way,” he says (John 14). So that the power of the demons might not obstruct those coming to the way by way of the way, and to God by way of God: one cannot reach God except through God.

But now let us hear what the demons cried out.

“What have we to do with you, Son of God?” This means: Author of life, what have you to do with the dead? Dweller in heaven, what have you to do with tombs? Fragrance of paradise, what have you to do with stench? You who cast us down from heaven, who expelled us from paradise, who now take away our cities and deny us habitable regions, allow us at least to inhabit the tombs. And if we are worthy of so great a persecution, you are not worthy of so great an injury.

[Note: [Col. 0241C] Because you mingle with stench and tombs. *Mita*.]

“What have we to do with you?” What? The relation of judge to defendant, avenger to one condemned, king to deserter.

“What have we to do with you, Son of God?”

[Note: [Col. 0241C] But how can someone continue to possess a thing that has been stolen from him? Because thieves do not remove the owner’s possession of the stolen thing, when possession itself is retained solely in intention; see Digest 41.2.3, § “In Admittenda,” and Digest 41.2.5, § final; and Code 7.32, “Licet,” on acquiring and retaining possession. When demons possess a human being, they are not owners but detainers and occupiers of what belongs to another; therefore they are rightly and deservedly called thieves. A human being is God’s creation and was made in his image; therefore, as thieves, they are kept from possessing the thing stolen, according to Code 6.2 and 6.6, on theft. *Mita*.]

This is what thieves say to the possessor, what plunderers say to the owner: they hold the spoils, carry away the booty, and ask what they have to do with the one who demands the return of his own.

“What have we to do with you, Son of God?” What? So that you may return human beings and restore the world to its creator; and when the Creator comes, you may know that you have no further authority over creatures.

“What have we to do with you, Son of God? Have you come before the appointed time to torment us?”

“What have we to do with you? And what have you to do with human beings?”

“What have we to do with you, Son of God?” They acknowledge him,

[Note: [Col. 0241C] Whether the demons truly recognized God, see Maldonatus on this chapter of Matthew 8:29. That they recognized him is clear from Luke 4:41. Yet this confession was not voluntary but extorted by necessity, as Lucas Brugensis explains from Jerome.]

they acknowledge God, confess him as judge, cry out that they are liable to judgment, and plead the limitation of time.

“What have we to do with you, Son of God? Have you come before the appointed time to torment us?” They set time against the author of time. “Have you come before the appointed time to torment us?” They complain about time as though they themselves had made time itself, in order to bury the living in tombs.

“Have you come before the appointed time to torment us?” Cruelty cuts short time, anticipates death, and through premature savagery buries the living; yet it complains about time,

[Note: [Col. 0241D] How corrupt and depraved this passage lies in the editions, and the manuscripts do not make it clearer. The Vatican manuscript reads: “And it complains about time, as though it ought to have time, so that when death had arisen it might be punished; it assigns punishment to time.” We have restored the text from the old Bolognese manuscript, Castillo, and Mita. The sense is still obscure. Perhaps Chrysologus is saying that the demons desired to harm human beings—something they unjustly desired before the appointed time, that is, before the human beings’ death—or because they did not think Christ would come so soon, and not that they wished to be punished immediately once their wickedness had been recognized.]

as though it ought unjustly to have what it desires before the appointed time, and not to be punished as soon as its wickedness had arisen.

[Note: [Col. 0241D] That is, he introduces time as a defense of his case. *Mita*.]

The hardened wickedness of the age pleads time as its excuse. Patience is brief toward the wicked, punishment is slow for the good; what is long for those who have been injured is narrow for those who inflict injury.

“There was, it says, not far from them a large herd of pigs feeding. The demons begged him, saying: If you cast us out, send us into the herd of pigs.” An unworthy servitude makes a worthy request. “Send us into the herd of pigs.” Wickedness begs to be sent from tombs into pigs, because it does not know how to abandon stench, only how to change it. “Send us into the herd of pigs.” They ask for mud as they fall from heaven; after heavenly dwellings they seek the wallows of pigs.

“Send us into the herd of pigs.”

[Note: [Col. 0241D] Where among the Jews was there such a large number of pigs, when the prodigal son had gone away into a distant country to feed them? Either because Jews were forbidden to eat pigs, not to raise them—and at that time they could have been raised by Jews to supply provisions to Roman soldiers, on which account many privileges granted to swineherds are recorded—or because many Jews living among Gentiles did not allow themselves to be bound by their own laws but subordinated them to their profit. For pork was highly valued by the Romans. Or finally, those animals did not belong to Jews but to Gentiles, who formerly inhabited the regions beyond the Jordan, including Gadara or Gerasa. Yet how Baronius confirms that the Gadarenes were Jews, under the year 31, §69, is still not clear. There were two Gadarae, and both were of Greek foundation. One was on the shore of the Mediterranean Sea, about which Strabo speaks in book XVI. The other was a city of Peraea, which Josephus, *The Jewish War*, book I, chapter 5, attributes to Greek inhabitants.]

The herd is sent into a herd so that the multitude of demons may be exposed,

[Note: [Col. 0242C] Jerome, *Life of Hilarion*, p. 95: “Those who saw it could not otherwise have believed that such a great multitude of demons had gone out from a man, unless a large number of pigs had also been present and, as though driven by many, had fallen together.” Thus the impiety of the Sadducees, who denied angels, was shaken.]

so that it may become evident that two men had borne what the multitude of pigs could not endure.

He said to them, “Go.” And they went out and entered the pigs; and behold, the entire herd rushed headlong

[Note: [Col. 0242C] This is what the possessed commonly do. Perhaps this sheds light on Hesychius: *edaimonizeto*, “to wander through trackless places.” Baronius thinks that this sea was the hot springs of Gadara, about which Epiphanius speaks, heresy 30, no. 7; but Jerome’s *On Hebrew Place Names* seems to show that they were submerged in Lake Tiberias.]

into the sea, and died in the waters. The worthless animals are said to have been handed over, not according to the demons’ will, but so that by this deed it might become known how

[Note: [Col. 0242D] Among the many reasons why Christ permitted this, Chrysostom and other commentators also mention the following. Certainly these demons would have preferred to enter another dwelling-place of the human body; but when they foresaw that they would never obtain this from Christ, they requested at least power over animals, either so that they might in some way harm human beings, or so that the owners, angered by the loss of their herd, would not receive Christ. Euthymius agrees with Jerome’s *Life of Hilarion*: “They seek to kill the pigs so that the owners, saddened by the loss, would not receive Jesus.”]

they rage against human beings, how they seek human deaths—those who sought to destroy pigs in this way. The demons burn to destroy everything that exists, moves, or lives; they do not desire to possess it. Therefore, let no human being presume to become like this: their ancient hostility toward the human race, fixed anger, and determined malice remain.

[Note: [Col. 0242D] The devil became the enemy of humanity so that human beings would not dare to become like him, but rather would shun his ways and suggestions as those of an enemy. *Mita*.]

Demons yield only when bound; they cannot injure unless commanded. The worthless animals are therefore handed over so that it may be clear that demons have no authority over human beings, since they were commanded to exercise it over pigs.

[Note: [Col. 0243C] For in this matter Christ did not exercise what they like to call an active force, but endured a force that wished to act. He wished the demons to be permitted to do what they otherwise could have accomplished, had they not been restrained by a greater power.]

Therefore, either through our vices we enable them to receive the power to do harm, or through our virtues, while Christ triumphs, we trample beneath us the necks of demons subjected to us.

## SERMON XVII. On the Demoniac

We have learned from today’s Gospel reading that the Lord crossed the sea into the region of the Gerasenes and, as soon as he came out of the boat, a man met him, emerging from the tombs, who had an unclean spirit and was bound with chains and fetters (Mark 5:3). He lived in the tombs: an author of death, he occupies death’s dwellings; greedy for human destruction, those whom he cannot kill by his cruelty he eagerly seeks to bury alive in a deathly manner.

The exacting collector of our destruction rages and storms, greedy for our ruin; it is punishment to him that a human being is born, and he is tormented that a human being dies only later. He strives to cast this very brief human life into dreadful tombs. The bewildered enemy, perverse in both directions, thrusts the living into tombs and places food before the dead,

[Note: [Col. 0243C] He condemns the practice of placing food on the tombs of the dead. Guilielmus Stuckius, drawing on Augustine and Cyprian, teaches in *Ancient Banquets*, book I, chapter 26, that the custom of funerary meals passed from the pagans—concerning whom see Kirchmann, *On Roman Funerals*—also into the Christian Church in its earliest period, and that over the passing years it was polluted by many abuses. Ambrose abundantly shows that this was also customary in Chrysologus’ time above the tombs of martyrs. Paulinus of Nola, poem XXVI, *Natalia*, 9, p. 642, verse 562:

> Yet I think such pleasures pardonable in the simple,  
> > pleasures they pursue with banquets; for error  
> > has crept into unlearned minds, and innocence,  
> > unaware of so great a fault, falls through piety,  
> > foolishly believing that the holy dead rejoice  
> > in tombs drenched with wine’s breathing flood.

Chrysologus condemns the pouring of unmixed wine as an invention of the devil; Paulinus excuses it as a lapse of simplicity. See Augustine, vol. X, sermon “On the Chair of Saint Peter,” which agrees with Chrysologus, and Tertullian, *On the Resurrection*, chapter 1, at the beginning.]

so that he may kill the living and disturb the dead. The man was being held bound with chains and fetters.

[Note: [Col. 0244C] Mita admits that this should be understood of the devil’s crime, by which he ruined the human race in Eve’s temptation; in comparison with it, the human being is innocent. Nevertheless, he interprets it mystically as referring to Eve’s crime and original sin. Thus this demoniac was innocent with respect to his own guilt, but liable with respect to the guilt of his parents.]

Bound by another’s crime and by the wickedness of his inhabitant, the innocent dwelling-place was being tortured. The devil’s guilt overflowed into the human being’s punishment, and the predator, enclosed within his prey, was fattened on the sufferings of the wretched man. Yet hateful envy exposes not the one who acts but the one who suffers,

[Note: [Col. 0244C] That is, the devil’s accursed envy does not allow him to appear as the torturer in this deed; it permits only the human being to be seen suffering such things, so that the human sin on account of which he suffers may appear, while the devil’s guilt remains unseen. *Mita*.—Many editions and the Vallicellian manuscript read *miserabilis invidia*, “miserable envy.”]

as though he were the perpetrator.

Wishing to help this sickness, the Lord crosses the sea. That is,

[Note: [Col. 0244C] That is, human sinners, according to Job 37:3: “His light is upon the ends of the earth.” Or rather, he crosses over to everything enclosed within his dominion: “I will give you the nations and the ends of the earth as your possession.”]

he crosses by the voyage of his body to the shores of the fluctuating world, reaches the shores of our salvation, filled with shipwrecks, and floods with the splendor of his light a region steeped in the blind darkness of ignorance. He is about to expose the snares of the crafty enemy and, by royal power, drive away the very prince of spiritual wickedness together with his legions, so that at last he may set free those whom hostile power had long held captive.

“Seeing Jesus from afar,” it says, “he ran and worshiped him, and crying out with a loud voice, said: What have I to do with you, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I adjure you by God, do not torment me.”

At Christ’s command the order of punishments is reversed. Formerly, while the devil was plundering, an innocent man was being tormented; now the man runs, but the devil rushes into danger. The flesh is bent down, but the unclean spirit lies prostrate and is thrown down.

“He ran and worshiped” (Matthew 4). What is this, devil? You challenged him three times to fall; by promising him a kingdom, you craftily sought to make him worship you. Now, trembling and pitiable, you fall down and worship. Behold: the one who promised all the honors and glory of the kingdom is found dwelling in tombs amid fetid corruption and corpses.

This is how, yes, this is how he deceives when he makes promises: he promises in order to drag his victims with him to the underworld, while the false promiser mocks those who consult him about heavenly things,

[Note: [Col. 0244D] From the Vallicellian and Vatican manuscripts. Some editions read *consolantes*, “those who console.”]

those who consult him about things above.

[Note: [Col. 0244D] Elsewhere, “false.” Those who consult heavenly matters, desiring to learn from a demon what is known only to God concerning the future, are deceived by a false promiser. It is well known that the ancient nations did this when they consulted idols about future events. *Mita*.—“What wonder is it,” says Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechetical Lecture*, p. 124, “if the father of lies observes the works of lying?”]

“What have I to do with you, Son of the Most High God?” For even now he worships as a flatterer, not as a devoted and obedient servant: he wants to escape punishment and fears losing his prey. The wretch believes that he can assault by flattery the one whom he could not conquer by temptation or bend with gifts. But that one is accustomed to release the bound, call back the captives, and restore to himself the boundaries not acquired but established by himself.

[Note: [Col. 0244D] See the preceding note 5. For the ancients distinguished one boundary from another and one limit from another; on this subject consult Hofmann, *Continuation of the Lexicon*, vol. III, p. 34, and Salmasius on Solinus, p. 680. I add that the Romans sometimes called the boundaries and limits of fields *arcae finales*, which served not only to delimit fields but also to bury corpses. You will find their shape represented from Hyginus in the Salmasius just mentioned.]

He strikes the enemy with unconquered virtue, and does not seek the possessor of his own people’s enemy by deceitful conspiracy.

[Note: [Col. 0245C] For Christ overthrew the devil by his own power, not by the deceitful art with which the devil himself had overcome Eve.]

“And crying out with a loud voice, he said: What have I to do with you, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I adjure you by God, do not torment me.”

What is happening? What is human frailty, subjected to such and so many miseries, suffering? Behold, the devil uses a human voice as his advocate and cries out to the Lord, seeking the human being; and all the human being’s limbs serve their enemy in his ruin.

[Note: [Col. 0245C] That is, the devil uses a human voice in order to cry out to the Lord.]

“What have I to do with you, Jesus, Son of the Most High God?” What have I to do with you? The relation of one to be punished to a judge, of a king to a deserter, of an invader to an owner.

“What have I to do with you, Jesus, Son of the Most High God?” If you acknowledge the Son, surely you do not fail to recognize the heir. If you know the heir, why do you presume to seize his inheritance?

[Note: [Col. 0245C] The human race is the inheritance of Christ the Lord. Psalm 2: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance,” where Augustine says: “The nations are your inheritance, which you possess for their salvation.” *Mita*.]

“I adjure you by God, do not torment me.” The evasive one is afraid and pretends. He confesses the Son, but by his customary art strives to prevent him from being understood as God. He adjures God by God,

[Note: [Col. 0245D] Vatablus reads the Gospel passage: “I ask you to swear to me by God,” as though Christ, according to Chrysologus here, were someone other than God.]

so that he may make him appear to be another, and deceive and mislead the ears of those standing nearby.

Jesus asked him, “What is your name?” He asks, not because he is ignorant, but to fulfill the role of judge and preserve the order of an examiner. He asks the name in order to investigate his condition, judge his guilt, condemn him for his crime, and demonstrate by the sentence pronounced that he is God.

[Note: [Col. 0245D] It is the judge’s duty first to interrogate the defendant; see the text in *Digest* 2.8.7, “Praescripta,” and Code 6.4, “Forus,” on the meaning of words.]

He answered, “Legion,” because we are many. Christ’s question dispels our ignorance in this way: it reveals to us what was hidden—the legion in the one.

It is clear cowardice in a soldier if he abandons the battle line, retreats, or fears to engage. Here he foresees that one captive is stronger than a numerous enemy.

[Note: [Col. 0245D] Either he says that one human being possessed by the devil is stronger than a legion of demons, or that a legion of demons was required to guard him. Basil seems to reveal Chrysologus’ meaning sufficiently in oration 23: “For he taught us that although the human race had been handed over to many demonic executioners, it did not perish, since a multitude of demons armed against one person was unable to destroy him.”]

What are these beings in the presence of the king, who gathered with the entire array of their cohort in order to seize one man, and not even a recruit?

[Note: [Col. 0245D] Some commentators think that one of the two demoniacs was a Gentile. Chrysologus seems to have followed this opinion when he writes that this man was not merely a recruit in Christ’s army.]

Where would they be if they had already seen the banner of the cross there, if they had seen Christ’s standards? Come, Christian, proceed confidently. That hand, so great and so numerous, which fears an unarmed man in this way, will flee far away if it sees, feels, and recognizes you as armed.

The spirits begged him, saying, “Send us into the pigs.” See where Satan desires to establish his dwelling: from tombs into pigs. Once infected with decay, he seeks foul and unclean dwellings. He delights in filth and mud, for he is always nourished by the stench of crimes and the squalor of vices.

But his Tartarean and cruel odor is so great that even the nature of pigs was unable to endure it. Finally, the pigs preferred to plunge into the sea and perish in the waves

[Note: [Col. 0246C] What if *maluere* should be read? The pigs preferred to drown rather than endure the Tartarean odor of the demons. Or he joined the verb *maluit* to *naturae*, taking it to mean “according to disposition, inclination, or some natural instinct.”]

rather than suffer his uncleanness and tolerate his decay.

[Note: [Col. 0246D] The Vatican manuscript reads this way. The printed editions have *aut quid*, “or something.”]

But what can demons presume, when they cannot even touch pigs unless divine power permits them? Miserable is the person who, having abandoned the judge, vainly seeks the favor of the executioner,

[Note: [Col. 0246D] Against those who, having truly abandoned God, are not ashamed to implore the demon’s help, as the ancient nations did.]

who can neither inflict nor spare, neither lessen nor increase punishments, but does everything while himself, the scourged one, is subject to the judgment and authority of the judge.

## SERMON XVIII. On Peter’s Mother-in-Law, Who Was Ill and Was Healed

In today’s reading the attentive hearer learned why the Lord of heaven, the restorer of all things, entered earthly and servile dwellings. Yet it is no wonder that he approached everything graciously, since he had come mercifully to help everyone.

“When Jesus had come into Peter’s house,” it says, “he saw his mother-in-law lying sick with a fever” (Matthew 8:14).

You see what had invited Christ to Peter’s house:

[Note: [Col. 0246D] This house seems to have been in Bethsaida, whose citizen Peter was (John 1:44). Since that city was only about an hour and a half from Capernaum, Jesus could have gone there after leaving the synagogue in Capernaum, either for lunch or for dinner. This is Chrysologus’ meaning, as will become clear below. Or this may have been the house of Peter’s father-in-law, called Peter’s because Peter was staying there. This is also the opinion of Brugensis and Maldonatus.]

surely not the pleasure of reclining at table, but the illness of the woman lying there; not the need for a meal, but an occasion for salvation; the work of divine power, not the display of a human banquet. In Peter’s house wine was not being poured, but tears; the household was disturbed not by concern for a feast but by concern for the sick woman; fever, not gluttony, was burning there. Therefore Christ entered it not to receive a meal but to restore life.

God seeks human beings, not human things; he desires to give heavenly things, not to find earthly things. Christ therefore comes to receive us, not to seek what belongs to us.

“When he had come,” it says, “into Peter’s house, he saw his mother-in-law lying sick with a fever.” Having entered Peter’s house, Christ saw what he had come to see. He did not look at the quality of the house, the crowds of those meeting him, the pomp of those greeting him, or the gathering of the household; certainly he did not inspect the adornment of the preparations, but he attended to the groaning of the sick woman and observed the burning fever.

[Note: [Col. 0246D] Chrysologus seems to have devised this from Galen’s *On the Differences of Fevers*, book II, since he repeatedly observes, with reference to Hippocrates, that a violent fever is called *pyr*, “fire.” Sedulius calls this fever the heat of a lamp, book III, p. 165.]

He saw the danger of one who seemed beyond hope and immediately extended his hand to the work of his divinity. Christ did not recline at a human table before the woman who was lying down had risen for divine service.

“He took her by the hand, and the fever left her.” You see how the fever leaves the one whom Christ has taken hold of: illness does not remain where the author of salvation is present; death has no access where the giver of life has entered.

“He took her by the hand.” What necessity was there for touching her, when the authority to command was present? Yet Christ took the woman’s hand for life, because Adam had received death from the hand of a woman.

“He took her by the hand,” so that what by the hand

[Note: [Col. 0247C] Adam is called “the presumptuous one” both here by Chrysologus and by Sedulius, book II, verse 4.

> Nor alone had the presumptuous one felt the deserved anger,

This is an expression scarcely Latin, with hardly a trace of it except in Sidonius. He is called “presumptuous” for no other reason than that a vain ambition to attain divinity had touched him. Alcimus Avitus, *Poem*, book II:

> He longs to be like the gods, and the poison creeps onward...

“Doing harm through ambition.”]—that the Creator’s hand might restore what the presumptuous person’s hand had lost. “He took her by the hand.” So that the hand which had snatched the sentence of death might receive pardon. “And she arose,” he says, and [Note: He follows the Greek reading, not that of Mark and Luke, which has *them*.] ministered to him. And did Christ need the service of a woman, and of a woman advanced in age, at the extreme of old age, weighed down by children? Was there then in Peter’s house no maidservant, no attendant, no member of the household, no relative, [Col. 0247B] certainly [Note: Peter alone among the apostles is recorded as having been married. This is also the opinion of many ancient Fathers. See Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* III, p. 448; Blessed Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 51, *Alogi*, p. 437 §22, and heresy 30, *Ebionites*, p. 147 §22; Jerome, book I *Against Jovinian*, p. 27, and in *Letter to Julian* 34; the author of the *Questions on the Old and New Testaments* preserved in Augustine, vol. III of the recent edition, question 127, p. 124E. Accordingly, in Ignatius’s *Letter to the Philadelphians*, which critics of more exacting judgment declare genuine, the words “and the names of the other apostles who devoted themselves to marriage” are judged to have been stitched in by some Greek interpolator. Nor does Chrysologus here deny that Peter had a wife; he merely asserts that she was not at home, since otherwise it would have been above all her duty to relieve the mother from the ordinary management of the household. Or because it is the common teaching of the Fathers that Peter and the others, if any of them had wives, had left them before the apostleship.] no wife who might anticipate the mother’s service? And, to sum up, did Peter himself not see the causes for his embarrassment—that this old woman, this mother-in-law, should do for the teacher what the disciple ought to have done?

Brothers, Christ did not demand human service from the woman to whom he had furnished the ministry of divinity; rather, he permitted her to minister as evidence that health had been restored. Christ drives away diseases in such a way that he immediately restores former strength: where medicine cures, the weariness of illness remains; where power heals, no trace of weakness remains. [Note: Since the Gospel says that she was immediately released from the fever, it implies that she was restored to health at once, without needing time to recover strength and vigor. “The health bestowed by God,” says Jerome in the passage on Matthew cited by Mita, “returns all at once.”]

But if we wish to know what spiritual understanding lies hidden in this passage, let us not seek little flowers of words: [Note: The printed editions read *maturitatis* (“maturity”); Meursius emended it.] whoever seeks the fruit of nourishment despises the pleasant fields. Violets, roses, lilies, narcissus—lovely flowers, but bread is lovelier. What fragrance is to the nostrils, ornamented speech is to the ears; what the bread of life gives, knowledge gives to salvation. The pleasure of eloquence must therefore be set aside when the strength of knowledge is demanded.

“When Jesus had come into Peter’s house.” Christ came to Peter’s house so that Peter’s house might come to Christ. Christ came to Peter’s house when he entered the dwelling places of our flesh. “When Jesus had come into Peter’s house” (Matthew 8). What is Peter’s house? That of which the Lord says: “And you, Bethlehem, house of Judah, are not the least among the rulers of Judah; for from you shall go forth a leader who will rule my people Israel” (Micah 5). Hence also the Apostle says: “From them is Christ according to the flesh, who is God, blessed for ever” (Romans 9).

“When he had come into Peter’s house, he saw his mother-in-law lying there and feverish.” [Note: Theophilus of Antioch, book III of the *Allegorical Interpretation*; Bonaventure on chapter 4 of Luke; Bede, vol. V, on chapter 8 of Matthew; and others likewise report that the feverish woman was a type of the Synagogue.] He saw the Synagogue lying in the darkness of its faithlessness, reclining beneath the burden of its sins, feverish with vices even to madness. And therefore he took her by the hand, because he works salvation for the Jewish people not only by word but also by his hands. Hear the prophet: “But God our King before the ages has worked salvation in the midst of the earth.”

“He took her by the hand.” So that her hand might first be cleansed by the blood of the prophets before it assumed the sacrament of ecclesiastical ministry. [Col. 0248B] “And she arose and ministered.” Hence it is that she who was lying down was raised and ministers to Christ, while now sanctifying her hands in good works—hands that she had previously polluted with evil works. [Note: She ministers to Christ and his disciples who had accompanied him.]

“When evening came,” he says, “they brought him many who had demons, and he cast out the spirits by a word.” How can this be understood in human terms? Why, disregarding the day, would those eager for salvation carry many, and those grievously wounded, to the remedies of salvation in the evening? But it is evening when the day of the world comes to an end, when the world declines from the light of the ages. The giver-back of light comes late, to restore everlasting day to us Gentiles who came in the night of the ages.

“When evening had come, they brought him many who had demons.” [Note: When Christ had come, many were tormented by demons, Satan raging more violently because he had foreseen that Christ would reign only briefly and that the worship of idols and the power of darkness would be utterly overthrown.] In the evening—that is, in the final age—the devout and solemn devotion of the apostles offers us Gentiles to God; and the demons who commanded us to worship idols are driven out from us. Hear the prophet: “All the gods of the nations are demons” (Psalm 95:5). For, ignorant of the one God, we served innumerable gods in sacrilegious and most filthy slavery.

“And he cast out the spirits by a word” (Romans 10:17). Because Christ did not come to us in the flesh, he came in the word. When, therefore, faith came from hearing, and hearing through the word, he made us free from demonic slavery and made the demons captives, removed from their impious domination.

Hence it is that demons are tortured beneath our hands, while we command them—demons that used to subject us to pieces of wood, attach us to stones, and terrify us daily through empty images with an empty fear. [Note: The particle *through*, which many editions lack, obscured the sense. The pagan belief in ghosts, apparitions, and lemures is otherwise well known. Perhaps, however, Mita’s interpretation comes closer to the author’s intention: by “empty figures” he understands statues of divinities, or idols, about which Wisdom 13:13 says, “He carefully carves through its emptiness.” Relevant to our subject is Cajetan’s reading of Psalm 95:5: “For all the gods of the peoples are emptinesses”—that is, they are like hollow vessels containing nothing within themselves.]

Now, brothers, let us take care that unbelief does not bring us back into their slavery: let us not be ensnared by auguries, let us not be deceived by divination, let us not be caught by lots, [Note: “Lots” was the term used for oracular responses, according to Valerius, book I, and Suetonius, *Tiberius* 63.] let us not be led astray by the Manes, [Note: Among the pagans, the Manes were called the souls of the dead, whom they believed sometimes moved among us.] let us not be seduced by the dead, [Note: That is, by apparitions of the dead. Castillo thinks that “the dead” refers to the deaths of pious men whom the common people readily believe to have been overtaken by sudden fate or some other misfortune as a punishment inflicted by God’s anger and as retribution for evil works.] let us not be taken captive by breathless plagues. [Note: Every pest, destruction, and calamity. Cicero, *Against Catiline*, speech 19: “That plague which you have long been plotting against us may be turned upon you.”]

Rather, let us commend ourselves and our actions to the Lord, entrust them to the Father, and believe in God; for, just as God acts in the time of human affairs, so the Father directs the actions of his children. [Note: This may perhaps mean the one who protects the goods and affairs of his children. An *actor* was one who, when a guardian was impeded, managed the affairs of minors (Digest 26.7.24 and 26.1.22 §). They were not called *actores* because they were appointed to records, as Theophilus thinks, but from *agere*, “to act”; hence in Greek they are also called πραγμάτονται, “managers of affairs.” The more immediate sense, however, is that Chrysologus understood *actus* as the actions and works of children.] And as Lord, he does not abandon care of the household.

## SERMON XIX. On the Scribe whom Christ did not permit to follow him

[Col. 0249B] Today the evangelist began in this way: “When Jesus saw,” he says, “great crowds around him, he ordered them to go across the sea” (Matthew 8:1). Whenever an unteachable crowd spreads itself around the Lord and is tossed upon the storm of conscience, it abandons calm, seeks the waves, [Note: Is this very close repetition of the word worthy of Chrysologus, whose verbal abundance was so great? What if we say that he wrote *it leaves the harbor, it enters shipwrecks*, etc., by the antithesis—a figure he greatly enjoyed?] abandons the harbor, enters shipwrecks, and, striving toward the heights, is submerged in the depths. Then Christ orders this sea, disturbed by such crowds, to be crossed.

“When Jesus saw great crowds around him, he ordered them to go across the sea.” Not because he was fleeing human beings, for he had come for the salvation of human beings, but because he grants the foolish a delay for believing and awaits the return of those who are wandering. He gives patience and pardon, for he does not wish to pronounce sentence; he bears with the obstinate, for he wishes not to destroy but to save what he made.

“When one of the scribes approached, he said to him, ‘Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go.’” [Note: The editions mislead. Corrected from the Vatican and Vallicellian manuscripts.] He departs, rather than approaches, who rashly promises to follow the Lord. But how can anyone promise that he can do everything? He should have said more cautiously, “I will follow you wherever you command”; more humanly, certainly, “Wherever you wish.”

“I will follow you wherever you go.” So speaks the man who does not understand the difference between himself and the Lord; so speaks the man who does not understand Christ as God, but as a teacher. “I will follow you wherever you go.” Peter follows across the sea, but he sinks; he follows to the Passion, but he denies him. And if Peter thus fails and gives way at the first difficulties, who is this man who promises so confidently to follow the Lord everywhere?

“I will follow you wherever you go.” This man speaks as though he could enter into conflict with Christ, [Col. 0250B] attain glory through the disgrace of the cross, enter the citadel of death, put death to death through death, and penetrate [Note: That is, among human beings. The ancients called anything suitable for receiving something else a “bosom.” Virgil: “To penetrate the Argolic bosoms.” Theophylact, on chapter 16 of Luke, p. 461: We also commonly call those places in the sea suitable for harbors and rest “bosoms.”] the unknown bosoms of Tartarus; burst the bonds of hell; bring back to their own bodies souls hardened for ages, forgetful of the light; shake the earth; split the rocks; open the tombs; lead the buried out from the underworld; and bring forth witnesses to his resurrection.

Let this man still add that he will go wherever Christ goes: let him recline upon the shoulders of angels, climb the heavens, sit beside the Father, and hold the summit of all heavenly dignities. Why does this foolish scribe, this proud servant, promise that he will follow Christ, the Lord, to such places? [Note: In sacred Scripture, scribes are the teachers of the law and wise men skilled in conducting affairs (1 Chronicles 27:32; Jeremiah 36:10, 12, 20, 26; Ecclesiastes 10:5; Ezra 7:61), as well as those who kept and reviewed the catalogue of enlisted soldiers (Judges 5:14; 2 Chronicles 26:11; Jeremiah 52:25; 1 Maccabees 5:45). But their office was honored and esteemed among the Hebrews, and would not permit them to be called fools and servants, a term Chrysologus so often uses in the sense of slaves. It is therefore easy to believe that, in the author’s understanding, this sort of scribe was a hired scribe, assigned to some private individual either as secretary or to keep accounts of receipts and expenditures. Jerome seems to agree with this, believing in the cited passage that the man was drawn to follow Christ solely by hope of profit. The name “scribe” is also used in this sense in Scripture. In 2 Samuel 7 appears David’s scribe Seraiah; in 1 Kings 4:3, Elihoreph son of Ahiah, Solomon’s; and in 2 Kings 22:8–9, Shaphan, Josiah’s. Since few among the Hebrews were skilled in writing, it could easily have happened that scribes of this kind belonged to another nation, hired by the Jews for wages and taken into service. Hilary supports this view in his commentary on Matthew, vol. I of the works, p. 702, Verona edition, teaching that the Gentiles and unbelievers are represented by the scribe.]

But he receives from Christ an answer worthy of such presumption: “Foxes have dens, and birds of the air have nests; but the Son of Man has nowhere to recline his head.”

What does this mean? [Note: Brugensis calls foxes useless and unwelcome beasts to human beings. In ecclesiastical writers, a fox signifies a deceitful person. Theophylact, on Colossians 3:9, p. 661: Scripture calls horses, dogs, and foxes those who, because of their desires and ways, have become like these animals. The same applies in Latin. Persius, *Satires* 5.115: “You keep a crafty fox beneath your reeking breast,” among whom *vulpinari* means to act deceitfully. See Augustine on Psalm 88 and Hilary’s commentary on Matthew, vol. I, p. 702.]

The fox is weak in strength but powerful in cunning, an inventor of deceit, an expert in fraud, a teacher of dissimulation, empty of simplicity, full of tricks, a predator of domestic birds, and hostile to familiar dwellings. With good reason Christ forms it as a type of Herod, the prince of the Jews, who, forgetful of his former freedom and remaining under Roman power, ruled by artifice, reigned by cunning, commanded through fraud, presided through deceit, and excelled in dissimulation. And because he could not bring back plunder from foreign nations, [Note: The Gentiles did not pay taxes; only the Jews did.] he devoured the common people, the native populations, as though they were domestic birds. [Note: Not because he was Jewish—for his father was an Ascalonite of Idumean descent—but because he ruled within the territories of the Jews and Galilee.]

Christ proves this when he sends word to Herod: “Go, [Col. 0251B] tell that fox” (Luke 13:32). [Note: Mita thinks that Chrysologus is speaking here of both Herods: the Ascalonite and his son Antipas, who was also called Herod: “Thus, because of the correspondence of name and blood, and because the principate which he attributed to one he also attributed to the other, we must believe that he understood one as well as the other—unless, as in many other passages, we are permitted here also to suspect a major corruption of the text.” But when he later adds that Herod was called a fox, the author seems to have spoken of Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great by Malthace. Antipas beheaded John the Baptist and mocked Christ; the Lord called him a fox, and Pilate sent Christ to him because he thought Christ was a Galilean and therefore subject to Antipas’s tetrarchy. After receiving the royal title from Gaius Caesar, Antipas was ensnared by Agrippa’s accusations and stripped of his royal name and dignity; he died at Vienne on the Rhône from grief of mind. Our author calls him the prince of the Jews: he was tetrarch of Galilee, who, forgetful of the Jews’ former freedom, obeyed the Romans under Roman rule and collected the taxes paid to Caesar, though by fraud and cunning, as appears from Josephus, *Antiquities* XVIII.1 and Origen on Matthew, tractate 22.]

Truly a fox, who seizes a kingdom by deceit—a kingdom he deserved neither by birth nor by his life. This Herod therefore established for himself, in the hearts of the scribes, dens of his crimes even unto the death of Christ; nor did he leave a place where Christ—whose head is God (1 Corinthians 11:3)—might recline.

“Foxes have dens and birds of the air have nests.” Here, too, he calls birds the demons flying about in the air, who likewise made nests of their wickedness in the breasts of the scribes, where they might produce all the offspring of their evil. Hence, when the devil inserted himself into Judas’s mind, he immediately conceived the fruit of deceit and brought forth the crime of the betrayer.

You see that Christ [Col. 0252A] did not reject the scribe when he wished to come, [Note: The Fathers dispute whether Christ expelled that scribe from discipleship or left him free to follow at his own discretion. Some hold the former view; others, with our author, hold the opposite. See Ambrose, book VI on Luke; Augustine, sermon 7 *On the Words of the Lord*; Gregory, homily 13 on Ezekiel; and Chrysostom, homily 28 on Matthew.] but exposed the pretender [Note: It is a common opinion among the Fathers, shared by Chrysologus, that Christ’s answer was adapted not to the sound of the scribe’s words but to their meaning, as Chrysostom says in homily 28 on Matthew. The mind of the impious and fraudulent scribe was to enter Christ’s service in order to obtain profit from it.] and recoiled from the presumptuous man. Or why would Christ—or why would the author and giver of salvation—prevent this man who wished to come, when he immediately restrained another disciple who wished to depart, so that he would not leave?

“Another disciple said, ‘Lord, permit me first to go and bury my father.’ But Jesus said to him, ‘Follow me, and let the dead bury their own dead.’” [Note: From ancient tradition he is said to have been John. But Matthew’s text does not have “a disciple,” as ours does, but “another of the disciples.” Hugh of Saint-Cher supplies “who was to become [a disciple],” since he was not yet a disciple.]

Does Christ thus deny the final service of piety? Does he forbid the last duty owed to parents? He does not deny the service of piety, but places divine service before human affections.

Listen to what the disciple said: “Permit me first to go and bury my father.” This should not have been first for him, but second; the earthly father must be placed after the heavenly Father. [Note: Ambrose, vol. II, on Psalm 1:1: “Piety toward God comes first, toward parents second.”]

“Follow me, and let the dead bury their own dead.” This means: Follow me into the disgrace of the Passion, so that with me you may reach the glory of the Resurrection.

“Let the dead bury their own dead.” Why should a child of faith return to the house of faithlessness? Why should an offspring of salvation mourn the lost among the lost? Why should the pledge of the Resurrection care for the tomb of its begetter? [Note: *Pignora* means “children”; this is a word familiar to Chrysologus. In Luke 20:36, “and they are children of God,” since they are children of the Resurrection.] [Note: The faithful of Christ is a child of the Resurrection—that is, a child of Christ himself, who said, “I am the Resurrection and the Life.” He has the right to rise to life together with Christ, his head. Other human beings, although they too will rise on the last day, cannot properly be called children of the Resurrection, since they will rise not to life but to punishment. Therefore the faithful should have no concern for the tomb of an unbelieving father, since the Resurrection will benefit not the father but the son. —Mita.]

“Follow me, and let the dead bury their own dead.” How do the dead bury their own dead? Brothers, he himself said: “I am life” (John 14:6). What the soul is to the body, Christ is to the soul; a body does not live without a soul, and a soul does not live without Christ. When the soul departs, immediately stench, corruption, decay, worms, [Col. 0253A] ash, horror, and everything hateful to behold follow in the body. When God departs, the stench of sins, the corruption of crimes, the decay of vices, the worm of conscience, the ash of vanities, and the horror of unbelief immediately enter the soul; and in the tomb of the living body there is formed a funeral for the already-buried soul. [Note: Thus the Vatican manuscript. Other editions read: “already buried.”]

The matter was further aggravated by the fact that the corpse of faithlessness [Note: Here he attacks the custom of employing songs, pipes, flutes, and musical instruments at funerals, which some believe passed from the Gentiles to the Jews. See Brugensis, Maldonatus, Tirinus, Schultetus, and especially Calvorius, *Ritual*, where he discusses funerals and funeral pipes, pp. 910 and 912. Just as Isidore notes that flute players were customary among the Greeks and Romans (*Etymologies* II.20, p. 90), so they were used among the Hebrews, as is evident from the Gospel history (Matthew 9:23). The singing of psalms and hymns while corpses are carried out is not condemned here; Chrysostom mentions it in homily 116, vol. VI, and homily 14 on 1 Timothy, p. 309; Gregory Nazianzen in his speech on his sister; Eusebius, book I, p. 121; Blessed Gregory of Nyssa, *Life of Saint Macrina*, vol. II, p. 201, concerning her funeral; and Macarius, homily 15, p. 184. Which psalms they sang may be learned from Chrysostom, homily 4 on the Epistle to the Hebrews, p. 454.] was being treated with faithless rites, and piety was being performed through the ministry of impiety.

“Jesus entered,” he says, “the house of the ruler and saw the musicians” (Matthew 9). Do those who hire foreign lamentations for mourning and music for the funerals of their own people not thus make an abomination out of piety? [Note: Ambrose, on chapter 7 of Luke, concerning the ruler’s daughter raised from the dead: “According to ancient custom, flute players were generally employed to kindle and arouse mourning.” Maldonatus explains more fully, on Matthew 9:23, that this was a Gentile custom which also passed to the Jews. Mita. —The author calls them “extraneous lamentations,” meaning a hired song performed inwardly by men or women employed for pay, so that, purchased with money, they would mourn the corpse being carried out. This is perhaps what is meant in Wisdom 19:13 by “mourning at the tombs of the dead.”]

Where there is no genuine lament, there is purchased and mercenary song. It is not the craftsman’s flute but simple affection that mourns the dead. Christ therefore did not wish his disciple to fail in the burial rites of his father, but did not wish him to take part in profane mourning.

## SERMON XX. On the Calming of the Storm at Sea

The ecclesiastical readings are distributed through a divine mystery in such a way that they both impart deeper knowledge to the learned and bestow the saving grace of understanding upon the simple.

“When Christ had entered,” it says, “into a small boat”—a bold storm is reported to have caused a great disturbance. “When he had entered the boat, his disciples followed him, and behold, a great storm arose on the sea, so that the boat was covered by the waves; but he himself was sleeping” (Matthew 8:23). [Note: Vatablus reads *navim*, “ship,” from the Greek text πλοῖον (*ploion*) used by the Evangelists, who wrote in Greek. Following Homeric example, Nonnus called this vessel πολυκήδα, “one of many cares”; such ships were generally of enormous size, built from strong timbers, and required many hands. To our author, however, πλοῖον seems to mean a small boat in which they crossed the lake. Sedulius expresses this well, book II, verse 15:

> “They climb aboard the timbers of a little skiff.”]

The sea that submitted its swelling back beneath Christ’s feet, [Col. 0254A] laid its peaks flat, restrained its movement, bound its waves, and served him on a flowing road with stony solidity [Note: Prudentius, preface to book II *Against Symmachus*: “And he stands and makes the wet sea enter beneath his back.” Arnobius, book I: “He trod upon the back of the sea, while the waters themselves stood amazed.” Claudian, *On the Gothic War*: “The icy backs of rivers.”] [Note: The difficult passage in the editions is restored according to Meursius’s punctuation. Some read: “the rocks serve with solidity.” Theophylact, on Matthew 6, reads Psalm 65 thus: “He walks upon the sea as upon pavement.” Latinius: “They serve upon the flowing way with the stony solidity of rock,” that is, the waves.] (John 6)—why does it rage, storm, and struggle almost to the peril of its creator? Why did Christ himself, foreknowing future things, appear so ignorant of the present that he did not guard against the approaching squall, the hour of the storm, and the time of danger, but alone among all who were awake was found asleep [Note: His sleep was natural, not voluntary or deliberately summoned, since he was weary from his labors; otherwise the storm would have seemed to arise without his intention.] when so great a danger threatened him and his own?

Brothers, a calm does not prove the skill of a helmsman, but a storm. When the breeze is flattering, even the least experienced sailor steers the ship; amid the confusion of winds, the skill of the master is sought first.

Thus, after the disciples saw that the skill of the sailors had failed them, that the seas were raging against them, that the waves were attacking them, and that the whirlwinds of the winds had converged against them, they tremblingly fled to the governor of all things, [Note: All printed editions and the Vallicellian and Cesena manuscripts have *vectorem mundi*, “pilot of the world.” The Vatican manuscript and Latinius’s reading have *rectorem*, “governor.”] the ruler of the world and master of the elements, asking him to calm the waves, remove the danger, and restore salvation to those who had despaired.

Finally, when a single command subjected the sea, [Note: So all witnesses. Latinius reads *retudit*, “beat back” or “rebounded.”] it drove back the winds, [Note: Meursius thinks the reading should be *sustulit turbines*, “lifted up the whirlwinds.”] removed the storms, and gave peace. The sailors perceive, believe, and confess that he himself is the author of all things.

But now let us bring forth what lies within. When Christ ascended into the boat of his Church to cross the sea of the world, the blasts of the Gentiles, the whirlwinds of the Jews, the storms of persecutors, the clouds of the populace, and the mists of demons rushed together, so that one storm arose throughout the whole world. The waves of kings foamed; the breakers of powers boiled; [Col. 0255A] the madness of subjects roared; the whirlpools of peoples revolved; the reefs of faithlessness were marked out; [Note: “The bellowing of the groves,” in Pliny, book XVII, chapter 35.] Christian shores bellowed; the shipwrecks of the fallen [Note: So Castillo and the Cesena manuscript. The editions and Mita himself have “were afflicted.”] were tossed about; and the whole world was one danger and one shipwreck.

Then the disciples approached the Lord and awakened him, saying: “Lord, save us; we are perishing.” And Jesus said to them: “Why are you afraid, you of little faith?”

Thus awakened by his disciples, Christ rebukes the sea—that is, the world—calms the globe, softens kings, appeases powers, stills the waves, composes the peoples, and makes the Romans Christians. [Note: Latinius reads this way, and the manuscripts support him. The editions have “and their very executioners.” Mita explains: He made Romans, or from Romans ministers who carried out the word of the Christian faith, which is belief.] From those very people he also made ministers of the word of the Christian faith who had been persecutors of the Christian name. This tranquility is preserved by Christian rulers, held by the Church, possessed by Christianity, and admired by paganism.

“Then,” it says, “he arose and commanded the winds and the sea, and a great calm came about.” But those men were amazed, saying: “What sort of man is this, that even the winds and the sea obey him?”

These are the disciples who approach the Lord, awaken him, and humbly beseech him to save them. [Note: Chrysologus seems here to follow those who think that the men who were amazed in the Gospel were not disciples, but either the sailors of the Gospel boat, men in other boats, or people standing on the shore. Origen and Maldonatus held this view, on Matthew 8, no. 27. But Jerome, in the same place; Basil, *Oration* 22 at the end; Hugh of Saint-Cher; Cajetan; and others thought that the apostles are called “men” here because of their little faith.]

Those men, however, who marvel that the elements obeyed Christ in this way are truly men—and men of the world. They marvel that the world was thus converted to obedience to Christ; they are astonished that the summits of temples, like swelling waves, were thus cast down; they see the foam of idols and the whirlwinds of demons flee in this way; and they are stunned by the profound and widespread tranquility of the Christian name throughout the whole world.

And truly, brothers, while Christ slept in death, a great storm arose in the Church; when Christ rose from the dead, great tranquility was restored to the Church, as it is written.

Now let us awaken Christ sleeping within us with all the groaning of our hearts, with the voice of faith, with Christian tears, with deep lamentation, and with apostolic cries, and let us say: “Lord, save us; we are perishing.”
