And because the reading aptly suits the present time, and as it is written: [Note: The marginal annotators of Chrysologus note this passage as if taken from the reading of the Septuagint. [Col. 0255D] But the passage there reads: “Yet the north wind raises clouds.” According to Castillo, the author’s reading refers to the effect of the north wind, which, being extremely cold, hardens snow and water into ice. Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, book VI:]

I harden the snows, and beat the lands with hail. 

Aquilo is a harsh wind (Prov. 28:23); but he is called “the Right-hand Wind” because he brings to us nations so savage, so bitter. This harsh wind, therefore, through the Right-hand Wind, the Southwest Wind, the South Wind, and the East Wind, spreads itself in a grievous whirlwind, confounds the seas, destroys the air, casts down mountains, swallows cities, submerges provinces, and compels the whole world to become one shipwreck. [Col. 0256C]

[Note: St. Augustine, volume IV, *On the Harmony of the Gospels*, book II, chapter 4: “The world itself is bounded by four regions, which Scripture sometimes mentions by the names of the winds: from the East, the North, and the South.” Thus our author understands the four regions of the world, in which during those times—though not always in the same years and months—there was the greatest shipwreck in the world. For the Angles, having subdued the Scots and the Picts, who originated from Scythia, conquered Britain. Africa was seized by the Vandals under Genseric, plundered, infected with the Arian taint, and consumed by fire and sword. Sicily was ravaged, and Palermo besieged. The Armoricans defected from the Western emperor. Attila, who was called the scourge of God, devastated Thrace and Illyricum, invaded Gaul, and finally prepared himself for the siege of Aquileia and the devastation of Italy. In Gaul the Western emperor lost his most distinguished army; commanders defected from the emperor to the enemy, so that the whole world was shaken by famine, war, pestilence, earthquakes, disasters, fires, and the barbarians’ violence, on account of pagan impiety and the heresy of the Christians. See above, Baronius’s *Annals*, volumes V and VI, from the year of Christ 430 to the year 450; Rubeus of Ravenna and Dolco of Tarquinia. MITA.—The author calls Aquilo “the Right-hand Wind,” perhaps because if you set your face toward the West—for that position is closer and more suitably aligned with the movements of the heavens—Aquilo will always be on your right.]

[Note: We have preferred this reading by conjecture, although more than ten editions that I have before me, as well as the Vallicellian and Caesena manuscripts, read *Christi turbine* (“by Christ’s whirlwind”).]

[Note: Latinius suspects that this may be the correct reading.]

From this comes the fact that Christ’s little boat is now lifted toward heaven, now descends into the depths of terror; now it is guided by Christ’s strength, now tossed about by fear; now it is covered by the waves of sufferings, now it swims out by the oars of confessions. But [Col. 0256B] let us, brothers, cry out again and again: “Lord, save us; we are perishing.”

And truly, brothers, if we were one body, a human body, and believed that those who are perishing are our own inward parts, we would continually cry out, amid the affliction of fasting, the groaning of prayers, and the outpouring of tears: “Lord, save us; we are perishing.” We would strive to help ourselves in our brothers. We would not see a sea of our own blood upon the earth while the sword raged; we would not experience such great shipwrecks of bodies—or even of souls—and we would humbly pray: “Lord, save us; we are perishing.”

Yet no compassion, no piety, no fear, whatever shame or remorse, rouses us to grief. It is God’s doing—God’s doing—that we are pressed by evils, that we are always scourged, that the nations prevail, that hail falls, that rust infects, that impiety [Col. 0256C] has power, that diseases rule, that death rages, and that the earth trembles. [Note: In the East there was a very great earthquake: indeed, Caesar Augustus, together with the people, spent the night in the open air, lest they be crushed by the collapsing buildings of Byzantium. Baronius, under the year 442. MITA.—We would be completely mistaken unless this sermon was delivered at the time when the Vandals were attacking the Roman empire and territory in a fierce war; or unless the event occurred in the year 430, when they gained possession of Africa; or a few years later, namely in 439, when they conquered Carthage by force of arms. Nor is the opinion of those to be rejected who, following Tillemont, thought that the losses and plunder perpetrated by the Vandals in Italy and Sicily in the year 440 are lamented here.]

Yet we neither tremble nor fear; neither do we turn away from evils nor seek good things. Greed rages, pomp pants for display, iniquity pleases, other people’s possessions delight us, while our own perish; God’s scourges come, but our sins provoke them.

If God is just, then surely he is merciful toward us. Brothers, let us return to the Lord, so that God may return to us; let us renounce evils, so that good things may answer us; let us serve the good God, so that we may not serve evil nations and unjust powers. With Christ the Lord and ruler helping us, may his honor and majesty endure without end, for ever and ever. Amen.

[Note: In this present sermon also the author continues to discuss the calamities of his own times. See the preceding note.]

## SERMON XXI. On the Same Subject

Whenever Christ sleeps in our boat and is lulled to sleep in the body by the slumber of our sluggishness, the whole confusion of the winds brings on a storm; threatening waves rage; and while they are repeatedly raised and fall back in foaming billows, they produce bitter shipwrecks for those sailing, as the present Gospel reading made clear when it said:

“And Jesus said to them on that day, when evening had come, ‘Let us cross over to the other side’; and leaving the crowd, they take him along, just as he was, in the boat” (Mark 4:35–36). [Note: The evangelist’s meaning is: on that day when he was about to preach twice. Although others think it was not the day on which Christ had taught the preceding things, but some other day.]

[Note: Chrysologus draws out the mystical meaning. Literally it says: “They took him into the boat, and he had settled himself”; that is, they either placed his cushion beneath his head or arranged some piece of wood in the stern where Christ could rest his head, as Theophylact understood it in his commentary on Mark, chapter 4. “Just as he was”: an elegant expression among the Latins, signifying the continuation of what had previously been the case: “as she was, with her hair disheveled.”]

“And Jesus said to them on that day.” On what day? On that day, namely, when, according to Isaiah, he rises up to shatter the earth (Isa. 2:20); on that day when all the brightness of the world’s light grows toward evening; on that day when, as the night of temptations approaches, the images of vanities that must be fled multiply.

“When evening had come.” It is evening when the final time and the last hour announce to human senses the confusions of events that are coming.

“Let us cross over to the other side”: from earthly things to heavenly things, from present things to future things. And appropriately “to the other side,” because divine things are always contrary to human things: while human things draw those subject to them toward frailty, divine things raise those who follow them toward virtue. [Col. 0257C]

“And leaving the crowd.” They leave the crowd who abandon popular favor and the common people, who are always wandering about with uncertain judgment. They are not held back from the road of virtue by human rumors, but, stable and secure in the goodness of conscience, they pass through the deceitful waves of praise and disparagement, with Christ accompanying them.

“And they take him,” he says, “just as he was, in the boat.” What does this mean? Christ is one way in heaven and another way he is held in the boat; one way in the majesty of the Father and another way he is perceived in human lowliness; one way coeternal with the Father and another way temporal, seen according to the stages of our ages; one way asleep in our body and another way awake in the holiness of his own Spirit.

“They take him,” he says, “just as he was, in the boat.” It is praise of faith to receive Christ as he is and is held in the boat—that is, in the Church: to confess, as a confession of singular salvation, that in it he was born, in it he grew up, in it he suffered, in it he was crucified, in it he was buried, in it he ascended into heaven, sat at the Father’s right hand, and from there will come as judge of the living and the dead. Whoever in this manner confesses and receives Christ in our boat, even if he is battered by the scandals of the waves, is not nevertheless drowned by dangers or submerged by the waters.

“And there arose,” he says, “a great storm of wind, and it was sending waves into the boat, so that the boat was being filled.” And there arose a great storm: it did not dare to test the power of the sleeping Lord, but to strike the disciples’ faith and reveal their fear, so that it might show its author how much service it owed him.

“And he was,” he says, “sleeping in the stern.” Those who are awake flee to the one who is sleeping; and they believe that the one whose sovereign mastery over sleep they behold can withstand the raging elements. They observe that the sleep of human necessity has so fallen upon him that neither the crashing of the sea, nor the shouting of the waves, nor the extreme danger of shipwreck could awaken him. [Note: Mita wrote this conjecturally, and thus it is read, although the manuscripts most consistently read *sua compassione* (“by his compassion”), as if to say that Christ was oppressed by sleep. What if sleep sympathized with Christ, already weary and exhausted? It is an unusual expression, but not so alien to Chrysologus’s style that someone might not accept it.] [Col. 0258B]

And where is that saying: “Behold, he will neither slumber nor sleep who guards Israel” (Ps. 120:4)? In himself he does not sleep, nor does his majesty, free from weariness and ignorant of rest, sleep for itself. Rather, he does everything through me and for me: whenever he changes the appearance of his action or his countenance, he reproves the variations and sins of our souls.

Hear the prophet saying: “His eyelids question the children of men” (Ps. 10:5). See how the eyes of God are closed, so that they may not see those who sin, in order to punish them. “Turn your face away,” he says, “from my sins” (Ps. 50:11). And again they are open, so that they may urge on those who run, raise up those who grow weary, and regard those who plead.

This sleep of the Lord, therefore, tests the disciples’ faith, exposes their doubt, and reveals them to be of little belief: they believe that the elements can rise not only against themselves but even against their author.

“The waves,” he says, “were sending themselves into the boat.” For just as the masses of the nations’ waves shake and pour themselves into the Lord’s boat from outside, so inside the swollen waves of heretics rush in and rage. [Note: Ambrose, in praising Paul’s words: “By these words he marks the doctrines of many heretics.”]

“So that the boat was being filled.” The evangelist rightly reports that the boat was filled with foaming waves, since the Church suffers almost as many heresies as there are questions that we read in the divine law.

And he was, he says, himself sleeping in the stern upon a cushion. They wake him and say to him: “Teacher, does it not matter to you that we are perishing?” And he arose, rebuked the wind, and said to the sea: “Be silent; be muzzled.” And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm. And he said to them: “Why are you fearful? Do you not yet have faith?”

While the reading discloses the event, the time commends it by its example. For a great and sufficiently grievous storm is threatening, while a raging and destructive whirlwind thrusts itself in from every side; the seas roar; the islands themselves are utterly overthrown, and every shore is struck with mournful sound.

But since, as we have said, Christ sleeps in our boat, let us approach him more by faith than by the body, and let us knock upon him more by the work of mercy than by the touch of those who despair. Let us awaken him not with insolent noise but [Col. 0259A] with the cry of spiritual songs; [Note: From this infer the ancient use of singing in the Church. Rupert, book V, *On Glory and Honor*: “The hearing of sweet music in psalm-singing and prayer serves to awaken in our breast the grace of the Holy Spirit.”] not with wicked murmuring but with watchful supplication. [Note: Aptly said. For Christ sufficiently explains that the cause of fear was *oligopistia* (ὀλιγοπιστία), “little faith.”]

Let us give God some portion of the time of our life, lest this wretched vanity and pitiable anxiety consume the whole day; lest destructive sleep and empty slumber spend the whole night. Rather, let a portion of day and night likewise be assigned to the author of time.

Stay awake, man, stay awake. You have an example, so that what the cock gives to its host, you may offer to your Creator. [Note: Cicero calls the cock a “night watchman” in book II of *On Divination*. See Ambrose, volume I, book V of the *Hexaemeron*, chapter 24.] Especially since he sounds his call for your benefit, rouses you to work, and announces that the day is already near: how much more fitting is it for you to awaken God by heavenly hymns from his heavenly seat, for your salvation?

Hear the prophet saying: “By night my spirit keeps watch for you, O God” (Isa. 26:9). [Note: Chrysologus’s marginal annotators note that this passage derives from the reading of the Septuagint translators. I would rather say that it derives from the Vulgate. Ambrose, who lived approximately fifty-three years before Chrysologus, explains it in his commentary on Psalm 118, eighth section, sermon 19, where he reads: “By night my spirit watches for you.” Perhaps these words were taken from some ancient reading that followed neither the Vulgate nor the Septuagint literally.]

And the Psalmist says: “With my hands by night before him, and I was not deceived” (Ps. 76:3). [Note: The Vulgate has *contra eum*, “against him.” Genebrardus likewise reads *contra* rather than *coram*, “before,” following a certain Hebrew particle that signifies both. The Gloss, Augustine, Cassiodorus, and others take the same view. Thus in Matthew 27:61, “sitting opposite the tomb” means “before the tomb.”]

The same Psalmist also admonishes us that three times of the day are to be assigned to God, saying: “In the evening, and morning, and at midday I will declare and announce, and he will hear my voice” (Ps. 54:13). [Note: See Isidore of Seville, *On the Ecclesiastical Offices*, book I, chapters 19–23.]

While Daniel diligently entreated God at these three times, he obtained not only foreknowledge of future events but also won liberty for his nation, long held captive (Dan. 6:10). Let us therefore say what the prophet said: “Awake; why do you sleep, O Lord? Awake, and do not reject us forever” (Ps. 43:23).

Let us say with the apostles: “Teacher, does it not matter to you that we are perishing?” And truly he is the Teacher, because he is not only the maker of all the elements but also their governor and ruler. When he hears us, when he deigns to awaken, the waves will be flattened, the swollen billows and the hills will be laid low, the winds will scatter, the storm will perish, and this tempest that threatens—this great tempest—will be changed into the greatest calm.

## SERMON XXII. On Despising Concern for Earthly Things and on the Watchful Servant

Rewards are always appointed for those to whom hard struggles are proposed, and the greatness of the reward is set forth in proportion to the greatness of the struggle. Hence Christ places the kingdom in the bosom of his disciples, so that in the struggle they may not yield to dangers or fear. Whoever strives toward the kingdom despises dangers; eager for victory, he does not know how to fear.

“Do not fear,” he says, “little flock, because it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom” (Luke 12:32). [Note: Maldonatus here wishes Christ’s disciples and all the faithful together to be called “little flock,” on account of Christian gentleness; following Mita.]

A little flock to the world, a great one to God; little because he calls them glorious whom he forms for the innocence of sheep and Christian gentleness. It is a little flock that is not diminished from something great but grows from something little. The little flock designates the infancy of the newborn Church, which he soon promises will come, through heavenly growth, to the insignia of his kingdom.

“Do not fear, little flock, because it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom.” He added what the one who is to reign must do: “Sell what you possess and give alms; make for yourselves purses that do not grow old, an unfailing treasure in heaven.”

“Sell what you possess.” No one can rule over all things unless he is not held by his own possessions. A fallen mind is the mind that remembers household property when it is called to the kingdom. A lowly, plebeian spirit prefers a little coin to royal treasures. A poor understanding, clinging to small things, loses great ones; and, gaping after temporal things, abandons the eternal.

“Sell,” he says, “what you possess and give alms; make for yourselves purses that do not grow old, an unfailing treasure in heaven.” Man, by such an admonition Christ wished to enrich you, not strip you; he wished your possessions to remain yours, not perish; he commanded that your purses be made everlasting, not emptied; he ordered you to transfer them, not lose them. [Col. 0260C]

“An unfailing treasure in heaven, where a thief does not approach and a moth does not corrupt.” [Note: Perhaps *veterasci* (“grow old”) ought to have been restored, so that the word might be more suitably set in opposition to *perpetuari* (“be made everlasting”), in accordance with Chrysologus’s style. Cicero, in the *Tusculan Disputations*: “None of those things in which the happy life consists ought to grow old.” Suidas calls purses *βαλαύτια* (*balautia*), which Matthew calls *ζαυνὰς* (*zaunas*).]

He acts more as a father giving counsel than as a ruler exercising legal authority: he rebukes you for storing your possessions amid the ambushes of thieves and the bites of moths; you are warned not to create sleepless nights, anxious days, and troubled times for yourself. The keeper of gold, the preserver of silver, has no security and knows no rest; and for one who lacks security, rest perishes. That rich man is rich in punishment, not in wealth.

“An unfailing treasure in heaven.” This means: “Where I am, there place your possessions; once given to me, I preserve them.” Man, give them to the Father; trust God, because the Father will not deny what has been entrusted to him, nor will God deny it to man. He cannot retain what is yours, because he has given what is his. Does the one who bestows divine things need human things? Is the one who made us heirs of his possessions greedy for ours? Certainly, to those to whom he has given the kingdom, what will he deny?

O man, if you are going to remain here, store here what is yours. If you are going there, why do you abandon here what is yours? Whoever stores what must be abandoned is a guardian of another’s property, not of his own.

If in this life, in which we are pilgrims, we live and grieve over being poor for a short time, sad, and without honor, what will it be in our perpetual homeland, among eternal citizens, to endure grief for contempt, punishment for low status, and disgrace for nakedness—and now to be assigned to punishments, while others are promoted to the kingdom? When the poor man is led to God’s seat and the rich man is dragged into the company of the punished?

Alas, how lamentable the reversals will be when the desperate possess divine hope among human beings, while those endowed with human goods are deprived of heavenly goods! And this is what the treasure does: it either lifts the human heart to heaven through almsgiving or plunges it into the earth through greed.

And therefore he said: “For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.”

Man, send and send ahead your treasure into the heavens, lest [Col. 0261B] you plunge your heavenly soul into the earth. [Note: The author calls our soul heavenly and from above because it is created immediately from nothing by God, as theologians commonly teach. MITA.—See Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, book VI, p. 641, where he expressly teaches these same things.]

Gold comes from the depths of the earth; the soul comes from the heights of heaven. It is therefore better for gold to be carried to the soul’s dwelling than for the soul to be plunged into a tomb of gold.

He therefore commands those whom he has granted to reign in heaven to serve him in the world, stripped of all concern for riches and already freed for every task.

“Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands, and be like people waiting for their master, when he returns from the wedding feast.” [Note: Having their loins girded belongs not only to soldiers and travelers but also to those who serve. See Luke 5:37 and John 13:4. Hence Phaedrus, *Fables* 2, called stewards *alte cinctos*, “highly girded.” Chrysologus explains the Gospel passage as referring to the girding and restraint of pleasures.]

“Let your loins be girded.” [Note: This we restore on the authority of the manuscripts; all editions, with Mita, have *voluntas* (“will”).] Virtue must be girded where pleasure must be restrained. Whoever removes the belt of virtue does not know how to conquer the vices of the body. Girded, therefore, with the belt of chastity, which is the insignia of Christian warfare, let us cut away the slack cowardice of the flesh. [Note: The belt was the chief badge of military service; anyone who took it off was compelled to leave military service. Thus in Prudentius, *Psychomachia*, v. 634, *discingere* means “to disarm”: “Every land is ungirded”; and at v. 824: “The ungirded youth hastens to the seat.” Aptly for our subject, Paulinus of Nola, epistle 25, p. 164: “Let us therefore follow him, that is, our Lord; let us serve as soldiers under him, whose soldier, once girded, is never ungirded.”] Let us remain watchful in expectation of our king and know nothing of the world’s wakeful sleep.

“They do not sleep unless they have done evil” (Prov. 4:16).

“And your lamps burning in your hands.” Blessed are those in whose hands the lamps of good works shine. For so it is written: “Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16). Just as a lamp shines before the eyes, so a good work shines in the mind. A lamp does not shine only for the one carrying it but for many; and while a good work shines through what one person has done, it enlightens many by its example. A lamp drives away the darkness of night; a good work puts to flight the darkness of wickedness.

Let us kindle the lamp of good works in our hands, if we wish to shine before the Lord and before men. [Note: Vatican manuscript: *Bonorum operum* (“of good works”).] “And be like people waiting for their master, when he returns from the wedding feast.” Since torches are always associated with wedding feasts, the chastity of marriage is celebrated by the testimony of lights. [Note: The torch-bearers included both those who awaited the bridegroom and those who followed him. See Luke 14:8 and Esther 9:22. To spare our pages, we refrain from profane testimonies. Torches were called companions of wedding feasts because they were joined or united with weddings. Mita thinks that Chrysologus is here alluding to the Novatians, who foolishly condemned marriage. There were also those who said that a demon was the author of marriage; Clement of Alexandria refutes them in *Stromata*, book III, p. 445.]

For just as the one who presumes upon what is unlawful flees the light, so the one who seeks what is lawful flashes with manifold light.

“And be like people waiting for their master, when he returns from the wedding feast.” Human beings are those who, in the manner of due service, await the arrival of their master with tireless watches. But those who serve their belly in such a way that they do not know divine service, and who, concerned with bodily pleasure, have lost concern for meeting the Lord, must not be called human beings but beasts. [Note: There were also servant-watchmen who, entrusted with the care of the doors, awaited their master until he returned.]

“And be like people waiting for their master, when he returns from the wedding feast.” [Note: Countless testimonies of the holy Fathers declare that Christ is called the bridegroom of the Church. If I wished to gather them, I would make a cloud. See Theophylact on John, chapter III, p. 602; Hammonius in the *Catena* on John, chapter III, p. 108; Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, book III, p. 446, etc.] From the time when Christ came to espouse his Church, the bridal chamber is adorned for the bride. [Note: That bridal chambers at weddings were like rooms with vaulted workmanship, or small tents constructed with special artistry. Claudian, *On the Marriage of Honorius*:

“Some of you, with skilful weaving, prepare the bridal chamber.

Let its roof be built with jewelled fabric

And painted columns,” etc.]

It is adorned with the gold of faith, the silver of wisdom, the jewels of virtues, the veils of holiness, roses of modesty, lilies of chastity, and violets of shame. [Note: The ancients customarily hung curtains in the inner rooms of a house. Ausonius may also allude to this in his *Epitaph on His Father*:

“Neither as one who rushes forward,

Nor as a babbler who notices what lies before him at the doors,

Did I enter what was hidden by a curtain.”]

For this matter Pignorius, in *On Servants*, cites these same words of Chrysologus; Calvorius likewise cites them in *Ritual*, volume I, book I, p. 145. The doors of the royal council chamber were also extended with curtains. Corippus, book III, *On Justin the Younger*:

“Curtains cover the doorposts; guards watch the lofty

Thresholds and bar the unworthy from entering.”]

And the pinnacle of virginity is raised to the high temple of heavenly chastity. Nor are there lacking the lyres of the psalms, the instruments of the prophets, the voices of the apostles, [Col. 0262C] and the complete harmonies of the heavenly wedding. [Note: Chrysologus, continuing his allusion, also mentions the music and harmony that we know were present at Christian weddings. Ambrose mentions a wedding song in sermon 25. Chrysostom, volume IX, p. 322, homily 42 on the Acts of the Apostles, reports that cymbals, pipes, and songs were used to gladden the guests at wedding banquets.]

He is sufficiently a servant of sleep who is not awakened by such a great and such a mighty cry to the wedding of the heavenly king.

“And be like people waiting for their master, when he returns from the wedding feast, so that when he comes and knocks, they may immediately open to him.”

When he comes, he knocks. A heart with a good conscience opens; one with a bad conscience closes. A just mind opens itself to reward; an unjust one, because it has not deserved it, shuts itself off.

Let us therefore keep watch, beloved, so that we may obtain the blessedness that follows.

“Blessed are those servants whom the master, when he comes, finds watching.”

These promises of blessedness would be sufficient, but because Christ speaks of the love belonging to that blessedness itself, let us postpone this today, so that we may hear more fully what such a Father has promised his children.

## SERMON XXIII. On Despising Concern for Earthly Things and on the Promise of the Kingdom
[Col. 0263B] Today you heard how the Lord joined the blast of the heavenly trumpet to pastoral rejoicing, so that he might lift the minds of the sheep, long bowed down, toward divine things and immediately advance the heavenly flock toward the kingdom. “Do not be afraid,” he says, “little flock, because your Father has been pleased to give you the kingdom” (Luke XII). Humility acquired what pride lost, and the little and gentle flock by its own meekness subdued every kind and variety of wildness. The little flock conquered and broke so many [Note: [Col. 0263D] Among Latins this term refers to people of a wild and uncultivated disposition; in this sense the Apostle called the Cretans “evil beasts.” Arianus, *On Epictetus*, book II, chapter 9: “Some of us are great beasts; others are malicious little beasts.” Theophylact, commenting on 1 Corinthians XV, 32, calls the struggle against the Jews a battle with beasts; and, commenting on Luke VI, calls the tax collector an evil beast.] kinds of beasts, as there are varieties of nations subjected to Christ’s yoke.

The little and gentle flock long remained content to be killed and allowed itself to be devoured, until gentile savagery, sated with blood or flesh and having tasted the sweetness of the Gospel pasture and the streams of the divine fountain, avoided the world’s entire contagion and [sought] pasture, and returned from beast to human being, though it had fallen [Col. 0263C] from human being into beast. That this was anticipated by the prophets, fulfilled by the apostles, and endured by the martyrs is clear from the testimony of him who says: “For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are reckoned as sheep for slaughter” (Psalm XLIII, 22).

But when this flock of the new order entered the battle—where the one who has been killed lives, the one who has fallen conquers, and the one who loses his life finds it—it imitated its king. It followed that sheep, that Lamb, who “was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer did not open its mouth” (Isaiah LIII). The one who suffers willingly is silent; the one who is torn apart unwillingly cries out. Nor can the one who willingly, not under compulsion, accepts death complain about death. It is a mark of power when someone dies willingly for many; when he dies unwillingly, it is the extremity of necessity, because the one case arises from contempt for death, the other from the condition of nature.

[Col. 0264A] Christ, therefore, like a sheep, both willingly and silently, is shorn [Note: [Col. 0263D] The Caesena manuscript reads, “so that he might will that one.”] in order to cover the nakedness that Adam first brought upon us; like a lamb he is killed, so that, sacrificed for the sin of the whole world, he might absolve it; he lays down his life for the sheep, so that he may fulfill both the shepherd’s devotion and his care. For you, therefore, he was made king, priest, shepherd, sacrifice, sheep, Lamb—he who had made everything was made everything for you. Though he never changes for himself, he so often changes for you and is shown in various forms, while he remains in the single form of his own majesty.

And what more? God the human being gives himself to you in a form that you can bear, because you cannot endure him as he is. But let us now hear what such a shepherd promised the little flock: “Do not be afraid, little flock, because your Father has been pleased to give you the kingdom.”

O overflowing goodness! O unheard-of devotion! O ineffable affection! In the fellowship of wealth the shepherd takes the sheep as his companions, and the master admits servants into partnership in his dominion; the king admits the flock of the whole people to a share [Note: [Col. 0263D] In Julius Capitolinus, *Life of Verus*: “After Pius’s death, Maximus bestowed on him everything belonging to the principate, including the grant of imperial power.” Isaac Casaubon judges that *participatum* (“a share”) should be restored, a reading supported by the Milan edition. Likewise in Spartianus, *Life of Didius Julianus*, where the words “he summoned Claudius Pompeianus from Terracina to the principate” are found, we learn from the Palatine manuscript, cited by Hofmann, that *participatum* should be read.] in the kingdom. Thus, thus he gives: the one who cannot suffer his wealth to fail, his kingdom to diminish, or his power to be emptied by giving.

The Lord wisely began by saying: “Do not be afraid, little flock, because your Father has been pleased to give you the kingdom.” It is not enough for a servant’s condition to hear the promise of the kingdom without fear, because one who is scarcely worthy of freedom cannot take up the insignia of rule. Therefore the Lord strengthens the minds of servants with this utterance, lest the sudden hearing of the promised kingdom overthrow them. For a servant to desire a kingdom is to incur the danger of a crime; not to fear is rashness.

But how great is this in relation to Christ? Or how astonishing that he gives servants a kingdom and makes servants partners in his dominion—he who washes the feet of servants, so that he may serve servants with the lowest form of service? [Note: [Col. 0264D] Against the heretics Aetius and Eunomius. See Augustine, *On Heresies*, 54. —Mita.]

Let those who question his power come here—let them come—and then dispute his equity when they have been able to grasp, express, and assess such devotion. Let them no longer slander if he says himself “less than the Father” in our body [Note: [Col. 0264D] The heretics perversely twisted several passages of Scripture. The anonymous author of the *Brief Summary of Faith against the Arians*, in Sirmond, vol. I, p. 225, explains their Catholic meaning. “For we Catholics say that our God Jesus Christ is both less than the Father and equal to him: less because of the humanity assumed, equal because of the eternal divinity.” See Basil, *Against Eunomius*, at the beginning of vol. II, p. 79, and book III, p. 35.], since by washing the feet of servants he subjected and humbled himself, in deed as well as in word, beneath the feet of servants.

Man, spare yourself now, because, so that you might spare yourself, your God washed your feet, held them, and embraced them. [Note: [Col. 0264D] Thus according to the manuscript tradition. The printed editions read, “so that you might spare yourself.”]

But let us return to what we began: “Do not be afraid, little flock, because your Father has been pleased to give you the kingdom.” See: the one who gives speaks of the Father as the giver. Does he deny his own generosity by speaking in this way? Far from it. He does not diminish his power, [Col. 0265A] but discloses his affection. By speaking thus, he does not establish a distinction, [Note: [Col. 0265C] Cyril of Alexandria, book IV, chapter 5, on John VIII, 17, p. 414, takes *from myself* in the sense of “particularly and properly,” according to the most perfect conformity and identity of the Father’s will.] but shows the Father’s will and his own, and confirms their unity.

When he said “has been pleased,” and did not say merely “was pleased,” he teaches the gift of the Trinity, because what pleased the Son concerning us pleased the Trinity. “Do not be afraid, little flock, because your Father has been pleased to give you the kingdom.” Therefore, after such generosity by the Lord, after his grace has been bestowed upon you so abundantly, he commands the one who is to reign to cast away the lowly and worthless possessions of servitude: “Sell what you possess and give alms.”

Royal power admits no plebeian dress; august honor is conferred only with diadem and purple. Therefore the one who believes himself divinely consecrated as king must cast off the clothing of servitude. This is why the heavenly King commanded that the man who dared to enter his banquet in an unworthy garment be bound, cast out, and thrust into the outer darkness (Matthew XXII), because the deformity of the invited guest redounds to the insult of the one who invited him.

The one who, enriched now with wealth and royal resources, preserves the former possessions of his freedom [Note: [Col. 0265C] The Vatican manuscript reads, “miserably captive.”] does not know that, in his misery, he is a captive and yet thinks himself happy. It is customary, and characteristic of a happy spirit, that one admitted to a kingdom immediately distributes generously to parents, relatives, and needy citizens whatever had been his own and private property, so that one who has acquired wealth and honor may not be a beggar in spirit. [Note: [Col. 0265D] A word familiar to Chrysologus. Mita’s text, perhaps through scribal carelessness, has *prorogare* (“to defer”); the Paris, Mainz, and other editions read *erogare* (“to distribute”).]

With such foresight, therefore, and by such counsel, the Lord commands us to sell and distribute and give away what is worthless and fleeting, since in the heavenly kingdom we wish to possess everything that is in heaven and on earth.

But if you want to preserve the value of your estates, and perhaps delight in what has been stored in your purses, make purses for yourself such as the one who is now the guardian and provider of your desire for wealth commanded. Indeed, when he saw that what he had said was harsh—“Sell what you possess”—he immediately added: “Make purses for yourselves that do not grow old, an unfailing treasure in heaven.”

Are you troubled again because you are compelled to place what you have in heaven? I beg you, trust your God, [Note: [Col. 0265D] He alludes to one of the offices of servants, that of the *arcarii*, or keepers of the treasury; compare Erastus, mentioned in the Epistle to the Romans VI. At least this passage of Chrysologus is interpreted in this way by Pignorius, *On Servants*. See Zeno of Verona, *To the Neophyte*, sermon 1.] you who trust a servant, and entrust it to God rather than to a human being.

But if you fear that he may take something from it or that the generosity of the giver may scatter something, seal your purses with the sign of faith by means of a ring, so that you may sleep securely under such a guardian, because where he is, there is no place for a thief. [Note: [Col. 0265D] The ancients used rings especially as seals. See Clement of Alexandria, *The Instructor*, book III, chapter 2. After saying that gold rings should be permitted to women not merely for adornment but so that things kept at home might be sealed, he disapproves of those who had figures of deities engraved on them. The passage deserves to be copied and explained: “Let our seals be a dove, in whose form the Holy Spirit descended; or a fish, by which name Christ was signified, as we shall see below; or a ship, which is carried swiftly by the wind and which, as has been observed, represents the Church; or the musical lyre used by Polycrates, which perhaps recalls David’s lyre, as the scholiast on Sidonius Apollinaris, in Sirmond, p. 909, no. 154, thinks. And if someone is a fisherman, let him remember the apostles and the children drawn from the water.”]

[Col. 0266A] He will not be able to deny you your money, he who has bestowed all his own things upon you and enriched you with the honor and glory of his kingdom.

## SERMON XXIV  
### On the vigilant servant and the blessedness of the kingdom of God

No one is unaware that vigilance is always and in every matter beneficial, because, in truth, to watch more is to live more. For what is so like death as the appearance of one who sleeps? What is so full of life as the form of one who is awake? Sleep should be granted so that the body may be restored, not dissolved, and regain strength, not be enervated.

No one, therefore, is unaware that vigilance is always and in every matter beneficial. What art, what work, what time, what power, what office does not seek the gains of life through labor by night? This is why the king, fully awake while on campaign [Note: [Col. 0266D] With the expedition itself imminent, as we have noted elsewhere.], guards against the cunning enemy and avoids ambushes. Then, in the camp, the soldier repels approaching night attacks by a cautious night watch.

Thus the sailor, keeping watch, enters the uncertain paths of the open sea, crosses trackless channels, and by a stealthy course reaches his desired lodging in the profitable harbor. Thus the shepherd adds nights to days and denies himself all time for sleeping, lest sleep, assisting the wolves, provide any opportunity for them to ravage the flock.

Thus the diligent traveler through the night air anticipates the heat of the sun and more prudently assigns the suitable day to his lodging. [Note: [Col. 0266D] Corrected by Latinius from the reading *actumque* found in the editions.]

Knowing this, the prophet cried out to the Lord not only by day but throughout the night: “Lord, God of my salvation, by day I have cried out, and by night before you” (Psalm LXXXVII). What more? The Lord himself “spent the night in prayer to God” (Luke VI), so that by prayer he might set us free before redeeming us through his passion. [Col. 0266C] [Note: [Col. 0266D] Christ’s prayer to the Father showed us to be free, as members joined to the head, the only-begotten Son. The passion, however, does not make everyone free absolutely, but redeemed: by taking us away from the slavery of the devil, he made us his servants, purchased at the price of such great blood. —Mita.]

And if the master keeps vigil for servants, rightly does he command servants to keep vigil for themselves. “Let your loins,” he says, “be girded and your lamps burning in your hands, and be like people waiting for their master when he returns from the wedding feast” (Luke XII).

“Let your loins be girded.” A new order of watches, a new dress, is commanded. “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands.” The vigilant servants are told nothing about clothing, nothing about footwear, nothing about preparations for the master’s arrival. All the care is commanded in girding the loins; all the force of the command is established in tightening the loins, with only the assistance of lamps added—without which neither is the darkness of night opened up nor does the appearance of the coming day grow bright.

“Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands.” [Note: [Col. 0267C] This was the garment of servants, which was girded so that it would not hinder them in carrying out what had been commanded. This has been noted elsewhere. I add from Horace, book II of the *Satires*:

> … a boy, tightly girded, passed by the maple table  
> in a purple shaggy cloak.

And from Juvenal, *Satire* 8:

> And with the for-sale flask, Cyane, tightly girded.

Pignorius, *On Servants*, cites Chrysologus’s words.]

A belt is properly an indication of servitude: it both makes one swift in movement and makes one obedient. [Note: [Col. 0267C] I preferred to restore this from the Vatican manuscript rather than retain the reading found in all the editions: *et discursus expedi os* [reading uncertain].] But it would have been enough to say, “Be girded.” Why does he specifically mention the loins? Why does the reverence of the one giving the command make such extensive mention of the loins?

Do you ask why? Because the whole cause of the body is in the loins; from the loins all the business of the flesh is aroused; in the loins lies the entire occasion of human falling and human weakness. From there comes what renders those ignorant of virtue and makes them more sluggish.

Therefore the Lord principally commands our loins to be tightened with the belt of chastity, and commands all that is loose, fluid, and relaxed in our flesh to be bound with an unbroken girdle of virtue, so that, with the flesh girded, the movement of our mind may be made free, swift, and unimpeded for meeting the Lord.

Yet, hearing this, man, you must know that the flesh does not delay your meeting with God, because it is the inseparable companion of that very meeting, provided that you arrange its baggage, uncover its burdens, and, as a prudent traveler, bind its hanging and winding coverings.

What more? Your association with it will be salutary if you are not a lazy and lax instructor of it. But how you ought to equalize its baggage and regulate its unjust burdens, the Apostle teaches by saying: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire, and avarice, which is the service of idols” (Colossians III, 5).

[Col. 0267C] The flesh must therefore be tightened with the belt of self-control, lest, poured out into vices and weighed down by the entire burden of sins, it be unable to stand upon the paths above and in heaven.

The Lord therefore rightly added: “And your lamps burning in your hands.” Lamps are always carried at night as a testimony of innocence. Just as darkness is always friendly to vices, so lamps are always hostile to crimes and always companions of good works.

But in the hands of the saints the good works themselves are lamps, as the Lord says: “Let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew V).

And truly they carry their lamps; truly, by the fuel of their works and by the oil of mercy, they set their lamps aflame. When their works lie hidden in place, purpose, and intention, they flash and shine through their action and virtue throughout the whole world.

And because the Lord knew that those awaiting him were very sorrowful and very anxious in their disposition—lest anyone be overcome by weariness, lest anyone grow tired of delay, lest anyone collapse from the fatigue of a long wait—he promises heavenly service to those who persevere toward heavenly blessedness.

“Blessed,” he says, “are those servants whom the Lord, when he comes, finds watching.” And lest the nature of that blessedness remain uncertain, he immediately added: “Amen, I say to you, he will gird himself, make them recline, and, passing by, minister to them.”

[Note: [Col. 0267D] Mita observes here three sources of astonishment. The first arises from the unheard-of reversal of things: that our Lord will provide service and ministry to the elect in heaven. The second arises from the terrifying suspension of his dominion. For he suspends—or sets aside—his dominion over human beings in order to offer them his service. The third arises from the fearful condition of servitude. How greatly should one fear a kingdom when one who is by nature a servant is suddenly taken up into kingship?]

God will gird himself, make servants recline, and minister to them. Behold the unheard-of reversal of things; behold the terrifying suspension of dominion; behold the fearful transformation of servitude. For a servant stands for a little while, girded, awaiting his master, and has endured the faithfulness of waiting through a brief fatigue. In order to repay him in kind, he conceals himself [Note: [Col. 0267D] According to the jurists, in § 7 of the *Institutes*, “On Injuries,” to repay by retaliation (*talionem reddere*) means to inflict upon someone the same punishment by which you yourself were punished by him. Thus our Lord has in some manner repaid you for the service rendered to him by a human being, while he himself serves that same human being in glory. —Mita. *Ταυτοκαθεῖα* is what the Greeks call this, and what we call the law of retaliation. See canon 4 of the Second Council of Nicaea, with Balsamon, p. 499, and the notes below on sermon 38.] in his very divinity. [Note: [Col. 0268C] Mita explains that this happens for two reasons, arising from the different meanings of the word *dissimulate*. First, *dissimulate* means to overlook or conceal something with closed eyes, as in Wisdom XI, 24: “you overlook the sins of human beings.” Here divine majesty acts as though it did not possess eternal dominion over human beings, both for its own sake, so that it may become the servant of its servants, and for the sake of human beings, lest, overwhelmed by such majesty, they be unable to bear being served by so great a lord. Second, *dissimulate* means to remain in a place, as in Genesis XIX, 16, when the angels wished to lead Lot out of Sodom. The text says: “While he lingered, they seized his hand,” that is, “while he remained at home.” Thus the deity remains within divinity, because, although God communicates blessedness to humanity, he does not bestow the entire abundance of goods, but only as much as the blessed person can bear. This is Mita’s opinion, which he develops at considerably greater length.]

“He will gird himself, make them recline, and, passing by, minister to them.” God stands beside the reclining human being—and he stands in the heavenly places; [Note: [Col. 0268D] What the blessed have at these banquets the author writes below in sermons 95 and 176. The blessed feast not by taste but by sight, for vision is the whole reward. —Mita.] [Col. 0268C] he serves the servant at the banquet, and he serves while girded to his little ones, his ministers. [Note: [Col. 0268D] If Christ, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, is the object of supreme glory, as the theologians hold, why is Christ alone said to perform ministry for the blessed? Because, as the author says above in sermon 22, “What pleased the Son concerning us pleased the Trinity.” Christ is said to minister blessed glory to human beings because he himself earned the banquet’s food and drink by his blood, as Barradas says in this passage of the Gospel. —Mita.]

Christ performs ministry, and he performs it already established in the glory of the Father.

Man, do you still slander Christ because he deferred to the Father? [Note: [Col. 0268D] We have restored an obscure passage found in some editions to its genuine reading, on the basis of Mita, Castillo, and the Caesena manuscript. Arius and others use this text—“The Father is greater than I”—to argue that the Son of God is less than the Father even in respect of divinity. But, unwilling sincerely to understand that passage with the Catholics, they do not interpret it in the common sense as referring only to his humanity. Our author is recorded as teaching this repeatedly in many places. Saint Ambrose, book II, chapter 2, on Luke, against the same heretics: “And we are astonished if Christ defers to the Father, when he is subject to his mother?” —Mita.] He who, by washing your feet on earth, displayed the lowest service [Note: [Col. 0269D] This lowest service performed by Christ the Lord for the disciples is called a prodigy by Blessed Lawrence Justinianus.] promises in heaven the final service?

Believe, heretic, and try also to repay him in kind. He prepares a banquet for you in heaven, with himself as its minister, while you on earth do not cease continually to heap up and generate blasphemies against him.

He too will make his transitions, because “passing by, he will minister to them”: from dominion he will pass and move into the loving service of his faithful; toward you he will pass from the Father of mercy into the most severe judge.

“And passing by, he will minister to them.” To those who confess and wait, he will minister food; he will minister to you as well, but a sentence worthy of your denial.

“And if he comes in the second watch, and if he comes in the third watch, and finds them so, blessed are those servants.”

If he comes in the second and third watch: the world knows more watches, but the expectation of the Trinity knows only three. Why, however, did he begin with the second and remain silent about the first? Because the first watch had already passed at the rising of the Lord’s birth.

The shepherds prove this. While they kept watch over their flock, they were found worthy to find, see, and hold in the manger the shepherd and author of the flock. But let us inquire what the second and third watches are.

Just as the first watch is certainly his birth in the flesh, so the second is the watch in which our flesh returns and is resurrected. Indeed, so that he might come to the risen one, the year is awakened [Note: [Col. 0269D] Thus according to the correction of Latinius and the Vallicellian manuscript. The editions read *annuus* (“yearly”).], and the world wakes.

The third watch is that in which the entire expectation of the one who is coming is brought to an end by his final arrival, so that, just as he rose for us, we too may rise for him to everlasting life. [Note: [Col. 0269D] *Jam*, “now,” here signifies future time, that is, “then”; compare Luke V: “From now on you will catch human beings,” and Exodus XIX: “Now I shall come to you in the darkness of a cloud.” —Mita.]

## SERMON XXV  
### On despising concern for earthly things and on the promise of the kingdom

Today you heard how the Lord consoled the small and earthly beginnings of the evangelical flock with gentle exhortation. “Do not be afraid,” he says, “little flock, because your Father has been pleased to give you the kingdom” (Luke XII). He removes anxious hopes, takes away uncertain outcomes, and drives away and excludes all fear when, at the very beginning, he promises the kingdom to those who are being born. [Note: [Col. 0270D] Christ addresses those who had given themselves, or were about to give themselves shortly, to his discipline.]

“Because your Father has been pleased to give you the kingdom.” Who sighs over food, clothing, plebeian wealth, and the lowliness of a spring turf when he is certain of the kingdom and secure in dominion? He does himself sufficient injury who, raised to the highest things, casts himself down to lowly things and reduces himself to poverty.

But it is fitting to know who this father is, what sort of father he is, and what kingdom he promises to his children. Who this father is you recognize as you confess him daily, when you cry: “Our Father who art in heaven” (Matthew VI, 9).

What sort of father he is you have clearly perceived from the greatness of his works: from nothing he made heaven, and he solidified the earth out of liquid matter. [Note: [Col. 0270D] He refers to Isaiah XL, 12: “and weighed the mountains in a balance, and the hills in scales.”] He established the mountains on a scale; [Note: [Col. 0270D] The reference is to Isaiah XL, 12: “and weighed the mountains in a balance, and the hills in scales.”] by the authority of his command alone he enclosed the seas within their lawful boundaries.

But if you desire to know the nature of the kingdom he promises to the little ones, he himself discloses it by saying: “Let the little children come to me, for of such is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew XIX, 14).

To be in heaven is astonishing; to live in heaven belongs to majesty. Now to reign in heaven is something mortal understanding ceases to measure. And yet, man, you have received what you cannot measure, as the Apostle says: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians II, 9).

And what you doubt that you deserve, you are compelled to confess that you already possess and hold. What, then, has one who possesses heaven to do with earth? What has one who has already obtained divine things to do with human things? Unless perhaps groans are pleasing, labors are chosen, dangers are loved, the worst death delights, and evils inflicted are preferred to goods bestowed.

But let us see what counsel so great a Father gives to those who are to reign: “Sell what you possess and give alms.” If you believe that you will live, that you will reign, that you are already rich in the heavenly places where you will be and to which you will migrate, let those things that are yours go before you. Count miserable riches as mercy; turn human things into divine things.

[Col. 0270C] And lest anyone perhaps lack transportation for carrying away what he leaves behind, the poor man has been pressed into service [Note: [Col. 0270D] On the *angariae*, see Stolbergius in the dissertation entitled “On the *Angariae* of the Ancients,” vol. X of *Sacred Criticism*, p. 101. In law, *angaria* is an unjust exaction; but the word is Persian, for among the Persians an *ángaros* was a royal courier. The Persians divided their routes into *parasangs*; when couriers and carriers reached each parasang, they rested and entrusted their burdens to others traveling farther, to be passed along in turn. If you desire more, consult Meursius, *Corrections*, chapter 29, p. 176.]: the poor carry our burdens, and they carry them willingly, because such a weight does not press them down but lifts them up.

“Sell what you possess and give alms; make purses for yourselves that do not grow old, an unfailing treasure in heaven, where no thief approaches and no moth corrupts.”

“Make purses for yourselves that do not grow old.” You see that this father wishes to enrich his children, not strip them naked.

“Make purses for yourselves that do not grow old.” In a new manner—or rather, in a heavenly manner—the one who hears this purchases by selling, stores up by distributing, and acquires while losing.

How eagerly does the one who says, “Make purses for yourselves that do not grow old,” wish money to endure, the purses of wealth to be made everlasting, and stored possessions to remain!

Behold: the one who had begun to commend contempt teaches avarice. “Make purses for yourselves that do not grow old.” And the one who had reproved those who stored up temporal treasures commands purses without end to be sought as fuel for every form of greed.

Christ, where does the love of your own lead you? To win the avaricious person, you make him hear what he desires, not what is necessary. You command that purses and eternal treasures that do not fail be prepared, so that, while the avaricious person pursues his customary profits, he may either grasp virtue or be grasped by virtue.

Truly you are a Father, who deals in this way with your little ones, whoever they may be. For we too sometimes give our little children, when they ask, harmful things that are beneficial under the appearance of harmful things, deceiving their foolishness without deceiving our affection.

You said: “Make purses for yourselves that do not grow old, treasures that do not fail in heaven.” Why is a purse prepared? What need is there for locks where innocence itself is the guardian? What need is there for a seal where no suspicion of fraud exists? If purses are needed even in heaven, concern is not lost but changed.

Lord, you saw that all faith and all hope lie in the purses of the avaricious person. Therefore you want purses that do not rot to be prepared in heaven, so that the one who does not follow you to heaven may at least follow his purses.

Avaricious man, make purses for yourself, and make them at God’s command, because divine majesty assents to your desires. But make purses for yourself by distributing, because whatever the poor person receives, the heavenly Father accepts.

And where does he store it? In heaven.

And lest you perhaps grieve that you have lost it or that you have not received interest, [Note: [Col. 0271C] See what we noted above on sermon 15. It should be added that Justinian’s law stipulated that even maritime interest should not exceed one percent per month, *Code*, book IV, title 32, § 26. On the method of obtaining interest among the Romans, after Salmasius, Gronovius, and Gravina, see Gottlieb Heineccius, *Roman Antiquities*, vol. II, p. 84, Venice edition of 1739.] you will receive a hundredfold interest on the heavenly loan—whatever you have sent into heaven by means of the poor person who carries it there.

The world’s interest is a hundred to one; God receives one and returns a hundred. And yet human beings do not want to enter into a contract with God.

Perhaps they are anxious about the guarantee? Why? Is not a human being bound to another human being by the obligation of a small document? God gives security in so many and such great volumes, and the debtor is not held?

But you say, “Granted that he owes it, who will demand repayment?” He himself, because he cannot lie to anyone; he is both the executor and the debtor. He will not be harsh in repayment, since he has been lavish in giving.

Believe God, man, in what God has given you. The giver wishes to return greater things when he wishes to become a debtor.

[Col. 0272A]

## SERMON XXVI  
### On the faithful steward

What the Lord is read to have answered Peter today, in the form of a figure addressed to the apostles themselves, to teachers especially, and to those [Note: [Col. 0271D] The Apostle truly calls these people “stewards of God’s ministries.” For, as Theophylact says here, p. 190, it is not necessary for everyone to supply the word of God, but only for those for whom it is needed, when it is suitable, and in the manner required. Gregory of Nazianzus, *Oration* 32, p. 518, calls the pastors of the Churches “οἰκονόμοι τῶν ψυχῶν καὶ τοῦ λόγου … ταλῶαι”—“stewards of souls and … dispensers of the word.”] who preside over the Churches, was heard by many.

Peter asks: “Lord, do you speak this parable to us or also to everyone?” The Lord answered him: “Who, then, do you think is the faithful and wise steward whom the master appoints over his household, to give them their measure of grain at the proper time? Blessed is that servant whom his master, when he comes, finds doing so. Truly I say to you, he will appoint him over all that he possesses.

“But if that servant says in his heart, ‘My master is delaying his coming,’ and begins to beat the boys and the female servants, and to eat and drink and become drunk, the master of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour that he does not know, and will cut him apart and appoint his portion with the unbelievers.”

This likeness first binds the rulers of the Churches, [Note: [Col. 0271D] Several commentators agree with Chrysologus in judging that “stewards of God’s grace” in Titus I, 7, refers to all the faithful, who ought to display the gifts received from God for the benefit of others.] but this figure excludes no human being, no mortal whatsoever. For while it speaks to the steward, it answers everyone through the one who asks.

If there is anyone who has received nothing from God, he will not fear the examination of his stewardship or the duty of a steward. But, man, if you received the very thing you give, how can you deny that you received what you possess?

From the heavenly stores, from the divine granaries, he will render an account; he will state his grounds [Note: [Col. 0272C] A term, as has been observed elsewhere, familiar to Chrysologus. It means the same as “steward.” For it was the steward’s customary duty to provide servants with their ration. An ancient inscription cited by Pignorius reads:

> SIGN OF HERCULES  
> DORUS, SLAVE OF LARCIUS, STEWARD,  
> WHO WAS FORMERLY THE FARM MANAGER OF THIS PLACE.

Chrysologus here speaks of the distributor of grain, who in ancient inscriptions was called the grain supplier or grain agent—unless this responsibility belonged to the supplier and agent because they sometimes performed this kind of office. Cassiodorus calls them treasury-keepers and procurators of grain. Another stone cited by the same Pignorius reads:

> To the divine spirits of the dead.  
> To Asclepiades Acthitus, freedman by birth,  
> grain agent.

]

According to Ennodius, *Book I, Letter 3*, one finds *prorogare litteras* (“to defer letters”); and in *Book III, Letter 14*, *prorogari scripta* (“writings to be deferred”).] [He is] the Church’s prolonger. And the greater the trust he undertakes, the greater the debt he does not hesitate to declare that he will repay [Col. 0272C], as the Lord says: “From the one to whom more has been entrusted, more will be demanded” (Luke XII). And elsewhere: “The powerful will suffer powerful torments” (Wisdom VI, 7). The higher a man has risen, the higher he will fall. What is higher than heaven? The one who sins falls from heaven while among the heavenly beings; the one who offends under the very eyes of the Ruler falls into despair; and the one who commits a crime with the Judge himself as witness has no excuse. Or what defense does he hope for whose accusation is supplied by the testimony of the one who knows him?

Thus, when the devil was an angel and lived in heaven, always most radiant in God’s presence, shining while he tested God’s ears and while he grew proud in God’s sight, [Col. 0273A] he fell to earth, was cast down to Tartarus, and was changed from an angel into a devil; and he who had been [Note: [Col. 0273C] Mita holds that the devil was once a minister of forgiveness, because the protection of human beings had been assigned to the angels. Quite rightly, indeed. Origen, in *Against Celsus*, Book VIII, p. 400, says that angels help human beings toward salvation. See Chrysostom, Homily 159, vol. V, p. 958; Basil, on chapter VIII of Isaiah, vol. I, p. 1012, where [Col. 0273D] angels are called guardians of the human race.] a minister of forgiveness [Note: [Col. 0273D] Of human beings, namely, and of angels: for under his leadership and persuasion angels who followed him, as well as human beings, sinned, as it is said in Revelation XXII, 14: “He dragged with him a third of the stars.” MITA.] became the leader of punishments.

Hence the Apostle warns a man of our order not to fall into pride and the devil’s snare. Therefore the steward of the divine word and the deferrer of heavenly doctrine, who continually stands before the Lord, always moves among the altars, and never withdraws from God’s eyes; who receives the cases of sinners and the people’s sorrows, presents and presses their prayers, accepts them, reports them, and restores what has been obtained; who, wholly transformed from a human being into an angel, can do nothing but sin in the very presence of God, among the holy of holies—so that he takes his crime from the very place from which he was accustomed to bring forgiveness to others.

Finally, when Nadab and Abihu, priests and sons of Aaron the priest, presumed to pollute the altars with foreign fire, they were themselves consumed by the fire of the altar, so that those who had made sin out of propitiation might receive punishment from the sacrifice (Leviticus X). Drunkenness had stirred up that sin in them: for the odor of wine had driven out the odor of incense, and the fire of drunkenness had provoked the flame of the altar. Therefore, because they had been estranged by wine and carried foreign fire, they were immediately extinguished by divine fire.

Drunkenness is a crime in another person, [Note: [Col. 0273D] See the canons ascribed to the Apostles, rule 42; *Adversaria to Barthius*, Book LV, chapter 1; and Valerian, Homily 19, in Sirmond, vol. I, p. 396.] but sacrilege in a priest, because while another kills his own soul with wine, a priest extinguishes the spirit of holiness, as the Apostle says: “Do not extinguish the Spirit” (I Thessalonians V, 19). Rightly, among the other things that today’s sermon condemns in the wicked steward, it condemns the madness of wine, saying: “But if that servant should say, ‘My master is delaying his coming,’ and should begin to beat the boys and the maidservants, and to eat and drink and become drunk.”

He specifically said: “to eat and drink, and [Col. 0273C] to become drunk, and to beat.” [Note: [Col. 0273D] So great a harvest of evils arises from drunkenness that, if even a few were listed, the limits of a note would be exceeded. See Gregory of Nyssa, *Homily on Baptism*, vol. II, p. 221; Basil, Oration 14, p. 489; Chrysostom, Homily 17 on First Corinthians, vol. V, where he enumerates many more harms of drunkenness, none very unlike those which Chrysologus mentions here; and Augustine, *To the Holy Virgins*, which Camerarius praises while pursuing this same subject, *Opera subcisiva*, vol. I, p. 443. For satiety, consult Stuckius, *Antiquitates convivales*, Book III, chapter 8.] Drunkenness is the mother of slaughter, the parent of quarrels, the begetter of madness, and a disgraceful teacher of shamelessness: whoever has it does not possess himself; whoever has it is not a human being; whoever has it does not commit sin, [Note: [Col. 0274C] A drunken person does not commit sin while drunk, because, through the failure of reason, he does not possess free will. But, as soon as he wished to become drunk, he was a sinner. St. Thomas, *Summa theologiae* II-II, question 150. Once drunkenness has been contracted, however, it becomes sin itself, because, while he is in the sin of drunkenness, he would in no way then wish to rise from it, since he neither understands it nor recoils from it by free choice. Hence a drunken person is called “sin”: that is, he is immovably turned away from the good of repentance while the drunkenness itself continues. MITA. — But perhaps Chrysologus did not need such distinctions, since here he used “sin” to mean abuse and reproach, etc.] but is himself sin.

Drunkenness is [Note: [Col. 0274D] The opinion that drunkenness can be likened to a demon is not Chrysologus’s alone. Basil, Oration 14, calls drunkenness a voluntary demon. Chrysostom, Homily 74, vol. V, p. 582, after himself calling drunkenness a voluntary demon, adds that a drunkard is worse than one possessed by a demon.] a pleasing demon, a sweet poison, voluntary madness, an invited enemy, a lure away from decency, and an injury to modesty. Let no Christian know it; let not even a priest touch it by hearing of it, lest one who is a model of virtues should thereby become an example of vices and be found to exemplify them.

But [Col. 0274A] since enough has been said about us and about ecclesiastical men, let us inquire how the Savior’s reply concerns everyone: that no one is found to be outside God’s stewardship. Let us examine the Apostle’s saying: “There is no authority except from God” (Romans XIII, 1). If all authority is from God, then the king too has received from God the dignity of royal stewardship. Thus the commander, the soldier, and the governors of provinces and cities—all these will have to render an account if in any respect they have exceeded the measure of the authority entrusted to them: whether the king guarded justice, whether he maintained equity, whether he moderated his power, whether he did not neglect mercy, whether he held the balance of his office so evenly that the scale of his authority did not incline to either side [Note: [Col. 0274D] I have preferred this form, following Latinius. The editions, after weighing the matter, read otherwise.], whether he cared for everyone, whether he secured the peace of the citizens, and whether he regulated the tax in such a way [Col. 0274B] that neither what was sufficient was lacking for the soldier nor the taxpayer was exhausted.

The commander, too, will give an account to God if he offered himself as an example of virtue to those who followed him; if he was ever-watchful on guard duty, tireless in his movements, and sought the peace of all through his own labor. The soldier also will render an account if he obeyed orders, extorted from no one, and repaid his wages through the most just labor.

The judge, too, will face the heavenly Judge of his own judgment. And you, who are master of your household: I want you to regard yourself as an appointed steward rather than a master, so that you may show your wife sincere affection and wisely pour into her the teaching you have learned in the Church. To her the Apostle commanded silence in the Church and instructed her to learn at home from you, saying: “Let women keep silent in the churches; but if they wish to learn anything, let them ask their husbands at home” (I Corinthians XIV, 34).

Give your children sober affection and attentive care, and faithfully raise them in the discipline of the Lord. Give your servants the food and clothing owed to them; forgive their faults; moderate threats; impose discipline; and regard as brothers in heavenly lineage those whom, in worldly servitude, you possess as subjects.

You servants, too, owe your master faithfulness in the very servitude you perform, because whoever, with a devout and pure heart, does not render the service owed to a human master is held accountable before God, who sees hearts, before he is accountable to man—the God who has made you equal by grace, though your condition had made you unequal through the degradation of servile status.

What shall I say about the rich man? The more he has, the more he owes.

Some material is missing.

Finally, he returns and hands over at the same time to another; if he does not wish to return it, let him entrust it to individuals in separate portions. And you, poor man, should not consider the stewardship entrusted to you a small one merely because it is poverty, if you bear it patiently, are not ungrateful, and are sober and frugal even in need; if you thank the giver and do not, in blasphemous abuse, heap insults upon the one who does not give; if you ask only as much as mercy gives, not as much as importunate desire compels.

Certainly you too, poor man, who readily ask, should also readily give to those who ask. But perhaps you say, “I have nothing.” Let there be the will to give, and the means of generosity will not be lacking. Set out your chair for the arriving guest; set out your table, your candelabrum, your lamp. At least gratefully offer something from what you have received.

Thus Elijah (I Kings XVII), and thus Elisha (II Kings IV), when they entered the empty and impoverished homes of widows, abundantly supplied what the widows lacked. But the Lord added the following to confirm this parable: “That servant who knew his master’s will and did not prepare himself and did not act according to his will will be beaten with many blows; but the one who did not know and did what deserved blows will be beaten with few.”

The one who sins knowingly [Note: [Col. 0275D] II Peter II, 21: “For it would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to turn back.”] rightly pays more grievous penalties of conscience; but this one, too, through faults of ignorance, will not avoid the blows of ignorance. Just as one may not despise God, so one may not be ignorant of him. [Note: [Col. 0275D] Tertullian, *On Repentance*, says that ignorance does not protect anyone from punishment.]

## SERMON XXVII. [Col. 0275C] On Removing Scandal

When battle is imminent, the soldiers’ watches are always distributed, so that nothing may be allowed to ambushes and nothing be exposed to deceit. A sudden enemy is exceedingly destructive: either he overtakes the uninformed, or he catches the careless unawares, or he crushes those who are asleep.

Hence Christ our King, from before the ages, throughout the night of this age, warned his soldiers, assigning beforehand successive watches, against the devil—that is, against the most subtle deceit of the ancient enemy; against the hidden assaults of vices; against the ambushes of crimes that rush upon us; against scandals that arise for us from various causes; against the temptations of the present life; and against the burning battle-lines of worldly pressures. He warned them thus: “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation” [Col. 0276A] (Matthew XXVI, 41).

[Note: [Col. 0275D] At the first watch people go to bed, and Christ does not name it. The second watch was the night watch, when deep sleep had already begun. The third watch was already in the middle of the night; toward its end the fourth approaches, which is the time for rising. Christ therefore wishes us to keep watch at the very time when everyone is asleep, namely, during the second and third watches.]

And, establishing how one should keep watch, he added: “And if he comes in the second watch, and if he comes in the third watch and finds them so, blessed are those servants whom, when he comes, he finds watching” (Luke XII, 39, 37). And plainly they are blessed, because those who keep watch and anticipate the enemy’s deceptions will rejoice in the coming of their Lord.

Today, however, the Lord aroused and armed the watches of our commanders against scandals, saying to the disciples: “It is impossible that scandals should not come” (Luke XVII). That is: it is impossible that enemies should not come. First, brothers, we must understand what these scandals are. [Note: [Col. 0275D] See Basil, *Shorter Rules*, response to question 64, pp. 550–551.]

There are different kinds of scandals. The first are those produced by the devil’s fraud. The second are those generated by human cunning. The third are those born from our own suspicious and unwary nature.

Those are from the devil which deceive by appearances, which present good things while bringing evil—as in the case of Adam, when the devil took away what was human from us while promising what was divine (Genesis III). So too in the case of Peter: “This shall never happen to you, Lord” (Matthew XVI). He attempts to empty the triumph of the cross, while pretending to burn with excessive love. For when the Lord was speaking of the glory of his passion, Peter answered: “This shall never happen to you, Lord.” How sweet is the serpent’s poison! Beforehand it makes the king’s soldier deny his victory, so that the servant himself would deny his Lord.

Therefore the Lord sends the servant behind him and sends the scandal back to its author, saying to Peter: “Get behind me,” and to the devil: [Note: [Col. 0275D] These words were not literally spoken to the devil, but to Peter by Christ. Chrysologus must therefore be understood as saying that they are addressed to the devil, who through temptation was suggesting to Peter that he should not think about the things of God but about the things of human beings, as Origen says in his commentary on Matthew, p. 286. [Col. 0276D] The name Satan, which means “adversary,” was applied to those who opposed the divine will. Origen, *Against Celsus*, Book VI, p. 306. Moreover, Satan, called *Satanas* in Hebrew and by some in the more Greek form *Satanas*, means “adversary.” As for the etymology of the word, Justin, in his *Dialogue with Trypho*, p. 331, indulges in astonishingly pleasant error.] “Satan, you are a scandal to me” (Matthew XVI, 23).

And Peter truly goes behind the Lord, because, in order to follow him to heaven, he climbed the cross with his face turned upward.

There is also that scandal of the same kind which he caused for the Jews. He scored the broad stone laid to steady their footsteps into a universal and sharpened stumbling-block; he turned the rock of the entire foundation into a scandal, so that it might become a cause of ruin for the wretched. “Behold,” he says, “I place in Zion a stone of offense and a rock of scandal” (Isaiah VIII, 14).

Hence the Psalmist asks in anxious supplication: “Guard me from the snare which they have set for me, and from the scandals of those who work iniquity” (Psalm CXL, 9). And because he had passed beyond offense and conquered scandal, he glorifies himself thus: “You have raised me up upon a rock and led me, because you have become my hope” (Psalm LX, 3–4).

We have described the first kind of scandal. Let us also describe the second, which we said arises from human cunning.
