Balaam the diviner placed a scandal before the Israelite people [Note: [Col. 0276D] When Chrysologus calls Balaam a diviner, he seems to agree with those who think that Balaam was not a prophet but a man devoted to magical arts. He is called a diviner in Numbers XXII, 5. See Origen, *Against Celsus*; the author of the *Opus imperfectum on Matthew*, Homily 2; Cyril of Alexandria, Books IV and VI of *Worship in Spirit*; Ambrose, *Letters*, Book I, recent edition, first class; Nicholas of Lyra; Cajetan; Brugensis; Jansen; and Tirinius. Jerome, however, following the opinion of the Hebrews, thinks that Balaam worshiped the true God. Certainly Moses explicitly testifies in Numbers XXII, 8, 9, 12, 18, 19, and 20 that he worshiped the true God, whom Balaam himself calls “the Lord my God” in Numbers XXII, 18. Augustine, in Book II of *Diverse Questions to Simplicianus*, article 9, question 46 on Numbers, left the matter, as he found it, still pending judgment.] [Col. 0277A] (Numbers XXXI; Revelation II, 14), when, instead of confronting the soldiers with armed men, he sent against them young women adorned with every kind of seduction, so that he might turn weapons into lust, change triumph into disgrace, summon the avengers of guilt upon guilt, and finally profane the whole of holiness through depravity.

Hence Moses marked him with this sentence when he punished him: “Kill Balaam the diviner, for he sent this scandal before the children of Israel.” [Note: [Col. 0277D] It is clear from Numbers XXXI, 16 that Balaam advised King Balak to send beautiful Moabite girls into the Hebrew camp to incite the Hebrews to fornication, on condition that they first eat food sacrificed to idols and worship their gods.]

Jeroboam devised a scandal (I Kings XII), when he placed golden calves among the people as gods through a lamentable fabrication, so that the people would not seek the living God, the true temple, the divine law, legitimate kings, or ancestral rites.

Thus a people enslaved to error creates scandal, according to the Apostle (I Corinthians VIII), when someone eats food sacrificed to idols as though it could do no harm, and by such an act judges that senseless stones and wooden gods—which can neither sanctify nor defile—ought to be despised. But what he regards as an example of faith becomes an occasion of error for the ignorant, because it provokes them not to contempt but to worship, and makes a religious feast appear to the uninformed, whom the informed person consumes with deliberate mockery.

Therefore the Apostle rightly concludes and explains: “And the weak brother will perish through your knowledge, for whom Christ died” (I Corinthians VIII).

The third kind is the scandal generated for us from our own senses, when we are deceived by our eyes, deluded by hearing, captured by smell, and corrupted by taste. Thus Eve was wounded by the forbidden and deadly food both through taste and through sight. “And the woman saw,” it says, “that the tree was good for food, and pleasing to the eyes, and beautiful to behold” [Col. 0277C] (Genesis III).

Therefore the Lord rightly added that we must scandalize—or cut off—those very senses, saying: “If your eye or your hand causes you to stumble, cut it off and cast it away from you. It is better for you to come into life without an eye or a hand than to enter Gehenna with your whole body” (Matthew V, 18; Mark IX).

And although the Lord commanded us thus to cut off falls and vices, not limbs, nevertheless, if Eve, the mother of the human race, had done this, she would have entered life without an eye or a hand rather than sending her entire posterity lamentably into death.

Therefore, brothers, we must beware lest we cause scandal to others, and lest we ourselves suffer scandal when another causes it. Scandal is what offends the senses, disturbs the mind, and confounds the purity of understanding. Scandal is what made a devil from an angel, what turned an apostle into a traitor, what brought sin into the world, [Col. 0278A] and what led humanity to death.

Hear the Lord saying: “Woe to the world because of scandals” (Matthew VI). Scandal tests the holy, exhausts [Note: [Col. 0277D] So Latinius. The editions read “the unwary.”] the cautious, casts down the unwary, confounds everything, and disturbs everyone.

Although in the present passage the Lord is speaking about the scandal of his passion and is marking out Judas, through whom the scandal of scandals came, nevertheless, lest anyone should bring this about, he warned them, saying: “It is impossible that scandals should not come; nevertheless, woe to the one through whom they come. It would be better for him if a millstone were hung around his neck and he were thrown into the sea than that he should cause one of these little ones to stumble” (Luke XVII).

Why not simply a stone, but a millstone? [Note: [Col. 0277D] It was the duty of slaves to turn millstones and to deliver a fixed measure of flour on appointed days. Sometimes horses or asses were also used. Thus a millstone turned by an ass indicates a very large stone, for which an ass was needed to turn it. Jerome here, Vatablus, Mariana, Maldonatus, and others thought that it was a form of punishment among the Hebrews to sink extremely wicked people into the sea with an ass-driven millstone hung around their necks. Lyra, however, and many non-Catholic interpreters—Grotius, Lightfoot, Clericus—call the matter into question; and Calmet asserts that not even a trace of such a punishment is found among the Hebrews. He nevertheless thinks that it may have been introduced into Palestine by the Syrians or Romans. For the Romans, see Casaubon on Suetonius, *Augustus*, chapter 67.] Because a millstone, while grinding wheat, pouring out flour, and separating bran from the meal, supplies bread to those who labor piously.

Therefore it is fitting that the one who chooses to be a minister of scandal rather than of peace should have a millstone fastened around his neck, so that what ought to have drawn him toward life may draw him toward death. He has turned the senses given for life into scandal, persuading one to see something else, hear something else, feel something else, and taste something else from what was in Christ and in saving knowledge.

Thus he has circumvented and drawn the little ones into scandal away from the cornerstone (Isaiah XXVIII, 16), the stone of help (I Kings VII, 12), and the stone cut out without hands (Daniel II, 45), which is Christ, so that he would prepare not the bread of life but the bread of tears and sorrow, as the prophet testifies, saying: “You who eat the bread of sorrow” (Isaiah XXVI, 2). [Note: [Col. 0278D] The Fathers often explain why Christ is called the cornerstone. See Cyril of Alexandria on verse 16 of chapter XXVIII of Isaiah; Oecumenius on First Peter II; Chrysostom, Homily 111, vol. V, and Homily 6 on the Epistle to the Ephesians; and through him Theophylact, on chapter II of Ephesians; Theodoret on Psalm CXVIII; and others.]

It is fitting, therefore, that for the one of whom he elsewhere said, “Let a millstone driven by an ass be fastened around his neck” (Matthew XVIII, 6), punishment should come from the very place from which understanding came; and that he should be made equal to foolish beasts, since he refused to be compared with human beings who possess heavenly wisdom.

## SERMON XXVIII. On the Calling of Matthew the Publican and the Rich Man, and on Christ Eating with Publicans and Choosing Poor Apostles

That poverty is akin to the virtues is demonstrated by both earthly and heavenly discipline. The athlete approaches wrestling naked; the sailor struggles with the waves naked; the soldier stands in battle only when unencumbered [Note: [Col. 0278D] The manuscripts of Cesena and Vallicella read *astat*, “stands.”]; and the one who strives toward philosophy first despises everything that belongs to worldly possessions.

Poverty, then, is akin to the virtues. And if poverty is the parent of the virtues and is held as their companion, it is worth considering why Christ chose the poor for the work of virtue in this way.

Peter and Andrew, James and John—a brotherhood joined, indeed a poverty doubled and redoubled—are chosen as the leading apostles [Note: [Col. 0279C] Either because they were chosen first, or because of their abundance of virtues. Theophylact calls Peter and John the summits of the apostles. For the word “apostle,” see Jerome, Letter 143 to Damasus, and Basnage, vol. I of the *History*, p. 288, at length; there he contends against Baronius that the term had not been adopted in Christ’s age. Yet we find it in John XIII, 16: *Οὐδὲ ἀπόστολος*—“nor is an apostle,” that is, one sent—“greater than the one who sent him.” Likewise in II Corinthians VIII, 23, brothers sent by the Church to collect alms are called *Ἀπόστολοι Ἐκκλησιῶν*, “apostles of the Churches”; and in Hebrews III, 1 Christ himself is called Apostle, either because he is the prince and head of the apostles, or because, as Theophylact says, he was sent to the sheep of the house of Israel.] : poor in wealth, lowly in station, insignificant in craft, obscure in life, [Note: [Col. 0279D] As if he were saying that they practiced some common and ordinary trade. We may assert, against Maldonatus and Theophylact, who did not exclude natural aptitude in them, that the apostles were deprived of all gifts of fortune and nature and were called solely by God’s nod and will, together with Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, Book VI, p. 480; Hilary, *On the Trinity*, Book II; and Origen, *Against Celsus*, Book II, p. 135.] common in labor, devoted to vigils, bound to the waves, denied honors, handed over to injuries, and seeking food and clothing solely through the catch of fish, with the support of a net.

But however contemptible they appeared to the world’s gaze, God’s regard then saw souls of such great worth in them. They were poor in wealth but rich in innocence; lowly in station but exalted in holiness; insignificant in craft but precious in simplicity; obscure in life but shining through the merit of life; common in labor but singular in purpose; devoted to vigils but already called to heavenly victories; bound to the waves but not drowned by the waves; denied honors but enriched with honors, not truly denied them; handed over to injuries but not abandoned to injuries; catchers of fish but already destined to be fishers of human beings.

“Come,” he says, “and I will make you fishers of human beings” (Matthew IV, 19), so that by casting living food and by the hook of the heavenly word they might raise souls from the gulf of death into everlasting light.

Catchers of fish become fishers of human beings. From one labor they pass to another, because labor, when practiced, does not know how to grow weary [Note: [Col. 0279D] That is, “trained.” For *meditari* can mean not only to turn over in the mind but also to practice. Thus Plautus says in *Stichus*: “And I shall practice preparing myself for the race at the games of Olympia” [Col. 0280C]. Labor practiced—that is, frequently undertaken and exercised—becomes lighter through use itself. MITA.]. Everything that comes through practice does not weary. Virtue persists through exercise.

Hence Christ wished to train his apostles through human labors, so as to make them tireless in divine labors. God wished strength to remain in them and virtue to be supplied through exercise. And because fruit comes from labor, he wished them not to lose their labors but to change them. He first granted them practice in labor, and afterward gave them endurance in virtue.

Hence they overcame kingdoms, nations, prisons, chains, tortures, deaths, and savage men throughout all the earth.

We have said that poverty, friendly to the virtues and dear to God, was chosen in the apostles. What shall we say of Matthew, whom Christ chose from the tax office as a rich man, wealthy through interest, and weighed down with the profits of the world? [Note: [Col. 0280C] Tribute is called *telos* in Greek; hence *telonium*. It was the place where public taxes were collected, situated near the sea so that they could be paid there by those crossing over.]

Today Matthew himself began his account in this way: “And as Jesus passed on from there, he saw a man sitting at the tax office, named Matthew; and he said to him, ‘Follow me’” (Matthew IX).

The term “publican” [Note: [Col. 0280C] This is what the Jews called those whom they detested as profane, either because of their way of life or because of the impurity of their conduct. It does not mean that all publicans were Gentiles, as Tertullian wrongly thinks in *On Modesty*, Book I, chapter 9; Jerome rightly attacks him in Letter 146 to Damasus, where he clearly proves that they were Jews, as is evident in Matthew from his father’s name, Alphaeus, and from his own name, Levi. If someone wishes to say that some publicans were Gentiles, I would grant this only of the chief publicans, whom the Greeks call *δημοσιώνας* (*dēmosiōnas*), that is, contractors for public revenues; not of their inferiors and assistants, such as Matthew. I think no one is unaware that publicans were honored among the Romans. Cicero, in his letter to the praetor Silo, calls them “very distinguished men” and praises them highly in his speech *For Plancius*. But among the Jews they were hated and despised because they served the greed and tyranny of the powerful.] presents us with no small question through his profits, and proposes a major difficulty through his business.

But someone says: “What question? What difficulty?” God receives the poor, but he does not reject the rich. He receives and draws to himself those who have, as well as those who do not. Abraham was rich (Luke XVI), Job was rich, and David was rich. And who was more blessed than Abraham? Who stronger than Job? Who holier than David?

For Abraham, after earthly sorrows, also gathers pious souls as they fly back to heaven into the bosom of his consolation. And Job, amid the very structures of his wealth, himself conquered the devil and left us an example for conquering him. Abraham possessed riches in such a way that he often both despised those offered to him and trampled upon those granted to him (Genesis XIV); he loved to possess riches, but not to be possessed by riches; to have them as material for generosity, not as fuel for greed.

But the answer to this is that the riches of the saints were innocent, since they were given by God and not acquired dishonorably; granted for the use of life, not for the interest of death.

In Matthew’s case, however, riches so proclaimed him a teacher of greed, so baked him in the furnace of avarice, and so bound him in the chains of obligations and weighed him down with the burdens of moneybags, that he could not rise toward innocence, stand upright in justice, or advance toward virtue.

Hence his sitting already meant sinking, not sitting. Why, then, did Christ call such a man to himself and choose him for divine things? Unless the matter is examined more deeply, it presents the deepest possible question—and not merely a question, but also a scandal, as the intention of those standing around made clear at that time.

For how could human weakness not be troubled when it saw money possessing such power with Christ that he gave trust to a fraudster, grace to a seller, the office of generosity to a teacher of greed, the mastery of holiness to a teacher of interest, and the heavenly secret to a publican of the world? It burned those who saw it that usury, which devastates the earth, was being taken up into heaven, and that the Godhead was summoning to itself the very thing people detest.

Matthew himself reveals that the onlookers thought this way at the time, for when he was about to tell the truth about himself, he could not remain silent about it: “And when Jesus was reclining at table in the house, behold, many publicans and sinners came and reclined at table with him and his disciples. But the Pharisees, seeing this, said to his disciples, ‘Why does your teacher eat with publicans and sinners?’”

The Pharisees said this so that it might be a great evil, something that even evil people could dislike. And if it was unlawful for publicans to share in Christ even at a meal, what was it for a publican to share in divine things? [Note: [Col. 0281D] It was a firmly established custom among the ancient Hebrews not to eat with adherents of another religion or with those who practiced some despised and degrading occupation, lest they should come into contact with anything unclean. See Genesis XLIII, 31; John IV, 9.]

Brothers, the interpreter’s ingenuity would labor over this question if the Lord himself, to whom the question is addressed, did not remove everything that makes it a question. Let us therefore return to the order of the reading and hear why Christ came to Matthew.

“As he was passing by,” it says, “Jesus…” He did not say, “when he was standing there.” Jesus passed and passed beyond that place [Note: [Col. 0281D] That is, having left the house and going out toward the sea.], lest Matthew remain there. Jesus passed beyond that place, lest Matthew remain there [Note: [Col. 0281D] We have retained this reading from the Vatican manuscript; some editions have a different reading.] in such a condition.

“He saw a man.” He did not say, “he saw Matthew,” because in Matthew he had liberated a human being. That is, those whom money possessed cannot serve God while serving money. “You cannot,” he says, “serve God and mammon” (Matthew VI).

“Come, follow me.” He did not say, “Bring it to me,” because he sought Matthew, not Matthew’s moneybags. “Come, follow me.” That is: lay down your burdens, break your chains, loosen your snares. Follow me. Seek yourself; lose your interest, so that you may be able to find yourself.

But let us now hear what he answered the Pharisees: “Those who are well have no need of a physician,” he said, “but those who are sick.” Behold why Christ had come to Matthew: to heal the wounds of avarice, to cure the pus of usury.

“Go,” he said, “and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy, and not sacrifice.’” He desired mercy so that Matthew might extend into acts of mercy what he had taken through misery, and redeem punishment from the very source from which he had acquired guilt.

“I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.” By saying this he did not reject the righteous, but excluded those who falsely claimed to be righteous [Note: [Col. 0281D] Pharisees of this sort.].

Therefore, in coming to sinners, Christ wished to erase sins; he did not wish to remain with sinners. Just as giving life to a dead person is [Note: [Col. 0281D] That is, just as it belongs to divine power, not to created nature, to restore the dead to life, so it is the work of the right hand of the Most High for a miser to distribute his goods. Therefore Matthew’s recall from usury and the distribution of his resources for pious uses was a divine gift. MITA.] giving life to the dead, so giving generosity to a miser is giving life.

Thus, in calling Matthew, Christ was not establishing an accounting of money but a whole accounting of virtue. Finally, Matthew immediately became poor on earth, so that he might be considered rich in heaven.

## SERMON XXIX. On the Same Matters, and on Gold
When the Lord calls and raises Matthew the publican to the summit of apostleship, he gives a hand to the fallen, restores hope to the despairing, and returns to life those whom death had already claimed for itself. “As he was passing by,” it says, “Jesus saw Levi, son of Alphaeus, sitting at the tax booth” (Mark 2). He was sitting, certainly, because he could not stand, crushed beneath the weight of greed and bent wholly inward by the consciousness of fraud. Gold is heavy by nature; through excessive avarice it becomes heavier still. Hence it weighs down the one who possesses more than the one who carries it, and burdens hearts more severely than bodies. It is born deep in the earth, follows the very foundations of the mountains, and runs through the lowest parts of the veins in blind winding passages; and, while it always seeks its own [Note: That is, since by its nature it loves obscure places and those buried deep.] nature, it lowers heavenly souls to the underworld. It continually darkens the senses and continually sinks the heights of the mind into earthly things.

To distribute gold is good; to hoard it is evil; to despise it is strength; to flee it is safety. For just as conquering it is a mark of virtue, so escaping it is a mark of happiness. The frenzy for gold burns more fiercely in the human breast than an entire furnace glows with fire, and it dissolves human beings into the earth more violently than heat melts things in flames. It is the master of cruelty, a savage enemy: by being loved it injures, by enriching it strips bare, it even captivates the gaze, breaks faith, violates affection, wounds charity, disturbs tranquility, removes innocence, teaches theft, advises fraud, and commands robbery. And why say more? This is what the Apostle said: “The love of money is the root of all evils” (1 Timothy 6).

There is, indeed, one exchange, if a prudent person sends it beforehand to heaven before he, like a fool, is sent by it to Tartarus. Let him send it through the hand of the poor, because whatever he gives to the poor for God’s sake he sends without delay to heaven. Rightly, then, the Lord, wishing Matthew to be released from such bonds, raises him, impeded as he was, saying: “Follow me.” That is: Follow me, who am advancing from the heights toward the heights, and do not plunge gold from the underworld into the underworld. “Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matthew 6).

Gold so corrupted the stock of the patriarchs, the holy offspring, that unique crown of kinship, and made it so completely alien to all piety, that they handed Joseph over to the Egyptians, their brother to barbarians, the innocent to criminals, and his free birthright to slavery (Genesis 37). [Note: The Vatican manuscript reads *ingenuum*, “the freeborn man.” Yet, in keeping with Chrysologus’s style, the editor has preferred the reading of the Caesena and Vallicellian manuscripts. It was not, however, the price of gold which they received from the Ishmaelites that brought Joseph’s brothers to sell him; rather, they were moved by jealousy because his dreams foretold that he would rule over them all. Nevertheless, there are Fathers who evidently shared Chrysologus’s opinion on this point.] Thus it dried up their minds, thus depressed their hearts, thus changed whatever human feeling had been in them into bestial frenzy, so that it did not allow them to remember either God’s offense, the grief of their holy father, or the awareness of their own blood.

Consider what is heavier than gold: when it destroys human character, it destroys nature as well. Gold so captivated the Jewish people by its appearance, conquered them by its allurements, and deceived them by its appearance, that they believed it to be God and denied the true God, whom they knew through so many benefits. It so transformed human beings into beasts that they believed the head of a calf to be their own head and set the head of a beast before the head of all things (Exodus 32).

[Note: Not all the holy Fathers thought that only a calf’s head had been fashioned by the Hebrews. Cyprian and Ambrose, Letter 62, and Lactantius, Book 4, chapter 10, hold this opinion. Some therefore report that from this arose the pagan slander that the Jews worshiped the head of an ass; it is sufficiently and abundantly established that this later passed over to the Christians of the earliest age, although it is more likely to have flowed from another source. Scripture, however, everywhere speaks of a calf and nowhere mentions the head alone. This was Apis, or Serapis, the Egyptian deity.]

[Note: More than one of the holy Fathers held that the Hebrews fashioned only a calf’s head. Cyprian, Ambrose, Letter 62, and Lactantius, Book 4, chapter 10, take this view. From it some derive the pagan calumny that the Jews worshipped an ass’s head—a calumny which, as is abundantly established, later passed to Christians in the earliest age, although it is more likely to have arisen from another source. Scripture everywhere says “calf” and nowhere mentions the head alone. This was Apis, or Serapis, the Egyptian deity.]

Observe how this evil must be avoided: after destroying human character, honor, and life, it even wished and endeavored to take God himself away from humanity. This is what made Judas a betrayer: it compelled a human being to deny God, sell the brother of his own blood, traffic in the Creator, and set a price even on the blood that the Lord was freely going to give for our redemption (Matthew 26).

But, lest a multitude of examples on this subject produce weariness, let us proceed to what remains.

“Follow me,” and rising, he followed him. Virtue is often found useful even in an enemy, and is often proved in an adversary. Matthew is not withdrawn from his work but changed; he takes up the tax booth rather than abandoning it, so that he may gather what would remain for God instead of perishing for humanity. He is not to be the gloomy accountant who reduces the thirtieth coin to the fortieth and the fiftieth, but is to store up, with joy, the thirtieth multiplied into a sixtieth and a hundredfold fruit, destined to benefit divine purposes.

And rising, he followed him. What a noble spirit, which so easily and, as though they were nothing, despised the things he had considered great! It is clear that through ignorance he had previously sought present profits; but as soon as he realized and saw himself freed from them, he was thus [Note: He felt himself moved by a hidden force, by which he was drawn gently and pleasantly, yet with the greatest intensity. See Augustine, *On the Grace of Christ against Pelagius*.] swept away toward divine things.

“And it happened, while he was reclining at table in his house, that many publicans and sinners were reclining with Jesus and his disciples.” Jesus was reclining more in Matthew’s mind than at the table [Note: That is, the table, as noted elsewhere. Concerning the Greek letter sigma, see Petrus Colum Brugensis, note on Sidonius, p. 19, where he corrects Lipsius, who was mistaken in *Lectures*, Book 3, in his exposition of a passage of Lampridius.], and he was feasting not on food but on the sinner’s return. Through fellowship at table, companionship, human affection, and the sweetest conversation with him, he sought to recall those reclining there—people whom he knew could be undone by recognition of the judge’s authority, struck by the terror of his majesty, and immediately cast down by his bare presence—though he was veiled in a human body, since he wished to assist humanity.

He concealed the Lord, who deigned not to deny servants confidence; he veiled his majesty, who sought to embrace the frail in a parent’s love.

But the Jews were offended, saying: “Why does your teacher eat and drink with publicans and sinners?” Do you marvel, Jew, that he mingles in the company of sinners, when for sinners he both wished to be born and did not refuse to be killed? You bark because he drinks the wine of sinners, though for sinners he poured out his own blood. And if you wish to understand further, he himself took sin upon himself so that he would not destroy sinners; as judge, he turned the sentence against himself, thereby revealing that he had loved sinners more by paying the debt than by simply forgiving it.

But let the Lord’s own answer to such people suffice: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick”; for “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.” And who was not sick, when the nature of the human race itself was so sick? He therefore came to all, since he found all in need of healing. But plainly the one deserved to die who despised the physician lest he accuse himself or confess that he was sick.

The Lord immediately discloses the meaning of his saying, declaring: “For I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.” Here the Lord does not reject the righteous but the proud [Note: The Pharisees were the most arrogant class of people: while they despised others as sinners, they proclaimed themselves righteous.], and he reproves those who, although they are not righteous, boast that they are.

And where were the righteous, when, according to the prophet, “There was none who did good, there was not even one” (Psalm 13)? Let them understand their sickness and admit the physician in order to be healed; let them confess that they are sinners, so that now Christ, as parent and host, may grant forgiveness [Col. 0284B], lest later, as judge, he impose on the obstinate the deserved sentence without end.

## SERMON XXX. On the Same Subject

Today’s Gospel reading so transformed Matthew the publican into an apostle that he who had been a defrauder of money became a distributor of grace, passed from the school of impiety to the teaching of piety, and became a teacher of mercy who had been an instructor in avarice. “As Jesus was passing by, he saw a man sitting at the tax booth, Matthew by name” (Matthew 9).

“As Jesus was passing by from there”: rightly, he was passing by from there. He was passing from Judaea in order to come to the Gentiles; passing beyond the Synagogue, so that the Church might endure; passing beyond the homeland of the flesh, in order to return to the seat of his divinity. In Christ, brothers, the injury of the flesh is transitory, while the honor of divinity is everlasting.

“As he was passing by from there, he saw a man.” He saw more with divine than with human eyes. He saw the man in order not to see the man’s sins. He saw his own work in order to disregard the works of sins. God saw him [Note: By his gaze God enlightens sinners, so that, once they recognize their most wretched condition, they may return to him through repentance. St Gregory: “No one sees God spiritually who lives carnally; for whoever has seen God thereby dies, wholly separated in mind from the delights of this life.” MITA.], in order that he might see God. Christ saw him in order that he might see the hiding-places of money no longer. Christ saw him sitting because, weighed down by greed, he was unable to rise.

Brothers, this publican sat more grievously at the tax booth than the paralytic of whom we spoke before lay upon his bed. For the latter suffered paralysis of the flesh, this man paralysis of the mind; in the former the framework of the limbs had been disordered, in this man the whole order of the senses had been scattered. The former lay captive in the flesh [Note: That is, deprived of all the powers of his limbs.]; this man sat captive in body and soul. The former unwillingly succumbed to pains; this man voluntarily served vices [Note: From these words it is abundantly clear that, in Chrysologus’s sense, Matthew was not some noble contractor of public revenues, of whom see the notes to the preceding sermon, but the servant of the public contractor—more aptly called a toll-collector or exacter, one of a class devoted to cruelty, avarice, and plunder. Chrysostom, vol. 6, Homily on Punishments, or 79, calls them traders in others’ misfortunes. Theophylact, Homily 15, p. 88, says that the term *portitor* includes an avaricious, unjust extortioner and lover of gain.]. This man regarded himself as innocent in the crime of avarice; the other recognized himself as a sinner amid his wounds. This man heaped up sins through profits; the other wiped out sins by groans of pain [Note: Although the Lord praised only the faith of those who carried the paralytic, it must nevertheless be said that the paralytic was undoubtedly so disposed by inward compunction of heart as to deserve both forgiveness of sins and bodily health.].

Rightly, therefore, the paralytic is told, “Take heart, son; your sins are forgiven you” (Matthew 9), because he had compensated for his offenses by pains; but the publican is told, “Come, follow me.” That is, by following me, repair what you lost by pursuing money.

But someone says: Why does the publican, who seems greater in guilt, receive a greater gift? For immediately endowed with the assured dignity of apostleship, he not only received forgiveness of sins himself but granted it to others; he illuminates the whole world with the splendor of Gospel preaching, while the paralytic is scarcely deemed worthy of forgiveness alone. Do you wish to know why the publican obtained more? Because, according to the Apostle, “where sin abounded, grace abounded still more” (Romans 5).

We know that the publican bears the type of the Gentile people, while the paralytic is the figure of the Jewish people, which even today is held upon the bed of ill health; unless it is carried by the faith of the Gentiles, presented to Christ through the compassion of the saints, and saved by the belief of the Christian people, it cannot come to the house of faith, to the house of its homeland.

“And while he was reclining in the house, behold,” he says, “many publicans and sinners came and reclined with him and his disciples.” But when the Pharisees saw it, they said to his disciples: “Why does your teacher eat with publicans and sinners?” God is accused because he bends down to humanity: why does he recline with a sinner? Why does he hunger for repentance [Note: Another reading: “the repentant person.”]? Why does he thirst for the return of sinners? Why does he accept the dishes of mercy? Why does he drink the cup of piety?

Brothers, Christ came to dinner; Life came to the banquet, so that he might make those destined to die dine with him. Resurrection lay down, so that those lying in tombs might rise; Forgiveness reclined, so that it might raise sinners to pardon. Divinity came to humanity, so that humanity might come to divinity. The judge came to the dinner of the accused, so that humanity might forestall the sentence of guilt. The physician came to the sick, that by dining with them he might restore the exhausted. The good shepherd bent his shoulders to carry back the lost sheep in safety to the fold.

Yet the Pharisee detests and condemns this, thinking the Lord’s meal to belong not to virtue but to the belly; not to the spirit but to the flesh; not to divine goodness but to human pleasure; to earthly luxury, not heavenly grace. Thus, thus does one see oneself who does not see God. Who condemns a physician lying beside those who lie ill [Note: Caesena manuscript: “lying with one who lies.”], unless he is an enemy of human salvation? Who reproves a shepherd supporting weary cattle, unless he knows nothing of love for a profitable flock? Who judges a judge for mercy unless he is hopeless? Who scorns communion with God, unless sacrilegious? Who shudders at forgiveness, unless cruel?

“Why does your teacher eat with publicans and sinners?” And who is a sinner except one who denies that he is a sinner? [Note: The Caesena manuscript reads: “the teacher himself is the teacher of sinners.” MITA accepts both readings: “He who denies,” he says, “that he is a sinner is called a sinner in the antonomastic sense, because comparatively he has a greater sin than others. For he contradicts God, who says in the sacred pages that no human being in this life is without sin.” Concerning the other reading, he adds: “He becomes a teacher of sinners by disseminating false doctrines, like the Pelagians and Caelestians in Augustine, Sermon 29 on the Words of the Apostle, who assert that there is a human being who is not a sinner and does not need Christ’s restoration. Indeed, from a sinner and teacher of sinners he becomes sin itself, because, unwilling to confess himself a sinner, he becomes finally unrepentant, rejoicing in his miserable condition and devoid of amendment.”] He is himself more of a sinner—and, to speak more truly, he is now sin itself—who no longer understands that he is a sinner. And who is unjust except one who judges himself just?

You have read, Pharisee, that “no living person shall be justified in your sight” (Psalm 142). As long as we are in a mortal body and frailty rules in us, even if we conquer sins in deed, we cannot conquer sins of thought and escape injustices. Even if we can avoid them in the body and overcome an evil conscience, how can we abolish the faults of negligence and the sins of ignorance?

Pharisee, confess your sin so that you may come to Christ’s table; so that Christ may be bread for you and that bread itself may be broken for forgiveness of your sins; so that Christ may become a cup for you, poured out for remission of your offenses. Pharisee, dine with sinners so that you may dine with Christ; acknowledge yourself a sinner so that Christ may dine with you. Enter with sinners into your Lord’s banquet, so that you may cease to be a sinner. Enter the house of mercy with Christ’s forgiveness, lest with your own righteousness you be punished, shut outside the house of mercy. Acknowledge Christ; hear Christ; hear your Lord; hear the heavenly physician decisively refuting your calumnies: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick.” If you desire healing, acknowledge your illness. “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.” If you desire mercy, confess your sin. “Go,” he says, “learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice’” (Hosea 6). Christ desires mercy and not sacrifice; or what sacrifice would he seek, who himself became a sacrifice in order to seek you? “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.” He did not reject the righteous, but no one is deemed innocent on earth without Christ. “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.” In saying this he did not reject the righteous, but found all to be sinners. Hear the Psalmist: “The Lord looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see whether there is one who understands or seeks God. All have turned aside; together they have become useless; there is none who does good, not even one” (Psalm 13). Brothers, let us be sinners by our confession, so that by Christ’s forgiveness we may not be sinners.

[Col. 0287A]

## SERMON XXXI. On the Fast of the Pharisees and John’s Disciples

Goodness is the mother of virtues, wickedness the source of vices; glory accompanies virtues, while kindred shame clings to vices. Just as vices are covered by deceit, so virtues are made radiant by freedom. Hence Christ, the light of virtues, acted freely, spoke purely, gave as God, suffered as a parent, and reproved as a lord. But the Jews, a viperous offspring, the death of their mother and the slaying of their father, while killing Christ tore open the womb of the Synagogue, their mother. [Note: He alludes to the commonly repeated claim that vipers come to life by gnawing through their mother’s womb. Chrysostom, Homily 11 on Matthew, p. 69: “This animal destroys its mother, devours her womb, and comes forth into the light.” Theophylact says the same on Matthew 3, p. 18, as do Isidore of Pelusium, Letter 105, Book 1, pp. 32–33, and others. See what will be said more fully in the notes to Sermon 138.]

Truly, as it is written, “Brood of vipers” (Matthew 3), they bowed their heads, flattered with their tongues, inflicted wounds by deceit, and poured out poisons through blasphemies [Col. 0287B]. And as though contempt had not been enough for hatred, nor disdain enough for injury, they thus pursued Christ with plots, tested him with deceit, attacked him with questions, assailed him with insults, and surrounded him entirely with greedy pretense.

They brought forward people to be healed on the Sabbath, so that, if he did not heal them, contempt might arise from his inability, while, if he did heal them, slander might flow from the law. They asked by what authority he performed miracles at his command (Luke 20), so that, if he said “by divine authority,” they might arouse envy, and, if he remained silent, charge him with magic. For they said: “By Beelzebub, the prince of demons, he casts out demons” (Matthew 12). And, as was read today, among the disciples they fabricated against the master an accusation concerning the meal with publicans.

Among the master’s disciples they accused those ignorant of fasting of being devoted to gluttony; but against the disciples because of the master, and against the master because of the disciples, they cast about causes of hatred and seeds of discord through envy.

“Then the disciples of John came,” it says, “saying: Why do we and the Pharisees fast frequently, but your disciples do not fast?” (Matthew 9)

And what fellowship was there between John’s disciples and the Pharisees? Only because envy had joined those whom discipline had separated [Note: John’s disciples, driven by a certain zeal for their master, had been led into envy of Christ. The Pharisees therefore sent them to attack Christ’s disciples. Or, as Chrysologus says here, in agreement with Augustine, *On the Harmony of the Gospels*, chapter 17, and as Chrysostom seems to think, they approached the Pharisees and joined themselves to them.].

Here zeal now forfeits its own rights: it has become accustomed to join what it ought to separate. The Jews could not bear Moses being placed after the Lord; John’s disciples would not tolerate Christ being placed before John in any respect. Thus both parties raged against Christ with a shared envy.

“Why do we and the Pharisees fast frequently, but your disciples do not fast?” Why? Because among you fasting belongs to the law, not to the will; fasting regards not the one who fasts but the one who does so willingly. And what fruit of fasting is there for you, when you fast an unwilling fast? [Note: This concerns not the public fasts prescribed to the Jews by the ancient law in Leviticus 1:29, but those which they observed on fixed days by private rule, by their teachers’ command, or by each person’s own decision. This was customary among Pharisees, who sought a reputation for it, twice every week and sometimes more often. John’s disciples also fasted, especially at the time when their master was detained in chains.]

Fasting is a singular plow of holiness: it cultivates hearts, uproots crimes, tears out transgressions, overthrows vices, sows charity, nourishes abundance, and prepares a harvest of innocence. The disciples of Christ, therefore, established in the entire field of holiness and gathering sheaves of virtues, already possessing the bread of the new harvest, cannot fast the obsolete fasts.

Fasts which are vaunted in words, displayed through pallor, and advertised by bodily weakness please human eyes, not divine ones.

“Why do we and the Pharisees fast frequently, but your disciples do not fast?”

The Lord answered: “Can the sons of the bridegroom fast while the bridegroom is with them?” [Note: Namely, those who had attended the wedding, whom Chrysologus appropriately calls the bridegroom’s friends. For just as virgins accompanied the bride, so companions and friends accompanied the bridegroom. See Judges 14:11. In Greek they are called ὁμήλικες (*homēlikes*), in Latin *aequales*, “equals.” From this Gospel passage the Montanists extended fasts and dry-food abstinence even after Pentecost, because, once the bridegroom had been taken away, the bridegroom’s sons ought to fast. See Jerome on Matthew 8. Perhaps Chrysologus is alluding here to their error.]

What does this mean? When John was asked, he testified that Christ was the bridegroom: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice” (John 3).

Appropriately, therefore, John answered the disciples concerning their master’s voice, so that they might either believe him and not force the joyful time of the bridegroom to enter sadly into fasting. For one who seeks a bride puts aside fasts, abandons austerity, gives himself entirely to joy, indulges in feasts, and proceeds wholly gentle, wholly attractive, wholly festive, doing everything that the bride’s tender affection requires.

Christ, therefore, who at that time was betrothing the Church [Note: It has been observed elsewhere that Christ is called the bridegroom of the Church. Grotius says, on John 3:29, that this follows the example of God, whom the prophets call the husband of the Hebrew people.], gave himself to meals, did not refuse those feasting with him, and made himself human, gracious, and charming through devoted love, until he joined human things to divine and transformed earthly fellowship into a heavenly union.

The Lord added, saying: “No one puts a patch of unshrunk cloth on an old garment; for it takes away its fullness from the garment, and a worse tear results” [Note: Among the Hebrews, “to join” means to mend or patch, and, by adding a piece of cloth, to repair a garment. Here “fullness” means the tear repaired by a sewn-on patch. A new loss will result if you join new cloth to old cloth; for when the patch does not hold, a new tear is made. See the same comparison in Luke 5:36. Philo has something similar when he explains the law that forbids weaving wool and linen together: “Not only,” he says, “does difference reject association, but the superiority of one causes tearing rather than union.”]

He calls the furniture of the ancient law worn out by Jewish observances [Note: Jerome, Euthymius, Chrysostom, Theophylact, and others likewise interpret the old law as a garment worn out through use, and the Gospel as unshrunk cloth. From this the Marcionites inferred that these two laws could not be joined together and that there was not one God, the author of both. See Tertullian, Books 3 and 4 *Against Marcion*; Epiphanius, *Heresies*, 42; Augustine, Book 4 *Against Faustus*.], torn by corrupt understandings, ripped apart by sects, and made threadbare by impure practices.

[Note: That is, new or never altered. Jurists too contrast new garments with garments that have been refurbished. Paulinus also uses *rudis* in the sense of “new” in Letter 31, p. 198 of the recent edition:

> “And surrounding the unshrunk lambs with festive altars,”  
> poem 27, *On the Nativity*, 10, p. 654.

> “A single beauty shines.”

> “In aged and unshrunk places.”]

He calls the unshrunk cloth the garment of the Gospel. But listen: the cloth is not a piece torn from a garment, but the beginning of a fabric. For then, for the first time, the fabric of a royal garment was being woven from Christ’s fleece—from the fleece given by the Lamb: “The Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1). The royal garment was being woven, its purple splendor to be dyed by the blood of the Passion.

Rightly, therefore, Christ forbade this unshrunk cloth to be put onto Jewish antiquity, lest a worse tear result if Christian newness tore apart Jewish old age.

He doubles the example, saying: “Nor do they put new wine into old wineskins; otherwise the wineskins burst, and the wine is spilled, and the wineskins perish. But they put new wine into new wineskins, and both are preserved.”

[Col. 0289B]

He calls the Jews old wineskins and Christians new wineskins. For just as leather wineskins are cleansed of every impurity and coated with fragrant substances so that no unpleasant odor may enter the wine [Note: Wineskins are goat skins prepared by craft, sewn together like a sack, thoroughly cleaned, and treated with fumigants so that no unpleasant odor may enter the wine. Hence the Greek expression ἀσκὸς αἴγειος (*askos aigeios*), “goat-skin vessel,” since the Hebrew *nebel*, “leather vessel,” is translated by the Septuagint as ἀσκὸς. Christ speaks in the Gospel according to the custom of the Syrians, who, especially when traveling, enclosed the wine they carried with them in wineskins.], so human bodies are cleansed by fasts of every defilement of carnal sins and become wineskins suited to the divine winepress, so that from the press of the cross [Note: The press and winepress are the same thing, suited for pressing grapes. The cross is often compared to a winepress, based on the words: “I have trodden the winepress alone.”] they may receive new wine and preserve its uncorrupted newness.

But just as Christians receive this, so Jews, unless they become Christians, will not possess it. Corrupted by vices and grown old in evils, they will receive the new wine, which is the word of the Gospel, in such a way [Note: The editions based on the Vallicellian manuscript read: “and they burst, and they spill.”] that they burst and spill it.

It must therefore be recognized that through these examples Christ did not refuse to have his disciples fast; rather, he refused to mix true fasting with fraudulent fasting.

## SERMON XXXII. On the Man Who Had a Withered Hand
All the works of Christ’s signs, astonishing in their powers, must be believed to have occurred not by human agency or chance, but through divine providence, as today’s Gospel passage demonstrated to us. “And he entered,” it says, “into the synagogue, and there was a man who had a withered hand” (Mark 3) [Either according to custom, because it was the sabbath; or he had entered in order to be healed by Christ].

Christ indeed enters the synagogue [Synagogues were academies or gymnasia, so called by the Hebrews from *beth hamidrash*, “house of teaching,” as Buxtorf teaches. For further discussion, see Lamy, *On the Temple*, p. 662], but the Jew neither receives him as he enters, nor recognizes him as present, nor, blinded, understands him as he acts [Athanasius, vol. 1, p. 1075: “The hand itself was restored; but the dryness of mind in the Jews was not healed”]. See how little bodily presence accomplishes where there is a pitiable separation of mind; and, conversely, how little bodily absence accomplishes where hearts have been joined through faith.

“And there was there a man having a withered hand.” In this man the image of all human beings is represented; in him the care of everyone is enacted; in him the long-awaited healing of all is restored. For the man’s hand had withered more through the stupor of faith than through the dryness of his nerves, and more through the guilt of conscience than through bodily weakness [We read in the Gospel of the Nazarenes, which Jerome translated into Greek, that this man was a mason. Indeed, from continual contact with the cold materials of cement, mud, and so forth, atrophy arises, by which the part is gradually wasted and, for want of nourishment, dries up and withers, as our author says].

This illness was exceedingly ancient, and had occurred at the very beginning of the world. It could not be cured by human skill or assistance; it had been contracted through God’s justified indignation. He had touched what was forbidden and presumed upon what was not permitted when he stretched himself toward the tree of the knowledge of good and evil (Genesis 3). He needed its maker—not one who would apply a *malagma* [plaster or medicinal preparation; *malagma* comes from Greek μάλαγμα, “something softened,” because it is softened and formed without fire, as Isidore says, *On Etymologies* 4.9. See Cornelius Celsus, *On Medicine* 5.17; Augustine, *Sermon* 38 *On the Seasons*; Salvian, *On the Government of God* 3; and Fortunatus, *Life of Saint Germanus, Bishop of Paris*, who uses this word]—but one who could release the sentence imposed and, by forgiving, undo what he had bound by his indignation.

In this man only the shadow of our healing is enacted; our perfect salvation, however, is reserved in Christ. For the withering of our hand is mercifully dissolved when it is drenched with the blood of the Lord’s Passion; when it is stretched out upon that life-giving wood of the cross; when it plucks fruitful power from suffering; when it embraces the entire tree of salvation; when the Lord’s body is fastened with nails—so that it may never again return to the tree of desire and withered will.

“The Pharisees watched,” he says, “to see whether he would heal on the sabbath, so that they might accuse him” (Mark 3) [For they watched to see whether he would heal, in order to denounce him thence to the court, where violators of the sabbath were punished]. To the disgrace of the judge and the wickedness of the examiner, healing is treated as a crime, piety as an accusation, virtue as guilt, and salvation as a punishment. But this is not surprising: good things always offend the wicked, pious things the impious, holy things the profane. Or when has the licentious not accused discipline, the vicious virtue, or the guilty innocence?

The priests watched anxiously on the sabbaths, not to see whether he would sin, but whether he would heal, so that they might accuse him. Lovers of crimes keep vigil and lay snares in order to accuse virtues, as though the sabbath had been established against salvation, rather than for salvation. “If he would heal on the sabbaths,” they watched. With such an interpreter of the law, I will not say that the sick man suffers greatly; rather, he completely expires.

The sabbath did not impiously deny care to the sick; in complete piety it sometimes granted rest to mortals wearied by excessive labor. And he said to the man who had the withered hand: “Rise into the midst”—you who proclaim your own weakness, exact the help of heavenly piety, bear witness to divine power, and assert Jewish unbelief. “Rise into the midst,” so that those whom such great signs do not pierce, whom such great works of salvation do not bend, may at least be constrained and softened by compassion for so great a weakness [Excellent. For he called him into the midst both to make everyone attentive and because the very sight of the wretched man might soften the hard hearts of those standing around].

Then he says to them [Since the Hebrews thought that it was not even permitted to attack an enemy on the sabbath, Christ here asks whether, if it is not permitted to do harm, it is at least permitted to do good]: “Is it permitted on the sabbaths to do good or to do harm, to save a life or to destroy it?” By saying this, he commends the goodness of his work and accuses their awareness of the malice they had conceived. For while he intended to save the man in body and soul, they, eager to accuse him, sought to destroy him. They were allowing him to heal on the sabbaths, lying in wait to see whether he would heal, so that, once he had healed, they might condemn him through the malignity of their judgment. Thus their endurance was worse than the malice itself, and they were more frenzied in deceit than they were demented in such a judgment.

“But they were silent. And looking around at them with anger, he was grieved at the blindness of their hearts.” He is said to have looked around at them, not merely to have looked at them: that is, he did not gaze upon only their faces as a human being, but, as God, contemplated their bodies, hearts, minds, thoughts, past, present, and future. “Looking around at them with anger, he was grieved” [Christ’s anger was not a desire for vengeance, but indignation against vices; and he was grieved over sins as a parent pities sinful children. A. Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* 4, p. 535, calls God ἄθυμος, “unmoved by anger.” In the Greek Gospel text, instead of “blindness,” some read πώρωσιν, “hardness”]. He grows angry as Lord, is grieved as parent, suffers as human being, and looks upon them as God.

He says to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” And he stretched it out, and his hand was restored. “Stretch out your hand”: by this command the hand that had been bound by a command is released [The Gospel explains only the atrophy; but Christ’s words, “Stretch out your hand,” show that he suffered from a double illness, namely contraction as well as atrophy. Chrysologus agrees with this view when he says that by Christ’s command the hand was loosened. For what the Gospel calls “withered,” Vatablus calls “contracted,” in Greek ἐγκύλτοσα, “bent inward,” with the nerves bending and contracting it].

“Stretch out your hand” [That is, the withering of the hand recognized through experience that the true judge was present, the one who had condemned it. *Mita*]. Punishment recognized the judge; the work revealed God; mercy disclosed the creator.

Pray, brothers, that only the Synagogue may be darkened by such a weakness, and that there may be no one in the Church whose hand greed withers, avarice contracts, robbery weakens, and covetousness constricts in sickness. But if the same thing should occur, let that person hear the Lord and quickly stretch out the hand in works of piety, loosen it, and extend it in mercy and almsgiving. The one who does not know how to lend to the poor does not know how to be healed.

Then the Pharisees went out and immediately took counsel with the Herodians about how they might destroy him. The Jew is always joined with the Herodians [Maldonatus, on Matthew 22, no. 23, argues that the three sects most divided from one another—the Pharisees, Herodians, and Sadducees—yet closely united to mock and deceive the Lord, prefigured the various sects of heretics: opposed to one another in religion, but nevertheless treacherously agreeing to persecute Christ, that is, the Catholic Church. *Mita.*] in order to attack Christians.

The Herodians were either servants, courtiers, or rather supporters of Herod—those who stood on his side. For many favored Herod as he planned to secure the kingdom for himself, while others opposed him. They seem to have been Sadducees by religion; for they wished Herod to consult with them so that they might establish his doctrine and he might establish their kingdom. If we accept the Talmudists’ view, who teach that they were the same as the Dositheans, the reason would become clear why they were angry with Christ over his violation of the sabbath. Their doctrine was that they should remain in the position in which the sabbath day found them until evening. But Origen contradicts this in *Against Celsus* 1 and 6, where he says that Dositheus came after Jesus and persuaded the Samaritans that he was Christ, the Son of God. Epiphanius likewise distinguishes the Dositheans from the Herodians: he says that the former were Samaritans and the latter Jews. Chrysologus agrees, saying that the Herodians were always allied with the Jews.

“Jesus,” he says, “with his disciples withdrew toward the sea.” [Mita explains Chrysologus’s thought through highly appropriate comparisons: “The sea destroys the one who rashly entrusts himself to it; the Jews voluntarily attack Christ in order to destroy him without cause. The sea submerges the body, not the mind, honors, or virtues; the Jews seek to destroy all these things in Christ. The sea does not always rage; the Jews rage continually. The sea acknowledged Christ as its creator when, at his command, a great calm arose and he walked upon it with dry feet; the Jews, though taught in the law to recognize the Word of God incarnate for us, refused to acknowledge him, and killed him.”]

Thus, by comparing the waves, he proved and displayed the Jews’ more wicked error. But because Jesus, with the boat serving him—that is, the Church [It is rightly said that the Church serves God. For this word means to remain in someone’s service, and is therefore commonly used of attendants]—withdraws from the confusion of the crowds; because the governor of the Christian people sits tirelessly at the helm, healing in various ways; and because he commanded the winds and the sea (Mark 4) [The manuscript of Cesena reads, “so that they may become quiet from their unrest through obedience”], until at last they become calm through the obedience of tranquility, in accordance with the prophet: “Let us break their bonds and cast their yoke away from us” (Psalm 2)—so that, remaining under the yoke of piety, we may be worthy to share in divine glory.

## SERMON XXXIII. On the Daughter of the Ruler of the Synagogue and on the Woman Suffering from a Flow of Blood

[Sometimes, and most often, the reading of sacred Scripture preceded the sermons in church. Examples are evident. We have discussed them elsewhere.]

Today, dear brothers, you will hear—and together with me learn from the holy evangelist Mark—how the authority of the Synagogue collapses and falls before Christ, and how it confesses him in two ways as God and Lord: when it adores him in accordance with the commandment of the law, saying, “You shall adore the Lord your God” (Deuteronomy 6), and when it identifies him as the restorer of life by pleading for the salvation of its dying daughter.

“A certain ruler of the synagogue named Jairus,” he says, “came to him; and when he saw him, he fell at his feet and begged him earnestly, saying, ‘My daughter is at the point of death; come, lay your hand upon her, so that she may be saved and live’” (Mark 5).

Before the Gospel discourse opens the sacred meaning, I would like at this point briefly to reveal the sufferings of parents, which they undertake and express through their affection and love for their children. With the household standing around amid the tender and gentle attentions of relatives, the delicate daughter lies sick in her little bed. The father, bowed down, lies prostrate and turns upon the ground. She is failing in body; he wastes away in mind and spirit. She endures the hidden sufferings of her illness; he, foul and mournful, is carried and tossed about publicly in the crowd. She dies for rest; he lives for punishment.

And indeed we have omitted the anxious vows of parents when they beget children [That is, the arrangements and positions of the stars at the time when children are born. He is speaking of human births according to astrologers, as below in Sermon 157 in the notes. *Mita.*—The orders of the stars are often mentioned in Scripture: Judges 5:20; Jeremiah 31:35; and Job 38:33: “Do you know the order of heaven?”], the perilous arrangements of the stars when they bring forth offspring, their sorrowful labors and continual pains when the children fall ill, and the day of death, worse still, when their dear ones precede them [That is, when the child dies before the father. Some manuscripts read *procedunt*, “go forth,” that is, when the corpses of the children are carried out for burial. *Mita.*].

Alas, why do children not know so much? Why do they not feel these things? Why do they not labor to repay their parents in kind? Yet the piety of parents endures, because whatever parents spend upon their children, God, the parent of all, will repay to the parents.

But let us return to the subject. “A certain ruler of the synagogue, named Jairus, came and, seeing him, fell at his feet and begged him earnestly, saying: ‘My daughter is at the point of death; come, and lay your hand upon her, so that she may be saved.’” That he laments the extremity of his daughter with tearful entreaty and so pleads for a remedy to her illness proves and demonstrates how utterly desperate his emotion was. Hence he asks for the order of the cure in this way: “Come, lay your hand upon her.” The sick man does not prescribe how he should be cured; he merely begs to be cured.

But since he was ruler of the synagogue, he possessed knowledge of the law; and, having read in the word that the human being had been formed by the hand of God, he believed that the same hand by which he had understood his daughter to have been created could restore and return her to life [The manuscript of Vallicella and Mita’s edition read “could do so”]. We understand what “Come, and lay your hand upon her” means: he asks that the one who voluntarily laid his hand upon her in creating her might, once again entreated, lay it upon her for restoration [Excellent. For more learned commentators wish “I beg and entreat you to come” to be understood here].

This is what the prophet acknowledges when he sings in the Psalms: “You formed me and placed your hand upon me” (Psalm 138). For the one who laid his hand upon me when he formed me from nothing placed it upon me again in order to reform what had been ruined.

Finally, when the same Psalmist felt the saving power of this hand and obtained its generosity, he broke forth again in song: “The right hand of the Lord has shown strength; the right hand of the Lord has exalted me; the right hand of the Lord has shown strength” (Psalm 117). And to demonstrate that he had obtained what the ruler of the synagogue had requested, he added: “I shall not die, but live.” When he asked, the ruler had said: “Come, lay your hand upon her, so that she may be saved and live”; now, having received it, the Psalmist rejoices: “I shall not die, but live.”

Christ is the right hand of the Lord, as we are taught by prophetic speech. Truly he has shown strength: he conquers the devil; he binds the strong man and, as he himself said, plunders the strong man’s vessels (Matthew 12); he destroys hell; he puts death itself to death. Truly he has exalted us, whom he has lifted from the depths and raised to heaven.

But now let the discourse pass to the woman who sought a remedy for a hidden wound and shameful illness in such a way that she both concealed her shame and preserved reverence for the one who was healing her. “And he went with him,” it says, “and a great crowd followed him and pressed upon him. And behold, a woman who had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years, who had endured much from many physicians and had spent all her resources without gaining any benefit, but had grown worse, when she heard about Jesus, came behind him in the crowd and touched his garment, saying: ‘If I touch even his garment, I shall be saved.’ And immediately the source of her blood was dried up, and she felt in her body that she had been healed of the affliction.”

Not even two seas are thrown into confusion by their waves as violently as this woman’s mind was tossed about by the conflicting mass of her thoughts. After the desperate struggles with physicians, after costly medicines, after an ancient and fruitless treatment, when the skill and expertise of the healer had now failed [Some printed editions and the manuscript of Vallicella read: “when the skill had already failed.”

“The physician’s art does not always suffice to relieve the sick;
sometimes the illness is stronger than learned skill”],

when all the substance of the suffering woman had already been consumed, a shameful wound came before the very author of healing—not by chance, but through divine providence—so that what human skill had been unable to cure for so many years might be cured by faith and humility alone [That is, a wound from which, according to the author himself, a certain shame arose].

The woman stood at a distance. Nature had covered her with shame, and on account of this the Jewish law had marked her unclean, saying: “She shall be unclean and shall not touch the holy thing” (Leviticus 15). She feared touching him lest she incur Jewish fury or undergo the sentence of the law.

She did not dare speak, lest she confuse those standing around and burden their hearing; lest she become the subject of the crowds’ talk, since for so many years she had been the stadium and the *skamma* of her sufferings [*Skamma*, an Italian term, “target.” Among the Greeks σκάμμα most commonly denoted the place in a stadium or circus where athletes competed. Saint Ephrem, near the beginning of his book *On Spiritual Struggle*, says: “The *skamma* is the central place in which athletes competed.” More often it denotes the place of the contest itself: Chrysostom, on Psalm 48, says, “The *skamma*, where the stadium and wrestling are.” Sometimes it denotes the contest itself. Hence, in Henschius, σκάμματα are ἄγμυνες, “contests.” Other Latin Fathers also retained the Greek word. Tertullian, *To the Martyrs* 3, p. 191, and Ambrose, *On Duties* 1, say: “The athletes are still in the *skamma,” proverbially meaning that the contest for the prize is still under way; similarly Tertullian says “to bring into the *skamma*.” Suicerus observes in *Thesaurus* 2, p. 996, that Erasmus incorrectly read *ad stamma* in this passage. Paulinus, Letter 24 to Severus, p. 161: “While we are in the *skamma*, while there are battles outside and terrors within, do not think or speak lofty things on our behalf.” I do not recall seeing Mita’s interpretation anywhere].

For long and continuous pain did not allow her to bear and endure more; the speed of Christ as he passed by cut short the time for deliberation; and, on the other hand, she knew that if she remained silent and concealed her illness, healing would not be given her.

Amid these battles of thought, the woman found the one path to salvation: she would steal a cure, silently seize what she could not ask for, both because of her shame and because of reverence for the one who was about to grant it. What she did not deserve to reach bodily, she would reach in heart. By faith she would touch God; with her hand she would touch only his garment. She knew that this theft would provide not merely pardon but also a remedy, since it had been generated not by willfulness but by ashamed necessity—especially since she sought the profit of the theft and caused no loss to the one from whom it was taken.

A pious robbery, committed by faith as its servant and drawn on by faith. Behold where power was sought through opposites, and where a fraud, harmonized with faith, obtained what it strove for.

The woman approached among those pressing upon him, so that her action would not be known, and presumed that she could steal a cure by faith alone, hiding through her clothing and body. She approached from behind, judging herself unworthy even to be seen. Faith cured in an instant what human skill had been unable to cure in twelve years.

After this example, the one who through his own fault drags out long periods in illnesses and suffers for a long time through his own negligence is responsible, if he does not know how to be cured by faith alone but instead burdens himself with the expense of spices and medicines.

The evangelist says “the fringe of his garment.” In Greek, however, the word κρασπέδων denotes those threads that hang from the fringes of garments. Moses had commanded in Deuteronomy 22:12 that the Hebrews wear strips and fringes at the four corners of their cloak. Christ, most observant of the law, used this kind of clothing. And if we seek hidden meanings, she touched this particular part of the garment because the fringe was an emblem of the Jewish people and a mark of holiness (Numbers 15:38).

The woman touched his garment and was healed, and was freed from her longstanding illness. Wretched are we, who daily handle and receive the Lord’s body and are not healed of our wounds. It is not Christ who is lacking for the sick, but faith; for he, now dwelling in us, can heal the wounded far more powerfully, just as he healed the woman while passing her by [Alternatively, “remaining”].

Today, brothers, it is enough to have recounted the theft of faith and the power of the passing Lord. Why, then, does the Lord, as though unaware, ask for the woman whom he knows to have been healed by the work of his power? We shall explain this in the following sermon, since it is too long to do so now.

## SERMON XXXIV. On the Same Matters

All Gospel readings, dearest brothers, bestow upon us great benefits both for the present life and for the life to come. But today’s reading has both supplied everything that belongs to hope and excluded everything that belongs to despair.

Our condition is harsh and to be mourned: inborn frailty compels us to sin [While it binds our affections through evil pleasures, so that we are compelled, as if necessarily, to fall into sin. How disordered passions entice and draw our will toward unlawful things is discussed below in Sermon 41. *Mita.*], and shame akin to sin prevents us from confessing. To do evil is not shameful, but to confess it is; we fear saying what we do not fear committing. But today the woman [Pseudo-Ambrose, Sermon 48 in the appendix to the new edition of the works of St Ambrose, teaches that this woman was Martha. See Calmet’s remarks here, rightly rejecting this opinion; see also Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* 3.18, and Sozomen, 5.21], while seeking a silent medicine for a shameful wound [Carthusianus wrongly persuaded himself that she suffered from a haemorrhoid of the nose. All agree, however, that she suffered from an importunate female flow. Brugensis, as also Chrysologus below in Sermon 35, calls it a foul and shameful illness], found in silence a way by which the sinner might reach pardon.

The first happiness is not to have fallen into the shamefulness of sins; but the second happiness is to have found forgiveness for sins while they remain hidden. The prophet had understood this when he said: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered” (Psalm 31).

“Behold,” says the evangelist, “a woman who had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years approached from behind and touched the fringe of his garment” (Matthew 9). The woman fled to sudden faith, after her longstanding treatment had failed. She was ashamed to ask for a cure and wished to steal health; she wanted to remain unknown to the one whom she believed could save her.

As the air is disturbed by a storm of winds, so the woman was troubled by storms of thought. The cause struggled with faith, hope with fear, necessity with shame. The cold of fear extinguished the heat of boldness; the force of shame obscured the light of faith [Mita agrees with the Vatican manuscript, the Vallicella manuscript, and some editions, which read “the force of love”]; ashamed necessity shattered the confidence of hope.

Thus the woman, like a great sea, was tossed by confused currents. She sought to make what was public secret and what was among the crowd private. She acted so that health might return to her and her modesty not perish. She took care that her cure should not redound to the injury of the healer; she arranged that salvation might be restored to her while the reverence due to the Savior remained intact.

With such a state of mind, the woman rightly reached from the top of the fringe to the fullness of divinity [Chrysologus above, Sermon 33: “By faith she believed in God; with her hand she touched only the garment.” Ambrose, *On Luke* 6.9: “Christ is touched by faith, Christ is seen by faith; he is not touched by the body or grasped by the eyes,” and so forth. He understands the woman as the Church coming from the Gentiles and recognizes the apostles and their successors through the fringe, as below in this same sermon. *Mita.*].

“She approached from behind.” But where was “behind”? “And she touched the fringe of his garment.” She approached from behind. But where? Where there was no “behind,” she found the face from which she was turning away.

In Christ there was a multiple body [Because of the various and numerous parts of which it consists. See *Theology*, part 1, distinction 8, letter D. Or because of the mystical body, in which the apostles, teachers of the Church, and others are counted. *Mita.*—A multiple body, because it was all eye everywhere and all hand everywhere, as below], but there was a simple divinity [Because God is spirit, utterly simple. *Mita.*]. He was entirely eye, and thus saw behind him the suppliant woman.

“She approached from behind and touched the fringe of his garment.” O what did this woman see dwelling in the inner parts of Christ, who saw the whole power of divinity dwelling in Christ’s fringe! O how much did the woman teach about the body of Christ, who showed that so much was present in Christ’s fringe!

Let Christians hear this [We have restored from the first Bologna edition a passage corrupted in the printed editions]—those who touch Christ’s body daily—and learn what medicine they can receive from that body, since the woman seized complete healing from Christ’s single fringe. But what we must mourn is that the woman carried medicine away from her wound, whereas the medicine itself is turned back upon us as a wound [Some manuscripts read: “She took medicine for her wound from the fringe”].

For this reason the Apostle warns and laments concerning those who touch Christ’s body unworthily: “Whoever touches the body of Christ unworthily brings judgment upon himself.” And to show that from the very source from which faith ought to receive healing, presumption receives weakness, he adds again: “Therefore many among you are weak and sick, and many sleep” (1 Corinthians 11). He calls those who are dead “sleeping,” mourning those already buried alive in the body.

Peter and Paul, the princes of Christian faith, spread knowledge of Christ’s name throughout the whole world. The woman first handed down the discipline of approaching Christ; the woman first supplied the model of how a sinner [Latinus says that these and the following words must either be read cautiously or properly interpreted. Mita exerts himself greatly to extract and demonstrate a Catholic meaning from them, and explains that Chrysologus is speaking here of the silent confession that the sinner must first make in his heart before confessing his sins. What doubt could there be? Could Chrysologus have condemned auricular confession, when shortly before in the same sermon he had said: “To do evil is not shameful, but to confess is; we fear saying what we do not fear committing”?] may erase sin through silent confession without shame; how one who has sinned and is known only to God need not be forced to strip his shameful conscience before human beings; how a person may forestall judgment through pardon.

“But Jesus,” it says, “turning and seeing her, said: ‘Take courage, daughter; your faith has saved you.’” Jesus turned, not through bodily movement, but through the gaze of divinity. Christ turned toward the woman so that the woman might turn toward Christ, so that she might receive from him the healing from which she had received life, and know that the cause of her present wound had been the enduring reality of salvation.

“Turning and seeing her.” He saw her with divine eyes, not human ones. He saw her in order to restore her to salvation, not in order to identify someone whom he already knew. He saw her; whoever God sees is endowed with good things and free from evils. The whole world understands this usage when it speaks of the fortunate by saying: “God saw him.” God therefore saw this woman whom, by healing her, he rendered so fortunate.

And what more need be said? Christ taught through the woman’s example how completely faith alone advances a person toward salvation. But let us now speak of the ruler of the synagogue, who, while leading Christ to his daughter, opened the way by which the woman might reach Christ.

Thus began today’s reading: “Behold, a certain ruler approached and worshiped him, saying: ‘Lord, my daughter has just died; but come, lay your hand upon her, and she will live.’”

Christ, who knew the future, was not unaware that the encounter with the woman would take place.
