Through her, the ruler of the Jews would learn that God is not to be moved from place to place, led along a road, or dragged by bodily presence, but that he is to be believed to be present everywhere—wholly everywhere, always everywhere—and that he can accomplish everything by command rather than labor; send forth powers rather than carry them; drive away death not by hand but by authority; and restore life not by art but by a command [Similar passages occur in Theodoret, *Oration 2 On Providence*; Isidore, *Etymologies* 8; and Tertullian, *Apology* 7. Especially notable is the passage in Arnobius, *Against the Nations* 1, where he addresses God].

“My daughter has just died, but come.” This means: “The warmth of life still remains; traces of the soul are still visible; the spirit is still on the way; the master of the house still has a daughter; Tartarus does not yet know the dead woman. Therefore hurry, so that you may retain the departing soul.”

The fool thought that Christ could not raise a dead woman unless he physically held her. Hence, when Christ reached the house and saw the girl being mourned as though she were lost, he said that she was sleeping, not dead, in order to move unbelieving minds toward faith: they would believe that she could rise from death more easily than from sleep [Mita removes this reading and replaces it with the easier statement that one can rise from sleep more easily than from death. The author’s meaning seems to be this: Christ said that the dead girl was sleeping to indicate that she would be restored to life as easily as another person might be awakened from sleep].

“It is not,” he says, “that the girl is dead, but she sleeps.” And truly, with God death is sleep, because God restores the dead to life more quickly than a human being awakens someone sleeping from sleep. God pours life-giving warmth into limbs chilled by death before a human being can infuse vigor into bodies buried in sleep.

Hear the Apostle: “In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, the dead will rise” (1 Corinthians 15). Because the Apostle could not express the speed of the resurrection in words, he adapted examples. Or how could he touch upon the speed of speech where divine power itself anticipates that speed? But how can time appear there where an eternal reality without time is given? Just as time introduced temporality, so eternity excluded time [A span of time].

## SERMON XXXV. On the Woman Afflicted with a Flow of Blood
What it means to touch Christ was taught today by the woman suffering from a flow of blood. When she touches Christ’s fringe, she strikes the secret place of the divine breast, and [Note: [Col. 0299D] Saint Fulgentius, *On the Treatise*, book II, chapter 15: “Secretly touching the fringe, by a faithful rapture she steals for herself the effect of healing.”] by a theft of faith she snatched the supreme power from the very tip of the fringe. A blessed deception, which both [Note: [Col. 0299D] Some editions read *lucrum salvis* (“profit for the saved”).] brought the profit of salvation and immediately removed the shameful loss. [Col. 0299B]

The hearing of the Gospel reading proves this. “Behold,” it says, “a woman who had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years, coming up behind him, touched the fringe of his garment, saying to herself: ‘If I only touch his garment, I shall be saved’” (Matthew 9). In difficult illnesses, the force of pain often gives counsel; in desperate circumstances, necessity is frequently a teacher; suffering itself discovers its own remedy. Hence this woman found how to aid her shameful wound, so that by silence she might suggest to faith what she could not suggest by a public cry; so that by a hidden path of the spirit she might reach the heavenly physician, whom she could not reach by the manifest route of the flesh.

The compassion of the one who healed gave her great boldness, but the necessity of her shameful illness took away her confidence. The magnitude of her pain compelled her to approach Christ, but [Note: [Col. 0299D] Several printed editions read incorrectly, “to hear.”] the offensiveness of the ulcer did not permit her to approach [Col. 0299C] Christ without hesitation. Thus the woman, uncertain and with the counsel of faith trembling, [Note: [Col. 0299D] That is, she preferred to be judged by Jews and Gentiles for the faith she had in Christ rather than to perish thus from her foul wound. On this kind of faith of the woman with the hemorrhage, see Chrysostom’s homily cited at length above in note 13 on Sermon 33.] preferred to be judged for her faith rather than perish from her foul wound in this way.

She came up behind him and touched the fringe of his garment. Knowing that God is neither polluted by touch, nor offended by sight, nor irritated by smell, nor wounded by hearing, nor defiled by human thought—for if the sun touches dung without being polluted by dung, how much more does the Creator of the sun touch all things and yet remain incapable of being polluted by any contact? And if a physician, when he handles the pus of wounds and treats the shameful parts of the body, does not count it an injury but an honor, how much more does God not regard it as an injury when, in healing our wounds, he looks upon them, touches them for a remedy, [Col. 0299D] and visits them for salvation?

It is the wounds of sins, not of sufferings, that offend God’s sight; the diseases of crimes, [Col. 0300A] not the afflictions of bodies; the pus of vices, not the flow of the entrails—for a person is held voluntary in offenses, but in illnesses is regarded as unwilling. Hence the sinner receives punishment, while the sick person receives care.

The woman, therefore, conscious not of her will [Note: [Col. 0300D] Latinius emends this as “of pleasure.” I have retained the common reading. The woman was conscious of pain, not of will. The evil she suffered was involuntary.] but of her pain, not confounded by crime but confounded by illness, came up behind him so as to avoid the eyes of the crowd, not Christ’s gaze. She wished to be unknown to the people, not to Christ; she eagerly desired not to hide from God but from human beings, because she could be seen while hidden, heard while silent, and healed while concealed by God alone.

She came and touched the fringe of his garment. For she believed that nothing in Christ was last, judged nothing to be extreme: God is not diminished in a human being, power is not attenuated in a fringe, nor is the heavenly nature altered by the functions of the limbs. Hence the woman [Col. 0300B] reached the face by way of the back, penetrated inward through the garment, and touched the summit of the head through the fringe.

Nor is this without mystery. Hear the prophet saying: “Like ointment that descends upon the hem of his garment” (Psalm 132). You see, brothers, that the whole fullness of the divine chrism and the whole power of the divine head passed into the fringe of this garment. Therefore the woman knowingly longed to touch Christ’s sacred fringe, so that from the hidden mystery she might take medicine for her wound.

Brothers, this woman is great and exceedingly worthy of wonder. By knowledge she conquered the teachers of the Law; by sacrament she surpassed all the Jews; by faith she went before an apostle. For Judaism, with its scribes and teachers, wholly despised God in the body. The apostle Thomas, in order to believe Christ to be God, put in his hands, inserted his fingers, and opened the wounds; and, in order to believe Christ, [Note: [Col. 0300D]

He speaks figuratively. With great patience he allowed his own wounds to be touched and opened again by the apostolic finger, although otherwise he possessed a glorious and impassible body. Mita.

After completing this discourse, Chrysologus remained silent for a long time; he touched upon the reason for this silence in Sermon 86. Mita holds this view.]

made Christ suffer again (John 20).

But let us seek, by spiritual understanding, whom this woman represents, whose type she bears, and whose image she presents. Who is this woman whom congenital blood, natural weakness, and original disease brought into the straits of death, to a lethal wound, to the extremities of a foul illness; whom vices so befouled and crimes so defiled, whom secret wounds so injured, that human skill could not cure her, nor even the eye merely look upon her, nor decency tolerate her, nor the Law itself prevail to cleanse her—but whom the Law commanded to be kept away from the temple, excluded from sacred things, and to abstain from everything holy; whom it declared so unclean that whatever she touched was considered unclean?

This is, brothers, this is the Church, which, wounded by the sin of the first human being, flowed wholly with blood and, by its origin, wholly ran toward death.

[Col. 0301A]

## SERMON XXXVI. On the Woman with the Hemorrhage and the Daughter of the Ruler of the Synagogue

At this point Saint Peter became silent; the reason for his silence is fully explained in Sermon 86.

It is characteristic of a bashful debtor to discharge promises at once, and neither to deceive the creditor’s mind nor to keep it suspended by prolonged expectation. Since the connected and extended account of the ruler of the synagogue and the woman with the hemorrhage was departing from the customary brevity of our discourse, we preferred to divide the treatment in half, so that your hearing might not be burdened instead of refreshed.

The ruler of the synagogue meets the Lord, falls completely to the ground, reports his situation, reveals his grief, moves the affection of the one who can help, and commands him to hurry and come to the aid. Conversely, the Lord, unasked, meets the woman; while passing by, he presents an opportunity for salvation; remaining silent, he recognizes the cause of one who is silent; and he sees the hidden wound even of the woman who conceals it.

Between the Lord and the woman there takes place an exchange of stolen salvation of immense significance. While the one summoned makes a way by a public request, the thought of faith penetrates the divine presence and reaches the secret place. Blessed is the woman who, amid such a great crowd, is alone with Christ, so that she alone is conscious both of the salvation restored and of the exalted power! Blessed is she who found such an approach that no one could obstruct it! Blessed is she who by such a way snatched herself away and slipped in to her author; who, before being shamed by a human being because of her wound, was freed from the foulness of the wound itself, knowing that among human beings and through human beings the entire path to healing was closed to her—those who are accustomed more to shudder at wounds than to cure them!

God wipes away human wounds; he does not despise them. He neither recoils from human illnesses but drives them away, nor detests the uncleanness of the human body but corrects it, because God, who is God, does not know how to be defiled by contact with his creature.

But the evangelist creates a question when he says: “And immediately Jesus, knowing in himself the power that had gone out from him, turned to the crowd and said: ‘Who touched my garments?’” (Mark 5). When he asks, he seems to confess ignorance: he feels that power has gone out from him, but does not know to whom it went? He knows what he granted, but does not know to whom he granted it? Does he doubt the person, although he is certain of the salvation bestowed? [Note: [Col. 0301D] Christ looked around and asked in the human manner.]

Yet the Lord asks here not through the error of one who does not know, but with the majesty of one who knows and foreknows. He does not inquire about something hidden from himself; rather, he demonstrates that it is well known to him by revealing to all who were ignorant what had remained hidden, through asking in this manner.

He brings into the midst the silent petitioner, who had communicated only through her thoughts and, behind his back, clung to the counsels of his power—not as an ignorant examiner, but as a foreknowing investigator. He makes her stand before his eyes, so that she who had carried salvation away for herself might bring it back to all, and faith also [Note: [Col. 0301D] In many editions “faith” is absent.]; so that she who had experienced the power might recognize the majesty; and so that she might not return unknown, as she supposed, although she had given full knowledge of herself [Note: [Col. 0301D] From the Caesenatensis manuscript. The printed editions read “to herself.”].

While she was ashamed of her wound, while she feared him as God in the very act of healing, the woman endured no small cloud over her faith, and the light of her mind itself was darkened by the fog of confusion. Therefore the voice of the inquiring Lord, like a saving breeze, drove away the clouds, scattered the mists, and illuminated her faith. It made her, who had been hidden in the darkness of night, brighter than the sun itself. Or is she less than the sun who shines throughout the whole world and gleams and sparkles throughout the assembly of the entire Church?

If she had returned unseen, forgive her: she would have eluded the physician, not honored him; and she could have attributed what she had obtained to herself rather than to the one who healed her. She had believed that she had snatched her healing from the fringe of the healer, not from his will; or what had she believed belonged to the one whose power she had felt within herself, while by her desire she nevertheless judged it to be external? [Note: [Col. 0301D] As has been observed elsewhere, she wrongly supposed with the Jews that Christ’s power was something flowing from his humanity, as in Luke 6: “Power went out from him and healed them all.” In truth, power went out from him when it was manifested by his deeds. Hence interpreters here explain “power” as the effect of power.]

And yet, even if what was hidden had previously been a matter of modesty, and her judgment that she was unworthy a matter of humility, why, after being healed, did she not come forward voluntarily to give thanks, render honor, and proclaim the glory of so great a work? But after she saw that the Lord persisted in his inquiry, and after she perceived that she could no longer remain hidden, since the disciples offered excuses and objected to the pressure of the crowd, and after fear and the trembling of her conscience began to accuse her, she came into the midst so that she might openly confess and worship as God the one whom she had secretly experienced as a physician. Thus, for those present and for those to come, she became a remedy for so great an illness. The evangelist says: “But the woman, fearing and trembling, knowing what had happened in her, came and, falling before his feet, told him the whole truth.”

Yet because historical narration must always be raised to a higher understanding, and future mysteries must be recognized through present figures, what sacramental meaning is held under the figures of these persons—the ruler of the synagogue, his daughter, or the woman suffering from a flow of blood—must now be disclosed in an allegorical discourse.

The daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, to whom Christ comes, toward whom he goes and hurries, traveling by human steps—for divinity cannot advance spatially—is unquestionably the synagogue, as the Lord says: “I was sent only to the sheep that had perished from the house of Israel” (Matthew 15).

But while Christ is moving toward her, the Church, established among all nations, was losing and shedding the blood of the human race after losing the good of its nature. While human expertise tried to cure its illness, it increased it. For the judgment of human weakness, the severity of worldly discipline, and the continual bloodshed of peoples could neither abolish enemies, nor restrain the wars of citizens, nor eradicate the madness of crimes.

Thus, when she had been pierced by such treatments, and saw that whatever substance had been hers [Note: [Col. 0302D] The allusion is apt to the woman with the hemorrhage, for the Gospel says that this woman had spent “all her substance” — Greek: πᾶσαν τὴν οὐσίαν αὐτῆς (*pasan tēn ousian autēs*). Older copies have ὅλον τὸν βίον αὐτῆς (*holon ton bion autēs*), which a more recent translator renders “her entire livelihood.” The word βίος (*bios*) means both livelihood and everything by which life is sustained. Luke uses this word, and the Latin translator correctly renders it “substance.”] [Col. 0303A] had been consumed—that is, her spirit, mind, understanding, talent, labor, diligence, and reason, which we entrust to rulers as though to physicians for our improvement—when she sensed the presence of Christ passing by, she came up behind him, because, polluted by blood, she was not worthy to see him.

She came up behind him—that is, she followed the report of faith—and touched Christ’s extremities as though they were his fringe, since she is not honored in the patriarchs, not sanctified in the Law, does not boast in the prophets, and is not honored in the Lord’s own body, since she is regarded as alien to him in the order of Christ’s generation.

Behind him—that is, at the end of time—she follows Christ, is sanctified by the hidden sacrament of faith, and truly touches the garment that she found in the tomb, through which she believed and proclaimed [Col. 0303B] the insignia of the risen Lord. [Note: [Col. 0303D] He calls the signs of the resurrection “the Lord’s garments,” in accordance with: “He saw the linen cloths, and believed.”]

But while Christ is occupied with her through his powers, the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue grows weak and dies, and the synagogue dies, so that it too may return to life through faith, having died through the Law and perished through nature.

Meanwhile people come from the ruler’s house and say: “Do not trouble the teacher; the girl is dead.” Even today the Jews do not wish Christ to be troubled, whom they desire not to come; and they pronounce dead the one whose hope of resurrection they have faithlessly lost.

But how fitting is this further point for our assertion: the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue is reported to have lived for twelve years, while this woman is remembered to have persisted in her wound for twelve years, with salvation and life being restored to both at the final and completed term. For this number concludes the period of human life; and, to make a year, it is divided and counted into twelve months. Hence the prophet [Note: [Col. 0303D] According to the version of the Septuagint.] indicates that Christ came at the accepted year of the Lord; and the Apostle confirms that Christ came in the fullness of time, saying: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son” (Galatians 4).

Pray, brothers, that just as the synagogue, having died to itself and to the Law, might live for Christ, so we too may die to sins and to the flesh, in order that we may live in Christ.

## SERMON XXXVII. On the Sign of the Prophet Jonah

Brothers, the deeds of the saints must not be attributed to accidents but to signs; and what are thought to be their faults must be applied to mysteries, not to [Note: [Col. 0303D] Thus the Caesenatensis and Vatican manuscripts. Latinius, and some editions with him, read “stones.”] falls. This is what the Lord’s instruction signified and revealed today, saying: “As the crowds were gathering, Jesus began to say: [Note: [Col. 0303D] Christ’s very reply testifies that this sign was sought with an evil intention, not with a desire to learn but with a purpose of contradiction.] ‘This generation is an evil generation; it seeks a sign, and no sign will be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah. For just as Jonah was a sign to the Ninevites, so also will the Son of Man be to this generation’” (Luke 11).

Behold, the prophet’s flight is turned into a figure of the Lord himself, and the shipwreck that is celebrated as fatal becomes a sacrament of the Lord’s resurrection. For the text of the history written about Jonah shows how, in every respect, Jonah held and fulfilled the type of the Savior.

“Jonah,” it says, “fled from the face of God” (Jonah 1). Did not the Lord, in order to bear the face and form of a human being, flee from the face and form of his own divinity? The Apostle says: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2).

The Lord assumed the form of a servant in order to remain hidden from the world, to forestall the devil, and to flee into humanity [Col. 0304B] from himself. [Note: [Col. 0304D] From the Vatican manuscripts. The printed editions read “he fled himself.”]

And appropriately Jonah’s type of Christ is preserved in the words themselves. He did not say, “I flee from God,” but “I flee from the face of God.” Since God, who is everywhere, has nowhere to which he can flee from himself, Christ did not flee from the place but, as it were, from the appearance—the face—of divinity; he took refuge wholly in the countenance of our servitude.

“Jonah went down,” it says, “to Joppa [Note: [Col. 0304D] A coastal town. It is now called Jaffa or Joppa by the barbarians. Strabo speaks of it in this way in book 16: “Those who go down to the sea use this harbor.”], in order to flee to Tarshish [Note: [Col. 0304D] A city of Cilicia, which Solinus calls the “Mother of Cities.”].” Hear the one who descended: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven” (John 3).

The Lord descended from heaven to earth; divinity descended to human things; heavenly dominion descended to our servitude. Yet the one who had descended to the ship went aboard the ship in order to sail. Thus Christ, who descended into this world, boarded the ship of his Church through powers and miracles.

But what does the storm confused by winds signify except the devil, who, entering the heart of Judas, stirred up and inflated kings, nations, peoples, soldiers, judges, and sailors into waves, so that the rising and falling waves might seek the author of the world for rest?

Hear the waves of the world; hear the prophet saying: “Why did the nations rage, and the peoples meditate vain things? The kings of the earth stood up, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ” (Psalm 2). And because the lot that would expose Jonah was not lacking, he fulfills over Christ David’s prophecy, which says: “And over my garment they cast lots” (Psalm 21).

But when Jonah declares himself the cause of his own being thrown into the sea, saying, “Take me and cast me into the sea,” he indicates the Lord’s voluntary passion. For why do those men bear being commanded to do this, when they could have saved themselves voluntarily from such danger?

Whenever the salvation of many requires the death of one, death is placed in the will of the one who is to perish, because the will can delay the one who is going to die from death, and [Note: [Col. 0305C] We have corrected this according to Latinius’s emendation. For what is “the delay of the one in danger,” as the printed editions read? Chrysologus’s meaning is: when the death of one is required for the salvation of many, and that death lies within his own power, his will can delay death, or his impending death can forestall the danger.] the death of the one in danger can forestall the danger [Note: [Col. 0305D] Some corrupt editions read “reach the danger.”]. Thus here, where everything concerning the Lord is enacted in figure, the authority of the one who is to die is awaited, so that dying may be not necessity but power.

Hear the Lord saying: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again; no one takes it from me” (John 10). How? Because although Christ released his spirit, he did not lose it. For the one who receives and holds the souls of all in his hand does not appear capable of losing his own soul.

Hear the prophet saying: “My soul is always in your hands” (Psalm 118). And elsewhere: “Into your hands I commend my spirit” (Psalm 30).

But why say more? A beast runs, rushes forward, and appears from the deep, destined to fulfill and disclose the whole mystery of the Lord’s resurrection, or rather to conceive and give birth to it. The beast appears; the dreadful and cruel image of hell appears. As it is borne with hungry jaws upon the prophet, it experiences and tastes the strength of its author, for in devouring him it encounters fasting.

But, trembling, it adapts and prepares the dwelling of its heart as a lodging for the heavenly guest, so that the very creature that had been the entire cause of the danger might become the unheard-of vehicle of the necessary voyage, preserving its passenger and carrying him back to heaven after three days. It thus gave to the Gentiles what it had taken away from the Jews, to whom, because they sought a sign, the Lord decreed that this alone should be given as a sign, by which they might know that the glory they had hoped for in Christ was to be conferred wholly upon the Gentiles.

“This generation,” he says, “is an evil generation; it seeks a sign, and no sign will be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah. For just as Jonah was a sign to the Ninevites, so also will the Son of Man be to this generation.”

Because Christ was submerged in the depth of hell amid the fluctuating unbelief of the Jews, and, traversing all the hidden places of Tartarus in a three-day journey, he gave an indication both of Jewish cruelty, of his own majesty, and of death defeated when he rose again.

Therefore the Ninevites will rightly rise in judgment and condemn that generation, because they were corrected by the preaching of one shipwrecked, foreign, and unknown prophet; whereas these, after such great powers and such great miracles, [Col. 0306A] and amid the entire splendor of the resurrection, [Note: [Col. 0305D] The Ninevites were barbarians in their customs and inhabitants of the city that was the capital of the Assyrian kingdom on the bank of the Tigris; they were Gentiles in religion and unrestrained in wantonness, and had not yet witnessed any miracle of Jonah, yet they prepared themselves for repentance. The Jews, by contrast, worshipers of God, nurtured among the Scriptures and fellow countrymen of the Messiah, did not believe in him despite all the miracles he performed.] do not come to faith and are not moved to repentance.

For they do not believe the sign of the resurrection itself, but eagerly seek to defame it. By paying the soldiers they close their eyes and corrupt their hearts, so that they may remain silent about what they had learned and seen; they purchase a lie in order to remove the truth.

They turned their own crime back upon Christ’s disciples when they said: “Say that his disciples came by night and stole him” (Matthew 28). You are mistaken, Jew: the disciples did not take him, but the teacher did; and he himself stole himself, who appeared to have been killed. [Note: [Col. 0306C] Ambrose, Sermon 57, “On the Lord’s Tomb”: “For he himself took his body”—namely Christ, who raised it. He himself took the body who, as it lay and slept, gathered it up by his breathing. He himself took the body who, bearing it by the power of his divinity, carries it to the heavens. Therefore the woman wisely asks: ‘If you have taken him, tell me where you have placed him.’ Mita.]

But I wonder that the Jew seeks Christ, whom he had placed in a cruel manner between two robbers: he commits him improperly, guards him impiously, and seeks him still more wickedly.

Jew, Christ cannot perish, but by your crime you have lost him for yourself. The queen of the South will rise [Note: [Col. 0306D] The evangelist says “will rise,” that is, as a witness before Christ the judge. Mark 14:57 and Acts 6:13 show that witnesses rose from their seats to give testimony both among the Romans and among the Jews.] in judgment [Note: [Col. 0306D] Many have been persuaded by Josephus, book 8, chapter 6, that the queen of the South, whose capital was Meroë in Ethiopia, ruled there. Juvencus agrees in book 2. It seems more probable to me that she came from Arabia Felix. The gifts offered to Solomon also support this.] with that very one who was thought to have been stolen as judge, and will condemn you [Note: [Col. 0306D] Not by possessing judicial power herself, but as an example of comparison. The corrupt passage is corrected by better punctuation.], because she came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom, [Note: [Col. 0306D] From Latinius and the Vallicellian manuscript. The printed editions read “and you, as she came.”] while you, most wretched of all, killed the wisdom of God when it came to you.

The Ninevites were provided as a figure of the Gentiles who would believe; the queen of the South, as a figure of the Church.

We are blessed, brothers, because what preceded in type, what was promised in figure, we worship, behold, and possess in its reality and truth.

## SERMON XXXVIII. On Enduring Insult with Equanimity

How great is the magnitude of heavenly philosophy, how great the power of Christian warfare, the Lord taught today when he said: “If anyone strikes you on your right cheek, offer him the other also” (Matthew 5).

Only one who does not know how great the rewards of patience are thinks this difficult. Do you suppose that someone can find victory through wounds if he does not wish to gain a crown even through a blow from the palm? Can someone seek glory through death when an injury inflicted by a human being seems burdensome to him for the sake of divine honor?

Human being, are not the beginnings of your childhood formed by such commandments? Blows of the palm are for children, not for men. Hence Christ’s childhood is animated by light commands, so that the evangelical youth, now possessing complete strength, may approach grave things; so that through labors, punishments, and death it may rejoice to obtain what in childhood it could not acquire through minor injuries.

To demonstrate that the commandments are not harsh, let the series of commands itself be repeated. You have heard that it was said to the ancients: “An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.” But I say to you: do not resist evil; rather, if anyone strikes you on your right cheek, offer him the other also; and to the one who wishes to contend with you in judgment and take your tunic, surrender your cloak as well; and to the one who forces you to go one thousand paces, go with him another two thousand (Exodus 21; Deuteronomy 12).

You have heard that it was said to the ancients. To which ancients? Certainly to the Jews, whom malice had made “ancient” more than age had, whom the fury of vengeance held so tightly that they demanded a head for an eye and a life for a tooth. Hence the Law restrained them to an exchange of vengeance, so that those who did not know how to understand forgiveness might at least understand the measure of retaliation, and might demand only as much vengeance as the force of rage had inflicted injury. [Note: [Col. 0307D] The law of retaliation, which is implied in these words and discussed elsewhere, is extremely ancient. Aristotle says that it was called the law of Rhadamanthus, described in this verse: “That he should suffer something which he has done is just.” Moses states this law explicitly in Exodus 21:24, Leviticus 24:20, and Deuteronomy 19:21. The legislator’s intention, however, was not that these things be carried out according to the literal sound of the words; rather, he either permitted or overlooked vengeance up to a definite limit. On this kind of law in later times, see canon 4 of the Second Council of Nicaea, where it is called by a term unknown to lexicons, ταυτοπάθεια (*tautopatheia*, “the same suffering”), and see Balsamon there.] 

But let us hear what divine goodness commands us, who have been renewed by grace, in contrast to the ancients. “But I say to you.” To whom? Certainly to Christians. “Do not resist evil.” By saying this, he wants us not to repay vices with vices but to overcome them with virtues; to extinguish anger while it is still a spark, for if it reaches the full blaze of fury, it is not quenched without blood.

Anger is conquered by gentleness; fury is extinguished by meekness; malice is softened by goodness; credulity is overthrown by compassion; impatience is punished by patience; contention is overcome [Note: [Col. 0307D] How badly, good God! Many editions read “by injuries.”] by kindness; pride is laid low by humility.

Therefore, brothers, whoever wishes to conquer vices should take up the weapons of compassion, [Col. 0307C] not of fury. And although a wise person can see clearly what the beginnings of Christian conduct through injuries are, nevertheless, because some do not understand that this is the summit of virtue, the height of goodness, the pinnacle of compassion, and the philosophy of God rather than of human beings—namely, not to resist evil but [Note: [Col. 0307D] What Christ and Chrysologus teach here is counseled rather than imposed. See Maldonado and Jansenius at this passage.] to overcome evil with good, to bless the one who curses, not to deny the one who strikes permission to strike again [Note: [Col. 0307D] Some editions, together with the Vatican manuscript, read “to the one who strikes.”], to leave one’s cloak to the one who takes one’s tunic [Note: [Col. 0307D] The Jews used two garments. Christ teaches that the one who takes the tunic, that is, the inner garment, should be given the outer cloak as well.], and to make generosity one’s response to the one who robs, [Note: [Col. 0308D] On forced service, see note 2 on Sermon 25. The customary distance for such forced service was one thousand paces.] to add one’s service to another two thousand paces for the one who forces one to serve—so that willingness may conquer necessity and compassion impiety; and so that the virtue of the one who suffers may do this which the force of the one compelling commands—therefore, although these teachings show how the soldier of Christ is strengthened for virtue through injuries, let us nevertheless inquire more deeply into the reason for which they were commanded, so that it may become clearer.

Brothers, when the disease of sins, the crime of vices, and the madness of impiety had poured themselves into human minds, extinguishing whatever knowledge, understanding, and reason there was, insane fury caused nations throughout the world to flee from God, follow demons, worship creatures, despise the Creator, desire vices, dread virtues, be driven by swords, fall through wounds, and perish while alive through deaths [Note: [Col. 0308D] Most editions read “by customs”; others “by diseases.” Mita, together with the Vallicellian and Caesenatensis manuscripts, has the reading we have retained.].

Therefore people could not be healed in any other way unless the heavenly physician, armed with complete compassion and patience, exerted himself. They had to endure the injuries of those suffering from such madness, carry their curses, bear their blows, and be cut by wounds, until they brought them back to soundness of understanding, purity of spirit, and health of mind; and thus enabled them to seek God, flee demons, recognize illness, understand health, cast off vices, take up virtues, avoid wounds, dread blood, reject death, and desire life [Note: [Col. 0308D] Perhaps “learn thoroughly.”].

And if you wish what we have said to become clearer, let us speak by examples from bodily physicians. Whenever the fire of bile inflames a wretched person and, with fever ruling, makes the sick person insane, are not the senses disturbed, the mind destroyed, savagery added, and humanity withdrawn? In short, while the person dies, madness lives. Hence the patient gnashes his teeth, tears at his parents, rends those nearby, strikes with his fist, attacks by biting, and injures those serving him.

Then the physician, armed with patience for the praise of virtue, the glory of his art, and the increase of his reputation, takes up endurance, disregards insults, bears bites, endures labor, [Col. 0308C] and suffers no slight punishments in order to free the sufferer from punishment. He soothes him with oil, applies himself to his care, supplies medicine, confident that the patient will repay his services with the reward of honor once he has regained health.

I ask: what greater madness, what more serious force of fury, what comparable insanity is there than to strike a holy person’s cheek? To beat the face of a gentle brother? To cover the grace of a peaceful countenance with a grim bruise? To strip a human being of the only garment by which he is covered? And, for the sake of a worthless spoil, to leave nothing to God, nothing to a human being, nothing to nature, nothing to modesty? To force into service a person occupied with his own duties [Note: [Col. 0308D] Du Cange praises this passage of Chrysologus in *Glossarium Mediae et Infimae Latinitatis*, volume I, column 234.]? And to count another’s suffering as one’s own consolation?

Therefore, brothers, since we recognize that those who commit such acts suffer from the gravest madness, let us obey Christ and bear the bites, blows, and burdens of our raging brothers with the entire strength of compassion, so that we may both free our brothers from punishment and obtain for ourselves the eternal reward of patience.

And let the servant not disdain to receive from fellow servants what the Lord graciously accepted from servants and for servants. He did not refuse his face to blows of the palms; to the one who took his tunic and cloak, he surrendered his body as well; and when one forced him into labor, he gladly and willingly followed him to death.

Therefore, brothers, if the Lord considered it worthy to suffer, how, how can it seem unworthy for a servant to suffer? We are mistaken, we are mistaken, brothers: whoever does not do what the Lord commanded vainly hopes for what the Lord promised.

## SERMON XXXIX. On Perseverance in Prayer
Per se, divine things always suffice for themselves; but for this reason they are frequently presented to human beings through human examples, because heavenly providence considers not what it can itself say, but what the hearer is able to grasp. Thus a spring first bursts forth through the slender passages of its veins, then gradually creeps through narrow streams, until in due course it breaks out into the full breadth of rivers and pours itself forth with force. And, to speak to you of matters familiar to us: when a little child is born, nature immediately prepares nourishment suitable to his age; it changes food into drink, and, by a long infusion of milk, trains the still astonished mouth and the sluggish passages within for the use of more solid food.

So the Lord raises and instructs us for receiving divine things by familiar examples, saying: “Which of you will have a friend and go to him at midnight and say to him, ‘Friend, lend me three loaves, because a friend of mine has come to me from the road, and I have nothing to set before him’; and he from within will answer, ‘Do not trouble me, because the door is already shut, and my children are with me in bed; I cannot rise and give you anything’? I tell you, even if he will not rise and give him because he is his friend, yet because of his persistence he will rise and give him as many as he needs” (Luke 11).

O how willing he is to give, who allows himself to be disturbed in such a manner and to be roused from sleep in such a manner! O how willing he is to appear to make his necessity what is in fact his power! O how eager he was to meet the one knocking, who placed the bed of his secret chamber at the very door! [Note: [Col. 0309D] In the Gospel, κοίτη can signify both “bed” and “bedchamber.” Chrysologus marvels at the unusual circumstance. No one places his bed at the door, but in the innermost parts of the house. It was the custom of servants, however, to sleep near the door. See Pignorius, *De Servis*, who quotes these words.]

O how unwilling he was to deny, who showed even one who was denying him how his refusal might be extorted! O how the Lord was not merely at the door, but was himself the door! “I am the door,” he says (John 10), who, while the servants slept, alone and first heard the need of the one knocking. O how devout, how merciful is he, who teaches by commands what he approves and inculcates by examples! “When you give alms,” he says, “do not sound a trumpet.” And again: “Let not your left hand know what your right hand is doing” (Matthew 6).

Which of you will have a friend and go to him at midnight? It is little that the night concealed the one performing the act of mercy, and that the petitioner’s persistence covered the generosity of the giver, unless sleep too were added to the concealment as an increase of his kindness. In this act of humaneness he introduces a twofold form of necessity, that of the petitioner and that of the sleeper, so that the guest might compel the one to ask and sleep might compel the other to give: for he says that the man will give him at that time in such a way that he seems not to come to meet his friend, but to return to sleep—and as though he would rather be permitted to sleep than be pleased to give to one asking in such a fashion. What more need be said? Behold, for the one knocking, sleep proved more helpful than sound.

Nor do I think it irrelevant that he discloses and specifies the hour of asking in this way, saying: “Which of you has a friend and will go to him at midnight?” [Note: [Col. 0309D] The Evangelist himself had marked the late hour of the night when he said, “The door is shut.” The Greeks call this hour κλαυσίθυρον, “the shutting of the door.”]

As though the first, second, and third hours of the night were not also disagreeable and harsh for the persistence of one disturbing another, when gentle sleep first pours itself pleasantly into the bodies of those sleeping and sweetly, completely, and without interruption enters their entrails wearied by the day’s labor. But this is the hour that demonstrates the judgment of one devoted to continual nightly vigil; this is the hour in which the spirit, burning amid the labors that have passed and those that are to come, yet directed toward divine things, allows nothing to the body and nothing to rest. Before it finishes the work of the day already completed, it begins and anticipates the work of the coming day. This hour is most effective for obtaining what is requested.

Knowing this, the prophet asserts that this was the very time of his supplication when he sings: “At midnight I rose to give thanks to you” (Psalm 118). At this hour the heavenly bridegroom always comes to those keeping vigil, who says: “At midnight there was a cry: Behold, the bridegroom is coming” (Matthew 25).

He could not fail to obtain what he desired, who, in order to receive a guest and refresh a guest, denied himself every kind of rest. Or how would that one not answer a man asking and knocking in this way, who confesses that he himself is received in the guest, when he says: “I was a stranger, and you welcomed me” (Matthew 25)?

I think that the one knocking said this, or perhaps expressed it somewhat differently: “I have done what you commanded; give back what you promised. I trusted you when you said, ‘Do not be anxious about tomorrow’” (Matthew 6). “Hence he left me nothing with which to set before yesterday’s guest. If I am troublesome to you, who have something, in this way, how much more troublesome was he to me, who had nothing? And yet I could not excuse myself to him, because I was striving to obey you. The embarrassment of the one who commanded is now weighing more heavily here than the embarrassment of the one who had nothing. The guest is in the house, and you sleep—or rather, you sleep although you are not asleep. I received the guest; unless you give the bread, you have denied bread to the guest.”

Rightly, then, to this man knocking in such a manner and asking in such a fashion, that Gospel lender gave as many loaves as he needed. What do those do who place themselves not in a bedchamber but in a tomb? [Note: [Col. 0309D] A metaphorical expression. Since lay Christians were required to rise at midnight to pray to God, or, according to the custom of those times, were bound to praise God in the churches through the four night watches as though through guard-posts, yet neglected this duty, the author rightly reproves them for lying in the tomb of death. For they have the ears both of heart and head so stopped that they would not hear even the cockcrow—that is, their own conscience calling them to rise—nor would they be awakened by the dawn—that is, by evangelical inspiration—nor recalled to the light by the sun itself, namely Christ. MITA.]

What do those do who surrender themselves not to sleep but to death? Whom the cock does not admonish, the morning star does not awaken, the sun itself does not recall and bring forth into the light? These have lost both the time for supplication, the guest’s reward, and the very works of the day.

We are saddened, brothers, when at dawn we stand before the Lord and do not see our children with us. He knocked in this way at midnight in whose house a guest had arrived. I ask you: why do you not keep vigil even at dawn, when you have a guest in your house? What he gave to grace, attribute at least to sloth; what he gave to humaneness, bestow at least upon necessity—you who love sleep more than yourself.

Certainly, so that you may be able to keep vigil for life, you who sleep toward death, listen to what follows: “And I say to you,” he says, “ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives; and whoever seeks finds; and to the one knocking it will be opened” (Luke 11).

But you say: “Granted that I can ask, how will I be able to knock upon the heavenly secret?” How? By repeating prayers, by awaiting the judgment of the giver, and by enduring with the greatest patience the delays of the one who gives. For whoever, after knocking once, becomes indignant at once if he has not been heard is not a suppliant petitioner but an imperious exactor.

Hear the prophet saying: “Wait for the Lord; act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened” (Psalm 26). And if he delays again into the future, wait patiently for your Lord.

But if you wish to know what you ought to seek, there are riches in the bosom of the poor, and the kingdom of heaven is within you. “The kingdom of heaven is within you,” says the Lord (Luke 17).

Who, then, is the friend who sleeps, and who is the friend who has come from the road; who are the children who sleep; who is this one who knocks; and why does he ask for only three loaves, according to a definite number? When I have asked, sought, and knocked, and when, as a sleepless disturber, I have deserved to receive, I will not conceal these things from you, the friends of my Lord. [Note: [Col. 0311C] The author either could not fulfill the promise he had given, or the sermon in which he had done what he here promises has been lost.]

But you say to me: “Behold, a friend of your Lord [Note: [Col. 0311C] Something is lacking here, and the sense is not complete. Yet the manuscripts provide nothing by which it can be either supplied or corrected. See below in the observations on Sermons 107 and 136. MITA.—For my part, I am certain that Chrysologus is speaking here of another bishop, who was then staying with him.] has come to you. He is accustomed to give, not to receive; indeed, this sitarcia—” [Note: [Col. 0311C] In 1 Kings 9:7 one reads: “The bread has failed in our sitarciae, and we have no bag”; the Septuagint reads: “For the loaves have failed in our vessels, and there is no more with us.” At this passage Abulensis says: “Sitarcium is a vessel woven from willow for storing bread, and by some it is called a basket.” The Interlinear Gloss explains: “In our sitarciae,” that is, in our pouches or bag. In corrected Bibles the reading is *sitarciis*, not, as in the older editions, *citarciis*. Maldonatus, on Matthew 10:10, understands *citarciis* to mean “a small basket,” and it should likewise be explained here. MITA.—With due respect, however, I would say that here, as above in Sermon 5, Chrysologus uses *sitarcia* to signify the daily allowance or daily ration. See what was said there.]

—this pastor has eagerly filled this sitarcia from the abundance of his own provisions, so that he might taste from the most meager preparation of our poverty; nor did he allow me, in the dead of night, to seek elsewhere for him what he, richest of hosts, possessed.” [Note: [Col. 0312C] The Vatican manuscript reads: “Nor did the richest of hosts allow me, in the depth of night, to seek elsewhere for him what he possessed.” Some editions read: “hospitality.”]

And this is not surprising, brothers: the rich man always wishes to give to the poor when he stoops down. He always remains at the door of that Gospel friend; in his bedchamber that Gospel giver remains with his children, in whose heart the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit always make and establish their dwelling.

What more need be said? He is the Father: I believed that I should ask from him, seek in him, and knock through him. Therefore I confidently declared that I would give him to you, not as an incautious promiser. [Note: [Col. 0312C] I would explain the obscure meaning as follows. The friend who is always accustomed to give and not to receive, eager to fulfill this familiar and daily custom from the abundance of his humility—which he brings with him as provisions customary to him—did so in such a way that he did not disdain to taste from the preparation of our most wretched poverty, nor did he allow me to seek elsewhere what he himself, richest of all hosts in virtue and humility, possessed. For why seek elsewhere how to entertain a guest splendidly, when one who is content with little has everything with him? From this point he briefly digresses in praise of the guest himself, aided by whose prayers he hopes that he will eventually fulfill the promise of another sermon.]

## SERMON XL. On the Good Shepherd

When the season of the spring breeze begins to open the annual births of the sheep, when across fields, meadows, and roads it begins to scatter the abundant offspring of the fertile flock, the good shepherd sets aside both leisure and song, [Note: [Col. 0312C] Namely, idleness and singing, by which he used to pass the time; he now gives himself entirely to labor.] and with anxious wandering seeks out, selects, and gathers the tender young. Then, rejoicing, he places the lambs upon his neck, shoulders, and arms, carrying them so that he may bring them all back safely and lead them unharmed to the folds. [Note: [Col. 0312C] The printed editions have, corruptly, *totas*.]

So we, brothers, when during Lent, with spring smiling upon us, we see the ecclesiastical flock bringing forth abundant offspring, set aside the songs of our sermons and the feasts of our customary discourse, [Note: [Col. 0312C] Among the holy Fathers this name was frequently used for sermons delivered in church. Optatus of Milevis repeatedly called the sermons of all the Donatists and of Parmenianus alone by the designation “treatises.” “None of you,” he says in Book 4, “begins the Sunday readings and unfolds your treatises to your own injury.” And in Book 5, addressing Parmenianus: “Although you treated these matters at the beginning of your speech, in the course of your treatise you have forgotten them.” See Ambrose, Letter 14 to Marcellina; Gaudentius of Brescia, Preface to Benivolus; Jerome, Letter 65; Augustine, Sermon 20 *On Various Subjects*; and Ferrarius, *On the Sermon*, who treats this matter explicitly.]

and devote all our care, with anxious and most arduous labor, to gathering and carrying the heavenly offspring. [Note: [Col. 0312D] From this passage of Chrysologus, I would infer that bishops abstained from preaching during Lent and devoted all their care to gathering and carrying the offspring of the Christian flock to the Church.]

But because we see the lambs restored to the flock and now entirely enclosed within Christ’s folds, [Note: [Col. 0312D] He calls those recently baptized “lambs.” During Lent our most holy shepherd was especially occupied with calling the Gentiles to the faith; and on Holy Saturday he instructed them in the catechism and baptized those who desired it. At that time it was customary for them to be baptized in the Church of God by immersion and emersion, as we learn from St. Augustine and others. Since our bishop performed this himself with his own hands, and since there were almost countless people to be baptized, he was compelled not only to give up preaching at that time but also to endure great anxiety and weariness because of the immense labor undertaken. Since he had consecrated men as companions in that labor, he preferred to have them share also in the joys of divine preaching. MITA.]

we are recalled, full of joy, to divine songs, setting before you, with the exultation of the Lord’s food, all our vital resources, so that those whom we have recognized as companions in labor we may have as participants in our joys.

And because this preface of ours has mentioned the good shepherd—him who alone is good, alone is shepherd, alone is shepherd of shepherds—let the whole purpose of our sermon and discourse be filled with and directed toward him. “The good shepherd,” he says, “lays down his life for his sheep” (John 10).

The force of love makes him strong, because true love counts nothing hard, nothing bitter, nothing burdensome, nothing deadly. What iron, what wounds, what punishment, what deaths can prevail to separate perfect love? Love is an impenetrable breastplate: it rejects arrows, shakes off swords, mocks dangers, laughs at death; if love is present, it conquers everything.

But let us ask whether this death of the shepherd is advantageous to the sheep—the death that abandons the sheep, delivers the defenseless flock to wolves, and leaves that beloved flock to the bites of beasts, gives it over to plunder, and exposes it to death—as is shown by the death of Christ himself, the shepherd. For once he laid down his life for his sheep and allowed himself to be killed by Jewish fury, his sheep, the Gentiles, were seized like prey in the attack of robbers; they were shut up to be slaughtered in prisons as in thieves’ dens; they were incessantly torn by persecutors like raging wolves; and they were gnawed by heretics with rabid teeth like alien dogs.

The slaughtered chorus of the apostles proves this; the blood of the martyrs, spread throughout the whole world, proclaims it; the limbs of Christians given to beasts, consumed by fire, and submerged in rivers plainly demonstrate it: all this, just as death brought it about, the shepherd’s life could certainly have prevented.

Therefore the shepherd proves his love for you by death, because, when he sees danger threatening the sheep and is unable to defend the flock, he prefers to die before seeing any evil befall his sheep.

But what shall we do, since Life could not die unless he had wished to? Who could take the soul from the giver of life if he did not wish it? He himself says: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again; no one takes it from me.” Therefore he wished to die, since, though he could not be killed, he allowed himself to be killed.

Let us therefore ask what the force of this love is, what its reason, what the cause of this death, and what the benefit of this suffering. And plainly its force is certain, its reason true, its cause radiant, and the benefit of so much blood entirely clear. For from the shepherd’s one death a singular power shone forth: the shepherd confronted the death that threatened the sheep, so that, by a new arrangement, he might capture the author of death by being captured, conquer him by being conquered, punish him by being killed, and by dying for the sheep open a way for them to conquer death.

For the devil, while he stretches himself against a human being, leapt against God; while he rages against the guilty, he rushed upon the judge; he found punishment while inflicting punishment; he himself received the sentence while passing sentence. And death, while living on the food of mortals, dies as it devours Life; death, while swallowing the guilty, is swallowed up as it devours the author of innocence; and death itself, which was destroying everyone, perishes while seeking to destroy the salvation of all.

Thus the shepherd went before the sheep in this manner, yet the shepherd did not withdraw from the sheep. He did not give them to wolves; rather, he handed over the wolves to those whom he granted the power to choose such plunderers, so that, though killed, they might live; though torn apart, they might rise again; stained with their own blood, they might shine in royal purple and gleam in snow-white wool.

Thus, when the good shepherd laid down his life for the sheep, he did not lose it; and by holding the sheep in this way, he did not abandon them. He did not leave the sheep in such a way, but invited them: through the mortal fields and along the road of death he called them to life and led them to the pastures.

But someone says: “When will these things occur?” Meanwhile, behold the sheep—that is, the apostles, prophets, martyrs, and confessors—lie buried: torn apart, they are scattered throughout the whole world; wrapped in blood, they are enclosed in gloomy tombs. And who doubts that the slain martyrs will rise, live, and reign, when Christ, having been slain, rose, lives, and reigns for them? [Note: [Col. 0314D] The Vatican manuscript has *ipse*, “he himself,” perhaps more correctly.]

Hear the voice of this shepherd: “My sheep hear my voice and follow me.” It is necessary that those who followed him unto death should follow him unto life; that those who accompanied him unto disgrace should accompany him unto honor; and that those who shared in his suffering should share in his glory. “Where I am,” he says, “there will my servant be also” (John 12). Where? Certainly above the heavens, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God.

Human being, let faith not disturb you, and let a more distant hope not weary you, because what is preserved for you in the author of all things himself is certain for you. “You have died,” he says, “and your life is hidden with Christ in God; but when Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Colossians 3).

The laboring reaper will see at harvest what he does not see in the seed, and he who weeps in the furrow will rejoice in the fruit. [Note: [Col. 0314D] We have corrected this from Latinius. All printed editions have *et quod*.]

## SERMON XLI. On Fasting and Almsgiving

We read that very many have conquered the battles of nations, yet we also read that they did not conquer the battles of the flesh; and we have heard that those who did not yield their backs to enemies gave their breasts over to sins. Alas! Conquerors of nations were captives to vices; masters of peoples served shameful crimes in slavery; they stood among raging swords and fell amid enervating seductions; they were a terror to kingdoms and a laughingstock to sins; fasting, they shattered opposing battle lines, yet, bloated with food and drink, they dissolved the camps of their own virtues; they lay helpless in spilled wine, though they had not known how to lie helpless in spilled blood.

Whence is this? Whence? Because this is not reason but sickness; not life but fever; frenzy, not nature. For whenever the undigested mass of foods weakens the vital organs, disorders the stomach, corrupts the blood, damages the humors, and inflames the bile, producing the final conflagration of fever, [Note: [Col. 0314D] See the annotations on Sermon 18.] so often the sick person loses his mind, forfeits his understanding, is driven by desires, is oppressed by contrary forces, rejects what is healthful, seeks what is harmful, and flees care.

Then physicians strive to bring aid through the remedy of abstinence, so that the sick person may be healed and abstinence may heal what gluttony had wounded. [Note: [Col. 0315C] We have judged that this should be restored from the manuscript of Cesena. The printed editions have: “They deliberately prepare to come to the aid of abstinence by a remedy.”]

And if, for the sake of temporal care, the sick obey physicians and maintain difficult restraint, why should it be burdensome, for eternal salvation, to obey Christ in moderate fasts, to govern the body by measure, to rule the mind by restraint, and to bridle the senses by sobriety?

As clouds darken the sky over the earth, so immoderate banquets obscure souls; as whirlwinds of wind confuse the elements, so piled-up dishes disturb the stomach; as waves sink a ship, so drunkenness plunges the body, casts a human being into the depths, takes away the profits of life, and makes him undergo the shipwreck of death.

There is therefore a fever—a fever which the blessed Apostle mournfully acknowledges to be burning within human entrails: “I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh” (Romans 7). If it is not good, then surely it is evil.

What evil? Certainly frailty, which, while it creeps through the flesh, boils in the veins, enters the bones, is hidden in the marrow, and burns in the blood, bursts forth in this way into the frenzy of vices. Frailty is the fever of nature, the mother of sicknesses, the begetter of passions.

It is frailty that imposes such necessities upon us; and where there is necessity, there is not will; where captivity arises from one’s condition, judgment based on power has no standing. Frailty is the means by which a person goes, not where his will invites him, but where necessity leads him. Hear the Apostle saying: “I do not do what I want” (Romans 7).

Frailty, while providing a person with what is necessary, brings him to what is unnecessary; while preparing food, it leads him to gluttony; while supplying drink, it encourages drunkenness; it offers sleep in order to deliver over to inertia; it tends the burdens of the belly so as to remove concern for salvation; it gives everything to the flesh so as to leave nothing to the soul. It makes the body a spectacle of passions; it makes a person his own death, the life of vices. [Note: [Col. 0315C] The printed editions have *jus necessitatis*, “the right of necessity.” Let others judge whether we have brought a remedy to this passage from the manuscript of Cesena. Mita retained the reading of the printed editions and added the following note: “This is our weakness, which is also called the tinder or fuel of desire. Human nature after the fall of our first parent became inclined toward evil; and where the Vulgate reading of Psalm 102 says, ‘For he himself knows our formation; he remembers that we are dust,’ the Chaldean paraphrast reads, ‘For he himself knows the evil tinder that suggests sin.’ Job likewise, speaking of human beings, says: ‘He will be consumed like a moth’; for just as a moth born from wood or woolen cloth gnaws the entrails of its mother like the offspring of a viper, so the fuel of sin, arising within us who are infected by original defilement, consumes, insofar as it depends upon itself, the radical spiritual moisture unless divine grace restrains it, and makes us weaker in overcoming difficulties and more feeble. The tinder of sin is the sensitive appetite deprived of original righteousness, which by its own nature inclines toward what is pleasant and delightful to it, even when these things are contrary to the dictate of right reason. It is called ‘sin’ by the Apostle in Romans 7, either because it proceeded from original sin or because it inclines vehemently, though not necessarily, toward sinning. That frailty imposes the right of necessity is shown by Bellarmine on Psalm 24:18, where David prays to God, saying, ‘Deliver me from my necessities.’ Bellarmine adds: ‘The necessities from which he wishes to be freed seem to be those most troublesome concupiscences which, whether we wish it or not, torment us and sometimes draw us into sin.’ St. Augustine says in Sermon 13 *On the Words of the Apostle*: ‘If God’s help is absent, you will be able to do nothing good; unless he rules you, you fall; unless he rules you, you lie prostrate.’ Viguerus, in his *Commentary on Romans 7*, near the end, should also be consulted.” “Necessities,” says Chrysologus in a broad sense, meaning those things that impel us, not those that compel us.]

Therefore, if a person feels himself sick in this way, let him surrender himself to the heavenly physician and safely obey his instructions; let him restrain himself from food, maintain measure in drink, [Note: [Col. 0316D] Some printed editions, together with the manuscript of Cesena, read “for the future.”] so that he may overcome the sickness of frailty, flee the passions of frailty, and avoid the fever and frenzy of vices.

Abstinence is the first medicine of the human being; but for complete healing it requires the expense of mercy. [Note: [Col. 0316D] For sins are to be redeemed through almsgiving.]

Abstinence extinguishes the fever, but limbs dried out by the burning of a long fever cannot return to complete health unless they are drenched with abundant ointment, unless they are moistened with the gentlest fomentations, unless they are aided by the expenditure required for medicine. So fasting, although it excludes the diseases of vices, cuts away the passions of the flesh, and drives away the causes of crimes, nevertheless does not restore perfect health to minds without the ointment of mercy, without the stream of kindness, without the expense of almsgiving.

Fasting heals the wounds of sins, but without mercy it does not cleanse the scars of the wounds. Hear the Lord saying: “Give alms, and behold, everything will be clean for you” (Luke 11).

Fasting, through its singular worship, uproots vices, eradicates crimes, and prepares the field of both mind and body for good fruits. But unless it lays the foundations of mercy, the devotion of the one fasting is an old age. [Note: [Col. 0316D] Old age here means decrepitude. Hence David: “Until old age and decrepitude.” Chrysologus compares fasting deprived of mercy to old age, the weakest of all ages and one needing a staff. Thus fasting totters and needs the foundation of mercy. MITA.]

Fasting is the sacrifice of holiness, the offering of chastity; but without the incense of mercy it cannot ascend into the divine presence as a pleasing fragrance. What the soul is to the body, mercy is to fasting. When fasting lives from mercy, then it gives life to the one who fasts.

Fasting is the ship of virtues; it carries the profit of life and transports the gain of salvation. But whoever enters the sea of the flesh, cuts through the waves of vices, passes among the reefs of crimes, and moves beyond the shores of passions cannot practice virtues or possess their gain unless he quickly enters the harbor of kindness.

Whoever knows that he stands upon the slippery ground of this life, whoever understands that he is crossing the road of the flesh through falling, whoever feels himself subject to the attacks of ignorance and the falls of negligence—let him hold fasting in such a way that he does not abandon mercy.

Fasting opens heaven for us; fasting admits us to God. But unless mercy, the patroness of our causes, is then present for us, we who cannot establish our innocence will not be secure of pardon, since the Lord says: “Judgment without mercy will be for the one who has not shown mercy” (James 2).

The day is pleasant, but the clear day is more pleasant. Therefore our fasting will be brighter than that day if the splendor of mercy makes the days of Lent clear for us.

God cries out: “I desire mercy” (Hosea 6). Human being, give God what he desires, if you wish him to give you what you desire. “I desire mercy” is the voice of God; God asks mercy from us. And if we give it, what will he say? What was read today: “I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink.” And what follows? “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom that has been prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25).

Whoever gives bread to the hungry will give himself the kingdom; whoever denies a cup of water to the thirsty will deny himself the fountain of life. For love of the poor, God sells his kingdom; and so that everyone may be able to buy it, he sets a fragment of bread as its price, because he wishes to have everyone who possesses as much of the price as he knows a human being possesses.

God sells his kingdom for a fragment of bread. Who will be able to excuse the one who does not buy it, when such a low price of sale accuses him?

Brothers, let our lunch be the poor person’s supper, so that Christ’s table may be prepared as our lunch, since he himself promises this when he says: “You will eat at my table in my kingdom” (Luke 22).

Brothers, let our fasts be the delicacies of the poor, so that our temporary fasting may be changed for us into eternal delights.

Human being, by giving to the poor you give to yourself; for whatever you do not give to the poor, another will have. You will have only what you give to the poor.

## SERMON XLII. On the Same Subject
The benefits of fasting, brothers, we have touched upon as best we could in the preceding sermon, and we disclosed in the very conclusion of the sermon what prayer is akin to fasting. But because fasting without mercy fails, fasting without piety fasts in vain, prayer without compassion grows weak, and prayer without generosity becomes weary, let us restore our fast by displaying mercy, and raise our prayer by hearing piety; let us attach mercy as a patron to our fasting. For fasting without mercy is the hunger of avarice; fasting without piety is the punishment of covetousness.

> [Note: As though, because of his avaricious covetousness, he were taking vengeance upon himself.]

It is vengeance, not devotion, to fast not for God but for one’s purse: to wear oneself down by abstinence while swelling with the dropsical disease of covetousness.

> [Note: Elsewhere, “covetousness.”]

To empty the belly of food while weighing down the mind with the burden of money. The man who does not know how to distribute money but only to lock it away reduces himself to a purse; he is the guardian, not the master, of another’s property. He prepares for someone else and denies himself, whereas the merciful distributes what the miser has hoarded.

He is a cultivated field without seed who fasts without compassion. A cultivated field is free of thorns, avoids weeds, and escapes everything that belongs to negligence and neglect. But just as, without seed, it becomes barren—its cultivation itself yielding no fruit, only labor, and unable to reach a good harvest—so the person who fasts cultivates the soul, purifies the senses, cleanses the heart, cuts away vices, uproots crimes, gives cultivation to the mind, and beauty to the body; yet without mercy he does not reach the fruit of life or proceed to the reward of salvation.

What a royal hall is without a king, such is fasting without generosity. A king’s hall gleams with gold, sparkles with marble, shines with paintings, expands in spaciousness, rises in height, and is made pleasant by green gardens.

> [Note: An unusual expression, meaning “it is made pleasant by verdant gardens.”]

It is itself terrifying in its private inner chamber.

> [Note: No one may enter the royal bedchamber without punishment unless admitted by order. This has been observed elsewhere.]

But without a king it possesses no honor, lacks glory, is an empty solitude, a closed wilderness, a dreadful desolation.

So fasting shines with innocence, radiates chastity, gleams in conduct,

> [Col. 0318B]

is painted with good morals,

> [Note: It is adorned with a variety of more refined manners.]

sparkles in its bearing, and is entirely magnified by the adornment of holiness. But without mercy it has no glory, lacks its reward, does not hold the palm of victory, loses confidence in prayer, and does not attain the merit of obtaining what it asks. Scripture bears witness when it says:

> [Note: According to the Septuagint version.]

“Whoever closes his ear so as not to hear the weak, he too will cry out, and there will be no one to hear him” (Prov. XXI).

How will he ask for mercy who has denied it? “Judgment without mercy will be shown to the one who has not shown mercy” (James II). Whoever does not give mercy to another takes it away from himself. Mercy will belong to the one who scatters it for the poor. “He scattered; he gave to the poor; his righteousness remains forever and ever” (Ps. CXI). Whoever sows mercy for the needy will reap it for himself. “Those who sow in tears will reap in joy” (Ps. CXV).

Rain does not soak the earth as the tears of the poor water fasting. Man, cast the seeds of your fasting into the tears of the poor, because the virtues of fasting dry up, and the harvests of those who fast wither if they have not been watered by the weeping of the poor. The rain of heaven waters the earth; the tears of the poor water heaven. Heaven, therefore, thirsts and awaits from the lamentation of the poor its measure of dew, because mercy plows the fields of heaven, and piety draws furrows through the heights; there mercy sows. For whatever the hand of the poor receives, there it reaps; there he gathers a harvest who entrusts his seed to the poor to be sown here.

Blessed is the one for whom, while he sows in this way, eternal barns are continually prepared for everlasting life. The blessed Apostle described this sower when he said: “This, however, I say: Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly; and whoever sows in blessings will also reap from blessings. Let each person give as he has resolved in his heart, not out of sadness or compulsion; for God loves a cheerful giver” (II Cor. IX).

Great are the works of the Lord, but the greatness of mercy surpasses their greatness. For when the prophet had said, “Great are the works of the Lord” (Ps. CX), he added elsewhere: “His mercies are over all his works” (Ps. CXLIV).

Mercy, brothers, fills heaven and fills the earth. “Lord,” he says, “your mercy is in heaven” (Ps. XXXV). And the same one says: “The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord” (Ps. XXXII). And truly, brothers, everything God had made would have perished unless mercy had come to its aid. Guilt and vengeance were carrying away everything that had entered this world, because frailty was always tending toward a fall, and the judgment of the one who judges was always being driven toward punishment.

Thus the angel is cast down from heaven (Isa. XIV); thus man is exiled from paradise (Gen. III); thus the world is destroyed by the flood (Gen. VII); thus the nations are confused in their languages (Gen. XI) and given over to the sword (Gen. XIV); thus cities are burned in a divine fire (Gen. XIX); thus the people led out of Egypt are concealed in the wilderness (Exod. XIX); thus the gaping earth swallows the people (Num. XVI); and, not to list everything, thus the Roman army destroyed Judea as the avenger of Christ’s blood (Matt. XXIV).

> [Note: He alludes to the destruction of Jerusalem under Titus and Vespasian.]

This is Christ’s great, abundant, and sole mercy, which reserved all judgment for one day and assigned to man the entire intervening time as a respite for repentance. Thus what infancy acquires from vices, adolescence seizes, and youth invades, even old age may correct; and one may repent of sin at the very moment when one realizes that one can no longer sin, and at least then abandon guilt when guilt has already abandoned him. Let him make a virtue of necessity; let the one who lived wholly in crime die innocent.

For this reason the prophet runs wholly to mercy, because he had no confidence in his own righteousness: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy” (Ps. L). And why “great”? “Because your mercy,” he says, “is great toward me, and you have delivered my soul from the lowest hell” (Ps. LXXXV).

And if God restores through mercy what had been lost through judgment, man, what did you think could stand or endure for you without mercy? It has therefore been proved to you that not only fasting, but all virtues, totter without mercy.

Abraham was made the master of the heavenly banquet by his burning hospitality, offered to God (Gen. XVIII). For because he received two earthly guests with God at his table, he received the people of the East and the West at the heavenly table. “They will come,” he says, “from the East and the West, and they will recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. VIII).

Lot, because he received angels as guests, forestalled judgment (Gen. XIX). Hence he overcame Gehenna in the flesh; the divine fire does not know how to strip the merciful man. Therefore the one who wishes not to fear the fire of Gehenna practices mercy.

Finally, when Christ comes, he discusses mercy before judging guilt. “When he has taken his seat,” he says, “upon the throne of his glory, he will say: I was hungry, and you did not give me food” (Matt. XXV). He did not say, “You murdered; you committed theft”; but, “I was hungry, and you did not give me food.” He will not have to give an account of his crime for whom the case concerning mercy will be established.

> [Note: To “give an account” is the same as to be brought before the judgment.]

Why? Because, “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke XI). The one whose generosity is praised by the judge will not be judged for guilt; the one who acknowledges the debt of humanity does not demand vengeance.

“I was hungry,” he says, “and you did not give me food” (Matt. XXV). God eats in heaven the bread which the poor man has received on earth. “As long as you did it for one of these least ones, you did it for me” (Matt. XXV). Give, then, bread; give drink; give clothing; give shelter, if you wish to have God as your debtor rather than your judge. Nothing will harm us on earth if mercy is our patron in heaven.

## SERMON XLIII. On Prayer, Fasting, and Almsgiving

> [Note: Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book XIV, chapter 15, says: “Unless popular matters were set before them, the faith of the simple would fail.” Observe how our author speaks suitably to his hearers, and how he uses the Latin tongue in delivering homilies, as in Sermon 159. MITA.]

One must speak popularly to the people; the community must be addressed in ordinary speech; necessary matters must be stated in the manner common to all. The natural language is dear to the simple and sweet to the learned. Let the teacher speak what will benefit everyone. Therefore, today let the learned pardon an unlearned expression.

There are three things, three things, brothers, by which faith stands, devotion is established, and virtue endures: prayer, fasting, and mercy. What prayer knocks upon, fasting obtains; mercy receives. Prayer, mercy, and fasting—these three are one; they give life to one another. For fasting is the soul of prayer, and mercy is the life of fasting. Let no one sever these things; they do not know how to be separated.
