Whoever has only one of them, or whoever does not have these things together, has nothing.

> [Note: We restore this passage, corrupt in the editions, from the Caesena manuscript.]

Therefore, let the one who prays fast; let the one who fasts show mercy. Let the one who asks to be heard hear the petitioner. He opens God’s hearing to himself who does not close his own hearing to the one who supplicates him. Let the one who fasts understand fasting; let the one who wishes God to feel what he suffers feel the hungry person. Let the one who hopes for mercy show mercy; let the one who seeks kindness perform it; let the one who wishes to benefit himself benefit another.

The petitioner is wicked who asks for himself what he denies to another. Man, be a model of mercy to yourself,

> [Note: Namely, a rule, example, or standard, as below.]

so that mercy may be shown to you as you wish, as much as you wish, and as quickly as you wish; show mercy to others yourself just as quickly, in equal measure, and in the same manner.

Therefore, let prayer, mercy, and fasting be one protection for us before God; let these three be one advocacy for us; let this one prayer for us be threefold.

These are the things, brothers—these are the things that hold the citadel of heaven, that knock upon the inner chamber of God the judge,

> [Note: The inner chamber, the innermost parts of the house, as above: “terrifying in its privacy.”]

that plead the case of the human race before Christ’s tribunal, that ask pardon for the unjust and obtain forgiveness for the guilty.

Whoever does not have these assisting him in heavenly matters does not stand on earth. Since these hold primacy in heaven, they govern the sum of affairs on earth. They direct prosperity; they drive away adversity. They extinguish vices; they kindle virtues. They render bodies chaste and hearts pure; they give peace to the limbs and rest to the mind. They make human senses a school of discipline. Through them human breasts rise into a temple of God. They make a human being an angel; through them they convey the honor of divinity to humanity.

Hence, through their support,

> [Note: Theodoret, *Dialogue* 2, p. 56: “That man, Moses, was a type and figure of the truth. A type does not possess everything that the truth possesses. Therefore he was not God by nature; yet he was called God, in order to fulfill the type.”]

Moses becomes God (Exod. III), and he commands all the elements to serve his military triumphs: he orders the sea to withdraw, the waves to become firm, and the depths to dry up (Exod. XIV); he commands the heavens to rain; he supplies grain and compels the winds to scatter the meat (Exod. XVI). He illumines the night with the splendor of the sun and tempers the sun with the covering of a cloud (Exod. XIII). He strikes the rock so that, from the fresh wound, it may give cool streams to the thirsty (Num. XX).

> [Note: Thus the Vatican and Vallicella manuscripts and Mita’s edition. The Caesena manuscript has *defluant flumina*, “let streams flow down.”]

He first gives the earth the law of heaven, writes the rule of life, and fixes the boundaries of discipline (Exod. XXIV, XXXV).

Through these things Elijah does not know death, leaves the earth,

> [Note: Other copies have “heaven.” The ancient authorities do not hold the same opinion concerning Elijah’s assumption. Some, following the Septuagint version, say that he was not taken up into heaven, but as though into heaven. See Theodoret on Psalm XXIV, p. 486; Athanasius, *Oration on the Assumption of Christ*, vol. II, p. 4; Oecumenius on Acts I, p. 4. Others teach that he was truly taken up into heaven: Chrysostom, *Homily 2 to the People of Antioch*, vol. I, p. 37 of the Paris edition; Nazianzen, Oration 34, p. 549; Tertullian, book V *Against Marcion*, chapter 12, p. 795. Scripture teaches the same.]

enters the heavens, dwells with angels, and feasts with God; and an earthly guest possesses the dwellings above (IV Kings II).

Through these things John becomes an angel in the flesh, heavenly on earth,

> [Note: Nyssenus, *Oration on the Nativity of Christ*, vol. III, p. 345: “Great among the prophets and a forerunner equal to the angels.” Theophylact on Luke VII, p. 352: “John was an angel, perhaps because he lived an angelic life, perhaps also because he announced the Redeemer’s coming.” But beware the error of those who, from John I.6, asserted that John was not a human being but a pure angel; Cyril refutes them in the *Catena* on John I.6.]

and, by hearing, sight, and touch, alone grasps, holds, and embraces the whole Trinity.

> [Note: That is, among human beings he alone, through the three senses—hearing, sight, and touch—holds and embraces the Trinity. In other words, as far as possible, he apprehends, understands, and comprehends the Trinity through the senses themselves: he touches the Son whom he baptizes; he sees the Holy Spirit descending upon the Son in the form of a dove; and he hears the Father’s voice thunder from the cloud: “This is my Son.” MITA.]

And we, brothers, if we wish to share in Moses’ glory, Elijah’s life, John’s virtues, and the merits of all the saints, let us devote ourselves to prayer, give ourselves to fasting, and serve mercy.

Whoever lives in these things, whoever is fortified by them, will not fear the darts of sin, the weapons of the devil, the machinations of the world, the wedges of vices,

> [Note: As he said in Sermon 13, “the camps of vices.” *Cuneus* means a multitude of infantry arranged in a wedge-shaped formation. Vegetius, book III, chapter 19. See below, Sermon 174, from Mita.]

the evils of the flesh, the snares of pleasures, or the weapons of death. As a Christian soldier and a warrior of the Lord, he will not fear them.

But we, who rise amid uncertainties, who pass the day among ambushes, who endure the changes of hours, the movements of moments, the slips of words, and the dangers of actions—why is it that we do not wish to enter the church in the morning? Why do we not wish to ask, by morning prayer, for protection throughout the whole day?

> [Note: It was the custom of the ancient Christians to gather in the churches before dawn and there devote themselves to prayer and divine psalmody. See Pliny’s letter to Trajan, illustrated by the observations of Vossius.]

Why do we gladly stand before a human being for an entire period of time, but do not wish to stand before God even for a moment? It is not ours, brothers; it is not ours. This is the enemy’s theft: he prepares to deceive those whom he does not allow to be fortified by prayers.

Why does one complain of adversity who does not pray for prosperity? Let us hear the voice of God warning us: “Pray, lest you enter into temptation” (Matt. XXVI). The one who does not go to prayer goes into temptation.

Knowing this, the prophet sang: “Come, let us worship and fall down before him; and let us weep before the Lord who made us” (Ps. XCIV). Do you think that the one who does not deign to utter words before God will deign to pour out tears?

Let us rise early and pray, whether from human fear if not from divine love, whether not invited by blessings, then compelled by evils.

> [Note: In several printed editions, corruptly, *magnificemus*, “let us magnify.” *Manicare* means the same as “to rise early.”]

Bad times are made for us by contempt of God; the passage of time does not make them. What we have therefore lost through contempt, let us recover through fasting. Let us sacrifice our souls through fasting, because there is nothing more excellent that we can offer to God. The prophet confirms this when he says: “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a broken and humbled heart God will not despise” (Ps. L).

Man, offer your soul to God, and offer the offering of fasting, so that it may be a pure victim, a holy sacrifice, a living offering—one that may remain with you and be given to God. Whoever does not give this to God will not be excused, because he cannot fail to possess what he is going to give himself.

But for these offerings to be acceptable, let mercy follow. Fasting does not sprout if it is not watered by mercy; fasting dries up from the drought of mercy. What rain is to the earth, mercy is to fasting. Although it cultivates the heart, cleanses the flesh, uproots vices, and sows virtues, if it does not provide streams of mercy, the person who fasts gathers no fruit.

O person who fasts, your field fasts when mercy fasts. O person who fasts, what you pour out in mercy returns to you in the granary.

Therefore, man, lest you lose by preserving, gather by distributing. Man, by giving to the poor, give to yourself; for what you leave to another, you will not have.

## SERMON XLIV. On the Counsel of the Ungodly, the Way of Sinners, and the Seat of Pestilence, on Psalm I

Whenever a skilled physician desires to apply a complete medicine to those exhausted by various illnesses, he uncovers the deep causes of diseases, exposes the hidden attacks of pestilence, warns that pestilential regions must be avoided, demonstrates very many kinds of remedies, reveals the powers of herbs, explains the qualities of medicines, and promises the obedient the longest-lasting health. In this way he persuades sick people to undertake difficult and harsh treatments and leads them through them.

For this reason the holy prophet, about to bring forth from heaven a medicine for body and soul, discloses the deep recesses of ungodliness,

> [Note: Elsewhere, “he disclosed.”]

lays bare the hidden diseases of sinners, displays iniquities, and draws forth, by wondrous reasoning, the secret poison, the natures of vices, the origins of transgressions, and the roots of crimes. Thus, with pious moderation, according to age, sex, time, and strength, he continually leads the sick minds of mortals to salvation through divine healing.

The psalm we have sung today

> [Note: In truth, many interpreters, and almost all of them, regard this psalm as the preface and summary of all the psalms.]

is the preface of the Psalms—indeed, the psalm of Psalms, the title of titles. It is the argument that generates arguments; it is the entire cause of the songs that follow. And just as the key to a royal hall, once it has opened the first door, makes accessible the innermost and manifold chambers,

> [Note: From the Vatican manuscript. All printed editions have *penetrales*, “inner chambers.”]

so this psalm, once it has unlocked the first entrances to understanding, unfolds the mystery and secret of all the psalms.

“Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of pestilence” (Ps. I).

“Blessed is the man.” Just as prizes, rewards, and crowns are announced beforehand to one about to fight beasts and undergo the dangers of the most serious contests, so the prophet placed blessedness first, in order to challenge a person to overcome the whole ferocity of the crimes that he later enumerates.

> [Note: The Caesena manuscript has *tantam*, “so great.”]

“Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners.” What he called walking in counsel and standing in the way may perhaps seem absurd, since in ordinary human usage one more commonly stands in counsel and walks in a way. But everything is perverse to the perverse, and those things that are not done in order cannot preserve order.

Nevertheless, the prophet is speaking here not of bodily movement but of the movement of the mind; he does not forbid slips of the feet but wards off the ruin of souls.

“Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly.” The ungodly man “walked”—he walked away from himself and from God when he withdrew. Nor does he stand in counsel who wanders through ungodly thoughts.

> [Note: Other interpreters likewise explain the psalm’s Hebrew phrasing as referring to the ungodly, who act wickedly restlessly and without ceasing, like the sea, which cannot be at rest; see Isaiah LVII.20 and Proverbs IV.16.]

At one moment he is carried toward heaven, at another brought back to earth; he is tossed across the seas, lifted by the waves, and plunged into the depths. And while he continually rolls about in his own mind like a drunken man, he does not count himself—and he counts heaven.

> [Note: Many make “heaven” the object of his worship, and so forth, although you make him nothing. MITA.]

He who thinks that he knows everything does not know himself. If he knew himself, he would never worship heaven, the sun, the moon, wood, or stones, all of which have been given and subjected to his service; but he worships stone and serves wood, because he has refused to serve the living and true God.

And, to recount the deeds of ungodliness from the very beginning of things, the counsel of ungodliness led to the depths of hell. It changed the angel from the heights, the messenger of the heavenly secret, into the devil; it transferred man from the governance of life into the exile of a mortal dwelling; it drove him from the delights of paradise into the wearisome labors of the world; and it cast woman down from the glory of virginity into conscious groans during childbirth.

Hence, before she rejoices, she already knows sorrows, and she pays the penalty for guilt before rejoicing in the birth of offspring. “Multiplying, I will multiply your sorrows and your groanings; in sorrow and groaning you will bear children” (Gen. III).

What kind of end can there be where the beginning is penal? What joy in life can hold one who takes the beginning of life from sorrow? The prophet knew this when he said: “I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother bore me in sins” (Ps. L).

If, brothers, we are thus thrown from the womb into the way of sinners, and run the path of transgressions through all our ages, let us consider the vanities of infancy, the falls of adolescence, the ruins of youth, and the diseases of old age. Then we shall see that we do not take the way of life, but the way of sinners.

Christ identifies this way when he says: “How broad and spacious is the way that leads to destruction, and many are those who enter through it” (Matt. VII). Broad with transgressions, spread wide with waves, spacious with crimes—and truly the present life is the way into which man comes and from which he goes.

“One generation goes,” he says, “and another generation comes, and the earth stands forever” (Eccl. VII). Therefore he said first: “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners.”

He did not say, “who has not come”; for no one fails to enter the way of sinners, into which the very law of nature leads us, and death. Rather: blessed is the one who does not stand in it.

He stands and lingers in it who takes up the burdens of sins; and the burdened traveler arrives slowly and finds the heavenly dwelling closed to him. The prophet, impeded by these burdens, lamented: “My iniquities have risen above my head, and like a heavy burden they have been made heavy upon me.” And because he bore them throughout his whole life, he cried out: “I have become miserable, and I have been bowed down to the end” (Ps. XXXVII).

That traveler passes through the way of sinners who sees the evils of this life but despises them; feels them but tramples them down; suffers them but conquers them. And while he flees from them, he runs all the more. Thus the heavenly doorkeeper meets him, and the heavenly dwelling does not close itself against him.

But why did he place the counsel of ungodliness before the way of sinners in this way: “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners”? Because although a human being, once born, immediately enters the way of sinners, he lies there at first. He does not immediately run along the way of sin; but when he begins to taste the poisons of ungodliness, he then draws nourishment from the richness of sins.

> [Note: “When the ungodly comes into the depths, he rejoices in his ungodliness and takes pleasure in it.”]

The ungodly man presses on against God and departs from God when he sins. God despises sinners, since he earlier commanded that they ought not to sin. Darkness flees the light; darkness returns when the light withdraws. Where God is, there is no sin; where sin is, God is not.

And so that you may know, man, that a human being runs along the way of sinners away from the presence of God, hear the prophet: “God is not in his sight; his ways are defiled at all times” (Ps. IX). A person therefore slips more grievously into the way of sinners when he plunges into it through the precipices of ungodliness.

“And he did not sit in the seat of pestilence.” The one who commits ungodliness proves it; the one who loves it cannot fail to teach it. Hence, while teaching ungodliness, he sits in the seat of pestilence and spreads the poison of deadly teaching among his listeners with honeyed speech.

> [Note: And thus he signifies that the man is a teacher of ungodliness. In the psalm, sitting indicates the teaching of the ungodly, whether hearing or teaching, since teachers and hearers sit. The progression occurs by degrees: walking is less than standing, and standing is less than sitting.]

The philosopher established the seat of pestilence, teaching either that there are many gods, or that the one who exists either does not exist or cannot be discovered; he attributed creation itself to nature in order to deny the Author of nature.

> [Note: He attacks the errors of the gentiles, who either denied one God, taught that he does not care for our affairs, or asserted that it cannot be known where he resides.]

The Pharisee set up the seat of pestilence, placing human traditions before heavenly decrees and thereby overthrowing the vast light of the Jewish people.

> [Note: That is, he overturned, scattered, and brought to destruction the immense light possessed by the Jewish people. MITA.]

The heretic sat in the seat of pestilence, dividing, tearing apart, and fragmenting unity under the appearance of faith.

Blessed, therefore, is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of pestilence. And plainly he is blessed, because by avoiding these three things he has deserved to reach the blessedness of the Trinity.

Let him therefore meditate on the law of the Lord, and meditate on it day and night, so that he may deserve to see in the future and hear more fully what follows at the proper time.

## SERMON XLV. On Frail Man Praying to God Not to Rebuke Him in Anger, on Psalm VI
[Note: [Col. 0325D] By this term they indicated a chant in which, while the cantor sang the individual verses of a psalm one by one, the choir responded by repeating those same verses. This practice seems to have been admitted at the beginning of the Church into Christian assemblies, since by it even the uneducated populace [Col. 0326C] could more easily learn to sing psalms together. This is clear from Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book II, chapter 17, in Rufinus’s translation, where, recounting what Philo the Jew reports about the Essenes, he concludes as follows: “All these things the aforesaid man described in the same order and with the same sequence as they are performed among us: one person rising from among them stands in the midst and sings a psalm in dignified melodies, and all respond to him, who leads the singing, with a single verse.” If you wish for examples, consult Martène, *De Antiquis Ecclesiae Disciplinis*, p. 19, no. 7.]

The responsory which today we have sung, as the prophet makes supplication, is appropriate to the present time and suited to present evils; your affection, together with mine, approves and recognizes this. “Lord,” he says, “do not rebuke me in your anger, nor chastise me in your fury” (Psalm VI). Does God then swell with anger? Does he grow hot with fury? Far be it, brothers. God is not subject to passion, is not kindled by anger, and is not disturbed by fury; rather, the anger of God is the punishment of those who transgress, and the fury of God is the penalty of sinners.

Brothers, formed from dust and fashioned from clay, we are trampled by vices, subjected to sins, exhausted by cares, withering in our limbs, dissolved by death, and horrified by stinking tombs; thus we are found incapable of virtues but capable of vices. The prophet, therefore, mindful of human frailty [Col. 0326A] and conscious of his fleshly substance, because he did not trust in his merits, hastened to the aid of mercy, so that God’s judgment concerning him might be shown to arise from compassion, not severity.

“Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger.” This is to say: rebuke me, but not in anger; chastise me, but not in fury. Rebuke me as a father, not as a judge; chastise me not as a master, but as a parent. Rebuke me, not in order to destroy me, but to correct me; chastise me, not in order to kill me, but to amend me. And why? “For I am weak.”

“Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak.” What is weaker than a human being, whom sensation deceives, ignorance misleads, judgment circumvents, splendor injures, time abandons, age changes, infancy dulls, youth rushes headlong, and old age breaks?

[Note: [Col. 0326D] He joins together the diseases of the soul and body. Genebrard explains the words of the psalm themselves in this way: “I am frail in body and, properly speaking, cut off in spirit.” One group of interpreters teaches that the passage concerns bodily infirmities, another that it concerns spiritual infirmities. Chrysologus embraces both.]

For God to be angry with such a person in anger and indignant in fury is not the action of a compassionate creator, but of a most severe examiner.

“Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak.” And what do you want?

[Note: [Col. 0326D] Augustine: “What, then, does this man pray for, who does not wish to be rebuked or corrected in the anger of the Lord? What else than that he may be healed?”]

“Heal me, Lord.” This man feels the wounds of his condition; he feels the bite of the ancient serpent; he feels the fall of the first parent; he acknowledges that he came into these infirmities by being born; he acknowledges that he naturally arrived at death. And since human skill could not remove death, he is compelled to seek divine medicine. To obtain the treatment of his sickness more readily, he discloses the causes of that sickness, describes its qualities, reveals its greatness, and expresses the force of his pain.

“Heal me, Lord.” Why? “For my bones are troubled.”

[Note: [Col. 0326D] Other interpreters likewise attribute this same explanation to David in words of this sort. And truly, the strength of the body is in the bones, without which it would have to crawl. Or “bones” is used for the whole body. Thus elsewhere the bones are said to praise the Lord, Psalm XXXIV, 10; to rejoice, Psalm L, 10; to be terrified, Job IV, 14; to waste away, Psalm XXXIII, 19; and to be deprived of peace, Psalm XXXVII, 4.]

The bones carry the whole structure of the body; and if the bones are troubled, what firmness remains in the limbs? What strength in the sinews? Where is the pitiable substance of the flesh?

[Col. 0326C]

The bones are troubled, brothers, by the weight of sins, by fear of death, and by dread of judgment. Hear him saying this elsewhere: “There is no health in my flesh because of your anger; there is no peace for my bones because of my sins” (Psalm XXXVII). And afterward: “My soul is filled with mockeries, and there is no health in my flesh.” He therefore rightly adds: “And my soul is greatly troubled.”

Between God’s commands and the passions of the heart, between virtues and vices, between adversity and prosperity, between punishments and rewards, between life and death, standing in battle array, enduring wars, receiving wounds, rarely standing firm, fainting in spirit, the soul is troubled [Col. 0327A]—greatly troubled—because, impeded by the burdens of the flesh, before it reaches virtue it first becomes captive to vices.

[Note: [Col. 0327D] Augustine, whom Du Hamel cites here: “Who does not understand the soul struggling with its own members?”]

The Apostle describes these wars when he says: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, so that you do not do the things you wish” (Galatians V). And elsewhere: “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin” (Romans VII).

The blessed prophet, therefore, alleging these infirmities, these wars, and these disturbances of souls, addresses God in such words: “And you, Lord, how long?”

[Note: [Col. 0327D] So Genebrard, Cocceius, Grotius, Pineda, and Vatablus. This is a familiar aposiopesis of one awaiting help and assistance. Compare Genesis XXV, 22; Luke XIX, 42.]

That is: How long will you tolerate this? How long will you pretend not to see? How long will you not come to our aid? How long will you permit your work to be scattered, your image to be destroyed, and your creature to perish from you?

[Col. 0327B]

Where is your Christ, so often announced through the Law, through us, and through the prophets, promised in many ways? Let him come, let him come, before the world perishes and finds nothing within the world to restore. Let him come, let him come, so that he may repair the flesh, renew the soul, and change nature itself into a heavenly substance. Let him come to remove sin, destroy death, overthrow hell, restore life, and grant heaven, lest earthly corruption be able to find in us anything more to destroy.

That the prophet is asking this, the following words demonstrate: “Turn, Lord.” Does a human being speak thus to God, the guilty person to his judge, the condemned person to his examiner? “Turn, Lord.” A human being sins, and God turns? Yes, brothers, because according to the prophet: “He bears our sins and suffers for us” (Isaiah LIII, according to the Septuagint). And blessed John says: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John I). He took sin upon himself in order to remove sin, not to possess it.

“Turn, Lord.” From where? To where? From God into a human being, from master into servant, [Note: [Col. 0327D] Pagninus, Arias Montanus, and others: “Turn away from the heat of your anger.”] from judge into father, so that your turning may show you to be compassionate, though your power threatens you as terrible.

“Turn, Lord; deliver my soul.” From the lower hell. “Save me for the sake of your mercy.” Not for the sake of my merit, since labor afflicts me, groaning wounds me, tears dissolve me, anger disturbs me, and the enemy attacks me. But to make this clear, let the prophet’s own prayer be sung:

“Save me for the sake of your mercy.” Why? “For in death there is no one who remembers you; and in hell, who will confess you? I have labored in my groaning; every night I shall wash my bed; I shall drench my couch with my tears.”

[Col. 0327D]

This is what holy David said while established at the royal summit. He exercised the authority of human power in such a way that he preserved in himself the holiness of the spirit and the grace of the prophet; yet we, placed wholly under the anger of God, do not know how to say: “Lord, do not rebuke us in your fury.”

[Note: [Col. 0327D] Chrysologus laments the afflictions and calamities of his own times.]

The earth refuses its fruits, the sky its temperate air, the atmosphere its healthfulness. Hence pestilence, spread everywhere through cities and fields, consumes the entire human race with various kinds of disease; yet we do not say: “Lord, do not rebuke us in your fury, nor chastise us in your anger.”

He, after triumphs, occupied nights and days with groans and tears; we, lying beneath the hostile sword, give God no time, pour out no tears to God even for an hour. Instead, continually through robberies, frauds, perjuries, deceit, and slander, we surrender and give ourselves over, so that by the provocations of our crimes we may kindle God’s anger against us more and more.

Come, brothers, come with the prophet: “Come, let us adore and fall down before him, and let us weep before the Lord who made us” (Psalm XCIV).

[Note: [Col. 0327D] Claudius Du Vert cites this passage in *Explication des cérémonies de la messe*, vol. I, p. 90, to prove that the clergy sang the psalms alternately with the people; I have noted this elsewhere. Hence Augustine, in Psalm CXIX, which we have just heard sung to us and to which we responded by singing.]

[Col. 0328B]

Come, let us say: “Lord, do not rebuke us in your anger, nor chastise us in your fury.” May he, mindful of his mercy, change anger into mercy, restore what has been lost, and free the captives; and may he now grant us to serve him with joy—he who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XLVI. On spiritual exultation and the confession of sins, on Psalm XCIV

Just as a cold spring, very refreshing and very wholesome, meets one who is burning with fever and consumed by a long thirst, so today, for us who are placed in grief and weighed down by an excessive burden of tribulations, the song of the prophetic voice [Col. 0328C] raises us toward joy:

[Note: [Col. 0328D] All printed editions have: “A song arose.” Mita has not applied medicinal hands to the open wound.]

“Come,” it says, “let us exult in the Lord” (Psalm XCIV).

[Note: [Col. 0328D] In the psalm this is the voice of one urging and rousing people to action. For among the Hebrews, “come” and “rise” are ordinarily expressed by particles equivalent to “come on!” and “go!”]

“Come”—where? Or from where? From yourself, human being, into yourself: not a change of place, but a change of the senses drives away adversities, dispels griefs, casts off despair, excludes distress, enters the dwelling of a sincere heart, and prepares an eternal abode for divine joy.

“Let us exult in the Lord.” And where is that saying, “Blessed are those who mourn” (Matthew V), and “Woe to you who laugh” (Luke VI)? Clearly, blessed are those who mourn for the world, and woe to those who laugh for the world; but blessed are those who exult in the Lord, who do not know how to rejoice in robbery, do not know how to rejoice in fraud, and do not know how to rejoice in the tears of their neighbors.

“Let us exult in the Lord.” He exults in the Lord who, in word, deed, and work, exults not in himself but in his author. “Let us exult in the Lord.” He exults in the Lord for whom God alone and wholly is always joy.

“Let us shout for joy,” he says, “to our saving God.” This is not the voice of sheep; it is the shepherd’s voice. With sweet jubilation and varied modulation, he either leads the flock out to pasture, keeps the weary sheep at rest beneath the shade of a grove, urges them to climb the slopes of high hills in desire for healthier grass, or gradually leads them down into the descending valleys as necessity requires.

[Note: [Col. 0328D] *Jubilus* is a piercing sound, whence *jubilare*, “to sing,” in Psalm LXV. We call the sound of a shepherd’s and countryman’s voice a *jubilus*. Du Cange praises this passage in his *Glossary*, vol. II, col. 139.]

But blessed are those sheep which heed the voice of their shepherd, are drawn by it, nourished, and gathered; which truly shout for joy to their shepherd and strive to multiply the shoots of their flock for the Lord.

Let us anticipate his face in confession. And who can anticipate the knower of sins, the searcher of hearts, the one conscious of thoughts, the foreknower of future things, who is always and everywhere present? Yet he must be anticipated not by nearness of the senses, but by the keenness of the mind; not by the speed of the feet, but by the prudent service of confession. For he did not say merely, “Let us anticipate him,” but, “Let us anticipate his face in confession.”

[Note: [Col. 0329D] The Lord is not to be anticipated in the Pelagian sense, according to which grace is thought to be anticipated by free will; rather, when the time of pardon has come and there is opportunity for repentance, as Chrysologus says a little above.]

That is: when there is hope of mercy, when there is a time for pardon, when there is an opportunity for repentance, let us confess to the Father, lest we experience him as judge. Let us expose what we have done to compassion, lest we be compelled to pay to severity what we conceal.

[Note: [Col. 0329D] By this and what follows, Chrysologus openly confirms the doctrine of auricular confession, whatever the heretics may chatter—those who twist these passages into an evil sense in order to seek shaky supports where their lies are utterly overturned.]

Let us declare our sins at the time of indulgence, lest, if we remain silent, we later lament when receiving the sentence. And what more, brothers? The most merciful prophet urges us to anticipate not the judge, but the judgment.

“And let us shout for joy to him in psalms,” he says. Lest an irrational jubilation be thought to have been proclaimed to our heart without instruction: “Let us shout for joy in psalms.” Thus [Note: [Col. 0329D] The Caesena manuscript has *in primis*, “especially”; the Vallicellian manuscript agrees. We have followed the first Bologna edition.] the divine mystery may resound in the psalms, and may it advance the minds of the hearers toward the progress of salvation.

“For God,” he says, “is a great Lord.” Here he discloses the mystery of the Lord’s body, because God is also a great Lord in our body.

“And a great king above all gods.” In accordance with the saying: “Who will be like God among the sons of God?” (Psalm LXXXVIII). For although all the heavenly powers rule others, they themselves are ruled by Christ.

“For in his hand are all the ends of the earth.” For whatever is in God’s hand cannot be obtained without God, if we desire to enlarge boundaries, extend limits, or call back what has been lost. Let us therefore beseech God with the strength of faith, through whose offense these things perish for us and by whose appeasement they return enlarged. He gives as he wills, takes away, and restores when he wills; if he could not restore, he would not be omnipotent. He does many things as a sign of his majesty and as an example of our amendment and correction. The assistance of others is useless if the help of our king does not come to us.

“For the sea is his, and he made it.”

Do not think that the sea was sought out, discovered, and not created by God. “The sea is his, and he made it, and his hands formed the dry land.”

[Note: [Col. 0329D] Tertullian testifies that Marcion thought the world had been constructed by God from pre-existent matter, in Book V, chapter 19, *Against Marcion*. Hermogenes likewise belonged to this seductive heresy, with Tertullian supporting the claim in *Against the Valentinians*, chapter 13, *Against Hermogenes*, chapter 1, and *On Prescription Against Heretics*, chapter 33; so did the Manichaeans. On these see Chrysostom, homily 1, vol. V; Theodoret, *Compendium of Heretical Myths*, Book I, chapter 26; Epiphanius, heresy 66; and Gregory of Nyssa, *On the Making of Man*, chapter 22, vol. I, pp. 105–106.]

Where are those who fabricate that God formed the world from matter, and especially from water?

[Note: [Col. 0330D] Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book II, chapter 10: “Thales of Miletus, who first inquired into such matters, said that water was the beginning of things, but that God was the mind which fashioned everything from water.” The philosopher seems to have drawn this from Moses’ passage: “The Spirit of the Lord moved over the waters.” Consult Huet’s letter to Gilbert Cuper in Tilladet, vol. II, p. 222.]

Our God, in heaven and on earth, not as the discoverer but as the creator of matter, accomplished all things from nothing.

“Come,” he says, “let us adore.”

The things that follow, brothers, show—as though the prophet had forgotten his exultation—that after summoning us to joy he soon calls us to tears.

“Come,” he says, “let us adore and fall down before him, and let us weep before the Lord who made us.”

He had said, “Come, let us exult.” But here the prophet desires us to pour forth tears from our very joys.

[Note: [Col. 0330D] It is already established that tears are poured forth unexpectedly from joy. Gaspar Barth praises and illustrates this passage in *Adversaria*, Book XLII, chapter 21, col. 1911.]

For tears are produced not only by great grief but also by joy; they disclose and testify to the feeling of the inner heart.

Those who had formerly prostrated themselves before stones and pieces of wood, now, having at last come to know the true God, he wishes us to adore and fall down before him and to repay our long neglect with tears and the continual obedience of devotion.

[Note: [Col. 0330D] Others observe, with Chrysologus, that by these three words of the Psalmist—“let us adore,” “let us fall down,” “let us weep”—we are taught, first, the veneration and worship owed to God; second, that this is to be expressed not only in the heart but also through outward posture; and third, through tears.]

Thus he weeps while repenting of the past, rejoicing over the present, and burning with concern and fear over the future.

That the weeping was one of perfect joy is demonstrated by what follows:

“Come, let us adore and fall down before him, and let us weep before the Lord who made us.”

And as though he were asked, “Why?” he gives the reasons and opens the explanations:

“For he is our God, and we are the people of his pasture and the sheep of his hand.”

From this it follows that, to the extent that the one who rejoices is devout, the one who is sorrowful is ungrateful.

But let us now listen more attentively to what he urges:

“Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts as in the provocation, according to the day of temptation in the wilderness, where your fathers tempted me; they tested me and saw my works. For forty years I was near that generation, and I said: They always go astray in heart; but they did not know my ways. So I swore in my anger: They shall not enter into my rest.”

When he says “today,” he addresses you; he speaks to you, whoever you are who hear, lest, after hearing his voice, you incur the guilt of contempt and the crime of obstinacy—he whom neither commands nor example has corrected.

For this reason he recounted Jewish hardness at such length: to make you, Christian, more cautious. God does not merely spend forty years among you and dwell with you; throughout the whole period of your life he attends you and works for your salvation.

[Col. 0331A]

## SERMON XLVII. On the parables of the pearl that was found and the net cast into the sea

Christ our God demonstrated wondrous proofs of his power by creating heaven, earth, the sea, and within them great, numerous, and varied creatures. But by taking on what is human, acting as a human being, entering time, [Note: [Col. 0331D]

Sedulius, Book I:

> “And he bore, in part,  
> the courses of the ages,  
> in human form.”

Augustine, *Sermon* 146, *On Time*: “He patiently awaited the ages; patiently he endured the times.”]

passing through the ages, teaching by his word, healing by his power, speaking in comparisons, proposing examples, and disclosing in himself the weight of our affections, he revealed that an ineffable love for humanity resides in him.

Hence he commends heavenly things through earthly examples, grants us to understand future things through present realities, and indicates invisible things by visible arguments. The comparisons that the Gospel reading proclaims to us today prove this:

“The kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking good pearls; but when he found one precious pearl, he went away and sold everything that he had and bought it” (Matthew XIII).

[Note: [Col. 0331D] Trade in pearls was familiar to the Jews because of the proximity of the Red Sea.]

Let no one who hears the name “merchant” take offense. Here he speaks of a merchant who gives mercy, not one who always charges the interest of usury; one who seeks the adornments of virtues, not the provocations of vices; one who bears the dignity of character, not the weight of stones; one who wears the necklaces of honesty, not luxury; one who carries not the pomp of pleasure but the insignia of discipline.

This merchant, therefore, offers these pearls of heart and body not in human commerce but in divine exercise; not for present profit but to purchase the future; not for earthly glory but for heavenly glory. In this way he may acquire the kingdom of heaven by the reward of virtues [Col. 0331C] and redeem, with countless goods, the one pearl of eternal life.

The Lord added another comparison, saying:

“Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea and gathering fish of every kind. When it was full, they drew it out; and sitting beside the shore, they selected the good into vessels, but threw the bad outside.”

“The kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea.” This comparison reveals why Christ chose fishermen for the apostolate and made fish-catchers into fishers of human beings: so that the type of divine judgment might be displayed through the art of fishing.

The catch gathers fish in confusion, but selection places the chosen in vessels.

[Note: What the Greeks call σαγήνη (*sagēnē*), and the Latins *sagena*, is called a dragnet (*everriculum*): its nature and operation are to draw along with itself whatever comes in its way. Grotius observes here from Plutarch and Homer that this very kind of net is called πάναγρον (*panagron*, “all-catching”).]

Thus the Christian calling gathers the just and unjust, the wicked and the good; but divine election distinguishes the good from the wicked.

[Col. 0332A]

“The kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea.”

Into the swelling sea of this age—puffed up with pomp, lifted high in its crest, wavy in its divisions, fluctuating in ignorance, loud with disputes, roaring with anger, savage through treachery, shipwrecked by sins, and sunk in impiety—Christ sent his fishermen: Peter, Andrew, James, and John, proven in their craft, when he said: “Come after me, and I will make you become fishers of men” (Matthew IV).

He therefore sent his fishermen bearing nets woven from legal and evangelical commandments, surrounded by admonitions, enlarged by the gifts and grace of virtues, gathering an endless catch in the bosom of the Gospel.

This is what is happening now, brothers. Throughout the nations and peoples, Christ’s nets are now being drawn, and they bring in confused catches throughout the whole world, without distinction of persons.

[Note: [Col. 0331D] From the Vatican manuscript: Mita and others read *credituras*, “those who would believe.” Perhaps not incorrectly.]

But because the end of the age is near, and the nets of our catch are now approaching the shore of judgment, the fish—that is, human beings—who wander freely and without restraint through the depth of the age are shaken by the dryness of the shore, that is, by the nearness of the end, and collide with the entire dispensation of things:

[Note: [Col. 0331D] That is, blind mortals, entirely incapable of understanding the just judgments of God, consider this administration of human affairs unjust and perverse. For “to collide with the entire dispensation of things” means nothing other than to be scandalized—that is, to be gravely offended because all things appear to them to have been badly distributed—when they see wicked nations grow stronger, and other things that are mentioned in the text. Those who are scandalized in this way are weak, not strong. Saint Hilary, *Commentary on Matthew* XXV, says: “Many will indeed be troubled by these vexations; when such evils arise, they will be scandalized and will be stirred up into mutual hatred, and there will be false prophets,” and so forth. Mita.]

They see impious nations grow through successive triumphs; Christian peoples throughout the world, though captive, suffer distress; the wicked rejoice in prosperous outcomes; the devout are trampled beneath an unbroken succession of evils; masters are subjected to slavery, servants rule their masters, rebellious children rise against their parents, the old are despised by the young, and the entire order of nature and arrangement of life has fallen into ruin.

But although these things are so, they do not disturb the strong; rather—

[Note: [Col. 0332D] Mita reads differently: “But although these things are so, they disturb the weak; they cannot disturb the strong, because…”]

they disturb the weak but cannot disturb the strong, because the strong draw strength from the comparison and courage from the figure.

[Note: [Col. 0332D] That is, from the Gospel net, which encloses every kind of fish, while it belongs to divine election to distinguish the good from the wicked.]

Fish drawn out from the deep roll about for a little while on the shore in their confusion; but swift separation casts away the wicked and chooses the good. It makes the good good; it does not disturb them. This confusion is brief and will soon pass.

[Note: [Col. 0332D] Below: “this brief mixture.” Augustine, *Sermon* 362, formerly 121 among the miscellaneous sermons: “The good tolerate the wicked until they are separated at the end.”]

This heavenly separation gives the wicked to punishments and carries the good to honor; leads the impious down to Tartarus and conveys the devout into the kingdom. It will console fathers, elders, the just, and the chosen—all of them—for a slight insult with everlasting glory.

The comparison itself proves this when it says:

“At the consummation of the age, the angels of God will go out and separate the wicked from among the just.”

“At the consummation of the age”: whoever believes in the consummation of the age, whoever complains about the diminution of the age, whoever trusts that what will remain is to follow—why seek to possess what is passing away?

Brothers, the world takes its beginning from its end; the creature is renewed by its end, not destroyed. The age comes to an end not for the Creator but for crime; the elements come to an end not for the just but for sinners.

“At the consummation of the age the angels will go out…”

[Note: [Col. 0333C] Some editions have: “to obey the just.”]

“…to separate the just.”

Let no one doubt that the angels will obey the saints, to whom Christ also promises their service. It is Christ’s voice: “I will gird myself and minister to you.”

“The angels of God will go out and separate the wicked from among the just” (Luke XVII).

Endure, just ones; endure—or rather, just ones, grant a delay. This brief mixture will be weighed against a long separation.

[Note: [Col. 0333C] That is, endure and support for a little while longer.]

“They will separate the wicked from among the just and cast them into the furnace of fire.”

Behold what dwelling those who drive out their neighbors and expel guests choose for themselves.

[Note: [Col. 0333C] Here and above he is speaking in this same sermon about enemies ravaging the Western Empire and refers to guests expelled from their own cities and provinces, as is clear from reading the histories. Mita.]

Behold those who here procure delights for themselves through the hunger of the poor and the sufferings of others; there they kindle for themselves a fire proportionate to the slight pleasure they enjoyed.

[Col. 0331B]

“There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” How badly the one who laughs badly here will gnash there! And the one who now rejoices in the misfortunes of the poor will then mourn over the prosperity of the poor, because he could have rejoiced with the poor but refused. But you, faithful ones, rejoice in the Lord always.

## SERMON XLVIII. On Christ being called the son of a carpenter, and on envy
The Evangelist, today intending to expose the envy of the Jews toward Christ, began in this way: “Jesus,” he says, “came into his own country and taught them in their synagogues, so that they were amazed and said: ‘Where did this man get this wisdom and these mighty works? Is this not the carpenter’s son? Is not his mother called Mary, and his brothers James, Joseph, Simon, and Judas? And are not all his sisters with us? Where, then, did he get all these things?’” (Matthew 13).

No cloud so darkens the sky, night the day, the sun mist, as envy blinds and obscures the mind. The Jewish spite proves this: they marvel at Christ’s wisdom, are astonished at his miracles, exalt his works, and accept his words; yet, so that divinity might not be seen in him and deity perceived, they recall and proclaim the names of his earthly parents.

“He came,” he says, “Jesus came into his own country.” Let no one wonder if the Creator of all things, the Lord of heaven, the God of all, [Note: [Col. 0333D] Christ’s homeland is in a manner threefold: Bethlehem, where he was born; Nazareth, where he was brought up; and Capernaum, where he established his dwelling. Here, all agree, Nazareth is indicated.] takes for himself a homeland and a place, when he confines himself in a womb, measures himself within a cradle, occupies a breast, is enclosed in an embrace, and is placed in arms; and, in order to remove human constraints, gives and adapts himself to human constraints. O man, through these things God lowers himself to you; through these things he follows you; through these constraints he seeks you, so that the one whom he formed by his work he might reform by his example; whom he rejected by judgment, he might restore by affection; and that in himself he might preserve the one whom, apart from himself, he sees to have perished. [Note: [Col. 0333D] Humanity had perished, for access to heaven was in no way open to it before God had assumed humanity. It is preserved by God himself when the Son of God hypostatically assumed human nature. MITA.]

“He came,” he says, “Jesus came into his own country and taught them in their synagogues.” Not in his own temple, but [Note: [Col. 0333D] In accordance with the Vulgate, the Greek text has: ἐν τῇ συναγωγῇ αὐτῶν, “in their synagogue.” And some rightly think this: for in Nazareth, a most obscure town, there could scarcely have been several synagogues.] in their synagogues. They could not have been his synagogues, since the crowds gathered there in unbelief, not in faith; there the people of envy assembled, not of love; there sat the council of the wicked, not the council of sound discipline.

He taught in their synagogues, “so that they were amazed.” They marveled in indignation, not in gratitude; they were astonished in spite, not in praise; they raged because what the proud benches could not comprehend, humble standing produced [Note: [Col. 0333D] From the Caesena and Vall. manuscripts. Very many printed editions read: “they produced.”], so that they marveled and said: “Where did this man get such wisdom?” [Note: [Col. 0333D] Novar. in Vall.: “As though they were being oppressed by some calamity,” because they looked with envious eyes upon Christ’s authority, which he had won for himself through so many miracles.]

Thus speaks the one who does not know God, from whom wisdom comes and from whom strength comes; thus speaks the one who does not know that Christ is the wisdom of God and the power of God. From whom wisdom comes is proved by Solomon. When, though still a child, he received the summit of the kingdom, so that he might govern the people entrusted to him with strength, not arrogance; with wisdom, not swelling pride; with the heart, not the head, he desired wisdom from God, asked for it, and received it.

“Where did this man get such wisdom and such power?” No one who begrudged salvation would deny that the power which gives eyes that nature had not given, restores hearing closed by weakness, loosens in the mute the bonds of speech, brings the lame back to running, and compels souls already bound in the underworld to return to their own bodies comes from God.

But the Jews knew that Christ’s works were works of divine power, not of human ability; yet [Note: [Col. 0333D] They were not slandering Christ as though all these things were performed by the power of trickery or sorcery. Christ does not reproach them with anything of that kind; rather, as Chrysologus rightly observes, they were driven by envy because one of such lowly birth had won so great a reputation.] the cloud of spite and the smoke of malice darkened the eyes of those who looked, so that they might not perceive the light of Christ or the time of the Gospel, as they said: “Is this not the carpenter’s son?”

They said, “This is the carpenter’s son,” but they did not say whose carpenter’s son he was. They said “the carpenter’s son” so that the craft might conceal the skill of its author, and the carpenter’s name hide the name of deity.

Christ was the son of a carpenter, but of the one who made the fabric of the world—not with a hammer, but by command; [Note: [Col. 0334C] A little farther below, he says that he did not forge it with charcoal. Chrysologus seems to think that Joseph, Christ’s putative father, practiced the craft of a smith. The phrase “carpenter’s son” in the Gospel produced various opinions about Joseph’s occupation. Pseudo-Eustathius, in the *Hexameron*, p. 37, considers him a builder of houses; Hugh, Cardinal, in his commentary on Mark 6, a goldsmith; nor does he condemn those who make him a mason. Hilary, on Matthew 15, p. 737, considers him an ironsmith: “Clearly he was the son of a smith, of one who conquers iron with fire, who melts down every power of the world by judgment and forms the mass for every work useful to humanity.” There was therefore no reason for Scultetus to mark Hilary’s opinion as a crime that could not be expiated by any flames of atonement. The same opinion seem to have been held by Theophilus of Antioch in his commentary on Matthew; Ambrose in *On Luke*, book 3, no. 2, where he copies the words of the aforementioned Theophilus; Bede on Mark 2; and Chrysologus here. The preferable opinion, however, is that he was a carpenter in wood. For when the word τέκτων is used absolutely, as in the Gospel, it has been observed from Book 5 of Xenophon’s *Cyropaedia* that it indicates a worker in wood. Consult Justin, that very ancient writer from Palestine, who regarded Joseph as a carpenter in his *Dialogue with Trypho*, p. 316. This was also known to that impious man Libanius, whose very witty reply, given by a schoolmaster, may be seen in Theodoret, book 3 of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 23, p. 142 of Valesius’s edition, and in Sozomen, book 6, chapter 2. But we have already exceeded the limits of the note.]

He joined together the members of the elements, not by skill but by command; he forged the mass of the world by authority, not with charcoal; he kindled the sun, not with earthly fire but with heavenly heat; he formed the moon, darkness, night, and the seasons; he distinguished the stars with varied light; he made everything out of nothing—and he made it, O man, for you, so that you might weigh the craftsman by the value of his work.

But you, Jew, recognize this carpenter’s son, to whom, for such great benefits, you ought to repay your duty as to a son. This is why you do not receive the things to come: because you are ungrateful for those that are present.

“Is this not the carpenter’s son? Is not his mother called Mary?” Again, Jew, you cry out the mother’s name [Note: [Col. 0335C] Most think this was done because Joseph was no longer alive.] and conceal the Father; you name the father but do not name him; you name the carpenter but do not name the work.

Jew, these things deceive you, but they do not deceive those who will believe.

“Is not his mother called Mary, and his brothers James and Joseph and Simon and Judas? And are not all his sisters with us?” If his mother, brothers, and sisters are with you, where is the father? He is not with you, because God hates the deceitful, abandons the envious, turns away from the ungrateful, and does not allow the cruel and impious to dwell with him.

“And his brothers and sisters—are they not all with us?” You cunningly thrust forward the brothers and display the sisters, so that by the numerous offspring of the holy mother the hidden virginity might be concealed, her integrity obscured, and everything human in the son be perceived, but nothing divine. [Note: [Col. 0335C] Although Chrysologus seems to be addressing Jews, he may perhaps also have had Ebionites, or Helvidius, who had lived in the preceding century, or Jovinian in mind. Both of the latter impiously blasphemed against the Virgin Mary, daring to say that she had borne other children after Jesus. See Epiphanius, vol. 2, book 1 of Petavius’s edition of the *Heresies*; Tertullian, *On the Veiling of Virgins*, chapter 6, p. 368 of the Paris edition.]

Jew, those whom you call Christ’s brothers and sisters are the sons of Mary, the sister of Cleophas [Note: [Col. 0335D] This is certainly the more probable opinion: namely, that those who are called the Lord’s brothers in the Gospel were his nephews through his mother’s sister, the wife of Cleophas or Alphaeus, although Chrysologus thinks that she was called Cleophas and not Mary. Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*: “James, who is called the Lord’s brother, as some think, was Joseph’s son by another wife; but, as it seems to me, he was the son of Mary, the sister of the Lord’s mother.” Consult Basnage, *Annals*, vol. 1, p. 91, more extensively p. 95. What Gregory of Nyssa relates in his sermon *On the Nativity of the Lord*, having been taken from apocryphal sources, deserves no credence.]—not Mary’s sons—and both divine law and human kinship call the children of brothers and sisters “brothers.” Thus Christ’s brothers were made so not by the virginity of his mother, who remained a virgin after giving birth, but by his maternal aunt; they were made brothers by the claim of kinship.

Blessed Mary, if she had had other sons besides Christ, at the very time of the cross, at the very point of his death, would not have been entrusted to a disciple or commended to a stranger. [Note: [Col. 0336C] Hilary uses this same argument to assert the Virgin’s purity in his commentary on Matthew, vol. 1 of his works, p. 671 at the end, from the Verona edition of 1730, although he believes that the Lord’s brothers were begotten by Joseph. If they had been Mary’s sons, rather than sons whom Joseph had had from an earlier marriage, she would never, at the time of the Passion, have been transferred as a mother to the apostle John, with the Lord saying to both: “Woman, behold your son,” and to John: “Behold your mother”—unless it was that, for the consolation of the desolate woman, he was leaving the affection of a son in the disciple. Hilary is joined by Chrysostom, *Homily 5 on Matthew*; Epiphanius, in the passage cited; and Ambrose, book 2 on Luke, although, as Hilary’s scholiast observes, Ambrose uses the point differently because he places Joseph as surviving until the time of the Passion. Paulinus likewise, in his letter to Augustine 1, otherwise 43, p. 295 of the Verona edition: “To show that, apart from him who had been born of that Virgin, she had neither had nor had any other son; for the Savior would not have cared so greatly for her desolation if he had not been her only son.”]

Envy cast an angel down from heaven (Isaiah 14); it excluded man from paradise (Genesis 3). It first stained the earth with a brother’s blood (Genesis 4). It compelled brothers to sell their brother (Genesis 37). It drove Moses into exile (Exodus 2); it stirred Aaron against his brother; it stained Miriam with envy of her brother (Numbers 12); and, not to prolong the account, it attended and reached the very blood of Christ—what the mind dreads, what the sight trembles at, what the ear cannot contain. [Note: [Col. 0336D] The Caesena manuscript has “itself.”]

Envy is worse than every evil: those whom it has seized cannot be freed; those whom it has wounded do not come to be healed and do not return to salvation. Envy is the poison of offenses, the venom of crimes, the mother of sins, the source of vices. Whoever has not seen it has not seen goodness; whoever has not known it does not know evil; whoever has fled from it lives. Envy can be avoided by flight; it cannot be overcome by combat.

But let us now hear what the Lord answered: “A prophet is not without honor except in his own country and in his own house.” Christ indeed came into his own country and into his own house, because it is written: “He came to his own, and his own did not receive him” (John 2). Yet by saying, “A prophet is not without honor except in his own country and in his own house,” he teaches that among one’s own there can be biting and burning; that to excel among fellow citizens burns those who are near; that when relatives owe honor to a relative, they count it as servitude.

“And he did not perform many miracles there because of their unbelief.” No miracle is performed where unbelief does not deserve it. Although Christ does not demand payment when he heals, he is nevertheless indignant when insult is offered him instead of honor—he who is God, blessed and glorious above all, forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XLIX. On the Same Subject, According to Mark

Whenever the holy Evangelist records that the Lord endured or did something in human fashion, he disturbs the senses of the flesh with something like the full agitation of waves. For feeble minds do not know how to hear, distinguish, and interpret the mysteries of the Lord’s body, as today’s reading shows when it says: “Jesus departed from there and went into his own country” (Mark 6).

From where does he depart, and into what does he enter, when no place contains or confines him? To what country does he go, when he made and possesses the whole world? As the prophet says: “The heavens are yours, and the earth is yours; you founded the world and its fullness” (Psalm 88).

Yet Christ does not depart from himself for himself, but from himself for you, and enters for you, until he brings you in, though expelled; calls you back, though exiled; restores and carries back the one cast out. Therefore Jesus went into his own country—not to restore a country to himself, but to restore to you the country that Adam had lost.

“He went into his own country.” If he was born, how is he not human? If human, how is he not a citizen? If a citizen, who would wonder that he has a homeland? But this is the condition of humanity, not the order of divinity, which he acknowledges; for he who is and who was our God and our parent before the ages willed to become the least throughout the ages, so that he might save by compassion those whom he had made by power; and by sharing their suffering receive those whom, by reproving and commanding, he had made exiles.

Whatever we read that Christ did or endured by assuming humanity, let us not hear it as an insult to divinity, but as contributing to the glory of humanity.

“And his disciples followed him.” Rightly do the disciples follow Christ returning to his country, since such great election and such fullness of grace had already made them citizens and townsmen of the heavenly country, enrolled in the register of the higher order. [Note: [Col. 0337D] Some manuscripts have “described in the higher order.”] The Lord says: “Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10).

“And when the Sabbath came, he began to teach in the synagogue, and many who heard him were astonished at his teaching, saying: ‘Where did he get all these things? And what is this wisdom that has been given to him? And such mighty works, which are performed by his hands?’”

Unhappy and detestable wickedness of the Jewish mind, always readier to examine than to believe! It is stirred up by divine miracles not toward faith but toward accusation, or because it deserved to hear such great wisdom. But from what source it is maliciously curious or querulous, suspicious of good things, readily inclined toward harmful ones: it despises the teaching it admires; it despises the commandments it approves; it hesitates before God but is exceedingly prone toward idols; clever in divine matters, yet wholly dissolved into wood and stones; rebellious against prophecy, opposed to truth, ruined by omens and lies.

I ask: for whom is it a matter of caution that the blind sees? For whom is it a concern that the dead rises? For whom is it doubtful that the mute speaks? Surely, who does not know that he is God whose command alone heals every weakness?

Moses had performed many signs; Elijah had displayed the greatest demonstrations of power; Elisha had performed works not unlike them. Why does no one examine their person? Why does no one raise a question about their status? Why did no one, in such ungrateful curiosity, inquire from where they were, who they were, where these things came from, or through whom they performed them? [Note: [Col. 0337D] From the Vatican manuscript. Alternatively, “ignorant.”]

Yet this man alone is judged—the one who alone refused to judge, lest he punish; he is scrutinized with wicked severity who, in order to grant pardon, asked nothing. And although, being the only innocent one, he found everyone guilty, he preferred, as a display of immeasurable mercy, to look upon them rather than revoke the sentence, so that he might restore to mortals the life once lost and revive the dead. [Note: [Col. 0337D] Printed editions incorrectly have “judgment.” Below, they have “to abolish”; the editions read “to ask.”]

Truly, as the Apostle said, “Great is the mystery of godliness, which is manifested in the flesh of our Christ” (1 Timothy 3). Yet this carnal rivalry extends its curiosity still further; its thought is always hostile to truth. [Note: [Col. 0337D] In many printed editions, “of truth” is lacking.] It does not allow Christ to be believed to be God in his miracles and wisdom, but asserts, desires, and understands him to be merely human on the evidence of his neighbors, parents, brothers, and relatives, saying:

“Is this not the carpenter’s son and the son of Mary, the brother of James and Joseph and Simon and Judas? And are not his sisters here with us?” [Note: [Col. 0338D] The Nazarenes were also offended by Christ’s mother. They objected to Christians that she had been a nurse, or had supported herself by some other manual labor, and had sought her livelihood through a trade.] [Note: [Col. 0338D] Perhaps they were paternal cousins, Joseph’s nieces through other brothers or sisters; that they were poor is clear from this very fact, that the Nazarenes reproached them for it.]

Caiaphas prophesies with a profane mouth (John 11); and although he was a priest, the sense of his falsehood was overcome by the function of truth: his sentence proves the power of the office assigned to him, not of his own person. [Note: [Col. 0338D] This passage may be corrupt, and we have not been able to heal it with the help of manuscripts. I would read: “the authority of the office entrusted to him proves it.”]

Balaam blesses with a cursing mouth, and, hired for wickedness, speaks a whole treasury of truths (Numbers 23–24). And just as among thorns—a flower of wondrous fragrance grows in a rough bush—so at times the thoughts of the worst people are driven toward good things by divine impulse against their will, so that what they speak is not a matter of merit but of mystery.

We see this happening then to the Jewish malice which, in insulting the Lord’s birth, while it magnifies the truth of Christ’s lineage through Joseph’s craft, confesses and proclaims the quality of his true parent, saying: “This is the carpenter’s son.”

It rightly kept the person silent, so that it might reveal the father through his craft, saying not “Joseph’s son” but “the carpenter’s son.” And what kind of carpenter is this, who fashioned such a world out of nothing? What kind of carpenter is this, who alone exists as the author and giver of every good craft?

Say, then, Jew, “the carpenter’s son,” so that you may confess unwillingly that he is the Son of God. Say “of Mary,” so that, compelled, you may confess him to be truly human, but the son of a Virgin. Say “brothers,” so that you may proclaim and make known the greatness of your Creator’s condescension.

And although by this you attempt to conceal the virtues of his holy mother, the truth of the Evangelist proves and declares that they were not the sons of Joseph and Mary but the sons of Cleophas, her sister, whom you call brothers; for the usage even of the present time is known to call the sons of brothers and sisters “brothers.”

The Lord would never, contrary to the order of piety, have commended his mother from the cross to an outsider, that is, to John, if she had had other sons besides him. [Note: [Col. 0339C] See the note at column 335 above in the preceding sermon.] Rather, he entrusts a virgin to a virgin, so that among such persons there might be only the care of the mystery and only the fellowship of religion; nor would so great a disciple serve worldly concerns, but, since he was going to preach the birth of virginity, he would have at home the means by which to prove it to those who doubted. [Note: [Col. 0339C] For in the Gospel he taught that the Word had assumed flesh and become human.]

But James [Note: [Col. 0339C–D] To distinguish him from James the Greater, killed by Herod’s command, he was called the Less. After Christ’s ascension into heaven, he was first consecrated bishop of Jerusalem by the apostles, Christ directing their hands, as Photius says in Letter 117. Under the agency of Ananus the Younger, high priest, he was condemned by the Sanhedrin and died after being cast down from the pinnacle of the Temple, in the thirty-first year of Christ, aged sixty-one.] could not have had the care of one woman and mother [Note: [Col. 0339D] Some hold that she was Mary, the sister of Jesus’ maternal aunt, the wife of Cleophas; and therefore he was called the Lord’s brother because he was his relative according to the flesh.]—he who, at the beginning and amid that Jewish fury, singularly governed the Church of Jerusalem.

The Lord rightly added: “A prophet is not without honor except in his own country.” Behold how those who are citizens by fleshly ties understand; behold how worldly relatives think and honor. Blessed is the one who, having deserved to have God as his Father, seeks nothing besides the heavenly homeland.

[Note: [Col. 0339D] See what we have said about this kind of sermon in the preface.]

## SERMON L. On the Paralytic Who Was Healed

Today’s reading has shown that Christ performed divine mysteries in human actions and carried out invisible operations through visible things.

“He went up,” it says, “into a boat, crossed over, and came to his own city” (Matthew 9). Is this not the one who, after banishing the waves of the sea, laid bare the depths, so that the Israelite people might pass through the astonished waters on dry feet, as through the hollows of mountains? (Exodus 14.) Is this not the one who bent the crests of the sea beneath Peter’s feet, so that the fluid path might offer solid service to human steps? [Note: [Col. 0339D] Some Bolognese and Cologne editions have “through the fluid.”] (Matthew 14.)

And what does it mean that he refuses the sea’s service in this way, so as to cross a very small lake by paying the fare of a boat? [Note: [Col. 0339D] He means the lake of Gennesaret, across which Jesus came to Capernaum. “As is clear to me from Mark 2:1,” says Grotius, “the evangelist reports that Christ had already moved there from Matthew.” This lake is sometimes called the Sea of Tiberias; in sacred Scripture a lake is sometimes called θάλασσα, “sea,” and conversely a sea is sometimes called a lake. The same usage occurs in secular writers. Homer and Sophocles call the sea λίμνη, “lake,” and Pliny calls the seven lagoons of the Adriatic Sea “seven seas,” as Fabricius observes in *Theology of Waters*, p. 178. See also Adrian Reland, *Palestine Illustrated*, book 1, chapter 38, p. 239. This shows how weak are the foundations of Porphyry’s criticism, concerning whom Jerome says in *Hebrew Questions on Genesis* 1: “In vain Porphyry slanders the evangelists, claiming that, in order to perform a miracle for the ignorant—that the Lord walked upon the sea—they called the lake of Gennesaret a sea.”]

“He went up,” he says, “into a boat and crossed over.” And what is surprising, brothers? Christ came to take upon himself our weaknesses and to confer his powers upon us; to seek human things, to bestow divine things; to receive insults, to return dignities; to endure weariness, to repay with healings. For a physician who does not bear weaknesses does not know how to heal weaknesses [Note: [Col. 0340D] Thus in some editions. MITA, from a very ancient manuscript breviary, has: “A physician who brings health does not know how to cure weaknesses.” The reading retained is more suitably connected with what follows and more plainly reflects Chrysologus’s style.]; and one who has not become weak with the weak cannot bestow health upon the weak. [Note: [Col. 0340D] According to the Apostle, 1 Corinthians 9. Saint Jerome, in Letter 11 to Augustine, volume 2 of Augustine’s works: “He becomes like a sick person who ministers to the sick—not by pretending that he has fevers, but by thinking, with a compassionate spirit, how he would wish to be served if he himself were sick.” Our author says below, Sermon 151: “He who does not suffer with another cannot cut away sufferings.” From MITA.]

Therefore, if Christ had remained in his own powers, he would have had nothing in common with human beings; and unless he had fulfilled the order of the flesh, his assumption of flesh in him would have been without purpose. He therefore endured these necessities so that, as a true man, he might be shown to be subject to human necessities.

“He went up,” he says, “into a boat.” Christ boarded the ship of his Church, intending always to calm the waves of the world, so that he might lead those who believe in him to the heavenly homeland by peaceful navigation and make citizens of his city those whom he made sharers in his humanity. Christ therefore does not need the boat, but the boat needs Christ, because without a heavenly pilot the ship of the Church cannot reach the heavenly harbor through the world’s sea amid such and so great a danger.

We have said this, brothers, as far as spiritual interpretation is concerned. But now let us follow the sequence of the history itself.

“He went up,” he says, “into a boat and crossed over, and came into his own city.” The Creator of all things, the Lord of the world, after, for our sake, constricting himself in our flesh, began to have a human homeland and to be a citizen of a Jewish city; he began to have parents, himself the parent of all parents, so that love might invite, affection attract, humanity persuade those whom domination had driven away, fear had scattered, and the force of power had made exiles. [Note: [Col. 0340D] “Capernaum” is meant, which the Evangelist calls his own city.] [Note: [Col. 0340D] Thus in Latinius and the Vallicellian manuscript. The printed editions have “the right of power.”]

He came into his own city, and behold, they brought him a paralytic lying on a bed. “And when Jesus saw,” he says, “their faith, he said to the paralytic: ‘Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven.’”

He hears forgiveness, and the paralytic is silent and offers no thanks, because he was more concerned for the body than for the soul; and he lamented the temporal troubles of his weakened body [Note: [Col. 0341C] Sedulius, book 3, p. 167, line 19, on this same paralytic: “And the loosened limbs lay there.” Vatablus also reads “loosened” for “paralyzed.” Paralysis is a loosening of the nerves, from which loosening the external limbs, deprived of strength, become tremulous. Hence the Hebrews call such sick people “loosened in their limbs,” and the Greeks say that those restored from this disease are “bound.” Guillelmus Ader describes the illness in *On the Diseases of the Gospel*, chapter 11: “For in paralysis the entire spine of the back is obstructed; because by nature it is cold, with its network of nerves, it is never freed from the very cold and icy disease of paralysis or convulsion.”] in such a way that he did not lament the eternal punishments of the soul’s dissolution, judging the present life more desirable for himself than the future.

Rightly, then, Christ looked not at the faith of those who brought him but at the senselessness of the man lying there, so that through the support of another’s faith the paralytic’s soul might be healed before his body. [Note: [Col. 0341D] In some copies, “of those acting.” Jesus looked at the faith of those who offered him. For just as the faith of his master’s friends benefited the centurion’s servant, so the faith of his friends, together with his own faith, benefited this sick man. It is also likely that the paralytic was not without faith, since he allowed himself to be offered in this manner; otherwise Christ would not have forgiven him his sins.] “When he saw,” he says, “their faith.” You see in this passage, brothers, that God does not seek the wills of the foolish, does not regard the faith of the ignorant, and does not scrutinize the foolish desires of the weak, but comes to the aid of another’s faith, bestowing by grace alone what he did not refuse, since whatever belongs to the divine will is not denied.

And indeed, brothers, when does a physician either seek or consider the wishes of the sick, when the sick person always desires and requests things contrary to health? This is why he sometimes applies iron, sometimes fire, sometimes bitter potions, and places them upon unwilling patients, so that they may experience the healing which, while sick, they could not perceive. And if a human being disregards insults and despises curses in order voluntarily to confer life and health upon those wounded by disease, how much more does Christ the physician, in divine goodness, draw to salvation—even unwilling and resisting—the sick with the diseases of sins and those suffering from the madness of crimes?

O if only we wished, brothers—if only we wished—to perceive all the paralysis of our mind, to see our soul lying deprived of virtues upon the bedding of vices [Note: [Col. 0342C] We have followed the Caesena manuscript. The printed editions read “we might see” (*cerneremus*).]! It would become clear to us how Christ daily regards our harmful desires, draws us toward saving remedies, and presses us forward against our will. [Note: [Col. 0342D] See the note at column 218, Sermon 10. He is said to press forward the unwilling when he chastises the obstinate or heaps benefits upon them, so that, recognizing God as their author, they may return to him through repentance. MITA.]

“Son,” he says, “your sins are forgiven.” In saying this, he wished to be understood as God, who was still hidden from human eyes through his humanity. In his powers and signs he was compared with the prophets, who had performed their miracles through him and for him; but because granting forgiveness of sins does not belong to man and is a distinctive mark of deity, he was impressing God upon human hearts.
