The Pharisaic spite proves this. For when he had said, “Your sins are forgiven,” the Pharisees replied: “He blasphemes.” [Note: [Col. 0342D] Not by cursing God, but by arrogating to himself what belongs to God—namely, the forgiveness of sins.]

“For who can forgive sins except God alone?” Pharisee, who know and yet do not know, confess and yet deny: if the one who forgives sins is God, why is Christ not God, who is shown, by the gift of his single act of forgiveness, to have taken away the sins of the whole world? “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1).

But so that you may grasp greater signs of his divinity, hear that he penetrated the secret of your breast; see that he reached the hiding places of your thoughts; understand that he lays bare the silent counsels of your heart. “And when Jesus had seen,” he says, “their thoughts, he said: ‘Why do you think evil in your hearts?’” [Note: [Col. 0342D] To inspect the secrets of the heart was among the recognized signs of the Messiah, as the Talmudists observe against Bar Kokhba under the heading *Sanhedrin*.]

“For which is easier to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Rise and walk’? But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority to forgive sins”—he said to the paralytic—“Rise, take up your bed, and go into your house.” And he rose and went into his house.

The searcher of souls anticipates the wicked counsels of minds and demonstrates the power of his divinity by the testimony of his work, while he restores the members of a shattered body, tightens the nerves, joins the bones, fills out the inward parts, strengthens the limbs, and raises feet already buried in a living corpse to running.

“Take up your bed.” That is: carry the one who carried you; change every relationship, so that what was a testimony of weakness may be proof of health; so that the bed of your pain may be evidence of my healing; so that the greatness of its weight may declare the magnitude of the strength you have recovered. [Note: [Col. 0342D] Lucas Brugensis used these same words in this passage.]

“Go,” he says, “into your house,” lest, having been healed by Christian faith, you should now die along the roads of Jewish unbelief.

## SERMON LI. On the Deaf and Mute Demoniac Who Was Healed
Because the heat had poured itself over the earth more intensely than usual, I remained silent for a long time, lest the compression produced by the desire to hear should itself kindle in us a *cynocauma* fire [Note: He indicates an extremely intense heat, which the crowds gathered to listen created by pressing their bodies against one another. For *cynocauma* means either the heat of the dog days or the bite of a rabid dog.]. Now, when the temperate air of autumn has mitigated the atmosphere [Note: Elmenhorst praises this passage in his note on Minucius Felix, p. 14, no. 1: “After the summer day, autumn was advancing toward mild weather.”], we are recalled, with the Lord’s help, to the Lord’s word.

When someone brought before the Lord for healing his son, possessed by the fury of a deaf and mute spirit [Note: He was descending from the mountain on whose summit he had been transfigured and was returning to the disciples.], the evangelist relates that the Lord was moved, contrary to his customary patience, so that he first attacked the father’s wound before turning to the care of the son. “One of the crowd,” he says, “answered and said: Master, [Col. 0343A] I brought my son to you, who has a mute spirit; and wherever it seizes him, it dashes him down, and he foams, gnashes his teeth, and wastes away. And I told your disciples to cast it out, and they could not.”

“Answering them, he said: O faithless generation” (Mark IX)!

“One of the crowd answered” [Note: Bachiarius says “to be struck by a question” in *On the Reception of the Lapsed*. Barthius cites and elucidates Chrysologus’s words in *Adversaria*, book XXXII.]: Why, when one asks the question, are many struck by it? Why, when one makes inquiry, are all marked as unbelieving? Why, at the voice of one man, is the whole generation called proud in its faithlessness?

Why? Because this man had not come to God but to a teacher; he was demanding a cure not from power but from skill; he attributed the delay of the cure not to the case but to the healer [Note: They were doubting whether Christ could heal him. Du Hamel, here.]; and he assigned the disciples’ inability to the teacher’s incompetence. Thus, by his outcry—“And I told your disciples to cast it out, and they could not”—he satisfied the envious malice of the Jewish scribes. This is what he was saying: that whoever did not believe in Christ was a devil, a demon capable of regarding the power of Christ’s name as insignificant.

The disciples drove demons from possessed bodies not in their own name but in Christ’s. Therefore, because the demon did not yield when the disciples commanded it, the man attributed this to the weakness of Christ’s name, not to the fault of the disciples [Note: And in fact, along with Chrysologus, some think that the faith even of the apostles, or disciples, wavered because of the difficulty of the matter, since so many evils had come together in one person.].

When the Lord saw the Jewish crowds gathered around them thinking in such a way, he thus brands the faithlessness of the fathers in their children and thus strikes the poisonous offspring in their parents.

“O faithless generation!”

“Coming,” he says, “the Lord to his disciples, saw a great crowd around them, and the scribes disputing with them; and immediately, when all the people saw Jesus, they were astonished, and they were afraid” [Col. 0343C]—fearing, of course, that what they had hurled as an insult at the disciples would be lost when the teacher arrived, and that, once so great a demon had been driven away, what had been an occasion of confusion for the disciples might itself become a cause of glory.

That is why the Lord, answering all by means of one man’s question, replied: “O faithless generation, how long shall I be with you?” Because of their unbelief, not even one demon is driven out from a captive body.

“How long shall I be with you?” [Note: From what follows Chrysologus’s meaning is clear: this rebuke, in his view, does not concern the apostles, as Origen says in Homily 4 on Matthew, vol. III, p. 13, column 1, of the old edition published by Giunta in 1536; nor the apostles equally with the surrounding multitude, as Lightfoot, Clericus, and the Gloss maintain; but the Jews alone, whom he compares with the Gentiles.]

“And shall I not send [you] to the nations?” Where, at the voice of one of my disciples, temples collapse, images flee, altars are consumed, idols fall, sacred groves are cut down; where the whole power of demons, groaning, trembling, and howling, is driven out from its ancient and age-worn dwellings; where shrines are changed into churches, pagan altars and sacrifices of slaughtered animals are transformed into the living sacrifice of the heart [Col. 0343D]; and omens, divinations, and dreams are placed solely at God’s nod and entirely under God’s judgment.

“How long shall I be with you? How long shall I endure you?” [Note: Aptly said. For Christ shows that the period of divine patience toward the Jews was drawing near its end, and he alludes to what is said in Deuteronomy concerning the calling of the nations.]

Patience endures them not through fear but through mercy; not from necessity but from compassion. In expectation, not dread, he endures, bears, and awaits them—he who wishes the wicked person to return rather than perish.

“Bring him to me”—as though he could not heal one who was far away; but bring to me yourselves [Col. 0344A], the cause of your unbelief, the title of your infidelity, the proof of your faithlessness. Bring him. Since you were unwilling to believe God, at least while he was teaching, believe when the demon confesses, and recognize that you are worse than the devil himself when you see him confess and immediately tremble in the presence of the one who knows him.

“And they brought him to him. And when he saw him, immediately the spirit troubled him, and, thrown upon the ground, he rolled about foaming.” The man rolled, but the devil was tortured; the affliction tormented the one possessed, but the majesty of the judge exposed the possessor; the captive was held in place, but the enemy was punished. The devil’s punishment was displayed in the torment of the human body.

Brothers, we need—indeed, we need—the light of God, lest human eyes be deceived in the work of God.

“And he asked his father, ‘How long has it been since this happened to him?’ But he said, ‘From childhood.’” The author of time asks about the duration of the affliction; the physician of the disease asks about the duration of the disease, not because he is ignorant, but because, knowing, he reveals the truth to those who do not know. Finally, by such questioning he discloses the time and reveals the age; he turns back to childhood, so that the cause of so great an evil may touch not the child but the parent. For the parent had given over, for the devil’s favor and to the honor of demons, the pledge entrusted to him by God, as Scripture says: “They offered their sons and their daughters to demons” (Psalm CV).

What crime had the child committed in infancy, in order to make a place for the devil within himself? What guilt? Yet little children are filled with a demon when they are offered by their parents to the devil and are handed over to the care of demons.

Finally, the father’s faith releases the one whom the father’s unbelief had bound. The father’s voice is: “If you can do anything, help us, taking pity on us.” That is: Help us, have mercy on us, whose guilt weighs down the innocent, and for whose punishment the child’s danger thus rebounds upon us.

And rightly the Lord demands faith from the parents, saying: “If you can believe, all things are possible to the one who believes.” And the father: “I believe, Lord; help my unbelief.” The father believes, and, as we have said, the one condemned by his father’s unbelief is freed by his father’s faith. For if the father’s faith benefited him, how could the father’s faithlessness fail to harm him?

How he was healed, and why the disciples, who had driven out many demons, could not drive out this one, we shall explain in the following sermon, with the Lord’s help.

## SERMON LII. On the same subject.

[Note: The designation “teacher,” or “one who teaches,” is common among Latin authors. Augustine, Sermon 122 *On Various Subjects*; the author of the *Commonitorium*, chapter 27; Gregory the Great, *Moralia*, book XVII, chapter 14.]

It is the teacher’s duty to explain what has been read and to clarify and demonstrate obscure matters of mystical meaning in lucid speech, lest inadequate understanding produce harm for the hearer precisely where the teacher ought and is able to impart salutary knowledge.

This, then, is the harmony of today’s reading:

“And one of the crowd answered and said: Master, I brought my son, who has a deaf and mute spirit” (Mark IX).

He did not say, “I brought my son, deaf and mute,” but, “I brought my son [Note: Certainly the Jews traced all the causes of diseases to spirits. In this case the boy was in fact possessed by a demon.] who has a deaf and mute spirit.”

Is spiritual wickedness distinguished according to human limbs and confined by human senses, so that it endures our weaknesses and undergoes our sufferings; so that it can see only through the windows of the eyes, receive hearing only through the openings of the ears, utter speech through the service of the tongue or mouth, and thereby endure the miserable condition of the deaf and mute? Yet its subtle, airy nature knows nothing of flesh, rejects bones, and, like a breath of air, passes through the whole world in a moment [Note: Almost all printed editions, which Meursius corrected, read *temporis* (“of time”) in the passage.], assumes different appearances, changes into various forms, penetrates hearts, mocks souls, breathes impious and most shameful thoughts into them, and cannot be perceived either from where it comes or to where it returns. Thus, like a flying javelin, it pierces innocent minds with a lethal wound and with complete ease.

It would have been a small matter if the father alone had said this in his supplication when he said, “I brought my son who has a deaf and mute spirit,” unless the Lord himself had driven away the unclean spirit with such a rebuke: “Deaf and mute spirit, I command you: come out of him.”

But let us now pursue the matters relevant to resolving the question.

God, who will burn the demons forever in an unending fire, who even now binds them with chains, afflicts them with torments, and presses them with punishments, can, whenever he commands, also deprive them entirely of every faculty and make them blind in the manner in which they see, deaf in the manner in which they hear, and mute so that they cannot speak [Note: See whether Chrysologus here falls into the opinion of the ancients that demons are even now suffering dreadful punishments, but are to be burned in the fire of hell only after the day of judgment.].

But in this passage let what the devil did to the man be made clear.

The ancient deserter [Note: He calls the devil a “deserter.” For *refuga* means a deserter and, as the *Glossary of Latin* manuscripts preserved by Du Cange says, an apostate—one who departs from the true worship of God. Zeno of Verona uses this word in his sermon *On Jacob’s Sleep*; Tertullian, *On the Apparel of Women*, chapter 5; Prudentius, *Peristephanon*, ode 1; and our author, Sermon 155, *On Herod*.], when he discovered that God had come among human beings, blocked the ears of men and bound their tongues. Having closed the doors of the human senses, he made and prepared the human breast as a hiding place for his cave, thinking that the hearing of the word and the power of the divine name would not reach there.

At the same time, crafty and cunning as he is, he thought that he could ensnare the father and deceive the parents through such a contrivance, so that they would despair of being able to cure one who could neither hear nor speak; and so that they would believe what was the devil’s work to be a weakness of human nature, attribute it to the child’s constitution, and ascribe to nature what the enclosed enemy had inflicted.

Finally, as Matthew reports concerning the same boy, the demon had deceived the father through another pretense. For he pleads in this way: “Lord, have mercy on my son, because he is lunatic and suffers terribly” (Matthew XVII).

The demon wished to appear either as a condition of human nature or as an effect of a heavenly body—this being his own trick [Note: Origen, Chrysostom, and Jerome agree: they do not recognize a natural cause of the disease in this boy, but, along with our author, believe that the demons tortured him so as to deceive human beings and pour insults upon the creator of the moon. Juvencus:

> By the demon’s art the moon’s course  
> Torments this child born to me.

Hence Origen attacks the physicians, vol. I, p. 311 of Huet’s edition, who think that this disease was not introduced by the demon’s art but by the moon’s moisture. He too is to be criticized, since, by departing too far in the opposite direction, he strayed from the straight path: he allowed everything to the demon and nothing to nature, whereas Euthymius, in his commentary on Matthew IV.24, refers it entirely to nature. Huetius is right, however, in *Origeniana*, p. 54, column 2, in thinking that the boy was epileptic, paralytic, and possessed. For it is certainly not unheard of that these two conditions should be confused. See Hesychius.]—adapting the boy’s sufferings to the courses of the moon [Note: Lunatics, or epileptics, suffer from a kind of comitial disease and are more violently agitated at the full moon. The reason is explained by the aforementioned de Ader, *On the Diseases of the Gospels*, and by Euthymius in the passage cited above. Rusticus Elpidius, book V, verse 243:

> A horrible frenzy—the blast of a demon’s madness—had crept over the wretched man;  
> the newly assailing spirit, by its own plague, dashed him down, seeking minds by a foul assault,  
> when the moon gathers again its monthly failing fires.]. He afflicted the body as the moon increased, so that people would believe that what was in fact the devil’s crime and madness belonged to the moon.

Thus he deceived human beings, misled the ignorant, and discredited among the heedless a creature which, created only for light [Note: That is, created to pour forth light at night upon things beneath the moon.], does not know how to harm the human beings whom it is compelled rather to help continually through its service.

But after the knower of hidden things and most powerful examiner of secrets had come—one whom the devil’s hidden contrivances could not oppose [Note: That is, “oppose.” Barthius explains the word in his notes on Claudius Mamertus, chapter 12, p. 384, and in *Adversaria*, book X, chapter 5, illustrating it with other examples from the Fathers; he collects fuller material in book XLVI, chapter 7, column 2132. Rudolphus Ardentius, Homily 19: “When the command of the earthly father does not oppose the command of God.”]—the boy was brought to be healed by divine command, so that whatever the devil had bound might be loosed by Christ.

The enemy did all he could to make what was seen appear to be natural. But why could the disciples not drive him out? Because this man represents the Gentile people in symbolic form. For, according to the Apostle, the Gentile people had “the spirit of this air.” “The spirit of the air,” he says, “which now works in the children of disobedience” (Ephesians II).

He, then, was deaf and mute: he could neither hear the law nor confess God. He was continually hurled into the fire of Gehenna and the waters of a bitter abyss; nor could he be healed by the disciples or by any human being, because Christ was formerly called the hearing of faith, the confession of salvation, the redemption and life of the nations.

Finally, when the devil had been driven out by Christ’s command, what had been closed was opened, bonds were loosed, speech was restored, hearing returned, and the man was restored. The devil alone lamented that he had been expelled from a long possession.

That is why the one coming from the Gentiles is first cleansed from the demon by the laying on of hands [Note: This alludes to the ancient Church rite of laying hands upon Gentiles who were coming to the faith.] and by exorcisms [Note: The First Council of Constantinople, canon 7, line 380: “On the first day we make them—whether Gentiles or Jews—Christians, and record their name in the registers; on the second, catechumens. Then, on the third day, we exorcise them, breathing three times together upon their faces and ears; and thus we catechize them, so that they remain in the church for a long time and hear the Scriptures; and then we baptize them.” From this it is clear that exorcism was a ceremony extending over several days before baptism, as Chrysologus rightly says.], and receives the opening of the ears [Note: Pamelius, in his commentary on Tertullian’s *On Baptism*, cites the words of the Council of Braga, chapter 3: “We absolutely command that catechumens come for twenty days before baptism for the purification of exorcism, and that during those twenty days they be instructed and consecrated according to the canonical precept. For the same number of days is counted from the Saturday of the third week.” This alludes to the same things, and especially to the third day, which was called the day of the opening of the ears. Blessed Ambrose alludes to it in *On Those Initiated into the Mysteries*, chapter 1, and *On the Sacraments*, book I, chapter 1; likewise Blessed Augustine, in his sermon to the candidates for baptism, and in the passage cited by Amalarius, *On Divine Offices*, book I, chapter 8; and Rupert, *On Divine Offices*, book IV, chapters 18–21. Thus far Pamelius.], so that he may receive the hearing of faith and, with the Lord leading the way, may reach salvation.

[Note: On this kind of sermon, see what was said at length in the preface.]

## SERMON LIII. On peace.

“Blessed are the peacemakers,” says the evangelist, “for they shall be called sons of God” (Matthew V).

Christian virtues rightly flourish in the person who possesses the unanimity of Christian peace, and no one arrives at the title “son of God” except through the name “peacemaker.”

Peace, dearly beloved, strips a person of servitude, gives him the name of a freeborn person, changes his status before God, and makes a son from a servant and a free person from a slave.

The peace of brothers is the will of God, the joy of Christ, the perfection of holiness, the rule of justice, the teacher of doctrine, the guardian of conduct, and a discipline praiseworthy in all things.

Peace is the support of prayers, an easy and attainable path of supplication, and the fitting fulfillment of every desire. Peace is the mother of love, the bond of harmony, and the evident sign of a pure mind, which demands from God whatever it wishes; which asks for whatever it wishes; and whatever it asks for, receives.

Peace must be preserved by royal commands, as the Lord Christ himself says: “I leave you peace; my peace I give you” (John XIV). That is to say: “I left you in peace; I shall find you in peace.” As he departed, he wished to give what, upon returning, he desired to find in all things.

It is a heavenly command to preserve what he gave: there is one voice—“I shall find what I left.”

To plant peace deeply is God’s work; to uproot it completely is the enemy’s. For just as brotherly love is from God, so hatred is from the devil. Therefore hatreds must be condemned, because it is written: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John III).

You see, therefore, dearly beloved brothers, why peace must be loved and harmony cherished: these are what generate and nourish charity. You know, according to the Apostle, that “charity is from God” (1 John IV); therefore the one who does not have charity is without God.

Peace among the people is, dearly beloved, the glory of the priest, and the joy full of peace is the perfect charity of sons. It is the priest’s task to admonish concerning what is fitting; it is the people’s task to hear what he counsels. Whatever is forbidden, it is the shepherd’s task to prohibit, and the flock’s to hear and desire that it not be done. If both agree, everything is safe: God finds nothing among the people to punish, nor can the priest have anything to grieve over.

Therefore let us keep the commandments, brothers, for they are commandments of life. Let the brotherhood remain bound together by the bonds of deep peace, and let it constrain itself in mutual love by the saving bond of charity, which covers a multitude of sins.

Love, therefore, must be embraced above all desires, for it can possess as many blessings as it has rewards. Peace must be guarded above all virtues, because God is always in peace.

Let us give no place to the enemy, lest he be able to sow weeds in the field of wheat and, when the farmer is already secure and deceived in his hope of long labor, ruin the expected fruits at the very ripeness of the harvest; or lest he disturb old wine, sweet with age, by changing it into the liquid of faithlessness through the admixture of sediment; or lest, among sweet honeycombs, he mix in poisons more bitter than gall.

Away with quarrels, away with disputes, away with curses! And because the tongue of the whisperer and the double-tongued person is a snare of death, let each person spare his own soul, lest he fasten upon himself the bonds of death for his own punishment.

Love peace, and everything will be tranquil. Thus you may reserve both rewards for us and joys for yourselves, so that the Church of God, founded in the unity of peace, may preserve perfect discipline in Christ.

## SERMON LIV. On Zacchaeus.

The blessed evangelist [Note: That is, a little earlier. Cicero, letter V to Lucceius: “The letters which I recently received from you.”], when shortly before he described the life and end of an inhuman rich man, moved and saddened human emotions; but today, by recounting the humanity and faith of the rich Zacchaeus, he lifted us heavenward and carried us forward into joy.

“And Jesus,” he says, “entered and was passing through Jericho” (Luke XIX).

Why does he pass through rather than simply walk? Because [Note: “To walk” signifies always being in motion; “to pass through” means to travel around but toward a goal and rest. Moses therefore walked, since he led the people only along the road; Jesus passed through, since he led the people to rest. Mita.—But Jesus did not traverse more of the city’s roads and streets, as some infer from the Vulgate meaning of *perambulabat*; rather, he passed through the middle of the city in order to proceed to Jerusalem, the destination of his journey.] what Moses had walked, Christ passed through; and the people whom Moses led into the way, Jesus led to the rest of the promised dwelling.

He was passing through Jericho. Jericho is the city itself which Jesus son of Nun overthrew with the sevenfold blast of trumpets (Joshua VI). But because Christ came to save what had perished, he enters Jericho so that what the Law had cast down with its terrifying cry, Jesus might raise up with the cry of pious preaching.

“Jesus,” he says, “entered and was passing through Jericho; and behold, a man named Zacchaeus, who was the chief of the tax collectors, and he was rich.”

[Note: The subordinate tax collectors brought their revenues to him as the prefect, or as the head and presiding officer, of the association that had gathered there.]

In the ruined city, Zacchaeus is said to have held the leadership of a ruined occupation. From the place, the person, and the office, the magnitude of his guilt is demonstrated, so that from the greatness of the crime the greatness of the one who forgives may shine forth.

“And he was seeking to see Jesus.” Whoever seeks to see Christ should look toward heaven, from which Christ comes, not toward earth, from which gold comes.

Therefore the rich man who looks upward does not carry riches but tramples them underfoot; he is not bent down by riches but lifted up by them. He employs riches in the service of the one who gives them, not in servitude to the greed of riches [Note: Barthius praises this passage, *Adversaria*, book XVI, chapter 20, p. 849.] [Note: Claudian:

> If you fear, if you desire what is wrong, if you are led by anger,]

Bear the yoke of service. ] The miser is a slave of riches, not their master; but the merciful man proves that he has as many servants as he has coins. He was seeking to see Jesus, but could not because of the crowd, since he was short in stature. Yet he was sufficiently great in spirit [Col. 0349B] who seemed small in body; for in mind he touched the heavens, though in body he did not equal other men. Let no one, therefore, concern himself with bodily shortness, to which he can add nothing; let him instead strive to excel in faith [Note: [Col. 0349D] Thus with the manuscripts and the Bononian and Mita editions; others read *immineat*.].

“And running ahead, he climbed a tree.” By what steps, do you think, did this man reach the branches of the lofty tree? He trod upon the earth, climbed above gold, rose beyond avarice, and surpassed the whole mass of riches, so that, leaping into [Note: [Col. 0349D] Mita supposes that Zacchaeus’s sycamore was called the tree of forgiveness because Adam and Eve, after the Fall, made girdles for themselves from its leaves, when they were ashamed that they had sinned. He praises Augustine, *On the Words of the Apostle*, sermon 8, vol. X. Hence that tree is called the tree of forgiveness, because beneath it forgiveness was pronounced by God himself upon our ancestors. I would think, however, that Chrysologus did not even dream here of Adam’s tree. He calls it the tree of forgiveness because, when Zacchaeus climbed it, he earned forgiveness from Christ the Lord.] the tree of forgiveness, he might seize the fruit of mercy, and from the [Note: [Col. 0350D] Again Mita divines: he thinks that this fig tree was called the watchtower of confession because beneath it our first parents, by covering their nakedness, confessed their sins. From this tree, as from a higher watchtower, Zacchaeus looked upon Jesus passing by and recognized him as the Lord and giver of mercy.] watchtower of confession might behold the giver of indulgence.

He climbed a sycamore tree. For a mystery, not for a natural cause, he climbed a sycamore tree [Note: [Col. 0350D] Various opinions concerning Adam’s tree may be found among the commentators. The sycamore is also called the Egyptian fig, which Pliny describes in book XI, chapter 7. Hence Chrysologus and others think that it is the same as the fig tree from whose leaves our first parents wove their first coverings. The Hebrew teachers and the Arabs, however, interpret it as “mulberry.” Its Greek name seems to indicate that the tree resembles the mulberry so closely that it also somewhat resembles the fig. Leo, in his *Description of Africa*, calls it by its proper name *giumum* and says that it is of extraordinary height.], so that from the place where Adam had covered the nakedness of his body, Zacchaeus might there conceal [Col. 0349C] the ugliness of his avarice.

He climbed a sycamore tree in order to see Jesus, because Jesus was going to pass that way. He truly said “to pass,” because Christ had not come to remain along earthly paths and amid human labors, but had come to pass through them.

“When Jesus came to the place, he looked up and saw him.” It is as though, if he had not turned his eyes there, he would not have seen him—though when Nathanael was absent, he saw him from far away beneath the same tree (John I). But he saw him in order to grant forgiveness; he looked upon him in order to show favor; he directed his gaze toward life; he contemplated him for salvation. God, when he sees someone, does not seek to recognize him as though ignorant, but, knowing him, wishes to see him for glory.

“He saw him and said to him: ‘Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for today I must remain in your house.’” If he had climbed well, why is he told [Col. 0349D] to come down? Earlier he said: “Running ahead, he climbed [Col. 0350A] the tree.” The servant ran ahead of the Lord, and Zacchaeus climbed the tree before the Ruler climbed the cross; therefore he is told: “Hurry and come down.”

If you are wise, hurry and come down: come down before the Lord from Adam’s tree, so that after the cross of the Lord’s Passion you may climb. “Unless someone takes up his cross and follows me” (Matthew X); he did not say, “goes before me.”

Come down, therefore, so that you may lay aside the burdens of such great fraud, the weights of greed, the mass of usury, the office of the publican, the authority of most cruel exaction; so that, unencumbered, you may enter the school of poverty, the discipleship of mercy, the practice of piety, the discipline of patience, the pursuit of virtues, the knowledge of divinity, endurance of sufferings, the philosophy of death; and, already perfected, may climb amid the steep places of the tree of life.

“Come down, [Col. 0350B] because today I must remain in your house.” Whoever Christ has not entered will not reach the divine dwelling; and at whose table Christ has not sat here, that person will not recline at the heavenly table.

“And he hurried down and received him joyfully.” He rejoices because he received his own Receiver; because he feeds his Shepherd; because the guilty man bends the Judge by the appeal of his humanity; because, through the loan of food and drink, he makes and acquires his Debtor as his own. Thus this publican does not lose his profit, but changes it.

“And when they all saw it, they murmured, saying that he had gone to stay with a sinful man.” And who is without sin? If no one is, the one who accuses God because he enters among sinners denies forgiveness to himself.

When God seeks the sinner, he seeks not sins but the human being: he despises the sin, which is the work of the human being, so that he may not lose his own work, which is the human being. Hear the prophet say: “Turn your face away from my sins” (Psalm L)—that is, from my works. But concerning himself he says: “Do not despise the works of your hands” (Psalm CXXXVII). When a judge wishes to forgive, he looks upon the person, not the offense; when a father wishes to show mercy to his son, he considers affection, not wrongdoing. So God remembers his own work in the human being, in order to forget the human work.

You, therefore, who criticize and murmur about why Christ went to stay with a sinner, take from such an entrance the way of salvation, the example of forgiveness, and the hope of mercy; and take care lest what is an occasion of salvation for you become material for blasphemy.

“To whom does a physician go,” except to the sick? “The healthy,” he says, “have no need of a physician, but those who are ill” (Matthew IX). To whom does the breathless shepherd go, except to the lost sheep? When does a king mingle with enemies, except when he wishes to free a captive? And the person who has lost a precious pearl does not disdain to enter filthy places, nor does he shrink from seeking it among the very dung.

Into what precipice does a mother not throw herself after her son? And yet God is reproached—the God who created the human being in his own image and likeness (Genesis I)—for seeking the human being amid sins with the love of the Creator. You murmur, human being, asking why God seeks a human being amid sins; what will you do when you see him penetrate the very darknesses of Tartarus for the sake of the human being?

Yet hear what Christ did when he entered among sinners.

“Standing,” it says, “Zacchaeus said.” You see how he who was lying down has been raised upright. We lie in vices, and we lie weighed down; we stand through good works and are raised toward progress.

“Standing,” it says, “Zacchaeus said: ‘Half of my possessions I give to the poor.’” This man believes that he will live after death, since he is already sending half his possessions ahead to the future life. Let the person be perfect who always sends everything he possesses to the place where he is going to live; yet this man is the companion of the virtues, the partner of prudence, the sharer in faith, who sends even half to God, because whatever a person leaves behind here, he loses.

And truly, brothers, just as this man believes that he lives there because he sends his possessions there, so he does not believe that you will live there who have prepared nothing for yourself there that you ought to possess. For if we can scarcely endure temporal poverty, who will endure becoming a beggar for eternity?

What soldier does not send to his homeland whatever he acquires through military sweat, so that old age may repay the labors of youth with comfort? And how can the Christian, whose military service is the life he lives in this world, fail to consider how to console earthly dangers with heavenly repose?

Zacchaeus himself teaches and shows by example how a Christian should do this: “Half of my possessions I give to the poor, and if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I repay fourfold.”

[Note: [Col. 0351C] Whoever gives alms from another person’s property takes more by giving alms than he took by stealing what belonged to another. The reason is that by stealing he inflicted fraud upon the human being; but by giving alms from the property taken by theft, he inflicted fraud upon himself, his neighbor, and God himself. Upon the human being, because he did not restore the property; upon himself, because by doing this he falsely persuades himself that he has satisfied justice; upon God, because, so far as depends upon him, he thus recalled his own crimes and displayed the theft to God the Judge. MITA.]

Whoever distributes what belongs to another steals more by giving than by stealing; nor does he thereby restrain the groans of the injured person, but prolongs them. I dare say that the person who offers God what he obtained by fraud heaps up crimes rather than cleanses them, because in such a gift God sees the spoils of his poor, not [Note: [Col. 0351D] “Mercies” in the sense of almsgiving. Thus Fulgentius, *On the Trinity*, book IV, chapter 24: “To distribute mercy to the poor.” Ducange praises this passage in the *Glossary*, vol. II, p. 638 of the old edition.] mercies.

He weeps to God without cause, against whom the poor person has rightly wept before God. God’s word is: “If you take your brother’s cloak as a pledge, you shall return it to him before sunset” (Exodus XI). As a lamp exposes a thief, so the sun accuses those who have been defrauded.

If we wish to offer God what is ours, if we wish to possess before God what belongs to us, let us also become worthy to hear what Zacchaeus heard: “Today salvation has come to this house, because he too is a son of Abraham.”

The inhuman rich man, although he was a son of Abraham, became a son of Gehenna; this man, although he was a son of robbery, by giving away his own and restoring what belonged to others [Note: [Col. 0351D] The ancients, with great agreement, held that Zacchaeus was a Gentile. Others think it more plausibly that he was a Jew, but a publican, and that, as a publican, he lived devoted to usury and profit-making. For the Jews did not reproach Christ because he dined with an uncircumcised person—something they certainly would not have omitted to mention—but because he dined with a sinner. Nor were Jews forbidden to contract public tax-farming arrangements. See Grotius here.] is adopted as a son of Abraham.

Nevertheless, let no one think that Zacchaeus reached the summit of perfection merely by offering half his possessions. He afterward gave both all that he possessed and himself to the Lord, so that, [Note: [Col. 0351D] The author of the *Constitutions of Clement*, book VII, chapter 46, p. 38a: “Zacchaeus, formerly a publican, was first ordained bishop of Caesarea in Palestine; after him Cornelius; Theophilus third.” The following should also be heard, from Latinius on this passage of Chrysologus: “It is established that the bishop of Jerusalem, named Zacchaeus, was called so, and that in the fourth year of Trajan, after the death of Justus, he undertook the governance of that Church—that is, in the year of Christ 114. But that this was the same man who is described in the Gospel as the publican is scarcely, or not even scarcely, believable. It is not easy to believe that, after so long an interval of time, the man who was still performing the office of publican when called by Christ both survived and was considered fit to govern the Church. The year of Christ 114 must be joined with the sixteenth year of Trajan’s reign, when Quintus Nicco Hasta and Publius Manilius Vopiscus were consuls. Other writings attributed to Clement agree concerning Zacchaeus’s episcopate, as do Rufinus in the preface to the *Recognitions* and the heresiographer of Sirmond, *Heresies* 11 and 12. Eusebius of Caesarea either did not read the writings of Pseudo-Clement or, having read them, rejected them; otherwise he would not have omitted from his works what would have been an ornament to his own Church. What is read in the forged third letter of Anacletus, in *Councils*, vol. I, p. 451, concerning Zacchaeus’s episcopate at Antioch is nonsense, against which all antiquity stands.] strengthened by the honor of the episcopate, he might pass from the table of the publican’s profits to the table of the Lord’s body; and, abandoning the fraudulent riches of the world, might find the true riches of the world in the poverty of Christ.

## SERMON LV  
### On God’s paternal love for us, on parents’ love for their children, and on the punishment of the Jews

After the precepts of the Law, spread through volumes and gathered into books, had not sufficed to commend divine love to us, God’s affection is inserted into and conveyed to the hard hearts of human beings through comparisons and examples.

“Who among you,” he says, “if his son asks for bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, will give him a serpent instead of a fish? Or if he asks for an egg, will offer him a scorpion? If you, then, although you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give the good Spirit to those who ask him?” (Luke XI).

“Who among you asks his father for bread, and will he give him a stone?” Love contains no deceit; piety admits no fraud, affection no falsehood. If he is a father, he cannot fail to love; if he loves, he knows how to give only what is good. The person who suspects his father’s generosity denies that he is a father; the person troubled by what his father gives does not know himself to be a son [Note: [Col. 0353D] Tilmanus cites this passage in his *Allegories* on Luke XI.].

He excludes everything belonging to piety who does not believe that whatever the father gives is beneficial; or how could a father give his children evils in place of good things, when he is always ready to endure evils for his children, when for his children he does not flee death or avoid danger?

For this reason God made you a father; for this reason he wished a human being to be begotten by you, although he could certainly have made very many from the earth from which he had made you. He acted thus so that, by begetting, you might know how great the affection of one who begets is, and so that in yourself you might prove as great a love for your Creator as the Creator himself strives to bestow upon his own offspring through you.

Certainly God wished you to feel in yourself not only what the affection of one who begets is, but also wished you to see it in wild animals, cattle, and birds. Although he produced them from the earth by command alone, afterward he compelled them to experience the labor of generation: to change their native places, seek dwellings suited to their lairs, protect their offspring against the difficulties of their surroundings, give birth amid groans, nourish them through immense labors, and refuse to spare themselves for death if they saw their young being seized.

Therefore, if not by comparison with human beings, then by the likeness of wild animals, the example of cattle, and the examples of birds, learn how sincere is the love within a father’s affection.

If you believe that God is a father and have confessed him as such, believe that whatever he commands and whatever he chooses for you is sufficiently beneficial for your salvation; believe that it is sufficiently life-giving. It is not permitted to scrutinize what a mother gives; it is not fitting to question a father’s instructions. Even if the appearance of a paternal command is sad, the reality itself is nevertheless beneficial and life-giving.

Thus Abraham, when he believed God to be his father, did not consider the forms of his commands harsh and bitter. He accepted the shameful circumcision (Genesis XVII); and what the heavenly Father commanded, he did not question but judged glorious. He regarded parricide as a most monstrous crime; but because God commanded it, he entrusted everything to piety.

Thus Isaac, when he saw his father’s sword over him—when he could have recoiled and grieved at being the victim—rejoiced (Genesis XXII). Thus Jephthah’s daughter fulfilled, with complete rejoicing through her death, her father’s gift and her father’s vows (Judges XI).

Why, then, now that he knows God, does anyone dispute what the Father gives, when a little and innocent child asks his father and receives from him things that are good and beneficial for himself?

But let us inquire why the Lord used these comparisons.

“Who among you,” he says, “asks his father for bread, and will he give him a stone?” He could have said, “A weed? A tare?”—something that, because of its closeness and resemblance, pretends to be bread but produces distress. But Christ had come for the children—that is, the Jews—whom he complained of having begotten with this cry: “I have begotten and raised children, but they have rejected me” (Isaiah I). He had therefore come for the children; he had come as the bread from heaven, who said: “I am the bread that came down from heaven” (John VI).

But for the Jews he was turned into a stone of stumbling (Romans IX) and a rock of offense (Isaiah VIII), as the Lord says: “Behold, I place in Zion a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense” (Isaiah XXVIII). Why a rock? Because they were eager to bite the rock rather than ask the Father for bread.

“Many dogs,” he says, “surrounded me” (Psalm XXI). Finally, after they were shown to have been changed from human beings into dogs, the heavenly bread was changed for them into a rock—not through any fault of the giver, but through the wickedness of the recipient. It would not refresh them but kill them; and, though placed as a foundation, it did not advance them toward the summit, but those who were striving toward the death of their own father it cast and rolled into deep ruin.

He added another comparison: “Will he give him a serpent instead of a fish?”

There was a fish—Christ—raised from the bed of the Jordan, who, placed upon the coals of suffering, after the resurrection provided his own people, that is, his disciples, with life-giving food. But for the Jews this fish is changed into a serpent, as the Lord says: “Just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up” (John III). The Jews saw Christ in the serpent, because an impious eye cannot see God; it cannot see piety.

He also gave a third comparison: “If he asks for an egg, will he offer him a scorpion?”

[Note: [Col. 0353D] Paulinus of Nola calls Christ by this name in letter 100 to Pammachius, p. 72: “Christ himself, the true fish of the water”; Rosweyde collects various material in his notes there. Tertullian, *On Baptism*, calls the newly baptized and Christians “little fishes” after Christ the Fish. Hence Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogus*, book III, advised them to engrave a fish on their rings in remembrance of Christ or of baptism. Optatus, book III against Parmenianus, in Chrysologus’s sense: “This is the fish who, in baptism, is introduced into the fontal waters through the invocation . . . In one name, through its individual letters, it contains a multitude of holy names: Ἰχθὺς. For ‘fish’ in Latin is Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior.” Augustine, *City of God*, book XVIII, chapter 23, p. 383, Antwerp edition, explains the mystery of these letters: “If you join the initial letters of the five Greek words Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς, Θεοῦ Ὑιὸς, Σώτηρ—Latin: Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior—the result is Ἰχθύς, that is, ‘fish.’” The Greek verses containing this acrostic, attributed to the Erythraean Sibyl, are found in Eusebius, *Oration of Constantine*, chapter 13.]

He also gave a third comparison: “If he asks for an egg, will he offer him a scorpion?” It is customary and usual for little children always to ask for an egg, and for parents not to refuse an egg to little children who ask for one. But because Christ had come to gather his children as a hen gathers her chicks (Matthew XXIII), he brought forth the egg of the word, by which the holy shoots of the Church might be nourished.

But because the Jew, through envy, wished rather to pour out than to take that egg, he found a scorpion there, so that, according to the Apostle, “the commandment that was intended for life” would be for them “unto death” (Romans VII).

In commendation of piety the Lord brought forward and displayed three examples, so that by three testimonies, as by three witnesses, he might both encourage the pious to faith in his love and refute the impious, who through no fault of the father but through their own fault had failed to receive the grace of love.

[Note: [Col. 0354D] It is clear from the reading that this sermon was delivered as Easter approached, when the solemn season for baptism had not yet arrived. The occasion was provided by the piety of certain persons who, longing for baptism, wished to anticipate the proper time. Chrysologus says nothing about the reason for their haste. Tillemont, vol. V, p. 188, believes that some among the hearers had been oppressed by an unknown calamity; among them, certainly, one of the leading members of the imperial court increased the number of listeners.]

## SERMON LVI  
### On the Apostles’ Creed

A sudden and confused storm of painful childbirth would trouble me, and the premature budding of shoots would disturb me, unless, with the customary times repeatedly broken apart, and with crude violence, and with the barriers of the womb burst open [Note: [Col. 0355C] “Painful, untimely.”], those about to be born sought and seized the sudden gains of life [Note: [Col. 0355C] From Latinius and the Vallicellian manuscript; elsewhere, “and having burst open.”].

This is why a human being, often disregarding the limit of the tenth month [Note: [Col. 0355C] Does a human being not come to birth after the ninth month has ended? He is perhaps speaking of a lunar month, or he is taking the time of birth in a broad sense.], rejects and abandons, in the seventh month, the narrow and confined dwellings of his first home and of the womb, so that, as a new soldier, he may rejoice that he has conquered time before he himself pays his service to time [Note: [Col. 0355D] That is, to have wrested time away by living as though by force. MITA.].

And if this is permitted to human nature, what can stand in the way of heavenly and divine nature? Or what can the Holy Spirit not do, if flesh can do this? Or how can heavenly grace fail to accomplish what frailty achieves and human weakness fulfills?

Did Paul not, in such premature travail, violently open the way for our birth and disturb the mother’s womb, so that, through a heavenly storm and the entire tempest of the Church, he might anticipate the time of the one giving birth and be born suddenly and [Note: [Col. 0355D] Thus Ananias testified when he said to Saul: “The Lord Jesus, who appeared to you on the road by which you were coming, has sent me.”] on the road (Acts IX)—he who was to provide the Gentiles with the way to faith?

He rightly calls himself “an abortion” (1 Corinthians XV) [Note: [Col. 0355D] 1 Corinthians XV, 8: “Last of all, as to one born out of due time, he appeared also to me.” Whatever is born outside the proper time is called an abortion. For another explanation of this designation, different from the one Chrysologus gives, see St. Thomas, *Works*, vol. VI, p. 394 of the recent Venetian edition.], and marvels that he was born, since he knows that he endured none of the periods of conception. For while he himself was still striking from outside the womb of the holy mother and, at the very moment of birth, was attacking her revered offspring, suddenly he was changed into a holy shoot, he who had been the fiercest persecutor of that very shoot.

The eunuch, too, is born on the road (Acts VIII) [Note: [Col. 0355D] Abbot Pezron believes that the spring from which the eunuch was baptized, while traveling along the road, flowed near the village of Beth-horon, twenty Roman miles from Jerusalem, toward Hebron.]. He whom human delicacy had castrated for service to a human being, and whom involuntary chastity had placed within the palace of a king, voluntary and vowed chastity advanced and transferred to the glory of the heavenly court and the service of the eternal King.

Blessed is this man, to whom it was granted not to lose the insignia of the palace but to exchange them.

This reasoning, little children, tells us that you, whom we received in sadness [Note: [Col. 0356C] Mita thinks that these sorrowful people were those preparing for baptism, because they repented of their former life in sins. Tillemont’s opinion is more reasonable: that they were driven by some misfortune or calamity.], we may bring to the womb of the mother in the greatest joy, in one and the same moment.

Hear the Creed; learn the prayer. But because, with time standing in the way, we can neither disclose the mystery to you [Note: [Col. 0356C] He perhaps touches upon the discipline of secrecy, by which it was forbidden, at the command of the Church, to disclose the more sacred mysteries of the religion to catechumens who had not yet been admitted among the competentes. The matter is sufficiently well known.], nor can you solemnly give back to us what is delivered [Note: [Col. 0356D] It was customary for catechists first to instruct the catechumens, who on an appointed day answered the bishop’s questions about what they had learned. Augustine, *On Faith and Works*, book I, chapter 2: “We deliver the Creed to those being baptized, and require it to be returned.”], act so that now you may learn the simple words of the Creed [Col. 0356A] [Note: [Col. 0356D] At first the catechumens received only bare instruction, and at that stage only the recitation of the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer was imposed. See Calvorius, vol. I, p. 314; Pamelius on Tertullian, *On Baptism*, no. 2; Augustine, cited above, chapter 6.], and at Easter, when these matters are delivered more fully, may be able to recognize the interior realities of the sacrament itself.

Receive what you wish; seize what you desire, because “the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and those who use violence seize it” (Matthew XI). Receive what you wish; and let grace bestow what force can seize.

The entrance of life, the gate of salvation, the entryway of faith—a singular, innocent, and pure confession—is fully taught, as the prophet says: “Enter his gates with confession” (Psalm XCIX).

Therefore the same prophet, instructed in this way, asks for access to the dwelling places of God, who speaks within him, saying: “Open to me the gates of righteousness, and entering through them I will confess to the Lord” (Psalm CXVII) [Note: [Col. 0356D] This passage, completely obscure in the editions, is clarified by Mita’s emendation.].

You see that no one can confess who has not entered this house of salvation and faith; just as confession admits a person into it, so denial certainly excludes him from it.

But let us hear how one must confess. “With the heart,” the Apostle says, “one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans X). And he shows what must be believed: “If you believe,” he says, “in your heart that the Lord Jesus is Lord, and confess him with your mouth, you will be saved.”

“With the heart one believes unto righteousness; with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.” Little children, through this we see that our faith contains a great abbreviation, since the entire mystery of human salvation is enacted and accomplished between the heart and the tongue.

You have the means by which you ought to believe: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness.” You have the means by which you ought to confess: “With the mouth confession is made unto salvation.”

And what shall I say? A human being possesses everything when he possesses himself; but he possesses himself who possesses God; and he possesses God who believes and confesses him as his Creator.

Sign yourselves. The faith that is received by hearing is believed in the heart and proclaimed by the mouth unto salvation. It must be placed in the secret chamber of the mind and entrusted to the very vital organs of our breast [Note: [Col. 0356D] The Creed was taught orally and in words; it was never recorded in books or writing. See the notes to the following sermon.], lest, while it is carelessly written down on parchment and in ink, it not be preserved for believers unto life but be betrayed to unbelievers unto ruin.

In yourself, human being, you must guard what, if placed outside yourself, could perish.

[Col. 0357A] ## SERMON LVII  
### On the Apostles’ Creed
Blessed Isaiah, [Note: [Col. 0357D] The principal reason is that the subject of his prophecy is the Babylonian captivity, the return from that captivity, and the kingdom of the future Messiah. Hence Augustine, in Book XVIII, chapter 29, of *The City of God*; Jerome, in Letter 17 and in the preface to Isaiah; likewise Theodoret in his preface; and others call him by this same name of “evangelist.”] no less an evangelist than a prophet, laments that he has unclean lips and dwells among a people possessing unclean lips, saying: “Woe is me, for I am pierced through, because although I am a man and have unclean lips, and dwell in the midst of a people having unclean lips, I have seen the King, the Lord of Sabaoth, with my eyes” (Isa. VI). He is struck here by a grief beyond human measure, because what he perceives and sees concerning God he cannot express, cannot announce, cannot confess. How narrow the flesh is! So narrow are the lips of his mind; so short is the tongue, the interpreter of his thought. Within the flesh a confined fire breathes, steams through the veins, inflames the viscera, boils in the marrow, and continually sets the whole interior of the human being ablaze, because what the mind contemplates with affection it cannot sufficiently bring forth from the mouth, pour out through the lips, distinguish with the tongue, or completely evaporate into speech.

Hence, when Isaiah saw the King of heaven—that is, Christ—and clearly perceived that he himself was the Lord of Sabaoth, he bewailed the uncleanness of his own lips and those of his people; for just as the divinity of Christ, when confessed, enlightens hearts, cleanses mouths, and purifies lips, so his majesty, when denied, pollutes them. But let us hear what this prophet’s lament accomplished. “And one of the seraphim,” he says, “was sent to me; he held in his hand a coal which he had taken from the altar with tongs, and he touched my mouth, saying: Behold, this has touched your lips, and it has taken away your iniquities and purged your sins.” [Col. 0357C]

It is not for the present occasion to say why one is sent, who this one is who is sent, or how great he is who so fearlessly carries the coal of heavenly fire in his hand—indeed, who so moderates it by his own touch [Note: [Col. 0357D] Latinius corrects this to *tempta*, “touch,” or “contact.”] that he cleanses the prophet’s lips without scorching them. But now let us also be pierced with the whole affection of our hearts; let us acknowledge that we are wretched in this misery of the flesh, and with devout lamentations let us mourn that we too have unclean lips, so that this one seraph, with the tongs of the law of grace, may bring us the sacrament of faith, taken glowing from the heavenly altar, and touch the mouths of our lips with such restraint that he may remove iniquities and cleanse sins, and kindle our mouths with the flame of full confession, so that this burning may be one of salvation, not of pain.

Let us also ask that the heat of this coal may reach our very hearts, so that from the great sweetness of the mystery we may receive not merely a taste with our lips, but receive its complete satiety with our very senses and mind. And just as Isaiah, after the cleansing of his lips, spoke of the ineffable birth from the Virgin, saying, “Behold, a Virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son” (Isa. VII), so let us proclaim the mystery of the Passion and the glory of the Resurrection: [Note: [Col. 0357D] Concerning this creed, which among us is called apostolic, many have composed many discussions. See Vossius, especially in his dissertation *On the Three Creeds*. Whatever others may babble, it is plainly very ancient; from the time of Rufinus long ago it was regarded as having been handed down by the apostles, and in that same period—namely, in the year 390—it had attained the same completeness that it possesses now. Compare Rufinus, *Exposition of the Creed*, among the works of Cyprian; Ambrose, *On the Apostles’ Creed*; Augustine, *On Faith and the Creed for Catechumens*, and *Enchiridion*; Pope Leo, sermon *On the Passion of the Lord*. Indeed, long before Rufinus, namely in the year 198, Tertullian is presented as a witness to its antiquity by Calvorius, vol. I, p. 505, § 3.]

“I believe in God the Father almighty.”

Today you rightly confess that you have believed in God, having gladly fled from gods and goddesses differing in sex, confused in number, popular in their throng, base in origin, disgraceful in reputation, monstrous in impiety, foremost in crime, and singular in wickedness—gods accused even by the faces of their own tombs [Note: [Col. 0358D] On the fronts, or façades, of pagan tombs, the crimes of gods and goddesses and the wicked deeds of myths are often seen carved. The surviving sarcophagi bear witness to this. Or rather, the reference may be to the faces of the tombs—to the sight of their own tombs—which proves that they had been human beings. “Euhemerus,” says Minucius in *Octavius*, p. 189, “enumerates their native lands and tombs.” See how similarly Augustine speaks of Euhemerus in Book I, chapter 23, of *The Harmony of the Gospels*, fol. 271.]—because it is misery, pain, and unhappiness to have as many such masters, and such masters as these, as you have hitherto endured. But rejoice that you have come to the one living, true, and only God—but not a solitary God, saying: “I believe in God the Father.”

Let him who names the Father now confess the Son also; for he who wished to be called and named Father has mercifully shown that he possesses a Son—not one whom he received in time, begot in time, or took up for a time. Divinity neither receives a beginning nor admits an end nor allows a successor, since it knows no setting. God does not bring forth the Son through pangs, but manifests him as existing through his powers; nor does he make outside himself what is from himself, but begets it; and while the Son is in him, he discloses and reveals him. The Son proceeded from the Father but did not depart; nor did he come forth from the Father to succeed the Father, but he came forth to remain forever in the Father.

Hear John saying: “This was in the beginning” (John I). And elsewhere: “That which was from the beginning” (1 John I). What was certainly did not come later; what was, plainly did not begin. “I am,” he says, “the first, and I am the last” (Isa. XLIV). He who is first is not after another; he who is last leaves no other after himself. Yet in saying this he does not exclude the Father, but includes all things in himself and in the Father.

But let us approach the words that follow: “And in Christ Jesus, his only Son, our Lord.” Just as kings are designated by the titles of their triumphs and accumulate countless surnames from the nations they have subjected [Note: [Col. 0358D] These titles occur frequently on coins and stones: Africanus, Germanicus, Parthicus, Dacicus, and so forth.], so Christ is designated by the titles of his blessings. He was called Christ from *chrism*, for he, the merciful healer, poured the anointing of divinity into the already withered limbs of mortals; and just as he was called Christ from *chrism*, so he was called Jesus from salvation, because for this reason he poured the divine anointing into us: to restore certain salvation to the sick and everlasting health to the lost.

“And in Christ Jesus, his only Son.” For although there are many sons by grace, this one is the sole and unique Son by nature.

“Our Lord.” He seeks us, liberated from the service of so many, so cruel, and so shameful masters, not to restore us to our former condition, but to set us free into perpetual liberty.

“Who was born of the Holy Spirit.” Christ is born in you in this way and with this character, until, as a human being, you change the order of your birth, so that you may have a new birth in life, whereas your former birth always ended in death.

“Who was born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary.” Where the Spirit generates, the Virgin gives birth: everything is divine; nothing is human. No weakness has a place where power has been joined to power. [Note: [Col. 0359D] The Septuagint, they say, reads “through a certain ecstasy and alienation of mind”; Symmachus reads “in the deepest sleep, with heaviness of the head.”]

Adam was put into a sleep so that a virgin might be taken from a man (Gen. II); now the Virgin was astonished so that a man might be restored from a Virgin (Luke I). [Note: [Col. 0359D] The Virgin is thought to have been overcome by a kind of stupor or sleep, just as Adam was put to sleep. MITA. I believe the reference is to the evangelist’s words: “She was troubled, and considered what kind of greeting this might be.”] What claim can nature make for itself concerning such a great and such a remarkable birth, when, as it sees its order being renewed, it perceives all its rights changed, and senses and marvels that its own author has come into its offspring? Let this seem worthless to unbelievers; to believers it is a great mystery.

“Who was crucified and buried under Pontius Pilate.” You hear the judge’s name so that you may recognize the time of the Passion [Note: [Col. 0359D] Augustine, *On Faith and the Creed*, chapter 11, vol. VI of the works, p. 115, old edition: “The judge’s name ought to have been added, for the knowledge of the time.”]; you hear that he was crucified so that you may recognize that our lost salvation was restored through the very means by which it had been lost [Note: [Col. 0359D] Augustine, sermon 77 *On the Seasons*: “For this is what the Savior does: that by the same tracks through which sins had entered, they might be cleansed.” Chrysologus himself, sermon 77: “By the same lines through which human salvation was lost, it is restored.” MITA.]; and so that you may see the life of believers hanging where the death of unbelievers had hung. [Note: [Col. 0359D] Adam and Eve, according to Mita; perhaps the Jews or pagans. For just as Christ was the life of believers, so he was the death of unbelievers.] You hear that he was buried so that his death may not be thought to have been mocked. [Note: [Col. 0359D] Christ truly died as a human being according to the form of a servant that he had assumed. This is directed against Nestorius, who said that only the human being died, or against Eutyches; see the notes on sermon 60.]

This is the mark of divine power: death dies by death, the author of death is cut down by his own sword, the captor is seized by his own prey, and hell is shattered by the life it had swallowed.

“On the third day he rose from the dead.” Christ spent three days in his burial, destined to benefit the three dwelling places—those below, the earth, and heaven: restoring what is in heaven, repairing what is on earth, and redeeming what is below, while at the same time revealing to humanity the grace of the Trinity bestowed through the mystery of the three-day period for salvation.

“He ascended into heaven.” He ascended, not to return to heaven—he who always remained in heaven—but to carry you with him, you whom, bound in this manner, he freed and withdrew from hell. Understand, human being, from where and to where you have been raised by God, so that you might be steadfast among heavenly things, although you were slippery and always wavering on earth. [Note: [Col. 0360D] Meursius, p. 178, chapter 30, thinks this ought to be written *mutabundus*, although he does not dare rashly to change the reading found in the printed editions, *nutabundus*.]

“He sits at the right hand of the Father.” But the Father has nothing on his left. Our confession does not assign places to the divine session, but indications of power: God knows no places; Divinity admits nothing left-handed.

“From there he will come to judge the living and the dead.” How can he judge the living and the dead? But those whom we count as dead are alive. Therefore you confess that those whom unbelief thinks to have perished will rise for judgment, so that both those who have died and those who are found alive may alike give an account of their deeds and their life. [Note: [Col. 0360D] Those who deny the immortality of souls. MITA.]

“I believe in the Holy Spirit.” After you have confessed the mystery of the flesh that was assumed, you must confess the divinity of the Spirit, so that the unity of the Trinity—of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—may in every respect and in all things preserve and maintain in our confession the complete truth of the faith.

“The holy catholic Church.” For neither are the members separated from the head, nor the bride from the bridegroom; rather, through such a union the Spirit becomes one, becomes all things, and God is in all things. Therefore he believes in God who confesses the holy Church in God.

“And the forgiveness of sins.” He grants himself forgiveness who trusts that his sins can be forgiven him through Christ.

“The resurrection of the flesh.” You believe well if you believe that through God you can rise from death, since the elements continually rise for you: time from time, day from night, and seeds from their burial. Nor can you perish when those things revive; nor is it difficult for God to make an old man of you what you yourself continually make of a seed.

“Everlasting life.” This faith, this mystery, is not to be entrusted [Note: [Col. 0360D] Augustine, *On the Creed for Catechumens*: “No one writes down the creed so that it may be read, but so that it may be recited, lest forgetfulness perhaps erase what diligence has handed down. Let your memory be your book.” Calvorius observes, vol. I, Book II, section 1, chapter 2, p. 312, Jena 1705, in *The Ecclesiastical Discipline of the Ancients*, that among the ancients oral instruction was called catechesis, so that κατηχέω or κατηκίζω signifies the same as ἀπὸ στόματος διδάσκω, “I teach from the mouth and with the living voice.” For κατηχίζω is the same as ἠχέω, “I resound.”] to paper or written in letters, because paper and letters proclaim caution more readily than grace; but where the grace of God and divine gift reside, faith in the covenant and the depth of the heart suffice for secrecy. Let the divine Judge know this symbol of salvation, this covenant of life, while the false witness remains ignorant of it. Sign yourselves.

May the Lord God himself guard your minds and your hearts, and in those things that he has commanded you may he himself stand beside you as your helper.

## SERMON LVIII. On the same subject

He who seeks faith [Note: [Col. 0360D] Not because the things faith teaches are contrary to reason, but because they are established above the capacity of our minds.] does not seek reasoning; he who asks for divine things lays human things aside; he who is born from God the Father transcends nature and owes nothing to time, because he merits the Author of time. [Col. 0361A]

Behold, we see the pious shoots of faith desiring to be born before you are conceived, to receive the kingdom of heaven before enduring the narrowness of the womb; so you reach toward the joys of the father while passing beyond the travail of the mother. Nor do you consider as abortive what you believe to be mature through Christ. Thus the apostle Paul is born mature through faith, although he declares himself to have been an abortion with respect to time (1 Cor. XV). Therefore receive faith by faith alone; and do not seek to have the rationale of faith itself opened to you, since by your haste you have closed it within faith so that you would not seek it.

Today faith, the faith of your author, invites you to faith, children. Before it receives the pledge of your faith, it fulfills the faith of its promise, and it restores to human affairs what it once promised through the prophet by his word. “Open wide,” he says, “your mouth, and I will fill it” (Ps. LXXX). That is: you open it wide in confession, and I will fill it with the sacrament of that very confession; I will enrich it with mystical speech and fill it with the whole utterance of the heavenly mystery. And truly, children, whatever the obedience of one who hears and whatever the obedience of one who responds professes, this overflows into the grace of God who gives and teaches.

Therefore, since you are about to receive the creed—that is, the covenant of life, the decree of salvation, and the unbreakable bond of faith between you and God—prepare your breasts, not paper; sharpen your understanding, not a pen; and inscribe what you have heard not with ink, but with the Spirit who ministers. For an eternal and heavenly secret cannot be entrusted to instruments that are fleeting and corruptible; it must be placed in the very ark of the soul, in the very library of the inner spirit, lest an irreverent judge or wicked examiner find what he may tear apart, and what was given for the salvation of one who confesses and believes become instead the ruin of one who despises and is ignorant.

But when the prophet says to you, “Open wide your mouth, and I will fill it” (Ps. LXXX), you can respond: “I have hidden your words in my heart, that I may not sin against you” (Ps. CXVIII).

“I believe in God the Father almighty.”

He who has confessed the Father also confesses the Son, because the Father cannot be called Father without the Son, and because nothing can be increased or added to God. The Son always was, because the Father also always was; the Son cannot begin, because the Father cannot fail; nor does the Begotten grow where the Begetter does not grow old. The eternal and coeternal substance of the Father and the Son must be judged not by human degrees but by divine powers.

“In Christ Jesus, his only Son, our Lord.” Receive Christ as anointed—not with ordinary oil, but with the holy oil with which he was born of the Spirit. [Col. 0361D]

“Who was born of the Holy Spirit.” Through such a consecrated birth, humanity was sanctified in God; divinity was not diminished in humanity by such condescension. [Note: [Col. 0362D] Leo the Great, sermon 1 *On the Nativity*: “The glorification would not consume what was lower, nor would the assumption diminish what was higher.”]

“Who was born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary.” Virginity believed in God, because the Virgin could be both virgin and mother only through God.

“Who was crucified under Pontius Pilate and buried.” He indicates the judge in order to designate the time; he mentions the crucifixion so that he may establish the character of the Passion. [Col. 0362A] From this, faith gathers an argument for divine power and true resurrection—from the very point where impiety presumed a basis for insult and an occasion for error. Crucified on the cross, raised up before all his enemies, with all their cruelty looking on and all their bitterness watching, he accepted death. He endured burial so that the impious might not say that he had not undergone death in order to conquer it, but had only pretended to undergo it in order to evade it.

“Buried, he rose from the dead on the third day.” Since in his Passion he proved that he truly possessed the substance of our flesh, through the figure of the three days the whole Trinity rises into glory.

“He ascended into heaven.” He ascended carrying us with him, not returning there himself, since he had never departed from heaven.

“He sits at the right hand of the Father.” The order there is divine, not human. The Son sits at the right hand in such a way that the Father does not sit at the left; the divine session is one and unique, and heavenly power admits nothing left-handed. [Col. 0362B]

“From there he will come to judge the living and the dead.” Let human beings cease, and let heretics cease, to judge their judge. Let them hope for pardon, lest they incur a sentence because of such presumption.

“I believe in the Holy Spirit.” Your confession in the Trinity is now complete, since with a faithful voice you have confessed the Holy Spirit to be of one substance with the Father and the Son.

“And the holy Church.” For it is joined to Christ in such a way that it is transferred wholly into the glory of divinity.

“The forgiveness of sins.” Acquire forgiveness for yourself through your faith; for he is sufficiently his own enemy who does not believe that what the most generous Forgiver promises to grant in complete kindness can be given to him.

“The resurrection of the flesh.” Believe in the resurrection of the flesh; for he who does not believe this has no faith in what was said earlier, as the Apostle says: “If the dead do not rise, neither has Christ risen” (1 Cor. XV). Whom will God judge, with whom will he reign, if the resurrection does not restore to life and judgment those whom death has taken from the world?

“Everlasting life.” It is evident that everlasting life succeeds when death itself dies.

## SERMON LIX. On the same subject

You have heard the Father’s voice; you have heard the voice of the one calling: “Come, children, come, come, because the time of faith has come, the day of belief, the hour of confession.” Come, petitioners for faith; bring a sincere breast, a clean heart, and a pure voice, so that you may receive with holy hearing what the saving word conveys through us. Faith comes from hearing, and hearing is established through the word.

Hear the decree of faith, the covenant of grace, the symbol of salvation, with complete simplicity of understanding, so that at the time of confession you may both hear it and give it back; for to give it back is to possess it. He who gives back the divine gift does not lose it.

When God was about to give the law, he commanded the people to wash their garments, wash their bodies, and cleanse themselves entirely from every contamination of the flesh, because a human being cannot approach God polluted by bodily filth and worldly squalor. That law, which held the shadow and figure of grace, rightly seeks such purification and rightly demands such purity. [Note: [Col. 0362D] It is well known how familiar ablutions and purifications were among the Hebrews. Hence, for those entering the temple, a bronze sea was provided nearby, where each person could wash. That such a custom also existed among the pagans—through the devil’s care, namely, so that practices ordained for the worship of God might be directed to idols—is attested by Herodotus, Book I. Among the offerings sent by Croesus to Delphi, he records two vessels in which people washed themselves before entering. In Book IV he also speaks of a vessel which he calls *chalkēion*, a bronze vessel capable of holding six hundred amphorae, which the natives said had been made from the barbs of arrows.] What purity is required for those who are about to hear the whole sacrament of Divinity? How great a purity of mind and body is necessary?

Therefore let us cleanse our hearts, purify our bodies, open our eyes, unlock our understanding, and throw open all the doors of our souls, so that we may be able to hear, receive, retain, and always preserve in the secret of our hearts the creed, which is the covenant of faith.

“I believe in God the Father almighty.”

We believe in God if we deny the gods, renounce idols, and reject the devil and his angels. “Hear, Israel,” he says, “the Lord your God is one” (Deut. VI; Mark XII).
