And again: “You shall have no other gods besides me” (Exod. XX). Therefore he possesses the true God, the one God, who possesses no other god.

We believe in God and confess him as Father, so that we may believe that he has always possessed a Son—not a Son conceived, begun, separated by birth, increased by time, diminished in rank, or changed by age, but a shoot remaining eternally within the eternal Begetter. “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John XIV).

We have heard the Father; let us believe in the Son through divine power, in an order not human, in the mystery of God rather than by worldly reasoning, not according to the law of the age but by heavenly power. What may be known may not be subjected to scrutiny; it is fitting to believe, not to investigate. For this reason we have called God almighty: so that we should consider nothing impossible for God.

“And in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord.” Christ was called from anointing; Jesus was called from salvation, because the anointing that once passed through kings, prophets, and priests [Col. 0363C] as a figure [Note: [Col. 0363D] See Augustine, *On the Harmony of the Gospels*, chapter 1; Epiphanius, *Against Heresies*, 19, in Baronius, year 57, no. 30, vol. I, p. 428, Lucca edition.] poured itself in its entire fullness of the Spirit of divinity into this King of kings, Priest of priests, and Prophet of prophets, so that the kingship and priesthood which he had formerly introduced temporarily through others might be poured back and rendered eternal in the author himself. [Note: [Col. 0363D] All these things were announced concerning Christ through the prophets. Luke I: “He will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.” Matthew XXVIII: “All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth.” Psalm CI: “You are a priest forever.” Deuteronomy XVIII, 15: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your people, from your brothers, like me; you shall listen to him.” John VI, 13: “This is truly the prophet who is to come into the world.”]

And Jesus—meaning “savior”—is rightly called salvation, because he both gave being to created things and gives salvation to those who are perishing. [Note: [Col. 0363D] The Caesena manuscript reads: “he himself.”]

“His only Son.” In himself he is the only Son; what he grants to others through his grace, he possesses uniquely in himself by nature. [Note: [Col. 0363D] Against Photinus, who rashly asserted that Christ was the Son of God by adoption, not by nature.]

“Our Lord.” As we said above, he is Lord God. God is one in Christ, because whatever he is, in divinity and humanity alike, he is one God.

The diversity of substances ceased in Christ [Note: [Col. 0364C] Mita reads “the diversity of subsistences” and adds: “One should not read ‘the diversity of substances,’ as in the printed editions, unless we wish to interpret *substantia* in a more strained sense. Therefore the diversity of substances ceased in Christ, because humanity in him does not have a subsistence of its own, but subsists formally through the subsistence of the Word. The printed reading, which says ‘of substances,’ conflicts with the Athanasian Creed, which says: ‘God is begotten from the substance of the Father before the ages, and man is born from the substance of his mother in the age.’ Thus the text seems corrupted through scribal error; indeed, we restore *subsistentiam* for *substantiam*, because where an error in Scripture is plausibly suspected, Bellarmine’s doctrine in Book III, chapter 15, *On Christ*, ceases to apply—that the Fathers did not always speak according to the exact rule of dialecticians, but sometimes used abstractions for concrete things and concrete things for abstractions. MITA. In truth, Chrysologus here, arguing against Nestorius, presses the point further than is proper; and without doubt the heresy of Eutyches was then unknown to him. Otherwise he would have proceeded more cautiously, as in sermon CXLIV, where he seems to have had this heresy before his eyes.]—where flesh began to be what the Spirit is, where the human being is God, and where there is one majesty of our body and of divinity.

“Who was born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary.” What earthly thing is born where the Virgin is called to childbirth by the Spirit as author? Who would not believe it divine, when she who gave birth experienced nothing human? A woman carried God in a virginal temple; hence she acquired the honor of a mother without losing the glory of virginity.

“Who was crucified and buried under Pontius Pilate.” We name the judge so that the time of the Passion and the truth of what happened may be made clear. He was crucified so that, because death had come through a tree, life might return through a tree. And he was buried so that he might fulfill all the duties of death, so that death might die by death, and so that from the seed of that bodily death the entire sowing of human bodies might rise and be raised into a life-giving harvest.

“On the third day he rose from the dead.” So that the benefit of the Trinity might be revealed in three days, and so that through the period of three days the human generation of three periods might be saved—that is, before the law, under the law, and under grace.

“He ascended into heaven.” Not as one seeking heaven, but as one reclaiming it. “No one,” he says, “has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven” (John III).

“He sits at the right hand of the Father.” But he does not have the Father at his left. The session of divinity admits nothing left-handed. He sits at the Father’s right hand as one with the Father in divinity. He sits at the right hand so that he may not be inferior in rank or later in order, but may reign with the Father, one in divinity and equal in power: “I and the Father are one” (John X).

“From there he will come to judge the living and the dead.” If we believe that the Judge will come, let us prepare ourselves innocent for the judgment. He denies that the Judge exists who does not believe that he will come; he shows sufficient distrust that he will be judged who lives wickedly. He judges the living, and he judges the dead—those whom he will certainly raise up for judgment.

“I believe in the Holy Spirit.” Having confessed up to this point the mystery of the Lord’s birth, Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension, we have now come to the confession of the Holy Spirit, so that just as we believe in the Father and the Son, we may believe in the Holy Spirit in such a way that we proclaim one divinity, power, and glory in the Trinity.

“And the holy [Col. 0365A] Church.” We also believe in the Church, which we believe has been received and established by Christ, and we confess it for glory.

“The forgiveness of sins.” What liability from an old offense or ancient sin will one who is about to be born as a new human being retain? He who does not believe that his past debts have been forgiven doubts that future debts will be forgiven.

“The resurrection of the flesh.” Believe, human being, that you can rise from death, because before you lived you were nothing. Or why do you doubt that you will rise, when everything that exists rises for you daily in this way? [Note: [Col. 0365D] The Fathers frequently use this comparison to establish faith in the resurrection: Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 48; Theodoret, *Oration 9 on Providence*; Prudentius, Book II *Against Symmachus*; Ambrose, *Hexameron*, Book III, chapter 8; Athenagoras, *Apology*, p. 49; and many others.] The sun sets and rises again; the day is buried and returns; months, years, seasons, fruits, and seeds die when they pass away, but when they return they revive from that very death of theirs. And so that you may be instructed by a continual and native example that you will rise again, as often as you sleep and awaken, so often you die and rise again.

“Everlasting [Col. 0365B] life.” Amen. It is necessary that he who rises should live forever; for if he did not live forever, he would rise not to life but to death.

Sign yourselves. Let the mind hold this covenant of hope, this decree of salvation, this symbol of life, this guarantee of faith, and let memory preserve it, lest the precious gift of divinity be cheapened by paper [Note: [Col. 0365D]

“Devalue it.” This expression is common in the reading of the holy Fathers. Thus in Paulinus, poem XIV, *depretiatus*:

“For when the glory of bodily pomp is cultivated,

a man, devalued, becomes cheap in worth.”

See the first note of the following homily.]—lest dark ink obscure the mystery of light, and lest an unworthy and profane hearer possess the secret of God.

If your charity always offered me silence in this way, your hearing would reach all the treatises of my discourse. But may our God deign to grant me confidence in speaking and you a desire to hear.

## SERMON LX. On the same subject
[Col. 0365C] If the Canaanite woman, by a sudden cry and sudden faith, with Christ’s help, both received what she asked and wrested away what was being refused (Matt. 15); if the Ethiopian eunuch, passing along the road, found the secret of the life-giving bath and seized it in passing (Acts 8); if the centurion Cornelius, before he entered baptism, reached Christ [Note: [Col. 0366D] The passage has been restored from the manuscript of Cesena. The printed editions read *ad spiritum*, “to the Spirit.”] (Acts 10); if the thief, at the very moment of death, stormed paradise (Luke 23)—who, then, will deny you the life you seek at the critical moment? Receive faith, therefore, from faith, and, so that you may be able to know the mystery of faith, labor through the passage of time.

Moses, about to deliver the Law, calls upon heaven and earth; what will a priest invoke when he is about to bring forth grace? He said: “Give ear, O heaven, and I will speak, and let the earth hear the words from my mouth” (Deut. 32, etc.). I shall say: “Give ear, O God; I will speak, and let the human being hear the words from my mouth.” He said: “Let my discourse be awaited like rain, and let my words descend like dew”; I shall say: “Let your Spirit come like dew, and let your grace pour down like a river, and let the heavenly wave of the Word now become a spring leaping up into eternal life.” He said: “Because he invoked the name of the Lord, give greatness to our God”; I shall say: “Because I have invoked faith, give credence to your God.”

And because the ships of our bodies have been refitted by the fast of Lent [Note: [Col. 0366D] This supports the opinion of those who believe that the catechumens were taught the creed on the three Sundays of Lent.], it is necessary that we now declare the agreement of faith, the symbol of the heavenly commerce, so that, under a firm hope, across all the seas of the world and the treacherous waves of the age, we may seek lasting gains for the ages. Receive faith, therefore; await the reality. For when faith does not precede as seed, the reality does not follow as fruit.

Sign yourselves. Speech creates hearing; hearing conceives faith; faith gives birth to belief; belief nourishes confession; confession grants perpetual salvation. Hence it is that the following comes forth from my mouth and yours: thus faith embraces belief, and belief embraces faith; thus salvation greets itself with the kiss of confession.

“I believe in God the Father almighty.” This utterance confesses and discloses the whole mystery of the Trinity. It says “God,” not “gods,” because Christian faith believes in one God in the Trinity: it knows the Father, knows the Son, knows the Holy Spirit; it does not acknowledge gods. Divinity is threefold in persons, but the divinity in the Trinity is one; the Trinity is distinct in persons, not divided in substance. God is one, but in Trinity; God is alone, but not solitary. Divinity is neither divided by threeness nor confused by unity. This is what faith means when it says, “I believe in God.”

Immediately it added, “the Father.” Whoever believes that there is a Father confesses the Son. Whoever believes in the Father and the Son should perceive no ages, conceive no degrees, suspect no periods of time, seek no conception, and inquire into no birth: whoever believes in God has confessed what is divine, not what is human.

[Col. 0366C] [Note: [Col. 0366D] Since many Goths and members of other nations accompanied the emperor Valentinian at Ravenna and were likewise afflicted by the Arian stain, Chrysologus was especially concerned to keep the people entrusted to him free from this poison. See Sermons 98 and 114.]

But the heretic says: “How is he Father, if he does not precede? How is he Son, if he does not follow? How does he who begets not give a beginning? How does what is begotten not receive its beginning from the begetter?” Reason teaches this; nature proves it. You are mistaken, heretic: human reason has this, but divine reason does not; the nature of the world receives this, but the nature of deity does not. Human frailty is conceived and conceives, is brought forth and brings forth, is generated and generates; it receives a beginning and gives an end, receives death and pours it forth again, and preserves in its offspring whatever belongs to its condition and nature.

God the Father, however, did not beget in time, because he does not know time; he did not give a beginning, since he knows no beginning; he did not pass on an end, since he has no end [Note: [Col. 0366D] Other manuscripts of Cesena and the Vatican read: “because he neither has an end nor a beginning.”]. Rather, he begot the Son from himself in such a way that everything that was in him was and remained in the Son. The honor of the begotten is the honor of the begetter; the perfection of the begotten is the form of the begetter; any diminution in the begotten discloses an injury to the begetter.

But, heretic, when you hear these things, do not say, “How can this be?” You said “God”; you believed “Father”; you confessed him almighty. If you doubt, you have lied. If you say “I believe,” how do you not believe when you investigate? If you think it impossible, you have removed the omnipotence you confessed.

But we, who confess the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit as possessing one majesty and glory, shall now speak of faith in the Lord’s body.

“And in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord.” After the Son of God, like rain upon a fleece, poured himself into our flesh with the whole anointing of divinity, he was called Christ from the anointing. The sole author of this name was he who was so overspread and filled with God that man and God were one God.

He poured the name of this anointing upon us, for we are called Christians from Christ; and what is sung in the Song of Songs was fulfilled: “Your name is poured-out ointment” (Song of Songs 2).

“And in Christ Jesus, his Son.” The former is the name of the sacrament, the latter of triumph. For just as the one anointed by God receives his name from the ointment, so, when he restored lost salvation to the world, he assumed from saving the name of Savior. We have often said that *Jesus* is called “Savior” in the Hebrew language, and that this is what the Latin word means.

“And in Christ Jesus, his Son.” Whose Son? Certainly, God the Father’s. When, therefore, you say “in Jesus, his Son,” you confess that Jesus, who was born of Mary, is the Son of God. Take care, then, not to think any longer in Christ merely that he was human, but always confess that he is God, as the Apostle says: “Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him no longer” (2 Cor. 3). [Note: [Col. 0367D] He touches on the heresy of the Ebionites, or rather—as was his custom—the Nestorian heresy.]

“His only Son, our Lord.” This applies to both: he is the Father’s only Son and our only Lord. Others have received by grace the status of sons; others have received the status of lords. Christ alone has and possesses by nature the status of Son and Lord.

“Who was born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary” (Matt. 1). If, according to the Evangelist (John 4), what was born in her is from the Holy Spirit, because God is spirit, let the heretic now confess that God was born from the Virgin’s flesh. Let him no longer drag the heavenly mystery, the birth from virginity, into the conception of the world and the injury of earthly frailty. [Note: [Col. 0367D] The Jovinianists destroy Mary’s virginity, saying that she was violated by giving birth. *Book on Heresies*, attributed to Augustine.]

“Who was crucified and buried under Pontius Pilate.” You hear the judge’s name so that you may recognize the time of the Passion; you hear “crucified” so that from the disgrace of death you may perceive the greatness of love; and know that the death which came through the wood was put to death through the wood, and believe that through the tree of the cross greater things have been restored to you than you lamented losing through the tree of paradise.

You say “buried” so that the confession of burial may prove Christ’s true flesh and his genuine, not merely apparent, death; that he received and conquered death, entered the underworld and returned, came under the rights of Tartarus and dissolved the rights of Tartarus. This is not frailty [Col. 0368A] [Note: [Col. 0367D] The error of Eutyches was that Christ’s flesh was not of the same nature as ours, and that the Word did not assume true flesh, but some other apparent and illusory flesh. Thus, rather than truly suffering and being buried as a man, the Word would merely have pretended to do so. See Flavian, Letter 9 among the letters of St. Leo, and Leo’s Letter 97 to the Emperor Leo; Theodoret, Book 4 of *On Heretical Fables*, at the end. Bellarmine, *On the Incarnation*, Book 3, chapter 2, p. 189, Venetian edition, notes that Caspar Schwenckfeld and Andreas Musculus, following the Lutherans, adopted this opinion from Staphylus in *On the Concord of Luther’s Disciples*.], but power.

You confess that he rose on the third day, so that you may understand that Christ’s resurrection was the victory of the whole Trinity. You say that he ascended into heaven so that you may believe him Lord of heaven and confess that he returned from where he had come. For, having overcome the devil, trampled down death, and liberated the world, Christ triumphs above the heavens—he who was thought to have been defeated on earth.

You cry out, “He sits at the right hand of the Father.” Since the divinity of the Father and the Son is one and their power equal, this means that in the heavenly session there is no dishonor of sitting on the left.

“From there he will come to judge the living and the dead.” When Christ comes, the dead will rise and the living will stand, so that together they may render an account of their deeds.

And since we have now spoken of the sacrament of the Lord’s body, let us proceed to confess the divinity of the Spirit.

“We believe in the Holy Spirit.” The divine voice proclaims him God for us when it says: “God is spirit” (John 4).

“We believe in the Holy Spirit.” The prophet celebrates him as the Father’s and the Son’s fellow worker: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their host” (Ps. 32). He is wholly God and wholly the power of God, proved to be the creator of the heavenly powers.

“We believe in the holy Church.” Christ received it into himself in such a way that he made it share in his divinity.

“We believe in the remission of sins.” Whoever has been born through Christ and the Church into the new human being will possess nothing of the former offense [Note: [Col. 0368D] Augustine teaches excellently that all sins are erased through baptismal regeneration, in Book 2, chapter 27 of *On the Merits and Remission of Sins*, against Pelagius, and in Book 1, chapter 12 of *Against the Two Letters of the Pelagians*. MITA.].

“We believe in the resurrection of the flesh.” Let us believe that the reason for Christ’s Passion, death, and resurrection was that we should rise from the dead. The flesh will rise—will rise as we ourselves are, so that recognition of persons may remain; so that the martyr may receive joy from the persecutor’s punishment, and the persecutor punishment from the martyr’s honor.

“We believe in eternal life.” For after the resurrection there is neither an end of the good nor an end of the wicked.

Sign yourselves. Let us entrust the faith we believe and teach not to ink but to the spirit, to the breast and not to paper; let us give it to memory, not to a book, lest human things violate the divine gift, lest a profane judge seize the heavenly secret, lest what is life for believers become ruin for unbelievers.

The sun gives not light but darkness to diseased eyes; wine does not restore the strength of fevered people but weakens it. Without a physician, the drink of life becomes deadly; so, without faith, the sacrament of faith is harmful to the faithless. As the Apostle says: “Let faith be received from hearing, and hearing be received from the word” (Rom. 10); and the agreement of life, the covenant of faith, the law of salvation must not cling to the dying, but must be fastened to living minds.

[Note: [Col. 0368D] From each sermon on the creed it is gathered that our most holy archbishop baptized very many adult unbelievers—both barbarians and Italians and people of Ravenna. They were so invited to receive the faith by the holy examples and sacred teaching of this shepherd that, because of the great stirring of the Holy Spirit in their hearts, they could not delay receiving baptism, as many used to do. When the blessed bishop inferred this from outward signs, he earnestly sought to baptize them, relying on the examples cited—namely, those of Paul, the eunuch, and the thief. At that time many in Rome also were being converted to the faith of Christ, as Pope Leo I testifies in Sermon 2 on the Nativity: “Since, of course, to those who first come to the faith we owe the service of our mouth.” MITA.]

## SERMON LXI. On the Same Subject

If the sudden and unexpected conversion of blessed Paul did not comfort me (Acts 9), I would scarcely believe that you could so easily be changed from earthly defilement into heavenly glory. For a sudden confession immediately made him an apostle from a persecutor, and gave the Church an eminent teacher whom it had found raging as a destroyer of the Christian name.

The example of that eunuch also encourages me no less, whom faith snatched away to grace before the chariot could return him to Ethiopia and his household (Acts 8) [Note: [Col. 0369D] He may truly have been a eunuch, since queens used such men to avert suspicion; hence Terence:

> “You said that you wanted a eunuch,  
> because queens alone use such men”;

or he may have been a royal minister and palace official. For in Scripture “eunuch” can mean the same as “official,” as in Daniel 1. Hence Potiphar, although married, is called a eunuch in Genesis 40.].

There is also that remarkable lesson of the thief, who seized paradise at the very moment when he was hanged to pay the penalty for his robbery, so that he might be released (Luke 23) [Note: [Col. 0370D] The Acts of the Apostles speak of the queen of Ethiopia and of the woman who was called African. What, then? Is Ethiopia in India? I believe Chrysologus used this name because Ethiopians were said to be at the farthest limit of humanity.].

Therefore, little children, because you have arranged the time of your regeneration so that neither can we say what is necessary nor can you hear what is required, we hand over faith to faith and briefly transmit what we cannot commend at greater length. For how can you, while we explain it, come to know the sacrament of the creed when you can scarcely retain the creed itself in memory? We give you only this warning: let no one commit to writing what he is about to entrust to his heart for belief, as the Apostle warns: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10).

As you are about to hear the form of faith, the standard of belief, and the order of confession, prepare the hearing of body and heart together. Just as a spring flowing from a narrow mouth expands into the broad waters of rivers, so the creed’s faith, expressed in brief speech, opens the widest channels of belief. And just as a root fixed deep in the earth extends itself into a lofty shoot, so faith rooted in the depth of the heart raises itself to the lofty summit of belief.

Therefore clear from your hearts the mud of faithlessness, so that the pure streams of faith may run through you; cut out by the roots the thickets of unbelief within you, so that the vigorous plantings of your belief may grow upward.

And because, according to the Apostle, “with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10), now give in the voice of confession what you already believe in your heart.

“I believe in God the Father almighty.”

Whoever believes in God must not presume to investigate God. It is enough to know that God is. Whoever asks where God is from, how great God is, or what God is, does not know him. The sun darkens an overbold gaze; unauthorized access to God is blinded. Whoever wishes to see his God must learn to observe the measure of his vision; whoever wishes to know his God must not know the gods of the nations. Whoever calls them gods contradicts God.

To serve one is freedom; to serve many is captivity. Believe the God whom you have confessed to be the Father, so that, believing the Father, you may learn that there is a Son; naming the Son, recognize that he was begotten from the Father; recognizing that he was begotten from the Father, do not ask how he was begotten, because you said, “I believe in God the Father almighty.”

The Almighty can do all things, and if he can do all things, who will deny that he has a Son who is in him, from him, and always with him? The generation of God has no beginning, knows no end, and permits no loss, since the Begotten persists in remaining in the Begetter, as the Lord himself says: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 10); “I and the Father are one” (John 10).

You have confessed the Father; you have confessed the Son; you have confessed the divine mystery. Confess the sacrament of the Lord’s incarnation.

“And in Christ Jesus, his Son.” Christ is called from the heavenly anointing, for he has been infused with the whole fullness of divinity. Jesus is a name derived from salvation; every being in heaven and in hell confesses this name with trembling, bending the knee and bowing the head (Phil. 2).

“And in Christ Jesus, his only Son, our Lord.” As the Father and Son have one divinity for us, so let their lordship be one for us [Note: [Col. 0370D] Ambrose, commenting on Luke 6, said: “There is one Lord because there is one God.” The cited passage explains this. MITA.].

“Who was born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary.” The union of Spirit and virgin is not an earthly union but a heavenly secret; hence what is born is divine. Therefore the fact that he was born must be confessed, but how he was born must be left unspoken. What is secret cannot be known; what is closed cannot be opened; what is unique cannot be explained by example.

“Who was crucified and buried under Pontius Pilate.” You hear the judge’s name so that you may not be unaware of the time; you hear “crucified” so that the character of his death may become known to you [Col. 0370C], and so that you may understand what he bestowed upon you who, for your sake, underwent the punishment of so great a death.

You hear “buried” so that you may know that the death was not superficial but real [Note: [Col. 0370D] St. Thomas aptly says in his commentary on 1 Corinthians 15, recent Venetian edition, vol. 6 of his works, p. 193: “For burial is an evident sign of someone’s death.”]. To be unwilling to die belongs to human fear; to rise from death belongs to divine power. Therefore, let the hearing of death not offend here, where the glory of resurrection conceals the dishonor of death.

“On the third day he rose.” What dies belongs to humanity; what rises belongs to the Trinity.

“He ascended into heaven.” He carried humanity there, where he had always remained.

“He sits at the right hand of the Father.” He sits at the right hand because divinity has nothing left-handed.

“From there he will come to judge the living and the dead.” He will judge the living and the dead, because those whom the pagans think perished with the world, and whom they do not believe exist after death, will rise for judgment.

“I believe in the Holy Spirit.” Believe and understand that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one divinity.

“I believe in the holy Church.” Confess that the Church of Christ will remain in perpetual fellowship with Christ.

“I believe in the remission of sins, the resurrection of the flesh.” Whoever does not believe in the remission of sins and the resurrection of the flesh removes forgiveness from himself and takes life away from himself.

What you have heard and believed, what you have confessed, let the heart possess and memory retain; let paper not know it, let the writer not know it, lest the sacrament of faith be spread publicly, lest the secret of faith pass over to the unbeliever.

May God, who has given you both to hear and to believe the sacrament of faith, himself bring you to eternal salvation.

[Col. 0371B]

## SERMON LXII. On the Same Subject

[Note: [Col. 0371D] The ancients called him a “nurse” (*nutricius*). Inscription:

> MEMMIA TERTULLA TO HER NURSER.

> Justinian, *Institutes*, title 6, § 5: “Either a pedagogue, or a nurse, or an educator.”

Pignorius, *On the Jernis*, p. 382, recent edition, praises these words of Chrysologus.]

Unless a devoted nurse has wholly reduced himself to the condition of a little child, he never brings a little child to full maturity as a man. Thus he makes his voice thin, simplifies his words, acts by gestures, sets aside understanding, weakens his limbs, casts away his strength, relaxes his members, slows his step, delights not to walk but to crawl. He pretends to laugh, feigns fear, falsely cries, because in him affection is a kind of falsehood, wisdom is a form of folly, and weakness is a form of strength.

I think blessed Paul did this when he said: “I became a little child among you, as a nurse cherishes her own children” (1 Thess. 2). But perhaps someone may be astonished when he sees a nurse doing such things. He does not laugh if he is a parent; if he is a father, he does not marvel. Whoever knows how to love cannot call this folly.

Therefore I beg you, already fathers, already strong, already wise, to permit me to discharge toward the little ones of my Lord the duties of the nourishment owed to them [Note: [Col. 0371D] The manuscript of Cesena reads “education.”]. Today let me bring forth words suited more to affection than to expertise; let me not square but smooth my speeches, and pour them like milk into their still-tender mouths, as the Apostle teaches: “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Cor. 3). Let me change my voice, love varied emotions—and what more? Let me occupy the minds of the little ones, weak in mind, heart, and body.

But now I address you as the holy offspring of the Church in prophetic speech: “Come, children; hear me” (Ps. 33)—or rather, hear through me and through my voice the commands of the true Father, because God calls you through my mouth.

“Come, children.” Where should you come, and for what purpose? “I will teach you,” he says, “the fear of the Lord.” Who should come to fear? The one who wants life; the one who desires to see good days; the one who wants to do good and flee evil; the one who desires to obtain the rest of divine peace after the struggle of flesh and spirit.

“Come, children; hear me: I will teach you the fear of the Lord.” Who is the person who wants life and desires to see good days? “Keep your tongue from evil, and your lips from speaking deceit.”

Just as sins corrupt the conscience, so deceit pollutes the lips, and curses contaminate the tongue; thus a person polluted in lips and tongue cannot confess God. Since “with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10), sanctify your hearts, cleanse your lips, justify your tongue, so that the voice bearing faith may come forth from a pure breast in every example of holiness.

Sign yourselves. An agreement or covenant that contains the hope of gain, whether present or future, is also taught by human contract to be called a *symbol* [Note: [Col. 0372D] Here the symbol is a document or handwritten instrument made between two contracting parties; or it is a pledge given by both sides, so that neither may withdraw from the original contract with impunity. MITA. I shall add Suidas as a witness in accordance with Chrysologus: “Symbols are agreements which cities made with one another and proposed to their citizens, establishing that they should render to others what had been decreed and in turn obtain it from others.”].

Yet such a symbol between two people is always secured by a duplicated written document, and human precaution makes it secure in the stipulation, lest it slip away from anyone or deceive anyone, since treachery is always the enemy of contracts.

But among human beings, where fraud always harms either the one who commits it or the one against whom it is committed, the symbol of faith between God and human beings is secured by faith alone. It is not entrusted to letters but to the spirit; it is committed to the heart, not to paper, because what God has entrusted needs no human security.

God neither knows how to commit fraud nor can suffer it, because time does not exclude him, age does not overcome him, concealment does not deceive him. He sees hidden things, retains stolen things, possesses things denied. His account is always safe with God, because what he has entrusted has nowhere to perish. If a person denies it, it is lost to the person, not to God; it does not perish for the lender.

But you say: “If he cannot be deceived, why does he require an agreement? Why does he seek a symbol?” He seeks it for your sake, not for his; not because he doubts, but so that you may believe. He seeks a symbol because he who has come to share your lot does not disdain to enter into your contract. He seeks a symbol because he who always lends himself entirely wishes to be owed something. He seeks a symbol because he now summons you not to the reality but to faith, and through the present agreement draws and invites you toward future profit.

The Apostle recalls this when he says: “From faith to faith” (Rom. 1); and elsewhere: “The just shall live by faith” (Heb. 10). Let no one, therefore, be forgetful of the symbol; let no one forget the agreement made with God. When someone has just received faith, let him not demand the reality; when he has come to hope, let him not complain that he does not immediately receive what he hopes for.

Hear the Apostle saying: “By hope we have been saved. But hope that is seen is not hope; for who hopes for what he sees?” (Rom. 8). “But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience.”

Hope reaches toward future things; faith carries us toward what has been promised. When the realities arrive, and the promises have arrived, hope ceases and faith comes to an end.

A letter is sweet, but only until the one who sent it comes. A handwritten bond is necessary, but only until the debt is repaid. Flowers are delightful, but only until one reaches the fruit. The presence of the sender destroys the letter; payment tears up the security; fruit consumes the flowers.

Therefore know that you have already been designated by faith as a son of the heavenly Father, heir of God, joint heir with Christ, sharer in the heavenly kingdom, confessor of the divine Judge, inhabitant of heaven, possessor of paradise. Know that you have been advanced now in hope, not yet in reality.

Therefore receive faith, hold fast hope, and recite the symbol, so that you may be able to reach the reality and those good things we have foretold.

Sign yourselves. Today, human being, your soul has been presented to God.

“I believe in God.” For a long time your soul spoke of God but did not know him; it called upon God but was ignorant of him. It was ignorant of the one whom it sought in this manner through stones and wood. Let it now say—let it say: “I believe in God the Father almighty” [Note: [Col. 0373D] The manuscript of Cesena reads “whom.”].

For a long time, while it saw stones, it did not see whom it should believe; but he truly is God who enabled you, without seeing, to see the one whom, while seeing, the gods of the nations had made you not see.

Hear the Lord saying: “For judgment I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9).

“I believe in God the Father.” Affection exists in God; affection is always in God; fatherhood remains with him. Therefore believe that he has always been the Son, lest by saying that he has not always been the Father you blaspheme.

But you say: “If he begot him, how has he always had him? How did he beget him?” You who ask in this way deny the faith that you confess. You said, “I believe.” If you believe, where does “how” come from? “How?” is the language of one who doubts, not of one who believes.

You said, “I believe in God the Father almighty.” If there is something he cannot do, he is not almighty. Yet you think that he begot the Son from something, although you confess that he made everything entirely from nothing. From something, certainly, if from time. But if the Father cannot be contained by time, the Son knows no beginning [Note: [Col. 0373D] The manuscripts of Cesena and the Vatican read “that he can.”].

How wretched, then, that you make him temporal who enabled you to be eternal. The Father does not generate the Son through a conception in time or through the travail of the womb; rather, he generates the Son while revealing him to us.

“And in Christ Jesus, his only Son, our Lord.” Observe, human being, with what reverence faith is conveyed and entrusted to you. Hear the Father so that you may perceive, understand, and believe the Son, not investigate him; confess that he exists, and do not rashly inquire where, when, or how he exists.

Hence the heavenly speech, in announcing the Father to you, immediately sends you with your whole mind to Christ, to Jesus, to the Son, to our only Lord, so that, when you see what belongs to his humanity and realize that you can neither attain, assess, nor comprehend it, you may not dare to touch what belongs to his divinity.

“Who was born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary.” Come, human being—if indeed you are human, and not rather an angel, in order that you may understand these things, or an irrational animal, or a devil employing malice, you who rashly investigate these things—advance in your heart, rise up in your mind, expand your understanding [Note: [Col. 0373D] Thus Latinius and the manuscript of Vallicella; the printed editions read “seize.”], sharpen the faculties of your intellect, awaken the powers of your knowledge. Awaken, examine, investigate, and scrutinize whatever reason there is in you; and now, in amazement, reveal by yourself what it means that the Spirit generates, the Virgin conceives, the Virgin gives birth, and remains a virgin after giving birth; how the Word becomes flesh, God becomes human, and humanity is transferred into God; how a cradle contains him whom heaven cannot contain; how he who sustains the whole is carried on shoulders; why he who made all things, established the universe, and governs everything wished to be born from you, to be ruled by you, and to be nourished, so that he might live by you as his parent, although he had previously disdained the servitude of one such as you.

And if you can grasp and express anything from the hidden things of divinity and the secret of deity, then come closer within, climb higher, look more boldly, and then explain, as a new investigator, a singular discoverer, and a betrayer of divinity, the Father’s times and the Son’s beginnings.

Be greater than Isaiah, who said: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he did not open his mouth; in humiliation his judgment was taken away. Who will declare his generation?” (Isa. 53). Whose generation? The generation of this one who was led like a sheep to the slaughter.

“If Christ’s human generation existed, if his divine generation existed; and if, as he is begotten, it cannot be narrated,” what wave, human being, what current carried you to this shipwreck? What spirit drove you through the air toward this ruin? [Note: [Col. 0373D] In all the manuscripts I consulted, the reading was *generatio exstitit si Divina*, “if the divine generation existed.” Unless properly divided and pronounced, the reading does not produce a suitable sense here. I therefore think it should be read: “If Christ’s human generation existed and his divine generation existed.” That is, if both generations have a place in him, and if in the one Christ, when he was led to slaughter, both the divine and the human are found, Isaiah called both beyond narration. The reading should not be changed, but properly divided. This is Latinius. Against the heresiarchs Arius and Eutyches, as in the Author’s letter to Eutyches and below, Sermon 145. MITA.]

The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one divinity, one power, one eternity, one majesty. Whatever diminution, reception, or increase belongs to the Son belongs to my body, not to his substance [Note: [Col. 0374D] I have followed Meursius’s correction. The printed editions read “he does not know.” The passages of Scripture—John 14 and 1 Corinthians 15, and any others—must be explained as meaning that the Son is less than the Father only with respect to the human nature. So Chrysostom, Cyril in Book 2 of *On the Treasury*, Augustine in Book 2 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 7, and Gaudentius in his letter to Paul, rejecting the earlier Fathers’ explanation concerning the principle rather than the nature, from which Chrysologus appears to have withdrawn as less suitable.].

Do you marvel, human being, that he calls the Father “in heaven” who deigns to have a mother on earth?

“Who was crucified under Pontius Pilate and buried.” Why, human being, do you accuse the one who is equal to the Father in himself for this one thing only: that in you he wished to be lesser? You hear that while Pilate sat he stood before Pilate; while Pilate examined him, he was judged. Why do you accept only this—that he was handed over to criminal accusers and condemned by the pronouncement of the accused?

He wished to be born from your flesh; he wished to be occupied at your breasts; he wished to lie upon your breast; he wished to be carried on your shoulders. He has always wished to be loved by you, not feared.

Examine what he first commanded in the Law, and then you will see what he sought in grace. When the Lord was asked, as the Evangelist relates, what the first commandment in the Law was, he said: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind” (Matt. 22). Hence he came to your heart and to your mind, because he sought to be loved by you from the beginning in soul, heart, and body [Note: [Col. 0374D] The manuscript of Cesena reads “he received your soul.”].

“Who was crucified under Pontius Pilate and buried.” [Note: [Col. 0375C] Mita observes that these words are absent from the manuscripts of Cesena and Urbino, but are present in the Vatican and Vallicella manuscripts, where they do not differ from the printed editions. Mita nevertheless extracts the Author’s meaning and says that here he is arguing against Jews and heretics. For although the Jew confesses Christ’s death and burial, he goes no further in faith; indeed, he denies Christ’s resurrection. The heretic likewise denied the future resurrection of the flesh. The Author rises against both in order to strengthen Christian hearers in faith in the resurrection of human flesh. From Mita.]

Up to this point the Jew has spoken; now the heretic follows—let him wait. Let no one who is nourished and fattened by Christ’s injuries approach their earlier position.

But you, little children, listen, so that after the suffering of death and the grief of burial you may dispel sorrow through the joys of resurrection.

“On the third day he rose.” So that the resurrection of our body might be the power, grace, and gift of the Trinity.

“He ascended into heaven.” Through me, who through himself was never absent from heaven.

“He sits at the right hand of the Father.” By the order of divine power, not by the honor of human rank. We have said that the Son sits at the right hand in such a way that the Father never sits at the left.

“From there he will come to judge the living and the dead.” And what does death owe the Judge? This is why a person rises: so that he may owe an account.

“I believe in the Holy Spirit.” Whoever denies the Holy Spirit denies the one in whom he believes.

“In the holy Church.” Because Christ is in the Church and the Church is in Christ; therefore whoever confesses the Church has confessed that he believes in the Church.

“The remission of sins.” Give yourself forgiveness, human being, by believing—you who have fallen into every sin through despair.

“The resurrection of the flesh.” This is the whole proof of faith. If you believe that flesh which has decayed, putrefied, and perished can, through God, rise, be rejoined, and return [Note: [Col. 0375D] “Be joined together again, fitted together.” Du Cange gives only one example of this word from Chrysologus.], then, when you confessed him almighty, you swore that he can do all things.

“Eternal life.” He rightly added “eternal life,” so that the one who will rise might believe that he will rise through him who lives and reigns with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always, and through immortal ages of ages. Amen [Note: [Col. 0375D] Ferrarius, *On the Rites of the Sacred Church*, Book 1, chapter 132, shows that the sermons of the ancient Fathers very frequently concluded under the invocation and glorification of the divine and most holy Trinity.].

[Col. 0375C]

## SERMON LXIII. On Lazarus Raised from the Dead
After the apostolic reading, as we desired to return to the evangelical virtues, Lazarus, who had soon returned from the underworld, meets us, bringing the pattern of death’s defeat and bearing an example of resurrection. If it pleases you, before we enter the sea of the reading, before we undertake the waves of its questions, before we penetrate the depth of such an event, let us contemplate the appearance of the resurrection, because we see in this the sign of signs, perceive the virtue of virtues, and discern the wonder of wonders.

**[Note: [Col. 0375D]** The same as Eleazar, by contraction of the Hebrew name. Grotius derives this from Tertullian and Prudentius. According to Bede, in St. Thomas’s *Catena*, Lazarus is interpreted as “helped.” Chrysostom, *Homily on Luke 16*, vol. II, p. 1171.]

The Lord had raised the daughter of Jairus, the ruler of the synagogue, but this was while the funeral was still warm, while death was still in progress, while the body was still present, while the human being still remained among human beings, while the spirit was still journeying,

**[Note: [Col. 0376C]** Everything here is expressed metaphorically and adorned with rhetorical coloring. Some writers of this period use *viare* in the sense of “to travel” or “to make one’s way.” Sidonius, book IV, letter 3; Fortunatus, book IX of the poems; Ambrose, book V of the *Hexameron*, chapter 10: “Who grants the arrangement of traveling.”]

while the soul did not yet know the prison of Tartarus—in short, he restored life to the dead girl in such a way that the claim of the underworld remained. He also raised a mother’s only son, but in such a way that he retained the bier, that he forestalled the tomb, that he suspended and anticipated corruption and stench, restoring life to one who had died before he entered wholly, as a dead man, into the rights of death.

But what happens in the case of Lazarus is wholly extraordinary. His death and his resurrection have nothing in common with those mentioned above. In him the entire power of death was fulfilled, and the complete pattern of resurrection shines forth.

I dare to say that Lazarus, had he returned from the underworld after three days, would have seized the whole sacrament of the Lord’s resurrection. For Christ returned after three days as Lord; Lazarus is recalled after four days as a servant.

**[Note: [Col. 0376D]** Since Christ’s three-day resurrection abounds in many mysteries and sacraments, if Lazarus had risen after three days, he would have taken for himself what had been reserved for the Lord’s resurrection and would have represented in himself what, indeed, was unbecoming to a servant. He is therefore raised before the Lord’s resurrection, but after four days, already stinking, so that he might not prejudice the sacrament of the Lord’s resurrection and, at the same time, so that he might not rob the disciples of their faith, as is explained below and in Sermon 81. —Mita.]

But to prove what we have said, let us now preview something from the reading. “His sisters,” he says, “sent to the Lord, saying, ‘Lord, behold, he whom you love is ill.’”

**[Note: [Col. 0376D]** Through messengers sent to Jesus, who was absent and across the Jordan.]

In saying this they strike at his affection, appeal to his love, address his charity, and strive by their need to move his compassion.

**[Note: [Col. 0376D]** Lazarus’s sisters do not extol either their own merits or their brother’s, but only Jesus’ love for him, as Brugensis observes here. “It is enough that you know,” says Augustine in the cited passage, p. 451, “for you do not love and abandon.”]

**[Note: [Col. 0376D]** Latinius reads *submonere* (“to remind” or “to urge”).]

But Christ, for whom it is greater to conquer death than to remove sickness, whose love consists not in relieving the beloved but in restoring him from the underworld, soon prepared for the beloved not the medicine of sickness but the glory of resurrection.

Finally, “when he heard that Lazarus was ill,” as the Evangelist says, “he remained in the same place for two days.” You see how he gives death its opportunity, grants permission to the tomb, allows corruption to exert its power, denies nothing to decay and nothing to stench; he even permits Tartarus to seize him, drag him away, and hold him. He acts so that every human hope may perish and the entire force of worldly despair may arrive, so that what he is about to do may be divine,

**[Col. 0377D]** This same interpretation—that Christ continued to wait and gave corruption its opportunity so that belief in the miracle might be more certain—is repeated in this passage by Cyril, Theodoret, Chrysostom, Euthymius, Alcuin, and others.

not human. Yet he remains so long in the place, awaiting death,

**[Note: [Col. 0377D]** For he remained at Bethabara.]

that he himself announces the man’s death and then declares that he is coming to Lazarus. For he says, “Lazarus is dead, and I rejoice.”

Is this what love does? Christ rejoiced because the sorrow of death was soon to be turned into the joy of resurrection. “And I rejoice for your sake.” Why for your sake? Because in the death and resurrection of Lazarus the entire figure of the Lord’s death and resurrection was being depicted, and what was soon to occur in the Lord already preceded it in the servant.

He said repeatedly to his disciples: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be delivered to the chief priests and scribes; and they will condemn him to death and deliver him to the Gentiles to be mocked, scourged, and crucified” (Matthew 20). As he said these things, he saw that they were becoming very uncertain, very sad, and deprived of all consolation. He knew that they would be so oppressed by the very weight of the Passion that nothing of life, nothing of faith, and nothing of light could remain in them, but that they would be almost completely darkened by the night of unbelief.

Therefore he prolonged the death of Lazarus until the fourth day and allowed stench to prevail, so that the disciples might have no doubt that the Lord could rise while still fresh after three days, when they had seen a servant rise after four days, already stinking; and so that they might believe that he could easily restore life to himself who had recalled another to life in such a manner.

This is why he says, “I rejoice for your sake, so that you may believe.” Lazarus’s death was therefore necessary, so that, with Lazarus, the faith of the disciples also might rise from the tomb.

**[Note: [Col. 0377D]** I have supplied a remedy for this corrupt passage in the printed editions from the manuscript of Cesena.]

“For I was not there.” Was there a place where Christ was not? And how was he not there, when he was announcing Lazarus’s death to the disciples?

Brothers, Christ God was there, but Christ the human being was not there.

**[Note: [Col. 0377D]** That is, he was not there in his humanity.]

Christ God was there when Lazarus died, but Christ was then going to come to the dead man, at the time when Christ the Lord was going to undergo death. Therefore he said, “For I was not there.” That is: I was not there in death, in the tomb, in the underworld, where by me and by my death the whole power of death must be overthrown.

“Martha,” he says, “when she heard that Jesus was coming, went to meet him, saying, ‘Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.’”

Woman, you confess God and say, “If you had been here”? Places do not make God absent, nor do times make him present. Lazarus would not have died if the Lord who was there had been there—namely,

**[Col. 0377D]** The printed editions read: “who was there, but if you, woman, had not been in paradise.” I have attempted, following Latinius, to shed some light on the rather obscure meaning. The Lord was there, and Lazarus would not have died if Eve had not sinned in the paradise of delight.]

if you, woman, had not been in paradise. Woman, you sought tears; you found groans; you purchased death at the price of your appetite; and you accuse God’s absence, when you do not deny that your presence was the cause of death.

When death was prepared by you,

**[Note: [Col. 0377D]** That is, equipped to do harm.]

then there was material for lamentation. But now it has become an opportunity for power: then it was given as punishment for the sinner; now it has been permitted for the glory of the one who raises the dead. Then Tartarus found a human being; now it loses one.

But now seek by faith what you lost through unbelief.

“Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died; but even now I know that whatever you ask of God, God will give you.”

This woman does not believe, but she tries to believe; her faith is confused by her unbelief. “Whatever you ask of God, God will give you.” God gives from himself; he does not ask from himself.

Why do you delay your petition, woman, when the one who is about to grant it already stands before you? Woman, the one whom you desire as your advocate is himself the judge. In this case there is the power of the giver, not the necessity of the one who asks.

“I know,” she says, “that whatever you ask of God, God will give you.”

Woman, to believe this is not belief; to know this is not to know. The Apostle proved this, because when a person thinks that he knows something, then he does not know (1 Corinthians 11).

But let us now hear what the Lord answered: “Your brother will rise again.”

And the woman replied: “I know that he will rise in the resurrection on the last day.”

Martha, once again you know what you do not know. You know that your brother can rise on the last day,

**[Note: [Col. 0378D]** Grotius thinks that Martha learned something obscure about the resurrection from the Pharisees. More careful interpreters, however, believe that belief in the resurrection was at that time common among the Jews. Among them see Calmet on Psalm 10 and on 2 Maccabees 12:43.]

but you do not know that he can rise here also. Or perhaps the God who can then raise everyone cannot now raise one dead man?

He can; God can raise one dead man for a temporal sign, the God who will then raise all the dead to everlasting life.

“I know that whatever you ask of God, God will give you, and I know that he will rise in the resurrection on the last day.”

Martha, the resurrection you send so far away is before you. “I am,” he says, “the resurrection.”

And what does “I am the resurrection” mean? Does it not mean “I raise the dead”? What does it mean? Because he assumed humanity, he assumed death, so that the one who raises one person by command might, by rising in himself, raise everyone; and so that Christ might become for those for whom Adam was the well of death the fountain of life.

**[Note: [Col. 0378D]** Brugensis explains the Evangelist’s words, “I am the resurrection,” as meaning “the author and fountain of resurrection and life.” The Hebrews often name causes by their effects. In this way Christ is called righteousness, sanctification, redemption, salvation, and so forth.]

And let what the Apostle said be fulfilled: “As in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive” (1 Corinthians 11).

“I am,” he says, “the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, even if he has died, will live; and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die. Do you believe this?”

And the woman replied: “Yes, Lord, I have believed, and I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of the living God, who has come into this world.”

He had come to Lazarus; why is he so occupied with Martha? Why? So that before these events she might rise in faith, before he raised Lazarus in the flesh.

**[Note: [Col. 0379D]** Chrysostom, Theophylact, Maldonatus, Grotius, and Brugensis likewise teach that by these words Christ strengthened Martha’s hope and faith.]

This is what he does who comes to help both the living and the dead. He is not afraid to delay the deed, for with him remain the act, its effect, and the power.

Brothers, bear with the word being delayed today, if you desire to hear more fully what follows.

## SERMON LXIV. On the Same Subject

If each word of Scripture were entrusted to separate books, even then the mysteries contained in those words would not shine clearly upon the hearers. What, then, will a sudden and brief sermon accomplish, one that, like lightning, retreats as soon as it has illuminated the eyes, giving not light to those who see but terror?

Pray, therefore, that because we move amid the darkness of the world, and, placed in the flesh, spend the time of night rather than of day, Christ may kindle for us the lamp of his word. With it going before us, may we enter the obscurities of heavenly mystery and advance slowly toward as much brightness of divine knowledge as we can attain.

So did those wise men, who measured the eyes of their minds and did not dare entrust themselves to the sun’s splendor or to the divine brightness, but, taking up by night the tender light of the star with eyes still more tender, reached Christ’s most tender cradle (John 11).

But now, as we promised, let us complete what remains of the evangelical reading.

“Martha,” he says, “when she heard that Jesus was coming, went to meet him.”

Thus the servant was not there, nor the neighbor, nor the friend—certainly not the comforter who was present—so that the woman alone, amid the crowds, through the whole town,

**[Note: [Col. 0379D]** Christ had not yet entered the town, but remained in the place where Lazarus’s tomb had been constructed, outside the town, according to Jewish custom.]

outside the city and at a time of mourning, should go to meet the Savior?

Brothers, in these persons it is not ordinary causes that are at work, but mysteries are signified. The woman runs on behalf of death, she who ran toward death; she hurries toward pardon, she who hurried toward guilt. She reaches the merciful Redeemer, but the worst deceiver had reached her first. She seeks the resurrection, she who sought ruin; and she who brought death to her husband now pants to bring life to her husband.

This is why Christ stopped in that place; why Christ waited; why he did not enter among the crowds; why he did not hurry to the house; why he did not turn aside to the tomb; why he did not hasten to Lazarus, for whose sake he had come. Rather, he supports the woman, delays for the woman, and first receives the woman whom the first persuader had infected. From the woman he drives away unbelief; to the woman he restores faith, so that she who had been the instrument of perdition might be its minister of salvation; and so that she might at last become, through the living God, the mother who had long been the mother of the dead through the devil.

And because the woman had been the source of evil, he takes up the cause of death, so that before he bestowed pardon he might wash away the crime, before he canceled the sentence he might remove the cause. He takes care lest the man refuse to accept as a participant in life the woman through whom he had once been deceived; lest, in short,

**[Note: [Col. 0379D]** Christ the Lord, the Wisdom of the Father, restores what was lost in the order in which it fell. The woman fell through sin before the man; therefore it was fitting that the woman should be restored before the man.

St. Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book II, chapter 34: “For the command was given by the Lord through the man down to the woman, but sin came from the devil through the woman down to the man.” And chapter 37: “Punishment was imposed on the woman before the man.” Thus, if the Redeemer had reached the man before the woman, the woman would have remained in her misery, and the customary order of restoration would not have been preserved. Or at least the man, in his indignation, might have refused to have as a participant in the life acquired through divine restoration the woman whom he had once experienced as the source of evil leading to death. See, nearly to the point at issue here, St. Augustine, *Eighty-Three Questions*, question 11, in the Master, part III, distinction 12, letter E.

“But how,” you ask, “or when did Christ reach the woman before the man?” When, in view of the foreseen merits of the coming Christ, the eternal Word chose the Blessed Virgin as his mother and made her free from every stain of sin. Or Christ reached the woman at the time when the angel Gabriel was sent by God. For at that time the Blessed Virgin was earnestly beseeching God to descend to redeem the human race, as he had promised through the prophets, and so forth. —Mita.]

the woman would have perished if Christ the Lord had reached the man first.

For this reason, brothers, Christ is born through a woman; for this reason a woman always raises a man from the tomb of her womb, so that by her pains she may recall him whom she drove away by her charms, and by weeping restore him whom she lost by eating.

**[Note: [Col. 0380D]** The Cesena manuscript reads *fastidiendo* (“by disdaining”).]

Finally, when Martha had confessed to Christ and had wiped away by her devout confession whatever guilt belonged to the woman,

**[Note: [Col. 0380D]** From the same manuscript. The printed editions read: “And whatever guilt of hers, not in the person of the woman,” and so forth.]

she is sent to Mary, because without Mary neither could death be driven away nor could life be restored.

Let Mary come; let the bearer of the maternal name come, so that the human being may see that Christ inhabited the secret place of the virginal womb, so that the dead may come forth from the underworld and the dead may leave their tombs.

“Jesus,” he says, “seeing Mary weeping, and the Jews who had come with her weeping, groaned in spirit and troubled himself, and said: ‘Where have you laid him?’ They answered: ‘Lord, come and see.’ And Jesus wept.”

Mary weeps, the Jews weep, and Christ also weeps. Do you suppose with a similar compassion?

Let it be granted that Mary, his sister, wept because she could neither retain her brother nor prevent death. Although she was confident about the resurrection,

**[Note: [Col. 0380D]** See note 8 of the preceding homily.]

she could not, deprived of present consolation, fail to weep over the delay of so long an absence and the sorrow of such a long separation. At the same time, the image of death—so savage, so mournful, so cruel—could not fail to touch and move even a faithful mind.

**[Note: [Col. 0380D]** The corrupt passage in the printed editions has been restored from Mita’s edition, the Urbino manuscript, and Latinius.]

The Jews wept, remembering their condition and possessed by despair of the life to come. Death is bitter enough to the living and sufficiently troubles them in the very act of dying; but it troubles them even more by its example. Whenever someone sees a dead person, he laments that he too has been destined for death. Thus a mortal cannot fail to grieve over death.

What of Christ? And if none of these things applied to him, why did he weep? Certainly he who had said, “Lazarus is dead, and I rejoice”—the one who rejoiced at his death—then lamented him when he raised him. When he lost him, he did not weep; when he received him, he lamented. Then he shed mortal tears, when he was restoring the spirit of life.

Brothers, human bodily nature possesses this quality: the force of joy and the force of sorrow produce tears. Whenever the inner organs are constricted by an excessive surge of either joy or grief, the eyes immediately burst into tears.

**[Note: [Col. 0381C]** These words are badly distorted by those impious minds that have tried to depict Christ to us as a Stoic, wholly devoid of emotions. Yet the ancients took offense at the statement in the Gospel that Christ wept. Hence, in Epiphanius’s age, as he himself testifies in the *Ancoratus*, chapter 31, p. 76, Cologne edition, the passage in very many manuscripts of Luke in which Christ is said to have wept at the sight of Jerusalem had been corrupted. Irenaeus nevertheless used it in *Against Heresies* to refute those who impiously taught that Christ had appeared only in outward semblance.]

This is why Christ wept not over the pains of death but in remembrance of that joy by which, with his voice—his single voice—he will raise all the dead to everlasting life.

He groaned in spirit and troubled himself with the whole movement of his inner being, because at that time he was raising only Lazarus and not yet all the dead.

What person, then, would think that Christ wept here from human weakness, when the heavenly Father does not lament the prodigal son while he is away, but laments him when he receives him (Luke 15)?

Christ wept for Lazarus when he received him, not when he lost him. Finally, Christ does not weep when he sees the mourners; he weeps when he asks and sees that no faith remains in those who answer him.

He had said, “Where have you laid him?” But they answered: “Lord, come and see.”

They thought that he did not know where the man had been placed on earth, though he knew where the dreadful underworld was holding him.

By asking in this way,

**[Note: [Col. 0381D]** Augustine, *On the Word of the Lord*, sermon 3: He should not have been thought ignorant of the place where the man was buried; rather, he wished to test the faith of the people.]

he demanded faith and offered knowledge, so that those standing there might know that death, the tomb, corruption, decay, and stench had come upon human beings not by God’s ordinance

**[Note: [Col. 0381D]** That is, by God’s covenant or decree.]

but through human sin.

For when he says, “Where have you laid him?” he rebukes the women and accuses the women. This is what he means: “Whom I placed in paradise, in the region of life—behold where you have placed him.”

But the Jews also answered the questioner’s supposed ignorance: “Lord, come and see.”

What? Did they think that he was ordering the man to death? What? Did they think that he was ordering him to the underworld, when they believed that he could not see what was before his eyes, and when they reasoned in such a way about his tears?

“He who could open the eyes of the blind—how could he not have done so that this man would not die?”

**[Note: [Col. 0381D]** This is sarcasm. They call the illumination of the blind into question, as though they were saying: “What do they proclaim about the miracle of the man born blind? Surely he would have preserved his friend if he had been able to give sight to the blind.” From this one can see how aptly Chrysologus attacks the Jews’ unbelief and infidelity in what follows.]

He could have made him not die, but the one who wished to raise the dead man for his own glory permitted him to die. He permitted him to descend to the underworld, so that it might be evident that God restores the human being from the underworld.

But, Jews, your hearts appear more obstructed than the underworld, your inner selves harder than the dead, your eyes more dreadful than tombs. The voice that opened your Tartarus did not open your hidden places; the command that awakens the dead did not awaken your minds; the law that illuminates the tomb did not enlighten your blindness.

But let these things suffice, so that with Christ we may see more openly the glory of Lazarus rising.

**[Note: [Col. 0381D]** In writing this, Chrysologus presents certain plausible matters under rhetorical coloring, so that, while he was treating the evangelical history, some might think that he had gone beyond proper bounds.]

## SERMON LXV. On the Same Subject.

Since we have already dealt, in a twofold sermon, with the death of Lazarus, Mary’s weeping, Martha’s tears, and the Jews’ lamentation, let us now relieve our minds, cast off our cares, and free our thoughts, so that with our whole minds we may both comprehend and hear the joy of so great a resurrection.

The Evangelist thus proclaims that the Savior came to the tomb:

> “Jesus, therefore, again groaning within himself, came to the tomb; and it was a cave, and a stone had been placed over it.”

Jesus came to the tomb groaning. Christ groans, so that the flesh may revive; Life groans, so that death may be driven away; God groans, so that humanity may rise again; Mercy groans, lest the sentence be contradicted. Christ groans as he conquers death, because one who wins a unique victory over an enemy cannot fail to groan.

[Note: This means that Christ the Lord cannot fail to be disturbed in the deepest feelings of his soul, and, once disturbed, to be stirred to the greatest indignation against the insolent enemy whom he is preparing to conquer in a special and extraordinary manner. Or Christ is indignant and cries out because he raises only one person, although he had come to restore all to life; meanwhile he was being held back, since the time fixed by divine foreordination had not yet arrived. MITA. Or rather, Augustine’s view should be embraced: he thinks that Christ groaned because of the sins of human beings, from which death arose.]

When he said “again groaning,” he groans again, to show by a doubled sign the marks of the resurrection: for, just as by Christ’s voice the dead in body are raised from their tombs to life, so the dead in faithlessness rise to the life of faith.

“It was,” he says, “a cave.” It would have been enough to say that he came to the tomb. Why does the Evangelist mention the cave so insistently?

[Note: In accordance with the custom of the Hebrews, tombs were excavated in caves.]

[Note: For by his deceits he stole from humanity the life of innocence and its other goods, and shut humanity itself into death’s cave, so that no one might see or discover the theft. MITA.]

Clearly, it was a cave in which the devil’s robbery had placed humanity; a cave in which deceit had buried the man through the woman; a cave in which the rapacity of death was enclosing God’s handiwork.

And a stone had been placed over it. The door of harsh death was closed by a harsher stone, itself most hard.

[Note: The stone had been placed at the entrance, by which one descended into the hollow of the cave. The mouth of the cave was higher on one side and lower on the other; therefore the stone is not here said to be rolled away, as in Matthew 28:2, but to be taken away.]

But what does weeping accomplish at the tomb, when the voice of one who weeps cannot penetrate such hard and piled-up barriers?

[Note: Anything that is placed in the way may be called an obstacle. Juvencus, Book IV, calls the wings with which a hen embraces her chicks “obstacles.” See Gaspar Barthius, on the verse, Book XIX, chapter 14, who illustrates this passage of Chrysologus.]

Christians, let us weep before God for our sins, and let us not weep with the Gentiles for those who do not hear.

[Note: The Caesena and Vatican manuscripts read, “hearing nothing.”]

Jesus said, “Take away the stone.” Does Christ require human assistance amid divine powers? Is he not sufficient to remove the stone, who is sufficient to drive away death? Is he unable to open the barriers of the tomb, who prevails to open the gates of hell?

He had said through the prophet: “I will take away the stony heart from their flesh, and I will give them a heart of flesh” (Ezekiel 11). Therefore he commands the Jews to remove from themselves the stony heart, to roll away the rock of faithlessness, and to exclude the flint of hard unbelief, so that souls dead through unbelief might leap forth from the tomb of the breast, and so that they might rejoice not merely that Lazarus had risen, but that they themselves had risen together with Lazarus.

[Note: Other Fathers agree: Isidore, Book IV of the Letters, 160; Theodoret on Ezekiel 11; Origen on Matthew 12, and elsewhere.]

“Take away the stone.” Take away the service owed by wretched humanity, so that the works of blessed divinity may now shine forth.

[Note: The final services performed for the dead are also called the last rites. Here the tomb is understood as the service owed by our humanity.]

“Take away the stone.”

[Note: Nearly all interpreters teach that Christ wished all those present to see with their own eyes Lazarus—not merely dead, but already stinking—so that the miracle of his resurrection might shine forth more clearly. See Ambrose, Book I of the Hexaemeron, chapter 73, and his discourse On Faith in the Resurrection; also Maldonatus and Brugensis, following Euthymius.]

[Col. 0383B] The stone that you placed, so that I may now restore the human being whom I placed.

Martha answered, “He already stinks.”

Woman, and whose is that stench? “He already stinks.” Now what came from you concerns you: you would not sense the stench at the tomb if you had not wished to listen to the tempter in paradise.

“He already stinks.” What stinks to the destroyer does not stink to the Creator.

“He already stinks.” What horrifies the overthrower of another’s work does not repel the lover of his own work.

But by speaking in this way, you testify to the death that you, woman, brought about. You cry out that there is a stench so that the fullness of death may be made known to those who hear, so that Lazarus’s resurrection may be understood to involve a returning spirit, not one that had remained hidden. Let it be the work of divine power, not of human skill. Otherwise the Jews, who say that we cast out demons by the ruler of demons (Matthew 9), may again say that we raise the dead not by God’s authority but by human assistance.

“He already stinks; he has been dead four days.”

[Note: He also states the length of time, so that they may know that he is the author of time, whom no times prescribe.]

“He already stinks; he has been dead four days.”

By speaking in this way, she intensifies their despair, so that those present may see that it is God who grants life to the hopeless dead and vigor to those who stink.

[Note: Because of the difficulty of the matter, Martha had not retained hope. Since the body was already foul and four days dead, all hope of resurrection had disappeared—especially if the old belief of theirs had by then gained force, namely, that the soul wandered around the body until the face and appearance of the dead person changed. Beresch Rabba, folio 114, in Lightfoot’s notes: “For three days the soul wanders around the body, waiting to return to the body; but when it sees that the appearance of the face has changed, it withdraws and leaves the body.”]

“Lifting his eyes upward,” he says. He lifts his eyes upward to give us a model for prayer,

[Note: Earlier Christ had given thanks to his Father because the Father had heard him before he prayed, so that they might understand that he was unlike the other prophets, who had to pray in order to be heard.]

not to prepare for himself a means of obtaining what he requests. For he looks upward who is always above with the Father; the Father is always in him, and he is always in the Father: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14).

“Father,” he says, “I give you thanks because you have heard me.” He gives thanks for what has already been granted. It is said that the Father has heard, while what the Son has asked is left unmentioned.

Brothers, between the Father and the Son there is affection in being heard, not necessity in petitioning; love is the assent, not the severity of a command. Everything is done there through love, where service is not needed, as becomes clear from what follows:

“Father, I give you thanks because you have heard me; but I knew that you always hear me.”

The need to call upon him exists where confidence in being heard is certain. Or what need is there for the labor of asking where the cause of granting is shared?

[Note: From words of this kind in the Gospel, the sons of Arius derived an argument by which they asserted that the Son of God was inferior to the Father. “Whoever,” they said, “is heard while asking for something is inferior to the one by whom he is heard and obtains what he asks.”]

Therefore let no one so diminish the Son by his prayers that he thereby diminishes the Father concerning the salvation of humanity.

[Note: As though the Father could not be moved to raise human beings up except by great prayers.]

But why the Son speaks in this way, he himself explains by saying:

“Father, I give you thanks because you have heard me; but I knew that you always hear me. Yet I said this because of the people standing around.”

You see that, by speaking in this way, he exalts, reveals, and displays the affection of himself and of the Father; he proclaims grace and speaks of unity.

[Note: For Christ was always chiefly intent upon ensuring that the people could never derive from his words that he was inferior to the Father. Therefore, when he prays—at which time he speaks as a human being—he always adds something, or after the prayer always does something, by which his unity and equality with the Father are shown.]
