He had said: “Everything that the Father has is mine” (John 16). And if everything is his, how does he ask? Whoever asks from what is his, asks not from necessity but from love.

“Father, I give you thanks because you have heard me; but I knew that you always hear me. Yet I said this because of the people standing around, so that they may believe that you sent me.”

He said that he had been sent, so that the people might know that Christ had come from heaven, not departed from heaven. Thus he is sent, and thus he also receives what he has, in such a way that he did not depart from where he had come.

[Note: Saint Augustine, Tractate 11 on John: “It should not seem incredible for this reason: that, in coming into the world, he went forth from the Father in such a way that he did not abandon the Father; and in going to the Father, leaving the world, he did not abandon the world. He went forth from the Father because he is from the Father; he came into the world because he displayed to the world his body, which he assumed from the Virgin. He left the world through bodily departure. He proceeded to the Father by the ascension of his humanity, and yet he did not abandon the world through his present governance. MITA.”]

Thus also the Son receives what he has, and the Father does not lose what he gives.

Brothers, what is heard, what is sent, what comes, what receives, what is born, what suffers, what dies, and what rises again—none of this belongs to his divinity; it belongs to our weakness, it belongs to our nature. All of this, for our sake, he took upon himself in our body; not for his own sake did he endure it in his majesty.

But let us return to the matter before us. What does he mean by saying, “Father, I give you thanks because you have heard me”? What does he mean?

When Christ began to strike at the doors of hell, to move the gates of the underworld, to open the doors of death, to release the ancient law of Gehenna, to overthrow the most ancient right of punishments, to reclaim Lazarus’s soul, and to renew the way of return from the underworld, the whole power of hell came raging against him. It displayed the edict of the heavenly ruler, carried the decree of the exalted King, and bore the sentence pronounced by God and made binding through so many ages. Seeing a human being, it asked who he was, what he dared to do, what he wanted, and why he alone, without trembling, challenged and approached the terrifying ways of death.

When it asked who he was, the ministers of the resurrection, the angels, answered with a prophetic voice: “He is the King of glory; he is strong and mighty in battle” (Psalm 23).

But hell replied: “I know the King of glory: in the heavens he presides over all the heavenly powers, and the whole creation cannot endure his command. But this man I see as one of those born on earth, formed from clay, enclosed in mortal flesh, and, in the very appearance of a human being, lower than human beings; soon to be handed over to the tomb and immediately subjected to my power.”

But while the angels persisted and repeated, “He is the Lord of hosts; he is the King of glory,” they added:

“He is the ruler of heaven, the creator of the world, the Savior of the age, the redeemer of all, and—the very author of the sentence concerning which you rage. He himself will trample your head; he himself will crush your dominion; he himself will destroy you by his judgment. You were ordered to seize the guilty, yet you drag away the innocent; you plunder the holy; you threaten the very Son of God. Therefore return this one, before you are compelled to release many.”

But hell, still not believing these things, hastened through its customary messengers back to heaven and lamented them in an envious complaint:

“I, Lord, although the lowest of your creation and although enslaved to a sorrowful service, observe your commands under an inviolable law. I keep watch lest some new transgressor alter the ancient right of your sentence. But a man has appeared who is called Christ. He boasts that he is your Son; he censures your priests, rebukes your scribes, violates your Sabbaths, abolishes your law, and compels souls removed from the flesh and assigned already to my punishment and custody to return to the bodies in which they had lived wickedly. Each day he advances with such audacity that he is now attempting to rescue Lazarus—already shut in our prison, already bound by our law, already remaining under our jurisdiction—by breaking open the barriers of hell. Come quickly to my aid; or, if he opens the doors even once, you will now lose all those whom we have kept for so many ages.”

To this the Son answered from the bosom of the Father:

“Father, it is just that a prison should hold not the innocent but the guilty; that punishment should torment not the just but the unjust. How long will this executioner continue to drag to himself, under the guilt of one man and because of the fault of Adam alone, patriarchs, prophets, martyrs, confessors, virgins, widows, those who remain in the chastity of marriage, people of every age, both sexes, and certainly little children who know neither good nor evil?

[Note: The Fathers of the Council of Florence held that the limbo of children, as Chrysologus here says, is in the underworld; in its final session it is expressly defined that both those bound by mortal sin and those burdened by original sin alone descend immediately to hell, though they are punished with unequal pains. Nevertheless, the common view of the scholastics, followed by Innocent III in chapter *Majores* from the treatise On Baptism, places the limbo of children in a higher location.]

Father, I will die so that all may not die. Father, I will pay Adam’s debt, so that through me those who die through Adam may live to you instead of perishing in hell. Father, because of your sentence I will pour out my blood; let it be enough that your creature return to you, and let the redemption of all the dead be the price of my blood, precious to you.”

At this, the whole Trinity consented. Lazarus was ordered to come out, and hell was commanded to obey Christ and return all the dead. Hence the Son cries out:

“Father, I give you thanks because you have heard me” (Hebrews 4).

The Apostle testifies that Christ is our advocate with the Father. Indeed, when he sits, he judges together with the Father; when he stands, he performs the office of an advocate.

Then Christ, his advocacy completed, cries out with a loud voice: “Lazarus, come out!”

Then hell, with hands and feet bound, returned Lazarus to the heights. It feared and trembled lest, while releasing him, while delaying, or while returning one too slowly, it should be compelled to bring them all forth. Thus the one who had been accustomed to seize the dead became the one who returned the living.

For why did Christ break the chains of hell and dissolve the bonds of death, unless to show us the dreadful slavery of hell? If the devil contradicted the angel concerning the body of Moses, how could hell not contradict Christ concerning the life and resurrection of Lazarus?

Pray, brothers, that we who have received a taste of the resurrection through Lazarus’s offering may, when Christ returns, be worthy to hear the voices of the universal resurrection.

## SERMON LXVI. On the Rich Man and Lazarus

Today we had two readings, delivered by two Evangelists, recited in such a way that your understanding might advance toward our sermon and hidden things might be opened.

[Note: Before a sermon was delivered to the people, readings from the Gospels—or passages of Sacred Scripture about which the sermon was to be given—were recited publicly. See Acts 13:14; the author of the Apostolic Constitutions, Book XI, chapter 14; Tertullian, Apology, chapter 39; and elsewhere. That two readings were sometimes recited is also taught by Augustine, Sermon 121, On Various Subjects. “Keeping our promise in mind, we had readings recited from the Gospel and the Apostle.”]

The occasion provided by the rising Lazarus has compelled us to mention another Lazarus. From what follows you will hear why. For now we desire to bring before you and set forth the astonishing reversals, fearful changes, and deeply lamentable conditions of the inhuman rich man and the poor Lazarus, because the rich man, who in our presence disdained to hear the poor man as his companion, did not deserve to find the poor man sympathizing with him amid future evils; nor did he receive the refreshment of water when he had denied the refreshment of bread to the poor man burning with hunger.

“When he was in torment,” it says, “he lifted up his eyes and saw Abraham from afar, and Lazarus in his bosom” (Luke 16).

He now looks freely upon Lazarus above whom he had previously disdained to see Lazarus below.

[Note: This refers to the Hebrew expression “lifting up the eyes.” Chrysostom, Homily 11 on Lazarus, in Saint Thomas, Catena, vol. V, p. 275, col. 1, of the more recent Venetian edition: “He lifted up his eyes in order to look, not in order to look down upon him. For Lazarus was above, while he was below.” Moreover, the Hebrews placed both Abraham’s bosom and hell in subterranean regions, so far apart that an immense abyss separated them, yet in such a way that one could look from one into the other. Compare Lightfoot’s discussion of the passage in the Apocalypse: “He will be tormented in the presence of the holy angels.”]

The prophet spoke of such people: “They set their eyes to turn them toward the earth” (Psalm 16).

“When he was in torment.” Punishment pierces him whom repentance did not pierce, and torments vex him whom Lazarus’s wounds did not move. Nor does he receive the stings of punishment for nothing, since he had rolled about ungratefully in purple.

He saw Abraham from afar. Abraham was far from him who had not been near to the poor man.

[Note: Chrysologus explains spiritual realities in words suited to the senses, for Christ treated this same matter. Tertullian and Irenaeus, however, wrongly derive from this passage the argument that after death certain outlines of the body and images of the limbs remain in the soul.]

He saw Abraham, a companion of the rich in wealth but excluded from his inhumanity.

[Note: Not a companion, not an associate.]

Abraham was rich, but richer in humanity than in possessions. You, by your inhumanity, proved greater than your riches. Abraham, a stranger, was a citizen among guests; you, possessing palaces, did not give the poor man a roof. Abraham, while receiving servants, received the Lord in this way, and, setting bread before all human beings, received the Lord himself at his table. You, while denying crumbs to a single poor man, lost even a drop of refreshment.

[Note: Some interpreters rightly think that Abraham rather than another patriarch is mentioned here because of his hospitality. Our author should be counted among them. The Evangelist’s expression, however, is figurative. By “Abraham’s bosom” the Hebrews understood the place where souls enjoyed a pleasant life. Muratorius rightly shows that Brunet misunderstood Chrysologus when he summoned him as a witness for his view of Paradise, p. 230.]

“And crying out, he said.” The one who here cries out once despised hearing those who cried out here; there his voice is empty, just as here his cry was useless.

Hear the prophet saying: “But in hell, who will confess you?” (Psalm 6). In hell, where is there a place for mercy? Amid torments, what hope of pardon? At the hour of judgment, who seeks a time for indulgence?

“Father Abraham, have mercy on me.” Cruel son, what mercy do you seek, which you denied to the poor man by denying it to him?

“And send Lazarus.” Wretched son, if Lazarus had come to your table, you would not have come to this banquet.

“That he may dip the tip of his finger in water.” The man who closes his hand to the poor now asks for the alms of a fingertip; he thirsts for a drop of water who shut up lakes of wine rather than give a drop.

“That he may dip the tip of his finger.” The man who did not give his wealth to the poor through mercy now diminishes mercy for himself in this way.

“And cool my tongue, for I am tormented in this flame.” It is as though he had the rest of his body immune from the fire. But the tongue burns more intensely because it neglected to command mercy to be shown; in the tongue he feels the greater burning because it cursed the poor and opposed mercy; the tongue is first in torment because, by denigrating the poor, it blasphemed the poor man’s creator.

But let us now hear what Abraham answered:

“Son,” he says, “remember that you received good things in your lifetime, and Lazarus likewise evil things.”

Let no one, hearing this, suppose that the rich man received good things in exchange for good things. Rather, he is guilty for this reason: although he received good things from God in exchange for evils, he refused to return good things to God for our sake. From such immense riches he gave neither food to the poor nor even the smallest offering as a sacrifice to God.

But the poor man, rich in wounds, naked of possessions, stripped of his body, clothed in punishments, continually offered to God as a sacrifice the soul that alone his wounds could not hold.

Therefore he receives, in exchange for his sufferings, rest; for disgrace, glory; for insults, honor; for contempt, favor; for punishments, immortality; for wounds, rewards; for thirst, a fountain of refreshment; for hunger, the everlasting delights of the heavenly table. And the one whom the rich man’s corner could not contain is enclosed in the bosom of divine consolation.

[Note: The Hebrews believed that those who had lived a life of luxury were punished after death, while those who had lived in affliction were heaped with blessings. Chrysostom held the same view in his homily on Luke 16, as did Maldonatus and Grotius.]

You, rich man, once shining in purple, must now be covered with filth; in place of scarlet, be clothed with flames; in place of soft reclining, endure the hard torments; in place of sumptuous dishes, feast upon punishments; compensate abundance with want; digest your drunkenness through thirst; in place of perfumes, be sprinkled with stench. Let the services of punishment now attend you, as the services of pleasure once attended you, because by despising the poor you have thus changed these things for yourself.

[Note: Under the name “purple” all the adornments of the rich are included. See Sidonius, Letter 10, and Lucan, in the “Hippica,” on the parts of the bath. On an onyx which Sirmondus had once possessed through the generosity of Cardinal Baronius, he read: “Εὐτίκει, Μακεδόν, ἡ πορφύρα τῶν ἀδελφῶν”—“Be fortunate, Macedon; purple, the glory of the brothers.” It happened later that only kings used purple, whereas earlier men of more prosperous fortune, such as our author, also wore purple garments. The proximity of Tyre gave the Hebrews a greater supply of purple. See Blasius Carophilus, Miscellanies, p. 43.]

[Note: Basil has similar words to those that follow in the Catena of the Fathers.]

Abraham added, saying:

“In all these things a great chasm has been fixed between us and you, so that those who wish to cross from here to you cannot, nor can they cross from there to us.”

[Note: Gregory, Book VI of the Moralia, chapter 27: “For those who followed the ways of the heavenly homeland were held, after their departure from the flesh, by the barriers of hell—not so that punishment might bend them as sinners, but so that, resting in more remote places, the guilt of original sin might keep them from entering the kingdom.”]

[Note: Theophylact: “*Chasma mega*, that is, a vast gulf,” signifies the distance of the just from sinners. Tertullian translates the Greek χάσμα (*chasma*) as “hell,” and says that it is an immeasurable distance between height and depth. Plutarch too, in *On the Delayed Vengeance of the Deity*, includes a *chasma* in his description of the underworld. See Lightfoot and Grotius on these Gospel passages, where they discuss much concerning Hebrew beliefs about the abodes of souls below. Chrysologus’s description supports the view of those who think that the Elysian fields were invented not by Greeks or Egyptians but by Hebrews. For rivers flowed in the Elysian fields among the pagans too, as among the Hebrews; see Ezekiel 31:15. Both peoples believed that the souls of the unburied wandered and did not reach Elysium. Elysium was separated from Tartarus by the vast circuit of impassable walls and by a fiery torrent; and we recognize from this Gospel passage that this was the Hebrew conception. This was no obstacle to those dwelling in Tartarus seeing and hearing those in Elysium:

> From here are heard groans, and cruel blows resound,
> then the clanking of iron and dragged chains.

And among the Hebrews: “Seeing, they shall be troubled with dreadful fear.” Be that as it may, the Hebrews used this word to indicate the underworld, as Chrysologus rightly does, where souls abode after death. Isaiah 14:9; Ezekiel 31:15; Job 26:5; 1 Peter 3:19.]

By saying this, he declares that before the coming of the Lord both the just and the unjust were in hell, and that they were separated only by places, not by regions.

[Col. 0389A] And when the Lord, rising from the dead, opened hell, disclosed the heavens, and unbarred the gates of paradise, he granted the saints entrance into the rest of paradise and access to the glory of heaven. Whoever believes these things in this way understands what Christ, coming among mortals, has given them.

The rich man therefore foolishly thinks that places are changed in hell, when here, by acting well or badly, a person determines for himself there either the end of punishment or the end of rest.

[Note: This is directed against Origen and his followers, who taught that an end would eventually be imposed upon eternal punishments. See Theophylact on this passage of the Gospel.]

The rich man who was foolish in life is found still more foolish in punishment. He who did not know the time of his good things does not recognize, even when deserving pity, the time of his evils.

“I ask you, father.” Now you ask; now it is time for you to suffer, not to ask.

“I ask you, father?” What?

“That you send Lazarus to my father’s house.”

How well Lazarus once lay before that door on which, through his hunger, he fixed the inscriptions of your inhumanity; where he crowned your doorposts with his sores; where, with his own pus, he painted your crumbs.

[Note: To fix titles on doorposts means to place inscriptions, stones, and statues there that indicate the nobility and offices of a family.]

[Note: In ancient times it was sometimes customary on feast days to decorate doorposts with flowers and laurel. With regard to the Hebrews, Persius is a witness:

> “The days of Herod have come; every window arranged,  
> its lamps vomiting forth rich clouds of smoke,  
> bearing violets,” and so forth.

By “Herod’s day” he means the feasts and Sabbaths of the Jews.]

[Note: Latinius: “How could he have depicted crumbs, if he denied crumbs?”]

Allow the reversals to stand; now put away your deceit. It is clear that you cannot bear to see Lazarus in this way: it is known, it is known, that Lazarus’s happiness torments you more than the fire of Gehenna.

Abraham answered: “They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them.”

That is: if they did not listen to Moses, who crushed the kingdoms of Egypt while the elements fought alongside him (Exodus 7), who dried up the sea (Exodus 14), who made the waves firm, who turned stones into streams (Exodus 17), who covered the sun with a cloud, who illuminated the night with light (Exodus 13), who made heaven rain flesh and dew bread (Exodus 16)—if they not only failed to listen to him but even plotted to kill him—will they deign to hear Lazarus, whom as many wounds enclose as miracles surrounded Moses?

[Col. 0389C] Let me feel what I have brought forth, and let you endure what you have done.

“No, father Abraham.”

Truly, he was not a father, because the rich man was not Abraham’s son but the son of Gehenna.

“No, father Abraham; but if someone should go to them from the dead, they will repent.”

[Note: Chrysostom, in his homily on Lazarus, Euthymius, Bede, Maldonatus, and Grotius explain this passage of the Gospel in this way.]

This the rich man says from the heart of everyone; this he requests from the desires of all; this is what all worldly people express in their wishes. For we are all accustomed to whisper: “If only someone would come from the dead and report here what is happening there, everyone would believe him.”

Certainly, doubters would say: “Who has come from there, from where no one comes?” After death, who will prove that anything exists? We all speak from what we have heard; we perceive through words what has been intimated. For what truth faith possesses has sunk into the depths.

But today the reading that followed from blessed John the Evangelist has shown that when we speak in this way, it is faithlessness, not ignorance, that is at work, since we do in fact believe.

For just as the rich man asks, God sent Lazarus.

[Note: That is, the Lazarus whom Christ raised from the dead. It is not unlikely that, when Christ expounded this parable, he had in view Lazarus raised from the dead. Many interpreters maintain this.]

But what the one who was sent, the one who was desired, and the one who rose again accomplished, hear patiently.

“They deliberated,” he says, “that they might kill Lazarus, because many of the Jews were going away on his account and were believing in Jesus” (John 12).

As though he had come in response to this request only so that he might endure the dangers of a second death. They do not want—no, they do not want—to report what they have seen, who want what has been heard not to be believed.

We know, we know, that life is prepared for the good and torments for the evil. But while we are held captive by our vices and do not wish the time of virtues to arrive, we pretend not to know what we know. We do not want someone to come from the underworld to tell us what exists after death, even though Christ, coming from heaven and himself returning from the underworld, has both taught by word and confirmed by example what awaits the good in heaven and what awaits the evil in hell.

But perhaps for this reason we neither believe these things nor wish Christ to come: because we do not wish the world to pass away. Or rather, it is not because we do not wish the world to pass away, but because we grieve that our vices will pass away.

Christ came not to drive away life but death; to drive away death, not life; to restore the world, not abolish it; to destroy vices, not to destroy his own creation.

But pray, brothers, that when he comes he may find us such as he desires and commands to be fellow-heirs of his kingdom.

## SERMON LXVII. On the Lord’s Prayer
You have received the hearing of faith, dearest brothers; hear the form of the Lord’s Prayer. Christ taught us to pray briefly, since he wishes to grant what is requested quickly. Or what will he not give to those asking him, who gave himself to those who were not asking for him? [Note: [Col. 0391C] Namely, to the Gentiles, who did not ask for him at all. For the Hebrews, instructed in the Law, prayed that Christ would come to humankind, saying: “Send, Lord, him whom you are going to send,” etc.; “Come, Lord, do not delay,” etc. MITA.] [Note: [Col. 0390D] When the apostles asked Christ to give them some formula for prayer, he taught them this one, the most excellent of all, which Tertullian calls “the brief summary of the whole Gospel.”] Or how could he delay in answering, who in dictating the prayers thus anticipates the wishes of those who plead? What you are about to hear today causes the angels to wonder, heaven to marvel, earth to tremble; flesh cannot bear it, hearing cannot contain it, the mind cannot reach it, nor can all creation sustain it. I dare not speak, yet I cannot remain silent. May God grant that you can hear, and that I can speak.

What is more awe-inspiring: that God gave himself to the earth, or that he gives you to heaven; that he himself enters into fellowship with flesh, or that he makes you enter into fellowship with divinity; that he himself assumes death, or that he restores you from death; that he himself is born into your slavery, or that he brings you forth as children for himself; that he accepts your poverty, or that he makes you heirs, co-heirs with his only Son? Surely the more terrifying thing is that earth is transferred to heaven, that humanity is changed into divinity, that the condition of slavery receives the rights of dominion.

But although this is to be feared, nevertheless, since the matter concerns not the one who teaches but the one who commands, let us approach, little children, where charity calls, love draws, and affection invites. Let our hearts feel God as Father; let the voice resound, the tongue speak, the spirit cry out; and let everything within us respond to grace, not fear—for he who changed the judge into a father wished to be loved, not feared.

“Our Father who are in heaven” (Matthew 6). When you say this, do not understand it as though he were not on earth; do not take it as though he were confined to a place, who confines all things. Rather, understand that you have your origin from heaven, whose Father is held to be in heaven; and act so that, by living holily, you may correspond to your holy Father. That man proves himself to be a son of God who is not obscured by human vices, but shines with divine virtues.

“May your name be sanctified.” [Note: [Col. 0391C] Maldonado and Brugensis: “may it become celebrated”; Bede and Menochius: “may it be loved and feared”; Tertullian: “may he reign most perfectly in all things through grace”; Augustine, formerly Sermon 48 on the Seasons, now Sermons 56 and 57: “This is what you ask: that what is always holy in itself may be sanctified in you.” Thomas Aquinas, Commentary on the Lord’s Prayer, first petition, *Opera*, p. 30, vol. VIII, Venice edition: “That his name may be manifested and declared in us.”]

We are reckoned according to the name of the one whose family we are; therefore we ask that his name, which is holy in itself and through itself, may be sanctified in us. For the name of God is either honored through our conduct or blasphemed through our actions. Hear the Apostle saying: “The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you” (Romans 2).

“May your kingdom come.” And when has God not reigned? We therefore ask that he who has always reigned for himself may now reign in us, so that we too may be able to reign in him. [Note: [Col. 0391D] That is, in the kingdom in which God reigns in the hearts of the righteous; this is truly called the kingdom of God by the Apostle in Romans 14:16. Ambrose, Hilary, Gregory, Maldonado, and others explain it differently. Cyprian, *On the Lord’s Prayer*, Sermon 6, p. 558: “Whoever dedicates himself to God and Christ desires heavenly kingdoms, not earthly ones.” Sedulius, Book 4; Chrysostom on Matthew; Augustine, formerly Letter 21, now Letter 130 to Proba, chapter 11, agree.]

The devil reigned, sin reigned, death reigned, and mortals were long held captive. We therefore ask that, when God reigns, the devil may perish, sin may fail, death may die, and captivity may be taken captive, so that we, set free, may reign forever in life. [Note: [Col. 0391D] Thomas Aquinas, at the place cited, p. 32: “When therefore we ask that his kingdom may come, we pray that sin may not reign in us, but God himself.” Ambrose, *On the Sacraments*, chapter 4, p. 341, Paris edition, 1551.]

“May your will be done, as in heaven so also on earth.” This is the kingdom of God: when God’s will alone exists both in heaven and on earth; when in all human beings “God is mind, God lives, God acts, God reigns, God is everything,” so that, according to the Apostle, “God may be all in all among you” (1 Corinthians 15). [Note: [Col. 0391D] The printed editions have, incorrectly, “my God.”]

“Give us today our daily bread.” He who gave himself to us as Father, who adopted us as children for himself, who made us heirs of all things, who exalted us by his name, who endowed us with his honor and kingdom—he himself commanded us to ask for daily bread. In the kingdom of God, amid divine gifts, what does human poverty seek? Does such a good, kind, and generous Father grant bread to his children only when it is requested? And what of the saying: “Do not be anxious about what you will eat, or what you will drink, or what you will wear” (Matthew 6)?

He commands us to ask for what he forbids us to worry about, so that the heavenly Father may urge heavenly children to ask for heavenly bread. [Note: [Col. 0392C] When some had observed that the word ἐπιούσιον (*epiousion*) is read in Hebrew as *mahar*, which in Syriac—the dialect they suppose Christ used—means “tomorrow,” rather than “daily” and “for today,” a question arose, the one Chrysologus raises here: namely, whether Christ taught in the Gospel two things that contradict each other. To resolve it, others followed the same path as Chrysologus, saying that the petition in the Lord’s Prayer concerns eucharistic bread. Ambrose, Book 5 of *On the Sacraments*, chapter 4; Cyprian, *On the Lord’s Prayer*; Augustine, formerly Homily 42: “Grant us your Eucharist, our daily food.” But explanations of this sort attend more to theological practice than to the literal wording. For in this petition we ask for everything we need to preserve life. Others, with Jerome, noted that the Hebrew word from which the verb ἐπιούσιον is thought to have been formed does not signify the next or immediately ensuing day, but whatever is future; and they said that ἐπούσια (*epousia*) means the whole span of life that remains for us to traverse.]

The Evangelist has “ἄρτον τὸν ἐπιούσιον” (*arton ton epiousion*); some translate it “supersubstantial,” “above all substances.” [Note: [Col. 0392D] Evangelist: “the supersubstantial bread”; some translate it “above all substances.”]

He himself said: “I am the bread that came down from heaven” (John 6). He is the bread who, sown in the Virgin, fermented in the flesh, prepared in the Passion, baked in the furnace of the tomb, stored in the churches, carried to the altars, supplies the faithful daily with heavenly food.

“And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” Man, if you cannot be without sin and you always wish everything to be forgiven you, always forgive; as much as you wish to be forgiven, forgive that much; as often as you wish to be forgiven, forgive that often. Rather, because you wish everything to be forgiven you, forgive everything. Man, understand that by forgiving others you have granted forgiveness to yourself. [Note: [Col. 0392D] “Debt” in Scripture is a figure for transgression, says Tertullian; and sins are called debts, adds Brugensis.]

“And do not lead us into temptation.” Because life in this world is itself temptation. “Life is a temptation,” he says, “for man” (Job 7). Let us therefore ask that he not leave us to our own judgment, but that in every action he may constrain us with fatherly mercy and strengthen us with heavenly guidance along the path of life. [Note: [Col. 0393D] God not only often abandons ungodly people to their own vices, as in Romans 1:24, but also those who trust their own strength more than is proper. According to Chrysologus, we avert this evil by constant prayers, especially by this very petition of the Lord’s Prayer.]

“But deliver us from evil.” From what evil? From the devil, certainly, from whom all evil comes. We ask to be delivered from evil, because whoever has not been freed from evil cannot enjoy the good. [Note: [Col. 0393D] Many of the holy Fathers can be cited in support of taking “evil” here as the devil. Yet “I would light a lamp at midday.” In the Greek text, ἀπὸ τοῦ πονηροῦ (*apo tou ponērou*) means “from that wicked one” or “from that evil one”; Tremellius, Montanus, and the Syriac translator render it in this way. The devil is commonly called by this name in Matthew 13:19 and John 11:13; 5:18.]

If, while they are not yet born, while they are still in the womb, they ask for bread and seek the kingdom, why is a question raised about the fact that the Son of God, always, remained in the mystery of God the Father? [Note: [Col. 0394D] This explains why we discuss what is firmly believed: namely, that the Son was always the Son of the eternal Father. See above, Sermons 58, 60, and 62; these passages were written against heretics. MITA.]

If the Church gives birth, there is no rational explanation; it is a heavenly mystery. That the Son of God was in God the Father cannot be handled by human reasoning; divinity must not be assessed in a human manner. You have heard “God”: think nothing earthly, nothing human. You have heard “the Father of Christ”: believe this according to substance. You have heard “your Father”: believe this through grace. He always had the Father, so that he might be Son; he has now given you to be a son.

Thus know yourself to be a son in such a way that you do not fail to know yourself a servant; hear that you have been restored to the likeness of Christ in such a way that you always recognize yourself as subject to Christ.

## SERMON LXVIII. On the same subject.

Mortal condition, earthly framework, muddy substance, a nature uncertain of life and death, worn down by labor, consumed by punishments, subject to decay and dust—such a nature cannot contain, cannot adequately estimate, dares not drive away, and fears to believe what today it is compelled to confess. From where human frailty could deserve such a great grace of God, such magnitude of promises, such abundance of gifts, it cannot discover.

I think the prophet Habakkuk foresaw this clearly with the mind’s eye when, describing himself as shaken by such great fear and agitated by the trembling caused by this hearing, he says: “Lord, I heard your report, and I was afraid; I considered your works, and I was terrified” (Habakkuk 3, according to the Septuagint). He feared the report—not because the great prophet then heard the Lord, but because then he found the Lord, his master, turned toward him, and heard him as Father; not because, contemplating the structure of this world harmonized from elements so discordant, he was terrified, but because, then considering the great works of divine mercy toward him, he was shaken by the trembling and fear of wonder.

“I considered your works,” he says, “and I was terrified.” He was then astonished that he had been adopted as a son, when he had lost the confidence of a servant. Finally, so that you may know the feeling of this prayer which Divinity today makes known and pours into you, observe what the prophet then dares to say, released, as it were, by fear of the gift received from heaven: “I kept watch,” he says, “and my belly trembled at the voice of the prayer of my lips.”

After he had felt the abundance of the divine gift, he guarded himself lest he should again find himself an enemy, an adversary, a thief, as in paradise. He becomes more vigilant, more concerned to guard himself; after the loss of so great a thing, he guarded the heavenly treasure in earthen vessels.

“And my belly trembled.” Here the prophet calls the inner part of the heart the belly; just as the belly is fed and filled by foods, so the heart is fed and filled by perceptions. “And my belly trembled at the voice of the prayer of my lips.” If the understanding of the heart had poured a voice into the mouth and given words to the lips, why did he tremble at his petitions, at his desires, at the very thing for which he was about to pray? Because he was speaking not by the prompting of his own heart but through the utterance of the divine Spirit.

Hear Paul saying: “God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father’” (Galatians 5). When he transmitted this hearing into the inner parts, he marveled that he had deserved so much, and all the inner faculties of the human being trembled. Rightly he added: “And trembling entered my bones,” because the prophet’s very inward parts were distressed.

“And beneath me,” he says, “my strength was shaken.” What does “beneath me” mean? It means that this same human being, already raised upward by grace, lay beneath his former nature; earthly strength could not sustain heavenly strength.

Mount Sinai already smoked when God descended upon the mountain to give the Law (Exodus 19). What would flesh do when God descended into flesh to bestow grace upon flesh? The Father came because human beings could not bear God, nor a servant his Lord. And because he is faithful in the words he spoke: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Psalm 80), open your mouths now, so that he himself may fill them with such a prayer and such a cry.

“Our Father who are in heaven” (Matthew 6). Where are those who distrust God’s promise? Behold how quickly the confession of faith is rewarded. As soon as you confessed the Father of God’s only Son, you yourself were adopted as a son by God the Father, so that you might be heir of heaven, though you had been regarded as an exile from paradise and from the earth. Therefore now you call him: “Our Father who are in heaven.”

Since once you had a father who dissolved you into mud, who led and dragged you to the prison of hell, let him who again seeks God the heavenly Father as his nature knows nothing of earth, ignore the love of the flesh, seek no father of dust, and permit no vice to have power in him.

And he who believes himself to be a son of God should correspond to so great a lineage in conduct, life, morals, and integrity, lest, descending again to earthly things, he advance toward an insult against so great a parent.

“May your name be sanctified.” If the name of Christ gives sight to the blind, gives movement to the lame, gives health to those exhausted by various illness, gives life to the dead, and sanctifies you, man, and the whole of creation, how do you pray and plead for the sanctity of that name? Because you have been called a Christian from Christ; therefore you ask that the privilege of so great a name may be strengthened in you by the merits that follow.

“May your kingdom come.” He himself commands devotion, demands desires, and seeks vows—the one who holds his coming within his own power. That soldier is faithful who thirsts for the presence of his king, longs for his kingdom, seeks and desires triumphs. But here you ask that he come to you and in you as the one who is to reign, in whom the devil once held his stronghold, death its dominion, and hell its power for a long time. [Note: [Col. 0395D] Elsewhere, “principality.”]

Let us therefore pray, dearest ones, that Christ may always reign in his soldier, [Note: [Col. 0395D] From the manuscript of Cesena. The printed editions have “that the soldier may…”] and that the soldier may always triumph in his king.

“May your will be done, as in heaven so also on earth.” Blessed is that day which joins, unites, and makes equal the wills of earthly beings with those of heaven, so that among substances unlike one another there may be one and the same will. This is faithful peace, unshaken concord, enduring grace: when, under the order of one Lord, a household of diverse natures becomes one in will and is found to be one in understanding.

“Give us today our daily bread.” After the heavenly kingdom, who would ask for temporal bread? But he wishes us to ask daily, and for the day, for the bread which is the provision for the journey in the sacrament of his body, so that through it we may reach the eternal day and Christ’s own table; so that from the place where we have here received a taste, we may there receive fullness and complete satisfaction. [Note: [Col. 0395D] Elsewhere, “from then onward.”] [Note: [Col. 0395D] “Viaticum” is the name given to the sacrament of the Holy Eucharist, which serves as provisions for us when we depart for the other life. See Basil Poncius of the Order of the Hermits of Saint Augustine, *Various Disputations*, question 2, part 1, no. 1. Compare what I said in the dissertation on the Silver Plate of Gorreorn, p. 96, in the notes.]

“And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” Whoever makes this request but does not release debts accuses himself by the very prayer he offers. Whoever asks God to grant and remit to him only as much as he himself remits and grants invites God to a pact on such terms. Let each person demand that as much be granted to him as he has himself granted to another. But debts, brothers, are to be forgiven not only in money, but in every kind of matter, fault, and crime. Whatever you, man, may be able to incur, when another incurs it against you, you will forgive him in these matters. [Note: [Col. 0395D] Elsewhere, “you may incur.”] He confidently asks forgiveness for his sins who willingly forgives the sinner.

“And do not lead us into temptation.” We are compelled to ask this a thousand times and in many ways, brothers: lest frailty, daring too much and rashly trusting in itself, without taking account of the measure of its strength, should fall through lack of caution in the struggle, and then, offended, God may hand over to temptations those who sin. [Note: [Col. 0395D] From the Vatican manuscript. The printed editions have “with swelling.”]

“But deliver us from evil.” He has a sufficiently humble opinion of himself and does not presume to be saved by his own power, who implores God to deliver him from evil. [Note: [Col. 0395D] Catholics drew from this same petition a very strong argument against the Pelagians, asserting that human beings cannot avoid sins by their own strength without the help of grace. For we ask in vain, “Do not lead us into temptation,” if this lies so entirely within our power that we can fulfill it without any help from God. Jerome, Book 3 against Pelagius; Augustine, formerly Letter 89, now Letter 157 to Hilary, and formerly Letter 74, now Letter 78 to the same.]

Mark yourselves. Understand, little children, how great the glory and power of the perfect and the strong must be, when such great power is revealed in conception itself and such majesty in birth. Not yet born, he calls upon the Father, asks for sanctity, seeks the kingdom, gives laws to the earth, makes earthly wills equal to heavenly ones, and already, devoted to labors that will bring benefit, demands his provision: “Give us today our daily bread.”

Blessed are you who have begun to conquer before the battle, to triumph before living, to reach the Father’s storerooms before reaching your mother’s bosom, to seize the food of the flock before entering upon the nourishment of milk, and to resound with the whole jubilation of victories before answering with the cry of the cradle. Truly, as the Apostle said, “the weakness of God is stronger than human beings” (1 Corinthians 1).

Or who could recount the mystery of so great a conception? [Note: [Col. 0396D] That is, the Church gives birth to children through baptism, whom she sends ahead to glory as they die; for the mother Church will remain here until the consummation of the age. Yet she sends Christian children daily ahead to the kingdom, as her elect children undergo death. MITA.] The Virgin Mother gives birth daily throughout the world, and does not leave descendants for labor, but sends her offspring ahead to eternal glory. [Note: [Col. 0396D] The manuscript of Cesena: “but from earthly offspring she sends them ahead to glory.”]

## SERMON LXIX. On the same subject.

Do you think that a mortal breast can grasp the greatness of the Lord’s love toward us? Do you think that a mind weighed down by an earthly body can understand and feel the divine affection toward us? For whatever shines, radiates, and gleams in the adornment of heaven; whatever gives fragrance in the flowers, taste in the fruits, and joy in living creatures—all was made for our love and assigned to our service.

Yet, however great these things are, they are small signs of the heavenly love shown toward us. For us the principalities of heaven, for us the ethereal powers, for us the heavenly dominions, for us the offices of angels labor in tireless watchfulness. Yet even these are still small and lesser things by which the divine relationship with us must be demonstrated—so much lower as the creature is than its Creator.

God, inaccessible to contemplation in his countenance, impossible to discern by sight, incapable of being measured by any sense, inaccessible to the mind, and not even fully known through hearing—how often, in what ways, how variously and differently has he adapted himself to human perception? How has he presented and surrendered himself to human fellowship and intimacy: when he makes Noah a participant in his counsel, warns him beforehand of the flood that will cleanse the world, and marks out the whole age in the seed of the small ark under his own guardianship (Genesis 6); when he comes to Abraham as a guest, graciously accepts his invitation, does not reject what is offered, receives what is set before him as though hungry and tired, and accepts and welcomes human things as though he were in need, through divine conversation (Genesis 18)?

Hence it is that the old man’s lifeless limbs soon revive, that the extinguished womb of the barren old woman is stirred to life, and that nature, buried in a living corpse, rises to bring forth its creator and, after the time for this has passed, bears many descendants through the one whom he had believed to be the Creator (Genesis 21). [Note: [Col. 0397D] Because Abraham believed that the one who had said that, though he and his wife Sarah were old, he would receive a son from her, who would become the father of many nations, was God and the Creator of all things; therefore, in reward for his faith, he obtained the grace of begetting even after the time of begetting had passed, and received many grandchildren through Isaac. MITA.]

For Moses, God gathers himself into a fiery form in the bush; then he discusses what must be done with his servant, exercises various powers in Egypt, and reveals himself at the servant’s command (Exodus 3). He inflicts plagues, or removes them (Exodus 8); and in the sea the obedient waves demonstrate how great he is and how much he has granted to humanity, when, after the waters have dried up, the wave yields to the holy ones, and, with the liquid hardened, provides a wall and protection for those being saved; then, with the whole power of its nature, it rushes forward to triumph over the fiercest enemy (Exodus 14). [Note: [Col. 0397D] The manuscript of Cesena and the Vallicellian manuscript have “had revealed.”] [Note: [Col. 0397D] Perhaps it should be read: “The wave yields to their feet.”]

God lived in wondrous fellowship with the Israelite camps (Deuteronomy 23). At one time he strikes numerous nations with lightning, at another he touches them with hail (Joshua 10); at another he overthrows them by the mere sound of trumpets (Joshua 6), so that without combat and without wounds God leads victorious armies, going before them.

He attends to the desires of individuals, responds to their prayers, answers their questions immediately, reveals hidden things, foretells the future, makes known what is sought, grants kingdoms, gives wealth, moderates the rains, makes lands fruitful, and adorns marriages themselves with the abundance and honor of children.

But he considered it still too little if he showed his affection toward us only by granting prosperity and not also by enduring adversity. After all these things, he enters his own world in poverty. He lies in swaddling clothes as a human being; by his crying he begs, seeks, and demands the very compassion that he himself has shown you. The parent of all used you as his parent; he was subjected to you, beneath whom every height is subject; he feared what those to be feared fear; he fled to the one to whom all things flee for refuge. The ruler of heaven is a guest in the houses of sinners; he is fed with bread who will feed everyone.

And what more? The Παντοκράτωρ (*Pantokratōr*, “Almighty”) of the ages is held; the founder of the earth is brought before an earthly tribunal; the giver of human forgiveness is judged; the searcher of the heart is examined; the giver and restorer of life is punished; the resurrection of all is buried—so that the sluggish mind and exceedingly slow understanding of humanity might at least through the death of God recognize the love he bears, since it had failed to understand or feel that love through the aforementioned and countless benefits of God toward it.

He therefore who made you be, gave you life, and taught you to pray—because he wished to grant everything—wished to be entreated by your prayer.

“Our Father who are in heaven” (Matthew 6). Behold, man: today, through your own voice, Christ adopts you as a son, so that he might make you a co-heir of God the Father, when he says, “Our Father.” What belongs to his gracious condescension he wished to belong to your power, according to the saying: “To all who received him, he gave power to become children of God” (John 1). Yet he commands you to say, so that the grace belongs to the giver and not the presumption to the one who dares: “Who are in heaven.” [Note: [Col. 0397D] Here the commentators appropriately observe that the petition says “Our Father,” and not “my Father,” so that we may understand that we are co-heirs with Christ and children of one Father.]

Not that he is not on earth, but he wishes you, who now call upon a heavenly Father, to strive toward and recover a heavenly nature, so that our life may correspond to so great a lineage and earthly conduct may not degenerate, since heavenly nature has already been bestowed and conferred upon us.

“May your name be sanctified.” It is not that your prayer must sanctify the name which sanctifies you. Rather, because you have been called Christian from the name of Christ, you must ask that this name be sanctified and honored in you through your conduct. For just as the fame of virtues corresponds to the glory of the name, so the disgrace of one who lives badly rebounds to the injury of that same name, as the Apostle says: “The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you” (Romans 2). And truly, children, a Gentile detracts from the Christian name when he sees a Christian living otherwise than he professes and is called.

“May your kingdom come.” You do not ask that the kingdom come to God, who has always possessed it; you ask that it come to you, who do not possess it, and that you may receive what the Lord promises you in his affection when he says: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25). “Come, blessed,” he did not say, “Let us come”; “receive,” he did not say, “Let us receive.”

Let no one wonder that he calls him Father who is not yet born. [Note: [Col. 0397D] Saint John Chrysostom, Homily 20 on Matthew 6, says that one not yet initiated by the sacrament of baptism cannot call God Father, which seems to contradict our author. But Chrysostom speaks in the human manner, whereas Chrysologus speaks in the divine manner. For although he is only designated as a son in the divine mind—and, as regards us, cannot physically be called a son because he still lacks the grace of baptism—nevertheless, in the divine manner he is called a son of God, for past and future are equally present to God. MITA. Chrysostom alludes to the custom of his own times, when catechumens were not openly permitted to recite the Lord’s Prayer. See note 4, Sermon 67. Augustine, *Enchiridion to Laurentius*, chapter 71: “It belongs to the faithful to say, ‘Our Father who are in heaven,’ since they have already been reborn as such a Father’s children from water and the Holy Spirit.”]

For if John rejoices (Luke 1) and Jacob wrestles in the womb (Genesis 25), a prudent person should consider what divine nature can do, if human conception can accomplish so much through God.

## SERMON LXX. On the same subject.

Everything that is reported as said and done divinely is miraculous, astonishing, and dreadful to mortals; even the heavenly beings tremble before it. Yet nothing so astonishes heaven, so terrifies earth, or so alarms the whole of creation as what you are today about to hear from us. A servant dares to call the Lord “Father”; the accused names his judge “Begetter”; earthly condition, by the voice of God, adopts itself as a son; the one who lost earthly things considers himself heir of divinity. But we dare to do this because the speaker’s presumption is not involved where the authority of the one commanding is present: for he himself has wished us to say this today, who taught us to pray in this way.

And what wonder is it if he consecrated human beings as sons of God, when he gave and adapted himself as a son of man? Then he transferred the nature of flesh into the divine nature, when he brought divinity into human nature; then he granted man to be his fellow heir in heaven, when he made himself a participant in earthly things. Or how could he deny man any love or gift, who assumed everything that belonged to man—even sin [Note: He assumed it in order to destroy it; he did not assume it in order to possess it, as he says above in Sermon 45. In the letter of Saint Leo to Flavian it is said: “He assumed the form of a servant without the stain of sin.” He assumed it for this purpose, as we read in 1 Peter 2: “He himself bore our sins in his body upon the wood.” And in 2 Corinthians: “He made him who knew no sin to be sin for us.” That is, God made God to be a sacrifice for sin. See Bellarmine, in his exposition of Psalm 21:1. Saint Ambrose, Book II on Luke, says of Christ’s baptism: “One person assumed the sins of all, so that in him all sins might die.” MITA.]—and death as well? Or how would he not have man as a companion in his prosperity, who made himself the companion of man in adversity?

Man, return to God, loved as you are by God; and give your whole self to his glory, who for your sake brought his whole self down to his own humiliation [Col. 0399B] [Note: The Caesenate manuscript reads, “to your humiliation.”]. Call him “Father” with confidence, whom you prove, perceive, and understand to be your begetter through such great love.

“Our Father.” Let no one wonder that the one not yet born calls him Father: what is to be born is already born for God; what is future is already accomplished for God. “What is to come,” he says, “has already been” (Ecclesiastes 3). Hence John in the womb already senses his author (Luke 1); and he who was unaware of his own life stands forth as a messenger to his mother. Hence Jacob is read to have fought before being born, and to have triumphed before living (Genesis 25). Hence those who are not yet for themselves already are for God—those who were chosen before the foundation of the world.

“Who are in heaven.” Not because he is not on earth, but so that through this you may know that you are a heavenly offspring. And if you confess yourself to be a son of God, live as a son of God, so that in conduct, life, and virtues [Col. 0399C] you may be able to answer such a begetter.

“Hallowed be your name.” Because you have been called a Christian by Christ, you ask that the privilege of so great a name be hallowed in you; for the name of God, which is holy in itself and for itself, is either hallowed in us by our conduct or blasphemed by our conduct among the nations.

“Your kingdom come.” He himself says: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17). If it is within us, why do we pray that it should come? It is present in faith, in hope, and in expectation; but we now pray that it may come in reality. Let it come to us—not to him who always reigns with his Father and always reigns in the Father—but let it come to us. “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 5).

We say, “Your kingdom come,” so that God may reign in us to the extent that death ceases to reign in us and sin ceases to reign. “Death reigned,” he says, “from Adam until Moses” (Romans 5). And elsewhere: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body” (Romans 6).

“Your will be done on earth as in heaven.” Now many things are done on earth according to the will of the devil, according to the wickedness of the world, and according to the desire of the flesh; but in heaven nothing is done except the Lord’s will. We therefore ask that, once the devil has been destroyed, the world renewed, the body changed, the dominion of death abolished, and the rule of sin removed, there may be one and the same will of God in heaven and on earth, in God and in human beings.

“Give us this day our daily bread.” After the heavenly kingdom, we are not commanded to ask for earthly bread, since he himself forbids this when he says: “Do not be anxious about your life, what you shall eat or what you shall drink” (Matthew 6). But because he himself is the bread that came down from heaven (John 6), we ask and beseech that we may receive the bread by which we shall live eternally every day—that is, continually: today, that is, in the present life, may we receive it from the banquet of the holy altar for the strength of body and mind.

“And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” By saying this, man, you have assigned yourself the manner and measure of forgiveness: you ask the Lord to forgive you only as much as you yourself have forgiven your fellow servant [Note: According to other interpreters, τοίως (“as,” “in the same way as”) does not signify the manner of forgiveness, for God forgives perfectly, but the reason or condition. It is not a rule that God forgives us greater things and more generously, but a condition: if we do not forgive others, neither will we be forgiven.]. Therefore forgive the one who has offended you completely, if you wish to owe the Lord nothing for your own offenses. Forgive yourself in the other, if you wish yourself to avoid the judgment of the avenger.

“And do not lead us into temptation.” God, as it is written, tempts no one (James 1); but he is said to tempt when he abandons those who stubbornly run toward the snares of temptation [Note: Augustine: “For God does not himself lead into temptation, but permits the one whom he has abandoned without his aid to be led into it.”]. Thus Adam fell into the ambushes of the tempter when he abandoned the commands of his creator.

But from whom and by whom man is tempted, he reveals by saying: “But deliver us from evil.” That is, from the devil, who is both the author and the origin of every evil. The devil was by nature a heavenly being; now he is spiritual wickedness, older in age than the world, worn smooth by the practice of harming, and most skilled in the art of injuring [Note: The Caesenate manuscript reads, “most ready.”]. Hence he is no longer called “evil” but “the evil one” [Note: See Note 13 to Sermon 67.], from whom everything that is evil proceeds.

Hence man cannot be delivered by his own strength, bound as he is by carnal bonds. We must therefore ask that God deliver us from the devil, who lent Christ to the earth so that he might conquer the devil [Note: Note the force of this word: he “lent” him, that is, granted him for use. In a loan, the very same thing in form and number that was lent is returned, as is clear throughout the title *De commodato* in the *Digest*. Thus Christ is said to have been lent to the earth because, after the devil was conquered and man redeemed, he was returned to heaven the same in form and number. MITA.].

Let man cry out—let him cry out to God—let him cry out, “Deliver us from evil,” so that, with Christ alone conquering, we may be delivered from so great an evil.

“Our Father who are in heaven.” In a very few words, the one whom you must entreat has himself granted you the theme of prayer, the material of petition, and the rule of supplication, so that from this you may draw the meaning of petition, gain understanding of asking, gather the measure of obtaining, and, through the briefest instruction in prayer, acquire the broadest discipline [Col. 0401A] [Note: Also because.]. At the same time, as a sign of love, the king himself performed the office of advocate, so that he might dictate the prayers to which he himself would respond [Note: Thus Meursius corrects the text, as it appears in the first Bologna edition. Nearly all printed editions have *responsus* (“answer”).].

All hesitation about obtaining has been removed; indeed, complete confidence in winning favor has been bestowed, since the one who is entreated reads himself in the prayers. Fear has no place where a son, with piety as interpreter, desires to obtain holy things from the Father.

## SERMON LXXI. On the Same Subject

Beloved brothers, the one who gave you faith taught you to pray as well, and fitted the entire form of petition into a few words. For when a son asks his father, the son does not labor with a lengthy prayer; just as necessity compels the begotten to ask, so love urges the begetter to give. Therefore the Father, who freely grants, showed not so much that he should be asked as what should be asked for, so that the son might please him by asking for what is right, though he could displease him by asking for foolish things.

Hear the Father, and now believe that you are sons, so that you may obtain without hesitation whatever you ask. What faith is worth, what belief can accomplish, and how precious confession is, is demonstrated today in you. Behold, the threefold confession of the Trinity has lifted you from earthly servitude into a heavenly offspring. Behold, the faith that called God Father has today obtained God as Father for you. Behold, the voice that confessed God the Son has adopted you as sons of God. Behold, the belief that proclaimed God the Spirit has changed you from the mortal substance of flesh into the life-giving substance of the Spirit.

Who will be found worthy to declare such great piety [Col. 0401C]? God the Father deigns to make human beings heirs; God the Son does not disdain to make servants his fellow heirs; God the Spirit assumes flesh as a companion of divinity. Heaven becomes the possession of earthly beings, and those consigned to the lower regions are received into the heavenly realm, as the Apostle proves when he says: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels?”

Therefore call God Father, and believe that, although you have not yet been born, you have already been designated as sons. Take care that you have a heavenly life and divine ways, and that the whole form of divinity be displayed in your form; for the heavenly Father enriches with divine gifts sons who correspond to their lineage, but recalls those who degenerate to penal servitude.

“Our Father who are in heaven.” A servile conscience would collapse and earthly condition would be dissolved, unless the authority of the Father himself and the Spirit of the Son himself aroused us to this cry [Col. 0401D]. “God sent,” he says, “the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father.’”

The mind grows weary and our flesh fails before divine things unless God himself, who commands what is to be done, also fulfills what he commands [Note: Meursius corrected the text to *flaccescit mens* (“the mind grows faint”). “Hallowed be it in us.” Augustine, Sermon formerly 48 *On Various Matters*, now 56 and 57: “You ask that what is always holy in itself may be hallowed in you”—that is, held holy and not despised.].

When would mortal humanity dare to call God Father except now, when the inner parts of man are animated by heavenly power?

“Our Father who are in heaven.” Man, what have you in common with earthly things, when you confess that your lineage is from heaven? Therefore display a heavenly life in your earthly dwelling. For if earthly thought has done anything in you, you have stained heaven and inflicted injury upon your heavenly lineage.

“Hallowed be your name.” We ask God to hallow his name, which by its holiness saves and sanctifies the whole creation. Brothers, this is the name before which the heavenly powers tremble, which they receive in fearful service; this is the name that gives salvation to a ruined world. But we ask that the name of God be hallowed in us by our conduct; for when we act well, God’s name is blessed through us, and when we act badly, it is blasphemed. Hear the Apostle saying: “The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you” (Romans 2).

We therefore ask—yes, we ask—that, to the extent that God’s name is holy, we may deserve to have his holiness in our minds [Col. 0402B].

“Your kingdom come.” As though it had not always been, and were not now, we ask that Christ’s kingdom come. And where is it? “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17). It is among us by faith, but we implore that it may come in reality.

Brothers, as long as the devil, through varied forms of wickedness and manifold arts of deception, disturbs the vision of things and confounds human senses and morals; rages through idols; storms through sacrileges; deceives through auguries; lies through divination; misleads through signs; mocks through the stars; occupies people with spectacles; besieges them with vices; wounds them with sins; injures them with crimes; and casts them down through despair, he prolongs Christ’s kingdom and keeps it away from us.

We therefore ask that the time may come when, with the author of so great an evil perishing, the whole world and the whole creation may reign and triumph wholly for the glory of Christ alone. And let what follows come to pass [Col. 0402C], so that, as in heaven, so also on earth, the Lord’s will may be one.

Let earth be heaven, life be God, time be eternity, homeland be rest, wealth be innocence, honor be immortality, glory be chastity, and God be everything [Note: How badly, good God! Many editions—those of Venice, Sarzina, Lyon (Durand), Cologne (Henning), and others—read *furia castitas* (“fury, chastity”). The Lyon edition of Landriani, edited by Theophilus Raynaud, has *cura custitas*; the reading is corrupt.].

He added: “Give us this day our daily bread.” After the fatherhood of God, after the holiness of the divine name, after the kingdom of heaven, we are commanded to ask for daily bread. Christ is not subject to forgetfulness; Christ does not command what contradicts his commandments. He himself said: “Do not be anxious about your life, what you shall eat or what you shall drink” (Matthew 6).

But because he himself is the bread that came down from heaven (John 6), which has been ground into flour in the millstone of law and grace, which has been prepared by the passion of the cross, which has been fermented by the sacrament of great piety, which raised from the tomb the relief of a light mixture [Note: In some copies, including the Vatican manuscript, *levis* (“light”) is absent.] [Col. 0402D], which, in order to be baked by the heat of his divinity, himself fired the furnace of hell, which is carried daily to the Church’s heavenly table as food, which is broken for the remission of sins, which feeds and nourishes those who eat him unto perpetual life—we ask that this bread be given to us daily, until we enjoy it on that everlasting day.

“And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” From the heart of the one who petitions, a fountain of forgiveness flows forth and flows back toward forgiveness: whatever abundance of piety he pours out upon another, he grants to himself in equal measure.

“And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” A merciful man can accomplish much, when he contends with God concerning piety: he desires to receive as much as he has given, and to be forgiven as much as he has pardoned. Man, let forgiveness always be in your heart, if you do not wish to fear crimes.

“And do not lead us into temptation.” This requires interpretation, because the devil’s temptation is his advance agent and bitter minister. But as long as we are enclosed in this fragile body, we rightly pray that neither an entrance be opened to temptation nor access be granted to the devil [Note: Truly, by these words we ask God not to allow us to be subject to temptation, as we indicated above. Cyprian, *On the Lord’s Prayer*; Augustine, Letter 157, chapter 2, and *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 6; Chrysostom, Tertullian, and others.].

“But deliver us from evil.” Here “evil” designates the author of evil, that is, the devil [Note: Mindful of our weakness, we ask not only that we may conquer, but also that we may not enter into the contest and perhaps be conquered. Maldonado, following Tertullian, Cyprian, Augustine, and others.]. We therefore ask that, by this one gift, we may be free from every evil by being free from the author of evil.

“Our Father who are in heaven.” When anyone calls himself a son, let him not wonder that he remains in the condition of a servant. Today you have been designated for divine offspring, not promoted into it; know that you have obtained hope, not the reality. Hear the Apostle: “We have been saved in hope; but hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Romans 8).

Today is the day of adoption; today is the time of promise. Hear, believe, and wait. Believe your creditor, who has trusted you, his debtor. Wait a little, until he comes who endured you for a long time until you came. Grant him a delay concerning what he promised, who has already forgiven you whatever debt you owed.

Or why are you wearied by hope in God, when the whole human race persists in hope and lives by faith? A farmer would never sow, exhausted by labor, if he did not hope in time to receive the fruit of his work. A traveler would not undertake the labor of a long journey unless he believed that he would reach his destination. A sailor would not enter the uncertain sea unless he hoped that the profits to come would compensate for the dangers of travel. A soldier would not spend all the years of his youth amid dangers unless he hoped for abundant honors in old age. A son would not endure the years of his father’s rule unless he hoped to become heir of his father’s property [Note: “[He] would not endure.” Horace, Book I, Ode 14:

“Hardly can the keels
Endure the sea’s more commanding force.”].

And you, if you already believe yourself a son of God, then, according to the prophet, “Wait for the Lord; act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened” (Psalm 26). Wait, so that you may obtain God’s inheritance through the faith of expectation and through the virtue of patience.

Hear the Apostle: “We are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be; we know that when he appears, we shall be like him” (1 John 3). And again: “Your life is hidden with Christ in God; but when Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Colossians 3).

Brothers, blessed are the children of God, because they will possess the inheritance of all things and will not experience the mourning of the ages at the passing of their Father.

## SERMON LXXII. On the Same Subject

What I am about to say with great trembling, what you are now about to hear—or rather, to call upon with terror—the angels are astonished at, the powers tremble before, the heavenly realm cannot contain, the sun does not see, the earth does not support, and the whole of creation cannot comprehend.

What can mortal breast do before this? What can the feeble mind of man do? What can the narrowness of human understanding do? What can the breath of a human voice do? What can the human tongue, soon to fall silent, do before this?

Paul, when he had seen this invisibly, revealed it without revealing it, saying: “Eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians 2) [Note: Paul saw invisibly because, without images, he saw hidden things in ecstasy, as Saint Thomas explains in his commentary on 2 Corinthians; and he saw invisibly because God is not seen by bodily eyes, as Fulgentius teaches from Augustine, *Response 3 to the Deacon Ferrandus*. From Mita.].

Isaiah, when he had scarcely begun to hear this with his own ears, doubted whether human faith could reach it, saying: “Lord, who has believed our report?” (Isaiah 53). Jeremiah, when he had conceived it through divine hearing, could not bear the birth of heavenly perceptions, crying: “My belly, my belly, I suffer, and the senses of my heart are troubled” (Jeremiah 4). Habakkuk proclaimed this under the inspiration of the divine Spirit when he said: “I watched, and my belly trembled at the voice of the prayer of my lips; trembling entered my bones, and beneath me my strength was shaken” (Habakkuk 3) [Note: Meursius corrects the text to “my strength was suddenly shaken.”]. Raised up by God’s power, he sensed that his own strength had fallen beneath him.

It would take too long to pursue further this sacrament of terror and to enumerate examples of the saints [Note: The Vatican manuscript adds “examples,” which is absent from the printed editions.]. Time does not allow me to linger long in this fear [Col. 0404C]; the urgent pressure of those being born with a heavenly birth cannot wait [Note: That is, you who, summoned by God, desire to be born spiritually as Christians, and who, in a kind of impulse, press upon the womb of Mother Church so that you may be born at once—you do not permit me to linger longer over the examples just begun. Observe how the nations desired to be baptized and renewed. MITA.].

Therefore I speak, and while you are still in the innermost womb I address you with a penetrating voice; I warn you beforehand with prudent exhortation: before you see your mother, call upon your Father; before your mother’s caresses, stretch yourselves out and hasten toward your Father’s kingdom; reach your Father’s bread before you hang upon your mother’s breasts. Let neither the necessity of the mother nor the stages of age claim anything for themselves in you; but in you everything should correspond and hasten toward the divine Father, the heavenly author (Matthew 6).

“Our Father who are in heaven.” This is what I was afraid to say; this is what I trembled to utter; this is what the condition of their own servitude permitted neither heavenly nor earthly beings to suspect: that such an exchange could suddenly arise between heaven and earth, flesh and God, that God might be changed into man, man into God, the Lord into a servant, and the servant into a son, so that, in an ineffable manner, there might arise one everlasting kinship of divinity and humanity [Col. 0405A].

Indeed, the condescension of the Godhead toward us is so great that creation cannot know what it ought chiefly to admire: whether that God humbled himself to our servitude, or that he snatched us up to the dignity of his divinity.

Hence, man, he divinely exhorts you [Note: Elsewhere: “Because he is so greatly.”], he who is now inflamed with such love for you; hence God, while you are still in the womb, adopts you by his voice as a son; hence he does not merely wish you to become free, but to be born; hence, for your sake, he himself emancipates nature, so that birth may impose no blemish or stain of its former servitude.

O blessed are you, to whom it has been granted to rule before being born, to reign before living, and to reach the glory of God the Father before recognizing the origin of your own lowliness!

Happy Church, the mother who beholds you as such, and who, although she remains a virgin, marvels that she has given birth to you, such and so great, in such a manner [Col. 0405B].

This birth was foreshadowed long ago by preceding examples. Hence Jacob wrestles with his brother in his mother’s womb (Genesis 25), and seizes triumphs in advance. Hence, in the womb of Tamar, twins contend over the honor of primacy; they delay the birth and do not wish to see the light before they have conquered (Genesis 38). Hence John exults beforehand and, from his mother’s womb, goes before and meets his author before he emerges (Luke 1).

And if human children thus fight for God before they are born to their parents and before they live in the world, what wonder is it if the divine offspring of the Church, if God’s children while still in the womb, already confess what they are—heavenly offspring?

“Our Father who are in heaven.” Astonishment rises up: Christ, from the breast of God the Father, calls the woman “mother” and confesses her on earth; and man, from his mother’s womb, calls God “Father” and confesses him in heaven: “Our Father who are in heaven.”

To what height has grace suddenly carried you, man? To what realm has heavenly nature snatched you, so that, while still placed in flesh and on earth, you no longer know flesh or earth when you say: “Our Father who are in heaven”?

Therefore, whoever confesses and believes himself to be the son of so great a Father should answer his lineage by his life, his father by his conduct, and should assert by mind and action what he has obtained—that he is heavenly by nature [Note: Elsewhere: “What you have obtained is fatherhood.”].

“Hallowed be your name.” Since we have begun to be his offspring, we are also reckoned by his name. Therefore we ask that the sanctification of that name may remain in us—the honor and privilege of the name that the exalted dignity of so great a Begetter has raised so high.

“Your kingdom come.” We do not ask this of him who has never lacked a kingdom, indeed, of him who himself is the kingdom and contains within himself the whole power of the kingdom; rather, because he wishes us to attain the promised glory of the kingdom, he urges us to seek it with every desire and wishes us to yearn for it with our whole minds.

How rash is the one who questions its lineage; so sluggish is the one who does not rejoice, burn, and pant when he directs and stretches himself toward the promised kingdom [Note: The Vallicellian manuscripts read “ignorant”; many printed editions have “who questions the lineage.”].

“Your will be done on earth as in heaven.” As in heaven, so also on earth: then the whole is heaven; then the one mind of God directs everyone; then all are in Christ and Christ is in all, when all think and do only the will of God; then all are one—or rather, one is all—when the one Spirit of God lives in all [Note: Brugensis thus explains the petition: “May what you will, command, and counsel be done by us and in us.”].

“Give us this day our daily bread.” As in the psalm: “Blessed is the Lord day by day” (Psalm 67), so here: “Give us this day our daily bread.” We call it daily because it is continual; that bread is continual which came down from heaven: “I am the bread that came down from heaven” (John 6).

This, then, is the bread of perfect blessedness. Today—that is, in the present—we begin already to live by the food of that bread, by whose perpetuity, which is “daily,” we shall be nourished in the future [Note: Mita explains this difficult passage from the Caesenate and Urbino manuscripts, adding that the bread is the sacrament of perfect blessedness, in which, by the force of the words, the body, blood, and divinity of Christ are present.
