Since in blessedness one divine person is not seen without the other, one may say with the theologians that the Father and the Holy Spirit are present in this sacrament by concomitance. Augustine, father and light of theologians, says in Sermon 3 *On Time*: “The Son assumed flesh and did not abandon the Father, nor did he divide himself from the Father: he assumed flesh in his own person, yet the Father and the Holy Spirit were not absent in majesty.” And as Christ is in the Incarnation, so he is sacramentally in the Eucharist. MITA.].

“And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” From the breast of the one who supplicates, a fountain of forgiveness flows out, and it will flow back toward forgiveness: whatever piety overflows and is poured out upon another, he grants to himself in equal measure.

“And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” A merciful man can do much, contending with God in piety, when he asks that as much be given to him as he has given, and as much be forgiven as he has pardoned. Man, let forgiveness always be in your heart, if you do not wish to fear crimes.

“And do not lead us into temptation.” These words require interpretation, because temptation is the devil’s forerunner and his bitter minister. As long as we remain enclosed in this fragile body, we necessarily pray that neither an opening to temptation nor access to the devil be granted against us [Note: Truly, by these words we ask God not to let us be subject to temptation, as we indicated above. Cyprian, *On the Lord’s Prayer*; Augustine, Letter 157, chapter 2, and *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 6; Chrysostom, Tertullian, and others.].

“But deliver us from evil.” May the Lord our God himself deliver us from evil and lead us to every good, he who lives and reigns as God, now and always, and through endless ages of ages. Amen.

[Note: In the Bologna manuscript this sermon bears the title: “Sermon of Blessed Peter of Ravenna on Easter Day.” Concerning it Mita says: “This sermon does not seem to be complete. Its subject concerns those who became Christians long ago and those who have only recently become Christians. The latter, hanging upon the necks of those who were baptized and confirmed long ago, ought to receive from the breasts of the Church, their common mother, the word of God and instruction in the faith, as though receiving milk. The former, however, ought to receive the body of Christ, and all together ought alike to hear the sacred teaching of God from the mouth of the shepherd.”]

## SERMON LXXIII. On the Paschal Solemnity

Today’s festival, beloved brothers, does not connect us with the old things, nor does it preserve the flesh of the lamb until tomorrow [Note: The Bologna manuscript reads “reserves it.”]. Rather, while it joins past things to present things through solemn devotion and unites our Passover with the returning Passover, it weans the infancy of the new birth, because, according to the Apostle, “The old things have passed away, and behold, all things have become new” (2 Corinthians 5).

The Lord’s year is completed through the seasons; it does not grow old [Note: The same manuscript adds “and.”]. It returns in its own circle for as long as it leads us toward the day of retribution.

Today’s Paschal solemnity now drives away from milk those whom it previously brought forth [Note: The same manuscript reads “has brought forward,” a corrupt reading. That is, it removes them from catechism and tender instruction so that they may share in the sacred Eucharist. MITA.—Among the ancients, honey was given to infants both as food and before food, and then milk, as learned men have observed: Salmasius, *On Transubstantiation*, p. 495; and Isaac Vossius, in his commentary on the Epistle of Barnabas, appended to the genuine letters of Ignatius. Hence the tasting of honey and milk in the ancient Church signified infancy, as Jerome says in one place.], so that, nourished by the food of greater solidity, they may be strengthened into the perfect man of Christ.

We know from the divine history that Abraham made a great feast and aroused the joy of his entire household when Isaac was weaned (Genesis 21). And if the offspring of old age, the only child of a barren woman, drew and stirred the hearts of the whole household into joy with dancing choirs, lyre and drum, and the whole resounding harmony of the psalter, how much more ought we [Note: The Bologna manuscript adds “today,” absent from the printed editions.] to rejoice today in spiritual hymns or songs, when all the fruitfulness born from the Virgin is weaned [Note: From the same manuscript, the printed editions read “of virginal offspring.”]?

If Anna, as barren as Sarah, who for so long had moistened the barrenness of her body and nature with the tears of her prayers, for as long as offspring had been denied her through the long course of her life, received Samuel as a divine gift, and, once he was weaned, immediately returned him as a divine gift, increasing her joy to the fullness of deliverance through sacrificial victims (1 Samuel 1), how much more ought we to offer a sacrifice of praise, fulfill our vows, burn incense of sweetness, and offer victims to God the Father with the entire richness of burnt offerings, when the Virgin Mother, nourished and weaned, presents to the Father throughout the whole world as many children as there are stars in the sky, so that the prophetic saying may be fulfilled: “You will bless the crown of the year with your goodness, and your fields will be filled with abundance” (Psalm 64 [in the source, Psalm XL])?

Therefore let no one think this saving mystery of our festival idle [Note: The same manuscript adds “to be.”], nor suppose that we are sewing a new patch onto an old garment [Note: That is, the Passover of the Hebrews is not sewn onto our Passover. He alludes to Matthew 9:16, discussed above in Sermon 31. MITA.], when we join nothing of Jewish antiquity to Christian newness. We know, as the Apostle says, that an entirely new creation has arisen for us in Christ; but we raise divine knowledge to the advancement of heavenly power (2 Corinthians 5), so that, while those newly born are instructed concerning what they ought to do, and those born earlier are taught how much gratitude they owe God for their perfection, those who have just been born may be hung upon the neck of the Church’s mother and wholly occupied with devotion at her breasts; may draw with tender mouths the food of innocence; may practice extending their arms in holy work; and may strive to steady their trembling footsteps in the course of faith [Note: All editions and the Vatican and Bologna manuscripts, among others, read *pactum* (“compact” or “agreement”). Latinius’s emendation has been preferred.].

Are those who have already been nourished to be abandoned, so that they are not governed by the father’s care, the father’s hand, and the father’s authority? And are they to be fortified by the mother’s counsel and the mother’s faith in such a way that they receive and anticipate what is salutary not only through human prudence but also through divine wisdom?

Thus Jacob, excessively fearful in himself but sufficiently bold through his mother’s counsel to seize his father’s blessing [Note: From the Vatican manuscript. The printed editions read “bold enough.”] [Col. 0408B], proceeded more as a mystic than as a deceiver (Genesis 27) [Note: Chrysologus is not the only one among the Fathers who excuses Jacob’s action from fraud and falsehood and insists that all these things ought to be referred to the mystery. See Augustine, *Against Lying*, chapter 10. But to excuse him from lying, it would not be enough to demonstrate a mystery in that action; it would also be necessary to prove that, in the historical and literal sense, no lie was put forward, as Estius rightly observes on this passage. This is chiefly what Theodoret undertook, *Questions on Genesis*, question 81; Gregory the Great, Book I, Homily 6 on Ezekiel, and *On Job*, Book XVIII, chapter 3 of the new edition; Saint Thomas, *Summa Theologiae* II-II, question 1, article 3, reply to objection 3; Melchior Cano, Book II, *On Theological Places*, chapter 4. It is more prudent, with the most learned Calmet, volume I, p. 216, column 2, to cite that wise principle of Augustine, Book III *On Christian Doctrine*: whenever Scripture relates the sin of some outstanding man in whom a figure and type of future things is displayed, the example nevertheless is not at all to be transferred literally into moral conduct. Augustine: “Refer the figure to understanding, but do not transfer the deed itself to morals.”].

For he did not lie in claiming to be the firstborn, because the firstborn is the one whom heavenly grace, not mortal nature, generates. He represented us beneath the skins of goats: in order that we may die to sin, at the exhortation of Mother Church we put on the garment of a mortified body; and we exude the fragrance of the field through the continual fruits and abundance of confessions, until, salutarily mocking Israel’s blindness, we seize the paternal blessing through the entire mystery of faith. The Apostle says: “A blindness has happened in part to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter” (Romans 11 [the source reads Romans I]).

[Note: See what we said in the preface.]

## SERMON LXXIV. On the Resurrection of Christ
[Col. 0408C] The labor of the vigils made us keep silent for a little while, dearest brothers, and [Note: The practice of vigils in the early Church, together with a more prolonged fast during Holy Week. Indeed, the very night of Easter is called the Night of Vigils by Gaudentius, *Treatise on Exodus*, p. 24; by Alcimus Avitus, *On the Institution of the First Rogation Festival*; and by Ado of Vienne in his *Chronicle*. See Lindenbrog’s *Observations on Marcellinus*, p. 545.] and the weariness of fasting compelled us. Therefore today we offer a sermon on the Lord’s Resurrection: if it is divine that Christ is born from a Virgin, how much more divine is it that Christ rises from the dead? What is therefore divine must not be received by human [Note: In the Bologna manuscript there is added: “You heard the evangelist say: ‘In the evening.’”] hearing.

“In the evening,” he says, “of the Sabbath, as the first day of the week was dawning” (Matt. 28). The evening of the Sabbath is unknown to the day of this world; the practice of the world does not possess it. [Col. 0409A] Evening ends a day; it does not begin one. Evening grows dark; it does not grow light. It does not turn into dawn, because it knows nothing of the rising of light. The evening, mother of night, gives birth to day; it changes the order of things when it recognizes its author. It radiates a mystery through novelty; it hastens to serve the Creator, not time.

“In the evening,” he says, “of the Sabbath, as the first day of the week was dawning, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to see the tomb.” Late the woman runs for pardon, though she ran early toward guilt. In the evening she seeks Christ, though in the morning she had known that Adam had been lost.

“Mary and the other Mary came to see the tomb.” She who had taken perfidy from paradise hastens [Note: This is almost the same as Gregory of Nyssa, *Oration 2 against Eunomius*, vol. III, p. 712: “Since, as the Apostle says, the woman was deceived into transgression and became the leader of the defection from God that came through disobedience, therefore she was the first witness of the resurrection, so that through faith in the resurrection the ruin that followed transgression might be repaired. And just as at the beginning of the discourse she became the serpent’s minister and adviser to the man, becoming the beginning of evil and introducing its consequence into life, so, bearing to the disciples the words of him who consigned to death the apostate dragon, she would become leader and guide of faith for human beings, through which the occasion of the first death might deservedly be undone.” From Suicer’s translation in his *Thesaurus*, vol. I, p. 807.] to draw faith from the tomb; she strives to snatch life from death, although she had snatched death from life. [Note: From what life? From the paradise of delights, where she ought to have lived? Or from the food that, restoring life, is said to provide life? Or because food is naturally made to preserve life? Thus she took life from death—that is, from the tomb, which is called the seat of death. MITA.]

Mary came. This is the name of Christ’s mother; therefore the mother came in name. [Col. 0409B] The woman came so that she might become the mother of the living, she who had become the mother of the dying, so that what is written might be fulfilled: “This is the mother of all the living” (Gen. 3).

“Mary and the other Mary.” He did not say “they came,” but “she came”: two women came under one name by mystery, not by chance. “Mary and the other Mary.” She came, the same yet another; another, yet the same, so that the woman might be changed in life, not in name; in virtue, not in sex. She who had been the intermediary of the fall and the ruin became the messenger of the resurrection.

“Mary came to see the tomb.” The sight of the tomb restored the woman whom the sight of the tree had deceived; the saving sight raised up the woman whom the enticing sight had cast down.

“Behold,” he says, “there was a great earthquake, for an angel of the Lord descended from heaven.” The earth trembled—not because an angel descended from heaven, but because the Ruler ascended from the underworld. [Col. 0409C] [Note: It is the common opinion of the holy Fathers that by this earthquake the Lord’s resurrection was especially announced to the world.] “Behold, there was a great earthquake.” [Note: In Greek, σεισμὸς ἐγένετο μέγας means “a great movement occurred”; some think that not an earthquake but a whirlwind is indicated—Hammond, Clericus, and others. But in the books of the New Covenant that word is used only for an earthquake, as here by Chrysologus. See Acts 16:26; Rev. 6:12; 11:13; Matt. 24:7; 27:54; Mark 13:8; Luke 21:11.]

Chaos is moved; the depths of the earth split apart; the earth is afraid. The masses of the mountains tremble; the foundations of the world are shaken; Tartarus is seized with fear; the underworld is brought to a halt. [Col. 0410A] Death is condemned [Note: The Bologna manuscript reads: “which, offending against the king.”]: while rushing upon the guilty, it encounters the Judge; having ruled over servants, it burned against the Lord; raging against human beings, it sprang upon God.

Therefore the law of Tartarus rightly perishes, the rights of the underworld are removed, the power of death is taken away, and, as punishment for its rashness, at the injury done to the Judge it raised the dead [Note: From the same manuscript: “it raised the dead.” “The underworld is provoked by the injury done to the Judge; bodies are restored,” and so forth.]. At last bodies are restored, the human being is made whole again, life is renewed, and pardon is now established in everything, because the sentence immediately turned against the author of life.

“Behold, there was a great earthquake.” Now there is a great earthquake. Oh, if then even a slight whirlwind had thrown down the deadly tree! Oh, if the smoke of a mist had darkened the woman’s sight! Oh, if a foul cloud had obscured the appearance of the deadly fruit! Oh, if the hand that touched what was forbidden had trembled! Oh, if an unjust night had darkened the day of sin [Note: But why is the night called unjust? Perhaps because it serves the unjust, who love darkness so that they may sin more freely; or because by its darkness it disturbs the order of things; or because it equally obscures what is beautiful and what is foul, good and evil? Certainly, because if it had made the day dark before its time, it would have acted unjustly. Or perhaps by “night” he understands death, as Bellarmine does in his commentary on Psalm 21:21, as though it would at least have been a lesser evil for Eve to die unjustly than thus to offend God. For if death, which is the punishment of sin, had befallen humanity before the sin itself, it could have been called unjust. MITA. The author earlier called Eve’s hand “forbidden,” because it was extended toward things that had been prohibited; now he calls the night “unjust,” because it had disturbed the rights of day.], and had then brought the world’s laments, the increase of death, and injury to the Creator!

But flatteries always serve vices; sweet things entice sins. To virtues, however, stern and strenuous things are friendly.

“For an angel of the Lord descended from heaven.” When Christ rose and death perished, heavenly commerce was restored to earthly things; and the woman who had shared a deadly counsel with the devil now has a life-giving conversation with an angel. [Note: The Bologna manuscript reads: “And the woman who had shared a deadly counsel with the devil had a heavenly conversation with the angel.”]

“For an angel of the Lord descended from heaven and rolled away the stone.” He did not say “rolled the stone,” but “rolled it away”—the stone that, when rolled toward the tomb, proved death, and, when rolled away, became the champion of the resurrection. [Note: That is, for those to whom the empty tomb was revealed—not because Christ’s rising body needed the stone to be rolled away, although some Fathers, namely Hilary here and Leo, *Letter 83 to the Monks of Palestine*, thought that the angels rolled away the stone as an honor to the rising Christ. See Grotius and Maldonado here.]

Blessed is the stone that was worthy both to reveal and to veil Christ; blessed is it, because it opens hearts no less than the tomb; blessed is it, because it gives faith in the resurrection and resurrection to faith, testifying that the divine flesh has risen. [Note: These words are absent from the Bologna manuscript.]

Here the order of things is changed: the tomb devours death, not the dead; the house of death becomes a dwelling of life; the womb in a new manner conceives the dead and gives birth to the living.

“For an angel of the Lord descended from heaven, and coming, rolled away the stone, [Col. 0411A] and sat upon it.”

And what reason did the angel have for sitting, since he possessed no weariness? [Note: Maldonado, Grotius, and others believe that the Greek word ἐπιστάναι, ordinarily understood as “to sit,” is also used in the sense of presenting oneself before someone.] He sat as a teacher of faith, as a master of the resurrection. He sat upon the stone so that [Note: The Bologna manuscript reads: “the solidity of the one sitting.”] the firmness of his seat might give stability to believers. [Note: From the same manuscript: “The angel sat upon the stone so that the solidity of the one sitting might demonstrate the foundations of the faith, upon which,” and so forth.]

The angel placed the foundations of faith upon the stone on which Christ was going to build the Church, for he said: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church.”

“His appearance,” he says, “was like lightning, and his clothing like snow” (Matt. 16). For the glory of the angel, brightness is not enough; for a heavenly nature, what purpose does clothing serve? [Note: From the same manuscript: “Lightning. What was done with the clothing for a heavenly nature?” The Caesena and Vallicelliana manuscripts read: “What need is there of clothing?”] Yet by such splendor he represented the appearance and form of our resurrection, because those who rise through Christ are changed into Christ’s glory. [Note: After this the Bologna manuscript adds: “The dark darkness of the flesh—thus the Lord says concerning the resurrection of the flesh in Hebrew: ‘Then the righteous will shine like the sun.’”]

But out of fear of him the guards were terrified and became like dead men. Wretched are those whom the dread of death strikes when the security of life is being restored. But how could the ministers of cruelty [Col. 0411B] and agents of another’s perfidy take confidence from heavenly things? [Note: The Caesena manuscript reads: “ministers of simplicity.”] [Note: The Bologna manuscript reads: “They themselves who were guarding the tomb.”]

They surrounded the tomb, blocked the doors against the resurrection, and guarded it so that no life could enter and death perish. [Note: In the aforementioned manuscripts, “death perish” is absent.] Rightly the angel’s arrival struck and cast them down—not the rising Christ, but the angels’ arrival. [Note: The angels’ arrival, of course, not the rising Christ. For it would not have been fitting for that impious crowd to be the first to see Christ returning from the underworld. Notice the persistent error of painters.]

Wretched mortality, always its own enemy, grieves that it is dying and attacks so that it may not be able to rise again. It should have opened the tomb and supplied everything that could facilitate resurrection, so that there might be a miracle from the deed, hope from the example, reality from the return, and faith from the living one. It is great madness for a human being not to believe what he desires to happen to himself.

Let this suffice for what we have said today about these guards. What our faith contains we shall discuss later, so that we may not be long-winded today, with the Lord Jesus Christ granting it, who lives and reigns with God the Father forever and ever. Amen.

[Note: This sermon is omitted in the Bologna manuscript.]

## SERMON LXXV. On the Same Subject

How far I had gone away from you, [Note: Chrysologus had departed from his own see and, a stranger to his people, had gone elsewhere—either to Rome for the synod held twice under Pope Leo against the Manichaeans, or to visit the same pontiff concerning the cause of the Eutychian heresy. From Mita. This conjecture is rejected by Abbot Bacchinius; see his *Observations on the Life of Chrysologus*, prefixed to this edition, no. 5.] so far had the sermon wandered from me. But pray, brothers, that just as God has restored me to you, so he may deign to restore and give my sermon back to me.

You heard the evangelist say (Matt. 28): “In the evening,” he says, “of the Sabbath, as the first day of the week was dawning.” What does human understanding comprehend here? What does human wisdom find intelligible here? “The evening that grows light.” Evening ends a day; it does not begin one, nor does it give birth to light, but to darkness. Here, however, the author of the elements changes the elements’ order, so that in the Lord’s resurrection you may perceive everything divine and nothing human.

Thus, when Christ rose, evening grew light for the faithful, while day grew dark for unbelievers. Night was changed into day for the disciples; for the Jews, day was turned and changed into night.

“From the sixth hour,” he says, “darkness came over the whole earth until the ninth hour” (Luke 23). [Note: This follows the reckoning of the Hebrews. Their first hour corresponded to six in the morning, the third to nine, the sixth to noon, and the ninth to three in the afternoon; thus they completed the twenty-four hours which make up our day.] The very thing that is wholly noonday brightness was darkened, and what is written was fulfilled: “The sun shall set for them at noon” (Amos 8)—“for them,” that is, for the Jews. But for us: “The night shall shine like the day” (Ps. 138).

For the evening, which always tends toward profound darkness, then stretched out and raised the whole of Christ into the light, and, when Christ rose from the underworld, filled the whole hearts of mortals with its complete splendor.

“The evening of the Sabbath.” The Sabbath is illuminated through Christ; it is not abolished. For he did not come to dissolve the Law but to fulfill it (Matt. 5). It is illuminated so that on the Lord’s Day it may shine, and so that what had been darkened in the synagogue by the Jews’ obscuring may become bright in the Church.

“Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to see the tomb.” The women precede the apostles in their ministry, women who follow men in sex and disciples in rank. But this does not make the apostles more sluggish, because these women bear not the forms of women but the type of the Churches to the Lord’s tomb.

Mary and Mary: one is another, and the other is the same; the other is the same Mary. Mary, the mother of Christ: one name is doubled in two women, because here the Church, coming from two peoples, is represented as one from two peoples—that is, from the Gentiles and the Jews—because “the first shall be last and the last first” (Matt. 20).

Mary came to the tomb; she came to the womb of the resurrection; she came to the birth of life, so that Christ might be born again from the tomb for faith, he who had been generated in the flesh from the womb. so that the closed tomb might restore to everlasting life him whom closed virginity had brought forth as life for the present age. [Note: It was the opinion of many Fathers and interpreters that Christ left the tomb in the same way as he came from his mother’s womb, with the opening untouched and intact: the author of the *Questions to the Orthodox* under Justin’s name, question 117; Chrysostom, *Homily 11 on St. John the Baptist*; Gregory Nazianzen, *The Suffering Christ*; Jerome, *Question 6 to Hedibia*; Augustine—or someone else—sermon formerly numbered 159, now 160, in the appendix.]

For divinity’s distinctive sign is that he left the closed virgin after childbirth; to have emerged bodily from a closed tomb is likewise a sign of divinity.

Mary and Mary came to see the tomb. You see that they came not to behold the Lord but the tomb; nor did they seek the living one among the dead, since they believed that the Lord had already risen.

“For an angel of the Lord descended from heaven, and coming, rolled away the stone.” He rolled away the stone not to provide the Lord, as he emerged, with an exit, but to show the world that the Lord had already risen; to give his fellow servants faith for believing, not to offer the Lord assistance for rising.

He rolled away the stone. What had been rolled toward the tomb for unbelief was rolled away for faith. He rolled away the stone so that the same object might be the title of life that had served as the guardian of death. [Note: The Caesena manuscript reads: “to hold the guard.”]

Pray, brothers, that an angel may now descend and roll away all the hardness of our heart; that he may open what is closed in our understanding; that he may testify even to our minds that Christ has risen. [Note: From the same manuscript: “and to our minds.”] For just as that heart is heaven in which Christ lives and reigns, so that breast is a tomb in which Christ is still held dead and buried.

Let Christ’s death be believed to have been as it was and also to have passed away. Christ the human being suffered, died, and was buried; he is, lives, reigns, remains, and endures as God.

Hear the Apostle say: “Even if we once knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him” (2 Cor. 5). And: “The death he died, he died to sin once for all; but the life he lives, he lives to God” (Rom. 6)—that is, God lives.

“And coming, he rolled away the stone, and sat upon it.” He sat to teach the resurrection, not to relieve weariness. Heavenly nature knows no weariness and does not know labor. But the stone became a vessel for angelic sitting, a chair of heavenly instruction, a school of life, because it had been placed by the Jews at the door of death, in the service of ashes, for sad silence. [Note: Some seem to have called large stones or pieces of columns suitable for sitting upon “vessels.” See Du Cange’s *Glossary*, vol. III, p. 1379.]

“His appearance,” he says, “was like lightning, and his clothing like snow.” The brightness of the face is distinguished from the whiteness of the garments; the angel’s face is compared with lightning and his clothing with snow, because lightning comes from heaven and snow from earth.

Hear the prophet say: “Praise the Lord from the earth, fire, hail, snow” (Ps. 148). Thus in the angel’s face the heavenly brightness of his nature is preserved; in his clothing the grace of fellowship with humanity is represented. The appearance of the angel who speaks is moderated so that bodily eyes may endure the gentle brightness of his garments, while from the lightning of his face they tremble at the message of its author and revere him.

“But out of fear of him the guards were terrified.” Why were they terrified? [Col. 0414A] Because they were guarding the tomb [Note: They followed the custom of the Jews and were therefore terrified lest they suffer bodily punishment for having guarded it carelessly. Maldonado and Brugensis.] out of zeal for cruelty, not in the service of piety. He falls, is destroyed, and cannot stand whom conscience abandons and guilt drives forward. Hence the angel strikes the impious but addresses and comforts the pious. [Note: Angels commonly console the pious who have been struck with fear by this formula of greeting.]

“Do not be afraid, you.” That is, let those men be afraid; let those who seek not be afraid, and let those who persecute be afraid. [Note: He aptly contrasts the women seeking Jesus with the soldiers pursuing him. Chrysostom, according to Maldonado, thinks that the word “you” was added emphatically to set them against the soldiers.]

“Do not be afraid, you, for I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified. He is not here.” That is: I have come to instruct you, not to remove him who is both the maker of all things and his own raiser. [Note: The Caesena manuscript reads: “and he is his own raiser.”]

“He is not here, for he has risen, as he said.” You see that the angel came so that the servant might affirm by deeds [Note: The same manuscript reads: “what the Lord had said.”] what the Lord had foretold in words, and might teach that the power of dying and living belonged to the one who had foretold his resurrection before his death. Indeed, the one who could know could also have avoided it; but because he could conquer, he scorned to evade it, because the glory of the one rising buried the injury of the one dying.

We shall treat of what follows, brothers, in the next sermon, because the weariness still fresh from the journey prevented us from prolonging and extending the sermon.

## SERMON LXXVI. On the Same Subject, and on Christ’s Second Manifestation to the Women Returning from the Tomb

In the preceding sermon we said that Mary and the other Mary bore the figure of the Church coming from two peoples. Today we wish to confirm this from what follows, if only your kindly hearing is granted to us.

“The angel answered,” he says, “and said: ‘Do not be afraid, you, for I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified. He is not here, for he has risen, as he said. Come, see the place where the Lord was laid’” (Matt. 28).

The angel proclaims the name, speaks of the cross, recounts the passion, acknowledges the death, but immediately confesses the resurrection—and immediately the Lord. [Note: For after the resurrection the reign of our Lord Jesus Christ began, and the angels too are subject to him.]

If the angel, after so many sufferings and after the tomb, recognizes him as Lord, speaks of his own servitude, and understands that the entire injury of the passion has passed into the glory of the resurrection, why does a human being either judge God diminished in the flesh, or think that his power failed in the passion, or believe that his dominion was consumed by servitude? [Note: See Epiphanius, *Against Heresies*, vol. I, part III, p. 1026, Cologne edition. In the Bologna manuscript “his” is absent.] [Note: For how obscure this passage was, consult the editions.]

Therefore the angel rightly says “crucified” and shows the place where the Lord had been laid, lest it be believed that another, and not the same one, had risen from the dead.

And if the Lord returns in the same flesh, carries back his wounds, takes up again the very holes made by the nails, and makes those very things the testimonies of his body and the signs of his resurrection which had been the disgrace of his passion, why does a human being suppose that he will return in another flesh, or not suppose that he will return in his own flesh? [Col. 0415A] Or does the servant perhaps disdain his own flesh, when the Lord did not change ours? [Note: The Samaritans and Sadducees were the first of all to deny the resurrection; the Epiphanius cited above refutes them, vol. I, part I, p. 25. So too the Origenists, Basilidians, Valentinians, Marcionites, and other people of this ilk.]

Accept, human being, that you yourself will be in your own flesh, lest you yourself not exist if you rise in another’s flesh.

The angel added, saying: “And go quickly, tell his disciples that he has risen and will go before you into Galilee; there you will see him.”

Here the angel sends not women but the Church in the two women. [Note: Absent from the Bologna manuscript.] He sends one, so that by sending her he may spread her far and wide. Here the angel sends the bride to the bridegroom. Indeed, as they went, the Lord met them and greeted them, saying: “Hail.” [Note: The same manuscript reads: “Hail,” that is, “Be well.”]

He meets them, and does not terrify them by his power; rather, he goes before them in the ardor of love. He does not disturb them by authority; he greets them according to the law of the bridegroom. He does not burden them with the right of a ruler; he honors them with the affection of a partner. He greets them: “Hail.”

He himself had said to his disciples: “Greet no one on the road.” What is it, then, that here on the road such a cheerful greeter comes to meet them? [Note: From Mita.] He does not wait to be recognized; he does not demand to be understood; he does not allow himself to be approached so that he may be questioned. He goes wholly into the greeting; he goes fervently, and by greeting himself fulfills his own command?

He did so, he did so, because the power of love conquers and surpasses everything. At the same time, Christ greets the Church in which he greets himself, since he has made it his own and has thus received his own entrails into his own body, as the Apostle says: “He himself is the head of the body, the Church” (Col. 1).

That the figure of the Church remains fully in these women is clearly shown by the reality itself, because Christ scarcely recalls his disciples, wavering about the resurrection, to faith: he reproves them when they tremble, strengthens them by showing his side and the cavities of the nails, and by eating food (Luke 24).

Therefore he deservedly calls them “little ones,” as children, saying: “Children, do you have anything to eat?” (John 21). Elsewhere he calls Mary herself, weeping as though for a dead man, “woman,” and denies her permission to touch him (John 20). But these women he finds so perfect, so believing, so free from trembling on account of their sex, so hastening in accordance with the mystery, so earnestly seeking the Lord with the whole ardor of faith, that he gives himself to be held by them with such a greeting, saying: “Hail.”

The angel had said: “I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified.” To those who seek him, Christ replied: “Hail.” Elsewhere Mary is not granted the opportunity even to touch him (John 20). [Note: Other interpreters reconcile these two Gospel passages, which Chrysologus introduces as though they conflicted. They say either that these were two different appearances; or that Mary Magdalene had touched him earlier; or that, despite Christ’s prohibition, she touched him nevertheless, as love is importunate and bold. Consult Maldonado.] Here she is granted not only the opportunity to touch him but every opportunity to hold him.

“But they,” he says, “came up and took hold of his feet.” These women hold Christ’s feet because in the Church they hold the type of evangelical preaching and are rewarded for their running. Thus they touch the traces of their Savior by faith and reach the glory of the whole Godhead and arrive at honor.

But she rightly hears: “Do not touch me” (ibid.), she who mourns the Lord on earth and seeks him in the tomb as a dead man, so that she does not know him reigning in heaven with the Father. [Note: Augustine appears to agree with Chrysologus in *Tractate 121 on John*, recognizing in this woman the Church from the Gentiles, which did not believe in Christ until he had ascended to the Father. Vol. III, p. 590, Antwerp edition.]

“Do not touch me”—that is, do not render him homage merely by the touch of flesh [Note: The Caesena manuscript reads: “to render homage only with flesh.”] when you ought to reach him by the touch of faith. Do not presume to touch on earth merely as a human being the one whom you do not yet understand as God and adore in the heavens. Let feminine concern cease; let womanly anxiety desist. Let manly faith ascend into your mind. Let the breadth of your heart comprehend my ascent, so that in heaven you may enjoy the eternal blessedness of touching me. [Note: Other interpreters, along with Chrysologus, teach that by the words “Do not touch me” Christ indicated that the woman would have the grace of embracing Christ in heaven, raising her mind from bodily things to spiritual ones. St. Leo, *Sermon 11 on the Ascension*, p. 72, Lyons edition, edited by Raynaud: “Do not touch me. I do not wish you to come to me bodily or to look upon me with the sense of flesh; I am directing you toward higher things. When I have ascended to the Father, then you will touch me more perfectly and truly, grasping what you touch and believing what you do not see.”]

In accordance with the prophet’s words: “Blessed is the man whose help is from you, O Lord; he has set ascents in his heart” (Ps. 83). Whoever does not ascend by faith to Christ in heaven does not touch Christ on earth.

Therefore, when this same Mary is now established at the summit of faith, now raised to the height of the Church, and touches Christ and holds him with the whole affection of holiness, while at another time she is cast down by the weakness of the flesh and feminine frailty, doubts, and is not worthy to receive the touch of her author, there is no contradiction. The former concerns the figure; the latter the sex. The former concerns divine grace; the latter human nature. For when we ourselves understand what is divine, it is God’s gift; when we understand according to what is human, we are blinded by ourselves.

[Note: Another version in the Bologna manuscript: “Thus blessed Peter, thus, when the Father revealed it, recognizes Christ as the Son of God.”]

Thus blessed Peter recognizes Christ when he confesses him as the Son of God, with the Father revealing it; when he denies Christ, he experiences and suffers the blindness of the flesh (Matt. 16).

Meanwhile the Jews either purchase their own crimes badly or sell another’s even worse, assigning a price to sins, weighing and balancing offenses with money, and pouring into their crimes what they had gathered through complete wickedness.

Thus they purchase Judas as the betrayer of his Lord, and weigh the blood of the world’s Redeemer against a price. Thus they close the faith of the opened tomb in a purse [Note: From the same manuscript: “in the world.”], so that with coins bought through crimes they might purchase the crime of denying the resurrection.

“They gave the soldiers a large sum of money, saying: ‘Say that his disciples came by night and stole him while we were sleeping. And if the governor hears this, we will persuade him and keep you safe.’ So they took the money and did as they had been instructed; and this story has been spread among the Jews to this day.”

Among the Jews—but surely not among Christians? Jew, what you darkened in Judea with gold has become bright and radiant through faith throughout the world. The disciples received Christ; they did not steal him. You purchased perfidy, but you did not steal the truth. Jew, Christ has risen; you have lost your money.

“His blood be upon us and upon our children.” Jew, Christ lives; you have killed both yourself and your descendants.

## SERMON LXXVII. On the Resurrection of Christ
Sufficiently full and perfect is the proof of devotion: at the time of the Passion, the whole creation suffers with its Creator. What flesh did not tremble when the earth trembled? What mind was not numbed? What intellect did not fail when the sun set before its time and the light withdrew? Finally, brothers, our own inward parts also fell then; our sense died with him, and our speech was buried with its author, so that it might now be raised wholly to his glory. This was the reason for my silence; this was the devout postponement of my obligation. Nor is it surprising, brothers, if my discourse, with the entire obedience of its affection, followed its benefactor even to the underworld, since without him I had nothing to render to creditors such as you, so numerous and so great. But if some covetous and greedy exactor complains about the delay in payment, let him cease bringing an accusation against time, because my rich Lord multiplies the interest of his own loan and repays it with increase.

[Note: An *actio in iure* is an action at law by which someone seeks to assert a thing as his through the formal formulas of law, or for which he institutes a suit. See Du Cange’s *Glossary*.]

Let the generous kindness of the Gospel reading now release us, whom the necessity of our office has led and bound to this debt alone.

[Note: That is, to mourning Christ’s death and grieving with the Church for so great a funeral.]

“In the evening of the Sabbath, as it dawns toward the first day of the Sabbath.” When the Lord rose, not only was the law of human nature transformed, but the very order of creation was remarkably changed. “In the evening of the Sabbath, as it dawns.” Behold: when the Lord rose, evening did not grow dark but dawned; and what was accustomed to be the beginning of night became the beginning of light. “In the evening of the Sabbath, as it dawns toward the first day of the Sabbath” (Matthew 28).

[Note: The meaning is difficult to explain. Given the limits of my understanding, I think the author is speaking of the resurrection of the human being through Christ on the last day. In that person’s flesh, mortality would be transferred into immortality, corruption into incorruption, and flesh into spirit through blessed glory. The darkness that will be changed into light is either all adverse circumstances, which are transferred into light—that is, into prosperity—or, certainly, death itself, which is called night and which, once its darkness has been laid aside, will be changed into perpetual light, that is, into perpetual life. Night—that is, death—does not disappear, since we all die; but for the righteous who die in the Lord, death is changed into life. Time does not fail, because the Author of time does not know temporal limitation. Night loses the role of its servitude, because death serves humanity and humanity serves death; but it is freed from servitude when the human being himself enjoys perpetual light in the resurrection.

The Author proves this from Psalm 138:10: “And night shall be illuminated like day,” and so forth. I explain it as follows. A person says: “Let darkness cover me in the night of death, so that I may no longer see the light.” This will indeed be the punishment of sin; but night—that is, bodily death itself—will be my illumination in my delights, because, raised up through Christ’s grace, I too shall rise from death, and through the way of death I shall pass from death itself into life, where, illuminated by the light of glory, I shall enjoy the delights of blessed vision.

See Maldonado on Luke 1, nos. 78 and 79, where he teaches that the Fathers understood darkness and light respectively as all prosperous and adverse circumstances. And on John 1:4, near the end, he says that Scripture calls life light and death darkness. Thus our author below, in Sermon 79, seems to indicate an explanation of this passage.

MITA. — Considering Chrysologus’ style, it is very easy to understand that here the resurrection of our bodies is compared with that same evening—or, as he likes to say, night—of the Lord’s resurrection, which turns the darkness of its nature into light, just as we too shall turn the corruption of our bodies into immortality.]

Just as mortality is transferred into immortality, corruption into incorruption, and flesh into God, so darkness is transferred into light, so that night itself may rejoice that it has not perished in this way but has been changed—night which has failed more through darkness than through time, which has more happily lost its intervals and its function of servitude, so that it might flow forth and break out into the freedom of perpetual light. As the prophet says: “And night shall be my illumination in my delights” (Psalm 138).

“In the evening, as it dawns toward the first day of the Sabbath.”

[Note: He calls the Lord’s Day, because of Christ’s resurrection, the primary Sabbath—that is, the chief and principal feast. He calls the Sabbath of the Hebrews secondary, that is, placed in a second and lower position, as signifying this primary Sabbath. On the transformation of the Hebrew Sabbath into the Lord’s Day, and on the sanctification of feasts, Augustine speaks beautifully, as usual, in Sermon 251 on the Seasons.

MITA.]

The Sabbath rejoices that it has been made secondary. It had lain inert in idleness by the command of the law, but through the primacy of the Lord’s Day it is wondrously roused to works of divine power—whereas the inertia of Jewish observance had made it alien to saving virtue. For the Lord says: “Is it not permitted on Sabbaths to grant the sick care, the afflicted help, the blind sight, and the dead life?” (Luke 6). By interpreting in this way the Sabbath day, assigned by God to the studies of the holy law, he had miserably subjected it only to the service of the belly.

“In the evening of the Sabbath, as it dawns toward the first day of the Sabbath, Mary Magdalene came, and the other Mary.” One comes under her name, while another is now read as a different person. “Mary came, and the other Mary.”

[Note: The Caesena manuscript has: “so that then the two might be one.”]

Thus the unity of the name might portray one in two, while the diversity of persons might reveal a woman transformed. For it says “she came,” not “they came”; and when it says “the other,” in both it mystically designates the same woman, showing that one had come before faith, while the other would return after faith had been received.

A woman came, but Mary returns. She came who brought death; she returns who gave birth to life. She came—the Adam who led to the underworld; Mary returns, who received Christ from the underworld. “Mary came, and the other Mary.” Why? “To see the tomb,” and not to seek Christ: merely to see the tomb, the title of her guilt, the sad evidence of her crime, the fatal transaction of her presumption with the devil, her deadly bargain, so that she might recover faith from the place where she endured the perpetual reproach of her transgression.

“And behold, there was a great earthquake.” If the earth trembled in this way when its Lord rose for pardon, how will it tremble when the guilty rise for punishment? As the prophet says: “The earth trembled and was still, when God rose up for judgment” (Psalm 75). And if it was unable to endure the presence of fellow servants—that is, of angels—how will it endure God the Judge?

Behold, along the same lines by which human salvation had perished, it is restored. The woman who was first to unbelief is first brought to faith; she who first ran to the author of death runs first to the destroyer of death; she who first conversed with the devil first hears from the angel.

“An angel of the Lord descended from heaven, and came and rolled back the stone, and sat upon it.” Not in order to confer resurrection through such an action, but to reveal it, as the Lord says: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10). For our sake he opens what was closed; for our sake he unlocks what was hidden. He does not lead his author, who was no longer in the tomb, out into the light; rather, he leads his fellow servants, who had been placed in the darkness of doubt, to faith in the resurrection. The Lord himself bears witness to this when he says: “He is not here; he has risen.”

“He rolled back the stone, and sat upon it.” Why does it say not that he rolled it, but that he rolled it back? So that what the perfidy of the Pharisees had intended for offense and scandal, the angel might roll back for faith and salvation, as the prophet says: “Behold, I place in Zion a stone of offense and a rock of scandal” (Isaiah 8; Romans 9). Therefore the stone is rolled back so that it might roll away death, having enclosed the life that had been sealed within it, as Scripture says: “You shall see your life hanging before your eyes, and you shall not believe” (Deuteronomy 28).

“And he sat upon it.” He was not refreshing himself from weariness; rather, by this he showed that he was the guardian of the sacred and life-giving tomb. The heavenly minister of the office declared, by this sign of his sitting, that death had been destroyed, and that the one who had suffered was God; that the one who had been received within the narrow confines of our body was God; that the one whom he, sitting in heavenly form, testified to was God.

And what more, brothers? He sits because no angel ever departs from that most venerable tomb.

“But from fear of him the guards were terrified and became like dead men.” Terror throws down the guilty; it soon returns to those who know what has happened. Thus, thus, when the innocent rise, terror and death will possess the unjust and ungodly.

“His appearance was like lightning, and his clothing like snow.” What purpose does clothing serve where there is no nakedness? What need is there for a garment where there is no necessity of covering? But the angel, brothers, prefigures in this way our condition, our form, and our likeness in the resurrection, when the human being is restored in the very brightness of his body. As the Lord says: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matthew 13).

“But the angel answered and said to the women: Do not be afraid; for I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified.” They were still seeking him as crucified and dead. The savage storm of the Passion had disturbed their faith and bent them down beneath the weight of temptation, so that they still sought the Lord of heaven in the tomb.

“He is not here.” He is not here according to what he was in that place; but he is here through the fact that he is everywhere and is not confined by the capacity of any place.

“Come, see the place where the Lord was laid.” The angel calls the women to see, so that the place of the sacred body might cleanse eyes which the sight of the forbidden tree had stained when the devil closed them.

[Note: The Caesena manuscript reads: “when the devil was persuading.”]

They enter the tomb so that, buried with the Lord, they might rise wholly into the salvation of faith. “If we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall be also in the likeness of his resurrection” (Romans 6).

“Go and tell his disciples.” Return to the man, woman now healed, and persuade him to faith—you who persuaded him to unbelief. Report the sign of the Lord’s resurrection to the man to whom you had earlier brought the counsel of temptation and ruin.

## SERMON LXXVIII. On the Seventh Manifestation of Christ, Made to the Disciples at the Sea of Tiberias

After that storm of the Lord’s Passion—unknown on earth, terrifying to heaven, unheard of through the ages, and intolerable to the underworld—the Lord came to the sea and found his disciples drifting in the darkness of night. For when the sun had fled, what of the moon’s brightness? What of the stars remained for the consolation of night? There was one earth and a confused darkness, which blinded not only bodily sight but the very vision of the mind; nor did it allow those sailing to seek, or to seek again, the shore of faith and the harbor of salvation.

“When morning had come,” says the Evangelist, “Jesus stood on the shore; yet the disciples did not know that it was Jesus” (John 21).

All creation had fled from the injury inflicted upon its Creator. The world tried to avoid the death of its Lord, knowing that vengeance extended to the whole household in which the Ruler had been killed through the crime of his servants. Hence, when its own foundations abandoned it, the earth trembled; the sun fled so that it would not see; the day withdrew so that it would not be present; the rocks, unable by nature to move apart, were split by a new wound, accusing so great a crime by their sound because they could not accuse it by speech; the underworld, overcome when it saw the Judge himself penetrating to it, and howling, lost those whom it held. Hence souls restored to their bodies announced to the living that the dead—whom the world had thought destroyed—would rise again.

Therefore, while the whole structure of the world was fluctuating in utter disorder and thought that, through the death of its author, it had been rolled back into the primordial darkness and ancient chaos, suddenly, by the light of his resurrection, the Lord restores the day and reforms the entire world into its former body, so that he might raise with himself to glory what he had seen suffering with him. As the Evangelist says: “When morning had come”—that is, when the night of the Lord’s Passion had passed—“Jesus stood on the shore.”

[Note: He brought all things back to their original state, from which they had departed.]

He did this to recall everything to its ancient boundary, strengthen what was doubtful, restrain what had been tossed about, compose what was disturbed, and by his standing stabilize the very foundations of the world, which had been so shaken, so that the world might immediately return to the service of its author, from whose injury it had fled.

“When morning had come, Jesus stood on the shore.” He did this especially to restore the Church, in which the disciples were then being tossed upon bitter waves, to the secure station of its faith.

[Note: Grotius says that Christ signifies by this that he is in the shallows, while they are struggling in the deep.]

Finally, because he had found them deprived of the power of faith and had discovered them cast down from manly strength, he rebuked them by calling them “children,” when he said: “Children, do you have anything to eat?” Peter was there, the one who had denied him (Matthew 26); Thomas, who had doubted (John 20); John, who had fled (Mark 14). Therefore he addresses them not as very strong soldiers, but as frightened children; and those whom he had not yet found fit for battle he invites, as tender ones, to the table, saying: “Children, do you have anything to eat?”

[Note: Chrysostom and others likewise teach that the apostles had been afraid.]

Thus he might recall them to grace through kindness, to confidence through bread, and to faith through food.

[Note: *Pulmentarium* is used for any kind of relish or provision; the Greek is προσφάγιον, “something eaten with bread.”]

For they would not believe that the body had risen unless they saw him eating in the full manner of a human being.

[Note: That is, in the same manner in which other human beings eat.]

Hence the fullness of all things asks for food: Bread itself eats, because he does not hunger for food, but always for the love of his own people.

[Note: Christ is called fullness either because he was full of all things and needed nothing, or because through him all are filled.]

“Children, do you have anything to eat?” They answered him, “No.” And what did those have who no longer possessed Christ with them, who still did not see with their eyes the Lord standing before them? “For the disciples did not know that it was Jesus.”

He says to them: “Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find.” He calls back to the right those whom the storm of the Passion had driven and reduced to the left.

“They cast it,” he says, “and they were unable to draw it in because of the multitude of fish.” They had cast it on the right; they had cast it on the manly side; but, still being children, they could not draw it in. Yet from its very weight they perceived that the fish had come at the command of the one who ordered them, not that the catch had resulted from human skill.

[Note: They had cast the net on the right, nearer the shore, where there was less hope of catching anything.]

“Then the disciple whom Jesus loved said: It is the Lord.” The one who is loved sees first, because the eye of love always looks more sharply, and the one who loves always perceives more vividly.

[Note: From the Latin; the printed editions read, “whom he loves.”]

Peter, when he heard this—what had so delayed Peter’s mind that he had to hear from another that it was the Lord, when he had been accustomed to announce the Lord to the others? Where is that extraordinary confession of his: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16, 26)? Where is it? It had fled from the house of Caiaphas, the ruler of the Jews. He saw his Lord more slowly, though he had easily heard the voice of a whispering servant girl.

“When he heard that it was the Lord, he girded his tunic around him, for he was naked.”

Wonderful, brothers! When the Lord was seized, John cast off his linen garment, and Peter was found naked. For flight clothed John, while denial stripped Peter naked.

[Note: In that warm climate Peter went about naked. Or, according to Bede’s interpretation, he is called naked in comparison with the other clothing he usually wore; or because, following the custom of fishermen, he had gone about naked while occupied in fishing.]

Wonderful, brothers, and truly wonderful: the one who was stripped naked in the boat plunges into the sea clothed (Matthew 14).

[Note: The Gospel says that he girded himself with his tunic. And indeed Peter, on seeing the Lord, put on an outer garment, as some think—a kind of cloak used by Phoenicians and Tyrians, says Theophylact—with which he girded himself in order to go more decently to the Lord. This garment, though ankle-length, could not impede swimming, for there was no need to swim: already near land, he could reach the Lord on foot, girded with the garment at his side.]

For innocence is never naked, and guilt always flees toward a covering.

[Note: Others agree. Theophylact, however, and many with him teach that Peter’s shame arose from nakedness, not from guilt.]

Thus, as Adam did (Genesis 3), so now Peter, after his sin, strives to cover his nakedness; both had certainly been clothed in holy nakedness before guilt.

[Note: In Adam there was original righteousness; in Peter, the grace of justification; in both, innocence.

MITA.]

“He girded his tunic around him and threw himself into the sea.” So that the sea might wash away what denial had stained in this way.

“He threw himself into the sea.” So that he who had received primacy in rank might be first in returning.

“And he girded his tunic around him.”

[Note: The Caesena manuscript has: “because.”]

He who was destined to be girded by the suffering of martyrdom, as the Lord says: “Another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish to go” (John 21).

“But the other disciples came in the boat, for they were not far from land, about two hundred cubits, dragging the net of fish.” The others arrive by boat and drag in the catch of fish, so that they might lead the Church, tossed by the storms of the world, and those whom they snatch from the depths and raise into the heavenly light through the Gospel net, together with themselves to the Lord through faithful labor.

“They were not far from land.” They were not far from the land of the living—those whom the end of the present life had already brought near to future things.

[Note: Either the end of the present life or the temporal goods which, by following Christ, they had abandoned.]

“About two hundred cubits.” He doubles the number one hundred from Jews and Gentiles, joining together the life and salvation of the two peoples.

The remaining part of the reading, with the Lord’s help, we shall discuss in the next sermon.

## SERMON LXXIX. On the Resurrection of Christ

Since we have already gone through Matthew’s and Mark’s readings concerning the Lord’s Resurrection, let us now inquire into what the most blessed Luke has proclaimed from this point.

“On the first day of the Sabbath,” he says, “very early in the morning they came to the tomb, bringing the spices they had prepared” (Luke 24).

We have often said that the events surrounding Christ’s resurrection were accomplished as a pattern of our own resurrection. Hence the Evangelists describe the sequence of Christ’s deeds in language that is more mystical than novel.

“On the first day of the Sabbath.” Fittingly “first,” because the day of resurrection knows no second day; the mother of eternal light knows nothing of the time of night; perpetual day perpetually dawns; the light of those who rise cannot die; the light that destroys night knows no extinction.

“They came,” he says, “to the tomb, bringing the spices they had prepared. And they found the stone rolled away from the tomb, and when they entered they did not find the body of the Lord Jesus.”

What is this? Those who earlier had fled from the tomb now return boldly to the sepulcher. Fearless, they return to the fearful burial; they confidently confront the sadness of the tomb. Not finding the Lord, they seek him steadfastly and remain even more steadfastly. Nor are they frightened by the fact that night had been added to the tomb, generating darkness and increasing fear.

[Note: This explains more fully what the Evangelist says occurred “very early”: he speaks of the beginning of their journey, not its end. For the women left Jerusalem on the Lord’s Day before sunrise and arrived about sunrise; John 20:1 says, Πρωῒ σκοτίας ἔτι οὔσης, “early, while it was still dark,” and Mark 16:2, Ἀνατείλαντος τοῦ ἡλίου, “when the sun had risen.”]

[Note: The Evangelist calls them “terrified in mind” because of the sight of the angels and because of the things that had occurred in Christ’s Passion. What is said here—that they had returned to the tomb after preparing spices—is stated by anticipation, since they would not have bought the spices until the Sabbath had passed, toward the evening of the following day.]

Brothers, woman is the cause of evil, the author of sin, the path of death, the title of the sepulcher, the gate of hell, and the entire necessity of lamentation.

[Note: This is the title of the sepulcher in Zamorra’s sense, in *The Mystical Monarchy*, chapter “On Evil Women”: since the title of a sepulcher is “Here lies,” the evil woman does not desist from wicked acts and deceptions until she has led her lustful lover to final destruction. But this is a moral interpretation.

MITA. — The matter may perhaps be derived from elsewhere. Whoever wished to indicate that some matter belonged to him would place a title before it. Augustine, on Psalm 21: “When a powerful person finds his titles, does he not rightfully claim the matter for himself and say: ‘I would not place my titles unless the matter were mine’?” See Du Cange in the *Glossary*. He therefore calls the woman the title of the sepulcher, because she prepared death and the tomb for the whole world. See below, Sermons 154 and 155.]

For this reason women are born for tears, assigned to sorrows, devoted to groans; and in laments they are as strong as they are found weak in bodily strength. As unprepared as they are for labors, so prepared are they for tears. Hence they conquer weapons with tears, bend kingdoms with weeping, and break all the strength of men with lamentation.

It is therefore not surprising if women appear here more ardent than the apostles in tears, at the burial, at the tomb, and in service of the Lord’s body. The woman who first ran to tears, having first run to the fall, runs first to the sepulcher; she who preceded to death precedes to the tomb; she becomes the messenger of the resurrection, who had been the interpreter of death.

[Note: Cyril, cited in Saint Thomas’s *Catena of Works*, vol. V, p. 374 of the recent Venetian edition: “For the woman who had been the minister of death first received and announced the venerable mystery of the resurrection.”]

She who had brought the message of such destruction to the man herself brings to men the report of great salvation, so that by the message of faith she might compensate for what she had taken away through the hearing of unbelief.

This is not a disorderly sequence but a mystical one. The apostles are not placed after the women as though inferior, but are reserved for greater things. The women receive Christ in service; the apostles receive Christ’s sufferings. They carry spices; the others carry scourges. They enter the tomb; the others enter prison. They hasten to service; the others fly toward chains. They pour in oil; the others pour out blood.

[Note: “Oil” is used for the spices that they had prepared for embalming Christ’s body.]

The women marvel at death; the men receive deaths. And what more is there to say? The women remain at home; the men advance into battle, so that as devoted soldiers they may prove their faith through adversity, their courage through labors, their patience through injuries, their willingness to die through dangers, their endurance through wounds, their devotion through punishments, and their steadfastness through the laceration of their inward parts.

Thus the women carry tears for Christ; the apostles, after conquering the devil and defeating their enemies, bring Christ both victory and triumph (Luke 24).

Yet no one should harshly blame the apostles because they are reported either not to have believed the women announcing that the Lord had risen or to have judged their report madness.

[Note: Luke 24:11: “And these words appeared to them as madness.”]

The one who believes more deeply doubts more profoundly; the one who is not a ready hearer cannot easily be deceived.

[Note: The Caesena and Vallicella manuscripts read: “A ready hearer.”] He is exceedingly sluggish who, after an example has been given, is found unguarded. An inexperienced soldier rushes into battle who does not know the cause of the war and is ignorant of the warrior’s strength. It is skill, not sluggishness, when a veteran soldier advances cautiously.

Thus the new Adam fell quickly because he believed quickly; and because he readily lent his ears to the woman’s report, he delivered himself and his descendants to the worst enemy.

[Note: Chrysologus seems to think that Peter, together with John, rose and ran to the tomb after hearing what the women had announced, according to Luke 24:12. He appears to have done this so that, instructed by experience, he would not rashly believe others but would examine with his own eyes whether these things were true. Mita adds that he was trusting not the women, by whose wile he had already been deceived in the courtyard, but only himself, deliberating about what should be believed concerning the resurrection. John 20:3 relates the first approach to the tomb, in which he himself took part. Here Luke speaks only of Peter setting out, or at least mentions Peter alone.]

But veteran Peter did not readily listen to the woman; he was slow to believe the women’s announcement; and as a veteran he deliberated, lest he rush forward like a child.

Finally, when two of the disciples, who after the resurrection had been granted Christ as their companion on the journey, returned and announced that they had seen the Lord, the apostles did not judge what they heard to be madness but recognized it as manly. They lend their ears, fix their mouths, open their eyes, and unfold their hearts; they so commend what is said to their senses that, after the fever of hesitation, they thirstily drink in the report of faith from the river poured forth by the tongue of their companions.

Just as cold drinks extinguish and refresh the heat of thirst, so the hearing of the mind becomes more joyful after grief.

Brothers, who can grasp the reasons for the Lord’s birth? Who deserves to understand the mystery of the Lord’s resurrection? No one can think, comprehend, or judge these things unless he has received that power from God himself: that the Creator of all things is born through a woman’s labor; that the Lord of the world is seen in human servitude; that the shepherd of all needs nourishment; that the one who absolves everyone is handed over to criminals; that the life of the world is punished; that the one who raises the dead dies; that the one who closes all things is enclosed in a tomb; that the Lord of heavenly things is found among the dead.

Who, then, can grasp these things without being surprised when he deeply considers the apostles’ hesitations, trembling, fears, flights, and hiding places?

Therefore, brothers, let us not be surprised that the apostles doubt, or that they receive these great things so slowly and with such belief. We ourselves have not believed even to this point. Let us pray that we may deserve to understand these matters only as much as he grants who enables human beings to perceive divine things.

What remains of the sequence of the reading we shall examine, with God’s help, in the next sermon.

## SERMON LXXX. On Christ’s Resurrection and His Second Manifestation, Made to the Women as They Returned from the Tomb
In the preceding sermon, since we touched upon the first part of the reading, let us today hear what follows.

The angel, it says, answered and said to the women: “Do not be afraid, you; for I know that you are seeking Jesus who was crucified. He is not here, for he has risen, just as he said. Come, see the place where the Lord was laid” (Matt. 28).

Do you suppose that the absence of Peter, John, and all the disciples is being censured, and their sluggishness rebuked, because, when Christ rose, the women alone were the first to meet him, watchful and ardent? Is even that manly portion being marked out in such a way that feminine weakness should hasten ahead toward the glory of the resurrection? Far be it from us, brothers: this has a reason, not an accident; a mystery, not a mere event; an order, not a fault. For here the woman follows the man, rather than precedes him, since the man rises in Christ.

[Note: Some editions read “is censured.” Others read “is burned.”]

[Note: Peter, that is, and the other apostles.]

[Note: This occurred on the very day of the Lord’s resurrection, according to Euthymius and Theophylact. — Mita. It is probable that this was the same manifestation that John records, although Thomas was absent; nevertheless, the apostolic college consisted of that number. Thus, before Judas’s fall, the college was called “the Twelve.” See Duhamel here, and Maldonatus.]

You should therefore understand that Peter did not yield to the women, but to Christ; not to a maidservant, but to the Lord; not to the sacrament, but to sleep; not to fear, but to the divinely established order. Indeed, the man was already in Christ when the angel came to the women, so that, to the degree that the Lord surpasses the angel, the man might precede the woman in honor.

[Note: That is, the male sex, which the Lord Christ assumed when he was born among us.]

[Note: The Caesena manuscript reads: “Therefore it is established.”]

[Note: The male portion of humanity had already been present not only at Christ’s tomb but also in Christ himself through the hypostatic union, when the angel, Christ’s minister, came to teach the women about Christ’s resurrection. — Mita.]

[Note: One should read “the Lord” or “Christ,” not “God,” as appears in the printed books. It would have been easy for the word “Lord,” written in an abbreviation, to be carelessly changed into “God.” Christ the Lord surpasses the angels, first because he is himself the head of the angels, according to the saying in Colossians 2: “who is the head of every principality and power”; and second because Christ, as man, is the eternal priest, who daily offers himself in the unbloody sacrifice of the Mass. From Mita.]

“Do not be afraid, you.” The good are possessed by love, the wicked by dread; fear terrifies the impious, while affection consoles the godly. “Do not be afraid, you.” This is to say: Let the Jew who betrayed him fear; Pilate, who condemned him; the soldier, who mocked him; the impiety that crucified him; the bitter cruelty that offered him the cup; the savagery that besieged him while he lay buried; the treachery that purchased the lie; the faithlessness that sold the truth; the inhumanity that grieves that its Lord has risen, though it does not grieve that it killed him. But you ought to rejoice, not fear, because he whom you sought as dead has risen, and he whom you mourned as slain is alive.

“I know that you are seeking Jesus who was crucified.” That is: Why do you seek the living among the dead? Why do you seek life in a tomb? Go instead to meet the living, and no longer hasten to perform the last service for one who is dying.

[Note: The Caesena manuscript reads: “who gives life.”]

“I know that you are seeking Jesus who was crucified: he is not here.” The angel spoke thus because he opened the tomb for this reason—not so that Christ might come out of it, since he was no longer there, but so that he might show that Christ was no longer there.

“He has risen, just as he said.” Here there is a double power: to return from the dead and to know the future beforehand.

“Come, see the place where the Lord was laid.” Come, women; come, see where you yourselves laid Adam; where you buried the man; where, by your counsel, you thrust the man into confinement; through which you caused the Lord himself to lie there on behalf of his servants. And understand how great is the magnitude of forgiveness granted to you, as great as was the magnitude of the injury done to the Lord.

“Come, see the place where the Lord was laid.” The angelic power confesses that the one who was crucified is the Lord; and human weakness investigates whether the one who rises is truly the Lord.

[Note: This may refer to the Manichaeans, who blasphemously claimed that Christ’s resurrection was fantastic rather than real. See Cyril of Jerusalem, Catechesis 14. Just as Eutyches denied the assumption of a body and impiously taught that the divinity of the Only-Begotten had been fastened to the cross, so he asserted that the divinity, having been committed to the tomb, rose again. Theodoret, *Haereticarum Fabularum* book 4, chapter 13, p. 246. Origen thought that Christ’s body after the resurrection was aerial or ethereal, as may be gathered from book 3 of his work *Against Celsus*, p. 136. Ostorodius, an unfortunate descendant of the Socinian stock, interpolated the same opinion, drawn from the foul pits of Origenist fragments.]

Christ assumed human sufferings in such a way that he did not lose anything belonging to his divinity. “And go quickly, tell his disciples that he has risen, and behold, he will go before you into Galilee; there you will see him.”

Here the apostles are not placed below the women. Rather, the woman is released from guilt, since she who had carried the report of death and ruin now carries the report of life and resurrection.

“And as they went,” it says, “quickly from the tomb, with fear and great joy.” The women enter the tomb so that they may become sharers in the burial and companions in the passion; they leave the tomb so that they may rise first in faith before rising in the flesh.

[Col. 0426B] They leave with fear and great joy. And where is the command, “Do not be afraid”? Fear was not taken away but changed. Fear had departed from guilt, but remained in service; there is an evil fear of fault and a good fear of reverence. They had lost the Adam who had been given to them, and they feared losing him who had been restored.

[Note: Namely, in Christ, who was the new Adam.]

“With fear and great joy.” It is written: “Serve the Lord with fear, and rejoice before him with trembling” (Ps. 2). “With fear and great joy.” For “the fear of the Lord is holy, enduring forever” (Ps. 18). Therefore he remains in holiness who remains in the fear of God.

They were running to announce it to his disciples, and behold, Jesus met them, saying, “Greetings.” Christ meets those who run faithfully, so that they may recognize by sight what they had believed by faith; and his presence may strengthen what their ears still possessed in trembling.

Jesus met them, saying, “Greetings.” He meets them as Lord and greets them as a parent; by affection he gives them courage, and by reverence he preserves them. He greets them so that they may serve through love and not flee through fear.

Then they approached and took hold of his feet. He who had suffered himself to be held wished to be held. They approached and took hold of his feet, so that they might know that the man is in the head of Christ and that they are in the feet of Christ; and that it had been granted them to follow the man through Christ, not to go before him.

[Note: Mita heaps up many arguments here and twists himself remarkably in order to persuade us that Chrysologus’s meaning is that the man is said to be established in the head, since the supreme pontiff is the head of the Church, while women are in the feet—that is, among the number of the faithful, who have been given to follow the man through obedience, but not through usurpation of priestly offices. The matter requires less effort. The man holds the superior place in the Church; the woman is subject to him and follows after him.]

He says to them, “Do not be afraid.” What the angel had said, the Lord also says, so that Christ might make those whom the angel had strengthened still firmer.

[Col. 0427A] But go, tell my brothers to go to Galilee; there they will see me. Rising from the dead, Christ took humanity back up; he did not abandon it. He therefore calls brothers those whom he made kin to his body; he calls brothers those whom he adopted as sons of his Father; he calls brothers those whom, in his goodness, he made his fellow heirs.

But hear how impiety also rises when Christ rises. “Behold, some of the guards came into the city and reported to the chief priests everything that had happened. And when they had assembled with the elders and taken counsel, they gave the soldiers a considerable sum of money, saying: ‘Say that his disciples came by night and stole him while we were asleep.’”

Those who give money do not purchase things to be lost, but things to be preserved. The Jews, when Judas was selling him, bought Christ in order to destroy him; now they poured out a considerable sum of money so that they might destroy themselves—the law, the temple, and their country. Men of blood and deceit establish a price for falsehood; they prepare an instrument of treachery; through a cruel transaction they market fraud against faith and robbery against truth.
