They corrupt the soldiers so that they may call theft what was the mystery of the resurrection: “His disciples came by night and stole him.”

Not content with killing the master, they contrive how they might destroy the disciples; they turn the master’s virtue into the disciples’ crime. “His disciples came by night and stole him.” The soldiers certainly lost him, and the Jews destroyed themselves; but the disciples carried away their master—not by theft, but by faith; by power, not by fraud; by holiness, not by crime; not dead, but alive. This is why they are sent to Galilee, so that they may see him, because God is not seen in the place of treachery.

[Note: For all who had accompanied Christ had come from Galilee, and from Galilee they had set out for the feast of Passover.]

But what he said—“All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth”—declares that he himself had given it to himself in himself, as the Apostle confirms when he says: “God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5). The Son of God gave to the son of the Virgin, God to man, and divinity to flesh what he had always possessed with the Father and the Spirit.

And therefore he says: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” Thus one and the same authority might recreate all nations for salvation, just as it had created them for life.

[Note: Among the Fathers, *to create* is a solemn expression meaning to change for the better. Chrysostom, Homily on 2 Corinthians 5:17: “God creates when he makes a bad man good.” Basil, Oration 4 against Eunomius; Gregory of Nyssa, *On the Aim of the Christian*, vol. 1, p. 224; Theodoret on 2 Corinthians 5:17, and Theophylact there.]

“And behold,” he says, “I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age.” He is always with us who is always with the Father, and he will come to us through that which he assumed from us.

And what more, brothers? What is born, what suffers, what rises, what receives—this is not, not at all, a matter of his own necessity; it is ours, for our salvation.

## SERMON LXXXI  
### On Christ’s fifth manifestation, made to the disciples when Thomas was absent

While rebellious Judea strove to subdue its Creator and raised impious hands against the death of its Author, it removed peace from the earth, dissolved the harmony of things, and broke the covenant of the elements so completely that it seemed to recall the whole world to its ancient chaos.

[Note: Mita says this is an amplification; or perhaps because, with so many prodigies occurring, people feared that it would then take place.]

Finally, it drives away the day, attacks the night, takes light from darkness and heaven from earthly things, makes the earth tremble, mixes the dead with the living, confounds the lower and the upper realms, and, with order dispersed to the injury of the Creator, leaves nothing wholly peaceful and nothing wholly friendly.

This is why Christ, returning from the underworld, cries out in order to restore peace to all things: “Peace be with you.”

“While they were speaking these things,” it says, “Jesus stood in their midst and said to them: ‘Peace be with you.’” He rightly adds “with you,” because now the earth had stood firm, the day had returned, the sun had come back, and the structure of the world had already regained its proper order.

But war still remained among the disciples, and the conflict between faith and faithlessness struck them fiercely. The storm of the passion had shaken the earth no more than it had shaken the hearts of the disciples. Therefore the battle-lines of belief and unbelief ravaged their spirits through persistent conflict. Hosts of thoughts pressed upon their minds, and, amid the sallies of despair and hope, even their sturdy hearts were broken.

Amid Christ’s innumerable miracles and the many forms of his passion; amid the signs of his divinity and the weakness of his flesh; amid the losses of death and the gifts of life, the disciples’ senses and minds were swept about. Now their spirits were lifted to heaven; now their souls collided with the earth. While such a storm raged within them, they could find no harbor of rest and no station of peace.

Christ, the searcher of hearts, saw this. He commands the winds, gives orders to storms, and by a mere nod changes tempests into calm. Immediately he confirms them with his peace, saying: “Peace be with you. It is I; do not be afraid.”

It is I, the one who was crucified, who died, who was buried. It is I. Through me, God; through you, man. It is I. Not a spirit in the appearance of flesh, but the very truth in flesh. It is I. From the dead I am alive; from the underworld I am from above. It is I, from whom death fled, before whom the underworld trembled; Tartarus confessed God when it quaked.

Do not be afraid, Peter, because you denied me; you, John, because you fled; all of you, because you abandoned me; because with all your thoughts you judged me unbelievingly; because even now you do not believe, though you see me (Matt. 26; Mark 14). Do not be afraid: it is I. I am the one who called you by grace, chose you through pardon, sustained you by mercy, carried you through love, and now receive you by goodness alone, because a father does not know how to see faults when he receives back a son, nor does affection see the faults of its own when it takes them back.

“Being troubled,” it says, “and terrified, they thought that they were seeing a spirit.” Why? Because the Lord had entered through closed doors.

[Note: These very disciples had confessed that Christ had risen: “The Lord has truly risen.” Why, then, do they now believe him to be a spirit? Chrysologus gives the appropriate explanation: he had entered through closed doors, and they had perceived no sound of his arrival. Consult Brugensis here.]

The disciples, therefore, overwhelmed by the sleep of sorrow, attributed to Christ not what divine power can do, but what human nature receives. “They thought they were seeing a spirit” (Luke 24). For the spirit of a human being passes through the barriers of the womb and penetrates walls, so that, while the body is closed, it may enter an enclosed body. Likewise, when the soul gives life its end and withdraws from the body’s beloved companionship, it is not held by the barriers of houses or by worldly obstacles. A heavenly substance cannot be confined in earthly prisons, according to the saying: “You do not know where the spirit comes from or where it goes” (John 3).

The disciples, therefore, after the resurrection, when the Lord entered through closed doors, did not believe that he had brought back the solidity of a body. They suspected that the soul had returned only in the image of flesh, as bodily images commonly appear to those who are asleep. “They thought,” it says, “that they were seeing a spirit.”

Thus, as we have said, the wars of thought in the disciples did not subside; rather, the wars of thought increased more and more, and the tumult of their minds was intensified even by the visions themselves. From the very source where faith in the resurrection was being asserted arose the scruple of complete hesitation.

What had come was a reality; that it had entered through closed doors was not faith. It was not faith, but power. It was not human, but it was a man, so that there might be a true body in the power of divinity, not an empty appearance of flesh to the detriment of the resurrection.

[Note: The evangelist’s passage quoted below—“a spirit does not have flesh and bones”—was interpreted differently from other Christians by the Marcionites. From it they inferred that the risen Christ did not have a true body but an imaginary one. Tertullian, book 6 of *Against Marcion*: “He therefore wishes it to be understood as though a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me having them”—that is, as not having bones, like a spirit.]

Therefore, to suppress the conflicts of thought arising from this, Christ answered: “Why are you troubled, and why do thoughts arise in your hearts?” He rightly says “arise,” not “descend,” because human thoughts, weighed down by the burden of flesh, strive to ascend to the height of God’s mystery; and in their very efforts they are broken, fall, and are cast down to earth, unless he helps who grants human beings the ability to think divine things.

“Why are you troubled, and why do thoughts arise in your hearts? See my hands and feet.” “See” means: Be vigilant. Why? Because what you see is not a dream. “See my hands and feet.” Since, with your eyes weighed down, you still cannot look upon the head, see the wounds of the flesh, because you do not yet see the works of God. Consider the marks of the enemies, because you have not yet considered the insignia of God. Touch, so that at least the hand may establish faith, since the seeing eye is so blinded. The eye does not see; let touch see. Let your fingers enter the traces of the nails; let your hands examine the depths of the wound; open the holes in my hands; furrow my side; renew the wounds. I cannot deny my disciples what I did not deny my enemies when they raged to punish me. Touch, touch, and advance as far as the bones, you lofty investigators, so that the bones of the flesh may at least affirm the truth, and so that either the preserved wounds may testify that I am the very same person.

I ask: Why do you not believe that I have risen, when I raised countless dead before your eyes?

[Note: Mita explains “countless” as meaning those who cannot easily be numbered.]

[Note: The apostles still doubted and their minds wavered, as Chrysostom says in Homily 83, and as others also hold.]

Unless, perhaps, the power that was present for others was absent for me, in accordance with that voice which insulted me as I hung upon the cross, saying: “He saved others; he cannot save himself. If he is the king of Israel, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him” (Matt. 27).

And what is greater: to shake off the nails and come down from the cross, or to trample death and ascend from the underworld? Behold, I saved myself; I broke the bonds of the underworld and ascended to the heights, and yet I found no faith in my divinity even among you.

Or perhaps a three-day death prevents belief? Did not my voice call Lazarus, dead four days and already smelling, back from the underworld before your eyes, and did not my command restore him to life (John 11)? If a servant rises after four days, why should the Lord not rise after three?

“While they still did not believe, because of joy, and were amazed…” Vowed-for joys are scarcely believed even when they are granted; when desired things arrive, they produce astonishment. This is why the apostles marvel that Christ’s resurrection came sooner than they had hoped. Their slower belief is not faithlessness but love. For, by examining faith in this way, they do not deny it but seek it; and, while they attend more deeply, they desire what they behold to be true.

Brothers, the disciples’ slowness before such things and their astonishment at such greatness were produced not by fear of faithlessness but by the magnitude of the matter. To see and yet not see, to be ignorant of what they knew, not to believe what they believed—this is caused not by unbelief but by a unique miracle.

Brothers, nature is exceedingly immature when it comes to divine powers. Unless God causes it to grow, it cannot become mature enough to comprehend; it cannot feel what is perfect. Therefore may God himself grant us to grasp through him what we cannot through ourselves, and to perceive what is divine.

## SERMON LXXXII  
### On Christ’s resurrection and his fourth manifestation, made to two disciples going to a village

Since the holy Matthew has already beneficially reported to us what he had learned concerning the Lord’s resurrection, let us today hear what the blessed Mark also relates.

“And when the Sabbath had passed,” he says, “Mary Magdalene, and Mary of James, and Salome bought spices, so that they might come and anoint Jesus” (Mark 16).

[Note: The Bononian manuscript reads “Salomene.”]

Here the women hurry about with feminine devotion. They bring ointments to the tomb not in faith that he is alive but for one who is dead; they prepare the services of mourning for one who has been buried, not the joys of divine triumph for one who has risen.

Christ accepted death so that death might die. When Christ was killed, he killed that which killed everyone. Christ entered the tomb in order to open the underworld. Therefore, once the law of Tartarus had been dissolved, the prison of hell destroyed, and the authority of death itself slain, Christ is no longer to be anointed as a dead man but worshiped as the victor.

[Note: At this passage of Chrysologus the evangelists may be reconciled. One must say that the devout women bought spices on the Sabbath evening itself, that is, after sunset, once the observance had ended (Matt. 28:1); they went outside the city and spent the night awake somewhere there, so that at the first light of the following day they might come and anoint Jesus; setting out on their way, they arrived at the tomb before sunrise (Luke 24:1).]

The women spend the night; they keep watch; they remain sleepless; they penetrate the darkness of the emerging dawn. Hence they seem to endure uncertain light no less in their hearts than in their bodies.

“And very early,” he says, “on the first day of the week, they came to the tomb after the sun had risen.” If it was very early, how had the sun already risen? Does the evangelist not know what he is saying? The evangelist knows what he is saying; but the person who has not learned what he hears does not know. This account is not an error but a statement of truth. It does not suffer from a lapse in human speech; rather, it reveals from heaven the truth of what happened.

He had said: “From the sixth hour until the ninth hour, darkness came over the land” (Mark 15). Therefore the sun, which had withdrawn before its proper hour in order to suffer with the Lord, came forth before its time with brightness when the Lord rose again. It had put its midday brightness to death so that it might mourn with its Creator; now, to rise with its Creator, it burst forth before dawn, overcoming the darkness.

[Note: From the Bononian manuscript: “The sun, which had withdrawn at the hour when the Lord was to suffer, came forth early in order to rise with the Lord.”]

“Very early.” For at that time the sun “made morning.”

[Note: Luke 21:38: “And all the people came early to him.” Peter Damian, book 6, letter 31: “As twilight declined, hastening immediately to the man, he made morning.” Some deny that this is a barbarous word, although Augustine, *Questions on the Book of Judges*, question 46, denies that it occurs among Latin writers. Chrysologus aptly uses it as derived from *mane* (“morning”), to designate a morning journey. Hence *manicationes*, “morning services,” in the Second Council of Tours, chapter 18; and *manicationes festivitatum*, “morning services of festivals,” in Haimo, book 4, section 81. Du Cange cites Chrysologus here in his *Glossary*.]

And the one who had fled before the night now himself anticipates the night in order to drive it away, so that night might restore to the light the hours that the terror of the Lord’s passion had seized.

“They said to one another: ‘Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb?’” From the entrance of the tomb—or from the heart? From the grave—or from the eyes? Women, your breast is shut and your eyes are closed. Therefore you do not see the glory of the opened tomb. If you desire to see, pour oil not upon the Lord’s body but upon the lamp of your hearts, so that through the light of faith what is closed by the darkness of unbelief may be opened.

“And looking up,” he says, “they saw that the stone had been rolled away, for it was very large indeed.” It was plainly large—very large—and now larger in merit than in form, since it had been sufficient both to enclose and to cover the body of the Creator of the world.

And entering the tomb, they saw a young man sitting on the right, clothed in a white robe. They entered the tomb so that, having been buried with Christ, they might rise with Christ from the tomb, and so that the Apostle’s saying might be fulfilled: “You were buried with him in baptism, in which you also rose” (Col. 2).

They see a young man so that they may behold the age of our resurrection. They see a young man because resurrection knows no old age, nor does eternal perfection admit of stages of life. Where a person does not know birth, he does not know death; and where he knows neither birth nor death, there he neither admits the loss of age nor requires its increase.

They see a young man sitting on the right, because resurrection receives nothing leftward. “The ways that are on the right,” says the Lord, “he knows” (Prov. 4, according to the Septuagint). And again: “Then he will place the righteous at his right hand” (Matt. 25, according to the Septuagint).

Pray, brothers, that we may die to vices and be buried with temporal pomp, so that we may rise to eternity in Christ and, placed at his right hand, deserve to hear: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25).

“Clothed in a white robe.” This robe is not made from mortal wool but from life-giving virtue; it shines with heavenly light, not earthly color; it is bright through the Creator’s gift, not through the fuller’s art. As the Prophet says: “You are clothed with light as with a garment” (Ps. 103), and concerning the righteous: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun” (Matt. 13).

Earthly people are clothed in earthly garments; therefore, just as they shine through newness, so they become filthy through age. The heavenly, however, are surrounded by the clothing of heavenly light; raised above earthly squalor, they are never defiled by age and are never darkened by any filth. Rather, the garments that resurrection gives once are clothed forever in perpetual light.

But the women, leaving the tomb, fled, for trembling and terror had seized them. The angel sits in the tomb, while the women flee from the tomb, because he trusts in heavenly substance, whereas they are troubled by their earthly condition. The one who cannot die knows no fear of the tomb, but the women still tremble at the event and, as mortals, remain mortally terrified of the tomb. Hence they say nothing to anyone.

“And they said nothing to anyone.” For women were given to hear, not to speak; to learn, not to teach, as the Apostle says: “Let women keep silence in the churches” (1 Cor. 14). Finally, that same Mary afterward goes and announces the news, but by then she no longer represents a woman but the Church: there, as a woman, she is silent; here, as the Church, she proclaims and speaks.

“After this,” he says, “he appeared to two of them as they were walking.”

Why not three? Why not four, but two? Because the faith of the resurrection is shown here as something to be preached to two peoples—that is, to the Gentiles and the Jews. Hence, as we said, it is demonstrated in the two women, so that one Church may be represented in the two disciples.

[Note: From Latinius; the printed editions read “or.”]

“He appeared in another form.” Let no one suppose that Christ changed the appearance of his face at his resurrection, so that the one who had been in the wound should be someone else in appearance. Rather, his form is changed when he becomes immortal from mortal and incorruptible from corruptible. Thus what changes is the substance, not the person; he acquires glory in his face but does not lose recognition of his face.

[Note: His former appearance remained, but more glorious and more beautiful, says Brugensis. That Christ retained his former appearance is clear from the fact that the disciples needed to recognize him with their eyes. Thus I think Mark is very well reconciled with Luke. The passage appears as follows in the Bononian manuscript: “Hence, as we said, it is shown in this way in the two women, so that one Church might be represented in the two peoples; he appeared by changing himself into another form.”]

And so that a hasty discourse may neither evade nor leap over the questions, let us, with the Lord revealing it, come to know what follows in the next sermon.

[Col. 0432D]

## SERMON LXXXIII  
### On Christ’s ninth manifestation, made to the eleven disciples while they were reclining
Today the blessed Evangelist reported that the apostles, at the very time of the crucifixion, were [Col. 0433A] devoted to tables [Note: [Col. 0433C] The manuscript of Cesena has “detained at the tables.”], intent upon banquets, occupied with feasts, and forgetful of the Lord’s Passion. “While the eleven were reclining,” he says, “the Lord appeared” (Mark 16). Reclining where? At the Lord’s tomb, and soon afterward at the servant’s table? Is this the faith of servants? Is this the love of disciples? Is this Peter’s fervor? Is this the devotion of John, who was taken from Christ’s own breast? Is this the affection acquired over so long a time, through such great gifts and such great virtues, so that [Note: [Col. 0433C] This took place on the very day of the Lord’s resurrection, as Euthymius and Theophylact state. MITA.—It is plausible that this was the same manifestation which John records, although Thomas was absent; yet the apostolic college consisted of that number. Thus, before Judas’s fall, the college was called “the Twelve.” See Duhamel here and Maldonatus.] at the very moment of the Passion, while death was still hot, the burial still recent, the enemies rejoicing and all Judea taunting them, the disciples should dine amid all the splendor of the couch and with all the pleasure of those reclining at table? [Note: [Col. 0433D] The couches on which tables were spread were adorned with every kind of decoration. On this subject see Philo, *On the Contemplative Life*, and Seneca, *On the Shortness of Life*, chapter 12, where he discusses it at length. Chrysologus, however, may perhaps have thought that the disciples used the same upper room in which Christ had eaten the Last Supper, since it had already been prepared. Grotius supports this view.]

[Note: [Col. 0433D] See the dissertation of the very learned Calmet on the death and burial of Moses, appended to the Epistle of Jude, *Dissertations*, vol. II, p. 304, Lucerne edition.]

When Moses died, angels attended him (Jude 9), and God himself took care of his burial; the Jewish camp was halted, the journey was interrupted, the harsh encampment in the wilderness was prolonged, thirty days of mourning were proclaimed, and a servant’s funeral was honored with a long observance of lamentation (Deut. 34). But Christ—the one true Lord, creator of all things, redeemer of all—after that tragic Passion, after death, and death on a cross, remaining three days dead, does not deserve tears from his disciples? The earth trembles, hell is thrown into confusion, rocks are split, tombs burst open, the sun flees, the day is buried, and everything becomes night; yet the disciples alone, at one great *sigma* table [Note: [Col. 0433D] It has been observed elsewhere that *sigma* signifies a table.], in one company, at complete leisure, secure in their pleasures, feast—and this, brothers, is how the Master himself found them when he returned from the underworld:

“While the eleven were reclining, the Lord appeared and reproached them for their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who had seen him risen.”

What shall we say to this, faithful Peter, most devoted Peter? “While they were reclining.” Were they dining? Brothers, this [Note: [Col. 0433D] Chrysologus rightly retracts his earlier statement. The disciples were reclining—that is, sitting together—not dining when Christ appeared to them, although this happened at mealtime, when they had food prepared, which the Lord wished to use to prove the truth of his resurrection, as Brugensis and Maldonatus say; or, according to others, at the end of the meal, when they were not so much eating as conversing with the two who had returned from Emmaus.] was not reclining at a feast, but lying down; that company was not a banquet, but an assembly of grief. There was no bread of joy there, but of sorrow; there the cups were mixed with the gall of the cross, not with the sweetness of wine.

“They were shut in because of fear of the Jews” (John 20). [Note: [Col. 0434C] Here Chrysologus maintains the opinion that this was the same manifestation of which John speaks. See above, no. 2.] If they were afraid, if they were shut in, certainly they were not dining; and if they were not dining, that house was not a dining room but a prison; that *sigma* was not a table but a tomb. Then the whole punishment of the Lord’s Passion had passed over to the disciples. The lance of grief was fixed not only in their sides but also in their hearts. Then the nails of sadness held fast their hands and feet. Then vinegar was offered them; then Jewish bitterness offered them gall. Then their sun set and their day fled. Then the deepest night possessed their minds and souls. Then the fiercest temptation of their thoughts dashed them against the rocks of treachery and into the shipwreck of faith. Then despair—the worst of all evils, which always comes last amid adversities—laid them out in sepulchers of death.

Therefore, as we said, the Lord found them not reclining at table, not feasting, but lying down—buried. And so he reproaches their unbelief, because they had believed despair so completely that they believed nothing of the resurrection foretold by the Lord; they would not believe the servants who announced it; [Note: [Col. 0434D] Augustine also, book III *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*; Euthymius, Brugensis, and Grotius write that Christ rebuked the apostles because they did not believe Mary Magdalene, Peter, the two disciples at Emmaus, and so many others who affirmed that they had seen him alive again.] [Col. 0434B] they left in themselves no faith and no hope of salvation, but, dead to the world and buried in it, all believed that they had only one house, one tomb for themselves. Hence, when the Lord saw that they had withdrawn from the world, he calls them back to the world and sends them into the world, saying:

“Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature.”

Come into the world, so that you who think that you are all already lying in one dwelling may suddenly see the whole world subject to you. Come into all the world; preach the Gospel to every creature. This means: Be yourselves the hope of all those for whom you were the cause of despair in yourselves. Then test how great your unbelief is, when you see the world believe your hearing, although you were unable to believe your sight; and then recognize how great is the hardness of your hearts, when, without seeing me, you perceive that the whole world confesses me—me whom you denied when I was placed before your eyes.

You will see people divided across the earth, shut away on islands, hanging from cliffs, withdrawn into solitude; the shallow dabblers in magic [Note: [Col. 0434D] For the astrologer presumes to know everything while knowing nothing.], the faultfinding Greeks [Note: [Col. 0434D] If one may use the term “soothsayers,” the Greeks are called *queruli* (“complainers”) because they are wordy; or, as Oecumenius has it in his commentary on Jude 16, p. 230: *Μεμψίμοιρος* (*mempsimoiros*), “one who is always eager to cavil at everything.” Hesychius translates *Μεμψίμοιρος* as “complainer.”], and the skilled Romans [Note: [Col. 0434D] Because they are experienced through long practice in human affairs. MITA.] seeking by faith alone the faith which you sought with hand and finger by tracing my wounds.

But because I send you as witnesses of my Passion, my death, and my resurrection, I grant that you have examined these matters more deeply—provided that [Note: [Col. 0434D] The apostles’ doubts strengthen you all the more. Radulphus Ardentius, homily 69: “He wished them to be unbelieving for a time so that we would not doubt.” See note 17 of the following sermon.] your hesitation becomes a foundation for those who will believe you.

“He who believes and is baptized will be saved.”

Brothers, what the soul is to the body, faith is to baptism. Hence he who is born from the font lives by faith: “The righteous man lives by faith” (Rom. 1). Therefore everyone who is without faith dies.

“He who believes”—because God is one Trinity; because in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit there is one majesty in complete equality; because the Godhead is distinct in the Trinity, not confused in unity, but is one in Godhead and three in persons; [Note: [Col. 0435C] The printed editions read “divided.” Above, in Sermon 60, he expressly said: “The Trinity is distinct in persons; it is not divided.” He also implies this in Sermon 88. The text is therefore thought corrupt through scribal carelessness. MITA.] because “God” is the name of the Trinity; because the Father and the Son are not to be ranked according to order but valued according to love; because the Holy Spirit must not be regarded as inferior, greater, or lesser; because he must not be regarded as more or less external, since the Godhead knows nothing external; because Christ became man in such a way that he remained what he is, God; because he died in such a way that throughout all ages he might raise the dead from death; because he did not rise for himself but for us; because he carried us into heaven when he raised himself to heaven; because he sits [Note: [Col. 0435D] The ancient theologians explain Christ’s sitting at the right hand of the Father after the Ascension as indicating his office as Judge. See Gregory the Great, p. 119, Paris edition, homily 29: “What does it mean that Mark testifies that he saw him seated, while Stephen testifies that he saw him standing? You know, brothers, that sitting is the posture of one judging, while standing is the posture of one fighting or helping.”] in the authority of a Judge, not in the rest of one who is weary; because he will come—not from a place, since he is everywhere and comes in order to move things; nor to hold his own world, since he possesses the whole world; but so that the world may now and forever deserve to behold its creator.

Let a person believe also in the forgiveness of sins, because although the heavenly realm is exceedingly vast, it does not admit a sinner; nor should anyone despair because of the magnitude of his sins, since if there were something God could not forgive, he would not be almighty.

Let him believe also in the resurrection of the flesh, so that the very person who rises may receive the penalty for his sin, and the very person who labors may receive the reward. [Note: [Col. 0435D] These words are absent from many editions.]

Let him believe in eternal life, so that the second death may have no place.

That demons—the ancient enemies—are driven from human bodies; that varied speech is poured forth from one mouth in many languages; that serpents, when touched through Christ, do not know their own poison; [Note: [Col. 0435D] The Greek words agree: *ὄφεις ἀροῦσι*, “they will take up serpents,” or “they will lift them with their hands.”] that those who drink poisoned cups are unable to be harmed through Christ; that diseases of the body are driven away when those who preach Christ touch the sick—this, brothers, is the supreme sign of faith.

“These signs,” he says, “will accompany those who believe: In my name they will cast out demons; they will speak in new tongues; they will pick up serpents; and if they drink anything deadly, it will not harm them; they will lay hands on the sick, and they will be well.”

Therefore, human being, become a physician to yourself through faith, lest you be forced, at your own expense, to submit to foreign physicians and buy dearly what you possess freely. [Note: [Col. 0435D] Not cheaply, but at great cost.]

Pray, brothers, that even in the present we may always experience the medicine of faith, and that, placed in expectation of Christ, we may at his coming rejoice, secure in our conscience.

## SERMON LXXXIV  
### On Christ’s fifth manifestation to the disciples when Thomas was absent, and his sixth when he was present

During the forty days in which the Lord is reported—and believed—to have appeared to his disciples in various ways after his resurrection, the sermon rightly serves those very readings and labors on those very mysteries, so that it may transform the sorrow of the Lord’s Passion, through the manifold evidence of the resurrection, into the joy of your love; and so that he who previously rose by his power in our body may now also rise by faith in our hearts.

“And when it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, and the doors were shut where the disciples were gathered because of fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood in their midst” (John 20).

“When it was evening”: it was evening more because of sorrow than because of the hour. Evening is the darkness of grief, with minds clouded by sadness. It was evening because, although twilight had offered some indication of the resurrection, the Lord had not yet shone upon them with the full brightness of his light.

“And when the doors were shut where the disciples were gathered because of fear of the Jews.” The magnitude of terror and crime, in so great a storm, had closed both the disciples’ house and their hearts, and had so completely excluded every entrance of light that, with their senses more and more occupied by grief, the blind darkness of night increased. No darkness of night can be compared with the gloom of grief and fear, because it cannot be tempered by any light of consolation or counsel.

Hear the prophet: “Fear and trembling came upon me, and darkness covered me” (Ps. 54).

“And when the doors were shut where the disciples were gathered because of fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood in their midst.”

Why should anyone doubt that absolute Divinity could penetrate the mystery of a closed body and a virginal dwelling sealed in complete integrity, when after the resurrection of our body—which has been thickened by the mystery [Note: [Col. 0435D] That is, divinity joined to humanity. “Absolute Divinity,” that is, simple Godhead. It should be noted that Christ’s person, considered precisely and in itself, is free from every composition; but Christ’s person considered as subsisting in a human nature, or as the terminus resulting from the union, is not simple but composite, just as the union of the Incarnation itself is a true composition, as Bonacina teaches theologically after others, *On the Incarnation*, disputation 2, question 5, point 3. MITA.]—he enters and leaves through closed doors, [Note: [Col. 0436D] Cyril of Jerusalem: “Let no one ask how the Lord’s body passed through closed doors, when he understands that these things are written not of a mere man, but of the almighty Son of God.” Calvin, Clericus, and other people of that faction interpret this passage as though Christ entered by opening the doors himself. But if Christ himself opened the doors, how can the Evangelist write that he entered while the doors were shut? They reply: the words “when the doors were shut” indicate the time when he entered, namely evening, when doors are shut, not the manner of his entry. But the Evangelist had already noted this: “When it was evening.” The pleonasm would therefore be useless here. These are false and futile inventions, because this passage was an argument for Catholics asserting Christ’s real presence in the Eucharist, and they used it, though not as an irrefutable proof, to establish it.] and by such a sign shows himself to be the creator of every creature, one whom no creature resists and to whom every creature serves in all things? [Note: [Col. 0437C] Alternative reading: “but if [there was] a conception.”]

But if virginity cannot excuse its conception and birth before its creator; if a closed door cannot deny its creator entrance and exit; how could the stone of the tomb, however large, however sealed by Jewish malice, resist the Savior rising?

Yet just as virginity and the door, by their barriers, give assurance of his divinity, so the stone rolled away confirms the resurrection. Though rolled away, it prepared no exit for its Lord, but affords and admits an entrance to the night of faith. [Note: [Col. 0437D] I corrected this from the manuscript of Cesena, where the earlier reading was *resolutus* (“loosed”). But that reading is corrupt. For the angel did not roll away the stone so that Christ could rise; rather, after he had risen from the closed tomb, the angel rolled away the stone so that people might see that Christ no longer lay in the tomb. Therefore the stone rolled away from the entrance of the tomb confirmed the disciples in faith in Christ’s resurrection. Another manuscript reads *resignatus* (“unsealed”). MITA.]

“Jesus came and stood in their midst, and said to them: Peace be with you.”

The hearts of the disciples were engaged in continual battles between faith and doubt, despair and hope, weakness and courage. Foreseeing the wars of such thoughts, he who saw their hidden places first returned to those who saw him the peace of their inner selves, so that he who had been taken away and left material for conflict, when restored to their eyes, might remove the whole cause of their struggle.

“The disciples rejoiced,” he says, “when they saw the Lord.”

They rejoiced: as light after darkness is more welcome, and calm after the gloom of a storm, so joy is more pleasing after sorrow.

He says to them again, “Peace be with you.” What does this repeated gift of peace reveal, except that he wishes the tranquility he had imposed upon the senses of each to be preserved among them also through a repeated gift of peace? He knew that afterward they would have no small struggles because of their hesitation: one would boast that he had remained steadfast in faith, while another would grieve that he had doubted.

Therefore, in order to cut away the arrogance and swelling pride of the boaster, and to heal and exclude the sufferings of the one who had been weakened, the merciful ruler attributed everything that had happened to the situation, not to the disciples, and by the command of his peace suppressed the wars that were about to arise, lest one reproach another for what he himself, to whom everything was owed, had granted in the future.

Peter denies, John flees, Thomas doubts, and all abandon him (Matt. 26; Mark 14; John 20). If Christ had not given them his peace, Peter, who was first among them all, might have been considered inferior, and the one who followed him might perhaps have been improperly raised up against the first.

“As the Father sent me, so I also send you.” [Note: [Col. 0437D] He is referring to the heretics who impiously dared to proclaim from this Gospel passage that the Son is inferior to the Father—Arius and the sons of the Arians.]

The statement “sent” does not diminish the Son; it declares that Christ wished us to understand here not the authority of the one who sends but the love of the one who is sent, when he says, “As the Father sent me.” Not “the Lord,” but “the Father.” “So I also send you.” Not yet with the authority of one commanding, but with the whole affection of one who loves: “I send you” to endure hunger, to bear the burdens of chains, to the squalor of prison, to undergo every kind of punishment, to lift from all people the accursed yoke of death. All these things love imposes upon human minds, not power. [Note: [Col. 0437D] See Gregory the Great, homily 27, p. 116, verso, column 1.]

“Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained.” [Note: [Col. 0437D] The unanimous consensus of the Fathers, the councils, and the whole Church is that Christ here communicated to the apostles the power to forgive sins.]

He gave the power to forgive sins—the one who by his breath infused himself into their hearts and bestowed upon them the Forgiver.

“When he had said this, he breathed on them and said: Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them.”

Where are those who prescribe that sins cannot be forgiven by human beings through human beings? [Note: [Col. 0437D] He is touching upon the Novatian heresy, which once denied pardon to the fallen. See note 7 of Sermon 94.] Where are those who crush people once they have fallen through the devil’s impulse, so that they cannot rise again; who, with a cruel spirit, withdraw care from the sick and treatment from the wounded, and deny them medicine; who impiously insult sinners with despair of returning? [Note: [Col. 0438C] Elsewhere: “so that they may not rise again.”] [Note: [Col. 0438C] Thus in Mita’s edition. Other editions read: “who impiously repel sinners through despair of forgiveness and return.” What if the reading should be: “who impiously press despair of return upon them”?]

Peter forgives sins and receives penitents with complete joy, [Note: [Col. 0438C] This was the view of the Fathers, the councils, and all Catholic commentators. See the Council of Trent, session 14, canon 3; and the Fathers cited by Bellarmine, *On Penance*; Menochius, Brugensis, and others.] and embraces for all priests this power granted by God. For if, after his denial, he had not sought repentance, he would have lost equally the glory of the apostleship and life itself. And if Peter returned through repentance, who can stand without repentance?

But Thomas, when he heard from his fellow disciples that they had seen the Lord, replied: “Unless I see the mark of the nails and place my hand in his side, I will not believe.”

Why does Thomas seek the traces of faith in this way? [Note: [Col. 0438D] The Greek *τὸν τύπον* means “the place of the nails”; our translator renders it quite appropriately “the traces of faith.”] Why does he examine so harshly the one who suffered so patiently and so piously, now risen? [Note: [Col. 0438D] Clericus denies, in his notes on this Gospel passage, that there were scars on Christ’s feet, because, he claims, nails had not been driven into them. But all antiquity cries out against him, for which there is no doubt that Christ’s feet too were pierced by nails. The only question is whether one nail was used or one for each foot. Drusius, a writer not unfriendly to Clericus, says that Christ was crucified with four nails, one through each hand and one through each foot. As for Clericus, we need no witnesses against him, since Luke says that Christ showed Thomas the marks of the wounds both in his hands and in his feet.]

Why does that devoted right hand so probe the wounds which impious hands inflicted? [Note: [Col. 0438D] Another reading has: “thus investigates.”] Why does his obedient hand strive to reopen the side which the lance of the impious soldier exposed? Why does the harsh curiosity of a servant renew the pains inflicted by the fury of persecutors? Why does the disciple seek to test the Lord by torments and God by punishments, the heavenly physician by a wound?

The power of the devil has fallen; the prison of hell has been opened; the chains of the dead have been broken; when the Lord died, the tombs were torn open; and when the Lord rose, the whole condition of death was changed. From the Lord’s most sacred tomb the stone has been rolled away, the linen cloths have been loosened, death has fled before the glory of the risen one, life has returned, and the flesh has risen, no longer destined to know falling.

Why, Thomas, do you alone demand that only the wounds be presented to you as proof of faith, too clever an examiner? What if those wounds had been erased along with the others—what danger would this curiosity have brought upon your faith? [Note: [Col. 0439C] Gaudentius uses this same word when speaking of Thomas, sermon 16, p. 189.] Do you think that no memorials of piety, no proofs of the Lord’s resurrection could have been found unless you traced with your own hands the entrails marked by Jewish cruelty?

This piety sought, brothers, this devotion demanded that even impiety itself should not afterward doubt that the Lord had risen. [Note: [Col. 0439C] Gregory, *Homily 26 on the Gospel*: “Thomas’s unbelief benefited us more than the faith of the disciples, because while he is led back to faith by touching, our mind is strengthened after every doubt has been set aside.” Gaudentius, in the same place: “The fact that he sought the Lord more eagerly both to see and to touch was entirely arranged for our salvation.”]

But Thomas was concerned not only with the uncertainty of his own heart, but with that of all human beings. As a vigorous executor who would preach these things among the nations, he sought how he might set forth the mystery of so great a faith. Certainly this was prophecy rather than hesitation. For why would he ask such things unless, by a prophetic spirit, he had recognized that the wounds alone had been preserved by the Lord as evidence of his resurrection? [Note: [Col. 0439D] Hilary and Leo also teach that Christ retained the marks of the wounds in his glorified body so that it might be clear that the body which had been crucified was the same body that rose.]

Finally, he freely provided the others with what this man had requested later.

“Jesus came and stood in their midst and showed them his hands and his side.”

For he who had entered through closed doors, and who was rightly thought by the disciples to be a spirit, could not otherwise prove to doubting people that he was himself except through the very suffering of the body and the marks of its wounds.

Finally, he came and said to Thomas: “Put your finger here and see my hands; bring your hand and put it into my side; and do not be unbelieving but believing.”

So that, when you open them again, these wounds may pour forth faith throughout the whole world—wounds which have already poured out water for washing and blood as the price of all. [Note: [Col. 0440C] Many commentators agree with Chrysologus that water mystically signifies baptism and blood redemption.]

Thomas answered and said: “My Lord and my God!”

Let the heretics come and hear this; and, as the Lord said, let them not be unbelieving but believing. Behold, Thomas’s cry manifests that Christ is not merely a human body but, through the sufferings of his punished body, God and Lord. [Note: [Col. 0440C] This is the first time in the Gospel that the title “God” is read as attributed to Jesus Christ. The Fourth Council of Constantinople branded Theodore of Mopsuestia with an anathema for interpreting Thomas’s words as though they arose from fear and astonishment and referred to God the Father, so that the glory due to him might be rendered for so great a prodigy, rather than referring to Christ. Our author, however, most explicitly teaches that the natures in Christ are unmixed, against Nestorius and Eutyches.]

And truly he is God, who lives from death and rises from a wound; for after undergoing such things, so great and so many, God lives and reigns throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 0440D] In some editions this sermon is entitled “On the passage of John: ‘Now it was the middle of the feast.’”]

## SERMON LXXXV  
### On Christ’s entrance into the temple and the Jews’ astonishment

Although some things appear hidden because of the depth of their mystery, no solemnity of ecclesiastical worship is without fruit. A divine feast is not to be consecrated according to our wishes, but cultivated for the sake of its own virtues. The Christian mind does not know how to drive into despair the things handed down by the Fathers and strengthened by the passage of time; rather, it desires to venerate them with the whole language of devotion.

“Now about the middle of the feast,” he says, “the Lord went up into the temple” (John 7).

Which temple? “Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (1 Cor. 3).

Today the Lord ascended into the temple of our breasts, having so mercifully descended into the form of our body. That God’s ascent takes place in the height of the human heart, the blessed prophet asserts when he sings: “Blessed is the man whose help is from you, Lord; your ascents are in his heart” (Ps. 83).

“Now about the middle of the feast, the Lord went up into the temple.”

The Lord rightly went up into the temple in the middle of the feast, because he was going to provide us from heaven with a perfect feast day. Whatever was sublime, whatever in human hearts reached toward heaven, the weight of the Lord’s Passion had bent down as far as hell.

This is why Christ remains and lingers on earth for forty days. If it may be said so, he delays meeting the Father and suspends the Father’s embrace until he reveals himself completely and [Note: [Col. 0440D] Saint Leo, sermon 1: “Christ delays his Ascension for the space of forty days so that the Lord Jesus might truly be recognized as risen, since he had truly been born, suffered, and died.”] refashions them into the glory of his ascension. [Note: [Col. 0440D] Christ is formed again in their minds—the same one who existed before his death, namely God and man in the unity of one suppositum. MITA.]

Therefore, in whose temple Christ has not ascended, that person will not ascend to heaven with Christ.

He ascended into the temple, taught, and the Jews were astonished, saying: “How does this man know letters, when he has not studied?”

They rightly marvel that Christ knows without having learned, when they themselves are shown to have learned and to teach the precepts of the law without knowing them, as the Lord says: “You are a teacher in Israel, and you do not know these things?” (John 3).

The Jews, already rebellious, were astonished and unwilling to believe. They know how to marvel; they refuse to understand and are able only not to know. [Note: [Col. 0441C] Other copies read: “they are able not to know.”]

“The Jews were astonished, saying: How does this man know letters, when he has not studied?”

You detract from the fact that a virgin gave birth, yet do not marvel. You reject that God feels and acts in our body, yet do not confess it. [Note: [Col. 0441C] In some editions, “is perceived.”] You do not marvel that the blind sees, the deaf hears, the lame runs, the dead rises, and Christ speaks the whole mystery of God; yet this alone—that he knows without having learned—is what astonishes you?

This is the one who did not learn letters but gave them. This is the one who created understanding, through which letters are formed. Why should anyone wonder that the one skilled in the law, the author of all things, did not learn letters? God is certainly present—the origin of all things—who makes what was not exist; though he has not learned, he teaches.

[Note: [Col. 0441C] Some editions note this omission.]

A considerable amount appears to be missing.

[Note: [Col. 0441C] A considerable amount appears to be missing. MITA.]

## SERMON LXXXVI  
### On the annunciation and conception of the blessed John the Baptist
Worldly speech, as it is uttered from human understanding, serves and accommodates human minds; divine speech, however, lies in the power of the one who gives it, not of the one who speaks it. You have heard how that Zacharias, [Note: [Col. 0441C] Chrysologus follows the opinion of those who think that Zacharias held the dignity of high priest, and not merely that of an ordinary priest, and that he belonged to the division of Abijah, as Luke I seems to suggest to some. Ambrose, on Luke I, under the heading “On Zacharias’s entrance into the Temple”: “It seems that this Zacharias is here designated as high priest, because once a year the high priest alone entered the second sanctuary.” [Col. 0441D] See Augustine, Homily 49 on John; Bede, Homily on the Vigil of St. John the Baptist; Theophylact, Brugensis, and others.] while he was entreating in the splendor of the high priesthood, became mute; the father of the voice fell silent. “I,” he says, “am the voice of one crying in the wilderness” (John I); the father of the cry became mute. And the man who had entered to return an answer came out bringing silence, [Note: [Col. 0441D] Drusius infers from several rabbinic writings that it was customary for priests to experience appearances of angels, who convey God’s commands to human beings, especially when they were burning incense. Zacharias, however, had not entered the inner sanctuary to receive God’s commands, but to burn incense.] having entered to bring back the response.

You see, therefore, that my silence, which previously saddened you, arose from ancient priestly custom, not from an unexpected occurrence. When he perceived that the bonds of his tongue had closed the door of his speech, he commanded by a sign that no one should inquire into the reasons for his silence, because he had not learned to speak the heavenly mystery, though he had learned to understand it. But this was only for a time, [Col. 0441C] because the priest’s speech is deferred, not taken away; hidden, not denied; suspended for the sake of the mystery, not driven away.

Finally, Zacharias’s silence itself is not a punishment but a sign; it is not an earthly weakness but a heavenly secret. God, who grants speech, causes silence; he commands silence who implants the word. Divine speech rules and does not serve, because God is the Word; and therefore it speaks not when it is commanded, but when it commands; [Col. 0442A] not when it is demanded, but when it gives; not when it is compelled, but when it comes.

Therefore, brothers, when it comes, listen; when it does not come, endure; when it gives itself, receive it; when it withholds itself, pray—for the teacher receives what the hearer deserves. Thus the speech that had been withheld from both you and me [Note: [Col. 0441D] Rubeus, *History of Ravenna*, book II, p. 109. Chrysologus: “Although he was exceedingly forceful in speaking and, as it were, carried away in divine fury, nevertheless, in the very heat of his discourse, his voice would be extinguished.” This occurred especially in the sermon he delivered about the woman suffering from a flow of blood. Tillemont, however, thinks that the reference is to Sermon 35, which is shorter than the others.] was withheld so that the woman’s flow, the cause of her shameful wound, and her modesty might be concealed by our own shame in such a way that what she kept silent would also be enclosed by our silence (Matthew IX). But let us return to the word with which we began.

The Jerusalem spring overflows when the angel stirs it (John V), not when the hearer thirsts; so the priest’s speech abounds when God gives it, not when the priest preaches. This is why Zacharias himself, who spoke prophecies to the people, is silent for himself, so that we may not be ungrateful to God if he has once willed us to be silent, [Col. 0442B] although he has always generously granted us unhindered speech. [Note: [Col. 0442C] Elsewhere: “to whom he has more frequently.”]

He does not disdain to receive a word from the Son to whom he had given light. And you, sons, pray for a voice on our behalf, so that you may be able to hear the word. Restore my joy, so that you may be able to possess the joy to which you are accustomed and fulfill the Apostle’s saying: “Who is there who can make me glad except the one who is saddened by me?” (II Corinthians II).

Let blessed Zacharias, then, come—let him come into our midst—who, by remaining silent, consoles us with a devout example and, by his silence, does not allow us to be sad about our own silence. Let him come, let him come: the forerunner of the Word, the mirror of the priesthood, the model of holiness, the first of the evangelists, [Note: [Col. 0442C] For prophecy had ceased with him. Chrysostom, drawing on various passages of Matthew, calls him “the silence of the prophets” in Homily 20, p. 1074 of the Paris edition.] the conclusion of the prophets.

“There was,” he says, “in the days of Herod, king of Judea, a certain priest named Zacharias” (Luke I). [Note: [Col. 0442C] This was Herod surnamed the Great, notorious for the murder of the Innocents and for other crimes. [Col. 0442D] He calls him king in order to distinguish him from the other Herod, the tetrarch of Galilee. John’s conception occurred in the twelfth year of Herod.] When it is stated under which king a priest lived, evils are tempered: consolation is always present in grief, and a consoler is not absent when a persecutor is near.

“There was in the days of Herod, king of Judea, a certain priest named Zacharias.” Until Herod, priestly holiness, the dignity of old age, and the piety of fathers presided over the Jewish people. The divine law was their rule; ambition had no power there, nor recklessness, nor presumption, because everything was conducted according to divine order, not human arrangement. But Herod, [Note: [Col. 0442D] For he was the son of Antipater and the grandson of Antipas. Antipas, a pagan by religion, was either born or raised at Ascalon and was the first to embrace the Jewish religion when he governed Judea under King Hyrcanus. Antipater, who followed the religion of his father Antipas, raised his sons Phasael and Herod the Great in the Jewish law. It is therefore strange that Hardouin maintains that Herod was a pagan, born at Athens and devoted to the Platonic school, which he himself transferred to the Herodians. Basnage removes these fables in his French *History of the Jews*, vol. I, p. 63.] coming [Col. 0443A] from a foreign people, invaded the kingdom, [Note: [Col. 0443D] After Antigonus II, son of Aristobulus, grandson of Alexander Jannaeus, and the last of the Hasmonean line, had died—having been beheaded or crucified at Antioch by order of Mark Antony, the Roman commander—Herod usurped the kingdom.] violated the priesthood, confused the order of things, changed customs, [Note: [Col. 0443D] He dethroned the aged King Hyrcanus and forced him to live as a private citizen.] despised the old, [Note: [Col. 0443D] Namely, Alexander and Aristobulus, his sons by Mariamne, whom he beheaded. Some printed editions incorrectly read: “He infected the young.” Chrysostom, in the passage cited: “Herod profaned the Temple, abolished the priesthood, confused the order, violated the kingdom, corrupted everything that belonged to religion, law, custom, and faith, and destroyed and confused it all … the murderer of his sons,” and so forth.] killed the young, mingled the tribes, erased genealogies, corrupted lineage, and utterly removed everything that belonged to divine and human discipline.

But what does this have to do with holy Zacharias? Therefore, so that no such deed might be thought to have been committed by Zacharias himself, the evangelist is compelled to report it in this way: “There was in the days of Herod, king of Judea, a certain priest named Zacharias, of the division of Abijah.” [Note: [Col. 0443D] The dignity of the royal priesthood had been assigned by God to the family of Aaron. The high priesthood, however, belonged to the firstborn. The other members of the family were ordinary priests who, from the reign of David onward, had been divided into twenty-four classes and served in their appointed rotations. Josephus observes that this division remained in use until the destruction of the second Temple at Jerusalem, *Jewish Antiquities*, book VII.]

Because his lineage had been transmitted to him from forefathers, grandfathers, and fathers, and had remained priestly down to him; because the entire discipline of the law and of sacrifice had been preserved; and because it restrained the impiety of the king, the wickedness of the age, the frenzy of ambition, and the madness of recklessness through the priest’s merit [Note: [Col. 0444D] The passage has been restored from the manuscript of Cesena; the printed editions read: “and surpassed merit and life.”] and life—let us hear what follows.

“It happened that, when he entered the Temple of the Lord, he was chosen by lot to burn incense, and the whole multitude of the people was praying outside at the hour of incense.” [Note: [Col. 0444D] There were two hours of incense. Grotius understands the morning hour; Chrysologus and the more careful interpreters with him understand the evening hour.]

At the hour of incense, brothers, the Jewish sun was already setting in the Temple, so that the morning might rise in the Church; evening was pressing upon Jewish teaching because the dawn of the Gospel was approaching; the day of the law was growing dim so that everything might shine forth in grace.

This is why Zacharias, at the hour of incense—that is, at the final period of the legal ceremonies—brings incense with prophetic Spirit: he offers prayers, presents desires, commends vows, recalls the time, repeats the promises, [Note: [Col. 0444D] Zacharias was praying. Was he praying for the birth of a child? Since both were already advanced in age, he scarcely hoped for this. His prayer therefore seems to have been for the salvation of the people and the coming of the awaited Messiah. Duhamel here. See note 4 on Sermon 88.] and demands Christ.

“And the whole multitude was praying outside.” Thus he entreats that the people standing outside may be admitted, because those whom the law brings to the door, grace admits into the Temple.

“And an angel of the Lord appeared to him, standing at the right side of the altar of incense; and when Zacharias saw him, he was troubled, and fear fell upon him.” Therefore it is not surprising if a priest is troubled, if a teacher is astonished, if a prelate is afraid, if the lesser becomes silent when he sees the greater, if he abandons words when he beholds signs.

And so that Zacharias may not seem to have been the only one who was afraid, hear another prophet saying: “Lord, I heard your report and was afraid; I considered your works and was terrified” (Habakkuk III). The one who speaks with God is overcome with fear; he does not know from where the angel is speaking. And what are we to understand? Why should the priest be silent? Let us now say.

“And the angel answered him: ‘I am Gabriel, who stand before the presence of God, and I have been sent to speak these things to you and to announce these things to you. And behold, you will be silent and unable to speak.’” [Col. 0444A] What fault is there in the one who is silent, if the power of the one commanding imposes silence?

Therefore, we who are so insignificant and have been silent: understand that our silence was not due to forgetfulness but to circumstance; it arose from divine business, not from human deliberation. Let us not be sad, then, because, by God’s gift, the silence of a moment will be repaid by continued speech, and our small measure of sadness will be turned into great joy.

I give thanks to my God, who has turned the loss of speech into a gain of love for me. For how great your affection for me is, your pallor revealed, [Note: [Col. 0444D] Rubeus, in the passage cited, draws from this how dear Chrysologus was to the people of Ravenna and how greatly they delighted in him.] your shouting testified, your tears showed, and your outpouring of prayer made evident.

## SERMON LXXXVII. On the same subject.

Just as light becomes harmful to eyes darkened by excessive pain and prolonged illness unless it is gradually poured back upon them—since light was created for the eyes alone and is friendly to the eyes alone, through which it is either conveyed to the rest of the body or withheld from it—so, when minds have been darkened by the long illness of unbelief, unless the brightness of faith is restored little by little, the very sudden brilliance of faith makes the darkness of unbelief grow thicker. By long habit, nature is always either extended or blunted. [Note: [Col. 0444D] With Latinus. The printed editions read “daytime.”]

This is why the Lord, wishing to shine upon hearts already blinded by the foul cloud of unbelief and to illumine the mystery of the Virgin’s childbirth, first sent ahead the conception of a woman afflicted by hopeless and longstanding barrenness. Thus the one who saw dry limbs revive after a long old age, and, when the course of an aged life had already passed, youth bloom again for the first time, and nature itself [Note: [Col. 0444D] The manuscript of Cesena. Other printed editions read “in declining age.”] rise in declining age to the dignity of bearing a servant who was to be born, might believe that the flower of chastity, the honor of modesty, the distinction of purity, and the enclosure of virginity could remain after childbirth and be preserved by the very author proceeding from the womb.

And so that the authority itself of which we are speaking might attend and support our preface and the comparison we have drawn from eyes wearied by an ancient illness, and might show that, for human eyes badly accustomed to night, darkened, and gradually brought forward and recalled to the light, the Lord kindled in John and sent ahead the lamp of his own light, so that, having tasted the light, they might already bear within themselves the very radiance of the divine Sun [Note: [Col. 0444D] From Latinus. The printed editions read “might bring forward.”] and grasp the brightness of the Godhead.

In accordance with what was said of John: “He was the burning and shining lamp” (John V), so that he might open the dense darkness of night with his gentle light, while he himself might restore to those already longing for light the day that knows no night.

This is why the magi, still inhabitants of night and astonished with all their eyes, are accustomed by a faintly shining star to the light and are gradually drawn to the very source of light and of days (Matthew II).

And truly, brothers, the season is fitting: the chariot of the seasons traverses the boundaries of the whole year, restores to us the festive celebration of the birth of our Lord, and brings back our joys. Let us now speak of John’s birth, of the childbirth of the barren woman, so that, by this brief lesson in belief, we may be able to reach that place where there is childbirth without childbirth, where the author himself is created by the one who gives birth, where the very origin of the begetter is born, amid wintry lights made uncertain by clouds and mists, with the preceding lamp and the star as guide.

“There was,” the evangelist says, “a certain priest named Zacharias, and his wife was Elizabeth; and they had no child, because Elizabeth was barren, and both were advanced in their days” (Luke I). [Note: [Col. 0445D] The manuscript of Cesena: “Old age doubled the miracle of barrenness.” Grotius says: “To the former defect of barrenness was added the impediment of age.”]

Barrenness is intensified by extreme old age, and everything belonging to the body and to nature is wholly withdrawn from the hope of begetting. And so that not even a thought of offspring might remain, they had reached that stage of time and age when, the vital heat having passed away, mortal cold possessed the barren womb, so that the father himself might recognize that a human being could no longer be born through human means from the place where human possibilities had departed.

Thus, brothers, thus belief is established in the hard hearts of human beings, and faith is planted and grafted. [Note: [Col. 0445D] That is, it is planted; and, like trees, faith itself is grafted into an already planted belief. MITA.] Then everything divine is believed, when there is nothing human.

“It fell to him by lot to burn incense when he entered the Temple of the Lord.” Well did he say “when he entered the Temple,” not “when he entered the temple,” because he himself was more truly the familiar temple of God, carrying in the purity of his breast all the mysteries of the law and offering not so much the incense of frankincense as the incense of pure supplication.

For God rests more graciously in his own work than in human work and does not smell as willingly the drop of an Arabian tree [Note: [Col. 0445D] In Exodus XXX four kinds of spices are enumerated, from which the incense to be burned to God in the Temple was to be made. Among them was *nataph*, that is, as Chrysologus correctly notes, a drop that flows from a tree; it was therefore called στακτή (*staktē*), because it flows or drips.] as the holiness of a sincere heart and breast.

“An angel of the Lord appeared to him,” he says, “standing at the right side of the altar of incense.” It would have been sufficient to say, “An angel appeared to him.” Why add “at the right side of the altar”? [Note: [Col. 0445D] Zacharias was serving on the eastern side of the altar and burned incense there. The western side was nearest the Ark; the angel would have turned his back indecorously toward it if he had stood on that side. Therefore he stood at the right side of the altar, namely, on the northern side.] So that the hearer might understand that there is nothing sinister in the holy angels, since Scripture says: “The Lord knows the ways that are on the right” (Proverbs IV, according to the Septuagint).

“An angel appeared to him.” When the whole human race had already failed, so that John might be born from a barren woman before Christ was born from a Virgin, it was said of John: “Behold, I send my angel” (Matthew XI).

Blessed is she in whom nature failed in old age so that she might grow toward God; blessed is she who exchanged the losses of barrenness for virginal fruitfulness; blessed is she who conceived in one childbirth what she lamented had been corrupted throughout the whole world; blessed is she who became the mother who brings forth living [Note: [Col. 0446D] The manuscripts of Cesena and Vallicella read “the mother of living offspring.”] shoots, though formerly she was the pitiable source of mortals—giving birth to them for pains, giving them forth amid groans, producing human beings at the risk of the one who gives birth, and announcing death at birth itself through lamentations and tears; always devouring her offspring, knowing that she generated beings destined to die amid such great sorrows.

Nature therefore was nourished more by barrenness, lest it rage more heavily through fruitfulness, destined to produce tears rather than children. For so long, through tears, grief, and groaning, she sought and appealed to her author, understanding that this had happened to her through guilt and had not been established by her most merciful author when she was created.

This is why the Lord himself, the creator of nature, passes by the path of virginal conception and virginal birth by an invisible footprint and an unknown way, and walks the road of human birth with a divine step, not a human one, so that by being born he might first free nature itself from the slavery of death to which it had been subjected in this way, [Note: [Col. 0446D] A metaphorical expression. He first liberates human nature as a fountain from which human beings flow like streams, so that the streams themselves may be cleansed of their impurities. MITA.] and, after cleansing the fountain, restore heavenly purity to its streams.

Rightly does John exult in the womb, who deserved to know the freedom of his origin before he deserved to exist, and deserved to feel it before he lived.

At the hour of incense, barrenness is opened through an angel, conception is commanded, childbirth is promised, and a sacred birth is prepared within the sacred precincts. Thus prophecy, while John is still in the womb and the structure of his limbs is almost formed, [Note: [Col. 0446D] See, appropriately on this subject, Cornelius à Lapide, Commentary on Luke V, 42–43, p. 24, col. 1, at the beginning.] is conceived in John, and before he reaches the office of the voice he speaks by God’s sign. [Note: [Col. 0446D] The manuscript of Cesena: “Before he is mute, he speaks.”]

But lest, while we strive to conclude the profound and marvelous matters of this very extensive reading in a brief discourse, I pass over what most needs to be said, we shall discuss the following points next time, if God wills.

## SERMON LXXXVIII. On the same subject.

It is always burdensome, brothers, always sad to be bound by the chains of debt. Yet I, whom my frequent promises to you often make your debtor, find the very nature and obligation of such a debt sufficiently consoling, because the one who promises gives rather than receives; and the one who incurs debt by giving makes the creditor himself more indebted to him. When the one who has lent is himself in debt, and the one who is in debt has himself lent, it is proved that the bond is one of obligation, not necessity; and in such a loan there runs for the soul an exceedingly sweet interest, not of burden but of honor.

After the Gospel account had described how an angel of the Lord appeared to the priest Zacharias, it added: “And Zacharias was troubled when he saw him, and fear fell upon him” (Luke I).

If one who is anxious about the authority of a judge is always disturbed and trembles at the arrival of an official, and assesses and measures the importance of the command by the person who comes—and, although conscious of doing well, remains afraid until he learns the reason for the visitor’s coming and understands his rank—what will a weak human nature do, with what fear will it tremble, when it senses heavenly power, when a human being looks upon an angel and sees a minister of the divine throne? [Note: [Col. 0447C] The Hebrews thought that such apparitions always foretold something deadly to those who saw them, and that they were certain omens of approaching death: Genesis XVI, 13; XXXII, 30; Exodus XX, 19; Judges VI, 21, 23; XIII, 22. See Euthymius and Maldonatus here.]

Flesh is never secure in its own conscience, as Zacharias himself, about whom we are now speaking, demonstrated. At the very moment of reconciliation he offended; while he believed, he doubted, as the angel said: “Because you did not believe my words.” While he was obtaining what had been requested, he stumbled; he was condemned when he received the gifts themselves; when he received a voice, he then lost his voice.

Therefore, before the angel disclosed his commands, bestowed his gifts, and reported that the petition had been granted, [Note: [Col. 0447C] Similar remarks are found in Origen, Homily 4: “For a new appearance, presenting itself to human eyes, troubles and terrifies the mind; therefore the angel, knowing this to be human nature, first heals the disturbance.”] he dispelled anxiety, drove away fear, and strengthened minds troubled by uncertain thoughts, so that the mind which had departed from itself through an excess of terror, returning to itself, might perceive and receive the abundance of blessings, as he said:

“Do not be afraid, Zacharias, because your prayer has been heard; and your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you will call his name John.”

Do you suppose that so great a priest had so forgotten the people, so forgotten the whole community, that he would ask for the conception of an aged wife, barren and despairing of childbirth, so that an envoy of all should be present for him alone, so that an advocate of all should pray individually on his behalf, so that he would confine so great an office of the high priesthood within domestic concerns, shut it up and occupy it within family anxieties, and, as an aged prelate, dedicate the incense of the whole people to the sole desire for his own child, becoming inflamed by such a desire in his advanced age and, already looking toward the end of his life, longing for an untimely childbirth? [Note: [Col. 0447D] Certainly the old man himself, married to a barren wife, was not even thinking about children, and it is easy to believe that he had not prayed for the removal of that barrenness, as Chrysologus also believed. Nevertheless, some think that Zacharias had long before prayed to God for the gift of offspring and that the angel was referring to that former prayer. See Ambrose on Luke I. On this matter Augustine, *Questions on the Gospels*, book XI, at the beginning, volume III of the works, part II, p. 179 of the Antwerp edition.] Far be it, brothers, far be it from the faithful soul to suspect this of holy Zacharias.

But the angel reports that the outcome of the entire supplication lay in this, saying: “Your prayer has been heard, and your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son.” If the angel answered what had been requested, the priest prayed for a child alone; if the priest’s prayer had acted on behalf of everyone, why did the angel report that only the request for a child had been granted? What are we to understand? Why do we keep the minds of our hearers in suspense for so long?

The point is that this venerable prelate had been present not for himself alone but for everyone; that the angel had answered on behalf of all; and that God had foreseen in this one offspring of the priest the one whom he had chosen for the parents and for nature itself for this purpose: to give him to the whole community, to bestow him upon the ages, to grant him to the peoples. He would become the son of the mystery, brought forth amid the sacred precincts, [Note: [Col. 0448C] The manuscript of Cesena reads “announced.”] granted amid the sacraments; he would be a prelate born from a venerable prelate; he would be an angel, conceived by the voice of an angel in holy entrails; he would be the voice of Christ: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness” (John I); he would be the voice of Christ, reserved for Christ until his appointed time; he would be the herald who would cry out the Judge’s arrival; he would be the repentance that would call the peoples of Christ to forgiveness.

What this priest, then, already forgetful of himself, already dead to himself, estranged from his wife, and already renounced by his offspring, had done for everyone and obtained for everyone, let us learn from the angel’s report.

“And many,” he says, “will rejoice at his birth.” He is not an only son who was created for the joy of all. “For he will be great before the Lord.” Who can establish how great he is among human beings if he is great before God?

“And he will drink neither wine nor strong drink.” He who was born from the holy body of a priest, in extreme old age, purified from every vice and removed from the fires of youth, knows neither wine nor strong drink, [Note: [Col. 0448C] *Sicera* was wine mixed with seasonings. On this, see Theophilus of Antioch, on Luke I, 15, p. 331, Paris, 1635. After wine, no drink is more ready or suitable for inducing drunkenness. Some distinguish *sicera* from wine and say that it means every artificial wine. Others teach that the word refers to everything that intoxicates except wine. See Theophylact and Balsamon on Canon 3 of the Apostles, p. 234, Paris, 1558. If you ask why this kind of drink was forbidden to Nazirites, the rabbis confidently answer that the tree forbidden to Adam was the vine-bearing grapevine. Nonsense. The Hebrew word *sekar* signifies everything capable of causing intoxication. See Duhamel here. Bede, on Luke I, gives the true reason for this prohibition.] which produce the extravagance of drunkenness and its vices and utterly scatter the ornaments of morality and the adornments of virtue.
