“And he will drink neither wine nor strong drink, but he will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb” [Col. 0448C]—in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “Brothers, do not become drunk with wine, in which is debauchery, but be filled with the Holy Spirit” (Ephesians V).

“And he will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb.” Blessed John, who deserved to thunder with God’s Spirit before he wailed in human crying; blessed is he who deserved to possess divine things before he received human things; blessed is he who deserved to know heaven before earth; blessed is he who, before seeing present things, deserved to announce future things; blessed is he who could receive God before he himself was enclosed by his own body; blessed, and uniquely blessed, is he who, before he knew how to seek, acquired merit; blessed is he who did not reach grace through labor, but descended into labor through the condescension of grace itself.

“And he will convert many of the children.” To whom? Let the angel speak, so that the heretic may fall silent because he blasphemes and denies; let the angel speak, so that the faithful may hear and rejoice, and so that the heretic may believe and return. “He will convert.” To whom? “To the Lord their God,” he says.

Who is this God? The one of whom the prophet says: “This is our God, and there is no other besides him, who found the whole way of discipline and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved” (Baruch III).

When did he give it? Certainly when, on the tablets of the law, he described the rule of the whole of life and the complete standard of discipline.

Pay attention, hearer, so that you may know who this God of ours is, besides whom there is no other. Who is he? “After these things he was seen on earth and lived among human beings” (ibid.).

Who else was seen on earth except Christ, who lived among us in the flesh? And who else lived among human beings except the one who dwelt with human beings in a human body?

And if this is our God, and there is no other besides him, heretic, when you do not have this one, whom will you have? “There is no other besides him,” he says. And now you do not say, “Then where is the Father?” The prophet says: “There is no other besides him.” And where is he? Certainly in the Son, because apart from the Son there is no Father. “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me,” he says (John XIV).

Therefore the prophet did not say, “There is no other,” but “There is no other besides him.” This means: He exists, but he exists in him.

But you say: “And if he exists in him, how is he another?” Heretic, he is another in person in such a way that he is the same in substance; he is the same in substance in such a way that there is no confusion of the Trinity; the Trinity is one in such a way that there is no separation in the Godhead; he is in himself, and the whole Trinity is not without him, in such a way that there is a defined personal distinction in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, but not a separated divinity.

“And he will go before him.” Before whom? Before Christ, who is their God—the God of ours, the God of all, the God besides whom there is no other—“in the power of Elijah.”

When anyone hears this, let him not attribute to it “transmigration of souls” (μετεμψύχωσιν). [Note: [Col. 0449D] He is referring to the transmigration of souls into other bodies. Some had invented the idea that Elijah’s soul had migrated into John; see Augustine, *Questions on Numbers*, question 17. Compare Tertullian, *On the Soul*. This, moreover, was the opinion of the Pharisees, who believed that the souls of the good could pass into another body, while the souls of the wicked were consigned to perpetual torment. See Calmet on Matthew.] Here he speaks of that spirit which he merited through divine grace, not of the spirit by which he obtained life through the flesh; and he speaks of that power which he possessed from above, not of the power he acquired because of the body’s physical strength.

John therefore came in the spirit of Elijah and walked in his power, representing Elijah and Christ in his whole way of life—in food, clothing, honor, chastity, abstinence, and every virtue.

“To prepare for the Lord a perfect people.” May God and our Lord deign to prepare and strengthen it in you, for the glory of his name.

## SERMON LXXXIX. On the same subject.

All things created by God are good for us, and very good, as Scripture says: “And God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good” (Gen. 1, according to the LXX). Therefore all things created by God are good, and very good.

[Note: That is, “best.” For the Hebrews lack a superlative.]

Yet creatures are regarded as lying between vices and virtues in such a way that from them the learned derive material for instruction, while the unlearned find a cause of error. For the wise recognize the Creator by contemplating creation; fools, however, while they suppose the creatures themselves to be gods, cannot know the Creator. Hence it is that the Gentiles made the sun, moon, stars, gold, stones, and [Col. 0450B] wood their gods—things which Christians understand to have been subjected to their service.

[Note: No one is unaware that these were the first beginnings of idolatry. See Diodorus Siculus, *Bibliotheca*, book 1. Thus the Athenians, guardians of their despised religion, judged that Anaxagoras, who babbled against the sun—which they themselves believed to be a god—ought to be punished by death. Wower, in the notes to Minucius Felix’s *Octavius*, p. 73, col. 1.]

Nor is it surprising that creation should thus be intermediate,

[Note: On the one hand an instrument of good, on the other of evil.]

since Christ himself, the Creator of all things, is salvation to believers and ruin to unbelievers, as the evangelist says: “This child is appointed for the falling and rising of many” (Luke 2). The apostles likewise are held by some to be a cause of death and by others of life, as Paul demonstrates when he says: “To some we are an aroma from death unto death, and to others an aroma from life unto life” (2 Cor. 2). Therefore the evangelical readings also become for the good a saving means of understanding, but for the wicked an occasion of error.

Earlier, when the most blessed evangelist reported that John the Baptist had been bound in Herod’s chains, slain because of Herodias’s adulteries, and beheaded as a reward for a dancing girl, we sensed that some were disturbed and asked why God had subjected a holy man to a sacrilegious woman, a virgin to an adulteress, an angel to a dancing girl. Brothers, we shall treat elsewhere of John’s virtues and Herod’s crimes;

[Note: Below, Sermon 127.]

for now let us explain the reason for John’s chains, the necessity of his imprisonment, and the usefulness of his death.

John could not die by the common lot,

[Note: The Caesarean and Vallicellian manuscripts read “by a common death.” Ambrose, Sermon 83, *On the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist*: “He who had been generated by promise beyond the birth of ordinary men deserved this from God: that he should not depart from the world by a common death with the rest, but that, confessing the Lord, he should lay down the body which he had received by the Lord’s gift. Thus John fulfilled the Lord’s will in everything, because he was both born and died for the Lord’s work.” Mita.]

since he was born by an exceptional privilege. When Christ God was born in the flesh, John was generated as an angel upon earth, so that earthly offices might be joined with heavenly offices, just as divine things were mingled with human things; and so that, on earth, the angel of God might serve the Lord, and the heavenly order of service might not be lacking.

But let us hear the account of John’s birth, so that we may discover the causes of his death. “There was,” he says, “in the days of Herod, king of Judaea, a certain priest named Zechariah, of the priestly division of Abijah; and his wife was of the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth. And they were both righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blamelessly” (Luke 1).

Orators, great men and outstanding in talent, whenever they prepare to recount the virtues of illustrious men, mention grandfathers and great-grandfathers, so that the dignity of their ancestors may contribute to the honor of those now living, and the praise of fathers may redound to the glory of their sons. Innate glory is greater than acquired glory; what comes from one’s origin precedes what follows from labor; it is more blessed to possess glory than to seek it. Hence, to exalt John’s glory, the evangelist names the lineage of Zechariah his father and Elizabeth his mother, recalls his ancestors, records their merits, speaks of their titles, arranges their ranks, lays open their life, enlarges upon their distinction, and proclaims their holiness.

“There was,” he says, “in the days of Herod, king of Judaea.”

He recalls the time of that impious king who violated the sacred dignity of the priesthood, confused its order, dissolved what had been established, and removed its institution. [Col. 0451B] This also contributes to Zechariah’s merit: although Herod had dared to extend his recklessness against almost everyone, he dared nothing against this man, being overcome by his virtues, so that the unblemished succession of the priesthood might preserve the glory of its lineage.

[Note: The priests of the Hebrews recorded their proper lineage, family, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers in public registers. There is a notable passage in Josephus, *Against Apion*, vol. 2 of the works, p. 440 at the end, Havercamp edition: “For whoever exercises the priesthood must have children by a wife of his own people; he must look neither to money nor to honors, but must investigate lineage according to the ancient succession, established by many testimonies.”]

[Note: Any priest was permitted to marry any woman, provided that she was born of Hebrew parents; for ordinary men were even allowed to marry foreign women, except women from certain nations with whom the Hebrews had no right of intermarriage. Therefore the fact that Zechariah married a woman from the stock of Aaron was not an observance of the law, as some maintain. For the law in Num. 36:8 applied only to virgins who were heirs of their paternal property. In any case, nothing could be nobler than the origin of John the Baptist: for he was descended through both royal Davidic blood and the priestly line of Aaron.]

“And his wife was of the daughters of Aaron.”

Aaron was the first high priest under the law and the origin of the priesthood. Therefore, rightly passing over all others, she is called his daughter, since the memory of one whose holiness she bore within herself most gloriously transmitted the pious guardianship of so great a lineage to her son.

But the evangelist describes the praises of this mother: “They were both,” he says, “righteous before God.” It is a new happiness, an extraordinary marriage, when one mind remains in two people, one holiness in two; when what differed in sex was united in mind, what doubled the appearance was one in conduct, and virtues made equal those whom nature had made unequal.

“They were both righteous before God.”

To please human judgments and to be righteous before men is a human virtue and a matter of great labor; but to be righteous before God, who searches hearts, examines thoughts, and sees the movements of minds, is not a human labor but a divine gift. If he is great who does not sin in the flesh, how great is he who does not sin in the heart? John, therefore, was born above the flesh from parents who had sinned neither in heart nor in body before God.

The evangelist added, saying: “Walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blamelessly.”

“Walking”: he walks who does not stand at the crossroads of sinners; who feels himself a stranger in this world; who fearlessly enters the harsh dwellings of the virtues; who, as an indefatigable traveler, climbs the mountains of ordinances and the hills of commandments,

[Note: Correctly so. For the commandments of God are called a way in sacred Scripture. Bede and Brugensis.]

so that he may enjoy the presence of God his Father in the blessedness of the heavenly homeland.

“Walking in all the commandments and ordinances.”

“In all”—in those things in which no one, or scarcely anyone, perseveres. “In all the commandments and ordinances.” Who, without knowing smoke, passes through the fires of desire? Who escapes the slippery course of life without ever falling? Who walks undefiled through the whirlpools of vices? Who carries out the affairs of the flesh, the causes of life,

[Note: He calls our life the business of the world, as though we were acting out a play here. Among writers of this age, *actus* means the same as action, office, and so forth.]

the business of the world, and is not subject to complaint, when birth itself is full of tears and complaints? A woman in labor complains because of pain, and one who has been born complains in tears because of nature.

But in Zechariah and Elizabeth guilt was slain, complaint perished, and every cause for accusation was cut away, because in them was being prepared the source from which complete holiness would be born. Let this, however, become clear from the reading itself.

“And they had no child,” he says, “because Elizabeth was barren.”

This barrenness was not accursed but mystical: in it childbirth was not taken away but delayed; she was not closed against offspring but reserved for the appointed time. It was cultivated by time, sown by virtue, ripened by age, and increased in old age, so that in one extraordinary son the whole of fertility might be reckoned, when in one child an accumulated abundance of virtues was born.

Blessed barrenness, which preserved one woman for one birth and awaited John, for whom, because all first things were due to him, the dignity of the firstborn would not perish.

“And they had both advanced in their days.”

They had advanced, not departed: age lived in the holy; it did not fail but advanced. Or what can be lacking to those who are always receiving increases of virtue? Thus, in Zechariah and Elizabeth, sex is astonished, the flesh grows cold, the limbs grow sluggish, time passes, age moves on,

[Note: The Caesarean manuscript reads: “everything has been wholly abolished.”]

and everything that belongs to human order and marital activity fades away,

[Col. 0452C]

so that by divine gift, and not through human procreation, an angel might be born.

We had promised to set forth the causes of John’s death by explaining his birth; but since our discourse has carried us farther today, and since what follows is sufficient for proving the matter, let what has now been said be counted to the glory of his birth. Let us not be ungrateful to you because we postpone what we owe you, though we do not deny it; for delay increases the debtor’s favor with the creditor. Await, then, what the debtor promises, and await it confidently, because promises cannot be denied when what was so generously denied to the barren is fulfilled.

## SERMON XC. On the Same Subject

The hesitation of the priest Zechariah has taught us today that we are raised up by the falls of the saints and strengthened by the trembling of the saints. When he did not believe God’s promises but questioned them, and received divine works not by faith but investigated them by human reasoning, he paid the penalty of unbelief through a long condemnation to silence.

He had heard from the angel: “Your prayer has been heard, and your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son.” He then replied: “How shall I know this? For I am an old man, and my wife is advanced in her days” (Luke 1).

Had the long duration of old age caused him to lose hope of descendants to such an extent that the long experience of his life had not taught him that nothing was impossible for God? The priest had read, and the veteran high priest knew, that nature could be constrained by law, but not the Author of nature; that time could impose limits upon man, but not upon his own Creator.

[Note: All these things, which were certainly not unknown to Zechariah, aggravated his guilt of unbelief. For whenever God reveals something, says Chrysostom, *Homily 2, On the Incomparable Nature of God*, it must be received in faith; to dispute about such matters belongs to a stubborn soul. See Note 4 here.]

He knew that, although the bodies of Abraham and Sarah were dead in extreme old age and their renowned barrenness had excluded them from the names of father and mother, Isaac had sprung forth into the full fertility of the Israelite stock (Gen. 21). It had not harmed him that nature had been so absent, since his birth profited from the beneficence of the Creator, not from nature. He had learned that God had granted to Rebecca (Gen. 25) and Anna (1 Sam. 1), long worn out and long deprived of nature’s assistance, what barrenness had denied.

Thus, taught by such examples, what does he mean by saying: “How shall I know this? For I am an old man, and my wife is advanced in her days”?

Brothers, human nature is sufficiently fearful before God and sufficiently weak before divine powers. It does not find itself in the cause to be what it judges itself to be before the cause; it knows itself insufficiently before it tests itself by events and learns through examples.

It seeks heaven, seeks the heights, searches the things above, moves heaven, and knocks at heaven; but when it has moved heaven, it cannot bear the weight of heaven. It attempts to climb the summit of faith and burns to penetrate heaven by its own strength; but when it begins to walk with human steps upon the ethereal paths, and looks back downward toward its own nature, it has not so much confidence in past things as it has fear of falling.

Thus blessed Peter, when he imitates the divine stride across the waters and, a new traveler, treads a soft path with hard steps, begs for protection against falling before he rejoices in the gift received (Matt. 14).

So too now Zechariah. For a long time he had lamented that the devil could prevail, that death could reign through the sin of one man, that human beings were born to labors, groans, and dangers; that, though they might long for offspring wretched and destined to die, they nevertheless could not obtain them; that they stood amid the battle lines of crimes, were besieged by hosts of vices, and were continually shaken and battered by the assaults of infirmities; that they saw from afar the standards of the virtues, the hope of the law, and the freedom of grace, yet no one could reach them by his own strength; that they wished to do good but did not do it, hated crimes but could not conquer them; that God ought by now to have mercy and ought by now to come to the aid of such captives.

Therefore, when this high priest continually knocked at God’s ears with such a complaint and such lamentation, God took from the very substance of his petition and established a wondrous proof for the one who was asking so piously and justly: a proof by which he might believe that God could give life to the dead and restore salvation to the despairing, if he gave offspring to dead old age and a son to hopeless barrenness.

Thus the evangelical sermon discloses the matter when it says: “Your prayer has been heard, and your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son”—the messenger of this redemption and the forerunner of this salvation. He will not, as you do, hear God with his voice or bend him by his groans. He will not, as you do, seek our intercessions in order to obtain something; rather, established within our order and supported by angelic honor, he will hold in his hands, embrace in his lap, and deliver into the world’s sight the God whom all desire but whom no one has ever known, whom even the angels have not seen—

[Note: That is, not known by a comprehensive vision.]

he will make God known to all through human eyes; he will bring the Lord into fellowship with servants; he will mingle the Judge with the guilty; he will testify that the Censor has taken upon himself the person of the guilty, as though proving that the sentence of human condemnation would cease when the one who was to deliver the guilty to punishment himself came forward, himself ran through forgiveness.

To make this mystery of boundless mercy shine forth, your son, Zechariah, immerses his Lord in baptism of repentance and washes him in remission of sins: because the Fountain wished to be washed, the Knower of all things to receive forgiveness, the Judge himself to undergo his own sentence, lest he condemn the guilty, lest he bring vengeance upon the wicked. He ascends the cross, tastes death, suffers burial, and enters the underworld—the one who chose to be punished so that he might not punish, who chose rather to be loved than feared.

When Zechariah heard this, brothers, he was terrified by the realization that he had obtained such a mystery through his prayers and disturbed by the contemplation of the mystery itself. He did not believe himself worthy of so great a thing, and he doubted that God would descend to such and so great a matter. Hence he says: “How shall I know this? For I am an old man, and my wife is advanced in her days.”

That is to say: “Just as human reason does not permit me to have a son, so everlasting majesty does not permit God to be born and die.”

[Note: Many infer, as Chrysostom does above, that Zechariah sinned by asking the angel for a sign, because the angel punished his hesitation. See Augustine, Homily 290, p. 1163 of the new edition. His fault of distrust was worse because the examples of divine power were not otherwise unknown to him; because he was a priest and teacher of the people; because at a time when prophecies and appearances had ceased, an angel had spoken to him; and finally because this occurred in the very place and time of prayer, at the place of the oracle. See Lightfoot, *Harmony*. Maldonatus, however, teaches that this was only a venial crime. Chrysologus perhaps says “venially,” that is, a fault worthy of pardon.]

To the unbeliever, the angel mercifully gave only the punishment of a sign, not of treachery. It is caution to believe humbly and slowly concerning God; it is contumely to think of him insultingly and even more slowly.

The angel added, saying: “I am Gabriel.”

[Note: Gabriel means “the strength of God,” or “my strength is God.” Since angels have no need of names, they receive names by which their ministries are indicated. The sons of the Hebrews say that Michael is the minister of severity, while Gabriel is the minister of mercy. Therefore Michael flies with one wing, because God is slower to punish; Gabriel with two, because he is swift to forgive.]

Thus, from so great a name and from the merit of so great a minister, the high priest might weigh and believe the character of the promise.

“I am Gabriel, who stand before God, and I have been sent to speak to you.”

When he says his name, he designates his merit; when he says that he stands before God, he declares that he has been sent.

[Note: A circumlocution for “servant,” as if he were saying: “I stand before God, serve God, minister to God.” The Latins likewise speak of “standing at someone’s feet,” “standing at the cups,” and so forth.]

He confesses his servitude, lest the prerogative of his name conceal the service that is owed.

“I am,” he says, “Gabriel, who stand before God, and I have been sent to speak to you and to announce these things to you.”

Truly great is the Lord, and of his wisdom there is no number (Ps. 146). He heals the one growing weak from his wound and strengthens the one wavering under punishment; from chastisement he fashions an argument for faith, saying: “And behold, you will be silent and unable to speak.”

[Note: It appears below that Zechariah was deprived not only of the ability to speak but also of hearing, since his friends are said to have addressed him by signs. The opinion of Theophylact is not implausible: that the word *κωφοί* used below signifies not so much “deaf” as “mute.”]

Thus, from yourself and in yourself, you may learn the rule of believing and believe by a familiar example that God can do what he promises. For when he wills, he closes the instrument of your voice; and when he wills, he can certainly open the function of your mouth. When he wills to make a fruitful woman barren, he can; when he promises to make a barren woman fruitful, he can. When he wills to grant the functions of childbirth, he prevails; when he wills, he can deny nature’s services.

The angel therefore acted so that the high priest, instructed by such a lesson, would no longer say: “How shall I know this?” He who had been able to prove by the evidence of the whole creation that God could do all things—and who had read that heaven, earth, the sea, and all that is in them had been established from nothing—ought to believe that God could make from something whatever he wished, and restore to the despairing what he promised. He who made the whole from what did not exist has no difficulty making whatever he wills from what does exist.

“And the people were waiting for Zechariah, and they wondered that he delayed in the temple. But when Zechariah came out, he could not speak to them, and they understood that he had seen a vision in the temple. And he was making signs to them and remained mute.”

The high priest comes forth carrying upon his lips the sign of barrenness and bearing in his breast the figure of conception, so that when the mother gave birth to a son, the son might give him a voice; then the father of the Word might utter the mystery, and the one who was born might grant forgiveness to his father before he washed away the ancient crimes of the peoples.

And because the one who did not believe became silent, rightly the prophet who believed exults, saying: “I believed, and therefore I spoke” (Ps. 115).

Brothers, faith gives speech; unbelief denies speech. Therefore, if, as I have said, the falls of the saints raise us up and the trembling of the blessed strengthens us, let us never judge anything to be impossible for God. Nor should we ask how he will do what he promises, since for him to will is to have done, and for him to give is to have promised.

[Note: See what we said in the preface.]

## SERMON XCI. On the Same Subject

Those who know how to extract gold from the earth, whenever they sense a rich vein, devote to it every skill and every labor. Since we know that a heavenly treasure lies hidden in holy Zechariah, let us occupy ourselves entirely with him—both with all that belongs to our discourse and with all that belongs to your hearing—so that what has been sought through common labor may become a common profit.

“There was,” he says, “in the days of Herod, king of Judaea, a certain priest named Zechariah, of the priestly division of Abijah.” We have already said this.

“And his wife was of the daughters of Aaron” (Luke 1).

The evangelist began in this way so that, in the priest’s wife,

[Note: The Caesarean manuscript reads: “so that the nobility preserved in the priestly lineage might be displayed.”]

the nobility preserved in the priestly line might be made evident.

“They were both,” he says, “righteous before God.”

Both righteous, because there was one righteousness in both. Both righteous, because their marriage was founded not merely on diligence but on holiness. Both righteous, because though unequal in sex, they were considered equal in merits. Both righteous, because just as there was one flesh in two, so there was one spirit in two.

Let married couples imitate them, so that those whom affection joins may also be joined by virtue.

“They were both,” he says, “righteous before God.”

Both righteous before God. And what of the statement: “No living person shall be justified in your sight” (Ps. 142)? Before men someone may perhaps be considered righteous, because just as men know the faults of bodies, so they are ignorant of the vices of the mind. But before God, to whom the barriers of the breast lie open and from whom the secrets of thoughts are not hidden, who is regarded as innocent and righteous? Is there a human being who does not sin in his heart, does not offend in thought, does not stumble through doubt, and does not suffer a fall through hesitation? Moses doubts (Num. 20), Aaron goes astray (Exod. 32), Peter denies (Matt. 26)—and who is righteous?

And how are they both righteous before God? Before God—but through God. Both righteous before God: not by labor, but by grace.

Hear the Apostle: “Being justified freely by his grace” (Rom. 3). And again: “It is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not from works, lest anyone should boast” (Eph. 2). And again: “What do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4).

The evangelist therefore reports not what they did not have, but what they received; not what was sought, but what was given.

“They were both,” he says, “righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of God blamelessly.”

He said “walking” to show that they had run in the virtues rather than stood still; that they had walked in the way of righteousness rather than sat down; that they had not remained on the road of the commandments but had reached the fullness of the commandments.

“Walking in all the commandments and ordinances of God blamelessly.”

Blessed, brothers, are those whom guilt does not strike and crime does not wound; but more blessed are those whom not even complaint has touched.

“Blamelessly.” If childhood, adolescence, and youth were without reproach—though that is the period in which every cause for reproach exists—what must the old age of these people have been like? If the beginning was such, what was the end? To have climbed the peaks of the ordinances and the hills of the commandments without stumbling in anything is the mark of singular grace and unique happiness.

“And they had no child,” he says, “because Elizabeth was barren.”

He did not say, “They had no children,” but, “They had no child,” because the one who was to be born from such parents would be unique.

Hear the Lord saying: “Among those born of women there has not risen anyone greater than John the Baptist” (Matt. 11).

“Because Elizabeth was barren.” Barren in body, but fruitful in virtues; slow to bear offspring, but not slow before God; not closed against offspring,

[Col. 0457A]

but reserved for the appointed time; not denied a child, but preserved for a mystery.

“And they had both,” he says, “advanced in their days.”

“Advanced”: this is how the mystery of old age is described—old age that has not yet fallen in merit or failed through age, but advances; that does not feel the losses of the body because it receives increases of virtue.

Brothers, Elizabeth’s holy childbirth was not taken away but delayed until the time of the flesh had passed: the suffering of the body, the necessity of marriage, the cause of pleasure, the impulse of desire, and everything human that confuses, burdens, and weighs down the conscience. For over a long period the house of sacrifice was being cleansed, the dwelling place of holiness,

[Note: This passage has been corrected from the Bologna edition 1 and from Mita. The others read *meatus metatoris*, “the passage of the quartermaster.” Chrysostom likewise calls the Baptist “Christ’s quartermaster” in a homily assembled from various passages on Matthew, vol. 2, p. 1074. Among writers of this age, *metatus* frequently means a dwelling; it occurs often in Gregory of Tours: “the burden of providing quarters,” and in the *Novels of Theodosius*, “On Quarters,” where more is said about this burden; and in the *Code of Justinian*, under the same title. Quartermasters (*metatores*) are preparers of lodgings. Mita rightly has *foriero*, “forerunner.” Cyprian, *Letter* 22, near the beginning, if we trust Pamelius in his notes, calls the emperor Decius “the quartermaster of Antichrist.” Chrysostom praises this passage. Du Cange in the *Glossary*.]

the abode of Christ’s forerunner, the dwelling of the angel, the court of the Holy Spirit, the temple of God.

“Do you not know,” says the Apostle, “that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you?” (1 Cor. 3).

Finally, when all complaint of the body had been quieted and they had become wholly blameless, barrenness immediately fled, old age revived, faith conceived, chastity gave birth, and there was born one greater than man, equal to the angels: the trumpet of heaven, the herald of Christ, the mystery of the Father, the messenger of the Son, the standard-bearer of the heavenly King, the forgiveness of sinners, the correction of the Jews, the calling of the nations, and, to put it precisely, the clasp of law and grace,

[Note: Some clasps were called *vestiariae*, “clothing clasps,” because garments were fastened with them. Among the ancients there is the expression “the one appointed over the clasps.” Chrysologus has this use in mind, as though John the Baptist were the one who united and embraced both laws.]

the clasp that joined the double robe of the high priest to the holy Father upon his breast.

The evangelist therefore describes the virtues of the father and mother, so that from the great merits of his parents the dignity of their offspring might be recognized, and so that he might be shown to be greater than man, since in his birth he exceeded the law of human birth.

But if John is about to come forth, let him now be born, because Christ’s birth is near; let the new Lucifer arise, because the radiance of the true Sun is already breaking forth; let the herald give voice, because the Judge is present; let the trumpet cry, because the King is coming; and because God is about to come forth, let the angel already go before him.

But since what is above human beings is beyond the ability of a human being adequately to recount—the virtues of the angel who is being born—let an angel now speak.

The angel said to Zechariah: “Do not be afraid, Zechariah; your prayer has been heard. Behold, your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you shall call his name John. And you shall have joy and gladness, and many shall rejoice at his birth. For he shall be great before the Lord; he shall drink neither wine nor strong drink; and he shall be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb. And he shall turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God. And he himself shall go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children and the disobedient to the wisdom of the righteous, to prepare for the Lord a perfect people.”

Human speech is silent; the preacher’s exposition is mute

[Note: *Tractator* means an expositor or preacher, one who explains the Scriptures in the Church. See Claudianus Mamertus, bishop of Vienne, book 1 *On the State of the Soul*, chapter 3; Sidonius, book 2, chapter 9; Cassiodorus, preface to *On the Institution*; Gregory the Great, in his letter to Bishop Leonard, chapter 11; Augustine, Sermon 19, *On the Words of the Apostle*; Paulinus—or whoever he may be—in the *Life of Saint Ambrose*; Jerome, *Against Helvidius*, and others.]

when the glory of John is proclaimed by an angelic herald; virtue resounds, praise is praised with praise,

[Note: The manuscript reads “is proclaimed.”]

and there is nothing for a human being to add to one to whom God has given everything.

“He shall be filled,” he says, “with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb.”

You see how John reached heaven before he touched earth; how he received the divine Spirit before he possessed a human spirit; how he received divine gifts before the limbs of his body; how he began to live for God before he lived for himself—indeed, he lived for God before God lived for him, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2).

[Note: Either from the time of the angel’s appearance or from the conception.]

In the sixth month he exults in his mother’s womb and announces that Christ has come into the Virgin’s womb. He is an ardent messenger, eager to announce before he could live; an impatient leader who reached the King before reaching his own body;

[Note: A king usually remains in the middle of the army, where, surrounded on every side by the best defenses, he may fight more securely. Mita.]

he seized weapons before limbs, sought the battle line before the light, and, in order to conquer the world, first conquered nature. Though he himself was without entrails, he stirs up the entrails of his mother; and because the body was delayed, he fulfills the office of an evangelist by spirit alone.

What shall I say? Before John went before Christ, he went before himself.

The hearts of father, mother, and son are filled by one and the same Holy Spirit, so that with one instrument of holiness the song of the Lord’s birth might resound.

Nor is it surprising, brothers, that royal births are always honored by celebration and sweetened by harmonious music. Let us too, brothers, glorify Christ’s birth with songs and honor it with gifts; for faith lies if what the magus does (Matt. 2) the Christian does not do.

## SERMON XCII. On the Same Subject
Gradually the evangelical discourse advances us to higher things and lifts us up to the heavenly realms. Nor is it surprising, brothers, that an ethereal chariot carried Elijah up to heaven (2 Kings II), since daily this four-horsed chariot of the Gospels carries the human race through heaven and conveys it to the kingdom. Behold, brothers, the Gospel itself has now brought us near—from the childbirth of a barren woman to the childbirth of the Virgin, and from the birth of John to the birth of our Savior [Col. 0459A]. But let us listen more patiently to what still remains concerning the high priest Zachariah, so that by a royal road we may reach the cradle of our King. For this reason we have mounted the secure seat of the heavenly chariot: to avoid the anxious and difficult paths of shortcuts.

It is written: “And it came to pass, when the days of his service were completed, that he went to his own house” (Luke I). Thus the whole tribe served at one temple; thousands of priests were in attendance. Consequently, the observance of the priestly office was divided among many, allotted to periods of time, [Col. 0459D] distributed by turns, lest either the multitude, confused, disturb the order of the priesthood, or one person, by reading continually, deny another the duty assigned to him.

The priestly families descended from Eleazar and Ithamar, the sons of Aaron, completed the number twenty-four, as we learn from 1 Chronicles XXIV. David had selected them by lot, so that each in its proper order might minister in the temple for successive weeks; thus, after 168 days had elapsed, the service returned to the first. It is clear that the division of Abijah, from which Zachariah came, was the eighth. These divisions are called in Greek *ephemeriae*. Luke has, in Luke I, ἐξ ἐφημερίας Ἀβία, “from the division of Abijah.”

After this, Elizabeth his wife conceived. They had the capacity for marriage; permission to beget children had been granted to them, [Col. 0459B] for the adolescence of the Law still remained among them, and the infancy of religion still endured. The Law, brothers, prohibited what was unlawful; it did not deny what was lawful. It kept humanity within the gift; it could confer nothing beyond the gift. It governed nature, but did not raise man above nature. The Law was the door of faith, the herald of grace, the forerunner of the Gospel, the tutor of religion in its infancy. In the legal priesthood it allowed the chastity of marriage, [Note: From Latinius. The printed editions read: “legal.”] [Col. 0459D] most appropriately foreshadowing the celibacy of clerics, so that in the high priesthood it might announce the glory of the perpetual virtue that was to come.

Accordingly, in keeping with this indulgence, Elizabeth, already dead through old age, revives into holy childbirth; and her dry limbs, parched and furrowed with wrinkles, become green again within her fertile womb through living marrow. Time itself—the very time in which she had ceased to bear—is recalled to the body; and when the house of the womb, collapsed through extreme age, is suddenly restored to a new appearance, [Col. 0459C] order is astonished, custom fails, nature herself wonders; and from the preparation of the dwelling the worth and dignity of its guest become known.

Yet John, in the common dwelling-place, marveled greatly that he was a stranger: he learned that he had been excluded by time, disowned by nature, and received there through the kindness of his Creator, not of his parent. “And she hid herself for five months, saying: ‘Thus has the Lord dealt with me.’” She rightly confesses that the Lord has done everything, since she saw nothing in what had been granted to her that came from man. And she hid herself for five months because, although what she possessed was a divine gift, it did not belong to her own time.

“She hid herself for five months.” [Note: The reason why Elizabeth hid herself is obscure. Some, such as Peter Chrysologus, think it was out of modesty. For fertility in a worn-out old woman was a disgrace, just as barrenness in a woman of full age was; others think it was so that the miracle might become more illustrious when she suddenly appeared before human eyes with her body swollen; or so that she might devote herself solely to praising God for so great a benefit; or finally, so that she might remain free from every impurity and withdraw from uncleanness. For her son was destined to be a Nazarene.]

The pregnant old woman is ashamed; the aged woman blushes at her first childbirth; and extreme old age conceals the woman in labor, lest the reproach of barrenness should be increased by the laughter directed at fruitful old age. That an aged and long-worn conception is subject to laughter is shown by Sarah, who was very much like this barren woman in age (Genesis XVIII). When she learned, at the Lord’s promise, that a child was being restored to her and a son granted to her, although her life was already nearly exhausted, she too laughed at her own childbirth. And that her pregnancy, her burdened gray hair, could be a source of laughter to everyone is testified by the name given to the child, as Scripture says: “And he called the name of his son Isaac” (Genesis XXI). Scripture teaches that this means “laughter,” adding: “The Lord has made laughter for me.”

Hence Elizabeth wishes to conceal the sacred mystery, saying: “Thus has the Lord dealt with me.” In this way the present conception might weary her with embarrassment for as long as the anguish of denied childbirth had afflicted her. The father remains silent because of punishment; the mother conceals herself because of shame.

O how great a voice is born from silence! O how great a trumpet, destined to cry out to the ages, is generated in quietness! O what a secret of the divine Judge produces a herald! “Thus has the Lord dealt with me in the days when he looked upon me, to take away my reproach among men” [Col. 0460B].

The honor of marriage and the dignity of wedlock consist in the begetting of beloved children. It is indeed very grievous and very sad both to lack the reward of virginity and not to have the consolations of children: to bear the burdens of marriage and not attain its fruit. Hence she rejoices that the reproach of barrenness has been taken away from her, saying: “Thus has the Lord dealt with me in the days when he looked upon me, to take away my reproach among men.”

For although this is counted miserable among human beings, before God [Note: From this Gospel passage Maldonado derives the point made by Chrysologus: namely, that barrenness was not a reproach before God, nor did it always proceed from an offended deity.] there is no guilt where there is no fault of the parent, but rather the judgment of the one who withholds. Certainly, if some bodily infirmity causes this, necessity is responsible, not the will.

But now let every sluggish understanding of the flesh be removed; let all weakness of bodily perception be cast aside. Let every limitation of human intellect be excluded; let the eyes of faith be opened, let the ears of the heart be unlocked, and let the movement of the mind run and rush forward, so that we may reach the mystery of the virginal conception and penetrate into the sacrament of virginal childbirth, with the help of the Lord Jesus Christ, who was born from her and now lives with God the Father and the Holy Spirit in the heavenly kingdom, throughout endless ages of ages. Amen.

[Note: In other editions this sermon is entitled “On the woman who anointed the Lord with ointment.”]

## SERMON XCIII. On the conversion of Magdalene

A listener may perhaps be surprised that Christ came to a meal, and to the meal of a Pharisee. Christ entered the Pharisee’s house not to receive Jewish food but to bestow divine mercy; [Col. 0460D] nor did he recline [Note: Honey was very familiar to the Hebrews, as to other Eastern peoples, as is clearly shown by many passages of Sacred Scripture. No one is unaware that the ancients used to adorn bowls with flowers and garlands.] in order to drink cups flavored with honey and scented with flowers, but to drink the tears of the penitent from the very fountains of her eyes. God hungers for the sighs of sinners; he thirsts for the tears of sinners.

“A certain Pharisee,” he says, “asked him to eat with him; and he entered the Pharisee’s house and reclined at table. And behold, a woman in the city who was a sinner, when she learned that he was reclining at table in the Pharisee’s house, brought an alabaster flask of ointment; and standing behind him at his feet, she began to bathe his feet with tears, and wiped them with the hair of her head, and kissed his feet, and anointed them with ointment” (Luke VII).

You see that Christ came to the Pharisee’s table not to be filled with bodily foods, but to display a heavenly work in the flesh; nor to approve what had been placed before him in human fashion, but to approve what had been done behind him in divine fashion. For we always recognize Christ as exercising divine powers through human actions, since everything he did bodily is shown to be new and beyond ordinary human practice.

The Pharisee invites Christ to eat. Why does an uninvited woman appear there? A stranger does not burst through the doors of the house; one who has not been invited does not presume to enter the privacy of the banquet; [Note: Among dining-room servants there was an *invitator* or summoner, so called from his duty. Athenaeus mentions the former in Book IV, Martial the latter in Book IX, as does an ancient inscription in Pignorius, *On Servants*: “AGATHOPUS, FREEDMAN OF THE AUGUSTI, INVITATOR.” Christ also expressly speaks of servant-inviters in Matthew XII and Luke XIV.] a luxurious arbiter does not dare disturb the prepared foods that relax the mind after labor. What, then, is this unknown—or rather, ill-famed—woman doing? Burdened with grief, full of tears, loud with lamentation, passing the doorkeeper without his knowledge, with no one aware and the shepherd himself ignorant, she runs through every entrance of the house, crosses all the [Col. 0461A] bands of servants, [Note: “All” may perhaps have to be corrected to “of the attendants.” For, as Pignorius says on page 47, this was the proper and legitimate terminology of the dining-room. Zeno of Verona, in his sermon “On Envy and Resentment,” says: “Joseph would not have come to Egypt, nor would he have arisen from among Pharaoh’s servants.”] and flies into the very privacy of the banquet. She turns the house of rejoicing into a house of lamentation and mourning.

Brothers, she came not because she was uninvited, but because she was commanded; she entered because she had been brought forward, not because she presumed. He himself caused her to be presented to him who, by a heavenly sentence, ordered her to be absolved.

Finally, while the Pharisee, splendid in his clothing, first [Col. 0461D] in the semicircular dining arrangement, [Note: “Sigma” takes its name from its semicircular shape, as in the portico of Constantinople built by Julian, mentioned by Zosimus in Book III; because of its semicircular form it was called *sigma*. Since the sigma had two ends, like horns, the man occupying the right-hand one held the first place at the banquet. The other place belonged to the man occupying the left-hand horn. Thus, if the Pharisee was first in the sigma, he held the right-hand horn.] swelling with pride in the very eyes of Christ, [Note: Gregory also calls this Pharisee proud and puffed up in Homily 33 on the Gospel.] intent on pleasing a man rather than God, is happily immersed in the feast, the woman comes—and she comes behind him, because a guilty soul stands behind the back of the one from whom it seeks pardon, knowing that through guilt it has lost the confidence to face him.

She comes to make satisfaction to God, not to please man. She comes to offer a banquet of compassion, not of pleasure. Finally, she sets a table of repentance, places dishes of remorse before him, brings the bread of sorrow, tempers the drink with tears in measured quantity, and, for the delights of the Godhead, makes the whole symphony of her heart and body resound, [Note: This is derived from the custom of the ancients, who delighted in the playing of instruments at banquets, especially the Jews. See Amos VI, 5. Pignorius quotes Chrysologus’s words in *On Servants*, page 162.] raises the voice of an organ through lamentation, plays the cithara with long sighs, and fits her groans to the flute. [Note: Hence the flute-players among the ancients. A girl also played reed instruments at a royal banquet, according to Abdias, *Apostolic History*, Book IX.]

And while her breast, accusing her own conscience, repeatedly strikes itself, she makes the cymbals resound in a way pleasing to God. [Note: These instruments were very widely used among the Hebrews. See Lamy, *On the Temple*, page 120.] While she brings such foods before the divine eyes, she carries away in return the whole abundance of mercy.

“Behold, a woman in the city who was a sinner.” The evangelist exaggerates the woman’s crime [Note: For she had been a prostitute or harlot. The Greeks call women of this kind ἁμαρτάδας, “sinners.”] so as to accumulate the indulgence of the one who grants it.

“In the city, a sinner.” [Note: Another reading has *civitati*, “to the city,” rather than *civitate*, “in the city.”] She had sinned against the city, because by her reputation she had touched the reputation of the whole city; and thus she had now become not merely a sinner herself, but the very sin of the city. [Note: Either because the city had acquired a bad reputation among others on account of Magdalene’s scandal, or because the whole city had been reduced to lust through this woman’s example, and so forth.]

She understood that the city’s sin could be taken away by no one except him who alone had come to abolish the sin of the world.

“And when she learned that the Lord was reclining at table in the Pharisee’s house.” The sinful woman dares not come to him standing, nor sitting. When God stands, he reproves; when he sits, he judges; when he reclines, he lies down beside those who are prostrate. When she learned that the Lord was reclining at table in the Pharisee’s house, she learned that the heavenly majesty was inclined toward mercy. Therefore she believed that the one who had come so readily to the Pharisee’s table would be ready to grant her pardon.

“She brought an alabaster flask of ointment.” [Note: She took oil for whatever kind of ointment was intended. The alabaster in which such oil was kept was an ordinary vessel, commonly used at banquets and suitable for storing ointments. See Pliny, Book XXXVI, chapter 8. Perhaps, however, the better view is that the name “alabaster” was applied to all vessels in which ointments were kept. See Epiphanius, *On Weights and Measures*; the scholiast on Theocritus, Idyll XV, page 188; and Aristophanes, *Acharnians*, page 302; above all William Stuckius, *Ancient Banquets*, Book III, chapter 15.]

She carried oil because she was seeking medicine for a deadly wound from the heavenly physician.

“Standing behind him at his feet.” Whoever seeks swift pardon always hastens to the feet. And rightly she stood, because the one who had managed to reach Christ’s feet could no longer fall. [Note: The Hebrews did not so quickly abandon their earlier manner of sitting at meals for reclining, as is customary with us today. Although Proverbs XXIII, 1; Amos IV, 7; Ezekiel XXIII; Tobit II, 4; and Esther I, 6; VII, 1 provide clear traces of reclining on couches or bedding, this practice had not yet become universal among them. Interpreters believe that it arose over time through imitation of the Persians and Chaldeans. Certainly, both at this Pharisee’s banquet and at the disciples’ final supper, the Savior reclined on couches. They lay so that their feet faced the table and their heads faced the forward part. They reclined after removing their shoes and sandals, which were afterwards guarded by a servant whom the Romans called *ad pedes*, “at the feet.”]

“Standing behind him at his feet.” She stood there so that, relying on Christ’s footsteps, she might travel along the road of life—the road along which she had previously run toward death.

“She bathed his feet with tears.” Behold, the order of things is changed. Heaven always gives rain to earth; but now earth waters heaven—or rather, above the heavens and as far as the Lord himself, a rain of human tears springs upward, so that, in accordance with the Psalmist, that saying may be sung even of the waters of weeping: “And the waters that are above the heavens, let them praise the name of the Lord” (Psalm CXLVIII).

“She bathed his feet with tears.” O how great is the power of sinners’ tears! They water heaven, wash the earth, extinguish Gehenna, and erase the sentence pronounced by divine proclamation against every crime.

“And she wiped them with the hair of her head.” She washes the Lord’s feet with tears and wipes them with her hair. [Note: Yesterday also, servants wiped the hands of their masters with their hair.] Poverty is no excuse; inhumanity will have no pardon, because nature in its entirety is sufficient for service to the Creator.

“And she wiped them with the hair of her head.” A stream flowed back upon the sinful woman’s head, cleansing her crimes, so that from her own fountain she might wash away the flood of her sins in a new baptism.

“And she wiped them with the hair of her head.” Thus, in accordance with the Psalmist’s “crown of hair” (Psalm LXVII), the head with which she had walked in her sins might be turned toward holiness through such service.

“And she kissed his feet.” Tears had come first, so that devoted kisses might follow, because tears are evidence of satisfaction, while kisses are signs of reconciliation. [Note: See Hebrews II, 21, and many other places; and consult Wowerus on Minucius Felix’s *Octavius*, page 18.]

“And she anointed them with ointment.” [Note: It is uncertain whether Chrysologus thought this was the same woman mentioned by Matthew XXVI. I would believe that he considered her a different woman. For he calls the other simply “a woman,” but identifies this one with the demonstrative “this,” as if he were saying: “this woman of whom we are speaking.” More discerning interpreters agree with Chrysologus. The setting here is different, and Christ’s speech is different. Here the Pharisee murmurs, not Judas; and the cause of the murmuring is almost entirely different: here the woman’s touch is criticized, there the waste of the ointment.]

We know from another evangelist that a woman poured oil upon the Lord’s head (Matthew XXVI). Therefore what this woman does is not a soft and merely bodily service, [Note: Among Eastern peoples it was an act of courtesy to anoint the head and feet of those who were eating and dining. Women especially performed this service, since the care of ointments was more particularly entrusted to them than to men. See 1 Samuel VIII, 13, and Maldonado here. Mita says that the oil poured upon the head signifies the service rendered to Christ the Lord, while the oil poured upon the feet signifies the courtesy rendered to the apostles and their successors. If the woman, representing the Church—as other interpreters also understand her—had given only half the service, she would not have anointed the whole mystical body of Christ. She performed it completely when she anointed Christ, the head of the Church, and the priests and preachers of the word of God, who are its feet.]

but a sacrament of complete human devotion. For [Col. 0464C] in Christ’s head is God; in his feet are those who proclaim peace. [Note: The same God who is in Christ’s head is also in the feet of the same mystical body, in which are the preachers of the Gospel. They are therefore called Christ’s feet because Christ, as the head, surpasses, illumines, and governs them, so that they may follow his footsteps, as is said below in Sermon 95. Nevertheless, it should be observed that God is present in different ways throughout this mystical body of Christ and the Church: most eminently in Christ’s head—that is, in Christ’s humanity through the hypostatic union; and in Christ’s feet—that is, in the Church, which is composed chiefly of Gentiles—through faith, grace, and inward illumination, directing their actions and steps, and so forth. This woman anointed Christ’s head and feet, that she might render the service of human devotion to the feet through the head and to the head through the feet; compare what the author says below in Sermon 173: “Just as the honor of the head,” etc. Mita.] [Note: This urges us to pray to God that we too may be anointed with the ointment poured upon the Savior’s feet—that is, that we may share in the sacraments of the Church.]

Pray, brothers, that we too may somehow be counted worthy of the Lord’s ointment and be anointed with the ointment poured upon the Savior’s feet. For just as there is an offering when the ointment is offered, so [Note: The manuscripts of Caesar read: “so certainly it is chrism.”] there is perfect chrism when it flows from the Lord’s footsteps.

Whom this woman represents, and what great mystery she foreshadows, we shall say, with God’s help, when we explain what follows.

## SERMON XCIV. On the same woman, the murmuring Pharisee, and Christ’s reply

Since in the preceding sermon we went through the first part of today’s reading, we were equally astonished by the fervor, faith, boldness, and unprecedented devotion with which the sinful woman touched the Savior’s feet. Now let us hear what the silent Pharisee said, and what Christ, to whom silent thoughts speak, replied.

“When the Pharisee who had invited him saw this, he said within himself: ‘If this man were a prophet, he would certainly know what sort of woman this is who touches him’” (Luke VII).

Pharisee, what you perceive is not ignorance but power; it belongs to divine judgment, not human error. Pharisee, you are mistaken. If he had been a prophet, he might rather have been unable to know, because prophecy does not belong to human choice; it is a divine gift. Hence a prophet [Note: Other commentators also note the Pharisee’s error here, as though prophets ought to know everything. See Grotius, the Bruges commentator, and Calmet.] knows not as much as he wishes, but as much as the one who grants prophecy has given him. [Note: Consult Maldonado on this passage.]

“If this man were a prophet, he would certainly know what sort of woman this is who touches him.” [Note: The Pharisees held the opinion that people were defiled by contact with immoral persons. See Isaiah LXV, 5.]

The touch of an evil woman burns the one who is evil in conscience, pollutes one who is like her, brands one who is suspected, and disgraces a man of evil will. But the sinful woman becomes good, holy, and innocent when she touches the one who grants pardon.

Filth touches the sun, but does not pollute it. [Note: Latinius reads: “When the wounds touch the physician, corruption does not defile him,” whereas the printed editions have: “When the physician touches the wounds, corruption does not defile him.”] When wounds touch the physician, corruption does not pollute him. Though a defendant touches a judge, he cannot stain him when he pleads. Thus, when a sinner touches the Lord, he does not soil the Lord; rather, he himself is suddenly freed from every sin and seizes holiness.

The woman suffering from a flow of blood proves this. When she touched the Lord’s fringe, [Note: Another reading has “touches.” Following Moses’ command in Numbers XV, 38, the Hebrews adorned the edges of square garments with narrow cords and attached little tassels or fringes to the corners, called in Greek κράσπεδα, made of linen or blue hemp. The woman with the hemorrhage testifies that Christ wore this kind of garment.] she did not pollute the fringe; instead, she herself was immediately freed from the defilement of her long-standing affliction.

“If this man were a prophet, he would certainly know what sort of woman this is who touches him.” The Pharisee would believe Christ to be a prophet if he saw him recognizing a woman exposed before his eyes and known to the people. What do you think he will believe when he soon learns that Christ is the arbiter of his mind, the judge of his heart, the witness of his conscience, and the knower of his thoughts? Will he then confess him to be God, whom even now, after such great miracles, he does not judge worthy to be a teacher? [Col. 0465B]

“If this man were a prophet, he would certainly know what sort of woman this is who touches him.” The woman had a wound and knew it; therefore she sought, in this manner, the physician for so great a wound. The Pharisee, wounded by the disease of faithlessness and fevered by the flame of pride, did not know through his madness that he was insane. Hence Christ first turned his healing toward the place where an unknown illness was raging, so that the heavenly physician might cure two sick persons with one medicine.

“When the Pharisee who had invited him saw this, he said within himself.” Because the Pharisee had thought within himself, Christ replied with a public voice. By revealing the secret of the Pharisee’s heart, he showed himself to be the author of all prophecy.

“Jesus answered and said: ‘Simon, I have something to say to you.’” To you who need medicine and do not know how to seek it; to you who call God your teacher and abandon God’s discipline. Do you not know that the teacher suffers great injury from one who declares himself his disciple but does not follow his teaching? For just as the uprightness of a disciple is the praise of the teacher, so the disciple who does not know the discipline brings reproach upon the teacher.

“Simon, I have something to say to you.”

He replied, “Teacher, say it.”

Again: “Teacher, say it”—and not “God, say it.” Yet he was already beginning to sense as God the one whom he called teacher.

“Two debtors,” he said, “owed money to a certain creditor. One owed five hundred denarii, the other fifty. Since they had nothing with which to repay, he forgave both. Which of them, then, will love him more?”

Simon answered, “I think the one to whom he forgave more.”

And the Lord said, “You have judged correctly.”

You have heard how the heavenly creditor compensates the entire debt with love, and, for the increase of the whole loan, demands and requires the interest of love alone. The debtor deserves punishment if, through love alone, he neglects to redeem his bond.

Do you wish to know, human being, what you owe God? That you were made is God’s deposit; that you possess rational capacity is God’s loan; that you have received the ability to distinguish good from evil is something you were given; and that you received a rule of life through the written bond of the Law—you cannot deny that you promised this to God as he demanded it.

But while you plunge yourself through the vices of the flesh into the mud like a swine, while you live like a four-footed animal and deprive yourself of the reason with which you are endowed, while in the whirlpool of crimes you confuse good and evil after losing the power of distinction, and while you squander the substance of the divine Law, [Note: Latinius thus corrects the text. Other editions have “captivated by worldly desire.”] captivated by worldly pleasure, you have become the sorrowful debtor of a glorious loan. As the profits of virtue fail, the interest of crimes multiplies.

But although you have fallen in this matter, although you have descended into this condition, [Note: He attacks the Novatians, who left no hope to those who had sinned even once, and impiously taught that sins could not be forgiven by men.] see that you do not despair. Human being, something remains by which you may satisfy your most merciful creditor. Do you wish to be absolved? Love. “Love will cover a multitude of sins” (1 John IV).

What is worse than the crime of denial? Yet Peter was able to erase this through love alone, as the Lord proved when he said: “Peter, do you love me?” (John XXI, 12).

Among all God’s commandments, love holds the chief place. “You shall love,” he says, “the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind, and with all your strength” (Matthew XII). Therefore love God, human being, and love him wholly, so that you may be able to conquer and erase all sins without labor. It is a gentle warfare, a delicate struggle, to carry away victory over every crime through love alone, as becomes clear from what follows.

“Turning toward the woman, he said to Simon.” Why does Christ, turning toward the woman, speak to Simon? Because when he looks upon the penitent, he rebukes the one who rails.

He said to Simon: “Do you see this woman? I entered your house; you gave me no water for my feet, but she bathed my feet with her tears and wiped them with the hair of her head. You gave me no kiss, but she has not ceased kissing my feet since I entered. You did not anoint my head with oil, but she has anointed my feet with ointment. Therefore I say to you: her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much; but the one to whom little is forgiven loves little.”

It has been proved that love erases and washes away all sins.

But what does he mean when he says: “The one to whom little is forgiven loves little”? Does this mean that one should commit more sins in order to acquire greater love? Certainly not. Love helps concerning past sins; it does not free one from future sins. Love does not know how to sin when it loves. Love is not love if it commits sin. Love is the guardian of holiness.

Brothers, if we know ourselves to be sinners but do not wish to remain sinners, let us offer tears at Christ’s feet, scatter our hair, press kisses upon them, and pour out the oil of compassion with complete devotion, so that it may be said to us: “Your many sins are forgiven, because you have loved much.” [Note: These feet are the priests who hear confessions. At their feet sins are to be laid down through confession; tears of contrition are to be offered, the hair of affection scattered, sins exposed with one’s own mouth, kisses of love impressed, God loved with the whole heart, the oil of compassion poured out, and satisfaction for sins presented. See below, Sermon 95. Mita.]

Let us imitate this woman, whom we see not only freed from sins but advanced to the summit of complete holiness. Who this woman is, however, since today’s sermon has delayed us with its treatment of love, we shall disclose in what follows, with God as our guide.

[Col. 0467A]

## SERMON XCV. On the same woman, concerning Magdalene’s allegorical conversion
Everything reported as having been bodily done by Christ is so supported by historical truth that it is always shown to be full of heavenly mysteries. And since we have already touched upon what lay on the surface of the reading in a repeated discourse, pray that, as we promised, we may unfold its inner meaning, with the Holy Spirit revealing it. Speech is dishonorable when it brings forth God’s deeds merely through a human interpretation.

“A certain Pharisee,” it says, “asked him to eat with him” (Luke 7).

The Pharisee, brothers, is called a catholic among the Jews; for he believes in the resurrection and disagrees with the Sadducee, who denies the resurrection.

[Note: The sect of the Pharisees is considered extremely ancient, although Jerome writes on Isaiah 8 that it arose from the school of Hillel and Shammai. Their customs, institutions, and superstitions may be found in Calmet’s *Dictionary of the Bible*. Moreover, that they believed the soul to be immortal, admitting a certain form of metempsychosis, and that angels exist and bodies will rise again, is established by Acts 23:8; Josephus, *Antiquities*, book 18, chapter 2, and *The Jewish War*, book 2, chapter 12.]

[Note: The Sadducees were stained by several errors. For they obstinately denied that the rational soul, whose existence in human beings they acknowledged, was immortal. Josephus, *The Jewish War*, book 2, chapter 12. They treated the existence of angels as a sort of fable: Acts 28:8 [an apparent textual error in the note]; Matthew 22:23; Mark 13:8; Luke 20:27. They also asserted that God is corporeal. Arnobius, book 3, p. 100. They had removed providence from him as well. Josephus, cited above. Hence they also denied the rewards and punishments of the other life. Above all, they vigorously opposed the resurrection of the body. Therefore, in the course of time—for after Jerusalem had been destroyed this pestilence subsided for a while, though it was destined to recover its strength—the emperor Justinian, by a promulgated law, drove them from the boundaries of the empire and condemned them to the ultimate punishment.]

This is why he asks Christ—that is, the author of the resurrection—to eat with him, because whoever feasts with Christ does not know how to die, but lives forever.

“He asked the Lord to eat with him.”

You ask, Pharisee, that you may eat with him; believe, become a Christian, and eat from him. “I am,” he says, “the bread that came down from heaven” (John 6). God always grants greater things than are asked: the one who was asked to eat with him gave himself to be eaten, so that he might bestow confidence in eating with him; and yet he gave this in such a way that he did not refuse what had been requested.

Does he not also promise this spontaneously to his disciples? “You who have remained with me will eat and drink at my table in my kingdom” (Luke 22). Christian, the one who here gave himself to be eaten by you—what of his can he deny you in the future? And he who prepared so great a provision for your sustenance—what has he not prepared for you in that everlasting dwelling?

“You will eat at my table in my kingdom.”

You have heard of God’s banquet; do not be anxious about the quality of the feast. Whoever is deemed worthy to reach the king’s table will eat whatever the dominion and power of the kingdom possesses. Thus whoever comes to the Creator’s banquet will have in his delights whatever is contained in creation.

But let us return to what we began.

“And he entered the house of the Pharisee.”

What house? Surely he entered the synagogue and reclined there. He reclined in the synagogue, brothers, when Christ died; but he transmitted his body to the Church’s table, so that it might be heavenly flesh for the nations who eat it unto salvation. “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6).

But how Christ’s flesh is eaten, and how his blood is drunk, those who have been instructed in the heavenly mysteries know.

[Note: For the sacred mysteries of religion were not disclosed to everyone. Augustine, *Tractate* 96: “The sacraments of the faithful are not brought forth to catechumens.” Everyone knows that the Eucharist in particular was kept under the discipline of secrecy. Consult Origen, *Against Celsus*, book 6.]

“Behold,” he says, “a woman who was a sinner in the city.”

What woman?

[Note: Ambrose also teaches that the Church is represented in this woman, *Commentary on Luke*, book 6, chapter 15; and Gregory, *Homily* 33 on the Gospels.]

The Church, without doubt.

“A sinner in the city.”

Which city? The one of which the prophet had said: “How has the faithful city, Zion, become a prostitute?” (Isaiah 1). And elsewhere: “I saw iniquity and contradiction in the city; iniquity and labor are in its midst and in justice” [the wording is uncertain]; “and usury and deceit have not disappeared from its streets” (Psalm 54).

Thus, in a city enclosed by the walls of infidelity, fortified by towers of pride, divided by the streets of iniquities, barred by the gates of contradictions, painted over with the cosmetics of deceit, hardened by the flint of usury,

[Note: Usurers, hard as flints, are condemned by the holy Fathers in Suicer, volume 2, p. 1275.]

burdened by the pains of commerce, and disgraced by brothels—that is, by temples of idols—this woman, that is, the Church, bore a very grievous guilt arising from such a mass of preceding sins.

But when she heard that Christ had come to the house of the Pharisee—that is, to the synagogue—and that there, that is, at the Jewish Passover, he had handed over the mysteries of his Passion, opened the sacrament of his body and blood, and revealed the secret of our redemption, she came, despising the scribes as the worst of doorkeepers:

“Woe to you lawyers, because you have taken away the key of knowledge!” (Luke 11).

Having broken through the doors of contradiction, disregarding the very leadership of the Pharisaic assembly, burning, panting, and eager, she reached the innermost chamber of the entire legal banquet. There she found Christ handed over amid the feasts of love and the sweet cups; she found the Jewish people fallen through treachery, in accordance with the prophet’s words:

“For if an enemy had reproached me, I would surely have endured it; and if the one who hated me had spoken evil against me, I would surely have hidden myself from him. But you, a man of one mind with me, my leader and my acquaintance, who together with me took sweet food, in the house of the Lord we walked with one accord” (Psalm 54).

When she recognized that the Lord was reclining in the Pharisee’s house—that is, in the synagogue—delivered over to every deceit and complete treachery, suffering, crucified, and buried, nevertheless none of this injury held her back from the ardor of faith. She carries ointment; she carries the oil of Christian chrism. And because she was not worthy to see Christ’s face bodily, she stands behind him—not in place, but in time—and clings to his footsteps so that she may follow him. Now she pours out tears of desire rather than of consciousness, so that the one whom she was not worthy to see departing she might be worthy to see returning.

She therefore bathes the Lord’s feet with tears poured forth from love. She holds the feet of those who evangelize his kingdom with the hands of good works; she washes them with tears of charity; she kisses them with the lips of confession; and she pours out the whole ointment of mercy.

Then, turning toward her—for what does “turning” mean? It means “returning”—he says to Simon, to the Pharisees, to those who denied him, and to the Jewish people:

“I entered your house; you did not give me water for my feet.”

And when will he say this? When he comes in the majesty of his Father and separates the righteous from the unrighteous, like a shepherd who separates the sheep from the goats, and says:

“I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink; I was a stranger, and you did not receive me.”

This means saying, “You did not give water for my feet.” But she, while washing my servants’ feet, anointing their feet, and kissing their feet, did for my servants what you did not do for the Lord; she did for the feet what you refused to do for the head; she bestowed upon the least what you denied to your own Creator.

[Note: According to the custom of the ancients, water for Christ’s feet was owed on three grounds: as to the Lord and to a guest, Genesis 18:4; 1 Samuel 25:41; 1 Timothy 5:10; and as to one reclining at table. See Athenaeus, book 14.]

Then he will say to the Church:

“Many sins are forgiven you, because you have loved much.”

For the forgiveness of sins will then take place, when every occasion for sinning has been removed; when corruption puts on incorruption; when mortality attains immortality; when the flesh of sin becomes wholly the flesh of holiness; when earthly servitude is changed into heavenly dominion; when human warfare is advanced into the divine kingdom.

Pray, brothers, that we, who have been placed within the Church, may also be worthy to reach the things we have enumerated, through Christ himself, to whom be honor and glory, together with the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0469C]

## SERMON XCVI. On the Parable of the Weeds

[Note: *Zizania* is a very common plant, with a thinner stalk than wheat; it is also a species of darnel that grows from corrupted wheat, and this is the Gospel’s *zizania*. See Julius Pomponius Sabinus, the old commentator on Virgil’s *Georgics*.]

If Christ’s sayings or deeds were everywhere subjected to carnal senses,

[Note: Alternatively, “were made subject to.”]

my mind would grow dull, my understanding would be idle and asleep, my heart would waste away, and everything belonging to human vigor and warmth would be extinguished.

“He proposed a parable to them,” it says (Matthew 13).

Just as fire is cold in a stone and fire lies hidden in iron, yet the fire itself is kindled by the striking of iron and stone, so an obscure word shines brightly through the comparison of word and meaning. Certainly, if these things were not mystical, no distinction would remain between the unbelieving and the faithful, between the impious and the devout; the devoted would be no different from the stubborn, the inactive from the laboring, or the wakeful from the one who sleeps.

But now, when the soul asks, the mind knocks, understanding seeks, devotion hopes, faith demands, and attentiveness deserves, there appears both the fruit of the one who labors, the punishment of the sluggish, and the justice of the giver—all at once—because things received are tasted more deeply than things possessed, and things discovered give more delight than things merely submitted to.

This is why Christ veils his teaching in parables, conceals it in figures, covers it with mysteries, and makes it obscure through sacred meanings.

“He proposed a parable to them.”

To them—that is, not to his own, but to outsiders; to enemies, certainly, not to friends; to those who looked on for accusation, not to those who listened for salvation.

“Therefore,” he says, “I speak to them in parables, because seeing they do not see, and hearing they do not hear, nor do they understand.”
