Why? Because whoever accuses the past is not worthy to see the present; nor is one worthy to recognize grace who hid the law so that it would not be understood.

“Woe to you,” he says, “lawyers, because you have taken away the key of knowledge; you yourselves did not enter, and those who were entering you prevented” (Luke 11).

“He proposed a parable to them, saying: The kingdom of heaven is like a man.”

And what offense is it if Christ became like human beings in order to help the human race that was perishing? Is the Lord a scandal if, in order to free slaves, he is found in the condition of slavery? For whatever belongs to the majesty of the future, whatever belongs to his coming and kingdom—behold, it is compared with a man.

“The kingdom of heaven,” he says, “is like a man who sowed good seed in his field. But while the men were sleeping, his enemy came and sowed weeds over the wheat, and went away.”

You have heard how the sower of the world sowed good beginnings of things, and that no evil proceeded from the author of their origin. Evil was sown over them by the enemy; evil was not produced by the parent of created things.

“God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good” (Genesis 1).

Good, and very good. For the one whom God, when making him, called the world, the enemy, by infecting him, made unclean; and the man whom God placed in the paradise of delight for life, the enemy dragged down in this life of labor to death; and the affection that God inserted into the flesh by nature, the enemy, through envy, changed into murder.

Cain proves this, for he was the first to stain the earth with a brother’s blood and became the one who first consecrated himself to fraternal death (Genesis 4).

[Note: Cain is called *πρωτοφόνος* (*prōtophonos*), “the first murderer.” Suicer says that the lexicons lack this word, volume 2, p. 884.]

Thus death, born from discord, always rends and separates human charity.

And because it would be lengthy to go through everything individually, we are compelled to explain at least briefly how the enemy has always sown evil among good things, vices among virtues, mortality among things that give life, for our ruin.

Did God not fill the whole earth from one human being, and did the one gracious sower not multiply the entire human race from one seed into so great a harvest? But the enemy soon brought all human beings into one mass; and by sowing evil over what had been well sown, he destroyed it by a flood rather than watering it.

Thus he disfigured the law, sown with divine and truthful commandments, with human and false inventions, so that a persecutor arose from a priest, a corrupter from a teacher, and an enemy from a defender of the law.

Thus, concerning creatures created for the knowledge of the Creator, he falsely claimed that there were gods, so that God would not be known. Hence he made the wise men of the world foolish; he taught the observers of the world to see nothing; he made those who professed knowledge possess no knowledge; and he left investigators of all things ignorant.

Thus the enemy, by sowing heretical weeds over the Gospel harvest sown with heavenly seed, confused it, so that he might make sheaves of faith into bundles for Gehenna and prevent the wheat from becoming part of the heavenly granaries.

And what more? After he himself had been changed from an angel into a demon, he strove by skill, tricks, devices, and fraud to prevent any creature from remaining in its proper state.

But now let us unfold the words of the present parable.

“The kingdom of heaven is like a man.”

Like whom? Certainly, Christ.

“Who sowed good seed.”

Because in the seed of created things the Creator’s nature knows no evil.

“In his field.”

That is, in the world, as the Lord himself says: “This field is the world” (Matthew 13:38).

“But while the men slept.”

That is, the holy Fathers—patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and martyrs—temporarily sleeping in the sleep of death, because the death of the saints is sleep. But the death of sinners is truly death, because in the punishment of hell they live while the sinners of life perish.

“His enemy came.”

That is, the devil.

“And sowed weeds over it.”

He sowed them over it; he did not sow them originally. The good things of the Creator come first; the devil’s evils follow afterward, so that the evil which comes from the devil is an accident, not a nature.

“He sowed weeds in the midst of the wheat.”

For the devil is accustomed to sow heresies among the faithful, sin among the saints, quarrels among the peaceful, deceit among the simple, and wickedness among the innocent—not in order to acquire the weeds, but to destroy the wheat; not to capture the guilty, but to deprive the innocent.

An enemy seeks the commander more than the soldier; he does not besiege the dead but attacks the living. Thus the devil does not seek to capture sinners, whom he already possesses in subjection; rather, he labors to capture the righteous.

“He sowed weeds in the midst of the wheat, and went away.”

For the devil indeed drives people toward ruin with his strength, but after he has thrown them down, he abandons them. The devil does not seek the human being; he seeks the human being’s destruction.

Brothers, he rejoices in our evils, swells with pride over our ruins, grows strong through our wounds, thirsts for our blood, is filled from our flesh, and lives from our deaths.

[Note: The Caesenatis manuscript reads: “He fattens himself on our deaths.”]

The devil does not want to possess a human being, but to destroy one.

Why? Because he does not want, does not endure, and cannot tolerate the human being’s reaching the heaven from which he himself fell.

And because today’s discourse is drawing us farther than intended, let us postpone the rest, so that we may lighten the common labor and explain more fully what must be said. May our God grant both me the grace of speaking and you the desire to hear.

[Col. 0471D]

## SERMON XCVII. On the Same Subject

Because the discourse previously delivered in haste, in order to moderate the common labor, was unable to reach the whole secret meaning of the passing parable, let us now unfold the remainder, with the Lord revealing it.

“He proposed a parable to them, saying: The kingdom of heaven is like a man who sowed good seed in his field; but while the men slept, his enemy came and sowed weeds over the wheat, and went away.”

“But while the men slept” (Matthew 13).

The ambusher lurks at night; by day he flees those who are awake. He attacks the sleeping; the strong seek conflict, challenge openly before all spectators, and want to win victory in the presence of the people.

To rush upon the sleeping is the clearest sign of weakness.

“But while the men slept, his enemy came.”

The wicked is never anything but foolish. What did the enemy accomplish here? Suppose the servants slept: was the Lord also sleeping? Suppose sleep closed the servants’ eyes after their labor: had any weariness overcome the eyes of their master?

Enemy, fugitive from the light, you watched and labored, but you did not remain hidden. For while the servants slept, the Lord himself saw you. Deserter from heaven, you anticipated them and acted, but you did not succeed.

What God himself guards cannot perish for God. Author of deceit, you do not commit your offense against the Lord but against the servants, since you make what is due to their negligence be attributed to your fraud. He—he himself—sees you, the witness both of every fraud and of every labor.

The fruits of their labor therefore remain for those who do good, and the punishment of their wickedness remains for those who deceive. They will carry their wheat to the heavenly granary; you will carry the bundles of your weeds to Gehenna.

“But while the men slept, his enemy came and sowed weeds.”

For what purpose? So that the Lord’s harvest might perish. And what did this have to do with the enemy’s gain, except that the spirit of envy counts human loss as its own gain, and considers that what has perished for human beings has been acquired by itself?

But, as we have said, the devil contrived this under cover of darkness so that the fault of the adulterated harvest might rebound upon the servants, and so that they might suffer punishment from the very source from which they had hoped for victory.

Accordingly, the watchful servants, terrified by fear, are alarmed at why this has happened. They fear that the growth of the weeds may return as an offense against those whose consciences possessed nothing except the sowing of good seed.

This is why they anticipated hearing their master, lest, secure in their innocence, they should bear guilt for their silence. When an innocent person is summoned to answer for a charge, while he strives to clear himself, he presses and urges the one who knows the truth.

“But when the grass had grown and produced fruit, then,” he says, “the weeds also appeared.”

What is hidden in the grass is revealed in the ear; what is concealed in the sprout is opened in the fruit. Thus we find those whom we think equal as believers unequal in faith; thus the harvest reveals what the Church’s growth conceals.

According to the Lord’s saying: “You will know them by their fruits” (Matthew 7).

Many blossoms promise a multitude of fruits, but once shaken lifeless by the blasts of the winds, very few persevere to fruitfulness. Thus many believers in Christ appear to be in the peace of the Church; but when the storm of persecution has blown through, few are found bearing the fruit of martyrdom.

But Saint Euphemia gave more in fruit than she promised in blossom; while preserving the blossom of virginity, she attained the abundant fruit of martyrdom.

[Note: In a constitution of Manuel Comnenus, cited by Suicer, *Ecclesiastical Thesaurus*, volume 2, p. 25, Saint Euphemia is called Καλλιμάρτυρ (*Kallimartyr*), “beautiful martyr.” Thus the Greeks generally called those women who suffered death for the Christian religion. Paulinus of Nola mentions her in poem 26, p. 638:

“And Euphemia, martyr on the Chalcidian shores,

marks the shore consecrated by virgin blood.”

Here “Chalcidian” means Chalcedonian. Euphemia suffered at Chalcedon in Bithynia, not at Chalcis in Euboea. Sidonius likewise says in poem 2, his panegyric on Anthemius, speaking of Byzantium, toward which the east wind blows from nearby Chalcedon:

“Nearby, the trumpet gradually tempers the east wind from Chalcedon.”

Euphemia is mentioned by Ennodius in Sirmond, volume 1, p. 110, hymn 17, and p. 1142, no. 130, where he records her epitaph; in Selden’s *Calendar*, p. 1339; in Mediolanese material preserved by Muratori; and in Fronto, p. 229. Saint Asterius, bishop of Amasea, also preached a sermon about her. At Ravenna there was a church dedicated to the blessed Euphemia, which Bishop Apollinaris, having returned after a long exile, properly consecrated. There he deposited the relics of the blessed woman, received from Hermacoras, bishop of Aquileia and disciple of Saint Mark, as Rubeus records in his *History of Ravenna*, and from him Bacchinius in Agnellus’s *Pontifical*, volume 1, p. 131. It is easy to believe that Chrysologus preached this homily in that same church. For there, and not in the other churches of Ravenna, Masses for the people were celebrated—that is, solemn services at which the bishop preached.]

“Then the servants of the master of the household came and said to him.”

They came, brothers, in mind, not in body; not in place, but in faith. They spoke not with the shouting of their voices, but with the silent grief of their hearts:

“Lord, did you not sow good seed in your field?”

“You sowed it; we did not sow it.”

[Note: The manuscripts of Caesena and Vallicella read: “What we perfectly accomplish, we always attribute to you, our author, and in the things you command us to do, you yourself stand as the worker.” The printed editions read: “What we do through you.”]

Whatever we do perfectly, we always assign to you, our author; and in the things you command us to do, you yourself are the one who works. Therefore, if in your graciousness you make us participants in your work, do not attribute the growth of the weeds to us alone.

Lord, either innocence protects us together with you, or guilt touches you together with us. We could not have envied our work; through great labors we could not have earned offense. You have whatever you wish, from whatever source you wish, whenever you wish. We possess nothing apart from your grace, through which we stand, live, move, and exist (Acts 17), and without which we lie fallen, fail, and perish.

Did we therefore labor for ourselves in such a way that these things might perish? But who did this? You, who alone do not sleep while we slept, saw it. And if you saw it, righteous Judge—for who knows the deed? The one who watches, not the one who sleeps (Psalm 126)—then expose him, so that you may make us, whom you see so anxious, secure.

The Lord said, “An enemy has done this.”

“An enemy has done this.” And why, Lord, did you permit it when you saw it?

Why? Because the one to whom nothing can be lost cannot fear fraud; and because distinguishing what is mixed is better than preventing the mixture, and restoring what has been lost is greater than preserving what is unharmed.

[Note: The edition of Mita reads: “It is better to distinguish what has been mixed than to prevent the mixture.” Other editions read: “It is greater to discern the mystical meaning than to forbid the mystery.”]

At the same time, it is necessary that there be weeds, so that those who are approved may become manifest (1 Corinthians 11).

The servants then said to him, “Do you want us to go and gather the weeds?”

Thus the devoted servants promise unwearied labor and cannot bear even temporarily to see the ugliness of the Lord’s harvest. But the Lord, whom time does not weary and who, whenever he wishes, can abolish the injury to his harvest, forbids them, saying:

“No.”

And he immediately reveals why he forbade them:

“Lest, while gathering the weeds, you uproot the wheat together with them.”

So inexperienced were the cultivators, so unskilled in the work, so lacking in the knowledge of discernment, that in uprooting the weeds they would also have torn up the wheat.

Where are the prophets prophesying through the Spirit of God? Where is Peter, to whom the Father reveals things (Matthew 16)? Where is Paul, in whom Christ works (Galatians 2) and speaks (2 Corinthians 13)? Where are all the saints—truly saints, but servants—knowing only as much as the giver of knowledge has granted to each?

But you say: “There was nothing hidden here; nothing was hidden when one thing appeared in outward form and another was contained in the blossom. What was a weed today was turned into wheat tomorrow. Thus today someone is regarded as a heretic who tomorrow becomes faithful; and one who is presently seen as a sinner stands forth in the future as righteous.”

This too is why the author referred both to the harvest: that is, until the judgment, the time of divine patience and our repentance. Whoever changes himself from evil to good is counted as the Lord’s wheat and gathered into the heavenly granaries; whoever changes himself from faithful to unfaithful is assigned to the fire of Gehenna.

And what more? If God’s patience did not assist the weeds, the Church would possess neither Matthew as an evangelist from a tax collector nor Paul as an apostle from a persecutor.

Indeed, Ananias was then seeking to uproot the wheat when, sent to Saul, he complained about Paul in these words:

“Lord, how much evil he has done to your saints!” (Acts 9).

That is, “Uproot the weeds.” What has a sheep to do with a wolf? What has the devout to do with the stubborn? Why has such a preacher been sent to a persecutor?

But while Ananias saw Saul, the Lord was already seeing Paul. While Ananias called him a persecutor, the Lord already knew him as a preacher. And while he judged him to be a weed destined for hell, Christ was already placing him as a chosen vessel, as wheat, in the heavenly granary.

“Go,” he says, “for he is a chosen vessel for me.”

[Note: Some material appears to be missing from this sermon.]

## SERMON XCVIII. On the Parable of the Mustard Seed

You have heard today, brothers, how the whole greatness of the heavenly kingdom has been compared with a mustard seed. And what is this, that so great a power is contained by something so small, so tiny—indeed, the smallest of small things?

For the Lord says:

“To what is the kingdom of God like? And to what shall I compare it?” (Luke 13).

When he says, “To what is it like?” he seems to indicate and bring forth the eagerness of one who is seeking. And is the Word alone—the fountain of knowledge, the stream of speech, who waters all hearts, opens understanding, and enlarges the mind—now laboring to discover a comparison?

But let us hear what he found.

“The kingdom of heaven,” he says, “is like a mustard seed.”

Searching in heaven and on earth, he finds nothing except a mustard seed in which to enclose the whole power of heavenly dominion. Does he compress and confine that kingdom, powerful in its uniqueness, blessed in its eternity, shining in its divinity, spread throughout the whole heaven and extended over the whole earth, within the narrowness of a mustard seed?

“The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed.”

Is this the whole hope of believers? Is this the supreme expectation of the faithful? Is this the happiness acquired by virgins through long labors of continence? Is this the glory won by martyrs through the outpouring of all their blood? Is this what “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart” (1 Corinthians 2)? Is this what the Apostle says has been prepared for those who love God, in an ineffable mystery?

Brothers, let us not be easily moved by the Lord’s sayings. For if what belongs to God is weak, it is stronger than human beings; and if what belongs to God is foolish, it is wiser than human beings (1 Corinthians 1). This least thing of God is found more magnificent than the entire greatness of the world—provided only that we sow this mustard seed in our minds in such a way that it grows for us into a great tree of understanding, that the whole mind may be lifted to heaven by the height of its meaning, and that it may spread throughout the branches of knowledge. Thus may it set our fervent mouths aflame with the living taste of its fruit; thus may it burn and blaze within our breasts with the fire of its seed; and through its taste may it take away from us all the weariness of our ignorance.

“The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed, which a man took and put in his garden; and it grew and became a great tree, and the birds of heaven rested in its branches.”

As he says, the kingdom of God is like a mustard seed. It is brought from above through the word, received through hearing, sown by faith, rooted through belief, enlarged by hope, spread through confession, extended through virtue, and expanded into branches. To these it calls the birds of heaven—that is, spiritual understandings—and in them it receives them into a peaceful dwelling.

Let the heretic come—let him come, because the entrance to the Church is always open to those who return. Let him come, let him hear, and let him cease now to bark against the Lord’s mercy:

If all the majesty of the heavenly kingdom has come in the likeness of a mustard seed, what is it that is being sought when God descends to humanity, and the Lord takes the form of a servant?

[Note: This passage rises against those who deny Christ’s humanity, especially Eutyches, who was a contemporary of the author. Saint Leo, writing to Julian, bishop of Cos, in what was formerly letter 11 and is now letter 25, says that Eutyches taught that the only-begotten Son of God was born from the womb of the blessed Virgin in such a way that he bore the appearance of a human body, but that the reality of human flesh was not united to God. Valentinus, Apollinaris, and the Manichaeans likewise denied that Christ possessed real human flesh.]

For he came in this way, heretic, so that everything might grow for you through faith, since everything had already failed you through nature.

“The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed.”

But let us return from the kingdom to the seed. Thus the whole fullness of the kingdom remains and consists in the kingdom of heaven.

Christ is the kingdom of heaven.

[Note: Hilary has similar remarks in his *Commentary on Matthew* 13, volume 1, p. 735 of the recent edition, where he compares Christ to a mustard seed.]

He, like a mustard seed, was placed in the garden of a virginal body, grew into a tree throughout the whole world through the cross, and, when crushed in his Passion, gave such a taste of his fruit that everything possessing life was flavored and seasoned by his touch.

[Note: The mustard seed is “least” in comparison with other things. But in warmer regions it rises far above human stature and grows into a tree. Herodotus testifies that this happens in the Babylonian countryside with sesame and millet.]

For just as the power of the mustard seed is hidden while the seed remains whole, but its power appears most forcefully when it is crushed, so Christ wished to be crushed in body, since he did not wish his power to remain hidden.

And we too, brothers, should crush this mustard seed, so that we may experience its power in this comparison.

Christ is king, because he himself is the whole origin of reigning. Christ is the kingdom, because in him is the whole majesty of his kingdom. Christ is human, because the whole human being is restored in Christ. Christ is the mustard seed, through which the whole greatness of God is reduced to the whole smallness of humanity.

[Note: That is, “he is abbreviated,” as in Psalm 88:14, “You have shortened the days of time,” where the Hebrew reads “you have abbreviated.” Mita.]

And what more? He himself became all things so that he might restore all things in himself. Christ the human being received the mustard seed—that is, Christ the human being received the kingdom of God, which Christ as God always possessed. He put it into his garden—that is, into the Church, his bride.

He often mentions this garden in the *Song of Songs*, saying:

“A garden enclosed” (Song of Songs 4).

The Church is the garden, spread throughout the whole world by the cultivation of the Gospel plough; enclosed by the goads of discipline; cleansed of every noxious weed through apostolic labor; made beautiful by the nurseries of the faithful, the lilies of virgins, the roses of martyrs, and the verdure of confessors; fragrant with everlasting flowers.

Christ therefore placed this mustard seed in his garden—that is, the promise of his kingdom, which was rooted in the patriarchs, born in the prophets, grew in the apostles, and made a great tree in the Church. It produced many branches through its gifts, which the Apostle enumerates, saying:

“To one is given the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge, to another the care of healings, to another the working of powers, to another prophecy, to another the discernment of spirits, to another different kinds of tongues” (1 Corinthians 12).

You have heard how this mustard seed burst into a tree; you have heard what roots it established; you have heard how great and how many are the branches into which it has now spread.

[Note: Christ predicts the future power and growth of evangelical teaching. How widely and how quickly the word of the Lord was spread may be learned from the Acts of the Apostles, Paul’s Epistles, and writers of the following century. Compare Irenaeus, book 1, chapter 3; Origen, *Homily* 4 on Ezekiel; Arnobius, book 2; Athanasius, in the synodal letter preserved by Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 4, chapter 3; Jerome, letter to Evagrius; Chrysostom, sermon on Pentecost. Tertullian, writing around the year 200, lists among the peoples subject to Christ “the varieties of the Gaetulians, the many regions of the Moors, places of Britain inaccessible to the Romans, the Sarmatians, Dacians, Scythians, and many peoples unknown to the Romans,” and so forth.]

The birds of heaven, not of the air, may rest in these branches, flying on the wings of wisdom and prudence, secure in faith.

And you, if you wish not to fear earthly beasts, if you wish to avoid predatory birds and ravenous vultures—that is, aerial birds, which are all spiritual wickedness—rise from the earth and abandon earthly things. Take the silvered wings of the prophetic dove (Psalm 67); take feathers radiant with the splendor of the divine Sun; fly forth in the appearance of gold, so that among such great branches you may always rest without any snare threatening you, strong in such a flight and secure in so great a dwelling.

We shall explain the following comparison in the following discourse, with the Lord as our teacher.

[Col. 0477A]

## SERMON XCIX. On the Parable of the Leaven
Well did today’s sequence of readings proceed, so that the woman of the Gospel, our mother, might receive from the Lord the leaven through which this temple might today be required of us in such holiness and rise into a mass. For the Lord began thus:

“To what shall I compare the kingdom of God? It is like leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, until the whole was leavened” (Luke XIII).

The good Lord, Christ, lover of his own, repeats the comparisons of his kingdom and varies his illustrations. He does not take them from hidden things or seek them from the heavens, but brings them forth from daily usage and proposes them from ordinary human life, so that what is beneficial to all may reach every kind of person, [Col. 0477B] in accordance with the prophet’s saying:

“Hear this, all nations; listen with your ears, all who inhabit the world, both earth-born and children of men, rich and poor alike” (Ps. XLVIII).

If he were to bring forward something from the hidden nature of divinity, something from royal secrecy, or something from the inner chambers of the wealthy, the poor would not know it, ordinary people would not grasp it, and simplicity would not recognize it. But now he speaks of what is familiar to the rich, customary to the poor, and native to all by the necessities of life [Note: [Col. 0477D] Derived from *verna*, that is, a household-born slave.], because in God’s call a human being is sought, not a person’s rank distinguished.

But let us repeat the comparison that has been read. “To what,” he says, “shall I compare the kingdom of God?” By saying this, he holds the minds of his hearers in suspense and makes them wonder completely what can be compared with the kingdom of God and with divine rule. While their thoughts wandered among many great things, the Lord of heaven found and fashioned an image of his kingdom in the lodging of a poor person, in the hand [Note: [Col. 0477D] So read very many editions. Others, with the Vallicellian manuscript, have *panicoctricis*. In the *Consuetudines of Toulouse*, Part II, under the heading “On Debts,” in Du Cange, there is *pancosteriae*. Pignorius marvels at the barbarous word, *De Servis*. Among the Latins they were called *a furno*. See Book XII, *De Fundo Instructo*, and elsewhere.] of a bread-baking woman, saying:

“It is like leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, until the whole was leavened.”

Previously he compared his kingdom with a mustard seed; now he makes it like leaven. Earlier he says that a man received the mustard seed; now he asserts that a woman received the leaven. Earlier he says that a man sowed a small seed so that it might grow into a great tree; now he makes clear that a woman hid a small quantity of leaven for the development of the whole mass.

Truly, as the apostle Paul said: “Neither is man without woman, nor woman without man, in the Lord” (I Cor. XI). A varied comparison brings the two sexes to the one kingdom. Christian calling does not separate man from woman: God joins them, nature associates them, [Col. 0478A] and a wondrous likeness makes their dispositions similar and their form harmonious. God makes one human being two, and two one; in the marital union one is the other self, so that there may be neither a deprived singularity nor a confused union.

But why does the Lord produce these comparisons of his kingdom through a man [Note: [Col. 0477D] In truth, the woman is not part of the parable unless one wishes to say, with Chrysologus and others below, that she signifies the Church. She is named rather than the man because the work of kneading is more characteristically woman’s than man’s.] and a woman? Why does he shape so great a majesty through examples so humble and so unlike it?

Brothers, a precious mystery lies hidden in this humility, as the Apostle says: “This is a great mystery, but I speak concerning Christ and the Church” (Eph. V). In these comparisons the principal affair of the human race is being handled. Through man and woman, the cause of the world, treated throughout the ages, is brought to its conclusion: Adam, the first man, and the first woman, Eve, are led from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil (Gen. III) to the fiery ardor of the evangelical mustard seed, so that [Col. 0478B] the eyes which that seductive tree had closed by opening them might be opened by the mustard tree’s collyrium and its very sharpness [Note: [Col. 0477D] When mustard seed is crushed, it becomes pungent and is aroused to its full force; by a natural sharpness it draws tears. Hence the Latin proverb: *Sinapi victitare*, “to lead a sorrowful life.”].

Thus the salutary tree might heal with the fiery taste of its fruit the mouths that the taste of the poisonous tree had infected; and this tree, by the fiery nourishment of its fruit, might kindle the conscience with the whole ardor of its way of life, whereas the other had made it completely cold through utter rigidity.

Nor is nakedness now either acted upon or confused, where pardon covers the whole human being and clothing of faith makes him warm. But this is conveyed by the mustard seed that the man received to the woman.

Let us examine more carefully what is conveyed to man through the leaven that the woman received.

“The kingdom of God,” he says, “is like leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of flour.”

The matter is drawn from ordinary practice. The man sows a mustard tree in the field; at home the woman prepares the leaven and makes loaves for food, because labor awaits the man outside, while domestic care confines the woman within. Hence Sarah, barren and elderly, from this preparation of leaven and [Note: [Col. 0477D] So, instead of “three seahs,” in Luke XIII, 21; Matthew XIII, [Col. 0478D] 33, Chrysologus reads it with the Arabic version. A *seah*, or *seach*, is a third of a *bath*, or *ephah*. It contains six *cab* measures, that is, one and a half Italian *modii*. But why does he say three? Because, apparently, three seahs were the measure of a single baking. Abraham baked three seahs, Genesis XXVIII, 6; Gideon the same number, Judges VI, 19; and Hannah, the mother of Samuel, one ephah, which amounts to the same, I Samuel I, 24.] from three measures offers and sets before the Lord’s hospitality three hearth-baked loaves as a mystical service (Gen. XVIII), so that the barrenness of the world, enclosed in the whole of old age, might place the leaven of faith in three measures [Note: [Col. 0478D] This is an older or similar exposition and interpretation, mentioned by Hilary, *Commentary on Matthew*, vol. I, chap. 13, p. 735: “Although I remember that many have understood the three measures of flour to refer to the mystery of faith, that is, to the unity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.” He rightly rejects and refutes this interpretation.], that is, in the equality of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and might set three loaves before her Lord in a confession of the Trinity; and through this gift might make the whole offspring of the Christian race fruitful.

But let us return to the subject. The woman received from God the leaven of faith, she who had received from the devil the leaven of unbelief. She hid it in three measures, that is, [Note: [Col. 0478D] Ambrose, Book VII on Luke, concerning the comparison of the kingdom of heaven with leaven, has something similar: “And because the leaven is said to have been hidden in three measures, it seemed fitting that we should believe the Son of God to have been hidden in the Law, covered in the Prophets, and fulfilled in the evangelical proclamations.”] in the three periods of humanity:

- from Adam to Noah;
- from Noah to Moses;
- from Moses to Christ.

[Col. 0479A] Thus the woman who had corrupted the whole mass of the human race with the leaven of death in Adam might restore the whole mass of our flesh through the leaven of resurrection in Christ; the woman who had prepared the bread of groaning and sweat might bake the bread of life and salvation; and through Christ might be the true mother of all the living, she who in Adam had been the mother of all the dead.

For this reason Christ wished to be born: so that, just as death came to all through Eve, life might likewise return to all through Mary. This Mary fulfills the type of this leaven, presents its likeness, and marks its figure, when she receives from above the leaven of the Word and kneads human flesh in the Virgin’s womb—indeed, in the Virgin’s womb she kneads the whole heavenly substance into a single mass.

But let us now reveal what allegorical meaning remains in this comparison. [Col. 0479B] [Note: [Col. 0479D] Ambrose, Book VII on Luke, in the chapter cited above, has the same interpretation. Bede likewise, on Luke XVII. Du Hamel, in order to prove that the progress of the Church is shown in this parable, cites these words of Chrysologus. This sermon, however, lacks its conclusion.]

The woman who received the leaven is the Church; the leaven that she received is the sacrament of heavenly doctrine; the three measures in which she is said to have hidden the leaven are the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospels. In them the divine meaning is mystically hidden and concealed in the word, so that it is not hidden from the faithful, though it is hidden from the unbelieving.

What he said—“until the whole was leavened”—is what the Apostle says: “We know in part, and we prophesy in part; but when that which is perfect has come, that which is in part will pass away” (I Cor. XIII).

In the kneading there is now divine knowledge: it sprinkles the senses, lifts the hearts, enlarges the intellects, and, in the manner of instruction, broadens, awakens, and spreads the increase of heavenly wisdom. The whole is leavened.

When? When Christ comes.

[Col. 0479C]

## SERMON C. On the Syrophoenician, or Canaanite Woman

Today Blessed Mark, while commending the prudence of the Syrophoenician woman [Note: [Col. 0479D] In Matthew this woman is called Ἑλληνίς (*Hellēnis*), “Greek.” The Jews called most of Syria “Greece,” especially because, after the Greeks had gained power, all peoples of other religions came to them under the name “Greeks.” See the Epistle to the Romans I, 16; II, 9; X, 12; and to the Galatians III, 28. Certainly, in the history of the Hebrews, when Antiochus returned from Judea to Antioch, he is said to have departed for Greece. She is also called Canaanite in Matthew XV, 22, because the Phoenicians were descended from the Canaanites.], recounting her faith, and exalting the ardor of her belief, raises no small question in anxious hearers by saying:

“And rising from there, the Lord departed into the region of Tyre and Sidon. He entered a house and wanted no one to know it, but he could not remain hidden” (Mark VII).

“He wanted to, but he could not.” To wish and not to be able is not a quality of divine majesty; it is [Note: [Col. 0480D] Hilary, on Psalm CXXXIV, vol. I, p. 530: “It belongs to a nature inferior to his that he should not both will and accomplish everything he wills.”] a weakness of human nature. For it is written: “All that the Lord willed, he did in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the abysses” (Psalm CXXXIV). And the Apostle says: “Who resists his will?” (Rom. IX, not XCV). Necessity overcomes a will that is not free and absolute.

The leper says to the Lord: “If you will, you can cleanse me” (Matt. VIII); and the evangelist says: “He wanted to, but he could not.”

What does blessed Mark mean? Must the woman’s faith be praised so highly that the Lord’s ability and will are made to bend? Or is faith’s cleverness so great that, against God’s will, it can investigate the divine secret?

The same seems to be meant by what occurred when the Lord wished to reveal and prove the Hemorrhoissa’s faith through the evidence of his power, asking: “Who touched me?” His disciples said to him: “The crowds press around you, and you say, ‘Who touched me?’” (Mark V).

The disciples thought that everyone was touching the Lord merely by pressing against him bodily, and that all were joined to him alike through such a physical contact. But he knew that the woman, who had felt and sought differently, had reached his majesty and penetrated his power—not bodily and not by an ordinary touch, but by faith [Note: [Col. 0480D] All printed editions have *ista sciebat*, “he knew this woman.”].

Therefore it is not a man but God, not flesh but spirit, who cries: “Who touched me?”—so that the power of the deed might reveal the one whom his humanity was then concealing.

But let us investigate more clearly what “he wanted to” and “he could not” mean. Remembering his promise, Christ had first come for the salvation of the Israelite people, so that he might faithfully fulfill what he had promised to Abraham (Gen. XXII), to David his offspring (Ps. CXXXI), and to his descendants. But because they had shown themselves unworthy through their unbelief, the faith of the Gentiles obtained, seized, and carried off what the unbelief of the Jews had rejected and lost.

Hear him saying it himself: “I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. XV).

But the sheep, already rabid from the contagion of wolves and fiercer than the beasts themselves in their own savagery, always wished to tear apart and violate their shepherd. Therefore Christ could not fulfill his will—not because of any inability in himself, but because of the wickedness of the lost. What he had assigned to some, he was compelled to confer upon others, as he himself says: “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and those who use violence seize it” (Matt. XI, 12).

The faith of the Gentiles used violence, so that it might seize the Father’s inheritance and wholly wrest the inheritance of the children from the children themselves, as the present reading shows more clearly.

For as soon as the woman heard about him, whose daughter had an unclean spirit, she entered and fell at his feet. She was a Gentile, a Syrophoenician by race. And she begged him to cast the demon out of her daughter.

He said to her: “Let the children first be satisfied, for it is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.”

He did not say, “It is not right to throw it to the dogs,” but “It is not right to take it from the children and throw it to the dogs,” because giving bread to dogs, although it is not an act of human kindness, is nevertheless consistent with human reason. [Col. 0481A]

When their masters are sleeping at night, the dog both guards and keeps watch: it exposes the stranger, disturbs the thief, and runs to meet the robber, relieving the servants of care and anxiety.

Yet how did he take the bread from the children, to whom he had so often and in so many ways offered, given, and supplied it? They tried to trample upon what had been offered, to their guilt rather than for their life; yet what had been broken and trampled by the children, the dog hastened to lick with complete faith and complete desire.

Hence she answered in this way: “Certainly, Lord; for even the little dogs under the table eat from the children’s crumbs.” [Note: [Col. 0481D] In antiquity, puppies too were counted among the delicacies of the dining room. See Ursinus, in the Appendix to Ciacconius, *De Triclinio*. This is also repeatedly attested by marble sculptures.]

Rightly, then, she who confessed herself a dog is changed into a human being; and those who refused to be children are justly turned into dogs [Note: [Col. 0481D] By this name he indicates the Gentiles, because they led impure lives and were involved with the blood of sacrifices offered to idols, says Theophylact, on Matthew XV; or because they were hated by the Jews, as he repeats elsewhere. See Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* II, p. 361; Chrysostom, Homily 23 on Matthew. The Theophylact cited above adds, on Matthew VII: “Dogs are ἄπιστοι (*apistoi*), unbelievers.” See Photius, Epistle 54, p. 107; Isidore of Pelusium, Book IV, Epistle 81.]; she is rightly adopted as a daughter, raised up, and honored at the table, she who cast herself beneath the table with praiseworthy and prudent humility. She now rightly feasts wholly on the crumbs from the bread, since by her merits she understood and confessed that she scarcely deserved them.

And what more is there to say? Hence, because of her righteousness, the Lord could neither give the bread to the Jews nor deny it to the Gentiles [Note: [Col. 0482D] Something seems to be missing from this homily. *MITA*.].

## SERMON CI. On the Contempt of Death by the Faithful, and Why God Permitted It

On the passage in Luke: “Do not fear those who kill the body,” etc.

You have heard, brothers, how Christ addresses his soldiers with royal exhortation, so that by despising death [Note: [Col. 0482D] The Caesena manuscript has “of their own bodies.”] they may not fear those who kill the body.

Finally, he enrolls among the rights of friends those who, [Col. 0481C] out of zeal for triumph and love of freedom, shed their blood joyfully and without trembling. For he says:

“But I say to you, my friends: Do not be afraid of those who kill the body, and after that have nothing more that they can do. But I will show you whom you should fear: fear him who, after he has killed, has power to cast into Gehenna. But I say to you, my friends: Do not be afraid” (Luke XII).

“But I say to you, my friends: Do not be afraid,” because courage proves freedom, while fear indicates servitude. The free person is born for glory; the slave is born for fear. Therefore he is rightly raised to friendship with God who, for God’s sake, despises human deaths and knows no fears.

If imitation of conduct makes friends, and likeness of conduct joins them together, Christ appropriately calls those his friends whom he sees and foresees, by imitating him, trampling underfoot the darts of the world and the very fear of death.

“But I say to you”—that is, [Col. 0481D] not to everyone, but to friends. Cyril, in the *Catena of the Greek Fathers*: “This saying does not seem simply to apply to everyone, but to those who love God with their whole mind, to whom it is fitting to say: ‘Who will separate us from the love of Christ?’]

“But I say to you.” To those whom death releases but does not destroy. “I say to you.” To those whom the dissolution of the body advances to something better, [Col. 0482A] and does not lead to punishment. “I say to you.” To those for whom life begins through death rather than ends. “I say to you”—to those whose death becomes precious not because of its nature, but because of its cause, since in it they find the gain of life rather than lose life’s interest.

But let us hear what he says to his friends: “Do not be afraid of those who kill the body.”

Let those who have worn out the ancient volumes of the pagans on the goodness of death hear this. They were nevertheless unable to draw from them any virtue or find any consolation. Even if, with all the strength of eloquence, they armed their minds for enduring death, dried their tears, removed their sighs, denied their groans, and enclosed their sorrows, they sought nothing for their readers either from certain hope, perpetual life, or true salvation.

Who could say to a human being—who could say to a wise man—“To die is natural; it is necessary to perish”? The ancients lived for us; we live for those who will come; no one lives for himself. To want what cannot be removed is a mark of virtue: willingly accept what you are compelled to accept unwillingly. Death does not exist before it comes; when it has come, one does not know that it has come. Therefore do not grieve that you have lost what, once you have lost it, you will not grieve over.

But when they have said such things, [Note: [Col. 0482D] Concerning the sentence passed upon human beings, namely, that they are mortal, not concerning life, etc. *MITA*. Or, concerning eternal life, which awaits us after death.] they speak entirely about the sentence, not about life. For they did not know from where, when, or how death came to you, or through whom it came. But the author of life revealed to us the author of death. For God did not make death (Wisdom I); but through the devil’s envy death entered the world (Wisdom II).

But you say: Why did God allow his work to perish through the devil’s work?

O human being, if you wished to know what you ask, you would pause a little, apply your mind, and open your ears, so that you yourself, as such a curious investigator, might recognize the principal affair. But you, always occupied with other things and never with yourself, because you do not know the causes of things, the whole course of the ages, the depth of judgments, or the impenetrable secret, lazily and idly bring accusations.

Did you not, in order to learn the letters and recognize their elements, submit yourself to a teacher and attach yourself to school, wholly enduring labor and hardship, so that you knew neither home nor parents? How useful to you is that to which a teacher assigns you, the school imposes upon you, and the instructor, through your own hardships and his labor, urges you, so that you may wish to know such things and deem yourself worthy to hear matters so great.

The apostles prove this, especially Paul, who taught by being beaten, not by beating others, so that as an excellent teacher he might undergo and endure as many sufferings as a human being has dispositions.

And are we to learn in a moment the principles of things and the causes of the world because we are commanded to do so? And how are we commanded? You hear, but not in the manner in which you ought. This servitude and such necessity excuse us [Note: [Col. 0482D] The Caesena manuscript has: “such necessity perhaps excuses.”]; but such great freedom and such a will unquestionably accuse you. What we say is our duty; what we say less fully is the result of your impatience.

You ask, human being, why God did not immediately destroy death together with its author, and why he did not then, through his providence, forestall its deadly poison, lest it reach the destruction of the whole world and especially of his own image.

The heaven that you see, human being, firmly established in the whole expanse of air, bears many waters, yet is itself borne by no one, because a command alone hangs it in place and the power of the decree alone sustains it, as the divine utterance reveals:

“He stretches out the heavens like a skin; he covers its upper regions with waters” (Psalm CIII).

The earth, trampled beneath so great a weight and solidified under the mass of mountains, floats upon a liquid foundation [Note: [Col. 0483D] Elsewhere: “element.”], as the prophet says:

“He founded the earth upon the waters” (Psalm CXXXV),

so that what stands is the result of a command, not of nature.

“He himself spoke, and they were made; he himself commanded, and they were created” (Psalm CXLVIII), so that what stands is the work of God, not the product of human reason.

The sea, carried along by the crest of its great agitation and raised toward the clouds, is restrained by slender grains of sand, so that we may see such great power [Note: [Col. 0483D] Caelius Sedulius, Book I:

“You who forbid the roaring storms of the sea, as the wave rises,
to engulf the neighboring boundaries of the land.”] yield not to dust but to a command.

Everything that is in these things moves and lives, made by command alone. The prophet again confirms that by a single command they will be dissolved when he says:

“In the beginning, Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They will perish, but you will remain, and all of them will grow old like a garment; and like a covering you will change them, and they will be changed” (Psalm CXI).

How? So that it is the creature’s old age, not the Creator, that perishes with time.

But now, whoever you are who ask, you say that we have wandered from the subject. When you ask why God allowed death to remain for the destruction of his creature, we have described at length how heaven, earth, and sea were made from nothing and will again be dissolved into nothing, and [Note: [Col. 0483D] With respect to old age, as he explains shortly above when he says: “So that it is the creature’s old age, not the Creator, that perishes with time.” The world must be cleansed and renewed through the burning of all composites existing on earth, in water, or in air, and the change will be accidental, as the theologians teach in Bonacina, *De Incarnatione*, disputation 2, question 5, point 5 and the last point. See Bellarmine on Psalm CI, verse 26. *MITA*.] have supplied you with ever more material for inquiry.

You say: “I asked why human beings perish, but you have established that you and the elements themselves will perish, so that you might provide weary mortal minds with consolation from the universality of perishing, not an explanation that would bring rest. As though it were not painful for heaven to perish, for earth to be dissolved, and for the whole appearance of things to be abolished by the law of mortality.”

You say, I ask: What is more beautiful than heaven? What more splendid than the sun? What more pleasing than the moon? What more adorned than the stars? What more healthful than the earth? What more useful than the sea? Or what old age is there in these things? They continue just as they were born or made; surely it would be more pleasing for them to remain than to perish.

Human being, perhaps it would be more pleasant, but it would not be more useful. For while these things stood, you stumbled; while they shone, you were blinded and could not see. The brightness of heaven stupefied your senses, and the sun blinded your eyes with its splendor. Deceived by their beauty, you denied their maker. You confessed as gods those rulers of the world whom the true God had subjected to your service. Therefore everything must be dissolved and all things renewed, so that at least then you may believe that they were made when you see that they have been restored.

Nor should you think that we have wandered, since you see that, as an argument for your understanding, we have traversed the whole of creation.

Human being, when your creator made you from dust, you did not see it. For if you had seen yourself being made, you would never have mourned yourself as destined to die. You saw yourself perfected; you saw yourself alive; you saw yourself beautiful; you already saw yourself like your creator. Since you had not seen yourself being born or dying, how could you know from where you would be or what you would be?

Hence you attributed everything to nature, yourself to yourself, and nothing to God. Therefore God brought you back through nature and allowed you to be recalled from nothing into dust, so that you might see what you had been and, when you rise again, give thanks—you who, having been made and created, proved yourself utterly ungrateful [Note: [Col. 0484D] Elsewhere: “restored.”].

Let us not fear, therefore, brothers, those who kill the body, as the Lord said, because they do not destroy this life; they destroy it only in such a way that they make it eternal from temporal life.

What more is there, brothers? He allowed to die the one whom he could raise up; he who is sufficient to give life allowed himself to be killed. To him be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON CII. On the Centurion.

Christ, remaining in our body, did not raise all the dead, nor heal all the sick. Let us believe that this was lacking not in his power but in the time appointed. Then he would have illumined the whole world with the full splendor of his power, removed the time of faith, and left nothing of his second coming for glory. Nor did he so moderate the signs of his powers that he failed both to reveal an indication of his divinity and to offer the fullest proof for believing, while removing every excuse for crafty unbelief—as the centurion whom the Evangelist Luke mentions demonstrated today by his faith and foresight.

“A certain centurion’s servant,” he says, “being gravely ill, was dying; and he was precious to him.” This centurion was a Roman; but in the hundredfold fruit he was more Christian.

[Note: For centurions commanded a hundred soldiers, and the hundredfold yield is greater in interest.]

He served God more than the world; and, brave in human warfare, he was braver in divine warfare, remaining a guardian of peace. “His servant, being gravely ill, was dying, and he was precious to him.”

[Note: Perhaps he was also a soldier. For among the Hebrews soldiers were sometimes called servants of their commanders.]

He was a servant, valued at a price. Let us therefore ask who this servant was who was precious to him.

[Note: Whom his master valued very highly.]

If the soul rules, the body serves; and to a human being nothing is more precious than the body. This servant of that centurion, precious to him, was sick unto death. Therefore the centurion asked that Christ alone might assist the mortal body by granting it perpetual life.

“When he had heard,” he says, “about Jesus, he sent elders of the Jews to him.”

[Note: Either the magistrates of the town or the heads of the synagogue. Both were called by this name.]

A Gentile sends Jews to Christ; and one who was outside the law points out to those placed within the law the author of the law. Let no one therefore be surprised if a Gentile—that is,

[Note: One summoned from paganism to the faith, or a Christian because of the faith by which he believed that Christ could heal his servant. And perhaps, as Grotius observes, this centurion professed the worship of the one God together with the Hebrews, or believed Christ to be the Messiah sent by God. Chrysostom, Homily 26, elsewhere 27, vol. VII of the works, p. 314, Monfaucon edition: “See that the centurion had a true opinion of Christ; for he did not say ‘Ask,’ nor did he say ‘Pray,’ ‘Entreat,’ but only ‘Command.’”]

a Christian—either calls, leads, or brings someone to Christ.

“He sent elders of the Jews to him, asking him to come and save his servant.” When they had come to Jesus, they earnestly begged him, saying: “He is worthy that you should grant this to him, for he loves our nation, and he himself built us the synagogue.”

The Jews plead for a Gentile who does not plead for himself; and they act sufficiently for the salvation of another’s servant, though they do nothing for the salvation of their own sons. They say: “He is worthy that you should grant this to him.” If he is worthy who hears, believes, and sends to Christ, how is the one who comes to Christ, sees him, and does not believe shown to be unworthy?

“For he loves our nation.” He loves your nation, since he makes it suppliant before Christ; but you hate it, since you make it obstinate toward Christ. Or how could a Christian not love your nation, when, by confessing Christ to have come from your nation, he raises and exalts everything belonging to your nation to heavenly glory?

“He loves our nation, and he himself built us the synagogue.”

[Note: Augustus had ordered—and Tiberius followed his institutions—that Jews should not be prevented from assembling in synagogues anywhere. It therefore cannot seem unusual that a Roman should have undertaken to restore a synagogue, perhaps using the labor of soldiers, whom the Romans customarily assigned to public works so that leisure would not turn them toward dissipation. Chrysostom, in the passage cited above, p. 316, at the end: “That Matthew declares him not to have been an Israelite himself, while Luke says that he built the synagogue, is not contradictory; for he could both be a non-Jew and have built a synagogue.”]

You have heard that the synagogue has always been destroyed and continually lies among the rubble, nor does it rise into a heavenly structure unless a Christian builder has fashioned it into the summit of the Church.

“Jesus,” he says, “was going with them.” But they were not going with Jesus, since they were not going with him in mind; nor were they with him, since they appeared joined to him in body while separated in heart.

“And when he was already not far away.” From whom? From the Gentile. However far the Jews separated themselves from Christ, Christ was nevertheless being joined to the Gentiles.

“And when he was already not far away, the centurion sent friends to him.” He had first sent Jews; now he sends friends. By calling the Jews this, he indicates them to be enemies, as the Apostle confirms when he says: “Enemies for your sake” (Rom. XI). While the Jews begrudged the Gentiles their having believed, they lost everything that belonged both to the law and to grace.

“He sent friends to him.” Hear the Lord saying to the apostles: “I no longer call you servants, but friends” (John XV). Just as faith promotes servants into friends, so unbelief reduces sons into punitive servitude.

[Note: The Caesena manuscript has: “Just as it promotes the faithful servants into friends, so it reduces the sons of unbelief into punitive servitude.”]

“He sent friends to him, saying: ‘Lord, do not trouble yourself.’” Why? “Because I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof.”

You see that Christ was leading the Jews more than he was led by the Jews, so that they might hear that in the centurion there was reverence for divinity, in the Gentile observance of the law, in the soldier the payment of grace, in the Roman the teaching of faith, in the pagan’s coldness Christian warmth, in an earthly breast a heavenly secret, and in the world’s entire servitude the complete knowledge of supreme dominion.

“Lord, do not trouble yourself.” This is to say: God, why do you trouble yourself in a human body? Why do you wear yourself out with earthly labor and fatigue yourself by the length of the road? Why do you travel through places, when you are wholly present everywhere and hold and possess the whole creation within yourself?

“Lord, do not trouble yourself; I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof.”

Brothers, what is the roof that either makes a human being worthy or renders him unworthy, that invites or repels divine approach? Brothers, this roof is the body that covers the soul, veils the perception of the spirit, conceals the dwelling of the heart, and shuts the mind’s freedom away from the heavenly vision. Under this roof, therefore, the centurion considers Christ unworthy to enter—that is, he considers it unworthy that divine majesty should enter the human body.

[Col. 0486B] “I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof.” But God, who, whenever he wills, makes what is human divine, and who, when he deigns, changes what belongs to our flesh into his spirit, does not disdain either to dwell in flesh or to enter beneath the roof of our body.

“Therefore,” he says, “I also considered myself unworthy to come to you.”

[Note: Both attitudes suit a pious, humble, devoted man: namely, to consider himself unworthy both that he should come to Christ and that Christ should approach him.]

This is the twofold attitude of the devout person: he considers it unworthy that God should come to him, and he knows that it is not fitting for him to approach God.

[Note: He considers himself unworthy. So the Caesena manuscript reads.]

Who enters a judge’s presence without being summoned? Who enters a king’s presence without being ordered? How much more, then, does no one come to God unless called? “Those whom he called,” he says, “he also justified” (Rom. VIII).

The centurion therefore does not shrink from the Lord’s coming, nor reject Christ’s presence; rather, he acts so that it may be the grace of the one who calls, not the presumption of one who ventures forward. For he suggests and illustrates what God can do by a human example, saying:

“For I too am a man placed under authority, having soldiers under me; and I say to this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.”

[Note: He indicates that he is subject either to a tribune or to a governor. Bede, here, chapter 25.]

That is: If I, who am placed under authority, make those subject to me obey by the command of a mere word, how much more can you, who are subject to no one and to whose authority all things are subject, heal by a word when you command? Can you not send health? Can you not command powers? Or can you not restore by a word what you made by a word? “He spoke,” it says, “and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. CXLVIII). Or are you not sufficient to restore something from something, since you prepared all things from nothing? Say therefore with a word, and my boy will be healed.

He fulfilled what the prophet sang concerning God: “He sent his word and healed them, and delivered them from their corruption” (Ps. CIV).

Brothers, this centurion, by saying, “I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof,” represents the Christian people, who judge themselves unworthy to merit Christ’s bodily presence, but by the word alone, by the message, by the mere hearing of faith, hear, believe, and behold all the Lord’s powers in their own healing.

For when he says, “I say to this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it,” he demonstrates the rejection of the Jews, the calling of the Gentiles, and the obedience of the Christian people in this way: “I say to this one”—that is, to the Jew who did not believe—“Go,” and he goes; “and to another”—that is, to the Gentile, because he believed—“Come,” and he comes; “and to my servant”—that is, to the Christian—“Do this,” and he does it.

Let us pray, brothers, that we may deserve to be Christians not in name only but in faith, and that we may not merely hear what is commanded, but do what we have heard. For just as it is the mark of a devoted servant to do what is commanded, so it is the mark of a rebellious servant not to do what is commanded.

Say therefore with a word, and my boy will be healed.

When Jesus heard this, he marveled.

The Creator of marvels marvels; the maker of ears, as though he did not know what he had not heard, is astonished at what he hears. But by marveling that the Gentile had believed in this way, he rebukes the unbelief of the Jews.

[Note: That is, he acted and spoke as one marveling, so that those standing by might marvel at and imitate the centurion’s faith. See Chrysostom, so often cited, Homily 26, formerly 27.]

Finally, speaking to the crowds following him and reproving the Jews who remained in death, he says: “Amen, I say to you, I have not found such faith even in Israel.”

It is true, brothers: faith alone lives, and will live among the Gentiles; signs and powers grow weary and accomplish nothing among the Jews.

# SERMON CIII. On the Son of the Widow Raised from the Dead, and on the Resurrection of Bodies

Today the blessed Evangelist, having announced that through Christ the only son of a widowed mother—already bound in the bonds of death, already placed upon a mournful bier, and already proceeding with the crowds from the prison of death toward the tomb—was restored to life (Luke VII), shook everyone’s hearts, moved their minds, and astonished their hearing.

But let the Gentiles marvel, let the Jews be amazed, let the world tremble. We, however, who believe that all the dead from the ages will be raised from their tombs at Christ’s single word—why should we marvel?

“ The dead will rise,” says Isaiah, “and those who are in the tombs will rise again” (Isa. XXVI, according to the Septuagint). And the Lord says: “The hour will come when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live” (John V). To this the Apostle adds: “In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet; for the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible” (1 Cor. XVI).

What is this trumpet that wages war upon the underworld, loosens the masses of the tomb, thunders life to the dead, and gives everlasting triumph in the light to those who rise? What is it? It is the one of which the Lord said above: “The dead will hear the voice of the Son of God” (John V).

It is not a trumpet that, with breath compressed through the hollow horn of wood or bronze, gives a mournful bellow to combatants,

[Note: He attributes the bellow to the trumpet, to which the reverberation belongs.]

but one that, from the Father’s heart through the Son’s mouth, gives a life-giving cry alike to those below and those above.

“And at the last trumpet” (1 Cor. XVI): the trumpet that at the beginning called the world out of nothing will at the end call the world back from ruin; and the trumpet that at the beginning raised the human being from clay will at the end raise the human being again from dust.

Brothers, this is what we believe, because the trumpet of the divine voice divided chaos, gathered the universe, cleansed the elements, distinguished the world, suspended the heaven, founded the earth, bound the sea, plunged down the infernal regions, assigned the changes of orders, and commanded the continual service of created things. And, lest the universe remain empty and dreadful, it fitted it with inhabitants and so distributed their dwelling places: in heaven it placed angels living by spirit alone; on earth it established various forms of life among earthly creatures; in the air it granted winged souls to fly through it; in the waters it made creatures both small and great, so that a multitude of living things might exist. In a wondrous manner it joined the world’s structure from separate parts, so that neither their commixture might confuse their distinction nor the distinction of things sever their unity.

Hence the union of day and night is so divided that labor arises from rest and rest from labor. Hence the sun and moon in turn circle the boundaries of the world, so that the sun, with a doubled light, may increase the brightness of day, and the moon, with a comparable light, may not leave the periods of night wholly blind.

[Note: Some printed books have “with germinating light,” but incorrectly. Latinius emends it in this way, and all the manuscripts and the first Bologna edition have this reading, as Mita observes, who offers various explanations here. The more suitable interpretation is that the sun is said to shine with doubled light: first, it shines from itself; second, through the moon and stars, which it illumines with its light.]

[Note: The moon then appears comparable to the sun when it is completely illuminated by it.]

Hence the stars, by their course, change their various risings, so that during the nights they both mark the hours and provide guidance to travelers.

[Note: Barthius praises these words as aptly expressed, Adversaria, book LVIII, chapter 5, p. 2730.]

Hence the seasons, as they pass, arrive; they begin to exist when they cease. Hence seeds are born, grow, mature, become youthful, grow old, fall, die, and then, buried again in life-giving furrows and released from decay, return from a saving death to their own life; raised from corruption, they are restored in an enduring form.

[Note: The Caesena and Vallicella manuscripts read this; the printed editions have “their own.” For the form of these seeds is perpetuated and continued in the world through corruption and vivification. Mita.]

And if, brothers, the voice of God—the trumpet of Christ—calls, recalls, leads, brings back, commands to exist, causes not to exist, gives over to death, and restores to life throughout days, months, seasons, and years, why should it not be able to do once in us what it always does in all things? Or does divine power grow weary in us alone, for whose sake alone the majesty of God has performed everything that has been foretold?

Human being, if all things belonging to you come to life again for you from death, why do you not come to life again from death for God? Or does God’s creation perish in you alone, for whose sake all creation subsists, operates, changes, and is renewed every day?

[Note: Elsewhere, “throughout the entire day.”]

Brothers, I say these things not wishing to diminish Christ’s powers in his signs, but urging that, by the example of one who rose again, we may be stirred to faith in the resurrection of all and believe that

[Note: Said symbolically. Moreover, some writers observe the figure of a plow in the cross. See Bosius, On the Cross.]

the cross is the plow of our body; faith, the seed; the furrow, the tomb; dissolution, the sprout; expectation, the season. Thus, when the springtime of the Lord’s coming smiles upon us, the ripened greenness of our bodies may then rise into a living harvest, knowing no end, knowing no gray hair, suffering no bundle, and feeling no scourge.

For when the chaff of old age has been laid down in death, the newness of the glorious body rises into fruit.

If Christ was so moved by the temporary tears of one widow that he met her on the way, stilled the streams of grief flowing from her eyes, struck down death,

[Note: Elsewhere, “overcame.”]

restored the human being, raised the body, returned life, changed mourning into joy, transformed a sorrowful funeral procession into a festal birthday, and returned alive from death to his mother the one placed upon the bier—what will he do now, when he burns with power against the enduring tears of his Church and the bloody sweat of his bride?

For through the praying Church he pours forth continual tears; through the martyrs he sweats sacred blood, until Christ, meeting his only son—that is, the Christian people, whom so many ages bear toward death—restores him from the mortal bier to everlasting life, for the eternal joy of the heavenly mother.

But since the time of the newborn Christ has arrived, and virginity about to give birth already shines with a heavenly miracle, and the rising of the divine King is now announced to us not by a star but by the rising of the sun, let us all hasten to meet him in worship, and with sacred gifts confess that God and King has proceeded from the virginal temple.

Let us offer gifts, because an offering is always publicly prepared for the newborn King. Let us offer gifts, because an empty worshiper is entirely lacking in devotion.

This the Magus proves: laden with gold, inflamed with incense, and consecrated with myrrh, he bows before Christ’s cradle (Matt. II). What is it, then, if a Christian does not do what the Magus did? What is it, if at the joy of Christ’s birth the poor man weeps, the captive groans, the stranger laments, and the traveler cries out?

The Jew has always honored the heavenly festivals with tithes.

[Note: Among the Hebrews there were two kinds of tithes: those paid to the Levites and those consumed in the temple on the occasion of festivals. Christian agapae seem to have succeeded them. The rabbis wish references to these tithes to be found in Deut. XIV, 22; XXII, 12; and XVII, 18. See Lyra on Deuteronomy XXVI.]

What does a Christian think of himself if he does not honor God even with hundredths?

Brothers, let no one suppose that I say this with the zeal of a declaimer rather than with the feeling of one who grieves. I grieve—indeed, I grieve—when I read that the Magi drenched Christ’s cradle with gold, and see that Christians have left the altar of Christ’s body empty, especially at this time, when vast famine,

[Note: Mita, together with the printed editions, reads “hunger lays waste,” and discusses the passage at length, as though hunger were devastating and destroying itself. Latinius emends it to “vast,” and admits that this is how it is read in the Caesena manuscript. The sense is: “When vast hunger and the lamentable crowd of captives pour themselves forth in tears.”]

when the lamentable crowd of captives pours itself forth.

[Note: That is, by wailing and tears it cries out so loudly for Christian compassion that the bowels of the poor seem to be poured out like metal. Mita. “The crowd pours itself forth,” that is, pours itself out, rushes together, and so forth.]

Let no one say, “I have nothing,” when God asks from what you have, not from what you do not have, and graciously credits the widow with her two small coins.

[Note: This agrees very well with Saint Leo, Sermon 3 on the Fast of the Seventh Month. Mita.]

Let us be devoted to the Creator, so that creation may be devoted to us. Let us support the distress of our neighbors, so that we may be freed from our own distresses. Let us fill God’s altar, so that the fullness of fruits may fill our barns. Certainly, if we do not give, let us not complain that we do not receive.

May our God himself grant you both present and future blessings, through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong all honor and perpetual glory, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# SERMON CIV. On the Rich Man Whose Field Was Productive

Whenever this rich man comes before us—the man whom, through all the ages, throughout the whole world, every day, the cry of the divine voice accuses—so often the deceptive allure of riches is driven away, so often the raging flame of desires is quenched, and so often the mad fury of avarice is calmed.

For today the Lord Jesus began in this way:

“The field of a certain rich man produced abundant crops; and he thought within himself, saying: ‘What shall I do, since I have nowhere to gather my crops?’ And he said: ‘This I will do: I will destroy my barns and make them larger, and there I will gather all the good things that have been born to me; and I will say to my soul: Soul, you have many good things stored up for many years; rest, eat, drink, feast.’ But God said to him: ‘Fool, this night they demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?’”

Wretched man, whom abundance made barren; whom plenty made anxious; whom riches made inhuman; whom wealth made a beggar. A human field endured an inhuman master. What the earth poured forth generously, he shut up and gathered narrowly, so that he might be the guardian of others’ possessions, since he refused to be a distributor of his own: ungrateful toward God, wicked toward himself, an enemy of the poor, a disgrace among the rich,

[Note: He enclosed the things that nature brings forth for the benefit of human beings. Basil, Homily 6, entitled “On Avarice,” says that such a rich man does not remember human nature.]

a prison for nature.

“The field of a certain rich man produced abundant crops, and he thought within himself.” As though anyone could think outside himself! Yet this man thought within himself because, having received an impious plan into his heart, he left himself nothing of piety and nothing of mercy.

“And he thought within himself, saying.” He used a counselor worthy of himself,

[Note: Our inner companion, with whom we ourselves take counsel, is the mind. But an evil mind can be neither a source of comfort nor a companion to us.]

for an evil mind could have neither comfort nor a companion.

“And he thought within himself, saying.” An impious mind was contending with piety, and he was suffering an inward war, because he had lost the peace and rest of mercy.

“And he thought within himself, saying: ‘What shall I do?’” This is the voice of one asking a question. And whom do you think he was asking? There was another within him, because the devil had already taken possession of the inner chambers of his mind and sat enthroned there,

[Note: Elsewhere, “was seated within.”]

and the one who had entered Judas’s heart held the secret place of his mind.

“What shall I do, since I have nowhere?” You have heard how the rich man says that he has nothing. Behold, he cries: “I have nothing.” It is true, for the one who always seeks never has enough, and the one who seeks in this way to gather has nowhere to gather.

But let us hear what his inner counselor answered him: “I will destroy my barns.” Clearly the one who was hiding appeared, because the enemy always begins with destruction. He acts, he acts, so that you may destroy what you have and fail to restore what you have desired.

Wretched rich man, ignorant of the present, you argue most foolishly about the future!

[Note: This wording comes from Mita’s edition and the Vallicella manuscript; it is absent in others.]

How much better you would have transferred your present possessions, where the soul has its dwelling!

But now

[Note: Basil says similar things in his Homily “To the Rich,” where he discusses avarice at length, vol. II of the works, p. 51: “Bring forth the wealth bound in prison.”]

the chains of your barns have tightened the throats of the poor, bound the necks of guests, and crushed the entrails of the hungry. Hence the groans of the poor go before you and follow you; the sallow faces of your guests accuse you; the crowd of those who ask attacks you with lamentation. Thus, condemned by the heavenly Judge, you will receive the full measure of punishments, since, by denying others, you have shut yourself inside the bolts of your barns.

To the rich man thinking within himself, he rightly replied who knows the thoughts of human beings, because “they are vain” (Ps. XCIII): “Fool, this night they demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?”

Well called a fool, because everything in him had been of the flesh and nothing of the heart. Well called a fool,

[Note: Gregory, Morals XXII, chapter 12: “He was taken away that same night who had been awaiting many years, so that the man who had planned for a long future by gathering for himself would not see even the following day.” Mita here praises a passage of Saint Maximus, Sermon on Saint Michael: “Naked we are born into the world, and naked we also approach the font. How incongruous, then, that she whom her mother bore naked and the Church receives naked should wish to enter heaven rich.”]

because he was preparing abundant stores for the soul that was soon to depart.

“This night they demand your soul from you.” Appropriately “this night,” because, fleeing the light of mercy, he had handed himself over to the darkness of avarice by saying: “Eat, drink, feast.”

That those who drink are sons of night, not of day, the Apostle makes clear in this way: “Those who become drunk are drunk at night” (1 Thess. V). Through obscurity he is carried, and through darkness he is received, who entrusted and stored the support of life in the enclosures of his barns.
