“They demand your soul from you.” Why did he not say, “the one who had given it demands it back,” but “they demand it”?

[Note: Others interpret it in the same way. Evil angels demand the souls of the impious; good angels demand the souls of the righteous.]

Because the God of the saints demands their souls and leads them back, while the ministers of Tartarus demand and drag away the souls of the impious.

“And he thought within himself, saying: ‘What shall I do, since I have nowhere to gather my crops?’ And he said: ‘This I will do: I will destroy my barns and make them larger, and there I will gather all the good things that have been born to me; and I will say to my soul: Soul, you have many good things stored up for many years; eat, drink, feast.’ But God said to him: ‘Fool, this night they demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?’”

Thus this rich man was overtaken, so that he lost what he had thought about more than what he had prepared. The prophet’s saying was fulfilled: “His spirit will go forth, and he will return to his earth; on that day all their thoughts will perish” (Ps. CXLV).

This man thought about what he would leave behind him, not what he would send ahead of himself. Hence, according to the Apostle: “They became vain in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened; claiming to be wise, they became fools” (Rom. I).

He is called a fool, and, awakened from the sleep of this present life, he found nothing in his hands in that eternity, as the Psalmist said: “They slept their sleep, and all the men of riches found nothing in their hands” (Ps. LXXV).

Wake, therefore, rich man, in good works; sleep in evil, so that your hand may not be empty toward the poor, but may always be full for you. For as much as a rich man pours forth generously, so much does it generously overflow into his affairs.

[Note: Elsewhere, “in streams.”]

Be rich, therefore, in mercy, if you always wish to be rich. Then your barns will be larger and full, if they are not emptied by generosity and closed by greed.

# SERMON CV. On the Woman Who Had a Spirit of Infirmity
Today Christ’s care both gave a remarkable proof of divine power, exposed the cunning of diabolical fraud, and released a woman wounded by a long and obscure affliction, as the Evangelist says:

> Jesus was teaching in the synagogue on the Sabbaths, and there was a woman who had a spirit of infirmity for eighteen years; she was bent over and could not look upward at all. When Jesus saw her, he called her and said to her, “Woman, you are released from your infirmity.” And he laid his hands upon her, and immediately she was straightened and glorified God (Luke 13).

She had a spirit of infirmity, and she was bent over. The wound was evident, but the author of the wound was not; everyone saw the illness, but they did not see the source of the illness. The punishment was openly visible, but within the punishment itself the executioner lay concealed. The body was seen to be curved, but the burden weighing upon the curved body was not seen. In the midst of her fellow citizens the woman carried her enemy, but the citizens did not see the enemy whom they might drive away.

[Note: Cyril of Alexandria, in the *Catena of the Greek Fathers*: “He says ‘a spirit of infirmity’ because the woman suffered these things through the devil’s cruelty, having been abandoned by God on account of her own crimes; or on account of Adam’s transgression, because of which human bodies incurred infirmity and death. In this matter God gives the devil power, so that people oppressed by the weight of adversity may wish to turn toward better things.”]

Bodily necessity was believed to be the artifice of the most wicked spirit—[Note: As though she had suffered *emprosthotonos*, a tension of the muscles that bend forward]—so that the crafty robber might hold captive by deceit one whom he was unable to hold by force.

The devil would be nothing if human beings were more watchful and cautious. For when has he ever prevailed over a human being by strength rather than by artifice, falsehood, ambushes, fraud, deceit, wickedness, the service of vices, or the fury of crimes? He always tests human wills: he flees good wills, but gives support to evil wills, so that he may be the servant of crimes, the procurer of offenses, and himself the parasite of vices. And because he cannot prevail by power, he rules over the basest minds by the basest servitude.

Thus he deceived Eve by falsehood (Genesis 3); thus he ensnared Judas by greed (Mark 14); thus he blinded the Jews by envy (Mark 15); thus he darkened the nations with the error of idols; thus he confused peoples with the pageantry of worldly things; thus he seized children through vanity, so that they would not think soundly. Finally, let us hear what he contrived concerning the woman before us:

> “And behold, a woman who had a spirit of infirmity for eighteen years, and she was bent over and could not look upward at all.”

You see that this woman, weighed down by the burden of the most wicked spirit, sighed—he who always crushes human beings beneath the burdens of sins and bends them toward the earth, lest they see heaven, lest they think on things above, lest they look upon God, lest they return to their liberty through their own Creator. Instead, with bowed head, fixed eyes, and downcast face, they are always held captive under the yoke of the ancient enemy.

Thus that tax collector was weighed down; he could not lift his eyes toward heaven, but beat the breast conscious of sin. And because there was no room for denial, he sought a place for mercy, saying:

> “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke 18).

Bearing this burden, the most blessed prophet sang:

> “My iniquities have risen above my head, and like a heavy burden they have been made heavy upon me” (Psalm 37).

And, elsewhere, to reveal the author of his work, he says:

> “The crown of the hair of those who walk in their sins” (Psalm 65).

For the devil both rides upon and runs over the head of those who do not resist their sins but walk in them, so that those who go toward evil by their own inclination may be led toward worse things by the devil’s impulse, as the Apostle says:

> “As though going, you were led” (1 Corinthians 12).

But let us examine what spiritual understanding lies hidden in this account:

> “And behold, a woman who had a spirit of infirmity for eighteen years, and she was bent over and could not look upward at all.”

Who is this woman whose illness is described even in terms of its duration? [Note: A passage worthy of Oedipus. Perhaps: “Whom a burning sickness strove not to lift from the earth but to bend toward it.”] Who is she whom a burning sickness strove not to lift from the earth but to bend toward it? Who is she?

She is now the mother of saints, the holy Church of her children [Note: The Caesena manuscript reads: “She herself is the holy Church, mother of holy sons.”], whom, as the Apostle says, “the spirit of this air,” the spirit of unbelief, and the spirit of error (Ephesians 6) afflicted with spiritual sickness, and so bent and cast down toward the earth under various burdens that she could never be raised to behold heaven.

But why is this woman, who bears the figure of the Church, found bent over in the synagogue? Why? Because, while she flees the sacrileges of the nations and turns away from the burdens of idols, she encounters heavier burdens and bears the weights of the synagogue [Note: Alternatively, “bore the burdens.” The Jewish precepts were heavier, threatening transgressors either with death or with more severe penalties.]. The Lord confirms this when he says:

> “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, who bind heavy burdens and place them upon people’s shoulders, while you yourselves are unwilling to move them even with the smallest finger” (Luke 11; Matthew 13).

Hence blessed Peter also says:

> “Now therefore why do you test God by placing upon the disciples’ necks a yoke that neither we nor our fathers were able to bear?” (Acts 15).

For this reason Christ, wishing to relieve people of these burdens, cries out:

> “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you, for it is gentle” (Matthew 11).

When he says “all,” he certainly calls both Jews and Gentiles.

But why is this woman’s illness said to have lasted eighteen years? Because unless the decade of the Law had come to the grace of the ogdoad, neither the holy Church nor this woman would ever have reached the fullness of time, the day of salvation, the acceptable time, or the presence of her Savior.

[Note: All printed editions and manuscripts have this reading. “Then the decalogus of the written Law reached the grace of the number eight when the Son of God assumed our flesh, and in it died and rose again for us.” *Mita*.]

That this woman bore the figure of the Church is indicated by the very character of her healing:

> “He called her to himself and laid his hands upon her.”

The one who has deserved to become a Christian and daily sees Christians being made knows well that this is how the Church is always healed. For a Gentile bent down by sins to be raised toward heaven, the wicked spirit must first be driven out of the Gentile through the laying on of hands.

[Note: Exorcisms and the laying on of hands upon the heads of the baptized are still customary in the Church.]

Since he had driven out demons by a mere word and healed all illnesses by a command alone, why does he lay his hands upon this woman? Why does he alter the customary order of healing in her case, unless because he is already healing everyone in one person? Indeed, he does not receive the Church beforehand unless he purifies her from the devil through the laying on of his hands and makes her Christian; and, moreover, he establishes and prefigures through this present healing the care involved in making Christians.

But the ruler of the synagogue is indignant that Christ heals on the Sabbaths; and even today the Jew is tormented by the frenzy of zeal in the Church’s care, while he turns heavenly meanings over with earthly understanding [Note: Thus in Latinius. The printed editions have *pervolvit* or *praevolvit*], thinking that the Sabbath was consecrated for beasts, not for human beings. He hastens to attend an ox or an ass in danger on the Sabbath, but grants nothing of compassion or mercy to a dying human being on the Sabbath.

And he does this in his senselessness: in his heart he violates the Sabbath, and in a human being he violates holiness itself. Thus he prescribes to God by God’s law; and by observing the Sabbath he gives the Sabbath back to God in such a way that God had mercifully granted the Jew the Sabbath in exchange for earthly labor and bodily work [Note: The Caesena manuscript reads, “carnal works”].

> “And they have become like a crooked bow” (Psalm 77),

because they so twist the law’s most upright commands against the Lord of the law.

O Jew, who [the defective text reads *te ab numanis*, evidently *humanis*; something is missing], so that you might cease—even for one day, or on the Sabbath—from the healing of your salvation.

And you, Christian [Note: Ignatius, in his *Epistle to the Magnesians*, p. 57 of the Geneva edition of 1623, calls this day “the day consecrated to the Resurrection and chief of all days.” Nicephorus is therefore mistaken, book 7, chapter 46, Basel edition of 1562, when he asserts that Constantine the Great was the very first to call this day “the Lord’s day.” Unless we say that Nicephorus here intended to suggest that this designation, already obsolete, was restored again by Constantine. This is also inferred from Sozomen, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 1, chapter 7, p. 13. But do not infer from this that Christians had not previously honored this day. See canon 29 of the Council of Laodicea, with Balsamon and Zonaras there; and consult the *Bibliotheca Juris Canonici*, p. 1242, Paris edition of 1661], keep the Lord’s Sunday for the Lord, if you wish to see the Lord’s day; if you wish to possess through the Lord whatever belongs to the Lord.

## SERMON 106. On the fig tree that produced no fruit

Just as a skilled teacher strikes the minds of students—those inexperienced in listening and slow to understand—with various kinds of instruction, awakening and kindling their intelligence, so the Lord, through various likenesses and different comparisons, calls and invites the sluggish and slow minds of the people to hear the Gospel. For today he began as follows:

> “A certain man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard, and he came seeking fruit on it but found none. He said to the keeper of the vineyard, ‘Behold, for three years now I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree and have found none. Cut it down. Why should it occupy the ground?’ But he answered and said to him, ‘Lord, let it remain this year also, until I dig around it and put manure on it; and if indeed it bears fruit—but if not, afterward you shall cut it down’” (Luke 13).

“A certain man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard.” I ask: what is as plain, as lucid, as common, as familiar to country people, or as clear to experts as the form of the comparison set before us? Coming from ordinary experience, it instructs and converts everyone both by its words and by its example.

An unfruitful tree entangles the turf, kills the available space, drains the strength of the soil, exhausts the cultivator through loss, and afflicts its owner with weariness. Thus it is profitable to cut it down; it is advantageous not to have it.

So too a human being who overturns, occupies, and buries the gift of nature, the gift of the soul, the benefit of reason, the excellence of perception, the judgment of the mind, the industry of skill, and the goodness of cultivation through barren and impoverished actions denies fruit to the Creator and gratitude to the cultivator. As the tree deserves to be cut off from the earth, so this person deserves to be cut off from life.

And just as an unfruitful tree, if it is in a vineyard, spreads a deadly shade over the plants beneath it and becomes hostile not only to itself but also to the fruitful vines, so a sluggish and idle person, if placed over peoples, becomes harmful not only to himself but to many, corrupting and destroying those who follow him by his example.

But let us hear why the Lord spoke this comparison. After the winter season has passed, the fig tree produces early figs, bringing them into bloom and pretending through its blossoms to bear fruit; it deceives the unwary and mocks the ignorant. Then it soon casts off the early figs; it makes slow progress and bursts into bud, becoming later in fruit than the other trees, although it had seemed to precede them.

The synagogue is therefore rightly compared by the Lord to a fig tree which, warmed during the legal season, blossomed temporarily in the form of ecclesiastical fruit. [Note: This is the common interpretation of the parable. Consult Ambrose, Bede, Theophylact, Euthymius, and Augustine, formerly *Sermon* 31, now 110, *On the Words of the Lord*.] Firmly established in the root of the patriarchs, elevated by the priestly summit, expanded through prophetic branches, and filled with the early figs of Jewish observance, it blossomed, then destined to give fruit through Christ alone—or rather, destined to give Christ himself as fruit [Note: The Caesena manuscript reads, “through the fruit”—] after the fruit, as the Psalmist says:

> “From the fruit of your womb I shall place upon your throne” (Psalm 131).

Therefore the saints, knowing these things, drew hope of fruit from the blossom and consoled the present with the future, seeing the eternal already about to succeed the mortal, the everlasting the fleeting, grace the Law, the Church the synagogue, heavenly things earthly things, divine things human things, and Christ all things. Because they awaited his coming with long patience, they rejoiced in faithful joy when he came.

Among these was Simeon, to whom it had been promised that he would not see death until he had seen the Christ of the Lord. Holding him in his arms, he broke into these words:

> “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word in peace. For my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2).

But the ignorant, while placing their confidence in the whole Law, were neither concerned about the expectation of Christ nor worthy to receive or recognize Christ. Thus they were deceived by the little blossoms of the Law, just as the fig tree deceives the ignorant with its early figs.

For this reason the Lord, wishing them to know the times of his coming, directs them to the fig tree, saying:

> “Look at the fig tree and all the trees. When they already produce fruit, you know that summer is near. So also, when you see these things happening, know that the kingdom of God is near” (Luke 21).

You see that the fig tree does not signify present things but indicates things that are to come.

But let us now continue the example according to the proposed order. “A certain man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard.” The synagogue is the fig tree; Christ is the owner of the tree; the vineyard in which this tree is said to have been planted is the Israelite people, as the prophet Isaiah says:

> “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isaiah 5).

“He came,” it says, “seeking fruit on it, and found none.” Christ came, and found no fruit of faith in the synagogue, because it was entirely shaded by the deceit of unbelief.

Christ came to the fig tree to which Adam is read to have fled naked after his sin [Note: The Hebrews, and many among the Greeks, report that this was the kind of tree forbidden to Adam. See Mariana here], as the book of Genesis says:

> “And they knew that they were naked; and they sewed fig leaves together and made themselves loincloths” (Genesis 3).

Christ therefore came to the fig tree to find Adam, to cover you who were naked with the pious garment of his body. The fig tree did not cover Adam’s shame but provoked it; and its fig tree—that is, the synagogue—through its circumcisions exposed the part of the body subject to shame rather than covering it.

“He came,” it says, “seeking fruit, and found none.” Then he said to the keeper of the vineyard:

> “Behold, for three years now I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree and have found none. Cut it down.”

The keeper of the vineyard who is commanded to cut down the fruitless fig tree is the angel presiding over the synagogue. Since he cannot excuse its barrenness, he obtains a reprieve by pleading.

We must not pass over the fact that he said, “Behold, for three years now.” The three years are the three periods during which Christ came to the synagogue seeking fruit: through the Law, through the prophets, and through his own bodily presence, so that the fruitless fig tree—which was already denying the Godhead what appeared to be unnecessary fruit—might not deny Christ, whether as a human being, as one who was hungry, or as one who was going to eat, the food he required.

[Note: Ambrose, Theophylact, and Gregory, *Homily 31*, repeat this same interpretation. Others explain the three years as the three forms of the Jewish state—under judges, kings, and high priests; others as the three ages of human life—childhood, maturity, and old age; and others finally as the three years during which Christ taught. These explanations are arbitrary. The more correct view is that the three years signify divine mercy toward the Jewish people. He says “for three years” because fruit-bearing fig trees do not delay their fruit longer than that.]

But now let us hear what the keeper of the vineyard answered:

> “Lord, let it remain this year also.”

The keeper of the vineyard asks that the year of Gospel time still be granted, of which Isaiah says:

> “To proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of recompense” (Isaiah 61).

“For what purpose?” “Until I dig around it.” He wishes to pierce it with the apostolic plow [Note: The Latins say *ablaqueare*, hence *ablaqueatio*, “to dig a trench around”], because it did not respond to the cultivation of the legal knife.

“And I will put manure on it” [Note: The fig tree, being colder than other trees, truly requires fertilization].

This was necessary for so great a root, which, although nourished by the heavenly rain because of the great richness of the holy soil [Note: From Latinius. All printed editions have, “the whole [soil] by heavenly rain”], did not deserve to be fruitful.

The sterile fig tree—that is, the wretched synagogue—is fertilized by the compassion of the nations, so that, aided by very humble means of nourishment, it may return to fruitfulness, though it has fallen away from fruit after having received such great and precious nourishment. If after this it remains in the same barrenness, it will then be cut down—not by the cultivator’s sickle but by the axe of the master himself, as hopeless and useless.

For this reason he did not say, “I shall cut it down afterward,” but, “You shall cut it down,” in accordance with John:

> “Now the axe has been placed at the root of the trees. Therefore every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matthew 3).

For after the period of Gospel cultivation, the axe of judgment will cut down the fruitless trees, and the final fire will receive and consume them.

[Note: See what we said in the preface and in the notes to Chrysologus’s *Life* by Castillo.]

## SERMON 107. On Saint Peter, bishop of Ravenna

Although a poverty of speech seems to impose silence upon me, the force and holiness of the one commanding compels me to speak. For it is better to expose an unskilled eloquence than to refuse a dutiful discourse.

Who, then, would reject the exhortation of so great a man, upon whom from heaven have fallen both the title “apostolic” and the privilege of the supreme priesthood? For it must not be thought that it happened without divine judgment that the rough infancy of his first way of life attained the dignity of so great a name. Whom else should we think was present but God himself, when his parents, ignorant of future merits, were judging him?

To be called Peter in others is merely the designation of a name; in him it is the prerogative of virtue.

Truly blessed Peter, immovable foundation of salvation, displays in the priesthood the kind of person those who desire the priesthood wish to appear. How, then, does he exercise the rule of holiness, formed by monastic disciplines? [Note: From these words it is easy to infer that Chrysologus composed this sermon in praise of Peter; we stated in the preface that the sermon was delivered in his praise, and that he spent his days within a monastery’s enclosure while still in vigorous youth. Or one should follow Tillemont, who is convinced that the word “monastery” here indicates either the house of Cornelius, bishop of Imola, or that bishop’s school.]

His face grows pale through fasting; emaciation weakens his body; almsgiving pleads for sins; tears baptize sins. [Note: Leo the Great writes in *Sermon 9 on the Passion of the Lord* that tears served the blessed apostle Peter in place of baptism. But Barthius is mistaken, *Adversaria*, book 55, column 2613, when he thinks that Chrysologus is speaking here of the apostle Peter; these words concern our Peter.]

And lest perhaps the devout crowd should marvel at this, Peter is accustomed to weep when Christ looks upon him (Matthew 26). Nor should anyone blame the apostle for the rain of his moist grief. The tears that purchased the joy of immortality are joyful (Mark 16).

He therefore is the guardian of the faith, the rock of the Church, and the doorkeeper of heaven. [Note: Adelphus calls our Chrysologus “the doorkeeper of heaven” because he brought innumerable people to the faith and gently led sinners to repentance.]

He is the chosen apostolic fisherman who invites to himself the crowds submerged in the waves of error with the hook of holiness and encloses them in the net of his teaching for a faith rich in the multitude of believers (Luke 5). He is also the most blessed apostolic fowler who touches with the reed of divine speech the souls of young people flying through the air. [Note: The Caesena manuscript reads, “with his nets.”]

Rightly, therefore, the venerable priest of God, having once obtained the name of apostle [Note: Alternatively, “having received by lot”], and now having also attained the merit, sows among the peoples the precepts of justice and reveals in manifest light the mystical questions of the sacred books. Such is his mastery in heavenly disciplines that whoever is converted owes his absolution to him, while whoever is not corrected bears the guilt himself.

From every direction, crowds come together to him from different regions, eager to see him. Whoever lived in pathless solitudes or in hidden retreats of the desert now comes rather to see the remarkable Peter than the world. [Note: This means the city of Ravenna, at that time made more distinguished by the imperial court, the influx of eminent men, and its noble retinue.]

At last they have been permitted to learn—more difficult indeed, but more glorious—that it is possible to struggle against the world while the world is present, and to array a kind of battle line of holiness against crowds of delinquents equipped for sin. For how great is the palm of victory for those placed in the world after combat, if crowns are owed without struggle to those established in solitude?

Therefore, brothers, since the most blessed Peter instructs you in all that belongs to divine virtue through the preaching of his teaching, and teaches you equally through his examples, let us beseech the Lord our God that, through a very long age, he may gladden you with the word of heavenly teaching.

## SERMON 108. On the human being as an offering and priest to God. On the words of the Apostle: “I appeal to you through the mercy of God,” etc.

Wonderful is the piety that, in order to be entreated, entreats; in order to give, begs. For today the blessed Apostle, not asking for human things but conferring divine things, entreats as follows:

> “I appeal to you through the mercy of God” (Romans 12).

When a physician persuades the sick to receive severe remedies, he proceeds by entreaties, not by command, knowing that whenever the sick reject what will benefit them, this arises from illness, not from the will. A father likewise draws his son toward the rigor of discipline not by power but by love, knowing how harsh discipline is to immature minds.

And if bodily illness is moved to treatment by entreaties, and if a childish spirit is scarcely led to prudence by such gentle persuasion, what wonder is it if the Apostle, who is always both physician and father, entreats human minds wounded by carnal diseases so that he may raise them toward divine remedies:

> “I appeal to you through the mercy of God.”

He introduces a new kind of entreaty. Why not through God’s power? Why not through his majesty or glory, but through the mercy of God? Through this mercy alone Paul both escaped the crime of persecution and attained the dignity of so great an apostleship, as he himself confesses:

> “I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man; but I obtained the mercy of God.”

And again:

> “The saying is faithful and worthy of all acceptance: Christ came into this world to save sinners, of whom I am the first; but I received mercy as an example to all who are going to believe in him unto eternal life” (1 Timothy 1).

“I appeal to you,” he says, “through the mercy of God.” Paul begs—or rather, through Paul God begs—because he wishes to be loved more than feared. God begs because he wishes to be a father rather than merely a lord. God begs through mercy, lest he punish through severity.

Hear the Lord begging:

> “All day long,” he says, “I have stretched out my hands” (Isaiah 65).

Does not one who stretches out his hands beg by that very posture? “I have stretched out my hands.” To whom? To the people. And to what people? Not merely to a people who do not believe, but to one that contradicts him.

He stretches out his limbs, enlarges his compassion, extends his breast, offers his bosom, and opens his lap, so that by the affection of such an entreaty he may show himself to be their father.

Hear God begging in another way:

> “My people, what have I done to you, or in what have I grieved you?” (Micah 6).

Does he not say: If the Godhead is unknown, at least let the flesh be familiar? Look, look upon your body in me, your limbs, your inner parts, your bones, your blood. And if you fear what belongs to God, why do you not love what belongs to you?

If you flee the Lord, why do you not return to your parent? But perhaps the greatness of my Passion, which you caused, confounds you. Do not fear. This cross is not mine but the sting of death. These nails do not fasten pain into me; rather, they fasten your love more deeply into me. These wounds do not draw out my groans; instead, they introduce you more deeply into my inmost being. The extension of my body enlarges you into my bosom; it does not increase my punishment. My blood is not lost to me; it is extended as the price of you.

Come, then; return, and by this very means test the Father whom you see returning good for evil, love for injuries, and such great affection for such great wounds.

But now let us hear what the Apostle entreats:

> “I appeal to you,” he says, “to present your bodies.”

By entreating, the Apostle raised all human beings to the summit of priesthood. [Note: Toletus, on 1 Peter 2:9, where he praises Chrysologus: “For this reason every Christian is a priest.”]

> “To present your bodies as a living offering.”

O unheard-of duty of Christian priesthood, when the human being is both offering and priest to himself; when the human being does not seek something external to sacrifice to God [Note: As formerly, when foreign animals were sacrificed], but brings with himself, within himself, and for himself what he is to sacrifice to God; when the same person remains both offering and priest; when the offering is slain and yet lives, and the priest does not know how to kill the one who will offer sacrifice. [Note: The sacrificed offering still lives when a person departs from this life and slays his carnal vices, mortifying his flesh with its sins and desires.]

A wondrous sacrifice, in which the body is offered without a body, and blood without blood.

> “I appeal to you,” he says, “through the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a living offering.”

Brothers, this sacrifice descends from the pattern of Christ, who offered his body vitally for the life of the world. He truly made his body a living offering, because, though slain, it lives. In such a victim death is expended, the offering remains, the offering lives, and death is punished.

From this martyrs are born through death: they begin at their end, live through execution, and shine in heaven, although on earth they were thought to have been extinguished.

> “I appeal to you,” he says, “brothers, through the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a living, holy offering.”

This is what the prophet sang:

> “You did not desire sacrifice and offering, but you fashioned a body for me” (Psalm 39).

Be, human being, God’s sacrifice and priest. Do not lose what divine authority has given and granted you. Put on the robe of holiness; gird yourself with the belt of chastity [Note: That is, the belt with which a priest’s thighs are girded]; let Christ be the covering of your head; let the cross remain as the protection of your forehead; place the sacrament of divine knowledge upon your breast; continually kindle the incense of prayer as a fragrant offering; seize the sword of the Spirit; make your heart an altar; and so bring your body confidently to God for sacrifice.

God seeks faith, not death; he thirsts for a vow, not blood; he is appeased by the will, not by slaughter.

God proves this when he asked the holy Abraham for his son as an offering (Genesis 22). For what else was Abraham sacrificing but his own body in his son? What else was God requiring from the father but faith, when he commanded the son to be offered but did not permit him to be killed?

Strengthened by such an example, therefore, offer your body, and not only slay it but also cut it apart through all the limbs of virtue. For the arts of vices die for you as often as the inner parts of virtue are sacrificed by you to God.

Offer faith, so that unbelief may be punished; sacrifice fasting, so that gluttony may cease; sacrifice chastity, so that lust may die; impose piety, so that impiety may be removed; invite mercy, so that greed may be destroyed; and, so that folly may be consumed, it is always fitting to sacrifice holiness.

Thus your body will become your offering, if it has not been wounded by any dart of sin. Your body lives, human being; it lives whenever the life of virtues is sacrificed by you to God in place of the deaths of vices. One who deserves to be slain by the living sword cannot die.

May our God himself, who is the way, the truth, and the life, both free us from death and lead us to life.

## SERMON 109. On rationally offering the body and soul to God as an offering. On the same words of the Apostle

Since the preceding sermon touched only the beginnings [Note: Alternatively, *cogit* (“gathers” or “treats”).] of the apostolic reading, let us now hear what the Lord inspires concerning what follows. For it began as follows:

> “I appeal to you,” he says, “through the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a living offering” (Romans 12).

Does the Apostle, by saying this, approve only bodies as worthy of divine offerings, and, as though rejecting souls, either remain silent about them, pass them over, or abandon them?

Is not the soul from heaven and the body from earth? The body is governed, while the soul governs; the soul rules, while the body serves; the body lives, while the soul gives life; the soul remains, while the body fails; the body undergoes the stages of life, while the soul knows none of them; and finally, death, which rules only over the body, does not touch the soul while it is present.

What, then, does it mean that the soul is silent and only the body is summoned as an offering to God?

Brothers, here the Apostle honors the body; he does not diminish the soul. For the body that sins seize, that offenses conquer, that crimes depress, that vices corrupt, and that passions cast down—this body the Apostle desires to release, strives to liberate, labors to raise, and endeavors to purify, so that the body may ascend toward the soul’s origin, rather than the soul descend to the body’s nature; so that the body may accompany the soul to heaven, rather than the soul follow the body to earth.

Hear Scripture describing the kinds and extent of bodily torments by which the soul is burdened:

> “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and earthly thought weighs down the mind that thinks on many things” (Wisdom 9).

Therefore the Apostle does not wish the soul to be cast down but the body to be raised; and he wishes both soul and body—that is, the whole human being—to come as a holy offering, as a sacrifice pleasing to God.

That the soul too is a sacrifice of God, the Psalmist declares:

> “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit” (Psalm 50).

> “To present your bodies as a living, holy offering, pleasing to God.”

For a human being is not pleasing because he lives, but because he lives well; nor does a person become an offering to God merely by offering himself to God, but by offering himself holily to God.

For as an unblemished victim pleases God, so a victim, if it is stained, provokes God.

Hear God saying:

> “You shall not offer me anything lame, blind, or polluted by the contamination of death, but a mature offering without blemish” (Leviticus 22).

For this reason the Apostle asks for a living offering to God.

Therefore, brothers, if we are the incense of that propitiation—[Some material is missing.]

This is proved by Cain, who, though he had received everything from God, as an ungrateful priest so divided his small offering with God that what was worst he burned upon the altar, while what was best he kept back for his own offense. Finally, when he wickedly shares his own possessions with their author, he deprived himself and his descendants both of life and of the human race (Gen. 4). Therefore let us follow Abel to his reward, and not accompany Cain to his punishment. Abel, carrying a lamb for God’s sacrifice, is received as a lamb; Cain, carrying straw for himself, finds fuel for himself, by which he would be consumed.

“Present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, your reasonable service.” The service that is supported by reason pleases as much as service without reason provokes God’s anger. Reasonable service is not disturbed by presumption, confused by rashness, violated by unlawful acts, or disguised by pretense.

At a king’s command, the military guard trembles; human authority demands attentive servitude; at the command of the one who gives orders, the fear of the obedient keeps watch. For cautious devotion acquires the reward of just recompense, while presumptuous servitude does not escape the punishment of rashness. Who, without being summoned, thrusts himself into service at a royal court? Who has dared to declare himself a soldier without authorization? Who, without the insignia of rank, seizes the name of a dignity?

[Note: The *infula* is sometimes used for an imperial crown, as in Book 1, at the end of chapter *De quadriennii praescriptione*, Mita. Hence it is used here for every ornament of rank.]

And if these things among human beings are conducted with care and caution, if they are established by reason, strengthened by order, and preserved with trembling, how much more cautious must devotion be before God, how much more awe-inspiring the service, how much more attentive the worship, so that one may render reasonable service to God? “Your reasonable service,” he says. Service informed by reason is ardor; what is not restrained by reason is frenzy.

Hence the Jewish people, while seeking God for themselves without reason, lost the God whom they had served with reason (Exod. 32). Hence the sons of Aaron, while forgetful of reason and presuming to bring earthly fires near the divine fires, changed the flame of a saving sacrifice into a punishment of fire for themselves (Lev. 10). Hence Saul, swelling with royal pride and thinking that he was permitted something even in the priesthood, lost the kingdom he had received because he profaned the altar (1 Sam. 15).

[Note: Some editions corruptly read *tremens* (“trembling”).]

Hence the Jew, while cultivating the law without the reason of the law, slew the author of the law. Hence the pagan, while serving the throngs of gods and the monsters called gods, ignorant of reason, did not deserve to attain the service of God, who is one and true.

[Note: No more fitting term could express the multitude of the pagan gods and their monstrous forms.]

[Note: Nothing is more opposed to reason than polytheism, as Arnobius and Minucius in the *Octavius* repeatedly show.]

Hence Arius thinks that he serves the Father by blaspheming the Son; and, while assigning a beginning to the Son, pitiably imposes an end upon the Father. Hence Photinus, by denying that the Son is coeternal with the Father, endeavors to establish that the Father was not always Father.

[Note: On the heresy of Photinus, see Epiphanius, vol. 1, book 3, *Against Heresies*, 61 or 71, p. 828.]

Hence all heresies, while they are directed toward an insult to the divinity and falsely name the Trinity with their terminology, serve it with blasphemies.

[Note: That is, they blaspheme deliberately, from the heart and with delight. Mita: They accommodate themselves to those who attack God with blasphemies.]

But let us, brothers, make our bodies a living sacrifice to God and cultivate our reasonable service, so that there may be true faith, a pure conscience, a sober mind, firm hope, a clean heart, chaste flesh, a holy understanding, a devout spirit, sound judgment, chaste love, abundant mercy, a holy life, modest bearing; and so that humility may always accompany our step in every service of Christ.

## SERMON 110

### On salvation placed under faith, justification by God through Christ, and undergoing death for Christ

On the words of the same Apostle: “Now it was not written for Abraham alone,” etc.

The blessed Apostle always raises one, unique, and singular banner of faith for the salvation of the first and the last—that is, for Jews and Greeks. Whoever has not deserved to possess and hold it will not be able to possess the glory of heavenly triumphs. For those fighting against faithlessness, it alone, brothers, directs the battle line; it points out the king, unites the allies, and by its very sight terrifies the impious enemy.

Thus he begins today: “Now it was not written for Abraham alone that it was reckoned to him as righteousness, but also for us who believe in him who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead” (Rom. 4). You see, brothers, that while the earlier generations believe in what is future and later generations in what is past, both arrive at salvation by the one road of faith: they profess that Christ will come, while we profess that he has already come. They marvel and believe that he would descend, in human fashion, even unto death; we glory in the fact that he died and rose again.

And what more, brothers? This salvation was denied to the eyes both of those who came before and of those who came afterward, so that it might be entirely grounded in faith. But when he says, “who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead,” let no one believe that this was done by another: he himself is the maker and raiser of his body, who said, “I have authority to lay down my life, and I have authority to take it up again” (John 10). For resurrection could not be raised by another, nor life be brought to life by another; nor could the same one deny himself what he was about to bestow upon everyone. For a spring does not thirst, bread does not hunger, the sun does not need light, and rest itself does not grow weary.

“He was handed over,” he says, “for our offenses, and rose for our justification.” He was handed over for our offenses, not so that life, which could not die, would be punished, but so that the offenses that had exiled us from life might alone be wiped away. “And he rose for our justification.” A condemned person cannot be justified while the condemnation remains. Therefore Christ, the heavenly and true parent, having dissolved the condemnation of death, justifies us by his own death and resurrection—us whom the guilt of our first parent had so bound that death was entitled to hold us subject to it. Thus it is not the guilty person who perishes, but guilt; and the punishment itself—that is, death—which had been ordered to strike the guilty, rightly fails and loses the insignia of its power.

Why did cruel and impious death dare to touch the innocent one, indeed the judge himself? And therefore he added: “Therefore, having been justified by faith, let us have peace with God” (Rom. 5). This is to say: let discord cease—cease, that mother of dissension and enemy of peace. Let the Jew not exalt himself through the law; let the pagan not grow proud through nature; let the philosopher subside from his frothy and empty opinions. Let no one glory in merits, no one in works, because divine peace restored and returned the life that the first transgression had taken away and furious contention had driven far from us.

“Let us have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.” Let earth not rebel against heaven; let flesh not rise up against the spirit; but let the humble person be joined perpetually to the peace above, for glory.

“Through whom we have access.” Why has he himself become our way? By faith into this grace. Faith, brothers, is the guide of this life. “In which we stand and glory in the hope of the glory of the children of God.” We stand by faith, certainly, not bodily; and we glory in hope, not in a reality already received.

“Not only that, but we also glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces endurance, endurance produces testing, and testing produces hope; but hope does not disappoint.” Behold by what stages the righteous person is strengthened into a mature man: through tribulation, endurance, testing, and hope.

Tribulation, brothers, like the first stage of a just man’s life, shakes and disturbs his infancy. But when it finds him enduring, it trains him, already growing toward greater goods, as one of good character. “Tribulation produces endurance.” Endurance, brothers, is what proves that Christ’s young man is suited to the virtues. “Hope does not disappoint.” Hope is what perfects the man and brings him unwearied to the measure of the fullness of Christ. It belongs to perfect virtue to possess through the strength of hope what one does not yet hold in reality.

[Note: For we have received the Spirit of the promise as a pledge and earnest of the heavenly kingdom. Duhamel.]

Because “the love of God has been poured out into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.” And to show the quality of the divine love poured into us, he added: “For why, while we were still weak, did Christ die for the ungodly at the appointed time? For scarcely would anyone die for a righteous person; perhaps someone might dare to die for a good person. But God demonstrates his love toward us in that, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”

If Christ loved the human race so greatly that he gave his death for the ungodly and sinners, what else do we believe that he will give the righteous except his life, his kingdom, and his glory? From you he received the death that he would expend upon the ungodly on earth; for you he reserves what he always possesses in himself and through himself, and possesses in heaven.

Let us therefore say with the prophet: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me? I will receive the cup of salvation” (Ps. 115). This means: I too shall die for him. And what comparison is there? He willingly died for the ungodly and sinner; I scarcely die for the righteous and good. I say “scarcely” because necessity rather than will leads me to death.

Hear him himself saying to Peter: “When you grow old, another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish to go.” In adversity, brothers, necessity cannot be compared with the will. To acquiesce is the mark of necessity; to will is the mark of virtue. Death itself is subject to the willing person, because death has always ruled the unwilling.

And yet, brothers, since a human being cannot offer anything comparable to divine love, let him give what he can, for he is accepted according to what he possesses. Let him fail for glory, die for life, perish for salvation. Let us glory, brothers, in this new exchange of commerce, because death, which had been the entire restoration of piety among human beings, has through Christ become a commendation of divine love.

[Note: The end and purpose of this sermon is to establish, against the Pelagians, the truth of original sin and the corruption derived from it, which can be healed by no other remedy than that God should have made himself human. Tillemont.]

## SERMON 111

### On original sin

On the words of the same Apostle: “Therefore, just as through one man sin entered into this world.”

The present reading from the Apostle, brothers, when it says that through one man the whole world received its sentence (Rom. 5), compels us not to deliver an oration but to weep with renewed and inward grief. If distinguished prophets have long lamented the misfortune of a single people, a single city, and sometimes even a single person, what mind would not be shrouded in complete darkness, what understanding would not be confused by utter dullness, what eyes would not be turned into springs and streams of tears, when the fall of one became the ruin of all, the guilt of one flowed down into the punishment of all, and the defect of a parent prepared deadly destruction for the entire race? The Apostle says: “Therefore, just as through one man sin entered into this world, and through sin, death” (ibid.).

Wretched me! He himself, who had been the cause of all good things, became the door of these evils. “Sin entered into this world.” Into this world? Do you wonder that he harmed his descendants who condemned the world by his crime? But you ask, “How did it enter? Through whom did it enter?” How? Through guilt. Through whom? Through a human being.

And what is sin? Is it nature or substance? It is neither nature nor substance, but an accident. This power, however, is hostile: it appears in its work, is felt in its punishment, attacks the soul, wounds the mind, violates nature itself, and throws it into confusion.

And what more, brothers? Sin is to nature what smoke is to the eyes, fever to the body, and bitter saltiness to the sweetest springs. The eye is naturally pure and clear, but it is disturbed and darkened by the injury of smoke. The body, through the parts and senses of its members, flourishes because it was created by God; but once the force of fever and the storm begin to rule, the whole body becomes weak. Then there is bitterness in the mouth, darkness before the eyes, unsteady traces of the feet, hostile air, burdensome loved ones, and even ordinary services seem hateful.

And just as springs are pleasing through their sweetness and nature, so they become unpleasant when they have received some defect through an addition.

But let us return to what we began: “Just as through one man sin entered into this world, and through sin, death.” Behold, brothers: the door is man; through sin we seem to have entered into death.

Sin, O cruel beast, not content to rage against the human race with one head! We have seen you devouring with three mouths the entire offspring of the human race, so precious: with three mouths, brothers, sin seizes, death devours, and hell swallows.

[Note: If the subject is original sin alone, it devours with a threefold mouth because of the three effects of evil: the diminution of natural good, the stain, and the liability to punishment. If he is speaking of actual sin, it devours with a threefold mouth—that is, through the threefold sin of thought, word, and deadly deed. Mita: Chrysologus explains himself. Adam’s sin afflicted us with three injuries: inclination toward evil, death, and eternal condemnation.]

And from what source of tears, as we said, must such a parent be fully mourned by us—a parent who left us heirs to such great miseries, who not only lost the goods that had been bestowed, but left all his descendants subject to such savage creditors? O harsh and cruel inheritance! O wretched people, who were neither permitted to accept nor permitted to renounce our status as heirs!

Hear what follows: “And so death passed to all human beings.” But lest this seem unjust—why through one person to all? Because all were through one person. You detest that you have been condemned through the one through whom you glory in having been brought forth into the light.

But you ask: “If I owe to my race the fact that I was born, do I also owe it my guilt, so that nature makes me guilty before my own guilt?” The Apostle’s next statement immediately answers your question: “In whom all sinned.” If all sinned in him, then all rightly received punishment through him.

“Just as through one man sin entered into this world, and through sin, death, and so passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned.” Whether “in the man” or “in sin,” through him and in him all sinned.

Sin, therefore, was not changed into nature; rather, since sin brings death, through nature it exacts the punishment owed to it. God had made nature so that human beings would be created for life. Yet when nature unwillingly gives birth to them for death, it confesses itself subject to the sin whose punishment it serves in life.

For who could imagine this, brothers: that nature would wish its offspring to be extinguished, and would wish its own dear descendants to be killed? Yet while it groans and suffers grief, it sighs for and longs to recover the freedom it has lost.

But John the first clearly shows through whom it received this freedom. When he saw Christ, he proclaimed and cried out: “Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1). The sin of the world—this is the sin, brothers, which the Apostle testifies entered through one man.

Rejoice, therefore, brothers, because the sin that was pressing us down with a heavy weight toward Tartarus has been taken away by Christ and already plunged into Tartarus. And us, whom the guilt of our first parent had condemned to death, the grace of the second and divine parent has recalled from punishment to life.

A human being, therefore, could not be saved without Christ, because the sin of the whole world remained before his coming.

[Note: The manuscripts of Caesena and Vallicelliana read, “no one could.”]

But you embrace the fact that you are justified through Christ, while you reject the fact that you were condemned through Adam; and you complain that another’s punishment has harmed you, even though you see that another’s righteousness has come to your aid.

Is not the whole tree present in the seed? The defect of the seed, therefore, is the defect of the whole tree. If nature could have helped itself by itself, the author himself would never have assumed it in himself for its restoration. Do you believe it was created for life while you still doubt that it was restored by its author?

“For until the law,” he says, “sin was in the world.” When you hear “until the law,” understand “until the end of the law”—that is, until the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. “Sin was not reckoned,” he says, “when there was no law.”

And when was there no law, since the law began with the human being himself? If there had been no law, Adam certainly would not have been a transgressor, as the same Apostle makes clear when he says: “But death reigned from Adam to Moses.”

Both had received the law. Adam immediately transgressed when he received it; Moses promulgated the law he had received for transgressors, as the Apostle says: “The law was established because of transgressions” (Gal. 3).

Death therefore reigned through the law, because it devoured transgressors more severely than sinners—not only those who had fallen through their parent’s defect, but also those who had already fallen through their own crime.

“But death reigned,” he says, “from Adam to Moses, even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression.” For death devoured not only adults but also little children; it ravaged not only the guilty but also the innocent—I mean innocent of their own guilt, not of their parent’s.

And this condition was all the more grievous to lament, because death exacted the punishment of a parent from one who had scarcely tasted life as an infant, and punished the sin of the world in one who had no knowledge of the world.

Let us therefore acquiesce, brothers, in the fact that death reigned through one person and through one person’s offense, if we desire to be absolved through one person and to exist through Christ. For whoever lives owes it to Christ, not to himself; and Adam will owe it that he dies.

## SERMON 112

### On death through man, life and grace through Christ, and the abundance of sin because of the law

On the words of the same Apostle: “For if death reigned through one person’s offense.”

If someone offers a cup of cold water to a thirsty traveler, he certainly refreshes the spirit of the one who is burning with thirst and fully assists his human need, but he does not completely extinguish his thirst. So too our discourse does not suffice for those who desire to know the secret of divine knowledge, since it serves the immediate occasion and the time available.

For if the whole brief life of a human being is too short to learn human matters completely, what time do we think can suffice for understanding divine things? Therefore, brothers, grant pardon if within a point of time and scarcely a moment of one hour I cannot illuminate obscure things, unlock what is closed, strengthen what is doubtful, touch what is profound, and disclose in every way the ineffable mystery of so many ages; and if we cannot speak cautiously to our rivals, securely to our children, confidently to believers, and steadfastly to unbelievers.

[Note: The time allotted for delivering a sermon was fixed at the length of one hour. See Origen, *Homily 3 on Genesis*; Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis 13*: “Although the subjects are many, and the time of an hour very brief”; also Augustine, *Sermon 237, On Time*; and our Chrysologus, Sermon 121, with its final note.]

Yet because today the apostolic discourse has poured itself wholly into the understanding of its hearers with clear light and has left nothing ambiguous to Catholic minds, when it says, “For if death reigned through one person’s offense” (Rom. 5), let us set aside the desire to declaim and rely in complete simplicity upon the apostolic words themselves, so that our speech may generate no obscurity for those who desire to know the truth.

“If death reigned through one person’s offense,” as he says, why does the authority of the Gospel labor to insinuate and establish that death was acquired for later generations from one and the first human being? And although the statement “God did not make death” is sufficient (Wis. 1), I cannot understand why some wish such a savage, cruel, and ruthless death to have been created by God.

No one can believe without sacrilege that so pious and good a God could have created death, whose author the whole world continually accuses and detests with grief, groaning, and tears. If even among human beings death is the punishment of crimes, by what audacity can it be believed that it was created along with humankind and implanted by God as a punishment in the innocent human being before life?

But let us hear the Apostle: “For if death reigned through one person’s offense, much more will those who receive the abundance of grace, the gift, and righteousness reign in life through the one Christ our Lord.”

Behold the one and the one: Adam and Christ. Through the former, sin reigned in death; through the latter, grace reigned in life. Finally, the Apostle’s following statement opens and declares these two principles of life and death, acquittal and punishment, desired freedom and ultimate condemnation:

“Therefore, just as through one person’s offense condemnation came upon all human beings, so through one person’s righteousness justification of life came upon all human beings.” Through one and one, either death reigns or life is granted.

What, then, can the interpreter’s discourse add here? If you add silence to these words, the entire purpose of the rivals collapses.

“Through one person’s offense condemnation came upon all human beings, so through one person’s righteousness justification of life came upon all human beings.” As a river serves its source, and fruit its seed, so a posterity is either bound to or freed from its origin, as is more fully established by what the Apostle added:

“For just as through one person’s disobedience the many were made sinners, so through one person’s obedience the many will be made righteous.”

Let the human being be a sinner, so that God may be just, because guilt rebounds upon the judge if punishment strikes the innocent.

[Note: God is entirely just because the human being is a sinner; God exercises justice upon the human being as upon one who is truly a sinner. Mita.]

And therefore he said: “Just as through one person’s disobedience the many were made sinners,” so that they might know themselves to have shared in the guilt of the one whose punishment they perceive themselves to share.

But now let the lovers of the law hear what benefit the law conferred, as the Apostle testifies: “The law entered so that the offense might abound.” Behold, as the Apostle says, the law did not bring about a diminution of offenses but an abundance—not through itself, brothers, but through the one who was unable to bear the law because of weakness.

The abundance of light does not weaken eyes for which the sun was created by God; rather, the weakness of the eyes cannot sustain the whole force of the light or endure its brightness. So too the law, brothers, which in itself was entirely just and holy, while demanding strict discipline from a frail human being, burdened and exposed the delinquent more and more.

And why was this, brothers? So that through the grace and pardon of the Creator the one who, through pride and ignorance, had been led into the punishment owed to his parent while boasting wrongly of his innocence might return to life.

[Note: The just person, still under the law of nature, saw himself doing what was right and, full of pride, rejoiced in the innocence he trusted himself to possess. Through ignorance he did not perceive that God was justly punishing him for his parent’s offense and for the innocence lost in that parent. The law of Moses came and exposed everything. Mita.]

The disease, therefore, had lain hidden. Through it, the secret channels of all the marrow and veins were tending toward the destruction of the vital organs themselves, and it generated a kind of *synchrisin* (συνχρίσιν) in all the interior parts—that is, a commingling or contagion.

[Note: That is, “contagion,” according to Mita. That is, the same condition. In other words, all the interior parts were similarly affected. This is written in the margin of p. 484 of the Cologne edition of 1627.]

The law came, exposing the wound and announcing that a heavenly physician would at last come to the ancient illness.

[Note: The Lord Christ is often called a physician by the Fathers. Chrysostom, vol. 5, Homily 31: “Do not say to me, ‘I have sinned; what shall I do?’ You have a physician superior to the illness; you have a physician who conquers the nature of the disease; you have a physician who heals by a nod; you have a physician who cures by his mere will, and who can do so if he wills. Basil of Seleucia, Oration 35, calls Christ a physician who heals without medicines. This may also be understood of bodily illnesses. Gregory of Nyssa, Oration 3 against Eunomius.”]

The law came, bringing to the surface through the soothing applications of its commandments what was lethally raging in the depths. The law came, opening with the sword of its precepts, like an abscess, what had festered for a long time, so that the healing discharge might subsequently dry up the pus that had accumulated.

Yet the law itself, brothers, could neither close the wound nor provide the sick person with complete health. When the sick person saw this and, at last, pitifully recognized his condition, he began hastily to make his way to the physician, so that what had been exposed by the law and long enlarged through it might be cured by the skill and grace of so great a physician.

We call the wound enlarged, brothers, because after the incision, putrefaction, stench, horror, and torment are generated in the wound itself by the cutting; and through the treatment the pitiable appearance of the illness becomes worse than the danger had been when it lay hidden from the ignorant person.

The physician therefore came, and, to one already exhausted by cares and utterly worn out by the afflictions of treatments, he gave aid by the authority of his word alone. As that centurion confesses when he says: “Speak the word, and my servant will be healed” (Matt. 8). And the prophetic statement was fulfilled: “He sent his Word and healed them” (Ps. 106).

And therefore it follows: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded even more.” It is as though he said: “Where the wound was enlarged, health was poured out in superabundance.”

Let no one therefore be ungrateful to the law. It had found him sick and lying helpless; it raised him up, cared for him, and, in order to hand him over to salvation, led him through a saving rejoicing all the way to the physician, so that, as the Apostle said, “just as sin reigned in death, so grace may reign in eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.”

Grace reigns for life; sin reigns for death. Right faith does not attribute death or the destruction of humanity to God the Creator, but salvation. Let death belong to humanity; let it belong to sin, so that life may be believed to have been created and restored solely through Christ.

[Col. 0510B]

## SERMON 113

### On not remaining in sin so that grace may abound, and on serving through the virtues

On the words of the same Apostle: “What then shall we say? Shall we remain in sin so that grace may abound?” etc.

The blessed Apostle, when he asks about what is known and inquires into what is evident, rebukes and censures those who corrupt the divine utterances by their own interpretation and, from the very place where they ought to have taken instruction in virtue, derive support for their crimes. Thus he begins today: “What then shall we say? Shall we remain in sin, so that grace may abound?” (Rom. 6). Above he had said, brothers: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more”; and therefore he began in this way, as though, in place of that divine and singular instruction, he were joining the unlearned to himself by means of a question, so that he might answer with the complete learning of heavenly wisdom.

For if, where sin abounded, grace also abounded all the more, what then shall we say? Shall we remain in sin, so that grace may abound? If compassion is inclined toward sinners, if grace is abundant toward those who sin, if divine generosity is friendly toward the unrighteous; indeed, if future blessings are acquired through present evils, why for us the difficult path of virtues, why the hard labor of obtaining righteousness, why the continual torment of preserving innocence amid the wicked? Let human crimes increase, so that heavenly goodness may overflow; “let us do evil, that good may come,” as he said (Rom. 3); let us remain in sin, so that grace may abound.

To this, brothers, the same Apostle who asks the question himself replies: “By no means.” [Col. 0510D] “For how shall we who have died to sin still live in it?” When he says “By no means”—the expression is that of one rejecting and abhorring something, as in Romans 3:31, as though he were saying: “This is the most absurd and detestable error”—he thus execrated the understanding and mentality of the foolish. [Col. 0511A]

For a physician is beneficial not to the wound but to its treatment and recovery; nor does he rejoice in putrefaction or disease, but only in health. So God, who, in proportion to the greatness of the wound, applied a medicine of corresponding magnitude and power, bestowed grace not upon sin but upon the human being, and poured out the rain of his mercy not to multiply offenses but to erase them. Let no one—no one—rejoice over sickness in such a way that he wishes to remain in the wound. He who always longs to be treated but never desires to be healed is ungrateful toward the physician and hostile to the treatment; and he who wants God’s grace to overflow through his sins desires his sins to be heaped up upon him. Miserable is the person who strives by such a wish to become guilty through pardon.

This madness must be fled, brothers—must be fled: the madness that, even after treatment, remains held captive by love of disease. For a relapse is often a deadly illness. But when he says, “For we who have died to sin,” he uses the form of the present tense: by saying that we have died to sin, he does not say that sin has already died completely in us. For although sin itself has died in the action of holy and faithful works, it nevertheless lives and still rages toward our death. [Col. 0511B]

[Note: According to the view of the ancient philosophers, a thing was said to die when it went out from its own limits and passed into another. For Plato, a human being was said to die both when the soul leaves the body and when the soul, situated in the body, puts off its passions and passes to virtues.]

Sin itself will die in us when “this corruptible has put on incorruption, and this mortal has put on immortality,” and the saying that is written has come to pass: “Where, O death, is your sting? Where, O grave, is your victory? The sting of death is sin” (1 Cor. 15).

But he lives for sin who, as the Apostle says in what follows, serves its desires;

[Note: When concupiscence is called sin, it is not called sin because it is itself sin, but because it has been produced by sin. St Augustine, vol. VII, Against Two Letters of the Pelagians, book I, ch. 12. MITA.] and pitiably submits to its goads who obeys vices, who yields to crimes in wretched and continual captivity, who supposes that what belongs to sin belongs to nature, and treats the disease that has come upon him as though it were the work and benefit of the Creator. And therefore, to rebuke the ignorance of such people, he added, saying: “Or do you not know that all of us who were baptized in Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were buried with him through baptism into death.”

Let the faithful hear and understand how the Lord’s three-day burial is represented in baptism by a threefold immersion, so that they may rejoice at having risen with Christ—not yet in the body, perhaps, but already in the newness of life—and so that the whole human being may be a dwelling place of virtues, though previously he had been a receptacle of vices. Thus, as he said, “just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too may walk in newness of life.”

Christ refers everything that belongs to his virtues to the glory of the Father; but the human being, who has nothing of his own, strives to claim for himself that he has risen through Christ. When he says, “Let us walk in newness of life,” he confirms what we said above: even if he has not yet been changed in this body, nevertheless let him already walk wholly transformed in life. Let him understand himself and rule the elements, though until now through ignorance he served the elements; let him give away his own possessions in glory, though previously he shamefully stole what belonged to others; and let him who practiced unlawful acts of the flesh despise even bodily permissions. Let him who until now wickedly sought to extinguish innocence himself die more gloriously on behalf of innocence.

And what more? If he has already been made new from the old human being, let him himself turn the whirlpool of vices into a fountain of virtues. To the end of the reading the blessed Apostle presses this point and demonstrates that the one can live with Christ and reign with Christ who follows the innocence of the risen Christ, imitates his life, and strives to fulfill holiness.

When he says, “so that the body of sin may be destroyed,” let it be destroyed, brothers, in action, not in substance; in practice, not in form. For he who said, “Consider yourselves dead to sin but alive to God,” wishes the human being to perish through sin, not through God. And with complete compassion he strives to restore the human being to heavenly freedom, saying: “Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body.” And again: “Let not sin have dominion over you.”

He did not say, “Let it not come to you”; he did not say, “Let it not provoke or prick you”; but, “Let it not reign; let it not have dominion.” Let it struggle for the glory of the one who conquers; let it fight and fall for the triumph of the victor. At last let the impious dominion of sin grieve that it is trampled with complete security by those who were once its slaves; and let the cruel tyrant groan that it has been subjected beneath the feet of its own captives. Let the veteran enemy lament that, for the triumph of those over whom it had long triumphed, it has been brought to its own defeat.

## SERMON CXIV. On the servants of the law and of grace

On the words of the same Apostle: “Shall we sin, because we are not under the law but under grace?” etc.

Just as return to one’s homeland is always sweet and dear to a traveler, and the vestibules of one’s native home are gracious after a period of absence, so for me, after intervals in preaching, return to the sequence of the apostolic readings is more delightful. For religious necessity often compels us to depart from the planned order of speaking and from the continuous path of discourse, since the order of instruction must be regulated so that one subject does not obstruct another. Let us therefore hear what the blessed Apostle said today.

What, then, does he say? “Shall we sin because we are not under the law but under grace? By no means” (Rom. 6). This question, brothers, exposes the ignorance of those who, held captive by the custom of the law, do not know how to recognize the virtues of grace; and those whom the sequence of legal precepts had revealed to be rebellious, the mere advantages of gifts and the pomp of festivals made and left obstinate in empty observances.

And when time has excluded the law, what will the worshiper of the law do, having been rejected by the law? Jew, what do you possess that you have not lost? But if you have lost it, why do you glory as though you had not lost it? Where is the temple, where the priest, where the sacrifice, where the incense, where your purifications, where the devotion to your solemnities that must not be omitted? But in order that you may be a Jew, you are rightly circumcised, because you have been cut off from all the good things just mentioned. [Col. 0513A]

For it is written: “Cursed is everyone who does not remain in all the things written in the book of the law” (Deut. 27). If the one who offends in a single matter is accursed, how many times accursed will be the one who is shown to have accomplished nothing at all of everything?

“Shall we sin,” he says, “because we are not under the law but under grace?” [Col. 0513D]

[Note: Latinius adds here: “See how far Chrysologus departs from the Apostle’s true reading and meaning. The Apostle’s sense is certainly different when he says, ‘We have sinned,’ etc. By the words ‘under grace’ he repeats, again and again, his refutation of the objection initially put to him in those other words: ‘What then shall we say? Shall we remain in sin, so that grace may abound? By no means.’”]

As though he were saying, brothers: Have we sinned because, once healed, we did not remain in treatment? Have we sinned because, once cured, we abandoned fire, iron, and medicines? Unhappy is the sick person who, after treatment, does not wish to endure the pain of treatment. And what more, brothers? Does anyone ever receive treatment who seeks and awaits the sick person’s own decision?

[Note: Fire is kindled in our body from cold but putrid moisture, which offers less resistance, and is nourished by that same cold, putrid moisture; for a contrary effect arises from its contrary, as is clear from Aristotle’s Physics. MITA.]

For when fire is continually kindled in the body from cold moisture, and excessive chill, while it torments and shakes the limbs, itself makes the fire more intense and generates it, so the sick person, to increase the flame that always burns and pants in his veins, impatiently waits for cold water to be given him, not knowing that at that moment heat is extinguished by heat, while cold feeds the fire. [Col. 0513B]

[Note: In the manuscript of Caesena: “Heat is not extinguished by cold; rather, the fire is nourished by cold.”]

Thus, while the law always awaits and tolerates the human will, and yet the human being, impeded by the burden of sin, is unable to obey the legal commandments adequately, the law does not absolve its worshiper from the bond of sin but binds him by the crime of transgression.

And therefore he added, saying: “Do you not know that to whom you present yourselves as slaves for obedience, you are slaves of the one whom you obey—whether of sin, which leads to death, or of obedience, which leads to righteousness?” What is this, brothers? When we were speaking about the law, why did he reveal that the human being had been a slave of sin? “Whether of sin,” he says, “which leads to death, or of obedience, which leads to life.” For above he had said, “Sin shall not have dominion over you, since you are not under the law but under grace.”

Those who are under the law of sin are oppressed and bent beneath its command, and these wretched people cannot be freed from the most shameful slavery of sin unless grace sets them free. “But thanks be to God,” he said, “that you were slaves of sin.” Does he give thanks as though he rejoiced that the human being had been a slave of sin? By no means. He gives thanks not because we were formerly slaves of so cruel a master, but because we have not remained subjected, as he makes still clearer in what follows, saying: “But you obeyed from the heart the form of teaching to which you were handed over; and, having been freed from sin, you became slaves of righteousness.”

We obeyed, brothers, through the grace of the one who called us, not through our own doing, because we were held captive in this condition by our own will. “But you obeyed from the heart the form of teaching.” What form? That of the Gospel, certainly. There, through a new kind of freedom, slavery has not been abolished but changed, because devoted service is better than wandering and presumptuous freedom.

“You became slaves of righteousness.” This slavery, brothers, does not bind but releases; it does not burden but honors; it wipes away the stain of slavery rather than imprinting it.

What here, I ask, is not divine—where slavery is driven out by slavery, where one condition is expelled by another condition, where death dies by death, where destruction is healed by destruction; or, to say it properly and briefly, where the whole of adversity is struck down by the sword of that same adversity?

But when he says, “I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh: just as you presented your members as slaves to impurity and to iniquity for iniquity, so now present your members as slaves to righteousness for sanctification,” he shows the greatness of his compassion, since he lowers evangelical teaching to examples so humble and almost shameful. He imposes and commands upon holiness as much as upon impurity, and upon righteousness as much as upon iniquity, the same measure of service.

The comparison seems absurd and indecent, brothers: it wishes the human being to be subjected to glory as much as to shame. But would that it were only so much! When does human weakness serve God as much as the world, heaven as much as earth, virtue as much as vices? The whole wretched human being is so given over to the flesh and so occupied with present things that he leaves nothing in himself to serve the future life or divine blessings.
