The blessed Apostle fittingly adapted and expressed the force of temporal allurements to human consciences in a single statement, so that human members might serve righteousness, chastity, and purity with as much will as they had given themselves with violence and madness to shame and vices.

He demands little, or perhaps nothing at all, who desires to surrender after his property has been conquered. [Col. 0514D]

[Note: Another reading is “held” or “retained.” This occurs when property is given in emphyteusis, where a small sum, regarded almost as nothing, is ordered to be paid as the rent by the emphyteuta. For ownership and direct lordship remain with the grantor, as in the Code, “On the Right of Emphyteusis,” and at length in Julius Clarus. MITA.]

And he removes an excuse who commands you to repay possible and customary things as though they were great. [Col. 0514D]

[Note: Here Latinius thinks the authenticity of the reading should be questioned. We have followed the first edition of Bon. The reading Latinius discusses is: “Who commands you to repay to him what is possible and customary as though it were great.”]

Give God, then, O human being, as much as you have given to the flesh and to vices. And what is this—that you should owe yourself first to vices and not to God, when God demands you from yourself solely out of love for you?

It follows: “For when you were slaves of sin, you were free in regard to righteousness; but now, having been freed from sin, you have become slaves of righteousness.” [Col. 0514D]

[Note: Chrysologus repeats here what the Apostle had said above, Romans 5:18.]

Formerly slaves of sin, now slaves of righteousness. Through the Apostle, behold, slavery succeeds slavery. You who are rebellious, now display the moment of your freedom. Sin falsely called you free, though it held you miserably captive;

[Note: For *miserē* (“miserably”). Nonius also has *miseriter* and *miserabiliter*.]

now grace calls you a slave whom, in order truly to make free, it adopted as a son of God himself.

Thus Christ’s saying has been fulfilled: “Whoever wishes to be master, let him be a servant” (Matt. 20). [Col. 0515A] Blessed is this slavery, which generates everlasting lordship.

For that freedom brought us the fruit of punishment and a shame we could not endure, as he says: “What fruit did you have then in those things of which you are now ashamed? For the end of those things is death.” Behold how that slavery of the devil manumits; behold with what reward it honors it: so that death at once ends life and begins punishment.

But those who serve Christ, brothers, with death and its wages put to scorn, are transferred into the everlasting life of holiness.

[Note: “The wages of sin is death.”] For Christ’s end does not receive an end; this end does not kill the human being but perfects him. [Col. 0515B]

## SERMON CXV. On the law abolished through grace

On the words of the same Apostle: “Or do you not know, brothers—for I speak to those who know the law,” etc.

After touching David’s spiritual harp with the plectrum and melody of spiritual understanding and soothing your minds and hearts, and after offering the fearsome beginnings of the resounding Gospel to awaken your perceptions, we have judged that we must soon return to the apostolic teaching, so that the threefold order of discourse may retain and provide the saving discipline of ecclesiastical teaching.

For song relaxes the mind from continuous labor, evangelical authority restores and awakens it for work, [Col. 0515D]

[Note: From Latinius.]

and apostolic vigor does not permit our senses to be removed from the straight path or to wander. Today we find that we are following the blessed Apostle’s reading in its proper order.

“Or do you not know, brothers,” he says—for I speak to those who know the law—“that the law has dominion over a person for as long as he lives? And he introduces an analogy. For a woman who is under a husband is bound by the law while her husband lives; but if her husband dies, she is released from the law of her husband. Therefore, while her husband lives, she will be called an adulteress if she is with another man; but if her husband dies, she is released from the law of her husband.”

You see, brothers, the great lesson of heavenly instruction given by the blessed Apostle: how he asserts by legal testimonies that the times of the law have passed, and how by the remarkable example of marriage he emptied its entire prerogative.

And rightly is the law compared with a carnal marriage, since it did not obtain a spiritual union with the synagogue. For when it had taken her to the observance of discipline, to the fruitfulness of holy offspring, to the increase of modesty, to the preservation of chastity, to the sacred and reverent mystery of the heavenly bridal chamber, to the mystical union of the heavenly marriage bed, it found in her an entire filth of prostitution. [Col. 0515D]

[Note: That is, of prostitution or adultery.]

For she came before so great a husband—that is, the law—neither adorned with moral conduct, nor decorated with the jewels of virtues, nor dignified in her bearing, nor covered by that true flame-colored veil of virginal modesty. [Col. 0516A]

[Note: The veil with which the bride’s head was covered. Jerome, in the Epitaph of Paula, says that it was reserved for her to be consecrated as a virgin under Christ’s auspices.]

Instead she was wanton in her eyes, loose in her steps, anticipated by allurements, and wholly painted over with deceits and pretenses.

When so great a husband saw her and, in justified indignation, despised her, drove her far from his fellowship, and condemned her with the full judgment of his severity, she, neither ashamed at being despised nor corrected by contempt nor brought to repentance, but rejected and rushing headlong, hastened to the brothels of idols. She preferred to incur the disgrace of fornication and the crime of adultery rather than to recoil from the shame of a displeasing appearance. [Col. 0516D]

[Note: He aptly develops the analogy from the Apostle. For one must not suppose that Paul is speaking of a woman dismissed by divorce who had married another—for this was permitted by the law—but of a married woman who had consorted with another man.]

Hence the blessed prophet rightly mourns for her, saying: “How has the faithful city, Zion, become a prostitute?” (Isa. 1). Holy Ezekiel too records her adulteries through almost his entire book.

This is why, brothers, when in the Gospel this adulterous woman was accused before the Lord by the scribes and teachers of the law, the Lord turned his face away and bent down toward the ground, lest he see the crime that he was to punish; and he preferred, brothers, to write pardon in the dust rather than to issue a sentence against the flesh (John 8).

The Apostle strives to restore this adulteress to fellowship with Christ, nor does he allow her to be held back by fear of her former fall. While her husband lived, she was rightly an adulteress because she was with another man; now, however, she does not abandon the law, since she returns to the author of the law. She dies to the law, being subject to the legal sentences, so that she may live to grace and rise again through pardon—she who had been killed and put to death by the law.

Finally, although he declares her released from marital right through the death of her husband, he testifies in what follows that she herself, rather than her husband, has died. [Col. 0516C]

[Note: Another reading, in accordance with the sacred text, is “having been released.”]

For it is not the law that dies to the human being, but the human being who dies to the law. [Col. 0516D]

[Note: Theodoret and Cajetan think that here the Apostle, accommodating himself to the Jews, preferred to say, “You have died to the law,” rather than, “The law has died for you.” The meaning is nevertheless the same; for if the Jews who have turned to Christ have died to the law, then the law has also died for them.]

Nor does the command pass away; rather, the one who falls away from the command fails with respect to the command.

Hear what follows: “Therefore, my brothers, you also have been put to death with respect to the law.” Does he say, “The law has died for you”? No: “You also have been put to death with respect to the law.” And he rightly added, “through the body of Christ.” For the law binds the guilty, constrains the liable, punishes and kills the criminal. Therefore, the one who through Christ’s body has been freed and rescued from every crime happily dies to the law, so that he may live to innocence and grace.

“So that you may belong to another, to him who rose from the dead.” “To another.” He himself became another when he changed our corruption into incorruption and carried mortality across into the glory of immortality. “So that we may bear fruit,” he says, “for God.” Through Christ we are sharers in the heavenly nature, belonging not to earth but to God, not to death but to life; and he asserts that fruit is offered to God, not to the flesh.

“For when we were in the flesh,” he says, “the passions of sins, which were through the law, were at work in our members, so that we might bear fruit for death.”

When he says, “When we were,” he indicates past time: while we were placed—and rather exposed—in the flesh alone, we were compelled to think, do, and desire only what belongs to the flesh, in accordance with the Apostle’s other statement: “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God” (Rom. 8).

“For when we were in the flesh,” he says, “the passions of sins, which were through the law.” I shall speak as the Lord spoke: “If the light that is in you is darkness, how great is the darkness!” (Matt. 6). If through the law the passions of sins dominate human members, what will the passions themselves do by their own power—those passions that unhappily and painfully serve the newborn human being from the moment of birth?

When someone is born in this condition and is generated in this condition, anxieties crush him, dangers press upon him, and punishments afflict him. These are the passions, brothers, through which infancy is weakened, childhood is dragged along, adolescence rages, and youth and old age are heaped with many struggles. They are the passions that, while the enemy disturbs it, accompany the whole life of the human being toward its fall.

When the law prohibited them, it warned of them; when it examined them, it increased them; when it accused them, it made them more attractive. What lay hidden through ignorance it made more conspicuous through knowledge. And just as thorns grow more abundantly when they are cut down by the sickle, so, when passions are cut back by the law, they put forth new growth, because inwardly they become fixed and solidified as though in the root of the flesh.

[Note: Through the corruption of our nature, which misuses God’s benefits, the law becomes fatal to us unless the Saviour’s grace accompanies it. First it inflames concupiscence, which, when restrained as by the barrier of an opposing law, bursts out with greater force into diverse desires; secondly, it rouses sin, which had lain dormant in the person living without the law. See Natalis Alexander, *On the Epistles of St Paul*, vol. I, p. 101.]

[Col. 0517C]

The law has a sufficiently just cultivation of faith within it, but it does not produce results. Hence, by its stimulation, it brings the very soil of human flesh to the harvest of death.

“The passions of sins,” he says, “which were through the law, were at work in our members, so that we might bear fruit for death.” The passions claim for themselves, in us, the instrument that was intended for life, turning it toward the harvest of death.

Wounded in this way, therefore, we are released through Christ’s grace from the law of death, and we receive the Holy Spirit within us as the conqueror and victor over vices, so that the passions, excluded outwardly, may strike, test, and provoke, but may fall to the glory of our triumphs.

He desires to conquer for us, for us, who, when he ruled over us, deigned to fight as our soldier, as I have said. [Col. 0517D]

[Note: Something appears to be missing here.]

Therefore let us serve in the newness of the Spirit, now freed from slavery to the flesh, because service to the Lord’s holiness is true dominion. For both the old human being and the old letter corrupted and destroyed the whole discipline. [Col. 0518D]

[Note: Adam and the ancient law of the Hebrews.]

## SERMON CXVI. On the knowledge of sin through the law

On the words of the same Apostle: “What then shall we say? Is the law sin? By no means,” etc.

Whenever the mystical song resounds in different forms but with a harmonious voice, it feeds and delights the hearing with wondrous sweetness. So, when divine and heavenly teaching is proclaimed in varied ways but by one Spirit and with the same meaning, it more willingly and with the greatest pleasure discloses and opens the mystery of evangelical knowledge.

And therefore, after the prophetic melody and the astonishing miracles of Christ’s virtues, let us return to the order of the apostolic readings. The substance of today’s reading was therefore this:

“What then shall we say? Is the law sin? By no means. But I did not know sin except through the law; for I would not have known desire unless the law had said, ‘You shall not desire.’ But sin, taking opportunity through the commandment, worked in me every kind of desire” (Rom. 7).

You have heard, brothers, with what disease the human condition suffered without Christ, how captive human weakness was without grace: the condition that was not prohibited by the law and its commandments but armed by them for crimes; the condition that heard and recognized them for this reason—not in order to overcome sins, but in order to commit them.

“I did not know vices except through the law.” Not to know vices is happiness; to know them is danger; to overcome them is virtue.

A noble and courageous king advances far against his enemies and forestalls the devices of those who are about to attack, so that the soldiers’ faith cannot be cast down and the citizens’ steadfastness cannot be disturbed. In the same way, a noble spirit, through Christ’s grace, passes beyond the miserable confines of its body, anticipates offenses in their entirety, tramples vices underfoot, and utterly destroys crimes, so that they cannot deceive the senses with disguises, corrupt the mind with tricks, dissolve wretched and feeble hearts with disturbances, kindle smoking opportunities through heat and bloodshed, or torment naturally weak members with various kinds of passion.

[Note: Although a deadly sin is buried beneath the ashes of repentance, if the sinner has not yet abandoned and cast away the immediate occasion for sinning, it is not said to be wholly extinguished, but only covered with ash, so that it may be kindled again when an opportunity arises. MITA.]

What fire is to dry grain, vices are to the human body. They are overcome and destroyed most safely by separation alone; through ignorance they perish, and what is not known happily vanishes. But if they reach the mind and senses, if they touch the spirit, if they once penetrate the members, an inextinguishable fire is generated and intensified. Unless heavenly water has refreshed the heart, poured into the mind, and moistened the members, everything in human strength is subjected and reduced to ash.

“Is the law sin?” he says. “By no means. But I did not know sin except through the law.” As though he were saying: Gold is not greed, but I did not know greed except through gold. Wine is not drunkenness, but I did not know drunkenness except through wine. Bodily beauty is not lust, but the splendor of physical form carried my desire away and led me to ruin.

Thus the things themselves are not evil, since they were created by God for usefulness, salvation, and grace; but through them an opportunity for wrongdoing is given. So the greedy person accuses gold, the drunkard wine, and the lascivious or frivolous person wants beauty to be responsible for what happened to his ruin.

So too the law, which had been given by God for salvation and was in itself heavenly and holy, was made by the human being into the ruin of the wretched human being, as the Apostle proves in what follows when he says: “Thus the law is indeed holy, and the commandment holy and just and good.”

Therefore what was good did not bring death; rather, sin brought death—sin that had principally brought death, that had made fragile and weak human nature inclined toward falls and vices. The law rebuked and exposed what lay hidden and was raging like an enemy in the human body: it did so by admonishing the human being concerning innocence, holiness, righteousness, virtue, and faith, and by reproving vices, offenses, and crimes.

But the human being began to hear about virtues and began to desire them, yet did not attain them; began to detest vices, yet followed them; to hate offenses, yet commit them; to recoil from crimes, yet fulfill them. Thus, only belatedly, he realized that he was a captive slave, handed over to evil madness, and began to cry out: “Wretched human being that I am! Who will free me from this body of death?” [Col. 0519B]

The answer is given: “The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.” Hearing this, he began to seek freedom through the author of freedom, salvation through pardon, and life through grace alone.

For a long time he had not known why innocence was difficult, righteousness laborious, holiness anxious, virtue arduous, and faith altogether full of dangers; why offenses possessed such great resources; [Col. 0519D]

[Note: In the manuscripts of Caesena and the Vatican: “why vices.”]

why crimes grew when they were cut down, while virtues diminished when cultivated. The law opened this up; the law taught it; the law showed it in full light: that crimes rule in human feelings and the human mind through sin, and virtues through God; and that offenses cannot be overcome before their author has been destroyed—that is, sin. Christ removed this sin, as John testifies when he says: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1).

“For without the law,” he says, “sin was dead. I was once alive without the law. But when the commandment came, sin revived, and I died; and the commandment that was intended for life was found to be for me the cause of death. For sin, taking opportunity through the commandment, deceived me, and through it killed me.”

Sin was dead—not because it did not exist, but because it was unknown. And it is properly said, “Sin revived,” because it had been buried in our ignorance. It was not the commandment that revived through sin, but sin that revived through the commandment: it made the one who had previously been a sinner become a transgressor; it made him fully guilty even when rebellious; it raised up the deserter and the rebel.

Therefore the human being rightly cries out that he is dead at the moment when he has learned from what, why, and through whom he was to die.

We now see, brothers, how cruel a tyrant sin is: “Through the commandment it deceived me, and through it killed me.” It turned an instrument of salvation into a snare; it made treatment into illness; it changed an instrument of health into a deadly wound; it turned life itself into a lethal sword: “Through the commandment it deceived me, and through it killed me.”

But how could one who was already dead provide for himself once he had learned that he was dead? For who could help the slain except Christ, who, having been slain, restored life? He repaid death in kind through death; he destroyed death and exposed its rebellion. Ordered to lie beneath the punishments of the guilty, death dared to attack the judge himself and presumed to assault the very author of innocence. Thus death rightly died, and in me it is not I who live, but Christ who lives, acts, reigns, and commands.

## SERMON CXVII. On the first and the last Adam

On the words of the same Apostle: “The first man Adam was made a living soul,” etc.

Two men, the blessed Apostle says today, gave the human race its beginning: Adam, namely, and Christ—two men equal in bodily form but unequal in merit [Col. 0520B]; wholly alike in the structure of their limbs, yet wholly unlike in the truth of their very origin. “The first man Adam,” he says, “was made a living soul; the last Adam, a life-giving spirit” (1 Cor. 15). The first was made by this last one, from whom he also received a soul in order to live; the latter was himself formed by his own author, but would himself alone bestow life upon all. The former was fashioned from the cheapest clay; the latter proceeded from the precious womb of the Virgin. In the one, earth was changed into flesh; in the other, flesh was raised into God.

And what more need be said? This is the Adam who, when he was then forming the other, placed his own image in him. Hence he assumes his person [Note: [Col. 0519D] Alternatively, “received.”] and received his name, lest what he had made in his own image should perish for him. The first Adam, the last [Col. 0520C] Adam: the first has a beginning; the last has no end. [Note: [Col. 0519D] The manuscripts of Cesena and Vallicella read: “That first Adam has no beginning; this last has no end; but that one is the last who is the first.”]

For this last one is truly himself the first, as he says: “I am the first, and I am the last” (Isa. 48). “I am the first,” that is, without beginning. “I am the last,” certainly, without end. But he says: “The spiritual was not first, but the natural, and afterward the spiritual.” [Note: [Col. 0519D] He says that the spiritual body was not made first, but the natural one, both in Christ and in us. For God customarily puts imperfect things first, so that perfect things may follow. Thus earth comes before fruit, and we are first children before becoming adults.]

Certainly earth comes before fruit; but the earth is not as precious as the fruit. The former demands groaning and labor; the latter grants substance and life. The prophet rightly glories in such fruit, saying: “Our earth has given its fruit” (Ps. 84). What fruit? That, surely, of which he says elsewhere: “I will place the fruit of your womb upon your throne” (Ps. 131).

“The first man,” he says, “was from the earth, earthly; the second man, from heaven, heavenly.” [Note: [Col. 0520D] He is taking a swipe at Cerinthus, Ebion, the Carpocratians, and other men of this sort. As to whether the most holy Virgin gave birth to Christ in the ordinary manner of women, see Mabillon, Preface 2 to the fourth century of the Benedictine era, p. 354 of the Trident edition, in connection with the discussion that arose between Ratramnus, a monk of Corbie, and Paschasius Radbertus, a fellow monk of the same place.]

Where are those who consider the conception of the Virgin and the Virgin’s childbirth equivalent to the processes of women, when the former is of earth and the latter of heaven; the latter is of divine power, the former of human weakness; the former [Note: [Col. 0520D] The manuscript of Cesena reads, “in the suffering of the body.”] involving bodily suffering, while the latter is entirely in the tranquility of the divine Spirit, in the repose of the human body? Blood was silent, flesh was astonished, the limbs were lulled to sleep, and the Virgin’s chamber remained wholly suspended in heavenly habitation, until the author of flesh took on the garment of flesh and became the heavenly man who would not only restore earth to humanity but also give humanity heaven.

The Virgin conceives; the Virgin gives birth; the Virgin remains. Therefore the flesh is conscious of power, not of pain: in giving birth it receives an increase of integrity and knows no loss of modesty. Rather, she is witness to her own childbirth, since she endured none of the pains of childbirth; and the new mother marvels that she has participated in heavenly mysteries, since she understands that the order of the one being born has nothing of ordinary human custom. [Note: [Col. 0521D] Our author uses this very argument for the same purpose in his letter against Eutyches.]

If the Magus confesses, by an offering, that God was so born, he confesses it while worshipping him. Consider what a Christian ought to think and believe. But let us hear what follows:

“Just as was the earthly man, so also are the earthly; and just as is the heavenly man, so also are the heavenly.” How can those who were not born in this manner be found to be such, by not remaining what they were born but continuing as what they were reborn to be?

Hence, brothers, the heavenly Spirit fecundates the womb of the virginal fountain by mingling within it the mysteries of his light, so that those whom the origin of a muddy stock had poured forth as earthly under wretched conditions, it may give birth to as heavenly and bring them into conformity with their creator. [Note: [Col. 0521D] Augustine says something similar in Book 13 of *The City of God*, p. 23: “We put on the image of the earthly man through the propagation of transgression and death, which generation brought upon us; but we put on the image of the heavenly man through the grace of pardon and everlasting life.”]

Therefore, now reborn and now reshaped according to the image of our Creator, let us fulfill what the Apostle commands: “Just as we have borne the image of the earthly man, let us also bear the image of the heavenly.”

It was necessary that, being formed from earth, we could not breathe heavenly things; that, being born from desire, we could not avoid desire; that, acquired under the domination of seductions, we were compelled to endure the shamefulness of seductions; that, received into the dwelling of this world, we were captives to its evils. But now, reborn in the likeness of our Lord—whom the virgin conceived, the Spirit made alive, modesty bore, integrity gave birth to, innocence nourished, holiness instructed, virtue trained, and God adopted as sons—let us bear the whole image of our Creator in complete likeness: not his majesty, by which he alone is what he is, but his innocence, simplicity, gentleness, patience, humility, mercy, and concord, by which he deigned to become and be shared with us.

Let the poisonous itch of vices cease; let the deadly blandishments of sins be overcome; let accursed rage, the source of crimes, be restrained. Let the whole darkness of worldly pomp be driven from our senses; let the illusion of worldly desire be cast out of our minds. Let the poverty of Christ be sought, for it possesses everlasting riches in heaven. Let complete holiness of soul and body be guarded, so that the image of our Creator may be borne and shine forth in us not by greatness but by conduct.

The Apostle confirms what we have said when he declares: “Now this I say, brothers, that flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God” [Col. 0522A]. See how the resurrection of the flesh is proclaimed: there the flesh will be possessed by the spirit, not possess the spirit, as becomes clear from what follows. “Nor will corruption possess incorruption.” You see that it is not the flesh that perishes, but corruption; not the human being, but guilt; not the person, but the crime—so that the human being, living in God and before God, may at last rejoice that the end of sins has been attained.

A separate discourse on the resurrection must be delivered, brothers, because it is not fitting to speak only in passing, at the very end of the sermon, about that which sends us forward to eternal ages and everlasting life.

[Note: [Col. 0521D] This sermon is elsewhere entitled: “On the words of the same: ‘Now I make known to you, brothers,’ etc.”]

## SERMON CXVIII. On the Death and Resurrection of the Flesh

Since the whole hope of the Christian faith rests upon the resurrection [Col. 0522B] of the dead, [Note: This is a commonplace among the holy Fathers. See Theophylact, *On 1 Corinthians* 15.1, pp. 291–292: “The whole of Christianity is founded upon the doctrine of the resurrection.”] so that no one might dare to doubt it, today we have had the very extensive reading of the blessed Paul recited to you—asserting it by authority, facts, and examples—to which our sermon could find nothing to add. [Note: [Col. 0522D] See Note 1 to Sermon 115.] But since your affection always demands the service of our office, we desire to repeat these same things and press them more forcefully, with the ardor of the resurrection itself.

Brothers, it is always pleasing to speak of the resurrection; it is continually delightful to hear of the resurrection, because no one ever wishes to die, while everyone always delights in living. Let resurrection, therefore, always resound in our mouths; let resurrection always be conveyed to the hearing of our minds, so that death, which always besieges our senses, may be driven from them together with its terror and lamentations.

Thus the farmer sings of abundant fruits and satisfying feasts, so that he may not feel the enormous labor and sweat of the plow. [Note: [Col. 0522D] By “satisfying things” we mean things in which our desires are abundantly fulfilled.] [Note: [Col. 0522D] The manuscripts of Cesena and the Vatican read “the enormous”; the printed editions, “the impending.”] Thus the sailor sings of harbors and profits, so that he may not fear the destruction of the waves or the dangers of the sea. Thus the soldier, so that he may not dread wounds and fear swords, sings of spoils and triumphs.

Therefore let the Christian behold, sing, and contemplate the resurrection with mind, mouth, and eyes, so that he may be able to despise and trample down the whole fear of death.

Death is, brothers, the mistress of despair, the mother of unbelief, the sister of corruption, the parent of hell, the wife of the devil, the queen of all evils. [Note: [Col. 0522D] Here *anima* (“soul”) is understood as bodily life.] It attacks the whole human race in an insatiable order, first sending ahead its whispering companion, despair, to persuade them in this way:

“Human being, why are you wasting your time? Behold, your mistress Death is coming, reducing your soul to nothingness, consuming your flesh with decay and your bones with age, so that she may make you, who did not exist before you were born, cease to exist after death. Therefore, before death, repay what you owe—to yourself and to your years, for you will soon die. Give infancy to games, adolescence to delights, youth to pleasures, and old age to me. Do not, in your despair, think of hope without reason.”

After this she sends her daughter, unbelief, threatening in these terms:

“Why, as though you were not going to die, as though you would escape death, do you arrange your life in this way? Human being, faith deceives you. You believe in faith, which, in order to take away the present, promises the future, and in order to remove what exists before death, promises I know not what invisible things after death. Who has come from there, or what wise person believes things promised for so many ages but never delivered? Oh, if only you would eat and drink! Eat and drink, for tomorrow you will die” (Isa. 22).

To the third sister of her wickedness—corruption—she gives such violent direction that it invades, draws in, and overwhelms human sight. Through the tombs, displaying the final prisons, she shows that her own victims lie there motionless and bound. And so that she may disturb human beings with the full horror and terror of human perception, she pours out decay, belches out pus, spreads stench, and proclaims that from herself she has given innumerable executioners—worms—to a single human body. [Note: [Col. 0523D] “Death itself is the executioner,” says Chrysostom, *Homily* 75, vol. 7.]

Why would Christians believe despair? Why would they believe unbelief? These are the wars of death. With these leaders, these counsels, and this conflict, it takes captive, lays waste, and kills all whom nature brings to present life. [Note: [Col. 0523D] Claudian, *The Rape of Proserpina*:

> Beneath your purple footsteps come kings,  
> Their luxury laid aside, mingled with the poor crowd.  
> Death makes all equal.

] It leads kings, drags peoples, drives nations; it could never be bought off by riches, bent by prayers, softened by tears, or overcome by strength. [Note: [Col. 0523D] Theodoret has similar words, *Oration 6 on Providence*, p. 387: “It does not pity the weeping, is not moved by prayers, is not corrupted by gifts,” and so forth. See Basil, Letter 185.]

They were mistaken, brothers, who attempted to write about the goodness of death. [Note: [Col. 0523D] Nearly all pagans praised death. King Ptolemy forbade Hegesias of Cyrene to praise it in the schools, because many who heard him killed themselves voluntarily.] And what is surprising? The wise men of the world then consider themselves great and illustrious if they persuade the simple that what is the greatest evil is the greatest good. Scripture rightly says of them: [Col. 0523C] “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil” (Isa. 5). “Woe to those who make darkness light and light darkness!”

And indeed, whom would they not deceive—whom could they not blind—when they persuaded the unwary that living is evil and dying good? [Note: [Col. 0523D] Alternatively, “whom did they not blind?”]

But truth drives these things away; light dispels them; faith attacks them; the Apostle marks them; Christ destroys them. For while he restores the goodness of life, he exposes, condemns, and excludes the evil of death.

Thus the Apostle began: “Now I make known to you, brothers, the Gospel which I preached to you, which you also received, in which you stand, through which you are also saved. By what reasoning I preached it to you, you must hold fast, unless you believed without reason. For I delivered to you first of all what I also received: that Christ died for our sins, that he was buried, and that he rose again on the third day according to the Scriptures” (1 Cor. 15).

God’s generosity enriches the one who is going to live, not the one who is going to die. For what good does anyone receive if the one who receives it will not himself exist? “In which you stand.” Surely the one who always lives stands, because the dead always lies there. [Note: [Col. 0524D] Most printed editions read, “who is going to die.”] “Through which you are also saved.” If someone dies, he perishes; [Note: [Col. 0524D] The manuscripts of Cesena and Vallicella read: “But he is saved through him who survives.”] the one who always lives, however, is saved.

“By what reasoning I preached it to you, you must hold fast, unless you believed without reason.” Not only did the one who believed that he was born solely in order to perish believe without reason, brothers; he also lived without reason.

Human being, what arises for you that does not die? What dies for you that does not rise again? The day rises in the morning and rises again in the morning; in the evening it is buried in night and rises again in the morning. The sun is born daily and dies daily; it rises again daily. The seasons perish as they pass; as they return, they revive. [Note: [Col. 0524D] The ancients often used this argument. Gregory of Nyssa, *Oration on the Resurrection of Christ*, vol. 3, p. 429. They considered night an image of death and day an image of life. Tertullian, *Against Marcion*: “But night is an image of death.” Hilary, *On Genesis*: “Day is an image of life; night is an image of death.”]

Therefore, human being, if you do not believe God, if you do not submit to the law, if you do not assent to what you hear, believe at least your own eyes, or submit to the elements, which continually proclaim your resurrection to you. Certainly, if these things are far inferior to you—things that are in your own hands and are raised from death by your work—let them teach you that you can be raised by God’s work.

Go to the seed, as the Apostle teaches (1 Cor. 15). Take dry wheat, without sensation or movement. Draw a furrow, dig the earth, make a grave, bury the wheat. Observe how it perishes through death, swells with moisture, and is corrupted by decay. When it has reached everything that despair, unbelief, and corruption previously thrust upon you, then suddenly it revives in a shoot, grows young in the grass, becomes youthful in the stalk, ripens in the grain, and rises again in that very appearance and form which you had mourned as lost altogether. Thus wheat teaches you, human being, not so much to eat as to understand, not so much to labor as to believe.

Let us be silent about the rest, because the blessed Apostle clearly, lucidly, and divinely declares both where, when, how, and through whom death came. Human being, receive faith, for it is given freely; believe in the resurrection, because the one who promises it asks no price.

## SERMON CXIX. On the True Race for the Crown of Glory. On the Words of the Same: “Do You Not Know That Those Who Run in the Stadium,” etc.

The blessed Apostle Paul exhorts us to the crown of heavenly glory not only through the teaching of the law but also through the example of this world. For among other things he says, as your affection has heard: “Do you not know that those who run in the stadium all run, but one receives the prize?” And he added: “Run in such a way that you may obtain it” (1 Cor. 9).

According to the earthly example, many, as the Apostle says, run in the stadium, but one receives the crown—that is, the one who runs best. So also in the stadium of the present life, many run, but one receives the crown. The Jews run through the law; the philosophers run through empty wisdom; the heretics also run through false proclamation; the Catholics run through the true preaching of faith. But of all these one receives the crown: the Catholic people, who, having received the course of faith, press on toward Christ, so as to reach the palm and crown of immortality.

Therefore Jews, philosophers, and heretics run in vain, because they do not walk along the straight path of faith. For what does it profit the Jews to run through observance of the law when they do not know Christ, the Lord of the law? The philosophers also run through the empty wisdom of the world, but their race is useless and empty because they do not know the true wisdom of Christ. For Christ is the true wisdom of God, which is recognized not by ornamented words or brilliant speech but by faith of the heart.

The heretics also run through the poisonous assertion of their faith; they run through fasts, they run through almsgiving, but they cannot reach the crown, because they do not run truly. Their false faith does not deserve to receive the grace of true faith. The Apostle makes this clear elsewhere when he says: “And if I distribute all my substance to the poor, and if I deliver my body to the fire so that it may burn, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13). For he does not have the charity of Christ who does not faithfully believe in Christ.

And therefore the Apostle rightly added, saying: “Run in such a way that you may obtain it.” We must therefore run the faithful race in the faith of Christ, in the commandments of God, and in works of righteousness, so that we may be able to reach the crown of eternal life.

Finally, how we ought to run the same Apostle subsequently shows, saying: “Everyone who contends in the contest exercises self-control in all things; and they do this to receive a perishable crown, but we an imperishable one.” [Note: [Col. 0525D] The Apostle seems to allude to the Olympic or Isthmian contests, which were celebrated at Corinth. The stadium was the place where contests were held on foot or with horses.]

See by what examples the Apostle invites us to the crown of promised immortality. [Note: [Col. 0525D] Alternatively, *promissam* (“promised”).] [Col. 0526A] [Note: [Col. 0525D] Following in Paul’s footsteps, Chrysologus passes from runners to contestants—that is, athletes and boxers.] In this earthly contest, those who wish to win abstain from certain foods and from excessive drink; they abstain from every impurity, practicing such chastity that they do not even seek their own marriages. Nor do they hope to win by any other means than by keeping their bodies chaste and pure. [Note: [Col. 0526D] Horace, on runners: “The boy has done and endured much, sweated and shivered, and abstained from Venus and Bacchus.” Chrysostom, on Paul’s words at 2 Timothy 2:5, “Unless one has competed lawfully,” says in agreement with our author: “It is not enough for lawful competition that the contestant has entered the contest, nor that he has been anointed . . . in addition, one who wished to obtain the crown had to observe every rule of the athletic profession, both concerning the foods from which athletes had either to abstain or which they had to eat, and concerning continence and decency.”] [Note: [Col. 0525D] Athletes—for among the Greeks this name included all who competed bodily, but among the Romans only boxers and wrestlers—although they were extremely voracious, were fed on dried figs, cheese, and nuts; and, if on meat, only meat that had much juice and fat, but without any seasonings. Their diet, called by the Romans *colephium* or *coliphium*, is called “dry fattening” by Tertullian, *On the Pallium*, chap. 4; see Salmasius, pp. 262, 267.]

And after so much labor, what else do they receive but a small, perishable, and indeed worthless crown? If, then, such labor is undertaken for a perishable crown, how much more ought we to endure every labor, to whom a heavenly reward and the crown of eternal glory are promised?

We must therefore contend in no light contest. For we contend against spiritual wickedness, against the devil and his angels; we contend against injustice, impiety, malice, immodesty, and the various seductions of sins. And if, while contending, we conquer, we receive as many crowns as the vices over which we have become victorious. [Note: [Col. 0526D] “If we conquer, we shall receive.”]

Great, then, is this contest, in which we present a spectacle to the Lord. We are watched while contending by the Lord; we are watched by his angels. On earth we conquer, but in heaven we receive the reward of virtue.

Finally, the holy martyrs, placed in the contest of combat, conquered not only the vices of sins but death itself, and received the rewards of immortality. [Note: [Col. 0526D] Muratori, p. 231, *On Paradise*, against Burnet, quotes this and several other passages.]

In this contest our Lord and Savior first both contended and conquered, so that he might show us an example of combat and victory. As we therefore discuss these matters with you, we cast the seed of good combat into your hearts, finding your breasts as though they had been furrowed by the plow of righteousness. [Col. 0526C] Cultivate, then, the word we have scattered among you, so that what has been sown may be able to germinate. May God, by his visitation, water you with the dew of his mercy, and grant increase to our seeds, so that, in gathered sheaves of merits, you may reach the hundredfold fruit.

## SERMON CXX. On Avoiding the Form of the World and Assuming the Form of the Savior. On the Words of the Same: “Do Not Be Conformed to This World,” etc.

Christ has today made clear that the apostles are salt, saying: “You are the salt of the earth” (Matt. 5). Let no one therefore take offense if we rub the words of the blessed Paul like grains of divine salt, so that, being more deeply lulled (*soporati*; the reading is contextually uncertain), we may be able to season the understanding of our minds.

For grains of salt season things that are whole, so that, more finely reduced, they may descend into the very marrow. [Note: [Col. 0527D] “Whole” means an uncorrupted thing, not violated by pus or consumed by decay. Thus the Author says that grains of salt season whole things, not yet corrupted, when the grains themselves, more finely reduced in the marrow, descend into it. Chrysostom, *Homily* 15 on Matthew, says: “How can things that have already been corrupted be restored by rubbing with salt?” The manuscript of Cesena reads, “into the very marrow.”] So the Apostle’s speech, read publicly, offers a simple meaning, supplies profound knowledge, and, through diligent reading, is repeated for those matters that we previously examined.

Today the blessed Apostle says: “Do not be conformed to this world” (Rom. 12). Do you suppose that, by saying this, blessed Paul the Apostle objects to our being conformed to the figures of the elements? Or does he forbid us to be like the Persian kings, who, with a sphere placed beneath their feet, so that they might be thought to tread upon the pole, pretend to take the place of God? Or does he forbid us, with radiant heads, to sit in the form of the sun, so that they might not be human beings; or, with horns placed upon themselves, to appear as though they lamented being men; or to make themselves effeminate in the moon; or to assume various forms like the stars, so as to lose the shape of a human being [Col. 0527B] and acquire none of the brightness from above? [Note: [Col. 0527D] The successors of Alexander, who pretended to be sons of Jupiter Ammon, appear on coins with horned foreheads.] [Note: [Col. 0527D–0528D] A coin of Gordian Pius, when he returned to Carrhae before attacking the Persians, displays his turreted head and, on the reverse, a crescent moon; see Patin, p. 373. In those regions the moon was worshipped religiously both in male and female attire. Spartianus, *Caracalla*: “When he again wished to wage war against the Parthians, and was wintering at Edessa, he came from there to Carrhae by the favor of the god Moon (*Lunus Deus*).”]

Although these practices descend from the vanity of the world and ought to be avoided—and laughed at—by the wise, nevertheless, when the Apostle says, “Do not be conformed to this world,” he corrects the life of the world, reproves its customs, judges its institutions, chastises its desires, condemns luxury, and drives, banishes, and excludes the whole pomp of worldly vanities from Christian minds.

But in this brief statement he recalls what he explained more fully at the beginning of this Epistle, where he depicts the form of the world in its vices: “Filled with all iniquity, malice, fornication, greed, wickedness; full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, malignity; whisperers, detractors, hateful to God, insulting, arrogant, proud, inventors of evil, disobedient to parents, foolish, disorderly, without affection, without mercy; who, although they knew the justice of God, did not understand that those who do such things are worthy of death—not only those who do them, but also those who consent to those who do them” (Rom. 1).

Brothers, you have heard the form of the world, learned its appearance, and seen its figure—if indeed it is a form and not a shapeless monster, where the whole face of things has been erased by the confusion of crimes; where the whole form of the world has been dissolved by the intermarriage of sins; where the image of the Creator itself has been taken away by the diseases of transgressions; where the human being is buried in vices; where the crimes of the corrupted body swarm; where one human being is the tomb of another; where in the human being no human being is seen, but only a corpse.

The Apostle therefore forbids us to be conformed to this form and prohibits us from being fashioned according to this figure. He does not permit us to resemble this likeness, but reforms us according to the form of God, recalls us to the likeness of Christ, and restores us wholly to the image of the Creator, saying: “But be transformed in the renewal of your mind.”

That is: let your minds be renewed through Christ, having cast away the form of this world; and, having wholly rejected the deformity of the old image, [Col. 0528A] restore your form to the form of your Savior. [Note: [Col. 0528D] Figure is fleeting, external, and apparent rather than substantial; form is more enduring and solid.] Thus the newness of your minds may shine forth in your actions, and the heavenly man may now walk upon earth in heavenly conduct.

How, then, he composes the form of the new man may now be made clear. “For just as in one body we have many members, and all the members do not have the same function, so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another. Having gifts that differ according to the grace given to us…”

He acts—he acts so that the body he places in heavenly conduct, in the life above, may consist in the agreement and union of its members through holy habits. Let not the foot, through perverse swelling, confuse the service of the eye, nor the eye the function of the foot. Rather, let the members of holiness be content with the gifts of the giver, and let them believe that all the members possess what he has made one member possess, because one member does not know how to diminish what is honored as a whole in the body.

Hence the Apostle depicts actions by members and members by actions in this way: “He who teaches, in teaching; he who exhorts, in exhortation; he who gives, in simplicity; he who presides, with diligence; he who shows mercy, with cheerfulness. Let charity be without pretense; hate evil, cling to what is good; in honor anticipate one another; be kindly toward one another; do not be sluggish in diligence; be fervent in spirit; serve the Lord; rejoice in hope; be patient in tribulation; persevere in prayer; share in the memories of the saints; pursue hospitality. Bless and do not curse; rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep; provide what is good, not only before God but also before human beings.

“Do not be wise in your own eyes; repay no one evil for evil. If possible, insofar as it depends on you, live at peace with all people. Do not avenge yourselves, but give place to wrath. If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink. Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.”

Above, brothers, the Apostle revealed the members of vices; now he has disclosed to us the members of virtues, so that the heavenly body, strengthened by so many members and reinforced by such sinews, may easily overthrow the battles of the world and overcome the conflicts of the devil.

And if one lives as the Apostle taught, does he not overthrow the world? Does he not trample down the flesh? Does he not conquer the devil? Is he not made equal to the angels? Is he not greater than heaven?

Indeed, he is greater than heaven, because heaven is not moved of its own accord, acts not by will, and does nothing by judgment; it always serves by necessity alone, because it was once commanded to serve. It does not preserve itself undefiled by strength or labor. Therefore, although it is not subject to punishment, neither does it stand for a reward.

But a human being, formed from earthly lowliness, while conquering earthly defilement, breaking the goads of blood, and overcoming the excesses of the passions of the flesh, transcends heaven and flies to the very seat of the Godhead. Thus he becomes greater than heaven and surpasses the angels in merits, not in nature.

The Apostle Paul proves this: while he thoroughly conquers earth, he entered heaven, passed beyond another, and merited to reach the third. And rightly so, for he ought to be the first to ascend the heavens who taught human beings to penetrate the heavens both by word and by example.

He will be greater than heaven who lives as Paul taught; brighter than the sun will be he who shines throughout the world with such rays of virtue that he permits himself to be darkened by no night of vices.

He will be brighter than the moon who tempers these shadows not with weakened light but drives away the whole night of the world with the full splendor of merits. Nor, like the moon, does he suffer daily losses of light; rather, by the perpetual lamp of his deeds he remains in the brightness of the heavenly light. Nor is he interrupted, as the moon is, by monthly darkness; he will remain continually in the brightness of God.

And if the moon is great because it softens the night, how much greater is the one whose life receives nothing from night? I say nothing of the stars, because as heaven shines with stars, so the saints shine with virtues, the Lord saying: “You are the light of the world; shine like lights in the world” (Matt. 5).

In sum, heaven, the sun, the moon, and the stars, as God says, will pass away (Matt. 24), but the righteous will remain in the continual brightness of God.

I would like, brothers, to draw out separate expressions from each word of the Apostle; but because repeated reading produces weariness in the listener, and because we cannot remain silent longer about the virtues of the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0529C] The bishop’s sermon sometimes preceded the reading of the Gospels.], may it please your affection that we have brought the present reading to a close in a concise sermon. May our God deign to impress upon your holy minds both what we have said and what we have left unsaid.

## SERMON CXXI. On the Rich Man and Lazarus

You have heard today, brothers, both the end of poverty and what the outcome of riches is, the Lord saying: “There was a certain rich man, and he was clothed in purple and fine linen, and he feasted splendidly every day” (Luke 16). “And there was a certain beggar named Lazarus, full of sores, who lay at his gate, desiring to be filled with the crumbs that fell from the rich man’s table, and no one gave them to him; but even the dogs came and licked his sores. It happened, however, that the poor man died and was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom. But the rich man died and was buried in hell.”

Behold, brothers, how lamentable is the change in circumstances: angels carry the poor man, while hell swallows the rich man. Behold, brothers, the poor man’s death conquered the rich man’s whole life, and the poor man’s single exaltation surpassed all the rich man’s pomp and glory.

Why does burial so deceive the eyes? Why does the pomp of funeral rites so lie? In the rich man’s funeral procession the whole city moves here, when the body is carried out; the poor man goes alone, and pity carries the poor man on the shoulders of two bearers. [Note: [Col. 0529C] Among the ancients, *obsequia* and *exsequiae* mean funeral rites. Pope Nicholas I, in his response to the consultations of the Bulgarians, quoted by Du Cange, *Glossary*, vol. 3, p. 32, cites this passage of Chrysologus: “He is not carried to the tomb with the customary funeral rites.”] [Note: [Col. 0529D] He touches on the ancient custom by which, when a funeral was carried out, relatives and friends, together with slaves, went ahead in honor of the deceased. See Jerome, to Paula, *On the Death of Blesilla*; Sulpicius, Book 2 of *The Life of Saint Martin*; Hegesippus, Book 5, chap. 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0529D] The two bearers here seem to be νεκροφόβοι (*nekrophóboi*), in Latin *vespillones*. Thus Augustine, Letter 19 to Jerome: “There will be no pious escort and bearer of the body.” Hence in Marcellinus, Book 14, p. 37, “the herald of the bearers”—that is, a flute player who played before the *vespillones*, or anyone else who urged them to their work, just as the *keleustai* encouraged rowers. Du Cange cites this passage in his *Glossary*, vol. 1, p. 482.]

[Note: [Col. 0529D] Men called *cuccullatores*, taken from the lowest servile condition, were assigned to funeral service; four of them placed their shoulders beneath the corpse. Martial, Book 8, p. 74:

[Col. 0530C]

> Four marked bearers carried the worthless corpse,

[Source ends here, incomplete.]

The unhappy pyre receives a thousand such things. See Pignorius, *On Slaves*.] Nor are four assigned to the dead man, but two under a single pole, as though unwilling bearers were being consigned to the task of throwing away a burden [Col. 0530B]. Rightly are angelic services and rightly divine ministrations soon assigned to him to whom even the final offices of humanity were so cruelly denied. A mournful crowd of servants precedes the funeral of the rich man; a multitude of singing angels goes before the bier of the poor man.

The rich man’s body lies enclosed in a marble tomb and in [Note: [Col. 0530C] Elsewhere, “gilded.”] carefully arranged clothing; the poor man’s flesh rests in natural mud [Note: [Col. 0530C] Caesenate manuscript: “in material mud and a natural position.”] and, by its material condition, knows neither the bites of worms nor putrefaction and stench [Note: [Col. 0530C] This could have resulted either from the beggar’s body being extremely dry, or from the nature of the earth, sandy and excessively arid; or because, as flesh begins to decay, the earth itself immediately consumes the decay—or rather, by its own power prevents the decay and keeps worms from being generated from it, which seems more likely. MITA.—There are many bodies of blessed men which, by God’s favor, are preserved incorrupt after death. The Author may perhaps have had this in mind.].

But let us ask, brothers, what fault, what crime, what offense consigned the rich man to the punishments of hell and, before the judgment of his condemnation, [Note: [Col. 0530D] Properly, *elogium* is a brief notation or heading of a crime, as in Book III: “Stellio was born”; and in the final law of the Theodosian Code, *On Shipowners*. Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XIV: “He ordered many to be killed under a single indictment.” Zeno of Verona, *On the Martyrdom of the Prophet Isaiah*: “When Isaiah preached Christ, or announced to the Israelite people the indictment of their future condemnation,” etc.] caused the indictment of so many ages to be sung, with the judge himself reporting it when the Lord said:

> “There was a certain rich man, and he was clothed in purple and fine linen, and he feasted splendidly every day. And there was a certain beggar named Lazarus, who lay at the rich man’s gate and desired to be filled with the crumbs that fell from the rich man’s table.”

Are riches, then, criminal in themselves alone? Or are garments, by themselves and alone, condemned by God? And are banquets to be punished in themselves to such an extent that they should not merely lack the reward of good things, but should bear and deserve [Note: [Col. 0530D] Elsewhere, “judgment.”] the destruction of all evils? Or has poverty been so approved and sanctified in itself, and its sores so consecrated, that Lazarus was snatched by the hands of angels into the bosom of holy Abraham?

And it is remarkable, brothers, [Col. 0531A] that Abraham, once a rich man, rejects this rich man, since Scripture says: “Abraham was very rich” (Gen. 30). He now condemns and allows to suffer punishment the man whom he once had as his equal in present goods, especially since the divine word disclosed neither the good qualities of this poor man nor the evil qualities of that rich man. Why, then, does Abraham now embrace the poor man, while fleeing from and rejecting the rich? Or how did riches make this man innocent, while riches made that man criminal; how did they advance the one to the repose of all the blessed, while assigning the other to the abyss of every evil?

But lest the sermon set before you weary your minds for long and suspend your hearing, we must hasten the solution of this question. Abraham, brothers, was rich not for himself but for the poor, and he strove not to possess wealth but to distribute it [Col. 0531B]. He endeavored to store his resources more and more in the bosom of the poor than in his own granaries, as his entire manner of life plainly teaches. For although he himself was continually a sojourner, he acted so that no stranger would feel himself a stranger (Gen. 18): while he himself lived under a tent, he did not allow a visitor to remain without shelter; and, always a host to a guest, though exiled from his homeland and ignorant of any permanent dwelling, he was himself both lord and fatherland for all.

He knew that he had been appointed not as one who “lies upon” [Note: [Col. 0531D] Basil of Caesarea, in the appendix to the Fourth Council, p. 26: “Those who wisely reflect upon the matter should consider that the use of riches consists in administration, not in enjoyment. For to do otherwise would be what Chrysologus means by lying upon riches.” The expression is commonly used in pagan sacred contexts of those who slept in temples to receive dreams from the gods. It occurs frequently among the poets. See Cicero, *On Divination*, Book II; Tertullian, *On the Soul*, ch. 27; Arnobius, Book I, etc.] wealth, but as a steward of divine generosity, so that he might vindicate the oppressed and release captives (Gen. 14); and, to rescue those already at the point of death, this new warrior himself gave himself over to death, for whom compassion for another’s sake was dearer than his own life.

Abraham stood beside the guest he had received; he did not sit beside him. He was not the guest’s fellow banqueter but his servant. [Col. 0531C] On seeing a stranger, Abraham did not know himself as lord; he himself brought the meal and, intent upon providing a sufficiently refined cuisine, assigned his wife to the kitchen. Though he entrusted and committed himself and all that was his to his servants, he scarcely dared entrust the guest to his proven wife.

And what more, brothers? In the end, his humanity was so holy and was always prepared by holy hands that it invited God himself to his dwelling and compelled him to become his guest. He came to Abraham, to the repose of the poor, to the shelter of guests—he who will confess in the future that he was received in the guest and the poor man, when he says: “I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was a stranger, and you welcomed me” (Matt. 22).

Now it happened that the poor man died and was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom. Not undeservedly, brothers, [Col. 0531D] he then received all the saints in his repose, [Note: [Col. 0531D] Here the Author changes the order and rises from the limbo of the Fathers [Col. 0532D] to the place of blessedness, where Abraham is said to perform the office of steward. MITA.] and in that very heavenly blessedness performs the office of steward: because, since he had always received strangers and poor people here, he deserved to receive God himself with the angels and to behold as a guest beneath his tent the one whom he had always possessed as his benefactor.

And truly, brothers, he would have considered himself only slightly blessed [Col. 0532A] if, in that very heavenly glory, he had ceased from the pious duty of hospitality. He would have enjoyed divine gifts alone, though here he had considered himself cruel toward anyone if he denied that person human goods.

Abraham, brothers, always went far out to meet those who were coming; he even calls passers-by with a request, and compels the unwilling, with great entreaty, to come to his table. [Note: [Col. 0532D] For “excellent.”]

> O first among beloved companions.  
> Ovid, Book IV of the *Tristia*, Elegy 9.]

He always sets before his guests the choicest and fattest animals from his herds, and with his own hands and those of his wife he continually offers freshly made, hot loaves—loaves which his constant hospitality certainly did not permit to be cold and from the previous day.

But that other rich man—rather, captive of riches, slave of wealth, and shackled by his very possessions—had only the pomp of an ignoble tomb, in which every manifestation and expression of compassion had entirely failed. He despises not merely a person or a poor man but compassion itself [Col. 0532B], while Lazarus lies at his gate in such a state.

With purple, fine linen, delicate clothing, and pleasant banquets, a cruel soul was nourishing iron entrails. God, eager to bring about human salvation and wishing to soften him, threw not so much Lazarus as the very furnace of his compassion [Note: [Col. 0532D] A vessel in which metals are melted. Yet Lazarus was unable to soften the rich man’s iron entrails.] at his gate. I call it a furnace because of his iron entrails.

Thus Lazarus the beggar is thrust before and brought near the impious eyes; and, so that the rich man might be able to give, the rich man’s wealth is increased more and more. But the rich man, harder than adamant, whatever God contributed to his wealth on account of the poor man’s nourishment, either shamefully squandered or cruelly stored away.

Again, so that God might not remain silent but cry out and admonish the rich man; so that the fasting poor man might show that he was seeking only bread; so that he might drive the rich man’s abundant soul to give even the smallest gifts, the poor man’s hunger is increased [Col. 0532C]. “He desired,” it says, “to be filled with the crumbs that fell from the rich man’s table.”

But the rich man, stuffed with various dishes, belched his indigestion toward heaven, lest he hear the voice of the poor man lying on the ground in such a condition. Again, because the voice of the one who cried out could accomplish nothing against ears that had been hardened, God opens the poor man’s whole body with wounds in order to open the rich man’s heart, so that, in admonishing the rich man, the poor man might have as many mouths as he had wounds.

The entrails are exposed, the sores are brought forth, the openings of the wounds are widened, pus pours out, and the poor man’s entire flesh is arranged as a stage of compassion, so that the one whom the voice of the hungry man had not moved might at least be moved by sighs, pains, groans, and the whole accumulation of misery. But the rich man, with his proud eye and insatiable heart, scorns both to hear, to see, and to feel all these things.

God still seeks how the rich man may be released from his obstinacy. He releases the poor man’s hands from his limbs, so that he might not drive away the rich man’s dogs—dogs which, by feeding on his wounds, would feed the rich man’s wound. And, in a new way, brothers, the order of humanity is reversed: human poverty becomes the means by which inhuman greed is exposed [Note: [Col. 0532D] Elsewhere, “might be revealed.”].

The rich man does not feed the poor man even with the crumbs falling from his table, and Lazarus the poor man, because he had nothing else, showed himself humane even toward the dogs with his own flesh. Miserable rich man! If you did not give bread, why at least did you not wish to drive away the dogs?

But your dogs are gentler than you—or rather, you are more savage than your dogs. While you rage, they spare him: they extend not their teeth for biting but their tongues for service, so that, like a sponge, they do not aggravate his wounds but wipe them clean.

Rich man, in your dogs hunger was overcome by compassion; in you, satiety did not overcome compassion. For what the dogs took care to do with such devotion [Note: [Col. 0533D] The printed editions, with Mita, read *fecere curantum*. We follow Latinus, which is better.] is confirmed by the practice always before our eyes. Dogs always heal their own wounds by licking them; dogs, taught by nature, care for the poor man, while a human being neglects another human being, with nature itself bringing the gravest accusation.

It is true, it is true: the rich man cannot give even crumbs, since the miser is always in need.

The sermon must be postponed, brothers, because we have both used up the time for speaking [Note: [Col. 0533D] That a fixed time for delivering a sermon was formerly established is demonstrated from the Fathers. Consult Origen, *Homily 21 on Numbers*; Augustine, *Homily 23 of the Fifty Homilies*, and Sermon 237, *On Time*; and Chrysologus again, Sermon 112; and the second note there.] and the passages of the reading that most especially require our treatment follow.

[Note: [Col. 0533D] From this sermon of Chrysologus, as from those of other Fathers—such as Chrysostom, in the Third Oration against the Jews; Augustine, in the Preface to his exposition of the Epistle of Blessed John; Gaudentius of Brescia; and others—Ferrarius, *On Sermons*, Book III, ch. 11, p. 363, inferred that among the ancient Fathers the practice of preaching was customary not only on Sundays but also on other festivals, especially those of martyrs.]

## SERMON CXXII. On the Same Subject

It would be fitting, brothers, for our sermon today to recount, insofar as is sufficient, the virtues of Saint Andrew. But since we said that we would return what remains concerning that rich man and Lazarus, the evangelical poor man; and since Blessed Andrew’s apostolate and the distinction of his martyrdom are sufficient, indeed abundant, for his glory, let us, if it pleases you, fulfill what we promised and what we owe, with the Lord himself granting its repayment.

Knowing that weariness always produces disgust both in the speaker and in the hearer, in our preceding treatment we postponed a large part of the proposed reading, so that, with the strength of our minds restored, we might receive the subsequent words of salvation with full vigor and attentive hearing [Col. 0533C] [Note: [Col. 0534D] Latinus reads “with devoted hearing.”].

For after what we have said, the following comes next:

> “And lifting up his eyes, while he was in torment, Abraham saw from afar, and Lazarus in his bosom. And he lifted up his eyes” (Luke 16).

Late does the rich man raise his eyes upward—eyes that he always kept lowered toward the earth. Rich man, the eyes you raise are your accusers; the eyes you raise do not appease the judge but inflame him; they bring not pardon but guilt, and demand an accumulation of punishments rather than consolation.

Where do you raise your eyes? What do you still cry out, rich man? What do you look toward, rich man? Lazarus is there; there is the betrayer of your impiety, the witness to your crime, the advocate of faith.

“And he cried,” it says, “Father Abraham, have mercy on me.”

Now you recognize a father, and now you do not know as your father the one whom you so despised as a father in the person of Lazarus. Now the just man comes before you, the man who then endured Lazarus’s long suffering so that he might be compassionate toward you.

Wretched is the man whom his very origin thus accuses [Note: [Col. 0534D] That is, Abraham himself, from whom you claim to derive your origin when you call him “Father.”]; whom the author of light himself [Note: [Col. 0534D] *Addicere* is a judicial term, used when a matter is assigned to the highest bidder. Here it means “to condemn,” “to devote,” and so forth.] thus condemns; wretched is he for whom, in judgment, the magnitude of his crime permitted neither a parent to show mercy, nor a father to forgive, nor affection to offer aid.

What do you still cry out, rich man? Rich still, but in crime, not in wealth; not in substance, but in guilt. Why do you cry out? What do you ask for?

Here there is no longer a petition but a legal dispute, where the one who suffered stands on the opposite side. Yet the places of the litigants are different: one pleads from nearby, the other from far away; one speaks from the bosom, the other cries out from Tartarus; one begs from repose, the other complains of punishment.

But what does the rich man say?

> “Father Abraham, have mercy on me.”

You would speak well if Lazarus, seated in the bosom, did not hold the very heart of the judge; you would speak well if Lazarus did not possess all the secrets of the most righteous judge. He begs the judge in vain, when an innocent witness accuses him in such a way; and he foolishly believes that the judge can aid him, when he who endured so much speaks through the judge’s mouth.

> “Have mercy on me, and send Lazarus.”

Are you still so cruel toward Lazarus? “Send Lazarus.” Where? From the bosom into hell; from the lofty throne into the deepest chaos; from holy quiet into the shriek of torments; from such silence among the blessed into punishment.

> “And send Lazarus.”

As I see it, what the rich man is doing arises not from a new pain but from an old envy, and he is more inflamed by heaven than by Gehenna. It is a grievous evil for them, an unbearable fire for them, to see those whom they once held in contempt become happy.

Even now malice does not abandon the rich man, whom punishment already possesses. He does not ask to be taken to Lazarus; he wants Lazarus brought to him.

Abraham, in his compassion, cannot send Lazarus to the bed of your torments, rich man—you who did not deem him worthy to admit to your table. Your circumstances have now been reversed: you see the glory of the one whose punishment you once so despised; he sees your torments, he who once marveled at you in your glory.

But let us see, brothers, why he so laments that Lazarus be sent to him.

> “Send Lazarus, so that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and refresh my tongue.”

You are mistaken, rich man. This flame belongs not so much to the tongue as to the mind; not so much to the tongue as to the heart. This is still the heat of conscience, not that final fire which remains and awaits you. [Note: [Col. 0534D] References to this occur everywhere among the ancient Fathers. Hilary, *On Psalm* CXVIII, no. 2: “When we are to render an account of every idle word, shall we desire the day of judgment, in which that unwearied fire must be undergone by us?” Origen, *Homily 3 on Psalm* XXXVI: “All of us must come to that fire.” Gregory Nazianzen, at the beginning of Oration 261: “That final fire by which our sins will be weighed or purged.” See Caesarius, in the appendix to the sermons; Augustine, Sermon 15, no. 4; Ambrose, Sermon 20, no. 4. Yet, in the passages cited, nearly all agree that the Fathers understood by the fire of judgment only expiatory flames. Chrysologus, however, seems to have meant hell. Tertullian too, *Apology*, no. 48, when discussing judgment, mentions “everlasting fire” and “fire of judgment”; yet there too he has in view only the reprobate. [Col. 0535D]]

For if the entire fire of the final judgment already surrounded you, and the sentence of that hopeless condemnation already held you, you would never raise your eyes, never address your father, never make a request for yourself, and never presume to intercede for your brothers.

Certainly, if the whole fire of hell already possesses you, if the flame of Gehenna embraces you, why do you desire relief from the heat of the tongue alone? Unless it is because, when your breast pants with the flame of its own crime and guilt, the tongue burns, blazes, and seethes more intensely—the tongue that insulted the poor man and denied mercy.

It goes first to judgment; it tastes and suffers the torments beforehand; it is the first part of the whole body to feel the heat—the tongue that, having first tasted various foods of luxury here and sampled fragrant drinks, refused to administer compassion and did not command mercy to be shown, but even disparaged it when others practiced it.

This is the man who was clothed in purple and fine linen [Col. 0535B].

What is this, rich man? Did fine linen not protect you from the heat? Does purple not resist hell? Those things remained behind; those things abandoned you. Now you sweat, burn, and seethe naked—you who once mocked the heat while clothed in an elaborate nakedness [Note: [Col. 0535D] The Author is speaking here about a garment of fine linen, which is a very delicate kind of linen from which extremely fine clothing is made. It does not cause heat for the body of the wearer but rather reduces it. From Mita.].

> “And send Lazarus, so that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and refresh my tongue.”

What is this, rich man? Where are the streams from your winepresses? Where are the granaries, expanded for the hunger of the poor no less by your desires than by your supplies? Where are the wines preserved for the poverty of the poor through long years and the very oblivion of time [Note: [Col. 0535D] See Law 113 of the Theodosian Code, *On Decurions*: “to protect oneself by age.” In the final law of the same Code, *On the Estates of Shipowners*: “the course of aging.” Peter of Celle, Book IX, Letter 5: “Our reed pen, shaken by age and disuse.”]?

Where are the outpourings, spillages, and rivers of your tableware [Note: [Col. 0535D] Pignorius notes, p. 101, that servants are sometimes called *ministeria*. Seneca, *On Benefits*, Book III, ch. 18; and among Latin and French writers, a household servant is *ministerialis*. Sometimes, too, by *ministerium* are understood all the silver vessels necessary for laying out a dining room. Paulinus of Nola calls the sacred vessels the “splendor of the sacred service.”]?

All these things have perished for you—not as a matter of guilt, though you thirst for a drop from the tip of a finger which, had you given even that alone to the poor man, you would not now thirst for.

The drop and the crumb made you merciless and inhuman, [Col. 0535C] though in them the poor man’s entire food and life consist.

I should like to know, rich man, whether, even while placed in punishment, you forgive yourself for this: you would not have come to these evils if, from such vast granaries, you had then given a crumb, and from such vast winepresses, a drop.

It is little enough that the flesh needs, that nature demands, that suffices for life. Greed is the reason why a person stores up great and many things—not for himself but for others, for his own evident torment, whether present or future.

But you say, rich man: “Even if I denied wine, I ask for water, which the author of all things himself has provided in common for every living creature, and which nature has provided.”

I think, rich man, that you also denied water to the poor man, for you placed before the door as many dogs as possible, so that he could neither enter your house nor reach your well [Note: [Col. 0536D] A dog was sometimes the companion of the doorkeeper servants. Plautus, *Mistel.*: “Tranio, drive the dog; remove the burned torch from the doors.” There were also people who kept a painted dog near the door, as Trimalchio did in Petronius. Seneca, *On Anger*, Book IV, called these “chain-dogs.” Pignorius rightly becomes angry at the ignorance of our painters, who depict Lazarus lying on the ground in the rich man’s very dining room: surely the doorkeepers would have admitted a man swarming with sores, and would themselves have paid on their backs whatever offended their masters’ eyes.].

But what is it that you say?

> “Send Lazarus so that he may dip the tip of his finger in water,”

and not bring the water? Then the water is nearby. And if it is nearby, why do you not take it from close at hand? Why? Because your hands are bound, rich man, by what you deserve, since you scorned to assist Lazarus when his hands had been loosened by weakness.

A person ought—ought—to divide his limbs among the weak. When Job did not merely give his limbs but returned them, he said:

> “I was the eyes of the blind, and the feet of the lame; I was a father to the weak” (Job 29, according to the Septuagint).

Human being, if you do not have a coin, give the poor man your hand, for the greater act of mercy is performed by the one who leads the disabled poor man to his table by the hand.
