He gave himself to the poor man who adapted himself to the service of the poor man and fitted himself for the poor man’s servitude.

Again, brothers, let us postpone the fullness of the present discourse, so that at a third hearing we may declare what sentence the rich man received from the most blessed Abraham [Col. 0536B].

## SERMON CXXIII. On the Same Subject
It is characteristic of a shameless debtor either to postpone what he has borrowed or to deny what he has promised; it is characteristic of an honorable man to pay both without delay and at once. We promised to render everything that remains concerning that rich man who, although he appeared pitiless toward Lazarus, proved still more savage and cruel toward himself. Thus far both the holy evangelist and our sermon, insofar as it could, have explained what the rich man said to Abraham. It was said:

“And lifting up his eyes, when he was in torments, he saw Abraham from afar and, crying out, said: ‘Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, because I am tormented in this flame.’”

[Col. 0536C] Abraham now answered him: “Son, you received good things during your lifetime” (Luke 16).

O marvelous compassion! He still calls him “son,” although he regards him as having degenerated through his own cruelty. O singular goodness! He still calls him “son,” although he saw him as hell’s servant, the offspring of punishments, the lowest slave of Gehenna. Yet he calls him “son” so that the son’s wickedness may be exposed all the more, since even in such a case the tenderness of paternal speech persists.

[Note: MSS Caesena and Vatican: “In such a man even the tenderness of paternal speech …”]

You call him father; [Note: In some printed editions: “I still …”] I call you son, so that you may bitterly grieve that you have lost what you were born to be. I still call you son, so that you may grieve more bitterly that you have lost what grace and nature had given you; for not having something is not as painful as losing what one has possessed. I call you son so that you may understand that what you suffer is a matter of judgment, [Note: Mita extracts a mystical sense and says that what the Jew, signified by the rich man, now suffers is not vengeance taken by Christ but the just judgment of the Godhead: since he refused to teach the Gentile the way of salvation, he himself must learn the way of salvation from a Gentile. He praises this interpretation in Sermon 102 and Sermon 171, though at a considerable distance.] not of rage. [Col. 0537A] I call you son so that in me my patience may remain, and in you your [Note: Elsewhere: “may remain.”] punishment.

But this man, brothers, understands that he is not a son, since he confesses and considers that his having lost what he possessed by nature from such a compassionate father is due to his own merit. He would certainly then have answered concerning his lineage if he had been pious, hospitable, merciful, and humane toward the poor. Whoever does not perform the works of his ancestor denies his lineage, as the Lord teaches: “If you were Abraham’s children, you would do the works of Abraham” (John 8). He proves the faith of his lineage who stands forth as the defender of his father’s work.

[Note: The passage has been restored from the Caesena manuscript.]

But what does Abraham say? “Son, you received good things during your lifetime.”

If this is the only crime of this rich man—that he received good things—how guilty is one who seizes what is not owed to him? If the one who shuts up his possessions and does not distribute what he has received is so criminal, how punishable is the man who both hoards his own goods and invades those belonging to others?

[Note: According to the various meanings of the verb *recipere* (“to receive”), the Author’s intended meanings are explained differently. Here I interpret *recepisti* as “you concealed,” in accordance with the final clause of the law concerning property made by the emperors Valens and Valentinian, from which there are the offenses of “receivers”—namely, those who take in thieves, robbers, and other malefactors in order to conceal them, as in the Digest, *On Receivers*, and the Code, *Concerning Those Who Receive Robbers*, and in the Canon *Sicut ait*, concerning heretics. Thus “you received good things during your lifetime” amounts to saying: “You reserved good things for yourself and your wicked uses, concealing them from others.” MITA.—Whether this is more ingenious or more truthful, let others decide. Here ἀπέλαβες signifies not merely “you received” but “you received fully.”]

[Col. 0537B] Brothers, let us give away what is ours—if indeed it is ours. Let us nevertheless give what we think is ours; let us avoid what belongs to others and shun what is foreign to us. Certainly, if we have taken anything from anyone, let us return it with all speed, lest, leaving everything behind here, we arrive there poor in possessions but rich in guilt, and so come before that rich man.

Yet let the rich man learn that he “received” good things, not that he “accepted” them.

[Note: “He received,” that is, he possessed good things so that he might return them to the Lord with interest or distribute them to the poor. “To accept,” however, means to have something from someone gratuitously, or to claim as one’s own what belongs to oneself. The rich man possessed good things because the Lord bestowed them, not because the Lord was returning them. From Mita.]

You see, brothers, how by Abraham’s holy words the mind of this rich man is exposed, his understanding accused, and his intellect punished: he believed that whatever he possessed through the Lord’s generosity had not been given to him but returned to him. Understand what kind of disposition he had and with what heart he lived, since he believed that God was his debtor, and, being wickedly rich, made his lord subject to his own usuries—ignorant that although the Lord came as a poor man on earth, he ascended rich into heaven.

And he gave, rather than received, at interest: to one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one. Hence he promises that he will demand, not repay, the interest, when he says to the servant: “You wicked and lazy servant, you should have given my money to the money-changers, and I, on coming, would certainly have demanded it with interest” (Matthew 25).

[Col. 0537C] This rich man was still more impious because he did not prove kind toward another. Even if he received good things, he received good things not in return for good deeds but, undeserving, in return for evil deeds.

But let us turn to Lazarus and ask what it means when he says: “And Lazarus likewise received evil things.” Let that alone suffice for merit and abound for glory: that he did not do good things but received evil things. Truly blessed, brothers, is the man who faithfully believes that he receives good things from God and evil things [Note: That is: while a just man is oppressed by evils, he faithfully believes that he is being oppressed by God, as a most loving son is oppressed by his father.] from God.

Blessed is the one who always repays what he owes to God; certainly, if he cannot repay, let him ask with complete humility that his debts be forgiven, the Lord himself teaching thus: “Say: Forgive us our debts” (Matthew 6).

Blessed is the one who repays his debts to God even when he does not understand that he incurred them, as the prophet teaches more profoundly when he says: “Then I paid back what I had not taken” (Psalm 68).

Blessed is the one who, in order always to excuse himself before God, accuses himself, as Scripture admonishes in these words: “The just man is his own accuser at the beginning of his speech” (Proverbs 18, according to the Septuagint).

And if he is just, why does the just man accuse himself? Because “no living person will be justified in your sight” (Psalm 42). A man may perhaps boast before another man of his justice, innocence, and merit; but before God, the man who boasts of his innocence and exalts himself over his justice is no man.

Hence that Pharisee, when he does not pray but counts, charges himself with, and belches forth his own acts of justice, departs unjust and worse than the publican [Col. 0538B] (Luke 18).

But let us approach what remains.

“Now,” he says, “this man is comforted, but you are tormented.” Observe, brothers; understand, brothers, from what has been said, that although the just and the unjust were distinguished by their locations, one region of hell still contained them both; and although a great chasm already separated them, a heavenly dwelling did not yet separate them; and although a grievous gulf divided them, the height appointed for the angels did not yet exist above them.

[Note: Elsewhere we have discussed these passages, on which Chrysologus has spoken, in accordance with the mind of the holy Fathers.]

[Note: The Vulgate has *flammeum gladium* (“a flaming sword”) in place of *flamma*, the flame being formed in the shape of a sword.]

“A flaming sword” (as the lawgiver reports) “was turned about at the gate of paradise” (Genesis 3), so that access there might not be open to man.

[Note: Origen agrees with this in his *Commentary on 1 Kings*, book 18, Huet’s edition, p. 36, where he teaches that our condition is more fortunate than that of those who lived before Christ, since none of them was granted passage beyond the place where the tree of life stood or passage through the flaming sword.]

The gates of hell were shut and barred with bronze doors and iron bolts, so that no exit might be open to the souls that had been hurled there from above. For the bond of the ancestral debt, which subjected each person to death, was held written in the stylus of guilt and the ink of that very liability; and a heavy interest continued to accrue over the generations toward the guilt of the offspring.

Nor was there anyone capable of entering paradise, extinguishing the divinely instituted flame, opening the gates of hell barred from heaven, or dissolving the bond that, by God’s command, was held enclosed in the legal archive.

This is why the Lord himself, the exile of the first man—that is, of the rebellious servant—came. The Lord himself, who had barred paradise and closed hell, descended to earth and to the lower regions with complete authority, so that he might extinguish what had been kindled, immediately open what had been closed, and wipe away the crime of the first-created man.

This is why, as he approaches hell, he bears the ram of his cross, so that he may crush and break the very gates of Tartarus, fortified with bronze and iron. From his side he pours water, so that he may temper the way to paradise, extinguish the fire of hell on the side of the saints, wash away the entire bond of debt, and dissolve the ancient bond; and by enduring this, he himself may forgive what he himself brought upon us by taking it upon himself.

[Col. 0538D] Recognize this, brothers; rejoice, brothers: after Christ’s triumph, the guardianship of the saints has been dissolved, and nothing further is owed by the saints to hell, since Christ penetrated even to the lower regions in order to release the just, not the unjust.

Let us understand, brothers, how much Christ accomplished—or rather, how there could have been no salvation at all without Christ, since, apart from the release of their bodies, the souls of the saints too were held bound in the lower regions.

Blessed, therefore, is Lazarus, who owed everything to God so that he owed nothing to guilt. Blessed is he because here he received so many evils that there he might possess every good.

And Abraham added, saying: “Neither can anyone pass from here to you, nor cross over from there to here.”

This utterance terrifies, brothers; its hearing terrifies greatly, since it shows that after death those assigned once and for all to a penal custody in the lower regions cannot be transferred to the rest of the saints, unless, already redeemed by Christ’s grace, they are released from this despair through the intercession of the holy Church—so that what the sentence denies, the Church may obtain, and grace may provide.

[Note: Mita thinks that Chrysologus is speaking here of the limbo of the holy Fathers, in which the Fathers were detained as punishment for original sin and from which they could be released only through Christ’s death.]

Yet this rich man still asks and says: “Father Abraham.” He still calls him father, although by his merits he has lost both father and fatherland in this way.

“Father Abraham, send him into my father’s house.” If he truly calls this man “father,” whose father’s house belonging to another does he then seek? Unless perhaps he thinks that he has as father in his absence the one whom he sees that he has lost in the present; and thus he believes that the house of that father is being guarded for him by the grace of the one whose bosom he sees denied to him there and whose rest he sees refused to him.

“Father Abraham, send him.” Whom? Lazarus, of course. Where? “Into my father’s house.” Now, and too late, the rich man—no longer merciful but pitiable—invites Lazarus to his father’s house, though throughout the whole period of his wealth he did not receive him as he lay at his gates; and under the appearance of piety he wants Lazarus to return to his former wounds and former groans, although he could not, by his first request, summon him to his own sufferings.

Before he said: “Send him to me.” Now he says: “Send him to my brothers.” He grieves and acts, the wretched man, lest he see fortunate the one whom he had once thought unfortunate. “Send him to my brothers.” Where? “Into my father’s house.” For what purpose? “For I have,” he says, “five brothers, so that he may testify to them, lest they too come to this place of torment.”

Who is compassionate toward others when he was so impious toward himself? Shamelessly he presumes to obtain repentance for others, though he made no provision for his own forgiveness with such cruelty.

“Send Lazarus into my father’s house, for I have five brothers.” And do you think that Lazarus will be sufficient for your five brothers, although he accomplished nothing for you through so long a time, with so many wounds of his, and with his whole body crying out?

Abraham rightly answered him: “They have Moses and the prophets; let them listen to them.” Leave Lazarus to rest after such great labors, and weep over your own punishments, which you endure because of your own merit.

God long ago provided salvation for your brothers and for everyone—not according to your advice but according to his own gift: through Moses he gave the law, through Elijah he bestowed prophecy. Let them listen to them, therefore, so that they may not experience your torments.

The rich man replied: “No, Father Abraham; but if someone rises from the dead, they will believe him.”

Abraham answered him: “If they do not believe Moses and Elijah, they will not believe even if someone rises from the dead.”

Nothing could be truer, brothers. The man who refused to believe Christ speaking from heaven through the law and coming from heaven will now not deserve to believe one returning from the lower regions.

[Note: MSS Caesena and Vallicella: “Nor will he believe Lazarus returning from the lower regions.”]

Christ himself, brothers, our God and Lord, spoke to Moses from heaven; he himself spoke on earth in an earthly body; he himself returned from the lower regions with an earthly body. And yet the brothers of that rich man—understood as those among the Jewish people—utterly refused to believe him when he reported what good things are in heaven and what evils exist in the lower regions.

But, brothers, since the time available does not permit us now to say who the rich man is, or who the poor Lazarus is, or who the rich man’s five brothers are, nor to reveal what spiritual understanding lies hidden in this story, let us, instructed by Christ concerning what awaits the just with him and what awaits the unjust in the lower regions, pursue and hasten toward the word, the work, and mercy, so that we may both grasp the good things above and, terrified by the evils, be able to avoid and shun them.

## SERMON CXXIV. On the Same Subject

Whenever God presents before us a rich man dressed in purple, whenever he places before us a poor man covered with wounds, so often is the arena (*σκάμμα*) of mercy opened to us, [Note: That is, the open place in which mercy may run. In the Greek-Latin Glossary *scamma* is rendered “a dug place” or “pit”; hence Mita, not implausibly, takes it as the arena of games, as do other editions: the central place where athletes wrestled, either because it resembled a slightly sunken pit or because among the Greeks it was customarily encircled by a ditch, as the Roman arena was by a Euripus. In Chrysostom, Homily 55, vol. V, Paris edition, p. 738, *scammata* are the limits or termini of a racecourse: “He made men angels, called them to hope for heavenly things, and extended the courses farther.” The translator less aptly renders this, “he set longer contests,” though I do not deny that in Chrysostom himself, Homily 1 to the people of Antioch, vol. VI, p. 458, in Isidore of Pelusium, and in others, *scamma* also means a contest. See the notes on Sermon 33.] so often is the course of piety laid before us, so that from this heavenly spectacle we may observe how, in a brief space of time, however poor he may be, the poor man reaches the prize, while the rich man comes to ruin.

The man, he says, “was rich, and he was dressed in purple and fine linen, and he feasted splendidly every day. And there was a certain beggar named Lazarus, who lay at his gate, desiring to be filled with the crumbs that fell from the rich man’s table” (Luke 16).

The rich man was dressed in purple, the poor man in lividness; the rich man in fine linen, the poor man in filth; the rich man in gold, the poor man in stench; [Col. 0540D] the rich man reclined on a feather-filled couch at a sigma-shaped dining couch, while the poor man lay on the hardest earth; the rich man belched up his feasts, while the poor man panted from his sores; the rich man poured out wines, the poor man tears; the satiated rich man threw away loaves, while the hungry poor man had not even crumbs; the rich man fed the barking dogs on his dishes while they harassed the poor man, and the poor man filled the rich man’s dogs with his wounds.

And, not to say more, we have read that all good things came to the rich man and all evils to the poor man; nevertheless adversity did not break the poor man, nor did prosperity in every form benefit the rich man. Rather, poverty advanced the poor man toward philosophy, pain toward virtue, contempt toward patience, necessity toward willingness, hunger toward fasting, thirst toward endurance, death toward life, punishment toward reward, earth toward heaven, and deprivation toward the kingdom.

And purple lifted the rich man toward pride, fine linen toward luxury, abundance toward inhumanity, plenty toward impiety, perfumes toward languor, splendor toward blindness, and exaltedness toward ruin.

Thus neither prosperity raises the lazy nor adversity casts down the strong, because neither riches nor poverty—but the mind—leads the grateful to reward or brings the ungrateful to punishment.

A poor man full of sores is placed at the rich man’s gate. This does not happen by human chance; it happens by divine judgment, so that the conflict between rich and poor might be on earth, while the spectacle remained in heaven.

The rich man stood fully clothed in the armor of riches, whereas the poor man lay clothed only in his flesh—unless, perhaps, his coat of mail was the single wound covering his whole body.

The rich man lingered amid choirs of servants, while the poor man, stripped of his skin, was driven on by the goads of his sufferings.

[Note: From Latinius.]

The rich man hurled the weapons of impiety; Lazarus opposed the shield of compassion. The rich man thrust his cruelty into the poor man’s wound; the poor man’s strength frustrated the rich man’s guilty soul, because, as his body failed him, he migrated wholly into his soul, and, with the flesh trampled down, the heavenly warrior ascended wholly in spirit, so that the rich man’s cruelty might find no place where it could strike.

[Note: From Latinius’s emendation; all printed editions corruptly read “to endure” (*ferre*).]

[Note: Latinius judged the passage corrupt and incomplete. It is now restored from the Caesena manuscript and Mita’s edition.]

For this reason God had arranged that the rich man and the poor man should always be before each other’s eyes, so that each might in turn care for the other’s different affliction. The poor man was sick in body; the rich man in mind.

This is why the poor man’s healing was delayed, so that the rich man might receive medicine from his wound, compunction from his groaning, repentance from his tears, an example from his patience, mercy from his hunger, and understanding from his thirst—in sum, a heavenly fellowship through earthly compassion. Certainly, the purpose was that, supported by such great blessings, the rich man might be pleasing to God, since the poor man, though surrounded by every evil, remained pleasing to God before the rich man’s eyes.

He was therefore rightly carried by angels, though he had lain there; he who had mourned was comforted in Abraham’s bosom; and he who did not even know how to live for himself in the world lives always for God.

“It came to pass,” he says, “that the poor man died and was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom. But the rich man died and was buried in hell.”

The wretched man received the burial of his soul before that of his body, and was delivered to a penal tomb before his body was delivered to rest, so that he might live forever in punishment, although he had died once to life.

“And he was buried in hell; and he saw Abraham from afar, and Lazarus in his bosom.”

What a transformation of circumstances! To what depths did the rich man descend! To what heights did the poor man ascend! There the rich man looks upward upon the one whom here below he had despised, and from hell sees him in Abraham’s bosom—the man whom, as he lay before the proud man’s couch, he had not seen.

“Father Abraham, have mercy on me.”

Foolishly he asks mercy from the father whom he had denied to his brother. “Have mercy on me.” What has he to do with mercy, since everything has now turned to punishment for him? Or what supplication before the father can help him when the accuser sits in the father’s bosom? Lazarus holds the father’s breast and beats upon the whole justice of his holy heart, so that he may preserve himself as the father of the good son and the judge of the evil one.

“Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, because I am tormented in this flame.”

“Send Lazarus”—so that the very man who is the cause of my torment may now himself offer the tip of his finger as a minister of refreshment, extending a small comfort to the one to whom I once denied the comfort of my whole hand while he lay there.

“And send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue.” Thus the man who, when the poor man thirsted, poured out lakes of wine now thirsts for a drop; and he believes that the tip of a finger can extinguish the flames of Gehenna, although he did not extinguish the fires of drunkenness with measures of wine throughout the day.

But he asks that this drop be given him for refreshment, for the heat of the poor man whom he had denied. This drop, rich man, is what makes you cruel; this drop is what dried Lazarus’s mouth because you denied it to him. For the refreshment of the body, both a drop and a crumb are sufficient.

“Desiring,” he says, “to be filled with the crumbs that fell from the table.” Bread was scattered, wine was poured out, and what was denied to the poor man for the preservation of his life was squandered by the rich man entirely for display.

“And send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue.”

The tongue is in the head, and the head is the source of evil. The tongue itself disparages the needy, insults the poor, barks against piety, and tears at mercy. It is therefore rightly first in Gehenna, the forerunner in torment, the leader of punishments, because it forbade mercy, although it had been given the power to command.

And although the sequence of the reading compels me to say, and invites you to hear, who the rich man in purple is, who the poor Lazarus is, who the rich man’s five brothers are, and how the rich man experiences the torments of Gehenna before the day of judgment, [Note: Latinius thinks that something is missing here. But the following should be restored: “Nevertheless, grief recalls me to say: ‘The rich man died and was buried in hell,’” which is absent from many printed editions.] nevertheless grief recalls me to say: “The rich man died and was buried in hell.”

[Col. 0542D] And if there is a prison beneath the earth, if there is a burning καῦσις [*kausis*, “combustion” or “burning”], if there is a lower region tormenting without end, if there is a sorrowful attendant [Note: Latinius reads *apparitor instans* (“an attendant pressing on”); corrupt editions have *apparitor istis*. In an older usage *apparitores* were called *limocincti* (“girded with an apron”): an ancient inscription reads, “Attendants and apron-girded men.” Here Chrysologus understands the attendant as death.] who will drag us there after the labors of this age, why are we amazed? Where are we? What is this sleep that deceives us? What is this deadly forgetfulness that holds us? Why is our sole concern not to escape such evils, after despising everything else, lest, while we live for the world and run after other things, we should suddenly be dragged to such great, such dreadful, such cruel punishments?

And if there is a possibility of ascending to the heights, if there is an opportunity to live among heavenly things, if Abraham’s bosom is prepared for the rest of all good people, if Lazarus is in the bosom of so great a father—indeed, since there is no doubt when places, persons, and names are described—why do we not exchange earth for heaven? Why do we not purchase eternal things with things that pass away? Why do we not acquire what endures in exchange for what perishes? Then we shall both avoid the punishments of hell and be able to see openly, possess, and hold what we now long to hear only obscurely.

## SERMON CXXV. On the Unjust Steward

Salt is indeed a wholesome seasoning for every food, provided that measure is not lacking; otherwise, without moderation, both salt itself perishes and what it has salted is spoiled. [Note: Theophylact, on Colossians 4:6: “Food without salt is unpleasant; but if it is too salty, it is altogether disagreeable to the taste.”] Excess makes bitter what moderation could have seasoned.

So too the understanding within us, if it keeps to moderation, gives flavor, produces intelligence, generates prudence, enlarges the heart, increases talent, ripens what is to be said, arranges what is to be heard, and becomes sweet to itself; to those who taste it, it becomes the fullness of every sweetness. Indeed, that understanding will be honeyed which utters nothing bitter with its mouth.

We have prefaced this so that our understanding may be restrained by a measure appropriate to evangelical meanings, so that it may not violate the life-giving food, the divine nourishment, or the heavenly flavor, but preserve them for us with the utmost cautious sobriety, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “Not to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think with sober judgment” (Romans 12).

But now let us hear what the Lord said: “There was a certain rich man” (Luke 16).

And who was this man except Christ? Who was rich except him, who in our poverty possessed all the riches of creation?

“There was a certain rich man.” He impressed this repeatedly upon the Jews, so that they might understand that the one whose human poverty they saw possessed a wealthy divinity within him.

“He was rich.” He was rich in his majesty, although he was poor in the eyes of the Jews. And how could he not be rich, when angels ministered to him, powers obeyed him, the elements served him, and things that did not exist came into being at his command and appeared when called?

“There was a certain rich man, and he had a steward.” Whom could this mean except man, to whom the entire possession of the world had been entrusted for cultivation?

[Note: There were two kinds of stewards. Some were sent to estates to preside over the other servants; Varro, book 1 of *On Agriculture*, chapter 13, and Columella, book 1, chapter 6, prescribe that their dwelling be established near the entrance of the estate. But they were also administrators of the entire household, called in Greek οἰκονόμοι (*oikonomoi*) and in Latin *actores*, as in the Digest, *On the Family*, book 40, section 7, *On the Status of Persons*. Leonidas in Plautus, *Asinaria* 2.4.53, pretended to be such a man. Others were assigned to estates to command the rest as deputies of their masters and to cultivate the land; these too were called *actores*, as in book 3 of the Digest, *On Pledges*. Chrysologus thought that the steward described by Luke belonged among the latter, since he compares him to a man to whom he says possession of the whole world had been entrusted. Cicero called magistrates of the state *villici*, and Arnobius, book 3 *Against the Pagans*, calls some deity a minister and steward of Jupiter.]

“There was a certain rich man, and he had a steward; and this man was denounced to him.”

[Note: This is a *catachresis*, for the denunciation was neither false nor defamatory but true. From this Calmet infers that this evangelical steward, who squandered his master’s goods, was not a farm steward but the administrator of a great household, with whom the accounts of receipts and disbursements were kept.]

As though he had not known beforehand, as though he had not foreseen it—the one to whom hidden things are known, before whose eyes even what is concealed lies naked.

“And this man was denounced to him.” Did he therefore believe the report? Did he learn it because rumor announced it? Far from it. But because the things he knew and had veiled with mercy, he then began to seek when the earth accused them: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to me from the ground” (Genesis 4). The earth cried out, heaven cried out, the angels grieved, when the whole report of the age was already speaking.

“And he was denounced to him as having squandered his substance.” The younger son was previously read as having squandered his substance; now the steward is said to have squandered his master’s goods. Just as Christ is the same God and man, the same father of the household and father, so it is clear that this same person is both steward and son. There is a diversity of circumstances and a change of names, but no difference of persons.

“And he was denounced to him as having squandered his goods, and he called him.” He called him through the Gospel. “And he said to him.” And what does he not do through the Gospel, by which he reproves conduct, uncovers hidden things, lays bare the conscience, chastises offenses, counts up evils, and [Note: Latinius corrected the corrupt printed editions, which read “presiding” (*praesistenti*).] threatens punishment to those who persist in them, although he promises forgiveness to the converted?

“And he called him, and said to him: ‘What is this I hear about you?’”

He charges him with things known as though they had merely been heard, because he does not wish to hasten the sentence against the accused. He summons the man convicted in his own presence as though he were merely accused, since he desires judgment to be preceded in this way by pardon.

“What is this I hear about you? Give an account of your stewardship, for you will no longer be able to be steward.”

Why does he join such severity to such compassion? Why does he remove him from stewardship before he has learned the account?

“Give an account; for you will no longer be able to be steward.” He demands an account now as man, but as God he announces what is imminent and what is to come. “Give an account; for you will no longer be able to be steward.” He asks for an account, not in order to exact payment but to grant release; he asks so that he may himself be asked; he asks here so that he may not ask you; he asks in this world so that he may not ask in judgment; he asks quickly so that the time of punishment may not exclude the time for satisfaction.

“Give an account of your stewardship; for you will no longer be able to be steward.” Why? Because the end of life has come, the time of death; heavenly summons already constrains you, and judgment already calls. Hurry, therefore, lest you lose the time for satisfaction, you who have lost the time for action.

“Give an account.” This means: Set your account in order; set your affairs in order, so that you may not have to repay what belongs to me. You will set them in order if you now cease to squander.

I took your earlier debts upon myself when I took you upon myself; I paid them when I absolved you; I stood as your advocate, to be heard before the advocate; I entered judgment as judge; I became a defendant for my defendant; I accepted punishment from those subject to punishment; I did not shrink from the sentence of the condemned; I, the destroyer of death, accepted death; I penetrated hell as the destroyer of hell, so that through these things I might not merely withdraw you from your punishment but also make you a participant in my dignity.

Therefore act, so that the eternity of my [Note: Thus in the Caesena and Vatican manuscripts; the printed editions read: “of my donation.”] condemnation may not enclose you whom the time of your stewardship has excluded.

But let us now examine what the steward answered.

He said within himself: “What shall I do? What shall I do now?” A man always desires to do good only when death has taken away the time for doing it.

“He said within himself.” He seeks counsel within himself, since outside himself he had no means by which he could now be helped.

“He said within himself.” He pricks his heart, goads his mind, and troubles all his inward parts, so that he may wring from himself the repentance he can offer on his own behalf.

“I cannot dig.” It was not strength but time that had failed him for labor.

“I cannot dig; I am ashamed to beg.” He fears the confusion of the future judgment, in which there is no longer a time for repentance but only for punishment, and where the accused is more ashamed of his conscience than of the fire of Gehenna.

“I am ashamed to beg.”

[Note: The Christian is so richly supplied with heavenly goods in the Church militant that he has no need to seek from elsewhere, for “glory and riches are in his house.” See how wrongly those act who, abandoning the sacred Scriptures and the teachings of the Fathers in their sacred sermons, search through all sorts of profane authors in order to extract from their sayings concepts that tickle itching ears and proclaim pleasing things to the people. MITA.]

And who is not ashamed to beg among heavenly things? Wretched is the man whom temporal life possessed as rich, but whom eternity will possess as a beggar. Tartarus will have him naked, although heaven could have received and retained him as wealthy.

The present figure points toward the people, but it is good for us—very good—if we apply these things individually to ourselves, if we refer them to ourselves, since on earth we ought to recognize ourselves as stewards, [Note: The Caesena manuscript: “to regard ourselves not as masters.”] not think of ourselves as masters; to understand that we have received the ministry of a temporary extension, not acquired a perpetual right of possession; to take care lest the report of a ruined estate precede us to the father of the household, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “The sins of some people are manifest, going before them to judgment, but the sins of others follow them” (1 Timothy 5).

He does not reach the appointed term of life who loses the time of his stewardship, once it has been announced that he has squandered what was entrusted to him. Hence comes premature departure; hence death before its day; hence a bitter summons; hence a return more bitter than itself, as the prophet laments, crying out: “Men of blood and deceit shall not halve their days” (Psalm 54).

Would that, when sickness warns us of our summons, when fever harshly excludes us from our stewardship, when the force of pain compels us to hasten toward rendering an account of our stewardship, we might follow the deed and disposition of the present steward! May we turn to the soul’s counsel, to compunction of heart, to repentance of mind, to the aid of mercy, to the protection of piety, and to the advocacy of confession.

Certainly we would ask for the Lord’s bonds of debt, [Note: The Vulgate has *cautionem*, “bond” or “security.” Jurists use the term in this way, as the Greeks use *syngraphē* or *chirographon*.] and, if not all of them, at least half, like this steward, we would discharge for our own forgiveness. Thus, although we are called stewards of iniquity because we squander the goods entrusted to us, at the end, through a pious fraud, we might obtain the praise of the judge himself.

“And he praised,” it says, “the steward of iniquity.”

And because the steward’s evangelical action gives rise to no small question—since he is guilty of many things yet is said to have pleased his master by means of one fraud—we shall reveal more fully in the following sermon, with God’s help, why he pleased him in this way and who this man was.

## SERMON CXXVI. On the Same Subject
How useful, how profitable it is to loosen the knots of debts and slacken the bonds of written acknowledgments, the example of the present steward teaches and instructs us. While he prudently regulates the heaps of promissory notes [Note: From Mita. Elsewhere: “pious.”], he not only escaped the tightest straits of examination [Note: From the same source. Elsewhere: “most certain.”], but also acquired enduring praise from the examiner for generations. [Note: See the preceding note. Tertullian and Salvian use this kind of expression in the same sense.]

And we, brothers, since I owe you what my promise concerning the present reading made [Note: Cesena manuscript: “I acknowledge that I promised.”], receive it with devout attention, lest a strict examination burden both you and me together—those whom understanding can graciously relieve. Let us therefore now follow what remains of the reading and hear what plan the steward discovered.

“He said within himself: ‘What shall I do, because my master is taking the stewardship away from me? I am unable to dig; I am ashamed to beg. I know what I shall do . . .’ And summoning each of his master’s debtors, he said to the first: ‘How much do you owe my master?’ He replied: ‘A hundred measures of oil.’ He said to him: ‘Take your bond; sit down quickly and write fifty.’ Then he said to another: ‘But you, how much do you owe?’ He replied: ‘A hundred measures of wheat.’ And he said to him: ‘Take your written acknowledgment and write eighty.’ And the master praised the unjust steward because he had acted prudently” (Luke 16).

It is now clear that the Gospel readings, obscured by divine mysteries and veiled in heavenly meanings, contain very many questions, and that what is uttered by Christ’s mouth from heavenly secrets does not easily submit to human understanding. “And the master praised,” it says, “the unjust steward because he had acted prudently.”

I ask: what does a worldly mind grasp in this passage? What does ordinary hearing understand and accept here, where the clever invention of fraud is praised between the steward and the master’s debtors, where the debtor’s honesty is removed, shame taken away, innocence violated, and modesty utterly buried? [Note: The entire force of the comparison lies in this shrewdness or cleverness, not in deceit or the wickedness of the act. Thus Genesis 3, according to the Septuagint, calls the serpent “most prudent”: it means not prudence as a virtue, but cunning. Origen—or rather Geometer, as Corderius observes in the *Catena of the Greek Fathers*—adds that it is remarkable for the resourcefulness and acuteness by which vigor of mind is elicited.] The steward, at the moment when he had to render an account, burns more eagerly for fraud than, during his stewardship, he had panted for luxury; at the moment of examination he inflicts more loss upon his master than he had poured out and squandered during the days of his administration; and he who had previously emptied the property by dissipating it now overturns still more by reducing what remained in the bond. He does not care where he might make good what was lacking, but devises how he might diminish what remained. [Note: The printed editions and manuscripts read this way. I would restore *velatur* (“is veiled”).]

He said to the debtor: “How much do you owe my master?” He did not say, “How much do you owe me?” By speaking thus, he confronted the man’s conscience and bore witness to the debtor’s mind. And why, without regard for his master, did the steward provoke the debtor to such fraud? “How much do you owe my master?” The man says: “A hundred measures of oil.” “Take your bond and write fifty.”

The steward was conspiring in and carrying out such fraud that he might lose all credit while he was planning precautions for himself. [Note: Cesena manuscript: “the debtor had conspired with the steward in such fraud”; the printed editions read as above. Here *meditabatur cautionem* means that the steward was considering how to safeguard and provide for himself; it is a frequent comic expression. Terence, *Andria*: “it is a precaution that he may not discover that the child is mine by her.”] “How much do you owe my master?” Both knew that the heavenly creditor was present everywhere and always, and could not be forestalled by fraud; yet the one who has once begun to steal does not cease even in the master’s sight.

Still, let it be human custom for the debtor to seek fraudulent advantages and for the steward to look after himself by stealing. Why, then, does the master again approve the fraud? Why does he applaud theft? Why does he praise falsehood? Why does he call wickedness prudence, and judge this to be pious though it offers many a most evil example of falsehood?

Let it have such meaning for carnal senses; for spiritual ones, let what belongs to divine light now shine forth. The parable is repeated through the steward, having previously been foreshadowed through the son. The Gentile people are called the steward of unjust mammon. [Note: *Mammon*, or *mammona*, is a Syriac word meaning “riches.” Since the Punic language arises from Hebrew, *mammona* also means “riches” in Punic. See Augustine, *On the Sermon on the Mount*, book II, chapter 21. Other interpreters hold that *mammon of injustice*, or *unjust mammon*, is a Hebrew expression meaning “mammon of vanity.” For among the Hebrews the same word means both “vanity” and “injustice.” See Natalis Alexander, Calmet, and others. Consult also Augustine, *Questions on the Gospels*, book I, question 34; Ambrose, book VI on Luke, at the final chapter; Theophylact on this passage, and so forth.]

“Make friends for yourselves,” he says, “from unjust mammon”—the people who, having abandoned the Creator, had surrendered themselves wholly to mammon’s slavery. Whoever is free from captivity to this mammon and is no longer weighed down by the cruel burden of money should stand upon the heavenly watchtower and from there look down upon mammon, ruling the world and worldly things with tyrannical fury.

It commands the nations, orders kingdoms, directs wars, equips warriors, sells blood, causes deaths, betrays homelands, destroys cities, subjugates peoples, assaults citadels, harasses citizens, presides over the marketplace, abolishes law, confounds right and wrong; and by pressing on even to death, it tests faith, violates truth, tears apart reputation, dissipates honor, dissolves affections, removes innocence, buries piety, severs family ties, and undermines friendship. And what more need be said? This is mammon, the lord of injustice, which unjustly rules both human bodies and human minds.

The steward of this mammon, that is, the Gentile people, guilty of having dissipated such property, is therefore summoned by the Lord through the Gospel to render an account of his stewardship—that is, of his natural good. Then it is said to him: “You can no longer be steward,” when the end of the world is announced to him. For he believes, in accordance with the Apostle, that “the form of this world is passing away” (1 Corinthians 7), and that the times of human stewardship are passing. Then, returning within himself, he asks what he ought to do.

He says within himself: “What shall I do?” His heart groaned, his mind grieved, faith answered, and belief offered saving counsel: that the steward should now return to the true master, and that by distributing mammon he should subjugate the cruel master, victoriously, to his own service, so that what had been an instrument of destruction might become an occasion of salvation. [Note: On this subject see Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, book IV, and Ambrose, book VII, no. 245. Salvian has much more, and of notable quality, on avarice in book I.]

The Gentile steward, once Gentile but now Christian, therefore proceeds to the first debtor of his master. [Note: Elsewhere: “namely.”] Whom? The Jewish debtor, whom he asks what and how much he owes his master—as though he did not know the measure of the debt. The bearer of the bond already knew it through the Gospel, but by asking he sought a confession in this manner. Finally, the debtor confesses both the kind and the amount of the debt, saying: “A hundred measures of oil.”

Why not a weight of silver or gold? Why not a hundred and ten, or ninety, but a hundred? So that a heavenly mystery might shine forth both from the debt and from the number.

The Jew owed oil, which through the written bond of the Law he had received as a figure for anointing kings, prophets, and priests, until he reached the very chief of kings, prophets, and priests, to whom the whole fullness of the hundredfold anointing had to be returned and poured out. But because the debtor, contrary to the bond’s terms, wickedly killed the creditor so that he would not repay the debt, the very legal bond passed to the Gentiles—that is, the Law—so that the Jew, convicted by the Gentile because he had turned his debt into a crime, might pay the interest through repentance.

You see, therefore, that the steward urges not fraud but repentance; he presses the debtor to obtain mercy, not to commit falsehood, when he says: “Take your bond, sit down quickly, and write fifty.”

David reveals that the number fifty pertains to mercy when he sings the fiftieth psalm, crying out: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy” (Psalm 50). The number fifty disclosed mercy when the Law prescribed that the fiftieth year, which is the jubilee, should erase and release the bonds of all debts and all contracts (Leviticus 25).

This steward therefore acts so that, through Christ’s mercy, the Jew may become capable of discharging the debt, though he had been held fast by the bond of the Law amid debts that could not be paid. The Jew owes oil: according to the Apostle (Romans 11), he had dried up within himself the richness of the fruitful olive through the barrenness of unbelief. Hence, warmed by the faith of the Gospel, he now wholly returns into Christian branches [Note: From the manuscript of Cesena. The printed editions read: “grows into the branches: entirely to the Christian,” and so forth.] and revives wholly into grace.

Then he said to another: “But you, how much do you owe?” He replied: “A hundred measures of wheat.”

After the grain of wheat, which is Christ, had been sown in the soil of our flesh and had been brought to heavenly fruitfulness through the Lord’s burial, it came about that a human being owed his Creator the hundredfold fruit. “Unless the grain of wheat, falling into the earth, dies, it remains alone” (John 12).

Seeing this, the steward acts with sufficient foresight when he says: “Take your bond and write eighty.” For just as fifty conveys mercy, so eighty prefigures the whole of faith and grace. This is the number in which the reader well acquainted with the Law understands the Decalogue to be present, and the reader devoted to the Gospel understands the ogdoad of grace. Thus, when the steward says, “Write eighty,” he acts so that by grace he may discharge what he could not repay by nature.

The steward therefore deserved his master’s praise, because in the written bonds he contrived not fraud but salvation.

But when he said, “The children of this age are more prudent in their generation than the children of light,” this is to be understood as follows: those who were once children of this age—that is, Gentiles—have now been chosen by God; and those who were children of God—that is, Jews—have now been left among the children of this age. “In their generation”: in the generation in which they were reborn, not in that in which they were born. “Let these things be written,” he says, “in the generation to come” (Psalm 101). This is the other generation, that of those who seek the Lord (Psalm 23).

May the God of knowledge and illumination illuminate your hearts and pour the whole fullness of his knowledge into the secret place of your minds.

[Note: See what is noted in the preface.]

## SERMON CXXVII. On the Beheading of the Blessed John the Baptist

Today, as John’s virtue and Herod’s savagery are recounted to us, our inward parts were shaken, our hearts trembled, our sight grew dim, our understanding was dulled, and our hearing fled. For what remains secure in human faculties when the greatness of crimes has destroyed the greatness of virtues?

“Herod,” it says, “seized John and bound him, and put him in prison” (Matthew 14).

John: a school of virtues, a teacher of life, a model of holiness, a rule of justice, a mirror of virginity, a title of modesty, an example of chastity, a path of repentance, forgiveness of sins, a discipline of faith; John, greater than a human being, equal to the angels, the sum of the Law, the sanction of the Gospel, the voice of the apostles, the silence of the prophets, the lamp of the world, the herald of the Judge, the forerunner of Christ [Note: The Lord’s forerunner or herald. Elsewhere there are several remarks on *metatores* (“path-markers” or surveyors).], the pathfinder of the Lord, God’s witness, the intermediary of the whole Trinity [Note: Mita explains *medius* as “messenger of the Trinity,” because through him, when Christ was baptized in the Jordan, the whole Trinity became known: the Father speaking, the Son receiving testimony, and the Holy Spirit descending in the form of a dove.]—he is handed over to an incestuous woman [Note: All the editions had *datur incestui* (“is given to incest”); Latinius corrected it.] and delivered to an adulteress, consigned to a dancing girl.

No wonder, then, that our inward parts were shaken and our hearts trembled.

But that Herod himself is the one who profaned the temple, abolished the priesthood, confounded order, violated the kingdom, and corrupted everything that belonged to religion, life, law, morals, faith, and discipline—he lost and confounded all of it. [Note: The Herod whose crimes the author enumerates was Herod surnamed the Great, whereas the other Herod was the one who ordered John the Baptist to be beheaded. He was the son of Herod the Great by the Samaritan Malthace, called Antipas, tetrarch of Galilee; Herodias, the daughter of Aristobulus and formerly the wife of his brother Herod Philip, had attached herself to him. Let us not accuse the learned Chrysologus of such extensive ignorance; perhaps he accommodated himself to the minds of the common people, in whom, as soon as the name Herod is heard, the image of that cruel and impious tyrant is immediately aroused.]

Herod was a murderer of citizens, a brigand toward nobles, a plunderer of his allies, a robber toward his household, a slaughterer of the populace, a killer of his sons, a homicide toward strangers, a parricide toward his own people; he drenched the earth in blood and remained athirst for blood.

Hence he absorbed John’s holy blood in the great cup of cruelty. But let the reading itself now speak.

“Herod,” it says, “seized John and bound him.” He who had loosed the bonds of sinners is bound by a sinner’s chains, so that forgiveness, once bound, might leave no place for forgiveness.

“He bound him and put him in prison.” [Note: Some believe—and from these words it is clear that our author must be counted among them—that Herod Philip was still alive when his wife Herodias married Herod Antipas.] Herod, you commit adultery, and John goes to prison? Is this how you judge, sitting as the guilty man in the judge’s place and as the persecutor of innocence in the avenger’s place? I ask: where is the face of justice? Where is reputation? Where is shame? Where is the standing of a public judge? Surely, where is God? Where is humanity? Where is right? Where is the law? Where are the very rights of nature? Through your action, Herod, through your judgment, through your command, all these things have been confused together.

“He seized John, bound him, and put him in prison.” Herod, the cause seeks you; the chains accuse you; the prison indicts you; the wrong done to John and brought into public view exposes you. Whoever seeks the reason for the imprisonment finds in you what must be punished and in John what must be mourned.

John, known throughout the world, renowned for the fame of his virtue, celebrated for his holiness—by drawing to himself those investigating the wrong done to him, he makes your incest known to everyone. [Note: In Herod the adultery was accompanied by the crime of incest, since the Law of Moses prohibited taking one’s brother’s wife, except in the single case where the husband had died childless. Herodias’s husband was still alive when Antipas took her, and she had received from him a daughter, Salome the dancing girl, who is mentioned in the Gospel. Moreover, Herodias had been not only the wife of Herod Philip, the brother—though not of the same mother—of Herod Antipas; she was also the daughter of Aristobulus, whom Herod the Great had fathered by Mariamne, the daughter of Hyrcanus and descended from the Hasmoneans. The Law prohibited marriages not only with a brother’s wife but also with a brother’s daughter (Leviticus 18:14), according to the opinion of many more discerning interpreters, although the matter is not without difficulty.]

He acts so that public disgrace may overwhelm you, whom private correction could not reform.

John attacked Herod with admonitions, not accusation; he wished to correct him, not destroy him. But Herod, burning with the torches of lust, preferred destruction to return, and preferred unlawfully to possess his brother’s wife.

To those captive to crimes, enemies of innocence, freedom is always hateful; virtue is opposed to the vicious; holiness is detested by the sacrilegious; chastity is an enemy to the shameless; integrity is a punishment to the corrupt; frugality is unbearable to the luxurious; mercy to the cruel; piety to the impious; justice to the unjust.

The evangelist proves this when he says: “For John said to him, ‘It is not lawful for you to have your brother Philip’s wife.’” Behold why John offended [Note: Other editions: “incurred.”]; behold why Herod raged: he who warns the wicked gives offense; he who rebukes criminals incurs hatred.

John was saying what belonged to the Law, what belonged to justice, what belonged to salvation—certainly what belonged not to hatred but to love. Behold what reward he received from the impious for his piety.

“Wishing,” it says, “to kill him, he feared the people.” The person who fears human beings rather than God in his affairs easily deviates from justice. Such fear can delay the opportunity for sin, but it cannot remove the will; indeed, it makes those whom it has held back from crime more eager for crime, and the mind burns until it accomplishes the evil it has conceived.

Only the fear of God corrects minds, drives away crimes, preserves innocence, and grants an enduring capacity for goodness.

But let us hear the passion of John himself, most blessed.

“On Herod’s birthday, the daughter of Herodias danced in the middle of the banquet hall and pleased Herod. Therefore he promised with an oath to give her whatever she might ask of him. But she, prompted beforehand by her mother, said: ‘Give me here on a platter the head of John the Baptist.’”

This is the ancient wickedness of woman, which drove Adam from the delights of paradise (Genesis 3); this made heavenly beings earthly; this sent the human race into hell; this took life from the world because of the fruit of a single tree.

This is the evil that leads human beings to death; the prophet Elijah fled from it (1 Kings 19). He whose tongue became a key of heaven [Note: Elijah called down fire from heaven, and rain descended from the clouds at his command; when flames fell from the air, they consumed God’s enemies. Chrysostom, *On Providence*, book III, chapter 12, calls him a heavenly soul who lived on earth as though he were simultaneously in heaven.] fled from the face of a woman as though he were guilty.

This is the evil that discovers true toil and oppression, which now kills John the Baptist, casts down childhood, destroys youth, seduces and disturbs exhausted old age.

“Prompted beforehand by her mother, she said: ‘Give me on a platter the head of John the Baptist.’”

A new beast, roaring from its mother’s breast [Note: Athenaeus, *Deipnosophistae*, book XIII, p. 414: “Of all beasts, no one is more destructive than a prostitute”; and a little earlier: “We may call all prostitutes Theban sphinxes.” From Mita.], disregarding the spoil of the body, advances to sever the head itself.

“And the king was grieved, but because of the oath and the guests reclining at table, he ordered it to be given. He sent and had John beheaded, and his head was brought on a platter, and it was given to the girl, and the girl gave it to her mother.”

You have heard, brothers, how great a cruelty was born from pleasure, how great an impiety from lust. “And his head was brought on a platter.” [Note: Pignorius praises and elucidates this passage of Chrysologus in *On Slaves*.]

The house is turned into an arena, the table migrates into a cage; diners become spectators; fury transforms the banquet; slaughter becomes food; wine turns into blood; an end is imposed upon a birthday; at the moment of birth a death is displayed; a banquet is changed into homicide; musical instruments resound a secular tragedy. [Note: It is called “secular” because it took place every hundred years. In these tragic games a herald announced: “The Roman people will see games such as no one of this age has ever seen or will ever see afterward” (Pliny, book VII, chapter 48). Thus the beheading of John the Baptist was a secular tragedy, because no one of that age had ever seen such a thing, nor would anyone afterward. Mita.—The secular games were not held at Rome every hundred years; rather, they were so called because common usage says that rare events occur only after a century. Ovid, *Tristia* II.25:

“He had ordered it to be proclaimed to Phoebus at the time when he held the games,
which one age sees only once.

Chrysologus calls John’s death a tragedy because tragedies present the mournful deaths not of people of ordinary condition but of illustrious persons. He calls it secular as though it were unheard-of and extraordinary.]

A beast enters, not a girl; it seeks to cut off, not to dance; a wild creature rushes about, not a woman; it scatters a mane over the neck, not hair [Note: Another reading: “over the crown of the head.”]; it spreads its limbs in coils; its savagery grows by degrees; it becomes great through cruelty, not through bodily size. This singular beast roars with its mouth until it seizes its prey and gnashes with its teeth; it does not receive iron but produces it.

But lest anyone think that we wish to declaim about such things, we do not wish to declaim but to cry out, so that the joys of your festivals may be guarded with caution. [Note: The days solemnly celebrated by the ancients are enumerated by Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 40. Among them the principal was the birthday, or *genethlia* (γενέθλια), which was celebrated with excellent and magnificent observance.] Let the solemnity of your birthdays maintain a measure in rejoicing; let Christ be present at our banquets; let us feast in the presence of the Creator; let nature herself, which brought you forth, be honored by the decency of the banquet; let the joy of your table reach the poor; let your household dance in the discipline of innocence; let luxury cease and extravagance be banished. [Note: Chrysologus censures the incitements to vice formerly customary at banquets. Singers were excluded from banquets by a law mentioned by Paul the Deacon, book I, *On Theodosius*, and touched on by Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, book III, chapter 1. Yet this excised luxury—which, Augustine testifies, *City of God*, book III, chapter 21, p. 63, had migrated from Asia to Rome—did not cease to reappear in turns, as Chrysologus here testifies. Sidonius Apollinaris has similar remarks, *Letters*, book I, letter 2, praising the banquets of King Theodoric: “No lyre-player, pipe-player, chorus-leader, female drummer, or female psaltery-player sings there,” etc. On *mesochori* see Pliny, *Letters*, book II, to Maximus.]

Let the plague of dancing girls, the pandering of singers, the fuel of pleasures, the burdens of the belly, and the shipwrecks of minds [Note: Another reading: “of the mind.” A more suitable term could scarcely have been used for drunkenness and its effects. See Hilary, *Tractate on Psalm 125*, p. 459, who says that in a drunk person a kind of death rules while nature remains intact. Basil, on Psalm 134, calls drunkenness “the destruction of reason.” He has much else worthy of reading in Oration 14, p. 489.] be cut away from the banquets of Herodias, so that your present joy may reach everlasting gladness.

Today, brothers, we have brought a sermon not only against Herod but also against Herodias, because the attentive hearer understands well how great is the martyr’s blessedness when he has heard of the persecutor’s misery. Yet we must know that John was born from his death, and Herod died from his birthday.

[Note: At first in the Church, the acts and deeds of martyrs were read amid the prayers of the Mass, in the confessions. They are called prefaces; this is how the passage of Hilduin, abbot of Saint-Denis, is to be understood in the letter prefixed to the *Areopagitics* and addressed to the emperor Louis the Pious, where he says that, during the celebration, the torments of the martyrs were recalled briefly. But since such acts were generally recited in a manner scarcely audible or intelligible to the people, it became customary for bishops to discuss them at greater length.]

## SERMON CXXVIII. On the Blessed Apollinaris, Bishop and Martyr

[Note: He was the first bishop of Ravenna, whom tradition says was a disciple of Saint Peter. You may find more about him in the distinguished Bacchinius, *Life of the Bishops of Ravenna* from Agnellus, volume I, p. 128. See the Florentine Martyrology, p. 667; Surius under 23 July, p. 275; the Bollandists, volume IV of July, 23 July, p. 341; Tillemont, volume II, p. 102; Baillet, on the same day. There is further material about him in the Martyrology of Ado, volume II, p. 349, and in the notes of the learned Georgius. The distinguished Father Sabbatini, in the Neapolitan calendar, observes that Pope Gregory, book VI, letter 61, to Castorius, at the end, p. 538, reports that the people of Ravenna considered it a religious duty not to fail to fulfill whatever they had promised over the body of Saint Apollinaris. Honoratus of Saint Mary, in *Critical Rules*, volume II, p. 66, considers what Chrysologus relates about this saint to be true for the reason that the learned men chosen to correct the Breviary of the Church of Paris judged it wrong to remove this homily. Let others judge how solid the argument is.]

Blessed Apollinaris, first in priesthood, alone [Note: From this it is inferred that, down to Chrysologus’s time, no archbishop of the Church of Ravenna except Saint Apollinaris had suffered martyrdom. This certainly refutes those who, on the basis of certain manuscripts, claimed that Saint Marcian, fourth in the order of the archbishops of Ravenna, had been crowned with martyrdom. Rubeus mentions him in book I of his *History of Ravenna* under the year 127; he does not, however, affirm the claim, and would certainly have denied it if he had considered the present sermon. Mita.—From our author’s words Fabrus and Henschenius also infer, in the *Acta Sanctorum*, 22 May, volume V, p. 127, Antwerp edition of 1685, that Saint Martian, whose memory is celebrated on 6 March and who suffered martyrdom under Trajan, was a different person from Marcian, the bishop of Ravenna. Rubeus, deceived by the similarity of their names, conflated the two. Peter Damian also asserts this in sermon 32 on Saint Apollinaris, no. 3, p. 222, although he lived six hundred years after Chrysologus.] adorned this Church of Ravenna with the native [Note: That is, “suffering at home.” Prudentius uses the expression similarly in the preface to *Psychomachia*. See the passage cited by Bartholomew in *Adversaria*, book XXIX, chapter 9.] and renowned honor of martyrdom.

Apollinaris rightly bears this name because, in accordance with the command of his God, he lost his soul here in order to find it for eternal life. [Note: Perhaps he is referring to the etymology of the name: *Apollou* (Ἀπόλλου), “I destroy.”]

Blessed is the man who so completed his course and kept the faith that he was truly found first among believers in his own place.

Let no one think him less than a martyr because of the title of confessor, when he sees him, by God’s will, returning daily and repeatedly to the struggle. [Note: Whether Apollinaris can be called a martyr, see the Bollandists at the cited place, p. 341, no. 76. Gregory the Great honors him with this distinguished title, book V, letter 22. In the litanies of the age of Charlemagne, in Mabillon, *Analecta*, volume II, p. 683, he is invoked among the martyrs after Timothy—unless, as Georgius observes in his notes on Ado at the cited place, the martyrs Timothy and Apollinaris of Reims are meant. In other litanies, in Martène, *On the Ancient Discipline of the Mass*, p. 630, he is listed among the martyrs after Protasius. But here in Chrysologus, and in the litanies reproduced by Thomasius in *On the Ancient Books of the Mass*, he is counted among the confessors after Saint Benedict. Although he did not suffer death by the sword, they nevertheless think that he may receive this title because he shed blood and burned with desire for martyrdom.]

Hear Paul saying: “I die daily” (1 Corinthians 15). To die once is too little for one who can repeatedly bring glorious victory over enemies to his king. It is not death so much as faith and devotion that makes a martyr. Just as it is a mark of courage to fall in battle, in conflict, for love of the king, so it is a mark of perfect virtue to wage and complete struggles over a long period. [Note: So read the Bologna edition and the manuscripts, and so Latinius read it; all the others have *pro re amata*, “for the beloved cause.”]

The persecutor did not persecute him as a martyr merely because he did not immediately inflict death; rather, he proved him a martyr because he did not draw faith from him. The crafty enemy hurled whatever weapons he could and exhausted every kind of armament, yet he could not move the mind of that most courageous commander or violate his steadfastness.

It is a great thing, brothers, to despise the present life for the Lord when necessity requires it; but it is glorious also, while still alive, to despise and trample the world together with its prince.

Christ was hastening toward the martyr, and the martyr was hastening toward his king. We rightly said “was hastening,” in accordance with the prophet’s words: “Rise to meet me, and see” (Psalm 58). But so that the holy Church might retain her champion, she ran vigorously to meet Christ, so that she might reserve the crown for victorious justice and obtain for herself the presence of her warrior during the time of battle.

The confessor often poured out his blood and, through his wounds, testified in the faith of his mind to his Creator. Looking up to heaven, he despised the flesh [Note: Another reading: “he despised.”] and the earth. Yet he conquered and endured, and tender infancy still delayed the martyr from his desire. [Note: He was crowned with martyrdom in the year of the Lord 74 and presided over the Church of Ravenna for twenty-eight years. Mita.—The number must be understood as a complete number, for from Agnellus’s *Book of the Bishops* we learn that he occupied the see for twenty-eight years, one month, and four days. This in no way supports the opinion that Apollinaris died in the year 74. Agnellus says that Apollinaris came to Rome with the apostle Peter and was ordained bishop by him and sent to Ravenna only after a very long time. Since Peter came to Rome in the forty-third year of the common era, if Apollinaris, who occupied the see for twenty-eight years, died in the year 74, he must have been sent in the second year of Peter’s pontificate. This does not agree with Agnellus, who says that he was sent to Ravenna long after Peter’s arrival in Rome. Since we know from the more exact chronological tables that Vespasian died in the common year 79, Bacchinius, p. 135, says that it is wrong to place Apollinaris’s martyrdom after that year, as Rubeus does, and thinks it more correct to place the death of Saint Apollinaris around the year of Vespasian’s death. Since Vespasian died, according to Suetonius, on the eighth day before the Kalends of July, however, Apollinaris’s death could not have occurred except in the preceding year. Once this chronology is accepted, Bacchinius concludes that the beginning of Apollinaris’s episcopate must be moved backward, while retaining the day on which his birthday is marked in all the Martyrologies—23 July, in the year 50 of the common era, though on 19 June according to the day-count.]

I speak of infancy, brothers—infancy, which always possesses the whole; which contends more through tears than through a calculation of strength. For the bodies of the strong cannot do as much as the tears of little ones, because there bodies are broken, whereas here hearts are broken; there the judgments of the mind are scarcely moved, whereas here all piety, bowed down, descends.

And what more, brothers? The holy Church acted and acted so that she might never be separated from her bishop.

Behold, he lives; behold, like a good shepherd, he stands among his flock, and the spirit that preceded the body for a time is never separated from it. I say “preceded” in condition; otherwise, he himself rests among us through the dwelling of his body. [Note: For he was buried at Ravenna, says Mita.]

The devil has been extinguished; the persecutor has fallen. Behold, he reigns and lives who desired to be killed for his king—who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever.

[Note: See what is noted in the preface.]

## SERMON CXXIX. On Saint Cyprian the Martyr
Since today we have gathered before God on the feast of the holy martyr Cyprian, in which he triumphed over the devil in a wondrous contest, and since he left us a glorious example of his virtues, it is fitting for us therefore to exult and rejoice.

[Note: Bingham praises these words, vol. IX, *Origines*, p. 134, as proving that the Church had long been accustomed to call the day of a martyr’s death the martyr’s birthday; Du Cange does likewise, vol. II, p. 808, at the end. Chrysostom has something similar in Homily 129; Origen—or an ancient author writing under his name—in *Commentary on Job*, vol. I, book III, p. 274 of the Paris edition of 1604; and nearly the same in Eusebius of Emesa, *On the Feast of St. Genesius*, *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. I, Lyons edition, p. 670; Augustine, vol. X, Sermon 95, *On St. Stephen*, fol. 567, col. 1; Maximus, *On the Feast of Saints Peter and Paul*, vol. VI of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*; and again Chrysologus, Sermon 133.]

Therefore, beloved, when you hear of the birthdays of the saints, do not suppose that this means the day on which they are born from flesh into the earth, but the day on which they are born from earth into heaven, from toil into rest, from temptations into peace, from torments into delights—not fleeting delights, but strong, stable, and eternal ones—from worldly laughter to the crown and glory. Such birthdays are rightly celebrated for martyrs.

When, then, such a festival is being held, beloved, do not think that the martyrs’ birthdays are celebrated merely through banquets and more lavish feasts.

[Note: It was customary among ancient Christians to celebrate solemnly the days on which martyrs died—days which, as I have said, the Church calls their birthdays. In former times banquets called *agapae* were held in honor of such days; these were different from those agapae known to the apostles. But when, because of the customary human inclination toward evil, they began to be polluted by excessive feasting and drunkenness, and the Manichaeans consequently seized the opportunity to slander the faithful, they were abolished by the common consent of devout people.]

Rather, what you celebrate in memory of the martyr is set before you for imitation. Look, then, beloved, at the enthusiasm of the people standing around. On this day, once, a crowd of impious people stood by when the holy Cyprian was struck down at the tyrant’s command; there were throngs of wicked men, waiting in choirs. Now a multitude of the faithful has gathered in devotion to rejoice together: then a crowd of raging people, now of exultant people; then of the despairing, now of those who hope.

For this reason, therefore, the birthdays of martyrs are celebrated each year with joy: so that what happened once may remain throughout all ages in the memory of the devout. It is an accomplished deed, beloved, so that you cannot say, “I did not know”; it is celebrated annually so that you cannot say, “I have forgotten.”

Be zealous, then, to imitate these things, beloved; desire this grace of greatness of spirit; ask that you may be granted what he deserved to attain. For all who desire heavenly things cannot be ensnared by the traps of earthly goods, because they have established their way of life in heaven, as the holy Apostle says: “But our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3).

Let the desire of our heart, therefore, be directed toward the heavenly dwelling, where, when your treasure has been distributed among the poor, your heart will also be. Christ is the treasure of all good things; may he deign to heap upon you and fill you with heavenly gifts, together with the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, both now and forever.

[Note: In some manuscripts this sermon is entitled “On the Consecration of a Bishop.” For bishops used to celebrate the feast of their consecration annually, just as emperors celebrated the birthday, or accession, of their imperial power. See Book II of the Theodosian Code, *On Holidays*. That panegyrics were customarily delivered on both occasions is shown, in the case of emperors, by those delivered at the quinquennial and decennial celebrations of the emperors; and, in the case of bishops, by this sermon, another among the Chrysologian sermons, number 107, one by Ennodius on the feast of Laurentius, bishop of Milan, and another by the same author on the feast of Epiphanius, bishop. Anastasius invited Paulinus of Nola by a most affectionate letter to the solemnity of his consecration, as Paulinus himself testifies in Book XVI. Ambrose, Book I, chapter 5, says to Felix, bishop of Como, that he had celebrated the latter’s feast with prayers. Hilary, writing to the bishops of the Church of Tarragona, says: “After your letter had been read in the assembly of the brethren whom the solemnity of my feast had gathered together.” If we are not mistaken, Damasus, who began to sit as bishop in the year 360, was the originator of this custom. See Basnage, *Annals*, vol. III, p. 518. As for this sermon, nearly all who have written about Chrysologus believe that he delivered it at Ravenna, not on the recurring anniversary of his own consecration, but at the very solemnity of his consecration. Rubeus, *History of Ravenna*, Book II, under the year 449; Mita in his *Life*; Bacchinius in his notes to Agnellus, vol. I, p. 315; Pastritius, *On the Paten*, etc., p. 98 and following.]

## SERMON CXXX. On the Consecration of a Bishop

Just as the long expectation of a great promise kindles the spirit and wearies the mind, so the desired fulfillment of the promise arouses all the senses and the inward power of the very heart. Hence it is that today, as Isaiah said (Isa. 52), the holy mother Church has come forth festive, wholly rejoicing and adorned; she has put on the tunic of her joy. Like a bride, she has placed a mitre upon her head,

[Note: Because, according to Pope Anacletus’s arrangement, three bishops, resplendent in mitres, consecrate another bishop. MITA. — Perhaps Chrysologus is referring to the mitre among the bride’s ornaments, as Onuphrius does at the end of his book *On More Obscure Ecclesiastical Terms*. Ovid, *Heroides* 9.63: “Dared even to bind my shaggy hair with a mitre.”]

and has arranged and adorned herself in varied ornament, as heaven glitters with the lights of its stars and earth blooms with its flowers; and as a garden produces its shoots, so she has produced joy in the sight of all her children.

For, in accordance with David’s promise, “Today a son has been born to her in place of a father” (Ps. 44): one who does not bend her down by his weight, frighten her by his authority, trouble her by agitation, or disturb her by severity, but supports her with faithful service; who, with sleepless care, makes provision for her when she is harassed; with attentive labor supplies what is necessary; orders her household through gentle instruction; meets her guests; serves her parents; obeys kings; cooperates with authorities; shows reverence to the elderly, kindness to children, love to brothers, and affection to little ones;

[Note: The Caesena manuscript reads *clamans*, “crying out,” instead of *cantans*, “singing.”]

and offers all people, through Christ, a free service.

David said: “Listen, daughter, and see” (Ps. 44).
