I shall say: “Listen, mother, and see: in place of your fathers, sons have been born to you.” May they be elders in wisdom, fathers in dignity, sons in charity, young men in strength, offspring in gentleness, infants in innocence, and little ones in ignorance of evil, knowing nothing of the world; possessing the whole presence of the kingdom of God, as the Lord bears witness when he says: “Let the little children come to me, for the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these” (Matt. 19).

Such children are generated by the union of perpetual virginity; such children are generated by the communion of heavenly life: a communion that knows no sex, is conscious of conception, understands childbirth, is ignorant of corruption, whole in modesty, enclosed in integrity, chaste in its pledges, and spread abroad in fertility.

While this devout mother today celebrates the birthday feast of one of her offspring,

[Note: Understand “birthday” not as referring to life, but to the episcopal see.]

she opens her bosom, extends her embraces, raises her voice, and sings in divine songs,

[Note: The Caesena manuscript reads *clamans*, “crying out.”]

so that she may summon everyone, receive everyone, and enclose everyone in the lap of charity, that they may rejoice together with her.

[Note: Mita thinks—and not without reason—that Galla Placidia, daughter of the emperor Theodosius and sister of Arcadius and Honorius, was present at this sermon. For Rubeus, in his *History of Ravenna*, tells us that the emperor Valentinian honored this solemnity by his presence. From this Mita infers that other words, mentioning the emperor himself, must have preceded the present passage; he also argues this from the particle *etiam*, “also,” which would necessarily have to be joined to words now missing. “This is perfectly clear,” he says, “from the end of the sermon, where the author asks the priests to pray for the Christian rulers who attended their solemnities.”]

The mother herself also of the Christian, perpetual, and faithful empire is present. While she follows and imitates the blessed Church in honoring the Trinity by faith, works of mercy, and holiness,

[Note: Since Chrysologus’s consecration took place on a Sunday, when the preface of the Trinity is customarily sung—“And because the Empress attended the sacred rites every Sunday, on which the preface of the most holy Trinity was sung,” says Mita, “therefore he follows and imitates the Church.” Or was she rather imitating the blessed Church by honoring the Trinity through the three virtues of faith, mercy, and holiness?]

she deserved to conceive, embrace, and possess the august Trinity.

[Note: Mita explains the obscure passage as follows. Placidia is said to have conceived the august Trinity because she was the mother of three emperors. First, on her account Constantius, formerly a commander of armies and now her husband, was shortly afterward declared Augustus by Honorius. Second, she bore a son, Valentinian, who was named Caesar by Theodosius the Younger and Augustus in his seventh year. Finally, she in a certain sense made herself Augusta, when Honorius, lest he should seem to have given his sister to Constantius beneath her dignity, declared both Constantius and Placidia Augusti. But, as Bacchinius says in his notes to Agnellus’s *Pontifical History*, vol. I, p. 315, Constantius was not made Augustus because of Placidia’s merits, but because of his own. Sozomen, Book IX, chapter 16: “The emperor honored Constantius, as a reward, with his sister, the crown, the purple, and partnership in the empire.” Therefore he could not be said to have been made Augustus by Galla Placidia. Nor was she herself proclaimed Augusta until Valentinian had been declared Caesar. Chrysologus must therefore be interpreted according to the proper force of the words: namely, that what Placidia deserved in relation to the august Trinity can be referred to the imperial dignity in three ways—she conceived it by giving birth to Valentinian; embraced it through her marriage to Constantius; and possessed it by attaining the honors of an Augusta.]

Thus the Trinity rewards those who burn with love and ardor for it. She deserved that the Trinity should grant her honor and rejoice that, by God’s grace, it had given her a religion like its own.

[Note: In Mita’s opinion, these words imply that Placidia was granted as her husband Constantius, a Catholic and one like herself in religion, whereas previously she had been married to the barbarian king Ataulf, who, even if not a pagan, was at least a follower of the Arian heresy. Some editions read: “That he had given her, by the grace of God, a similar religion.”]

She deserved that the dignity of the mother should, through the mother, flow down to her descendants.

[Note: In my view, the reading should be either “the dignity of the parent” or “the imperial dignity.” For through Placidia the imperial dignity passed to her descendants—that is, to the sons and grandsons born from her and Constantius; and this imperial dignity proceeded from Theodosius Caesar, Placidia’s father, through whom it afterward passed to those descendants. MITA.]

Pray, brothers, that the Christian rulers, who in pious devotion deign to attend our joys and be present at our solemnities, may themselves also, through the equal favor of all the priests, be commended by the devout prayer of the Church for a long time to come.

[Note: This sermon is elsewhere entitled “On the Words of John: ‘If anyone keeps my word.’”]

## SERMON CXXXI. On God, That He May Be Seen; on the Envy and Obstinacy of the Jews, and on Human Death

We have often said that God is not seen with bodily eyes; that the divinity is not enclosed by a carnal mind; that human reason cannot grasp the Creator of all things; but that faith alone reaches God, that the whole of belief perceives him—not what he is in magnitude, but simply that he is—and that the human gaze, however great its capacity, contemplates him.

Thus Moses, who was advanced from servant to friend and from human being toward God, seeks the face of God but does not find it; he asks but does not receive it. He is warned that he may see only God’s back (Exod. 33), so that a human being may learn to seek to follow God, not to precede him; and may not presume to ask what lies before God, but may acknowledge, as a worshiper, that all things exist through God.

God frequently displays to human beings the form of a human being, and gathers his own greatness into so small a figure of our work that our weak eye may behold the divine presence and our narrow sight may receive it.

Thus God came to Abraham in human form, assumed the appearance of a guest, and, as a weary traveler, accepted water for his feet (Gen. 18). Invited to the table, he was also satisfied by the serving of a calf and bread. In this way he entrusted and committed himself wholly to human service, so that, by touch and sight, he seemed to fulfill the reality of a true human being—at the very time when the true God came to grant offspring in childbirth to extreme sterility by opening the long-closed womb of an old man’s wife.

Thus Jacob encountered a fellow traveler on his journey (Gen. 32), and presented himself as a companion among human beings, so that God, challenged by a human being, entered wholly into the struggle; and he then appeared to conquer with sinews and muscles when, as victor, he bestowed heavenly gifts and divine rewards.

Thus Isaiah saw God seated in royal attire (Isa. 6), so that he might recognize that unless kings are ruled by God the King, they, though human beings, have no power to rule.

Thus Daniel sees God the Father seated in judgment, with snow-white hair, venerable with age, terrifying in antiquity, surrounded by angels, and seated upon a fiery throne (Dan. 7). Thus he sees the very Son of God coming with the clouds of heaven in the form of the Son of Man,

[Note: Latinius suspects that this may not be the genuine reading.]

so that he may understand that Christ, previously unknown to so many unbelievers, has always been known to the faithful.

If God is so often seen by human beings in human form, why is it that the Jew, now seeing the human being Christ, becomes so enraged? Unless, perhaps, what is regarded as an image, an honor, and truth is considered an insult.

The evangelist reported today that Christ said: “If anyone keeps my word, he will never see death” (John 8). To this statement the Jews replied: “Now we know that you have a demon. Abraham our father died, and the prophets; yet you say, ‘If anyone keeps my word, he will never taste death.’ Are you greater than our father Abraham, who died? Whom do you make yourself?”

What perfidy there was in their response! How envy closes the eyes! How much the forejudgment of wickedness confuses the judgment of the heart! How harshly obstinacy cuts off reason! A perverse human mind cannot hear what it has once decided to hate: goodness is hateful to the wicked, and justice is hostile to the unjust.

Hence liars cannot recognize the truth; a judging mind cannot discover what is true amid reports of falsehoods.

[Note: Variant reading: “A messenger among falsehoods.”]

The person who has decided to err always hears what he wants, not what is actually said.

Christ had said: “If anyone keeps my word, he will never see death.” The Jew does not examine what he has heard or seek to interpret the words for himself. What he considers impossible, he demands that the one who makes the promise establish. But immediately he gives birth to blasphemy from the conception of his mind, sows insults, pours forth curses, and strives so to empty the speaker’s authority through abuse that he refuses to believe that the one who appears so subject to human conditions can give mortals eternal life.

“Now we know that you have a demon.” A demon is the author of evil; he promises evil, not good. He is accustomed to killing, not to giving life; nor does he wish human beings to be eternal, since he does not even allow them to remain temporal.

Therefore Christ is not a demon but God, who restores the life he had given, and by his word makes eternal those human beings whom the devil, through his persuasion, had made temporal.

[Note: The Caesena manuscript reads: “Therefore Christ is God, not a demon, for he restores what he had given.”]

“Abraham,” he says, “died, and the prophets; yet you say, ‘If anyone keeps my word, he will never see death.’”

Let the faithful hear, so that faith may reveal and make known what the unbeliever does not know how to hear, what the person who has plunged himself into the darkness of unbelief cannot see.

Christ said: “He will not see death.” Your obstinacy, Jew, rightly seeks to declare this false. Abraham and the prophets heard the word and kept it steadfastly, yet they died—but not forever. Therefore, when he says, “He will not see death,” and adds, “forever,”

[Note: Read similar remarks in Augustine, *Tractates on John* 43, p. 425 of vol. III of his works: “What does the Lord’s saying mean, ‘He will not see death forever,’ except that the Lord saw another death, from which he came to free us—the second death, eternal death, the death of Gehenna, the death of condemnation,” and so forth.]

he promises resurrection; he does not deny that they will die temporally.

Jew, those whom death in the present age caused not to exist, resurrection restores to us as perpetual beings in the future.

Hear him say this more openly: “Everyone who believes will not die forever, but will pass from death into life” (John 5 and 11). How does he not die? Because he passes from death into life.

Everyone who is born from mortal condition dies—yes, he dies; but everyone who is reborn from a life-giving generation lives, and lives forever.

But I ask: if he could take death away, why did he wish human beings to pass through death? For a physician who anticipates illnesses appears more gracious than one who administers medicine late and not without pain.

Jew, Christ the physician would have done this also, if the sick person had not been ungrateful to the physician. He gave life and foretold that death would come to the human being; but the one who had not experienced adversity did not know how to preserve prosperity.

We cannot know how good good things are except through knowledge of evils. Therefore Christ will be magnified: he both gave life before it had been possessed and now restores life that had been lost. And the human being, now more knowledgeable about life, will be more cautious for himself and more grateful to his creator.

“Are you greater,” he says, “than our father Abraham?” Certainly—and so much greater as a lord is greater than a servant, God than a human being, the maker than what is made, the one who gives life than the dead,

[Note: Latinius corrects the reading found in the printed editions, *suscitando suscitatus*, “raised by raising,” to the present reading.]

and the one who raises than the one who has been raised.

Jesus answered: “Abraham rejoiced that he might see my day; he saw it and was glad.”

To show that Abraham lives, he said that Abraham had seen his day—that is,

[Note: Augustine, in the passage just cited, p. 427, no. 16: “It may be uncertain what day he meant: whether the temporal day of the Lord, on which he was to come in the flesh, or the day of the Lord that knows neither rising nor setting. But I have no doubt that the father Abraham knew the whole.”]

the day on which Christ was born into the world.

The maker of days is not confined by a day; the author of time does not know temporal limits. But Christ, born as a human being for the sake of humanity, received both a day and a time.

“Abraham rejoiced that he might see my day.” If Moses and Elijah came to meet him on the mountain so that they might behold the promised Christ, how could Abraham not also come to meet him at the Virgin’s childbirth, as the most patient of watchers awaited and contemplated the promised blessing among the nations—that is, in his seed?

“Amen, amen, I say to you: before Abraham was, I am.”

If all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made (John 1), and if this is the one to whom the Father said, “Let us make humanity in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1), how could Abraham not have seen him?

“Let us make humanity in our image and likeness.” As the substance of an angel and of God is different, so too is their image.

[Note: St. Barnabas has the Father speaking to the Son: “Let us make humanity,” and so forth; likewise Justin Martyr in his *Dialogue with Trypho*; Theophilus, Book II *To Autolycus*; Origen, Book II *Against Celsus*; Eusebius of Caesarea, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book I, chapter 2; and others.]

Therefore the Father speaks only to the Son when he says, “Let us make humanity in our image and likeness,” since they have the same image and the same substance.

They took up stones in order to throw them at him. And, as builders of a tower so that they might fall from a greater height, they themselves provided the stones for themselves. These wretched men brought stones not with which to kill God, but with which they would kill themselves.

Jesus hid himself—not because he was afraid, but because he forgave. When God flees from the sinner, he spares him; when God withdraws from the rebellious, he does not wish to destroy him.

## SERMON CXXXII. On the Unity of the Faithful

If nature generated and brought forth everything perfect, robust, and needing nothing, devotion would surely be abolished, ingenuity would fail, art would perish, gold would lie hidden in the earth, and a gem concealed in the stone. Yet skilled training finds, cleanses, distinguishes, and polishes both; and the same art brings them to the appearance and beauty of a precious little ornament. What the earth produces from nature’s abundant spring is either roughened by thorns or, under the rule of wild luxuriance, grows uncultivated in the woods, unless the diligent industry of the farmer restores it to cultivation.

But, lest we wander too far, let us give one familiar and domestic example of the matters on which we rely. A human being, once born, is already in the human being in the cradle,

[Note: For he is imperfect and not complete. From Aristotle, Books II and III *On Generation*. MITA.]

but lies hidden; there is a body, yet it is not yet there; the limbs appear, yet are not there; what live do not flourish in perception. Devotion bends over him, industry toils, art labors; and, to say it more fully, as many as are the limbs of a human being, so many arts labor to perfect the human being. What more need be said? Everything that nature generates or produces, devotion nourishes, industry cultivates, and art adorns.

And what wonder, brothers, if God, who chose to suffer for humanity in order to honor human industry, chose also to make nature weak in present things?

[Note: For the course of life is prescribed in labor for the human being alone, so that he may exercise the rational faculty which he has received. St. Ambrose discusses this excellently in the preface to his Gospel of Luke, near the middle, where he also gives the fittingness of this matter. MITA.]

Hence meaning lies hidden in the letter, and a divine mystery is concealed in human speech, so that things already evident to believers, though still future, may be obscured to the faithless and unbelieving—as though the punishment of unbelievers redounded to the glory of the faithful. For it is no slight torment not to discern what is seen, not to understand what is heard, to reject saving things as though harmful, and to avoid virtues as though they were vices; as the Lord himself says: “I speak in parables, so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not hear” (Mark 4; Luke 8); and to the faithful: “But to you it has been given to know the mystery of God” (Matt. 13).

Therefore, brothers, let no one regard the evangelical discourse as common or cheap because of its simplicity, especially since the very trumpet sounding in the Gospel reading has foretold that nothing will be denied to those who ask rightly and desire devoutly, saying:

[Note: These words are explained in wonderful ways by the Fathers, as Maldonatus does on this text, Matt. 18:19. MITA.]

“Because if two of you agree on earth about anything whatsoever that they ask, it shall be done for them by my Father” (Matt. 18). You have heard how much the agreement of a holy petition can do and prevail: he did not say this or that, but promises to grant whatever the unity of their request desires, when he says: “Concerning anything whatsoever they ask, it shall be done for them.”

Yet this safeguard and reverence must be preserved: that things worthy of God be asked from God.

[Note: James 4:3: “You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly.”]

For one who asks evil from God judges and considers God the author of evil; and one who prays for base and unworthy things, being an unworthy petitioner, does not understand the power and might of the giver. Therefore what must always be sought from such a giver is not impious but pious, not earthly but heavenly, not suited to enticements but to virtue, not deserving hatred but fitted for concord.

Where are those who presume that the assembly of the Church may be despised, and claim that solitary prayers should be preferred to the venerable congregation, when, with two or three assembled,

[Note: The faith of our Church rests upon this promise, believing most firmly that the Holy Spirit presides over assemblies and councils of the faithful, and over every place where the Catholic flock gathers.]

he promises that he will be in their midst and will grant whatever is asked of him (Matt. 18)? He who denies nothing to so few, what will he deny to those asking in councils and in the congregation of the saints? Believing thus, the prophet boasts that he obtained this, saying: “I will praise you, Lord, with my whole heart, in the council of the righteous and in the congregation” (Ps. 110). He praises with his whole heart who hears that everything he has asked in the council of the saints

[Note: From the Caesena manuscript; the printed editions read *audet*, “dares.”]

is to be granted him.

But some, under the appearance of faith, try to excuse their own sloth through contempt for the congregation. Neglecting the ardor of the venerable gathering and congregation, they pretend that they have assigned to prayer the time which they have given and devoted to domestic concerns; and while they become enslaved to their own desires, they scorn and despise divine ordinances. These are they who scatter the body of Christ and disperse the members. They do not allow the form of the Lord’s garment to attain its proper beauty—a form which the prophet, seeing in the Spirit, sang thus: “You are fairer in form than the children of men” (Ps. 44).

The individual members indeed each have their own function of service; yet they can fulfill it only if, joined and fitted together, they attain the beauty of the perfect body. This, then, is the difference between the glorious fullness of the congregation and the presumed vanity of separation arising from ignorance or negligence: in the health and honor of the whole body lies the beauty of the unity of the members; in the separation of the inward parts lies a foul, deadly, and dreadful destruction.

Human being, what else has your own body taught you—or what has such division joined together, or such union divided—except that you should live as one from many, and as one among many? The eye is precious through the salutary interchange of the members, but only if it remains in the body; otherwise, when it fails the body, it will not be of use to itself. All the members owe it the service of their light; but the eye itself recognizes that it owes the body its light, since it provides for the service of the members with all the members.

[Note: From the Caesena and Vatican manuscripts; the printed editions read *ministratum*, “provided.”]

Torn from the body, it does not see. Whoever he may be who thinks himself something, instructed by such an example let him remain in the Church so that he may be something; otherwise, when he has left it, he immediately ceases to exist for himself. Whoever desires to know this more fully should read through the teachings of the Apostle speaking about Christ’s body, because the brevity friendly to a sermon does not permit us to run through them (1 Cor. 1).

The law was given not to one but to all. Christ came not for one, nor to one, but to all and for all, in order to restore all into one. The prophet, foreknowing the sole good and sole delight, thus proclaims: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in one” (Ps. 132). For singularity is not acceptable to God, but unity. The Holy Spirit flows upon the apostles gathered together as one with the full abundance of his spring (Acts 2); and they were reminded by the Lord’s command to await his coming together.

Brothers, whoever, injurious to himself and foolishly self-sufficient through his own defect, seeks life outside the Church, loses divine gifts, forfeits the abundance of grace, is deprived of the goods of charity, and will not retain the blessing of unity. Yet the prophet testifies that life exists only in the Church, saying: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in one” (Ps. 132), because “there the Lord commanded blessing and life for evermore.”

[Note: In the Vatican manuscript this sermon is entitled: “Here begins the sermon on the feast of St. Andrew.”]

## SERMON CXXXIII. On St. Andrew the Apostle

Blessed Andrew is rightly believed to have been born today, when he was not brought forth from his mother’s womb into this present life,

[Note: In the margin of this manuscript, in a later hand, *materno*, “maternal”; in the text, *merito*, “rightly.”]

but is known to have been begotten for heavenly glory by the conception of faith and the birth of martyrdom.

[Note: In the same manuscript, *conceptu Dei*, “by the conception of God.”]

It was then that maternal cradles did not receive him crying, but the heavenly mysteries received him triumphant; when he did not draw from his mother’s breast the nourishment of milk,

[Note: Vatican manuscript: *lactis potum*, “a draught of milk.”]

but, as a most devoted soldier for his king, shed the blood of valor. He lives because the warrior of heavenly service killed death.

Burning and panting, he follows his dying Lord; with every step of courage he strives to cling to the Lord’s footprints, lest his course make him unequal to the brother whom nature had made like him, calling his companion, and grace itself his equal. At one word of the Lord, like him he left father, country, and property. Through labors, reproaches, journeys, insults, and vigils,

[Note: From Mita’s edition. *Largiente se*, “granting himself,” is absent from the Vatican manuscript and the other printed editions. Mita testifies that he corrected this sermon—which was more corrupt than any other in the printed editions—according to the authority of the manuscripts. It is also corrupt in the Vatican manuscript and in the Vallicellian manuscript, where it is likewise entitled “On the birthday of St. Andrew.” On this manner of speaking, see the remarks of the learned Meursius in his *Glossary on the Birthdays of Martyrs*; of Gaspar Barth, *Adversaria*, Book XIX, chapter 3; and in the *History of the Two Soldiers of Christ* ascribed to Damascene. Hence the ancients also called the passions of martyrs a baptism. See note d to Sermon 135.]

by Christ’s gift he devoted himself untiringly to his brother’s companionship. Only in this was he inferior: at the time of the Lord’s Passion he fled; yet even in this he was not unequal, because he fled. But if denial is thought any fault, flight is no more serious than denial. But let other matters be passed over: brothers, pardon made equal those whom fault had so distinguished. The subsequent ardor of martyrdom proved devoted those whom the preceding fear had disapproved.

For the cross which they had fled, they afterward eagerly assail with joined strength, so that from that from which they had incurred guilt, they might ascend to heaven and receive reward and crown. Peter indeed climbed the cross; Andrew climbed the tree, so that those who longed to suffer with Christ might express in themselves the figure and form of his Passion; and, redeemed by the wood, might be perfected unto the palm. Thus our Andrew, although he yields in rank, does not yield in reward or labor.

[Note: The title of this sermon in the Caesena manuscript is: “On the feast of St. Felicitas.” Blessed Felicitas suffered martyrdom with her sons at Rome under the persecution of the emperor Severus, about the year of the Lord 200, or somewhat earlier under Marcus Aurelius, in the time of Pope Soter, about the year 176. MITA.—The passion of St. Felicitas, with her seven sons, occurred at Rome about the year 150, under Publius, prefect of the City, and the emperor Antoninus Pius. Under that most peaceable prince, martyrdoms were nevertheless not lacking. Both the ancient martyrologies and the Sacramentary of blessed Gregory distinguish her feast from that of her sons: they commemorate the latter on 10 July, and her on 23 November. That Felicitas’s commemoration was once celebrated at Rome is shown especially by the fact that Pope St. Gregory preached a homily to the people on the day sacred to her passion, in which he extols this woman’s steadfastness with many praises; Baronius further notes in his annotations on the Martyrology that a cemetery at Rome once existed under her name. Ruinart gives her genuine acts on p. 26. See also the Martyrology of Ado for 10 July and 23 November, and the very learned notes of Georgius there.]

## SERMON CXXXIV. On St. Felicitas the Martyr
Since time does not permit us to enumerate the various and manifold triumphs of the martyrs, which the cruelty of the persecutor, so often defeated, amassed, our whole discourse turns to that woman who deserved to have as many sons as the days [Note: That is, as many as the days consumed in the creation of the world. For she bore seven sons, who suffered martyrdom together with her; and the world was completed on the seventh day.] that the world received. Truly a mother of lights, a source of days, who shines throughout the whole world with the sevenfold radiance of her offspring. Blessed is she who [Note: He alludes to that mother of seven sons in 2 Maccabees 7, who, for the laws of her fathers, together with her sons, most courageously endured the most atrocious tortures and death at the hands of the tyrant Antiochus. Saint Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 20, *On the Maccabees*, speaks beautifully of them. MITA.] not only suffers for the law, but a holy mother deserved to generate the heptalism (sevenfoldness) [Note: So all the editions. Mita adds in the margin of the book: “*Heptalismus* is used for the number seven.” Macrius, however, in his *Ecclesiastical Notes*, observes that there is an error here; one should read *heptalychnum*, from the Greek word ἐπταλύχνος, “a lamp,” namely one filled with seven lights, which burned in the Temple of Jerusalem and to which Chrysologus is referring.] of the law itself [Note: [Col. 0564C]]: the heptalism, brothers, which would not illuminate the hidden meaning of one temporary tabernacle, but would illumine the everlasting Church with sacred incense.

Blessed is she who deserved to carry as many pledges of virtue as that ark [Note: In the ark of the covenant there was, according to Tostatus, the book of Deuteronomy written on stone tablets. Perhaps the Author’s meaning is that there were seven stones on which Deuteronomy was written, containing the commandments. [Col. 0565C] Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book IV, chapter 8, writes that the book of the law stood beside the ark, but outside it, and that it was read every seventh year at the Feast of Tabernacles by the high priest. See, if desired, Saint Jerome’s *Commentary on Deuteronomy*. MITA.] carried the sacred volumes of the commandments [Col. 0565A] (Exodus 25); and just as that ark taught by the word, so she would teach by her example. Even then she gave birth to martyrs, brothers, when she consecrated them in the mystical number of seven at their birth.

Let Saint Paul come here—here indeed—who is still in labor until Christ is formed in a human being (Galatians 4). Behold, a woman again and again in labor until weakness is transformed into strength, flesh passes over into spirit, and earth is transferred into heaven. She burned and panted to give birth in a single day to those whom, while they were little ones, she had scarcely brought forth over the course of years. Behold the woman; behold the mother, whom the life of her sons made anxious, but their death made secure. Blessed is she before whom in future glory stand as many candelabra as she has offspring; blessed is she who sent so many on ahead to the kingdom; more blessed still is she who lost nothing of her own in this world [Note: For she did not lose her sons, but sent her pledges on ahead to heaven, as blessed Gregory says in the homily mentioned above.].

[Note: Ruinart praises these words in the place cited above, p. 25.] She moved more joyfully among bodies pierced through than among the dear cradles of her sons [Col. 0565B], because with her inward eyes she saw as many rewards as wounds, as many prizes as tortures, as many crowns as victims. And what more, brothers? She is not, she is not a true mother who does not know how to love her sons in this way.

[Note: See the Preface.]

# SERMON CXXXV. On Saint Lawrence.

This present day, the baptism of the martyr Lawrence [Note: We indicated above, in the note to Sermon 133, that the day on which martyrs die was also called their baptism by the ancients. Chrysostom, Homily 75, volume V: “Do not be surprised that I have called martyrdom a baptism; for the Spirit is also abundantly present here, sins are removed, and the soul is wonderfully purified. Just as those who are baptized with water, so those who attain the crown of martyrdom are washed in their own blood.” In this same sense Chrysostom notes that the word *baptism* is used of Christ’s death in Matthew 20:22; Mark 10:38; and Luke 12:50, in Homily 32, volume V. See also Theophylact on Matthew 20, p. 117.] is illumined by the crown of the martyr, whose outstanding merits [Note: Ruinart published these words in *Acts of the Martyrs*, on Saint Lawrence, p. 188. Augustine, Sermon 303 of the new edition: “As Rome cannot hide it, so it cannot hide the crown of Lawrence.” Leo the Great, in a sermon on this saint, says: “As Jerusalem was glorified by Stephen, so Rome was made illustrious by Lawrence.”] no part of the Roman world is unaware of. He suffered in the very capital of the nations, that is, in the city of Rome itself. There the deacon served, and in the very flower of his youth he dyed the beauty of his youth purple with his blood. His passion is renowned and exceedingly wondrous; with the Lord’s help, I shall recount it briefly.

[Note: Prudentius also suggests this in his hymn on Saint Lawrence, in Book II of *The Crowns* (*Περὶ Στεφάνων*):

> He is first among the seven  
> Who stand nearest the altar,  
> A Levite exalted in rank,  
> And superior to the others.]

At that time the blessed Sixtus was bishop, with this man as archdeacon [Col. 0565C]; Sixtus’s triumph of martyrdom had occurred three days earlier. When, therefore, Saint Lawrence followed his bishop Sixtus as he proceeded to martyrdom—sustained by faith, sorrowful in feeling, not because Sixtus was suffering, but because he himself was being abandoned by him—the venerable old man looked back at the venerable young man and said to him: “Do not be sad, son. In three days you will follow me.” Then, having drunk in the prophecy, already fully prepared in heart and intoxicated with the Spirit, he confidently hoped that what the one who knew had foretold would come to pass.

Afterward he was seized and brought forward. Since he was archdeacon, it was naturally believed that the Church’s wealth was in his keeping [Note: This was the duty of archdeacons. In the same passage:

> He presided over the sacred precincts,  
> Governing the heavenly mystery of the house  
> With faithful keys,  
> And distributing the dedicated resources.]

The persecutor desired this wealth—not so much because he was avaricious as because he was mad. He hated the man he was killing, but loved in him what that man despised. Saint Lawrence was poor in wealth but rich in character. He did not deny that the Church possessed riches; rather, so that he might display them, he asked for a delay of three days, and then ordered the ranks of the poor to be gathered.

Then, on the very day of his crown, when he was brought before the tribunal, as though he were going to show what the persecutor sought, he showed what he possessed. The persecutor then said: “Where are the Church’s resources?” Extending his hand toward the poor, Lawrence replied: “These are the Church’s resources” [Col. 0566B]. He spoke truly, but bitterly. And what wonder if truth increased hatred?

The cruel and avaricious tyrant, grieving that he had been mocked—an enemy who had perhaps contemplated the milder punishment of killing the venerable young man with the sword—ordered flames to be prepared. He burned more than he scorched; he scorched the flesh, but burned in his heart. His punishment was all the heavier because it was inward.

Then that famous gridiron of Lawrence was brought forth to roast him—or, to speak more accurately, to roast the martyr [Note: This relic had long been celebrated at Rome. Gregory the Great, in the eleventh indiction, Letter 33 to Dynamus, patrician of Gaul, sent a small cross into which benefits from the chains of Saint Peter had been inserted, “and on its four surrounding sides are contained benefits from the gridiron of blessed Lawrence, on which he was burned.” It is still preserved at Rome outside the walls, at Saint Lawrence’s, in the Verano district.]. He was fastened with iron, but he regarded the gridiron of punishment as a bed of rest. I said “punishment” in accordance with the mind of the one inflicting it, not in accordance with the conscience of the one suffering it. For there is no punishment for a condemned man where there is no punishment for sin.

Thus the most blessed martyr, showing how peacefully he lay upon that burning iron [Col. 0566C], said to those standing around: “Turn me over now, and if one side is cooked, eat it” [Note: Augustine, Sermon 303: “Now,” he said, “it is cooked; what remains, turn me over and eat.” Prudentius:

> Then he said: “It is cooked; devour it,  
> And test whether it is more pleasing  
> Raw or roasted.”]

We marvel at his endurance; let us marvel at the gift of God. There faith not only did not burn, but also comforted the one who was burning. Why did faith comfort the one who was burning? Because it held fast to the Promiser as faithful. That faith should not fail, that hope should not turn away, that charity should burn more intensely amid bodily, fiery torments [Col. 0567A]—these were gifts of God.

My brothers, let no one claim for his own power what only God gives. With good reason, when the Apostle addressed the martyrs—as you heard today when his Epistle was read—he said: “To you it has been granted for Christ’s sake not only to believe in him, but also to suffer for him” (Philippians 1). Therefore let us praise and love the merits of the martyrs as gifts of God, let us pray, and let us add our will beneath them. For the will follows; it does not precede. Yet charity is not absent if the will is not absent, for the ardent will itself is called charity.

Who is there who fears while willing? Who is there who loves unwillingly? Let prayer burn fervently, and let the martyr’s feast be celebrated; but so that the one who celebrates may not do so in vain, let him imitate the martyr.

[Note: In the manuscript of Cesena this sermon is entitled “On the Praise of Saint Adelphus, Bishop.” We know that among the ancients it was customary for bishops, as a sign of mutual respect, if a bishop of another see happened to be present at their sermons, to digress into his praise; there are many obvious examples of this. One particularly notable example occurs in Ennodius, *Discourse* 2, volume I of Sirmond’s works, p. 1053, where Laurentius, bishop of Milan, who was present, is praised at length. Nevertheless, Honoratus, bishop of Novara, delivered this sermon as his own, as Ferrarius notes was formerly customary, *On Sermons*, p. 203. Nazianzen praises Nyssenus when present in Oration 6, Basil in Oration 17, Eulalius in Oration 30, and one hundred and fifty bishops in Oration 32. Augustine praises the bishop of Carthage in his commentary on Psalm 92; Gaudentius of Brescia praises Ambrose of Milan, and so forth.]

# SERMON CXXXVI. On Adelphus, Bishop.

This is a quality of the holy spirit and devotion-filled condescension of Bishop Adelphus: that a rich man should enter a poor man’s dwelling, sit at a poor man’s table, and make himself accessible to the humble—he whom wealth, power, and honor had made and rendered distinguished. For this willingness must be counted among the greatest virtues: despising the arrogance of his own attendance, disregarding the reverence owed to a magnificent house, trampling even upon the eminence of his own power, and casting aside the inward awareness of his wealth—the source from which the greatest pride always dominates human minds—he bent down to the most wretched circumstances of the poor, so that by his companionship he might exalt the poor man.

Blessed indeed is that disposition, removed from every disease of arrogance, which first entered the poor man’s lodging so that it might become a debtor in humanity before becoming a giver [Note: Variant reading: “might have become.”]. This man plainly desired to imitate God: before granting divine benefits to humanity, God first accepted human services in the body.

We see that the present Adelphus, pontiff of the Most High God, has done this. Though rich in speech, abundant in knowledge, and great in intellect, first in rank [Note: Chrysologus here plainly indicates that Saint Adelphus—whoever he may have been—was superior to him in order and rank. Before the Church of Ravenna was endowed with metropolitan rights, it acknowledged no superior in Italy other than the bishop of Milan, or perhaps of Aquileia. There was no Adelphus in those sees in Chrysologus’s time. It is therefore easy to conclude that the man about whom this sermon is concerned was merely an older bishop than Chrysologus. Although some believe that the Church of Ravenna had already been made metropolitan while Chrysologus’s predecessor occupied its see, this cannot be asserted with certainty or security. It is therefore quite plausible that Chrysologus was the first among the bishops of Ravenna to receive this dignity.], he desired to hear the words of our poor understanding and modest eloquence, like that prophet who hungered for the last portion of the widow’s food and, by his own hunger, afflicted the poverty of her little ones, postponing his request for a new ministry so that by asking he might give, by hungering he might satisfy, and by exhausting the storehouse of those in want he might fill it through divine generosity (1 Kings 17).

[Col. 0568A] And we, little children, do not regret having given what we possessed; for although what happened troubled us for a time, the example both relieves and consoles us. Soon, through the word of this man of God, the smallness of our understanding will advance through heavenly increase like the widow’s food; and thereafter the substance of life will not fail from the storehouse of our heart, but poverty itself and want will be abolished.

Blessed is the spring that is enriched by its own irrigation and gains and draws in all the streams of its well through abundance [Note: We correct this from the Vatican manuscript and from Latinius. The printed editions erroneously read *libertate*, “by freedom.”]. Behold, he has come, and the heavenly rain has drenched your exalted minds. With the full force of the upper river, he has watered by his descent the city of God that is in you, so that our earth, moistened with divine dew, may become fruitful even to a hundredfold yield.

Open your understanding, enlarge your hearts, and extend the lap of your mind, so that whatever he pours forth generously for you from these heavenly treasures [Col. 0568B] [Note: It appears clearly from this that Adelphus himself was also going to address the people of Ravenna, as was then customary; this has been observed elsewhere by us, in Sermon 138, note e.] you may possess for eternal glory and everlasting wealth.

# SERMON CXXXVII. On the Preaching of Saint John the Baptist.

After the fertility of the Jewish soil had been exhausted by the plowshare of the law and by continual cultivation, blessed John, flying to the wilderness of the Gentiles, kindled the thorns of sins with the fire of the Spirit, cut down fruitless trees with the axe of vengeance, leveled the rough hills of pride, raised and equalized the valleys of humility, and prepared the whole plain of the earth, stripped of its grass, by laying beneath it the irrigating streams of the Jordan, thus preparing new fields spread out for the evangelical seed and arranging them to be fertile.

“It came to pass,” he says, “that the word of the Lord came upon John, the son of Zechariah, in the desert” (Luke 3). “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1). Upon John? Why not “to John,” but “upon John”? Because what is from above is above all. “The word of the Lord came upon John.” Because John is the voice, while God is the Word. “The word of the Lord came upon John.” God above John, the Lord above the servant, the Word above the voice.

But you say to me: What of the fact that the voice precedes the Word? It precedes, but does not surpass. It goes before in service to what follows, not as an indication of its own power. The voice is not itself the judge, but the herald of the judge; the Word judges, the voice proclaims beforehand; authority belongs to the one who commands, not to the one who cries out.

Let the voice itself, the herald himself, who cries out, acknowledge, testify, and affirm this: “He who comes after me,” he says, “is mightier than I” (Matthew 3). Why? Because terror is in me, but judgment is in him.

“He came into the whole region of the Jordan” [Note: Either the region around Jericho, on this side of the Jordan and toward the west of the Jordan; or Bethany, that is, Bethabara, beyond the Jordan; or Aenon near Salim, on this side of the Jordan. It is certain that John exercised his preaching in these places.]. He came to the Jordan because a jar could no longer wash away Jewish uncleanness, but a river could. As it is written: “There were,” he says, “stone jars for the purification of the Jews” (John 2).

He came to the Jordan to carry repentant people by water, not by wine. He came into the whole region of the Jordan, preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. Forgiveness was present with John, but not without repentance; remission was present, but purchased with mourning; there was care for the wound, together with pain; there was a baptism that removed guilt but did not [Note: Variant reading: “display the conscience.” Those who were baptized with John’s baptism were baptized only for the forgiveness of sins through an intermediate repentance, so that by the power of repentance the guilt of the baptized person was forgiven through that baptism. But whenever sins forgiven in that baptism came back before their minds, those who had been baptized in this way were bound again to be contrite and repent in their hearts. Therefore that baptism did not erase the conscience—that is, it did not remove the conscience’s *synderesis*—or, according to the manuscript, it did not remove guilt but displayed the conscience. For an explanation of the effect of the baptism of Christ and of John, see Suárez, in the third part of Saint Thomas; from him you may draw an explanation of this passage of Saint Chrysologus below Sermon 13, somewhat before the middle. MITA.] erase the conscience.

And what more? Through John’s baptism [Note: John’s baptism was truly a preparation for Christ’s baptism: it prepared people to hear the Messiah and to receive forgiveness of sins through baptism. Gregory, Homily 20 on the Gospels, p. 110, verso 50, Paris edition of 1551: “It should therefore be noted that it says, ‘preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins,’ because, since he could not give the baptism that would release sins, he preached it.” I refrain from quoting Chrysostom’s passage on Matthew, Homily 10, although it would fit here perfectly, because it is rather long.] a person was purified for repentance, but was not [Col. 0569B] advanced to grace. Christ’s baptism, however, regenerates and transforms a person so thoroughly, and makes the old person new, that he knows nothing of what is past and does not remember former things; once earthly, he now possesses heavenly and divine things.

For this reason, when the son returns after dissipation, the father restores to him the first robe of immortality [Note: This was especially the distinguishing mark of freedmen: that they were presented with a white garment and a ring. Tertullian, *On the Resurrection*, chapter 57; Lipsius, *Electa*, p. 1108; Johann Kircham, *On Rings* XV.16; Thomas, *On Practical Usage*, distinctions on ingenui and liberti XXVI.27, p. 14; Justinian, Novel 78: when he removed the distinction between freeborn persons and freedmen, he excepted the use of rings, which he wished to remain intact for them.], puts upon him the ring of freedom, kills the fattened calf, and changes the waters of repentance into the wine of grace, so that the pure cups of grace may now satisfy the banquet (Luke 15), and the sober intoxication of the Lord’s chalice may abolish the pains of conscience, the groans of repentance, and the laments of sins. As the prophet says: “And your intoxicating cup—how splendid it is!” (Psalm 22). For as earthly drunkenness is deformed, so heavenly drunkenness is splendid and beautiful.

He therefore said to the crowds going out to be baptized by him: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath? Therefore produce worthy fruits of repentance, and do not begin to say, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For I tell you that God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. For already the axe has been laid at the roots of the trees. Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire.”

“Brood of vipers.” He rebukes them by example, marks them by comparison, and reveals them through a figure, so that he may now change not merely their conduct but the very nature of their poisonous offspring. “Brood of vipers.” Those whom God had created human beings and made children of Abraham, wickedness brought forth and changed into vipers [Note: Christ calls the Jews “sons” or “offspring of vipers” by a Hebraism, as in “sons of rams.” Hence Chrysologus rightly calls them vipers. See Suicer, volume I, p. 754, where he explains the passage.]. Those whom the heavenly Creator had filled with the sweetness of compassion, impiety made capable of pouring forth deadly, bitter venom; and, with an unspeakable beginning of cruelty, made them conceived from the death of their father and born from the death of their mother.

“Brood of vipers.” An ungrateful offspring toward nature, whose birth is the destruction of its parent, whose life is the death of its parent.

“Brood of vipers.” At the time of conception, the viper is said to receive the head of its mate within its mouth and to bite it off, so that through bloody kisses it conceives not offspring but crime [Note: These things were once commonly asserted about the viper. Now hear more recent writers, for whom such claims have the character of a fable. Consult, if you wish, Mattioli on Dioscorides, where you will observe that this account arose from a misinterpretation of a passage in Aristotle. Basil also teaches similar things about the viper, volume II, p. 91C of the recent edition.]. It seems to give birth to the children of its crime like executioners, according to the order of vengeance, not of nature.

For offspring conceived from the father’s slaughter demand nourishment of blood before milk, and seek revenge. For vipers are said to tear open their mother’s womb and, in mature fury, to shatter the dwelling of their conception, still immature in its organs, so that for them life consists in not seeing their mother—the mother who gave them birth as such.

We have described and developed the type and figure more broadly than Saint John did, so that what the Jews are called by him in this manner may be a matter not of cursing but of truth.

“Brood of vipers.” This demonstrates, brothers, that the synagogue and its children were such. When Christ came to it with the affection of a husband, as John says, “He who has the bride is the bridegroom” (John 3), amid the embraces and bloody kisses of Judas the head of Christ was sought, and it was sought with the mouth when they said, “Crucify, crucify” (John 19).

Thus offspring conceived in blood are immediately armed for the destruction of their mother, so that, when the womb of the synagogue was torn open, they might run at John’s voice and be regenerated into the offspring of God.

“Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?” What is this coming wrath? It is the wrath that has no end, which does not release a person through death but binds him, nor permits him any longer to have hope of forgiveness once hell has assigned him to punishment.

Warned in this way, they recognize both their lineage and their crime, and therefore they answered, saying: “What shall we do in order to be saved?” He answered and said to them:

What he is about to say, brothers, I fear to say, lest the number of contemptuous hearers I see today should cause him to make an equal number of obstinate people. What shall I do? I fear to speak, but I cannot remain silent. One thing forbids me, another drives me: compassion, lest the hearer, while despising the warning, fall into ruin [Note: Many editions erroneously read: “lest the hearer, while despising, be unheard.”]; usefulness, lest someone who is going to act fail to hear, and thus the teacher give offense.

I say, brothers, so that the naked man may clothe himself and I may strip myself. “He who has two tunics,” he says, “let him give to one who has none; and he who has food, let him do likewise.”

Do you think he asks enough when he asks for one of two tunics? He does not ask enough, because he asks not for a jewel but for a tunic, not for gold but for bread. And if someone who has two tunics does not give one, he is guilty; what shall we say of one who refuses one out of many, who locks up his clothing and shuts away his bread so that the poor man may perish of hunger and be consumed by cold?

Such a man buries his clothes; he does not store them. He entrusts them not to careful keeping but to tombs: what he refuses to the poor, he gives to moths. He himself becomes the devourer of his own clothing, as the Lord says: “Their worm shall not die” (Isaiah 66), because the hunger of the poor has assailed Christ; the suffering of the human being has leapt into the inmost parts of God; the groaning of the captive has penetrated into Christ’s interior; the contempt shown to the needy has rebounded as an insult against his Creator. He himself declares this when he says: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was naked, and you did not clothe me” (Matthew 25).

Tax collectors also came, saying: “What shall we do?” Let the tax collectors hear: “Demand nothing more than what has been appointed for you.” He revealed what makes a tax collector guilty: demanding more. Whoever demands more is an exactor of fraud, not of tribute. Let them consider how guilty before God is the man who taxes one already exhausted and burdened, presses and fatigues him further through his fraud, adds to the debts of one scarcely able to meet what is owed, and increases what is not owed [Note: Correctly so: Christ does not condemn the taxes and lawful tributes imposed by rulers, provided that they are levied according to the laws of justice and equity; rather, he condemns exceeding the proper measure in exactions and extorting more than is just. See Grotius on this passage.].

Soldiers also came, saying: [Note: The soldiers whom John addressed were either from the forces of Herod Philip, or of Herod Antipas, or Jews serving in Roman camps. Those whom Chrysologus addresses were soldiers receiving pay under the emperor and stationed at Ravenna.] “And what shall we do?” And he said to them: “Do violence to no one, accuse no one falsely, and be content with your pay.”

The true soldier is the one who does not use violence but protects; who does not inflict false accusation but drives it away; who hastens to the king’s pay, not one who hastens to plunder.

Blessed John taught divine things in such a way that he did not disturb human institutions. He established the commonwealth; he did not remove it. He demonstrated that what he taught had been ordained by God, and that it was possible to practice and preserve justice.

But what difference there is between John’s baptism and Christ’s baptism, since it must be explained at greater length, we now leave unsaid.

[Note: See the Preface. That it was customary in the Church for visiting bishops to be invited to preach is shown by numerous examples; this custom was established by canon 33 of the Fourth Council of Carthage, *Councils*, volume II, p. 1440. Baronius, year 36, no. 13, p. 337 of the Lucca edition, and Ferrarius, *On Sermons*, Book II, chapter 5, p. 178, give many examples, which there is no time to reproduce here. Tillemont notes that this sermon may perhaps have been delivered outside the diocese of Ravenna.]

# SERMON CXXXVIII. On Peace.

It would indeed have been better, dearest brothers, if our common father and teacher had allowed our ignorance to remain concealed and had not exposed the poverty that until now has been covered in us by the veil of our own modesty [Note: Some think that the prelate praised here was the archbishop of Milan; but Tillemont likewise observes that this conjecture rests upon a failing support.]. It would have been better if one who abounds so richly in the spiritual treasures of teaching had not demanded the far-from-meager tribute of speech from a poor man’s little boat.

For what can a poor man offer to the rich, a stranger to citizens, or an uncultivated and ignorant man to the learned? Yet because we are compelled to obey commands, the same humility that seems to excuse us compels us to speak; it compels us to obey.

What, then, O devout people of the Lord, can we, poor and most unlearned though we are, offer you decently? Without doubt, peace, which our Lord Jesus Christ commands us to offer as we enter every house (Luke 10). Therefore, at the beginning of our greeting, we have entreated peace for you from the Lord [Note: Chrysostom’s practice of announcing solemn peace to the people is attested by Socrates, Book VI, chapter 14; Sozomen, Book VIII, chapter 18; and, from him, Nicephorus Callistus, Book XIII, chapter 16.], peace which must always be possessed and always prayed for [Note: The Vatican manuscript reads “always to be prayed for.”].

Not that faithless and unstable peace of this world, which is either sought for the sake of advantage or preserved out of fear, but the peace of Christ, which, according to the Apostle Paul, surpasses every mind and guards the hearts of believers (Philippians 4); peace nourished at the fruitful breasts of charity; peace, foster-child of faith and pillar of justice; peace, a suitable pledge of future hope; peace that unites those present and invites those absent; peace that reconciles earthly things with heavenly things and human things with divine things.

For thus the Apostle says: “Our Lord Jesus Christ has made peace through his blood, not only for the things on earth but also for the things in heaven” (Colossians 1).

This, dearest brothers, is what the wandering traveler has set before you, according to the strength of a poor traveler’s provisions, awaiting that he may be nourished together with you at the table of the powerful teacher by abundant and sumptuous dishes.

May the God of peace, who has joined earthly things to heavenly things, grant that we may think the same things toward one another and rejoice in complete unanimity, through Christ our Lord, through whom there is glory to God the almighty Father, for ever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON CXXXIX. On Forgiving a Brother’s Offense.

[Col. 0572D]

As gold lies hidden in the earth, so divine meaning is concealed in human words [Col. 0573A]. Therefore, whenever the Lord’s words are disclosed to us, let the mind awaken and the spirit attend, so that the understanding may enter the secret chamber of heavenly knowledge.

Let us hear why the Lord began today in this way. “Pay attention,” he says, “to yourselves” (Luke 17:3). What is the point of this unusual expression? Where is this admonition, contrary to ordinary usage, leading? “Pay attention,” he says, “to yourselves.” He pays attention to himself who does not intrusively, shamelessly, and inquisitively observe the actions of others. “Pay attention,” he says, “to yourselves.” The wandering eye, [Note: [Col. 0573D] The Caesena manuscript and the first Bologna edition read *passivus intuitus* (“passive gaze”).] the lustful gaze, the shameless look, does not notice its own ruin; it runs toward the falls of others and rushes upon them. Blind to its own crimes, it shines a light upon the errors of others; ignorant of its own evils, it is the accuser and witness of those belonging to others; lukewarm toward its own guilt, it burns and blazes against the examination of another, even an innocent person.

And, not to say much, as the Lord said [Col. 0573B]: “The eye, not seeing the beam in itself, sees the splinter in another” (Matthew 7:3). Is not the eye the author of transgression? “And the woman saw,” he says, “that the tree was good for food and pleasing to the eyes to behold” (Genesis 3:6). The gate of death, the torch of envy, the furnace of spite, it races through what belongs to another with the whole conflagration of desire, more swiftly than fire runs through dry and earthy grasses.

It is God’s work that the eye, opened in such a circular form, is narrowed into the extremely small pupil, so that it may see with moderation, not envy; foresee, not seize; look upon, not look down upon. Let it be the window of the soul, the mirror of the mind, the light of the body, the guide of the limbs—not the entrance of vices.

But let us return to what was said before. “Pay attention,” he says, “to yourselves.” He did not say “to yourself,” because whatever a person pays attention to in others, he pays attention to himself; and as much as one person sees in another, the other will see in him, as becomes clear from what follows: “If your brother sins against you,” he says, “rebuke him; and if he repents, forgive him.”

Come, man: at God’s command, forgive—yes, forgive sins. Be merciful toward offenses; toward sins committed against you, be the one who remits them. Only do not lose in yourself the insignia of divine power. Whatever you do not forgive in another, you will deny to yourself through another.

“If your brother sins against you,” he says, “rebuke him.” Rebuke him as a judge; forgive him as a brother. For charity joined to freedom, and freedom mingled with charity, both restrains terror and raises up a brother. A brother is in fever when he harms; he is near madness when he commits an offense; he is unaware of himself; he is alienated from humanity. Whoever does not assist him through compassion, whoever does not treat him through patience, whoever does not heal him through forgiveness, is not healthy: he is sick, he is infirm, he has no inward compassion, and is shown to be alien to human feeling.

Your brother rages: attribute it to illness, and help him as a brother. Attribute what is happening to fever, and you will not be able to charge the offense to your brother. Thus, prudently, you will assign blame to the infirmity and forgiveness to the brother, so that his health may return to your glory and his forgiveness redound to your reward.

“If your brother sins against you,” he says, “rebuke him; and if he repents, forgive him.” Let no one hearing these words assume a judgment for himself while remitting it, and in empty presumption impose a role upon the offending brother, thereby thinking it harsh to forgive offenses. Let a person consider himself a sinner and one who will sin; then he begins to love forgiveness rather than revenge.

You hear that you ought to forgive, but you do not hear that you ought to be forgiven. Tomorrow you too will sin against the one who sinned against you today. The one who was previously guilty before you will become your judge, and he will return forgiveness to you if you gave it. If you did not give it, he will either deny you forgiveness or, if he grants it, he will charge it more heavily to your account and place it among your debts rather than truly forgive it. [Note: The reading means that he will charge it more heavily to your account and place it among your debts than he will forgive it. MITA.]

Forgive the sinner; forgive the penitent, so that when you sin, forgiveness may be repaid to you rather than merely granted. [Col. 0574B] Forgiveness is always good, but then it is sweetest when it is owed. The one who forgives in advance has conquered punishment, forestalled the judge, escaped judgment, and already secured forgiveness for himself before he committed the offense.

“And if he sins against you seven times in a day, and seven times in a day turns back to you, saying, ‘I repent,’ you shall forgive him.” Why does the law bind forgiveness, restrict it by a number, and enclose it within a limit, when it so powerfully urges mercy and so graciously releases the debt? [Note: In the sense of sacred Scripture, the number seven is used for an indefinite number. See Maldonatus, observations on Matthew XVIII, nos. 21 and 22.] If seven times—why not eight? Does a number defeat grace? Does calculation obstruct goodness? Does one offense condemn to punishment the person whom seven offenses already entrusted to forgiveness? By no means. For just as the person who forgave seven times is blessed, so the person who forgave seventy times seven is more blessed.

Peter, forgetful of this commandment, asks the Lord: “If my brother sins against me, how often shall I forgive him? Seven times?” (Matthew 18:21). The Lord answered: “Not only seven times, but seventy times seven.” The prescribed number therefore does not narrow forgiveness but expands it. What the commandment limits, it leaves without limit to free choice, so that if you forgive as much as he commanded, there may be both obedience and reward. [Note: That is, the Lord’s command is that one forgive a sinning brother, and so forth. But suppose it is only up to the number seven: the one who forgives up to that number will receive the reward of obedience; whoever forgives beyond that number will receive the reward of supererogation, which is greater than the reward of obedience. For if it is good to forgive seven times, it will be best to forgive always and whenever a brother needs forgiveness. MITA.]

Yet the seventh number, which seems small, is found to be immense in its mystery. For the seventh number, proceeding through the days, makes the Sabbath, which the Lord blessed and appointed for rest, both from his own work and from human labor.

The seventh number, proceeding through [Note: Latinius reads “through weeks.”] octads, multiplies the weeks sevenfold, so that it concludes Pentecost for us with the solemnity of its mystery and then pours out the whole rain of the Holy Spirit upon the ecclesiastical harvest with heavenly sound.

When the seventh number hastens through the months, it consecrates the feasts of the seventh month for us with the complete holiness of fasting (Leviticus 23).

When the seventh number moves through the years, it makes weeks; it makes the year that grants rest to the earth and releases every bond of fraternal obligation (Deuteronomy 15).

When the seventh number of years completes its cycle of weeks, it brings the fiftieth year, called the jubilee, to the full measure of forgiveness and remission (Leviticus V), so that slavery may be removed and freedom return; so that the documents and records of debts may be broken; so that the debtor may rise again and the debt be buried; so that the field may return to the poor man, while everything the rich man has contracted through greed may perish.

And if the seventh number, multiplied through days, months, and years, has brought about the fullness of remission and forgiveness, let the Christian hearer consider and understand what the seventh number, multiplied by seventy times seven, can bring. Then truly the contract of credit and debt will cease; then the entire condition of slavery will truly be abolished; then that freedom, freedom without end, will come; then the eternal field, destined always to live, will return.

True remission will come then—yes, it will come—when even the necessity of sinning itself is abolished; when, impurity having perished, the world will truly be called clean; when life returns and death no longer exists; when Christ reigns and the devil has already perished.

Pray, brothers, that the Lord may increase our faith, so that we may be able to believe, see, and possess these good things.

[Note: That a feast of this kind, the Annunciation, was already celebrated in the Church from the third century is demonstrated by the many sermons preached on it by the holy Fathers: namely by Epiphanius, bishop of Constantia on the island of Cyprus; Chrysostom; Saint Acacius, bishop of Melitene; Saint Basil, bishop of Seleucia; Titus, bishop of Bostra; Anastasius, archbishop of Antioch; Hesychius, a presbyter of Jerusalem; and many others. On these, consult Combefis in the *Bibliotheca Concionatoria*. That it fell on 25 March is inferred from the Menologia, the Menaea, and the calendars of the Churches of the Russians, Egyptians, Syrians, Copts, and other Eastern peoples. The most ancient martyrologies of the Latin Church likewise have it; and Henschenius, besides the martyrologies from the age of Charles the Bald, such as those of Wandelbert, Ado, and Usuard, mentions others that record it. Thomasinus, *De Festis*, vol. II, book II, chapter 12, p. 299, followed by Baillet in the *Lives of the Saints* under 25 December, says that 25 March was established by the Fathers merely by common opinion, because the Conception precedes the Nativity by nine months. Father Honoratus attacks both positions in *Animadversiones in Regulam et Usum Critices*, vol. II, pp. 271–272. I do not know whether his arguments are strong enough to overturn the contrary opinion. The Tenth Council of Toledo transferred this feast to the eighth day before the Nativity of the Lord; the Spaniards celebrate that day under the title “Expectation,” and it is called the Feast of the O’s from its antiphons. The Church of Toledo retains both solemnities: the one in March, in order to follow the most holy institution of the Roman Church, and the other on the eighth day before the Nativity of the Lord. Whoever wants more about the feast of the Annunciation should consult the most eminent Lambertini, now Benedict XIV, *De Festis B. M. V.*, p. 11, § 29.]

## SERMON 140. On the Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin Mary

Let the clear sight of our eyes [Note: [Col. 0576C] The Caesena manuscript reads *purus intuitus* (“pure gaze”).] now be pure enough to gaze upon the radiance of the divine birth. For if the full health—or even purity—of our eyes scarcely endures the ray of the rising sun, how great a sincerity of inward sight must be prepared to bear the splendor of the Author who rises and radiates?

“But in the sixth month,” he says, “the angel Gabriel was sent to a city of Galilee named Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph” (Luke II). [Note: The one sent to Daniel and Zechariah was also sent to the Virgin, so that the whole task of announcing Christ’s coming to mortals may seem to have been entrusted to him alone. See Saint Gregory, *Homily 34 on the Gospels*.] The holy Evangelist identifies the place, the time, and the person, so that the truth of the account may be confirmed by the manifest indications of the events themselves.

“He was sent,” he says, “to a betrothed virgin.” To a virgin God sends a winged bearer. For the one who bears grace gives a pledge and receives a dowry; he brings back faith and bestows gifts of virtue, while immediately dissolving the pledge of the virginal consent. [Note: Nazianzen, in his oration on Christ’s Nativity, says that she was shown worthy of betrothal when Gabriel called her “FULL OF GRACE”: her abundance of graces is displayed, as it were, as the bridegroom’s pledge or dowry.] [Note: Or perhaps more clearly, “he releases the betrothal”—that is, he opens it by removing what was, as it were, a bond; or he returns the pledge of the virginal consent to God. MITA.]

The messenger flies swiftly to the bride, so that he may keep and withdraw from God’s bride the attachment of human betrothal. He does not take the virgin away from Joseph, but returns her to Christ, to whom she was pledged in the womb when she was being formed. [Note: From this passage Mita derives evidence for the doctrine of the Immaculate Conception of the Mother of God. He wishes Mary to be said to have been pledged to Christ as soon as she began to be formed, so that she might never be said to have been pledged to the devil, even for a time.]

Christ therefore receives his own bride; he does not seize another’s. Nor does he cause a separation, [Note: The manuscripts of Caesena and Vallicella read: “he suddenly joins the creature to himself in one body.”] when he joins the whole of his own creation to himself in one body.

But let us hear what the angel did. “Entering to her, he said: ‘Hail, full of grace; the Lord is with you.’” In this utterance there is an offering, an offering of a gift, [Col. 0576B] not merely the duty of a simple greeting. [Note: Others, on the contrary, think that this was a simple greeting. See Lightfoot in his *Harmony*.]

“Hail.” That is: receive grace. Do not tremble; do not be anxious about nature.

“Full of grace.” Because in others there is grace, but in you the fullness of grace will come entirely. [Note: Thus Arias Montanus, from the Syriac, Arabic, and Persian versions: *Κεχαριτωμένη*, “full of grace and favor.”]

“The Lord is with you.” What does “the Lord is with you” mean? He does not come to you merely to visit, but enters into you in the new mystery of birth.

He appropriately added: “Blessed are you among women.” For in the very wombs where Eve, accursed, suffered punishment, blessed Mary then rejoices, is honored, and is held in esteem. And by grace she truly became now the mother of the living, though by nature she had become the mother of the dying.

“When she heard this, she was troubled at his saying.” What does it mean that she sees the person but is troubled by the words? The angel had come gentle in appearance, [Note: So read several editions and the Vatican manuscript. Mita reads *fortis in verbo*, “strong in speech.” I have retained the editors’ reading because of Gregory’s statement, *Homily 34 on Luke*, vol. II, p. 124 of the Paris edition: “Gabriel is sent to Mary, who is called the strength of God. He was coming to announce the one who, for the defeat of the powers of the air, deigned to appear in humility.”] strong in battle, gentle in manner, terrifying in speech, displaying what was human and promising what was divine. [Note: Showing something human to the light and to human sight, but promising divine things in words—that is, promising them in reality. MITA.]

Thus the hearing greatly troubled the virgin whom the sight had lightly disturbed; and the authority of the sender, with its full weight, shook the woman whom the presence of the one sent had moved only slightly.

And what more? She immediately felt the heavenly Judge being received within her, where earlier she had already seen and contemplated the heavenly surveyor. [Note: He calls the angel a *metator*, for a *metator* is a forerunner who goes ahead of a leader and marks out the places where dwellings and camps are to be established. See the notes on Sermons 91 and 127.]

Although by a gentle movement and with pious affection God was turning the virgin into his mother and the Lord was turning his servant into his parent, nevertheless her womb was troubled, her mind recoiled, and her very condition trembled, when God—whom all creation cannot contain—received and concealed himself wholly within a human breast.

“And she was considering,” he says, “what kind of greeting this might be.” Let your charity attend, as we have said, to the fact that the Virgin consented to the greeting—not merely to the words but to the realities—and that the voice was not an act of ordinary courtesy but possessed the whole force of heavenly virtue.

The Virgin therefore considers, because to answer quickly is characteristic of human superficiality, whereas to consider is the mark of the greatest deliberation and mature judgment. [Note: The Geometer in the Greek *Catena*: “Having heard the joyful message, she examined it; she neither openly resisted through unbelief nor immediately obeyed out of thoughtlessness.”]

He does not sufficiently know how great God is who does not marvel at this Virgin’s mind and wonder at her spirit. Heaven fears, angels tremble, creation cannot bear it, nature is not sufficient. Yet one young woman so receives and contains God in the chamber of her breast and delights in giving him hospitality [Col. 0577B], that for the rent of that house she demands peace for the earth, glory for the heavens, salvation for the lost, life for the dead, kinship between earthly and heavenly things, and the commerce of God himself with flesh; that for payment of the womb she acquires and fulfills the prophet’s saying: “Behold, the inheritance of the Lord is children, the fruit of the womb his reward” (Psalm 126:3). [Note: The Caesena manuscript reads: “She receives him in the chamber of her own breast and delights in his hospitality.” Other copies read: “She contains him in the little treasury of her own breast and delights in him.”]

But let the sermon now come to an end, so that, with God granting it and time allowing, we may speak more pleasantly about the Virgin’s childbirth.

## SERMON 141. On the Incarnation of Christ

How secret is the royal bedchamber; with what reverence and trembling the place is regarded where the very power of the prince rests; how no outsider, no unclean person, no unbeliever is granted or permitted access there; how pure, chaste, and faithful are the services that await there—all this is taught by the manifest insignia of the imperial court. [Note: Chamberlains stood ready to keep the unworthy away; at times they also performed the functions of armed guards. See Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXVII.]

Who is base enough to approach the very doors of the palace? Who is unworthy enough to draw near? Certainly no one is admitted to the bridegroom’s chamber unless he is sufficiently close, sufficiently intimate, of good conscience, reputable, and of a credible life.

Within the bedchamber itself, God admits only the virgin; only unviolated virginity is received. Therefore, O man, instructed by these examples, consider who you are, how great you are, and what kind of person you are. Then at last consider whether you can penetrate the secret of the Lord’s birth; whether you deserve to reach the chamber of that breast where the entire majesty of the heavenly King, the whole majesty of divinity, rests; whether you ought rashly, as an investigator, to examine with human eyes and bodily senses the conception of the virgin; whether you can, as a bold and inquisitive observer, look upon the very hands of God forming for himself a holy temple of the body within the mother’s womb; whether you can strip bare before your eyes a mystery hidden for ages and reveal to yourself the sacrament invisible even to the angels. [Note: The angel possesses no natural knowledge of the mystery of the Incarnation, but knows it through God’s revelation. Ambrose, *On the Faith to Gratian*; Augustine, book IV, chapter 1. MITA.]
