Can you preside over the heavenly work in such a way that you clearly discover how God entered the inner chamber of closed flesh; how he painted the features of the sacred body within that venerable womb [Col. 0578B] without the Virgin’s awareness; how he solidified bones destined to remain for ages without the consciousness of the woman conceiving; how, beyond the order of man, he produced the true form of man; how, beyond the concern of flesh, he assumed the whole truth of flesh; how, beyond the nature of our flesh, he received its complete condition? [Note: Variant reading: “the nature of our flesh.”]

And if free access to these things is not opened to you, was God then unable to assume from flesh what in the beginning he assumed from clay? Certainly not. For since everything is possible for God, while you cannot reach even the smallest of God’s works, do not investigate the Virgin’s conception; believe instead. Piously understand that God willed to be born, because you do him an injury if you demand an explanation. Receive the great mystery of the Lord’s birth by faith, because without faith you cannot attain even the least of God’s works, as Scripture says: “All his works are in faith” (Psalm 32).

But here you want everything to stand by reason. [Note: The first Bologna edition reads: “You strive to establish everything by reason.”] Yet everything rests upon faith—not without reason, but by God’s reason, not by yours, O man. What is more reasonable than that God should be able to do whatever he wills? If he cannot do what he wills, he is not God.

Therefore what God commands, [Note: Other copies read: “the angel announces.”] the angel carries out; the Spirit fulfills; power accomplishes; the Virgin believes; nature receives; the heavens proclaim; the firmament announces; the stars display; the Magi preach; the shepherds adore; the animals recognize, as the prophet bears witness: “The ox knows its owner, and the ass its master’s manger” (Isaiah 1:3). [Note: From these words some have been persuaded that Isaiah was not reproaching the slowness of the Jews and their ingratitude toward God, their benefactor, by the example of the ox and the ass as slower animals; rather, they thought he was pointing specifically to an ox and an ass that recognized the Lord of all, newly born in the manger. Chrysologus must be counted among these, as you see. Other Fathers interpret the passage very differently, especially Jerome, most explicitly, in his commentary on Isaiah 1. They also attribute similar words to Chrysostom’s Homily 32, volume VI of his works. But no critic who has touched the matter even lightly has failed to class that homily among the spurious. Nevertheless, Chrysologus should be excused if he held the same view that we read in Origen, Ambrose, Gregory Nazianzen, Gregory of Nyssa, Cyril of Jerusalem, Paulinus, Prudentius, and others. More discerning critics know that those Fathers spoke figuratively and allegorically, understanding by the symbol of the ox and ass, beasts accustomed to the yoke, the shepherds—Jews by race and religion—accustomed to bearing the burden of the Mosaic law; they understood from the sign given by the angel that the Lord had been born.]

You, O man, if you do not recognize him immediately with the angels, recognize him at least, however slowly, with the beasts, lest while you delay you be placed below the very animals with which you were formerly compared.

Behold, the animals fawn with their tails, flatter with their ears, lick with their tongues, and by whatever movement they can confess that their Creator has come, contrary to nature, into your nature. Yet you, together with the Jews, examine and criticize him—those who excluded their Lord from their inns, while the animals received him in their own mangers.

Therefore, if at last you are going to offer a pious hearing even to the angels, accept what must be said by the angel, if not happily then at least reverently. This sufficiently necessary sermon, holy brothers, compels us to defer it today and set it forth in the following sermon. [Note: This was formerly a title by which the faithful were honored.]

[Note: This sermon is entitled “On the Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin Mary,” a feast that Pope Sergius seems to have remembered: “He established that on the days of the Annunciation of the Lord, the Nativity, and so forth …” Rosweidus argues that this refers to the Nativity of the Lord, not to the angel’s Annunciation to his Mother, but others note that he made a serious and shameful error. Gregory Thaumaturgus, in his second oration on the Annunciation, seems to place it before all other solemnities. Yet men of sound judgment rightly doubt whether these three orations are genuine. See Sermon 140, note a.]

## SERMON 142. On the Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin Mary

You have heard today, dearly beloved brothers, an angel treating with a woman about the restoration of humanity. You have heard that the matter was arranged so that man might return to life by the same steps [Note: Other copies read: “by the same degrees.”] by which he had slipped away into death. The angel deals with Mary concerning salvation because an angel had dealt with Eve concerning ruin.

You have heard an angel constructing, by an ineffable art, a temple of divine majesty from the clay of our flesh. You have heard God placed on earth and man placed in heaven through an incomprehensible mystery. You have heard God and man mingled in one body by an unheard-of process. [Note: This is directed against Eutyches, as has often been observed, and against the errors of Valentinus, Manes, and Apollinaris, none of whom admitted the reality of Christ’s human flesh. See similar passages in Hilary, *On Psalm 6*, no. 12, and *On the Trinity*, no. 11.]

You have heard the fragile nature of our flesh strengthened by an angelic exhortation to bear the whole glory of divinity. Finally, lest the delicate sand of our body in Mary should collapse beneath so great a weight of heavenly construction, [Note: The Caesena manuscript reads: “and lest the slender virgin rod bearing the fruit of the whole human race should break.”] and lest the slender branch, in the virgin who was to bear the fruit of the whole human race, should break, the angel’s voice immediately preceded it to drive away fear, saying: “Do not be afraid, Mary” (Luke 1:30).

Before announcing the matter, the dignity of the virgin is proclaimed through her name. For *Maria* in Hebrew, in Latin, is called “lady.” [Note: Some derive the name Mary from the Syriac word meaning “lady”; others from the Hebrew *marum*, meaning “excellent” and “sublime.” See Suicer, *Thesaurus Ecclesiasticus*, vol. II, p. 303.] The angel therefore calls her “lady,” so that the trembling of servitude may leave the mother of the Lord; the authority of her own offspring caused and obtained that she should be born and called “lady.”

“Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found grace.” It is true: whoever has found grace does not know how to fear.

“You have found grace.” With whom? With God. Blessed is she who alone among human beings deserved to hear this above all others.

“You have found grace.” How much? As he had said earlier: full. And truly full, for she would pour out and infuse all creation with a generous rain. [Note: Alternatively: “with whom.”]

“For you have found grace with God.” When he says this, even the angel marvels—whether that a woman alone, or that all humanity, has deserved life through a woman. The angel is astonished that the whole of God should enter the narrow confines of a virgin’s womb, though all creation is narrow for him.

This is why the angel lingers; this is why he addresses the Virgin in terms of merit and grace; this is why he scarcely reveals the cause to the listener, so that he may advance her understanding, and scarcely composes his speech after her long trembling. [Note: Do not say that the conversation lasted until the ninth hour; that was an invention of Antonius Belingerus in his book *On the Guardian Angel*. Even more laughable is Rutilius Benzonius, who dreamed that Gabriel, in greeting Mary, had sung musically a most sweet and rather lengthy hymn or song. These are truly absurd fantasies.]

Consider, brothers, with what reverence and trembling it is fitting and proper for us to stand before so great a mystery, when the angel himself dispels the hearer’s fear only with fear.

“Behold, you will conceive in your womb.” You will conceive well: something unknown to flesh, impossible to ordinary condition, and not admitted by nature.

“Behold, you will conceive in your womb.” Who has reached fruit before experiencing the labor and sweat of the earth? Who gathers apples before the plant contributes and expends its own effort? [Note: Suicer praises these words in the *Thesaurus Ecclesiasticus*, vol. II, p. 415, at the end.] Who reaches any dwelling apart from the road? Who receives growth beyond nature and outside nature?

Blessed, therefore, and truly blessed is Mary, who, beyond the cares of generation and beyond the distress of maternal pain, attained such glory of offspring. Blessed is she who received and preserved the divine pledge in her breast in such a way that the whole exterior of her body did not know it. Blessed is she who entrusted and committed to her mind alone what she had received from above through the angel’s report. [Note: Alternatively: “through the one who conveyed it.”]

Within the Virgin’s house the heavenly work is carried out in such a way that, while the barriers remain, the enclosed house itself does not perceive it.

“You will conceive and bear a son.” He who enters and departs, leaving no trace of his entrance or exit, is a divine inhabitant, not a human one; and he who preserves the virgin through his conception and leaves her a virgin through his birth is not an earthly man but a heavenly one.

Let the order of our flesh therefore withdraw. Here our nature may claim nothing for itself, where, for the divine offspring, a heavenly order is being established within the divine nature. Let the words “conception” and “birth” not weary the hearer’s mind or lightly move the Christian’s understanding [Note: Other copies read: “the Christian [understanding].”], where the divine signs of God’s power are being accomplished for the heavenly offspring. [Note: Alternatively: “where the insignia of divine power are being performed.”]

“You will conceive and bear a son.” He did not say “to you”; he said “yours” [reading uncertain]. Why? “Because he will be called the Son of God.”

Grace made you a mother, O Virgin, not nature. Piety wished you to be called mother, though integrity did not permit it. In your conception, in your childbirth, modesty increased, chastity grew, virginity was strengthened, and every virtue endured. [Note: The most common opinion among the ancient Fathers acknowledges the Blessed Virgin’s perpetual integrity. See Jerome, *Against Helvidius*, chapter 9; Origen, *Homily 7 on Luke*; Constantine the Great, *Oration to the Assembly of the Saints*, chapter 19; Epiphanius, *Against Heresies*, 78.7; Augustine, if the work is his, *On Heresies*, chapter 56. Basnagius refutes Helvidius’s argument, vol. I, p. 106. Tertullian, *On the Veiling of Virgins*, says that this is established even if Hebion resists. After Helvidius and Hebion, we know that Jovinian uttered the same things.]

Virgin, if everything remains safe for you, what have you given? If a virgin, how are you a mother? If a bride, how are you a mother? The one through whom everything was increased for you diminished nothing, O Virgin.

Virgin, your Creator is conceived from you; [Note: Barthius praises these words and illustrates them with almost identical expressions from other Fathers in *Adversaria*, book I, chapter 7, p. 14.] your origin arises from you; [Note: Alternatively: “in your womb.”] your begetter is in your offspring; your God is in your flesh; and he himself, who gave light to the world, received through you the light of the world. [Note: Some editions read: “He gave it to us through you.”]

Warned, therefore, by the angel, O Virgin, do not presume to call this one your son, but as soon as you have given birth, invoke the Savior. [Note: Latinius observes that these words must be read and explained cautiously: do not presume to regard him as a son in the manner of a humanly begotten child; rather, invoke and beseech him as your Savior.]

For virginity does not give birth to a son for itself; it gives birth to the pledge of its Creator, and integrity bears its Lord, not its foster-child. As the angel says: “And you shall call his name Jesus,” which in Latin is called “Savior.”

Then Mary said to the angel: “How will this happen?” Behold, Mary asks. If the person who asks doubts, why does only Zechariah incur blame as a querulous questioner? Because the knower of hearts examined not the words but the hearts; he judged not what they had said but what they had felt. For the cause of the questioners was different, and their outward appearance entirely unlike.

She believed what was contrary to nature; he doubted what concerned nature. She sought the order of an intact reality; he declared that what God commanded could not happen. He did not approach faith despite the examples urging him toward it; she hastened to faith without an example. She marveled at the birth of a virgin; he argued about conception within marriage.

Therefore she rightly speaks, rightly recognizes and confesses God in her body; he is silent until, convicted, he restores John—whom he had denied—from his own body. [Col. 0581C]

“How will this happen?” Why? “Because I do not know a man.”

Woman, what man are you seeking—the man whom you lost in Paradise? Restore the man, woman; restore God’s deposit; restore from yourself the one whom you lost through yourself. Set aside the order of nature; recognize the order of the Creator.

He will assume from you and make a man, the one who in the beginning made you and assumed you from a man. Do not seek a man; let the work of man cease, because divine skill is sufficient for the restoration of humanity.

This is why God himself comes to you: because you regretted having approached a man. [Note: Mita vainly twists himself into knots here, for the Author is speaking of Eve, not Mary.]

No longer flesh to flesh; rather, “the Holy Spirit will come upon you.” For “what is born of flesh is flesh, and what is born of Spirit is spirit” (John 3:6). Therefore the one who is born of the Spirit is without controversy God, because the Spirit is God.

“The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.” The power of God overshadows her, lest human frailty, bearing God, collapse. [Note: According to some, by the words “the power of the Most High will overshadow you,” the angel explains the mode of the operation: it consists in God’s divine protection, without which the divine Majesty would have consumed her; this is Chrysologus’s meaning. See *Synopsis Sacrorum Criticorum*, vol. IV, p. 817, at the beginning.]

“The power of the Most High will overshadow you.” [Note: See Saint Thomas, part III, question 27, article 4, where he teaches that the Blessed Virgin had no inclination toward sin.]

The heat of our body does not know how the shadow of divine power protects her; nor does she inquire into the secret of earthly dwelling, for she sees herself enclosed beneath the covering of heavenly splendor.

“Therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God.” Let no one understand “holy” here in the ordinary sense, but in that singular sense in which it is proclaimed in heaven: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts” (Isaiah 6:3).

Mary is sent to Elizabeth: a virgin to a barren woman, an infant to an old woman, so that in a pious contest both may receive and attain alike—the one faith from novelty, the other strength from necessity.

After hearing these things, Mary replied: “Behold, the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word.” She whom the angel calls “lady” recognizes and confesses herself to be a handmaid. For a devoted spirit grows toward service through the bonds of benefits; it increases toward grace, does not leap into arrogance, and does not swell into pride. [Note: “The bonds of benefits”—that is, the bands or cords of favors.]

“Let it be done to me according to your word.” [Note: Alternatively: “because she believes.”] Because she believes the word, she rightly conceives the Word: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). She reaches the whole reality because by hearing she consents to the secret of faith. [Note: The Blessed Virgin reached the perfect incarnation of the Word and became the Mother of God, because by her own hearing she ascended, as though by the steps of a ladder, to the summit of faith. MITA.]

How great is the sin of the heretic who does not believe after the event, when he sees that she believed before the event!

[Note: Consult the preface.]

## SERMON 143. On the Same Subject
You are indeed owed a sermon for the Nativity, but it is more fitting to believe the ineffable mystery of the Lord’s Nativity than to recount it. A virgin gave birth. What nature does not possess, custom does not know, reason does not comprehend, the mind cannot grasp, heaven is awestruck by, earth is astonished at, and creation marvels at—how will human speech narrate it? In the end, just as the Evangelist discloses the Virgin’s conception and the Virgin’s childbirth in human language, so he closes them with a divine mystery, and he does this so that a human being may not presume to investigate what he has been commanded to believe.

Who can approach the mystery of God: the Virgin’s childbirth, the causes of things, the working of the ages, the union of divinity and flesh, one God who is both human and divine? The Evangelist says:

“An angel Gabriel was sent by God to a city of Galilee whose name was Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph; and the virgin’s name was Mary” (Luke 1).

An angel was sent by God.

[Note: Barthius, *Adversaria*, book 58, chapter 6, column 2733, gives this passage and says that *mediator* (“mediator”) was also used by others for *legatus* (“envoy”).]

Where the angel is the mediator, let human opinion fall silent; where the messenger is heavenly, let earthly interpretation be driven away. Let human curiosity grow numb where an interpreter from above is present. An angel was sent by God. Whoever listens more attentively, because he was sent by God, shrinks from probing the secret of the Godhead. What God commands through an angel deserves to be known by the one who fears to know it.

Hear the Lord saying: “Upon whom shall I look, if not upon the humble, the gentle, and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isaiah 66, according to the Septuagint). Humble and gentle: as gentle as the one who obeys commands, so harsh is the one who scrutinizes commands.

An angel was sent to a virgin. For virginity is always akin to angels. To live in the flesh beyond the flesh is not an earthly life but a heavenly one. And if you wish to know: to acquire angelic glory is greater than to possess it; to be an angel is a matter of blessedness, to be a virgin a matter of virtue. For virginity obtains by strength what an angel possesses by nature. Thus the angel and the virgin perform a divine service, not a human one.

“The angel entered,” he says, “and said to her: ‘Hail, full of grace; the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women.’”

“Hail, full of grace; the Lord is with you.” You see with what gifts the virgin has been entrusted.

“Hail, full of grace; the Lord is with you.” “Hail”—that is, “receive.” What? The powers of gifts, not the loss of modesty.

“Hail, full of grace.” This is the grace that gave glory to heaven, God to the earth, faith to the nations, an end to vices, an order for life, and discipline for conduct. The angel brought this grace; the Virgin received salvation, which she would return to the ages.

“Hail, full of grace.” Grace has been bestowed upon individuals in portions, but upon Mary the fullness of grace gave itself wholly and all at once. “We have all received,” says the Evangelist, “from his fullness” (John 1). Hence David also says: “He descended like rain upon fleece” (Psalm 71).

Although fleece comes from the body, it does not know the sufferings of the body; so virginity, although it exists in the flesh, is ignorant of the vices of the flesh. Thus the heavenly rain poured itself upon the virgin fleece in a gentle descent, and the entire wave of divinity concealed itself in the absorbent fleece of our flesh, until, expressed upon the cross, it poured forth upon all the earth as a rain of salvation.

“And like drops that drip upon the earth” (ibid.), so that, distributed in life-giving drops, the seasons might water the shoots of faith rather than destroy them.

“Hail, full of grace; the Lord is with you.” An angel was sent by God, and what does he say? “The Lord is with you.”

[Note: Someone might perhaps suppose that Chrysologus believed Mary had already conceived the Lord Christ when the angel greeted her; they think this may be inferred from Jerome’s Letter 190 to Principia: “Holy Mary, because she had conceived him in whom all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily, is greeted as full of grace.” Yet I would find it very difficult to believe that Jerome, Chrysologus, or any others, if there are others, departed from the correct sense of the Gospel in so clear a matter and contradicted other Fathers who believe that Christ was conceived by the Virgin only at the close of the conversation and after the Virgin’s assent—namely Augustine, *Sermon 18 on the Saints*; Gregory the Great, *Moralia*, book 18, chapter 27; Basil of Seleucia, *Oration on the Annunciation*; John Damascene, *On the Orthodox Faith*, book 3, chapter 11; Bernard, *Sermon 4 on “Missus est”*; Sedulius, book 11 of the *Paschal Poem*; Prudentius, in the poem *Against the Homuncionites*; Rupert, book 1 of *On the Works of the Holy Spirit*, chapter 9, and others. Therefore Chrysologus’s, Jerome’s, and similar testimonies must be softened and redirected to the orthodox sense. Consult the very learned Serry, *Exercitation* 27, page 180, where he discusses these matters at greater length.]

Therefore he was with the Virgin who had sent him to the Virgin. God preceded his messenger, but did not withdraw from God: he cannot be confined by places who is present in all places, and who is wholly everywhere, without whom nothing is whole.

“Blessed are you among women.”

Truly blessed is the virgin who possesses both the glory of virginity and bears the dignity of a mother. Truly blessed is she who earned the grace of a heavenly conception and carried away the crown of integrity. Truly blessed is she who received the glory of a divine offspring and became queen of all chastity. Truly blessed is she who was greater than heaven, stronger than earth, and wider than the world; for she alone contained the God whom the world cannot contain. She carried him who carries the universe, gave birth to her own begetter, and nourished the nourisher of all living things.

But let us see what the Evangelist says: “When Mary saw the angel, she was troubled at his word.” The flesh was troubled, the inward parts were shaken, the mind trembled, and the entire depth of the heart was stunned, because at the angel’s entrance the virgin sensed the entrance of divinity. The temple of the human body was troubled, and the confines of the bodily dwelling were shaken, when the whole greatness of God concealed itself in the virgin breast.

But, if you please, before we penetrate the mystery of Christian faith, let us address those who refer the virgin’s childbirth, the great mystery of piety, and the restoration of human salvation to an injury inflicted upon the Godhead.

God came to the Virgin—that is, the craftsman to his work, the Creator to his creature. When does the restoration of a work not redound to the craftsman’s honor? When is honor not reckoned as glory, if the maker repairs his handiwork? To prevent anyone from losing his work, does he not restore it when it grows old, raise it when it falls, and reform it for the better when it is destroyed?

Therefore what takes place in the Virgin’s childbirth is not an injury to the Creator but salvation for the creature. If God made the human being, who can accuse him for remaking him? And what is rightly believed to have been formed from clay—why should it be judged unworthy to have been re-formed from flesh? What is more precious, flesh or clay? Therefore, the more precious the material of our restoration, the greater its glory.

Or when is God not the fashioner of a human being in the womb? Hear Job: “Your hands made and fashioned me. And afterward: ‘As cheese you curdled me; you clothed me with bones and sinews; you granted me life and mercy’” (Job 10). And David: “You fashioned me and placed your hand upon me” (Psalm 138). And God says to Jeremiah: “Before you were in the womb, I knew you, and in the womb I sanctified you” (Jeremiah 1).

If, then, he painted Job’s features in his mother’s womb; if he joined David’s limbs together in his mother’s womb; if he sanctified Jeremiah in his mother’s womb; if he filled John, though his mother was barren, with the Holy Spirit in the womb—what is surprising now if he dwelt in a virgin’s womb, who took a woman from the side of a man? The same one who formed a virgin from a man’s body took a man anew from a woman’s womb. Thus, human being, what seems new to you is ancient with God.

But you say: What necessity of being born could God have, when he possessed the power to create?

What necessity? So that by being born he might restore the very nature that he had made by his work. For the nature that had been made in order to generate for life was itself generating for death. Through the sin of the first human being, nature received a deadly wound and began to be the origin of death, although it had been the beginning of life.

This, then, is the purpose of the birth that compelled Christ to be born: that the birth of the author might provide care for nature, and that the healing of nature might be the enlivening of his children.

## SERMON CXLIV. On the Same Subject

The greatness of the subject and the magnitude of the mystery make us postpone our sermon on Christ’s birth until the day after tomorrow. A virgin gave birth—who will speak? The Word became flesh—who will narrate it? If the Word of God gives an infant’s cry, how will an imperfect human being cry out in speech?

As great a light as a star gave those seeking light in the night, so great a clarity does the teacher’s discourse on the Lord’s birth offer its hearers, so that they may rejoice at having found Christ, but not presume to run about in search of him; so that they may honor infancy with gifts, not diminish it.

But pray, brothers, that he who gradually grew in our body may also graciously grow gradually in our speech.

Today the Evangelist reported that the angel spoke as follows: “Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found grace with God” (Luke 1).

“Do not be afraid, Mary.” Why? Because you have found grace. The one who has found is not afraid; the one who has lost is afraid. She found—she found grace by conceiving a heavenly offspring, and by giving birth she did not lose the insignia of virginity.

“Do not be afraid, Mary.” What does she fear, who conceives the security of all things and gives birth to the joys of the ages? There is no fear where the work is divine, not human; where there is consciousness of power, not of shame. What does she fear, who received him whom all feared things fear? What does she fear,

[Note: That is, she who has obtained the Judge to whom the perpetual defense of her same freedom has been entrusted from heaven.]

whose judge is the advocate of her case, whose integrity is the witness of her innocence?

“Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found grace with God” (John 1).

The Word who was in the beginning with God,

[Note: Latinius’s emendation. The printed editions have: “the Word God.”]

the Virgin found within herself; and she who was a small lodging for humanity became a great temple of divinity. What the smallness of the human body could not contain, the greatness of the virginal womb began to contain.

“Behold,” he says, “you will conceive in your womb.”

For the sake of reverence, it would have been enough to say “you will conceive.” What does the addition “in your womb,” which he emphasizes, mean? It means that the conception would be a reality, not a figure; that the childbirth would be actual, not an image; that just as true God was born from true God, so the truth of a human body would be born from a true conception.

At Christ’s birth, brothers, the injury to the human body was removed, not its nature; the creature was not destroyed, but sin was condemned.

There is therefore a heresy

[Note: The impious doctrine that Christ put on an aerial body, compacted from the substances of the higher world, belonged to Apelles, a disciple of Marcion. Tertullian rose against him in *On the Prescription of Heretics*, chapter 51, page 343, and in *On the Flesh of Christ*, chapter 8, calls his followers Apellitans. Augustine calls them Apellitae in *On Heresies to Quodvultdeus*, chapter 23; Epiphanius calls them Apelleians in heresy 44, page 166. Theodoretus says of the same doctrine in *Compendium of Heretical Fables*, book 1, chapter 25, page 211: “He attributed to Christ a body not human, but from the substance of the world.”]

that falsely claims Christ assumed an aerial body and invents that he did not possess flesh but merely pretended to be human.

[Note: Various persons fostered this heresy: Simon, Menander, Marcion, Valentinus, Basilides, Bardesanes, Cerdo, Manes. See Theodoretus, *Compendium of Heretical Fables*, book 4, chapter 11, page 278; the same author, Letter 104, page 975; Chrysostom, *Homily 8 on Matthew*, page 52; Ignatius, *Letter to the Trallians*, page 13; Basil, *On the Human Generation of Christ*, page 589, on Matthew 1:20; Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 1, chapter 22, page 185; Photius, final letter, page 381; Leontius, *On the Sects*, act 3, page 434. The Gnostics must also be included here, since Epiphanius, heresy 26, page 45, writes that they taught that Christ was not born from Mary but manifested through Mary; that he did not assume flesh, but that he was merely an appearance or an illusion.]

“You will conceive in your womb and give birth to a son, and you will call his name Jesus.”

What is called *Jesus* in Hebrew, and *Sōtēr* (Σωτήρ) in Greek, is called *Salvator* in Latin—that is, “Savior.”

[Note: See *Synopsis Sacrae Criticae*, volume 4, pages 34–35. In sacred usage, *Sospitator* (“Preserver” or “Deliverer”) is more customary.]

Rightly, then, all things are safe for the Virgin, who gave birth to the Savior of all. “And you will call his name Jesus,” because in this name the whole majesty of the Godhead is adored. All who dwell in heaven, all who inhabit the earth, and all who are held in the depths of hell bow before this name and adore it.

Hear the Apostle saying: “So that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Philippians 2:10). This name gave sight to the blind, hearing to the deaf, walking to the lame, speech to the mute, and life to the dead; and by the power of this name it drove out the whole power of the devil from possessed bodies. And if the name alone has such power, how great must the power itself be?

But who is this one who is called by this name? Let the angel now say it.

“And he will be called Son of the Most High.”

[Note: God is called “Most High” here, and also in Genesis 14:18; Psalm 82:7; and Mark 5:7.]

You see that what the Virgin conceives is not an earthly offspring but a heavenly one. The Virgin gave birth, but God received the Son. Therefore whoever argues about this birth in a human manner aims at every possible injury to such a parent.

“And the Lord God will give him,” he says, “the throne of David his father.”

[Note: He is striking at the Arians.]

Here the heretic gives birth to the clouds of his unbelief; here he fabricates material for his error. “Behold,” he says, “I am not speaking, but the angel is: ‘The Lord God will give him.’ Is the one who gives not greater than the one who receives? And the one who receives did not possess before he received.”

But let us hear these things, brothers, not as unbelievers but as faithful people; and let what is an occasion of error for them be an argument of faith for us.

“The Lord God will give him.” Who gives, and to whom does he give? Clearly, God gives to the human being; divinity gives to flesh.

“The Lord God will give him.” Which God? Clearly, the Word who was in the beginning and was always God. To whom does he give? To him who became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1).

Hear the Apostle saying: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (1 Corinthians 15)—to himself, certainly, and not to another.

Therefore this God, who was in Christ, gave the kingdom to himself in Christ and conferred upon the body he had assumed what he had always possessed through his divinity, as is demonstrated by the angel’s own words:

“The Lord God will give him the throne of David his father.”

You see that when he receives, he is called David’s son; when he gives, he is called the Son of God. He himself said: “All things that the Father has are mine” (John 16). And what necessity is there for receiving where there is the power of possessing? He says, “All things that the Father has are mine.” Who receives what is his own? Or is it a gift of the giver if what is given belongs to the recipient?

We confess that he received—but let the one who was born, who assumed flesh, who assumed infancy, who endured the cradle, who assumed the stages of life, who endured labor, who felt hunger, who suffered thirst, who did not shrink from so many kinds of injuries,

[Note: According to Latinius. The printed editions have: “every kind of injury.”]

who climbed the cross, who underwent death, who entered the tomb—heretic, ascribe to this one what he received.

Do you think that he disdains receiving honor from God, who received such injuries from human beings? Or do you suppose that he is reluctant to receive a kingdom from the Father, who received punishments and death from his enemies?

Heretic, if you understand that what belongs to injury, infancy, age, time, giving, receiving, diminution, and death belongs not to the divinity but to the body, you will inflict no injury upon the Son and will create no distinction within the Trinity.

But let us return to ourselves and now speak of what belongs to us.

“He will give him,” he says, “the throne of David his father, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.”

[Note: The Fathers agree in wishing “the house of Jacob” to signify the Church and the faithful.]

He who has always sat with the Father in heaven has now received David’s throne on earth; he who will always reign for himself has now received an eternal kingdom for us in the house of Jacob.

Let us rejoice, brothers, because he who has reigned for himself is going to reign for us. Let us rejoice, because he came to reign on earth so that we might reign with him in heaven.

Hear the Apostle: “If we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him” (2 Timothy 2). He was born for us—certainly to come and give us the kingdom, as he himself promised when he said: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25). He said “for you,” not “for me.”

He came so that he might always be with us, so that he who is now present in our hearts alone might always be before our eyes. He will come so that those whose glory comes from the kingdom may also have confidence from intimacy with him.

“And of his kingdom there will be no end.”

If you believe in his coming, rejoice, because he promised a kingdom without end, where there is a host without a successor and perpetual dignities.

[Note: You may understand this either of the host of the stars or of the angels; in either case it will always remain the same and will never fail. From Mita.]

But what is this? Those who seek what passes do not desire what will remain. What is it? What is it that they purchase fleeting honors with gold and refuse to receive eternal ones freely?

Brothers, here offices are prepared, here places are assigned, here honors are designated. Whoever has not received his credentials here on the faith of the Gospel will not possess the eternal insignia of dignity there.

Therefore, if military service delights us, if we wish to serve forever, let us seize Christ’s weapons; let us keep watch and remain sober; let us conquer the devil and overthrow vices, so that we may receive both rewards

[Note: Similar passages occur in Theophylact on 2 Timothy 2; Saint Athanasius, question 120 on the *Parables of Scripture*; Gregory of Nazianzus, *Oration 11 on Pentecost*; Augustine on Psalm 60; and Ambrose, *Duties*, book 1, chapter 10.]

and crowns from our Lord Jesus Christ himself, who reigns with God the Father now and forever, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Note: In some manuscripts the heading reads only: “On the Generation of Christ”; the rest is lacking.]

## SERMON CXLV. On the Generation of Christ and on Joseph’s Wish to Dismiss Mary

Today, brothers, you will hear how the blessed Evangelist reported to us the mystery of Christ’s generation.

“Christ’s generation,” he says, “was as follows: When his mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together, she was found to be with child by the Holy Spirit. But Joseph her husband, being just and unwilling to expose her, wanted to dismiss her secretly” (Matthew 1).

And how was he just, since he decided not to investigate his betrothed’s conception? He does not seek the cause of a suspected dishonor, he does not defend the reputation of the marriage, but he seeks—

[Note: Alternatively: “abandons.”]

—to dismiss her secretly.

This seems more fitting to piety than to justice, but only according to human judgment, not divine judgment. With God there is neither piety without justice nor justice without piety. According to heavenly understanding, equity without goodness and goodness without equity do not exist. If the virtues are separated, they fall apart: equity without goodness is savagery, and justice without piety is cruelty.

[Note: As a just man—that is, one observing ancestral rites—he did not at all judge that the wife should be retained; as a pious man, he considered dismissing her, but without legal commotion or the disgrace of a charge.]

Joseph, then, was rightly just because he was pious, and pious because he was just. Indeed, while considering piety, he was free from cruelty; while moderating the case, he preserved judgment; while postponing vengeance, he escaped guilt; while refusing to become an accuser, he fled the sentence.

His holy mind was in turmoil, struck by the novelty of the matter. His betrothed stood pregnant, yet a virgin; she stood full of the pledge, yet not empty of modesty; she stood anxious about the conception, yet secure regarding her integrity; she stood clothed with the gift of motherhood, yet not excluded from the honor of virginity.

What was the fiancé to do in such circumstances? Should he accuse her of a crime? But he himself was a witness to her innocence. Should he declare her guilty? But he himself was the guardian of her modesty.

[Note: Augustine did not hesitate to say that Joseph suspected nothing other than adultery. Justin likewise writes in his *Dialogue with Trypho*, page 303D, Cologne edition of 1686: “The reason Joseph considered dismissing her secretly, rather than exposing her publicly, was certainly that he did not know her to be an adulteress but merely suspected it; indeed, he was moved rather by the wavering and agitation of his mind.”]

Should he press a charge of adultery? But he himself was the defender of her virginity.

What was he to do in such circumstances? He considered dismissing her, because he could neither expose outside the house nor contain within it what had happened. He considered dismissing her and told everything to God, because he had no one else to whom he could speak.

And we, brothers, whenever circumstances trouble us, appearances deceive us, and the outward character of a matter causes us not to know its inner reality, let us withdraw judgment, restrain vengeance, flee the sentence, and tell everything to God, lest, while rashly seeking to punish the innocent, we pronounce a harmful sentence upon ourselves. For the Lord says: “With whatever judgment you judge, you will be judged” (Matthew 7).

Certainly, if we remain silent, God will speak; the angel will answer. To prevent Joseph from abandoning the innocent woman, the angel forestalled him:

“Joseph,” he said, “son of David, do not be afraid to receive Mary as your wife; for what has been born in her is from the Holy Spirit. She will give birth to a son, and you will call his name Jesus; for he will save his people from their sins.”

“Joseph, son of David.” You see, brothers, that a whole lineage is called by the name of one person; you see that the entire ancestry is named in one man; you see that the line of David’s stock is already invoked in Joseph.

[Note: “Thirty-eighth” was corruptly read. It was easy for scribes to write “thirtieth” instead of “twentieth.” Matthew 17 says: “All the generations from Abraham to David are fourteen generations; from David to the Babylonian captivity, fourteen generations; and from the Babylonian captivity to Christ, fourteen generations.” Therefore Christ was born in the twenty-eighth generation from David. From Mita.]

“Joseph, son of David.” Born in the twenty-eighth generation, how is he called David’s son, unless the mystery of his lineage is being disclosed, the faith of the promise fulfilled, and the heavenly conception and virginal birth already signified in the flesh?

“Joseph, son of David.” In such words the promise of God the Father had been given to David: “The Lord swore truth to David, and he will not frustrate him: ‘From the fruit of your womb I will set one upon your throne’” (Psalm 131).

This is celebrated in a song of such significance: “The Lord said to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand’” (Psalm 109).

“From the fruit of your womb”—appropriately, “the fruit of your womb,” appropriately “from the womb,” because the heavenly guest and inhabitant from above descended into the dwelling of the womb in such a way that he did not know the body’s enclosure. He came forth from the dwelling of the womb in such a way that the virginal door did not open, and what is sung in the Song of Songs was fulfilled: “A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride; a garden enclosed, a sealed fountain” (Song of Songs 4).

“Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid.” The fiancé is warned not to fear the circumstances of his betrothed; and truly, a pious mind fears more when it shares another’s suffering.

“Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid.” Do not, while secure in conscience, fail under the knowledge of the mystery.

“Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid.” What you see is power, not crime; here there has been no human fall but a divine descent; here is a reward, not guilt; here is an increase of heaven, not an injury to the body; here is not the betrayal of a person but the secret of the Judge; here is the palm of the one who recognizes it, not the punishment of a penalty; here is not a human theft but God’s treasure; here is not the cause of death but of life.

Therefore do not be afraid, because she who gives birth to life does not deserve to be killed.

[Note: According to the law of Moses, Deuteronomy 21:20, stoning was prescribed for wives guilty of adultery.]

“Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid to receive Mary as your wife.” It is the law of divine speech that a betrothed woman should be called a wife. Thus, just as she is a mother while her virginity remains, so

[Note: A betrothed woman is one who has been promised to someone as a wife. For one who had been betrothed was regarded as a wife by designation and was therefore called a wife in Genesis 29:21 and Deuteronomy 22:24, where the man who violated another’s betrothed is punished as an adulterer. In ordinary human speech, however, the word “wife” does not fit a betrothal concerning the future. Therefore a valid but unconsummated marriage existed between the Virgin and Joseph. See Duhamel’s notes here, and Augustine, *Against Julian*, book 5, chapter 12. Augustine answers Julian, who sought refuge in this point and foolishly claimed that the Evangelist spoke according to popular opinion when he called Mary Joseph’s wife, with this acute observation: “Let us suppose that the Evangelist could have done this when he was reporting his own words or those of another human being, so that he might speak according to popular opinion. But could the angel, speaking privately to a private person, have spoken against his own knowledge and that of the one to whom he spoke, according to opinion rather than truth, when he said to him: ‘Do not be afraid to receive Mary as your wife’?”]

she is called a wife while modesty remains.

“Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid to receive Mary as your wife; for what has been born in her is from the Holy Spirit.”

Let those who ask who the one whom Mary bore is come and hear: “What has been born in her is from the Holy Spirit.”

Let those who strive to cloud Latin purity with a Greek storm come and hear—those who, blaspheming, seek to suppress *Theotokon* (θεοτόκον, “bearer of God”) in favor of *anthrōpotokon* (ἀνθρωποτόκον, “bearer of a human being”) and *Christotokon* (χριστοτόκον, “bearer of Christ”).

[Note: Theodore of Mopsuestia, who was Chrysologus’s contemporary, had taught according to this erroneous doctrine: the Word God was in the man whom the Virgin bore *kat’ axian* (κατ’ ἀξίαν), “according to worth”; *kat’ anaphoran* (κατ’ ἀναφοράν), “according to relation”; and *kat’ energeian* (κατ’ ἐνέργειαν), “according to operation.” Hence the Virgin Mary could be called *anthrōpotokos* (“bearer of a human being”) and *Christotokos* (“bearer of Christ”), but not *Theotokos* (“bearer of God”). More probably Chrysologus is attacking the heresy of Eutyches, as Bacchinius thinks in Agnellus, volume 1. From this the very learned scholar infers that Peter, bishop of Ravenna, was different from our Peter, who lived in a later age; Tillemont also observed this, volume 5, page 864, column 2. Note that in this sermon several expressions also occur in Chrysologus’s letter against Eutyches.]

“What has been born in her is from the Holy Spirit.”

And what is born from the Holy Spirit is spirit, because God is spirit (John 3 and 4). Why, then, do you ask who was born from the Holy Spirit, when God himself answers you that he is God? When John reproves you, saying: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God”; and, “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we saw his glory” (John 1).

John saw the glory; the unbeliever looks for an injury.

“What has been born in her is from the Holy Spirit.” “And we saw his glory.” Whose glory? The glory of the one born from the Holy Spirit, the glory of the one who became flesh and dwelt among us.

“What has been born in her is from the Holy Spirit.” The Virgin conceived, but by the Spirit; the virgin gave birth, but to the one whom Isaiah foretold: “Behold, a virgin will conceive in the womb and give birth to a son, and they will call his name Emmanuel,” which is interpreted, “God with us” (Isaiah 7; Matthew 1).

“God with us,” while with them he is human. And accursed is the human being who places his hope in a human being (Jeremiah 7).

Let those who ask who the one born from Mary is hear. “You will give birth to a son,” says the angel, “and you will call his name Jesus.”

Why Jesus? The Apostle says: “So that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Philippians 2). And you, deceitful investigator, now ask who Jesus is?

Every tongue now confesses that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father; and you still ask who Jesus is?

“You will give birth to a son, and you will call his name Jesus; for he will save his people.” He will save them—not another’s people.

From what? “From their sins.”

If you do not believe Christians who say that he is God, believe, most unbelieving one, at least the Jews who say: “Although you are a human being, you make yourself God” (John 10). “Who can forgive sins except God alone?” (Mark 2).

They denied that he was God because they did not believe that he could forgive sins. You believe that he forgives sins, and yet you hesitate to confess that he is God?

“The Word became flesh”

[Note: The manuscripts of Cesena and Vallicella read: “so that the human flesh might be advanced.”]

so that human flesh might be advanced into the glory of God, not so that God might be changed into an injury of the flesh, as the Apostle says: “Whoever is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Corinthians 6). And how much more so when God joins himself to a human being: there is one God!

[Note: He refers to the law given by Valentinian when Arturus and Protogenes were consuls, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July, concerning the thirty-year limitation of legal actions, in the *Code*, title “On Limitations.”]

Human laws extinguish all disputed questions within thirty years, and Christ, nearly five hundred years after his birth, is still required to furnish the causes of his birth, still suffers disputes about his origin, and still bears questions about his status?

[Note: Some had improperly inferred Chrysologus’s age from these words. See Mita’s responses to the objections concerning the life of Chrysologus. Everyone admits that the ancients devoted little care to calculating years, especially Father Le Ceiller, *General History of Ecclesiastical Authors*, volume 4, page 13. Indeed, this very sermon disproves that calculation. It was written in the same style as the letter to Eutyches, unquestionably sent in the year 449. Unless we wish to say that fifty years had already passed since that letter, Chrysologus was still engaged in preaching to the people.]

Heretic, stop judging your Judge, and adore in heaven the God whom the Magus adored on earth (Matthew 2).

[Note: Alternatively, the title reads “On the Same Subject.” The rest is lacking.]

## SERMON CXLVI. On the Same Subject, and on Joseph the Betrothed and Mary the Betrothed Mother
Whenever, after the boundaries of the year have passed, the day of the Lord’s Nativity arrives, and the splendor of the virginal birth is spread throughout the whole world in flashing radiance, it is by choice, not by fear, that we keep silent. [Note: [Col. 0592D] Alternatively: “It is from fear, not choice, that we have kept silent.” In Tillemont’s view (vol. V, p. 187), these words seem to suggest that Chrysologus refrained from preaching on the day of the Lord’s Nativity.] What mind would dare to thrust itself forward at the very birth of the divine King? When the sun’s rays burst forth, human sight is dulled; when God shines forth, how could the whole vision of our souls not be wounded?

Therefore, once our senses have been restored after the stupor caused by the new light, the time has come for us, having now seen Christ’s generation according to the flesh, to contemplate also the mysteries of his divinity. “The generation of Christ,” says the evangelist, “was thus” (Matthew I). Brothers, if we wish to understand what is being said, let us not weigh divine words by human standards; human understanding must be set aside where everything that is said is divine. Thus, Christ’s being born is not custom but a sign; it is not nature but power; it is not an order but authority; it is a heavenly miracle, not a human explanation.

What can worldly knowledge grasp here? What can understanding of the flesh seek here? “The generation of Christ,” he says, “was thus.” He did not say, “Thus it happened,” but “Thus it was,” because Christ’s generation was with the Father when he was generated from his mother. What was, always was; what was made was rendered as such: he was God, and was rendered human. From the womb he received us—the one who had fashioned us [Note: [Col. 0592D] Alternatively, “from clay.”] from the mud.

“When his mother Mary had been betrothed.” It would have been enough to say, “when Mary had been betrothed.” What does “the betrothed mother” mean? If she is a mother, she is not a bride; if she is a bride, she is not yet a mother. “When Mary, his mother, had been betrothed”: a bride in virginity, a mother in fruitfulness; a mother who knew no man, yet knew childbirth.

Or how could she not be a mother before conception, she who after childbirth remained a virgin mother? Or when was she not a mother who gave birth to the Author of the ages and bestowed a beginning upon created things? [Note: [Col. 0592D] The Caesena manuscript reads: “Virgin nature, violated, brought an end to nature: just as the nature of things was a virgin mother, so corruption was always a stepmother of things.” That is, when nature, which had been created a virgin by God, remained corrupted because of the sin of the first parent, it brought an end to virgin nature itself, which thereafter could no longer give birth as a virgin, but only as corrupted—so that, as many say, the generation of one thing is the corruption of another. For this reason nature is no longer called a mother but a stepmother. MITA.]

Virgin nature is always a mother; thus corruption is always a stepmother. It is therefore the gift of virginity that a virgin should regenerate through God what a virgin generated through God. God and integrity form a heavenly partnership; virginity joined to Christ is a perfect union of virtue.

What the Virgin conceives is the honor of the Spirit, not a burden of the flesh; what the Virgin gives birth to is God’s secret, not a marital function; what is born is Christ, the glory of divine majesty, not the weakness of humanity. It is the whole glory of the Godhead, where no injury to the flesh is perceived.

“When Mary his mother had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together she was found to be with child from the Holy Spirit.” Why is this heavenly mystery entrusted to a betrothed woman rather than to an unmarried one? Why is the bride’s danger arranged in such a way as to arouse the bridegroom’s jealousy? Why is so great a power regarded as a crime, certain salvation as a peril? Why, among the innocent, does modesty labor in this fashion, shame succumb, chastity grow weary, faith become wounded, accusation arise, the case press forward, and every opportunity for defense disappear?

Who can excuse the bride whom conception accuses? Or what benefit will an external defender provide when an internal witness of the deed stands present?

What are we holding to, brothers? Not a stroke, not a letter, not a syllable, not a word, not a name, not a person in the Gospel is empty of divine figures. The bride is sought so that even then the Church of Christ might be designated as his bride, in accordance with what the prophet Hosea says: “I will betroth you to myself in righteousness and judgment, in mercy and compassion, and I will betroth you to myself in faith” (Hosea II). Hence John says: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom” (John III). And blessed Paul says: “I betrothed you to one man, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (II Corinthians XI).

Truly she is a bride who, through a virginal birth, regenerates Christ’s infancy anew.

Joseph the bridegroom is a guardian, so that this Joseph might fulfill in himself the figure of Christ’s passion. Joseph, through prophetic dreams, encounters jealousy; Christ, through prophetic visions, receives envy. Joseph, cast into a pit of death, emerges alive from the pit; Christ, placed in the tomb of death, returns alive from the tomb. Joseph was sold, and Christ was assigned a price. Joseph was brought into Egypt; Christ is driven into Egypt. Joseph abundantly supplies bread to starving peoples; Christ, with the bread of heaven, satisfies the nations dwelling throughout the whole world.

Thus it shines forth why this Joseph prefigured the heavenly bridegroom, bore his image, and walked as his figure.

Mary is called “mother”; and when is Mary not a mother? “He called the gatherings of waters ‘seas’ (*maria*)” (Genesis I). Did she not conceive, in one womb, the people departing from Egypt, so that a race reborn into a new heavenly creation might emerge, in accordance with the apostle’s words: “Our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea” (I Corinthians X)?

And so that Mary might always go before human salvation, she rightly preceded in song the people whom the life-giving wave brought forth into the light. “Mary,” he says, “the sister of Aaron, took a tambourine in her hand and said: ‘Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously exalted’” (Exodus XV). [Note: [Col. 0593D] Mary, Aaron’s sister, was distinguished by the gift of prophecy.]

This name is akin to prophecy; it is salutary to those being reborn; it is the mark of virginity, the adornment of chastity, the sign of purity, the sacrifice of God, the virtue of hospitality, the fellowship of holiness. Rightly, therefore, this maternal name belongs to the mother of Christ.

We have explained why she is a mother and bride, why Joseph is the bridegroom, and why Mary bears a maternal name, so that we might reveal that everything surrounding Christ’s birth was mystical. Now, for other reasons, let us disclose why a bride was sought for Christ’s birth.

Isaiah had foretold that a virgin would give birth to the God of heaven (Isaiah VII), the King of earth, the Lord of the world, the restorer of the world, the slayer of death, the giver of life, and the author of eternity. How grievous this would be to worldly powers, terrifying to kings, and frightening to the Jews, the event of the Lord’s Nativity itself demonstrated.

For when Judea heard from the Magi that Christ had been born, Herod learned of it; immediately the Jews sought to destroy him, and Herod plotted to kill Christ (Matthew II). While fearing a successor for himself, they all tried to destroy the Savior.

Finally, because they could not find him, they destroy his homeland, mingle milk with blood, and in murderous fury strike down those of his own age. They tear apart the companions of innocence because they could not find participants in guilt whom they might punish.

And if they do these things once Christ has been born, what would such savagery have done to Christ while he was still conceived? This is why a bridegroom is provided, why the appearance of marriage is supplied: to conceal the miracle, cover the sign, veil the Virgin’s childbirth, leave no room for accusation, and thus elude the plots of the raging enemy.

Although Christ had been destined for death, if he had been killed in the womb, death, in its haste, would have taken away what he had come to bring for our salvation. And because this passage can offer us much if it is expounded, let it suffice, brothers, that today we have given a preliminary taste of the Lord’s sacrament.

## SERMON CXLVII. On the Mystery of the Incarnation

What moved the Lord Christ, brothers, to enter into association with an earthly body, to enter the narrow confines of human flesh, and to dwell in the habitation of a virginal womb? Since we have begun to hear about this before, let us hear it more fully today. You are my life, you are my salvation, you are my glory; and therefore I cannot bear for you not to know what God has granted me to know. [Note: [Col. 0594D] The Caesena manuscript reads, “what God has granted me to know.”]

The evangelist knew God when he said: “No one has ever seen God” (John I). Therefore, he recognized and perceived the God whom he knew: because the creature could not see him, it was carried under harsh servitude and offered sorrowful service in place of invisible majesty. Fear had besieged everything; terror had loosened all bonds; dread had shaken everything. In heaven, divine splendor had prostrated the angels; on earth, thunder and lightning shook the hearts of mortals.

Thus excessive fear excluded love of the ruler; it drove angels to earth, drew human beings to idols, and occupied the world with empty errors. It made everyone flee the Creator and worship creatures. No one who fears greatly can love. Hence the world preferred to perish rather than to fear; even death seemed lighter than terror.

Finally, when Cain began to be tormented by murderous terror, he sought death, believing that he would find rest if he perished (Genesis IV). And why should I speak of Cain? When Elijah felt himself entirely enveloped in fear, he sought again the death from which he had fled, judging it better to succumb to death than to fear (III Kings XIX).

Peter too, disturbed by fear of the Lord’s power, begged Christ to depart from him: “Depart from me,” he said, “for I am a sinful man” (Luke V). He said this because the weight of fear had extinguished whatever love and faith there was in him. Thus, unless fear is tempered by love, it makes even devoted service rebellious.

Therefore, seeing the world shaken by fear, God immediately acts to recall it with love, invite it by grace, hold it by charity, and bind it by affection.

Hence he washes the earth, grown old in evils, with a punishing flood; calls Noah the father of a new age; addresses him in gentle speech; grants him familiar confidence; instructs him kindly about present matters; consoles him by grace concerning the future; and no longer by commands alone, but through shared labor, closes in the ark the offspring of the whole age, so that the love of fellowship might remove the fear of servitude, and what had been saved through common labor might be preserved through common love (Genesis VII).

Hence he calls Abraham from among the nations, enlarges him by his name, makes him the father of faith, accompanies him on the road, preserves him among foreigners, enriches him with possessions, honors him with triumphs, guarantees him by promises, rescues him from injuries, wins him over by hospitality, and glorifies him through offspring when offspring seemed impossible, so that, filled with so many blessings and drawn by such great sweetness of divine charity, he might learn to love God rather than fear him, and to worship by loving rather than by trembling (Genesis XII).

Hence he consoles Jacob in flight through dreams, challenges him to a contest when he returns, and binds him in the embrace of a wrestler, so that he might love the father of the struggle rather than fear him (Genesis XXVIII).

Hence he calls Moses in the language of his homeland and addresses him with fatherly affection, inviting him to be the liberator of his people (Exodus III). And why say more? He makes him a god—he gives him as a god to Pharaoh. He makes him a god, strengthens him with signs, arms him with powers, conquers battles by commands, grants him the power to defeat the enemy by the very word, permits him to triumph through orders, and advances him through every crown of virtue into his friendship. He grants him a share in the heavenly kingdom, and, although he graciously allows him to be a legislator, he accepted everything so that Moses might love him.

Finally, he was so inflamed with love of God that he himself loved ardently and urged others to love in these words: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength” (Deuteronomy VI). Whatever belongs to the heart, whatever belongs to the mind, whatever belongs to human strength—he wished it to be possessed in such a way by love of God that worldly human affection would have nothing left to violate.

But through these things we have recalled, when the flame of divine charity had kindled human hearts and the intoxication of love for God had poured itself fully into human senses, wounded minds began to desire to behold God with bodily eyes. How could a narrow human vision contain God, whom the world cannot contain?

Love does not consider what will be, what ought to be, or what can be. Love knows no judgment, lacks reason, and knows no limit. Love does not accept impossibility as consolation or difficulty as a remedy. Unless it reaches what it desires, love kills the lover; and therefore it goes where it is led, not where it ought to go. Love gives birth to desire; desire grows hot; ardor presses toward what is not permitted.

And why say more? Love cannot fail to see what it loves. Hence all the saints considered everything they had deserved to be little if they did not see the Lord. And indeed, brothers, how can one render service for benefits if one does not see the giver of the benefits? Or how can one believe that one is loved by God if one is not granted his sight?

Hence love, which longs to see God, although it does not possess judgment, nevertheless possesses zeal for devotion. Hence Moses dares to say: “If I have found favor before you, show me your face” (Exodus XXXIII). Hence another says: “Show us your face” (Psalm LXXIX). Finally, even the Gentiles fashioned images for this reason: so that amid their errors they might see with their eyes what they worshiped.

Therefore, knowing that mortals were tortured and wearied by the desire to see him, God chose a means by which he could make himself visible—something great to earthly beings and by no means insignificant to heavenly ones. For what was made by God on earth in his likeness could not fail to be regarded as honorable in heaven.

“Let us make man,” he says, “in our image and likeness” (Genesis I). Perfect devotion is owed to the image just as it is owed to the king. If he had taken an angel from heaven, he would nevertheless have remained invisible; if he had taken something less than a human being from earth, it would have been an injury to divinity, and he would have cast humanity down rather than raised it up.

Therefore, beloved, let no one regard it as an injury to God that God came to human beings through a human being and took from us what would allow him to be seen by us—God who lives and reigns now and throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 0595D] Ferrarius, *On Preaching*, book I, chapter 32, p. 153, testifies that it was customary for the Fathers to conclude sermons with this formula; there he also praises Chrysologus himself.]

## SERMON CXLVIII. On the Same Subject

Today, brothers, we must take up yesterday’s discourse again; today we must repeat the joy of the Lord’s Nativity. When the Virgin conceives, the virgin gives birth, and remains a virgin, it is not custom but a sign; it is not reason but power; it has an author, not nature; it is not something common but unique; it is divine, not human. [Note: [Col. 0595D] Nothing is more common among the ancients than to express divinity, and especially Christ’s divinity, by the name “power.” The testimonies collected by Theodoret at the end of Dialogue 3 against the Theopaschites are more than sufficient. I add that of Ambrose, Book II On the Faith, chapter 7, no. 56: “Christ is troubled as a human being; his power is not troubled, his divinity is not troubled.”]

Therefore let the labor of empty philosophy cease. Christ’s birth was not necessity but power; it was honor, not injury; it was the mystery of piety, not a diminution of divinity; it was the restoration of human salvation, not a reduction of divine substance.

He who, without being born, made man from untouched clay, by being born himself made man from an untouched body. The hand that graciously took up clay for our formation also graciously took up flesh for our restoration. Therefore, when the Creator is found in his creature, when God is found in flesh, it is the creature’s honor, not an injury to the Creator.

But the one who believes that clay is more precious than flesh regards this as an insult. Does he perhaps regret having been changed from clay into the honor of flesh, into the glory of humanity? Human being, why are you so contemptible in your own eyes, when you are so precious to God? Why do you dishonor yourself in such a way when God has honored you so greatly? Why do you seek to know from what you were made, but do not ask for what you were made?

Is not this entire world, which you see, made as a house for you? For you the infused light drives away the surrounding darkness; for you night has been tempered; for you day has been measured. For you the heavens have been lit by the varied radiance of the sun, moon, and stars. For you the earth has been decorated with flowers, groves, and fruits. For you a beautiful and marvelous multitude of living creatures was created in the air, on the fields, and in the water, lest the joy of the new age be disturbed by sad solitude.

Hence he made you from earth, so that you might be lord of earthly things and might share with them in the communion of the same substance. Yet he did not so equal you, an earthly being, to earthly things that he did not also make you, animated from heaven, equal in heavenly origin to heavenly things. And so that you might share a common relation with God, while sharing a body with animals, he gave you a soul from heaven and a body from earth, so that within you the harmonious bond of heaven and earth might be preserved.

Even now your Creator devises what more he may add to your honor: he places his image in you (Genesis I), so that the invisible Creator might be made present to earthly beings through a visible image; and among earthly things he gave you his own vicegerency, so that so vast a possession of the world would not be deprived of the Lord’s representative. [Note: [Col. 0597D] Mita reads *fundaretur* erroneously.]

And if these things are so, why is it now considered an injury when God mercifully received into himself what he had made in you, and wished truly to be seen in a human being, in whom previously he had wished to be seen only figuratively? And he granted that he himself should be *proprietas*—God’s own possession—who had earlier received the status of likeness. [Note: [Col. 0597D] Previously, man was only the likeness of God; now, after humanity was assumed by the Word, he is also called *proprietas* (God’s own possession). MITA.]

The virgin conceived, the virgin gave birth. Do not let conception trouble you; do not let childbirth confuse your hearing, since virginity excuses whatever belongs to human modesty. Or what injury to modesty was there, where divinity entered into partnership with the integrity that had always been its friend; where the angel was the interpreter, faith the bride-woman, betrothal chastity, the gift power, conscience the judge, God the cause, integrity the conception, virginity the birth, and the mother a virgin?

Let no one therefore judge in a human manner what is accomplished in a divine sacrament. Let no one examine a heavenly mystery by earthly reasoning. [Note: [Col. 0597D] Casaubon undertook to examine the meaning of this word in *Exercitationes* 16, p. 542, and thought it derived from *claudere*, “to shut.” The whole doctrine of Christ and concerning Christ is called a mystery. In I Corinthians IV.1 the apostles are called stewards of God’s mysteries. Nor would I deny it if someone maintained that the word came from the pagans, for some of their rites too were called mysteries, or hidden rites.] Let no one treat the secret of novelty according to ordinary usage. Let no one measure what is unique by example. Let no one construct an insult out of piety. Let no one incur danger through salvation.

Certainly, whoever desires to know higher things should return to the Law; through the Law, let him seek knowledge of the Law; by the authority of the author, let him recognize the author’s deed.

The Law relates (Genesis II) that God created man for a life of his own; that he commanded the earth to produce fruits for man in spontaneous service; that he commanded wild beasts, cattle, and herds to be subject to human authority, not to human skill, so that man, knowing neither labor nor pain, might possess delights in blessedness.

But so that man would not possess all these things, an angel, who was held among the first, became envious and preferred to be changed into the devil rather than see man so full of glory. [Note: [Col. 0598D] Alternatively, “rather than see man in this condition.”] Finally, inflamed by this envy, he attacked the woman by deceit and led the virgin to taste the forbidden fruit. Once led astray, the virgin soon led astray her husband; and while she ministered death’s condition, the food of death, and the nourishment of sin, she brought down the state of life. She herself became the material of the whole ruin, although she had been made for unique consolation.

Hence came the first sin; hence the origin of death; hence labor, pain, groaning, and the bitter condition of our servitude, propagated from it. [Note: [Col. 0598D] We have corrected the editions from the Caesena manuscript, in which *propagata est* is absent.] For the human being who had previously been lord of all was cast down into servitude to all; and he fears everyone who had previously been feared by everyone, and can scarcely prevail by skill who had reigned by power.

Hence, brothers, hence it is that Christ’s order of birth is such: the devil had come to a virgin; an angel came to Mary, so that what the evil angel had cast down, the good angel might raise up. The one persuaded disbelief; the other faith. That woman believed the persuader; this woman believes the author.

Christ is born so that, by being born, he might restore corrupted nature. He assumed infancy, endured nourishment, and passed through the stages of life so that he might restore the one perfect and abiding age that he himself had made. He carries humanity so that humanity can no longer fall. He made heavenly what he had made earthly. He gives divine life to the spirit that had been animated by human breath. And thus he takes the whole person up into God, leaving in him nothing that belongs to sin, death, labor, pain, or earth.

This is granted by our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father lives and reigns, God in the unity of the Holy Spirit, now and always and throughout immortal ages of ages. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 0598D] In some editions this sermon bears the title “Sermon on the Nativity of the Lord”; some think it belongs to D. Severian of Gabala, but falsely. Consult the notes in the preface.]

## SERMON CXLIX. On the Nativity of Christ and the Peace of Christians

At the coming of our Lord and Savior, and at his bodily presence, angels leading heavenly choirs evangelized to the shepherds, saying: “I announce to you great joy, which will be for all the people” (Luke II).

Therefore, borrowing our voice from those holy angels, we too announce great joy to you. For today the Church is at peace, and the heretics are in anger; today the ship of the Church is in harbor, while the fury of the heretics is tossed upon the waves; today, brothers, the shepherds of the Church are secure, while the heretics are in confusion; today the Lord’s sheep are safe, while the wolves rage; today the Lord’s vineyard is in abundance, while the workers of iniquity are in want; today the people of Christ, beloved, are exalted, while the enemies of truth are humbled; today, most beloved, Christ is in joy, while the devil is in mourning; today the angels are in exultation, while the demons are in confusion.

And why say more? Today Christ, who is the King of peace, proceeding with his peace, has driven away every division, removed dissension, and disturbed discord. Just as the sun’s splendor illuminates the heavens, so he illuminates the Church with the radiance of peace.

“For today,” he says, “a Savior of the world has been born for you.” O how desirable is the name of peace, how firm a foundation of Christian religion, and how heavenly an adornment of the Lord’s altar! And what worthy thing can we say about peace?

Peace is the name of Christ himself, as the Apostle also says: “For he is our peace, who made both one” (Ephesians II)—those who were divided not by opinions or faith, but by the devil’s envy.

Indeed, just as when a king proceeds, the streets are cleansed and the whole city is crowned with various flowers and ornaments, so that nothing may appear less worthy of the king’s face, so now, as Christ the King of peace proceeds, let everything sorrowful be taken away from our midst. As truth shines forth, let falsehood be driven away; let discord flee; let harmony shine.

And just as we often see when the images of kings or brothers are painted, so that the signs of unanimity between them may be displayed: the painter places Concord, in female attire, behind both of them, embracing each with her arms [Note: [Col. 0599D] This appears on a coin of Julia Paula and in ancient monuments.], to indicate that those who appear separated in body agree in judgment and will, so now the Lord’s peace, standing in the midst and connecting both of us with a caressing embrace, teaches that bodies separated from one another are brought together by arms joining their minds. In this, without doubt, the prophetic saying is fulfilled: “There shall be peaceful counsel between the two” (Zechariah VI).

Yesterday, indeed, our common father began with a Gospel word of peace. [Note: [Col. 0599D] Namely Chrysostom, who had himself preached on peace the day before Severian.] Today, however, we bring forth words of peace. Yesterday he received us with uplifted hands in the word of peace; today we run to him with gifts of peace, our chests expanded and our arms open.

Now wars have been destroyed. The beauty of peace has prevailed over everything. Now the devil is in mourning, and the entire troop of demons in lamentation; now there is joy in the heavenly places and exultation among the angels, for peace is especially familiar to them. Even the heavenly powers admire it, among whom its fountain is everlasting, from which earthly beings too are sprinkled by drops that trickle down from it.

And therefore, even if peace is praised by the saints on earth, the radiance of its praise overflows into heaven. The heavenly angels praise it and say: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.”

You see, brothers, how all heavenly and earthly beings send one another gifts of peace: the heavenly angels announce peace to the earth; the saints on earth praise Christ, who is our peace, as he is established in heaven; and they cry out together in mystical choirs: “Hosanna in the highest.”

Let us therefore also say with the angels: “Glory to God in the highest,” who humbled the devil and exalted his Christ; “glory to God in the highest,” who drove away discord and established peace.

See, brothers, the exultant angelic voice: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace.”

For I shall tell you about the devil’s artifice, whose cunning you yourselves do not fail to know.
