Satan saw the firmness and stability of the faith; he saw it fortified by the piety of its doctrines; he saw it abounding in the fruits of good works. And therefore he went mad over all these things and burned with furious frenzy, so that he might tear apart harmony, overthrow charity, and shatter peace. But may peace always be with us.

## SERMON CL. On Christ’s Flight into Egypt
If discourse does not disclose the Virgin’s conception and the Virgin’s childbirth, sense does not receive them, the human mind does not comprehend them; who would speak of God’s fleeing as a human being? “The angel of the Lord,” it says, “appeared in a dream to Joseph, saying: Take the child and his mother, and flee into Egypt” (Matthew 2). If we have said that Christ was born as an act of divine mercy, what shall we say of Christ, who is read to have fled? Perhaps, just as we said that he was born in order to restore nature, let us say that he fled in order to call back those who flee. And indeed, if he himself wanders in the mountains in order to call back the wandering sheep, how could he himself not flee from the fleeing peoples in order to lead them back?

[Note: [Col. 0599D] Mita repaired from the Caesena and formerly Urbinate manuscripts a passage badly damaged in the printed editions.]

“Take the child and his mother, and flee into Egypt.” Why is this heavenly event handled in such a way that the human understanding is confused, the mind wearied, intelligence strained, hearing dulled, faith shaken, hope made to stumble, and belief itself brought low? “Take the child and his mother, and flee into Egypt.” With a human being pursuing, God flees; with the earth raging, heaven trembles; and as dust flies, the angels are thrown into alarm, while, as the Son flees, the Father’s fear is displayed.

“Take the child and his mother, and flee into Egypt.” When Saul pursued David, he fled for refuge to Judea, and the neighboring region received him (1 Samuel 21–22); the house of a single widow sufficed to conceal Elijah (1 Kings 17). When Christ flees, there is no place for him; the province fails him, his homeland does not come to his aid. As he migrates, neither neighboring peoples nor bordering regions suffice; instead, Egypt provides a sorrowful exile—foreign in appearance, barbarous in language and customs.

[Note: The manuscript of Cesena reads: “but Egypt’s sorrowful place is procured as an exile, foreign in appearance, unknown in language, barbarous in customs.”]

[Note: [Col. 0600D] Latinius emends the text thus; the printed editions and manuscripts read procuratur, “is procured.”]

“Take the child and his mother, and flee into Egypt.” If the refuge of all things flees, the aid of all lies hidden; if the strength of all fears; if the defense of the whole universe does not defend itself, why is human flight marked with blame, trembling arraigned, and fear condemned? Why is Peter charged because he denies, John because he is terrified and flees, and all the disciples because they desert him through fear (Matthew 26; Mark 14)?

And if these things, brothers, did happen, why are they committed to writing, why are they reported in books, why are they recited through the ages, why are they made known in daily readings, why are they proclaimed to all nations? Is it so that tongue, place, age, time—in a word, everyone—may recognize divine fear? For just as virtues, when read, lift the spirits toward progress, so weaknesses lower the spirits when they are recited. What, then, does the evangelist intend by writing these things for everlasting remembrance?

It is the duty of a devoted soldier of the king to conceal his flight, report his steadfastness, speak of his virtues, suppress his fears, disclose his courageous deeds, keep his weaknesses silent, erase his defeats, and proclaim his victories—so that he may break the enemy’s boldness and rouse the valor of his comrades. The evangelist, therefore, by reporting such things, seems to have provoked the barking of heretics and removed the means of defense from the faithful.

[Col. 0600D] “Take,” he says, “the child and his mother, and flee into Egypt.” Flight is commanded, not a journey; necessity is imposed, not free choice. The angel orders a concealed exile, not an unimpeded passage, so that a road already burdensome in itself might always be made more burdensome by fear.

It is therefore time for us to ask why these things were written for us.

“Take the child and his mother, and flee into Egypt.” For the warlike, fleeing in battle is a matter of strategy, not fear; when God flees from a human being, it is a mystery, not panic. When the powerful withdraws from the weak, he does not fear the pursuer but brings him into the open. For he who wishes to conquer openly desires to report a public victory over his enemy; he who wishes to entrust his triumph to the ages does not allow the conflict to begin in secret. A secret victory and hidden valor leave no example for posterity.

This is why Christ fled: to yield to time, not to Herod. He did not flee death, since he had come to win victory over the enemy; he did not fear human snares, since he had come to expose all the devil’s deceits. Nor did he fear then, when he was an infant—when, as a human being, he did not yet know how to fear, and, as God, could not fear.

Brothers, if Christ had then been slaughtered among that flock of suckling infants, death would have befallen him by accident, not by his will; it would have been weakness, not power; necessity, not authority. It would have been a reward for innocence, but not the glory of majesty. Certainly, where would there have been what God said: “You shall not boil a kid in its mother’s milk” (Exodus 13 and 34)?

“It will happen,” he says, “that Herod will seek the child.” Herod sought him, but the devil sought him through Herod. The devil saw that the magi whom he possessed as leaders in their errors had departed.

[Note: That is, in the errors into which those devoted to astronomical observations are generally led. From this and what follows it is sufficiently clear that Chrysologus held the magi to have been diviners and students of the appearances of deceptive stars; below he calls them “standard-bearers of the devil.” Yet no one now doubts that these magi were wise men, philosophers, and skilled in astral science. Chrysologus perhaps adhered to the bare meaning of the word. For Hesychius says that they called a deceiver or enchanter a magus, and Suidas says that sorcerers were called magi. Balsamon is closer to Chrysologus, in his commentary on canon 36 of Laodicea, p. 842: “Magi are those who approach Satan.” Nor were there lacking among the Fathers those who, like our author, judged harshly concerning the Gospel magi: Hilary, Commentary on Matthew, chapter 1, no. 5, p. 672, vol. I of the Verona edition, calls them “men whose profession was far removed from knowledge of divine understanding”; Ignatius, Letter to the Ephesians; Justin, Dialogue with Trypho; Origen, Book I Against Celsus; Ambrose, Book II on Luke, nos. 47 and 48; Jerome, on Isaiah 19, §47, who finally seems to sing a palinode in Daniel 11.]

If Christ, bound in swaddling clothes, occupied at his mother’s breast, silent in speech, hidden in action, and not yet walking, transformed the devil’s standard-bearers—that is, the magi—into most faithful leaders, the devil already saw what Christ could do at mature age. Therefore he stirred up the Jews and incited Herod, so that he might forestall Christ’s infancy, which he regarded with suspicion; anticipate the insignia of his future power; and cunningly remove from us the most victorious and decisive banner of the cross.

[Note: Another reading: “the most salutary banner.”]

[Note: The manuscript of Cesena reads “that he might empty.”]

The devil perceived—yes, perceived—that Christ would soon restore life through teachings and miracles, and would occupy the whole world, which was still wailing, even the world’s summit, according to the prophet’s saying: “Before the child knows how to call father or mother, he shall receive the power of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria” (Isaiah 8).

And, as the Jews themselves testify when they say, “You see that we are accomplishing nothing; behold, the whole world has gone after him” (John 12), Christ had promised through the law and the prophets that he would come in the flesh, ascend through the stages of age, announce the glory of the heavenly kingdom, preach the teaching of faith, and by the mere command of his word drive out demons, give sight to the blind, the power to walk to the lame, speech to the mute, hearing to the deaf, forgiveness to sinners, and life to the dead.

[Note: Another reading: “pardon.”]

Accordingly, Christ, who was to fulfill these things as a man,

[Note: Another reading: “at a more vigorous age.”]

postponed death as an infant; he did not flee. Finally, the evangelist asserts that his flight arose not from fear of danger but from the mystery of prophecy, saying: “Take the child and his mother, and flee into Egypt.” And afterward: “So that what was spoken by the Lord through the prophet might be fulfilled: ‘Out of Egypt I called my son’” (Hosea 11).

Christ therefore fled so that the truth of the law, the faithfulness of prophecy, and the testimony of the Psalmist might stand, as the Lord himself says: “It was necessary that everything written about me in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms be fulfilled” (Luke 24).

Christ fled for us, not for himself. Christ fled so that he might preserve the mysteries to be administered in their proper times. Christ fled so that he might assist the virtues destined for the future, deprive the faithless of material for excuse, and grant believers confidence in faith—because in persecution it is better to flee than to deny.

Finally, Peter, because he did not wish to flee, denied him (Mark 14); John fled so that he would not deny him.

## SERMON CLI. On the same subject

Today’s reading has moved our hearts, shaken our inmost parts, and stunned our hearing. “Behold,” it says, “the angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream, saying: Rise, take the child and his mother, and flee into Egypt” (Matthew 2).

He at whose birth virginity offers no resistance, reason no obstacle, and nature no contradiction—what power, what force, what danger prevails so as to compel him to flee?

“Take the child and his mother, and flee into Egypt.” More reverently he might have said, “Go into Egypt,” so that it would be a journey, not a flight; a choice, not a necessity; judgment, not fear—human at least, if not divine. But now flight is commanded, commanded from heaven, commanded through an angel, so that heaven may appear to have held fear before the earth did.

“Take the child and his mother, and flee into Egypt.” Flee into Egypt—from your own people to strangers, from the holy to the sacrilegious, from your own temple to the shrines of demons, to the homeland of idols.

[Note: No one doubts that Egypt was the seat of idolatry; and Isaiah had already foretold, in chapter 19, that at Christ’s coming the images of Egypt would fall. Baronnius discusses this prophecy in his Annals. But the distinguished Serry, Exercises 38, pp. 261 ff., holds that the most holy prophet intended something else; I would recommend consulting him, so that one may finally abandon the opinion commonly held.]

Thus Judea’s breadth is insufficient; thus the wide possession of the world is narrowed; it cannot contain the secrecy of the temple. The crowd of priests does not receive him; the numerous, readily traceable company of relatives does not conceal him; so profane Egypt is made suitable for the hiding-place of the deity.

The situation presses in this way, if there is no opportunity to consider the modesty of the virgin, the labor of the mother, the decency of her sex, the danger to Joseph, the fatigue of the long journey, the destruction of the whole household, and—harder than all these—the Jews’ becoming exiles among nations with which they have no fellowship, indeed with which there is the profound shipwreck of transgressing the law.

[Note: The Jews were forbidden to travel abroad among foreigners.]

O how harsh is exile, even among fellow citizens and brothers! He who feels what is alien knows what his own home is. And where is that saying: “Lord, you have become our refuge” (Psalm 89)? And: “Our God is refuge and strength” (Psalm 45)? If refuge flees, if strength fears, if protection migrates, what life, what hope, what security, what defense remains?

One widow sufficed for Elijah against the plots of a free king (1 Kings 17); all Judea did not suffice for Christ against the threats of captive Herod. Elijah consumes those sent against him with heavenly fire (2 Kings 1); Christ is saved by flight alone.

Up to this point, it is enough to have magnified the complaints concerning Christ’s flight.

Brothers, Christ’s flight was a mystery, not fear; deliverance, not danger to the Creator; divine power, not human weakness. He did not flee because of the death of the Author of life; he fled because of the life of the world. For he who had come to die—why would he flee death? Christ would have destroyed the whole cause of our salvation if, as a little child, he had allowed himself to be killed.

Christ had come to strengthen by his examples those whom he had taught by his commands, and himself to do what he had commanded to be done; to prove by sight possible what had seemed impossible by hearing. He had come to pour the knowledge of his divinity into the world and to remove the ignorance of the human race. He had come to rouse sluggish mortal hearts to faith through miracles. He had come to overcome the devil in a public conflict, so that the devil might be conquered by all through a divine command and cast down through a human example.

[Note: Another reading: “by human beings.”]

He had come to fulfill the promises of his presence, granting those to whom he had made himself known the permission to see him. He had come so that the Jew might depart from contempt of the law. He had come to bring the nations into faith. He had come to choose apostles as teachers of the world, fill them with heavenly teachings, fortify them with virtues, arm them with signs, so that by signs they might tame the wild, by virtues heal the sick, and by teachings instruct those who were ready to learn.

Finally, he had come to destroy death by dying, dissolve the underworld by penetrating it, unlock the tombs by rising again, and, by ascending to heaven, grant heavenly gifts to those of earth.

All these things would certainly have perished for us if Christ, while still in the cradle, had not fled.

But you may say, hearer: “Since he could have acted otherwise, why did he submit himself to such great and such grievous injuries?” Why? First, because neither could the human being be saved without the human being, nor could human injuries be cut away without human injuries. He who wishes to guard another makes that other’s cause his own; he who does not suffer together cannot cut away sufferings. Christ took us into himself in order to give himself to us; he endured our sufferings in order to remove our sufferings.

This is why Christ fled: to moderate our own flights in persecutions. A martyr who has been seized ought to maintain steadfastness; one who has not been seized ought to flee from the persecutor—both to grant the persecutor time to repent and not to deprive himself of time for prayer, as the Lord says: “If they persecute you in this city, flee into another” (Matthew 10).

He provokes the persecutor who challenges him; he corrects him who withdraws. We must therefore flee; we must not provoke, if we wish our persecutors to be saved—for them we have been commanded to pray. “Pray,” he says, “for those who persecute you” (Matthew 5).

We must pray and flee, so that the one who rages through ignorance may be healed, and the one who suffers may receive the palm of patience rather than incur danger through rashness.

[Note: In many editions this passage is corrupt and needed a careful emendation. When he says “and made a martyr,” he perhaps has Saint Stephen in mind.]

Brothers, if the martyrs had not fled from Saul, they would not have made Paul a martyr.

Christ taught that this should be done; he left us this example, so that when the Lord flees, the servant should not consider fleeing disgraceful.

There is another reason why Christ fled: as an infant he postponed the time of his passion, and he mounted the cross after the thirtieth year of his bodily life, so that he who had made the perfect human being for life might restore him to perfect life, and might return to heaven the one whom he had given to earth in the same condition.

And the fact that he fled into Egypt proceeds from another reason.

[Note: Literally: Christ withdrew into Egypt, where Herod possessed no authority or power. He would not have escaped either Herod’s fury or that of the scribes and Pharisees, as Jerome observes in his Commentary on Matthew, Book I, if he had fled only beyond the borders of Galilee. For at that time Herod, the persecutor, held the whole kingdom of the Jews; only after his death was it divided into tetrarchies.]

[Note: [Col. 0603D–0604D] This does not mean that Christ’s faith was then received in Egypt, as some undistinguished mystical writer suggests. More accurate writers teach that idolatry endured there until A.D. 329. Those who relate that the idols’ images in that region fell at Christ’s coming, if they mean the casting off there of the demons’ dominion, relate events of later times, not things occurring then. Although in the preceding note I said that the whole question of the overthrow of those images should be examined with better judgment, I have not therefore expunged every miracle reported to have been seen in Egypt at that time; that would be the audacity of Casaubon and other Protestants, based solely on the assertion that Christ performed the beginning of his signs at Cana of Galilee.]

He fled into Egypt so that he might chastise the Jews’ unbelief through the faith of the nations. For Egypt obediently received its Lord, whom Judea had driven away, so that by this figure it might disclose that the Church and the nations were to be preferred in faith to the synagogue and the Jews.

[Note: Some editions place before this sermon the title “On the same subject,” though incorrectly, under the name of the blessed Severian. See the preface.]

## SERMON CLII. On the slaughter of the infants

Today Herodian brutality revealed where jealousy tends, where spite leaps forward, and where envy is carried. While it envies the narrow limits of a temporal kingdom, it attempts to extinguish the birth of the eternal King, as the evangelist says: “Then Herod, seeing that he had been mocked by the magi, was exceedingly angry; and he sent and killed all the boys who were in Bethlehem and in all its districts” (Matthew 2).

“Seeing that he had been mocked by the magi.” Impiety grieves at having been mocked; cruelty, delayed, rages; deceitfulness roars at having been deceived; and fraud, turned back upon itself, is shattered. Herod hisses as he falls into the snare that he himself had set. Here he draws the sword of the wickedness he had fashioned; from faithlessness he takes up weapons against faith. With earthly fury he seeks the one whose heavenly birth he does not believe. He compels soldiers to march against mothers’ breasts; among nursing breasts he attacks the citadel of piety; he hardens iron against tender breasts; he pours out milk before blood; he makes them experience death before life; he brings darkness upon those entering the light.

Such is the teacher of evil, minister of deceit, craftsman of wrath, inventor of crime, author of impiety, plunderer of piety, enemy of innocence, foe of nature, bad toward all, worse toward his own, worst toward himself. Christ fled from him—not in order to escape, but so as not to see him.

Reaching upward, he falls from on high; striking at heaven, he enters the depths; he goes toward himself who goes against God. He kills himself who attempts to kill life,

[Note: Another reading: “to extinguish.”]

[Note: The manuscript of Cesena reads: “because salvation cannot be seized by destruction, life by slaughter, or eternity by an end.”]

because salvation cannot be captured by destruction, life by slaughter, or eternity by an end.

O blind ambition, always! O worst presumption, always! How he loses what has been granted who grasps at what has not been granted!

While besieging an earthly kingdom, Herod attacks the heavenly one. Gaping after earthly things, he rushes upon divine things, and with complete impiety persecutes piety itself. He had heard that a king had been born; he had asked where, when, from where, and for what purpose. But he did not ask how he ought to have done so, because in him there was a love of sinning, while love of innocence did not remain.

[Note: [Col. 0605D] The Caesena manuscript reads “fear of sinning.” Incorrectly.]

[Note: That is, one determined by a perverse will to commit crime; for destinare means “to deliberate” or “to resolve.”]

Determined upon crime, ready for sacrilege, prepared for wrongdoing, he does not seek the grounds of innocence; he abolishes right; he confounds what is lawful and unlawful. For him wickedness is a companion, justice hateful, and injustice always a friend. He lives by slaughter, fortifies himself with blood, pursues cruelty, and rests entirely upon fear, while nothing rests upon love.

Then, blind Herod, he seeks Christ with swords, investigates him through blood, searches him out through cruelty. Fearing a successor, he attacks the Author; he destroys the innocent, wishing innocence itself to perish.

The ruler of the people, guardian of morals, censor of discipline, investigator of justice, defender of equity, preserver of innocence, enlarger of the people—he makes the cause of the innocent a crime against the innocent. He turns the gift of the diviners

[Note: That is, of the magi, who had informed him of Christ’s birth. I judged that “the gift of the ones born” should be emended from the manuscript of Cesena, although Mita, with the printed editions, retains that reading.]

into punishment; he orders the rising of the Author to become a setting; he commands the work of the Savior to become a danger to those to be saved.

The judge summons those who have heard; he interrogates those who speak; he accuses those who deny; he presses the guilty; he strikes the offenders; he rebukes those who know; he adds accomplices;

[Note: Perhaps: “he condemns.”]

he delivers the exposed to sentence.

But what of the infants? Their tongues were silent; their eyes saw nothing; their ears heard nothing; their hands did nothing. Since they had no action, where was their guilt?

[Note: Another reading: “They underwent death.”]

Those who did not know how to live underwent death. Time did not help them;

[Note: From the Vallicellian manuscript. The printed editions read: “time was present.”]

age did not excuse them; silence did not defend them. Before Herod their only crime was that they had been born.

And indeed, how could they not repay what they had received from nature, when a cause was demanded from them on behalf of the Author? Unhappy man, who prepared everything for his own accusation and left no room for excuse, but prepared everything for punishment! Who will excuse the one whom innocence assails, infancy attacks, and milk accuses like blood?

This is directed against Herod.

But Christ, who knew the future, who was aware of hidden things, judge of thoughts and searcher of minds—why did he abandon those whom he knew would be sought because of him and knew would be killed because of him? Born a king, and a heavenly king, why did he disregard the soldiers of his innocence? Why did he despise those of his own age?

[Note: He calls the number of infants killed in Herod’s persecution an army. The Greeks in their menologies and the Ethiopians in their liturgies extend the number to fourteen thousand, quite beyond all plausibility. For who could believe that, in so narrow a part of the earth and within only two years, so many thousands of boys were born into the light, females being excluded as well, against whom Herod would hardly have raged, since he feared nothing from them—and since those born before that time would presumably have died peaceful deaths? These matters should therefore be assigned to Greek fables.]

Why did he leave the watches assigned to his cradles in such a way that, while the enemy sought only the king, he might rage through the whole army?

Brothers, Christ did not despise his soldiers but advanced them. He gave them triumph before life; he enabled them to seize victory without combat; he bestowed crowns upon them before limbs; he willed them to pass beyond vices through virtues, to possess heaven before earth, and to be joined first to divine things rather than to human ones.

Christ therefore sent his soldiers ahead; he did not lose them. He received his ranks; he did not abandon them.

Blessed are those whom we have seen born for martyrdom, not for the world. Blessed are those who exchanged labors for rest, pains for refreshment, and sorrows for joy. They live—yes, they truly live—who deserved to be killed for Christ.

Blessed are the wombs that bore such children; blessed are the breasts that poured themselves out for such children; blessed are the tears shed for such children, which, through the mothers’ weeping, conferred the grace of baptism. For in different ways, through one gift, the mothers are baptized in their tears, and the sons in their own blood.

The mothers suffered in the martyrdom of their sons. For the sword passing through the sons’ bodies reached the mothers’ hearts, and those who shared the suffering must necessarily share the reward.

The little boy smiled at his killer; the infant played with the sword; the nursing child, in place of a nurse, fixed his attention on the terror of his assailant; an age ignorant of light rejoiced as it was dying; the infant son looked upon every human being not as an enemy but as a parent.

The mothers endured whatever anguish and pain there was, and therefore they will not lack the joy of martyrdom—the martyrdom whose tears they shed.

Here let the hearer attend—attend, so that he may understand that martyrdom does not depend upon merit but comes through grace. In the infants, what will, what choice was there, when nature itself was captive? Concerning martyrdom, therefore, we owe everything to God and nothing to ourselves.

To conquer the devil, hand over the body, despise one’s entrails, endure torments, weary the torturer, receive glory from injuries and life from death—this is not human virtue but a divine gift.

May he bring us to the heavenly nourishment who deigned to lie in our stable, Jesus Christ of Nazareth, our Lord, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON CLIII. On the same subject

Brothers, it is not within human understanding to disclose the mystery of a virgin birth. What nature does not possess belongs to the Author, not to nature; it is the work of the heavenly Spirit, which flesh cannot comprehend. Where there is no sign of humanity, there is a sign of divinity, as the prophet says: “The Lord God himself will give you a sign. Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb” (Isaiah 7).

Where there is nothing belonging to earthly custom, everything belongs to the heavenly order. What is not of the world cannot be subject to worldly understanding. A conception that preserves the virgin, and a childbirth that leaves the virgin

[Note: Another reading: “that does not violate the virgin.”]

a virgin—what generates is divine, not human. God walks where no trace whatsoever of human passage is found. Custom fails when miracles occur; customs do not govern signs; uniqueness admits no precedent.

This is revealed by today’s reading, which recounts the divine warfare of the little ones. A cohort arose for its king, and the whole band eagerly desired rather to die before him than to die with him. Soldiers dedicated to Christ began to serve as soldiers before they began to live; to fight before they began to play; to pour out blood before they desired the breast’s milk.

Burning souls could not endure the delays of the body. Flying from the lap toward the raging battle-lines of the enemy, they anticipated the world’s caresses with virtues, kisses with wounds, and ointments with iron, so that they might inhabit heaven before earth, bear the rewards of the spirit before the body, and render triumphs to God before enduring human nourishment.

Truly, truly, brothers, these are martyrs of grace. They confess while silent; they fight without knowing it; they conquer without understanding; they die without consciousness; unaware, they take up palms; ignorant, they seize crowns.

Therefore, just as virginity, knowing nothing of corruption, bestowed honor upon the mother, so infancy, knowing nothing of suffering, seized the palms and crowns of martyrdom.

But what shall we say of the fact that the king himself, who ought to have stood firm, fled alone—and fled at the Father’s command? This flight is one of intimate love, not cowardly fear.

[Note: From the manuscript of Cesena. The printed editions read: “not the cowardice of fear.”]

If Christ had stood firm, the synagogue would have had them as sons, and the Church would not have had them as martyrs.

## SERMON CLIV. On Saint Stephen, the first martyr

[Note: [Col. 0607D] Titulus properly means an inscribed stone, or the inscription on a stone itself. In this sense an old inscription in J. Spon, Itinerarium, vol. III, pt. 2, p. 5, has lapideum titulum, “a stone inscription.” See Du Cange, Glossary, vol. III, p. 1252, where he cites this passage of Chrysologus.]

Just as inscribed markers fixed at the boundaries of estates proclaim the names of their owners, so names themselves often indicate and attest the merits and distinguishing marks of the saints.

Thus Abraham displayed through the addition to his name what he believed by faith, when he was divinely called Abraham instead of Abram: so that, since he was to be enlarged in descendants, he might first be enlarged in name, as the Lord says: “Your name shall no longer be called Abram, but Abraham shall be your name, because I have made you the father of many nations” (Genesis 17).

[Note: Mariana here: “Abram, exalted father; Abraham, father of a multitude.”]

So his holy wife, when she became fruitful from being barren, was called Sarah instead of Sarai, so that she too might first grow in name before she grew in offspring.

[Note: Since she was to become the mother of many nations, she was therefore adorned with an appropriate name. Sarai indicated “my princess” or “my lady,” since she was superior to one man and one family; but that name responded too narrowly to her future dignity. Therefore God commanded that she thereafter be called Sarah—that is, “lady” without limitation, or “princess”—so that she might be called the stock and origin of many nations. Mita. —Sara, “my princess”; Sarah, “princess” absolutely, because of the abundance of her descendants. Mariana here. See Philo, On the Change of Names.]

And because, with the Lord permitting it, she gave forth laughter when she conceived in old age, already furrowed with wrinkles;

[Note: [Col. 0608D] We corrected a seriously defective passage from Latinius. The printed editions, and Mita himself, read: “with the Lord promising, she believed laughter.”] by giving birth when fertility had already been despaired of; by becoming pregnant when barrenness had reached the extremity of old age—she immediately named what she had borne “laughter,” and fitted the name to what she experienced when she laughed: “And she called his name Isaac,” which is interpreted as “laughter” (Genesis 21).

So Jacob, who began to struggle in the womb before he began to live, and to prevail by strength before he had limbs, also received within his mother’s womb the name of “supplanter,” because before he was born he is known to have supplanted the brother divinely rejected (Genesis 25).

And because it would take too long to go through each case, just as Peter received his name from the rock because he first deserved to establish the Church through the firmness of faith, so Stephen was called from a crown because he first deserved to undergo conflict for Christ’s name, and first deserved to dedicate martyrdom through the blood of Christ’s soldiers.

[Note: Ennodius, poem 44:

> What is more powerful than Stephen?  
> Call him a crown: he is a martyr.  
> The fruit of his labor is his name.

]

[Note: Cain is called the dedicator of death, as is said in Sermon 96. Stephen is the dedicator of martyrdom, because he was the first to shed blood for the name of Christ, who had already suffered, died, and risen for us. Saint Fulgentius, sermon on the same subject. Mita. —Dedicare means the same as “to give a beginning.” Saint Cyprian, Letter 33: “On this day he began it, while he dedicates the reading.” Acts of Constantine: “He carried the palace through to completion, which he did not dedicate”—that is, “began.” The word is familiar to Tertullian.]

Let Peter hold the ancient primacy of the apostolic choir,

[Note: Barthius, Adversaria, Book V, chapter 2, p. 2148, presents the passage and observes that choir was used by the ancients for a most joyful company, rarely or never for a sorrowful one. He supplies examples.]

open the kingdom of heaven to those entering, bind the guilty with authority, and mercifully absolve penitents. Let Stephen be the first of the martyrs; let Stephen lead the purple-clad army,

[Note: Another reading: “leads” or “led.”]

who, for the sake of his Lord,

[Note: Some say that he suffered on 3 August of the same year, A.D. 34, in which Christ was crucified for the salvation of all. But according to the tradition of the Church, confirmed by the testimony of the Fathers, he was crowned on the seventh day before the Kalends of January, in the year A.D. 34 completed and the very day beginning A.D. 35 from the Lord’s birth. Mita. —The Martyrology of Ado, edited by the distinguished Georgius, vol. I, p. 7: “The feast of Saint Stephen the first martyr, who suffered not long after the Lord’s ascension, namely in the same year as Christ’s passion.” Whether Saint Stephen’s feast is celebrated on 26 December, or whether that date marks his discovery or the translation of his relics to Constantinople, which is said to have occurred on that day in A.D. 439, Baronius should be consulted in the Martyrology under 3 August, as should Sollerius on Usuard, under 3 August.]

as an eager warrior pours out his blood while the blood of his Lord is still warm. And because he himself won purple stained with his own blood, he deservedly received from his king, after the crown, the name that he had already received at birth from the crown. Truly, the one whom he foreknew and predestined, he now called first to the glory of martyrdom.

[Note: This sermon is praised by Martène, On the Antiquity and Discipline of the Church, vol. I, p. 104. It is known to all that the Kalends of January—whose third day, or the day before the Nones, was called the Vota, because on that day vows were received for the safety of the emperor—were still observed among Christians with immoderate freedom and excess. For this reason the ancient Fathers and councils fiercely attacked their observance. Chrysostom, Homily 23, Against Those Who Observe the New Moons, vol. I, p. 264, Frankfurt edition of 1698, says that many on that day were devoted to superstitious observance and omens, and believed that they would spend the rest of the year happily if they passed this new moon happily. Augustine makes similar complaints in Sermon 5, On the Kalends of January, vol. X, p. 621; Asterius of Amasea, Homily 4, On the Feast of the Kalends, in Combefis’s New Additions, p. 65; Ambrose, Sermon 17 throughout. Prudentius, Book I Against Symmachus:

> …Janus too is propitiated in the accustomed manner  
> With auspices and sacred banquets, which, alas, wretched people,  
> Under an age-old honour celebrate, and make their joyful  
> Festival the feast of the Kalends. Thus the observance grew,  
> Once wrongly begun by ancestors; then handed down  
> Through succeeding ages and enlarged for their late descendants.  
> Unthinking hearts drew out a long chain,  
> And a shadowy custom flowed into corrupt ages.

See Martène, On the Antiquity and Discipline of the Church, vol. I, p. 104; Durant, Book XI, chapter 48, p. 380; Du Cange, vol. II, p. 13; the distinguished Sabbatini, Calendar, p. 12; the Council of Trullo, canon 62, in Councils, vol. VII, p. 1375; Bingham, The Origins of the Church, vol. IX, p. 6, §3, where he cites Chrysologus.]

## SERMON CLV. On the Kalends of January, which were polluted by the various superstitions of the nations
When Christ was piously born for our salvation, immediately the devil generated numerous and pernicious portents from divine goodness, so as to make religion ridiculous, turn holiness into sacrilege, and prepare an injury to God from the honor due to God. Hence, brothers, [Col. 0609B] hence it is that [Note: [Col. 0610C] From this text I judge it worthy of observation that at that time many commoners and nobles at Ravenna still lived according to pagan custom and worshiped idols. MITA.—But these entertainments were also customary among Christians. For the Ravennates, consult Rubeus, *Historia*, book II, p. 106.] today the pagans drag out, parade, and pull along their gods to be seen in carefully devised obscenities, in contrived disgrace, and in a very shamefulness more shameful than itself [Note: [Col. 0610C] The printed editions read: “They drag out their gods to be seen in the very shamefulness itself.” Meursius uselessly deletes the repeated words “their gods” [Col. 0610D].], whom they make unfit to be seen. What vanity, what madness, what blindness: to confess that they are gods, and to disgrace them with wretched mockeries! Those who mock the gods whom they worship are mockers, not worshipers; they dishonor, rather than honor, the gods whom they venerate; they deform and confound, rather than glorify, the gods from whom they suppose themselves formed, when they compose them out of that very confusion. Truly, as the Apostle says, “Because they did not approve of retaining God in their knowledge, God handed them over to a debased mind, to do what is improper” (Rom. I): when they assign divinity to those whom they deprive of humanity, when they judge them worthy of heaven, when they make them unworthy even of the earth itself, truly they have been handed over to a debased mind. And [Note: [Col. 0610D] Latinius rightly observes that the truth of this reading is doubtful, for in his manuscript he had read: “This is not the judgment of God.” We have restored the genuine reading.] this is not a judgment of human beings; it is the wisdom of God that those who are proved to be the authors of injury should themselves be the avengers of God’s injuries. What anger, what vengeance, is this—that the offense against God should be punished through idols in such a way that those whom antiquity falsely claimed to be gods through altars, incense, sacrifices, jewels, and gold, posterity should judge to have been the most disgraceful of human beings, and should mark their life, character, and deeds upon their very faces, teaching that such beings ought rather to be shunned than worshiped!

Let us mourn, brothers, both for those who pursued such things and rejoice that, by heaven’s mercy, we have escaped them. Those whose adulteries they shape in statues, whose fornications they entrust to images, whose incest they title in paintings [Note: [Col. 0610D] “They adorn.” Tertullian, in the poem *On the Judgment of God*:

> Who will fit rustic Muses to my song  
> and title the rose-colored airs with spring flowers?], whose cruelties they commend in books, whose parricides they hand down to the ages [Col. 0610B], whose impieties resound in tragedies, whose obscenities they enact—through what madness would they believe such beings to be gods, unless they are possessed by a desire for crimes and a love of wickedness, and wish to have criminal gods? [Note: [Col. 0610D] The printed editions read, “They desire gods of crimes.” Meursius again deletes the word *crimes*, repeated twice.] Whoever wishes to sin worships and venerates the authors of sins. Hence it is that the adulterer gives himself over to Venus; hence it is that the cruel man dedicates himself to Mars. [Note: [Col. 0610D] Mita restored the entire sentence from manuscripts and conjecture. Other editions have a longer night.]

We have said these things, brothers, to expose the reason why the pagans today make their gods commit such deeds as we endure, and make them such that they are both objects of horror and shame to those who see them; why they make them such that, eventually, even those who make them may themselves dread and abandon them, while Christians may glory in having been freed from such things through Christ—provided only that they are not defiled by these spectacles, that they do not defile their incense by touch, that they flee the danger of assent to such things, since assent is always equal to the deeds themselves, as the Apostle proves when he says: “Not only those who do them, but also those who consent to those who do them” (Rom. I).

And if condemnation for assent is so great, who could sufficiently mourn for those who [Note: [Col. 0611D] For they proceeded in costume, disguised as gods and goddesses. See especially Augustine, or any other author, *Sermon* 29 in the appendix. The note’s longer passage would exceed its limits. Hear only Rubeus, p. 106, concerning Ravenna: “They ran about the city dressed in the images of the gods, and in such gestures and manner that nearly all the things handed down about their incests, adulteries, and other wicked deeds seemed to be placed before one’s eyes.”] make images of themselves? Have these people not lost the image of God, forfeited his likeness, and stripped themselves of Christ’s clothing, who have fashioned themselves in the sacrilegious forms of idols?

But someone may say, “These are not pursuits of sacrilege; these are the vows of play. This is the joy of novelty, not the error of antiquity; this is the beginning of the year, not an offense against paganism.” You are mistaken, man: these are not games but crimes. Who plays with impiety? Who jokes with sacrilege? Who calls an abomination laughter? He greatly deceives himself who thinks this way; whoever assumes the attire of a tyrant is a tyrant. Whoever makes himself a god stands opposed to the true God; whoever wishes to wear the persona of an idol has refused to bear the image of God; whoever wishes to play with the devil will not be able to rejoice with Christ. No one plays safely with a serpent; no one jokes with the devil with impunity.

Therefore, if there are in us any bowels of piety, if there is in us any regard for humanity, if any concern for our brother’s salvation possesses us, let us pull back those who run headlong toward destruction, are snatched toward death, dragged toward Tartarus, and hurry toward Gehenna. Let the father pull back his son, the master his servant, the parent his relative, citizen his fellow citizen, one human being another, and the Christian all those who have compared themselves with beasts, made themselves equal to cattle, [Note: [Col. 0611D] This too was an infamous custom of those profane games: assuming the forms of sheep and deer, they ran here and there and behaved with greater wantonness. See the Council of Toledo IV, canon 10; Augustine, *Sermon on the Seasons* 225; the Council of Auxerre, canon 1; Ambrose, on Psalm XLI; Maximus of Turin, *Sermon on the Kalends of January*: “Is not everything there false and insane, when human beings, formed by God, transform themselves either into cattle or into wild beasts?” [Col. 0612D]], and fashioned themselves in the likeness of demons [Col. 0611C]. The one who frees another finds a reward; the one who neglects him incurs offense. Blessed is the person who is guardian of his own life and provider for another’s salvation.

## SERMON CLVI. On the Epiphany and the Magi

Just as the careful skill of physicians prepares an antidote from health-giving juices against deadly diseases, yet, if a sick person presumes to take what has been prepared for health outside the rules of the art, outside medical treatment, and outside the proper time, what was provided for salvation becomes the cause of danger, so the word of God, if a reckless hearer presumes to know it outside instruction, teaching, and the dogma of faith, though it is the substance of life, becomes an occasion of destruction. [Note: [Col. 0612D] Elsewhere: “It must be attended to.”] We must take care, brothers, lest through incompetence in hearing what has been divinely written for our advancement become harmful to our souls. Do you suppose [Note: [Col. 0612D] He is attacking judicial astrologers and the Priscillianists, who thought that the magi had inferred Christ’s birth through natural astronomical knowledge; Augustine, Chrysostom, and Gregory often refuted them. Since our author denies that the magi found Christ by the guidance of a star, he speaks of natural and human knowledge of the stars, as he indicates in the following sermon. Mita. — More learned men regard the idea that the magi were Chaldeans as a fabrication. For Chaldea lies north, not east, in relation to Judaea; hence the prophets so often say that the evil to be inflicted upon the Jews by the Chaldeans would arise from the north. It is more plausible that they were Persians and came from Persia. The tale of one magus having a dark complexion arose from collections falsely attributed to the Venerable Bede.] that the Evangelist has taught today that Chaldeans, star-watchers, magi wandering among the constellations, investigating the affairs of heaven amid the darkness of night, assigning the causes of birth and death to the courses of the stars, and determining human good and evil by the will of the heavenly lights, found the birth of Christ, hidden for ages, under the guidance of a star? Far from it.

Thus the world thinks; thus the pagans understand it; thus the surface of the reading appears to make it. But the evangelical message speaks not human things but divine ones; not customary things but new ones; not things deceiving through art but things supported by truth; not things that play upon the eyes but things fixed in the heart; not things wavering through conjecture but things confirmed by authority; things coming from God, not from fate; not things collected through numbers but acquired through powers.

“When Jesus was born,” he says, “in Bethlehem of Judaea in the days of King Herod, behold, magi came from the East to Jerusalem, saying: ‘Where is he who has been born King of the Jews? For we saw his star in the East and have come to worship him’” (Matt. II).

When Jesus is born, the origin of all things arises; the giver of generation is brought forth; the author of nature is born, so that he might restore nature, restore the race, and renew its origin. Adam, the first human being, father of the race, origin of generation, the good of nature, lost the freedom of the race and the life of his offspring through his transgression in such a way that the succession of generations had to lamentably bear the evil of nature, the slavery of the race, and the death of its offspring. Hence Christ, by being born, restored nature; by dying, removed death; by rising again, recalls life. And he who had given the human being a soul from heaven then made the human being also consist of flesh, lest earthly corruption should again drag heavenly understanding down into the fall of the flesh, as the Apostle says: “The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man from heaven, heavenly. As was the earthly, so also are the earthly; and as is the heavenly, so also are the heavenly” (I Cor. XV). And the evangelist John says: “Everyone who is born of God does not sin, but the generation of God preserves him” (John V). This, then, is why Christ is born: so that he might raise those lying in an earthly offspring to a heavenly nature.

“When Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judaea.” Bethlehem, brothers, is called in Hebrew “house of bread.” By these names, then, Judaea is marked as a house and called a race, so that the faithfulness of the promise and the truth of prophecy might be fulfilled, as Jacob says: “Judah, your brothers shall praise you; your hands shall be upon the backs of your enemies; your father’s sons shall worship you” (Gen. XLIX, according to the Septuagint). And afterward: “A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs, until he comes to whom the things laid up belong, and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations.” Hence David also says, “Judah is my king” (Ps. LIX).

“When Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judaea in the days of King Herod.” What does it mean that [Note: [Col. 0613D] It is now agreed among the principal chronologists that Christ was born in the year preceding Herod’s death. According to Flavius Josephus, *Jewish Antiquities*, XVII.8, Herod died in the thirty-seventh year after Judaea had been taken under Roman rule. Christ therefore must have been born in Herod’s thirty-sixth year and Augustus’s fortieth year, since Augustus was in the fifth year of his reign when he appointed Herod king of the Jews. Cardinal Norisius demonstrates this at length in *Cenotaphium Pisanum*, dissertation 11, chapter 6, p. 128, Lyon edition by Van der Aa.] at the time of a wicked king God descended to earth? Divinity is joined to flesh? A heavenly exchange is made with an earthly body? What does it mean—and when does the true king not come to expel the tyrant, avenge his homeland, restore the world, and return freedom?

Herod [Note: [Col. 0613D] Hence “renegade”: unless from the camp of the Jews to the religion of the gentile emperors? See note 4 on Sermon 52.]—a renegade from the Jewish nation—invaded the kingdom, took away freedom, profaned holy things, and confused the order of things; he abolished everything belonging to discipline and worship. Therefore, rightly, since human help is absent from the holy nation, divine aid comes to it, and God is present to the very people for whom no human being was present.

So also Christ will come again, so that Antichrist may be overthrown, the world may be freed, the homeland of paradise restored, the freedom of the world perpetuated, and the slavery of the age entirely removed.

“Behold, magi came from the East.” The magi come from the East toward the East, so that the one who had commanded them to come might himself receive them as they came. For when would a magus seek God unless God commanded him? When would an astrologer find the king of heaven unless God revealed him? [Note: [Col. 0613D] He calls the magi wise men, astrologers; and he explains himself, should he perhaps have caused anyone scruple, in Sermon 150. [Col. 0614D] Yet he never calls the magi kings, nor did the ancients ever honor them with such a title, apart from Tertullian alone and a few others. Noteworthy is Origen’s third homily, which calls the magi miserable men.] When would a Chaldean worship the one God on earth without God, when in heaven he served as many gods as there were stars? [Note: [Col. 0614D] No one is unaware that the stars were once regarded as gods.]

There is a more heavenly sign concerning the magi than concerning the star: the magus knows the king of Judaea, the author of the law, while the Jew does not; Chaldea brings him forward, Judaea does not; Jerusalem turns away and flees, Syria follows and worships.

“Behold, magi came from the East, saying: ‘Where is he who has been born King of the Jews? We saw his star.’” And yet what is this thing that is seen? Truly, as the Apostle said, “Though he was rich, he became poor” (II Cor. VIII): though he was rich in his divinity, he becomes poor in our flesh; and the one who made and contains the whole creation began to have one star.

“We saw his star.” At last the magus sees the one who has the star, not one who is possessed by the star; nor is he himself driven by the course of the star, but he directs the star’s course—the star whose movement through heaven he directs, regulates, and guides along its way in such a manner [Note: [Col. 0614D] Origen, on John, p. 27, calls the star the magi’s servant and the handmaid of the knowledge of Jesus.] that it serves the magi and is sent to accompany their steps. For when the magus walks, the star walks; when the magus sits, the star stands; when the magus sleeps, the star keeps watch. Thus the magus understands that, since their conditions of travel are alike, their necessity of service must also be alike. He no longer believes the star to be a god, but judges it to be a fellow servant, since he sees it so completely devoted to his service.

“Where is he who has been born King of the Jews? We saw his star [Col. 0613D] in the East, and we have come to worship him.” By saying, “Where is he who has been born King of the Jews?” they are not asking but taunting: when those who know question those who do not know, [Note: [Col. 0614D] The manuscript of Cesena reads, “They are not ignorant while those whom they question are ignorant, but they accuse the negligent.”] they themselves are not ignorant, but rebuke the negligent, reproach the sluggish, expose the wicked, chastise the obstinate, and accuse the servants of not having gone out to meet their Lord.

For why do they ask human beings about what they had learned through God? Why do they need human assistance in pointing out the way, when the stars of heaven served this purpose for them? Why do they need the temple lamp, when the wondrous star of heaven shone brightly for them?

“Where is he who has been born King of the Jews?” This is what they mean: Why does the King of the Jews lie in a manger and not recline in the temple? Why does he not shine in purple but lie rough in swaddling clothes? Why is he hidden in a cave and not held openly in the sanctuary? You received animals in a manger, but you refused to receive in your own house the one whom they received. “The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger,” as it is written (Isa. I); but you, Israel, did not seek your Lord.

“We saw his star.” The star appeared unwillingly, but under command; not by the nod of heaven, but by the impulse of Divinity; not according to the law of the stars, but through the novelty of the signs; not by the climate of heaven, but through the power of the one being born; not by art, but by God; not through the astrologer’s knowledge, but through the foreknowledge of the Creator; not by arithmetical calculation, but by divine decree; through heavenly administration, not Chaldean curiosity; not through magical art, but through Judaean prophecy.

Thus, when the magus saw that human concerns had perished, that his own arts had failed, that the labors of worldly wisdom had been emptied, that the efforts of all the schools had stiffened into lifelessness, that the treasures of all philosophy had been exhausted, that pagan night had fled, that the clouds of opinions had collapsed, and that even the shadows of the demons had hidden themselves, he saw the star—not, as a comet, concealing what it announces with its uncurled hair [Note: [Col. 0614D] Mita reads, “with its curled hair.”] and darkening what shines—and said: [Note: [Col. 0614D] Mita: “It is right that I should follow you as my guide, and by a new …”]

“It is right that I should see you shining toward Judaea with a new ray, a light bearing a sign, and a sure brilliance, and there show the King born there, beyond the law of the world, beyond the order of flesh, beyond human nature.”

Thus, laying aside his error, he follows, runs, arrives, finds, rejoices, falls down, and worships, because, not through the star and not through art but through God, he marvels that he has found God in human flesh.

Therefore, brothers, the present reading has not confirmed magical error but dissolved it. But let these things suffice for today, so that through God the matters that follow may shine forth clearly.

## SERMON CLVII. On the Same Subject

The festivals of the Lord express their causes through their names. For just as by being born Christ gave the day of his birth, and by rising again gave the day of resurrection, so by the light of the signs he displayed the day of his manifestation. For the one who, by being born, first veiled himself in a human body afterward revealed himself through the heavenly mystery of his works: afterward God himself appeared in a threefold manner, who had appeared as a single human being in birth.

Rightly, therefore, this present solemnity is called by the name Epiphany, in which the divinity that was hidden from us in our flesh shone forth. This is, brothers, this is the festival which, conceived at different times, brought forth three signs of divinity. Through the Epiphany the magi confess Christ the Lord by mystical gifts [Note: [Col. 0615D] Elsewhere: “Christ God.”], and the worshipers of the stars [Note: [Col. 0615D] Either because they were devoted to the study of the stars, or mystically because they lived their lives in the night of paganism. From Mita.], inhabitants of the night, find the author of light in the thick darkness, so that this may be the grace of the author, not the achievement of those seeking in this way; it may belong not to the star but to God; it may be the Creator’s gift, not a benefit bestowed by a creature; it may not be human art but a divine gift.

“Behold,” he says, “magi came from the East, saying: ‘Where is he who has been born King of the Jews? For we saw his star in the East, and have come to worship him’” (Matt. II).

“We saw his star.” And what is not his? It is his star, not that he is the star. “His star”: the star that received existence but did not give it; the star whose rising the author held in his power, not the star that held the author’s rising. “His star”: coming not from a nativity, but from a begetter; by command, not by fate; from the author, not from the calculator; not one that would give birth, but one that would sustain its setting. A star not law-giving but sign-bearing, carrying not the order of days but the light of nights. This star is a servant of the way, not of life; companion of the magi, not kin to Christ; not mistress of the Lord, but a little maidservant of servants.

But someone may say: Why magi? Why by means of a star? If the matter has nothing to do with stars or origin, why is there any cause or reason connected with nature? Why magi? Why a star? So that through Christ the very material of error might become an occasion of salvation, just as through Christ the cause of death became the cause of life. It is a singular mark of virtue to confuse an enemy with his own sword.

Among the magi, ignorance was at fault, not the will; what was criminal was not devotion but error. [Note: [Col. 0615D] The manuscript of Cesena reads: “To seek God whom they did not know, and not to know how to seek him, is more a matter of necessity than of guilt. For they were not seeking God in the stars through obstinacy but through ignorance,” says Mita.] To seek God and not know how to seek him is more a matter of necessity than of guilt. It was therefore pious that God should both grant himself to be found by those seeking him and attribute the fault to their error.

Accordingly, Paul was made a preacher from a persecutor by such a judgment, because through zeal for the law he attacked the law, and through love for the God he did not know he sinned against God. [Note: [Col. 0615D] For, through zeal for the divine law, he persecuted Christ, whom he did not know to be God.] Hence faith runs to Paul, while unbelief returns to ignorance.

But the hearer still says: Suppose that the star, not by its own command but by God’s order, showed the magi who were seeking the way; whence came such knowledge of mystical gifts, such profound sacramental significance in their offerings? Not from Chaldean art, but from the ancient tradition of the holy ancestors. They were [Note: [Col. 0615D] Many authors report that the magi were worshipers of the true God but ignorant of the Jewish law. The Fathers commonly call them the firstfruits of the nations. In 1636, a frivolous author published an entire volume in France to demonstrate that the magi who worshiped Christ were none other than Enoch, Elijah, and Melchizedek. He is accustomed to such madness:

> “A people lacking reason and feeding their minds on chimeras,” says Serry, p. 336,

who mocks rather than examines this opinion. In any event, what our author asserts—that the magi were descendants of Abraham, through his concubine Keturah—can also be found in Maldonado, on Matthew II.] of the lineage of Noah, sons of Abraham, who had learned through God, not through art, that Christ would be born; and by a profound mystery they knew him to be human, God, king, and destined to die.

Hence they carried gifts suitable to the faith of the fathers, knowingly offering gold to the king, incense to God, and myrrh to the one who would die, and by such a gift satisfying both piety and honor.

But let this suffice concerning the magi. Through the Epiphany Christ changed water into wine at the wedding (John II), so that Christ’s presence at the wedding might be a matter of power, not pleasure; not of humanity, but of authority; for the sake of a sign, not the belly; not an arrangement for drunkenness, but a manifestation of divinity. Accordingly, when the water changed its nature, it immediately disclosed its author, and the Creator of the elements was revealed to the creature through the transformation [Note: [Col. 0616D] Because it happened so quickly and so completely that one must judge it possible only for God the Creator.].

Blessed is the wedding, blessed is that wedding at which Christ is present, which is consecrated not by luxury but by virtues. What did not pass into grace there, where water passed into wine?

Through the Epiphany Christ entered the channel of the Jordan, consecrated as our baptism (Matt. III), so that those whom he had received on earth by being born he might raise to heaven by being born again; that in himself he might have as free people those whom he had seen to be captives apart from him; that he himself might make living those whom guilt had made mortal; that he might make everlasting those whom death had made temporal; and that those whom the devil had made exiles from earthly things he might himself make his companions in heavenly things.

Hence, brothers, the Holy Spirit then poured himself out in a complete descent, when the Father cried from heaven, “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. III), so that the operation which had been one with the Son in creating us might become one with him in restoring us. Thus, at different times but on one and the same day, through the gift of the magi, the transformation of water, and the Father’s voice, Christ was recognized as God by a threefold testimony, and from the threefold manifestation of Christ there came one sacred solemnity of the Epiphany.

[Note: [Col. 0616D] Observe here the golden stream of Roman eloquence: the subject is Christ the newborn king and the magi seeking Christ; the hearers are the emperor Valentinian, his mother, the Augusta Galla Placidia, and the leading men of the court; the setting is a time when human morals were corrupt and depraved; and the learning consists in reproving them with complete calm of mind through a comparison drawn from the subject of the speech, while instructing them in holy precepts. Mita.]

## SERMON CLVIII. On the Same Subject

Often we ask why Christ enters the world in such a way that he experiences the narrowness of the womb, suffers the hardship of birth, endures the bonds of swaddling clothes, tolerates the weakness of a cradle, seeks nourishment from the breast through tears, and experiences the stages and necessities of human age. And how ought the one who wished to bring grace, drive away fear, and seek love to come?

Nature teaches everyone what infancy can accomplish and what it deserves. Infancy—what barbarity does it not overcome? What savagery does it not tame? What cruelty does it not restrain? What fury does it not check? What power does it not lay down? What harshness does it not soften? What hardness does it not dissolve? What love does it not demand? What affection does it not extort? What grace does it not impose? What charity does it not obtain? Fathers know that this is so, mothers feel it, everyone approves it, and human hearts bear witness.

Thus he wished to be born who wished to be loved, not feared. Yet among human wickedness, although infancy is so gentle, pious, and dear, hear what benefit it produced.

“When King Herod heard this,” he says, “he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him; and gathering together all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he asked them where Christ was to be born” (Matt. II).

If Jerusalem, the king, the scribes, and the chief priests are so troubled by Christ’s infancy, what would they have done if Christ had come immediately as a full-grown man, supported by riches and a multitude, accompanied by those regarded with suspicion and by strangers? They give nothing to time, nothing to age, nothing to poverty, nothing to a parent. As soon as they hear that he has been born, they prepare death for the newborn, deceit for the innocent, crime for the pious, swords for the defenseless, soldiers against the lone child, slaughter for the crying infant, and punishment for the parent. And, so that violence might be mingled with blood, bitter cruelty declares war on cradles, presses breasts with weapons, strikes shields against laps, so that it may make both human and divine offspring enter the tomb before entering the world.

Granted that King Herod was compelled to contrive such things by his love of the kingdom and fear of a successor; why Jerusalem, why the chief priests, why the scribes? Because the profane does not want God to be born, the servant does not want the master, the guilty person does not want the judge, the rebel does not want the ruler, and the faithless person does not want the one who knows him.

Jerusalem had drenched itself in various forms of contamination; the priests had profaned holy things, selling sins and turning forgiveness and piety into profit. [Note: [Col. 0618D] For they claimed for themselves the sacrifices offered for the expiation of sins, or stored away for themselves the price that had been claimed.] The scribes had changed heavenly doctrine, saving knowledge, and life-giving instruction into a cruel understanding, a lapse into faithlessness, and deadly empty talk.

Hence they do not want Christ to be born and fear him living, [Col. 0617D] because they knew that they would soon be handed over to disgrace, dragged into reproach, expelled from the temple, deprived of the priesthood, and stripped of the revenues from offerings. Once inflamed by greed, captured by pomp, wounded by vices, drunk with vanity, and soaked in luxury, they could think of no correction and hope for no forgiveness.

A good steward, when he has obtained abundant fruit through continual labor, desires his master to come for his profit and longs for his arrival with joy. A diligent worker, when he has completed the work he undertook, desires the head of the household to arrive so that he may receive his wage. A devoted soldier, after conflict and victory, longs for the king’s presence, so that his sweat and wounds may be repaid with rewards. Thus the one who overthrows the wars of the world with tireless strength desires Christ to come for his victory-palm; but the one overcome by the allurements of the age does not want Christ to come, trembling at punishment and expecting no forgiveness.

Brothers, let us do good and turn away from evil; let us flee vices and follow virtues; let us disregard present things and think about future ones; let us seek our kingdom, come to our crown, desire glory, and direct all our hopes toward the crown. But now let the sermon return to the matters that follow.

“Then Herod,” he says, “secretly summoned the magi and carefully learned from them the time when the star had appeared to them. Sending them to Bethlehem, he said: ‘Go and inquire carefully about the child, and when you have found him, report back to me, so that I too may come and worship him.’”

He secretly summons the magi because a feigned mind and deceitful conscience dare nothing openly. He secretly summons the magi because a thief loves the night and a robber lays ambush in secret. He carefully inquires about the time of the star; yet, while he fears for his kingdom, he does not fear the sign of heaven or dread the author of the time.

Why are you troubled, Herod? Why are you so concerned about a successor? The one whom the stars serve is not held by an earthly empire.

“Go and inquire carefully about the child, and when you have found him, report back to me.” Herod, you are mistaken: the magus was ordered to worship, not to betray; he came to bear witness, not to denounce; it was granted to him to see, but not granted to you to find.

“Go and inquire.” As though asking the magi once were not enough. To those who asked in piety, a response was given [Note: [Col. 0618D] For while Herod, with courtly kindness, allowed the magi to depart, he was impiously plotting Christ’s death.] without piety; the message of salvation became ruin to those who heard it wickedly.

The obstinate servant hears that the Lord has been born, but prepares snares, not honor, for the Lord who is being born; he prepares death so that he may escape servitude. But since God could neither be ended, salvation perish, nor life die, the Lord remains in honor while the servant remains in guilt; the one who refused to come for service is dragged to punishment, and the one who did not wish to reach grace is seized for judgment.

“Go and inquire carefully about the child, and when you have found him, report back to me.” He appropriately said, “Report back to me,” because whoever hastens to reach Christ always renounces the devil. When a Christian is to be baptized, he hears from the priest, “Do you renounce the devil?” and replies, “I renounce him.” Herod therefore specifically says that the magi must renounce to him, because he knew that he held the devil’s place and fulfilled Satan’s role.

“So that I too may come and worship him.” He wishes to lie, but he cannot. He will come, so that he may be bent down to torments, cast into punishments, and stretched out in penalty—the man who had pretended to worship in order to rage.

But the magi, when they had passed through the clouds of Jewish faithlessness and again saw the star they had seen in the clear sky of Christian faith, with the star itself going before and guiding them, reached the most sacred place of the Lord’s birth. [Note: [Col. 0619D] Some interpreters of Sacred Scripture reasonably suspect that the star seen by the magi in the East went before them as far as Jerusalem, serving as their guide; that its light was then withheld while they remained there; and that it appeared again when they departed, leading them as far as Bethlehem.]

“And opening their treasures, they offered him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh.” They offer gold to the king, frankincense to God, and myrrh to the one who would die, offering these gifts in devotion to the Lord and entrusting great treasures of knowledge to those who would believe afterward. Thus they return by the road of innocence to their own country, while they have trodden Herod’s fraudulent path toward ruin.

## SERMON CLIX. On the Same Subject
A few days ago—that is, on the eighth day before the Kalends of this month, when the days began to grow longer, because the true Day dawned—those who have read, or who have lent their ears to readers, readily recall that the Lord Christ Jesus was born in the flesh, as it is written in the Gospel (Luke 2). The Israelite shepherds, keeping watch over their flock, learned this when the angels announced it; today the Gentile Magi, pursuing their quest with curiosity, found him when signs pointed him out. To the shepherds, the voice of the spiritual ministers spoke, announcing the birth of the Lord; to these men, a star, as it were the tongue of heaven.

The shepherds say, to whom the prophets had so often been sent: “Let us go as far as Bethlehem and see this word that has come to pass for us.” The Magi say, to whom no prophet had ever spoken:

> “Where is he who has been born king of the Jews? We saw his star in the East, and we have come to worship him” (Matthew 2).

[Note: Neither by a word reaching their ears, nor in writing and through prophecy. Although the Magi may have known through Balaam’s prophecy and the ancient tradition of their ancestors what is said in the text, Balaam was not a prophet but a diviner; and he prophesied like Caiaphas, not like a prophet. See Maldonado, on Matthew 2, question 4, and Numbers 22:5. — MITA.]

Thus the shepherds approach from nearby, while these come from far away; nevertheless, both converge in pious devotion upon one and the same place of faith. There they behold, admire, and recognize Christ the King laid before those two prophetic animals, which bear the type and figure of the two peoples.

[Note: From the passage of Isaiah cited below, which is commonly applied to Christ at his birth:]

> “The ox knows its owner, and the ass its master’s manger” (Isaiah 1).

The ox, the Jew, recognized him, having shaken off the yoke of the Law; the ass, the pagan, also recognized him, having laid aside the brutishness of folly. The one abandoned the superfluous labor of observance; the other left behind the wandering error of superstition.

[Note: This is the genuine explanation of this prophecy. See Jerome, most explicitly, on Isaiah 1.]

Both recognized him, because both approached the one manger of the Lord in order to feast—not on the hay of death, but on the food of salvation. Eat, eat, devout animals, the food of eternal life; with eager mouths, seize as much as you can of the food of everlasting recompense—not dividing it into pieces, but taking it whole and entire. For Christ cannot be eaten and divided: believers receive him whole, and whole he is received into the mouth of the heart.

> “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1);

he dwelt among us from the moment he graciously filled the Virgin’s womb.

They offered him, as it is written, gold, frankincense, and myrrh. We offer the frankincense of a faith that has come from a distant region; we offer the myrrh of a confession that is near at hand; we offer the sweet-smelling gifts of charity.

[Note: For our faith journeyed to us from the Hebrews.]

[Note: For from the Law the sacrament of repentance and the confession of sins flowed forth to us—unless one should rather understand this as referring to the confession of faith that we elicit with heart and mind. — From Mita.]

We offer these three things whenever we confess Christ as King, Lord, and man. But let us worship Christ in spirit and in truth, if we have offered him the gifts of faith and confession. And, like those Magi—who are guides of our faith and leaders of our belief—having been warned in a dream, that is, in this life, which is like a dream, let us elude Herod the king, that is, the devil, prince of this world, and return by another road—that is, through another life—to our homeland, from which we were unhappily expelled through Adam but have now been mercifully led back through Christ.

[Note: Through the amendment of the present life.]

## SERMON CLX. On the same subject

Although clear signs of divinity were always present in the very mystery of the Lord’s incarnation, today’s solemnity nevertheless discloses and reveals in many ways that God has come in a human body, lest mortal humanity, perpetually enveloped in darkness through ignorance, lose what it has merited to hold and possess through grace. For he who wished to be born for us did not wish to remain unknown to us; and therefore he reveals himself in this manner, lest the great mystery of piety become the occasion of a great error.

Today the Magus, whom he had sought shining in the stars, finds him wailing in a cradle. Today the Magus marvels at him, radiant amid swaddling clothes, whom he had long endured as obscure among the stars. Today the Magus turns over in profound astonishment what he sees, and where: heaven on earth, earth in heaven, man in God, God in man, and, throughout the universe, one who cannot be contained enclosed within a tiny body.

Therefore the Magus, who cannot investigate and cannot comprehend, immediately worships. For he sees that the stars, moon, and sun do not shine in heaven as brightly as he beholds the flesh shining on earth; he sees the commerce of divinity and humanity brought together in one and the same body. Here, while he believes him to be God, he recognizes him as king and understands that he will die for love of the human race. With fearful thought he considers how God can die, how the restorer of life can be killed.

And so the Magus ceases to seek by his art what his art cannot discover. Because he sees that he had long wandered in heaven among wandering stars, he rejoices that on earth he has reached God under the guidance of a single star. The Magus discovers that all the things seen in heaven with human eyes are obscured by profound mysteries.

[Note: The Caesenatian manuscript reads: “He believes and does not investigate, but confesses through mystical gifts.”]

Now, seeing that he must believe and not investigate, he confesses through mystical gifts: by frankincense, that he is God; by gold, that he is king; by myrrh, that he is destined to die. By frankincense, God; by gold, king—so that he might placate by a rich act of service the one whom he had assaulted and offended through his inquisitive and presumptuous undertaking.

And he fulfills what many suspect concerning the eunuch from Ethiopia:

> “Ethiopia will stretch out its hands to God” (Psalm 67).

[Note: In this prophecy many recognize the conversion of the Gentiles, especially the Egyptians and Ethiopians, whose first fruits many identify in the eunuch of Queen Candace. Hilary, however, together with Chrysologus, supposes that the Magi who worshiped Christ in the manger came from those regions.]

The Magus anticipates the Jew with his hands toward Christ, because when the Jew was treacherously betraying Christ to Herod, the Magus was confessing Christ as God through his gifts. Hence it is that the Gentile, who was last, became first: for then, through the faith of the Magi, the belief of the Gentiles was consecrated, and the cruelty of the Jews was exposed.

Today Christ entered the channel of the Jordan, to wash away the sin of the world. John himself testifies that he came for this purpose:

> “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1).

Today John, a servant, holds the Lord; a man holds God; John holds Christ. He holds him in order to receive forgiveness, not to give it.

Today, as the prophet says:
