> “The voice of the Lord is over the waters” (Psalm 28).

What voice?

> “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3).

Today the voice of God is over the waters, because God the Father, in order to test the faith of the human race, himself stands as witness to his Son, himself as his advocate.

[Note: The Caesenatian manuscript reads: “He himself is his own witness, the witness of his Son.”]

“This is my beloved Son,” because he had no other to bear witness; the Father’s secret had no arbiter. Divine generation knows no external witness; divinity admits no external recognition, as the Son himself says:

> “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son” (Matthew 11).

Today the Holy Spirit hovers over the waters in the form of a dove, so that, just as Noah’s dove announced that the flood had departed from the world (Genesis 8), so this dove might indicate that the world’s perpetual shipwreck had ceased. Nor does it carry, like that earlier dove, a sprig of the old olive; rather, it pours the whole richness of the new chrism upon the head of the new parent, so as to fulfill what the prophet foretold:

> “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 44).

[Note: That is, of Christ, who is the parent of all who are to be saved and restored. — MITA.]

Today the Lord is above the waters. Properly above the waters, and not beneath the waters, because Christ does not serve the sacraments of baptism but commands them.

Today the God of majesty thundered. If the Father thunders from heaven, if the Son stands upon the flowing waters of the Jordan, if the Holy Spirit appears bodily from above, what is the meaning of the fact that the Jordan, which fled at the presence of the legal ark (Joshua 3), did not flee at the presence of the whole Trinity?

[Note: Most deny that this was a real and natural dove. Nevertheless, St Augustine affirms that it had a body, but a body of air in the form of a dove. Yet that body, whatever it was, was not hypostatically assumed by the Holy Spirit, as Tertullian falsely supposed; rather, the Holy Spirit was in it as signified in a sign, just as angels, in order to be seen by human beings, have often assumed human bodies. See Maldonado on Matthew 3, no. 16. — MITA. — “In this matter,” says Calmet, “the Fathers were not so scrupulous as our modern writers; nor did they judge a dove’s form unworthy of the Holy Spirit, since throughout Scripture the Son of God is described by the names Lion of Judah, Worm of Jacob, Lamb, Stone, etc.”]

What does it mean? It means that whoever obeys piety begins not to be subject to fear. Here the Trinity exercises the whole of grace and speaks with itself of the whole of charity. There, the elements are rebuked, so that servants may be trained in fear.

Yet amid such and such great realities John stands fearless, because one who has been born wholly for the love of God, as the angelic testimony confirms, cannot fear.

Today Christ gives the beginning of heavenly signs when he changes water into wine (John 2), so that the one whom the Father had already proved to be his Son by his voice might himself prove himself to be God by his works.

[Note: The Caesenatian manuscript reads: “Might manifest himself.”]

He is the author of the elements, who changes the elements; he himself made nature, and therefore does not struggle to act against nature. He changes water into wine so that the dullness of our nature may advance through the power of divinity.

[Note: The same manuscript reads: “through the wine of divinity.”]

For he who, through a hidden and furtive increase, extended and multiplied five loaves into a filling meal for five thousand people (Matthew 14),

[Note: That is, concealed and inaccessible to human eyes.]

could, through successive increases, enlarge and perpetuate the measures of wine for the wedding feast.

But the water was to be changed into the mystery of blood,

[Note: Namely, in the sacrifice of the Mass. — MITA.]

so that Christ might offer pure draughts to those drinking from the vessel of his body, fulfilling the prophet’s words:

> “And your cup that intoxicates—how splendid it is!” (Psalm 22).

Today the divinity of Christ was proved in three ways: by the gift of the Magi, by the testimony of the Father, and by the changing of water into wine. For the authority of Scripture established that every matter stands by three witnesses when it says:

> “Let every matter be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Matthew 18).

But since the festival itself summons us to the Lord’s table and to the joy of this cup, it is enough to have concluded these great matters in a brief sermon, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns now and forever, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Note: From this the editor infers that our author preached the divine word to the people before the sacrament, or before he celebrated it. — MITA.]

[Note: Or rather, during the solemnities of the Mass, immediately before the Gospel reading, before the sacred mysteries were distributed to the people.]

## SERMON CLXI. On the parable of the servant returning from the field, and on human gratitude toward God

You have heard, brothers, how the Lord demands divine service by the example of human servitude, saying:

> “Which of you, having a servant plowing or tending sheep, would say to him when he returned from the field, ‘Come at once and recline at table’? Would he not instead say to him, ‘Prepare what I am to eat, gird yourself, and serve me until I have eaten and drunk; afterward you will eat and drink’? Does he thank that servant because he did what he had been commanded? I think not. So you also, when you have done everything that has been commanded you, say: ‘We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we were obliged to do’” (Luke 17).

“So you also.” What is similar? Rather, it is vastly dissimilar. Does man owe God as much as man owes man? Far from it. The order is different, the cause different, the faithfulness different.

God made man exist, commanded him to be born, granted him life, allowed him understanding, gave him times, distributed the ages, admitted him to glory, opened the way to honor, placed him over living creatures, and established him as lord of the whole earth under a defined law and appointed period.

And when those first benefits of God to man—so many and so great—had perished, he restored them a second time, all the greater in proportion as they were divine, all the more excellent in proportion as they were heavenly. For he gave him heaven as an inhabitant after having first given him the earth as a dwelling place, so that no hostile attack and no serpent lurking amid earthly goods could any longer creep upon man.

[Note: The older editions have here a profound obscurity. We have supplied the light from Mita.]

A now-established condition would preserve the one whom uncertain freedom had lost.

[Note: “Uncertain” and “wavering,” because it rested upon the mutable judgment of man. — MITA.]

Man would be free of all things, subject only to the service of the Lord, to whom he owes the condition in which he was made and owes his origin. Since he was redeemed and purchased, he certainly owes service, as the Apostle says:

> “You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of human beings” (1 Corinthians 7).

And the prophet, confessing his condition and origin, says:

> “I am your servant and the son of your handmaid” (Psalm 115).

Man owes these things to God. What does man owe man that is comparable? And yet God asks even so much, because man is unwilling to give anything to God, to whom he owes everything.

But let us return to the reading and set the likeness itself before our eyes; then what we have said will become clear: we render no complete service to God, while we render complete servitude to man.

> “Which of you, having a servant plowing or tending sheep, would say to him when he returned from the field, ‘Come at once and recline at table’? Would he not instead say to him, ‘Prepare what I am to eat, gird yourself, and serve me until I have eaten and drunk; afterward you will eat and drink’?”

How familiar, how homely, how drawn from daily experience, how common this teaching is. If the hearer is a master, he recognizes that he demands such things from a servant; if he is a servant, he recognizes that he performs such things for his master.

[Note: Pignorius, *On Slaves*, p. 68, commends these words.]

After the watches before dawn, after the various and arduous labors of the entire day, after fearful and anxious tasks, the servant prepares supper for his master, and, girded, serves what he has prepared. He is not elated because he has done it; rather, as he performs each task with devotion, he trembles. He sets before his master numerous foods, seasoned with every skill and every flavor, while he himself perhaps will taste only an undercooked and unsalted little supper.

He offers cup after cup, changes the goblets, changes the wines; he stands fixed throughout the long conversations of the very lengthy banquet, standing motionless, as though he were not permitted to grow weary in his servitude.

[Note: The Caesenatian manuscript reads: “Various cups.”]

[Note: Either because conversations frequently take place at banquets, or because this refers to the custom of the ancients, at whose banquets games and theatrical performances were held, or because riddles were proposed for the guests to solve.]

And while the master spends part of the night in sleep and passes it in rest, the servant gathers, cares for, arranges, places, organizes, and puts things away. He remains occupied with necessary matters so completely that he reserves little or no part of the night for food and sleep.

After all this, unless he keeps watch into the following day and rises before his sleeping master, he will face the morning exhausted yet unable to rest, exposed to blows and immediate punishment. None of yesterday’s labor benefits him, because whatever the master does to the servant—without due cause or in anger, willingly or unwillingly, forgetfully or deliberately, knowingly or unknowingly—is judgment, justice, and law. The anger of the one who commands is the right of the subordinate, and the condition of servitude has no voice against the master’s will.

[Note: Pignorius says that these servile hardships are elegantly touched upon by the Terentian Geta in *Phormio*, Act 2, scene 1:

> “If the master returns,
>
> I must keep grinding at the mill, be beaten, wear the chains,
>
> Do the work in the fields, and so forth.”]

If, then, a servant understands what he owes man by serving in this way, and if a master who rules understands what kind of service he owes the Lord of lords, he is taught and understands himself through the teacher.

Paul fulfilled this. He wrote the titles of his servitude in this way:

[Note: I do not know what Mita is imagining about men commonly styled *principes*. The titles of servitude were tablets on which were inscribed slaves’ diseases, defects, and whatever else purchasers had an interest in knowing; such titles hung from their necks. Propertius, *Elegy* 5, Book IV:

> “Or those whose title hung from barbarian necks.”]

> “To this very hour we hunger and thirst, we are naked and are struck with blows” (1 Corinthians 4).

And elsewhere:

> “I bruise my body and subject it to servitude” (1 Corinthians 9, according to the Septuagint).

He exacted punishment from himself, like a good servant who, treating himself thus until he was bruised, continually scourged himself; nor did he loosen the reins on his body, lest flesh relaxed through indulgence should incur another’s servitude.

But, man, give to the one who made you master what you demand from a servant. You who are always asleep, while demanding tireless watches from your servant, keep watch at least sometimes for your Lord, who watches without ceasing for your sake. Attend, even for a single moment, upon your Lord while he fasts, although your servant always attends upon you while you eat.

Forgive the innocent servant, while your Lord shows indulgence to you when you sin.

[Note: God is gentle with the sinner either by not punishing him immediately, by granting him temporal goods, or, like the best of parents, by smiling at the curses of his little children in order to make them good; or, as Augustine said when speaking of Saul, he is “fierce and merciful.” See Augustine, *Sermon 15 on the Words of the Apostle*. — From Mita.]

Grant meanwhile forgiveness to the one whom your Lord always forgives. Certainly, if you do anything good, believe that you have paid a debt to the Lord, not rendered him a benefit.

[Note: Another reading: “to the ruler.”]

> “When you have done everything that has been commanded you, say: ‘We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we were obliged to do.’”

When is man useful for divine things, when he is so useless for human things to himself? Let man consider the evils of the heart, the vices of the flesh, the waves of pleasures, the storms of desires, the reefs of anger, and the shipwrecks of crimes. Then whatever useful thing is in him he will assign to God,

[Note: That is, he will ascribe it to God.]

and whatever is useless he will attribute to himself.

But let us return to the subject, so that the reason why the Lord admonished his disciples may now become clear. When Christ sent his Apostles to peoples afflicted by various sufferings,

[Note: Alternatively, “when he was sending them.”]

he gave them the power of the Spirit; he gave them heavenly authority; he gave them the grace of healing. As they went about, they restored sight to the blind, movement to the lame, hearing to the deaf, and, not to delay you by listing each case, they gave health to all who were ill. On their return they boasted, saying:

> “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name.”

The Lord restrains them, saying:

> “Do not rejoice that the demons are subject to you; rejoice rather that your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10).

Therefore, lest through pride they lose what they had acquired through labor and claim for themselves what they had obtained from God, he calls them back to humility, which is the mother of instruction, by this example:

> “Which of you, having a servant plowing or tending sheep, would say to him when he returned from the field, ‘Come at once and recline at table’? Would he not say to him, ‘Prepare what I am to eat, gird yourself, and serve me until I have eaten and drunk; afterward you will eat and drink’?”

After their completed labors and their many great demonstrations of virtue, the Apostles seemed sufficiently useful to themselves. But they did not know that they were still moving about in the mud of the flesh and the mire of this body, and that they were useless. This was exposed when Judas betrayed him and Peter denied him (Matthew 26), when John fled and they all abandoned him (Mark 14), so that the whole usefulness that was in him and proceeded from him might appear in him alone.

When he said, “And afterward you will eat,” he urges the disciples to desire, after his ascension, to be joined immediately to the Lord in that heavenly blessedness. For in the end he approves that they will leave everything here,

[Note: In all printed editions the word “everything” is missing, to the considerable detriment of the passage. Latinius supplied it.]

girds them for endurance of the Passion, and completes them for the labor of his ministry.

For the Apostles served the one reclining at table for as long as they prepared the Lord’s supper upon the tables of the Church, amid the kitchens of sinners and the hearths of the Gentiles, as an everlasting memorial.

This supper is known by the one who is faithful. Let the one who does not know it, but desires to know it, become faithful.

[Note: Namely, the sacred Eucharist, which in that age was concealed beneath the darkness of secrecy from unbelievers and catechumens.]

[Col. 0625D]

## SERMON CLXII. On the man who wished to divide an inheritance

You have heard, brothers, what the heir of worldly goods asked from the Lord today:

> “Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me” (Luke 12).

Rash and heedless greed believed that the Lord himself, the knower of the world, should arbitrate a worldly dispute. It wanted him to become the author of a division who had come to restore the unity of the human race.

> “Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.”

Here he is not a teacher of profit, but of love.

[Note: The printed editions incorrectly read: “but [a teacher] of love.”]

> “Tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.”

When he says, “Tell my brother,” he has prefaced what appeals to charity, invokes nature, and strikes the heart.

> “Tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.”

He cannot say “brother” and then “divide,” when through the prophet he taught:

> “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is when brothers dwell together as one” (Psalm 132).

> “Tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.”

What inheritance is greater, what inheritance better, than the bond of divine charity? An inheritance sometimes perishes; charity never does, as the Apostle says:

> “Charity never fails” (1 Corinthians 13).

But someone may say, “Then charity never perishes and is never violated?” Certainly never. For if charity exists, it remains; if it does not remain, it is not charity.

Just as a barren tree, though it becomes entirely white with blossom in springtime, does not produce fruit but deceives, so too there is a charity that is thought to exist but does not. Shaken by the waves of circumstances, it vanishes, and thus injures those who rely upon it and deceives the unwary.

[Note: The Caesenatian manuscript reads: “It bears no fruit.”]

But let us return to what we began:

> “Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.”

A worldly inheritance brings quarrels to descendants before it brings them wealth. Before it divides possessions, it splits the heirs; before it hands each person his due portion, it cuts the successors themselves apart and sends them in different directions.

Therefore this is not an inheritance but a conflict; it is a stepmother to children, not a possession. The one who enriches children is he who leaves them a charity that is complete.

But you, whoever you are, who address the Lord with such a petition, provoke the Lord and bring the Lord into litigation, although the Apostle teaches and shows you that the inheritance is shared with him:

> “We are heirs of God, and fellow heirs with Christ” (Romans 8).

Here is your heir; here is your brother, who wished to be found like you in every respect: in the lot of birth, in the condition of growth, in the order of life, and in the end of death. For although he alone was God’s heir and, by nature, the only Son, he wished and caused you to be his participant and fellow heir by grace—although you were wretched and subject to the lowest servitude.

You will possess what has been bestowed, and will be able to possess it happily, if you remain in the Father’s palace and share in the divine inheritance. The divine portion can be given but cannot be divided: he who gives heavenly things does not lose them, and he who receives them does not store them up for himself alone.

Therefore, man, why do you call him to division? Why, in your misery, do you invite him to an investigation? Why do you ask a portion from him who sought and bestowed the whole for you?

At least learn from experience and repent now that you asked such things. For you received a portion of the principal substance, and, as a stranger, wanderer, and prodigal, you squandered what you had received with the prodigals and gluttons (Luke 15). Hence you became an exile from paradise; hence you were deprived of the inheritance; hence you were banished from life.

Christ says to you:

> “Man, what you have obtained from me and through me you will not be able to possess without me, because you have already seen what you were without me.”

Knowing this, I asked the Father for you, ungrateful as you are, in these words:

> “Father, I will that those whom you have given me should be where I am, and that they should be with me” (John 17).

And because even this could not be sufficient protection for you—for although you were with me in paradise, you perished outside me—

[Note: Alternatively: “You perished utterly.”]

I added:

> “Father, just as you are in me and I am in you, so may these also be one in us.”

I proceeded from the Father in order to possess the Father’s goods; I did not altogether depart from the Father. Therefore I wish you to have in us as much as we ourselves are and remain in ourselves.

Cease, then, either dividing heavenly things or litigating over earthly things while I hear you, lest you find the one whom you now hold and possess as a pious giver to be afterward a most severe examiner.

But let us now hear what the Lord answered:

> “Man, who appointed me judge or divider over you?”

“Who appointed me judge?” And what of what you yourself said, Lord?

> “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5).

“Or divider over you?” And who will divide the righteous from the unrighteous, as a shepherd separates sheep from goats (Matthew 25)?

If judgment over humanity belongs to you, and through you the division of the whole world is to be carried out, how do you say, “Who appointed me judge or divider over you?”

All judgment is indeed with Christ, and was, and will be. But at that time he had not come to judge; he had come to be judged. He had not come to condemn the guilty, but to be declared innocent by the guilty. In the man he was acting as God; in the servant, as Lord—the servant of time, though he was also the maker and judge of the ages.

Therefore he rightly answered:

> “Who appointed me judge or divider over you?”

And who could appoint as judge the one who appointed and restored all things? Christ could not be an arbiter at the litigant’s bidding, since he is the fullness and power of all judgment.

[Note: The entire period is remarkably riddled with errors in all editions. Since the manuscripts too are corrupt, we have restored it conjecturally from Mita.]

But why did that quarrelsome man not object: “How did you ask thus without having been invited by your brother? Do you not know that a just mediator is not one chosen by only one side?” He did not say this; rather, he stood there uninvited, so that it might be lawful for Christ, the adjudicator, but not for the brother, to withdraw the judgment.

And because Christ had come to correct, not to condemn the guilty, he removes the fuel of quarrels by commanding:

> “Be on your guard; beware of greed.”

This is what he means: Let greed be cast away, and there will be no dispute over inheritance.

Greed, brothers, denies parents, divides siblings, separates companions, dissolves friendship, and excludes affection. Whoever harbors it within himself will belong to no one and will not belong even to himself.

Greed, brothers, as the Apostle says,

> “is the root of all evils” (1 Timothy 6);

when it begins to take root in the heart, it destroys the adornments of character just as a harmful tree, bound by deadly roots, loosens and scatters the monuments of one’s ancestors.

[Note: Mita observes that the passage refers first to monuments, which in ancient custom were built in the fields from stone and brick. If trees had truly been planted near them, their roots, inserted among the joints of the stones, would have thrown down indiscriminately both the inscribed stones and the bricks composing the tomb. — MITA.]

## SERMON CLXIII. On despising concern for earthly things
Blessed are those whose hearts the hearing of the Lord’s discourse today has penetrated. Blessed are those whose minds so great and so remarkable a promise of the Savior has advanced toward faith. Blessed are those who, through belief in the heavenly commands, have been released from the harsh cares of the present. For today the Lord addresses his disciples—or rather, all his hearers—with such a voice: “Do not be anxious about your life, what you shall eat, nor about your body, what you shall wear. [Col. 0628B] Life is more than food, and the body more than clothing” (Luke 12). [Note: [Col. 0628D] Latinius asks what the reading is.]

Who is so hostile to his own blessings, who so inimical to his own delights, that he despises what has been prepared spontaneously and from heaven, and craves what has been acquired through worldly labors and pains? An utterly degenerate spirit, a wholly servile mind, is the one that searches out dishes smelling of yesterday’s foulness, the fumes of cooks [Note: [Col. 0628D] The Caesenian manuscript and the printed editions read *affatus* (“addresses,” “words spoken”).] and the filth of the kitchen, while the royal apparatus is continually serving it and lying at its side.

Therefore, human being, do not groan by making provision for empty things; do not labor to prepare what perishes, because God, the provider of your meal, is always and everywhere present. What king does not secure the proper ration for devoted soldiers? What master does not supply such food to faithful servants? What father does not give bread to his children? If, then, God is for us both king and master [Col. 0628C] and father, what will he deny?

A soldier serving under his wages disparages his king; a servant living at his master’s expense accuses his lord; a son anxious for himself blames his surviving father. Therefore, human being, do not expose God thus by thinking in this way: he who, through the justice of a reigning king, the diligence of a master, and the affection of a parent, has taken upon himself the whole of your anxiety and assumed your care, saying: “Do not be anxious about your life, what you shall eat.”

But perhaps the honeyed rain and the unique food deter you by the example of Jewish distaste, and you do not believe that flesh, compacted from a variety of humors, could be sustained by manna alone [Note: [Col. 0628D] The Author of Wisdom 16:20–21 states that manna was customarily adapted to everyone’s taste, so that it tasted different to each person. Saint Augustine, *Retractationes* II.10, aptly observes that this power was given to the food—that it should accommodate itself to everyone’s taste—only for the sake of the children of God. See Gregory, *Moralia* VI.9.] according to its own will. You say: “Just as God wished the body to consist of different members, so he wished and commanded it to be nourished with varied dishes.”

This fear that agitates you is needless, human being. For the whole of creation hastens and flies together to the Creator’s meal. Therefore, if the uniqueness and frugality of lawful food frighten you, let the overflowing heavenly banquet of the Gospel invite and summon you: in one dish prepared for Peter to eat, it sets out every kind of creature (Acts 10).

For whatever Noah [Note: [Col. 0628D] The Fathers adorn him with various epithets. Chrysostom calls him, *Homily* 110, vol. V, p. 711, “the good pilot of nature as it was being shipwrecked”; Nazianzen, Oration 18, p. 297, “the father of this second world”; Theodoret, on Psalm 90, “the spark of our race”; and again, *Oration 5 on Providence*, “the second ruler of the human race,” and so forth.] the bearer of the new age preserved for the seed of the age, whatever flies and moves through the air, whatever is born and lives upon the earth, whatever exists and moves in the waters—this is slaughtered and presented from heaven as one meal for Peter. If, then, you wish to receive and eat everything, human being, scorn providing humble storerooms for yourself.

We strive to prove to you, when you are thinking of heavenly things, that bodily necessities will not be lacking, by means of great examples. But God, in accordance with the marks of his majesty, sends one who doubts his promises back to humble and extreme examples, so that by such an examination he may convict you, whom [Note: [Col. 0629D] I have chosen to restore this reading with Latinius. All the printed editions read: “with so great a change.”] he has not drawn by so great an imitation.

“Consider,” he says, “the ravens: they neither sow nor reap; they have neither storeroom nor barn, and God feeds them. How much more valuable are you than they?” He rightly sends the doubting unbeliever to a bird that is an ally in war, a companion of fury, insatiable for blood, and more savage with the sword against the dead themselves. For when the sword has ceased, the most wicked executioner attacks the lifeless body, tears it, scatters it, and throws it about, lest anything found of the corpse should be entrusted to peaceful burial as an act of mercy. Thus the Lord, by such an example, intensifies the madness of the doubter, who thinks that God would deny to pious children what he supplies to impious birds [Note: [Col. 0629D] Ambrose, cited here by Du Hamel: “The birds of heaven claim nothing special for themselves; and therefore they do not know that they need fodder, because they cannot envy others.”]; and who supposes that he will not provide food for those who leave homeland, house, parents, children, and spouses for his sake, although he has allowed the newborn to grow and has set a limit to the body’s increase.

O wretched person, utterly deserving of every misery, to whom, when a kingdom is given, bread causes sighs; when perpetuity is granted, drink causes lamentation; when clothed with the glory of immortality, clothing for the body causes grief. Conscious of his native misery, he does not believe that he can become happy; nourished in earthly dust, he doubts that he will become an inhabitant of heaven.

The Lord therefore appropriately added what follows: “And which of you, by thinking, can add one cubit to his stature?” He reveals the thoughts of the human mind, whose inmost searcher he is. For every person, while desiring the beauty of his body, wishes to be tall. A human being can think about this, but cannot obtain it by himself; he attains it by believing, but cannot attain it by thinking.

Hence, because he knew human desire, the Lord extended humanity into the form of Christ, so that the person who in his own shortness was deformed, even ashamed of himself, might become entirely beautiful in the stature of Christ. Therefore he rightly added: “If, then, you cannot do even what is least, why are you anxious about the rest?” That is: Why do you presume to undertake greater things in thought, human being, when through faith you despair of lesser ones? What is less than clothing, and what is greater than bodily growth? Believe, then, that God can provide clothing for your body, since through faith he promises you the increase of your body.

But because God loves the human race so greatly that, although he rebukes those whom he rules by right of dominion, he immediately consoles and soothes them with paternal tenderness, he leads those whom he seemed to have provoked by comparison with the most disgraceful bird back to the example of a flower fragrant and exceedingly beautiful.

“Consider,” he says, “the lilies, how they grow: they neither labor nor spin. But I tell you, not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these.”

O how deeply heavenly mercy lowers itself out of love for humanity! For he who could have strengthened his commands by authority alone explains and establishes them with the whole labor of a teacher; and he who could have placed the fulfillment solely in faith in his promise leads his hearers to faith in the promise by the example of persuasion. He confirms the doubtful by comparison with the lily, and exalts the lily by comparison with Solomon. For, as the Lord himself testifies, among all the kings of the world Solomon shone with singular glory and unique adornment, beautiful in appearance; yet the lily surpasses and excels all the flowers of the earth in beauty. The lily differs from the whole of vegetation by as much as it is established that the king excels all others in appearance and glory.

Nor need we describe the beauty of the lily at greater length, since the Lord’s testimony makes its excellence unique. Certainly those things should be repeated which the Lord commended to strengthen our faith by a twofold example: because a Christian, certain of life, the kingdom, and immortality, [Note: [Col. 0630D] The Caesenian manuscript reads: “should not doubt concerning nourishment and clothing.”] ought not to be troubled by the necessity of food and clothing, when he sees that God has bestowed such glory of clothing upon a plant born today and destined to perish tomorrow. But just as these things are dried up and assigned to the burning of the furnace, so those who doubt that God will provide present things for them, although they already perceive that future things have been granted to them, are destined for the fires of death and Gehenna.

“And you, do not seek what you shall eat or [Col. 0630C] what you shall drink, and do not be lifted up to lofty things; for all these things the nations of the world seek. But your Father knows that you need them. Nevertheless, seek the kingdom of God, and all these things shall be added to you.”

When he calls himself our Father, he proves that his loving care for us is not lacking. When he commands us to seek the heavenly kingdom, he shows that everything else must be subordinate and indicates that whatever the heavenly order requires will be supplied to us.

## SERMON CLXIV. On the heavenly fire, the separation made by Christ, and the division between the Church and the Synagogue. On the passage in Luke: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth,” etc.

Just as nourishing food is always bitter to those suffering from fever, so the Lord’s discourse is often offensive to the unlearned. Yet in both cases this happens for different reasons: in one case because of bodily weakness, in the other because of weakness of mind.

Today the Lord seems to have irritated the hearing of some people by saying: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I wish except that it be kindled?” And later: “Do you think that I have come to bring peace upon the earth? No, I tell you, but division” (Luke 12).

And where is this saying: “Behold the Lamb of God” (John 1)? Where is this: “He was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer he was silent, so he did not open his mouth” (Isaiah 53)? And also this: “Tell the daughter of Zion: Behold, your king comes to you, meek” (Matthew 21)? What, then, does it mean that this Lamb strikes so harshly in his preaching? Why does he butt so forcefully in his speech, when in his passion he is silent with such patience [Note: [Col. 0631D] The Vatican and Vallicellian manuscripts read: “when in such great patience he hastens toward death,”] and in death submits with complete humility?

And indeed, brothers, Christ entered his world gentle and meek in every respect: when, born among us, he came forth sweetly in our human stock; when, lying in the cradle, he himself was tenderly cherished; when, as a little child, he poured himself out and relaxed in a human lap; when he was held around the neck of his parent and held the parent in the full embrace of love.

And so that he might nourish others with complete affection while himself being nourished, he gradually passed through and matured through every age. He always lived as a poor man; he always walked alone, because he was always poor in common with others, always alone and open to everyone.

What, then, does it mean that he scatters so much fire in his words, that he inflames and expands such great fires, saying: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth”? What does it mean?

Whenever a field, through prolonged neglect, grows wild and becomes filthy with the whole horror of uncultivated luxuriance, it is always opened and cleansed by the fire of a most skilled cultivator. Through kindly diligence the cultivator applies fire, so that, once the thorns have been burned, the field’s original appearance may be revealed [Col. 0631B]. [Note: [Col. 0631D] That is, freed from brambles and thorns. We have emended the text in this way with Latinius. All the printed editions read: “freedom may be granted to the farmer.”] The farmer is given free access, an easy way is made for the plow, the long-sterile earth becomes productive of seed, and after its long and sorrowful idleness it now repays him with the most joyful fruit.

Therefore, when the Jewish turf, continually exhausted by the plow of the Law and by unceasing cultivation [Note: [Col. 0631D] Thus with the same Latinius. The printed editions read: *effectus*.] to the point of poverty, failed to respond to seed or labor, but produced darnel instead of wheat and brought forth thorns to the extent of its strength, Christ turned the industry of divine cultivation toward the fields of the nations.

Desiring to clear the new fields of the nations, long oppressed by thickets, he first sends the greatest teacher, fire, upon the earth; and whatever natural luxuriance had made foul, whatever winter’s severity had dried out, he cleanses and consumes by skilled burning. Thus, having long been exhausted by fasting and fattened by its own ashes, the earth might grow rich; after its prolonged hardness, it might become tender and soft; and so, made suitable for evangelical cultivation, it might be prepared for seed and, through a fortunate furrow, yield thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold fruit.

But this very cultivation is not new to the ancient and heavenly farmer, for he has always been accustomed to set down the Law, sow grace, and employ the work of fire. When he was about to give the Law, he sent fire beforehand into the bush; but the bush bore the divine fire and did not conceive it within itself (Exodus 5), prefiguring a people already full of the thorns of wickedness and ungrateful toward the cultivation of the Law. [Note: [Col. 0631D] The Jew did not conceive the divine Law, but bore it only externally, like the bush that burned only on its outer side. From Mita.]

And now, when he was assigning the apostles to the fields of the nations, he drenched them with fiery rain, and fire settled upon them, so that they could dry what was wet, moisten what was dry, cook what was raw, warm what was cold, kindle what was extinguished, burn what was harmful, and, through diverse works but one and the same fire, refine all the deserted places of the earth into heavenly abundance, as the prophet says: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm 18).

But let us now proceed to what follows: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I wish except that it be kindled? But I have a baptism with which I must be baptized, and how I am constrained until it is accomplished!””

Water presses upon fire; such a conjunction, so divided, must be contemplated. The water presses upon the flame, and the flame multiplies the water. What is this harmonious discord, so great and so strange?

Here, as we have said, the figure of the divine farmer is being enacted. Everything germinates when full of warmth and is nourished by moisture. Therefore God, the parent of all things, causes us to germinate and nourishes us through the commerce of fire and water, with such affection that he burns, glows, boils, and breathes for us.

“I have a baptism with which I must be baptized.” Christ is baptized in his own blood, so that whatever he assumed from our flesh might be washed, renewed, and brought wholly into the form of his divine majesty. Christ is baptized with the baptism of his Passion, he who washed away the sin of the whole world, which could be abolished only by him who had made the world.

“Do you think,” he says, “that I have come to bring peace upon the earth? No, I tell you, but division.” Why? Because heavenly union exists within this earthly division. No one can be joined to earth and united to heaven. Therefore let this earthly separation be welcome and dear: it separates us from earthly things in such a way that it grafts us into divine things.

“There shall be,” he says, “from this point onward five in one house divided, three against two and two against three: father shall be divided against son and son against father; mother against daughter and daughter against mother; mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law and daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law.”

Although he said that five people would be divided from one house, six names are divided: father, son, mother, daughter, mother-in-law, and daughter-in-law. But because the mother-in-law is herself the mother, it is certain that only five persons are found under these names.

Three are divided against two when the bride, joined to the bridegroom, remains united, while the mother-in-law, who is the third, remains divided within the household. Thus the division in which the Church is joined to Christ takes place: the Synagogue, which is both mother and mother-in-law, remains separated from her own husband.

Two, then, are divided against three in this way: from the fellowship of Christ and the Church, another sect [Note: [Col. 0632D] Latinius reads, with possible justification, “another heresy.”] is cut away and the Synagogue is divided, so that Christ and the Church, separated from the heretics [Note: [Col. 0632D] Elsewhere: “from the Jews,”] may remain one and be joined in the Spirit.

Father is also divided against son, and son against father: the Jewish people, which through Christ’s fleshly generation received the name of father, is separated from Christ the Son through envy. The livid father turns affection into hatred; the glory of the son is for him a continual punishment and unending torment, as the Apostle says: “Whose are the fathers, and from whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever” (Romans 9).

Mother is also divided against daughter. The Synagogue is a mother, from whom the daughter Church is born through Peter and the other apostles. Once the Church deserved to share the fellowship of the divine king Christ, she found in her mother a rival and a stepmother.

And what kind of mother is such a mother to her daughter, what kind of mother-in-law to her daughter-in-law? For when this mother Synagogue saw that the daughter-in-law Church had come from the nations, the wicked woman killed her son so that she would not see the daughter-in-law’s fellowship. She killed Christ, if by this furious act she could in any way extinguish the love of the daughter-in-law.

But through death Christ rose again wholly into marriage with the Church, to prove that love is not separated by death but grows.

The Lord rebukes those who study with excessive curiosity the face of the sky, the rising of clouds, the courses of the stars, and the regions of the world, but make no effort, by any study or indication, to recognize the time of their salvation.

“Hypocrites,” he says, “you know how to interpret the face of the sky and the earth; and how is it that you do not interpret this time?”

An eye that is spread out loses its light, because the whole of a person’s vision is contained within the pupil. Therefore, do not strive to see many things in order to see yourself; do not presume to gaze upon lofty things, nor seek to observe distant things, because a narrow eye cannot contain many things, does not penetrate lofty things, and does not discern distant things. Thus the person who thinks he sees everything sees nothing.

Recognize, then, the day of salvation, the acceptable time through Christ Jesus our Lord, if you wish, from yourself.

*The end is missing.*

[Note: [Col. 0633D] In the Caesena manuscript this sermon is prefaced by the title: “At the ordination of Bishop Projectus of Forum Cornelium.”]

## SERMON CLXV. On the consecration of the blessed Projectus, bishop of Forum Cornelium

I confess that I owe veneration and most faithful service to all the Churches; but I am compelled to serve the Church of Cornelium with particular devotion, out of love for its very name. [Note: [Col. 0633D] See the observations in the notes to the Life of Chrysologus drawn from Castillo, no. 5.]

For Cornelius, illustrious in life and of most blessed memory, shining everywhere with every title of virtue and known to all for the greatness of his works, [Note: [Col. 0633D] Perhaps through baptism, certainly through education, ordination, and consecration. Concerning Saint Ambrose, Saint Augustine says in his book against Pelagius: “I venerate the baptizer as a father; through the Gospel he himself begot me in Christ Jesus.” From Mita.] was a father to me. He himself begot me through the Gospel; he himself, in pious affection, most lovingly nourished me; he himself, as a holy man, instructed me in holy service; he himself, as bishop, offered and consecrated me at the sacred altars. Therefore the name of Cornelius is illustrious, venerable, and wondrous to me.

Love for one who shares his name therefore compels me to meet eagerly the desires of the Church of Cornelium and to consecrate the venerable man Projectus as bishop with even greater affection.

I have said “Projectus,” but not “cast away,” in accordance with the saying: “Upon you I was cast from the womb; from my mother’s belly you are my God” (Psalm 21). And truly this Projectus, cast forth from the womb of a human mother, remained continually in the womb of the divine mother; ignorant of his own house, he persisted as an inhabitant of the house of God.

But how he climbed, brothers, from the very beginnings of his ecclesiastical service through its stages and offices—because it would take me too long to tell it—let him speak for himself, as the Lord says: “He is of age; let him speak for himself” (John 2), through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 0633D] Mita reports that Projectus was dedicated to the sacred altars and ordained a deacon together with Chrysologus by Saint Cornelius. When Chrysologus was thereafter elevated to the see of Ravenna, another succeeded him in the dignity of archdeacon; later, when he himself was elected bishop, he yielded it to the blessed Donatus, a deacon of Cornelium. He appears to have been adorned with the episcopal insignia in the year 431. Baronius believes him to be the same Projectus whom Pope Celestine chose as his legate to preside in his name over the Council of Ephesus. *Annales*, vol. VII, year 431, no. 22. But if this were true, the common opinion concerning Chrysologus’s ordination would collapse, and the anniversary of his accession to the see would have to be placed before the days and year of Sixtus, 431. Yet Baronius does not appear consistent with himself, for elsewhere, following Rubeus, he places Chrysologus’s ordination in the year 433, under Pope Sixtus II, in the same volume, no. 24 of the year 433. The martyrologies are silent about Bishop Projectus. Ferrarius alone mentions him, in *The Saints of Italy*, under September 23, a day sacred to him in the Church of Forum Cornelium. Strange things are reported about him; whoever wishes to know them should consult the Author himself concerning their reliability.]

## SERMON CLXVI. On the Lenten fast

[Note: [Col. 0634D] In this sermon, says Castillo, Chrysologus restrained the faulty and excessively corrupted fasts of the people of Ravenna. For the citizens sometimes embraced the Lenten weeks with excessive severity, and at other times favored them with excessive indulgence and laxity.]

Simplicity certainly possesses the grace of its innocence and bears the fruit of its faith; but it cannot possess the reward of knowledge or the palm of the virtues. It is one thing to live in leisure and security for oneself; it is another to endure watches and labors for everyone. Simplicity makes a good citizen; it does not make a strong soldier. Hence one person pays a tax, while another receives pay and honors. The citizen either yields or succumbs to adversity; the soldier endures and repels adversity. The former has not learned to fight; the latter has learned not to fear. The former is always on guard; the latter conquers.

We have said this to show what difference there is between one who simply receives and follows the sacrament of the Christian faith and one who strives both to grasp the faith intelligently and to understand its mystery.

Behold the fast of Lent, which the universal Church will undertake tomorrow with solemn devotion. Many think that it was handed down to us, or performed by the Lord for us, merely as an exercise in abstinence; they think that it contains no deeper mystery, but was provided solely for chastising the body, cutting away vices, and disciplining the mind.

Yet this number forty is found to have been so sacred through the ages and so mystical that, whenever divine things are to be accomplished and God’s greatest works carried out, it is prescribed by an inviolable law.

To make this fully clear, let us review a great many examples. When, in the earliest beginnings of the human race, the world had become filthy with the deplorable foulness of sins, stank throughout with the horror of crimes, and almost strove to darken the great brightness of heaven with the very smoke of its iniquity, heavenly rain was poured out for forty days and nights to cleanse the earth (Genesis 7). Since the world, though made, now had to perish through its own fault, it could rejoice that through such a baptism it had been reborn, and know that it owed its existence no longer to nature but to the grace of its author. The earth, origin of our body, had already foreshadowed the form of our baptism, so that what before the birth of human beings had brought forth creatures for death might now bring forth the reborn for life. [Note: [Col. 0634D] Elsewhere: “was lamenting.”]

Attend, brothers, to how great this number forty is: then it opened heaven to cleanse the earth, and now through the fountain of baptism it opens the whole world to the nations being renewed. Rightly do we run through forty days by fasting, so that we may reach the fountain [Note: [Col. 0635D] After the Lenten fast had been completed and fulfilled, a solemn baptism was celebrated at Easter.] of baptism and salvation.

For forty years the rain that provided bread fed the Jewish people in the wilderness (Exodus 10). It did not produce the growth of plants from the earth by its customary service; rather, it itself flowed upon the earth as grain. It removed all the labor of human servitude and, through its gentle dew, offered and lifted up heavenly food to the hungry.

For forty days, an exploration sent by divine command traversed the promised land (Numbers 13), so that this sacred number might summon the people of Israel to the promised lands. It summons us and leads us to heaven through the forty-day course of fasting.

For now heavenly inspection explores and traverses the earth of our body for forty days, so that, once the nations of vices have been conquered and expelled, the multitude of virtues may possess the region of our heart.

And because nothing must be omitted, Moses himself, through a fast of forty days, was so purified and emptied of his body [Note: [Col. 0635D] That is, of the divine essence, or by the word of the Lord, who had renewed Moses twice in the air for forty days, as the author of *On the Marvels of Scripture* says in volume III of the works of Saint Augustine.] that he was wholly transformed into the glory of divinity; and even in the darkness of our body he still shone with the entire light of deity. The eyes of mortals could not look upon him, because, having long been nourished by the substance of God, he had forgotten all mortal food and its assistance. [Col. 0635C] Thus he learned that before God and among those who dwell with God the necessities of life are not lacking.

And indeed, brothers, the one whose bread and life is God does not know weariness and cannot die. Rightly did such a man deserve to establish the Law, since he had removed everything that the Law could impose upon a human being.

Perhaps continual fasting had produced this effect in Moses; but it would not have made him such a man if this sacred number forty had been absent.

Fasting lifted Elijah to heaven (2 Kings 2), and to his purified body it assigned the service of a fiery chariot, to show that Gehenna, which consumes the guilty, serves the innocent. But before Elijah reached this, the mystical path of the number forty ran ahead of him (1 Kings 19). [Note: [Col. 0635D] On the etymology of this word, see Hofmann in his lexicon; Fungerus, *On Gehenna*; Selden, *On the Syrian Gods*, *Syntagma* 1.6.]

Ezekiel, the most distinguished of the prophets, lying for forty days on one side—I speak to those who know the Law—while prefiguring the future captivity, brought it to an end (Ezekiel 4). [Note: [Col. 0635D] Ezekiel, the most ancient of the prophets, lay on his left side for 390 days and on his right side for 40 days. Altogether, by the forty days and the 390 days—each number signifying the same number of years—the iniquity of Israel is defined; by the forty, the duration of the captivity of Judah is indicated. Concerning Ezekiel’s lying down, and whether one should have recourse to a portent, see Chrysostom, *On Providence*; Basil, on Isaiah 8; Theodoret, on Hosea 1; and the other commentators.] This sacred number takes on iniquities in order to erase them; it enters into captivities in order to release them; it suffers bonds in order to loosen them.

Hence the Lord, the author from the ages of the sacrament hidden in this number, within the very number of forty days fasted (Matthew 4), so that Truth itself, now present in person, might bring to completion what he had foreshadowed in his servants, things done and begun; so that he might strengthen tender things, supplement what had been begun, and reinforce by example what he had established by commands. For it would not have been enough merely to impose this sacrament of so great a number in words, unless he had also commended it by deed.

And yet, brothers, from the time of the Flood onward we have attempted to open the mystery of this sacrament, not daring to touch what came before, to search out what lies above, or to speak what has been silent and reveal what has certainly been hidden for so long. Especially since it seems to me rash and unnecessary for you to investigate the origins of such great and numerous causes.

It belongs to true devotion, to most faithful service, to inquire what the ruler wishes to be done, not why he wishes it.

If, then, the simple, pure, uniform fast of forty days, handed down to us by the Lord through so many testimonies and under the sacrament of so great a number, is thoroughly taught, whence comes this variation? Whence this novelty? Whence the weeks now relaxed, now rigid, now excessively indulgent, now severe? Whence this practice of intemperate fasting, which either afflicts without pardon or relaxes into gluttony?

That is, to assign separately the remedies of hot things, cold things, salt, and food to their respective uses, while altogether neglecting the creator of life. Certainly those who season food for the body should wisely learn to regulate nourishment for the soul, lest either food that is too heavily salted or food that is completely tasteless produce a deadly disgust for salutary nourishment.

Let the fast be uniform; and, as it has been handed down to us (Matthew 2), [Col. 0636C] let it be observed for the discipline of body and soul. Certainly one who cannot fast should not presume to introduce a novelty. Rather, let him acknowledge that what he relaxes proceeds from his own weakness, and let him redeem through almsgiving what he cannot fulfill through fasting. [Note: [Col. 0636D] See how excellently Saint Leo treats this in his sermon on the fast of the seventh month.] For the Lord does not seek the groaning of one who has redeemed the groans of the poor for himself.

## SERMON CLXVII. On Saint John the Baptist preaching and on the necessity of doing penance
Opportunely, blessed John comes to us during the season of fasting as a teacher of repentance: a teacher in word and deed, a true master, demonstrating by example what he asserts in speech. A teacher’s office rests upon knowledge, but the authority of teaching is established by life; doing what must be taught makes the hearer obedient. Teaching by deeds is the sole standard of instruction: teaching in words is knowledge, but in deeds it is virtue. That knowledge, therefore, is true which has been joined to virtue; it is divine, not human, as the Evangelist proves when he says: “What Jesus began both to do and to teach” (Acts I).

When a teacher does what must be taught, he instructs by hearing and forms by example. “In those days,” he says, “John the Baptist came preaching in the wilderness of Judea and saying: Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. III).

“Repent”—why do you not rather rejoice? Rejoice rather, because divine things succeed human things, heavenly things earthly things, eternal things temporal things, good things evil things, security anxious things, blessedness misery, and lasting things perishable things. “Repent.” Let the one who preferred human things to divine things repent—yes, let him repent; the one who wished to serve the world and not to possess dominion over the world together with the Lord of the world. Let the one who preferred to perish with the devil rather than reign with Christ repent. Let the one who fled the freedom of virtues and chose to be captive to vices repent. Let him repent—let him repent deeply—who surrendered his hands to death so that he might not preserve life.

“For the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.” The kingdom of heaven is the reward of the righteous and the judgment of sinners; for the impious, it is punishment. Blessed, therefore, is John, who wished judgment to be forestalled by repentance; he wished sinners to have not judgment but reward, and the impious to enter the kingdom, not punishment.

John proclaimed the kingdom of heaven near when the world was still a child, gathering the growth of its ages. Now we know how very near the kingdom of heaven is, when the world, exhausted by extreme old age, is emptied of strength, lays down its limbs, loses its senses, is oppressed by pains, rejects care, dies to life, lives amid diseases, cries out its decline, and bears witness to its end.

We, then, are harder-hearted than the Jews: we pursue the fleeing world, forget the times to come, gape after present things, do not fear although we are already placed within judgment, do not go out to meet the Lord who is already coming, wish death to remain, do not desire the resurrection of the dead, wish to serve and refuse to reign, so that we may delay the kingdom for our Lord. Where is the saying: “When you pray, say: Thy kingdom come” (Luke XI)?

We therefore need greater repentance, and the remedy must be proportionate to the wound. Let us repent, brothers; let us repent quickly, because the span of time is already being denied us, the very hour is already closing in upon us, and the presence of judgment already excludes for us the opportunity for satisfaction. Let repentance run ahead, lest the sentence run ahead of it. For the Lord, who has not yet come, who still waits, who delays, desires us to return to him, not to perish—us to whom he has continually spoken with such compassion: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that the wicked turn from his way and live” (Ezek. XXXIII).

Let us therefore return in repentance, brothers, and let us not fear the shortness of time, because the Author of time cannot be confined. The Gospel thief proves this: on the cross and at the hour of death, he seized pardon, took hold of life, broke into paradise, and entered the kingdom (Luke XXIII).

And we, brothers, who have not sought merit by our will, let us at least acquire virtue from necessity. Let us not be judged; let us be our own judges. We owe repentance to ourselves, so that we may remove the sentence from ourselves.

The first blessedness is to rejoice in the security of perpetual innocence: to preserve the purity of mind and body inviolate; to feel none of the unclean contaminations of the world; not to possess a conscience burdened by guilt; not to know the wounds of sin; always to possess the grace of the virtues; always to live in hope of heavenly rewards.

But if perhaps our mind has been pierced by the dart of sin, if the flesh swells with crime, if human frailty is corrupted by the festering matter of vices, then let the medicine of repentance come to the sick, not to the healthy; let the iron of contrition be applied; let the cautery of pain be placed upon them; let the consolations of sighs be brought; let the heat of the swollen conscience evaporate. Then let the ulcers of guilt be washed away with tears; then let haircloths cleanse the uncleanness of the body.

Let the one who refused to preserve the health owed to him bear—yes, bear—the bitter care of repentance. For one whose life is dear to him, no care is too harsh.

[Note: Elsewhere, “delicate.”]

[Note: The manuscript of Cesena reads: “to whom his life is dear, no impure care is burdensome.”]

Let the physician not be resented who recalls a person to health through pain. Whoever preserves the trust committed to innocence does not pay the interest of repentance.

The Lord makes this clear when he says: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick.” And he disclosed who the sick were when he said again: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners” (Matt. IX).

John recalls through repentance; Christ calls through grace. Hence John proceeds wholly formed by repentance—in clothing, food, and place. “John the Baptist came,” he says, “preaching in the wilderness of Judea and saying: Repent.”

John cries out repentance through the deserts of Judea, which by their barrenness were destroying the observance of the Law, the labor of the prophets, the fruitfulness of the fathers, and the harvest of God. Hence the deserts of discipline, not of people or places, are rightly called to repentance: the cry calls where no hearer is present.

John himself “had clothing made of camel’s hair.” He could have worn goat’s hair, but haircloth was not required; instead, he took the hair of the most twisted animal, which has nothing straight, nothing graceful, nothing beautiful—an animal whom nature gave over to hard labor, subjected to a great burden, and assigned to the extremity of servitude.

[Note: He calls the camel a crooked animal, perhaps because the camel alone, according to Horus, book II, chapter 95, bends its thigh; for it has four joints in the thigh, with an equal number of bones interposed. Nazianzen describes a camel maddened by anger in this way:

“What if some savage camel roars  
from its throat and thrusts its hostile head at you?  
Will you stand and fight? Will not the wise man flee?”]

The teacher of such repentance had to be clothed in such a garment, so that those who had turned away from the discipline of what is straight and had made themselves wholly deformed by the shapes of sins might be subjected to great burdens of repentance and added to the harsh agonies of satisfaction; so that they might carry the laborious sighs of contrition; so that, straightened and made thin like a needle, they might enter through the narrow opening of repentance into the wide expanse of forgiveness; and so that the Lord’s saying might be fulfilled:

“It is possible for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle” (Matt. XIX).

[Note: In these words of Christ many think that the reference is not to the animal camel but to a *camelus* or *camilus*, a nautical rope. Theophylact notes, in his commentary on Matthew XIX, p. 113, that *camilus* means a thick rope used by sailors for casting anchors. The more learned are rightly divided here. The acceptance of the word and a Talmudic proverb, long ago used by Caninius concerning one who undertakes a difficult task, favor understanding it of the animal: “Perhaps you are from the city of Pombeditha, where they send an elephant through the eye of a needle?” Christ, however, used “camel” instead of “elephant,” an animal more familiar to the Jews. The analogy between a rope and a thread, which is customarily passed through the eye of a needle, favors the reference to a rope. Certainly the Syrians and Arabs understand it as a rope. Nor should anyone object with the Talmudists, for they too have a proverb about a rope passing through a narrow opening such as the eye of a needle. See Suicer.]

“His food was locusts and wild honey.” The locust, assigned to the chastisement of sinners, is rightly represented as food for repentance, so that, leaping out from the place of sin, it may be able to fly on the wings of forgiveness toward the place of repentance and heaven.

[Note: From this it is clear that Chrysologus believed the locusts (*akrídes*) of which the Evangelist testifies that John ate were truly locusts, not fried cakes in honey, as the Ebionites held, according to Epiphanius, *Against Heresies*, book II, heresy 30, p. 65; nor the tips of trees and grasses, as Theophylact on Matthew XI, Nicephorus Callistus, *History*, book I, chapter 14, p. 79, and Paulinus of Nola, in his poem on John the Baptist, held:

“Wild honey provided an easy food,  
and fruits and herbs growing from uncultivated rocks.”

Nor was it some other kind of herb called *melagram*, as Theophylact reports in the passage cited, and James of Vitry, *History of the East*, book I, chapter 53; nor little birds nor sea-fish, which would be utterly absurd. Chrysologus agrees with the more common opinion of the authorities: for, as Jerome says in *Against Jovinian*, book I, chapter 7, it is customary among Eastern peoples to eat locusts. Hence, according to Eustathius, in his commentary on *Odyssey* θ, people who eat locusts were called *akridophagoi*, “locust-eaters.” The distinguished Bochart is rightly consulted, *On Animals*, part II, book IV.]

The prophet had this in mind when he said: “Like a shadow when it declines, I have been carried away, and I have been shaken off like a locust; my knees have become weak through fasting, and my flesh has been changed because of mercy” (Ps. CVIII).

You hear how he was shaken from sin into repentance like a locust, and how he bent his knees to carry the burdens of repentance. Honey is then added as food, so that sweet mercy might temper the bitterness of repentance.

## SERMON 168. On the Parable of the Hundred Sheep

Just as a skilled traveler finds a way to enter the depths of the sea and cross the trackless paths of flowing water, so divine law has granted and taught us to hear something from the words of God and to penetrate the secret of divine meaning.

Hence, releasing the vessel of our mind from the shore of the flesh, we enter the open sea of the Gospel discourse, trusting that, with the Holy Spirit blowing, we shall reach the harbor of heavenly understanding.

Our Lord today advanced the hope of sinners toward forgiveness and most mercifully silenced the murmuring of the proud by an example. “There were,” he says, “tax collectors and sinners drawing near to the Lord to hear him; and the Pharisees and scribes were murmuring, saying: This man receives sinners and eats with them” (Luke XI).

They derived their malice from the Lord’s goodness, being no less envious than proud. From God’s compassion they became impious; from Christ’s mercy they became cruel; from heavenly healing they took sickness; and they turned the forgiveness of penitents into the guilt of a judge.

[Note: Elsewhere, “forgiveness of sin.”]

“He receives sinners and eats with them.” This is how the envious person sees it; this is how the proud person feels it; this is how the greedy person understands it; this is how the malicious person interprets it.

“He receives sinners.”

[Note: That is, the Pharisees, failing entirely to consider that Christ the Lord, needing nothing from us, seeks us solely through mercy and compassion, say: “He receives sinners”—that is, he recovers sinners as something useful to himself that had been lost, as though they wished to say that the divinity had suffered some loss through our destruction. They would have spoken correctly had they said: “He accepts sinners”—that is, he freely and gratuitously admits sinners into his grace, as below in Sermon 170. MITA.]

They do not say, “He accepts.” What had he lost, that he receives? Whoever finds what he had lost forgives sins, turns anger into joy, changes grief into grace.

“God receives sinners,” but God does not allow those whom he receives to remain sinners. The sinner does not violate God by drawing near; God sanctifies the sinner when he draws near.

Pharisee, Christ does not receive sins when he receives the sinner, because God is the receiver not of crime but of the human being. Therefore the Pharisee ought to have considered not what kind of people the sinners had come, but what kind they returned. Certainly they had sent out Paul as a persecutor, but they soon saw him return as a preacher.

But let us now hear by what comparison and likeness God reveals his joy over the sinner’s return.

“And he said to them this parable: Which of you is the man who has a hundred sheep, and if he loses one of them, does he not leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness and go after the one that was lost until he finds it? And when he has found it, he places it on his shoulders, rejoicing; and when he comes home, he calls together his friends and neighbors, saying to them: Rejoice with me, because I have found my sheep that was lost. So, I tell you, there will be joy in heaven over one sinner who repents, more than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of repentance” (Luke XV).

Whenever we find what was lost, we always receive a new increase of joy; and it is more pleasant for us to have found what was lost than not to have lost what was preserved. But this parable speaks more of divine compassion than of human custom, and expresses the truth.

To leave great things and love lesser things belongs to God’s power, not to human greed, because God makes even what does not exist exist; he pursues what is lost in such a way that he retains what he left; and he finds what was lost without losing what was preserved.

This shepherd, therefore, is not earthly but heavenly; and the whole parable is not represented by human labors but shadowed by divine mysteries. This becomes clear at once from the number itself, when he says: “Which of you is the man who has a hundred sheep, and if he loses one of them?”

Why not fifty? Why not two hundred? Why a hundred? Why not four or five, but one? So that he might show that the greater grief arose not from the loss itself but from the number.

[Note: Elsewhere, “greater pain.”]

The loss of one had dispersed the whole number of a hundred; it had reduced the whole number from the right hand to the left, so that through the loss of one it closed all on the left and left nothing on the right.

[Note: Irenaeus, *Against Valentinus*, book I, chapter 13, says that “the number ninety-nine, which is on the left, is transferred to the right by the addition of one, and there the hundred is formed.” Pierius Valerianus cites this passage and explains at length that this method of counting was customary among the ancients, and how it worked. Referring to this custom, our author says that “the number ninety-nine lies enclosed on the left.” For when the left hand was displayed with the fingers folded and the thumb pressed over the middle finger, the number ninety-nine was indicated. If one unit alone is added to that number, it immediately becomes a hundred; and the hundred is shown not by the left hand, compressed as described, but by the right hand, with the little finger pressed toward the palm. Thus, if the number ninety-nine becomes a hundred by the addition of one, it passes from the left to the right. From Mita.]

The number ninety-nine lies hidden on the left, constrained, clinging, held down and oppressed. Yet as soon as it receives and feels the increase of one, it passes from the left to the palm of the right hand, and immediately reaches the crown of the number one hundred. If not having a hundred is a cause of grief, what grief is it to have lost one?

You see that through the loss of one sheep this shepherd grieved that the whole flock had fallen from the right and entirely slipped back to the left. Therefore, leaving the ninety-nine, he follows the one and seeks the one, so that in the one he might find all and restore all.

[Note: The ninety-nine sheep are the lost human race; the one sheep is Adam. Once this one is recovered, the number one hundred is complete, and all are recovered.]

But let us now disclose the secret of the heavenly parable.

The man who has one hundred sheep is Christ: the good shepherd, the compassionate shepherd, who had placed the whole flock of the human race in one sheep, that is, in Adam; he had set this sheep amid the delights of paradise, in the region of living pasture. But it forgot the shepherd’s voice when it trusted the howls of wolves, lost the saving folds, and was wholly wounded by deadly injuries.

Therefore, when Christ came into the world to seek it, he found it in the womb of the virgin’s region. He came in the flesh of his birth, lifted it onto his shoulders upon the cross of his Passion, and, rejoicing with the complete joy of the resurrection, carried it through his ascension and brought it to the heavenly dwelling.

“And he called his friends and neighbors”—that is, the angels—saying to them: “Rejoice with me, because I have found my sheep that was lost.”

The angels rejoice and share Christ’s joy over the return of the Lord’s sheep, nor do they begrudge his presiding over them from the entire throne of his majesty, because envy from heavenly places had already been driven away together with the devil.

[Note: The author favors the opinion of certain theologians who assert that Lucifer was shown the hypostatic union of human nature with the divine Word, and that from this arose the pride and envy that cast down the devil and his followers. See Suárez, vol. I, disputation 42, section 1.]

Nor could the sin of envy penetrate heaven any longer through the Lamb who had taken away the sin of the world.

[Note: That is, through the grace granted to the good angels; or because envy had been driven from heaven through the eternal expulsion of the devil and his followers; or because the Lamb, by his own death, had restored peace to the heavenly beings. MITA.]

Brothers, he sought us on earth; let us seek him in heaven. He carried us to the glory of his divinity; let us carry him in our bodies with complete holiness. “Glorify,” says the Apostle, “and carry God in your body” (I Cor. VI).

He carries God in his body who carries no sin in the activity of his flesh.

## SERMON 169. On the Parable of the Lost Drachma

Only those who have received the grace of the divine Spirit know that mystical meanings lie hidden throughout all the Gospel readings and that secrets of heavenly understanding remain within them.

Behold: after the heavenly Shepherd had sought out the lost sheep of the flock of a hundred, found it, and brought the complete joy of the angels back to the heavenly fold, an evangelical woman is introduced as a figure. Having lit a lamp, she seeks one lost drachma from ten drachmas in such a way that, once it is found, her profit and joy become the cause of heavenly joys.

For she says: “Or what woman, having ten drachmas, if she loses one drachma, does not light a lamp, sweep the house, and search carefully until she finds it? And when she has found it, she calls together her friends and neighbors, saying: Rejoice with me, because I have found the drachma that I had lost. So, I tell you, there is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents” (Luke XV).

Do you think this woman is an ordinary woman? Is it thought, in a human sense, that she had ten drachmas? Is it believed that she lost one by some worldly accident? Does what happens here occur simply because she seeks it at night? Does she light a lamp according to ordinary human custom? Is it merely the familiar circumstance that she lost and found it inside the house, or that she calls her friends and neighbors to joy—although she is not said to have called them together in grief when she lost it?

This is a new kind of loss, one that shows that the drachma was not taken away but slipped away, and that it was hidden in domestic darkness, not buried through the deceit of outsiders.

You see how singular the whole matter is, how it surpasses and transcends human custom, how it breathes and exudes a divine meaning, how it raises the understanding of the mind to heaven, places it among heavenly things, compels it to light the lamp of the heavenly heart, and, like the evangelical woman, to seek the drachma of saving knowledge through the obscurities of the Lord’s reading.

Before Christ came to the wandering sheep and, worn out by its pitiable wanderings, lifted it to heaven upon his merciful shoulders, and, bearing his pious flock, reached the folds inaccessible to wolves, the woman who had ten drachmas endured prolonged darkness. She not only mourned one lost drachma but could not see the nine drachmas that remained to her.

It was perpetual night for her, a deep and enduring darkness; no lamp shone for her, without divine fire, as comfort in the night.

But after the heavenly fire—the fire of the Holy Spirit—had poured itself like a flame-bearing rain upon the apostles, and had kindled the cold and no less gloomy hearts of mortals with the full warmth of its fire, the woman—that is, the Church—lit her lamp, that is, the inward sight of her heart, namely, as the Apostle says, “the eyes of your heart, enlightened” (Eph. I).

She therefore lit her lamp and, after apostolic labor, overturned that Jewish house of ignorance, blinded by darkness, until she found in Christ the lost drachma among the ten drachmas—that is, the Decalogue of the Law.

[Note: Thus read several editions: Cologne 1627, Venice 1636, Lyon 1636, and the Lyon edition of Raynaud, 1633. In several others, the reading is *everrit*. Older Latin books, manuscripts, and the edition of Sixtus V (1590) read *evertit* in the sacred text. But that is erroneous. It should be read as the Greek has it, *everrit*. Some ancient copies, around the time of Gregory the Great, read *emandat*. Ambrose agrees with these in Letter 11, at the beginning. La Haye, disregarding the corrections, wishes to read *evertit*.]

Christ is the complete coin of divinity; Christ is the drachma of our redemption and price; Christ is the one who both was present in the Decalogue of the Law and lay hidden there; Christ is the one whom the Synagogue possessed but could not see because of the darkness assailing it.

We have said that the ten drachmas are the ten words of the Law, from which the Synagogue lost the Word—one drachma. Which one?
