The one that John first found in the Church, because he was a burning lamp, as the Lord says: “He was a burning lamp” (John V); and as the Evangelist says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I).

Let it now become clear that this was in the Decalogue. “Hear, O Israel,” he says, “the Lord your God is one God” (Deut. VI; Mark XII).

When the Synagogue does not see this in the Son, it loses it in the Father; when it does not believe in Christ, it lethally crucifies Christ. Therefore it is deservedly told next through the Decalogue: “You shall not kill” (Exod. XX).

For when the Jew mutilates the very sequence of the commandments by cutting off its head, he became Christ’s murderer before becoming the Law’s murderer, and consequently turned the whole body of the Decalogue against Christ.

[Note: The manuscript of Cesena has the opposite reading: “It became the Law’s murderer before becoming Christ’s murderer; hence it turned the whole body of the Decalogue against Christ” (*Legis antequam Christi exstitit homicida*). Which reading is more genuine I leave to the reader to judge. I prefer the printed reading. This means that when the Synagogue, joined to the gods of the Gentiles, committed adultery and rejected Christ, the true bridegroom, it then cut off the head of the ten commandments of God, namely: “I am the Lord your God,” and so forth. Thus it first killed Christ in its mind before killing the Law, and turned away and rejected the whole body of the Decalogue from itself—or rejected it against Christ, that is, against Christ and his Church, abandoning the observance of the Decalogue that it had repudiated. MITA.]

“You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery.” The Synagogue is condemned: joined to the gods of the Gentiles, it rejected Christ, who, setting aside the authority of a ruler, descended to it in the affection of a husband.

“You shall not steal.” It stole the Lord’s resurrection, giving money to the soldiers so that they might bury and conceal the truth of the resurrection (Matt. XXVIII).

“You shall not bear false witness.” This is the one that sought false witnesses (Matt. XXVI), to fulfill the saying: “Unjust witnesses rising up against me questioned me about things I did not know” (Ps. XXXIV).

And truly it could not hand over the author of truth in any other way, because falsehood alone always attacks truth.

Thus the one who slips on the stairs of the commandments falls; thus it collapses step by step. For if it had believed that the Lord God was one, it would not have come to this abyss of ruin.

But let us now follow the lamp of Mother Church, and, walking in the light of the Lord’s face, let us reach Christ’s drachma. Let us call together the friends and neighbors—that is, the Churches of the Gentiles—so that they may not fail to know that our mother has found her drachma. Let us say with the prophet: “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ” (Ps. CXXXI).

And let us hear what benefit the lamp provided: “Behold, we heard of it in Ephrata; we found it in the fields of the wood. We shall enter into his tabernacle; we shall worship in the place where his feet have stood” (ibid.).

Behold what we sought through extended fields and forests: let us find this in the Lord, this of our mother, by the lamp.

At this let heaven also rejoice, because, when one sinner repents, the fullness of the entire Christian people has shone forth, and the whole form of Christ’s divinity has gleamed for us in the drachma.

## SERMON 170. On Christ’s Assuming Various Forms for Our Sake, Calling the Apostles, Sending Them to Cure Diseases, and Commanding Poverty

Blessed Mark today, when he reports that the Lord went around the villages of Galilee, revealed his ineffable compassion toward us. “And Jesus went around the villages in the surrounding region, teaching,” he says (Mark VI).

You have heard how he goes around, how compassion tirelessly seeks you everywhere and does so for your sake. He who contains all things, while himself being contained by no creature, enters; he is confined within your body and contracts himself within your dwelling places.

He whose majesty the daily voice of the faithful proclaims, crying: “Heaven and earth are full of your glory” (Ecclesiastical Preface), goes around for your sake, appears, is seen, and is held in places.

Where does immovable fullness move? Where does it approach, or from where does it withdraw, when all things are full of it? Yet he goes, returns, descends, ascends; and God, becoming human, suffers all this for you and because of you,

[Note: The manuscript of Cesena reads: “who suffers you.”]

because he loves you exceedingly, because he loves you very much.

He assumes appearances, changes forms, and alters his offices. Now he shines for you like fire in the bush (Exod. III), so that he may kindle you, cold in faith, with the warmth of faith. Now he shines like a heavenly, fiery flame in a pillar (Exod. XIII), so that, when the darkness of your ignorance has been removed, you may travel through the solitudes of this world along the path of saving knowledge.

Now he himself becomes for you a pillar of cloud, so that he may temper the burning passions of your hearts. Now he protects you like an eagle with the wings of wisdom and invites you to heavenly flight, as Moses says:

“As an eagle protects its nest and hovers over its young, spreading its wings, it took them up and carried them upon its shoulders; the Lord alone guided them, and there was no foreign god with them” (Deut. XXXII, according to the Septuagint).

Now, like a hen, he leads out, guides, calls, receives, protects, carries, cherishes, surrounds, and embraces; forgetting its own flight and temporarily unmindful of its freedom, he moves about in your inner chambers and in your dust, so that he may nourish, educate, and instruct you with familiar, intimate, household nourishment (Matt. XXIII).

Now, as the good shepherd, he alone seeks the one wandering on the highest mountains, alone finds it, alone places it upon his shoulders, and, so that you may no longer be exposed to the bites of wolves in earthly pastures, carries you upward and leads you to the heavenly folds (Luke XV).

Thus, as we have said, he assumes appearances, changes forms, and, to change you for the better, changes and alters his offices so many times.

And because the enemy had long gone around in order to snatch and devour, Christ now necessarily goes around in order to defend and rescue you, as Scripture says: “Your adversary, like a roaring lion, goes around seeking whom he may devour” (I Pet. V).

“And he called the twelve.” After the long ages of the dark night, Christ our eternal day shone forth in the desired splendor of his dawn, illuminating the world; and he signified that he was fitting his twelve hours to his twelve apostles.

The blessed Psalmist saw this day in prophetic spirit when he sang: “This is the day that the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it” (Ps. CXVII). Hence the Apostle also calls believers sons of light and of the day: “You are sons of light and of day” (I Tim. V).

“And he called the twelve.” This number twelve, divided into three parts by the number four, shows and forms for us a four-horse chariot. Through it, the whole Trinity is carried throughout the whole world in the apostolic courses: so that the gentle warrior may conquer the devil; so that the meek victor may bend the pride of the world; so that the peaceful fighter may remove the dissensions of the nations; and so that, once hell—that is, the pit of sin—has been destroyed, he may lead the captivity of the human race, long imprisoned in the jail of souls, free into the glory of his triumph.

The blessed Psalmist saw this chariot of the Trinity in prophetic spirit when he said: “You ascended on high, you led captivity captive, you received gifts among men” (Ps. LXVII).

The Lord was preparing this chariot for himself, his Father, and the Holy Spirit when he said: “Take my yoke upon you, because my yoke is sweet and my burden light” (Matt. XI). The bearer of mercy, the vehicle of compassion, does not know how to grow weary.

We leave it to the investigator of the Law to prove more deeply that the twelve patriarchs, the twelve tribes arranged distinctly (Gen. XLIX), the twelve springs of the wilderness (Exod. XV), and the twelve stones of the Jordan lifted from its bed (Josh. IV) were described as figures and forms of the apostolic number, because the sequence of the reading before us attempts to explain why he sent the disciples to preach two by two.

“And he began to send them two by two.”

[Note: Matthew is silent about their having been sent in pairs. He sent them so that, as Brugensis says, they might help one another by their combined labor; and also, as Grotius holds, to provide complete testimony.]

He sent them in pairs so that their isolation, left without support, might not either deny Christ, as Peter did, or flee, as John did (Mark XIV). Human frailty quickly falls when, proudly trusting in itself, it despises companions and refuses to have a colleague, as Scripture says: “Woe to the one who is alone when he falls, and has no second to raise him” (Eccles. IV).

How much one person is strengthened by another’s help the same Scripture testifies when it says: “A brother helped by a brother is like a fortified city” (Prov. XVIII).

“And he began to send them two by two.”

Nor is it surprising, brothers, that the Trinity, which from the number twelve mounts a four-horse chariot divided into three parts, now mounts a two-horse chariot as well, so that the calling of the two peoples might be shown by the two messengers, and so that the Apostle’s saying might be made clear: “Is God the God of Jews only? Is he not also of the Gentiles? Indeed, of the Gentiles also” (Rom. III).

Thus the prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled: he testifies that he saw a rider upon a two-horse chariot when he heard himself asked: “What do you see?” And he answered: “I see a rider upon a two-horse chariot” (Isa. XXI). Immediately afterward he proclaims that Babylon and all its carved images have fallen.

Who, brothers, can doubt that Christ rode through these chariots on saving journeys, when he sees temples overturned by apostolic preaching, idols destroyed, the lowing of cattle and sacrifices brought to an end, and the altars themselves with their incense wholly vanishing in smoke through the ages?

Habakkuk had seen these chariots when he cried: “You mount your horses, and your riding is salvation” (Hab. III).

“And he gave them power over unclean spirits.” This is the mark of divine power; this is the trophy of a singular triumph: that the plunderer himself should be handed over as the spoil of his own prey, that the devil himself should become captive to those whom he had taken captive, and that he who had formerly bound them should now himself be bound, so that he might be subjected to the authority of those whose mighty master he had previously been.

He rightly grieves, rightly groans, rightly gnashes his teeth when he sees himself struck down by human judgment and human power—he who for so long had falsely persuaded human beings that he was God.

“And he commanded them to take nothing for the journey except a staff: no bag, no bread, and no money in their belts.”

When a human being invites workers to labor, he pours out not only the necessities of food but also abundant banquets, so that the weight of the work may be surpassed by the lavishness of the hospitality and the labor may be exceeded by the feast.

[Note: It is clear that in this first mission the Lord wished to give the apostles a demonstration of divine providence. This is the common opinion of the holy Fathers, shared by Chrysologus.]

How inhuman does he think God to be who, invited to his work, goes burdened and anxious with bag, bread, and money, so that the laborer, faithless because he is tired or slow, may arrive at the work—or perhaps may not be able to arrive at all?

A human employer promises abundant rewards; with so many written guarantees and so many witnesses he pledges generous pay. Do you, with an impious spirit, think that God will provide you neither bread nor clothing?

When you did not exist, he gave you existence; whatever you possess as a human being, he himself gave you; and while you were living for yourself and your pleasures, he did not deny you the necessities of food. Do you think that he will give neither bread nor clothing to one who serves him in his virtues and works?

Who gave you this very thing that you carry in your bag and belt? Why do you come to insult him with what belongs to him? He knows that you are rich.

[Note: This passage is corrected from Mita. Other editions read: “Cease, man, from your works.”]

Yield, man, to your possessions. Divine poverty is sufficient for you. Lay down the burdens of your riches. Burdened, you cannot reach the work of the Lord’s harvest by the narrow way. Come unencumbered; come free to the work, before, naked and stripped, you are seized as an unfaithful laborer and carried away to punishment; for, as it is written: “When a man dies, his riches do not follow him” (Ps. XLVIII).

Let your bag be your conscience; let your life be your bread, so that Christ may be the true bread in your life—he who said: “I am the bread” (John VI).

Let your reward be your payment, for the one who confidently demands his reward from Christ is the one who, in order to follow Christ, nakedly and faithfully rejected what he possessed.

[Col. 0647A]

## SERMON 171. On the Disciples Eating with Unwashed Hands
Like lightning bolts that shatter rocks, mountains, trees, and the very roofs of houses in a terrifying collision, they seize the senses and minds of human beings: so, whenever the Lord thunders against the Pharisees, he corrects and reforms his own with salutary fear. Thus today’s Gospel passage has thoroughly shown that the Pharisees and scribes reproached some of the Lord’s disciples because they ate without washing their hands.

When anyone hears this, let him not suppose that the Lord’s disciples ate with unkempt and muddy hands under the pretext of contempt, or that they failed to preserve and honor either the propriety of the Lord’s table or that of an ordinary meal. Neither nature permits such a thing, nor does the feeling of hospitality allow it. Who would not immediately offer water to serve someone who has arrived? Who would immediately refuse the one offering it, to the latter’s distress—especially since the Lord himself rebuked Simon when he had been invited to the table? “You gave me no water for my feet,” he says (Luke 7).

What he is shown to demand, therefore, he wishes to be done. But the Pharisees were seeking in the Lord’s disciples not bodily attentiveness but the baptisms of their own superstition. They did not know the one baptism that the Lord had established—not merely for washing, but for renewing souls and bodies: one that cleanses not the body for the conduct of life, but the conscience for salvation. The prophet was praying for this when he said: “Wash me more from my iniquity” (Psalm 50). That is: “How long will you wash me legally, yet not wash me? Wash me once by grace, me whom the innumerable washings of the Law did not wash.”

But let the Gospel passage itself, which follows, disclose this to us: “The Pharisees,” it says, “and all the Jews, unless they wash their hands frequently, do not eat, holding to the tradition of the elders; and when they return from the marketplace, unless they have been baptized, they do not eat, observing the baptism of cups and pitchers and bronze vessels and couches” (Mark 7).

Pharisee, who believe yourself clean, when everything of yours is polluted by your own banquet?

**[Note: Because of the Pharisaic conscience, defiled by sins, as below. MITA.]**

In the marketplace you argued over the blood of the innocent; you investigated how to seize a poor man’s property; you scrutinized how you might sell freedom into slavery. Since your interior is consumed by such great crime, how can water suffice to wash and cleanse your exterior? This water will be able to cleanse our hearts and bodies when it too has been purified through the fellowship of the Holy Spirit, so that by its visible ministry it may accomplish the sacrament of our invisible purification.

But you, Jew, baptize cups, pitchers, bronze vessels, and couches—things which, being without movement or sensation by nature, just as they do not know guilt, so they do not feel it. You honor these things, yet do not cleanse yourself, through whom everything has been contaminated. You purify them, enslaved to your uses and services, yet do not purify yourself, enslaved to divine offices and divine ministries.

But let us hear, brothers, not what the Lord answered the Jews, but what he answered his disciples: “He was saying that the things which come out of a person are what defile a person. For from within, out of the human heart, proceed evil thoughts, adulteries, fornications, murders, thefts, avarice, wickedness; deceit, shamelessness, an evil eye, blasphemies, pride, folly. All these evils proceed from within and defile a person.”

What expanse of earth, what size of cities, what breadth of regions could bear so many enemies, contain so many adversaries, or endure so many nations as the number of vices, offenses, and crimes that seize human senses and afflict human hearts?

You saw, brothers, an entire breed, the whole savagery of beasts, approach one sheep—beasts that rage all the more because they cannot fill themselves and cannot be satisfied by the capture of a single victim with their ravenous teeth. They burn and waste away more intensely because they cannot seize and devour it; just as against one dove there runs together such a multitude of kites, eagles, and greedy vultures—so many filthy birds.

The prophet had perceived this number and multitude when he sang: “Evils without number have surrounded me; my iniquities have seized me, and I could not see” (Psalm 39).

“They proceed from within, out of the human heart.” An enemy is bearable when he batters the walls from outside, when, stationed beyond them, he sometimes yields to combat. But the one whose enemy is within, whose adversary already rages in the innermost chambers—such a person understands and feels himself oppressed; he sees himself captive and bewails it; he cannot be his own conqueror, nor can he be his own liberator. He requires outside assistance and seeks another defender.

**[Note: The Caesenate manuscript reads: “He can be his own conqueror, but he cannot be his own liberator.” That is, he can indeed overcome by fighting on his own, but he cannot rescue or completely free himself from troubles, losses, and dangers. *Expugno* signifies “I conquer by fighting”; a *liberator* is one who rescues from danger and trouble. MITA.]**

“They come out from within, out of the heart.” Here is a new order of warfare: from the human being, nations go forth against the human being to wage war—not content to conquer and overthrow secretly, in hidden places, as though they sought human fame from his ruin.

Let the Jews, who are concerned with what is outward, wash themselves outwardly. But let us, brothers, be cleansed inwardly from these filths of vice. Let us conquer these nations of wickedness in our minds, with Christ fighting on our behalf; let us drive these beasts of offenses from our hearts by dread of the Lord’s name; let us strongly repel these frenzies of crime and these most ravenous birds from our senses with the spear of the cross. Thus the splendor of our city, the holiness of our temple, and the complete and distinctive adornment of our house may always summon and invite its creator to dwell within us.

Vices cannot return to the place where Christ dwells together with his virtues.

## SERMON CLXXII  
### On Envy and Hypocrisy

You have heard today, brothers, how, while he excluded others, the envious gatekeeper excluded himself. “Woe to you, lawyers,” he says, “because you took away the key of knowledge. You yourselves did not enter, and you hindered those who were entering” (Luke 11).

You have therefore heard how, while he excluded others, the envious gatekeeper excluded himself. The Pharisee had received the keys not in order to shut, but to open for those desiring to enter. Yet, so that another might not enter, he preferred to remain outside through jealousy.

All vices indeed always aim and rush toward harming those who possess them, but envy always consumes its own more thoroughly. Envy has always been the executioner of its own kind: it stretches the senses, tortures the soul, torments the mind, and corrupts the heart. And what more need be said? Whoever has admitted it endures punishments without end, because he always loves to have within himself a domestic torturer.

What end can there be to evils where another’s good is another’s punishment? Where another’s happiness is another’s torment?

**[Note: The Caesenate and Vallicellian manuscripts read “honor.” But envy, as John of Damascus says (*On the Orthodox Faith*, Book II, chapter 14, p. 128), is sorrow arising from another’s goods. Basil the Great likewise says at the beginning of his *Oration on Envy*, p. 445: “Envy is pain conceived at a neighbor’s prosperity and success in affairs.”]**

The evil is multiplied: as many as are the prosperities of human beings, so many are the torments of the envious.

A Christian spirit may be able to struggle with other vices, but whoever does not flee envy before he feels it will not escape it. It persuaded the lawyers not to open the Law but to close it; not to lend the teaching of a saving command but to deny it; to bar the fountain of knowledge and obstruct the riches of the life-giving stream at its source.

**[Note: “To obstruct the source of the life-giving stream through his envy.”]**

This disease must be fled with speed, because once it has touched someone, it no longer allows him to be healed.

Envy assailed heaven; for there it made the devil out of an angel. It burned the earth, which, through the flaming guardian, barred us from the delights of paradise.

It presses kings, because it compelled Herod to rage against Christ’s contemporaries so savagely that, before blood, milk was poured from tender limbs (Matthew 2).

It violates charity, for it made Cain a fratricide and stained the earth—still innocent—with the blood of a new murder (Genesis 4).

**[Note: “New,” that is, recently introduced into the world by human beings. The Caesenate manuscript, perhaps more correctly, reads: “He stained it with the blood of the innocent.” Similar remarks are made by Chrysostom, *Homily 40 on Matthew*, p. 269: “This made the demon savage. By this means the first murder was committed; thus nature was disregarded; thus the earth was polluted.” Basil the Great’s homily *On Envy* deserves to be read in full.]**

It lays waste to peoples, for it made the Jews—if it is lawful to say so, if the language can bear it—deicides. We call them deicides not according to the outcome but according to the direction toward which the crime was aimed. For in Christ the Jews attempted to crush not merely a human being but God, the Son of God; they sought to kill the virtues when they said: “This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours” (Mark 12).

**[Note: Mita argues at length here that the Jews, instructed in the Law, knew Christ to be the Messiah and Son of God, yet, blinded by envy and malice, condemned him to death. He says that Chrysologus’s judgment should be explained in these terms, although not all the Fathers and scholastic theologians agree with it. To establish it more firmly, he relies chiefly on Christ’s testimony in John 7:28: “You know me, and you know where I am from.” The Hebrew Scriptures presented a twofold generation of Christ: one eternal and unknown to human beings, the other temporal and assigned to a definite time, place, and family. Hence disputes arose among the crowds. In Christ’s words just cited, many understand a reference to his human generation; Christ answered them appropriately: “You know where I am from, and you recognize me only from the Father; but I have another origin, which is hidden from you.” The Greek Fathers interpret the passage in different ways. According to Mita’s understanding of Chrysologus: “You know what I am—not only according to human nature, but you also know that I am the Messiah and Son of God, although you conceal this through the extremity of your malice.” Maldonado approved this explanation. In any case, Origen, *Treatise 19 on Matthew*; the author of the *Opus Imperfectum*, *Homily 40*; Jerome in his commentary; Bede, Book III on Matthew; Thomas Aquinas, *Summa theologiae* III, question 47, article 5, in the body of the article; and others cited by Mita maintain that the Jews knew Christ.]**

But what power does the devil have against God? What power does envy have against the Lord’s charity? The devil envied us the earth, but God gave heaven; the lawyer took away the keys of knowledge, but Christ, through Peter, bestowed the keys of the heavenly kingdom (Matthew 26).

Thus envy was stripped of its own advantages, and the human being was enriched by the very necessity of his losses.

**[Note: That is, because through the devil’s envy the human being necessarily fell into temporal losses, Christ the Lord therefore enriched him with spiritual goods, which are of a higher order. MITA.]**

The Lord therefore rightly added in what follows, saying: “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees” (Luke 12).

For in leaven there is not mass through greatness but swelling through inflation; and the dough, inflated in this way, has not been enriched but puffed up. The more violently it ferments, the more the mass of flour swells, filling its entire shape with lightness and swelling.

Therefore the Lord appropriately said: “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy.”

What is hypocrisy except an appearance artificially composed, which does one thing in reality and promises another in its expression? Among the Pharisees it swelled through knowledge, as the Apostle says: “Knowledge puffs up” (1 Corinthians 8). Knowledge puffed them up toward pride; it did not instruct them for life. It corrupted them toward malice; it did not advance them toward prudence.

There was hypocrisy on their faces; in their minds there was the dropsy of envy; in their breasts there was a thirsty fountain; there was a burning flood, which grew ever more inflamed by its own streams, so that it did not extinguish the thirst of the drinker but increased the fire.

Thus, yes, through the ministry of hypocrisy, envy always serves its own kind a drink.

The Apostle withdraws us from this disease when he compels us to celebrate the Lord’s holy Passover “not in the old leaven, nor in the leaven of malice and wickedness, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1 Corinthians 5).

Truth knows no swelling; simplicity utterly ignores hypocrisy.

“In the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.”

**[Note: The Caesarean manuscript reads: “Truth is the unleavened bread of the heart, prepared with heavenly sweetness, seasoned with the richness of grace,” and so forth.]**

These are the unleavened breads of the heart; these are prepared with heavenly sweetness; these are seasoned with the rich savor of grace; these are cooked by the fire of the Holy Spirit. Eating them, we solemnly sacrifice the Lamb of God—“the Lamb who takes away the sin of the world”—for our Passover. Through these, Christ has been born and transformed entirely for our joy and entirely for our glory.

## SERMON CLXXIII  
### On Saint John the Baptist and Herod

The good shepherd spends sleepless nights and anxious days, lest the cunning thief or the crafty savagery of wolves contrive anything harmful against the dear flock, or lest anything injurious be attempted.

The good shepherd, as the Lord said, “lays down his life for his sheep” (John 10). The good sheep also listen to the voice of their shepherd with attentive ears, always follow their shepherd’s direction, and do their shepherd’s entire will. They climb hills, seek high places, often change regions; and thus they enter places suitable for pasture, watered by streams, shaded, convenient, and secluded for rest. They discover pleasant places and enjoy their delights.

And you also, little children, a numerous portion of the Lord’s flock, already clothed in a snowy and divine fleece, fertile with tender offspring and heavenly growth—if through hearing our voice you have often reached health-giving places and health-giving pastures; if through the streams of our discourse you have moderated the heat of your souls and the ardor of your thirst; if beneath the shelter of our teaching you have reclined with some comfort—pay attention to what we prescribe, listen to what we say, approve what we do. Receive the reasoning of our preaching not according to your own will but according to our arrangement.

Whether we speak from this step, or whether, according to the circumstances of the time, we address you from the priestly seat—

**[Note: Ferrarius, *On Preaching*, cites these same words from Chrysologus, Book III, chapter 7, p. 347, to support his claim that sermons were delivered from the steps of the altar. Sidonius, *Eucharistic Poem to Faustus of Riez*, at the end, writes:

> Whether the attentive crowd surrounds you as you are about to preach from the conspicuous steps of the venerable altar.

Note: Bishops also spoke from the episcopal exedra. See Ferrarius, cited above, Book III, chapter 5, p. 338. Aurelius Prudentius, describing the basilica of Saint Hippolytus, writes:

> Beneath the opposite façade a lofty tribunal rises on steps, from which the bishop proclaims God.]**

—as good sheep, as dear flocks, beloved offspring, come together and hasten without arrogance, diligently, with the entire course of faith.

Nor should the proximity of the change of place, the confined spaces, or the restricted distance make you sluggish or cause you to murmur. A sheep does not reach the fold if it wanders according to its own pleasure; a disciple cannot acquire knowledge if he insists on being taught according to his own will; nor can a sick person ever recover health if he is treated according to his own preference.

But since our discourse today is against a raging wolf, let us take up the shepherd’s staff and pass to the Gospel reading.

“King Herod heard,” it says—“for the name of Jesus had become known”—and he said: “John the Baptist has risen from the dead; therefore powers are at work in him” (Mark 6).

The fool piously believes of the dead man whom he savagely persecuted while alive. “John has risen,” he says, yet he confesses unknowingly that the one killed rises in Christ and for Christ.

Herod, what did your sword accomplish? What did your cruelty achieve? Where did your impiety advance, if, as you yourself say, he who was thought to have been extinguished by your fury has returned to the powers and risen again for divine works?

John has risen, as you yourself confess. Here it is not the person but weakness that perishes; not John, but death itself, has succumbed to such a death. Punishment has been mocked; the executioner is held up to ridicule; the judgment of the wretched judge himself has been deceived. It did not destroy the man it killed but advanced him.

“John has risen from the dead; therefore powers are at work in him.”

Although he was an enemy of the Law, he had nevertheless learned through the Law that resurrection from the dead had been promised.

**[Note: Herod seems rather to have believed in a kind of metempsychosis. We are also taught that this belief had been persuaded upon the Jews, especially by Philo, *On Dreams*. The Hebrew rabbis, whom Grotius cites in his note on Matthew 14:2, report that whatever Plato, Pythagoras, and others discussed was drawn from the prophets.]**

If he knew that John would rise, why did he madly kill him? If he knew that through such a death John would be raised to the summit of all divine power, to the full distinction of everything that belongs to authority, why did he make himself the author of so great a death?

**[Note: The Caesarean manuscript reads: “Why did he dare to be the author of his death?”]**

Impiety is always fevered; cruelty is always possessed by frenzy; madness does not know how to be without dementia.

For whenever it reaches toward another, it rages against itself; it punishes itself while striking the innocent; it is wholly deadly to itself whenever it is cruel toward the just.

Behold, John, as you yourself say, now lives in Christ. He returns for your punishment, having come by heavenly gift for the healing of all.

“But others were saying, ‘He is Elijah’; and others, ‘He is a prophet, or like one of the prophets.’ When Herod heard this, he said: ‘John, whom I beheaded, is the one; he has risen from the dead.’”

With a malicious yet truthful understanding, he himself stands as witness to his crime, defender of his wickedness, and accuser of his own deed.

“John, whom I beheaded, is the one; he has risen from the dead.”

He speaks the truth. For just as the members of Christ rise in Christ, so Christ himself suffers in his members; and just as the honor of the head extends to the members, so the punishment of the members flows back into the suffering and injury of the head.

“John, whom I beheaded, is the one.”

This wise king, this distinguished judge, this censor of morals, guardian of discipline, avenger of innocence, and punishment of crimes says that he beheaded John but remains silent about why he beheaded him, lest the shamefulness of so great a deed expose the royal power. But the evangelist reveals it, so that the disgrace of the murderer may lead the murdered man to glory.

“For Herod himself,” he says, “had sent and seized John and bound him in prison because of Herodias, the wife of Philip his brother, because he had married her. For John was saying to Herod: ‘It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife.’”

Herodias, who, out of love for crime, sought to be the wife of two brothers—

**[Note: By loving Herod, she had violated the active and passive affection of her lawful husband Philip; and through her affection for Herod she had violated the mutual affection between the brothers Herod and Philip. MITA.]**

—in order to violate affection and join herself to Herod; so that those who were alike in crime, morals, and life might not be different even in name, and so that those whom the shamefulness of their crimes had joined might be joined also by their title—this Herodias therefore plotted against John.

Herod did not overcome the mind of the adulteress, yet he postponed the adulteress’s wicked demand. She, so that she might no longer be reproved, directed her attack toward the death of the reprover. He, in order to please the incestuous woman, himself a captive, merely held the just man and bound him in confinement, because, being guilty against an innocent man, he could not easily pronounce sentence.

**[Note: Because Herodias surpassed Herod in her eagerness for incest, yet Herod did not drive her away. Alternatively, with the Caesarean manuscript: “Herod did not master the adulteress’s mind,” that is, he did not restrain Herodias’s mind, which had been forcibly subjected or prepared for his use, so that he could not withdraw from her. MITA. Perhaps the meaning is that Herod did not overcome Herodias’s mind by striving to turn her away from her purpose, but merely postponed the Baptist’s death, which she demanded.]**

“When an opportune day had come,” he says, “Herod made a banquet on his birthday for the leaders, tribunes, and first men of Galilee. When the daughter of that same Herodias had entered and danced and pleased Herod, and also those reclining at table, the king said to the girl: ‘Ask me for whatever you wish, and I will give it to you.’ And he swore to her: ‘Whatever you ask, I will give you, even half my kingdom.’”

An ungrateful and inhuman king, who gave such virtue, such glorious labor, and such a memorable deed not his entire kingdom but half of it! And why did he preserve even part of it for himself, when, after such glory for his house, after such holiness for his family, after such an example of chastity, he ought not to have existed, appeared, or lived?

That girl, then, a daughter of crime rather than of nature, ran immediately not so much to her mother as to the very sewer of her wickedness. She had gone forth wholly fluid and wholly dissolved; she now flew back savage and cruel. To speak in terms of the arts themselves, she returned to sing the wicked tragedy that had most shamefully completed the comedy.

When she had gone out, she said to her mother: “What shall I ask?” And the mother said: “The head of John the Baptist.”

She immediately entered with haste to the king and asked, saying: “I want you to give me at once, on a platter, the head of John the Baptist.”

The king was distressed because of the oath and because of those reclining at table, and he did not wish to distress her. Immediately the king sent an executioner and ordered John’s head to be brought. The executioner went and beheaded him in prison, brought his head on a platter, gave it to the girl, and the girl gave it to her mother.

Thus acts a mind burdened with gluttony, loosened by wine, and in every respect submerged in the shipwreck of drunkenness.

**[Note: Chrysostom, volume I, homily 84, judges: “Drunkenness is nothing other than disturbance of the mind, overturning of reason, abandonment of understanding, and absence of intelligence.”]**

“I want you to give me at once, on a platter, the head of John.”

The serpent’s offspring seeks the head of the human being, whose own head it knew had been condemned by the principal sentence, when God said:

**[Note: Some Latin copies read *Ipse* (“He himself”), together with Chrysologus, Jerome in *Hebrew Questions*, Irenaeus, Book IV *Against Heresies*, chapter 78, and Pope Leo, Sermon 2 *On the Nativity of the Lord*. Onkelos, cited here by Calmet, has: “You will remember what he did to you from the beginning, and at the end you will watch for him”—namely, the son who will be born from that woman will exact vengeance for the injury inflicted on him by you; but you will nurse from the beginning a rage conceived against him, or against the woman.]**

“He himself will watch over your head, and you will watch his heel” (Genesis 3).

The length of the reading draws us onward, and the immense depth of the passage advances us far below the surface. Let us defer what follows today, lest, while the discourse hastens toward its end, it pass over what ought to be discussed at length.

In the conclusion of our speech we commend this point: the serpent ran for no purpose. For this John of ours destroyed all the offspring of the ancient serpent and, killed, extinguished it by the pouring out of his own blood.

## SERMON CLXXIV  
### On the Beheading of Saint John the Baptist

The bloody courses of Herod’s banquet, such a savage feast—then the earth, then heaven—today your hearing has shuddered and trembled with me.

“Herod,” it says, “made a banquet on his birthday” (Mark 6).

It rightly calls it a banquet, because this birthday belongs not to light but to darkness: in it the son of night, not of day, was born.

“He made a banquet on his birthday for the leaders, tribunes, and first men of Galilee” (Mark 6).

What has reckless and ever-blind impiety done? It summons every authority, so that it may acquire not so much many companions of its banquet as innumerable witnesses to its crime, and have as many judges of its deed as it had guardians of discipline.

“When the daughter of Herodias herself had entered,” he says, “and danced and pleased Herod.”

She answered her own shameful origin while pleasing a more shameful father; for from adultery only a shameful child ought to have been born. With broken steps, loosened body, and the structure of her limbs disjointed, her inner parts flowing through artifice, she became more beautiful to her father through her entire deformity.

**[Note: Mita rightly says that Chrysologus was mistaken. Salome, the dancing daughter, was not born to Herodias from this Herod, but from Herod Philip the tetrarch.]**

And indeed Herod believed her to be his own when he saw such a girl; he would have thought her someone else’s if he had perceived even a little modesty in her.

The serpent was then hiding in the woman. Crawling with winding steps, she poured deadly poison through her entire body, so that frenzy wounded the minds of those reclining at table, venom wounded their bodies, and human beings were turned into beasts. They were no longer drinking wine but blood; they were no longer eating bread, but, rabid, feeding on human flesh.

**[Note: This alludes to rabid dogs, which do not and cannot eat bread but, because of their rabies, strive to bite human beings and all living creatures and infect them with the disease. Saint Augustine discusses them in *The City of God*, Book XXII, chapter 22, in the middle.]**

Such people she made them—such people indeed—when she brought John’s head to them, with the blood still smoking, so that the Psalmist’s song might be fulfilled: “They gave the flesh of your saints to the beasts of the earth; they poured out their blood like water” (Psalm 78).

Behold what banquets prolonged through entire nights produce; behold what wine produces when it is bought with restraint and drunk without restraint. Behold where the flesh is hurled when pleasure inflames it with the fires of lust.

I ask: why is the unhappy flesh confined within such great wedges? It is enough for it, through its own falls, to be brought down to ruin, as the prophet testifies when he says: “Why do you all rush upon a human being? You kill him as though he were a leaning wall and a tottering fence” (Psalm 61).

In Herod, the flesh lay oppressed by gluttony and captive to drunkenness. Lust tickled it, and wantonness—not so much playing as deceiving—made it promise that it would give whatever shamefulness demanded.

“Ask me for whatever you wish,” he says, “and I will give it to you”; and he swore to her.

The wretch swears while forswearing everything that belongs to honor and virtue.

“Ask me for whatever you wish.”

What would lust ask for except the destruction of chastity, the death of modesty, and the death of the holiness that is always opposed to it?

“I want you to give me the head of John on a platter.”

If Christ is the head of the man, according to the Apostle (1 Corinthians 11), then even at that time the ancient serpent was stretching out its hand toward the death of Christ the Lord through a new mouth.

“I want you to give me the head of John on a platter.”

Even then the eager dragon, in the head of the servant, was tasting the Lord’s passion with thirsty appetite.

“I want you to give me the head on a platter.”

Why on a platter? Why do you carry with honor the one whom you kill dishonorably, unless it is because “precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Psalm 115)?

You do not accomplish even what you want in the way you yourself want, because heavenly reason causes you to act otherwise than you wish.

In that savage cave—not a royal court—frenzy then thought it had found its food when it saw the martyr’s head. It sensed that its fill had come when it gazed thirstily upon the stream of sacred blood. With its whole mouth and all its jaws it strove and struggled to swallow the dish of its own cruelty.

But John came set on high, like a lamp upon a lampstand, to drive away the darkness, as the Lord said: “He was the burning and shining lamp” (John 5).

John came as a judge shining on the tribunal, so that he who had reproved adultery might expose and condemn the murderer; and he who, living piously, had called incest to repentance and reserved it for pardon might, once killed, also condemn murder.

What pardon, I ask, does the one deserve who so credulously killed repentance itself in John’s death?

You ran pointlessly, Herod and Herodias—names joined not by affection but by crime—

**[Note: Another reading: “who believed most foolishly that the voice could be cut off.”]**

—you who most foolishly believed that the voice could be cut off.

“I am,” he says, “the voice of one crying in the wilderness” (John 1).

A voice cannot be killed; freed from the restraints of the body, it cries out more loudly. Thus Abel’s voice, already poured out in his blood, sounds more loudly, penetrates more deeply, and reaches more insistently toward heaven (Genesis 4).

So now John cries out throughout the whole world; through all ages he reports and displays your crime to everyone among the nations.

Behold, John glories in the head of Christ, though he was thought to have been condemned because of the head. Behold, on the day when you ended your own life, he acquired a birthday in heaven. For when your birth sank into its end, his end arose into a birthday.

The just person begins to live precisely when he deserves to be killed for Christ. Through this death the martyr’s life is transferred, not taken away. He became more glorious through the death by which he died so that he might live forever.

Behold, you lie in death; John lives though killed. You lost purple dyed with artificial crimson; John forever glories, clothed in shining purple through his own blood. Your banquet companions now become partners in punishment; John feeds at the heavenly table with choirs of angels.

He continually hears the heavenly harmony; you continually hear the groaning and grinding of hell. He, who was handed over as the price of your prostitute and dancing girl, is now honored with a kingdom and heavenly rewards; you received in Tartarus, together with your daughter, the payment of your sentence.

Joseph, when he fled from the adulteress, left his garment behind (Genesis 39); John, so that he would not see the adulteress, cast away even his body. Joseph willingly accepted prison so that he would not commit adultery; John exchanged the wilderness for prison so that he might reprove adultery.

Joseph escaped death while revealing dreams; John, in order to reveal the Son of God, accepted death. Joseph, while preparing temporal bread, earned a golden necklace and honor; John, in order to show believers the heavenly bread (Matthew 11), earned a necklace of martyrdom from blood.

John is rightly greater than all those born of women. He not only reproved adulteresses but, through love of virginity, trampled underfoot even lawful companionship with women.

And if John, so great and so distinguished, separated from women in such a vast wilderness, did not escape the dangers of women,

**[Note: The Vallicellian manuscript reads: “the snares of women.”]**

who is there who, living among women, can confidently believe that he will escape without the greatest effort and the greatest caution—unless he is one who is nourished by the Holy Spirit, who, together with the Father and the Son, orders all ages through every span of time?

## SERMON CLXXV

**[Note: This title appears in the Caesenate and Vallicellian manuscripts. Mita and Tillemont believe that this sermon was delivered at Ravenna on the Sunday of the Lord’s Nativity, on the occasion of the ordination of Marcellinus, bishop of Vicohavenna. He was the first to be consecrated by the bishop of Ravenna, as metropolitan. The see of Vicohavenna, which in the thirteenth century is found under the name Ferrariola and is now the parish of Saint George on the northern bank of the lesser Po, did not remain there long after the Lateran Council; the people of Ferrara want Vitalian, pope in the year 657, to have been responsible for its transfer. Henschenius, volume II of the May collection, p. 154, suspects that the cause was the arrogance of Maurus, archbishop of Ravenna, who, defecting from the Roman see, advanced so far in insolence that he dared to summon the Roman pontiff to judgment before his own tribunal. He had Reparatus as successor both to his throne and to his offense. When Reparatus quickly repented, he obtained pardon from Pope Deodatus, the successor of Vitalian, on no other condition than that Maurus’s name be erased from the diptychs. Henschenius thinks it likely that the bishop of Vicohavenna, having cursed the arrogance of his archbishop, went to Rome and requested and obtained permission to transfer his see to Ferrara. That is his account.]**

### On Marcellinus, Bishop of Vicohavenna, and the Birth of Saint Mary the Virgin
The beginnings of all things are indeed difficult, but the beginnings of one who gives birth are more difficult than all others. The holy Church of Ravenna, when she was to give birth for the first time, made a way, endured anguish, and felt pains. And she did this, brothers, in order to preserve the order of the divine birth along the whole course of truth: for after the Virgin Mother, in order to bear the firstborn of all creation, had traversed the road throughout the whole land, so the virginal birth, so the birth of the firstfruits, was consecrated. And necessarily, brothers, the Way is generated on the way. “I am the Way,” he says (John 14), so that every entrance to error might be shut out, and the traveler might at last seek heaven—he who had long endured the sweat and labors of an earthly journey.

[Col. 0656C] “And it came to pass in those days,” says the Evangelist, “that a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be registered. Joseph also went up from Galilee, from the city of Nazareth, into Judaea, to the city of David, which is called Bethlehem, because he was of the house and family of David, to register with Mary, his betrothed wife, who was pregnant. And it came to pass in those days that the days were fulfilled for her to give birth, and she bore her firstborn son” (Luke 2).

It is pleasing here to say something about the pain. The Lord of all, in obedience to the decree of Caesar and of a pagan, comes forward to obey; and does some servant still irreverently resist the decree of blessed Peter, the decree of a Christian ruler? But since neither prosperity should be mingled with adversity nor sadness with joys, let us set these matters aside and proclaim the joy of today’s offspring.

[Note: [Col. 0656D] Here the author seems to be speaking of Saint Apollinaris the martyr, who, as the first offspring of the Church of Ravenna mentioned above, deserves reverence. If one prefers to understand him as speaking of Marcellinus, it should be known that Vicohaventia had as the first bishop of its Church Oltradus, a foreigner immediately elected and consecrated by Pope Saint Sylvester in the year of Our Lord 330. After him it had a second bishop, likewise a foreigner, and in third place this Marcellinus was appointed in his stead. He was not, like those mentioned above, an outsider, but was Vicohaventinus by origin and upbringing. Thus the author’s meaning seems to be: Let that bishop who was the firstborn of the Church of Vicohaventia have the reverence due to the firstborn, [Col. 0657B] because he was a foreigner, made the journey, and endured the anguish proper to firstborns. But Marcellinus today, not indeed as a firstborn and a child of anguish, but as a son born at home and a domestic offspring, free from a journey—for that Church was already firmly established in the Catholic faith—wins for himself all the affection of his people. Perhaps the author also understood [Col. 0657C] Christ himself, Mary’s most sacred firstborn, who is said to have been born before Marcellinus, since his annual feast of the Nativity had already begun and was almost halfway completed when Marcellinus was consecrated bishop. MITA.]

[Col. 0657A] Let him who has now been born, who was born first, have the reverence and retain the honor of the firstborn. Marcellinus today, a native offspring, has seized and won all affection. Sons stand around, relatives are present, the whole kindred gathers, the entire household rejoices, and the innermost chambers of the house themselves leap and exult: because today they have been privileged for the first time to see with their eyes and receive in their hands the offspring and child of the holy mother. The mother herself—bride, mother, and virgin—marvels with new rejoicing that she has given birth in the very chamber of her union.

[Note: [Col. 0657C] Perhaps the people had been disturbed by this kind of election: namely, that he was not a foreigner, nor otherwise immediately elected and consecrated by the supreme pontiff, but a citizen elected by citizens, of humble skill as a fisherman, perhaps married and devoted to his sons, and not sufficiently learned in letters. For this reason there could have been suspicion, especially among the envious, who never die, and among the misled populace, that some stain of wrongdoing had intervened. But our Chrysologus, by arguments and examples drawn from Saint Joseph and the most blessed Virgin, suggests that this should by no means be suspected, especially since Marcellinus himself is the bridegroom, witness, and guardian of the integrity of his bride, the Church. For he knew very well that divine counsel had been present in such an election, and that it is wicked to oppose it. How, however, Marcellinus’s election was more precisely carried out, I cannot conjecture, and from the very ancient records of Ferrara I have been able to learn nothing else. One thing is known: there were five bishops of Vicohaventia from the year of Christ 330 to the year 657, at which time the see is said to have been transferred to Ferrara, according to Rubeus, *History of Ravenna*, book 11, p. 109, second edition. Those who add this Marcellinus to the Martyrology of Usuard place him among the saints of God; but whether this was commonly received by the Church of God is not sufficiently clear. MITA.—And indeed there is profound silence about Marcellinus in the other ecclesiastical registers.]

But let no one be troubled, let no one be disturbed, by the fact that the bride herself is seen to have given birth in the very bridal chamber: this is not a matter of guilt, but of a conception arising from virginity, since in such an offspring the birth is heavenly, not human. Nor is there any place here for sinister suspicion, where the bridegroom himself is held to be the witness and guardian of his bride. Whoever is anxious about the event, let him pursue the greatest example, and let the trembling of what preceded contribute to your caution and protection.

That Joseph, a husband in name only but a bridegroom in conscience, gazes in agitation and anxiety upon his pregnant bride, because he could neither accuse an innocent woman nor accuse a pregnant woman; silence was unsafe, while speech was dangerous. He admits the matter but does not betray it: an accuser of the innocent, he does not expose the alleged offense. He himself was the testimony of chastity; he was the guardian of modesty. He knew one thing but saw another; his sight confused him, though the Virgin’s faith did not confuse him. His conduct and life were at a crossroads; his just mind and holy spirit were tormented by divided thought. He perceived the matter, but could not penetrate the mystery, because he could neither accuse her nor defend her before men.

[Col. 0658A] Rightly, then, an angel immediately appeared; rightly, a divine answer at once came to his aid. When human counsel failed, justice did not fail. And what does he say? “Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid.” He had done nothing: what was he afraid of? He was afraid because, although there was no guilt in the deed, there was immense fear in the circumstance. A holy mind is terrified by whatever it does not comprehend.

[Note: [Col. 0657D] A passage badly corrupted in many editions is restored from Mita and the Vallicellian manuscript.]

Beware, therefore, man, of discussing the birth of our mother in such a way, since it is enough that the angel answered: “Do not be afraid to take Mary your wife; for what has been born in her is of the Holy Spirit.”

[Col. 0658B] Happily she gives birth who, by giving birth ever more fully, has won the crown and glory of virginity.

[Note: [Col. 0657D] The Caesena manuscript reads: *cum sibi angelum*, “since the angel [answered] him,” adding *sibi* (“to him”).] But this man who has been born for us today has always cast his nets into the sea.

[Note: [Col. 0657D] Or Marcellinus was a fisherman, or, as Tillemont supposes, he held some administrative office over public fishing.]

Let no one, therefore, wonder if Peter eagerly desired to have a fisherman as his colleague. Pray, then, brothers, that he may be worthy to fish for human beings, he who until now has labored to catch fish for the life of human beings.

[Note: [Col. 0657D] It will not now be a fruitless labor to append what Pastritius wrote about the explanation of this sermon in his little work *On the Paten of Chrysologus*. It is as follows.]

## Explanation of the Obscure Sermon 175 of Saint Peter Chrysologus, So That It May Become Clear That He Himself First Exercised Metropolitan Dignity and Authority

[Col. 0658C] “Chrysologus’s sermon 175, which concerns Marcellinus, bishop of Vicohaventia, consecrated by him, prompts us to consider another delay, and indeed a longer one. For there he shows that resistance was made against the decree of blessed Peter the Apostle and the edict of the emperor. But who was this resister? Let us hear the words of the sermon.

“He first states that these were beginnings and a first generation, which does not occur without pain. ‘The beginnings of all things are difficult, but the beginnings of one who gives birth are more difficult than all others.’ He takes up the Gospel for exposition, when the Virgin Mother of God gave birth to her firstborn, beginning with the words: ‘A decree went out from Caesar Augustus.’ In his customary manner, as the Gospel proceeds, he contemplates present circumstances, applying both the words and the events of the Gospel to them, and therefore demanding the reader’s or hearer’s keen attention.

“After the prologue concerning the hardness, difficulty, and pain of the one who gives birth for the first time—when the hearers had not understood where he was going—he removes all doubt by continuing: ‘The holy Church of Ravenna, when she was to give birth for the first time, made a way, endured anguish, and felt pains.’

[Col. 0658D] “Therefore the words and events of the Gospel and of the Mother of God must be explained with reference to the Church of Ravenna at the ordination of the bishop of Vicohaventia. Just as the Mother of God had previously given birth to no one, but brought forth Christ Jesus as her firstborn, so the Church of Ravenna had previously consecrated no bishop and had not exercised the office of a mother; but then, at the consecration of the bishop of Vicohaventia, she first demonstrated herself to be a mother, when she gave birth for the first time and brought forth her firstborn.

“The Mother of God did not endure pains in giving birth, because the holy Virgin conceived through the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit and gave birth as a virgin—unless we say that the difficulty and pain consisted in the journey undertaken from the house at Nazareth to the cave at Bethlehem. But the Church of Ravenna, which is also a holy mother and undefiled virgin, like every other Church of Christ, truly endured pains and anguish before she gave birth.

“For when she became a mother through the decree of the apostolic see and the edict of the emperor Valentinian [Col. 0659A] III, the metropolitan who governed the cities subject to the Church of Ravenna by virtue of those decrees resisted, asserting his rights and refusing to be deprived of metropolitan authority over those same cities. Hence the Church of Ravenna was compelled to defend her new privilege against the former metropolitan. The words ‘she endured anguish and felt pains’ sufficiently indicate with what zeal and through how many difficulties she did so. For what purpose? In order that she might give birth for the first time.

“[Col. 0659B] The bishop of Vicohaventia had previously belonged to the archbishop of Milan. For Saint Ambrose of Milan wrote Letter 19—in other editions, Letter 44, and in the latest edition, Letter 2—to Constantius, bishop of Vicohaventia, commending to him the Church of Forocornelium as belonging to his jurisdiction and subject to him. But this Church, like Vicohaventia, together with other cities, was subjected to the bishop of Ravenna in the edict of Valentinian III, as may be seen there; consequently those cities had belonged to the archbishop of Milan.

“Vicohaventia is now called Ferrara. Since there were many villages there along the Po, the city was called Vicohabentia, as though it were ‘a place possessing villages’; then, through corruption of the name, it passed into various forms. The city itself was eventually completely destroyed by the Goths, and when its inhabitants crossed to the other bank of the Po and founded Ferrara, the episcopal jurisdiction was transferred there by Pope Vitalian.

[Col. 0659C] “We thus have a metropolitan who was fighting with the bishop of Ravenna and was inflicting anguish and pains upon that Church, already constituted as a mother and metropolitan, before she gave birth to her firstborn. Therefore Chrysologus continues his sermon: ‘And she did this, brothers, in order to preserve the order of the divine birth along the whole course of truth. For after the Virgin Mother, in order to bear the firstborn of all creation, had traversed the road throughout the whole land, so the virginal birth, so the birth of the firstfruits, was consecrated.’

“He emphasizes the likeness between the birth of the firstborn of the Church of Ravenna and the birth of the firstborn of the Mother of God, both in that before the birth it was necessary to travel and traverse many roads, and to labor by traveling along the Aemilian Way and the Flaminian Way, which joins Rome—or rather, which begins there—beseeching the apostolic see and imploring its assistance and authority in order firmly to defend the privilege that had once been granted, and recently so; just as it was necessary for the Mother of God to travel as far as the borders of Jerusalem, or all the way to Bethlehem.

[Col. 0659D] “It is also alike in this respect: the Mother of God gave birth to her firstborn on the road, or beside the road, while the Church of Ravenna gave birth to her firstborn on the Aemilian Way, in the territory of the metropolitan of Ravenna. ‘And necessarily, brothers,’ Chrysologus continues, ‘the Way is generated on the way. “I am the Way,” he says, so that every entrance to error might be shut out, and the traveler might at last seek heaven, who had long endured the sweat and labors of an earthly journey.’

“Christ is not only generated, or born, on the way; he is himself the Way. Consequently, no one can go astray while on the way, for whoever goes astray does so because he leaves the way, and undergoes many labors in order to be brought back to it.

“The Church of Ravenna was indeed situated on the Aemilian Way, but did not have the Aemilian region subject to her, since that region acknowledged the Church of Milan as its mother. But after she received the privilege of a mother and metropolitan, together with the power to give birth, she had a way and made a way, as Chrysologus had said at the beginning of the sermon. Thus the bishoprics situated on the Aemilian Way would not be in error if they obeyed Ravenna, because the privilege was valid and legitimate and had not been taken from Milan by robbery, having been granted through the ordinary channel—namely, by apostolic and imperial authority.

“The likeness is not yet complete between this birth of the bishop of Vicohaventia, consecrated by the metropolitan of Ravenna, and the birth of Christ the Lord from the Mother of God. For in the latter case there intervened the decree of Caesar:

[Col. 0660A] “‘And it came to pass in those days,’ says the Evangelist, ‘that a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be registered. Joseph also went up from Galilee, from the city of Nazareth, into Judaea, to the city of David, which is called Bethlehem, because he was of the house and family of David, to register with Mary, his betrothed wife, who was pregnant. And it came to pass in those days that the days were fulfilled for her to give birth, and she bore her firstborn son.’

“This is what happened in the birth of the Mother of God. But what happened in the birth of the mother of Ravenna? ‘It is pleasing here to say something about the pain: the Lord, in obedience to the decree of Caesar and of a pagan, comes forward; and does some servant still irreverently resist the decree of blessed Peter, the decree of a Christian ruler?’

“In both births, therefore, a decree of Caesar and a promulgated command were involved: there, that of Caesar Augustus; here, that of Valentinian III Augustus. There, the Lord of all obediently and without any delay or resistance complied with the decree and edict of a pagan emperor. Here, it is not the Lord but a servant and subject bishop of Milan who dares, without any reverence, to resist the edict of a Christian emperor, and to resist for a long time, thereby causing anguish and pains to the Church of Ravenna so that she might not give birth.

[Col. 0660B] “This is plainly a matter for sorrow, and for the greatest sorrow, all the more because in granting this privilege of a mother or metropolitan there intervened not only the edict of the emperor, but also the decree of blessed Peter—and the latter ought to be named first, since this prerogative derives its firmness from it as from its first root.

“From this, surely, the archbishops of Ravenna who succeeded Chrysologus could have learned reverence toward the apostolic see, and should not have sounded the trumpet of autocephaly, or independence from the Roman pontiff, while fortifying themselves with Valentinian’s privilege. For in this sermon of Chrysologus attention should have been paid not only to the decree of Caesar, but also to the decree of blessed Peter, and indeed to the decree of Caesar in its proper place.

“From this too those who ridicule Valentinian III’s edict as spurious and reject it must be refuted. The authority of Chrysologus compels every sane person to admit that the privilege of the emperor Valentinian was promulgated, as was also the decree of the supreme pontiff, by which such authority was granted to Ravenna. But since this second document has perished, the first too may perhaps have perished, or may be read in a corrupted form through some addition. Nevertheless, it cannot be denied that there was an imperial edict by which the bishop of Ravenna was constituted archbishop and metropolitan, with authority over the cities situated on the Aemilian Way and formerly subject to the bishop of Milan, who did not contend for this matter without labor and pain, resisting both the decree of blessed Peter and the edict of the emperor Valentinian.

[Col. 0660C] “But at last, victory having been won after so much anguish, Chrysologus was the first to exercise the primary office of the metropolitan by consecrating the bishop of Vicohaventia as a firstborn and ‘son of sorrow’—since a mother experiences greater pain in giving birth to her firstborn than when she gives birth to the others. Thus was the virginal birth; thus was the birth of the firstfruits consecrated.

“It also seems necessary to conclude that Valentinian’s privilege was granted to John of Ravenna, surnamed Angeloptes, the predecessor of Chrysologus, toward the end of his episcopate, so that in this dispute the bishop of Milan died. For after his election Chrysologus, preaching in the metropolitan see, complains in the words we have quoted—and indeed in the present tense: ‘Does some servant still irreverently resist?’ This clearly suggests that, after the victory had been obtained so successfully that Ravenna proceeded to the consecration of the bishop of Vicohaventia, the unwilling bishop of Milan still grumbled, as though he had not yielded; just as, after a judge’s sentence in a case long contested, the defeated adversary commonly continues to complain and mutter.

[Col. 0660D] “But since neither prosperity should be mingled with adversity nor sadness with joys, Chrysologus continues: ‘Setting these matters aside, let us proclaim the joy of today’s offspring.’

“‘Let him who has now been born, who was born first, have the reverence and retain the honor of the firstborn.’ Certainly the see of Ferrara had this distinction: not only was its bishop, called Vicohaventinus, the first among those consecrated by Chrysologus; he was also the firstborn of the metropolitan Church of Ravenna. Hence he could demand from men this reverence and honor as a firstborn.

[Col. 0661A] “‘Marcellinus today, a native offspring, has seized and won all affection.’ The birth of the Mother of God, when she bore Christ, was the Lord’s birth, because the Lord of all was born. The birth of Bishop Marcellinus at his consecration is the birth of a native and a servant. The first birth seized and won all the affection of the Christian people—an affection, I mean, owed to the Lord, who is worshiped with the adoration of *latria*. The birth of Marcellinus seized all the affection that can belong to a native and human offspring. One affection does not displace the other, since they belong to different orders and worship in different ways; nor does affection for the Creator exclude affection for creatures.

“To seize shows force and efficacy; but to win shows that affection is drawn from every heart. The expression ‘native offspring’ seems also to have indicated Marcellinus’s servile condition and humble family of origin, as may be inferred from what follows. But in ecclesiastical ranks and dignities, the splendor of birth and the smoky images of a celebrated household are not considered; rather, the radiance of piety and the ardor of virtue and religion are considered. Therefore, although Marcellinus was of humble birth, just as this did not prevent his consecration, so it did not prevent the joys and full rejoicing of the people.

[Col. 0661B] “‘Sons stand around, relatives are present, the whole kindred gathers, the entire household rejoices, and the innermost chambers of the house themselves exult and rejoice, because today they have been privileged for the first time to see with their eyes and receive in their hands the offspring and child of the holy Mother.’

“Since the eye of the mind and the speaker’s intention look toward two firstborn births, these words should be understood more of Marcellinus’s birth than of the Lord’s, since neither sons nor relatives gathered at the birth of the Mother of God to see and receive the child with their eyes and hands.

[Col. 0661C] “Therefore, by ‘sons’ may be understood the suffragan bishops, who are like the sons of a mother and metropolitan; by ‘relatives,’ the bishops of another province subject to a Roman metropolitan or to another. For not a few prelates gathered at Ravenna, where the emperor and Augusta were present; when they saw this first solemnity and the exercise of the office of a newly created metropolitan, they applauded Marcellinus’s consecration in greater numbers and with greater joy and exultation. Citizens and outsiders alike displayed signs of joy and congratulated Marcellinus.

“Yet we can also explain ‘sons’ as sons actually begotten by Marcellinus, who had previously been married, and ‘relatives’ as his blood relations. Examples are not lacking even in those times of men who, after their wives had died or been separated from them and after they had devoted themselves to a religious life, were promoted to episcopal honors because of their excellence in piety, learning, or merit. Salvianus alone would suffice in Gaul; but in Emilia Severus, the bishop of Ravenna, had preceded him.

[Col. 0661D] “The gathering of sons, relatives, and the whole household and family easily took place in Ravenna itself, the metropolitan city. For it is not the mother who should hasten to the son, but the son to the mother. Thus the holy Mother is the holy Church of Ravenna, the mother of the other Churches subject to her.

“‘The Mother herself—bride, mother, and virgin—marvels with new rejoicing that she has given birth in the very bridal chamber of her bridegroom, in the very chamber of her union.’

“These words cannot be understood of the Mother of God and her virginal birth. They must therefore also be explained of the Church of Ravenna, which is not only a holy mother but also a virgin, having Christ the Lord as her bridegroom, just as the Mother of God had a bridegroom. There is, however, this difference: the Mother of God was not united to her bridegroom in order to give birth to her firstborn—for otherwise she would not have remained a virgin—but so that he might be the witness and guardian of her virginity.

[Col. 0662A] “The Church, however, because she does not give birth carnally but spiritually, needs her bridegroom and his bridal chamber—or rather, their union—in order to give birth to her firstborn. In and through that union she remains ever a virgin while bringing forth children, since at consecration she communicates spiritual gifts from the grace of the Holy Spirit, which is invoked in every operation of the Church.

“The bridegroom’s bridal chamber is clearly the greater Church, and the metropolitan Church. Thus it can also be established from this that Marcellinus’s consecration took place at Ravenna, and that Chrysologus recognized this privilege—that the bishop of Vicohaventia was consecrated in the metropolitan Church—as a new cause for rejoicing.

“But because the names ‘bridal chamber’ and ‘union’ at first sight seem opposed to virginity, the holy orator and pastor resolves the difficulty in this way: ‘But let no one be troubled, let no one be disturbed, by the fact that the bride herself is seen to have given birth in the very bridal chamber: this is not a matter of guilt, but of a conception arising from virginity, since in such an offspring the birth is heavenly, not human; nor is there any place here for sinister suspicion, where the bridegroom himself is held to be the witness and guardian of his bride. Whoever is anxious about the event, let him pursue the greatest example, and let the trembling of what preceded contribute to your caution and protection.’

[Col. 0662B] “This birth, namely, at the consecration of the bishop, is not carnal, nor is the union carnal, but spiritual. Virginity excludes carnal union; therefore, in this generation or birth, the bridegroom who is spiritually united—namely Christ—is the witness and guardian of virginity. We are taught this by the greatest example, the virginal birth of the Mother of God, in which Joseph the bridegroom was the witness and guardian of his bride’s virginity.

“Everyone should therefore be secure that no stain or disgraceful mark intervened here, and that the birth of Marcellinus as a firstborn did not lack a likeness to the virginal birth of the firstborn of the Mother of God.

“‘That Joseph, a husband in name only but a bridegroom in conscience, gazes in agitation and anxiety upon his pregnant bride, because he could neither accuse an innocent woman nor excuse a pregnant woman; silence was unsafe, while speech was dangerous. He admits the matter but does not betray it: an accuser of the innocent, he does not expose the alleged offense. He himself was the testimony of chastity; he was the guardian of modesty. His conduct and life were at a crossroads; his just mind and holy spirit were tormented by divided thought. He perceived the matter, but could not penetrate the mystery, because he could neither accuse her nor defend her before men.

[Col. 0662C] “‘Rightly, then, an angel immediately appeared; rightly, a divine answer at once came to his aid. When human counsel failed, justice did not fail. And what does he say? “Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid.” He had done nothing: what was he afraid of? He was afraid because, although there was no guilt in the deed, there was immense fear in the circumstance. A holy mind is terrified by whatever it does not comprehend.’

“Since the Gospel had been expounded in the part that corresponded to Marcellinus’s consecration, and since many people knew it, Chrysologus—lest he appear too favorably disposed toward his own cause—pauses over the principal matter contained in the Gospel oracles, which he had not abandoned in examining their mysteries, and makes a transition from Marcellinus’s consecration to Joseph, the most holy bridegroom of the Mother of God. By recalling Christ’s bridegroom during the virginal birth of Marcellinus as a firstborn, he strives to dispel suspicion of a carnal union and non-virginal birth, on the grounds that Christ the bridegroom was both the guardian and witness of virginity, just as Joseph had been the witness and guardian of the Virgin’s virginity.

“He therefore describes Joseph’s suspicion without allowing justice to be lost, and describes how that fear was removed by divine intervention. He now returns and concludes with the consecration of the bishop of Vicohaventia.

[Col. 0662D] “‘Beware, therefore, man, of discussing the birth of our mother in such a way, since it is enough that the angel answered: “Do not be afraid to take Mary as your wife; for what has been born in her is of the Holy Spirit.” Happily she gave birth who, by giving birth ever more fully, won the crown and glory of virginity. But this man who has been born for us today has always cast his nets into the sea. Let no one, therefore, wonder if Peter eagerly desired to have a fisherman as his colleague. Pray, then, brothers, that he may be worthy to fish for human beings, he who until now has labored to catch fish for the life of human beings.’

“Returning to the consecration, Chrysologus shows that he is concerned with it alone, and perhaps hints that there would be some who might suspect such a birth was not virginal, since the bishop of Milan was still muttering and still resisting the pontifical and imperial decree.

[Col. 0663C] “Therefore, not without reason, he treats at length the fear of the blessed Joseph and explains fully how that fear was removed from him through the angel’s heavenly message, as if he were saying:

“‘The birth of our mother, the Church of Ravenna, established in the office of mother and metropolitan, is legitimate. Therefore, whoever you are, suspect nothing evil; do not be afraid, whatever Church among the suffragans you may be, that this mother is not genuine, or that any force or fraud intervened against imperial majesty. The Church of Ravenna has won the crown and glory; she has prevailed in a case contested while her opponent protested, and she has happily given birth to this firstborn offspring, Marcellinus, who has been born for us today and who practiced the art of fishing.

[Col. 0663D] “‘Yet this did not make him unworthy of episcopal honors. On the contrary, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, whose see is at Rome, through his successor Sixtus III admitted this fisherman to the episcopate.
