And he who had been called from fishing for fish to fishing for human beings did not disdain to have the fisherman Marcellinus as his colleague, so as to make him likewise a fisher of human beings.

“‘What do I mean by “did not disdain”? Rather, he eagerly desired it and was exceedingly glad when he found in him a likeness of his own calling, which commonly produces joy.’

“From this it seems possible to infer that this first consecration took place after the victory in the dispute with Milan, with the consent of the supreme pontiff, and was thereby made safer and more secure, so that no one would dare to suspect anything evil.

“It may also be explained that Chrysologus is speaking of himself: since he was metropolitan and was also named Peter, he rejoiced at the consecration of a fisherman, having recognized in him the lot of the apostle whose name he bore.

[Col. 0664C] “This, then, is the whole sermon of Chrysologus, with no word omitted, so that the truth proposed may shine forth through the entire context of the sermon: blessed Peter, archbishop of Ravenna, was not indeed the first to shine with this dignity, but he was the first to exercise it in the chief metropolitan office of consecrating the bishops of his province.

“We also have another sermon, 165, on the consecration of Bishop Projectus of Cornelium. Yet it contains nothing similar, nor does it ever suggest pain or anguish in giving birth, or before the mother Church of Ravenna gave birth, as it does not suggest such immense joy when she gave birth. This seems a plainly evident indication that at that time the bishop of Milan had ceased from raising complaints and disturbances, and that Chrysologus was in peaceful possession of the right to consecrate and exercise archiepiscopal functions. Therefore, the sermon delivered at the consecration of the bishop of Vicohaventia unquestionably preceded it in time, although it is later in numerical order.”

.

[Col. 0663A]

## SERMON 176. On the Blind Man.

God, whenever he heals the hopeless diseases of human bodies, reveals so often the power of his divinity; but when, in one and the same illness, he changes the order of his healing, he makes us search more deeply for the reasons why he does so. For to the blind man sitting beside the road he restored sight by command alone; but to another, blind from birth—born not for light but for darkness, one from whom nature had withheld sight, and whose eyes nature itself, which prepares and opens them, had closed and denied—Christ applies mud and, by means of a material ointment, fashions, makes, and provides eyes, [Note: That is, he did not restore eyes to their former light, because the man had never possessed light but had been born blind. MITA.] not healing him (John 9), so that by a hand creating rather than healing he might supply the man with lights from the same source from which he had made the whole man.

But this blind man, whose healing the evangelist Mark reported to us, is cured in such a new manner that he compels everyone to ask why stubborn blindness dares thus to delay before its author, at whose nod, sight, and command illnesses perish, health returns, life arises, death ends, all things stand, and everything dissolves. “Jesus,” he says, “came to Bethsaida, and they brought a blind man to him and begged him to touch him; and taking the blind man by the hand, he led him outside the village” (Mark 8). It was as though he could not cure him in that place, or as though the place’s benefit were needed by the one who had bestowed sight on everyone.

This was Bethsaida, whose faithlessness the Lord reproves when he says: “Woe to you, Chorazin; woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works that were done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes” (Matthew 11). Therefore, taking him by the hand, he leads him out of the house of unbelief; he raises him from his seat of faithlessness, so that before giving sight to his eyes, he might give faith; before restoring health to the body, he might restore it to the mind; before displaying the sign of divine power, he might provide the service of human guidance. [Note: In us we experience nature before God, and grace afterward: for the natural man is created first, and thereafter, through the grace of Christ’s baptism, he is regenerated and reborn as spiritual. MITA.]

They begged him merely to touch the man. But Christ, who does not know how to recoil from the poor and knows how to love the poor, gave the whole of his hand to the poor man; and God offered public service to weakness, so that a human being might not recoil from another human being, and that one who sees might see one who does not see, and, by leading the blind by the hand, might make him ignorant of blindness through the light. Let no one say: “My hand has nothing to give the poor.” Let him give the poor his very hand; it will be more to have given a hand to the poor than a coin, to have provided the poor with a road than to have given him a fragment of bread.

“And he led him outside the village, and spat into his eyes.” By the Lord’s spittle he fills the empty hollows of the eyes; from the divine mouth he gives life-bearing saliva, so that a drop of holy dew might baptize the sinner’s eyes, and forgiveness might open those which guilt had closed. Let no one doubt, therefore, that by divine rain all the dried-up members of mortals can revive, when he sees that a small drop of the Lord’s spittle suddenly raises eyes parched by blindness into the light.

“‘The dead shall arise,’ says Isaiah, ‘and those who are in the tombs shall rise, and those who are on the earth shall rejoice.’ How so? ‘For the dew that is from you is healing for them.’” What rain is to seed, the Lord’s rain is to those who will rise.

“And he laid his hands upon him.” In making, restoring, and shaping the human being, the Lord’s healing hands are always present to humanity. “Your hands,” he says, “made me and fashioned me.”

“And he asked him whether he saw anything.” He asks as a human being; he acts as God. He who sees the hidden things of the earth, who looks into the secrets of the heart, for whom everything concealed is naked, seeks in his work and in the man’s eyes to see, labors to know, and learns by another’s report? Far from it. Rather, he asks so that those present might understand, and those to come might know, that this healing of blindness was not simple but mystical.

Finally, the man who was being healed, while the Lord was questioning him, answered that he had been given not light but a kind of dawn and an emerging brightness: “‘I see,’ he said, ‘people like trees walking about.’” [Note: “From an abundance of crystalline humor,” says Mita.]

With imperfect eyes, forms appear enlarged, appearances are confused, and the very things seen are mistaken, because the eyes do not yet grasp vision itself but still endure the shadow of vision. But why “like trees,” rather than like columns or something else? And why not standing, but walking? Because after Christ’s healing he had seen that human beings passed through this world like trees and did not remain; he immediately saw that human growth was a temporal planting in this life, once Christ had healed him.

Christ’s healing must therefore be repeated, so that perfected eyes may see things that are certain, abiding, and eternal. “Again,” he says, “he laid his hands upon his eyes, and he began to see; and he was restored, so that he saw everything clearly. And he sent him to his house, saying: ‘Go to your house, and if you enter the village, tell no one.’”

Let spiritual understanding now be opened, so that we may recognize who this blind man is, and why he does not come of his own accord but is brought by others; why he is led by Christ’s hand and led outside the village; why he receives sight elsewhere, although he had long endured among his own people the prolonged blindness of himself; why Christ spits into his eyes; why the laying on of the divine hand is repeated; and why, although he is given sight outside the house, he is not permitted to tell his own people what he saw, how he saw it, or through whom he saw it.

Brothers, this blind man is the Jew, who in the Synagogue—that is, in the house of faithlessness—and in the village—that is, in the assembly of the wicked—was held in the blindness of ignorance and sat there oppressed. Hence he did not come to Christ; rather, Christ came to him and took him by the hand, so that he might glory in having been healed by the gift of the one who calls, not by the benefit of the Law, nor by the glory of his own choice.

He leads him outside so that, through the freedom of grace, he may see the light of faith in the Church—he who had seen nothing beneath the veil of the Law. He first lays his hand upon him so that he may see the shadow of the Law passing away; so that he may see priests, scribes, Pharisees, and the whole form of Jewish observance passing by like trees, which, as they belong to time, grow old with time: they are born, grow green, blossom, bear fruit, perish, and vanish.

Again he lays his hand upon him, so that, rising again, he may no longer see what is perishable but what is eternal, and may see whatever belongs to divine light, honor, [Col. 0666B] and glory. Such was the great Paul, one of their own, who fell outside the village and on the road as a Jew, so that he might rise again as a Christian; and who was blinded in the Law (Acts 9), so that he might see in grace, as he himself testifies: “Now we see in a mirror and in an enigma; but then we shall see face to face” (1 Corinthians 13). Then, when what has been buried in death rises in life, and whatever has been sown in dishonor rises in glory.

# APPENDIX

[Col. 0665B]

## Seven Sermons of Saint Peter Chrysologus, Archbishop of Ravenna, formerly rejected as belonging to the holy Father [Note: See above, column 179, the censure of all the sermons.] (C, G, S)*

[Col. 0665C]

## SERMON I. On the Lord’s Prayer

You have received the hearing of faith, dearest brothers; hear the form of the Lord’s Prayer. Christ teaches us to pray briefly, since he wishes quickly to grant what is asked. Or what will he not give to those who ask him, who gave himself to those who did not ask? Or what delay will he make in answering, who so anticipates the prayers of suppliants in dictating their petitions?

Today, what you are about to hear makes the angels amazed, heaven wonder, earth tremble; the flesh cannot bear it, the ear cannot contain it, the mind cannot reach it, the whole creation cannot sustain it. I do not dare to speak, yet I cannot remain silent. May God grant that you can hear and that I can speak.

What is more dreadful: that God gave himself to the earth, or that he gives you to heaven; that he himself enters into fellowship with flesh, or that he makes you enter into fellowship with divinity; that he himself took on death, or that he takes you back from death; that he is born himself in your servitude, or that he begets you for himself as free children; that he assumes your poverty, or that he makes you his heirs, coheirs with his only Son?

Certainly more terrifying is that earth is transferred into heaven, that the human being is changed into divinity, and that the condition of servitude receives the rights of dominion. Yet although this is fearful, because the matter concerns not the one who speaks but the one who commands, let us approach, little children, where love calls, affection draws, and devotion invites. Let the heart feel God as Father; let the voice resound, the tongue speak, and the spirit cry out. Let everything within you answer to grace, not fear, because he has changed the judge into a Father: he wished to be loved, not feared.

### “Our Father who are in heaven” (Matthew 5:9; Luke 11:2)

When you say this, do not understand it as though he were not on earth; do not take it as though he were enclosed in a place, he who encloses all things. Rather, understand that he has a nature from heaven, whose Father is regarded as being in heaven. And act so that, by living holily, you may answer the holy Father. He proves himself a son of God who is not darkened by human vices but shines with divine virtues.

### “Hallowed be your name”

We are reckoned according to the nature and name of the one whose kind we are. We therefore ask that the name which is holy in and of itself may be hallowed in us; for God’s name is either honored by our conduct or blasphemed by our actions. Hear the Apostle saying: “The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you” (Romans 2:24).

### “Your kingdom come”

And when has God not reigned? We ask, therefore, that the one who has reigned for himself may always reign in us, so that we too may be able to reign in him. The devil reigned, sin reigned, death reigned, and mortality was long held captive. We therefore ask that, when God reigns, the devil may perish, sin may fail, death may die, captivity may itself be taken captive, and we, set free, may reign forever in life.

### “Your will be done, as in heaven so on earth”

This is the kingdom of God: when in heaven and on earth God’s will alone is done, when God lives, acts, reigns, and is wholly present in all human beings, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying, “that God may be all in all in us” (1 Corinthians 15). [Note: In this place we deleted the word *est* (“is”), which disturbed the sentence before the word *Deus* (“God”). Below, where *qui nos nomine* occurs, since we understood that something was missing, we added points to show the reader that this had not escaped us.]

### “Give us today our daily bread”

He who gave himself to us as Father, who adopted us as sons, who made us coheirs with himself, who exalted us by his … name, who endowed us with his honor and kingdom—he himself commanded us to ask for daily bread. In the kingdom of heaven, what does human poverty seek among divine gifts? Does not such a good, loving, and generous Father grant bread to his children when asked? And where is the saying: “Do not be anxious about what you will eat, or what you will drink, or what you will wear” (Matthew 6:31)?

The Father commands what he forbids us to worry about. What do we understand? The heavenly Father urges us to ask for the heavenly bread of the heavenly Son. He himself said: “I am the bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:51). He is the bread that, sown in the Virgin, fermented in flesh, prepared in suffering, baked in the furnace of the tomb, and stored in the churches, is brought to the altars and daily supplies the faithful with heavenly food.

### “And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors”

Human being, you cannot be without sin; and if you wish always to be forgiven, forgive everything always. As much as you wish to be forgiven, forgive that much. As often as you wish to be forgiven, forgive that often; indeed, because you wish everything to be forgiven you, forgive everything. Human being, understand that by forgiving others you have granted yourself pardon.

### “And do not lead us into temptation”

For in this world life itself is temptation. “Temptation is the life of a human being” (John 7:1). We ask that he not leave us to our own judgment, but that in every action he constrain us with paternal compassion and strengthen us on the path of life with heavenly moderation.

### “But deliver us from evil”

From what evil? From the devil, of course, since all evil comes from him. We ask to be delivered from evil, because one who has not been without evil cannot enjoy the good. If those not yet born, still in the womb, ask for bread and seek the kingdom, why is there dispute over the mystery that the Son of God is always in the Father’s mystery, and that the Son of God has been in God the Father? How is this treated by human reasoning? Divinity must not, must not, be assessed in a human manner.

You have heard “God”: think nothing earthly, nothing human. You have heard “the Father of Christ”: believe this according to substance. You have heard “your Father”: believe this according to grace. He has always possessed the status of Son; now he has given himself to be Son. Know yourself, therefore, to be a son in this way, and do not fail to know yourself to be a servant. Hear that you have been restored to the likeness of Christ in such a way that you always recognize yourself as subject to Christ.

## SERMON II. On the Same Subject

Mortal condition, earthly structure, muddy substance, worn down by the uncertain labor of life’s burdens and death, consumed by punishments, a nature subjected to the rottenness of dust—cannot grasp and fears to believe what it is compelled to confess today. Human frailty cannot discover the greatness of such gifts, [Note: These homilies are riddled with as many corruptions as even the most perceptive person could not remove by conjecture. Therefore let no reader expect anything here to be entirely emended—I would not wish that. We did restore quite a few passages that were disgracefully corrupt, but we did not even attempt to restore them all, for there are some that cannot be corrected without the aid of a manuscript codex. Here I read: “such great grace of God, of promised gifts, …” Below we printed *auditu* (“by hearing”), where *auditus* (“hearing”) stood; shortly afterward *conservum* (“fellow servant”), where *conversum* (“converted”) had been read. The rest seems to me to be read as follows: “he found and heard God the Father.” Nor because …]

of the greatness of our neighbors, or of the abundance of gifts. I think that the prophet foresaw this mystery with the insight of his mind when, shaken by such fear and agitated by hearing of it, he said: “Lord, I heard your report, and I was afraid; I considered your works and trembled” (Habakkuk 3:2).

He feared the report, not because the great prophet had then heard the Lord, but because the servant then found his Lord to be his fellow servant and heard him admitted to a share; [Col. 0668C] or because, contemplating the structure of this world harmonized from elements so discordant with one another, he trembled. But because he considered such great compassion shown toward him, he was then shaken by the trembling and fear of wonder. “I considered,” he says, “your works and trembled.” He trembled to find himself adopted as a son when he had lost the confidence of servitude.

Finally, so that you may know that the prophet then received by heavenly hearing the affection of this prayer, which divinity today reveals and pours into you, observe what he said when released, so to speak, by fear of this gift: “I kept watch over myself,” he says, “and my belly trembled at the voice of the supplication of my lips” (the same, verse 16).

After he had felt such great generosity in the divine gift, he kept watch over himself, lest he again find himself an enemy, an adversary, or a robber in paradise. He becomes more vigilant, more attentive as his own guardian, having realized after the loss of so great a thing that he had found a heavenly treasure, as Paul says: “We carry this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Corinthians 4:7).

“I kept watch over myself, and my belly trembled.” By “the belly of the heart” the prophet names the heart’s inner parts, because just as the belly is nourished and filled by food, so the heart is nourished and filled by perceptions. [Note: No sane person will deny that the earlier word was rightly added. Immediately afterward, where it reads “ex hoc est exhortaturus” (“from this he will exhort”), the most disgraceful error of the copyist seems capable of being corrected as follows: “he recoils from the supplication”?]

“And my belly trembled at the voice of the supplication of my lips.” If the understanding of the heart poured a voice into the mouth and had given words to the lips, why did he tremble at his prayers, his desires, and his … from this he will exhort? He trembled because he was speaking not by the prompting of his own heart but by the utterance of the divine Spirit.

Hear Paul saying: “God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father’” (Galatians 4:6). When he transmitted this sound inwardly, he marveled that he had deserved so much, and all the inward parts of the human being trembled. He rightly added: “And trembling entered my bones,” because the prophet’s own inward parts were being disturbed; “and beneath me,” he says, “my strength was shaken.”

What does “beneath me” mean? The one and same human being, once again lifted up by grace, lay beneath his former nature, and earthly strength could not sustain heavenly strength. [Col. 0669B] Mount Zion smoked when God descended onto the mountain to give the Law; what would flesh do when God descended into flesh?

The Father came to bestow the grace of flesh, because the human being could not bear God, nor the servant his Lord. And because the one who said, “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Psalm 80:11), is faithful in his words, open your mouths now, so that he himself may fill them with such a prayer and such a cry.

Where are those who distrust God’s promise? Behold how quickly the confession of faith has been rewarded. As soon as you confessed the Father of the only Son to be God, you yourself were adopted as a son by God the Father, so that you might be an heir of heaven, although you had been regarded as an exile from paradise and from the earth. And therefore now you call out: “Our Father who are in heaven.”

For once you had a father who dissolved you into mud, who led and dragged you to the prison of hell. Let him know nothing of earth, ignore the love of flesh, seek no father of dust, and permit no vice to have authority over him who seeks from God the Father a heavenly restoration to nature, so that he who believes himself a son of God in conduct, life, character, and integrity may answer a lineage so great, lest, descending again to earthly things, he direct himself toward an offense against so great a parent.

### “Hallowed be your name”

If the name of Christ gives sight to the blind, restores the power of walking to the lame, gives health to those exhausted by various illness, life to the dead, and sanctifies you, human being, and the whole creation, how do you pray and plead for the sanctity of that very name? Because you have been called a Christian by Christ, you therefore beseech him that the prerogative of so great a name may be strengthened in you by the merits that follow.

### “Your kingdom come”

He himself commands devotion, demands desires, and seeks vows—the one who holds the life of his coming in his own power. That soldier is faithful who thirsts for the presence of his king and seeks and longs for the triumphs of so great a kingdom. But here you ask that he come to you and in you as king—the one in whom the devil held a stronghold, death held dominion, and hell long exercised and possessed power. Let us therefore pray, dearest ones, that Christ may always reign in his soldier, and that the soldier may always triumph in his king.

[Col. 0670A]

### “Your will be done, as in heaven so on earth”

Blessed is that day which joins, unites, and makes equal the will of earthly things with heavenly things, so that among different substances there may be one and the same will. This is faithful peace, unshaken concord, enduring grace: because within the order of the one Lord, a household distributed among diverse wills is found to be one and the same in its understanding.

### “Give us today our daily bread”

After the heavenly kingdom, who would ask for temporal bread? Yet it is daily bread. And for this reason he wishes us to ask in the sacrament of his body for the bread of the journey, so that from here we may reach the everlasting day and Christ’s own table, and so that from the place where we have received a taste here, we may there receive the fullness of food and complete satiety.

### “And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors”

Whoever asks in this way but does not release debts accuses himself by the very thing for which he prays. He asks that only as much be given and forgiven him as he himself forgives, and by granting according to his pleasure he invites God into such a pact: let as much be rendered to him as he himself has granted to another.

Debts must be forgiven, brothers—not merely financial debts, but everything belonging to matters, faults, and crimes into which a human being can fall. When another falls into these against you, forgive him. The one who willingly forgives the sinner faithfully asks forgiveness for his own sin.

### “And do not lead us into temptation”

We are compelled, brothers, to ask this in many ways, lest frailty, daring too much and presumptuously relying on itself, gathering none of its own strength in the conflict, fall through poor caution; and lest God, offended, then hand over to temptations those whom he abandons.

### “But deliver us from evil”

He has a sufficiently humble opinion of himself who begs to be delivered from evil by God. Sign yourselves. Understand, little children, how great is the glory and power of the perfected and the strong, when such power is revealed in conception itself and such majesty in birth.

Not yet born, he calls upon the Father, asks for holiness, and seeks the kingdom. He gives laws to earth, makes earthly wills equal to heavenly ones, and, already devoted, demands provisions for future labors: “Give us,” he says, “today our daily bread.”

Blessed are you who have begun to conquer before the battle, to triumph before living, to reach the Father’s embrace and the Father’s storehouse before reaching the mother’s embrace; to seize the nourishment of the flock before taking in the whole supply of milk; to sound forth victory with a joyful cry, to answer with a wail before reaching the cradle … truly, as the Apostle said, “the weakness of God is stronger than human beings” (1 Corinthians 1:25).

But who could recount the mystery of so great a conception, where a virgin mother gives birth daily to the world and does not leave descendants for labor, but sends them ahead from an earthly germ to glory?

## SERMON III. On the Same Subject

Everything that is reported as spoken and done by divine power is miraculous, astonishing, and dreadful to mortals; it is even terrifying to the heavenly beings themselves. But nothing so amazes heaven, makes earth tremble, or causes the whole creation to shudder as what you are about to hear from us today.

A servant dares to call the Lord “Father”; the accused names his judge “begetter”; an earthly condition adopts itself by its own voice as a son; one who has lost earthly things considers himself an heir of divinity. Yet we dare because the speaker’s presumption is absent wherever the authority of the one commanding is present. For he himself wished you to say this today, who today taught us to pray in this way.

And what wonder is it if he then consecrated human beings as sons of God, when he gave and adapted himself to human beings as a son? He transferred the nature of flesh into the divine when he brought divinity into human nature. Then he made the human being his coheir in heavenly things, when he made himself a participant in earthly things.

Or what love, gift, or honor could he deny to the human being who assumed everything that belonged to the human being—even sin and death? Or how will he not have the human being share in his prosperity, when in adversity he made himself the human being’s companion?

Human being, return to God, so loved by God; give your whole self to his glory, since he led his whole self, for your sake, into your injury. And confidently call “Father” the one whom, with such love, you prove, feel, and understand to be your begetter. [Note: It had been printed *tum probas* (“then you prove”). Below, in the verse “and forgive,” we printed *si vis ipse* (“if you yourself wish”), where *suis ipse* (“with his own … himself”) had been read. Near the end we likewise wrote “so that the prayers with which,” where it had previously been printed “so that by the prayers with which.” Immediately afterward Acherius did not understand “his author,” when the interpreter conjectured that it should be read “by the Father the Son,” where the reading is “the Father, through the interpreter.”]

### “Our Father who are in heaven”

Let no one wonder that one not yet born calls upon the Father. Things that are to be born are born to God; future things have become accomplished things for God. “He made,” it says, “the things that will be” (Ecclesiasticus 16:10).

Hence John felt his author while still in the womb, and he who did not know life stands forth as a messenger to his mother. Hence Jacob is read to have fought before he was born and began to triumph before he lived. Hence those who are not yet themselves are already present to God, since you were chosen before the foundation of the world.

“Our Father who are in heaven.” This does not mean that he is not on earth, but that through this offspring you may know yourself to have a heavenly origin. And if you confess yourself to be a son of God, live as a son of God, so that by conduct, life, and virtues you may be able to answer such a begetter.

### “Hallowed be your name”

Because you have been called a Christian by Christ, you ask that the prerogative of so great a name may be hallowed in you, since the name of God, holy in itself and for himself, is either hallowed in us by our conduct or blasphemed among the Gentiles by our conduct.

[Col. 0671D]

### “Your kingdom come”

He himself says: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17:21). If it is within us, why do we pray that it may come? It is in faith, in hope, and in expectation; but we pray that it may now come. Let it come to us—not to him who always reigns with his Father and always reigns in the Father—but let it come to us: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:34).

We say, “Your kingdom come,” so that God may reign in us in such a way that death may cease to reign in us, and sin may cease to reign. “Death reigned,” he says, “from Adam to Moses” (Romans 5:14). And elsewhere: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body” (the same, verse 15).

### “Your will be done, as in heaven so on earth”

Now on earth many things happen according to the devil’s will, according to the wickedness of the world, and according to the will of the flesh. But in heaven nothing is done except the Lord’s will. We therefore ask that, once the devil has been destroyed, the world renewed, the body changed, the dominion of death destroyed, and the rule of sin abolished, there may be one and the same will of God in heaven and on earth, in God and in human beings.

### “Give us today our daily bread”

After the heavenly kingdom, we are not commanded to ask for earthly bread, since he himself forbade it when he said: “Do not be anxious about what you will eat or what you will drink” (Matthew 6:13). But because he himself is the bread that came down from heaven (John 6:50), we ask and pray that we may receive for the nourishment of body and mind in eternity that very bread which we take daily—that is, continually.

### “And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors”

By saying this, human being, you have established the measure of indulgence and the limit of forgiveness. You have given it to yourself, since you ask the Lord to grant you as much as you yourself have forgiven your fellow servant. Therefore forgive the one who has sinned against you completely, if you yourself wish to owe the Lord nothing for your sins. In the other person, forgive yourself, if you yourself wish to avoid the sentence of the judge.

### “And do not lead us into temptation”

God tempts no one, as it is written; but he is said to tempt when he abandons those who stubbornly proceed to the snares of temptations. Thus Adam fell into the tempter’s ambush when he abandoned the commands of his creator.

But from where and by whom the human being is tempted he revealed when he said: “But deliver us from evil”—that is, from the devil, who is both the author and origin of every evil. The devil was heavenly by nature, but now he is spiritual wickedness; older than the world, worn smooth by the practice of harming, and most skilled in the art of injuring. Hence he is called not merely “evil” but “the Evil One,” from whom everything evil comes.

Therefore the human being, bound by carnal chains, cannot be freed by his own powers. We must ask that God deliver us from the devil, for he gave Christ to the earth so that Christ might conquer the devil. Let the human being cry out—let him cry out to God: “Deliver us from evil,” so that from so great an evil we may be freed by Christ alone as victor.

[Col. 0672D]

“Our Father who are in heaven.” The one whom you must entreat himself granted, in very few words, the theme of prayer, the subject of petition, and the rule of supplication, so that from this you may derive the meaning of asking, gain understanding of petitioning, gather the measure of obtaining, and, through this brief instruction in prayer, receive the most extensive discipline of praying.

At the same time, because the king himself undertook the office of advocate for the judgment of love, he dictated the prayers to which he himself would respond. All hesitation about winning favor has been removed when the one who is invoked is read in the prayers themselves. Fear has no place where a son desires, through the Father as interpreter, to obtain holy things.

## SERMON IV. On the Same Subject

Dearest brothers, the one who gave you faith also taught you to pray, and fitted the entire form of petition into a few words, because when a son asks the Father, he does not labor over many prayers. For just as necessity compels the begotten to ask, so love urges the begetter to give.

The Father, therefore, who grants willingly, shows not so much that he should be asked as what should be asked, so that the Son may please him by asking for what is right, whereas he might displease him by asking for what is foolish. Hear the Father, and believe already that you are sons, so that you may obtain without hesitation whatever you ask.

What faith is worth, what belief can accomplish, and how great a confession is, is shown in us today. Behold the threefold confession of the Trinity: it has lifted you, an offspring from earthly servitude, into heavenly birth. Behold the faith that confessed God as Father: today it sought God the Father for you. Behold the voice that confessed the Son of God: it adopted you as sons of God. Behold the belief that proclaimed God the Spirit: it changed you from the mortal substance of flesh into the living substance of the Spirit.

Who can be found worthy to assert such great compassion? God the Father deigns to make human beings heirs; God the Son does not disdain to make little servants coheirs; God the Spirit receives flesh as a companion of divinity by right of dominion in the heavens, as the Apostle proves when he says: “Or do you not know that we shall judge angels?” (1 Corinthians 6:3). [Note: Thus we printed *vocate* (“call”), where *vocat* (“he calls”) stood. Immediately afterward, in the earlier edition: “who is heavenly.”]

Therefore call the Lord “Father,” and believe that you, although not yet born, are already designated as sons. Take care that your life be heavenly, that your conduct be divine, and that the whole form of divinity be displayed in you as a son. For the heavenly Father enriches with divine gifts sons who answer to their lineage, but recalls those who degenerate to penal servitude.

### “Our Father who are in heaven”

Conscience would succumb in little servants and earthly condition would be dissolved unless the authority of the Father himself and the Spirit of the Son himself stirred us to this cry. “God sent,” he says, “the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father’” (Galatians 4:6).

The mind grows weary and the flesh fails before divine things unless God himself fulfills what he commands to be done, the one who commands it. When has mortality dared to call upon the Father, except now, when human beings on earth are animated by heavenly power?

“Our Father who are in heaven.” Human being, what have you in common with earthly things, since you confess that your origin is in heaven? Therefore display a heavenly life in your earthly dwelling. For if earthly thought has done anything within you, you have brought a stain upon heaven and an offense upon your heavenly lineage.

### “Hallowed be your name”

We do not ask that God hallow his own name, which by its holiness saves and sanctifies the whole creation. Brothers, this is the name before which the heavenly powers tremble, which they receive in fearful service; this is the name that puts demons to flight; this alone is the name that releases souls held captive by the devil’s ferocity; this is the name that gives salvation to a ruined world.

But we ask that God’s name be hallowed in us by our conduct. When we act well, God’s name is blessed through us; when we act badly, it is blasphemed through us. Hear the Apostle saying: “The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles” (Romans 2:24). We ask, therefore—we ask—that, insofar as God’s name is holy, we may deserve to possess his holiness in our conduct.

### “Your kingdom come”

Although Christ’s kingdom has always existed, we now ask that it come. And where is that kingdom of God? “It is within us.” It is within us by faith, but we implore that it may come in reality.

Brothers, when the devil, through various kinds of wickedness and manifold arts of deception, distorts the appearance of things, confuses human senses and morals, rages, raves through sacrilegious idols, deceives through omens, lies through divination, misleads by signs, mocks through arts, occupies through spectacles, besieges through vices, wounds through sins, injures through crimes, and casts down through despair, he delays Christ’s kingdom and keeps it away from us.

We therefore ask that the time may come when, with the author of such great evil destroyed, the entire world and the whole creation may reign and triumph wholly for the glory of Christ alone, and that what follows may be fulfilled:

### “As in heaven, so on earth”

Let there be one will of the Lord: earth; heaven; life—God; time—eternity; homeland—rest; wealth—innocence; honor—immortality; [Note: I do not sufficiently understand what “fury—chastity” means, nor do I think this passage is adequately emended if it is read “luxury—chastity.”] fury—chastity; God—everything.

He added: “Give us this day our daily bread.” [Col. 0674C] After the fatherhood of God, after the holiness of the divine name, after the kingdom of heaven, we are commanded to ask for daily bread. Christ is not subject to forgetfulness; Christ does not command anything contrary to his commandments. He himself says: “Do not be anxious about what you shall eat or what you shall drink” (Matt. 6:31). But since there is a bread that has descended from heaven, which has been ground into the form of law and grace, which has been prepared in the flour of the cross, which has been prepared through the suffering of the cross, which has been fermented with the great sacrament of piety, which has raised up from the tomb the leavening of the dough, which, when it was [perhaps: “cooked”] with the heat of its divinity, itself baked the furnace of hell, which is brought daily to the Church’s table as heavenly food [Note: In the earlier edition, *quotidianis* (“daily,” plural). Below, therefore, I read *unum* (“one”); accordingly I now read *ergo* (“therefore”).], which is broken for the remission of sins, which nourishes and feeds those who eat it unto everlasting life—we ask that this bread be given to us daily, until on that day we may enjoy it forever.

“And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” Man, the power of forgiveness lies with you; its indulgence is in your hands; you have been appointed the author of your own remission. You ask forgiveness freely, while you refuse to forgive another. Man, you yourself have become the measure of mercy for yourself: show as much mercy as you ask for.

[Col. 0675A]

“And do not lead us into temptation.” Temptation, brothers, is deceptive in appearance: it prospers amid adversity, conceals adversity amid prosperity, and leads human ignorance into deceitful falls. Therefore we ask that, when sins drive us forward, we may not fall into the pits of temptations. The Lord is said to lead us into them when, as we run toward crimes, he abandons us.

“But deliver us from evil.” Here “evil” designates the author of evil, that is, the devil. Therefore we ask for one thing: that by this gift we may be freed from all evils together with the evil one who is their author.

“Our Father who art in heaven.” Let no one be surprised, when he proclaims himself a son, that he remains in the condition of a servant. Today you have been designated for divine sonship [Note: Or “taken up”? It seems so to me; and below, where *sed promissori* (“but to the promiser”) is read, I think that, with no intelligible sense, one ought to read *se promittenti* (“to him who promises”).]; know that you have not yet attained the hope—or the reality. Hear the apostle: “You have been saved in hope; but hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Rom. 8:24). Today is the day of adoption; today is the time of promise. Hear, believe, and wait: believe your creditor, who has believed in you as his debtor; wait a little while for him to come, since he endured you for so long so that you might come; grant him a delay—but to the promiser, who has already forgiven you whatever debt you owed.

So that you who are wearied by hope in God may live by faith. [Note: This too is corrupt, but in such a way that it cannot be restored without the help of a manuscript. Below, *ut haeredem*, Acherius rightly conjectured *ut haereditatem* (“as an inheritance”).] A farmer would never sow while exhausted if he did not hope in due season for the fruit of his labor; a traveler would not undertake the labor of a long journey unless he believed that he would reach his destination; a sailor would not enter the uncertainties of the sea if he did not reckon that the dangers would be compensated by the profits to follow; a soldier would not spend all the years of his youth amid dangers if he did not hope for the richest honors of old age; a son would not endure the period of his father’s rule if he did not hope to become heir to his father’s property. And you, if you now believe that you are a son of God, say with the prophet: “Wait for the Lord; act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened; wait for the Lord” (Ps. XVI, 20). Wait to become God’s heir through the faith of expectation, and attain it through the strength of patience. Hear the apostle: “We are children of God, but it has not yet appeared what we shall be. When he appears, we shall be like him” (1 John 3:2). And again: “Our life is hidden with Christ; when Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear in glory” (Col. 3:3). Brothers, blessed are the children of God, because they will possess the inheritance of all things and will not experience the times of mourning at the passing of the Father.

[Col. 0675D]

## SERMON V. On the same subject

What I am now about to say with great trembling, what you are now about to hear—or rather, what you are about to invoke with terror—the angels marvel at, the heavenly powers fear, heaven cannot contain, the sun does not see, earth does not sustain, and the whole of creation cannot comprehend. What can mortal breast do in the face of these things? What can the feeble human mind do? What can the narrowness of human perception do before this? What can the breath of the human voice do? What can the human tongue, soon to fall silent, do before this?

When Paul had invisibly seen this, he disclosed it without disclosing it, saying: “Eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2:9). When Isaiah had scarcely begun to receive this through hearing, he doubted whether a human being could yet attain it, saying to the hearing of all: “Lord, who has believed our report?” (Isa. 53:1). When Jeremiah had conceived it through divine hearing, he endured the birth-pangs of heavenly perceptions, crying: “My belly, my belly! I am in pain, and the senses of my heart are troubled” (Jer. 4:19). Habakkuk proclaimed this under the breath of the divine Spirit when he said: “He watched over me, and my belly trembled at the voice of the prayer of my lips; trembling entered my bones, and beneath me my strength was shaken” (Hab. 3:16). Raised up by the power of God, he perceived that his own strength had fallen beneath him.

It would take too long to pursue and enumerate the fears of the saints concerning this mystery; time does not permit me to enumerate them while speaking of this fear, and the force of the heavenly birth cannot delay those coming to birth. Therefore I speak, and while you are still in the womb I address you with an inward voice; I warn you beforehand with prudent exhortation: before you see the mother, call upon her Father; before the mother’s caresses, stretch yourselves and hasten toward the Father’s kingdom; reach the Father’s bread before you hang at the mother’s breasts. Nor should the need of the mother or the periods of age claim anything for themselves in you, but in you may everything answer to the divine Father and everything belonging to the heavenly Father respond and hasten to meet the author. [Note: Anyone can readily understand that this passage is badly corrupt. We remedy it as follows: “let everything answer to the divine Father, let everything belonging to the heavenly Father respond, and let it hasten to meet the author.” In what follows, “From this it is that, etc.,” there is also some corruption, which others may perhaps correct.]

“Our Father who art in heaven.” This is what I was trembling to utter; this is what the condition of their own servitude allowed neither the heavenly nor the earthly to suspect: that such an exchange could suddenly arise between heaven and earth, flesh and God, that God might be changed into man, man into God, the Lord into a servant, and the servant into a son, and that an ineffable and everlasting kinship of divinity and humanity might come to be.

The condescension of the Divinity toward us is so great that creation cannot know what it ought chiefly to marvel at: whether that God humbled himself to our servitude, or that he snatched us up to the dignity of his divinity. Hence it is that man—man who has also been divinely worshipped—is now inflamed by so great a love of his own; hence it is that, while still in the womb, he adopts himself as a son through your voice [lacuna]

O you blessed ones, to whom it has been granted to rule before being born, to reign before living, to reach the glory of God the Father before recognizing the lowliness of your own lineage. Blessed Church, a happy mother, who looks upon you as such and, while remaining a virgin, marvels that she has borne so many of you and borne you in such a manner.

In former times this birth was indicated by preceding examples. [Col. 0677A] Hence Jacob and Esau, twins in the womb, contend for the honor of primacy; they delay birth and do not wish to see the light before they conquer. Hence John rejoices and meets his creator from his mother’s womb before he emerges. [Note: In the earlier edition, *Joanne exsultante* (“with John rejoicing”), wrongly. Immediately below, where *Deus sua sobole* (“God with his offspring”) stands, I read *Deo destinata soboles* (“offspring destined for God”).] Human pledges likewise serve God in advance of being known to their parents, in advance of living in the world.

What wonder if the Church [bears] divine offspring, if God, while his offspring is still in the womb, already acknowledges that it is of heavenly stock: “Our Father who art in heaven”? Astonishment arises: Christ, from the breast of God the Father, calls [her] mother and acknowledges [her] on earth; and man, from his mother’s womb, calls the Father and confesses him in heaven: “Our Father who art in heaven.” To what heights, man, has grace suddenly raised you? To what heights has heavenly grace snatched you? To what heights has heavenly nature snatched you, so that, while still placed in flesh and on earth, you no longer knew either flesh or earth when saying: “Our Father who art in heaven”? Therefore, whoever confesses and believes that he is the son of so great a Father should answer the lineage with his life, the Father with his conduct, and assert by mind and action that he has attained what is heavenly by nature.

“May your name be sanctified.” Since we have begun to be of his lineage, we are certainly reckoned by his name also. Therefore we ask that the sanctification of that name may remain in us—the honor and prerogative of the name that the majesty of so great a begetter has exalted in this way.

“May your kingdom come.” We ask this of the one whose kingdom is never absent and never has been absent; indeed, he is himself his own kingdom and contains in himself the whole power of the kingdom. But because he wishes us to attain the promised glory of his kingdom, he urges us to seek it with all our prayers and wants us to long for it with all our minds. For how rash is he who argues about lineage? He is like fire that does not burn, yet seethes, when he fixes his attention upon the promise and presses onward toward the kingdom. [Note: I restore this entire passage as follows: “He who argues about lineage is fire that does not burn; he seethes.” Below, where *tunc autem Dei* is read, I read *coelum, cum Dei* (“heaven, when God’s …”).]

“Your will be done, as in heaven so on earth.” Then all is already heaven; then the mind of God is one in all; then all are in Christ and Christ is in all, when all perceive and do the will of God alone; then all are one—indeed, one is all—when one Spirit of God lives in all.

“Give us this day our daily bread.” As in the psalm: “Blessed is the Lord day by day” (Ps. LXVII, 22), so here: “Give us this day our daily bread.” We call it continual daily bread. That bread is continual which has descended from heaven: “I am the bread that came down from heaven.” Therefore that bread is the bread of perfect blessedness. “Today”—that is, in the present—to live already by the food of that bread whose perpetuity, which is “daily,” will fatten us in the future.

“And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” From the breast of the one who prays, a fountain of forgiveness flows; whatever of compassion overflows and pours itself into another will flow back toward forgiveness, when one forgives himself as much as he has forgiven another. [Note: Perhaps *exhibebit* (“will show”)? If anyone maintains that this author uses the verb *exuberare* (“to overflow”), I shall not object, but I would at least prefer him to read *exuberabit* (“will overflow”). Below: *praevia et amara* (“preceding and bitter”); I would prefer *praevia mali* or *malorum* (“the precursor of evil” or “of evils”).] “Forgive us our debts as we also forgive our debtors.” A merciful person can do enough—a person who contends with God in compassion, desiring that as much be given to him as he has given, and as much forgiven as he has forgiven. Man, let forgiveness always be in your breast, if you do not wish to fear crimes.

“And do not lead us into temptation.” These words require no interpretation, because temptation is the devil’s preceding and bitter servant. Yet as long as this fragile being is contained in the body, it necessarily prays that neither an entrance to temptation be opened against us nor access be granted to the devil.

“But deliver us from evil.” May our Lord Jesus Christ himself deliver us from evil and lead us to every good, God who lives and reigns now and forever, through endless ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0678B]

[Note: This appears as no. 73 in the appendix to the works of St. Augustine, vol. V.]

## SERMON VI. On the words of the Gospel of Matthew 17: “This kind is driven out by nothing except prayer and fasting.”

We must certainly retain the weapons that the Lord has shown us against the wickedness of demons. “This kind,” he says, “is driven out by nothing except prayer and fasting” (Matt. 17:20). When these are practiced with full faith, they constitute piety. Piety, moreover, is useful for all things, holding the promise of the present life and of the future life (1 Tim. 4:8).

Let us therefore profitably examine the fruits of prayer and fasting, since these themselves are weapons against wicked thoughts. Fasting purifies the mind, lifts up the understanding, and subjects the flesh to the spirit. Fasting makes the heart contrite and humbled, and God does not despise such a heart. Fasting disperses the clouds of desire, extinguishes the fires of lust, and kindles the true light of chastity. Fasting does not love verbosity; it judges the excess of riches, despises pride, commends humility, and enables a person to understand himself as he is—weak and fragile. And while he thus understands himself to be feeble, he more readily seeks and receives the help of God’s power; he seeks it through frequent prayers and supplications.

Prayer is indeed the refreshment of fasting and summons the grace of the Holy Spirit. Prayer softens hardness of heart, moderates austerity, and sweetens fasting. For just as refreshment is not complete without drink, so fasting cannot perfectly nourish the soul without prayer. What is prayer, moreover, except the ascent of the soul from earthly things to heavenly things, the seeking of what is above, the desire for invisible realities? Let the discord of worldly customs, by which the human mind is daily oppressed, depart. Prayer is union with the Holy Spirit—provided that the mind is intent in prayer—as the prophet cries: “My soul thirsted for you; how manifoldly my flesh longs for you” (Ps. 63:2). What one ought to thirst for follows: “that he may see your power” (ibid., 3).

Believe me: if a human soul of earthly substance thirsts fully to see the full power of God, and does not conceal its desire through weariness, it will be filled with spiritual fat and richness; and, thirsting for that visitation of God, it will cry out in its own understanding with faith: “My soul clung after you; your right hand received me” (ibid., 9).

Fasting removes sluggishness and takes away bodily impediments from the mind. Persevering prayer, however, joins one to God, and thus, rejoicing to stand before the Lord, one glories in it. When the soul clings to the Lord, it begins to possess security and freedom; it endures neither terrors nor fears. Having received so great a protection from the right hand of God, how could it be harmed by any power, as it is written, that no one snatches it from the hand of the Father (John X, 19)? This is what fasting provides; this is what prayer provides.

[Note: This appears as no. 97 in the appendix to the works of St. Augustine at the end of vol. V, where a fuller version is also repeated from the Royal manuscript and the Colbert manuscript. For the convenience of readers, lest anything seem lacking in this latest edition, the booksellers decided to insert it here.

“This is the Lord’s saying: ‘I give you my peace; I leave you my peace’” (John 14:27). Since we are about to speak of peace, let us first hear what benefits peace possesses. Peace is serenity of mind, tranquility of soul, simplicity of heart, the bond of love, and fellowship in charity. It is peace that removes hostilities, restrains wars, suppresses anger, tramples the proud, loves the humble, calms disagreements, reconciles enemies, and is pleasing to all. It does not seek what belongs to another; it counts nothing as its own. It teaches one to love what it does not know how to hate. It does not know how to exalt itself or be puffed up; it is humble toward all and gentle toward all. In peace there is rest; in peace there is tranquility.

Peace that is practiced in a Christian is perfected in Christ. Whoever loves it is an heir of God; whoever despises it is a rebel against Christ. For when the Lord Christ returned to the Father, he left his worshipers an inherited good—that is, his peace—saying: ‘I give you my peace; I leave you my peace.’ Whoever has received this peace should hold it; whoever has lost it should seek it again; whoever has forfeited it should search for it. For whoever is not found in that same peace is rejected by the Father and disinherited by the Son; stripped and naked, he will be found alienated from that same Lord.

He who has despised the good of the law that was given will reject the gift offered; nor will he be able to reach the Lord’s inheritance who has been unwilling to serve the testament. Christian, embrace the peace that Christ left; as a worshiper, cling to God’s inheritance; show that the Lord’s will has been poured into you. ‘Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God’ (Matt. 5:9).

It is written for the quarrelsome; it is written for enemies: no one can be a son unless he is a peacemaker. He rejected enemies and made peacemakers his sons. Either preserve the peace given to you, Christian, or recognize that the glory of salvation has been taken from you if you do not love peace.

He cannot receive Christ’s promises who has been unwilling to be reconciled with his brother; he cannot have harmony with Christ who has wished to be at odds with a Christian. If Christ had demanded from us a vicarious suffering, and the blood of the Son of God, poured out for us, had been sought to be weighed against our blood, with what urgency and devotion ought we to have hastened, so that we might fulfill the commands of so great a Majesty, rejoice to pay the debt through vicarious suffering, acquire life in exchange for death, and make compensation through reciprocal suffering? But now how can you lay down your life for Christ if you are unwilling to preserve the peace entrusted to you by that same Christ?

It is the crime of obstinacy to despise what is ordered, to refuse what is commanded, and to avoid what is imposed. The peace of Christ is good; discord is the devil’s evil. He answers to the author from whom he chooses one or the other. What have you to do with discord, Christian, which has destroyed its own prince, the devil? Why do you love hostility, which could not please its author? Why do you practice enmities, which even the one who first discovered them could not escape?

While the serpent exercised enmity against the first man, he was killed; while he envied man, he himself was overthrown; while he deceived Adam, he was strangled. Christ, on the contrary, clung to man with such great charity and loved him with such singular kindness that he commended him to the Father and joined him to himself, descending for his sake and putting on flesh.

It is written: ‘Through the envy of the devil, death entered the world’ (Wis. 2:24). Those who belong to his party imitate him. Let what falls upon the devil not fall upon a Christian, for it befits a Christian to preserve what he is known to have learned from the Lord. We ought therefore to embrace the charity of Christ, so that we may be able to live with him in eternal blessedness. Amen.”)]

## SERMON VII. On the words of the Gospel of John 14: “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace.”

[Col. 0679B]

It is the Lord’s voice, dearly beloved brothers: “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace” (John 14:27). Since we are about to speak of peace, let us first consider what benefits peace possesses. Peace is serenity of mind, tranquility of soul, simplicity of heart, the bond of love, and fellowship in charity. It is peace that removes hostilities, restrains wars, suppresses anger, tramples the proud, loves the humble, calms those in disagreement, reconciles enemies, and is pleasing to all. It does not seek what belongs to another and counts nothing as its own; it teaches one to love what it does not know how to hate. It does not know how to exalt itself or be puffed up.

Therefore, whoever has received peace should hold it; whoever has lost it should seek it again; whoever has forfeited it should search for it, because whoever is not found in that peace is rejected by the Father, disinherited by the Son, and nevertheless made alien to the Holy Spirit. For he rejects the gift offered who despises the good of the law that was given; nor can he reach the Lord’s inheritance who has been unwilling to observe the testament. He cannot have harmony with Christ who has wished to be at odds with a Christian.

It is therefore the crime of obstinacy to despise what is ordered, to refuse what is commanded, and to avoid what is imposed. What have you in common with discord, Christian? Why do you love hostilities, which could not please the author of peace? Why do you practice enmities, which even the one who first discovered them could not escape? For when the serpent first exercised enmity against the first man, he was killed; when he envied man, he himself was overthrown; when he wished to deceive Adam, he was himself first strangled. Therefore either embrace the charity of Christ, Christian, or recognize that, through the similarity of your actions, you are equal to the author of discord. [Note: All manuscripts add the word *ipsius* (“his own”), but some place it after *operum* (“actions”), others after the particle *te* (“you”).]

## SAINT VALERIAN, BISHOP OF CEMELUM

[Col. 0681]

## LETTER OF J. SIRMOND TO FRANCIS CARDINAL BARBERINI, ON THIS EDITION OF SAINT VALERIAN

[Note: This letter, together with what is appended to it in the manner of a brief dissertation, was taken from Sirmond’s autograph.]

MOST EMINENT LORD,

Shame and reverence prevent me from daring to do this too often; but now the logic of my office, and—if I am not mistaken—the same devotion toward Your Eminence, persuade me to address Your Eminence in writing. For when I heard that the reputation of Valerian, the bishop, was once again being placed in jeopardy, I thought that it was not merely my duty not to abandon the cause I had previously undertaken on his behalf, but also that it concerned the Holy Office and the Roman name that it should not overturn its former judgment and decision concerning him.

I believe that Your Eminence remembers—for Your Eminence could not have been unaware of it, although you were then away from Rome—that six years ago, when the same informer was pressing the censure of these Homilies, the sacred tribunal, after hearing and approving the author’s defense contained in our letter, judged that nothing else should be decided than that I should prepare notes for a new edition in which both heads of accusation would be answered: namely, the saintly title attributed to him and the suspicion of Semi-Pelagianism with which he was charged.

Father Theophilus Raynaudus, a theologian of our Society, has recently accomplished both tasks in a work published at Lyon for Valerian’s vindication, and has done so so fully and accurately that I think the case has been admirably handled, since by his zeal and diligence he has anticipated my efforts in this matter, from which nothing of this kind could have been expected. If nothing new has since been brought forward that requires a more severe judgment, I think it would be worthy of Your Eminence’s singular piety to ensure that the decree of the Holy Office remains undisturbed and that the reputation of an otherwise innocent and useful writer be preserved intact.

In this matter, I trust that there is still less reason to fear that I shall appear an importunate intercessor, since, besides the common judgment of learned men, who have hitherto read Valerian with approval, I understand that Your Eminence yourself—who are not usually pleased by anything except what is right—have at some time taken delight in the taste and flavor of his work.

Paris, 16 August 1632.

### On the two charges brought against the Homilies of Valerian

#### I

One charge concerns the name “Saint,” which they deny is appropriate to this author. Yet it is clear that this did not originate with me, because many years earlier, when his first homily, *On the Good of Discipline*, was published in Germany before the others had been found, the same title was prefixed to it according to an old copy, reportedly from the monastery of St. Gall, in which the inscription reads as follows: “The book of Saint Valerian, bishop of Cemelum.” Since I observed that others had called him this without rashness, and since I had no certain evidence to the contrary, I did not think that I ought—or could—remove this title from him without annotation.

Whether this name was formerly attributed to Valerian because of a particular reputation for holiness or merely because of the dignity of his episcopal office would be difficult to determine, since scarcely any monuments of the city of Cimela remained after its destruction. Conversely, however, the suspicion brought forward concerning Semi-Pelagian doctrine would not be sufficient to remove the title from him, if it properly belongs to him, especially since that doctrine had not yet been condemned by the authority of the Church at the time in question. For we see that Cassian and Hilary of Arles, who professed this doctrine more prominently than others, are nevertheless called saints—the former by St. Gregory in Letter 12 of Book VI, the latter in the Roman Martyrology—and both are honored among their own people with the customary worship of saints.

#### II

The second charge concerns the accusation that this doctrine is found in certain passages of these Homilies. In this respect, apart from the fact that there seems to be no passage of this kind that cannot be defended and interpreted in a better sense—as is customary in this very matter when Chrysostom and other Fathers, both Greek and Latin, are explained—and apart from the fact that Father Theophilus, in the work he wrote in defense of Valerian, shows him to be free from every stain, one further point must be observed.

Even if we conceded that Valerian, together with other Gallican bishops who lived in the same century and in the same province, had embraced this doctrine, they still could not have been considered heretics on this account before the Second Council of Orange, which condemned that doctrine and was confirmed by the Apostolic See more than sixty years after Valerian.

As for Valerian once again, whatever the controversy concerning the name and title “Saint,” it cannot be denied that throughout his life he remained in peace and communion with the Catholic Church. The evidence of this is Letter 52 of St. Leo the Pope, written to him and other bishops of Gaul, as well as another letter from these bishops to St. Leo. The Council of Riez, too, at which he was present and signed together with the others, bears witness to it. So does the honorable mention made of him in the convoking letter [Note: Vol. I of the Councils of Gaul, p. 120.] of the Third Council of Arles, at which an agreement was reached between Faustus, abbot of the island of Lérins, and three neighboring bishops, one of whom was Valerian.

These Homilies, moreover, were first printed at Paris twenty years ago, subsequently reprinted in Germany, and printed more than once at Lyon. They have been read by everyone without offense and with profit, and they truly contain pious and religious doctrine, especially useful for establishing the invocation of the saints and the veneration of sacred relics. Indeed, there was no shortage of a man of great reputation who said and wrote, when they were brought to Germany, that it seemed to have happened through divine providence that they had been discovered at precisely this time for the refutation of heretics. Nor have we hitherto heard of anyone other than the informer who failed to approve their reading.

[Col. 0683]

# HISTORICAL-LITERARY NOTICE ON SAINT VALERIAN

(From Gallandius, *Bibliotheca Maxima Veterum Patrum*, vol. X, and Schoenemann, *Historical and Literary Bibliography of the Latin Fathers*, vol. II.)

[Col. 0683A]

## § I. Life (Gallandius)

Among Gennadius, Isidore, and other cataloguers of ecclesiastical writers, there is complete silence concerning VALERIAN. We must therefore recover from other ancient records whatever may in some way make our author known to us. First, his episcopal see must be investigated; from this it will at the same time become clear during what period the holy bishop flourished.

Pliny says that Cemelion was a town of the Vediantii [Note: Pliny, *Natural History*, book III, chapter 5.]; and, together with Ptolemy, he assigns it to Italy, because both of them make the river Var the boundary of Italy—not the summit of the Alps, as the itinerary of Antoninus more correctly does, where the town is assigned to Gaul. For this point, see Wesseling [Note: Wesseling, *Ancient Roman Itineraries*, p. 296.].

“And indeed,” says Sirmond [Note: Sirmond, preface to Valerian’s Homilies.], “apart from the itinerary just mentioned, the fact that Cemelium belonged to Gaul is established beyond controversy by the ancient *Notice of the Cities of Gaul*, which, among the cities of the Maritime Alps reckoned under the metropolitan see of Embrun, lists the city of the Cemelenians in sixth place. Usuard likewise, in his Martyrology, on the day before the Ides of May, notes that on that day the feast of Saint Pontius the martyr was solemnly celebrated in Gaul, in the city of Cimela [Note: Usuard, *Martyrology*, authentic edition, p. 81, Paris, 1718.]—the very saint whom our author repeatedly commemorates, though always without naming him, in three homilies on the good of martyrdom [Note: Valerian, Homilies 15–18].”

To these may be added the Acts of the same Saint Pontius, published through the efforts of Baluze, where the following passage is relevant to our subject [Note: Acts of Pontius, chapter 15, in Baluze, *Miscellanea*, vol. II, p. 134.]: “Crossing the boundaries of Italy, Pontius sought a city situated far away beneath the Alps, called Cimela.”

This city, moreover, as Sammarthanus writes [Note: Sammarthanus, *Gallia Christiana Nova*, vol. III, p. 1268.], “which was once most renowned, was so worn down by so many disasters at the hands of the Vandals, Lombards, and Saracens that it preserved not even the shadow of its former greatness” [Note: Sirmond, cited work]. “To this day, only ancient traces of ruins and the name remain not far from Nice, on the hill called Cemela.”

Valerian’s episcopal seat having thus been established, it remains for us to investigate with Sirmond the period in which he lived. [Note: The same work.]

“But I seem to discover from the Cemelene see itself,” he says, “that he flourished around the year 450, that is, in the time of Leo the Great. For after Leo, by Leo’s own decree, as we learn from the words of Pope Hilary in Letter 4, the bishops of the city of Cemelum and of the fortress of Nice were no longer distinct, but the same men were simultaneously bishops of Cemelum and, as long as Cemela stood, of Nice. This can be seen in the Fifth Council of Orléans, where Aetius the presbyter, sent by Magnus, bishop of the Church of Cemelum and Nice, is said to have subscribed in the ancient copies that preserve the complete subscriptions of that council; for they are mutilated in the printed editions.

“Therefore Valerian, who is called only bishop of Cemelum, must have governed that see before Leo’s decree. And, to state my view, I infer that this Valerian is the same man to whom Leo himself wrote, together with other bishops of the neighboring provinces of Gaul, concerning the ordination of the bishop of Vaison [Note: Leo, Letter 66, works, vol. I, p. 998, latest edition of the Ballerini.], a letter which Cardinal Baronius of blessed memory published from a codex of Arles [Note: Baronius, under the year 450, § 57.].

“I am confirmed in this opinion because among that number of bishops I see Ingenuus, bishop of Embrun—that is, Valerian’s metropolitan. There are also two other letters: one from Leo to forty-four bishops of Gaul, and another from those same bishops to Leo [Note: Leo, Letters 99 and 102, pp. 1107 and 1136 of the edition cited.], in which Ingenuus and Valerian are likewise joined together.”

Thus far Sirmond; Tillemont [Note: Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*, vol. XV, p. 125.] and the authors of the *Literary History of France* [Note: *Literary History of France*, vol. II, p. 329.] agree with him.

Concerning Valerian’s deeds, Sammarthanus writes as follows [Note: Sammarthanus, cited work, p. 1270ff.]: “In the year 439 he was present at the Council of Riez, at which the affair of Armentarius was discussed. After receiving St. Leo’s letter to Flavian (in the year 451), he wrote to him with many others, extolling it with the highest praises and professing his agreement with him in all things [Note: Among Leo’s letters, no. 99, p. 1107 of the edition cited.]. He was also one of those to whom the holy pontiff replied (in the year 452), congratulating them on their orthodox faith and indicating that Eutyches and Dioscorus had been condemned at the Council of Chalcedon [Note: Leo, Letter 102, p. 1136 of the edition cited.].

“When a serious dispute arose between Theodore, bishop of Fréjus, and Faustus, abbot of Lérins, which at that time depended upon that diocese [lacuna] and when our Valerian and Maximus of Riez, the bishops, had taken the side of the Lérins monks in that quarrel, Ravennius, bishop of Arles, convened a council in his city on 30 December to bring a remedy to so great an evil [Note: Councils, vol. V, p. 23, Venice–Labbe edition.]. Eleven bishops attended with him, including Rusticus of Narbonne. Maximus and Valerian likewise assembled with the monks of Lérins; they are not, however, named among the judges, perhaps because they were present as parties. The dispute was nevertheless settled amicably.

“The precise year in which this council was held is unknown; certainly it was between the years 449, when Ravennius was raised to the episcopate, and 451, when he departed for immortal life. Sirmond assigns the year 455; Tillemont earlier assigned it [Note: Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*, vol. XV, p. 125.]. The Carthusian Rivierus notes that mention is made in the year 451 of Valerian, bishop of Nice.”

Thus far Sammarthanus. The Benedictines, however, because Valerian took the side of Lérins in this matter together with Maximus of Riez, do not hesitate to maintain that he was the same person as Valerius, the monk of Lérins, who was venerated as a bishop at Nice on 24 July [Note: *Literary History of France*, vol. II, p. 329. On this Valerius, see Vincent Barralis, *Lérins Chronology*, part I, p. 203, where he is said to have been taken from the monastery of Lérins to the episcopate of Nice in the province [Col. 0686D]. But concerning his letter, which the authors of the *Literary History of France* call his, there is complete silence both in Barralis and elsewhere.]. When he died is uncertain.

## § II. Writings (Schoenemann)

These are attributed to this Valerian: twenty Sermons and a Letter to the Monks, concerning the virtues and order of Apostolic teaching. The Sermons are entitled: I, On the Good of Discipline; II, III, On the Narrow and Constricted Way; IV, On Promises Made and Not Kept; V, On Insolence of Speech; VI, On Idle Words; VII, VIII, IX, On Mercy; X, On Parasites; XI, “Let Whoever Boasts, Boast in the Lord”; XII, XIII, On the Good of Preserving Peace; XIV, On the Good of Humility; XV, XVI, XVII, On the Good of Martyrdom; XVIII, On the Maccabees; XIX, On Lent; XX, On Greed.

§ III. Editions. (Schoen.)

Melchior Goldast of Haiminsfeld restored Valerian’s name by attributing to him, on the authority of manuscript copies, the Sermon On the Good of Discipline, which had previously circulated among Augustine’s works under an uncertain author’s name. Goldast published it in a separate volume, with notes and corrections, in 1601. Ten years later Jacobus Sirmond added nineteen other homilies, together with the Letter, which he had found in a Corbie manuscript written with considerable corruption—not because the manuscripts bore Valerian’s name, but because the style and eloquence of both collections were alike.

Although this judgment was somewhat precarious, everyone immediately accepted it. Hence these works of Valerian were reprinted both in the Bibliothecae Patrum and several times together with the works of Leo the Great, as well as with some additions in the collection of Sirmond’s works, and finally by Gallandius.

Scarcely had Valerian’s Homilies appeared when their orthodoxy began to be called into question, and they were brought before the sacred tribunal at Rome as akin to the Pelagian heresy. At the same time Sirmond was challenged over the title “Saint,” which he had bestowed upon Valerian. He answered both accusations in a brief writing sent to the Holy Office. After it had been read and approved, the authorities decided that nothing further was necessary except that he should prepare notes for a new edition in which both charges would be answered.

The more extensive defense was undertaken either at Sirmond’s request or on his own initiative by Theophilus Raynaudus, a theologian of the same Society. Certainly, when Sirmond heard that Valerian’s reputation was again being placed in danger, he referred to Raynaudus in a letter written on this matter to Cardinal Francesco Barberini. He stated that Raynaudus had dealt with both points so fully and accurately that he considered the case admirably handled: Raynaudus had anticipated, through his own zeal and diligence, the work which Sirmond himself could not reasonably have been expected to undertake. Unless something new were later produced requiring a stricter judgment, Sirmond requested that the decree of the Holy Office remain undisturbed.

Whether that Raynaudian writing was first published separately, or appeared together with some edition of Valerian at Lyon, I confess is not sufficiently clear.

[Col. 0686D] **Note:** Such an edition, unless an earlier one is to be placed before it, must have been produced between 1626 and 1632. For Sirmond’s letter to Cardinal Barberini is dated at Paris, 16 August 1632. In it he writes that Valerian had been brought before the Roman judges six years earlier. Certainly the edition of 1623 does not contain it; and Sirmond himself, in the brief chapters appended to the cited letter in defense of his position, repeatedly asserts that Valerian had been printed at Lyon for twenty years—that is, from 1612, when these Homilies were first printed at Paris, to 1632.

Nevertheless, it was inserted by the bookseller into the Lyon edition of 1633 and those following it up to 1671, and also into the Venetian edition of 1742. But let us now examine Valerian’s individual editions.

## SEVENTEENTH CENTURY
