**1601.** Geneva, printed by Petrus de la Rouiere; octavo. *Sermon of Saint Valerian, Bishop of Cimiez, On the Good of Discipline.* *Fragment of Saint Isidore, Bishop of Seville, On Prelates.* Melchior Hamenuelto Goldastus published it together with his *Collectanea*, in which many passages of many authors—especially of the Fathers—are either explained from earlier editions or newly published.

In two prefaces addressed to the reader—one preceding the text and the other prefixed to the *Collectanea*—Goldast discusses the importance of these books, namely ecclesiastical discipline. He partly explains the system of ancient discipline and partly gives instructions for preserving it or recovering it once lost.

The same subject is treated in a letter likewise prefixed to the *Collectanea*, addressed to Theodore Beza and dated at Lectius’s house on the fourth day before the Ides of Quintilis, in the year [infinity sign]. In the beginning of the *Collectanea* he explains what moved him to place Valerian’s name before this sermon.

Erasmus, to be sure, had already understood that Augustine was not its author. But Goldast was the first to explain and support this opinion with arguments. He proves that the style of the two authors differs extremely. He also maintains that the sermon is not suited to Augustine’s intelligence or learning, and does not consider it plausible that Augustine would have treated one subject and one argument in various and different books, since he has a more extensive work on the same subject, *On Christian Discipline*.

Finally, he says that the ancients neither recognized this work nor brought it to light; this is clear from even the single catalogue of Possidonius—or Possidius—in which it is not mentioned, and from the fact that it is nowhere cited in the *Sentences* collected by Prosper, in Eugippius’s *Excerpta*, in Peter Lombard’s *Sentences*, or, finally, in the *Augustinian Confession* of Jerome of Tortona, that most zealous and distinguished defender of Augustine’s works.

After presenting these arguments, he continues as follows:

> Thus I believe that by my own efforts and courtesy I have now done enough to ensure that you will never again say that this sermon belongs to Augustine as its author. As for its true and legitimate father, you can easily arrive at a conjecture if you admit a fifth γνώρισμα (*gnōrisma*, criterion), by which, as though with a sundial, we distinguish genuine and native books from spurious ones. For this is no less useful or safe—so I understand the matter—than what several highly learned men have told me, provided that the reliability of the manuscripts is sound and their authority worthy.
>
> I found the oldest and most ancient copy of this sermon in the library of the noble jurist Bartholomaeus Schobinger, splendidly furnished with both handwritten and printed books. Its title is:
>
> **“Here begins the book of Saint Valerian, Bishop of Cimiez, On the Good of Discipline.”**
>
> As soon as I first read the title and the name of the little book, I was so astonished that I said of the libraries of Conrad Gesner, Josua Simler, and Jacob Frisius: “You would say they were Neptune’s cattle”—so greatly do they change.
>
> In the archive of the monastery of Saint Gall, from whose property this codex once came, there are very ancient book catalogues that mention this author. One is the catalogue of Saint Othmar, the first abbot under Pepin, father of Charlemagne: “Saint Valerius, Bishop of Cimiez,” and so forth.
>
> At the Council of Constance, Poggio of Florence carried off to Rome and Florence the finest and most excellent portion of the manuscripts, while Aeneas Silvius—later destined to become pope—sold them at Basel by fraud and trickery. Warned and angered by this crime, the brothers sealed the remaining codices against seizure with the monastery’s mark and recorded them in a catalogue. There one reads: “Saint Valerius’s book On the Good of Discipline,” and so forth.
>
> You can also see the same inscription on the binding of the book itself. Either I am mistaken, or the error arose from the similarity of the names. There was Valerius, Bishop of Hippo and Augustine’s predecessor, who, according to Volaterranus, still has a book *On the Life of Monks*. There were also others of the same name, whom it is unnecessary to list.
>
> He next indicates that he has discovered nothing certain about the age of this Valerian or about the location of his bishopric of Cimiez.

In arguing the case, Goldast used the later Basel edition of Augustine’s works. At the very beginning, however, on the authority of the manuscript codex, he removed the divisions into chapters as inelegant and as frequently disturbing the author’s sense. Erasmus had already noticed this, and, rejecting the chapter headings, had been content to add only the numerical markers in the margin. The Lyon—or rather, probably, the Geneva—edition later restored them.

Goldast then admits that he corrected very many things in the sequence and context of the discourse, either because they seemed absolutely certain to him or because they were too slight and trivial to deserve notation. Nevertheless, he explained the basis of most of his corrections. His notes are exceptionally choice and filled with rare learning.

**1604.** The Island at Lake Constance, from the workshop of Johannes Ludovicus Brem; quarto. *Sermon of Saint Valerian, Bishop of Cimiez, On the Good of Discipline*, among the *Ancient Paraenetic Writers*, with the notes of Melchior Haiminsfeld Goldast, from the library and at the expense of Bartholomaeus Schobinger, jurist, pp. 7–39.

**1612.** Paris, from the Nivellian press; octavo. *Twenty Homilies of Saint Valerian, Bishop of Cimiez.* Also, *Letter to the Monks, On the Virtues and Order of Apostolic Teaching.* All published for the first time, except for the single homily, after approximately twelve hundred years, by Jacobus Sirmond, priest of the Society of Jesus, in 1612.

> “Apart from the homily of the Bishop Valerian On the Good of Discipline,” says Sirmond, “which had previously circulated under an uncertain name and was restored to its author a few years ago, we have hitherto received nothing of his into print. The remaining nineteen which we now publish we owe to the celebrated ancient monastery of Corbie. The single copy which alone we used was a copy in a very ancient, but insufficiently corrected, hand. Although it did not contain the homily On the Good of Discipline and did not indicate the name of the city in which Valerian served as bishop, it was nevertheless easy, from the similarity of style and subject matter, to conjecture that these were its genuine sisters, all issued by one and the same Valerian, Bishop of Cimiez. Nor, I believe, will anyone object to this conclusion.
>
> “For style is the best teacher of judgment, and the character of Valerian’s diction—the grave and splendid eloquence, full of dignity and vigor, which shines forth in these Homilies—sufficiently reveals the period of his life I have mentioned: the period in which Eucherius of Lyon, Hilary, Bishop of Arles, Vincent of Lérins, Prosper, and the presbyter Salvian were adorning our Gaul with a comparable reputation and glory for eloquence.
>
> “I only wish that we had been able to publish them in a more corrected form, such as the most eloquent bishop himself had delivered them. But in the face of such extensive corruption of the codex, that was more to be desired than hoped for. Perhaps, however, what this first edition could not accomplish will be achieved by a second.”

He also discussed the bishopric of Cimiez with the greatest care and, as far as possible, Valerian’s person. He dedicated the work to Henri-Louis Castan, Bishop of Poitiers.

**1618.** Cologne, from the press of Anton Hierat; folio. *Twenty Homilies of Valerian, Bishop of Cimiez*, from the edition of Jacobus Sirmond; his *Letter to the Monks*, in the *Great Library of the Fathers*, vol. V, part III.

**1623.** Lyon, at the expense of Claudius Landry; folio. *Twenty Homilies of Saint Valerian, Bishop of Cimiez near Nice in Gaul, with the Letter to the Monks, On the Virtues and Order of Apostolic Teaching*, together with Leo the Great, Maximus of Turin, Peter Chrysologus, Fulgentius, and Asterius, Bishop of Amasea. Sirmond’s preface is placed first, but without his name. Fabricius incorrectly reports that Sirmond himself prepared this edition.

**1633.** Lyon, [details omitted in the source]; folio. *Twenty Homilies of Valerian, with the Letter to the Monks*, and so forth. Theophilus Raynaudus defended Valerian in a careful defense against Parcus, the accuser of charity, in the *Heptad of Bishops Distinguished for Christian Wisdom and Eloquence*. See the works of Leo the Great.

**1661.** Paris, at the house of Simeon Piget; folio. *The Twenty Homilies of Valerian*, and so forth, with Raynaudus’s defense; in the same collection.

**1671.** Paris, at the expense of Petrus Variguet; folio. The same works, among the same authors.

**1677.** Lyon, at the house of the Anissons; folio. *Homilies of Saint Valerian*, from the edition of Jacobus Sirmond; his *Letter to the Monks*; in the *Greatest Library of the Fathers*, vol. VIII, pp. 498–523.

**1685.** Paris, at the house of François Muguet; folio. *Sermon of Saint Valerian On the Good of Discipline*, in the Appendix to vol. VI of the works of Saint Augustine, edited by the Benedictines, in the Antwerp copy, cols. 775–777.

**1696.** Paris, from the Royal Printing House; folio. *Twenty Homilies of Saint Valerian*, and so forth, among the works of Jacobus Sirmond, vol. I, pp. 604–702. Added from the papers of the deceased were his letter to Cardinal Barberini, with certain notes addressing the two points of objection, and also certain testimonies of the Fathers transcribed by him at the end of his copy. By these he wished to make clear that in Homily 11, where some thought Valerian appeared to agree with the Semi-Pelagians, he nevertheless spoke no differently from those unquestionably Catholic holy Fathers.

## EIGHTEENTH CENTURY

**1742.** Venice, at the house of Augustinus Savioli; folio. *All Extant Homilies of Saint Valerian, Bishop of Cimiez, a Most Worthy Writer.* Also included are the *Letter to the Monks* and the defense of Theophilus Raynaudus, together with the works of Peter Chrysologus, reprinted by this bookseller according to the edition of Dominicus Mita, pp. 213–291.

Raynaudus’s name is nevertheless absent—not through any deception, but perhaps through the bookseller’s ignorance. For Raynaudus’s name had been written only in the general title of the Lyon and Paris editions; the bookseller, or the person to whom he had entrusted the copying, apparently did not think it worth his attention to notice it. This nevertheless misled Oelrichs, who attributed that edition to the Venetian editor of 1742.

**1774.** Venice, from the printing house of Giovanni Battista Albrizzi; folio. *Twenty Homilies of Saint Valerian, Bishop of Cimiez.* Also, *Letter to the Monks On the Virtues and Order of Apostolic Teaching.* Revised from the distinguished Sirmondian edition and corrected in several places, in the *Library of the Fathers and of the Ancient Saints of the Church* of Andrea Gallandius, vol. X, pp. 123–158.

This is a reproduction of the 1696 edition. Accordingly, Sirmond’s letter to Cardinal Barberini and other material were added, and the corrections of Baunaeus (de la Baune), together with some of Caspar Barth’s corrections from his *Adversaria* and Cotelerius’s from the *Ecclesiastical Monuments of the Greeks* and the *Apostolic Constitutions*, were interspersed, along with several conjectures of Gallandius. Chapter III of the Prolegomena is devoted to Valerian.

[Col. 0689C]

# TESTIMONIES CONCERNING SAINT VALERIAN

In the copy of **Valerian published by Sirmond**, we found the following testimonies of the Fathers, later transcribed at the end in Sirmond’s own hand. By them he wished to make clear that, although some thought Valerian appeared in Homily 11 to agree with the Semi-Pelagians, he nevertheless spoke no differently from those unquestionably Catholic holy Fathers.

[Col. 0689D]

## Methodius of Patara, in Damascus’s *Parallels*

> Πάσης ἀγαθῆς πράξεως ἡ καταρχὴ ἐν τῇ ἡμετέρᾳ βουλῇ κέκτηται· τὸ δὲ συμπέρασμα ἐν τῷ Θεῷ.

“The beginning of every good action is possessed by our will; its completion, however, is in God.”

## Chrysostom, Homily 12 on the Letter to the Hebrews

> Δεῖ γὰρ ἡμᾶς πρῶτον ἑλέσθαι τὰ ἀγαθὰ, καὶ ὅτε ἑλώμεθα ἡμεῖς, τότε καὶ αὐτὸς τὰ παρ᾽ ἑαυτοῦ εἰσάγει. Οὐ προφθάνει τὰς ἡμετέρας βουλήσεις, ἵνα μὴ λυμήνηται τὸ αὐτεξούσιον ἡμῶν.

“For we must first choose the good things; and when we have chosen them, then he too contributes what comes from himself. He does not anticipate our wills, lest he destroy our free choice.”

## The same, Homily 2 on the Second Letter to the Corinthians

> Ἀπὸ τούτου τοίνυν μανθάνομεν, ὅτι κᾂν ἐλεεῖσθαι μέλλωμεν, ἀξίους πρότερον παρέχειν ἡμᾶς ἑαυτοὺς χρή· κᾂν γὰρ ἔλεος ᾖ, τοὺς ἀξίους ἐπιζητεῖ· οὐ γὰρ ἁπλῶς ἔπεισιν ἅπασι καὶ τοῖς ἀναισθήτως διακειμένοις.

“From this, then, we learn that, even if we are going to receive mercy, we must first make ourselves worthy of it. For even when there is mercy, it seeks those who are worthy; it does not simply come upon everyone, including those who are insensible.”

“From this we plainly understand that, although God intends to show us mercy, we must first do this: make ourselves worthy of mercy. For although it is mercy, it seeks the worthy; it does not come indiscriminately even to those who are afflicted with insensibility, and so forth.”

## Hilary, on Psalm 118, on *Nun*

“Our will must possess from itself the power to will. God will give increase to one who begins, because our weakness cannot obtain completion by itself; nevertheless, the merit of attaining completion proceeds from the beginning of the will.”

[Col. 0691B]

## Optatus, Book II

“For it belongs to the Christian to will what is good and to run in that which he has willed well; but it has not been given to man to bring the matter to completion. Thus, after the stages which a person must complete, something remains for God, whereby he may come to the aid of one who is failing. For he alone is perfection, and Christ, the Son of God, alone is perfect. All the rest of us are only partly perfect, because it is ours to will and ours to run, but God’s to perfect. Hence the blessed Apostle Paul also says: ‘It depends neither on the one who wills nor on the one who runs, but on God’s grace.’”

## Jerome, Book III Against the Pelagians, almost at the beginning

“Know that baptism forgives past sins, but does not preserve future righteousness; this is guarded by labor, effort, diligence, and always above all by God’s mercy. Thus it is ours to ask, his to grant what is asked; ours to begin, his to complete; ours to offer what we can, his to fulfill what we cannot.”

## Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 32

“Everything must be given to God, who both prepares the human will for assistance and assists it once prepared. For a good human will precedes many gifts of God, but not all; and in those gifts which it does not precede, it is itself also present.”

From an old Floriacian codex containing various works or fragments of ancient Fathers:

“Valerian, Bishop of Cimiez, likewise says in his book *On the Good of Discipline*: ‘Well does fear obey discipline in every matter; because it knows how to avoid imminent dangers or the anger of judges, it has obtained the power of preserving safety,’” followed by what appears in Homily 1, no. 2.

[Col. 0691B]

# TWENTY HOMILIES OF SAINT VALERIAN, BISHOP OF CIMIEZ (C, S)

[Col. 0691C]

## HOMILY I. On the Good of Discipline

### 1

Many who oppose sound doctrine blame justice, judge discipline to be tyranny, and assign rational correction to pride, although there is tyranny only where something unjust is commanded, and pride only where discipline is neglected.

Discipline, therefore, is the teacher of religion, the teacher of true piety. It neither rebukes in order to injure nor chastises in order to harm. Finally, it corrects human conduct when angered and preserves it when inflamed, as Solomon says:

> “My son, do not reject the discipline of the Lord, and do not grow weary when he rebukes you. For whom the Lord loves, he rebukes; and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Prov. 3:11).

There is certainly nothing that discipline does not either correct or preserve. Whoever wisely embraces it neither loses the favor of friendships nor incurs the danger of condemnation.

Let no one consider discipline irrational when he sees that, while all things in heaven and beneath heaven have been ordered by the operation of the Word, the plan of almighty God stands firm. At the beginning of his work God made nothing before discipline. For when, with Wisdom standing beside him, he suspended the heavens, prepared the earth, enclosed the seas, and assigned the courses of the sun and the sphere of the moon to their proper places and times, he established everything under discipline.

What would not be dark, what would not be disordered, what would not be judged absurd, unless all the elements stood firm under established laws? Is the course of the sun managed without discipline? Although it tirelessly completes the obligation of its daily journey, it nevertheless appears each morning for its appointed service, displaying itself daily in a region of the sky to survey the expanses of the earth.

So great is the order of discipline that, within the limits of time prescribed by law, the courses of the stars are driven through alternating turns of tireless motion, so that neither the moon escapes the eclipse and losses assigned to it, nor is the sun deprived of the flame of daylight.

[Col. 0691D] **Note:** This phrase seems awkward and intrusive.

Is it without discipline that the waves of so vast a sea are contained by the low shore of the earth, and that the wave, frequently driven higher by the winds, is enclosed within its own basin by a raised embankment? Foolish nature would surely throw everything into confusion unless the order of discipline governed the world.

### 2

We have set these things forth so that you may learn to obey the evangelical precepts and submit to the heavenly commands. What benefits a rational soul made in the image of God a person can easily understand when he sees that even the elements serve the constitutions of discipline established by God’s will.

Hear the prophet saying:

> “Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling. Embrace discipline, lest the Lord become angry and you perish from the righteous way” (Ps. 2:11–12).

Fear rightly obeys discipline in every matter. Because it knows how to avoid impending dangers or the anger of judges, it has obtained the power to preserve safety.

What would be safe for an adulterer? What would be secure for a thief? What path would not be open to a robber? Who would not fear the hollows of the shores and the hidden places of the forests? What would presumption not seize, unless discipline restrained the fury of human minds under fear of punishment?

And unless an established order of life existed, nature would never put an end to the practice of sinning. There is nothing that gluttony would not advise if discipline agreed with gluttony. There is nothing that luxury would not destroy if discipline departed from you through love of vices. There is nothing that the mind would not seize through desire to have and possess, unless discipline condemned the vice of greed.

All vices lie beneath the fear of discipline. Faith will never have cause to blush if a person looks toward God’s future judgment and considers the account he must render. Nor will the avenging flame of crimes rage where, with discipline in view, one either contemplates what is honorable or chastises what is shameful.

Many call it cruelty when the crime of a robber is punished in the name of discipline, although the sentence of the judge serves just laws by attacking what is shameful and cutting away what is criminal. It extends a hand not only to those who are present but also to those who are to come.

### 3

Who, then, would not believe that he might rightly sin if a judge did not prescribe discipline for shameless and impious acts? Let us see what the law says:

> “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness” (Exod. 20:13, 16).

[Col. 0693D] **Note:** I read *hae sunt* (“these are”).

These are the disciplines of the law, to which even the strictness of secular judgment obeys by attacking shameful acts and cutting away crimes. For Scripture adds:

> “The judge is appointed not as an avenger of good conduct but of evil” (Rom. 13:3).

Thus it even requires a corresponding form of punishment when it says:

> “An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth” (Lev. 24:20).

But we can easily avoid the severity of that ancient sentence if we consider the flames of the future judgment.

The Apostle teaches plainly that the weapons of secular judgment can be despised when he says:

> “If you do not wish to fear the authority, do what is good” (Rom. 13:3).

But these matters must not be treated superficially. For when the Apostle’s teaching mentions earthly authorities, it insinuates into our understanding the elements of heavenly judgment. When he teaches that one must obey the laws of the world, he necessarily warns a person to guard against future times.

“If you do not wish to fear the authority,” he says, “do what is good.” This means: “Do you wish not to fear the future judgment? Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 36:27).

Therefore we must guard against and overcome this first form of legal order, which lacks the laws of the world, so that we may exclude from ourselves the sentence of future death. For those whom temporal punishment does not afflict are pursued eternally by that other punishment, with the insatiable pain of torments.

No one should think that a person has escaped the crime of homicide merely because a corrupt secular judgment excused and acquitted him. Nor should the one who escaped detection under a law of indulgence think that the crime of adultery has been overlooked.

No one, seeing a sound right hand, should judge that the punishments legally due to the culprit for falsehood have been waived. When bodies have died, the crimes remain, unless they have first been cleansed before God through the intercession of tears. For hell awaits its guilty victim, armed with punishments appropriate to his offenses.

The authority of secular judgment serves rather to disgrace the present life than to absolve crime. We must therefore think above all of those punishments where a person lives while the punishment continues, where the body lacks neither torments nor limbs for the torturer.

Yet we can easily avoid these punishments if we hold the reins of discipline, as the Apostle says:

> “If you do not wish to fear the authority, do what is good, and you will receive praise from it” (Rom. 13:3).

### 4

What wise person would not gladly devote his mind to these benefits of discipline, where one can not only avoid punishment for a crime but also gain the favor of praise?

Hear the prophet saying:

> “Embrace discipline, lest the Lord become angry and you perish from the righteous way” (Ps. 2:12).

I think this sentence applies here to those to whom discipline has not yet come, who still linger on crooked paths, captured by the ancient error of superstition. They are shown never to have lived under the law, since they are admonished to embrace the pursuit of discipline.

The psalm continues:

> “Lest the Lord become angry and you perish from the righteous way.”

If, then, the prophet declares those to be guilty to whom discipline has never come, what do we think should be judged of those whom discipline has abandoned? The authority of the prophetic reading condemns the conduct of both groups, plainly judging it a lesser fault not to have reached discipline than to have rejected the law of discipline.

Behold, the prophet says:

> “Whoever rejects discipline hates his own soul” (Prov. 15:32).

And truly, as he said, so it is. For an enemy and adversary of his own soul is the person who, having rejected the admonitions of discipline, is occupied with diabolical services.

[Col. 0693D–0694D] **Note:** I am inclined to suspect that *offuciis* was written by Valerian instead of *nugis*, meaning trifles and vanities that obstruct the truth. **Barthius**, *Adversaria*, p. 898.

### 5

Some say that discipline has been established by laws that are excessively harsh. Let those miserable people say this—those whom the devil, the author of death, invites to every crime, whose minds insatiable gluttony possesses, over whom drunkenness reigns, whom shameful lust holds captive, and from whom thankless pride never departs.

For those who are devoted to preserving the faith of honorable continence and to serving humility and piety, the burden of discipline is sweet and the yoke of the Lord is light; it burdens only the lost or those about to perish.

I am ashamed to say, for the disgrace of human negligence, why discipline makes so little progress among some people, when we see that the instruction of a master is not lost even among mute animals.

Let the docile spirits of horses teach us to preserve the order of discipline. Led in a circle, they arrange their limbs in winding steps and, under the restraint of a single rein, consent to slacken themselves in such a way that both running and standing are governed under a certain arrangement of laws.

Thus those whom nature divides by species, discipline unites in purpose.

See how the strong bodies of oxen submit to the wagon. They prepare their minds so completely for command that they place their naturally swelling necks beneath a light yoke. Thus even creatures born to ferocity serve the regulations of discipline.

I therefore marvel that a human being endowed with wisdom and understanding of prudence sometimes carelessly neglects the precepts of discipline, when we see a mute animal avoid vices, obey commands, serve authority, and adapt its mind to every obedience, so that, when required, it will confront armed legions and, when ordered, expose itself to enemy weapons.

Hear the prophet saying here:

> “The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger; but Israel does not know me” (Isa. 1:3).

I fear saying that this sentence strikes at our negligence. Yet a person does not know the Lord if he does not know the duty of his own condition.

### 6

I shall show how the Lord can be found or known, provided there is a desire to see him.

If you wish to see the Lord, seek out a beggar, receive a stranger, visit the sick, run to the prison. If you wish to see God, release the bonds of captivity and cut through the knots of iniquity.

Hear the Lord speaking about this:

> “I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was a stranger, and you welcomed me; I was naked, and you clothed me; I was sick, and you visited me; I was in prison, and you came to me” (Matt. 25:35–36).

I therefore warn you: do not despise the naked, do not withdraw your hand from the blind, do not scorn one wrapped in rags. For in this garment the Lord was first found when he was sought by the Magi.

And since we have mentioned the discipline under which Christian faith flourishes, it is necessary to bring all the adornments of life to your ears, so that each person may understand that the reputation of conversion benefits him little unless, in contempt of the world, he has loved discipline.

Therefore whoever is devoted to honoring Christ should first assume the garments of the heart [and] likewise those of the body.

[Col. 0695D] **Note:** Perhaps *sicut* (“as” or “in the same way”).

The whole life of professed religion must bear the reputation of integrity, lest the one expecting the crown of virtue be struck by the loss of modesty. Bodily integrity must fortify life; unblemished faith must guard integrity, so that, while the benefit of both parts remains, it may make the blameless person reign with Christ.

### 7

But the principle of our conversion consists solely in this: that we should be good. Therefore the person who pursues goodness must first of all labor to be judged good.

For although a person may preserve a pure and unblemished body, he brings to God a torn life if his conduct stains his appearance, even though we know that conscience alone can suffice for good deeds.

But how much better it is that the person who frequently suffers from empty suspicions around your door should always think well of you! For it is naturally implanted in the common crowd always to judge good people badly.

But you who cultivate concern for a good reputation should by your devotion acquire the favor of an unblemished opinion. Let our life, then, be so luminous that it is known to everyone. Let integrity serve religion and modesty serve humility.

Whoever is devoted to preserving integrity must above all not admit into himself the reputation of a false error. It is indeed a great and glorious thing, worthy of being proclaimed by everyone’s mouth up to heaven, never to have given place to evil deeds; but it is far stronger never to have suffered under false suspicions.

What good does sobriety do you if you practice the vices of drunkenness? Who would not judge you drunk if, among wine-filled cups being poured and the circles of dancers, you imitated their whirling movements?

Who would think you chaste if he saw you mixed up with the stories of prostitutes, speaking in theatrical phrases, uttering obscene things, or echoing what is dishonorable? I praise in you the conscience of chastity, but I hate the conversation of the prostitute.

### 8

At this point someone may perhaps say, “A pure conscience is enough for me.”

As far as innocence is concerned, it is enough for you alone. But care must be taken lest, through your indulgence, another person sin and another’s sin rebound upon you, according to what Scripture says:

> “Woe to the one through whom scandal comes” (Matt. 18:7).

Even if you clothe your body in costly silk and arrange your limbs in snow-white fleece, you do not pass the day without stain if you have touched the mouth of a burning furnace.

Let discipline, therefore, accompany your life in every action. If you wish to please Christ, strive so that faith may support your profession and reputation commend it.

Let patience, the companion of humility, go before you; let chastity, the teacher of integrity, stand beside you. Let greed flee, drunkenness blush, luxury mourn its actions, and confused pride depart.

Whoever, then, hastens to know God will be able to find our Christ under this order of discipline.

There were still many things, beloved, which the order of discipline urged us to explain. For the present, however, we thought they should be postponed, lest a lengthy account produce weariness in idle ears.

Yet, so that we may not appear to have omitted anything from this work, we shall strive to discuss at a later time those matters that belong to religious conduct.

## HOMILY II. On the Narrow and Constricted Way

### 1

By many and innumerable laws of discipline, beloved, as you have heard the Evangelist say, our Christ established the order of life. In various ways he showed the reborn people the way of salvation, and he did not wish anything to remain hidden that might either save or destroy the soul, lest a possession purchased at so great a price should serve demonic superstitions after being deceived by the fault of ignorance.

But what is worse, medicine benefits the dying little. The way of salvation is therefore difficult because the exit into death is always easier, as Scripture says:

> “How broad and spacious is the way that leads to death, and many are those who enter by it! How narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life, and few are those who find it!” (Matt. 7:13–14).

Some perhaps wonder why the Evangelist calls the way of death broad and easy, when the path of life is narrowed at every approach.

Who has ever found descent to lower places difficult, where a person is dragged down by his own burden and borne down by the weight of his pack? Many things obstruct the way of prosperous salvation.

At this point the injury of death especially pursues those over whom vanity and cruelty rule. Moreover, dissensions, rivalries, lawsuits, quarrels, sacrileges, adulteries, homicides, fraternal hatreds, parricidal schemes, and perjuries armed with falsehoods converge to the prejudice of life. They not only obstruct one who is ascending but also plunge him into the depths of Tartarus.

How, then, can the person whom so many vices obstruct ever easily reach the heights? Narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life.

This is that way, beloved, along which the righteous proceed and the holy and blameless walk; the way belonging to those endowed with humility, integrity, and holiness who tirelessly follow our Christ.

2. Therefore, we must both choose and fortify the approach to this road, because although it is arduous, it is also passable. It makes itself easy for those who are willing, provided that vanity does not hinder them or the deceptive splendor of this world obstruct them. Whoever undertakes the journey up a steep mountain ought to be free and stripped of every impediment. Just as we see footsteps falter beneath an unjust burden, so the soul is subject to many falls if it is occupied with wicked deeds. Therefore the body encumbered by worldly desires must be unburdened, lest, as one strives through steep and lofty places, either the danger of death overtake him or despair of the labor increase. What wise person would direct a burden-laden animal along a narrow path, when on one side the mass of a lofty mountain presses it and on the other a precipitous cliff stands before it? If recklessness prevails there, one must either turn back or escape.

The same is true of the person who has entered upon the way of religion. It is therefore necessary for anyone who desires to bring his soul to heavenly glory always to cut away whatever appears dishonorable or shameful. The Lord does not say without reason: “Leave your possessions and follow me” (Matt. XIX, 21). These possessions, beloved, are our evils, nourished by earthly actions. While some serve them with excessive devotion, they have lost heavenly things.

3. If you therefore wish the heavenly door to be opened to you, everything must be removed, and whatever has been negligently and improperly practiced to the destruction of life must be assigned to repentance. It is difficult for you to gain access to what the Lord has prepared for those who believe in him unless you unload your breast, burdened with vices, and restrain all the guilt of injustice by the authority of religious discipline. You think in vain that you are following the paths of a steep journey and a harsh road if your soul is impeded by error.

Finally, if you wish, place before your eyes two men striving upward. Let one proceed weighed down by a heavy burden, while the other advances leaning only on a light staff; and you will see which reaches the heights more easily. Look first at the one burdened with the load, and you will see that his footsteps, hanging backward, hurry behind him, and that he walks with bent knee in such a way that he seems to be returning. Now like one descending, now like one falling, he is tossed with his whole body from moment to moment toward the opposite side of the sloping path, so that the very necessity of walking seems almost to contain more despair than labor.

Now turn your eyes to the one whose neck bears no weight, and you will see how freely he walks, how easy it is for him, with unburdened feet, to go through steep places and to cling with his footsteps to rugged slopes. Now he rises tall in a light run; now he is carried through the various places with complete eagerness of spirit, showing that the difficulty of the terrain does not hinder free bodies and that journeys, however steep, are not laborious for anyone if the mind occupied by unjust burdens is relieved.

[Note: [Col. 0697D] The scribe: “submerged.” Barth.]

The situation is similar, beloved, both for those whom wicked deeds burden and for those whom the tears of repentance commend after being stripped of their former guilt. Therefore the one who wishes to come confidently to judgment must lay down what is burdensome and despise earthly things if his mind is set on possessing heavenly things.

4. Certainly, beloved, if we wish more easily to overcome the narrowness of that arduous journey, we must apply the efforts of a sincere mind. Anything produced by quarrels, unhappy speech, or a tongue that has perhaps stirred up the poisonous offense of injury against another’s household must be removed. It cannot be estimated how greatly the vices of an undisciplined tongue obstruct the way of life. While it exercises the instrument of its mouth by speaking too much, it has aroused hatred against itself even through idle words. For the Lord says that an account must also be given of idle words (Matt. XII, 36).

Consider, therefore, what awaits the person whom the cause of guilt attacks before the principal [reading uncertain], since it is not without danger to the soul to carry even the slightest matters to judgment. Narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life. Whoever is wise, therefore, should first cast away from himself the impediments of the world and fortify his road through devotion to discipline. With repentance intervening, let him remove whatever seems to have been imposed through negligence, and let him not think that he must carry with him whatever secular glory has imposed; for although such things are heavy in themselves, they become heavier still through the difficulty of the journey.

Perhaps, for some who are excessively delicate in this world, the necessity of a narrow and arduous journey gives rise to despair. And indeed it is natural that an inexperienced mind should dread whatever is harsh and difficult. But what are we to do, when no door of virtue is open to soldiers who are too delicate? What reward would there be for labor if you ran across level ground? Or when would you rejoice that you had reached the prepared place if you arrived without bodily injury? Who has ever assembled trophies while idle? Or who has reached victory by sleeping while legions of enemies surrounded him on every side?

[Note: [Col. 0697D] The word “virtues” seems superfluous. It is contrary to the author’s meaning to recognize virtues in someone without labor. Barth.]

The crown of virtues that does not arise from labor possesses little praise. It may have the palm, but it does not have glory. When has a farmer ever filled his barns while idle? Or who has ever received the fruit of his field at the proper time unless he had first worked the rough earth with repeated furrows? This is the principle of great virtues: the more a person labors, the more reward he gains.

5. Let us nevertheless consider what sort of road of death this is which the evangelist calls broad and spacious and full of waves. Although it is crowded with deaths, it never ceases to receive criminals. Its nature is such that it quickly invites those who are destined to perish; it presents itself as easy to those whom discipline has abandoned. In comparison with the level and narrow journey, nothing is more dangerous for a traveler than spacious roads, because one runs without discipline where the reins of the horses are loosened. Thus it happens that the gate of death receives many, because where one proceeds more freely, one arrives more easily.

Hear the Lord saying: “Take up your cross and follow me” (Matt. XVI, 24). Surely a person does not fear the approach of that arduous journey when another extends a hand to him. Each person, therefore, is guided through the steep places by the side of another and is encouraged to undertake what he has begun by sharing the labor of the journey. Thus it can happen that the person who hastens upward with the Lord accompanying him reaches without hesitation the promised rewards of the kingdom.

But first, beloved, as we said above, everything that the unhappy error of the world has imposed upon human bodies must be laid down, lest the mass of sins placed before us prevent us from reaching that time of reward—or, if we do reach it, prevent us from entering the gates of the heavenly kingdom.

6. But you say, “We cannot reach it.” The matter is demonstrated by certain examples: we often see many depart without greeting the master of the house, with the gate bearing witness; yet wickedness, malice, treachery, luxury, or pride makes them hateful. Let each of you contemplate the offense of diabolical presumption, and he will understand how greatly pride weighs down the person striving upward, or in what condition the person is placed over whom a spirit of arrogance rules.

Hear the Lord speaking about this: “God gives grace to the humble and resists the proud” (James IV, 6). The necessity of this journey is no less impeded by the vice of greed. While greed wishes to rejoice in an excessive mass of money, it does not permit the rich person to enter the kingdom of heaven, as the Lord says: “Amen, I say to you, it is difficult for a rich person to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XIX, 23).

From this, drunkenness, conscious of the evils of lust, lays no small burden upon human bodies. While it serves immodest acts, it excludes the wretched person from fellowship in the heavenly kingdom. Cruelty, joined with impiety, also besieges the hidden narrowness of the journey. While it establishes bloody laws of death,

[Note: [Col. 0699D] Examine more carefully what those laws of death are and what their establishment is. You will entirely agree with us that *Martis* should be read. Just as he has thus far inveighed against the greedy, lustful, and drunken, so now under the heading of cruelty he comes to military men. Barth.]

[Note: [Col. 0700D] Or *institit*?]

it closed the way to heavenly glory, as the Apostle says: “Neither thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor the rapacious shall possess the kingdom of God” (I Cor. VI, 10).

Against the things we have mentioned, therefore, we must fight through devotion to discipline, so that we may reach the place of life. Piety, mercy, humility, integrity, chastity, sobriety, peace, faith, and charity must rather be brought to our journey. You will not reach the place of the promised inheritance, however, unless under this devotion to life you first strip off the body burdened with vices.

[Col. 0700A]

# HOMILY III. Likewise, on the narrow and constricted way

1. Every person who is concerned to see God and attain the heavenly kingdoms can readily understand that the demands of a narrow and arduous journey contribute to the attainment of life, and that hope of obtaining glory consists in labor. For there is nothing that labor cannot overcome, provided that the mind does not turn aside in the other direction, as it is accustomed to do. It is clear that all difficulties confront the person who takes pleasure in the error of that spacious road.

Hear the evangelist saying: “How broad and spacious is the way that leads to death, and many are those who enter through it! How narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life, and few are those who find it” (Matt. VII, 13, 14)!

[Col. 0700B]

I do not doubt that, for some established in the ranks of the heavenly soldiery, despair arises because access to the arduous road of the heavenly soldiery is constricted. And truly, beloved, for those striving toward higher things the way is not only arduous but also difficult and more than laborious. Yet, against the unwilling lazy and the occupied negligent, the necessity of labor undoubtedly increases even across level ground. Although whatever is placed on the heights may be harsh and difficult, it nevertheless comes into an open field if no cause for despair confronts those traveling.

Every work, therefore, beloved, in which diligence watches over human conduct requires voluntary service. For it is immeasurable how much difficulty increases if a person’s will deceives him in the greatest necessity of affairs. He never undertakes the journey up an arduous mountain well over whom despair rules. How can the body become accustomed to labor unless the will obeys the one who labors? Look and see how quickly he rebounds to the ground who climbs onto a horse in fear; or how many anxieties afflict the person who unwillingly enters the high sea in order to sail.

2. The religion of the Christian name, to which we have been called, has undertaken the duty of free choice. If anyone comes to it unwillingly, he adds burden to burden and, having stripped his body of the old law, imposes upon himself the weight of a hopeless life. Hence it is that the gate of death receives many, because the difficulty of life always confronts those destined to perish.

It is therefore necessary that the person who has reached the way of freedom cut away whatever infidelity there is in him and accumulate a heavenly testimony through the diligence of voluntary service, lest a person indebted to God for such great benefits be found ungrateful in small duties. By the negligent and inexperienced, the service owed to God may perhaps be judged burdensome because it excludes no time of respite.

God called every person not only to freedom but also established him in the highest dignity of affairs. The person who serves unwillingly imposes service upon himself. For if you adapt service to your will, you will find yourself not a servant of God but a son. For thus the prophet speaks in the voice of the Lord: “I will be a father to you, and you will be sons and daughters to me, says the Lord Almighty” (Jer. XXXI, 9; II Cor. VI, 18).

3. The service of our condition, beloved, is such that we always praise our Lord in his works and exalt him in the glory of his majesty with an unceasing voice. What, beyond this, does the invisible, incomprehensible, immeasurable power of glory require from a human being? Or in what does it require bodily service, when a choir of angels attends it?

That service is intolerable which the pride of tyrannical—that is, diabolical—dominion imposes, through the injury of impious captivity. To offer service voluntarily to a superior person belongs to duty, not servitude. Hear the prophet saying: “I will sacrifice to you willingly, O Lord” (Ps. LIII, 8).

Learn how great is the difference between imposed and voluntary servitude. It can never happen that the person whom negligence accuses of imposed service passes the day without offense. The person who obeys his lord by vow acquires grace; the unwilling person accumulates injury, as the prophet says: “Cursed is the person who performs the works of the Lord negligently” (Jer. XLVIII, 10).

If each of you considers the grace of the freedom bestowed by Christ our Lord on faithful peoples through the regeneration of the life-giving bath and the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, he understands that one must not serve the Lord idly. Although we offer him some honor or gift each day, we nevertheless never repay what we owe. When can the person repay his debt whom it is clear has been matched with the substitute payment of punishment, unless perhaps, for love of his Redeemer, he accepts a similar sentence either of death or of condemnation?

But while such things befall the bravest, let us at least offer Christ our Lord daily sacrifices of thanksgiving, so that, if the merits of virtues commend others, the duties of voluntary service may at least make a place of grace for us.

4. Let us first of all unload our hearts from impious contamination, so that we may be able to nourish the fruits of righteousness. The person who wishes to fulfill the heavenly commandments must renounce earthly actions completely. For just as a person never serves well unwillingly, so neither does an occupied person guard well what has been entrusted to him.

“I will sacrifice to you willingly.” The prophet does not commend himself to the Lord in these words without reason. He knew that many necessarily served with a doubtful heart, promising one thing with their mouths while arranging another in the secret places of their hearts.

“I will sacrifice to you willingly.” Although small, gifts offered by one who makes a vow become great; but benefits that have been extorted consume their author. Thus the person who has established a banquet unwillingly always laments what he has spent.

“I will sacrifice to you willingly”—that is, with a voluntary sacrifice. So that you may gladly present daily offerings of your mouth to your Creator, compose his sacrifice of praise with the sweetness of words, and devotedly attend to the duty of the work assigned to you.

Hear the prophet saying: “Make acceptable, O Lord, the voluntary offerings of my mouth” (Ps. CXVIII, 108).

5. When, therefore, we gather in church, beloved, above all let faith possess the secret places of our hearts, fortified by the aid of truth:

[Note: [Col. 0701D] I would indeed prefer “one,” or “for one”; otherwise the text seems abrupt.]

for God loves what is pure and undefiled—not what is possessed by falsehood, occupied by perjuries, fabricated, or doubtful. For these are indications of perfect fickleness [the wording is uncertain], or of love of holiness, or of devotion to discipline: namely, to present an immaculate victim in sacrifices and to have served the Lord faithfully with one’s whole mind.

This is the order of our service: always to recall the benefits of Christ our Lord and to ascribe to the author of your freedom whatever progress you have made through the labor of religious faith. Among all things, keep the precepts of justice; serve the one God, while preserving the honor of the Trinity.

Believe one faith and one baptism; confess the Father, the Son, [Note: [Col. 0701D] The word *vel* (“or”) is objectionable. It seems that *et* (“and”) should be restored, as below at [Col. 0702D].]

and the Holy Spirit to be one essence of glory; let no person, by a divided will, either precede or rule over another person; but believe the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit to be of one power and one virtue.

Thus, then, you will overcome that arduous and narrow road and live forever; and you will undoubtedly obtain what has been promised to the just in the heavenly realm, if you run through these stages of discipline and order the seasons of your life under this rule of living.

# HOMILY IV. On promises that have not been fulfilled

1. If a person indebted for benefits, beloved, fulfilled his promise and showed good faith in carrying out his pledges through devoted diligence, no one would ever be troubled by the unpleasant repetition of a debt. Nor would there be any occasion for accusation if the fulfillment of the promise were immediately followed by the result of the vow.

Hence it is that the trust of friendships sometimes wounded sighs, because it is occasionally necessary either to reproach a person for delaying repayment or to condemn the treachery of a debtor. To declare hostilities is to deny one’s promises [perhaps: “to have declared hostilities”], because the matter belongs to litigation if one person unwillingly returns something or another, embittered by delays, demands it.

You have heard the prophet saying: “Thus I will sing praise to your name, O God, forever and ever, that I may pay my vows from day to day” (Ps. LX, 9).

It is immeasurable, beloved, how much benefits of grace gain when a debtor anticipates the day of his creditor by making payment. Whoever freely returns money that was lent stores it up for himself. A person readily obtains whatever he needs if he answers his lender with prompt satisfaction.

But the person whom treachery condemns always finds his creditor’s door closed. Although he frequently knocks and pleads, he departs sad, empty-handed, and rebuked. If, therefore, a person by lying to another stirs up hatred against himself, how much more so if he deceives God and cheats the Lord of heavenly majesty with a slippery promise?

2. We have set these things forth, beloved, because some people, when dangers threaten, arrange the vows of their minds in such a way that, when the time has passed, they forget that they promised something to the Lord. One offers the sacrifice of his body; another promises tears of repentance; another becomes bound by a vow in love of the churches, another in honor of the saints.

But these things are as easy to promise as to deny. In such people, the hope of fulfilling their devotion lasts only as long as pain is felt in the head. Little by little they become accustomed to denying their promises once they have ceased to fear death.

And we wonder why the Lord sometimes answers so slowly with streaming tears and does not heed the voices of those who plead with righteous sorrow. We wonder why cultivation does not make itself more fruitful than usual for the diligent farmer; why a many-grained ear does not burst forth from fertile soil; why rich olive trees do not produce valuable commodities; why abundant vintage does not sweat through full winepresses.

Let no one here blame the earth; let no one accuse the weather. A dry hand gathers nothing—or, if it gathers something, soon loses it. The barns of unfruitful farmers are always empty and idle.

For this too follows from it: sometimes medicine finds no one whom it can heal. It is difficult for a physician faithfully to apply his hand when the sick person’s empty promise has often disappointed him.

3. Here a man sighs over the illness of his son and troubles the doors of the saints day and night with prayers. This woman, afflicted by her husband’s illness, and that man by his wife’s, knock at the secret place of their hearts and implores the help of heavenly mercy with tearful prayer, offering himself and his gift to God.

But when their vows have met with success, we sometimes see everything suddenly escape the mind, so that you might think that the wretched have drunk rather the cup of forgetfulness than that of health. Thus their deceitful vows do not always receive a beneficial response.

When, then, will the person who does not return what he owes find a benefit? It cannot happen that the person who has often mocked the judge’s patience with empty words does not at some time pay the penalty for his treachery.

Hence it is that human prayers vanish into the idle ears of God, and the intercession of tears has no effect, because it is difficult for those to be heard who frequently flatter their God with empty promises.

4. Blessed are those among whom fidelity to a pledge remains, with no inclination to lie. It is certainly better not to promise than to defraud one’s promises. Although a person may be marked by the fault of inhumanity, he is nevertheless not burdened by the injury of deceitful circumvention.

Return, finally, to the Acts of the Apostles, and you will find that breaking faith with one’s promises brings harm to the soul. We read that Ananias and his wife Sapphira, having sold their property, brought part of the money to the apostles for distribution while keeping the part reserved at home. Saint Peter said to them: “Ananias, in lying to the Holy Spirit, iniquity has filled your heart. While the estate was in your power, you have not lied to human beings but to God” (Acts V, 3, 4).

Thus, while they practiced fraud, they purchased death; and while they served greed, they lost eternal gifts.

The prophet says: “I will pay my vows to the Lord in the courts of the house of the Lord” (Ps. CXV, 18). The person who is convicted of having promised something to the Lord is unquestionably bound by a lawful debt through an agreement; and the person who says that he will repay necessarily confesses the debt.

Your property remains yours only so long as it has not been bound to another by the faith of a written obligation. In every pledge, therefore, whether friendship has offered it or willingness has assigned it, repayment must not be delayed. For all the grace of a gift offered perishes when the necessity of demanding it arises.

Thus the person who must unwillingly return what he promised has accomplished nothing for his vows. For we read in Solomon: “If you vow a vow to your Lord God, do not delay in paying it; for your Lord God will surely seek it from you, and what proceeds from your lips will become sin for you unless you repay it” (Deut. XXIII, 21).

5. Therefore, beloved, I admonish you: whoever knows that he has promised a vow to the Lord should pay it immediately. Certainly, whoever is not able to pay should not promise.

Here we do not, as some suppose, exaggerate the vices of inhumanity; we are speaking about faith, which we see endangered among some by the pestilence of vanity. For many, what is worse, having withheld the price of their freedom, have brought to the Lord not the whole sum but an incomplete payment—that is, a half-complete religious faith.

Hear the prophet saying: “Vow and pay gifts to your God” (Ps. LXXV, 12). “Vow”—by this he gives the counsel of conversion. “Pay”—from these people he demands the debt of the holiness they promised.

The person whom you see striving for the world and favoring the present life more than eternal glory possesses little religion. You prove that you have defrauded the Lord of nothing through your offering if you cultivate justice, love integrity, and exhibit the holiness you promised.

The person who understands that he has lied to the Lord must dread the end of Ananias or his wife.

“Vow and pay gifts to your Lord God.” In this passage he does not press the matter of generosity inappropriately, since we are admonished by suitable testimonies. If we listen to unfruitful people, perhaps this saying indicates the disposition of the one who asks.

Does God demand anything from you because he lacks it? What does the one who possesses everything not have? Is gold, which you promise in your tribulations, or silver, which you pledge in your pain, necessary for God’s uses? Or does anyone offer precious stones or garments because God needs them?

Your gift is therefore sought from you so that you yourself may shine in your gold, you yourself gleam in your silver, you yourself be adorned with your gems, and you yourself be clothed in your silk. The Lord wishes your soul to be arranged by your gifts, since he sees it disfigured by the vice of pride, wickedness, greed, or lust.

“Vow and pay gifts to the Lord your God.”

6. But you may perhaps say, “God does not need our gifts.” He does not indeed need gifts; but he seeks the fruit which, for the redemption of your soul, he has assigned to mercy.

For, apart from that sacrifice of your body which ought to be presented incorrupt and undefiled upon the altars, and apart from the duties of the voice that we owe to our Creator, this is the sacrifice acceptable to the Lord: that you devote yourself to goodness and mercy, that you favor the cause of justice, and that with undefiled faith you continually strive to please the Lord; that you clothe the naked willingly, that you feed the needy willingly, that you voluntarily ransom captives, and that you remember your redemption and release the person held in bondage.

To this you may perhaps reply, “What shall I do for the poor? What shall I leave to my son?” Hear the Lord saying: “Whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. X, 37).

You see, therefore, that nothing must be preferred to God and that a son must not be considered more important than God.

You say, “What shall I leave to my son?” If, when you have one son, the birth of your wife, while you despair, presents you with another, does not paternal affection commend both to you in one degree of succession? And, to make room for the newcomer, do you not even revoke the provisions of your will?

Thus we frequently see the inheritance to which one heir is accustomed to succeed prove sufficient for many as their number increases. Therefore, the person who has one son should think of Christ as having been born for him and should divide his resources among two, three, or more in such a way that Christ our Lord does not depart disinherited.

If you take such joy in the number of your children, I admonish you to admit your Redeemer to a share in the inheritance and to regulate the division of your property as though you judged that one child had been born fewer to you—or rejoiced that one had been added.

Make a place, therefore, for your beloved Christ among your children.

[Note: [Col. 0705D] Perhaps, “for you.”]

Why should those who are awaited in heaven by the same share of the promised inheritance not remain together through one division of property on earth? Whoever has withheld from the needy and wretched the necessities of life has denied the portion assigned to the firstborn—and indeed the better—among all his children.

Hear Scripture saying in this passage: “Whoever has mercy on the poor lends to God” (Prov. XIX, 17).

7. Many people think that the need of the wretched should be mocked by deceiving them with daily promises; and this belongs to those vows which, as we said above, are consumed by forgetfulness. What benefit is there in delaying the wretched person if abundant resources are available? Where you see that someone can immediately do good but postpones almsgiving through delayed kindness, understand that only the will to give was lacking.

Hear the Psalmist saying in this passage: “Thus I will sing praise to your name, O God, forever and ever, that I may pay my vows from day to day” (Ps. LX, 9). Did he say, “from year to year”? No, he said, “from day to day.”

Every day, therefore, beloved, we must work. The debt owed to God and the promised gift must not be prolonged in time. The person who has fulfilled his vows daily owes nothing to the future judgment; nor is there any account left for the future from the person who, enriched by just labor, has offered the Lord from day to day the fruit of good works.

He says: “Whatever you have done for one of these least ones, you have done for me” (Matt. XXV, 40). Whether someone has done good or evil, let him know that it belongs to the Lord’s majesty; for the recompense of either side awaits the human being.

Therefore we must devote ourselves to mercy and almsgiving, lest, when the Lord of heaven and earth comes, he set before us, among the other errors of our soul, the nakedness of the poor and force the wretchedness of the needy upon our eyes.

Let no one despise the naked; let no one trouble the beggar with harsh speech. This is, among all offerings, the sacrifice pleasing to God; this is the order of saving sacrifices: to assist the wretched in their need. And, lest you fall under the reproach of infidelity, as one who has fulfilled his vow, release your promise’s claim upon you.

# HOMILY V. On insolence of speech

1. It is not without purpose, beloved, that among all the vices which attack human life the prophet especially chastises the insolence of the tongue. He knew that, through zeal for bitter speech, poisons are often compounded and that the excessive ease of the lips frequently acquires hatred.

And truly, beloved, so it is. For the naturally restless tongue brings no small loss of life to mortals: when things have been well arranged, it scatters them, and when they have long been at peace, it disturbs them.

When can a quarrel arise if the tongue restrains itself? Or what place is there for enmities where the poisons of words cease? For the malicious tongue always has this commerce: to sow quarrels, stir up hatred, and acquire deaths, as Solomon says in this passage: “The tongue has disturbed many who were at peace; it has destroyed cities and dug up houses” (Ecclus. XXVIII, 16, 17).

Those who think that nothing is stronger than iron and nothing more violent than poison are certainly mistaken. Although these things possess a special natural power in accomplishing deaths, they nevertheless yield in the contest of words. For nothing is so harmful or malicious that it is not weaker than its own forces once an aroused tongue has stirred itself.

There are indeed many vices of the human body, and sufficiently serious ones; but they can accomplish little through their own counsels and powers unless they are armed with the crimes of others. Such is cruelty, which serves impiety and guards the gates of hell with the bloody law of death.

What could falsehood accomplish if greed slept idly? Indeed, death itself would be less destructive if either iron failed or poisons ceased.

2. The tongue, however, is a unique evil. In it such strength of wickedness exults that, in accomplishing its work, it requires no assistance from another. We must therefore restrain it, as the prophet admonishes, lest, when it bursts forth, it either injure when aroused or strike when provoked.

For it is not accustomed to withdraw without penalty once it has displayed itself in the boldness of words. When stirred, it vomits flames; and when it seeks to harm another, it sets fire to the entire inwardly guilty breast.

Hear the prophet saying: “You will not escape sin from much speaking” (Prov. X, 19). If necessary, anyone can more easily endure ranks armed with iron and legions equipped with instruments of war. But who could withstand the weapons of the lips fixed in the breast?

Bodies torn by iron undoubtedly recover health more easily. Or why should anyone impose so great a burden of cruelty upon the death of those killed by the sword, when sometimes the dangers are less where the resentment over bloodshed is greater? Whatever is enclosed by an external collision is always more difficult to heal.

It is certainly not difficult for a physician to soften ulcers, however swollen, when they are located in the eyes, by the benefit of herbs. The force of poison also has its remedy. Although it rules in the furthest recess of the viscera once swallowed, the wave of a healing draught can nevertheless seek it out. So much so that the craftsman of crimes sometimes marvels that, when medicine arrives, the incantation of his mouth has accomplished nothing.

But the wound of the tongue is incurable. Although it may strike lightly, it always moves deep sighs of pain from the breast. The prophet undoubtedly knew how great an evil the tongue was when he cried: “Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth and a door around my lips, so that my heart may not incline to evil words” (Ps. CXL, 3, 4).

If anyone is wise, let him set a guard over his mouth and fasten his lips with the bond of silence.

3. Nor does envy attack only one side of the concerns raised by the insolent tongue. We must act so that this tongue speaks nothing injurious; but no less must provision be made so that the words of a raving person may be answered with a reasonable reply.

It is a great effort in preserving peace if you pursue the bitterness of another’s tongue with gentle speech; but friendly conversation quickly confounds the lips of the wicked.

Yet, what is worse, you will more easily find someone who either always wishes to speak evil or willingly wishes to hear evil. Nothing is fiercer, nothing more violent, than bitter and harsh speech. Its wounds are healed with greater difficulty in proportion as the words are spoken more easily.

You readily disregard the darts of iron hurled through the air by the opposition of a shield; but a shot of words can neither be recalled nor prevented, for words are much swifter than arrows.

What defenses could help there, or what fortification could be ready enough to come to the rescue, where a weapon released almost strikes before it advances? It cannot be counted how many verbal darts the tongue carries, darts sufficiently ready to strike even the more secret places of the soul.

Whatever injury the ears receive, they immediately transmit to the secrets of the heart. Once it has entered there, it does not depart without a deadly outcome. Whatever cannot be discovered and expelled by any remedies of medicine produces perpetual pain.

Therefore the sound of the tongue must be chastised, lest through the ease of words it make poison.

### 4

If we consider, dearly beloved, all the pains that afflict the body, you will find nothing that cannot be healed either by the knife or softened by the gentle preparation of a medicine. No one can be unaware how grievous are the bites of wolves and how dangerous the venom of serpents; yet these can easily be resisted either by the juice of herbs or by the skill of physicians. The wound inflicted by words, however, is intolerable; and another can scarcely heal a cause of pain once it has been driven into the breast and has secretly invaded the dwelling-place of the soul. Hear the prophet saying: “Death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Prov. XVIII, 21). Truly, dearly beloved, if you look into the inner self and carefully investigate the swelling of an embittered heart, you will find that wounds inflicted by words bring about death.

Why should anyone reproach the art of poison-making in comparison with a malicious tongue, or accuse the preparation of harmful potions? That thing has surpassed every kind of poison which can be restrained only by death. Every wickedness, indeed, descends from the heart; but although this wickedness is harmful, it can easily be endured if what has been nourished by an evil plan is not provoked into a quarrel, but either silently grieves or rests, rolled back within its own recesses. For as long as what is conceived in the heart is held back by a silent mouth, the disease of wicked thoughts can be healed. But once it has burst forth through the rolling tongue, it seeks a physician in vain; the guilt of words is without remedy, because whatever injury, having entered through the ears, has spread cannot be erased by tears. Hear the Lord saying: “Make doors and bars for your mouth, and make a balance for your words” (Eccli. XXVIII, 28).

### 5

Perhaps you will reply to this: “Who can restrain the lips of his mouth so completely that he passes the day in silence?” This statement does not impose the bond of silence upon an honorable tongue. It plainly wishes a person to speak, but to utter honorable things and think peaceful thoughts. Words acquire much greater dignity if no bitterness of mind confuses their sweet-sounding music.

We have set these matters forth, dearly beloved, because we have found many people sometimes mixing poisons with sweet words in one and the same speech and entering into the battles of lawsuits under the false charm of peace. What could be more wretched or more dangerous than those who, through the activity of a deceitful tongue, lie in wait for another’s life? Why do they not heed that prophetic psalm which says: “May the Lord destroy deceitful lips” (Ps. XI, 4)? Do you see under what sort of curse the person lives who sows one thing in his heart and arranges another upon his tongue?

The Lord of heaven and earth knew very well that evil people sometimes deceive the pursuits of the holy by a pretended humility; therefore, he says in the language of the Gospel: “They come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves” (Matt. VII, 17). It is unquestionably an inextricable evil to mix deceitful designs with flatteries. I do not want the suspicious sweetness of gifts. Who would willingly have sour milk seasoned with the bitter taste of herbs? It is therefore difficult for someone who offers both sweet and false water to be pleasing to anyone. When does taste fail to be offended if any bitterness is mixed with a honeycomb? The human heart itself, although living and wise, lacks sound judgment once the bitterness of gall has infected it.

All the vices of a treacherous mind must therefore be restrained, lest, when they have begun to prepare something bitter outwardly, they also begin to make displeasing those things that are sweet in our mouth.

### 6

Hear the prophet saying: “Set a guard, O Lord, over my mouth.” This is the useful guardianship of our mouth: that our heart may not readily turn toward words which either a shameful speech utters or a worthless act of a person devises for overthrowing the cause of peace. Among the confused sounds of the tongue, no one has ever regretted having remained silent.

For we frequently see even deeds of speech become a crime, and hatred succeed friendships through excessive readiness to speak. How can a person who is either boastful or abusive fail to be regarded as offensive? If you investigate this vice, it abounds especially in certain women, who, just as they do not hesitate to say shameful things, are likewise not embarrassed to hear what ought to cause modesty.

Yet we do not say these things so that someone should always hold back his voice with compressed lips and enclose the sound of his tongue in perpetual silence. Just as it is unpleasant for the excessively wicked to speak, so it is useless for the good always to remain silent. Therefore, whenever necessity requires, let us utter words of justice; let our mouth be seasoned.

### 7

But perhaps you say: “A person who is provoked cannot help responding at times.” One must plainly be silent when an improper speech troubles quiet lips, and one must speak when a friendly mouth commends the cause of peace. Thus both speaking and keeping silent are forms of perfection. In either case, the reason for words is to have maintained moderation.

It is a great thing to be silent, and a great thing to speak; but it belongs to the wise to govern both. For sometimes excessive silence is attributed to folly, just as excessive speech is referred to madness. If you ask my judgment on this matter, I would already prefer that someone be judged foolish through silence rather than insane through speaking too much.

Let us therefore speak, but with fear and trembling, remembering that an account must be rendered for every word (Matt. XII, 36), so that nothing unjust may come forth from our heart, nothing blasphemous proceed from our mouth, and nothing harmful remain in our thoughts. For besides those things by which the hearing is offended, the prophet chastises the inner conscience of certain people: “They spoke evil with deceitful lips and heart” (Ps. XI, 3).

Among the faults, therefore, of an insolent tongue are thoughts. For whatever you speak in your heart, you confess to the Lord, because God is the searcher of the heart. Consider, then, whether what you cry aloud can be hidden or excused from the one who cannot be unaware of what you think.

Therefore, dearly beloved, let our mouths be restrained by an equal bond with every care. Let the tongue utter nothing offensive; let no improper speech devise anything injurious; let there be nothing deceitful or treacherous in our heart, nothing harsh, nothing idle. For the Lord also said that an account must be rendered for idle words (Matt. XII, 36). Even if someone fortifies his life with faith, governs it by knowledge, and orders it with chastity and sobriety, there is nothing pleasing in a person if, throughout the whole body, the tongue alone is displeasing.

## 9. HOMILY VI. On Idle Words

### 1

Whenever, dearly beloved, in accordance with the duty entrusted to us, we have treated a matter of discipline, while wishing to pursue weightier concerns we have neglected certain lesser ones. Although these may seem easy to some, if you investigate them more carefully, they are found to be liable to many crimes. We must now extend a hand to them and labor with the diligence of medicine, so that each matter may recognize the faults arising from its own weakness.

Run, then, if you will, through each of those things that either serve punishment or flatter joy, and you will find that harmful venom reigns not only in fierce dragons but also lies hidden in the small bodies of bees. We have often said, dearly beloved, that drunkenness and desire are certain fountains of vice, from which some torrents of sin rush headlong and drag a very large part of the human race with them into the depths. From one side drunkenness feeds the whirlpool of gluttony; from the other, desire kindles the fury of wicked seizure. The former is the mother of pride, the latter of lust; one is the companion of falsehood, the other of deformity. Their concern is to commit murders, contrive adulteries, and destroy the foundations of friendships, while desire, through a kind of commerce in shamefulness, supplies payment for secret love, and drunkenness provides the opportunity.

### 2

But these things, dearly beloved, as we have sometimes said, you will be able to restrain with little effort if you first wish to cut away those things that provide fuel for sinning. It will not be difficult for you to suppress what follows if the vices at the beginning are condemned after being chastised. For the whole structure of the body will quickly fail if there is no one to supply food to the wicked belly.

Therefore, above all, the vices of drunkenness and desire must be chastised; among the rest, they claim the position of leadership, so that those things which serve them may be endangered by their own function. It is easy to dry up the water of even a very deep whirlpool if its source can be shut off.

Many things, dearly beloved, still come to mind concerning those matters we recall; but because we have sometimes fulfilled our duty in chastising them, we think that what has been said today may suffice by way of remembrance. Therefore, for the present, we shall refrain from those matters that appear to belong to the subject at hand, until we set forth the faults of those parts which seem easy to some.

### 3

You have heard the evangelist saying that an account must be rendered to the Lord for idle words (ibid.). If you look, dearly beloved, at the matters we have set forth and at those things we have sometimes said in chastising an undisciplined tongue, you understand that this statement concerns the insolence of the mouth. Although its utterances are called idle, they must not therefore be treated idly.

Let no one believe that the fault is trivial which the heavenly sentence of strict judgment attacks so forcefully. From this, finally, comes all that rumor falsely reports: idle words are always fruitless conversations recounting invented tales. What speech, however, should be considered idle except that which is ignorant of reason and a messenger of falsehood, whose concern is either to invent ridiculous stories or to regard uncertain things as though they were certain?

There is a kind of person who, while nourishing tales, does not know how to avoid lying. Let such people hear the Lord saying: “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. I, 11).

Idle words are figurative insults, devised with foolish exertion, sweet—as some think—but furnished with many blows and further armed with deadly punishments. For although they arouse merriment, they frequently give rise to hatred.

There are many things like these, dearly beloved, which perhaps should not be passed over, although among all the vices of words they may seem the least important.
