For example, if you call a dark-complexioned person “silvery,” the idle word commits an insult against his appearance: if you have spoken truthfully, you have accused him; if you have reported what is false, you have mocked him. When you call a person of tall stature and advanced age a child, do you not commit an insult if, suppressing the truth, you lie with childish intent? It belongs to insult if by your words you add anything to or take anything from the human body.

### 4

But perhaps you say that these things are sufficiently trivial and easy to bear. It is true. Such kinds of names are like inserting light feathers into someone else’s hair, or sprinkling flowing ashes or something dusty and white over the whole crown of a youthful head shining with the honor of its first growth. You do not weigh down the head, certainly, but you disfigure it.

Likewise, when hair is pulled out in jest, although it causes no pain, it nevertheless displays much ugliness. We must therefore be on guard, dearly beloved, lest one person injure another with theatrical speech and inflict shame upon a brother through stage-like words that damage his reputation.

Excessive cleverness of the mouth is accustomed to stir the movements of minds, and speech girded with laughter prepares a reciprocal insult. Thus even a small spark spits out flames, and, arising from nothing, frequently kindles great fires.

Idle speech is adequately nourished by an idle author. Therefore, since we have mentioned theatrical words, perhaps in the interest of discipline I should not keep silent about those things that capture curious ears with idle words and shake the secrets of the deepest breast while they flatter with rhythmic blows. These are the vices we mentioned earlier, composed with a certain sweetness of honey; this is the work by which, as we said, the bitter pains of wounds are produced with sweetness mixed in.

### 5

At this point someone may perhaps think that, for the sake of discipline, he should ask what those idle voices are that arouse insult and bring danger to those who hear them. You ask rightly, lest hearing be endangered through ignorance.

We frequently find, then, that the path of immodesty is fortified in this way and that fuel for adulteries is supplied from it: while one person brings forth the sounds of a ringing zither with an agile plectrum, another composes the alluring sounds of a laboring organ with a skillful finger. These are the snares by which the devil, employing them among his other wounds, brings about the deaths of human beings.

For whenever hearing is caressed by a sweet voice, the sight is invited to a shameful deed. Let no one trust seductive songs or look toward the incitements of a lustful voice: when they delight, they rage; when they flatter, they kill. Thus we frequently see birds deceived by gentle whistles and dull beasts driven into the snare of death by the sweetness of a voice.

The case of mortals is similar, dearly beloved, when care for sweet-sounding songs occupies them. In this way variations of voices and words prolonged without syllables serve so that a person may either be captured or capture another.

It cannot be explained, dearly beloved, how dangerous snares are displayed by the pursuits of mimetic pleasure. For if someone could search out the secrets of the human breast, he would find the hearts of the wretched sighing at each sound of the flute.

Understand, then, what excessively familiar and secret conversation between men and women can do; what joined proximity can do; what conversations mixed with jokes can do; what the appetite invited by delicacies can do; what hunger for gold, exposed to every crime of prostitution, can do—if even the flatteries of a mute voice deceive another’s madness.

### 6

This error of vocal sound must therefore be shunned: it has made bitterness for human breasts through its sweetness and has frequently mixed deadly poisons into the sick through the persuasion of honey-flowing song.

At this point, first of all, the ears must be closed, holding up the shield of faith, so that the hearing of every seductive voice may more easily be shut out. Discipline must also be applied, so that it may repel the desires of the eyes and restrain the incitements of the wasting heart.

For the evangelist teaches in this way, saying: “If your eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out” (Matt. V, 29). Let no one, dearly beloved, think that the meaning of this statement is that the Lord wishes to deform the human body, which he fashioned in his own likeness and established according to the form of his dignity. To pluck out the eyes means to cut away the shameful things in a person and restrain worthless acts through correction; to cut off lust by chastising its allurements; and to cut off the hands of wicked desire through the goodness of conscience.

The person who has cut off his hands is the one who has shattered within himself the weapons of unbelief and, by a just judgment, cut off the reeds of unbelief. It therefore contributes to the soul’s salvation if vices nourished by wicked acts are weakened and the sight of the impious eyes is torn out by the roots. The sting of death quickly finds rest in these things if you permit the matters I mentioned above to dominate intact and unharmed.

But so that we may accomplish these things more easily, Christ must be heard, for he says: “Leave all your possessions and follow me” (Matt. XIX, 21).

### 7

I know, dearly beloved, that those who are occupied with the affairs of the world undertake these things with difficulty; the use of this life is sweet to them. But if you investigate carefully, the world, full of vanity and clothed, so to speak, in a thin shadow, serves for a time, and this deceitful pomp of riches that you see flatters us.

Holy David knew this well, for he says: “Turn my eyes away, O Lord, lest they see vanity” (Ps. CXVIII, 37). What is this vanity except the cult of riches and the pursuits of worldly pleasures? Solomon confirms this when he says: “Vanity of vanities, every rich person” (Eccles. I, 2).

Therefore, dearly beloved, let no one trust in the vanity of this world, which he sees standing upon feeble foundations. Its display is temporary and empty, and its adornment is like smoke and wind. Such is the beauty of its face, as though you were looking upon the appearance of that vine which, adorned with the flower of the summer solstice, does not know how to produce the fruit of the promised vintage; while it labors excessively to give birth, it incurs the stain of perpetual barrenness.

### 8

A very different adornment is promised us, dearly beloved, for the time of eternal life, provided that a person walks poor in sins. The one who goes to Christ rich is the person who gathers the fruits of mercy and attacks the pursuits of foolish desire. He goes most wealthy to the heavens who excludes from himself the pomp of temporal vanity. He carries great riches with him to paradise who unloads his breast, burdened with vices, through devotion to religion.

Finally, he escapes all the poverty of beggary who daily sows the commandments of our Christ in his heart and fills the granaries of his breast, through vigilant faith, with the seeds of divine instruction. Thus, above all, restrain the freedom of that idle speech which, if it settles in among the pursuits of a religious life, will unquestionably prejudice holiness at the examination of the future judgment.

The best things in a person quickly become worthless unless, among the other matters requiring correction, the vices of the tongue mentioned above are diligently cut away.

[Col. 0713A]

# HOMILY VII. On Mercy

### 1

If we consider, dearly beloved, all the degrees of justice by which the work of religion is constructed, you will find no form of devoted service that does not acquire for its servant a place of honor before the Lord. Yet these very things, which faith works within us, although they advance through human labor, must be referred to the Lord, through whom and in whom whatever has been done well both stands firm and is preserved for future benefit.

Therefore, let no wise person attribute God’s gifts to his own virtues, lest he hear the Apostle’s statement: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (I Cor. IV, 7).

We know, dearly beloved, that according to the faith of the Gospels, which recalls the promises of blessedness, justice has made a place for human beings in heaven. That is, the grace of gentleness and humility obtained the promise of paradise and the promised land; purity of heart merited seeing Christ; mercy received a corresponding reward in return; the joy of peace prepared a place among the children of God for many; and the suffering of the saints acquired, through the merits of virtue, the crown of victory and the glory of the heavenly kingdom.

But all these things are wrought within us by one and the same power of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, which grants perfection to righteous labors and supplies whatever is best to a good will.

There is, however, one thing—indeed, a very great thing—that descends from the seat of mercy, in which mortal human beings may daily glory with justice: the refreshment of the poor and the redemption of captives, provided that neither boasting dissipates it nor thankless sadness disturbs it.

### 2

You have heard the evangelist saying: “Come, you blessed of my Father; possess with me the kingdom of heaven promised to you from the foundation of the world. I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was naked, and you clothed me” (Matt. XXV, 34–36).

You see, therefore, that if anyone ought to glory, he should glory only in this work, in which the Lord commands that he himself be fed and clothed, and each day asks that his hunger be satisfied by a small portion of broken bread.

If you wish your glorying not to be empty, let us first redeem the friendship of the supreme King through abundant almsgiving; and, so that the heavenly kingdom may be opened to us, let us direct every work of mercy toward the Lord. In love for him, the tears of the poor must not be treated idly or negligently, lest the one who is accustomed to feed the whole world appear, to our shame, to be hungry among beggars.

Consider, finally, the needs of each person and the concern of our Savior for the wretched; then you will understand that our Christ is there where you see an abundance of tears. You need not seek the Lord far away if you are not greedy. Behold, he awaits us outside with that crowd of his servants.

You need not wander with your eyes, uncertain about where you should principally expend the work of compassionate generosity. Know that the one is our Christ whom you see naked, whom you behold blind, whom you encounter lame, whom you see wrapped in rags, whom you see covered with filthy clothing.

It was in this clothing, finally, that he was found when the Magi were seeking him; and when he lay placed in the manger, wearing this appearance he received the gifts offered when the treasures were opened.

To this corresponds the evangelical statement that says: “Store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth destroys nor thieves break in and steal” (Matt. VI, 20). These are those treasures assigned to heavenly merits, which no adversity contaminates: that is, the substance of one’s resources distributed through the poor.

### 3

Hear, then, first in this matter my advice, whoever glories in an abundance of riches. If you fear the moth, entrust your riches; if you fear the thief, entrust them above. Behold, you have a trustworthy guardian who will preserve your wealth for you, destined to profit you forever and throughout the ages of ages.

He adds: “Do not store up treasures for yourselves on earth” (ibid., 19). It is not without reason, dearly beloved, that the Lord warns no one to entrust his treasure to the earth. For we frequently see hoarded things endangered by the faults of the earth and riches buried too deeply consumed by a kind of decay in the mud.

Therefore, I judge it more useful to lend than to hide, and to entrust something at interest rather than assign it to the earth. It is a form of foolishness to keep locked away what can prosper through manifold labor and provide the fruit of justice for the use of eternal life.

I warn, therefore, that no one should hide his treasure in the earth; that is, no one should think that the dignity of his heavenly soul ought to be assigned to earthly actions. The moth consumes the treasures of the person who serves vanity and establishes his life in the pomp of this world.

The moth, then, dearly beloved, is the worm of envy and avarice. It alone possesses the secret places of the heart; it alone consumes what has been heaped up in hidden places. Believe the thief to be the devil, who, in order to lie in wait for good works, flatters with the pomp of the world set before us. To exclude a person from fellowship with the heavenly kingdom, he places gold in his hands, sets silver before his eyes, and fastens gems around his neck.

Thus he nourishes pride and kindles the desires of the flesh with the spur of greed; these, as Scripture says, “sink a person into destruction” (I Tim. VI, 19).

Without doubt, the person who sends his treasures ahead to heaven relieves the abyss of punishments. Hear what the Lord offers: “Come, you blessed of my Father; possess with me the kingdom promised to you from the foundation of the world. I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was naked, and you clothed me” (Matt. XXV, 34, 36).

After this voice, who would doubt that he should depart from this world with the whole pomp of his patrimony? Vanity is plainly a folly, a vice in the choice of merits: to choose the world rather than the heavenly kingdom, and to please the world rather than Christ.

Therefore, if anyone wishes to find a place in the heavenly dwelling, let him not cease to supply what is necessary to those in need.

### 4

But perhaps someone will say: “My resources are small; they do not permit such great expenses of generosity.” If someone offered you a splendid house belonging to this temporary possession, would you not heap up money from every side to pay the price? And if perhaps the weight of your purse were insufficient, would you not acquire what you needed with borrowed money until you could rejoice in possessing an estate enlarged with new ground?

Behold, possession of the heavenly kingdom is offered to you, and it is assessed at a small price—one that can easily be paid even by the person who is not accustomed to plead poverty. Let us see, then, what is demanded from you as the price: food, drink, and clothing. In these matters, I find no one who does not possess something that can be distributed daily.

If you investigate, perhaps your granaries abound in kinds of grain, and new wine cellars are commended by the reputation of their old flavor. What good does it do you to preserve these things if you do not know how to pursue profitable commerce?

But you say: “I am poor.” Will you be able, under this plea, to excuse yourself before those for whom you set aside the prices of provisions because of the scarcity of the times? You accuse the smallness of your resources without cause: can you have something to sell, but not something to give?

It was not said without reason: “Break your bread for the hungry” (Isa. LVIII, 7). I think this statement applies to inhuman people, whose stored and untouched loaves decay and are consumed by rot. Break your bread, therefore, for the hungry, lest it perish and exclude you from fellowship with the heavenly kingdom.

He adds: “And do not despise those of your own seed” (ibid.). Who are those of our household? Necessarily, all those joined to us by the law of birth.

Why is it that, in giving alms, no person is to be excluded and no selective judgment is to be made? Because a thing that serves necessity does not require an order of distribution. Why do you need to ask whether the person who requests is Christian or Jew, heretic or pagan, Roman or barbarian, free or enslaved? Where necessity presses, there is no need to examine the person, lest, when you exclude those deemed unworthy of mercy, you likewise lose the Son of God.

How, moreover, can we know in what part of the earth Christ dwells? He must be believed to be everywhere, since he is known to possess the whole world.

### 5

The preceding passage continues: “Then your timely light will break forth, your garments will rise before you, justice will go before you, and the glory of God will surround you. Then you will call, and the Lord will answer you. While you are still speaking, he will say, ‘Behold, here I am’” (ibid., 8–9).

And all this is because of a piece of broken bread. How much more do you think you will acquire if you provide greater things?

Hear the evangelist saying: “Blessed are the merciful, for God will have mercy on them” (Matt. V, 7). There are indeed many degrees of mercy, but we must ask which are the chief ones.

The highest forms of mercy are to extend a hand to the fallen, to show the erring the way of salvation, to visit the sick, and to remain beside those in tribulation with consolations. But what must especially be expected is to feed the hungry, clothe the naked, redeem the captive, and lend what is necessary for a time to one who does not possess it.

We also sometimes find many kinds of mercy by which human endeavors commonly commend themselves. Although these offer no fruit of mercy, they nevertheless pretend to be motivated by mercy. Of these James says in his Epistle: “If a brother or sister is naked and lacks daily food, and one of you says to them, ‘Go in peace, be warmed and filled,’ but you do not give them what is necessary for the body, what good will it do you?” (James II, 15–16).

Who would not hate such a kind of mercy, in which the elegance of the mouth idly flatters the weak with piety and fruitless tears are offered to heaven? What good does it do to weep over another’s shipwreck if you neglect the exposed body? Or what benefit is there in torturing your spirit with grief over another’s wound if you deny the cup of healing?

Smooth words do not feed the hungry, nor do fruitless counsels clothe another’s nakedness. What good does it do to caress a beggar with gentle soothing if you do not refresh someone dying of hunger? What kind of mercy is it to wish a person to live but not to wish to preserve him in his necessity? Truly cruel is the piety that knows how to grieve for the wretched but does not know how to aid those who are perishing.

### 6

What more do you seek, dearly beloved, in exchange for the distribution of broken bread? Even if the portion of the heavenly kingdom had not been promised to you, that statement should be sufficient for sinners which has brought mortals the hope of future salvation and the joy of perpetual security.

For if you consider the fruits of your labor and the indulgence of heavenly mercy, you receive much more than you give. Behold, in the Gospels the kingdom of heaven is promised to you in exchange for feeding the poor; in exchange for distributing broken bread, offering lodging, or clothing the naked body, the Lord promises, through the prophets, his aid to those who call upon him (Isa. LVIII, 9). In the Psalms, the justice of your mercy is established forever and ever (Ps. CXI, 9).

If we compare earthly things with heavenly ones, so precious a matter is obtained at a sufficiently small price; or how large a part is your almsgiving in comparison with what the Lord appears to have granted mortals? Behold, we give earthly things, while he gives heavenly things; we offer temporal things, while he bestows eternal ones.

Do you wish to know how far your wealth falls short of heavenly gifts? In comparison with these benefits, it is not the same thing to receive everlasting riches and to give what was destined to perish.

Above all, we must attend to those tears which the fury of cruel hostility recently caused. There is no lack of work in which good will may exercise itself. Indeed, what is worse, we see many people anxious for the redemption of themselves and their own, and we must extend a hand to them.

But you say: “I am poor.” We do not urge anyone to give what he does not have. But if someone’s resources are so limited that he cannot redeem a captive, let him at least add what is very little to the price, so that, even with a small coin, he may appear to have fulfilled the command.

# HOMILY VIII. Also on Mercy

### 1

Many matters arising from the evangelical reading draw the mind in different directions. If we wished to arrange them under the presentation of a single subject, it would be necessary for one matter to impede another and for the understanding of one concern to exclude that of another. How could the intelligence either of the speaker or of the hearer avoid being hindered by great confusion among many matters?

Among the other things, therefore, dearly beloved, which the evangelist recalls as having received the grace of blessedness according to their merits, we have meanwhile thought it right to set forth among you the matter of mercy, which requires the fruit of daily work. We shall treat the rest at their proper times, when necessity requires, so that each matter may stand firmly established with its own powers and not require the subject matter of another.

Behold, the Lord says: “Blessed are the merciful, for God will have mercy on them” (Matt. V, 7). I am astonished if, after this statement, anyone hesitates to spend his money, when he sees that profits answer just acts of kindness.

What good does it do to guard a mass of accumulated gold in a purse, when you can daily both do good and receive interest on money spent? “Blessed are the merciful, for God will have mercy on them.” Rejoice, dearly beloved, and give securely; spend without hesitation.

Who would not distribute his wealth eagerly through generous gifts to the poor, when he understands that he will receive manifold fruits and double gifts? Finally, the Lord judged those people blessed in this life to whom he promised mercy in the future.

### 2

Hear the Lord saying elsewhere: “Give to everyone who asks you” (Luke VI, 30). It is not without purpose, dearly beloved, that the Lord commands alms to be given to everyone who asks. He knew that sometimes good people necessarily lie hidden even among the wicked; and for that reason he mingled the good and the wicked together, lest, when an excessively cautious distribution passed by those deemed unworthy, someone worthy of mercy should also depart without a gift.

There is no distinction to be made among those who ask, nor is the poverty of the poor person to be investigated. The fruit of the giver, not of the recipient, is being sought. It does not matter to whom you give when he asks; the Lord does not inquire whether the person who requests deserves it, but asks how much the giver provides.

Hear the Apostle speaking on this matter: “Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly” (I Cor. IX, 6). We benefit ourselves whenever we assist the wretched; the distribution of our resources is our profit.

For if you look to the hope of future recompense, whatever is supplied to the hungry is lent at interest, as the prophet says: “Blessed is the one who understands concerning the needy and the poor; on the evil day the Lord will deliver him” (Ps. XL, 1).

Christ is guarantor of all these things, for he says: “I will repay you a hundredfold” (Matt. XIX, 29). In addition, eternal life is promised, while the severity of judgment is reserved for impiety and greed. Thus the evangelist says:

“When the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all the angels with him, then he will separate all from one another, the sheep on the right and the goats on the left. He will say to those on his right: ‘Come, my children, possess with me the kingdom of heaven. I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was a guest, and you welcomed me; I was naked, and you clothed me.’ He will say to those on his left: ‘Depart from me, accursed ones, into eternal fire. I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink’” (Matt. XXV, 31–32, 34–36, 41–42).

Let us therefore reflect, dearly beloved, and take care lest the recompense of impiety find us. For just as the Lord is appeased when the poor are fed and clothed, so he is injured by contempt for the wretched. His concern for the unhappy is so great that he considers whatever clothes or refreshes a needy person to have been given to himself.

[Col. 0718A] **3.** Hear Solomon saying: “My son, do good to yourself; shut up almsgiving in the bosom of the poor” (Ecclus. XXIX, 15). Therefore, whoever wishes to provide for his own interests should feed the poor willingly. There is no lack of opportunity for you to make a daily profit, if you consider the need of another’s poverty. For Scripture says: “Almsgiving and faith purge away sins” (Prov. XV, 27). Behold, one asks for food with a famished mouth; another, in his nakedness, testifies that he lacks miserable clothing. He is sufficiently cruel and exceedingly hard whom pain does not touch when some part of his body is tormented by weakness, nakedness, or poverty. He clearly looks poorly after himself who does not attend to the cause of another’s need.

Your riches are of no benefit to you if you do not make use of the benefits of riches. For it is a form of beggary to possess money accumulated in secret. Do you not know that whoever does not sow receives no harvest, according to the statement we mentioned above: “He who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly” (II Cor. IX, 6)? This, then, is the principle of cultivating the soil: the more seed a person entrusts to the earth, the greater the hope that grows for future harvests. He who does not sow watches others reap with idle hands. For whoever has labored more than the other farmers will store up more.

How can it happen that one who has entrusted seed continually to the earth through multiplied furrows should look upon his granaries as empty? What profit is it for you to lie upon accumulated riches if you gain no return from them? Finally, we often see a mass of grain consumed by long age, and wines spoiled by time thrown away because they will be useful for nothing in the future. We understand that the one thing which has sometimes benefited its owner more is that which the farmer is accustomed to lend to the needy for the sake of renewing his stock. Whatever avarice has preserved is either ruined by excessive heat, consumed by thankless age, or corrupted by destructive moths. A person stores up for himself only whatever he has spent for the sake of compassion. For thus the Lord says: “Store up treasures for yourselves in heaven, where neither moth consumes nor thieves break in and steal” (Matt. VI, 20).

**4.** Let us therefore take care, beloved, lest the worm of avarice destroy our resources. Let us send our wealth ahead to that place where no thief may break in and no attacker set it on fire. Let us entrust our riches to the Lord, who says: “Do not store up treasures for yourselves on earth” [Col. 0718D] (ibid., 19). Whoever has faithfully spent his resources in God’s work keeps them stored and deposited in heaven under a trustworthy guarantor.

Let no wise person look toward the ornaments of this age: while they temporarily serve human desires, they mock the souls of their possessors. There are two kinds of riches: one that persuades toward death, and another that leads to life. The riches of death are to lie upon another’s resources and to count money amassed through the tears of the wretched as destined to benefit the inheritances of this world. There are also those whole and incorruptible riches by which souls are redeemed and sins are cleansed. Those riches are acceptable to God by whose generosity the poor are fed, the naked clothed, captives redeemed, the bound [Col. 0719A] released, and the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom acquired. I do not want those riches which, through their daily increase, produce hunger and, stripped in the future of the flower of their dignity, make their lovers suffer hunger.

**5.** Let us finally return to the Scriptures, and you will understand that, in comparison with riches, poverty stands in the better condition. For, in condemning avarice, the Lord represents a certain rich man in the underworld as pleading with Abraham our father that he send the beggar Lazarus, seated in a higher place, to cool his mouth and quench his lips burning with thirst. The answer given to him is recorded as follows: “Son, remember that you received good things in your lifetime, and Lazarus likewise evil things; but now he is comforted, while you are suffering torment” (Luke XVI, 25).

You see that certain reversals await the pursuits of good and evil people, and that it is fitting to forestall them through the practice of mercy, lest unprofitable riches kindle against themselves the flames that avenge their crimes. Let us therefore prepare for ourselves, beloved, a place of grace before the Lord, and fortify the road of our life with generosity and liberality. Let us cleanse the stain of our affections before the Lord by offering satisfaction in advance, looking toward that prophetic saying which declares: “Those who sow in tears will reap in joy” (Ps. CXXV, 5).

If anyone carefully questions his own conscience, let him not think that these words may be received with idle ears. For on that day of the future judgment you will be unable to find refreshment in any other way unless you have either healed your wounds by restoring the poor or washed them in a flood of tears. Weep more abundantly yourselves, and distribute your resources to those who weep, so that in the time to come, among the others who reap joys, you may gather the fruits of mercy.

# HOMILY IX. On the Same Subject of Mercy

**1.** Whenever, beloved, it is necessary to admonish your charity in the pursuit of religion, that saying from the Gospel reading repeatedly comes before us which distinguishes between the good and the wicked at the future judgment. Whoever neglects it will reap tears; whoever cultivates it will acquire exceedingly abundant fruits of joy. Thus the evangelist says: “When the Lord comes in his majesty and separates the wicked from the good, he will say to those who are on his right: Come, possess with me the kingdom of heaven. I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink.” He will also say to those on his left: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into eternal fire. I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink” (Matt. XXV, 31 ff.).

Therefore, beloved, whoever among you desires to come to the fellowship of the heavenly kingdom should first extend a hand to poverty and not idly look upon another’s tears, because a sentence of recompense awaits each person, whether for good work or for evil, as the Lord says: “Whatever a person sows, that he will also reap” (Gal. VI, 8).

Among the other things, beloved, to which we devote our efforts in the zeal of a religious life, let us not neglect the needs of the poor, lest we lose the commerce of the wretched’s tears. For this is the principle governing money distributed through the miserable before the Lord: the more a person spends, the more interest he stores up. Thus many seeds produce many crops, and multiplied harvests rise from many sowers. Hear the Lord also saying concerning this: “He who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly” (II Cor. IX, 6).

If, then, you see that the one who sows little will reap little, so also the one who spends little will receive little; the one who sows nothing stores up nothing. Thus it happens that the one who stores up little is often unwillingly hungry. How can a person see his granaries full of great crops if he entrusts no seed to the earth? If you wish, then, to gather the fruits of joy, let us sow more generously in tears: “He who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly.”

**2.** We frequently find a person who, after giving alms once to someone who is hungry, believes that he has fulfilled the commandment. It is not enough, therefore, to restore limbs weakened by hunger with the food of a single day; a person is good to no purpose on one day if on the next he becomes ungrateful. For he has lost the benefit of his preceding mercy who thinks that what he gave once is sufficient for the hungry person.

But the one who sends whole fruits of mercy ahead to the Lord is he from whom the poor never depart sorrowful. A physician needs continual medicine so that the groans of another’s pain may be driven away, because an illness that grows day by day requires medicine day by day. Nor should we take less care to ensure that, through abundant almsgiving, we cure whatever is bloody or filthy in us. Wounds are not immediately healed merely because you have washed them once. Often the treatment of an excised part of the body must be repeated.

If you wish, beloved, that no day of our lives be stained by the guilt of avarice, let us not close our ears to the cry of the wretched, nor turn our eyes away from the nakedness of the miserable. Let no one think that what he has given to the poor is lost. For just as beggary follows inhumanity, so wealth is acquired through the practice of humanity, as the prophet says: “He who gives to the poor will never lack; but he who turns away his face will be in the greatest poverty” (Prov. XXVIII, 27).

Behold, the cry of the hungry rebukes your ears, and the sound of a failing voice assails your door with its famished mouth. Why does that saying not come to your mind: “Blessed is the one who understands concerning the needy and poor; on the evil day the Lord will deliver him” (Ps. XL, 1)? It is clear that the merchant who keeps a coin hidden in a purse, from which he can conduct no transaction, is a very foolish one.

**3.** But what is worse, many things agree with avarice. One person, to prevent himself from having pity on the poor, drowns out the voice of those asking with a disturbance of words; another, so that he will not hear, pretends to have heard something else. It is a sufficiently wretched condition of life that, while a person is devoted to avarice, he tries to impose heaviness upon his own ears.

Look to the saying that declares: “He who has mercy on the poor lends to the Lord” (Prov. XIX, 16). Why, then, should anyone hesitate to feed the needy when he sees that, in feeding the poor person, he is contributing this to Christ our Lord?

There are some who mock miserable beggary with the hope of delayed kindness. When they are ashamed to make excuses to those who ask, they deceive the wretched by making promises. Behold, one says: “The key is missing; the steward is absent. As soon as you return, you will receive it.” Do you not consider Solomon’s saying: “Do not say, ‘Go and come back; tomorrow I will give,’ when you can do good at once” (Prov. III, 28)?

How do you know what may happen on the following day? You say, “As soon as he returns, you will receive it.” When will that be—for the hungry person, until your steward returns, though perhaps he is frequently absent because you wish it? When will it be that those tiresome bolts of your private chambers, which serve your will and do not know how to open, spring apart before the one who cries out?

You say, “When you return, you will receive it.” But what if a storm harsher than usual beats upon the naked person? What if the limbs weakened by hunger are overtaken by the approach of death? Who would not judge that the person whom he sees could have been saved by your kindness was consigned to death by your judgment?

“When you return, you will receive it.” On whose word does one return whom all strength has abandoned? Or with what hope does one return home who departed confused the day before?

**4.** Let us suppose that he returns in a condition that enables him to satisfy your promise, perhaps under the same terms as yesterday. It is plainly much more just to deny alms at once than to deceive a hungry person with a promised hope.

Hear the Lord saying: “Break your bread for the hungry” (Isa. LVIII, 7–9). If you wish, beloved, let us ask with what reward broken bread is repaid. Behold, the Lord says: “Break your bread for the hungry; if you see someone naked, clothe him; and do not despise those of your own flesh. Then your timely light will break forth, your garments will quickly arise, righteousness will go before you, and the glory of God will surround you. Then you will cry out, and God will hear you; and while you are still speaking, he will say, ‘Behold, I am here.’”

See, beloved, how little the expenditure of a small gift costs us, so that the Lord of such majesty may deign to come to our petition. For elsewhere he also says: “Whoever gives one of these least ones a cup of cold water, truly I tell you, his reward will not perish” (Matt. X, 42).

Here, willingness is required, not means. In great matters, the person who displays a vow of compassion in small things shows the fullness of his devotion. Therefore, beloved, let each person distribute, give, and spend according to what he has and is able.

Let no one shun the lame; let no one pretend not to have heard the deaf person; let no one withdraw his hand from the weak, because all these things have their place in recompense. To clothe a poor person is to cover the nakedness of his body; to refresh a beggar, however, is great profit. For thus the Lord says: “Whatever you have done for one of these least ones, you have done for me” (Matt. XXV, 10).

For such is the care of the miserable before our Lord that he considers whatever compassionate generosity has bestowed upon the needy to have been bestowed upon himself. We sometimes see, amid the commerce of abundant wine and grain, needy widows whom sex and old age have overcome and who possess neither the strength to work nor the power to provide for themselves. He is sufficiently impious whom neither the unhappiness of desolation nor the weakness of old age moves to mercy.

We see, and what is worse, that frequently a multitude of captives wander about with naked bodies. What benefit is your abundance of riches to you if, in your presence, one person is cold and another hungry?

[Col. 0722A] **5.** Behold, beloved, the time of just recompense and the promised gift of inheritance in heaven is approaching. Let us therefore distribute and spend in this world, if you wish to possess a share of riches in heaven. Hear the Lord saying: “Store up treasures for yourselves in heaven” (Matt. VI, 20); and elsewhere: “Make for yourselves purses that do not grow old” (Luke XII, 33).

Well, beloved, Christ our Lord has arranged the fruit of good works according to the measured quality of one’s resources, so that in giving alms neither rich nor poor can excuse himself. Thus he commanded the one who possessed very much to distribute treasures, while he commanded the one whom he knew to be filthy with the squalor of poverty to break bread for the hungry.

What granaries are so empty that they cannot bear so small an expense of giving? What resources are so meager that a beggar could disturb them? The person upon whom nothing beyond his ability has been imposed can easily and without difficulty fulfill the commandment.

I know that scant resources often obstruct good will, so that there is no room in which a person may extend the work of a precious intention. But if we cannot fulfill the things that are greater, let us at least not neglect those that are small and easy: “Break your bread for the hungry.”

Who could fail to answer this with a devoted heart, even if he is oppressed by poverty and groans beneath the whole burden of beggary? Otherwise, he is either excessively poor or exceedingly vain who, in giving alms, is not content with the distribution of broken bread.

But you say: “Many small portions distributed little by little make a whole.” It is true. But how much is this compared with what the Lord says: “I will repay you a hundredfold, and, in addition, eternal life” (Matt. XIX, 29)?

Yet you, who so unwillingly extend a little portion of broken bread, what would you do if a weight of gold, a precious talent of silver, or something whole were requested of you? I do not know whether you would ever redeem a captive at a great price, since you groan over so small a matter.

“He who has mercy on the poor lends to the Lord” (Prov. XIX, 16). Therefore, beloved, I urge you: let no one withhold from God a portion of his riches. Through just labors he receives without difficulty the fruit of a good work, when he repays the reward of mercy with multiplied compassion. Let us therefore not hesitate to distribute; let us not pretend not to spend. For among those who cultivate the earth there has always been the greatest hope of sustaining life by sowing abundantly.

[Col. 0722D]

# HOMILY X. On Parasites

**1.** Whenever, beloved, in the interest of discipline and for the shame of the wicked, it has been necessary to set forth the virtues of the good, we have shown great honor to friendships, praising each one according to its merits and preferring the practices of fraternal union, which, joined in the fellowship of peace and charity, establish a life of perfect religion.

But while I persistently investigate the causes of individual matters and adapt the duty of speech to honorable actions, I have found much in these very friendships that displeased me. Therefore, lest I seem to have subtracted anything from discipline while praising good associations, I have dared to rebuke even friendships among the faults of enmity—if they are to be called friendships where injury operates through many wounds.

Here, perhaps, some may put forward a game as an excuse for the hateful disgrace of the practice, and give the name of joy to matters deserving punishment. Let whoever is accustomed to suffer such insults bear this with whatever attitude he wishes. I consider friendships to have surpassed every kind of captivity where it is proper neither for the injured person to grow angry nor for the angry person to seek vengeance.

Here, beloved, I do not know which of two wretched men to judge the more unfortunate: the one who lives by another’s disfigurement, or the one who exposes his own body to ridicule and delivers it over to mockery. Let no one impose upon me the name of patience in such matters. The punishment that the injury of an angry enemy does not extort certainly belongs to lust.

Perhaps pardon should be granted to those whom poverty drives into every insult and wretched want compels to submit to luxurious beatings—those who, while serving necessity, yield to abuse. Grant that the cause of depraved poverty teaches these people patience; what are we to judge concerning those whom another’s insult feeds? What kind of friendship is this, bound by punishment and made harsh by injury? Or what affection of familiarity can there be where punishment is daily for sale?

**2.** I am indeed ashamed, beloved, at the confusion of the wretched whom hunger has lured into depraved desire; but I sigh much more over the conduct and companionship of those among whom punitive friendship has removed sadness, and bloody love of familiarity has demanded joy.

I judge those unfortunate whom the belly invites to continual insult and gluttony, never to be satisfied by drinking, provokes to every injury. But I consider those much more unfortunate who, at the instigation of a friend, arrange fights and, among cups flowing with wine, are sated with another’s blood.

Behold, one has established a banquet and, with a kind of ceremonial preparation, has gathered crowds of flatterers from every side. Among them proceeds the appetite of the parasites, whose custom it is to sell injury for wine and mend garments torn by blows with drinking cups.

See, then, how these people endure the causes of hatred, among whom it is pleasing that friendships should be bloody. What does wretched and destructive luxury not discover? Behold, one human being becomes a spectacle for another, and, to arouse amusement, either shameful speech or a face deliberately made hideous is demanded.

Finally, one person’s beard is plucked while he eats; another’s seat is taken away while he drinks; one is fed with split wood, another with fragile glass. So great is the lust for laughter that these wretched people think no banquet passes without joy unless they have turned either the clothing of bodies or the service of drinking vessels into food.

How many miseries do you think these things cost? Whatever damage the table has done, the insatiable belly acquires. For the person who serves such pleasures either destroys the reward of his labor by drinking or consumes it by being beaten.

**3.** But above all these things must be charged to those who, for the sake of amusement, incline friendship and familiarity toward such a foul service. Before the Lord, the servitude that obeys an assigned duty according to the law of standing is certainly in a better condition. Among those reclining at table, there is a place for laughter, yet no guilt of sin is imposed upon the person standing by and waiting.

Behold, a battle line of drinking vessels is drawn up, armed with weapons. First, victory in a contest of words is awaited; nor is an end put to it until every harshness is tempered by abundant cups. To await the fights of wretched friends is rather to pollute than to adorn a banquet, if indeed those are to be called friends who serve under the law of captives and are fed in the manner of gladiators.

Amid the novelties of foods and the fluids of wine, whatever is cheaper and whatever is harsher is given to the wretched, so that amid such abundance of things it is uncertain whether it is better to hunger or thirst.

Captivity assigned to dark dwellings is plainly less exposed to mockery. Although a person there endures the harsh command of domination, he nevertheless receives consolation from the very necessity of his circumstances. For the one who must serve unwillingly has nothing in which he can be ashamed.

Yet I should like to know, beloved, in what way injury inflicted through another’s deformity refreshes the mind of the person who waits. Perhaps the lovers of this practice will claim that such things are provided as jokes—as though there were truly any lack of material from which a person might seek amusement.

**4.** I will show you, if you please, wholesome entertainments that can easily remove all the sadness of a languishing spirit. Consider the marvelous beginnings of speech in infants: when the first shapeless letter forms the word “mother,” and the separated syllable’s cry begins the name of “father.” Who would not be joyful there, when, amid the hard rudiments of speech, an untrained tongue stumbles over struggling sounds, and a trembling mouth fails to produce its drooping words?

If you happen to delight in spectacles, you have horse races—though sometimes dangerous, nevertheless sufficiently pleasing—when, with swift strides, the horses either fear the winds or carry them away beneath the blows. Nor do the pursuits of hunting contribute little joy, with contests carried on by dogs, which are exposed neither to danger nor to loss: one, in the struggle of rival courses, presses upon the long-eared hare; another, with keen nostrils, searches out the tracks of a hidden stag.

Yet such things should be left to the world, in which luxury burns with its ancient error. We, however, ought to live differently, for Christ our Lord has bound us by his laws and separated us from the folly of superstitious paganism. Nor are spectacles lacking for us—spectacles that relieve sadness and sufficiently entertain a mind anxious with cares.

**5.** Let us place before our eyes those battles of the martyrs and contemplate examples of admirable virtues; then you will see all the heat of wretched spirits suddenly yield as joy increases. Who would not find joy in a battle in which victory succeeds on the side of justice, a battle which the savage enemy prepared in the persecution of the saints by applying the goads of torments?

Who, then, would not laugh, who would not be joyful, when he sees a soldier of Christ our Lord exulting amid punishments, while the author of the persecution blushes and the torturer, overcome by blows, gives way?

If anyone happens to delight in the sound of sweet singing, let him turn his attentive heart more widely toward the choirs of the prophets as they sing psalms. Let our mouth be filled with the heavenly exultation of psalms, giving thanks through Christ our Lord, who, by restoring the hope of salvation, willed us continually to exult in honor of his name.

Let this be the exultation of our heart: that day and night we rejoice in the Lord. To exult, however, means to serve the Lord’s commandments with one’s whole mind. And the person who guards his life from every contagion of vices serves the Lord’s commandments.

He guards his life who shows faithfulness to his neighbors, loves peace, and cherishes friendships. To cherish friendships means to endure another’s anger with the discipline of moderation and to temper a brother’s heated spirit through patience.

Thus it is: you will walk blameless among others at the future judgment if, in all these matters we have mentioned, you prove yourself corrected through Christ our Lord.

# HOMILY XI. “Let the One Who Boasts Boast in the Lord”

**1.** They do not think rightly, beloved, who suppose that the ornaments of life are fashioned by personal labor and that the merits of virtue can be acquired without the assistance of almighty God. If the fact that we are good belongs to us alone, why are we subject to vices? Or if everything that can adorn or save a person proceeds from us, why are we confined under the law of perishing?

He has certainly exceeded every measure of sacrilegious superstition who takes away from God a share in righteous labors—God from whom we have received the spirit of wisdom, who governs the whole person and kindles the minds of mortals toward every good work, and to whom belongs whatever descends from that seat of righteousness.

Therefore all the distinctions of our labors must be referred to God, lest anyone destroy the gifts of the Holy Spirit. It is a fault of excessive presumption for a soldier to wish to carry off the palm of victory alone while the emperor is fighting.

Certainly, if you wish, you can recognize to whom evils and to whom good things ought to be attributed, as the prophet says: “You have dealt graciously with your servant, O Lord” (Ps. CXVIII, 65). And elsewhere: “The fool said in his heart, ‘There is no God’” (Ps. XIII, 1).

You see, therefore, that we ought to ascribe our good things to the Divinity, but attribute evil to human conduct, because just as good things are created by the Lord’s provision, so evil things arise through the devil as their author.

**2.** But so that you may understand that life is God’s gift and death is subject to the devil, hear the evangelist saying: “Come, children, possess with me the kingdom promised to you from the foundation of the world. I was hungry, and you gave me food” (Matt. XXV, 34, 35). But to others he says: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into eternal fire, because you did not give me food” (ibid., 41).

See, therefore, that good deeds serve heaven, while evil deeds are assigned to the dwelling places of hell. The division of our actions is this: when we do good, we belong to Christ; when we do evil, we pass into the power of the devil.

The Lord never abandons a will flourishing through zeal for religion; nor are the consolations of divinity absent where there are acts of good conduct. Good things abandon us only when worse things succeed them, because we are plainly deprived of divine help after we have become occupied with desires of iniquity.

When God and our Savior assist us, the dominion of diabolical power is undoubtedly absent. But when the Lord of virtues departs, the enemy easily invades the palace of an empty possession. There is therefore one hope of our salvation: that we attribute the order of evil acts to ourselves and ascribe good acts to God’s virtues. The person who has not deserved to obtain the consolations of divine majesty quickly admits into himself the rule of diabolical power.

**3.** We must therefore hope in the Lord that we may be good; and when we have become good, we must boast in the Lord. Hear the Apostle saying: “What do you have that you did not receive? If you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (I Cor. IV, 7).

This is the perfect glorying of our actions: to glory in the Lord, with whom the crown of victory is prepared for those who conquer through virtue. A person ought indeed to glory in himself where voluntary punishment of the cross succeeds for the name of the Lord. Yet this glorying bears fruit only if, with Christ’s help, it achieves its purpose.

For the prophet says here: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain; those who guard it keep watch in vain” (Ps. CXXVI, 1). You see, therefore, that what is good cannot be built without the Lord, nor can what has been built be guarded without the Lord.

The building of this divine house is the building of our life, which must be fortified by the help of the divine majesty. Christ our Lord must therefore always be entreated to nourish good things in us and besought to guard what he has nourished; and he must so order the hearts of our understanding that all good things may be assigned to the power of heavenly glory.

**4.** It is a kind of foolishness for a person to judge that what he has labored for belongs to him when he remains in another’s power. Behold, one moment he exults in riches, the next he sighs in poverty. If our good things are in our hands, why does want not cease when we wish, or riches endure when we wish?

One moment a person is lifted up by the strength of health, the next he is afflicted by the pain of illness. If the safety of our life were in human power, a beggar would never be endangered, nor would the sick person die.

Finally, let each person examine the beginnings of his own life and seek the author of the human race: who formed the body, who fashioned the limbs, who caused earthly matter to grow for human use. Did not the Lord establish all these things through the provision of Wisdom?

Since what we are is not ours, how can what we possess be ours? It is a kind of foolishness that, while owing the benefit of life to another, a person ascribes to himself the ornaments of virtue.

Behold, one is exalted by honor; another flatters himself over the integrity of his body; one attributes riches to his labor; another assigns knowledge to the vigils of study. Nor can we deny that the ornaments of a religious life are acquired through the practice of vigilance. But God is present where the mind possesses complete religion, as the Apostle says: “Are you seeking proof of the Christ who speaks in me?” (II Cor. XIII, 3).

Human effort plainly falters where God’s help is not sought. For faith is undoubtedly endangered if it is not fortified by the protection of divinity.

[Note: [Col. 0725D] See below the letter of Sirmond placed after these homilies of Valerian, § 2, together with the sayings of the earlier Fathers appended to it.]

It is ours to will what is good; it is Christ’s to bring it to completion. For the Apostle speaks thus: “To will is present with me, but to accomplish the good I do not find” (Rom. VII, 18).

You see, therefore, that the will for a good work ought to proceed from us, but its perfection depends upon God’s power. Why, then, should any mortal attribute the doing of good solely to his own effort, when the prophet says: “There is none who does good, not even one” (Ps. XIII, 3), and the Evangelist likewise teaches that there is none good except God alone (Matt. XIX, 17)?

Therefore you see that whenever we seem to be good, we are carrying out the goodness of God. Hear the Apostle saying: “You are the temple of God, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you” (I Cor. III, 16). We are certainly God’s temple—but when we do good. If a human being is God’s temple, then necessarily what we possess in the temple belongs to God.

**5.** But we have said these things concerning the good. Yet it is not God’s temple where a multitude of vices has gathered. For wherever crimes are practised, there the devil rules.

The pomp of riches belongs to the one who claims the position of master for himself in a great house. We act in the place of stewards: if we have made a profit, it will be reported to the master; if there is a loss, it will be reported to the steward’s destruction. Whatever a servant placed under his master’s power has labored over necessarily belongs to the master.

The servant indeed has the master’s favor for his labor, but he owes the fruit of the completed work to the master. Finally, money is entrusted to a useful servant for this purpose: that the profits of doubled interest may be counted out to the master.

**6.** Look, then, to the custom of human affairs, and you will understand that money is entrusted to a useful servant for this purpose: that the profits of doubled interest may be counted out to the master. For thus the evangelist says here that the servant brought to his master, returning from abroad, the profit of money made fourfold (*quadruplicatae*; the accompanying note corrects this to “doubled,” *duplicatae*):

“‘Well done, good servant, because you were faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your master’” (Matt. XXV, 23).

Thus the master is praised in the good servant, and the good servant is commended in the master. Therefore we must beware lest we ever ascribe to our own virtues what belongs to the glory of a good work, knowing that the crown of victory is not prepared through boasting, but through faith and confession of the Lord’s Passion, to which the pursuit of good works responds.

This is the money to which we said the benefits of the heavenly kingdom correspond. This is the business multiplied at just interest. This is the recompense owed to merits and promised to blessed labors.

[Note: [Col. 0727D] Correct with me and read “doubled,” from the text of Scripture itself. COTELER, *Monumenta Ecclesiae Graecae*, vol. II, p. 545b. The restoration is confirmed by what the author soon adds [Col. 0728D]: “This is that business doubled at just interest.”]

**7.** Let piety, faith, mercy, and goodness therefore be multiplied in us, so that when the Lord comes to settle accounts with his servants, we may enter into the joy of the Lord our God. We can easily obtain this if we preserve the heavenly commandments to the end.

But we must not labor carelessly, so that we may be judged worthy of the reward. Honorable things easily follow righteous actions, provided that depraved pleasures do not seize the mind—pleasures that readily vanish into the winds if the consolations of the divine majesty are not sought.

Whoever, therefore, has been established in the order of religion, in which human salvation consists, must not be lifted up by the glory of holiness. Rather, let him reserve the fruit of his labor [Col. 0728A] for the Lord, who prepares heavenly gifts for each person according to his merits.

Therefore, “Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord” (I Cor. I, 31). Every effort must accordingly be made, beloved, so that pure faith may commend our life to the Lord in such a way that human pride claims nothing for itself or attributes anything to its own labors. He has lost everything he labored for who has ascribed the fruit of holiness to his own virtues.

# HOMILY XII. On the Good of Preserving Peace
1. Some may perhaps be anxious to reproach with malicious words the pursuit of good will, and to attribute it to fear or cowardice, whenever a person yields in disputes and, wounded by injuries, takes refuge in complete patience for love of peace. To refute such judgments of a depraved mind, [Col. 0728B] the admonition of the Gospel ought indeed to suffice. But, for our part, we shall pursue the truth of the matter, even if in a brief discourse; and whatever the fullness of religion demands, we shall support with appropriate prayers, in accordance with the affection with which we devote ourselves to charity. I know, however, that under the ancient laws many serve conquered love in such a way that they always oppose with hatred whatever concern for preserving peace has suggested. For we shall approve the very point we are about to make by many testimonies of the divine Scriptures, since the Lord says in this passage: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Matthew 5:44). I do not doubt that to some it seems sufficiently idle and impossible to offer love in return for enmity, or gratitude in return for insults. And indeed, beloved, it is difficult for the pain of an injury received not to rage in some part [Col. 0728C] of the body. But it is the mark of a wise person either patiently to endure an arising pain or to moderate it with gentler remedies. It is an immeasurable virtue to overcome hatred with kindnesses. Among all others, that person surely wins the palm of perfect virtue who responds to cups of poison with sweet honey.

2. The first degree of love, therefore, is to nourish affection through friendship; the summit of complete love, however, is to repay hatred with love. The former is reckoned among benefactions; the latter among virtues. Moreover, this saying is added to the height of perfect love: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink; for by doing this you will heap burning coals upon his head” (Romans 12:20). Whoever you are, then, whom injury caused by another’s insolence disturbs, and whom pain [Col. 0728D] aroused by insults goads: if you wish to be perfect, restrain the anger of your spirit with moderation, and exclude from yourself the hatred of wrongful indignation by the virtue of patience. Or certainly, if you desire so greatly to exact vengeance, pity those who are ignorant that the salvation of their soul depends upon this perfection of love. Perhaps hatred is repaid with hatred, and one injury with a corresponding offense, in order to return the deed. To provoke a brother to anger is indeed a crime; but, once provoked, not to cease is disgraceful. Thus the seeds of hatred yield very abundant fruits of iniquity and produce the punishments of crimes, while the author [Col. 0729A] of the quarrel blushes to make satisfaction to his brother, and the injured party demands vengeance for the injury inflicted, according to the judgment he himself considers just.

3. Behold, beloved, you have heard with what fruits the pursuits of peace are greeted; now learn by how many crimes hatreds are condemned. For the evangelist sets it forth in this way, the Lord saying: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15; the printed citation reads “III, 51”). Observe the recompense of both parties. To one, for hatred of his brother, the stain of murder is attributed; for the other, a recompense is prepared in return for a small act of charity. Finally, consider and see with how great an honor friendship, tranquility, and peace surround you, and how much favor they bring you, if you contend against enmity with love. “Love your enemies” (Matthew 5:44). The fruit is much less if you love one who loves you. The person who does not love one who loves him serves another’s character; [Col. 0729B] the person who loves one who loves him serves his own. The grace of charity necessarily belongs to the one who first displayed affection between two people; the one who loves a lover merely returns what is owed. There is no new merit where the other’s service comes first; nor should it be attributed to perfection where gifts are repaid with gifts and services with services. “If your enemy is hungry, feed him” (Romans 12:20). Did he say, “If your friend is hungry, feed him”? Feed your enemy; a friend himself sees to it that he does not go hungry. What work does your charity perform there, where friendship feeds your friend?

4. Let us nevertheless see what difference there is between the person who feeds a friend in need and the person who refreshes a hungry enemy. The former repays a debt of gratitude; the latter displays an example of compassion and virtue. [Col. 0729C] It is glorious to feed a needy brother, but it is stronger to come to the aid of an enemy placed in need. “Love your enemies.” Perhaps these words seem contrary to reason to one whom a recent injury still afflicts. But whoever he is should look to the tranquility of his own life, and he will understand that to have loved an enemy is to have conquered. Immeasurable, moreover, is the danger that threatens a person when that devil, the master of quarrels, arms two people alike in rival fury for battle; it is his custom to carry bitter words to inflame hatred and to bring them back again. When will that person spend a day without tribulation, or when will night depart from him without impious thought, whom anger goads with indignation? He will certainly never lead his life without suspicion if he must always think about and fear the person he has injured. [Col. 0729D] Therefore, the harshest pains must be tempered with the soothing medicine of words, so that the hardness of the heart, disciplined by the pursuit of peace, may grow gentle. In this matter I judge blessed those who guard the words of their lips with silent speech and, mindful of the heavenly commandments, do not seek an insult from another’s voice. Hatreds cease where an injury is not held against someone; and anger has no strength if one of the parties to the contention is absent. Thus a twofold victory awaits patience: to conquer one’s own passions and to moderate the conduct of another.

5. We know, beloved, that at times, during verbal disputes, hearts sigh when their ears have been wounded. [Col. 0730A] But the person who preserves the words of a quarrelsome man does injury to himself; the person who complains that another’s words were directed against him stains himself. It is complete victory to remain silent toward one who shouts and not to answer one who provokes. You receive a reward both for your patience and for your brother’s healing if the injury is consigned to oblivion; for when words follow words, fuel is supplied to the fire. Just as nothing is more disgraceful than answering furious people, so nothing is more useful than remaining silent toward those who provoke. Enmities grow when, while one person defends himself with words, the other accuses him for his words. There is no end to enmities unless we yield for a time to those who are angry.

You may say, “There is no fault if you do what the prophet says: ‘Set a guard, O Lord, over my mouth, and a door around my lips’” (Psalm 140:3). If you do not wish to suffer insult, [Col. 0730B] bind the plectrum of your mouth and close your ears, lest the words of your angry brother reach you; or certainly, if they do reach you, let them be consigned to silence. Thus it happens that the fury conceived loses its power if one person remains silent while the other rages alone.

6. Hear the Apostle saying: “Love of neighbor does no evil” (Romans 13:10). Do you wish to know what this evil is that excludes the grace of brotherly love? Hatreds, quarrels, hostilities, disputes, and rivalries, which disgrace the entire course of the present life. The person who serves charity is therefore freed from this evil; the ruin of vices has no place in one who, having trampled hatred underfoot, preserves an undiminished affection of charity.

Behold, the evangelist adds an increase to love, saying: “Love your neighbor as yourself” (Matthew 22:39). [Col. 0730C] Let us see who this neighbor is whom the evangelist commends with such zeal. The prophet did not define the degree of kinship or the bond of blood relationship in such a way as to exclude strangers from the grace of brotherly love. Your neighbor is every person joined to you by the same law of Christianity; your neighbor is the one who does not appear alien to the fellowship of the Church; your neighbor is anyone who is near to Christ. Therefore, whoever loves his neighbor loves God. Thus whoever loves God ought to honor the neighbor of his Christ.

The prophet, praising brotherly union, says: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is when brothers dwell together in unity!” (Psalm 133:1). What is good in human life except peace, under which all honorable things prosper and religious things are nourished? What is more pleasant [Col. 0730D] than for all nations to serve the one God in peace and for the prayers of all peoples to converge in praise of one Lord? To dwell together in unity means to believe in one God and to remain faithfully in the one Son of God. This is a useful and pleasant union for mortals: that we not divide the Father from the Son, as heretics do, nor the Son from the Father, nor the Holy Spirit from both; but that we believe these three names, divided according to their persons, to share in the fellowship of one divinity. Thus it comes about that, when they have come together in unity, no dissension of charity exists in the Church.

7. Let us therefore always avoid hatred, beloved; but, if we wish to avoid hatred, let us above all avoid the causes of hatred. First of all, let envy cease, for it inflames the minds [Col. 0731A] of human beings toward every quarrel. Let no one disgrace another’s origins by comparison with his own person, and let there be no one whom the insolence of his own mouth accuses. Above all, we must beware lest anything be increased through the rivalry of hostility. For an incurable enmity commonly descends from contention. Here patience is needed, and you obey it not without the fruit of your own salvation. For just as grave guilt awaits the person who inflicts injury upon his brother, so the greatest crown of virtue protects you if you do not become angry at an injury received. That affection is full of love if, once insults have been blotted out, you show compassion toward another’s weaknesses.

We know that it seems glorious to some to await with benevolent eyes the punishments of bodies or the loss of the miserable possessions of others. But if there are such people, let them hear the Lord saying: [Col. 0731B] “Pray for those who slander you” (Matthew 5:44). Many, after receiving an injury, prepare a retaliatory insult and, with a predatory spirit, await an opportunity for vengeance. And where is what the Lord says: “Repaying no one evil for evil” (Romans 12:17)? And lest anger claim anything for itself, he even removed the hope of taking vengeance by saying: “Vengeance is mine; I will repay, says the Lord” (ibid., 19). Let each person therefore forgive his brother from his whole heart. Let no one recall an injury; let no one seek vengeance with enduring anger. Let your conversations with your enemy always be gentle but sincere; let backbiting cease, and quarrels will cease. You show that your enemy is loved by you if you do not add causes by which his anger may continually be inflamed.

[Col. 0731C]

[Col. 0731C]

# HOMILY XIII. Likewise, on the Good of Preserving Peace

1. Some perhaps think, beloved, that the justice of the ancient law—which the guilty judge sufficiently harsh—was trampled down by an excessive presumption in favor of goodness, because the Lord says in the Gospel: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who slander you” (Matthew 5:44). He is sufficiently cruel, beloved, who thinks that goodness is incompatible with justice, since the ordering of Providence is one and the same: to restrain the wicked by goodness and to guard the good by the bond of the law.

Go, finally, to holy David, and you will find that the fountain of justice and goodness belongs to one virtue. He says in one of the Psalms: “You are good, O Lord, and in your goodness teach me your ordinances” (Psalm 119:68). Therefore, beloved, let no one think that the exposition of the law is anything other [Col. 0731D] than a partnership of goodness and piety. When it devotes itself to discipline, it forms character through honorable actions and restrains hearts stirred by wicked thoughts through severity. For, so that you may know that nothing was taken away from the ancient law, hear the Lord saying: “I have not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it” (Matthew 5:17).

2. It was not without reason, beloved, that our Christ willed the precepts of the present and ancient Testament to be one body. He knew that one part could not stand without the assistance of the other; and so it truly is. For where there is the strictness of the judge, the moderation [Col. 0732A] of goodness is always necessary.

Indeed, every potion, beloved, through whose aid medicine works toward the hope of human salvation, consists of bitter and sweet ingredients. If a physician ignorant of reason cannot blend them properly and, while seeking a remedy, compounds deadly poisons for the sick, he inflames all their external pains because he does not know how to mix the bitter juices of herbs in equal measures. So too the law, beloved, which regulates Christian principles, has been composed of bitter and sweet—that is, of ancient and present ordinances. For although it is displeasing to sinners, it is wholly composed, for the just, with the sweetness of its words: to such an extent that it promises the heavenly kingdom to some and threatens others with the fire of Gehenna. If, in this law, some wise person knows how to preserve the proper measure of the compound by adding humility and peace, [Col. 0732B] he will thereafter suffer no injury from the stricter law. For just as it is easy to soften any harsh potion with the sweetness of honey, so it is not difficult to temper the bitterness of the ancient law with honorable actions.

3. Therefore, if any of you love justice, let him strive to preserve the commands of both Testaments.

[Note: After this word, “to preserve” may perhaps need to be added. (Col. 0731D)]

Let him serve the newer laws in such a way that he does not neglect what was established in ancient times. Thus you will fulfill the law of Christ if you subtract nothing from the truth of either the ancient or the present ordinances. What wise person, hearing the prophet say, “It is good for me that you have humbled me, so that I might learn your ordinances” (Psalm 119:71), would deny that the work of justice is the fruit of goodness?

I do not doubt, beloved, that there are some who think perfect justice is contained in this saying: [Col. 0732C] “An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth” (Leviticus 24:20). This once prevailed among the people of the world, but only because the author of goodness had not yet come. What kind of justice do you suppose that was which brought about only the injury of death? Certainly there would still be no end to punishment unless our Christ had mixed the oil of mercy into the bloody laws—that is, unless he had truly fulfilled justice without deceit and displayed the teaching of goodness.

Therefore, instructed by these teachings, beloved, let us temper the bitterness of the ancient law through the pursuit of love, lest the person who returns the equivalent of an injury inflicted appear to have exceeded the measure of perfect justice.

4. Behold, the evangelist says: “Love your enemies” (Matthew 5:44). Perhaps to some it seems absurd [Col. 0732D] to repay an insult with love. It is not impossible to love an enemy if you consider what benefits your own side. “Love your enemies.” Let no one, under the heading of this command, think that he is conferring some benefit upon his enemy. Whoever loves an enemy loves himself. He spares himself who restrains the robber’s right hand with the spoils of a great gift; and he protects his own body who meets an armed enemy with prayers, attempting by a certain transaction to preserve respect for the fighter. For it is plainly a part of victory to buy off battle by offering a weight of gold.

“Love your enemies.” This is what it means to love enemies: not to respond to hatred, to bear patiently an insult received, [Col. 0733A] and to forgive an injury inflicted either by the hand or provoked by the goads of words. For the Lord says: “Whoever strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the left also” (Matthew 5:19; the printed citation). I know that this offering is unwelcome to some who do not know how to avoid quarrels or to restrain the impending penalties of punishment by moderation.

5. Immeasurable is what a person’s patience accomplishes for him if the other rages alone. For just as the person who resists provokes doubled blows against himself, so the person who keeps his hands restrained when another strikes gains the profit of a greater quarrel. “Do good to those who hate you” (Matthew 5:44). The first degree is the one we mentioned: that you love your enemy; the second is to do good to your enemy. There affection is taught; [Col. 0733B] here a work of compassion is required. It is one thing to love an enemy, another to have helped a wretched person. Your love therefore accomplishes little for your enemy if you allow the person whom you claim to love to go hungry.

Hear Paul saying: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink; for by doing this you will heap burning coals upon his head” (Romans 12:20). Here, as far as I can see, mercy serves cruelty. Why, then, should the person who awaits the time of promised vengeance not safely spend money on his enemies? The person who hesitates to show mercy undoubtedly does not know how to be angry. Beyond the fortune of victory, it is surely a thing to have saved an enemy and to have avenged an injury.

The passage continues here: “Pray for those who slander you” (Matthew 5:44). Without doubt, [Col. 0733C] here the Lord warned the conscience of a deceitful heart. For he knew that love could be composed in words and, although generous expenditure might be made, could frequently prove unwelcome. Thus you show that you did not unwillingly perform that charity which avenges you, if you commend the wounds of your enemy to the heavenly physician in humble prayer and seek the aid of salvation with abundant tears.

“Love your enemies.” If we are commanded to love enemies, what condition do you think the person is in who pursues his brother with impious hostility, though provoked by no injuries? The Apostle seems to me to have spoken of him: “Whoever hates his brother without cause is a murderer” (1 John 3:15). And indeed it is so: the person who persecutes an innocent man with hatred is as though he had killed him.

6. But let us nevertheless see who those people are whom Saint John judged deserving [Col. 0733D] of condemnation because of fraternal hatred. I think they are those of whom the prophet says: “Their heart has been struck by envy.” These are the people who undertake battles against themselves and set their own houses on fire with their own fire, keeping a flame enclosed in their bosom for the burning.
