For here there is nothing that can be charged to another, where there is no conflict with an opposing party, since nearly all disputes and all hatreds rage between persons challenged for battle.

If this is credible, behold, we have found the guilty person who has no adversary: we have someone who can be punished, but we do not find anyone who ought to be avenged. I judge that person truly happy whose [Col. 0734A] glorious life another has regarded with hostile eyes. His case is in a sufficiently good state if he suffers from another’s envy, because no one is envied except those who are better; nor is anyone subject to envy unless an advance in the better conduct of his life has raised him to higher things.

But I consider those more than wretched whom another’s prosperity agitates, and whom impious anger, conceived through rivalry, disturbs with hidden darts of the heart. Their own weapons rightly punish them, so that envy itself seems to me to possess a certain discrimination: it strikes back at the heart of its author and continually consumes the guilty breast with bloody jealousy.

7. Envy must therefore first be disciplined, for once conceived in the mind it produces pains. Certainly, whenever another’s glory and happiness comes before our eyes, let the zeal of emulation seize us rather than jealousy, in accordance with what the Apostle says: [Col. 0734B] “Emulate the better gifts” (1 Corinthians 12:31). The person who emulates another’s good without envy takes nothing away from true friendships; nor does he injure another who strives toward better things by following examples.

If anyone is wise, let him imitate the fruits of justice, follow the practices of self-restraint, grasp the grace of humility, and run alongside good people with emulous love, so that he may reach better things, looking to that apostolic saying: “Run in such a way that you may obtain” (1 Corinthians 9:24). Whoever, then, is moved by another’s glory should run after the good and labor to overtake them. I am willing for him to go ahead, provided that he strives without jealousy of heart. This is truly to exercise an unblemished virtue: to conquer a better person without injury.

Let us give the proud their place, provided that we surpass them in humility. [Col. 0734C] Let the profit of secular service not provoke us to rivalry. Let those whom concern for their children admonishes retain the pomp of riches, although the person who practices the cultivation of compassion gains and stores up far greater profit for himself. Nothing is safer than to place part of one’s resources in the mouths of the poor. For Scripture says, the Lord speaking: “Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly” (2 Corinthians 9:6). Whatever you reserve, you defraud yourself of.

Let us therefore give generously, beloved, so that we may gather multiplied fruits of mercy. Money kept shut up in a purse is without profit; but if it is devoted to investment, it soon returns fourfold.

Whatever you give to the poor, you undoubtedly assign as interest, to be repaid to you in the future, when each person’s labors are assessed with multiplied [Col. 0734D] honor. A recompense for his work awaits each person, whether religious faith adorns him or a generous hand commends him. For the evangelist says: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matthew 5:7, 9).

Let peace therefore be our first concern, beloved, and compassion our second. Let our hearts suggest nothing false to our lips; let our mouths answer nothing doubtful, looking above all to that saying: “What you do not wish for yourself, do not do to another” (Tobit 4:16).

[Note: For “to another,” as I have observed Cotelerius reads *pro alii* in the Apostolic Constitutions, book I, chapter 1. (Col. 0733D)]

This is the perfect love of which we spoke, which establishes the affection of complete love. [Col. 0735A] Thus the strictness of the ancient law has no power over you if you obediently observe what the fullness of the law demands.

[Col. 0735A]

# HOMILY XIV. On the Good of Humility

1. Beloved, whenever necessity requires us to proclaim the merits of virtues, it is not without injury to the other side, because when a person praises better things, he rebukes worse ones. A fool surely thinks that he is being marked as such if he departs praised as wise by the judgment of good people. But what are we to do, since we can neither set forth good things without reproving evil ones nor condemn evil things without recalling good ones? Let the person who thinks he has suffered injury in this work grant pardon. It is better for evils to depart, confused by an inward sense of shame, [Col. 0735B] provided that the things worthy of praise are not hidden.

Two causes therefore come together here: humility and pride. The nature of things does not permit one to be explained without the shame of the other, because the one is displayed by its own acts, while the other is put to shame by those of the former. We must therefore explain how much usefulness humility possesses, so that you may understand how much unhappiness weighs upon pride; and we must set forth how much hatred pride produces, so that you may learn how much love the grace of humility acquires. In this way each of you may more easily recognize what he ought to correct in himself and what he may choose.

Pride must not be chastised in such a way that the grace of humility is neglected; nor must humility be preferred to such an extent that the vices of pride remain unmentioned. For what does it profit to know the cause of sickness if you do not know the medicine? Or what good is it to know the remedy for health [Col. 0735C] if there is no concern to restrain the disease?

2. Hear Scripture speaking of these things: “God gives grace to the humble, but resists the proud” (James 4:6). Learn now, beloved, the recompense of both sides, and you will understand what you ought to love and what you ought to hate. Behold, one is invited to grace for the love of humility; the other is assigned to punishment for the crime of pride. Let each person therefore discipline himself if a swelling of spirit has grown in him, lest he stir up against himself the weapons of heavenly justice. A person whose cause of combat lies against a higher power passes his life with difficulty and danger. The mind must therefore be inclined toward all humility, so that there may be a place [Col. 0735D] for grace to be obtained from the Lord.

You can understand how grave is the guilt of a swollen brow, which must be restrained by so great an exertion of the Divinity. Humility is always safe and unharmed; for the person who has no cause for fighting knows nothing of defeat. Pride, however, is subject not only to hatred but also to danger. It is difficult for the person who imposes an injury not to endure a struggle. But we easily exclude every danger of this necessity from ourselves if we fight the vices of pride with humility. “God gives grace to the humble, but resists the proud.”

3. If you inquire carefully, beloved, into all the things by which we began to displease the Lord from the beginning of the world, you will find that pride was the prince of all vices; and you will easily recognize in what respect humility deserved heavenly grace or pride incurred the offense of the Divinity.

The Devil’s downfall teaches, finally, that pride endangers a human being. [Col. 0736A] Established in a higher place, he despised lower things; and, cast down from angelic dignity because of the vice of a presumptuous mind, he received the sentence of tyrannical condemnation. You see, therefore, that the person who devotes himself to pride plays the part of pride. What remains for him except a sentence of condemnation, when arrogance rules him?

If you please, let us compare good things with evil, and better things with worse; and you will understand how much a person suffers daily from the envy produced by the vice of pride. Nor need we seek far for an example. Assume the office of a free person, and at once you will recognize the mind of the proud. What kind of life, I ask, do those people have whose days are filled with hatred? The person who walks with an arrogant brow never passes a day without either his own sin or another’s, because among those above and below him he is always either despised or feared. [Col. 0736B] Pride is a vice of baseness and a sign of ignobility; nobility of mind, however, does not know how to exalt itself. Among the unworthy, arrogance always increases with power; but where there is splendor of life, humility quietly gives delight.

4. I call true and holy that humility which religion and love of God recommend, not that which fear of domination extorts. We speak of the humility joined to the fellowship of charity, which is not extorted by the authority of command but nourished by a law of conduct. Let no one think that the habits of nature alone are to be blamed for vices, when arrogance is nourished by wealth and command grows with power. [Col. 0736C] When would medicine suffice for weakened bodies if wounds were born together with the human being?

Pride is nourished when one person judges himself wiser in speech and another better by birth; when one does not wish to be moved from his position and another thinks he can be despised. Thus we see hatred growing through the vice of pride in comparisons between persons: one heaps the weight of gold and silver before the eyes of flatterers, while another sets ambition for honor against it; one displays an abundance of riches, another of words; one wants to be sought out for his advice, another desires to be greeted for his banquets.

The vices of pride can scarcely be enumerated. If a person could overcome or avoid them, he would fall into no snare of the devil’s condemnation. Behold, one, so that he may always seem novel, sends an excuse to those who come to greet him; [Col. 0736D] another falls ill so that he may be greeted every day; one, in order to find an opportunity for accusation, pretends to be concerned about everything—not because he misses an absent person, but so that he may accuse him of failing in duty. He asks which visitor has occupied the doorway since the morning hours, so that he may charge someone with the absence of the procession of friends. Thus, when the person who is present is not admitted to the greeting, the one who is absent is made guilty; and when the door is closed to the person who has arrived, offense is prepared for the one who is absent.

I do not wish to speak of the arrogance of those who go out with a long-prepared haughtiness and establish arrangements according to their own places and merits, so that when one offers kisses, the other presents his breast. No conversation pleases him; no affection of friendly exchange is preserved. He passes some by with his eyes and despises others in speech; [Col. 0737A] he loves another, that he may show himself angry with the other.

[Note: Perhaps, “he loves one, so that he may show himself angry with another.” BAUN. (Col. 0737D)]

What hope of living is there, I ask, where one person, under the appearance of friendship, presumes to exercise domination, while another, by obeying too much, endures servitude?

5. Let us see what this proud person is like when, seated among equals, he perhaps sits ready to give judgment. I seem to see verbal battles composed through eruptions of speech, when one professes devotion to mercy and another pretends to favor justice—not to preserve fidelity to a right judgment, but to await the preferences of the superior person. He pretends to think something else in order to disagree through another’s disputation. He considers nothing right in counsel except what he alone has thought; he considers nothing just except what he himself has persuaded himself of. He wants to be heard alone and praised alone by everyone’s mouth; and, what is worse, [Col. 0737B] there is no lack of someone on this side to support him.

For pride quickly gives way to flattery, when one person seeks favor or another fears offense. Nor is pride absent from banquets, when a higher place is prepared on the couch and the bed is spread so high that the person seems to hang rather than lie down. Thus pride submits to injury in order not to appear to suffer injury. It is asked who will offer a hand to one rising, who will support his shoulder, who will prop up his side. No one can excuse to me the claim that this vice is not a form of tyrannical domination. For the service which one human being offers another, if it is not rendered solely to support the weak, is plainly servitude.

Here I praise the patience of poverty, which, when abandoned by its own virtues, serves the conduct of others. But why should we place such a weight of pride only upon the rich, [Col. 0737C] when we frequently see people established in the deepest poverty stained by the same wretchedness of spirit? Of such people that most wise Solomon says: “There are three things that my soul hates … a proud poor man,” and the rest that follows (Sirach 25:3–4).

Without doubt, that person exceeds the measure of pride who possesses no awareness of his resources. In the greatest and highest things, humility is to be preferred; no one admires a humble poor person, for the person whom the necessity of poverty bends humbles himself unwillingly. Humility is pleasing in a poor person and glorious in a rich one; humility is gentle among enemies, while pride is unwelcome even among friends.

6. Let us, by contrast, inquire, beloved, what the goods of humility are. Humility is always gentle and obliging, pleasing in friendships and quiet amid insults. It is not [Col. 0737D] lifted up by prosperity; it is not changed by adversity. It does not impose service or extort it. It is first in the duty of offering greetings and slower to take a seat. It does not expect to be led about by a crowd of flatterers; it does not ambitiously desire to be greeted; it does not demand praise or await the favor of public approval. It hates the choruses of acclamation, because a good conscience is not praised without shame.

It does not seek the voices of flatterers except for the person who knows himself unworthy of praise; but the person who deserves praise is always praised more modestly through the devotion of friends. Yet where unworthiness rules, a person thinks his actions are being marked if he departs without praise.

Humility is surrounded by goodness. Just as it does not know how to inflict injury, so it does not seek redress for an insult. [Col. 0738A] A humble man, in disputes, prefers to remain silent rather than to win; in judgments, he is content to appear inexperienced rather than be judged shameless. He is not quick in speech or ready with an answer.

The speech of the proud, however, is rapid and facile, full of insults and packed with injuries, never sent forth without wounding, never hurled without pain. Its wound is incurable and its stain irremediable. But wherever the fault of words has reached, healing soon follows through satisfaction.

7. It is fitting for us, beloved, to love this humility, to seek it, choose it, and hold fast to it, so that we do not lose the grace promised as a reward. Hear the evangelist saying: “Whoever humbles himself will be exalted, and whoever exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke 14:11; 18:14). [Col. 0738B] This exaltation is condemnation, which exercises the power of future judgment over the arrogant and proud.

Our mind must therefore be inclined downward, so that, once every mark of pride has been crushed, the pursuits of hatred may come to rest. Thus it will happen that a person reaches higher things from a lower place and, rewarded with fitting honor, obtains the grace of heavenly power.

# HOMILY XV. On the Good of Martyrdom
1. I have much confidence in speaking before you, beloved, whenever it is necessary, in love for the blessed martyr, to recall in his memory the praises of martyrdom—praises that courageous faith brought forth when stirred by profitable sufferings—although the tongue is not sufficient for as much as martyrdoms [Col. 0738C] demand. For when could the service of the human mouth adequately recount all that heavenly virtue accomplished in preparation for battle? Therefore, since this is all we can do, we offer the favor of our lips to his merits, since no one could remain unaware of the deeds of the struggle that renew for us each year examples of virtue.

You have heard the Psalmist say: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. 115:15). What could be more precious than that death which, in the conflict of battle, does not know how to yield to the enemy’s weapons? It is certainly clear that the soul which, undeceived by impious laws, refuses to submit to servitude carries away the greatest palm of victory. This is truly the mark of outstanding virtue: in a time of persecution, to favor death more than life. Although it makes room for eternal life, the voluntary punishment of the cross commended by the confession of our Christ does so, as the Lord says: “Whoever loves his life will lose it; and whoever hates his life will find it in eternal life” (John 12:25). What wise person, despising the use of this present light, would not, when the occasion arose, hasten eagerly to martyrdom, seeing that consigning the soul to death belongs to the profit of life? Why, then, should a person not devotedly hasten to so precious a work and boldly place himself in the way of impious hands, when the grace of heavenly reward awaits him, in accordance with what the Lord recalls in that description of blessedness: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” [Col. 0739A] (Matt. 5:10)?

2. You see how many fruits faith, tested by sufferings, has brought to humanity, and in what position stands the victory acquired through contempt for the body. Who could doubt the reward we have mentioned, when one sees that throughout the whole world devotion converges in love for the saints and that people come from everywhere to the annual solemnity? We readily understand what place in the heavenly dwelling is being prepared for those whose memory is pursued with such great acts of service. Let us therefore prepare our souls for the future glory that has been stored up for us, and place heavenly things before earthly things, so that we may attain those promises of eternal life.

Let no one flatter himself with the ambition of this world, which he sees failing day by day through the advance of age and time. If, finally, we compare present things with eternal ones, it is clear that what we possess temporally is sufficiently worthless and useless. Seek, then, the grace of the inheritance that is owed, and you will understand that the riches of this world are displeasing; you will judge that nothing is darker than gold, nothing dirtier than the splendor of silver. In comparison with paradise, the most precious gem is like glass. Such is the dignity of this present light and of the future age: it is as though, while the moon stood in heaven, a morning ray had poured itself into human eyes. For the moon’s light is pleasing only as long as, under the established order, it performs its service for the dark night. Although it pleases by the whiteness of its nocturnal light, it is nevertheless obscured by the brightness of a better star that comes upon it [Col. 0739B].

3. The present time of life has only this to commend it: that we do what will not be subject to accusation at the future judgment and cannot be convicted when accused. But so that no soul hereafter may suffer before God from the reproach of injustice, that psalm must certainly be embraced which says: “Those who sow in tears shall reap in joy” (Ps. 125:5). To sow in tears and reap joys means to refute by one’s own judgment the deeds of one’s earlier life, and to subject a wanton soul to just punishment. Joy quickly follows sadness if you forestall the strictness of the judge by satisfaction and overwhelm the guilt of a committed crime by constant correction.

But lest you think that you have thereby acquired a lesser grace, assist those afflicted and worn down by grief, and settle your own case before the poor by generous distribution. For the Lord says: “Blessed are the merciful, for God will have mercy on them. Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” [Col. 0739D] (Matt. 5:7, 5). Therefore, if any of you, beloved, earnestly seeks the consolation of Christ, let him cut away the pains of others by almsgiving, and diligently commend his own tears to this patron in whose honor we have gathered; let him commend himself through frequent acts of patronage, so that he may more easily obtain whatever he has brought before the Lord for his own benefit. We must always hasten to the friends of God, serve our neighbors, and pray without ceasing, so that we may obtain the support of holy intercession. What place for pardon, then, will there be before the just Judge if you do not know how to entreat the king’s friends?

4. Finally, look to the order of secular discipline [Col. 0740A], and you will understand what concern ought to remain among you regarding service to the saints. Without doubt, unless the disposition of the one who guards the secrets of the palace has first been appeased, one does not easily reach friendship with the higher power. The support of patrons must certainly be sought eagerly; to them alone it has been granted to know how to soften the disposition of the angry Lord and moderate his wrath.

In a great household, after the master, the friends always hold the second rank. Through them alone there is offered before the master both free opportunity to make requests and easy access for obtaining what is sought. We must therefore cultivate the memory of the saints with special veneration, so that they may open the door of salvation and cause the desires of our service to reach the knowledge of the Lord.

It is a great share of security, amid difficult circumstances, to have support from the king’s household [Col. 0740B]. For the reproach of a crime somehow diminishes when the accused has begun to belong to the friendships of the royal family. A person passes his life without danger if there is someone who can excuse the sinner’s negligence before the Lord. Yet no one is so secure that he does not need the support of a more powerful person, even at the height of security. For although tested faith sanctifies some in this number, it is nevertheless necessary that there be someone who commends that very faith to the Lord through humble intercession. You will not find anyone so strong that he does not need the help of one stronger.

As one fights well beneath a shield, so a matter is safely conducted under a patron with witnesses; and there, although punishment threatens, if someone intercedes, the offense liable to the laws is undoubtedly pardoned. What limit could there be to death if, when the Judge strikes with his sentence, no one is present to assist the accused through humble intercession [Col. 0740C]?

5. If we considered, beloved, how much the virtue of our fellow-citizen martyr has provided for us, the devotion of our tongue and the service of our mouth would never cease from praising our God. Look at the zeal of those who drink foreign waters and, thirsting, seek springs located far away; you will see how much value a possession flooded with its own waters has. It cannot be estimated how much useful increase accrues to a patrimony when what is eagerly sought elsewhere is born within one’s own possession.

Behold, the Lord of hosts, on whom you should rely each day, has given you a living fountain—not failing, not harsh, not bitter—from which, if anyone wishes to drink, he will always thirst for righteousness and will never depart from the law of the heavenly commandments [Col. 0740D]. If, then, beloved, you want us to have a share in the heavenly dwelling that the Lord promised to victors, let us first imitate the faith of the holy martyr in confession, follow his path in virtue, and not hesitate, in love for the Lord, to expose our breast to the bloody hands of the executioner. A willing soldier in the conflict of battle is soon protected by the crown of victory.

But while these things come upon the blessed and are conferred upon the merits of the fortunate, let us meanwhile resist adversity insofar as it concerns the present salvation of the soul. There is no lack of something in which you can conquer daily, if you wish to resist the desires of the flesh. Look and see how many battles of sins rage around you, and how many ranks of vices are drawn up. On one side pride, on the other envy, attacks our faith [Col. 0741A]; now drunkenness supplies material for lust, now greed inflames the soul toward every kind of falsehood. Its pursuit is, among other things, to sow quarrels, stir up disputes, and acquire hatred.

Against these legions, therefore, we must fight with spiritual weapons and stand in the battle line day and night, until either the vices yield or, brought low, flee for refuge to repentance. Once these have been overcome, we can undoubtedly also enter the conflict that seeks the supreme palm of martyrdom. Who would not wish to fight there, or who would not try to conquer, where a person is taught not only by the merits of preceding labors but also by present examples of virtue?

## HOMILY XVI. Also on the Good of Martyrdom

[Col. 0741B] 1. As the event itself shows, beloved, this world greatly needed the knowledge of so splendid a victory to awaken the glory of virtue. It would still be lying in dark bonds, without doubt, if it had not been illumined by the renowned examples of the saints; and it would be fighting amid crooked and uncertain paths unless the crown of martyrdom, spread throughout the whole world, confounded the unbelieving minds of humanity.

For this reason thanks must be given to God, who armed mortal minds for such great endurance and did not look upon the labors of a great work idly. He imposed the necessity of battle upon his lovers and prepared a fitting reward for the victors, as the evangelist says: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (ibid., 10).

Therefore, whoever wisely strives upward through devotion to religion should first learn from where the crown comes to the virtues. We do not have to search far for someone whom we should follow. Behold, he is before our eyes: every day he urges us on by saving examples and, with fatherly affection, invites us to share in holiness. Therefore, if you wish, you can readily grasp what is worthy of the heavenly kingdom, since every day you have someone whom you can follow and whom you ought to imitate.

Look, beloved, at the devotion of other regions, which we see flourishing more widely through foreign journeys in love for the saints; and you will understand how much the Lord has granted us, or how much concern and love he has expended upon us. Among the other nations he has regarded with the desire to save them, he has also drenched our own places with the blood of martyrdom. Seek, and you will find how eagerly almost the whole world desires the patronage of holiness [Col. 0741D], so that the merits of such great virtues are continually pursued by competing vows and frequent acts of service.

You readily recognize, then, how particular the care of service owed to the martyrs must be among us, when you see even foreign nations gathering here through the love of devoted hearts and, as the need requires, seeking the consolation of the holy martyr. You plainly have something for which to rejoice especially. [Note: In the 1677 Bibliotheca maxima Patrum, volume VIII, the reading is: “You plainly have things for which you may rejoice especially.”]

For whatever religion is drunk everywhere arises from your fountain, and whatever is supplied elsewhere to the thirsty is born from you. Learn from this, beloved, to love God, who commends himself daily through the pouring out of his blood by heavenly authority [Col. 0742A]; and recognize how much endurance contributes to the lovers of Christ and how much sorrow in persecution contributes to acts of religion.

2. Behold, as the reading teaches, possession of the heavenly kingdom receives the victor. It is plainly a great thing to have endured the executioner, when punishment itself opens the way to reward. What wise person, if the occasion arose, would not, conscious of such great virtue, seek to undertake it and boldly place himself before his enemies? Why should one who is awaited by such a precious grace of reward not look upon the flames without fear, or why should he dread the executioner’s claws?

It belongs to perfect faith to give place to profitable sufferings, especially when you are taught by such great examples of preceding virtues. You can readily understand what it benefits the bravest to have conquered in persecution when you see the sentence of spiritual judgment raging daily against the wickedness of diabolical presumption in each of the saints’ places.

It is not an idle matter, beloved, that we frequently see human bodies tormented in the chastisement of an unclean spirit, and that, when the names of the saints are invoked, they confess that the author of crimes is responsible for their acts. When would mere reading suffice for unbelieving minds? When would ancient knowledge implant the complete faith of truth in human senses? Or when would the soul descend to belief in such great things if, for the affirmation of past events, it awaited hearing alone?

Therefore, that person is sufficiently wretched and alien from Christ whose heart is still occupied by the error of foolish unbelief, when he sees the merits of the saints standing in such great powers [Col. 0742C]. For this is directed toward them: we often see an aerial spirit singing under another person’s identity and uttering words of trembling confession through another’s mouth. Although the flame is at work in this, no injustice is seen: one person is beaten, and another confesses.

3. The Lord works so much virtue through his saints that he confounds the deeds of diabolical wickedness by the hidden wounds of injuries and invisible tears, through the authority of judgment; and he restrains the concealed blandishments of crimes, chastised under a certain torturer. What wise person would wait for these things and not immediately accuse whatever unbelief there is in himself, and, mindful of his condition, prepare fitting honor for the memory of the saints through constant service?

He can readily understand what place those persons have with the Lord, and with what honor they ought to be held by us [Col. 0742D], to whom he sees judgment entrusted through the examination of palms. Therefore, beloved, their examples must be followed, their faith pursued, their virtue imitated. It is not difficult for anyone to accomplish these things. For if you consider the crown of the promised reward, it will be easy for you to overcome the violence of persecution.

Behold, the Lord says: “Whoever perseveres, I will give him the crown of victory” (Rev. 2:26). Therefore, if the occasion arises, let no one shrink from the sound of chains or from the idle punishments of dark prisons, prepared for the use of the impious, or from the torment of sinews. Without doubt the entire apparatus of death yields, provided that the will to fight grows [Col. 0743A]. All hope of obtaining victory, therefore, rests in faith and will. For if the will follows faith, faith never abandons the will.

It is difficult for the person who has accepted the injury of voluntary suffering to feel the punishment of the body. Certainly, so that you may walk securely when stationed in the battle line, the deeds of the saints must always be placed before your eyes. In the greatest battles, a fighter is not without consolation if he seeks the examples of the bravest men.

Behold, the Lord says: “Take up your cross and follow me” (Matt. 16:24). But perhaps these things do not suit everyone, because a pampered body frequently yields to injury. Whoever despairs because of the frailty of his body should flee to the weapons of righteousness, which are reckoned as voluntary service. He readily withstands the attack of an invading enemy whom the will has armed for battle [Col. 0743B]; nor does he fear the sword of the bloody executioner whom the virtue of souls protects.

4. But those to whom these things seem burdensome, beloved, should undertake easier ones. There is indeed one arduous road, as the evangelist says, which leads to life (Matt. 7:14). Yet if we inquire, there are many roads by which one comes to glory. Behold, lust presses upon us, pride dominates, greed rages. We must fight against these through the discipline to which all heavenly glory of virtue gives obedience.

Bend down pride, and immediately you will obtain a crown of graces. Restrain greed, and without doubt you will be able to gain victory over all vices. First conquer, then, the desires of the flesh, and it will not be difficult for you to conquer the tortures of the executioner [Col. 0743C].

You know how many evils envy is subject to: while it begrudges others, it strikes itself. You also know how greatly the soul is endangered by the burning of desire. You know how oppressive the gaze is in arousing desires, how swift are the darts of the eyes, how shameful drunkenness is, how dangerous the arrows of words are—arrows that strike not without pain and depart not without weariness.

Against these things, therefore, the battle of the cross must be prepared for us. As many times in a day as you conquer the desires of your souls, so many times you will take up the reward.

5. Moreover, beloved, there are many things that frequently show us the necessity of battle. Once these have been defeated and overcome, you will obtain no small palm through the labor of a just victory. For just as there are as many vices in a person as there are wounds, so there are as many rewards as battles and as many crowns as victories [Col. 0743D]. The person who proceeds with a purified mind after chastising his vices does not pass a day without a small triumph.

Behold, the Lord says: “Take up your cross and follow me” (Matt. 16:24). I know that the crown of martyrdom is owed to few, since the Lord himself says: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 20:16). But while these things come upon the fortunate, faith must be stirred in the matters explained above, so that, when necessary, the hostile attack may find us prepared by the assault of a religious life.

Virtue always tests itself in small matters. Thus an inexperienced soldier, before entering battle, exercises his strength against a felled tree and, playing, fashions wounds with his trained hands. Now he raises his feet; now, through the swift running of horses, he imitates the winds [Col. 0744A]. Finally, his zeal advances so far that it is almost less difficult to conquer the enemy than to exercise his virtue.

In such matters, therefore, beloved, we must rehearse beforehand, and the soul must be fitted by discipline for the greater things that are to come. For the virtue promised in small matters is displayed more easily in great ones. Thus, while we accustom ourselves to conquer lesser things, we learn to endure greater ones.

## HOMILY XVII. Also III, on the Good of Martyrdom

1. Anxious farmers affirm, beloved, that rough land, never tested by any furrows, does not immediately respond to suitable seeds, nor nourish a germ properly conceived in the furrow unless it is first split open and softened by repeated plowing. The owner of his little field must then await its fruit with confidence, when the bitterness of the ancient turf has ceased. If the zeal for plowing is suddenly abandoned by cultivation, the earth is nearly certain to become foul again with its former appearance.

This is the distinction between good and evil: diligence conquers nature, while negligence recalls one to nature. Under this rule of life, beloved, the cultivation of Christian religion either grows or declines. The work requires no less care from the one who must soften the hardness of the human heart through constant correction and cultivate, by frequent exposition, a breast besieged by vices. Without doubt, among the negligent, the zeal of religious profession is endangered, especially if an embittered mind receives the seeds of heavenly words and unteachable souls do not know how to nourish the fruits of righteousness.

For just as, when diligence ceases, fields commonly become overgrown with thorns [Col. 0744C], so, when the cultivation of religion is neglected, the vice of nature is renewed.

2. Among those nations, perhaps, beloved, it would be difficult to set out the way of salvation in a suitable discourse—nations to whom the faith of the Christian religion has become known only by word. Perhaps such people may find, though vainly, an excuse: they may say that no examples worthy of imitation were ever presented to them. The prophet refutes their voice, saying: “Their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 18:5).

What excuse can we offer, beloved, if the Lord finds in us either negligence or unbelief—among whom the Christian name began with miracles, and in whose ears and before whose eyes the faith of religion is daily implanted in the presence of so great a martyr? And whose martyr? Necessarily, the one who first exercised the battle of renowned virtue in this place, showed by what order we might obtain possession of the heavenly kingdom, teaches us daily by his example what we ought to do, and asks what progress we are making.

Let no one doubt that he is concerned for his own deeds, since he sees himself joined to him by the kinship of relationship.

3. First of all, therefore, we ought to make ourselves known to this patron through frequent acts of service, so that he may watch over us as a special intercessor before the Lord and commend our life through the favor of his approval. There is nothing that a person placed in any necessity cannot obtain if he does not cease to entreat the friends of the supreme Emperor [Col. 0745A].

Look, beloved, at the zeal of those who, thirsting, seek water from foreign springs: that is, those who, moved by religious devotion, search across extended regions of the earth for the holy and venerable relics of martyrs and pursue, through particular acts of service, the merits of their virtues spread throughout the whole world. You will understand with what honor we must regard the one who, in the conflict of heavenly battle, drenched the place of this city with his victorious blood.

For we have seen, in various and distant regions, the wounds of his torn body divided everywhere, and the precious evidence of his wounds carried throughout the world close at hand, so that those who possess only the tokens of martyrdom are no less concerned for the saints. The Lord of majesty has therefore freely provided us with the patronage that faith has provided to others.

The one whom we should follow is not to be sought far away. Here we have a teacher of endurance; here, examples of rewards; here, the form of virtues; here, demonstrations of merits. Let us therefore prepare our soul for every kind of endurance, if the occasion arises; and, mindful of the one whom we honor through his merits at the annual solemnity, let us follow him also in his examples.

4. Look at the ornaments of the breast that you cover with precious silk, as though with the work of God, and at the starry face that you burden with yellow gold. Learn what the pageantry of wounds is, what the crown of tears is, what it means to have endured the executioner, how much it costs to conquer the torturer, and with what exultation a victory gained through sufferings descends, as the prophet says: “Those who sow in tears shall reap in joy” (Ps. 125:5).

What wise person, instructed by these matters, would not judge that the use of temporal life ought to be despised in comparison with martyrdom? But if you look to the services offered daily to the saints, you will recognize that, in a time of persecution, it is better to perish than to live.

Why, however, do we say “perish,” when the prophet says: “The righteous shall live forever” (Ezek. 18:9)? Let us therefore entreat this teacher of virtues, beloved, with tears poured out each day, so that he may teach us to serve wounds that will profit us; let him show us how to expose the breast against the battles of adversity and endure every conflict of injury.

It is not difficult to enter battle where you see that victory has gone before. What is taught by examples quickly settles in the minds. But, what is worse, because of the vanity of this world it is difficult for anyone to reach heavenly things. The promised kingdom is not obtained through the delicate care of the body, nor does one easily reach the crown of virtues who has not fought in a legitimate contest [Col. 0745D]. Therefore, the body must bend to every injury if one intends to reach the place of victory. The place of attaining glory consists in this: that the person who wishes to please Christ must first learn to displease the world.

5. Hear the Lord saying in this place: “Whoever loves his life will lose it; and whoever hates his life will find it unto eternal life” (John 12:25). There are many kinds of sufferings by which mortal humanity may commend itself to our God under the law of life. Although they do not possess the crown of martyrs, they nevertheless possess no small palm of virtues.

Indeed, beloved, since the crown of which we have spoken has been stored up for victors, let us meanwhile resist, as far as we can, the sins that surround us [Col. 0746A]. Whoever is not entrusted with that first pageantry of martyrdom should at least strive to obtain, among the bravest, the rewards of an honorable and religious life.

You are not unaware, therefore, how many shipwrecks the human mind is subject to. Behold, the desire of our eyes continually knocks at the doors and disturbs human hearts with the goads of riches. From one side the mind, from the other the sight, invites a person to every crime. There is no lack, then, of something in which you can conquer, if you do not cease to fight and, stationed as though in the battle line, contend moment by moment against hostile weapons.

6. To conquer these things, certainly, we need the evangelical instruction that says: “If your eye causes you to stumble, tear it out” (Matt. 5:29). To tear out the eye means to chastise vices, extinguish the desires of the flesh, and suppress the wantonness of life through zeal for discipline.

Behold, the field is prepared for you: you are challenged by the enticements of lust, and, as usually happens, you are deceived by appearance and adornment. If you wish to overcome these things, you must fight through zeal for chastity. Let the chastity of Thecla, guarded amid flames and raging beasts, come before you. She so despised the ornaments of this world that, out of love for preserving chastity, she rejected the marriage chamber to which she had been betrothed, and by fighting nourished and by conquering preserved the integrity of her professed virginity.

Anger and the fury of the soul frequently challenge us to battle. We are provoked by injuries and assaulted by insults. Learn with what zeal we should conquer these things: let us arm our souls for patience. What we cannot obtain through prayer, let the evangelical saying teach us in this matter: “If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the other also” (Matt. 5:39).

You see that to submit to injury is to conquer [Col. 0746C]. For it is clear that the person carries away no small crown of victory who, in accordance with the words of the commandment cited above, knows how not to become angry when injured.

At times our eyes suggest things that the mind does not seek; frequently the tongue itself betrays its errors, bursting into a voice that sounds out shameful and dishonorable things. Here the method of applying virtue is this: through the discipline of silence, let the words of love be enclosed. In an altercation of words, restraint in speaking is the summit of virtue.

Hear the prophet saying about this: “Set a guard, Lord, over my mouth, that my heart may not turn aside to evil words” (Ps. 140:3). Greed must therefore be conquered, anger refuted, lust chastised, and the mouth restrained by the bond of restraint. By these steps one reaches paradise; by these merits of virtue one arrives at fellowship with the saints.

## HOMILY XVIII. On the Maccabees

1. The soul is certainly kindled by much hope for eternal salvation whenever the deeds of individual martyrs are recalled. But the soul is moved with a joy somehow multiplied, toward love and favor for the Lord, whenever the mother of the Maccabees comes to mind. By her exhortation she clothed seven sons in the crown of martyrdom in a single day, stronger in faith in proportion as she appears to have been more fruitful in childbirth. In her there were as many demonstrations of virtue as there were children.

For she handed over to almighty God as many martyrs in one day as she had acquired sons through the successive intervals of time. Blessed among all mothers, and even more fortunate in her bereavement, she received such a gift from faith that in a single day she passed into the glory of the heavenly kingdom with the whole fruitfulness of her womb.

Here consider that evangelical sentence which says that neither parents nor children are to be preferred to our Christ (Matt. 10:37). Among some people it may be considered glorious and worthy of being offered as a saving example to have presented one son as a sacrifice to God. She surpassed every strength and aspiration of souls, so that, amid the pain of raging punishment, the affection of maternal devotion did not spare any of her sons.

Consider through how many steps of virtue her precious faith grew. Where it is sufficient to have consented once, she seven times punished her maternal affection through voluntary bereavement for the love of the Lord; fully conscious of what was good for her, knowing that the whole fruit of her womb consisted in that eternity of life, in accordance with the saying: “Whoever loves his life will lose it, and whoever hates his life will find it unto eternal life” (John 22:11).

2. The reading of the Old Testament teaches that our father Abraham offered his only son Isaac as a sacrifice to God, to be sacrificed. This is acknowledged throughout the whole world as a memorable demonstration of faith. Although no blood was poured upon the altars, victory existed in the will, because before the Lord wanting is equivalent to doing. Thus we read that the angel cried out to him: “Abraham, Abraham, do not lay your hands upon the boy; it is enough that I have learned that you love the Lord your God” (Gen. 22:11–12).

If, then, our father Abraham offered one son as a sacrifice and pleased God, how much more did she please him who at one time sacrificed seven, with seven vows consenting, and offered herself to God as the eighth victim—so that she who had been a teacher urging on the glory of heaven for so many courageous men might herself also become an example of outstanding virtue?

But if it pleases you, beloved, let us recall the order of the battle itself, so that parents may learn to love their children and children to obey their parents, while the love of our Christ is placed first. He prepares the crown of life with heavenly flowers for victors who fight in a legitimate contest, as the Lord says: “Whoever conquers, I will give him the crown of life” (Rev. 11:11).

Behold, beloved, as the faithfulness of the event itself declares, a battle is instituted for the ancestral laws between the ministers of almighty God and the devil, equipped with many and countless punishments. Armed with these, the author of iniquity was accustomed to exercise the poisons of his wickedness.

Although hostile fury rages against the ministers of righteousness with many terrors, the conflict takes place without trembling. At this point the craftsman of crimes and enemy of the good attacks their hearts with a deeper plan. He therefore prepares the weapons of his impiety against each one individually and, according to his custom, arranges single combat through a punitive strategy. He believes that the brotherhood, divided into separate parts by adversity, can easily be disturbed and not difficult to conquer if punishment exhausts each person placed under interrogation.

3. Therefore the eldest is brought forward first, while on every side the services of impiety stand around and roar with the entire apparatus of death. The persecutor proceeds deliberately, thinking that once the head of the united virtue had been removed, the whole war could be ended [Col. 0748A]. But the plans of one excessively schooled in cruelty deceived him, to his misfortune.

For the enemy is defeated all the more shamefully the greater the crowd of attendants serves the tyrant against one righteous man. It is the greatest indication of cowardice that, amid compacted masses of enemies, one person should carry away the palm of victory.

When the enemy’s fury was wounded, and various kinds of tortures served it, the executioner’s bloody hand ran through them one by one. To instill the fear of death, he carried their brother’s blood to each of them, searching out, through the fear of death, evidence of his cruelty. But while he attempts to obtain a place of victory over one, he confesses himself conquered by another.

Their strength nevertheless stood unshaken in all of them, animated by the sufferings of their own brothers. The second enters the battle line; not after a long interval, the third follows [Col. 0748B]. When these had been crowned, the fourth undertakes the battle; neither the fifth nor the sixth was deterred by deadly death.

There is finally one faith, one virtue, one conscience in them all, so that you would think them all one and believe them all to be one, although injury tore each of them apart individually. Thus the brotherhood, animated by sharing in victory, while serving the ancestral laws, carried away the insignia of manifold virtue.

4. Amid so many pageants of funerals, the mother runs about stunned, anxious with cares, crushed by fear and terror. But let no one be deceived by this. She trembles indeed, but over the outcome of the victory, not over the death of her sons. At each interrogation the mother stands anxiously, lest faith deceive anyone, lest human frailty separate anyone from the fellowship of holiness.

Against the enemy’s bloody threats [Col. 0748C], she diligently encourages each one, so that he would not wish to be anything other than a brother. Each suffers individually, but she suffers with each one and, in spirit, is tortured alone with each one.

Thus she takes up the palm of her own virtue in love for almighty God. But if you consider individually all that maternal devotion endured, she shared a portion of martyrdom with all her sons.

After so many countless palms of virtue, behold, they come to the one whose age had given the enemy hope of obtaining victory. When the enemy saw that his threatening interrogation had achieved little with men stronger by age, he attacks the boy’s mind with the soothing language of gentle exhortation and, finally, by every path of crafty persuasion. He judges him worthy of riches and honor and thinks that she can be caressed through the release of her one son. But the mind, now wholly directed toward heaven, does not readily accept counsel from the earthly side; the spirit of fearless childhood is kindled still more toward the summit of virtue by the exhortation of his mother.

5. O new and wonderful example of virtue! In her bereavement the mother rejoices; and from the very thing through which affection suffers loss, she derives gain. Having sent ahead even this son whom she loved more tenderly, she too enters upon the path of glorious death; and, not long afterward, harassed by countless tortures, having followed her sons in triumph, she rushed away to the heavenly and eternal realms, despising this temporal light. Therefore, beloved, whoever cares for the pledges of her womb should imitate the example of this mother—so numerous, so courageous. Whoever fixes his attention upon her with a desire for victory will undoubtedly proceed adorned with the honor of manifold glory. Let every mother, therefore, judge her sons worthy of this honor, and by the exhortation that you have heard teach them to learn to observe the institutions of the heavenly laws.

Those, however, who serve our Christ should imitate the battles of the bravest men. That mother proves that she loves her sons who, having driven away this error by which the world strives, has offered to God a sacrifice from the fruit of her womb and willingly presented herself and her children, intending daily to sacrifice them to the Lord. But so that we may more easily obtain the insignia of that heavenly virtue, the gifts and honors of this age must be despised, since, with vanity persuading them, they deceive human eyes. It is established that this sacrifice is acceptable to the Lord: if, after heavenly honor has been preferred, you begin to despise the world.

[Col. 0749B]

HOMILY XIX. On Lent.

1. If we consider, beloved, the reason for the present solemnity, which commends to us the hope of eternal salvation through the law of the future resurrection, it is not inappropriate for us to spend all these days in rejoicing and to moderate those practices of the stricter life. Yet in this the chorus of rejoicers sometimes displeases me: a person thinks that everything is permitted to him that, during Lent, he had assigned to religious discipline. Hence no one can doubt that his previous observances come to nothing if he does not know how to preserve whatever he had acquired for the purification of his soul through the labor of fasts and vigils. He quickly destroys what he has acquired who, forgetful of spiritual gifts, gives way to carnal desires.

For amid the joys of which we have spoken, that path of religious discipline must be maintained which undoubtedly commends a person of good will to the Lord. If we knew how to observe toward it the reverence owed according to its laws, Gehenna would receive no one, nor would the punishment of perpetual death condemn anyone. We must therefore make every effort, beloved, lest indulgence through excessive relaxation attack the conscience of a purified body; we must not be content merely with observing those days which the annual care of fasting commends. Although this very observance is known to be displeasing to some because of useless sleep and insatiable gluttony. While they hurry toward the days of holy Easter, spurred on by desire, they accuse the practices of vigils, the good things of continence, [Note: [Col. 0749D] The whole of this sentence is made very obscure both by omitted punctuation and by one corrupt word, which we now emend as follows: “Accusing the practices of vigils: the good things of continence, frugal banquets, and abundant fasts, etc.” When the word *Pascha* is changed to *parca* (“frugal”), the elegance of the sentence is restored. BAUN.] Easter [Col. 0749D] banquets, and abundant fasts. As though, in truth, what the days of Lent prohibit were permitted by a votive solemnity to be done lawfully, and as though permission to sin had been granted with the release from fasting.

2. Therefore let no one think that everything is permitted to him because he sees that the period of stricter living has passed. Careless relaxation is accustomed to deceive every condition of honorable life. Let no one think that drunkenness has been permitted because he sees fasting cease at the appointed time. Let no one believe that human minds have been assigned to sleep because he sees continual vigils suspended when the solemnity arrives. A servant is not useful who waits for holidays merely in order to sleep.

The farmer’s anxiety is greater after he has touched the earth with prolonged labor. He must therefore first keep watch lest the seed entrusted to the furrows be either claimed by a savage, presumptuous creature or disregarded by a treacherous bird. Next, in leisure time, a ditch must be led to serve as a channel for water, lest an approaching storm either destroy or carry away the growing shoots. Weeds must also be pulled up, and the dry turf softened by the work of the hoe; and throughout those twenty-seven days which farmers claim as holidays for themselves, a troublesome animal must be kept away by means of a surrounding fence. For so great is the love of nurturing life, so great the care of foresight, so great the devotion to cultivation, that no one ought even then to be idle when the farmer entrusts the fruit to the ear of grain in its perfected bloom.

For mature harvests are often hindered by growing thorns, and those things established in the hope of ripeness are choked by foreign seed. Thus one must understand that many things grow through the farmer’s diligence, while the greatest things are lost through negligence.

3. But perhaps you say: “All negligences are excused by the solemnity.” Without doubt, everyone is exposed to dangers who at any time has surrendered his life to negligence. In the end, the reins are never loosened well for horses assigned to idleness. So, after winter’s rigor, the earth, quickly drunk with waters, luxuriates. We also frequently see ships, near the closest harbor of the sea, suffer sudden wrecks while their oars lie still.

Looking to these examples, therefore, beloved brothers, let us arrange the order of our life so that, in the first place, we chastise the luxury of banquets, until the fleeting desires of the flesh withdraw from us. I do not say this as though one must abstain from food to such an extent, or entirely spare drinks; for although bodies are prepared for the cross, they must nevertheless always be sustained. What displeases me in these days is only insatiable gluttony and those unproductive transactions of the belly; I dislike a banquet poured out in drunkenness and exposed to ridicule throughout the entire night. A person certainly exceeds the measure of discipline if he drinks more than he thirsts.

What, then, is so hateful in those banquets where, besides the vice of drunkenness, the loss of property also comes together? Who could endure the losses of drunkenness, where more is spent for the sake of drunkenness than is drunk? Or who would willingly look upon the arrangement of that dining room in which everything is soiled by the odor of wine being squandered? For when unmixed wine runs over, the banquet necessarily bristles with disgraceful filth, and whatever a full wine-jar has received is utterly wasted.

4. Let the person who delights in drunkenness, then, consider what his future will be, and let him wisely apply his mind to what we are about to say; he will not find it difficult to recognize the cause of his unhappiness. If you fill a vessel with too much oil, the boiling wave of the vintage returns to its open mouth, and with filth it vomits out whatever it has received in excess. We also frequently see vessels of goat-skin spoiled by overflowing wine, and earthenware jars open cracks when their struggling contents surge against them.

Death would have no power at all if wretched people knew how to avoid the causes of perishing. But the person who places an additional burden upon weakened bodies fortifies the way of weakness. Thus the person whose unjust burden accuses him completes a journey that was doubtfully begun.

I therefore urge you, beloved, that if anyone intends to please our Christ, he should first chastise the desires of the stomach, which, with drunkenness serving as its mistress, is accustomed to be the cause of losses. From this, finally, comes nakedness; from that, beggary; from another source, impoverished destitution—just as Solomon says: “Every drunkard will be clothed in rags” (Prov. XXIII, 21).

Rather let the fruits of continence persist in those things by which we seem to serve the Lord continually with devoted mind during the days of Lent. Let us not, when perhaps we have surrendered ourselves to be possessed by negligence, appear to have devoted ourselves to the pursuit of honorable living only in particular seasons, and not in our conduct.

What does it profit you to present yourself as good to the Lord for forty days, and to offend him on a single day through the fury of impious cruelty? What good is it to have preserved reverence for chastity through long stretches of time, if afterward you are carried away to a shameful deed at the prompting of lust? What does it profit you to have cheated greed for a time, if, after the many fruits of mercy that a generous hand has bestowed upon you, you take delight in the losses and tears of others? Whatever a person has acquired through just works over many years is certainly lost if, within the space of a single hour, he is corrupted by some disgraceful error of life.

5. This, then, is the principle of preserving discipline: nourish integrity within yourself, love chastity, cultivate peace, and, under the fear of discipline, bring to confusion everything that serves iniquity. Let mediocrity not grow proud over the superior, nor poverty be despised in comparison with persons of rank.

Just as it is a great thing always to have served those who are better, so it is useful and glorious to have shown reverence toward a humbler person. For insofar as a person endowed with dignity humbles himself, he is raised up, as the Lord says: “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Matt. XXIII, 11).

The path of humility must therefore be chosen before all else. It is subject neither to hatred, and it always acquires much love, as the Apostle says: “God gives grace to the humble, but resists the proud” (Jas. IV, 6). Let the person who sees the punishment of heavenly wrath stirred up against himself consider whether he can doubt the punishment of the future judgment because of such wicked labor. If anyone forestalls that punishment through humility, it will not be difficult for him to find in the heavenly dwelling a place of eternal possession—from which that devil, expelled through the working of pride, received the sentence of perpetual condemnation.

Let us therefore pursue humility, sobriety, continence, and chastity; let us labor with devoted zeal to obtain holiness, so that our life may be shaken by no losses to the soul and may never sigh under any hatred before the Lord.

HOMILY XX. On Avarice.

1. Beloved, the authorities on all cures assert that different medicinal benefits correspond to different pains, and that each illness receives its own particular remedy. Thus they teach that swellings must either be restrained by the knife or softened by the preparation of a medicine; that hidden conditions are better investigated through potions; that cold parts of the body should be nourished with hot things, and hotter parts tempered with colder ones.

I, however, think differently in the work of divine instruction. For if you review that Epistle written to Timothy, you will find that many illnesses can be cured by one medicine and the cutting away of one wound. What that wound is, in which diverse diseases meet and produce deadly pains, the holy Apostle Paul clearly explained when he said: “The root of all evils is greed; in reaching for it, some have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many pains” (I Tim. VI, 10).

We must therefore consider, beloved, by what work and labor so great a forest of crimes should be cut down. But first you must recognize the causes of all the vices that converge from every side into one, and diligently investigate from what each descends, where it goes, and what deformity and pain it produces. For the greatest hope of recovering health is to know the source of the disease.

2. The root of all evils is greed. And truly, beloved, if we consider the various ways in which, from the beginning, the human condition has prostituted its life to the desire for possessions, there is no evil that greed does not either conceive, give birth to, feed, or nourish. From this fuel we see the causes of hatred spring up; from here arise the battles of crimes; from here brotherly lines are drawn up for battle; from here the bonds of friendships are shattered.

Let no one therefore assign the guilt of a particular pain to each individual illness. For although all vices stand under their own names, they nevertheless depend upon the crimes of others. We see, then, pride brought into order by the swelling of vanity, and every humble person moved by the contagion of arrogance.

If you suddenly observe such a person placed among equals, you judge him to be someone other than he was: so elevated does he walk in his words, so swollen is his appearance as you see him carry his neck toward heaven, and with the benefit of poverty long keeping his path closed, fortify the road of his tongue with the burdens of words. He arranges the words of his disdainful mouth to such an extent that, when he himself wishes to speak, he does not wish to listen to another.

Yet although these things are serious in themselves, it is clear that they are animated by the allurements of greed. Finally, when the pomp of wealth ceases, you will not so easily find someone laboring under the envy of pride.

[Col. 0752D]

3. The root of all evils is greed. Let us run through the individual cases, if you please, and you will find how many evils the vice of greed produces.

Look: neighbors are often armed for litigation. Why is this, unless one of them is thinking of crossing the boundaries and occupying a piece of another’s lawful ground? Why does that saying not come before their eyes: “Do not cross the boundaries that your fathers established” (Prov. XII, 28)?

Look: contention over ownership first arises in this place; and while each person nourishes his own greed with words, he kindles the spark of litigation. Then accusation grows out of contention—and would that this alone were enough for greed! The more serious matter is that, while no one wishes to suffer the loss of the slander he has begun, the affair reaches a quarrel.

Servants are armed, relatives are incited, and one person’s breast is exposed to another’s gain. Fury hired for the purpose is stirred by wine, and shed blood becomes the price of possession. The forum is then opened to the laws; and while a place for vengeance is sought, murder is doubled.

We also frequently see battle lines formed by greed, when one man wants to appear richer or another is ashamed to be poorer. While these people rival one another, the security of neighboring property is endangered, as each seeks to invade first and plans how to possess with impunity. Thus, while greed seeks increase, another person’s patrimony totters.

4. Why do these people not consider the saying that declares: “Fool, this night your soul will be required of you; and these things that you have prepared—whose will they be?” (Luke XII, 20). Truly, nothing is more foolish than seeking uncertain things and acquiring things destined to perish.

What benefit do riches bring a person when they are gathered only so that they may perish? Certainly, when you die, the plot of land propagated by greed remains; the enlarged property is left behind. Although it has passed into another’s power, it will nevertheless preserve testimony to your crime.

Here one must always consider that prophetic saying: “Woe to him who joins house to house and field to field” (Isa. V, 8).

But you say: “I read that parents ought to store up treasures for their children” (II Cor. I, 24). From this very saying you can recognize what your devotion has accomplished. Look: the adornments of your wealth pass to another, while envy born of your persuasion remains with you. The pomp of your resources settles with another, while punishment migrates with you. It is a kind of folly to have made profit for others and prepared punishment for oneself.

For the Apostle says: “Those who wish to become rich fall into temptation and a snare of the devil” (I Tim. VI, 9).

5. Nor does the heavenly sentence delay long in extending the severity of its power. In a certain manner, the growth of vices proceeds by stages toward a kind of vengeance for past acts.

At last, a person with a parricidal mind either censures his father’s life or awaits his mother’s death. Let the rightful claim of inheritance perhaps protect him from this crime. It is true: yet although he may be a legitimate heir, he does not arrange his hopes of succession without the vice of greed. In the end, he would wish to be an only child if he could; now he thinks of his father’s death, now he sighs for his brother’s life. This is not without the great crime of impiety.

For whoever nourishes his soul by awaiting a parent’s death succeeds to the inheritance through the crime of parricide. Here, driven by greed, hatred is nourished among co-heirs. The funeral has not yet left the house, and already the validity of the will is emptied by legal interpretation. One disputes the father’s signature; another despairs of the brother’s standing. One asserts that the document cannot stand under the witnesses; another declares that the will does not correspond to the circumstances.

Thus the estate totters amid the collision of claims; and what the avarice of the parents acquired, the greed of the children destroys.

Hear Scripture saying: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property” (Exod. XX, 17). It is impossible to enumerate the ways in which greed rages. Look: when the will is produced, falsity is immediately suspected. People ask who heard a mute person speak, who knew a dead man appointing heirs. Nor is it difficult—what is worse—for anyone to find persons either joined to the crime or purchased for a price. This wretched man imitates another’s handwriting. Thus greed, repeatedly guiding the pen, composes a document that the testator did not establish.

6. The root of all evils is greed. One person arms falsehood with perjury to confirm fraud; another sometimes places a corrupted heart at the service of other people’s lawsuits. Thus, under the vice of a single greed, property is both acquired and torn apart.

Where is what Scripture says: “A false witness will not go unpunished” (Prov. V, 19)? Whom should we hold responsible for this—that among those whom we hear have sometimes been involved in crimes, even the innocent are summoned into the accusation? Suspicion frequently enters the inquiry; and while the guilt of theft rests with one person, the disrepute of appropriation passes to another. Thus, while an increase of possessions is sought, even things honestly acquired are torn apart.

So it happens that sometimes falsehood descends from greed, and poverty from falsehood.

The root of all evils is greed. Why do we often see armed legions standing against one another? What else is it except that one seeks to seize another’s property, or another guards what has been seized? Hence comes the fact that people sometimes contend over imperial power and compete for primacy. Everything would certainly remain at peace if the desire to rule did not remove a person from peace.

7. The root of all evils is avarice. Let us ask whose vice it is that human life is entrusted to a frail plank and the uncertainties of the sea are tested amid doubtful dangers. Is it not to be attributed to greed when, as a storm approaches, the sailor’s cry assails the deep sea? Does it not return to the envy of greed when a shipwrecked body is dashed against jagged rocks and limbs swollen by the waters are hurled by the waves of the sea onto unknown shores?

A sailor would never have entrusted himself to a ship if the desire to sail had not been driven on by the greed of trade. In the end, a person is carried over the waves by the hope of quadrupling his money; gold is transported so that it may be brought back with the falsehood of perjury. For no commercial transaction is conducted without fraud when something is bought more cheaply for the sole purpose of selling it more dearly.

Even if, in this matter, a voyage should succeed according to human wishes in calm conditions, it is not without shipwreck when, between seller and buyer, someone either commits or suffers injustice through dishonest weights or measures. Why do these people not consider the saying that declares: “As you have measured, so it will be measured to you” (Matt. VII, 2)?

8. We are ashamed to speak of those things, beloved, that are brought about by lust, from which the traffic of greed descends. Thus marital modesty frequently becomes cheap through a monetary assessment, and virginity long kept undefiled, prostituted for a small weight of gold, loses the trust of its integrity.

Greed is so great among some people that purchased modesty finds a price for its disgrace. Money is carefully weighed out for the corruption of the body as though something worthy were being bought. Truly wretched is the person who takes greater care of greed than of modesty. He has condemned the gift of the promised inheritance and suffered the loss of integrity.

See, under a single crime, how different is the exchange of greed. One person gave money in order to purchase corruption; the other lost modesty in order to acquire money. Nothing is done without greed whenever sin is committed. For if you remove the adornment of ornaments, you will suffer no shipwreck in the contamination of the body. Let the desire for gold cease, and neither marital fidelity will perish nor virginal integrity blush with shame.

9. The root of all evils is avarice. One person is accused of betrayal; another, as an informer concerning another’s crime, is accused. Who could doubt that the weight of offered money has broken into the secret of the heart? Nothing is closed that gold and silver cannot open; nothing is hidden that money, investigating it, cannot discover. Hence the trust of conscience is dangerously placed in those whom greed rules.

Integrity would certainly possess the whole secret if treacherous money did not gain entry into another’s house.

The root of all evils is greed. Look: our Lord and Savior fulfilled the outcome of his voluntary Passion through the vice of another’s greed. We read that the condemnation of our Redeemer was purchased for thirty pieces of silver. But just as you have seen betrayal arise from greed, so you must recognize condemnation descending from betrayal. The betrayed man is led to punishment, but the betrayer runs to the noose.

Look at what fruit greed bears: money set aside for the purchase of condemnation and assigned to a burial—that is, devoted to funeral expenses. Understand, then, the condition of the guilt of greed, when the price of betrayal has come to condemnation. The Apostle Peter also says: “May your money be with you for destruction” (Acts VIII, 2).

Perhaps there is some foolish and avaricious person who flatters himself because of this saying and prefers to hear that his money will migrate with him. We do not take away from his wishes in this respect. It will indeed come with you—not, as you think, for the adornment of your body, but as testimony to your falsehood.

This does not, however, apply to those whom mercy accompanies. One destiny awaits those whose money the Lord commends through generous distribution to be spent among the poor; another awaits those whom their resources, stored up through crime, accuse. For the latter, it is counted toward punishment; for the former, it is prepared for the kingdom, as the Lord says: “Come, children, possess with me the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was naked, and you clothed me” (Matt. XXV, 34–36).

10. Let each one of you, beloved, therefore be content with that kind of money which acquires the grace of salvation, not with that which kindles the cause of condemnation.

Let us first chastise greed, if we wish to overcome the error of all vices. Let no one desire what belongs to another, and no one will suffer the resentment of enmities. Let no one attack another’s partnership, and there will be no dispute over seizure. Let each person be content with his own, and there will be no accusation concerning occupied property.

Despise gold, and murder, already prepared, vanishes; nor are parricidal hatreds sown if the eye of greed is chastised. There is no matter in which an heir need blush if he approaches content with the modesty of his share. Let no one seek an increase of money, and no one will be accused of the guilt of betrayal.

If you do not seek profit, you will suffer no shipwreck in a storm; and while you quietly guard the hidden places of your own small field, you will look securely upon another’s danger.

To avoid these things one by one may perhaps be difficult, beloved, and it is laborious to confront many enemies simultaneously through their various errors. We must therefore seek a shortcut in the battle and look for the author of the quarrel, so that our fight may be with the one from whom the injury proceeded.

For you cannot doubtless defeat legions equipped with weapons unless you can overcome the tyrant. The person who overcomes the author of the battle has brought the entire cause of the war to an end.

Let us therefore draw up the ranks of the virtues against the prepared legions of crimes. But before all else, let us fight, with faith assisting us, against greed itself, which is the head of the battle. Thus victory over that stain of the vices of which we have spoken will not be difficult, once the mother has been captured.

[Col. 0755]

LETTER OF ST. VALERIAN, BISHOP OF CEMELIUM, TO THE MONKS. On the Virtues and the Order of Apostolic Teaching. (C)

[Col. 0755D] 30 The burdens of your vows concerning me have been imposed upon me; and although for the present I am absent in body, as it is written, I nevertheless come to you present in spirit and mind (I Cor. V, 3; Col. II, 5). Nor, as I think, do I offer little in duty and affection to your love, because I trust that you too act in spirit, not in the flesh, as the Apostle says: “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God. But you are not in the flesh, but in the spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you” (Rom. VIII, 8–9).

Nor do I follow an unfamiliar path among spiritual people when I express my concern for your edification in the words of epistolary eloquence; I have before my eyes the outstanding example of the blessed Paul, whom we desire to follow, even if we cannot equal him. For although comparison with him admits us nowhere, your obedience must nevertheless be equal to that of those whom he instructs.

Thus, with the order of teaching established, and desiring that your faith be proclaimed throughout the whole world, as it was among the ROMANS (Rom. I, 8), corrected by a second emendation, with complete peace and unfeigned charity, greet one another with a holy kiss, as it is written (I Cor. XVI, 20; II Cor. XIII, 12), as among the CORINTHIANS. With the GALATIANS (Gal.
