IV, 10, 30–31), rejecting the observance of months, seasons, and days, repudiating the world and following God, understand that you are not children of the slave woman but of the free woman.

Remaining in the word of truth with the EPHESIANS (Eph. I, 13; IV, 5), know one Lord, one faith, one God and Father of all, who is above all, through all, and in us all. With the PHILIPPIANS (Phil. II, 14–15), blameless and simple, doing everything without murmuring and hesitation, shine like lights in the midst of a crooked nation.

With the COLOSSIANS (Col. III, 16), with the word of Christ dwelling abundantly in you, teach one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs. With the THESSALONIANS (I Thess. IV, 1, 3; V, 17), abstaining from fornication, pursue the will of God, pray without ceasing, test everything, and hold fast to what is good.

Thereafter, following the order of the commandment with every effort, so that “if anyone is unwilling to work, neither let him eat” (II Thess. III, 10). For he is the bread that came down from heaven (John VI, 51, 59); no one ought to be mingled with him unless he practices the works that please him.

Let TIMOTHY be a model for you: he was commanded, even after prolonged use of water, to use a little wine for the support of his stomach (I Tim. V, 23), not for its oppression; for although he is instructed by repeated admonitions, unless a person is sober he will not be able to fulfill his ministry (II Tim. IV, 5).

Let the example of TITUS shape you: you must not only be sober but also continent, since “all things are clean to the clean, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean” (Titus I, 8, 15).

Finally, this conclusion of the whole apostolic teaching completes the sum of the mystical number through purification of the body, because nothing is so close to God as a person who is not corrupted.

Let us therefore observe more carefully what follows after these things. A servant once a fugitive returns to his master, and his condition is changed by conversion (Philem.). Born through apostolic bonds, the formerly useless man becomes useful; and not merely as a brother, but as a beloved brother, he surpasses the rank of related names by the elevation of souls. He merits not only the bond of the name but also the affection of love.

Pure chastity, nourished by sobriety, is brought by the Lord’s gracious favor to this point: what moderation in wine accomplished in Timothy, and what abstinence and continence purified in Titus, grows into the most indulgent freedom in ONESIMUS.

These things must be carried out by the learned and recognized by the unlearned, because, as it is written, “ignorance too is death” (I Cor. XIV, 38), and “faith without works is dead” (Jas. II, 26). A double obligation of observance rests upon you: care to know, together with labor to fulfill. For what is commanded in the divine utterances is sin not only to fail to do but also to fail to know.

Finally, taking the HEBREWS as an example of consummate perfection, I commend contempt for present things through love of heavenly rewards. If perhaps someone should impose upon you the burden of persecution or plunder everything that belongs to you, may you too pursue, with no different devotion to holy imitation, that noble and singular testimony which Paul, speaking with venerable mouth, proclaimed in their highest praise: “For you had compassion on those in bonds, and you joyfully accepted the seizure of your possessions” (Heb. X, 34).

[Col. 0757]

THEOPHILUS RAYNAUD, S.J., APOLOGY FOR ST. VALERIAN, BISHOP OF CEMELIUM, AGAINST NICOLAS CHICHON.

[Col. 0757C]

PROLOGUE. The Purpose and Method of Acting on Valerian’s Behalf.

33 It must be considered that the following saying or command of the excellent mother to her beloved Samuel, her child, in the vision in which she instructs him—“Open your mouth for the mute and for the causes of all the children who pass by” (Prov. XXXI)—applies equally to everyone whenever the occasion arises and the ability is not lacking.

If we seek the genuine meaning of this otherwise obscure passage, whoever preserves an innocent person—one who nevertheless cannot speak on his own behalf or defend his case—from the attacks directed against him opens his mouth for the mute. This is precisely to undertake and open one’s mouth in defense of the causes of passing children—that is, the weak and those incapable of defending themselves (as passers-by and resident aliens generally are). Their mother wished this to be commended to her beloved son as a distinguished work of charity, and it is to be expressed by anyone else through imitation.

With this purpose, since Valerian of Cemelium, a bishop recently brought forth from long darkness, has endangered—and continues to endanger—his reputation through the sharp accusation and most fervent zeal of a certain theologian, whom not even the rigors of the Alps could temper, and since the man I have called the “SPARSE CHARITY” accuser [Note: [Col. 0757D] This was the aforementioned Nicolas Chichon.] everywhere attacks Valerian as discovered and convicted of Semi-Pelagian error and strives with every cry he can raise to have Valerian’s work and name returned to their former tomb and darkness, I have judged it consistent with charity to open my mouth on behalf of a man who is, if not holy—for even this honor is endangered for him through the accuser’s zeal—at least mute and no longer able to speak for himself, and to assist the cause of one who is passing by and the hard-pressed reputation of Valerian.

For although the blemishes sprinkled upon him by the accuser are not merely great but even the smallest, nevertheless even little stains darken exquisite brightness, and flies—even tiny ones—destroy the sweetness of the ointment in which they die.

[Col. 0759A] Besides the common reason proposed above, a private reason also impelled me to this duty: the fragrance of these flowery homilies, “verdant with every charm,” as Hilary of Arles aptly said of the writings of Eucherius, once wafted many centuries ago over our neighborhood, which Valerian governed as bishop, and therefore also over our own region, although belonging to another diocese and province yet not very far removed. It seems worthy to dispel every trace of shame from them so that they may continue to breathe their fragrance.

I seem likely to accomplish this conveniently if, after presenting what concerns Valerian’s person—something that will appear necessary for removing the stain from his teaching, as will become clear from what follows—I diligently and carefully examine these homilies, which the accusation of “SPARSE CHARITY” attacks by denying them a favorable interpretation, bringing forward everything from which any blemish appears to have been cast upon the sincere and wholly Catholic teaching of this writer.

After these matters have been explained and carefully adjusted to the standard of sound doctrine, let the other head of the accusation also be addressed: an investigation of whether Valerian ought henceforth to retain the title of saint with which very ancient manuscript codices honor him.

[Col. 0759B]

CHAPTER I. Valerian’s See.—Concerning His Age, Nation, Family, Private Condition, and Conjectures.

1. Theodoretus, as elegant in this as in everything, in his ninth oration *On Providence*, imitating Chrysostom’s seventh homily on the Epistle to the Colossians concerning the words “Your life is hidden,” observes that most of the saints, although illustrious before God and already crowned with glory, may nevertheless, so long as they are tossed upon the waves of the world, be compared to a pearl. They are hidden, as it were, within an oyster, and human beings remain without glory; therefore, he concludes, God provided the condition of another age, in which each person’s honor and worth would be established openly and it would become clear what they had been even while they were pressed down in obscurity and unknown.

This can be discerned not only in countless other most holy men but specifically in Valerian. Although some small remnant of antiquity preserves him as illustrious under the name of holiness, a great obscurity has nevertheless until now covered him in most respects, together with the common, so to speak, envy of the age. Thus, of the matters proposed, only his see is certain; in the others, conjecture must generally be used. Nevertheless, we shall try to creep from the see, which is established, toward the remaining matters.

### 34. 2. Valerian’s See

Valerian’s see was Cemelium, also called Cella or Cemelinus. I find the city designated by all these names. Now scarcely any ruins remain of it, near Nice, at Salyum, on a hill which still bears the name Cemelium; the memory of the once-flourishing city, however empty of actual things, also endures. For if one removes the shrine of the Mother of God and the abbey of Saint Pontius, everything else is merely fields and vineyards where Cemelium once stood.

Truly, as Seneca says in Letter 91:

> Nothing is stable, whether privately or publicly. The destinies of both human beings and cities roll onward.

And as he aptly says in Letter 71 [Col. 0759D]:

> Everything proceeds at appointed times: it must be born, grow, and perish. Every individual has his own old age. The whole human race, and everything that is and shall be, has been condemned to death. All cities that anywhere possess power over things, and that are the great ornaments of foreign empires—of each of them it will one day be asked where it has been.

Antonius also wisely wrote about death in Book IV of *On His Life*, no. 38:

> How many cities, so to speak, are dead? Helice, Pompeii, Herculaneum, and countless others.

Similarly, Saint Ambrose, in Letter 8, addressed to Faustinus, speaks of the corpses of half-ruined cities and the funerals of lands displayed beneath the same sky. To these I add Cemelium, whose former existence and not inglorious status are indicated by its ruins and are clearly attested by Pliny and the ancient geographers.

### 3.

[Col. 0760A] From the established location of Valerian’s see, a fairly strong conjecture can be drawn concerning his period. For from a letter of Pope Hilary to certain bishops of Gaul, it appears that, by decree of Saint Leo the Great, the bishopric of Cemelium was joined to the bishopric of the *castrum*—for that is how he calls it—of Nice, plainly because of the great proximity of the two places and the narrow extent of their dioceses.

From that time, therefore, the same man was both bishop of Cemelium and bishop of Nice. He was not called merely Cemelian or merely Nicene, but was designated by the combined name of both cities, as is clear from the Fifth Council of Orléans, to which the presbyter Aetius subscribed in the name of Magnus, bishop of Cemelium and Nice. In the printed copies of that council, however, the subscription is mutilated, as the Reverend Father Jacques Sirmond, who published Valerian, observed.

From this observation he further infers that, since Valerian is read as having been called simply bishop of Cemelium, he must have presided over the Church of Cemelium before Saint Leo united the two sees, and therefore cannot have been later than Saint Leo the Great. I would readily concede this. He adds that Valerian should be placed around the year 450, that is, regarded as a contemporary of Saint Leo. [Col. 0760B] He bases this on the fact that there exists a letter of that same Saint Leo, published by Cardinal Baronius from a manuscript of Arles, addressed to Valerian and Ingenuus of Embrun, Valerian’s metropolitan, and to the other bishops of the neighboring provinces of Gaul, concerning the ordination of the bishop of Vaison. There is also another letter among Saint Leo’s letters, no. 42, addressed to all the bishops of Gaul, in which Valerian and Ingenuus are mentioned among the Gallic bishops whose letter to Saint Leo had immediately preceded it.

Likewise, Valerian is said to have subscribed, together with the other bishops of that region, to a council held at that time at Riez in Gaul. Finally, Valerian the bishop is honorably mentioned in a recently discovered Council of Arles under Ravennio, a contemporary of Saint Leo, in these words:

> The case that arose between the holy bishop Theodore and the holy Valerian, or the holy Maximus, likewise bishops, and Abraham Faustus, as well as the other brothers of the island of Lérins, [Col. 0760C] plainly cannot be deferred by all of us who are one in Christ, unless we act in such a way that it may be settled and cleansed.

Theodore was bishop of Fréjus, while Maximus was bishop of Riez; Faustus later succeeded him—indeed, succeeded him twice, as Sidonius sings to him. Thus, when a dispute arose between Theodore, who was near Lérins, and Faustus, abbot of Lérins, Maximus, formerly abbot of Lérins and then bishop of Riez, took the side of Faustus and the people of Lérins. The times and places agree, so that the bishop Valerian who likewise supported Faustus’s party was this same bishop of Cemelium whom I shall later show to have once lived as a monk in the monastery of Lérins.

Although I do not deny that these conjectures are highly probable, I nevertheless see that they are only conjectures and unlikely to persuade an unyielding mind, especially because in the letters and councils cited Valerian is nowhere called Cemelian. Nor is Ingenuus, who is listed after Valerian in the cited letters, said to have been metropolitan of Embrun. [Col. 0760D] This seems to be weakened by the position in which Ingenuus is listed later. I will not press the further point that this may be attributed to the completeness of the council or to a defect in a title added later: namely, that those bishops belonged to the metropolitan see of Arles, distinct both from Embrun, to which Cemelium was subject, and from Aix, to which Riez was subordinate.

Finally, that several bishops named Valerian flourished at the same time in that region of Gaul is shown by the letter of the Gallic bishops to Saint Leo and by that pontiff’s reply to them, which is among Letter 52. It must therefore be entirely uncertain which of them can be identified with our Valerian. Nevertheless, since there are several considerations in favor of Valerian and the other circumstances agree, it is not unreasonable to think that one of them was this very Valerian whom we seek, the bishop of Cemelium. I am altogether convinced of this. Enough concerning Valerian’s period.

### 4.

His nationality is less obscure. From what has been said, it appears evident that he was a Gaul, and his see agrees with this. [Col. 0761A] For although Cemelium is placed in Italy by Pliny, Ptolemy, Leander, and several other geographers, this was evidently because they regarded the Var as the boundary of Italy. In former times, however, when the boundaries of Gaul extended as far as the highest Alps, Cemelium was enclosed within the territory of Gaul. This is also affirmed by the ancient itineraries and by the *Register of the Cities of Gaul*, which counts Cemelium among the cities of the Maritime Alps subject to the metropolitan see of Embrun.

Moreover, in the Roman Martyrology, on the day before the Ides of May, Saint Pontius—who had brought the two emperors named Philip to Christ—is said to have suffered in Gaul under Valerian and Gallienus. It is certain that he suffered at Cemelium; and both facts, namely that he suffered at Cemelium and in Gaul, are explicitly affirmed by Usuard on that day. Peter of Exquilinum, bishop, also agrees in his *Catalogue*, where he likewise makes Pontius bishop of Cemelium. The ancient Acts published by Surius agree as well.

Valerian celebrated this Pontius, beheaded at Cemelium for Christ, in three homilies *On the Praise of Martyrdom*, as a particular glory of his Church. This is shown by the familiar passage from Homily 17 on that subject [Col. 0761B]:

> Of that martyr who [35] first exercised in this place the contest of renowned virtue.

Although in that region—indeed, at Nice, which stood immediately beside Cemelium—others had shed their blood for Christ before Saint Pontius, such as Saint Bassus under Decius on 5 December, Pontius was nevertheless the first to complete the struggle of martyrdom at Cemelium.

Therefore Cemelium was enclosed within the boundaries of Gaul, since, as you have seen, the Martyrologies and Acts commonly report that Pontius suffered at Cemelium in Gaul, and state that he came from Italy to Cemelium. No different conclusion can be reached concerning Cemelium from that concerning Nice, which, as I said, stood immediately beside Cemelium. The Roman Martyrology, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of June, places Nice within the boundaries of Gaul when it speaks of Saint Hospitius the confessor; Gregory of Tours does the same on that occasion in Book VI of his *History of the Franks*, chapter 6; so does Sigebert under the year of Our Lord 581, and many others elsewhere.

[Col. 0761C] Valerian, therefore, was a bishop in Gaul and may reasonably be conjectured to have been a Gaul, since there is nothing to suggest that he came there from elsewhere and obtained the see of Cemelium. From this new constellation, added to the many brilliant stars of the Gallic Church of the age I have mentioned—Eucherius of Lyon, Hilary of Arles, Salonius, Veranus, Claudian, and other bishops, as well as the presbyters Gennadius, Vincent, Salvian, and Prosper—we may recognize the remarkable splendor that already belonged to the churches of Gaul in those times.

### 5.

Since Eucherius has been mentioned, I should not pass over another conjecture concerning Valerian, suggested by Heribert Rosweyde in his notes on Eucherius’s *Paraenesis*: namely, that this Valerian was a relative of Eucherius himself—the same man whom Eucherius, then devoted to secular philosophy, invites to despise the world in that work of exceptionally florid writing. If we accept this, light is cast upon Valerian’s family and nobility.

For the very opening of Eucherius’s *Paraenesis* indicates that the Valerian to whom he writes was related to him by blood. [Col. 0761D] Since it is established that Eucherius was distinguished by an extremely illustrious birth, the same distinction is transferred to Valerian. Eucherius addresses him in the passage I have marked as follows:

> Although you have been raised to the highest summits of the world through your father and father-in-law, and are surrounded by illustrious titles from both lines, I nevertheless desire for you the heights of a far higher honor.

You see that his family was exceedingly illustrious. Notice in passing also the word “father-in-law,” which reveals that this Valerian was bound by marriage.

That fact might seem to destroy the force of the conjecture, since Valerian of Cemelium was a bishop and had lived as a monk before his episcopate, as is plainly stated at the beginning of the letter to the monks who, although he was absent, had chosen him as their superior. Yet it is clear that nothing is thereby removed from the proposed conjecture. Eucherius’s invitation to the holy institution itself shows either that Valerian’s marriage had merely been contracted but not consummated, and that he was therefore still free to turn to another way of life; or, as happened to many others, that Valerian, [Col. 0762A] with his wife’s consent—or because she was no longer living—was free to undertake the holy institution, and subsequently attained promotion to monastic leadership and the episcopate.

### 6.

From this point a path is opened, at least to some extent, toward recognizing Valerian’s holy death and blessedness. For in those times Lérins—“the plain that nurtures great mountains,” as Ennodius calls it—was very probably the most frequented refuge in Gaul for distinguished men withdrawing from the storms of the world. It is therefore highly probable that Valerian lived as a monk on that island. From there he may first have been requested by the monks, while absent, to become their superior; then, distinguished by holiness of life joined to the splendor of his birth, he may have been transferred to the see of Cemelium, situated on that coast, where he rested after a holy death.

This agrees with what Arnauldus records in his *Monastic Martyrology* concerning the deposition of Saint Valerius, once a monk of Lérins:

> On the ninth day before the Kalends of August, at Nice in the province, the deposition of Saint Valerius, bishop and confessor, who, taken from the monastic life of Lérins and raised to the episcopate, strove to fulfill the office of a good [Col. 0762B] shepherd and, admitted into the joy of his Lord, deserved to hear: “Well done, good servant,” and so forth.

The same is recorded in the Lérins registers on that day. Some people of Nice believe that this was our Valerian. Among them was the distinguished D. Honoratus Leotardus, highly learned not only in both branches of law but also in every form of refined literature. In letters written on this subject, he indicated that this was his opinion.

It is no objection that the saint who was made bishop from a monk of Lérins is called Valerius, not Valerianus. In the older registers from which that Martyrology was compiled, scribes hastily pursuing abbreviated forms—as is customary—may have written *Valerius* for *Valerianus*, using an abbreviation mark that was omitted in another transcription, leaving *Valerius*. For this reason, or for some similar one, Valerius is confused with Valerianus in most manuscripts of the subscriptions to the Council of Orange.

It is even less of an objection that the place of his deposition is marked in those registers and in the Martyrology as Nice, not Cemelium. [Col. 0762C] Since at that time Saint Leo had united the episcopates of Cemelium and Nice, it could easily have happened that Valerian, bishop of both sees, deposited his bodily remains at Nice rather than at Cemelium. Given the great proximity of Nice and Cemelium, it would not be surprising if Valerian died at Nice while Cemelium was still standing, even though he remained constantly at his post watching over his flock.

Moreover, by the time that Martyrology was compiled—or the ancient register from which it was copied—it may have been the case that Cemelium no longer stood. The person who inserted Valerian into the register, wishing to avoid obscurity, could easily have omitted mention of the ruined Cemelium and designated the neighboring city, to which Cemelium, its people, its episcopal see, and its other rights had passed, as the place where that holy bishop died. What if the register did not even mark the place of his death, but rather the place where his deposition was commemorated on the day of his death—something that, after the destruction of Cemelium, necessarily had to be done at Nice?

### 7.

[Col. 0762D] I am tired of continuing to act as a conjecturer concerning such obscure matters about Valerian. I would be still more tired if I had not observed that his accuser, relying on much weaker evidence—or rather on manifest errors—boldly portrays the author of these homilies in colors entirely different from those in which I have presented him.

He takes it as self-evident, and supports it with the testimony of the most illustrious Cardinal Baronius, that this man was a most impious heretic, a partisan of Pelagius and Coelestius, who came from the West to Alexandria. This is supposed to appear from a letter of a certain Eusebius to Saint Cyril of Alexandria, which Baronius publishes under the year 417, no. 15.

In that letter, the Eusebius I have mentioned protests amicably to Saint Cyril that Pelagius and Coelestius—“cut down by the sword of the apostolic see”—enjoyed communion with the Church of Alexandria through the intervention and activity of a pestilential man, Valerian, their ally in the chief points of their heresy, a ventriloquist, a slave of his throat and belly, of low birth and actually servile condition, belonging to the estate of the most illustrious Count Valerius of Ariminum.

[Col. 0763A] Baronius adds that he conjectures this to be the same Valerian mentioned by Saint Jerome in Letter 79. In the common manuscripts, the man there called Annianus, a false deacon of Celeda, whose books published against him Saint Jerome says he received through the presbyter Eusebius, is mentioned when Jerome, in reply to Saint Augustine and Alypius, who had asked whether he had refuted those books, testifies that he received them through the presbyter Eusebius. Baronius suspects that *Annianus* is corrupt and that *Valerianus* should be read instead.

Since it is likely that this was the same Eusebius who had accused Valerian before Cyril, Baronius accordingly suspects that the Annianus whom Eusebius hated was also none other than Valerian. He likewise holds that the man is corruptly called a deacon of Celeda, since no Church of Celeda is ever mentioned, and that he should instead be called Cenetensis. Baronius makes this substitution, reporting that the Arles manuscript has the other reading.

[Col. 0763B] But what if the reading were *Avellanensis*, a designation derived from the homeland of Julian, formerly bishop of Capua and a fierce Pelagian, as Prosper testifies? What if it were also *Celanensis*? For at the very beginning of Book I of his commentary on the *Song of Songs*, Bede calls this Julian bishop of Celana in Campania.

The accuser of our Valerian sings his triumph and considers it obvious that, by the authority of Cardinal Baronius, Valerian is plainly burdened, indeed crushed.

### 8.

But this opinion is so foolish that it seems not worth refuting even with a bushel of salt. The entire force of the argument on which it rests turns on this: Cardinal Baronius, while saying nothing at all about Valerian of Cemelium, these homilies, or their author, reveals that in the time of Jerome and Augustine there lived a certain Pelagian named Valerian, a deacon of Ceneta. From this the accuser infers that this man was Valerian, bishop of Cemelium and author of these homilies.

[Col. 0763C] If I tried to demonstrate what sort of inference this is, I would only demonstrate its absurdity. I will therefore say merely in passing that, if some heretic named Alexander, John, or Sergius existed, it would not immediately be permissible to transfer everything he did or said perversely to anyone else of the same name flourishing in the same period, even if the offices and other circumstances of the persons were not different—as here they are plainly different.

By this freedom to infer and accuse, the author of the Catholic Epistle, blessed Jude, would be in danger of being charged with the betrayal and sale of the Lord Christ, carried out by the most wicked of men, who shared with the holy Apostle the same name, office, and age. I shall stop wearing out a pen already shaken enough.

[Col. 0763D] I can easily demonstrate that nothing in what has been brought forward either from that Eusebius or from Jerome provides any further grounds for condemning our Valerian. I will not insist on the reliability of certain writings circulated under the name of that Eusebius concerning the life of Saint Jerome, or of other products of the same kind addressed to Cyril and Augustine. These writings are stuffed with heresies and absurdities, as the Louvain scholars observed in volume II of their edition of Augustine; Baronius agrees under the year 420, no. 42 onward, and in the Roman Martyrology on 30 September.

Even if I wished to pass over this point, who does not see that the Valerian whom that Eusebius calls an *engastrimythus*—a “ventriloquist”—was a disciple and ally of Pelagius and Coelestius, whereas this Valerian, whose homilies we preserve intact, was their sworn enemy, as he was also an enemy of the other Semipelagians, to whom a less attentive opponent later joined him?

The Semipelagians were otherwise good and learned men, but they detested Pelagius and Coelestius, whose ally that ventriloquist Valerian is said to have been, as I shall report below. Thus, in reality, our Valerian has nothing in common with the Valerian whom Eusebius attacked before Cyril, except the name.

By what right, then, does the accuser attach the infamy of the heretic Valerian to our Valerian merely because they had the same name? If one wished to be foolish in the same way, our Valerian could equally be heaped with the praises with which Prudentius celebrates the bishop Valerian in Hymn 10 of the *Peristephanon*, or with which Saint Jerome, Rufinus, and others honor Valerian, bishop of Aquileia, who flourished [Col. 0764A] at approximately the same time.

### 9.

Although it does not harm the present case if that ventriloquist Valerian is the same person as Annianus, deacon of Celeda, as Baronius conjectured, there are nevertheless many considerations suggesting that they were entirely different men and weakening the conjecture of that most learned writer.

All the ancient manuscripts of Jerome and Augustine—for this letter of Jerome is also found inserted in volume II of Augustine—consistently read *Annianus*. No variation of reading is recorded in that name in the manuscripts used by Marianus Victorius and Augustine’s editors.

The fact that some Eusebius—whether he was the same man who wrote to Cyril is uncertain—sent Annianus’s writings to Jerome is not enough to transform Annianus into Valerian. Indeed, if we grant that this was the same Eusebius who wrote about Valerian to Cyril and sent the writings of that heretic to Jerome, then, because the testimony of several manuscripts is stronger than that of a single recent manuscript, we should rather conclude [Col. 0764B] that the error lies in the recently published letter of Eusebius, and that it should read *Annianus* there instead of *Valerianus*.

But let us grant that an error entered the manuscripts of Jerome and Augustine, and that *Annianus* was corruptly written there for *Valerianus*. What connection is there between Valerian the deacon of Celeda and Valerian the bishop of Cemelium? What connection is there between a blasphemous writer who, after deceiving the Council of Diospolis together with Pelagius, turned his pen against Saint Jerome, and a writer whose every line breathes piety, humility, charity, and the other Christian virtues?

The other supposed corruption in Jerome’s manuscript, even if it were admitted, would cleanse rather than defile Valerian of Cemelium, since the disgrace attributed to him would be transferred, on the basis of conjecture, to another Valerian, perhaps the one of Ceneta, or, as one reading has it, of Arles.

Yet the most diligent writer overlooked [Col. 0764C] the fact that no Church of Celeda exists—the sole reason offered for explaining the corruption—although Jerome’s Letter 77, which is almost immediately adjacent to what is numbered 79, was written to Marcus, a presbyter of Celeda. From this it seems clear that there was a Church of Celeda in Syria, since Saint Jerome asks that Marcus, who had considerable influence in the Church of Celeda, assist him against those who were attempting to drive him from the Syrian desert where Jerome was then living.

Once the identity of the Valerian about whom Eusebius wrote to Cyril and the Annianus about whom Jerome wrote is gratuitously granted, there is nothing surprising in the possibility that a man born in the West—as the reference to the estate at Ariminum indicates—was enrolled in the Church of Celeda in Syria. For in those times it was extremely common for people born in the West, when traveling to the East, to be ordained there. Saint Jerome himself, although of Dalmatian origin, was initiated into the priesthood at Antioch.

[Col. 0764D] I see that I am wasting time, and that the poorly supported defamation of our Valerian based on that letter of Eusebius has already been sufficiently—indeed, more than sufficiently—refuted. It is entirely clear how justly the accuser has sung his triumph over our Valerian on the basis of that letter, and how much more probable our conjectures are when they are set against the accuser’s arguments.

Whatever the conjectures I have set forth may be worth, I have chosen not to omit them, both because they possess some probability and because they may contribute something, among sensible and impartial readers, toward suspending or moderating judgment concerning Valerian’s orthodoxy in the accusation to which I now proceed.

## CHAPTER II. Matters that Have Appeared, or Could Have Appeared, to Tell against Valerian

### 1.

The accuser censures two things in Valerian: Semipelagian doctrine and the title “saint.” I shall begin with the first part of the accusation, and shall add to it whatever else in Valerian’s doctrine may appear unhealthy or [Col. 0765A] capable of arousing suspicion of some hidden evil.

In this matter I was not satisfied either with the accuser’s diligence or with my own indignation and investigation. I also wished to add to my effort the judgments of exceptionally perceptive critics and the insight of men possessing the keenest discernment.

What is scattered through various passages of these homilies makes Valerian suspect of Semipelagianism—or, if we listen to the accuser, proves him plainly to have been a Semipelagian. I shall mark everything that came to my attention.

The first homily is, in everyone’s judgment, sound in every respect. For that reason, when it was long ago included under Augustine’s name in volume IX of Augustine’s works, under the title *On the Good of Discipline*, it escaped not only Erasmus’s attack but also the judgment of the Louvain theologians. Although they rightly declared that the little work should be removed from its place as not having been written by Augustine, they nevertheless found nothing to criticize in it. Nor did Cardinal Bellarmine do so in his assessment of volume IX of Augustine, although he was uncertain about the author of the work and did not dare decide whether it was someone other than Augustine or Augustine himself.

After Bellarmine wrote, this doubt entirely disappeared when later scholars, through their diligence, brought forward ancient manuscripts from the libraries of Fleury and Saint Gall, in which the work is explicitly attributed to Valerian of Cemelium [Col. 0765B]. Even without the testimony of the ancient manuscripts, the style clearly proclaims that its author was not Augustine but the same man to whom the remaining eighteen homilies are attributed—that is, Valerian.

Yet from the fact that so great a man did not dare reject the little work from Augustine, it is evident that he detected nothing unsound or tainted in it. That first homily could therefore have been left untouched, unless Valerian’s accuser, with his keen instinct for detecting other people’s errors, had also fastened upon it because its opening words were taken from Pelagius, whom he says repeatedly complained in that manner of speaking.

### 2.

At the beginning of the second homily, Valerian speaks of the narrow way as follows:

> This is that way, beloved, [Col. 0765C] along which the just proceed and the holy and undefiled walk.

It is clear that he is speaking of the narrow, righteous way, not merely philosophically but also in a Christian sense. Yet the following passage appears to smell of the Massilian ferment, by which the will is said, as it were, to take hold of God’s hand and raise itself toward him:

> We must therefore choose and fortify our approach to this way, because although it is difficult, it is passable; and it makes itself easy for those who desire it, provided that vanity does not impede them or the deceptive adornment of this world obstruct them.

This seems to be precisely what Cassian and others of the same flour repeatedly insist upon, and what is condemned in Canon 6 of the Second Council of Orange: that God’s mercy is granted to those who desire it.

In the same sense, Homily 3 says:

> Every work, beloved, in which zeal for human preservation keeps watch requires a voluntary service.

And shortly afterward:

> The religion of the Christian name, to which we have been called, has undertaken the service of free will.

These voluntary services of free will reproduce both the language and the soot of Cassian and Faustus. Faustus plainly says in his letter to [Col. 0765D] Lucidus, attributing the beginning of salvation to the powers of nature, that it is “a matter of service, not merit.”

Again, later in the same homily:

> Let us daily sacrifice to our Christ the offerings of thanksgiving, so that, if the merits of virtues commend others, the voluntary services of our slavery may at least make room for grace for us.

What could be clearer in favor of the error of the same Massilians, since human servitude is said to summon grace and make room for it?

Moreover, the term “service” designates an honorable work within the order of nature and therefore signifies nothing other than human service rendered to God by a human being. This is taught by Cicero’s books *On Duties*, which Lactantius repeatedly mentions; likewise by the books of Panaetius and his son, and also by Aristotle’s *On Duties*, as Saint Ambrose reports in Book I, chapter 7 of his *Duties*. The same is true of the work of Nicolaus of Damascus on this subject, bearing the same title, praised by Simplicius in chapter 37 of his commentary on Epictetus’s *Enchiridion*. Finally, it is true of the writing of the Stoic Zeno, whose title employed the word translated into Latin as *officium*, as Diogenes Laertius reports [Col. 0766A] in Book VII, in his life of Zeno.

It is established that these pagans rose no higher than merely natural moral goodness. Therefore, whoever asserts that grace is given room through voluntary or free-will services—as Valerian appears to do here—attributes to human labor the summoning of grace. That is the Massilian error.

### 3.

Homily 7 is equally slippery. After enumerating many holy works by which heaven may be purchased through the merits of virtues, it adds:

> But all these things are produced in us by one and the same power of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, which grants perfection to righteous labors and supplies to the good will whatever things are best.

Let the reader recognize the familiar formula by which Semipelagianism is expressed among its undisputed adherents: God grants perfection, while the human being provides the beginning. God indeed supplies all the best things—namely, heavenly assistance and grace, both actual and sanctifying—yet the good will mentioned beforehand proceeds from the human being through the powers of nature.

Was the same not meant by the words of Homily 9?

> See, beloved, [Col. 0766B] how small an expenditure is required from us, so that the Lord of such great majesty may deign to come to our petition?

He says that the Lord comes, but only when summoned and invited by human wishes. This is the small beginning that the Massilians insisted must be granted to nature’s powers in the matter of salvation, so that they would have a basis for freeing God from the charge of partiality, since he appears to assist some and reject others. Valerian applies the passage from Isaiah, chapter 15, to this point, as Cassian also does in Conference 13, chapters 8 and 11.

### 4.

In Homily 11 the error under discussion is first presented somewhat obscurely, in these words:

> God never abandons a will that flourishes through zeal for religion, nor are divine consolations lacking where there are acts of good conduct.

There you have it: God strengthens and advances a will that is zealous of itself by superadded assistance, and the acts of our human conduct receive the consolations of grace.

Soon afterward, however, Semipelagianism is expressed so openly that it appears [Col. 0766C] to have been written by the rays of the sun themselves:

> Nor can we deny that the adornments of a religious life are acquired through vigilant zeal; but God is present where there is a mind devoted to complete religion, as the Apostle says: “Do you seek proof of Christ speaking in me?” Human zeal is sufficiently unstable where God’s help is not sought. For faith is plainly endangered if it is not fortified by divine protection. It is therefore our part to will what is good, but Christ’s to bring it to completion. For the Apostle speaks thus: “To will is present with me; but I do not find how to accomplish the good.” You see, therefore, that the will for a good work must descend from us, while its perfection depends upon God’s power.

And again, below:

> The servant indeed has the grace of his labor, but he owes the master the fruit of completed labor.

Valerian may be regarded as plainly convicted, and it seems that no Chiron could provide a remedy sufficiently suitable for so diseased a passage. What else had the remnants of the Pelagians imposed upon us?

Listen to Cassian, Conference 13, chapter 9, at the end:

> That it may become more evident that, even through the good of nature, which was granted by the kindness of the Creator [Col. 0766D], the beginnings of good wills sometimes arise—although, unless they are directed by the Lord, they cannot reach the completion of virtues—the Apostle is witness when he says: “To will is present with me, but I do not find how to accomplish the good.”

Saint Augustine likewise, in his exposition of certain propositions from the Epistle to the Romans, no. 60, when he was younger, had written:

> That we believe is ours; but that we do good is the work of him who gives the Holy Spirit to those who believe in him.

Later, when reviewing this work in Book I, chapter 23 of the *Retractions*, and in *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 3, he rejected that proposition. The Semipelagians commended it as impregnated with Semipelagianism and objected it to Saint Augustine, as Hilary reports in his letter to Augustine.

Indeed, Julian of Capua, the standard-bearer of the Pelagians, against whom Saint Augustine fought a twofold battle, was finally driven to assert nothing other than what Valerian says in the passage just cited. Augustine reports his position [Col. 0767A] in Book IV, chapter 3, of the first series of his *Replies*:

> He wanted it to be understood that a human being begins by himself without grace what grace completes.

And in Book II, chapter 8:

> The adherents of Pelagius, of whom he is speaking there, want the desire for good to begin in a human being from the human being himself, and for the merit of this beginning to be followed by the grace of completion.

Thus Valerian may now seem capable of being called not merely a drinker of Semipelagianism—that is, diluted Pelagianism—but of Pelagian dregs themselves.

### 5.

What if paganism is involved as well?

Hierocles, certainly a thoroughly pagan man, confirms at length in his commentary on verse 47 of Pythagoras that the choice of good things lies in good people, while their perfection comes from God. He says that our zeal is like the extension of our hands to grasp good things, while God is the one who is present to those who stretch out their hands and gives to those who are willing and ask.

He therefore teaches that prayers must be impressed upon our work and effort as form upon matter, so that, with this intermediate element placed between us who ask and God who gives, we may complete, with the help of the deity, what we could not bring [Col. 0767B] to perfection by ourselves. He calls the virtue of the person who trusts only in his own works and does not expect perfection from God through the exercise of his natural power “impious virtue,” if it may be called virtue.

Seneca says the same in Letter 73, at the end:

> The gods are not disdainful; they admit people and extend a hand to those who climb.

As if he were saying: the gods certainly admit human beings, but only those who come. They extend a hand to those who climb, but only to those who attempt by themselves to accomplish what they can by nature.

He therefore adds that no mind is good without God, yet he does not fail to mention that the natural seeds of goodness are to be advanced through cultivation into fruit. He says almost exactly: “It is ours to will, but God’s to perfect.”

He has essentially the same statement at the beginning of Letter 41, where he declares that no one is a good person without God and that no one can rise unless helped by him [Col. 0767C]. He likewise says that so great a thing cannot stand without the support of the deity, yet that we must make the beginning, because God treats us as we have treated him. A good mind, or the beginnings of good willing, must therefore be obtained from ourselves, and God will add completion to them.

This is that Stoic model which Saint Augustine repeatedly traces among the enemies of grace, especially in Sermon 13 *On the Words of the Apostle* and in his treatise *On the Stoics and Epicureans*.

Philo, most beautifully, in Book *On the Sacrifice of Abel and Cain*, commenting on the words “and it came to pass after some days,” says that Cain labored under this very error and therefore permits us to regard the defenders of this most hideous doctrine as Cain’s kinsmen. For Philo distinguishes three classes of those who do not give thanks to God.

The first consists of those who sin less gravely than the others—namely, those who, through forgetfulness of benefits, omit the giving of thanks, than which nothing is more precious. The second, and worst, consists of those who, through excessive arrogance, regard themselves as the authors of their own good things. The third is a kind of intermediate malignity: those who refer their good things to God as their author, but do so in such a way that they think they obtain them by their own merit, drawing God to themselves by some good work of their own and supposing that through it they have been made worthy of divine grace [Col. 0767D].

One might say that Philo has plainly portrayed the Pelagians and Semipelagians who would arise many centuries later. For that second class corresponds very well to the Pelagians, while the third corresponds to the Semipelagians. Philo shows that both are overthrown by the clear oracles of the Old Testament that he adduces, and confirms that they belong to the followers of Cain. Saint Ambrose likewise agrees, as is his custom, in Book I, chapter 1, *On Cain and Abel*, although at the beginning of chapter 2 he approves another allegory of the same two brothers more strongly, without rejecting this one.

Behold, then, how much poison lies hidden in the passages cited from Valerian—if indeed it is hidden, rather than revealing itself openly—when he so explicitly attributes to man the beginning of his good works, while assigning only their perfection to God, just as the remaining Semipelagians do.

### 6

“Now this is the Catholic faith,” says Chrysostom—or whoever else was the author of the homily *On Adam and Eve*, a portion of which may also be read in Celestine’s letter to the bishops of Gaul [Col. 0768A]:

> That we should profess God to be the author of all good effects and works, of all endeavors, and of all virtues by which, from the beginning of faith, one moves toward God; and that we should not doubt that all human merits proceed from his grace, through whom it also comes about that we are found both willing and doing something good.

From this plainly Catholic rule, John Maxentius—otherwise a bad author and not entirely without cause accused of Eutychianism—attacks, at the end of his profession of the Catholic faith, those who approve the words attributed to Valerian:

> We abominate those who dare to say, contrary to the voice of the Apostle, “It is ours to will, but God’s to perfect.” The same teacher testifies that both willing and perfecting are divine gifts, for he says: “For it is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish according to his good pleasure.”

Thus he speaks consistently with the Catholic doctrine that God is the initiator of human salvation. For those who become children of God are born in imitation of the natural Son—as Fulgentius rightly observes in Book *On the Incarnation and the Grace of Christ*, chapter 20—not from the will of the flesh or of man, but from God. And although [Col. 0768B] each person, with God going before, may become his own father and make himself a mother or a woman—that is, a holy or an evil person—as Nyssenus teaches most beautifully in Homily 6 on Ecclesiastes and in the book *On the Life of Moses*, and Bernard in Sermon 57, nevertheless, as Bernard teaches in Sermon 57, *On Small Things*, unless God goes before, man must remain eternally in nothingness—much more with respect to the being of grace, which is higher, than with respect to natural being.

He himself is, as Fulgentius above insists from the Apostle, not merely the completer but also the initiator and author of our faith and of our entire holiness. According to Saint Augustine, Homily 14 on Psalm 50, by repaying good for evil he found a way to repay good for good, and so forth. Therefore, when he repays good, he goes before himself by giving the good things with which he may repay good.

According to the same Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 32, he both prepares the human will for assistance and assists it when prepared. For the human good will precedes many gifts of God, but not all. In those things which it does not precede, it is itself also present [Col. 0768C].

This is the sweetest of the threefold blessing poured out upon us for salvation, and, in Bernard’s judgment in Sermon 39, *From the Small Things*, the most agreeable and most delicious to the palate of the meditating soul. There he distinguishes the mercy and blessing of God as preceding us, assisting us, and bringing us to completion:

> In these three things, he says, it is not without reason that the one which precedes not only those who are undeserving but even those who are ill-deserving tastes more sweetly: while we are still children of wrath and are performing works of death, he himself thinks thoughts of peace concerning us; and, although we do not ask, indeed although we resist; although we do not invoke, but provoke; although we do not intercede, but even repel him, he bestows upon us the good Spirit, the Spirit of life, the Spirit of adoption. What sweetness can be tasted by that soul to which such great mercy is not sweet? Therefore that blessing is rightly called the blessing of sweetness—the blessing that precedes us.

Valerian must therefore have possessed a very corrupt, or no, spiritual capacity for tasting, since that blessing of sweetness not only did not taste sweet to him, but was not perceived by him in any way. We Catholics think otherwise. I say that we do not [Col. 0768D], as Valerian asserted, go before God and, as it were, urge him to come as helper and completer of the work begun by us. Rather, he himself anticipates and goes before us. Richard of Saint Victor, Book *On the Degrees of Charity*, chapter 3, at the beginning, should also be consulted.

I conclude this point with the truly remarkable discussion of the Church of Lyons in its work against John Scotus, near the end of its fourth chapter, where Scotus’s proposition is reported:

> Nature can always begin, but can complete only through grace.

The Church of Lyons rejects this in the following words:

> If he says this as though human nature, through its own free will, could always begin the good, but could complete it only through the grace of God—so that the beginning of every good would always be attributed to man, but its perfection only to God; so that man would claim for himself the first part of doing good and God the second—such a view is altogether Pelagian and contrary to evangelical and apostolic truth. For the Lord himself, [Col. 0769A] to show that the beginning of our good is not from ourselves but from him, says: “You did not choose me, but I chose you.” And the Apostle says to the faithful: “He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion until the day of Christ Jesus.” And again: “To you it has been granted for Christ’s sake not only to believe in him, but also to suffer for him.” And blessed John the Apostle says: “Not as though we loved God, but because he first loved us and sent his Son as an expiation for our sins.” And again blessed Paul the Apostle says: “Let us run with endurance the contest set before us, looking to Jesus, the author and completer of our faith.”
>
> If, then, we truly wish to be Catholics, we must faithfully attribute everything to divine grace—both the beginning and the end of our good work. For, as is most clearly demonstrated by the foregoing testimonies of Holy Scripture, the Lord chose his saints; they did not choose him. God both begins and completes the good in his faithful. From him the faithful who suffer for him receive both the beginning of faith and the end of martyrdom. He first loved his saints, so that they too might be able to love him. [Col. 0769B] And our faith has the Lord Jesus as its author: he begins it in us and brings it to completion by perfecting it.
>
> Let us therefore hold these things faithfully, so that, founded upon true faith, we may be protected from heretical error. No stronger or clearer refutation of Valerian’s error can be sought with respect to the beginning of supernatural work being from us and its perfection alone being from God.

### 7

I have also heard that Valerian was charged by his accuser with other errors against sound doctrine. Yet a friendly man of sharp and penetrating intellect, whom I employed to examine Valerian by lamplight, indicated one or two additional passages, in another matter, that might appear harsh to a less attentive reader, or harsher than is fair.

Moreover, so that I may omit nothing that could contribute to Valerian’s condemnation, I mention that, after these matters had long since been published once and again, I came across a work by Bernard Vinding, entitled *The Augustinian Critic Chastised*. There, in the observations on the ninth volume of Augustine [Col. 0769C], which contains the book *On the Gift of Discipline*—the same work as Valerian’s first homily—that composition is denied to Augustine, and nothing else in it is criticized except that in chapter 1 it says:

> There is no authority unless something unjust is commanded.

And in chapter 8 it is said very obscurely:

> Let him whose desire is to worship Christ first take on the garments of heart and body.

But these matters need not trouble us. For when the author of that work—which is rightly denied to blessed Augustine—says that there is no authority except when something unjust is commanded, this must be understood according to the phraseology of the grumblers whom Valerian rebukes: those who accused the concern and exactness of superiors of tyranny and arrogance. Valerian shows that this is perversely said when he argues that a well-mannered and humble subject, so long as nothing unjust is commanded to him, ought not to accuse the superior’s harsh and tyrannical order of being an injunction.

The passage from chapter 8 is perfectly clear. There Valerian is speaking of a convert who, having been kicked about in the world, became a monk and accordingly changed his clothing. He therefore admonishes him that, just as when undertaking [Col. 0769D] the service of God and entering religious worship he changed the clothing of his body, so he should assume a new garment of the soul through his purpose and will. What is obscure or unclear there?

Therefore, leaving aside these preliminary matters, let us examine the two passages that I said had been noted by my friend John Garatius, a man of exceptionally discerning judgment.

The first passage occurs in Homily 3, where he denies that other Christians can ever repay God what they owe, but professes that the martyrs paid their debt to God exactly:

> The Lord is not to be served carelessly. Although each of us may daily offer him some honor or service, we never repay what we owe. But when does one repay the debt, who is clearly assigned to the office of a substitute punishment, unless perhaps, for love of the Redeemer, he accepts a similar sentence of death or condemnation?

It is certainly bold to compare the blood of a pure man poured out for God with the precious blood of the spotless Lamb, when it is said that the debt by which Christ bound us to himself is [Col. 0770A] repaid and, as it were, extinguished by that repayment in blood. Chrysostom—or whoever else was the author of the homily on Adam’s precedence over the other creatures—more wisely considers the indissolubility of the names by which we are bound to God.

Saint Ambrose, as usual, speaks most gently in the book *On Virginity*, near the end:

> The good servant strives to prepare for his Lord the price that was paid for him. Do not prepare gold, daughter; do not prepare silver. Christ did not redeem you with these riches. Have the price ready—not because it is always demanded, but because you always owe it. He paid blood; you owe blood. He paid for you; repay for yourself.
>
> We were pledged to an evil creditor by our sins. We contracted a bond of guilt and owed the penalty of blood. The Lord Jesus came and offered his blood for us. But he cannot return the blood—his own blood, I mean—for he is speaking of it and denies that it can be returned or compensated. The good servant ought to restore his price to his Lord. But if he cannot repay the price, let him at least do this, so that he may not appear unworthy of the price. Therefore conduct yourself as worthy of such a price.

As though he were saying [Col. 0770B]: “You must despair of compensating for it; at least, then, strive so that so great a price may not have been offered in vain.”

Salvian likewise speaks most eloquently and truthfully in Book II *To the Church*:

> Let a man endure whatever he will for God; what God endured for man cannot be repaid at all. For even if the suffering itself does not differ in kind of punishments, the difference between those who suffer must nevertheless be very great.

The second suspect passage of Valerian occurs in Homily 5. Valerian seems to assert that the sin of the tongue is a wound without remedy. For he speaks as follows:

> The sickness of wicked thoughts can be healed so long as what is conceived in the heart is kept contained while the mouth is silent. But once it has burst forth through the rolling tongue, it seeks a physician in vain. The guilt of words is without remedy, because whatever injury, inserted through the ears, has spread cannot be erased by any tears.

### 8

[Col. 0770C]

These, apart from the Semipelagianism for which Valerian is attacked by his accuser, are the matters that I said might appear harsh in him, but which are nevertheless easily softened. For the first passage contains only that glory of the martyrs by which they repay the Savior’s death with their own death and, by divine concession and the privilege of martyrdom, wipe away every guilt and stain, paying to the last farthing what they owe, in accordance with Tertullian’s words at the end of the *Apologeticus*:

> Who would not desire to suffer, so as to redeem the whole grace of God and obtain complete forgiveness from him by the compensation of his blood? For all sins are forgiven to this work.

Saint Cyprian likewise says in Letter 52 that the martyrs purged all sins by their suffering and immediately after death attained glory. Consequently, as Pope Innocent said, they cannot be helped by the prayers or sacrifices of the living without injury; a necessity to which almost all adults who depart this life in another manner are bound. For there are few adults whose sins are wiped clean by another route in its entirety—that is, through baptism, the most complete contrition, or perfect satisfaction—without the addition of purifying fire.

Valerian therefore was not thinking [Col. 0770D] of a comparison or equivalence between the blood of Christ and the blood of the martyrs. Even if he had expressed something of the kind, it could be explained no more difficultly than the words of Saint Cyprian at the end of his book *On the Praise of Martyrdom*:

> When you lay down your soul according to the example of the Lord’s passion and for the whole testimony of Christ, and do not fear to pour out your blood, everything must necessarily yield to martyrdom. The glory of martyrdom is inestimable, its measure infinite, its victory spotless, its virtue noble, its title beyond price, its triumph immeasurable—for by it the praise of the one who confesses is itself exalted, adorned as though by fellowship in Christ’s blood.

And shortly afterward:

> O blessed ones, whose sins have truly been forgiven!—if indeed you, who are Christ’s companions, ever sinned.

### 9

In the later passage [Col. 0771A] Valerian did not wish to assert that the sin of the tongue is incurable. He intended only to show how great is the harm usually caused by a word uttered without due care, and how often that wound is healed only with difficulty—or, indeed, is frequently never healed at all: the one who has been pierced not only failing to draw out the dart fixed in his heart, but driving it in more deeply and firmly.

> As an arrow fixed in the flesh of the thigh, so is a word in the heart of a fool.

Our author argues the matter altogether excellently in Homily 5.

Leaving aside, then, these matters, which are plainly trivial and are not brought forward by the accuser, we must concentrate on removing the charge of Semipelagianism, with which Valerian is accused sharply and vehemently. From this charge the accuser also infers his deposition from the rank of a saint. Since it is impossible to please God without right faith, he considers it altogether rash to bestow the title “Saint” upon a man whose faith is doubtful, or rather openly impaired.

There is also Valerian’s profound silence in ecclesiastical records and in all earlier lists of the saints. It is not plausible that Valerian would have been omitted so universally and consistently if, while alive, he had shone with the praise of holiness and had departed this life worthy of the name “Saint.”

[Col. 0771B]

## CHAPTER III. The first defense of Valerian with respect to Semipelagianism, and its rejection

### 1

Before I retrace the steps taken against Valerian and show how vainly the foul stain of Semipelagianism has been attached to him, it is useful to report what might be proposed in his defense; indeed, this is necessary for the vindication of other very serious Fathers.

There will therefore be those who think that the stain in Valerian is less serious than his adversaries suppose, because Valerian lived in an age when Semipelagianism had not yet been recognized as an error, and in a region where almost all the bishops and men distinguished for holiness and learning, though shipwrecked upon the same reef, dissented from Saint Augustine with impunity regarding the beginning of faith as arising from some effort of the human will by its own power, regarding the grace of God as subordinate to the human invocation, and regarding all persons as equally sprinkled, insofar as anything proceeds from God, with the dew of divine grace.

This continued until approximately sixty years and more later, when, by the definition of the Second Council of Orange, the error was condemned and Catholic truth was firmly established. According to the latest opinion of Cardinal Baronius—for he changed his view many times on this point—this occurred in the year of Christ 529, under the consulship of the younger Decius, the date assigned to the council, although Valerian had flourished long before that.

Thus, from this standpoint, Valerian might appear to have erred only slightly, indeed only materially, even though the entire charge of Semipelagianism being mingled into his homilies rested upon truth. Nothing, then, would seem to warrant detracting from his holiness, since it is clear that very holy men, without forfeiting their holiness, have stumbled over much more obvious matters, led not by a common error but by their own private opinion and judgment.

“For it is not error that makes a heretic, but obstinate persistence,” says Peter Damian in Book I, Letter 13, “nor are all who hold an error to be called heretics, but only those who pertinaciously and boldly preach falsehood.”

### 2

I pass over the others, since in this very matter of Semipelagianism the conspicuous examples of Cassian and Faustus of Riez are available. For Cassian, even after he had written and published his *Collations*, enjoyed the closest familiarity with Saint Leo, as is shown by the letter in which Cassian dedicated his work *On the Incarnation* to Saint Leo.

How great a reputation for holiness he enjoyed is shown not only by his writings, which one might rightly call the marrow of Christian perfection, but also by the memory in which he is held at Marseille, where for so many centuries he has retained the title of Saint and is honored with heavenly rites. His head, enclosed in a silver reliquary among the sacred relics of the Abbey of Saint Victor, where Cassian once lived, is displayed for veneration; a sacred office, and one proper to him, is celebrated in his honor; he is honored on his feast day; and finally he is devoutly accorded every form of worship customarily offered to the saints in heaven.

This seems to have been why Peter de Natalibus, Book VII, chapter 59 of the *Catalogue of the Saints*, numbered him among the saints. Alenardus noted the various dioceses in which Cassian is venerated as a saint in the prefaces to the *Concordance of the Rules of Saint Benedict of Aniane*, when treating the authors of monastic rules. Paulinus, bishop of Aquileia, when citing Cassian in Book I *Against Felix of Urgel*, near the end, and in Book II once and again, as well as at the beginning of Book IV, calls him “blessed Cassian.”

Thomas Waldensis likewise, most explicitly, in Book III, Article 3, chapter 28, no. 2 of the *Doctrine*, citing Cassian, calls him “Saint Cassian” and argues, with an eloquent encomium, that Catholics ought to recognize him as such. In the *Concordance of the Rules* by Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniane, the rule of Saint Cassian is cited very frequently, and the title “Saint” is rarely omitted.

The same honors are accorded to Faustus at Riez in Provence. There a church erected long ago in honor of Faustus as a saint is still to be seen, and each year a feast is celebrated for him, with an octave, as for an eminent saint. John Molanus was the first, not long ago, to remove him from the Gallican Martyrology, in which he had until then been listed as a saint—an example by no means commendable in the case of a private scholar.

Although Cassian and Faustus were therefore such men, it is nevertheless so firmly established that both supported error and were materially heretical that there is no room for evasion.

### 3

For Cassian, as I shall demonstrate most clearly later, conceded to some of those who undertake the path of salvation that the beginning of salvation comes from the powers of nature. Nor should we listen to either Henry Cuychius or Peter Ciaconius in their annotations on Cassian.

Cuychius admits that *Collation* 13 is heretical because of Prosper’s attacks and the decree of Gelasius, but he exempts Cassian from the stain, saying that Cassian merely reported, and did not approve, the opinion of the abbot Chaeremon. He maintains that Cassian’s other books are free from error; and wherever Cassian seems to teach the contrary, Cuychius interprets him as speaking of a good will aroused by grace and preceded by more abundant helps, and in some manner meriting those helps.

Ciaconius, however, excepts propositions 2 and 10 from Cassian and, throughout the remaining propositions relating to the question of grace, also clears *Collation* 13 of the charge, on the ground that in that *Collation*, and much more clearly elsewhere, Cassian asserts only some remote natural merit, or a remote natural disposition toward sanctifying grace—not a proximate disposition, which alone Ciaconius considers admissible without error.

### 4

Neither defense of Cassian is adequate. For Chaeremon’s mind is no different from Cassian’s own. To speak with Prosper, in the preface to his book *Against the Collator*, Cassian showed that he approved and accepted Chaeremon’s opinion in every respect.

Indeed, unless we admit that this was Cassian’s mind, we shall have to say that everything contained in the *Collations* concerns only those who are introduced as speaking. That would be no less beside the point than if someone denied that Plato’s *Dialogues* contain Plato’s mind, or if someone said that Saint Jerome’s *Dialogues Against the Pelagians* do not reveal what Saint Jerome truly thought about grace.

Cassian is therefore plainly convicted of error with respect to *Collation* 13, which has been condemned by the authority of the Church. To say that what is asserted in that *Collation* is diseased, while what is taught elsewhere by the same author in nearly the same words must be understood in another sense, is to divine—or rather gratuitously to spread darkness. Thus the whole of Cassian’s earlier defense disappears.

### 5

Nor is the later defense any more adequate. For to admit some remote natural merit, and even a remote natural disposition, toward sanctifying grace is rejected and almost accursed. Although that disposition would be remote with respect to sanctifying grace, it would nevertheless be proximate with respect to some assisting grace, through which the step toward sanctification is made.

But to concede that a help of grace can be naturally acquired and fall under merit is a Semipelagian error. Whoever clears Cassian on that basis therefore attaches the same error to himself.

If the term “remote disposition” were taken improperly, in the manner in which many Scholastics use it—admitting a remote natural disposition, that is, the mere removal of an obstacle without the introduction of any proportion or any morally suitable adaptation of the subject to supernatural form, whether attractive to God, in any sense meritorious, or even commanding—then Ciaconius’s doctrine would be free from fault, but would not address the issue.

For Cassian plainly speaks of a natural disposition that is indeed slight, but nevertheless properly so called and endowed with some merit toward grace. It must therefore be admitted that Cassian erred concerning the beginning of salvation.

Those works of his that remain, and that contain the error Prosper criticized in Cassian, teach this. For that reason Cardinal Baronius’s statement in the year of Christ 433 is displeasing: namely, that Cassian was sound at that time, but had formerly been diseased, before the labors of Eucherius of Lyons, Victor of Martyritana, and Cassiodorus purged him by cutting out whatever did not cohere with the doctrine of the Catholic Church.

I reject this, since, as I have said, the passages Prosper quoted from Cassian verbatim and condemned are still found in Cassian.

### 6

Peter the Deacon also expressly asserts, in the final chapter of his book *On the Incarnation and the Grace of Christ*, that Faustus labored under the error of the Semipelagians concerning the beginning of salvation. He says that Faustus cannot be freed from that charge, although he generally betrays the error rather obscurely, yet in such a way that it is difficult to grasp. Nevertheless, from the attacks made upon Faustus by so many Catholic teachers of that age, it seems to me indubitable that he held it.

For Saint Avitus, bishop of Vienne—of whom Ennodius says in the *Life of Epiphanius* that “he enclosed himself in him as in a lodging of a luminous house through his knowledge”—together with Saint Fulgentius, Saint Caesarius, and, in the East, John the presbyter of Antioch, rose up against Faustus, who was partly still alive and partly had died not long before. This is taught by Isidore, Book *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 14; Gennadius, chapter 86 of the *Catalogue*; the author of the *Life of Saint Fulgentius*, chapter 28; Ado of Vienne in his *Chronicle*, under the year of Christ 492; and John Maxentius in his reply to the letter of Hormisdas.

Consequently, modern writers who defend Faustus labor in vain when they try to persuade us, so long afterward, that he was wholly Catholic. They have been deceived by the slightness of the natural merit that he admits with respect to grace—merit that, because of its smallness, he sometimes scarcely dignifies with the name of merit at all—so that, although he insists that grace must be acknowledged despite that partial merit, he seems to affirm grace sincerely.

### 7

Cassian and Faustus, then, were pious and holy men, distinguished by the reputation of piety not only during life but also after death, commended for holiness in the places where they spent their lives and illustrious with the honors of the saints. Having suffered something human, they wrote concerning the beginning of salvation otherwise than sound doctrine permits, since the matter had not yet been clearly defined by the Church. Nevertheless, for that reason they were not altogether proscribed. On the contrary, what they wrote usefully is read with profit, and their memory is blessed.

There will therefore be someone who decides similarly concerning Valerian.

To me, however, such an excuse seems in reality to differ little or nothing from the true accusation on the point under discussion. For by this means the homilies, whose authenticity and sound doctrine are in question, are not demonstrated to be free from error; instead, the author’s probable ignorance and involuntary stumbling are alleged.

This is the one refuge available for Cassian, once—because of Prosper’s authority, supported by the Roman Church—all the kindly ways of interpreting Cassian in a Catholic sense have been closed, ways that some previously attempted without success, as I have shown. Yet there are still those who think the same, with, as I foresee, no different outcome and with scarcely persuasive reasoning.

For what purpose does it serve to retract Prosper’s attack on Cassian, an attack praised by Gelasius together with Prosper’s other little works, and even to attempt, by undermining—or rather badly tampering with—the decisions established against Cassian, to preserve Cassian himself harmless in the full and uncorrupted editions of the decree?

Those who clear Cassian seem finally to reach the point of accusing Prosper—who is distinguished by the praises of Celestine and Gelasius—either of slander in twisting Cassian’s meaning or of ignorance in understanding it. How unsafe and unjust this is need not be explained.

Cassian himself, although he took Prosper’s attack badly, as Prosper reports near the beginning of his letter to Rufinus, did not charge him with slander; such a charge would have been most suitable for turning Prosper aside.

In the case of Faustus, although his delusion might seem less certain and his case somewhat more doubtful because several Catholic writers stood in his defense—for Synodius certainly regarded Faustus as a man of sound and exceptional learning; Ruricius called him an outstanding teacher and excellent pastor; Hilary of Arles, while Faustus was still abbot, honored him so highly that he placed him between himself and the bishops Theodore and Maximus; and Pope Hilary deemed him worthy to preside with him at the Roman synod—nevertheless, it seems to me that the same rule applies, and Gelasius the pope rejected him equally.

### 8

It therefore does not seem advantageous to Valerian’s cause or reputation that he should be grouped with Cassian and Faustus both in error and in the similarity of their defense. The claim that the Semipelagian error was common in that age and region concerns the greater diffusion of the stain, not Valerian’s immunity from it.

For just as good, according to Seneca, Letter 73; Dio Chrysostom, Oration 40; and Tyrius, Dissertation 33, is greater in proportion as it is more common and widespread, so also evil, which the same Dio elegantly develops in his customary manner in Oration 32, is more foul and more serious the farther it spreads.

“Things which are equal in merit,” says Prosper, speaking of evils in chapter 9 *Against the Collator*, “are not diminished by coming together, but increase.” Saint Hilary likewise, at the beginning of Book VI *On the Trinity*, shows most beautifully how great is the gravity of an error once it becomes widespread and common.

Another course must therefore be taken to clear Valerian solidly and truly, so that we may be judged not to wish to arouse pity for him or plead against a just censure, but to show him innocent and, after a just judgment has been rendered and the case examined, to establish his innocence.

[Col. 0774C]

## CHAPTER IV. The true exposition of Semipelagianism is set forth, as a prelude to Valerian’s legitimate exemption from that stain

### 1

Because the accuser directs the charge of Semipelagianism against Valerian above all, while being less concerned with the remainder of the accusation, it is worthwhile to establish first what the genuine error of the Semipelagians was. Opinions about it differ, and I fear that Valerian’s accuser may perhaps interpret Semipelagianism otherwise than is proper and than truth permits, thereby deceiving the inexperienced.

It seems all the more necessary to examine this in a matter that is not especially straightforward. For the same critic of Valerian—so skilled and astute in ecclesiastical antiquity and heresies, and so capable of penetrating to the very lairs of errors—contends that Arianism, although scarcely any error in the Church was less ambiguous, should be understood not as concerning the divine Word subsisting only in the divine nature, but as concerning Christ composed of divinity and humanity. He argues as though Arius erred, and were crushed by the thunderbolts of so many councils, for saying that Christ is lesser than the Father. How serious this stumbling is, to put it as mildly as possible, need not be exaggerated.

### 2

To obtain a true knowledge of Semipelagianism, one must consult Prosper and Hilary, who, while Saint Augustine was still alive, sent him letters concerning that error; these letters are extant prefixed to Saint Augustine’s book *On the Predestination of the Saints*.

To mention first a point that may have some usefulness in this matter: I think it is clear that this Hilary was not only not Saint Hilary of Poitiers—as some thought, whom Baronius reports under 5 May in the Roman Martyrology, letter I—and was not merely mistakenly identified as such by the Cassian glossator, through a blunder of pen or printer, in Book XII *On the Institutes*, chapter 13—an error plainly twin to that into which Erasmus stumbled in his notes on Eucherius’s *Paraenesis*—but also was not Hilary, bishop of Arles, as is commonly asserted.

For Hilary, bishop of Arles, was one of those who brought complaints against Saint Augustine. Hear Prosper at the end of his letter to Augustine:

> We hope not only that our insignificance will be strengthened by the support of your discussions, but also that those themselves whom the darkness of this opinion obscures, though distinguished by merits and honors, will receive the clearest light of grace.
