For let your blessedness know that one of them, a man of exceptional authority and spiritual pursuits, the holy Hilary, bishop of Arles, is, in all other matters, an admirer and follower of your teaching, and that concerning the matter over which he complains he has for some time wished to communicate his view to your holiness by letter. But since it is uncertain whether he will do this, or for what purpose he will do it, and so forth.

Consider the phrases “one of them”—plainly one of those acting against Augustine, who were under discussion—and “in all other matters.” For with respect to the matter about which Prosper’s entire letter is concerned, and therefore with respect to the Semipelagian error, Hilary was not an admirer of Augustine’s teaching; indeed, he held it as a grievance.

Prosper clearly testifies that he regarded Hilary with suspicion, since he doubts with what purpose Hilary would correspond with Augustine, despite having undertaken to do so. For this reason, it plainly seems that Hilary of Arles was the man outstanding in the merits of his life and recently exalted to the highest priestly dignity; Prosper acknowledges in the same letter that he was not his equal in authority.

The plural number, which Prosper likewise uses in that passage, can easily be referred to the common manner of speaking about someone when his name is suppressed for some reason.

But that Hilary whose letter to Augustine survives was not merely not a bishop when Prosper wrote to Augustine about this matter and about Hilary, bishop of Arles; he also seems to have been a layman. For he gives as the reason for writing to the blessed Augustine that the opponents of the blessed Augustine were, in part, people to whom ecclesiastical custom required that laymen show the highest reverence; and he adds that he observed this custom, while nevertheless acting modestly on Augustine’s behalf in a manner plainly appropriate to a layman. What of the fact that Hilary, bishop of Arles, was both a highly learned man and—as some surviving works of his reveal—an extremely eloquent one? Yet this Hilary does not at all display himself as stylistically similar to Hilary of Arles in the cited letter. At its conclusion he even admits that, compelled by consciousness of his own inadequacy, he is dealing with a man “distinguished both in character, eloquence, and zeal,” so that he might communicate in his letter whatever he could gather, and that he had taken care to send the letter together with the present one. “For he is such a man that even apart from this necessity he should be judged worthy of knowledge by Your Holiness.” These words plainly apply to Prosper, who testifies at the beginning of his letter that he was personally unknown to Augustine, and who later stood with Hilary on Augustine’s behalf before Pope Celestine. Since Celestine calls both of them “son” in that very letter, whereas the other Gallic bishops to whom it was written are called “brothers”; and since the blessed Augustine likewise calls both of them “son” at the beginning of his book *On the Predestination of the Saints*, it seems clear that Prosper was not even a bishop at that time, and perhaps not afterward either, since Gelasius, Fulgentius, Marcellinus Comes, and others who followed them never call him bishop, as they commonly call others in Gelasius’s decree, but only “a religious, learned, and holy man.” Even if he had been bishop of Riez, would he nevertheless seem likely to have been placed before Hilary of Arles, the prelate of a far more exalted see, and one elevated first to religion and then to the Arlesian episcopal insignia from the fullest seat of worldly power, as Eucherius says in his *Paraenesis*? This plainly confirms the distinction we have established between Hilary, prelate of Arles, and the man who stood with Prosper on Augustine’s behalf.

What must be corrected, however, in an otherwise very careful writer is the assertion that this Hilary, a student of Augustine, became bishop of Arles—not indeed when he appealed to Augustine, but later—and that he was the same Hilary who excelled no less in learning and eloquence than in nobility and holiness. Yet when he appealed to Augustine, the writer says that Hilary was merely a presbyter. This is stated in the year of Christ 426, no. 20; in the year 430, no. 89; and in the year 441, no. 3; and it is set out fully in the *Roman Martyrology* under 5 May, letter I. These points collapse of themselves in light of what has been said. For it has been shown that, when Augustine was appealed to by Hilary and Prosper, that famous Hilary of Arles had already obtained that see and had been brought under suspicion by those very appellants of Augustine. It has likewise been demonstrated that the Hilary whose letter to Augustine is directed against the Semipelagians was, when he wrote it, no more than a layman, and therefore was not at that time a presbyter.

From this it may incidentally also be perceived that it is open to question whether this Hilary should be regarded as different from that Hilary of Syracuse who, much earlier, when Pelagius was then staying in Sicily, challenged Augustine with the questions recorded in Augustine’s Letter 88 and resolved in Letter 89, where Augustine always calls him “son.” Having acquired such a taste of Augustinian doctrine, this Hilary could have gone to Augustine in Africa to be nourished in person at his life-giving breasts. He laments bitterly at the end of his letter against the Semipelagians that he had lost this benefit, adding that this had happened to him especially on account of a brother whom he reports to have professed continence together with his matron. He writes from the maritime coast of Gaul, and thus he could have written to Augustine either while passing through or while turning aside there for some other reason.

Although this may seem uncertain, I nevertheless consider it established that the other Hilary whom the blessed Augustine warns in Letter 94 about the recent error of Pelagius was different from Hilary, the accuser of the Semipelagians. For in that Letter 94 Augustine calls the other Hilary his fellow priest and pastor, whereas Hilary, Augustine’s friend, was—as I have said—a layman at the end of the blessed Augustine’s life. He therefore seems to have been Hilary, bishop of Narbonne I, who was flourishing at that time. The chronology does not allow me to grant that he was Hilary, bishop of Arles. For that letter of Augustine was written under Innocent I, in the year of Christ 417, as Baronius observes there, no. 5, at which time Hilary had not yet been appointed to the see of Arles. He succeeded Saint Honoratus, who had sat after Patroclus. But Patroclus, according to Prosper in his *Chronicle*, was killed at Arles in the year of Christ 426, while Celestine was bishop at Rome; before Celestine had been Innocent, and before him Zosimus and Boniface. It is therefore clear that in those days Augustine could not yet have addressed Hilary with the title “fellow priest and pastor.” But enough of this.

**3.** From the letters of these contemporaries and devoted followers of Augustine it is therefore evident that toward the end of the blessed Augustine’s old age, in Narbonese Gaul and especially at Massilia, most people—and among them at least one man pre-eminent both in life and merits and in the dignity of the highest priesthood, that is, a bishop—resented the fact that Saint Augustine, having retracted his earlier teaching that the beginning of grace and justification arises from natural effort—a teaching he had transmitted when young and less knowledgeable about the matter of grace—now taught plainly that the very first beginning of our salvation must be attributed to divine prevenience. Saint Prosper gives a lengthy account of their complaints in his response to the first three extracts of the Genoese opponents.

Although at first they opposed Augustine almost only by whispering and secretly, as Prosper testifies in his letter to Rufinus, they gradually—something Prosper expressly records in the preface to his book against the *Collationes*—became inflamed by great agitation against the later doctrine of the blessed Augustine. They thought that by this doctrine the ruin of the sinner was thrown back upon God and that human salvation was not placed in the human being’s own hand, contrary to what the ancient sense of the Church had maintained down to that time.

Others among those same rivals of Augustine added other charges. “Some of our people,” Prosper says in his letter to Rufinus, after first setting forth Augustine’s most illustrious eulogy, “slander him, saying that he completely removes free choice and, under the name of grace, preaches a fatal necessity; they further add that he wishes two masses of the human race and two natures to be believed, so that the impiety of pagans and Manichaeans may be attributed to a man of such great piety.” They also added other harsh and dreadful accusations, which may be seen in their chapters preserved in Prosper. The numerous and monstrous calumnies with which they burdened Prosper himself, the defender of Augustine, are recorded in the preface to the *Vincentian Objections*, in the same Prosper.

**4.** I would judge that the first origin of all these movements against Augustine and his followers was an error spreading among many weak minds, arising from a badly understood doctrine of the blessed Augustine concerning the calling of the elect according to purpose, and concerning the non-uniform election of all people to the same helps of grace, and therefore not to glory either.

For it is clear from the blessed Augustine’s Letters 46 and 47, and from his books *On Grace and Free Choice* and *On Rebuke and Grace*, that certain monks were greatly disturbed by this. The despair of that monk in the blessed Augustine’s own monastery, which he describes in *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 15, seems to have belonged to the same matter. Although the blessed Augustine refers it solely to foreknowledge of causes, these two matters are sufficiently closely connected, and weak minds are almost always dashed against both rocks. They attribute the reason why such people are foreknown to the fact that those greater and more hidden benefits which fall to the elect have not been supplied to them.

These and other weak persons therefore took offense at the doctrine proposed by the blessed Augustine. The matter reached the point—if we listen to Sigebert—in the year of Christ 415, and the same account appears in Prosper’s *Chronicle* published by Pithaeus, under the twenty-third year of Honorius, that a heresy of the Predestinarians arose. They weakened the hearts of God’s servants and denied that concern for salvation ought to be entertained, maintaining that unless someone belonged to that fortunate little group of elect for whom God had antecedently decreed glory, and prepared special helps and a deep and secret calling, such a person would necessarily be lost; whereas those who belonged to that number and blessed possession of God would necessarily be saved.

Others, however, place the heresy of the Predestinarians much later and explain a large part of it differently. They attribute it to its author, Gottschalk, a monk of Soissons, who lived around the year of Christ 800. His error is reported in these words by the Church of Lyons, in its work against John Scotus, during its examination of the fourth chapter of Scotus’s book:

> “He sets forth a third heresy, one that introduces necessity and compulsion through a twofold predestination. He does not conceal the author whom he believes responsible, calling it Gottschalkian, after a certain wretched and most unhappy monk, long ago condemned there—for we do not know in what manner—and for many years confined in a prison dungeon, named Gottschalk.”

The same Church reports this man’s other errors, together with those of Gottschalk, at the beginning of its book *On Three Letters*, drawing, I believe, from a letter of Hincmar. It adds that when Gottschalk had gone from Gaul to the remotest regions of Germany for the preaching of the Gospel, the beginning of his preaching arose there: God had predestined from eternity those whom he wished, either to glory or to punishment, in such a way that neither the elect could perish nor the reprobate be saved; nor did God wish all to be saved, but only those who in fact attain salvation, for whom alone Christ had also come and suffered.

Because of these and similar propositions to which he obstinately clung, Gottschalk is said, according to the same book, after the middle of the work, to have been condemned to scourging by monks and abbots, almost torn apart without pity until near his death, and compelled with his own hands to throw into the flames the book he had written in support of those propositions.

See Pithaeus on Gottschalk in the *Annals*, Trithemius in the *Hirsau Chronicle*, Frodoard in Book III of his *Ecclesiastical History of Rheims*, chapter 14, and above all Hincmar, who was present, in his letter about him to Nicholas I. Hincmar rightly observes there that Gottschalk was not truly the original author but merely the restorer of the Predestinarian heresy, which we trace back to its first origin.

Much is also read about Gottschalk’s wickedness and the punishments inflicted upon him in Rabanus’s letter to Hincmar himself and in another letter to Count Eberhard. In another letter, addressed to Noringus, Rabanus rejects Gottschalk’s error while saying nothing at all about him. Likewise, the author of the recently published work against the Predestinarian heresy, who adduces in full a book falsely attributed to Augustine in order to bring the inner chambers of this heresy into public view, nowhere mentions Gottschalk. He acknowledges that the Predestinarian heresy arose in the very time of the blessed Augustine, and places it immediately after the Nestorian heresy and before the rise of the Eutychian heresy, of which he says nothing.

**5.** Some people, therefore, wishing to withdraw as far as possible from this heresy, which was then spreading for the reason I have explained—as error’s madness is always abrupt—turned aside to the opposite extreme, in accordance with Novatian’s statement on the Trinity, chapter 20. They denied God’s special benevolence toward the elect and their calling according to purpose. They also rejected divine election to glory as having been made without any consideration of merits acquired through grace. The more turbulent among them compounded that antecedent election, in order to increase its infamy, with a great addition of lies.

They also rejected the antecedent preparation of the grace that awakens and every prevenience of the human will made by God, the author of grace, as hostile to human freedom. With the intention of proving that God is the common Father of all and shows no partiality, and likewise of placing the power of human salvation in each person’s own hand, they joined the helps of grace to the will naturally exerting itself and to one who, by natural powers, implores assistance and strives toward salvation.

Some who were more thoughtful, calmer, and also more religious—Cassian, for example—did not base the subordination of awakening grace to the human will on a subsequent violation of freedom through prevenient grace, or on the loss of the human being’s power over his own salvation if he is first preceded by grace. They seem in fact to have recognized that none of these consequences truly follows, whether from eternal election to glory and special grace or from temporal prevenience effected by the power of the eternal decree; and therefore, in the case of some who are freely saved, they acknowledged gratuitous prevenience.

Instead, they based the subordination of grace to the will on certain passages of Scripture that they had wrongly distorted and that pertained to subsequent grace. In those passages God is said to await the sinner and to be preceded at the time of maturity.

**6.** To make it evident and established that matters stood in this way—for there are people who contradict it and report the error of the Massilians differently—and also to make clear the variety of opinions and foundations that we have mentioned among the Massilians, we must approach and hear Prosper and Hilary, who first reported their nascent error to Augustine and then to Pope Celestine.

Prosper therefore writes in his letter to Augustine, after presenting at length the Massilians’ complaints against Augustine’s assertion of the special election of certain persons and their calling according to purpose, not common to others:

> “They say that, insofar as God is concerned, eternal life is prepared for all; but, insofar as free choice is concerned, it is apprehended by those who have freely believed in God and have received the help of grace as a reward for their belief.
>
> “They turned especially to this preaching of grace—which offended them by their contradiction—although they had previously held better views, because, if they professed that all good merits are preceded by grace and are granted by grace so that they may exist, they would necessarily concede that God, according to the purpose and counsel of his will, by a hidden judgment and manifest work, makes one vessel for honor and another for dishonor, since no one is justified except through grace and no one is born except in transgression.
>
> “But they shrink from confessing this and fear to attribute the merits of the saints to divine action. Nor do they accept that the predetermined number of the elect can neither be increased nor diminished, lest the exhortations of those who encourage unbelievers and negligent persons have no place, and lest the command to industry and labor be superfluous, since its pursuit would be frustrated if election ceased.
>
> “For they think that each person can be called to correction or improvement only if he knows that by his own diligence he can become good, and that his freedom is therefore to be aided by God if he chooses what God commands.
>
> “Thus, since in those who have received a time of free will there are two things that bring about human salvation—namely, God’s grace and human obedience—they wish obedience to precede grace, so that the beginning of salvation may be believed to depend on the one who is saved, not on the one who saves; and so that the human will may procure for itself the help of divine grace, rather than grace subjecting the human will to itself.”

You see the beginning and progress of the error, enclosed at last in an abyss and gulf.

**7.** Hilary says similar things at the beginning of his letter to Augustine, more briefly indeed concerning the origin of the error, but more distinctly concerning its progress and its various circumstances:

> “They say,” he writes of the Massilians, “that it is a new and useless form of preaching to say that people are chosen according to purpose, so that they can neither seize nor retain this gift unless the will to believe has been given. They think that all force from preaching is excluded if it is said that nothing remains in human beings which preaching can arouse.
>
> “They agree that every human being perished in Adam and that no one can be freed from this by his own choice. Yet they assert that it is consistent with the truth, or appropriate to preaching, that when the opportunity of obtaining salvation is announced to those who are prostrate and will never rise by their own powers, they can be healed from their illness by the merit with which they have willed and believed, and can obtain both an increase of faith itself and the entire effect of their healing.
>
> “For the rest, they agree that no one is sufficient for any work, whether for beginning it, much less for completing it. They do not think that the terrified and suppliant will of each sick person, in wishing to be healed, should be counted as one of the works of their cure. For when it is said, ‘Believe, and you will be saved,’ they maintain that one of these is demanded and the other offered, so that, on account of what is demanded, what is offered may be granted thereafter if it has been supplied.”
>
> And shortly afterward:
>
> > “They do not think that grace is denied if a will of this kind is said to precede—a will that merely seeks the physician but is itself already capable of nothing. For they wish those testimonies, such as ‘as God has apportioned to each the measure of faith,’ to mean that the one who has begun to wish is helped, not that he is also given the will to wish; while others, equally guilty and who could likewise be freed, are excluded from this gift if the will to believe, which is bestowed equally upon the undeserving, were also bestowed upon them in the same way.
> >
> > “But if it is said, they say, that a will remains in everyone by which a person can either despise or obey, they think that an account of the elect and the rejected is conveniently supplied by the fact that each person’s own merit of will is added to him.”

Again, farther below:

> “What Your Holiness said, that no one perseveres unless he has received the power of persevering, is understood by them in this sense: that for those to whom it is given, even though they may be sluggish, it is nevertheless attributed to their preceding personal choice. They maintain that free choice is retained only to the extent that a person may wish or refuse to admit the medicine.
>
> “For the rest, they testify that they themselves abominate and condemn anyone who thinks that any strength remains in a person by which he may progress toward health. They do not wish perseverance to be preached in such a way that it cannot either be acquired through humble entreaty or lost through stubbornness. Nor do they wish to be reduced to uncertainty about God’s will, since, as they think, the beginning of the will—whatever its character—by which one obtains or loses salvation is evident.”

For a complete examination of the error under discussion, Hilary’s words above lack some illumination on two points: namely, concerning that “whatever kind of beginning” which the Semipelagians expected from choice arising from itself, and concerning the work for which they admitted that grace was necessary.

[Col. 0780A]

**8.** In fact, by the word “beginning,” in the very cradle of their error, they designated the beginnings of every good work, so that they attributed to bare free choice not only the first free good act, whether of faith, but also the beginnings of all good works necessary for perseverance.

Later, however, after being refuted—as the blessed Augustine reports in *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 2, at the end of that book, and in *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 17—they sang a recantation and restricted themselves to the beginning of salvation alone and to perseverance in it, as the blessed Augustine testifies twice in that chapter 17.

It is useful to append his actual words, since some more recent writers confidently declare that the Semipelagians went astray only concerning the beginning of salvation, not concerning perseverance. Augustine therefore speaks as follows, reporting the Semipelagian position:

> “But those who place only the beginning of faith and perseverance in it to the end within our power, in such a way that they do not think these are gifts of God, nor that God works our thoughts and wills so that we may possess and retain them, concede that he gives the other things when they are obtained from him by the faith of the believer.”

And shortly afterward:

> “These, then, are gifts from God—namely, to say nothing of the others, wisdom and continence.”

The Semipelagians agree with this. For they are not Pelagians, so as to contend against this evident truth with harsh and heretical perversity. “But these things,” they say, “are obtained from God by faith, and faith begins from us.” They insist that both to begin to possess this faith and to remain in it to the end belong to us, as though we did not begin them from the Lord.

You see the straits to which the Semipelagians finally came: they were compelled to attribute only the beginning of faith and perseverance in it to the bare will, and thus took refuge in order to remove God from blame and human beings from necessity in the matter of salvation.

But Scripture cries out innumerable times that this refuge was wholly unsafe with respect to perseverance. Equally clear testimonies exist for conceiving the beginning of faith from supernatural helps alone, as for the beginning of the other supernatural works. This may be seen in the long and notable discussion undertaken by Saint Augustine in *On the Predestination of the Saints* and, especially, Sermon 15 *On the Words of the Apostle*; by Prosper in *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, chapter 23; and by Fulgentius in Book I of *On the Truth of Predestination*, to prove that faith is a gift of God.

The issue is not merely the addition to faith, as the blessed Augustine calls it in that book, chapter 2, but also the beginning of faith, concerning which alone the Semipelagians opposed the argument there directed against them. Although the Council of Orange, which dried up the dregs of Semipelagianism, condemns not only those who claimed the beginning of faith for themselves but also those who in the same way claimed the beginnings of other good works for bare choice and natural powers, this does not mean that the Semipelagians reasoned in this way about the beginning of every good action outside faith. Rather, since they had thought this way concerning the beginning itself, the Council rejected that point as well, lest any spark of the error remain.

Nevertheless, since faith is the first root in the matter of salvation, and since the case for it is much stronger than the case for subsequent acts, once it has been proved that its beginning comes from God, it should also seem to follow with much greater right that the beginnings of all the others come from God. It would therefore not be surprising, even if one admitted that the Semipelagians had always persisted in the same error concerning the beginning of every work, that the blessed Augustine nevertheless concentrated especially on demonstrating that the beginning of faith comes from God and not from bare free choice.

**9.** Since, however, the testimony of the blessed Augustine in *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 2, establishes that the Semipelagians could not withstand the clearest passages of Scripture showing that faith is a gift of God, it seems evident that by “the beginning of faith” they did not understand faith while still raw and slight. Rather, by “the beginning of faith” they understood that willing to believe which precedes faith, which the Second Council of Orange, canon 5, calls “the inclination toward belief” (*credulitatis affectus*). Saint Fulgentius, plainly refuting the Semipelagians concerning the will to believe, which they insisted came from human beings, calls it “the beginning of belief” (*initium credulitatis*) in Book *On the Incarnation and Grace of Christ*, chapter 18.

It follows that the faith begun, for which the Semipelagians—as the blessed Augustine says in that chapter 2—claimed that increased faith was repaid, is not faith essentially constituted although imperfect in intensity. Rather, it is an antecedent inclination, a kind of prelude to faith, although morally it is counted as one act with it and is therefore commonly granted the same name.

Likewise, it follows that the increased faith, which is called there “the increase of faith,” is not an enlargement or addition to faith already begun in the same genus. It is faith of a higher order, succeeding that imperfect beginning, which was regarded as belonging to human effort.

They said that the increased faith was granted in response to that begun faith because they thought that, once a human being had furnished the beginning, he could in some way merit the interior help of grace necessary for believing. They held that the human being first contributed the willing on his own side, but that, once it had first appeared, God nourished and advanced it. They expressed the same idea in another way, saying that human beings provide the beginning, but that completion belongs to God.

Likewise, as Prosper reports in the cited letter, they said that holiness was conferred upon those who had used well the good of nature, which they called “initial grace,” and had thereby, through some kind of merit, summoned divine supernatural benevolence upon themselves.

**10.** To this natural inclination toward belief, posited as coming from ourselves, by which they asserted that the assistance of divine grace was elicited and which they said was awaited by divine calling, the Semipelagians added all the remaining things to which they gave the name of works. They even said that the assent of faith itself came from divine grace.

They affirmed this when they said that grace was necessary for every work of human healing, both for beginning and for completion. They excluded from the catalogue of works only that natural inclination toward belief of which I have spoken, which in some way disposed a person toward grace.

They wished this alone to remain available to the bare will in the matter of salvation, because they considered it so necessary that salvation would thereby be placed within the power of every adult, while God would be freed from partiality toward persons. They alleged that the later doctrine of the blessed Augustine was burdened by these two difficulties; they thought that they avoided them by admitting on the human side some kind of beginning, or by attributing to the good use of bare free choice some merit, however slight and negligible, so that the whole subjection of grace to the will might have its foundation in that beginning.

They said that this beginning, purely natural and drawn from our bare choice, was awaited by God as a little handle by which he might receive the will clutching at the divine helps.

**11.** Those who interpret this expectation differently are altogether ridiculous and foolish. They say that the error consists in maintaining that consent, insofar as it is freely supplied by the will to the antecedently given grace that calls, is awaited by God as the reason why God himself should also wish that the consent proceed from the will.

Thus, since these two causes concur in producing that consent, the will, already preceded by grace, is prior in reason. God waits for it and, at its nod—and therefore later in the order of reason—applies himself to cooperate and to give consent.

The critics mentioned above consider this to be the condemned doctrine that God awaits our will, a doctrine which Cassian wrongly founded in *Conference* 13, chapter 12, on the words of Isaiah, chapter 30: “The Lord waits to have mercy on you,” and which was condemned by the Second Council of Orange, canon 4, and refuted by Prosper, Fulgentius, and the other defenders of grace against the Semipelagians.

This is what it means to misplace the account of ancient errors and to misinterpret the definitions of the councils against them, when it is perfectly clear that the Semipelagians excluded the divine grace that awakens and the first beginning placed by God, fearing that prevenience would harm human freedom and using God’s exemption from the fault of partiality toward persons as a pretext.

They are therefore condemned in this sense: they affirmed that the will is awaited by God, although God does not await the will in order to call it—even though he truly does await it with respect to the production of free consent once he is calling. That is, God does not wish to seize it unconsulted and carry it away to cooperation, or compel it to forge consent; rather, he leaves this to its freedom and does not come to cooperate until he has been preceded by it.

He is called, I say, not by a prior act of divine cooperation—which is known to be incapable of being affected—but by the exigency of a nature then about to act, in such circumstances, and after the preceding divine fertilization, which would produce the action if it could produce it without God joining himself to cooperate.

For the will, setting before God this exigency of its own and presenting it objectively, not formally, summons God to cooperate and to produce the free consent together with it.

Thus that expectation by God of the human will which the Council of Orange rejected is none other than the expectation posited by the Semipelagians themselves: an expectation of the will in order that it might be called. In their view, the human being first produced from himself and by his own powers some kind of effort, while God had not yet undertaken anything concerning the human being’s salvation; and by that effort, in some way, the human being merited that God—who had been awaiting only that effort, however weak and powerless—should immediately come as the promoter and perfecter of our beginning, displaying supernatural assistance to it as to a certain kind of merit and morally moving cause.

**12.** I always say that, according to the Semipelagians, that beginning of salvation which they asserted came from us was something slight and negligible, containing no more than some kind of merit of the helps of grace.

For it seems clear that they did not assert that such a beginning possessed merit *de condigno*—merit in strict proportion—in relation to the salvation toward which they said it disposed a person. Cassian teaches this most explicitly in *Conference* 13, chapters 9, 13, and 16, and in Book XII of *The Institutes*, chapters 11, 13, and 14.

The same meaning is conveyed by those words of the Semipelagians which we quoted above from Hilary: that this beginning, or the will by which the physician is sought, is of no avail—that is, that it is of extremely slight force and merit. In this the Semipelagians differed from Pelagius, who granted merit proportionate to the natural transaction of salvation.

Nor are those writers convincing who assert that in this respect the Semipelagians adhered to Pelagius and introduced merit *de condigno*, such as Vega in Book VIII, question 5, and Toletus in his annotation on Romans 8, annotation 31, and on Romans 11, at the words, “But if by grace, then it is no longer of works.”

I do not find them convincing, I say, because Saint Augustine, who in the passages cited rejects this Semipelagian merit, nevertheless in those same places, in Letter 105, section 48, and often elsewhere, grants to the sinner divinely preceded by grace a merit *de congruo*—a fitting merit—for the remission of sins, while denying that a similar merit can be granted on the basis of natural powers with respect to first grace.

Therefore he recognized that grace is overturned not only by the concession of natural merit *de condigno*—although especially by that—but also by the concession of natural merit *de congruo*, however slight and negligible, such as the Semipelagians introduced.

Because they considered the smallness of this merit, the Semipelagians reached the point of professing that what is repaid to that beginning of ours, whatever its character, is a gift of grace, and that the beginning itself is not merit in the absolute and straightforward sense.

Some people, not penetrating this distinction, condemn Cassian and Faustus for inconsistency, since expressions of this kind frequently occur in their works, as though they had forgotten their error in this respect. In fact, however, they persisted in the error and denied only merit in the absolute sense, whereas every natural disposition toward salvation, and every power that is in any way meritorious, which they admitted, must be denied as destructive of grace. Toletus wrongly denies this above.

**13.** Nor did the Semipelagians rightly think that by this error they were safeguarding human freedom in the matter of salvation and God’s exemption from the stain of partiality toward persons—the twofold rock of error which, as I said earlier, they regarded as at stake. They were wrongly avoiding one error by means of another.

For although it is entirely true that salvation lies within the power of every adult and that God is far removed from partiality toward persons, it is utterly false that God is preceded by the human being, or that the human being begins the matter of his salvation by a good use of bare free choice.

To place salvation in the hand of every adult, it is entirely sufficient that a person, preceded by God, can consent or dissent from the one calling him. Fulgentius teaches this with perfect clarity in *On Predestination and Grace*, chapter 9, following Augustine in *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 34.

Although this prevenience is not an equal benefit to all upon whom it is bestowed, but in some it is of such a kind that it makes them act—even though with struggle—because it becomes a victorious sweetness and delight, as the blessed Augustine calls it in *On the Merits and Remission of Sins*, chapter 27, it is nevertheless always sufficient for action and is of such a kind that it fails to achieve its effect only through human negligence and fault.

The selective and special character of this prevenience does not impose upon God the stain of partiality toward persons. Such partiality has no place in matters that are purely gratuitous, even when the distribution is unequal and no cause whatsoever has intervened on the part of those who receive it.

Yet there remains there a cross fixed for every intellect, and one must cling to the divine, just, but hidden judgment, in accordance with Augustine’s statement in *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 34 [Col. 0783B]:

> If anyone presses us to investigate that depth—why one person is persuaded in such a way that he is convinced, while another is not persuaded in the same way—two answers alone occur to me for the moment, which I am glad to give: “O the depth of the riches,” and, “Surely there is no injustice with God?” Let anyone who is dissatisfied with this answer seek out those more learned than I; but let him beware lest he find people who are presumptuous.

He likewise warns that one must beware of precipice in this question in *Sermon 20 on the Words of the Apostle*, and beautifully in *Sermon 11*:

> It troubles me, he says, that one person perishes and another does not. It troubles me as a human being—if you wish to hear the truth—and it troubles me because I am human. But although you are human and I am human, let us hear the one who says: “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” If an animal could speak and say to God, “Why did you make this man and me an animal?” would you not justly be angry and say, “O animal, who are you to answer back to God?” You are a human being, but in relation to God you are an animal; and may you be his animal, and the sheep of his pasture!

See also *Letter* 105 on the same subject, and Prosper, *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, book II, chapter 30, at the end, and Saint Chrysostom, *Homily* 26 on the Epistle to the Romans, in the moral section (*in mor.*). Thus the contrivances set up by the Semipelagians are overturned without difficulty. Some think that they can demolish these contrivances by a profound argument, but in reality the argument is neither solid nor free from error. For I do not see how the author of the work *Against the Predestinarians* can conveniently be cleared of the stain of Semipelagianism. Throughout his third book he often grants that grace precedes the will, but understands this of the Incarnation already accomplished, and of Christ, given by the Father as the source of grace for our salvation. By this reasoning he could have demolished the arguments of the Semipelagians from the necessary precedence of grace. Yet this is not sufficient for that beginning which must be acknowledged against the Semipelagians as properly belonging to prevenient grace. For it must be understood of actual grace, which is an act received in us and which arouses us to act. This author does not seem to acknowledge such grace as preceding on God’s part and anticipating our action. The same seems to be suggested by Arnobius the Younger in his commentary on Psalm 147. Therefore the only Catholic and solid argument for overturning the Semipelagian contrivances is the one I have proposed.

### 14

The other calumnies against Augustine, which I mentioned as having been disseminated at Massilia and throughout that coastal region of Gaul, partly disappear of themselves with respect to election to glory, as Prosper rightly demonstrates when reporting them in his *Book on the Vincentian Objections*. In part, however, they seem to me most suitably dispelled if we say that Saint Augustine did indeed admit in God a formal intention of the glory of the elect, prior to foreseen merits, from which the preparation of a fitting calling and one according to purpose derives its origin. For this is plainly conveyed by what he discusses in *On Rebuke and Grace*, chapters 7 and 12; in *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 3; in *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 9; and in other places. The special care and love of God for the elect, so often celebrated in Scripture and so frequently examined by Augustine, also supports this view.

Nevertheless, according to that same Saint Augustine, this intention must not be regarded as effective except through its ordering toward the suitable aids procured by it. For the choice of suitable and therefore effective means is so connected with that divine election and intention that the intention ought not to be conceived as effective before those means, and the ordering toward them, have been considered. Since, however, those means are not irresistible but, absolutely speaking, can fail to produce their effect—as is demonstrated elsewhere, and as Saint Macarius teaches most splendidly in *Homily* 37, where he discusses the grace given to the apostles, already confirmed in grace, so that they might not commit grave sin—and since that grace was certainly effective, we rightly infer [Col. 0784A] from these means that the efficacy of the intention introduced by Saint Augustine was not more unshakable.

Thus all the contrivances collapse that were brought forward on the grounds that, according to Saint Augustine, the salvation of the elect is entirely necessary and incapable of being overthrown. [49] For it is one thing that it certainly and infallibly will not be overthrown, and another that it cannot be overthrown even if a person wished it. The first is entirely true; the second is entirely false.

Although I would not think that anything need be feared for the mutable condition of human freedom [Col. 0784B] even if I admitted that, according to Saint Augustine, election to glory is entirely effective—but only within the order of intention—for God, because of the conditionally foreseen cooperation of the human will if it is assisted by such or such pleasant means, did not wish to decree that the will should be carried away by irresistible aids, would nevertheless, consistently with that robust and wholly antecedent election which he conceived from himself, decree this if he had foreseen the human will’s unwillingness and obstinacy against those gentler and milder means.

For in this way human freedom and its capacity for turning in matters concerning salvation remain intact, notwithstanding that iron decree which wholly persists and leaves the will as it was in itself, and therefore wholly released. Salvation nevertheless becomes indefectible, because although the divine intention is a pure intention based on the foreknown free turning of the will through rejectable grace, nevertheless, if the will wished to be otherwise disposed, it would be compelled to take this or that path, in accordance with the antecedent divine decree that is presupposed. [Col. 0784C]

But since I do not approve that indefectibility of salvation, although it is compatible with present freedom, for other reasons, it is preferable to explain Saint Augustine’s proposed position in the manner I have described, so that it may be established as less exposed to quibbles and calumnies. It is enough for now to have touched upon these matters, which have been fully discussed elsewhere, in order to expose the emptiness of the complaints voiced by the Massilians. So much for them.

### 15

Cassian saw that the error of the remaining Massilians, explained above—according to which the first grace is always subordinated to the human will and invocation—could not be reconciled with most of the passages of Scripture in which we are taught that God makes himself known to those who do not know him and appears to those who were not asking for him. Accordingly, he devised something else. Namely, that sometimes a human being does precede God and, by a good use of free will, somehow merits the grace of God, superadded to natural petition and striving. This was the error of the Semipelagians, or the common Massilians. At other times, however, God precedes us, and, though not yet called by us, knocks at the door and anticipates the will. [Col. 0784D]

Cuychius, in annotation 20 on Cassian, and Ciaconius, in his observations on the same author, noted that this was Cassian’s view; and it is plainly found in Prosper’s *Book Against the Collator*, especially chapters 5, 9, and 38. “You have no full agreement,” Prosper says in chapter 5, “neither with the heretics nor with the Catholics. They defend the beginnings of free will in all the just works of human beings; we always believe that the beginnings of good thoughts proceed from God. You have discovered some shapeless third position, wholly unsuitable to either side, by which you could acquire neither the agreement of your opponents nor a place among those who understand us.”

But why should we try to discover Cassian’s mind elsewhere, when there are clear passages in Cassian himself in which the opinion I have described is plainly evident? Most clearly, *Conference* 13, chapter 7:

> When God’s goodness perceives that even the smallest spark of good will has appeared in us—or one which he himself has struck from the hard flint of our heart—it fosters and rekindles it, and confirms it by his inspiration. [Col. 0785A]

And in the following chapter:

> When he perceives that some beginning of good will has arisen in us, he immediately enlightens and strengthens it, giving increase to that which either he himself has planted or has seen emerge through our effort.

The whole of that *Conference* teems with similar disjunctions. Therefore the Second Council of Orange, canon 8, distinctly and separately condemns his error, although Cassian’s name is suppressed: the error by which some are said to approach God by preceding God through free will, while others are said to accomplish the same thing after being preceded by God through divine mercy. The council says that this is cut off by that universal declaration: “No one can come to me unless my Father draws him.” It is likewise cut off by the apostolic saying, which embraces everyone equally: “No one—absolutely no one, as the council explains, not merely some people—can say, ‘Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit.”

Therefore, when Cassian in one place mentions only God’s being preceded by the created will, whose movement he awaits, [Col. 0785B] while elsewhere, and specifically in *Conference* 3, he repeatedly mentions only the divine precedence by which every movement of the will is anticipated, he should not be accused of inconsistency, as some do even here. Rather, since his distinctive error maintains that sometimes God and sometimes the will establishes the beginning of justification, he consequently sets forth sometimes one kind of precedence and sometimes the other, according to his purpose and the subject under discussion, as Prosper also noted in *Book Against the Collator*, chapter 38.

### 16

Although these things are so, Cassian’s error is nevertheless commonly branded with the mark of Semipelagianism, and Cassian himself is counted among the Semipelagians, because insofar as he held that the will sometimes precedes God in the matter of salvation, he followed Semipelagianism. Similarly, the Semipelagians themselves, because insofar as they held that human precedence comes before God’s help, followed Pelagius; for this reason they are often branded with Pelagianism [Col. 0785C] and called Pelagians by Augustine, Prosper, Fulgentius, and other ancient writers.

Cassian, however, did not labor under the other errors found in others who bear the same label. And although he covertly opposed Saint Augustine, as Prosper extensively records in his *Letter to Rufinus*, he did not fasten upon or disseminate the monstrous calumnies against Saint Augustine that we reported above. This is indicated by Prosper’s *Book Against the Collator*, chapter 2:

> Lest we seem to be attacking, in order to obscure the knowledge of learned men, the things which the ignoble common crowd and the shameless chatter of fools pour forth without restraint, we shall report chiefly the definitions of one man whom there is no doubt surpasses all of them in devotion to the study of the sacred Scriptures.

This refers to Cassian, whom Prosper shortly afterward again calls “a man of the priestly order who excels in the practice of disputation among those with whom he lives.” As you see, Prosper frees him from the charge of shamelessness toward Augustine. Then, throughout the work, he refutes only Cassian’s error concerning divine precedence through the human being, while passing over all the other matters mentioned above with which, as we stated, Saint Augustine had been burdened by some people of that age and region. [Col. 0785D]

### 17

We have therefore established what the true error of the Semipelagians was, both insofar as it was common chiefly to the Massilian party and insofar as it was peculiar to Cassian, and we have established why it is called Semipelagianism. Since the proponents of the proposed error did not adhere wholly to Pelagius but only in part—namely, by denying that the first beginning of justification comes from divine grace, although they otherwise acknowledged grace—they are called Semipelagians.

They would more appropriately be called the remnants of the Pelagians, and they are sometimes named this for that very reason. For in reality they did not embrace half of Pelagius’s error; rather, they agreed with him on only one point, rejecting so many other errors in which Pelagius had additionally gone astray. They retained that one portion of proud teaching—that is, Pelagian teaching—while renouncing the rest, as Prosper says in his *Letter to Demetriades*.

Indeed, even on that single point [Col. 0786A] they did not wholly follow Pelagius, but only as if from one half. For Pelagius acknowledged a condign merit in natural works with respect to human salvation. They, by contrast, philosophized much more moderately and admitted only some sort of natural merit, which would be the foundation of our salvation and would reconcile grace to the human being, although they considered it so slight that they scarcely deemed it worthy of the name of merit.

Yet because this error of theirs was, as it were, a portion of the fullness of the errors introduced by Pelagius, and because that advocacy of grace—which, to use Faustus’s expression, “seizes the handle of the will”—laid the way through human labor for renewing Pelagius’s principal error, by which he contended that divine grace is given on account of natural merits, they were therefore called the remnants of the Pelagians. “In their mutilated remains,” Prosper says in his *Letter to Rufinus*, “the Pelagian heresy was still palpitating.” And in his *Letter to Augustine*: “In these remnants of Pelagian depravity, a considerable fiber of its poisonousness is being nourished.” In *Book Against the Collator*, chapter 11, he calls the proponents of this error [Col. 0786B] people who, “by rekindling the ashes of the already extinguished Pelagian doctrine, attempted to kindle the failing smoke of its stench into a renewed flame.”

### 18

They are called Massilians by most writers because, in fact, at the beginning of his *Letter to Augustine*, Prosper says that those whose error the entire letter reports were established in the city of Massilia. He testifies that they were distinguished and eminent men in every pursuit of virtue—clearly because that city was then most fully supplied with monks highly trained in ascetic practice and virtue according to Cassian’s discipline. Among them Cassian himself, “like the bright moon among lesser fires,” as Prosper Tiro says in his *Chronicle* under the year of Christ 436, shone forth as distinguished and renowned both for learning and holiness.

For this reason Saint Prosper, in his *Letter to Rufinus*, laments the danger that had arisen from the Massilians’ reputation for virtue and the threat posed by their moral integrity: the peoples would easily follow them when they saw that so illustrious a portion of Christ’s flock had approved the error. Hilary, however, at the beginning of his *Letter to Augustine*, reporting the same matters [Col. 0786C] that had been brought before Augustine by Prosper, says that they had been discussed at Massilia and also in other places in Gaul.

Prosper was not unaware of this; he likewise did not suppress the complaints of Hilary of Arles, as we saw above, nor the doubts of the Genoese. From this it is clear that that Massilian plague spread throughout the entire region and coast of Gaul, and even assailed Genoa and the approaches to Italy.

If, however, it is to be called the Massilian plague, although it seems first to have arisen in Africa, this applies not only to the disputes concerning calling according to purpose, which compelled Saint Augustine to write *On Rebuke and Grace*, as he states at the beginning of that work and in *Letter* 47, and as Prosper also states at the beginning of his *Letter to Augustine;* it applies also to the Semipelagian opinion that arose from this dispute concerning special calling, namely, that the first grace is subordinated to human invocation. [Col. 0786D]

For before the Gauls were brought to his attention by Prosper and Hilary, Saint Augustine plainly reports in *Letter* 107 and in *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book II, chapter 8, that, after Pelagius had been crushed, there arose people who defended the error that the first grace is expended upon human labor, while abandoning the remaining errors of Pelagius. This was that diluted Pelagianism which the Massilians, together with nearly all the neighboring Gauls, admitted for some time—late in acquiring wisdom among the Africans, and not without a degree of obstinacy.

Thus, although after Saint Augustine had been warned by Prosper and Hilary, and after his wholly divine books *On the Predestination of the Saints* and *On the Gift of Perseverance*—which one may rightly call Augustine’s swan songs and testament—it might have seemed that the error had been utterly crushed, it was nevertheless later necessary for Pope Celestine, approached by those same Prosper and Hilary, to restrain, by a serious rebuke, the bishops who survived Augustine and who professed Semipelagianism in Gaul, or who were indulgent toward its error or even supported it. This was not a task of small importance with respect to that error.

For many additional years it flourished in that region because the Gauls were not greatly moved in this matter by the authority of Saint Augustine [Col. 0787A] in this matter, since he had formerly thought otherwise on this point, and because they calumniated his later position as harsh and unmerciful. They nevertheless thought that they could sufficiently evade Celestine’s authority by alleging that the books *On the Predestination of the Saints* and *On the Gift of Perseverance*, in which Semipelagianism is overturned, had not been approved by Celestine; rather, they claimed, Celestine had commended only the teaching of Augustine’s earlier works, by which he had reduced Pelagianism to ashes. Prosper reports at length that the Gauls made this claim at the end of his *Book Against the Collator*.

### 19

Nor was this Pelagian ember, still smoking, entirely extinguished before the apostolic see, by sending to the bishops of that region the chapters that had been publicly proposed at Orange, at the dedication of the basilica of Liberius, and confirmed and proclaimed by the assembled Fathers, successfully suppressed every spark of that conflagration, placed beneath the deceptive ash in defense of human freedom and divine justice. This occurred in the year of Christ 529, according to the latest calculation of Cardinal Baronius, under Felix IV, long after Saint Leo, Cassian’s contemporary; a title gratuitously attached by a compiler attributes the transmission of those apostolic chapters to Leo. [Col. 0787B] A notable confirmation of the same chapters was also added by Boniface II, in letters sent to Saint Caesarius, which are found in volume I of the Councils of Gaul, page 223 in my edition.

It is also worthy of consideration that in those chapters, or canons, only those matters are defined that concerned excluding the subjection of divine grace to the human will and affirming the necessity of grace throughout the entire progress of justification. Matters concerning election to glory, as well as most of the points that had displeased people in Saint Augustine’s doctrine, were left untouched.

Similarly, at the end of his letter, after establishing the Catholic faith concerning the truth of original sin and the necessity and primacy of grace, Celestine professes that the remaining questions about which people had harassed Saint Augustine were neither neglected nor decided by him, but were left to the free disputation of teachers, within the limits prescribed by Christian charity and modesty. [Col. 0787C]

I would judge this to pertain to the question of absolute election to glory, whether before or after foreseen merits produced through grace. Since Saint Augustine had many serious opponents on this point, and since the earlier Fathers had not clearly handed down anything in this matter as something to be held as a matter of faith, while on the other hand a certain fatal necessity, under the name of election and predestination to glory wholly antecedent to human consent, seemed likely to be introduced to the fearful, the pontiffs thought it better not to enter into unnecessary questions. They were content to transmit what could not be denied without violating the faith; with respect to the unnecessary questions, they enjoined modesty and prohibited the disparagement of Saint Augustine, which dishonored the merits of so great a man and the labors he had expended for the Church.

Moreover, Saint Prosper, although the most steadfast defender of Augustine’s positions, nevertheless, in his *Letter to Augustine*, after reporting the Semipelagian complaints concerning various elements of the doctrine handed down by Saint Augustine, and after showing that the extreme boundary of their contrary position was the subjection of grace to the bare human will, seems to reject only this as imbued with Pelagian poison, leaving the rest untouched [Col. 0787D]:

> If the beginning of salvation is wrongly placed in the human being; if the human will is impiously preferred to the divine will, so that a person is helped because he willed, rather than wills because he is helped; if one who is evil by origin is wrongly believed to begin the reception of good not from the supreme Good but from himself; if God is pleased for any reason other than that which he himself has given.

It is clear that these statements concern only the primacy and necessity of grace.

### 20

I do not see how some people, leaning against a tilting wall and a displaced ruin, have detected in the Semipelagians, so long afterward, several errors openly opposed to the faith that the pontiffs, councils, and Fathers of those times did not perceive.

For [Col. 0788A] they attribute to the Semipelagians the removal of the internal aids of grace and of the true assistance of the Spirit. They also claim that the Semipelagians said that a human being is immediately raised to sanctifying grace by the powers of nature, with no free deliberations intervening. Others add that they denied sanctifying grace and divine cooperation in free actions. By what right all these things are attributed to the Semipelagians, I certainly do not see.

As for sanctifying grace, not even Pelagius openly abolished it, as seems clear from the fact that the councils and Fathers who opposed Pelagius are wholly silent about habitual grace. The exaggerations of the powers of nature that Pelagius inserted in his *Letter to Demetrias* and in the surviving commentaries on Paul, as well as the alleged injury to freedom by grace that he proposed—as appears from Saint Augustine, *Against Julian*, book IV, chapter 8, and from *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book II, chapter 5—concerned only actual grace, not habitual grace.

How much more, then, must the Semipelagians, who were both learned and upright men, be judged not to have abolished sanctifying grace? [Col. 0788B]

As for internal actual grace, distinct from revelation and from the external proposal of the object, it is certain that Pelagius denied it, first absolutely and simply, and afterward as necessary. He maintained that it was, at most, useful and helped one to perform more easily what could absolutely be accomplished by the bare powers of nature. Saint Augustine recalls this in *Letter* 106, explains it clearly in *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, chapter 14, and it is found in Pelagius himself, in his *Letter to Demetrias*.

Unless, as Augustine sufficiently suggests in the same *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, chapter 31, Pelagius, following the custom of heretics, deceitfully admitted, when circumstances demanded it, what he otherwise denied. Bellarmine confirms at length in *Recognitions*, chapter 13 of the first book of *On Grace and Free Will* that the Pelagians, being less concerned about their teacher’s later position, denied internal awakening grace. Saint Augustine explicitly states this in *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book I, chapter 19 [Col. 0788C], and in the second response against Julian, book I, chapter 93, where he reports that they called internal grace “necessity.”

Thus Pelagius and the Pelagians held this view concerning the internal aids of grace, whatever verbal coloring they used to conceal the heresy. The Semipelagians did not. For this reason Saint Augustine, in *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 1, praises them because, admitting grace in the simple sense, and therefore internal grace, they departed from Pelagius.

Why, then, should we attribute the opposite to them and classify them, not as Semipelagians, but as pure Pelagians with respect to the matter of grace?

I say the same regarding the denial attributed to them of divine cooperation with us in free acts. Although there is a question whether Pelagius excluded divine cooperation with secondary causes, specifically with free will—and although not a few authors present the affirmative position while most present the negative, as may be seen in Salas, *1, 2*, treatise 5, disputation 3, number 9, and in the other authors whom I cited in *Natural Theology*, disputation 8, number 338—nevertheless, nowhere in the ancient writers is it read that the Semipelagians opposed divine cooperation.

Nor, in truth, was such a position relevant to their case, as is clear from what has been said. [Col. 0788D]

### 21

I say nothing about the foolishness that some recent writers condemn in the Semipelagians: namely, that they admitted purely natural acts concerning those material objects with which supernatural acts are distinguished. For example, that they admitted that there could be a natural assent to objects to which the intellect, strengthened by supernatural faith, gives assent, and a natural love proportionate in its own order to theological charity, yet without any ordering toward grace and justification.

To turn this into a fault of the Semipelagians and fasten it upon them is foolish. Nor is it permissible to insult the very grave ancient and modern theologians who held this view.

Enough has now been said about the error of the Semipelagians: if one considers the complexity of the matter among most writers and the fruitfulness of the argument, it has been said in very few words; if one considers our purpose here, it has been said at considerable length. Let us now consider whether this same error is rightly charged against Valerian, by revisiting and examining the passages that we saw above had caused offense.

## CHAPTER V  
### It is directly demonstrated that Valerian was wholly alien to the Semipelagianism just described

[Col. 0789A]

### 1

I shall show by two methods [52] that Valerian was wholly alien to the proposed error. First, directly: by showing how devoted he was to asserting divine grace and how he always assigned primacy to it. Second, indirectly: by suitably explaining and adapting those passages that seemed to savor of Semipelagianism, so that they accord with Catholic doctrine.

Various passages plainly express a Catholic affirmation of divine grace in Valerian. Thus he speaks in *Homily* 3, at the end:

> This is the principle of our service: always to recall the benefits of our Christ; and whatever progress you have made through the labor of religious faith, to assign to the author of your freedom.

And in *Homily* 7, at the beginning:

> The very things that faith works in us, although they advance through human labor, must be referred to the Lord, through whom and in whom whatever has been rightly done subsists, and is preserved for future usefulness. Therefore no wise person should reckon the benefits of God as attributable to his own virtues, lest he hear that sentence of the Apostle: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?”

From this passage of the Apostle, Venantius Fortunatus, in his exposition of the Lord’s Prayer concerning the third petition, argues in a notable digression against the Semipelagians that their error is plainly and explicitly overturned. Thus whoever humbly confesses this with the Apostle—whom Fortunatus aptly calls the eye of the Church—thereby confesses that good will and the beginning of salvation also come from God. This is just as the first lighting of a lamp comes from within. By that example he admirably shows that the human being is preceded by God, imitating Augustine, *Tractate* 23 on John.

Valerian therefore held the same view when he applied that passage to the same purpose. Immediately afterward, having listed various supernatural good works, he adds:

> But all these things are brought about in us by one and the same power of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, which grants perfection to righteous labors and supplies to the good will whatever things are best.

He plainly alludes to the Apostle’s words, which one might rightly call a brief summary of the entire doctrine of grace:

> Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights.

### 2

This is expressed most splendidly in *Homily* 11, almost throughout. Specifically, at the very beginning of the homily, in these words:

> He wholly exceeds every measure of sacrilegious superstition who subtracts from God his share in righteous labors, although from him we have received the spirit of wisdom, which governs the whole human being and kindles the minds of mortals for every good work. Therefore all the honors of our labors must be referred to God, lest he withdraw the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

And shortly afterward, after bringing forward several testimonies from Scripture:

> You see, therefore, that our good things must be ascribed to the Divinity, while our evils must be attributed to human conduct, because just as good things are created with God as their provider, so evils arise with the devil as their author.

The claim that a share in righteous labor, and in labor that advances toward righteousness, must not be taken away from God; that we receive from God the spirit of wisdom, as it were the first breath of supernatural life; that God kindles our minds for every good work; and that everything of this kind is created with God as its provider, and therefore must all be ascribed to him—how far this is from Semipelagianism, according to which the human being is established as the first root of a good work and its production is attributed to him!

In particular, what he says—namely, that good things are created in us with God as their provider, while evil things arise with the devil as their author—contains an extremely effective argument for our position. It is drawn from the fact that, just as a fetus cannot give itself its own first existence but necessarily presupposes a father, so the spiritual fetus—that hidden human being of the heart which is formed in us—although it can contribute something to its own increase and preservation, nevertheless necessarily proceeds from elsewhere with respect to its first beginning: namely, from God, who voluntarily begets us through the word of truth, so that we may be a kind of first fruits of his creation. [Col. 0790A]

That Valerian spoke in this very sense, wholly cutting off Semipelagianism, is clear from these other words of the same homily:

> Let each person inquire into the beginnings of his life and seek the author of the human race: who formed the body, who arranged the limbs, who caused earthly matter to become fruitful for human use? Did not the Lord establish all these things through his wisdom? Since, therefore, what we are is not ours, how is what we have ours? It is a form of folly that, when you owe the benefit of life to another, you ascribe the adornments of virtues to yourself.

Here is an entirely explicit overthrow of Semipelagianism, founded upon the argument I mentioned, and also employed by Saint Augustine in his commentary on Psalm 144, on the words, “And they shall exult in your righteousness.”

Nor should I leave unexamined the force of the word by which Valerian said that, just as evils arise in us with the devil as their author, so good things are created with God as their provider. Whether we take the word “create” in its precise and strict sense or in a looser sense, something relevant to this matter will be available.

The strict interpretation, in which the word “create” signifies production from nothing [Col. 0790B], directly attacks Semipelagianism and every beginning of salvation derived from the powers of nature. For this reason Saint Augustine often uses, to confirm Catholic truth on this point, the words of the Psalm: “You will save them for nothing.” He does so clearly in his commentary on Psalm 55, and likewise uses the Apostle’s words: “We are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works,” together with similar passages that he presses into service for this purpose in *On Grace and Free Will*, chapter 8.

In the same sense, Saint Basil, in his commentary on Psalm 32, treating the words, “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created,” brings forward various Scriptures in which creation, because it is production from nothing, signifies that our spiritual begetting took place without any beginning from us. He adds that the verse of the Psalm may be understood, in its first part, of natural formation, by which the world was made when God spoke; but in its second part it may be understood of generation in Christ, which is a moral creation, with every moral influence of the subject excluded with respect to the first assisting grace.

Similarly, Anastasius of Sinai, in book VII of the *Hexaemeron*, at the beginning, says [Col. 0790C] that in the second chapter of Genesis the account of the creation of things is repeated. This might seem superfluous unless it had been instituted anew to signify a second and far more sublime creation, which is in Christ and through Christ.

Finally, this must have been what those ancient scholastics intended who, either in book I, distinction 26, or in book IV, distinction 1, held that grace is produced in us through creation. For, speaking in strict physical terms, this is improbable if the subject is habitual grace: it is very unnatural for an accident to be produced without a subject, and therefore from physical nothingness. It is even more improbable when the subject is actual grace, which perhaps cannot be produced in this way by any power.

The meaning of those scholastics must therefore be the one Saint Thomas clearly expressed in *Summa Theologiae* I–II, question 110, article 2, reply to objection 2: namely, that sanctifying grace is created morally, because, considered with respect to its first root, it comes from the mere liberality of God who precedes us. The same must be said of actual grace.

Thus this first sense of our creation through the Spirit sent forth by God, and accomplished with God as its provider, plainly overturns Semipelagianism. [Col. 0790D]

### 3

If, however, the word “create” is taken somewhat more broadly [53], so that good things are said to be created with God as their provider, while evil things arise with the devil as their author, because those who act well supernaturally are born not from blood, nor from the will of the flesh, nor from the will of man, but from God—as from a father who makes fruitful and imposes the first beginning of the entire begetting—then Semipelagianism likewise collapses through these words.

For this purpose it is useful to cite the exceedingly elegant doctrine with which William of Paris, in *On the Sacrament of Marriage*, chapter 5, constructs the marriage of the human soul with God for conceiving and giving birth to the offspring of good works, together with the entire array that accompanies such a marriage, by analogy with human marriages.

This doctrine belongs to Richard of Saint Victor in his commentary on Psalm 28 [Col. 0791A], on the words, “Beloved, like the son of unicorns,” and to Bernard, *On the Interior House*, chapter 68, who plainly developed his account from Richard.

These teachers observe that, although we can be fathers of Christ by cooperating in another person’s salvation and begetting him in another’s heart, nevertheless each of us in whom Christ is formed and generated does not stand toward the Christ thus begotten as a father, but only as a mother who conceives from another’s seed.

For this reason they consider the unqualified curse in Scripture upon the barren woman and the woman who does not give birth, while Scripture does not similarly say, “Cursed is the man who does not beget.” For it is not equally within our power to be preceded by a holy thought through which truth is perceived, as it is within our power to adhere to truth once understood and inwardly tasted, with the Lord giving sweetness.

That precedence, which confers the first beginning of salvation, is entirely from God. Therefore he is rightly said to have the role of Father in this spiritual birth—contrary to the Semipelagians, who arrogated to themselves the beginning of that birth without the grace of birth.

It is therefore clear how far Valerian was from them.

Also below, in the same Homily 11, after citing the beginning [Col. 0791B] of Psalm 126, “Unless the Lord builds,” etc., he says:

> You see, therefore, that neither can what is good be built without the Lord, nor can what has been built be preserved without the Lord. The building of this divine house is the building of our life, which must be fortified by the aid of the divine majesty. Our Christ must therefore always be asked to nourish what is good in us, and entreated to preserve what has been nourished, and so to dispose the hearts of our understanding that we may attribute everything good to the glory of the heavenly Power.

I understand the building of the divine house—that is, the beginning and commencement of justification—to be attributed to God no less than the preservation of that same house once built. For from the fact that it is God’s work to build our inner house, it follows that the beginning of justification too must be derived from grace. This is taught admirably by Nazianzen in Oration 31, section 8; and by Nazianzen’s hearer, St. Jerome, in his commentary on Jeremiah 18. Likewise by John, bishop of Jerusalem, cited and commended by St. Augustine in *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, chapter 14, and also by Prosper in the *Genoese Extracts*, doubtful passage 8.

[Col. 0791C]

I further observe that the aids of prevenient divine grace are expressed in the very words of Valerian by which they are designated in the Church’s prayer for the sixth Sunday after Pentecost, in which God is asked to nourish what exists and, in the zeal of piety, to preserve what has been nourished. Moreover, in the same passage Valerian attributes not some but plainly all Christian goods—including the beginning of justification—to God, the author of grace, and urges that God be asked to dispose the hearts of our understanding so that we may acknowledge this and demonstrate it in action. All of this is utterly foreign to the remnants of Pelagianism.

For from such a statement one may draw the inference of St. Augustine, which he makes in *Retractions* I, chapter 9. Considering what he had said in Book III of *On Free Choice*, namely, that all good things are from God, he concludes:

> Since all good things are from God, it follows that the good use of free choice, which is a virtue and is counted among the great goods, is also from God.

### 4.

[Col. 0791D]

Below too, Valerian, drawing from those passages of Scripture, “There is no one who does good,” and “No one is good except God alone,” reaches a conclusion parallel to the argument which Prosper constructs from the same passages in chapter 20 of *Against the Collations*, to prove that the beginning of our salvation is from God. He concludes in this way:

> Therefore you see that, whenever we appear to be good, we are carrying out the goodness of God.

He adds that, when we do good with reference to salvation, God dwells in us as in a temple, and consequently works in us that very good which, although it is ours, is nevertheless called by Valerian “the good of God,” because it depends radically and principally upon God. He uses the same sense that St. Gregory expressed admirably in *Morals* XXXIII, chapters 25 and 26, while treating the words, “Who has given to me, that I may repay him?” and in Homily 9 on Ezekiel, at the words, “The spirit entered into me after he had spoken to me, and set me upon my feet.”

I offer part of that most illustrious passage, as a ray by which Valerian’s true and Catholic teaching here may be illuminated:

> It must be known that our evils alone are ours, whereas our goods belong both to us and [Col. 0792A] to almighty God. For by inspiring us, he goes before us so that we may will; and by helping us, he follows after us, so that we may not will in vain but may be able to fulfill what we will. Thus, when grace goes before and good will follows, what is the gift of almighty God becomes our merit.
>
