> Paul explains this well in a brief sentence when he says: “I labored more than all of them.” But, lest he seem to have attributed what he had done to his own virtue, he added: “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me.” Because he had been preceded by a heavenly gift, he acknowledged himself as foreign to his good work, saying, “not I.” But because prevenient grace had made free choice good in him, and because in action he followed that same grace with free choice, he added, “but the grace of God with me.” It is as though he were saying: “I labored in the good work—not I, but I also.” Insofar as I was preceded by the Lord’s gift alone, it was “not I.” But insofar as I followed the gift by my will, it was “I also.”

[Col. 0792B]

Here St. Gregory gathers and proves prevenient grace and the beginning of salvation from God from the fact that our good work is called the good of God, and that we are said to perform a good foreign to ourselves—precisely the manner of speaking that, as you have seen, Valerian also uses. These seem to me adequate arguments for attributing even the first good movement of any will to the help of grace in the matter of salvation.

### 5.

Finally, at the end of the same Homily 11, he has these words:

> Therefore, “the one who boasts, let him boast in the Lord.” It must therefore be our utmost concern, beloved, that pure faith commend our life so to the Lord that human presumption claim nothing for itself or attribute anything to its own labors. He has entirely lost what he labored for who has attributed the fruit of holiness to his own virtues.

This plainly corresponds to the saying of St. Cyprian that one must boast in nothing, since nothing is ours. On the basis of this testimony, St. Augustine confesses in *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 3, and *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 14, that he was led to retract his earlier opinion concerning the beginning of salvation.

[Col. 0792C]

How, then, could Valerian, speaking in the same manner, arrogate the beginning of salvation to man? Indeed, when he denies that it is lawful for human presumption to claim anything for itself from its own labors, 54 this seems directed against the error of the Semi-Pelagians, who added grace to human labor and attributed grace to that labor by which the will, through asking, knocking, and seeking, calls upon God. Thus one may suspect that this entire homily, in which Valerian expressly rejects those who exclude God, the author of grace, from any partnership in their own labor in good works, is directed not only against Pelagius, who denied grace absolutely, but also—and indeed much more strongly—against the Semi-Pelagians, whose embers still smoked after Pelagius’s ashes.

### 6.

[Col. 0792C]

Finally, it is utterly foreign to the sense and manner of speaking of the Semi-Pelagians that which appears in Homily 16:

> Therefore all hope of obtaining victory consists in faith and will. For if the will follows faith, faith never abandons the will.

The very flower—or rather the dregs—of the Semi-Pelagian error is the following and subordination of faith to good will. Valerian, however, expressly subordinates good will to faith, so that even the first will to believe does not arise from the bare power of the will but follows the divine seed of faith, [Col. 0792D] or grace preceding the will. This is Catholic doctrine against the Semi-Pelagians.

For this reason St. Peter Chrysologus, rebuking them in Sermon 135, after praising St. Lawrence’s steadfastness in the burning alive, admonishes his hearers that, while admiring St. Lawrence’s faith and endurance, they should admire the gift of God. Such faith and such strength of spirit amid such torments had been God’s gift. He concludes:

> Therefore let us praise the merits of the martyrs as gifts of God; let us love them, let us pray, let us bring forward our will. For the will follows; it does not go before. Yet charity is not absent if the will is not absent. For that ardent will itself is called charity.

[Col. 0792D]

## CHAPTER VI. The passages in which Valerian seemed earlier to suggest Semi-Pelagianism are shown to be Catholic

### 1.

I proceed to Valerian’s indirect vindication, [Col. 0793A] which consists in explaining the passages proposed above. I shall treat each individually, in the order in which they were cited; this is also the order and sequence of the homilies whose disease or ulcer was suspected.

One point must nevertheless be stated in advance—not only for Valerian’s vindication, but also because it is worth observing for the protection of many of the Fathers. Namely, if the Fathers sometimes omit mentioning the aid of grace in a work requiring such aid, it does not immediately follow that they excluded it, since it is often understood and it is not always necessary to express everything. The most serious Fathers have observed that the Holy Spirit preserved this practice even in Scripture itself.

Thus St. Basil, in his commentary on Isaiah 6, treating the words, “Behold, I send”; and St. Ambrose, in the preface to Luke, considering the words, “It seemed good also to me,” observe that even if the evangelist did not mention the Spirit speaking within him, he did not therefore deny it. Similarly, if a Christian speaks in the same way about a work pertaining to salvation and remains silent concerning divine cooperation, he does not thereby deny that cooperation. St. Augustine transcribed this passage of St. Ambrose in *On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 46, and *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 19.

[Col. 0793B]

St. Anselm teaches the same point especially clearly in the second part of the *Concord*, chapter 15, among other things:

> When Sacred Scripture says something on behalf of grace, it does not remove free choice altogether; nor, when it speaks on behalf of free choice, does it exclude grace—as though grace alone or free choice alone were sufficient to save a human being, and so forth. Divine statements must be understood in such a way that, except for what I said concerning infants, neither grace alone nor free choice alone accomplishes human salvation.

He illustrates this with several passages of Scripture and then offers an excellent comparison:

> Therefore, just as natural intercourse does not produce offspring without a father, nor except through a mother, yet no understanding removes either the father or the mother from the generation of the child, so grace and free choice do not conflict but cooperate in justifying and saving a human being.

Most aptly so. What could be more familiar than simply saying, “This [Col. 0793C] man is the son of that woman,” while the father is unmentioned but not thereby excluded? Similarly, although our will conceives from the Spirit of God, and cannot bring forth the child of salvation unless it has been made fruitful by heavenly seed and impregnated by the conception of divine illumination—as St. Fulgentius puts it at the beginning of his second book to Trasimund—nevertheless the work of founding that child is often mentioned as belonging to free will alone, without the divine seed by which the will was made fruitful being expressed, though it is not denied. Without that seed, the will could no more conceive or give birth to the offspring of salvation than a woman could naturally become a mother without the action of a man.

Accordingly, those who mention the will alone merely express what this cause contributes, according to its own kind and order, to the effect it shares with grace; they do not deny the cooperation of grace, even though they do not express it. As I said, we see this practice preserved in Scripture itself.

It is also entirely reasonable to understand similar statements of the Fathers in the same way, especially in longer discussions or when they are addressing the people. For the careful and anxious expression of both cooperating [Col. 0793D] causes would either produce nausea and weariness or cause offense by suggesting an ingrained distrust of the understanding or security of the hearer or reader. Thus St. Augustine himself softens, in *Retractions* I, chapter 9, certain statements in Book III of *On Free Choice* that appear somewhat harsh concerning the powers of human freedom. He shows that grace was then silent but not excluded.

Faustus of Riez commends this rule—as he calls it—after citing Augustine, in Book I of *On Grace*, chapter 6:

> Among the regenerate, when grace without labor, or labor without grace, is set forth in Scripture, one is suppressed, not separated. When one is mentioned without the other, the other is kept silent, not denied, according to that rule which Bishop Augustine suggests: “Not everything that is kept silent is denied.”

I am not unaware that the Pelagians insistently employed this very argument. Thus Critobulus, defending Pelagius [Col. 0794A] before Jerome in Book I *Against the Pelagians*, near the beginning, replies to the Catholic Atticus, who objected that he had not mentioned grace and therefore seemed to deny it:

> From the fact that I did not deny it, I should be considered to have said it; for we ought not to think that whatever we do not say, we deny.

And Paul Orosius, in his *Apology for Free Choice*, records these words written against Pelagius himself:

> Although you repeatedly say concerning the grace of God, “I did not deny it for the reason that I did not mention it,” you must be understood to have said it for the reason that you did not deny it—as though Susanna ought to be believed to have confessed adultery merely because she did not deny it when others accused her; or as though the Lord Jesus, because he remained silent, had approved the testimony of false witnesses.

I do not deny that the Pelagians said these things. Nevertheless, the rule proposed does not therefore totter, since not everything heretics say must immediately be opposed. What they say may—as is certainly the case here—not be a product of their own doctrine but something borrowed from the Church and approved teachers. Therefore, when the Fathers establish this as a kind of canon, it must rightly be accepted as valid.

[Col. 0794B]

Moreover, as St. Augustine also observed in *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 14, the Fathers, being intent upon the subject they are treating, are generally not so concerned to express and distinctly and explicitly set forth everything which faith certifies to be involved in a matter. Speaking with confidence, they carry on their discussion. Thus they generally presuppose the aids of grace immediately and incidentally, or touch upon them rather than treat them, without thereby denying them or rejecting God’s prevenience of our will. Instead, they press what belongs to our task and lies within our power.

### 2.

What I have stated generally concerning the Fathers’ manner of writing and speaking in this matter could apply entirely to Valerian. [Col. 0794C] We therefore need not deal with him too rigidly or harshly if, among the two causes involved in the matter of our salvation, he sometimes mentions only one and does not express the other, since he does not thereby deny it.

With this precaution established—which can equally assist us in dealing with many statements of the Fathers on other subjects, such as the suppression of mention of one of the divine Persons in a work common to all three, as Paschal the Deacon uses it at the end of Book II *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 4—we may proceed to examine individually the passages in Valerian proposed above as suspect.

[Col. 0794D]

The first homily was fastened upon and condemned on the ground that its very first words had been taken from Pelagius, who, it was said, had “often complained in this manner of speaking.” I cannot help suspecting a remarkable degree of cleverness in sniffing out Pelagius’s tracks.

The beginning of that first homily reads:

> Many who oppose sound doctrine blame justice and judge discipline to be a form of tyranny; they assign reasonable correction to pride, although there is tyranny only where something unjust is commanded, and pride only where discipline is neglected.

A lengthy encomium of discipline immediately follows. What Pelagian ferment is perceptible here? Or what, at least in appearance, does this principle have in common with Pelagian impiety?

Augustine gives a catalogue of Pelagius’s errors in *Heresy* 88 and in *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, chapters 11, 14, and 35. What affinity is there between those errors and this commendation of regular discipline? The author is speaking of discipline while addressing monks, as is sufficiently clear from his warning that the reputation of conversion is useless when one has professed religion unless zeal for discipline is added.

Are we therefore to accuse St. Cyprian, at the beginning of his book *On the Discipline and Conduct of Virgins*; Chrysostom, in his homily *On the Training of Discipline*; Hugh of St. Victor, in Book I of *The Formation of Novices*, from chapter 10 onward; St. Bonaventure, in *The Mirror of Discipline for Novices*; Lawrence Justinian, in his book *On Monastic Discipline*; and others who celebrate discipline no less than Valerian does, and who complain that its serious yoke is regarded as burdensome by the disorderly, of Pelagian soot on this account?

How truly the accuser adds that Pelagius often complained in this manner will be understood by anyone who observes that, apart from the pamphlets preserved by Augustine, the only writings of Pelagius that remain [Col. 0795A] are the letter to Demetrias, wrongly attributed by some—since the time of Bede—to St. Jerome, and attributed by Bede in Book I of his commentary on the *Song of Songs* to Julian of Eclanum, the bishop who opposed Augustine; the brief commentaries on Paul, also attributed to Jerome but expressly ascribed to Pelagius by St. Augustine in *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, chapter 16, and in Book III of *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, chapters 1 and 11; and finally the second creed, found in volume IX of Jerome, which begins, “We believe in God the Father,” and concludes with the words, “he proved him to be a heretic.” St. Augustine shows in *On the Grace of Christ*, chapters 32 and 33, and *On Original Sin*, chapters 1 and 21, that Pelagius sent this profession of faith to Innocent.

[Col. 0795B]

Nowhere in those works do Pelagius’s complaints appear concerning the neglect or harshness of regular discipline among certain unrestrained persons intolerant of its yoke. And even if those complaints were found somewhere in Pelagius, it would matter very little, since not everything said by heretics ought to be cut away—unless we want nearly all the doctrines of the faith cut off with the same blade, as Cardinal Deacon Rusticus properly warned in his *Dialogue against the Acephali*.

### 3.

In Homily 2, attention was drawn to the fact that, while speaking about the Christian way, Valerian says that he makes the entrance upon the Christian way easy for those who wish to undertake it. This seemed to suggest a Semi-Pelagian subordination of grace to the effort of the will.

But this is plainly an empty accusation. What is more frequently celebrated among the Fathers and teachers of morals than the saying, “Nothing is difficult for one who wills”? And if we wish to cooperate with the divine grace by which we are preceded, the ascent to virtue, however steep and difficult, will not merely become gentler but will even be overcome with joy. This alone is what Valerian affirms.

With equal clarity, and without any charge or suspicion of error, the same thing was taught by Clement of Alexandria in Book II of the *Stromata*, chapter 7; by St. Augustine in Book I of *On Free Choice*, chapter 13; and by St. Chrysostom in various places, to pass over others for the moment.

Clement, discussing adoption as children of God, says:

> Willing, therefore, precedes everything. For rational [Col. 0795C] faculties are ministers of that which consists in willing. “Will,” he says, “and you will be able.”

St. Maximus conveyed the same teaching in precise words in *On the Scope of the Incarnation*. Eucherius expressed this very sweetly in his *Exhortation to Valerian*, section 7:

> If some distinguished and wealthy person were inviting you to be adopted as a child in his place, you would go through every difficulty and hurry toward him by every distant road, carried across the long journey. God, the Lord of the universe and of all things, calls you to adoption; if you wish, he will bestow upon you the cherished name of son, by which he names our one God his own. Yet are you not inflamed? Are you not driven to hasten, lest sudden death snatch away so great an opportunity before you can reach it?
>
> To obtain this adoption, however, you will cross neither impassable deserts nor the uncertain expanses of a distant sea. Whenever you wish, this adoption is with you.

Laurence of Novara likewise explains the point clearly in his homily *On Penance*:

> Man, 56 do not delay. The matter is at hand; life is in your power; victory lies within your choice. If you have willed it, you have conquered; if you refuse to will it, you will be left defeated. Whoever wishes [Col. 0795D] to conquer strives so as to conquer; whoever despairs has lost the victory.

Thus he plainly states that it lies in each person’s power to conquer sins, and that this victory brings holiness. Yet no one on that account marked Laurence or accused him of Semi-Pelagianism because he suppressed mention of prevenient divine grace.

St. Augustine, in the passage cited, concludes his lengthy discussion of the power of the will for Christian living with these words:

> It follows that whoever wishes to live honestly and rightly, if he wishes to will this rather than passing goods, may attain so great a thing with such ease that having what he willed consists for him in nothing other than willing it.

When reviewing this passage in *Retractions* I, chapter 9, Augustine acknowledges that it is Catholic and completely sound, although it mentions only the action of the will, while grace is left unmentioned but not excluded, since it was irrelevant to the purpose of that passage. Moreover, since the Pelagians had not yet arisen, it did not then seem necessary to speak more carefully and anxiously.

Similarly, in Sermon 31 [Col. 0796A] of the forty new sermons, after exhorting his hearers to hold fast to justice and freedom from the second death, he adds:

> If you do not wish it, it will not be; but that by which you redeem yourself from this death will be yours if you wish it. The will obtains justice from the Lord and drinks it as from its own fountain, and no one is forbidden to approach that fountain if he approaches worthily.

A little later he says:

> The blood of your Lord, if you wish it, was given also for you; if you refuse to will it, it was not given for you.

And again shortly afterward:

> The blood of Christ is salvation for one who wills it, punishment for one who does not.

Finally, in his commentary on Psalm 102, at the words, “He heals all your diseases,” after saying much about God the physician and the healing of souls, he adds:

> Will he heal you? You must wish to be healed. He certainly heals every sick person, but he does not heal one who is unwilling. What could be more blessed for you than to have your health in your will, just as you have life, as it were, in your hand? If you wished to hold some high office on earth—to desire a military command, a proconsulate, or a prefecture—could you immediately possess what you wished? Would power follow your will?

[Col. 0796B]

No one has ever accused these and many similar statements, frequent in Augustine, of error or of affinity with the soot of Semi-Pelagianism.

St. Chrysostom speaks in nearly the same manner in Homily 5 on the First Epistle to the Thessalonians, at the very end, insisting that to become good and acquire Christian virtues it is enough to wish it, in accordance with the passage of Isaiah that he cites: “If you are willing and hear me.”

Elsewhere he is also often concerned with this point; but he speaks most explicitly in Homily 18 on the Epistle to the Romans, shortly before the moral section. After presenting the salvation of the remnant through the election of grace, whose role in human salvation he says is the greater part, he raises the objection:

> Why, then, are not all saved, if salvation is from grace?

He answers:

> Because you were unwilling. For although grace is freely given, it saves only those who are willing, not those who are unwilling—those who immediately turn away and resist. As he says at the beginning of Homily 19, grace is indeed the greater part, but it is not the whole.

A long and beautiful passage on this subject may be read in Theodore the Studite’s *Catechesis* 43, near the end.

[Col. 0796C]

### 4.

Therefore it is entirely right and Catholic to say that the way of salvation lies open to those who are willing and is easy for them. The aid of grace, which strengthens the will, is not excluded; rather, it is equally understood, as in that statement of St. Ambrose near the end of *On Widows*:

> Each person’s will is the author of his prosperity. From the will wisdom is born.

He is plainly speaking of supernatural wisdom.

The same is true of those other statements:

> One’s own will is the cause of each person’s salvation.
>
> Good will brings God down to us and directs us toward God. Through good will we love God, choose God, run toward God, reach God, and possess him. Through it we are remade in the likeness of God and made like him.

All these statements are found in the *Manual* circulated under the name of St. Augustine, chapter 23. Very similar statements are found in St. Bernard’s *On the Interior House*, chapter 8.

Nazianzen speaks no less similarly, and even more boldly because of the added exclusive particle, though with a similar implicit qualification, in Oration 40:

> Go and buy, and [Col. 0796D] drink wine without paying a price? O immense swiftness of goodness! O easy means of acquisition! This good is offered for sale to you for the will alone; God regards the desire itself as the price of great value. He thirsts to be thirsted for.

The exclusive particle must be understood as applying only to what is to be contributed on the part of the will.

Finally, the words of St. Justin in his *Apology to Antoninus* must be understood in the same way. He recalls Isaiah’s passage on the justification of the sinner and the second birth, which he had already cited: “If you are willing and hear me.” Contrasting this second birth with the birth that takes place through the baptism of an adult, he says that the apostles taught that the first birth of man was a work of necessity, since it took place without a person’s knowledge or will. God nevertheless provided that we should not remain children of necessity and ignorance, as we were by our first birth, but should become children of will and knowledge, [Col. 0797A] obtaining forgiveness of sins and being reborn in holiness by our own will.

Here it is certain that birth is expressed as arising from the choice of free will, by which a person is formed and born anew willingly and knowingly; yet divine grace, both preceding and advancing the will, is not excluded.

The same intention unquestionably belonged to Gregory of Nyssa in Homily 6 on Ecclesiastes, at the words, “A time to give birth and a time to die”:

> In a certain sense we ourselves are our own fathers, whenever, through a good disposition of soul and free choice, we have formed, begotten, and brought ourselves into the light. We do this by admitting God into ourselves and becoming children of God, children of virtue, and children of the Most High.

The same author explains birth by grace excellently in *The Life of Moses*:

> Human life is always subject to change. Since it is not eternal and immovable, it must therefore always be born. This birth does not occur through another’s desire, nor externally, as in bodily birth, but each person is born through his own choice. Hence it comes about that we ourselves are our own fathers, giving birth to ourselves according to whatever we wish to become by our choice, and shaping ourselves as male or [Col. 0797B] female according to vice or virtue.

He could not have presented the intervention of good will in the matter of our salvation more magnificently. His statement could therefore rightly seem more rugged than Valerian’s statement that the way of salvation lies open to those who are willing.

Nevertheless, Nyssa has not been burdened with the charge that he denied gratuitous prevenient grace, and rightly so. To pass over his other passages, he asserts prevenient grace most explicitly in his *Catechetical Oration*, chapter 30. And when, in chapter 39 of the same work, he carefully teaches what I have drawn from the other passages cited—namely, that a human being is begotten of God by the choice of his free will and becomes a child of the Most High—it seems clear that these two statements do not conflict: that the second birth comes to those who are willing, and that what the will wishes to obtain comes from God who calls and prepares it. 57

Some Fathers, considering this, said in chapter 5, section 3, that no one in spiritual birth is his own father but only his own mother, because the mother is made fruitful solely through another’s prior action.

[Col. 0797C]

### 5.

In the third homily, the first suspect passage was the one in which it was asserted that a Christian is required to offer voluntary service. But we are wrongly troubled by fear where there was no fear.

Either the word “voluntary” is suspect in the matter of salvation, or the word “service.” Neither deserves accusation.

[Col. 0797C]

David, who promised that he would sacrifice voluntarily, is not considered suspect of error. Nor is the prince of the apostles accused, although he exhorts Christians to voluntary servitude. St. Ambrose is not accused either. In Book I of *On Jacob*, chapter 3, while commending our zeal and saying that everything depends upon it, so that it either brings guilt or grace, he adds:

> Why do we transfer this to others? Christ chooses for himself a voluntary soldier; the devil buys a voluntary servant for himself.

Nor is St. Paulinus accused, whose words in Letter 2 to Severus are:

> What grace is there for us if we are faithful only in what belongs to another, unless we serve from what is our own—that is, from the free choice of our will—loving God with all our heart and with all the powers of our soul? The prophet challenges us to this disposition when he says, “I will sacrifice to you voluntarily.” For this is acceptable and pleasing before God: that our good be voluntary.

The very nature of service requires that all our obedience offered to God be voluntary, even though divine prevenience is required for supernatural obedience. Indeed, because that prevenience summons us to voluntary obedience, Isidore of Pelusium, in Book IV, Letter 51, treating the words, “Those who are called according to purpose,” wisely says that the calling is not violent or forced but voluntary and spontaneous. He calls it voluntary from the effect that follows it, or from our own voluntary purpose, to which he applies the Apostle’s words. He was therefore far from denying to human consent and obedience the character of voluntariness.

### 6.

[Col. 0798A]

The word “service” is just as easily vindicated. Although it is not as customary in ecclesiastical books, as St. Augustine says in Letter 19, and although pagans used it to designate the natural nobility of actions honorable within the limits of nature, St. Ambrose teaches in Book I of *The Duties*, chapter 8, that it is not suited only to the philosophical school but may also be used in a Christian sense.

He says that “service” may be derived from *efficere*, “to accomplish,” as though it were *efficium*, with one letter changed for the elegance of speech; or from the fact that those things are done which harm no one and benefit everyone. Whichever derivation and meaning of “service” is accepted, he insists that the term applies equally to Christian and supernatural honorable acts as to natural ones.

For this reason the same holy Father, in Book IV of his Commentary on Luke, at the words of chapter 4, “None of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian,” confidently uses the word “service” while speaking of supernatural obedience:

> Clearly this saving discourse of the Lord instructs us and urges us to the zeal of venerating the Godhead. No one is shown to have been healed, and no one afflicted with bodily disease is shown to have been freed from it, except the one who devoted himself to healing through religious service. For divine benefits are not bestowed upon those who sleep, but upon those who keep watch.

[Col. 0798B]

Nor, merely because Cassian and Faustus used the expression “voluntary service,” should it immediately be condemned as rejected and pregnant with Semi-Pelagianism. Not everything heretics say is fabricated or to be rejected, says St. Cyril in Letter 30, with Origen in Homily 9 on Numbers and Jerome in Letters 75 and 152 agreeing.

### 7.

The slander constructed around the other passage of the same homily is dispelled no less easily.

[Col. 0798C]

Valerian says that, when the merits of others’ virtues are being commended, care must be taken that the services of voluntary servitude make room for grace in us. This does not mean what it was twisted to mean.

His meaning is this: when the crown of martyrdom, which he was discussing, is not always at hand—and it certainly was not at the time when Valerian delivered these homilies, during the Church’s then profound peace—we must strive so that voluntary servitude may supply what externally inflicted punishment, patiently endured, could have accomplished if it had been imposed. In this way, access to the grace of God may be opened.

This is equivalent to saying that we must strive, through good works, to make an addition to sanctifying grace already possessed, in accordance with St. Ambrose’s words in Sermon 14 on Psalm 118:

> Christ filled the voluntary instrument with a more abundant grace of his Spirit.

Or it may mean that, through good works conceived from the inspiration of the Holy Spirit—namely, perfect contrition and the most ardent love—we call forth God’s sanctifying grace after the sin by which the soul had perhaps previously been stained has been driven away.

### 8.

[Col. 0798D]

In Homily 7, attention was drawn to the passage in which divine power is said to grant perfection to the labors of the just and to supply the good will with whatever things are best.

So far from deserving censure, this was spoken by Valerian in a highly pious and Catholic manner. His purpose in that passage, as the immediately preceding words show, is to humble human pride and to acknowledge God’s beneficence toward us, since every perfect gift and every excellent endowment is from God, according to the Apostle’s statement to which Valerian plainly alludes.

Accordingly, when he says that perfection is granted by God to the labors of the just, he does not mean that a human being merely begins while God completes. He means that the whole perfection and worth of righteous works flows from God, and that the glory of righteous works must be attributed wholly and without reservation to him.

This agrees with St. Macarius, whose striking words are found in Homily 26:

> A person must diligently and deliberately cultivate the soil of his heart and labor. For God requires labor, weariness, and action from a human being. But unless heavenly clouds and rains of grace appear from above, the farmer’s labor will be of no benefit.
>
> This is the mark of Christian worship: no matter how much someone labors or how many acts of righteousness he performs, he should conduct himself as though he had accomplished nothing, attributing everything rightly and well done through us to grace.

St. Leo speaks similarly in Sermon 2 on the Epiphany, chapter 3:

> Let us bring forth from our hearts what is worthy of God. For although he himself is the giver of all good things, he nevertheless seeks the fruit of our labor as well. The kingdom of heaven does not come to those who sleep, but to those who labor and keep watch in God’s commandments, so that, if we do not render his gifts fruitless, through the things he has given we may deserve to receive what he has promised.

He says similar things in Sermon 5 on the Epiphany, chapter 3.

When Valerian likewise says that whatever is best is supplied to good will, this must not be interpreted as the provision of the aids of grace on account of a preceding volition that was naturally good. 58 [Col. 0799A] Such an interpretation would plainly contradict Valerian’s purpose and would not suppress human pride but increase it. Rather, the statement must be understood of the provision of every excellent gift made by God to a will that is needy in itself and would never rise to supernatural things unless it were divinely raised up and preceded by grace.

### 9. From Homily 9

The passage was alleged in which it is said that the Lord deigns to come to meet our petition. But this is a very foolish accusation, one that could equally be brought against Isaiah himself, and even against the Holy Spirit. For Valerian there treats Isaiah’s words: “Then you shall call, and the Lord will answer; you shall cry out, and he will say: Behold, I am here.” From this he infers the ineffable condescension of God, who deigns to come to meet our cry and petition and to show himself ready to help—something which the prophet in that passage, or rather the Holy Spirit through the prophet, openly declares. Valerian could rightly be regarded there as not merely suspect but demonstrably erroneous if he said that this cry was conceived solely by the powers of nature, or if he intended the petition to which the Lord comes to meet as proceeding from the bare force of nature. That would be the error condemned at the Second Council of Orange: that grace is made subordinate to human invocation. But Valerian gives no other indication of this perverse meaning than does the prophet whose words he employed.

Other Fathers plainly agree with him, such as St. Chrysostom in Homily 27 on Genesis. He is treating a similar passage of the same prophet, from chapter 65: “While you are still speaking, I shall say: Behold, I am here.” After exhorting his hearers to rely upon divine grace, and enlarging upon God’s supreme benevolence toward us—which does not, as commonly happens among human beings, first demand services and then lavish its benefits, but first does good and by its prior benefits arouses us to render holy service—he adds that, for the attainment of holiness and the remission of sins, much time is not required. He confirms this by the example of the thief, who did not even need an hour for complete cleansing. So great is God’s mercy toward us. For when he sees that the purpose of our will is firm and that we approach him with ardent desire, he does not delay or defer, but hastens; displaying his customary generosity, he says: “While you are still speaking, I shall say: Behold, I am here.” He confirms this at length by the example of that servant who, when asked to render an account and unable to pay, became a suppliant before his lord, begged forgiveness of an immense debt, and obtained even more than he had asked.

Similar words occur in Ambrose at the end of Sermon 47:

> There are many diabolical waves in this world, many shipwrecks of temptations, from which we can be freed if the Savior extends his hand to us when we cry out. Let us therefore not cease crying to the Lord; he will not deny his customary help.

More harshly, likewise, in book 3 *On Virginity*, he says:

> You have learned where to seek Christ; learn also how you may merit that he should seek you. He stirs up the Holy Spirit, saying: “Rise up, O North Wind, and come, O South Wind; blow upon my garden, and let my spices flow forth. Let my brother come down into his garden and eat the fruit of his fruit trees.”

The garden of the Word is the flourishing affection of the soul, and in the fruit trees there is the fruit of virtue. Come, therefore; and whether you eat or drink, if you invoke Christ, he is present, saying: “Come, eat my bread and drink my wine”; and even if you sleep, he knocks at the door.

These final words plainly convey God’s gratuitous prevenience, by which God himself solicits and entices human beings toward the good, even though they have not yet opened the door of their hearts. Yet in the earlier words St. Ambrose teaches that the sinner, by invoking God, merits that God should seek him, and that he should stir up the Holy Spirit. If these statements were taken crudely, they would not only fail to agree with the Catholic truth taught elsewhere so often by St. Ambrose, but would also conflict with those final words, in which God is said to knock at the door of the heart—that is, to precede and move a person toward the good. It therefore remains that St. Ambrose should be understood as attributing to the person who invokes God a merit by which he is sought by God and stirs up the Holy Spirit—not speaking of a human invocation by which the first aid of grace is obtained, but of an invocation made through earlier helps of grace in order to merit a further and more abundant grace. In precisely this way, it is entirely reasonable to understand Valerian’s milder words, which we are now defending.

Finally, St. Macarius agrees with these Fathers, both in various other passages, especially Homilies 16 and 23, and most clearly in Homily 46. There he speaks much more harshly than all those mentioned above, although in many—indeed, very many—places he strongly asserts prevenient grace, as I shall show below. I quote the passage so that those who see a speck in Valerian’s eye may first remove this beam from St. Macarius’s eye:

> Just as, if someone is held by illness or fever, although his body has been thrown upon a bed and he is unable to accomplish any earthly task, his mind nevertheless does not remain at rest, but, distracted and concerned about the things that must be done, seeks a physician and sends his friends to him; so also the soul, after transgressing the commandment and being reduced to weakness and made feebler in its affections, when it approaches the Lord and believes, receives help from him. Although it has renounced its former evil life, although it lies sick with an old illness and is unable to perform the works of true life, it nevertheless both can and does attend diligently to the things that pertain to life, earnestly entreat the Lord, and seek the true Physician. It is not, as some people misled by perverse teaching say, that the human being is completely dead and therefore wholly unable to do anything good. For an infant, although unable to accomplish anything or to approach its mother on its own feet, nevertheless turns, cries, and weeps while seeking its mother; and the mother is moved by the greatest compassion toward him, and rejoices at the infant’s seeking her with effort and crying. When the infant cannot reach her, nevertheless, because of the child’s persistent seeking, the mother herself goes to it, seized by love for the child, embraces it, holds it close, and provides nourishment with the greatest affection.

The benevolent God does the same in the soul that approaches him and is held by desire for him.

Whether St. Macarius is speaking of the soul’s weakness and illness resulting from the fall of the first parent, or of weakness and illness resulting from its own earlier fault, the point is the same. He holds that the soul, in either of these conditions, can cry out and seek a physician, and he calls those who deny this, as people instructed in perverse teaching, what they are. For he is speaking of a soul that cries out and seeks while heavenly prevenience and solicitation have already been supplied, although he does not express that fact here. Moreover, as you see, he employs the very example of the sick person that the Semipelagians later used to explain their error, as we learn from Hilary’s letter to Augustine. For this reason I said that St. Macarius speaks more harshly than the others already mentioned, although a favorable interpretation is not to be denied him; and consequently it must not be denied to those who speak more mildly, including Valerian. 59

### 10. Homily 11 seemed especially diseased

Two passages were noted in it. The first says:

> God never abandons a will flourishing through devotion to religion, nor are the consolations of the Divinity absent where there are acts of good conduct.

This passage, however, is entirely sound. Who but an impious person, utterly ignorant of divine benevolence, would say that God abandons a will flourishing through devotion to religion? Who is unfamiliar with the statement handed down by the Council of Trent, Session 6, chapter 11, following St. Augustine, *On Nature and Grace*, chapter 26; Prosper, in his responses to Objections 7 and 13 of Vincent, and in book II *On the Calling of the Nations*, chapter 12; and in response to the seventh chapter of the Gauls: “God abandons no one unless he is first abandoned by that person”? But God does not abandon a will flourishing through devotion to religion. Therefore, the grace God had bestowed upon it, by which it conceived and flourished in devotion to religion, he willingly and gladly prolongs; and he does not allow the intention of the human being to lack heavenly aids and consolations for producing good acts through divine generosity. Thus the first passage has, as I said, an easy explanation—or rather, it was needlessly brought forward.

Because the second passage is thought hopeless, it must be addressed separately.

[Col. 0801A]

## CHAPTER VII

### It is shown in many ways that Valerian’s statement—“It is ours to will, but God’s to perfect”—is entirely Catholic

1. The whole weight of the battle against Valerian rests upon the second passage noted from Homily 11. There Valerian expressly teaches that it is ours to will the good, but God’s to perfect it; that the will for a good work must descend from us, while its perfection depends upon God’s power. He says that a human being receives credit for the labor, but owes the fruit of completed labor to the Lord.

This appears to be the very poison of Semipelagianism: a person admits God as a subsequent co-worker, yet, as St. Augustine admirably noted in *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 2, claims the first place for himself in the work of his salvation, granting God only the second place; as though he were making an agreement with God, claiming one part for himself and leaving another to God. And, what is more presumptuous, he takes the first part for himself and gives the subsequent part to God; in what he says belongs to both, he makes himself prior and God subsequent.

Yet this passage is so far from being hopeless that it can instead be shown, and shown in more than one way, to assert nothing inconsistent with sound doctrine.

The Church of Lyons appears to have recognized this in its book against John Scotus, near the end of its treatment of his fourth proposition. After rejecting that proposition at length—“It is ours to begin, but God’s to perfect by grace”—the Church of Lyons adds:

> If his words have another meaning, let the author himself who wrote them show it.

These words plainly imply that, besides the openly heretical meaning that may appear to lie beneath those words when considered merely on their external surface, another meaning can be found that is Catholic and free from error. We shall endeavor to present such a meaning in Valerian, whatever may be said of John Scotus, who may appear to have denied prevenient grace, although he used similar words; and, I hope, it will not be difficult to present it—indeed, in more than one form.

First of all, Valerian’s purpose must be considered, along with the coherence and structure of the opinion that is being brought into disrepute, in relation to what precedes and follows. The general principle applies here that St. Chrysostom admirably noted concerning the passage of Jeremiah: “I know, O Lord, that a person’s way is not his own.” There is no more dangerous or misguided interpretation of a passage than one given to a single place after it has been torn away from the body of the discussion entrusted to it, with the coherence and *ἀκολουδεία*—that is, the sequence—and the author’s purpose in what precedes and follows being neglected.

Valerian’s purpose in that passage was to impress upon his readers, as he says, that it is a kind of folly to ascribe to oneself the adornments of virtue when one owes the benefit of life to another. In other words, although you acknowledge that you have from God what you possess according to nature, you nevertheless deny that you have from the same God what enables you to fare well above nature, namely infused virtues and the other supernatural adornments of the soul.

Valerian confirms this in such a way that he does not deny that the adornments of religious life are acquired through the effort of vigilance, and that we contribute something toward this adornment of the soul and supernatural beauty—namely, the free assent by which we agree with God when he admonishes us, although it lay within our power to resist and to reject the divine solicitation and movement that precedes us, as the Council of Trent expressly teaches in Session 6, chapter 4.

But lest the human spirit become inflated because of this, Valerian adds that the assent and volition of the good exercised by the will provide no occasion for empty boasting. For even that manifestation of our effort, although drawn forth by grace and, so to speak, struck from the flint of the will, first required God’s help in order to be struck out. Moreover, once struck out, it is still incomplete and exposed to danger unless it is divinely strengthened and fortified against the difficulties that arise, which are always numerous and serious in the exercise of supernatural works.

2. The first motive of humility proposed by Valerian—that our assent is not offered by us except through the help of grace, both prevenient and cooperating—is contained in the words that the accuser calls suspect, although they are entirely Catholic and sound in every respect.

Nor can we deny that the adornments of religious life are acquired through the effort of vigilance. But God is present where there is a mind devoted to integral religion, as the Apostle says: “Do you seek proof of him who speaks in me, namely Christ?” These words are called suspect and judged diseased by the accuser, who thinks their meaning is that the effort of human vigilance, with God’s help excluded, prepares the adornments of religious life, because God comes where the mind’s religious devotion, conceived by the powers of nature, calls him.

But this meaning is plainly contrary to Valerian’s purpose and conflicts with the reasoning drawn from the passage of the Apostle just cited.

Valerian’s genuine meaning must therefore be recovered from what immediately precedes. He had said that it is a kind of folly to ascribe one’s first natural beginnings to God, but not one’s supernatural beginnings. Then, silently answering an objection that could be raised by a proud person—namely, that the adornments of virtue are acquired through human effort—he adds that he certainly cannot deny that human effort contributes to acquiring those adornments; but that this effort is not from us, but from God, who both precedes and cooperates.

For where there is a mind devoted to integral religion, there God is—not consequently, but antecedently. It is as though he were saying: Indeed, whoever you are who silently raise this objection, you have done something through watchful effort; but by whose help, and from where did that effort come? Was it not from God? The Apostle spoke of God’s zeal for the good of souls when he said: “Do you seek proof of him who speaks in me, namely Christ?”

Thus vigilance is indeed to be praised, and the effort summoned forth for the exercise of a good work is to be commended; but unless divine prevenience had come first, that effort and striving of the will would not merely have been weak and fruitless, but wholly nonexistent.

This same meaning concerning human vigilance and justification is expressed in these words of Augustine, Sermon 15, *On the Words of the Apostle*, chapter 11:

> Let us possess justification insofar as we possess it, increase it insofar as we are lacking, and perfect it, and so forth. But everything is from God—not as though we were sleeping, not as though we did not strive, not as though we did not will. Without your will, the justice of God will not be in you. The will is indeed yours alone; justice is God’s alone. The justice of God can exist without your will, but it cannot exist in you except through your will.

And shortly afterward:

> Without you God made you; for you gave no consent for God to make you. How could you consent, when you did not yet exist? Therefore, he who made you without you does not justify you without you. He made you without your knowledge; he justifies you with your will.

Enough has been said about the first motive of humility proposed by Valerian.

He adds a second motive of humility, already touched upon, intended to suppress human pride arising from the free contribution of human effort toward acquiring the adornments of the soul. Namely, besides the divine help that precedes and cooperates, we need subsequent divine help by which we are strengthened and fortified in the good conceived through divine inspiration.

Human effort is quite unstable where God’s help is not sought. Faith is plainly endangered unless it is fortified by divine protection. It is therefore ours to will the good, but Christ’s to perfect it. For the Apostle speaks in this way: “To will is present with me, but I do not find how to perfect the good.”

Valerian warns us that we are not sufficient for ourselves, even when God is already inspiring us to aspire to a conceived good, because, given our weakness, we are easily liable to waver amid so many waves and storms and with such great frailty. Therefore, God’s subsequent and strengthening help must be sought and humbly implored amid so many dangers.

This is particularly appropriate for restraining the inflation of pride arising from a good work and from the free assent of a will solicited by God. For it shows that, although we have already been preceded by grace and have contributed something—namely, the free assent by which we adhered to God calling us—nevertheless, unless God heaps upon the earlier benefits of prevenient and cooperating grace a new and special benefit of subsequent and persevering grace, our labor will be fruitless and by no means lasting. It is in this sense that Valerian understands the Apostle’s words: “To will is present with me, but I do not find how to perfect the good.”

3. Prosper understood the same passage in this way in book *Against the Collator*, chapter 8:

> When it has been granted to us to will the good, we do not immediately find that we can also do it, unless the one who gave the desire supplies its effect to those who seek, ask, and knock. For that saying of the one who says, “To will is present with me, but I do not find how to perfect the good,” belongs to one who has been called and established under grace, who indeed delights in the law of God according to the inner person, but sees another law in his members, resisting the law of his mind and taking him captive under the law of sin. Although he has received the knowledge of willing rightly, he nevertheless does not find within himself the strength to perform what he desires, until, in return for the good will he has received, he merits to find what he should do.

St. Gregory likewise understood the Apostle’s passage in the same way in *Morals*, book XXIX, chapter 25, where he treats the words: “From whose womb came the ice, and the frost from heaven—who gave it birth?”

He shows that many people, after holy desires have arisen, become troubled in carrying them out and cannot advance the seeds of virtue that have been conceived into the fruits of works, because they are struck back by intervening temptations, lest they become proud of the good purpose divinely implanted in them and forget their own emptiness and poverty. He judges that this is what the Apostle intended in the passage I have mentioned:

> What else is produced from the true womb of God than ice, when a dispensation proceeds from the inner secret place and our wills, even in their good desires, are restrained? Let us see how greatly the ice of discipline presses upon the infused earth, when he says: “To will is present with me, but I do not find how to perfect the good.” For when someone asserts that he possesses the will, he already shows, through the infusion of grace, what seeds lie hidden within him. But when he does not find how to perfect the good, he clearly indicates how greatly the ice of the heavenly dispensation presses upon him.

St. Thomas interpreted the Apostle in the same sense in his commentary on Romans 7, lecture 7. He rejected the interpretation of that passage which he reports, just as St. Augustine rejected it even more strongly in *Retractions*, book I, chapter 23.

4. Valerian therefore employed the Apostle’s passage in this sense, and, speaking together with the Apostle, said that it is ours to will, but God’s to perfect.

That is, the assent offered by us to God calling us is indeed supplied by us—for, having been preceded and divinely helped, we contribute that assent from ourselves—yet the assent offered to God who solicits us must not be rendered fruitless or dissipated into the air, nor must the desire conceived by us vanish before it is carried out. It is furthermore necessary that it be strengthened by divine protection and by the constant fortification of subsequent help.

The other words spoken near the end of the homily convey the same meaning:

> The servant indeed receives credit for his labor, but owes the fruit of completed work to his master.

Thus no stain reveals itself in Valerian, but rather radiance and purity everywhere.

5. To make this clearer: since this is the adversary’s most powerful battering ram, by which, once it is cast down, the rest will collapse, two things must be distinguished in Valerian’s present statement.

First, he says that it is ours to will—that is, that in the work of salvation the human being’s role is to offer assent to God who precedes. Second, he says that it is God’s to perfect and to dispel the difficulties that arise.

The second point causes Valerian no difficulty, because everyone agrees that subsequent grace and God’s strengthening of what he has worked in us are not merely useful but necessary. Leaving aside other evidence for the moment, St. Ephrem, a frequent herald of the praise of grace, expressed this very beautifully in his treatise *On Fleeing Evil Habits*, found in volume I:

> Let us hear the Apostle himself saying: “Work out your salvation with fear and trembling.” Let no one, even if still young, regard this lightly, nor let the elderly neglect it. For the end of each is uncertain.
>
> Let us therefore contemplate farmers. They level the earth and sow; and when the fields have become green, they carefully guard them, driving away birds and quadrupeds, lest, while the seed is still tender and soft, it be torn out by such creatures and yield no good crop. When it has grown as far as the harvest, they are not even then free from care and anxiety; rather, they remain apprehensive lest the crops be battered by hail, or locusts devour the harvest, or a scorching wind ruin the fruit. Consequently they continually offer vows to God and appeal to him with suppliant prayers, asking that the Lord may deign to grant them their fruits safe and unharmed. Then, when they have stored the fruits in their barns, they celebrate a festival with great joy.
>
> In the same way, those who undertake the spiritual life must be watchful and sober and guard the seed of the divine word, and so forth.

He could not have declared more familiarly the necessity of divine help to perfect what has been begun under God’s inspiration.

For this reason other Fathers frequently employ this comparison when explaining the work of salvation. They compare our heart to a field and soil; grace to heavenly seed and divine clouds; the Scriptures to a mattock; the fervor of the Holy Spirit to manure; our effort to cultivation performed by the farmer; and, finally, the care that continues until the harvest and the bringing of the fruits into the barn to subsequent divine grace.

See especially the same Ephrem, *Ten Chapters on Virtue*, chapter 10; Macarius, Homily 26, final and penultimate questions; Paulinus, very aptly, Letter 30, or Letter 2, to Aper and Amanda, and Letter 35, near the end; and Prudentius, book III *Against Symmachus*, near the end.

The first statement—that it is ours to will—is entirely pure in the sense I attributed to Valerian. That this is truly its genuine meaning is shown by a notable passage from a homily on the words of Isaiah, “If you are willing and hear me,” and so forth. The homily is attributed to Chrysostom, although it may perhaps have another, and indeed Latin, author.

At the beginning of the homily it says:

> If willing or unwilling were not ours—that is, if the freedom to live rightly or wrongly had been taken away from us—then the good person would never worthily receive the heavenly gift, nor would the evil person incur the punishment he deserved; rather, everything would be attributed to God as its author.

The homily soon explains this more fully. It states that willing is called ours insofar as each person, by the free choice of the will, either fulfills or despises the commandments. Thus each person establishes for himself what he deserves and cannot deserve anything other than what he wills, since the tenor of the law has been set before him, from which he chooses what he wills and despises what he does not will. In this way God’s judgment is celebrated through human judgment: the person who gives his granted freedom to obedience is rewarded, while the one who turns it toward contempt is condemned.

What this author says so explicitly—that willing is ours in the work of salvation insofar as we freely offer assent, which we could deny if we wished—is entirely Catholic and certain. For this does not exclude prevenient grace; rather, it clearly implies it in the word “assent,” which connotes an antecedent invitation and solicitation. The person who consents thereby adopts that same judgment and disposition.

Thus the words attributed to Valerian have an entirely Catholic meaning. They say only that it is ours to will—that is, as the author just cited explained these words, it is ours to consent to and carry out, or to refuse, the divine command.

“For us,” says Bernard in *On the Interior House*, chapter 68, “there remains, in seeking salvation, the freedom of choice; but God first admonishes and invites us to salvation, so that we may either choose or follow. It is within our power to acquiesce in divine inspiration and to choose and follow the things that pertain to our salvation; but it is a divine gift that we are able to attain what we desire to obtain by following.”

These words are plainly twin to those that were regarded as suspect in Valerian.

Bernard copied the passage from chapter 21 of Gennadius’s *On Ecclesiastical Dogma*—if it is indeed Gennadius’s passage and not that of someone who inserted the addition into Gennadius’s book, since Gennadius himself, from his praise of Cassian and Faustus and his rejection of Prosper, rather plainly reveals himself to be a Semipelagian. Whatever the case may be, Bernard approved and copied the passage, as did Rabanus in book IV *On the Universe*, chapter 10, and the author of the book *On the Spirit and the Soul*, chapter 48.

I regard this first interpretation of the statement—which, throughout Valerian’s work, appears at first sight extremely difficult—as clear and most convenient, and as cohering especially well with what precedes and with the entire structure of the homily. Nor do I doubt that it should be accepted by anyone who investigates Valerian’s meaning in that passage with a mind directed solely toward the truth, teachable, and free from preconceptions.

6. I shall add a second interpretation, equally Catholic. According to it, Valerian intended only this: the free volition by which we offer assent to God calling us belongs simultaneously to us and to God, yet in the order of reason it proceeds from us before it proceeds from God. The reason God cooperates with us in freely forming it is that, making good use of divine prevenience, we will to act, although we could kick against the goad.

Nevertheless, the entire supernatural character, or perfection of the higher order, that is seen in this free assent, to which our free determination and application gave the beginning, is from God.

According to this interpretation, “perfection” does not mean the completion of a thing already begun and therefore still imperfect, but the dignity and eminence of the higher order that is present in the act, by which the act has proportion to further grace and glory.

To make this answer clear, two points must first be established.

7. First, it should not seem strange that our convert—or converted will—into a free act is posited as prior in reason to the divine concurrence in that same act, or to divine cooperation with us. For the discussion here is not about the divine excitation that God produces in us without our free cooperation, and therefore without us, an excitation that clearly precedes our supernatural assent. Rather, the discussion concerns the concurrence by which God produces a free action together with us.

It lies within the power of the will, sprinkled with prior divine dew and supported by divine help and grace, either to posit or to omit that action, or free assent. But God, out of the great reverence with which he disposes created will, does not in this respect precede it, as St. Chrysostom often says. That is, he does not compel it or use force so that it is turned in one direction rather than another. He would do this by operating beforehand and, so to speak, acting and running ahead; instead, he permits the will, strengthened by his grace, to choose this or the opposite action, or action and omission.

The reason God himself applies himself to cooperate with us and to produce this or that action together with us is that he sees our determination to imply that here and now there is not a suspension in the will, but the exercise of some action, and likewise that an action of this particular kind, rather than another, be exercised. However he sees our determination to imply this belongs to another inquiry.

The fact that divine concurrence with our free operations follows our determination in the order of reason has been explained extensively elsewhere. It is rightly taught by Scotus, book IV, distinction 1, question 1, letter Ss, and book II, distinction 37, single question, letter V; Ockham, book I, distinction 42, single question, letter F; Gregory, book II, distinction 34, question 1, article 3, response to objection 8; Gabriel, in book II, distinction [unspecified], question 2, letters F and M; Capreolus, book IV, distinction 12, single question, response to objection 1; Scotus, *Against the Second*; Major, book II, distinction 37, final doubt; Almain, *Moral Treatise*, book II, chapter 10, at the end; Ruardus, article 7, proposition 10, near the end; and others cited in discussions of divine concurrence, the coherence of human freedom with divine decrees, and the cooperation of the first cause with us.

In particular, the same conclusion follows clearly in supernatural cooperation from the fact that God professes himself our helper and co-worker. But whoever is helped, insofar as he is helped, is at least presupposed in reason to have first girded himself for action. The same applies to the person with whom God cooperates, according to St. Augustine, Sermon 15, *On the Words of the Apostle*: “If you were not an operator, he would not be a co-operator.”

Nevertheless, in Question 15 on Deuteronomy, taking account of prevenient grace, Augustine says that God operates while the human being cooperates.

8. I also establish beforehand that “perfection” can be used in two ways.

First, it can connote a prior imperfection that is completed by some addition or supplementation. In this sense, when a small child grows, he is said to be perfected by acquiring a new size beyond his earlier size; and habitual grace is said to be perfected whenever it is increased by some new addition.

In this sense St. Thomas, *Summa theologica* I, question 4, article 1, response to objection 2, says that God, considering the meaning of the word, cannot be called perfect.

Perfection is then taken in a second sense, as denoting the nobility and dignity of the thing said to be perfect. In this way, the smallest degree of grace is said to possess the greatest perfection in comparison with all natural goods. In this sense God, to whom nothing can be added or taken away, is called perfect, although no beginning of goodness preceded in him that would have to be completed and consummated by the arrival of something else.

St. James likewise used “perfect” in this sense when he said that every perfect gift is from above. The Apostle did not mean that only those gifts are sent down from heaven to which no further addition can be made. If that were his meaning, every grace we acquire here, so long as it is capable of increase, would have to be excluded from the register of perfect gifts descending from the Father of lights.

The Apostle’s meaning, therefore, was that every gift of the higher order proceeds from God, the author of grace; and in these gifts there shines a very great perfection—that is, an entitative dignity and nobility.

[Col. 0806B]

9. With these points established, the second interpretation of Valerian that I proposed becomes clear.

When he says that in the work of salvation it is ours to will, but God’s to perfect, as though free assent were formed in such an order that we first will and God then adds perfection, his meaning may be this: in the free assent that proceeds from a will divinely preceded and assisted, there are two elements. First, it is free assent; second, it possesses a certain perfection and dignity and has proportion to sanctifying grace, toward which progress is made through that assent, and also to glory, which is the goal of the entire supernatural progress.

Therefore, insofar as that free assent is established in reality, it derives both from our will, divinely preceded by exciting grace, and from God cooperating with us. Nevertheless, in the order of reason, our willing to act comes first, before God’s willing to cooperate.

Nor does God apply himself to produce that free act together with us unless, with his divine perspicacity, he sees that the will in these circumstances will act—that is, will burst forth into an act of a determinate kind if it could burst forth into it by itself alone. This is what the words “it is ours to will” convey.

But the fact that our assent possesses the dignity and perfection that it truly has—that is, that it is supernatural—it receives from God, the author of grace. God initiates this act both by the help of prior and cooperating grace and by the supernatural cooperation and application through which divine power, in carrying out the act, cooperates with the human will above the will’s connatural requirement. This is what the words “it is God’s to perfect” express.

For just as the determination to exercise a free act is attributed to a created will divinely preceded, as to the direct and proximate cause of such an exercise established in the hand of that will, which has been divinely fertilized, so also the supernatural character and perfection of the higher order—in virtue of which this assent has proportion to human holiness and glory—belongs to God as its direct and proximate cause.

This does not mean that the degree of supernaturalness is not jointly from the will and from God; rather, if we consider the aspect and cause from which the act has its supernatural character, that cause is none other than God.

For example, in supernatural intellection, such as the assent of faith: that it is an expression of the object comes from the intellect; but that it is an expression of this particular kind comes from the impressed species, which determines the universality and indifference of the power. Nevertheless, the whole intellection, in its entitative reality, comes both from the intellect and from the impressed species, which, as the Philosopher says, equips the power and determines it to an act of this essence, or to the presentation of such an object.

To condense this second interpretation of Valerian into a few words: it is ours to will—that is, the fact that a free operation is exercised proceeds from us, divinely preceded, as from its direct cause. But the fact that this operation, exercised at the will’s command when the will has been divinely preceded, possesses supernatural perfection is from God, as from its direct cause.

[Col. 0807A]

10. We can strengthen this doctrine by the authority of the Fathers. St. Macarius presents it clearly in Homily 37, explicitly teaching that the exercise of a supernatural work belongs to the human will, and that God operates nothing in this sphere except according to the requirement of the will that has been preceded by grace. I shall give the passage below, in chapter 9, section 3.

The Author of the Imperfect Work on Matthew, homily 32, examining those words of chapter 19, “Not all receive this saying, but those to whom it has been given,” has these words:

> By saying “to whom it has been given,” he does not mean that it is given to some and not given to others; rather, he shows that unless we receive the help of grace, we can accomplish nothing by ourselves. Since grace is not denied to those who are willing, the Lord says in the Gospel: “Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives; and whoever seeks finds; and to the one who knocks it will be opened.” The will, however, must precede, and then grace follows. For neither does grace accomplish anything without the will, nor can the will do anything without grace. For the earth too does not germinate unless it has received rain, nor does rain produce fruit without the earth.

[Col. 0807B] Here this Author explicitly teaches the indivisible partnership of grace and will in producing a supernatural work, although prevenient grace must precede before it actually co-produces that work, and must, as it were, water the aridity of the will, as happens in the example of rain and earth. Therefore, when he says, “The will must precede,” so that no manifest contradiction may be admitted between one line and the next, and so that the reasoning which follows may cohere, this must necessarily be understood of that precedence in the order of reason which we have explained: will and grace co-produce the free act in such a way that, once the will has first been touched by prevenient grace, the free will acts first in the order of reason with respect to the actual co-production of the work. For the reason why God applies himself to co-producing that work with the will is the determination of the will, foreseen conditionally. Thus that passage of the Author of the Imperfect Work most explicitly contains the interpretation of Valerian that has been set forth.

[Col. 0807C] It may be objected that this work is corrupt and stuffed with errors. But that objection has no force here. For when St. Bonaventure, *Pharetra*, book II, chapter 26, and St. Thomas in the *Catena*, while reproducing the quoted words of Matthew 19, encountered them, they detected nothing corrupt or suspicious in them. It is indeed established that the Arians interpolated that work and corrupted it by mixing in the leaven of their heresy. But the matter with which we are concerned had nothing to do with Arian impiety.

**11.** Nor are there lacking comparable passages from the unquestionably genuine and, so to speak, unadulterated works of Chrysostom. For in homily 23 on Matthew, in the *Perfect Work*, while investigating the cause of Manasseh’s cleansing, he answers that it was accomplished by the tears of repentance and the earnestness of the will, and adds:

> For there is not—there is absolutely not—any sin that does not yield to the power of repentance, or rather, to the grace of God. When we turn toward better things, he immediately becomes our fellow-worker. For if you prefer to be good, there is absolutely no one who can prevent you. Indeed, the devil does try to prevent you, but he will certainly be able to do nothing if you choose better things; and even more so when God joins himself to you as your helper.

[Col. 0807D] The Latin translation incorrectly has “when God is joined” (*Deo copulante*), whereas it should read “when God joins himself to you” (*Deum copulante*), as the Greek witnesses indicate and the sense requires.

> But if you certainly do not wish this and turn back, who will protect you? For he does not wish to save you by necessity and force, but with your own will.

He then adds very many things to the same effect, confirming that God certainly does not wish to constrain us by force:

> If, nevertheless, we show him only our willingness to please him, he will in no way abandon us, but will come to fight alongside us—as the Greek expression has it—and will join himself to us when we ask, as our fellow-worker and protector.

And shortly afterward he says:

> Would that we preserved such affection toward him that his inmost parts might be set aflame with love for us. But God seeks only an occasion for this fire; and if you yourself offer even a tiny spark, you will kindle within yourself an immense flame of his benefits.

Immediately afterward, closing off the vain fear of those who are afraid that by approaching God they may seem importunate toward him, he denies that any uncivilized insistence need be feared in approaching God:

> Just as breathing is never altogether an improper act, so likewise it is not asking, but rather failing to ask, that is improper. For just as we continually need to breathe, so too do we need the help supplied by God. If we are willing, we shall easily be able to bend him toward us.

And to make this clear, showing that God is always ready to bestow benefits, he said that we shall find him prepared like the dawn:

> Whenever we wish to come and approach him, we shall immediately discover that our prayers have been awaited by him.

You see how explicitly Chrysostom requires that prior application of the will divinely prevened, so that God may join himself to it as a fellow-worker in the struggle against Satan and in the formation of free consent, which our enemy strives to intercept.

The following words from homily 15 of the same work must be understood in the same sense:

> If only you yourself provide the beginning of the undertaking, you will have the God of peace helping you above all things, and you will dispel that flame, with him first cooperating.

And these words from homily 16:

> God makes virtue easy by cooperating with us and always helping us in good actions. For wherever you wish to bring even a little devotion, everything else will quickly follow. This is why he wishes you too to undertake some labor, so that your victory may also be yours.

Finally, there are these words from book I *On Compunction of Heart*, which some incorrectly take as referring to those who are “incurably ill”:

> The grace of God alone does not make each person perfect. For it is also required that we accomplish what lies within our purpose and our powers. Therefore the grace of God does come to each person, but among those who worthily fulfill what has been commanded, it remains in them. From those, however, who act less worthily, it quickly departs. But to those who do not even begin to turn toward the Lord, it does not come at all. For it loves upright minds and an unfeigned purpose.

These words would indeed be irreparably difficult if their meaning were that the first help of grace does not come to a person unless that person, by an honorable action drawn from the powers of nature—in other words, by a natural turning toward God as an initial act of salvation on his own part—first elicits it. But this meaning is utterly foreign both to Chrysostom and to the truth.

The genuine meaning, therefore, is that the grace which fights and cooperates, and which makes a person perfect, does not come at all to those who do not even begin to turn toward the Lord. For grace to come as a cooperating and fighting force, and to elicit with us the consent by which we are dispositively brought to final perfection, it is necessary that we first, in the order of reason, make a beginning of conversion. This is fully sufficient to stop the mouths of those who speak wickedly—namely, heretics, against whom Chrysostom is incidentally arguing in that final passage—and of sluggish Christians who attributed the blame for their failure to attain perfection to grace, as though grace spurned them and did not come to them.

Chrysostom says that they advance this claim wrongly, because the grace that fights alongside us and assists in attaining perfection comes, insofar as it depends on itself, to everyone. To those who wish continually to use it, it is always readily and steadfastly available. But from those who first use it and then recoil, turning their efforts elsewhere, it too ceases to be present until they again require its co-operation; and by that requirement of an active will they summon that divine grace to fight and [Col. 0808D] cooperate.

Finally, to those who, utterly inert and languishing in idleness, refuse to elicit the first free act of turning toward God, it wholly denies itself. For, as this same holy Father most wisely weighs in homily 83 on Matthew and homily 60 *To the People*, at the very beginning, Divine Wisdom wished to preserve both our humility and our honor: not everything was to belong to freedom, lest we become proud, nor everything to grace, so that virtue might be our good in some measure—namely, insofar as the prevenient will freely admitted and summoned grace as it actually cooperated and co-produced the act. For the will, after the heavenly inspiration had been given, determined itself to act first in the order of reason.

**12.** Finally, I add a notable passage from St. Bernard, in the treatise *On Grace and Free Choice*, somewhat near the beginning, where he extensively confirms that willing belongs to us through free choice, and therefore that willing is ours, although willing well, in the Christian sense, is not ours but belongs to grace.

> Willing is present in us through free choice; not, however, the ability to do what we will. I do not mean willing good or willing evil, but simply willing.
