For willing good is progress; willing evil is failure. But willing simply is itself what either progresses or fails. Moreover, grace as creator made it exist; grace as savior makes it progress; it casts itself down into failure. Thus free choice makes us willing, while grace makes us well-disposed; willing is from ourselves, willing good is from grace.

He explains this at much greater length and, among other things, understands in this sense the Apostle’s words: “To will is present with me, but I do not find how to perform the good.” He teaches that the Apostle recognized that willing was present in him through free choice, but that, for this willing to be a supernaturally good willing, it derived from grace, which makes a person Christianly well-disposed, or willing well in relation to salvation.

Bernard therefore acknowledges that willing is ours, and indeed prior in the order of reason to the point at which cooperating grace co-produces free consent with us. For, at least in the order of reason, the willing that is ours is prior to the willing well that comes from grace and from God, its author, who operates above what nature is owed.

I seal this second interpretation of Valerian with the words of Prosper, *On the Calling of the Nations*, chapter 26, elsewhere numbered 9, in which the doctrine so far proposed is contained and admirably illustrated:

> The grace of God, he says, takes precedence principally in all acts of justification: persuading by exhortations, moving by examples, frightening by dangers, urging by miracles, giving understanding, inspiring counsel, illuminating the heart itself, and filling it with the affections of faith. But the human will is also added and joined to it; it has been aroused for this purpose by the aforesaid helps, so that it may cooperate in the divine work within itself and begin to exercise toward merit what it conceived through heavenly seed as an inclination toward action: if it fails, it has this from its own mutability; if it progresses, from the assistance of grace. This assistance is supplied to all in innumerable ways, hidden or manifest. What is rejected by many is due to their own wickedness; what is received by many belongs both to divine grace and to the human will.

That, once the human being has been aroused, the free consent added to non-free grace is prior in the order of reason on the part of the human being to grace as it actually co-produces the act, Prosper makes clear in what he adds at the end of the chapter:

> Grace first of all does this: in the one whom it calls, it prepares for itself a will that receives it first and serves its gifts. For there is no virtue in those who are unwilling.

Grace, I say, strives beforehand to lead the will, once the will has offered its free consent, to admit cooperating grace and its further gifts. Without that consent, the remaining progress in the work of salvation is completely blocked; and consequently the first step after prevenient grace belongs to the will in the order of reason. Similar passages may also be drawn from Richard of St. Victor, book III *On Contemplation*, chapter 16.

**13.** I now set forth a third Catholic interpretation of Valerian, while at the same time illustrating the two already given from Anselm—or rather, Hervaeus—in his commentary on Philippians 1, on the words, “He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion.”

He explains the passage in these words:

> I pray to God for you, trusting in this very thing because of his goodness: he who began a good work in you through prevenient grace will bring it to completion through subsequent and cooperating grace, granting perseverance until the day of Jesus Christ—that is, until the final day of each person’s life, when the soul, departing from the body, is presented before Christ’s tribunal to be judged. By cooperating in us, God brings to completion what he begins by working, because he himself works in us as he begins, so that we may will; and he cooperates with those who are willing as he brings the work to completion. For he works without us so that we may will; but when we will, and will in such a way that we act, he cooperates with us.

In these words both of the interpretations of Valerian already proposed are contained, and the third is also indicated. The first is presented when it is said that it belongs to God to bring to completion what, through his prevenient action, we have willed well—bringing it to completion, that is, by granting perseverance.

The second is presented when it is said that God cooperates when we will, and therefore, because we will, works with us and in us to produce the act by which we are brought to the highest perfection, since this act is the best gift and the perfect gift, surpassing everything capable of arising from the fruitfulness of nature.

I derive the third from the statement that God, by cooperating, brings to completion what he begins by working. Here the verb “to bring to completion” must be used with the connotation of a prior imperfection, which is completed and consummated through the addition of a subsequent perfection.

Since, therefore, divine cooperation and our supernatural free consent, when compared with divine prevenience, stand to one another as the imperfect and the perfect, or as seed and fruit, as St. Anselm beautifully explains in *On the Harmony*, part II, chapter 16, it is rightly said that, insofar as God invites and arouses us toward the good, his work in us is imperfect.

But the human being who has thus been prevened must, by willing, bring it about that God completes through cooperation what he began to do alone. For it belongs to us to will and to make use of the seed of grace divinely implanted. By recognizing the determination of the will, God joins himself to it—not now as its arouser, but as its fellow-worker—and brings to completion what he had begun by inspiring it; otherwise it would have remained imperfect because our earth did not yield its fruit.

Hervaeus reproduced verbatim St. Augustine’s book *On Grace and Free Choice*, chapter 17; this third interpretation of Valerian therefore rests more upon Augustine than upon Hervaeus. It can also be grounded in the words of Fulgentius, book *On Predestination and Grace*, chapter 11, where he teaches that God is the one who is said to bring to completion in us what calling had begun, because it belongs to us to strive after the good, which he also gave us the will to desire. He thereby shows that, without him, what he wills to belong to human striving cannot be brought to completion.

**65 14.** I append a fourth interpretation of Valerian, one conforming to the interpretation which most Catholic authorities give to that passage of the Apostle on which Valerian relies: “To will is present with me, but I do not find how to perform the good.”

For not a few, and not undistinguished, authorities understand those words as referring to the sinner’s willing, operating from bare nature. This willing is present with him—that is, according to them, it lies weak and prostrate, as though infirm, unless grace comes and gives the will efficacy for bringing the matter to completion.

Those authorities therefore say that the Apostle has assumed in himself the person of the sinner deprived of the strength of grace and groaning: that he naturally sighs for the good and wills it ineffectively under the aspect in which it is presented to him; and that it is proportionate to the dart of natural light and to the appetitive will. But that willing is weak and lies prostrate, and cannot rise to Christian good unless completing grace comes, by which an undue vigor is infused into the will and the good is thus brought into effect.

Nicholas Gorran elegantly pursues this interpretation of the Apostle in Romans 7. It may accordingly be said that Valerian humbles human action in this respect and strives to persuade people that “whoever boasts should boast in the Lord”: although, through the powers of nature, we possess some imperfect and ineffective willing of the good, and in this respect willing is ours, nevertheless it belongs to God alone to bring it to completion—that is, to effect in us something as it ought to be effected.

For that willing which we have from ourselves must be regarded as entirely worthless in the matter of salvation, and does not dispose us to grace and justification even remotely. But the divine gift—first the arousing grace and then the cooperating grace—brings to completion what had been outlined and in some way begun through that natural and languid willing of the good.

This is not because grace and that willing belong to the same order, but because grace stands as that which forms and actualizes the natural roughness and potentiality. In this respect grace may be said to bring the work of salvation to completion, since that imperfect willing could not consummate it. In this very sense grace is said to perfect nature, raising it to a different order.

And St. Bernard, in a sermon on Palm Sunday recently added, beginning “Our Redeemer,” says near the end that the good things of nature are begun by creating grace, but increased and brought to perfection by saving grace.

**15.** The distinction used by the recently cited Gorran, in 2 Corinthians 1, is relevant to the present matter. He employs it while treating a difficulty concerning the words of that same chapter: “We are not sufficient,” and so forth.

He opposes to it the Gloss on Ezekiel 3, which says that the beginning of a good will comes from us. The Gloss’s statement he disentangles in this way:

> There are two kinds of beginning. One is natural, namely, the natural and actual inclination toward the good, and this comes from us. The other is formal, which is part of a good work, and this comes from God.

He calls this latter beginning, which supervenes upon the former, “formal,” as perfecting and actualizing the potentiality of the earlier beginning; and for that reason he calls the earlier beginning “material.”

It is easy to adapt this same distinction and interpretation to Valerian by saying that he admits a natural willing from us, as the material beginning of the good, which in no way disposes one toward grace and does not even congruently obtain it; but that the perfection of that natural beginning of the good—which alone contributes to salvation—is assigned not to the human being but to God, the author of grace.

It is indeed much cruder to say, as the Gloss above did, that the beginning of salvation comes from us and its perfection from God, than to say with Valerian that willing is ours but bringing to completion belongs to God. Therefore, if we give the harsher words that interpretation, we should not deny the same interpretation to these milder words.

**16.** A fifth interpretation could be added, one suggested by St. Optatus, book II *Against Parmenian*, where he says that willing and running are ours, but bringing to completion belongs to God—that is, removing imperfections and coming to the aid of a human being who is always deficient in many respects—because he alone is perfect, whereas all of us are only partly perfect, however well and piously we may run.

I shall cite Optatus’s words below, in chapter 9, from which this interpretation will be more clearly understood. Nor are there few passages in St. Jerome’s book I *Against the Pelagians* that serve to illustrate it, where he discusses at length how, although we may all wish to attain complete goodness and righteousness, perfectness nevertheless belongs properly to Christ alone.

[Col. 0811B]

# CHAPTER VIII  
## Valerian Imitated the Manner of Speech of Scripture and Was Therefore Wrongly Branded

[Col. 0811C]

**1.** I think that everything which could be brought forward, even by the most suspicious person, in order to brand Valerian with the stigma of Semi-Pelagianism has been sufficiently and more than sufficiently dispelled.

Now, in order that Valerian’s innocence may be made even clearer, especially at that final point which was thought to be most slippery, it is useful to show that the very manner of speech which caused the accuser to take offense at Valerian, and other expressions plainly similar to it, are found as accepted expressions in Scripture. Consequently, it is unjust to mark him as erroneous on account of his use of an expression suggested by the Holy Spirit to the canonical writer—unless it were established from some other source that he was twisting the genuine meaning of Scripture, as all sectarians customarily do. That, however, has no place in the present case, since nothing opposed to Valerian remains that has not been suitably dismissed and explained.

**2.** The Apostle’s passage in Romans 7 therefore supports Valerian above all, and he himself cited it: “To will is present with me, but I do not find how to perform the good.”

Various interpretations of this passage are commonly found among interpreters, but the two which St. Thomas reported there are especially suitable.

According to the first, the Apostle understands it to mean that the willing of the good, as it ought to be willed, is free for a human being helped by grace, although further grace is required for perseverance, which must be awaited from God. God is therefore said to bring it to completion because our choice, although conceived through grace, would not be brought to consummation, since difficulty would supervene from outside. Even if those difficulties were absent, the weariness that naturally creeps in through continual struggle and striving against the current often disrupts the best plans and breaks the will’s earlier resolve.

The author of the *Soliloquies*, wrongly attributed to St. Augustine, expressed this excellently by using this very passage of the Apostle. In fact, the work belongs to St. Anselm, at least for the most part. He speaks as follows in chapter 4:

> Lord, if you will, you can save me; but although I might wish it, I could not. A great multitude of my miseries is with me. For “to will is present with me, but I do not find how to perform the good.” I cannot will what is good unless you will it; nor can I do what I will unless your power strengthens me; and what I can, I sometimes do not will unless your will is done, as in heaven and on earth. And what I both will and can, I do not know unless your wisdom enlightens me. Even when I know, sometimes willing and sometimes being able, my wisdom passes away imperfect and empty unless your true wisdom helps me.

And shortly afterward:

> I said, “I shall do this; I shall bring that to completion,” but I did neither this nor that. The will was present, but not the ability. The ability was present, but the will was absent, because I trusted in my own powers. But now I confess to you, Lord my God, Father of heaven and earth, that a human being will not be strengthened by his own strength, so that the foolish presumption of all flesh may not boast before you. For it is not a human being’s to will what he can, or to be able to do what he wills, or to know what he wills and can do; rather, a human being’s steps are directed by you. They confess, I say, that their steps are directed not by themselves but by you.

These and other statements in that passage clearly express not only human weakness in willing the good by the bare powers of nature, but also human weakness in persevering with the assistance of grace, which was sufficient for willing. They allude to the Apostle’s passage under discussion, understood in the sense I have presented.

**3.** According to the second interpretation, that passage means that the natural willing of the good comes from us, whereas the perfection of the good—that is, the execution of the disposition by which we are led to salvation—from the first willing that disposes us in some way toward supernatural good all the way to the summit of attained glory, comes from God and from those helps by which he raises nature to goods of this higher order.

This interpretation has some foundation in the word “to bring to completion,” which in Scripture, when the matter is the work of salvation, has the same force as execution and accomplishment. Adamus noted this—or rather, as I read it in the preface to Hesselius’s book *On the Case of Nestorius*, John Hesselius, Adamus’s fellow student—when commenting on Philippians 2, on the words, “He who works,” *energōn* (ἐνεργῶν), “in you both to will and to bring to completion,” *thelein kai energein* (θέλειν καὶ ἐνεργεῖν). There the verb which the earlier translator rendered “works” he immediately renders “brings to completion.”

According to this interpretation, therefore, it is as though the Apostle had said in the passage under discussion:

> By bare nature and from myself I possess some willing of the good, wholly useless for salvation. But to carry out in fact, as is necessary for salvation, that good which I am moved by myself to conceive and in some way will within the lower order, I possess only through grace.

**4.** Of these interpretations of the Apostle’s passage, the first seems to me more suitable; St. Thomas approved it, as did Catharinus and other more recent authorities. Valerian plainly seems to have embraced it when he used this passage of the Apostle.

Nevertheless, for Valerian’s purpose it makes no difference which interpretation of the Apostle we accept. On either interpretation, Valerian, who used the Apostle’s expression, must be pronounced free from error.

Valerian’s purpose was to show that in the work of salvation a human being must lay aside pride and glory in the Lord rather than in himself. Either meaning of the Apostle’s words as used by Valerian is extremely well suited to this purpose.

For what room for pride can remain amid such wavering and weakness of human efforts, even when those efforts have begun rightly and with the help of grace? What material for boasting can be available to one who knows that all his strength is like the ash of tow, and that whatever he can do by his natural powers has absolutely no significance for salvation, so that everything belonging to the order of grace comes from God?

“By every means,” says Richard of St. Victor, book III *On Contemplation*, chapter 23, “the mind advances both toward love of God and toward contempt of itself when it fully recognizes how little it can do by itself. How marvelous is his grace, through which he works all our works in us in such a way that they are both his and ours—his gifts and our merits.”

St. Gregory strongly presses this incentive to humility in *Moralia* XXII, chapter 10, when treating the words, “If I kissed my hand with my mouth.” He says that this is equivalent to Job’s saying:

> I do not put forward my works as my own, because whoever attributes to himself what he accomplishes is convicted of denying the grace of its author.

For this reason he had first stated that the saints are utterly foreign to such arrogance, because they know clearly what they possess from themselves and what from God. Whatever good they discern in themselves, they recognize as the gift of immortal grace, and they become debtors to him for the gift received: he gave them, by preceding them, the will to desire what they had not wanted, and, by following them, granted them the ability to do what they will.

Hence John rightly says:

> They worshiped the one who lives forever and ever, casting their crowns before the Lord’s throne, so that they might refer the glory of praise to him from whom they know that they received the strength for the struggle.

St. Augustine inculcates the same point countless times, especially in book *On Rebuke and Grace*, chapter 12, and in his commentary on Psalm 58, near the end.

The Apostle wished to impress this very point through the words cited, and Valerian intended and said nothing else. Therefore, whoever attacks him on this account should take care lest, with the same battering ram, he attack the Apostle.

**5.** St. Thomas observes that a passage in Scripture parallel to this one is another passage from chapter 16 of Proverbs: “The human heart disposes its way, but it belongs to the Lord to direct its steps.”

St. Thomas considers it equivalent to say that a human being disposes his way and, as is said shortly before in the same place, prepares his soul, and to say that willing belongs to a human being but bringing to completion belongs to God.

Or, as St. Augustine reads it following the Greek text, “from God is the answer of the tongue”—that is, the inward, steadfast, and perfect consent continuing to the end.

Therefore, just as that expression of the wise man—“It belongs to a human being to dispose his way and prepare his soul, but it belongs to the Lord to direct his steps”—is entirely pure, since it was suggested by the Holy Spirit and is as far as possible from Semi-Pelagian error, so too the other expression used by Valerian is wholly sound and Catholic. For, in St. Thomas’s judgment, both expressions, beneath the different covering of their words, carry the same meaning.

The Semi-Pelagians indeed abused that disposition of the heart and preparation of the soul which Solomon attributed to the human being. From this they inferred that the beginning of salvation, or a good will, belonged to the human being from himself, whereas the perfection and completion of the work of salvation belonged to God, the author of grace, as St. Augustine reports in book II *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, chapter 8.

Nevertheless, if their understanding had not been distorted, they would easily have perceived that a human being prepares the heart, but not without the help of God, who touches the heart, as St. Augustine rightly argues in the cited passage.

**67 6.** What Solomon taught in that passage was not weakened by Jeremiah in chapter 10, in these words:

> I know, Lord, that the way of a human being is not his own, nor does it belong to a man to walk and direct his steps.

St. Chrysostom splendidly discussed Jeremiah’s statement in an entire homily devoted to it. He first noted that in his own time it was customarily circulated everywhere—in houses, marketplaces, villages, cities, on land, at sea, on islands, and wherever one might go. He also observed that not a few people, gathering aconite from the sweetest flower, had inferred from it that nothing lay within our power.

St. Chrysostom reports that they did this because, without examining the structure and sequence of the whole chapter, they rashly seized a few words, cut off and torn from their surrounding context, and twisted the prophet’s statement into absurd meanings foreign to the writer’s intention. He gravely complains that this is the source of much foolishness and error.

St. Chrysostom therefore confirms that Jeremiah does not weaken what we reported as having been taught by Solomon. He does so on the ground that in that very passage the prophet attributes his steps to the human being himself and acknowledges that the way he takes is his own—something he would not say if it did not lie within his power.

Moreover, the prophet immediately adds supplicatory prayers to God, asking him graciously to moderate the punishment. There would certainly be no place for this prayer unless the human heart disposed its way, as the Wise Man affirmed.

Having thus flattened the difficulty arising from that passage, St. Chrysostom gives its genuine meaning in these words:

> What he says has this meaning: everything does not lie within our power, but one thing lies within our power and another within God’s power. To choose the best things, to will them, to strive to do them, and to expend every effort, belongs to our free choice. But to bring them to their outcome, not to allow them to fail, and to reach the end of right actions—this belongs to heavenly grace. God has divided virtue between himself and us. He did not wish the whole matter to lie within our power, lest we be lifted up into pride; nor did he take the whole matter upon himself, lest we surrender to inactivity. Rather, leaving a small part to our labors, he himself accomplishes the greater part.

And below:

> This, then, is what the prophet says: the successful outcome of actions does not lie within our power, but depends upon divine help; yet choosing lies within us and within our free choice.

In the remainder of the homily he confirms the genuine meaning of the prophet at greater length. In particular, he blocks the vain excuse which some seemed able to derive from the passage: that a human being should not be blamed if he does not act, since willing and choosing alone belonged to him, whereas bringing the matter to completion belonged to God.

St. Chrysostom proves that this excuse is frivolous on the ground that, if we are willing, choose, and resolve, it is impossible for God to abandon us. For if he exhorts those who are unwilling and advises them to will and resolve, he will much less abandon those who willingly choose.

From all this it is more than sufficiently clear how Jeremiah’s passage both contributes to clearing Valerian and does not conflict with the Wise Man’s passage, which we likewise showed to be relevant to the present matter.

### 7.

In the same sense, in that passage St. Chrysostom adduces the famous text from Romans 9, which he had likewise mentioned at the outset as having been misused by those who pleaded the Scriptures in support of their own sluggishness: “It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy.” Yet he demonstrates that this passage is compatible with freedom, even if it reveals that willing and running belong to man, whereas showing mercy and bringing the matter to completion belong to God, after discussing the cited passage from Jeremiah:

> “The same may also be said of this: ‘It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy.’ ‘Why, then,’ you ask, ‘do I run, or why do I will, unless the whole matter lies within my own power?’ So that, while you will and while you run, you may win for yourself divine assistance and benevolence, so that he may help you, stretch out his hand, and bring you all the way to the end. For if you remove this, and cease both to run and to will, God will not stretch out his hand, but will himself also withdraw. And how is this established? Hear what Jerusalem says: ‘How often I wished to gather your children, and you were unwilling? Behold, your house will be left desolate.’ Do you see that, because they were unwilling, God also withdrew? Therefore it is necessary for us likewise to will and to run, so that we may also win God’s favor.”

Man therefore wills and runs, according to the Apostle’s teaching, and this is plainly man’s act, although he has previously been touched and anticipated by God. Nevertheless, unless he were pleased to do so, neither would he will nor run; yet the successful outcome and completion of the undertaking must be awaited from God who shows mercy. For this reason the completion of what we have willed and chosen through his inspiration is said to belong to him.

To demonstrate, therefore, that only assisting grace is being expressed, he says that this serves to indicate how insignificant everything we contribute to salvation is when compared with the perfection and completion that comes from heaven and advances our efforts—efforts that otherwise would come to nothing:

> “Human willing alone is not sufficient for bringing salvation to completion, nor is mortal running capable of attaining heavenly things and receiving the crown of God’s heavenly calling, unless this very good will, this ready purpose, and whatever industry there may be in you are either helped or fortified by divine assistance.”

And therefore, he says, the Apostle speaks very appropriately: “It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy.” It is as if we were to say of agriculture what is written: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth.” Thus neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the growth.

Just as, therefore, when a crop has brought forth good and abundant fruits to perfect maturity, no one will piously and appropriately say that the farmer made those fruits, but will acknowledge that they were granted by God, so likewise our perfection is indeed not produced while we are inactive and idle; yet its completion is attributed not to us but to God, who is the first and principal cause of the work.

And after much else he concludes:

> “In the course of our life, the labor must indeed be undertaken by us, and effort and diligence must be applied; but salvation, the fruit of our labor, must be hoped for from God.”

Thus the Apostle’s passage, properly explained, agrees beautifully with the passage we are clearing of suspicion in Valerian.

### 8.

I append a passage from Psalm 80, which St. Augustine, *On Two Letters against the Pelagians*, book II, chapter 7, says is the counterpart of the passage we already cited from Proverbs 16: “The heart of man directs his way, but it belongs to the Lord to direct his steps.” Namely, the passage from the psalm: “Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it.”

The same author considers these words to mean the same as those which we cited from the Wise Man in Proverbs 16, and we saw that they amount to what was first proposed from the Apostle and employed by Valerian. Therefore, since things that are identical with one third thing are also identical with one another, we must admit that all these passages amount to the same thing.

In this passage from Psalm 80, then, the opening and widening of the mouth are attributed to man, but its filling to God. This does not mean that God himself does not open the mouth and lips of our heart—for he is said to open them in Exodus 4, as St. Augustine noted in *Questions on Exodus*, question 9, and Fulgentius in *On Predestination and Grace*, book I, chapter 11—but rather that we ourselves, divinely anticipated, begin the fabric of the work of justification in such a way that God, repaying grace with grace and heaping an earlier grace upon us through a new benefit of grace, comes as the consummator of the good which, because of our frailty, our many hindrances, and the very sublimity of the work, we would not have brought to perfection unless the strength of new grace had intervened from heaven, necessary both for filling us and for enabling perseverance.

In this sense, we are the ones who, having been divinely touched and anticipated, willingly open our hearts to God. He, entering through the free consent granted by us, and drawing near as we approach him, as James 4 says, fills the open mouth; he directs the steps of the man who has ordered his heart and prepared his soul, and perfects and completes what our weakness rightly willed but could not complete.

This is the full and perfect gift of grace which God is said to give when the will has been applied through consent and the bosom of the heart has thus been opened, as the author of the *Ladder of Paradise* elegantly explains, chapter 10, volume IX of Augustine:

> “What does it profit a man, if through meditation he sees what must be done, unless through the help of prayer and the grace of God he grows strong enough to obtain it? ‘Every good gift and every perfect gift,’ he says, ‘comes down from above, from God.’ Without him we can do nothing, but he himself performs works in us—not, however, entirely without us. We are God’s fellow workers, as the Apostle says. For God wishes us to pray to him, to open to him, when he comes and waits at the door, the bosom of our will, and to consent to him. He demanded this consent from the Samaritan woman when he said, ‘Call your husband.’ ‘I wish to pour grace into you; you apply your free will.’”

Yet just as the infusion of sanctifying grace follows that application of the will as its disposition, so the opening of the heart through free consent, and that supernatural approach of ours to God, was preceded by a purely gratuitous anticipation and by a knocking upon the human being that was not free. Thus our willing—that willing which is like a rudiment placed by us, whereupon God approaches as the one who perfects and completes—has its origin in the same source from which it receives perfection. For unless God had been present to those who were not thinking, and still less to those who were willing, stirring and moving them beforehand, our willing would not have arisen in a form capable of being perfected by God.

### 9.

Nor should that other passage in the Psalmist be understood differently: “Draw near to God, and be enlightened.” Nor should the other passage in James be understood differently: “Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you.”

God is said to draw near to us when, after man’s prior approach and free dispositions, he adds what belongs to himself and, to that extent, enlightens the man who until then had remained in darkness—man illuminating himself with the light of knowledge by his own free will, as St. Jerome explains in his commentary on Ecclesiastes 2, concerning the words “It is not good for man,” and so forth.

The same thing is expressed in another way: because man willed, God adds completion and perfection; or, as Isaiah says in chapter 30, we wait for the Lord to have mercy on us; or man prepares his heart for the Lord, as we are admonished in 1 Samuel 3; or, finally, man anticipates him in the morning and cries out, as is said in Psalm 118.

Just as, therefore, no one would mark as erroneous these expressions, suggested by the Holy Spirit to the canonical writers, or declare man’s approach and free drawing near contrary to divine grace that anticipates him—for it is certain that, although divine anticipation is not expressed in those passages, it is not thereby denied in them but understood—so the expression which we are clearing of suspicion in Valerian, since it is akin to those expressions or even genuine in meaning, could, without inconvenience, and indeed ought, to be granted the same charitable interpretation rather than made an occasion of accusation.

I think that these examples from Scripture are sufficient for the present to provide some taste of the matter and to show how weak Valerian’s accusation is, especially at the point where it is most vehement.

---

## CHAPTER IX. Fathers of the highest authority would have fallen under the same accusation as Valerian.

### 1.

Nothing can show more clearly how empty Valerian’s accusation of Semipelagianism was than demonstrating that Fathers of the highest authority, whose doctrinal orthodoxy is beyond doubt, spoke in precisely the same way, without complaint, as Valerian spoke in the passage where there seems to be the greatest opportunity for charging him with Semipelagianism—namely, where he said that willing belongs to us, but completion to God. For everyone can see how empty the other accusations are.

I shall not produce every Father whom I could cite, but only certain selected ones. Nor shall I heap together everything in their writings that might serve this purpose; I shall merely offer a few individual passages, so similar to the statements condemned in Valerian that an egg is not more like an egg, nor a drop more like a drop.

What weight the judgment of the Fathers ought to carry with any prudent theologian in the matter of grace, and how cautiously one must proceed in condemning what the Fathers have used concerning it, however slippery or ambiguous it may appear, is evident from the matter itself. St. Fulgentius teaches the same in book I of *On the Truth of Predestination*, chapter 15:

> “It is fitting that, in each of those statements in which we are uncertain because of some cloud of obscurity, we should cling to the definitions of the holy Fathers, whom God’s anticipating mercy freely enlightened so that they might believe, and whom his following mercy spiritually instructed so that they might teach.”

### 2.

Let Origen be the first to enter the field. His thoroughly Catholic judgment concerning grace can be gathered from many other passages, but it is expressed most clearly in book VII of *Against Celsus*, page 414, column 1. Origen wrote no differently from Valerian in homily 12 on Numbers, concerning the words “Having departed from the well, they came to Mattanah,” and says, among other things:

> “From Mattanah we come to Nahaliel, which is interpreted as ‘FROM GOD.’ What does ‘FROM GOD’ mean? After we have offered what comes from ourselves, we come to obtain what comes from God. For when we have offered him our faith and affection, then he also bestows upon us the various gifts of the Holy Spirit, concerning which the Apostle says, ‘But all things are from God.’”

There Origen calls “faith and affection” the free assent of the will, by which we cooperate with God as he urges us toward the good, as is clear from what immediately precedes. Thus this passage from Origen plainly amounts to the passage which appeared diseased in Valerian.

The same Origen, in homily 24 on the same book, argues clearly in the same sense concerning the words “Whatever man makes a vow,” and says, among other things:

> “God therefore wishes first to receive something from us, and then himself to bestow something upon us, so that he may appear to bestow his gifts and favors upon those who merit them, and not without reason.”

He makes clear that what God asks to be placed first by us is a voluntary turning toward God with groaning, and a turning toward the heart; this turning is placed first by us before God’s subsequent gifts, although we are nevertheless anticipated beforehand.

St. Hilary has much greater authority. He is, as St. Jerome aptly called him, “the Rhône of Latin eloquence,” and the same Jerome, writing to Laeta, bears abundant witness to the complete sincerity of his doctrine and its freedom from error on every side.

Hilary, therefore, in his commentary on Psalm 118, on the letter *nun*, concerning the words “I have acquired by inheritance,” and so forth, speaks as follows:

> “So that the statement often made by many may have no authority of reason—when they assert that it is God’s peculiar gift that anyone should be occupied with God’s matters and works, excusing their unbelief by saying that, since God’s will toward them has ceased, they remain unbelievers—there is indeed from God the gift of remaining in faith, but the origin of beginning is from us. Our will must have this as its proper contribution from itself: that it should will, so that God may give increase to the one who begins; for our weakness cannot obtain completion by itself, yet the merit of attaining completion comes from the beginning of the will.”

A corrupt edition prepared by Erasmus gives the words “the origin of beginning is from us” in the form “the origin of hindering is from us.” It is evident in itself that this does not agree with Hilary’s purpose, and the point is confirmed by what follows: “so that God may give increase to the one who begins,” and “it comes from the beginning of the will.” These expressions plainly support the reading of the earlier words that I have given.

As those earlier words stand, Hilary’s passage is just as favorable to Valerian on account of the later statements, which are found everywhere in the same form. They may seem to express the exclusion of gratuitous anticipation; in reality, however, they do not exclude it. They merely show what man must contribute from himself to salvation after divine movement, with God’s help.

This is admirably illustrated by what the same Hilary says on the same psalm, on the letter *he*, concerning the words “Incline my heart to your testimonies,” where he addresses the same difficulty: how can the man who does not attain salvation be at fault if salvation is from God?

> “The prophet has removed every occasion for this impious excuse. First, when he prays, he performs the duty appropriate to his weakness; then he joins human devotion to divine gifts. For when he says, ‘Establish your law for me, O Lord, the way of your commandments,’ he shows, in accordance with the humility of our prayer, what belongs to God. But when he adds, ‘And I shall seek it always,’ he promises the duty of his devotion. In the other passages too he joined both elements together in a kind of mutual embrace, when he asked to be led in the path and also willed that very thing. First he placed before God, with honor, the things that come from God; then, in pure confession, he added what came from himself. He therefore prays that God may grant. Thus, when we pray, the beginning is from us, but the gift is from him. Then, because the gift of our beginning is his, it is again from us that it should be sought, obtained, and preserved. Here, then, is a beginning from us, so that the gift and completion may be from God.”

Just as St. Hilary, while acknowledging that beginning of ours, did not overturn what he had immediately before conceded—namely, that the first place in the matter of salvation must be given to God—so neither should all who speak similarly, or even more mildly (as Valerian in fact did), be accused of denying divine anticipation or of defending Semipelagianism.

The same St. Hilary, in canon 6 on Matthew, concerning the words “Many will say to me,” and so forth, rebukes vain boasters of their works, as though anything they say or do belonged properly to them and not everything were accomplished by the invoked power of God. He then adds:

> “That blessed eternity must therefore be merited by us; and something must be supplied from what is our own, so that we may will the good and avoid every evil.”

He expressly says that willing the good is from what is ours and proper to us, while affirming that the invoked power of God accomplishes everything. This is precisely the same sentence of Semipelagianism that was marked against Valerian. Whatever gloss, then, the accuser applies to these words of Hilary, we shall apply to Valerian.

### 3.

St. Macarius the Egyptian, disciple of St. Antony and contemporary of St. Hilary, explicitly and clearly attributes the beginning of salvation to God in homily 37. After saying many things in this sense, he writes:

> “Do not therefore suppose that you anticipated the Lord in virtue, in accordance with the one who says, ‘He himself is the one who works in us both to will and to accomplish according to his good pleasure.’”

He immediately adds a question and answer which explain the matter under discussion with great clarity.

> “What, then, does God command man to do?”
>
> “We said earlier that man has a readiness of spirit from nature, and God also requires this. He therefore commands him first to know; when he has known, to love; and by his will to apply himself. But for the mind to be exercised, to endure labor, or to accomplish some work, the grace of the Lord is granted to the one who wills and believes.”

The human will is therefore like assistance implanted in us by nature; but in the absence of the will, God himself does nothing, although he could, precisely because of the freedom of free choice.

> “The perfection, then, of the work of the spirit is situated in the human will.”

And shortly afterward:

> “He himself says: ‘How often I wished to gather your children, and you were unwilling?’ Let us therefore believe from this that he himself gathers us, but requires from us only the will. And what indication of the will can there be except voluntary labor?”

He adds a remarkable comparison between an instrument of art and man in the work of his salvation. Just as an instrument remains unmoved unless it is set in motion by the craftsman, so the soul, although it labors in doing what is good, requires God to be secretly working within it.

Similar statements occur in part in homily 4, near the middle. Everything for which Valerian was blamed is contained in these passages. Macarius mentions voluntary or spontaneous labor, and the consent of the will which is required from us so that God may work in us. God arranges our freedom with such reverence that, although he is able, he nevertheless does not wish to bestow the grace by which the work of the spirit is perfected except upon one who wills.

This does not concern the first and anticipatory grace, which he had established most explicitly a few lines earlier and also acknowledged with complete clarity in homily 1, page 6; homily 11, page 143; homily 15, page 180; homily 26, pages 345 and 347; and homily 29, page 388. It concerns cooperating grace, by which free consent is brought forth—consent which God does not produce together with us except because we will.

St. Macarius therefore rightly concludes that, although we do not anticipate God in the work of virtue, the perfection of the work of the spirit—that is, the spiritual work to which we have been anticipated and urged by God, and which God brings to its perfection and completion—rests in the human will.

According to St. Macarius, the perfection of the work is supplied by God, but in response to the demand of the human will, divinely anticipated; yet God did not await a demand of the will before anticipating it.

St. Macarius may have learned this doctrine from his teacher, the great Antony. For, according to St. Athanasius, chapter 15 of the *Life*, section 33, Blessed Antony affirmed that in this matter nothing but our will is awaited.

Nothing more suitable to the supposed stumbling blocks in Valerian can be brought forward.

### 4.

St. Optatus of Milevis, *Against Parmenianus*, book II, near the middle:

> “You yourselves, who wish to appear holy and innocent before men, tell us from where comes this holiness which you appropriate to yourselves so freely. The Apostle John does not dare to profess it, for he says: ‘If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.’ The man who said this wisely reserved himself for the grace of God. It belongs to the Christian to will what is good, and, in God, to run well in what he has willed; but it has not been given to man to bring it to completion, so that, after the stages which man must complete, something may remain for God, where he may come to the aid of one who is failing. For he alone is perfection, and the only one who is perfect is God’s Son, Christ. All the others are only partially perfect, because willing is ours, running is ours, but completion is God’s. Hence blessed Paul the Apostle says: ‘It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of him to whom God’s grace belongs.’ For perfect holiness was not given by Christ our Savior but promised. Finally, he says: ‘You shall be holy, because I also am holy,’ he who alone is holy and perfect. He did not say, ‘You are holy,’ but said, ‘You shall be holy.’ Why, then, do you arrogantly claim perfect holiness for yourselves?”

It would be superfluous to demonstrate how closely these statements agree with what was viewed with suspicion in Valerian.

Nor can St. Optatus’s authority be evaded by admitting that he fell into error. For St. Augustine, in book I of *Against Parmenianus*, chapter 3, and book III of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 4, and Fulgentius, book II *To Monimus*, cite him with praise as a writer who is Catholic in every respect.

### 5.

St. Cyril of Jerusalem, at the end of the preface to the *Catecheses*:

> “It is mine to speak, yours to act, but God’s to bring to completion.”

And in *Catechesis* 1, after he had stated that the flowers of the mystical plants had appeared and had added his desire that the fruit also be brought to perfection—plainly by God—he continues:

> “For God is generous and inclined to beneficence; he waits only for each person’s own will. Therefore the Apostle added, ‘Those who are called saints according to the purpose.’ When the purpose is present as one’s own, it makes you called.”

What Cyril says God awaits—our purpose and our will—is precisely what Valerian said: willing belongs to us. And when Cyril desires our beginnings to be perfected, and the fruit to follow from the flowers, through God’s generosity and beneficence once our assent and purpose have been supplied, he acknowledges what Valerian affirmed: completion belongs to God.

Cyril says that God awaits the will, not a bare will giving the beginning to human salvation from itself, but a will that has been anticipated and cooperates with grace already at work. To the will that thus follows divine anticipation, the most generous giver returns richer assistance, completion, and every good thing.

The same Cyril teaches most splendidly that the anticipation of the human will comes from God in *Catechesis* 16, where he speaks of the Holy Spirit. He elegantly describes the Spirit as the “Great Superintendent” and “dispenser of graces”—an appellation corresponding to the one by which he is called “Superintendent of God’s blessings” in St. Ambrose, book I *On the Holy Spirit—as breathing upon our wills and anticipating us in every work of piety.

### 6.

St. Basil, in his commentary on Isaiah 6, concerning the words “Whom shall I send?” speaks as follows:

> “Observe the exact discipline and cautious wisdom of speech appropriate to a truthful prophet. Two questions are answered by a single response: ‘Whom shall I send, and who will go?’ ‘Behold, here I am; send me.’ He did not add, ‘And I will go.’ For undertaking this apostolic mission lies with us and depends upon our choice; but strengthening it unto perfection belongs to him who fortifies us by the infusion of grace, namely God.”

Isaiah therefore replied according to what belonged to free and elective will: “Behold, here I am; send me.” But what belonged to grace he left to the Lord, since, conscious of his own weakness, he did not dare to promise that he would go.

What is this other than what Valerian said: willing belongs to us, but completion to God?

### 7.

Gregory of Nyssa, brother of Basil the Great—the man whom everyone calls “the father of the Fathers,” as Epiphanius the deacon says at the council, session 6, part 5—gives an excellent account of the necessary connection between free will and grace in his little work *On the Purpose of the Christian*. He clearly teaches that willing belongs to us and completion to God.

While exhorting many people to grow in holiness and to cooperate with the assisting Spirit of grace, he says, among other things:

> “Certainly, the increase of the body, so that it may grow, does not lie within us. Nature does not measure a man’s stature according to his judgment and desire, but according to its own impulse and necessity. But in the renewal of the soul’s growth, its measure and beauty, which the grace of the Spirit bestows, depend upon our purpose, through the zeal of the one who has received it. For the more he extends his labors for piety, the more the greatness of his soul is also extended. And the grace of the same Spirit grants eternal life and the ineffable joy that is in heaven; but love, through faith and labors, obtains the reception of these gifts and the dignity of enjoying grace. When the justice of works and the grace of the Spirit, in which the soul has cooperated, advance together toward the same end, they jointly fill the blessed life; but when separated from one another, they provide no benefit to the soul. For the grace of God cannot frequently be present in souls that flee salvation, while the power of virtue by itself is not sufficient to raise men to the complete form of life. ‘Unless the Lord builds the house and guards the city, those who build it have labored in vain.’ Here we are taught that we must not imagine that the whole crown is placed in human effort, but must refer our hope of attaining the end to the will of God.”

Thus speaks Nyssa, in complete agreement with Valerian. He acknowledges that God’s call to help us depends upon our being moved beforehand, and expressly establishes that completion comes from God.

### 8.

St. Gregory Nazianzen, whose authority in Christian doctrine is such that no one has ever dared to bring an accusation against his words—as these are the words of St. Thomas, *Summa Theologiae* I, question 61, article 3—and whom St. Augustine expressly sets against the Semipelagians with respect to the beginning of salvation in *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 19, writes as follows in Oration 31.

There he discusses Christ’s statement “to whom it has been given,” and dispels the manifold heretical inclination hidden beneath the wicked distortion of those words:

> “I too grant that some people have greater aptitude than others, and some less. But I insist that aptitude alone is not at all sufficient for attaining perfection. There must be a reason that arouses it, so that nature may come forth into action, just as flint struck by iron produces fire. When you hear ‘to whom it has been given,’ add, ‘It has been given to those who are willing,’ and to those who possess such an inclination of spirit. For when you hear, ‘It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy,’ I think you should understand the same thing.”

When he says that the attainment of salvation is given by God to those who will, this is equivalent to saying that willing belongs to us, but completion to God. Yet it is clear that these words do not conflict with the beginning of salvation being from God, from what he immediately adds, proving, and drawing from Romans 9, that our very willing is also from God.

### 9.

St. Ambrose, for whose sound assertion of grace St. Augustine often bears witness—for example, in Letter 107, in *On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 44, and in *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapters 8, 13, 19, and 23—speaks most appropriately to our purpose in Sermon 10 on Psalm 118, concerning verse 4:

> “God says to Moses: ‘I will have mercy on whom I have had mercy, and I will show mercy to whom I have shown mercy.’ Therefore it is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy. Perhaps you will say, ‘Then we ought neither to will nor to run.’ Yet God is accustomed to abandon the negligent. He does not say this, therefore; let us consider what he does say. Perseverance is not of the man who wills or runs. It is not in man’s power, but it belongs to God who shows mercy, so that he may complete what he has begun.”

You see that Ambrose attributes willing to human power, but assigns completion, or perfection and perseverance, to God. Valerian says no more and nothing different.

There is another excellent passage in St. Ambrose, at the end of his letter to Justus—Letter 63, otherwise book I, letter 10:

> “Increases come through nature, which possesses the grace of a divine gift; God—namely, that most excellent and divine nature and substance of the Trinity—gives completion and perfection.”

He does not use “increase” for the augmentation or progress of something already created, but for its beginning and first production. He used it in this sense shortly before, concerning the Apostle’s words in 1 Corinthians 3: “Neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase.”

St. Ambrose therefore acknowledges that this increase of holy works occurs through nature, which possesses the grace of a divine gift. For the very freedom by which we wish to act and follow God is plainly a great gift of God, even though it is known to us by nature; but God gives completion and perfection.

Beyond what nature performs by its spontaneous capacity, so that divinely implanted seeds may rise—as Ambrose had said shortly before—that is, beyond what nature can contribute from itself, the prevenient grace of God is required. By this grace God completes and perfects our imperfect work; he advances us toward the fruits of supernatural works, which we could not even begin through bare nature.

This is precisely what Valerian said: willing belongs to us, completion to God. An egg is not more like an egg.

### 10.

St. Chrysostom, in his first homily on the Epistle to the Hebrews, speaks in this way:

> “We must first choose what is good, and then God introduces what belongs to him. He does not anticipate our wills, lest our free choice be harmed. But when we have chosen, he then brings us abundant assistance.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Our part is only to choose and to will; God’s is to accomplish and bring to perfection.”

The same is meant by what he says in homily 17 on John, concerning the words “Jesus turned and saw them following,” and so forth:

> “From this we may be admonished that God, in his benefits toward us, does not anticipate our wills, but that the beginning must be from us. Yet when we present ourselves with a ready and prepared spirit to receive grace, he then offers us many opportunities for salvation.”

And in homily 42 *To the People*, treating the words “Do not give your foot to be moved”—for this is how he reads the passage—he says:

> “He did not say, ‘Do not be moved,’ but, ‘Do not give.’ Therefore giving lies with us, not with anyone else. For if we wish to stand firm and unmoved, we shall not be moved. What, then? Is nothing in God? Everything is in God, but not in such a way that free choice in us is violated.”

If, then, the wicked are in God, why does he not accuse? “For this reason,” he says, “I stated that free choice in us must not be violated. Thus they are in us and in God. We must first choose what is good, and then he introduces what belongs to him. He does not anticipate our wills, lest he violate our freedom. But when we have chosen, he then brings us great assistance.”

From this he resolves the difficulty arising from the Apostle’s words in Romans 9: “It is not of him who wills,” and so forth, which seem false if our salvation is also in us. In addition to his first explanation of those words—namely, that the Apostle uttered them in the person of an opponent, putting them forward as an objection and question rather than as an assertion—he adds a second:

> “It can also be said that the one to whom the greater part belongs is said to possess the whole. For it is ours to choose and will, but God’s to make effective and bring to completion. Since the greater part is his, he testifies, speaking according to human custom, that the whole is his. Let us act in the same way. Consider what I mean. We see a house that has been well built, and we say, ‘It is all the work of the builder,’ although it does not belong entirely to him, but also to the laborers, to the master who supplied the materials, and to many others. Nevertheless, because he contributed more, we say that the whole belongs to him. So it is here as well. Again, where there are many, we say that everyone is present; where there are few, we say that no one is present. So Paul too says: ‘It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy.’”

Here he attributes great things to God for one reason: so that we may not become exalted.

> “Whether you run or hasten,” he says, “do not think the merit is yours. For unless you obtain favor from above, everything is in vain. Yet it is clear that you will attain what you desire so long as you run, so long as you will. He did not therefore say that we run in vain, but that we run in vain if we think the whole belongs to us, unless we assign the greater part to God. Nor did God wish the whole to be his, lest it appear that he crowns us without cause; nor, again, did he wish the whole to be ours, lest we fall into arrogance. For if, while possessing the smaller part, we think highly of ourselves, what would happen if we were the authors of the whole?”

Finally, while treating the words “Wash yourselves, be clean; and if your sins are like purple, I will make them white as snow”—for this is how he reads the passage—he adds:

> “You see that we must first cleanse ourselves, and then God cleanses us. For after he had first said, ‘Wash yourselves, be clean,’ he then added, ‘I will make you white.’”

I have already cited, in chapter 7 above, the passage from homily 32 of the *Imperfect Work*, which Doctors Thomas and Bonaventure cite as Chrysostom’s. There is also another beautiful passage in the homily on the seven Maccabees, which is number 44 in volume I of the Greek-Latin edition. There God is introduced as speaking in this way:

> “I am not such a director of the contest as to place the outcome of the struggle in the virtue of any of the contestants. Rather, I myself stand beside those who wrestle, provide assistance, and stretch out my hand to my athletes. What they receive through the freedom of their own choice, from the inclination of a good will, so that they may fight for my laws and my name—that it should advance in them to victory belongs to my assistance.”

Similar statements are found more than once elsewhere in Chrysostom, plainly resembling the statements for which Valerian is accused of error.

I fear, however, that someone may think me insufficiently cautious in bringing Chrysostom forward to clear Valerian and to establish that his doctrine is free of Semipelagianism. Chrysostom has long been attacked by Thomas Bradwardine, in book II of *The Cause of God*, chapter 11, as covered with this foul soot and, indeed, as the teacher of error to his disciple Cassian. Some more recent writers have made the same attempt, such as Anianus in the preface to Chrysostom’s homilies on Matthew, whom Sixtus of Siena cites and approves in book V of the *Bibliotheca*, annotation 101—although, for my part, I find nothing of the kind in Anianus himself, but rather detect the contrary quite plainly—Molina, part I, question 14, article 13, disputation 41; Toledo on John 6, annotation 20; and Vasquez, who turns a deaf ear to every defense of Chrysostom, part I, disputation 89, chapter 4, and disputation 91, chapters 8 and 9.

Nevertheless, it has always seemed remarkable to me that Chrysostom did not suffer this accusation from the Pelagians themselves, yet should endure it from Catholics after so many centuries—especially since, although the Pelagians collected Chrysostom’s passages concerning original sin so zealously on behalf of their error and opposed them to Catholics [Col. 0822B], as St. Augustine testifies in his work *Against Julian*, they nevertheless became so blind in this particular respect that they failed to recognize an error which, according to the doctors cited, is so frequent in Chrysostom. What is more, Chrysostom contains such frequent, repeated, and lucid assertions of the wholly gratuitous beginning of salvation that they entirely remove any suspicion that he held this error. I pass over the homily on Adam and Eve, which contains, with complete clarity, the Catholic doctrine of grace against the Pelagians and their remnants. I say that I pass over this homily because its attribution to Chrysostom is doubtful and—at least in some respects, insofar as it is inserted in Celestine’s letter to the bishops of Gaul—spurious.

Yet one may read in most of Chrysostom’s unquestionably genuine works, and expressly and distinctly, a gratuitous prevenient grace—particularly in Homilies 19, 22, 23, 28, and 38 on Genesis. In these passages he openly admits a grace that precedes and anticipates our prayers; and beautifully so in Homily 12 on First Corinthians [Col. 0822C], on the words, “What do you have that you did not receive?”; also in Homilies 13, 44, and 71 on John; Homily 4 on the Praise of Paul; Homily 5 on the Second Epistle to the Thessalonians; Homilies 1 and 8 on the Epistle to the Philippians; and most clearly in Psalm 143, on the words, “Lord, what is man, that you have made yourself known to him?” Likewise in Homily 70 on Matthew, on the words, “Go out quickly into the streets,” where he holds that only what follows the calling made and freely bestowed by grace pertains to our diligence. Homily 24 on the Epistle to the Hebrews likewise says that the observance of the commandments ought to be valued more highly by a Christian than miracles, and gives as the reason that miracles are purely God’s gifts, whereas the observance of the commandments, after God’s gift, is also a matter of our own effort. He says, “after God’s gift”—that is, after divine prevenience. For concerning accompanying grace, precisely because it accompanies us, it could not properly and truly be said that doing good is our effort after God’s gift. Likewise, Homily 28 on the Epistle to the Hebrews, on the words, “Looking to the author of faith.” Most magnificently and explicitly, however, he teaches divine prevenience in Homily 83 on Matthew, on the words, “Before [Col. 0822D] the cock crows.”

Accordingly, the following have rightly contended to clear Chrysostom of this accusation in this respect: Jeremias of Constantinople, in *Censura Orientalis Ecclesiae* 18; Driedo, *Concordia*, chapter 4, in the middle; Bellarmine, *On Grace and Free Choice*, book VI, chapter 6; Fonseca, *Metaphysics*, book VI, chapter 2, question 5, section 10; Suárez, *On Predestination*, book II, chapter 8; Justinian, on chapter 2 of the Epistle to the Philippians, on the words, “God is the one who works”; and many others. Indeed, Dominicus Soto, commenting on chapter 1 of the Epistle to the Romans, on the words, “Who was predestined,” condemns Chrysostom’s accusers on this point as impious; Driedo, in the place noted, condemns them as displaying great shamelessness. Thus there seems to be no reason to doubt the soundness of Chrysostom’s doctrine on this matter. Consequently, the explanation which we grant for the passages cited from Chrysostom cannot fairly be denied to one similar passage in Valerian.

### 11. St. Isidore of Pelusium

St. Isidore of Pelusium, a disciple of Chrysostom, writes as follows in Book IV, Letter 171:

> Not only those things which are not [Col. 0823A] in our power, as you, wise man, suppose, but also those over which we are masters: unless a great abundance of assistance comes to us from divine Providence, we shall not be able to bring them to a perfect end and completion. This assistance, however, will certainly be present to those people who, without evasion or any pretext, undertake the things that lie within their power and omit nothing that seems conducive to obtaining it.

The first words clearly attribute completion to God; the latter, however, attribute willing to us. But lest one think that Isidore ascribes this willing to the powers of nature, hear what he adds:

> For divine Providence, which arouses those who are unwilling and urges them to become willing, will surely raise those who are willing and do everything, acting with diligence, to the summit of excellent deeds.

And most explicitly, in Book II, Letter 72:

> Once the power of preceding divine assistance is recognized, whoever wills, labors, and sets everything in motion—for bare willing is not enough—then learns, then bears fruit, then attains salvation.

See also Book II, Letter 266, and Book III, Letter 271.

### 12. Hilary the Deacon

Hilary the Deacon—whom St. Jerome, in the *Dialogue [Col. 0823B] Against Lucifer*, called “the Deucalion of the world” because he introduced rebaptism—clearly anticipated Valerian in his *Commentaries on Paul* on the words of Philippians 2, “God is the one who works in you both to will and to act according to his good pleasure.” These commentaries are wrongly attributed to Ambrose, since they belong to this Hilary, as an erudite man noted in the Louvain edition, in Book IV of St. Augustine’s *Against Two Letters*, chapter 4. Hilary writes:

> The Apostle testifies that God assists good endeavors. For he always refers every grace to God, so that willing is ours, but bringing to completion is God’s.

Nor can Hilary’s schism or even his heresy be brought against him here. For regarding the matter of grace, and the issues relevant to the Pelagians, he held Catholic doctrine. Otherwise St. Augustine, in Book IV of *Against Two Letters*, chapter 4, would not have brought forward against the Pelagians a passage from these *Commentaries* on chapter 5 of Romans, in his explanation of the words, “In whom all sinned.” And since Augustine cites these commentaries under the name of St. Hilary, one may reasonably conjecture that this Hilary repented and returned to the Church and to the entirely true [Col. 0823C] faith.

That St. Augustine, deceived by the similarity of names, attributed these commentaries to Hilary of Poitiers, and therefore called their author Saint Hilary, is too crude an explanation and unworthy of Augustine’s discernment and acumen, given the great difference in style and composition—especially since Augustine knew that the author of those commentaries, in chapter 3 of the First Epistle to Timothy, disclosed himself to be a contemporary, or nearly a contemporary, of Pope Damasus. This agrees well with the age of Hilary the Deacon, but not with that of Hilary of Poitiers.

### 13. St. Jerome

St. Jerome’s doctrine of grace—against Rufinus, who was suspected of Semipelagianism—was approved by Gelasius in the decree *The Holy Roman Church* and in Letter 7, addressed to the bishops of Picenum; Jerome likewise professes in *Dialogue 3 Against the Pelagians* that he adheres to St. Augustine’s doctrine of grace; and Augustine, in turn, presents Jerome as a defender of Catholic doctrine against the Pelagians in Book I of *Against Julian*, chapter 2, and near the end of Book II, where he discusses the false rumors spread by Pelagius [Col. 0823D] against St. Jerome, as though Jerome, out of rivalry, had envied him. Jerome, then, writes as follows in *Dialogue 3 Against the Pelagians*:

> Let it be granted that baptism forgives past sins but does not preserve future righteousness, which is guarded by labor, effort, diligence, and, above all, always by God’s clemency—so that asking is ours, but granting what is asked is his; beginning is ours, completion is his; offering what we can is ours, fulfilling what we cannot is his.

Again, farther on in the same dialogue:

> Where mercy and grace are present, free choice ceases in part; it consists only in our willing and desiring and giving assent to what is pleasing. It is now in the Lord’s power to enable us, through his aid and assistance, to accomplish what we desire, what we labor for, and what we strive toward.

The same author writes in his commentary on chapter 3 of Ezekiel, on the words, “And I opened my mouth”:

> “I opened my mouth,” says the prophet, “because I was told, ‘Open your mouth and eat.’” With his mouth opened, the Lord bestowed food, [Col. 0824A] so that the beginnings of willing might be in us, while we receive perfection from the Lord. For it is not of the one who wills, nor of the one who runs, but of God who has mercy. Nevertheless, both willing and running belong to our free choice.

And in Book II *Against Jovinianus*:

> Just as God is the one who perfects good works—for it is not of the one who wills, nor of the one who runs, but of God who has mercy and assists us so that we may reach the finish—in evil things and sins, our seeds are the incitements, but their completion belongs to the devil.

In a letter to Theodosius and the other anchorites, speaking of the effort to escape the darkness of the world through supernatural acts, he says:

> I said this before in person, and now I do not cease to express in writing my desire: my mind is swept toward this pursuit by every form of longing. It is now yours to make the outcome follow my will. It is mine to will; it belongs to your prayers that I may both will and be able.

For you will obtain for me the help of God, whose role it is to bring to completion.

What could be more genuinely like Valerian’s passage? Again, in Letter 8:

> It is not of the one who wills, nor of the one who runs, but of God who has mercy. And yet willing and not willing are ours; and even that which is ours is not ours without God’s mercy.

[Col. 0824B] No one has ever accused Catholic doctrine of opposing the wholly gratuitous beginning of salvation, even though St. Jerome so consistently fights for grace against its enemies. In Letter 8, near the middle, he clearly teaches Demetrias how these words are to be understood when they say that willing is ours, but completion belongs to God:

> Willing and not willing are ours; yet even that which is ours is not ours without God’s mercy.

And in his letter to Ctesiphon:

> Willing and running are mine; but this very “mine” will not be mine without God’s continual assistance. For the same Apostle says, “God is the one who works in us both to will and to accomplish.”

### 14. St. Augustine

St. Augustine, in Book I of the *Retractions*, chapter 23, and in *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 3, in both places examining a passage from an exposition of certain propositions of the Epistle to the Romans which he had published when younger, expressly admits that it can truly and Catholicly be said that willing is ours, but completion belongs to God. He does correct, however, what he had additionally said in those propositions—namely, that believing is ours—because, as he admits, he had not yet [Col. 0824C] adequately examined the mysteries of grace. When explaining those propositions, he had believed that the act of faith did not arise from grace but was a product of nature.

Thus he absolutely retracts what he had said in that exposition, proposition 61: “What we believe is ours; but what we do well belongs to him who gives the Holy Spirit to believers.” Yet he admits as Catholic what he had added there:

> Believing and willing are ours, but giving believers and those who will the ability to do good is God’s.

For concerning willing, although it is supernatural—as is the willing involved in believing—it is correctly said to be ours because of freedom of choice. As he adds in the same place:

> Although it is also God’s, by reason of divine grace preparing and strengthening the will.

Insofar as believing is subordinate to our willing, through which it is brought about, believing itself is also ours, because it occurs only when we will it. In this sense, and subject to this rule, Augustine acknowledges in the passages cited that it is entirely true to say that willing is ours, but that God grants the ability to complete or perform the act.

[Col. 0824D]

In the same passages he confirms and strongly commends what he had said in proposition 62:

> When, after the calling, we have willed, our willing and running are not sufficient unless God also supplies strength to those who run and brings them to the place to which he calls them.

He then added:

> It is therefore evident that what we do well is not of the one who wills, nor of the one who runs, but of God who has mercy.

This is entirely true. But it is precisely the same as the opinion which was accused of error in Valerian. For Augustine acknowledges our willing, or our will, in the work of salvation, and wishes perfection to be added to this willing by God, the author and consummator of grace. This is the one thing Valerian said. Consequently, if the accusation against Valerian stands, then—God forbid—St. Augustine must be condemned for Semipelagianism in that judgment of his, recorded in the *Retractions*, concerning a proposition entirely genuine to him, which is both argued and confirmed in *On the Predestination of the Saints*, where the agitation against the Semipelagians was at its height. [Col. 0825A] That book was written expressly against them at the end of St. Augustine’s life.

Another passage of St. Augustine, in Questions 68 and 83, is especially clear:

> If someone, through great groaning and the sorrow of repentance, has become worthy of God’s mercy, this is not his own doing—for if he were abandoned to himself, he would perish—but the doing of the merciful God, who comes to the aid of his prayers and sorrows. For willing is not enough unless God has mercy; yet God does not have mercy on one whom he calls to peace unless the will toward peace has gone before.

That this precedence of the will toward God’s peace does not exclude God’s prevenient mercy is declared by St. Augustine himself in Book I of the *Retractions*, chapter 26, when he revisits the passage in question. Thus, when he says that the will must precede the perfect peace of the soul divinely bestowed, while that peace follows, this is plainly the same as saying that willing is ours but completion is God’s. St. Augustine therefore understands that a gratuitous divine gift precedes our willing, and that this is not denied when it is said that we freely take the beginning of willing, or that willing [Col. 0825B] is ours.

There is also a distinguished passage from St. Augustine in Question 9 on Exodus. He is discussing God’s words to Moses, “But now go, and I will open your mouth and instruct you in what you shall say,” and comparing this with Psalm 80, where God invites a person to enlarge and open his mouth, promising that God himself will fill the opened mouth. He argues as follows:

> It is sufficiently clear here that not only the instruction of the mouth but its very opening belongs to God’s will and grace. For he did not say, “Open your mouth, and I will instruct you,” but promised both himself: “I will open and I will instruct.” Elsewhere in the psalm he says, “Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it.” There he signifies the human being’s willingness to receive what God gives to one who is willing. “Open your mouth wide” pertains to the beginning of the will; “I will fill it” pertains to God’s grace.

Here the beginning of free consent is expressly assigned to the will—one already antecedently prevented and concomitantly assisted—while completion is assigned to God. That this prevenience and assistance are not explicitly stated in that [Col. 0825C] psalm passage, as they are in the words from Exodus 4, is of little importance: what is left unspoken is not for that reason denied. Thus, according to the Holy Spirit speaking through the Psalmist and interpreted by St. Augustine, once antecedent and accompanying divine assistance has been placed at hand, the will provides the beginning of forming free consent, by which it wills to receive what God gives to one who is willing. Once this beginning of the will has been established, and the human being has opened and widened his mouth in this way, God does not fail to fill or complete it.

See Augustine arguing excellently in the same direction in Sermon 7 on the *Words of the Apostle*, near the beginning. There, for the reception of the grace of divine goodness, he wishes the human being to open the bosom of his will, and he teaches that the person must adapt his will to receive what he asks God to give him. At the very end of *Against the Fundamental Epistle*, chapter 1, he writes:

> It was ours to will to seek these things; it is God’s to give what is good to those who will and ask.

These statements are so genuinely like those which are exposed to accusation [Col. 0825D] in Valerian that I cannot see whether one drop resembles another more closely.

### 15. Eucherius of Lyons

Eucherius of Lyons—or whatever other author composed Homily 11 on Easter, wrongly attributed to Eusebius of Emesa—responds to the question why God ordained that human salvation should be accomplished in the manner by which it is accomplished, rather than, by right of his supreme dominion, freeing the human being and carrying him, stiff and prostrate, to glory. Among other things, he writes:

> It seems most unjust that one who fell voluntarily should be raised unwillingly. Do you see that the care of the most compassionate physician requires the assent of his sick patient?
