Captivity was entered into through free choice; through free choice freedom was likewise to be restored. For the Lord, who opens the door, also awaits the concern of the one who knocks. I say, of the one who knocks; for unless he strives through labor to recover what he lost, he will experience neither the loss of what was lost nor the benefit of what has been restored. One who does not know how to desire a benefit cannot preserve it. The gift of the giver [Col. 0826A] is endangered if it does not find an effect in the recipient.

And shortly afterward:

> Divine Providence labors at this: because consent brought guilt to the one who was lost, let the will confer merit upon the one who has been recovered, and let the devotion of the restored person display the righteousness of the restorer—namely, while God kindly acts for the human being according to the human being’s good will, and completes and perfects what the human being had begun with affection alone, granting what belongs to him.

Thus the passages we have cited say, if not in words, at least in meaning, the same things as those which we are defending in Valerian. The meaning of both sets of passages is the one I have so often stated: the human being, divinely invited, first offers consent, knocks, and wills; and God, observing this, cooperates with the human being and completes the work to which he has drawn the will. He also provides heavenly assistance lest the person be turned from the right path by dangers that arise, so that the will may be strengthened and supported against hostile assaults and inner conflict.

But lest anyone accuse Eucherius—if he is indeed the author of the homily—of Semipelagianism [Col. 0826B] because of his affinity with Hilary of Arles, consider the passages from Homily 9. There, presenting the same doctrine more briefly, he says that the human being was not to be compelled but led to salvation: the person who had fallen by his own will was to be restored by his own will, so that there might be room for virtue and reward. Therefore God does not seize the human being by force, but by benevolence solicits and instructs him toward life:

> For the kindness of the one who invites also desires the merit of the one who assents, and the care of the most compassionate physician requires the assent of his sick patient.

He could not have borne clearer or more harmonious witness to divine prevenience, or more effectively freed himself from the stain of the Semipelagianism then at its height.

Another passage of Eucherius, relevant to this matter, deserves consideration at the end of Homily 3, addressed to monks. Among other things, he writes:

> When God sees devotion of mind, he will inspire a more ardent affection; and as much as we add [Col. 0826C] to our effort, so much will he add to our assistance; as much as we add to our diligence, so much will he add to our glory. “To the one who has, more will be given, and he will abound.”

Elsewhere he says:

> “I have placed assistance upon the mighty.”

These passages may appear open to the same criticism as the words in Valerian that are regarded with suspicion. For God’s assisting the mighty, seeking assistance for one’s effort, and inspiring affection when he sees devotion seem to have the same meaning as Valerian’s statement, “Willing is ours, completion is God’s.”

Yet Eucherius’s meaning is entirely Catholic and coheres perfectly with gratuitous prevenience. His aim is to teach that the more a human being cooperates with God’s grace, the greater the gain he makes, and the more continually he grows rich. He nevertheless wishes the beginning of the labor to have been made by God, who precedes us, and therefore wishes the entire fruit and gain of the human being’s labor to be attributed to God. For shortly before the words quoted above he says:

> Let the holy person become still holier; let us add daily to our merits, and let us presume nothing of ourselves, because everything we can do belongs to God.

Immediately after the words we previously cited as suspect, he concludes as follows, clearly removing every suspicion from those words:

> Thus grace is born from grace, and [Col. 0826D] advances serve advances, profits produce profits, and merits generate profit upon merits, so that the more someone begins to acquire, the more he strives and delights in acquiring, and the profit of acquisition nourishes the appetite for acquiring.

Since the later and earlier words of Eucherius clearly convey this Catholic meaning, despite the intervening words which we said were similar to Valerian’s passage, why should the same meaning not also be applied to Valerian’s words, when nothing in him stands in the way?

### 16. St. Dorotheus

St. Dorotheus, a frequent assertor of divine grace, is attested by St. Theodore the Studite—a man both most holy and most learned, and in his time a pillar of the faith in the East—in his *Testament*, number 4, as teaching the most sincere and Catholic doctrine throughout all his writings. Dorotheus speaks as follows in *Doctrine* 10, section 2:

> God looks upon and gladly assists the one who fights bravely and does violence to himself. Therefore, brothers, let us compel and force ourselves, lay a firm foundation, and at last will what is good. For although we are not yet [Col. 0827A] perfect, to will perfection itself and to desire what is good is the beginning and foundation of our salvation. As soon as we begin to will, we have also begun, with God’s assistance, to fight. The one who assists us in acquiring virtues will not be lacking, provided that we ourselves fight. Hence one of the Fathers used frequently to say: “Give blood and receive spirit.” That is: fight, contend, strive, and without doubt you will acquire the habit of virtue.

These words contain, in many ways, the opinion which was badly received in Valerian. For Dorotheus wishes the human being to lay the foundation of his salvation, to will and desire what is good, so that God may look upon him, divine assistance may be added, God may give him rest, and he may reach perfection. He promises that God will not be absent from this willing; and, once we have given our blood—that is, our sweat and effort, as he himself interprets it in *Doctrine* 11—he testifies that divine grace and the Spirit will not be lacking and that perfection, toward which we were striving, will follow.

Likewise, in *Doctrine* 14 he says:

> Begin with a courageous spirit and steadfast faith toward God. [Col. 0827B] Show him the resolve and effort of your mind, and you will undoubtedly feel his assistance present there for acting rightly and virtuously.

If these words were accepted in St. Dorotheus with the same severity with which his accuser wishes them to be accepted in Valerian, and if their meaning were that God is joined as helper to an effort conceived solely from the power of free choice and from human strength, being moved by that disposition and bringing it to perfection, then St. Theodore the Studite would have left a wholly false testimony to the Church at his death when he declared that nothing contrary to right and sound faith was contained in St. Dorotheus’s teachings.

For it was an established and well-known error in St. Dorotheus’s time—that is, around the year 360—and even more so in the time of St. Theodore the Studite—that is, around the year 800—to assert that divine grace is subordinated to human labor as to a disposition. Dorotheus’s meaning is therefore the one we assigned to Valerian when he spoke similarly: namely, that the human being, acting by grace and through divinely pre-given grace, lays the foundation for further [Col. 0827C] and richer assistance through the good use of earlier assistance; and that God repays him with the Spirit, approaching as the consummator of the work by supplying more abundant grace and granting perseverance. This is something the human being must await from God beyond the calling.

Pope St. Gregory, according to St. Zachary, Roman pontiff, in Letter 6 to St. Boniface of Mainz—which is extant in volume II of the *Decretal Letters of the Supreme Pontiffs* and among St. Boniface’s letters after number 137—has these words:

> Let a good work be in the will, and with God’s assistance it will be brought to perfection.

I am entirely convinced that St. Zachary is citing there no other Gregory than Gregory of Rome. For a Roman pontiff, when writing, would not introduce another Gregory without some distinguishing addition. Moreover, Zachary was exceedingly devoted to Pope Gregory and translated his *Dialogues* into Greek, as Photius reports.

I was once uncertain where this passage might be found in St. Gregory the Great. The two passages of Gregory which Serarius notes as containing these words in his scholia on the letters of St. Boniface actually contain nothing of the sort. Later, [Col. 0827D] however, I discovered that the passage occurs at the beginning of Homily 21 on the Gospels. Even if the passage were found nowhere in Gregory, it would nevertheless have to be regarded as genuinely Gregory’s, because there can be no doubt about the faith of Pope Zachary when he cites a passage of Gregory. And even if someone should stubbornly dare to deny that the words belong to Gregory, the sole authority of Pope Zachary would be more than sufficient to secure their complete vindication.

Thus the cited passage is fortified by the authority of two most holy pontiffs. It is unnecessary to explain how much protection this gives Valerian, who said nothing other than what these teachers of the faith said. In Letter 40 of Pope Hormisdas, addressed to Anastasia and Palmatia—number 34 in volume I of the *Decretal Epistles*—there are words in this pontiff’s series of letters very similar to the passage just cited:

> The effort of a good will is always accompanied by the effect of divine success.

[Col. 0828A]

### St. Ildephonsus

St. Ildephonsus writes at the beginning of Sermon 1 on the Assumption:

> Let us have good will in our affection; certainly God’s assistance will be present in the outcome.

What could be clearer? What could be more similar to Valerian’s statement?

### Bede

Bede, highly experienced in the matter of grace and an exceptionally devoted student of St. Augustine, was so far from detecting any fault in the Valerian passages under examination that in Question 13, among the various works found in volume VIII, he actually presents such a statement from the Book of Wisdom. He writes:

> God made the human being perfect, that is, one who could will the good and not will it. This is free choice: an absolute willing and not willing. Thus the human being’s willing is said in the Book of Wisdom to be natural: “Willing is ours, but completion is God’s.” Ours, that is, by nature. And the Apostle says, “Willing is present in me” by nature. But human beings corrupted this willing and this good by sinning and, as it were, extinguished it—not entirely, however, because some spark of good always remained in them. And when the Apostle says, “God works willing,” we do not understand this to mean that he first places willing in the human being, but that he awakens and revives the will which exists in the human being by nature, though corrupted [Col. 0828B] and almost extinguished. In this way we reconcile the two statements: what Scripture says, “Willing is ours,” and what the Apostle says, “God works willing,” together with free choice.

The wording “Willing is ours, but completion is God’s” does not appear in the Book of Wisdom. It is therefore necessary that Bede expressed its meaning. Perhaps he was expressing the passage from chapter 12, where it is stated that God disposes us with great reverence. That is, after he has first prevented and moved us by thought and sweetness, he does not leave us to ourselves without freedom, but awaits our free willing, or our determination of consent to an elicited act, in order to complete what it brings forth.

Perhaps he was expressing the celebrated passage on free choice from chapter 15 of Ecclesiasticus, a book which, because it is sapiential, is sometimes called “Wisdom.” Whatever may be the scriptural passage in which Bede thought the proposed statement was expressed, for the present it is enough that the statement was certain and wholly Catholic for Bede, since he also believed it to have been dictated by the Holy Spirit [Col. 0828C]. For what he had first said was found in Wisdom he immediately afterward says is found in Scripture. Thus no one can suppose that by “Wisdom” Bede initially meant the book of some noncanonical wise author.

### 17. St. John of Damascus

St. John of Damascus, in Oration 3 *On Images*, presenting the first class of those to whom worship may be offered, says that it includes the saints:

> Those who have made themselves like God as far as humanly possible, by their own will and deliberate purpose, through God dwelling and cooperating with them; they are also truly called gods, but by adoption, not by nature, and so forth.

This depends first upon the freedom of purpose and will. Then, to everyone who proposes the good with firm deliberation and determination of mind, God cooperates for good.

Likewise, in Book II of *The Orthodox Faith*, chapter 29:

> One must know that the choice of what is to be done lies within our power, but the good end lies in God’s cooperation, who rightly cooperates with those who choose what is good with a right conscience, according to his foreknowledge.

The translator renders *finem bonorum* as “the end of good things,” but he could equally, or even more properly, have translated it as “perfection.” For in that passage of Damascene there can plainly be no discussion of a final cause. The Greek word τέλος (*telos*), which Damascene uses [Col. 0828D] there, signifies not only a final cause but many other things as well, including perfection. Stobaeus noted this in the opening of chapter 3 of the *Ethical Eclogues*, where he discusses the polysemy of the word. He adds that marriage is called τέλος in the Doric dialect either because it perfects youth or because it perfects the man joined to the woman; for this reason he observes that Juno, as the patroness of marriage, was called “perfect.”

Thus Damascene plainly says the very thing Valerian says: willing and choosing are ours; completion is God’s.

### Mark the Ascetic

Mark the Ascetic, in his treatise *On Paradise*, at the final question, writes:

> God commands that a human being first know, and, having known, love and express the will. But, so that the mind may be exercised, endure labor, or complete some work, the Lord’s grace is bestowed upon the willing and believing. Therefore the human will is like an assistance implanted by nature [Col. 0829A], without which not even God does anything, although he does not lack the power to act. This is because of the freedom of human choice. Thus the perfection of the work belongs to God; the will belongs to the human being.

There is no need to compare Mark’s words with Valerian’s: they are so genuinely alike, indeed so identical. The only objection that can be made is that this Mark too is considered highly unsound. I will not examine that question here with respect to other matters. On this point, however, he is entirely sound. For when he almost copied St. Macarius in Homily 37, in the words found immediately before this final question, he clearly taught prevenient glory:

> Never think that you have preceded the Lord in virtue, according to the one who says, “He is the one who works in us both to will and to accomplish according to his good pleasure.”

### 18. Strabo of Fulda

Strabo of Fulda, in the *Ordinary Gloss* on chapter 3 of Ezekiel, on the words, “And I opened my mouth,” reproduces St. Jerome and writes:

> With his mouth opened, the Lord bestows food, so that the beginnings of willing may be in us, and we may receive the perfection of blessedness from the Lord. For it is not of the one who wills, nor of the one who runs, but of God who has mercy. [Col. 0829B] Nevertheless, willing and running belong to our free choice.

These are plainly the same as the words found in Valerian. Since Strabo made them his own after reading them in Jerome, he sufficiently showed that he detected no error in them.

### Theophylact

Theophylact, as is clear from his preface to the Gospel of Matthew and from his commentary on chapter 22, on the words “Many are called,” held thoroughly Catholic views concerning the beginning of salvation and prevenient grace. Nevertheless, in chapter 9 of his commentary on Romans, on the words “It is not of the one who wills,” he has the following:

> The Apostle seems here to abolish free choice. But he is not doing that. It is like saying of a house, “The whole thing belongs to the craftsman,” even though the work requires material and cooperators who assist him. Yet because the completion of the work depends on him, we say, “This whole thing belongs to him,” namely, to the builder; or, “This builder constructed the house.” In a similar way, God also needs our will. Yet because he completes and perfects the work, we say, “This whole thing belongs to God.”

Thus, according [Col. 0829C] to Theophylact, God completes and perfects the work of salvation; yet the consummator does not act without our will intervening. Without that will presupposed, he would not cooperate with us or complete and perfect our salvation. What else does Valerian say? Let the passage cited above, in number 9, from Chrysostom’s Homily 42 *To the People* be recalled. Theophylact clearly drew from it, and it will be beyond doubt that this was his meaning.

### 19. Philotheus of Constantinople

Philotheus of Constantinople, in his sermon for the Third Sunday of the Fast, on the Adoration of the Cross, examining Christ’s words, “If anyone wishes to come,” explains at considerable length the divine plan by which human beings retain the power of their own will in the matter of salvation. He finally concludes:

> The supreme dignity and preciousness of the good things prepared for us when we obey God is the reason why we are not dragged by force, especially since what is received by necessity and force does not endure for long.

He then adds:

> For this reason Christ does not compel, but, if someone wishes to follow, he calls him and admits him. “If [Col. 0829D] you are willing,” he says, “and listen to me.” First comes willing, and then listening. If we are unwilling, we will not be able to listen either; for all the activities of virtue and vice are situated in our will.

John Xiphilinus likewise, patriarch of Constantinople, in a sermon on the same subject, uses nearly the same words, citing that passage from Isaiah to illustrate Christ’s purposes:

> Through Isaiah, he says, God declares, “If you are willing and listen to me.” For one must first will and then listen, so that on our part we may be free. For when we are unwilling, the result is that we do not listen. Thus all blessedness and the endurance of punishment and sorrows proceed from our free power.

Both of them clearly drew upon Chrysostom’s sermon on the same subject.

In the statements of these authors that I have cited, not only is free willing placed first, which is called into suspicion in Valerian, but, what is more serious, calling seems to be made subordinate to free volition, insofar as [Col. 0830A] they have placed the hearing—which appears to follow calling—after volition. It is as though volition summons or obtains calling, as Saint Ambrose also said, *On Cain*, book I, chapter 8, when discussing the calling of Zacchaeus, whom he says obtained that he should be called. These things are much harsher than those which, in some measure similar to them, are treated so severely in Valerian.

In the expressions of these authors, therefore, “to will,” which is cast down as the first foundation of the entire subsequent structure, is not so absolutely first that it is not built upon an earlier divine movement from which it was produced. It is said to be first only in relation to the divine grace that cooperates and to the remaining consequent progress. In reality, it is subsequent to the divine grace that arouses one to will—that is, to the calling which is not obtained insofar as it is wholly first, but only insofar as it is more explicit or more abundant, or insofar as it urges one toward further good works connected with the first, which was granted by divine grace in sheer liberality and obtained by no antecedent good works. To that first volition, God joins what belongs to him, and brings to perfection [Col. 0830B] the beginning that is ours—namely, cooperating and subsequent grace—by which that rudiment of ours, aroused through divine prevenience, is fostered and brought to completion. I do not see why we may not understand Valerian, who spoke much more gently, in the same way.

### 20. Saint Bernard, *On the Interior House*, chapter 68

“It is within our power to acquiesce in divine inspiration, and to choose and follow what pertains to our salvation. It is the gift of God, however, that we may attain what we desire to achieve by following.”

These words, which they wish to hear spoken of unfavorably in Valerian, are so genuine that no dispute should be raised about them. Nor does it matter that, in the same chapter, Bernard so expressly asserts the necessity of grace and teaches that there is no human effort without God’s grace, and that freedom is in us so that we may either choose or follow, but only after God has first admonished us and invited us to salvation. For what Saint Bernard explicitly said, the other Fathers, when speaking in the same manner concerning those later words, did not [Col. 0830C] exclude but implicitly understood, as we have often shown.

Hugh of Saint Victor, *On Spirit and Soul*—for he himself is regarded as the true author of that work—chapter 48, uses the same words that we have just quoted from Bernard, and may therefore be pressed into service for the same point. Before both of them, Rabanus spoke in the same way in book IV of *On the Universe*, chapter 10. All of them, as I also noted above, chapter 7, number 5, drew from the book *On Ecclesiastical Dogma*, chapter 21, whose author was Gennadius. Gennadius, therefore, could equally have been cited, if it were certain that this chapter was not an addition to Gennadius by some Catholic writer, or one requiring correction—for it is suspected of Semipelagian taint—or completion.

I can imagine the experts laughing at me if I point out that this Gennadius is the Massilian who flourished around the year of Christ 490, and not Gennadius Scholarius, who occupied the see at Constantinople approximately two hundred years ago, around the year of Christ 1440, and worked vigorously for the concord of the Roman and Greek Churches at the Council of Florence. Nevertheless, it is not entirely superfluous to mention the point in passing, because of the expertise of the accuser, [Col. 0830D] for whom a thousand years are like a single day; and for that reason he calls Gennadius, the author of the book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, “Gennadius Scholarius.”

Rupert, in his book on Joshua, chapter 10, while treating of the scouts sent out by Joshua, writes as follows:

“Let no one, therefore, in any matter presume so greatly upon heavenly assistance that he does not also first attend to himself, watching according to the ability of his understanding and laboring according to his share of human effort. For just as it is a sign of very little faith to doubt the divine promises, so it is a sign of excessive rashness or presumption to await heavenly aid through miracles while sitting idly with folded hands. It belongs to man to begin, but to God to bring to completion.”

What could be clearer? What is closer to the statements of Valerian that are being called into suspicion? Yet Rupert was never marked, or in any way accused, of Semipelagianism. On the contrary, one finds in him, most explicitly [Col. 0831A] and repeatedly, the Catholic doctrine of the perpetual prevenience of divine assisting grace. His book X, *On Offices*, chapter 8, is written as though expressly for this question: there he splendidly explains both how God’s prevenience is necessary and how willing belongs to us, while bringing to completion belongs to God.

### 21. Laurence Justinian

Laurence Justinian, *On Contempt of the World*, chapter 3, after stating that we must recognize free choice alone as properly ours, while everything else, whether natural or gratuitous, is a gift of God, concludes in these words:

“Virtues are produced both by the accumulation of merits and by the assent of free choice, yet with the power of God cooperating, which assists free choice.”

Here this blessed teacher says that free choice, and its offspring—choice—are our own; but he attributes to God the perfection of it through cooperating and assisting grace. This is plainly the same as if, with Valerian, he had said: “Willing belongs to us, but bringing to completion belongs to God.” Yet that Laurence Justinian was entirely sound and Catholic in the matter of grace is evident from that very [Col. 0831B] chapter which has been cited, and also most clearly from *The Bundle of Love*, chapter 8, toward the end, and from *On Discipline and Perfection*, chapter 23.

It will not be unwelcome to add the testimony of so many holy doctors that of a holy virgin taught by God, since before God there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, and likewise neither male nor female. Blessed Hildegard, whom Saint Bernard, many great prelates, and even supreme pontiffs honored, because of her heavenly wisdom, by letters addressed to her, in her replies to the questions of Wibert, a monk of Gembloux, openly acknowledges that bringing to completion the good works we will belongs to God.

Thus she writes in response to the question, “What do grace and free choice possess as their own, and what do they possess in common?”:

“Grace and free choice have this in common: that a human being, in the knowledge of good and evil, can choose either good or evil to perform; and whatever he chooses through the property of free choice, according to the taste and desire of the flesh—which he can never be compelled to abandon—he chooses, [Col. 0831C] he brings to completion with the devil’s assistance; but whatever he chooses according to the will of the soul, he brings to completion with the assistance of the grace of the Holy Spirit.”

Here free choice can choose what it brings to completion with God’s assistance. This is precisely what Valerian said: “Willing belongs to us; bringing to completion belongs to God.”

Everyone understands the statements we have cited, and similar ones found among the Fathers, in such a way that they do not condemn the most weighty Fathers—that is, the flower of ecclesiastical learning—as Semipelagians, but charitably explain them in various ways according to the subject they are treating.

For example, they may understand the statements in this way: that willing belongs to us, but bringing to completion belongs to God, insofar as, having been divinely called and preceded by grace, we freely assent, although we could refuse to assent. For even after calling, as Chrysostom explicitly said in homily 4, *On the Praises of Paul*, we remain masters of our own consent; although, for the good purpose to be brought to perfection and fully carried out, grace must necessarily be bestowed by God.

Or certainly they may understand them in this way: that a person preceded by divine grace freely gives consent to God, and thus willing belongs to that person, while God, cooperating with the person who wills freely, [Col. 0831D] brings the effect of the first calling to completion.

Or again, they may understand them in this way: that they grant to a person working from himself and by the bare powers of nature only an imperfect willing of the good, which does not dispose him even remotely toward righteousness; and therefore that it belongs to God, through grace, to dignify our poverty and bring to completion in us what nature could never accomplish by itself.

All these interpretations, and any others mentioned above, remove the Fathers from the charge, even though they do not always remember gratuitous prevenience, because they were not treating that subject—as Saint Augustine said of himself in *Retractations*, book I, chapter 9, excusing his silence, or at least his sparing mention of grace, in the books *On Free Choice*, which he wrote before the Pelagian heresy had arisen.

The Fathers are not, I say, trying to say everything everywhere. Rather, according to the subject before them, they set forth what contributes to the edification of the reader or hearer. Though they leave other matters unmentioned, they do not thereby deny them. The writings of the Fathers must be measured by this rule [Col. 0832A] whenever, intent upon the argument they are treating, they undertake to explain some associated matter less fully. Saint Anselm noted that this was extremely common among them in his book *On the Sacrament of the Altar*, chapter 13. Nor can this reverence or charitable interpretation be denied them without the gravest injury to men equally learned and holy, and without dishonor to the Church.

### 22. Valerian to be treated in the same way

What we are necessarily compelled to do with other Fathers—why should we not do equally with Valerian? The objection that we saw applied to Cassian and Faustus does not work against him: namely, that Fathers who lived at that time and were well aware of the mind and meaning in which a somewhat slippery statement, capable of being turned toward a good or bad interpretation, had been uttered, protested against him.

The same judgment, therefore, must be pronounced concerning Valerian as concerning so many other Fathers who spoke in a similar or even harsher manner. Indeed, although Valerian was not sailing in the same vessel as so many other Fathers, it would be fair to interpret a statement capable of being understood in a true as well as a false sense in a good and Catholic [Col. 0832B] sense. Christian charity and gentleness require this.

As Nazianzen rightly judged in oration 8:

“He does not readily suspect evil in another who is not readily driven toward evil.”

Likewise, someone who loves truth and sincerity himself, and wishes to deal candidly with others as he wishes them to deal with him, will not easily be persuaded that falsehood lies in the words of others, especially words that have grown gray with age.

## CHAPTER X. Whether Valerian should be stripped of the title “Saint,” which he has long possessed in manuscripts

### 1.

What the philosopher of Madaura once said in his own case may be said in the matter of Valerian by changing one or two little words. Have you ever seen a flame arising from straw, crackling loudly, blazing brightly, and growing rapidly? Yet it is merely light fuel, a fleeting fire, leaving no remains.

Such is that accusation: begun in quarrels, enlarged by words, weakened by arguments, languishing in substance, [Col. 0832C] vigorous in noise, but destined, after the judgment of fair-minded arbiters, to leave behind no remains of calumny.

Those who have learned the origin and progress of the charge brought against Valerian concerning his doctrine will understand that I have exaggerated nothing and said nothing rhetorically or with any parsimony toward truth or charity. From this little work they will judge the justice and outcome of the accusation—or rather its emptiness and weakness.

There remains now the second head of the accusation proposed above, concerning the title “Saint.” We may be briefer in this part, not only because the accuser offers as its sole foundation Valerian’s allegedly corrupted doctrine, which we have sufficiently dismantled, but also because this part of the accusation attacks not so much Valerian himself, whom we are undertaking to defend and clear, as those who conferred that title upon him.

Nevertheless, the accuser’s severity, and his lack of charity in a matter that could have been received benevolently, counsels us to touch upon this head of the accusation also, briefly and in passing.

[Col. 0832D]

### 2.

The accuser therefore infers that Valerian bears the title “Saint” improperly and to the injury of the Catholic faith, because, having been a Semipelagian, he must be acknowledged to have been without true sanctity, which has no place outside the Catholic faith.

What Saint Irenaeus wrote concerning the heretics of his own time, book IV, chapter 60, may equally be directed against all such people with respect to piety and holiness:

“Everything among them is appearance, not truth.”

Origen noted in homily 7 on Ezekiel that nothing is more familiar to heretics than to deceive the simple by the shadow of holiness. Augustine confirmed in book II against the *Letters of Petilian*, chapter 18, that this is characteristic of the devil and his chosen instruments.

Yet those who, according to the true definition given by Epictetus in chapter 36 of the *Enchiridion*, are merely apes of honesty and holiness, and who are actually marked by the Fathers with that name—especially by Saint Ignatius in letter 9 and by Saint Cyprian in his letter to Jubaianus—readily reveal [Col. 0833A] what kind of holiness it is whose mask they place over a life most hideous and foul in every respect.

They are like that Alexandrian ape who, according to Gregory of Nyssa in his book to Harmonius *On the Christian Name*, when nuts were offered to it, put on a mask and displayed itself as what it was.

Thus Valerian certainly falls under this objection if he lived his life and possessed his soul outside the Catholic faith, which is the one true and Christian faith.

For this reason Saint Maximus the monk and martyr, in his letter to Peter the Illustrious, argues that the title “Saint” must be denied to Pyrrhus, who had fallen into heresy. “He has fallen,” he says, “from all holiness who has voluntarily leapt away from the Catholic Church.” He adds:

“Only through pious confession and orthodox faith does he receive sanctification and the name ‘holy.’”

Here one may surely say what Emperor Frederick said, according to Tageno, to the envoys of the emperor of Constantinople during the Asian expedition:

“Your lord calls himself ‘Holy.’ Wonderful is the holiness that customarily imprisons holy, honest, and religious men—faithful envoys [Col. 0833B] kindly received with the kiss of peace, in whose mouths no falsehood or iniquity was found—and then suddenly torments them with hunger and nakedness unto death. May God keep such holiness far from us!”

I say that one may similarly say, on the assumption of Valerian’s Semipelagianism:

“Away with holiness polluted by a foul heresy! Away with the holy heretic!”

### 3.

It is not difficult, however, to demonstrate how feeble this accusation is. It is beyond dispute that outside the true faith there is no place for holiness, so that there is no need to wander into the commonplaces by which it would be made clear that the holy Catholic Church is one and unique, while the dens of heretics are hiding places of wickedness and depravity.

What had to be demonstrated, therefore, was that Valerian had departed from the true faith—a faith which, as I have proved, was taken from him only by calumny and wholly empty suspicion.

And, to deal generously with Valerian even in the face of the accuser’s very sparing charity, let us grant that Valerian was convicted by him of Semipelagianism, [Col. 0833C] so that he must be regarded as unquestionably and inexcusably stained by that defect.

What I stated above concerning Faustus and Cassian in the matter of grace; concerning Saint Cyprian with respect to the rebaptism of heretics; concerning Saint Chrysostom with respect to slight faults attributed to the Mother of God; concerning Saint Irenaeus with respect to the Millennium; and concerning many other most holy men with respect to other subjects, is acknowledged. The same may also be said of Valerian: he may have erred materially and without pertinacity, before the matter had been clearly defined by the Church.

For it is not a false assertion that makes someone a heretic and truly outside the faith, but obstinacy and stubborn resistance to the Church, the teacher of the faith, according to Augustine’s notable teaching to Vincentius Victor. Vincentius had related many serious errors in book III of *On the Origin of the Soul*, chapter 15.

“Far be it from you,” Augustine says, “to think that by holding these opinions you have departed from the Catholic faith, although these opinions are opposed to the Catholic faith, if before God—whose eye is deceived in no one’s heart—you truthfully repent of having said them, not trusting yourself, but desiring that what you have said be capable of being proven, and always striving [Col. 0833D] not to defend even your own opinion if it is exposed as untenable; since you care, once your own judgment has been condemned, to pursue what is better and what is more true.

“For that disposition, even in statements that are non-Catholic through ignorance, is itself Catholic through the very forethought and readiness to be corrected.”

And in *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 21, Augustine likewise explains the reason for the decision by which he had resolved to revise what he had written up to that time. He admitted that some errors might have slipped from him while writing—of which the very error with which we are concerned here, concerning the beginning of the act of faith and salvation from the powers of nature, was certainly one, an error which he had taught when younger and inexperienced in matters of grace.

“But it makes a difference,” he says, “how much and in what matters one errs, and how readily each person corrects himself, or with how much pertinacity he attempts to defend his error. A person is one of good hope if the final day of this life finds him progressing in such a way that what was lacking in his progress is added to him, and he is judged more likely to be perfected [Col. 0834A] than punished.”

Let no one who wishes to be a fair judge of human frailty in falling and of divine kindness toward us consider this excuse unsuitable, especially when there is no hardening of the mind in an error which one has imprudently embraced but does not knowingly and willingly retain. We wish this excuse to remain available to Valerian’s honor.

### 4.

But I would urge the rigid censor of hoary antiquity, who in the matter before us has resolved to deal with it according to the strictest law and with scant charity, to consider carefully lest, along with that lack of benevolence, he join an injury—not merely any injury, but an irreligious one and one hostile to heaven itself.

On this matter, I ask him to recall what we established in chapter 1 by no implausible conjectures: that this is the same Valerian who was promoted from abbot to bishop, instructed the people entrusted to him in every form of holiness—as these homilies teach—and frequently [Col. 0834B] corresponded with Saint Leo by letters of ecclesiastical communion. He subscribed to most of the Catholic councils and transmitted his reputation to posterity, if not brilliant, and undeniably somewhat obscure, at least untouched by any sinister rumor.

No one has ever reported, even by conjecture, that anyone in all the ages past spoke an evil word about him. Indeed, we established by indications no less weighty and clear than those which secure for many ancient men peaceful possession of the title and distinction now disputed in Valerian’s case, that he died a holy death and was entered as a citizen of heaven on a fixed day, 24 July, in the Lérins records and the monastic martyrology.

But why should I press further the ancient and exceedingly strong testimony in favor of Valerian’s sanctity? Ancient manuscript codices, drawn from the library of Saint Gall and other distinguished libraries, explicitly designate Valerian of Cimiez, the author of these homilies, as “Saint.”

Is it not therefore an unsound example, and one attempted without danger of rashness, for Valerian’s accuser to try to drive from ancient possession a man whose sanctity he has weakened by no firm argument and by no even probable reasoning, but only by unjustly invoking the obscurity of his circumstances—the same [Col. 0834C] obscurity which time has cast over so many other holy and learned men?

### 5.

The reader sees how easily, to use Mamertus’s words, the warmth of truth melts the frost of chilling words. Nor is it necessary here to resort to another possible evasion of the charge against Valerian, which someone might regard as not wholly unsafe: namely, that the ancient use of this title should not be admitted for present ecclesiastical usage.

For today, to use Saint Cyprian’s expression, only those who have been plainly vindicated are honored with this title. Thus even those whom the Church honors with heavenly distinctions subject to some restriction are not called “Saints,” but only “Blessed,” so long as that restriction has not been removed; and by that postponement the full and complete glorification of their sanctity is held back.

No one is so unfamiliar with the books of the Fathers or with ecclesiastical history [Col. 0834D] as not to know that this designation once prevailed for another purpose as well.

In the very cradle of the Church, all Christians were adorned with this name, as is often clear from the Apostle, from chapter 9 of Acts, and from the writers of that age, especially Ignatius. In his letter to the Magnesians, he earnestly exhorts Christians to show themselves worthy of the title they had received, and applies to this subject Isaiah 62:

“He shall be called by a new name, which the Lord shall name him, and he shall be a holy people.”

Indeed, Philo the Jew, a contemporary of the Apostles, appears to confirm that the common designation “Saints” was at that time generally applied to all Christians. He describes Christian institutions and customs under the name of the Essenes in his book *On the Contemplative Life*, as Eusebius and Jerome assert, along with many others cited by Baronius under the year of Christ 64.

That the name “Essene” and the name “Saint” are equivalent is found in Philo himself, in his book *That Every Good Person Is Free*, and in Chrysostom’s homily 44 on Acts.

[Col. 0835A] Thus all Christians in ancient times were called “Saints,” since by their institutions, profession, and their head, Christ, they were holy; they were bound to aspire to all holiness and dedicated in so many ways to divine obedience and worship. For this is properly what it means to be holy, according to the most common manner of speaking in Scripture, as Origen observed in homily 11 on Leviticus:

“For this reason even mute animals and vessels of ministry were called holy; garments also were called holy, and likewise places situated in cities or beneath cities and assigned to the priests.

“Among the many animals, the firstborn of cattle or sheep are commanded by the law to be sanctified to the Lord, and it is said: ‘You shall do no work with them, because they are holy to the Lord.’

“As for vessels, in the tabernacle of testimony the vessels of ministry—censers, bowls, and other vessels of this kind—are called holy.

“As for garments, Aaron’s high-priestly robe, his linen tunic, and other garments of this kind are called holy.”

Origen develops many other points in that passage, showing at equal length that a Christian may be called holy and is bound to aspire [Col. 0835B] to holiness in as many ways as there are kinds of inanimate things to which the name “holy” is given because of some special connection with divine worship.

You can therefore see that the designation “Saint,” once applied to all Christians, must be traced much farther back than the source from which Pamelius, in his notes on Tertullian’s *To His Wife*, book II, chapter 1, number 3, derived it. He believes that it was first taken from the Apostle’s statement in 1 Corinthians 7, where the children of Christians are called holy.

All Christians, then, were called “Saints,” although it is certain that not all of them at that time lived according to the exact standard of solid holiness. Nevertheless, no one may rightly argue that the title should now be removed merely because greater strictness is now exercised in conferring it.

Nor does anyone accuse the holy Fathers, or argue that a sponge should be applied to erase the title “Saint” when they occasionally bestowed it upon heretics or persons of suspect faith, whether because of the office they held or because of the glory of their confession, even though a subsequent [Col. 0835C] stain seemed to darken it.

Certainly Saint Augustine calls the Luciferian deacon Hilary “Saint Hilary,” although it is not certain that he repented and returned to the Church. Very often, too, he bestowed the title “Saint,” as a mark of honor, when addressing bishops whose faith had been wounded or corrupted, so long as their case was not considered hopeless.

Saint Gregory, book VI of the *Registers*, letter 6, calls John the Faster—whom Baronius believes died in his sins in the year 596—“John of holy memory.”

The emperor’s title in Liutprand, book I, chapter 3, is Greek: **δεσποτεία σοῦ ἁγία**—“your holy dominion.”

Saint Cyril, book II against Nestorius, chapter 4, acknowledges what Nestorius had said there: that the Medes and Persians are called “holy” in Isaiah 13, even though they were impious and idolatrous. Nevertheless, Cyril acknowledges that they are called holy because, just as a sacrifice set apart for God—whether it happened to be a calf or a sheep—was called holy, so they too were called holy in prophetic speech because they had been set apart and dedicated by divine ordinance for the capture of Babylon.

It is also established that Alexander III, [Col. 0835D] in a rescript to the heretical king of Ethiopia reported by Baronius under the year of Christ 1177, bestowed upon him in the inscription the title “Most Holy,” by which, according to the custom of the region, he was habitually honored by everyone.

In certain manuscript codices of the Sixth Council of Constantinople, Alemanus testifies in his notes to Photius’s *Secret History*, page 73, that Justinian is read as **ἐν ἁγίοις**—“among the holy ones.” Likewise, in the preface to the Trullan Canons, [80] it is said, **τῆς θέως λήξεως**—“of the divine departure/death” (the transmitted Greek reading is uncertain); the same expression is also used of the empress Theodora by the Fathers of the Sixth Council of Constantinople.

Yet Procopius, in that history, reported the scandalous life of this Alectus and Justinian’s monstrous crimes, which were farther removed from true holiness than heaven is from earth.

Likewise, the Roman council called the Palmary Council bestowed upon Theodoric [Col. 0836A], the Arian king of the Goths, the title “Saint”—some codices read “Most Pious”—not out of a desire to flatter, but according to the custom of honoring the princes of that age with that magnificent title.

Dionysius of Alexandria, as cited by Eusebius, book VII of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 10, went even further: he called Valerian and Gallienus, pagan emperors exceedingly hostile to the Christian name, “Most Holy.” He was plainly following the example of the Apostles, who called an exceedingly wicked man “Most Excellent” because he held the office of prefect.

On the contrary, we learn from Saint Chrysostom’s treatment of the words of Psalm 13, “There is no God,” that the heretics of ancient times acted in the opposite way. He writes:

“Any extremely vehement heretic, during a time of persecution, when speaking with a bishop, does not call him bishop, nor archbishop, nor most religious, nor Saint. What does he say? ‘Your Reverence,’ ‘your wisdom,’ ‘your prudence,’ ‘your justice’; and he applies common names to him, denying his authority.”

The reason, of course, was that ecclesiastical authority was being indicated by such titles, especially by the title “Saint,” which is now restricted to the bishop of bishops, and which heretics detested.

Finally, that the dead too were called “Saints” by the ancients [Col. 0836B] is taught by Martial, book XI, epigram 30, elsewhere numbered 54:

> “Speak well of the woman who bore children to her holy husband.”

Raderus comments: “The dead were holy to the ancients.”

Virgil writes:

> “Hail, holy father; hail, ashes received.”

And the Twelve Tables say:

> “Let those given over to death be held as gods.”

### 6.

This defense, therefore, of retaining the title “Saint” prefixed to Valerian’s name, based upon the ancient custom of honoring bishops with that designation, would have nothing to fear from the accuser’s sponge.

For if the accuser, judging the matter according to present ecclesiastical usage, were to argue that all the titles I have mentioned should be wiped out in the writings of the Fathers or the acts of councils whenever they are not plainly applied to persons who have been vindicated, he would offer himself up to be laughed at and hissed off the stage by the prudent, [Col. 0836C] rather than achieve his aim.

One may therefore reasonably think that he has made adequate provision for the security of the title in question.

Those who have adorned so many persons not yet vindicated with the titles “Saint” and “Blessed”—despite the objections raised against the practice—have no better grounds than John, abbot of Cîteaux, in his *Compendium of the Saints of His Order*; Chrysostom Vander Sterre, in the *Lives of the Saints of Premontre*; Molanus, in the *Catalogue of the Saints of Belgium*; Arnold de Raisse, in his supplement to that work; Augustine de Witte, in the *Genealogy of Saint Francis*; Hyacinthus Coquetus, in his book *On the Saints of Belgium of the Order of Preachers*; and Chrysostom Henriquez, in the *Cistercian Menology*.

As I stated at the outset, I set aside this defense as unnecessary. I consider that I have done enough, and more than enough, for any fair-minded and prudent person, since there is no occasion for innovation. The question is not whether Valerian should be entered into the Church’s records, nor whether any new honor should be decreed for him, but whether matters should be left in the position in which they have long stood.

The earlier authorities wished this author to be what he has been called: an author whom no accusation has proved guilty, and for whom the compelling conjectures I set forth at the beginning speak—especially his frequent communion with the head of the Church, his subscription to most of the Catholic councils, the testimony of the Lérins records and the monastic martyrology, and his long-established possession of the title now recently disputed in the inscriptions [Col. 0836D] of the most ancient codices.

No one respecting the prescription of so long a period has troubled the matter until now, after so many editions of Valerian had been produced in so many places, except for the one accuser who has shown so little fairness toward Valerian’s doctrine and so little charity toward him.

Therefore, so long as the Church and wise men permit it: let him who holds it retain it. Possession has force.

# SAINT NICETAS, BISHOP OF AQUILEIA

## EDITOR’S NOTICE

Although the surviving testimonies of the ancients concerning Saint Nicetas establish with the utmost certainty that the holy bishop was the author of several writings, the republic of letters had long and fruitlessly desired an edition of them that could properly bear that name. From all the ages before the year 1833, scholars had been able to discover nothing beyond certain very brief fragments and a short work entitled *Exposition of the Faith*.

For the little book *To a Fallen Virgin*, which was counted among the literary remains of Saint Nicetas by Peter Braida in 1810, belongs with equal or even greater right to Saint Ambrose; for that reason we have given it a place among the works of that Father. [Note: [Col. 0837] See volume XVII of our *Patrology*, column 367.]

Approximately thirteen years ago, however, what had so long eluded the investigations of scholars presented itself almost spontaneously to the eminent and exceptionally learned Cardinal Mai. It happened that this most learned man encountered several treatises preserved in the Vatican Library, over which he most happily presides. Not only the extremely strong authority of the manuscript but also its manner of writing and the analogy of its subject matter most clearly establish these works as belonging to Saint Nicetas.

We shall therefore adhere to Mai’s text in publishing the works of this Father. Braida’s explanations from other sources will illuminate it, and it will be preceded by an account of Saint Nicetas taken from Schoenemann’s *Historical-Literary Library*.

## PREFACE OF PETER BRAIDA TO HIS RECENSION OF THE LITTLE WORKS OF SAINT NICETAS

### [Col. 0837A]

We present to you, excellent reader, a writer and Father of the fifth century of the Church, hitherto scarcely known except by name—indeed, not even sufficiently known by name.

This is Niceas or Nicetas, bishop of the Church of Aquileia, who, according to the better authorities, governed that most celebrated Church from the year 454 until the year 485. He left monuments of his pastoral care, piety, and intellect in several short writings, of which ecclesiastical authors have preserved the memory; but, so far as we know, only one or two of them have come down to us, apart from a few fragments that survived as though from the wreckage of other works.

Only one of these little works had been known to the scholars of an earlier age. It had also provided material for dispute concerning its true author, and for that reason it was attributed now to one, now to another, of the principal Fathers of the Latin Church. Scholars suspected that its author was some Niceas or Nicetas, although they always remained uncertain which one.

Only in our own final age has another work become known under the name of Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia. It had lain hidden in Rome in the Ghislieri Library and was brought to public attention through the work of that eminent prince of the Church and ornament of all letters, Cardinal Stephen Borgia—alas, how prematurely taken from life!

Not long afterward, fragments of the lost works also appeared. They were contained in an ancient codex of the Palatine Library at Vienna and were published through the efforts of the distinguished Michael Denis, prefect of that same library, who likewise had recently been taken from the world of letters.

It will therefore be very pleasing to you to possess in a single volume all that survives of this Niceas or Nicetas, so that the succession of the lesser—as we may call them—ancient Fathers may be enlarged by the addition of this one as well. This is especially welcome because in our own age there is little hope that, after the last Venetian edition of the Library of the Fathers by Andrea Gallandi, new editions of the Fathers will be published, or that those already issued will so quickly grow through additional volumes.

You will surely be astonished, whoever you are who first examines this volume of ours, that we have composed a book of no small size for only two little works and a few fragments, which we present as though they constituted the complete works of this Niceta of ours. “But what,” you will say, “if it had been possible to publish everything wholly and intact?” [Col. 0838B] Yet when the thought of publishing and adorning Niceta first entered our mind, we discovered that the matter was hazardous in more than one respect and would therefore require much work and labor.

First, no bishop of Aquileia named Niceas or Nicetas was admitted by scholars as the author of any works. When Baronius, in his annotations on the Roman Martyrology, declared that the Niceas or Nicetas whom Gennadius and others call the bishop of the city of Romatiana and the author of various little works should be regarded as Niceas or Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, nearly all scholars, with only a few exceptions, rose up against Baronius as though in battle array and reproached him for having openly done violence to the historical records.

Then the little works which Gennadius attributes to Niceas or Nicetas, bishop of the city of Romatiana, were assigned by almost universal scholarly agreement to another Niceas or Nicetas, who was a bishop among the barbarous people of Dacia at the end of the fourth and the beginning of the fifth century and who is known to us chiefly from the testimony of Paulinus of Nola, whose closest friend he was. The city of Romatiana mentioned by Gennadius and others was understood by them to be the city which, situated in new Dacia on this side of the Danube, is called by ancient geographers and writers—by a word not very different from that used by Gennadius—Remesiana, or Romesiana, or Remissiana.

What more need be said? When a work of Niceta newly discovered at the seminary of Padua was published in 1799—the work mentioned by Gennadius in his account of the bishop of Romatiana, namely, *On the Creed*, or *Explanation of the Creed Delivered to the Candidates for Baptism*—when, I say, this work appeared under the name of blessed Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, as the Ghisian manuscript presented it, the distinguished Michael Denis, who at that time was bringing to light Niceta’s fragments from another Viennese manuscript, did not hesitate to write that he could not agree with the word “Aquileiensis” (*of Aquileia*), which in the Ghisian manuscript must certainly be an error (*σφάλμα*), and that it ought to have been written either “of Dacia,” or “of the city of Romatiana,” in agreement with Gennadius, or “of Romesiana,” in agreement with the Peutinger Table, or “of Remesiana of Dacia” (*Ρεμεσιάνης τῆς Δακίας*), in agreement with the first act of the Council of Chalcedon, volume IV of Labbe’s Venetian edition of the Councils, column 892. This may be seen in volume II, part III, page 2041, of the work entitled *Theological Manuscript Codices of the Palatine Library of Vienna: Latin and Other Western Languages*, reviewed by Michael Denis, Vienna, 1802. [Col. 0839C]

Nor was that all. Shortly afterward, the distinguished Giovanni Prosdocimo Zabeo, a doctor of sacred theology and at that time professor in the royal gymnasium of Venice, now the royal lyceum there, without yet knowing anything about Michael Denis’s judgment, independently adopted the same opinion. He also composed a most learned dissertation in its defense and published it at Venice in the printing house of Antonio Rosa in 1803, under the following title: *Dissertation: The Explanation of the Creed, Published at Padua in 1799, Is More Probably to Be Attributed to Saint Nicetas, Bishop of the Dacians, than to Blessed Nicetas, Bishop of Aquileia*.

You see, therefore, excellent reader, what a difficult undertaking we have begun. You see how many and what kind of adversaries, both of our own age and of an earlier one, it was necessarily our task to confront, since our purpose was to write in support of our Niceas or Nicetas of Aquileia and thus, in some fashion, to establish in him a new fifth-century writer and Father from works commonly attributed to another person living far away from these regions. [Col. 0839D] It was consequently necessary to say much, both in support of the new opinion and in weakening the old one. We had to meet many difficulties raised by earlier scholars, and especially those which Zabeo most recently gathered, together with his newly devised arguments, as the strongest supports of the opinion he defended, in the cited dissertation of fifty-one quarto pages, as they say. Nor could we neglect a particular observation of Michael Denis, which might easily have appeared exceptionally solid.

What, however, if we consider that an argument of this kind—resting on the poverty of the ancient records and on the absence of statements that are clear and unambiguous—is, by its very nature, chiefly open to conjecture? When conjecture is under discussion, an extended treatment is necessarily appropriate. [Col. 0840B] This, then, is the principal reason why our work has in some measure exceeded the limits of deliberate brevity.

There are nevertheless other matters which have driven us, as it were, to loosen the reins of our running pen. Several topics of varied learning arose which, although not entirely new, did not reject a new elucidation in relation to our subject; and we thought that such discussion might perhaps not be unwelcome to readers. Certain new matters also presented themselves which deserved to be treated from the beginning, so that our purpose might be fulfilled.

The matters relating to Aquileia—both those concerning the Church and those concerning the city and its territory—repeatedly demanded our attention. Some of them were relevant to our subject, others touched it closely, and still others required either a new or a fuller investigation. [Col. 0840C] Moreover, the little works and fragments of our Niceas or Nicetas are a rich treasury of ecclesiastical learning. In them the principal doctrines of religion are asserted, precepts of morality are taught and impressed upon the mind, and many aspects of ecclesiastical discipline are elucidated.

Who, when he was required to discuss a fifth-century writer and Father and to publish what he left in writing, would not undertake to examine these matters individually in such an author? Nor were the matters concerning Niceta himself to be regarded as less important: his name, lineage, homeland, age, deeds, extant writings, lost writings, and other matters touching him; likewise his holiness and veneration, as well as the integrity of his doctrine in certain expressions which might perhaps trouble someone. You have, then, excellent reader, reasons why you may endure without displeasure the bulk of the volume, even though the sacred store which it presents is small. You also have reasons why, as it were, from the threshold you may perceive both the seriousness and the subject matter of our Dissertation. Now, in accordance with your good nature, kindly examine each matter.

## [Col. 0839]

# HISTORICAL-LITERARY NOTICE ON SAINT NICETA, BY SCHOENEMANN

*(From Schoenemann, Historical-Literary Library of the Latin Fathers, volume II.)*

## § I. Life

The name of that bishop of Romatiana, whom Gennadius calls Niceas, seems properly to be written in this way. [Note: [Col. 0839D] The names vary on almost every occasion and in nearly all the manuscripts: *Nicaeas, Niceas, Nicetas, Nicetus,* and *Nicetius*. Meanwhile, the name of the Dacian bishop appears more frequently as *Nicetas* and *Nicetius*, just as the Hypodeacon of Aquileia is invariably called *Niceas*. Holstenius testifies that even in Gennadius, in the admirable manuscript at Saint Andrew “of the Valley,” *Nicetas*, not *Niceas*, is written, in the posthumous notes on the Roman Martyrology published by Florentinius and the continuators of Bollandus, as cited by Rubeus.] He was a Dacian by nation and bishop in his homeland, the city of Romatiana.

From Paulinus of Nola we know that, when he passed through Rome on a journey to Italy, he attracted the admiration of many there. Then, too—this occurred in 398—he went to Nola, proceeded to the tomb of Saint Felix, and visited Paulinus. He so entered the mind of that exceptionally candid man that Paulinus later celebrated his return to Dacia in a poem which still survives. The poem extensively displays Niceta’s distinguished gifts of mind and spirit and especially praises his ardor in preaching the Gospel among the barbarian peoples who occupied Dacia.

Nor could Niceta refuse his friend’s request that, on his second journey to those lands in 402, he should again stay with him. From the letters of Innocent I it is clear that he was still alive in 414. [Note: [Col. 0841D] Not only in the letter to Marcianus of Naissus, dated at Ravenna in 409, where Tillemont judges that Innocent speaks of him as living—for which see Coustant, where the passage appears as no. XVI, page 822—but he is also listed among the Macedonian bishops in the heading of letter 17, dated 414, according to Coustant, page 833.]

In other respects Baronius greatly confused his memory. He judged the Dacian Nicetas mentioned in the Roman Martyrology on 7 January to be different from the Niceas whom Gennadius calls bishop of the city of Romatiana. He considered the latter to be identical with Niceas, the Hypodeacon of Aquileia, who received letters from Leo the Great in 458, thus placing a considerable span of time between his service as hypodeacon and his elevation to the episcopate. In this matter he strained himself remarkably to demonstrate that Aquileia had been called by the name of the city of Romatiana.

But learned men long ago recognized that all this was groundless. Through their careful investigations it has now been established that the city of Romatiana must be sought in Dacia Mediterranea, or Moesia, between Naissus and Sardica, and that Nicetas of Romatiana, born in Dacia, was not—according to Tillemont’s intermediate opinion—summoned from the clergy of Aquileia to the episcopate of that city. [Col. 0841C] [Note: [Col. 0842D] Among these must be counted Holstenius in the work cited, Quesnellus in his notes on Letter 79 of Leo the Great, Tillemont in volume X of his *Memoirs*, pages 621 and following, and most recently Rubeus in *Ecclesiastical Monuments of Aquileia*, chapter 17, pages 151 and following. Nevertheless, setting these authorities aside, Oudinus embraced Baronius’s opinion and simply transcribed it into his *Commentaries*, volume I, pages 1249 and following.]

## § II. Writings

According to Gennadius, he composed in a simple and polished style six little books of instruction for candidates for Baptism and a little book to a fallen virgin, an incentive to amendment for nearly all who fall. The former have been lost and are known only from the subjects indicated by Gennadius. The latter is thought to survive among the works of Ambrose and Jerome.

Indeed, among Jerome’s letters there is one bearing the title *Rebuke to Susanna, a Fallen Woman*, manifestly spurious; for it evidently was composed by a bishop, a dignity which Jerome never attained. The same work is found among the writings of Ambrose under the title *Treatise to a Fallen Virgin*. Yet because its wording differs from Ambrose’s, and because its ideas, in their severity, approach almost the Novatian heresy—which Ambrose attacked in his books *On Repentance*—scholars who have examined his works have long believed that it cannot properly be attributed to him. Bellarmine, Possevinus, Riverus, and later writers of this kind agree with them.

If I am not mistaken, Giovanni Battista Cotelerius was the first to attribute it to Niceta. [Note: [Col. 0842D] In his notes on the *Apostolic Constitutions*, book II, chapter 57. In the latest edition of the *Apostolic Fathers* by Jean le Clerc, Amsterdam, 1724, volume I, page 268, note 14. The first edition had appeared at Paris in 1672.] Since then no one, apart from the learned Maurist Fathers mentioned above, has dissented.

To defend its attribution to Ambrose, they brought forward the following arguments. To remove the charge of heresy, they said that the harsher expressions found in the work had been employed for no other purpose than to inspire more intensely the works of repentance by instilling a greater horror of the shame committed, and to prevent the woman from being recalled from the austerity she had once embraced either by her own softness or by the indulgence of some more lenient teacher. Thus, they maintained, the author had stimulated her to public repentance while at the same time raising her spirits with the hope of avoiding eternal punishments.

They added that it had once been the custom of the Church to refuse even at death pardon and reconciliation to those guilty of certain atrocious crimes; consequently, the author could have included this crime of Susanna among those offenses without thereby falling under any charge of error. They conceded that the style was not entirely Ambrosian, since Saint Ambrose, even when he adopted a highly impassioned mode of speech, used less dense and less abrupt clauses. They also judged that a certain opinion which Robert Cocus, in his *Censure*, had attacked as diametrically opposed to Christian doctrine is found in nearly the same words in book I *On Virginity*.

Furthermore, they thought it irrelevant that a letter with a similar subject was attributed to Niceta. An occasion for writing such a letter, they argued, could just as well have arisen for Ambrose; Basil, too, has a letter on the same subject and with the same heading. And if, in Ambrose himself, the virgin Indicia could be accused of a false crime, as in the letter to Syagrius, another virgin could also have been accused of a real one. Finally, all the manuscript books agree in assigning the work to Ambrose, except one more recent manuscript which attributes it to John Chrysostom.

Induced by these arguments, they have retained the work among the genuine offspring of Ambrose. Although Tillemont and Vallarsius rejected their position, I do not see that they have brought forward anything of new weight against it.

## § III. Editions

We have stated that this work is read both among the writings of Jerome and among those of Ambrose. Since it is often found in different volumes of different editions, however, we shall endeavor to provide some indication to assist readers who are curious about it.

I wish to point out above all that in the editions of Jerome the work begins with the words, “I think the offense is lighter,” and continues through the words, “evaporating, it supplies refreshment to suffering.” These passages are absent from the Ambrosian editions, where the work ordinarily begins, “Hear, you who are near.”

In Erasmus’s edition of Jerome, Basel, 1516, it appears in volume II, folios 81–85. “It is astonishing,” Erasmus writes, “how different this book was found in the copies. It did not have the same beginning, and in some copies various passages survived or were missing; moreover, most things were different. The style plainly proves that it is not Jerome’s, although I do not consider it unworthy of being read. The flavor of its phrasing is not unlike the speech of Saint Augustine.”

In the second Frobenian edition of 1537 it appears in volume IV, pages 139–143; in the Antwerp edition of Marianus Victorius, 1579, volume IX, pages 104–107; in the Paris edition of 1609, volume IV, pages 865–871; and likewise in the edition of 1643, volume IX, pages 88–91. In these editions Erasmus’s judgment has been omitted.

In the Frankfurt edition of 1643 it is found in volume IV, pages 92–96; in the Benedictine edition, Paris, 1706, volume V, pages 176–182; and in Vallarsius’s edition, Verona, 1742, volume XI, pages 178–192, and Venice, 1771, volume XI, part II, pages 245–263.

Vallarsius orders the author to be written as *Nicaea* and considers him identical with the Hypodeacon of Aquileia. Since that man had been a friend of Jerome, Vallarsius thinks that it could easily have happened that his book found a place among Jerome’s writings, just as it may have been attributed to Ambrose because of the similarity of its subject, since it often discusses virginity and the instruction of virgins. Everyone understands how weak the first argument is; the second applies equally to Jerome and Ambrose. In any event, Vallarsius treated the work with great care, examining also the various readings and observations of the Benedictines and of the editors of Ambrose.

In the Basel edition of the works of Ambrose, 1527, it appears in volume I, pages 178–186. Through a typographical error, the final chapter, which contains consolation for the fallen woman, was copied as a new little work under a separate title. Erasmus, in a brief notice to the reader printed on the reverse of the title page, says that it is a declamation like Jerome’s work on the reconciliation of mother and daughter, and that, among the writings of Jerome, it had been interpolated from the beginning, middle, and end by the deceit of a scribe, lest its true nature be detected.

In the Paris copy of the Sixtine edition, 1603, it appears in volume IV, pages 449–456; in the Benedictine edition, Paris, 1690, volume II, pages 301–320, under the title *Book on the Fall of a Consecrated Virgin*.

## [Col. 0843B]

# TESTIMONIES OF THE ANCIENTS CONCERNING SAINT NICETA

## Letter of Saint Leo the Great to Niceta

“Having returned to us,” etc. *(See the remainder in volume LIV of our edition, Letter 159.)*

## Gennadius of Massilia, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 22

Niceas, bishop of the city of Romaciana [Note: [Col. 0843D] Elsewhere, incorrectly, *Romana*. Suffridus Petri testifies that in other copies he found *Romanicia*.], composed in a simple and polished style six little books of instruction for candidates for Baptism. The first of them contains how candidates who desire to attain the grace of Baptism ought to conduct themselves. The second is on the errors of paganism. In it he says that, almost in his own time, a certain Melodius [Note: [Col. 0843D] The Corbie manuscript has the corrupt fragment: “in which, ‘almost time, a certain Meigidius, a head of household … and Gadarius, a peasant,’ etc.”] was transferred by the pagans among the gods because of his generosity, and Gadarius, a countryman, because of his courage.

The third book is on faith in the one Majesty; the fourth is against *Genethliology* [Note: [Col. 0843D] Elsewhere, *Genethlogy*. In the Corbie manuscript it is corruptly written *Genoclia*.]; the fifth is on the Creed; the sixth is on the victim of the Paschal Lamb. He also published a little book to a fallen virgin, an incentive to amendment for nearly all who fall. [Note: [Col. 0843D] The same manuscript reads: “a book, an incentive to those who fall *humane* (‘humanely’).”]

## Honorius of Autun, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, book II, chapter 22

Niceas, bishop of the city of Romaciana, composed in a simple and polished style six little books of instruction for candidates for Baptism. The first is on candidates for Baptism; the second on the errors of paganism; the third on faith in the one Majesty; the fourth against *Genealogy* [Note: [Col. 0843D] *Genethliology*.]; the fifth on the Creed; and the sixth on the victim of the Paschal Lamb. He also composed a little book to a fallen virgin, an incentive to amendment for nearly all who fall.

## Johannes Trithemius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, § 118

Niceas, bishop of the city of Romaciana, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, sharp in intellect, clear and polished in speech, wrote for the edification of readers little works worthy of serious reading, of which the following are reported:

- *Preparatory Instruction for Candidates Being Prepared for Baptism*, book I;
- *On the Errors of Paganism*, book I;
- *On Faith in the One Majesty*, book I;
- *Against Genealogy*, book I [Note: [Col. 0843D] Rather, *Genethliology*, or *Against the Astrologers of Nativities*. [Col. 0844D]];
- *On the Creed*, book I;
- *On the Victim of the Paschal Lamb*, book I;
- *To a Fallen Virgin*, book I [Note: [Col. 0844D] In the volume of the works of Johannes Trithemius from the library of Marquard Freher, Frankfurt, Wechelian press, 1601, folio, the following words appear after the final little work, *To a Fallen Virgin*: “And certain other works.” He flourished in the time of the emperors Theodosius and Honorius, in the year 420.]

## Cassiodorus, *On the Institution of Divine Scripture*, chapter 16

If anyone prefers to touch briefly upon something concerning the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and would rather not weary himself with lengthy reading, let him read the book of Bishop Niceta [Note: [Col. 0844D] Elsewhere, *Nicaea*.] which he composed *On Faith*. Filled with the clarity of heavenly doctrine, he will be led by its concise brevity into divine contemplation. This book is associated with the volumes of Saint Ambrose which he sent to the Emperor Gratian.

## From a parchment Martyrology

From a manuscript Martyrology of venerable antiquity belonging to the monastery of Saint Gall of Mosac, formerly in the diocese of Aquileia and later in that of Udine, probably compiled from Notker and Usuard. A copy made from the original and illustrated by the hand and scholarly work of the distinguished Joseph Bini, archpriest of Glemona and vicar-general in spiritual matters of that monastery and abbey, is preserved in the inner archive of the Metropolitan Chapter of Udine.

Saint Niceas, bishop of the Roman city.

This Martyrology was first published by Dacherius from a manuscript of the monastery of Corbie, approximately six hundred years old, in volume II, page 1, of the folio edition of the *Spicilegium*. Vallarsius later included it in his edition of the works of Saint Jerome, volume XI, page 457.

This was published in its entirety by Francesco Maria Florentinius of Lucca, chiefly from his own manuscript, from that of the Major Church of his homeland, and from several other codices of proven reliability. In the title of the volume he declared that substantial arguments suggested that it should be called the Roman Martyrology described by Gregory the Great, praised by Ado, and neglected and later sought out in subsequent centuries. Lucca, 1668.

Burial of Niceas, of holy memory, bishop.

That is, of the monastery of Saint William of the Desert, of the Order of Benedict, in the diocese of Lodeve. It appears in volume II, page 25, of the aforementioned folio edition of Dacherii’s *Spicilegium*, and is believed to have been written about the year 804, as appears from the preceding notice.

Bishop Nicaea.

This Martyrology was published from the manuscript of Monsieur Chauvelin, keeper of the royal seals, by Martene and Durand in volume VI, column 658, of *Ancient Writers and Monuments*, etc. They state in their preliminary observation that it was written approximately seven hundred years ago.

**10 Kalends of July**

Saint Nicetas, bishop.

This Martyrology was published from a Colbert manuscript by the same Martene and Durand in volume VI, column 685, of *Ancient Writers and Monuments*, etc.

# PROPER READINGS

For the use of the archiepiscopal diocese of Udine, approved by the Sacred Congregation of Rites on 23 August 1794, for the feast of Saint Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, on 22 June.

## Reading IV

Niceas, or Nicetas, bishop of the city of Romatiana—a name which some think signifies Aquileia, or Portus Romatinus, not far distant from it—is said to be that same Nicetas of Aquileia to whom the letter of Saint Leo the Great survives.

When he had assumed the episcopate, after the Huns under the leadership of Attila had devastated that region, and while the condition of affairs had scarcely begun to improve, some citizens who had been carried away into captivity by the barbarians returned free to their homeland. He immediately discovered that, as a result of the enemy’s invasion, numerous wounds had been inflicted upon his flock, wounds which seemed likely to present great difficulty in treatment.
