Some of the women whose husbands were believed to have been killed had become entangled in new marriages. Some men were said to have been polluted by food sacrificed to idols. Others had received Baptism a second time, or at least once, but from heretics.

Accordingly, through Adeodatus, a deacon of the Roman Church, he reported all these matters to Saint Leo the Great, so that he might be instructed, by Leo’s authority and direction, what ought to be done. In this he displayed a splendid proof both of his exceptional love for his people, his mature judgment, and his dutiful obedience to the principal see.

## Reading V

The holy pontiff replied to each of the concerned bishop’s questions in a special letter addressed to Nicetas of Aquileia, and he also wished it to reach, through Nicetas, all his brethren and fellow-provincial bishops.

Regarding the women who had married other men, he decreed that the bonds of legitimate marriage should be restored. Those who had used food offered to idols were to be cleansed through the satisfaction of repentance, which was to be measured not so much by the length of time as by the contrition of the heart.

Those who had been compelled by fear or led astray by error into repeating Baptism were likewise to be received back into the unity of communion through the remedy of repentance, with moderation and according to the judgment of the bishop. Finally, those who had been baptized only once, but by heretics, were to be confirmed solely by the invocation of the Holy Spirit through the imposition of hands.

Thus instructed by the doctrine received from the Roman See according to ancient custom, Nicetas, impelled by his ardent zeal to restore discipline and by the reverence he bore toward the chair of Peter, is rightly believed to have devoted himself entirely to wiping away the stains of past errors inflicted by the ravages of war, so that he might restore the face of his Church to the dignity of its former observance.

## Reading VI

The works of his intellect that display more and more clearly his vigilance in caring for the flock entrusted to him, while at the same time commending his learning together with the praise of his evangelical preaching, are those monuments of his genius which, according to the testimony of Gennadius of Massilia and Honorius of Autun, he left written in polished and simple language. [Col. 0848B] Yet scarcely one or two of them have survived.

He had published instruction for candidates for Baptism, works already highly esteemed at that time and associated with the labors of other distinguished Fathers. In them he discussed the conduct of candidates who desire to attain the grace of Baptism, the errors of paganism, faith in the one Majesty, opposition to *Genethliology*, the Creed, and the victim of the Paschal Lamb.

He also composed a little book to a fallen virgin, which the same writers call an incentive to amendment for nearly all who fall.

Amid these cares of pastoral office, after administering the episcopate of Aquileia for about thirty years, distinguished for learning and holy conduct, he departed to the Prince of Shepherds in the year 485.

---

## [Col. 0847]

# ON THE PRINCIPLES OF FAITH BY SAINT NICETAS, BISHOP OF AQUILEIA

*(S)*

### 1

To human beings reborn through faith and sanctified according to the form of the Gospel in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and who through this confession hope for the heavenly kingdom, the Apostle declared that nothing is more useful than that they should devote themselves to good works.

Thus he writes to Titus: “And concerning these things I wish you to affirm, [Note: [Col. 0847D] The Vulgate edition of the New Testament reads: “that those who have believed in God should be careful to preside over good works.” Nicetas therefore uses an older translation of the Bible, which often departs from the Vulgate. Those who diligently collect the remnants of that translation will now also consult our Nicetas with benefit. For this reason I have indicated in the margin the passages of the Vulgate edition. [We have placed them in parentheses in the text. Editor.]] that those who believe in God should take care of good works. These things,” he says, “are good and useful to human beings. But avoid foolish questions, genealogies, quarrels, and disputes about the law, for they are useless and vain” (Titus 3:8).

In writing this, the blessed Apostle already foresaw that people would arise who, through curiosity and useless questions, would neglect the care of good works and destroy the peace which the Lord had left to his Church.

For people who, while attempting to think lofty thoughts, are not even permitted to understand humble ones, have forgotten the Apostle’s saying, “Do not be high-minded, but fear” (Romans 11:20). Thus, while they presume upon what is unlawful, they have also lost what is lawful.

These are the people who, although they cannot gather together or comprehend by their senses the structure of heaven and earth, nevertheless attempt to grasp and measure God himself, their creator and maker. Instead of simply and solely worshiping the One whom they ought to adore through the greatness of his works and the immensity of such mighty things, they bring him into question and debate the quality and magnitude of his mystery, saying: “How great is the Father? What is the Son like? Of what kind is the Holy Spirit?”

O human being, who do not yet know yourself, do you dare to measure divine things?

### 2

I say nothing about Sabellius the Patripassian, who in foolish presumption dared to say that the one who is the Father is himself the Son, and that he is also the Holy Spirit; that the Trinity exists in name only and not in reality; that the Persons do not subsist, but exist solely by designation. In this way he confounds everything, pretending that the Father himself assumed a body and suffered.

I say nothing about Photinus [Note: [Col. 0849D] The manuscript has *Photinianus* here incorrectly, but correctly elsewhere.], who, hearing of the incarnation of the only-begotten Son of God, his humility, and also that saving passion which he endured for us, thought that Christ was merely a human being. He denied the God whom he ought to have recognized from the works themselves, forgetting the Apostle’s statement:

“Since Christ was in the form of God, he took the form of a servant, so that he might give us, as servants of sin, the truest freedom” (Philippians 2:6). [Note: [Col. 0849D] So the manuscript reads, not *qui* (“who”).]

And to the Corinthians he says: “You know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that for our sake he became poor, although he was rich, so that by his poverty you might become rich” (2 Corinthians 8:9).

I say nothing, then, both of Sabellius and of Photinus, because nearly all the churches have pronounced a judgment upon them worthy of their error.

### 3.

You have asked me to say a few things about this heresy, which now maligns the Catholic faith—about that heresy, certainly, which arose from Arius as its author. For he was not content with the words of the Gospel or the preaching of the apostles, which clearly proclaim the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Nor did he deign to believe as he ought that the Father has a Son and that the Son truly has a Father. Instead, when the wretched man stretches himself beyond his limits and wishes to investigate how and in what manner God could beget, he failed to grasp the manner—which cannot be grasped—and fell into error, denying both the Father and the Son.

[Note: The manuscript has *haerese* here, but *haeresi* above.]

He denies the Father in this way: he says that the Father could not beget from himself a proper and true Son. He denies the Son in this way: he says that the Son was made from elsewhere and from things that did not exist, rather than begotten; that he is some sort of creature who deserved to be called “Son” because of his love, but is not truly the Son begotten from the Father. Hence he devised the claim that the Son is of another substance, so that he would not be believed to be the Father’s true Son.

[Note: Ambrose, *Against Palladius*, book II, chapter 8: “This is the cause of the error, this is the origin of the Arian heresy: they do not understand the power of God, nor recognize the ordering of so great a mystery, but compare God with human conditions.” Phoebadius transcribes all these words exactly in *Against the Arians*, little work II, chapter 8. See our *Patrology*, volume XX.]

Against this perversity and novel teaching of his, therefore, the Council of Nicaea was held, where, after all the Scriptures had been brought together and examined, the truth was made manifest and written down.

[Note: The manuscript has *nicea*, “Nicaea.”]

For Arius had said that the Son was from elsewhere and not from the Father, nor from the substance of the Father—that is, from that very reality which is God. But our holy fathers professed that he was born from the Father, that is, from the substance of the Father: God from God, light from light, true God from true God, born, not made, of one substance with the Father. Thus no difference at all is to be believed to exist in the Son.

[Note: After this word, the manuscript writes: “that is, from that very reality which is God.” A line is then drawn beneath the phrase, indicating that it is to be deleted as a mistaken repetition of the preceding clause.]

Indeed, if he is the true Son of God and truly begotten from God the Father, he must not be believed to be of another substance than that of which he is the Son. Thus, just as the Father is God, so the Son is God; and just as the Father is light, so the Son is light.

### 4.

But this very confession—that the Son is believed to be of the same substance—has offended some people, and the holy confession is twisted by slanders. They interpret “of one substance” as though we were saying that the Father had been divided; that the Son were a part of the Father; and that God the Father had been diminished in the Son. Or else they suppose that, through some flowing or derivation, the Son retains the unity of the Father’s substance.

May such a notion be far from Christian minds—and even from Christian ears. We believe the Son to be of one substance with the Father in such a way that we believe the Father to be perfect in his eternity and to remain in his impassibility, and to have begotten the Son without experiencing any passion or diminution of his nature or majesty. Being himself perfect, he begot from himself, before all ages, the perfect, true, almighty Son, through whom all things were made and without whom nothing was made. Thus he is believed to be the true Father of his only-begotten Son and the true Son of the Father—not confused, but distinct—while the Son possesses in himself all that belongs to the Father, as he himself says in the Gospel: “All that the Father has is mine” (John 16:15).

What are those “all things”? Certainly power, might, goodness, incorruptibility, glory, and eternity, just as the Father has them. Otherwise, if these things are not in the Son, I hesitate to say that the Father would seem to have degenerated in the Son.

[Note: Rufinus notes in his explanation of the creed that the epithet “impassible” was added to the words “God the Father” in the creed of Aquileia. Nicetas of Aquileia is therefore speaking here according to the creed of his own church.]

And if the Son is thus judged degenerate, how can the same honor be given to him when the Lord himself says that “all should honor the Son just as they honor the Father” (John 5:23)? This is what the Lord requires; this is what the faithful display. They are not scandalized by the humility of the Son, our Savior, nor by his words spoken according to his humanity, nor by the sufferings which he deigned to undergo for the salvation of the world. Rather, through these very things they recognize that they owe Christ greater grace and greater honor. Even if the Gospel had not commanded that all should honor the Son just as they honor the Father, the more faithful would do so of their own accord, because the one who deigned to humble himself ought to be exalted, as it is written: “Whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11).

### 5.

But when the Father says, “This is my Son; hear him” (Matthew 3:17),

[Note: Nicetas now joins the other New Testament manuscripts that contain the addition “hear him”; this was how he read the passage in his own manuscript.]

and the Son says, “All should honor the Son just as they honor the Father” (John 5:23), what blindness of mind is it to set aside honor and devise insults? What forgetfulness of hope is it to consider weak, inferior, and contemptible Christ, who, according to the will of his Father, has bestowed strength, greatness, and glory upon us?

[Note: The manuscript has *errare*, “to err,” instead of *aestimare*, “to consider.” The latter reading seems to me the one that should be restored.]

Believe me: the honor given to the Son is the dignity of the Father. The more honor you show the only-begotten Son, the more you increase the Father’s glory. A good Father does not begrudge glory to the Son, because all the Son’s glory returns to the Father. This is the Catholic understanding; this is the devotion of the faithful; this is the zeal of the saints. According to these principles they understand all the Savior’s words and deeds, and, understanding them, they speak of them.

Nor are they at all hindered in this devotion by those passages that seem to reveal the Lord’s will: “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28); “I have not come to do my own will” (John 6:38); “The Son can do nothing of himself” (John 5:19); and many other statements of this kind. None of these weakens or diminishes the Son; they distinguish him from the Father.

[Note: The manuscript has *distingunt*, “distinguish,” in an older orthography.]

Indeed, these statements have been set down so that his true divinity should not be denied:

“I came forth from God the Father” (John 16:28);

“I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 10:38);

“I and the Father are one” (John 10:30);

“Whoever sees me sees the Father” (John 14:9);

and, “Just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wishes” (John 5:21).

### 6.

Nor do those things scandalize the faithful soul by which the Lord is reported to have hungered, slept, and wept; nor his sorrow even unto death, his cross, passion, and burial. These things were written and done so that examples of endurance might be provided and his true incarnation made known.

When the Lord is said to have hungered, understand the assumption of a true body. But when he feeds five thousand people with five loaves and two fish, recognize his true divinity.

[Note: The manuscript has *milia* with a single *l*, an older orthography.]

Certainly, when he says, “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:41), it does not accord with our understanding to believe that bread could hunger.

The same should be understood of sleep. Just as the reality of his body is recognized through sleep, so his true divinity is demonstrated by the fact that he immediately commands the winds and the waves.

[Note: The manuscript has *somnium*, “dream,” instead of *somnum*, “sleep.”]

When he shed tears over Lazarus, suspicion of a phantom is removed, for tears are fluids of a true body. But when he says, “Lazarus, come out” (John 11:43), and immediately the man who already stank emerges alive as the earth opens, this is a great indication of his divinity.

The statement, “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matthew 26:38), can likewise be understood from this resurrection of Lazarus, so that we may know how it ought to be interpreted. The divinity did not fear death; rather, he revealed a human feeling through the sorrow of his soul.

[Note: Nicetas also mentions together the miracles of the multiplication of the bread, the calming of the storm, and the restoration of Lazarus to life in his explanation of the creed. There too he makes the same comparison between Christ’s weak humanity and his powerful divinity. He has imitated Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 35.]

The cross, passion, and burial are likewise answered by one or another saying of the Lord, so that weakness or incapacity may not be attributed to him.

[Note: The manuscript has *una vel altera*, “one or another.”]

When he says to the Jews, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19), he was speaking of his own body. Again he says, “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10:18).

[Note: The manuscript reads *sic*, “thus.”]

If he raises the temple of his body, if he has the power to lay down his soul through passion and take it up again through resurrection, then the idea of weakness in Christ comes to an end, since the sublimity of such great power is revealed.

### 7.

Everything, therefore, must be understood devoutly; everything must be treated honorably. Both realities must be confessed in the Lord: the form in which he always existed and the form of a servant, which he assumed for the sake of servants. His passion according to the flesh and his impassibility according to his divinity must both be believed, lest we be judged either impious or ungrateful.

[Note: The manuscript has *conficiendum*, “to be completed/confessed.”]

[Note: The manuscript lacks the second *aut*, “or.”]

Whoever denies that the Son of God, in what he is, is impassible, and says that he is unlike God the Father, is impious. Whoever is unwilling to confess his sufferings according to the flesh is ungrateful.

Let us therefore glory in the cross of Christ, as Paul was accustomed to glory:

“Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Galatians 6:14).

Let us confess the unity, so that we may not be separated:

[Note: Read *commortui*, “having died with him.”]

“If we have died with him,” says the Apostle, “we shall also live together; if we endure, we shall also reign with him. If we deny him, he will also deny us” (2 Timothy 2:12).

If we do not believe what he himself says—“I and the Father are one”—he remains faithful; he cannot deny himself. He is in the glory of God the Father; he lives with the Father; he reigns with the Father by one and the same authority.

As the Apostle says, speaking of every immoral, unclean, and greedy person:

“He will not be an heir in the kingdom of Christ and of God” (Ephesians 5:5).

He calls the kingdom one, belonging both to Christ and to God, because the will of the Father and the Son is one; their cooperation is one; finally, their grace and governance are the same.

The same teacher of the nations teaches this when he writes:

“Grace to you and peace from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ.”

And again:

“May God himself, our Father, and the Lord Jesus direct our way to you” (1 Thessalonians 3:11).

He did not say “may they direct,” lest he introduce a difference between the Father and the Son either in will or in power. Rather, he said “may he direct,” in order to demonstrate unity.

In this faith, therefore, using these same words, let us also pray that the one grace, one peace, and one governance of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit may always protect and direct us.

I could not refuse you these few remarks in return, by way of a little commentary, since you asked that they be written for you. I trust that, although brief, they will be able to provide faithful souls with complete joy in God.

**The book of Nicetas, bishop, on the Account of the Faith, ends.**

[Note: Here the word “bishop” correctly appears in the manuscript, though the copyist carelessly omitted it in the title of the little work before its beginning. Conversely, the same copyist omitted “holy” before “Nicetas” in the title here, although he had correctly included it at the beginning of the work.]

**The same author’s work on the Power of the Holy Spirit begins.**

[Col. 0853]

## The Power of the Holy Spirit, by Saint Nicetas, Bishop of Aquileia

[Note: Victorinus, in the commentary on Galatians 4:6 which I published in earlier years, and in *Against the Arians* III.17, calls the persons of the Holy Trinity “powers.” Nicetas should therefore be understood in this title in that sense.]

### 1.

It remains for me to explain, according to the capacity of my mind, what I think about the third person, that is, the Holy Spirit. I understand that many people are especially doubtful about this matter.

[Note: Gregory of Nazianzus speaks similarly near the end of his panegyric on Saint Athanasius. For the history of the ancient errors concerning the Holy Spirit, beginning with the Sadducees, see Petavius, *On the Trinity* I.14. The same author should also be read in II.13 and III.7. Among the ecclesiastical Fathers who explicitly defended the divinity of the Holy Spirit, the principal surviving authorities are Didymus, Saint Basil, Saint Ambrose, Saint Athanasius, Theodoret, Saint Cyril of Alexandria, and Paschasius, deacon of the Roman Church. Nicetas of Aquileia now joins them. I have recently published in this volume Jerome Donatus’s extensive treatise on this subject.]

Although it is rash to debate about one who is joined with the Father and the Son in the confession of faith, according to the Lord’s command and our confession in baptism, nevertheless, since many people think differently and an explanation is demanded of us, an answer must be given. It must be drawn from no other source than the fountains of the divine Scriptures.

I am certain, however, that ears already preoccupied and minds burdened by another opinion can scarcely be pacified, for prejudice is dangerous. Human nature is such that, if something bad has been whispered to us about a good man, and a false report has preceded our knowledge of the truth, we relinquish the opinion we have accepted only with difficulty and labor, even when reliable witnesses instruct us otherwise.

I suspect that this will now happen to many who, having been anticipated by the perverse interpretation of teachers, have believed the Holy Spirit to be a creature and have despised him as a minister. Let us therefore return to our subject.

### 2.

In the Nicene statement, according to the form of the creed, it is written: “And we believe in the Holy Spirit.” This was certainly sufficient for the faithful, because at that council the question concerned the Son, not the Holy Spirit.

Would that those who later introduced the question concerning the Spirit—such as the Macedonians and those who shared in their curiosity—had simply believed in the Holy Spirit with the Father and the Son, just as the faith had been handed down!

For while they ask, “What sort of being is the Holy Spirit? From where is he? How great is he? Was he born, or was he made?” they have again divided the people and, truly, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying (1 Timothy 1:4), introduced an endless question into the churches.

Was it not sufficient that they honor him whom they had once believed to be holy and begotten, together with the Father and the Son, rather than associate him with creatures?

[Note: The heretics said that the Spirit was “born”; Nicetas is now reporting their opinion or words.]

But they continue to introduce questions and strive, through tortuous interrogations, to rob the simple of their faith. I think no one doubts that a malicious question, unless the person questioned is cautious, plunges him into ignorance and blasphemy.

Hence Paul gives this warning:

“See that no one robs you through philosophy and empty deception” (Colossians 2:8).

For those rebellious against the Holy Spirit ask: “Was the Holy Spirit born or unborn?” Behold two snares stretched out to right and left. Whichever way you extend the foot of your answer, you will be caught.

If you say, “He was born,” they will say that the only-begotten Son of God is no longer unique, since there is another who was born. If you say, “He was not born,” they will tell you that there will then be another Father who is unbegotten, and that God the Father, from whom all things are, is no longer one.

After blocking the path of your answer on both sides, they then lead you, as though along a straight course, into a pit, saying: “If the Spirit was neither born from the Father nor unbegotten, it remains that he must be called a creature.”

### 3.

What will the faith of the Church do amid these enclosed passages? Should it yield to tortuous philosophy and, contrary to the opinion of all the Scriptures, both Old and New Testaments, believe that the Holy Spirit of God was created, although nowhere could it read that he is a creature?

[Note: The manuscript has *credit*, “believes,” for *credat*, “should believe.”]

Away with such a thought. It will do far better to reject such human conclusions and the chains of interrogation and turn to the words of its Lord.

For in the Gospel he himself says where the Holy Spirit comes from; he himself sets an end to a question that has no end. He says to the apostles:

“I will send you from the Father the Paraclete, the Spirit of truth” (John 15:26).

But from where is he? You do not know. If you wish to know, hear him himself saying:

“He proceeds from the Father.”

What ought we to do now, brothers? Hear Christ or human beings? Christ did not say that the Holy Spirit was made, but only that he proceeds from the Father.

[Note: The manuscript repeats “What ought we to do now, brothers?” and then crosses out the repeated line.]

His opponents say that he was made and created. I think it would be better to believe what Christ the Lord revealed than what human presumption has contrived.

But if we ask them from where they can prove that the Holy Spirit was made, since they have no certain and evident testimony from Scripture, let them take up what is said in the Gospel:

“All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:1).

They therefore say: “If all things were made through him, then the Holy Spirit must be believed to have been made among all things.”

This is not a suitable proof, but rather a scrupulous inference. I ask, therefore: in what Spirit was the mouth of John, who said these things, speaking? Was it not in the Holy Spirit? If he was speaking in the Spirit, then the Spirit himself was speaking.

John was speaking of those things that were made through him—that is, all things established in the multitude and order of creatures. He was not speaking of the Holy Spirit himself, so that the Spirit too might be believed to have been made from nothing among the other creatures.

[Note: The manuscript lacks *de*, “of,” in this clause.]

### 4.

Blessed Paul the Apostle is also a witness to this matter, for he specifically lists the things that were made through Christ:

“In him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones,

[Note: The manuscript has *sedes*, “seats,” rather than *throni*, “thrones”; Victorinus also has *sedes* in *Against Arius* I.24. In chapter 36 he has *throni*, which is certainly a variation introduced by copyists.]

or dominions, or principalities, or powers. All things were created through him and in him” (Colossians 1:26).

[Note: Victorinus has *constituta*, “established.” The copies of the Old Latin version also varied. Victorinus himself has *creata*, “created,” in chapter 36; these are decisions of scribes.]

Did he mention the Holy Spirit among all things heavenly and earthly? Certainly he would have mentioned him first if he had known him to be created or made like the rest.

But if you insist on understanding the statement “all things were made through him” so rigorously that you do not except the Holy Spirit, I ask what you think of the prophet David’s words addressed to God the Lord:

“All things serve you” (Psalm 118:91).

Do you say that the Holy Spirit serves among all things, or do you call him a servant, when he is not a servant but the Lord who frees creation from slavery?

That the Holy Spirit is Lord, Paul says in his letter to the Thessalonians:

“May the Lord direct your hearts into the love of God and the endurance of Christ” (2 Thessalonians 3:5).

He clearly calls the Spirit “Lord,” for the Savior himself had said to the apostles that the Spirit “will guide you into all truth” (John 16:13).

Paul teaches this still more clearly when he says:

“The Lord is the Spirit; and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Corinthians 3:17).

And to the Romans:

“You did not receive a spirit of slavery again for fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption” (Romans 8:15).

If he is the Spirit of adoption and makes human beings children of God, how can he be placed in the condition of a servant, when a servant cannot legitimately set free?

“For because you are sons,” he says, “God sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father.’ Therefore you are no longer a servant but a son; and if a son, also an heir through God” (Galatians 4:6–7).

If Christ makes me free, a son, and an heir of the divinity of his proper name, I would be impious if I called him a servant who makes me free.

The freedom of the Spirit is also revealed in what the Apostle says:

“One and the same Spirit accomplishes all these things, distributing to each person as he wills” (1 Corinthians 12:11).

Where voluntary distribution is proclaimed, a condition of slavery cannot be seen. In a creature, slavery is to be understood; in the Trinity, however, there are dominion and freedom.

Therefore, if the statement in the Psalm, “all things serve you,” refers to creatures and not to the Holy Spirit, then the statement “all things were made through him” also does not include the Holy Spirit among all things. For he is not read to have been made from any material or from nothing, since he proceeds from the Father.

[Note: Nicetas also writes simply “from the Father,” without adding “and the Son,” in his *Explanation of the Creed*. Other Fathers likewise often spoke in this way before the controversy arose. On this matter, see the distinguished Braida’s commentary on the aforementioned work of Nicetas, p. 270.]

### 5.

It is sufficient for the faithful to know this: the Son was begotten, whereas the Spirit proceeds from the Father. Let us use the very words which divine Scripture intended us to use.

Whoever loves life and knows the author of life, and has received the three names with equal honor in the sacrament of baptism, does not seek a limit there where he believed that no beginning existed.

We therefore believe that the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, proceeds from the Father. He is not the Son, nor the Son of the Son, as foolish people habitually investigate.

[Note: The manuscript has *stulta*, “foolish things.” It would also be possible to write *stulti*, “foolish people.”]

He is the Spirit of truth, whose manner and extent of procession no one is permitted to know. For concerning the incomprehensibility of the Spirit, the Lord also said in the Gospel:

“The Spirit blows where he wills, and you hear his voice, but you do not know where he comes from or where he goes” (John 3:8).

We know that this Spirit exists in his own true person: the fountain of sanctification, the light of souls, and the distributor of graces. This Spirit sanctifies; he is not sanctified. He illuminates; he is not illuminated. Without this Spirit, no creature can attain eternity or truly be called holy.

I dare to say that the Lord’s own temple—that is, the body which he received from the Virgin—was certainly equipped by this very Spirit.

The angel Gabriel said to Mary:

“The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the one who will be born from you is of the Holy Spirit” (Luke 1:35).

Behold, we find that the very temple in which the word of the Lord dwelt was sanctified by the Spirit.

Although the Lord himself says of himself, “The one whom the Father sanctified and sent into this world” (John 10:36), and again, “The Son of God can sanctify both his own body and all things” (John 17:19), nevertheless, to reveal to the world the power and distinct identity of the Holy Spirit, at the time of his baptism he himself received the Holy Spirit into his own body in the form of a dove.

Thus, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement, “all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily” in him. From this fullness the apostles afterward receive grace upon grace, as the Lord breathed upon the apostles’ faces and said:

“Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive anyone’s sins, they are forgiven; if you retain anyone’s sins, they are retained” (John 20:22–23).

And since it is written, “Who can forgive sins except God alone?” (Luke 5:21), behold, the apostles are shown to forgive sins by Christ’s authority.

The greatness of the Spirit’s sanctification is therefore known, since it is shown to have been applied to the Lord’s own body; and the Spirit’s power is also known, since he forgives sins.

### 6.

Let us therefore come to his other powers and works, so that what the Holy Spirit is and how great he is may be recognized. For just as the Father and the Son are known through their works, as the Lord himself says, “Believe because of my works” (John 10:38), so the Holy Spirit cannot be fully known except through the marks of his works.

Let no one be anxious when we present passages concerning the power of the Holy Spirit. Let no one close his ears when the divine words are recited. They ought to believe the heavenly testimonies more than earthly inventions.

What, then, do we intend? Without doubt, we wish to follow the tradition of the Lord’s signs. If we are reborn in the name of the Father and the Son, not without the Holy Spirit; if we are sanctified and proceed toward eternity, not without the Holy Spirit; then we wish to show that the Holy Spirit has worked and always works with the Father and the Son not only in baptism but also in everything else.

### 7.

Indeed, this one fact would be sufficient: he is found to have cooperated in the sacrament of baptism. From this it is also understood that other things were not created without the Spirit.

For how could the renewal and restoration of a human being take place with the Spirit, while the formation and creation of the human being are believed to have occurred without the Spirit? Is there any doubt that the sacrament of baptism is greater than the very beginnings of creation? In baptism eternity is perfected, whereas at the beginning death reigned from Adam.

Let us therefore hear David prophesying about creation:

“By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their host” (Psalm 32:6).

This “word” must certainly be understood as the Son, according to John’s proclamation, through whom all things were made. The “breath of his mouth” is none other than the one believed to be the Holy Spirit. In one verse, therefore, you have the Lord, the word of the Lord, and the Holy Spirit, fulfilling the mystery of the Trinity.

If someone should impudently wish to interpret this “word,” through which the heavens were established, as merely a command, and should likewise call the Spirit dissolvable air,

[Note: Nicetas recognizes the grammatical sense of the word “spirit,” but gives precedence to its sacred meaning.]

he must gradually fall into Judaism, since neither Photinus nor the Jews allow anything to have been created through the substantive Word and the Spirit.

### 8.

But you will say: “It is clear concerning the Word that he created; what about the Spirit?” Receive another testimony from that most righteous and ancient man, Job:

“The divine Spirit who made me” (Job 33:4).

And David, singing praises, says to God:

“Send forth your Spirit, and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth” (Psalm 103:30).

If creation and renewal occur through the Spirit, then unquestionably the beginning of creation did not occur without the Spirit.

But those who resist the truth habitually turn the word and person of the Spirit into a reference to the Son wherever the Spirit is found to be Creator. They do this because the Son too is Spirit, just as the Father is Spirit.

This must certainly not be believed as a result of their perverse argument. It is disproved by the fact that David mentioned both the word of the Lord, which is the Son, and also proclaimed the Spirit, who is holy: the Word establishes the heavens, and the Spirit establishes all their host—that is, their adornment.

[Note: The manuscript has *ornatuum*, “of adornments.”]

So let those who read these things believe; or, if they do not wish to believe, why do they read them?

But let no one think that this faith concerns an insult to God the Father. Rather, it redounds to his glory if all things are said to have been created by his Word, whose Father he himself is, or by his Spirit, whose author he himself is. For he himself creates all things when his Word and Spirit create them.

[Note: The manuscript has *erat*, “was,” instead of *creat*, “creates.”]

[Note: Nicetas also uses “faith” in the sense of firm belief in his *Explanation of the Creed*. On this word, see Braida, pp. 264 ff.; Salvianus, *On the Government of God* III.2: “What is faith or belief? I think it is for a person faithfully to believe Christ,” and likewise Paulinus in a poem published by me in *Classical Authors*, volume V, p. 378.]

### 9.

After creation, let us show that the Trinity gives life.

Regarding the person of the Father, the Apostle says:

“I testify before God, who gives life to all things” (1 Timothy 5:21; 6:13).

Christ gives life:

“My sheep hear my voice, and I give them eternal life” (John 10:27).

We are given life through the Spirit, as the Lord himself says:

“It is the Spirit who gives life” (John 6:64).

Likewise Paul says to the Romans:

“He who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies, because of his Spirit dwelling in you” (Romans 8:11).

[Note: The manuscript has *vivificavit*, “gave life,” instead of *vivificabit*, “will give life.”]

Behold, the one life-giving work of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit has been plainly demonstrated.

### 10.

Foreknowledge of all things is in God, and he is the knower of hidden things. Although no Christian is ignorant of this, it must nevertheless be demonstrated from the book of Daniel:

“O God, knower of hidden things, who see all things before they come into being” (Daniel 13:42).

This same foreknowledge is in Christ, as the Evangelist says:

“From the beginning Jesus knew who it was that would betray him, and who those were who did not believe” (John 6:65).

That he is the knower of hidden things was made manifest when he exposed the secret designs of the Jews, saying:

“Why are you thinking evil in your hearts?” (Matthew 9:4).

### 11.

God has likewise shown that the Spirit foreknows all things, saying to the apostles:

“When the Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all things and announce to you the things to come” (John 16:13).

Since he is said to announce things to come, surely no one will doubt that he foreknows all things, because he searches the depths of God and knows all that belongs to God.

[Note: The manuscript has *scruptatur*, an obvious error for *scrutatur*, “searches.”]

He also reveals God’s mysteries. Daniel bears witness:

“He is God of gods and King of kings, who reveals mysteries” (Daniel 2:47).

All things are revealed through Christ, as he himself says:

“No one knows the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wishes to reveal him” (Luke 10:22).

Every revelation, however, is in the Spirit. Paul testifies:

“God has revealed to us through his Holy Spirit” (1 Corinthians 2:10).

Behold, there is the revelation of the one God of the Trinity.

### 12.

That he is present everywhere and fills all things is shown by Isaiah:

“I am God who draws near, and God from afar” (Isaiah 30:27).

“If a person is hidden in secret places, will I not see him? Do I not fill heaven and earth?” (Jeremiah 23:24).

What does the Savior Christ say in the Gospel about his own presence, since he is everywhere?

“Wherever two or three are in my name, there I am in their midst” (Matthew 18:20).

[Note: Nicetas’s text lacks the word *congregati*, “gathered together.”]

Concerning his fullness, the Apostle says:

“The one who descended is also the one who ascended above all the heavens, in order to fill all things” (Ephesians 4:10).

The prophet likewise says of the Holy Spirit, that he is present everywhere:

[Note: The manuscript has *assit*, “is present,” a reading that can be accepted.]

“I am among you, and my Spirit stands in your midst” (Haggai 2:6).

And Solomon says:

“The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world” (Wisdom 1:7).

God dwells in his saints, according to the promise he gave:

“I will dwell in them and walk among them” (2 Corinthians 6:16).

And what does the Lord say in the Gospel?

“Remain in me, and I in you” (John 15:4).

Paul confirms this:

“Do you not know that Jesus Christ is in you?” (2 Corinthians 13:5).

All this is fulfilled through the indwelling of the Spirit, as John recalls:

“By this we know that he is in us: by the Spirit which he has given us” (1 John 3:24).

Likewise Paul says:

“Do you not know that you are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (1 Corinthians 3:16).

And immediately afterward he says:

“Glorify and bear God in your body” (1 Corinthians 6:20).

13. For that the Father rebukes, the Son also rebukes, and the Holy Spirit likewise rebukes, must be proved as follows. In Psalm 49 it is written: “But to the sinner God said, ‘Why do you recount my ordinances?’” (Ps. 49:16). And below: “I shall rebuke you and set it before your face” (ibid., 21) [Note: Thus the manuscript.]. David likewise, praying, says to God: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger” (Ps. 6:2). And because he himself is to come to rebuke all flesh (Jude 15). But what does the Savior say about the Holy Spirit in the Gospel? “When that Paraclete has come,” he says, “he will rebuke the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment” (John 16:8). Foreseeing this, David cried out to God: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence?” (Ps. 138:7).

That there will be one judgment from God through Christ, blessed Paul demonstrates [Note: The manuscript has *ad eum*, “to him,” for *a Deo*, “from God.”]: “God will judge the hidden things of human beings through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 2:16). And that the Holy Spirit will judge Antichrist, Paul says when speaking of him: “The Lord Jesus,” he says, “will kill him with the Spirit of his mouth” (2 Thess. 2:8). If Antichrist is killed by the Spirit of the Lord’s mouth, then every creature will also be judged by the Spirit, as Solomon says: “The Spirit of power will stand against them and divide them like a whirlwind” (Wis. 5:24).

14. That the Father is good, the Son is good, and the Holy Spirit is good is likewise proved as follows. Concerning the Father, the Only-Begotten said in the Gospel: “No one is good except the one God” (Matt. 19:17). Concerning himself: “I am the good shepherd” (John 10:11). Concerning the Spirit, David likewise says in song: “Your good Spirit will lead me on a straight path” (Ps. 142). And just as it is said of the Son, “The word of the Lord is upright” (Ps. 32:4), so also it is said of the Spirit: “Renew an upright spirit within me” (Ps. 50:10).

15. Who could remain silent about the dignity of the Holy Spirit? For the ancient prophets cried out, “Thus says the Lord.” Christ, when he came, appropriated this utterance to his own person, saying: “And I say to you.” But what do the new prophets proclaim? As Agabus, prophesying in the Acts of the Apostles, says: “Thus says the Holy Spirit” (Acts 21:11).

And again the Apostle Paul says that he was called and sent by God the Father and by Christ (Gal. 1:1), not from human beings nor through a human being, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father. In the Acts of the Apostles, however, it is written that he was set apart and sent by the Holy Spirit. For thus it is written: “And the Holy Spirit said, ‘Set apart for me Barnabas and Paul for the work to which I have called them’” (Acts 13:2). And shortly afterward: “And so, sent by the Holy Spirit, they went down to Seleucia” (ibid., 4).

16. But let no one, because the Holy Spirit is called the Paraclete, regard him as something contemptible [Note: The manuscript reads “contemptible things.”]. For in the Latin language Paraclete means advocate or comforter. This title is also shared by the Son of God, as John teaches: “I write these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (1 John 2:1).

When the Lord himself says to the apostles, “The Father will send you another advocate,” undoubtedly, by naming another Paraclete, he thereby also identifies himself as a Paraclete. Nor is the name Paraclete foreign to the Father: it is a name of benevolence, not of nature. Finally, Paul writes to the Corinthians: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, who consoles us” (2 Cor. 1:3). In Greek this is expressed as: “and God of all consolation” (*καὶ Θεὸς πάσης παρακλήσεως*) [Note: The Greek words were absent from the manuscript, which left a blank space; I supplied them to fit the space.].

And when the Father is called the Comforter, the Son the Comforter, and the Holy Spirit the Comforter, nevertheless one consolation of the Trinity is bestowed upon us. “But you were washed, sanctified, and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God” (1 Cor. 6:11).

17. Perhaps these gentle and benevolent things do not stir the mind to understand the power of the Holy Spirit; let us bring forward a few things of a terrifying character. Ananias had sold a possession, as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles, and had kept back part of the money for himself, laying the remainder at the feet of the apostles as though it were the whole amount. He offended the Holy Spirit, from whom he had thought he could hide. But what did blessed Peter immediately say to him? “Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart, so that you should lie to the Holy Spirit?” (Acts 5:3). And immediately he said: “You have not lied to human beings but to God.” And so, struck down by the power of the one to whom he had wished to lie, he breathed his last.

What does blessed Peter intend the Holy Spirit to be understood as here? [Note: Thus the manuscript, which has *blessed*, although shortly before it has *most blessed*.] It is certainly clear when he says: “You have not lied to human beings but to God.” It is therefore evident that whoever lies to the Holy Spirit lies to God; and whoever believes in the Holy Spirit believes in God. Likewise Ananias’s wife, who had shared in the deceit, also became his companion in death.

The Lord shows something similar, indeed something more forceful, in the Gospel, saying: “Every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven human beings; but whoever speaks blasphemy against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come” (Matt. 12:32; Mark 3:28–29; Luke 12:10). A terrifying sentence! He declares that the sin of one who blasphemes against the Holy Spirit is unforgivable [Note: Nicetas expresses, or rather writes, this judgment absolutely also in his *Explanation of the Creed*; Braida discusses the passage, pp. 289 ff.].

Compare this sentence with what is written in the Book of Kings: “If a man sins against a man, they will pray for him; but if he sins against God, who will pray for him?” (1 Kings 2:25). Therefore, because to sin against the Holy Spirit and to sin against God is the same, it is an unatonable crime. They can now perceive how great is the majesty of the Holy Spirit: whoever rebels against him will be thrust into everlasting punishments.

[Note: Yet sins against God are expiable before God, although here the contrary seems almost to be said. Therefore nearly the same answer applies to sin against the Holy Spirit—namely, that Nicetas has spoken more severely than he would have wished himself to be understood.]

18. I could produce more testimonies from the divine Scriptures which, in accordance with the sacrament of Baptism, would reveal the Trinity as possessing one operation and power. But since even in these matters the understanding of the wise is complete, I pass over many things. I shall therefore make a recapitulation, saying:

If the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father; if he liberates; if he sanctifies; if he is Lord, as the Apostle said; if he creates with the Father and the Son; if he gives life; if he possesses foreknowledge, as the Father and the Son do; if he reveals; if he is everywhere; if he fills the world; if he dwells in the elect [Note: The manuscript erroneously reads “in the heights”; compare p. 325]; if he will rebuke the world; if he judges; if he is good; if he is upright; if it is proclaimed of him, “Thus says the Holy Spirit”; if he appoints prophets; if he sends apostles; if he is the Comforter; if he washes and justifies; if he kills those who tempt him [Note: The manuscript reads “his tempters”]; if the one who blasphemes against him has no forgiveness, neither in this age nor in the age to come—which is certainly proper to God [Note: The manuscript reads “for whom, indeed, I command”; in another Vatican manuscript I read *devote*, “devoutly,” for *dubie*, “doubtfully”]—if these things are so, indeed because they are true, what is being asked of me when I am asked to say what the Holy Spirit is, since through the greatness of his works he reveals what he is?

He is certainly not alien to the holiness of the Father and the Son, since he is not alien to the power of their works. In vain is the name of divinity denied to him whose power cannot be denied. In vain am I forbidden to worship him with the Father and the Son, when the truth itself compels me to confess him with the Father and the Son. If he grants me, with the Father and the Son, forgiveness of sins, sanctification, and eternal life, I shall be exceedingly ungrateful and impious if I do not render glory to him together with the Father and the Son.

Or if he is not to be worshiped with the Father and the Son, then neither should he be confessed in Baptism. But if he must be confessed in every respect, according to the Lord’s command and the apostles’ tradition, so that faith may not be partial and imperfect, who will be able to restrain me from his worship and veneration? For in whom I am commanded to believe, to him I shall also pray devoutly.

19. Therefore I shall adore the Father, I shall adore the Son, I shall adore the Holy Spirit, with one and the same veneration. If anyone thinks this harsh, let him hear how David urges the faithful toward the worship of God [Note: Here *cultura* undoubtedly signifies religious worship. Nicetas uses the same word in his *Explanation of the Creed*, clearly, in my judgment, in the same sense, since it there concerns renouncing the worship of the devil. I therefore cannot agree with the learned Zabaeus, in his edition of Nicetas’s *Explanation of the Creed*, who thinks that *cultura* there signifies elegance of dress. Saint Ildefonsus of Toledo also says, in *On Ecclesiastical Writers* 3, “the worship of idols.” Indeed Lactantius, *Institutions* V.7: “the pious and religious worship of the one God.” So Tertullian, *Apology* 21: “He denies what he worships and transfers worship to another.”]: “Adore the footstool of his feet, for it is holy” (Ps. 98:5). If the Lord’s footstool is to be adored as an act of religious worship, how much more religious will it be to adore his Spirit?

That is the Spirit whom blessed Peter proclaimed with such exalted praise, saying: “They announced to you the Holy Spirit sent from heaven, into whom angels long to look” (1 Pet. 1:12) [Note: There is a notable variant: “They evangelized the Holy Spirit sent,” instead of “the Holy Spirit sent,” as in the common edition and likewise in the Greek text, *ἐν Πνεύματι ἁγίῳ ἀποσταλέντι*. Thus, if the manuscript’s reading is sound, Nicetas says that the Holy Spirit himself was preached by the apostles.].

If angels desire to gaze upon him, how much more ought we mortal human beings not to despise him? [Note: The manuscript reads “to regard with contempt.”] Otherwise it might also be said of us, as was said to the Jews: “You always resist the Holy Spirit, just as your fathers did” (Acts 7:51) [Note: So the manuscript reads. Eugenius of Carthage likewise shows that he read it in this form in his *Book of Faith*.].

20. But if these great and weighty considerations do not incline the mind to venerate the Holy Spirit, receive something still more forceful. Paul thus instructs the prophets of the Church, among whom and through whom the Spirit himself was speaking:

“If all are prophesying and some unbeliever or uninitiated person enters, he is convicted by all, he is examined by all, and the secrets of his heart are made manifest. And then, falling on his face, he will adore God, declaring that God is truly among you” (1 Cor. 14:24).

He certainly intended the Holy Spirit, who was speaking in the prophets, to be understood. If, then, unbelievers fall on their faces and adore the Holy Spirit—adoring in terror and confessing unwillingly because of the greatness of his works, that is, the abundance of spiritual grace—how much more is it fitting for believers voluntarily and devotedly to adore the Holy Spirit!

21. The Spirit is not adored as though separately, in the manner of the pagans; nor is the Son adored separately, since he is at the right hand of the Father. Rather, when we adore the Father, we faithfully believe that we are adoring the Son and the Holy Spirit together as well. For when we invoke the Son, we believe that we are invoking the Father; and when we beseech the Father, we believe that we are heard by the Son, as the Lord himself promises: “Whatever you ask of the Father in my name, I will do, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son.”

So also, when the Spirit is adored, the one whose Spirit he is is thereby adored.

22. No one is unaware that nothing can be added to or taken away from the divine majesty by human supplications. But each person, according to the purpose of his will, either acquires glory for himself by faithfully venerating it, or brings confusion upon himself by stubbornly resisting. For it is certain that both contention and pride produce condemnation, while honor looks for the fruit of devotion.

Why, then, should the faithful not honor the Trinity in its entirety, to which they trust they belong, in whose name they glory to have been reborn, and by whose title they glory to be called? For just as human beings are called people of God from the name of God the Father—thus Elijah was called a man of God, and Moses a man of God, and Timothy was called a man of God by Paul—so Christians are named from Christ; and so also those who are spiritual are named from the Spirit.

Therefore, if you are called a man of God but are not a Christian, you are nothing. Likewise, if you are called a Christian but are not spiritual, do not place excessive confidence in your salvation. Let there therefore be for us, according to the Savior’s Baptism, confession, the faith of the complete Trinity, and one devotion of piety. Let us neither, in the manner of the pagans, suppose differences among the divine powers, nor suspect a creature within the Trinity.

Nor let us succumb to the stumbling block of the Jews, who deny the Son of God and do not adore the Spirit. Rather, let us adore and magnify the perfect Trinity, and, just as we say with our mouths in the mysteries, “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth,” so let us hold this in our conscience:

“One is holy”—namely, the Spirit; “one is God”—Jesus Christ in the glory of God the Father; “one is omnipotence,” because the worship of the Trinity is one.

Then, pursuing peace and love, let us always abound in good works; and let us hear from the Apostle, as the Corinthians heard in the first Epistle [Note: Rather, the following words are found at the close of the Second Epistle]: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all. Amen.”

Here ends Saint Niceta, Bishop, *On the Power of the Holy Spirit*.

Here begins his treatise *On the Various Titles Appropriate to Our Lord Jesus Christ*.

[Column 863]

SAINT NICETA, BISHOP OF AQUILEIA, ON THE VARIOUS TITLES APPROPRIATE TO OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST. (C)*

[Note: Damasus treats the same subject in poem 11 of Sarazan’s edition (in our volume XIII, col. 378, *St. Damasus, poem 6*), although in the very ancient Vatican manuscript 353 these verses are attributed to a certain Silvius. In the Vatican manuscript, *via* appears for *vita*, “life”; *columba* for *columna*, “column”; and *panis* for *paries*, “wall.” The poet Orientius should also be consulted in the Pisaur collection, vol. VI, p. 89, and Phoebadius, *Against the Arians*, chapter 6; I scarcely doubt that the latter was read by Niceta.]

1. Many names and many titles are found in the holy Scriptures that are appropriate to the Lord Jesus and our Savior. He is called the Word; he is called Wisdom, Light, Power, Right Hand, Arm, Angel; he is called Man. He is called Lamb, Sheep, Priest, Way, Truth, Life; he is called Vine, Righteousness, Redemption; he is called Bread, Stone, Physician, Fountain of Living Water, Peace, Judge, and Door.

You will find many other names for Christ in the holy Scriptures [Note: The manuscript reads *in* for *de*, “concerning.” Another manuscript lacks several words here], although he is one and the same Son of God, our God, so that the nature of his power and dispensation may be understood. You have heard the titles; now seek the meanings of the titles.

He is called the Word either because he was begotten impassibly by God the Father, or because his generation came forth without diminution of the Father’s substance. For a human being also does not seem to suffer any diminution when he utters a word. Or certainly he is called the Word because through him God the Father has always spoken both to angels and to human beings.

He is called Wisdom because in the beginning all things were wisely ordered through him. He is called Light because he himself illuminated the world’s primordial darkness and, by his coming, drove away the nights of human minds. He is called Power because no creature can overcome him. He is called Right Hand and Arm because all things were created through him and all things are held together by him.

He is called the Angel of Great Counsel because he is the messenger of the Father’s will. He is called the Son of Man because, for our sake, he graciously consented to be born human. He is called Lamb because of his singular innocence. He is called Sheep so that his passion might be shown.

He is called Priest either because he offered his own body to God the Father as an offering and sacrifice for us, or because he graciously consents to be offered each day on our behalf [Note: Let us note the use of the daily Mass in Niceta’s time.]. He is called the Way because through him we proceed to salvation. He is called the Vine because, stretching out the branches of his arms on the cross, he bestowed upon the world the abundant fruit of sweetness.

He is called Righteousness because through faith in his name he justifies sinners. He is called Redemption because once lost, he redeemed us by the price of his blood. He is called Bread because through his Gospel he refreshed the hunger of the nations [Note: One manuscript reads *famis scientiam*; another, *scientiae*. I have corrected the text.]. He is called Stone because the serpent left no trace upon him, and he himself provided us with a defense.

He is called Physician because by his visitation he healed our illnesses and wounds. He is called the Fountain of Living Water because through the washing of regeneration he both cleanses and gives life to sinners. He is called Peace because he gathered those who were divided into one and reconciled them to God the Father. He is called Resurrection because he himself will raise all bodies from their tombs. He is called Judge because he will judge both the living and the dead. He is called the Door because through him entrance into the kingdom of heaven is opened to the faithful.

2. Therefore, since the Lord is called by so many names and titles, have confidence, faithful one, and establish your hope in him with all your strength. For if you wish to know the Father, he is the Word for you. If you wish to possess true wisdom, seek him, because he is Wisdom. If your understanding suffers some darkness, seek Christ, because he is Light. Are you ill? You have a refuge, because he is both Physician and Power.

Do you wish to know through whom the world was created and by whom all things are held together? Believe in him, because he is proclaimed to be the Arm and Right Hand. Do you endure some fear? He will be present to you in all things like an angel. If it is difficult for you to approach visually such great majesty of the Only-Begotten, do not despair, because he also became human, so that humanity might have easy access to him.

If you are innocent, he will join himself to you like a lamb [Note: Another manuscript reads “he will associate himself with you”]. If some persecution by the pagans troubles you, take courage, because he too was sacrificed like a sheep; and as Priest he will receive you to be offered to the Father.

If you do not know the way of salvation, seek Christ, because he is the path of souls. If you wish to know the truth, listen to him, because he is the Truth. Do not fear death at all, because Christ is the life of believers.

Does the sweetness of the world delight you? Turn rather toward the cross of Christ, so that you may be refreshed by the sweetness of his Vine, which hung upon the cross. Are you a lost sinner? You ought to hunger for righteousness and thirst for the Redeemer, who is Christ; for he satisfies, because he is Bread.

If you waver in anything, make your step firm in him, because he is the Stone, and he will make you secure like a wall. Are you weak and infirm? Seek healing from him, because he is the Physician. Do you suffer the burning of sins, especially if you are a catechumen, whoever you are? Run to the Fountain of Life, so that your burning may be extinguished and your soul may attain eternity.

If anger torments and discord drives you on, approach Christ, because he is Peace, so that you may be reconciled to the Father and love every human being as you judge that you ought to be loved [Note: I have supplied the word “judge.” In the manuscript a blank space exactly the length of one word is left.].

If you fear the decline of the body and dread the death of this life, remember that he is the Resurrection; he can raise up what has fallen. If the pleasure of sin entices you and the vices of the flesh provoke you [Note: Another manuscript reads “invite you”], consider with foreknowledge that he is the just Judge, the strict Examiner, and the one who prepares the eternal fire; and sin will never delight you.

Finally, brother, if despair has invaded you concerning the reward of righteousness or your hope of heavenly glory, presume with a faithful mind [Note: Another manuscript reads “with a believing mind”] that he is the Door. For through him, raised from the dead, you will penetrate the secrets of heaven and attain the fellowship of angels. And you will hear that desirable voice:

“Well done, good and faithful servant, because you have been faithful; enter into the joy of your Lord. Possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” [Note: Another manuscript reads “because you have been faithful in little.” Another reads “prepared”].

Through the gift of him who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns forever and ever (Matt. 25:23). Amen.

[Column 865]

SAINT NICETA, BISHOP OF AQUILEIA, *EXPLANATION OF THE CREED*, DELIVERED TO THE COMPETENTES

[Note: In an ancient Bobbio manuscript, preserved by Muratori, *Antiquitates Italicae Medii Aevi*, vol. III, p. 819, the title appears as follows: “Book One of the Instruction of Niceta, Bishop.”]

[Note: To explain this term, here is a passage from an ancient exposition of the Mass that I read in a Vatican manuscript. What is the difference between a catechumen and a *competens*? What a catechumen is has been sufficiently explained above; but what a *competens* is must be stated briefly. A *competens* is someone carefully instructed in the faith and attentively imbued with belief who, after receiving the teaching of Christianity, the mystery of the Creed, and the tradition of the Lord’s Prayer, asks and begs to be able to attain the mysteries and grace of holy Baptism, to become a participant in the holy Church, and to be with Christ among the faithful in his service. Hence they are called *competentes*, from asking.

Likewise, in an old manuscript sermon I read: “The requested Easter, or the Easter of the *competentes*, is so called because on that day the Creed—that is, the belief of the holy faith—was handed over to the *competentes*, the newly baptized, so that those who hastened to receive God’s grace at the solemnity of Easter might recognize the faith they ought to confess. For *competentes* means, as it were, ‘those asking together.’ Finally, in an ancient Vatican sacramentary manuscript I read: ‘The first rank: of catechumens; the second: of *competentes*; the third: of the baptized.’ There is a brief and light exhortation addressed to the *competentes* among the spurious sermons of Saint Fulgentius, no. 78. Augustine also has a good sermon addressed to the *competentes*, namely the second sermon for Palm Sunday.]

1. Whoever believes in Christ and follows him as he leads to true life, just as the people of Israel followed Moses and entered the promised land, this person, trusting in Christ as guide, renounces the enemy, his angels, and every form of magic, which is constituted through the angels of Satan [Note: The manuscript wrongly reads “curiosity.”].

Then he renounces the enemy’s evil works, his worship, idols, lots, and auguries, public spectacles and theaters, fornications [Note: The word *renounces* was wrongly omitted in the editions, but is present in the manuscript.] [Note: The particle “and” has been intruded here in the editions], drunkenness, dances, and lies. These and other serpentine things bind human souls and lead them to the prison of hell.

Thus, freeing himself from these evils and throwing these chains behind his back, as it were, into the face of the enemy, a person now makes his declaration with a sincere voice [Note: The editions wrongly read “symbolic.” The true and evident reading of the manuscript is confirmed by a fragment of Niceta preserved at Vienna.].

2. “I believe in God the Father almighty.”

The confession rightly begins with belief, because blessed Paul expressed it in this way: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10:10) [Note: Above, p. 15, note 1, I said that I believe the Aquileian Creed was written *in Deo*, “in God,” rather than *in Deum*, “in God” with motion toward him. Why, then, do we read *credo in Deum* in Niceta of Aquileia? The learned Braida has already demonstrated very skillfully in his dissertation, p. 64, that in Niceta’s time the formula of the Aquileian Creed had nearly become obsolete and that the Roman formula had come into use in its place.].

You therefore believe in God the Father almighty [Note: Fea showed me in his notes a remarkable, so to speak, spoil taken by Alcuin, who silently copies this chapter word for word in part III, chapter 20, of his confession of faith, as far as “nothing was made.” I observe, however, in Braida’s edition of Saint Chromatius, p. LXXIX (*Patrologia*, vol. XX, col. 315), that Alcuin also copies a passage of Saint Chromatius, though naming its author. Alcuin therefore seems to have had Aquileian Fathers at hand.]: God unbegotten, who arose from no one and began from no one [Note: Alcuin inserts “and”]; God invisible, whom no eye of flesh is sufficient to see; God incomprehensible, who comprehends all things; God immutable, who is not changed by the passage of time and does not grow old with age, but is always the same; who did not begin to live in time, but, always living, suffers no successor; God good and just, Creator of heaven and earth.

You confess this one to be God, but you must also confess him to be the Father of the Son, for no one is Father without a Son. The Father therefore exists through the Son, having a Son of whom he is Father [Note: Alcuin omits the words from “and” through “know him also as Father.”].

And this is the pious confession concerning God: that you should know him not only as God but also recognize him as Father [Note: Alcuin adds, “I mean, Father”], the Father of the living Word, of his own Power and Wisdom [Note: In Alcuin: “who [referring to the Word] ineffably, before all things—indeed, without beginning—begot from himself the Son, Spirit from Spirit, etc.”], who before all ages, before the beginning of everything, before absolutely all time, begot from himself the Son: Spirit from Spirit, God from God.

In him all things were established that are in heaven and that are on earth, visible and invisible, as Paul teaches (Col. 1:16), and John confirms: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3) [Note: Alcuin reads *et quae*, “and which,” before “are in heaven,” and *omnia, inquit*, “he says, all things,” before “were made.”].

3. Therefore, believing in God the Father, you will immediately confess that you also believe in his Son Jesus Christ. This is the Son of God, Jesus Christ.

“Jesus,” interpreted in the language of the Hebrews, means “Savior”; “Christ,” however, is a title of royal dignity. Thus Savior and King are one and the same: Christ Jesus.

For our salvation he descended from the Father from heaven and assumed a body like ours. He was born from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary without any action of a man. A body was generated from a body through the power of the Holy Spirit; remaining God, he became human [Note: Thus the manuscript reads; so too the editions], so that he might be both visible to human beings and bring salvation through his teaching, since otherwise the Godhead could not have been borne by human beings unless it became visible through the assumption of a body.

4. Therefore he was born from the holy and undefiled Virgin, so that he might provide us with the beginning of a holy birth. He was born according to what had previously been spoken through the prophet: “Behold, a virgin will conceive in the womb and bear a Son, and his name will be called Emmanuel,” which is interpreted, “God with us” (Isa. 7:14; Matt. 1:23) [Note: So the editions read; the manuscript has the less satisfactory form with a single *m*.].

Believe, therefore, that this one who was born from the Virgin is God with us: God from the Father before the ages, human from the Virgin for the sake of human beings.

He was truly incarnate, not merely in appearance, as certain erroneous heretics, ashamed of the mystery of God, say that the Lord’s incarnation occurred as a phantom. For, they claim, what appeared was not real but deceived human eyes [Note: The manuscript has *qui*, followed by an abbreviation that appears to require expansion as *dicunt* or *dicuntur*. In fact an earlier copyist wrote only *quideam*, which a later scribe did not understand. The editions wrongly print *quidam dicunt*, “certain persons say,” since *dicunt* follows shortly afterward. I have therefore altered their punctuation.]. Let this be wholly absent from the truth of God [Note: The editions wrongly repeat *absit*, “far be it.”]. Let this be wholly absent from the truth of God. For if the incarnation is false, human salvation will also be false. But if salvation is truly in Christ, the incarnation is likewise true.

In him both realities exist: human, in what was visible; God, in what was not visible. He ate as a human being and fed five thousand people with five loaves, because he was God. He slept as a human being in the boat, but commanded the winds and the sea, because he was God. He fastened his hands to the cross like a human being, but granted Paradise to the thief who confessed him, because he was God. Finally, he accepted death, laying down his body for a short time, as a human being, but raised the four-days-dead man from the tomb, because he was God [Note: The manuscript and editions read *suscitat*, “raises,” a reading I have emended on the basis of the certain parallel structure above.].

Christ must therefore be believed to be both God and human: just as he is recognized as human from his sufferings, so he is revealed as God from his divine works.

You have, then, grounds on which to reject teachers of falsehood. If anyone should attempt to whisper into your ears that Christ was merely human [Note: The manuscript reads “should attempt”], say that he became human through the things stated above; the one whom I have already recognized through his powers and declarations, since the Savior himself says to the Jews: “If you do not wish to believe me, believe the works. And know that I am in the Father and the Father is in me” (John 10:38) [Note: The manuscript has *qm*, with a contraction mark; thus either *quem*, “whom,” or *quoniam*, “because.”].

5. It follows that you should believe in the Lord’s passion and confess that Christ suffered, crucified by the Jews, according to the predictions of the prophets. And see to it that you are not ashamed of the passion of your Lord.

If perhaps Jewish unbelief or pagan folly should wish to blaspheme against Christ’s glorious cross, always remember the Lord’s saying: “Whoever confesses me before human beings, I also will confess before my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 10:32).

There is certainly no reason for you to be ashamed if you understand in what manner Christ suffered. He suffered not in his divinity but in the flesh. For God is always incapable of suffering. He suffered in the flesh, as the Apostle teaches (1 Pet. 4:1), so that salvation might come to the human race through his wound, just as the prophet Isaiah had also foretold: “He himself suffered for our sins, and by his wound we were all healed” (Isa. 53:5).

Christ suffered because of our sin, so that righteousness might be given to us. Therefore he suffered under Pontius Pilate. The time is indicated when Pontius Pilate was governor of Syria and Palestine. This is carefully stated because certain heretics, deceived by demonic frauds, babble about various Christs.

You are therefore also taught the time of the passion, so that you may not confess that someone else suffered, but that the Christ who truly suffered under Pontius Pilate for the salvation of the world suffered. Therefore he died in order to dissolve the rights of death.

6. On the third day he rose alive from the dead, as the prophet says: “Free among the dead” (Ps. 88:7). Nor could Christ be held by death, since he possesses complete authority over both death and life.

He ascended into heaven, from which he had also descended. For he says: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who was in heaven” (John 10:18; 3:13).

He sits at the right hand of the Father, according to what was said in the Psalms by David, from the person of God the Father to the Son: “Sit at my right hand until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet” (Ps. 109:8).

From there he will come to judge the living and the dead [Note: The editions wrongly add *est*, “is.”]. Believe that this same Christ our Lord will come with the angels and their powers to judge both the living and those who were formerly dead [Note: The learned Braida discusses at length how this passage of Niceta should be understood, dissertation, pp. 266 ff. Indeed, no theologian, whether an expositor of the Creed or of Paul (1 Thess. 4), has left this passage untouched. I must therefore refrain from further comment], so that he may repay each according to his works: that is, establish the righteous in eternal life but subject the impious to eternal punishment.

### 7

You believe also in the Holy Spirit. This Holy Spirit is one, sanctifying all things; he proceeds from the Father, alone searches out the mysteries and depths of God, and came from heaven upon Christ in the form of a dove. This Holy Spirit is indeed one, but manifold in his powers and operations. He distributes the gifts of grace to each person as he wills (1 Cor. 12:11). He appointed the prophets and filled the apostles; and at the time of baptism he sanctifies the souls and bodies of believers. Without his operation no creature can attain eternity; and into his glory even the angels long to look (1 Pet. 1:12). By his majesty he sanctifies thrones, dominions, and all the powers of heaven.

[Note: Thus literally also Niceta in his treatise *On the Power of the Holy Spirit*, p. 16, line 11.]

[Note: Compare *On the Power of the Holy Spirit*, p. 28, line 1.]

[Note: Thus Niceta also in *On the Power of the Holy Spirit*, p. 13, three lines from the end.]

[Note: Was there then a copyists’ error in *On the Power of the Holy Spirit*, p. 25, line 18, which reads “shall have blasphemed in the Holy Spirit”?]

If anyone blasphemes against the Holy Spirit, he has no forgiveness either in this age or in the age to come, as the Lord himself declared (Matt. 12:32).

### 8

Brothers, establish this faith of the Trinity firmly in your hearts: believe in one God the almighty Father, and in his Son Jesus Christ our Lord, and in the Holy Spirit, the true light and sanctifier of souls, who is the pledge of our inheritance. If we are intent upon him, he will lead us into all truth and make us adhere to heavenly things. For the apostles received this rule of faith from the Lord, so that in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, they might baptize all believing nations (Matt. 28:19). Let this faith remain in you; guard this deposit, dearest ones, avoiding profane innovations in speech and the oppositions of falsely named knowledge (1 Tim. 6:20).

### 9

If the Gentiles persuade you to worship many fathers again, hold fast to your blessed profession, because you have confessed one God the Father.

[Note: The edition reads *qua*.]

Nature itself does not allow one man to have several fathers.

[Note: For *enim* is absent in the editions.]

If a Jew tries to persuade you not to believe Christ to be the Son of God, let him be to you as an enemy: either attack him, if you possess such knowledge of the Scriptures, or at least avoid him, if you lack training.

If some heretic, under the Christian name, tells you either that Christ is a creature or persuades you that the Holy Spirit is alien to the glory of the Father and the Son, let him be to you as a pagan and a tax collector, because he leads you toward idolatry when he persuades you to worship a creature.
