[Note: The manuscript reads *idolatriam*. I am uncertain whether this is a scribal error or reflects a usage already current at that time, since modern Italians likewise speak in this way—perhaps because it has been transmitted to us from earlier generations.]

[Note: The manuscript reads *deducunt*, and shortly afterward *persuadent*.]

When he tries to entangle you in tortuous questions, take refuge behind the wall of your faith and say with the Apostle: “I have been acquitted; I have been sanctified; I have been justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of my God” (1 Cor. 6:11).

[Note: The manuscript and editions read *absolutus sum* (“I have been acquitted”). But Niceta himself, *On the Power of the Holy Spirit*, p. 24, line 16, shows that this is an error for *ablutus* (“I have been washed”). The standard Latin edition of Paul has *abluti*, as does the Greek archetype, ἀπελούσασθε (“you have washed yourselves”).]

I will renounce nothing of this profession of the Trinity, lest I bring harm to my salvation and cause detriment to my faith.

[Note: The learned Braida has observed that *nuntiare* is used for *renuntiare*, “to renounce” or “deny,” also in Tertullian.]

[Note: The manuscript reads *dampnum* (“loss” or “harm”).]

### 10

After professing the blessed Trinity, you now profess belief in the holy catholic Church. What else is the Church than the assembly of all the saints? From the beginning of the world, whether patriarchs—namely Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—prophets, apostles, martyrs, or the other righteous who have been, who are, and who will be, they are one Church, because they have been sanctified by one faith and manner of life, sealed with one Spirit, and made one body. Christ is the head of this body, as is affirmed and written (Col. 1:18).

I say something further: even the angels, even the heavenly powers and authorities, are united in this one Church, as the Apostle teaches, because all things have been reconciled in Christ, not only those on earth but also those in heaven (Col. 1:20).

Therefore believe that in this one Church you will obtain communion with the saints. Know that this one Church is the catholic Church established throughout the whole world; you must hold firmly to communion with it.

There are indeed other pseudo-churches, but you have nothing in common with them—for example, the churches of the Manichaeans, Cataphrygians, Marcionists, and the other heretics or schismatics. These churches have ceased to be holy, because, deceived by demonic doctrines, they believe and act otherwise than Christ the Lord commanded and than the apostles handed down.

Next you believe in the forgiveness of sins. This is the grace by which believers, confessing Christ as God, obtain through baptism forgiveness of all their sins.

[Note: The editions read *Dominum* (“the Lord”).]

[Note: The manuscript reads *consecuntur* (“they obtain”).]

For this reason it is also called regeneration, because a person is restored innocent and pure—indeed, more so than when he is born from his mother’s womb.

Consequently, you believe also in the resurrection of your flesh and in eternal life. For if you do not believe this, you believe in God in vain. Everything we believe, we believe for the sake of our resurrection. Otherwise, if our hope in Christ extends only to this life, then, as the Apostle says, “we are of all people most pitiable” (1 Cor. 15:19), since Christ assumed human flesh precisely in order to grant participation in perpetual life to our mortal nature.

### 11

There are indeed many heretics who distort the faith of the resurrection, claiming salvation for the soul alone while denying the resurrection of the flesh. But you, who believe in Christ, profess the resurrection of your flesh. For Christ died and rose for this purpose: that he might rule over both the living and the dead (Rom. 14:9).

Nor do you believe this without good reason. You have suitable authorities. Hear the prophet Isaiah clearly proclaiming: “The dead will rise, and those who are in the tombs will rise, and those who are in the earth will be raised” (Isa. 26:19).

You also have the Lord himself, the prophet of prophets, promising in the Gospel: “I am the resurrection and the life; whoever believes in me, even if he has died, will live” (John 11:27).

And elsewhere: “Amen, I say to you, the hour is coming when the dead who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God; and they will rise—those who have done good, to the resurrection of life, but those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment” (John 5:28–29).

You have the Apostle Paul affirming: “This corruptible body must put on incorruption, and this mortal body must put on immortality” (1 Cor. 15:53).

Know that we consist of two substances, namely body and soul. The body is mortal, but the soul is immortal. When a person departs from this life, the soul does not die; rather, when it departs, only the body dies. While the body decays in the earth, the soul, according to its merits, is kept either in a place of light or in a place of darkness.

[Note: The learned Braida discusses at length how this passage of Niceta is to be understood, and how the words “in a place of light” clearly indicate a heavenly dwelling. Thus Niceta is not among those who have thought that heavenly blessedness is assigned to the righteous only after the universal judgment. See his dissertation, pp. 274 ff.]

This continues until the day of the Lord’s coming from heaven, when he comes with his holy angels, all having been raised, and the souls are recalled into their bodies, so that there may be a just separation between the good and the evil.

[Note: The editions improperly read *distinctio* (“distinction”).]

Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father; but the impious and wicked will be in the darkness of hell, where there will be weeping of the eyes and gnashing of teeth, as it is written.

### 12

So that you may not doubt the resurrection of the body, receive at least one example from the things of this world, as the Apostle teaches (1 Cor. 15:36). Look at a grain of wheat: dead and dry, it is sown in the earth; watered by the dew of heaven, when it has decayed, it is then brought to life and rises.

I think that the one who raises a grain of wheat for the sake of man will be able to raise the man himself who has been sown in the earth; indeed, he both can and wills to do so. For just as the grain is brought to life by rain, so the body will be brought to life by the dew of the Spirit, as Isaiah cries out to Christ: “For the dew that is from you is healing for them” (Isa. 26:19).

It is truly healing, because the resurrected bodies of the saints no longer fear death. They will live with Christ in heaven—those who lived according to Christ’s commands and righteousness in this world. This is that eternal and blessed life which you believe in; this is the fruit of the whole faith and of a good manner of life; this is the hope for which we are born, believe, and are reborn.

For this hope the prophets, apostles, and martyrs endured inextricable labors and gladly embraced death. This life will be possessed neither by the pagan nor by the unbelieving Jew, nor by the Christian who serves vices and crimes, because it has been prepared only for the faithful and those who live chastely.

### 13

Since this is so, dearest ones, remain in what you have learned and what has been handed down to you. Always retain the covenant that you made with the Lord, namely this creed, which you confess before angels and human beings. The words are few, but they contain all the mysteries.

[Note: The learned Fea observes that St. Ildephonsus of Toledo appropriated this passage almost word for word in *On the Knowledge of Baptism*, chapter 33 (Madrid edition, *Fathers of Toledo*, vol. I, p. 185). His words are: “In this creed, for this reason, the apostles briefly collected passages from all the Scriptures, so that, since many believers either did not know letters or, although they did know them, could not read the Scriptures because of worldly occupations, by retaining this in heart and memory they might possess sufficient saving knowledge.” Ildephonsus flourished approximately two hundred years after our Niceta.]

For these words have been collected from all the Scriptures for the sake of brevity, like precious gems arranged in a single crown, so that, since many believers do not know letters, while those who do know them cannot read the Scriptures because of worldly occupations, they may have sufficient saving knowledge for themselves.

### 14

Therefore, dearest ones, whether you are sitting, working, sleeping, or awake, let this saving confession revolve in your breasts. Let your mind always be in heaven, your hope in the resurrection, and your desire in the promise. Let the cross of Christ and his glorious passion be carried before you with confidence.

Whenever the enemy has disturbed your mind with fear, greed, or anger, answer him threateningly, saying: “I have renounced you, and I renounce you, together with your works and your angels, because I have believed in the living God and in his Christ. Sealed with his Spirit, I have now learned not to fear death.”

Thus the hand of God will protect you; thus the Spirit of Christ will guard your holy entrance, from this time forth and forever. As you meditate on Christ, say to one another: “Brothers, whether we are awake or asleep, let us live together with the Lord,” to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

## Fragments of the Same Saint Niceta: Six Fragments (C)

[Note: The learned Michael Denis published these fragments from a tenth-century Viennese manuscript in his work entitled *Manuscript Theological Codices of the Palatine Library at Vienna*, vol. II, part III, pp. 2042 ff. In the aforesaid Viennese manuscript there is, among other things, a little work entitled *The Order or Brief Explanation of the Instruction of the Unlearned in the Faith*, with the authorities of the Fathers, among which are those of Niceta. It appears that these fragments are sometimes recited in their pure form, but at other times their meaning is presented, with the wording occasionally altered.]

### I

Niceta, in the first book addressed to the Competentes.

[Note: For Niceta had written six books of instruction for the Competentes, which Gennadius enumerates.]

It is necessary, therefore, for those hastening toward the faith to examine the instructions they require—teachings which rustic souls can both understand and retain—not composed from private ingenuity, but collected from the preaching of the divine Scriptures. Through them the elect are instructed concerning baptism, so that they may know what they have abandoned, understand better what they desire, and recognize more certainly what they will receive and what they must observe. For what they desire is great; what they are beginning is substantial—whether God has inspired them or a human being has admonished and persuaded them.

### II

In the same work.

A catechumen, like a guest and neighbor of the faithful, hears the mysteries from outside without understanding them; he hears of grace without perceiving it. From this point, however, he begins to be called faithful.

[Note: The manuscript reads *hospis* (“guest”); shortly before, *caticuminus*.]

[Note: That is, baptism.]

### III

In the same work.

No one comes to confession unless he has first renounced the devil. Just as a gold-seeker does not put gold into a purse unless he has first washed away all the earth or mud.

[Note: The manuscript reads *aurilicus*.]

Therefore one must first declare repudiation of diabolical vanity and cast away, by renouncing them, its bitter pursuits. One must renounce not with empty speech or the lips alone, but with the strongest faith and unwavering knowledge—that is, a person must commit himself to Christ with the full power of his soul, trusting that, having become Christ’s, he will cease to fear the devil.

Then he also renounces the devil’s wicked works: cults and idols, lots and auguries, entertainments and theatres, thefts and frauds, murders and fornications, pride and boasting, anger and greed, banquets and drunkenness, dances and lies, and other evils of this kind.

What shall we say about those who wish to flaunt themselves in excessive bodily adornment and to appear extraordinary? I say nothing about the elaborately fashioned refinements of clothing, uselessly contrived. I ask you: what is the point of men’s hair curled with a needle—locks covering the neck behind but completely hiding the forehead in front, so that not even a place is left free on the forehead for the sign of Christ? And why is it that from what they suppose gives them some glory or beauty, they acquire disgrace and dishonor?

[Note: The manuscript reads *aquo*.]

[Note: The manuscript reads *eumdem*.]

Similarly, women bind their heads like a shield, so that the forehead sinks like a valley between two hills; they hang weights of little stones bound with gold from their ears; they burden their arms with gold; they press chains or stones upon their necks; and on their feet crimson shoes gleam with little flames.

What use or benefit is found in these things except empty display and a mind corrupted by childish desire?

[Note: This passage is especially noteworthy concerning the custom, in Niceta’s time, of adorning the bodies of men and women. As still happens today, ecclesiastical writers severely criticized this vanity.]

### IV

Also in Book II.

Certainly no sin occurs without the devil’s operation; all such works we understand to be the works of the devil or his pomps. Therefore, freeing himself from these evils and throwing these chains behind his back, as it were into the face of the enemy, a person now declares with a sincere voice: “I believe in God the almighty Father,” and the rest.

Concerning the faith, as it is contained in the same creed, everyone who desires to come fully to faith and baptism must be instructed and taught, so that he may retain the brevity of the creed in his heart and memory; he should recite it to himself every day before going to sleep and after rising from sleep, and keep it in mind at every hour. Likewise he should retain the Lord’s Prayer and the sign of the cross, by which he fortifies himself against the devil.

### V

In the book addressed to the Competentes.

The creed is a reminder of the faith and a holy confession, which is held and learned jointly by all.

### VI

In the first book.

Why is a person exorcized, unless he is being prepared to receive grace? Through exorcisms they are cleansed as though by fire, because the sayings of the Lord, from which the exorcisms have been composed, are fiery.

# Dissertation of Peter Braida on Saint Niceta

## 1. Preface

### Aim and Structure of the Dissertation

I undertake to elucidate Niceas, or Niceta, bishop of Aquileia—namely, the man to whom the celebrated letter of the blessed Leo the Great concerning certain difficulties is extant. Above all, I maintain that he is the very person whom Gennadius calls the bishop of Romatiana, and therefore also the author both of the recently discovered and published booklet entitled *Explanation of the Creed of the Blessed Niceta, Bishop of Aquileia, Delivered to the Competentes*, and of the other work which the same Gennadius calls *The Booklet Addressed to a Fallen Virgin* and which until now has occupied a place among the works of the holy doctors of the Church, Ambrose, Jerome, and sometimes even Augustine.

My principal opponent, therefore, is the distinguished man who has deserved so well of the holy Fathers of the Church through his published studies and other merits, and who is also highly regarded for other reasons, namely John Prosdocimus Zabeus. In a special dissertation published at Venice by the press of Antonio Rosa in 1803, he wished Niceas, or Niceta—the bishop of the Romatiana city mentioned by Gennadius and famous for these and other written works—to be someone other than the Niceas or Niceta of Aquileia. He defended him as the bishop of a city in Dacia which ancient writers call Remisiana, Romessiana, or Remesiana, and therefore as the man who lived somewhat earlier than the bishop of Aquileia bearing the same name and who became famous through the friendship and hospitality of Saint Paulinus, bishop of Nola.

Although I now take up my pen against a man distinguished for learning and scholarship, whom I esteem highly and whose study of our Niceas or Niceta I have truly admired, I do not intend to detract in any way from his reputation. He undertook to write solely from a desire to uncover the truth and adopted the opinion which he judged more probable.

Let the distinguished man retain his honor. In his opinion, before the earlier of these booklets had recently been discovered, he had as predecessors the most eminent leaders of ecclesiastical scholarship, as well as, more recently—after the same booklet had already been published at Padua—the man of illustrious memory, Michael Denis, prefect of the Palatine Library at Vienna. His work is certainly worthy of reading, both for the polish of its language and for the selection of its scholarship, and especially for the clarity that is not rarely lacking in this kind of recondite learning.

Meanwhile, let me also defend the opposing view, which I consider plainly more probable and, if I may say so without offending anyone, sufficiently established. I trust that it will appear so to gracious readers who are entirely free from partisan zeal. In pursuing this argument, I am confident that the character of so upright and accomplished a man, his breadth of mind, and his desire to attain the truth are such that he will not hesitate to withdraw from an opinion once he finds it supported by less solid arguments, even though he may perhaps have worked with no small expenditure of effort for the opinion itself.

Here, then, is the progress and structure of this dissertation.

1. Whether he was bishop of the Church of Aquileia or of another city situated in Dacia, the man whom Gennadius calls bishop of Romatiana was unquestionably the author of both the *Explanation of the Creed Addressed to the Competentes* and the *Booklet Addressed to a Fallen Virgin*. We now publish these two works together for the first time under the name of Saint Niceta, bishop of Aquileia.

2. Niceas or Niceta, famous for his friendship with Saint Paulinus, bishop of Nola, was not bishop of the city of Romatiana in Dacia situated this side of the Danube; rather, he held a bishopric beyond the Danube.

3. The Niceas or Niceta whom Gennadius mentions as bishop of the city of Romatiana was not that Dacian Niceas or Niceta who was the friend of Saint Paulinus, bishop of Nola, and celebrated in his praises.

4. The Niceas or Niceta whom Gennadius mentions as bishop of Romatiana was beyond doubt Niceas or Niceta, bishop of Aquileia, who flourished in the time of Saint Leo the Great and to whom a letter of that holy pontiff is extant.

5. The Romatiana city mentioned by Gennadius is not to be sought in Dacia, but in the ancient diocese or province of Aquileia. It was probably the place which Pliny called Portus Romatianus, Romatinus, or Romatius, from the river of the same name, not far from Concordia; or the place now called Portus Gruarius, situated on the same river Romatius, Romatinus, or Romatianus, which flows through it.

6. Niceas or Niceta, bishop of Aquileia, was probably called bishop of Romatiana either because, before he ascended the episcopal see of Aquileia, he was auxiliary bishop of the Church of Aquileia at the harbor of Romatius or Romatinus, or because he frequently held his seat at the harbor or city of that name even while he held the helm of the Church of Aquileia.

7. A sufficient answer is given to the arguments of the distinguished Zabeus against the episcopate of the Gennadian Niceas or Niceta of Aquileia. The authority and observations of the distinguished Michael Denis are also addressed.

8. Concerning Saint Niceta, bishop of Aquileia, and his works, both those now published and those either lost or still hidden, as well as concerning the fragments made known to us through the study and industry of that most learned man, Michael Denis. Also concerning his sanctity and veneration.

9. Certain matters worthy of notice are presented concerning doctrine and morals, as well as discipline, from the works and fragments of Saint Niceta.

10. Certain statements are also examined which might appear to have been expressed by Niceta either less precisely or too harshly.

## Chapter I

Whether he was bishop of the Church of Aquileia or of another city in Dacia, the man whom Gennadius calls bishop of the city of Romatiana was unquestionably the author of both the *Explanation of the Creed Addressed to the Competentes* and the *Booklet Addressed to a Fallen Virgin*. These two works we now publish together for the first time under the name of Saint Niceta, bishop of Aquileia.

This discussion of Niceas or Niceta, bishop, and of his written works must originate with Gennadius of Massilia. For those who followed him and spoke about this Niceas or Niceta—Honorius of Autun and John Trithemius—borrowed their material from Gennadius.

Gennadius therefore writes the following in chapter 22 of *On Illustrious Men*, according to the edition of Johann Albert Fabricius:

> “Niceas, bishop of the city of Romatiana, composed six booklets of instruction for the Competentes preparing for baptism, in a simple and polished style. The first of these explains how the Competentes who desire to attain the grace of baptism ought to conduct themselves. The second concerns the errors of paganism; in it he says that, almost in his own time, a certain Melodius, a head of a household, was transferred by the pagans among the gods because of his generosity, and a rustic named Gadarius because of his courage. The third book is on the faith of the one Majesty; the fourth is against genethlology (natal astrology); the fifth is on the creed; the sixth is on the victim of the Paschal Lamb.

[Note: Other copies read *Genethlogiam*; the Corbie manuscript, corruptly, reads *Genocliam*.]

He also published a booklet addressed to a fallen virgin, an incentive to correction for almost all who fall.”

[Note: Another reading has *Romana*, improperly; in other copies Suffridus Petri records that he found *Romanicia*.]

[Note: Corbie manuscript: “in which almost [at] the time a certain Melgidius, a householder ... and Gadarius the rustic,” and so forth.]

[Note: The same manuscript reads: “a book, an encouragement for those who fall humanly.”]

This, then, is what Gennadius says.

It is therefore clear from Gennadius that Niceas or Niceta, bishop of the city of Romatiana, among the other works he wrote in a simple and polished style, also wrote a booklet on the creed addressed to the Competentes, which Gennadius lists fifth, and in addition another work addressed to a fallen virgin, which he lists last.

Since this last booklet was the only one of the seven works composed by Niceas or Niceta to become known to the ecclesiastical world in earlier times, many experts in textual criticism suspected, on the basis of Gennadius’s testimony, that this booklet belonged to that Niceas or Niceta, even though it was counted among the works of other holy Fathers. The most learned Benedictine editors of the works of Saint Ambrose, however, wished to enumerate it among Ambrose’s genuine writings, being scarcely moved by the authority of Gennadius or of those who relied upon his testimony.

The very first person to attribute this booklet addressed to a fallen virgin to the Niceas or Niceta of Gennadius was the distinguished John Baptist Cotelerius. In the final note to chapter 57 of Book II of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, volume I, p. 268, of the 1724 Amsterdam edition of the *Apostolic Fathers*, he writes:

> “Since in this note and elsewhere I cite the book addressed to a fallen virgin, which learned men indeed deny to Ambrose, Jerome, and Augustine, but assign to no one, I shall reveal whose offspring I think it is. I believe it belongs to Niceas, led to this opinion by the authority of Gennadius and of those who copied him, Honorius of Autun and Trithemius.”

The chief distinction of this Niceas or Niceta is surely that his booklet was at one time considered worthy of the intellect of both Jerome and Augustine; and still more that, even in what may be called our own age, it was listed by the Benedictine monks among the genuine works of Saint Ambrose.

“For a book,” John Clericus says in *The Art of Criticism*, part III, section 2, chapter 6, no. 12, “can be attributed to a certain writer, and falsely so, if it has been written in a style not wholly unlike his diction; it may actually have been written by another author of the same or a nearby age ... Nor is it surprising that in recent centuries various learned books have been attributed to Ambrose and Jerome, books which they themselves could scarcely have written better.”

While that single work of Niceas or Niceta, among the seven known to have been written by him, was the only one known, and while it especially enjoyed the name of Saint Ambrose, the authority of Gennadius was not considered sufficient to settle the matter and remove the booklet from the catalogue of Ambrose’s works in order to assign it to Niceas or Niceta, a writer who at that time was insufficiently known.

For what could prevent Ambrose himself—who wrote such distinguished books on virgins, virginity, the instruction of a virgin, and exhortation to virginity—from composing another work, as circumstances required, addressed to a fallen virgin, or rather concerning the fall of a consecrated virgin, as it is entitled in the edition of his works prepared by the Benedictine monks?

Ambrose’s dignity is certainly not lacking in this booklet: episcopal authority shines forth; the strength of discipline is vigorous; scriptural learning gleams everywhere; and the seriousness of the subject wonderfully accords with the power of the expression.

There was, however, no touchstone, so to speak, against which the booklet could be compared according to the judgments of critics, so that its author might be determined without ambiguity. What was lacking was another of the six booklets mentioned by Gennadius that bore the name of Niceta and against which the work addressed to a fallen virgin—or concerning the fall of a consecrated virgin—could be compared, about whose authorship opinion had remained uncertain.

For this reason the editors of Ambrose’s works were permitted to apply against the defenders of Origen what Saint Jerome had written against them. Those defenders relied upon a certain apology for Origen under the name of the martyr Pamphilus, although no other work of Pamphilus was available by which the apology could be proved to be the genuine offspring of that martyr:

> “Produce any other work of Pamphilus; nowhere will you find one. This alone exists. How, then, do I know that it belongs to Pamphilus? Surely style and saliva will be able to teach me!”

Saint Jerome, *To Pammachius and Oceanus, Concerning the Errors of Origen*, Letter 84, in Vallarsi’s edition, no. 11.

But after one of the six booklets addressed to the Competentes for baptism, which Gennadius attributed to his Niceas or Niceta, finally emerged from the library of Ghis, was first printed at Padua in 1799 through the work of the eminent Cardinal Stefano Borgia—alas, how quickly he was taken from the Church and from all literature!—namely, the fifth booklet, *On the Creed*, and after it bore a title which removed every doubt that it was indeed the work of the author mentioned by Gennadius, *Explanation of the Creed of the Blessed Niceta, Bishop of Aquileia, Delivered to the Competentes*—whatever may be thought of the word “Aquileia,” which does not now affect the substance of the matter and which will be discussed more fully below—then we possessed a critical rule by which we could safely judge even the other booklet, *Addressed to a Fallen Virgin*, or *Concerning the Fall of a Consecrated Virgin*, and determine whether it should be regarded wholly as the work of this Niceas or Niceta or rather left to Saint Ambrose.

We now have a very reliable rule of style, wisely transmitted by all writers on criticism. Nor was it invented in our age or the preceding one; it was drawn from the ancient Fathers of the Church, who often used the same method—Saint Dionysius of Alexandria, Eusebius, Jerome, Augustine, and others—as may be seen in John Clericus at the place cited above and in Honoratus of Saint Mary, *Observations on the Rules and Use of Criticism*, dissertation 3, article 7.

Since, therefore, no doubt exists that the *Explanation of the Creed Addressed to the Competentes* is the work of the bishop Niceas or Niceta concerning whom Gennadius speaks, whatever one may meanwhile think about the city of Romatiana—whether it is to be understood as Aquileian or as another city in Dacia—that *Explanation*, which certainly offers every reader the simple and polished style defined by Gennadius, also reveals the style of this Niceas or Niceta in such a way that we may say of our Niceta what Saint Augustine said of Saint Cyprian in Letter 93, no. 39:

> “His style has a certain distinctive character by which it can be recognized.”

From the style of the *Explanation of the Creed Addressed to the Competentes*, therefore, one may rightly judge also of other booklets of the same Niceas or Niceta, should any emerge into the light after so many centuries, even if they lack the author’s name.

Meanwhile, we must examine the *Booklet Addressed to a Fallen Virgin*, or *Concerning the Fall of a Consecrated Virgin*, which for so many centuries has circulated without the author’s name and relies solely upon Gennadius’s testimony for its attribution.

The distinguished Zabeus himself recognized the kinship of these two booklets in the notice appended to his dissertation and placed after the *Explanation of the Creed*, which he published again. He wrote:

> “If anyone weighs these works, he will recognize that their clothing is different, but that their verbal ornament and the polish of their sentences are the same. Consequently, even in the difference of their style, they reveal such a character as befits sisters.”

I am glad to have Zabeus as a companion in my opinion, which sixteen years ago I defended in a special observation before the Congregation of Sacred Rites, when, at the command of our distinguished and most reverend archbishop—and afterward cardinal of the Holy Roman Church—Peter Anthony George, a man of illustrious memory, I acted as advocate for Saint Niceas or Niceta, bishop of Aquileia, for the purpose of augmenting that office with proper readings. This was also carried out according to our wish.

But since Zabeus there abstained entirely from any investigation of this matter, as it did not belong to the purpose of his work, the matter itself is of such a nature among us that it deserves to be explained clearly.

Nor should it be denied that, at first sight, these booklets may appear to have been produced by different authors, since the kind of eloquence is not the same in both—in fact, it is as different as heaven from earth. For, as Zabeus himself observed, the style of expression in the *Explanation of the Creed* is familiar and restrained, whereas in the other booklet, *Addressed to a Fallen Virgin*, the language is elevated, forceful, and impassioned.

This, however, is no reason to abandon comparison of the two works. The style can be the same in different works even though the face, so to speak, of the style is different. A person himself can be recognized very well and distinguished from anyone else even if he presents an appearance that varies with his inward emotions—now calm, now troubled; now pleasing, now offended; now cheerful, now severe; now peaceful, and now even agitated.

Thus Niceas or Niceta does not have the same appearance in these two booklets, but the style in both is the same: the same manner of expression, the same movement of language, the same joining of words, and other features of this kind. From these things it is evident that, although he was not, so to speak, of the same temperament and disposition in both works, he nevertheless remained in both the same speaker.

We confirm this, for example, by a few comparisons that follow. Meanwhile, we ask the indulgence of learned readers if we descend to such small details, which nevertheless, in this new argument, we do not believe should be despised.

We read, then, in the *Explanation of the Creed*, chapter 1: “These and other serpent-like things constrict the souls of human beings.” In the little book *To the Fallen Virgin*, or *On the Fall of a Consecrated Virgin*, chapter 9, no. 39: “What shall I say of you, son of the serpent?”; and no. 42: “Therefore exclude . . . the serpent’s allurements from your heart.” Here we see the same author’s use in both works of a metaphor that seems, in a certain sense, to have been characteristic of him.

Again, in the *Explanation of the Creed*, chapter 2: “He who was born of no one.” But in the little book *To the Fallen Virgin*, chapter 2, no. 5: “You who are the head of these things and the cause of evils”; and chapter 6, no. 22, according to the reading of Vallarsius’s edition of Jerome: “You who have suffered the forgetfulness of such great blessings and have become a receptacle of such great evils.” Again, in the *Explanation of the Creed*, chapter 8: “Make this faith firm, brothers, in your hearts.” But in the little book *To the Fallen Virgin*, chapter 5, no. 19, according to the reading of the previously cited edition of Jerome: “6 Always consider to whom you have pledged your virginity” [Col. 0880B].

Again, in the *Explanation of the Creed*, chapter 10: “For they had been deceived by demonic doctrines”; and chapter 12: “We believe in our resurrection”; and shortly afterward: “For this Christ assumed human flesh.” But in the little book *To the Fallen Virgin*, chapter 6, no. 25: “The labors which he endured for the sake of your reputation”; chapter 8, no. 32: “He excluded the aid of human medicine”; and no. 36: “He escaped the destruction that hung over him.” Here, in both works, we find the same cultivation of style and the same arrangement of words. The same style is therefore evident in both works; and, with the authority of Gennadius added—Gennadius assigning both works to Niceas or Nicetas—their authenticity is thoroughly confirmed.

But there is another remarkable feature in these same works that must by no means be passed over in silence. Style is indeed a sufficiently good and sufficiently secure rule for recognizing and distinguishing works, as we have already seen. Nevertheless, something additional is usually desired—something that has a certain affinity with style—so that the argument drawn from style may become still firmer and clearer [Col. 0880C]. For it cannot be denied that even this argument, although scarcely any argument is either safer or more wisely devised, can sometimes be mistaken, as the highly praised Honoratus of Saint Mary observes and proves by arguments and examples in the passage cited above. Thus Saint Jerome too, writing to Augustine in a letter numbered 102 among Jerome’s letters in Vallarsius’s edition and 68 among Augustine’s, concerning another letter given to him by the Bishop of Hippo—a letter about whose authenticity he nevertheless remained uncertain—although he recognized its style and method of argument, desired something more than style itself, so that he might become more certain of the genuine character of the writing. For he said: “I frankly confess to your graciousness that, although your style and arguments [ἐπιχειρήματα, arguments] seemed to me to be present, nevertheless I thought that copies of letters ought not to be trusted rashly.”

What we have, then, in these two little books that is distinctive and confirms the unity of their style, so that their authenticity may shine forth still more clearly [Col. 0880D], is that certain words of Sacred Scripture are reported in exactly the same way in both, and differ from the text of the common reading. These are the words that in our Vulgate are always read without any variation in Matthew 8:12; 13:50; 22:13; and 25:30, as well as in Luke 13:28: “There will be weeping and the gnashing of teeth.” In both of these little books, however, the words appear enlarged by the addition of a single word wherever the passage is cited—once in the first work and twice in the second. For in the *Explanation of the Creed*, chapter 13, we read: “There will be weeping of the eyes and the gnashing of teeth”; and in the little book *To the Fallen Virgin*, chapter 8, no. 34, likewise: “There will be weeping of the eyes and the gnashing of teeth”; and chapter 10, no. 44, according to the same reading of the text: “The gnashing of teeth and the weeping of the eyes followed.”

It is well known among scholars that in the early centuries of the Church, down to the age of Gregory the Great, that Latin version of the Sacred Scriptures which was called the Old Latin, or *Itala*, prevailed in the West [Col. 0881A]. In the course of time, however, with the Vulgate gaining supremacy, it became obsolete and finally even disappeared, so that the distinguished scholar Pierre Sabatier, of the illustrious Maurist congregation, who had undertaken to restore that most ancient version for us, was compelled to extract it, with immense labor, from the works of the Latin Fathers of the Church of those centuries—though gaps nevertheless remained here and there, gaps that perhaps it will never be possible to fill by any means.

This old Latin version was the one used in common practice throughout the Western Church. It was not multiple but always single, as the most learned Benedictine proves against Joseph Blanchini in his preface, no. 64, although the manuscripts of that one version used by the individual Fathers differed from one another. Hence, when they cite Scripture, they do not always all agree with one another, and sometimes one differs from another; at one time one writer uses one wording and another a different wording, as he himself observes [Col. 0881B].

What, then, does the Old Latin have in the aforementioned passages of Matthew and Luke, where our Vulgate, without the addition “of the eyes,” simply reads: “There will be weeping and the gnashing of teeth”? The same Old Latin agrees perfectly with our Vulgate in each of the passages mentioned and everywhere supplies precisely the words: “There will be weeping and the gnashing of teeth,” completely omitting the word “of the eyes.”

The highly learned editor Sabatier, however, who constructed this Old Latin text after consulting all the Fathers and writers of those centuries, as well as all the manuscripts that he could obtain relevant to the matter, did not leave the addition of the word “of the eyes” unnoticed. In the note placed beneath this text, he remarks that the reading containing the word “of the eyes” is exceedingly rare and that he encountered it only twice: once in a certain manuscript of Saint-Germain, and again in Faustinus the presbyter, in his book *Against the Arians*, volume 5, page 644, h. of the Lyon Library of the Fathers. I will add that [Col. 0881C] I also encountered the word “of the eyes” in the Gospel text cited in Victor of Vita’s *History of the Vandal Persecution*, book 5, chapter 1, and nowhere else.

It is therefore clear that the reading containing the word “of the eyes” in the Gospel text, “There will be weeping and the gnashing of teeth,” was the reading of exceedingly few manuscripts in that Old Latin version of the Bible which prevailed in the early centuries of the Church. For among all the writers of those centuries whom the distinguished Sabatier had before him in reconstructing that version, he admits that he encountered the word only twice; and it can scarcely be found elsewhere, except in the one passage of Victor of Vita that I have added.

If, then, that reading was found in exceedingly few manuscripts of antiquity, and if the very same reading is found in two works which are otherwise demonstrably of the same style, and whose subject matter and very inscription attribute them to one and the same author, whether contemporary or nearly contemporary, the works themselves must rightly and deservedly be regarded as genuine, even on the basis of this new proof [Col. 0881D]. It has therefore been sufficiently demonstrated, as was desired, that both the *Explanation of the Creed to the Competentes* and the little book *To the Fallen Virgin*, or *On the Fall of a Consecrated Virgin*, which we are discussing here, are the works of one author—whoever, finally, that bishop Niceas or Nicetas of the city of Romatiana may have been to whom Gennadius assigned the two works.

One matter concerning this subject still remains, which we shall settle briefly: the authority of those who formerly assigned the little book *To the Fallen Virgin* to Jerome and Augustine, and especially the Maurists, who assigned the book itself to Ambrose so decisively that they wished to place it among his genuine works concerning virgins and virginity, prefacing it with a notice that bears witness to their conviction.

Now, if the *Explanation of the Creed to the Competentes* undoubtedly belongs to that Niceas or Nicetas whose name it bears—whether he was the Romatian in Dacia or the Aquileian in Italy—and if, on the basis of what has been said, the little book *To the Fallen Virgin* also belongs to the author whose *Explanation of the Creed* is known to be his, then the little book *To the Fallen Virgin* can be neither Jerome’s nor Augustine’s, and indeed not even Saint Ambrose’s, whatever the Maurists, the editors of his works, may have thought [Col. 0882A].

But what seems entirely to settle the matter—and what is truly astonishing that it has thus far escaped the careful attention of learned men who have so often mentioned this little book *To the Fallen Virgin*—is the addition of the word “of the eyes” in the Gospel text of which we were speaking. As we observed, this addition is used not once but twice in the same book under discussion.

Where, then, is this addition, “of the eyes,” found in the many genuine works of Saints Jerome, Augustine, and Ambrose, when they happened to quote the words of that Gospel passage? Indeed, Jerome, in Letter 14 to Heliodorus, no. 8, reports the words of the Gospel in precisely this form: “Where there will be weeping and the gnashing of teeth.” Augustine likewise, in Sermon 31 *On the Words of Psalm 125*, chapter 5 [Col. 0882B]: “There there will be weeping and the gnashing of teeth”; and in *On True Religion*, chapter 54: “So that they may be there where there is for them weeping and the gnashing of teeth.”

As for Saint Ambrose, who, in addition to works of various kinds, explained the Gospel of Luke in a special commentary entitled *Exposition of Luke*, where the Gospel text under discussion occurs, this holy teacher, in book 7 of that work, no. 204, renders the text simply according to the common reading, without the addition “of the eyes”: “There will be weeping and the gnashing of teeth.”

It is therefore certainly astonishing that the Maurists, especially the editors of Ambrose’s works—otherwise men as diligent as they were learned—either failed to notice this difference in the text in the little book *To the Fallen Virgin*, or *On the Fall of a Consecrated Virgin*, which they joined to the other works of Saint Ambrose, or regarded the difference as wholly insignificant.

This difference, when all the other considerations are also weighed, is so important to us here that we judge the matter to be beyond dispute [Col. 0882C]. We may confidently say that, just as that little book *To the Fallen Virgin*, which twice reports the Gospel text in an entirely different form from that found in the other genuine and authentic works of those Fathers, cannot be called Jerome’s, Augustine’s, or Ambrose’s, so the same little book must be regarded as the genuine companion of the other little book *On the Creed to the Competentes*, also because it presents the same Gospel text with precisely the same and sufficiently uncommon addition that appears there.

[Col. 0882C]

## CHAPTER II

Niceas or Nicetas, famous for his friendship with Saint Paulinus of Nola, was not bishop of the city of Romatiana situated in Dacia on this side of the Danube; rather, he held an episcopate beyond the Danube.

Having examined the authenticity of the two little works, *On the Creed to the Competentes* and *To the Fallen Virgin*, we now approach their author—namely, Niceas or Nicetas.

The distinguished Zabeus, who devotes himself entirely [Col. 0882D] to demonstrating that this Niceas or Nicetas was the same person as Niceas or Nicetas, the intimate friend of Saint Paulinus of Nola, who is known to have exercised the office of bishop with great distinction in Dacia, agrees with those writers who confidently identify the city called Romatiana by Gennadius with Remisiana, or Romessiana, or Remesiana. This city was certainly situated in Dacia Mediterranea on this side of the Danube, as the geographers establish. For this reason, together with Crevier and with Anville’s geographical map of both Dacias, situated on this side of and beyond the Danube, he provides us with an account of both Dacias, to prevent ambiguity concerning places and names.

We, however, who have adopted an entirely different opinion—namely, that this Niceas or Nicetas, who was joined in friendship with Saint Paulinus of Nola, was neither bishop of Remisiana, Romessiana, or Remesiana, nor held an episcopate anywhere in Dacia on this side of the Danube, but rather in that Dacia which extended very broadly beyond the Danube, without any particular title of a see or city—we, I say, together with Daniel Farlatus, author of the *Illyricum Sacrum*, who expressly discussed these Dacias with reference to the Christian religion and added a new map of those regions, present here an account of both Dacias [Col. 0883A]. We shall then prove, chiefly from the very words of Paulinus of Nola, that his Nicetas was neither bishop of Romessiana, Remesiana, or Remisiana, nor held an episcopal office anywhere in Dacia situated on this side of the Danube, but that he became distinguished beyond the Danube in the office of bishop and in apostolic ministry.

From this it will become clearer that the name of the city Romatiana, used by Gennadius in connection with Niceas or Nicetas, provides no support for supposing that this Niceas or Nicetas mentioned by Gennadius was both the friend of Paulinus of Nola and the bishop of that city in Dacia which was called Romessiana, Remesiana, or Remisiana.

Thus, in volume 1 of the *Illyricum Sacrum*, in part 1 of the prolegomena, chapter 5, Farlatus gives the following account of the Dacias:

“Trajan, having assumed supreme power at the end of the first century after Christ [Col. 0883B], extended the boundaries of the Roman Empire—or of Illyricum—beyond the Danube. He threw across the Danube a stone bridge, completed with immense foundations and remarkable workmanship and skill, so that he could lead his army across. After defeating Decebalus, king of the Dacians, he added Dacia to the Roman provinces, placing garrisons and Roman colonies there in the year 103 after Christ.

“‘He subdued Dacia,’ says Eutropius in book 8, ‘after defeating Decebalus, making it a province beyond the Danube in those lands which the Taiphali now possess, as well as the Victophali and the Tervingi. That province extended for a circuit of one million paces . . . . . From the entire Roman world he transferred countless numbers of people there to cultivate the fields and cities . . . . .

“‘Dacia extended far and wide from north to south, between the Carpathian Mountains and the Danube; from west to east, between the course of the Danube, which bends from north toward the south, and the river Tyras, which rises in the Carpathian Mountains and flows above the mouths of the Danube into the Black Sea. This region contained the three provinces which we today call Transylvania [Col. 0883C], Moldavia, and Wallachia.’

“‘But as the third century after Christ was drawing to a close, Dacia was permanently lost through Gallienus’s negligence, and the Roman Empire, and Illyricum likewise, contracted their boundaries to this side of the Danube. “Gallienus,” says Eutropius in book 9, “long mild and tranquil, afterward having given himself over to every form of licentiousness, loosened the reins of governing the state through disgraceful indolence and despair. The Alemanni, after ravaging Gaul, penetrated into Italy. Dacia, which Trajan had added beyond the Danube, was lost.”

“‘Nevertheless, the Romans still held certain cities and regions with their colonies and garrisons when Aurelian began to rule, around the year 270 after Christ. He perceived, with his customary prudence, that neither could Roman citizens safely remain among the barbarians, nor could that region be defended against enemy incursions or peacefully retained. He therefore judged it preferable to leave it to the barbarians than to recover it through useless labor and expense.

“‘Accordingly, he withdrew the Roman garrisons from those towns and transferred to this side of the Danube [Col. 0883D] the Roman colonies brought there by Trajan. Having settled them between the two Moesias, he assigned them enough fields and land to support and maintain them, and enough to equal a province of proper size. This province was formed from the intermediate cities and lands taken partly from Upper Moesia and partly from Lower Moesia.

“‘He gave the name Dacia to this province, which extended from the Danube to the borders of Macedonia between the two Moesias; and it was called Aurelian’s Dacia, the new Dacia, Dacia on this side of the Danube, and finally Roman Dacia, so that it might be distinguished not only by location but also by name from the other Dacia, which was customarily called Trajan’s Dacia, ancient Dacia, Dacia beyond the Danube, and Barbarian Dacia.

“‘He later divided it into two parts. The portion adjoining the banks of the Danube toward the north he called Ripensis; the portion that turned toward the south and extended as far as Mount Haemus he called Dacia Mediterranea.

“‘These matters are reported by Eutropius, Vopiscus, Jordanes, and many others. Trajan had established the province of Dacia beyond the Danube, but it was abandoned after all Illyricum [Col. 0884A] and Moesia had been devastated, since there was no hope of retaining it. The Romans removed from the cities and fields of Dacia were settled in central Moesia, and he called that territory Dacia which now divides the two Moesias and lies on the right of the Danube as it flows toward the sea, whereas previously it had lain on the left.’

“Eutropius, book 9: ‘When he saw that Illyricum had been devastated and Moesia destroyed, he abandoned the province beyond the Danube which Trajan had established as Dacia, withdrawing the army and the provincials, since he despaired of being able to retain it. He transferred the peoples removed from it to Moesia and called that territory his Dacia, which now divides the two Moesias.’

“Vopiscus, in his *Life of Aurelian*.

“Jordanes, however, in *On the Succession of Kings and Times*, adds that Aurelian also made Dardania, situated below Upper Moesia to the south, into a province. It bordered the new Dacia Mediterranea on the east and extended westward and southward as far as the mountains Scardus and Haemus.

“‘But while Gallienus was ruling, he lost the Dacians. The Emperor Aurelian, having summoned the legions from there, settled them in Moesia, and there established one part as Dacia Mediterranea and another as Dacia Ripensis [Col. 0884B], and joined Dardania to them. Moreover, Aurelian ordered Trajan’s bridge over the Danube to be cut apart, so as to bar the barbarians from every approach to the new province.’”

Thus far Daniel Farlatus, author of the *Illyricum Sacrum*, concerning the Dacias, their situation, and their changes.

We must now examine the episcopate of Niceas or Nicetas: namely, whether Niceas or Nicetas, famous for his friendship with Saint Paulinus of Nola, was bishop of the city that Gennadius calls Romatiana, which is said by ancient authors and geographers to have been Remisiana, Romessiana, or Remesiana in Cisdanubian Dacia, also called Aurelian’s new and Roman Dacia; or whether he was bishop of another place in the same region; or rather whether he held an episcopate in the other ancient Dacia situated beyond the Danube, which was called Trajan’s, ancient, and Barbarian Dacia.

In poem 17 of Saint Paulinus of Nola, entitled *To Nicetas Returning to Dacia*, which extends quite extensively over six pages in the folio edition of Saint Paulinus’s works published at Verona, and in which [Col. 0884C] many places along that journey and many names of peoples among whom this holy Nicetas had propagated the name of Christ are mentioned—in this poem, I say, there is absolutely no mention of the city of Romatiana, Remesiana, Remisiana, or Romessiana, which is asserted to have been his episcopal see in Cisdanubian Dacia under the metropolitan see of Sardica.

If Nicetas had truly been bishop of that Cisdanubian city, Paulinus of Nola would certainly not have forgotten it in so long a poem accompanying him as he returned to Dacia. That city should have been the poem’s chief subject and, likewise, the destination of Nicetas’s journey. Yet Paulinus did not pass over other places lying along so distant a route, such as Thessalonica, Tomi, and Scupi—the last of which he also calls near Nicetas’s homeland, as we shall see below.

This Dacian Nicetas therefore seems not to have been bishop of any particular see at all. Rather, we should reasonably judge him to have been one of those bishops who, according to the ancient discipline of the Church, were called bishops of the nations and were consequently [Col. 0884D] sent to preach the Gospel among the nations. They were therefore bishops of several peoples and regions before episcopal sees were established there.

Concerning these bishops, the distinguished Abbot Bacchinius writes in part 1, chapter 3, no. 19, of his *On the Origins of the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*:

“We know that in the earliest times of the Church bishops were ordained in the West not only for a particular people that was to be instructed in the faith, but also as bishops of no particular people and no particular region. They preached to the nations and, wherever they settled, established a definite see for themselves.

“Photius provides a clear testimony to this practice—which was established in custom after apostolic times and undoubtedly derived from the apostles—in the *Bibliotheca*, codex 48, where it is related that Gaius, a presbyter of the Roman Church, under Victor and Zephyrinus, was ordained bishop of the nations; they judged that he had been ordained [χειροτονηθῆναι, to be ordained] ‘bishop of the nations’ [ἐθνῶν ἐπίσκοπον].

“From the beginning, then, it had been established that through such emissaries of the Gospel the world of the Gentiles should be converted to Christ, and that they should found colonies in the West belonging to the Roman see [Col. 0885A] as to a metropolis.”

We therefore believe that this Nicetas too was one of these episcopal emissaries of the Gospel. Indeed, he was probably ordained bishop of the particular people of the Dacians, in order to establish colonies of the Roman see, as of a metropolis, in those regions.

Since Saint Paulinus himself, in Letter 29 to Severus, no. 14, calls Nicetas “a venerable and most learned bishop who had deservedly come from Dacia to the admiration of the Romans,” why should he not have intended to indicate that Nicetas’s journeys from Dacia to Italy had been undertaken for this very purpose—or rather, chiefly for this purpose: that, on coming to Rome, he might report to the Roman see the progress in the faith achieved there through his labors, as to the see from which he had been sent as apostle of those peoples to found a new Christian colony?

That Nicetas had been ordained bishop of that particular people newly to be instructed in the faith, according to the aforementioned practice of apostolic bishops, and not bishop of some already established individual see [Col. 0885B]—as Remesiana was, or Remisiana or Romatiana under the metropolitan see of Sardica—Paul himself also seems to suggest. In the same poem, when he touches upon the place of this Nicetas’s episcopal care, he does not designate any one place but speaks generally of regions over which he had been appointed priest. For he says:

> But once the strait has been crossed, there remains  
> Again, on land, the labor of the journey, that you may be carried  
> As far as the happy regions over which you have been appointed  
> Priest . . .

Indeed, from the same poem of Paulinus we may rightly, if I am not mistaken, determine that the field of this Nicetas’s apostolic labor was not on this side of the Danube, where the city of Romessiana, Remissiana, or Romatiana was situated, but beyond the Danube. In reality, it was Transdanubian Dacia—namely, the region called Trajan’s Dacia—an extensive territory on the left bank of the Danube [Col. 0885C] and inhabited by various barbarian peoples, that he undertook to cultivate.

See the geographical map of the Dacias and Moesias in Cluverius, *Introduction to Universal Geography, Ancient as well as Modern*; and also the other map in volume 1 of Daniel Farlatus’s *Illyricum Sacrum*, showing universal and modern Illyricum. What, then, does Saint Paulinus say?

“You will go far away to the northern Dacians”: thus, shortly after the beginning of the poem, Paulinus addresses his Nicetas. Who are these northern Dacians, situated so far away, unless they are plainly the inhabitants of Transdanubian Dacia, who at that time no longer belonged to the Roman Empire and were rightly called “northern” by Paulinus in comparison with the other Dacians situated on this side of the Danube between the two Moesias—namely, in that part of Moesia taken from Upper and Lower Moesia which was called Aurelian’s Dacia? Those Dacians, situated on the right bank of the Danube, formed part of the Roman Empire [Col. 0885D].

Furthermore, that the Dacians whom the Paulinian Nicetas undertook to cultivate were Transdanubian is suggested more and more by other passages in the same poem. For he said to his Nicetas as he returned to Dacia:

> You will walk through the Philippian fields of the Macedonians,  
> Through the city of Tomi;  
> And you will go to Scupi, near your homeland,  
> As a Dardanian guest.  
>   
> O how great joys will then resound through that land  
> Where you teach the stiff-necked peoples [Col. 0886B]  
> To submit their savage necks  
> To gentle Christ!

That this Nicetas was a Dardanian—that is, descended from Dardania, the province Aurelian had joined to the new Dacia, as Jordanes testifies in the passage cited above from Farlatus—is evident from Paulinus’s words. That he had his native soil not far from [Col. 0886A] Scupi, the chief city of Dardania or Upper Moesia, is likewise clear from the same passage.

He was evidently a man wisely chosen by the Roman Church to preach the Gospel in Barbarian Dacia, a man who was native to regions not very far from those peoples; who, being himself a Dacian, would be heard by them, although he came from Roman Dacia situated on this side of the Danube; who, for that reason, would also have a sufficient command of the language of those barbarians, as of neighboring peoples, and would not be ignorant of their institutions and customs; and who would easily know the very places situated chiefly on the left bank of the Danube.

Accordingly, after his arrival at the city of Thessalonica, Paulinus follows the course of his journey on land. He accompanies him, as it were, as he proceeds through the fields of Philippi in Macedonia and through the city of Tomi, and as he also goes to Scupi, a city near his homeland, before he reaches the land where he taught the stiff-necked peoples to submit their savage necks to gentle Christ.

What, meanwhile, does Paulinus do? Moved by poetic inspiration, he exclaims: “O how great joys will then resound through that land where you teach the stiff-necked peoples to submit their savage necks to gentle Christ!”

But what does “then” mean in Paulinus’s poem if, when Nicetas was at Scupi, he was still not far from those peoples whom he taught to submit their savage necks to gentle Christ? If Paulinus wished to express the longing of those peoples for Nicetas’s arrival, he sings of their joy at his approaching arrival even while he was still a considerable distance from them.

If Nicetas had been very near them when he was at Scupi, Paulinus would surely have used “then” less appropriately. There is nothing surprising in our rejoicing when we understand that someone whom we ardently desire is near us; but it is certainly surprising to rejoice even when we know that the person is still far away, though we know that he is hastening toward us [Col. 0886C].

The peoples, then, whom the Paulinian Nicetas taught to submit their savage necks to gentle Christ seem not to have been Cisdanubian but Transdanubian. Nor should the expression “savage necks” be passed over in silence, since through it Paulinus describes the character and disposition of those peoples to whom Nicetas was returning.

The Cisdanubian Dacians certainly did not display savage necks, since they were not barbarians but Romans, descended from Roman colonists whom the Emperor Aurelian had summoned from Transdanubian Dacia. Aurelian left the whole of that region to its ancient inhabitants—those who truly possessed savage necks, as Paulinus rightly sang, because of their innate barbarism and their aversion to the Roman Empire.

Paulinus continues:

> And where Boreas, on the Riphaean shores,  
> Binds the rivers with dense frost,  
> There you dissolve minds stiff with ice [Col. 0886D]  
> By heavenly fire.

Previously Paulinus had said that those peoples were stiff and frozen, those who rejoiced at Nicetas’s imminent arrival. Now he expresses more fully the rigidity of that land, and especially marks the force of Boreas blowing upon the rivers in the Riphaean regions.

But Cisdanubian Dacia, situated between the forty-third and forty-fourth degrees of northern latitude, as is clear from Anville’s own map, and therefore placed farther south than we Forojulians, who live between the forty-sixth and forty-seventh degrees and nevertheless experience no such force of Boreas in our rivers—Cisdanubian Dacia, I say, is by no means compatible [Col. 0887A] with what Paulinus notes here concerning the Riphaean shores, where Boreas binds the rivers with dense frost and where Nicetas also dissolves minds made rigid by ice with heavenly fire.

Indeed, the rigidity of the land that Paulinus notes in the region under Nicetas’s episcopal care is even less compatible with Cisdanubian Dacia, which was formed chiefly from parts of Upper and Lower Moesia by Aurelian, as we saw earlier. For it is well established that Moesia was once exceedingly fertile in grain and was called by the Romans “the granary of Ceres” because of the fertility of its soil, as is shown in the work of Cluverius cited above, book 4, chapter 16, no. 1.

But why say more? Paulinus here mentions the Riphaean regions, which lay extremely far north from the left bank of the Danube, and even farther from Aurelian’s Cisdanubian Dacia and from the city of Remesiana, Remisiana, or Romessiana, situated in the Mediterranea part of this new Dacia. By this one expression, therefore, he clearly indicates Nicetas’s Transdanubian episcopate, which extended, as it were, from the greater Dacia of Trajan beyond the Danube as far as the Riphaean regions.

Nor should anyone say that Paulinus is speaking poetically here and has substituted one place for another in a kind of hyperbole, for the ornament and dignity of the poem. Whatever at that time was understood by the name “Riphaean regions” or “Riphaean Mountains,” when those vast [Col. 0887B] and remote stretches of barbarian lands lying to the north were less known to Roman people, Paulinus expressly describes the Riphaean regions—or at least places tending toward the borders of the Riphaean regions—as locations undoubtedly situated not on this side of the Danube but beyond it, subject to Nicetas’s episcopal care. He immediately names the inhabitants of those places whom Nicetas himself had brought forth for Christ, saying:

> For although hard in lands and minds,  
> And harder than their own snow, the Bessi,  
> Now, made sheep under your leadership, are gathered  
> Into the hall of peace.  
>   
> Their necks, which, unconquered in war,  
> They had always refused to yield to slavery,  
> Now, subdued beneath the yoke of the true Lord,  
> They rejoice to lay low.

Here, then, we have the Bessi as inhabitants of the Riphaean regions beyond the Danube, and therefore situated very far from Aurelian’s new Cisdanubian Dacia [Col. 0887C], whom Paulinus presents as subject to the care of his Nicetas.

There were also other peoples beyond the Danube who, together with the Bessi, were open to Nicetas’s care, and whom Paulinus likewise names in the same poem: namely, the Scythians, the Getae, and especially the Dacians, who gave their name to the entire immense region. Thus Nicetas’s apostolate extended broadly from the left bank of the Danube as far as the Riphaean regions, always among barbarian peoples, without any mention appearing of the new Dacia on this side of the Danube or of the Romans who had been summoned from Barbarian Dacia and established their dwelling there.

Here again is Paulinus:

> The whole northern region calls you father;  
> The Scythian is softened by your words,  
> And the savage heart, discordant with itself,  
> Lays itself aside under your guidance.  
>   
> The Getae run to you, and both Dacians—  
> He who dwells in the middle of the land,  
> Or he who, wearing a cap, is the inhabitant  
> Of the riverbank rich in many cattle. [Col. 0887D]

There are therefore Bessi, Scythians, Getae, and Dacians whom Paulinus says were cultivated in the Christian religion by his Nicetas. Since they were neighboring peoples, they formed, beyond the Danube and outside Aurelian’s Dacia, the entire northern region that called Nicetas its father.

Although in Strabo’s time—that is, at the beginning of the first century after Christ, when he flourished—the Bessi occupied the greater part of Mount Haemus between Lower Moesia and Thrace, as he himself writes in book 7, they seem later to have established their dwelling beyond the Danube, perhaps because Trajan compelled them to do so, or even under Aurelian, when he contracted the boundaries of the Roman Empire to that river, in the region near the Black Sea that is still called, with its name slightly extended, Bessarabia.

As for the Scythians, without saying anything of Lesser Scythia on this side of the Danube—which was also called Roman Scythia, since it was part of the Roman Empire, and where Tomi [Col. 0888A], the city famous for Ovid’s exile, was located and is also mentioned here by Paulinus in connection with Nicetas’s journey—the barbarian Scythians at that time inhabited vast stretches of land to the north beyond the Danube and occupied a considerable part of Asia there as well.

The Getae were the most powerful part of the Scythians. They were also called Goths and were neighbors of the Bessi and Scythians, whose principal dwelling at that time was beyond the Danube, although on some occasions they were admitted into Roman territories if they wished to be initiated into Christian rites, as we shall say below.

Finally, the Dacians were themselves a Scythian people. Their territory, joined to the Getae beyond the Danube to the south and east, was enclosed by the Carpathian ranges to the north. It was divided into Mediterranean, Ripensis, and Alpine regions, just as that new Roman Dacia on this side of the Danube, established by Aurelian, was likewise divided—apparently in imitation of it—into Mediterranean and Ripensis.

See Cluverius, *Introduction to Universal Geography, Ancient as well as Modern*, book 4, chapters 16, 17, and 18.

From this, the character of Nicetas’s episcopate [Col. 0888B] becomes clear from Paulinus’s poem: it was entirely among barbarian peoples, beyond the Danube on the side opposite the new Dacia, although Nicetas himself was a Dardanian and was born near Scupi.

Something further, however, must still be said about the same poem of Paulinus, in order to confirm our case more decisively.

Speaking above of the Bessi whom Nicetas was instructing, and embracing under the poetic name of the Bessi that entire people subject to Nicetas’s episcopal care—which, as we have seen, consisted of Bessi, Scythians, Getae, and Dacians—he said, in praise of the people themselves and in commendation of Nicetas, that those who, always unconquered in war, had refused to offer their necks to slavery now rejoiced to bow them, subdued beneath the yoke of the true Lord.

Those, moreover, who were unconquered in war and had always refused to offer their necks to slavery were certainly not the Dacians on this side of the Danube, all Roman both by origin and by culture. After abandoning the old Dacia beyond the Danube, these had settled, at Aurelian’s direction, on the right bank of the river. Rather, they were truly those unconquered in war and perpetually hostile to servitude, whatever name they might bear, who inhabited the vast region beyond the Danube: their native land, for which they had so often and so bravely fought against the Romans. Although at times conquered and reduced by Trajan into a Roman province, they nevertheless always remained unconquered and later shook off the yoke, so that Aurelian, having summoned across the river all the Romans there—soldiers and colonists alike—judged it preferable to leave the entire region to them, as it had been before Trajan’s time, rather than undertake new wars against them in order to subjugate them again.

But let us hear Paulinus once more, addressing his Nicetas and defining, as it were in a single mode of expression, that entire region which obeyed him in religious matters:

> Through you, the Barbarians in the mute region of the world  
> Learn to make Christ resound  
> With a Roman heart and, made chaste,  
> To live in tranquil peace.

Paulinus would never have called the “mute region of the world” (whatever he understood by the word “mute”) a Roman province; never would he have called Roman Dacia on this side of the Danube—situated between Upper and Lower Moesia, populated by Roman colonists, crowded with cities and fortified towns, and bordering other distinguished regions—nor would he have called the Dacians on this side of the Danube “Barbarians.” He could not have been unaware that they belonged to the Roman Empire and had sprung from colonists formerly brought by Trajan from throughout the Roman world.

What, moreover, of his statement that through Nicetas those Barbarians learned to make Christ resound with a Roman heart? By this manner of speaking he undoubtedly designates peoples who, although they were not subject to Roman rule, nevertheless rightly bore a Roman heart—that is, the Roman faith—through Nicetas; people who were Roman in heart, even if not in body. [Col. 0889A] These Barbarians, then, who learned to make Christ resound with a Roman heart, and indeed in Dacia where Nicetas exercised his apostolate, could be none other than the Dacians and other peoples situated beyond the Danube, who from Aurelian’s time no longer obeyed the Roman eagles. Nevertheless, after accepting the religion of Christ through Nicetas’s preaching, they appeared to bear a Roman heart, since they were joined to the Romans by faith, although alien from the Roman Empire.

Why should Paulinus not also have intended by this manner of expression—“Through you Barbarians learn to make Christ resound with a Roman heart”—to indicate that Nicetas, born in Roman Dacia and therefore ordained by the Roman Church as bishop to preach the Gospel among the Barbarians situated opposite it among the Dacians, was the very person whom we conjectured above? It would be as if he had said: “Through you, a Roman man sent from the Roman see, the Barbarians, although hostile to the Romans, nevertheless learn to make Christ resound in the same manner in which he resounds in your Roman mouth and in the Roman Church—having again become Roman in heart, although barbarian by nation and culture and not subject to Roman laws.” But this is said in passing, taking the opportunity, and more by conjecture than by assertion. Let us now return to our subject.

We therefore have Nicetas’s episcopate as described by Paulinus: extending northward from the Danube as far as the Euxine Pontus, through the Dacians, then through the Getae, and afterward through the Scythians and Bessi, in a continuous course and almost a straight line, since these peoples bordered one another, or perhaps were intermingled in more than one place. We have the customs of these peoples, whom Paulinus describes indiscriminately as rustic, hard, and savage, and the whole nation defined by the name “Barbarians.” We have also the “mute region of the world,” meaning that entire expanse of territory—apparently both because of the severity of the cold and, above all, because of the harshness of its inhabitants and their way of life, entirely deprived of every form of cultivation and alien from the Romans both in political rule and in disposition.

Nicetas, therefore, the man praised by Paulinus, was not bishop of the city of Romessiana, or Remesiana, or Romatiana, nor of any other city in new, Roman Dacia situated on this side of the Danube. Rather, he seems undoubtedly to have been one of those bishops of the nations who were distinguished by no title belonging to a particular see and who, on the left bank of the Danube, exercised not so much an episcopate as an apostolate among those barbarian peoples called by the names of Dacians, Getae, Scythians, and Bessi. For this reason we rightly read of this Nicetas in the Roman Martyrology, on 7 January, without any title belonging to a particular see and with a commendation fully equal to his apostolic labors:

> In Dacia, Saint Nicetas, bishop, who through the preaching of the Gospel rendered savage and barbarian peoples gentle and peaceful.

This agrees perfectly on both sides with the poem of Saint Paulinus of Nola.

But what we have thus far discussed concerning Nicetas the Dacian’s episcopate among the Dacians beyond the Danube, on the basis of the knowledge of the places and peoples which Paulinus of Nola supplies so abundantly, ought in part also to be confirmed by other records of ecclesiastical history. These show us the condition of Christianity on this side and beyond the Danube—namely, in both the old and the new Dacia, and in both Moesias—at the time of Nicetas the Dacian’s apostolate, that is, at the end of the fourth and the beginning of the fifth century.

Indeed, the records show that in Nicetas the Dacian’s time Christianity had long been firmly established on this side of the Danube—in new Dacia, in the Moesias, and in Roman Scythia, as well as in the neighboring regions, namely Dardania, Thrace, and Macedonia, and also around Mount Haemus—and that many episcopal sees, together with their metropolises, already existed there. This appears especially from the subscriptions of the bishops to the First General Council of Nicaea and later to the Council of Sardica, held there in new Dacia. It is also explained more clearly elsewhere by the highly learned Lequien in his *Oriens Christianus*, volume I, in the Thracian Diocese, where he treats of the provinces of Thrace, Haemimontus, Scythia, and Lower Moesia, and so forth; and volume II, in the Illyrian Diocese, where he treats of the provinces of Macedonia, Mediterranean Dacia, and Dardania, and so forth.

Either, then, no barbarian peoples devoted to the worship of profane deities, and therefore in need of being brought to the Christian religion, existed in Nicetas’s time in Dacia on this side of the Danube or in the neighboring regions; or else there was no reason for Nicetas, if he had actually been bishop of the city of Remesiana in new Mediterranean Dacia, either to leave his own particular Church in order to instruct Barbarians situated here and there elsewhere, or to put his hand, as it were, to another’s harvest and invade the dioceses of other bishops in some fashion by undertaking an apostolate among barbarian peoples there.

Nicetas must therefore have exercised his episcopate beyond the Danube, where there certainly were barbarian peoples devoted to the profane worship of deities and therefore in need of conversion to the Christian religion, and where particular Churches, furnished with their own bishops, had not yet been established.

What, then, do we learn from the records about those peoples beyond the Danube in the age of Nicetas the Dacian, and about the introduction of the Christian religion among them? We said that the peoples beyond the Danube were those whom Paulinus lists as having been brought by his Nicetas to the Christian religion—namely, the Dacians, Getae, Scythians, and Bessi. We proved that these were peoples beyond the Danube in Nicetas the Dacian’s own time from Paulinus’s manner of expression, which could in no way apply to peoples and regions situated on this side of the Danube.

The names of those peoples beyond the Danube are often used indiscriminately by writers. Other barbarian peoples united with them are often indicated under one or another of these names, although the proper distinction of the terms is not thereby eliminated. Nevertheless, those whom the Romans called Getae are the same as the Goths, as scholars commonly observe. Having emerged from the more remote regions of Germany toward the north, they first settled in various areas beyond the Danube under different leaders or kings. They were called partly Ostrogoths and partly Visigoths, according to the eastern or western region which they occupied, and afterward they seized various stretches of territory throughout Europe.

Some of these—or a portion of them—as Philostorgius reports (*Ecclesiastical History* II.5, and Saint Basil the Great also mentions, Letter 165, alternatively 339 in the Maurist edition), during the reigns of the emperors Valerian and Gallienus entered Asia, Galatia, and Cappadocia by way of the Euxine Pontus for the sake of plunder. They carried away many Christian captives, among whom were not a few priests and clerics of the Christian law. From these captives they learned the true worship of God. This worship became so widespread among them, especially in the time of Constantine the Great, that they had bishops, among them that Theophilus who attended the Council of Nicaea and subscribed in the name of the province of Gothia: “Theophilus, bishop of the metropolis of Gothia.”
