Nevertheless, in the same passage Philostorgius records that under the rule of Constantine the Great a great multitude of the Getae or Goths was expelled from its native homes on account of its piety. The emperor received them kindly and settled them in Moesia. Thus the greater part of the Getic or Gothic people situated beyond the Danube remained devoted to the worship of empty gods even under Constantine’s rule.

What happened afterward? A most savage persecution also arose against the Christians among that people, as Sozomen reports (*Ecclesiastical History* VI.37. The author of the persecution was one of the Gothic kings, named Athanaric, who attacked the Christian religion not only out of zeal to defend the superstition of his ancestors, but also because he could scarcely endure that his people should follow the religion of the Romans, of whom he was an especially bitter enemy.

On that occasion the Church was enriched with many Gothic martyrs, among them the celebrated Saba, whose life and martyrdom are related in a letter of the Gothic Church preserved by Ruinart in the *Acta Martyrum*, Verona edition, p. 527. Scholars assign his martyrdom to the year of Christ 372.

Meanwhile, many Gothic Christians withdrew across the Danube to the Romans and to the ancient Christian Goths who had long before been given hospitality by Constantine in Moesia, in order to escape the persecution; Athanaric himself also drove them to this course, as Isidore relates in his *Chronicle*. At last weary of his own cruelty, Athanaric preferred to expel the Christians from his kingdom rather than kill them.

Thus pagan Goths truly held dominion beyond the Danube, except for those who occupied the region from the river Tanais as far as the river Tyras, where the aforementioned Lequien considers a Gothic Church to have been established (*Oriens Christianus*, I, col. 1241, “The Church of Gothia”), and where the undefiled Catholic faith continued to endure.

Toward the end of the reign of the Emperor Valens Augustus, when the Hunnic people—more savage than every form of savagery, as Jordanes writes in *On the Gothic Affairs*, chapter 24—had emerged from other northern regions of greater Scythia beyond the river Tanais and were advancing toward Dacia beyond the Danube, part of the Goths, defeated in war and overwhelmed by the multitude, was compelled to yield its territory and, after seeking permission, cross into Roman territory on this side of the Danube.

This was not done without agreements and conditions between the Romans and the Barbarians, as Socrates writes (*Ecclesiastical History* IV.33). The chief conditions were that they should live according to Roman laws and give their names to Christ. The Romans granted the new settlers Moesia, Thrace, and new Ripense Dacia.

In this, however, the unhappy new settlers suffered the misfortune that a large part of them, through the deceit of the Emperor Valens, an exceedingly obstinate champion of the Arian party, received stones instead of bread and serpents instead of fish: that is, they received the Christian religion not pure and orthodox, but defiled by the impiety of the Arians, which they afterward transmitted to their descendants and spread widely.

Let us not here trace the later fortunes of the Goths and of the other Barbarians, or their wars with the Romans, sometimes successful and sometimes disastrous. It is meanwhile clear from what has been said that the barbarian people of the Getae or Goths, established beyond the Danube, was for the most part pagan at the end of Valens’s reign, or shortly afterward, under the rule of Gratian and Theodosius; and the same was true of the Huns, who conquered them and were later mingled with them.

It is further clear that at that time no Churches and no episcopal sees existed in those regions beyond the Danube, if we except that Gothic Church mentioned above with Lequien, which, from its location, did not properly belong to the Dacia of which we are speaking.

As for the Dacians, Scythians, and Bessi, whom Paulinus mentions together with the Getae or Goths—names perhaps belonging to the original peoples of those regions before the Getae or Goths and later the Huns descended into those places, and by which he also understood new inhabitants mingled with the old, or bordering upon them, or at any rate ruling in their territories—who would dare assert that before the time of Valens or Theodosius the Great they were not all pagans? Who could point out there any Churches or bishops other than the Church and bishop of Tomi in Minor or Roman Scythia, situated on this side of the Danube beside the Euxine Pontus? That Church, consequently, had no connection whatever with barbarian old Dacia or with the other barbarian peoples beyond the Danube.

If, therefore, that Nicetas, Paulinus of Nola’s own Nicetas, exercised an episcopate among the barbarian peoples as Paulinus describes them; if he truly taught them to make Christ resound with a Roman heart and now for the first time to bow their necks beneath the yoke of the true Lord—those necks which, always unconquered in war, they had refused to offer to servitude, as Paulinus sang, as we saw earlier—then this means nothing other than that he brought them to the Christian religion, which they had not previously known.

These barbarian peoples, therefore, could be none other than those who inhabited barbarian Dacia beyond the Danube. For that reason we may rightly say that Paulinus’s Nicetas exercised his episcopate beyond the Danube, even after weighing, besides Paulinus’s own words, the other records of ecclesiastical history which disclose to us the condition of Christianity on this side and beyond the Danube in Nicetas the Dacian’s own age—that is, at the end of the fourth and the beginning of the fifth century.

[Col. 0892A] Yet Lequien himself, cited above, admits that the peoples beyond the Danube were brought to the Christian faith by this Nicetas the Dacian, in *Oriens Christianus*, volume II, in the Eastern Illyrian Diocese and the province of Mediterranean Dacia, col. 306. Nevertheless, he makes him bishop of the Church of Remesiana, or Romesiana, or Remessiana, on this side of the Danube in new Mediterranean Dacia under the metropolitan see of Sardica, saying:

> At the same time as Saints Jerome and Paulinus, Nicetas, or Nicetius, bishop of the city of Remesiana, flourished. He preached the word of God to the Bessi, Dacians, Goths, and Scythians living beyond the Ister.

What, then, are we to say to this? The authority of Lequien certainly favors our opinion, since he acknowledged that the Bessi, Dacians, Goths, and Scythians to whom this Nicetas preached were situated beyond the Danube. But while he nevertheless asserts that Nicetas, the instructor and father of those barbarian peoples, was bishop of the city of Romatiana in new Mediterranean Dacia on this side of the Danube, he grants too much to a certain San-Germain manuscript of Gennadius, which he cites and which is certainly not known from any other source. Elsewhere it will be mentioned that Nicetas is called bishop of the city of Remesiana, which certainly lay in Dacia on this side of the Danube.

In this respect also he follows the practice of so many learned writers who, against Baronius, have wished to understand Gennadius’s city of Romatiana as Remesiana, Romesiana, or Remessiana in new Roman Dacia. These writers too will be discussed at length in their proper place.

Moreover, since Paulinus was entirely silent—as we noted earlier—about any city called Romatiana, Remesiana, or by any other name in his poem when he praised Nicetas; since he said absolutely nothing about Nicetas’s merits in governing a particular Church where there were no barbarian or pagan peoples; and since he places all Nicetas’s praise in the conversion of Barbarians from pagan superstitions, who could make him bishop of some particular Church outside barbarian Dacia, indeed in new Mediterranean Dacia, merely on the basis of a similarity in the place-name, an identity of names, or even a coincidence of time?

Furthermore, Paulinus’s praises of Nicetas in that same poem, when Nicetas returned to Dacia, are plainly such—as anyone reading the entire poem can see—as to indicate that Nicetas spent his whole life in the conversion and instruction of barbarian peoples. He would therefore have had no time remaining to govern another particular Church, especially one separated from those barbarian peoples by the Danube and by some additional stretch of land.

Unless we gratuitously assert that this Nicetas abandoned his particular Church, situated in Roman Mediterranean Dacia, as it were, in order to undertake an apostolate among the barbarian peoples in Dacia beyond the Danube—a course which, we do not know whether the discipline of that age would have permitted, or whether it could readily be attributed to Nicetas’s merit.

The age of this Nicetas the Dacian, the period of his episcopate, and the year in which we suppose him to have died, more or less, will be discussed at length in the following chapter, to which we refer the reader. In the meantime, from what we shall say there, we may reasonably assert here that this Paulinian Nicetas began his episcopate and apostolate among the barbarian peoples beyond the Danube under the Emperor Valens, around the year 375, when he was about thirty or perhaps thirty-five years old; and that he completed it with his life around the year 420, at the age of seventy-five or perhaps eighty.

Accordingly, the merits of this Dacian Nicetas among those barbarian peoples beyond the Danube were praised by Saint Jerome at almost the same time as Saint Paulinus. In Letter 60 in Vallarsi’s edition, addressed to Heliodorus, no. 4, and assigned to the year 396, Jerome wrote from his Bethlehem retreat that:

> The savagery of the Bessi and the multitude of fur-clad peoples, who once sacrificed human beings at the funeral rites of the dead, have broken their shriek into the sweet melody of Christ.

But he expressed the progress of those peoples beyond the Danube in the Christian religion even more clearly in the same edition, Letter 107 to Laeta, no. 2, assigned to the year 403:

> The Huns are learning the Psalter; the frosts of Scythia glow with the warmth of faith; the red-haired and golden-haired army of the Goths carries the tents of the Churches about with it. And perhaps for this reason they fight against us in an equal battle line, because they trust in the same religion.

Here, however, we must also address an objection raised by the distinguished Dominicus Georgius, who in his *Martyrology of Ado*, on 22 June, p. 288, cites two letters of Pope Innocent I, which may be seen in volume III of Labbe’s edition of the Councils, published at Venice under the care of Coleti: Letter 21 to the bishop of Naresis or Naissus, and Letter 22 to the bishops of Macedonia. In these letters mention is made of a bishop Nicetas, whom Georgius unquestionably understands as Nicetas, bishop of Romatiana in Dacia on this side of the Danube.

However much the date of this Nicetas, Saint Paulinus’s friend, may agree with the age of Pope Innocent I and with the time of the letters mentioned, I must nevertheless say, with due respect for the great man, that Pope Innocent calls Nicetas in neither of those letters bishop of the city of Romatiana, nor of Romisiana or Remissiana, and so forth, but simply “bishop.”

Perhaps he was the same person as the friend of Paulinus mentioned in the first letter, where the person and condemnation of Bishop Bonosus are discussed. But what does that imply against us, if it does not follow either that he was actually bishop of Romatiana or that he was not a bishop in Dacia beyond the Danube?

As for the other letter of Innocent, who does not see that it was addressed to the bishops of the province of Macedonia under the metropolitan see of Thessalonica? Consequently, the Nicetas mentioned there among the other bishops of Macedonia was a bishop of that province, named Nicetas but entirely different from the other Niceas or Nicetas of whom we are speaking here. He could not in any way have been counted among the bishops of the province of Macedonia, whether he had possessed the episcopal see of Romatiana on this side of the Danube—for then he would have been counted among the bishops under the metropolitan see of Sardica, in the province of Mediterranean Dacia, and therefore could not be confused with the Macedonians—or whether he had exercised an episcopate beyond the Danube, since he would then either have belonged to no province at all or certainly to the neighboring province of Mediterranean Dacia, whose metropolis was Sardica.

It therefore seems right to conclude once again that Niceas, or Nicetas, the friend of Saint Paulinus of Nola, was not bishop of that city in the new Dacia established by Aurelian on this side of the Danube, which was called Remesiana, Romissiana, or Romatiana, and so forth. Rather, he undoubtedly exercised an episcopate beyond the Danube among barbarian peoples, in that Dacia of Trajan which at that time did not belong to the Roman Empire and was therefore called barbarian Dacia.

There is consequently no basis for anyone to take comfort in the name of the city “Romatiana” used by Gennadius and thus claim that the Gennadian Niceas or Nicetas was the same as Niceas or Nicetas, the friend of Saint Paulinus, who was celebrated by his praises. On that assumption he could conveniently be placed in Dacia on this side of the Danube and assigned the city of Remesiana, Romesiana, or Remissiana, and so forth—a city which could easily be understood under Gennadius’s slightly altered name “Romatiana.”

## CHAPTER III

**The bishop of the city of Romatiana, Niceas or Nicetas, mentioned by Gennadius, is not that Dacian Niceas or Nicetas, the friend of Saint Paulinus of Nola, who was celebrated by his praises**

I now proceed to more inward and more serious matters, undertaking in this chapter to prove that Niceas, or Nicetas, the bishop of the city of Romatiana mentioned by Gennadius, was not that Dacian Niceas or Nicetas, the friend of Saint Paulinus of Nola and celebrated by his praises.

Here his little works must be examined more closely. Here it must be investigated whether the distinctive features presented in these works concerning dogmas, heresies, and discipline agree with Saint Paulinus of Nola’s holy friend Nicetas—or do not agree with him—according to the standards which sound reasoning requires and experts in criticism transmit. Here, consequently, we must also discuss the age of this Nicetas, Paulinus’s friend, and whether he was exactly Paulinus’s contemporary, nearly his contemporary, or later than him. All this requires careful investigation, so that the broad proposition may proceed from it as though spontaneously.

Both of these works, which we have proved to be genuine, supply the strongest arguments for demonstrating that their author, Niceas or Nicetas, bishop of the city of Romatiana mentioned by Gennadius, cannot be that Dacian Niceas or Nicetas, the friend of Saint Paulinus of Nola and celebrated by his praises. But both for the sake of brevity and because it is preferable to select the more certain evidence, it will be sufficient for now to dwell on the *Explanation of the Creed* addressed to the catechumens, reserving the *Booklet to a Fallen Virgin* for another occasion.

As for the dogmas transmitted in certain insufficiently examined works of the holy Fathers, from which critics commonly draw arguments for identifying their authors, I am not unaware that the conclusions drawn from certain dogmas are not sufficiently firm when those are dogmas which the Church later explained in councils against heresies that had arisen. For since the Church never introduced new dogmas, but merely explained more fully and confirmed by its definition those things which had been revealed from the beginning and preserved by constant tradition, but which were later violated by the sophistries of innovators, it is necessary that the same dogmas should also be found asserted in the works of the holy Fathers that preceded the councils in which those dogmas were defined. From this, however, it cannot be inferred that those works ought to be judged the works of authors of a later age rather than of the Fathers themselves.

Who, for example, is unaware that the Catholic dogma concerning the divinity of the Son and his consubstantiality with the Father was both believed and transmitted by the Fathers before Nicaea? Therefore, the mere assertion of a dogma which the Church later sanctioned by a formal decree is not sufficient reason for judging that a work must be later than that ecclesiastical definition.

[Col. 0894C]

There are nevertheless often certain accompanying features which make arguments drawn from dogmas firm and irresistible. This occurs, for example, if the dogma is asserted with a particular force not employed before the Church was challenged concerning it; or if it is announced in virtually the same words, or in words only slightly different, from those used by the Church assembled in ecumenical councils when defining it, or from those employed by the Roman pontiffs in their dogmatic constitutions; or if it is supported by the same considerations commonly used by those who, amid the heat of controversy, defended Catholic truth with greater force; or if, in announcing the dogma, words, arguments, and modes of expression are employed which became common among the Fathers after its definition.

The weight and strength of arguments drawn from dogmas increase if the contrary error is indicated in the announcement of the dogma, even when the name of the erring person and his followers is left unspoken; and if a dogma is proposed whose contrary error has broken out more than once in the Church and has been overthrown more than once. Then, in judging works on the basis of an assertion of this kind, other features of the same works must be sought which may bring light into the darkness. Almost never are certain distinctive features lacking that remove ambiguity. Nor should the variation in the manner of writing and arguing be considered insignificant: this variation distinguishes one age from another and one century from another, as though by some particular color and characteristic mark of its own.

Having considered these matters, here is Niceas, or Nicetas, called by Gennadius bishop of the city of Romatiana, addressing his catechumens in the *Explanation of the Creed*, chapter 4, concerning the mystery of the Incarnation:

> Believe that this one who was born from the Virgin together with us is God: God from the Father before the ages; man from the Virgin for the sake of human beings. Truly incarnate, not merely apparently so, as certain misguided heretics say, ashamed of the mystery of God. They say that the Lord’s incarnation occurred only in appearance, because what was seen was not real, but had deceived human eyes. Far be this—far, utterly—from the truth of God. For if the incarnation is false, human salvation will also be false. But if salvation is truly in Christ, then the incarnation is likewise true. In him both are present: man, in what was seen; God, in what was not seen. Eating as man, and feeding five thousand people with five loaves, because he is God. Sleeping as man in the boat, but commanding the winds and the sea, because he is God. Fastening his hands to the cross as man, but granting paradise to the thief who confessed him, because he is God. Finally, accepting death, having laid aside his body for a little while, as man, but raising a four-day-dead man from the tomb, because he is God. Christ must therefore be believed to be both: God and man. For just as he is recognized as man from his sufferings, so God is manifested through his divine works. You therefore have grounds for rejecting teachers of deceit.

Thus far blessed Nicetas.

Here, then, is the Catholic dogma of Christ’s true humanity asserted by our Nicetas—not merely asserted, but also clearly and energetically explained and most solidly defended against those who violate this dogma. He marks their error and, without expressing their name, calls them in general misguided heretics and teachers of deceit.

This Nicetas therefore belongs not to a time before the errors concerning Christ’s true humanity arose, but to a later period. Consequently, the assertion of this dogma by our Nicetas is of such a kind that some opinion concerning his age may be formed from it.

Yet error concerning Christ’s true humanity has broken out in the Church of God more than once. The author of the *Catalogue of Heretics*, which follows Tertullian’s book *On the Prescription Against Heretics*, mentions the heretic Saturninus, who under the Emperor Trajan or Hadrian disseminated his heresy at Antioch, asserting among other things that Christ had not existed in the substance of a body and had suffered only apparently, as though in a phantom.

He also mentions Basilides, who likewise proclaimed that Christ had come in appearance only and had lacked the substance of flesh. He lists the Ophites as well, who arose around the year 150 and asserted among other things that Christ had not existed in the substance of flesh.

Then he mentions Valentinus, who taught that Christ had not existed in the substance of our body, but had brought down from heaven some kind of spiritual body, passing through the Virgin Mary like water through a pipe, receiving or borrowing nothing from her.

After others he mentions Cerdo, who denies that Christ existed in the substance of flesh and declares that he existed only in appearance; that he did not truly suffer, but suffered as though he did; that he was not born from the Virgin, indeed was not born at all.

Finally he mentions Marcion, Cerdo’s disciple, who attempted to approve Cerdo’s heresy and to say the same things which that earlier heretic had said.

To these may be added the Apollinarians and Manichaeans, none of whom believed in the reality of human flesh in Christ, as Saint Leo the Great states in Letter 35 to Julian, bishop of Coensa, chapter 1, in the edition of the Ballerini brothers, which we shall use throughout this dissertation.

This error, long since condemned by the Fathers in these heretics and therefore almost obsolete, was recalled from the underworld in the middle of the fifth century by Eutyches, archimandrite of Constantinople. For this reason Saint Leo the Great says in Letter 124 to the Palestinian monks, chapter 2, that Eutyches had been tossed about through the impious errors of the ancient heretics.

Of him Saint Leo likewise wrote in Letter 79 to Pulcheria Augusta:

> If he had possessed any soundness of heart, he could easily have avoided the error—once struck down and long ago overthrown in its authors—in order not to attempt to stir up revived fires from buried ashes and thus enter the company of those whose example he had followed.

It is nevertheless worthwhile to consider Eutyches’s error more closely. For I do not think that our Nicetas had those ancient heretics in mind when, in asserting the Catholic dogma concerning Christ’s true humanity, he calls those opposed to it misguided heretics and teachers of deceit. Rather, I maintain that Nicetas intended especially Eutyches and his followers by those words, as I shall explain below.

Let blessed Nicetas therefore speak once more to his catechumens concerning the Catholic dogma of Christ’s true humanity, and fortify them against the opposing error:

> Believe, he says, that this one who was born from the Virgin together with us is God: God from the Father before the ages; man from the Virgin for the sake of human beings. Truly incarnate, not merely apparently so, as certain misguided heretics say, ashamed of the mystery of God. They say that the Lord’s incarnation occurred only in appearance, because what was seen was not real, but had deceived human eyes. Far be this—far, utterly—from the truth of God.

What, then, of Eutyches and his followers? Let us first hear a contemporary historian and the notary of Saint Leo, Pope Leo I: Saint Prosper of Aquitaine in his *Chronicle*. Under the consulship of Asturius and Protogenes he writes:

> At this time the Eutychian heresy arose, its author being a certain presbyter named Eutyches, who presided over a highly renowned monastery at Constantinople. He preached that Jesus Christ our Lord, the son of the blessed Virgin Mary, possessed nothing of his mother’s substance, but that in him there was only the nature of the Word of God under the appearance of a man.

Here, then, is Christ, according to Eutyches’s error, incarnate not truly but apparently, just as those misguided heretics said in Nicetas; here is one who possessed nothing of his mother’s substance, as Saint Prosper reports from Eutyches; here is the Lord’s incarnation occurring only in appearance, with what was seen not truly being himself but deceiving human eyes. This is undoubtedly equivalent to saying that in Christ, under the appearance of a man, there was only the nature of the Word of God—the heresy of Eutyches as Saint Prosper presents it.

But as regards the heresy of Eutyches, nothing is more precise, nothing more solid, nothing more comprehensive [24] than the teaching of Saint Leo the Great, who both understood that heresy thoroughly from its very origin, assailed it with the greatest vigor, restrained it with the utmost vigilance, and crushed it by apostolic authority. Let Saint Leo, then, be heard as he explains the error of Eutyches—not in one place only, but in several, out of the zeal with which he burned for Catholic truth.

[Col. 0896C] “Nor would he [Eutyches], speaking deceptively, say that the Word was made flesh in such a way that Christ, born from the Virgin’s womb, possessed the form of a man but did not possess the reality of a body derived from his mother.” Thus in the celebrated letter to Flavian, which is Letter 28 in the cited edition of the Ballerini brothers, chapter 2.

“As far as Nestorius fell away from the truth when he asserted that the Lord Jesus Christ was born from his Virgin Mother as man only, so far also did this man [Eutyches] deviate from the Catholic path when he believed that he who was born from that same Virgin was not of our nature: so that what he bore was the form of a servant, and what he possessed was likeness and conformity to us, but was only a kind of image of our flesh, not its reality.” Thus Letter 30, to Pulcheria Augusta.

[Col. 0896D] “As far as Nestorius departed from the truth by separating the divinity of the Word from the substance of the assumed man, so far also did this man [Eutyches] depart from the right path, who preached that the only-begotten Son of God was born from the womb of the blessed Virgin in such a way that he bore the appearance of a human body, but that the reality of human flesh was not united to the Word.” Thus Letter 35, to Julian of Cos, chapter 1.

“Just as Nestorius . . . so also Eutyches, following the error once condemned and blaspheming with another profanation, was cut off from the structure of Catholic firmness. For he attempted to persuade certain people who were unlearned and excessively simple that the Word of God was made flesh in such a way that he did not take true flesh from his mother; nor did he possess a body of our race; rather, the divinity and flesh of the Word were one nature, so that he would say that our one Lord Jesus Christ was both a false man and a passible God. This neither the piety of faith nor the reason of the mystery accepts: either that the divinity was passible in its own nature, or that the Truth lied in assuming humanity.” Thus Letter 102, to the bishops of Gaul.

“The rock of the Catholic faith . . . likewise execrates Eutyches, who, emptying out the reality of human flesh in the Lord Jesus Christ, asserts that the Word itself was transformed into flesh, [Col. 0897A] so that birth, nourishment, growth, suffering, death, burial, and resurrection on the third day belonged solely to the divinity, which did not assume the reality of a servant’s form, but only its appearance.” Thus Letter 119, to Maximus of Antioch, chapter 2.

Thus far Saint Leo the Great concerning the error of Eutyches. Now, what the holy pontiff records concerning Eutyches’ error—namely, that he taught Christ to have the form of a man but not the reality of a body derived from his mother; that in him there was an image of our flesh, not its reality; that he bore the appearance of a human body, not the reality of human flesh; that he did not take true flesh from his mother and did not possess a body of our race, and therefore proved to be a false man; that he assumed the appearance of a servant’s form, not its reality—are these not precisely the same things that blessed Nicetas reported concerning his erroneous heretics and teachers of deceit: namely, that they taught the Son of God to have become incarnate notionally, not truly, and that they said the Lord’s incarnation had taken place in a phantom, because what appeared was not real, [Col. 0897B] but had deceived human eyes?

Let us now consider even clearer statements [25] concerning the error of Eutyches in the writings of the same Saint Leo, and the word “phantom,” used by Nicetas, as well as that illusion intended to deceive the eyes, expressed by the equivalent term “simulation.” Thus the same error will appear to have been indicated by our Nicetas through the very same usage of words as that employed by the holy pontiff. Below we shall state what, once these points have been established, no one, as we believe, will deny to settle the matter completely.

“For plainly . . . they [Eutyches and his followers] ally themselves with the error of the Manichaeans, who deny that a true man of our nature was assumed by the only-begotten Son of God, and who want all his bodily actions to have been those of a simulated phantom.” Thus Saint Leo, Letter 59, to the clergy and people of Constantinople.

“Let Eutyches also be struck with the same anathema as Nestorius: he who, having been carried through the impious errors of the ancient heretics, chose the third doctrine of Apollinaris, so that, denying the reality of human [Col. 0897C] flesh and soul, he asserts that our entire Lord Jesus Christ is of one nature, as though the divinity of the Word itself had changed into flesh and soul; and that conception and birth, nourishment and growth, crucifixion and death, burial and resurrection . . . belonged solely to that essence which does not receive any of these things in itself without the reality of flesh . . . Therefore, if this heretic departs from the perversity of Apollinaris lest he be convicted of considering the divinity passible and mortal, yet if he dares to declare one nature of the incarnate Word—that is, of the Word and flesh—he plainly passes into the madness of Manichaeus and Marcion, and believes that the mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, performed everything by simulation, and that no human body was in him, but that a phantom-like appearance of a body was presented to the eyes of those who saw.” The same Saint Leo says this in Letter 124, to the monks of Palestine, chapter 2, and in exactly the same words in Letter 165, to Leo Augustus, chapter 2.

In Sermon 65, On the Passion of the Lord 14, chapter 1, he says:

[Col. 0897D] “My beloved, I understand that the sermon promised concerning the glorious passion [Col. 0897D] of our Lord Jesus Christ must be delivered in such a way that the duty of exposition may both serve the paschal feast and confront the daring of impious error [the Eutychian error]. For those who deny that the Son of God assumed the true nature of our flesh are enemies of the Christian faith, and they attack the evangelical proclamation with excessive shamelessness, so that, according to them, Christ’s cross was either the simulation of a phantom or the punishment of the divinity.”

Here, then, is the word “phantom,” used by Saint Leo when explaining the error of Eutyches, in precisely the sense of blessed Nicetas; likewise the word “simulation,” which expresses that illusion intended to deceive human eyes, as blessed Nicetas understands it. Who, moreover, does not detect exactly the same meaning in those words of the Roman pontiff: that Eutyches “believes Christ Jesus to have done everything by simulation, and that no human body was in him, but that a phantom-like appearance of a body appeared to the eyes of those who saw him”—and in these words of blessed Nicetas: “They say that the Lord’s incarnation took place in a phantom, because what appeared was not real [Col. 0898A], but had deceived human eyes”? Let us add also that, in the same sermon of the holy pontiff just cited, chapter 4, the followers of Eutyches are called “phantom-Christians,” just as those same men are attacked in exactly the same words in Letter 124, chapter 6, where the holy pontiff says:

“Let these phantom-Christians, then, say what substance of the Savior was fastened to the wood, what substance lay in the tomb, and what flesh rose on the third day when the stone of the monument had been rolled away, and so forth.”

Nor does the correspondence of words and meanings end here between Saint Leo [26], speaking of Eutyches and the Eutychians, and blessed Nicetas, admonishing his own hearers concerning those erroneous heretics and teachers of deceit whom he mentions. Therefore, in a matter that is especially important for this argument, nothing must be omitted that can shed even the smallest amount of light or, as it were, prepare the way for what will be made clear below.

Blessed Nicetas, then, speaking of his erroneous heretics, says: [Col. 0898B] “As certain erroneous heretics say.” They were therefore not numerous at that time, since they are said to have been merely “certain” individuals. But what does Saint Leo the pope say about the Eutychians?

“This confession”—namely, of true divinity and true humanity in Christ—“although it is now impiously injured by a few individuals, and so forth.” Letter 43, to Theodosius Augustus.

And again:

“Because this mystery”—of true divinity and equally true humanity in Christ—“is now impiously opposed by a few imprudent persons, and so forth.” Letter 44, to the same Theodosius Augustus.

Likewise:

“So that ecclesiastical peace may be renewed, which appears to have been disturbed by the dissensions of certain persons.” Letter 70, to Pulcheria Augusta.

Pulcheria Augusta herself, who was present in opposition to the Eutychian faction, wrote as follows to the same Saint Leo in the letter that is numbered 77 among the letters of the holy pontiff:

“That error having been removed which has now arisen among certain persons.”

Blessed Nicetas continues, and calls those certain erroneous heretics of his who said that Christ had not truly become incarnate [Col. 0898C] “ashamed of the mystery of God.” What, then, does the holy pontiff Leo say here also about the Eutychians? Let us recall what he writes in Letter 165, to Leo Augustus, chapter 9:

“The impiety of the heretics reveals that they are engaged in great sacrilege when, under the pretext of honoring the divinity, they deny the reality of human flesh in Christ; and they consider it a religious belief if it is said that what saves is not true in our Savior. For, according to the promise extending throughout all ages, the world has been reconciled to God in Christ, so that unless the Word deigned to become flesh, no flesh could be saved. For the entire mystery of Christian faith is greatly darkened, as the heretics wish, if the light of truth is thought to have lain hidden beneath the falsehood of a phantom. Therefore no Christian should consider himself ashamed of the reality of our body in Christ . . . Since no part of the sacred writings is silent concerning him, it is enough to set forth certain signs consonant with the truth, by which the diligence of faith may be directed into the most splendid breadth and, in the sincere light of understanding, may perceive that, in the Son of God, [Col. 0898D] who unceasingly professes himself the Son of Man and man, Christians ought not to be ashamed, but ought most steadfastly to glory.”

You see, then, that according to Leo the Great the Eutychians were ashamed of the reality of our body in Christ, and indeed under the pretext of honoring the divinity; just as according to Nicetas those erroneous heretics, themselves ashamed of the mystery of God, said that the Lord Christ had become incarnate not truly but supposedly, as though a true incarnation of God were unbecoming to him.

How immense, moreover, was the enormity of that error in the eyes of Nicetas, the error against which he admonished those preparing for baptism, and how great a destructive danger it threatened to Christian faith and to the salvation of humanity, appears from what immediately follows his indication of that error in the Explanation of the Creed. For he says:

“Far be it, far be it altogether from the truth of God. For if the incarnation is false, salvation also will be false. [Col. 0899A] But if salvation is truly in Christ, then the incarnation is equally true.”

Is there anything similar concerning the Eutychian error in Pope Leo? Letter [27] 60, to Pulcheria Augusta, contains the following:

“For it is an exceedingly impious heresy, and hostile to the Gospel of truth, which attempts not merely to injure some portion of the faith, but to tear out the very foundations of the Christian religion, by denying that the eternal Son of the eternal Father took true flesh of our nature from the womb of the blessed Virgin Mother.”

And in Letter 165, to Leo Augustus, chapter 5, he writes:

“What hope, then, do they leave for themselves in the protection of this mystery who deny the reality of a human body in our Savior? Let them say by what sacrifice they were reconciled; let them say by what blood they were redeemed.”

Thus far we have seen the Eutychian heresy fully exposed through its principal opponent [Col. 0899B], Saint Leo the Great, and we have seen the remarkable similarity of this heresy to that concerning which Nicetas spoke in the Explanation of the Creed. Indeed, by comparison we have learned that both writers used the same meanings, phrases, and even words in identifying the heresy in question.

We must now proceed to what was proposed at the beginning: namely, that our blessed Nicetas did not at all have in view the error of those ancient heretics who, as it were, foreshadowed Eutyches, although their error agrees entirely with that of which Nicetas speaks, and although words are not lacking that establish the identity of the matter—words which undoubtedly deceived even the most learned Zabeo, so that, suspecting nothing whatever about Eutyches, he recognized only his predecessors there, in the second part of his dissertation, number 16. Rather, Nicetas was actually speaking of the Eutychian error, and by the erroneous heretics and teachers of deceit mentioned in the Explanation of the Creed, Eutyches himself and his followers must certainly be understood.

I undertake to prove this by conjectures, since no arguments of another kind are available; but, unless I am mistaken, these conjectures are of such weight that, whether taken together or individually, I am confident they will establish the matter [Col. 0899C] completely.

We must turn to the celebrated dogmatic letter of Saint Leo the Great to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople. From the very beginning, this letter struck down the error of Eutyches with such force of reasoning and such power of authority and eloquence that nothing was judged more robust or more effective against that impiety, amid the common applause of the entire Church.

From the year 449, when this letter was issued, in the consulship of Asturius and Protogenes, until the Council of Chalcedon, where it was reverently received as a rule of faith delivered, as it were, from the very mouth of Peter, it spread throughout all the Churches of both East and West. It consequently came to be on everyone’s lips, so that not only did individual bishops throughout the world always keep it before their eyes, but the faithful also commonly committed it to memory as though it were a creed of faith.

It is fitting to offer on this matter the most illuminating testimony of the Church of Gaul, which, in a synodal letter sent to Saint Leo himself and numbered 99 among the letters [Col. 0899D] of this holy pontiff, wrote in chapter 2:

“Your apostolic writings are inscribed upon the tablets of the heart, just like the creed of faith, by everyone who does not neglect the mysteries of redemption; and they have been entrusted to a tenacious memory, so that he may be more prepared to confound the errors of heretics.”

What the bishops of Gaul, assembled in synod, testified concerning the Gallican Church may rightly be judged concerning the other Churches throughout the world—especially since it is certain that, in professions of faith, nothing was more common in antiquity than, after the general councils, to profess the doctrine of this letter as well. The letter held a place even among the divine offices during Advent, both [28] in the Roman Church and in other Churches of Italy and Gaul, as the Ballerini brothers learnedly point out in their admonition to this same letter.

As regards these regions of Upper Italy, there exists a letter to the same holy Pope Leo from Eusebius, bishop of Milan, and other bishops of the province, numbered 97 among Leo’s letters. [Col. 0900A] In it, the blessed pontiff’s letter to Flavian is received with the greatest veneration and celebrated with the praise it deserves.

As for the province of Aquileia, adjoining that of Milan, where we live, the same learned Ballerini brothers refer to the Pledge (Sponsio) of the Bishops of the Province of Aquileia to Paulinus, patriarch, in the year 801, cited by de Rubeis in the Monuments of the Church of Aquileia and extracted from Vatican manuscript 1322. There the provincial bishops professed the rule of the Catholic faith according to the definition of the Council of Nicaea and “as the volume of blessed Pope Leo declares.”

Although this is a monument of a later age, there is nevertheless no doubt that it too flowed from the original discipline of the people of Aquileia, and from that same ancient source of veneration for this letter—a veneration which the Gallican and Milanese bishops left attested in their writings, and which, as both the gravity of the matter, the circumstances of those times, and reason itself suggest, existed in full measure throughout the universal Church.

What, then, does this dogmatic letter [Col. 0900B] of Saint Leo contribute to our case? Since the letter was held in such veneration throughout the Catholic world from the time it was issued that it was accepted by everyone as a kind of creed of faith and also committed to memory, whenever the meaning of this celebrated letter, whenever its arguments directed against the Eutychian error, whenever even its words and, as it were, its very manner of expression are found in another work—especially one that treats of faith in some way or, above all, explains the creed itself and warns its hearers not to be carried away by erroneous heretics and teachers of deceit who teach contrary doctrines—we must have no doubt that the author of that work had in view the same Eutychian error that the holy pontiff refuted in that letter, even if neither Eutyches nor the Eutychians are mentioned there by name.

That the Explanation of the Creed for Those Preparing for Baptism is such a work—that it contains meanings expressed in Saint Leo’s letter against the error of Eutyches, that it employs the same arguments, [Col. 0900C] and that it even exhibits the same words and, as it were, the same manner of expression—the texts from both works, set before our eyes, will demonstrate with complete force, as I believe.

Let Saint Leo the holy pontiff, then, first be heard in the same letter to Flavian, which is numbered 28, chapter 4:

[Col. 0900D] “Each form acts in communion with the other in what properly belongs to it: the Word performing what belongs to the Word, and the flesh carrying out what belongs to the flesh. One of these shines forth in miracles; the other submits to insults . . . To hunger, thirst, grow weary, and sleep is evidently human. But to satisfy five thousand people with five loaves . . . to walk upon the back of the sea with feet that do not sink, and, after rebuking the waves, to lay low the surging waters in the storm: this is without doubt divine.

“Thus, to pass over many examples, it is not of the same nature to weep for a dead friend as an act of compassion and, removing the barrier of a four-day burial, to raise that same person alive at a command; or to hang upon wood and, when night has been changed into light, make all the elements tremble; or to be pierced with nails and open the gates of paradise to the faith of the thief. Likewise, it is not of the same nature to say, [29] ‘I and the Father are one,’ and to say, ‘The Father is greater than I.’ For although there is one person of God and man in the Lord Jesus Christ, one thing is the source of their common humiliation, another the source of their common glory. His humanity, by virtue of our nature, is less than the Father; his divinity, by virtue of the Father, is equal with the Father.”

Thus far Saint Leo.

Now observe blessed Nicetas in the Explanation of the Creed, chapter 4, immediately after those words cited above to demonstrate the danger threatening Christian faith from the error that he was attacking in his erroneous heretics. He explains himself in precisely the same sense as the holy pontiff when speaking of the error of Eutyches:

“In him [the Lord Jesus Christ],” says blessed Nicetas, [Col. 0901A] “both realities exist: man, in what was visible; God, in what was not visible. He ate as man; and he fed five thousand men with five loaves, because he was God. He slept as man in the boat, but he commanded the winds and the sea, because he was God. He fastened his hands to the cross as a man; but he granted paradise to the thief who confessed him, because he was God. Finally, he accepted death, laying down his body for a short time, as man; but he raised a man who had been dead four days from the tomb, because he was God.

“Christ must therefore be believed to be both God and man, because just as he is recognized as man through his sufferings, so God is revealed through his divine works. You therefore have grounds on which to reject the teachers of deceit.”

Thus far blessed Nicetas also.

Now, if we set aside the distinctive character of the style—which is not the same in the two writers, since Nicetas is simple and lucid, while Leo is weighty and splendid—and if we set aside a certain lengthiness of discourse apparent in Saint Leo’s text, since throughout that entire letter he was asserting the Catholic dogma concerning true humanity in Christ and overthrowing the error of Eutyches, whereas a more concise manner of expression suited Nicetas, [Col. 0901B] who was delivering to those preparing for baptism an explanation not of that one dogma but of the entire creed, and one intended to be readily received by the ears of his hearers rather than presented to the eyes of readers, as in a letter or another kind of treatise—a work which, when circumstances demand it, need not be ashamed to be somewhat long—if these differences are set aside as necessary variations arising from the diversity of style and manner of expression, who, I ask, cannot see that the meanings of the two texts are entirely conformed in their exposition of the dogma; that the same arguments, drawn from evangelical history, are employed to pierce the error opposed to the dogma; and that the words also, more than once, and as it were the very manner of expression, correspond completely in both?

The two texts just cited require no more minute discussion. I may not improperly call them parallel texts, and they plainly reveal themselves as parallel to the eyes of anyone who looks at them. From them we may conclude that, in chapter 4 of his Explanation of the Creed for Those Preparing for Baptism, blessed Nicetas had in view the same error of Eutyches that Saint Leo addressed [Col. 0901C] in his letter to Flavian, and that, consequently, by those erroneous heretics and those teachers of deceit whom he rebukes, he undoubtedly intended to indicate Eutyches and his followers themselves.

Nevertheless, it will not be tedious to illuminate the matter still more fully and to confirm it more forcefully. The same manner of confronting the Eutychian error that appears in our Nicetas—whether from the meaning and arguments presented in Saint Leo’s dogmatic letter to Flavian, or from its very manner of expression, and almost from its words themselves, as we have seen—shines forth also in other Fathers of the same age, concerning whom there is no controversy that they had the Eutychian error in view.

What follows from this? [30] It is thereby established more firmly that the bishops of the Church at that time generally drew from the source of that dogmatic letter what they handed on to the faithful in order to confirm the truth of Christ’s humanity as well as his divinity, and to refute the opposing error. It is therefore plainly the heresy of Eutyches that Nicetas was addressing [Col. 0901D] in the Explanation of the Creed when he admonished those preparing for baptism, since the same manner of expression appears in Leo and in Nicetas, and also in other Fathers whom no one doubts either to have lived into the time of Eutyches’ error or to have followed closely after it.

Let us now see.

Among others, Saint Maximus of Turin is at hand. As appears from his Life, composed for the latest Roman edition of his Works, he was still alive in the year 465; and in the year 451, at the Council of Milan, he had subscribed, together with the other bishops of that province, to Saint Leo’s letter to Flavian, as is clear from the synodal letter cited above of Eusebius, bishop of Milan, to the same holy pontiff, which, as stated, is found among his Letters, numbered 97.

Thus Saint Maximus, in Sermon 37, On the Solemnity of Easter 9, from the same latest Roman edition, says:

“Who could doubt that he is ineffably both the Son of God and the Son of Man, who was able both to undergo death and, having conquered death, to raise himself [Col. 0902A] from the tomb? For, having assumed flesh from the Virgin, lest we suffer any clouding of the faith of our confession, throughout the entire period of his preaching he revealed himself to be truly God and showed himself to be perfect man.

“He wept, as though mourning in our sorrow; yet, powerful in his own virtue, he had compassion on the darkness of the blind: for some he made eyes that had not yet been formed, for others he restored eyes that had been lost. Sailing with his disciples, he slept in the stern with the sleep of a man; but at the command of his majesty, conscious of itself he immediately restrained the mass of the rising waves and the threatening winds in serene calm.

“As a man of temporal life, he repeatedly testified that he would die; but as eternal God, sending back the vital spirit into bodies, he commanded the dead to return to the light. As the Son of Man he was subjected to the insults of blasphemers; but, so that mortal ignorance might learn the hidden truth of faith, the Father addressed him from heaven as his only Son.”

And in Sermon 102, On the Words of the Gospel, and so forth, he speaks as follows: [Col. 0902B]

“In this reading we must consider together, in one and the same Redeemer, the distinct operation of divinity and humanity, as well as the altogether detestable error of Eutyches, who dares to dogmatize that there is only one operation in Christ. For if anyone sees only one side, he who says that Christ was man only will deny the glory of the Creator, while he who says that he was God only will deny the mercy of the Redeemer.

“When the Lord has compassion on the crowd, lest it fail either through hunger or through the toil of a longer journey, let us recognize in this the feeling and compassion of human weakness; but when he satisfies four thousand men with seven loaves and a few fish, we believe this to be the work of divine power.”

Homily 49 contains the following:

“The Lord accomplished this kind of mystery in his flesh, so that, just as he is believed to be God through divine powers, so also he may be recognized as man through human weaknesses. Hence Christ, as man, hungers; and as God, feeds the hungry. Hence he grows weary from the journey; and grants the lame [Col. 0902C] the power to walk. Hence he loosens his eyes into tears; and wonderfully restores sight to the blind. Hence, as death approaches, he is troubled; and raises Lazarus, who had died, from the tomb.

“All these things, brothers, our Creator [31] and Redeemer does as God and man—not because such was a necessity imposed upon him at birth, but because he willed such a mystery to reign in heaven and on earth.”

Thus Saint Maximus of Turin concerning the Catholic dogma of true humanity in Christ, just as of his divinity, against the Eutychian error—and entirely in accord, indeed almost word for word, with both Saint Pope Leo and our blessed Nicetas.

After Maximus of Turin, it is also worthwhile to hear Saint Peter Chrysologus, whose celebrated letter to Eutyches himself is extant among the Letters of Saint Pope Leo, numbered 25, belonging to the beginning of the year 449, as the Ballerini brothers note in their preliminary admonition. In that letter he admonished Eutyches to attend obediently to what had been written by the most blessed pope of the Roman city, since blessed Peter, who both lives and presides [Col. 0902D] in his own see, provides the truth of faith to those who seek it.

Although the death of Chrysologus cannot be placed later than the year 451, as the distinguished Abbot Bacchinius observes in his Notes on the Life of the same man, given to us by Agnellus in his Pontifical Book, even within this very short period—approximately two years—from the emergence of the Eutychian error, which he himself had come to know, the most holy bishop of Ravenna did not cease, when occasion arose, to attack it in his sermons. He did so in such a way that it is plainly evident that he depicted that error in the very colors used by Saint Leo and our blessed Nicetas, and refuted it with a similar manner of expression and with arguments of the same weight and kind.

In Sermon 21 of the edition of Sebastian Paulus, Augsburg, 1758, in folio, he says:

“And they take him as he was in the boat. What does this mean? Christ is one way in heaven and another way in the boat; he is perceived one way in the majesty [Col. 0903A] of the Father and another way in the humility of man; one way as coeternal with the Father, another way as temporal, seen through the stages of our ages; one way he sleeps in our body, another way he remains awake in the holiness of his spirit.”

In Sermon 58 he says:

“He [Christ] undergoes burial, lest the impious should say that he did not approach death in order to conquer it, but simulated it in order to evade it . . . And if in his passion he proved that he possessed the true substance of our flesh, through the figure of three days he rises into the glory of the whole Trinity.”

In Sermon 60 we read:

“You say that Christ was buried, so that the confession of burial might prove that Christ possessed true flesh and that his death was not merely feigned; that he accepted death and conquered it; that he entered the underworld and returned; that he came under the jurisdiction of Tartarus and broke the laws of Tartarus—this is not weakness, but power.”

Finally, in Sermon 144 he writes:

“‘Behold, you will conceive in your womb.’ For the sake of reverence it would have been enough to say, ‘You will conceive.’ Why does he add ‘in your womb’? So that the conception might be a reality, not a figure; so that the birth might be an actual event, not an image; so that just as true God was born from true God, so from a true conception the reality of a human [Col. 0903B] body might be born.

“In Christ’s birth, brothers, the dishonor of the human body was removed, not its nature; the creature was not destroyed, but guilt was condemned. Therefore there is a heresy that falsely claims that Christ assumed an aerial body; it invents that he did not possess flesh, but merely simulated a man.”

These are the words of Saint Peter Chrysologus in his Sermons. Who, then, does not see that the Eutychian error is expressed here in the very words “simulation,” “figure,” and “image” of human flesh in Christ—words that Saint Leo used in so many of the texts cited above, and which fully correspond to the other expressions concerning a supposed incarnation and a phantom-like appearance intended to deceive human eyes [32], found in Nicetas? Who likewise does not understand that Saint Peter Chrysologus here adduces certain points, as the occasion of his discourse required, to assert human operations in Christ distinct from the divine—points that Pope Leo set forth in his letter to Flavian and that blessed Nicetas also reviewed in the Explanation of the Creed?

To add something further, after Saint Maximus of Turin and Saint Peter Chrysologus, let us also bring forward from the bishops of the Gallican Church some material relevant to our case. It will be permissible to add here [Col. 0903C] a few passages from Faustus of Riez and from Saint Avitus, bishop of Vienne.

The following passages belong to Faustus, who ascended the see of Riez shortly after the condemnation of the Eutychian error, around the year of Christ 455, as the Maurist editors of the Augustinian works note in connection with Sermon 176, included among the Augustinian appendices. Its title is “On the Ascension of the Lord I.” The following words are appended there, and are most improperly attributed to the holy bishop of Hippo, who had died long before and thus preceded the error under discussion.

Faustus says:

“Therefore, by every possible means, the poisons of the Eastern error must be detested—an error which, in impious novelty, presumes to assert that the Son of God and the Son of Man are of one nature . . . Let us therefore recognize in Christ a twofold and double substance: heavenly, from the Father; earthly, from his mother. It is easy to explain both in one and the same Redeemer by his own testimonies. [Col. 0903D]

“As man he said, ‘The Father is greater than I’; but, as God, the same man declared, ‘I and the Father are one.’ As man he said, ‘My soul is sorrowful even unto death’; but, as God, he spoke confidently: ‘I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again.’ As man he hung upon the cross; but, as God, he bestowed the heavenly kingdom.”

These are the words of Faustus of Riez. That he spoke in accord with the sense of Saint Leo the Great in the passage cited from his letter to Flavian is sufficiently clear, although in some other doctrine he did not think with complete orthodoxy, as is known. That matter, however, does not concern the issue now under discussion.

But Saint Avitus, somewhat later in age than Faustus—for he held the see of Vienne toward the end of the fifth century—attacked Eutyches’ error with a more expansive pen, both in Letter 3, entitled “To Gundobad, the King,” and also in other works, of which now only fragments survive; especially in those formerly bearing the title *Against the Phantom*. For Avitus called Eutychianism by this name, and likewise called Eutyches himself a preacher of phantoms. Here, then, are some passages from the bishop of Vienne, as printed in volume X, pages 709 and following, of the *Bibliotheca Veterum Patrum*, edited by Andrea Galland; first, excerpts from the same letter to Gundobad, which is wholly directed against the Eutychian error, an error which at the end he also calls a depravity that is still being inflamed by further growth, thereby showing the necessity, even in his own time, of fighting against it:

> “Now, moreover, since the passion that has taken place teaches us that the man was real—tormented by sufferings, reckoned among thieves, exhausted by punishment, and buried in a tomb—through all these things the reality of the assumed body contradicts the advocates of a phantom.”

Saint Avitus continues, touching upon the wickedness and ruin of the Eutychian error in a manner entirely consonant with both Saint Leo and blessed Nicetas, whom we compared with one another earlier on this very matter. He adds the following:

> “Since, moreover, we place all that is hoped for in the sole mystery of our redemption, and since our rising again is nothing other than that the Lord endured death, it is false that he saves us by his incarnation if it is also called into question that he assumed in the flesh what he had to endure for us.”

As for Leo’s principal text, parallel to Nicetas’ text concerning the true humanity in Christ just as much as his divinity—and to which, as I said, those Fathers who pursued Eutychianism after Leo appear to have looked, so that it may become still clearer that Nicetas fully understood the Eutychian error and opposed it with the very ideas and almost the very words of Saint Pope Leo—Saint Avitus explains himself as follows:

> “Here one must consider how much more deeply the Eutychians are plunged than the Bonosians’ abyss. The Bonosians merely deprive Christ of the honor of divinity; the Eutychians deprive him also of the reality of his body. Photinus mocks us for worshiping the person of a man; this one mocks us for worshiping a cloud. Or perhaps the beginning of this heretical illusion starts from the very swaddling-clothes of Christ’s sacred birth, so that it will likewise be false that he lay in cloths, appeared to the Magi, and cried in the cradle? I say nothing of the remaining developments of his growing age, in which, embracing both the divine and human nature, refreshment endured weariness, consolation poured out tears, light slept, bread hungered, and the fountain thirsted. I say nothing of that weeping which he displayed over the dead Lazarus, before he showed by the effect of raising him that God had first manifested the feeling of human condition.”

Nor should we omit, on this occasion, what we have seen Saint Leo say in more than one place about the Eutychians: namely, that by denying true humanity in Christ, they claimed that Truth itself had lied in assuming humanity and was concealing itself beneath the falsehood of a phantom. Our Nicetas likewise did not remain silent about his own erroneous heretics, whom he accused of saying concerning Christ that what appeared had not truly existed, but that he had deceived human eyes. In this sense Avitus himself wrote most excellently:

> “Consider to what degree this pertains to an insult against divinity, if the teacher of truth, who even forbids us falsehoods in words, is himself believed to have been able to lie in deeds. For it would unquestionably be a kind of falsehood if he wished his followers to believe him to be what he was not, and if Christ were thought to have done what a Christian is not permitted to do.”

Thus far Saint Avitus in that Letter 3 to King Gundobad. I have judged that what follows should be added, not because I think anything is lacking for fully grasping Saint Avitus’ mind concerning our subject and the Eutychian error attacked by him in the same manner in which it was pressed by Saint Pope Leo, but because his position is explained there still more fully, and because these passages are properly taken from the surviving fragments of his books *Against the Phantom*, that is, against the Eutychian error. He says:

> “Who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh.”

He asserted, in a full description, a twofold nature: one in which, according to divinity, he is the maker of all things, and another in which he was made from the seed of David according to the flesh. In neither substance can any suspicion of a phantom be found. For just as the divinity that descended from heaven was invisible in itself, so the reality of Christ’s flesh, descending from David’s stock, could possess nothing deceptive. This reality is traced not only through his forefathers back to David, but through David himself back to Adam, with the names of his ancestors expressly set out. Therefore the Apostle says that he is from the seed of David according to the flesh, in order to declare him consubstantial with his mother, from whom he certainly also received death; for a phantom can neither be born nor die, but its beginning is to deceive, and its end to vanish into nothing.

This is Saint Avitus of Vienne in the fragments, and so forth, number 1, from the same volume X of Galland’s *Bibliotheca*, page 749.

It must therefore now be concluded that our Nicetas, the bishop of the city of Romatiana mentioned by Gennadius, in his *Explanation of the Creed*, chapter 4, where he teaches his catechumens the catholic doctrine that Christ possesses humanity just as he possesses divinity, and where he refutes those erroneous heretics and teachers of deceit who, as he said, declared Christ to have been incarnate not truly but apparently—and therefore claimed that the Lord’s incarnation took place in a phantom, because what appeared had not truly existed but had deceived human eyes—must, I say, be understood not to have had in mind those ancient heretics who preceded Eutyches in their inventions and phantoms, but Eutyches himself and his followers.

For he explains that error throughout in precisely the manner and in the very forms in which we find it in Saint Leo the Great in the many letters he issued to overthrow it, both in the East, where it had erupted, and in the regions of the West, where it was attempting to gain supporters. And because the same Nicetas uses against that error the same ideas and arguments, indeed almost the same words, with which the holy pontiff himself proceeded in his celebrated doctrinal letter to Flavian—a letter that was circulated throughout the catholic world and universally regarded as a rule of faith even before the general Council of Chalcedon, where Eutyches’ error finally received its deathblow—and because, moreover, the very same method of confronting the growing error that appears in Nicetas is also commonly evident, from that letter to Flavian or from its ideas, arguments, and almost its very words, in Fathers who were either contemporaries of Eutyches or flourished not long after him, and who are known actually to have attacked the Eutychian error:

What, then, follows after this lengthy investigation concerning the true and proper Eutychian error attacked by our Nicetas in his *Explanation of the Creed*? Clearly, this follows: that this Nicetas, the author of the *Explanation of the Creed*, cannot be earlier than the Eutychian error. And if this Nicetas cannot be earlier than the Eutychian error, it is now clear that the bishop of the city of Romatiana, Niceas or Nicetas mentioned by Gennadius and author of the *Explanation of the Creed*, is not that Dacian Niceas or Nicetas who was a friend of Saint Paulinus of Nola and celebrated in his praises. This is the proposition of the present third chapter, which I have undertaken to maintain against the opinion of the most distinguished Zabei.

For that Dacian Nicetas, the friend of Paulinus of Nola and celebrated in his praises, unquestionably preceded the Eutychian error, which first erupted only after the Dacian Nicetas had long been dead. We must therefore now move from the Eutychian error to a careful investigation of the age of this Dacian Nicetas, who was joined to Paulinus of Nola by friendship. This was my second aim at the beginning of this chapter, and it is the only point remaining for completing the matter now under discussion.

The Dacian Nicetas, then, was no longer alive when the Eutychian heresy arose. This heresy originated in the East around the year of the Lord 448, under Eutyches the archimandrite, already an old man, as is evident from several passages in the Letters of Saint Leo the Great. In that same year, at a gathering of bishops and abbots held at Constantinople by Flavian, bishop of that imperial city, Eutyches was first accused by Eusebius, bishop of Dorylaeum and formerly his friend, who had also warned him in vain, of spreading through the monasteries a new doctrine that he had published in a book. Eutyches was convicted of error, condemned as obstinate in that error, and deprived of the honor of the priesthood.

In the following year, 449, Saint Pope Leo sent his celebrated letter to Flavian against the Eutychian error. In it he set forth with such clarity the catholic doctrine concerning the Lord’s incarnation and the two natures in Christ, and so vigorously overthrew Eutyches’ error. Finally, in 451, the ecumenical Council of Chalcedon was held. There, after everything done through violence and fraud by Eutyches’ supporters and patrons at the Robber Council of Ephesus had been rescinded, that letter of Saint Pope Leo to Flavian—already circulated throughout the world, everywhere received with reverence, and regarded as a kind of rule of faith against the Eutychian error—was acclaimed by the Fathers as though it had been spoken from the mouth of Peter.

We have no certain information concerning the year of Nicetas the Dacian’s death. But the Dacian Nicetas unquestionably flourished in the time of Paulinus of Nola, with whom he was also extremely close, and whom he visited twice by traveling from Dacia to Nola, as is evident from Paulinus’ writings.

Paulinus of Nola, moreover, departed to heaven in the year 431, at the age of seventy-eight. He had been a presbyter at Nola for several years before his episcopate and had been appointed to that episcopal see around the year 409, as the learned editors of his works have observed. We may reasonably infer from several of Paulinus’ own expressions concerning him that this Dacian Nicetas was older than Paulinus.

For Paulinus repeatedly calls him both his father and his teacher, and in Poem 26, on Saint Felix, *Natale* 9, composed on the occasion of Nicetas’ second arrival at Nola around the year 402, when Paulinus was then approximately forty-nine, he calls himself not only, out of humility, poor and foolish, but also, in comparison with Nicetas, a little child. Other passages establish the same point even more clearly.

Four years earlier, namely in 398, Nicetas had first arrived at Nola, when Paulinus was forty-five. Paulinus’ Poem 17, addressed to Nicetas on his return to Dacia, is extant; more was said about it in the preceding chapter. Learned scholars consider that it refers to his return after his first visit, not after his second.

In this poem Paulinus pursues, in a more expansive style, Nicetas’ praises, which rested chiefly on the fact that he himself had first led the peoples of the Bessi, the Getae, and the Scythians, as well as both Dacias—the Ripensian and the Mediterranean—to the sheepfolds of the Lord, and had transformed the savage customs of those peoples into the gentle character of Christians. It is best now to hear Paulinus himself:

> O land, with what joys will it then resound,  
> where you teach fierce peoples  
> to submit their stiff necks to gentle Christ!
>
> And wherever Boreas binds the rivers  
> with dense frost on the Rhipaean shores,  
> there you dissolve rigid minds  
> with heavenly fire.
>
> For although hard in lands and hearts,  
> and their Bessi harder than their own snow,  
> now, made sheep under your leadership,  
> they gather into the hall of peace.
>
> Those necks which, always unconquered in war,  
> refused to submit to servitude,  
> now, subdued beneath the yoke of the true Lord,  
> rejoice to bow down . . .
>
> O changes of things! O form well transformed!  
> Mountains formerly inaccessible and bloodstained  
> now shelter robbers transformed into monks,  
> pupils of peace . . .
>
> Where once the custom of wild beasts prevailed,  
> now the practice of angels flourishes;  
> and the righteous man dwells in the caves  
> where the robber himself once lived . . .
>
> Hail, Nicetas, good servant of Christ,  
> who grants you to turn stones into stars  
> and to build sacred temples  
> from living rocks . . .
>
> The whole region of the North calls you father;  
> at your words the Scythian is softened,  
> and the savage, divided against himself,  
> lays down his heart under your instruction.
>
> The Getae run to you, and both Dacias:  
> both he who inhabits the middle of the land  
> and he, the cap-wearing inhabitant of a bank rich in many oxen,  
> dwells beside the riverbank . . .
>
> Through you, in the silent region of the world,  
> barbarians learn to make Christ resound  
> with a Roman heart  
> and to live the peaceful life of chastity.
>
> Thus the wolf is gentle in your fold;  
> the calf feeds peaceably beside the lion;  
> the little one, drawn from savage caves,  
> plays with the serpent.

From these verses it is evident what sort of man that Dacian Nicetas was, of whom Paulinus sings so greatly. It is also evident how much he had already accomplished in those regions in the year 398, when Paulinus was forty-five: through Nicetas’ care, those lands had been recalled from barbarism and had progressed so far in Christian instruction and worship that they scarcely envied anything in the Christian regions long since cultivated elsewhere.

If there were gatherings of monks in the mountains, cells of solitaries in caves, and everywhere the practices of angels, then Christian religion must certainly already have been established everywhere at that time through Nicetas’ apostolate in barbarous Dacia beyond the Danube. Sacred buildings had already been erected everywhere, and priests and ministers of that religion had everywhere been instituted through his work. Thus, without any harm to that new flock, he was able to undertake a long journey, and not long afterward to make the journey again, in order to visit Paulinus and venerate the tomb of Saint Felix of Nola.

To achieve such great things in those regions—regions made extraordinarily difficult by their extent, the multitude of their peoples, the harshness of the climate, the savagery of their customs, and the unfamiliarity of the places—who does not see that Nicetas must already have spent the greater part of his life? Therefore, when Paulinus was in his forty-fifth year at the time of Nicetas’ first arrival, we rightly infer that Nicetas himself was older, having already become renowned among those barbarous peoples for such great apostolic merits.

Paulinus himself also suggests in the same poem, not obscurely, that his guest and friend was older. For, in poetic fashion, after accompanying him through so many labors and merits toward the reward of the heavenly kingdom, he represents him—clearly with the ordinary course of life in view—as destined to precede Paulinus himself in death, and therefore asks him to obtain divine assistance for him, out of regard for a friendship that no force can break. He continues:

> Having stored up these riches for the everlasting Lord,  
> and with these profits having increased the sacred talent,  
> you will hear: “Enter gladly into the joys  
> of the everlasting Lord.”
>
> When the blessed house, filled with a great company  
> of holy brothers in their choirs,  
> receives you, I beg you:  
> keep us hidden, dear through the affection of your heart.
>
> For thanks be to God that he bound us to you  
> by so great a love through hidden bonds,  
> so that no force may be able  
> to break the inward chain.

Since Paulinus of Nola died, as we indicated above, in the year 431, not yet eighty and two years short of that age, we may infer with no slight probability from these statements that the Dacian Nicetas had been called to heaven at least a decade earlier, around the year of Christ 420. This is so even if we grant that he reached the age of eighty—something that does not seem easy to admit in an apostolic man who was the father of so many peoples, was worn down by innumerable labors, and was presumably weakened by long journeys.

Since, then, the life of the Dacian Nicetas did not extend beyond the year 420, when the Eutychian heresy was still nearly thirty years away from its origin; and since the Eutychian heresy is so clearly indicated—and even attacked—in the *Explanation of the Creed* by Niceas or Nicetas, bishop of the city of Romatiana and mentioned by Gennadius, as we have seen; and since it is attacked with the same ideas and arguments, indeed almost the very words, with which it was attacked and utterly overthrown by Saint Leo the Great with such authority and eloquence in his letter to Flavian, written in 449, and with which it was likewise commonly attacked in the same and the following age by the bishops of the Church, among whom Leo’s letter was reverently regarded as a rule of faith—it is therefore clear, I say confidently, that the Dacian Nicetas is not the author of the little work *Explanation of the Creed* addressed to the catechumens. Consequently, the Niceas or Nicetas of the city of Romatiana mentioned by Gennadius, and the author of the *Explanation of the Creed*, is not that Dacian Niceas or Nicetas, the friend of Saint Paulinus of Nola and celebrated in his praises. This was the proposition of the present third chapter.

Before proceeding, however, it is useful to anticipate one or two difficulties that might be raised, and that may perhaps appear to someone to carry some force against what has been said.

Let the two texts quoted from Saint Leo the Great and blessed Nicetas be, someone might say, truly parallel, so that they lend weight and strength to our proposition. Let it be that one of these two writers received from the other the ideas and arguments, as well as the very words, with which they attacked the error against which both were fighting. What, then, assures us that blessed Nicetas drew from Saint Leo the Great’s letter to Flavian what he wrote in chapter 4 of his *Explanation of the Creed* against those erroneous heretics whom he names, as we have tried to prove? Why could it not instead be that Saint Leo the Great took his ideas from a pre-existing work of blessed Nicetas, who therefore really was that Dacian bishop, the friend of Saint Paulinus of Nola and also his senior in age, and who consequently attacked not Eutyches but Eutyches’ ancient predecessors and teachers in the words quoted from the *Explanation of the Creed*, as the distinguished Zabei maintains? Saint Leo might then have used those words quite appropriately to pierce the error of those ancient heretics, revived in his own age by Eutyches.

I can meet this difficulty appropriately by saying, first, that it is certain that Saint Leo the Great attacked Eutyches’ error in his letter to Flavian. It is equally certain that the ideas, arguments, and almost the very words of our Nicetas correspond completely with the ideas, arguments, and almost the words of Saint Leo, both in that letter and in other passages where he explains and overturns the Eutychian error, as has already been demonstrated at length.
