There can therefore be no doubt that Nicetas, together with Saint Leo, had the Eutychian error in view, since he expresses and overturns it with him so perfectly. Consequently, it was not Saint Leo who drew from Nicetas, but Nicetas who took from Saint Leo what he wrote. Saint Leo was the first person in the West to attack and pierce the Eutychian error, immediately after its emergence from Eutyches, already an old man.

Second, it should not readily be supposed that Saint Leo copied virtually word for word from someone else’s writings what he composed in that letter to Flavian; no example of this kind is found elsewhere in Saint Leo’s other writings. By contrast, whoever Nicetas may have been—if he was someone later than the Dacian whom we have discussed—he would have served both himself and the subject he was presenting very well if we say that he took almost word for word from the Roman pontiff’s letter to Flavian what he used to attack the error against which he was teaching his catechumens to guard. For that letter was well known and celebrated throughout the Christian world and was regarded in the universal Church as a rule of faith in setting forth the mystery of the incarnation, as we have already seen.

Saint Leo may perhaps have preferred to use the same ideas, arguments, and almost the same words that an earlier writer had used, in order to confirm the doctrine he defended in that letter. But would the holy pontiff have remained silent about the writer’s name? Certainly not. It was in the interest of the Christian world to show that the doctrine he set forth in that letter was the doctrine of the Fathers, and that Eutyches’ fabrication, which he refuted there, was far removed from the tradition of the Fathers. It was therefore his duty to identify those whose doctrine and almost whose very words he was repeating.

Yet perhaps Saint Leo remained silent about Nicetas’ name in the text of that letter so that, in a matter where either several Fathers had to be mentioned in order for the tradition to appear, or certainly none, he would not mention Nicetas alone. But would he have omitted Nicetas’ text from the collection of testimonies that the holy pontiff sent through his legates to the East after the Council of Ephesus and before the Council of Chalcedon, in order to show that the doctrine of his letter to Flavian agreed with the doctrine of Latin and Greek Fathers?

Later he sent this collection, enlarged, to Leo Augustus, together with his own special letter to him, numbered 165, so that the catholic faith confirmed at Chalcedon would not be endangered by fresh machinations of the heretics after Marcian, the emperor and defender of the faith, had died. Would he, I say, have omitted from this collection the text of Nicetas, so outstanding and so clear—indeed, I would say plainly clearer than all the others—and failed to insert it to display the tradition of the Fathers, if he had truly benefited from this text of Nicetas in his letter to Flavian?

Let the testimonies of the Fathers be consulted that the holy pontiff collected and that may be read in the editions of the councils, in the second act of the Council of Chalcedon after the letter to Flavian, and also in fuller form after the other letter already cited, to Leo Augustus, in the edition of the works of the holy pontiff by the Ballerini brothers. The preliminary remarks to this same letter and to the preceding Letter 28, to Flavian, may also be read concerning these testimonies.

In this series of testimonies we shall see many passages collected by the holy pontiff from Hilary, Ambrose, and Augustine among the Latin Fathers, and many also from Athanasius, Chrysostom, Gregory of Nazianzus, Basil, Theophilus, and Cyril of Alexandria among the Greek Fathers. They were collected for the purpose of making it clear to everyone that we agree with the preaching of the venerable Fathers, that we preach nothing other than what our holy Fathers taught throughout the world, and that no one differs from them except the impious heretics alone, as the same holy pontiff professed in chapter 10 of that letter to Leo Augustus.

Saint Leo would certainly not have omitted the testimony of our Nicetas from these testimonies of the Fathers if that testimony had existed at the time, and much less if he himself had used it in his letter to Flavian.

Therefore Saint Leo did not draw from an earlier work of Saint Nicetas, or from Nicetas’ statements directed against the predecessors and teachers of Eutyches. Rather, Saint Nicetas took from Saint Leo’s letter both the ideas and arguments, and almost the very words, with which he attacked the same error of Eutyches that Saint Leo had overthrown.

The holy pontiff himself, therefore, who included nothing at all from our Nicetas among the testimonies of the Fathers that he collected to confirm his own doctrine, is the one who truly assures us that he took nothing in his letter to Flavian from Nicetas, bishop of the Dacians and friend of Saint Paulinus of Nola. Rather, he assures us that another Nicetas, later than the Dacian, drew from that letter the material with which he most securely set forth and most invincibly defended catholic doctrine in his own ideas and almost his own words.

Nor should anyone perhaps add that Nicetas ought at least to have mentioned Saint Leo’s letter in his *Explanation*, if he had truly taken from that letter what he said against those whom he calls erroneous heretics.

For the *Explanation of the Creed* of our blessed Nicetas, addressed to catechumens, is of such a character—both by its nature and because of the audience of catechumens for whom it was delivered—that it admits a simple exposition and even elucidation of doctrine according to the order of the articles of which the Creed consists. It should not be stuffed with references to any work or author, except the book of sacred Scripture, since the Apostles’ Creed is, in the principal matters of faith, a kind of abridgment, as all the Fathers say, and as Nicetas himself says in chapter 15 of the same *Explanation*, in accordance with the common judgment of the Fathers.

It was therefore not appropriate to burden the minds of the catechumens with indications of any author or work. It was enough for them simply to understand the divine oracles and the Gospel testimonies relevant to this matter, so that they might attain catholic truth and protect themselves against the snares of the heretics.

As for those who would read Nicetas’ *Explanation*, what need was there to identify this passage from Saint Pope Leo’s letter to Flavian if, as has been said, that letter had spread throughout the world, was regarded by all Catholics as a rule of faith, and was then on everyone’s lips? Saint Leo’s ideas from the letter to Flavian would sufficiently identify themselves among Catholics wherever they were expressed, without the author’s name needing to be supplied.

Moreover, the entire authority of Saint Pope Leo in that passage from the letter to Flavian rests upon the facts and texts of Gospel history that he cites and brings together, in order to establish the two natures in Christ and to distinguish the different operations in him according to the difference between the two natures. It was therefore less necessary for Saint Leo to be mentioned by Nicetas, since it was not so much Saint Leo’s authority as the authority of the Gospel, presented by Saint Leo and taken up by Nicetas into his own discourse, that settled the matter against Eutyches.

Finally, Saint Leo himself, who composed that celebrated letter to Flavian against Eutyches’ blasphemies, and who boasted that he was preaching in it the faith of the earlier Fathers—which of the Fathers did he name there individually, although he had before his eyes their testimonies, deliberately collected and made public, as we have seen, and although he unquestionably drew in that letter from their ideas and from arguments taken by them from the Gospel?

But we must now proceed to the second difficulty, which may perhaps appear to someone to have greater force. If Nicetas truly intended, in chapter 4 of the *Explanation of the Creed*, to attack Eutyches’ error and to identify him and his followers by the words “erroneous heretics,” someone may object, why did he never call Eutyches himself or the Eutychians by their proper name? Indeed, when in chapter 10 of the *Explanation* he names the pseudo-churches of various heretics that a Christian must avoid—namely, those of the Manichaeans, Cataphrygians, and Marcionists—why did he entirely omit the pseudo-church of the Eutychians? Surely it ought especially at that time to have been explicitly named, so that Christian catechumens might be warned above all against it and might not allow themselves to be deceived by Eutyches’ followers, who were attempting to spread their poison under the appearance of piety even after the supreme blow by which they had been struck at the Council of Chalcedon.

As for the first point: what is surprising if Nicetas did not identify Eutyches and the Eutychians by their proper names in chapter 4 of his *Explanation* while attacking their error? The matter concerned the error, not the author of the error or his followers, who were already sufficiently well known at that time because their error had stirred up disturbances in the Church.

Since this error had recently erupted and Eutyches’ name was already known everywhere, it was certainly unnecessary for Nicetas to announce to the catechumens the name of the author of an error that already revealed itself through the error he was indicating.

Nicetas also spoke in his *Explanation* about other errors that preceded the Eutychian error—for example, the error of the Arians against the Son of God and that of the Macedonians against the Holy Spirit, in chapter 9, where he says:

> “If any heretic, under the Christian name, presents Christ to you as a creature, or persuades you that the Holy Spirit is alien to the glory of the Father and the Son, let him be to you as a heathen and a publican, because he leads you into idolatry by persuading you to worship a creature.”

But where did Nicetas, either here or elsewhere in his *Explanation*, name Arius or Macedonius, or the Arians or Macedonians? There is therefore no reason to claim that Nicetas did not have the Eutychian error in view in chapter 4 of the *Explanation* merely because he did not identify Eutyches or the Eutychians by their proper name.

But why did he at least not name the pseudo-church of the Eutychians in chapter 10, where he expressly mentioned the other three pseudo-churches? The answer to this second part of the difficulty is easy.

In the age of Saint Leo the Great, and likewise in the time of our Nicetas of Aquileia, the disciples of Eutyches had not yet established for themselves particular societies and churches distinct from the Catholics. Rather, scattered here and there in the Catholic churches themselves and living among Catholics, they spread their error while always wishing to appear Catholic.

There was therefore no reason for Nicetas to mention the pseudo-church of the Eutychians, as he mentioned the pseudo-churches of the Manichaeans, Cataphrygians, and Marcionists—ancient heretics who had long since defected from the catholic fellowship. The Eutychians had only recently arisen and had not yet coalesced into a separate sect, distinct from the catholic flock and devoted to its own separate rites.

Saint Leo himself supplies us with this answer in Letter 157, which he wrote in 457 to Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople. Someone in Anatolius’ clergy, a presbyter named Atticus, was following and teaching the doctrine of Eutyches. Leo writes:

> “I recall having written to Your Charity some time ago that you should allow no one in the clergy of your Church to agree with the Eutychian heresy, since danger to the head is involved if anything diseased is found in the members. But since this has not yet been remedied by any correction, and since I learn that your presbyter Atticus has advanced to such insolence that he dares to dispute in the Church against the catholic faith and the Council of Chalcedon, I am compelled to complain more vigorously about your dissimulation . . .  
>
> “And therefore I warn you more sternly and declare that no further concealment is permissible if you decide to retain that pestilential man in your communion. We would prefer, if possible, that he be corrected rather than perish. If he wishes to appear corrected and to remain in ecclesiastical fellowship, then, from that place where he argued at length against the catholic faith, let him openly become a preacher of that very faith, and let him condemn, by a public profession before the Christian people, every element of Eutychian doctrine that he previously failed to condemn. Otherwise, as I have said, this concealment will greatly stain you, if either this highly culpable man or Andrew, his companion in that impiety, is neither corrected nor expelled.”

The Eutychians were therefore still mixed with the Catholics at that time, and did not constitute another particular Church or society from which Catholics ought to have recoiled, and from which our Nicetas would have taught his catechumens to recoil after receiving baptism.

If this particular society and pseudo-church of the Eutychians had already existed at that time, there would have been no reason for the presbyter Atticus to belong to the Constantinopolitan clergy. He would already have gone with Andrew, his companion, to their pseudo-church or society and would have celebrated the rites separately from the Catholics. In that case, as one who was outside, there would have been no reason for Bishop Anatolius to be accused by Saint Leo of dissimulation on his account.

But if this particular Eutychian society or pseudo-church had no place in the eastern regions, or even in the city of Constantinople, from which the Eutychian error had erupted, it certainly had even less of a presence in the West and in the regions of Italy. There was therefore still less reason for Nicetas of Aquileia to mention this society of heretics as a pseudo-church.

It should also be added that Saint Leo, in the following year, 458, wrote in Letter 161 to the presbyters, deacons, and clergy of that same Church of Constantinople:

> “Do not allow anyone infected with Nestorian or Eutychian perversity to associate with you.”

Thus they were attempting to maintain fellowship with the Catholics, and therefore had not yet formed any society or pseudo-church of their own. Here we must also observe that not only the recently arisen Eutychians, but even the Nestorians, who had preceded them by approximately twenty years, were not yet at that time so united in a society and so distinct from the catholic Church in a separate communion as to form a church or pseudo-church different from the catholic one, from which the faithful would consequently have had to be warned to protect themselves.

And indeed, either none or almost none of the heretics who assailed and disturbed the Church by their errors effected a separation from it either from the very beginning of their errors or during the first period, so to speak, of their revolt, in order to establish for themselves a particular church separate from the Catholic Church—even though, by a sentence of anathema issued either in provincial or in general councils, they might be excluded from communion with the Catholic faithful and from entry into the sacred buildings. For heretics have always shuddered at the establishment of another body distinct from Catholic communion, as though it were an absolute condemnation of their impiety; and meanwhile they left no stone unturned to have the sentences passed against them amended or revoked. Only at length, when their impiety had been hardened by the passage of time, all shame had been lost, and—usually—the influence of deceived royal authority had also intervened, did they reach the point of openly separating from the Catholics, of assembling for divine worship apart, and of constituting another church, as it were, in the likeness of that from which they had defected.

Let the history of the Arian heresy and of the Arian Pseudo-Church serve as an example for all. From the origin of this most dreadful plague until the Council of Nicaea, and from the Council of Nicaea until the Council of Sardica, which was held in 347, the Arians had never formed among themselves any particular Pseudo-Church separated from the Catholic Church. On the contrary, they always sought union with the Catholics, by their deceitful interpretation of their error in a Catholic sense and by making numerous crafty professions of faith to deceive the simple, as is well known.

For this reason that most pious Augustus Constantine 42, who enacted a law against all sects of heretics and schismatics—as Eusebius mentions in *The Life of Constantine*, Book III, chapters 64 and following—does indeed mention the Novatians, Valentinians, Marcionites, Paulianists, and Cataphrygians, who were perhaps at that time the principal groups raging in the East against the Catholic Church; but he makes no mention whatsoever of the Arians. This can have had no other reason than that the Arians, although even then strong in numbers, boldness, and influence, nevertheless continued to enter Catholic sacred buildings while claiming Catholic unity and feigning the faith, and took the greatest care not to establish a body bearing the name of the condemned author of their error, as Sozomen also observes in *Ecclesiastical History*, Book II, chapter 32.

For this reason, too, Pope Julius, who around the year 341 wrote to the Eastern bishops of the Eusebian faction—as reported by Saint Athanasius, *Apology against the Arians*, no. 21—treats them in his letter as brothers and addresses them as members of Catholic communion. This shows that, according to Socrates himself, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book II, chapter 18, the Arians had not yet at that time established another church for themselves, separate from the Catholic Church.

Accordingly, as Socrates states in the same work, chapter 22, and Sozomen, Book III, chapter 13, open separation between the Arians and the Catholics occurred only after the Council of Sardica and after the conciliabulum of Philippopolis—that is, after the year 347. From this separation the Pseudo-Church of the Arians arose, and it spread so widely in the East, especially through the favor of the two Augusti Constantius and Valens, and for a long time also prevailed extensively in the Western regions, chiefly through the agency of the barbarians who, after the fall of the Roman Empire, gained power in the West while infected with this doctrine.

The earliest mention, perhaps, of separate sacred buildings in which the Arians met apart from the Catholics is found in the *Ecclesiastical History* of Socrates, Book II, chapter 23; of Sozomen, Book III, chapter 20; and of Theodoret, Book II, chapter 12. There it is related that in the year 349 the emperor Constantius, through the intervention of Constans—who had pleaded with his brother on Athanasius’s behalf—requested from the great Athanasius, when he was returning from exile to his Alexandrian see, one of the sacred buildings in Alexandria for his Arians, where they might hold their sacred assemblies apart from the Catholics. Yet, through Athanasius’s remarkable skill, this did not turn out according to his wishes.

Therefore, the objection that someone might raise against what we have established concerning the Eutychian error indicated and attacked by our Nicetas in chapter 4 of his *Explanation of the Creed*—namely, that in chapter 10 he said nothing about the Pseudo-Church of the Eutychians, although he mentioned the Pseudo-Churches of other heretics—has no force whatsoever. Let us now proceed to the remaining matters.

## APPENDIX TO CHAPTER THREE

We have thus far shown, on the basis of the Eutychian error which Niceas or Nicetas, bishop of the city of Romatiana, mentioned by Gennadius, attacks in this work, that he is not the same Niceas or Nicetas the Dacian who was a friend of Saint Paulinus, bishop of Nola, and celebrated by him in his praises. In this work, the author of the little book *On the Creed for the Competentes* attacks the Eutychian error in a manner corresponding to the teaching of Saint Leo the Great and of others of his own and the following age; whereas that Dacian Nicetas, who died nearly thirty years before the rise of the Eutychian 43 error, could not have attacked it in precisely this way.

We therefore consider the matter settled in such a way that it requires no support from any further proof. Nevertheless, since other considerations also present themselves which, according to the principles of critics, are especially useful for attaining the truth when the question concerns authors bearing the same name and determining which works belong to which of them, we must linger here somewhat, so that we may omit nothing that can not only confirm our case more and more, but also clarify it.

What has been said thus far concerns the period in which that Dacian Nicetas flourished, so that he simply cannot be the same as Nicetas, bishop of the city of Romatiana, whom we know to have transmitted in his *Explanation of the Creed* matters that did not at all belong to the age of the Dacian Nicetas.

What must now be added concerns the place in which that Dacian Nicetas exercised his episcopate. Thus certain things are found in the statements of the Romatian Nicetas which would in no way suit Nicetas the Dacian, the friend of Saint Paulinus of Nola, or the Dacian peoples living beyond the Danube, where we have shown that this Nicetas exercised his episcopate.

The evidence to be brought forward here has been drawn not only from the *Explanation of the Creed*, but also from one of the fragments of the Vienna manuscript which we publish after the little works. From it we shall also draw certain other points which will more strongly confirm our argument based on location and will prepare the way for what we shall say in the following fourth chapter, where we shall openly prove that Niceas or Nicetas, bishop of the city of Romatiana, was Niceas or Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia.

Niceas or Nicetas, bishop of the city of Romatiana, says the following in chapter 1 of his *Explanation of the Creed for the Competentes*:

> “Whoever believes in Christ . . . renounces the enemy and his angels . . . Then also his evil works: cults and idols, lots and auguries, entertainments and theaters, fornications and drunkenness, dances and lies.”

But in the third of the *Fragments* he has the following similar passage, explained somewhat more fully:

> “For one does not come to confession before the devil has first been renounced . . . Therefore one must first repudiate diabolical vanity . . . Then one renounces his wicked works—that is, cults and idols; lots and auguries; entertainments and theaters;  [Col. 0914A] thefts and frauds; murders and fornications; pride and boasting; anger and avarice; banquets and drunkenness; dances and lies; and evils of this kind.”

Saint Nicetas said these things to remind his faithful what the renunciation meant and how broadly that renunciation extended which, according to the most ancient custom of the Church, is required of those who desire to be received into the bosom of the Church through baptism and who are about to make their profession of faith immediately before being washed in the saving waters.

Here everyone can see that in both passages the holy bishop is not reciting the simple formula of the Church by which renunciation was required of those seeking baptism, but rather presenting an explanation of that formula, so that they might understand that its force extended to every manner of life and that, under the single expression “the works of the devil,” everything opposed to the Christian name was included.

In the early centuries of the Church, the custom of renunciation was indeed the same throughout the Church, but the formula itself was not identical everywhere—that is, it was not expressed everywhere in the same words.

The distinguished Joseph Vicecomes, who in his learned work *On the Ancient Rites and Ceremonies of Baptism*, Book II, chapter 20, discusses the forms of renunciation and shows that the ancient form of renunciation agreed with ours, adduces much evidence from the Fathers of the Church. Although the meaning of renunciation is everywhere the same, the words nevertheless do not everywhere appear identical.

Joseph Catalanus did the same thing and for the same purpose in his *Commentaries on the Roman Ritual*, volume I, title 2, chapter 2, § 13. The devil’s *pompae*, which had to be renounced, are expressed in the ancient formulas of renunciation, although not always and everywhere, nevertheless very frequently. There is no doubt that this renunciation derived its origin from the *pompa* in the proper sense, which, while the worship of idols prevailed in the Roman Empire, constituted a major, indeed the principal, part of the circus.

Tertullian speaks of this in *On the Spectacles*, chapter 7:

> “But the display of the circus is somewhat more elaborate; the name *pompa*, in its proper sense, precedes it.”

He continues by explaining what this procession was:

> “What it consists of is shown by the series of images, the procession of statues, the chariots, the sacred platforms, the carriages, the seats, the crowns, and the spoils; how many sacrifices precede, intervene, and follow; how many guilds, priesthoods, and offices are set in motion—all this is known by the people of that city in which the assembly of demons has taken its seat.”

It is therefore established that the *pompa*, in the true and proper ancient sense, was the solemn procession of images which, for the sake of honoring them, was conducted along the public streets of the City as far as the circus before the circus games were held. On this point Onuphrius Panvinius also gives a full account in *On the Circus Games*, Book II, chapter 2.

Hence, in those first centuries of the Church when the worship of idols prevailed, nothing was more solemn in Christian initiation than to add to the renunciation of the devil, his angels, and his works a renunciation of the *pompa*—that is, of the procession of images properly so called which was customary at the circus and through which the greatest religious honor was paid to the pagan divinities.

Origenes must certainly be understood as referring to this circus procession in homily 10 on the Book of Numbers, where he says:

> “Let every believer remember, when he first came to the waters of baptism, when he received the first seals and approached the saving font, what words he then used there and what declaration he made to the devil: namely, that he would not use his *pompae* or his works.”

Tertullian must likewise be understood as referring to this same circus procession when, in *On the Soldier’s Crown*, chapter 3, he says:

> “When we are about to enter the water, and indeed somewhat earlier in the Church, under the hand of the bishop, we testify that we renounce the devil, the Procession, and his angels.”

And in *On the Spectacles*, chapter 4:

> “When we enter the Christian water and profess the Christian faith in the words of its law, we testify with our mouths that we have renounced the devil, the Procession, and his angels.”

The circus procession, however, ceased after the beginning of the fourth century, as the aforementioned Panvinius observes in the cited Book II of *On the Circus Games*, chapter 18:

> “For Constantine,” he says, “having been initiated into the sacred rites of the Christians, weakened as far as he could, and as the circumstances of the time allowed, around the year of Christ 325, the ancient superstition which was chiefly preserved by this procession of supplications.”

Nevertheless, the renunciation of the devil’s *pompa*, or *pompae*, continued in Christian initiation. What, then, was understood by the devil’s *pompa* if the properly so-called procession was no longer practiced at the circus?

After the circus procession—that is, the carrying of images—had been omitted, the entire remaining apparatus and entertainment of the circus continued for a long time, even under Christian rulers, although contrary to religious principles. Such entertainments included naval battles, equestrian and pedestrian combats, hunts with wild beasts, races of quadrigas and horses, and other things of this kind.

These were the amusements understood by the name of the devil’s *pompa* or *pompae*, which those approaching baptism renounced. Some of them displayed a certain vanity unworthy of a Christian; others presented to the eyes of spectators a brutality abhorrent to the Christian religion; and all were regarded as defiled by their origin in pagan superstition.

In this sense, as the fourth century was drawing to a close, Saint Cyril of Jerusalem explained the renunciation of the devil’s *pompa* or *pompae* in *Mystagogical Catechesis* 1, no. 6, where he said:

> “Afterward you say: ‘And every procession of his.’ The devil’s procession is the madness of the theaters, the races of horses in the hippodromes, the hunts in the circus, and the rest of this kind of vanity . . . Let not the madness of the theater be your concern or delight, where you behold the shameless behavior of the actors . . . nor the behavior of those who expose themselves to wild beasts in circus hunts . . . Flee also the races of horses, a spectacle that is utterly insane and casts down souls lying on their backs. For all these things are the devil’s procession.”

Thus it is clear what was included under the name of the *pompa* in the renunciation preceding baptism after the procession properly so called, which had taken place in the circus, had been abolished.

In precisely the same sense, in the fifth century, Salvian also spoke of the *pompae* which those being initiated renounced. By them he understood not the now-obsolete carrying of pagan images in the circus, but the other circus spectacles that remained, as well as the theatrical stages. He bitterly lamented that Christians, contrary to their solemn profession, yearned for these with such eager and vehement desire, especially throughout Book VI of *The Government of God*, and most particularly chapter 6.

Now let us return to the discourse of our Nicetas. As we have seen, he twice mentions *pompae* and theaters when speaking of the renunciation made to the devil by those seeking baptism. By the name of *pompae*, distinguished especially from theaters, he evidently understood the circus spectacles that still remained after the removal of the image-processions and for which the people of that age burned with the most ardent passion. No one will deny this.

Nor will anyone deny that from the passages of Nicetas cited above it can sufficiently be inferred that in the formula of renunciation used by him according to the custom of his Church, the specific word *pompa* was absent and was supplied by the general designation “the works of the devil.” From this we correctly infer that both circus spectacles and theaters flourished among those to whom he was speaking, since in explaining the works of the devil which those giving themselves to Christ renounced, he did not omit to mention the *pompae* then in use, and also listed the theaters—all of which were regarded as characteristic amusements, or rather seductive corruptions, of the Roman world.

But who would ever say that such circus spectacles, which were explained by the name *pompae*, and theaters existed in Transdanubian Dacia among those barbarian peoples who were designated by the names Dacians, Scythians, Bessi, and Getae?

Salvian, certainly, whom we cited above and who devoted himself entirely to rebuking the Christians of his age for their delight in circus games and theatrical spectacles—by which, he declared, they were lying about the faith given to them in baptism—reproached them by adducing the example of barbarian peoples. Among these, he confidently asserted, there were neither circuses nor theaters by which their morals could be corrupted.

> “What comparable thing exists among the barbarians?” he says in Book VI, cited above, chapter 7. “Where among them are the circuses? Where are the theaters? Where is the crime of various impurities—namely, the destruction of our hope and salvation?”

There was therefore no reason for that Dacian Nicetas, the friend of Saint Paulinus of Nola, when explaining the works of the devil which those new Christians renounced as they prepared to receive baptism, to mention *pompae* and theaters, so that they might understand that they had also renounced these inventions of the devil, which did not exist among them.

Even if we grant that among those barbarian peoples there existed certain things resembling the circus games and theatrical spectacles of the Romans, and which could properly be called works of the devil, so that they too might have renounced them in baptism, why would that Dacian Nicetas have used the Roman words *pompa* and *theatrum* to designate them? Among peoples unaccustomed to Roman ways, those words would certainly have had no significance.

Since, therefore, we see that Niceas or Nicetas, bishop of the city of Romatiana, mentioned by Gennadius, used in his little work *On the Creed for the Competentes* and in the third surviving fragment of his works words that would not at all have been appropriate among the barbarian peoples living in Transdanubian Dacia, where Nicetas, the friend of Saint Paulinus of Nola, exercised his episcopate, we rightly infer from the location of this Dacian Nicetas’s episcopate also that Niceas or Nicetas, bishop of the city of Romatiana, of whom Gennadius speaks, was not Niceas or Nicetas the Dacian, the friend of Saint Paulinus of Nola and celebrated in his praises.

Who, then, was this Nicetas, bishop of the city of Romatiana, who mentioned circus games and theatrical spectacles in his little works?

This investigation belongs not to the present chapter but to the following one, where we openly assert and prove that Niceas or Nicetas, bishop of the city of Romatiana, as Gennadius calls him, was Niceas or Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia.

Nevertheless, it will not be inappropriate to anticipate the following chapter to some extent by asserting that, from the words *pompae* and *theatra* used by Nicetas, it can readily be inferred that this Nicetas, whom Gennadius calls bishop of the city of Romatiana, was Niceas or Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia.

First, an Aquileian bishop could properly mention *pompae* and theaters, which Christians renounced in baptism, since there can be no doubt that in the once most celebrated city of Aquileia there had been a circus in which processions were held, together with other spectacles of that place, both before Constantine the Great and afterward, and that there had likewise been theaters in which stage performances were presented.

That Aquileia once possessed a circus in which processions of images were conducted on appointed days is not clearly expressed anywhere in the surviving monuments of those times. Nevertheless, many considerations support it.

The people of Aquileia were once worshipers not only of Jupiter and Belenus, or Apollo, but also of the Sun, whom they designated under the name Mithras, as the distinguished bishop Filippo della Torre demonstrated in his dissertation on Belenus, p. 281, which is found together with his *Monuments of Ancient Antium*.

Moreover, the Sun was worshiped especially through circus games, as the same learned bishop proves at length in *On Mithras, etc.*, chapter 6, in the same *Monuments*, p. 219. It therefore appears that the city of Aquileia was not without a circus.

Furthermore, the same distinguished bishop, in his dissertation on the Aquileian gods, p. 315 of the same work, showed that a famous temple of Jupiter and a Capitolium, modeled on that of the mistress-city, also stood at Aquileia. The learned Marcus Velserus likewise concludes in *History of the Vindelicians*, Book V, p. 259 of the final edition, as he himself says, that the distinguished cities Ravenna, Florence, Milan, Carthage, and several others possessed Capitolia, and above all his own Augsburg.

Della Torre also deduced from Aquileian inscriptions elucidated by him that the city of Aquileia was not without a college of Augustales, as he states in his dissertation on the Colony of Forum Julii, p. 366 of the same work.

He adds, p. 359, that the order of decurions which existed at Aquileia and which was equivalent to a senate was called “the most splendid order” in the inscriptions where it is mentioned. It was therefore probably, like the decurions of Capua mentioned by Cicero in *Agrarian Law* 2, composed of one hundred members, which was certainly considered a very large number.

Indeed, consuls of the city of Aquileia are also mentioned fairly frequently in inscriptions explained by the same author in the same work, although learned men are reluctant to permit the dignity of consul to colonies and municipia, as he himself says on the following page, 360.

Why, then, should Aquileia not also have possessed a circus in which circus games were held and in which the devil’s *pompae* were carried about while idolatry prevailed?

The learned Panvinius also observes that other cities of the Roman world, besides Rome, were adorned with circuses, in *On the Circus Games*, Book II, chapter 17: namely Milan in Italy, Antioch in Syria, Arles in Gaul, and others elsewhere.

John Argolus lists most of these, both in Italy itself—such as Anagni, Assisi, and Alatri—and throughout the world, in his notes on this passage of Panvinius. He adds generally that there were many circuses: wherever Roman power manifested itself, they were erected.

Since the city of Aquileia was not inferior to Milan, and since it far surpassed Anagni, Assisi, and Alatri, it is not unreasonable to conjecture that Aquileia possessed a circus, along with the other buildings that adorned a very large, splendid, and wealthy city.

This conclusion must be drawn with still greater firmness if we consider what authors who were either contemporaries of that great city or lived not long after its destruction left in writing about it.

Our learned Nicolaus Madrisius collected this material in an Italian booklet entitled *Apologia per l’antico stato e condizione della famosa Aquileja*, published at Udine in 1721, p. 31.

There we read Herodian, who called Aquileia the greatest city of Italy; Julian Augustus, who called it a wealthy emporium; Procopius, who called it a very rich and immense city and shortly afterward described it as remarkable for its size and the number of its citizens; Justinian Augustus, who testified that Aquileia had been the greatest of all the cities under the West; Luitprand, who said that it had been a great city and extraordinarily populous; and other more recent writers who, led by the authority of the ancients, pour out praises of its magnificence.

Who, then, would deny that so distinguished a city possessed a circus, both before the age of Constantine the Great and afterward, even though no certain, particular documents from those times survive in the writings of the ancients?

Nevertheless, although certain and particular written documents concerning the Aquileian circus are lacking, there are not altogether lacking indications by which our conjecture may be strengthened.

The most holy bishop of Aquileia, Chromatius, who governed the Aquileians at the end of the fourth and beginning of the fifth century, spoke as follows to the people of Aquileia in tractate 1, chapter 2, on the Gospel of Matthew, which is found in Andrea Gallandi’s *Library of the Fathers*, volume VIII:

> “In the role of the president of the games or the provider of the contests, Christ sets before the competitors in this spiritual stadium a great prize, so that, while they look upon the prize, they may neither fear the labors nor dread the dangers.”

Unless we wish to say that Chromatius presented to his Aquileians an example drawn from matters unknown to them—which would certainly be absurd—we must admit that the Aquileians knew the *agonothetai*, that is, the judges of contests; the *munerarii*, namely, those who sponsored contests; and the stadium, that is, the place where contests were held. Consequently, such events were held at Aquileia, and Aquileia possessed a stadium where they took place.

The stadium was also called a circus because of the similarity of the thing, just as the Circus Maximus at Rome was sometimes called a stadium, although the word is more properly Greek. For what the Latins called a *circus*, the Greeks called a *stadium* or *agon*, as the aforementioned Panvinius observes in *On the Circus Games*, Book II, chapter 1.

We may therefore readily infer from Chromatius himself that in his time Aquileia possessed a circus which was also called by the Greek word *stadium*.

If, after Chromatius, a contemporary and fellow-countryman, there is room in such an argument for Procopius of Caesarea, who wrote his histories in Greek in the sixth century, then he certainly mentions an Aquileian hippodrome in *The Vandalic War*, Book I, chapter 3, among the Byzantine historians, volume I.

He used the term *hippodrome* in accordance with the custom of Constantinople, which called the circus existing there a hippodrome, as the same Panvinius also notes in Book I, chapter 27 of the work cited.

Procopius, I say, mentions an Aquileian hippodrome, which his Latin translator rendered as *circus*, when he relates that John the Tyrant, captured at Ravenna in war by Theodosius the Younger and led to Aquileia, was carried there on a donkey through the hippodrome before he was killed, as an object of disgrace and a spectacle for the mockery of the watching crowd. This occurred in the year 424 or 425.

Although Procopius’s mention of the Aquileian circus came after an entire century had elapsed since the catastrophe of Aquileia at the hands of Attila, and even longer after the event he was recounting, and although he was an author who lived far from these regions, it nevertheless strongly reinforces our conjectures concerning the Aquileian circus.

Moreover, the exceptionally diligent investigator of Aquileian antiquities, Canon Bertoli, in his work entitled *The Antiquities of Aquileia*, p. 254, infers from an old indication of a place in the city of Aquileia called “near the Tower of the Arena” that an amphitheater existed at Aquileia.

Perhaps this building did indeed exist at Aquileia, although such massive structures, especially those made of stone, were not so common, as the distinguished Scipione Maffei observes in *On Amphitheaters*, chapters 7 and 9. Maffei himself admits that he had never encountered anything in ancient monuments concerning an Aquileian amphitheater.

But what if by the name “Arena” a circus should rather be understood? A circus was also not infrequently called an arena, as Maffei observes in the same work, chapter 10.

The tower also seems to indicate a circus rather than an amphitheater, as is clear from the images that represent circuses to us, especially in Panvinius’s *On the Circus Games*, and from the coins that represent amphitheaters.

The conjecture concerning an Aquileian circus is therefore strengthened still further.

These remarks concern the existence of a circus at Aquileia. Since the subject has been treated, it was not entirely inappropriate to discuss it somewhat more fully, as we believe it has not previously been addressed.

Since we have established that a circus existed at Aquileia, it is unnecessary to add much about a theater. A theater was a smaller and less expensive building and was therefore common even in smaller cities and municipia, and sometimes not unusual in villages themselves, as is clear either from the distinguished Mazochi’s work *On the Campanian Amphitheater*, chapter 8, or from the monuments—whether the theater was built of marble, of wood, or of both marble and wood.

In that very large and wealthy city, which was also filled with foreigners because of commerce and was often honored by the presence of the Augusti, both before Constantine’s age and afterward, as the histories relate and the laws issued there show, nothing seems to have been lacking that belonged not only to amusement but also to luxury, or that could in any way satisfy the multitude, which was especially devoted to spectacles and theatrical performances.

This, then, shows how Nicetas of Romatiana, Gennadius’s Nicetas, reveals himself through his use of the words *pompae* and *theatrum*, which prevent him from being that Dacian; rather, he reveals himself as an Aquileian—especially since there is no other Niceas or Nicetas whose episcopate must be investigated.

In the meantime, no one should object that Aquileia had been destroyed by the time of Nicetas of Aquileia, so that it no longer possessed either a circus for games or theaters for stage spectacles.

It is enough that these buildings had existed shortly beforehand, so that the Aquileian bishop could mention *pompae* and theaters in his explanation of renunciation as things wholly familiar to his hearers.

Moreover, Aquileia may not have been so completely destroyed that its larger and more solid buildings, such as circuses and theaters, especially in the principal cities, were immediately leveled to the ground. Nor was it certainly destroyed so utterly that, at least after the Huns had departed from Italy, it could not again be inhabited to some extent. A letter of Saint Leo the Great addressed to Nicetas of Aquileia seems to indicate this to some degree.

In addition, the madness and folly of the peoples of that time concerning circus games and theatrical stages were so great that the few citizens who survived the disasters of their cities demanded and procured these spectacles for themselves as a kind of remedy for their sufferings.

For this reason we must consult Salvian, a contemporary writer of Nicetas of Aquileia, in the aforementioned Book VI of *The Government of God*. He devotes himself entirely to rebuking the madness of those who, even after cities had been destroyed, citizens carried off or killed, and regions laid waste, nevertheless pined for circus and theatrical spectacles.

This is how he speaks of those who, after losing their theaters and circuses in the devastation wrought by the barbarians, nevertheless demanded theatrical and circus spectacles elsewhere for themselves:

> “The inhabitants of any city who come to Ravenna or Rome become part of the Roman populace in the circus, or part of the people of Ravenna in the theater.”

So he says in chapter 9.

Of those who survived the destruction of their cities and nevertheless desired spectacles in those same cities as before, he says in chapter 15:

> “A few nobles who had survived the destruction were asking the emperors for circus games as though they were the supreme remedy for the ruined city.”

The city of Trier, described by the author as the greatest and wealthiest city of Gaul, suffered this fate at the beginning of the fifth century and begged this consolation from the emperors Honorius and Constantius, as Baluzius and Valesius note in their annotations on this passage.

Salvian therefore discusses the destruction of this city at length and finally turns his speech to it in a manner highly relevant to our subject:

> “So, Trier, you desire circus games—and this after being devastated, after being conquered, after disaster, bloodshed, punishments, captivity, and so many destructions of your city? What is more tearful than this folly, what more grievous than this madness? . . . You seek theaters, then, and ask the rulers for a circus? For what condition, I ask, for what people, for what city? For a burned and ruined city, for a captive and slaughtered populace, which has either perished or mourns; and even if anything remains of it, everything is calamity, with all either anxious from grief, exhausted by tears, or prostrate through bereavement, so that you can scarcely know whose lot is worse and harder, that of the dead or that of the living. For the sufferings of the survivors are so great that they have surpassed the misery of the dead. You ask, then, for public amusements, Trier? Where, I ask, are they to be held? Over graves and ashes, over the bones and blood of the slain? For what part of the city is free from all these evils? Where has blood not been shed, where do bodies not lie stretched out, where are the torn limbs of the mutilated not found? Everywhere there is the face of a captured city, everywhere the horror of captivity, everywhere the image of death. The wretched remnants of the people lie upon the tombs of their dead, and you ask for circus games? The city is black with fire, and you assume the expression of festivity? Everything mourns, and you are cheerful?”

This is what Salvian said about the city of Trier and to its citizens.

What wonder, then, if, given the madness of those times concerning spectacles and the depravity of morals which provoked God’s anger and drove the hands of the barbarians toward the destruction of the West, Aquileia itself, after experiencing the fate of Trier, should, following its example, have yearned for its former circuses and theaters among the few citizens who survived and escaped the swords of the barbarians after the disaster inflicted by Attila?

Thus Nicetas the bishop, in explaining the works of the devil which those seeking baptism renounced, would have had to mention both *pompae* and theaters.

But enough of this—and perhaps we have said more than was necessary.

Yet the very formula of renunciation used by our Nicetas in administering the sacrament of regeneration must not be omitted. We have already noted that, in the passages cited above from the *Explanation of the Creed to the Candidates for Baptism* and from the third Fragment, Nicetas did not report the simple formula customarily used in his Church, but rather an explanation of that formula for the instruction of the faithful, so that they might understand how far-reaching was the renunciation they made in receiving baptism. He himself clearly suggests this by the expression “that is,” which he places before the enumeration of those things he taught were included under the name “works of the devil,” and also by the words “and such like evils,” with which he concludes the enumeration.

If Nicetas’s words are examined more carefully, it certainly appears that the formula customarily used in his Church was the one consisting of a twofold renunciation and was almost the simplest of all, namely: “the devil [Col. 0920B] and his angels,” and then “his works,” without any further addition of words. From the works cited above by Josephus Vicecomes and Josephus Catalanus, who examined the rite of renunciation, it is clear that in some places a single renunciation was in force, embracing everything that elsewhere was divided into several renunciations; in certain other places a double renunciation was customary, more commonly a triple one, and in some places even a quadruple one, according to the division of the matters and words. It is further clear that the wording used in eliciting the renunciation was not uniform everywhere but varied.

The renunciation in use in the Milanese Church under Saint Ambrose was twofold and itself expressed in few words; moreover, the word “pomp” was entirely absent, although it was commonly used elsewhere. It is worthwhile to hear that holy teacher writing on this subject in more than one place.

“After this, the holy of holies was opened to you; you entered the sanctuary of regeneration. Repeat what you were asked; recall what you answered. You renounced the devil and his works, the world and its luxury.” Thus in the book *On the Mysteries*, chapter 2.

Ambrose speaks more clearly in the work *On the Sacraments*, which circulates under his name, book I, chapter 2:

“When he asked you, ‘Do you renounce the devil and his works?’ what did you answer? ‘I renounce.’ ‘Do you renounce the world and its works?’ what did you answer? ‘I renounce.’ Remember your pledge.”

In the *Hexaemeron*, book I, chapter 4, bringing all the words of the renunciation together into one formula, he wrote:

“He who is washed abandons that intelligible Pharaoh, the ruler of this world, saying: ‘I renounce you, devil, and your angels, and your works, and your dominions.’”

Whatever may be said about the slight difference of wording that appears between Ambrose and Ambrose himself in the formula of renunciation which he presents to us in the passages cited—and which must be regarded as having then belonged to his Milanese Church—no one, I think, will deny that the formula of renunciation handed down to us by Ambrose corresponds most closely, and is almost identical, with that which belonged to Nicetas, the author of the *Explanation of the Creed to the Candidates for Baptism* [Col. 0920D] and of the third fragment from his lost works. In both cases, namely, a double renunciation appears; in both, the devil and his angels are renounced; in both, his works [Col. 0920C] are also renounced; and in both alike the word “pomp,” or “pomps,” is absent, although otherwise it was so frequent and almost universal in formulas of renunciation.

This similarity between Nicetas’s formula of renunciation and that of the Milanese Church under Saint Ambrose offers considerable evidence for recognizing in this same Nicetas the bishop of Aquileia. For who is unaware of the close relationship that existed at that time between the Aquileian and Milanese Churches—indeed, of something like kinship between them? The bishops of these Churches had long been conferring episcopal ordination upon one another and supporting one another by reciprocal services, as we learn abundantly from the histories; the distinguished De Rubeis has noted this in more than one place in his *Monuments of Aquileia*, as has also the most learned Oltrocchi in his *Ligustic History of the Church of Milan*, [Col. 0921A] published a few years ago. But we must hasten to other matters.

In the same third fragment, immediately after the words cited above, in which he explained the works of the devil, blessed Nicetas proceeds by rebuking those who, contrary to the renunciation made of the devil’s works, were entirely devoted to excessive adornment of the flesh and to procuring for themselves an extravagant cultivation of the body.

“What are we to say,” he asks, “of those who wish to parade themselves in excessive adornment of the flesh and to appear remarkable? I say nothing of the unnecessarily elaborate refinements of clothing. I ask you: what purpose do hair curled with a needle serve on men, with locks covering the neck behind but completely hiding the forehead in front, so that no free space remains on the forehead for the sign of Christ [the cross], and so that from the very feature by which they think they possess some glory or beauty they derive disgrace and shame? Likewise, women bind their heads like a shield, so that the forehead stands like a valley between two hills; weights of little stones [Col. 0921B] fastened with gold hang from their ears; their arms are burdened with gold and chains or stones press upon their necks; and on their feet, in blood-red footwear, little flames gleam. What use or benefit is found in these things, except empty display alone and a mind corrupted by childish desire?”

This is what Nicetas says in the cited Viennese fragment.

The first point here deserving attention is the rebuke with which Bishop Nicetas censures both men and women who, through elaborate bodily grooming and excessive luxury in adornment, displayed that pride and ostentation which he had previously enumerated among the works of the devil and which those being initiated into the Christian faith had renounced in the sacrament of baptism.

If we now consult what we previously reported from the poem of Saint Paulinus of Nola concerning the peoples of the Dacians, Scythians, Bessi, and Getae, recently converted to the faith through Nicetas’s preaching; if we recall what that same holy bishop celebrates there, in great and wondrous terms, in praise of his Nicetas, concerning the holy conduct of those nations, [Col. 0921C] by which they rivaled the primitive age of the nascent Church—who could believe that the face of that new Church had suddenly changed, under Nicetas’s own eyes, so that he had to rebuke those faithful so severely because they had, as it were, departed from the faith pledged in the sacrament of regeneration, through their renunciation of the works of the devil?

Those words, therefore, do not seem to belong to Nicetas of Dacia, but rather to another Nicetas who was cultivating a Church already mature, in which abuses had gradually crept in and needed to be marked by the pastor’s rebuke. Accordingly, it was rather that Nicetas of Aquileia who was attacking these practices in his Aquileian Church.

Moreover, several individual observations deserve to be made concerning the expressions cited from this fragment of Nicetas.

“I say nothing,” he says, “of the unnecessarily elaborate refinements of clothing.” What are these unnecessarily elaborate refinements of clothing? The garments, it appears, were acquired not for use but solely for luxury; garments, I think, not merely of complete perfection and elegant workmanship, but also [Col. 0921D] of remarkable fineness, such as those made of extremely light fabrics prepared with great skill and labor from very finely drawn threads of wool, cotton, linen, or silk.

The abuse of such fine garments, which often offended not only Christian moderation but also modesty and decency, may perhaps have been in Jerome’s mind in his letter to Laeta, which is number 107 in Vallarsi’s edition, section 10. In instructing her about the discipline of her little daughter, he said:

“Let her prepare such garments as will drive away the cold, not such as will expose the bodies clothed in them.”

Nicetas may perhaps have taken this word “fineness,” when applied to clothing to denote luxury unworthy of a Christian, from prophetic expressions. For in Isaiah, chapter 19, verse 9, where the burden of Egypt is described, the prophet says:

“They shall be confounded who work in flax, combing and weaving the fine fabrics.”

By “fine fabrics” the prophet chiefly means linen garments of extreme delicacy, such as were woven in Egypt. [Col. 0922A] Similarly, in Ezekiel, chapter 16, verse 10, the same word is used when the subject is Jerusalem, the city whose dignity and beauty the Lord had increased in the sight of all nations:

“And I clothed you in embroidered garments, and shod you with violet; I girded you with fine linen, and clothed you with delicate garments.”

Here interpreters understand “delicate garments” generally as thin and refined clothing, and especially as a silk mantle made with an exceedingly fine thread.

Whatever Nicetas understood in this fragment by “the unnecessarily elaborate refinements of clothing”—whether garments of linen or of another material, worked with such extreme delicacy—no one will easily persuade himself that such refined garments could have been found, in the time of Nicetas of Dacia, among the savage and barbarous peoples living beyond the Danube; still less that those peoples were so devoted to the luxury of such clothing that Nicetas, their bishop and spiritual father, deserved to rebuke them for it.

Let us again recall what can readily be inferred from the verses of Saint Paulinus [Col. 0922B] cited above concerning the barbarism and rustic manners of those peoples. Everyone will see, unless I am mistaken, that all the arts associated with luxury and with excessive cultivation of life and body were entirely foreign to those regions, as was also the taste for such delicate objects and the ease of obtaining them from other regions of the Roman Empire—regions which for the most part had no, or at least very little, commercial intercourse with barbarian peoples outside Roman rule.

On the contrary, how entirely suitable would such things have been to the people of Aquileia, inhabitants of a city which, when prosperous, was the greatest of all the Italian cities after Rome and the richest emporium, where merchandise from the whole East and West flowed together in abundance! Even after the disaster inflicted by Attila, the city was not immediately so completely cast down from its former condition and dignity, and from the constant presence of foreigners, that its inhabitants could not for some time retain in their manner of life and dress either their former luxury or at least some likeness of that former luxury—[Col. 0922C] indeed, a form worthy of rebuke among Christians.

Other matters worthy of notice occur in the same fragment of Nicetas. They are those elegant and vivid descriptions by which he placed before their eyes, while at the same time condemning it, the superfluous cultivation of the hair, first among men and then among women, whom he also reproves for burdening their necks, ears, and arms with varied and costly adornment.

“I ask you,” he says, “what purpose do hair curled with a needle serve on men, with locks covering the neck behind but completely hiding the forehead in front, so that no free space remains on the forehead for the sign of Christ [the cross]?”

Here Nicetas is speaking of the most ancient sign of the cross—not the sign by which the forehead was touched and the hand afterward brought down to the breast and then carried to both sides of the shoulders, a sign that may be called the greater sign of the cross and which Christians commonly use today—but rather of the sign of the cross that was completed entirely on the forehead, the thumb being drawn across the forehead in the form of a cross. [Col. 0922D] We may properly call this the lesser sign of the cross, whose use is also found among us, though less frequently.

It is certainly of this lesser sign that Tertullian must be understood in the well-known passage read in *On the Crown*, chapter 4:

“At every step forward and every movement, at every entrance and exit, when putting on shoes, at baths, at tables, when lights are brought, when going to bed, when sitting down, whatever occupation engages us, we rub our foreheads with the sign of the cross.”

Saint Augustine also speaks of this same sign in his *Exposition on Psalm 50*, section 1, where he complained that Christians marked themselves with this sign on the forehead even in the circus whenever they were frightened for any reason, without meanwhile realizing from the sign itself that they ought not to have a place among the vanities and madnesses at which they were present as spectators.

“How many of our brothers today, we think and lament, go after deceitful vanities and madnesses … If by chance they are frightened in the circus for some reason, they immediately sign themselves and [Col. 0923A] stand there carrying on their forehead the very thing from which they would withdraw if they carried it in their heart!”

Since Nicetas too is speaking of this sign, which was made entirely on the forehead—by rubbing the forehead, as Tertullian says, and therefore carrying on the forehead something impressed there, as it were, according to Augustine—it is clear that the forehead of Christians had to be bare and uncovered, and by no means concealed under the hair, so that Christians could easily fortify themselves with that sign at every action.

Blessed Nicetas therefore rightly complained about his Christians, who, loving a novel fashion in their hair and locks, covered their foreheads so completely with their hair that they left no free space for the sign of the cross to be made upon it.

Could one really suspect that such an abuse had arisen during the episcopate of Nicetas of Dacia, among those peoples living beyond the Danube who, before Nicetas’s preaching, had been strangers to all more cultivated refinement, and who through Nicetas’s apostolic labors had been numbered among Christ’s flock and had advanced so far in the Christian religion that Paulinus of Nola could celebrate such wonders [Col. 0923B] about them?

This abuse rather belongs among those that easily creep into peoples devoted to excessive refinement, who possess everything that pertains to the comfort, luxury, and splendor of life; and also among peoples in whom Christian religion cools with the passage of time, and among whom Christians, becoming more wanton, easily depart from their former habit of stricter living.

These rebukes therefore fit Nicetas of Aquileia rather than Nicetas of Dacia: they are addressed to Christians who indulged excessively in the cultivation of their hair, so that they left no room for making the sign of the cross on the forehead.

What confirms this conjecture still further is an ancient Aquileian stone [Col. 0923B] carved in relief and published by the canon Bertoli in his *Antichità d’Aquileja*, on the page cited above, number 16. There one can see a young man holding a horse with his left hand and having his forehead covered by his hair, exactly as Nicetas describes in his fragment.

[Col. 0923C] The stone is pagan, not Christian, as appears from the inscription on the other side of the stone; and therefore it probably does not belong to the age of Nicetas of Aquileia. Even if idolatry had not then been entirely abolished, it was nevertheless no longer of such a kind as could easily express and reveal itself through inscriptions and reliefs.

It is enough, however, that such a manner of wearing the hair once existed among the Aquileians, even the pagans, for it later to have been taken up again by the Aquileian Christians themselves, who, led by vanity, sought out and revived obsolete forms of adornment and, through a certain lukewarmness in religion, did not entirely recoil from the old practice of their pagan ancestors.

So much concerning the men. What does Nicetas next criticize in the women in the same fragment?

Nicetas continues his rebuke, saying:

“Likewise women bind their heads like a shield, so that the forehead stands like a valley between two hills; weights of little stones fastened with gold hang from their ears; their arms are burdened with gold; chains or stones press upon their necks; and on their feet, in blood-red footwear, [Col. 0923D] little flames gleam.”

Then he concludes both rebukes, that addressed to men and that addressed to women, as follows:

“What use or benefit is found in these things, except empty display alone and a mind corrupted by childish desire?”

Here too one sees that Nicetas has depicted the women’s elaborate and showy adornment in such a way that it is extremely difficult to believe that it existed among the barbarous Dacian peoples living beyond the Danube; more difficult still to believe that it existed among those new believers who had recently been added by blessed Nicetas to the Christian people.

But what if an Aquileian stone also happens to appear at this point, from which we might infer that the adornment of Aquileian women corresponded to Nicetas’s words, and therefore that the words cited from the Viennese fragment belong not to Nicetas of Dacia but rather to Nicetas of Aquileia?

Such a stone does indeed exist in the work just mentioned, *Antichità d’Aquileja*, page 253. There one sees a woman carved in relief as far as the breast, [Col. 0924A] by an artist who, apparently, was not especially accomplished; so that the work seems to belong to a period of decline in the fine arts and perhaps even to a time when Christianity had matured at Aquileia, since there is nothing in it that suggests idolatry.

You can see this woman with her hair braided crosswise and her head bound like a shield. You can see her forehead, like a valley, standing between two hills rising on either side from her hair. Perhaps you can also see weights of little stones hanging from her ears, certainly fastened with gold. Finally, you can see her neck pressed by chains or stones in the middle between the two hills.

Let this suffice as a preface to the following chapter, in which we undertake to prove by stronger arguments that Niceas, or Nicetas, that Romatian whom we have shown thus far could not have been a Dacian—first by considerations drawn from time and then by considerations drawn from place—is in fact Niceas, or Nicetas, called by Gennadius a Romatian, and is truly Niceas, or Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, who flourished in the time of Saint Leo the Great and to whom a letter of that holy pontiff [Col. 0924B] is extant.

[Col. 0924]

## CHAPTER IV

Niceas, or Nicetas, bishop of the city of Romatiana, mentioned by Gennadius, is beyond doubt Niceas, or Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, who flourished in the time of Saint Leo the Great and to whom a letter of that holy pontiff is extant.

The question now chiefly requiring investigation is who, finally, was that Niceas—or Nicetas, bishop of the city of Romatiana—mentioned by Gennadius [Col. 0924C] and author of the two short works which we have shown to be genuine. We have hitherto proved that he was not Niceas, or Nicetas, the Dacian friend of Saint Paulinus of Nola, nor the bishop of that city in Dacia on this side of the Danube called Romesiana, Remesiana, Remissiana, or Romatiana. We now assert that he was in reality Niceas, or Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, who flourished in the time of Saint Leo the Great and to whom a decretal letter of that holy pontiff is extant.

We now pass from a serious inquiry to one of the greatest importance. It would indeed be desirable for clearer arguments to be available, arguments that would settle the matter with complete openness. Nevertheless, the considerations we shall bring forward, even though conjectural, are such that, if we are not mistaken, they will readily deserve assent.

To say a few preliminary words about the period of Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, which are beyond dispute: first, as the distinguished Bernard Maria De Rubeis correctly observed in the *Monuments of the Aquileian Church*, chapter 17, column 152, this Nicetas is not the man who was a subdeacon of the Aquileian Church in the time of Saint Jerome, to whom a familiar letter of that holy teacher is extant and which belongs approximately to the year 374, according to the editors of Jerome’s works. A proper consideration of that man’s age does not permit him to occupy the position of our Nicetas in the pontificate of Leo the Great.

Second, in the year 454, two years after Attila’s destruction of Aquileia, our Nicetas succeeded a bishop named Secundus in the see of Aquileia, not Chromatius, as some have thought; [Col. 0924D] Chromatius had five other successors before Nicetas. Then, in the year 458, Saint Leo the Great sent the letter in response to the consultations, which is number 159 among the letters of that holy pontiff in the Venetian edition of the Veronese brothers Ballerini. Finally, Nicetas departed this life in the year 485, as we learn from the Aquileian Chronicles, in which learned men have by no means refused their agreement on this point.

Was this Aquileian Nicetas, therefore, a contemporary of Leo the Great, the same as Niceas or Nicetas, bishop of the city of Romatiana, mentioned by Gennadius and author of the two short works which we proved genuine in chapter 1?

Indeed he was. For, I ask, if the author of the *Explanation of the Creed to the Candidates for Baptism* cannot be Niceas or Nicetas the Dacian, the friend of Saint Paulinus of Nola and celebrated in his praises—and there is only one question concerning that point, since, as we have seen, the *Explanation* speaks of the Eutychian heresy, [Col. 0925A] which Nicetas of Dacia could not have encountered in his lifetime, and from which we have shown that he was still far removed when he departed this life—what is there that compels us to depart from the authority of the Roman manuscript recently discovered in the Ghisian Library?

That manuscript states plainly and clearly, with no difference of script, no sign of corruption, no erasure, and no trace of a later hand: “The *Explanation of the Creed of blessed Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, delivered to the Candidates for Baptism.*” Why should we read it, or conceive it in our minds, as the distinguished Zabeus maintains, as the work of blessed Nicetas, or Niceas, bishop of Romatiana in Dacia?

That Dacian Nicetas, the friend of Saint Paulinus of Nola, cannot be the author of that work. No other Nicetas is extant, or at least no other has been established, who could have delivered an *Explanation of the Creed to the Candidates for Baptism* and spoken in it of the Eutychian heresy, and thus compete with our Aquileian Nicetas with even a semblance of probability.

[Col. 0925B] The authority of the Roman Ghisian manuscript therefore stands firm and unshaken: it makes Nicetas of Aquileia the author of the *Explanation of the Creed to the Candidates for Baptism*. Since the author of the other work is likewise the author of the work addressed “To the Fallen Virgin,” our proposition remains valid: the Niceas, or Nicetas, bishop of the city of Romatiana mentioned by Gennadius, is beyond doubt Niceas, or Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, who flourished in the time of Saint Leo the Great and to whom a letter of that holy pontiff is extant.

If it is desirable to add further authority, we may note that the learned Carlo Fea, who first informed us in 1790, in his *Miscellanea Filologica Critica Antiquaria*, volume I, page 7—a work which, however, for some reason unknown to me did not proceed beyond its first volume—of this recently discovered work on the Creed addressed to the Candidates for Baptism, concealed in the Ghisian Library at Rome, and who also promised to show it to us at a suitable opportunity, though we did not see that promise fulfilled—[Col. 0925C] Carlo Fea, I say, did not hesitate, with his expertise in such matters, to assert clearly that, according to the rules of criticism, this work belonged to that Nicetas of Aquileia who submitted various questions to Saint Leo the Great.

It is worthwhile to hear him writing briefly in the place cited, as the simple indication of the matter required:

“Explanation of the Creed of blessed Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, delivered to the Candidates for Baptism; of that same Nicetas who proposed various questions to Saint Leo the Great concerning the marriage of the Arian Goths, whose response exists among his works. De Rubeis, Liruti, and others speak at length about him; but they do not speak of this short work, which I believe to be his, insofar as this can be asserted according to the rules of criticism.”

Thus he wrote. Certainly he did not judge without knowledge of the case, since he was able—and in all probability did—look upon that Ghisian manuscript with his own eyes; and he names Liruti and De Rubeis, who, along with several others, certainly were not supporters of his opinion before the discovery of this manuscript. Would that he had given us that work! He would certainly have strengthened his opinion in such a way that it would now be entirely unnecessary for us to contend for it, though our powers are unequal to the task.

[Col. 0925D] Let us therefore continue the inquiry and clarify it with some observations.

Either Gennadius of Massilia was mistaken when he wrote that our Nicetas was bishop of the city of Romatiana, when he should have written that he was bishop of Aquileia; or the Roman manuscript was mistaken when it presented Nicetas as bishop of Aquileia, when it should have stated that he was bishop of the city of Romatiana.

If there is in fact an error in one or the other, to whom should we rather give credence, Gennadius or the Roman manuscript?

Gennadius, however careful and perceptive he may be considered, was nevertheless a writer neither closely connected with the Aquileian Church nor Italian, and not free from error in every respect, as we shall say in its proper place. He was also a writer who reported what he received from others and who perhaps had not himself seen everything about which he wrote; indeed, he may have known more by report [Col. 0926A] than he had personally investigated.

The Roman manuscript, on the other hand, is itself Nicetas’s work; it reveals the name of its author and identifies the place of his episcopate. The manuscript, as it were, bears witness about itself; Gennadius bears witness about another. Who would not rather trust a genuine work that presents its author’s name than a distant and unrelated writer reporting something different?

Although the Roman manuscript shows the appearance of a fourteenth-century script, there can be no doubt that it was copied in the fourteenth century from an older manuscript, perhaps even one contemporary with the author himself.

Since we learn from the letter of Saint Leo the pope cited above that a deacon of the Roman Church named Adeodatus, returning from Aquileia to Rome, brought the consultations of Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, to the pontiff, it would not be unreasonable to conjecture—or rather, in view of the discipline of that age, it would be equally reasonable to judge—that he brought to Rome Nicetas of Aquileia’s work on the Creed and selected this work from among Nicetas’s other writings to present to Pope Leo and all the Romans, since it was a witness to the faith publicly taught in the Aquileian Church. [Col. 0926B]

This would be especially appropriate in view of the new Eutychian error, which Saint Leo had recently and vigorously refuted in his celebrated letter to Flavian, and which Nicetas had attacked using the very reasoning and arguments of Leo, indeed even his words, as we have seen, taken from that same letter.

Here, then, perhaps, is a copy of the *Explanation of the Creed* belonging to the fifth century itself, from which the Ghisian copy was later produced in the fourteenth century. That copy lay hidden for so long in the recesses of libraries and finally emerged into the light in our own age, increasing the ecclesiastical collection of books with this precious new treasure, more powerfully confirming the transmission of Catholic doctrines, and shedding new light upon ecclesiastical history.

[Col. 0926C] The inscription of the Roman manuscript should therefore not be corrected from the work of Gennadius—wherever the error lies, it cannot be removed by any reconciliation—but Gennadius should rather be corrected from the Roman manuscript.

Before any manuscript had appeared that could resolve Gennadius’s difficulty concerning the city of Romatiana in the case of Nicetas, and that could clearly and explicitly call him bishop of Aquileia, I admit that the most serious scholars acted with great prudence. They did not dare to infer an Aquileian episcopate from the name “city of Romatiana,” nor did they think it right to follow Cardinal Baronius and a few others who, with arguments not sufficiently firm at that time, defended the Aquileian episcopate of this Nicetas of Gennadius, confidently asserting that Aquileia was in reality the city intended by Gennadius instead of Romatiana.

Indeed, I think they should also be forgiven for finding among geographers and other ancient writers a Remisiana, Remesiana, or Romessiana in Dacia, as well as another Dacian bishop Nicetas, the friend of Saint Paulinus of Nola.
