They therefore supposed, without doubt, that this man was the Nicetas mentioned by Gennadius, and that Gennadius’s Romatiana could easily, because of the similarity of the names, have been Remisiana, Remesiana, or Romessiana in Dacia on this side of the Danube, which ancient writers and geographers mention.

[Col. 0926D] But once a manuscript previously unknown to all finally appeared—a manuscript bearing no mark of falsification or interpolation, indeed possessing so strong a character of authenticity and making so simple an assertion that it assigns one of the seven short works attributed by Gennadius to Nicetas of Romatiana to Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia—and once it was found also to contain matters within that work which cannot at all suit Nicetas of Dacia, the friend of Paulinus of Nola—who would not judge the matter settled by this manuscript of such excellent quality? Who would any longer seek in Dacia, in Remisiana, Romessiana, or Remesiana, a bishop of the city of Romatiana mentioned by Gennadius, when the Roman manuscript asserts that he was bishop of Aquileia? Accordingly, who would not conclude that the Niceas or Nicetas, bishop of the city of Romatiana, is himself Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia?

[Col. 0927A]

The distinguished Zabeus believes that the inscription, or title, of the work was falsified by its copyist. He supposes that the copyist, perhaps reading in an older manuscript “Explanation of the Creed of blessed Nicetas, bishop,” added the word “Aquileian” on his own initiative, from whatever information he may have possessed that one of the bishops of Aquileia had borne the name Nicetas. Thus he argues in part I of his dissertation, number 20.

This, evidently, Zabeus had to devise in order to defend his own opinion and to evade the exceedingly clear authority of the Roman manuscript. Yet I do not know with what justification he lays the charge of arbitrary action upon that worthy copyist, to whom we owe the preservation of so precious a work of Nicetas, since no trace of fault or of any other arbitrary intervention occurs throughout the transcription of the work.

Indeed, I do not consider that the supposed arbitrary addition of the word “Aquileian” to the title of the work is even plausible. Moreover, I think that the inscription, or title, is of such a nature as to display its original and authentic character. This must now be demonstrated.

[Col. 0927B] First: either Zabeus supposes that the word “Aquileian” was arbitrarily added in an older manuscript of this *Explanation of the Creed*, for example, one written in the fifth century itself; or in another manuscript of a later period; or finally by the last copyist in the fourteenth century, the copyist responsible for the Roman manuscript recently discovered in the Ghisian Library and still unique in the whole world.

Now, in the fifth century—namely, in the age of Nicetas of Aquileia, and not long after the death of Nicetas of Dacia—there could not have been such ignorance concerning these two Nicetases, especially in the Churches of Italy, that a copyist, through lack of knowledge, would arbitrarily write one in place of the other.

Certainly Nicetas of Aquileia could not have been unknown at Rome, both because of the letter of Saint Pope Leo addressed to him and because of the testimony of Adeodatus, deacon of the Roman Church, who, returning from the Aquileian Church, brought the requests of Nicetas of Aquileia to the pontiff. Without doubt, he also spoke concerning Nicetas and concerning his Church, recently emerged from the distress caused by Attila’s disaster, [Col. 0927C] with the Roman clergy and people.

Nor was Nicetas of Dacia, the friend of Saint Paulinus of Nola, an unknown person. Paulinus himself, in Letter 29 to Severus, testifies that Nicetas, a most learned man and rightly admired by the Romans, had come from Dacia. Thus a copyist would not have inserted Nicetas of Aquileia in the inscription of the *Explanation of the Creed* in place of that Nicetas.

If, therefore, we suppose that this *Explanation*, with its inscription, emerged from a fifth-century manuscript, and that this manuscript was also located at Rome—as must be considered more probable, since nothing contradicts it—no such ignorance can be attributed to the copyist of the manuscript that he would have written one Nicetas in place of the other, arbitrarily, in the title of the work in that very fifth century.

There can be less suspicion of that intrusion if we suppose that the Explanation was copied from a codex written after the fifth century. For after the fifth century the usage also arose in the West of calling those prelates archbishops who possessed metropolitan authority—a usage that by the eighth century had already become very common [Col. 0927D] throughout the Western Church, as is clear to scholars. The most distinguished Abbot Fumagalli most recently noted this in his *Diplomatic Institutions*, published in Italian, vol. II, book II, part II, chapter 14, no. 8, and also in the *Santambrosian Diplomatic Codex*, p. 60, note 2; likewise the equally distinguished Gaetano Marini recently noted it in his most learned work, *The Diplomatic Papyri*, p. 289, annotation 15 to papyrus 87. A copyist later than the aforesaid fifth century, and insufficiently familiar with the two Nicetases, would not so readily have added *Aquileiensis* after the words “Bishop Nicetas,” since the Aquileian prelates had long before, even before Nicetas himself, been metropolitans and, with the introduction of the title “archbishop,” enjoyed that title along with the others. He would rather have added *Romatianae in Dacia*, which at that period better suited the simple title “bishop.” Or, if he had deliberately wished to insert the word *Aquileiensis*, he would not [Col. 0928A] have omitted the preceding title “bishop” and changed it to “archbishop,” in order to conform to the custom introduced after the fifth century and not diminish the honor of so distinguished a see.

But what if the insertion of the word *Aquileiensis* in the title of the little work is judged to have arisen in the fourteenth century itself, when the Roman codex of the Ghislieri Library is said to have been written? At that time, the Aquileian prelates used neither the title “bishop” nor “archbishop,” but, according to the long-established custom of preceding centuries, were called “patriarchs,” as is sufficiently well known from the ecclesiastical history of Aquileia. The copyist of the little work, therefore, would have inserted the word *Aquileiensis* after “Bishop Nicetas” still less appropriately, at least without changing the preceding word *episcopi* (“bishop”) into *patriarchae* (“patriarch”), which was the sole designation of the Aquileian prelates and which is read as having been used even for Nicetas himself in the printed calendars of the Aquileian Church—calendars that I myself have seen—from at least the year 1651 to the year 1753. There, under 22 June, the office is appointed for “Niceas, patriarch of Aquileia, confessor.” [Col. 0928B] In no way, therefore, does the addition of the word *Aquileiensis* in the Roman codex of the Ghislieri Library appear probable as something made by its copyist, as the most distinguished Zabeus judges. Rather, that word must be regarded as having originated with the codex itself, as must the entire title, which lends authority to the same word, as will shortly be seen.

The title of the Roman codex is as follows:

> *Explanation of the Symbol of blessed Nicetas, Bishop of Aquileia, delivered to the candidates.*

The polish and simplicity of this title strongly suggest the fifth century, and wonderfully agree with the polish and simplicity of the entire little work, qualities for which Gennadius commends it. For that reason, this very title of the work, on account of its polish and simplicity, may rightly be compared with the title of the letter of the holy Leo the Great to Nicetas himself, which runs as follows:

> *Leo, bishop, to Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia: greetings.*

I might reasonably conjecture [Col. 0928C] that the title “blessed,” which we see prefixed to Nicetas’s name, was attached from the beginning by the first copyist of the little work, and perhaps by Adeodatus himself, the deacon of the Roman Church, who probably brought the Explanation of the Symbol of Bishop Nicetas with him from Aquileia to Rome, as I indicated earlier. Certainly, the designation “blessed” was a title of honor that in that period was commonly bestowed even upon living bishops, as many monuments of the same century teach us, especially a number of epistolary titles preserved in the *Works of the Holy Fathers*. In that same period, men distinguished for learning and piety who had died were also honored with this title, particularly those whose works stood forth for the edification of the Church. Famous in this connection is the decree of Pope Gelasius, belonging to the year 494, concerning authentic books and apocryphal writings, issued at a council of seventy bishops held at Rome. It may be seen in the councils edited by Labbe under Coleti’s care, vol. V, col. 387, and in Fontanini’s *Antiquities of Horta*, appendix, no. 1. There, all those whose works are commended [Col. 0928D] as worthy of acceptance are individually listed under the title “blessed”: namely, blessed Cyprian, martyr and bishop; blessed Gregory of Nazianzus, bishop; blessed Basil, bishop of Cappadocia; blessed Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria; blessed Cyril, bishop of Alexandria; blessed John, bishop of Constantinople; blessed Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria; blessed Hilary, bishop of Poitiers; blessed Ambrose, bishop of Milan; blessed Augustine, bishop of Hippo; blessed Jerome, presbyter; blessed Prosper, a most religious man; and blessed Leo, pope. If, then, we see Nicetas of Aquileia marked by the title “blessed” in the title of the same little work—whether he was still living or was so called by the copyist shortly after his death—that title unquestionably exhibits the writing practice and discipline of the same fifth century, in which Nicetas of Aquileia flourished.

This becomes still clearer from the fact that blessed Nicetas himself is designated simply by the title “bishop.” That too [Col. 0929A] belongs to the practice of the same century, although the Church of Aquileia had long before shone with the honor of a metropolitan see. For around the year of Christ 369, under Valerian, the holy bishop of Aquileia who vigorously defended the Catholic cause against the Arians, it was the first of all the Churches of Italy to be honored with this dignity, under Damasus the Supreme Pontiff, as our most learned Innocentius Maria Lirutus, recently a member of the Paduan Benedictine family and now bishop of Verona, has newly written, together with many other works, in his *Dissertation Printed at Padua in 1787 on the Late Origin of Ecclesiastical Metropolises in the West*, chapter 2.

Although examples exist from the seventh and even the sixth century in the Western Church showing that metropolitan bishops had already begun to be elevated by the title “archbishop,” as the above-mentioned Gaetano Marini, among others, has noted in the cited passage, no such example from the fifth century can be found in genuine documents. The same distinguished scholar, while illustrating his papyrus 86 from the year 553, in which the bishops of Ravenna are mentioned with the title “archbishops,” observes [Col. 0929B] in annotation 31 to that papyrus, p. 287, that the prelates of that Church had always been called simply “bishops” in papyri earlier than the year 553. Yet the unanimous testimony of scholars establishes that the Church of Ravenna had become an ecclesiastical metropolis at least from the time of Saint Peter Chrysologus, also because Ravenna was then the imperial city, as we find in the same Lirutus at the cited place.

Since, then, we see our Nicetas of Aquileia, although a metropolitan, called simply “bishop,” exactly as were other metropolitans of the East and West—for example, Athanasius and Theophilus, bishops of Alexandria, and Ambrose, bishop of Milan, along with the others listed in the aforesaid decree of Gelasius—and exactly as the same Nicetas was called by Leo the Great in the letter sent to him, who would not also conclude from this that the title or heading [Col. 0929C] of the little work on the Symbol is such as to display its primeval authenticity and its original fifth-century character together with the work itself, and consequently to make the intrusion of the word *Aquileiensis* devised by the most distinguished Zabeus altogether less probable?

But let us now pass from the title of the little work to the work itself. First, we must weigh those features that in some way indicate the period of Nicetas of Aquileia; then those that show the little work to be a product of the Church of Aquileia. We have already noted above that the episcopate of Nicetas of Aquileia began in the year 454 and continued to the year 485. He began his episcopate in the fifth year after the letter of the holy Leo to Flavian, and in the third year after the Council of Chalcedon—at a time when, although the Eutychian error had everywhere been rejected by the Church and struck with anathema, it had nevertheless neither lost its strength nor lost its followers.

When, therefore, Bishop Nicetas ascended the Aquileian see, [Col. 0929D] the Eutychian error was above all the one against which the pastors of the Church had to fight with the sword of the word of God. They also had to fortify the faithful people with particular zeal and eloquent words, so that they would not allow themselves to be carried away by the new seducers. The danger from these men was not then merely like that posed by the earlier heretics; they were even more dangerous because, under the appearance of defending the faith and overthrowing the Nestorian heresy, they spread their own error.

What, then, does Nicetas do in the little work on the Symbol addressed to the candidates, where in reality those novel shoots were expressly to be imbued with Catholic doctrines and consolidated in the profession of the true faith? He teaches, in chapter 4, the doctrine of Christ’s true humanity as well as his divinity—a doctrine that we have reported earlier and shall also set out below. The force of the expression, the weight of the arguments, the urgency of the discourse, and a certain expansiveness of speech sufficiently show that [Col. 0930A] this, more than anything else, was the matter about which at that time it was necessary both to speak at somewhat greater length and to insist with more ardent zeal, lest the candidates be led into error by adversaries ready to deceive their minds if they found them unprepared and insufficiently cautious.

Moreover, when Nicetas there identifies Eutyches and the Eutychians as teachers of falsehood, he does not designate them by their proper name, as he does certain other heretics or schismatics, calling them by the names of their founders. Rather, as though they were well known to everyone and present with their deceptive doctrine, he mentions them by a common designation, calling them “erring heretics and teachers of deceit.”

What follows is still clearer in indicating the period of Nicetas of Aquileia—indeed, in my view, even the first years of his episcopate. In the cited chapter 4 of the *Explanation of the Symbol*, [Col. 0930B] Nicetas attacks not only the error of Eutyches, as we have seen, but also the error of Nestorius. Although the latter was about twenty years earlier than the Eutychian error, it is placed second. And while Nicetas seems perhaps overly expansive in discussing the former, beyond what a simple explanation of the Symbol requires, he is, by contrast, extremely brief concerning the latter, as though little or nothing needed to be said about one who, when the new opposing error of Eutyches had broken out, had already almost lost his strength.

Here are his words, which we set out concerning both errors so that they may more easily be compared:

> “Believe that this one who was born from the Virgin is God with us: God from the Father before the ages; man from the Virgin for the sake of human beings. Truly incarnate, not merely apparently so, as certain erring heretics say, ashamed of the mystery of God. They say that the Lord’s incarnation occurred in an apparition, because what was seen was not real but had deceived human eyes. Far be it—far be it altogether—from the truth of God. For if the incarnation is false, the salvation of human beings will also be false. But if salvation is truly in Christ, then the incarnation is likewise true. In him both exist together: man, in what was seen; God, in what was not seen. Eating as man, and feeding five thousand people with five loaves, because he is God. [Col. 0930C] Sleeping as man in the boat, but commanding the winds and the sea, because he is God. Fastening his hands to the cross as a man, but granting paradise to the thief who confessed him, because he is God. Finally, accepting death and laying aside his body for a short time, as man, but raising the four-day dead man from the tomb, because he is God. Christ must therefore be believed to be both God and man: for just as he is recognized as man through his sufferings, so God is manifested through his divine works. You have, then, grounds on which to reject the teachers of deceit.”

Thus far Nicetas against the Eutychian error. What he immediately adds is directed against the error of Nestorius. For he says:

> “If anyone should attempt to whisper in your ears that Christ was merely a man, say that he became man through the things mentioned above. From his powers and declarations I have already recognized him, since the Savior himself said to the Jews: ‘If you do not wish to believe me, believe at least the works, and recognize that I am in the Father and the Father is in me.’”

[Col. 0930D] What, I ask, is the meaning of this reversal of order and this difference in speech concerning the Eutychian and Nestorian errors? Why does Nicetas here begin his warning not with the Nestorian error, which had broken out first, but with the Eutychian? Why does he explain the Eutychian error so carefully and provide such a diligent and powerful antidote against it, drawing arguments from the Gospel history, while conversely marking Nestorianism more briefly and in only a few words—unless it is because the Eutychian error was then the one against which the faithful most urgently needed to be fortified, whereas the Nestorian heresy had already lost its patrons and followers, at least those of great renown?

Let us also examine more closely the actual expressions used in identifying the two errors. They were certainly not placed there accidentally but deliberately; for nothing in an explanation of the Symbol can be considered not to have been carefully weighed in every respect. When he first speaks of the Eutychian heresy, he says that the heretics [Col. 0931A] “say” this, and repeats the same verb twice. This is to be understood of their public and open manner of speaking, for although they had already lost much favor and authority, especially after the letter of the holy Leo to Flavian had been published throughout the world and after the ecumenical Council of Chalcedon, they nevertheless, as is characteristic of all heretics and always has been, did not cease to proclaim their error.

When he turns his speech to the Nestorian heresy, however, he says that the Nestorians no longer speak openly but whisper in the ears, and indeed not without a certain caution and hesitation, trying to proceed secretly and gradually, as do those who are less confident and who approach someone with fear concerning some matter. Such people do not do this immediately or at just any time, but when the opportunity of person, place, and time is given.

What does this mean? Clearly, the Nestorians lost their strength immediately after the Eutychian heresy arose, since they had both the Catholics and the Eutychians against them: the Catholics, because of the integrity of the faith, which they defended against [Col. 0931B] every heresy; and the Eutychians, because of the very character of their new error, which arose from an excessive and imprudent zeal in attacking the Nestorian heresy.

Once the Eutychian heresy had arisen, therefore, the Nestorian heresy had lost its strength and no longer dared to reveal itself as before. What could Nestorianism then have dared to do in the Catholic world, when Catholics themselves—those same vigorous defenders of Catholic truth against the attempts of Eutyches—were everywhere most shamelessly accused by the Eutychians of Nestorianism, as is well known to all who are acquainted with the history of those times and errors?

Nicetas therefore did not distinguish the conduct of the Eutychians from that of the Nestorians without reason: the former openly declared their particular error, while the latter attempted to whisper it in people’s ears. This difference in their manner of expression in the *Explanation of the Symbol addressed to the candidates*, with respect to the Nestorian and Eutychian errors; this apparent reversal of order in [Col. 0931C] describing the two; this greater force and intensity in refuting the latter—all these things, I say, wonderfully prove and confirm that Nicetas, the author of this *Explanation*, properly belonged to the period in which the Eutychian heresy had to be overthrown with greater force. Accordingly, this Nicetas is in reality our Nicetas of Aquileia, as the title of the little work in the Roman Ghislieri codex indicates: namely, the Nicetas who ascended the episcopal throne of Aquileia in 454, who therefore lived in the age of Leo the Great, and to whom a decretal letter of that holy pontiff is extant.

Why should not this same manner of speaking also indicate the first years of Nicetas’s episcopate, as we suggested earlier? At that time Eutychianism was still being defended with greater obstinacy by its first advocates and propagators, while Nestorianism—which was by no means extinguished and later recovered its strength—was then, as though yielding to circumstances, forced to lie concealed. But we must hasten to other matters that will confirm more and more strongly what has been said.

[Col. 0931D] In that *Explanation of the Symbol* we possess not only features that in some way indicate the period of Nicetas of Aquileia, as we have already seen, but also features showing that the little work is a product of the Church of Aquileia. I do not wish to appear overconfident in first undertaking to show that this little work is a product of the Church of Aquileia from the very point from which the most distinguished Zabeus affirmed in his dissertation that it was not. In part II, no. 3 and following, of his dissertation, that learned man endeavored at length to prove that the *Explanation of the Symbol* was not a product of the Church of Aquileia because that Nicetas did not undertake to explain the particular Symbol of the Church of Aquileia, but the common ancient Symbol of the Roman Church, with the addition of the word “catholic” to “Church” and of the final article, “life everlasting.”

I, however, argue that the *Explanation* is a product of the Church of Aquileia because clear traces [Col. 0932A] of the distinctive Aquileian Symbol appear in it. The matter must therefore be examined closely.

What the distinctive Symbol of the Aquileians was, as distinguished from the Roman—or rather, what distinctive additions the Aquileians made to the Roman Symbol—we learn from Rufinus of Aquileia in his celebrated *Commentary on the Apostles’ Creed*, which antiquity commended with so many praises; and also from Fontanini’s *Literary History of Aquileia*, book V, chapter 14; from De Rubeis’s *Monuments of the Church of Aquileia*, chapter 7; from his work *On Liturgical and Other Sacred Rites*, etc., chapter 8; and from his dissertation *Various Learning*, chapter 2.

There were three such Aquileian additions to the Roman Symbol. The first consisted of the words “invisible” and “impassible,” added to “God the Father almighty.” The second was “he descended into hell,” added after “crucified and buried” in reference to Jesus Christ. The third was the word “this,” added to “the resurrection of the flesh”; for they said, “the resurrection of this flesh.” These additions were accompanied by some less significant variation, such as “I believe in God the Father” instead of “I believe in God the Father” with the different case distinction in Latin—*Credo in Deo Patre* rather than *Credo in Deum Patrem*—and likewise [Col. 0932B] *in Christo Jesu* rather than *in Christum Jesum*, and so forth.

No one doubts that these three additions were in use among the Aquileians in Rufinus’s time. How long they continued after Rufinus is what must now be considered.

The most distinguished investigator of the affairs and antiquities of the Church of Aquileia, Bernardus Maria De Rubeis, whom Zabeus very frequently and deservedly praises, holds that in the sixth and even the fifth century, especially in public explanations of the Symbol during examinations, the Roman Symbol may have prevailed completely even among the Aquileians, without the three additions we have mentioned.

> “Once the additions have been set aside,” he says in his dissertation *Various Learning*, chapter 2, no. 5, “I have no doubt that the simpler formula of the Roman Church prevailed in the Church of Aquileia; and this is inferred from a remarkable ancient monument, namely, the Aquileian examination of catechumens. It has been published in print in my cited dissertation [Col. 0932C] on liturgical and other sacred rites, chapters 9 and 11, and elsewhere.””

From this examination at Aquileia, he says, two explanations of the Symbol are extant, belonging to the final examination, as he calls it: one brief and the other more extensive. Neither of them displays the additions noted by Rufinus. After the more extensive explanation, which he presents in full and which he supposes to have been composed by Saint Peter Chrysologus, he adds:

> “The more attentively I consider this explanation of the Symbol in the Aquileian examination, the more inclined I am to think that it could occupy a place among the sermons of the same Chrysologus and be regarded as an unpublished sermon of that holy Father; for its style agrees perfectly. I must therefore conclude that this explanation of the Symbol, and the Roman Symbol that it explains, may already have been in use in the Church of Aquileia in the fifth or sixth century.”

Now, if Saint Peter Chrysologus began his episcopate in the year of Christ 439 or 440—the last year of Pope Sixtus III, in which Saint Peter is said to have been elected and ordained to the see of [Col. 0932D] Ravenna, according to the distinguished Abbot Bacchini in dissertation 3, part II, no. 6, of his *Agnellus*, and in his observations on the *Life of Saint Peter Chrysologus—and if we suppose that he continued to live until the year 451, as has been stated elsewhere on the authority of the same Bacchini, that more extensive explanation of the Symbol could already have been in use among the Aquileians in the examinations of catechumens several years before the episcopate of Nicetas of Aquileia—that is, while his predecessor Secundus was seated in the see—and even several years before the devastation of Aquileia by Attila.

If these things are true, there is therefore no reason for Zabeus to deny that the *Explanation of the Symbol of Bishop Nicetas* could be a product of Bishop Nicetas of Aquileia merely because it explains not the Aquileian Symbol with its three additions but the common Roman Symbol.

But what if the Roman [Col. 0933A] Symbol probably began to prevail in the Church of Aquileia much earlier than the time of Nicetas, while those three additions, together with a few other variants, gradually fell into disuse? In the Maurist edition of Augustine’s works there is a sermon numbered 242, placed in the Appendix for the first time. In earlier editions it had occupied a place among the other genuine sermons under Augustine’s name. This sermon is about the Symbol. After a brief preface, it also presents the Symbol itself in full before undertaking to explain it in sections.

What is distinctive about this Symbol is that, although it almost entirely agrees with the ancient Roman Symbol—with the addition of the word “catholic” to “Church,” the final article “life everlasting,” and certain other wording found in the present Apostles’ Creed, which may perhaps have been inserted from memory by a later copyist’s careless pen—it nevertheless contains two of the three distinctive additions of the Aquileian Symbol that we have noted: “he descended into hell” and “the resurrection of this flesh.” It omits [Col. 0933B] the earlier addition, “invisible and impassible,” and likewise leaves aside the slight variation noted above, namely, the use of the ablative case instead of the accusative, which existed in the Aquileian formula.

Since this sermon is not by Augustine, bishop of Hippo, as the common judgment of scholars establishes, why should it not have belonged, at least in part, to Augustine, bishop of Aquileia, who succeeded Saint Chromatius in the episcopate and who lived in the time of that same Saint Augustine, bishop of Hippo? Certainly this would not be the first confusion to have arisen from the coincidence of name and period. Indeed, to take an example from the very matter before us, Augustine of Hippo himself was believed to be the Augustine to whom a certain book of the Pelagians’ faith is recorded as having been presented. That work was published in the Augustinian appendices, and according to the judgment of learned men reported by De Rubeis—and according to the judgment of that most distinguished man himself in the *Monuments of the Church of Aquileia*, chapter 14—it was in reality presented to Augustine, bishop of Aquileia and successor of Saint Chromatius, by [Col. 0933C] presbyters and others of the clergy of the province of Aquileia who had been infected with the Pelagian stain and were refusing to subscribe to the *tractoria* or *tractatoria* letter of Pope Zosimus, in which Pelagius and Coelestius had been condemned.

If that sermon belongs to Augustine, bishop of Aquileia, as those two distinctive Aquileian traces suggest, then already in the time of this Augustine—at the very beginning of the fifth century, and shortly before or shortly after the death of Rufinus, who died at the age of seventy in Sicily in the year 410, as we learn from Fontanini’s life of him—the practice began in the Church of Aquileia of delivering and explaining the Roman Symbol, with the ancient Aquileian formula set aside. It began, however, not all at once, so to speak, but gradually, since here only one of the Aquileian additions appears to have been omitted, whereas in the other explanations of the Symbol that occur in the Aquileian examination of catechumens mentioned above—both the brief and the more extensive, which could have prevailed in the Church of Aquileia around the middle of the same fifth century—all three additions had completely disappeared.

What may now be inferred from these considerations is that, in the time of Nicetas of Aquileia, the ancient formula of the Aquileian Symbol, with its three additions, had [Col. 0933D] undoubtedly fallen entirely into disuse, at least in public explanations of the Symbol. Consequently, Zabeus does not correctly infer that the *Explanation of the Symbol*, recently brought to light under the name of Bishop Nicetas of Aquileia from the Roman Ghislieri codex, cannot be a product of the Church of Aquileia because it presents not the ancient Aquileian formula with its three additions but the Roman one throughout.

Someone might perhaps object: if Zabeus is wrong to conjecture that the *Explanation of the Symbol* recently brought to light from the Roman codex cannot be a product of the Church of Aquileia because it gives the Roman rather than that ancient Aquileian Symbol to the candidates, how can anyone infer that the *Explanation* truly [Col. 0934A] is a product of the Church of Aquileia because clear traces of the distinctive Aquileian Symbol appear in it?

This is precisely what must now be noted, in order to show that the *Explanation of the Symbol* truly is a product of the Church of Aquileia. For it is one thing for the ancient practice of delivering and explaining the Symbol according to the old Aquileian formula, with the three additions distinctive of the Church of Aquileia, not to have remained in force in the time of Nicetas of Aquileia; and another thing for certain traces of the ancient Aquileian Symbol still to have existed in the time of Nicetas of Aquileia, traces by which a work could be recognized as truly an Aquileian product, provided that nothing else made it impossible to ascribe it to that Church and that it was otherwise shown to fit it. This is what I meant when I said that I would show the *Explanation of the Symbol addressed to the candidates* to be a product of the Church of Aquileia from the very point from which the most distinguished Zabeus affirmed that it was not.

Even if it had not been sufficiently proved from the foregoing that the ancient formula of the Symbol was not abandoned all at once but gradually in [Col. 0934B] the public explanations of the Symbol in the Church of Aquileia, I shall confidently add that this may be inferred by conjecture almost to the force of proof. Even if this were not fully evident from what has been said, the very nature of such matters would teach us so. From that nature we learn that in such cases one must always proceed gradually, in order to avoid the offenses often provoked by innovations introduced suddenly, as though forcefully imposed upon public opinion and public instruction.

Who, then, would not understand that the ancient Aquileian formula of the Symbol, together with its additions, must have continued among the Aquileians for a long time, even if it was no longer publicly transmitted in ecclesiastical instruction? Thus the old formula would at least have continued to be recited privately by those who had received baptism especially in Rufinus’s time and who were still alive under Chromatius, Augustine, and perhaps other bishops; and it would have been taught by them to their sons and grandsons for memorization. In this way, [Col. 0934C] during those early periods, the descendants would have known both formulas perfectly and would have used either one at will.

We may reasonably conjecture that this is what then occurred, since in our own age we have seen something similar—not at one time only or in one place only—if not with respect to the formula of the Apostles’ Creed, which has remained the same for centuries, then certainly with respect to those professions of faith circulated both in Italian and in the vernacular, commonly called “acts of faith.” These were later issued in shorter form to assist the memory of less educated people than the forms recited by our fathers and grandfathers from the famous and widespread Christian instruction of the venerable Bellarmine.

What happened as a result? The old acts of faith continued to live on the lips of our fathers and grandfathers, who had learned them from childhood; many people afterward learned both the old and the new; and finally, even after the new forms had become generally prevalent, the old ones did not entirely fall into oblivion. This is known to everyone.

[Col. 0934D] Nothing, therefore, is more consistent with the nature of such matters than that, once the Roman Symbol had been introduced for public use in the Church of Aquileia, its ancient Symbol with its additions should still have remained on the lips of the Aquileians, and that those three additions should have been known to everyone and even commonly used as a kind of clearer explanation of the Roman formula.

If we readily understand that this could have remained in use among private individuals, why should it not also have existed—or even deliberately been maintained—among the prelates of the Church of Aquileia in the explanations of the Symbol that they publicly gave for the instruction of catechumens or candidates? Wherever such traces of the Aquileian Symbol appear in explanations of the Symbol that transmit the Roman Symbol itself, those explanations may rightly be considered products of the Church of Aquileia. They possess, so to speak, a certain form and a kind of face that indicates the stock from which they derive.

[Col. 0935A] What, then, appears in the *Explanation* of our Nicetas that can be considered a trace of the ancient Aquileian Symbol, so that from it we may infer that the *Explanation* truly is a product of the Church of Aquileia?

From the first addition of the Aquileian Symbol, for the sake of easier understanding and fuller explanation, the word “invisible” appears in reference to God the Father in chapter 2. Likewise, the word “impassible” appears in chapter 5, where we read:

> “For God is always impassible.”

Zabeus did not notice this latter word as used by Nicetas in the *Explanation*. Indeed, in part II, no. 6, of his dissertation he wrote that this word “impassible” is not even mentioned there.

From the third addition, our *Explanation* certainly does not contain the exact word “this” in “the resurrection of the flesh.” But it contains twice the word “your”—that is, “the resurrection of your flesh”—in chapters 12 and 13, as required by the connection and character of the discourse. There, the individual hearers were addressed one by one by the bishop, as it were. Everyone can see that the word “your,” placed there, derives from the word “this” in the Aquileian Symbol and is used in the *Explanation* for the same reason: so that the Aquileians, drawing from the treasury of their own Church and from an addition well known to them, might grasp more easily and more deeply the force of the article concerning the resurrection of the flesh.

The traces of the ancient Symbol of the Church of Aquileia therefore appear sufficiently in the *Explanation of Bishop Nicetas* for us to infer that the *Explanation* is a product of the Church of Aquileia and consequently reveals its author to be our Nicetas of Aquileia, as the title of the little work indicates.

The most distinguished Zabeus also understood something of the force of these Aquileian traces in the cited passage of his dissertation and in the following no. 9. But since he was persuaded that an Aquileian bishop, without regard to differences of period, ought to have transmitted the Aquileian Symbol rather than the Roman, he thought he could easily dispose of this objection by asserting that the word “invisible”—the only word connected with God that he himself noticed there as coming from the Aquileian Symbol—and also the other word “your,” used in reference to the resurrection of the flesh, had not been employed by Nicetas in his *Explanation* according to the intention of that same Aquileian Symbol or for the reasons on account of which, as Rufinus said, they had been introduced into the Symbol by our ancestors. He did not fail to support this also from Rufinus’s own *Commentary*, which indeed conveys to us there the rationale of the Aquileian additions.

But if, in the time of Nicetas of Aquileia, the public use of the Aquileian Symbol had fallen into disuse in the Church of Aquileia, then those reasons for which the additions themselves had originally been introduced into the Symbol by their ancestors no longer existed in the Church of Aquileia. Consequently, there was no reason why Nicetas, in inserting into his *Explanation* those traces of the Aquileian Symbol, should have directed his attention to the reasons that, according to Rufinus, had originally occasioned these additions among the ancestors of the Aquileians of his own time.

Rufinus’s name here reminds us that, while we assert that the [Col. 0935D] Explanation of the Creed by Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, is a product of the Church of Aquileia because it exhibits traces of the ancient Aquileian Creed, even though that Creed had by then already ceased to be publicly used, Rufinus’s name, I say, reminds us not to omit this further way of strengthening our argument: that the Explanation contains many passages entirely conformable to Rufinus’s Commentary, and conformable in such a way that one could easily persuade oneself that Nicetas, the bishop, derived them from it.

### 68

Accordingly, before saying something about Rufinus of Aquileia’s Commentary on the Creed, we should not neglect the testimony of Gennadius, who asserted that in those ancient times that Commentary was held in such high esteem that, by comparison with it, other writers are scarcely thought to have expounded the Creed at all (*On Illustrious Men*, chapter 17). It also contributes to the praise of this work of Rufinus that it was at one time considered worthy of being counted among the writings of Cyprian and Jerome.

No writer has preserved any reliable information as to in what year, or in what place, Rufinus published that Commentary, since he spent most of his life abroad. Who, however, was that Laurence, the pope—that is, bishop—to whom Rufinus dedicated his Commentary? Although this cannot be established with certainty, the conjecture of the most distinguished Fontanini (*Literary History of Aquileia*, book V, chapter 14, no. 1) [Col. 0936A] nevertheless seems to me by no means contemptible: namely, that he was one of the bishops assigned to the metropolitan church of Aquileia, perhaps the bishop of Concordia, whose see is vacant in Ughelli before the sixth century.

That learned prelate infers this from the expressions Rufinus uses in his Commentary. These seem to indicate that both Rufinus and the man to whom he dedicated the work belonged to the same Church of Aquileia. Thus, for example, in no. 6, where he discusses the words “invisible” and “impassible,” used in the Creed among the Aquileians, he says:

> “It is established among us that these expressions were added on account of the heresy of Sabellius, that heresy, certainly, which is called Patripassian by our people.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Therefore, in order to exclude such impiety concerning the Father, our forefathers seem to have added these words.”

Similarly, in no. [Col. 0936B] 43, where he presents the Aquileian addition of the expression “the resurrection of the flesh,” he says:

> “With sufficient caution our Church teaches the faith of the Creed: whereas what is handed down by the others is ‘the resurrection of the flesh,’ she has handed down, by adding a single pronoun, ‘the resurrection of this flesh.’”

What else can “our Church” here mean than the Church of Rufinus and, at the same time, of Laurence, to whom Rufinus was writing? What else can “among us” and “our forefathers” mean there—Aquileians, plainly, and not others, as the text shows—if Laurence did not belong to the same people as Rufinus, and if Laurence too did not have, in the Church of Aquileia, the same forefathers as Rufinus?

I am not unaware that the most distinguished De Rubeis is less favorably disposed toward conjectures of this sort by Fontanini, in his *Dissertations in Various Learning*, chapter 3. He argues that the expressions quoted from Rufinus can stand even without reference to Laurence, and that the same modes of expression are familiar to Rufinus in the same Commentary even where they cannot be referred particularly to the Church of Aquileia.

With due respect, however, to so great a man, [Col. 0936C] these considerations do not seem to me capable of entirely weakening Fontanini’s conjecture—which is, after all, a conjecture. Nor does it matter that Rufinus’s expressions could stand without reference to Laurence, provided that in reality they fit much better if they are also referred to him, as anyone reading them can see. It is also sufficiently well known that expressions, even when familiar to a given author, always derive from their context a force by which they are understood one way in one place and another way elsewhere, without any ambiguity. Consequently, conjectures are not thereby weakened when critics derive them, in the absence of more compelling evidence, from modes of expression encountered in various passages.

With regard to Rufinus’s Commentary, we should further note here, together with De Rubeis in the place cited, that in the sixth century Venantius Fortunatus, in his *Exposition of the Creed*, which stands at the beginning of book XI of his *Poems and Proses*, borrowed from Rufinus of Aquileia what he wrote there in such a way that he seems deliberately to have condensed Rufinus’s Commentary itself [Col. 0936D]. The same distinguished scholar also demonstrated this by collating the passages in the same place.

### 69

Now, to approach our subject: it must indeed be admitted that the argument would not be conclusive for proving that the Explanation of the Creed by Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, is a product of the Church of Aquileia merely because certain passages appearing here and there in it conform to the Commentary of Rufinus of Aquileia. Rufinus’s Commentary was not known exclusively to Aquileian bishops, so that only they could have used it; nor was it so peculiar to the Church of Aquileia that other bishops could not also have used it if they wished.

Nevertheless, after what has so far been said about our Nicetas’s Explanation—considerations which demonstrate from more than one standpoint that it is a product of the Church of Aquileia—who will deny that the agreement of subject matter, ideas, and words detected between the Explanation of the Creed by Nicetas, [Col. 0937A] bishop of Aquileia, and the Commentary on the Creed by Rufinus of Aquileia increasingly confirms that the Explanation may truly be regarded as the work of some Aquileian bishop, and therefore, beyond doubt, of the man whose name it bears?

There can be no doubt that Rufinus of Aquileia’s Commentary on the Creed became known in the Church of Aquileia from the beginning. There is even less reason for doubt if we suppose that Rufinus wrote that Commentary while living at Aquileia under Bishop Chromatius, and that the Laurence to whom he dedicated it belonged to the Church of Aquileia.

Moreover, even if Rufinus wrote his Commentary at a great distance from the city of Aquileia, and dedicated it to that Laurence, who perhaps was not an Aquileian, two things can scarcely be imagined: either that the Church of Aquileia failed to acquire so distinguished a work by her son and presbyter, one that expounded the Christian faith’s Creed and offered such illustrious testimony to the Aquileian additions; or that Rufinus himself did not promptly send it [Col. 0937B] to the Aquileian Church, his mother, where—as he himself testifies in book I, chapter 4, of his *Apology*—while living there as a monk under Bishop Valerian, he had been regenerated through the grace of baptism and received the seal of faith, and where he proudly declared that he had had as father and teacher of the Creed and the faith a deacon of that very Church, a man of the highest reputation.

Furthermore, if Rufinus composed that work before the year 407, while Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia, was still alive and with whom Rufinus enjoyed the closest friendship—that is, if he composed it, wherever he may have been, before that date, as seems more probable—it is scarcely credible that Rufinus’s Commentary did not immediately become known to the Aquileians, at least through the efforts of Chromatius himself.

That Rufinus’s Commentary became known to the Aquileians, and that at the same time the Aquileian bishops used it as the most complete and approved exposition of the Creed—perhaps the only work of its kind then existing in the Western Church—is very easy to understand for those who are not unaware of Rufinus’s reputation, which he enjoyed even during his lifetime [Col. 0937C] among the more eminent men of his age, and especially among the clergy of the Church of Aquileia. According to Jerome’s own testimony, that clergy flourished at that time with such distinction in learning and holiness, notwithstanding the disagreement between Jerome and Rufinus over the works of Origen, a matter about which scholars have so extensively debated on both sides.

And if, even in the sixth century, Venantius Fortunatus—not indeed an Aquileian, although by birth a neighbor of the Aquileian province—drew from Rufinus’s Commentary the material from which he composed his own Exposition of the Creed, perhaps while he was in Gaul, what would the Aquileians themselves not have done in the fifth century? They could rightly glory, above the other Churches of the West, in so distinguished a Commentary on the Creed by one of their own presbyters.

We must now proceed [70] to a comparison of the passages between Nicetas and Rufinus. “Confession begins well with belief,” Nicetas says in his *Explanation of the Creed*, chapter 2. “Nothing can be done in life unless belief has first preceded it,” Rufinus said in no. [Col. 0937D] 3 of his *Commentary on the Creed*; and both writers are explaining the same first word of the Creed, *I believe*.

Nicetas continues in the same place:

> “You believe, therefore, in God the Father almighty: God unbegotten, who derives his origin from no one and began from no one; God invisible, whom no eye of flesh is sufficient to see; God incomprehensible, who comprehends all things; God unchangeable, who is not changed by time and does not grow old with age, but is always the same. He did not begin to live in time, but, always living, suffers no successor.”

What does Rufinus say? In no. 4 of his *Commentary* he stated:

> “When you hear ‘God,’ understand a substance without beginning or end, simple, without any admixture, invisible, incorporeal, ineffable, beyond estimation, in which there is nothing added and nothing created. For he who is altogether the author of all things exists without an author.”

Nicetas continues in the same place:

> “You confess this one to be God, but you also confess him to be Father. He must [Col. 0938A] be the Father of a Son, for no one is a father without a son. The Father, therefore, exists through the Son, possessing a Son of whom he is Father.”

Rufinus had anticipated this in almost the same words, in the same no. 4, saying:

> “When you hear ‘Father,’ understand the Father of the Son [lacuna] for just as no one is called lord, etc. [lacuna] so no one can in any way be called father unless he has a son. Therefore, by the very name by which God is called Father, the Son too is shown to subsist together with the Father.”

Again, Nicetas says in chapter 3:

> “Jesus, interpreted in the language of the Hebrews, means ‘Savior.’ Christ, however, is a designation of royal dignity: thus Savior and King, one and the same, is Christ Jesus.”

Rufinus had written in no. 6 of his *Commentary*:

> “Jesus is a name of Hebrew origin, which among us is called ‘Savior.’ Christ is called from *chrisma*, that is, from anointing . . . Christ is also either a priestly or a royal name.”

In chapter 5 of his *Explanation*, Nicetas spoke as follows about the Lord’s passion:

> “And see that you are not ashamed at the passion of your Lord . . . Nor is there any reason for you to be confounded if you understand in what sacramental manner [Col. 0938B] Christ suffered. He suffered not in his divinity, but in the flesh.”

Rufinus had said the following about the same passion, earlier than Nicetas, in nos. 16 and 17 of his *Commentary*:

> “But perhaps someone is frightened by this kind of teaching: that the one whom a little earlier we said was eternal with God the Father and begotten from his substance [lacuna] we now discuss in relation to his death. But I do not want you to be frightened, faithful hearer, etc. [lacuna] Christ therefore suffers in the flesh without any harm or injury to his divinity, etc.”

Nicetas says the following about the Holy Spirit in chapter 7:

> “This Holy Spirit is one, sanctifying all things . . . He appointed the prophets and filled the apostles.”

In no. 35 of his *Commentary*, Rufinus had written about the same Holy Spirit:

> “This Holy Spirit [lacuna] sanctifying all things;”

and in no. [Col. 0938C] 36:

> “This is the Holy Spirit who in the Old Testament inspired the Law and the prophets, and in the New, the Gospels and the apostles.”

Nicetas says the following about the holy Church in chapter 10:

> “What else is the Church than the assembly of all the saints?”

And Rufinus had written in no. 36 of his *Commentary*:

> “The holy Church is to be believed, not as God, but as the Church gathered by God.”

Nicetas continues in the same chapter:

> “There are indeed other false churches, but you have nothing in common with them—for example, those of the Manichaeans, the Cataphrygians, the Marcionites, or the other heretics and schismatics, because these churches are already ceasing to be holy.”

Rufinus had also anticipated this in no. 39, though he pursued the matter more extensively in accordance with the purpose of his work:

> “For many others too have gathered churches, such as Marcion, Valentinus, Ebion, Manichaeus, Arius, and all the other heretics. But those churches are not without stain or wrinkle of unbelief [lacuna] For the assembly which Marcion conducts is an assembly of vanity, etc.”

In chapter 12, Nicetas instructed his catechumens concerning the resurrection of the flesh as follows:

> “Consequently, you also believe in the resurrection of your flesh;”

and in chapter 13:

> “You who believe in Christ profess the resurrection of your flesh.”

Rufinus had written in no. 43 of his *Commentary*:

> “Without doubt, of this flesh, which the one who professes possesses [lacuna] so that each of the faithful [Col. 0938D] may know that his flesh, if he keeps it pure from sin, will become a vessel of honor.”

Nicetas gave the following warning about the same matter in chapter 13:

> “There are indeed many heretics who distort the faith in the resurrection, claiming salvation for the soul alone while denying the resurrection of the flesh. But you who believe in Christ profess the resurrection of your flesh. For Christ both died and rose again for this purpose: that he might be Lord of the living and of the dead.”

By the word “living,” Nicetas understood souls, and by the word “dead,” bodies. He proved the resurrection of the flesh from the authority of the Apostle which he cited in Romans 14, against those who admitted salvation for the soul alone while denying the resurrection of the flesh.

In this interpretation of souls and bodies by the words “living” and “dead,” Rufinus had preceded Nicetas. Rufinus, however, wished to understand the living as souls and the dead as bodies—not in order to establish the resurrection of the flesh, but to explain, in a singular manner of interpretation, the final judgment of the living and the dead. In no. [Col. 0939A] 33 of his *Commentary* he says:

> “When it is said that he will judge the living and the dead, this is not said because some living and others dead will come to judgment, but because he will judge souls and bodies together; and by ‘living’ he named souls, and by ‘dead,’ bodies.”

Thus far Nicetas and Rufinus have been compared together.

To meet an objection that might be raised: it must certainly not be denied that, in the same subject—especially in an exposition of the Creed—it is easy for authors to agree with one another not only in ideas but sometimes to some extent even in words, although one has never seen the other. This does not, however, usually happen frequently; it occurs only occasionally. Nor does one find in the same work a kind of sequence of matters that provides, so to speak, a continuous parallel with another work on the same subject. For this reason I have not compared only one or two passages of Nicetas with Rufinus, but deliberately selected many.

It is therefore plainly evident that these writers [Col. 0939B] agreed with one another in matters, ideas, and even words—not ambiguously or by mere chance, but as a result of a kind of correspondence in their subject matter—and that Nicetas actually transferred much from Rufinus’s Commentary, as from a fuller and more complete treatise, into his own *Explanation of the Creed for Candidates for Baptism* for the instruction of candidates for baptism. He nevertheless preserved, along with the brevity of expression required by the place and occasion, the simplicity and polish of his own style. These two qualities are not found to the same degree in Rufinus, a man who, because he had spent many years in the regions of the East, was accustomed to Greek literature and had lost the use of the Latin language through so many years that, as he himself wrote to Chromatius of Aquileia in the preface to his Latin translation of Eusebius’s *History*, which he had undertaken at Chromatius’s urging, he spoke of his diminished command of Latin.

### 72

What, then, should we conclude concerning our subject? In the preceding chapter we already proved, from the error of Eutyches clearly mentioned and refuted in the little work *Explanation of the Creed for Candidates for Baptism*, as well as from the known period of Paulinus, bishop of Nola, [Col. 0939C] and from the material we added in the appendix, that Niceas or Nicetas, bishop of the city of Romatiana, mentioned by Gennadius, was not that Niceas or Nicetas the Dacian who was a friend of the same Saint Paulinus and celebrated by him in his praises.

Since it is now additionally clear that, concerning the author of that little work, there is no reason for us to depart from the authority of the Roman Ghisian codex—the sole source from which we possess the work—and to accept Nicetas the Dacian, or anyone else, in place of the Nicetas who is there written as bishop of Aquileia; since the title of the work contains nothing that suggests interpolation or error, and indeed displays throughout the marks of a fifth-century date, when one Nicetas could not so easily have been written for another; since the work itself unmistakably indicates the period of Nicetas of Aquileia and also contains other features showing it to be a product of the Church of Aquileia; and since all this is reinforced by the work’s clear agreement in subject matter, ideas, and words with the Commentary on the same subject by Rufinus, presbyter of Aquileia [Col. 0939D]—it follows that the Niceas or Nicetas, bishop of the city of Romatiana, mentioned by Gennadius, was beyond doubt Niceas or Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia: namely, the man who flourished in the time of Saint Leo the Great and to whom a letter of that holy pontiff is extant.

This was what had to be demonstrated in this fourth chapter of the dissertation.

## APPENDIX TO CHAPTER FOUR

For the sake of further clarification, I wish nevertheless to add to this chapter an appendix which may perhaps not be unwelcome to readers. They may reasonably say that up to this point they have learned many things relevant to the proposed subject from the little work *Explanation of the Creed for Candidates for Baptism*, but nothing from the other work *To the Fallen Virgin*, or *On the Fall of a Consecrated Virgin*. Yet since this too is by the same author, as was demonstrated in chapter 1, it may easily contain something that reveals the Aquileian see of its [Col. 0940A] author. So indeed it seems to me, unless my opinion deceives me; and this is what must now be examined.

The first things that present themselves to a reader of the little work *To the Fallen Virgin* are those which not only provide an excellent example of the well-ordered and flourishing Church of the place where the author exercised his episcopate—evidenced, namely, by the solemn assembly of the Church of God on the holy day of the Lord’s Resurrection, by the light of the vigils, by the singing of spiritual hymns, and so forth—but also specifically mention a community of sacred virgins established there. These women, solemnly dedicated to God and professing virginity, were nurtured by the bishop’s particular care and brought honor to the Church of God through their reputation for piety and holiness.

All the learned men who have sought to illuminate the subject of communities of sacred virgins existing in the Western Church during the early centuries of the Church drew from this work *To the Fallen Virgin* much of what concerned their institution: the rite of veiling, their clothing, their procession into the Church, and other matters of this kind.

In this work, at no. 28, [73] we find a virginal monastery indicated [Col. 0940B], to which the sacred virgins went to live after leaving their father’s house behind. From no. 12, we may readily infer that it was located in the middle of the city, at least in the case of the virgins about whom our work speaks.

From nos. 19 and 20 we learn that the holy day of the Lord’s Resurrection was assigned for the consecration of virgins. On that day they offered themselves at the divine altar among the lights of the newly baptized and among the candidates for the heavenly kingdom; after the bishop had addressed them, they were covered with the sacred veil, while all the people cried out, “Amen.”

The virginal habit is also indicated in no. 22, as is the procession of the virginal choir into the Church for the nocturnal vigils, the singing of spiritual hymns, and the heavenly readings.

In no. 24 we are also informed that this community of sacred virgins had a place in the church separated by screens. There they stood, segregated from the other faithful as a mark of honor. Religious and noble matrons also hastened eagerly [Col. 0940C] to that place to seek their kisses. On the wall, before the eyes of the virgins, were written commandments taken from the holy apostle Paul and concerning virgins and virginity.

Finally, from nos. 28 and 29 it is clear that the bishop showed particular solicitude toward this virginal community: both in the spiritual love there indicated and in his holy admonition, as well as in his exposition of the hymn of virginity, in which they were to sing alike the glory of their calling and the observance it required.

These are the features found in the work *To the Fallen Virgin* concerning the community of sacred virgins established there, all of which were said in order more effectively to rebuke the fallen virgin. They are truly splendid evidence for forming an exalted conception of the condition of that Church in which such an institution flourished with such orderly arrangement and such disciplined cultivation.

Was this community of sacred virgins, gathered in a virginal monastery and instructed in the discipline that we have seen expressed in our work, established under that Niceas or Nicetas who was bishop in Transdanubian Dacia, the man of whom we spoke above?

There is certainly nothing [Col. 0940D] in Paulinus of Nola about such a community of sacred virgins in the care of his Nicetas in Dacia. Yet Paulinus sings of so many and such remarkable things concerning the Christian cause in his poem entitled *To Nicetas Returning to Dacia*, as we saw in chapter 3. Since the holy Fathers of the Church considered consecrated virgins one of the Church’s principal ornaments, measuring the merit of virginity by divine praises, if such an institution had flourished under the episcopal care of Nicetas the Dacian, Paulinus would certainly not have been silent about it. Yet, in his great praise of Nicetas, he did not fail to mention both brigands converted to monks who lived in the mountains and the hidden righteous man in whose caves the former robber had lived, as we learn from the passages of the same poem cited there.

Moreover, what place would there have been in Dacia beyond the Danube—called by Paulinus a silent region of the world—for such expressions as “noble matrons” seeking the kisses of sacred virgins? What place, [Col. 0941A] among the Dacians, Bessi, Getae, and Scythians, where, according to the same testimony, the way of life had once been that of beasts before Nicetas’s preaching?

These are not expressions belonging to barbarian peoples who had scarcely laid aside their animal-like customs, but expressions belonging to the Roman world. Nicetas the Dacian would have used them with still less appropriateness in those regions beyond the Danube, even if some distinction of families and social orders had actually existed among those peoples. Such a distinction, however, being always far removed from Roman customs and institutions, would not have been expressed in Roman language.

These considerations plainly teach us that the work or booklet *To the Fallen Virgin*, of which we are now speaking, cannot belong to Nicetas the Dacian. At the same time, they sufficiently show that the work is certainly by Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, if we also recall what we proved earlier: namely, that this little work is genuinely by the same author as the other *Explanation of the Creed for Candidates for Baptism*; that, just as that Explanation is foreign to the period of Nicetas the Dacian, so it accords with the period of Nicetas of Aquileia; and that it bears the distinctive [Col. 0941B] mark of the Church of Aquileia.

What is most important for us in this appendix, however, is the evidence that can be detected in this same work, through which its Aquileian origin, even if it does not clearly emerge, may at least be recognized to some extent.

There is abundant general evidence. Who would not understand that the bishop who rebukes the fallen virgin in this work presided over a long-established Church, one that, through the merit of its earlier bishops, had grown into such an extraordinary splendor of form that it equaled the more distinguished Churches of the world?

What we have reported above about the virginal monastery situated in the city; what we have said about the rite and form of veiling virgins; and what we have said about their clothing, their procession, and their place within the church—all these things amply prove what we are asserting.

Who could doubt that in the time of our Nicetas the Church of Aquileia was such a Church, shaped by the care of the holy bishops Valerian, Chromatius, and others, and elevated through their merit to the dignity of a metropolitan see?

It is certainly established from Saint Jerome himself, an eyewitness, in his *Chronicle*, and from Rufinus in book I, no. 4, of his *Apology*, that already in the fourth [Col. 0941C] century, or at the beginning of the fifth, there existed in the Church of Aquileia a highly celebrated community of clergy, worthy of being praised above others by Saint Jerome, and from which later emerged bishops of the highest reputation and excellence, appointed to govern other Churches as well.

We likewise learn from Jerome and Rufinus that, at the same time, a most distinguished monastery of men flourished at Aquileia. There Rufinus himself and Jerome for some time honored one another through their mutual services and vied with each other in piety and learning. Other highly esteemed men also distinguished themselves there, mentioned by Saint Jerome in his letters: Chrysogonus and Heliodorus, one of whom later became bishop of Altinum.

Nor did virtue shine less brightly among Aquileian women in the same period. There were women who guarded their commitment to virginity in their own homes and thus aspired to the better gifts, as we learn from Saint Jerome’s Letter 7. In it, the brothers Chromatius and Eusebius, together with their friend Jovinus, their mother, and their virgin sisters, all living holy lives in [Col. 0941D] the same house, are extolled with deserved praise.

Why, then, should a virginal monastery not also have existed in the Church of Aquileia at that time, established to receive and nurture virgins who would be covered by the bishop with a sacred veil according to a special rite?

If it can be established that such a monastery existed in the Church of Aquileia, at least in the time of Nicetas, then we have the evidence we seek—indeed, distinctive evidence—so that we may judge the work *To the Fallen Virgin* from its very innermost character, so to speak, and recognize the monastic discipline of virginity detected in that work as the discipline of the sacred virgins of the Church of Aquileia.

There are indeed no surviving explicit monuments from that same period that teach us about a virginal monastery then standing in the Church of Aquileia. Nevertheless, we possess some evidence with which to make up, to a certain extent, for the lack of monuments.

Andreas Dandulus reports in his *Chronicle*, book VI, chapter 1, in Muratori’s *Scriptores rerum Italicarum*, volume XII, column 103, that Helias, the Aquileian bishop who governed that Church toward the end of the sixth century, transformed a certain pagan temple [lacuna], situated on the adjoining shore, into a monastery for girls [lacuna]. [Col. 0942A]

If an author of the fourteenth century may be trusted concerning a matter belonging to the sixth century—an author otherwise extremely weighty, approved by critical scholars, and one who may have had before his eyes many ancient documents that have not come down to us—then here is a mention of a virginal monastery in the Church of Aquileia in the century after Nicetas.

Yet this cannot be called the first foundation of a virginal monastery among the Aquileians. It was rather an addition of premises for the convenience of the sacred virgins, whose number perhaps required new buildings.

In the words cited, Dandulus seems to have attributed to Helias the conversion of a pagan temple to Christian use rather than the establishment of a monastery for girls. If Helias had truly been its first founder and originator in the Church of Aquileia, he would not have failed to indicate that in explicit terms at that point.

Let us now turn our attention to another monument—and indeed a thoroughly certain one—of that same Church of Aquileia.

The Council of Forojuli, celebrated in 796 by Saint Paulinus, patriarch of Aquileia, is extant [Col. 0942B]. It took place in the third century after the period of Nicetas of Aquileia had elapsed. It can be found in collections of councils and among the works of that holy prelate, edited by our distinguished Giovanni Francesco Madrisio, priest of the Nerian Oratory, on page 65. There, canon 11 reads:

> “It has pleased us concerning women of every condition—namely, girls or widows—who, spontaneously promising a commitment to virginity or continence, have been emancipated to God, and who, as a sign of continence, have put on a black garment, as though religious women, according to the ancient custom in these regions: although they have not been consecrated by a priest, we nevertheless command that they persevere perpetually in this commitment.”

The following canon, 12, also decreed:

> “We have deemed it right to sanction in this inviolable form that the monasteries of girls who live under a rule of discipline [Col. 0942C], fortified by more securely closed enclosures, shall be open to the entrance of no men, except perhaps when the greatest necessity compels it. But neither priests nor deacons, etc. [lacuna] Indeed, not even the bishop without his priests or clergy, etc. [lacuna] But whether it is he himself or any religious person who is deemed worthy to visit these places dedicated to God, they shall do so only with suitable witnesses, lest through incautious presumption the angelic order of the holy Church be defamed.”

From these two canons of the Church of Aquileia, issued toward the end of the eighth century, we may infer the following: that one thing existed in the Church of Aquileia—the simple commitment to virginity or continence which girls or widows voluntarily promised—and another, so to speak, solemn commitment belonging to those virgins who were consecrated by a priest, that is, by a bishop.

The assertion that this was “the ancient custom in these regions” may, without any violence, be referred to both institutions: namely, that both had flourished from ancient times in the Church of Aquileia, that is, for several centuries before Paulinus himself; and also that both institutions involved wearing a black garment as a sign of continence.

The statement that those virgins or widows mentioned in the first canon had not been consecrated by a priest [Col. 0942D] seems to suggest that, following the custom of consecrated virgins, other women who had made only a simple commitment had also adopted the black garment from ancient times, although perhaps they did not likewise use the veil. The veil belonged properly to consecrated virgins: the bishop covered them with it in the very act of consecration. It was, as it were, the matter and sign of their consecration, just as it continued to be in later times.

But what chiefly concerns the monastery is what is decreed in the other canon: namely, that the monasteries of girls who live under a rule of discipline, fortified by more securely closed enclosures, shall be open to the entrance of no men.

These girls who live under a rule of discipline are undoubtedly consecrated virgins, distinct from the other women—whether virgins or widows—mentioned in the preceding canon. The latter had made a simple commitment to [Col. 0943A] virginity or continence and, from the very distinction between these canons, do not seem to have been subject to any particular rule of discipline, but to have lived freely in their own homes.

Now, the fact that the other canon decrees that these monasteries of girls living under a rule of discipline should be fortified with more securely closed enclosures and open to the entrance of no men clearly shows that monasteries of this kind had long stood in the Church of Aquileia. At that time they were evidently not closed to everyone as they ought to have been, and their enclosures were even less securely fortified so as to be entirely inaccessible.

That monasteries of this kind had existed in the Church of Aquileia for centuries before Paulinus is shown by the very concern expressed in this canon, which undoubtedly arose from some abuse. For this is the general nature, so to speak, of abuses: they are introduced only gradually, over a long passage of time. The process must take still longer among persons, communities, and places dedicated to God, since there abuses encounter, from the institution of the places and persons themselves, a particular resistance [Col. 0943B] which they can overcome only through prolonged effort and gradual persistence.

What wonder, then, if from such canons of the Church of Aquileia, issued toward the end of the eighth century, we infer that a monastery of consecrated virgins existed in that same Church of Aquileia even in the fifth century, under the episcopate of Nicetas? And therefore, that the virginal monastery mentioned in the little work *To the Fallen Virgin* was a monastery of consecrated virgins standing in the Church of Aquileia while Nicetas was bishop; and that the little work itself bears this indication of Aquileian origin, just as it displays other indications of the same kind, which we have already seen in the other little work, the *Explanation of the Creed*?

Moreover, Saint Paulinus’s canon 12 also adds the reason for his particular concern, expressed in these words:

> “Lest through incautious presumption the angelic order of the holy Church be defamed.”

Why should the holy bishop not then have had before his eyes both the particular fall of that virgin about whom Nicetas wrote and the little work of rebuke composed [Col. 0943C] by his predecessor? In that work the author vehemently lamented that the Church had been stained by the crime of the fallen woman and that almost all its light had been darkened. The fallen virgin herself, brought forward to speak, confessed that because of her, disgrace had been brought upon all the servants of the Lord and upon all who worshiped him worthily.

Yet there are by no means lacking monuments from the age of Nicetas himself of Aquileia that remember the consecrated virgins of the Aquileian Church and, consequently—as may be inferred from what has been said—those who lived also in a virginal monastery. Since papyri, parchments, and documents fail us, there remains a stone more precious than any bronze: it preserves the funerary inscription of one of these consecrated virgins, named Columba, who also enjoys immemorial veneration in the province of Aquileia, especially among the inhabitants of the district of Forojuli, called Osoppo. There, together with her relics, a small chapel dedicated to God in her name stood until our own times in the fortress above the town.

The illustrious Fontanin saw and transcribed this inscription in that same chapel in the year 1717; afterward he published it engraved in copperplate and explained it in an extremely learned commentary, published at Rome in Italian in 1726. The same inscription—perhaps engraved somewhat more accurately after Fontanin—may also be seen in Giovanni Domenico Bertoli, who, as Fontanin testifies, inspected it again, in his Italian work *Antichità d’Aquileja*, p. 333. It begins with the sign of the saving cross, repeated above and below in the middle of the tablet. When the two engravings are compared together, it is as follows:

> + + HIC IN PACE REQVIESCIT COLVBA VIRGO SACRATA DI QVE VIXIT IN DNO ANNOS PL M NONAGINTA [Col. 0944A] DP SVB Ds VIII IDVS AGVSTAS OPILIONE VCCONSl INs SECl +

The illustrious prelate read the inscription in this way:

> Here in peace rests Columba, a consecrated virgin of God, who lived in the Lord approximately ninety years. She was buried on the eighth day before the Ides of August, in the consulship of Opilio, a man of highest rank. For the ages.

From the consulship of Opilio mentioned here—and the illustrious scholar proves that it belongs to the first consul of that name, not to the second, which was seventy-one years later—he infers that the burial of this consecrated virgin belongs to the year of Christ 453, that is, to the year immediately following the destruction of the city of Aquileia by Attila. That event likewise immediately preceded the episcopate assumed by Nicetas at Aquileia in the year 454, as we indicated above.

A local tradition among those inhabitants maintains that the consecrated virgin, who was ninety years old, actually completed the course of her life there. Even now, in the rock of that fortress, an inaccessible cave is shown—or rather pointed out—where she hid for as long as she lived there in the Lord. The learned prelate therefore infers that this consecrated virgin belonged to the company of virgins of the Aquileian Church, who, when Attila’s invasion threatened, fled from the city of Aquileia to avoid the disaster they foresaw, and concealed themselves in this distant and secluded place, situated thirty-four miles from that city toward the northwest.

Why should this virgin not also perhaps have had her birthplace here, and therefore, when placed in such great necessity, have fled more safely to places that were not wholly unknown to her, where she could also enjoy the consolation of her fellow countrymen? I too, I think not unwillingly, may venture this conjecture.
