In order to explain the inscription on this stone, and to prove that consecrated virgins of this kind were already accustomed at that time to live in monasteries, the illustrious Fontanin, as was his custom, produces several monuments from ecclesiastical tradition. These establish that the discipline then prevailed both in the East and in the West. Among them the first place belongs to our little work *To the Fallen Virgin*, or, as it is designated there, *On the Fall of a Consecrated Virgin*. Fontanin did not doubt that this work belonged to Nicetas, bishop of Romatiana in Dacia, just as the nearly universal opinion of scholars held, since all the other little works that Gennadius mentions as having been written by Nicetas of Romatiana were completely hidden from view.

It must nevertheless be acknowledged that Fontanin’s interpretation of the funerary stone of Columba, the consecrated virgin of Forojuli, found opponents. They said that the illustrious prelate had been deceived when, taking the final inscriptional abbreviation **INs SECl** as a pious acclamation or prayer, he chose to interpret it as *in saecula*, “for the ages.” They maintained instead that the words should be understood as an abbreviated chronological indication in the inscription. Accordingly, they said, the phrase should not be read *in saecula* [Col. 0944D] but *indictione secunda*, “in the second indiction.” This would mean that the year indicated was not the consulship of the first Opilio but rather that of the second; consequently, the date would not be A.D. 453 but A.D. 524, which was in fact the year of the second consulship of Opilio and also coincided with the second indiction.

This alteration would not be so great as to overthrow entirely the conclusion that we draw from the inscription for our present purpose. For if the inscription belonged even to the year 524, it would still provide evidence for the institution of consecrated virgins in the Aquileian Church not long after the age of Nicetas of Aquileia. We could therefore still reasonably conjecture that the same institution existed during Nicetas’s episcopate and that a virginal monastery also existed at that time, although it was not yet enclosed by cloisters, as Saint Paulinus prescribed toward the end of the eighth century. From that monastery Columba, the consecrated virgin, might perhaps have gone out freely, in order to lead, no doubt, a stricter and holier life as a solitary in the cave at Osoppo.

Taken in this second way, the same inscription would likewise enable us to recognize clear indications of Aquileian origin in the work *To the Fallen Virgin*. That is the purpose of this appendix, even if the inscription itself did not in fact belong to the very age of Nicetas.

Nevertheless, our fellow Fontanin’s interpretation seems to me wholly deserving of acceptance, so that we should say that the inscription properly belongs to the age of Nicetas of Aquileia, taking Opilio as the first consul, in the year 453, not the second, in the year 524.

I shall say nothing about the criticism of the otherwise illustrious and highly deserving scholar Francesco Antonio Zaccaria in his Italian *History of Italian Literature*, vol. VIII, book III, chap. 4. In attacking Fontanin sharply over his interpretation of this inscription, Zaccaria was beating the air, for he attributed to Fontanin errors that he had not committed. He showed clearly enough that he had never had before his eyes either the Forojulian inscription, Fontanin’s interpretation, or the commentary that Fontanin published on it.

It is rather necessary to answer those who object to the singularity of the acclamation *in saecula*, and who wish to understand in the upright line, bent somewhat upward and downward, which appears after the monosyllable **INs**, an abbreviation of the letters needed to complete the full word *indictione*. They consequently insist that the following letters **SECl** must mean not *saecula* but necessarily another word, *secunda*.

But Fontanin himself sufficiently explained and illustrated the use of Christian acclamations or prayers in funerary inscriptions in chapter 21 of his commentary. Although he produces no other inscription having exactly the same acclamation as our stone—namely, *in saecula*, which is equivalent to *in saecula vivas*, “may you live forever”—he points to many others very similar to it: *vibe* or *vive in aeterno*, “live eternally” (with *vibe* apparently an inscriptional spelling); *bibas* or *vivas in Deo*, “may you drink” or “live in God”; *vives in Deo*, “you will live in God”; and *bibas* or *vivas in Domino*, “may you drink” or “live in the Lord.” All these expressions lend authority to the acclamation *in saecula* on our Osoppian stone. Its uniqueness therefore should not be alleged against it, except perhaps with respect to the form of the letters from which it is composed; but since the meaning remains the same, that matter is entirely negligible.

As for the little line placed after the monosyllable **INs**, which is said to have been placed there to signify the completion of the word *indictione*, I would venture to say that this is certainly an invention unsupported by any evidence or by any example from ancient inscriptions. There are indeed many stones in the collections of the scholars available to us that display the notation of indictions. In some one sees the word *indictionis* written out in full; in others, only its first three letters, written separately; in others, the same letters joined in the monogram **ND**. Likewise, the number of the indiction is sometimes expressed by the word written out in full, sometimes by its initial letters alone, and sometimes by numerical signs. But, I say confidently, nowhere will one find the word *indictionis* represented without at least the third letter, **D**, in some form, so as to remove every opportunity for doubt that the inscription is speaking of an indiction.

That little line on our stone must therefore be considered worthless. Perhaps it was added through the carelessness—or at the whim—of an unskilled and certainly very inelegant stonecutter, as anyone who examines the inscription in Fontanin or Bertoli can see. Or perhaps we should say that it was added to give a certain festive flourish to the joyful acclamation expressing the perpetual life of the virgin Columba with God.

Furthermore, in this very inscription the line is absent in places where it ought to have been placed—for example, above the letters **DI**, used for the word *Dei*, just as it appears above the abbreviations **DP**, signifying *deposita*, “buried,” and above other abbreviations indicating other words. Who, then, could reasonably be surprised that the line should instead have appeared unnecessarily and superfluously after the monosyllable **IN**, where it was not needed—especially since the line also appears, and quite ineptly, above the letter **C** in the half-word **CONS**, although the other part of that word was already represented by another upright line placed nearby and appropriately?

We may set aside the difficulty caused by the omission of the diphthong in the syllable **SEC**. That diphthong might be thought necessary for pronouncing the word *saecula* rather than *secunda*. For the word *saeculum* is found among writers both with and without the diphthong; and collections of ancient inscriptions, both pagan and Christian, sufficiently show that the rules governing diphthongs were very frequently disregarded on old stones. This was especially noted, with new examples, by the illustrious Antonio Maria Lupi, in his *In Epitaphium Severae martyris*, pp. 132 and following, in the Panormitan edition of 1734.

Moreover, there is no reason to investigate the diphthong in *saecula* by examining an inscription that also gives the word **QVE** without a diphthong. These are the points that had to be said concerning the funerary inscription of this consecrated virgin of the Aquileian Church. For the moment, however, let this suffice.

Since, then, nothing at all may be asserted concerning a company of consecrated virgins among Nicetas of Dacia; since it is established from what has been said—and specifically from the precious stone that we have produced and discussed—that there were consecrated virgins in the Aquileian Church in the time of Bishop Nicetas; and since there is no reason to doubt that a virginal monastery existed in the Aquileian Church even in Nicetas’s time, both because of the nature of the matter itself, because of the flourishing renown of that Church, and especially because of the evidence that we have produced from the council of Forojuli under the holy patriarch Paulinus; if, moreover, we recall the demonstrated kinship of the work *To the Fallen Virgin* with the other work *Explanation of the Creed*, which—God forbid that envy should object—is fully established as the work of Nicetas of Aquileia, then the indications we sought are already conspicuous in this work *To the Fallen Virgin* as well. They show Aquileia to have been the seat of its author’s ecclesiastical parentage and reinforce the conclusion that we stated above: that the Nicaea or Nicetas mentioned by Gennadius as bishop of Romatiana was without doubt Nicaea or Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia—the very man who flourished in the time of Saint Leo the Great and to whom a letter of that holy pontiff survives.

**80** One further objection might perhaps be made to what we recently conjectured, chiefly on the basis of the funerary stone of the consecrated virgin Columba, read together with Fontanin. It might be said that we wrongly infer that the author of the work *To the Fallen Virgin* was Nicetas of Aquileia merely because consecrated virgins and a virginal monastery existed in the Aquileian Church at that time. It might instead be argued from that same stone that, even if consecrated virgins and their monastery had previously existed there, at that time, with the virgins scattered everywhere by Attila’s disaster and the virginal building—as is credible—destroyed and overturned, a sacred company of virgins could not have survived in the Aquileian Church.

What consecrated virgin of God, then, could Nicetas of Aquileia have rebuked, while also reproaching her with the virginal monastery where she could have been safe had she wished, thereby increasing the gravity of her crime? [Col. 0946D]

However severe the disaster caused by Attila may have been in the city and Church of Aquileia—bringing about the dispersion of the sacred company of virgins and also the destruction of the virginal monastery—it was nevertheless not such a disaster that restoration afterward would have been impossible. Already in the year 458, when Pope Saint Leo sent his Decretal to Nicetas of Aquileia, the condition of affairs in that same letter was said to have turned, with the Lord’s help, toward better things as far as the Aquileian Church was concerned. This is confirmed also by Adeodatus, a deacon of the Roman Church mentioned there, who had recently returned from Aquileia. Just as he had brought Nicetas’s consultations to the pontiff, so he had undoubtedly informed him about the condition of that Church.

Perhaps, then, in the year 454—immediately after the death of Columba, the consecrated virgin, and the year in which he assumed the episcopate of Aquileia—Nicetas found the consecrated virgins dispersed and their monastery destroyed. Nevertheless, all these things may perhaps already have been restored to their former condition in that same year, 458 (the supplied text reads 438), since Saint Leo’s letter clearly establishes that the vigilance and pastoral care of Bishop Nicetas were directed especially toward carefully repairing the losses inflicted by the war.

Moreover, during the approximately thirty years of Nicetas’s episcopate, from 454 to 485, both the company of consecrated virgins could be restored in the Aquileian Church and the virginal monastery rebuilt. Thus the unfortunate occasion could arise for Nicetas to rebuke the fallen Virgin and to say all those things that belonged to the institution of consecrated virgins in that same century.

And what of the fact that this virgin’s fall, brought about by the insolence of a young man whom Nicetas likewise gravely rebukes in the same work, in its own way indicates a period following the hostile incursions—incursions that are always especially hostile to religion, morals, and discipline?

But enough of this, lest the common saying prove applicable:

> The appendix defeats the main course.

[Col. 0947]

## CHAPTER V

The city called Romatiana by Gennadius is not to be sought in Dacia, but in the old diocese or province of Aquileia; probably it is the place that was called Portus Romatianus, or Romatinus, or Romatius, not far from Concordia, after the river of the same name mentioned by Pliny; or else it is the place now called Portus Gruarius, situated on the same river Romatius, Romatinus, or Romatianus, which flows through it.

From what was said in the third and fourth chapters of this dissertation, it may now be considered beyond dispute that the Nicaea or Nicetas mentioned by Gennadius as bishop of the city of Romatiana was not Nicaea or Nicetas of Dacia, the friend of Saint Paulinus, bishop of Nola, and celebrated by him in praise. Rather, he was in fact Nicaea or Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, who flourished in the time of Saint Leo the Great and to whom a letter of that holy pontiff survives.

Did Gennadius himself, then, err when he called this man not the bishop of Aquileia, as he should have done, but the bishop of the city of Romatiana? A few things must therefore be said about Gennadius of Marseille, so that it may become clear how highly his authority should be valued and what place should be assigned to it.

Lest we prove ungrateful to those through whom we have advanced, we must acknowledge that we owe Gennadius much gratitude. As a kind of continuator of Jerome’s work *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, he too left us a book *On Illustrious Men*. From it all those who have undertaken to adorn the literary history of those times drew many pieces of information about authors, their works, and also the public opinion then held about them.

We ourselves, in treating of Nicetas, bishop of the city of Romatiana, could not, without Gennadius’s *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*, have said enough about the *Explanation of the Creed for the Competentes* and the little work *To the Fallen Virgin*. Nor could we have known about the other works written by that same bishop, works that have either perished entirely or perhaps lie hidden somewhere, destined to benefit the investigations and studies of later generations.

Saint Isidore of Seville, writing about the blessed Jerome and Gennadius in book VI, chapter 6, of the *Etymologies*, and referring to the little works that we have mentioned, says:

> “Jerome and Gennadius likewise, seeking out ecclesiastical writers throughout the whole world, followed them in order and included their studies in a single little volume.”

The illustrious Arevalo, who recently prepared the Roman edition of the works of Saint Isidore, thought that these words should be annotated as follows:

> “Isidore implies that Saint Jerome and Gennadius spoke in their catalogues about those writers whom they had in their own libraries. I think that this is true to a considerable extent.”

The fault charged to Gennadius of Marseille in this work is that he showed excessive favor toward the party of the Semi-Pelagians, to which he was attached. This is certainly a sufficiently serious fault in a historian, for it damages sincerity, the principal duty of a historian.

The venerable Bellarmine speaks of this fault of Gennadius in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*:

> “Gennadius also wrote a book *On Illustrious Men*, in which he left considerable suspicion of the unsoundness of his faith. For he praised Cassian and Faustus, who were Semi-Pelagians, and disparaged Saint Prosper, who fought most vigorously for the grace of God against Pelagius.”

Natalis Alexander likewise wrote in his *Ecclesiastical History*, century five, chapter 3, article 7, § 9:

> “That Gennadius of Marseille, a presbyter, was attached to the Semi-Pelagian faction is sufficiently proved by his book *On Illustrious Men*, written about the year 490. In that book he attacks Saint Augustine and his outstanding disciple and defender, Saint Prosper, as though they were guilty of error, while he extols Cassian and Faustus, the leaders of the Semi-Pelagians, with praises.”

The learned scholar proves the same point clearly by adducing passages from Gennadius.

But learned men have not noted only this fault in Gennadius’s *Catalogue*. There are other errors, and not insignificant ones. Some must be attributed to the judgment and ignorance of copyists, others to Gennadius’s own carelessness.

As for the copyists, there is certainly no work more exposed to the arbitrary decisions and carelessness of scribes than any historical or biographical work. It is very easy for one of them, under the pretext of correction or clarification, to insert something of his own that had never occurred to the author, or to alter or remove whatever pleases him more or less.

As for the author’s carelessness, historical works, and especially biographical works, are likewise such that sleep must at times creep in, particularly when the author’s attention is exhausted by collecting from every quarter the writings of the authors about whom he must speak and then reading and weighing those writings themselves, while other matters continually intervene, time is lacking, or the mind is unequal to the task.

This certainly applies to Gennadius. Learned men who have devoted themselves to editing the works of certain writers whom he discusses in his *Catalogue* have repeatedly complained that he made mistakes there—whether concerning chronology, the substance of events, or the identification of places.

Who, for example, would not be astonished that Gennadius, in chapter 70, records only a single letter of Saint Leo the Great, namely the letter to Flavian, which has been mentioned so often in this dissertation, while omitting all his other letters, both on that subject and on others? He does not even mention all those sermons of Leo that earned him, among everyone, such great renown for truly divine eloquence.

Although this concerns the fame of that celebrated letter, as the Ballerini brothers note in their admonition to it, no. 4, it nevertheless does little to support the accuracy and diligence of the author of *On Illustrious Men*. He ought not by any means to have omitted, without even a general mention, so many excellent works through which the renown of that most wise pontiff was raised to the stars.

This serious omission is an error of Gennadius, not of his copyists. When speaking of Maximus of Turin, in chapter 40, he had by no means failed to list his sermons and homilies on various subjects, so fully that one might almost say he enumerated them individually. In the case of Leo the Great, therefore, Gennadius acted very carelessly and negligently.

But was he at least entirely accurate concerning Saint Maximus of Turin? The illustrious Bruno Bruni, of the Order of the Piarist Fathers, editor and compiler of the works of Saint Maximus of Turin, which were published at Rome by the authority and under the patronage of Pope Pius VI of immortal memory, noted in the life of that holy bishop that Gennadius said Maximus died while Honorius and Theodosius the Younger were reigning, although it is certain that he lived long after those emperors, at least until the year 465, as Bruni himself demonstrates.

Here, then, is Gennadius’s carelessness even in the case of Maximus of Turin, and it cannot be attributed to the arbitrary judgment or ignorance of copyists.

What is read in some manuscripts of Gennadius—“He died … in the year 420 from the redemption of the world”—is an addition by ignorant copyists of a later age, for Gennadius certainly never wrote it.

Nor should we pass over the note that the author of that Life added on p. 133 in order to establish Gennadius’s carelessness more firmly:

> “I could produce from the same Catalogue many examples of Gennadian errors, *ἁμαρτημάτων*—that is, mistakes—but, lest I seem excessive, I shall omit them. Let one example be Julian of Eclanum, whom Gennadius, in error, says was a bishop of Capua. Another is Atticus, bishop of Constantinople, whom he says attacked the Nestorian doctrine. This cannot be granted, since Atticus died long before Nestorius began to spread his perverse doctrine.”

So he wrote.

I consider it worthwhile to offer another example of Gennadian negligence from the dissertations of our illustrious Francesco Florio on the little works of the monk Bachiarius, which Florio published at Rome in 1748.

The learned man identifies not one but three errors of Gennadius in a single article on Bachiarius, which forms chapter 24 of Gennadius’s *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*.

The first is an error against chronology, on p. 28. Gennadius places Bachiarius before Augustine and Orosius and Helvidius the heretic after Bachiarius, although Helvidius was the younger. Bachiarius expressly mentions the error of Helvidius in his own little work on the faith. Consequently, Gennadius does not provide sufficient grounds for accurately determining the period in which Bachiarius himself flourished, and the necessary information must therefore be sought elsewhere.

The second is an error against the substance of the matter, on p. 47. Although Gennadius admits that he had read Bachiarius’s book *On the Faith*, he reports its subject as something completely opposed to Bachiarius’s actual purpose and undertaking.

The third is an error against the correct identification and designation of the man to whom Bachiarius’s little work is addressed, on p. 49. Gennadius says that he was the bishop of the City—that is, the bishop of Rome—although from reading the little work itself it can clearly be inferred not only that he was not the bishop of Rome, but that he was not distinguished by episcopal rank at all.

After these blemishes in Gennadius’s work, which we have so far noted chiefly on the testimony of the most learned men, who could not reasonably suspect that Gennadius also made an error in his account of the bishop Nicaea or Nicetas? He may have mistakenly called him the bishop of the city of Romatiana, when he should have called him the bishop of Aquileia.

We, who have already brought forward so many and such strong arguments for the Aquileian episcopate of this Nicetas, whom Gennadius calls Romatianus, might above all accuse Gennadius of an error like the one he committed concerning Julian of Eclanum, when he described him as bishop of Capua.

But perhaps Gennadius did not err. Rather, those who forced his words in another direction may have erred twice: against Gennadius’s purpose and meaning, they sought that Romatiana city not merely outside the diocese and province of Aquileia, but far away in Cisdanubian Dacia under the metropolitan see of Sardica—namely, in that Remisiana, Remesiana, or Romessiana mentioned by ancient geographers and others there. They thus made the question concern not only the name of the city but also the person of the bishop, so that Gennadius’s bishop would not be the same man who was bishop of Aquileia in the time of Saint Leo, but another person separated from him by approximately half a century.

But since that Dacian Nicetas, according to their own assertion, flourished in the time of Paulinus, bishop of Nola, and was bound to him by the closest friendship; and since we showed in chapter 2 that Nicaea or Nicetas, famous for his friendship with Saint Paulinus of Nola, was not bishop of a city of Romatiana situated in Dacia south of the Danube—indeed, that this Nicetas exercised his episcopate beyond the Danube, in those extensive regions and among barbarian peoples who did not obey Roman laws, where it is not clear that any city existed bearing the name Romatiana or any similar name—there is no reason to debate here over a city of Romatiana situated in Cisdanubian Dacia.

We must rather now determine where, in the diocese or province of Aquileia, this city of Romatiana was situated, since from what was said in chapters 3 and 4 it can no longer be doubted that Nicaea or Nicetas, whom Gennadius calls the bishop of the city of Romatiana, was not that Nicaea or Nicetas of Dacia, the friend of Saint Paulinus of Nola, but was in fact our Nicaea or Nicetas, who occupied the Aquileian see during the latter part of the fifth century.

In the meantime, who would not be astonished that the city called Romatiana by Gennadius was sought in Cisdanubian Dacia because of a certain similarity of name with the city that existed there and is named by geographers and other ancient authors?

The city of Dacia is called **Romesiana** in segment 7, letter A, of the *Peutinger Table*, in the beautiful Vienna edition of 1753. In the *Itinerary of Antoninus*, p. 135 of Peter Wesseling’s Amsterdam edition of 1735, it is called **Remisiana**.

The illustrious Zabeus himself, in part I, no. 18, of his dissertation, asserts that the forms found in ancient monuments for designating one and the same city of Cisdanubian Dacia are as follows: **Romissiana, Remissiana, Remessiana, Romantiana, Romesiana, Romessiana**. The illustrious De Rubeis presents all these forms, marked in the places where they were excavated, in his *Various Dissertations of Learning*, chapter 19, p. 194.

Where, then, among all these names—or rather, among all these inflections of one name—where, I ask, is the true and proper name **Romatiana** used by Gennadius? By what reasoning, by what rule of criticism, can it be inferred that Gennadius’s Romatiana is the city in Dacia that appears under various names in ancient monuments, but is never truly and properly called by Gennadius’s word *Romatiana*?

The illustrious Wesseling himself, in the note that he appends to the word *Remisiana* in the aforementioned *Itinerary of Antoninus*, criticizes the opinion of Antonio Pagi. In his *Baronian Criticism*, under the year 396, Pagi wished to see in the word *Remisiana*, which appears in that *Itinerary*, the word *Romatiana* used by Gennadius, so that he too might place his Nicetas in Dacia.

And rightly so. For if we once admit this rule for reconciling matters—that one and the same thing may be understood from the similarity of one word to another—how many new errors do we open the door to while attempting to remove ambiguities and errors?

Here, however, it must be especially observed that one might perhaps concede to some extent that, because of the similarity of the names, Gennadius’s *Romatiana* appears to be one and the same place as the city marked by ancient geographers in Dacia—if those same geographers were consistent in pronouncing the name of that place; or at least if among the various forms we have seen there also occurred Gennadius’s own **Romatiana** or **Romaciana**.

But what argument for identity can be drawn where there is such variety, and where, amid all that variety, the very word that is central and whose identity is in question is nowhere found?

We must now approach the proposed subject more closely and examine whether we can find in the diocese or province of Aquileia the city of Romatiana that, as we have said, is sought in vain in Cisdanubian Dacia.

Here Cardinal Baronius must first be heard. In his notes on the *Roman Martyrology*, under June 22, which is sacred to Nicaea or Nicetas, bishop of the city of Romatiana, he writes:

> “What city this was, whose bishop Nicaea was, I confess that I sought for a long time and with great labor. At last, if I am not mistaken, I seem to have grasped the matter. For I think that it was Aquileia, and that Nicaea, or Nicetas, was the bishop of this city, to whom the letter of Saint Leo the pope survives, and so forth.”

After some further remarks he continues:

> “Why, then, is the bishop of Aquileia found written as the bishop of Romatiana, or Romana, or Romanicia? The reason seems to be the one that we drew from the aforementioned *History of Aquileia*: because Aquileia had been a most illustrious Roman colony, the city is found called Roman or Romatian. Thus Ausonius, in his poem *On Famous Cities*, calls Arelate ‘Gallic Rome.’ … Leander, the recent cosmographer, says that when he discusses the city of Aquileia, it was called the second Rome.”

Thus Baronius.

Along with Baronius, several ecclesiastical critics readily adopted this view, both among Protestants—for example, Cave, Oudinus, and Johann Albert Fabricius—and among Catholics, such as Vallarsi and our own Johann Joseph Liruti.

Cave, in his *Literary History of Ecclesiastical Writers*, p. 399 of the Basel edition of 1741, writes:

> “Nicaea of Romatiana—that is, as Baronius correctly interprets it, of Aquileia—and so forth.”

Oudinus, in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. I, p. 1248 of the Frankfurt am Main edition of 1722, has the following:

> “Nicaea, bishop of Romatiana—that is, as Caesar Baronius correctly interpreted it in his notes on the *Roman Martyrology* under June 22, the bishop of the city of Aquileia—and so forth.”

Johann Albert Fabricius wrote in the first edition of his *Bibliotheca Graeca*, vol. VI, p. 439:

> “The Dacian Nicetas is mentioned in the *Acta Eruditorum*, vol. II of the Supplement, p. 212, from Gennadius. But in chapter 23 of Gennadius’s *On Ecclesiastical Writers*—as it is there given—we find Nicaea, bishop of Romaciana or Aquileia, or, as Martianaeus found it in an extremely ancient manuscript, bishop of the city of Romana.”

Vallarsi likewise observed in his note, no. 8, on Saint Jerome’s letter to Nicaea, the subdeacon of Aquileia:

> “This Nicaea is commonly believed to be the same man whom Saint Paulinus repeatedly praises under the name Nicetas, and who afterward became bishop of Dacia. But he is certainly not the same man. Rather, he is the one whom Gennadius, in chapter 22, reports as Nicaea, bishop of the city of Romatiana—that is, of Aquileia, as Baronius correctly interprets it, and so forth.”

Finally, our own Liruti pursues this matter at very great length in his Italian work *Notices of the Lives of the Learned Men of Friuli*, vol. I, chapter 11—indeed, at such length that he might even seem excessive. For this reason, he effectively excuses us from reproducing his words here.

These, then, are the writers who either openly agreed with Cardinal Baronius or at least did not contradict him. They accepted the view that Gennadius’s city of Romatiana was Aquileia and adopted his explanation based on the renown of the Roman colony established there, as well as on the dignity of the City, which deserved to be called by that name—a name derived from the chief city of the Roman Empire.

Far more numerous, and indeed men of great renown and learning, are those who, as though forming a column, called Baronio’s opinion and his reasoning into question, and rejected them with one voice, so that they might jointly adopt the view that Gennadius’s Romatiana was located in Cisalpine Dacia. These are Tillemont, *Mémoires pour l’histoire ecclésiastique*, vol. X, pp. 621 and 826, Venice edition by Pitteri; Baillet, *Lives of the Saints*, 22 [Col. 0951D] June, no. 2; Dupin, *Bibliothèque des auteurs ecclésiastiques*, vol. III, p. 154, Paris edition, 1693; Quesnel, *Notes and Observations on the Letter of Saint Leo the Great*, no. 129 in the same work; Holstenius, *Remarks on the Roman Martyrology*, 22 June, p. 80 of the first edition; Florentinius, *Martyrology of the Ancient Western Church*, illustrated by his notes, 10 days before the Kalends of July; Pagi, *Baronian Criticism*, for the year 396, no. 4 and following; Henschenius, vol. IV of the Bollandist *June*, pp. 243 and following of the Antwerp edition; Georgius, *The Martyrology of Ado*, illustrated by him, at 10 days before the Kalends of July; and, among our fellow inhabitants of Friuli, Fontanini, *Commentary on Saint Columba*, chapter 18; and de Rubeis, *Monuments of the Church of Aquileia*, chapters 16 and 17, as well as *Dissertations of Various Learning*, chapter 19.

I omit the statements of each of them, which it would take too long to report, content merely to indicate most recently the distinguished man Bernardo Maria De Rubeis, [Col. 0952A] who can stand for them all, since he devoted himself to illuminating the affairs of the Church of Aquileia with much credit for learning and critical judgment. In his often-cited *Monuments of the Church of Aquileia*, chapter 17, no. 4, he writes as follows:

“Baronius’s arguments do not establish that Aquileia was at some time called the city of Romaciana. It was a most distinguished Roman colony. No one will deny that. But who would infer that the city was therefore called Romaciana? We read of no other city, among the many that were most distinguished Roman colonies, being called by a similar name. Ausonius calls Arles the Gallic Rome. The author appropriately calls this famous city Rome, not Romaciana; likewise, he calls it Rome with an adjective, namely Gallic, or “little Gallic,” as he says; not simply and absolutely . . . . Leander, a recent cosmographer, says, when discussing the city of Aquileia, that it was called a second Rome. This recent cosmographer asserts the point without a witness; for no ancient historian, rhetorician, or poet is reported to have spoken in this way concerning a matter so old. Finally, the issue concerns the city of Romaciana, not a new or second Rome.” [Col. 0952B]

Such is De Rubeis’s argument against Baronio’s opinion.

What, then, are we to do now? Must Baronio be defended, together with his few followers, or abandoned, following the authority and example of those who unanimously departed from him? If there were time for it, Baronio’s opinion could certainly be defended, though not entirely, or at least illuminated to some extent, from what the distinguished Faustinus Arevalus reports on a similar matter in part I, chapter 23, of the Isidorian works recently published by him in volume I of the works of Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville, printed in Rome in splendid type through the authority and at the expense of the illustrious late Cardinal Lorenzana.

The most learned editor examines the inscription of a certain Isidorian work entitled *On the Order of Creation*, which in a particular manuscript is said to have been addressed by its author to Braulio, bishop of the city of Rome. To these words the distinguished D’Achery, by way of explanation, added: “Of the city of Rome, that is, Zaragoza, of which Braulio was bishop.” Arevalus then cites the interpretation of Nicolás Antonio, who observed that by the name “city of Rome” the royal court in Spain had been indicated, that Toledo too had been called the Romulean seat, 87 and that generally any royal city could, by antonomasia or by excellence, be called Rome; precisely as among the same Spaniards any metropolitan church was also called Jerusalem in ecclesiastical documents.

Since, however, Zaragoza was never a royal city during the Gothic period, Nicolás Antonio seems not to have been far from accepting the further opinion that cities which had at some time exercised some prerogative—sacred or secular—of the city of Rome had likewise earned the name of a second Rome or another Rome, as examples are given there concerning Trier and other places. The authority of the distinguished Flórez also supports this view. In volume V of his *Sacred Spain*, p. 512, no. 15, he defends D’Achery’s very interpretation of “the city of Rome,” that is, Zaragoza. Why, then, could Aquileia not sometimes have been called the Romatian or Roman city, in accordance with Baronio’s conjectures, because it had been a most distinguished Roman colony and had become famous for other prerogatives of the city of Rome, as was fully observed in the *Appendix to Chapter Three*?

Thus Baronio’s opinion could, even in this new light of scholarship and after the dissent of so many distinguished men, find some support, if we wished to contend for it; but that is not at all our purpose. Indeed, we judge that Baronio’s interpretation of “the city of Romatiana” as Aquileia itself must be wholly abandoned, just as the explanation he himself newly devised must be considered worthless, since it rests upon no foundation and is supported by no authority of the ancients.

I do, however, think that Baronio should be defended in this respect: by the name “city of Romatiana” he understood the bishopric of Aquileian Nicetas, although he may have arrived at this opinion through a preconceived error. Others who followed him likewise derived that error from him—namely, that the Nicetas whom we read of as a subdeacon of the Church of Aquileia in Saint Jerome’s letter 8, in Vallarsi’s edition, belonging to the year 374, was himself later the Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, who received a decretal letter from Leo the Great in the year 458 and lived until the year 485. We had already pointed out that this is wholly inconsistent with the chronology.

I therefore think that Baronius shed light upon the truth when he understood Niceas or Nicetas, whom Gennadius calls bishop of the city of Romatiana, to be Niceas or Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia. But what wonder if the light which Baronius brought forward for discovering the truth was then surrounded by little clouds, which would finally be scattered when a new light was added? For what if the city of Romatiana—which cannot be the city in Cisalpine Dacia and which, contrary to Baronio, must not be understood as Aquileia properly so called—what if, I say, it can best be understood as another place within the diocese of Aquileia at that time, situated not far from the city of Aquileia, toward which none of the many learned men praised above, whether those who followed Baronio or those who attacked him, directed their attention? [Col. 0953B]

We must now return again to Gennadius. Just as we have noticed varying pronunciations of the name of that city in Cisalpine Dacia among ancient geographers and writers, so we must understand that Gennadian manuscripts vary in the name of the Romatiana city which Gennadius mentions, so that we may more easily discover which city he could truly have intended within the Church of Aquileia.

“Niceas, bishop of the city of Romaciana, etc.” Thus we read Gennadius in the edition of Johann Albert Fabricius, which I used from the beginning, and in volume II, p. 962, of the works of Saint Jerome in Vallarsi’s edition. At the bottom of the page both editors note that in some copies, instead of *Romaciana* or *Romatiana*, one finds *Romana*, and also, according to Suffridus Petri, *Romanicia*. Baronio had likewise noted this in the *Roman Martyrology* for 22 June, saying:

“Different readings are also found in different manuscripts concerning the name of the city: in some he is called bishop of the city of Romatiana, as it is written here, while in others he is called bishop of the city of Romana or Romaniciana.”

Lequien cites and follows the San-Germain Gennadian manuscript, as we indicated in chapter two, in his *Christian East*, vol. II, col. 306, where he discusses the bishops of the Church of Remesiana in the Cisalpine province of Mediterranean Dacia under the metropolitan see of Sardica. In this manuscript the passage reads:

“Nicetas, bishop of the city of Remesiana, etc.”

To these words Lequien adds:

“Thus expressly reads the ancient San-Germain manuscript, not ‘of the city of Romaciana,’ as was formerly printed.”

By this manner of speaking he wishes to confirm his opinion—which was also the opinion of most scholars—that Gennadius’s Nicetas was bishop of the city located in Cisalpine Dacia which in fact was called by ancient geographers and writers Remesiana or Remessiana, as in the manuscript cited, and Romissiana, Remissiana, or some scarcely different form, but never Romatiana, Romana, or Romaniciana, as the manuscripts long known and the editions of Gennadius have it. [Col. 0953D]

Let Lequien himself see, however, whether, according to the rules of criticism, a single manuscript, even if ancient—as he himself says, though neither its proper age nor the other necessary marks for establishing its authority are indicated—should be trusted so far that it may be absolutely preferred to all the other Gennadian manuscripts known until now. Above all, let him consider the Vallicellian manuscript, formerly belonging to a monastery in Rome and later to the Vatican Library, which the most learned Holstenius and Georgius praised so highly for its remarkable antiquity. They discuss Nicetas there: the former in his *Remarks on the Roman Martyrology* for 22 June, the latter on that same day in the *Martyrology of Ado*; as do Florentinius and Pagi, cited there by Georgius. None of these manuscripts ever presents the word *Remesiana*, or any similar form corresponding to the ancient geographers and writers in their notices of Cisalpine Dacia.

Let him also see whether his San-Germain manuscript can likewise be preferred to all the editions of Gennadius that we owe to highly learned men, editions prepared according to their purpose after examining and collating all the manuscripts of Gennadius that they could find anywhere. For us, it is enough at this point to have mentioned the San-Germain manuscript; no consideration of it need here affect our argument.

It is useful here to add a new variant concerning the episcopal seat of Nicetas, which I recently obtained from a parchment Gennadian manuscript dating approximately from the twelfth or thirteenth century and of fairly good quality. It is preserved in the chapter archive of the distinguished collegiate church of Cividale, through the assistance of the most courteous man and most diligent investigator of manuscript books, Michael della Torre, formerly a member of the counts of Vallisaxina and a canon of that church. I wish to mention him here as a mark of honor and gratitude.

In the article concerning this Nicetas, this Gennadian manuscript displays several variations from the common reading, and indeed some quite unusual ones, which will be discussed at the appropriate place below. As regards the episcopal city of Nicetas, it reads:

“Niceta, bishop of the city of Romathiciana, etc.”

I later discovered this same reading, *Romathiciana*, in another paper manuscript, apparently of the fourteenth century or the end of the thirteenth, marked L, preserved among the Guarnerian manuscripts of the library of the town of San Daniele. The same unusual variants also appear there as in the Cividale manuscript, so that it may readily be conjectured that, considering their apparent home in the same diocese and province, one was derived from the other, and the latter therefore from the former.

We therefore have the following variant readings for the one episcopal seat of Niceas or Nicetas in the editions and manuscripts of Gennadius, with the exception of the San-Germain manuscript:

*of the city of Romaciana, Romatiana, Romana, Romaniciana, Romanicia,* and finally *Romathiciana.*

What place, then, in the extensive diocese of Aquileia at that time corresponds to these names?

We may willingly hear our Lucretius Treus, a man endowed with much and varied learning, who in 1724 published at Udine, in a brief and simple style modeled on Gennadius’s catalogue, the *Sacred Monuments of the Province of Friuli*. I am surprised that our later writers, especially in connection with the matter before us, have never, or almost never, remembered him. He was certainly a man deserving a better fate, and in a work of no great size he embraced many things most worthy of being known, although, given the circumstances of the period in which he wrote, it contains certain judgments requiring criticism—judgments which he himself would have avoided had he lived in a broader light of learning.

He was therefore the first to identify Gennadius’s and the Roman Martyrology’s city of Romatiana within the Church of Aquileia. In the notes which he appended to chapter 36 of his work, entitled *On Saint Niceas, Bishop of Aquileia*, he writes:

“Niceas or Nicetas was perhaps called bishop of the city of Romatiana because in the province of Friuli this word was commonly heard in those times, especially of the Port of Romatinus, now Portogruaro, near Concordia, and of the river Romatinus, now called the Lemene, which flows there, as Pliny witnesses in book III, chapter 18. Roman governors sent by the emperors resided sometimes at Aquileia and sometimes at Concordia; it is therefore probable that the bishops of Aquileia did likewise. Indeed, after Aquileia had been destroyed, Niceas perhaps fled to the Port of Romatinus, and for this reason was called a Romatian bishop.

“Another argument also favors this view: certain bishops of Aquileia were likewise so designated, as Saint Chromatius does of himself in his *Commentary on the Eight Beatitudes* . . . . Although there may indeed be another episcopal city of Romatiana elsewhere, no one can deny that Niceas was bishop of Aquileia, etc.”

Such is our Treus’s account of the city of Romatiana, situated not very far from Aquileia. [Col. 0955A]

Whatever may be said meanwhile about several things Treus ventures here—for example, about the Roman governors who supposedly resided alternately at Aquileia and Concordia, and about Saint Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia, who supposedly called himself a Romatian bishop—all of which, since they are advanced without an authority, we leave to him: the Romatian place, certainly, attested by the Port of Romatinus and likewise by the river Romatinus, and supported by Pliny’s authority, ought both to be accepted and carefully considered.

Pliny therefore writes in book III, chapter 18, of his *Natural History*, in Harduin’s edition:

“The tenth region of Italy follows, bordering on the Adriatic Sea . . . . The town of Altinum; the river Liquentia from the Opitergine mountains, and a port of the same name; the colony of Concordia; the rivers and the port Romatinum; the greater and lesser Tilaventum; the Anassus, into which the Varramus flows; the Alsa; the Natiso with the Turro, flowing past Aquileia, etc.”

Thus Pliny. At the bottom of the page the editor added:

“Romatinum. 90 Now the Lemene: it flows past Concordia and finally forms a port, Porto Lematino.”

Something should also be added concerning the word *Romatinum* in this edition. In the very rare Venetian edition of Pliny printed by Johann de Spira in 1469, which I consulted in the exceptionally well-stocked library of the distinguished and thoroughly learned Philippus Florius of Udine, who most courteously made many books available to me, the reading is *Romantinum*. In another Venetian edition, printed by Paulus Manutius in 1559, with Manutius’s emendations and the corrections of Sigismund Gelenius, the reading is *Romatium*.

Philippus Cluverius also examined the passage of Pliny concerning the Port of Romatinus—or, as one may say, Romantinus or Romatium—in a special discussion in book I, chapter 18, of *Ancient Italy*. There he also rearranges the words of Pliny relating to Romatinum, which, as he conjectures, had been somewhat inverted by copyists. He writes:

“The river flows past Concordia, now called by the common name Leme or Lemene. Its mouth forms a port near the island town of Caorle, commonly called Porto Lematino. From this name it is clearly evident that this is Pliny’s river and port Romatinum in the passage just cited. ‘The town of Altinum,’ he says, ‘the river Liquentia and a port of the same name; the colony of Concordia; the rivers and port Romatinum; the greater and lesser Tilaventum; the Anassus, into which the Varramus flows; the Alsa; the Natiso with the Turro, flowing past Aquileia.’”

After some intervening matter he continues:

“If I am reluctant to accuse Pliny of errors, I would judge that he wrote as follows: ‘The colony of Concordia; the rivers and port Romatinum, greater and lesser; the Tilaventum, into which the Varramus flows; the Anassus, the Alsa, and the Natiso.’ For the greater Romatinus is the river which rises higher up, above the town of Valvasone, and is commonly called the Lemene. The lesser Romatinus should be called the river that descends from the town of San Vito and joins it near the town of Portogruaro, commonly called the Lemetto—a diminutive in Italian from Leme—so that you correctly interpret it as ‘the lesser river Romatinum.’”

Such is Cluverius’s account.

Other geographers must now be heard on this matter. First, Johann Jacob Hofmann, in his *Universal Historical-Geographical-Chronological Lexicon*, writes:

“Romatiana, a city of the Carni, Concordia according to Ortelius, or the Port of Romatinus, so called from the river.”

He also writes:

“Romatinum, a river of the Carni according to Pliny, now in Venetian territory and called Limino, as Leander writes.”

Baudrand treats the same matter somewhat more fully in volume II of his *Geography*. After discussing the city of Romatiana, or Remisiana, in Dacia, he writes of our river and port Romatinus:

“Romatinum, a river of the Carni according to Pliny, now the Lemene, which, according to Leander and others, flows from the Carnic Alps between the Liquentia and the Tilaventum and enters the Adriatic Sea beneath the city of Concordia.”

He continues:

“Portus Romatinus, a place of the Carni according to Pliny, now Porto Lematino, in the province of Friuli, according to Cluverius; according to others, Portogruaro.”

He adds immediately:

“Portus Romatinus, a town of the Carni in Italy according to Pliny, now Portogruaro, the Italian Porto-Gruaro, a town of Italy in the province of Friuli, on the river Romatium, in the territory of the Venetian Republic, only two miles north of the ruined city of Concordia, from whose ruins it grew. The seat of the bishop of Concordia is there. It is forty Roman miles east of Venice, twenty-five toward Udine, and twenty-five west of Aquileia.”

This is what he says there.

What may therefore be inferred from the text of Pliny just cited, from Cluverius’s remarks 91 on the same text, and finally from the geographical writings of Hofmann and Baudrand is this: in the ancient episcopal territory of Aquileia, before any trace appears of the more recent episcopal sees of Concordia or Caorle, there existed a place called Romatinum, or Romantinum, or Romatium, situated approximately twenty-five miles from Aquileia. [Col. 0956B] That place was also a port, named from the river Romatinus, Romantinus, or Romatius. It is believed still to exist in the present Portogruaro, whose inhabitants are therefore also very proud of its Plinian designation.

Why, then, should this not have been the very city of Romatiana—or Romanicia, or Romanicia, or Romathiciana, or even Romana—which appears in the editions and manuscripts of Gennadius? Certainly, from Pliny’s *Romatium* as it appears in Manutius’s edition, Gennadius’s *Romatiana* and *Romaciana* follow naturally. From *Romatinum* or *Romantinum*, *Romatiana*, *Romanicia*, *Romaniciana*, and even *Romathiciana* likewise arise without difficulty.

From what has been said, then, it seems sufficiently clear, unless I am mistaken, that the city of Romatiana mentioned by Gennadius should not be sought in Dacia but in the diocese of Aquileia; and that it may probably be the place which Pliny named Portus Romatianus, Romatinus, or Romatius, not far from Concordia, from the river of the same name. [Col. 0956C]

But I also said in the heading of this chapter that Gennadius’s city of Romatiana might be the place now called Portogruaro, situated on the same river Romatium, Romatinum, or Romatianum, which flows through it. We must now ask whether the Portus Romatius or Romatinus mentioned by Pliny in the passage cited above—and consequently whether the city of Romatiana mentioned by Gennadius in connection with Nicetas—is entirely identical with the present Portogruaro, which is likewise situated on the Romatium or Romatinus, but on this side of Concordia, about two miles from it, and where the bishop of Concordia now has his seat.

It is certain from the historians that the site of present-day Portogruaro grew from the ruins of the city of Concordia after the disaster caused by Attila. While Concordia still stood and flourished, the site of Portogruaro existed in the condition of a village or hamlet. But I would not at all say that the port itself was the Romatinus mentioned by Pliny, since Pliny’s Portus Romatinus probably stood at the mouth of the river Romatinus beyond Concordia, and was in a certain sense the port of that city, situated at the estuary.

Pliny’s words cited above seem certainly to indicate this: “The colony of Concordia; the rivers and port Romatinum”—that is, first Concordia, then the river that flows past it, and afterward the port beyond Concordia, at the river’s mouth, where the river’s course ends. The words of Pliny were also understood in this way by writers most skilled and authoritative in such matters.

We have already seen that Harduin, in his note on the passage of Pliny, wrote that the river Romatinus flows past Concordia and finally forms a port. Thus, according to Harduin, the Portus Romatinus was situated downstream from Concordia; indeed, at the mouth of the river, where the river itself formed the port.

Moreover, in book I, chapter 17, of Philippus Cluverius’s *Ancient Italy*, there is a map of Venetia, Istria, and the territory of the Carni, on which Pliny’s Portus Romatinus is marked beyond Concordia, at the mouth of the river Romatinus where it flows into the estuary. An island can also be seen before the mouth itself, which probably constituted the same port.

When explaining his map in chapter 18 according to Pliny’s account, Cluverius wrote, as we saw above:

“The river flows past Concordia . . . and its mouth forms a port near the island town of Caorle, which is commonly called Porto Lematino. From this name it is clearly evident that this is Pliny’s river and port Romatinum in the passage just cited.”

The same is also shown on the map published by the distinguished Filiasi of Upper and Lower Venetia, or the terrestrial and maritime regions, in volume III of his recently published Italian work entitled *Historical Memoirs of the Early and Later Venetians*. He writes that both the shores and the islands of this estuary, into which the Romatinus flows, were already abundant in inhabitants before the time of the Venetians—that is, while the Roman Empire still stood and before the barbarian invasions of Italy.

Speaking of the location of this Portus Romatinus, Filiasi writes in chapter 13 of the cited volume III:

“The Lemene, then called Romatinus, formed at its mouth the Portus Romatinus according to Pliny, which must have been the maritime port of Concordia . . . . Whether this port was the port of Caorle, or that of Santa Margherita, or some other nearby place, is difficult to know, because enormous changes also took place in that estuary.”

Thus Filiasi. It is therefore established that the Portus Romatius or Romatinus mentioned by Pliny is not properly and exactly the present Portogruaro, although the latter too is situated on the same river Romatium or Romatinus.

But if Pliny’s Portus Romatius or Romatinus cannot be the present Portogruaro, could this Portogruaro at least have been the city of Romatiana mentioned by Gennadius in connection with Nicetas? I consider that quite probable.

It is a common opinion that Portogruaro, situated on this side of Concordia and not far south of the little village of Gruaro from which it took its name, grew from the ruins of Concordia. Concordia, then, was destroyed in the disaster of Attila together with Aquileia and Altinum, distinguished cities situated on either side of Concordia. Portogruaro quickly coalesced into a new city, which perhaps received inhabitants from the Portus Romatinus. That port had undoubtedly suffered destruction by the barbarians together with Concordia, of which it was the port and from which it was not far distant.

After the date of Attila’s disaster, that is, after the year 452, the Portus Romatinus mentioned by Pliny—whether situated on an island or on the inner shore of the estuary—perhaps under the subsequent pressure of the waters, as frequently happens in such places when human hands are absent to repair them promptly, vanished, as it were, from the world. In its place, in a certain sense, Portogruaro arose. By Gennadius’s time, as the fifth century was drawing to a close, it could easily have been called both a port and a city: Portogruaro, and the city of Romatiana.

It was a port because it retained the name of the ancient Portus Romatinus which had stood at the river’s mouth; and it bore the additional name of the city of Romatiana from the form of a city which the port had newly acquired and from the river Romatinus or Romatius, which flowed through it.

In any case, Filiasi, cited above, says in volume III, chapter 12:

“In the barbarian centuries, the name ‘port’ was given to all places of trade situated on rivers; thus Porto-Buffoleto, Portogruaro, and so forth received the name.”

Dufresne, in his *Glossary*, under the word *Civitas*, observed:

“By the name *civitas*, the ancients designated not only a city that was the head of a people, or one of its chief cities, but also the entire territory of a city, a district, or a diocese.”

The Portogruaro port could therefore have been called by the inhabitants, though less precisely, after the nearby village of Gruaro following the disaster of Attila. It ought rather to have been called the new Portus Romatius or Romatinus, after the older port which it had replaced, and so in fact it was. Better still, it could have been called the city of Romatiana, after the new civic form which it had acquired. 93

Why, then, should Gennadius not have understood this place as the actual city of Portogruaro when he wrote that our Nicetas was bishop of the city of Romatiana? Why should he not deliberately have called it the city of Romatiana, from a place perhaps known to him whose common name, Portogruaro, he nevertheless did not know among its inhabitants? He would thereby have designated the place as a city which he knew to be a city and which he knew to be situated on the river Romatinus—the same river which had already given its name to the old port situated at its mouth in the nearby estuary.

Gennadius’s city of Romatiana in the passage concerning Nicetas, then, which is not to be sought in Dacia but within the ancient diocese or province of Aquileia, was either the port mentioned by Pliny at the mouth of the river Romatius or Romatinus, or else the city situated on that same river and called Portogruaro, which grew after the destruction of Concordia and in a certain sense occupied the place both of Concordia itself and of the Portus Romatinus that had stood at the river’s mouth. [Col. 0958A]

This chapter should not, however, be closed before we say something also about the word *Romanae*, which, as we saw above, occurs in one Gennadian manuscript in place of the more common *Romatiana*, so that the text appears to read: “Niceas, bishop of the city of Romana,” as Fabricius also noted in the passage cited above.

From those Gennadian manuscripts which present the word *Romanae*, the same reading may perhaps have entered one or another of the martyrologies. This was sufficiently clear to the distinguished De Rubeis, who did not fail to note the singularity of this reading both in *Monuments of the Church of Aquileia*, chapter 17, no. 4, and in *Dissertations of Various Learning*, chapter 19, no. 4.

The same misfortune which befell Niceas or Nicetas also befell Chromatius, the predecessor of Aquileian Nicetas, who was likewise called a Roman bishop in a very ancient manuscript from which Johann Sichard first published his works at Basel, in the press of Adam Petri, in 1528, in octavo, under the title *Chromatius, Most Learned Roman Bishop, etc.*

Since scholars disagreed over the novelty of this title in the case of Bishop Chromatius, whom they knew to have been not Roman but Aquileian—and indeed a most distinguished bishop, according to the testimony of both Jerome and other outstanding men of that age—let us see how De Rubeis explained the matter, in accordance with his learning and his exceptional knowledge of Aquileian affairs.

“I offer another conjecture concerning the homeland of Chromatius, based on the title prefixed to the works of Chromatius listed below in certain editions. His treatises are entitled, namely, *of Chromatius, Roman bishop* . . . . There occurs the Portus Romatius, which Pliny mentions in book III, chapter 18, in Venetia, the tenth region of Italy, as follows: ‘The colony of Concordia, the river and port Romatium.’ We also read of the Portus Romatinus, which is a town—today Portogruaro according to its inhabitants—on the river Romatium, commonly called the Limino, near the ruined city of Concordia. Why should Chromatius not have been called Roman, or rather have been called Romatius and Romatinus by homeland, while being bishop of Aquileia?”

So he writes in *Monuments of the Church of Aquileia*, chapter 10, no. 2.

Then, in chapter 17, no. 4, where he responds to Baronio’s note concerning Saint Nicetas of Aquileia, he says of the title “Roman bishop” applied to Saint Chromatius:

“Saint Chromatius, the predecessor of Saint Nicetas, is found entitled ‘Roman bishop’ in his commentary on the Eight Beatitudes.”

He adds the following in the same sense:

“Saint Chromatius may perhaps have been called Roman from the place of his homeland. He ought rather to have been called Romatinus, from the Portus Romatius or Romatinus which Pliny places near Concordia.” 94

Finally, in *Dissertations of Various Learning*, chapter 18, no. 6, he wrote of this conjecture:

“Amid so many conjectures, I too was permitted to put forward one that occurred to my mind in *Monuments of the Church of Aquileia*, chapter 10, no. 2: namely, that by that designation—‘Roman’—the homeland of Chromatius was indicated, and that it was Concordia, concerning which Pliny writes in book III, chapter 18: ‘The colony of Concordia, the river and port Romatium.’ Accordingly, Chromatius ought rather to have been called Romatius or Romatinus by homeland, and afterward bishop of Aquileia.”

We have therefore seen how aptly the most learned De Rubeis resolved the difficulty of the title “Roman bishop” in the case of Chromatius of Aquileia, and how appropriately he found within the boundaries of Aquileia a place to which, through the slightest difference or rather a small inflection of the word, that Roman designation could be referred—a designation which, as he supposed, indicated Chromatius’s native land.

Why, then, did this distinguished scholar devise nothing similar by which to claim for Aquileia Gennadius’s Nicetas, whom Baronio had attributed to the Church of Aquileia with arguments that were not sufficiently firm, but whom De Rubeis could have claimed with greater confidence, since he had already succeeded in doing so with Chromatius?

Indeed, it was not merely the reading *Romanae civitatis* found in certain manuscripts concerning Bishop Nicetas, but the more common and explicit reading *Romatianae*, found in all printed editions, that should have directed him more effectively to the river Romatius or Romatinus and to the Portus Romatinus, to which he could also have referred Nicetas, at least as regards his homeland, just as he had done with Chromatius—especially after the work of Lucretius Treus in the *Sacred Monuments of the Province of Friuli*, which preceded him, as was said above.

But there was no other Chromatius bishop besides the Aquileian one in the ecclesiastical records of that period to whom the designation “Roman” could be fitted. Meanwhile, two Nicetases flourished, though not precisely in the same period, yet separated from each other by no great interval of time. If the city in Dacia could in some measure suit one of them, there was no reason to labor on behalf of the other, whom no one would deny to have been bishop of Aquileia.

Without doubt, the distinguished man would now prefer another opinion after the discovery, under the title of Nicetas the bishop, of the *Explanation of the Creed for the Competentes*. Since that work cannot belong to Nicetas the Dacian, the friend of Saint Paulinus of Nola, and clearly bears indications of Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, as well as of that Church, as we have seen, he would have found Gennadius’s city of Romatiana, even for Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, within the borders of Aquileia, just as he had done for Chromatius.

But someone may say: What does the city of Romatiana situated on the river Romatius or Romatinus contribute toward fully resolving our difficulty, if this city of Romatiana is not itself Aquileia? Someone might add: Perhaps the city of Romatiana near the river Romatius or Romatinus was the homeland of Gennadius’s Nicetas. Certainly, if this Nicetas was in reality bishop of Aquileia, there was no reason for him to be called bishop of the city of Romatiana on the basis of his homeland.

Once, therefore, Gennadius’s city of Romatiana has been found and established within the boundaries of the ancient diocese of Aquileia, one knot still remains to be untied before the Aquileian bishopric of this Romatian Nicetas can be fully demonstrated. Yet, unless I am mistaken, the following chapter will conveniently dissolve it through conjectures drawn from ecclesiastical learning.

[Col. 0959]

95 **CHAPTER VI**

**Niceas or Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, was probably called bishop of the city of Romatiana, either because, before ascending the episcopal see of Aquileia, he was an auxiliary bishop of the Church of Aquileia, stationed at the Portus Romatius or Romatinus; or because he frequently resided at the port or city of that name, even while he held the helm of the Church of Aquileia.**

**PART ONE**
Why this Niceas or Nicetas Gennadianus—whom we have already shown not to have been that Nicetas who became renowned through the friendship of Saint Paulinus of Nola and held a bishopric in Dacia, but rather to have been a bishop of the Church of Aquileia, as we have endeavored to establish by various arguments under Pope Saint Leo the Great—why, I say, this Niceas or Nicetas could have been called by Gennadius not a bishop of Aquileia but of the city of Romatiana, is now to be investigated. I shall not linger over the search for this Niceas’s or Nicetas’s homeland; and even if Romatinus or Romatianus may perhaps have been his homeland, I would not for that reason believe that Gennadius called him bishop of the city of Romatiana, but for an entirely different, stronger, and more suitable reason—first, probably because, before ascending the episcopal see of Aquileia, he had been an auxiliary bishop of that same Church of Aquileia, stationed at the port of Romatium or Romatinum.

That port of Romatium, which is commonly called Portus-Gruarius today, is now subject to the bishop of Concordia—indeed, it is the seat of the bishop of Concordia—while Concordia, once a Roman colony, now consists of only a few inhabitants and a few dwellings, scarcely forming a small hamlet or village. It offers nothing else particularly worthy of attention except an ancient cathedral and a few ruins, monuments indeed of its former name, but not so distinguished that they can even be compared with what still survives of the very extensive city of Aquileia, which, together with Concordia, suffered the same fate [Col. 0960B] from Attila’s savagery.

Nevertheless, the port of Romatium, and Concordia itself, which lies scarcely two miles from the modern port of Romatium, was once part of the very extensive diocese of Aquileia—both before Nicetas’s time and afterward, down to the very end of the sixth century. At that time a bishop of Concordia appears, famous for his name, who opens the series of the bishops of Concordia in Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, volume V, and in De Rubeis, *Monumenta Ecclesiae Aquileiensis*. The highly learned bishop Fontanini, in *Historia Literaria Aquileiensis*, book V, chapter 14, no. 1, conjectured that Laurentius, to whom the presbyter Rufinus had dedicated his *Commentary on the Creed*, might be counted among the bishops of Concordia.

Yet although that Laurentius seems to belong to the Church of Aquileia—as we previously remarked, following Fontanini himself—there is no reason why he should be assigned specifically either to the Church of Concordia or to another of the Churches belonging to the metropolitan province of Aquileia. More probably [Col. 0960C] he should be called one of those bishops who served as auxiliary bishops of the greater dioceses, with whom we must now deal. Perhaps he too may have been stationed at Concordia or at the port of Romatium on behalf of the bishop of Aquileia, but with an authority quite different from that enjoyed by the later bishops who, in the course of time, were established there in their own title, as the expression goes.

Nor was it only the territory of Concordia and the modern territory of Romatium that, both in Nicetas’s time and before and after it, was immediately subject to the bishop of Aquileia. The port of Romatium itself, Pliny’s port, which we saw was probably once situated beyond Concordia at the mouth of the river Romatium, near the island of Caprula, was likewise subject to him. For at that time the care of the bishop of Aquileia extended widely, even along the same shores of the Concordian—or, more properly, Romatian—lagoon and through the surrounding islands, as is also maintained by the very weighty opinion of the eminent Flaminius Cornelius in volume XIII of *Ecclesiae Venetae*, p. 5.

At that time, of course, the many episcopal Churches in maritime Venetia had not yet been established with their own independent jurisdiction—some of which still survive, while others have disappeared. Nor did the Church of Caprula yet exist near Pliny’s port of Romatium, or near the place where Pliny’s port of Romatium had stood. That Church arose only toward the end of the sixth century, under Pope Saint Gregory the Great, as the most eminent Cardinal Norisius demonstrates in his historical dissertation *De Synodo Quinta*, chapter 9, § 5, contrary to what Ughelli had maintained in volume V of *Italia Sacra* under the Church of Caprula. De Rubeis explains the matter more fully in *Monumenta*, chapter 32, no. 5; and most recently it has been demonstrated in a special dissertation written in Italian and published at Venice by Coleti in 1796, entitled *Sopra a’ primi vescovi Caprulensi, etc.*, by our likewise previously mentioned Innocentius Maria Lirutus, now bishop of Verona.

Therefore, since in the fifth century the territory of Concordia, and also the territory of Romatium, extending as far as it did in every direction, still lacked a bishop of its own see, and consequently formed part of the special and very extensive diocese of Aquileia in Venetia, it is highly probable that an auxiliary bishop was placed there by the bishop of Aquileia, to care, by the authority of that bishop, for the flock established in that region. It was therefore perhaps our Niceas or Nicetas who held this position before ascending the episcopal see of Aquileia, and who was consequently called bishop of the city of Romatiana by Gennadius because of the place where an auxiliary bishop of the Church of Aquileia was accustomed to reside.

We must therefore discuss auxiliary bishops of the greater dioceses in general, and in particular the auxiliary bishops of the Church of Aquileia. If it can be established that, while the territory of Concordia and the territory of Romatium had not yet been constituted as a separate diocese, the institution of auxiliary bishops nevertheless flourished in the ancient Church of Aquileia, and not long before Nicetas’s time, then, amid such great obscurity of circumstances and such chronological distance, this will be enough for us to infer with greater force that our Niceas or Nicetas at some time served as auxiliary bishop of the Church of Aquileia at the port of Romatium, and that Gennadius therefore called him, not without reason, bishop of the city of Romatiana.

I do not intend to repeat what has already been done by proposing here to write something about auxiliary bishops of the greater dioceses. After the investigations of earlier scholars, this subject has been treated with great fullness by very many more recent writers on ecclesiastical hierarchy and polity, so that there is scarcely any hope of contributing from the treasury of ecclesiastical history anything that their diligence has overlooked. Nevertheless, concerning the subject in general, it will be permissible to gather ears of grain, as it were, after the harvest; nor will readers find it unwelcome if we draw from the antiquity of Aquileia something on the same matter that may perhaps be entirely new, or at least not yet sufficiently considered.

## 97

It is an established fact, sufficiently demonstrated by Christian Lupus in his introductory dissertation on the Nicene canons, chapter 5, and abundantly by others as well, that in ancient times it was customary in the greater dioceses of the Church for all, or nearly all, of the priests of the episcopal presbyterate to be distinguished also by episcopal ordination. Some of them were even stationed in towns and villages where there were larger gatherings of the faithful. Although afterward the episcopal ordination of priests was not as frequent as at first, there were nevertheless in each of the greater Churches certain men endowed with episcopal character. They resided with the chief bishops and were prepared, when necessary and at their command, to serve as their delegated hands. The same bishops sent them to distant and more populous places within their dioceses to perform episcopal functions, so that the faithful might have access to those means of salvation which can be provided only by one marked with episcopal ordination, and which the diocesan bishop himself could have supplied only with great difficulty in those places.

Examples of both forms of this ancient institution are not lacking in the ecclesiastical monuments of earlier centuries, and it is useful to present some of them here.

That holy martyr Hippolytus, bishop of Portus, about whom learned men have written much and variously, and most recently the eminent Simon de Magistris of the Neronian Congregation of the Oratory of Rome, himself bishop of Cyrene—that holy martyr Hippolytus, I say, is found called “bishop of Rome” in ancient manuscripts. In the edition of *Daniel according to the Septuagint* published at Rome by that same most learned man in 1772, there is, on p. 95, a work of the same holy martyr in Greek and Latin under this title: *The Solutions of the Two Visions of Daniel and Nebuchadnezzar by Hippolytus, Bishop of Rome* (*Hippolyti episcopi Romae*, ἐπισκόπου Ῥώμης).

In his preface, p. 28, the distinguished editor made the following observation concerning this special title, which we quote here to illuminate the entire subject:

“After the opinions of many learned men concerning the title of Hippolytus, by which he is called ἐπίσκοπος Ῥώμης, *bishop of Rome*, it seemed to us more probable that it should be understood in this way: since he had been ordained bishop of the gentiles at Rome, he was a bishop in the city of Rome; hence the expression ‘bishop of Rome’ became common, although it is incorrect. In Hippolytus’s time there lived the presbyter Caius, likewise bishop of the gentiles at Rome . . . . . Since at that time the City was flourishing with an immeasurable multitude of people, and the number of Christians was increasing daily, the Roman pontiffs took as assistants men of the highest ability and learning, whom they employed in the administration of the Church, and whom they wished to be in the episcopal rank.”

This is de Magistris’s first of the two explanations that seemed possible to him concerning the matter, and it is enough for us to have reported it here.

Another bishop of the same kind in the city of Rome, named Macedonius, during the pontificate of Saint Cornelius, was presented in certain lost *Acts*, or *Commentaries on the Novatian Sect*, refuted by Eulogius, patriarch of Alexandria, toward the end of the sixth century. Several excerpts from that refutation, likewise lost, have been preserved for us by Photius in codices 182 and 280 of his library.

Whatever may be thought of the truth of the event reported by those *Commentaries*—which, in order to stir up hatred against the Catholics and magnify the strength of the Novatian party’s faith, accused this Macedonius, bishop of the city of Rome, of the following: after Novatian, the author of the schism, and his followers had boldly confessed the faith during the persecution, Macedonius had shamefully yielded in the same struggle and violated the holy faith—an accusation that Eulogius said had been falsely invented by the Novatians—it nevertheless seems impossible to deny that, at the time when Saint Cornelius was pontiff, there was in Rome a certain Macedonius distinguished by episcopal rank, who was called “bishop of the city of Rome.”

Although those *Commentaries* on the Novatian sect, refuted by Eulogius, were full of lies and fabrications—as is characteristic of those who undertake to defend a bad cause—the person of this Macedonius, and likewise his episcopal rank in the city of Rome, cannot be dismissed as fictitious. For it is generally characteristic of falsehood that it does not invent everything out of nothing, which would make it entirely unfit to deceive; rather, it preserves above all the truth of persons, places, and times, so that it may more effectively disguise its fabrications and stamp them with some mark of probability.

This Macedonius, then, may have been bishop of the city of Rome during the pontificate of Cornelius. Certainly he was no other than one of the auxiliary bishops of Pope Cornelius, precisely as were the martyr Hippolytus and Caius, whom we have already discussed.

A third bishop of the city of Rome, a certain Felix, during the pontificate of Saint Innocent I, is reported in the *Acts of the Carthaginian Conference* between the Catholics and Donatists in 411, first session, which are preserved in the collections of the councils and in Dupin’s edition together with Saint Optatus, bishop of Milevis.

This Felix, a refugee from Rome with almost the entire Roman nobility, as the *Acts* state, had fled the barbarity of the Goths under King Alaric and withdrawn to the African shores. On the occasion of this celebrated conference he had come to Carthage and attached himself to the Donatist party.

Balduinus, in the notes appended to this conference, thought that he was one of the Donatist pseudo-bishops who, as we learn from Optatus, presided at Rome over their Donatists, who were called the Montenses there, and that he had therefore usurped the title “bishop of the city of Rome.”
