Yet since the conference itself shows that the Catholic bishops made no such accusation against him—in fact, that he was admitted to the conference under the same title, “bishop of the city of Rome,” with only the addition that this was to be understood without prejudice to the chief bishop of the city of Rome, Pope Innocent, who was then living at Ravenna at the imperial court, lest Felix’s authority, as bishop of the city of Rome, should appear greater than it ought to have been—it is much more probable that this Felix too was one of the auxiliary bishops in Rome belonging to Pope Innocent.

Felix himself, driven by the same storm of the Goths and carried to Africa, may have allowed himself to be expelled from Catholic unity by the frauds of the Donatists; and he may have added this favor to their efforts at deception, wishing that, although separated from Roman communion, he should nevertheless be called by his former title, “bishop of the city of Rome.”

Thus the auxiliary bishops of the Roman pontiffs are clearly attested—men who were present with them at Rome and were therefore called “bishops at Rome” or “bishops of the city of Rome.” In later centuries, however, we do not find this designation, “bishop of the city of Rome,” applied in the same way to the auxiliary bishops of the Roman pontiffs who lived with them at Rome.

The reality nevertheless remained the same. For the sake of illustration, it is worth mentioning a bull of Pope Stephen II from the year 753, preserved in Ughelli’s second edition of *Italia Sacra*, prepared by Coleti, volume II, col. 86. There one finds a certain Anastasius, called “the first bishop of the diocesan bishops of the holy apostolic see,” without the addition of any title indicating a particular and proper see.

Here, unless I am mistaken, we have auxiliary bishops of the supreme pontiff in the eighth century, belonging to the number of those who lived with him at Rome. They were called not, as in earlier times, “bishops of the city of Rome,” but “diocesan bishops of the holy apostolic see.” This Anastasius, who is called “the first,” may have been the senior among such auxiliary bishops by ordination, or may have held precedence over all the others for some other reason.

There are also traces of this discipline at other major sees throughout the world, and it will suffice to present one or two examples.

In the first session of the Council of Ephesus against Nestorius, in Labbe’s edition of the councils, volume III, Venetian edition prepared by Coleti, col. 1090, one reads a letter of Saint Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, to certain members of the clergy of Constantinople concerning the deposition of Nestorius. The letter is addressed to Comarius and Potamion, bishops; to the lord Dalmatius, archimandrite of the monasteries; and to Timothy and Eulogius, priests.

The Church of Constantinople therefore had in its clergy, besides its archbishop—the prelate of that imperial city—bishops whom we may properly believe to have been auxiliary bishops of that same bishop of Constantinople. They could not have belonged to the clergy of Constantinople for any other reason.

In the fourth session of the same Council of Ephesus, in the cited volume, cols. 1166 and 1174, we read twice among the supporters of Nestorius and the followers of John of Antioch, who defended Nestorius’s cause and held a special assembly of his adherents at Ephesus in Nestorius’s favor, that there were also “bishops in name only,” that is, men who possessed no cities. In the fifth session, col. 1182, they are named individually together with other bishops of the same faction who possessed proper sees. These bishops of name only, without a see or any city, numbered six.

Cyril of Alexandria and Memnon, bishop of Ephesus, brought this, among other charges, against John of Antioch, in order to make the sentence of deposition that John had dared to pronounce against them appear all the more invalid, since it had also been issued by men whose authority in the Church was slight and negligible: although they were bishops in name only, they possessed no jurisdiction of their own.

But who could these six bishops have been—bishops in name only and possessing no cities—unless auxiliary bishops of that same John of Antioch, or of some other bishop among his followers, whom they had brought with them to Ephesus in order to perpetrate their crime against the holy ecumenical synod assembled there under the presidency of Cyril to condemn the blasphemies of Nestorius?

These, then, are two examples from the Eastern Church in the fifth century.

When I now produce another example from the same century in the Western Church, and outside the boundaries of Rome and Italy, I do not wish to appear to be acting too boldly if I venture to oppose the opinion of the very learned Sirmondus, to whom such auxiliary bishops were less acceptable.

Sidonius Apollinaris, a writer of the fifth century, wrote the following in the epitaph of Claudianus Mamertus, the brother of Saint Mamertus, bishop of Vienne, preserved in book IV of his letters, letter 11 [Col. 0964A]:

> He was a prelate of the second rank,  
> Relieving his brother by bearing the episcopal burden.  
> For, after the fashion of the supreme pontiff,  
> The one took the insignia, the other the labor.

Under the expression “a prelate in the second rank,” Sirmondus, in his notes on this letter, understands Claudianus to have been the presbyter of his brother Mamertus, the bishop, and not a bishop himself. He sharply criticizes those who already at that time distinguished bishops of the first and second rank in the same see—that is, bishops proper to the see whose title they bore, and auxiliary bishops.

In Sirmondus’s time the matter of auxiliary bishops had evidently not yet been sufficiently clarified. But what prevents us from understanding this Claudianus, called “a prelate in the second rank,” to have been an auxiliary bishop of his brother Saint Mamertus in the Church of Vienne?

Sidonius had already stated in the same letter that Mamertus had in his brother Claudianus an adviser in judicial matters, a substitute in the churches, an agent in business, and so forth. In the epitaph he adds that this prelate of the second rank relieved his brother by bearing the episcopal burden and took upon himself the labor of his brother’s episcopate, while the latter possessed the insignia of that same office.

Although these expressions are not wholly incompatible with Claudianus’s having been a presbyter, who does not see that they fit much better with Claudianus as the auxiliary bishop of his brother? The word “prelate,” applied also to Claudianus, indicates that he was a bishop, not merely a presbyter; and the task of raising his brother by his own labor under the episcopal burden suggests that he performed even those duties which are proper to episcopal character.

Moreover, when Sidonius wished to indicate a presbyter, in letter 25 of the same book, he did not call him “a prelate in the second rank,” but “a priest of the second rank.” In the same letter, after first speaking of the bishop of the diocese of Cabillonum who was to be ordained, he called that same man “the supreme prelate.”

Thus, in Sidonius’s usage, *antistes* means a bishop, not simply a presbyter: “supreme prelate” means one who presided over a diocese; “prelate in the second rank” means one who assisted the supreme prelate in the episcopal office.

Claudianus Mamertus, therefore, called “a prelate in the second rank” beside his brother Saint Mamertus, bishop of Vienne, seems to have been an auxiliary bishop of that same Church. This is so whatever the learned Sirmondus may think to the contrary, on the basis of his preconceived opposition to bishops of this kind existing within one and the same diocese, as though they were seated in one see together with the principal bishop.

Nevertheless, Gennadius, in *De Viris Illustribus*, chapter 83, calls this Claudianus a presbyter of the Church of Vienne. Perhaps he was called a presbyter because he was not the chief prelate of the diocese, and because such auxiliary bishops were for the most part not distinguished from presbyters.

Let us now pass to another kind of auxiliary bishop: namely, those who were established by bishops in large dioceses as though in a stable see, in distant and more populous places within their episcopates, wherever the needs of the faithful required them.

In my judgment, canon 6 of the Council of Sardica must be understood as referring to these bishops. In Gentianus Hervetus’s translation, preserved in Labbe, edited by Coleti, volume II, col. 662, it reads:

> “It is not permissible simply to establish a bishop in some village or small town for which even one presbyter is sufficient. For it is not necessary to establish a bishop there, lest the name and authority of a bishop be held in contempt.”

This sixth canon corrects the abuse that had arisen of establishing bishops in villages or small towns where even one presbyter was sufficient. The abuse did not consist in establishing, through the placement of bishops in villages and small towns, a great number of tiny dioceses, since dioceses at that time were generally of very great extent; nor can one imagine that the discipline of that period had suffered such a collapse that the smallest and lowest dioceses were being established everywhere, to the disgrace of the Church.

Rather, the abuse consisted in this: instead of presbyters, who could have sufficed in those villages and small towns, bishops were placed there by the diocesan bishops—men subject to their authority, that is, simply bishops, [Col. 0965A] as the Greek reading of the canon also has at the cited place: ἁπλῶς καθιστᾶν ἐπίσκοπας, “to appoint bishops simply.” These men were to preside there under the authority of the bishop who sent them.

While the Sardican canon corrects this abuse of establishing such simple bishops in villages and small towns, it already presupposes the practice then existing in the Church of appointing these simple bishops here and there in places within the dioceses of the greater bishops. In rejecting such an excessive multiplication of bishops even in small places, it consequently does not reject the establishment of such simple bishops when this was done selectively—in the more populous places of dioceses and in cities that were not so small and where presbyters would not suffice. For it adds in the very same passage:

> “But if some city should be found to become so populous that it is judged worthy of a bishopric, let it receive one.”

Here, then, we have auxiliary bishops of another kind in the greater dioceses about which we are now speaking.

These bishops were commonly called *chorepiscopi*, especially among the Greeks, from the nature of their office. At least during the first five centuries, all of them stood in the rank of true bishops, though this was not so in later times, even though they retained the name *chorepiscopi* for a long period, both among the Greeks and among the Latins.

Such bishops, established in various places within dioceses, sometimes used simply the name *chorepiscopus*, without the addition of the place where they resided by authority of the diocesan bishop. They were also often called bishops with the place added, so that they were scarcely or not at all distinguished from bishops of proper sees.

Many bishops sat at the ecumenical Council of Nicaea under the title *chorepiscopus* without any place being added, constituting the number of the 318 Fathers. They are listed under the simple title of *chorepiscopus*, in distinction from bishops of proper sees, in Labbe’s cited edition, volume II, col. 55 and following.

No one, however, is read under the title *chorepiscopus* at the general Council of Constantinople II, attended by 150 Fathers, in the same work, col. 1134 and following. Among these, certain men appear under the title of presbyter with the addition of a place. Perhaps they stood in the rank of presbyters in their own Churches but were also marked by episcopal ordination and presided over the specified place as auxiliary bishops.

In the first session of the Council of Ephesus, in the same Labbe, volume III, col. 1079, among the subscriptions of the bishops to the sentence of deposition pronounced against Nestorius, one also reads “Perebius” (elsewhere “Parebius”), bishop of the Thessalonian forests.

Why should he not have been an auxiliary bishop of the metropolitan Church of Thessalonica, established by the diocesan prelate in the wooded districts of his own diocese, and for that reason having written himself “bishop of those forests”?

It is now necessary to investigate the custom of the Roman Church also with respect to auxiliary bishops of this second kind, established in particular places, of whom we have just spoken. We have already observed the same custom in the auxiliary bishops of the other form: those who were not placed over any particular location, but depended entirely upon the will of the principal bishop who governed the whole diocese and who, as it were, almost always kept them near himself.

While I had in hand the learned work of the distinguished Dominicus Georgius, entitled *Historical Dissertation on the Episcopal Cathedra of the City of Setia in Latium*, published at Rome in 1727, I came upon words in chapter 4 worthy of careful consideration. The author there calls the attention of readers to the fact that “the Roman pontiffs established bishops everywhere not only in Latium and Campania but also in suburban Tuscany, even in the more insignificant little towns, so that they might employ their work and counsel in the Roman councils, which they often held to establish matters of faith and ecclesiastical discipline.”

The purpose for which this was said by the distinguished author—to prove that in such places, in the Church’s earliest times, actual episcopal sees had been established, in accordance with the practice of our own age, namely, fully independent sees with their own dioceses like ours—is abundantly revealed by what follows there.

For in order to demonstrate that genuine episcopal cathedras had existed in ancient times, practically from the very origin of Christianity, in the places he enumerates and even in places that had always been almost entirely without distinction—such as, for example, the very small place called the Three Taverns, which had never been anything other than three inns or three public lodging houses; and likewise places that were, as it were, attached to the walls of a city, such as the place called Subaugusta, together with many others of the same kind, which he discusses individually there with great learning—he cites the names of the bishops of those places, drawn from the subscriptions preserved from Roman synods of the same period.

Thus, for example, Felix of the Three Taverns, from the Roman council held under Pope Miltiades in 313, as recorded by Optatus of Milevis, book I, chapter 23; and Crispianus of Subaugusta, from the Roman council held under Pope Hilary in 465, in volume IV of the councils, Paris edition of 1715, p. 1060, and in Labbe’s councils, edited by Coleti, volume V, col. 86, where another bishop of the Three Taverns, named Lucifer, is also listed.

He adds further, after reviewing such sees from chapter 5 through chapter 47, in the following chapter, 48:

> “Not only were episcopal cathedras established in ancient times by the Roman pontiffs in the distinguished cities of Latium and suburban Tuscany, and established so thickly that they seemed almost to touch one another, but bishops were also assigned to towns of almost no distinction.”

Certainly, episcopal cathedras may have been established by the Roman pontiffs in individual cities that still flourished in the earliest centuries of the Church and were notable for the size of their populations. Yet, with due respect to so worthy a scholar, I would not be equally inclined to think that genuine and proper episcopal cathedras, possessing their own jurisdiction, were established by those same Roman pontiffs in Latium, Campania, and suburban Tuscany so densely that they seemed almost to touch one another.

Still less would I suppose that bishops were assigned even to towns of almost no distinction, if by such bishops one understands bishops of a true and proper see, with those insignificant places regarded as their own special and tiny dioceses.

Who would not more easily and plausibly understand such bishops—at least the great majority of them—as merely auxiliary bishops of the Roman pontiffs, whom the pontiffs placed in Latium, Campania, and suburban Tuscany almost in the place of presbyters, within the very extensive diocese of the city of Rome, which they had reserved for themselves to govern in a special manner?

I do not deny that some of these bishops, in the course of time and with the authority of the Roman pontiff, became bishops of a proper see and of a proper diocese. But I believe that this should be conceded only to those places that were more distinguished, richer in population, surrounded by a more extensive territory, and also more distant from the city.

For the rest, I seem to see here only auxiliary bishops of the Roman Church, who remained in places assigned to them by the Roman pontiff and who, when necessary, were summoned from there to attend the Roman councils, where they subscribed with the addition of the name of that place in which, by the designation of the Roman pontiff, they sat as auxiliary bishops in his place and by his authority.

My conviction is strengthened still further by the fact that in ancient times the authority of bishops who depended immediately upon the authority of the Roman pontiff was confined within extremely narrow limits. Many things were not permitted to them without authorization granted by him—things that today, and for many centuries, bishops called ordinary bishops of Churches perform everywhere by their own right. It is reasonable to believe that all those who were situated far from Rome and did not belong to the special synod of the Roman pontiffs already performed such functions at that time, since they enjoyed ordinary authority in their own Churches.

There exists a book entitled *Liber Diurnus Romanorum Pontificum*, first published, as is reported, by Holstenius and afterward by Garnerius. It is generally thought to have been compiled in the seventh or early eighth century, although in substance it is considered much older, since in many respects it reflects the discipline that had prevailed among the Roman pontiffs several centuries earlier.

In chapter 5 of Garnerius’s edition there are various formulas concerning the suburban bishops—that is, those whom we have recently mentioned, of Latium, Campania, and suburban Tuscany, and perhaps also of other neighboring provinces—who were specifically subject to the consecration of the Roman pontiff.

These formulas present petitions of the bishops and the responses of the pontiffs, by which the bishops were granted authority to consecrate basilicas, oratories, baptisteries, and altars; to raise the bodies of saints and reinter them in a more honorable place; to ordain priests to be placed over oratories and basilicas; and to perform other such acts, which they had not previously been permitted to carry out until the supreme pontiff had granted them the privilege.

Even if this discipline was in use during the seventh, eighth, and also ninth centuries, and bishops specifically subject to the Roman pontiff sought his permission on each occasion to perform all these acts when necessary, although they were already the ordinary bishops of their Churches, it can nevertheless easily be conjectured that the very restricted authority of these suburban bishops originated in earlier times, when they exercised entirely delegated authority in those Churches, as merely auxiliary bishops of the Roman pontiffs in that part of Italy which the pontiffs had reserved to themselves to govern as though it were their own special diocese.

Consequently, the narrow authority of these bishops, which continued through the seventh, eighth, and even ninth centuries, confirms the opinion that, among the many bishops of those regions before the fifth or sixth century, the Roman pontiff had none but auxiliary bishops—men without independent rights, who therefore depended upon him in everything and entirely upon his will, as it were.

The same discipline likewise prevailed in the fifth century in the regions of Egypt, Libya, and the Pentapolis, which were subject to the bishop of Alexandria.

For the thirteen bishops of those regions who were present at the Council of Chalcedon, in the fourth session, declared, also in the name of the other fellow bishops who obeyed the Alexandrian see, that nothing in general could be carried out by any of the bishops subject to the Alexandrian see without the authority of the archbishop—as they called him—of the famous city of Alexandria.

They based this on the celebrated Nicene canon of the 318 Fathers, which is the sixth canon and may be found in the collections of the councils and in Christian Lupus, *Opera*, volume I, p. 244, Venetian edition of 1724, where it had been decreed:

> “Let the ancient custom prevail throughout Egypt, Libya, and the Pentapolis, so that the bishop of Alexandria may have authority over all these places, since a similar custom also belongs to the bishop of Rome.”

This parity of custom with the Roman Church, which the Fathers of Nicaea adduce as an argument in favor of the archbishop of the city of Alexandria; this ancient custom by which the Nicene canon confirms the authority of the bishop of Alexandria over the bishops of Egypt, Libya, and the Pentapolis; and finally this, so to speak, nullity of authority which those same bishops confessed before the Council of Chalcedon on the basis of the Nicene canon—all these considerations taken together lead us easily to believe that the same discipline which prevailed in the Roman Church also prevailed in the Alexandrian Church: that in ancient times, and even in the fifth century itself, all or nearly all the bishops of those regions were merely auxiliary bishops of the archbishop of Alexandria, who exercised full authority over everyone in those regions.

But now we must turn our discussion to the African prelates who assembled for the aforementioned Carthaginian conference in the year 411, together with the bishops of the Donatist faction. Since at that time in most of the African churches there were two bishops—one Catholic, the other Donatist—several Catholic bishops, moved by the zeal for unity with which they burned, and in order to oppose more attentively and effectively both the violence and the seductions of those schismatics, had appointed certain bishops in the more dangerous and remote places of their dioceses. These bishops were to assist the Catholic cause by their presence, prevent the defection of the faithful, and be available to those who were recovering their senses. The Donatists likewise, driven by resentment and wishing in some manner to oppose force with force, did not fail to do the same on the opposite side, although they dared to charge the Catholics with having done this not out of zeal for unity but under the impulse of vanity, namely, to increase their number.

The soundness of the Catholics’ policy is sufficiently clear from Saint Augustine’s Letter 209. Not long after the Carthaginian conference, he himself established a bishop in his own diocese at a place called Castellum, recently converted from the Donatist schism through no small exertion on his part and lying forty miles from the see of Hippo. He appointed there a man named Antonius, drawn from his own monastery, so that he might provide, as Augustine himself put it, the necessary care for those faithful whom Augustine doubted he could adequately serve because of the distance of the place [Col. 0968A]. Yet Antonius later responded so badly to the holy prelate’s expectations that Augustine discusses the matter at greater length in the same letter.

What, then, do those records say about such bishops? In Action 1 of this conference, no. 117, Petilianus, a Donatist bishop, complained against the Catholics, saying: “In the one people of our present colleague Januarius, in one diocese, four have been appointed against him, plainly so that the number might be increased.” Likewise, in no. 121, Verissimus, another Donatist bishop who said that he was bishop of the city of Tacarata, where Aspidius was the Catholic bishop, also complained, saying: “There are four in my people: Datianus, Aspidius, Fortunatus, and Octavianus.”

The Catholics, then, so as to repel the accusation directed against them and to show their opponents that there was no ground for complaint on this matter, did not fail, when the occasion arose, to report the bishops whom the Donatists themselves had similarly added in their dioceses for the advancement of the schism. Accordingly, in the same Action 1, no. 121, Victorianus, the Catholic bishop of the people of Mustitana, said: “I have Felicianus of Mustitana and Donatus of Turres against me.” Likewise, in no. 126, Asmunius, the Catholic bishop of Tiguala, said: “There are two in my diocese, Gaianus and Privatus.”

It should further be observed that these bishops of both parties, whom I have called new and additional bishops, were not designated in the nominal listing by the simple title of bishop when each was summoned and recorded at that conference. Rather, the name of the place over which each presided was added, as, for example, in the case of the Catholics Octavianus and Fortunatus, about whom the Donatist Verissimus complained: one was later called bishop of Ressiana, the other bishop of Casa, as appears in the editor’s note in Saint Optatus. Similarly among the Donatists there was that Donatus whom the Catholic bishop Victorianus calls “of Turres” [Col. 0968D], and Privatus, who was perhaps the man called “of Auzaga” in the same records. The same is true of all the others present at that conference: none appears without the name of a place of which he was said to be bishop.

But were those additional and new bishops, in the places over which they had been appointed, of the same condition, rank, and authority as the earlier bishops of the old sees in whose dioceses they had been established? I would add another question: were those communities entrusted to these additional bishops? Were so many new dioceses of the same order as the original dioceses, within whose bounds they seemed to exist?

This has appeared so to many who have thought it proper to compile a vast number of African dioceses from the many episcopal names which, together with the designation of an episcopal place entrusted to their care, appear in the acts of the African Church. But, to state my own view confidently [Col. 0969A], without intending to detract in any way from the authors or defenders of the opposing position, whom I confess that I respect: I would not say that the multiplication of bishops in the African provinces amounted to the establishment of so many new churches within the boundaries of the ancient dioceses; nor would I say that those additional and new bishops—at least for the greater part of them—were of the same condition and authority as the bishops of the ancient sees that existed in Africa before the spread of the Donatist schism.

That Petilianus, the bishop of the Donatist party, in Action 1 of the conference, no. 165, reproached the Catholics for the following: “In our absence, they set up many images here and there, in places, cities, or dioceses, so that they may appear numerous.” However insolently that abusive ranter may have wished, according to his custom, to insult the Catholics, he would certainly never have dared so brazenly to reproach them with their many “images,” whether of dioceses or of bishops, if those had been genuine dioceses comparable to the ancient ones, and if those men had been bishops possessing full rights like the others who could enumerate a long succession of predecessors [Col. 0969B].

Moreover, in no. 181, when Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, had heard the names of many bishops on Donatus’s side recited together with their communities, he said in the same conference: “Let it be recorded that all these men”—the Donatist bishops—“were ordained bishops in villages or on estates, not in any cities.”

What did Petilianus reply in the following section? The leader of the schismatics immediately answered him: “So you too have many scattered throughout all the countryside. Indeed, you have them in abundance, and plainly you have them without peoples.”

Who could possibly regard these as true dioceses in the proper sense, whether on the Catholic or on the Donatist side, when they were counted according to the number of estates or villages, and when their bishops were described, because of the smallness of their dioceses, as virtually being without peoples?

But what was the condition and authority of these bishops? I shall say again with confidence that such additional and new bishops, established in villages and on estates and scattered throughout all the countryside, were, at least for the greater part, simple auxiliary bishops appointed in certain places by the primary bishops, almost in place of presbyters who had previously been there but who, because of the schism, were no longer sufficient for the needs of the people. Their purpose was plainly that, by virtue of the dignity of a higher order, they might care for the Catholic cause more effectively and energetically.

Further evidence is available from the same Action 1 of the proceedings of the conference, and it seems to me to suggest this quite clearly. When, in no. 182, Rogatianus, the Donatist bishop of Idassa, had said, “I have no opponent”—that is, “I have no other bishop from the Catholic side in my diocese”—Aurelius, the Catholic bishop of the Church of Macomades, immediately replied: “I have Florentinus, a presbyter, in the church. There were three Catholic bishops; they have now died. We have not yet been able to ordain another.”

The Church of Idassa, therefore, belonging to Rogatianus, the Donatist bishop, was part of the diocese of Aurelius, the Catholic bishop of Macomades. When Aurelius says, “I have Florentinus, a presbyter, in the church,” this sufficiently shows that the church belonged to him, that the presbyter was subject to him, that he had sent him there, and that the presbyter presided there in Idassa by Aurelius’s authority [Col. 0969D].

The next statement—“There were three Catholic bishops”—refers to the period before that presbyter Florentinus. It shows that those bishops had been placed there by Aurelius or by his predecessors, not as diocesan bishops but as auxiliaries of his Church of Macomades, in place of the presbyters who had previously been in the community of Idassa. After those three bishops, another presbyter, the aforementioned Florentinus, had been sent there to take their place and govern that community on behalf of Aurelius until another bishop should be ordained. That bishop, therefore, just as much as the presbyter, would occupy the place of Aurelius and exercise his authority, not as the bishop of an independent diocese but as Aurelius’s auxiliary bishop.

There is another passage, in sections 187 and 188. Victor, the bishop of Rotaria on Donatus’s side, likewise cried out [Col. 0970A]: “I have no opponent.” One of the Catholic bishops answered him: “We had a bishop there. You killed him and seized his place.”

Another Victor, the Catholic bishop of Azura, immediately replied to the Donatist: “He says that he has no opponent. I have a church there, a fact of which you are not unaware.”

But if Victor of Azura had a church in the alleged diocese of Rotaria belonging to the other Victor, the Donatist bishop, then the Catholic bishop who presided there and was killed by the Donatists presided over a church or community that belonged to Victor of Azura. Therefore that bishop killed by the Donatists—perhaps called the bishop of Rotaria—was by no means the bishop of an independent diocese, but only the auxiliary bishop of Victor of Azura, the Catholic bishop.

I shall add a third passage, from sections 203 and 204 of the same first Action. There the name of a certain Donatus, a bishop on the side of the schismatics, was recited. He had subscribed himself bishop “of Medianis Zabuniorum,” although no Donatist existed there at all, and although that bishop, so designated from the place, had never been present there [Col. 0970B].

Victor, the Catholic bishop, first answered him as follows: “Let him prove that he went to the one house he mentioned.” Then Novatus, himself also a Catholic bishop of the Church of Sitifis, immediately added: “Let it be recorded that Medianis Zabuniorum has a presbyter. He now holds the community and the basilica. He has the unity. There is no Donatist there. Over the body of the Catholic bishop I ordained a presbyter, and, God willing, a bishop will be ordained there. There is no Donatist bishop in that place.”

What, then, should be inferred from this? What else can the bishop of Sitifis mean when he says, “Over the body of the Catholic bishop I ordained a presbyter, who now holds the community and the basilica in Medianis Zabuniorum,” except that he clearly indicates that Medianis Zabuniorum belonged to Novatus, the bishop of the Church of Sitifis? For that reason, over the body of the bishop who had died—that is, immediately after his death—Novatus, by his ordinary authority, ordained a presbyter there [Col. 0970C], and that presbyter then held the community and the basilica.

But if Novatus ordained a presbyter in place of the deceased bishop, as he was doing so in a place subject to himself, what else could that bishop have been except what the presbyter was after him and in his place: that is, a bishop in rank but not in independent jurisdiction, and therefore simply an auxiliary bishop of Novatus of Sitifis? He too, nevertheless, like the others, would have held the title of the place which he governed.

So much thus far, if I am not mistaken, is sufficient to establish that the discipline of auxiliary bishops existed in the African Church in the fourth and fifth centuries—namely, bishops who were placed by other bishops in places within their dioceses and were called by the names of those places no less than the prelates of the primary sees.

I do not, however, deny that abuses also entered the Catholic Church of Africa itself concerning the appointment of bishops of this kind. Thus, in fact, bishops were commonly ordained, as we have seen, even in the smallest and most insignificant places, without any particular selection and contrary to the discipline of the canons [Col. 0970D]. Nor were they always appointed for the necessity or benefit of the people, but sometimes at the request of the communities or because of the ambition or importunity of certain presbyters. The African Church endeavored to remedy these abuses in several councils held both before and after that Carthaginian conference, as is especially clear from canon 5 of the Council of Carthage of the year 390, in Labbe, edited by Coletus, volume II, column 1245, and also from sections 53, 56, and 98 of the Code of the Canons of the African Church, which is printed in Greek and Latin in the same work of Labbe, at column 1251.

Nor should it be denied that, with the passage of time, some of these portions of ancient dioceses, which had been entrusted to particular auxiliary bishops, eventually became dioceses with proper names. The earlier bishops later retained little or no authority over them, so that those who undertook their governance were no longer auxiliary bishops of other bishops but bishops with independent jurisdiction, like those from whom they had originally derived their existence. This could have happened for more than one reason, and indeed for legitimate reasons; but I shall refrain here from examining them, lest I seem to wander too far from the subject, concerning which I may perhaps say something below and at a more appropriate point.

Meanwhile, we must not omit the authority of Saint Leo the Great in the letter which he addressed to the African bishops of the province of Mauretania Caesariensis—or, as it is stated elsewhere, to all the bishops established throughout Africa. This is Letter 12 in the Venetian edition of the Ballerini and belongs to the year 446.

Perhaps, after the Carthaginian conference of 411, the abuse in Africa of multiplying bishops in small and obscure places had grown beyond measure, with the greatest loss to episcopal dignity. The bishops of some ancient dioceses themselves brought complaints about this matter to the apostolic see. They apparently belonged to those who were no longer free, on their own initiative and by their own will, to refrain from ordaining bishops [Col. 0971B], since these places already had predecessors and an established see, and the bishops there exercised not auxiliary but diocesan authority.

What, then, did the holy pontiff say in the cited letter?

“Certainly, as regards sacerdotal dignity, we wish the statutes of the canons to be observed in all things: that bishops not be consecrated in just any places, nor in whatever fortresses, nor where there had previously been none; since, where the communities are smaller and the assemblies less numerous, the care of presbyters is sufficient. Episcopal governance, however, ought to preside only over larger peoples and more populous cities, lest—as the divinely inspired decrees of the holy Fathers have forbidden—the sacerdotal eminence be bestowed upon villages and estates, obscure and solitary townships, and the honor which ought to be entrusted to superior places be cheapened by its very proliferation.

“Bishop Restitutus has complained that this has now been done in his diocese, and he has reasonably requested that, if the bishops of those places in which they ought not to have been ordained should die according to the course of nature, the places themselves should return to the jurisdiction of that same prelate to whom they formerly belonged either as his own or as adjacent territories. It is useless for sacerdotal dignity to be diminished by excessive multiplication resulting from the thoughtless ease of the ordaining bishop.”

This is what the holy pontiff said to the African bishops. Who does not see that, in the first part of the text, the holy pontiff drew both the ideas and, above all, the wording from the ancient councils—especially from canon 6 of Sardica cited above—in order to restrain that excessive readiness in the African churches to ordain bishops in places by no means worthy of such honor?

Since these bishops are compared by the holy pontiff with presbyters in those same smaller places, where he says that the care of presbyters is sufficient, it is rightly understood that the bishops who were thus abusively chosen for smaller places had no authority other than that of presbyters, without any diminution of the authority of the bishops in whose dioceses they had been established [Col. 0971D]. This is characteristic of merely auxiliary bishops: they possessed the power of order, but not of jurisdiction, except whatever the diocesan bishop might have wished to impart to them.

In the second part, however, when he speaks of Bishop Restitutus, who had complained to him that such bishops had also held places in his diocese, and who reasonably requested—apparently both for himself and for others—that, when those bishops died who had been established in places where, according to the canons, they ought not to have been ordained, those places should return to the jurisdiction of the earlier bishops to whom they had once belonged either as their own or as adjacent territories, the pontiff seems already to be speaking of places which, over the course of time, and with a succession of bishops in them—perhaps supported by circumstances and without opposition from those whose interests were involved—had eventually become distinct new bishoprics, at the expense of the older diocese.

The original bishops had therefore, as it were, lost their right over them. For that reason they required the superior authority of the Roman pontiff, so that, when those bishops died, the places themselves might be reclaimed for their ancient and proper jurisdiction [Col. 0972A].

Having thus discussed the auxiliary bishops of both kinds who existed in the early centuries of the Church—namely, those attached to no particular place, who were called simply bishops without any addition of a place, or who were called bishops of the place where they served as auxiliaries at the will of the principal bishop, such as the bishops of Rome or of the city of Rome, as we have seen; and also those who were assigned by diocesan bishops to certain particular places and were commonly called by the names of those places—the first part of the proposition set forth in this chapter appears sufficiently supported by the ecclesiastical discipline of the earlier centuries of the Church. Namely, Niceas, or Nicetas, was probably called bishop of the city of Romatiana because, before ascending to the episcopal see of Aquileia, he had been an auxiliary bishop of the Church of Aquileia, situated at the port of Romatium or Romatinum.

Our conjecture becomes still more probable if we demonstrate, from the surviving monuments of the Church of Aquileia, that the same discipline concerning auxiliary bishops which we have thus far gathered piecemeal as having generally existed in the ancient Church also existed in the Church of Aquileia. This is what must now principally be done.

We must return once more to the Library of Photius. In the codices cited above, 182 and 280, he reviews a work of Eulogius, patriarch of Alexandria, divided into six books and directed against the sect of the Novatians, which in his own time—namely, toward the end of the sixth century—still harassed the Church of God in more than one place.

While Photius preserved for us excerpts from Eulogius’s lost work, those same excerpts also preserve information about certain commentaries, likewise lost, belonging to the Novatian sect, which Eulogius himself had deliberately refuted in Book VI.

We have already said that in those commentaries a certain Macedonius, called the bishop of the city of Rome, was accused by the Novatians as a deserter from the faith in a contest held before the persecutors of the Church, while, by contrast, Novatian and his followers are said to have emerged victorious after boldly professing the Christian faith.

But who were those who adhered to Novatian and were said to have boldly engaged in the struggle with him? Those commentaries present three bishops as Novatian’s associates: namely Marcellus and Alexander, whom they call bishops of Aquileia, ἐπισκόπους Ἀκυληίας, and Agamemnon, bishop of Tiberis or Tibur—commonly Tivoli.

The same commentaries, according to Photius, added that those three bishops laid hands on Novatian so that he might undertake the pontificate at Rome against Pope Cornelius. They also said that the three lived together with him in a small building which they had constructed themselves, because they refused to use it or to perform sacred rites together with those who had sacrificed to idols.

Here, then, we have two bishops, Marcellus and Alexander, existing together and at the same time, who are called bishops of Aquileia, just as Macedonius is called bishop of the city of Rome. Whatever may be thought about the truth of the event or events, as we previously observed concerning Macedonius, persons themselves, their names and places, and their offices, even in fictions, are generally free from fabrication, so that the fictions themselves may more easily be made credible.

The illustrious De Rubeis, however, in his Monuments of the Church of Aquileia, chapter 4, section 7, is entirely occupied with excluding these two bishops, Marcellus and Alexander, from the series of Aquileian bishops which he himself arranged.

Nor shall I insist that these two must be included in the series of Aquileian bishops, although the series of the Aquileian bishops of that period, down to Theodore, whom we see subscribed to the Council of Arles against the Donatists in 314, is extremely uncertain and confused and is not without gaps and lacunae, as the learned author himself observes.

Nevertheless, even if those bishops, Marcellus and Alexander, do not belong to the series of Aquileian bishops, they were certainly not called Aquileian bishops without reason, nor were they described as though they were exercising the episcopate in the same church at one and the same time [Col. 0973A]. No reason is more probable or more consistent with the discipline of those times than that they were so called because they were both auxiliary bishops in the vast diocese of Aquileia, serving the man who at that time was the chief bishop of the Aquileians, whoever he may have been.

I confirm this from the very evidence by which De Rubeis attempted to exclude them from the Church of Aquileia. He says that Theodoret, in Book III, chapter 5, of the Heretical Fables, asserts that those three ordainers of Novatian were bishops of πολιχνίων—that is, of small towns.

“But,” adds the distinguished author, “the writers of that age unanimously present and praise Aquileia not as a small town, not as a little city, but as a very great city.”

Quite rightly, then, he uses this to keep Marcellus and Alexander out of the catalogue of Aquileian bishops. But it is equally right and highly appropriate to understand them as auxiliary bishops in the Church of Aquileia, sent here and there by the principal bishop throughout that very extensive diocese and perhaps situated in small towns. They would nevertheless not be designated by the titles of those unknown small towns, but by the name of the great and celebrated city whose bishop they served.

The Christian cause at that time especially required that the ministry of bishops should not be lacking to the faithful, who were frequently subjected to persecution. The Church was still far removed from that security of peace in which, once established, it was later able to provide for the dignity of the episcopal office by decreeing at the Council of Sardica and elsewhere that bishops should not be placed so indiscriminately in villages or small cities, much less in hamlets and estates or obscure and solitary townships, as we have seen.

De Rubeis continues, and introduces Pope Cornelius as saying in his letter to Fabius of Antioch, preserved by Eusebius in Ecclesiastical History, Book VI, chapter 43, that two men of ruined condition sent by Novatian had been dispatched εἰς βραχύ τι μέρος, καὶ ἐλάχιστον τῆς Ἰταλίας—that is, as he himself interprets the words, “into a narrow and very small part of Italy”—from which three bishops would be brought to Rome to lay hands on Novatian [Col. 0973C].

“But,” adds the author of the Aquileian Monuments, “would anyone in his right mind say that the places of Aquileia and Tibur, which lie so far apart, could be contained within a narrow and very small part of Italy?”

I would not indeed say that the places of Aquileia and Tibur were contained within a narrow and very small part of Italy, or even, as Valesius there and Coustant in the Letters of the Roman Pontiffs interpret the words, within a “small and most insignificant” part. I would, however, point out that Rufinus, the ancient translator of Eusebius’s History, praised even by Valesius in his notes on this chapter, rendered the words of Cornelius’s letter in Cacciari’s edition, Book VI, chapter 33, in such a way that he spoke not of a narrow and very small part, nor of a small and most insignificant part, but rather of a remote part of Italy, from which those three bishops who ordained Novatian had been summoned.

I would also say that the Greek words which now appear in the text of Cornelius’s letter, and which De Rubeis translates literally as “a narrow and very small part of Italy,” were perhaps translated more accurately and more in keeping with the author’s intention by Cacciari himself in his notes on this passage, so that it would be understood that those three bishops summoned by Novatian had come from the remotest corners of Italy [Col. 0973D].

Who, moreover, will deny that Aquileia and the surrounding territory lay in a remote part of Italy, both in relation to Rome, which was situated virtually in the center of Italy, and in itself, since it lies at the extreme northern and eastern edge of Italy?

As for “corners”—a name applied to places that are usually smaller, or even very small, and situated at the outermost edges of provinces—such corners certainly existed in the Aquileian region too. There were places distant from the city of Aquileia, lowly in condition and situation, and distinguished by no fame, where Christians may perhaps have hidden more easily and safely during times of persecution, and where lesser bishops, so to speak, may have resided to attend to matters of religion and faith among the Christians, in place of the bishop of the whole region, who could not be present everywhere [Col. 0974A].

The Aquileian province, therefore, would have had corners of this kind, as did the neighboring territory of Tibur near Rome, from which those three bishops were deceitfully summoned by Novatian.

Let us even grant that the literal interpretation of the Greek text, as it appears in all the editions, may be accepted, and that with De Rubeis we may speak of a “narrow and very small part of Italy,” or, with Valesius and Coustant, of a “small and most insignificant” part, from which those three bishops were brought to Rome. It does not follow that the dignity of Aquileia and Tibur should therefore be diminished, contrary to the truth of the matter, by such terms in the most insulting manner.

It means rather that those cities, however celebrated, had in their surrounding territories narrow and very small districts, indeed small and most insignificant places, where bishops may have existed at that time. Such bishops, being simple and inexperienced—as Pope Cornelius calls them—Novatian could easily deceive through his messengers, depraved and exceedingly crafty men.

For example, who would not have called the shores of the lagoons, or the many islands within the lagoons themselves, a narrow and very small part of Italy, indeed a small and most insignificant part in relation to Aquileia and its flourishing territory, at that time? They had no particular renown then; they acquired it only later, when the Venetian state emerged, as it were, from the waters of those lagoons amid the ruins of the Roman Empire.

Who would not understand by that term the wooded and nearly inaccessible parts of the region here and there, which even now our diocese of Udine—formed from the Aquileian diocese—includes toward Germany and Noricum?

There is therefore no difficulty, and no reason to prevent us from holding that Marcellus and Alexander, called Aquileian bishops, really were Aquileian bishops at the same time—namely, auxiliary bishops established in the distant and remote places of the Church of Aquileia on behalf of the Aquileian bishop who then governed the whole of the extensive Aquileian region.

I said above that, whatever may be thought about the truth of the event or events reported in those commentaries, scholars agree that the two Aquileian bishops Marcellus and Alexander mentioned in the commentaries of the Novatian sect preserved by Photius—and perhaps not even the bishop of Tibur—were not the men who laid hands on Novatian. Instead, they were three others, two of whom the same scholars name as Trophimus and Evaristus.

Perhaps these two Aquileian bishops, Marcellus and Alexander, were never on Novatian’s side, nor did they hold a meeting with him at Rome, as the commentaries assert. Those commentaries undoubtedly introduced these two Aquileians, together with the bishop of Tibur, in order to lend the Novatian sect a kind of honor and authority from the very extensive and almost apostolic Church of Aquileia and from another church close to Rome. They did so in precisely the same manner in which they falsely displayed Novatian as having been regarded by the Alexandrian Church as the Catholic bishop of Rome, as we understand from the same Photius.

It is nevertheless preferable to have removed this stain from the Church of Aquileia by a method different from that used by De Rubeis: preserving, that is, the Aquileian bishops Marcellus and Alexander, who at that time were auxiliary bishops in the same Church together, and whose office there at the same time is by no means incompatible, as we have seen, with the historical monuments of that period. Indeed, it accords perfectly with the methods of forgers. We must now proceed to other matters.

Among the more distinguished monuments of the Church of Aquileia is the council held at Aquileia in the year 381 against Palladius and Secundianus, bishops in Cisdanubian Dacia and followers of Arian impiety. It may be found in Labbe’s Councils, edited by Coletus, volume II, column 1163, and among the Works of Saint Ambrose prepared by the Maurist monks.

The importance of this council lies not in the number of its bishops but chiefly in the fact that the more distinguished men of the Western Church of that age, renowned for learning and holiness, assembled there. Most of them have been entered in the catalogue of the saints and enjoy public veneration in the Church [Col. 0975A].

There were thirty-two bishops, almost all of them, with few exceptions, from Upper Italy. The first was Valerianus, bishop of Aquileia, followed by Ambrose of Milan, who moderated the entire council and was, as it were, its soul and voice among all the bishops.

What is especially relevant to our subject in this council is that several bishops were present who were undoubtedly auxiliary bishops of other bishops, whether present or absent. For while some are designated by the name of their proper sees, these men are called only bishops, without any indication of the place to which they were attached.

We possess a list, or subscription, of all the bishops who attended the council in the same council, under section 76, among the Works of Saint Ambrose, and at the beginning of the council itself in the cited Collection of Labbe. It is useful to keep this list, or these subscriptions, before us, so that, after comparison with the other material to be set out below [Col. 0975B], no reason may remain for doubting that these men were truly bishops, although without proper sees. For some have been mistaken, taking these bishops to have been presbyters, as we shall see.

### Names of the Bishops and Presbyters Who Were Present at the Council

This is the title of the list, or statement of the subscriptions. The list then follows, in both places, with only a few alterations, as follows:

> “Valerian, bishop of Aquileia; Ambrose, bishop of Milan; Eusebius, bishop of Bologna; Limenius, bishop of Vercelli; Anemius (also Armenius), bishop of Sirmium in Illyricum; Sabinus, bishop of Piacenza; Abundantius, bishop of Trent; Philaster, bishop of Brescia; Constantinus (also Constantius), bishop of Orange, legate of the Gauls; Theodorus, bishop of Octodurum; Dominus (also Domninus), bishop of Grenoble; Amantius, bishop of Nice; Maximus, bishop of Emona; Bassianus, bishop of Lodi; Proculus, bishop of Marseille, [Col. 0975C] legate of the Gauls; Heliodorus, bishop of Altinum (Altiniensis; also Altinensis); Felix, bishop of Jadera (Jadertinus; also Jadrensis); Eventius, bishop of Ticinum (Ticiniensis; also Citiniensis); Exsuperantius, bishop of Tortona; Diogenes, bishop of Genoa; Constantius, bishop of Siscia (Scisciensis; also: Sciscianensis, legate of the Gauls); Justus, bishop of Lyon, another legate of the Gauls; Felix, legate of the Africans; Numidius, legate of the Africans; Evagrius, presbyter and legate; Artemius; Almachius; Januarius; Jovinus; Macedonius; Cassianus; Marcellus; Eustathius; Maximus; Chromatius, presbyter.”

Thus runs the list of those who were present at the Council of Aquileia, bishops and presbyters alike. But were those last men, who are designated without the title “bishop,” and who, together with the two African legates—likewise named without the title “bishop”—make eleven in all, bishops or presbyters?

At the title “presbyter,” which is given in the list to Chromatius—then certainly a presbyter of Aquileia and placed last—we read an annotation in the cited Venetian edition of the Councils, apparently supplied by the editor: [Col. 0975D] “perhaps presbyters.” According to that editor, then, it would have to be understood that all those whose names are given simply before Chromatius were presbyters together with him; and that, for this reason, they were called presbyters in a single designation placed after all the names.

The matter, however, is not so. It is clearly established that all were bishops, with the sole exceptions of Chromatius of Aquileia and Evagrius the legate, who alone are specifically called presbyters in the list. This is evident from the opening of the council itself, which reads as follows:

> “In the consulship of Syagrius [113] and Eucherius, most illustrious men, on the third day before the Nones of September (also: on the Nones of September), while they were seated in the church at Aquileia, with the bishops (also: with the bishops seated) of the city of Aquileia—Valerian, Ambrose, Eusebius, Limenius, Anemius, Sabinus, Abundantius, Artemius, Constantius, Justus, Philaster, Constantius, Theodorus, Almachius, Domninus, Amantius, Maximus, Felix, Bassianus, Numidius, Januarius, Proculus, Heliodorus, Jovinus, Felix, Exsuperantius, [Col. 0976A] Diogenes, Maximus, Macedonius, Cassianus, Marcellus, and Eustathius, bishops—Ambrose the bishop said, and so forth.”

Thus begins the Acts of the council. The order of the names here is not the same as in the list, as becomes clear when one compares them; nor is there any place here for the two presbyters named in the list, Evagrius and Chromatius.

Along with the bishops who are named in the list with their proper sees, eleven others are included, whose proper names alone we discover from the list. All of these, as genuine bishops, are called bishops indiscriminately and without distinction together with the others—not once but twice: namely, both at the beginning and at the end of this opening passage. Moreover, those who had no see are not all placed here at the end, as they are in the list; instead, they are intermingled with the others who had their own sees, as anyone can see by observing the names deliberately printed in a different type.

[Col. 0976B] All these men, therefore—both the two African legates and the other nine—were bishops, although they possessed no proper see of their own. Furthermore, when some of them began to state their opinions in the council, the recorders of the Acts designated them by the title “bishop.” Thus, for example, Felix the African legate is described in the Acts, section 16, as follows: “Felix, bishop and legate, said”; and Januarius, one of the nine, is described in section 64: “Januarius the bishop said.”

The two presbyters, Evagrius and Chromatius, however, whenever they said anything in the council, were both consistently identified by the recorders with the title “presbyter.” Thus, for example, section 11 reads: “Evagrius, presbyter and legate, said”; and section 45, as well as elsewhere: “Chromatius the presbyter said.”

We must therefore conclude once again that those eleven who are listed later in the list, or subscriptions—namely, the two African legates, Felix and Numidius, and the remaining nine, Artemius, Almachius, Januarius, Jovinus, Macedonius, Cassianus, Marcellus, Eustathius, and Maximus—were by no means ordinary presbyters, but bishops in the true sense, although they were bishops of no proper see.

[Col. 0976C] These men, then, who had no see—what bishops could they have been except assistants to other bishops who possessed proper sees, bishops whose fields of pastoral labor were either difficult or very extensive? Setting aside the two African legates, with whom we are not presently concerned, I may reasonably conjecture that the other nine belonged to the bishops of the greater sees who were present at this council, especially Valerian of Aquileia and Ambrose of Milan, who at that time were the first in Italy to begin enjoying metropolitan rights as well.

As regards the Church of Aquileia, the name of Jovinus certainly belonged to the most distinguished clergy of that Church, in the office of archdeacon: first in the year 370, when Rufinus received baptism in the Church of Aquileia, as appears from book I, section 3, of his *Invectives*; and again in the year 373, when Jerome wrote from the East to the brothers Chromatius and Eusebius, as well as to their friend Jovinus, as appears from letter 7 of Vallarsi’s edition.

In the year 399, when Rufinus undertook the composition of his *Invectives*, he called Jovinus himself, together with Chromatius and Eusebius [114], [Col. 0976D] “already at that time highly renowned and highly approved bishops of God,” in the cited section 3. That archdeacon Jovinus, therefore, had long since been raised to the honor of the episcopate; and, together with the other two, was already then regarded as a most approved and distinguished man in episcopal dignity.

Why, then, should it be surprising that this same Jovinus, who had previously been archdeacon of the Church of Aquileia under Valerian in 370 and 373, was already in 381 a bishop assisting that Church under the same Valerian, and that he attended the council together with the other bishops?

Among the bishops without sees who were present at this council, besides Jovinus, were also Januarius and Maximus, as appears from the passages cited from the council. A certain Maximus is listed among the bishops of Aquileia after Valerian, Chromatius, Augustine, and Adelphus; immediately after this same Maximus comes Januarius, who was succeeded by Secundus, [Col. 0977A] the immediate predecessor of our Nicetas. De Rubeis shows in chapter 15 of his *Monuments of the Aquileian Church* that Maximus died before the year 444, while Januarius lived at least until the year 447.

Were this Maximus and this Januarius the very same men who, among the bishops without sees, attended the Council of Aquileia under Valerian, who at that time assisted Bishop Valerian in administering the Church of Aquileia, and who later, after Chromatius, Augustine, and Adelphus, held that very see, one immediately after the other? I consider this highly probable; nor do I think that the age of either man can obstruct this conjecture.

For if we suppose that both Maximus and Januarius were thirty years old in the year 381, when the Council of Aquileia was held and they themselves attended it after receiving episcopal rank, then in the year 443 Maximus, if he lived that long, would have reached the age of ninety-two; and Januarius in 447 would likewise have completed his ninety-sixth year. Their ages would indeed have been exceptionally advanced and uncommon; nevertheless, they would in no way be impossible or easily rejected. [Col. 0977B] For when we admire an almost hundred-year lifespan in other bishops of that age or of the nearby period—for example, Hosius of Cordoba, Remigius, bishop of Reims, Simplicianus, the successor of Saint Ambrose, the presbyter Salvianus, and others—why should we not accept it equally in the two Aquileian bishops Maximus and Januarius?

There is nevertheless a way, if one wishes, to reduce the age of both without forcing the evidence. In a matter that is wholly open to debate, there is room for conjecture, so that every difficulty may, if possible, be removed.

We said with De Rubeis that Maximus died before the year 444 because Januarius was bishop of Aquileia in that same year; and, as the same most learned scholar proves, Saint Pope Leo wrote a letter to him in that very year. This letter is now first in order in the Venetian edition of the Ballerini, although it does not explicitly give the name Januarius.

[Col. 0977C] But who would infer from this that Maximus died in 443, rather than in 440 or 435? That Maximus died several years before the indicated date of that letter—namely, the year 444—is demonstrated, unless I am mistaken, by another letter of Saint Leo to Januarius, which explicitly gives his name and was written in the year 447. In the cited edition it is eighteenth in order, and Leo addresses him as follows:

> “Having read the letter of your brotherhood, we have recognized the vigor of your faith, which we had known long ago.”

I will leave aside for the moment the controversy among critics concerning this letter. It is enough to say here that I strongly approve the opinion of the distinguished scholar, defended with great force, as I believe, in the chapter cited above. Rejecting another letter of exactly the same wording, which is there second in order and is addressed to Septimus, or Septimius, bishop of Altinum [115], he accepts this one alone as addressed to Januarius.

What, then, does the phrase “which we had known long ago,” used in this letter with reference to the vigor of Bishop Januarius’s faith, imply, unless Januarius had held the see of Aquileia not long before the year 447 and at least as early as the year 440, when Leo himself began his Roman pontificate?

The date of the death of Maximus, bishop of Aquileia, must therefore be moved farther back. He would consequently have died at more than eighty, but certainly several years before reaching ninety.

[Col. 0977D] What, then, of Januarius, whose age—even if it did not exceed the year in which Leo’s second letter to him was written, 447—would have to be reckoned as having reached ninety-six? There is, however, another consideration that works equally well for Januarius and Maximus, and that, if necessary, reduces the age of both by five years or more.

We assigned both of them the age of thirty in the year 381, when they sat as bishops at the Council of Aquileia, assuming, of course, that both had been raised to episcopal rank at approximately that time. For the thirtieth year was sufficient, as it is today, even according to the more common discipline of those times, for a person to be ordained to the episcopate, as appears from canon 11 of the Council of Neocaesarea. It is true that Pope Siricius, not long after the Council of Aquileia, established the forty-fifth year in his decretal letter to Himerius, bishop of Tarragona, chapter 9, in Coustant; and it is true that the age of fifty is prescribed in the *Apostolic Constitutions*, book II, chapter 1. Yet, as most critics observe, these Constitutions may not at that time have been generally known in the Church.

The age of thirty, however, was not then so firmly established in the Church’s discipline for episcopal consecration that men often younger than thirty were not raised to the episcopal dignity, especially when necessity demanded it or exceptional merit of life supported it.

Examples of such exceptions abound in ecclesiastical history. Their origin goes back to the holy apostle Paul, who had ordained Timothy, still quite young—or even adolescent—as a bishop; hence, among other things, he admonished him to conduct himself in all things with such prudence and instruction that no one might despise his youth.

While still young, therefore, according to Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, chapter 30, Gregory Thaumaturgus and his brother Athenodorus, hearers of Origen, were ordained bishops of the churches in Pontus.

Likewise, Acholius, bishop of the Thessalonians, according to Ambrose, letter 16 to Anysius. [Col. 0978B] Socrates reports the same concerning Paul, bishop of Constantinople, in *Ecclesiastical History*, book II, chapter 6; and Theodoret concerning Athanasius of Alexandria, book I, chapter 25.

Gaudentius of Brescia also strongly reproached the immaturity of his age, at which he had been almost compelled to accept the episcopate, in sermon 16 of the Cominian edition of his works.

Antonius, whom Augustine had appointed bishop of Fussala, a town in his diocese, was likewise young, indeed adolescent, as Augustine himself testifies in the letter cited above, letter 209. Antonius had previously held only the office of lector in the Church of Hippo.

Furthermore, we know from Nicephorus, *Ecclesiastical History*, book III, chapter 29, that Eleutherius, not more than twenty years old, was chosen bishop in Illyricum; from Hincmar, in Baronius under the year 470, that Remigius was, as it were, seized for the episcopate of Reims in his twenty-second year; and from Ennodius, in the *Life of Epiphanius of Ticinum*, that Epiphanius himself was ordained bishop in his twenty-eighth year.

After examples of this kind, from both the Eastern and Western Churches, examples that are either not far removed or scarcely removed at all from the age of Valerian [116], [Col. 0978C] bishop of Aquileia, and from the council held in the city of Aquileia in the year 381—who could ever be accused of excessive laxity in criticism if, in order to lessen a difficulty, when only a few things are known and certain, many are doubtful or obscure, and when on the other hand nothing prevents the conjecture and no one is wronged or subjected to violence, who, I say, could be accused of excessive critical laxity if he wished to suppose that Maximus and Januarius received episcopal ordination from the same Bishop Valerian around the year 381, so that they might serve as his assistants throughout the diocese, when they were no more than twenty-four or twenty-five years old?

On that assumption, Maximus would have died in the see of Aquileia at scarcely eighty, and Januarius perhaps would not have exceeded ninety—a conclusion that is hardly at variance with the ordinary course of human life.

[Col. 0978D] We have therefore discovered three auxiliary bishops at the Council of Aquileia in 381 whom it is highly credible belonged to the Church of Aquileia: Jovinus, Maximus, and Januarius.

I would not venture to say anything about the other six, since I presently have nothing to offer concerning their names. Nevertheless, speaking generally, I might conjecture that, besides the three named, others among their number also belonged to the Church of Aquileia, since that diocese itself extended far and wide, was very extensive and among the more distinguished of the West, and at that time especially populous, before the barbarian armies entered the Aquileian territory to the ruin of Italy.

It is also highly probable that the bishops of Aquileia appointed bishops in several places within their own diocese to act in their stead, especially in those places where, in the course of time, certain cathedral churches later arose and were called suffragans of this first see.

Here, then, is a new kind of problem concerning our Church of Aquileia, [Col. 0979A] with respect to its auxiliary bishops—a problem that deserves to be examined in detail, and which I shall therefore endeavor to address by presenting new documents and new conjectures.

From those earliest times of the fourth or fifth century, then, in examining the ecclesiastical monuments concerning the Church of Aquileia that have survived, it is useful to make not a step but rather a leap to the later age of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries.

Indeed, customs of earlier centuries that, because of the loss through the injustice of time of monuments contemporary with them, we cannot derive from contemporary writers, we often infer most successfully from the traces of those same customs preserved intact for us by a later age.

I believe that this is what happened with the auxiliary bishops of the Church of Aquileia. At first they were established here and there throughout that vast diocese; eventually they gave way to genuine suffragan cathedral churches, which were erected in the places where these auxiliary bishops had formerly been accustomed to reside.

What traces, then, survive in the suffragan cathedral churches of the Church of Aquileia that may show us that bishops once existed there who were merely auxiliary bishops of the Church of Aquileia, before those same churches were raised to the dignity of distinct sees?

[Col. 0979B] Two autograph documents, among others, survive in the archive of the chapter of the former patriarchal Church of Aquileia, now the archiepiscopal Church of Udine. One belongs to the year 1183, the other to the year 1260. We shall provide them here as an appendix at the end of this dissertation.

The first to mention all of them was the distinguished provost of the Church of Udine, Francesco Florius, in his booklet entitled *Preliminary Discourse on the Life of Blessed Bertrand, Patriarch of Aquileia*, which he published in the second edition of that Life in 1791, pages 25 and 26. 117

A remarkable fact that we learn from these two documents, with that most learned man leading the way, is that four suffragan bishops of the Church of Aquileia are here listed as born canons of that same Church, as the expression goes—that is, as men who were always both bishops of those sees [Col. 0979C] and canons of the metropolitan Church.

They were the bishop of Concordia, the bishop of Trieste, the bishop of Emona, and the bishop of Justinopolis. The first two are presented in the first document, the latter two in the second.

In the first document, the bishops of Concordia and Trieste appear among the canons of Aquileia through their vicars, whom they deliberately appointed to fulfill the canonical office in the Church of Aquileia, precisely as the patriarch and the count did. According to the usage of those times, the count was the advocate of the Church of Aquileia.

The presence of vicars for these bishops in the Church of Aquileia proves that it was characteristic of the sees of Concordia and Trieste that their bishops were habitually, as the expression goes, reckoned among the clergy of the Church of Aquileia, as its canons. They were so reckoned no less than the patriarch himself and the count, who likewise were regarded as perpetual canons of the Church of Aquileia and discharged the duties of canons through their vicars.

The same appears to be true of the bishops of Emona and Justinopolis, who are shown in the second document not through vicars but present in person with the other Aquileian canons at a chapter act concerning future provision for the number of canons.

[Col. 0979D] The first document now provides authority for the second, enabling us to understand that the bishops of Emona and Justinopolis, no less than those of Concordia and Trieste, were born canons of the Church of Aquileia. The very wording of the second document seems to assert the same without ambiguity; and, if further proof were needed, it is amply confirmed by other earlier documents of the same Church, indicated there by the highly praised scholar, an expert in Aquileian antiquities.

[Col. 0980A] It is not new in ecclesiastical discipline for bishops of cathedral churches to have been at the same time canons of some distinguished church situated even outside their own diocese, and especially of their own metropolitan church.

In Gaul, the bishops of Angers and Poitiers, as well as the archbishops of Sens and Bourges, were canons of the Church of Saint Martin of Tours, as appears from Thomassinus, *Old and New Ecclesiastical Discipline*, part I, book III, chapter 64, section 3.

In England, all and each of the suffragan bishops of that province were canons of the metropolitan Church of Canterbury, according to the same Thomassinus, in the same place, section 7.

As for the aforementioned Gallic archbishops and bishops, the reason for their canonry in the Church of Tours appears to have been nothing other than the sanctity of the place, owing to the fame and merit of Saint Martin, bishop of Tours, celebrated in the praises of all writers of his own and later ages.

For the bishops of the province of Canterbury in England, the reason was wholly particular to that place and its circumstances; it may be seen in the same Thomassinus.

[Col. 0980B] As for the Church of Aquileia, however, where the four bishops mentioned were canons, where all were bishops of the province of Aquileia, and where it is entirely unclear when they began to be both bishops of those four suffragan sees and canons of the metropolitan Church, it may be conjectured that this points in a particular way to the ancient Aquileian origin of those bishops.

For this reason, the beginning of their canonry in the Church of Aquileia may very probably be traced back to the time when these four bishops were simply auxiliary bishops 118 of the Church of Aquileia, perhaps established in those very places where, in the course of time, cathedral bishops with proper sees and proper jurisdiction later came into existence.

At that time, when they were auxiliary bishops of the Church of Aquileia, there can be no doubt that they belonged, as the expression goes, to the bosom of the Church of Aquileia and formed part of the greater clergy of that Church. Consequently, they would also have received from the common ecclesiastical treasury stipends for their support and for carrying out the duties entrusted to them.

[Col. 0980C] No one, then, will deny that they were already in reality canons of that same Church, even if not in name—for the name “canons” is not older than the ninth or tenth century—in fact and substance.

But what if, once the name “canons” had been introduced, they too were called canons of the Church of Aquileia, just like the others who lived there in person and continuously, and were actually regarded as such, while the ancient custom attesting their origin was retained, and perhaps also their share of the stipends common to the other canons of the same Church?

Here, then, is how from the surviving monuments of the later Church of Aquileia an ancient form of that Church’s discipline emerges in a certain sense—a discipline that, because of the scarcity of contemporary monuments, could not have been derived with equal clarity from elsewhere.

Here is how we infer that auxiliary bishops, whom we called bishops of the second kind, established here and there in various places of the principal dioceses, also existed in the Church of Aquileia in ancient centuries, probably in those same places where these bishops were once regarded as perpetual canons of that Church.

[Col. 0980D] The matter, however, can be explained more clearly by further observations and conjectures.

Someone may perhaps ask how widely the care of the bishop of Aquileia extended. On this subject we must consult the eminent Cardinal Norisius, in his dissertation *On the Fifth Synod*, chapter 9, section 4.
