We must also hear the distinguished De Rubeis, who in chapter 20, section 3, of his *Monuments of the Aquileian Church*, and in chapter 22, section 2, of his *Dissertations on Various Erudition*, assigns to the Aquileian metropolitan, under the bishops Valerian and Chromatius—that is, toward the end of the fourth century and at the beginning of the fifth—not only Istria, but also the Church of Trent and the Church of Sabiona in Raetia II, as well as perhaps Augusta in Vindelicia; and even Celeia, Emona, Scarabantia, and Tiburnia in Noricum and Pannonia, together with all of Venetia, as far as it extended to the borders of Insubria and Emilia.

Concerning Noricum, [Col. 0981A] Marcus Hanzisius, in volume I of *Sacred Germany*, chapter 12, stated candidly and confidently, as reported by the same De Rubeis:

> “The churches of Noricum took their origin from Aquileia; even the situation of the places seems to suggest this, for the Noricans and the Aquileians are contiguous.”

What Hanzisius acknowledged concerning the churches of Noricum must also be said of the others then situated in Istria and in parts of Pannonia, and even more so of Venetia: all must have received their origin in the same way from Aquileia.

From this the extent of the Church of Aquileia is evident, before the other churches arose that derived their beginning from it. For the care of the bishop of Aquileia must have spread throughout all these places before particular churches bearing their own names were established there.

From this anyone can easily infer that one bishop of Aquileia could hardly have been sufficient for a pastoral care extending so widely; and that, consequently, from the very beginnings of the Christian faith in those regions, he must have needed the assistance of auxiliary bishops—not only men who would remain with him in a stable residence, always ready at his command, but also men who would preside here and there [119] over particular and distant regions, as though themselves set over so many secondary dioceses.

These regions eventually developed into dioceses with their own names and jurisdiction, some sooner and others later, and thus formed the primitive suffragan dioceses of the same Church of Aquileia.

What, then, do the surviving Acts relating to the beginnings of the Church of Aquileia report on this subject?

I mean the Acts of the holy martyrs of Aquileia, Hermagoras, the first bishop of Aquileia in the apostolic age, and Fortunatus, his deacon. They are found in the third volume of the *July* of Bollandus, page 251 of the Antwerp edition.

[Col. 0981C] These Acts were entirely rejected by the distinguished scholars Papebrochius and Tillemont, but with a critical severity that was surely excessive, as the Bollandist associates themselves—who succeeded Papebrochius—point out in the preliminary commentary on these same Acts. De Rubeis likewise treats the matter at greater length and with greater precision in chapters 1 and 3 of his *Monuments*. There he examines and defends the Acts individually, concluding that critics have so far been unable to produce anything that destroys their principal points or undermines their credibility. Those features of the Acts that can be defended only with the greatest difficulty, he says, prove the addition of interpolations in a later age; these interpolations do not overturn the sincerity of the Acts as a whole.

In these Acts, chapter 1, section 4, after what has been said above, the following passage is relevant to our subject:

> “Then, journeying with blessed Mark to the city of Rome, and there receiving from blessed Peter the staff of the pontificate and the veil of the sacrament with a blessing, he became proto-bishop (*proton episcopus*) of the province of Italy, and returned to the city of Aquileia, and ordered the administration of his Church; and he ordained elders and Levites (*levitas*, i.e. deacons) there. After this he sent a presbyter and a deacon to the city of Trieste; and he acted similarly in the other cities. He did these things in the city of Aquileia, which is first among the cities of Italy.”

[Col. 0981D] It is useful to agree with De Rubeis, in the chapter cited above, that this passage of the Acts, which he examines with particular attention, is free from interpolation, at least in substance.

Here we see how extensive a province of episcopal care Hermagoras was the first to assume in this part of Italy, which at that time was properly regarded as Italy, as we learn from the distinguished scholar mentioned above; and which extended by way of the Alps to the neighboring regions beyond them, where in the fourth and fifth centuries we know that the jurisdiction of the Aquileian metropolitans was extended.

We also see how diligently Hermagoras sought to ordain elders and Levites for the work of the ministry. Finally, we see such ministers sent by him throughout the cities, specifically to the city of Trieste, which perhaps was the first of all to experience the pastoral care of the proto-bishop of Aquileia, and whose bishops in later centuries we have seen to be born canons of the Church of Aquileia.

Here, indeed, [Col. 0982A] the Acts speak of presbyters and deacons sent by Saint Hermagoras to the cities. But these presbyters may also have been endowed with episcopal rank, or at least may have received it not long afterward from the successors of Hermagoras, as the harvest of Christians grew more abundant everywhere day by day.

From the very beginning of the Church of Aquileia, as these Acts report it, the necessity of auxiliary bishops for the Church is thus made still clearer, given the breadth of the care entrusted to the bishops of Aquileia. The opinion is also strengthened that such auxiliary bishops were placed especially in those locations—or at least not far from them—where, with the passage of time, churches with their own names and jurisdiction later arose as suffragan sees.

Someone may now ask also about the origin [120] of the suffragan Churches, as they are now called, and especially about the suffragan churches of Aquileia. I shall confidently disclose my view on this matter.

[Col. 0982B] I would not deny that metropolitan Churches in the full sense, and with their proper legal rights, arose late in the West. Together with the most distinguished scholars, I have said that under Bishop Valerian of Aquileia and Bishop Ambrose of Milan—with only a short interval between them—Aquileia and Milan were regarded as the first metropolitan Churches in the West.

Nevertheless, I believe that a kind of image, or rather certain beginnings, of metropolitan Churches had already shone forth in the greater dioceses of the West before the time of Valerian and Ambrose. For those Churches seem to me to have existed in the likeness of metropolitan Churches whose bishops established auxiliary bishops, as it were suffragans, here and there throughout their own dioceses—dioceses of greater extent, so to speak, and more difficult to traverse—and entrusted to them the exercise of their pastoral office among the flock.

Was not the Church of Lyon in Gaul, under Bishop Irenaeus, already in the second century itself a kind of metropolitan Church with its suffragans? Eusebius speaks of it in *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chapters 23 and 24.

Eusebius calls the districts of Gaul “parishes” which Irenaeus, bishop of Lyon, governed:

> **ἅς Εἰρηναῖος ἐπεσκόπει**  
> “which Irenaeus supervised.”

Those parishes situated in Gaul and under Irenaeus’s oversight [Col. 0982C] were not administered by presbyters but by bishops whom Irenaeus himself called brothers, and over whom, according to Eusebius, he presided. This was proved conclusively and clearly, against Massuetus, Quesnellus, and Coustantius, by our distinguished Francesco Florius in his most learned dissertation *On the Martyrs of Lyon*, chapter 5, following the opinion of Petrus de Marca, Henricus Valesius, Guilielmus Beveregius, and Stephanus Baluzius. Nothing further need be added here for the sake of confirmation.

Why, then, should Irenaeus not have exercised, already in the second century, the appearance of a metropolitan bishop in Gaul, with the other bishops of the parishes of Gaul over whom he presided serving as his suffragans?

Why should Irenaeus not have presided over the other bishops of the parishes of Gaul because the Church of Lyon was, as it were, the mother of the other Churches in Gaul; and because Irenaeus himself and his predecessor, the most holy old man and martyr of Christ, Pothinus, had established auxiliary bishops there, who eventually became bishops of their own sees and, in succeeding centuries, themselves became founders and parents of other Churches?

[Col. 0982D] The same, I believe, must certainly be said of the very extensive and ancient Church of Aquileia, which, besides the broad boundaries of Venetia, embraced Istria and Noricum and also held part of Pannonia.

This Church bore the appearance of a metropolitan Church even before it was called metropolitan and exercised all metropolitan rights. In a certain sense it could call the Churches of Venetia, Istria, Noricum, and Pannonia its suffragans, since it was itself the first to introduce the name of Christ there and to establish auxiliary bishops—men who eventually became bishops of distinct dioceses. Those distinct dioceses, with their own jurisdiction, constituted the suffragans in the true sense of the same Church once it had been raised to metropolitan dignity. Thus the Church of Aquileia did not so much extend metropolitan authority over them as preserve it by a certain original right.

[Col. 0983A] We have therefore established the primitive origin of the suffragan Churches: it must be traced back to that, so to speak, maternal authority which the principal Churches exercised over them, and from which those suffragan Churches themselves derived their beginning.

To investigate at least somewhat the manner in which those suffragan sees121 came into being, it will not be inappropriate to infer the unknown from known facts and, by a certain analogy between suffragan bishoprics and our parishes of the second order, to imagine that their origin was not unlike that of those same parishes—which certainly did not arise very long ago and which we often see emerging daily before our eyes.

I therefore believe that what happened, and continues to happen, in every diocese with respect to ancient churches called baptismal churches, or pleban churches, in the multiplication of parishes that took place within their bounds, happened likewise in larger dioceses with respect to the multiplication of bishoprics within their limits. We have seen, namely, that baptismal churches [Col. 0983B] situated in the countryside long presided over many churches or chapels called succursal churches. These had their own priests, but were nevertheless wholly subject to the authority of the priests of the baptismal churches. Then, after divisions had followed, with the permission and consent of the bishops, the priests of the succursal churches themselves became priests of independent jurisdiction; and thus, within the territory of a single parish, many smaller parishes emerged from portions severed from the old baptismal church. The latter consequently lost its former authority over them, retaining only the prerogative of primacy and a certain mark of honor, which it is always fitting that daughters should show toward their mother.

In a manner apparently not unlike this, large ancient dioceses and their bishops placed auxiliary bishops here and there in the more important places of their territories; there the auxiliary bishops administered, as it were, succursal churches of a higher order; yet they themselves, together with those churches, remained wholly subject to the bishops. In the course of time, [Col. 0983C] as the harvest of the faithful multiplied and other needs arose, these auxiliary bishops, together with their territories—whether with the support of the people and the indulgence of the principal bishop, or through the intervention of councils, or finally by the authority of the Roman pontiff, whose power in these matters was always supreme throughout the Church, and especially in the regions of the West—constituted certain particular dioceses within the bounds of the ancient dioceses, formed from portions severed from those primary dioceses.

Thus, within the very same area of territory where formerly there had been a single bishopric and a single true authority, several bishoprics were afterward created, separated from the principal Church and possessing their own jurisdiction. The ancient Church therefore retained only the title of superior Church, and the new churches rendered to it those signs of obedience that are naturally customarily and properly offered to those from whom one derives one’s origin.

Here, then, we have also the manner in which the primitive suffragan Churches arose throughout the Christian world, so that we may understand that the suffragan Churches of the Church of Aquileia were formed in much the same way in Venetia and Istria, as well as in parts of Noricum and Pannonia. They did not all arise at one time: some arose earlier, others later; some before the ecclesiastical form of metropolitan provinces was introduced in the West, around the end of the fourth century, and some afterward. For the present I say nothing of suffragan Churches of another kind and origin, which a later age produced according to the needs of places and times, the erection of new metropolitan sees, and the variety of human circumstances, to which the holy Church has often been accustomed to adapt herself when guided by a desire for peace.

Someone may finally ask by what marks of honor the suffragan Churches, and especially those of the province of Aquileia, anciently honored the metropolitan. The most illustrious Mabillon, in the preface to the fifth century of the Benedictine history, no. 22, points out to us a certain Folc, archbishop122 [Col. 0984A] of Rheims in the tenth century, who called his suffragan bishops by the name of “sons.” Although this was an unusual practice on the part of that archbishop—for, as Mabillon writes, he was either the first, or certainly among the first, to call suffragan bishops “sons” by virtue of metropolitan jurisdiction—and although it conflicts with the discipline of the Church, according to which bishops even of the smallest places, and even those bearing only a simple title, have always been called “brothers” by every bishop, just as the Roman pontiffs themselves have been accustomed always to call even the least of bishops “brother,” this nevertheless indicates both the great authority that metropolitan bishops anciently exercised over their suffragans, as over the bishops of daughter Churches, and the exceptional honor with which those metropolitan bishops were honored by their suffragans. For this reason the metropolitans were regarded, as it were, as the parents and founders of the suffragan Churches.

As for the suffragans of Aquileia, I shall briefly mention [Col. 0984B] some very well-known facts, sufficiently familiar from De Rubeis and other investigators of Aquileian affairs: namely, that from ancient times these suffragans received from the metropolitan both confirmation of their election and the imposition of hands. To him also they promised faith and obedience by a special formula written in their own hand and confirmed by oath.

I shall add that the Aquileian suffragans were accustomed every year to go to the threshold of the metropolitan Church on the feast of the holy martyr-patrons Hermagoras and Fortunatus; they also frequently stayed with the same metropolitan bishop and attended him at solemn ceremonies as a mark of honor and obedience. This is evident from nearly countless solemn diplomas and other documents in which the names of the individual participants are recorded. These diplomas and documents are not, indeed, of the earliest antiquity; nevertheless, most precede the year 1000 or follow it shortly thereafter, and [Col. 0984C] I have no doubt that they reflect the discipline not only of that age but also of preceding centuries. It is enough to have touched on these matters in passing, since they help to clarify what has been said thus far about the auxiliary bishops, first, and then the suffragan bishops of the Church of Aquileia.

Now, therefore, to come to the conclusion of the first part of this sixth chapter, whose purpose was to show that Niceas, or Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, was probably called by Gennadius bishop of the city of Romatiana because, before ascending to the episcopal see of Aquileia, he had been an auxiliary bishop of the Church of Aquileia situated at the port of Romatium or Romatinum: now, I say, to reach the conclusion at last, what has been said concerning our argument is not sufficiently probable, whether we consider the general discipline of the twofold institution of auxiliary bishops that prevailed in the Church in ancient centuries, or the specific practice of precisely this kind demonstrated in the Church of Aquileia by particular documents?

The probability of this auxiliary episcopate of Niceas [Col. 0984D] or Nicetas, derived from these sources, admits no exception. But in a matter so remote and obscure, where nothing is sufficiently established and investigated, and where there is room only for conjecture, what can ever be hoped for that exceeds the limits of mere probability? In matters of this kind, where it is not granted us to attain what is true and certain, we have enough if we put forward what is at least most like the truth, probable, and consistent with reason.

Nor should it cause any difficulty that our Nicetas, after holding an auxiliary bishopric at the port of Romatinum, subsequently obtained supreme governance in the very [p. 123] see of Aquileia. Since purely auxiliary bishops had neither a diocese of their own nor a proper title, it was not contrary to the canons that, when the principal episcopal see was vacant, they should be chosen to occupy it. Indeed, since, as auxiliary bishops, they were chief members of the clergy of the principal Church, or of the episcopal presbyterium, [Col. 0985A] it was in accordance with the canons that they in particular should ascend to a vacant episcopal see.

When, therefore, I said that our Nicetas later exchanged his auxiliary bishopric at the port of Romatinum for the see of Aquileia, I meant precisely that this was not contrary to the ecclesiastical discipline of those times; that learned men have made the same assertion concerning other auxiliary bishops; and especially that the most distinguished investigators of such matters, Peter Coustant, *Epistolae Romanorum Pontificum*, pp. 3 and 6 of the Paris edition, and Francesco Bianchini, vol. II of Anastasius, in the historical notes to the Life of Pope Saint Eleutherius, p. 142, devised the same explanation concerning certain Roman pontiffs of earlier centuries in order to remove certain difficulties of place and time. It is enough to have indicated this in passing.

One further point should be added concerning the place of Romatium, or the port of Romatinum, where we have said that our Niceas or Nicetas probably resided before undertaking the episcopate of Aquileia. From the monument of the first part of the twelfth century mentioned above [Col. 0985B] we learn that the bishop of Concordia was one of those among the suffragan bishops of this metropolitan province who were called “born canons” of the Church of Aquileia. We conjectured that this was because the bishops of Concordia, too, were successors of those auxiliary bishops who in ancient times occupied that place on behalf of the bishop of Aquileia. Since at that time they belonged to the presbyterium of Aquileia, they therefore continued to be listed among it—even after the name “canons” had been adopted, once that term first came into use in the Church—even after they had been elevated to a genuine cathedral see, with a particular diocese formed from a portion severed from the mother Church.

Now, since the present port of Romatium or Romatinum, commonly called Portus-Gruarius, is scarcely two miles from the destroyed city of Concordia, which likewise stood on the Romatium River, by which there was a direct route back and forth; and since Pliny’s port of Romatinum stood at the mouth of that river, through which it flowed into the lagoon, [Col. 0985C] and was once the port of the city of Concordia, it is probable that the auxiliary bishops of Aquileia situated in this part of Venetia, who doubtless had responsibility here and there for the whole region traversed by that river, sat at the port of Romatium or Romatinum—and perhaps more probably at Pliny’s port of Romatinum for as long as it continued to exist, before its own destruction and the destruction of the city of Concordia—as a place perhaps more convenient for their vigilance. Thus they may commonly have been called bishops of Romatinum or Romatianum from that place.

Later, however, when a cathedral see of its own name and jurisdiction arose there in the sixth century, those new suffragan bishops assumed the name of bishops of Concordia, after the principal city of that place. Although the city had then been destroyed and had fallen from its former dignity, it perhaps had not yet been cast down and ruined to the extent that it is in our own age, so that it was not without some hope of recovering its former splendor. Meanwhile, it retained a sufficiently famous name in the ancient records to seem worthy of adorning the new episcopal cathedral.

[Col. 0985D] This concludes what concerns the first probable reason why Niceas or Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, was called by Gennadius bishop of the city of Romatiana. We now turn to the second.

[p. 124]

## SECOND PART OF THE SIXTH CHAPTER

In the second place, the purpose was to show that Niceas or Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, may perhaps also have been called bishop of the city of Romatiana, and thus have been named by Gennadius of Marseilles and by the others who copied him among ecclesiastical writers, because he probably sat at the port of Romatium or Romatinum quite frequently while he held the helm of the Church of Aquileia.

It must therefore be shown that this could have happened, and that it was probably also practiced by Niceas or Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, both on the basis of the ecclesiastical discipline of those times and on the basis of the historical monuments that display to us the condition of Aquileia and of the whole of Venetia at that time.

What if [Col. 0986A] there is nothing contradictory in saying both that Niceas or Nicetas was first an auxiliary bishop at the port of Pliny’s Romatinum, perhaps, on behalf of the bishop of Aquileia, and that afterward, having become bishop of the Church of Aquileia, he also frequently resided at the new port of Romatinum, or rather in the city of that name? We shall therefore investigate the matter proposed in the second place with greater confidence, so that everyone may choose either explanation, or embrace both if he wishes.

But what if neither should please? So long as this does not cast doubt on the fact that Gennadius’s Niceas or Nicetas really is our Niceas or Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, for whom we have hitherto contended, we shall meanwhile await better explanations of this difficulty with willing minds. We must now proceed to the matter proposed.

It is the opinion of learned men, vigorously and at length defended by Michael Antonius Frances in his work *De Cathedralibus*, chapter 2, no. 37 and following, that until the peace given to the Church by Constantine the Great, no sacred building existed anywhere in the Christian world that could truly and properly be called a cathedral church, or that could be regarded as the special seat of a bishop, in distinction from other churches that were considered of an inferior order and dignity.

[Col. 0986B] For the bishop presided equally over all the churches or places that then existed for the celebration of the sacred assemblies of the faithful, insofar as the times of persecution permitted, either personally or through others, without any church or episcopal seat being capable of being called truly and properly such, as later happened through ecclesiastical organization and custom.

It is best to hear him writing at the cited place:

> “I firmly judge that it does not follow merely from the fact that there was a bishop in some city and that a church was built there that the church itself was therefore the cathedral of that city, even if it was erected by the bishop of that place . . . . . There can be no doubt that bishops existed in the Catholic Church before cathedral churches were erected . . . . . It is established that in those earliest times, at the beginning of the emerging Church, bishops were [Col. 0986C] in all the Churches, not as in cathedrals, since cathedrals did not yet exist at that time . . . . . It is clear that cathedral churches are of later date and arose long after the bishoprics from which they derive their origin; nor can a sound argument be drawn from the establishment of a bishopric to a cathedral church supposedly erected at that time, before the division of the Churches.”

These words are excerpted from Michael Antonius Frances, who nevertheless pursues the matter more fully throughout that chapter and elsewhere, even confidently asserting that before the peace given to the Church by Constantine there was absolutely no cathedral in existence.

[p. 125] The learned Benedictine monks of the Cistercian congregation, authors of the Italian work published at Milan in four quarto volumes, entitled *Delle Antichità Longobardico-Milanesi*, have most recently made the same claim concerning cathedrals. Thus they write in dissertation 31, no. 12:

> “What we can affirm is that cathedral churches originated only after the beginning of the [Col. 0986D] fourth century. Before this period, during the storm of the persecutions, Christians were accustomed to assemble with their bishop and clergy for the exercise and worship of religion in cemeteries, caves, and other secluded retreats. When calm returned, they did so in houses or in places designated for that purpose, which acquired the names of churches and basilicas. Whatever many learned writers may say to the contrary, writers perhaps too much predisposed toward their own opinion, cathedrals, metropolitans, distinctions, and prerogatives are of later date and must be called effects of the peace granted to the Church by the emperor Constantine—a peace that did not dawn until after the beginning of the fourth century.”

So they write.

Cardinal De Luca, however, in *De Praeeminentiis*, disputation 3, no. 15, goes even further and writes that cathedral churches, at least with respect to the use and suitability of the designation, came [Col. 0987A] into general use long after the peace granted by Constantine. This occurred when, after several churches had been built here and there throughout the dioceses, both in cities and in the countryside, and after the parishes had been divided, it became necessary to distinguish that church which was, as it were, the mother of the others and in which, once peace had been granted, the bishop had finally established the seat of his government in some manner.

> “This name,” he says, “or designation, ‘cathedral,’ came into use long after the Church’s tranquillity, when, after parish and other inferior churches had been constructed throughout the cities and the remaining places of the diocese, it became necessary to distinguish the mother church, which was the seat of the bishop, and from which the other inferior churches, like daughters, received their rule and professed their subjection to it.”

Cathedral Churches, then, with respect to the reality and substance of the matter, began to exist only after the fourth century had begun, or even after it had already advanced; perhaps later still. Certainly they originated earlier in some places and later in others, according to the diversity of places and the varying speed with which ecclesiastical affairs could prosper in accordance with the suitability of circumstances. [Col. 0987B] As for the terminology, however, they became commonly known in ecclesiastical organization much later still.

Why, then, have these preliminary remarks about cathedral churches been made? They have been made so that we may understand what the discipline was in those earlier centuries, even with regard to the places where bishops sat. Cathedral churches and fixed episcopal seats in cities or places where cathedral churches had been established advanced everywhere at the same pace, as the Benedictine monks also observe in the passage cited above, saying:

> “This was the period in which episcopal sees began to be established in the cities, the bishop assigning cathedral dignity to the church that he had chosen for this honor.”

If, then, no cathedral church existed before the peace granted by Constantine—or indeed if the designation “cathedral” came into use only long after the Church’s tranquillity—then there was likewise no fixed episcopal seat in the cities before that time; and perhaps fixed seats in cities did not begin to exist until long after [Col. 0987C] the Church’s tranquillity.

It follows from this that, even if most bishops from the earliest times [p. 126] bore the name of the principal city of the province or region in which their episcopal care was exercised, they did not therefore always reside in that city as though it were a fixed and stable place of residence, as later usage came to express it. Rather, they might also stay in lesser places, either according to their own choice, or for convenience, or as a matter of prudent administration. Thus it also happened that doubts later arose as to which place in particular a given bishop should be said to belong to. Likewise, many bishops were named and themselves called and subscribed not by the name of cities and places, but by that of provinces or peoples.

Ecclesiastical history abounds in examples of this kind. The learned Foggini, in his work *De Romano divi Petri Itinere et Episcopatu*, exercise 14, where he discusses the first apostles of the Florentines, observes that the holy [Col. 0987D] Paulinus, one of the apostles of Tuscany, concerning whom Tuscan writers dispute which particular place there he was bishop of,

> “is that same Paulinus who was bishop of Lucca, whom it is easy to believe was bishop of nearly the whole of Tuscany, although the people of Lucca make him bishop only of their own city, in which he died, and perhaps because, as a more convenient or more frequented place, he stayed there longer.”

Here, then, according to Foggini, we have a bishop of nearly the whole of Tuscany who had no place in that region that we would call his proper residence, although he may perhaps have lived longer at Lucca; and who was called bishop of Lucca only at a later time because he ended his life there.

In Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, chapter 26, there is a letter of Saint Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, addressed to Basilides, bishop of Pentapolis—or, as the Greek words read, “bishop of the parishes throughout Pentapolis.” Here there is certainly no mention of a place where Basilides, bishop of the Pentapolitan [Col. 0988A] region, resided as though it were his ordinary place of residence and from which he took the name of his bishopric. Yet he was probably not a bishop of independent jurisdiction in the Pentapolitan region, but merely an auxiliary bishop for the bishop of Alexandria, who possessed full authority in that region, as we noted above.

To come down also to the later period after the peace, among the subscriptions of the bishops to the Council of Nicaea, found in volume II of Labbe’s *Councils*, edited by Coletus, column 55 and following, one reads “John of Persia,” that is, a bishop in the kingdom of the Persians, without any title indicating a particular see or residence in any city of Persia.

In the subscriptions of the bishops to the Second Ecumenical Council of Constantinople, in the same Labbe, in the same volume, column 1134, one reads of Agapius and Bagadius, bishops designated as belonging to the province of Arabia, likewise without the name of a place where they possessed an episcopal seat.

Among the bishops of the Council of Chalcedon, in Labbe’s *Councils*, volume IV of the same edition, [Col. 0988B] column 855, one reads of John, bishop of the people of the Saracens, and likewise of Eustathius, bishop of the people of the Saracens; both are named without the name of any see or place that might be regarded as the center of their episcopal care.

These examples will now suffice to illustrate the point at issue: namely, that in the ancient centuries of the Church bishops had no place within their own dioceses that, in the manner of our times, was the place of their constant residence, just as they had no properly so-called cathedral church. Nevertheless, for the most part they took their name from the chief city or more celebrated place of their episcopate, as we also see in the earliest examples of the bishops of the Churches of Asia in the book of Revelation, as well as of others in the Acts of the Apostles and in the Epistles of Saint Paul.

[p. 127] The first mention that perhaps appears in ecclesiastical monuments of cathedral churches and of an episcopal residence, or, as we say, a place of residence, concerns the African Church and reaches the year 398. In that year two Councils of Carthage were held under Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, and Augustine also took part in them.

In the first of these, in Labbe, edited by Coletus, volume II, column 1438, canon 14 was established as follows:

> “That the bishop should have a lodging not far from the Church.”

In the later council, in the same place, column 1455, canon 5 decreed:

> “It was decided that no one should have permission, after leaving the principal see, to go to any Church established in the diocese, or, while remaining longer than necessary on his own property, to neglect the care or visitation of his own see.”

These two canons of the African Church of the year 398 therefore present both the command given to bishops to have their lodging—that is, their dwelling—not far from the church, and the designation “principal see” and “own see,” indicating the chief church of the diocese at which they ought to remain, distinguished from the other lesser sacred buildings in the diocese. At the same time, they testify to the former freedom of bishops to stay wherever they wished within their own diocese [Col. 0988D] and also to go to whichever church of the diocese they preferred.

These canons, I say, also mark the period toward the end of the fourth century when mention of cathedral churches began in ecclesiastical organization and when a law was simultaneously promulgated requiring bishops to establish a permanent dwelling, that is, to fix their residence, at those churches.

Although the discipline of one ancient century or one period cannot be confused with that of another century or period, even when they are close to each other—for it would be an error to view ancient centuries generally under a single aspect, without distinguishing one from another and without considering the changes that repeatedly occurred within them—the discipline that bears the name of a particular century or period is not so exclusively proper to that century or period that it does not in some way also touch the [Col. 0989A] century and period immediately preceding it, nor does it fail at the same time to extend into the century and period immediately following.

It would therefore equally be an error either to try to confine a particular ecclesiastical discipline that prevailed in a given century or period within the chronological limits of that century or period, or to refuse to observe that the change in discipline attributed to such a century or period occurred earlier in some places and later in others, as we noted above—fully and completely in some places, while elsewhere not without some exception that combined and blended the discipline of one century or period with that newly introduced in another.

It is useful to have said this, so that it may be clear how broad a field remains for conjecture concerning what we have stated, whether about the establishment of cathedral churches after the peace of the Church, or about the consequent custom, not introduced into the Church before that time, whereby bishops ordinarily established their permanent seat at cathedral churches, usually situated in the principal cities of the dioceses.

What, then, if we say that the bishops of Aquileia [Col. 0989B] only late established a permanent seat in the city of Aquileia, so that thereafter they all took their name from it without reference to any other place, while in the meantime some might not improperly have called them bishops of the city of Romatina or Romatiana, after the place where they frequently stayed, when no truly and properly so-called cathedral church had yet been established anywhere?

I certainly would not say that the city of Aquileia, distinguished by the extent of its site and the multitude of its people, [p. 128] lacked a sacred building under the predecessors of Bishop Nicetas, any more than it lacked a church house or church houses where the bishop would live when staying there, together with the company of clergy that ought to be with the bishop.

What was said above about the monastery of men that existed at Aquileia, as well as about the monastery of virgins, abundantly proves that a sacred building had existed at Aquileia for a long time, in which the assembly of Christians gathered, ecclesiastical solemnities were celebrated, and the bishop performed the sacred rites.

[Col. 0989C] Moreover, from Saint Athanasius, in his *Apology to the Emperor Constantius*, nos. 3 and 15, we understand that during the time of Fortunatianus, whose guest he had been at Aquileia, a sacred building there began to be newly constructed. From this we infer that it was built in place of an older one, which by then no longer sufficed for the multitude. In that new building, although it was not yet completed—and perhaps because the old one had been demolished so that the larger new one might rise in its place—an assembly was nevertheless held, in which Athanasius himself also took part, as did the emperor Constans, brother of the aforementioned Constantius, who was then himself residing at Aquileia. This belongs to the year 348, as De Rubeis records in the *Monumenta*, chapter 6, no. 5.

Likewise, in the Council of Aquileia held in the year 381 under Bishop Valerian, the successor of Fortunatianus, which we discussed above, the Church of the city of Aquileia is named as the place where the thirty-two bishops, the Fathers of that council, sat. It must therefore be regarded as the very same church that was being built in Athanasius’s time, according to his testimony concerning Fortunatianus, and perhaps the only one then [Col. 0989D] existing in that city, since no distinguishing designation is given there.

That sacred building was certainly worthy of being regarded as the principal church throughout the entire diocese of Aquileia: first, because of the splendor of the city; also, without doubt, because of the majesty of its structure, which was not unequal to the size and dignity of the city; and still more because of the distinction of the council held there. Although not ecumenical, that council can certainly be regarded as equivalent in importance to a general council, and it acquired the greatest renown from the fact that the leading men of the Western Church and men eminent both in holiness and in learning assembled there.

This, however, is not enough to make that church a cathedral in the manner of our churches, nor to show that the city of Aquileia had by that time become so fixed a place of residence for the bishops of Aquileia that it was no longer permissible for them, whether according to their choice, convenience, or the circumstances of changing conditions, to reside freely elsewhere and to make use of other sacred buildings, which even then were not uncommon in smaller cities, [Col. 0990A] as well as in more populous villages and rural settlements.

The bishops of Aquileia, and indeed very frequently—plainly, I would say, more frequently than the other bishops of all Italy—had reasons to withdraw from the city of Aquileia and seek quieter and safer residences elsewhere within the extensive boundaries of their own diocese. However much we may concede that the bishops of Aquileia, down to Valerian, resided chiefly at Aquileia, I would venture to say that after Valerian the bishops of Aquileia, the predecessors of our Nicetas, lived not chiefly at Aquileia but elsewhere, and more often elsewhere than at Aquileia.

The first after Valerian was Chromatius. He is said to have been ordained at Aquileia in the year 388, the very year in which Valerian died, by Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan, according to the custom of those two Churches, namely, that their bishops should ordain one another in the city and church of the person who was to be ordained. We know from the histories—and Muratori reports it in the *Annals of Italy*—[Col. 0990B] that in that very year the city of Aquileia suffered a siege at the hands of the army of Theodosius the Great Augustus, who was pursuing the tyrant [129] Maximus, after Maximus had entered Aquileia with his forces in order to defend himself there after the defeats he had previously suffered in battle.

It is uncertain whether this siege of Aquileia occurred before or after the ordination of Chromatius. It is certain, however, that the siege was brief; that Theodosius entered the city; that Maximus was captured; and that, at the emperor’s command, he was beheaded three miles from the city in July or August of that same year, as the historians variously report.

After Maximus, when the emperor Valentinian had been killed and Eugenius had seized power as a usurper, the same Theodosius came again from the East through Illyricum into Italy in the year 394 with a great force of soldiers. He opened for himself the roads through the Julian Alps, which were fortified by the enemy, and reached the territory of Aquileia, where the immense army of Eugenius was stationed. There, then, a battle was fought that brought ruin and death to the new tyrant and a new and [Col. 0990C] complete victory to Theodosius, who, entering the nearby city of Aquileia, was there also greeted by Saint Ambrose, who had deliberately come from Milan to Aquileia.

Here, then, was the territory of Aquileia, within no more than six years, twice overflowing with an immense force of soldiers; and twice battles were fought there with opposing armies, in such a way that the struggle was no less than one for the Western Empire between the legitimate emperor and two usurpers.

Not long afterward, however—namely, in the year 400, six years after the destruction of Eugenius—the region of Aquileia was again exposed to still greater misfortunes. Who does not know of that first invasion of Italy by the Goths under the leadership of Alaric, which was undertaken at that time not so much to acquire dominion as to carry away booty? The territory of Aquileia was the very first to lie open to the voracious jaws of the barbarians. It must therefore be believed that they left nothing undone in order, amid the ruin of the Aquileians’ possessions, to satisfy the long-conceived greed for every kind of property.

What, then, did Bishop Chromatius do in these straits? There is certainly nothing surprising in [Col. 0990D] in his withdrawing once, and even twice, from the city and territory of Aquileia; and especially on this second occasion, in prolonging his stay for a longer period in a place that he had preferred as his residence; indeed, in such a way that he seemed, in some manner, to be the bishop of that place rather than of the city of Aquileia.

Anyone who knows the Roman roads that were then in use will readily understand, if I am not mistaken, that the port called Romatium or Romatinum on the river of the same name was in fact a place well suited at that time to Chromatius’s withdrawal—whether by the name of that port we understand the place now called Porto-Gruaro above Concordia, or another place beyond Concordia, mentioned by Pliny, at the mouth of the same river, where it flows into the lagoon, which seems the more probable identification.

This place, I say, was well suited to Chromatius’s withdrawal both for avoiding the military disturbances of the Romans and for escaping the incursions of the barbarians. It lay apart especially from that road—whether one calls it the Flaminian or the Postumian—which led from Aquileia through [Col. 0991A] Venetia and Aemilia to the chief cities of Italy and finally to the capital of the world itself; and from which both the port of Romatium or Romatinum and the river lay to the left of the same road for those traveling from Aquileia. They were almost unknown, or at least less attractive to the barbarians, who were then directing themselves elsewhere.

See the map of ancient Italy published by Muratori at the front of the first volume of the *Writers on the Affairs of Italy*, as well as the other map of Upper and Lower Venetia, that is, of inland and maritime Venetia, published by Filiasi in volume III of his *Historical Memoirs of the First and Second Venetians*. It is therefore also probable that Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia, was called not “Roman,” as De Rubeis himself also observed, but “Romatinian” or “Romatian” bishop.

In the year 407 or 408, Chromatius exchanged mortal life [130] for heavenly glory. Alaric, the leader of the Goths, having apparently reached at least a temporary settlement with the emperor Honorius, was stationed in Noricum, pressing upon the borders of Aquileia and [Col. 0991B] longing for a new ruin of Italy. He soon attained his desire. For in that very year, descending into Italy, he again shook the territory of Aquileia with terror, although he passed by Aquileia and the other cities of Venetia at that time, in order to proceed by a direct route to Rome. Rome he finally captured in the following year, 409, or, as others have thought, in 410, after first reducing it by famine, and then cruelly plundering it.

Meanwhile Augustine had succeeded Chromatius. The years of his episcopate are variously given in catalogues and chronicles. Augustine was then succeeded by Adelphus, Adelphus by Januarius, Januarius by Maximus, Maximus by Secundus, and Secundus finally by our Nicetas, as appears in De Rubeis’s *Monuments*.

While Augustine was bishop, Dandulus reports in his *Chronicle*, book V, chapter 1, part XII, that “the nobles of the city of Aquileia came to the Waters of Grado and built on the shore a conspicuous fortress, which was called Grado from the name of the waters.” The Aquileian nobles established this refuge not far from their ancestral homes against the incursions of the barbarians, to whom the territory of Aquileia was almost always [Col. 0991C] the first to lie open.

Thus, even after Chromatius, the Aquileian bishops continued to have both occasion and necessity to withdraw to safe and peaceful places. We may therefore readily conjecture that the successors of Chromatius also often stayed outside the city of Aquileia, probably at the same port of Romatinum, situated on the inner shore of the Concordian lagoon at the mouth of the Romatinum River.

Nor, meanwhile, were the Aquileians without what I might call domestic troubles, in addition to the foreign troubles caused by the barbarians, which repeatedly supplied the bishops of Aquileia with reasons for withdrawal. For when, after the death of the emperor Honorius, the tyrant John seized the Western Empire, and the emperor Theodosius the Younger consequently moved his army from the East to overthrow him, the territory of Aquileia again overflowed with military forces, around the year 424 or 425. Aquileia itself, which had obeyed the invading John, was besieged and captured, and returned to the power of Theodosius. There also, shortly afterward, [Col. 0991D], John paid the deserved penalty for his rebellion.

But we must now approach the principal reason that Secundus, the immediate predecessor of Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, had for withdrawing from the city and territory of Aquileia, in the year 452. That was the year in which the famous king of the Huns, Attila—born, as Jornandes or Jordanes said, for the convulsion of nations, and deservedly called the scourge of God—burst from Pannonia into Italy with an immense multitude of barbarians. At his first assault he invaded the territory of Aquileia, and, after harassing Aquileia with a dreadful siege, finally captured, plundered, and burned it. Proceeding from there, and carrying off captives, he inflicted the same disaster on Concordia, Altinum, and the other cities of Venetia, the first of which were never afterward able to rise again to their former dignity.

What Bishop Secundus of Aquileia did in these straits, where he was, or to what refuge he fled, is entirely uncertain. No one, however, will deny that this was by far the greatest occasion and necessity that Bishop Secundus had for withdrawing from the [Col. 0992A] city and territory of Aquileia—and not merely for withdrawing, but also for remaining for a longer time elsewhere, far from the city and territory of Aquileia.

Pliny’s port of Romatinum, situated at the mouth of the river and not far from Concordia, could not have been a safe place of refuge because of the immense multitude of barbarians. When the city of Concordia was destroyed, they certainly cannot be thought to have left unharmed the port belonging to it, situated on the Romatium River, where it was undoubtedly necessary that many goods of every kind, brought from all directions, had been collected—goods that would stimulate their desire for plunder.

Indeed, it seems most probable that the port of Romatinum itself, situated at the river’s mouth, suffered at that time the same fate as Concordia, whose port it was, and that it finally perished completely when the waters, restrained by no one, freely overflowed it, so that it disappeared, as happened also to other once-famous places and cities situated near the waters.

Bishop Secundus undoubtedly mourned so great a disaster [Col. 0992B] of the province of Aquileia and the destruction of so many cities. Finally, in the year 454, as Dandulus writes in De Rubeis, worn out perhaps more by grief than by age, he yielded to nature.

In that same year our Nicetas is said to have been proclaimed bishop of Aquileia in Secundus’s place. But what was the city of Aquileia then—still, so to speak, smoking from its fires, wet with the blood of its citizens, deprived of inhabitants, and fallen from all the splendor of its former dignity? At least during the first years of his Aquileian episcopate, it may reasonably be conjectured that our Nicetas did not remain in the city of Aquileia but rather stayed elsewhere, wherever a larger number of the terrified and fearful population that had escaped barbarian slavery had gathered.

Nor could the islands situated in the lagoons have so suddenly become sufficiently full of inhabitants and people that the bishop of Aquileia could easily, or would have thought it expedient, to establish his seat there. Nor was the fortress of Grado, built under Bishop Augustine, [Col. 0992C], as we have seen from Dandulus, suited to anything more than temporary defense rather than permanent habitation; it was not capable of supporting a population of sufficient size.

The new port of Romatinum, however, which was called Gruarius and was situated this side of Concordia, had perhaps already begun, owing to the suitability of the river and the place, to abound in both population and resources and to display the appearance of a new city, as if taking the place of Aquileia and Concordia.

Why, then, should Bishop Nicetas of Aquileia not have established something like a fixed seat in this port of Romatinum from the beginning of his assumption of the Aquileian episcopate, until the city of Aquileia, as circumstances improved, had recovered at least to some extent? And why should he not meanwhile have been called bishop of the city of Romatiana, and have been called so also by Gennadius?

By the time of Nicetas and Gennadius, the name of “city,” rather than “port,” suited that place situated on the Romatium or Romatinum River. For that reason Gennadius himself called it the city of Romatiana: a city, because it was rising like a new city [Col. 0992D] after the destruction of Concordia; Romatiana, because it was washed by the Romatian River.

Why, moreover, should Nicetas not have frequently visited this new port of Romatinum, or city of Romatiana, even after the city of Aquileia had raised its head somewhat from its own ruins? It was a place that was growing daily and that offered the bishop of the diocese frequent and abundant opportunities for pastoral work. From this, too, the designation “bishop of the city of Romatiana” may have become widely attached to our Nicetas.

To illustrate by an example from both his own age and the period that followed what we have not unwillingly conjectured about Nicetas of Aquileia on the basis of the vicissitudes of those times and the ruin of the city of Aquileia, the Church of Milan, related to Aquileia, is at hand. Its city suffered from Attila’s savagery the same fate as Aquileia, although not so deadly, since, with almost its entire population saved and unharmed, it was able quickly to recover its former dignity after the ruins and fires.

Eusebius, the most holy bishop of that city at the time, heard of the disaster of the Aquileians [Col. 0993A] [132] and saw the army of the Huns approaching the cities of Insubria, or Upper Liguria. He left Milan with the clergy and people and withdrew to mountainous places unknown or inaccessible to the enemy. There he remained until the barbarian leader, overcome by the eloquence of Saint Leo the pope, abandoned Italy and returned to his ancestral seats in Pannonia.

On this matter one may consult the very distinguished Oltrocchi in his recent work entitled *The Ligustic History of the Church of Milan*, book III, chapter 1. Worthy also of being read is a homily of Saint Maximus, bishop of Turin, which he delivered at Milan before Eusebius himself on the occasion of the restoration of that church, which had been destroyed by Attila’s fire together with the other houses of the citizens. This homily first appeared in its entirety in the splendid Roman edition of the works of Saint Maximus published in 1784, where it is numbered 94.

Eusebius of Milan, although at one time a fugitive from Milan, was never called by any title other than that of bishop of Milan. Indeed, he could not have been called otherwise, since he had been bishop of the Milanese before Attila’s disaster; after a brief emigration he returned to Milan with the clergy and people and devoted himself entirely there to restoring the sacred building and rebuilding the city; nor did he ever have occasion or need to go elsewhere, up to the year 462, when he departed to heaven, according to the chronological summary of the bishops of that Church found at the end of Oltrocchi’s work mentioned above.

The occasion for withdrawing from the chief city of their provinces was plainly the same for the bishop of Milan as for the bishop of Aquileia. But the condition of the city of Aquileia amid the same calamity was far different. Consequently, the bishop of Aquileia, Nicetas, who succeeded almost immediately after the destruction of that city, may have had to begin his episcopate elsewhere rather than at Aquileia, to stay elsewhere more frequently, and probably to stay at the new port of Romatinum, from which, [Col. 0993C] through a prolonged or frequently repeated residence, he would have acquired the designation “bishop of the city of Romatiana.”

[Col. 0993D] The Church of Milan itself offers us another example, and a singular one, much more significant than the one just cited, concerning the latter part of the sixth century and the Lombard invasion of Italy.

For when this people added to the native ferocity of its character and customs both the stain of pagan superstition and the profession of the Arian error—both of which intensified an ancient hatred of Christians and Catholics—it shook all Italy with fear when it learned that they were approaching the Alps, not merely as an army but as almost an entire nation, eager to seek new settlements within Italy.

Paul the Deacon writes in *On the Deeds of the Lombards*, book II, chapter 10, that the bishop of Aquileia at that time, Paul or Paulinus, struck with fear, abandoned the city of Aquileia and withdrew to the island of Grado with the treasures of his Church, in order to avoid the first arrival—or rather the first attack—of the new guests, or new enemies. We know that other bishops did the same whenever they had the opportunity to escape.

The singular circumstance reported concerning Saint Honoratus, the bishop of Milan at that time, in those straits, is that he left Milan together with the greater part of the clergy of his Church, abandoned his entire diocese, and went down to the maritime coast of Liguria. Entering Genoa, he established his seat there, where it continued not only during his lifetime but also for seventy years and more under several of his successors. These successors are believed to have been bishops both of the Church of Milan and simultaneously of the Church of Genoa, since no memory survives of any particular bishop of Genoa [133] having been appointed at that time.

The same Oltrocchi explains the entire matter in the work and place cited, with much praise for his learning and diligence.

[Col. 0994A] What therefore happened to the bishops of Milan in the century after Nicetas—that, driven by circumstances into prolonged exile from their own see, they were bishops of the Milanese Church but at the same time were bishops of, and were called bishops of, the Church of Genoa, where they had established their seat—why should it be surprising if the same thing happened also in the case of Nicetas? Although he was a bishop of Aquileia, he was nevertheless called bishop of the city of Romatiana, after the place where he may have begun his episcopate following the ruin of the city of Aquileia and where he may have resided frequently.

There is, however, this difference between the two cases: the bishop of Milan residing at Genoa and governing the Genoese Church was bishop of two distinct Churches. At that time, because of the circumstances, they were united under one prelate; when the reason for the union later ceased, each received its own bishop again, as before. The Aquileian bishop Niceas or Nicetas, on the other hand, even when he frequently resided at the port of Romatinum or Gruarius and consequently received the designation “bishop of the city of Romatiana,” was solely the bishop of his own Aquileian diocese, [Col. 0994B] to which the port of Romatinum then belonged to that diocese, since it had not yet been detached from the mother Church of Aquileia to form a separate suffragan Church and diocese of Concordia.

We cannot mention this diocese of Concordia without drawing from it another example—one that remains in force in our own time and is placed before everyone’s eyes and ears—in order to confirm still further what we have conjectured about Nicetas of Aquileia.

The city of Concordia, once a most distinguished and celebrated Roman colony, now consists of only a few buildings and a few inhabitants, as we have already noted above. Although it possesses a cathedral church distinguished by great and venerable antiquity, as well as an old episcopal residence situated nearby, it sees its bishop only at fixed and few times during the year—not indeed for days, but merely for hours. He therefore has a permanent and fixed residence in the nearby city of Porto-Gruaro, where there is another sacred building that serves as the cathedral, together with another episcopal residence containing the episcopal curia [Col. 0994C] and the seminary for clerics, and where the episcopal household is established.

The bishop of this diocese is always called “bishop of Concordia” in public documents, as he really is. But the more frequent, indeed common, usage, both within the diocese itself and among the neighboring peoples outside it, always calls him “bishop of Porto-Gruaro,” after the place where he permanently resides and from which his episcopal care flows out over the entire diocese.

Something nearly similar could have happened in the case of our Nicetas of Aquileia. Although he was certainly bishop of Aquileia, he might nevertheless also have been called bishop of the city of Romatiana, after the place where he frequently resided following the destruction of Aquileia. Thus, precisely as bishop of this city of Romatiana, he became known to Gennadius, a writer situated far from the province of Aquileia, who consequently wrote much according to popular report, especially at a time when the ancient fame of Aquileia had disappeared.

[Col. 0994D] Besides the example of Concordia just cited, the Church of Aquileia itself offers a similar fact that cannot be passed over. It is established that the bishops of Aquileia long maintained a stable seat in the city of Forum Julii, especially in the eighth and ninth centuries, as De Rubeis demonstrates in his *Monuments*, chapter 36.

What, then, if, because of the residence of the Aquileian bishops at Forum Julii, they themselves were sometimes called bishops of Forum Julii rather than [134] bishops of Aquileia, and if the Church of Aquileia received the designation “Church of Forum Julii”?

We know that this did indeed happen. For Pope Gregory II, in one of his letters to Donatus, the bishop of Grado, and Marcellus, duke of Venetia—reported by Baronius under the year of Christ 729, no. 4, although it must have been written several years earlier, as De Rubeis proves in the place cited—Pope Gregory, I say, calls Serenus, [Col. 0995A] the Aquileian bishop or patriarch of that time, who lived in the city of Forum Julii, the bishop of Forum Julii.

And Charlemagne, who in his testamentary documents of the year 811, reported by Einhard in his *Life*, chapter 33, bestowed alms from his own treasury upon twenty-one metropolitan churches of his kingdom—Charlemagne, I say, in those documents, without making any mention of Aquileia, named Forum Julii in place of Aquileia, because the Aquileian metropolitans were still residing in the city of Forum Julii.

On this matter consult the much-praised De Rubeis, *Monuments*, chapter 46, no. 1, and *Dissertations of Varied Learning*, chapter 20, no. 3.

If, therefore, because of the residence at Forum Julii of the Aquileian bishops during the eighth and the beginning of the ninth century, the bishops of that period were called bishops of Forum Julii, and if their Church of Aquileia was designated under the name of Forum Julii, why should it be surprising that in the fifth century Niceas or Nicetas, likewise bishop of Aquileia, could, because of a probable residence at the new port of Romatinum, or rather at the city of Romatiana, commonly be called bishop of the city of Romatiana, [Col. 0995B] and thus also be named by Gennadius and by later writers?

But enough now of this, as far as concerns what was to be investigated in the second part of the sixth chapter.

It is useful here to add one point from what has been said thus far, both in the first and in the second part of this chapter: namely, that it is by no means improbable that Niceas or Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, had first served as an auxiliary bishop for his predecessor Secundus, or even for another Aquileian bishop before Secundus, at the port of Romatinum—the same port of Romatinum that was indicated by Pliny and situated at the mouth of the Romatinum River.

Afterward, once Secundus had died and Nicetas had been appointed to govern the Church of Aquileia, he may also have frequently resided at the port of Romatinum. That port was then the new port situated on the same Romatinum River and located this side of Concordia. Consequently, it was commonly called at that time—and therefore also by Gennadius—not “port,” but rather, by the more appropriate name, “the city of Romatiana.”

In a matter so distant and obscure, we have done enough when we offer probabilities. These probabilities, however, are more than sufficient once the principal point of the dispute has been securely established—as we trust has been done in the preceding chapters.

[Col. 0995C]

## CHAPTER VII

The arguments of the most distinguished Zabeus against the Aquileian episcopate of Niceas or Nicetas of Gennadius are answered. The authority and observations of the distinguished Michael Denis are likewise addressed.

After establishing in the preceding chapters the Aquileian episcopate of Niceas or Nicetas of Gennadius—which is the principal aim of this entire discussion of ours—and after examining and explaining the difficulty concerning the city of Romatiana, which was the chief reason [135] that led the distinguished Zabeus to adopt another opinion, so that, together with the learned men of an earlier age, he maintained that the same Niceas or Nicetas was not Aquileian but Dacian [Col. 0995D]—although those scholars had not known of his recently discovered little work *On the Creed to the Competentes*, in which that same Nicetas is presented as bishop of Aquileia, and from which we first discovered that he was not the Dacian—we are required by the order of the argument, and the importance of the matter itself demands, to examine also the arguments advanced by Zabeus himself against the Aquileian episcopate of this Niceas or Nicetas in the dissertation that he placed before that little work.

Zabeus divided his dissertation into two parts. In the first he gathers what he calls external considerations in support of his opinion; in the second he investigates more deeply, collecting from the little work itself, the *Explanation of the Creed*, those points which, in his judgment, would show that its author was not Aquileian but Dacian.

Beginning with the second [Col. 0996A] chapter of this study, we have already refuted many of Zabeus’s arguments from both parts of his dissertation—and certainly the principal ones—as we think will be evident to anyone who has carefully read our discussion in its entirety. Some we attacked directly; most we dealt with as they arose here and there, blocking the path before us, which had to be cleared so that the argument could proceed freely on its course.

Nevertheless, some matters remain, especially in the second part of the distinguished man’s dissertation, which require particular attention for the complete confirmation of our position. These matters, then, will provide the subject of this seventh chapter. At its end we will also address the points whose author is the most learned prefect of the Vienna library.

Since nearly all the external arguments presented in the first part of Zabeus’s dissertation in favor of Nicetas the Dacian and against Nicetas the Aquileian are based either on the distinction [Col. 0996B] between the two cities, Aquileia and Romatiana; or on the Romatiana situated in Dacia on this side of the Danube; or even on the testimony of learned men who asserted that Gennadius’s Romatian Niceas or Nicetas was the man who became famous through his friendship with Saint Paulinus, bishop of Nola, and was consequently distinct from our Aquileian in both place and time—since all these points have already been resolved and explained in the preceding chapters, we begin this seventh chapter with that observation of Zabeus which is the first in the second part of his dissertation, under number 1, and therefore the first of those deeper matters by which he attempts to confirm his opinion.

“The Nicetas of Gennadius who was Romatian,” says Zabeus, “wrote a book on the errors of paganism.” He then adds:

> “Indeed, he spoke of an error that could have had a place only among barbarous and savage peoples. For thus we read in Gennadius: ‘The second book, On the Errors of Paganism, in which he says that, almost in his own time, a certain Melodius, a head of household, because of his generosity, and Gadarius, a peasant, because of his courage, were transferred by the pagans among the gods.’
>
> “But what need was there for such things to be proclaimed at Aquileia, where, from the time of Saint Mark the Evangelist, the temples of idols had begun to be demolished and the idols themselves [Col. 0996C] overthrown from their profane altars? Perhaps some remnants of paganism still survived there in the fifth century; but certainly very few, and not of such a kind that this foolish opinion could take root—namely, that bodily courage was the reason why someone could become a god.
>
> “For when we mention Aquileia in those times, we are speaking of the city that, among the cities of Italy after Rome, was the most cultivated; that flourished in the sciences and letters; and that, in every age, had been instructed by the teaching of great [136] men.
>
> “Rufinus had preceded Nicetas of Aquileia . . . Rufinus too explained the Creed, as is known to all the learned . . . Yet Rufinus speaks of the unity and existence of the true God in such a way that, even while silent, he seems to indicate that paganism in his region and in his time did not require careful refutation.
>
> “Are we to say that over the course of the years it had acquired an increase of strength, and that it grew while Nicetas was seated as bishop? But this is contrary to history. For three letters of Saint Leo the Great to Aquileian bishops survive; the last of them is addressed [Col. 0996D] to blessed Nicetas. From these we learn that there were not a few priests in those regions and that the Christian religion was held in great honor there.
>
> “Moreover, there were monasteries at Aquileia in which men distinguished for learning and piety lived and worked by their speech and writings for the preservation and advancement of Christianity . . .
>
> “In such an abundance of light and learning, how can it be believed that ignorance prevailed to such an extent that it led a number of people to believe what is refuted in the second book of Saint Nicetas? Shall we say that over the course of five centuries the Christian religion preached by Saint Mark made so little progress?”

Thus far Zabeus in his first observation, drawn from the deeper indications of this argument against the Aquileian episcopate of Niceas or Nicetas of Gennadius—and indeed he writes learnedly and eloquently.

To answer this observation, it must first be noted that it was not only among barbarous and savage [Col. 0997A] peoples, but among all kinds of pagans, including those who lived in a refined and respectable manner, that people sometimes enrolled among the gods those who had excelled in some virtue—whether a social virtue, such as generosity, or a bodily endowment, such as courage.

Nor does the designation “barbarous and savage peoples” in any way suit the Dacian population situated on this side of the Danube, where the city of Romesiana, Remesiana, Remissiana, or Romatiana was located, and where, rather than at Aquileia, Zabeus thinks these events and statements took place. For this people was subject to Roman rule and Roman civilization—indeed, it was of Roman origin, since it descended from the Roman colonies summoned by the emperor Aurelian from the other side of the Danube, as was said in the second chapter.

Furthermore, the Nicetas of Gennadius wrote a book not about one “error” but about the “errors” of paganism—that is, about the superstitious worship of idols and the falsehood of pagan religion, considered not from a single aspect but from every direction.

What, then, is surprising if, in order to attack more vigorously the ancient monstrosities of this false religion, [Col. 0997B] he chose, when he came to attack and ridicule deification, to make use—on the occasion of a recent and ridiculous example—of those two men, Melodius the head of a household and Gadarius the peasant, who, almost in his own time, had been transferred by the pagans among the gods because of their generosity and courage?

This example naturally served Nicetas to demonstrate more fully the emptiness and frivolity of pagan worship, which was the subject of his book. It did not, however, show that this foolish opinion—that bodily courage was the reason why someone could become a god—could actually have been spreading in the very city or region where Nicetas was preaching.

But since Zabeus’s observation is directed toward establishing that preaching against idolatry was altogether unnecessary in a fifth-century bishop of Aquileia—as is also clear from another observation in the second part of his dissertation, under number 14, concerning the little work *Explanation of the [137] [Col. 0997C] Creed*—and since he wishes from this to conclude that Nicetas of Gennadius, who attacked the errors of paganism in a separate little book and also attacked them in the *Explanation of the Creed* itself, was not Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, but rather Nicetas the Dacian, the friend of Saint Paulinus of Nola, the matter requires somewhat fuller explanation.

Although pagan superstition, as a result of the preaching of the Gospel, had lost much of its dignity and influence during the first three centuries, even while the drawn swords of the emperors were wielded in its defense, through the daily and abundant increase of Christians—so that Tertullian, in the *Apologeticus*, chapter 17, could confidently reproach the pagans by saying that, although Christians were, as he put it, “of yesterday,” they had already filled in his time every place belonging to the pagans: cities, islands, fortresses, military camps, tribes, divisions, the palace, the senate, the forum—in a word, everything except the temples of the idols;

and although this same pagan superstition received, at the beginning of the fourth century, with the peace granted to the Church by the emperor Constantine, [Col. 0997D], what may be called its final blow, so that the Christian religion occupied throughout the Roman world the place of the error everywhere subdued and had become the religion of the Roman Empire;

nevertheless, paganism did not then, nor for a long time afterward, reign alone and undisturbed, so that Christianity was not continually compelled to struggle against a multitude of people who, even amid such abundant Gospel light, stubbornly loved the darkness of their former superstition.

The contemporary records provide abundant evidence of this multitude of pagans existing everywhere throughout the fourth century of the Church, even in the principal Churches of the world founded by the apostles themselves. This evidence is supplied especially by the most holy bishops of the Churches of that age. In their surviving works, the pagan superstition attacked by those bishops is plainly seen to have still been active and by no means without strength.

For the present it is enough for us to recall the reign of the emperor Julian Augustus, as well as the efforts of the senator Symmachus on behalf of the [Col. 0998A] Altar of Victory under the emperors Valentinian and Theodosius. These examples make clear how many worshipers of idols there still were at that time, and how considerable their remaining power was.

What now of the fifth century? The fifth century was, as it were, ushered in by all those calamities which, first shaking the Roman Empire to its foundations, finally hastened its collapse in the West, as the barbarians everywhere gained the upper hand. Who is unaware of the outcries raised throughout the world by the pagans of that age against the Christian religion, and in favor of restoring the public worship of idols, to whose suppression they attributed all the troubles by which the Empire was afflicted? Hence arose the distinguished work of the blessed Augustine, *The City of God*; hence also Orosius’s *Histories against the Pagans*. These two works were two new *Apologetics* of different kinds, suited to those circumstances, written on behalf of the Christian religion to repel the odium which the worshipers of pagan superstition, still present everywhere in great numbers, stirred up against it on every side by their denunciations, and also to strengthen the will and faith of Christians [Col. 0998B] amid so many adversities.

The multitude of pagans is therefore evident even at the beginning of the fifth century, when Churches already stood everywhere throughout the world, and when they flourished not only through bishops outstanding in learning and holiness, but also through illustrious examples of every virtue and through the holiest institutions. It is indeed true that by the laws of Theodosius and Honorius the temples of idols were closed and public sacrifices prohibited, and therefore every form of worship properly belonging to idolatry, from which the pagan religion consisted, was prohibited as well. Yet the laws themselves did not everywhere achieve their full effect, and at times they had to be silent even before the eyes of the Augusti by whom they had been enacted.

While Theodosius the Younger was ruling—that is, when the fifth century was already mature—pagan superstition still flourished in the imperial city itself, Constantinople. It was credited to him that the temples of the idols were utterly destroyed, so that no trace of the former superstition remained. He also dedicated to the true God, in honor of the martyr Ignatius, a temple in that city which had been consecrated to demons and called the Tychaeum, placing there the martyr’s relics, transferred from the cemetery outside the Daphnitic Gate, as Evagrius Scholasticus writes in Book I, chapter 16.

In the year 451, as Muratorius notes in the *Annals of Italy*, the Emperor Marcian enacted a law against the pagans, which is preserved in the Justinian Code, Book VII, under the title “On Pagans.” But in the year 467, when the Emperor Anthemius entered the city of Rome, the Lupercalia were still being celebrated there in honor of the god Februarius, as is clear from a letter of Pope Gelasius I against the senator Andromachus, preserved in Labbe’s *Councils*, edited by Coletus, volume V, col. 359.

It is further clear from the same letter that even during the pontificate of Gelasius himself, who governed the Church from 492 to 496, many people in the city of Rome were still eager to restore the Lupercalia, which had been abolished not long before. I certainly do not deny that in this same letter the supreme pontiff reproves Christians who supported and sought to restore this pagan celebration of the Lupercalia. Nevertheless, the same letter likewise makes clear that at that time there were still pagan people in the city of Rome who took precedence over the Christians in this celebration, and who could have celebrated the Lupercalia among themselves without the company of Christians.

At the end of that letter the same pontiff Gelasius says:
