> Finally, as far as concerns me, let no baptized person, let no Christian, celebrate this; let only the pagans, whose rite it is, perform it. It is proper for me to declare that these things are unquestionably harmful and fatal to Christians.

Here one sees the distinction made by Gelasius between Christians and pagans. He maintains that spectacles of this kind are not fitting for Christians. But he names as pagans those who were then carrying them on; and since he could not prevent them, he at least wished them to perform them alone, without the attendance of Christians. Pagans, therefore, still existed at Rome even in the time of Pope Gelasius, following the licentiousness of the Lupercalia [Col. 0999A] and enticing the Christian people also to imitate them.

When we speak of Rome, however, what Church are we discussing? Surely that most fortunate Church to which the apostles poured forth their entire teaching together with their blood, as Tertullian expressed himself no less magnificently than truthfully in *On the Prescription against Heretics*, chapter 36. We are speaking of that Church whose succession of bishops from Peter, continuous and without any interruption, had already been set before the heretics by Irenaeus, Augustine, and other Fathers as proof of the transmission of undefiled doctrine.

We are speaking of that Church which gloried in an immense number of holy martyrs and which had already become abundant in men of outstanding holiness. We are speaking of that Church of which Pope Innocent I had already written in Letter 25, in Coustant’s Paris edition, col. 856, to Decentius of Gubbio: through priests appointed by the venerable apostle Peter and his successors, it had established Churches throughout Italy, Gaul, Spain, Africa, Sicily, and the intervening islands [Col. 0999B].

If, then, such a great Church—taught by the very leaders of the apostles, illustrious with such glory, laden with such merits, and the mother of so many Churches—if this Church, I say, still had pagan people in her bosom and within the walls of the City even as the fifth century was passing away, against whose insane superstitions and obscenities Pope Gelasius had to warn the Christian people, there is no reason why the most distinguished Zabeus could write that it was wholly incompatible with the claim that at Aquileia, in Niceta’s time—that is, in the already advanced fifth century—there were idolaters who deserved to be reproved by him in an appropriate discourse and against whom the faithful needed to be admonished. Zabeus argues that Aquileia was at that time, after Rome, the most cultured of the cities of Italy, flourishing in the sciences and letters, and that it had received the Christian religion from Saint Mark and had already been instructed in every age by the preaching of great men. From this he concludes that this Nicetas Gennadius, author of the book *On the Errors of Paganism* and of another *Explanation of the Creed*, was not our Nicetas of Aquileia, but rather Nicetas the Dacian, the friend of Paulinus of Nola. But we must now draw nearer to the Church of Aquileia itself; after a further excursion from our direct route, we shall then examine it more conveniently.

As we travel from Rome toward Aquileia, let us halt at Ravenna, which was then another royal city, powerful in population and resources, where the court of the Western Empire was established and where the imperial family itself spent almost all its time around the middle of this fifth century. At that time Saint Peter Chrysologus was the chief glory of this city and its Church; he flourished and illumined the whole Church by the holiness of his life and the excellence of his teaching.

If we examine his sermons, especially those which he delivered on the Apostles’ Creed, and also another entitled *On the Kalends of January*, which were polluted by the various superstitions of the nations, numbered 155 in the edition of Sebastianus Paulus, we shall clearly understand from them that pagan worshipers of idols existed even in that part of Italy and in the territory of the diocese of Ravenna itself. The zeal of the holy bishop was directed toward them, both for their conversion and for the constancy of Christians in faith and discipline of life.

It is useful to sample a few passages from these sermons, lest we seem to have made our assertion without evidence.

> This is why the one who comes from the nations is first cleansed from the demon by the laying on of hands and by exorcisms, and receives the opening of his ears, so that he may be able to receive the hearing of faith and, with the Lord guiding him, may be able to attain salvation.

So Saint Peter Chrysologus says in Sermon 52. There were therefore Gentiles known to the people of Ravenna who sometimes came to the church, since on an appropriate occasion the holy bishop addressed his faithful concerning their entrance into the church and the value of the ceremonies performed for them.

That Gentiles actually came to the church from the territory of Ravenna is further shown by what follows:

> Therefore cleanse from your hearts the mire of unbelief, so that the streams of faith may run purely through you [Col. 1000A]; cut out from the roots within you the growths of unbelief, so that the strong plantings of your credulity may grow upward into the heights. … Let the one who wishes to know his God not know the gods of the nations: whoever calls them gods contradicts God. To serve one is freedom; to serve many is captivity.

Thus he speaks in Sermon 51, *On the Apostles’ Creed*:

> Today you rightly confess that you have believed in God, when you rejoice that you have fled from gods and goddesses differing in sex, confused in number, common in the crowd, base in origin, foul in reputation, supreme in impiety, first in crime, singular in guilt, accused even by the very faces of their own tombs. For it is misery, pain, and unhappiness to have had as servants such and so many beings as you have hitherto endured as masters. But rejoice that you have reached the one living, true, sole God, yet not a solitary God, saying: “I believe in God the Father.”

The holy bishop himself says this in Sermon 57 on the same Apostles’ Creed. To whom could these words of both sermons have been addressed except to catechumens, or those seeking baptism, who came to the Church from paganism? Certainly, if they had been children of Christians, the holy bishop could not have said to catechumens or candidates for baptism that they had fled from gods and goddesses whom they had until then endured as masters, and who had possessed such people as servants.

I pass over many other passages that I could cite from the sermons of this holy bishop on the Apostles’ Creed, which are numerous, and from all of which it may be concluded, as Dominicus Mita, the old editor and commentator on Chrysologus, observes:

> Our most holy archbishop baptized very many adult unbelievers, both barbarians and Italians and people of Ravenna, who were so invited to embrace the faith by the holy examples and sacred teaching of this shepherd.

That the holy bishop also had to warn the Christian people not to allow themselves to be carried away by the example of idolaters and not to involve themselves in their spectacles is clearly shown by the following passages from the aforementioned sermon *On the Kalends of January*:

> This is why, brothers, this is why today the Gentiles drag, pull, and haul their gods out to be seen amid carefully devised obscenities, with contrived shamefulness, and made more shameful by the very indecency itself; they make them such that they ought not to be seen, and so forth.

He then continues:

> We have said this, brothers, in order to make clear the reason why today the Gentiles make their gods commit such acts as we endure, and make them such that they are both a source of horror and a cause of shame to those who see them; let them make them such that eventually even those who make them themselves will loathe and abandon them, and let Christians glory in having been freed from such things through Christ—provided only that they are not polluted by their spectacles, that they do not defile their incense by touching it, and that they avoid the danger of consenting to such things. For consent is always equal to the deed, as the Apostle proves when he says: “Not only those who do them, but also those who consent to those who do them.”

So Chrysologus speaks. Who, from these and the other words of the holy bishop cited above, could fail to understand clearly enough both that pagans existed in his diocese and that there were many of them, against whom Christians needed to be warned, and from whom very many also, with some frequency, came over to the Christian faith?

[Col. 1000D] From the Church of Ravenna, Saint Maximus, bishop of Turin in the Subalpine region and of approximately the same age, invites us to make a brief detour; afterward we shall resume our journey to Aquileia by the direct route. The sermons of this holy bishop also survive, and from them we clearly understand that there was then a large supply of pagans in those regions, especially among country people settled in villages and rural districts. Let the reader therefore not be reluctant to weigh his words:

> We are therefore commanded to prepare the way for the Lord by the purity of our faith—by a purity with which we oppose not only empty idols and superstitious inventions, but also detest and correct them in our brothers.

So he says in Sermon 58, which is Sermon 7 *On the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist*, in the latest Roman edition. Why would Saint Maximus have named here empty idols and superstitious inventions against which the faithful ought to oppose themselves, if such things had not existed in those regions? Why would he have taught his faithful to detest them, and even to correct them, in their brothers, if pagans—whom he calls brothers—had not actually been present among them?

Against the purifications or lustrations of the pagans, which still prevailed in his diocese, he speaks as follows in Sermon 77, which is Sermon 2 *On the Holy Martyrs Alexander and His Companions*:

> And because we have heard that a lustration is customarily sent out by certain sacrilegious people in imitation of the saints, let us rebuke the impious and chastise those who err. … But if, when we see this, we remain silent, and by keeping silent endure it, we make ourselves guilty—not, perhaps, by carrying out the crime, but at least by consenting through our concealment. … How often has God commanded that the sacrileges of idols be destroyed, and yet we never wish to be concerned with this matter? We have always concealed it; we have always despised it. Subsequently the imperial command admonished us. See how great a derogation from divinity this addition of human authority is. … The rulers, indeed, being such good Christians, promulgate laws on behalf of religion, but the officers do not properly enforce them.

Here Saint Maximus points to an imperial law, perhaps the one mentioned above, that of the Emperor Marcian enacted in the year 451. He also bears witness to the lax and incomplete observance of this law, just as of the preceding laws of the Augusti, exactly as we likewise noted in order to demonstrate the ineffectiveness of these laws for the complete extinction of pagan superstition [Col. 1001B].

Two other sermons of this holy bishop are extant, namely Sermons 96 and 97, under the title *On Removing Idols from Private Estates*. From them it is clear that the worship of idols still prevailed to a considerable extent in those regions at that time, especially among country people, as we pointed out above. Wooden altars, stone images, and the corresponding ministry are mentioned here; here the soothsayer, here the *dianaticus*—the person associated with Diana or her rites—and here their dress is described.

But let us cite a few words from each sermon that deserve consideration as evidence for our argument:

> A few days ago I admonished your Charity, brothers, that, as religious and holy people, you should remove every pollution of idols from your estates and uproot from the fields the whole error of the Gentiles. For it is not permissible that those who have Christ in their hearts should have Antichrist in their dwellings, that while you worship God in the Church, your people should venerate the devil in shrines. Let no one think himself excused by saying, “I did not order it to be done; I did not command it.” … You therefore, brother, when you see your farm laborer sacrificing and do not prohibit him from making the offering, sin; even if you have not supplied the opportunity, you have nevertheless permitted the license. … Great, therefore, is the evil of idolatry: it pollutes those who perform it, pollutes those who live there, pollutes those who look upon it; it penetrates to the ministers, it penetrates to those who know of it, it penetrates to those who keep silent. For when the farm laborer sacrifices, the *domnedius* [estate-owner; the printed reading is uncertain] is defiled, and so forth.

This is from the first sermon. From the second are the following words:

> We believe that you have made no small progress through the treatment of the preceding Lord’s Day, since by our preaching we have cleansed your hearts from every defilement of idols. … But whoever knows that sacrifices are being made to idols in his field and does not prohibit them, even though he himself lives far away in the city, is nevertheless touched by that foul pollution. And although a farm laborer stands beside the altars, the accursed contamination returns to the *domnedius* [estate-owner; printed reading uncertain]. For he becomes a participant in it, if not by awareness, certainly by knowledge.

Thus far Saint Maximus. How many pagans there were, and how widely pagan superstition extended in the diocese of Turin around the middle of the fifth century—or rather, once that century was already half over, when Saint Maximus held the episcopate—appears abundantly from his zeal in attacking this superstition, both in the sermons devoted to it and in the opportunities he took to speak about it as circumstances required. Now let us proceed directly from the Subalpine regions to the Church of Aquileia.

As we travel, the Church of Brescia, situated approximately halfway along the route, compels us to pause briefly. From the sermons of its holy bishop Gaudentius it has something to tell us about the paganism of its region. He flourished at the end of the fourth and the beginning of the fifth century: according to some, he died in 410; according to others, in 427, as is stated in the preface by Paulus Galeardus to his works, published at Padua by the Cominian press.

What, then, do these sermons present to us? The fourth treatise, *On a Reading from Exodus*, contains the following:

> You therefore, neophytes, who have been invited to the banquet of this blessed and spiritual Passover, see to it that you preserve your souls from every pollution of foods infected by pagan superstition. Nor is it enough for a Christian to guard his life from the deadly food of demons; he must also flee, as though from certain serpentine poisons of the devil, every abomination of the Gentiles and every path of idolatry. For the parts of idolatry are sorcery, incantations, binding-spells, vanities, auguries, lots, observation of omens, and funeral rites—in short, all those things from which the evil of idolatry first raised its head of error. For at first people began, on account of their appetite, to prepare meals for the dead, which they themselves would eat; afterward they even dared to celebrate sacrilegious sacrifices for them. … Beware, I beg you, of all these things, and so forth.

Treatise 13 of the same holy bishop Gaudentius, delivered on the Nativity of the Lord, presents this further passage:

> Do you think that the lukewarm and negligent Christian loves God, who allows idols to be worshiped on his estates, who permits the shrine of a demon and the altar of the devil to stand as an insult to God?

The sermons of Saint Gaudentius of Brescia therefore show us that in his time the worship of pagans still existed in the diocese of Brescia as well, especially on estates—in other words, among country people in villages and rural districts—as we recently saw in the Subalpine regions. Nor was it merely a form of worship that could be called some surviving remnant of pagan superstition to be despised. It was a form that still had idols exposed to everyone’s eyes, with altars and shrines, and even animal sacrifices, from which foodstuffs may perhaps have been offered for sale; it also fostered further abominations. The bishop therefore had to warn Christians repeatedly about all these things.

Instructed by this information as well, not inappropriately, along our route, and having departed from the territory of Brescia, behold, we are now at Aquileia, which is the goal of our entire journey or excursion through various parts of Italy.

As soon as we enter the diocese of Aquileia, Saint Chromatius, bishop of the Aquileians, comes before us. He is the author of the surviving sermons or treatises on Matthew, and governed the Church of Aquileia toward the end of the fourth century until the seventh or eighth year of the fifth.

What, then, does Saint Chromatius reveal to us about the pagans who were present in his time within the territory of Aquileia? He does not speak expressly about paganism; perhaps he also wrote other works that have not reached us. But when an opportunity arose to mention pagans in Treatise 7 on Matthew, chapter 1, preserved in Andrea Gallandi’s *Bibliotheca Veterum Patrum*, volume VIII, he made the following few remarks, which are extremely worthy of notice:

> We have adversaries, the Gentiles, who oppose our faith, and who sometimes, during the time of persecution, compel us to make abominable sacrifices.

These words certainly show that Gentiles existed in the very diocese of Aquileia, where Chromatius was speaking at the end of the fourth and beginning of the fifth century, as the words themselves indicate, referring as they do to the time and place of the speaker. Nor do they show them to have been so few in number that they could perhaps be described as merely a few remnants of paganism, as Zabeus thinks. For people could not have been extremely few who had to be named as our adversaries and opponents of our faith, and still less could they have been so few if they were capable, as Chromatius thought might happen, of compelling us to sacrifices during a time of persecution [Col. 1002D].

Nevertheless, clearer evidence remains to be presented, and it must be sought from the same source to which the distinguished Zabeus himself directs us.

He directs us, of course, to Rufinus of Aquileia, who was a contemporary of Chromatius and died in 410, as Fontaninus demonstrates in the biography he composed of him, with De Rubeis also agreeing in the final chapter of his dissertation on Rufinus:

> “Rufinus,” says Zabeus, “preceded Nicetas of Aquileia. … Rufinus himself also explained the Creed. … Now Rufinus speaks of the unity and existence of the true God in such a way that, even while silent, he seems to suggest that paganism in his region and in his time did not require careful opposition. Are we to say that over the course of the years it acquired an increase of strength and grew while Nicetas was seated [as bishop]?”

Rufinus of Aquileia was indeed a contemporary of Chromatius. After returning to Aquileia from the East, he was admitted by Chromatius to the company of the Aquileian presbyters, as the same De Rubeis writes in the aforementioned dissertation, chapter 14. Rufinus, I say, probably composed his *Commentary on the Creed* while serving as a presbyter at Aquileia, a position he held until the death of Chromatius. He dedicated it to a certain bishop Laurence, whom we conjectured above to have been one of the bishops attached to the Church of Aquileia and one of those who assisted the bishop of the diocese.

Rufinus’s authority in this *Commentary*, in matters concerning his own Church of Aquileia, must therefore be regarded as very great. Indeed, since he was himself an Aquileian presbyter writing to a bishop attached to the diocese of Aquileia, he must be held to have written there what would be especially necessary for the use of his own Church of Aquileia.

Yet Zabeus must have read this *Commentary on the Creed* very cursorily when he wrote as he did about Rufinus—or else he read it while occupied with one thought after another. For Rufinus’s *Commentary* is very far from suggesting, as Zabeus claims, even silently, that paganism in his region and time did not require careful opposition. On the contrary, Rufinus is wholly engaged there in attacking paganism as well, and doing so carefully, wherever an opportunity presents itself.

The matter must therefore be examined in detail. In doing so, we shall answer Zabeus in two ways: first, by showing that Rufinus deliberately attacked paganism in his *Commentary*; and second, by showing that paganism actually existed in the Aquileian region in Rufinus’s time in such a form that it deserved to be attacked expressly and carefully.

I have before me Rufinus’s *Commentary on the Creed*, as presented to us by the distinguished editor and commentator on the works of Rufinus, Dominicus Vallarsius. The first point that must be made against Zabeus’s observation is that Rufinus discussed little or nothing in his *Commentary* about the unity and existence of the true God, and certainly nothing that would serve to prove or demonstrate that unity and existence. Thus he had no occasion on this account to attack paganism.

The existence and unity of the true God was already, at that time, a settled matter, especially among those elder Christians of ours; Christians no longer needed to be fortified against paganism concerning it. As for the pagans themselves, or any unbelievers who held the contrary view, they were more deserving of ridicule than refutation.

Nevertheless, Rufinus deliberately attacks paganism at the very beginning of his *Commentary*. Explaining, in section 3, the opening words of the Creed, “I believe in God the Father almighty,” he spends some time examining the first word, *I believe*. He therefore demonstrates its force and necessity by adducing various highly appropriate analogies from human life and ordinary conduct. He says that he has done this in order to meet the objection of the pagans, who, as he himself says, accuse us of excessive readiness to believe.

Let us therefore hear him speak:

> We prefaced these matters at the beginning for this reason: pagans are accustomed to object to us that, because our religion lacks rational proofs, it consists solely in the persuasion of belief. We have therefore shown that nothing can either be done or stand unless the power of belief has preceded it.

Here, certainly, from the beginning of his *Commentary*, Rufinus carefully attacks paganism and implies that paganism existed in his own time in the province of Aquileia in a form that required such careful opposition.

Let us proceed from section 3 of this *Commentary* of Rufinus to sections 11 and 12. Here Rufinus treats the article of the Creed that proposes belief in the Virgin’s childbirth: “Who was born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary.” In the preceding section he had brought forward the prophets’ oracles concerning this ineffable mystery [Col. 1004A], together with the testimony of the Gospel, which declares that what those earlier writings had once foretold would happen had been fulfilled.

In these two sections, the eleventh and twelfth, which make up almost three complete columns of the folio edition of the aforementioned *Commentary* of Rufinus, Rufinus is entirely occupied with refuting paganism, whose adherents mocked the Virgin’s childbirth in opposition to the faithful of Christ.

He begins as follows:

> But since these things are asserted from the prophetic Scriptures, they may perhaps refute the Jews, although they are unbelieving and incredulous. Pagans, however, are accustomed to mock us when they hear us preach the birth from a Virgin. For this reason we must respond briefly to their criticisms.

Rufinus then continues throughout section 11 and the following section, answering the objections of the pagans with force and learning, as was appropriate in dealing with pagans who did not acknowledge the authority of our sacred writings. He responds partly by reason, insofar as is sufficient in so great a matter; partly by arguing on their own ground, taking the opportunity provided by the many monstrous and incredible births of pagan religion, to which blind paganism nevertheless refused to deny belief; and partly by familiar examples and analogies, showing that an event set above the human mode of understanding need not be contrary to reason, and explaining it to some extent.

How Zabeus failed to see all these matters, set out at such length against paganism in Rufinus’s *Commentary*, I confess that I simply do not understand.

It is also worthwhile to cite another passage from the same *Commentary*, where Rufinus attacks paganism expressly. It occurs under section 40, where he treats the article “The forgiveness of sins.” In this part Rufinus’s entire discourse is directed against paganism. This is how he speaks:

> Pagans are accustomed to say mockingly against us that we deceive ourselves when we suppose that crimes committed in deed can be cleansed by words. And they say: “Can the man who committed murder cease to be a murderer, and can the adulterer who committed adultery fail to appear as an adulterer? How, then, will one guilty of such crimes suddenly appear holy to you?”

Rufinus responds to this pagan objection against the Christian faith, and then concludes against them as follows:

> In this way our faith is not found to be opposed to natural reasoning, since the forgiveness of sins is attributed not to deeds, which cannot be changed, but to the mind, which can certainly be converted from evil to good.

Rufinus of Aquileia himself therefore shows our distinguished opponent Zabeus that in his *Commentary on the Creed* he did not speak against paganism only once or superficially, but repeatedly and at considerable length. He also shows that paganism itself was present in the territory of Aquileia in his time in such a form that it required careful and persistent opposition, both to overthrow it continually and to strengthen and confirm the faith of Christians.

From Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia, and Rufinus the presbyter, down to Nicetas—from the year 410, that is, to 454—there are no surviving Aquileian documents by which pagan superstition in the diocese of Aquileia can be demonstrated [Col. 1004D]. The works of the bishops and presbyters of Aquileia after Chromatius and Rufinus and before Nicetas, if there were any, have not reached us, apart from two or three small works published here and there, about which scholars inquire and dispute.

Only Sermon 242 *On the Creed*, addressed to candidates for baptism and preserved among the Augustinian appendices, makes mention of pagans. As we said above in chapter 4, it probably belongs to Augustine, bishop of Aquileia, the successor of Chromatius. From this sermon one might perhaps infer that pagans still existed there at that time. For, in treating the article “From there he will come to judge the living and the dead,” it says:

> He judges Christians and pagans, the just and sinners, the faithful and the impious.

Why would pagans be mentioned here in an explanation of the Creed addressed to candidates for baptism, if pagans had not existed in that region and were not already known to those candidates—indeed, if some of those candidates had probably themselves come from their number? The candidates could then understand the difference between divine judgment upon them and upon Christians from this simple indication, just as they understood the distinction between the just and sinners, the faithful and the impious, categories from which the Lord’s threshing floor has never been free. But let these remarks be regarded as incidental, so that nothing that can be brought forward in support of this argument may be omitted.

For the rest, what need is there of documentary evidence to conjecture that paganism continued to flourish in the Aquileian region even after the time of Rufinus, when we have seen that during Rufinus’s lifetime it was so widely diffused that he too was compelled to attack it at length? It is therefore no wonder that paganism still existed among the people of Aquileia even more than forty years later, so that Nicetas himself was compelled, both in his specific little book and when the opportunity arose to address candidates for baptism, to turn his discourse toward it and to instruct them expressly concerning it.

Paganism was eradicated only by slow degrees. It reached not only through the entire fifth century, but even into the sixth, when that century was already mature and passing away, in the very heart of Italy, as we shall soon see.

Moreover, could Aquileia in the time of Nicetas have been in a better condition than Rome under Pope Gelasius, Ravenna under Chrysologus, and Turin under Bishop Maximus, all of whom flourished at the same time or even later, as we have seen in each case? Even if pagans were perhaps not so numerous in Nicetas’s time in the city of Aquileia itself, they unquestionably abounded in the territory of Aquileia, especially among country people settled in villages and rural districts, just as we saw that they were likewise abundant at the same time in the fields of the Subalpine region, and not long before on the estates of the people of Brescia under Bishop Gaudentius.

Indeed, since pagan superstition had its principal home among country people in the fifth century, it should not seem surprising if those same idolaters, naturally more superstitious than others and of coarser understanding, sometimes descended into portents and monstrosities, so that even for a slight reason they wished to enroll among the gods especially those of their own people whom they saw to excel in some virtue [Col. 1005C]. Why, then, should Nicetas not have cited in his little book *On the Errors of Paganism* an example of an apotheosis carried out by pagan country people of the province of Aquileia itself, when he mentions that Melodius and Gadarius had, almost in his own time, been enrolled among the gods by the pagans?

But we acted too liberally when we said that perhaps there were not so many pagans in Niceta’s time within the city of Aquileia itself. For from the fact that in those times Aquileia was, after Rome, the most cultivated of the cities of Italy and flourished in sciences and letters, as Zabeus very rightly reminds us, and also from the fact that, while its fortunes were favorable, Aquileia was regarded in Italy as a second Rome, as we infer from the histories, we must conclude that pagans were also more numerous there than in the other cities of inferior rank and dignity. The most distinguished Innocent Ansaldus supplies us with this observation in his most learned work, entitled *The Very Great Multitude of Those Who Professed the Christian Religion in the Earlier Centuries of the Church*, chapter 16, page 343 of the Turin edition. [Col. 1005D] For he says:

> “That particular kind of struggle and contention which existed in the fourth century between the vicissitudes of the Christian religion and idolatry did not arise from the opposition, resistance, or instability of the provinces and regions, whether of the East or of the West, but from the principal cities of the empire alone. A considerable part of these was so entangled and enveloped, through the connections of social position, business, and public offices, with the sacred rites of the pagans, that it could be freed from that impediment only with the greatest difficulty. … Bossuet shows that the entire Roman empire had already become Christian, while at Rome a large part of its inhabitants were still devoted to the gods, whose divinity it dreamed was the source of its victories, power, and glory. … You might say nearly the same about the other cities that ruled the provinces: they rivaled Rome not only in greatness and ostentation, but also in superstition [Col. 1006A] and vices. … Since religion therefore encountered greater obstacles in the cities that ruled the provinces than in provincial cities, towns, villages, and hamlets, it should not seem surprising that even in the fourth century idolatry had a rival in the chief city of all, although religion had already almost extinguished it in all the lesser cities and places of the Roman empire.”

This is what Ansaldus said about the fourth century of the Church, which was the period under discussion. That his words can also properly be extended to the fifth century is sufficiently clear from what has so far been said about the pagan superstition of the fifth century, especially in the principal cities of Italy, Rome and Ravenna. Nor does it contradict this conclusion that the same may be said of Aquileia shortly after the disaster inflicted by Attila, when Niceta was bishop. The city was not immediately deprived of its former dignity by that catastrophe, but only gradually; and it was especially later, when new calamities overtook it after Niceta, that the efforts of its citizens to restore it to its former condition finally proved fruitless. [Col. 1006B] But we must proceed further in this argument, which is the first among Zabeus’s objections that we are deliberately attempting to answer, and which, given the importance of the matter, deserves to be examined with care.

To show that, in the time of Niceta of Aquileia, it was unnecessary for the things which Gennadius says his Niceta preached against paganism to be preached at Aquileia, Zabeus says that, from the time of Saint Mark the Evangelist, the temples of the idols began to be destroyed at Aquileia, and the idols themselves to be overturned from their profane altars. No one will deny that this may be said in a broad sense, although Zabeus produces no evidence for the claim; and although it is more probable that, among the Christians of those first three centuries, the temples of the idols were abandoned rather than demolished, and the idols despised rather than overturned from their altars, as appears from the words of Tertullian quoted above.

Whatever may have happened at Aquileia, from the time of Saint Mark down to Niceta, with respect to the temples of the idols and the idols themselves—for on this subject the histories are profoundly silent—we have from the *Chronicle* of Andrew [Col. 1006C] Dandulus, book VI, chapter 1, as we also reported earlier, while treating another matter in chapter 4, the following information. Helias, bishop—or patriarch, as he is called there—who governed the Church of Aquileia as the sixth century was drawing to a close, transformed a certain pagan temple situated on the neighboring shore into a convent for women under the name of Saint Peter the Apostle. Learned local scholars, in De Rubeis’s *Monuments*, chapter 26, no. 2, wish the name “Bethel” that we read here to be understood as “Belenus,” because Belenus had been a famous deity of the people of Aquileia.

As the sixth century was therefore drawing to a close, a temple of idols still stood in the territory of Aquileia, and not far from Aquileia itself, which could be converted to Christian use. Did the worship of idols therefore also continue in the territory of Aquileia down to that time? We certainly know that the survival of a temple of idols somewhere cannot be certain evidence that idolatrous worship was still active there at the same time. The matter may perhaps be judged differently, however, when numerous indications of idolatrous worship are found in the same period [Col. 1006D], even if not in the very place where we know that the temple stood, but in other places neither very distant nor less distinguished by reputation and renown.

To continue along the path of our evidence, what does the city of Ravenna, for example, show us concerning idolatrous worship during the sixth century? From Cassiodorus’s *Variae*, book I, letter 6, it is clear that in the city of Ravenna, not long after the beginning of the sixth century, King Theodoric built a spacious temple of Hercules. For that reason he ordered Agapitus, prefect of the city of Rome, to send from Rome the most skilled marble-workers to complete the work. He says:

> “Having undertaken in the city of Ravenna the spacious work of the basilica of Hercules, whose name antiquity appropriately assigns to whatever it established in that celebrated hall as an object of admiration, we most earnestly entrust this to Your Greatness, so that … you may send us from the City the most skilled marble-workers, and so forth.”

Thus, at the beginning of the sixth century, there were still pagan people in the royal city of Ravenna [Col. 1007A] who followed the ancient worship of idols. King Theodoric, although by no means a pagan, though infected with the Arian stain, built a spacious temple of Hercules in the royal city itself for their benefit and adorned it with much expense in marble, as is also stated in the same letter. Hercules had been the tutelary deity of the people of Ravenna, as the learned commentators on Cassiodorus note at this passage.

After Ravenna, what does Rome show us concerning idolatrous worship in that same sixth century? Helias, the bishop of Aquileia who converted the temple of idols to Christian use, had already departed this life in the year 586, as appears from De Rubeis’s *Monuments*, chapter 29. After his death, as the sixth century was drawing to a close, Saint Gregory the Great had ascended the Roman see, which he adorned so remarkably by the holiness of his life, his learning, and his zeal for religion.

There survives a letter of this holy pontiff, written around the year 597 or 598 to Agnellus, bishop of Terracina, a place situated not far from the city of Rome. In it he writes that he had learned that idolatrous worship was still surviving there [Col. 1007B], and he expresses surprise that Agnellus had delayed correcting it; finally, he urges him to investigate carefully and punish the offenders:

> “It has come to our attention that certain people there, which it is unlawful to say, worship trees and perpetrate many other unlawful acts against the Christian faith. We are amazed that Your Fraternity has delayed correcting this by a strict punishment. Therefore, by this present letter we exhort you to have these people sought out through diligent investigation and, once the truth has been discovered, to see that vengeance is exercised upon them in such a way that God may be appeased and the punishment inflicted on them may serve others as an example of correction.”

This is letter 18 of book VIII in the latest Venetian edition of the holy pontiff’s works, edited by Gallicciolli. Perhaps those Christians of Terracina had either fallen or relapsed into idolatrous superstition; for that reason Saint Gregory writes that they had to be dealt with so strictly, as with a matter belonging to the jurisdiction of the Church, so that they might be recalled to their proper duty.

Whatever the case may be, as far as we are concerned it is certainly established that, in that very region of Italy of which we spoke above, and not far from the city of Rome [Col. 1007C], as the sixth century was passing, either idolatry properly so called, or at least idolatrous worship, was flourishing. The Roman pontiff was so concerned to extinguish it.

Nor did such worship exist only at Terracina. In the larger islands adjacent to Italy—Sicily, namely, Sardinia, and Corsica—idolatry in the proper sense still existed in the same age of Saint Gregory, as is plainly evident from other letters of that holy pontiff. To avoid quoting too many of his words, let the case of Sicily be represented by letter 62 of book III, addressed to Eutychius, bishop of Tyndaris. In it Gregory urges him to persevere in converting the worshipers of idols, and informs him that he has also sent a letter to the praetor of Sicily, so that the praetor might join him with his own authority in so distinguished a work.

With respect to Sardinia, one may consult letters 24 and 25 of book IV, the first addressed to Zabardas, the governor of Sardinia, and the second to the nobles and landowners in Sardinia, as well as letter 65 of book IX, addressed to Januarius [Col. 1007D], bishop of Caralis. In each of these Gregory vigorously attacks the worship of idols, which was still flourishing there, especially among the rural population. It was principally on their account that he wrote to the nobles and landowners, their masters.

For Corsica, one must consult letter 1 of book VIII, addressed to Peter, bishop of Corsica. There too he similarly urges the bishop to continue turning the inhabitants away from the worship of idols.

Since this, then, was the state of idolatrous worship throughout Italy and the neighboring larger islands at the end of the sixth century, what wonder is it if it also existed in the territory of Aquileia in the time of Bishop Helias, where a temple of idols still survived? Indeed, may it not properly be attributed to Helias that, toward the end of the sixth century, when that idolatrous temple was converted to Christian use, the worship of idols finally ceased altogether in the province of Aquileia?

Would that this Helias, who appears to have been an outstanding champion of religion, had likewise been a defender of ecclesiastical unity [Col. 1008A], which his obstinacy in the celebrated controversy of the Three Chapters then did too much to injure.

But enough has now been said concerning the first observation of the distinguished Zabeus. Against it we may rightly conclude that there is absolutely no contradiction in supposing that Niceta of Aquileia, either around the middle of the fifth century or as the fifth century was drawing to a close, deliberately composed a little work against idolatry, or attacked it elsewhere as circumstances required. Consequently, there is no reason on this account [149] why the Niceta or Niceas mentioned by Gennadius should be understood rather as that Dacian who was a friend of Saint Paulinus of Nola than as our Aquileian Niceta, who flourished in the time of Saint Leo the Great.

Zabeus’s second observation, drawn from considerations more closely connected with the argument, is as follows. First, Aquileian bishops, he says, were not accustomed personally to deliver an explanation of the Creed to catechumens. He proves this by the example of Rufinus, who, writing about himself—he had been baptized at Aquileia—in book I of his *Invectives against Saint Jerome*, said:

> “I … nearly thirty years ago, when I was already living in a monastery, was regenerated by the grace of baptism and received the seal of faith through the holy men Chromatius, Jovinus, and Eusebius, most renowned and highly approved bishops of God. One of them was then the presbyter under Valerian, of blessed memory; [Col. 1008B] another was archdeacon; another was deacon; and at the same time one of them was my father and teacher of the Creed and of the faith.”

At the passage where Rufinus says, “one of them was then the presbyter,” and so forth, Zabeus inserts these two words within little lines—“note the words”—as if pointing with his finger to the fact that Valerian, bishop of Aquileia, did not take part in this act or these acts. Rufinus therefore received the Creed itself and the explanation of the Creed either from Chromatius, then a presbyter, or even from Eusebius, then a deacon, of whom Rufinus himself said, “he was my father and teacher of the Creed and of the faith.”

Zabeus immediately admits that in earlier times bishops themselves had occasionally been accustomed to perform these duties. He adds, however, that he knows this was not the custom of all bishops, and that there is certainly no evidence [Col. 1008C] establishing this custom among the Aquileian bishops in the fifth century; indeed, there is evidence to the contrary.

Second, he observes that only those bishops were accustomed personally to deliver the explanation of the Creed to catechumens who were accustomed to speak publicly extemporaneously, or whom the practice of writing had made more ready with the pen. But nothing of this kind, Zabeus adds, can be said of Blessed Niceta, bishop of Aquileia, concerning whose learning there are no clear and distinguished testimonies, as Henschenius says. If this Niceta had written anything of this sort, Gennadius’s book would have prevented learned men from forgetting the books of Niceta of Aquileia, and the highly learned clergy of Aquileia would have carefully preserved copies of his writings in their archives and handed them down to posterity.

Third, Zabeus turns to the style of Blessed Niceta’s *Explanation of the Creed*. He asserts that this style proves that Niceta could not have been its author, since the style is polished, elegant, and Latin, and therefore requires extensive practice in writing and an extensive knowledge of the Latin language [Col. 1008D]. Such knowledge, he says, cannot be attributed to Niceta of Aquileia, for, according to Dandulus, Niceta was Greek by origin rather than Aquileian, as our own John Joseph Lirutus judges. Lirutus, however, relies on arguments that do not establish certainty.

Finally, as a fourth argument by which Zabeus denies Niceta of Aquileia practice in writing, he observes that, if we pay attention to the letter addressed to Niceta by Saint Leo the pope, Niceta himself was sparing even in writing. When he wanted to ask the supreme pontiff what he ought to do in extremely difficult circumstances, he did not send a letter, as we know other bishops commonly did; instead, he used the voice of Adeodatus, a deacon of the Roman Church, as is clear from the very opening of Saint Leo’s letter to him. Just as it is certain, he says, that Niceta of Aquileia did not obtain this letter from Saint Leo by a written request of his own, so it is equally certain that no trace survives of a written reply by Niceta to that same letter [Col. 1009A].

After this, Zabeus concludes as follows:

> “How, then, shall we affirm that the man who did not write even to the supreme pastor of the Church when necessity itself urged him, but used another’s voice, personally did and wrote those things which his predecessors entrusted to the industry of others?”

This is the whole of Zabeus’s second observation. I have chosen to divide it into four parts so that, once each has been examined separately, the reply may become clearer.

Let us therefore take up the first part. Zabeus certainly asserted far too confidently that the Aquileian bishops were not accustomed personally to deliver the explanation of the Creed to catechumens, relying solely on what Rufinus reports about himself—even if he were to admit no explanation of the Creed having been given to Rufinus. Who would dare infer the discipline of a particular Church from one simple and isolated fact, especially a discipline entirely unlike that of the other Churches situated around it, as the discipline Zabeus proposes would be, as we shall soon explain?

[Col. 1009B] How completely unsuitable Rufinus’s experience is as a basis for extracting from it the custom which Zabeus wishes to attribute to the Church of Aquileia is plainly apparent from the very facts about Rufinus brought to light by the distinguished De Rubeis. In his dissertation on Rufinus, chapter 2, De Rubeis examines these same words from Rufinus quoted by Zabeus and investigates the year in which Rufinus was regenerated through baptism at Aquileia. Against Fontanini, who had previously examined the same argument, De Rubeis establishes two points: Rufinus received baptism at Aquileia not in the year 371 but rather in 372; and he received it not from Valerian, then bishop of Aquileia, but from Chromatius, then presbyter of that Church, as is also easy to understand from Rufinus’s own words.

Inquiring why Rufinus received baptism from the presbyter Chromatius rather than from Bishop Valerian, whose proper duty it would in fact have been to confer baptism on an adult man according to the discipline of that period, De Rubeis first observes:

> “The customs of that age did not forbid baptism to be conferred by presbyters, either when the bishop was absent or when, for other reasons, the bishop had granted presbyters the authority to perform that duty.”

He then adds that perhaps [Col. 1009C] “the most holy Valerian was absent from Aquileia at that time, since he was devoting all his efforts to opposing Auxentius of Milan and the Arians. He also took part in the Roman synod celebrated under Pope Damasus, which some assign to the year 371, while others, with more probable conjecture, assign it to the following year, 372, in which we believe Rufinus received baptism. … The synodal letter of the Roman council, which is counted as the second under Damasus, begins: ‘Damasus, Valerianus,’ and so forth.”

There is therefore no reason for Zabeus to infer from Rufinus’s experience that Aquileian bishops were not accustomed personally to deliver the explanation of the Creed to catechumens. Valerian was probably absent from Aquileia at that time, either because of the Arian controversy or, more likely, because of the Roman council under Damasus. What took place without the bishop at Rufinus’s baptism should therefore not be said to have taken place because of a custom of that Church, but only accidentally, because the bishop was absent or prevented for some other reason.

But if from this fact about Rufinus we infer that Aquileian bishops were not accustomed personally to confer the explanation of the Creed on catechumens, why should we not similarly conjecture that, in the same age, Aquileian bishops were not accustomed personally to confer baptism either? Let Zabeus see where this excessively easy method of conjecturing from a single fact, considered in isolation and illuminated by no explanation of either the actual or probable circumstances, leads us [Col. 1009D].

Was it therefore the presbyter Chromatius who, on that occasion, delivered the explanation of the Creed to Rufinus [151] in place of the absent or impeded Bishop Valerian? This certainly seems consonant with reason: the presbyter named by Rufinus would have performed this task in place of the bishop, rather than the archdeacon or the deacon, whom Rufinus likewise mentions.

But since Rufinus writes of Eusebius, then a deacon, that “he was my father and teacher of the Creed and of the faith,” Zabeus probably judged [Col. 1010A] that Eusebius had delivered the explanation of the Creed to Rufinus. For this reason, and because he was a deacon, Zabeus also believed that Eusebius was one of those who, in the Church of Aquileia, delivered the exposition of the Creed to catechumens before baptism in place of the bishop.

Here, however, with all due respect to so eminent a man, I would say that private and public explanations of the Creed, domestic and solemn ones, must by no means be confused. One kind took place within the domestic walls of those who were to be enlightened, or in buildings of the Church separated from the church proper; the other took place in the church before the people, or in baptisteries near the church. Nor should catechumens in general be confused with the *competentes*: the former were those who had enrolled themselves under the name of the Christian faith but were still far from receiving baptism; the latter were those who were soon to be washed in the sacred waters. To the former only the principal elements of the Christian faith were entrusted; to the latter alone the Creed was delivered, and they were also required to recite it on appointed days before they were admitted to baptism.

From this it is evident that, in those early times, it may not have been possible for the bishop alone to perform all these tasks when there was a large number of people to be baptized and adults came from every direction to receive baptism—even if the bishop had wished to devote himself to that one task. For this reason, lower-ranking clerics, and especially deacons, were chosen in every Church, as is well established and abundantly demonstrated by writers on such matters. Private instruction was entrusted to them, whether of catechumens or of the *competentes*. They taught the former the first rudiments of the faith, so that, once sufficiently instructed, they might be admitted into the number of the *competentes*. To the latter the Creed was entrusted, and they recited it on appointed days, so that at last they might be fit for the saving bath [Col. 1010B].

With respect to the Creed, let me touch here on something that will have to be discussed more fully in its proper place. Who does not know that it was customarily delivered to the *competentes* orally and recited by them orally, without any assistance from writing? Consequently, the sustained labor, constant effort, and frequent repetition of those clerics were necessary, especially for those who did not possess a strong memory or were not particularly quick-witted.

[Col. 1010C] This private and laborious instruction, then, whether of catechumens or of *competentes*, which was performed by lower-ranking clerics, must be distinguished from the instruction that was later given, especially to the *competentes*, by the bishop in a public place. To that instruction they had to come already sufficiently instructed in the words and to some extent also in the meaning, so that they could profit from it.

Rufinus himself speaks of the first, private instruction that he had received from the deacon Eusebius before baptism when he said of that same Eusebius that “he was my father and teacher of the Creed and of the faith.” As for the word “father,” I agree with the distinguished De Rubeis, in the passage cited, that here it signifies a sponsor, guarantor, and one who received the candidate into the baptismal rite. Eusebius the deacon must have been this to Rufinus in the saving bath, according to the rites of that period, after having instructed him in the faith and the Creed.

But since Rufinus notes that he had in the deacon Eusebius a teacher of the Creed and of the faith, and thus not without reason distinguishes the Creed from the faith [Col. 1010D], why should he not have wished in this way to distinguish his two conditions before baptism: first, that of a simple catechumen, and afterward that of a *competens*? In both conditions he had a teacher or instructor in the monastery at Aquileia where he was living, namely the deacon Eusebius: during his catechumenate, a teacher of the faith with respect to the first rudiments of Christian faith; and, when he had become a *competens*, a teacher of the Creed, which was delivered only to *competentes* who were approaching baptism.

This may be conjectured from Rufinus’s words and from the discipline prevailing in that same period, which plainly does not seem to have been foreign to the Church of Aquileia.

But what shall we now say concerning the public and solemn explanation of the Creed which bishops customarily gave to the *competentes* preparing for baptism, whether in the church or in the baptisteries? No mention of this appears in the monuments of the ancient centuries of Aquileia. From this absence Zabeus asserted that Aquileian bishops were not accustomed personally to deliver the explanation of the Creed to catechumens [Col. 1011A].

To omit many examples of such solemn explanations of the Creed given by bishops that I could produce from the Eastern Church, and many others furnished by the Western Church from the numerous regions where this same discipline once prevailed, it will be enough to recall two or three from Churches situated near Aquileia or not far distant from it. From these examples it will be evident how much, or rather how extreme, force would be required to assert that the Aquileian bishops—surrounded by the discipline of all the other Churches—were not accustomed personally to deliver the explanation of the Creed to catechumens, or rather to *competentes*.

Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan, certainly lived in the very age of Valerian and Chromatius of Aquileia, with whom he also had a certain relationship, indeed something like a spiritual kinship, because of the episcopal ordination they had given and received according to the ancient custom of those two Churches, a matter mentioned elsewhere. Saint Ambrose, I say, bears most explicit testimony about himself in his letter to his sister Marcellina, which is letter 20 in the latest Venetian edition of his works. There he says: [Col. 1011B]

> “On the following day, which was Sunday, after the reading and the sermon, when the catechumens had been dismissed, I delivered the Creed to certain *competentes* in the baptisteries of the basilica.”

The bishops of Milan, therefore, were accustomed personally to deliver the Creed—or the explanation of the Creed—to the *competentes*. Ambrose writes of the matter in such a way that there can be no doubt that he is both recalling his own action and asserting an episcopal duty confirmed by the custom of his Church.

But let us now approach the very age of our Niceta and examine the episcopal explanations of the Creed that still survive, witnesses to the discipline prevailing in that same period in the Churches whose bishops were the authors of those explanations.

Several sermons of Saint Peter Chrysologus, bishop of Ravenna, whom we have mentioned elsewhere, survive [Col. 1011C] concerning the Apostles’ Creed for the instruction of the *competentes*. They may be seen in the edition of Sebastianus Paulus, where they are presented one after another. There one may also see several sermons of the same bishop on the Lord’s Prayer, likewise addressed to the *competentes*, to whom that prayer, together with the Creed, was delivered to be learned and recited.

Saint Maximus, bishop of Turin, about whom we have presented other material elsewhere, also has a distinguished sermon on the Creed addressed to the *competentes*. It is entitled a homily, and in the latest Roman edition of his works it is numbered 83, under the title *On the Delivery of the Creed*, or, in other copies, *On the Explanation of the Creed*, or even *On the Delivery of the Creed, on Its Explanation* [153].

What follows, then? Since the Church of Milan, the Church of Ravenna, and the Church of Turin present us with bishops personally delivering the explanation of the Creed to the *competentes*, was the Church of Aquileia alone—surrounded, so to speak, by these Churches—one whose bishops were not accustomed personally to deliver the explanation of the Creed to catechumens, as Zabeus believes?

[Col. 1011D] I would also have you observe how far Zabeus departed from the truth when he said, speaking generally, that bishops themselves had occasionally been accustomed in earlier times to perform these duties, and that he knew this was not the custom of all bishops. Even the evidence we have so far produced from this one region of northern Italy—deliberately omitting the testimonies of the other Churches throughout the world—is sufficient to show that in earlier times bishops were accustomed to perform these duties not merely on occasion, but everywhere and commonly, both in accordance with prevailing discipline and as part of their own episcopal office.

Thus, even if some bishops should be found of whom it were certain that they did not perform these duties, it should by no means be said that this happened according to custom. It would have occurred for an entirely different reason, which could have been serious and various according to the character of the persons, places, and times.

[Col. 1012A] To touch also on something from the Church of Aquileia in the fifth century, so that what Zabeus adds may not be left entirely unanswered—namely, that there are no monuments establishing this custom among the Aquileian bishops in that same century—here once again before our eyes is sermon 242 in the Augustinian appendices. As we said earlier, it probably had as its author Augustine, bishop of Aquileia and successor of Saint Chromatius.

The title of this sermon is *On the Creed for the Competentes*. After a complete recitation of the Creed, in which some trace of the distinctive Aquileian formula, already then disappearing, can be seen, each of its articles is also explained individually, as may be observed in the other explanations of the Creed that we possess, including those recently cited, by Saint Peter Chrysologus and Saint Maximus of Turin.

We now come to another part of Zabeus’s second observation, where he says that only those bishops were accustomed personally to deliver the explanation of the Creed to catechumens who were accustomed to speak publicly extemporaneously, or whom the practice of writing had made more ready with the pen [Col. 1012B].

We deny both points to Zabeus, with the same freedom with which he asserts both. For the public delivery of the explanation of the Creed to catechumens, or rather to *competentes*, it was not necessary that a person be accustomed to speak publicly extemporaneously, nor that practice in writing had made his pen more ready.

Of all the public speeches by which bishops performed the duties of their office, none was more frequent in subject matter than the explanation of the Creed, and certainly none was easier. There was no other in which they had to labor less with memory, effort, talent, or study. Thus, even if a bishop were found who was unequal to public addresses and homilies, either because he could not speak extemporaneously or because he had little practice in writing, there could certainly have been no one who, for these reasons, could properly be judged unequal to giving explanations of the Creed to catechumens or *competentes*.

Whoever glances even hastily at the explanations of the Creed that we possess, or merely at those that we ourselves have cited, will easily understand that the style varies according to place and time, and that the material is not arranged in precisely the same way in every instance: one point is treated more briefly in one place, another more fully elsewhere [Col. 1012C]. Nevertheless, the same order of subjects is present everywhere—not deliberately devised or artistically invented, but derived from the very sequence of the articles of the Creed. The same doctrines of faith, the same mysteries of religion, and everywhere the same explanations of those mysteries and doctrines are found.

Accordingly, no bishop whose memory was weak, or who lacked practice in extemporaneous speaking or writing, could rightly be judged unfit to perform this duty. The matter is of such a kind that we need not linger over it any longer.

What, then, does Zabeus add? He says that nothing of this kind can be said about Blessed Niceta of Aquileia: neither that public extemporaneous speaking was familiar to him nor that he had a ready pen through practice in writing, because, as Henschenius says, there are no clear and distinguished testimonies to his learning [Col. 1012D]. Even if this were true and established, it would not follow that Niceta of Aquileia could not be the author of that *Explanation of the Creed for the Competentes* which bears his name, and therefore that the Niceta mentioned by Gennadius was not Niceta, bishop of Aquileia.

What more does Zabeus add? He says that, if this Niceta had written anything, Gennadius’s book would have prevented the learned from forgetting Niceta’s books. Yet there are, in fact, clear and distinguished testimonies to this Niceta, and Gennadius mentions them in his book under the name of Niceta, bishop of the city of Romatiana, as has been expressly explained and demonstrated in the preceding chapters.

As for Zabeus’s further statement concerning the clergy of Aquileia—that they would carefully have preserved copies of Niceta’s writings in their archives and handed them down to posterity if he had really left anything in writing—this shows that, when Zabeus made these observations, he did not have before his eyes [Col. 1013A] all the misfortunes to which the Church of Aquileia in particular was exposed even after Niceta’s death, nor all the calamities that the whole world experienced from the fifth century down to our own time. These caused an almost immeasurable number of ancient works to perish everywhere, with the result that among the works of authors whose memory survives there are perhaps more writings desired by scholars than those that are acknowledged to exist.

Yet perhaps the clergy of Aquileia did preserve the writings of Niceta, their bishop, for the benefit of posterity. Of these, however, only two have been made publicly known: one recently discovered at Rome and bearing the name of Niceta of Aquileia himself; the other known for a much longer time and likewise attributed by scholars to Niceta of Gennadius, besides certain fragments that have been discovered only very recently.

Who, then, would dare deny that all these works originally came from the Church of Aquileia, where they originated—whether they were circulated by Niceta himself or, after him, reproduced by the Aquileian clergy—and were thus brought out [Col. 1013B] from the very archives where the original manuscripts were preserved?

In the third place, in his second observation concerning the style of the *Explanation of the Creed* of blessed Nicetas, Zabeus turns to the matter of style. He says that this style sufficiently proves that Nicetas of Aquileia was not the author of that *Explanation*, since the style is polished, refined, and Latin—a style requiring very extensive practice in writing and the greatest knowledge of the Latin language. Such knowledge, he maintains, certainly cannot be granted to Nicetas of Aquileia, who, according to Dandulus, was rather Greek by origin than Aquileian, as Lirutus holds. Anyone possessing sound judgment, however, will certainly judge the style of this *Explanation* to be polished, refined, and Latin. What follows from this? It may therefore be argued that the Nicetas who was the author of this *Explanation* was Aquileian rather than Dacian.

We know from Paulinus himself that the Dacian Nicetas, the friend of Saint Paulinus of Nola, was a Dardanian, and that his homeland lay not far from Scupi, in Dardania itself, which constituted part of new Dacia on this side of the Danube. No one will deny that the Greek language formerly prevailed in Dardania, indeed that it was the indigenous language. It also seems certain that in the time of the Dacian Nicetas both Greek and Latin were in use there.

The Roman colonies summoned from Dacia beyond the Danube by the emperor Aurelian and settled in new Dacia—and consequently also in Dardania—introduced Latin there. It is extremely probable that they transmitted that language to their descendants. That Greek likewise continued there among the ancient inhabitants of the region cannot be doubted; and thus Greek and Latin were used equally in the same places.

But what was the situation in the two Moesias, Upper and Lower—parts of both of which, with their outermost portions removed where they touched one another, principally constituted Cisdanubian Dacia along the right bank of the Danube, as we saw in the second chapter from ancient monuments? The most learned canon Mazochius, in volume III of the *Neapolitan Calendar*, p. 663, concluded from the coins of both regions that Lower Moesia used Greek, just as Upper Moesia used Latin. He adds:

> “As far as I have been able to observe, I find coins bearing Greek inscriptions above all from the famous cities of Marcianopolis, and also from Nicopolis, Istrus, Tomi, Callatis, and Serdica, which are cities of Lower Moesia; nor have I seen any Latin coins from that region. By contrast, the coins of Naissus and Pincum, which are in Upper Moesia, bear Latin inscriptions.”

If this is so, then not only in Dardania, the homeland of the Dacian Nicetas, but also in those parts of the two Moesias—Upper and Lower—from which, together with Dardania, Cisdanubian Dacia was constituted, both languages, Greek and Latin, prevailed during the lifetime of the Dacian Nicetas. I think this should also be understood in the sense that both languages prevailed equally in those border regions on either side, owing to the condition of neighboring territories united by every kind of bond, especially political and natural. For this is what happens: the language of one region, throughout at least some area shared by both places, becomes also in some sense the language of the other, so far as ordinary speech is concerned, although each language remains proper and distinctive to its own region.

What, however, occurs when two languages prevail equally in one and the same region, owing to the very disposition and character, so to speak, of its inhabitants? Neither language remains perfectly pure and undefiled; neither is wholly free from foreign influence, nor immune to the gradual and corrupt admixture of the other—not necessarily in vocabulary, but at least in modes of expression and syntax.

If, therefore, the style of the *Explanation of the Creed* of blessed Nicetas is, in Zabeus’s own judgment, polished, refined, and Latin, and thus testifies that its writer possessed the greatest knowledge of the Latin language, how can this *Explanation* so readily be attributed to the Dacian Nicetas, the friend of Saint Paulinus of Nola and, as Zabeus supposes, bishop in this new Dacia, rather than to Nicetas of Aquileia, who flourished in the time of Saint Leo the Great?

This *Explanation of the Creed* can be attributed even less to that Dacian Nicetas, the friend of Saint Paulinus of Nola, if we recall in what Dacia this bishop actually served. It has already been stated, and demonstrated at length—and, unless I am mistaken, sufficiently—in the whole of the second chapter of this discussion, that Paulinus’s Nicetas did not hold the episcopate in new and Roman Dacia situated on this side of the Danube, but in the old barbarian Dacia beyond the Danube. That region contained the Dacians, Getae, Bessi, and Scythians—barbarian peoples—and extended far and wide toward the north. There Nicetas himself was not the bishop of a particular see, but the bishop of that entire immense region of peoples, that is, an apostolic bishop.

What, then, is one to make of the *Explanation of the Creed* being polished, refined, and Latin in the bishop Nicetas who served there? Those barbarian peoples had always recoiled from Roman laws and from Roman customs alike, so long as they remained beyond the left bank of the Danube. Were they so devoted to the Latin language that they needed to hear their bishop speaking in polished, refined, genuinely Latin speech?

Indeed, I would dare to say that those peoples—especially those inhabiting the old Dacia somewhat far from the left bank of the Danube, namely Mediterranean and Alpine Dacia—had, in Nicetas’s time, that is, more than a hundred years after the reign of Aurelian, when they had once again recovered their ancient settlements in full right, not even the slightest knowledge of the Latin language, even if we concede that they had previously known it to some degree. For that reason they then used their native barbarian language. Thus Nicetas the bishop, who had probably come from new Dacia and had been sent there to preach the Gospel because of the suitability of the place, even if he did not entirely lack knowledge of their language, nevertheless had to labor to learn it more fully and to become acquainted with its various dialects individually. He also had constantly to deliver sermons, exhortations, explanations, and other such things in that same barbarian language.

We understand this quite clearly from the poem of Saint Paulinus, poem XVII, addressed to Nicetas as he returned to Dacia, where he says:

> In a mute region of the world, through you  
> the barbarians learn to make Christ resound  
> with a Roman heart.

What is that “mute region of the world” except a region that seemed in some sense mute to the Roman world because of the unfamiliar sound of the barbarian language, wholly inaccessible to Roman ears, resembling the harsh noise often emitted by the mute without any articulation of voice and without distinct expression of meaning?

And when Paulinus adds that the barbarians learned from Nicetas to make Christ resound with a Roman heart—that is, with the mind, feeling, and faith of the Romans—and does not say “with a Roman voice” or “in the Roman language,” this confirms more and more strongly that their language was entirely different from Latin. Therefore the Nicetas mentioned by Gennadius, who wrote the *Explanation of the Creed* for the competentes in polished, refined, Latin speech, was not Nicetas, the instructor of the barbarian peoples in Dacia and the friend of Saint Paulinus of Nola. Rather, he was our Nicetas of Aquileia, who flourished in the time of Saint Leo the Great.

I do not dwell on the difficulty which Zabeus adds from Dandulus’s assertion that Nicetas of Aquileia was Greek by origin. For now it is enough to say that Dandulus may perhaps have inferred from the Greek derivation of the name Nicetas that the Aquileian Nicetas was Greek by origin.

Who, however, prevents us from understanding that this Nicetas was both genuinely Greek by origin, as Dandulus says, and nevertheless Aquileian by nationality, as Lirutus holds? He may have been born at Aquileia to parents or ancestors who came from Greece, and may therefore have been raised and educated at Aquileia, so that he absorbed the native Latin language of the Aquileians as though with his mother’s milk. He could later have cultivated it through use and study, eventually producing the kind of style that, together with Zabeus, we admire in the *Explanation of the Creed*: polished, refined, and Latin. But I shall discuss the origin of this Aquileian Nicetas below, in its proper place.

I come to the fourth part of Zabeus’s other observation. To tell the truth, he might here appear somewhat injurious to the memory of our holy Aquileian bishop Nicetas, were it not that elsewhere we know his mind to have been full of moderation and religious restraint.

Zabeus represents Nicetas of Aquileia as sparing in writing. Even when the needs of his Church pressed urgently upon him, he supposedly avoided the labor of writing a letter to the supreme pastor of the Church and instead used another person’s voice to implore that pastor’s authority. Moreover, after receiving a letter from Saint Leo the Great providing for the needs of his Church—the letter numbered 159 in the Venetian edition of the Ballerini—he supposedly gave no reply.

Thus, in the main, Zabeus accuses our Nicetas of Aquileia, whether deliberately or not, of sluggishness in action, negligence in his pastoral office, and even discourtesy and irreverence toward the Roman Pontiff, in order thereby to prove that he also lacked practice in writing Latin. His purpose is to confirm the proposition he had set himself: namely, that Nicetas was not the author of the *Explanation of the Creed for the Competentes*, since a work so polished, refined, and Latin required extensive practice in writing from anyone who composed it.

To answer these objections as well—although otherwise they might seem not to require an answer—several points must be considered. If we recall the opening lines of the previously cited letter of Saint Pope Leo to Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, we understand that Adeodatus, a deacon of the Apostolic See, had returned to Rome from the Aquileian Church and from Nicetas’s own company and conversation, and had reported Nicetas’s requests to the holy pontiff. But we cannot conclude from this that Adeodatus himself brought with him no writing by Nicetas containing those requests, which he could report to the pontiff.

Indeed, from Saint Pope Leo’s letter itself we can, unless I am mistaken, understand clearly enough that the deacon Adeodatus brought with him some written document by Nicetas of Aquileia, from which he reported Nicetas’s requests to Saint Leo. In chapter 1 of that letter to Nicetas, the holy pontiff writes:

> “Since, therefore, you say that certain marriages have been so divided by the calamity of war and by the gravest incursions of the enemy, etc.”

The plural verb *dicatis*—“you say”—when the Roman pontiff was writing to one Nicetas, certainly seems to refer not only to Adeodatus reporting the matter orally, but also to Nicetas himself saying the same thing in some fashion in his written document.

Perhaps what follows is even clearer for demonstrating that our Nicetas committed something to writing and gave it to the Roman deacon Adeodatus, something which Saint Leo had before his eyes while composing that letter to Nicetas. Such, it seems, are the words we read in the same chapter 1:

> “It is rightly apparent that your Charity is uncertain what we ought to determine concerning women who have been joined to other men.”

Saint Leo could have detected this uncertainty of Nicetas only from some writing of Nicetas himself in which Nicetas had expressed that uncertainty in suitable words. This also seems to be confirmed by another expression. For he would not appropriately have said, “your Charity appears to be uncertain,” if he had not read something written by Nicetas on this matter, to which the expression “appears” could properly be applied. In response merely to the deacon Adeodatus’s oral report, the word “appears” would certainly have been less suitably used by Saint Leo.

There are also other points relevant to our case. In chapter 5 of that letter Saint Leo writes:

> “Concerning those Christians who, among the people by whom they had been taken captive, are said to have been defiled by sacrificial foods, we have also thought it necessary to respond to the consultation of your Charity.”

Likewise, in chapter 6:

> “Concerning those matters about which your Love likewise thought that we should be consulted.”

Finally, in chapter 7 he concludes:

> “You shall ensure that this letter of ours, which we have sent in response to the consultation of your Fraternity, reaches all your brother bishops and fellow provincials.”

Since Saint Pope Leo so frequently asserts in his reply that Nicetas of Aquileia had consulted him, it seems less probable that no written document of this consultation by Nicetas himself existed—one which the holy pontiff had before him when he was replying.

Furthermore, if we recall the subject of Bishop Nicetas’s consultations, which was certainly of the greatest gravity—namely, the marriages of those who returned from captivity and sought to reclaim their own wives, who had meanwhile married other men; and the case of those who, while in captivity, had eaten sacrificial foods or had been compelled to undergo baptism again—it can scarcely be believed that Nicetas of Aquileia entrusted such matters merely to the memory of the deacon Adeodatus and did not explain them in some written document of his own, so that they might become known to the pontiff clearly and distinctly, with all the circumstances and the sequence of events.
