If Nicetas of Aquileia had in fact been so negligent, it could scarcely be believed that Saint Leo the Great—who, as his letters show, was so attentive in censuring the negligence of priests—would not have admonished our Nicetas in this very letter to provide more carefully and diligently, at least in the future, for himself and his Church.

“But other bishops,” Zabeus insists, “consulted the Apostolic See in doubtful matters belonging to their own office by sending letters. Why did Nicetas of Aquileia not do the same?”

But if Nicetas set out his consultations to the supreme pontiff in some written document, as seems to have been the case, what difference does it make if he did not send him a separate letter? There was, in fact, a reason why Nicetas did not send a separate letter—a reason that scarcely existed for any other bishop. Adeodatus, a deacon of the Roman Church, was present. He had probably been sent to Aquileia by the holy pontiff himself, or perhaps had even been requested by Bishop Nicetas himself, so that he might learn the condition of that Church at first hand and report it as an eyewitness to the Apostolic See.

What need was there of a letter when the person who represented the recipient of the letter was present? With Adeodatus present, nothing else was needed except some written work setting out the condition of the Aquileian Church and the gravity of the circumstances, to be submitted to apostolic authority. It is probable that Nicetas did this, and no one could have done it more accurately than Nicetas himself.

But why, at least, did Nicetas not reply to the letter of Saint Leo the Great? Yet Saint Leo’s letter itself was a response to Nicetas’s consultations, which had probably been written out by him, as we have seen. What need, then, was there for a response to a response, without some new necessity for writing?

Let this suffice concerning the fourth part of Zabeus’s second observation. These considerations also amply suffice to clear Nicetas of Aquileia from the accusations brought against him.

Zabeus begins his third observation, drawn from the deeper aspects of the case, with number 3 of the same second part of his dissertation, and continues it through number 11. The whole discussion concerns the formula of the Apostles’ Creed formerly used among the Aquileians, distinguished by three unusual additions and by another variation.

Since Zabeus does not find this formula in precisely the same form in the *Explanation of the Creed* of Bishop Nicetas, he consequently denies that *Explanation* to Nicetas of Aquileia. He does so at considerable length, and from his discussion we understand that this is one of the principal arguments of his case.

We answered this argument expressly in the fourth chapter of our discussion. There we also asserted, on the basis of the clear indications of the ancient Aquileian formula found in this very *Explanation of the Creed* of Bishop Nicetas, that the work belongs to Nicetas of Aquileia. For that reason we refrain here from any further investigation of the matter, which was discussed there sufficiently and more than sufficiently.

In numbers 12 and 13, Zabeus proposes to resolve objections which he anticipates might be raised against him, namely, objections based on the Latin language in which Nicetas’s *Explanation of the Creed* was written and on the cultivated style of that *Explanation*.

These are objections to which Zabeus’s entire response appears inadequate. We too have just shown that cultivation of style in Latin eloquence could not have existed among the Dacians on this side of the Danube in the time of the Dacian Nicetas, because Greek and Latin had long coexisted in one and the same province. Still less could refined Latin speech have had a place in barbarian Dacia beyond the Danube, where that Dacian Nicetas actually held the episcopate.

To add something here, as the occasion requires, in confirmation of what was said above: Zabeus opposes to us the action of Bishop Ulfilas, who, in the fourth century, translated the four Gospels into the language of his Goths or Getae. These peoples had obtained, by the concession of the emperor Valens, a part of Moesia on this side of the Danube and also part of Thrace, as is known from history. The Gospels were published at Dordaci from a precious codex in 1665 by Francis Junius and Thomas Marshall.

This action, whatever Zabeus may say, proves that the Latin language at that time was not the language in which religion could be preached to barbarian peoples, even to those who had crossed the Danube and entered Roman territory.

What, then, should we say if we cross the Danube, where the episcopal care of the Dacian Nicetas extended far and wide, even through the northern regions toward the Riphaean lands, places to which Roman footsteps had never reached? There the barbarian peoples—including those settled on the left bank of the Danube—had long remained on their own soil and separated from Roman society.

Here, however, we must also turn our attention to the fate of the Latin language after barbarian forces from the regions beyond the Danube invaded the Roman Empire on every side and changed the face of the world in the fifth and sixth centuries.

Without doubt those peoples found the Roman world speaking Latin everywhere, especially in its western regions. If we suppose that those peoples were not ignorant of Latin speech, so that in the fourth and fifth centuries the Dacians and Getae, Bessi and Scythians could everywhere understand Bishop Nicetas speaking polished Latin in their own regions, could in some manner cast off their barbarism at his voice, and could approach the profession of the true religion, why did they not immediately learn the Latin language, which dominated so widely throughout the West and especially in Italy, where it had its native soil and principal seat?

Why, rather, did they everywhere infect Latin, which was in such broad use, with the barbarism of their own speech, so that, because of those very peoples, the Latin language gradually ceased to be common everywhere and was finally devoted only to sacred matters and confined within the narrow limits of the schools? Why was it, as though compelled, to give birth to a new form of language for general use—the kind we now speak in Italy and the kind we know to be used in Gaul and Spain?

But let us proceed to Zabeus’s other observations.

Zabeus continues to investigate the deeper issues. In number 14 he says that the following point must be noted above all: in the *Explanation of the Creed* of blessed Nicetas there is discussion of idolatry and especially of the heresies of the Arians, Marcionites, Cataphrygians, and Manichaeans.

“Moreover,” he says, “these absurdities ought to have been absent from the highly cultivated province of Aquileia at that time, as we indicated above; whereas they suited the character of barbarous and savage nations”—that is, the character of those Dacians, as he supposes, who on this side of the Danube were subject to the bishop of Remesiana.

For the moment it is useful once again to point out that Zabeus wrongly calls those peoples “barbarous and savage” who in Nicetas’s time inhabited the right bank of the Danube, especially Dardania, or new Mediterranean Dacia, where, according to Zabeus, the Dacian Nicetas’s episcopate was situated.

Throughout his dissertation Zabeus frequently confuses the Roman Dacians with the barbarians, and consequently Cisdanubian Dacia with Transdanubian Dacia. This confusion was necessarily required by the opinion he had adopted: that the Dacian Nicetas, the friend of Saint Paulinus of Nola, was bishop of the city of Remesiana, situated in Roman Dacia.

For since it is clear from Saint Paulinus that the peoples subject to his friend blessed Bishop Nicetas were genuinely barbarous and savage, those peoples situated on this side of the Danube and settled in Dardania, or new Mediterranean Dacia, had unquestionably also to be called barbarous and savage within the imagined episcopate of Nicetas of Remesiana.

But Zabeus himself, who is compelled to assert against the clear testimony of Paulinus of Nola that Nicetas was not the bishop who first introduced the religion of Christ into Dacia—as he openly states in the second note to the first part of his dissertation—also admits and proves there that, already from the time of the Council of Nicaea, several bishoprics had been established in that same Dacia, namely in Dardania and also in Moesia, with their bishops under the metropolitan see of Sardica. This is plainly established by ecclesiastical records, and we too demonstrated it at length in the second chapter of this dissertation.

How, then, did he fail to understand that the peoples governed by Nicetas, bishop of Remesiana in Roman Dacia, could be called barbarous and savage only improperly and unjustly?

But let us now approach his new observation.

Nothing need be added here concerning idolatry to what we said at the beginning of this chapter, where we showed that the bishops of Aquileia themselves genuinely had reason to struggle against the remnants of idolatry even in the fifth century.

What shall we say now about the heresies of the Arians, Marcionites, Cataphrygians, and Manichaeans? We must briefly observe that there was scarcely any heresy against which the bishop of Aquileia at that time would not have had to fortify his faithful, whether he sat at Aquileia or elsewhere in his diocese, even at the port of Romatinum, as we suppose happened more than once.

For it is known from history that at that time, and long before, people of every religion and every error arrived from the whole East—from Greece, Asia, the Pontus Euxinus, Egypt, and also from other parts of the world—for purposes of commerce. They came to the shores of maritime Venetia and especially to Aquileia, where many even maintained permanent residence, since it was a most prosperous emporium and, for purposes of trade, a kind of center of union for the whole world, both Western and Eastern.

On this subject consult the distinguished Filiasi, *Historical Memoirs of the Early and Later Venetians*, volume II, chapter 22, where he treats the matter learnedly and at length.

To confirm that this was truly the situation of the Aquileian bishops, we have the Aquileian Church’s presbyter Rufinus, who in his frequently cited *Commentary on the Apostles’ Creed* bears remarkable witness concerning the Aquileian Church with respect to heresies—a matter for which scarcely any other example remains in the whole Western Church.

He presents us with the additions which the ancient bishops of the Aquileian Church, whom he there calls our ancestors, inserted into the Apostles’ Creed in order to confront certain heresies. These heresies had certainly not arisen on Aquileian soil—for no heresy had in fact originated among the Aquileians—but had been brought from afar by foreigners who undoubtedly came to Aquileia for commercial purposes.

Thus, concerning the addition of the two words “invisible” and “impassible” to the first article of the Creed, “I believe in God the Father almighty,” he says that this was done among us—that is, among the Aquileians—to oppose the heresy of the Sabellians, who affirmed that, together with the Son, the Father too had been born and suffered:

> “It must be known,” he says in the cited *Commentary*, section 5, “it must be known that these two expressions, ‘invisible’ and ‘impassible,’ are not found in the Creed of the Roman Church. It is established, however, that among us they were added because of the heresy of Sabellius, that heresy which our people call Patripassianism: namely, the doctrine which says that the Father himself was born from the Virgin and became visible, or affirms that he suffered in the flesh. In order to exclude such impiety concerning the Father, our ancestors seem to have added these words and declared the Father invisible and impassible.”

Likewise, another addition, the word “this,” was included among the Aquileians in the article “the resurrection of the flesh,” in order more openly to reject the heresy of the Valentinians and Manichaeans:

> “For Valentinus,” our Rufinus adds in the same work, section 41, “entirely denies the resurrection of the flesh, and so do the Manichaeans, as we have shown above.”

Therefore he adds in section 43:

> “And for this reason our Church”—that is, the Aquileian Church—“teaches the faith of the Creed with sufficient caution. In the statement handed down by the others, ‘the resurrection of the flesh,’ she has handed it down with one pronoun added: ‘the resurrection of this flesh.’ ‘This,’ unquestionably, which the one who professes it possesses, with the sign of the cross placed upon his forehead, etc.”

Here, then, is what the Aquileian bishops were compelled to do, even before the time of Rufinus, against the absurd errors of the Sabellians and Valentinians. Those errors had certainly arisen far from the Aquileian Church, yet they nevertheless stirred the zeal of the Aquileian bishops because they had begun to be disseminated within their territory by foreigners infected with the same errors, who came from every part of the world to the borders of Aquileia.

There is therefore no reason for Zabeus to deny, on the grounds of official duty, that certain absurd ravings of heretics had a place in the highly cultivated province of Aquileia. It is established that they did have a place there, just as they did elsewhere, and that they had such a place in a manner requiring the Aquileian bishops to fight against them in a distinctive way—namely, by deliberately adding clauses to the Creed of the faith—and to safeguard among their own people the integrity of the Christian profession.

What is surprising if, in the course of time, the Aquileian bishops also encountered other heretics besides the Sabellians and Valentinians, against whom they were compelled to warn their faithful to guard themselves? At the time of Nicetas these may especially have been Arians, Marcionites, Cataphrygians, and Manichaeans.

Rufinus himself explicitly names Arians, Marcionites, and Manichaeans in section 39 of his aforementioned commentary on the Creed, which he wrote for Laurentius, a bishop attached to the Aquileian see, as we indicated above, and at Laurentius’s request for his use. We therefore consider it highly probable that such heretics existed in the Aquileian province at that time, or at least were commonly known there, without our thereby casting any reproach upon that most noble Church.

It was certainly not within that Church’s power either to prevent foreigners infected with these errors from coming to Aquileia and residing in the Aquileian province, or to ensure that their wicked doctrines did not become known in so large and cultivated a city, even at the peril of the faithful.

In the same passage Rufinus also names, together with the heretics mentioned above, the Ebionites and Eunomians. He names the errors of Paul of Samosata and Photinus; he names the schisms of the Donatists and Novatians. And so that we may understand that he did not list all these names of the erring without reason, nor do so merely for the sake of learning or as though to complete his work, but because it was genuinely necessary that in the Aquileian province the faithful be deliberately warned, when occasion arose, against such errors and their teachers, consider how confidently he addresses that bishop Laurentius.

He does not necessarily do so in order to teach Laurentius, but certainly to instruct him concerning the manner in which the Christian people subject to him ought to be taught:

> “Therefore, whoever receives this faith in the Church must not turn aside into the council of vanity, nor enter in with those who do evil. For it is a council of vanity that Marcion promotes . . . It is a council of vanity that Ebion teaches . . . It is a council of vanity that Manichaeus teaches . . . It is a council of vanity that Paul of Samosata and, after him, his successor Photinus asserted . . . It is a council of vanity that Arius and Eunomius taught . . . But it is also a council of vanity that Donatus brought together throughout Africa by accusing the Church of betrayal, and that Novatus stirred up . . . Flee, then, all these gatherings of the wicked. And if there are any who are said to assert that the Son of God, etc. . . . From all these, I say, let the hearing of the faithful turn away, etc.”

What would Rufinus have meant by telling Laurentius to flee from these gatherings of heretics and erring people, and by telling the faithful to turn their hearing away from them, if such people had not existed in the Aquileian province itself, or if their corrupt doctrines had not at least been sufficiently known there?

We do not flee from those who are far from us, nor do we turn our hearing away from speeches which we cannot easily hear.

But let us now consider individually some of the heresies which our Nicetas mentions in his *Explanation*.

Nicetas Gennadius never explicitly indicates the heresy of the Arians by name in the *Explanation of the Creed*, whereas he does in fact name the Marcionites, Cataphrygians, and Manichaeans. Nevertheless, he inculcates the Catholic doctrine concerning the divinity of the Word, as was required, and warns his competentes to guard themselves against those heretics who, under the Christian name, teach that Christ is a creature, as in chapter 9 of the *Explanation*.

These were plainly the Arian heretics, against whose snares those who stood in the rank of the competentes and were learning the Creed had to be fortified.

Why, then, would a fifth-century bishop of Aquileia say nothing against the Arians, after the Aquileian bishops Valerian in the fourth century and Chromatius at the beginning of the fifth had rendered such great service to the Church by suppressing the Arian heresy within the Aquileian territory?

Why would an Aquileian bishop in the fifth century say nothing against Arian errors, when the memory of the famous Council of Aquileia held in 381 was still fresh? At that council the two Arian bishops of Cisdanubian Dacia had been condemned while present—specifically, as Saint Ambrose wrote in letters 11 and 12, from the corner or side of Riparian Dacia and Moesia. I mean those two bishops, Palladius and Secundianus, whom we have mentioned elsewhere.

Why would an Aquileian bishop in the fifth century say nothing against the followers of Arius, when Arianism was still raging everywhere and exercising its power in many places, as history shows?

But we must observe several other matters which will establish and illuminate more clearly what is otherwise sufficiently evident.

We know from history that in the final period of the Roman Empire, especially at the close of the fourth and the beginning of the fifth century, barbarian peoples served for pay in the Roman armies under commanders of their own nation. These were chiefly the Goths, also called Getae by the Romans. They were brought repeatedly from the regions beyond the Danube into Roman territory for various reasons, as we indicated in chapter 2—first especially through the indulgence of the emperor Valens, and afterward through the more extensive concession of Theodosius the Elder. They inhabited the new Dacia Ripensis, as well as a certain part of Lower Moesia and Thrace, on the further condition that they provide military service to the Roman Empire.

These Goths—whether they were those who had long before arrived from the Christian Gothic Church situated between the Tanais and the Tyras rivers [Col. 1021A], or those who had afterward been converted from idolatry to the Christian faith so that they might settle in Roman territory on this side of the Danube, as Valens had imposed by law upon them—these Goths, I say, not long afterward defected in large part from the Catholic Church to Arianism, especially under the influence of the emperor Valens, who vigorously defended the Arian cause, so that, as the fourth century advanced, nearly all became followers of the Arian perfidy.

The Roman armies, however, together with auxiliary barbarian forces—namely, the Goths and the other peoples who had joined themselves to the Goths—invaded the territory of Aquileia and occupied Aquileia itself not once but repeatedly during the fourth and fifth centuries. This happened especially when the emperor Theodosius the Great pursued first the tyrant Maximus and afterward Eugenius, and later when Theodosius the Younger took up arms against the tyrant John, who was captured at Ravenna, brought to Aquileia, and there condemned to death.

What, then, would the bishops of Aquileia not have said against the Arian impiety [Col. 1021B], whose preachers were so often present in the Roman armies in the form of Gothic auxiliary troops? Those Goths, however, stained with Arian perfidy, entered Italy under their commander Alaric not as Roman auxiliaries but as enemies of the Roman Empire, intending to plunder it. They invaded the territory of Aquileia again in the year 400, and again in 409 or 410, when at last they gained possession of Rome itself and enriched themselves with its spoils. Anyone who knows the restless character of the heretics of that period, especially the Arians, and their zeal for propagating their own sect, will easily understand with what vigilance the watchmen of the house of Israel must then have watched—and consequently the bishops of Aquileia as well—lest the poison of false doctrine, strengthened even by the force of victorious arms, spread into the breasts of Catholics.

But as the fifth century advanced, the bishops of Aquileia had increasing occasion and necessity to oppose not only Arianism but also every other heresy requiring attack. As soon as rumor became widespread in the regions of Pannonia that Italy was to be invaded and devastated under Attila’s leadership, swarms gathered from every direction—not so much of barbarian peoples differing from one another in place and name as of the heresies and errors prevailing among those various barbarian groups—so that one might reasonably doubt whether war was being brought against the religion or rather against the material possessions of the Italians, and one could clearly recognize that danger threatened their possessions no less than their religion from that most dreadful preparation.

When the immense barbarian host burst into Italy through the Alpine passes and first brought ruin or utter destruction upon Aquileia, and then upon the other cities of Venetia, Emilia, and Liguria—buildings being burned or plundered, fields being laid waste, and an immense multitude of captives being led away into distant regions—only then did it become apparent that this military incursion had also inflicted a great disaster upon religion, a disaster that could afterward be repaired only by the diligent care of the bishops.

As regards the Church of Aquileia, there is the often-cited letter of Saint Leo the Great to Nicetas of Aquileia, written in the year 458. From it we understand that those Aquileian captives who, after several years, were able to return to their native homes had been tested by the barbarians on religious grounds. Some of them, who had served idolatrous masters, had been polluted by sacrificial food; others, who had fallen under the power of heretical barbarians, had been compelled by fear or led astray by error into repeating baptism.

To say nothing now of idolatry, which held a large part of those barbarian peoples in its grip, who does not see that followers of the Arian cause were among those who either compelled the Aquileian captives, through fear and force, to repeat baptism, or enticed them by persuasive insinuations? Certainly the Arians, even if at the beginning they had not possessed this detestable practice of baptizing again those who had fallen away from the Catholic faith and joined their sect, adopted it from the Eunomians, an offshoot of the Arians themselves. According to Epiphanius, in heresy 76, the Eunomians were accustomed to rebaptize not only Catholics but also Arians themselves, including their own teachers, when they came over to them. This was also the common abuse of the Arians in the time of Augustine, who attacks them for this reason more than once; and Victor of Vita likewise bears witness to this abuse in his *History of the Vandal Persecution*.

After the fall of Aquileia in Attila’s invasion, what was the condition of the Western Empire, for as long as it continued, down to Romulus, called Augustulus—that is, down to the year 476, when even the shadow of the Western Empire disappeared? Did not the supreme power and authority, despite the Roman names of so many emperors who lasted scarcely a day, lie with barbarian men alien to the Catholic confession? Having gained control of the court and relying upon the power of the barbarian armies they commanded, did they not everywhere direct all affairs according to their own will, sometimes even against the wishes of the emperors themselves?

Thus the Roman Western Empire was subject to barbarian domination even before it perished completely through their violence. It perished in the aforesaid year 476, when Odoacer, having led into Italy a new multitude of every kind of barbarian from the most remote regions of Pannonia—Heruli, Turcilingi, Rugians, Scythians, and others—deprived Romulus Augustulus of all power and established a new principality for himself. This principality passed from barbarian to barbarian in uninterrupted succession down to the eighth century.

Meanwhile Nicetas of Aquileia, amid such a collapse of human affairs, such variety among rulers, and such great peril to the rulers themselves, governed his Church and continued his life down to the tenth year of Odoacer’s principate. Odoacer himself, although not hostile to Catholics, was by confession an Arian, as were his Arian countrymen and a large part of those barbarian peoples whom he brought with him into Italy to abolish the Western Roman Empire [Col. 1022B].

What shall I say about the many other columns of barbarian peoples who, having entered into an alliance with one another, flooded into Italy on that occasion? To say nothing of those who still remained devoted to idolatry, about whom there is no reason to inquire here, we certainly do not venture to say anything contrary to probability if we affirm that, besides Arianism, other errors proscribed by Catholic doctrine also flourished among those peoples, especially those which had their authors and propagators in the regions of the East [165]. Such were the errors of the Marcionites, Cataphrygians, and Manichaeans, expressly mentioned by Nicetas Gennadianus in his *Explanation of the Creed*.

Zabeus, however, directly supports our argument when, in numbers 15, 16, 17, and 18, he proves that the errors of the Marcionites, Cataphrygians, and Manichaeans existed in the barbarian regions of the Dacians on the basis of a certain proximity between the places from which those errors originated and the barbarian peoples of Dacia. He nevertheless maintains that it was Cisdanubian Dacia, which certainly was not barbarian, as was stated elsewhere. Moreover, with respect to the Marcionites, who differed from the Catholic faith in many respects, he wished to identify one of the errors of the Marcionites rather than the Eutychian error, in those matters which Nicetas Gennadianus in the *Explanation of the Creed* presents so openly against Eutyches himself, as we expressly demonstrated above in chapter 3.

If, then, among the barbarian Dacians the errors of the Marcionites, Cataphrygians, and Manichaeans existed in those times, as Zabeus himself testifies—errors suited, as he had previously maintained, more to the character of barbarian than of civilized peoples—those barbarian peoples undoubtedly also brought these errors with them into Italy, even in the course of their immense invasion under Odoacer. Consequently the Italian bishops could not have lacked the opportunity to warn their faithful, and especially those preparing for baptism, to guard themselves not only against these errors but also against their gatherings and their very association.

But what if we add that those barbarians who invaded Italy under Odoacer, stained by so many errors, were at that time not guests and newcomers, as they had previously been, but had already become citizens and inhabitants from the first years of Odoacer’s principate? According to Procopius, *Gothic War*, book 1, chapter 1, they had been given, as a reward for their victories, a third part of the lands of Italy everywhere, taken from their former owners [Col. 1023A].

The province of Aquileia perhaps had more than other regions of these new inhabitants and owners of a third part of the land. It had shortly before suffered such a great collapse of its affairs under Attila’s leadership, and had consequently endured this further and most serious calamity: the reduction of its former citizens and inhabitants. Its population could therefore be supplied without great difficulty by barbarian families who were introduced into possession of a third, and perhaps even a larger part, of the territory of Aquileia.

What, then, would the bishop of Aquileia not have said even against the Marcionites, Cataphrygians, and Manichaeans who might be present here and there in these new barbarian settlements, necessarily joined in human affairs with the Catholics themselves, to the serious danger of their corruption—both because of the weakness of human nature and because of the perverse character of all errors, by which truth is more often and more easily corrupted by them than errors are suppressed by truth, unless the unceasing vigilance of pastors remains constantly active [Col. 1023B]?

But with regard specifically to the Manichaeans and Manichaeism, Zabeus himself, in the previously cited number 18, does not deny that in the age of Saint Leo the Great—and therefore even before Odoacer’s invasion, indeed before the final old age of the Roman Empire in the West—there were many Manichaeans in Italy. For that reason they may not have been from the barbarian group along the Danube. They had been discovered at Rome itself through the zeal and diligence of the holy pontiff and compelled to leave, with the laws of the emperors Theodosius and Valentinian supporting the action; those laws had been issued through the care of the same holy pontiff.

The bishops of Italy had therefore long had reason to act and take precautions against the Manichaeans. It should consequently not be doubted that those writings could also have belonged to the Italian bishops in which Manichaeans were discussed. Much more, however, should the zeal of the bishops of Italy have flared up against the Manichaeans after Saint Leo the Great, in the year 444, sent letters to all the bishops established throughout the provinces of Italy and specifically summoned them to share his vigilance against the sacrilegious followers of this perversity. Some of them, as he himself said, had fled from Rome, and there was reason to fear that, to the danger of their own flocks, they would find opportunities to hide themselves here and there [Col. 1023C].

What, then, was the Manichaean heresy of that time against which the zeal of Saint Leo the Great burned so earnestly? Let the holy pontiff himself be heard. In sermon 16, *On the Fast of the Tenth Month* (V), chapter 3, he spoke as follows:

> “By this one’s [that is, the devil’s] art Basilides is skilled; by this one’s cunning Marcion acts; under this guide Sabellius proceeds; under this director Photinus is overthrown; to this one’s power Arius is enslaved; to this one’s spirit Eunomius is subject. Finally, the whole host of such beasts, under this ruler, departed from the unity of the Church; under this teacher, it deviated from the truth. But although he holds a many-formed dominion over all perversities, he built his citadel in the madness of the Manichaeans and found among them an exceedingly broad court in which he might display himself more exultantly. There he possessed, in general, not merely the appearance of one perversity but a mixture of all errors and impieties together” [Col. 1023D].

Here, then, is the extent of the impiety of the Manichaeans and Manichaeism, which embraced, as it were, all the errors of the other heretics. The bishops of Italy therefore ought at that time to have fought especially and more vigorously against this sect.

There is consequently no doubt that the previously cited letter of Saint Leo to all the bishops established throughout the provinces of Italy—which is the seventh letter in the Venetian edition of the Ballerini—reached, in that same year 444, the metropolitan bishop of Aquileia, who was then either Maximus or Januarius. Nor is there any doubt that that bishop of Aquileia took every possible care to discover any Manichaeans who had secretly crept in and to expel them from the territory of Aquileia, employing the authority of the imperial laws and obtaining the assistance of those laws, which declared that the Manichaeans were to be driven from the entire world, in accordance also with the enactments of all earlier emperors.

Since Saint Leo’s exhortatory letter to the bishops of Italy against the Manichaeans, written in the year 444, was famous and circulated throughout all Italy, and since the law of the emperors Theodosius and Valentinian was promulgated in the same or the following year and became no less widely known, what is surprising if, ten, fifteen, or even twenty years later, Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, named the Manichaeans together with the other heretics as people to be avoided, even if perhaps no one of them then remained in Italy?

Yet who could deny that Manichaeans again infiltrated Italy at that time, amid such a disturbed condition of all affairs—when the laws were silent, barbarians ruled everywhere, and everything was permitted to everyone that would have been entirely forbidden in a peaceful state? These are precisely the times, as is sufficiently clear, in which wicked men, bursting forth from the hiding places where they had previously lurked, raise themselves insolently and shamelessly; and those who had formerly been accustomed to live in fear now boldly strive everywhere to rule through corrupt doctrines and depraved morals [Col. 1024A].

There is therefore no reason for Zabeus to evade this objection by briefly asserting that we cannot affirm that Manichaeans were present at Aquileia. Although there are no monuments available by which we can affirm it, there certainly are no contrary ones by which we can deny it. Meanwhile, what we have brought forward is sufficient for us to judge that Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, could in his own time have named the Manichaeans as people to be avoided, even if they had perhaps never existed in his province or diocese.

But Zabeus proceeds further in the same number 18. While he treats the mention of the Manichaeans in that little work, which he attributes to Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, as superfluous, he argues on the other hand that the Pelagians are not mentioned there. In his view this omission certainly ought not to have occurred in the work of Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, because in reality the Pelagian heresy had followers at that time in the province of Aquileia among presbyters, deacons, and clerics of various orders [Col. 1024C], as appears from the letter of Saint Leo the pope addressed to the bishop of Aquileia, which is the first in the cited edition of the Ballerini.

To satisfy this objection as well—an objection of that most distinguished man, and the last of the deeper arguments he draws from the case—some points must be noted from the preliminary notice of the same Ballerini to the first and second letters of that holy pontiff, as well as from chapter 14 of the *Aquileian Monuments* by our most learned De Rubeis.

It cannot be denied that Pelagian errors entered the province of Aquileia perhaps from the beginning of the fifth century, and that from then onward they had followers there among members of the ecclesiastical order, among whom this heresy chiefly found easier access. For it is established among scholars, under the leadership of Cardinal Norisius, that the little book of the Faith, teeming with Pelagian chaff, which Sirmond transcribed from a manuscript codex at Verona, which Garnerius published in his edition of Marius Mercator, and which the Benedictines of Saint Maur subsequently published again in the Augustinian appendices—that is, in the appendix to volume 10 of the Paris folio edition—belonged to men of the ecclesiastical order in the province of Aquileia under Augustine, the metropolitan bishop of Aquileia and successor of Chromatius, who flourished under the Roman pontiffs Innocent I and Zosimus [Col. 1024D].

Zosimus, the Roman pontiff, was the one who in the year 418 published that celebrated dogmatic letter of his against the errors of Pelagius and Coelestius, called the *Tractoria* or *Tractatory Letter*. He sent it throughout the entire world so that it might be confirmed by the signatures of all the bishops and the universal agreement of the Church in condemning the Pelagian doctrines might become evident.

Zosimus’s *Tractoria* therefore undoubtedly reached Augustine, bishop of Aquileia and, as Norisius calls him, primate of Venetia, Istria, both Noricums, and Raetia Prima. As seems most probable, Augustine, in the performance of his office, sent the *Tractoria* to his provincial bishops so that it might be confirmed by the signatures of each of them and of the presbyters. From some of those men infected with the Pelagian taint he received the aforesaid little book, from which he clearly understood both that they had refused to sign Zosimus’s *Tractoria* and that they had dared to appeal to a plenary synod [Col. 1025A].

It is uncertain who those men were, and equally uncertain whether they were presbyters or whether some bishops were also included—perhaps some of the eighteen who, under the leadership of Julian of Eclanum, alone in the whole Church refused to sign the *Tractoria*. Nevertheless, after the judgment of so many learned men, it seems entirely certain that they belonged to the province of Aquileia and were also of the priestly order; the metropolitan bishop, by order of Pope Zosimus, had required their signatures.

What happened after this? There is the previously cited letter of Saint Leo the pope addressed to the bishop of Aquileia and assigned to the year 442. In it he says that, from the report of Septimus or Septimius, who was bishop of Altinum [Col. 1025B] in the province of Aquileia, he had learned with indignation that certain presbyters, deacons, and clerics of various orders whom the Pelagian or Coelestian heresy had involved had been admitted in the province of Aquileia to Catholic communion without any condemnation of their own error being required of them. Because pastoral watchfulness had been excessively asleep, wolves covered with sheep’s clothing had entered the Lord’s fold without laying aside their bestial dispositions.

Therefore he commands the metropolitan bishop of Aquileia, after convening a synod of the provincial bishops, to compel all—whether presbyters, deacons, or clerics of whatever order—who had been received from the fellowship of the Pelagians and Coelestians into Catholic communion with such imprudence that they had not first been compelled to condemn their own error, now at least, after their hypocrisy had been partly exposed, to submit to true correction, which could benefit them without harming anyone. They were to condemn openly, in their own professions, the authors of their proud error and detest whatever the universal Church had rejected in their teaching, and so forth [Col. 1025C].

These presbyters, deacons, and clerics of various orders about whom Saint Leo wrote to the bishop of Aquileia seem to have been among the ecclesiastics of the province of Aquileia—or among their followers—who approximately twenty years earlier, devoted to Pelagian errors, had refused to sign Zosimus’s *Tractoria* and had presented that little book of the Faith concerning this matter to Augustine, the metropolitan of Aquileia. They had consequently already been rejected by Augustine from ecclesiastical communion because of their obstinacy in condemned errors, but afterward they had been received by one of his successors, after giving some proof of their faith, perhaps inadequate or insufficiently explicit. For that reason they had given no slight grounds for suspecting that their minds were still occupied by their former errors.

Zabeus will therefore confirm even more forcefully that if Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, was truly the author of that *Explanation of the Creed* addressed to those preparing for baptism, he ought at that point specifically to have mentioned the Pelagians, as heretical men who were probably still present in his time in the province of Aquileia and from whom the Christian flock faced danger even more than from the Manichaeans and the other heretics mentioned there [Col. 1025D].

But we must add certain points which, unless I am mistaken, completely resolve Zabeus’s objection. In Nicetas Gennadianus’s *Explanation of the Creed*, these are the words in chapter 10, where he names the heresies individually in connection with the article “the Holy Catholic Church.” Nowhere else in the whole *Explanation* is any heresy mentioned by its proper name:

> “There are indeed also other pseudo-churches, but you have nothing in common with them—for example, those of the Manichaeans, Cataphrygians, Marcionites, or the other heretics or schismatics; for these churches have ceased to be holy.”

The purpose of the author of this little work, then, was not to name each individual heresy and each individual pseudo-church, as becomes clear when one weighs the very words. He was not naming each heresy, because the discussion here was not about heresies; nor was he naming each pseudo-church, because his concern was simply to speak about the Catholic Church. If he names the pseudo-churches of the Manichaeans, Cataphrygians, and Marcionites, it is plainly evident that he names them solely as examples of false churches, so that the truth of the Catholic Church might shine more and more clearly by comparison with those false churches.

He therefore fulfilled the purpose toward which he directed his thought when he named some. He did not fail in his duty because he passed over others, since his subject was not each one individually but only the presentation of some examples. Yet after naming those three pseudo-churches—the Manichaeans, Cataphrygians, and Marcionites—does he not also speak of all of them when he adds, “or the other heretics or schismatics” [169]?

Nevertheless, Zabeus would have wished to see a distinct mention of the Pelagians here if this *Explanation* truly belonged to Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia. But even if the Pelagian heresy had had followers in the province of Aquileia in Nicetas’s time, a matter we shall discuss below, there was certainly no place here for Pelagianism. Nicetas was indicating pseudo-churches, whether of heretics or of schismatics.

The Pelagians, as everyone who has read their acts can recognize, never, from the beginning of this heresy to its end, established a distinct church or pseudo-church by which they would be distinguished from the Catholic Church and from which Catholics would have to abstain. Other disturbers of ecclesiastical peace established pseudo-churches for themselves, either at the beginning of their errors or, rather, after some time had passed. Such were the Manichaeans, Cataphrygians, and Marcionites, whom the *Explanation* names; likewise the Arians, Eunomians, and others among heretics, and the Novatians, Donatists, and others among schismatics.

For as long as their error prevailed, the Pelagians certainly did not cease, as far as they could, to spread their poison, recruit companions in error, acquire patrons for themselves, fight with sharp disputations, mock through deceitful arguments, mislead through crafty professions, demand a plenary council, win over not a few bishops—especially in Gaul and Britain—and sometimes stir up disturbances and commit crimes. But they never went so far as to create a schism, separate themselves from the Catholic Church, and establish a distinct church or pseudo-church for themselves. This was so although they were repeatedly condemned by episcopal councils in Asia and Africa; although they were struck with an anathema by the *Tractoria* of Zosimus on behalf of the universal Church and deprived of ecclesiastical communion; and although they were repeatedly punished by the laws of the emperors, expelled from Italy, and persecuted everywhere.

The very character of Pelagianism, as others also observe, was such that it could not easily win popular favor for the formation of a separate people opposed to the Catholics. For although it exaggerated and defended the powers of free will beyond what its system warranted, it did not do so in order to accommodate human weakness—the aim usually desired by the masses in new religious controversies—but rather to rise more vehemently and sharply against careless Christians who extended human weakness into their vices and, in the Pelagians’ view, failed to recognize the powers of their own nature, by which they could strive toward the perfection of Christian life even without the assistance of divine grace [Col. 1026D].

There was therefore no reason for Nicetas of Aquileia to mention the Pelagians here among the pseudo-churches whom he cited as examples in explaining the article concerning the Catholic Church, even if Pelagians had in reality existed in his province at that time.

But were there Pelagian heretics in the province of Aquileia during the time of Nicetas of Aquileia? This remains to be investigated, so that our response to Zabeus may be complete in every respect.

Among the imperial laws against the Pelagians there is a constitution issued in the name of Valentinian III by his mother, the empress Placidia, against them. It was issued at Aquileia in the year 425, on 9 July, while she was living there with her son after the death of the tyrant John [Col. 1027A]. It does not follow from this that Pelagians were then at Aquileia or in the province of Aquileia, because that constitution was addressed to Amacius, prefect of the Gauls, on the occasion of a disturbance stirred up by the Pelagians in the Gallic regions.

The previously cited letter of Saint Leo the Great addressed to the bishop of Aquileia—who may perhaps have been Adelphus or Maximus, as the Ballerini brothers conjecture in their preliminary notice—belongs approximately to the year 442, as indicated there.

Those presbyters, deacons, and clerics of various orders mentioned in the same letter, whom the Pelagian or Coelestian heresy had involved and who afterward reached Catholic communion in the province of Aquileia without being required to condemn their own error—thereby giving rise to the suspicion, once their hypocrisy had been partly exposed, that they had entered the Lord’s fold without laying aside their bestial dispositions—those men, I say, do not appear to have been numerous, since the holy pontiff says: “We have learned that certain presbyters, deacons, and clerics of various orders,” and so forth.

For this reason that most distinguished Cardinal Norisius seems to have written less accurately in book 2, chapter 12, of his *History of Pelagianism*. In recounting the matter from this same letter of Saint Leo, he does not say “certain,” as the holy pontiff does, but “many clerics,” thereby excessively increasing the number without a suitable witness—namely, by as much as “many” exceeds “certain.”

The suspicion of Pelagianism appears to have concerned only those few members of the ecclesiastical body, not the subordinate laity as well. The same letter says absolutely nothing about the laity, except that there was a danger of their contracting the disease from those whose repentance was not sufficiently certain.

Thus, in the province of Aquileia in the year 442, it was only clerics, and not many of them, who gave grounds for suspecting Pelagianism. It should also be noted above all that they gave grounds for suspecting the Pelagian error with which they had previously been involved because, before they were received into Catholic communion, they had not condemned that same error in explicit words and by some particular formula, and because something of the same chaff perhaps appeared—or rather seemed to appear—in their speech. This often happens with those whom we formerly regarded as adversaries, whose sincerity we easily doubt even after reconciliation.

They were not, however, absolutely Pelagians even after being admitted to communion, as they had previously been. For the holy pontiff himself says that “their hypocrisy is partly exposed,” which indicates nothing other than that they had given grounds for suspicion and had also raised doubts about the genuineness of their repentance. This was not because genuine repentance did not sufficiently appear in them, but chiefly because they lacked the particular and open condemnation of the errors and their authors of which he was speaking. That condemnation alone was ultimately required as a remedy for completely wiping away the suspicion and doubt they had occasioned.

From this it is clear that Saint Leo’s zeal against Pelagianism was truly great and worthy of so great a pontiff, who stood ready everywhere with his authority and teaching against every danger. But it is also clear that Pelagianism was not in reality of such importance in the province of Aquileia at that time that it could be regarded as an error openly and widely prevailing, against which a battle line had to be continually drawn.

What, then, was the situation in the province of Aquileia after the year 442? There are two other letters of Saint Leo the pope—the second and the eighteenth in the frequently cited edition of the Ballerini—which scholars have discussed at length. The first is addressed to Septimus or Septimius, bishop of Altinum or Altinate; the other to Januarius, bishop of Aquileia.

The occasion for the debate was the nearly complete agreement of the sense, and even of the wording, of the two letters [171]. The purpose of the debate was to determine whether one of them, and which one in particular, should be regarded as spurious, or whether both should be judged genuine and legitimate.

In chapter 15 of his *Aquileian Monuments*, the distinguished De Rubeis, with very strong arguments capable of winning assent, rejected the second letter as addressed to the bishop of Altinum and admitted only the eighteenth as addressed to Januarius, bishop of Aquileia [Col. 1028A]. But if we collect the judgments after the matter has been debated on both sides, we believe the conclusion should be that, whatever one may think about the second letter to Septimus of Altinum, the other, addressed to Januarius of Aquileia, can in no way be rejected.

This letter of Saint Leo the Great to Januarius of Aquileia belongs to the year 447 and is properly a reply to another letter that Saint Leo had received from Januarius, which is no longer extant. From the response of the holy pontiff we can reconstruct the letter of Januarius. It seems entirely beyond doubt that Januarius, who held the see of Aquileia after Adelphus and Maximus, informed Saint Leo the pontiff about the work and care he had undertaken so that the measures which Leo himself had ordered in his first letter to the bishop then presiding over that Church might be fully carried out. Those measures concerned the presbyters, deacons, and clerics of various orders who had previously been infected with the Pelagian taint and afterward received into Catholic communion without sufficient safeguards [Col. 1028B].

Perhaps after the death of Maximus the holy pontiff had again sent a letter full of concern about this same matter to Bishop Januarius, who consequently replied to the pontiff in such a way that he deserved to receive from him this second letter of praise and congratulation.

What, then, does this letter of Saint Leo to Januarius say?

> “Having read the letter of your Fraternity, we have recognized the vigor of your faith, which we had known long ago, and we congratulate you because you are carrying out the pastoral care of guarding Christ’s flock with vigilant attention, lest the wolves who entered under the appearance of sheep tear the simple ones apart with bestial savagery, and lest they not only themselves make no progress through correction but also corrupt those who are sound.
>
> “To prevent this viperous deceit from succeeding, we have thought it necessary to admonish your Belovedness, making clear that it endangers the soul if anyone who has fallen from us into the sect of heretics or schismatics and has in some way stained himself by the contagion of heretical communion is, after repenting, retained in Catholic communion without a proper declaration of satisfaction.
>
> “For it is most salutary and full of the benefit of spiritual medicine that presbyters, deacons, subdeacons, or clerics of any order who wish to appear corrected and seek to return to the Catholic faith, which they previously lost, should first acknowledge without ambiguity that they condemn their errors and the very authors of those errors, and so forth.”

And later:

> “Therefore let your Belovedness, whose devotion gives us joy, join its care to our arrangements and take care that the measures which have been proposed commendably and ordained salutarily for the safety of the whole Church be carried out carefully and promptly.”

What we can rightly gather from this letter of Saint Leo to Januarius of Aquileia, dated in the year 447, is the following: Bishop Januarius had long before demonstrated the vigor of his faith in the matters discussed in this letter, and therefore, before he perhaps ascended the episcopal [Col. 1028D] see of Aquileia, while he was still exercising in that same Church the office of auxiliary bishop, either under Maximus, or under Adelphus, or under still earlier bishops—for above, at §172, chapter 6, we had not unwillingly conjectured that this same Januarius held this office—his vigor had already become known to Pope Leo. We also gather that this Januarius, who earned from Saint Leo such high praise for pastoral care and vigilance, even after receiving the see of Aquileia devoted himself admirably to ensuring that the measures so beneficially ordained by the Roman pontiff were carried out; and indeed, when Saint Leo sent that letter to him, little or nothing was lacking for the completion of the work in these matters.

Who, then, would say that in the time of Bishop Januarius there were still Pelagians in the province of Aquileia, or persons suspected of the Pelagian contamination, after such vigilance and devotion on the part of Bishop Januarius, commended with such praise by [Col. 1029A] Saint Leo? Indeed, since this letter contains no specific mention of Pelagians or Coelestians, as does the first letter to the bishop of Aquileia that we examined earlier; and since it is moreover plainly evident that Saint Leo spoke in this letter in general terms about any heretics and schismatics of the ecclesiastical order who were returning to Catholic communion, we think it may be inferred from this very letter that, at the time when it was sent—namely, in the year 447—no remnants of the Pelagian error remained in the province of Aquileia, nor any suspicion of Pelagianism [Col. 1029B] among the priests, deacons, and clerics of various orders who had returned from the party of Pelagius to Catholic communion. Either they had, after furnishing guarantees, complied with the metropolitan bishop who obeyed the instructions of the Apostolic See—as seems more probable—or they had preferred to leave the province of Aquileia and lead a wandering and exiled life, following the example of their teachers.

If, therefore, in the year 447 Pelagianism and the suspicion of Pelagianism had been banished from the province of Aquileia through the vigilance of Pope Saint Leo, and especially through the efforts of Bishop Januarius, Secundus, Januarius’s immediate successor, undoubtedly received the Church of Aquileia entirely cleansed of this contamination. In the same condition Nicetas, who assumed the bishopric of Aquileia in the year 454, received it—namely, in the second year after the destruction of the city of Aquileia by Attila.

Here we must also consider that the barbarian peoples who at that time invaded Italy from the north under the leadership of Attila, bringing with them the contagion of the errors with which they were infected, must undoubtedly have inspired great fear even in Pelagian persons, if any happened to be hiding in some corner of the province of Aquileia. It is therefore likely that they fled far away, just as they had also fled from Rome, withdrawing first to Sicily and then to Africa, in the time of Alaric—their principal leaders being Pelagius and Coelestius, as is known from the history of Pelagianism.

From what has been said thus far, it is sufficiently clear [Col. 1029C] that not very many people, even among the ecclesiastical community alone, gave grounds for suspicion of the Pelagian error in the province of Aquileia around the year 442, when Saint Leo, Pope, sent his letter to the bishop of Aquileia, Maximus; and that certainly only a few, or perhaps none at all, remained around the year 447, when the same pontiff wrote his second letter to Januarius, bishop of Aquileia. It is entirely certain that none existed in the time of Bishop Nicetas, who held the bishopric of Aquileia from the year 454 to 485. Thus he had no occasion to name the Pelagians or their errors in his *Explanation of the Creed*, even if he had intended to treat heresies there specifically.

Thus far, then, concerning the observations of the most distinguished Zabeus, drawn by him from the deeper aspects of the matter.

It remains now for us to turn our discourse to the most distinguished Michael Denis, a truly learned man, prefect of the Palatine Library at Vienna, and one who rendered outstanding services to the entire world of letters. His death, which we formerly mourned, although [Col. 1029D] perhaps not excessively premature in view of his age, was nevertheless a loss to the best studies and to all students. Among the monuments of his intellect, by which he benefited the learned and enriched the republic of letters, there is a work entitled *Latin Theological Manuscript Codices of the Palatine Library at Vienna, and of Other Western Languages*, Vienna, 1802.

In volume II, part three, of this work—whose editor after the author’s death was Baron de Müller—a certain Latin parchment codex is described on page 2041: a tenth-century manuscript of 119 leaves, in octavo, written in a clear and well-formed hand, distinguished with red, and ornamented with many headings, the square letters enclosed in various colors, as it is described there.

At its beginning this codex presents an order, or brief exposition, concerning the catechizing of the uneducated, which therefore also treats of baptism and its rites. It consists entirely of words and ideas drawn from the holy Fathers, as happens in canonical collections [Col. 1030A], according to Denis himself in that place; and the Fathers from whom the ideas and words are taken are indicated at the appropriate points. The Fathers named there are Nicetas, Clement, Isidore of Spain, Albinus (Alcuin) the Master, Jerome, Gregory the Great, Bede, Augustine, Athanasius, Leo, and Origen.

“But concerning the others,” the distinguished man adds, “the matter is settled … only Niceta—Nicetas, Niceas—pulls my ear.”” He therefore investigates who this Nicetas, or Nicetas/Niceas, might be, and immediately adopts the opinion that he is in fact the Gennadian author of the six little books of instruction for baptismal candidates. He calls him bishop of the city of Romatiana in Mediterranean Dacia, and therefore the same person as Nicetas, the friend of Saint Paulinus of Nola.

Accordingly, in order somehow to lessen the loss caused by the disappearance of these books, he presents from that codex at least their *λειψανα*—their relics or fragments—which can be nothing but most welcome to all students and learned men. We ourselves gladly present them after the two complete works of the same Nicetas, in the form in which we received them through Denis’s diligence [Col. 1030B].

These Nicetian fragments are six in number. From the third of them Denis draws an argument that is indeed attractive and at first sight extremely powerful, to confirm his opinion: namely, that Nicetas the Gennadian is the same as Nicetas, bishop of Dacia, and the friend of Saint Paulinus.

For Nicetas says there:

> “One does not come to confession before having first renounced the devil. Just as neither does a gold-washer (*aurilicus*, or *aurilegus*) put gold into a little bag before first washing all the earth or mud.”

What does Denis say to these words of Nicetas?

> “You see,” he says, “the custom of Dacia confirmed by a local bishop of the fifth century, about which Samuel Koeleserus has written more fully in *Roman-Dacian Gold-Mining*, Sibiu, 1717, in octavo. Paulinus, in poem XVII addressed to our Nicetas, calls them gold-washers: ‘You turn clever gold-washers into gold,’ that is, by instructing them in Christian life; and in the same poem: ‘The Bessus rejoices because what he once sought with hand [Col. 1030C] upon the ground he now gathers with his mind in heaven.’”

Thus, and very ingeniously, the distinguished author uses the matter for his own purpose.

After the fragments he adds the following, which we reproduce in full, lest our fidelity in explaining the views of so great a man be lacking. Denis had preceded Zabeus himself both in his opinion concerning the episcopate of this Gennadian Nicetas and in the emendation he proposes for the title of the little work *Explanation of the Creed*, in the word “Aquileian”—although, when Zabeus wrote, he knew nothing of Denis’s opinion or of the Viennese codex.

Denis therefore says:

> “The following remains in the codex concerning Nicetas … For the moment, let us turn our attention to Nicetas. While I was writing these things, a little work was brought to me at Padua, recently printed in 1799 by the seminary press, in quarto, entitled *Explanation of the Creed of Blessed Nicetas, Bishop of Aquileia, Delivered to the Candidates*, transcribed, as the Italian preface states, by the most eminent Cardinal Stefano Borgia, the most learned patron of learned men, from a Chisian parchment manuscript in quarto of the fourteenth century.
>
> “I was delighted that the memory [Col. 1030D] of the holy bishop should at nearly the same time be revived both by me and elsewhere. Nevertheless, I could not agree with the word ‘Aquileian’ (*Aquileiensis*). If the Chisian codex contains it, it is certainly an error; it should have been written either ‘of Dacia,’ or ‘of the city of Romatiana,’ as in Gennadius, or ‘of Romessiana,’ as in the Peutinger Table, or ‘of Ῥεμεσίανα τῆς Δακίας’—‘Remesiana of Dacia’—as in the first act of the Council of Chalcedon, volume IV of Labbe’s edition of the Councils, Venetian edition, column 892.
>
> “Cardinal Baronius attempted to identify this city with Aquileia; but Papebrochius corrected him in the notes to the *Martyrology* on 22 June, in the *Acta Sanctorum*, volume IV of June, in the critical dissertation for that day, page 245; Pagius, in the critical notes to the *Annals*, volume II, under the year 396, page 8; De Rubeis, in *Monuments of the Church of Aquileia*, chapter 17, column 152; and Quesnellus, in the notes to Letter 129 of Leo the Great, volume II, page 506.
>
> “If, then, the city of Romatiana is not Aquileia, it is clear that the bishop of Aquileia [Col. 1031A] did not write what the bishop of Romatiana wrote. Indeed, no ancient writer reports that an Aquileian bishop, almost a whole century later than the Romatian, left anything in writing. But Gennadius, whom I cited above, and who was contemporary with the Aquileian, expressly attributes to Romatian six instructional books for baptismal candidates, following Honorius of Autun, book II, chapter 22, and Trithemius, number 118. Among these was the fifth, concerning the Creed.
>
> “I have even less doubt that this is the same work which has recently come to light at Padua from the Chisian codex, because, at the beginning of the printed Paduan edition, on page 7, its author soon repeats the same words that I cited above from its second little book: ‘Thus, freeing himself from these evils, and throwing these chains behind his back, as it were into the face of the enemy, a man now pronounces with a sincere voice: I believe in God, etc.’
>
> “Let the reader weigh these matters, and without reluctance decide with me that, if this *Explanation of the Creed* is to be reprinted, either separately or in some supplement to the *Library of the Fathers*, ‘Dacian Nicetas’ or ‘Nicetas of Romatiana’ ought to be substituted for ‘Nicetas of Aquileia.’”

Thus far the distinguished Michael Denis.

What are we now to make of the authority of so great a man? What of the arguments he adduces to establish that Nicetas the Gennadian is the same as Nicetas the Dacian, the friend of Saint Paulinus of Nola; and consequently to assert that the title of the newly published work should be corrected, the word “Aquileian” being deleted and “Dacian,” or “of Romatiana in Dacia,” substituted for it, as Zabeus himself proposed?

I had already written a good deal against Zabeus’s dissertation when word reached me that he had already been anticipated by the distinguished man in the same line of reasoning. I was certainly taken aback by the unexpected news, and did everything possible to obtain as quickly as I could what Denis had written on the subject. Then, behold, Zabeus himself, who had learned of my desire, on 26 September 1805 freely sent me, in the most courteous letter, a copy of Denis’s entire article on Nicetas, which he himself had shortly before transcribed from the printed copy that had already reached Venice and the Marciana [Col. 1031C] Library.

When I had eagerly read it, the authority and renown of the man greatly impressed me, especially when I realized that he had not learned of the new little work merely by report, but had actually examined it with his own eyes, and thus could recognize the genuine relationship of his fragments with it.

Nevertheless, I saw absolutely nothing in Denis’s article that contradicted what I had already worked out, especially in chapters two and three: namely, that Nicetas the Dacian, the friend of Saint Paulinus of Nola, was not bishop of the city of Romatiana situated in Cisdanubian Dacia, but held a bishopric beyond the Danube; and that Nicetas the Gennadian referred in a particular way in his *Explanation of the Creed* to the error of Eutyches, an error of which Nicetas the Dacian, the friend of Saint Paulinus of Nola, could not have spoken.

Moreover, I found nothing that contradicted what I had intended to establish in chapter four in support of the Aquileian episcopate of this Gennadian Nicetas. I therefore asked the distinguished man’s pardon—he may perhaps have been distracted by various other concerns and overwhelmed by a multitude of manuscripts [Col. 1031D] to examine—and resolved to stand by what I had begun.

Nor could Denis’s arguments move me. For what is there in his entire observation that we have not examined and treated with an even fuller pen when we argued against Zabeus, especially in chapters four and five, where we reconsidered the opinion of Cardinal Baronius, which the most learned men had rejected with such a clamour? Nothing, therefore, remains to be added here to Denis’s observation, which rests entirely upon the authority of those men who rose up, as it were in a united army, against Baronius, and to whom Denis himself subscribed without making any distinction of the facts. And Denis himself, if he were still alive, would not take it amiss if I departed from him, just as I thought it necessary to depart from the entire body of learned men who preceded him in this opinion.

Nevertheless, the distinguished man has one particular [Col. 1032A] observation of his own, which he skillfully drew from his third fragment, as we have reported above; and this must be answered.

This Nicetian fragment mentions gold-washers, whether those who gathered gold from the veins of the mountains or, more probably, those who collected it from the gravel and mud of rivers. Nicetas appropriately used them for his purpose, saying that just as a gold-washer, or gold-washer-worker, does not put gold into a little bag before first washing all the earth or mud, so a Christian confession of the truth contained in the articles of faith is not pronounced by a candidate before he has first renounced the devil.

Since Paulinus of Nola also mentions gold-washers more than once in his poem addressed to his own Nicetas, as inhabitants of Dacia, where that Nicetas, the bishop of the Dacians, lived—and whom Nicetas himself, as he said, had won for Christ and turned into gold—Denis argued from this that Nicetas, the author of that fragment and therefore also the author of the other little works for baptismal candidates mentioned by Gennadius, was in reality that Nicetas the Dacian, the friend of Saint Paulinus [Col. 1032B] of Nola. For that reason, he placed the example of gold-washers in his sermon because they were well known to those to whom he was speaking; and, by naming gold-washers, he sufficiently indicated that he was bishop in Dacia, not bishop of Aquileia.

This observation of the distinguished man, drawn so felicitously and naturally from a comparison of the Nicetian fragment with Paulinus of Nola’s poem about Nicetas the Dacian, may at first sight create a plausible appearance, but it cannot by any means settle the matter or compel belief. It might serve to confirm and illuminate an opinion founded upon stronger arguments; it cannot itself serve as an argument by which to defend and establish that opinion.

Denis himself used this observation for the purpose of confirming and illustrating his opinion, which he already considered firmly established by other arguments, and especially by the authority of those men who rose against Baronius, on the assumption that Baronius had confused the city of Romatiana, or Remesiana, or Remisiana, or Romessiana [Col. 1032C] in Dacia with the city of Aquileia.

Since these arguments have been fully answered, what force can Denis’s observation retain, however natural and spontaneous it may be? Nevertheless, it is worth examining it.

Nicetas, as Denis thinks, appropriately used the example of gold-washers in his address to the baptismal candidates because gold-washers were found in Dacia, where Nicetas, bishop of the Dacians and friend of Paulinus of Nola, lived, as is evident from Paulinus himself. “You see,” he says, “the custom of Dacia confirmed by a local bishop of the fifth century.” Nicetas was therefore bishop of the Dacians, Denis concludes—the Nicetas who spoke in this way to his baptismal candidates—not bishop of the Aquileians.

But why could Nicetas of Aquileia not also have used the example of gold-washers, even if there were perhaps no gold-washers in the province of Aquileia? It is enough that the name and activity of gold-washers were commonly known, so that anyone could draw examples from them in speech as circumstances required.

Virgil, certainly, when he once happened to be holding Ennius in his hand and was asked what he was doing, is said to have replied that he was collecting gold from Ennius’s [Col. 1032D] dung. Here Virgil takes the practice of gold-washers as an example, although he was as far removed as possible from the gold-washers [Col. 1033A] of Dacia.

Saint Jerome likewise, in his letter to Laeta concerning the education of her little daughter Paula—letter 107 in Vallarsi’s edition—speaking in section 12 about apocryphal books, whose reading he sometimes did not forbid to a virgin girl, says: “Let her know that many corrupt things are mixed into them, and that great prudence is required to seek gold in mud.”

It was therefore a common figure of speech, used everywhere among all peoples, to draw an example, as the occasion demanded, from the activity of gold-washers, as from a matter known to everyone. There is consequently no reason why that Nicetas had to be a Dacian merely because there were gold-washers in Dacia and Paulinus of Nola mentioned them; for a bishop of Aquileia could equally have taken an example from gold-washers whenever the discourse required it, just as we read that Maro first did, and Saint Jerome afterward, not to mention many other writers whom it would be possible to cite at an appropriate point, if the matter were not already sufficiently and abundantly established.

But the bishop of Aquileia could also have mentioned gold-washers in a particular way, and perhaps even the gold-washers of Dacia, who might have been known to his Aquileians, since it is established that Aquileia was a market for peoples situated along the Danube.

For Aquileia, as Strabo testifies in book V of the *Geography*, “was open as a market to the Illyrian peoples dwelling along the Ister.” Herodian likewise says, in book VIII, in his account of Maximinus:

> “In addition to a vast number of citizens, a great multitude of foreigners and merchants also frequented that city [Aquileia]; and, situated by the sea, it was like the boundary of Illyria.”

Why, then, might the people of Aquileia not often have seen either the Dacians themselves, who were gold-washers, selling the products of their labor at Aquileia, or other peoples neighboring the Dacians, who brought to Aquileia for sale the gold, or gold-bearing mud, purchased from the Dacians?

Why might the inhabitants of Roman Dacia [Col. 1033B] not have bought from the barbarian Dacians living beyond the Danube sands rich in gold particles, or golden earth dug from the depths of the mountains, and themselves brought these materials to the goldsmiths of Aquileia for purposes of trade?

I have said “sands rich in gold particles,” or “golden earth.” For however well those barbarian gold-washers may have been able to separate gold from mud and earth by washing it, so that they could put it into a little bag, they did not render the gold so pure that it contained no many particles of sand or earth clinging to it. These had to be separated entirely by the more laborious work of goldsmiths.

Thus there was an occasion for trade, first between the barbarian Dacians and the Romans, who, so to speak, purchased the raw material from the barbarians; and then between the Roman Dacians and the merchants or goldsmiths of Aquileia, who acquired from the Roman Dacians the raw material brought to Aquileia, in order to obtain new profit through the work required to purify the gold completely.

Let this suffice concerning the authority and observations of the distinguished Michael [Col. 1033C] Denis.

[Col. 1033C]

## CHAPTER VIII

On Saint Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, and on his little works, both those now published and those either lost or still concealed; also on the fragments that became known to us through the study and diligence of the most learned Michael Denis. Likewise, on his sanctity and veneration.

Since, as it seems, there can no longer be any doubt that Nicetas the Gennadian is in reality Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia; and that this Nicetas of Aquileia is the author of the two little works which we now publish together for the first time, as well as of the fragments remaining from other works either lost or still concealed, we now think that we may freely discuss this Nicetas of Aquileia as the author of the works that Gennadius attributes to Romatian.

But what can we say about this Nicetas of Aquileia [Col. 1033D] that might shed some light on knowing him more deeply? Leo Allatius had composed a dissertation on the Nicetases, which has perished, as Johannes Albert Fabricius reports in volume VI of the *Greek Library*, page 429 of the first edition. Allatius likewise published similar works that survive, concerning Psellus and his writings, the writings of the Methodiuses, the writings of the Simeons, Nilus and his writings, and also Georgius and his writings.

Nothing is more useful, certainly, than that, when many men of the same name have become famous through their lives and writings, someone should be found who treats each one distinctly, so that the opportunity and danger of confusion and error may be removed.

For this reason, following the example of this learned man, others too have written about persons with the same name: for example, Anselm Banduri about the Nicephoruses and their writings, although his dissertation was never published; and recently Franciscus Fontanius about the illustrious Remigiuses and their writings, in volume III of *The Delights of the New Erudite*, Florence, 1793, and elsewhere.

Why, then, [Col. 1034A] among those Nicetases illustrated by Allatius should there not also have been a place for our Nicetas, the bishop of Aquileia mentioned by Gennadius? Why should Allatius not have said something there about this Nicetas as well, which we seek elsewhere in vain? It is truly regrettable that the work of that distinguished man has perished, since our discussion might perhaps have been assisted by it.

We have many persons named *Nicetae*, *Niceti*, *Niceae*, *Nicae*, and *Nicetii* in the martyrologies of the Latin Church, both in those published separately—the Roman, Hieronymian, Ado, and Usuard martyrologies—and in those that appeared in collections of ancient monuments: namely, in D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, Canisius’s *Ancient Lessons*, and the *New Treasury of Anecdotes*, as well as in Martène and Durand’s *New Collection of Ancient Writers and Monuments*.

But what do these works contain beyond a name and sometimes a brief eulogy—testimonies, certainly, to their sanctity and even to the veneration accorded them in the Church, but generally nothing about their deeds and nothing about their time, unless other monuments are available to supplement their deficiencies?

The Greek menologies also [Col. 1034B], such as that outstanding one magnificently printed at Urbino in three folio volumes in 1727, and the calendars—for example, the Constantinopolitan calendar illustrated and published at Rome by the distinguished Stefano Antonio Morcelli, in two quarto volumes, 1788—present several Nicetases to us as martyrs and confessors. But these belong to the Eastern Church and have nothing in common with our Aquileian Nicetas, about whom Gennadius speaks, except the name.

Our investigation of this Aquileian Nicetas and his works must therefore proceed entirely from Gennadius. To this must also be added what learned men have so far transmitted concerning the Aquileian Nicetas, both from the letter of Saint Leo the Great to him and from the monuments of the Church of Aquileia itself, as well as from the more ancient trustworthy records that survive.

But should our investigation of this Aquileian Nicetas not begin rather with Saint [Col. 1034C] Jerome than with Gennadius?
