Saint Jerome is certainly the first to mention a certain Niceas, a native of Aquileia, his friend, and even his companion in his travels. While this man was then residing at Aquileia and exercising the office of subdeacon in the Church of Aquileia, Jerome sent him from the East a letter full of friendly complaints. It is Letter 8 in Vallarsi’s edition and belongs, as noted there, to the year 374.

Baronius and others thought that this was the same Niceas or Nicetas who, having first been a subdeacon of the Church of Aquileia, later became its bishop and received from Saint Leo the Great that well-known [Col. 1034D] letter. They further added that he succeeded Chromatius immediately in the Aquileian see.

We have already indicated elsewhere, and must again point out here in accordance with our purpose, that Baronius and those who followed him were mistaken in two respects concerning this subdeacon of the Church of Aquileia, Niceas or Nicetas. First, Niceas or Nicetas, the bishop of Aquileia who received the notable decretal letter from Saint Leo the Great, was not the immediate successor of Chromatius, but the successor of Secundus, who held the Aquileian see fifth after Chromatius. Second, Niceas or Nicetas, who was a subdeacon of Aquileia in Saint Jerome’s time, could not have lived long enough to become bishop of the Church of Aquileia later, receive the cited letter from Saint Leo the Great, and complete the years of his episcopate that the ancient records assign to the Aquileian bishop Niceas or Nicetas.

The distinguished De Rubeis explains and proves both points in *Monuments of the Church of Aquileia*, chapter 17, section 3, in such a way as to leave no room for doubt:

> “The immediate succession of Nicetas after Chromatius is overthrown by the two chronicles, the Aquileian and the Gradensian, and by the Forum-Julian catalogue of patriarchs.”

For after Chromatius several successors are numbered in this order: Augustine, Adelphus or Delphinus, Maximus, Januarius, and Secundus; then [Col. 1035A] Nicetas takes his place.”

Regarding the second point, he continues:

> “The subdeacon Niceas must be distinguished from the bishop Nicetas by consideration of the chronology. Jerome wrote to the former around the year 374, and Leo the Great wrote to the latter in 458. Thus more than eighty-four years would already be counted in the age of Nicetas himself. Add the years he had reached when, as subdeacon of the Church of Aquileia, he received Jerome’s letter; add again the years during which he continued to govern the Church at Aquileia after the year 458; and the total becomes so great—or rather exceeds all bounds—that no prudent person could attribute so advanced and prolonged an age to one Nicetas, or Niceas.”

Thus he.

Two persons named Niceas or Nicetas must therefore necessarily be distinguished in the Church of Aquileia. One was a subdeacon of that Church; he certainly did not succeed Chromatius in the Aquileian episcopate, and nothing is known about him except what we read in the cited letter of Saint Jerome to him. The other was certainly bishop of Aquileia in the time of Saint Leo [Col. 1035B] the Great; the decretal letter of Leo to him survives, and Gennadius speaks of him in chapter 22 of *On Illustrious Men*, under the name “bishop of the city of Romatiana,” as was demonstrated in the preceding chapters.

Since our concern is solely with Niceas or Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, after distinguishing the two Aquileian Nicetases as was necessary, we leave the subdeacon to Saint Jerome and take up the bishop mentioned by Gennadius for elucidation.

But should this Aquileian bishop mentioned by Gennadius be called Niceas, or rather Nicetas? It is necessary to establish, insofar as possible, something even about the propriety and true pronunciation of the name of the man whose office, age, writings, and deeds are under discussion.

If we follow Joannes Josephus Lirutus, who discussed the two Aquileian Niceases or Nicetases at length in his *Notices of the Lives of the Learned Men of Friuli*, volume I, chapters 10 and 11, we should without doubt call the man who was a subdeacon in Saint Jerome’s account “Nicetas,” [Col. 1035C] and the man who was bishop of Aquileia “Niceas.”

But—and it is useful to note this once here—Lirutus ventures a great deal in these chapters, both concerning the proper names of these two Niceases or Nicetases and concerning their deeds and other matters relating to them, as he also frequently does elsewhere. All this certainly displays the man’s considerable learning; but, as the greatest judges of such matters have thought, it does not equally demonstrate in him a sound use of criticism.

We must therefore approach the matter by another route. The subdeacon whom we recently mentioned is commonly presented under the name Niceas, not Nicetas, in the editions of Jerome’s letter through which he is known to us. It therefore seems beyond doubt that the proper name of that subdeacon, the friend and companion of Saint Jerome, was Niceas.

Our bishop likewise appears under the same name, Niceas, both in the published works of Gennadius, Honorius of Autun, and Johannes Trithemius, and in the similarly published martyrologies of Ado, Usuard, and [Col. 1035D] the Roman Martyrology.

The older calendars printed for the Church of Aquileia likewise called him Niceas; and the calendars of the Church of Udine still call him Niceas. Following the ancient custom of the mother church, they announce the feast of that holy bishop on 22 June.

But because the ancients were persuaded that Niceas, the Aquileian subdeacon and friend and companion of Saint Jerome, was the same man who afterward became bishop of Aquileia, it easily came about, we think, that he was more commonly called Niceas, both in the published works of Gennadius, Honorius, and Trithemius and in the martyrologies and calendars.

Nevertheless, we think there are several considerations that clearly recommend calling the Aquileian bishop of this name not Niceas but rather Nicetas, and that he was in fact so called in his own time.

Certainly Saint Leo the Great addressed his decretal letter not to Niceas but to Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia [Col. 1036A], as we have it in the editions of Quesnellus, Cacciarius, and the Ballerini brothers, with no variant reading appearing anywhere. This holy pontiff could well have known the bishop’s true and genuine name, even from the report of Adeodatus, a deacon of the Roman Church named in the same letter, who had previously been with Nicetas at Aquileia and, returning from there, had brought Nicetas’s inquiries to the Roman pontiff, which Leo answered in that letter.

Moreover, the *Explanation of the Creed for Baptismal Candidates*, recently brought to light from the Chisian codex, has not “Niceas” but “Nicetas” in its title:

> “The Explanation of the Creed of Blessed Nicetas, Bishop of Aquileia, Delivered to Baptismal Candidates.”

The celebrated Vallicellian codex of Gennadius, cited by Holstenius in his observations on the Roman Martyrology under 22 June, also by Florentinius in *The Ancient Western Church Martyrologies* under 10 Kalends of July, and by others, has:

> “Nicetas, bishop of the city of Romatiana.”

The San-Germanensis [Col. 1036B] Gennadian codex likewise has “Nicetas.” Michael Le Quien cites it in his *Christian East*, volume II, column 306, and calls it ancient.

The tenth-century Viennese codex must also be added here. It preserved for us fragments of the works missing from Nicetas’s corpus, and for these we are indebted to the diligence and merit of the distinguished Michael Denis, who published them for the benefit of the ecclesiastical republic. In this codex the author of those fragments is called Nicetas, not Niceas.

Nor are domestic, so to speak, testimonies to the same matter lacking. Two Gennadian codices are available: one a parchment manuscript, apparently of the twelfth or thirteenth century, belonging to the distinguished Collegiate Church of Cividale; the other a paper manuscript, apparently of the thirteenth or fourteenth century, among the Guarnerian codices of the public Fontaniniana Library at San Daniele.

In both we read:

> “Niceta, bishop of the city of Romathiciana.”

Niceta, or Nicetas, rather than Niceas, therefore appears to have been the proper [Col. 1036C] and genuine name of our Aquileian bishop, although the difference between the two is very slight and of no importance, so that either may easily be used for the other without harm to the identity of the person.

Indeed, although, as we noted, our bishop was continually called Niceas in the calendars annually published in the diocese of Aquileia—and was therefore also called Niceas in the lessons of the second nocturn, which had previously been taken from the common office of a confessor-bishop, as well as in the prayer similarly taken from that common office, both for the office and for the Mass—he was nevertheless called Niceta or Nicetas in the Greater Litanies of the saints formerly sung in the same Church of Aquileia.

These litanies were published at Udine in 1602 by order of the celebrated Aquileian patriarch Francesco Barbaro, after the diocesan synod held by him at Gorizia that same year on 25 June. Among the holy pontiffs and confessors invoked in these supplications, after Saints [Col. 1036D] Sylvester, Gregory, Ambrose, Augustine, and others, and among the particular saints of the Church of Aquileia—Valerian, Chromatius, Paulinus, and others—we read also:

> “Holy Nicetas, pray for us.”

After the name of this Aquileian bishop—whom henceforth we shall rightly call not Niceas but Nicetas—what should now be thought about his homeland? We touched briefly on Nicetas’s homeland a little earlier, when replying to Zabeus; but the matter must be taken up again here, so that the discussion may proceed in due order.

Dandulus asserts that he was Greek by origin; against Dandulus, however, Joannes Josephus Lirutus defends his Aquileian origin. What might I myself dare in so remote and obscure a matter, where there is room not for arguments but only for conjectures? Lirutus affirms that our Aquileian and Gradan Chronicles convey absolutely nothing about Nicetas’s origin, whereas Dandulus, who drew his information from no other source than these Chronicles, added the Greek origin on his own authority [Col. 1037A], probably from the Greek derivation of Nicetas’s name. But who does not know that Dandulus enjoys the reputation of being a diligent and precise writer, who, not only in matters belonging to his own age but also in reporting ancient memories, transmitted nothing rashly or without due consideration? Moreover, no one will deny that in Dandulus’s time there existed many ancient monuments that have by no means survived to us, from which he could draw the material that he left in writing.

Lirutus adds that even in the time of Nicetas of Aquileia the custom prevailed that bishops were generally chosen from the clergy of the vacant Church, and especially from those who had served there in the lower orders. Why, then, would the Church of Aquileia have taken a foreigner and newcomer as its bishop, when it is especially clear that this same Church often nurtured within its own bosom men distinguished for holiness and learning, whom it gave to other Churches to be raised to the honor of the episcopate? Yet if other Churches received bishops from the Aquileian clergy, the history of the Aquileian Church itself, as reported by Lirutus [Col. 1037B], already shows that this custom was not so firmly established by common practice that it did not often admit exceptions—especially when an exception contributed to the greater advantage of the Church, which was the chief rule of discipline in every age and place. Why, then, could the Church of Aquileia not have had as its bishop a Greek, or rather a man Greek by origin?

Nevertheless, I am pleased to accept Lirutus’s own opinion that Nicetas, our bishop, was in reality Aquileian by homeland. There is no contradiction in his being at once Greek by origin, as Dandulus records, and Aquileian by homeland, as Lirutus argues. The name Niceas itself also suggests Greek origin in that Aquileian subdeacon, the friend and companion of Saint Jerome, whom we mentioned shortly before. Yet who could doubt that he was in reality Aquileian by homeland, after the testimony of the same holy teacher in the above-mentioned letter addressed to him, in which Jerome wrote to him amicably while he was living at Aquileia [Col. 1037C]: “Do you sometimes sigh amid the delights of your homeland and the journeys we undertook together?”

Here, then, we have the subdeacon Niceas, at once Aquileian by homeland and, probably, also Greek by origin, as his name indicates. Surely the ancestors of this Niceas, originally from Greece, migrated to Aquileia and settled there, making it their new homeland, while nevertheless preserving their ancestral names, which continually indicated their Greek origin. Why, then, could Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, not have belonged to those who were born at Aquileia of ancestors originating in Greece, and thus have been both Greek by origin and Aquileian by homeland? [182]

Let us venture a little further into conjecture. Why could this Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, not have been related by blood to the subdeacon Niceas, indeed a member of the same family—perhaps Niceas’s nephew or great-grandson—who retained the family name, though slightly altered for the sake of distinguishing one from the other? In place of established truth, which we cannot ascertain because of the lack of monuments [Col. 1037D], we offer a conjecture, or even a guess; yet one that in no way conflicts with the truth.

We must next inquire into the year in which our Nicetas assumed the episcopate of Aquileia, and also the year in which he departed to heaven. With regard to these dates, there is no reason to linger over the chronological note found in Trithemius’s works, in the Frankfurt edition of 1601, printed by Wechel, in folio, where we read: “He flourished in the time of the emperors Theodosius and Honorius, in the year 420.” Whether these words belong to Trithemius or, as seems more likely, are an addition by a later copyist of his works, they certainly cannot be regarded as deserving consideration after what has been said thus far.

As for the first date, namely the year in which Nicetas assumed the episcopate of Aquileia: since Nicetas was the immediate successor not of Saint Chromatius but of Secundus in the Aquileian episcopate [Col. 1038A], we must determine whether he entered upon the episcopate before or after the destruction of Aquileia, and, more probably, in what year.

We place the destruction of Aquileia, following the common judgment of historians and chronologers, in the year 452; and, with the common agreement of more recent writers, we reject the three-year siege of that city asserted by some ancient historians. We also consign to the realm of fable the account that Nicetas the bishop was killed by the Huns during the very destruction of the city, an account that we find in one of the ancient monuments; relying on the contemporary authority of Saint Leo the Great’s letter to Nicetas himself, we consign it to the realm of fable.

When, then, did Nicetas assume the Aquileian episcopate after Secundus? The distinguished De Rubeis, in his *Monumenta*, chapter 16, following Dandulus’s chronology, links the beginning of Nicetas’s episcopate to the year 454 of the common era, explicitly marked by Dandulus, and therefore the second year after the destruction of Aquileia.

[Col. 1038B] Yet Dandulus erred at this point in that, relying on the authority of Gotfridus of Viterbo, whom he names there, he narrates the destruction of Aquileia after the date at which Nicetas assumed the Aquileian episcopate, so that he appears to be one of those who accepted the three-year siege of Aquileia. Moved by this error of Dandulus, Joannes Josephus Lirutus persuaded himself that he had to depart from the date assigned by Dandulus for the beginning of Nicetas’s Aquileian episcopate, and devised another which he thought better suited the facts: namely, that Nicetas assumed the Aquileian episcopal see in the closing year 451, before the city of Aquileia was captured by Attila, indeed before it was pressed by the siege of his army. He attempts to demonstrate this at length.

The distinguished De Rubeis, nevertheless, was not at all moved by the learned man’s observations. In his dissertations *Variae Eruditionis*, chapter 20, § 2, he defends Dandulus’s date for the beginning of Nicetas’s Aquileian episcopate, maintaining that it must be distinguished from the sequence of other events and actions in which Dandulus may have been mistaken.

The veteran chronologer may perhaps also have been mistaken in assigning the date of Nicetas’s accession [Col. 1038C], as De Rubeis candidly admits. For no contemporary monuments are available on this matter, nor is there any evident way by which a certain year for the beginning of Nicetas’s Aquileian episcopate can be found amid so much darkness. But since, as De Rubeis adds, Dandulus’s chronological order of the Aquileian bishops [183] displays no gross defect during this period—and since certain synchronisms founded on more reliable monuments seem to support its sufficient plausibility, as he clearly demonstrates in the same place—why should we depart from him in assigning the date of Nicetas’s accession merely because he erred in placing the Aquileian disaster after the date he had assigned?

We therefore think that we should, with greater probability, stand by Dandulus’s chronology, insofar as this is permitted, together with the same distinguished De Rubeis: namely, that our Nicetas both assumed the Aquileian episcopate after the destruction of the city of Aquileia and that the date of his accession should be assigned to the year 454 of the common era, the year marked by Dandulus himself.

What, then, of the year in which Nicetas departed to heaven? Here too we have conflicting ancient monuments—or rather, because of the loss of the monuments, conflicting opinions of the ancients. One account is utterly absurd. De Rubeis also records it in the cited passage of his *Monumenta*: it reports that Nicetas was slaughtered in the destruction of Aquileia, yet assigns him thirty-two years in the episcopal see.

Another account, found in certain lessons for the office of Saint Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, published by the Bollandist hagiologists in volume IV of the June *Acta Sanctorum*, under 22 June, is more moderate. Those lessons, however, are neither very ancient nor, certainly, were they ever used in the ecclesiastical liturgy of the Church of Aquileia, whatever the aforementioned Lirutus asserts to the contrary without an adequate witness. They may therefore be regarded rather as a private attempt to increase devotion to our Saint Nicetas, just as other examples of the same kind survive concerning other heavenly patrons [Col. 1039A] of the Aquileian diocese, in a non-ancient manuscript preserved in this public archiepiscopal library.

These lessons assert that Nicetas “departed at Aquileia to the Lord in the year of Christ 458, on the tenth day before the Kalends of July.” At least this date of Nicetas’s death does not conflict with the date of the letter sent in that same year by Saint Leo the Great to Nicetas, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April. That date is the only completely certain and contemporary date connected with Nicetas’s Aquileian episcopate.

But from where did the author of those lessons—plainly a writer of a later age—derive the claim that Nicetas died three months after Leo’s letter was dated? Who, then, would not follow Dandulus rather in assigning the year in which Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, departed to heaven, just as the distinguished De Rubeis followed him? For the Venetian Chronologer writes as follows on this matter: “Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, surrounded by such great hardships and labors, oppressed also by old age, died in the year 485, thirty years and nine months after his enthronement.”

[Col. 1039B] The day of his death must not be passed over either. By the agreement of all the Martyrologies that mention this Nicetas, beginning with that most ancient one bearing the name of Saint Jerome, it can be none other than 22 June. On that day not only is his memory commemorated, but, as can be seen in many sources, his deposition also is indicated. Let this suffice concerning the principal dates of Nicetas of Aquileia, both his assumption of the episcopate and his death, matters about which something had to be said.

It is now pleasing to advance to the indisputable—and indeed illustrious—date of his episcopate, namely the aforementioned letter of Saint Leo the Great to him, bearing this date: “Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of Majorian Augustus.” It therefore belongs to the year 458, which was the fourth year of Nicetas’s episcopate.

Among the many duties of pastoral office by which Nicetas’s thirty-year episcopate must have become renowned during those most difficult times, this one, after the little works of which we shall speak below, [Col. 1039C] remains for us the most certain monument of his episcopal concern. What a monument, and how distinguished! Here is the beginning of this letter, which is numbered 159 in the Venetian edition of the Ballerini, 133 in Cacciari’s Roman edition, and 129 in Quesnell’s edition:

> “My son Adeodatus, a deacon of our see, has returned to us and reported that Your Love had requested that you receive from us the authority of the Apostolic See concerning matters that appear to present great difficulty in judgment. But care must be applied in view of temporal necessities, so that the wounds inflicted by the adversity of hostility may be healed chiefly by religious means.”

After this introduction, the letter proceeds through seven chapters, whose substance is as follows:

1. Concerning women who, because their husbands had been taken captive, married other men.
2. Whether the man who took the place of a captive husband is blameworthy.
3. That the wife must be restored to her first husband.
4. That women unwilling to return to their first husbands must be excommunicated.
5. Concerning those who, [Col. 1039D] while captive, ate food sacrificed to idols, compelled by hunger or fear.
6. Concerning those who were rebaptized through fear or error.
7. Concerning those who had once been baptized, but by heretics.

After giving his response to these questions, Saint Leo closes the letter as follows:

> “You shall cause this letter of ours, which we have sent in response to the consultation of your brotherhood, to reach all your brother and fellow-provincial bishops, so that the authority given may benefit all through their observance.”

The first thing that presents itself to us in this letter of Saint Leo to Nicetas is the unfortunate condition of the Church of Aquileia following Attila’s disaster. It consequently required extensive and exceptional care—care that the bishops could safely and uniformly provide only after consulting the Apostolic See, amid so many grave matters then arising.

Nicetas’s pastoral concern for treating the illnesses and assisting the needs of his people is also evident, as is his great prudence and obedience toward the Apostolic See [Col. 1040A]: distrusting his own judgment, he sought its authority in difficult matters. Perhaps he himself requested a deacon of the Apostolic See who could be present, inspect the condition of his Church with his own eyes, and hear with his own ears especially the complaints of husbands who had returned from captivity and found their wives married to other men.

Perhaps Saint Leo himself, moved by compassion for the calamities of the people of Aquileia and impelled by zeal for restoring discipline, sent that deacon Adeodatus on his own initiative, as his legate and visitor, to the Church of Aquileia and to other Churches throughout Italy, to remedy and relieve the losses that the barbarian upheaval had left in matters of faith and morals.

These consultations of our Nicetas and this letter of Saint Leo testify, meanwhile, to the fact that the practice was still in force at that time whereby bishops everywhere consulted the Roman See on more serious and doubtful matters, whether of doctrine or of the common ecclesiastical discipline. Numerous other examples exist from both earlier and later centuries [Col. 1040B], demonstrating in these matters the authority inherent in the Apostolic See.

Saint Jerome himself mentions the synodal consultations of the East and West that came to Damasus, bishop of the city of Rome, and in drafting the replies to which Jerome helped him. [185] He does so in his letter to Ageruchia, number 123 in Vallarsi’s edition, § 10. Learned writers on ecclesiastical discipline have treated the whole matter with the greatest fullness, and most recently the exceptionally diligent Selvagius illustrated it in book I, chapter 16, § 7, of his *Institutions of Christian Antiquities*. Nothing need be added here.

[Col. 1040C] The final words of Saint Leo’s letter deserve consideration because of the “brother bishops of Nicetas’s province” mentioned above, to whom the holy pontiff ordered that his letter should be conveyed through Nicetas, so that, as he himself says, “the authority given may benefit all through their observance.”

The distinguished De Rubeis writes as follows concerning these same words in his *Monumenta*, chapter 17, § 1:

> “The bishops of the metropolitan province of Aquileia at this time were those of Istria and Venetia, as well as others from Raetia Secunda and Noricum.”

It is therefore probable that either all the bishops of the province of Aquileia, or at least most of them—especially the bishop of Altinum and the others of inland Venetia who existed at that time—were involved in the same necessity as the metropolitan of Aquileia, and that Nicetas bore responsibility for all these Churches when he sent his consultations to the Apostolic See through the deacon Adeodatus.

Let us now turn to the little works mentioned by Gennadius, and examine each of them individually.

“Niceas,” says Gennadius in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 22, from the *Ecclesiastical Library* of Joannes Albertus Fabricius, “bishop of the city of Romaciana, composed in simple and polished language six little instructional works for those preparing for baptism. The first of them explains how those preparing for baptism ought to conduct themselves. The second is on the Errors of Paganism, in which he says that, almost in his own time, a certain householder named Melodius was transferred among the gods by the pagans because of his generosity, and a rustic named Gadarius [Col. 1040D] because of his courage. The third book is On the Faith of the One Majesty; the fourth, Against Genethliology; the fifth, On the Creed; the sixth, On the Victim of the Paschal Lamb. He also published a little book addressed to a fallen Virgin, an incentive to amendment for nearly all who fall.”

After Gennadius, with a few changes and omissions, Honorius of Autun writes in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, book II, chapter 22, likewise from Fabricius’s *Library*:

> “Niceas, bishop of the city of Romaciana, composed in simple and polished language six instructional works for those preparing for baptism. Of these, the first is On Those Preparing for Baptism; the second, On the Errors of Paganism; the third, On the Faith of the One Majesty; the fourth, Against Genealogy [another reading: Genethliology]; the fifth, On the Creed; the sixth, On the Victim of the Paschal Lamb. He also composed a little book addressed to a fallen Virgin, an incentive to amendment for nearly all who fall.”

After Gennadius [Col. 1041A] and Honorius, Joannes Trithemius writes in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, no. 118, again from Fabricius’s *Library*:

> “Niceas, bishop of the city of Romaciana, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, sharp in intellect, and clear and polished in speech, wrote little works of respectable literary value for the edification of readers. The following are attributed to him: One preparatory book for those preparing for baptism; one book On the Errors of Paganism; one book On the Faith of the One Majesty; one book Against Genealogy [another reading: Genethliology]; one book On the Creed; one book On the Victim of the Paschal Lamb; and one book Addressed to a Fallen Virgin.”

These are the works that antiquity has preserved for us concerning the writings of Nicetas of Aquileia.

It is evident from these accounts that, with the single exception of the little book addressed to the fallen Virgin, all the works of Nicetas of Aquileia were addressed to those preparing for baptism [186]. But who in ancient times were the *competentes* in the Church? We are touching upon a well-established matter, but one that is by no means foreign to our present undertaking; indeed, it is necessary to the subject, since it is extremely useful for understanding nearly all of Nicetas’s little works.

[Col. 1041B] The sacrament of baptism, which at the beginning of the nascent Church was administered to all without delay as soon as they had shown a mind full of piety and religion and had grasped the principal mysteries of the faith, as is clear from Acts chapters VIII and X, later began to be administered with careful caution. The life and faith of those who requested it were first diligently tested, because experience had shown that the faith of all those who had been baptized immediately after expressing their willingness to embrace Christian life was not sufficiently secure.

Accordingly, for the sake of this testing, the catechumenate was established in the Church. It was divided into two, three, or four stages, depending on differences of place or time. Those who enrolled themselves in the Church had to pass through these stages before being washed in the saving bath. A suitable period was also assigned to each stage, though it was sometimes lengthened or shortened according as the zeal and diligence of the catechumens—or, conversely, their lukewarmness and sluggishness—seemed to require.

The highest stage of the catechumens was that of the *competentes*: those who, after completing the other stages of the catechumenate, making sufficient progress in Christian instruction, giving unmistakable signs of piety, religious commitment, and steadfastness, and undergoing the required examination, were close to receiving the bath of regeneration.

“*Competens* means one examined according to the legitimate procedure of examination,” said Saint Zeno of Verona in book II, treatise 27. “The saving day has arrived, rich in every kind of gift through the offices of the Lord’s sacrament. For it grants a reward to devout priests … and remission of all sins to those preparing for baptism.” The same author says in treatise 50, *On Easter* 6: the *competentes* were baptized especially during the Easter Vigils, and thus obtained remission of all sins.

Why, however, were the catechumens close to baptism called *competentes*? The Latin Fathers unanimously explain the reason, especially Saint Augustine in several passages [Col. 1041D]: the name derives from requesting baptism, and requesting it together as a group, among those who were soon to be baptized.

“As Easter approached, he enrolled himself among the other *competentes*.” Thus writes the holy teacher in *On the Care for the Dead*.

“Those who shortly before were called *competentes* are now called infants. They were called *competentes* because, by asking to be born, they were knocking at the maternal womb; they are called infants because they have now been born to Christ, having previously been born into the world.”

Thus he writes in Sermon 228 to the people and infants—that is, to the newly baptized—on Easter Day, § 1:

> “What else are *competentes* than those asking together? For just as *condocentes*, *concurrentes*, and *considentes* mean nothing other than teaching together, running together, and sitting together, so the term *competentes* is formed from no other idea than asking together and desiring one thing.”

The same holy Father says this in Sermon 216 to those preparing for baptism, chapter 1. Saint Caesarius has nearly the same words in Sermon 68, which is numbered 267 in the Augustinian appendix to the sermons.

[187] The distinguished Mazochius, explaining the matter with his customary comprehensive learning in volume III of the Neapolitan Calendar, p. 678, writes:

> “Because their names were not given separately but together in one place, they were called *competentes* from asking together. This did not take place until they had absorbed catechetical instruction among the hearers for a sufficiently suitable period. A trace of this ritual petition is preserved even today in the words, ‘What do you ask of the Church of God?’”

We therefore know who the *competentes* were, both in reality and by name, those to whom our Aquileian Nicetas addressed his six numbered works. They were people already sufficiently instructed in the principles of the Christian religion and the precepts of Christian life, who requested baptism and had been placed among those soon to be baptized. They were therefore nourished with a more substantial kind of divine Word, separately from the other catechumens. They received the Creed to learn by heart and later recite [Col. 1042B] on appointed days before baptism. Certain other teachings of the Christian religion were also disclosed to them, teachings that previously had not been entrusted to them.

This explains the purpose of Nicetas’s works addressed to those preparing for baptism: the first, “How those preparing for baptism who desire to attain the grace of baptism ought to conduct themselves”; the second, On the Errors of Paganism; the third, On the Faith of the One Majesty; the fourth, Against Genethliology; the fifth, On the Creed; and finally the sixth, On the Victim of the Paschal Lamb.

Let us now come to them individually.

The first of Nicetas’s works addressed to those preparing for baptism, which Gennadius indicates and which we regret to have been lost together with four others, contained, as he writes, an account of how those preparing for baptism who desire to attain the grace of baptism ought to conduct themselves.

Two Gennadian manuscripts from our region, cited earlier—the parchment manuscript from Forojulium, or Cividale, and the paper Guarnerian manuscript from the town of San Daniele—present the title somewhat differently. Both similarly read [Col. 1042C]:

“How those preparing for baptism who desire to attain the grace of baptism ought to believe and act.”

That is, they specify how those preparing for baptism who desire to attain its grace ought both to believe and to act. I would not dare say which reading should be preferred. I will say only that the reading of our manuscripts more openly and clearly indicates the subject of the little work, as it probably was; this is not sufficiently apparent from the excessively general reading found in the editions of Gennadius.

Meanwhile, one can see what the first instruction of our Nicetas to those preparing for baptism was directed toward: namely, that those who had been placed in the rank of the *competentes* and were close to receiving baptism should understand how great a faith they ought to display and in what manner of life they ought to excel, so that they might worthily attain the grace of regeneration.

Joannes Trithemius, who may perhaps have had the work before his eyes and consequently known what it actually was, called it by the single and simple term “preparatory”—either because it served as an introduction to the other works addressed to those preparing for baptism, or because it constituted a general preparation for baptism, or even because it included both, as seems highly probable.

Since, however, it has not been granted to us to know that work, let us at least derive some idea of it from a work by one of the holy Fathers on the same subject.

[Col. 1042D] Among the sermons delivered by Saint Augustine to those preparing for baptism, there is one numbered 216 in the Maurist edition, which seems to be preparatory both to the baptism they were about to receive and to the instructions by which they were to be trained in that stage. In it, they are reminded of the condition and name of the *competentes*, and of their progress through listening to sermons. It speaks of contempt for the world and the acquisition of the heavenly kingdom; of restraining the senses and fighting against the devil; of their cooperation with Christ the Father and the Church the Mother in the new birth received through baptism, and of the desire they should have for this regeneration [188]. It also contains other matters appropriate to the subject, so that they might preserve the grace they were to receive and be worthy to approach the Lord’s table after the bath.

This is what Saint Augustine teaches. Probably in the same or a scarcely different sense, blessed Nicetas also taught in that preparatory work which we have lost and whose title alone Gennadius preserved for us.

Among the catecheses of Saint Cyril, archbishop of Jerusalem, called *phōtizomenōn* (φωτιζομένων), or “of those being illuminated”—the name given to those who were close to baptism and were called *competentes* among the Latins—there is a first catechesis, indeed placed before the first itself, called the *procatechesis*, or preliminary discourse to the catecheses. In Trithemius’s sense, it too might have been called preparatory.

The purpose of Cyril’s *procatechesis* is to warn those being illuminated with what sincerity of mind, fervor of spirit, purity of heart, and cleanness of soul they ought to approach baptism. It also teaches them to understand the higher rank to which they have ascended from the other stages of the catechumenate [Col. 1043B], in which they will be able to receive matters not entrusted to the others; to hasten to hear the catecheses, persevere in them, preserve forever what they hear and learn in them, and meanwhile disclose nothing to those beneath them who have not yet been illuminated; and finally, to maintain order in the assembly and while listening to the catecheses, persist in prayer, and overcome the snares of the devil and the temptations of unbelievers.

When Saint Cyril exhorts those being illuminated to persevere in hearing the catecheses, the following words, highly pertinent to our subject, are found in § 10 of the same *procatechesis*, according to the edition and translation of the distinguished Touttée [Col. 1043C]:

> “Persevere in the catecheses; even if our discourse should become lengthy, never lose heart. For you will receive weapons against the opposing power; you will take up weapons against heresies, against Jews, Samaritans, and pagans. You have many enemies; receive many weapons. Since you are fighting with many, you must learn how to pierce the Greek, how to fight against the heretic, the Jew, and the Samaritan. The weapons are ready, and the sword of the Spirit is most prepared; but your hands must strive through good will, so that you may wage the Lord’s war, defeat the opposing powers, and show yourself unconquered by all the schemes of the heretics.”

Thus Saint Cyril.

Why, then, should our Nicetas of Aquileia not have had the same purpose as Cyril of Jerusalem in his *procatechesis*, or at least a similar one, in his first preparatory work for those preparing for baptism? According to Gennadius, Nicetas discussed in it how those preparing for baptism ought to conduct themselves—or how they ought to believe and how they ought to act—if they desired to attain the grace of baptism.

You should also observe that the purpose of Cyril’s subsequent catecheses, as expressly indicated in this *procatechesis*, was that those being illuminated should take up from them weapons with which they could appropriately fight against heretics and pagans, as well as against Jews and Samaritans, who were regarded there [Col. 1043D] as the indigenous enemies of Christians.

After his first preparatory work for those preparing for baptism, did not our Nicetas act in the same way as Cyril in his other little books—namely, in the second, On the Errors of Paganism; the third, On the Faith of the One Majesty; and the fourth, Against Genethliology—[189] providing those preparing for baptism with weapons so that they could defend themselves against pagans, heretics, and Jews?

The one surviving fifth work, On the Creed, in which those preparing for baptism are so frequently and deliberately warned and instructed against errors and the teachers of error, sufficiently indicates that this was indeed Nicetas’s purpose: to make those preparing for baptism ready, through his instructions, to resist the enemies and violators of Christian doctrines.

It is therefore probable that in his first preparatory work for those preparing for baptism our Nicetas also warned them beforehand, after Cyril’s manner, that the instructions they were about to hear were directed toward enabling them to take up weapons with which they could fight bravely for the faith they had embraced against every kind of adversary [Col. 1044A].

Yet Nicetas’s first little work contained something distinctive that does not appear in the comparable works of Saint Augustine and Saint Cyril. The four fragments of that same work that fortunately survive, and which will be discussed below together with the others, clearly demonstrate this.

From the first fragment we understand that the subject of the work really was what we have conjectured thus far from Gennadius’s statement and from a review of other sermons of this kind. From the other three—namely, the second, third, and sixth—we further discover that, besides the principal matters belonging to that subject, Nicetas also explained certain other matters to those preparing for baptism, especially the renunciation that had to be made and the significance of that renunciation, as well as exorcisms and their purpose. All these topics suited a preparatory sermon for those preparing for baptism just as well as the other matters we have mentioned.

There follows Nicetas’s second work, likewise lost, On the Errors of Paganism. [Col. 1044B] Gennadius writes of it as follows, from the edition we are using by Joannes Albertus Fabricius in the *Ecclesiastical Library*, and from other sources as well:

> “The second [little book] is On the Errors of Paganism, in which he says that, almost in his own time, a certain householder named Melodius was transferred among the gods by the pagans because of his generosity, and a rustic named Gadarius because of his courage.”

Two of the Gennadian manuscripts cited above differ slightly from the editions here as well, reading:

> “The second is On the Errors of Paganism, in which he indicates that, almost in his own time, a certain householder named Melchidius [or Melgidius] was counted among the gods by the pagans because of his generosity, and a rustic named Garadius [or Graduim] because of his courage.”

The variation in the names is slight and appears to be of no importance; it is therefore enough merely to point it out.

As to the matter itself, there is no doubt that those preparing for baptism received special instruction on the Errors of Paganism, even while they were still serving in the preceding stages of the catechumenate. [Col. 1044C] Whether they had come to the Church from paganism, or whether they had been born to faithful parents but postponed receiving the sacrament of regeneration until adulthood—as seems to have been customary at that time except in danger of death—it was appropriate that the catechumens should be expressly fortified against pagan errors, because pagan superstition was still powerful and widespread everywhere.

The bishops of that age labored so strenuously to extinguish it completely, even in the heart of Italy and in the most distinguished cities, as was shown in the preceding chapter when we replied to Zabeus concerning this very matter.

It is nevertheless clear that the catechumens in the lower stages of the catechumenate did not receive from their instructors everything concerning the errors of paganism. For pagan errors also consisted in corrupting certain Christian truths that, according to the discipline of the Church at that time, could not be disclosed to catechumens—at least not fully and perfectly—and in mockingly attacking the holier matters of the Christians [190], which likewise, under that same ecclesiastical discipline, had not yet been explained to those catechumens [Col. 1044D].

Therefore the catechumens must have received more extensive instruction from the pastors of the churches, even concerning the errors of paganism, once they had reached the rank of the competentes, so that they might approach baptism better prepared and more fully instructed. The sole exceptions were matters taught only to those who had already been baptized.

When, for example, the pastors spoke to the competentes about God in opposition to pagan errors—about God’s existence, unity, omnipotence, providence, justice, mercy, and other matters pertaining to these or resembling them—these things had already been taught to them during their preceding apprenticeship. The pastors could therefore lead them freely into deeper matters, explaining and commending to them Christian doctrine concerning, for instance, the Trinity; disclosing to them the names of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, in whom they were to be baptized; and teaching them the other things concerning this subject that a Christian must know and believe. The ecclesiastical discipline of secrecy then in force had not previously permitted these matters to be handed on to them, at least not in an explicit form [Col. 1045A].

Here, too, the occasion was provided for distinguishing the three Persons in the one God and explaining their relations, and for attacking more broadly the error of the pagans, who not only worshiped several gods received from their ancestors, but also dared to count among the gods human beings who had been taken from the living with some reputation for eminence or some reputation for virtue. Here, moreover, the faith in eternal life was to be disclosed to the competentes, and their hope of attaining it was to be raised: Christians trust that they will become not gods, indeed, but participants in divine glory.

Here also the article concerning the resurrection of the flesh was to be introduced in due time into the minds of the competentes, to be handed on later in its proper order in the Creed. Thus the excellence of Christian faith would become known as surpassing pagan expectation: for it believes and expects not only the blessedness of the soul but also the perpetual blessedness of the body.

But when the errors of paganism had to be attacked in all the absurdities that paganism, no less falsely than maliciously, charged against Christians [Col. 1045B], it was no longer enough to show the competentes that the Christian religion was pure and free from every defilement and disgrace, since it required purity of life and innocence of conduct from its adherents—something they had learned abundantly from the very first instructions they had received upon entering the discipline of the catechumens.

Rather, they had to be led to know more intimately the institutions of the Christian religion, full of a higher wisdom and completely inaccessible to pagans. These institutions prescribe, for example, the guarding and restraint of the senses, bodily discipline, hatred of oneself, love of enemies, and other such practices. Through them, for those who strive after greater perfection, the way of heavenly counsels is opened, so that even while living on earth they may seem in some manner to live the life of angelic spirits.

By these teachings, all the accusations of the pagans against the Christian religion were thoroughly refuted, and the competentes themselves advanced toward a more intimate perception of the purity and excellence of the Christian religion [Col. 1045C], so that they might finally become daily better prepared to obtain the grace of baptism.

These, then, or nearly similar matters, were what the pastors of the churches, according to the discipline of those times, would say to the competentes against the errors of paganism. Why should Nicetas of Aquileia not have taught the same things to his own competentes in the work on *The Errors of Paganism* that we have lost?

Third in Gennadius’s list is Nicetas’ little work *On the Faith of the One Majesty* [*De Fide unicae Majestatis*]; 191 which is identified in precisely the same way by Honorius of Autun, Trithemius, and our Gennadian manuscript codices. We too lament that this little work of Nicetas has been lost; nevertheless, something survives in ancient records from which we can gain at least some knowledge of the work’s purpose and merit.

In the *Diario Italico* of the most distinguished Montfaucon, on page 81, a letter was published from Henry, a cleric of the monastery of Pomposa, to a certain Stephen, concerning the library of that monastery. It was written in the year of Christ 1093. Appended to it is a catalogue of the books that then made up the library, a very rich catalogue indeed for the circumstances of that age. John Albert Fabricius also mentions this letter in volume VI, page 429, of the first edition of his *Bibliotheca Graeca*.

Now, in one of the volumes of this Pomposian library, listed on page 84 of the same *Diario*, after twelve books, as it says there, of Ambrose *On the Trinity*, and likewise book I of Fulgentius *On the Trinity*, and so forth, there is also listed “one book of Bishop Nicetas *On the Method of Faith*” [*de Ratione Fidei*]. Since no works of any Bishop Nicetas are known in ecclesiastical antiquity during the first five centuries, apart from those that Gennadius, the first of all, attributes to his Nicetas, bishop of the city of Romatiana, the single book *On the Method of Faith* listed here by Henry, the Pomposian cleric, simply as the work of Bishop Nicetas, appears to be the same as the single book *On the Faith of the One Majesty* mentioned by Gennadius. It is therefore a work of our Nicetas of Aquileia [Col. 1046A].

Thus, toward the end of the eleventh century, this book of our Nicetas still existed in the monastery of Pomposa, though it later perished. It also bore the title *On the Method of Faith*, a title that somewhat explains the other title transmitted to us by Gennadius, *On the Faith of the One Majesty*. We may therefore understand that this book dealt not only with faith in the one God, but also with the manner of believing, so that the competentes might receive complete instruction concerning faith in God—both as regards the inward act of belief and as regards the outward confession of faith—in accordance with the Apostle’s words: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10:10).

Let us now examine still more notable and clearer evidence concerning this work from a more ancient source. Cassiodorus, in chapter 16 of his book *On the Institution of Divine Scripture*, writes:

> “If anyone wishes to touch briefly upon something concerning the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and does not prefer to weary himself with lengthy reading, let him read the book that Bishop Nicetas (or, in another reading, Nicaeus) wrote concerning the faith. Filled with the clarity of heavenly doctrine, it will lead him by its concise brevity into divine contemplation. It is joined to the volumes of Saint Ambrose that he sent to the emperor Gratian” [Col. 1046B].

This book concerning the faith of Bishop Nicetas, cited by Cassiodorus, can be considered none other than the same book *On the Faith of the One Majesty* mentioned by Gennadius as the work of his Nicetas, whom we have already established as Bishop of Aquileia.

The most distinguished Tillemont, in *Mémoires pour servir à l’histoire ecclésiastique*, volume X, page 626, Venice edition by Pitteri, likewise asserts that Cassiodorus’s words refer to the Gennadian Nicetas—although he himself considers Nicetas not an Aquileian but a Dacian. He adds, however, that he does not know whether the little work of Nicetas indicated there is the third work, *On the Faith of the One Majesty*, mentioned by Gennadius; or the fifth, *On the Creed*; or all six works collected together, which are addressed to the competentes; or rather another book, distinct from those six, unknown to us.

But we know Nicetas’ fifth book, *On the Creed*. Cassiodorus would more readily have said *On the Creed* 192 than *On the Faith*, had he intended to indicate this fifth work in that passage [Col. 1046C]. Nor could he have meant all six works taken together as addressed to the competentes, because the six together would have contained, as is clear from Gennadius’s description, much more than what concerns the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Moreover, reading all six books in order to touch briefly upon something concerning the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit would not have been that concise brevity by which someone would be led into divine contemplation, but rather a lengthy reading suited to wearying the mind. It was precisely to avoid such fatigue that Cassiodorus proposes reading Nicetas’ book *On the Faith*.

Nor is it permissible to infer from Cassiodorus’s words that he meant another book distinct from the six. The book on the faith that he cites, and that Gennadius mentions under the title *On the Faith of the One Majesty*, or *On the Method of Faith*, as in the catalogue of the Pomposian library, must expressly have provided in summary form the matters that every Christian wishes to touch upon concerning the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit [Col. 1046D]. These are the first and principal rudiments of Christian faith, which were also given to the competentes according to the established practice, and indeed with concise brevity.

Since, then, Cassiodorus undoubtedly refers here to Nicetas’ third book, *On the Faith of the One Majesty*, how excellent is the evidence we possess from Cassiodorus’s words concerning this work of Nicetas! Cassiodorus simply calls it *On the Faith*. Yet from the same passage we understand more clearly that the book dealt with the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, since Cassiodorus invited his readers to draw from it what pertained to this faith.

Why should Nicetas’ instruction concerning faith in the Trinity not have had as its principal purpose not only to teach his competentes what they ought to believe concerning this mystery of the Christian religion, but also above all to make them steadfast against heretics, those most audacious violators of this mystery [Col. 1047A]? Thus, once fully instructed in all things, the competentes would be capable of giving, as far as required, an account of their faith and hope, in accordance with the words of the Apostle Peter: “Always ready to make a defense to anyone who demands from you an account of the hope that is in you” (1 Pet. 3:15).

Cassiodorus here asserts and commends the concise brevity of this book of Nicetas. Such brevity was appropriate in a discourse addressed to competentes, who were not to be wearied by excessively extended speech, so that they might more easily retain in memory what they had heard. Cassiodorus also notes the clarity of the heavenly doctrine contained in this little work. This clarity appears to pertain to its style—simple and lucid—as Gennadius himself had indicated in the case of Nicetas’ little works, a clarity that brings illumination to the subject matter.

Cassiodorus further praises the work’s chief merit when he asserts that it contains heavenly doctrine and possesses the power to lead the reader into divine contemplation.

The circumstance that Cassiodorus mentions last increases both the merit and the praise of this little work: namely, that Nicetas’ book *On the Faith* was joined to the volumes of Saint Ambrose that he sent to the emperor Gratian [Col. 1047B].

The books of this holy teacher addressed to the most Christian emperor Gratian Augustus are very well known: specifically, five books *On the Faith*, together with three others *On the Holy Spirit*, written at different times and on different occasions, in order to comply with the pious will of the Caesar, who had requested this writing from him more than once. In these works the holy bishop is wholly occupied with establishing the Catholic faith concerning the Trinity and defending it against the sophistries and calumnies of the heretics—especially the Arians, who were then insolently growing bold, 193 by their sophistries and calumnies [Col. 1047C].

The similarity and nature of their subject matter was doubtless what brought about this association of the books of Ambrose and Nicetas. It is therefore probable that Nicetas’ book both handed on the Catholic doctrine of the Trinity to the competentes and defended it against the distortions of the heretics of that age. Moreover, Nicetas’ little work *On the Faith* must have possessed such distinction that it strengthened this association with Ambrose’s books more and more.

We also possess a record of this association of the books of Ambrose and Nicetas, which Cassiodorus stated had already taken place in the sixth century, in the catalogue of the library of the monastery of Pomposa mentioned shortly before, dating from the end of the eleventh century. There, one book of Bishop Nicetas *On the Method of Faith* is cited immediately after twelve books of Ambrose *On the Trinity* and one book of Fulgentius likewise *On the Trinity*. It is also cited as though contained and bound in the same volume with those books of Ambrose [Col. 1047D].

There are, strictly speaking, no books of Ambrose *On the Trinity*. But under this title *On the Trinity*, the same five books of Ambrose *On the Faith* addressed to the emperor Gratian, together with the three books *On the Holy Spirit*, were formerly catalogued, as the distinguished Benedictine editors of Ambrose’s works explain in their preliminary notices to those books. Thus, even at the end of the eleventh century, the book of Nicetas of Aquileia *On the Faith*, or *On the Method of Faith*, or *On the Faith of the One Majesty*, was found joined to the same volumes of Saint Ambrose that he had sent to the emperor Gratian, just as Cassiodorus, in testimony to his own age, had reported.

Since these books number only eight, they may perhaps have been counted as twelve at that time either because the same books had been divided into twelve parts at the discretion of the scribes, as often happened then, or because four other works by the same Ambrose had been added to those eight, even though they did not have a similar subject. In that period of great obscurity in literary affairs, such an arrangement could very easily have occurred.

Why, then, did this book of Nicetas perish, when it was preserved at the end of the eleventh century in the celebrated monastery of Pomposa? The monastery of Pomposa, once situated not far from the sea, enjoyed an exceptionally healthy climate. Later, when the sea withdrew from the shore, it began to lie among forests and stagnant waters, and gradually became so harmful to health that for nearly three hundred years the monks have abandoned it and transferred themselves to the new and much more magnificent monastery of Saint Benedict at Ferrara. D. Placidus Federicius wrote this in his *History of Pomposian Affairs*, published at Rome in 1781, book I, § 76, page 78 [Col. 1048A]. What wonder, then, if amid that upheaval of circumstances and the transfer of the dwelling many codices of that exceptionally well-stocked library perished, including Nicetas’ book *On the Faith*?

A fourth book of Nicetas addressed to the competentes is now added. It is uniformly entitled by Gennadius, Honorius, and Trithemius *Against Genethlialogy*—with variant forms *Genethlogia*, *Genethliologia*, or even *Genealogia*; but properly and correctly *Genethlialogia*. Our two previously cited codices, which also report this work of Nicetas, both add, in precisely the same words, something rather unusual and worthy of attention:

> “The fourth [book of Nicetas] is *Against Genealogy*, in which he attributes more to free will than it is capable of.”

We must first discuss Nicetas’ book, and then the addition—or rather the judgment—of our Gennadian codices concerning the book.

Γενεθλιαλογία (*genethlialogia*), the proper term for this subject, is “prediction of births” according to Suidas [Col. 1048B], in the *Lexicon*, letter G, L, volume I, page 472 of the Cambridge edition of 1705. The practitioners of this art—or, more truly, this deception—were called *genethliaci*. In antiquity they were also called 194 astrologers and mathematicians, and sometimes Chaldeans. From the position of the stars, which they investigated as it stood on the day someone was born, they dared to predict all his future circumstances.

“Genethliaci were those who gathered everything from the natal constellation and made predictions.” So Pitiscus writes in his *Lexicon* under this word.

Because of the natural human curiosity to know the future, especially matters concerning the course of each person’s life, genethlialogy held great influence among the pagans. Yet even among them there were people who vigorously attacked this art, and the laws of the pagan emperors themselves prohibited it as harmful both to private morality and to the state. This can be seen in Gellius, cited by Pitiscus; in Tacitus, *Annals* II.32; and in the Justinianic Code, book IX, title 38, *On Sorcery and Mathematics* [Col. 1048C].

When the Christian religion had been introduced into the world and large numbers of pagans who detested false gods were daily joining the Church, many of them nevertheless remained so attached to this genethliac superstition that they were unwilling to abandon it. Even among those born to Christian parents and long enrolled among the Christians were people who willingly lent their ears to genethliac deceivers. These men sold oracles concerning the course of their clients’ lives, their condition, their fortunate or unfortunate circumstances, the length of their lives, the manner of their deaths, and so forth.

I shall pass over what the ancient writers tell us about the heretical Priscillianists, who, among the other monstrous errors taught in their foul society, added this madness concerning the influence—or rather the dominion—of the stars over human life. I shall instead say that even men of culture and respectable conduct, raised and nourished within the bosom of the Catholic Church, were sometimes deceived by this fraud.

In the very fifth century in which our Nicetas flourished, Sidonius Apollinaris, in book VIII, letter 11 of his *Letters* [Col. 1048D], reported that a certain Lampridius, his friend, a man endowed with no ordinary learning, highly accomplished in oratorical and poetic ability, and beloved for his social virtues, had once consulted mathematicians about the end of his life. At last, by God’s permission, he was killed by the very violent death that the mathematicians had predicted for him, and at the time they had designated:

> “For whoever,” he added, “presumes to investigate forbidden matters and probe prohibited secrets, I fear that such a person will depart from the rules of the Catholic faith and become worthy of entering a condition in which misfortunes correspond to the things unlawfully sought.”

How important it therefore was in those times for Christian doctrine to fight against the predictions of the genethliaci and to instruct the faithful and the competentes not to lend them hearing or belief, everyone can see.

For besides the fact that genethlialogy was burdened by pagan origin and superstition, like the other divinations of various kinds that formed part of idolatrous worship, it was also wholly directed toward actually destroying all religion, overturning the entire force and rationale of order and discipline, and abolishing every distinction between good and evil. It removed divine providence from human affairs, denied human beings freedom of choice, rejected the power of divine grace, exalted fatalism, and introduced into action a dreadful necessity imposed by the will of the stars [Col. 1049A].

Accordingly, the Fathers frequently spoke against the genethliaci—whether they called them mathematicians, astrologers, or Chaldeans—and against those who made use of their services. I mean frequent admonitions, reproaches, and also disputations, both when the opportunity arose in their sermons and in books expressly written for the purpose. Tertullian, 195 Origen, Lactantius, and Eusebius diligently attacked this art of the mathematicians in their works.

Under the name of Saint Pamphilus the martyr, in Rufinus’s translation, there is a book *Against the Mathematicians* among the works of Origen in Grynaeus’s edition, volume I, page 758 [Col. 1049B]. Macarius the Roman monk, mentioned by Gennadius in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 28, and by Rufinus in book I, chapter 11, of his *Invectives or Apology*, wrote at Rome itself, around the year 401, as Ursius notes in *Ecclesiastical History*, book XXII, no. 26, a book or books *Against Fate or the Art of Mathematics*, that is, *Against the Mathematicians*. Rufinus, who was then living there, assisted him.

What more is needed? Christian emperors also repeatedly and severely acted through their laws against such deceivers. For example, the emperor Honorius, by a law issued in the year 409 and preserved in the Theodosian Code, ordered that they be expelled from Rome and the other cities. Valentinian III likewise, in another law relating to the year 425, issued at Aquileia on 9 July to Amacius, prefect of the Gauls, declared that mathematicians, together with Pelagians, Manichaeans, all heretics, and schismatics, were to be expelled not only from the cities but even from the sight of the various cities.

Since it is sufficiently clear what genethlialogy and the genethliaci were in the ancient centuries of the Church, and since it is also evident how harmful they were considered to Christian faith and how opposed to the Christian name, so that the utterly foolish vanity of the genethliaci was rightly attacked everywhere [Col. 1049C], we now also understand well enough what our Nicetas of Aquileia’s fourth book addressed to the competentes, *Against Genethlialogy*, mentioned by Gennadius, must have been—even though we possess nothing concerning it beyond the bare title, as with the preceding works.

One point here appears worthy of notice: scarcely any other work, or perhaps no other work at all, in the whole of antiquity can be found or identified as having been addressed to the competentes and as having dealt expressly and systematically with genethlialogy and the genethliaci.

Nearly all who wrote instructions for the competentes sharpened their style against this impious folly and its impious practitioners or adherents—whether in explanations of the Creed, explanations of the Lord’s Prayer, or other addresses given before baptism [Col. 1049D]. This can be seen in the many surviving sermons of both Latin and Greek Fathers, especially in the sermons of Saint Peter Chrysologus and in the *Catecheses for the Illuminated* of Saint Cyril of Jerusalem. Yet, I venture to say, among them there is absolutely no sermon or treatise delivered to the competentes whose sole purpose was to attack genethlialogy and the genethliaci deliberately and expressly.

Thus the loss and sorrow caused by this lost little work of Nicetas are increased: from the treasury of ecclesiastical matters there is missing, as it were, a link that would join the sequence of events in this part of the discipline.

We must not, however, conceal the excellent treatise of Saint Zeno of Verona on this subject, which is book 43 of book II in the edition of the Ballerini brothers. But this work is not addressed to competentes before baptism; it is addressed to neophytes after baptism, as is indicated there, and bears the title *On the Twelve Signs*—that is, the twelve signs of the zodiac, from which the genethliaci drew their divinations of future events [Col. 1050A].

This treatise is not properly directed against genethlialogy, which it rather assumes had already been renounced and despised by his neophytes before they were washed. It is instead an elegant and ingenious conversion of the profane observations that the genethliaci made from the signs of the zodiac into sacred use, applied to those who had recently been born through baptism from the womb of Mother Church and still remembered the former superstition of genethlialogy. 196

It is worthwhile to hear the holy bishop addressing his neophytes for a little while, so that it may become clear what ought to have been taught concerning such a subject to the competentes and what to the neophytes:

> “Behold, boys, adolescents, young men, and old men of both sexes, who were guilty of … [lacuna], you are clean infants; and what is wonderful and pleasing, in a single moment you have suddenly become contemporaries despite your different ages. But I know well your curiosity, acquired through your former life; indeed, you will no longer be permitted to indulge it. Perhaps you also ask us by what birth or under what sign [Col. 1050B] your mother, in one single labor, gave birth to so many, so different, and so unlike persons. I shall humor you as one humors little children, and in the briefest possible manner disclose the secrets of the sacred horoscope. Therefore, brothers, this is your nativity. The first to receive you was not Aries but the Lamb, who rejects no one who believes in him and clothed your nakedness in the snowy whiteness of his fleece … [lacuna]. The same One, not the swollen-necked, grim-browed, horn-threatening Bull, but the excellent, gentle, kindly, and mild Calf, admonishes you: do not seek omens in any work, but, following his yoke without malice, tame and cultivate the earth of your flesh, so that you may carry a joyful harvest of divine seeds into the heavenly storehouses, and so forth.”

Thus Saint Zeno speaks to the neophytes. He proceeds in the same manner through the remaining signs of the zodiac, turning the profaneness of the genethliaci into instruction for the neophytes.

So much concerning Nicetas’ little work *Against Genethlialogy*, or rather concerning the subject on the occasion of this little work [Col. 1050C].

What are we now to say about the judgment of our manuscript copies of Gennadius concerning this same work—namely, that Nicetas “attributes more to free will than it is capable of”? This addition is so peculiar to our two manuscript copies of Gennadius, by which Nicetas’ little work *Against Genethlialogy* is charged with an excessive exaltation of free will, and the author is therefore tacitly branded with the fault either of Pelagianism or of Semipelagianism, that it is found nowhere in the printed editions. Nor is it indicated anywhere as having ever been read, at least in any manuscript codex—except for John Joseph Liruti, who reproduces the whole article of Gennadius on Nicetas from one of these two codices, in volume I, page 113, of his previously cited work *News of the Lives of the Men of Letters of Friuli*. There, following his own inclination, he discusses Nicetas the Dacian, without adding any comment on this singular judgment.

What, then, should be said either for Nicetas or against him on this matter, since the little work is not available, and it alone could provide grounds either for convicting Nicetas of error or clearing him of blame [Col. 1050D]?

For the present, what seems highly probable to us concerning this addition is that it is not a writing of Gennadius, but rather the work of some reckless interpolator, or even of a copyist—probably one from this region—since we know that the addition exists only in the manuscript codices of this area, of which one also appears to have been derived from the other.

Certainly Gennadius, who was in no way hostile to Pelagianism or Semipelagianism, would never have censured this work of Nicetas for excessively exalting free will beyond its proper powers, since, in the view of Pelagians and Semipelagians, those powers are great and endowed with much virtue.

Moreover, if Gennadius had actually appended this judgment to Nicetas’ little work *Against Genethlialogy*, Honorius of Autun—who copied Gennadius almost word for word everywhere in his work *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, and who mentioned our Nicetas there in nearly the same words as Gennadius [Col. 1051A]—would not have been silent about this distinctive point. It was certainly of great importance and useful for understanding the author’s mind.

Trithemius, too, who took from Gennadius and Honorius what he reported in his own similarly titled book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, and who, from the manner in which he wrote about our Nicetas and his works, seems also to have had the little works themselves before his eyes, would have mentioned this judgment if he had actually found it in the older authors.

This censorious addition to Nicetas’ little work *Against Genethlialogy*, which our two Gennadian codices present to us, therefore does not appear to be the offspring of Gennadius.

Nor does our Nicetas appear in any way to deserve accusation of Pelagianism or Semipelagianism because he may perhaps have seemed to exalt the powers of free will further than was proper. Since neither Honorius nor Trithemius says anything against the soundness of our Nicetas’ view concerning the power of human choice, why should we trust an uncertain author—or rather an irresponsible interpolator—of this Gennadian section on Nicetas, 197 or even a copyist, who arrogated to himself the authority to injure Nicetas’s reputation?

Besides, our Nicetas, who was fighting genethlialogy in that work, necessarily had to attack fatalism and the fatalists expressly. Their doctrine was to make the human will purely passive and to introduce into human actions a genuine necessity that individual human beings, according to the genethliaci, had received from their very origin through the commanding and inescapable influence of the stars.

Nicetas therefore had to defend the power of free will with all his strength in that work, if he was to engage genethlialogy and the genethliaci in battle with an ordered line. He had to explain the limits of this power and show how far and how widely they extended, so that people could not acquire an excuse for evil actions under the pretext of an innate necessity.

What wonder, then, if, as an advocate for free will against fatalism, Nicetas seemed to have magnified the power of free will [Col. 1051C] even beyond what was reasonable, in order to overthrow fatalism more completely? This often happens when a cause of this kind is being argued: someone may appear excessive on his own side while defending the truth against an opponent who has injured it.

Saint Augustine likewise made this observation concerning free will, as regards grace, in book 47 of *On the Grace of Christ*, against Pelagius and Coelestius:

> “This question,” he said, “in which free choice of the will and the grace of God are debated, is so difficult to distinguish that when free will is defended, God’s grace seems to be denied; but when God’s grace is asserted, free will is thought to be taken away.”

Nicetas was not speaking here, while acting against genethlialogy and the genethliaci, about the grace of God, but only about free will in opposition to fatalism and the fatalists, for whom freedom of choice did not exist.

Although Nicetas therefore magnified the powers of human choice against such adversaries, he did so only in order to destroy the fatalism of genethlialogy, not to weaken the grace of God. There was no reason at that time for him to debate the rights of grace, which, in the presence of free will, seemed in some manner to vanish, as Augustine testifies [Col. 1051D].

Who, however, does not know that the power of human choice is indeed extensive, and such that God can justly inflict punishment on sinners for the abuse of their freedom and confer rewards in justice for its proper use? The only thing to be feared is what the same holy teacher said in book 4 of *On Grace and Free Will*: that statements made in defense 198 of free will

> “be understood in such a way that no place is left for the help and grace of God in the pious life and good conduct to which eternal reward is owed; and that miserable human beings, when they live well … dare to glory in themselves rather than in the Lord and place in themselves the hope of living rightly.”

Thus, even if Nicetas was perhaps more expansive, given the nature of his subject, in defending free will against genethlialogy, which entirely abolished freedom of choice, who [Col. 1052A] could ever persuade himself that he had in reality left no place for the help and grace of God, so that a person living well by his freedom must nevertheless glory not in himself but in the Lord and place in him the hope of living rightly?

The judgment of that unknown interpolator of the Gennadian text must therefore be rejected. He certainly investigated Nicetas’ little work with more scrupulousness and subtlety than was appropriate, and, while intending to point out an error, actually brought a false accusation.

We now come to the fifth little work.

When we deal with Nicetas’ fifth little work, *On the Creed*, there is no room for conjecture concerning its subject and contents. We possess the little work itself complete. It was unearthed at Rome from the Chigi Library, and we owe it to the generosity of the most eminent cardinal, patron and leader of all the learned men of Italy, whom we still mourn as prematurely taken from us, Stefano Borgia. While he was living at Padua in the ninety-ninth year of the previous century—that is, 1799—he entrusted it there for publication and made it available for the enlightenment of scholars [Col. 1052B].

It is, specifically, an *Explanation of the Creed for the Competentes*, in which the Creed itself is expounded, explained, and illustrated point by point. Each section is furnished with appropriate admonitions, as the circumstances of the time and the capacity of the hearers required.

This little work is of the same nature and purpose as so many other sermons on the Creed addressed to the competentes, which are read throughout the works of the holy Fathers, especially in Saint Augustine, Saint Peter Chrysologus, Saint Maximus of Turin, and others.

The Creed of faith was not handed over or explained to catechumens before they had reached the highest rank of the competentes. At that point, while the scrutinies continued—scrutinies held shortly before baptism to examine the capacity and progress of the competentes—the Creed of faith was solemnly handed over to them. A sermon was usually added to stir their diligence in learning, memorizing, and retaining it, together with an explanation of the same Creed that would in some manner assist their memory and open their understanding [Col. 1052C].
