In the final scrutinies, which immediately preceded the reception of baptism, the competentes also solemnly recited from memory the Creed of faith they had learned—once, twice, or even more often, according to the differing custom of the churches in this matter. A sermon by the bishop then followed, in which the Creed they had recited was explained at greater length. The sermon also contained admonitions, whether concerning faith or conduct, as the matter required and the needs of the hearers demanded.

On the handing over of the Creed and on the recitation of the Creed, one may consult sermons 212, 213, 214, and 215 of Saint Augustine in the Maurist edition, as well as sermon 58 of Saint Peter Chrysologus and other sermons on the Apostles’ Creed. Other matters concerning the ancient practice of handing the Creed over to the competentes and receiving it back from them are explained throughout the works of those who treat ecclesiastical affairs, and they are more familiar to scholars than to require explanation here [Col. 1052D].

[199] Yet concerning this Explanation of ours by Saint Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, one might reasonably ask whether it should be regarded as having been delivered by him at the handing over of the Creed to the competentes, or rather at their recitation of it. The Explanation itself must therefore be consulted, so that the matter in question may be discerned. What first appears in the Explanation of the Creed by Bishop Nicetas is the renunciation, which is indicated as already having been carried out by those to whom the Creed was being explained there. For Nicetas says:

> “He who believes in Christ . . . renounces the enemy, his angels, and every form of magical curiosity . . . Having therefore freed himself from these evils, and having thrown these chains behind his back, as it were, into the face of the enemy, he now declares in the language of the Creed: ‘I believe in God the Father,’ etc.”

The same fact—that the renunciation had already been made by those to whom this sermon was delivered—is also confirmed at the end of the Explanation in these words:

> “Whenever the enemy has touched your mind with fear, [Col. 1053A] or greed, or anger, answer him threateningly, saying: ‘I have renounced you, and I renounce you, together with your works and your angels, because I have believed in the living God and in his Christ,’ etc.”

According to the ancient custom of the Church, renunciation was made not only at the time of baptism—that is, immediately before the saving bath—but also before the solemn profession of faith, which consisted in the recitation of the Creed that had been received, as well as in the repeated answer “I believe” to each of the questions concerning the articles of the Creed. This took place several days before baptism, during the scrutinies that preceded it.

> “For what is the first confession of Christians in saving baptism? What else, indeed, except that they declare that they renounce the devil and his pomps, spectacles, and works? . . . ‘I renounce,’ you say, ‘the devil, his pomps, spectacles, and works.’ And what afterward? ‘I believe,’ you say, ‘in God the almighty Father, and in Jesus Christ his Son.’ Therefore one first renounces the devil in order to believe in God, because whoever does not renounce the devil does not believe in God.”

[Col. 1053B] Thus wrote Salvian in the fifth century itself, in *On the Government of God*, book VI, chapter 6. Saint Isidore likewise wrote, in the century after the fifth, in book II of *Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 24:

> “The first compact is that by which one renounces the devil, his pomps, and his entire way of life.”

See Joseph Vicecomes, *On the Ancient Rites of Baptism*, book II, chapter 24, on this subject.

But what in particular may be said about the Church of Aquileia? Our own Saint Nicetas provides the clearest testimony on this matter in the third of the surviving Viennese fragments. This fragment seems to belong to his first little work, mentioned by Gennadius, about which we spoke above. There, while instructing his competentes also about the manner of renunciation, he says plainly:

> “For one does not come to confession before the devil has first been renounced. Just as a goldsmith does not put gold into a purse before he has first washed away all the earth or mud.”

It is also useful to look briefly at the Rituals of this same Church [Col. 1053C], so that its concord with the other churches in the discipline under discussion may become still clearer. I do not mean Rituals from that same fifth century, in which Nicetas flourished, but certainly Rituals which, although of a later age, preserved traces of the ancient discipline of Nicetas’s own time.

The distinguished De Rubeis, in his dissertation *On the Sacred Rites of the Forojulians*, chapter 26, first from codices of various antiquity belonging to the notable Collegiate Church of Cividale, and then also from other codices of this province, as well as from the *Agenda* of the diocese of Aquileia printed at Venice in 1575, produces the rites that were in use in the Aquileian diocese in [200] the administration of baptism, especially baptism administered to children, after the orders of catechumens and competentes, as well as the order of the scrutinies, had already fallen into disuse. This is believed to have happened after the ninth, or certainly after the tenth, century throughout the Western Church, although not everywhere at the same time, as normally happens in similar matters.

[Col. 1053D] The rite of administering baptism introduced in this later period is composed of all the rites that formerly prevailed among catechumens and competentes and that took place during the scrutinies preceding baptism. De Rubeis also notes this in his *Dissertations of Various Learning*, chapter 31, no. 5. Thus it may rightly be said that this later rite, both in substance and in order, is a kind of abridgment of the ancient rite, inasmuch as what formerly constituted a long course of activity and an exercise extending over many days was completed within the space of a short hour. The same must likewise be said of the Roman order now in force, both for the baptism of children and for the baptism of adults: this abbreviated order too may be regarded as a condensation of the ancient rites that prevailed in earlier centuries.

In these later rites for administering baptism, which were in force in the Church and diocese of Aquileia, renunciation always preceded both the recitation of the Creed and the profession of faith from the Creed—whether [Col. 1054A] renunciation took place only once, or whether, according to the ancient custom of the Church, it was repeated, as may be seen there and especially in the *Agenda* cited above. We must therefore believe that the discipline of the Church of Aquileia in the fifth century was also of this kind: namely, that renunciation always preceded the profession of faith of the competentes, so that only after renunciation had been completed did they recite in the scrutinies the Creed that they had previously received for learning, and answer the questions concerning the articles of the Creed about which they were questioned individually.

Since, therefore, it appears in the Explanation of the Creed by the blessed Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, that the competentes with whom he was then speaking had already made their renunciation, that Explanation may reasonably be believed to have been delivered to the competentes during the scrutinies, at the time of their recitation of the Creed—or rather immediately after its recitation—in order to strengthen their resolve in the faith and fortify their virtue.

[Col. 1054B] What confirms the matter still further, which we infer from the discipline of that period and also from the particular discipline of the Church of Aquileia, are the words of our Nicetas in chapter 15 of the Explanation. There, bringing his sermon to a close, he says:

> “Since this is so, beloved, remain in what you have learned and what has been handed down to you. Always retain the compact that you made with the Lord—that is, this Creed, which you confess before angels and human beings.”

Here, unmistakably, the Creed had previously been handed over to the competentes: “what has been handed down to you”; afterward it had been committed to memory by the competentes: “what you have learned”; then it had been solemnly recited by them in a profession of faith: “which you confess before angels and human beings.” They were therefore admonished to retain it as a compact made with the Lord: “Always retain the compact that you made with the Lord—that is, this Creed.”

This Explanation of the Creed, then, was delivered by our Aquileian Nicetas to the competentes during the scrutinies, at the time of the recitation of the Creed. We now come to the sixth little book or work.

[Col. 1054C] The sixth book of Nicetas addressed to the competentes has everywhere the same title, *On the Sacrifice of the Paschal Lamb*. Since this book is among the lost works, its subject must to some extent be conjectured. Nevertheless, under the metaphorical title *On the Sacrifice of the Paschal Lamb*, we can have no doubt that it dealt explicitly with the most holy sacrament of the Eucharist.

[201] Although the competentes were not admitted before baptism to the knowledge of the innermost mysteries of the Christian religion, they nevertheless had to be instructed at some point, at least in part, concerning this most august mystery, before they approached the saving bath. For who does not know that the competentes, reborn through sacred baptism and called neophytes, the infants of Mother Church, were admitted on that very night of Easter, immediately from the sacred font, as though still wet with the saving water, to the most sacred table of the heavenly Lamb?

The distinguished Vicecomes cited above, in *On the Ancient Rites of Baptism*, book V, chapters 34 and following, demonstrates this with extensive learning, both with respect to adults and with respect to children themselves who were washed in sacred baptism. Other later interpreters of ancient discipline likewise demonstrate it, so that there is no need to add more.

[Col. 1054D] Nevertheless, anyone would gladly hear Saint Augustine speak on this matter in the following way, in sermon 227, which is sermon 4 *On the Day of Easter* and bears the title *To Infants, on the Sacraments*:

> “I remember my promise. For I promised you who have been baptized a sermon in which I would explain the sacrament of the Lord’s table, which you now also see and of which you became participants last night. You ought to know what you have received, what you are about to receive, and what you ought to receive daily, etc.”

Here, then, on the very night of Easter, are the competentes, already made infants of Mother Church through the baptism they had received, immediately becoming participants in the Lord’s table, at which they had received in reality the body and blood of Christ.

The competentes therefore had to be instructed at some point, at least to the extent necessary, concerning the sacrament of the Eucharist, so that they might know what they were about to receive after baptism on that very [Col. 1055A] night of Easter. This, therefore, must have been Nicetas’s purpose in the little work *On the Sacrifice of the Paschal Lamb*, the sixth and last of the books or sermons that he delivered to the competentes.

There is scarcely any other mention—or perhaps not even scarcely any—in all antiquity of a sermon expressly delivered to the competentes concerning the sacrament of the Eucharist, apart from this one by Nicetas, which too has perished and whose title alone Gennadius preserved for us. Why is this so?

Certainly, in ancient times a full and complete instruction concerning the sacrament of the Eucharist was not given to those who had not yet been initiated, because the discipline of secrecy was then carefully observed. Those who had not yet been initiated were considered to be all who had not yet been washed in the saving bath, whether they were catechumens or competentes.

For this reason Saint Ambrose, [Col. 1055B] who wrote a book *On the Mysteries* for the newly baptized and and also treats expressly, in the third place, of the sacrament of the Eucharist—which he asserts they had received immediately after baptism—spoke to them in this way in chapter 1, section 2:

> “The time now urges us to speak about the Mysteries and to set forth the very meaning of the sacraments. If, before baptism, we had thought that this should be disclosed to those not yet initiated, we would be judged to have betrayed rather than revealed it.”

He then gives another reason for his silence about these mysteries before baptism and continues:

> “Moreover, the very light of the mysteries would have poured itself more effectively into those who were unaware, than if some discourse had preceded it.”

It is therefore clear that even the competentes themselves were to be understood as not yet initiated before baptism. Consequently, the meaning of the sacraments was not yet to be disclosed to them, and no sermon concerning these same mysteries had preceded their initiation, so that the mysteries themselves were presented to them while they were unaware.

Indeed, the sermons delivered by Saint Augustine on Easter *On the Sacraments* were not addressed to competentes but to infants—that is, to those already baptized. Such are, for example, the recently cited sermon 227 and also sermon 229, in which he treats the sacrament of the Eucharist and speaks of it as something they had received after baptism on the preceding night.

[Col. 1055C] Saint Gaudentius of Brescia likewise addressed his treatise—or second sermon—*On the Meaning of the Sacraments*, not to competentes but to neophytes who had left the font, that is, to those immediately baptized. In it he addresses them concerning the sacrament of the Eucharist, which they were about to receive.

What, then? Shall we say that our most holy Nicetas disclosed the mystery of the Eucharist when he wrote a book, or sermon, concerning it for the competentes?

I think the matter must be distinguished and clarified, so that we may understand what Nicetas’s sermon or book *On the Sacrifice of the Paschal Lamb* for the competentes actually was, or could have been.

Although the mystery of the Eucharist was among those things that ought not to be disclosed to the uninitiated, and therefore not even to the competentes, nevertheless, since they were to become participants in that same mystery on the very night of Easter, when they were regenerated through the bath, they could not be admitted to the sacred table as entirely ignorant and unprepared.

[Col. 1055D] The arrangement of those times therefore seems to have been as follows: throughout the entire period during which the competentes were preparing, even immediately, for baptism, they were to understand absolutely nothing concerning the mystery of the Eucharist; as the day of Easter approached, they were to be instructed about it only very briefly, and only in what concerned simple faith in so great a mystery; finally, once they had become neophytes, they were to be instructed more fully and extensively, during the remaining days of Easter week, about this mystery and about the other matters which, according to the discipline of the Church, were communicated only to the initiated.

We understand this arrangement clearly from the Catecheses of Saint Cyril of Jerusalem, and it is not out of place to recall it here. In Catechesis 13 for those being enlightened—that is, those being baptized, who, as we noted above, among the Greeks were the same as the competentes in the Latin Church—when, in chapter 19, the subject briefly concerned the body of Christ under the appearance of bread, on the occasion of that prophetic text, “Come, and let us [Col. 1056A] cast wood into his bread,” he addressed those being enlightened as follows:

> “If the Lord should judge you worthy, you will learn hereafter that, according to the Gospel, his body bore the figure of bread.”

Thus the mystery of the Eucharist was not yet disclosed to those being enlightened—that is, to the competentes—because of the reverence owed to silence. It was promised that it would be disclosed afterward, if the Lord should deem them worthy; that is, if they should prove worthy of sacred baptism after hearing the catecheses and completing the scrutinies.

But what did Saint Cyril mean by “hereafter”? The holy Father explains himself concerning the appropriate time for disclosing the mystery of the Eucharist to those being enlightened in Catechesis 18, which likewise was addressed to these same persons. In chapters 32 and 33, in the conclusion of the catechesis, he addresses them as follows:

> “Beloved brothers, this discourse of instruction exhorts all of you to prepare your soul for the reception of heavenly gifts. Concerning the holy and apostolic faith handed down to you for confession, which, by the grace of the Lord, we have expounded in catecheses during these past days of Lent . . . As the holy [Col. 1056B] day of Easter approaches, when your love in Christ will be enlightened through the bath of regeneration, you will again, God willing, be instructed concerning matters that accord with this—with how much devotion, etc. . . . and with what reverence and order it is necessary to proceed from baptism to the holy altar of God, and to partake of the spiritual and heavenly mysteries distributed there, so that your soul, first enlightened by the discourse of instruction, may individually recognize the greatness of the gifts bestowed upon you by God. After the holy and saving day of Easter, beginning on the second day of the week, you will hear further catecheses on each succeeding day of the week, God willing. In them you will again be instructed concerning the meaning and reasons of each of the things that will have been accomplished in you . . . and concerning the mysteries of the New Testament that are present upon the altar, which began here, what the divine Scriptures have handed down concerning them, and what their power and efficacy are; also how one ought to approach them, when, and how they are to be received . . . These matters, if God wills, will be explained by us.”

[Col. 1056C] Thus Saint Cyril of Jerusalem.

Here, then, is what he understood by “hereafter” with respect to explaining the mystery of the Eucharist to those being enlightened with whom he was then speaking—or, as one might say in Latin usage, to the competentes.

He indicated two occasions for speaking about this mystery. The first was as the holy day of Easter approached, when they were about to be enlightened through the bath of regeneration in Christ. This could consist only in a brief and condensed discourse, intended to arouse faith in and reverence for so great a mystery; for among the competentes, who had recently been initiated in religious matters, a more elaborate discourse would not have been possible.

The second occasion was a fuller treatment after the holy day of Easter, in the other catecheses, where he promises to speak about the mysteries of the New Testament present upon the altar, what the divine Scriptures have handed down concerning them, and what their power and efficacy are.

[Col. 1056D] As the distinguished editor of Cyril’s works, Touttée, also notes:

> “Since in the catecheses before baptism it was forbidden to disclose the mysteries to those being baptized, but it was nevertheless necessary not to admit them to those mysteries unprepared and entirely ignorant of them, their fuller exposition was postponed to the subsequent period; on the very night of Easter they were instructed briefly about them, as far as the time permitted, before they approached them.”

We possess the fuller explanation of the mystery of the Eucharist that Cyril had promised his candidates after baptism. It is Catechesis 22, or Mystagogical Catechesis 4, which, according to the preceding notice of the distinguished editor, he delivered on Holy Thursday of Easter week.

But we desire the briefer discourse that he promised to deliver as the holy day of Easter approached, that is, on the very night of Easter:

> “But these instructions of Cyril, given at the time of baptism itself, seem more like timely admonitions than sermons delivered from the pulpit,”

as the same most learned interpreter likewise notes. It is therefore not surprising that they have not come down to us, since perhaps Saint Cyril did not even commit them to writing.

[Col. 1057A] What, then, should we think about our Nicetas’s little book or sermon *On the Sacrifice of the Paschal Lamb* addressed to the competentes?

If this discourse of Nicetas on the Sacrifice of the Paschal Lamb was truly delivered to the competentes, we may say that it was a brief address to them concerning the mystery of the Eucharist, delivered immediately before they proceeded to the baptistery, and therefore as the day of Easter approached, when they were already about to be enlightened. Thus, after receiving regeneration, they could approach the sacred altar sufficiently instructed concerning the Sacrifice of the Paschal Lamb, of which they were to become participants.

But was this instruction on the Sacrifice of the Paschal Lamb addressed to the competentes properly so called? Or rather was it addressed to neophytes or infants, [204] whom Gennadius and Honorius did not distinguish from the competentes in their catalogues of Nicetas’s books, because this last little work has such close affinity with the five preceding works that were truly delivered to the competentes, and because it was delivered to the same audience who had [Col. 1057B] shortly before been competentes?

This could very easily have happened. In that case, this little work of Nicetas, or sermon *On the Sacrifice of the Paschal Lamb*, may have been delivered to competentes who had already become infants of Mother Church, on the very day of Easter after they had received the Eucharist, as in the sermons of Saint Augustine mentioned above; or on the other days of Easter week, as in the sermons of Saint Ambrose, which later coalesced into the cited book *On the Mysteries*, and as in Mystagogical Catechesis 4 of Saint Cyril of Jerusalem.

Why should it not rather have been delivered to competentes who had already become neophytes, immediately after they had left the font, like the second sermon of Gaudentius of Brescia cited above? According to the same author’s testimony in his fifth sermon or treatise, that sermon was delivered on the most splendid night of the Easter vigil, so that the inexperienced neophytes might learn the discipline governing the eating of the paschal sacrifice. It was therefore delivered immediately after they had received baptism and before they consumed the Eucharist.

[Col. 1057C] The same seems to be true of another sermon of Augustine, entitled *On the Sacrament of the Altar for Infants*. This is the third in order among his unpublished sermons, which the distinguished Michael Denis, otherwise often praised, first published in 1792 from the manuscripts of the Palatine Library of Vienna, in a Viennese edition. He also calls this sermon an excellent preparation for holy Communion and assigns it a place in the Maurist edition after sermon 228.

I shall add one point here concerning this little book or sermon of Nicetas, whenever it was delivered and to whatever audience—whether competentes, neophytes who had left the font, or infants. The title it bears, *On the Sacrifice of the Paschal Lamb*, corresponds perfectly to the subject of the entire second treatise or sermon of Saint Gaudentius of Brescia addressed to neophytes who had left the font.

Since that sermon concerns the mystery of the Eucharist, it is wholly occupied with explaining the allegory of the Jewish paschal lamb, which had been a type of the body of Christ that we were to receive in the mystery of the altar. From the laws written in the Book of Exodus concerning the sacrifice and eating of that typical lamb, Gaudentius most elegantly extracts, illustrates, and commends the dispositions of soul [Col. 1057D] with which the faithful, once instructed, ought to approach the sacred table of the new covenant prefigured there.

Why should Nicetas’s little book *On the Sacrifice of the Paschal Lamb* not likewise have had the same purpose in instructing its hearers about the mystery of the Eucharist as the sermon or treatise of Saint Gaudentius of Brescia?

It could also have happened that the title of Nicetas’s sermon was supplied either by the author himself, or by Gennadius, or by others, as *On the Sacrifice of the Paschal Lamb* rather than *On the Sacrament of the Eucharist* or *On the Mystery of the Altar*, so that the ancient discipline of secrecy might be observed more cautiously. Meanwhile, initiates already understood the subject of the sermon sufficiently under this veil, whereas the uninitiated would not have grasped it at all, even if they had heard of it by report.

But what if we say that Nicetas’s little book or sermon *On the Sacrifice of the Paschal Lamb* was merely an explanation of that typical Jewish rite, intended to prepare the minds of the hearers for learning the mystery at the proper time, without the discourse meanwhile descending to any [Col. 1058A] explanation of the mystery itself?

In that case, this sermon could have been delivered to the competentes properly so called before baptism, without any violation of the discipline then in force. No occasion for the difficulties that we have so far labored to unravel would consequently arise from it, although, even [205] on this hypothesis, I do not regret having said what I have said about them.

The last book of Nicetas listed by Gennadius and others is no longer concerned with competentes but with penitents. It is a certain rebuke—and a very vehement one—addressed to a fallen virgin, who is presented as being then receiving public penance from the bishop for a publicly known offense.

Gennadius and Honorius indicate this little work in the following way:

> “He also published—or composed—a little book addressed to the fallen Virgin, an incentive to amendment for nearly all who fall.”

The two native copies of Gennadius mentioned earlier, omitting the word “nearly,” read:

> “He gave a little book addressed to the fallen Virgin, an incentive to amendment for all who fall.”

This little book had long been known—in fact, for a long time it was the only work among the seven [Col. 1058B] mentioned by Gennadius that was known to scholars—although it did not reveal itself with certainty as a genuine product of Nicetas and wandered about with an uncertain parentage. Nevertheless, it had the fortunate distinction of being judged not unworthy of inclusion among the writings of both Augustine and Jerome; above all, it occupied a place among the genuine works of Ambrose, even in the most complete Maurist edition of the works of Ambrose.

The recent emergence of the Explanation of the Creed for the competentes under the name of Bishop Nicetas finally solved the problem and shed light upon it. The work of Gennadius’s Nicetas, to which that Explanation of the Creed was without hesitation attributed, and the little book addressed to the fallen Virgin, were now recognized as belonging together. This seemed so to learned men, and to Zabeus himself; we too expressly confirmed it in chapter 1 of this dissertation.

[Col. 1058C] In the Veronese edition of the works of Saint Jerome prepared by the distinguished Vallarsi, this little book occupies a place among the spurious works, volume XI, column 178, under the title *Rebuke of the Fallen Susanna*. Among the genuine works of Saint Ambrose, however, where the Maurist editors placed it with other known writings by the same holy doctor on the same subject, concerning virginity and virgins, in volume II of the Paris folio edition of 1690, it bears the title *On the Fall of a Consecrated Virgin*.

This variation in titles does nothing to injure the little book; indeed, when the subject is considered in both titles together, it explains the content more precisely. It is a genuine rebuke addressed to a consecrated virgin named Susanna, who had fallen.

It is preferable to transcribe an epitome of the little book from the admonition that the most learned Benedictine editors prefixed to it:

> “This work contains a most vehement reproach by which the bishop, with the deepest sorrow of heart, rebukes a girl who, after promising virginity at the altar, had repeatedly allowed herself to be violated by an impudent young man and was said to have killed the child conceived by him. The offense was enormous by its very nature, but it was made much more serious by many other circumstances, especially the offense that followed from it among the people. Susanna—for that was her name—was [Col. 1058D] descended from a noble family. When she had resolved to preserve perpetual chastity, she was unable to overcome the contrary wishes of her parents until, as she solemnly affirmed, she was moved to do so by certain terrifying visions.

> “On the very feast of the Lord’s resurrection, in the principal basilica, near the altar to which crowds of neophytes had led her with lighted candles, she pronounced her vows, the entire people responding, ‘Amen.’ Immediately afterward, following the customary exhortation, the bishop placed the veil upon her and admitted her, together with the other holy women, into the convent. There he did not neglect to instruct her frequently with suitable admonitions.

> “Yet she did not lead a life so remote from every appearance and likeness of wrongdoing that, not long afterward, her chastity was not attacked by hostile rumors. Susanna bore this with the utmost impatience. The bishop, joining his efforts with those of her parent, labored in vain to discover the authors of the slander and subject them to canonical penalties.

> “Since this ought to have made her more cautious, nevertheless, after three years [Col. 1059A] had passed, she truly committed the crime of which she had previously suffered the false accusation, and did so amid great scandal among both Jews and pagans. She moved every stone in order to conceal it, and she could not be brought by any means to confess it.

> “At last, convicted before the bishop, she was assigned to public penance. When she had already begun to perform it, the same bishop set out to confront her with the most severe address, of which this writing consists. Having placed before her eyes the enormity of the crime, both by enumerating its circumstances and by removing her excuses, he taught her that the one remedy remaining to her was penance equal to her sin.

> “If she bore its labors and disgrace nobly to the end of her life, he promised that she would escape the unceasing punishments of hell that were due to her. He also addressed the corrupter of this falsely named virgin and, by the example of Balthasar as well as of the Sodomites and Gomorrhans, declared what punishments awaited him unless he showed corresponding fruits of repentance. He urged him to do so by setting before him the unavoidable necessity of the final judgment.

> “Finally, returning to Susanna, [Col. 1059B] he prescribed for her the daily recitation of Psalm 50 and further suggested various dispositions of mind by which she might move herself to sorrow and God to mercy.”

Thus far the Benedictine editors; and such, indeed, is the little book of our Nicetas.

In praise of this little book Gennadius writes that it is an incentive to amendment for all, or nearly all, who fall. We most willingly subscribe to Gennadius’s commendation, which estimates the book’s intimate merit, and anyone who has read the book itself will subscribe to it as well.

Yet this book deserves from us and from students of ecclesiastical affairs more than any commendation, on account of the precious monuments of fifth-century rites that it contains: both as regards the intention of virginity and the discipline of sacred virgins, and as regards the order of penance imposed, according to the institution of the Church, on those guilty of more serious offenses, who were to be punished by public humiliation and affliction.

[Col. 1059C] All learned men who have undertaken to illustrate either the history of the sacred virgins of the ancient Church or the public penance performed for public sins have regarded this little book addressed to the fallen Virgin as a treasure from which they could extract useful information for their subject—information most of which they would scarcely have found elsewhere. It is enough for us, while hastening on to other matters, to have indicated this much.

Having examined the seven little books of Nicetas listed by Gennadius, of which only two survive complete, we now proceed to certain fragments or remains of the lost works. The sole consolation in such a loss is one of which scholars have until now been deprived, and of which we too might have been deprived had not the love of letters and the skill of the distinguished Michael Denis, formerly prefect of the Palatine Library of Vienna and recently deceased, provided for the advancement and adornment of ecclesiastical scholarship.

The learned man knew that only one or two of the seven little books of Nicetas mentioned by Gennadius survived complete. He therefore judged that it would be most welcome and useful if we possessed at least some *leipsana*—λείψανα, “remains”—of the lost works. He found these in one of the ancient Latin codices of the same library, which he had undertaken to examine and illustrate.

These remains of Bishop Nicetas, six in number, were made publicly available in volume II, part 3, [Col. 1059D] of Denis’s work, published at Vienna in 1802, entitled *Theological Manuscript Codices of the Palatine Library of Vienna: Latin and Other Languages of the West*. We now proceed to examine them individually.

[207] Not all these *leipsana*—λείψανα, “remains”—of our Nicetas can properly and strictly be called fragments of his lost works. Some truly are fragments: passages of the works as they appeared in them, and as they were written and uttered by the author, reproduced in full in the work of which that codex consists and whose title is *The Order, or Brief Explanation, of Instructing the Unlearned in the Faith*.

Others, however, are not so much complete passages of the works as their meaning, which the author of the codex [Col. 1060A] adapted to his own discourse and, as it were, claimed for himself, while nevertheless retaining, insofar as the subject and course of the discourse permitted, the author’s own words. These, rather than fragments of Nicetas’s lost works, might perhaps more suitably be called “remains,” so as to distinguish them from genuine and proper fragments.

The first fragment—or rather remain—of this second kind appears to be the first. In it Nicetas is not speaking; rather, the author of *The Order, or Brief Explanation, of Instructing the Unlearned in the Faith* draws upon Nicetas and upon Nicetas’s thoughts and words. For it is this author himself who is speaking—not instructing competentes, as Nicetas did, but admonishing those who had to instruct beginners in faith and religion concerning the manner and method of teaching. He has taken Nicetas’s doctrine and adapted it to his own purpose, as will be evident to every reader:

> “It is necessary to examine the instructions required by those who are running toward the faith . . . Through them those chosen for baptism are taught, so that they may know what they have abandoned, understand better what they desire, and recognize more certainly what they are about to receive and what they ought to observe. For what they desire is great; what they are beginning is magnificent, whether God has inspired it or a human being has admonished and persuaded them.”

[Col. 1060B] This remain, if I may use the term, unquestionably belongs—as the codex itself also indicates—to Nicetas’s first little book addressed to the competentes, also called *The Preparatory Work*. According to Gennadius, in it Nicetas taught his competentes how they ought to conduct themselves—or rather, how competentes who wished to attain the grace of baptism ought to believe and act. The words of this remain are most appropriate to that purpose.

The second fragment, which is properly a fragment and therefore belongs to the first category, appears to be that very brief second fragment of Nicetas in which it is explained who a catechumen is. It too very probably formed part of Nicetas’s first little book addressed to the competentes, as the author of the codex himself indicates by the word placed before the fragment.

The third fragment follows, longer than both those preceding and those following it, and superior both in the weight of its subject matter and in its very diction. It consists entirely of Niceta’s own words; and therefore it is truly and properly a fragment excerpted from Niceta’s writings [Col. 1060C] and inserted into the work of which the codex consists. If we examine the diction of this Fragment, it is an exceedingly elegant discourse, sufficiently demonstrating how capable Niceta was even in secular literature and in the art of speaking. But if we consider the subject of the discourse, it is an excellent instruction for the competentes concerning the time, manner, and significance of renunciation; and it is also a serious rebuke of the men and women of that period who, by the foreign fashion of arranging their hair and by excessively elaborate adornment of head and body, contradicted the renunciation made at baptism. The description of such abuses in this fragment is so vivid and truly pictorial that each reader seems to see before his eyes the men and women rebuked by Niceta, present in the very adornment that provided the occasion for the rebuke. The codex’s author marks this fragment as belonging to that same first book of Niceta addressed to the competentes, to which the preceding two are assigned; and this is also highly probable from the known subject of that book, indicated by Gennadius [Col. 1060D]—namely, how the competentes who desire to attain the grace of baptism ought to conduct themselves. For this reason they had to be instructed, in the preparatory address itself concerning the renunciation they were to make, so that they might attain the grace of baptism before proceeding to the renunciation itself and being admitted to the other matters proper to the competentes.

The fourth fragment is assigned in the Vienna codex to Niceta’s second book, which, as we saw above, concerned the Errors of Paganism. We do not, however, think that this fragment belongs wholly to Niceta’s second book, nor that it is a fragment in the full sense, but rather a number of excerpts which the codex’s author adapted to his own discourse from various passages of Niceta. Those words—“Certainly no sin occurs without the operation of the demon; and we understand all such works to be works of the devil, or his pomps”—can readily be recognized as possibly belonging to Niceta’s second book on the Errors of Paganism. But the words that immediately follow [Col. 1061A], without any indication of the place from which they were extracted, are these:

> “Thus, having freed himself from these evils and cast these chains behind his back, as it were into the face of the enemy, the man now declares with sincere voice: ‘I believe in God the Father almighty,’ and the rest.”

These are the very words of Niceta’s fifth book, On the Creed, chapter 1, except for the word *sincere*, in place of which the edition based on the Ghisian codex reads *symbolica*—“creedal” or “pertaining to the Creed.” What we read afterward is as follows:

> “Concerning the Faith, therefore, as it is contained in the same Creed, everyone who desires to come fully to faith and to baptism must likewise be instructed and taught, so that he may retain the brevity of the Creed memorized in his heart, reciting it daily to himself before he goes to sleep and when he rises from sleep, and keeping it in mind at every hour.”

All this is rather Niceta’s thought than his wording. The author of the Vienna codex drew it from Niceta’s fifth book, On the Creed, chapters 15 and 16, where these admonitions are given to the competentes. The remaining words are:

> “Likewise, the Lord’s Prayer, and the sign of the cross [Col. 1061B] by which he may fortify himself against the devil.”

These words do not occur in Niceta at that place, nor does their substance; nor can we easily conjecture where they might have existed, unless we say that Niceta wrote another distinct book for the competentes, also concerning the Lord’s Prayer, which was unknown to Gennadius, and that he discussed the sign of the cross either in his first book or in another of those books listed by Gennadius.

The fifth fragment, the shortest of all and a fragment in the true sense of the word, consists of these words:

> “The Creed is a reminder of the Faith and a holy confession, which is held and learned in common by all.”

These words are not found in the *Explanation of the Creed*. They seem to be words by which the notion of the Creed is introduced to those to whom the subject of the Creed is first presented. Why should this not have been said by Niceta at the handing over of the Creed? And why should he not thereby have written another book for the competentes, concerning the handing over of the Creed, which likewise was unknown to Gennadius? This fragment is indeed marked in the Vienna codex under Niceta’s name in the book addressed to the competentes [Col. 1061C], but the number of the book is not given.

The sixth and final fragment, likewise genuinely a fragment and also brief, is a certain exposition of exorcisms—quite neat and well suited to presenting the general rationale of exorcisms—but it appears to have been spoken in passing in a discourse that embraced several other matters. It therefore probably belonged to Niceta’s first book addressed to the competentes, called the *Preparatory Book* by Trithemius, as the codex also records. And this is sufficient concerning Niceta’s fragments, or remains.

The style of our Niceta’s little works deserves consideration; for the ancients who remembered Niceta did not remain silent about it. “He composed,” says Gennadius, “six instructional books for the competentes preparing for baptism, in simple and polished language.” Honorius of Autun repeats the same statement. Two of our Gennadian codices read: “in simple and pure language.” Trithemius writes somewhat more fully:

> “Niceas … a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, keen in intellect, clear and polished in speech [Col. 1061D], wrote, and so forth.”

Cassiodorus too, as we saw above, mentions one of these books of Niceta—namely, the book *On Faith*—and commends it for the clarity of its heavenly teaching and for the concise brevity in which it was written. In addition to these earlier testimonies of the ancients concerning Niceta’s style, we now admire four qualities in his little works that concern style or are closely related to it: simplicity and polish of language, learning in the Scriptures, keenness of intellect, and concise brevity in writing.

The simplicity and polish of his language shine clearly from the reading of the little works that survive, as well as of the fragments; but especially from the reading of the third fragment, which, being longer than the others, is also more illuminating. Although there is some difference of expression between the little work *On the Creed* and the other addressed to the fallen Virgin, as the different nature of the subject required, as was explained more fully in chapter 1 [Col. 1062A], the style nevertheless appears to be the same: simple in both, polished and pure in both, and carrying a certain sweetness—indeed a distinctive sweetness—which so separates our Niceta’s style from that of the other writers of his age that it cannot be fully and exactly compared with any of them.

When our Niceta’s book addressed to the fallen Virgin circulated in earlier times without a certain author’s name, a certain affinity of style at one point associated it with the works of Saint Jerome and Saint Augustine. But the evident difference did not remain hidden for long; consequently it came to be regarded as belonging wholly to neither of them. The editors of Jerome’s works therefore, at last persuaded by the rules of criticism, placed it among the spurious works, while the Augustinian editors granted it no place in editions of Saint Augustine. The editors of the works of Saint Ambrose likewise, although they inserted the same book among the genuine offspring of the holy bishop of Milan, as being worthy of so great a prelate, do not deny that the style of this book [Col. 1062B] is not entirely consistent with that of Ambrose’s other writings. They say in the preliminary note to this book:

> “Since this is so, nothing now can be brought against Ambrose except the style. For although the diction of this work may not seem to some to differ greatly from the Ambrosian style, it must nevertheless be admitted that the holy bishop, even when he employs a discourse of the greatest force, uses fewer dense and brief clauses.”

If the editors of Ambrose’s works were compelled to acknowledge this difference of style between this book and Ambrose’s other undisputed writings, even though their purpose was to attribute the book to Ambrose, they would have acknowledged it still more clearly from the other book, *On the Creed*, if it had been known to them. For someone’s style is recognized better and more clearly in calm and simple discourse, when he explains matters naturally and uses language familiar to him, than in an impassioned discourse, where the style itself necessarily assumes something of the disturbance arising in the mind of the speaker.

Our Niceta’s style, therefore—rightly called simple and polished by Gennadius [Col. 1062C]—is a style of its own kind. It bears a face of its own, by which it can readily be distinguished from that of other writers, and especially from that of the three great Latin Fathers, Jerome, Ambrose, and Augustine. Nevertheless, we are pleased that it was at times attributed to them, even though mistakenly.

Closely related to style is learning in the Scriptures. This learning is displayed extensively in the two books of Niceta that survive: they teem everywhere with the meanings and words of Scripture, aptly and elegantly employed and inserted. The keenness of his intellect also shines forth, especially in the book addressed to the fallen Virgin, where he gathers together so many and such appropriate arguments for repentance that he drives the fallen woman’s mind toward detestation of her guilt and toward undertaking the labors of penitence.

Finally, concise brevity distinguishes Niceta’s style. This undoubtedly applies to the books he wrote for the instruction of the competentes, who were not to be wearied by prolonged discourse. For the concise brevity of the book *On Faith*, we have Cassiodorus as a witness [Col. 1062D], whose words we quoted above. We ourselves see concise brevity in the very broad subject of the Creed in his *Explanation of the Creed*; and thus we may rightly infer the same concise brevity in the other works addressed to the competentes.

The book addressed to the fallen Virgin uses a more expansive discourse and more abundant eloquence, as the matter required. This demonstrates that our Niceta possessed ability in more than one kind of expression; indeed, that he was endowed with an intellect by which he could adapt his manner of speaking most suitably both to the capacity of his hearers, to the matter under discussion, and to the time at which he was speaking, as did the more eloquent Fathers of the Church.

After reviewing Niceta’s little works and fragments, and after investigating the character of his style, it would not be inappropriate to ask when and where the works attributed to the holy Aquileian Niceta were written: whether before or after Attila’s destruction of Aquileia [Col. 1063A]; whether at Aquileia or at the port of Romatinum.

We must first distinguish Niceta’s books written for the competentes from the one he composed for the fallen Virgin. The cause of the latter book was the special occasion of rebuking that fallen virgin, an occasion that probably arose only once during the entire thirty-year period of Niceta’s episcopate. The other books, however, arose from his customary episcopal duty of instructing the competentes each year through appropriate sermons as the Paschal solemnity approached. At that time people came to baptism in adulthood from every quarter: from paganism, from Judaism, and even from Christian parents.

If we assign the origin of these works addressed by Niceta to the competentes to the earliest years of his episcopate, we shall be saying something entirely consistent with the truth and very much in keeping with Niceta’s episcopal zeal. Certainly he must have begun his pastoral ministry by instructing the competentes as well.

What, then, are to be regarded as the early years of Niceta’s episcopate? We have already inferred, from conjectures drawn also from the records of the Church of Aquileia [Col. 1063B], that before ascending the episcopal throne of Aquileia our Niceta may have been one of the auxiliary bishops of the Aquileian Church, seated at the port of Romatinum and exercising there the vicariate functions of the bishop of Aquileia in the administration of the very extensive diocese, before the distinct bishoprics of Concordia and Caprula arose. From this he could commonly have been called bishop of the city of Romatinum, and thus also be called by Gennadius.

Why, then, should Niceta not have written the six instructional books for the competentes preparing for baptism at that time, and therefore at the port of Romatinum—and more probably even before Attila’s destruction of Aquileia? Nevertheless, if matters occurred in this way, a limit must still be established, or a date fixed, before which at least Niceta’s fifth book *On the Creed* could not have originated.

We have seen that Niceta’s fifth book *On the Creed* clearly remembers the Eutychian heresy and attacks it [Col. 1063C] with the very arguments, and almost the very words, used by Saint Leo the Great in his famous letter to Flavian, which, by the common judgment of scholars, was issued in the year 449. Therefore our Niceta’s fifth book *On the Creed* could not have been written before that same year, if he wrote it before the destruction of the city by Attila and if he was situated at the port of Romatinum, where he performed the office of auxiliary bishop of the Church of Aquileia—unless we prefer to say that, after Saint Leo the Great’s letter to Flavian had been published, Niceta inserted into his fifth book *On the Creed*, which he had completed some time earlier, those passages intended to strike down the new heresy by means of that letter.

But what if our Niceta, before assuming the episcopate of the Church of Aquileia, never sat as bishop at the port of Romatinum in succession to one or more bishops of Aquileia? In that case Niceta began his Aquileian episcopate only two years after the destruction of the city, namely in 454, before [Col. 1063D] Aquileia could in any way lift its head from its ruins and probably before the Aquileian citizens who had returned from barbarian captivity were present—those of whom Saint Leo the Great speaks in his letter to the same Niceta in 458, as mentioned above.

The six instructional books he wrote for the competentes must therefore be assigned to the early years of Niceta’s Aquileian episcopate after the destruction of Aquileia and after the year 454. It nevertheless remains uncertain whether they were delivered at Aquileia or elsewhere, especially at the new port of Romatinum, or rather in the city of Romatinum, which by then had grown sufficiently from the ruins of Concordia and of the old port of Romatinum, as inhabitants from both places streamed there. Niceta probably spent his early episcopal years there more frequently, while Aquileia still lay prostrate; and from there he could also have been called bishop of the city of Romatinum.

Amid such uncertainty, it will not be inappropriate to discuss here at some length [Col. 1064A] the condition of the city of Aquileia after its destruction and throughout the entire thirty-year period during which Niceta lived as its bishop. Whatever, then, the most savage king of the Huns may have done to captured Aquileia with sword and fire, slaughter and ruin, I would not nevertheless suppose that he raged against it so violently as to level completely to the ground and render wholly uninhabitable a city as strongly fortified, extensive, and populous as the ancient historians describe Aquileia—one filled and equipped with the most solid public and private buildings, as the ruins still being excavated after so many centuries demonstrate.

This would plainly have been a work of immense scale and labor. Even if the immense barbarian army might perhaps have been sufficient for it, the army’s eagerness to plunder and advance prevented it from being so: that eagerness was carrying it headlong toward other cities of Venetia and Emilia as well, which it similarly destroyed in that same year, 452. Therefore, although we may say that Aquileia was burned and overthrown by Attila’s ferocity [Col. 1064B], and emptied of its citizens—some killed, some carried into captivity, and some scattered in flight—we should not understand it to have been so utterly laid low and cast down that, once the Barbarians had left Italy in the course of that same year, many of its citizens returning from flight could not again inhabit it, at least in part, and restore it in some fashion not long afterward, aided also by those who, after Attila was removed from the living in the following year and the power of the Huns was thereby broken, eventually returned unharmed from captivity to their ancestral homes.

The ancient historians described Aquileia’s fate, but not with such unanimity of narration as to leave no room for later generations to debate and conjecture. Muratori, in the *Annals of Italy* under the year 452, cites several historical records concerning Aquileia’s destruction. The distinguished De Rubeis offers more in his *Dissertations on Various Learning*, chapter 20, no. 3, where he investigates particularly, and very appropriately to our subject [Col. 1064C], the place in which Adeodatus, a deacon of the Roman Church, visited Niceta. Adeodatus is mentioned in the previously cited letter of Saint Leo the pope to Niceta. De Rubeis asks whether Adeodatus visited him at Aquileia, which may have been restored within six years after the disaster inflicted by Attila.

Muratori’s opinion is that Aquileia was in fact restored at that time, at least in part, though at other times it suffered further ruins from which it ultimately could not recover. De Rubeis, however, after citing the authorities of the historians, turns finally to the last authority he adduces, Liutprand of Ticinum, a deacon and later bishop of Cremona who wrote in the tenth century. Liutprand asserted that Aquileia was utterly destroyed by King Attila and never raised up again. De Rubeis says that Liutprand meant this not to imply that Aquileia in fact was never raised again after Attila’s devastation, but rather:

> “that it never returned to its original greatness, nor could it be restored in such a way that it could be compared with the other cities that had been repaired and could raise its head as the capital of the province of Venetia.”

Aquileia may therefore rightly be considered to have been restored after Attila’s devastation and again inhabited by its own citizens who had escaped the ruins [Col. 1064D]. This nevertheless could not have occurred so suddenly, with both resources and labor exhausted, nor so rapidly that no interval of time—indeed a sufficiently long one—intervened between the destruction itself and whatever restoration enabled it rightly to be said to have emerged from its former condition of desolation and ruin.

What, then, is more probable than that Niceta scarcely sat at Aquileia during the early years of his episcopate, but was more frequently elsewhere, especially in the city of Romatinum? If this line of conjecture is accepted, then, as regards Niceta’s six books for the competentes, we shall certainly more easily say that they originated in the city of Romatinum than at Aquileia. For when Niceta was appointed to the episcopate, the sacred buildings there probably still had to be repaired, as did the other buildings of the Church: the episcopal residence, the dwellings of the clergy, the monastery of men, and also the monastery of the holy virgins [Col. 1065A]. None of these had undoubtedly escaped the common fate of the city two years earlier. Their restoration required not only willingness, funds, and labor, but also sufficient time.

Something different must now be said about the book addressed to the fallen Virgin. Although the institution of holy virgins had flourished from the very beginnings of the Church, so that each diocese, once somewhat developed and imbued with the principles of Christian perfection, could number companies of them to the singular glory of our religion, there were not yet several *asceteria*—ascetic houses or monasteries—established to contain all of them together. Usually there was only one under each bishop, in the principal place of his diocese, where he himself customarily resided most often. Meanwhile, the others either lived in their own homes or were gathered together in private houses, though still in a private capacity.

We inferred abundantly above, in the appendix to chapter 4, where much is said on this subject, that a monastery of holy virgins had long existed in the celebrated Church of Aquileia and in the city of Aquileia itself, indeed in the middle of the city [Col. 1065B]. There we also noted that, even if the monastery of the holy virgins situated at Aquileia probably suffered the common loss in Attila’s destruction, it could have been repaired not long afterward, so that its former discipline might revive in every respect—the discipline that shines so splendidly in the book addressed to the fallen Virgin.

We therefore believe that our Niceta’s book, or rather his sermon of rebuke addressed to the fallen Virgin, most probably originated and was delivered at Aquileia. Indeed, to add something about the time when it was more probably delivered, we would readily say that it belongs rather to the final years of Niceta’s episcopate. By then, through Niceta’s own pastoral concern, everything or nearly everything relating to the Church, to the assemblies of the faithful, to the order and dignity of the liturgy, to the solemnity of the feasts, and to the other matters mentioned there had been restored to its former condition, so that they presented the appearance of a flourishing Church [Col. 1065C]. The memory of Attila’s destruction would scarcely have remained there any longer, and in fact not even the slightest indication of it appears throughout that entire work.

But did Niceta, who governed the Church of Aquileia for thirty years, compose nothing else besides the seven works mentioned by Gennadius and by his copyists Honorius and Trithemius, concerning which we have been speaking? We consider this question also worthy of investigation, so that we may examine everything relating to our Niceta as far as possible.

Above we quoted what Trithemius says about Niceta, bishop of the city of Romatinum, in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, no. 118, from the *Ecclesiastical Library* of Johann Albert Fabricius, published at Hamburg in 1718. There only the seven works of Niceta are listed, following Gennadius and Honorius. But in the earlier edition of Trithemius’s works, from the library of Marquard Freher, printed at Frankfurt by the Wechel press in 1601, in folio, immediately after Niceta’s final work addressed to the fallen Virgin, these words are read [Col. 1065D]:

> “And certain other works.”

Thus from Trithemius himself we understand that Niceta wrote other works besides the seven mentioned ones, whose titles he had supplied. I would not venture to say what authority should be assigned to this edition of Trithemius, which contains the additional words at this place and presents Niceta to us as the author of other works as well. Nevertheless, Trithemius’s preceding statement itself, which is the same in both editions—namely, “He wrote, for the edification of readers, works of not contemptible value, of which the following are transmitted”—sufficiently suggests that Trithemius certainly believed Niceta to have written other works besides those he himself then listed from Gennadius and Honorius.

I would add that in the *Roman Martyrology* of Peter Galesinius, printed at Milan in 1578, our Niceta is also mentioned in this eulogy:

> “In the city of Romatinum, Saint Niceas, bishop [Col. 1066A] and confessor, who, having composed many books and lived a religious life, flourishing in the praise of holiness and learning, departed to the Lord.”

If Niceta therefore composed many books, it is probable that he should be said to have written others in addition to the seven mentioned by Gennadius [214] and the others.

Indeed, in the letter of Henry, a cleric of the monastery of Pomposa, cited above from the *Italian Diary* of the distinguished Montfaucon—or in the catalogue of that monastery’s books appended to the same letter—there is listed on page 84 a book by Bishop Niceta *On the Reason of Faith*. This certainly seems to be the same as Niceta’s third book, *On the Faith of the One Majesty*, which was discussed earlier in its proper place. In this catalogue of Pomposan books, immediately after the listing of one book by Bishop Niceta *On the Reason of Faith*, the following is added:

> “By the same—namely, Bishop Niceta—one book *On the Power of the Holy Spirit*. By the same, *On the Various Appellations Appropriate to Our Lord Jesus Christ*.”

Here, then, are probably two further works of our own Aquileian Niceta [Col. 1066B], not mentioned by Gennadius or Honorius. In the eleventh century they were preserved in the richly supplied library of the monastery of Pomposa, together with his book *On the Faith of the One Majesty*, bound in one and the same volume. They perhaps later perished completely along with that book, since, so far as I know, no mention of them is found anywhere, nor is there in collections of ancient records or appendices to the Fathers any work of this kind that truly identifies our Niceta as its author.

Why should these two works of Niceta not also have belonged to the instruction of the competentes—or rather to the instruction of the neophytes after baptism, to whom more profound aspects of the Christian religion were explained, having previously not been entrusted to them?

Johann Albert Fabricius writes in the first edition of his *Bibliotheca Graeca*, volume 6, page 430, that “in Labbe’s *New Library of Manuscripts*, page 27, two treatises are mentioned belonging to Saint Niceta, bishop of the Dacians [Col. 1066C], about whom Paulinus of Nola often writes, and to whom the *Roman Martyrology* assigns 7 January: the first, *On the Vigils of the Servants of God*, the second, *On the Good of Psalmody*, from the Vatican codices and from the library of Saint Maximus of Turin.”

Labbe did indeed find these two treatises among the Vatican codices and in the library of Saint Maximus of Turin under the name of Bishop Niceta. But who made him certain that they belonged to Niceta the Dacian, about whom Paulinus of Nola often writes and whom the *Roman Martyrology* commemorates on 7 January? Labbe undoubtedly designated Niceta as “the Dacian,” the author of these two treatises, on the basis of a preconceived opinion that at that time was held by nearly all scholars against Baronius: namely, that the Dacian Niceta, the friend of Saint Paulinus of Nola and the person placed in the *Roman Martyrology* on 7 January, was the same as Niceta, bishop of the city of Romatinum, first named by Gennadius and afterward by Honorius and Trithemius; and that the Aquileian Niceta was entirely different from Gennadius’s Niceta and was not regarded as the author of any work [Col. 1066D].

I would not, however, say that our Aquileian Niceta was the author of these two treatises. Dacherius published the two treatises—*On the Vigils of the Servants of God* and *On the Good of Psalmody*—not under the name of Bishop Niceta but under that of Bishop Nicetius, having extracted them from a manuscript of Saint-Germain. He published them in volume 3 of the first edition of the *Spicilegium*, and in volume 1, page 221, of the second folio edition. In the notice prefixed to them, he attributed them, on the basis of very sound conjectures, to Saint Nicetius, bishop of Trier, who flourished around the middle of the sixth century and had earlier been abbot of a certain monastery. Dacherius supposes that Nicetius addressed these treatises to his brothers in order to instruct them concerning vigils and the manner of singing psalms.

Whatever may be said meanwhile about Dacherius’s conjectures and opinion, these two treatises—which otherwise reveal their author as a learned man, versed in the divine Scriptures, and fervent with a deep affection for piety and devotion—are in no way the work of our Aquileian Niceta [Col. 1067A]. We can now recognize this with the utmost certainty, especially from the style of our Niceta, which is sufficiently known.

It was the name of Niceta, assigned in the titles of these two little works in Labbe’s *New Library of Manuscripts*, that compelled us to say this. For the rest, the purpose and object of our present investigation concern not what Niceta did not write, but rather what we believe our Aquileian Niceta wrote in addition to the seven books mentioned by Gennadius and the others.

Why, then, should Niceta of Aquileia not have composed other works during the thirty years in which he held the episcopate of Aquileia, besides the books mentioned from the former library of the monastery of Pomposa—*On the Power of the Holy Spirit* and *On the Various Appellations Appropriate to Our Lord Jesus Christ*—especially amid the greatest difficulties of circumstances and times, after the devastation of war, when the evils inflicted by the enemy had to be removed and the wounds inflicted upon religion healed, as Saint Leo, the supreme pontiff, wrote to him in his well-known decretal letter?

The consultations that Adeodatus, a deacon of the Roman Church, brought to the apostolic see [Col. 1067B] on behalf of Niceta of Aquileia were therefore written down by Niceta himself in some form, although perhaps not in the form of a letter, as we conjectured in chapter 7 against Zabeus. He undoubtedly also wrote to his fellow provincial bishops when, at the command of Saint Pope Leo himself, he sent them Leo’s decretal letter concerning his consultations.

Why should he not also have composed special treatises for the people of Aquileia concerning marriage, according to the authority received from the apostolic see, so that women who had married other men, believing their former husbands to have perished in captivity, might more easily return to them? Why should he not also have offered suitable exhortations concerning the other subjects of that decretal letter, while he strove to apply healing hands to the illnesses of his people?

The style of Niceta’s surviving works abundantly demonstrates in him ease of writing, fullness of expression, extensive learning in the Scriptures, and a fervent zeal for the house of God [Col. 1067C]. From this we may readily infer that Niceta wrote other works as well—and not a few of them—during the thirty years that were unknown to Gennadius and his other copyists and that perished through the injury of time.

Moreover, from the same six instructional books for the competentes preparing for baptism that we know, we can easily conjecture that he wrote others for their instruction in the same way, as the discipline of those times required. Since the *Explanation of the Creed* that we possess was, as we saw above, delivered at the rendering of the Creed, Niceta surely did not omit to give another address at the handing over of the Creed itself [Col. 1067D]. The fifth Vienna fragment may perhaps relate to this, as we indicated in its proper place.

Since the recitation of the Lord’s Prayer is inculcated in the fourth fragment, or remnant, according to Niceta’s thought, why should he not also have composed a little work or book for the competentes explaining the Lord’s Prayer, as was customary—whether when it was handed over to the competentes or when it was recited by the competentes at an appointed time, just as the Creed of the Faith was recited by them?

After baptism, likewise, Niceta probably composed other works for the infants or neophytes, providing full instruction in the divine mysteries that was not given before baptism—for example, concerning the rites of baptism itself and the sacraments of confirmation and the Eucharist. This would accord with the discipline of that period and with the example of the more celebrated Fathers of the Church, Ambrose, Augustine, Cyril of Jerusalem, and others whom we mentioned earlier in this very connection.

But what of the book addressed to the fallen Virgin? In that book, section 19, Niceta himself testifies that he addressed the Virgin on the solemn day on which she received the veil of virginity. In section 28 he testifies that, in fulfillment of his pastoral office, he had not failed her or the others with holy admonition—that is, apparently, with sermons delivered expressly to virgins. Finally, in the following section, 29, he testifies that he expounded a hymn of virginity [Col. 1068A]. By this title we may perhaps understand homilies on a psalm concerning virginity, probably Psalm 44, from which the dignity of the brides of Christ shines forth.

How many works, then, may we readily infer that Niceta of Aquileia composed beyond the seven books mentioned by Gennadius during the thirty years in which he governed the Church of Aquileia!

It remains, for the completion of this chapter, to speak of the holiness of Niceta, bishop of Aquileia, and of his cult, both generally in the Church and among the people of Aquileia. First, however, we must not omit here a rather insufficiently considered observation by the distinguished Muratori in the *Annals of Italy* under the year 401 concerning the title “saint” as applied to the bishops of Aquileia in earlier centuries.

He was indicating the death of the holy Roman pontiff Anastasius, who is mentioned in the ancient catalogues with the title “saint,” as he says. His memory is certainly also celebrated in the *Roman Martyrology* on 27 April, and on that same day a feast is held at Rome with proper readings in the patriarchal basilicas of the Vatican, the Lateran, and Saint Mary Major, as is evident from the proper books of saints belonging to those basilicas [Col. 1068B].

“Living bishops of those times,” he says, “were also given the title ‘saint,’ just as Roman pontiffs are now; and for that reason we know all the Roman pontiffs of earlier centuries to have been called saints, as also the bishops of Milan, Ravenna, Aquileia, Verona, and so forth. Nevertheless, this title should not be regarded as an absolute proof of their holiness, comparable to the decrees later established for the canonization of saints.”

Here the distinguished man seems to have intended to criticize a certain excessive readiness in the churches mentioned to venerate all, or nearly all, of their ancient bishops under the title “saint,” simply because they saw their names adorned with that title in ancient records.

Whatever may be the case regarding the other Churches whom he names—for it is not the place here to discuss them individually—as far as we are concerned, there was no reason for him, on this account, to include the Church of Aquileia among them. Apart from the Aquileian bishops crowned with the glory of martyrdom, of whom only two or three are known to us, and to whom veneration is rightly due on this ground alone, how many of the others, although perhaps adorned with the title of saint while still alive, in accordance with the custom of those times, subsequently obtained the cult of sanctity from that fact? We have passed through the whole of the first five centuries, and know only three non-martyr Aquileian bishops who were venerated under the title of sanctity: namely Valerian, Chromatius, and Nicetas, of whom we are speaking. Muratori therefore ought rather to have numbered the Church of Aquileia among those Churches which, not without considerable selectivity and restraint, chose to bestow upon their bishops both the title of saint in the proper sense and the cult of sanctity from the earliest times.

Among the Aquileian bishops of the fifth century there is Augustine, successor to Saint Chromatius. While still alive, he is seen adorned with the title of saint and of sanctity in that little book of Faith [Col. 1068D] which was presented to him by certain followers of Pelagius and which has a place among the Augustinian appendices; this is the only surviving monument of this matter as far as he is concerned. Nevertheless, it is sufficient for us to understand that Augustine himself was commonly honored with the title of saint, in accordance with the custom of his age. Yet this Bishop Augustine never received any cult whatsoever among the people of Aquileia.

Adelphus, or Delphinus, successor to Augustine in the same see, was celebrated with the highest praise, including praise of his moral life and pastoral office—not by some ordinary street-corner speaker or by chance, but by the most holy and learned man Peter Chrysologus, Bishop of Ravenna, in a sermon delivered expressly in Adelphus’s presence. That sermon is number 136 in the latest edition of his works. There Adelphus the bishop is praised as having a holy spirit and, indeed, a blessed spirit, and is commended as a “man of God.” Yet Adelphus never obtained among the Aquileians the title and honor of a saint in the proper sense.

What, then, of the centuries after the fifth? After Nicetas, only two Aquileian bishops—or patriarchs, as the custom later came to call them—were endowed with the title and honor of sanctity down to our own times: Saint Paulinus, who flourished in the time of Charlemagne, and Blessed Bertrand, who brought distinction to the Church of Aquileia in the middle of the fourteenth century. Thus, apart from the martyrs, only five Aquileian bishops are found to have obtained the cult of sanctity from the Church’s apostolic, as it is said, beginning down to our own times. Which of the other Churches mentioned, or which Muratori might have mentioned, does not boast a larger number of saintly bishops? Muratori therefore ought to have excluded the Church of Aquileia from his censure, whatever that censure may be: certainly, in honoring its bishops with the title and cult of saints, it was not excessively liberal.

[Col. 1069B] With these points established, in order to bring the truth concerning the holy bishops of the Church of Aquileia into the light, we now come to the sanctity and cult of our Nicetas. We have already sufficiently proved in its proper place that the Bishop Niceas, or Nicetas, of the city of Romatiana mentioned by Gennadius was not Nicetas the Dacian, the friend of Saint Paulinus of Nola, but was in fact our Nicetas of Aquileia, who flourished in the time of Saint Leo the Great and to whom a decretal letter of that same pope survives.

It is therefore already sufficiently clear that this Nicetas of Aquileia was holy, since everything that ancient writers and martyrologies have hitherto said about Nicetas of Romatiana applies in reality to this Nicetas of Aquileia. As for proving the sanctity of one of the ancient servants of God, who does not know how greatly the ancient martyrologies contribute when they remember such men with praise—especially when neither the memory of antiquity nor public report says anything against them? Such ancient martyrologies, insofar as they concern the servants of God who have a place in them, are testimonies of the greatest weight. They establish the reputation for holiness in which those men were held at the time when they were entered in the martyrologies; nor do they permit us to doubt that, according to the custom of those times, that reputation properly and legitimately took hold and spread in the Church. This remains true whatever differences there may be in the pronunciation of the name or in the designation of the place—differences that can easily arise from the diversity of regions, periods, and authors, and that in no way affect the substance of the matter or the identity of the person.

Among the testimonies concerning Nicetas of Romatiana—that is, concerning our Nicetas of Aquileia, as we may freely assert—which we have assembled at the beginning of this volume, no fewer than eighteen are drawn from various martyrologies of the Western Church and from various, more important editions of them. Their procession is led by a particular testimony from an ancient manuscript copy of a martyrology, said to have been compiled from Notker and Usuard and formerly used by the monks of Mosacum in the Diocese of Aquileia. In all these witnesses Nicetas is mentioned on the tenth day before the Kalends of July [Col. 1069D], almost always with the title “blessed,” “saint,” or “of holy memory,” and also with some particular encomium of sanctity, as appears in the latest of them. This is the martyrology now in common use throughout the Western Church, which, after the revisions of Gregory XIII, Urban VIII, and Innocent XI, possesses the outstanding authority of the most learned as well as most erudite Pope Benedict XIV, through whose work it was enlarged and corrected.

When, then, should Nicetas be said to have acquired a place in the martyrologies? I am approaching a difficult matter, one hard to resolve by argument; nevertheless, I think that something should be attempted by conjecture, even if perhaps nothing certain and established will follow from it.

By the common judgment of scholars, the oldest of all the martyrologies is certainly the one attributed to Saint Jerome, of which two or three copies have emerged from various manuscripts of varying antiquity. In 1717 Edmund Martène and his associate Durand published, in volume III of the *Thesaurus novus Anecdotorum*, col. 1547, from a manuscript of the monastery of Saint-Germain of Auxerre, an ancient martyrology compiled approximately a thousand years earlier under the name of Saint Jerome, as its title states. Yet it contains no mention of our Nicetas, either on the tenth day before the Kalends of July or anywhere else.
