Another extremely ancient martyrology, bearing the name of Jerome the presbyter and, as he then stated, written about six hundred years earlier, had been published before Martène and Durand by Dachery in 1661 from a manuscript of the monastery of Corbie: in volume IV, p. 517, of his old edition of the *Spicilegium*; in the second folio edition it appears in volume II, p. 1; and Vallarsi included it in his splendid edition of Saint Jerome’s works, volume XI, p. 475. In this martyrology our Nicetas is mentioned on the tenth day before the Kalends of July as follows: “The deposition of Nicetas, bishop, of holy memory.”

Franciscus Maria Florentinius published another martyrology in 1668 from other Italian manuscripts of the tenth or eleventh century, both ancient and of proven reliability—although, as he himself asserts in his sixth preliminary admonition, their exemplar was considerably more ancient. This was an older martyrology of the Western Church attributed to Saint Jerome. He states that no slight arguments suggest that it should be called the Roman martyrology, described by Gregory the Great, praised by Ado, and neglected and sought out in the intervening centuries. In it, likewise on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, our Nicetas is mentioned in this way: “The deposition of Niceas, bishop, of holy memory.”

What at first sight seems worthy of some observation is the designation of Nicetas the bishop in these older martyrologies without any indication of the place of which he was bishop. This is contrary to what Ado, Notker, and Usuard later did, as did the others who compiled their martyrologies from theirs: there Nicetas is always, or almost always, designated as bishop of the city of Romatiana, of the town of Romatiana, of the city of Rome, or as the Romatian bishop, as appears from the testimonies of the martyrologies cited at the beginning of this book.

Why should the first compilers of the Hieronymian martyrology—or those who enlarged it not long afterward—not have wished to designate him absolutely and properly as the Aquileian, without any reference to the city of Romatiana, if Nicetas was perhaps, as the nearer figure, also sufficiently well known to them? And why should Ado, Notker, and Usuard, strangers to our regions and later in time, whose knowledge of Nicetas’s reputation and see was less certain, have freely added “the city of Romatiana” from Gennadius and Honorius, thereby providing later scholars with the occasion for such disputes? But these remarks may be regarded as incidental.

As for the time when our Nicetas acquired a place in the martyrologies—namely, in the martyrologies commonly called Hieronymian, which were primitive and which, as Dachery observed in the notice prefixed to the one he published, originated shortly after the death of Saint Jerome—who does not see that this time was extremely remote, long preceding the age of Usuard, Notker, and Ado? This is evident both from the very designation of Nicetas’s name without an appended place and from the antiquity of the Hieronymian manuscripts themselves, as assessed by the learned men through whose work and study they were published.

In the genuine and original Hieronymian martyrology, therefore, the name of Nicetas is undoubtedly a later addition, as is clear from the martyrology of the monastery of Saint-Germain of Auxerre, described at that time as approximately a thousand years old and now, speaking absolutely, more than a thousand years old, as well as from the other martyrologies published continuously in the same volume III of Martène and Durand’s *Thesaurus novus Anecdotorum*. There, only a small number of saints is presented for each day, and the name of our Nicetas is everywhere absent. Yet the addition of Nicetas’s name must itself have been extremely ancient, as is likewise clear from the other Hieronymian martyrologies published by Dachery and Florentinius, in which Nicetas’s name is present. These too are of very remote antiquity, so that they seem not to be far removed from the fifth century, the century of Nicetas—especially if one supposes that they are not autographs but rather copies, as Florentinius conjectured concerning his own manuscripts.

The sanctity of our Nicetas therefore shines forth more clearly even from this very ancient addition of his name to the older martyrologies. We may thus reasonably conjecture that he departed this life with the fragrance of sanctity among his own people and among outsiders as well, and that for this reason he was regarded, in accordance with the custom of those times, as numbered among the citizens of heaven. His memory, together with that of other holy men of an earlier age, was to be recalled on the anniversary of his deposition.

There is no need here to add anything concerning the designations “blessed,” “saint,” and “of holy memory,” with which the name of our Nicetas is honored in the martyrologies just mentioned. The mere inclusion of a person’s name in martyrologies, even without any proclamation of “blessed,” “saint,” or “of holy memory,” sufficiently testifies to that person’s sanctity. Our Nicetas likewise sometimes appears under such a designation in the testimonies of the martyrologies cited at the beginning of this book: for example, in the Gellonian Martyrology published by Dachery and composed around the year 804, as Dachery himself observes in the preceding notice. There the mention is simply of “Nicae, bishop,” on the tenth day before the Kalends of July.

Such honorifics are now commonly used in the Roman Martyrology that we employ, but formerly they were not used in this way in every Church. Indeed, with particular regard to the prefix “blessed” or “saint,” the learned Joannes Baptista Sollerus observed in his learned preface to Usuard’s Martyrology, section 4, printed in volume VI, part I, of the Bollandist *Acta Sanctorum* for June, that the rarer the prefix “saint” or “blessed” is, the greater is the antiquity of the manuscripts of the martyrology.

Nevertheless, I think it must be admitted that such honorifics, even when applied in ancient martyrologies to the names of certain saints, probably indicate a greater renown of those persons and a more firmly established knowledge of their sanctity; this was in some way marked by the addition of these designations.

As for the designations “blessed” and “saint,” as well as “of holy memory,” there is no reason to seek in the ancient martyrologies a distinction based on the ecclesiastical discipline that has been in force for several centuries, by which the blessed are considered inferior in degree to the saints with respect to cult. Among the ancients, the words “blessed” and “saint” were used indiscriminately to designate men distinguished by virtue who were regarded as numbered among the citizens of heaven. Fontaninus, in his dissertation on Saint Peter Urseolus, chapter 25; Mazochius, *On the Cult of the Bishops of the Neapolitan Church*, part II, chapter 5, no. 2, note 30; and Pope Benedict XIV, in his distinguished work *On the Beatification of the Servants of God and the Canonization of the Blessed*, among others, have learnedly illustrated this matter.

An observation must nevertheless be made here, one commonly raised by nearly all the distinguished men who opposed Baronius’s opinion concerning this Nicetas, the bishop of the city of Romatiana mentioned by Gennadius. They reason that it was not our Aquileian Nicetas but that Dacian Nicetas, the same man who is celebrated with so many praises by Saint Paulinus of Nola. “In the martyrologies,” they say, “on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, there is no mention of Nicetas of Aquileia, but of Nicetas, bishop in Dacia. Thus the older martyrologies that simply remember Nicetas the bishop on that day must be understood; and likewise the later ones that add the title ‘bishop of the city of Romatiana,’ or ‘of the Roman city,’ or ‘Romatian bishop.’”

On the same day the martyrologies also mention Paulinus of Nola. Nicetas the Dacian may therefore rightly be considered to have been added to him, since the two men were very closely joined in friendship while alive, and since perhaps the natal day, or day of death, of this Nicetas of Dacia was unknown to the martyrologists. For the very mention of Nicetas, bishop of the Dacians, which is now read in the Roman Martyrology on 7 January, is a later addition made arbitrarily by Baronius in his revision of the Roman Martyrology under Pope Gregory XIII [Col. 1072A], in order to serve his own opinion: namely, that he wished Niceas, or Nicetas, bishop of the city of Romatiana, to be regarded as Niceas, or Nicetas, Bishop of Aquileia.

What argument for the sanctity of our Aquileian Nicetas, then, can we derive from the martyrologies that either simply present Nicetas the bishop or present Nicetas as bishop of the city of Romatiana on the tenth day before the Kalends of July?

But the distinguished proponents of the opposing position, who wished to explain Gennadius’s statement that Nicetas was bishop of the city of Romatiana as though he had said “Nicetas, bishop in Dacia, of that city”—a city which, as we saw in its proper place, was called by writers and ancient monuments not “Romatiana” but by another name not very different from it—ought also to have given the martyrologies that repeat the same words of Gennadius the same interpretation. They should likewise have drawn the older martyrologies, which simply remember Nicetas the bishop on the same tenth day before the Kalends of July, into the same meaning.

But what is there new in this observation about the martyrologies that deserves consideration? We explained Gennadius earlier, against these same distinguished men, when he said that Nicetas was bishop of the city of Romatiana. We have likewise interpreted the martyrologies that contain the same wording in the same sense, so that there is no need here to go over the same ground for the sake of the martyrologies. The other points that are added are mere conjectures, and they are easily overturned by other conjectures, if I am not mistaken, stronger ones.

First, we saw that the mention of Nicetas on the tenth day before the Kalends of July is absent from the oldest Hieronymian Martyrology, as well as from the others that we cited generally from volume III of Martène and Durand’s *Thesaurus novus Anecdotorum*. To these it is now appropriate to add Bede’s genuine Martyrology, together with the additions of the deacon Florus, printed in a distinct type in the Bollandist *Acta Sanctorum*, volume II for March; and Rabanus’s Martyrology, found in the *Thesaurus Monumentorum*, or among Canisius’s *Antiquae Lectiones*, in Basnage’s edition, volume II, part II, p. 314; and Wandalbert’s metrical Martyrology, which appears in Dachery’s *Spicilegium*, volume V of the first edition and volume II, p. 40, of the second folio edition; as well as the old Roman Martyrology of Heribert Rosweyde, which may be seen at the beginning of Ado in the edition of Dominicus Georgius. Likewise there are two other very ancient martyrologies, the Fulda Martyrology and the Ottobonian Martyrology, found in the same Georgius, at the end of his work.

In all these martyrologies, then, in which the name of Nicetas is absent on the tenth day before the Kalends of July—in all of them, I say, or almost all, since, on recent occasions, the rules of certain of our libraries prevented me from examining one or two of them again—the same day contains a mention of Paulinus of Nola. Thus we can assert without danger of error that every martyrology which has Nicetas on the tenth day before the Kalends of July also has Paulinus of Nola, whereas not all, indeed very many, of those that have Paulinus of Nola have Nicetas.

From this we may easily conjecture that, although the name of Nicetas was inserted into the martyrologies in ancient times, as we conjectured above, it nevertheless occupied a place in them at least one generation after Paulinus of Nola, or even an entire century later.

Since those two holy men, Nicetas the Dacian and Paulinus of Nola, were contemporaries and joined in friendship, and since each of them also bears witness to the sanctity of the other, it is highly probable that one could not have been known in the Church without the other, and therefore that one was not to be entered in the martyrologies without the other. Or, if one ought to have preceded the other as a sign of honor, Nicetas the Dacian, who died before Paulinus, as we showed in chapter 3, ought certainly to have been entered in the martyrologies—or rather in the ecclesiastical registers from which the martyrologies arose not long after Jerome’s time—before Paulinus. He should at least have been entered through the efforts of Paulinus himself, who had been so lavish in praising him while he was alive.

But if, as is established, Nicetas’s name was inserted into the martyrologies after Paulinus, this Nicetas can no longer seem to be Nicetas, bishop of the Dacians and friend of Saint Paulinus of Nola, even though the name was inserted into the martyrologies under the same day. Another Nicetas must therefore be understood, one who has no connection with Saint Paulinus of Nola; and consequently our Nicetas of Aquileia, who was later in age than Saint Paulinus of Nola and for whom so many arguments previously advanced stand, must be intended.

Furthermore, how could the natal day of that Nicetas whom they added to Paulinus of Nola on the tenth day before the Kalends of July have been unknown to the martyrologists, when several martyrologies—some of them cited by us among the testimonies—remember him on that same day, and some are of great antiquity and belong to authors of illustrious name among the martyrologists, such as Ado, Usuard, and Notker? These martyrologies, I say, explicitly recorded the deposition of the Nicetas whom they remembered—that is, the day of his departure, on which, his body having been laid down, his spirit flew upward to the heavens [Col. 1073B].

Nor, thirdly, can we accept the attribution to Baronius of an arbitrary act in the correction, or rather restoration, of the Roman Martyrology: namely, that he was the first to insert on 7 January the memory of Nicetas, bishop in Dacia, who, according to those scholars, is not another person but the very same Nicetas as the bishop of the city of Romatiana—the one person who, on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, has a place in all the martyrologies earlier than Baronius.

Baronius himself explained the purpose of his work, or rather the purpose of the Roman Church, in that undertaking, in chapter 8 of his treatment of the Roman Martyrology: it was not to compose a new martyrology, but to restore the old one from ancient copies. It is therefore necessary to suppose that Baronius, together with the most select and learned men who assisted him in his work, drew from the old manuscript copies of the martyrologies existing at Rome, which he himself had consulted in the task entrusted to him—especially, perhaps, from the manuscript martyrology of the Vatican Church that he names there—the names of the two Nicetases, their distinct episcopal sees, and also their different natal days.

Thus, after leaving the Romatian Nicetas on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, he named another bishop of Dacia on 7 January, as the instructor of the barbarous and savage peoples there. He did not so much place him there for the first time as restore him to that place. This is the proper way to think about so religious and learned a man and his highly skilled associates in a matter of such importance—even if we were to regard as utterly worthless what Baronius later wrote under Sixtus V in his notes on Romatian Niceas, or Nicetas, by way of illustration and with no authority other than that of a private writer. For in that case, rather than expunging Nicetas the Dacian from the Roman Martyrology on 7 January, another location would have to be sought for Nicetas of Romatiana on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, if the circumstances required it—though that location would not be Aquileia, for which we argue.

What finally contributes most strongly to the defense—or rather restoration—of Baronius’s correction of the Roman Martyrology are the revisions of that same Martyrology carried out in later times. I say nothing of the most careful revision undertaken by Pope Urban VIII, with many learned and highly experienced men also summoned at that time; nor do I say anything of another revision under Pope Innocent XI. Let us turn our attention to the latest revision, completed by the most learned and erudite pontiff of them all, indeed easily the foremost of all the learned and scholarly men of his age and beyond it, Benedict XIV.

The complaints of several critics concerning Baronius’s opinion of Nicetas of Romatiana on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, as well as concerning the addition of Nicetas, bishop in Dacia, on 7 January, had long since become generally known to scholars. In 1745 the distinguished Dominicus Georgius had dedicated to that same pontiff his Ado, printed at Rome; on p. 288, under the tenth day before the Kalends of July, he indicated the critics’ censures on this matter, to which he himself also adhered.

In this revision of the Roman Martyrology, the most wise pontiff had resolved—as appears from his Apostolic Letter of 1 July 1748, no. 2, to John V, King of Portugal—that whatever was found superfluous after the published corrections should be cut away, while whatever was lacking should be added. We know that this was done in many places, and not without mature consideration of the matters, as we understand from the same Apostolic Letter.

What, then, was done with the memory of Nicetas, bishop in Dacia, on 7 January—the memory that Baronius had first introduced into the Roman Martyrology and that, according to the position of his critical opponents, was certainly superfluous, since the older entry on the tenth day before the Kalends of July under the name Nicetas, or Niceas, bishop of the city of Romatiana, should have sufficed, that bishop being precisely the same as Nicetas, bishop in Dacia?

Nothing at all. From this we understand that the most wise pontiff detected nothing superfluous in Baronius’s addition of Nicetas, bishop in Dacia, on 7 January. Consequently, in his judgment also, there is one Nicetas, bishop of the Dacians, who is recorded in the Roman Martyrology on 7 January, and another Nicetas, bishop of the city of Romatiana, whose memory is recalled on the tenth day before the Kalends of July—whatever the critical scholars who attacked Baronius’s opinion on this ground may have thought.

Since the memories of these two Nicetases must not be confused, and therefore Romatian Nicetas on the tenth day before the Kalends of July is different from Dacian Nicetas on 7 January; and since Romatian Nicetas, or the bishop of the city of Romatiana, is beyond doubt Nicetas, Bishop of Aquileia, as was discussed at length in its proper place, the martyrologies—whether the older ones that simply remember Nicetas the bishop on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, or the later ones that on the same day identify Nicetas as the bishop of the city of Romatiana—and thus bear witness to the sanctity of this Romatian Nicetas, are thoroughly well-founded proofs of the sanctity of our Nicetas of Aquileia, as we observed earlier.

But can the sanctity of our Nicetas be demonstrated in no other way [Col. 1074C] apart from the authority of the martyrologies just mentioned? Many things can certainly now be said in praise of our Nicetas’s sanctity that were not established in earlier times: namely, when it was not sufficiently clear whether the Nicetas of Gennadius was the same as the Aquileian; when the little book addressed to the fallen virgin was circulating under an uncertain author; and when the *Explanation of the Creed for Catechumens*, which has brought such great illumination to the recognition of our Nicetas of Aquileia, still lay hidden in obscurity.

Nicetas’s pastoral care in the most difficult circumstances of his Church certainly shone forth from the letter of Saint Leo the Great addressed to him. From this letter it appears that Nicetas’s consultations had been brought before the Apostolic See; these are undeniable proofs of his zeal in repairing the losses inflicted by the devastation of war and in curing the diseases contracted through barbarian incursions and association with barbarians, so that, when the state of affairs had turned for the better, that Church might return to the dignity of its former observance.

But how much more can we now add in praise of this man’s sanctity from the two treatises that survive and that, as we have proved, are genuinely his offspring [Col. 1074D]?

On this matter we follow the example of the most wise and highly praised pontiff, Pope Benedict XIV, in the Apostolic Letter cited above to the King of Portugal concerning the new edition of the Roman Martyrology. In order to demonstrate the sanctity of his most ancient predecessor, Pope Siricius, whose name he himself had decided to introduce into the Roman Martyrology for the first time on 26 November, with an encomium of learning, piety, and zeal for religion, he proposed especially to examine Siricius’s letters as edited by Pierre Coustant in the *Collection of the Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, so that from them he might draw proofs of that pontiff’s sanctity.

What, then, is there in our Nicetas’s *Explanation of the Creed for Catechumens* that does not likewise breathe learning, piety, and zeal for religion, and thereby establish the man’s sanctity? Learning shines forth in the explanation of the mysteries and articles of faith, as well as in his knowledge of the Scriptures; piety appears in the words of heavenly grace with which the prayer abounds; zeal for religion appears in defending the truths of the Church against the deceptions of heretics and in instructing people in innocent living and true piety.

What, moreover, does the little book addressed to the fallen virgin not contain in support of Nicetas’s sanctity? The integrity of his morals, the holiness of his life, and the rigor of his discipline are sufficiently demonstrated by those fiery words with which he was able so freely to rebuke the fallen virgin and her seducer. For who, unless he were entirely irreproachable and most steadfastly offered himself in all things as an example of good works—in teaching, integrity, and seriousness, as the Apostle says to Timothy—would have dared to rise against sinners with so vehement an address? And he did so in such a way that this address was commended by ecclesiastical writers with singular praise as an incentive to correction for all who were falling.

That same work provides another striking proof of his zeal in the fact that, setting aside human considerations, he publicly rebuked that fallen virgin—although she was of noble birth—with pastoral firmness and apostolic freedom, out of zeal for the house of God, and subjected her to the labors of public penance.

How many proofs of Nicetas’s sanctity would the other works of his that are now lost have supplied us, especially that work *On Faith in the One Majesty*, or *On Faith*, or *On the Reason of Faith*, which Cassiodorus praised so highly in chapter 16 of *On the Institution of Divine Scripture*, as we saw above? But the sanctity of our Nicetas of Aquileia shines forth sufficiently even from the very few works that survive. From this we may also readily conclude that the reputation for his sanctity properly and deservedly took root in ancient times, from the very time of his death, and not without the authority of the Church according to the discipline of those times. Hence his name had a place in the martyrologies and there received the praises “blessed,” “saint,” and “of holy memory.”

What has been said thus far concerning the sanctity of our Nicetas of Aquileia, especially on the basis of the testimonies of the martyrologies [Col. 1075C], may also be regarded as sufficient for recognizing his cult in the Church generally. For a cult is the very entry of a saint in the ecclesiastical registers and the recitation of his name together with those of other holy men in the public assemblies of the Churches; and it was for this purpose that martyrologies were written from the earliest periods of the Church.

But what shall we now say concerning the cult of our Nicetas of Aquileia in the Church of Aquileia itself? The distinguished Alexander Politus, a cleric regular of the Pious Schools, did not hesitate to assert in his *Roman Martyrology Illustrated with Commentaries*, printed at Florence in 1751, under 7 January, that the reputation and opinion of the sanctity of Nicetas, Bishop of Aquileia, had arisen and spread among the Aquileians only in the most recent times after Baronius. He even does not hesitate to accuse them of imprudence and rashness on account of the solemn and annual cult that they rendered to Nicetas on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, if they did so without some certain judgment of the Roman Church and solely on the authority of Baronius, which he called a mere and wholly false conjecture.

Zabeus likewise asserts, in part I, no. 15, of his dissertation, that the Church of Aquileia began very late to venerate its Nicetas with a proper office and Mass on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, since there is no mention of this saint in the ancient calendars of the Aquileians and none in the missals of the old Aquileian rite, whether written by hand or printed. He demonstrates this by adducing the authority and very words of the distinguished De Rubeis, who had deliberately investigated certain Aquileian calendars and missals precisely for this purpose, as we learn from chapter 17 of his *Monuments* and from chapter 19 of his *Dissertations on Various Erudition* [p. 225].

What, then, after all this, are we to say about the cult of Nicetas among the Aquileians?

Both Politus and Zabeus infer the recent origin of Nicetas’s cult in the Church of Aquileia from the absence of Nicetas’s name in the calendars and missals proper to the Church of Aquileia and to the Aquileian rite, which were in use in the Diocese of Aquileia and throughout almost the whole Aquileian province before the year 1596. In that year, by decree of the provincial Council of Aquileia, the old rite that had long prevailed was abolished, and the Roman rite was everywhere prescribed and introduced.

But in those old calendars and missals of the Church of Aquileia, not only is our Nicetas absent; so also are Saint Nicetas’s predecessors, Valerian and Chromatius, who are very well known in the calendars of the Western Church and whose connection with the Church of Aquileia is beyond any doubt.

There are, in fact, three printed missals according to the custom of the holy Church of Aquileia. The first, by far more valuable than the others and in my possession, apparently belongs to the year 1490—it is mutilated both at the beginning and at the end, and therefore the year of its publication can be conjectured but not stated with certainty. The second belongs to the year 1517, and the third to 1519; these two are preserved in our public archiepiscopal library.

In addition, there is a ritual book of the same Church of Aquileia under the title *Agenda of the Diocese of the Holy Church of Aquileia*, printed in 1575. One copy is in the same library and another is in my possession.

In these four liturgical books of the Church of Aquileia—the last of which is not far removed from the period when the distinctive Aquileian rite ended and made way for the Roman rite—in each of them, I say, there is a calendar at the beginning. Our Nicetas, the subject of this discussion, is always absent from it, as are Valerian and Chromatius; they are likewise absent from the entire body of the missals.

The evidence that, according to Politus and Zabeus, tells against a distinctive cult of Nicetas in the Church of Aquileia would therefore equally tell against the cult of the Aquileian bishops Valerian and Chromatius, concerning whom there is likewise no mention in the Aquileian calendars or missals, all the way to the end of the sixteenth century.

It should therefore be noted, along with the most distinguished men—Joannes Fronto, in the preliminary observations to the Roman Calendar, nine hundred years older, which he published [Col. 1076C], §§ 1, 4, and 11; Theodoric Ruinart, in the general preface to the *Acts of the Martyrs*, no. 18; Stefano Antonio Morcelli, in the preface to the *Calendar of the Church of Constantinople*, § 1, p. 6; and frequently elsewhere throughout his work—that no sound inference can be drawn concerning the cult, or lack of cult, of any holy man from the inscription or omission of his name in the ancient calendars either of his city or of his diocese.

For calendars, both in the Eastern and in the Western Church, were intended in each locality to announce the feasts of saints who were customarily honored with a special office and Mass. Yet not all saints were honored with a special office and Mass, but only those whose monuments existed there—namely, relics, or sacred places dedicated to them, such as chapels, basilicas, or cemeteries. Other saints, although they had no feast day in the calendar with an office and Mass, were nevertheless regarded as saints and honored: they were invoked [Col. 1076D] in the litanies, represented in paintings and in the ornaments of altars, and entered in the ecclesiastical registers. This was a sign of the cult rendered to them, even without a special feast day assigned to that cult with an office and Mass. 226

As for Nicetas, and likewise for Nicetas’ predecessors, the saints Valerian and Chromatius, who had no feast day assigned to them with an office and Mass in the ancient calendars of the Church of Aquileia: the litanies mentioned above are extant—proper to the Church of Aquileia, ordered to be published by Francesco Barbaro, Patriarch of Aquileia, after the diocesan synod held by him at Gorizia in 1602, and printed at Udine in the same year. In these litanies, together with the other saints of the universal Church and with the particular martyrs, confessors, and virgins of the diocese or province of Aquileia, Saint Valerian, Saint Chromatius, and Saint Nicetas are also invoked in their proper places.

In the recently mentioned ritual book, *Agenda of the Diocese of the Holy Church of Aquileia* [Col. 1077A], the proper litanies of the Church of Aquileia are recited twice: namely, in the rite for anointing the sick, as the book itself states, and in the blessing of the font at the vigils of Easter and Pentecost. Although some of the martyrs and confessors of Aquileia appear in these litanies, Valerian, Chromatius, and Nicetas are absent.

Nevertheless, with the distinguished De Rubeis, in his dissertation *On the Sacred Rites of Friuli*, chapter 31, no. 2, we call these the lesser litanies—that is, the less extensive ones—in distinction from the other litanies used in other ecclesiastical functions, especially processions. Those may be called the greater litanies, both because they were longer and because they contained invocations of more saints; De Rubeis also provides there a specimen of these litanies from Aquileian manuscripts that he had examined.

There is therefore nothing surprising in the fact that some Aquileian saints are absent from these lesser litanies who may have been invoked in the greater ones [Col. 1077B], just as very many saints of every order are absent from those litanies of the modern Roman Rite, which may likewise be called lesser litanies and which are recited in the same functions—the blessing of the font and the commendation of the souls of the dying—although those saints are invoked in the full and greater litanies of the Rogation Days and of the penitential psalms.

Although no ancient Aquileian manuscript is now available from which those greater Aquileian litanies ordered to be published by Patriarch Barbaro together with the Synod of Gorizia can be said to have been extracted—and in which the three Aquileian bishops and confessors, Valerian, Chromatius, and Nicetas, are invoked among the saints—sound reasoning nevertheless urges us to infer that those litanies had long been customary in the Church of Aquileia.

This is suggested by chapter 24 of the same synod, where the Aquileian prelate calls them litanies formerly published by us, and where he orders them to be recited on appointed days in that part of his diocese of which Gorizia was the capital, on account of the particular and urgent needs then arising from the war against the Turks [Col. 1077C]. He says nothing about the names of the Aquileian saints as though they had been newly added and inserted there. He certainly would have done so if that had actually been the case; for such novelty would have deserved to be noted, supported at least by some explanation, and commended to the people, who are always astonished by novelties.

Here, then, is the cult rendered in the Church of Aquileia to Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, although nothing concerning him appears in the ancient calendars of the Church of Aquileia and nothing in its missals.

Moreover, it is not unworthy of notice that the ancient calendars and missals of the Church of Aquileia display the ancient custom of the universal Church—a custom brought to light by all learned men who have discussed these matters. On this subject one may consult, in particular, the same Joannes Fronto in the place cited; Sarnelli, *Ecclesiastical Letters*, vol. VI, letter 37, no. 4; Mabillon, preface to the fifth century of the Benedictine order, nos. 93 and 97; Muratori, preliminary dissertation to the ancient Roman liturgy edited by him, chapter 3 [Col. 1077D]; and Pope Benedict XIV, *On the Beatification of the Servants of God and the Canonization of the Blessed*, book I, chapters 5 and 6.

The custom was this: only martyrs were honored with a feast day appointed together with a special office and Mass; only gradually were a few confessors, and those the more celebrated, introduced. In the calendars and missals of the Church of Aquileia mentioned above, if two are excepted—namely, Saint Zoilus, a presbyter and confessor, so called there, but nevertheless treated as a martyr because of the acts of devotion that he performed toward the Aquileian martyrs during the persecution under Diocletian; and Saint Syrus, a bishop and confessor, a native of the Church of Aquileia and given as bishop to the people of Ticinum by Saint Hermagoras, the first bishop of the Church of Aquileia, according to the tradition of the Aquileians, a tradition also confirmed by the Roman Martyrology on 12 September—if these two, I say, are excepted, the only saints from among the Aquileian blessed who have a place in the calendars and missals of the Church of Aquileia, with a feast day, office, and Mass, are the holy martyrs who shed their blood for Christ.

Saint Syrus, because he was regarded as the founder of the Church of Ticinum and as the apostle of that region, almost in the apostolic age, amid the persecutions of the pagans, deserved a special cult even without martyrdom in the strict sense [Col. 1078A]. Not until a late period, however, was one of the Aquileian confessors who died in the peace of the Church inserted: Saint Paulinus, Patriarch of Aquileia, who flourished in the time of Charlemagne, since his sacred body is piously venerated in the distinguished Collegiate Church of Cividale.

He was inserted after the thirteenth century, because in the calendar of the Church of Aquileia from that same century, published by the distinguished Fridericus Althanus in his work on calendars, the name of our Saint Paulinus is not found. He was therefore inserted only after the custom of honoring confessors also with special feasts, office, and Mass had become established throughout the Church, and after the Church of Aquileia itself had given a place to the principal confessors and virgins who, because of the renown of their names throughout the universal Church, already enjoyed a common cult [Col. 1078B].

When the highly praised Patriarch Francesco Barbaro, a distinguished restorer of ecclesiastical discipline among us, had abolished the ancient Aquileian rite and adopted the Roman rite, he then began to consider how he might fully conform himself in every respect to the Roman rite, which had existed for centuries and included the honoring of confessors also with an office and Mass.

He therefore began to think of inserting into the diocesan calendar—which at that time first began to be printed annually among us—the ancient confessors of his diocese who, as was said, were already commonly regarded as saints and invoked, and who had places in the Roman Martyrology and elsewhere. He wished them, too, together with our martyrs, to have feast days, offices, and Masses.

This was indeed done. But not all our Aquileian confessors obtained a place in the new [Col. 1078C] calendars at the same time. Rather, one appeared after another, and not without the omission of certain names for a time, whether intentionally or by accident.

In the first Aquileian calendar printed by Barbaro himself, after he had introduced the Roman rite into his particular diocese even before the provincial council of 1596, by which it was prescribed for the entire province—namely, in the calendar for the year 1595, a very rare and perhaps unique copy of which is preserved in the archive of the distinguished Collegiate Chapter of Cividale, and which begins on 1 November of the preceding year, 1594—in this first separately printed Aquileian calendar, I found among the saints of November and December of both years the Aquileian bishops Valerian and Chromatius, taken, as the calendar says, from the Martyrology, that is, from the Roman Martyrology, which at that time were first transferred into our calendar, each on his own day. But I did not find Saint Nicetas.

In the second Aquileian calendar that I was able to consult, in the extensive [Col. 1078D] library—now no longer existing—of the distinguished man Carlo a Pace, namely, the calendar for the year 1598, after having searched in vain for the two intervening calendars, I found Saint Valerian, but not Chromatius or Nicetas. In the third calendar, for the following year, 1599, I found Valerian and Chromatius, but not Nicetas. Finally, I found Nicetas, Valerian, and Chromatius in another calendar, for the year 1606, since I can say nothing about the six intervening calendars, which I was unable to obtain. Thus they appeared thereafter throughout the entire subsequent series of our calendars, which, apart from a few missing items, had recently remained complete in the distinguished library of the Congregation of the Oratory of Nerio in this city of Udine.

Nothing, therefore, can be alleged against the cult of Nicetas among the Aquileians on the ground that Nicetas himself obtained a place in the calendars of the Church of Aquileia only late. This recent addition of his name to our calendars was not the beginning of his cult, but rather the completion of a cult already flourishing [Col. 1079A], through the addition of a special feast day, office, and Mass, just as had also been done in the case of Chromatius and Valerian, whose ancient cult in the same Church no one has ever questioned.

Why, then, throughout the course of so many centuries, did the Aquileians never think of entering those three bishops and confessors into their own calendar and honoring them on a sacred day with an office and Mass, while they honored others from other Churches with the same cult? Why did this not occur to them even when they introduced Saint Paulinus, the Aquileian patriarch, into the calendar?

No reason seems to us more suitable or probable than the one employed by the distinguished canon Mazochius in his work, cited elsewhere here, *On the Cult of the Saints Who Were Bishops of the Church of Naples*, part II, chapter 8, in a matter not altogether dissimilar.

He was discussing a certain Probus, a bishop of Naples in the earliest age, who is said to have flourished from the time of Antoninus Verus to that of Septimius Severus. Mazochius was surprised that Probus had found no place among the holy [Col. 1079B] bishops and confessors of the Church of Naples, his predecessors and successors, either in the celebrated Marble Calendar of the Church of Naples that he had elucidated, or in other calendars of an earlier or later age. Nor was Probus listed anywhere among the saints in other liturgical books, although ancient records of his holiness were not lacking, considering the circumstances of those times.

The situation was almost the same as that which we ourselves, and with even greater justification, have wondered at: that in our ancient calendars the three Aquileian bishops and confessors—Valerian, Chromatius, and Nicetas—were absent for so long, although among us, too, both the cult of their sanctity and their inclusion among the saints had existed from the earliest antiquity.

Mazochius therefore proposed to resolve the difficulty in this way, in accordance with his learning:

“The reason why Probus, and perhaps several others, are not found to have obtained ecclesiastical honor seems to have been simply that their bodies, lying hidden in obscurity, never came to light [Col. 1079C], so that on that occasion their abbreviated canonization, according to the custom of those times, could be promoted. For, as far as I can discern from the facts … and from the entire sacred history of the later age, the canonization of saints of somewhat earlier times took its beginning from the discovery of their bodies.

“Then, if the holiness of those whose relics had been discovered was already established by reputation, the people’s zeal was kindled so that they might be enrolled among the saints. At that point the pastors of the Church, judging the people’s desires—like a divine voice—not to be disregarded, investigated the life and holiness of those in question. If their holiness was then established by ecclesiastical judgment, proceedings were undertaken for the elevation of their bodies and their translation to more worthy places.” 229

He then concludes:

“Therefore, for this one reason it seems to me that both Probus and perhaps others … failed to shine with ecclesiastical cult: plainly because, since their bodies were never discovered, there was no occasion for the zeal of the faithful to be inflamed so as to seek from the bishops an inquiry into the cause, followed by [Col. 1079D] canonization, the elevation of the body, and its translation. Their names are now written in the Book of Life.”

Thus far Mazochius, who on this subject also refers to what he had written in note 13 of the dissertation prefixed to his commentary on the aforementioned Marble Calendar of the Church of Naples. He also cites Mabillon’s dissertation on the canonization of saints in the later period. The same matter may be found in Morcelli’s *Calendar of the Church of Constantinople*, vol. I, p. 134, where he discusses Eudoxius the martyr on 6 September.

Returning, then, to our three Aquileian bishops and confessors, Valerian, Chromatius, and Nicetas: it is certain that they belong to the fourth and fifth centuries of the Church, when the practice of granting even confessors the full public cult of a feast day, office, and Mass was only beginning, and, as learned men observe, was followed only in certain places [Col. 1080A]. This was not done without great selectivity, so that only those whose eminence in virtues and merits in some way equaled the glory and renown of the martyrs were elevated to this honor. Previously, the martyrs alone had enjoyed this full public cult.

This is clear from what was done in the case of Saint Martin, bishop and confessor of Tours. He is regarded as one of the first among the confessors who died in the peace of the Church and are found to have been granted this full ecclesiastical cult. For that reason, contemporary writers deliberately compared him with the martyrs in the merit of his life, as Pope Benedict XIV most learnedly observes in the place cited above.

In the meantime, there can be no doubt that our three bishops and confessors initially received at least some cult of sanctity in the common opinion—an opinion which, with the permission or even the approval of the bishops, was equivalent to legitimate canonization for those times. Thus they found a place in hagiologies or martyrologies and were used by the faithful in invocations [Col. 1080B].

Furthermore, it is certain that no relic of the sacred ashes of these three Aquileian bishops—Valerian, Chromatius, and Nicetas—is possessed today. Nor is there any evidence that such relics ever existed in the celebrated treasury of the Church of Aquileia, which was rich in the relics of the holy martyrs of the Church of Aquileia and of other Churches, as can be seen from the ancient inventory of relics of that most celebrated Church in our Bertolus, *Antiquities of Aquileia*, p. 366.

From this it may easily be inferred that the memory of their sacred ashes was lost from the earliest times, while only the reputation of their names and sanctity survived. 230 It may therefore rightly be said that, after that first age had passed—an age in which confessors who were saints were still very rarely granted the public cult of a feast day, office, and Mass—and since the places where the bodies of the holy Aquileian bishops Valerian, Chromatius, and Nicetas had been buried remained unknown, especially in view of the disastrous vicissitudes to which the city of Aquileia and the whole province of Aquileia were so frequently subjected at that time and thereafter [Col. 1080C], it may rightly, I say, be said that, in Mazochius’s words, there was no occasion for the zeal of the faithful to be inflamed so that these holy bishops and confessors might receive that fullness of public cult which otherwise was due to them.

That fullness consisted in their inscription in the calendar of the Church of Aquileia, with the appointment of a feast day and also of an office and Mass. Thus they remained deprived of this honor until the end of the sixteenth century, when they were finally enriched with it by their distinguished successor, Patriarch Francesco Barbaro, whom we mentioned above.

As for our Nicetas in particular—the only one under discussion here, whose name we have seen listed in the martyrologies from ancient times—who would not be astonished that he had held a place in the martyrologies for so many centuries before being entered in the calendar of his own Church, when, conversely, as learned men observe, martyrologies in antiquity were formed chiefly from the calendars of particular Churches? The distinguished Morcelli, whom we have praised above, recently made this observation in the preface to the *Calendar of the Church of Constantinople*, § 1, pp. 6–7 [Col. 1080D].

Unless our opinion deceives us, this is the fullest possible proof that our Nicetas had long been known everywhere and that his sanctity had been established, as well as that a cult had been rendered to him widely among his own people and among outsiders. With this we gladly conclude our discussion of his sanctity and cult, and at the same time bring to an end the eighth chapter of our dissertation, whose purpose was to discuss Saint Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, together with his short works and fragments, as well as his sanctity and cult.

[Col. 1080D]

## CHAPTER IX

### Certain noteworthy matters concerning doctrine and morals, and concerning discipline, are presented from the short works and fragments of Saint Nicetas

There is no greater delight for a Christian who has been imbued from childhood with the dogmas, precepts, and institutions of the holy [Col. 1081A] Catholic religion—no greater delight, I say—than, when the opportunity presents itself and the powers of his intellect permit, finally to learn and perceive from the ancient works of the holy Fathers, whether long since published or brought to light later, that he has learned nothing in the arena of Christian doctrine which was not guarded and handed down by those first teachers of our religion through every age.

This is indeed the excellence of this religion, by which it is distinguished from all the so-called religions introduced by the spirit of error: it has never handed down anything new, nor taught anything new, whether in the rules of faith or in the precepts of morality; and, amid the variations of discipline itself, it has always and everywhere preserved one and the same spirit.

For this reason, all who have devoted care to publishing the works of the holy Fathers have thought it worthwhile to include in [Col. 1081B] their prefaces those matters concerning dogma, moral precepts, and rites that were especially exposed either to the calumnies of innovators or to the insults of wicked men. They did so to promote both the usefulness and the convenience of theologians, preachers, and all readers, and to set before them, as though in a single view, the perfect agreement of our doctrine and institution with the teaching of antiquity.

Following in their footsteps, although with unequal ability, we too shall investigate here certain matters from the two short works of our Nicetas that survive, as well as from fragments of his lost works, concerning dogma, moral precepts, and discipline. We shall do this so that, insofar as lies within our power, nothing may be lacking even in this modest attempt that others, with greater precision and fullness, have supplied according to the strength of their intellect and the abundance of their material.

Yet what need is there for our observations if the subject is the dogmas that we profess or the more important precepts governing life? For the *Explanation of the Creed* by our Nicetas is clear in itself and sets out in order everything that we ourselves received in the instruction of our earliest years. Let the fair-minded reader therefore judge kindly the few things that we add on these subjects, as well as those that will follow [Col. 1081C].

The foundation and at the same time the pillar of the entire Christian formation is faith; for it is from this that Christian believers are called Christians, by a kind of antonomasia. Therefore, when someone approaches the doors of the Church to receive the washing of regeneration, and the priest asks what he seeks, he answers: faith.

This is the first act of obedience owed to the Divinity by a creature endowed with reason: by it the creature professes both the supreme excellence of God and its own servitude, giving assent without any hesitation whatever to those things that are proved to have been revealed by God to humanity, even though they wholly surpass the reach of the human mind and at times may appear contrary even to reason.

This, then, is the purpose of the entire little book, the *Explanation of the Creed*: the principal dogmas of the Christian faith contained in the Apostles’ Creed are handed down and explained. They are treated individually and at somewhat greater length, either because they had been violated by the heretics of that period—such as the dogma of the true humanity of Christ our Savior, which Eutyches and his followers had then [Col. 1081D] recently denied—or because they seemed more difficult to secure assent to in human minds, such as the doctrine of the future resurrection of our true flesh, which, one might almost say, has never lacked opponents, whether among pagans, Jews, or heretics.

But what is there here that requires our particular attention? Nicetas our author asserts in his *Explanation*, chapter 9, that integrity of faith in every single article is necessary for eternal salvation, just as we are still taught today in the Catholic Church by perpetual tradition. Therefore those who boast of professing the whole Catholic faith cannot flatter themselves if they stumble in even one dogma of the faith:

“I will proclaim nothing concerning this confession of the Trinity, lest I cause harm to my salvation and injury to my faith.”

Thus Nicetas instructed his catechumens to answer those—whether pagans, Jews, or heretics—by whom they might perhaps [Col. 1082A] be tested concerning the dogmas of the Christian faith.

“Always retain the covenant that you made with the Lord, namely, this Creed which you confess before angels and human beings.”

Thus also to the same people, in chapter 15. Nor does our Nicetas merely impress upon them the absolute integrity of faith; he also admonishes them to remember continually the confession of faith spoken by the mouth and contained in the Creed. This serves not only to proclaim the matters of faith by oral confession, but also diligently to meditate upon them and frequently to elicit inward acts of faith, which has always been a principal element of Christian instruction and profession. For he says in chapter 16:

“Therefore, beloved, whether you are sitting, working, sleeping, or awake, let this saving confession revolve in your hearts.”

So much for faith and the dogmas of faith taken together. Let us now turn to certain matters individually.

What the Catholic Church has always taught and continues to teach concerning the operation and power of the Holy Spirit, with respect to the gift of divine grace—namely, that this grace is gratuitous and [Col. 1082B] altogether necessary for salvation—Nicetas himself also taught his catechumens in chapter 7 of the *Explanation*, where he says:

“He [the Holy Spirit] distributes the gifts of grace to each as he wills … without whose operation no creature can attain eternity.”

Can this eternal life, for whose expectation we are comforted, on account of which we are neither elated in prosperity nor cast down in adversity, and which is equally believed and hoped for by Catholics and by all the communities under heaven that dissent from Catholic communion—can this eternal life ever be attained outside the one Catholic Church? Certainly not, according to Catholic dogma.

Whatever those separated from Catholic communion have uttered at any time, and whatever they still chatter, there is perhaps no doctrine of the Catholics that is more offensive to them than this. It has therefore always been the doctrine of Catholics of every age. Our Nicetas also offers a clear testimony to it in the fifth century, in chapter 10 of the *Explanation*, where, on [Col. 1082C] the article of the Creed concerning the holy Catholic Church, he says:

“Therefore, believe that in this one Church you will obtain communion with the saints. Know that this is the one Catholic Church established throughout the whole world; you must firmly retain communion with it. There are indeed other pseudo-churches, but you have nothing in common with them, such as those of the Manichaeans, Cataphrygians, Marcionites, or the other heretics or schismatics; for these Churches have ceased to be holy. Deceived by demonic doctrines, they believe and act otherwise than Christ the Lord commanded and the apostles handed down.”

What could be clearer for confirming the Catholic dogma concerning the communion of saints and the attainment of eternal life in the Catholic Church alone, with all pseudo-churches—whether of heretics or schismatics—entirely excluded?

Yet Catholic believers must not flatter themselves that they belong to this one true Catholic Church, as though for that reason alone they might dare to promise themselves eternal life, without striving with all their strength to be free from vices, to avoid sins, and to live piously and chastely [Col. 1082D].

This is what the guardians of souls teach daily in the Catholic Church from divinely revealed doctrine. Nicetas himself taught the same thing to his catechumens in chapter 15 of the *Explanation of the Creed*, saying:

“No pagan will possess this life [eternal], nor will the unbelieving Jew possess it; nor will the Christian who serves vices and crimes, because it has been prepared only for the faithful who live chastely.”

What does Nicetas think, then, concerning the eternity of the punishments that await the wicked? This eternity of punishment, so frequently and unanimously proclaimed in the Catholic Church, greatly troubles lazy people and those enslaved to sins, so that they are not ashamed easily to persuade themselves that preachers have magnified the matter in order to instill fear rather than proclaiming a dogma divinely handed down.

What do they not invent [Col. 1083A] concerning divine goodness and divine mercy, so that they may imagine that the place of punishment will certainly not be eternal? But what can they say against the perpetual faith of this dogma, which the Fathers handed down to us with one voice and with which our Nicetas also agrees?

“But let him subject the wicked to eternal punishment,” he says in chapter 6 of the *Explanation*.

“I know that more severe torments are reserved for criminals, and that impious souls must remain in torment without end—not temporal torments, certainly, but eternal ones.”

Thus in the little book addressed to the Lapsed, chapter 8, no. 32:

“Be willing to undergo whatever affliction, whatever labor, provided that you are freed from eternal punishments.”

Thus in the same work, no. 34, and frequently elsewhere.

Heretics are angry with the Catholic Church because it teaches that the merits of the saints and their prayers in heaven are highly effective for obtaining the forgiveness of sins; for this reason they ridicule our invocations of the saints. Yet the Church has always maintained both propositions, and both are dogmas of faith, to which our Nicetas also bears witness.

“If you had died according to the common [Col. 1083B] lot”—he said to the lapsed virgin in chapter 8, no. 16—“your parents … would have rejoiced greatly, because they would have sent an unstained virgin before them, a living sacrifice to the Lord, an expiation for sins.”

Here, then, are the merits of the saints and their prayers as an expiation before God for sins.

“Seek the help of the saints.”

Thus he says to the same woman in chapter 9, no. 40. Here is the invocation of the saints proposed and impressed upon the lapsed virgin by our Nicetas as effective for obtaining from the Lord forgiveness for the crime she had committed.

These few observations from Nicetas concerning the dogmas of faith and matters related to dogma should suffice.

Let us now proceed, as far as our purpose permits, to matters concerning morals: the manner in which life is to be conducted; sins and the various degrees of their gravity; penance to be performed after sins; and the institution of sacred virgins.

What is more frequently on the lips of all our preachers and parish priests, as well as of teachers, especially in the earliest instruction in Christian life [Col. 1083C] that most of us receive from childhood, than the remembrance of the renunciations made at baptism—renunciation of the devil, his works, and his pomp?

There is certainly no easier way to keep Christian minds within their duty than to place before their mind’s eyes the promises they made so solemnly at baptism. Nor is there a more powerful argument with which to rebuke a Christian life that has departed from its appointed purpose than to compare that life with the promises made at baptism.

This was therefore a very common reproach among the Fathers, especially against those who pursued vanity through excessive bodily adornment and displayed pride in their way of life, and particularly against those devoted to spectacles, dances, and theaters, followed for the most part by luxury and drunkenness, and who thereby openly falsified the Christian commitment.

You may now see our Nicetas preaching the same things in the fifth century, both in the *Explanation of the Creed*, chapters 1 and 16, and especially in the third fragment. There, while instructing his catechumens, he urged and [Col. 1083D] taught them not to renounce these things with bare words or with their lips alone, but with the strongest faith and certain knowledge, as he himself put it. There, too, he most elegantly rebukes before them Christians—men and women—who, contrary to what they had promised, pursued excessive refinement in their way of life and more splendid bodily adornment.

“What shall we say,” he asks, “about those who wish to flaunt themselves in excessive adornment of the flesh and to appear marvelous? I say nothing of the unnecessarily elaborate fineness of their garments. I ask you: what purpose do curled and artificially arranged hair serve on men, with locks covering the nape of the neck behind and completely hiding the forehead in front, so that no room is left on the forehead even for the sign of Christ’s cross? From the very thing by which they think they possess some glory or beauty, they derive disgrace and dishonor.

“Likewise, women bind their heads like a shield, so that the forehead stands like a valley between two hills; so that jeweled pendants fastened with gold hang from their ears; so that their arms are [Col. 1084A] burdened with gold; so that chains or stones press upon their necks; and so that crimson little flames of footwear gleam upon their feet.

“What use or benefit is found in these things, except empty display alone and a mind corrupted by childish desire?”

It should not therefore be considered excessive severity on the part of our times if we preach these same things to the people frequently. This is the moral teaching that has flowed down to us together with the articles of faith, and which, from the tradition of our ancestors, will always be preached in the Catholic Church for the correction of human conduct and the formation of a life worthy of the Christian name.

What shall we now say about sinners, sins, and the penance to be performed for them? We are daily warned that sins lead to death and that sinful souls are under the dominion of the devil, so that we may abstain from sins and mourn over sins committed.

The same doctrine existed in every age. The bishop Nicetas of Aquileia also bears witness to it in the fifth century, in the little book addressed to the Lapsed, chapter 1, no. 4, where he says:

“Truly this is captivity: souls [Col. 1084B] are led captive by sin to death and are possessed by diabolical domination.”

That sins are more serious when they give scandal to the faithful and cause unbelievers also to blaspheme the name of the Lord is not a fabrication of certain stricter theologians, but the teaching of Scripture, commended to the Church by the harmonious tradition of the Fathers.

Imbued with this doctrine, the Aquileian Nicetas also stirred his lapsed virgin to greater penance because of the crime she had committed, which had been a scandal to many and had given unbelievers an occasion for blasphemy.

For in the same little book addressed to the Lapsed, chapter 7, nos. 30–31, he said:

“Indeed, if you had harmed only yourself, there would have been sorrow, but perhaps it would have been bearable. But now, how many souls have you wounded by your crime? How many souls have you caused, because of you, to repent of their purpose? How many lips even of the faithful have been defiled by blaspheming the way of the Lord? The Gentiles have opened their mouths against us; through your disgrace [Col. 1084C] the synagogue of the Jews has rejoiced against the holy Church.

“And if one who has caused a single person to stumble ought to be thrown into the sea with a millstone fastened around him, what sentence will you pronounce concerning yourself, through whose crime every soul has been wounded and the name of the Lord has been blasphemed among the nations?”

Moreover, certain sins are more common among people, and indeed are deadly sins, in which sinners nevertheless wish very easily to secure indulgence and impunity for themselves from the multitude of their associates. Who does not hear avaricious men, rapacious men, fornicators, and others of this kind even today flattering themselves because of the crowd of their companions, and striving to lessen the gravity of their sins by appealing to the very multitude of sinners? We respond to them daily and expose their deceptions; but how elegantly and firmly our Nicetas does so in the same little work *To the Lapsed*, chapter 9, no. 41, addressing his words to the violator of a virgin:

> “Nor should you flatter yourself because of the multitude of similar sinners and say: ‘I am not the only one who has done this; I have many companions.’ Rather, reflect that a multitude of companions does not make crimes go unpunished.” [Col. 1084D]

A judgment truly worthy of a learned and holy man, one that establishes an entire moral doctrine on this matter.

From sinners and sins, let us turn to repentance. “Repentance,” he says, “is necessary for the lapsed, just as medicines are necessary for the wounded.” Thus *To the Lapsed*, chapter 8, no. 33. “The greatness of repentance must be proportioned to the weight of the conscience . . . and after the one baptism no other remedy has been established than the consolation of repentance.” Thus in the following no. 34:

> “Therefore, if the sinner does not spare himself, God will spare him. And if, in this brief span of life, he compensates for the future everlasting punishments of Gehenna, he will free himself from the eternal judgment.”

Thus in the same place, no. 36. These are the things that all the Fathers taught concerning repentance insofar as it is a virtue, and concerning penitential works insofar as they are the fruits of the virtue of repentance and actions satisfying to God; and these are the things that we ourselves preach daily to the faithful.

[Col. 1085A] Let us now consider what Nicetas thought about the profession of virginity and about virgins. In a certain sense the ancient Fathers compete with one another when they speak of the profession of virginity and of virgins, in celebrating the praises of virginity and virgins—as must be well known to anyone who is not unfamiliar with the reading of the holy Fathers. This is a distinctive glory of the Christian religion, wholly unknown to human philosophy and entirely unrecognized even by the Synagogue itself. Nevertheless, from the very beginning of the world God, in his supreme wisdom, did not cease to prepare his Church for it, as though by certain steps, as Saint Methodius, bishop and martyr, eloquently explained in the *Banquet of the Ten Virgins*, pp. 16 and following of the Roman edition, prepared by Leo Allatius in 1656.

Thus our Nicetas too agrees with the other Fathers of the Church and with the Church’s common proclamation. He had a particular occasion to write about the profession of virginity and about virgins, although on that occasion it was a very unhappy one: in the frequently cited little work of reproof addressed to a certain virgin of his Church who had fallen. Speaking of the institution of virgins in chapter 2, no. 5, of that same work, he calls the virginity that the wretched woman had lost a “glory,” and he often recalls this glory throughout the work, so that it is sufficiently clear how highly he valued this institution.

What, then, was a consecrated virgin according to Nicetas? Let him speak for himself. Addressing the same woman in the same place, no. 6, he says:

> “You were a virgin in the paradise of God, surely among the flowers of the Church; you were the bride of Christ, you were the temple of God, you were the dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit . . . . You walked in the Church like that dove of which it is written: ‘The wings of the dove are silvered, and the hinder parts of its back are like gold.’ You shone like silver, you gleamed like gold, when you came forth with a pure conscience. You were like a star shining in the hand of the Lord; you feared neither any wind nor any clouds of war.”

These statements concern the consecrated virgin with respect to the excellence of her state and the dignity of her soul. But what does Nicetas say about the virgin body? In chapter 4, no. 13, he declares the members of consecrated virgins to be members dedicated to Christ. Saint Ambrose had called the body of a virgin “sacred” in *On Virgins*, book II, chapter 3, no. 20. Saint Hilary of Poitiers had called virgins “bodies consecrated to God” in his letter, or book I, *To Constantius Augustus*, no. 6. Saint Cyprian, in letter 60 of the edition of Baluze, had called virgins “members dedicated to Christ,” using the very words of our Nicetas. Tertullian had written of “sanctified flesh” and “flesh given over to Christ” in *On the Veiling of Virgins*, chapters 3 and 16.

But what was the common opinion of people at that time concerning the glory of virginity and virgins consecrated to God—an opinion that, certainly, even among Christians was not always the same as the sound teaching of bishops and eminent men? The most devout Helena, mother of Constantine Augustus, had left the whole world a splendid example of this matter not long after the beginning of the fourth century. Rufinus of Aquileia, our own countryman, reports in book I, chapter 8, of his *Ecclesiastical History* [Col. 1085D]:

> “When she was at Jerusalem, she is said to have invited to dinner the virgins whom she found there consecrated to God, and to have cared for them with such devotion that she considered it unworthy for them to make use of servants’ services. Instead, girded in the dress of a maidservant, she herself with her own hands would set out the food, offer the cup, and pour water over their hands; and she, the queen of the world and mother of the empire, counted herself the servant of Christ’s handmaids.”

What, then, did the fifth century think about these virgins and their virginal profession? From our Nicetas we understand that Christian families considered it a supreme honor and glory for themselves to have given some consecrated virgin to the Church. For in the chapter cited above, chapter 4, no. 15, he asserts that the father of that fallen virgin had counted her, while she was still undefiled, as his particular glory, and that her mother too found consolation through her virginity for the pangs of her childbirth. This was certainly the common opinion everywhere among Christians of that age. To illustrate it, it will not be out of place to insert here what Saint Augustine wrote in 413 or 414 about the consecrated virgin Demetrias, from the illustrious Roman family of the Anicii. He wrote in letter 150 of the Maurist edition, addressed to the noble widows Proba and Juliana—one the virgin’s mother, the other her grandmother—who had informed him by letter about the solemnity of the veiling of their daughter and granddaughter:

> “Who,” he says, “could explain in words, who could celebrate with fitting praise, how incomparably more glorious and fruitful Christ finds the virgins among women of your blood than the world finds consuls among men? For if it is a great and splendid thing to mark the records of time with the dignity of a name, how much greater and more splendid is it to surpass others in purity of heart and body? Let the noble girl, noble by birth and nobler by holiness, rejoice more that through divine fellowship she is to attain a distinguished elevation in heaven than if through human marriage she were to produce an exalted offspring. For the Anician posterity more nobly chooses to bless so illustrious a family by refusing marriage than to multiply it by childbearing, and already in the flesh to imitate the life of angels rather than still to increase from the flesh the number of mortals.” [Col. 1086B]

Thus the holy teacher. Saint Jerome agrees with him in letter 130 of Vallarsi’s edition, addressed to Demetrias herself, whom in no. 1 he calls first in the Roman world in nobility and wealth. In no. 6 he introduces her mother and grandmother rejoicing that “the virgin [Demetrias] by her virginity made a noble family nobler.” Likewise, in no. 3, he had called Demetrias’ father Olybrius, already dead, more fortunate because “he made the nobility of Demetrias’ great-grandmother more distinguished through the perpetual chastity of his daughter Demetrias.” From all this it is even clearer that the most illustrious Christian families also counted it as their greatest glory whenever they had offered a consecrated virgin from their offspring to the Church. This common estimation of virginity in earlier times rightly lifts us up, since among us too, in accordance with the Church’s perennial teaching, no lesser account is made of this angelic state. But let us proceed further.

Although the glory of virginity was regarded as splendid and exalted, professing virginity was nevertheless considered a difficult and arduous undertaking. Thus girls were not merely subjected to no compulsion to enter upon this course; rather, the difficulties of the life they were to undertake were set before their eyes. Only after a long delay, after many examinations had been conducted, the divine will had been tested for the gifts of grace necessary for so great a work, and the girls themselves had freely desired it—indeed, had in a certain sense pressed for it—were they permitted to profess virginity in the presence of the Church. Nicetas himself testifies in the same little work, chapter 4, nos. 17–18, that all these procedures had been carried out with the fallen virgin before she was admitted to be solemnly dedicated to God in virginity.

The same principle has always prevailed in the Catholic Church in establishing consecrated virgins: their free will had to be approved, and the signs of a divine vocation made evident. If, on occasion, the outcome did not correspond to such great care—which, under the protection of the divine Spirit, happened very rarely—this was certainly to be attributed less to the negligence of superiors or parents than to the devices of that ancient and most crafty serpent who deceived even the virgin of our most holy Nicetas.

What, in reality, did the teaching of those times hold concerning girls who professed virginity, with respect to their resolve or promise to preserve chastity? Here we mean virgins belonging to the institution to which Nicetas’ fallen virgin belonged: consecrated virgins who had not merely privately expressed their intention of virginity and made a promise to the Lord in their hearts, but who had publicly professed the institution of virginity in the presence of the Church—having received the veil from the bishop of the Church, and having undergone the other customary rites on a solemn day and before the assembled people, rites that will be discussed below. They therefore ought not to be said to have made a simple vow of continence, but a wholly solemn one, if those terms—introduced later to indicate the same reality—had then been in use.

The teaching of those times concerning these virgins certainly held the same thing that was afterwards always taught and observed concerning virgins who bound themselves by a solemn vow to preserve chastity, when they made solemn profession in one of the virginal institutions approved by the Church. Namely, that this resolve to preserve purity imposed a truly serious obligation, affecting both soul and conscience; that the resolve was perpetual, indissoluble, and irrevocable; and that it rendered invalid any subsequent bond attempted against it.

For this reason, consider our Nicetas in the same work *To the Lapsed*, chapter 5, no. 19, where he calls the solemnity of that virgin’s veiling her marriage with her Spouse and Lord, and later recalls the fidelity that she then promised him—a fidelity corresponding to that made after a marriage had been completed, and therefore indissoluble and perpetual. In the following no. 20, consider how Nicetas calls that act of veiling a spiritual union made by the virgin with Christ, among the innumerable witnesses of the Church, before the angels and the armies of heaven.

But when the holy bishop had proposed to himself, in no. 21, in excuse for the fallen woman, the Apostle’s words in 1 Corinthians 7, “It is better to marry than to burn,” see how correctly he interprets the authority and at the same time explains the whole matter concerning the profession of virginity by those who had received the veil:

> “This saying of the Apostle applies to one who has not made a promise, to one who has not yet been veiled. But she who has promised herself to Christ and received the holy veil has already married; she has already been joined to an immortal man. And if she should now wish to marry according to the common law of marriage, she commits adultery and becomes a servant of death.”

Nicetas again speaks in the same sense in chapter 9, no. 39, when, addressing the young man who had corrupted that virgin, he rebukes him for two crimes committed in a single offense—namely, adultery and sacrilege:

> “But what shall I say about you, son of the serpent, servant of the devil, violator of God’s temple? In a single offense you committed two crimes: adultery and sacrilege.”

The holy bishop thus sufficiently confirmed what he meant by the solemn veiling that the fallen virgin had received, since he distinguishes two crimes in her corrupter: adultery and sacrilege. It was adultery because she was already married and joined to an immortal man—a man, that is, who is never subject to death and therefore never leaves his bride a lawful and valid opportunity to enter a new marriage. It was sacrilege because she was married and joined to the immortal man Christ the Lord, whose spiritual union he himself ought also to have revered in a particular way for its excellence and holiness.

Furthermore, the very word “adultery,” used by Nicetas in both places after he had taught about marriage and spiritual union, conveys this as well: that the marriage accomplished by the veiling is not abolished and that the marital bond is not dissolved, in accordance with the Catholic doctrine concerning the sacrament of marriage.

Nicetas therefore judged that the profession of virginity publicly made by virgins, together with the solemn reception of the veil, was perpetual, indissoluble, and irrevocable, just as it was later in the case of virgins consecrated by a solemn vow; and that it also rendered invalid any bond attempted against it. Since Nicetas makes these assertions so confidently concerning the profession of virginity and its force in virgins who had solemnly received the veil, there can be no doubt that he was speaking from the common teaching of the Church at that time on so grave a matter.

This teaching, which in the fifth century appears entirely common from Nicetas’ manner of speaking, was undoubtedly also the teaching of earlier centuries. Learned men have demonstrated this by adducing numerous documents from those times, so that we may rightly say that those who denied that, during the first five centuries, the marriages of those who had solemnly vowed chastity were invalid in the judgment of the Church were mistaken. But let us now turn to matters of discipline.

As we attempt here to extract the discipline of the fifth century from Nicetas’ works and fragments, with respect to those customs or rites of the Church that are mentioned there, it is not our intention to show that the same discipline still prevails in every respect today, as was done concerning the dogmas of the faith and moral teaching.
