Some elements of the discipline of those times still continue; others are traces of that discipline; still others of that ancient discipline have become entirely obsolete, making way for new institutions appropriate to the circumstances of the times.

Yet even amid this variety of discipline, we admire one remarkable fact: the spirit of the Church was always one and the same. By that spirit she regulated everything, both collectively and individually, according to the diversity of places and times; she was most indulgent toward the needs of her children, now maintaining strictness, now relaxing it, now restoring ancient practices, now substituting new ones for the old. In all this conduct she was concerned with one thing alone: always to win all people for Christ, and above all to preserve among them the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. Let us therefore review each matter in order.

The first discipline that we observe in Nicetas’ works concerns the *competentes*, those preparing for baptism. We already said much about this in the preceding chapter, when we reviewed Nicetas’ individual works. But here we should recall a particular rite concerning the Creed, which was handed over to the *competentes* and recited by them in return.

Addressing the *competentes* in his *Explanation of the Creed*, chapter 8, after setting forth the doctrine of the Trinity, Nicetas spoke as follows:

> “Establish this faith of the Trinity firmly, brothers, in your hearts.”

In the same sense, we have the following in a fragment, or remnant, of Nicetas, no. 4:

> “Everyone who desires to come to the faith and to baptism must alike be instructed and taught, so that he may retain the brevity of the Creed by heart and from memory.” [Col. 1088C]

Here, unless we are mistaken, an ancient discipline of the Church is indicated—a discipline still in force in Nicetas’ time—according to which the Creed of the faith, in accordance with the still more ancient discipline of the *arcana* or secrecy, was handed over orally to the *competentes*. According to the same discipline, the *competentes* also recited the Creed orally, with every aid of a written page entirely forbidden, even as an otherwise useful assistance to memory.

Saint Augustine certainly offers an outstanding testimony concerning this discipline in sermon 212, *On the Tradition of the Creed*, no. 2:

> “I have rendered back to you the brief discourse owed to you concerning the whole Creed . . . . You must in no way write down the same words of the Creed so that you may retain them; rather, learn them thoroughly by listening. And when you have learned them, do not write them down, but always retain and recall them in your memory. For whatever you are going to hear in the Creed is contained in the divine writings of Scripture. But the fact that it has been collected in this way and reduced to a certain form, which it is not permitted to write down, serves as a reminder of God’s promise. Through the prophet, when he foretold the New Testament, he said: ‘This is the covenant that I will establish with them after those days, says the Lord: giving my law into their minds, and I will write it on their hearts’ (Jeremiah 31:33). To signify this, the Creed is learned by listening; it is not written on tablets or on any material, but on the heart.”

Other words of the same holy teacher on this very matter also deserve to be recalled, from the sermon entitled *On the Creed to the Catechumens*. In reality, it ought to have been delivered at the handing over of the Creed to the *competentes*, and in the latest edition of his works it appears outside the numbering of the other sermons:

> “Receive, children, the rule of faith, which is called the Creed. And when you have received it, write it on your heart, and say it every day among yourselves: before you go to sleep, before you go out, arm yourselves with your Creed. No one writes down the Creed so that it may be read; but, lest forgetfulness erase what diligence has handed over, let your memory be your book for reciting it. What you are going to hear, you will believe; and what you have believed, you will also return with your tongue . . . . For this is the Creed that you are going to recite and return.”

Thus the holy teacher. It should be observed here that, on the basis of the more reliable editions of Augustine’s works, the words quoted must in fact be read with a short line—the mark we call a comma—between the word “diligence” and “let your memory be your book,” not with a full stop after the word “diligence,” as we have seen the same text of Augustine quoted in some places, as will be seen below. The full stop placed there entirely changes the meaning of the text and makes it wholly contrary to Augustine’s earlier, most unambiguous passage.

Saint Peter Chrysologus offers another distinguished testimony to this discipline in force around the middle of the fifth century, in his celebrated Church of Ravenna, in sermon 58, *On the Apostles’ Creed*. There he instructed the *competentes*, who were about to receive the Creed:

> “You who are about to receive the Creed—which is the covenant of life, the pledge of salvation, and the unbreakable bond of faith between you and God—prepare your breasts, not paper; sharpen your understanding, not your pen; and write what you hear not with ink, but with the Spirit as your minister. For an eternal and heavenly secret cannot be entrusted to perishable and corruptible instruments; it must be placed in the very ark of the soul, in the very library of the inward spirit, lest a profane judge or an unscrupulous examiner find something to tear apart; and lest what was given for the salvation of one who confesses and believes become, to the ruin of one who despises and is ignorant, an occasion of destruction.”

Thus the holy teacher.

The Roman Church also supplies a document from the end of that same fifth century in support of this discipline concerning the Creed, in the *Gelasian Sacramentary*, in Muratori’s *Ancient Roman Liturgy*, volume I, col. 540 of the Venetian folio edition. In the preface of the Creed addressed to the elect, we read:

> “Therefore, with attentive minds learn the Creed; and what, as we have received it, we hand over to you, write not upon any material that can be corrupted, but upon the pages of your heart.”

What, then, of the Church of Aquileia? Our Rufinus is available in his celebrated *Commentary on the Apostles’ Creed*, no. 2 [Col. 1089C]. There he also calls this discipline—the prohibition against writing down the Creed—an apostolic tradition, saying:

> “For this reason they [the apostles] handed it down that these things should not be written on little sheets or parchments, but retained in the hearts of believers, so that it might be certain that no one had learned them from reading—which sometimes reaches even unbelievers—but from the tradition of the apostles.”

Furthermore, there is an old Aquileian liturgy in De Rubeis’ dissertation *On the Sacred Rites of Friuli*, chapter 11, extracted from ancient codices of the Church of Aquileia. In the office of examination for the *competentes*, called the opening of the ears, the very words that we quoted above from the Gelasian Sacramentary are first repeated to the elect. That office closely resembles the Gelasian one. Then another admonition is added, absent from the Gelasian Sacramentary: a particular warning to them not to write down the Creed, among the repeated recitations of the Creed prescribed there for this reason:

> “But it has been commanded that this Creed not be written on paper, wax, or a fragile reed, or with a mortal stylus; rather, it must be fixed in our minds with the stylus of faith and the pen of the divine word, which penetrates the veins and searches out every secret.”

So it says there. These words, we may venture to say, have the character of a certain antiquity, and are older than the Gelasian Sacramentary. Why should these not have been the older and, as it were, proper words of the Church of Aquileia in this very office of examination—words that were retained even after the Gelasian material had been received and inserted into it?

Thus it was the discipline of all the Churches generally in the fifth century that the Creed of the faith was handed over orally to the *competentes*, learned orally by the *competentes*, and recited orally by them, with every form of writing it excluded. Nicetas had this discipline in view in the words quoted above from chapter 8 of his *Explanation* and from fragment—or rather, remnant—4.

We must not entirely pass over here the unusual opinion of the distinguished Pierre Lebrun, in volume II of his *Liturgical Dissertations*, concerning the Apostles’ Creed. He maintained that during the first four or five centuries of the Church the Creed was not written down at all—not even by the *competentes*—but was entrusted only to the memory of Christians.

The distinguished Muratori refutes him admirably in his dissertation *On Liturgical Matters*, chapter 1, prefixed to the work cited above, *Ancient Roman Liturgy*, to which we refer the reader. Yet Muratori himself was somewhat mistaken there when, relying chiefly on the passage of Augustine quoted above from the sermon *On the Creed to the Catechumens*, and reading it incorrectly—with a full stop closing the sentence after the word “diligence,” where, as we noted there, there should be only a comma—he attempts to show that it had always been freely permitted to anyone without distinction to write down the Creed. He concedes that it was not to be recited by reading, but maintains that it could at least be written down so that, if necessary, it might be recalled from the written text for the sake of memory.

According to him, the Fathers’ warnings against handing the Creed over in writing meant nothing more than that the Creed was so precious that every believer was ordered to commit it to memory and recite it frequently, retaining it written in the mind rather than on paper.

But the passages cited, both from Augustine and from the other Fathers, undoubtedly confirm the ancient rite by which the writing of the Creed was altogether forbidden to the *competentes*. Thus they were to possess faith, in accordance with the Apostle, “from hearing”; and, deprived of the hope of assisting their memory by a written text, they were to learn the Creed more carefully and retain it more firmly. The discipline of secrecy was also to be preserved. Just as care was taken that the Creed not be handed over to catechumens before they had reached the rank of *competentes*, so care had to be taken lest, among the many copies of it that *competentes* might write, one should happen to fall into the hands of those who were not yet permitted to possess it.

This was also required by the reverence due to the Creed: it was fitting that the *competentes* should receive it from the mouth rather than from a sheet of paper, as we understand from the texts cited.

We must therefore say, both against Lebrun and against Muratori, that in antiquity it was indeed forbidden for the *competentes* to write the Creed even for their own use, so long as they remained in the order of the *competentes*. It was not, however, forbidden for bishops, priests, and others of the clergy, upon whom the duty of teaching rested, to write it; nor was it forbidden to any believers who had passed beyond the apprenticeship of Christian instruction.

One may now ask how long this discipline continued in the Church. The documents we have cited show that it was in force everywhere throughout the fifth century, when many Jews and pagans were coming daily and everywhere to the Church, and the instruction of catechumens and *competentes* was a principal concern of bishops and clergy. It may therefore have ceased when, with the Christian population increasing everywhere—and indeed with whole provinces throughout the world becoming completely Christian—the discipline of the catechumenate, as it had originally been established, gradually became obsolete.

[Col. 1090D] To touch more specifically on the Church of Aquileia, on the occasion of this rite mentioned by our Nicetas: in certain *Collections on the Ancient Rites of Baptism and Their Meaning*, which appear together with a letter of Maxentius, patriarch of Aquileia, to Charlemagne on the meaning of the rites and ceremonies of baptism, in Bernard Pez’s *Newest Treasury of Anecdotes*, volume II, we may say—not implausibly—that these collections were compiled by Maxentius himself for his own use and that of his Church. As the distinguished editor points out, they were contained in the very same codex and alongside the same letter of Maxentius.

In these so-called *Collections*, under no. 4, we read the same passage of Rufinus that we quoted above, concerning the Creed not being written on parchment but retained in the heart. From this we infer that the same practice was still in force among the people of Aquileia at that time, with respect to the *competentes*: namely, that the Creed was not to be written, but received only orally.

Maxentius governed the Church of Aquileia from approximately the eleventh year of the ninth century, as De Rubeis records in his *Monuments*. Moreover, the Aquileian order of examination at the opening of the ears, mentioned above, provides the warning from the Gelasian Sacramentary and adds another of its own concerning the Creed not being written by the *competentes*, as we have seen. This order bears a certain chronological mark, which the same De Rubeis examines in chapter 10 of his cited dissertation; from it he concludes that this examination was in use at Aquileia certainly in the ninth, or even the tenth, century.

Thus even at this late period those warnings were given in the Church of Aquileia during the examinations of those about to be baptized, concerning their not writing down the Creed. This is sufficient to say about this rite.

Another rite likewise concerned the *competentes*: the renunciations they were to make before returning the Creed they had received. Nicetas mentions this rite in chapter 1 of his *Explanation* and in fragment 3. But since we discussed it more fully in the preceding chapter, when reviewing Nicetas’ fifth work, *On the Creed*, it is sufficient here merely to recall the rite.

Nicetas calls the Creed of the faith a covenant (*pactum*) made by the *competentes* with the Lord, using a manner of speaking then common among the Fathers and drawn from the divine Scriptures, where it was also exceedingly familiar. By this expression he indicated a faith as though given to the Lord by the *competentes* in the recitation of the Creed before witnesses, and from which they were therefore not permitted to depart.

> “Always retain the covenant that you made with the Lord—that is, this Creed, which you confess before angels and human beings.”

Thus *Explanation*, chapter 15. The *competentes* were to be bound by this particular bond: the faith once given and the solemn preservation of the Christian religion, because of the grave danger of apostasy that then threatened, especially from the considerable number of pagans among whom they had to live.

Nicetas also says in fragment 5 that the Creed is a “reminder of the faith” (*commonitorium fidei*), and that it is to be held and learned by everyone in common. He called the Creed by the very suitable term “reminder of the faith,” whether with reference, as we have already said, to the faith given for the preservation of the Christian religion in the recitation of the Creed, or also with reference to the profession of the mysteries of the faith contained in it.

When he adds that the Creed is to be learned and held by everyone in common, he confirms the Church’s perpetual practice: we hand the Creed over to children themselves, reborn through baptism, to learn as soon as they begin to speak, and we require absolutely everyone to make the same profession.

How frequent is the mention in the writings of the Fathers of exorcisms before baptism! Nicetas also mentions them in his fragment 6, where he briefly and elegantly indicates both what exorcisms are and for what reason they are administered before baptism. We therefore retain this rite of exorcisms in the administration of baptism as a sacred practice handed down through the Church’s perpetual tradition.

As for the neophytes—that is, those recently baptized—on the holy Sunday of the Lord’s Resurrection, here too we have Nicetas’ testimony concerning the rite of lights, namely, burning candles that they carried in their hands until the order of the liturgy had been completed, and concerning the white garments that they then put on as a sign of the grace and innocence received in baptism:

> “In so great and so solemn an assembly of the Church of God, amid the brilliant lights of the neophytes, amid the candidates for the kingdom of heaven, and so forth.”

Thus *To the Lapsed*, chapter 5, no. 19. We still preserve both these rites to some extent in the baptism of infants, and we retain them in full in the baptism of adults.

Other matters now call us, matters that concern the worship of the sacred buildings of that time and offer us some information about what was done there in the assemblies of Christians.

Nicetas mentions the custom of vigils as fully prevailing in his own age, in the work *To the Lapsed*, chapter 6, no. 22: namely, the custom of spending in sacred buildings, amid divine praises, the nights preceding the principal festivals of the year. This was the practice not only of the clergy but also, as is very well known, of the entire people. Some trace of it now survives for us only on the night of the Nativity of the Lord.

> “You have turned night into day through these sacred vigils. Do not again turn day into night through drunkenness and gluttony and the songs of prostitutes,”

said Saint John Chrysostom to the people in homily 59, *On the Martyrs*.

In the Western Church, Sidonius Apollinaris provides a splendid example of these vigils in Nicetas’ own fifth century, in book V, letter 17, of his *Letters*. There he mentions vigils for the annual solemnity of Saint Justus, bishop of Lyons. A great crowd of both sexes is said to have been present at these vigils, so large that the immense basilica could not contain it, even though it was surrounded by crypts and porticoes extending widely.

But let us return to our Nicetas. He mentions there not only the vigils but also the light of the vigils, and such a quantity of light that it could dazzle the eyes:

> “How did the light of the vigils not dazzle your eyes?”

Who would not see here the worship of the Church of Aquileia—truly dignified and splendid, and already at that time lavishly displayed, especially in the lights of the sacred buildings? Sidonius himself mentioned the numerous lights at the vigil of the solemnity of Saint Justus in the passage recently cited.

Nicetas also mentions the singing of spiritual hymns there as a practice maintained in his Church:

> “How,” he says, “did the singing of spiritual hymns not penetrate your ears?”

Thus, already at that time, the rite of singing psalms and hymns in sacred assemblies prevailed in the Church of Aquileia. This rite, adopted from the East, had first been introduced in the West by Saint Ambrose, and the other Churches afterward immediately made it their own as well, because of the spiritual benefit that flowed from it, as we understand from Augustine, *Confessions*, book IX, chapter 7.

Nicetas describes the singing of his Church not as something that merely soothed the ears, but as something that penetrated them and thereby affected the innermost heart and generated holy affections. This was indeed the manner of singing that Saint Ambrose introduced into his Church of Milan, and whose marvelous effects Saint Augustine himself experienced. In the cited book of the *Confessions*, chapter 6, he confessed to God:

> “How greatly I wept amid your hymns and songs, deeply moved by the voices of your sweetly sounding Church! Those voices flowed into my ears, and your truth was dissolved into my heart; and from it there arose an ardent feeling of devotion, and tears ran down, and it was well with me because of them.”

This, then, is what Nicetas meant by the singing of which he speaks in the Church of Aquileia: singing that penetrated the ears.

Finally, Nicetas also mentions, in the passage cited, the heavenly lessons that were given at the gatherings of his church—that is, readings from the sacred books, which formed part of the sacred Liturgy—and he notes as well the power of these readings: “How . . . did the power of the heavenly lessons not stir your mind?” From the beginning of the Church, readings from the Old Testament were employed in the ecclesiastical Liturgy, and afterward also those from the New Testament, as soon as the Gospels and the other apostolic writings had appeared, as we learn from the ancient records. But in the fifth century, as Mabillon and others observe, a certain book was already in use among the Churches and their ministers, called the *Comes*—because it was always at hand for the ministers of the sacred temple—and it was indeed ancient, so much so that some, though incorrectly, attributed it to Saint Jerome. This book indicated the readings to be used on each day in the sacred services. Was this book also in use in the Church of Aquileia in Nicetas’ time? Quite probably. For, in the same passage, Nicetas mentions particular readings from the New Testament, which, in his view, ought to have stirred the mind of that fallen woman; then, in number 23, he adds: “Did such great and terrifying things not come to your mind when your limbs were being sought for that abominable deed, etc.?” Those words must therefore have been read in the Church of Aquileia at fixed times during the year; and, since the same words had repeatedly been read in the Church in previous years when their appointed time returned, the fallen virgin deservedly merited Nicetas’ reproach for having forgotten those heavenly lessons. [Col. 1093A] This seems readily to suggest that a certain order was also in use at Aquileia, indicating the readings to be used in the sacred services throughout the annual cycle; and that this was none other than the *Comes*, whose use had already become common in that same century.

At that time the *Comes* was of the greatest utility—I would add, necessity—to the ministers of the Church, so that they might read the divine Scriptures in the sacred gatherings, in due order and proper fashion, at each appointed time, and those passages appropriate to each day. Copies of the Scriptures were then preserved in the sacristies of the churches, undivided and complete, with great reverence for this very reason. We have for centuries had no need of this *Comes*, since we possess the readings from Scripture already divided into sections, arranged in their proper order, and distributed by individual days in our ecclesiastical books, which, thanks to printing, circulate in everyone’s hands.

But what is the power of those heavenly lessons that Nicetas notes? Without doubt he is indicating the power inherent in them, in accordance with the Apostle’s words (Hebrews 4): “The word of God is living and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart.” Yet that power probably also arose from the pronunciation of the ministers who read them, whether the lessons were simply read, or whether they were also sung with a clear voice and suitable melody, as they are still customarily sung in the Churches; and Saint Augustine acknowledged the great usefulness of such singing in *Confessions*, book 10, chapter 33.

But now the institution of sacred virgins calls us back—the subject of what Nicetas’ teaching was in his time we have already considered above—so that we may now investigate what also pertains to discipline. We are speaking, then, of those same sacred virgins who publicly professed chastity in the Church, having solemnly received the sacred veil from the bishop, together with the other ceremonies performed for such a sacred rite.

Thus, Nicetas first mentions a virginal monastery in his treatise *To the Fallen Woman*, chapter 7, no. 28: “You forgot the house of your father, as it is written, and went over to the virginal monastery.” Where, then, was this virginal monastery of the Church of Aquileia under Nicetas situated? At Aquileia, certainly, and in the middle of the city, as we can readily infer from the same work, chapter 4, no. 12.

It seems clear among learned men that sacred virgins who had professed the solemn purpose of virginity existed in the Church before there were residences for them in which they might dwell together and live under a common rule. Numerous examples of consecrated virgins in the earliest period are known who remained in their own homes, either alone or at least joined to a few companions. Nevertheless, learned writers likewise endeavor to show that certain asceteries—places of ascetic retreat—for sacred virgins existed from the earliest times of the Church, especially in the regions of the East.

The distinguished Alteserra made an excellent observation concerning the first and most ancient communities of sacred virgins in his work entitled *Asceticon*, or *On the Origins of Monastic Life*, book 3, chapter 2, where he writes: [Col. 1093D] “In the time of the apostles the name ‘monks’ was by no means heard; nevertheless, through the apostles themselves, communities of sacred virgins and widows began to exist in the Church.”

Whatever may be the case concerning these apostolic communities of sacred virgins, which may have resembled the asceteries of a later age—a matter that has not yet been sufficiently investigated—it nevertheless now appears certain from the ancient records that, after the peace granted to the Church by Constantine, communities of sacred virgins existed publicly also in the West. These virgins lived together under a certain rule of discipline in buildings established for that purpose, which were called monasteries. At the same time, the custom also continued that some of these sacred virgins, even after receiving the sacred veil from the bishop, lived within domestic walls, as is evident in the case of the famous Demetrias, descended from the family of the Anicii, whom we mentioned above on the basis of the letters of Saints Augustine and Jerome, and likewise in the case of Marcellina, the sister of Saint Ambrose, and others.

A book written in Italian appeared a few years ago, entitled *Delle Monache di Sant’ Eusebio, primo monastero d’ Occidente* (“The Nuns of Saint Eusebius, the First Monastery of the West”). We saw its second edition, printed at Vercelli in 1785, in the format commonly called octavo. Far be it from us to weaken here what its learned author asserts in the first and second chapters of this work concerning the foundation and location of this monastery, as well as its rule. Nevertheless, we would wish those claims to rest upon firmer records, so that they might persuade everyone, just as they certainly instruct and delight. If this is a defect, it is not a defect of the work but of the particular subject, which, because of the lack of native records in this area, suffers from a certain barrenness that must therefore be supplied from elsewhere. In fact, the author supplies it abundantly through his comprehensive learning, drawn from all antiquity, with which he has furnished the little book and made it pleasing to students of sacred antiquity.

Let us nevertheless grant that, toward the end of the fourth century, or even around the middle of that century, the Church of Vercelli, through the merit of Bishop Eusebius, possessed a monastery of sacred virgins, just as it possessed one for men, who were at once monks and clerics; hence the memory of Bishop Eusebius is celebrated with such distinction. Let us further grant that this was in fact the first monastery of sacred virgins in the regions of the West. What, meanwhile, shall we think of the virginal monastery at Aquileia, first mentioned by our Nicetas only after the middle of the fifth century? We may certainly conjecture, and not unwillingly, that the Aquileian virginal monastery also belonged to the fourth century of the Church, indeed to the very age of Eusebius of Vercelli, if we recall what we touched upon in the supplement to chapter 4 of this dissertation, and especially if we consider the ninety-year lifespan of that consecrated virgin Columba, whom we discussed there on the evidence of our inscription from Osoppo, and who probably belonged to the Aquileian virginal monastery.

[Col. 1094C] We have already seen there the highly celebrated clergy of the Church of Aquileia under Bishop Valerian, who assumed the Aquileian episcopate around the year 368 or 369. We likewise recognized at that same time a very famous monastery of men flourishing at Aquileia, renowned for holiness and learning; and, on the testimony of Saint Jerome, we learned of the cultivation of the praise of virginity among the female sex. Why, then, should a virginal monastery not already have existed at that time, through the merit of that clergy celebrated with such great praises—especially if we recall that it has always been more important, for the protection and honor of virgins, to provide a common dwelling for them than to establish the discipline of monks? Furthermore, that ninety-year-old consecrated virgin Columba, who died in 453, as we indicated there from Fontanini’s observations, and who probably belonged to that same Aquileian virginal monastery of which our Nicetas speaks—as the learned prelate himself would undoubtedly have inferred in that passage from what he had previously stated, had he not embraced, with the common judgment of scholars at that time, an opinion concerning the author of this treatise *To the Fallen Woman* different from ours concerning Nicetas—that ninety-year-old virgin, I say, by her very age shows that the Aquileian virginal monastery belonged to the fourth century.

Certainly, in chapter 16 of his *Commentary*, Fontanini conjectures that Columba was consecrated by Valerian, Bishop of Aquileia, who departed this life around 388 or 389, as recorded by De Rubeis in the *Monuments*. Even if we suppose that she did not receive the sacred veil of virginity before her twentieth year—for, given what was asserted there and the discipline prevailing in these regions, girls of even younger age who displayed maturity of judgment could attain this vow, as is clear from the records produced by the same author, especially from an inscription at Vercelli in Gruter, p. 1170, no. 1, where a certain deceased virgin is said to have been thirteen years old and already then “covered . . . her hair with a chaste veil”—we thus approach, insofar as conjecture allows, the age of Eusebius of Vercelli with the Aquileian virginal monastery, the latter part of whose life reached into the first years of Valerian’s Aquileian episcopate. But something further must still be attempted.

Who was it that introduced monastic discipline for both sexes from the East into the West—or at least made it more commendable and extended it? Surely it was that great Athanasius, as Saint Jerome testifies in letter 127, no. 5, to the virgin Principia, when Athanasius, exiled from his Alexandrian see, was traveling through the regions of Italy.

Athanasius was also then at Aquileia, as the guest of Fortunatianus, Bishop of Aquileia and predecessor of Valerian, in the year 348, according to De Rubeis in the *Monuments*, chapter 6, no. 5; and he took part with Bishop Fortunatianus in the ecclesiastical gatherings of the Church of Aquileia. Why should he not at that time himself have persuaded that same Fortunatianus of Aquileia to invite the sacred virgins living there into one place and instruct them in the monastic discipline of the East? In this way, might not the Aquileian virginal monastery have arisen at that very time through the efforts of Athanasius of Alexandria and the care of Fortunatianus, Bishop of Aquileia? It is enough to have said this about the Aquileian virginal monastery mentioned by Nicetas, so that we may understand it to be much older than Nicetas and certainly not much later than the virginal monastery of Eusebius of Vercelli—even if the latter was perhaps the first in the West, as the author of the aforementioned little work preferred to maintain.

But how many sacred virgins should we suppose constituted the Aquileian virginal monastery under Nicetas? He himself mentions the virginal choirs of this monastery in *To the Fallen Woman*, chapter 6, no. 22, saying: “How did there not come to your mind . . . your procession into the Church among the virginal choirs?” This manner of speaking undoubtedly indicates that the number of sacred virgins living in that virginal monastery was not small. Indeed, since at that time there were not yet, as there later were, numerous monasteries of sacred virgins in one and the same Church or one and the same city, at least in the West, the one or two that existed must have abounded in virgins gathered there from the whole [Col. 1095C] diocese.

Now, to say something also about the number of sacred virgins who lived in monasteries in antiquity: if we speak of the Eastern Church, where monastic discipline for both men and women first flourished, the ecclesiastical records provide extraordinary information about the number of virgins living in monasteries even in the fourth century of the Church. Saint Ambrose, in *On Virginity*, chapter 7, no. 36, a work which the Maurist editors judged to have been written around the year 378 on the basis of indications supplied by Ambrose himself, says: “Learn how many virgins the Alexandrian Church, the whole Church of the East, and the African Church customarily consecrate each year. Fewer men come forth here than virgins are consecrated there.”

Indeed, from Palladius’ *Lausiac History*, chapter 34, we learn that in the solitude of Tabennesis, which lies in the Thebaid, there was a monastery of three hundred virgins under the abbot Elias, who laudably cared for them for forty years. Nor do we learn without the greatest astonishment, from our Rufinus’ *Lives of the Fathers*, book 1, chapter 5, that the single city of Oxyrhynchus in Egypt, according to the report given to him by the local bishop, contained twenty thousand sacred virgins, as well as ten thousand monks.

What shall we say of the virginal monastery that the celebrated Roman widow Paula had founded in the holy city of Bethlehem? She was distinguished by the blood of the Gracchi and Scipios, but far more distinguished by Christian humility and piety. Concerning her, Jerome writes in letter 108 to her daughter Eustochium, according to the aforementioned edition of Vallarsius: “She divided the many virgins whom she had gathered from different provinces, both noblewomen and those of middle and lowly birth, into three groups and monasteries; only in such a way that, though separated in work and food, they were joined in psalmody and prayers . . . . Each company followed its own mother, etc.” From this very manner of speaking we certainly recognize the great number of virgins in the Bethlehem monastery. In the course of time this virginal monastery grew so greatly under Paula that Jerome could say in the same place, no. 30, that at her death Paula left behind an immense multitude of brothers and sisters—that is, monks and virgins.

But at that time there was not an equal abundance of virgins in the virginal monasteries of the West, or in Italy itself. Saint Ambrose delivered highly distinguished sermons on virginity to his people, which were later collected by the same author into short works entitled *On Virgins, to His Sister Marcellina*; *On Virginity*; *On the Institution of a Virgin*; and *Exhortation to Virginity*. Yet the holy bishop complained that his sermons accomplished little or nothing among his Milanese people, where, even through the efforts of their mothers, virgin girls were prevented from coming to hear him speak about virginity. He asserted instead that virgins came to him from Piacenza, Bologna, and even Mauretania, in order to receive the veil, as he says in *On Virgins*, book 1, [Col. 1096B] chapter 11.

In the same passage he extols above all the virgins of Bologna, who, renouncing worldly pleasures, inhabit the sanctuary of virginity—that is, the virginal monastery—and, leaving their parents’ dwelling, proceed to the tents of Christ, tireless soldiers of chastity. But how many virgins, finally, constituted this monastery of the Bolognese virgins, so highly praised by Ambrose in order simultaneously to stir shame and fervor among the Milanese? Certainly no more than twenty, as he himself admits, although he strives to magnify this small number by the abundance of its fruits: “Without companionship with the other sex, advancing in the companionship of modesty to the number of twenty and to the hundredfold fruit,” said the holy teacher.

What of the Roman Church itself, the foremost Church of all, at approximately the same time? Saint Jerome testifies in the aforementioned letter 127 to the virgin Principia, *On the Praises of the Widow Marcella*, no. 5, that in Marcella’s time—that is, around the middle of the fourth century—“no noblewoman in Rome knew of the monastic way of life, nor, because of its novelty, dared to assume among the people a name that was then considered disgraceful and contemptible.”

Accordingly, the first noble virgin of the city of Rome, according to the same Jerome in letter 22, no. 15, to Eustochium, written in the year of Christ 384, was Eustochium herself, Paula’s daughter, who lived with her mother in the Bethlehem monastery. As far as Rome itself is concerned, then, where, according to Jerome, the monastic way of life was still a novelty, there seem to have been no virginal monasteries there before Marcella. These monasteries finally began after Athanasius’ arrival there, and indeed also after the arrival of Peter, who succeeded Athanasius in the episcopate and was himself at Rome in the year of Christ 373 or 374. From Peter, more probably, Marcella “learned the discipline of the monasteries in the Thebaid, of Pachomius, and of virgins and widows,” as Jerome himself says in the aforementioned letter to Principia, no. 5, and as Vallarsius explains in his notes.

How small, however, was the beginning of that first Roman monastery for women! It consisted of only one or two persons: the widow Marcella and the virgin Principia, who used a suburban estate as their monastery and chose the countryside as their solitude, as Jerome says in the same place, no. 8. Yet the example of these two was like a most fertile seed, from which monasteries of virgins soon arose in Rome and grew in the number of their members: “You lived in this way for a long time,” Jerome adds, “so that, through imitation of you, we rejoiced that Rome had been made Jerusalem through the conduct of many. There were frequent monasteries of virgins and an innumerable multitude of monks; so that, because of the multitude of those serving God, what had previously been a disgrace afterward became a glory.”

Thus, shortly afterward—that is, already by the year 412, when Jerome was writing these words—the West, from so small a beginning, possessed in its communities of sacred virgins what would no longer leave it envious of the East. In Rome especially, monasteries began to abound in virgins, so that they far exceeded the number of a thousand; and in the age of Gregory the Great, that is, at the end of the sixth century, there were found no fewer than three thousand, as appears from his letter 26 of book 7, elsewhere numbered 23 of book 6. It is therefore no wonder that at Aquileia also, in the time of our Nicetas—that is, toward the end of the fifth century—the virginal monastery located there abounded in sacred virgins who truly formed virginal choirs.

But we must proceed to other aspects of virginal discipline. We must now examine the initiation of the virgins themselves, which our Nicetas specifically describes in *To the Fallen Woman*, chapter 5, nos. 19 and 20. He mentions the solemn veiling, in which lay the public and complete profession of the virginal purpose; the divine altar, where the ceremony of veiling was performed; and the holy day of the Lord’s Resurrection, on which, after the solemnity of baptism, the virgins proceeded among the lights of the newly baptized candidates in order to receive the veil, by which their spiritual marriage with Christ the King was signified:

“Did you not remember the holy day of the Lord’s Resurrection, on which you offered yourself at the divine altar to be veiled? In so great and solemn an assembly of the Church of God, amid the splendid lights of the neophytes, you came forward among the candidates for the heavenly kingdom, as though about to marry the King.”

The Apostle commanded the veiling of women in church in a grave passage, 1 Corinthians 11. That this command concerned not only married women but also unmarried women, and especially virgins who had made such a profession, was demonstrated at greater length by Tertullian at the beginning of the third century in his book *On the Veiling of Virgins*, written in the year 210, as Pamelius judged, against an abuse that had arisen in some places at that time, whereby sacred virgins went about unveiled. Among other things, he says in chapter 16—words especially worthy of notice and appropriate to our subject:

“Complete the attire of a woman”—that is, by veiling yourself, O virgin—“so that you may preserve the status of a virgin. Conceal something of what is within, so that you may present the truth to God alone. Yet you are not pretending to be married; for you have married Christ. To him you have given your flesh; to him you have betrothed your maturity. Walk according to the will of your Bridegroom. Christ is the one who commands even the brides of others and married women to be veiled; certainly, he commands his own brides to be veiled much more.”

So much for Tertullian.

The records testify that, even from the earliest times of the Church, the public and solemn initiation of virgins was carried out through veiling. The veiling of virgins indicated the spiritual marriage that the virgin entered into with Christ the Bridegroom, just as the veiling of a new bride was also employed among the Romans in wedding rites, as is sufficiently well known to scholars.

Although an example of such veiling may appear in the divine Scriptures in the case of Rebekah, when she first saw Isaac, her bridegroom, in Genesis 24, and although the practice still exists among the Hebrews, as we know from Buxtorf’s *Jewish Synagogue*, chapter 39, on the example of Ruth the Moabite in Ruth 3:19, I would nevertheless more readily believe that the custom of veiling virgins was introduced into the Church to signify their spiritual marriage from the secular custom of marriage then prevailing throughout the Roman world. That custom also had a place among Christians in ancient times, once every superstition of idolatry had been removed, and the same use of veiling had even been sanctified to demonstrate the divine origin of marriage.

This is especially clear from the first letter of Pope Siricius to Himerius, Bishop of Tarragona, chapter 4, preserved by Constantius and written around the year of Christ 385, where the nuptial veil among Christians is mentioned. It is likewise evident from letter 19, class 1, of Saint Ambrose, written at the same time to Vigilius, Bishop of Trent, no. 7, where he speaks of Christian marriage, which ought to be sanctified by a priestly veil and blessing—that is, by a veil placed by the priest upon the bride’s head, as the Maurist editors note at this passage.

Among the ancients that nuptial veil was called the *flammeum*, or *flammeus*. Because of the similarity, the virginal veil was likewise called the *flammeum* among Christians, as in Jerome’s aforementioned letters, in Ambrose’s works on virginity and virgins, and frequently in other writers, as is likewise well known to scholars.

For what purpose, then, was the nuptial veil originally used among the Romans? “The bride is clothed with the *flammeum*,” said Festus Pompeius the Grammarian, “as a favorable omen, because the *flaminica*—that is, the wife of the *flamen*—always wore it, and she was not permitted to divorce.”

What could be more similar to the indication of that same reality—namely, the perpetual and indissoluble union of sacred virgins with Christ the Bridegroom—in the prayers of the Church even to the present day, when a veil is placed upon the head of virgins at their initiation?

“Receive the sacred veil, by which it may be recognized that you have truly and humbly, with the whole striving of your heart, submitted yourself perpetually as a bride to Christ Jesus.”

Thus it is found in the Roman Pontifical, *On the Blessing and Consecration of Virgins*. There can be no doubt that this formula derives from more ancient Orders, even if it is perhaps absent today from the liturgical collections we possess of the ancient Roman rite; nor can there be any doubt that it derives entirely from the primitive discipline of the Church.

It therefore seems not unreasonable to conclude that the ceremony of veiling virgins derived its origin from the nuptial veiling of the ancients, both pagans and Christians, to indicate the spiritual and also indissoluble marriage of virgins with Christ. Among the Romans, the nuptial veil had first been introduced as a favorable omen, so that, according to Festus, it might at least auspiciously signify the indissoluble bond of marriage, after the example of the wife of the *flamen*, who always wore that veil and was not permitted to divorce. The same veil was also used in Christian marriages to signify, in accordance with the institutions of the Christian religion, the absolute perpetuity of the marriage bond.

As for the more ancient records of the veiling of virgins, there is, for the first century of the Church, a commemoration in the Martyrologies on 7 May of the most blessed and illustrious servant of God Flavia Domitilla, as we read in Ado. There she is also said, as elsewhere, to have been “consecrated by Saint Clement with the sacred veil for perseverance in integrity.”

Here we have two points: Christian virgins were consecrated with the sacred veil in the Roman Church from the very beginning of the Church; and the sacred veil itself was in fact employed to signify perseverance in integrity—that is, the perpetual union of such virgins with Christ the Bridegroom. This corresponds to the custom among the pagans, which we mentioned earlier, whereby brides were veiled for the sake of a favorable omen, at least to inaugurate the perpetuity of the marriage begun or entered into; and likewise to the Christian use of the veil to assert that same perpetuity in fact and absolutely.

We are certainly not unaware that Ado and the other martyrologists drew the lengthy eulogy they present for Flavia Domitilla, virgin and martyr, from the *Acts of Saints Nereus and Achilleus*. Among scholars those Acts appear to falter in authenticity, and Tillemont is said to have treated them with unusual severity in volume 2, as the distinguished Dominicus Georgius warns in his edition and commentary on Ado’s *Martyrology* for this very day, 7 May.

Following Georgius, however, those Acts certainly deserve a more charitable assessment. Baronius judged them interpolated in places rather than false, while Henschenius the Bollandist considered them highly trustworthy. There is no reason to suspect interpolation in the statement that Flavia Domitilla was consecrated as a virgin by Saint Pope Clement with the sacred veil, if, after what we have said above about the use of the veil, we consider what the devotion to and zeal for virginity in the Roman Church were even at that time.

What those conditions were is sufficiently shown by two letters of the same Saint Pope Clement, *On Virginity*, or *To Virgins*. John Jacob Wetstenius first published them from a Syriac manuscript, together with a Latin translation, at Leiden in 1752; Andreas Gallandius inserted them in his new *Library of the Fathers*, as though they were the genuine offspring of that same holy pontiff, in volume 1, in Syriac and Latin, and added to them two other letters of the same Saint Clement, long known, *To the Corinthians*, in Greek and Latin.

In these newly discovered letters—the first of which is addressed “To Virgin Brothers and to Virgin Sisters,” that is, to virgins of both sexes, and concerns the manner of leading a virginal life, while the second concerns the precautions to be observed in conduct with virgin sisters—the zeal already then burning among Christians to profess virginity shines forth, as does the care of the bishops that virgins should lead a life equal to their professed virginity.

In view of such a great body of material concerning virginity and virgins already present in the first century of the Church, who could reasonably suspect that the mention of the sacred veil was a later addition to the initiation of Flavia Domitilla the Virgin?

The Roman Church itself supplies us with another most ancient example of this veiling in a certain painting that Bosius and Aringhius discovered in the cemetery of Priscilla on the Salarian Way. It is reproduced in an engraving in volume 2 of Aringhius’ *Subterranean Rome*, p. 395, and was again published and illustrated by the distinguished Francesco Blanchinius in his notes to Anastasius the Librarian, volume 2, p. 128.

The painting depicts a pontiff seated and apparently laying his hand upon a sacred virgin standing before him with a veil, which she holds with both hands as though she had just received it from him. It also depicts a certain presbyter standing beside the pontiff and apparently offering his assistance in this sacred rite.

For students of sacred antiquity, many things here deserve consideration: the pontifical chair and the pontiff’s clothing, the garments of both the virgin and the presbyter, and also the gestures and manner of bearing of each of the three persons. But what concerns us now is that the learned men mentioned above, together with others who support them, agree that this painting represents the initiation of a Christian virgin through the giving of the sacred veil. They identify the seated pontiff as Saint Pope Pius I, by origin an Aquileian, who held the Roman see around the middle of the second century; the standing presbyter as Hermas, or Hermes, also called the *Shepherd*, the brother of that same Pope Pius; and the virgin as Saint Praxedes, or her sister Saint Pudentiana.

With these two monuments from the first and second centuries before us, we see how great is the antiquity enjoyed by the ceremony of veiling virgins mentioned by our Nicetas and transmitted to us through the centuries by the Church’s continual practice.

This veil, which we still hear called sacred, Nicetas likewise called sacred in the same work, chapter 5, no. 20, saying: “You are covered with the sacred veil.” All antiquity similarly called it sacred and holy. Jerome, in his letter to Demetrias, letter 130, no. 2, called the virginal *flammeum* holy; Ambrose, in *On the Institution of a Virgin*, chapter 17, no. 108, wrote of hair “to be consecrated with the sacred veil”; and others likewise speak in the same manner throughout.

From where, then, did the virginal veil receive this holiness? Certainly from the divine altar, from which it was taken in order to be placed upon the head of the virgins, and probably also from a particular supplication by which its sanctification was requested from God. Both practices continued afterward and may be seen in the Roman Pontifical, *On the Blessing and Consecration of Virgins*. Hence a certain girl who had fled to the altar when her parents were pressing her against her will to marry said to Ambrose, *On Virgins*, book 1, chapter 12, no. 66: “Could a *maforte* veil me better than the altar itself, which sanctifies the veils?”

Many further questions could still be raised concerning this virginal veil among the ancients: what its form, material, quality, price, and color were. But, to avoid excessive length, it is enough here to indicate generally that, although the virginal veil derived its origin from the *flammeum* of brides, it nevertheless differed from it, especially in that the virginal veil was intended in every respect to signify humility, devotion, poverty, and chastity.

Saint Ambrose demonstrates this difference in *On Virginity*, chapter 5, no. 26. While exhorting girls to virginity and expressing his desire to consecrate virgins, he wrote: “Would that I could exchange the nuptial *flammeum* for the devout veil of integrity!”

Here, then, is the veil of sacred virgins, distinct from the nuptial veil—and certainly distinct in form, material, quality, price, and color.

Moreover, we understand somewhat more clearly from Tertullian, in the book already cited, *On the Veiling of Virgins*, chapter 15, what the virginal veil actually was, especially with regard to its form and material, its color and adornment, and its principal purpose of covering the face:

“She flees,” he says, “to the veil of her head as to a helmet, as to a shield that protects her good against the blows of temptations, against the darts of scandals, against suspicions, whispers, rivalry, and even envy . . . . Who would dare press his eyes upon a closed face, a face that does not respond, a face, so to speak, made sorrowful? Every evil thought will be broken by that very severity.”

Here, then, is the veil of virgins covering and closing the entire face; indeed, not merely the face but also the whole upper part of the body, as though it were a shield. Here is a virginal veil expressing a certain sadness and also displaying severity—and therefore offering neither nobility of material, nor splendor of ornament, nor the allure of a gleaming color. Who would not recognize here the veil of virgins in later centuries, and especially of cloistered virgins, already described by Tertullian at the beginning of the third century?

This solemn veiling of virgins is called consecration by Nicetas, in the same place, no. 20: “On that day of your consecration, etc.” Speaking also of virgins, Tertullian, in the book cited above, chapter 13, said that by their virginal purpose they consecrated nature itself to God [Col. 1100C]. Saint Ambrose likewise mentions the consecration of virgins in *On Virginity*, chapter 7, no. 36, and often elsewhere. In the Gelasian Sacramentary, in Muratori’s *Ancient Roman Liturgy*, volume I, col. 632 of the Venetian folio edition, this secret prayer is found in one of the Masses that also bear the title “Consecration of a Sacred Virgin”:

> “May the gifts, we ask, O Lord, which your servant and consecrated woman N. offers to you for the consecration of her body, likewise advance toward the healing of her soul.”

The same manner of speaking about solemnly veiled virgins remains in use even now; and a title of this kind is found in the Roman Pontifical, namely, “On the Blessing and Consecration of Virgins.” There, after the ceremony has been completed, this admonition of the bishop to the superior or abbess of the monastery is also included:

> “See to it how you preserve these women consecrated to God and present them immaculate, etc.”

This consecration of virgins, through the imposition of the sacred veil, was performed at the divine altar, as we have shown from Nicetas [Col. 1100D]; and thereafter it was always performed in this way, according to the Roman Pontifical at the place recently indicated. Saint Ambrose also mentions this consecration at the divine altar in *On Virgins*, book I, chapter 12, no. 66. There, recounting the noble deed of the girl mentioned above, who was being compelled by her parents and relatives to marry against her will, he says:

> “She fled to the most holy altar. For where could a virgin go better than where the sacrifice of virginity is offered? Nor was this the end of her boldness. She stood at God’s altar as a sacrifice of modesty, a victim of chastity: now placing the priest’s right hand upon her head and asking for prayer, now impatient of rightful delay and laying the crown of her head upon the altar. ‘Will anything veil me better than the altar, which itself consecrates veils? Such a bridal *flammeum* is more becoming, in which Christ, the head of all, is consecrated daily, etc.’”

In the sermon which Ambrose delivered to the virgin Ambrosia [Col. 1101A], who was shortly to be consecrated with the sacred veil, in *On the Institution of a Virgin*, chapter 17, no. 108, he addressed God in prayer as follows:

> “By these examples, may this servant of yours also, stirred toward the grace of such virtue, stand before your altars—not carrying, with shining golden hair, a blond lock dedicated to the bridal *flammeum*, but that lock with which the woman of the Gospel, holy Mary, diligently wiped Christ’s feet and filled the whole house with the outpoured perfume, offering it to be consecrated under the sacred veil.”

Moreover, Nicetas identifies the holy day of the Lord’s Resurrection as the day on which the solemn veiling of virgins took place after the conferral of baptism, with the newly baptized present, dressed in white garments and carrying their lamps. The solemnity of the veiling of virgins was therefore reserved for the Church’s greatest festival, so that the Church’s rejoicing might be increased both by the arrival of a new offspring and by the marriage of virgins, in the utmost chastity, with the same immortal Bridegroom, Christ. Indeed, the veiling of virgins was in a certain way especially connected with this festival of the Lord’s Resurrection, because of the condition of virgins, by which they were made, as it were, daughters of the resurrection. The divine Cyprian said to them in *On the Dress of Virgins*, toward the end:

> “What we shall be, you have already begun to be. You already possess the glory of the resurrection in this world; you pass through the world without the world’s contamination . . . . You are equal to the angels of God.”

And certainly the holy day of the Lord’s Resurrection, even in the age of Saint Ambrose, was throughout the world the solemn day for the veiling of virgins, as the same witness states in the book entitled *Exhortation to Virginity*, chapter 7, no. 42, where we read:

> “The day of Easter has come; throughout the world the sacraments of baptism are celebrated; sacred virgins are veiled.”

Nevertheless, Easter was not so designated for the veiling of virgins that this rite could not also be appropriately performed on other principal festivals of the year. Certainly, from the same Saint Ambrose we learn in *On Virgins*, book III, chapter 1, that Marcellina, a virgin and his sister, made her profession of virginity at Rome in the basilica of Saint Peter on the birthday of our Savior. Approving the appropriateness of that day, he added:

> “For on what better day than the day on which a virgin acquired posterity?”

Besides Easter and the day of the Lord’s Nativity, antiquity assigned other days as well for the veiling of virgins. In the Gelasian Sacramentary cited above, where the blessings, prayers, and Masses for this rite are given, we read the following title:

> “Consecration of a sacred virgin, which is celebrated on the Epiphany, or on Easter Monday, or on the feast of the apostles.”

Finally, the Roman Pontifical prescribes today that “the blessing and consecration of virgins should take place on the Epiphany of the Lord, or during the Easter season in white garments, or on the feasts of the apostles, or on Sundays.”

Although the imposition of the veil was the principal ceremony of the initiation of virgins, that initiation did not consist solely in this; a change of clothing was also added. Accordingly, our Nicetas mentions the virginal habit in *To the Fallen Virgin*, chapter 6, no. 22—that is, the distinctive habit of sacred virgins [Col. 1101D], certainly distinguished by the simplicity of its material, its color, and its form. Saint Ambrose likewise said in *On Virginity*, chapter 14, no. 88:

> “The mantle of virgins is one thing; that of worldly adolescence is another.”

In *On Virgins*, book III, chapter 1, when describing the initiation of his sister Marcellina at Rome, he mentions this change of habit as having been carried out at the same time as the initiation:

> “When, on the Nativity of the Savior, you marked your profession of virginity before the Apostle Peter, together with a change of clothing.”

It is also probable that these virginal garments were already then blessed by means of a particular prayer. Certainly, a formula for such a blessing appears in the Gelasian Sacramentary at the place cited above, under the heading “Blessing of the Garments of Virgins,” followed by “Prayer over the Handmaids of God, when their clothing is changed.” The purpose of this change is indicated in the first prayer, where these garments are said to signify humility of heart and contempt for the world [Col. 1102A]. This same blessing of virginal garments, together with the taking up of those garments in the ceremony itself, is still practiced today, as prescribed in the Roman Pontifical. Indeed, the same blessing of the garments of virgins found in the Gelasian Sacramentary is also included there, so that from this we may understand how much authority from antiquity this rite enjoys.

But who, at that time, initiated the sacred virgins? Nicetas makes it sufficiently clear that the bishop was the initiator of the fallen virgin of Aquileia, in his little book addressed to her, chapter 5, nos. 19 and 20. That the initiation of sacred virgins was in fact the office of bishops, as it afterward always remained, is attested by ancient records.

> “It was decreed by all the bishops: The preparation of chrism and the consecration of girls are not to be performed by presbyters.”

So says canon 3 of the Second Council of Carthage in the year 390, in Labbe, *Councils*, edited by Coleti, volume II, col. 1245. The Third Council of Carthage in the year 397 had likewise decreed in canon 36:

> “A presbyter is not to consecrate virgins without consulting the bishop.”

This is found in the same Labbe, same place, col. 1404. It therefore belonged by ordinary right to bishops to consecrate virgins, since presbyters were forbidden to do so, and since they were altogether unable to do it without consulting the bishop.

Moreover, the consecrator of virgins is called “the bishop,” almost as an antonomastic title, by Jerome, letter 69 to Oceanus, no. 9, in Vallarsi’s edition. In letter 130 to Demetrias, no. 2, the holy doctor addressed the same sacred virgin as follows:

> “I know that, at the invocation of the pontiff, the sacred virginal *flammeum* covered your head”—

that is, of the pontiff Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, from whom Demetrias, while living in Africa, received the veiling of virginity.

The virgin Marcellina, sister of Saint Ambrose, had likewise received the veil at Rome from Pope Liberius of blessed memory, as Ambrose himself testifies in *On Virgins*, book III, chapter 1. Ambrose also reveals that he himself solemnly veiled at Milan the Bolognese virgin Ambrosia, niece of the distinguished man Eusebius [Col. 1102C], to whom he dedicated his book *On the Institution of a Virgin* for this reason. Finally, those virgins who came to Milan from Bologna, Piacenza, and the remotest regions of Mauritania on both sides, so that they might be veiled there because they eagerly desired to be consecrated there, all unquestionably regarded Ambrose the bishop as their veiler, as the same Ambrose testifies in *On Virgins*, book I, chapter 11. Unless, that is, we prefer to say that Bishop Ambrose, through his sermons and books already widely disseminated everywhere, had labored so greatly to kindle love of virginity in the hearts of girls, and afterward showed less eagerness to take the fruit of his work into his own hands, as it were.

At that time bishops did not merely consecrate virgins; they also honored the ceremony of consecration with an address or sermon to the virgins present, before they received the veil. That this was done on the day of her veiling with the fallen virgin of Aquileia is attested by Nicetas in chapter 5, where he says:

> “Do you not remember what sort of address was made to you on that day: ‘Look, daughter; behold, Virgin, etc.’ . . . . After these words had been spoken to you on that day of your consecration, and after many praises of your chastity, you were covered with the sacred veil.”

This had also been done with the sacred virgin Marcellina by Pope Liberius. Ambrose preserved the address delivered at that time—not almost in its actual words, but at least in its meaning, expressed in his own style—in book III, chapters 1–3, of the work cited above, *On Virgins*. Ambrose himself, rightly called by learned men the doctor of virginity, maintained this practice of delivering an address at the veiling of sacred virgins. He preserved for us the sermon he gave at the solemn consecration of the aforementioned Bolognese virgin Ambrosia, while she stood before the altar before being covered with the sacred veil, in the previously mentioned book *On the Institution of a Virgin*. Apart from one or two chapters, that book consists entirely of the same sermon, as the Maurist editors note in their preliminary notice.

This rite also remains in force today: at the solemn veiling of virgins, the bishop—or anyone else acting in the bishop’s place—addresses them, either before they receive the veil, as prescribed in the Roman Pontifical, or after they have received it, according to the custom of certain places. Sermons delivered to virgins at their nuptial celebrations have also been published in print, both by bishops and, with episcopal authority, by presbyters; they all breathe the fragrance of the earliest institution. Among these are sermons altogether worthy of cedar, which we consider it worthwhile to mention here and which were recently published posthumously at Udine: those of the most distinguished Francis Florio, provost of this metropolitan church and vicar general of our bishops, whom we have already deservedly praised elsewhere in this work.

And thus much concerning the ceremonies and solemnity of the initiation of virgins.

We must now consider something about the conduct of those same sacred virgins in the matters mentioned by our Nicetas. First, Nicetas mentions the virgins’ procession into the church, not individually [Col. 1103B], but in a group and in choir: to the sacred gatherings of the faithful, to the singing of spiritual hymns, to hear the heavenly readings—in short, to the entire order of the Liturgy—as well as to the nocturnal vigils, in accordance with the custom of all Christians at that time, as stated in *To the Fallen Virgin*, chapter 6, no. 22.

At that time there were not yet enough sacred buildings in one and the same city, nor was any particular church assigned to the virginal monasteries. Moreover, the virginal monasteries themselves were not yet entirely enclosed, as was later wisely done for the greater protection of sacred virgins. Sometimes the virgins were free to leave the monastery for a necessary reason, and they also had to go out in order to approach the sacred buildings and take part there in the divine mysteries with the Christian people.

Saint Jerome therefore gave a general rule concerning any departure of sacred virgins from the monastery in his frequently cited letter 130 to Demetrias, no. 19, writing:

> “Those who live in a monastery and are numerous together should never go out alone, never without a mother. From a flock of doves the hawk often separates one, which it immediately attacks and tears apart, feeding itself on its flesh and blood.”

This concerns the virginal monasteries of Africa, where the virgin Demetrias lived, although, as we noted above, she herself preserved her virginity in her own home, living with her mother and grandmother. Saint Jerome also commended there those virgins who, out of modesty and reverence, did not even go to the church on certain feast days when there was a greater crowd of people:

> “I know sacred virgins who on feast days, because of the crowds, keep their feet at home; nor do they go out when greater watchfulness is required and the public must be entirely avoided.”

Perhaps this concerned sacred virgins who lived not in a monastery but in their own homes, either alone or with a few companions, and who went to church on other days of the week rather than on feast days in order to participate in the sacred rites. Saint Ambrose likewise impressed this precaution upon sacred virgins, especially young women, in *Exhortation to Virginity*, chapter 10, no. 71: they should rarely even go to church. I would readily judge that this was said both to virgins living in monasteries and to those living in their own homes:

> “Take heed, virgin, especially one of a sacred profession . . . . Let no going out of yours take place without your mother, who is to be an anxious guardian of modesty. Let your going to church also be rarer for young women.”

By “mother” he may have meant the natural mother, who at home and everywhere was to be the guardian of her virgin daughter endowed with the sacred veil, although he could likewise have meant the superior of a virginal monastery, in the sense intended by Saint Jerome.

The same Saint Jerome presents the discipline of the virgins’ monastery at Bethlehem under the direction and care of the elder Paula in letter 108 to Eustochium, no. 19:

> “They went out to church only on Sunday; they lived beside it.”

Two aspects of prudence deserve notice here, to the praise of the elder Paula, as well as of Saint Jerome and the local bishop, who were undoubtedly her advisers in establishing the monastery. She had taken care that her virginal monastery be located not far from the church, so that the virgins would have the shortest possible route for going there; nevertheless, they did not go to church daily, or even several times a week, but only on Sunday, so that their modesty might certainly be safeguarded more carefully.

If conjecture is permissible, the virginal monastery of Aquileia under Bishop Nicetas, which we said above was situated in the middle of the city, was also close to the local church—especially if we recall that those virgins were present in the church even for the vigils with the rest of Christ’s faithful. They therefore had to go there at night, and it would have been less suitable for sacred virgins to attend if they could not reach the church by the shortest possible route. If, then, the virgins of the Aquileian monastery also went out to the church for the sacred vigils, they perhaps took part in the church’s sacred services more frequently than on Sundays alone.

In later times, provision was made fully both for the devotion and for the modesty of virgins, when each monastery, and even each community of them, was allowed to have its own sacred buildings from which it could receive the consolations of religion without setting foot beyond its enclosure.

Nicetas nevertheless reports something distinctive concerning the residence of sacred virgins in the sacred church of Aquileia, something perhaps found nowhere else in all antiquity, and something that greatly commends the institutions of the Church of Aquileia and its prelates. The most holy discipline of the ancient Church is well known: it took the greatest care that women should stand apart from men in the sacred buildings. Sacred virgins were also given, in that part of the sacred buildings belonging to women, a place distinct from the others of the same sex, where they could attend the sacred mysteries together. Hence Saint Augustine wrote to them in letter 211, no. 10:

> “When you are together in the church . . . guard one another’s chastity.”

But what does Nicetas tell us about the virgins gathering in the Church of Aquileia? Not only did they have a special place in the Aquileian church, as they did everywhere in the world, but they also had a place separated by railings, and perhaps raised somewhat above the floor, so that the honor of their dignity might be evident even from the distinctiveness of the place:

> “Should you not at least have remembered that place separated by railings, where you stood in the church? . . . . You have forgotten your profession . . . . You have forgotten the whole Church; you have forgotten the glory of virginity; you have forgotten the honor of your dignity, etc.”

Thus Nicetas, *To the Fallen Virgin*, chapter 6, nos. 24 and 27 [Col. 1104D].

What, moreover, did the custom of the Church of Aquileia in the time of Nicetas—or, to use a more appropriate term for the matter itself, its refinement—provide for the benefit of sacred virgins? That place in which the virgins stood during the sacred rites was decorated with admonitions taken from divine Scripture and written on the wall. These referred to and commended the profession of virginity. From this alone one may understand how highly the profession of virginity was esteemed among the Aquileians:

> “Should you not at least have remembered those admonitions which the written wall itself placed before your eyes, etc.?”

So Nicetas continues in the same passage.

Nicetas also notes another sign of the special honor bestowed upon sacred virgins in the Church of Aquileia during the divine mysteries: the kiss of peace. They unquestionably received this from the sacred altar during the divine mysteries, as was customary; and afterward devout and noble matrons who were present at the sacred rites eagerly desired to receive it from them, as from the purest channel of holiness:

> “To that place devout and noble matrons ran eagerly, seeking your kisses, although they were holier and more worthy than you.”

These are the notable details concerning the discipline of sacred virgins in the sacred buildings which Nicetas alone preserved for us, from the custom of the Church of Aquileia, in his little book addressed to the fallen virgin. Perhaps we would never have learned them from him had he not been given the occasion—though certainly an unfortunate one—to write that little book, in which he reproved the fallen virgin with arguments drawn from every quarter.

Moreover, this same little book reveals the care which the bishops of that time exercised toward sacred virgins. It consisted in the spiritual love shown to them, as well as in the holy admonition specifically given to them:

> “Certainly you have no grounds for complaining about our negligence; for whatever belongs to the office of a pastor has not been withheld either from you or from anyone else. Spiritual love has been shown; holy admonition has not been lacking.”

Thus Nicetas writes in chapter 7, no. 28.

Such was Nicetas of Aquileia toward his sacred virgins; such had the more celebrated prelates of the Churches been toward them before him, and such afterward were all those who regarded the sacred virgins of the Catholic Church as its ornament, companions of angels, and brides of Christ. “Now our discourse is addressed to virgins; and the loftier their glory, the greater also is our care,” Saint Cyprian began his sermon to virgins, thereby testifying to his particular care for them in the special little book he wrote, *On the Dress of Virgins* [258]:

> “Listen to me, virgins, as to a father; listen, I beg you, to one who both fears for you and admonishes you; listen to one who faithfully gives counsel for your usefulness and welfare.”

Thus, in the same passage, he showed toward his virgins both spiritual love and holy admonition.

There is no need to add anything about Saint Ambrose, whose views we have so often reported here, since it is clear that his books on the subject of virginity grew out of sermons which he delivered either when exhorting people to embrace and honor virginity or when he approached virgins in order to instruct and educate them. Who, moreover, is unaware that Saint Augustine gathered a community of virgins in his Church at Hippo and organized it under excellent rules, with his sister as superior and a presbyter also appointed to provide their spiritual care? He certainly showed them love and offered them admonition. His previously cited letter 211 survives as an exceptionally full witness to his concern for them, and it was always regarded in the Church as an unsurpassed model for forming communities of sacred virgins according to monastic perfection.

Finally, Nicetas asserts in the same place, no. 29, that he had also expounded to his virgins a “Hymn of Virginity,” so that they might sing both the glory of their profession and its observance. Perhaps by this Nicetas meant homilies which he delivered to sacred virgins on some psalm, probably Psalm XLIV. From the tenth verse to the end, as the Maurist editors of Ambrose’s works also note at this passage, that psalm contains much relating to the glory and observance of the virginal profession [Col. 1105D]. By being attracted through this spiritual interpretation of the psalm, the virgins could sing it more joyfully and sweetly in their spiritual exercises.

Since nothing appears here concerning a presbyter or another member of the clergy who was in charge of the virginal monastery of Aquileia, as there was in Augustine’s community at Hippo, it remains for us to conjecture, to Nicetas’s credit, that he had reserved this task especially for himself: namely, to cultivate and water, as though with his own hands, this spiritual garden of holiness and modesty. We may readily gather this also from several expressions used throughout the little work.

Thus much concerning the discipline of the fifth century among the Aquileians as it relates to sacred virgins.

Nicetas’s little book addressed to the fallen virgin now leads us to another kind of discipline, namely, the system of public penance that then prevailed for sins, especially public and more serious sins. For the whole purpose of Nicetas’s little book is to urge and instruct the fallen virgin—and also the man who corrupted her—to undertake public penance for the grave crime committed.

The first matter that presents itself in this little book of Nicetas concerning the penitential discipline of that time is a practice then prevailing in both the Eastern and Western Churches. According to this practice, a sin was considered greater and more serious, and therefore to require greater penance for its expiation, when it became known after an investigation had been conducted than when the sinner had voluntarily confessed it. Thus Nicetas addressed the fallen virgin who had tried to conceal her crime, which became known only after an investigation had been made, in chapter 8, no. 37:

> “For a great wound, deep and prolonged medicine is needed; a great crime requires great satisfaction. For there is no doubt that a crime is lighter when a person voluntarily confesses his sin and repents; but when he conceals his evil deeds, is exposed against his will, and is unwillingly made public, that crime is more serious.
