You cannot deny that this has happened to you. Therefore you must grieve more intensely, because the sin is more serious.”

Morinus proves and illustrates this ancient discipline, as is his custom, with many testimonies of both Greek and Latin Fathers, as well as with this very passage of our Nicetas—which he believed to be by Ambrose—in his *Historical Commentary on the Sacrament of Penance*, book II, chapter 6.

For confirmation, and because it is related to the matter at hand, we shall offer one passage from Augustine in the previously cited letter 211, in which he instructed the virgins of his monastery and taught how the offenses of those who violated their virginal profession should also be punished:

> “If any woman,” he says in no. 11, “has advanced so far into evil that she secretly accepts letters or any little gifts from someone, then, if she confesses this voluntarily, let her be spared and let prayer be offered for her. But if she is discovered and convicted, let her be corrected more severely, according to the judgment of the superior, the presbyter, or even the bishop.”

Thus, according to the practice of those times, a sin that was discovered as though against the sinner’s will was in fact considered more serious and punished with greater severity than one that became known because the sinner voluntarily disclosed it.

It is also clear from this discipline that at that time there were certain hidden sins which nevertheless had to be disclosed through public confession, so that the sinner might undergo the public remedy of penance, as was the case with the fallen virgin in Nicetas, and as would have been the case in the situation mentioned by Augustine. It is likewise clear that investigation into Christian conduct was then in force, in order to discover its stains, and that accusations were brought to the prelates of the Church, so that they might, according to their authority and prudence, examine, correct, and punish.

Morinus illustrates this matter in the work cited above, as does Juenin in his *Historical and Dogmatic Commentary on the Sacraments*, dissertation 6, “On Penance,” question 5, “On Confession,” and question 6, “On Satisfaction,” followed by others whom, in our opinion, those who adopted the contrary position did not adequately answer.

From this entire ancient discipline—which gradually declined together with the penitential order, first in the East and then in the West—one form of investigation into Christian conduct still remains with regard to the bishop. It belongs to the pastoral office by which he is bound to safeguard the well-being of the people entrusted to him and to provide for the salvation of individuals, especially as appears from the Roman Pontifical in the order for visiting parishes. With regard to the laity, however, there remains, by virtue of the precept of charity through which God has commanded each person to care for his neighbor, the obligation to report to the prelates of the Church or to pastors of the second order, according to the seriousness of the matter, those Christians who either speak against the integrity of the faith or injure the Christian profession through depravity of conduct.

But what are we now to say about the particular sin of the sacred virgin who had secretly allowed herself to be violated and was afterward discovered against her will? What penance was owed for the expiation of this sin?

Nicetas distinguishes between the sacred virgin who, after receiving the holy veil—that is, after entering into marriage with Christ—nevertheless wished to marry according to the common law of marriage, and the sacred virgin who had been defiled by hidden and furtive shame and afterward pretended to be what she truly was not. He says that the former committed adultery and became a servant of death; but he calls the latter “twice adulterous,” both because she had truly violated the faith given to Christ and because she nevertheless pretended to be a virgin, although she was no longer one:

> “And if the sacred virgin should wish to marry according to the common law of marriage, she commits adultery and becomes a servant of death. If this is so, what must be said about the woman who is defiled by hidden and furtive shame and pretends to be what she is not? A virgin in habit, not a virgin in deed: twice adulterous, both in action and in appearance.”

Thus Nicetas, *To the Fallen Virgin*, chapter 5, no. 21.

We are now concerned with this sacred virgin, whom Nicetas calls twice adulterous because she secretly committed the crime while nevertheless feigning virginity through her virginal habit; and with the sacred virgin who in no way voluntarily disclosed her wound but, after being convicted, was finally compelled against her will to confess.

No one should be surprised that Nicetas makes so much of this fallen woman’s deception, so that he calls her twice adulterous, since it is well known with what religious care the ancient Fathers always guarded the special honor of preserving intact virginity. They ensured that no widow, even if she professed continence, should receive the veil; and they ensured that virgins who, without any fault of their own—for example, through barbaric violence—had suffered the loss of virginity, though polluted in body but not in mind, should no longer be counted among the number and community of sacred virgins. Ferdinand de Mendoza demonstrates this by adducing many testimonies of councils and Fathers in *On the Council of Elvira*, book II, chapter 27, in Labbe’s *Councils*, edited by Coleti, volume I, col. 1152 and following.

With all these circumstances taken into account, therefore, nothing could be more serious in this sacred virgin than this crime. She could not even offer the excuse that violence had been done to her; indeed, she had been convicted of voluntary consent by the repetition of the crime, as stated in chapter 4, nos. 12 and 13.

For how long, then, did Nicetas impose penance upon this fallen virgin, and how did he instruct her to perform it?

As regards its duration, Nicetas imposes penance upon the fallen virgin until the very end of her life, and, at first sight, apparently without hope of obtaining absolution and forgiveness except from the mercy of the Lord alone:

> “But you,” he says in chapter 8, no. 38, “who have already entered the contest of penance, persevere, wretched woman. Hold fast firmly as to a plank in a shipwreck, hoping through it to be rescued from the depths of your crimes. Hold fast to penance until the end of your life, and do not presume that forgiveness will be given to you by any human authority; for anyone who wishes to promise this to you is deceiving you. Since you sinned specifically against the Lord, you ought to expect the remedy from him alone on the day of judgment.”

Nicetas’s judgment concerning his fallen woman—that she should await mercy and forgiveness from God alone, without any assistance from the Church’s power of the keys—certainly appears rather severe. There will be an opportunity to discuss this judgment in the following tenth chapter.

For the rest, we should not be surprised that Nicetas imposes penance upon this fallen woman until the end of her life for the crime committed. Antiquity always subjected sacred virgins who, through their own fault, had failed to keep their pact of virginity to more severe penalties, according to the discipline prevailing in different places and times. It showed itself somewhat milder only toward those who displayed the weakness of their sex more than a depraved intention of mind.

Perhaps such were the virgins about whom Cyprian wrote to Pomponius in letter 62 of Baluze’s Paris edition. Accordingly, he decreed concerning their penance:

> “If any one of them is found to have been corrupted, let her perform full penance, because she who has committed this crime is an adulteress not of a husband but of Christ; and therefore, after a suitable period has been determined and confession has been made, let her return to the Church.”

“Full penance” in Cyprian’s sense must be understood as full even with regard to the duration of the appointed period, which at that time would have been the most rigorous of all, although it was not extended until the end of life. It was distinguished in this way from other lesser penances, which were not full and were therefore completed within a shorter period.

But what did the same Cyprian say about other sacred virgins who by their perverse will had overcome the weakness of their sex? He was unquestionably more severe toward them, to the point of testifying that he would never admit them to reconciliation. For he added:

> “But if they persist obstinately and do not separate from one another, let them know that, with this shameless obstinacy of theirs, they can never be admitted by us into the Church, lest they begin, through their offenses, to become an example leading the others to ruin.”

The celebrated Council of Elvira presents this twofold classification of sinful virgins, and accordingly a twofold manner of proceeding against them, in canon 13. It is worthwhile to reproduce the canon here in an amended form from the previously praised work of Ferdinand de Mendoza, in Labbe at the place cited above:

> “It has been decided that virgins who have dedicated themselves to God, if they lose their virginity pact and give themselves over to the same lust, without understanding what they have lost, are not to be given communion even at the end of life. But if they should persuade themselves that they fell through bodily weakness, and such women should perform penance for the whole time of their lives and abstain from intercourse, since they appear rather to have fallen through weakness, it has been decided that they ought to receive communion at the end of life.”

Here, then, within one and the same kind of fault, there is a twofold degree of guilt, to be punished by a different form of discipline. Yet the milder punishment is the one that requires the fallen virgin to spend her entire life performing penance, so that she may finally deserve to receive forgiveness at the end.

The fall of the Aquileian virgin in Nicetas was certainly extremely serious for many reasons, as we have seen. Therefore it was not unjustly that penance was imposed upon her until the end of her life, so that she might hope for forgiveness from the Lord.

But in what particular way, and by what practices, was this penance to be performed? Nicetas calls the penitential course already entered upon by that fallen virgin the “contest of penance”; and he does so in accordance with the common manner of speaking at that time, by which the labors, afflictions, and, as it were, struggles of penitents—both of soul and body—were most aptly indicated, undertaken to render satisfaction and obtain pardon. In this contest of penance, Nicetas, in chapter 8, no. 35, prescribes chiefly the following for the fallen virgin. First of all, every concern with this life had to be extinguished in her, and she was to think of nothing except the spiritual death into which she had fallen through her sin and the means of coming back to life. Next, she was to put on mournful clothing, and her mind and each of her limbs, as deserving punishment, were to be chastised. Here the virginal habit is changed into a penitential one, whose particular color and form, customary among penitents, are indicated to some extent by the word “mournful.” The cutting of the hair is also prescribed as a sign of penance; from this it appears that at that time our consecrated virgins wore their hair uncut, contrary to the practice elsewhere, especially in Egypt and Syria, as Jerome teaches in his letter to Sabinianus, 48. “Let her eyes, moreover, stream with tears,” Nicetas said to the fallen woman; “let her face grow pale” [Col. 1108D]. Nor was this enough. “Finally, let the whole body be worn down by injuries and fasts, let it shudder, sprinkled and covered with ashes and clad in sackcloth . . . Let the senses also be tortured.” These are what Nicetas prescribed to the fallen woman concerning the outward signs of penance and the affliction of the body, to be undertaken for the sake of doing penance. If, by injuries inflicted upon the body for its mortification, you understand flogging as well as other harsher punishments of that kind—so frequently mentioned in the Lives of the saints who crucified their flesh with its vices and desires—you will certainly understand nothing that does not accord perfectly with the penitential discipline of that time. Although this discipline later declined in the expiation of penitents’ crimes, it always remained among the more fervent Christians who joined innocence with penance and employed penitential afflictions in order more easily to cultivate Christian virtues.

What, then, should be done to conceive inwardly and nourish grief for the disgrace that had been committed? Nicetas gathers excellent material in chapter 10 from the divine Scriptures, in order to fill the fallen woman’s mind with sentiments of repentance and to direct her tongue—both the tongue of her mouth and that of her heart—to implore the Lord’s mercy. Worthy of notice, however, is what he first recommends to her: that she recite the fiftieth psalm every day up to verse 19:

“And first of all, let the fiftieth psalm never be omitted on any day, because it was sung in such a matter; and let her proceed through it up to that verse: ‘A contrite and humbled heart God does not despise,’ with tears and groaning.”

Here we see how ancient was the recitation of this fiftieth psalm among the afflictions and prayers of penitents. Even today it is so frequently assigned to penitents by priest-confessors as part of their satisfaction after hearing their confession. Yet Nicetas does not prescribe the whole fiftieth psalm to the fallen virgin, but only through verse 19, omitting the two other verses with which the psalm is completed. For the penitents were not assigned a wordy and bare recitation of psalms, as though merely for a pious exercise of the lips, but rather meditation upon the meanings contained in the psalms. Therefore the psalms were assigned to them only up to that part which most forcefully expressed grief of soul and implored mercy, lest, being distracted by other meanings, however holy, they should in some way interrupt the compunction once aroused in the heart.

Concerning this same fiftieth psalm, not recited in its entirety, and likewise concerning other psalms to be cut short as the circumstances of the action required, we have examples in the ancient penitential books which Morinus added to his work On the Sacrament of Penance. In the ancient Roman Penitential, in the same work, p. 565 of the Venetian edition, under the heading “Here begins the procedure for giving penance,” we read:

“First, he says the whole thirty-seventh psalm, ‘O Lord, rebuke me not in thy fury,’ and afterward says, ‘Let us pray.’ And he says the hundred-and-second psalm, ‘Bless the Lord, O my soul,’ up to ‘your youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s.’ And he says the fiftieth psalm, ‘Have mercy on me, O God,’ up to ‘blot out my iniquities.’ After this he says the fifty-third psalm, ‘O God, in your name,’ and says, ‘Let us pray.’ And he says the fifty-first psalm, ‘Why do you glory,’ up to ‘the righteous shall see and fear,’ and says, ‘Let us pray,’ etc.”

In another likewise ancient Penitential, in the same work, p. 581, under the heading “The order of a penitent at the point of death,” after prayers and other material, we read:

“Then the psalms: ‘O Lord, rebuke me not in your fury,’ up to ‘My heart is troubled within me, and the light of my eyes is not with me.’ ‘Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy,’ up to ‘Turn your face away from my sins.’ ‘Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me,’ up to ‘Youth like the eagle’s.’”

Here, then, are the fiftieth psalm and others employed in penitential practice in ancient times according to Nicetas’ custom, as circumstances required, without regard for their complete recitation [263].

But if the consecrated virgin who had broken faith was subjected to such great penance [Col. 1109D], what of the man who had violated her, being at once guilty of adultery and sacrilege, as we indicated above? Nicetas also turned his pen severely against him in chapter 9 of the same little work, striking him with this sharp address:

“But what shall I say of you, son of the serpent, servant of the devil, violator of God’s temple—you who in one crime have committed two offenses, namely adultery and sacrilege?”

When he proceeds to the penance to be imposed upon this violator, he likewise assigns him perpetual penance:

“By mourning and continual tears, while that dark soul remains in your unclean body, acquire for yourself a remedy for the day of necessity.”

Thus he writes there, no. 42. Nicetas appears harsher toward the ravisher of the virgin than toward the fallen virgin herself, perhaps also for this reason: that the man did not readily present himself for undertaking penance. Thus he addressed him as well:

“Lest anything be withheld from a sick or dying sheep by its shepherd in the way of medicine, I give this counsel: voluntarily seek the prison of penance.”

The violator of the virgin, therefore, had not yet approached penance, unlike the fallen woman, who had already entered the contest of penance when Nicetas addressed her.

What, then, was this man to do in the course of penance, both for the affliction of the body and for the compunction of the heart? Nicetas proposes that he use chains to bind his bowels—something evidently more severe and harsher than what he had imposed upon the fallen woman, whose sex entailed physical weakness. From this one may infer that in the penances formerly imposed, or rather in the penitential afflictions, consideration was given both to sex and to strength. How frequently, moreover, is the use of chains read of in the Lives of the saints, among their voluntary torments for chastising the body and reducing it to servitude, lest it ever rise up rebelliously against the spirit!

Let our delicate and idle men cease to receive with laughter what religious men and those devoted to Christian perfection sometimes adopt for themselves, even in our own age, from the most ancient institutions of penitents—not indeed to correct what they have done wrong, but certainly to restrain something in themselves lest they sin, and to carry always in their body, exultantly, the mortification of Christ’s cross [Col. 1110B]. Nicetas imposes upon this corrupter of the virgin not only chains but also fasts and groans, to torment the soul. These things were common to those doing penance, whether women or men. “Let him also seek the help of the saints,” Nicetas added, “and let him lie beneath the feet of the elect”; all this is found in the same chapter 9, no. 40.

By “the help of the saints,” Nicetas most probably understood the assistance of the saints dwelling in heaven, which, he says, should be invoked in order more easily to obtain from the Lord the forgiveness of sins. Yet by “saints” he could also have meant priests and other members of the clergy, to whose intercessions the penitent might commend himself. To lie beneath the feet of the elect was the prostration of penitents before the doors of the church, before each of the faithful entering the church, and, as it were, their falling at the feet of those people, so that they might be aided by their prayers. These matters have been amply explained by writers on such subjects, and we shall not linger over them here.

Here, finally, ends the discussion of discipline, or of matters pertaining to discipline, undertaken on the occasion of the little works and fragments of Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia.

## CHAPTER X

### Certain matters are examined which might seem to have been stated by Saint Nicetas either less exactly or too harshly

Other matters now remain which concern Nicetas himself, namely, the correctness of his manner of thinking and teaching. There are certain statements in Nicetas’ little works which might seem to have been expressed by him either less exactly or too harshly; and for that reason Nicetas must either be defended or explained.

Speaking of faith in chapter 2 of his Explanation, Nicetas calls it “credulity”:

“Confession rightly begins with credulity,”

he says as he begins to explain the opening words of the Creed: “I believe in God the Father almighty.” Likewise, in chapter 8, when he names the nations that had believed the Gospel, he calls them “credulous nations”:

“The apostles received this rule of faith from the Lord, so that they might baptize all credulous nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”

What does this “credulity” mean in Nicetas’ mouth? In ordinary speech the word suggests a defect and a certain weakness of mind opposed to true faith, since it is taken either for excessive readiness to believe, which is an act of frivolity, or for a weak and feeble opinion, which has no place in the doctrines of faith without grave sin. This same point, with respect to the first meaning of the word, was once brought against Augustine by his friend Honoratus, deceived by the frauds of the Manichaeans, in the book which the holy doctor wrote to him, On the Usefulness of Believing, chapter 9, no. 22:

“Credulity itself,” he said, “from which people are called credulous, seems to me to be a kind of vice; otherwise we would not usually hurl this name as an insult. For if a suspicious person is at fault because he suspects what he has not ascertained, how much more a credulous person, who differs from the suspicious person in this: that the former grants some doubt to things unknown, while the latter grants none.”

Yet let us by no means understand the words “credulity” and “credulous,” as used by our Nicetas, in this or in any other erroneous sense. “Unbelief” is often named in the New Testament to indicate a lack of faith; and in both the New and Old Testaments we frequently read of “the unbelieving,” as those who err in faith. If Nicetas used the contrary terms “credulity” and “credulous,” we shall rightly say that he did so in accordance with the sense of Scripture, to signify what was contrary to unbelief and to the unbelieving—namely, complete faith and the perfect believer.

In this very sense, in accordance with the usage of Scripture, Saint Zeno used the words “credulity” and “unbelief” in Book I, Treatise 1, On Faith, according to the Veronese edition of the Ballerini brothers, saying:

“Abraham pleased God by credulity without the Law, and the Jewish people displeased God by unbelief with the Law.”

Here “credulity” is used in a sense wholly contrary to unbelief, and therefore not to indicate a fault in faith but to display the fullness of faith.

Moreover, among the Fathers—both those before Nicetas and those living in Nicetas’ own age—the word “credulity” is frequently used to signify true and perfect faith and, especially, it seems, the inner act of faith itself, by which we adhere to divine truths and from which we proceed to make confession with the mouth.

“You are accustomed to laugh at our faith, and at credulity itself.”

Thus Arnobius, Against the Nations, Book II [265], distinguishing faith from credulity—that is, the thing to be believed from the very act of believing.

“It is enough for us to say: one substance, three subsistent persons, perfect, equal, coeternal . . . Let the credulity already mentioned be enough,”

said Saint Jerome in Letter 15 to Pope Damasus, no. 4, according to Vallarsi’s edition.

Pope Sixtus III, in his letter to John of Antioch, in Coustant’s Letters of the Roman Pontiffs, spoke of “the credulity of our forefathers,” meaning right faith and the act of believing those things which we received from our ancestors [Col. 1111C]:

“Since by the coarseness of our carnal understanding we are unable to comprehend the mysteries of his passion, let us hold fast by the credulity of right faith, which has been granted.”

Thus Saint Maximus of Turin, Sermon 38 on Time, plainly taking “credulity” for the interior act of faith by which we hold the mysteries of religion without doubt.

Nothing, however, is clearer or more explicit in this matter than Saint Peter Chrysologus, Sermon 60, in the edition of Sebastianus Paulus. There he establishes, as it were, the stages of the profession of faith, and clearly distinguishes where credulity belongs and what credulity actually means:

“Speech creates hearing; hearing conceives faith; faith gives birth to credulity; credulity nourishes confession; confession grants everlasting salvation.”

Credulity, therefore, is that which embraces and follows the faith once conceived in the mind through hearing, by an inward assent; and from this it precedes and nourishes the confession to be uttered by the mouth. It is therefore properly the internal act of faith, by which firm assent is given to the things that must be believed and from which one proceeds to external confession.

Hence Nicetas aptly said in the Explanation that “confession rightly begins with credulity”—that is, with the intimate persuasion of the mind by which we believe without doubt, and from which the word “I believe” bursts forth, by which we confess outwardly what we hold inwardly in our hearts. He also aptly called “credulous” the nations that were to be baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: credulous not because of any frivolity in granting or having granted assent, nor because of a mode of opinion exposed to hesitation, but because of the firm inward faith that would precede confession and was necessary for receiving baptism.

It is precisely in this sense that the word “credulity” is also found used in liturgical acts. Thus in the old Gallican Missal, in the rite for the handing over of the Creed, in Muratori’s Ancient Roman Liturgy, vol. II, col. 710 of the Venetian folio edition cited above, we read:

“Therefore the salutary summary of credulity must be employed, where the weak mind cannot grasp the heavenly secret.”

Credulity, then, is an activity of the mind, supplied as a support to the weak mind. It is stated even more clearly in the old liturgical books of the Church of Aquileia, cited by De Rubeis in his dissertation On the Sacred Rites of the People of Friuli, chapter 11. In the scrutiny called “the opening of the ears,” the following invitation was given to the candidates:

“Come, children; come, for the time of faith has come, the day of credulity, the hour of confession.”

Then, in the subsequent exposition of the Creed:

“If you have believed, do not doubt. Do not turn credulity into unbelief. Do not join vice to virtue.”

Here credulity, in Chrysologus’ sense, is distinguished from faith and confession; here credulity is called a virtue and is separated entirely from doubt.

The distinguished De Rubeis observes in the same work, chapter 12, that the Aquileian scrutiny just mentioned is almost the same as that found in the Gelasian Sacramentary. Yet in the Gelasian book, in Muratori’s work cited above, both the aforementioned invitation to the candidates and the subsequent exposition of the Creed, in which credulity is mentioned, are entirely absent [266]. Why should the word “credulity” not have passed from Nicetas’ Explanation of the Creed into the Aquileian liturgy? Nevertheless, this same word also had a place in the ancient Roman Orders, and even today it is read more than once among the prayers of the Roman rite commonly in use, including in the administration of baptism.

We now proceed to another doctrine of our Nicetas, which he teaches in chapter 6 of the Explanation, where he discusses the article of the Creed: “From there he shall come to judge the living and the dead.”

“Believe,” he says, “that this same Christ our Lord will come with his angels and their powers to judge both the living and those who were formerly dead, so that he may repay each according to his works.”

By the words “to judge both the living and those who were formerly dead,” Nicetas might appear to teach that those whom the Judge’s coming at the end of the world finds alive will come to the universal judgment without a preceding death. We know that this is contrary to the common view, by which we are taught that all human beings without exception must undergo the punishment of death, and that all human beings, according to the Apostle, will rise again—something that can happen only after death has intervened.

Our Nicetas’ doctrine would, indeed, tolerate a certain explanation by which we might judge him to have understood by “the living,” whom he names in opposition, so to speak, to those formerly dead, people who would not come to judgment until they too had undergone death, even if only for a brief—or rather, the briefest—period of time. Thus those living people would be understood as about to die immediately, so that together with those formerly dead, and themselves now newly dead, they might all finally be brought back to life and stand before the judgment.

Yet Nicetas’ doctrine, even when understood according to the first and obvious sense of his words, does not require explanation here, but defense. In a matter never defined by the Church in a particular canon, and especially at that time debated in both directions, Nicetas was permitted to hold and teach the doctrine—or rather, the opinion—which the distinguished Touttée of the Congregation of Saint Maur, in his notes on Saint Cyril of Jerusalem, whom he had edited, at Catechesis 15, no. 23, said was a common opinion among the Greek Fathers and also among very many Latin Fathers:

“Namely, that at the Lord’s second coming many will still be found alive, and that they will be brought to his judgment together with those restored to life, without first undergoing death.”

Let us set aside the Greek Fathers, for whom the same Saint Cyril, in the cited catechesis on the Last Judgment, may suffice. There, in no. 23, he adheres most openly to this opinion as thoroughly established and entirely familiar to his hearers. For the sake of illustration, let us dwell somewhat on the Latin Fathers, so that our Nicetas’ position may appear free from every censure.

Saint Augustine certainly wrote in chapter 8 of On Faith and the Creed, which he composed while still a presbyter, around the year 393:

“We also believe that he will come from there at the most suitable time and will judge the living and the dead. Either by these names the righteous and sinners are signified, or those whom he will find on earth still alive before death are called the living, while the dead are those who will rise at his coming.”

Likewise, in the Enchiridion on Faith, Hope, and Charity, judged to have been written after the year 420, or in that same year, he says in chapter 55:

“That he will judge the living and the dead can be understood in two ways: either we understand by the living those whom his coming will find here not yet dead but still living in this flesh, and by the dead those who have departed or will depart from the body before he comes; or we understand by the living the righteous and by the dead the unrighteous, since the righteous too will be judged.”

Thus Saint Augustine explained the article of the Creed concerning the future judgment of the living and the dead, so that it was entirely free from censure for anyone to include among the living even those whom Christ’s final coming would find alive and who would come to judgment together with the dead raised up, without undergoing death.

Nevertheless, when the opportunity arose, the holy doctor proposed to investigate the matter more deeply. He did so especially in Letter 193 to Mercator, chapter 4, concerning the year 418, and then also in Book XX of The City of God, chapter 20. That book, as we may infer from what the Maurist editors note in their places, was certainly written after the year 425.

In that letter, after citing the Apostle’s words in 1 Thessalonians 4—“And we who are alive, who remain, shall be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord”—he wrote the following in support of an opinion he had elsewhere explained:

“Indeed, so far as the words of the blessed Apostle are concerned, he seems to assert that at the end of the age, when the resurrection of the dead is to take place, certain people will not die but, being found alive, will suddenly be changed into that immortality which is also granted to the other saints, and will be caught up together with them, as he says, in the clouds. Nothing else has seemed to me whenever I have wished to reflect upon these words.”

Yet the holy doctor was troubled when he considered other words of the same Apostle, in 1 Corinthians 15: “Fool, what you sow is not brought to life unless it first dies,” and also the words found there: “We shall all rise again,” or, as some manuscripts read, “We shall all sleep.” From these passages no human being at all seems to be exempt from undergoing death in order to attain perpetual immortality.

What, then, did the holy doctor do amid this apparent conflict in the Apostle’s words? After again reporting the words from 1 Thessalonians, which seem to keep death away from those living at the end, at the coming of the divine Judge, he said:

“I would like to hear from those more learned than I, if these words can somehow be explained so that it may be understood from them that all human beings who live now or will live after us are going to die; and, if so, I would correct what I have at some time thought otherwise about this. For we must not be teachers who refuse to learn.”

Nevertheless, he continued to reveal his inclination in favor of the immortality of those living at the end. Believing that there was greater force in the words of the Apostle to the Thessalonians, he instead sought to determine how the other words reported from 1 Corinthians could be reconciled with the sense of his earlier opinion. Therefore he continued:

“For if no other meaning can be found in these words of the Apostle”—those to the Thessalonians—“and if it becomes clear that he intended them to mean what the words themselves seem to proclaim, namely, that at the end of the age and at the Lord’s coming there will be people who will not be stripped of the body but clothed over with immortality, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life, then this opinion will undoubtedly agree with what we confess in the rule of faith: that the Lord will come to judge the living and the dead. In that case, by ‘the living’ we would not understand the righteous and by ‘the dead’ the unrighteous, although both righteous and unrighteous will be judged, but rather those whom his coming will find not yet departed from their bodies, and those whom it will find already departed from their bodies. If this is established, then those words”—in 1 Corinthians—“must be examined: how shall we understand, ‘What you sow is not brought to life unless it first dies,’ and ‘We shall all rise again,’ or ‘We shall all sleep,’ so that they do not conflict with the opinion that some are believed to live eternally even with their bodies, without tasting death?”

Nevertheless, Saint Augustine remained uncertain about this difficulty. Thus, turning to Mercator in the conclusion of the letter, he addressed him so that he might understand something more clearly concerning the matter:

“But as regards the question of the resurrection, on account of those who are believed not to die but to pass from this mortality to immortality without an intervening death, a more diligent inquiry must be undertaken. If you have heard, read, or yourself been able to consider any reasonably argued and fully worked-out solution concerning this matter—or if you can still hear, read, or consider something of the kind—I ask you not to hesitate to send it to me. For I”—as I must confess to your charity—“love learning more than teaching, etc.”

Thus Saint Augustine, in the year 418, investigated at length the meaning of “the living and the dead” with respect to the judgment.

But what did he write in Book XX of The City of God, about seven years later, when he again undertook to clarify the same matter? After once more citing the Apostle’s words both to the Thessalonians and to the Corinthians, he seems here to withdraw somewhat from his earlier opinion. He now appears to assert that the words to the Thessalonians, in which the immortality of those living at the end seems to be affirmed—as Augustine himself had said—should instead be explained by the other words to the Corinthians, where the death of all human beings without exception and the resurrection of all are proclaimed.

The whole purpose of the holy doctor here is to assert the possibility that those last living people will die and rise again, even within that briefest and smallest interval of time, and to reconcile with this the other words of Scripture that seemed to argue against their death.

“It is usually asked,” he says, “whether those whom Christ will find alive here . . . will never die at all, or whether, at the very instant when they are caught up with those rising again in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, they will pass through death into immortality with marvelous speed. For it must not be said that it is impossible that, while they are being carried aloft through the air, they should in that interval both die and come back to life.”

Then, after some further discussion:

“If, therefore, we believe that the saints who will be found alive when Christ comes and who will be caught up to meet him will, in that same rapture, depart from their mortal bodies and immediately return to those same bodies made immortal, we shall encounter no difficulty in the Apostle’s words, whether where he says, ‘What you sow is not brought to life unless it first dies,’ or where he says, ‘We shall all rise again,’ or ‘We shall all sleep.’ For they too will not be brought to life through immortality unless they first die, however briefly; and thus they will not be excluded from the resurrection, which is preceded by sleep—although that sleep will be exceedingly brief, it will not be nonexistent.

“Why, moreover, should it seem incredible to us that that multitude of bodies should in some manner be sown in the air and there immediately come back to life immortal and incorruptible, when we believe, as the same Apostle most plainly says, that the resurrection will take place in the twinkling of an eye, and that the dust of the bodies of the ancient dead will return to limbs destined to live without end with such ease and at such immeasurable speed?”

Finally, always maintaining this opinion and responding to another difficulty—which we omit here for the sake of brevity—he concludes that chapter 20 and the whole matter as follows:

“But how what we now conjecture as best we can with the limited powers of our reasoning will actually occur”—namely, how those last living people will both die and rise again within so short a space of time, as he had previously shown could happen—“will then be understood, so that we may know it. We must believe, if we wish to be Christians, that the resurrection of the dead will take place in the flesh when Christ comes to judge the living and the dead. Our faith concerning this matter is not therefore empty merely because we cannot fully comprehend how it will occur” [269].

Thus far the holy doctor on the question of how to understand those living and dead whom the coming Lord will judge at the end of the world—namely, whether those living whom he finds will die or not before they come to judgment. Here it is sufficiently clear how uncertain he was between the two positions, and finally how he inclined more toward the one that admitted even the death and sudden resurrection of those last living people.

What, then, if our Nicetas, after the middle of the fifth century—that is, not long after Augustine’s time—adopted, in a matter insufficiently established and debated in both directions, the opinion common among the Greek Fathers, toward which Saint Augustine himself had at times also inclined?

Yet in Nicetas’ own age, and within Italy itself, other Latin Fathers also taught what our Nicetas appears to have taught concerning the living at the Last Judgment: namely, that they would pass into perpetual immortality without death. Thus Saint Peter Chrysologus explained the same article concerning the judgment of the living and the dead in three of his sermons on the Apostles’ Creed:

“From there he will come to judge the living and the dead. Let us grant that there are living; how can he judge the dead? But those whom we count as dead are alive. Therefore you confess that those whom unbelief considers to have perished will rise again for judgment, so that those who have died and those who will be found alive may equally give an account of their deeds and their life.”

Thus in Sermon 57.

“He judges the living; he also judges the dead, whom indeed he raises up in order to judge.”

Thus in Sermon 59.

“From there he will come to judge the living and the dead. For when Christ comes, the dead will rise and the living will stand before him, so that together they may give an account of the character of their deeds.”

Thus in Sermon 60.

Saint Maximus of Turin also appears to express the same opinion as our Nicetas and Saint Peter Chrysologus in his Homily 83, entitled “On the Handing Over of the Creed”:

“Thus the living are said to be judged, and the dead, so that it may be believed that God is concerned for all human beings.”

That is, he is concerned both for those who have undergone death and for those whom the coming of the Judge will overtake before they undergo death, as the obvious sense of the words appears to indicate.

Accordingly, in Nicetas’ time the more common opinion among the Latin Fathers was still that, under the name of “the living” in the Creed, those should be understood whom the coming of Christ the Judge would find alive and who would undergo judgment without a preceding death, together with the other living who had been raised from the dead.

This opinion also continued for some time in the West after Nicetas’ age. It gradually and almost step by step fell out of use, until another opinion finally prevailed completely—one that affirmed that those whom the last day would find alive would also die, in accordance with the view now commonly held. That view undoubtedly gained greater force from the discussions of Saint Augustine in the cited Book XX of The City of God.

Evidence of this is supplied by the book entitled On Ecclesiastical Dogmas, chapter 8, in the Isidorian appendix 13, vol. VII, p. 322 [Col. 1115D], of the Works of Saint Isidore of Seville, in the latest Roman edition of the distinguished Arevalus, where we read:

“When we say in the Creed that at the Lord’s coming the living and the dead are to be judged, we believe that this signifies not only the righteous and sinners, as Diodorus thinks, but also those living whom he will find in the flesh, who are believed still to be destined to die—or, as others hold, to be changed, so that, immediately raised up or transformed, they may be judged together with those who died beforehand.”

The author of this book, which was first attributed to Saint Augustine and then to Gennadius of Massilia, is thought by more recent investigations to have been a certain Bracharius, a bishop of Seville, fourth after Saint Isidore, who lived at the end of the seventh century. See Arevalus’ Isidoriana, chapter 83, in the aforementioned Works, vol. II, pp. 31 ff.

Thus, even in the seventh century, although the opinion of those who held that the living whom Christ the Judge would find would not be brought before the judgment until they too had undergone death, however brief, so that they might be raised together with those who had already died, was regarded as the stronger—as appears from the text cited—the other opinion was not entirely rejected. This second opinion asserted that those living people would be brought to judgment without a preceding death, undergoing only a change or transformation corresponding in some way to resurrection. It was at least proposed in second place, as an explanation for understanding the article of the Creed.

Let this suffice for the elucidation of this matter and at the same time for the defense of our Nicetas concerning it.

A third difficulty arises from what Nicetas says in chapter 7 of the Explanation, where he expounds the article of the Creed: “I believe in the Holy Spirit.”

“You believe,” he says, “also in the Holy Spirit. This Holy Spirit is one, sanctifying all things, who proceeds from the Father.”

What do these words—“he proceeds from the Father”—mean? Did Nicetas hold and teach that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone, and not also from the Son?

Nicetas, however, was not the only one who spoke in this way in an exposition of the Creed, omitting mention of the procession of the Holy Spirit also from the Son. Other Fathers, both before Nicetas and in Nicetas’ own age, spoke in much the same way in their expositions of the Creed addressed to the candidates:

“We believe in the Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Father, yet not [himself] the Son,”

said Saint Augustine in Sermon 214, “On the Handing Over of the Creed,” no. 10.

“According to evangelical truth, just as the Son came forth from the Father, so also the Spirit proceeds from the Father,”

taught Saint Maximus of Turin in the aforementioned Homily 83, “On the Handing Over of the Creed.”

The difficulty that arises for us from Nicetas’ words had already been noticed, before us, in the comparable words just cited of Saint Maximus of Turin by the distinguished Bruno Brunius, the editor and commentator of the latest Roman edition of his works, whom we praised above. On the basis of his learning, Brunius undertook to resolve it in a special note which he appended to that homily. His discussion also bears most fully upon our present subject in defense of Nicetas. We may therefore appropriately borrow certain points from it which, we believe, will be agreeable to readers and necessary for the argument [Col. 1116C].

“Let no one be surprised,” he says, “that Maximus said that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and did not add that he also proceeds from the Son; for in this he acted together with the other Fathers who opposed those heretics who made the Holy Spirit inferior to the Son. Eunomius taught that the Spirit proceeds at the Father’s command, through the Son’s operation and power. Therefore, at that time Catholic teaching concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit was chiefly concerned with his procession from the Father; and the Church did not require an explicit [271] confession that he also proceeds from the Son. It was enough for her that all should believe and worship the Holy Spirit as true God.

“Afterward, however, when the error was raised up by the Greeks from the ashes of Macedonius and Nestorius—an error in which they denied that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son—the Church judged it necessary to proscribe the heresy that had arisen and to confess his procession from both the Father and the Son. This confession was first received in Spain, where several councils were held for this reason [Col. 1116D] and the phrase *Filioque* was added to the Creed. Three further synods—the Synod of Gentilly, the Synod of Friuli, and the Synod of Aachen—approved it while condemning the error of the Greeks.”

After other material Brunius continues:

“To speak of Saint Maximus’s teaching concerning this dogma: he mentions the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father; but he does not explicitly mention it from the Son. Nor was it necessary for him to make explicit mention of this when handing on the Creed, since at that time no controversy had been raised by innovators against Catholic dogma, and the teaching of all—especially of the Westerners—was that the Holy Spirit also proceeds from the Son.”

Then the distinguished commentator continues. In order to defend Saint Maximus even more clearly against the suspicion that he denied the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son as well, he turns to similar expressions of Augustine—one of which we too have cited in support of our Nicetas [Col. 1117A], from Augustine’s Sermon 214, *On the Tradition of the Creed*:

“Certainly,” says Brunius, “if Saint Augustine, apart from his treatise *On Faith and the Creed*, chapter 8, and his sermon *On the Tradition of the Creed* . . . in which he discusses the matter exactly as Maximus does, mentioning the Spirit proceeding from the Father while omitting an explicit mention of that same Spirit’s procession from the Son—if, I say, apart from those treatises he had written no others on the Trinity, and someone had consequently concluded that Augustine did not grant the Spirit’s procession from the Son, that conclusion would have been gravely mistaken. For although in the works mentioned he does not mention this procession from the Son, he nevertheless truly believed that the Holy Spirit likewise proceeds from the Son, as is clear from Book II of *Against Maximinus*, chapter 14, and from Book XV of *On the Trinity*, chapter 27. Therefore, if Maximus had written a treatise on the Trinity and had encountered this question in it, I have no doubt that he would have affirmed that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son . . . . Otherwise, this further consequence would remain: that the Fathers of the First Ecumenical Council of Constantinople, because they mentioned in the Creed [Col. 1117B] the Holy Spirit’s procession from the Father, but remained silent about *τὴν* [the procession] from the Son (see volume I of the Councils, under the year 381, p. 814, Paris edition of 1714), would be accused of the crime of denying his procession from the Son. What could be more unjust than that?”

This learned author wrote these things in defense of Saint Maximus of Turin. We judge that they apply equally to our Nicetas, a bishop of the same period, so that we should not at all be surprised that he too, when explaining the Creed to the catechumens, mentioned the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father but said nothing explicitly about his procession from the Son.

If it is not superfluous to add something here on behalf of our Nicetas to the observations of this distinguished writer, let the reader accept in good part the few points that remain. If we see Nicetas, Augustine, and Maximus, while explaining to the catechumens the article of faith concerning the Holy Spirit, mentioning only the Spirit’s procession from the Father and omitting an explicit profession of his procession also from the Son, we shall judge that they did so not without reason [272]: they were explaining the Apostles’ Creed [Col. 1117C], and in this matter they wished to clarify no more than the additions found in the Constantinopolitan Creed. They imposed upon themselves, as it were, a scruple against adding anything belonging to an explicit formulation of faith that was not found there—especially since at that time no attempt had been made in the workshops of heretics against the particular doctrine of the Holy Spirit’s procession also from the Son.

For who does not know how often heretics accused the Catholic Church of tampering with the Nicene faith of the three hundred and eighteen Fathers in its explanations of the sacred dogmas, and likewise with the faith of the Constantinopolitan Creed of the one hundred and fifty? Who also does not know how much labor and opposition preceded the addition and general acceptance of the word *Filioque* in the Creed to indicate the procession of the Spirit also from the Son—out of reverence, namely, for the Nicene and Constantinopolitan Fathers and for their creeds of faith, in which nothing was said about this procession of the Spirit from the Son?

[Col. 1117D] There remains the celebrated response of Pope Saint Leo III on this matter to the legates of the Council of Aachen, who were asking him to approve the addition of the word *Filioque* to the Creed. He approved the procession of the Holy Spirit also from the Son, as it had been declared at that council, and said that it was to be retained in a holy manner; but he did not approve the addition of the word *Filioque* to the Creed. He did so, first, because he judged that nothing should be added to what the Nicene and Constantinopolitan Fathers, enlightened by divine wisdom, as he put it, had admitted in their creeds; and, second, because he added that it was not necessary for every dogma of faith to be inserted into the Creed. Nor had those Fathers inserted in their creeds absolutely everything that was already known and firmly established at that time.

See the Acts of the conference of those legates with Leo III in Sirmond, volume II of the *Councils of Gaul*, under the year 809, and also in Labbe’s *Councils*, edited by Colet, volume IX, column 278 and following.

[Col. 1118A] Moreover, in order to vindicate even more clearly Nicetas’s faith concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit—not from the Father alone but also from the Son, although he says nothing explicitly about it in his *Explanation of the Creed*—it is useful to observe how common this faith then was in the Church, so that we should in no way think him alien to that common belief.

We have seen the divine Augustine cited by the distinguished Brunius from Book II of *Against Maximinus*, chapter 14, and from Book XV of *On the Trinity*, chapter 27. To these we can add chapters 26 and 28, where he speaks expressly and clearly of the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son. The holy doctor treats the same subject no less clearly and fully in his *Tractates on John*, tractate 99, numbers 6, 7, and 8. There, by bringing together and carefully weighing the testimonies of the New Testament, he impressed upon the hearts of his faithful hearers the Catholic dogma of the Holy Spirit’s procession also from the Son—without making any mention of the contrary error. Thus this procession was evidently regarded as part of the common faith at that time, even though the Constantinopolitan Creed mentioned only procession from the Father.

[Col. 1118B] Saint Leo the Great likewise mentions the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son as a doctrine received everywhere, in Letter 15 to Turibius of Astorga, chapter 1, which belongs to the year 447:

“How impiously,” he says, “do they think about the divine Trinity who assert that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one and the same person . . . so that there is not one who begot, another who was begotten, and another who proceeded from both [or: proceeds from both], etc.”

Who, then, could persuade himself that, amid such brilliant clarity concerning this [273] doctrine among Catholics, Nicetas was blind to it, so that he would not admit that the Holy Spirit proceeds also from the Son merely because he did not teach it in explicit words in his *Explanation of the Creed*? Indeed, Nicetas had a witness to this faith within his own household: Rufinus, formerly a presbyter of his own church. In his exceedingly full explanation of the Creed, so highly commended by writers and known everywhere—namely, his *Commentary on the Apostles’ Creed* [Col. 1118C], no. 35—Rufinus speaks most explicitly of the procession of the Holy Spirit also from the Son, as of a doctrine known and established by everyone:

“Let ‘the Father’ be understood as the one from whom all things are, and because he himself has no Father; ‘the Son’ as the one who was born from the Father; and ‘the Holy Spirit’ as the one proceeding from both and sanctifying all things.”

Nicetas therefore could neither have been ignorant of this dogma of the procession nor disagreed with it. At that time its profession had no particular opponent, and it was the common doctrine of the Church.

Moreover—and this may be added—Nicetas himself appears to have made a certain profession of this dogma in the same *Explanation*, although not at the place where he speaks specifically about the Holy Spirit, namely, chapter 7, but elsewhere, in chapter 9, where he briefly presents and inculcates the doctrine of the Trinity. He says:

“If any heretic, under the Christian name, either makes Christ a creature for you, or persuades you that the Holy Spirit is alien to the glory of the Father and the Son, let him be to you as a pagan [Col. 1118D] and a tax collector.”

Nicetas’s purpose in these words is indeed to establish the divinity of the Holy Spirit, which had long before been called into question and was finally asserted by the Fathers of Constantinople and disclosed in the Creed through an explicit confession of his procession from the Father, whose divinity no one was then, or had formerly been, calling into question. Yet when Nicetas asserts that the Holy Spirit is not alien to the glory of the Father and the Son, and thus adds the Son to the Father in confirming the Spirit’s divinity, he seems to have spoken from an inward conviction that the Spirit proceeds from both—from the Father and the Son. Through this, no doubt, the divinity of the Holy Spirit is more clearly manifested.

[Col. 1119A] On this occasion I wish to add one point that does not immediately concern Nicetas, but which strongly confirms the faith of the Church of Aquileia concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit also from the Son, and which may in some way have a bearing on Nicetas as well, since the tradition of this faith came from bishops of that church.

The word *Filioque*, which was eventually inserted into the Creed with the consent of the Apostolic See and the approval of the whole Western Church in order to profess solemnly and explicitly the procession of the Holy Spirit also from the Son, was first adopted in Spain toward the end of the sixth century and then, in the seventh century, in Gaul and Germany as well, according to the learned. By whom is it first recorded as having been introduced into Italy?

It was Saint Paulinus, patriarch of Aquileia, at a synod held by him at Friuli in 796, concerning, as the title states, the most sacred Trinity and the Incarnation of the divine Word. There we read the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed with the word *Filioque* inserted in its proper place. Immediately after the Creed we also find an explanation of the Creed, in which it is similarly said:

“The Holy Spirit is true God; the Holy Spirit is truly and properly [the Holy Spirit]: not begotten and not created, but proceeding timelessly and inseparably [Col. 1119B] from the Father and the Son.”

This synod appears in Labbe’s *Councils*, edited by Colet, the aforementioned volume IX, column 31 and following, and also among the works of Saint Paulinus collected and annotated by Giovanni Francesco Madrisi, p. 65. With regard to the word [274] *Filioque* and its first introduction into Italy by Saint Paulinus of Aquileia, Madrisi’s fifth dissertation in the same work, p. 229 and following, is also worth reading.

The fourth difficulty that could arise from expressions of our Nicetas is found in chapter 13 of his *Explanation*, where he speaks of the resurrection of the flesh. He says:

“When a human being departs from this life, the soul does not die; but when it departs, only the body dies. When the body has decayed in the earth, the soul is kept according to its merit either in a place of light or in a place of darkness, so that on the day of the Lord’s coming from heaven, when he comes with his holy angels, after all have been raised, the souls may be restored to their bodies and there may be a just distinction between the good and the wicked. Then the righteous will shine like the sun [Col. 1119C] in the kingdom of their Father; but the impious and wicked will be in the darkness of hell, where there will be weeping of the eyes and gnashing of the teeth, as it is written.”

When Nicetas says that after the death of the body the soul is kept according to its merit either in a place of light or in a place of darkness until the day of the Lord’s coming from heaven with his angels, does he establish some place distinct from heaven where the souls of the righteous are placed until that day, and likewise some place distinct from hell where the souls of the wicked remain until then? When he also says that on that day, after all have been raised and the souls restored to their bodies, there will be a just distinction between the good and the wicked, and that then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father while the impious and wicked will be in the darkness of hell, did Nicetas perhaps think that before that day the distinction between the good and the wicked was not sufficiently just or according to merit? Did he likewise think that before that day the righteous would not shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father, and therefore that the impious and wicked were not yet to be thrust into the darkness of hell?

[Col. 1119D] Was Nicetas therefore among those who thought that the crown of glory would not be given to the righteous according to the merit of their life until the day of judgment, nor punishment to the wicked; and that meanwhile the souls of the righteous, released from the body, would be deprived until that day of fellowship with Christ and of the blessed vision of God, just as the souls of the wicked would meanwhile be spared the fires of Gehenna?

If this work of Nicetas of Aquileia had been known to the learned when the Englishman Thomas Burnet was writing his book *On the State of the Dead and the Resurrected*, which saw the light at London in 1726, he would surely not have omitted this text of Nicetas as a support for his own opinion—an opinion which he revived from the long-obsolete views of certain ancient writers: namely, that rewards are to be given to the righteous and punishments to the unjust only when Christ brings the entire human race to judgment, and that meanwhile the souls of all the dead and dying will remain until that final day in a state of rest, silence [Col. 1120A], and something like sleep.

He certainly left no argument unused and scarcely spared any of the holy Fathers or ancient authors from being pressed into service, in order to show that this opinion was the common teaching of the ancient Church and to accuse Catholics who, in accordance with the definition of the Council of Florence, firmly maintain:

“The souls of those who, after receiving baptism, incurred no stain of sin at all, and likewise those who, after contracting the stain of sin, have been purified either in their bodies or after being stripped of their bodies . . . are immediately received into heaven and clearly behold the triune and one Lord as he is, though one more perfectly than another according to the diversity of their merits. But the souls of those who die in actual mortal sin or in original sin alone immediately descend into hell, though they are punished with unequal [275] punishments.”

For a long time Catholic theologians after Saint Thomas—Sixtus of Siena, Alfonso de Castro, Cardinal Bellarmine, Vasquez, Petavius, and others—have clarified this question against those who dissent [Col. 1120B] from the faith of the Catholic Church, producing and explaining many statements of the Fathers, from which the tradition of the Catholic dogma, clearly and firmly grounded in the Holy Scriptures, emerges. This remains so despite the fact that some of those writers may have been influenced by the error of the Millenarians or indulged their particular opinions on a matter not yet defined by the Church.

But the distinguished Muratori reviewed, illuminated, and completed the entire matter most carefully from the beginning in his book published against Burnet, entitled *On Paradise and the Glory of the Heavenly Kingdom, Granted by God to the Just without Awaiting the Resurrection of Their Bodies*. There he demonstrates from Scripture the evident revelation of this dogma and shows, from the teaching of the Fathers and other monuments of the Church, its perpetual profession in the Church. There too, after maturely examining the sayings and opinions of the holy Fathers, he reduces the number of those formerly thought to have departed into the opposing view. In particular, he explains the statements and distinctive modes of expression of Saints Hilary, Ambrose, Augustine, and [Col. 1120C] Bernard, who have sometimes seemed to differ in this matter not only from the dogma later defined by the Church but also from themselves.

What, meanwhile, shall we think about our Nicetas, whose words could be adopted neither by Burnet in support of his opinion nor by Muratori and other Catholic writers? No stain would indeed be cast upon the integrity of Nicetas’s faith even if he had actually held, with the Millenarians or with a few others, that the blessedness of the righteous and the punishments of the wicked were to be postponed until the end of this world and the day of the final judgment. For anyone was permitted to abound in his own opinion on a matter not yet defined by the Church and harmlessly debated in both directions.

But our Nicetas was far from holding that opinion; indeed, the very words of the text cited demonstrate that he held the opposite. Nicetas says that after the death of the body the souls are kept according to their merit, either in a place of light or in a place of darkness, until the day of the Lord’s coming, on which [Col. 1120D] the souls will be restored to their bodies. There is therefore a certain keeping of souls separated from the body—whatever their state may be while they remain separated from the body—for the entire period between their separation from the body and their new union with it. For it is precisely for this new union, which will take place in the resurrection, that they are truly and properly kept.

The souls of the departed are not kept only for this new union with the body; they are also kept for the universal judgment to be undergone together with the body. For in relation to this judgment as well, the souls are truly kept [Col. 1121A] until the day appointed by the Lord arrives. Nicetas did not use this word “kept” as a product of his own ingenuity. To whom would the same expression, repeated in the Epistles of Peter and Jude, not immediately present this meaning: “kept for judgment”; “to reserve for the day of judgment”; “he has kept for the judgment of the great day”?

What, then, does Nicetas mean by the place of light and the place of darkness in which souls are kept according to their merit? We have no doubt that by these words Nicetas understood the true blessedness in heaven already obtained, or to be obtained, by the souls of the righteous as soon as they have departed, or shall depart, from the body; and likewise the true punishment of suffering in hell into which the souls of the wicked are cast at the very moment of their departure from the body.

We must not overlook even the word “place” itself, which Nicetas uses in a sense undoubtedly [276] familiar to him from Scripture. As it concerns the souls of the righteous, it recalls Christ’s words to his disciples in John 14: “I go to prepare a place for you.” As regards the souls of the wicked, it perhaps recalls what the apostles unanimously said about Judas the traitor in Acts 1: “That he might go to his own place.” Here, then, are the places or receptacles of souls after death, in which, according to Nicetas, they are kept according to their merit until the day of the Lord’s coming.

But what precisely is the place of light for the souls of the righteous? The very mention of a place for righteous souls separated from the body—a place which Nicetas could have understood as none other than that which the Lord promised to prepare [Col. 1121B] for the apostles in his Father’s house—immediately brings to mind that indescribable blessedness in heaven with Christ, in the presence of God the Father, which those happy souls must enjoy as soon as they are separated from the body, provided that nothing remains to be expiated.

For Nicetas was not unaware of the rest of Christ’s words in the same discourse:

“And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and take you to myself, so that where I am, you also may be.”

These words, plainly spoken of Christ’s coming at the death of each of his disciples and of their perpetual fellowship with him then to be undertaken, as well as of their dwelling with him where he is—that is, in the glory of God the Father, who is the true light and dwells in inaccessible light—can suggest no other meaning than eternal blessedness with Christ in heaven, without any postponement after death, as the Catholic faith teaches.

Here, then, is the place of light in Nicetas’s natural and obvious [Col. 1121C] sense, for the souls of the righteous separated from the body.

That the place of light indeed has this meaning in Nicetas’s mouth is demonstrated by other words used in a similar way by the holy Fathers, even in the earliest centuries of Christendom.

“He endured many labors; and thus, having become a martyr, he departed to the place of glory” (*τόπον τῆς δόξης*, “place of glory”).

Thus Saint Clement, the disciple and successor of the holy apostle Peter, speaks of Peter in his First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 5, in Cotelerius, *The Apostolic Fathers*, volume I, p. 150 of the second Amsterdam edition of 1724.

“Let me breathe in the pure light. When I am there, I shall be a man of God.”

Thus Saint Ignatius the Martyr speaks of himself, destined for the death of martyrdom, in his *Epistle to the Romans*, chapter 6, in the same work, volume II, p. 28.

“I am persuaded that all these did not run in vain, but in faith and righteousness, and that they are in the place appointed for them with the Lord, with whom they also suffered.”

Thus Saint Polycarp speaks in his *Epistle to the Philippians*, chapter 9, [Col. 1121D] in the same work, p. 189, referring to Saint Paul and the other apostles who had died.

“Place him in the bosom of the patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and all who have pleased you from the beginning of the age; where there is neither sorrow, pain, nor groaning, but the tranquil place of the pious and likewise the peaceful land of the upright, and of those who there behold the glory of your Christ.”

Thus reads the prayer for the brethren who have fallen asleep in Christ in Book VIII, chapter 41, of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, in the same work, likewise volume I, p. 423. Although these *Constitutions* do not belong to Clement, whose name they bear, they nevertheless appear, according to the judgment of the learned, to have been composed in the earliest centuries of the Church, and they are mentioned by Athanasius, Eusebius, Epiphanius, and others.

Here, then, is the place; here is the light, for the souls that have departed from the body: words which, as these testimonies themselves establish, indicate heavenly glory, dwelling with the Lord, and the vision of Christ’s glory—obtained immediately after death, provided that nothing remains to be expiated. [277]

Who could persuade himself that Nicetas did not use “place of light” in precisely the same sense, as the place in which the souls of the righteous, stripped of their bodies, are kept?

Furthermore, does not the Catholic Church, which so often offers prayers for the souls of the righteous who are subject to purifying punishments, asking that, once freed from them, they may obtain as soon as possible the reward and glory due to them in heaven, use Nicetas’s words every day: that they may approach the holy light and ascend to the place of light?

“May the holy standard-bearer Michael lead them into the holy light, which you once promised to Abraham and his descendants . . . . May eternal light shine upon them, Lord, with your saints forever.”

Thus in all the Masses for the dead.

“For them, Lord, and for all who rest in Christ, we ask that you grant the place of refreshment, light, and peace.”

Thus every day in the canon of the Mass at the commemoration of the dead.

The place of light, therefore, according to Nicetas, in which the souls of the righteous are kept after their departure from the body until the day of the resurrection and universal judgment, is not some place [Col. 1122B] distinct from that happy blessedness which is the reward of the righteous and the crown of righteousness that the just Judge will give on that day. Rather, it is blessedness itself, which the souls of the righteous who have nothing left to expiate obtain immediately after the destruction of the body. It consists in this: that they enjoy the vision of God and, in God’s light, see light itself, as the royal Psalmist proclaims.

We must speak similarly, by contrast, of the place of darkness in which, according to Nicetas, the souls of the wicked are kept. Nicetas uses the word “darkness,” in opposition to light, in the sense intended by the apostle Jude in his Epistle, verse 6. Speaking of the rebellious angels, Jude says that they are kept in eternal chains under darkness for the judgment of the great day. The word is also used in the sense intended by the Apostle Peter in 2 Peter 2:17. Attacking heretics, he calls them “waterless springs and mists driven by storms, for whom the gloom of darkness is reserved.”

What is that place of darkness where the rebellious angels, already condemned to eternal chains, are kept for the judgment of the great day, and where wicked people, too, who have been driven away from the true faith, are to be cast after death [Col. 1122C]? What is that place, I ask, except the place to which Judas the traitor went to pay the penalty for his betrayal? And what is Judas’s place except the place of torments, anguish, and flame among the dead, in which, immediately after death, that rich man was buried who was clothed in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day while despising the beggar Lazarus lying at his gate, as in Luke 16?

The place of darkness, therefore, mentioned by Nicetas for the souls of the wicked who have departed from the body, does not differ from hell. It does not differ from the Gehenna of fire, where souls are tormented immediately after the death of the body, without awaiting the day of the universal judgment.

Yet further difficulty might seem to arise from what Nicetas adds: that on the day of the Lord’s coming from heaven with his holy angels, after all have been raised and the souls restored to their bodies, there will be a just distinction between the good and the wicked; and that then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father, while the impious and wicked will be cast into the darkness of hell [Col. 1122D], where there will be weeping of the eyes and gnashing of the teeth.

But Nicetas’s words present no difficulty against the present blessedness of the souls of the righteous or the present punishment of the souls of the wicked, if we remember that these words refer only to the resurrection of the bodies and the restoration of the souls to their bodies. For then, and only then, will there be a just distinction between the good and the wicked, when this distinction itself has actually fallen [278] under everyone’s gaze—namely, when the good and the wicked have again become human beings through the new conjunction of their souls with their bodies, from which the human constitution exists by reason of its original formation.

Then too there will be a just distinction between the good and the wicked—that is, a perfect and complete one—because of the association of their bodies either with glory or with punishment, whereas previously only their souls were affected.

As for what Nicetas adds: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father, but the impious and wicked will be in the darkness of hell, where there will be weeping of the eyes and gnashing of the teeth,” this likewise refers, in the case of the righteous, to the condition of glorified bodies, and, in the case of the impious and wicked, to the misery of condemned bodies. For it will properly belong to the glorified bodies then to shine like the sun in the kingdom of the Father, just as it will then belong to the condemned bodies [Col. 1123A] to weep with their eyes and gnash their teeth in the darkness of hell.

Moreover, when Nicetas says that on the day of the Lord’s coming from heaven, after all have been raised and the souls restored to their bodies, there will finally be a just distinction between the good and the wicked, and that then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father while the impious and wicked will be thrust into the darkness of hell, where there will be weeping of the eyes and gnashing of the teeth, he has by this very manner of speaking referred to the opinion common among the holy Fathers, sacred interpreters, and our theologians. According to that opinion, we are taught that before the resurrection of the bodies and the universal judgment the souls of the saints do not yet possess that perfect and consummated happiness which is due to them, just as the souls of the wicked [Col. 1123B] are not yet afflicted with the full weight of judgment that they deserve. Therefore, after the resurrection and universal judgment, the blessedness of the saints and the punishment of the wicked must increase—whatever the ultimate reason for this increase may be; it is not our task here to investigate that question.

Meanwhile, concerning this increase—whether of blessedness in the righteous or of punishment in the wicked—see how Saint Augustine understood it:

“All souls, when they depart from this world, have their different receptions. The good have joy; the evil have torments. But when the resurrection has taken place, the joy of the good will be greater and the torments of the evil more severe, when they are tormented together with the body.”

Thus in *Tractate on John* 49, no. 10.

The holy doctor pursues the same matter even more clearly in Sermon 280, on the feast of the martyrs Perpetua and Felicity, no. 4, where he establishes a comparison between the present state of souls separated from the body and their state after the resurrection of the bodies and the universal judgment:

“What, then, [Col. 1123C] when the souls of the martyrs, released from these bonds after the labors of a perilous struggle, have been received and refreshed by angelic triumphs . . . ? With what joy do they now feast spiritually! How secure they are in the Lord, and with what exalted honor they glory—who could teach this by any earthly example? This life, then, which the blessed martyrs now possess, although it cannot be compared with any happiness or delight of this world, is only a small part of the promise; indeed, it is a consolation during the delay.

“But the day of retribution will come, when, once their bodies have been restored, the whole person will receive what he deserves. Then the limbs of that rich man, once adorned with temporal purple, will be scorched by eternal fire, while the flesh of the poor man covered with sores will shine, transformed among the angels. Even now, however, the rich man thirsts for a drop from the poor man’s finger in hell, while the poor man rests delightfully in the bosom of the righteous.
