“For just as there is a very great difference between the joys and miseries of those who dream and those who are awake, so there is a great difference between the torments or joys of the dead and those of the risen. This is not because the spirits of the dead must be deceived, as sleepers are [Col. 1123D]; [279] rather, because the repose of souls without any bodies is one thing, while the splendor and happiness of the angels in heavenly bodies is another. To this the multitude of the faithful who rise again will be made equal. In that multitude the most glorious martyrs will shine with the exceptional light of their honor, and the very bodies in which they endured unworthy torments will be transformed into adornments worthy of them.”

Such is Saint Augustine. Similar material may also be found in his Sermon 328, on the feast of the martyrs, but we omit it here so as not to become too lengthy.

It is clear from this what Augustine’s opinion was concerning the state both of the righteous and of the wicked after the resurrection, although he acknowledged the blessedness and glory of the righteous even before the resurrection to be indescribable and incomprehensible, and likewise regarded the torments of the wicked as exceedingly severe.

In a similar way Nicetas, after saying that souls are kept according to their merit either in the place of light or in the place of darkness—that is, either in the place of blessedness with Christ in heaven or in hell, in a place [Col. 1124A] of torment, anguish, and flame—asserted in his remaining words an increase, after the resurrection and judgment, both of blessedness and of torment. He explained this increase through the just distinction that would then occur between the good and the wicked, through the righteous then shining like the sun in the kingdom of their Father, and through the impious and wicked being thrust into the darkness of hell, where there would be weeping of the eyes and gnashing of the teeth.

With a view to this increase, which would be received on the day of the Lord’s coming from heaven with his holy angels, he rightly said that the souls were meanwhile being kept. For, in the case of the righteous, however happy their state may be, it is still a kind of keeping until the fullness of happiness is added to them. In the case of the impious and wicked, their present state is likewise a keeping, although their present condition of torment and anguish is exceedingly bitter, until on the last day all the sinners of the earth drink from the dregs of the cup of God’s wrath, which has not yet been emptied.

The fifth difficulty is presented by other words of Nicetas in his little book *To a Fallen Virgin*, chapter 8, [Col. 1124B] no. 36. After exhorting the fallen woman to perform public penance according to the form he had prescribed for her, and finally raising and inviting her to hope for forgiveness from God for the crime she had committed, he says:

“Such a life, such an act of penance, if it perseveres, will dare to hope—even if not for glory, certainly for exemption from punishment.”

For Nicetas seems here to imply that for certain people—for penitents who have committed more serious offenses, as that fallen virgin had, or even for lukewarm Christians who have earned little in the Christian service—there is, so to speak, an intermediate state in the next life between eternal blessedness and damnation, where there is neither glory nor punishment.

Although such a state is granted, according to the more lenient opinion of theologians, to little children who die without baptism, with no opposition from the Church, it is certainly not granted to adults, for whom, according to the merit of their life, either punishments or rewards await them—with the single exception of that temporary state of purification for the souls of the righteous who, when they depart this life, still have something [Col. 1124C] left to expiate.

What, then, are we to say about this opinion of Nicetas, which the Church in no way supports?

It must first be observed, with theologians and scholars, that similar modes of expression are sometimes found among the ancient Fathers, both Greek and Latin. Saint Gregory Nazianzen, in his celebrated Oration on the Moderation to Be Observed in Disputations, etc.—Oration 26 in the Paris edition of Fed. Morellus, 1609—writing through the translation of James Billy, said on page 458:

> “You seek something greater than salvation, namely, the glory 280 and splendor of the other life; but for me, attaining salvation is the greatest thing, and avoiding future punishments. You enter upon a road that is scarcely trodden and inaccessible; I enter upon one that is trodden and worn, and by which many have reached salvation.”

In Oration 40, On Holy Baptism, where he also appropriately rebukes those who delayed receiving baptism until the very end of life—when, that is, little or no time intervened between baptism and death—he says on page 644:

> “Let some time intervene between grace [Col. 1124D] and death, so that not only may the evil writing be erased, but better writing may be inscribed in its place; so that you may not only possess grace, but also obtain the reward; so that you may not merely escape the punishment of fire, but also receive the inheritance of glory, which the transaction joined to the gift secures. For to small and lowly souls it seems a great and splendid thing to avoid punishment; but those endowed with a great and lofty spirit aspire also to the reward.”

Here, then, are sentiments of Gregory Nazianzen similar to those of our Nicetas. In them he seems to assert some state that is indeed a state of salvation, insofar as it is not condemnation, but nevertheless a state without the reward and recompense of glory, just as it is without the punishment of fire and other penalties. Similar passages are also reported from Athanasius, in his *Exhortation to Monks*, and from Origen, in Homilies 17 and 35 on Matthew; it is enough here merely to indicate them.

[Col. 1125A] As for the Latin Fathers and writers, there is Saint Ambrose, who says in Letter 71 of Class II, addressed to Horontianus:

> “He who is converted under the stroke of death and confesses the Lord Jesus deserves a dwelling in paradise”—like the thief, of whom he had spoken earlier. “But he who exercised himself long beforehand and served as a soldier for Christ, acquired the souls of peoples, and offered himself for Christ: let him have God’s kingdom prepared in accordance with his services, and let him rejoice that he has been granted its recompense. Therefore it is said to Peter: ‘To you I will give the keys of the kingdom of heaven.’ The man converted from robbery has rest; the one proved in the apostolate has received authority.”

In the book *On Faith in the Resurrection*, no. 93, he likewise says:

> “In death itself, some rest, while others live. Rest is good, but life is better.”

Here paradise is distinguished from the kingdom of God, and a state of rest and repose from a state of life and glory. Ambrose therefore seems to assert a third, or middle, state for certain souls who have departed from the body, without glory and without punishments—if we take his words as they stand.

Moreover, in the Augustinian appendices, volume XVII [Col. 1125B] of the Venetian quarto edition of Augustine’s works, column 1951, there is a sermon entitled *Sermon on the Creed*, compiled—as the Maurist editors observe—chiefly from excerpts of Rufinus and others. In chapter 18, column 1966, the same opinion concerning this middle state seems to appear. For its author, or compiler—whoever he may finally have been—says:

> “Yet we can not only escape these punishments and these torments—the fire of eternal Gehenna—but also attain eternal blessedness, provided that we repent of our evils.”

Here he seems to establish an escape from punishments distinct from the attainment of eternal blessedness, and thus to indicate some middle state in the other life in which there is merely escape from punishments and torments, without attaining eternal blessedness.

Aurelius Prudentius may also be added, in the *Hamartigenia*. Near the end of the book, while pouring out prayers to God for his soul after it has been separated from the body, he says:

> O God, father of all, giver of the soul . . . . . [Col. 1125C]  
> I confess—willingly forgive and spare the one who confesses—  
>   
> 281 I deserved every evil; but you, good judge, remove  
>   
> What I deserved; favorably grant better things to one who prays.  
>   
> Grant gifts at some time to my soul, when it has left  
>   
> The shelter of this body . . . . .  
>   
> May it not behold some savage one from the race of robbers,  
>   
> Cruel, raging, terrible in face and threatening in voice,  
>   
> Who may drag me, stained with the sprinkling of my conduct,  
>   
> Headlong, like a plunderer, and plunge me as I fall  
>   
> Into the black caverns, exacting every debt  
>   
> Of my ruinous life down to the smallest farthing.  
>   
> There are many dwellings in the Father’s treasuries, Christ,  
>   
> Distinguished in different places. I do not ask for a blessed  
>   
> Dwelling in that region: let the chaste companies of men  
>   
> Be there, disdaining earthly wealth  
>   
> And seeking your riches . . . . .  
>   
> But for me it is enough if no face of a Tartarean minister  
>   
> Meets me, and if the flame of greedy Gehenna  
>   
> Does not devour this soul, sunk in the deepest furnaces.

Prudentius immediately continues:

> Let it be, since this is necessary [Col. 1125D] for bodily guilt, that the cavernous  
>   
> Sad fire of Avernus consume me:  
>   
> At least let the slow fires breathe forth soothing vapors,  
>   
> And let the heat grow mild as its intensity languishes.  
>   
> Let immense light glorify others, and let brows bound with crowns  
>   
> Glorify them; let a gentle, light punishment burn me.

Scholars, both Catholic and heterodox, refer this entire passage of Prudentius to the punishments of purgatory, which Prudentius evidently asserts. The most recent editor of Prudentius’s poems, the distinguished Faustinus Arevalus, agrees in his learned *Prolegomena* to his most complete Roman edition, which he entitled *Prudentiana*, chapter 17, page 151 and following, of volume I.

Indeed, if the subject is the later verses of Prudentius—“Let it be, since this is necessary for bodily guilt,” and so forth—there is no doubt that he had the punishments of purgatory in view. But in the preceding verses his language is sufficiently clear concerning the heavenly glory of the blessed and the infernal punishments of the condemned. When, therefore, he said [Col. 1126A] that he did not ask for a dwelling in the blessed region, and that it was enough for him if no face of a Tartarean minister met him and the flame of Gehenna did not devour his soul, sunk in the deepest furnaces, he seems undoubtedly to have indicated some middle state between heavenly glory and the punishments of Gehenna. He desired this state for his soul after death and even after his bodily stains had been expiated in purgatory by the gentle vapors of a slow-burning fire, because in his humility he felt that he was not permitted to ask for anything greater.

Accordingly, Prudentius’s meaning seems to us to have been understood by the author whom Arevalus himself cites in the same place: a certain note in Fabricius’s *Bibliotheca Latina Veteris*, book IV, chapter 2, Venetian edition of 1728, where he says that at the end of the *Hamartigenia* there are prayers “in which the author says that it is enough for him if he is not thrust into Tartarus, even though punishments must be endured in purgatory.”

Since, moreover, from the very notion of purgatory Prudentius could not have been unaware that purgatory would not be eternal, what does it mean to say that it is enough for him if he is not thrust into Tartarus, unless it means that he is in fact satisfied, even after purgatory, with some middle state [Col. 1126B] between heavenly glory and the flame of Gehenna? All this, however, is said without any wish to detract from the observations of the aforementioned 282 Arevalus, who strives to explain Prudentius’s words in their proper sense and to refer everything exclusively to purgatory, lest we regard the most devout Christian poet as though he had abandoned hope of attaining heavenly glory.

To Prudentius we may append Salvian, a writer of the same century as Nicetas. In book III of *Against Avarice*, chapter 18, rebuking the rich who were concerned with increasing their property and enriching their heirs, and who, even when close to death, thought nothing of redeeming their sins by offering some portion of their wealth as a remedy for their souls, he attacks them as follows:

> “What reason is there, then, that, even when dying and lying at the very end, you should not at least perform that final duty of offering, and do everything within your power, so that, if you can merit to be rich and blessed with God, you may be so; but if you cannot do that, at least merit this much: that you may not be wretched, certainly not burned, certainly not tortured, certainly not cast into outer darkness [Col. 1126C], and not boiled in flames burning without end?”

What does it mean, for one who cannot merit being rich and blessed after death—that is, enjoying the joys of heaven—to merit at least not being wretched, not being burned, not being tortured, and so forth, unless it means to merit at least being in some third state where there is neither blessedness nor condemnation, neither glory nor punishment? Salvian, therefore, who wrote in the same century as our Nicetas, also seems to have admitted this third state for baptized adults. It should consequently not seem strange if, in this same sense of Salvian, as also in the sense of the other writers and Fathers we have cited, both Greek and Latin, our Nicetas could in some measure have gone astray and himself believed in a certain third state for baptized adults who were neither worthy to become participants in heavenly blessedness nor worthy to be consigned to the eternal punishments of hell.

But did Nicetas really go astray? Did other writers and Fathers also go astray with Nicetas, whose words we have found to conform to his? This is the second point that it is useful to consider: whether the words reported from Nicetas, as well as those of others that we have cited, can be given a reasonable interpretation, so that they may present not the meaning they outwardly seem to bear, but a true meaning conformable to Catholic doctrine.

We certainly should not say that all the ancient Fathers and writers were free from certain peculiar opinions that did not entirely agree with the universal doctrine of the Church and that later completely fell out of use. Thus we need not be greatly concerned if our Nicetas and others with him really admitted, for baptized adults, that third state of which we have spoken in the future life, as a result of a mistaken interpretation—as scholars point out—of a passage of the Apostle, Romans 10:9. At that time, evidently, not everything that did not constitute one of the principal articles of faith had yet been explored as thoroughly as it later was, when, through the disputations of learned men, matters that had previously lain concealed, as it were, were brought into the light.

[Col. 1127A] But, as regards our present subject, the opinion of the most learned James Billy in his scholia on the above-mentioned twenty-sixth Oration of Gregory Nazianzen is especially welcome. Considering Gregory’s sentiments there, as well as those of Oration 40 as cited above, Billy is inclined to think that the holy Doctor did not at all separate salvation, or avoidance of punishment, from heavenly glory, and thus did not admit some middle state between blessedness and condemnation for adults baptized; rather, by the word “salvation” and other similar expressions, he wished to signify the lowest degree of blessedness and the lowest dwelling in that heavenly house, for those who had deserved nothing more 283 than exemption from punishment.

By this manner of understanding—which in no way conflicts with Nazianzen’s words—the statements of the other authors whom we have cited can easily be explained in their proper sense, especially those of our Nicetas in his work *To the Lapsed*, which is the reason we are writing this. The glory which he doubted that his lapsed virgin could merit—or rather, which, as he said, she would scarcely dare to hope for through her penance, however sincere and persevering—he undoubtedly understood as some higher degree of glory reserved for the innocence that she had lost. By exemption from punishment he understood [Col. 1127B] that lowest degree of blessedness, below which there is nothing in heaven, where dwellings are assigned according to the measure of merits; and thus he understood that degree which, if one may speak in this way, by reason of its lowliness is almost adjacent to the final degree of the punishments of the condemned.

Furthermore, are there no other expressions of Nicetas himself on this subject from which we might perhaps explain more clearly the obscure matters that now concern us, as learned men have successfully done in the case of other ancient Fathers and writers of the Church? The observations made by the Maurist editors of Ambrose’s works concerning the two passages of Ambrose that we have cited are certainly worthy of notice, especially concerning the second passage from the book *On Faith in the Resurrection*, [Col. 1127C] where, to those who look only at his bare words, he seems to suggest the middle state of which we are speaking. They say:

> “Certainly those are wrong who fabricate from such expressions an opinion concerning a state intermediate between glory and punishments and attribute it to the holy bishop. For in countless passages he opposes immortality directly (ἀμέσως) to punishments, as in this very oration, no. 8, contrasting those consigned to punishment with those destined for immortality. If John Daille had considered this more carefully, he would have treated the same formulas of speech with less hostility in book II, chapter 4, of *On the Use of the Fathers*.”

Salvian also—to pass over the others for the moment—who flourished in the same age as Nicetas, had expressed his mind more clearly on this very subject in the same book cited above, *Against Avarice*, chapter 3. Speaking there about the state of souls separated from the body, he acknowledged no middle state whatever between condemnation and glory. He says, addressing a greedy man:

> “Behold, you are going away—you are going away, most wretched of all—to the sacred tribunal, to that dread and unbearable judgment, where for the traveling and anxious soul [Col. 1127D] there can be no consolation at all except a good conscience alone . . . where for the guilty man there is no help except a generous mind, except fruitful repentance . . . where, finally, according to the diversity of merits, you will find either the highest good or the highest evil, either an immortal reward or torment without end.”

Where, then, is that middle state, neither of glory nor of punishments, which Salvian seemed in the passage cited earlier to imply so absolutely? Thus obscure statements are best clarified by clear ones, if we compare writers with writers, whenever several works of one and the same writer are available, or whenever the same work is more extensive and the writer has not lacked occasion to address the same subject repeatedly. Something of this kind should therefore also be attempted with our Nicetas. It might perhaps be easier if other works of his, which have perished, were still extant.

[Col. 1128A] Nevertheless, even among those writings of Nicetas that escaped destruction there is not altogether lacking a means by which we may ascertain his correct mind on the matter under discussion, and by which we may give a true interpretation to the ambiguous statements in his work *To the Lapsed*, chapter 8, from which that middle state appears at first sight—a state that is neither one of glory nor one of punishment, but merely an exemption from punishment.

In the words of the *Explanation of the Creed* considered above, chapter 13, where he speaks of the future universal judgment, he says:

> “Then 284 the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father; but the impious and wicked will be in the darkness of hell, where there will be weeping of the eyes and gnashing of the teeth.”

Here Nicetas distinguishes two states: that of the righteous in their Father’s kingdom, and that of the wicked in the darkness of hell. Where, then, even here in Nicetas, is that third or middle state without glory and without punishment, in which there is only exemption from punishment?

It should be noted, however, that Nicetas speaks in this way in the *Explanation of the Creed*—that is, in a work that sets forth the dogmas of the faith and that is at the same time an especially rich testimony to the faith of its author. Nicetas therefore did not at all acknowledge this third or middle state for baptized adults. [Col. 1128B] Accordingly, his words in *To the Lapsed*, chapter 8, should properly be interpreted in the manner of the most distinguished Billy: he wished to suggest that the lapsed woman, through her sincere and persevering penance, might indeed dare to hope not for that glory which awaits the innocent in heaven and those who have greatly merited it, but nevertheless for some glory of the lowest degree, which he signified by exemption from punishment.

That Nicetas intended to indicate some degree of glory by this exemption from punishment is also sufficiently shown, unless we are mistaken, by the words that he poured, as it were, into the mouth of the lapsed woman whom he was addressing, and with which he concluded his discourse, teaching her to implore mercy from the Lord amid the labors of penance:

> “I desire this gift, this grace, to be granted to me from your fountain, O God, that I may confess you forever.”

Now, what does one who asks to confess God forever ask for, unless she asks [Col. 1128C] that, after the course of this life, she may possess at least some share in the glory of the blessed in heaven? For it is properly said, according to the language of Scripture, that only the blessed confess God forever.

Nicetas therefore seems to have sufficiently explained exemption from punishment even in the work *To the Lapsed* itself—not by some middle state between glory and condemnation, but by the very state of glory in heaven with the blessed, though perhaps glory of a small or lowest degree.

Why, moreover, should Nicetas not have intended by the words “even if not glory” merely that particular and more exalted glory in heaven destined for virgins—a glory which that violated virgin would certainly never have dared to hope for after her fall, however great her penance, as the aforementioned Maurist editors of Ambrose’s works rightly observe concerning this passage?

We should therefore find and accept the words of our Nicetas even more readily in the proper sense of the common doctrine, and conclude that he did not at all admit that third state after death for baptized adults.

We now undertake, as the sixth point, to examine something more serious [Col. 1128D] concerning Nicetas’s orthodox faith in an important matter. Some have suspected that Nicetas favored the error of the Novatians and Montanists concerning the remission of sins in his work *To the Lapsed*, chapter 8, no. 38, where he addressed his lapsed woman as follows:

> “Hold fast to penance until the end of life, and do not presume that forgiveness will be granted to you by the human day; for the one who wishes to promise you this deceives you. Since you have sinned specifically against the Lord, you ought to await the remedy from him alone on the day of judgment.”

Let it be granted that this lapsed virgin ought to perform penance until the end of life, according to the discipline discussed in the preceding chapter. What, then, is meant by her not presuming that forgiveness should be granted to her by the human day—that is, that she could not hope for help from the Church’s keys or absolution from sins, and that anyone who wished to promise her this would deceive her—because, since she had sinned specifically against the Lord, she ought to await the remedy from him alone, and not from any human being, on the day of judgment? 285 Are there, then, according to Nicetas, certain sins not subject to the Church’s keys, as the Montanists and Novatians taught, and therefore reserved to God’s judgment alone even after penance had been given and performed until the end of life?

Theologians and scholars alike have perceived this difficulty in Nicetas’s words. If desired, one may consult Natalis Alexander, *Ecclesiastical History*, century III, dissertation 22, near the end, as well as the Benedictine editors of Ambrose’s works in their admonition concerning this book *To the Lapsed*. Bellarmine and Possevinus, especially, considered this difficulty so serious that they found in these words a wholly Novatian sentence, which Ambrose attacks in two books *On Penance*, and for this reason they also rejected the attribution of this work to Ambrose.

[Col. 1129B] But, in order to investigate Nicetas’s mind more closely at this point and ascertain it more securely, and also to clear him entirely from every Montanist and Novatian error, we must distinguish doctrine from discipline in a matter of this kind. It is one thing to deny the Church the power to forgive certain grave sins—such as adultery, murder, and apostasy into idolatry—which was the fundamental position of the Montanists and Novatians and in which they chiefly dissented from Catholic doctrine. It is another thing to deny peace and communion to those guilty of certain such crimes even after they have performed penance, according to the institution of the Church, until the end of life. That was the stricter discipline of certain Churches and certain bishops in the early centuries of the Church, including the fifth century, the age of our Nicetas.

Who, then, would say that the words of Nicetas under discussion reflect the condemned doctrine of the Montanists and Novatians rather than the Catholic discipline that was still in force in certain places, even in the age of Nicetas?

[Col. 1129C] Meanwhile, a common distinction is found among the Fathers, based on the sense of Scripture, between sins against God and sins against brothers or human beings, as may be seen in Morinus, *On the Sacrament of Penance*, in several places. There one may also understand how sternly they spoke against those who sinned against God and how much more difficult a forgiveness they always presented to such sinners, so as to arouse in them a greater sense of sorrow for such sins and require greater labors of penance.

Nicetas rightly counted the fall of his virgin among sins against God. In the same book he so often called it adultery against the Lord and a failure to keep faith with the Lord. Moreover, there can be no doubt that, in Nicetas’s judgment, this woman’s sin belonged among the graver sins against God—whether because it plainly bore the marks of a perverse will rather than of human weakness, or because it had resulted in other sins as well, or because she had ultimately been forced, wholly against her will, to disclose the matter, as was said in its proper place in the preceding chapter.

[Col. 1129D] Who, then, should be surprised that Nicetas, following the judgment of canon 13 of the Council of Elvira, which we cited in the preceding chapter when discussing penitential discipline—who, I say, should be surprised that our Nicetas counted this lapsed virgin among those concerning whom the Fathers decreed in these words:

> “It has been decided that communion is not to be given to them even at the end,”

that is, absolution from sins, as learned men understand the word “communion” in that place, and that he therefore told her not to presume that forgiveness would be granted to her by the human day, since, having sinned specifically against the Lord, she ought to await the remedy from him alone?

Should we say that the Fathers of Elvira were infected with the error of the Montanists or Novatians because they deprived virgins who had fallen through perverse will rather than weakness of communion—that is, absolution—even at the end of life? Certainly not. That they did not decree this because they recognized no power in the Church to release such sins is sufficiently shown by the very word they use, “it has been decided.” Their particular intention on this matter therefore emerges: it concerns discipline alone, not doctrine. It is as though they had said: “It has been decided”—that is, it has seemed expedient—that henceforth communion should not be given even at the end to those guilty of such crimes, although otherwise it could have been given by the authority of the Church and had previously been given.

[Col. 1130A] Theologians and scholars have found much material for discussion both here and in other canons of Elvira, where a stricter discipline was established in penitential matters and where communion—that is, absolution—is denied in more than one place to those guilty of certain crimes even at the end of life.

The common opinion, however, is that this was done for no other reason than to deter people more effectively from these graver sins, concerning which they could hope for no indulgence from the Church, and so that in practice there might be no, or almost no, occasion for applying such severity.

Today no trace of this severity remains. Yet it seems that the discipline currently in force developed in part from this ancient severity, whereby the absolution of certain sins, outside the moment of death, was reserved to the supreme pontiff alone, and that of certain others to individual bishops in their own dioceses. Thus some degree of difficulty—greater or lesser—in obtaining forgiveness from the Church might make people more ready to avoid these crimes, and the holiness of the Christian name as a whole might thereby be beneficially safeguarded.

[Col. 1130B] Other stricter points of discipline likewise prevailed in the early centuries and later fell partly or entirely into disuse. Explaining the general rationale of these, Saint Augustine said in Letter 185 to Boniface, no. 45, that “the experience of many diseases compels us to discover many remedies.” Speaking there also about a certain rigor of discipline toward clerics who had performed penance for some crime, he wrote:

> “That it was established in the Church that no one, after penance for any crime, should receive clerical office, return to clerical office, or remain in clerical office was done not from despair of indulgence but from the rigor of discipline. Otherwise an argument would be made against the keys given to the Church, concerning which it was said: ‘Whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven.’”

[Col. 1130C] The rigor of discipline, therefore, which for the common good of the Church moved the Fathers of Elvira to deny communion—that is, absolution—to virgins who had fallen through perverse will even at the end of life, although they did not doubt the power of the Church’s keys: this rigor of discipline, and not adherence to a Novatian or Montanist dogma, also compelled our Nicetas to remove from his lapsed woman the hope of obtaining communion—namely, any forgiveness at all—from the Church, and to reserve her to the mercy of God alone.

This stricter discipline, although approved by the authority of the Fathers of Elvira, was never the common discipline of the Church, as scholars observe, nor did it remain in force for long. Indeed, the abuse of this severity—which would ultimately have harmed discipline—perhaps caused it eventually to fall into disuse, and led the Roman pontiffs in particular, who always favored mercy over severity, to reject it on more than one occasion.

[Col. 1130D] Nevertheless, we gather from the letters of those same Roman pontiffs, who in that century replied to inquiries from bishops on this matter, that it still existed in the fifth century, so that Nicetas could use it with his lapsed woman without censure, since it still had a place in certain regions.

Thus, at the beginning of the fifth century, in the year 403, Saint Pope Innocent I wrote to Exsuperius, bishop of Toulouse, in Letter 6, in Coustant’s *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, column 792 of the Paris edition. Exsuperius had asked him what should be observed concerning those who, after baptism, had devoted themselves throughout their lives to the pleasures of sexual excess and, at the very end of life, requested both penance and restoration to communion. The canons of Elvira in particular seemed to stand against them, as the learned editor observes at this point.

Saint Innocent writes:

> “Concerning these persons, the earlier practice was stricter; the later, with mercy intervening, more lenient. For the earlier custom held [Col. 1131A] that penance should be granted but communion denied. Since in those times persecutions were frequent, communion was rightly denied, lest the ease of its being granted should keep people secure in reconciliation and fail to recall them from falling; penance was granted so that everything might not be entirely denied. The circumstances of the time made the remission stricter. But after our Lord restored peace to his Churches, when terror had now been driven away, it was decided that communion should be given to those departing, both because of the Lord’s mercy, as a viaticum for those about to journey, and lest we should appear to follow the harshness and severity of the heretic Novatians, who deny forgiveness. Therefore communion is to be granted together with final penance, so that such people, even at the end of their lives, may, with the permission of our Savior, be rescued from everlasting destruction.”

Here, in Innocent’s words, are two forms of discipline concerning the same matter: the older and stricter, and the other more lenient. Both are praiseworthy according to the differing circumstances of the time in which each was introduced. The former, although harsh and outwardly similar to Novatianism, was in reality entirely foreign to the positions of the Novatians. [Col. 1131B] Here too is evidence that the stricter practice still existed in certain places in his own time, since Innocent recommends the later, more lenient practice to the inquiring Exsuperius as preferable at that time.

Another letter of the same pontiff to Decentius of Gubbio may also be consulted, Letter 25, concerning the year 416, in the same edition of Coustant, column 862. In chapter 7 he shows him the custom of the Roman Church: namely, that no one should be permitted to depart from this world without communion.

There is also another letter of Pope Celestine I, Letter 4, from the year 428, to the bishops of the provinces of Vienne and Narbonne, in the same work, column 1067, where in chapter 2 he severely rebukes those who deny penance to the dying.

But the letter of Saint Leo the Great, no. 108 in the edition of the Ballerini, addressed to Theodore, bishop of Forum Julii in Gaul, and belonging to the year 452—that is, to the very age of our Nicetas—must be examined. It sheds much light [Col. 1131C] on Nicetas’s own defense concerning the stricter discipline that he follows, namely, the denial of forgiveness in certain grave offenses against God, even after penance has been performed throughout the whole course of life.

Saint Leo says in chapter 4:

> “To those who, in a time of necessity and under the pressure of imminent danger, implore the help of penance and immediately afterward reconciliation, neither satisfaction is to be forbidden nor reconciliation denied. For we can impose neither measures nor time limits upon the mercy of God, with whom true conversion tolerates no delay in forgiveness . . . Therefore, in distributing God’s gifts, we must not be difficult, nor neglect the tears and groans of those who accuse themselves, since we believe that the very disposition to repent has been 288 conceived through God’s inspiration.”

In the following chapter, after noting the carelessness of those Christians who put off conversion to the Lord from day to day and set the time for their satisfaction at the end of life, choosing the narrow confines of that moment in which scarcely any time may be found either for the penitent’s confession or for the priest’s reconciliation, he continues:

> “Yet, as I have said, their necessity must also be assisted in such a way [Col. 1131D] that penance and the grace of communion are not denied to them if, even after losing the power of speech, they request them by signs indicating an unimpaired mind. But if the force of illness has so aggravated their condition that they cannot indicate, in the presence of the priest, what they had shortly before requested, the testimony of the faithful standing around them ought to benefit them, so that they may obtain both the benefit of penance and of reconciliation. Nevertheless, the rule of the ancient canons must be preserved concerning those who have sinned against God by departing from the faith.”

Thus far Saint Leo’s instruction to the bishop of Forum Julii concerning the reconciliation of sinners before they depart from life.

[Col. 1132A] At this point it may be permitted to observe in passing that, from this text of Saint Leo, as also from the earlier text of Saint Pope Innocent I to Exsuperius of Toulouse, when these passages are rightly considered, it is confirmed that the word “communion,” used by the Fathers of Elvira in canon 13 and also elsewhere, and often repeated in the same sense in later ancient times, meant the same as forgiveness and absolution from sins, as was said earlier.

On this subject, if desired, one may consult especially Selvagius, *Institutions of Christian Antiquities*, book III, chapter 9, section 4, and chapter 11, sections 4 and 5, as well as the distinguished prelate John Devoti, *Canonical Institutions*, book II, title 2, section 4, *On Penance*, § 87.

Returning now to St. Leo and to the purpose of the authority cited from him on behalf of our Nicetas: the matter here is not, strictly speaking, identical with Nicetas’s case, as is clear; nevertheless, the disciplinary principle is the same—namely, whether pardon is to be granted or denied to sinners at the point of death when they simultaneously request penance and pardon, as the bishop of Fréjus had consulted the Roman pontiff. Here there is expressly mention of penance, and at the same time of reconciliation to be granted immediately after penance has been administered at the end of life. Thus it should never happen that penance is then given but reconciliation and pardon nevertheless denied, so that the sinner must await a remedy from [Col. 1132B] God alone—except only in the case of those who sinned against God by abandoning the faith; with regard to them alone, it is said that the rule of the ancient canons must be observed, namely, a more rigorous procedure prescribed by the ancient canons, discussed above by Innocent. This was perhaps the very rule that Nicetas observed in the case of his fallen woman, according to those canons, as we have said. We possess it in the first and second canons of the aforementioned Council of Elvira, and also in the final, twenty-second canon of the First Council of Arles in 314: namely, that such apostates should not receive Communion even at the end of life, as may be seen in Labbe’s *Councils*, edited by Coleti, vol. I, cols. 992 and 1453.

Let us therefore conclude that the words of our Nicetas addressed *To the Fallen Woman*, chapter 8, no. 38, do not in the least savor of Montanism or Novatianism, but merely display a certain rigorous discipline. This discipline had formerly been introduced for just reasons, in the case of more serious offenses against God, in certain Churches; it enjoyed the authority of venerable Councils, as well as [Col. 1132C] the practice of bishops of no inferior rank throughout the world; it still prevailed in Nicetas’s own time, especially in Gaul; and, according to the judgment of St. Leo, it was still to be retained in the case of apostates who sinned against God by abandoning the faith, even if no longer in the case of all the crimes contemplated by the ancient canons, nor perhaps in the particular case of a fallen consecrated virgin, which was Nicetas’s case.

What if we were to say that Nicetas may have mentioned that more rigorous ancient discipline in the case of his fallen woman in order both to frighten her further—although she had confessed her sin unwillingly—and to compel her to produce greater fruits of penance, while nevertheless not intending to dismiss her without sacramental reconciliation at least at the end of her life, or even after a suitable period spent with the utmost fervor in the labors of penance? In any event, no difficulty remains in Nicetas’s words under discussion that could in any way appear to undermine his orthodoxy. [Col. 1132D] This was what we had to demonstrate.

As a seventh and final difficulty, one might raise the words of Nicetas that we read in chapter 7 of the *Explanation*. There, while discussing the Holy Spirit, he seems to hold that sins against the Holy Spirit are altogether unforgivable, both in this age and in the age to come, so that they are subject neither to the keys of the Church nor can ever obtain mercy and pardon from God himself. For he says:

> “Whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit has no forgiveness, neither in this age nor in the age to come, as the Lord himself declared.”

But our Nicetas needs no defense here. The very Gospel text that he sets forth defends the statement—indeed, the very words of Christ the Lord, which Nicetas takes from the Gospel into his discourse, adding and subtracting nothing so as to present a harsher judgment according to his own interpretation. Thus our Lord says in Matthew [Col. 1133A] 12:31–32:

> “Therefore I say to you: Every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven people, but blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven. And whoever says a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come.”

John Morinus, in his previously cited *Historical Commentary on the Sacrament of Penance*, book 9, chapter 28, set out, on the basis of many testimonies from the ancient holy Fathers, to prove that most of the ancient Fathers judged a single crime so execrable that they said its perpetrators could never be granted pardon either by the Church or by God; and that this crime was principally the one called in the Gospel the sin against the Holy Spirit. Natalis Alexander, in *Ecclesiastical History*, third century, dissertation 22, shortly before the middle, demonstrated against Morinus that the Fathers in reality acknowledged no sin that could not be forgiven by God and by the Church, however much the wording of some of them may seem on the surface to suggest otherwise. [Col. 1133B] He does this by examining most of the passages from the Fathers cited by Morinus himself, adding what Morinus more than once omitted, and comparing and explaining obscure passages by clearer ones, so that nothing remains to be desired on this matter.

Since our Nicetas says absolutely nothing in the cited passage of his *Explanation* from his own opinion, but merely reports the words of Christ that we have quoted, there is no reason gratuitously to attribute to him a view alien to the common teaching of the other Fathers, as though he wished to teach that sins against the Holy Spirit are altogether unforgivable, both in this age and in the age to come. Nicetas therefore, in accordance with the common mind of the other Fathers, could not have failed to understand that sins against the Holy Spirit are called unforgivable in this age and in the age to come—not because some such sin truly cannot absolutely be forgiven by God and by the Church, nor because it is never in fact pardoned, but because it is forgiven with greater difficulty. Those who sin against the Holy Spirit—whether by voluntarily abandoning, without persecution, the faith once received; [Col. 1133C] by denying the works of God and attributing them exclusively to the powers of nature; or by blaspheming against the Spirit in any other way and failing entirely to acknowledge God’s gifts of grace—all place a greater obstacle in the way of grace in obtaining mercy. They have no excuse for their sin, whether through ignorance or weakness, as other sinners do. Consequently, for the most part, they are abandoned by divine justice to final impenitence; and for this reason they cannot have forgiveness, neither in this age nor in the age to come.

What if Nicetas intended by those words to indicate the Macedonian heretics, who truly blasphemed against the Holy Spirit because they denied his divinity and equality with the Father and the Son? It seems more probable that in this passage, after asserting the divinity of the Holy Spirit and his procession from the Father, and after explaining the works of the Holy Spirit for the sanctification of souls and the attainment of blessed eternity, as is evident in that passage, Nicetas finally wished to arm his hearers against such heretics and against their error, [Col. 1133D] which is direct blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. Through this blasphemy the human creature so excludes the Spirit from itself that, while persevering in this impiety, it is rendered incapable of the disposition toward penance, of heartfelt contrition, and therefore also of the remedy of pardon.

In precisely this way, and in the same age as Nicetas, St. Leo the Great explained the same words of Christ in Sermon 75, *On Pentecost I*, chapter 4:

> “We likewise detest the Macedonians, who, although they ascribe equality to the Father and the Son, nevertheless believe the Holy Spirit to be of an inferior nature. They do not consider that they have fallen into that blasphemy which will not be forgiven either in the present age or in the judgment to come, since the Lord says: ‘Whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come.’ Therefore, the person who remains in this impiety is without pardon, because he excludes from himself the one through whom he could have confessed; [Col. 1134A] and he will never reach the remedy of pardon who does not have an advocate to plead for him. For from him comes the invocation of the Father; from him come the tears of penitents; from him come the groans of those who implore; and no one can say, ‘Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:4).

Thus far the holy pontiff. There is therefore no reason to suspect that our Nicetas departed from the common judgment of the Fathers and of the Church when, on the authority of Christ the Lord, he asserted that sin or blasphemy against the Holy Spirit has no forgiveness, neither in this age nor in the age to come.

Here, then, let this be the end of our dissertation on St. Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia. At first sight, as we anticipated in the preface, someone may criticize its length, especially in the case of an author whose surviving works, now published together for the first time, amount to only a few pages. We too willingly admit its length, although when we first applied our hand to the task we had not foreseen it at all. Yet, in any event, no one will readily judge that the labor was entirely wasted in elucidating a [Col. 1134B] fifth-century Father of the Church who is not yet sufficiently known.

Would that our work suffered from this one fault alone. The reader will certainly discover many things worthy of correction; nor are we people who rashly imagine that we have never erred, although we have always intended to guard against error. Since the subject is by its nature barren and has not hitherto been fully treated on either side by a more productive pen, we have wandered here and there for the sake of pleasantness, and sometimes discoursed at greater length than might have been fitting. Nevertheless, we think that even the lines we have extended in various directions ultimately return, as they say, to the center. In this course of exposition, to have stumbled occasionally would in some measure have been no disgrace to our weakness.

We are confident that we have accomplished the principal aim of the work: namely, to demonstrate—especially against the opinion of the most distinguished Joannes Prosdocimus Zabeo, whom, also at the conclusion of this writing, we wish to name in his honor—that the Niceas [Col. 1134C] or Nicetas whom Gennadius and later writers call bishop of Romatiana, and whom they identify as the author of the recently discovered *Explanation of the Creed addressed to the Competentes*, as well as of the long-known little work *To the Fallen Virgin* and other similar brief works listed by Gennadius, whether lost or still hidden, is not Niceas or Nicetas the Dacian, the friend of St. Paulinus of Nola and celebrated by him in his praises. Rather, he is in reality our Niceas or Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, who flourished in the time of St. Leo the Great and to whom the celebrated letter of that holy pontiff is extant.

The difficulties opposed to this judgment had to be resolved—both those produced by the same distinguished man in his dissertation and those produced by the most learned Michael Denis, recently prefect of the Palatine Library at Vienna, as well as those that might plausibly be produced against the arguments on which our proposition rests. This was done as the matter required, especially by weighing various [Col. 1134D] points of learning and examining certain particular monuments of the Church of Aquileia which, perhaps even after the investigations of distinguished men, did not reject further inquiry.

The person of Nicetas, moreover—his age, homeland, and other matters relating to him that could be investigated—had to be treated here systematically, as did his brief works, both those that survive and those that are missing, together with whatever was worthy of notice in the surviving works and in the fragments of those that are lost, so that nothing would be lacking that bore upon the dignity and importance of the subject. This too we have done, within the limits of our ability, and in such a way that we may easily seem to have erred more through excess of material than through excessive brevity.

Whatever, then, may be the value of what we have labored over thus far, may the reader receive this effort, whatever it is, with an indulgent mind, and know that we are always ready to abandon our own views and pursue better ones.

[Col. 1135]

## APPENDIX

### Two Ancient Documents of the Chapter of Aquileia

One from the twelfth century and the other from the thirteenth, mentioned in the dissertation, chapter 6, part 1, p. 116 (Col. 979).

[Col. 1135A]

### I. From the original document of the archive of the Canons of Aquileia, dated 1183

We, Liuprandus, dean of the Church of Aquileia; Oto, deacon; Joannes, deacon; Hermannus, deacon and treasurer; Gompertus, deacon; Joannes, deacon; Rambaldus, deacon; Otacus, deacon; Mainardus, subdeacon; Artuicus, subdeacon; Rempotus, priest; Petrus, subdeacon; Hermeinardus, subdeacon; Wernerius, priest; Rodulfus, deacon; Megenardus, priest; Eliseus, priest; Leonardus, deacon; Master Aldigerius, acolyte; Thomas, acolyte; Petrus, priest of Udine; and Vodescalcus, subdeacon—all canons of the same Church of Aquileia—together with Bertoldus, vicar of the lord patriarch; Natalis, priest and vicar of the bishop of Concordia; Dominicus, priest and vicar of the bishop of Trieste; and Joannes, priest and vicar of the count, just as we proposed long ago, so now before God and his saints we promise to uphold the justice of the Church of [Col. 1135B] Aquileia and to pursue it before the lord pope against Gabriel, the provost.

He has acted against the privilege establishing common life, drawn up by Vodalricus, patriarch and legate of the Apostolic See, with the consent of the entire chapter, and against the privilege of our blessed father Pope Lucius confirming that same common life, which was sent to us through our messengers. By means of threats from his relatives, while we consented out of fear for our persons, he removed and unjustly retains the administration of the entire common life. Whatever the lord pope may decide concerning this dispute, we wish to receive with complete obedience and devotion.

And I, Liuprandus, priest and dean of Aquileia, declare, etc. [The remainder is omitted.] I, Dominicus, priest and vicar of Wernardus, bishop of Trieste, declare, etc. [The remainder is omitted.] I, Natalis, priest and vicar of the bishop of Concordia, declare, etc. [The remainder is omitted.]

[Col. 1135C]

We, all the canons named above, add the following and testify with one voice that through our mediators we offered the provost annual revenues of twelve marks if he wished to cease and not take away the administration from us. But he replied to us, on the advice of his brothers and of others who now lord it over our [Col. 1136A] peasants and have plundered their property, that he would accept nothing unless we handed over the administration to him.

The provost stripped the peasants by an unlawful exaction beyond what was owed, and did the same to the priests after he had received the administration. Consequently, as many of our peasants themselves said, they would already have fled from our holdings if they did not hope someday to return to our hands and authority. And we give the messengers permission to swear this on our souls.

+ Sign of the above-mentioned canons, who requested that this be done.

Petrus Vener., priest and canon of the Church of Caorle, and notary of the Venetian palace, requested by the dean and the other aforesaid brothers, have written, completed, and authenticated this document just as I heard each of them speak, in the year of the Lord 1183, on the eighth day before the end of October, in the second indiction, at Caorle.

### II. Act of the Chapter of Aquileia, dated 1260

[Col. 1136B]

We, Asquinus, dean, together with the chapter of Aquileia—namely, the venerable bishops Bonacursius of Cittanova and Conradus of Capodistria; Articus de Castelerio; Vuodolricus, dean of Cividale; Vuarnerius de Cucanea; Master Henricus de Pulcinico; Master Valterus; Albericus, cantor; Rozius de Osopio; Bonafides; Rodulfus de Moruzio; Master Villielmus, scholasticus; Conradus de Brazaco; Ricoldus, provost of Concordia; Vuodalricus de Cucanea; Ferrarinus; Leonardus de Feugnaco; Berardus, provost of San Felice; and Hermannus of Udine, canons of Aquileia—establish and firmly promise under oath to observe the indulgence by which the number of canons in the Church of Aquileia was reduced to twenty-four by the venerable father Lord G. patriarch of Aquileia, by authority of the Apostolic See.

We further promise not to act or proceed against it in any way or by any device, by choosing or receiving anyone as a canon or brother, collectively or individually, or by assigning to anyone any prebend, place in the choir and chapter, or stall, to the prejudice of the aforesaid number of canons. Rather, in good faith and to the best of our ability, insofar as we can by right, we shall defend the aforesaid indulgence by which the number of canons was reduced to twenty-four.

If any canon acts against this provision or presumes to attempt it, he shall be suspended from his prebend at Aquileia for one year. For the certainty and lasting stability of this matter, we have caused the present statute to be strengthened by the protection of our hanging seal.

Done in the chapter of Aquileia, in the year of the Lord 1260, on the sixth day of March, in the sixth indiction.

[Col. 1135]

# INDEX OF THE GOSPELS AND EPISTLES EXPOUNDED IN CHRYSOLOGUS

*(From the Cologne edition.)*

Since we understood, most gracious reader, that the learned sermons of St. Peter Chrysologus could be of considerable service to Christian clergy if everything were arranged in the order in which it is to be explained in churches according to ecclesiastical custom, we wished to apply some of our diligence to spare you labor. We have therefore compiled for you this index of all the Gospels and Epistles whose exposition you will find in Chrysologus.

On the holy day of the Nativity of the Lord. Gospel of Luke 2: “A decree went out from Caesar.” Sermon 175.

On the day of St. Stephen the protomartyr. Sermon 154, without the Gospel reading.

On the day of the Holy Innocents. Gospel of Matthew 2: “An angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph.” Sermons 150, 151, 152, 153.

On the day of the Lord’s Circumcision. Sermon 155, without the Gospel reading.

On the Epiphany of the Lord. Gospel of Matthew 2: “When Jesus had been born.” Sermons 156, 157, 158, 159, 160.

Sunday within the octave of the Epiphany. Epistle to the Romans 12: “I appeal to you, brothers, by the mercy of God.” Sermons 108, 109, 110.

Fourth Sunday after the octave of the Epiphany. Gospel of Matthew 8: “When he had entered the boat.” Sermons 20, 21.

Fifth Sunday after the octave of the Epiphany. Gospel of Matthew 13: “The kingdom of heaven is like a man.” Sermons 96, 97.

Sunday in Septuagesima. First Epistle to the Corinthians 9: “Do you not know that those who run in a race.” Sermon 119.

Wednesday, Ash Wednesday. Gospel of Matthew 6: “When you fast, do not become.” Sermons 7, 8, 22, 166. [Col. 1140]

Thursday, at the beginning of the fast. Gospel of Matthew 8: “When he had entered Capernaum.” Sermons 15, 102.

Friday, at the beginning of the fast. Gospel of Matthew 6: “Take care not to practice your righteousness.” Sermon 9.

First Sunday in Lent. Gospel of Matthew 4: “Then Jesus was led.” Sermons 11, 12, 13.

Monday after the First Sunday. On Psalm 40. Sermon 14.

Wednesday after the First Sunday. Gospel of Matthew 12: “Then certain people answered him.” Sermon 37.

Thursday after the First Sunday. Gospel of Matthew 15: “Jesus went out and came into the region.” Sermon 100.

Thursday after the Second Sunday of Lent. Gospel of Luke 16: “There was a certain rich man.” Sermons 60, 121, 122, 123, 124.

Saturday after the Second Sunday of Lent. Gospel of Luke 15: “A certain man had two sons.” Sermons 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.

Tuesday after the Third Sunday of Lent. Gospel of Matthew 18: “If your brother sins against you.” Sermon 139.

Wednesday after the Third Sunday of Lent. Gospel of Matthew 15: “Then they approached him.” Sermon 171.

Thursday after the Third Sunday. Gospel of Luke 4: “Jesus rose from the synagogue.” Sermon 18.

Tuesday after the Fourth Sunday. Gospel of Luke 7: “Jesus went to a city called.” Sermon 103.

# VERY FULL INDEX OF NOTABLE SUBJECTS AND WORDS IN THE SERMONS OF ST. PETER CHRYSOLOGUS

The number indicates the sermon; where it is omitted, understand the number of the immediately preceding entry.

[Note: In this index, Arabic numbers refer to sermon numbers.]

### A
## A

Aaron, the first high priest under the Law, was the origin of the priesthood, 89. The sons of Aaron are punished, 109.

Habakkuk. Why he was terrified, at length, 68.

Abel, carrying a lamb to God’s sacrifice, just as the Lamb is taken up, 109. His voice, poured out in his own blood, sounds all the more loudly, 174.

Abraham. In his son the priest was slaughtering himself, and the sacrifice, 10. His beloved was the victim. Prince of the heavenly banquet because of his humanity, 42. Obedient to God the Father, 55. His praises, 66. He receives God and His favors, 69. After Isaac was weaned, he prepares a feast, 73. Though decrepit, he begets Isaac, 90. He was offering himself in his son, 108. He condemns the rich banqueter, 121. Innocent and rich, 121. A stranger and guest who helps strangers, 8. He receives God as a guest. He is a steward in glory. His table is prepared for the needy. He does not pity the banqueter, 122. He calls the banqueter “son,” 123. He saw God in human form, 131. He dies, but not forever. He saw the day of Christ’s birth, 17. Dead in body, he lives in spirit. From what he should not fear but love God, 147. His name is changed, 154. The hand of the poor man is Abraham’s bosom, 8. Offering his son, he binds him, 10. He accepts faith, 14.

Departure. It is spoken of both mind and place, 1. What evils departure from the father produces, 2. Let him who has withdrawn from his father return confidently to him, 3. The son departed from his father rich, and returned without shoes, 3.

[Col. 1142]

To conceal virtues is good, 7. To place one’s resources in the bosom of the poor is beneficial. To conceal one’s possessions and not distribute what has been received is a crime, 123. Why Jesus hides Himself from the Jews, 131.

The absence of the body does no harm where hearts have been joined through faith, 32.

Absolution of sins is granted through love, 94. In the underworld it is granted by Christ to the just, not to the unjust, 123.

Abstinence is the first medicine of human beings, if it is accompanied by almsgiving, 41. It heals what greed has wounded. What one should do when entering upon the way of abstinence, 8.

We must draw sinners away from sins, if we do not wish to sin, 155.

Abundance exalts one into impiety, 124.

To receive. We receive what we did not previously possess, 144.

To acquiesce in adversity is a matter of necessity; to will it is a matter of virtue, 110.

To accuse. Blessed is the one who accuses himself before God even of offenses of which he is unaware, 123. To accuse the innocent is to commit crimes, 175. One meets the convicted man as though he alone were accused by the gods, 125.

What are the actions of the members in the mystical body? 120.

Adam was preserved in paradise by fasting and expelled by gluttony, 12. He is clothed from the shearing of Christ the Lamb, 23. He was granted a homeland by Christ, 49. Zacchaeus is ordered to descend from the Adamic tree, 54. He was put to sleep so that a woman might be taken from the man, 57. The well of death, 63. He fell quickly because he believed quickly, 79. He is led from knowledge to the mustard tree, 99. He was found by Christ at the fig tree, 196.

All are subject to death through Adam’s guilt, 110. Life was lost through his transgression. Adam’s fall, which was the ruin of all, is to be lamented, 111. And how the inheritance of Adam was neither pleasing nor permitted for us to renounce. In Adam all sinned. Death came through Adam, life through Christ. Sin reigned through Adam unto death, 112.

Adam and Christ gave the human race its beginning, 117. The first Adam was made by Christ, the last Adam, and was fashioned by Him as a figure. Formed from clay, he is changed into flesh. A figure of Christ, the first, yet possessing a beginning. Adam is earth; Christ is fruit. The record of Adam’s debt is canceled by Christ, 123. What he did to nature and to his descendants, 156. In Adam is the whole flock of the human race, 168. He received death from the hand of the woman, 18. He was excluded from paradise through envy, 4. Created at perfect age, and how he is recreated, 151.

Adelphus, the bishop, is praised, 39 and 136, throughout.

Help from another is useless apart from God, 46. The one who has an enemy within requires help from another, 171.

“Adolescent” is said of sense and age, 1. It is not years but conduct that makes someone younger, 5.

An empty worshiper is an irreverent one, 103. The exhortation of a good and great man should not be refused, 107. How one may be a worshiper in hell, 13.

When adversities are turned into prosperities, the Lord turns our bed, 14. Let the one who does not pray for prosperity not complain about adversity, 43. In adversity, necessity is not comparable with the will, 110. Adversities do not cast down the strong, 124. Whoever does not experience adversity does not know how to preserve prosperity, 131. Prosperities must not be mixed with adversities, 175. All adversities rely upon their own strength, 7. In adversity a person has Christ as his companion, 70.

Adversity. In the Gospel one is struck down by the sword of adversity, 114.

Flattery is the devil’s fourth and final temptation, 27.

The synagogue was adulterous, 115. The adulterer serves Venus, 155. John rebukes adulterers, 174, where more is said on the subject.

Christ is our advocate, 70. In heaven there should be prayer, fasting, and mercy, 43. The effects of this advocacy. Advocacy for poverty at the judgment, 14. See Patron.

Illness arising from weakness is healed by abstinence and almsgiving, 41. By God’s command it is cured, 49. Why the bent woman’s illness lasted eighteen years, 105. One must not rejoice over illness in such a way that one remains in the wound, 113. A relapse is often fatal. What should be done if it reminds us to render an account, 125. See Infirmity.

The sick person implores healing, not the manner of healing, 33. Why he accepts treatment, 35. The sick person is described as suffering from cholera, 38. His treatment is described from the physician, 2. Let him obey the spiritual physician, 41. Why the physician does not consider his will, 50. Two sick persons cured by one medicine, 94. The sick person, through delirium, does not know that he is insane. Why not all were healed by Christ, 102. He rejects remedies because of weakness, not because of will, 108. Unfortunate if, after treatment, he does not treat his torment, 114. The sick person suffering from fever, and the increase of his fever. He asks for what harms him. Ungrateful to God the physician, 131. One who harms his neighbor is sick with fever and madness, 139. He must not receive an antidote for illnesses apart from medical skill and the proper time, 156. How the medicine of repentance should assist the sick, 167; the one who is cured according to his own choice does not receive health, 173. See Sick.

Egypt receives Christ as He flees, 150. Why He flees there, 151.

Equity without goodness, in the heavenly sense, is cruelty, 145.

The air is disturbed by winds, 34.

Heat is mocked by one who is dressed in artificial nakedness, 122. One who is protected by the shadow of divine power does not feel bodily heat, 142.

Our age is disturbed by passions into falling, 115. He lived, and did not fail, among the saints, 89. The ages of human beings and the vices to which they are subject, 118.

Eternity, eternal. It excludes time, 34. He grieves over eternal evil, 22. Eternal things must be purchased with passing things, 124. The devil does not allow human beings to be eternal, nor even temporal, 131. We must pray that we may be able to believe in eternal goods, 139. Human beings do not want eternal things, 144. How eternal things are signified here.

The Ethiopian. The eunuch seized baptism while passing by, 40. Faith seized him for grace before the chariot reached India, 61.

Affection does not admit falsehood, 55. He violates affection, 173. What befalls the deserter of affection, 1. What proves a despairing affection, 33. He is violated through affection, 173; affection naturally implanted in the flesh is changed by the devil into parricide, 96. See Passions.

Africa has martyrs of the devil, 13.

The human field endured a human master, 106. The eternal field will be in heaven, 139. Why it is purified by fire from the burned thorns, 164.

Struggle. What must be avoided in the earthly struggle so that we may conquer, [Col. 1144] 119. What must be done in the spiritual struggle. What takes place in it; see Contest.

The Lamb of God is shorn so that Adam may be clothed, 23. So that the lambs may be gathered by the shepherd for judgment, 60. At Easter the flesh of lambs is not kept for the following day, 73. Abel carries a lamb to God’s sacrifice, 109. Why the Lamb of God strikes in preaching, 164. Through the Lamb of God envy does not enter heaven, 168. So that those who eat may sacrifice the Lamb of God, 172.

Who is the farmer who, while cultivating the field, abandons himself? 4. The one who cultivates badly causes harm to himself, not to the earth, 7. He rejoices in the fruit over which he weeps in the furrow, 40. Sowing fruit, he hopes, 71. He sings of abundant fruits to lighten the labor of the plow, 118. Industry brings wild things back to cultivation, 132. To extend what belongs to another is to seize more by giving than by stealing, 54. See Almsgiving. To invade what belongs to another and brood over one’s own possessions is criminal, 123. Whoever does not restore what belongs to another will descend to the underworld with the banqueter. How harmful it is to attend to the evils of others, 139.

High. Whoever aims at a high place falls from a high place, 151.

Let the altar of Christ’s body receive almsgiving, 103. Let God’s altar be filled, so that our storehouses may abound.

Ambition is always blind, 152.

Friendship. We are raised to God’s friendship when we despise death for His sake, 101. Money destroys friendship, 126.

Friend. One is regarded as a friend through similarity of conduct, 101. A person becomes God’s friend. See Friendship, Saints, Martyrs, Just.

Love conceals sins, 3. It does not see them. It recognizes even a disobedient son, 4. Love is recognized from gifts, 10. It is proved by sufferings, 14. It conquers all things and performs other works, as at 40. The eye of love looks more sharply and feels more vividly toward the one who is loved, 78. It possesses the good, 80. How the contract of love exists between debtor and creditor, 88. No one loves unwillingly, 135. The one who fears greatly cannot love, 147. Through it the world is recalled. The law of love does not consider what will be, where more is said about the nature of love. Unless love reaches what is desired, it kills the lover. One cannot fail to see what one loves. Love must be embraced, 53. Through love the son is drawn toward the rigor of discipline, 108.

The love of God. It is a burden, and removes the burden of sins, 3. Toward us, 23. It brings back the one whom judgment had rejected, 48. It is recognized from the generations of animals, 55. How it reduced a man to a little child, 62. Everything between God the Father and the Son is carried out through love, 65. It is not grasped by human beings, 69. God’s love remits every debt to a human being, 94. God wishes to be loved more than feared, 108. What our love toward God should be, 147. Those who love God began to desire to see God. The one who desires to see God possesses devotion. One born for the love of God cannot fear, 160. God’s love for the human race through reproof and tenderness, 163. How it is displayed toward human beings in various ways, 170.

Andrew the apostle has sufficient glory in the prerogative of apostleship and martyrdom, 122. He is born on the mountain for Christ, 133. He is praised throughout, 133.

An angel sinned through envy, 4. He is given for our defense, 13. Sinning before God, he is changed into the devil, 26. The counsel of impiety led the angel to the underworld, 44. At the consummation of the age the angels will obey the saints, 47. An angel converses with Tartarus, 65. He keeps watch for us, 69. He does not know labor or weariness, 75. He both flatters and terrifies. He does not know from where he should speak with God, 86. There is nothing sinister in angels, 87. At the judgment there will be fear for the flesh, 88.

He drives fear from Zechariah, 4. Why he answers him concerning the obtaining of a son alone. He points out Christ. The angel on earth. See John the Baptist.

God is unseen by the angels, 90. He speaks of John’s virtues, 91. The ruler of the synagogue obtains a postponement, 106. We are watched by angels while contending, 119. The just surpasses angels by merit, 120. Angels carry the poor man to burial, 121 and 124. The heights are assigned above to the angels, 123. They ministered to Christ, 125. They grieve over public sin. Their substance and image are different from God’s, 131.

The angel to the Virgin Mary, 140. He is called a measurer, and other matters concerning him. The mystery of the incarnation is invisible to the angels, 141. He speaks to Mary, 142. He marvels, and why. With fear he dispels the Virgin’s fear. Virginity is akin to the angels, 143. To acquire angelic glory is greater than to possess it. The angel explains doubts to us, 145. He speaks to Joseph.

The angels cast down in heaven by the divine splendor, 147. They are driven to earth by excessive fear. The angel was among the first to envy the human being, 148. He preferred to be changed into a devil rather than see a human being filled with glory. Why the angel comes to Mary. They announce joy at the Savior’s arrival, 149. While they rejoice, the demons are in confusion. When the angels are disturbed by flying dust, 150. They announce the Lord who has been born to the shepherds, 149. They rejoice with Christ over the return of the Lord’s sheep; and, when indignant, do not consider themselves rulers, 168. One becomes a devil because of scandal, 27.

The angel of the resurrection. He sits upon the stone at the tomb as a teacher of the resurrection, 74. His glory reflects the splendor of our resurrection, [Col. 1145] 75. Why he rolls away the stone, 75. He sits in order to teach her. Why he has the appearance of lightning and white clothing. After the tomb he recognizes the Lord, 76. He sends the Church, represented by two women, to the bridegroom. He rolls away the stone for the sake of our faith, 77, and against the faithlessness of the Pharisees. Some reasons why he sits upon the stone. He never departs from Christ’s tomb. Clothed, he represents our form in the resurrection. Why he calls the women to see the tomb, 80. He confesses as Lord the one who was crucified. Why he sits in the monument, 82.

The troubles of one’s neighbors must be relieved so that we may be freed from our own troubles, 103.

The soul. The salvation of souls must be sought even for one’s own benefit, 10. To the end, the hunger of Christ is the salvation of souls, 11. Something must be given to the soul, 12. It lies in the body as in a bed of pain, 14. It is described as dead without Christ, 19. It must not be brought down from the heights of heaven into a tomb of gold, 22. Why it should be offered to God with fasting, 43. How it is disturbed while standing between vices and virtues, 45. Abandoned by virtues, it lies in the beds of vices, 1. It should recite the creed, 62. Long before, it called upon the God whom it did not know. At the time of Christ’s Passion souls announced the resurrection of the dead, 78. It passes through walls, 81. The migrations of souls are rejected, 88. The soul is from heaven; it rules the body, gives it life, and is everlasting and immortal, 109. By what bodily torments it is weighed down. It is God’s sacrifice. It did not leave Tartarus before Christ’s resurrection, 123. The saints lose their soul here so that they may find it in heaven, 128. The soul’s nourishment must be moderated, 166. Souls drawn by Christ from the pit of sin to the glory of His triumph, 170. It is renewed by Christ’s baptism, 181. It mortifies the body when it departs from it, 8. Desiring to return to heaven, it is pressed down by the earth of the body, 14. How it may be harmed by banqueters, 91. It has an ark and a library, 58. When the soul rules, the body serves, 102.

Two animals in the manger: how they signify Jew and Gentile, 159. Let them approach the Lord’s manger for the food of life. But let them receive it whole.

Let the mind persevere in the heavenly watchtower, 12. The mind occupied with small things loses great ones, 22. It is disturbed by divided thought, 88. The minds of hearers must not be kept in suspense for long. Suspended by Christ in the discovery of the likeness of the kingdom, 99. Through grace the mind transcends the body’s narrowness and tramples sins underfoot, 116. Once touched by vices, it burns. It leads the grateful to reward and the ungrateful to punishment, 124. Devotion grows from benefits into service, 142. He is servile who seeks foul-smelling things when he could have royal delicacies, 163. In spirit we make our pilgrimage, 5.

Anna sacrifices and rejoices after Samuel is weaned, 73; her tears.

The Lord’s year is completed in its seasons but does not grow old; it runs in a circle so as to lead us to the day of retribution, 73. What are the three years in which Christ sought fruit in the synagogue? 106.

How antidotes against illnesses should be received, 156.

Antichrist will be overthrown by Christ, 156.

The Jews are called “ancient” more because of malice than because of age, 38. And why they were restrained from returning vengeance. The ancients willingly received what was harsh when it came from God, 55. Their dignity, so that it may approach the honor of those now living, 89. To investigate more ancient things is rash, 166.

An old woman, pregnant, is ashamed, hides her childbed, and is exposed to laughter, 92 and 154.

Apollinaris, the first martyr among the bishops of Ravenna, 128. Why he was so called, and other matters concerning him to the end of the sermon.

The apostles offer the nations to God, 18. Why the poor were chosen, 28. Their poverty and spiritual riches are described, 28. From labor they pass to labor. They will rise in glory when killed together with Christ who was killed, 40. Why fishermen were chosen, 47. Why women precede the apostles to the tomb, 75. They are called “children” because of timidity, 78. They would not believe that the body had risen unless they saw the Lord eating. They are recalled to the right side. Like children, they could not draw the net. The apostle who is loved sees the Lord first. Why they drag the fish they have caught by boat. How far they are from land. They are not placed behind the women, but reserved for greater things, and what those things are, 79.

They bring victory to Christ. They are defended for not believing the women concerning the resurrection. They believe it when reported by the disciples. They believe slowly because of the greatness of the mysteries. The women’s announcement of the resurrection does not prejudice them, 80. Whether they were reclining at table or in mourning when the Lord appeared to them, at length, 83. Despairing and without faith. Invited to the world so that they might be hope for all. They are regarded by some as bringing death, by others life, 89.

The synagogue must be dug up with the apostolic plow for fruit, 106. They are the salt of the earth, 120. John’s voice was the voice of the apostles, 127. For what they were chosen by Christ, 151. From Him they receive the power of healings, 161. Recalled by example to humility. They were thought useful to themselves, but appear useless. Why they leave the Lord. How long they ministered to Him while He reclined. [Col. 1146] Warned about future blessedness. Why they were drenched with a rain of fire, 164. They are the twelve hours of Christ’s day, 170. Where the twelve are represented.

Cold water increases fever, 114. A cup of water does not quench the traveler’s thirst, 112. Heavenly grace extinguishes the burning of vices, 116. Water is denied by the banqueter to Lazarus, 122.
