He sowed evils among good things for our ruin—and what evils. By fraud he strives to prevent the creature from remaining in its proper state, 96. He sows heresies among the faithful, sin among the saints, quarrels among the peaceful, deceit among the simple, and wickedness among the innocent—why, 96. He labors to seize the righteous, not to possess sinners. Driving a human being toward ruin, he abandons him so that he may perish. He rejoices in our evils, and other things. He does not want to possess the human being but to destroy him—why. While the servants sleep, he sows weeds, 97. He slanders God’s servants so that they receive punishment in place of reward. He counts our loss as his profit. Demons are called predatory, voracious, aerial birds, 98. He plotted against life, 101. He begins with destruction, 104. His description in the bent woman, 105. He complies with evil wills and rules through the vilest servitude. He deceives by craft. He presses human beings down to the earth under the burdens of sins. He rides on the heads of those who walk in offenses. He drives toward worse things those who go to evil by their own purpose. How he honors the servitude rendered to him by a human being, 114. He disturbs human passions toward a fall, 115. He has death as his spouse, 118. Whoever acted against the blessed Apollinaris, 128.

He promises evils, not good things; he wants human beings neither eternal nor temporal, 131. An angel preferred to be changed into the devil rather than see a human being filled with glory, 148. He attacks the woman Eve with deceit. He rages against the firmness of faith and attempts to split concord, 149. He wanted to take the banner of the cross away from us, 150. What he thought about Christ’s virtues after he became human. When the Savior was born, he produced numerous portents—and why, 155. Herod was the devil’s representative, 155. He prowls about to devour, 170. He had lied that he was God. Envy made the devil from an angel, 172. He tasted Christ’s passion in the head of John, thirsting for it, 174. How he is an over-sower [reading uncertain], 96.

The demon’s theft is that we do not enter the church in the morning when we are going to pray, 43.

### Christ and the human being toward the devil

Whoever joins himself to the devil is one demon, 5. Our good deeds should be unknown to the devil, 7. Once vices are conquered by him, they have no power, 11. He must be attacked while Christ fights. He is conquered by Christ so that he may yield to Christians, 2. He is caught in his own snare when his first temptations are resisted. Before Christ he loses his arts, 16. Signs are given to the devil for his ruin. He does not prevail over those who are watchful and sober, 12. When we fast, he hungers. God descended so that the devil might be conquered. Christ restrains his boldness, 12. He is exposed through his counsels, 13.

Demons must be guarded against, not feared, 16. They are driven away by Christ’s name alone. Human beings drag them into Christ’s presence. Demons do not yield unless defeated; they do not harm unless commanded. They derive the power to harm from our vices and lose it through our virtues. Christ’s crossing over freed us from the demon, 17. At Christ’s command the demon is tortured and the human being is freed. It suffers evil from the possessed. See *Possessed*, *Demoniac*. It fears the unarmed and flees the armed, 17. Unless God permits it, it cannot prevail even against pigs.

When a human being begins to follow demons, 38. There is no demon that does not yield to Christ, 51. The demon is tortured in the possessed person. The devil is confounded by Christ, 52. He is driven away and bonds are loosed. Let no place be given to the devil, 53. He immediately obeys Christ, lest delay be harmful to him, 65. On earth the devil’s will is done, 70. The Lord, remaining watchful, exposes the demon’s ambushes, 97. How the evils of demons are to be avoided, 98. He can do nothing against the more cautious, 105. When Christ reigns, the devil will perish, 139. He is overcome by Christ in open conflict—why, 151. Whoever plays with the devil will not rejoice with Christ, 155. Those who hasten to reach Christ renounce the devil, 158. The gentle warrior conquers the devil, 170. He is overcome by those whom he once conquered. What he is worth before God, 172. It belongs to divine power to cut down the demon with his own sword, 57. The demon was held captive by the human being from Christ’s advent, 18.

### Speak

Because of religious necessity, we often cannot speak in the order originally intended, 114. The authority of the speaker is emptied by insults, 131. The preacher is afraid to speak lest he harm contemptuous hearers, 137.

### Day

What day it was when Jesus spoke in the evening, 21. A pleasant day, but a clear one more pleasant, 41. The Lord’s Day must be observed by a Christian, 105. The day dies and rises again, 118. The Creator of days is not bound by a day, 131. For our sake Christ assumed day and time. The day is illumined by the martyr’s crown, 135. The true day dawned when the Lord was born, 159. The day of salvation must be recognized, 164. Christ is the eternal day, 170.

### Dignity

Whoever is without the insignia of dignity does not invade dignity, 109. See *House*.

### Gods

The gods of the nations are criminal, 57. They should be unknown to the one who wishes to know God, 61. Captivity in serving many gods had made human beings unable to see the God whom they saw, 62. How they were publicly disgraced on the Kalends of January, 155. Many gods were fashioned by the demon so that the one true God might not be known, 16. The nations served innumerable gods because they did not know the true God, 18.

### Slip away

At God’s command all things slip away, 176.

### Delay

Delay granted to debtors increases the creditor’s favor, 89. Speech is delayed when the time for speaking has passed, 121.

### Love

See *Love*, *Peace*, *Enemy*.

### Flood

The Flood was for the expiation of the world, 69 and 165. From that time the mystery of the Lenten fast is opened—and not beyond it—why.

### Forgive

By God’s command we must forgive the sins committed against us, 139. Otherwise they will not be forgiven us. How they are to be forgiven. One must forgive one’s neighbor, 68. See *The Lord’s Prayer*.

### Learn

The whole of life is short for learning human things; how much more so for learning divine things, 112. So that it may be learned, 101.

### Departure

God’s departure from the soul causes its death, 19.

### Discipline

Harsh discipline is received by immature senses through love, 108. Discipline, the craftsman, comes to the aid of imperfect nature, 132. In Lent, discipline is the square of faith, 11. [Col. 1161]

### Disciples of Christ

The disciples take refuge in Christ during the storm, 20. They awaken Christ. Why they flee to the sleeping one, 21. Why they follow Christ as he returns to his homeland, 49. Their inability to heal the demoniac is attributed to the master, 51. Why they are to drive demons from the nations. Why they do not heal the demoniac, 52. Those wavering about Christ’s resurrection are recalled to faith, 76. They are called children because they were small in faith.

The Lord’s disciples were left in the darkness of the passion, 78. They are called the Lord’s brothers, 80. By faith they raised up the living teacher. The conflict between the disciples’ faith and faithlessness, 81. They were strengthened by the Lord with peace. They were comforted. They believed that Christ had returned from the dead in his soul with only the appearance of flesh. The battles of the disciples’ thoughts. Christ’s words to the disciples, “See my hands and feet,” explained through a golden discourse, 81. They are invited to renew their wounds. They believed more slowly out of love, and because of the greatness of the matter. The punishment of the Lord’s passion had passed to the disciples, at length, 83.

They were sent throughout the world to be a hope for all who had been a cause of despair to themselves. Their delay in believing is a support for us. Terror from the Jews and the crime of Christ’s death had shut up the house and the hearts of the disciples, 84. Struck down when Christ was taken away, but made peaceful when he was restored. Christ offers them inward and eternal peace. They are sent by Christ’s love to endure evils, and even to forgive sins.

A disciple is an injury to his teacher if he does not follow the teacher’s instruction, 94. The disciple’s integrity is the teacher’s praise. The disciples believed that the Lord had been touched only in the body, 100. The disciples’ labor and punishment in learning letters, 101. Christ’s disciples are armed for the destruction of the Synagogue—why and how, 137. Their flight is excused by Christ’s flight into Egypt, 150. Whether it was blameworthy, 133. Blessedness was promised to Christ’s disciples, 161. Why Christ sent them two by two, 170. Why they are forbidden to take anything on the road. How they ate with unwashed hands, 171. A disciple does not obtain knowledge if he insists on being taught according to his own will, 173.

### Discord

Harmonious discord between fire and water, 164. The peacemaking warrior removes the discord of the nations, 170. The devil arouses discord and quarrels during Lent, 13.

### Discernment

The distinction between the faithful and the unfaithful is determined from this, 96. See *Separation*.

### Examine

To examine offenses is to expose them, 3. To examine something is to enlarge it, 115. Severe examination burdens both speaker and hearer, 126.

### Steward

The parable about the steward of faith concerns everyone, 26, throughout. See *Leader*, *Churchmen*, *Master of the Household*, *Poor*, *Servant*. A steward of good things is not a rich man who hoards them, 121.

### Rich

A rich man is rich in punishment, not in wealth, if he is the guardian of gold, 22. He will be confounded in the other age. His heart is either in heaven or on earth. The more he has, the more he owes, 26. How holy rich people possessed riches, 28. The rich man always wishes to give when he turns toward the poor, 39. How the evil rich man is punished, 47. The merciful rich man has as many servants as he has coins, 54. The inhuman man, from being a son of Abraham, becomes a son of Gehenna, 54. The rich man should give to the poor and to God, 66. What he possesses by despising the poor. Concerning him, 104.

The rich man is described as gathering wealth. How he thinks within himself, using himself as adviser. The devil, who was in his heart, is questioned by the rich man. The greedy rich man does not possess forever. Ignorant of present things, he debates future things, 104. By closing his storehouses to the poor, he closes them to himself. Why he is foolish. He loses what he has thought out. Let him be watchful in good work. Let him be rich in mercy so that he may be spiritually rich.

Hell swallows the rich man, 121. He is a steward, not a hoarder, of riches, 121. He is a slave of wealth. An ignoble tomb of pomp. Harder than diamond. The miser is always in need. His conflict with the poor, 124. Let the rich man see the poor, and conversely. What is denied to the poor or scattered for display perishes for the rich man. Christ was a rich man—and how, 125. The rich man who is rich in time will be a beggar forever; the evil rich man. The rich man’s virtue lies in humility, 136. What a rich person serving Christ ought to have by way of bag, bread, and money, 170. See *Avarice*, *Miser*, *Feaster*.

### Divine things

Divine things are contrary to human things, and conversely, 21. Why they are conveyed through human examples, 39. Divine generosity, at length throughout, 39. To know divine things is God’s gift, 76. Likewise to perceive them, 79. When divine things were mingled with human things, 89. What amount of time is sufficient for understanding divine things, 112. The divine meaning is concealed by human words, 139. Divine words must not be weighed in human ways, 146. Divine things come to the aid of good people when human things are lacking, 156. Divine generation knows no witness, 160. Divine benefits given to humanity are natural and supernatural, 161. Why the divine inheritance is given and cannot be divided, 162. The law taught penetration into the secret of the divine meaning, 162. The law taught penetration into the secret of the divine meaning, 168. Those assigned to divine offices and ministries must be purified, 171. Divine service must be preferred to human affections, 19. What is divine must not be received by human hearing, 74. See *Trinity*.

### Divination

Divination must be avoided—why, 18. See *Astrologer*. [Col. 1162]

### Divinity

Divinity neither begins nor receives an end, 57. It receives nothing sinister, 57 and 59. It is neither divided by the Trinity nor confused by unity, 60. There is one Godhead in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, 61. It must not be assessed in a human fashion, 67. The everlasting kinship of divinity and humanity is to be feared, 72. Which is more wondrous: that God is human, or that the human being is God? 72. The Godhead, distinguished in the Trinity, is not confused in unity, 83. It does not know external things. It entered Mary’s womb without damage to virginity, 84. The Godhead is not enclosed by a carnal mind, 131. It is made known through Christ, 151. It does not receive an external lineage, 160. Where the fullness of the Godhead dwells, 6. How the Godhead was thickened through mystery, 84. See *Trinity*, *God*.

### Division

Cain offended God in sacrifice through an evil division, 109. Desire would make Christ the author of division, 162. The division of heavenly goods must not be requested, 162. How three are divided into two and two into three mystically according to Christ’s teaching, 164.

### Riches

What evils riches do, and the desire for them. How they are to be preserved, 23. How they ought to be possessed, 28. What riches did for Matthew the publican. How they may benefit those who look toward heaven, 54. They must be abandoned by the one serving God, 170. They are burdens that weigh one down. When their deceptive allure is driven away, 104. Their end, 121, throughout. Whether they are inherently criminal. Why they produced different effects in Abraham and the rich feaster. In hell, riches perish for the human being, not for the crime, 122. It is the mind, not riches, that leads the ungrateful to punishment, 124. From them comes swelling of the mind, 136. They do not follow
dying, 170. Here we are their prolongers, 125.

**Docere [To teach].** Women ought not to teach, but to learn, 82. How Paul taught, 101. Teaching is labor, 163. A teacher should speak what will benefit everyone, 43. He discusses what has been read so that it may be understood as well as possible, 52. A kindly hearing should be given to the teacher, 76. The teacher receives what the hearer deserves, 86. How he may become an intercessor, 96. He entreats the disciple to wish to know, 101. When he may obscure Sacred Scripture, 112. The teacher of the word of God should ascend into heaven before teaching human beings to penetrate heaven, 120. Let him maintain measured interpretations of Scripture, and why, 125. He is wicked if he does not teach the obedient; he is pious by not teaching the contemptuous, 137. Let Christ be our teacher in making the commandments understood, 163. Let the teacher do what he teaches, 167. See *Concionator* [Preacher], *Scriptura sacra* [Sacred Scripture], *Evangelium* [Gospel], *Magister* [Teacher].

**Doctrina [Teaching].** Christian teaching must first be learned word for word, so that afterward its mysteries may be understood, 56. Why Christ’s teaching becomes obscure through its mysteries, 96. In teaching the uneducated, let it be varied, 106. How it should be explained in various ways, 112. Its order must be regulated, so that one matter is not impeded by another, 114. The Gospel is beneficially presented in a threefold order of discourse, 115. Heavenly teaching, drawn out in various ways, more sweetly discloses the sacrament of ecclesiastical knowledge, 116. Let it be received in measured form from the meanings of Scripture, 125 and 126. Heavenly teaching corrupted by the scribes, 158. Familiar teaching handed down by Christ, 161. It is the daughter of humility. The teaching of faith is more useful through simplicity, 166. In sayings, teaching is knowledge; in deeds, virtue, 167. See *Verbum Dei* [Word of God], *Concio* [Sermon], *Scriptura sacra* [Sacred Scripture], *Evangelium* [Gospel].

**Dolor [Sorrow].** Sorrow compensates for and erases sins, 30. The force of sorrow in severe illnesses often gives counsel, 35. Sorrow recalls what flatteries have driven away, 64. It is sorrow to lose heaven, etc., 101. It is a greater sorrow to have lost what one possessed than not to have possessed it, 123. Sorrow advances one toward virtue, 124. At times it recalls the speaker from the sequence of the election. When sorrow compels us to give an account, what must be done, 125. What things caused our author sorrow, 175. Sorrow is superhuman when it is on account of God, 57. See *Afflictio* [Affliction], *Moeror* [Grief].

**Dolus [Deceit].** Deceit pollutes the lips, 62. Deceitfulness rages that it has been deceived, 152.

**Dominari [To rule].** He rules over everyone who is not held captive by his own possessions, 22. Let the Christian rule over the elements, 113. Everlasting dominion arising from servitude to Christ, 114. True dominion is service to the Lord’s holiness, 115. The Father and the Son have one dominion for us, 61. See *Praesidere* [To preside].

**Dominus [Lord/Master].** When the Lord is killed at home through the crime of his servants, punishment extends to the whole household, 78. Manumitting servants, 96. The earthly master demands attentive service, 109. Here each person should recognize himself not as master, but as steward, 125. He is above the servant, 137. Let him withdraw the servant from sins, so that he himself may not sin, 155. Traps are prepared by a rebellious servant for the Lord at his birth, 158. The Lord dining and the servant ministering are described, 161. Whatever he does concerning the servant is justice. From the service rendered to him, let him understand how he ought to serve God. He supplies faithful servants with their proper food, 163. He is our God. One must inquire not why, but what the Lord wishes to be done, 166. The servant’s property belongs to the master, 15.

**Domus [House].** A large house cannot contain two brothers because of envy, 4. Let the sons dwell in their father’s house, where there are many good things, 1. Why and when the Lord of heaven enters an earthly house, at length, 18, throughout. Let Christ enter our house, 54. From the furnishings of a dwelling the dignity of the guest becomes known, 92. Elizabeth’s house, mystically: how it is restored. An outsider does not break through the barriers of the house, 93. One’s own house is more pleasing after a period of time, 114. By what payment satisfaction was made to God for the dwelling of Mary’s womb, 140. No one reaches it except by the way, 142. The house of the world touched for the sake of humankind, 148. He who experiences another’s house knows what his own house is, 151. Its adornment invites its author to dwell there, 171. The inner rooms of the house are said to dance and rejoice, 175. Why the prophet is without honor in his own house, 48. See *Habitaculum* [Dwelling], *Hospitium* [Lodging].

**Donatio [Gift].** Christ’s gift is perpetual, 125. Let each person be content with the gift of the generous God, 120. Nor should he wish to seize another’s gift. See *Munera* [Gifts].

**Dormire [To sleep].** A person is sleeping when he does evil, 22. He sleeps deeply who is not awakened to the sound of the heavenly wedding. The sinner is said to sleep, 34. What those sleeping deeply throughout the whole night lose, 39. Bodily images commonly appear to those who are sleeping, 81. To rush upon sleepers is a sign of weakness, 97. When the servants were sleeping, the Lord was keeping watch—when? The lost and found drachma is described, 169. Many questions concerning it are resolved.

Doubts must be firmly established, 112. In doubtful matters, judgment must be avoided and the matter entrusted to God, 145.

**Dubitans [The doubter].** He is reproved concerning the divine promises, 163. Why he is sent to the raven. An invective against him. He is assigned to the fires of death and of Gehenna, and why.

**Duodenarius [The number twelve].** The number of the Apostles, through the fourfold grouping, forms a threefold four-horse chariot, and for what purpose, 170. The twelve patriarchs, distinguished into twelve tribes, are another figure of the apostolic number, 170.

**Dux [Leader].** What account a military commander must render to God, 26. Leader of the vices. See *Mercenarius* [Mercenary].

## E

**Drunkenness.** Drunkenness weakens the bodily powers, 12. Our drinking is spread into drunkenness by the demon, 12. Drunkenness plunged the world into ruin and caused other evils. The devil threatens the drunken, 13. Drunkenness is sacrilege in a priest, 26. What drunkenness is and its effects, 26. It drowns the body, 41. It comes from wine, and the Holy Spirit is not in it, 88. It makes people children of the night, 104. It is recognized through wine, 116. The drunkard accuses the wine. The fires of drunkenness in the glutton, 124. The sober drunkenness of the Lord’s cup wipes away the lamentations of sinners, 137. Earthly drunkenness is disgraceful, heavenly drunkenness beautiful. What divine love has accomplished, 147. The drunken mind judges badly, 173.

**Church.** The Church prays for the giver of alms, 14. When Christ entered the ship of the Church, the sea of the world was thrown into turmoil, 20. It is calmed. The Church’s tranquility. The storm. The bride of Christ, and how she is an adorned bridal chamber, 22. When the Church was betrothed to Christ, 31. She is represented in the woman with the flow of blood, 35. While Christ was going toward the synagogue, the Church was pouring out human blood, 36. How the Church approached Christ from behind. What kind of garment she touched. While Christ attends to the Church, the synagogue dies. We ought to enter the church in the morning to pray, 43. And why this is not done. So that the Church may be made from the temples of idols, 51. The Church is directed toward God, 57. Joined to Christ, 58. The glory of Christ, 59. Sharing in Christ’s divinity, 60. The perpetual bride of Christ, 61. She is in Christ, and Christ in her, 62. If she gives birth, it is a heavenly mystery, 67. How much glory she gives the Son in the very act of birth, 68. The virgin mother gives birth to us as blessed, and how, 72. Her figures. She weans her children at Easter, 73. How her children of different ages are nourished. She urges us to repentance. In the Church the Sabbath shines forth on the Lord’s Day, 75. The two Marys bear the type of the Churches to the Lord’s tomb, 75. The Church, coming from two peoples, is one. Why the bride is greeted by Christ, 76. Brought back by Christ to the station of the faith of her faith, 78. She speaks represented in a woman, 82. The one Church represented in two women and two disciples. She has Christ’s body to eat, 95. Represented in the sinful Magdalene, 95. She weeps because she did not see Christ as he was departing, 95. At the judgment Christ returns to the Church, rebuking the synagogue. She always receives those who return, 98. The bride and the garden; in her the mustard seed is sown, 98. She receives leaven from the Lord, 99. The Church’s tears will obtain the resurrection of the dead, 103. Represented in the bent woman, 105. The Church heals through the laying on of hands. So that she may bear children for Christ, 117. How her intercession freed souls from the lower places, 123. What she obtained from Christ for Apollinaris, 128. She rejoiced at Chrysologus’s consecration, and why and how, 130. Her assembly must not be despised, 132. Let everyone remain in her, so that he may be something. What evils result from seeking life outside the Church. Enlightened by the sevenfold incense (*heptalismus*) of Saint Felicitas, 134. The Church as bride represented in the virgin Mary, 146. The peace of the Church and the anger of heretics, at length, 149. Her figure, in that she was to be preferred to the synagogue, [Col. 1164] 151. From Christ’s flight she has innocent martyrs, 153. She has tables on which the apostles prepared the Lord’s supper, 161. The Church and Christ are divided by heretics and are united in one Spirit by the synagogue, 144. The Church is the daughter of the synagogue and its daughter-in-law. From Christ’s resurrection she is wholly in his marriage. Why the Cornelian Church was dear to Chrysologus, 165. The Church was the woman of the drachmas, and how, 169. She is the burning lamp by which we find Christ. At the beginning of her birth the Church made a journey, 175. How the Church of Vicohaventina joyfully gave birth to Bishop Marcellinus, 175. By giving birth she wins the crown of virginity all the more. In her the Jew sees the light of faith through the freedom of grace, 176. Before ecclesiastical administration, hands must be cleansed of blood, 18. **Church of Ravenna.** See *Ravenn.*, *Temple*, *Festival*.

**Ecclesiastics.** They are bound to dispense the word of God and heavenly teaching, 26. What danger those who sin from the beginning in matters concerning heaven incur, 26. Sinners derive their crime from the very source from which others obtain pardon. They touch Christ’s body, yet are not healed because they lack faith, 33. See *Preacher*, *Christian*, *Priest*, *Reading*.

**Edict.** By the emperor’s edict, and with the pagan obeying the edict, the Lord comes forward, 175.

**Almsgiving.** Let it accompany fasting, and let great benefits result from it, 8, throughout. It obtains divine mercy. It has been proclaimed as hostile, etc., 9. It is sold, not given. It must be practiced everywhere, provided that it is known not to the earth but to God. Let it be secret, out of regard for the poor person’s modesty. In almsgiving, let the right hand not know what the left is doing, and how. The devil discourages almsgiving during Lent, 13. A full treatment of it occurs in sermon 14. Almsgiving is the first subject treated in heaven, 14. It makes one blessed. It is a remedy against the evils of the world. The whole Church prays for the giver of alms. Almsgiving makes rich, and how, 22. It safeguards our possessions. God stores it up for us, 22 and 23. Let a poor person gladly place almsgiving in heaven, 25. What is distributed is stored up. It heals the withered hand, 32. What virtues and benefits almsgiving together with fasting brings, at length, 41. Let it always be joined with prayer and fasting. Where its effects are discussed, at length. How the giver of alms may believe that he will live after death, 54. What is done from all or from part of one’s possessions. It is harmful to the giver when it is made from fraud or from another person’s goods, 54. God seeks almsgiving only from what you possess, 103. How it benefits us. Whoever does not give alms from his own possessions is guilty, 123. We must give what is ours and avoid what belongs to others. Almsgiving should be practiced by one who cannot fast, and why, 166. It should be practiced during birthday celebrations, 127. It pleads for offenses, 107.

**Elements.** When the elements of sinners will come to an end, 47. The elements of the world are destined to perish, 101. They continually proclaim the resurrection of human beings, 118. They served Christ, 125. God is the author of the elements, 160. The whirlwinds of the winds throw the elements into confusion, 41.

**Elijah.** What he accomplished through the aid of prayer, fasting, and almsgiving, 43. A heavenly chariot carried him to heaven, 92. His tongue is the key of heaven, 127. As though guilty, he fled from the face of a woman. He met Christ on the mountain in order to see the one who had been promised, 131. He hungers for the widow’s food, so that he may be filled, 136. Out of fear he sought death, which he had earlier fled, 147. For his hiding place, the house of a single widow is sufficient, 150. He consumes those sent against him with heavenly fire, 151. He was raised to heaven by Lenten fasting, 166, 12. Why the fiery chariot does not harm him, 166.

**Elizabeth.** Why a barren and aged woman gives birth, 87. Her barrenness is opened at the hour of the incense. Her praises, 89. She is called the daughter of Aaron, and why. In her the nobility of the priestly lineage is preserved, 91. Both are righteous. This is explained in various ways. Barren in body, fruitful in virtues, 91. Why her childbirth was most fittingly delayed. She conceives. Her virtues and those of Zechariah are recounted for the glory of John, 91. How she is prepared for conception, 92. She attributes everything to the Lord and conceals herself. She is silent out of modesty. From her silence a voice arises. Why Mary is sent to her, 142. See *Zechariah*, *John the Baptist*.

**Eloquence.** The pleasure of eloquence must be laid aside when strength of knowledge is demanded, 18. Secular eloquence discovered superstition, and lost natural substance and the knowledge of God, 5. To reveal an unskilled utterance is preferable to refusing a dutiful speech, 107.

**Buying.** We are accustomed to preserve what we buy, not to lose it, 80. The human being was bought by God, 161.

**Epiphany.** It is called *Epiphany* because the divinity of Christ shone forth in it in a threefold manner, 157. In it the Magi confess God through their gifts. In it Christ changed water into wine at the wedding. He is also baptized in the Jordan, and why. It is one solemnity of the threefold manifestation of Christ. It reveals in many ways God made human, and why, 160. It reveals him in three ways. See *Magi*.

**Bishop.** When Chrysologus is consecrated, he delivers this sermon in order, 130. In it he also describes the bishop’s office, [Col. 1165] and virtues. Read the whole sermon. The bishop says that his subjects are his life, salvation, and glory, and that he must teach them what he knows, 147. How the bishop is the bridegroom and the son of his Church, both bride and mother, 175. Bishop Zacchaeus, 54. Cornelius, Projectus, Marcellinus. See their respective entries.

**Letter.** Sweet until the one who sent it comes, 62.

**The devil’s feasts.** What they are, 12. Are feasts in themselves to be condemned? 121. The feasts of the rich man and the poor man, 124. Let Christ be present at our feasts, 127. The feasts of the saints are not solemnized in banquets, 129. Feasts are given to the laborer to lighten his work, 170. The bloody feasts of Herod’s banquet, 174. See *Banquet*, *Drunkenness*, *Supper*. *Drink*.

**The rich banqueter.** His astonishing reversals with Lazarus, 66. He looks up at Lazarus in vain. He is pierced by his punishment. Why he cries out. He seeks the mercy that he had denied, 66 and 124. He received good things from God in exchange for evil things, 66. But now evil things in exchange for good. A fool, thinking that he can change his place in the underworld. He was tormented by Lazarus’s happiness. In vain he asked that someone be sent to his own people. Abraham is called his own, not his father. In the rich banqueter we all ask, “Oh, if only someone would come from the dead”; but that would be in vain. The rich banqueter is swallowed up by hell, 121. His death and life are overcome by the life and death of Lazarus. The funerals of the rich man and Lazarus are described. His guilt. Why riches made him guilty. A captive of riches. God cast the poor man’s furnace into his iron entrails. He disdains hearing the poor man’s voice. The dogs are kinder than the banqueter, and other descriptions of him. He raises his eyes upward, but against himself, 122. He calls Abraham “father,” but in vain, 4. The dispute between him and Lazarus, differing in place and position. Why he cannot obtain mercy from Abraham. Still cruel toward Lazarus, and why, 4 and 123. He envies Lazarus, 122. Why Lazarus is not sent to his couch. By what flame he would be tormented. He had not been condemned at the final judgment. The tongue that insulted the poor man burns more fiercely, for it had enjoyed taste here. His temporal goods perished, but not as a crime. A drop and a crumb would have made him merciful. He denied Lazarus water from his own well. Why he has his hands bound so that he cannot take water. He was cruel toward Lazarus, and more cruel toward himself, 123. Why he is called a son by Abraham. Guilty because he received good things. He believed that God was his debtor. Impious because he was not pious toward another. Unworthy, he received good things in exchange for evil. He calls the father whom he lost; in his punishment he lies. Lazarus would not have been sufficient for the benefit of his brothers. These brothers represent the Hebrews. A descriptive contrast between the rich man and Lazarus, 124. He received the burial of his soul before that of his body. He lives forever in punishment. His reversal with Lazarus. Foolishly he asks the father for the mercy which he had denied to his brother. Why he asks that Lazarus be sent. He thinks that a drop can extinguish the fire of hell, although he did not extinguish the fires of drunkenness with many wines.

**Desert.** What the cultivators of the desert learn when they see Bishop Peter, 107. Deserts are called desolate, 13.

**To err.** Whoever has decided to err always hears what he wants, not what is true, 131.

**Error.** Through Christ, the material of error becomes an occasion of salvation, 157. God comes to the aid of error through a judgment of mercy, using examples.

**The hungry.** The hungry commit more sins, 2. To feel hunger and overcome it belongs to human labor; not to have hunger belongs to divine power, 11. The devil tempts the hungry.

**Eucharist.** It must be received with humility and fear, 15. Why receiving it daily does not heal us from sins, 33. How it provides medicine for sins, 34. Received unworthily, it inflicts a wound. Here we receive a taste of it, and in the homeland fullness, for it is a foretaste of the blessed table and a viaticum, 68. Here it is received on the altar, and through it one lives in eternity, 70. It is the strength of body and mind. How the Eucharistic bread was made, 71. And its effects. It is called “daily bread” because it is continual, 72. It is the bread of perfect blessedness. If Christ gave himself here to be eaten, what will he do in glory? 95. It is a viaticum. It is a royal banquet. It is given in the Church for salvation. How Christ’s flesh is eaten is known by the devout Christian. It was prepared by the Lord’s apostles upon the tables of the Church, 161. Only the faithful know it. How it must be received, 172. The purity required of us in receiving it is indicated, 91. See *Bread*, *The Lord’s Prayer*.

**Eunuch.** Through voluntary chastity the eunuch is transferred into Christ’s service and exchanges the insignia of the palace, 56.

**Euphemia.** She paid more in the fruit than she promised in the blossom: while retaining the blossom of virginity, she reached the fruit of martyrdom, 97.

**Eve.** Eve received a scandal through the eye, 27. It would have been better for her to have been without an eye and a hand than without original righteousness. Likewise, it would have been better if she had been prevented in paradise, 74. Let the one who saw the tree of knowledge look upon the mustard tree, so that she may be healed, 99. Through her, death came to all. Eve was cursed, the mother by nature of the dying, 140.

**Gospel.** The Gospel is called an unprocessed cloth and the beginning of weaving from the fleece of the Lamb of God, 31. A cloth dyed with Christ’s blood. For this reason the cloth is not inserted into Jewish antiquity. The Gospel readings bestow advantages for the present and future life, [Col. 1166] 34. They are to be preached by the disciples to everyone, 83. When its dawn occurs, 86. Its readings are beneficial to the good for saving understanding, but to the wicked they become an occasion of error, 89. It gradually advances toward higher things, 92. The chariot of the four Gospels carries human beings to heaven. The enemy mixes the Gospel’s harvest with heretical weeds, 96. Its divine meaning is concealed within it, 99. Our obedience to the Gospel comes from God, who calls us, 114. What service to the Gospel accomplishes in us. The marvelous piety arising from evangelical teaching, and why. Its fearful beginnings thunder forth to awaken human senses, 115. Its authority restores minds for labor, 115. It is heard more willingly when explained in various ways, 116. It must be explained with moderation of understanding, and why, 125. What the Gospel does among human beings. Many questions are veiled within it, and they are not easy for a human being to resolve, 126. Its sanction was John, 127. The evangelical sermon must not be considered worthless because of its simplicity, 132. It was prepared for the Gentiles by John, 137. From it come eternal crowns, 144. Its points, letters, syllables, word, names, and persons are filled with divine figures, 146. What the Gospel says and does not say, 156. Women are a type of evangelical preaching, 76. It is entirely full of mystical meanings, 169. The evangelists use mystical speech, 79. The profundity of the Gospels has advanced us into the heights, 173. Those who evangelize peace are Christ’s feet, 95. And his footprints, 76.

**Bearer.** The bearer of piety does not know how to grow weary, 170.

**Exacting creditor.** The greedy creditor complains about delay in payment, 77. See *Publican*.

**High things.** Do not presume to gaze upon exalted things, and why, 164.

**Guards.** The Innocents were assigned as guards for Christ’s cradle, 152. See *Watchings*.

**Excuse.** There is no excuse when customary commandments are to be repaid as the greatest things, 114. The excuse of one speaking at the beginning of a prayer, 138. No excuse was left to Herod, 152. He lacks it who commits a crime with the judge himself as witness, 26.

**Example.** A good example is beneficial, 34. By familiar examples the Lord instructs us to grasp divine things, 39 and 47. Christ reforms the human being by his example, 48. God’s disposition is insinuated through examples, 55. An example gives hope, 74. We are strengthened by example, 108. Singularity does not admit of an example, 153. Why God gives external and humble examples, 163. Why Christ descends from the example of a most foul bird to the example of a fragrant flower, 163. Examples reinforce commandments, 166. They confirm an action, 175. Let the Jew be a useful example for Christians, 46. Many examples produce weariness, 29.

**Experience.** Experience demonstrates the powers of nature and of the human being, 90.

**Scout.** What the scouts who went around the land for forty days signify mystically, 166.

**To expound.** We ought to expound Christ’s deeds literally and mystically, 95.

**Conqueror.** One cannot be his own conqueror if he has an enemy within, 171.

**To await.** The servant awaiting the Lord here will receive retribution in glory, 24. Long waiting for a great promise wearies the mind, 130.

**Exultation.** Whoever enters exultantly before God is free from guilt, 6. And why he dares to do so. Who can exult in the Lord, 46. And how. Exultation should be shared at the birthdays of the saints, 129.

**Stranger.** A stranger does not intercede with the father, 2. What the person who denies himself to his father and entrusts himself to a stranger finds, 1.

**Ezekiel.** An eminent prophet: by lying on one side for forty days, while prefiguring the future captivity, he completed it, and the reason is given, 166.

## F
Faber. Christ was called the son of a craftsman, and why, 48. And whose craftsman’s son he was, 48 and 49. We must do what we have heard commanded by the Lord, 102. Christ did what he commanded, 151. See Facta Christi.

Facies. Things must not be judged from appearance alone, 145. A feigned appearance is excluded by God in fasting, and why, 7.

Facultates. See Divitiae.

Falsitas. Why an example of falsehood is called pious in the case of the steward, 126. Amid reports of falsehoods, the mind acting as judge does not find the truth, 131. Falsehood arising from obstinacy. Falsehood alone always attacks truth, 169.

Fama. Christ does not trust reputation but investigates when the earth accuses, 125. If the reputation of our altered substance precedes us to the Father, we shall die before our time. Reputation is criticized on account of money, 126. Who would seek fame from another person’s ruin? 171. Almsgiving performed for reputation is hypocrisy, 9. The fame of virtues answers to the glory of the name, 67. Through disgrace and infamy reputation is buried and glory perishes, 1.

Fames. Hunger is the torturer of gluttony and lust, 1. It brings the son back to the father, 11 and 5. Fasting without mercy is an image of hunger, 8. Christ did not experience hunger during the forty days, 11. To overcome hunger is human; not to experience it is divine. [Col. 1167] From hunger the devil judges that he can tempt. Hunger in Chrysologus’s time, 45. Christ’s hunger is not for food but for charity toward his own, 78. It advances one toward fasting, 124.

Fastidium. Weariness is produced by repeated discourse, 120. It arises from the fatigue both of the speaker and of the hearer, 122.

Febris. How it is kindled from cold humor, 114. What should be done when fever excludes us from stewardship, 125. The brother who injures his brother burns with fever, 139. For those suffering fever, nourishing food is bitter, 164. Fever was burning in Peter’s house, 18. See Phrenesis. Aegrotus, Infirmus. How dried-up limbs may be healed by a long fever, 41.

Felicitas. Holy Felicitas had as many children as the world has days, 134. Mother of lights, fountain of days, and other things concerning her, throughout, with note. The first happiness is not to have sinned; the second is to have found forgiveness for sins, 34. The one true happiness is to be just in all things, 91. The first happiness is perpetual innocence, 167. Another person’s happiness is torment to the envious, 172.

Felix. Envy arises from another’s happiness, 122. It is painful to see someone happy whom we once thought unhappy, 123.

Ferculum. Cruelty was the platter bearing the head of John the Baptist, 174. Countless wild beasts against one sheep are more cruel because they cannot seize and devour it, 171. Savageness is softened by gentleness, 6.

Fermentum. Leaven is an image of the kingdom of God, 99 and throughout; and why the grain is said to be received from a man, but the leaven from a woman, 99. The three measures of flour are applied to the Trinity. Faith, unbelief, and resurrection possess leaven. It is a sacrament of heavenly doctrine. It is not a mass of size but of swelling, 172.

Ferrum. Hardened iron against tender breasts—when, 152.

Fertilitas. He who is generous toward the poor will be fruitful, 104.

Fervor. Fervor is rational service, 109.

Festivitas. An ecclesiastical festival is not fruitless, 85. Festivals are not to be consecrated according to our wishes but according to their own virtues. God grants us a feast day from heaven. The Lord’s Nativity recalled by the sun, 87. The joy of a festival should include mercy toward the needy, 103. The Jew honored heavenly festivals with tithes; let the Christian honor them with hundredths. Their pomp made the Jews obstinate, 11. At the festivals of the saints their praises should be recounted insofar as sufficient, 122. What caution should govern human festal joys, 127. The festivals of the saints are not celebrated in extravagant banquets but in imitation of the saints, 129. Annual festivals are celebrated for our remembrance. The Church rejoices in the festival of her son, 130. How the festival of a martyr should be celebrated, 135. The festival of the seventh month, 139. The Lord’s festivals disclose their causes through their names, 157. The Epiphany occurs each year for the remembrance of humankind, 160. At festivals care must be taken that everyone turns to God’s grace, 10. See Solemnitas, Sabbatum, Epiphania.

Fenus. It is always grievous to be bound by the chains of interest, 88. Christ gave, rather than received, at interest, and promises that he will collect, 123. See Usura.

Fetor. What stinks to one who destroys another’s work does not stink to one who loves his own work, 65. Lazarus’s stench demonstrates the divine miracle. God gives strength to those who stink. See Lazarus, Martha.

Ficus. How it covers Adam and Zacchaeus, 54. The tree is given as a likeness, 106. It produces figs in blossom but casts them off, 106. A symbol of the Synagogue. It does not signify the present but indicates the future. After his sin Adam runs to it, and under it Christ seeks him. It did not cover the shamefaced man, but exposed him and spurred shame. Barren, though manured.

Fiducia. Confidence in obtaining what is requested exists when the king dictates a petition to the petitioner, 70. Our confidence arises from intimacy with Christ, 144. Confidence given to believers from Christ’s flight, 150.

Fidelis. Christ will serve a banquet to the faithful and sentence to the unfaithful, 24. For them evening becomes light, 75. Let him rejoice at having found Christ, the true God, 88. The divine meaning concealed in God’s word is not hidden from them, 99. The faithful person is said to be worthy of God’s help, 102. Christ is always known to the faithful, 131. God is with the faithful, man with the unfaithful—how, 145. Christ meets those who run faithfully, 80. The faithful person is brighter than the sun, 36.

Fides. The divine Father, sought in faith, is immediately present, 3. Faith does not require witnesses, 9. Unbelievers must be led to faith, 10. Who they are, and by whom they are to be led. By whom and in what manner signs of faith should be given, 11. Through faith comes the salvation of the nations, 18. And the defeat of the demon. Why the disciples’ faith in Christ was little, 21. Faith immediately heals what art does not heal for a long time, 33. It gives salvation, 34. The clouds of the hemorrhaging woman’s faith are dispelled, 36. Faith stands through prayer, fasting, and almsgiving, 43. Why Christ looks upon the faith of those who offer the paralytic, 50. The father’s faith benefits his son; unbelief harms him, 51. Faith and confession are the sacrament of salvation, 56. They must be placed in the heart, not on tablets. Faith is grasped by hearing. The summary of faith is to believe with the heart and confess with the mouth, 56. The sacrament of faith cleanses unclean lips and accomplishes other things, 57. It must not be committed to tablets, 57 and [Col. 1168] 58. Whoever seeks faith does not seek an argument, 58. God compensates for it. From where faith gathers the proof of Christ’s resurrection. Faith comes from hearing, and hearing from the word, 59. The thing follows in the fruit if faith has preceded in the seed, 60. Faith is to be entrusted to memory, not to a book. To the treacherous the sacrament of faith is destructive. Rooted faith in the depths of the heart rises to the summit of belief, 61. The confession of faith is made with the mouth for salvation. Through faith a person is marked out as an inhabitant of heaven, and so forth, 62. It is to be embraced reverently. The confession of faith is quickly rewarded, 68. What faith can accomplish, 71. The women’s faith at the tomb, 74 and 77. The foundations of faith upon the rock, 74. It taught the resurrection of Christ, 76. It received Christ from the dead, 77. The women’s faith was shaken during Christ’s passion. It was established, 18. The disciples’ faith in Christ was sought at a deeper level, 81. The women’s faith was blind, 82. Those who would receive faith were prophesied from peoples divided from the earth, magicians, Greeks, and Romans, 83. He who is without faith dies, and how. Faith heals diseases, 83. It must be gradually infused into the treacherous, 87. Faith begins from belief. Faith gives the word; unbelief denies it, 90. He lies against faith if what a magician does a Christian does not do, 91. Faith is required in the Virgin’s conception and childbirth, 92. Those considered equal in faith are sometimes unequal, 97. By faith we approach God. Faith has its own leaven, 99. It inclines God’s will to reveal secrets, 100. Through it we are joined to God. The faith of the nations seized what the unbelief of the Jews rejected. And it used force to seize the Father’s inheritance. Christ manifests himself as God in such a way that he is also a place for faith, 102. Faith advances servants into friends. It lives and flourishes among the nations. God seeks faith, not death, 108. Faith must be offered to God for the destruction of unbelief. The banner of faith was raised for the salvation of Jews and nations, 110. Salvation is entirely in faith. Faith is the guide of Christ’s way, in which we stand. How the Law disclosed that faith would be wholly full of dangers, 116. The whole hope of faith is in the resurrection of the dead, 118. Faith must be accepted because it is given freely. Faith and devotion make a martyr, 128. Faith alone touches God, 131. The faithful person recognizes what the unfaithful does not know. Faith did not burn in Lawrence but consoled him while he burned, 135. Faith holds the one who promises to his word. We must pray that faith may be increased for believing eternal goods, 139. Through faith the incarnation of the Word is known, 141. Without faith we cannot attain even the least of God’s works. Faith rests upon God’s reason, not upon human reason. From the Gospel, notes concerning faith are to be taken for eternal crowns, 144. The faith of the promise made to David is fulfilled in Joseph, 145. Through Christ the hearts of mortals are aroused to faith, 151. It is signified by incense, 159. The faith of the nations is consecrated through the belief of the magi, 160. Faith reaches where human thoughts do not reach, 163. It increases us to the measure of Christ, 163. Christ leads hearers to faith in the promise by an example. The difference between one who is simply faithful and one who is knowingly faithful, 166. For the strengthening of faith the demon rages, 149. See Perfidia, Confessio. Whoever ascends to the secret of faith through hearing reaches the whole reality, 142. So that the shoots of faith would not be destroyed, the seasons were divided into drizzles, 143. He does not touch Christ with his hand who has not first touched him by faith, 76. The hearing of faith is drunk from the river of the tongue, 79.

Figura. The figure, or parable, of the prodigal son is set forth for three reasons, 1. Figures are spoken by the Lord for our correction, 2. How the figure of the prodigal applies to us. How it is attributed to the Hebrew and to the Gentile, 5 and throughout. The figure of the faithful steward concerns everyone, 26. The paralytic is a figure of the Jews, the tax collector of the nations, 30. Whose figure is represented by the man with the withered hand, 32. The hemorrhaging woman is a figure of the Church, 35. Future mysteries are born from present figures, 36. John is a figure of Christ; Jacob of Christians, 73. Why Christ speaks in parables and obscurely, 96. The figure of the mustard seed, 98. Of the leaven, 99. Parables are handed down concerning things known to everyone, and why, 99. They are spoken to instruct the minds of peoples, 106. Adam is a figure of Christ, 117. The figure of the unjust steward pertains to the people, 125. It is a figure of the Gentile people, 126. The returning son signifies the baptized person, 137. The figure of the Church as bride is the Virgin Mary, 146. Joseph is a figure of Christ. What the figure of Christ fleeing into Egypt signifies, 151. The two animals of the manger are figures of the two peoples, 159. The bramble is a figure of the Jewish people, 164. Figures must be fulfilled, 166. The figure of the lost sheep is explained, 168. Of the lost drachma, 169. The brothers of the rich banqueter are a figure of the Hebrews, 123. The demoniac is a figure of the Gentile people, 52. See Forma.

Filius. The son who is unworthy of the son’s privilege: when he does not possess goods with his father, 1. With what audacity the prodigal asked his father for his portion. Blessed if his father retains his substance. Unhappy—and how—if he possesses it without his father. What good comes from living with parents and relatives. Ungrateful toward his father, he turns into a beast, 2. He does not need an advocate before his father. Why he says, “I am not worthy to be called your son.” In freedom, toward what evils he tends. Let him avoid the devil and remain with his father. And let him always enjoy his father’s goods. The sins of sons are redeemed by a kiss, 3. Let sinful sons return to the father. The son who left his father rich [Col. 1169] returns barefoot. The elder son, through envy, lost the good of frugality, 4. The ignorant son judges his father’s piety, 4. The son is the substance of the father. The elder son is the Jew; the younger, the Gentile—how, 5. Let the heavenly Father’s son ask for forgiveness and bread. A son is not generated without God’s authority, 6. Not believing his father, he does not know himself to be a son, 7. He is ungrateful to his father if he does not honor him with gifts, 10. Let sons be grateful toward their parents, 33. The son of the craftsman. See Faber. The Son of God seeks nothing except the heavenly homeland, 49. The son when filled by a demon, 51. What a son suspected of his father’s generosity should do, 54. The Son of God is proved by not being darkened by vices, and so forth, 67. Let the son correspond to his lineage, 68. He obtains from the Father the things that are holy, 70. He is not wearied by much prayer, 71. The son asks from necessity; the father gives from charity. He pleases when asking for what is just; he displeases when demanding what is foolish, 71. Degenerate sons are punished. The harsh period of paternal rule, because of hope of inheritance, 71. The sons of God will possess the inheritance while the Father lives. The sons serve God before they are born to their parents, 72. The Son was not begotten for one person alone; he was created for the joy of all, 88. The son of the old man does not know wine. He is praised from the glory of his father, 89. A person is called the son of one whose vices or virtues he possesses. That parents judge from the merits of their sons comes from heaven, 107. The son is more impious because of the father’s piety, 123. Called by the name of son and severely condemned, he suffers greatly. What the son suffers belongs to judgment, not rage. Whoever does not perform the works of his father denies his lineage. The son who leaves the fullest charity enriches, 162. The son concerned for himself blames his surviving father, 163. The father did not allow the prodigal to remain in prosperity, 3. See Pater.

Fimbria. The fringe of Christ’s garment, which the hemorrhaging woman touched. See Haemorrhoissa. What this fringe is mystically, 34.

Finis. The end that Christ gives to the righteous in death does not receive an end and does not kill but perfects, 114. The end of sins will be at the resurrection of the flesh, 117.

Flagellum. The scourge of God is on account of our sins, 20. It floods over us. God is said to sleep and therefore must be awakened—how. People scourged by God with scarcity and pestilence nevertheless clung to their sins, 45. It comes from contempt of God, 43. God’s scourges will cease if we turn to God, 20.

Fletus. We must weep that the whole world was condemned through the sin of one person, 111. See Lacrymae, Planctus.

Flores. The flowers of the fields are pleasing, but bread is more pleasing, 18. Flowers are pleasing, but only until one reaches the fruits—why, 62. Many flowers promise a multitude of fruits; but, exhausted by the blasts of the winds, very few persevere to fruit, 97. When something else appears, let it be regarded as its outward form. The garden of the Church burns with everlasting flowers, 98. Fragrant flowers are taken by Christ as an example for us, 163. See Lilium, Rosa.

Flosculi. Little flowers of words are not to be sought; rather, the fruit in the explanation of Sacred Scripture, 18. In a thorny shrub, little flowers of wondrous fragrance grow, 49. The little legal flowers deceived the Jews, 106.

Femina. Women precede the apostles in their ministry; in rank they follow the disciples, 75. They bear the type of the Churches to the Lord’s tomb, 75. Why they came to see the tomb, not the Lord, 75. Through a woman Christ is generated for us from the tomb. The two women are a figure of the Church, 76. They bear the type of evangelical preaching. By faith they touch the Savior’s footprints. A woman, interpreter of death, becomes the messenger of the resurrection, and other matters, 79. They are not placed above the apostles. Through man and woman the cause of the world is brought to an end, 99. Through a woman we have merited life, 142. A deceived virgin woman induces her virgin husband to eat food, 148. She becomes the cause of the whole ruin that had been made for singular comfort. Hence the first sin of humanity. If John did not escape the dangers of women, who among those living among them will escape safely? 174. See Mulier.

Fons. A cool spring is joyful to the thirsty, 46. Flowing from a narrow mouth, it expands more greatly into the waters of rivers, 61. How it gradually grows, 39. The spring of Siloam abounds when the angel moves it, not when the one drawing water is thirsty, 86. The spring itself is not thirsty, 110. Springs are pleasing by nature but displeasing through saltiness, 111. The river serves the spring, 11. If its channel is enriched by its own irrigation, it is blessed, 136. A thirsty spring in the breast of the Pharisees, 172. The fountain of forgiveness. See Veniae. Christ wished to be washed as a fountain, 90.

Forma. The form or figure of the world censured by the Apostle, 120. What it is is explained by that same Apostle. The Apostle recalls us to the form of Christ, and how. Various forms assumed by the kings of the Persians are ridiculous, 120. Peter and Andrew expressed the form of Christ’s passion in themselves, 133. Why forms are varied by God, 170. Forms grow large to imperfect eyes, 176.

Fortis. The strong person is not disturbed by evils, 47. The brave soldier challenges openly, with everyone watching, 97. The strong are not overthrown by adversity, 124. The sweat of the strong is overcome by the tears of little ones, 128.

Fragilitas. Fragility is a fever that breaks out into the madness of vices, 41. What it is, and much concerning it, 41. The evils that arise from it. How it may be cured. Fragility always tends toward a fall, 42. What effects human fragility produces, 45. Its description, 68. How it succumbs in conflict, 68. How great human weakness is concerning divine matters, 90. Human weakness is commanded to give God as much as it gave the world, 114. How human weakness is disturbed by passions at every age toward a fall, 115. Human weakness succumbs while bearing God, 142. It is corrupted by the pus of vices, 167. What despises its companions falls quickly, 170. Innate weakness compels us to sin, 34. See Infirmitas, Passiones.

Frater. A brother is to be helped by prayer, fasting, and tears, 20. He who assists his brother assists himself. Who is called a brother among the Hebrews, 49. Why the disciples are called brothers by the Lord, 80. The brothers of the rich banqueter are a figure of the Hebrews, 123. A brother is in fever and madness when he injures his brother, 139. A brother’s anger toward his brother is to be attributed to illness. Madness does not know how to be without insanity, and how, 173. Christ became our brother, 162. An envious mind is not grateful to a brother or to a father, 4. The envious person believes he has suffered loss when he sees a coheir. The Hebrew wishes to destroy his brother through envy, 5. What a painting of brothers in harmony signifies, 149. Brotherly charity prays to the Lord in the dangers of brothers, 20. Through it sinners must be drawn away from destruction, 155. Where it is absent, there is also no gratitude toward the father, 4. See Unio, Concordia, Amor, Proximus.

Fraus. Deceit harms people, 62. The penalties of deceit remain, 97. He cannot fear deceit for whom nothing can perish, 97. When deceit is pious, 125. The steward’s deceit, 126. Through it faith is entirely lost. The heavenly Creditor is not forestalled by deceit. Why the steward’s actions were approved by the Lord, 126. Deceit turned back upon itself is shattered in Herod, 152. Blessed is she that—, 35.

Fremere. Why Christ groaned at the resurrection of Lazarus: various explanations, 65.

Fructus. Fruit, once produced after the earth, gives life and substance, 117. When the hundredfold is owed by a person to his creator, 126. A person does not receive fruit from the earth before labor, 142. When a steward has abundant fruit, he desires the lord to come for his profit, 158. The fruit of the interpreter of mystical Scriptures, 96.

Frugalitas. Frugality is the highest good, 4.

Fuga. Flight must be taken from hypocrisy, otherwise we shall fall, 7. We must flee from the face of a woman, 127. Our flight is excused by Christ’s flight, 150. Flight in warfare is a skill, not fear. Why the flight of the powerful person withdrawing for the weak is appropriate. In persecution it is better to flee than to deny, 150. Flight is useful, 151. Flight is necessary for a martyr who has not been captured. Flight from envy must be taken immediately, 172. It is not the duty of a devoted soldier to describe the flight of his commander, 150. Whether the flight of Christ’s disciples while he himself was being captured was blameworthy, 133. Christ flees in order to recall those who are fleeing, 150. Human beings who flee are excused by Christ’s flight. When the Lord flees, it is not unworthy for the servant to flee, 151. God, fleeing the sinner, spares him, 131.

Fulgur. Lightning does not illuminate but produces fear, 64. The lightning of the angel of Christ’s resurrection, 74. When lightning dissolves something, it seizes the senses and minds of human beings, 171.

Funus. The funeral of the rich man and of the poor man is described, 121.

Fures. Thieves arise from necessity, 7. Let those who stole what belonged to others give away their own possessions, 113. Whoever has once begun to steal will not cease even in the sight of the Lord, 126. The thief loves the night, 158.

Furor. Rage is irrational service, 109. A brother’s rage occurs when he himself has sinned against his neighbor, 139. A brother’s rage toward his brother should be attributed to illness. Rage does not know how to be without madness, and how, 173.

Furtum. The hemorrhaging woman’s theft caused no loss to the one robbed, 33. It was pious because it was committed with faith drawing her onward. It was blessed, 35. Theft must be returned with all speed, 123. See Latro.

Futurum. The future is understood from present things, 47. The Jew does not receive future things because he is ungrateful for present things, 48. Future things are already accomplished for God, 70.

# G

Gabriel. The angel Gabriel appeared and spoke to Zechariah, and is a servant of God, 90. See Maria virgo, Angelus.

Galla Placida. Galla Placidia, mother of the emperor Valentinian, was present at Chrysologus’s consecration as archbishop, 130. She possessed the august Trinity—and how, and why. Priests are asked to pray for her and for her son, the Augustus.

Gallina. Gallus. God raises us, leads us, and calls us like a hen, with the associated description and reasons, 170. What the cock offers his guest, 21.

Gaudium. The father has greater joy over forgiveness granted to his son than over justice, 3. We should rejoice when others rejoice, 6. Why the earth is called to joy. David’s joy when the Christian lambs were nourished with milk, 6. Our joy is to cooperate with God in the salvation of souls, 10. A fellow worker must also be regarded as a companion in joys, 40. How joy should accord with tears, 46. Joy at the poor man’s misfortune will be balanced by grief, 47. [Col. 1171] Joy after tears, 65. From the resurrection of Lazarus. Desired joys are scarcely believed and produce astonishment, 81. Joy is more pleasing after sorrow, 84. The joy of a festival should be accompanied by mercy toward the needy, 103. Joys at festivals should be cautious, 127. Joy should be taken from the victory and example of the saints, 129. Joy with the Church exists in peace; heretics are in anger, 149. Sadness must not be mixed with joys, 175.

Gazophylacium. Christ’s treasury is the hand of the poor, 8.

Gehenna. Gehenna, which burns the guilty, serves the innocent, 166. Who are assigned to its fires, 163. See Infernus.

Gemitus. Our groaning is unnecessary—when, 166.

Generatio. The generation of human beings and animals displays divine love, 55. There are two kinds: the generation by which we are born and that by which we are reborn, 126. Divine generation knows no witness, 160. The beginnings of one who begets are harder for everyone, 175. How a way is generated from a way. A human being must not exist without God, 6. The divine generation of the Word. See Trinitas, Divina.

Generosus. A noble spirit easily despises what it considers great, 29. How it may prevent sins and trample them down, 116.

Gentilis. The Gentile people are called the younger son, 5. Five natural benefits were his portion of the substance. These could lead him to knowledge of the heavenly Father. At the beginning of the world he was an idolater. He was a stranger to God, not in place but in mind. Through secular learning he dissipated his father’s substance, 5. An idolater of demons. He did not learn the truth. His foolishness. His withdrawal from God toward gluttony. God allowed the Gentile so that good might come from evil. He returned to the Father. By idolatry he sinned against heaven. To gather the scattered nations, God assumed the role of a shepherd, 6.

The Gentile is healed in the evening, 18. He is an idolater. Christ came to the nations not in the flesh but in the Word. The Gentile beats against the outside of the Lord’s boat, 21. How he rises up against the faithful, 40. Represented in the demoniac, he is not healed except by Christ, 52. The Gentile coming to faith in Christ is first cleansed by exorcisms. The Gentile rejoices that he has fled the profane gods, 57. He detracts from the Christian name, 69. A partial blindness has occurred in Israel until the fullness of the nations enters, 73. The salvation of Gentiles and Jews is joined by Christ, 78. The Gentile believes without seeing Christ, 83. Foreign nations that received the faith. The Gentile made creatures into gods for himself, 89. The faith of the nations seized what the unbelief of the Jews rejected, 100. And it used force upon Christ. How the dog licks Christ, the bread, 100. The Gentile—that is, the Christian—leads others to Christ, 102. He loves the Hebrew people. Christ is joined to the Gentile to the extent that he is separated from the Jew. The Gentile is praised for faith. The calling and obedience of the nations. The sacrilegious Gentile, 105. Obedient to monstrous gods, he is ignorant of the true God, 111. Why he ought not to be proud by nature, 110. The Gentile is represented in the unjust steward, 126. He is summoned to render an account of natural goodness. The Gentile, now a Christian, questions the Jew. How Gentiles who have become Christians are wiser than the Jews. John prepares the nations for the Gospel and repentance, 137. Why they fashioned images, 147. Christ came to bring the nations into faith, 151. The Gentiles are to be placed before the Hebrews, 151. The Gentiles drag their gods into view through obscenities, 155. The Gentiles are avengers of injuries against God, and how. The Gentile donkey recognized its Lord, and how, 159. The belief of the nations is consecrated through the faith of the magi, 160. The sown fields of the nations are purified by Christ with refining fire, 164. What sort of conversion of the Gentiles was accomplished by the apostles, 51. He was a beast—how, 23.

Genus. He is rash who investigates lineage, 72. Whoever does not perform the works of his father denies his lineage, 123.

Gladius. The life-giving sword, when it kills, does not give death, 108.

Gloria. Glory accompanies virtues, 31. The glory of the risen Christ buried the injury of the dying Christ, 75. The glory of the son is the praise of the father, 89. Innate glory is greater than acquired glory, 89. He who is free is born for glory, 101. A person should be subjected to glory to the same extent that he was subjected to disgrace, 114. The Apostle urges us toward the crown of glory, 119. The Hebrew, philosopher, heretic, and Christian strive for it, but only the Christian receives it. We must contend for eternal glory, and against whom. How, in glory, the saints practice the pious duties that they performed here, 121. In glory the saints see the torments of the wicked, 122. Let us labor to possess eternal glory, 124. How eternal glory is prepared here, 144. Let our glory be buried, 1. In it the saints see whatever belongs to divine light, honor, and glory, 176. See Beatitudo, Aeterna. In glory there will be no time, 82.

Glorificare. We must glorify God publicly after receiving benefits, 36.

Gratia. God’s grace leads us into his presence, 6. How it is given by God to the infirm, 50. How it justifies the aborted sinner, 56. By God’s grace we hear and respond concerning faith, 58. Thanks must be given for what has been granted, 65. Grace makes an earthly person heavenly, 72. We are called by grace, 81. It admits into the temple what the Law leads to the door, 86. How John the Baptist attained grace, 88. Grace should be referred to the glory of God’s name. Through it we are justified, 91. It is a singular grace to be just in all things. Preventing and effective, it leads to Christ, 93. He is unworthy to recognize grace who conceals the law, 96. The just confess that they possess grace, by which they stand and without which they perish, 97. Grace is also offered to the reprobate, 100. Grace rejected by the master is given to the servant. Grace calls to God, 102. Through Christ’s grace we return to life, 112. So that grace may abound, we must not remain in sin, 113. It was given by God to the human being, not given to sin. Through emancipating grace, those who are under the Law are freed from slavery to sin, 114. Grace calls a person a servant who is truly free. It adopts a human being as a son of God. Through grace one must settle what cannot be settled by nature, 126. The effects of baptismal grace, 137. Whoever finds grace knows no fear, 142. The grace of the Holy Spirit teaches that mystical meanings lie hidden in the Gospels, 169. It washes with the one bath of grace, 171. The freedom of grace, 176. Everyone should be led to God’s grace, 10. Mary’s grace. See Maria virgo. Concerning her generous grace, at length, throughout. The magnitude of grace is known from the magnitude of guilt, 54. When grace perseveres, 68. Let the rich be grateful to God, when the poor person is grateful amid evils, 124. Things received are more pleasing than things possessed, and things found more than things subjected, 69. The human being who will rise again should be grateful to God, 101.

Gratus. The grateful person is pleasing to God, 124.

Grex. The herd of demons is sent into a herd of swine—why, 16. Why Christians are called a little flock, 22. How a gentle flock conquered various kinds of beasts, 23. It imitates Christ. It conquers when it loses.

Gula. Gluttony leads to hunger, 1. Epicurus is an authority for despair through gluttony, 5. Do not please gluttony while you fast, 12. Gluttony drove Adam from paradise, 12. At the price of gluttony the woman bought death, 63. What the drop requested by the rich banqueter is for, and what it accomplished, 124. A drop and a crumb suffice for the poor man’s refreshment. A drop of holy dew baptizes the sinner’s eyes in Christ, 176. From it the credibility of the resurrection is demonstrated. See Mica.

# H
## H

To have lost what one possessed is a greater grief than never to have possessed it, 123.

An innocent dwelling is tormented by the sitting of its inhabitant, 17. See **House**.

**Form / habitus.** For what purpose it is changed by God, 170.

**The woman with the hemorrhage.** She seeks a remedy for a hidden wound, 33. Burdened with conflicting thoughts. She is cured by faith. Why she stood at a distance and did not speak. Why she steals healing. She resorts to faith and theft, 34. How she was driven about by storms of thought. From the summit of the fringe she reached the summit of Divinity. How she approached from behind. Her faith, 34–35. She taught how greatly it matters to touch Christ’s body, 35. How she obtained pardon through silent confession, 34. How Christ turned toward her. What she did between the wound and shame, 35. Conscious of pain, not of sin, she approached from behind. Why she touched the fringe. Great in knowledge, sacrament, and faith. She is a figure of the Church. The Lord, though not sought by her, meets her, 36. Between her and the Lord there is an exchange of stolen salvation. In the crowd she is alone with Christ. Why Christ asks who touched his garments, 36. God is praised in her. Before healing she hides from shame; afterward she comes into the midst so as to return glory to God. Why she had suffered twelve years of illness. Her shame, concealed even by Chrysologus’s silence, 86. In touching the Lord’s fringe she did not pollute it, but was herself healed, 94. Concerning her, 100.

The inheritance of the children—that is, of the Jews—transferred to the Gentiles, 100.

The cruel inheritance of our father Adam, which neither pleased one to acquire nor allowed one to renounce, 111.

No inheritance is better than the bond of divine charity, 162. The worldly inheritance and the evils it retains with itself. It is a battlefield; it is a stepmother to its children. The divine inheritance may be given but cannot be divided. In an inheritance there is no strife if greed is removed. The Christian will be a blessed heir while his father always lives, 71. Human beings are heirs of their father Adam, and heirs by necessity, 111. They lost the goods bestowed on them and acquired evils. What the heir of worldly goods asked from the Lord, 162. He enriches heirs who leaves them the fullness of charity. Through grace we are co-heirs with Christ. The heir is impatient when he grows weary of his father’s life, 1.

The Church suffered almost as many heresies as there were questions concerning the divine law, 21. Why the heretical weeds sown over the Gospel by the demon exist, 96. The heresies of Arius and Photinus, 109. They all blasphemed God. It is heresy to say that Christ assumed an ethereal body, 144. Likewise, that the Father is greater than the Son, 2. Heresies concerning Christ’s birth, 145.

The heretic shakes the Lord’s ship from within, the Gentile from without, 21. He blasphemes Christ, 24. Like foreign dogs, they snap at Christians with rabid teeth, 40. He sat in the seat of pestilence, 44. He opposes the eternal generation of the Son, 60. After Christ’s burial he says: “Let him wait,” 62. He feeds on injuries done to Christ. Let him believe that Christ is God, and understand in what manner, 88. Let him return to the Church, 98. Let him recognize that the Lord has come to his servants. He loses God by nature but will find him through faith. He runs for the crown of glory but does not receive it, 119. The heretics’ profession of faith is poisoned: they fast and give alms, but in vain. The heretic does not believe after the cause has been demonstrated, 142. Where he generates the clouds of his faithlessness, 144. How they are in anger while the Church is at peace, 149.

**Hebrew / Jew.** His envy is shown in the figure of the prodigal son, 1; likewise, passim at 4. The Jew was the elder son, 5. His portion of the substance was the divine law, 5. He does not enter the Church because of envy. Judging the Gentile by his former conduct, he deprives himself of his father’s joys, 5, 31. He speaks but does not act. He is with the father through the holy Hebrews. He possesses everything that belongs to the father, including Christ. Yet through envy he loses everything.

Christ works salvation with the hands of the Jewish people, 18. Their unclean hands are cleansed by Christ. He wonders why Jesus associates with sinners at table, 29. He is represented by the paralytic, 30. The Jews are a brood of vipers, 31. Their plots and deceits against Christ. They are old wineskins. They will not have the new wine of the Gospel unless they become Christians, 31.

The Jew does not receive Christ when he enters the synagogue, 32. The Jew joins the Herodians in order to attack the Christians. The Jews’ error is more perverse than the waves of the sea. The Jew defames Christ’s resurrection, 37. How he might seek Christ. He will be condemned by the Ninevites and the queen of the South. How he would exact vengeance, 38. Let him be a useful example to Christians, 46. How the spiritual law of the Jews was lost, 44. He wonders indignantly at Christ, 48. He attempts to obscure Mary’s virginity. The wickedness of the Hebrews against Christ, at length, 49. He confesses the truth unwillingly. What he says about Christ and his disciples, who were unable to cure the demoniac, 51. More wicked than the devil. Transformed from human beings into dogs, 55. They see Christ as the rock, the serpent, and the scorpion. Beyond burial they offer Christ nothing else, 62. They are not converted when Lazarus is raised, 64.

The Jews’ Passover is not joined to ours, 73. Day is turned into night for them, 75. The blind man assesses sins at a price: he buys the blood of the Redeemer and the treachery against Christ’s resurrection, 76. But he loses the money, kills himself and his descendants. He grieves that Christ rose rather than that he killed him, 80. He buys in order to destroy. He wants Christ’s resurrection to be theft. He seeks to destroy the disciples. What he caused at Christ’s death, 81. Why he is surprised that Christ knows, although he has not learned, 85. The holiness of the Hebrews until the time of Herod, 86. Why Christ preaches to them in parables, 96. He tears the shepherd, 100. They ask on behalf of the Gentile, not for themselves or their children, 102.

The beloved Jew, praised by Christians, hates his own people. He went bodily, but not mentally, with Christ. To the extent that the Hebrew separated himself from Christ, Christ was joined to the Gentile, 102. An enemy to the Christian. The Jews’ rejection. Signs and miracles among them accomplish nothing. Earthly understanding rushes over heavenly meanings, 105. In seeking God contrary to reason, he lost him, 109. Cultivating the law without understanding the law, he killed the author of the law.
