He should not be cultivated through the law, 110. He lost the temple, priesthood, sacrifice, incense, purifications, and devotion to solemn festivals, 114.

He is circumcised because he has been cut off from present goods. He is accursed because he offends in everything. Through the law he runs for the crown of glory, 119, but does not receive it. He refused to believe Christ concerning the goods of heaven and the evils of hell, 123. He is questioned by a Gentile who has become a Christian, 126. Why he would owe a hundred measures of oil. Abandoned to be a son of this age, he is less prudent than the Gentile Christian. He is enraged when he sees God as man, 131.

All the Hebrews were marked by faithlessness. His jealousy and blasphemies against Christ teaching: “They took up stones,” so that they might kill themselves, not God. Their filth can be washed away by a river, 137. They are called “offspring of vipers,” 137. The Jews excluded the Lord from inns, while animals received him in their mangers, 141. The Jew fears that Christ may be born, 146. The Virgin’s childbirth is concealed from the Jew, lest he be killed.

Christ came so that the Jew might come out of contempt for the law, 151. Their faithlessness is chastised by the faith of the Gentiles. The Jew drove away the Lord; Egypt received him. The Gentiles are to be preferred to the Jews in faith, 151. Christ’s infancy is troubled. They hope neither for pardon nor correction. The message of salvation, when badly received by the Jew, is turned into ruin. He prepares death for the newborn Lord. How the Hebrew ox recognized his Lord, 159. The cruelty of the Jews is indicated by the faith of the Magi, 160. Jewish soil gave weeds instead of wheat and thorns instead of vines, 164.

Allegorically, how the father is divided against the son and the son against the father. Christ’s glory is punishment for him. The Jewish father is separated from Christ the Son through envy. Judaea is preached to by John, 167. The Jewish house is blind, 169. He was a murderer of the law before he was a murderer of Christ. He turned the body of the Decalogue against Christ. If the Jews had believed that the Lord was God, they would not have come to the abyss of ruin. He washes vessels for purification, but not himself, 171. Through envy they were killers of God—not by deed, but by will, 172. The Jew is the blind man healed by Christ: how, 176. See **Pharisee**, **Scribe**, **Law**.

**Herod.** Like a fox, 19. An enemy of Christ. The evils he inflicted on the Hebrews, 86. He violated the sacred custom of the priesthood, 89. He did not dare to act against Zechariah. An impious king. Twenty of his reproaches are enumerated, 127. He swallowed John’s blood. A perverse judge, and in what manner. He rages because he is reproved. His dancing girl, 5. See below **Dancing girls**. He died on his birthday. He killed the infants, 146.

Through Herod the devil sought Christ’s death, and why, 150. For the sake of a temporal kingdom he seeks to extinguish the eternal one, 152. He grieves that he was deceived and kills the innocent. His vices. Christ flees from him. The evils into which he falls. He seeks Christ with swords. What evil a ruler of the people does. He prepared everything for accusation and punishment, nothing for defense.

What the tyrant Herod did to the Jews, 156. Troubled by Christ’s infancy, described at length, 158. Why he secretly summons the Magi. He fears the kingdom, not God. Why he says, “Report back to me.” He was the devil’s lieutenant. Why he wished to go to the child. He signifies the devil, 159. Through envy he rages against the children, 172.

In ignorance he confesses, because the one he killed rises again in Christ, 173. Why did he kill John, who was to rise again? A witness to his crime. He is praised ironically. Why is he silent—why did he behead John? Herod and Herodias are alike in name and life. What she did, and what Herod did because of her. He judges according to drunkenness. Earth and heaven shuddered at the bloody dishes of Herod’s banquet, 174.

A son of night, not of day. He calls all the powers to share his banquet and witness his crime. Herod believes his daughter is dancing when he sees her behaving shamelessly. The flesh overwhelmed by drunkenness in Herod: what it promised, and why. What his banquet caused. While he forswears decency, he swears to virtue. He killed repentance in John’s death. Herod and Herodias—names joined in crime—believe that they kill a voice: their contrasts with John. The Herodians joined with the Hebrews, 32. See **Dancing girls**, **Drunkenness**, **Fasting**, **John the Baptist**, **History**.

A historical account is to be raised to a higher understanding, 36. Whoever clings only to bare history dishonors God by his expression, 95.

A murderer has no love, 152. The murdered John condemned murder, 174.

**Human being / man.** Namely, the good things of a human being. He is called the Son of God, 10. Whatever is born and whatever exists owes everything to God, 6. Let him answer to his nature, 10. Let stones be changed into human beings, 13. At Christ’s presence he is freed from punishment, 16–17. Let him keep watch day and night, and for what purpose, 21. Let him store his treasure in heaven, 22. Let him spare himself, 23. He is bound by a small document, 25. He possesses what he can give to the poor, 41. Let him flee to God, 45. Let him be converted at God’s voice, 46. Salvation comes to him from the Lord’s going out and coming in, 49. Through birth he is born so that he may recognize divine love, 55. He is often born in the seventh month, 56. From Christ he receives a new birth, 57. Let him be cleansed as he approaches God, 59. In the darkness of night let him seek the lamp of Christ’s Word, 64.

That a human being should be given to heaven is more terrifying than that God should be given to the earth, 67. He is God’s son by grace and a servant, 67. All created things were made for the human being, 69. Let him return to the God who loves him, 70. Let him cry to God: “Deliver us from evil.” He calls God “Father” after God has commanded it, 71. Let him display heavenly life. The Son of God is designated in the form of a servant. That the human being is God, the creature marvels, 72. From his mother’s womb he acknowledges the Father in heaven. Since God always spares him, let him not fear accusations.

Human thoughts. See **Thought**.

Let the human being be his own physician through faith, 83. How much he owes God, 94. He is acquitted by love. The kingdom of heaven is compared with a human being, 96. In God’s calling, the human being is sought; persons are not distinguished, 99. The human being is more delightful to the world, but not more useful—and why, 101. How he ought to give thanks. At the beginning he was raised from clay; at the end he will be raised from dust, 103.

Let all human beings be both sacrifice and priests, 108. Let him bring a sacrifice pleasing to God, 109. He pleases God by living well. He becomes a sacrifice if he offers himself in holiness. If he gives what he can, he is accepted, 110. Let him die for Christ. Let him be a sinner, so that God may be just, 112. Through the grace of the Creator he returns to life. In baptism he becomes a dwelling place of virtues, 113. Let the new human being exchange vices for virtues.

God seeks the human being solely out of love for the human being, 114. The human being dies to the law, 115. Let him bring fruit to God, not to the earth. Let him anticipate and trample down sins, 116. Through Christ he began to seek freedom. Taught by the law how difficult virtue was, and how numerous the sins, and so forth. Two human beings—namely Adam and Christ—gave the human race its beginning, 117.

Let the earthly human being become heavenly and bear the image of the Creator, 7. The just human being is greater than heaven and the angels, 120. If he has no coin, let him give the poor a hand, 122. Let him accuse himself as a debtor to God and pray that God forgive him, 123. Before human beings he boasts of his justice and so forth, but not before God. He is Christ’s steward, appointed to cultivate the world, 125. He desires to do good when death takes away the time for doing it. Let human beings acknowledge themselves stewards, not masters.

Let him follow God and not seek to go before him, 131. God is shown in human form so that he may be seen. Human piety and skill perfect the human being, 132. His diligence is to be honored by God. By the same courses he returns to life by which he had slipped away toward death, 142. Made from untouched clay, 148. Precious to God. For what purpose he was made. The house of the world was made for him. Made from earth so that he might be lord of earthly things and share in heavenly things—how. The image of God, God’s deputy in earthly matters. The human being is God’s property, whereas previously he was God’s likeness. Created with dominion over the earth so that he might possess delights.

Without the human being, the human being could not be saved, 151. Made perfect for life, restored to perfect life. Let him draw human beings away from sins, 155. He owes more to God than to a human being, 161. What God has done for the human being in natural things; what in supernatural things. Freed from servitude to all, let him serve God alone, 161. The Lord gently encourages the sinful human being. Through grace he is a co-heir of God, 162. Let him not seek a division of heavenly things. How he ought to possess the inheritance with Christ. What he should do if he eats everything, 163.

God stretches the human being into the form of Christ so that he may be beautiful. Once corrected by God, he immediately receives consolation. He has God as Father and a heavenly dwelling prepared. Formerly brought forth for death, now brought forth for life, 166. God’s benefits toward human beings, in the various forms and appearances of God, at length, 170. What he gives to those invited to works. How he triumphs over the devil. Let one human being not shrink from another, 176. By leading the blind man by the hand, let him make him, through light, unaware of blindness.

The human being always lives by the heavenly Word, but not always by earthly bread, 11. From what he becomes an angel and receives the honor of Divinity, 43.

**The evils of the human being.** He sinned through envy in paradise, 4. A slave of cruel masters, 6. After fasting he seeks bread, 12. Easily falls, difficult to rise. He falls, and God ascends, 13. Human servants lie prostrate and suffer evils as punishment, 15. In despair the human being cannot help his own servants. He is buried alive by the demon, 16. The demon prevents him from going to God. How the possessed person is tormented by the devil, 17.

He marvels at Christ’s power, 20. He is scourged by God because of sins, 20. When he is idle and asleep, Christ is said to sleep in his ship, 21. He is a beast, and in what manner, 23. The clever man generates scandal, 27. He is represented by the man who had the withered hand, 32. What his harsh condition is, 34. Voluntary in offenses, involuntary in punishments, 35. Accustomed to dread wounds more than to cure them, 36. Driven from paradise by a counsel of impiety, 44. What is weaker than a human being, and in what way, 45. He sins, and God turns toward him—how, 45. He is in the darkness of night, 64.

Nature cannot receive the grace of the Lord’s Prayer. See **The Lord’s Prayer**. Raised upward by grace, he lies below by nature, 68. He cannot grasp the greatness of divine charity, 69. By his own strength he is not freed from the devil, 70. He grieves at his death and attacks so that he may not be able to rise again, 74.

The human being feared the angel when he looked back, 88. He is never secure concerning his conscience, 88. His nature is weak in relation to divine virtues, 90. Before experience he presumes too greatly on himself. He is born for labors, groans, and dangers; he wants good things but does not do them, along with his other evils, 90. He knows the faults of bodies but is ignorant of the vices of the mind, 91. He sins in heart, thought, doubt, and trembling, 91. What is above human beings the human being cannot adequately report. Human speech is useless where an angelic proclamation is present. He has been dragged from the paradise of delights to death, 96.

Why he perishes by death, 101. He made creatures into gods for himself. Made from dust, he gave everything to nature and himself, nothing to God; and why God permits him to be returned to dust, 101. Sterile or ungrateful, the human being deserves to be cut off from life, 106. If an idle human being rules peoples, he becomes harmful to himself and many others. A human being scarcely dies for a just person, because necessity drives him to death, 110.

Through the human being sin entered the world, and through sin death, at length, 111, passim. He could not be saved without Christ, and why, 111. Human beings share Adam’s guilt and punishment, 112. Formerly a receptacle of vices, 113. He possesses nothing of his own. He is not strong enough to obey the commandments of the law, 114. Devoted to flesh and the world, he leaves nothing in himself that belongs to the life to come. His whole life is disturbed by passions, 115. The old human being lost all discipline, 115.

Without Christ the human being knew sins not so as to conquer them, but to commit them, 116. The human being’s strength is reduced to ashes by the burning of vices. He began to desire virtues but to follow vices. A captive and slave under the law. How he is born in sins, 117. Buried in vices, 120. The human being is the grave of the human being. The human being neglects the human being, 121. The same person is the son who squandered his substance, 125. Let human beings acknowledge themselves stewards, not masters. Whoever fears human beings rather than God in legal matters easily departs from justice, 127.

The human being does not consider how great God is, but only that he exists, 131. The demon does not want human beings to be eternal—or even temporal. Why the human being dies. In the cradle the human being lies hidden within the human being: he is a body and is not, 132. Out of fear human beings were drawn to idols, 147. He is worthless to himself who is precious to God, 148. What good things he lost through the devil’s envy. His evils from original sin. Enveloped in the darkness of ignorance, 160. Why he owes more to God than to a human being, 161.

He renders no service to God. He is useless for divine and human things. He moves about in the mud of the flesh, in the clay of the body. He lost part of his substance, and hence became an exile from paradise, 162. The most ungrateful of all human beings. He was with Christ in paradise and perished outside Christ. Doubting the divine promises, he is rebuked, 163. Those born before the Flood were brought forth for death, 166. The minds and senses of human beings are struck by the evil lightning, 171. From human beings, against human beings, nations go forth to war. They seek a human being’s reputation from his ruin. Human beings are like walking trees, 176.

An hour is called a point and a moment of time, 112. The twelve hours of Christ’s day are the twelve apostles, 170.

**Garden.** How the garden of the Church is mystically cultivated and sown, 98. It produces its shoots, 130.

**Guest.** Christ is received in the guest, 39. Once the guest has been received, Christ is bound to assist the one who received him. The merit of the host is made known by the preparation of the lodging, 92. In the figure of a guest God appeared to Abraham, 131. Chrysologus was a guest, 138, passim. What a worldly guest, once received, is accustomed to do, 18. Those who unjustly drive guests from their own dwellings, so that they may be punished, 47. The hospitality of humanity becomes a temple of Divinity, 144. Its indignity remains in the guest’s injury, 15. God entered the lodging of our flesh. See **Dwelling**, **House**.

**Sacrifice.** The human being is both sacrifice and priest: he is slain and lives, and how, 108. Christ is a living sacrifice, and in what manner. Let the whole human being be a sacrifice pleasing to God, 109. And he will be so if he offers himself to God in holiness. The spotless sacrifice pleases God; the stained one provokes him. How the living sacrifice and rational service are to be offered to God. How the sacrifice of fasting is to be offered, 13. What sacrifice we ought to offer to God, which also remains for us, 43.

An earthly enemy cannot prevail against heavenly things, 12. A sudden and destructive enemy, 27. He seeks a commander rather than a soldier, and does not besiege the dead but the living, 96. It is better often to bring victory over enemies to one’s king than to die once, 128. To trouble the enemy with his own sword is a mark of courage, 157. An enemy is more tolerable when he batters the walls from outside, 171. Whoever has an enemy within cannot free himself by his own power. The wicked act against others so that they may be punished, 67.

When we understand human things, we are blinded by ourselves, 76. Human salvation is restored along the same lines by which it was lost, 77. The human becomes divine, God willing, 102. The whole life of a human being is brief for learning human things thoroughly, 112. The things of God cannot be grasped by us, 62. Christ’s humanity displays charity, 47. Where there is no sign of humanity, there is a sign of Divinity, 153. There is no human understanding in one who does not forgive his brother’s sins, 139.

**Humility.** The humility of the centurion, 15. Humility toward others should be learned from our own weakness, 88. It raises us to the heavenly table, 100. Voluntary humility is a great virtue, 136. It excuses one from speaking and compels one to obey, 138. It is the mother of teaching, 161. It acquired what pride lost, 23.

**Dropsy.** The dropsical man thirsts by drinking, 7.

**Hypocrisy.** What it is, its effects, names, and evils, 7. It labors in vain. It is shipwrecked in harbor. The hypocrite is a usurer. From remedies he creates diseases. He causes harm to himself, not to God. Hypocrisy is fasting without mercy, 8. What hypocrisy does, 9. It is blind and blinds the eyes. It must be avoided, and why, 9. It is an appearance composed by art: in reality it does one thing, while by his expression he promises another, 172. What hypocrisy does together with envy. In secret the hypocrite does nothing secretly, 9.

## I
## Idol

The burdens of idols are heavier than those of the Synagogue, 105. The Synagogue flees to the brothels of idols, 115. Idols perished at the preaching of the apostles, 170. On idolatry, 5, at the end.

The ignorant speak foolishly, 19. They are deceived by coarse figs, 106. The ignorant do not receive Christ.

## Sloth

The sloth of human beings is called sleep, 21. He is excessively slothful who, after an example has been given, is found careless, 79. The slothful person does not understand Christ’s obscure sayings and deeds, 96. Prosperity does not raise up the slothful, 124. How the slothful person harms others while presiding over them, 106.

## Fire

Divine fire does not know how to burn the merciful, 42. It pants while enclosed in flesh and performs other evils, 57. Heavenly fire cleanses the lips and satisfies the heart. It grows cold in stone and lies hidden in iron, 96; and it is kindled by their striking together. Earthly fires must not be brought near divine ones, 109. Feverish fire is kindled in the body from cold moisture, 114. What fire is to grain, vices are to the human body, 116. What sort the rich man’s fire was, 122. The fire of hell was extinguished in part by Christ for the saints, 123. A drop of water does not extinguish the fire of hell, 124. Fire is scattered by Christ through his words, 164. The cultivator purifies the field with fire. By it the crops of the nations are purified. Why it is applied to the apostles. Water presses fire, and fire multiplies the wave. The fire of Gehenna, burning the guilty, serves the innocent, 166. Fire in the bush and in the pillar, 170. The fire of the Holy Spirit. See Holy Spirit.

## Ignorance

One who sins through ignorance will not escape his punishment, 26. Sins of ignorance are not avoided, 30. It carries disgust within itself, [Col. 1177] 98. What the ignorance of human beings has done, 112. Vices are killed by ignorance, 116. Human ignorance is removed by the law, 116. Sin buried in our ignorance. God comes to the aid of ignorance out of pity, 157. Mortal humanity wrapped in the darknesses of ignorance, 160.

The Apostle adapted the enticements of temporal things to human consciences, 114. We must struggle against the enticements of sins for heavenly glory, 119. One overcome by enticements does not want Christ to come, 158. Why a person is compelled to endure them, 117.

Illumination comes from God, 126. The illumination of the Church was accomplished by the children of Saint Felicity, 134. The illumination of the Magi. See Magus.

## Image

How Christ’s image must be borne by us, 117. Perfect devotion gives to an image what it gives to a king, 147. The human being is the image of God, 148. Why images painted of kings or brothers are made with concord, 149. Whoever bears the person of an idol did not wish to bear the image of God, 155. See Magus.

## Sacrifice

We ought to sacrifice the inward parts of virtues to God, and how, 108. The life of virtues is sacrificed to God through the death of vices. The best things must be sacrificed to God, 109. See Offering; Sacrifice.

## Ruler

The anger of a ruler is law to the subject, 161. He who shamelessly presumes to obtain repentance for others, while having provided nothing for his own pardon, 123.

## Impiety

What impiety has done to the already-created human being, 137. It is always feverish, 173. It incautiously takes witnesses of the crime and judges of the deed, 174. How it teaches, 44, and concerning it throughout the series.

The impious person, departing from God, dies away from himself and does not stand in the council, 44. He is carried now toward heaven, now toward earth, and does not know himself. What the counsel of impiety has done. He derives a taste from the fatness of sins. He departs from God when he sins. When the impious person rages, the pious person is disturbed, 47. He turns away from God, 48. Sometimes he speaks the truth against his will, 49. God wants the impious person to return, not to perish, 51. It must be charged against the impious if they do not receive the grace of charity, 55. The impious person falls, is destroyed, and cannot stand, 75. Possessed by the earth, and by death in the resurrection of the just, 77. Fear terrifies the impious person, 80. He is assured by Thomas concerning Christ’s resurrection, 84. He will fear heavenly power, 88. He stands at the crossroads, 89. Counselor of himself. See Counsel.

Their souls are reclaimed by the ministers of Tartarus, 104. The son’s impiety is revealed more clearly by the father’s piety, 123. One is not pious who is not pious toward another. The impious and the just were in hell before Christ’s Resurrection, 123. If one is impious toward himself, toward whom is he pious? Piety must not be shown to the impious, 127. What reward his character gives him. If the impious person is against the just, he is deadly to himself, 173. See Sinner.

## Immodest

Chastity is hostile to the immodest, 127. An immodest woman born from an immodest woman, 174.

## To Walk

Whoever does not stand at the crossroads of sinners walks on and does other things, 89. Those who run by means of virtues walk onward and attain the fullness of the commandments, 9.

Arabic incense is not smelled by God as willingly as the holiness of a sincere heart, 87. Incense consists of frankincense and pure supplication. What kind of incense mystically illuminates the Church, 134. It is owed to God, 157.

## Fire, Conflagration

A feverish conflagration is extinguished by heat and nourished by cold, 114. It is unquenchable because of the burning of vices, 116. Who, ignorant of the smoke, passes through the conflagrations of desires, 89.

## Unbelief

Unbelief is the daughter of death: what it persuades a person to do, 118.

Unworthy things must not be requested from God, and why, 132. A promise is not given to the unworthy, 100.

## Unteachable

The unteachable person, striving toward lofty things, is plunged into the depths, 119. Christ avoids him for his salvation. He tires the teacher’s intellect, 106.

## Indulgence

One must repent during the time of indulgence, 46. The indulgence of the ancient law toward priests, 92. Great indulgence arising from great guilt, 93. See Pardon; Remission; Repentance.

Indulgence lies down so that it may raise sinners to pardon, 30. The right of indulgence belongs to the person who forgives his neighbor’s debts, 71. What things seek the indulgence of the just, 43.

## Skill

So that human industry may be honored, God conceals the divine mystery in human speech, 132; and elsewhere, etc., 96, from the beginning.

## Infancy; Infant

How the children were once handed over to the devil, 51. An infant is filled with a demon when he is offered by his parents to the devil for healing. The glory of Christian infancy, 68. The infancy of the Church in the time of Saint Apollinaris, 128.

Infancy possesses everything, more through tears than through the measure of strength. The human being lies hidden in the infant, and is developed through human labor, 132. He has a cry derived from the word of God, 144. Infants are not condemned, descriptively, 152. An infant is described as dying joyfully. The infant regards every person not as an enemy but as a parent. Unacquainted with suffering, he seized the palms of martyrdom, 153. The infant seeks nourishment from the breasts with tears, 158. He conquers barbarism, power, and so forth, and demands love.

The infancy of Christ troubles Jerusalem.

## Hell

By devouring Christ, hell incurred a fast, 37. [Col. 1178] It gives Christ, taken away from the Jews, to the nations. It prepares a dwelling for Christ. The life swallowed down is torn apart, 57. Its dreadful servitude, 65. There is no pardon in it, 66. Christ teaches us its evils. When the Lord rises, the realms below are halted, 74. It lost its prisoners when the Lord descended to it, 78. Its prison is destroyed, 82. In it sinners live for punishment and perish from life, 96. Its flame belongs not so much to the tongue as to the mind and conscience, 122. The members that sinned more greatly here are tortured more greatly in hell. Purple does not withstand it, and the naked person sweats in it. Before Christ’s resurrection it held the impious and the just, 123.

Its gates were closed against souls by bronze doors and iron bars. Christ opened it. Death is the parent of hell, 118. The condemned lie in it, 123. We would not believe one returning from the dead. Let us strive to avoid its evils, 123 and 124. It is the pit of sin, 170. It snatches sinners naked toward punishment. In it there are groaning and gnashing, 174. See Condemned; Gehenna; Fire; Tartarus.

## Unbeliever

For unbelievers, the sacrament of faith without faith is destructive, 60. The sacrament of faith must not be disclosed in writing among unbelievers, 61. For them the day grows dark, 75. He is unworthy, 102. He plunges himself into the darkness of unbelief, 131. He neither hears nor sees what the believer hears, and so forth. Their punishment overflows into the glory of the faithful, 132.

Those baptized and instructed by Chrysologus, 58, 57, throughout, and 56–62, 67–72. See Faithless.

Unbelief must be avoided, lest it bring us back under the power of the devil, 18. Because of the Hebrews’ unbelief, not even one demon is driven captive from the body, 51. It harms the son through the father. Cunning has no excuse, 102. See Faithlessness.

## Weak Things

When they are recited, they cast down the spirit, 150.

## Weakness

Weakness does not stand where Christ is, 18. Nothing is weaker than the human being, and why, 45. Let the weak person return to the heavenly physician. There is no place for weakness where virtue has been joined to virtue, 57. Where weakness is unknown, Christ first directs his care there, 94. Human weakness wants but cannot, 100. It bent the woman down, 105, throughout. It cannot bear the greatness of light with the eyes, 112. Weakness must be blamed so that forgiveness may be given to a brother, 139. One weakness belongs to the body, another to the mind, 164. Why the same weakness was healed in different ways by the Lord, 176. At Christ’s nod weaknesses perish.

What is familiar, when it becomes public, brings pain and shame, 15. Its weariness remains where art heals but virtue does not, 18. See Sickness; Frailty; Fever.

The weak person is disturbed by evils, 47. He does not heal the weak person who seeks and awaits his will, 114. He lies in bed, 14. His desires are foolish, 50.

## Head-Dress; Insignia

Whoever does not possess the insignia of dignity does not usurp the name of dignity, 109. When death lost the insignia of its power, 10. Whoever does not forgive his neighbor’s sins loses in himself the insignia of divine power, 139. Who possesses eternal insignia, 144. The eunuch exchanged the insignia of the palace, 56.

## Intellect

How the intellect of an experienced teacher is wearied in teaching uneducated students, 106. It is corrupted by deceits, 116.

## Ingratitude

What the ingratitude of a sick person toward God the physician has caused, 131. The ungrateful person is led to punishment, not by wealth or poverty but by his spirit, 124. The human being is the most ungrateful of all, 162. How he may rightly be punished, 66.

## Enemy

One must spare an enemy, extensively, 38, also by Christ’s example. Forgiving him is beneficial, 67. His sins must be forgiven, and so forth, 68. Whoever forgives an enemy everything owes the Lord nothing concerning his own offenses, 70 and 71. See Pardon; Devil.

The enemy’s sins must be forgiven, extensively, 129. What harm an external and an internal enemy cause, 171.

## Iniquity

Iniquity established by Herod is unsheathed, 152. Iniquity is always friendly to the one who hates righteousness. It is in the streets, 95.

## Injury

Injury must be endured with an even mind, throughout, 38. To endure injury is divine philosophy. Those who inflict injury on their neighbor are mad and must therefore be healed through piety, 38. Christ grows indignant when an injury is said to be inflicted upon him in place of honor, 48. The injury to the Creator is avoided by the whole creation, 78. The injury to the human body was removed in Christ’s Nativity, 144. Without human injuries, human injury could not have been cut away, 151.

## Innocent

An innocent person is not regarded as such on earth without Christ, 30. The resurrection of the innocent will be a terror to the impious, 77. Who is innocent amid the whirlpools of vices and the slippery course of life? 89. An innocent person summoned to guilt, while eagerly seeking purification, provokes the investigator, 97. While an innocent person is punished, guilt rebounds upon the judge, 112. When an innocent person accuses the guilty, the judge is freely entreated for mercy, 122. An innocent person is not easily condemned by the guilty, 173. If he is accused, what then? 175. What will one innocent from the beginning be at the end? 91.

The innocent martyrs killed by Herod, 146. Why, 146 and 152, throughout, very fully. Their only crime was that they had been born, 152. They are soldiers of Christ’s innocence, the guards of the cradles. Born for martyrdom, not for the age. They changed mourning into joy. They themselves were baptized in blood, their mothers in tears. They die rejoicing. They desire to die before their king rather than to die with him, descriptively, 153. How they are martyrs of grace. Their martyrdom compared with virginity. Christ flees so that he may have them, lest the Synagogue hold them. Killed because of Christ’s infancy, 158.

Our innocence comes not from ourselves but from the pardon of the heavenly Father, 4. It admits us to God’s presence, 6. It is never naked, 73. A person who wrongly glories in his innocence is led into the debt and punishment of his parent, 112. Let the one who has hitherto tried to extinguish it die for it, 113. It must be embraced in the risen Christ. For a long time humanity did not know how innocence could be difficult, 116. It is taken away by money, 126. Freedom becomes hateful to its enemies, 127. Innocence is the first happiness, and how, 167. Whoever preserves what has been entrusted to innocence does not pay the interest of repentance. See Just; Integrity.

## Ambusher

The ambusher hides in the nights, attacks sleepers, and flees the watchful, 97.

## Folly

Folly is sometimes deceived, but affection is not deceived, 25.

## Instrument

The instrument that was an occasion of destruction can become an occasion of salvation, 126.

## Understanding

Understanding concerns hidden things, not things seen, 14. Its power lies in seeing the nakedness of the poor. Christ is understood to be present in the poor person. A lesser understanding of the Scriptures produces destruction, 52. The human understanding is sharpened by the Lord’s obscure words, 96. It is a great tree, 98. By the height of understanding, the whole person is raised toward heaven. Human and divine matters are not perfectly grasped throughout the whole of human life, 112. Let the Christian understand himself, 113. Understanding can kindly lift up those whom severe examination burdens, 126. Human understanding does not easily grasp evangelical meanings.

## Intention

God judges from intention, not from works, 9. How inward sins may be cleansed and driven away, 171.

## Interpreter

What the interpreter of the letter does, 32. Of the word of God. See Word of God.

## Integrity

Integrity is punishment to the corrupt, 127. Integrity, as a witness to innocence, drives away fear, 144. The integrity of Mary. See Virgin Mary.

## Intercession

The intercession of the Church. See Church.

## To Enter

We can enter God’s presence, if not by place, then by the heart, 6.

## To Find

Whoever finds what he lost gives away his faults, turns anger into joy, and changes grief into grace, 168. It is more pleasing for us to have found lost things than not to have lost what was preserved. Things found delight us more than things subjected, 96.

## Envy

The envy of the Hebrews toward Christians, 4, throughout. It admits neither piety nor charity. It disperses the reason of nature: the ancient evil, and other things; the evil of the angel, the human being, and the Hebrew arms itself against Christ and shakes the heart and soul. It must be avoided. It drives away joy. It tolerates no companion. It pretends; it lies. It grieves over another’s good, not over its own loss. The envious person is greedy. Envy destroys all good things, 5. Whoever, raised to the highest things, casts himself down to the lowly envies himself, 25. How, in order to join, it separates accustomed things, 31. It blinds and darkens the mind, 48. Its evils are shown by examples, 48. It is an incurable evil, and many other things concerning it. It is avoided by flight.

The envy of the Hebrews toward Christ, 49. What the spirit of envy, the devil, does, 97. The envy of the Jews deprived them of law and grace, 102. The rich man’s envy toward Lazarus, 122. It is grievous to the wicked to see those happy whom they once held in contempt. Envy closes the eyes, 131. Where it leads is shown by Herod’s savagery, 152. What evil the envious person does, 168. It was driven away from heavenly things together with the devil, 168. The envy of the Pharisees, 172.

What evil envy, the executioner of its own people, does. Whoever admits it endures his own punishments. Another person’s good is punishment to the envious; it is a manifold evil and must immediately be fled. It is a disease. What it persuaded the experts in the law to do. The evils envy caused, extensively through examples. Christ stripped it of its advantages. What it did among the Pharisees. Envy serves its own people together with hypocrisy. The torch of envy. See Malice; Zeal. It is an evil eye, 139.

## Anger

Anger must be extinguished in its very sparks, 38. Otherwise it is not calmed by blood. How it is conquered. What it is like in God, 45. Why David asks to be reproved by God, but not in anger. The wrath to come will be eternal condemnation in Tartarus, 137. The anger of a ruler is law to the subject, 161. How it is nourished by a demon, 16.

## Isaac

Isaac rejoices when he becomes a victim, 55.

## Isaiah

Isaiah is an evangelist no less than a prophet, 57. He is touched by grief because he cannot proclaim what he has perceived concerning God. He is purified by a seraph. Why he saw God in royal attire, 131. He foretold that a virgin would give birth to God, 146.

## Journey

The journey to God is made not by the steps of the feet but by the movement of the mind, 3. The journey to God the Father is a shortcut of the way of salvation. The journey of the nations from God to the devil was in the mind, not in place, 5. When entering upon the journey of fasting, one must lay aside other concerns, 8. Christ’s journey to death and glory, 19. The human being endured the sweat and labors of the earthly journey fruitlessly for a long time, 175. To provide a journey for a poor person is more than to give him a fragment of bread, 176. [Col. 1180]

# J

## To Lie

The servants of human beings lie prostrate, and why, 15. We lie in vices, and lie oppressed, 54.

Jacob was more mystical than deceitful; he represented us beneath goatskins, 73. God, traveling with him as a companion, met him as he journeyed and wrestled with him, 131. What God does with him so that he may be loved rather than feared, 147. Why his name was changed, 154. Jacob triumphs before he lives, 70.

Why the blessed Virgin was not entrusted to the apostle James, 49.

A closed door does not deny its creator entrance and exit, 84. The human being was the door of death through which sin entered, 111. The gate of hell. See Hell. The gates of the lower world were shattered by the ram of the Lord’s cross, 123.

## Fasting

What fasting can do is shown by the hunger of the prodigal, 2, and by other examples. It is the first virtue for us, 7. During fasting, what it means to anoint the head and wash the face. Fasting without mercy hungers and grows cold, 8. Mercy is the springtime of the land of fasting, and other things. Various definitions or epithets of fasting, 8. It conquers under the leadership of mercy. Its wings are mercy and piety. Without mercy it is an image of hunger, greed, and hypocrisy.

Fasting is lifted up by heavenly harmony, 10. The weapons of fasting must be taken up against the devil, 11. What must be done during fasting, 12, throughout. Our fasting is the devil’s hunger. Its essence and power. It conquers the devil, 12 and 13. The person who fasts is believed to be God, 13. It is placed before all virtues. It is feared by the devil. What the devil’s temptations are during fasting. How the sacrifice of fasting must be offered to God. Let it be voluntary, 31. It is the plow of holiness. Why Christ’s disciples do not fast, etc., extensively throughout, 31.

Fasting cleanses bodies of the filth of carnal sins, 31. True fasting must not be mixed with deceitful fasting. One must fast at Christ’s command, 41. Let it be accompanied by mercy. Thus it will possess many virtues. At length: fasting without piety fasts, 42. Without mercy it is the hunger of greed, and other things, 1. The seeds of fasting must be cast into the tears of the poor, 42. It totters without mercy. Let it be accompanied by mercy and prayer, 43, throughout. Fasting has weariness. It must be offered to God so that gluttony may cease, 108. Why Lent was instituted and how it ought to be observed, extensively, 166. See Abstinence; Lent.

## Jephthah’s Daughter

Jephthah’s daughter dies rejoicing, 55.

## Jericho

Why Christ walks through it, 54.

## Jeroboam

Jeroboam caused a scandal among the people, 27.

## Jerusalem

Why Jerusalem is troubled at Christ’s birth, 158.

## Jesus

Why Jesus is called the son of a carpenter and of Mary, 48. Jesus is called from salvation, 57 and 59. The only Son by nature. Jesus in Hebrew; *Salvator* in Latin, 60. Born of Mary, he is the Son of God. The name Jesus is confessed submissively by heaven and hell, 61. He is called Savior, 142 and 144. In that name the whole majesty of the Godhead is worshiped by all, 144. His power and authority. Who Jesus born of the Virgin is, 145. He lies in a stable, 152. What Jesus’ Nativity is, and for what purpose, 156.

## John the Baptist

What John the Baptist accomplished through the power of fasting and prayer, 43. His epithets, 86. He was a lamp gradually showing the Lord, 87. When he is called an angel. He exults in the womb. A prophet in the womb. Son of the sacrament, and his other epithets, 88.

The joy of all, great before the Lord. Why he would not drink wine. His privileges. The forerunner of Christ. He possessed the spirit of Elijah. He represents Elijah and Christ through his virtues. Bound in chains, extinguished through adulteries, 89. Why he did not die an ordinary death. An angel on earth rendered obedience to God. Praised through the original glory of his parents. He is wholly holiness, 89. All first things, including firstborn things, ought to be owed to him. What happened for an angel to be born. His praises derived from the angel, 90. What he did for Christ, and why, 90. He is born from a barren woman, and why, 90. He granted his father pardon before he washed away the sins of the peoples. He is called “son” because of his uniqueness, 91. Greater than a human being, equal to the angels, and other things, 91.

Lucifer, herald, trumpet, angel; and the other things that he, the morning herald, did, 91, very fully. The stranger marvels at himself in the womb, 92. Voice, trumpet, and herald are born from silence, 92. His praises, 127. He is handed over to the adulterous woman. He is bound so that there may be no place for pardon. He rebuked Herod lest he perish. He gives offense because he reproves. His beheading is described most fully. He was born for his own death, 127.

He prepares new fields of the Gospel for the nations, 137. Why the word of the Lord was upon John, not to John. Why “voice,” not “word.” Why he came to the Jordan. What his baptism was like. He reproves by example so that he may change morals and nature. He calls the Hebrews broods of vipers. He holds Christ in the Jordan for those about to receive pardon, 160. Fearless among heavenly things. Born for the love of God, 2. Teacher and master of repentance, 167. He urges repentance. Through what deserts he preached. He received a garment of camel’s hair. When he fed on locusts and honey. The burning lamp finds Christ, the drachma, 169.

How he rose again from Herod’s statement, 173. He came for the healing of all. By the outpouring of his blood he extinguished the whole brood of the ancient serpent. His head is carried on a costly platter, 174. He was like a lamp upon a lampstand and like a judge on a tribunal. Killed, he condemned homicide. Though killed, he cries throughout the whole world. He is born when Herod perishes. Contrasts between John and Herod. In many respects he surpasses Joseph. Greater among those born of women because he reproved adulteresses and trampled underfoot licit intercourse with women. He did not escape the dangers of women. Greater among those born of women because of fasting, 12. Recognizing God in the womb, he reports him to his mother, 70. See Herod.

## John the Evangelist

He fled so as not to deny Christ, 150. Why the blessed Virgin was entrusted to him, not to James his brother, 49. During the Passion he fled naked, but his flight covered him, 78. Why he fled during the Passion, 170.

## Jonah

The prophet Jonah was a figure of the Lord, 37, throughout.

## Jordan

Why Christ enters the channel of the Jordan, 160. What things took place in it. If the Jordan fled at the presence of the legal Ark, why did it not flee at the presence of the Trinity?

## Joseph

Whether the Virgin lost her virginity through the incarnation of the Word, 140. How he was just if he did not wish to investigate his betrothed’s conception, 145. He was pious and just. His troubled mind is described. In him the whole lineage of David is named, 145. Born in the twenty-eighth generation from David. In him the faith of the promise is fulfilled. He is admonished not to fear the circumstances of his betrothed. He was secure concerning Mary’s conscience. The angel’s speech with Joseph concerning the Virgin’s conception.

How Joseph, the bridegroom, fulfills the figure of Christ the bridegroom of the Church; in the other Joseph he foreshadows the Passion of Christ, 146. Joseph, husband in name, bridegroom in conscience, anxious about his pregnant betrothed, descriptively, 175. Immediately an angel meets him, and why. He was afraid because, in the matter, there was very great fear, 175. Joseph the patriarch is compared with John the Baptist, 174.

## Jubilation

Sweet jubilation leads sheep to pasture, 6. How one must rejoice before God, 46 and following. What kind of jubilation David invites us to, 6. Pastoral jubilation inclines sheep toward pasture, 23. The jubilee brings one to the complete fullness of pardon and remission, and how, 139.

## Judas

Judas caused the scandal of scandals, 27. He dragged the stone, Christ, into the scandal of the weak, so that he might prepare not the bread of life but the bread of sorrow. What gold did to him, 29. How he shakes Christ’s ship, 37. In his mind the devil, conceiving the fruit of deceit, gave birth to the crime of betrayal, 19.

## Jew

See Hebrew.

## Judge

The judge acts from his own judgment; the executioner from another’s, 17. The judge will endure the heavenly Judge of his own judgment, 26. When he wishes to forgive, he looks at the person, not the fault, 54. Why God the Judge assumed the person of the guilty, 90. Touched by a supplicant defendant, he is not defiled, 94. One does not enter before the judge without being summoned, 102. Guilt rebounds upon him if he strikes an innocent person with punishment, 112. The person whom an innocent confessor accuses freely entreats the judge for mercy, 122. God the Judge was seen by Daniel, 131. Which persons the Judge reproves and judges, 152. John’s head on a platter was a Judge shining on a tribunal, 174.

## Judgment

At the final judgment, while God is silent about other matters, he will cry out concerning mercy toward the poor, 14. The poor person will be an advocate on the day of judgment. The Judge is a debtor to the person who lends to the poor. Through judgment everything had perished, but mercy came to the aid, 42. It was preserved for the day of death so that we might repent. The person who practices mercy is not judged for his crime.

What the approaching judgment accomplished among human beings, 47. Separation at the judgment consoles the saints, 47. Why Christ is judged by the Hebrews, 49. Judgment will be made of the living and the dead, and how, 57. The person who lives badly does not believe in judgment, 59. At it the earth trembles, 77. It is the terror of the impious. Judgment will reveal what each person was, 97. God’s judgment is the harvest-time of human beings. How God’s profound judgments can be known, 101. His axe will cut down and burn sterile trees, 106. Wretched is the person whose parent does not show mercy to him in judgment, 122. God eagerly wishes to anticipate judgment with pardon, 125.

We are summoned to judgment at the time of death. In judgment there is no time for repentance, but for punishments. Herod’s perverse judgment, 127. The coming anger will be the judgment of the impious, 137. The person who provided himself with pardon before the offense escapes judgment, 139. To preserve judgment, the cause must be moderated, 144. In doubtful matters judgment must be avoided and left to God. Judgment must be anticipated by repentance, 167.

Christians would not wish to come to judgment. Because it has not yet come, the reason is that the Lord desires us to go to him. So that we may not be judged, let us be our own judges. What judgment belongs to gluttony and wine, 173. The confusion of the impious at the Judgment, and the causes from which it will arise, 22.

## Animals

Animals confess that Christ has been born, 141. They receive him in their own mangers, 141 and 156.

## Command

The command of a superior removes the rashness of the speaker, 70. By God’s command heaven is suspended, 101; likewise the earth and sea. Everything was created by command alone and will be dissolved by command alone. The command and holiness of the ruler compel even one whose speech is barren to speak, 107. At the will of the commander, the fear of the obedient person keeps watch, 109. To obey a command is virtue, 138. See Precept.

## Just

The just disdain popular applause, 21. Those just in name only but unjust in deed are rejected by Christ, 28 and 29. Christ does not call the just because he finds everyone sinful, 30. [Col. 1182]

The just rejoice in the Lord, 46. Let them grant the wicked a respite, 47. The just person is disturbed by the appearance of an angel, 88. To be just among human beings is a human virtue; before God it is a divine gift, 89 and 91. From what are Zacharias and his wife called just?

The just person is strengthened into a perfect man by tribulation, patience, testing, and hope, 110. Christ will give the just life, a kingdom, and glory. How the just person says, “I will die for Christ.” The just mock death in dying and are transferred to life, 114. The just are greater than heaven, equal to angels, indeed superior in merits, 120. A just person is sometimes allowed to be tormented by poverty and miseries for the sake of the piety of the wicked, 122. They accuse themselves before God so that God may excuse them, 123.

The just and the impious were in hell before Christ’s resurrection, although in different places. They were released when Christ descended to hell. Their death is precious before the Lord, 174, and their death is life. They desire Christ to come for their palm of victory, 158. See Saints; Confessor; Innocent.

## Justification

The mountains of justification must be climbed by us so that we may enjoy blessedness, 89. Few walk in all the justifications. While condemnation remains, the condemned person cannot be justified, 110.

We have been justified through Christ’s resurrection. How it is to be understood that our righteousness should not be before human beings, 9. Through itself it abounds for its own glory. Born from God, it awaits heaven. Whether it can be hidden. Hypocrisy is not righteousness. Whoever displays himself to human eyes should not expect the reward of the divine Father.

Righteousness must be served as much as iniquity has hitherto been served, 114. It is laborious, 116. It cannot be tolerated by the unjust, 127. Whoever fears human beings rather than God in legal cases deviates from righteousness. It is hostile to the unjust, 131. Without piety, it is cruelty before God, 145. Whatever the Lord does toward a servant is justice, 161. If human counsel fails the just person, divine counsel immediately comes to his aid, 175. God shows mercy while preserving justice, 6.

## Young Man

A foolish youth is called a youth even if he is old in age, 5. See Adolescent.

Unclean lips Isaiah had, 57. We must mourn that we have such lips. With lips cleansed, let us proclaim Christ’s passion and resurrection. Lips polluted by deceit, 62.

**Labor**

See *Philosophy*. A song is raised up, 10. Where there is no labor, there is no fruit either, 14. It is overcome by use and practice, 28. Human labor benefited the apostles’ divine labor. From labor comes fruit. John descended to labors through the condescension of grace, 88. Glory derived from labor is surpassed by glory derived from origin, 89. Common labor should have a common profit, 91. The labor of one who interprets the Scriptures mystically, 96. See *Sweat*. What is acquired through labor is more pleasing. Labor is required for recognizing the depths of judgments, 101. Labor and punishment in learning letters. Labor from rest, and conversely, 103. The labor undertaken by those contending in the arena for a crown, 119. The teacher’s labor is derived from Christ’s labor for us, 163. The traveler’s labor on a human journey is long unavailing, 175. Why God is a companion in our labor, 147. No one begrudges his own labor, 97.

**Tears**

The tears of the poor water their fasting, 42. They water heaven. Whoever does not pray to God with words will not pray with tears either, 43. Blessed are those who mourn for the world, 46. Tears are produced by joy and grief, 46 and 64. They testify to the heart’s affection, 46. The wicked man will weep in the other age over the poor man’s good fortune, 47. They restore what was lost through food, 66. The tears of Magdalene, the Jews, and Christ arose from different causes, 64. We must weep before God for sins, 65. Tears obtain children, 73. Women’s tears are most powerful, 79. They are their weapons. Children’s tears arise from nature, 89. God thirsts for sinners’ tears, 93. The tears of sinners water heaven, flood the earth, extinguish Gehenna, and erase the divine sentence. They are sinners’ baptisms. The widow’s tears obtain the resurrection of her son, 103. They are pleasant—the tears that purchase the joy of immortality, 107. The tears of little children are the most powerful weapons, and why, 128. Tears are the drink of penitents, 137. The tears of the mothers of the innocent slain were baptisms, 152. He who shed the tears of martyrdom does not lack the joy of martyrdom. The infant searches out nourishment from the breast with tears, 158. Tears wash away the wounds of guilt, 167. In Peter’s house it was not wine that was poured out, but tears, 18.

**Injuring**

To cut down the one who injures with his own sword is a sign of divine power, 57.

**Injured**

For the injured, what is long is short when compared with those who injure, 16. The injured person should forgive his brother, 139.

One who willingly receives death cannot lament it, 23. A woman in labor laments from pain; the one born, from nature, 89.

A lance of sorrow fixed in the hearts of Christ’s disciples, 83.

**The stone**

The stone rolled against Christ’s tomb proved death; when rolled away, it proved the resurrection, 74. Praises of the tombstone. Rolled away by the angel for belief in the resurrection, 84 and 75; and for other matters, 75. Set by the Jews at the door of death, it becomes the chair of life. Rolled away by the angel for salvation, faith, and the rolling away of death, 77. The angel sits upon it as presiding over it, and for other reasons. The stone closed the door of the women’s hearts, 82. The great stone is greater in significance than in appearance. It cannot resist the rising Christ, 84. The builders of the tower provided themselves with stones so that they might fall from a greater height, 131. The Jews brought stones in order to kill themselves, not God.

**Snare**

Herod fell into the snare he had laid, 152. The devil’s snare, 11.

The lustful man blames beauty for his own fall, 116. See *Lust*.

**Weariness**

It produces disgust both in the speaker and in the listener, 122. He cannot grow weary whose bread is God, 166. Nor does the bearer of mercy grow weary, 170.

**Thief**

The Gospel thief invaded paradise at the very moment of death, 60. He seized pardon, 167. When he was paying the penalties for robbery, 61. The thief secretly lays ambushes, 158. The thief is called clever, 173.

**To wash**

Before the table, hands must be washed, 171. The many washings of the Law wash, yet do not cleanse; the washing of grace cleanses. And how. What is devoted to the divine mysteries must be washed. Hearts must be washed from sins—how.

Laurence, a martyr distinguished by his passion, 135, throughout.

The praise of fathers redounds to the glory of their sons, 89. How the orator ought to praise illustrious men. See *Sacrifice of praise*.

**Lazarus of Bethany**

He is a figure of death to be conquered and an example of resurrection, 63. His resurrection is the sign of signs, 63. He is raised after four days, as a servant, and why. His illness is reported only to Christ, who loves him. Christ gives death a place in him. Why Christ rejoices at Lazarus’s death. If the woman had not been in paradise, Lazarus would not have died. Lazarus was mourned by three, in different ways, 64. His death was for the glory of God. Joy from his resurrection, 65. Why Christ groans. What the cave signifies, 65. Why he commanded the stone to be removed. Martha said that he stinks. That he had been four days dead. In Lazarus’s resurrection, a dialogue between Tartarus and the angel, and other matters at length, 65, toward the end. Why he rises with his hands and feet bound—beautifully explained. Lazarus offered us a foretaste of the resurrection. He is an argument for Christ’s resurrection, 81.

**Lazarus the poor man**

His astonishing reversals with the rich man, 66. He received good things in return for evil. He offered his wounds to God as a sacrifice. How he lay at the rich man’s gate. His death and burial compared with the rich man’s burial, 121. He is presented as the rich man’s smelting furnace, and other matters wonderfully and descriptively, 14, toward the end. He possessed the judge’s breast and secrets, 122 and 124. He did not do good deeds, but received evil, 123. Why he is blessed. The misery of mortals is recognized from Lazarus and the rich man, 124. The contrast between Lazarus and the banqueter. He was not broken by evils. Why he ought to be cured by the banqueter. See *Banqueter*, *Rich man*.

**Reading**

Ecclesiastical reading benefits the learned and the simple, 20. What it discloses by word, time commended by example, 20 and 21. Gospel reading is a saving understanding for the good, but an occasion of error for the wicked, 89. Careful and repeated reading produces profound knowledge, 120. When frequently repeated, it produces disgust in the listener. Part of it is deferred lest its length produce disgust in the hearers, 122. Prolonged reading draws things out at length, 173. To read or to lend one’s ear to those reading is the same thing, 159.

The bed of our sorrow is our body, 14. The paralytic is commanded to carry his bed as a testimony of health, 50.

**Law**

What the law of nature is, 5. What the law of God was at the beginning of the world. The divine Law taught what human wisdom did not know, 11. It exposed the devil as the author of evil. The equipment of the ancient Law, worn down by Jewish studies, 31. The Law of the Gospel is called an unprocessed cloth and is the beginning of weaving—how. The precepts of the Law were not sufficient to commend divine love to us, 55. The Law brings those whom grace admits into the temple to the door, 86. In legal tablets God inscribed the standard of discipline, 88. The ancient Law prohibited what was unlawful but did not deny what was lawful; it could do nothing beyond nature, 92. The law of faith, the door of grace, the forerunner of the Gospel, and so forth. Why the devil disguised the Law, sown with truthful precepts, with lying inventions, 96. Why the divine meaning is concealed in the Law, 99. The one who was without the Law demonstrates, through those placed under the Law, the author of the Law, 102. Compared with little flowers, 106. The Law began with man himself; but Adam immediately transgressed when he received it. Moses proclaimed it to transgressors who had received it, 111. Through the Law death reigned, because it devoured transgressors more severely than sinners. It increased rather than diminished offenses, 112. It exposes man’s wound and announces the coming of the heavenly physician. It draws the internal wound to the surface and opens the ancient abscess with the sword of its precepts. It was able neither to close the wound nor to give perfect health by itself. It enlarged the wound, and how. It raised up and cared for the sick person and led him to the physician. When the Law is excluded, its worshipers are convicted, 114. The Law, awaiting man’s will, does not free its worshiper from sin; rather, it binds him by the crime of transgressions—how. Those who are under the Law are bent beneath sin. The Law did not obtain a special partnership with the Synagogue, 115. The Law looked down upon the Synagogue. He does not abandon the Law who returns to its author. It is not the Law that dies for man; rather, man dies to the Law. The Law binds the guilty and punishes the criminal. Through the Law, the more conspicuous passions of sinners dominate the human limbs, 115. The Law does not advance a person but leads to death. Without Christ, man was armed by the Law for crimes, not to conquer but to commit them, 116. The Law was given by God for salvation but was turned by man into his own ruin. It exposes what was lurking in hostility within the human body—how. From it man began to desire virtues but to pursue vices. Under the Law, man is a slave and a captive. Why the Law reached the Gentiles, 126. John was the culmination of the Law, 127. It was given not to one person but to all, 132. Through the Law, knowledge of the Law must be sought, 148. What Christ promised through it, 150. Christ fled into Egypt so that the truth of the Law might stand. Paul attacked the Law out of zeal for the Law, 157. The divine Law taught penetration into the secret meaning of the divine sense, 168. Christ lay hidden in the Decalogue of the Law, 169. The many washings of the Law do not cleanse what the one washing of grace cleanses, 171. It was concealed by the Pharisee out of envy, 172. Under the veil of the Law, the Jew saw nothing, 176. Its shadow passes away. See *Synagogue*, *Hebrew*.

**Generosity**

God’s generosity is displayed abundantly, 39.

**Freedom**

Freedom is a slave in the power of a stranger, 2. The freedom of man from the servitudes of his enemies is to be celebrated, 6. Freedom is proved by virtue, 101. The free person is born for glory. The freedom of nature was restored through Christ when he took away the sin of the world, 111. Presumptuous and wandering freedom is placed after devoted service, 114. Freedom lies in sin. The freedom of sin gives punishment and shame as its fruit. When and how freedom was sought by man, 116. Freedom is hateful to captives of crimes and enemies of innocence, 127. Freedom should be mingled with charity when correcting a brother, 139. Freedom without end in heaven. Uncertain freedom destroyed man, 161.

**Lust**

See *Luxury*.

Whoever seeks what is lawful shines with manifold light, 22.

**To bind**

Whoever binds pardon leaves no room for pardon, 127.

**Wood**

From wood hangs the life of believers, where the death of the faithless had hung, 57. Through wood come death and life, 59. Through wood death came and is put to death, 60. Redeemed through wood, Peter and Andrew are brought to perfection through wood for the palm of victory, 133.

**Lily**

Its glory and pre-eminence, 163. It asks for tomorrow. They assign it to dryness and the fire of the furnace. An epithet of virginity and chastity, 22 and 98.

**Boundaries**

The inscriptions fixed to boundary markers indicate the lords of estates, 154.

**Tongue**

Natural language is dear to the simple and sweet to the learned, 43. For the whisperer and the double-tongued person it is a snare of death, 53. The sacrament of salvation lies between heart and tongue, 56. If the tongue, interpreter of the mind, cannot release speech, we are tormented by sorrow, 57. A cursed tongue defiles, 62. Why the rich man’s tongue is tormented more severely in hell, 66, 8 and 122. The tongue in the head is the head of evil, 124. The tongue is the river of faith, 79. See *Banqueter*.

Let lawsuits be far from us, so that we may preserve charity, 53. They are barred by the passage of thirty years, 145. Greed believes that the Lord is the judge of lawsuits, 162. At the litigant’s discretion Christ could not be the judge, 162. There are no lawsuits where greed is absent.

Letters are sweet, but only until the one who sent them arrives, 62. How letters are learned by pupils through labor and punishment, 101. The old letter destroyed the whole discipline, 115. Why meaning lies hidden in the letter, 132. What the mere interpreter of the letter does, 32.

**Envy**

See *Envy*, *Zeal*.

**Place**

God gathers the quality of deeds not from places but from their meaning, 9. Change of place is useless where there is no change of mind, 46. God is not confined by the capacity of a place, 77. The diet of locusts as a figure of penance—why, 167. Like the locust, we must leap from the place of sin to the place of penance. Do not desire to gaze upon distant things, and why, 164. What the distant and foreign things of the world are, 2.

We must speak according to the time, 57. Women are not permitted to speak in the Church, 82. We are afraid to speak with God, 86. We ought to speak, even if unlearned, when the command of the one giving orders is present, 107. We must speak at length about the one who makes us eternal, 117.

Love is an impenetrable breastplate, 40. What sort of breastplate the poor Lazarus had, 124.

**Lot**

Lot fled the fire through mercy, 42. He was drawn out of the flames by the hands of angels, 10. Through fasting he extinguished the conflagration—the one who through drunkenness had been burned in the fire of incest, 12.

**Lamp**

A burning lamp signifies good works that edify others, 22. It should be held in the hands, 24. A testimony of innocence. It is a good example. The lamp of Christ’s word displays the heavenly mysteries, 64. It exposes the thief, 54. John was a lamp, 87, 127, and 169. Those for whom the star of heaven shines through do not need the lamp of the temple, 156. The lamp of the heart must be kindled so that we may seek the drachma of saving knowledge, 169. The Church did not shine without divine fire. The mother Church is a lamp. John’s head on the platter was a burning lamp upon a lampstand, 174. The richness of oil kindles the lamp’s light so that it may shine as a comfort in the night, 8.

**To wrestle**

More difficult in the presence of the world, but more glorious, 107. How one must wrestle spiritually in Lent, 13.

Profane mourning is to apply foreign lamentations to a corpse, 19. Blessed are those who mourn for the world, 46. The game of the present life is recognized from the altered fortunes of Lazarus and the banqueter, 124. No game should be made of impiety or sacrilege, 155. No one plays safely with a serpent.

The loins of watchful servants must be girded, with lamps in their hands, 24. And why the loins must be girded.

**Light**

God’s light is needed in God’s work, 51. Gentle light for gentle eyes, 64. Light is supplied by Christ to the man born blind, 176. See *Eyes*.

The moon has been slandered by the devil, 52. It does not harm man but serves him. Why those obsessed by the moon’s phases are tormented. What is more pleasing than the moon? 101. The moon is equal in brightness to the sun, 103. The saint will be brighter than the moon, and how—descriptively, 120.

**Wolf**

The fierceness of wolves is called crafty, 173. Their contagion, 100.

The clay from which man was made restores sight to Celidonius, 176. Man was made from untouched clay; Christ was born with an untouched body, 148.

**Light**

The many forms of light are sought by one who does what is lawful and avoided by one who commits what is unlawful, 22. When the light withdraws, darkness returns, 44. Light in the night of the resurrection, 77. More pleasing after darkness, 84. When the eyes have been darkened, light must gradually be restored; it was created for the eyes, 87 and 112. The light of mercy, 104. The martyrs shine in heaven who on earth were thought to have been extinguished, 108. Its greatness does not weaken the eyes; rather, the weakness of the eyes can scarcely endure its brilliance, 112. God, the author of light, is found by the Magi in the thick darkness, 157.

**Luxury**

What evils it gives birth to and what evils it extends, 21. It resembles despair, 5. It is called a contagion, 59. It profanes all holiness, 27. The luxurious person should despise even bodily permissions, 113. Whoever burns with luxury would rather perish with it than turn back, 127. Frugality is adverse to the luxurious. From luxury impiety arises. A luxurious person—that is, one who pours himself out immoderately, a glutton—has lost the principal part of his substance, 162. Luxury seeks the destruction of chastity, the death of modesty, and the death of holiness, 174. It tickled Herod. The luxurious are called the devil’s swine, 2. One who leads others into luxury is called the devil’s hireling. The luxurious are never satisfied, and why. Luxury is curbed by rustic food, 13.

Magister. Christ is called Teacher because he is the maker and ruler of the elements, 21. Whoever wishes to know is devoted to a teacher and attached to a school, 101. How Paul taught. See Paul. Skilled, so that he may teach untrained disciples, 106. To the teacher who opens the questions of Scripture, the convert owes absolution, 107. Teaching rests upon knowledge; but its authority is established by life, 167. See Doctor, Preacher, Instructor. Master of crimes. See Mercenary, so that the disciple may do injury to the teacher, 94. See Disciple.

Magnus. Someone is called great in spirit, even if small in body, 54. How great before God—how great will he be among human beings? 88. To leave great things and love lesser things belongs to God’s power, not to human desire, 168.

Magus. Why he entrusts his eyes to the star, 64. The inhabitant of night is led by the star to the light, 87. He waters Christ’s cradle with gold, 103. By his gift and adoration he confesses that God has been born, 117. He received from the star the splendor of the Lord’s birth, 144. He worshiped God on earth, 145. At the Magi’s announcement Herod plots to destroy Christ, 146. The Magus, the standard-bearer of the devil, becomes Christ’s leader, 150. He wanders among the stars, 156. He did not recognize Christ’s birth under the guidance of the star. He came from the East toward the East, commanded by God to come. The sign from heaven concerning the Magi is greater than the sign from the star, and why. He recognized the star as servant and fellow-servant. He insults the Jews. The Jews do not ask the Magus about Christ. Explanation of the words: “Where is he who has been born king of the Jews?” From the commanded star, though unwilling, the Magus recognizes Christ. He marvels to find God in human flesh. By gifts he confesses Christ to be God, 157.

The worshiper of the stars, an inhabitant of night, finds Christ, the author of light, by grace. He is led by the star, so that what had been material for error may through Christ become an occasion of salvation. In his case ignorance and error were culpable, but not the will. The Magi were of Noah’s race, and had learned through God that Christ would be born. The Magus is commanded to worship, testify, and see, 158. To him, piously asking, an impious answer is given. In the serenity of Christian faith they came to the Lord. They give gifts to the Lord and treasures of knowledge to those who will believe. By the way of innocence they return to their own [Col. 1186]. The Gentile Magus recognized from the star that the Lord had been born, 159. They find Christ between two animals. Leaders of our faith and princes of belief. How the Magus may seek and find God, 160. He beholds on earth flesh brighter than the sun, moon, and stars. He does not investigate, but believes that he is God, king, and destined to die, and rejoices that he has found him. By confessing God with his hands, he precedes the Jew. From the faith of the Magi the belief of the nations was consecrated.

Evil. One’s own evils are heard with grief, but external evils eagerly, 2. Evils are permitted by God so that good may follow from them, 5. Which evils come from the devil, 11. Evil is an accident, not created, and how this is so. Temporal evils come from God because of our faults, 20. If temporal evils cause grief, what of eternal ones? 22. To whom evils seem more pleasing than goods, 25. Evils arise from the illnesses of sins, 38. Let contempt of God make our times evil, 43. Evils are tempered, 86. Evils were introduced into the world by the devil, 96. Evil is accidental, not natural. How the passions of sinners were increased by the law, 115. The believer thinks that receiving evils and receiving goods from God are alike, and in what sense, 123. How good it is to receive evils. The poor man’s evils benefited him, 124. Christ enumerates evils, threatens punishment, and permits pardon, and how, 125. The demon does not promise good things, 131. Through knowledge of evils we recognize how good goods are. Evils are not to be requested from God, and why, 132. Evils are to be avoided, 158. All are delivered from evil. See the Lord’s Prayer.

Malediction. If he is cursed who offends in one matter, how often is he cursed who offends in everything? 114.

The wicked. They seek evil from the good, and other matters, etc., 32. What dwelling they choose for themselves, 47. Torments are prepared for them, 66. Always foolish, 97. They envy the good of those whom they despised, 122. They are tormented to see happy the one whom they once thought miserable, 123. Whoever admonishes the wicked offends them, 127. Goodness is hateful to them, 131. Herod was wicked toward everyone, worse toward his own, and worst toward himself, 152. See the Lord’s Prayer. The malicious interpret everything for evil, 168.

Malice. The origin of vices, 31. It is not abandoned even in punishments, 122. It turns human beings into vipers, 137.

Mammon. How Mammon—that is, money—rules, very fully, 126.

The commandments of God. Their hills must be climbed fearlessly, so that we may enjoy glory, 89. No one, or scarcely anyone, walks in all the commandments and ordinances. The commandment does not pass away; rather, the person who slips from the commandment fails in respect of it, 115. From them the sinner takes the opportunity to become also stubborn and a transgressor, 116. See Law, Precept.

Manna. It fed the Hebrews for forty years, 166.

Dwelling. See House, Habitation.

The withered hand. The man’s withered hand healed by Christ represents the human race, extensively, 32. It had touched what was forbidden. When the withering of our hand will be dissolved. And many other matters. How and when the hand became withered. Why the one with the withered hand comes forward. By a command the withering of the hand, which had been conquered by a command, is removed. What the withered hand is in the Church, and how it is to be healed. Human beings were created and recreated by the hand of God, 33. The right hand of the Lord is Christ. The laying on of hands heals the Gentile in the Church, 105. To stretch out one’s hands is to pray by one’s posture, 108. Why the glutton’s hands were bound, 122. Let the person who cannot give money give his hand to the poor at table, 122 and 176. The hand of God assumed flesh for our restoration, 148. How hands speak among the Magi, 160. Hands must be washed before the table, 171. The hand of the Lord in making, restoring, and shaping the human being, 176. God measures deeds not by hands but by hearts, 9. Why Christ held the hand of the fever-stricken man in various ways, 18. Hands are sanctified in good works and polluted in evil ones. The Lord fashioned the human being with his hand, and with his hand supplied light to the human being, 176.

Marcellinus. Bishop of the Church of Vicohaventia, praised, 175.

The sea. What those who enter the sea of fasting should do, 8. The sea becomes a path for Christ, descriptively, 20. Why it rages even to Christ’s danger. From the calming of the sea Jesus is believed to be God. The sea of the world is troubled when Christ enters it, and is calmed. The sea of human blood on earth—when? 20. When the sea is a mother, 146. A storm at sea was made for faith, 21. The error of the Jews is more perverse than the waves of the sea, 32. What the sea of the world mystically is, 47. Description of the sea when it drowned the Egyptians. The sea washes away Peter’s filth, 78. It has a gentle passage, 90. By God’s command it is restrained by fine sands, 101. What is more useful than the sea? The evangelical sea, to be navigated, 168. See World, Age.

Pearls. What the evangelical pearls are. A pearl is also sought among dung, 44.

Mary Magdalene. She bore the name of the mother of Christ, 74 and 64. Her tears for Lazarus’s death, 64. Why she came to the tomb, 74. She came as herself, but as another; the same woman transformed. She is forbidden to touch Christ because she did not believe that he was God, 76. What it means that Mary touches and does not touch, distinguished, 76. Mary comes, and the other Mary is revealed, 77. The woman comes back as Mary. What is she seeking in the Pharisee’s house when she was not [Col. 1187] summoned? 93. Commanded by the Lord, she comes. She comes behind him for pardon. How she prepares the table of repentance with music. In her there was great guilt and great indulgence. She was a sinner in the city because of her bad reputation. Why she approaches the one lying down. She believes Christ favorable to her because he eats with the Pharisee. She carries oil because she needs medicine. Why she stood beside his feet. She moistens them with tears. How she was baptized by her own tears, and how her hair was sanctified. Her tears are an example of satisfaction. She anoints him through the sacrament of his humanity. Recognizing her own wound, she sought the physician. Why Christ, turning toward Magdalene, speaks to Simon, 94. The sinner should imitate Magdalene in repentance. Magdalene is a figure of the Church, 95.

Mary the Virgin. Her virginity was obscured by a Jew; but it is explained what brothers Christ had, 48 and 49. If Mary had had sons, Christ would not have commended her to John; and why to him rather than to James. Mary marveled that the human being should be restored from a Virgin, 58. She could not be both virgin and mother except through God, 58. As a virgin she carried God in the temple, 59. The Virgin gave birth, 60. The salvation of women, because she first received Christ, 64. Before the human being was freed from sin, Mary had already been received by Christ through grace. She hastens to restore life to the man. Without Mary, death is neither driven away nor life restored, 64. Christ dwelt in the Virgin’s womb so that the dead might rise—how. She conceived in complete virginity, 84. So that birth from a virgin might be believed, a barren conception is set forth beforehand, 87. To reach the Virgin’s conception and birth, bodily understanding must be removed, 92. Through Mary life returned to everyone, 99. She fulfills the type of the evangelical leaven. Why the conception and birth of the Virgin Mary must not be equated with women’s births, 117. How she was a virgin before, during, and after childbirth.
