The Holy Spirit makes her womb fruitful by a mysterious mingling of his light. Why she is greeted by a winged angel, 140. In the salutation the fullness of grace is offered to her. The Lord is in her. Mother of the living by grace. She is troubled by the speech, not by the sight, of the angel. She reflects prudently. What payment for the house and the womb she demands from God received within her. Mary’s spirit is wondrous. What is necessary for a human being to penetrate Mary’s secret heart, 141. In her breast the entire majesty of the Godhead rests. The Virgin’s conception is to be believed, not investigated. The angel drives away Mary’s fear, which arose for two reasons, 142. Maria means “Lady” in Hebrew, in Latin, and why. She was full of grace so that she might pour it over the whole creation like abundant rain. The angel marvels and fears, and why. She gave birth to Christ without the distresses of maternal pain. The Virgin conceives and gives birth. Her virginity was strengthened in conception and childbirth. She gave birth to the Savior. Why she does not incur blame by asking a question, as Zechariah did. From her a man was made. She vowed virginity; a note explains why God’s power overshadowed her. What holy one she was to bear. She is sent to Elizabeth. She confesses herself a handmaid. She believes the word and conceives the Word. Since an angel is sent to her, let no one seek anything else, 143. How great her virginity was. What sort of grace. The fullness of grace. The Word descended like rain upon fleece. Before the Forerunner, the Lord was with her. Blessed because she is virgin and mother. Greater than heaven, stronger than earth, broader than the world. She is troubled because she senses the entry of the Godhead. God is not injured by the incarnation, and how. By conceiving she found grace, and by giving birth she did not lose virginity, 144. Why she ought not to fear. She finds the Word within herself. The temple of the Godhead was great. She conceives in the womb so that the conception may be reality, not a figure. Everything is safe in her, because she gave birth to the Savior of all. The Virgin conceives and gives birth to a heavenly offspring. Christ is called the fruit of Mary’s womb because of her perpetual virginity, 145. She is called mother while virginity remains and spouse while modesty remains. She gives birth to a human being, Christ God. She conceives from the Spirit and gives birth to Emmanuel. Christ did not receive from her womb [146]. Virgin as bride, mother in fruitfulness. Mother before conception, virgin mother after childbirth. What she did while being a virgin. Why Christ is born from a betrothed woman. Mary represents the Church as bride. Why Christ is born from Mary his mother. How Mary is always mother and the forerunner of human salvation. What the name Mary means, at length. What “the Virgin conceives and gives birth,” and so forth, means, 148. That Christ might be born from a Virgin. Because he was conceived from a Virgin, human shame is abolished. Why the angel is sent to Mary. To disclose the mystery of virginal birth is beyond human understanding, 153. That the Virgin should conceive and give birth is divine. In Mary’s womb Christ finds the lost sheep, 168. To give birth to the firstborn of all creation, she traverses the whole road to her homeland, 175. See Birth, Christ’s Nativity, Christ’s Incarnation, Virginity.

Martha. What she said to Christ at Lazarus’s death, and his reply, 63, 64. How useful it was for Martha to meet Christ, confess her faults, and await his response, 64. Why she said, “Lazarus stinks,” 65.

Martyrs. They undergo death voluntarily, 23. They heal the illnesses of sins, 38. What they suffer for Christ, 79. Few martyrs in persecution, 97. Their glory is won by the shedding of blood, 98. They are roses. They are written in the catalogue of God’s friends [Col. 1188], 101. They are born through death, begin at the end, and shine in heaven, 108. In the contest of the arena they conquered vices and death, 119. Their happiness comes from the persecutor’s savagery, 127. They are born from death. It is not so much death as faith and devotion that makes a martyr, 128. At a martyr’s death a crowd stands by, as at the annual festival, but in a different manner, 129. The birthdays of martyrs are celebrated with annual joy in memory of the event. His birthday is the day on which he sheds blood for the king, 135. The persecutor’s cruelty, mocked, accumulated multiple triumphs for the martyrs, 134. Their merits are gifts of God, 135. Their festivals should be celebrated with fervent prayer, and they should be imitated. A captured martyr should maintain steadfastness; one not captured should flee the persecutor, and why, 151. Let him attain the palm through endurance, not expose himself to danger through rashness. Fleeing martyrs made Paul the martyr Paul. Those who deserve to be killed for Christ truly live, 152. Martyrdom comes through grace, not merit. It is a divine gift. One who runs to martyrdom by his own strength does not possess a crown through Christ. The innocent martyrs belong to grace, 153. From Christ’s flight. A martyr begins to live when he deserves to be killed for Christ, 174. Martyrs of the devil in Africa—who they are, 13.

Mother. A mother labors in vain when the authority of the Creator is absent in the offspring, 6. She rushes headlong after her son, 54. It is not permissible to scrutinize a mother’s gifts, 55. She is not a true mother who does not know how to love her children, as Felicitas did above, 134. How Mary is always a mother, 146. Camps against the mothers’ breasts; iron hardened against their breasts; milk poured out before blood, 152. The mothers of the innocents were baptized in their own tears. Having suffered in the martyrdom of their sons, they ought to have been companions in the reward. See Innocents, Father, Son.

Marriage. Its dignity is the procreation of children; otherwise it is a serious thing to be without virginity and children: to bear the burdens of marriage but not attain its fruit, 92.

Matthew. How he was called by the Lord as a disciple. Why he was called, since he was rich, to the end. Why he was sitting, 29. He does not abandon the tax office but changes it. A usurer through ignorance. His conversion is the more marvelous, 30. He is compared with the paralytic. A figure of the Gentiles.

Medicine. The strength of medicine is proportioned to the size of the wound, 113. The poor man’s medicine is wealth, and conversely, 124. A late remedy is not without pain, 131. Let it correspond to the wound, 167. The medicine of repentance comes to the aid of the sick.

Physician. From touching wounds he counts not insult but honor, 35. His care for the deranged person, 38. One must obey both the bodily and the spiritual physician, 41. The physician’s care in healing the sick, 44. A physician who does not bring health and is not made weak with the sick person does not know how to treat, 50. He goes to the sick person, 54. Without a physician, the cup of life becomes deadly, 60. Through faith a person is his own physician, 83. Touching wounds, he is not polluted by putrefaction, 94. He asks rather than compels the sick to accept harsh remedies, 108. He benefits not the wound but the treatment and health, 113. He rejoices with health, not putrefaction. The sick person is ungrateful who is always eager to be treated but not to be healed. He does not await the sick person’s choice in treatment, 114. He anticipates it. The physician who heals diseases is more welcome than one who applies late medicine to diseases, 131. The one who recalls a person to salvation through pain does not become hateful, 167. See Sick Person, Disease, Wound.

Members. They are not separated from the head, 57. Those that served the demon should serve God, 93. The weak are troubled by various kinds of passions, 116. Let them agree with one another, and let one not occupy another’s function, 120. All the members should believe that what one has done belongs to them all. The members of vices and virtues are explained by the Apostle. Let a person share his members with the weak, 122. Each member has its own function, 132. In their separation is destruction; in unity, beauty. Their punishment rebounds upon the pain and injury of the head, 173. See Body.

Liars. In what case they are rejected by Christ, 28, 29. They cannot know the truth, 131.

Beggary. It becomes human so that inhuman greed may be exposed, and how, 121. Rich for a time, the beggar is eternally miserable, 125.

The mind. How our mind becomes mindless, 12. The weak person does not know how to dispense the mysteries of the Lord’s body, 49. Sin takes away the mind, 78. The mind’s hearing is happier after grief, 79. Through an excess of fear it departs from itself, 88. When one mind is in two persons, 89. It is sharpened by obscure words, 96. Description of the mind’s understanding, 98. We reach God by the mind, not by the body, 97. With the same mind as Jesus, 102. Money rules unjustly over minds, 126. It is wearied by the long expectation of the great promise, 130. A simulated mind dares nothing openly, 158. It is pierced by the arrow of sin, 167. The human mind is struck by the evil of splendor, 131. A drunken mind judges badly, 173. In the house of the mind an unorganized household of thoughts moves about, 15. Bodily presence is nothing where there is separation of mind, 32. See Spirit, Sense.

Table. Let Christ sit at our table, 54. The table acquires a debtor for us. If Lazarus had been at the Rich Man’s table, he would not have been in torments, 66. To sit at table after the Lord’s death is not the behavior of a son of servants, 83. The king’s table. See King. Lazarus was not admitted to the rich man’s table, nor is he admitted to the bed of his torment, 122. The poor and disabled person must be led to the table by the hand. The table of the poor and the rich by contrast, 124. How our table is to be prepared, 127. Hands must be washed before the table, 171. See Banquet, Meal, Food, Wine, Glory, Blessedness.

Mercenary. The hard servitude of the mercenary, 2. Who become mercenaries of the demon, and what they do. Why the demon sends his mercenaries to the pigs. A wage is owed to the mercenary for his labor, 5. See Laborer. What payment the impious receives for piety, 127. The laborer who will receive his wage desires the father of the household’s arrival, 158. In serving God, let your wage be your price, 170.

Prostitute. How the Synagogue became one, 115. When it lost hope of salvation and life, it became the devil’s mercenary, and what evils it does, 2. See Mary Magdalene.

Merit. Our merit does not save us, but divine mercy does, 45. John the Baptist acquired merit before he knew how to seek it, 88. A guest’s merit becomes known from the preparation of his dwelling, 92. Let no one boast of merits or works, 110. From collected handfuls of merits one reaches a hundredfold fruit, 119.

Forerunner. John the Baptist was the Lord’s surveyor, 127, 91. He was an angel to Mary, 140.

God measures by cradles, 48.

Fear arouses our senses, 115. See Fear.

Crumb. Whoever gives a crumb to the poor receives everything, 8. See Drop, Coin.

Soldier. A soldier is led to war by the trumpet, 6. Here one must fight alongside the poor, 9. Combatants are encouraged by song, 10. In spring the soldier goes out to the field, 13. The experienced soldier receives discipline from the trumpet, 14. When a soldier’s laziness occurs, 17. Freed from the cares of wealth, he can serve as Christ’s soldier so that he may reign, 22. What account he must render, 26.

Soldier of Christ. See Christian. He sends what he has acquired to his homeland, 54. The believer who thirsts for the presence of his king, 68. He hopes for honors in old age, 71. He spends his youth amid dangers. Why the soldiers at Christ’s tomb were terrified, 75. The Christian soldier prays not to be led into temptation, 68. The inexperienced soldier runs into battle; the veteran advances slowly, 79. Christ urges his soldiers not to fear those who kill the body, 101. When the soldier’s pay was the wage of grace, 102. He does not dare to call himself a soldier who lacks a military title, 109. Christ deigned to serve as our soldier, 115. Let the soldier not fear wounds; he proclaims spoils and triumphs, 118. What he should do to be saved, 137. Devoted, he does not conceal the flight of his king and reports his steadfastness, 150. The innocents were soldiers of Christ’s generation, 152. Why after victory he desires the king’s presence, 158. The soldier campaigning for his own pay diminishes the king’s honor, 163. He receives pay when a citizen pays tribute, 166. The difference between citizen and soldier. The cohort of soldiers eagerly desires to die before its king, not with him, 153. See Lurker, Brave Man, Centurion.

Christian warfare. How great its virtue is, 38. It is the mark of tender warfare to win victory over all crimes by love alone, 94. What it is like with Christ’s weapons, 144. Fasting is the invincible command of Christian warfare, 8. The true insignia is the belt of chastity, 22. Warfare without a successor exists in Christ’s kingdom, 144.

Minister. Every human being is the minister of his possessions, not their possessor, and how, 125. See Wealth.

Miracle. Its powers come from God, 48. A singular miracle is to see what one has not seen, know what one has not known, and not believe what one has believed, 81. Faith is evidence from the miracles of Christ’s disciples, 83. They show that Christ is God, 100. Miracles weary the Jews and do not benefit them, 102. What Christ’s miracle accomplished, 105. When miracles occur, ordinary custom ceases, 153. What signs or miracles must be performed, 11. See Sign.

Mercy. God’s and human mercy. Through it the world’s most bitter sentence was taken away, 6. God’s mercy is not without justice. It is also the companion of fasting, throughout the discussion of fasting, 8. Through earthly mercy one reaches divine mercy. It recalls the sentence of condemnation. It frees sinners and restores saints. Divine mercy is sent through those who show mercy to the poor. Hypocrites sell it rather than give it, 9. How it is to be practiced in every place and at every time. God is witness and rewarder of mercy. Mercy is confidently requested from the merciful, 14. How “I desire mercy” is to be interpreted, 28. How it benefits when joined to fasting, 41. It is the soul of fasting. God desires it. For it he will give the kingdom. Let it accompany prayer and fasting, at length. Whoever does not give to another takes away from himself; whoever sows for the poor reaps for himself, 42. It plows the fields of heaven. It is the greatest of God’s works. If mercy had not intervened, God’s work would have perished. He postpones judgment until death so that we may do penance, 42. Through mercy God restores what had been lost through judgment. In judgment Christ first argues about mercy before judging guilt. Nothing harms on earth when mercy is an advocate in heaven. It must be practiced with prayer and fasting, at length, 43. How a human being may be a model of mercy to himself, 43. The merciful person has as many servants as he has coins, 54. When the peace of mercy is lost, civil war is at hand, 104. Fleeing the light of mercy, a person enslaves himself to the darkness of greed, 104. Why Paul entreats us by the mercy of God, 108. By it Paul escaped crime and became an apostle. Through it God asks human beings not to avenge themselves with severity. It must be taken up so that greed may be destroyed. It was despised by the Rich Man, 121. It does not stand for the accused who is accused by the innocent, 122. Mercy is to divide one’s own members with the weak. Giving a hand to the poor at table is greater than giving money. Mercy is foolishly sought from a father after being denied to a brother, 124. At life’s end one must have recourse to mercy’s aid, 125. It must not be sown among the cruel, 127. It sweetly tempers the bitterness of repentance, 167. Its bearer does not grow weary, 170. See Pardon, Indulgence, Piety, Almsgiving, Charity.

Mass. See Eucharist, Sacrifice.

Mixture. It is more important to distinguish mixtures than to prohibit mixture, 97.

A pious governor attributes whatever happens to the cause, not the person, 48.

Grief. The disciples, overcome by the sleep of grief, 81. But grief is turned into joy, 84. Out of grief comes delay. No darkness of night can be compared with the darkness of grief. Consolation is present in grief, 86.

To admonish the wicked is to offend them, 127. See Correct.

The monuments of the ancestors are loosened and scattered by the harmful roots of trees, and how, 162.

Delay makes the one waiting sad; but a great promise lightens the burden of expectation, 24. The delay of the one who pays is compensated by interest, 77. On the delay of expectation, 130.

Moral matters should be explained to the people more than doctrinal matters, 2.

Disease. What the disease of sins has done to human beings, and how it is healed, 38. Even after the disease has been healed, one must remain under treatment, 104. See Weakness, Illness, Physician, Care.

Conduct. Conduct makes someone younger or older, not age, 5. If we judge someone by former bad conduct, we recoil, 5. The bad conduct of human beings in Chrysologus’s time, 47. Persons of different sexes are made one by conduct, 89. Imitation of conduct makes friends and joins them together, 101. As many habits as a person has, so many passions did Paul have. Conduct is reproved through the Gospel, 125. The death of the calf is the life of the son and the fattening of the whole household, 3.

Death. Death is from the devil, 11. The author of death dwells in death’s habitations, 17. Death does not approach where Christ is, 18. The death of the soul is God’s departure from it, 19. The death of the just is willing; that of the unjust is not, 22. Whoever dies voluntarily does not complain, 23. Voluntary death belongs to power; forced death to necessity. With God, death is sleep, 34. The death of one for the salvation of many, 37. Is the shepherd’s death beneficial to the flock? 40. How the innocent person dies who lived in crime, 42. Death dies by death, 57. It was put to death through the wood, 60. Death leading to the glory of the one who raises up is not to be lamented, 63. It was given as punishment for sin. Death came from the woman, from whom life also came, 64. It troubles us more by example. A mortal cannot fail to grieve over death. It comes from human transgression. Death is hard, but its gate is harder, and so forth, 65. The rapacity of death shut God’s creation in a cave, 65. What death lost in Christ’s resurrection, 74. How the increase of death would not have occurred. What it is unseemly for a servant to do at the Lord’s death, 83. The second death is not in eternal life. Whoever lives from death is God, 84. It reigned because of human guilt, 90. Born from discord, death divides human charity, 96. The death of the saints is sleep; the death of sinners is death. Death came to all through Eve, 99. Despising death, one becomes God’s friend, 101. The death of the saints. See Saints, Martyrs, Just. The ancients who wrote about the good of death did not attain their aim, 101. The devil is the author of death. Why God did not immediately destroy death together with its author. A person dies so that he may see what he has been. The death of bodies makes life eternal from life temporal. Death is permitted by God because he can raise the dead. Our body is weakened for death, 102. In death we put down the chaff of old age, 108. When death is imminent one must not gather possessions, 104. Death is expended and punished in Christ’s sacrifice, 108. Martyrs are born through death. He cannot die who deserves to be killed by the life-giving sword, 108. Through Adam’s fault we are held liable, 110. Death is the punishment of sin, so that he may lose his insignia. A person scarcely dies for the just, because necessity rather than will leads to death. Death is subject to the willing and rules the unwilling. Among human beings, death becomes through Christ a restoration of piety and a commendation of divine charity. Nature, unwilling, gives birth to death, 111. What it means that a person dies, he owes to Adam, 20. Death was acquired by a human being for his descendants; it was not made by God, 112. Among human beings death is also punishment for crimes. It comes from human sin. Let the person die to sin, not to God, 113. How and for what cause death dies by death, 114. The death of sinners ends life and begins punishment. That of the just does not kill but perfects. Death dies through Christ, 116. No one ever wishes to die, 118. Fear of death is trampled down by resurrection. Death is the mistress of despair, mother of unbelief, sister of corruption, parent of hell, spouse of the devil, queen of all evils, attacking every class of human beings, and in what order, at length. Its wars, most fully. It is invincible. Inflexible. Why those writing about the good of death went wrong. Death advances to life, 124. At its time the supreme apparition constrains and summons judgment, 125. In death a person wishes to do good. Whom it overtakes, 125. From what untimely death proceeds. In danger of death let us turn to repentance. From his own death the martyr is born, 127. What it means to die once for the king, 128. Death comes from the demon’s persuasion, 131. Everyone born under mortal conditions dies. Because of human ingratitude God wills that the human being pass through death. Death was killed by the warrior of the heavenly army, 133. She who gives birth to life does not deserve death, 145. Death would have taken good from us if Christ had been killed in the womb, 146. Death itself is lighter than fear, 147. The innocents experience death before life, 152. See Innocents. Through Christ the cause of death became the cause of life, 157. Charity is not separated by death but increases, 164. Whoever has God as life cannot die, 166. Even at death’s moment there is room for repentance, 167. The death of the just is precious before the Lord, 174. Their death is life. Death ends at God’s nod, 176.

Death is to be philosophically considered, 54.

Mortal. Why our life is called mortal, 1.

The dead. The dead are to be mourned, not sung for, 19. How the dead bury the dead. A dead person is raised by God more quickly than a sleeping person is awakened by a human being, 34. The dead who are to be judged will rise, 62. The dead are not to be mourned like the Gentiles, 65. They have life from God. The dead would not benefit sinners by rising, 66. Those raised by Christ are an argument for his resurrection, 81. Whoever does not know that they were created from dust mourns the dead, 101. Why Christ did not raise everyone to life, 102. How we are dead to sin, rather than sin being dead, 113. A raven more cruel than iron rages against the dead, 163. Why Christ did not permit the disciple to bury the dead, 19. The Gentiles used to place food beside the dead, 17.

Moses. He becomes God through the support of prayer, almsgiving, and fasting, and what wonders he performs, 43. His wonders again, 66. God communicates himself to Moses, 69. The honor of his funeral, 83. Why he sees not God’s face but only his back, 131. He meets him on the mountain so that he may behold the promised Christ. What he receives from God so that he may love God and teach others to love him, 147. By a forty-day fast he is completely transformed into the glory of divinity, 126. Why he deserved to establish the law. Moses’s fasting made him shine through with the light of divine fervor, 12.

Woman. Let her be silent in the Church and learn from her husband at home, 26. What war lascivious women waged, 27. A woman provided the model for erasing sin by silent confession, 34. What punishment the counsel of impiety gave the woman, 44. If the woman had not been in paradise, Lazarus would not have died, 63. She sought tears and purchased death at the price of appetite. She runs for death, having run toward death, 64. She who had sinned first is healed first. Mother of the living through God, mother of the dead through the devil. The woman would have perished if Christ had reached the man first, and how, 64. She raises the man from the tomb of her womb. She is rebuked by Christ. The woman’s deceit placed the man in a cave, 65. Why the woman senses stench at the tomb. She comes late for pardon, though she had run early toward guilt, 74. In the evening she seeks Christ, although in the morning she had lost Adam. From paradise she had taken faithlessness, but from the tomb she takes faith: she seizes life from death, having snatched death from life. How she becomes mother of the living, 74. She is the messenger of resurrection, who had been the cause of ruin. Deceived by the sight of the tree, she is restored by seeing the tomb. If only she had had the impediment of sin in paradise. She has a life-giving conversation with the angel. She comes to the tomb, but returns as Mary—why, 77. Adam led her to the underworld; she received Christ from the underworld. The tomb is the woman’s reproach, 77. From it she received faith. First to faithlessness, to the author of death, to the devil; and first to faith, to the Savior, to the angel, 77. She enters Christ’s tomb so that she may rise to faith. The evils that came from the woman, and why she is so ready for tears, most fully, 79. Why the women weep at the tomb. They bear tears for Christ. How her running ahead to the resurrection does not detract from the apostles, 80. In the tomb they see the effect of sin. She is absolved from guilt. She is not placed before the apostles. She becomes a companion in the Passion and rises through faith. She fears and rejoices. The women are greeted by Christ and hold his feet. The woman is at Christ’s feet. She follows the man; she does not go before him. Devoted toward the dead, 82. They endure doubtful light in body and spirit. Why they flee from the monument. They are silent because they were given to hear, not to speak; to learn, not to teach; and when a woman speaks, she represents the Church, 82. The touch of an evil woman burns the one conscious of evil, pollutes her equal, brands the suspect, and disgraces a person of evil will, 94. A sinful woman becomes good if she touches the Lord. Neither woman without man nor man without woman in the Lord, 99. Domestic care confines the woman at home, 99. She receives from God the leaven of faith, which she had received from the devil as faithlessness; and why she hid it in three measures of flour. The woman who received the leaven is the Church. The woman who had a spirit of infirmity is described, 105. She is a figure of the Church. Why she was bent over in the Synagogue. What her wickedness was, and the evils she did to Adam and his descendants, 127. She took life from the world because of the fruit of one tree; she is to be avoided according to Elijah’s example. The woman becomes a new beast when she cuts off John’s head. Let her restore to himself the man whom she lost through herself, 142. The woman with ten drachmas is explained, 169, throughout. See Female, Tomb, Woman with the Issue of Blood.

World. Its entire breadth, through envy, is narrow for two brothers, 4. It is a field of battle with the devil and vices, 14. Its shipwreck—when? 20. Converted to obedience to Christ, 20. Its end, 47. Sinners would not wish to pass through the world, 66. The structure of the world harmonizes elements that are dissonant, 68. In Noah’s ark was the seed of the world, 69. The evening of the world. See Evening. The world strives to avoid the death of its Lord, 78. The whole structure of the world believed itself to have rolled back into the first chaos at Christ’s death, 78. But the Lord raises it up to glory, 78. The disciples are sent into the world to preach the Gospel, 83. It believed only what it heard. The one whom God, in making him, called “world,” the enemy, by infecting him, makes unclean, 96. The barren becomes fruitful, 99. Made by a command, it will be dissolved by a command, 101. It is more difficult but more glorious to struggle while the world is present, 107. Its figure and reformation, extensively, 120. The world is the game of princes, 124. The world is the human being’s field, 125. In the world he seeks...

That God may not demand an account from us at the judgment. Money rules the world, 126. It is glorious to despise the world together with its prince, 128. It receives seven days, 134. The world will truly exist when death no longer exists, 139. In the world are prepared the things we ought to have in heaven, 144. Christ’s birth is grievous to worldly people, 146. It preferred to perish rather than to fear, 147. Occupied with empty errors because of fear. It is brought back by love. Made for the sake of humanity, 148. That which is not from the world cannot be subject to the world’s understanding, 153. The dove in the Jordan indicates that the world’s shipwreck has ceased, 160. Becoming filthy with the foulness of vices, it is washed by the Flood, 166. It dies in the Flood and is reborn through such a baptism. It is wholly opened up by the baptismal spring for the renewal of the nations in the number forty. Once a child, now old and close to destruction, 167. Christians follow the fleeing world. Its pride is brought low by the gentle victor, 170. At Christ’s second coming it will always have the vision of its author, 83.

Gifts prove love, 10. Whoever does not honor the Father with gifts is ungrateful to him. Divine things terrify a person, and for that reason he ought to be more cautious, 68. Zechariah is condemned for looking upon divine gifts, 88. Whoever gives back divine gifts does not lose them, 59.

The proud murmuring of the Pharisees and scribes is silenced by the Lord; from which vices it increases, 168.

Music is not to be used at funerals, 19.

Change in this life may be from heretic to believer, from sinner to righteous person, and conversely, 97. It is to be lamented in the rich man and the poor man, 121. The change of the rich man and Lazarus, 124. The change of God’s offices occurs in order to change a person for the better, 170.

Myrrh is offered to one who is dying, 157.

The heavenly mystery should not always be made public when it is known, 86. The precious lies hidden in what is vile, 99. The Gospel readings are obscured by divine mysteries, 126. Why the divine mystery is concealed in the human, 132. Its greatness and height compel postponement, 144. Things that appear clear to human eyes in heaven are obscured by profound mysteries, 160. What benefit comes from mysteries of the Christian faith investigated knowingly, 166. The disclosure of the heavenly mystery is to be sought from God in prayer, and how it is to be made, 64. Why Christ’s words and deeds are mystical, 96. A mystical exposition of divine Scripture is to be undertaken, 95.

A human being’s birthday abounds in tears and complaints, 89. The birthday of the saints is when they are transferred from earth to heaven, 129. This day is not celebrated with feasts but by imitation. It is celebrated every year for our remembrance. The saints’ birthday arises from martyrdom or death, 133. The solemnity of birthdays should maintain moderation in rejoicing, 127.

Savage nations are brought back to gentleness by Christ the shepherd, 6. The king’s birth is honored with festivity and music, 91. From John’s birth we draw near to the Savior’s birth according to the Gospel, 92, 88. See Christ’s birth, the Virgin Mary. Why the author is silent about Christ’s birth, 146.

We are born for sufferings, with suffering, and so forth, 87. See Son.

Born. How one who has not yet been born calls someone father, 67. See Catechumen. The one born weeps by nature, 89. Those born from earthly Adam, so that they may become heavenly, 117. Born from desire, so that we may be reborn through Christ. “Born of flesh is flesh; born of spirit is spirit,” 142. Why John is greater among those born of women, 174. Those born in different months, 56.

Nature. The natural portion and the law of nature given to humanity by God: what it is and what kind, 5. It marvels at the Virgin’s childbirth, 57. Nature [Col. 1193], an infant in relation to virtues, grows through God, 85. Through long use nature is either developed or blunted, 87. Happy is the nature that conceives God, and why, in various respects. It gives birth to sufferings and devours its offspring. Why it was nourished by sterility. It was freed from slavery to death through the Lord’s birth. Human nature, sensing a power from above, will tremble in its weakness, 88. Nature is constrained by the law, not the author, 90. Trembling before God, weak in relation to divine virtues. It presumes great things about itself before testing itself by deeds. God commands it. It marvels at Elizabeth’s conception, 92. It is sufficient for the service of its Creator, 93. What sin is for nature itself, 111. Made by God to create human beings for life, it gives birth to death because it is subject to sin. It would not wish its offspring to be destroyed. While grieving, it sighs for the freedom it has lost. But it regained that freedom when Christ took away the sin of the world. It could not help itself on its own; therefore the author takes it up into himself to restore it. To attribute sins to nature is to live in sin, 113. Human nature, made prone to falling through sin, 116. Through grace it should bear the image of Christ, 117. Content with little, 122. It did not perfect everything, so that it might leave something for art, 132. It is adorned by art. It is weakened in present circumstances. John wishes to change the nature of a poisonous offspring, 137. Human nature is strengthened to bear the glory of the Godhead, 142. Who would accept its growth beyond nature? 142. Mortally wounded, it began to be the source of death, although it had been the beginning of life, 143. It is healed by Christ’s birth and becomes the enlivening of children, 143. Virgin nature, mother of things, 146. Whatever nature does not possess belongs to the author, 153. It teaches what infancy is capable of, 158. God created nature, 160. How the dullness of our nature may advance into the vigor of the Godhead. The Holy Spirit indicated that the world’s shipwreck had ceased by appearing in the form of a dove, 160.

Ship. When Christ enters the Church’s ship, how the sea of the world is disturbed, 20. Yet it is calmed by Christ. When Christ’s ship was tossing. Whenever Christ sleeps in our ship, a storm breaks out, 21. The Lord’s ship is shaken from outside by a pagan, within by a heretic. The Church’s ship needs Christ, 50. Why he himself boards it. The ship of our body is to be equipped during Lent, 8. The waves overwhelm the ship. When the sailor enters the sea, why he lays aside his other concerns, 8. An experienced sailor steers a ship in a storm; in calm weather anyone can do so, 20. He enters the sea hoping for profit, 71. He sings of the harbor and profits so that he may not fear shipwreck, 118. He discovered the art of sailing, 168. By song he overcomes the dangers of the sea, 10. He keeps watch, and why, 24.

God provides what is necessary for his workers, 170. Necessity makes a thief, 7. In desperate situations it is often a teacher, 35. In adversity it cannot be compared with the will, 110. It is necessity to acquiesce; to will is virtue. Religious necessity compels the speaker to depart from the planned order of discourse, 114. What necessity of nature has done for humanity, and what grace has done, 117. It advances toward the will, 124. The necessity of sinning will be abolished in glory, 139. It is more necessity than guilt to seek God and not know how to seek him, 157. Frailty imposes the law of necessity, 41.

To deny God what he wills is to deny oneself what one desires, 8, 38. God does not deny favors to those who ask, 39. The petitioner is wicked who denies something to others while asking it for himself, 43. Promises cannot be denied when, once denied, they are fulfilled: how this is so, 89.

Negligence. The sins of negligence cannot be avoided, 30.

Merchant. The Lord is a dealer in pearls, and how, 47.

Spiritual wickedness described, 52. It binds the hands of the lost to Christ, 100. It confounds the judgment of the heart, 131. Whoever has wickedness as a companion confounds right and wrong, 152. The nations are to be conquered in their wickedness with Christ fighting on their behalf, 171.

Ninevites. Why they will rise in judgment against the Jews, 37. Saved through mercy, 8.

Noah, the parent of the new age, has in the ark the offspring of the entire age, and why, 147. What his dove indicated, 160. Carrier of the new age, 163. What was saved by Noah is placed before Peter’s supper. Kept in the ark by fasting, 12. He saved the world, 14. The seed of the age, 69.

A name is bestowed on kings from their triumphs, 57. How God’s name is to be hallowed in us. See the Lord’s Prayer. A change of names can occur where there is no variation of persons, 125. Different names can be assigned to the same persons. The names of saints often indicate their merits and distinguishing marks, 154. The glory and disgrace of a name arise from good and bad reputation, 69.

The number ninety-nine lies hidden and closed in the left hand; with one added, it immediately passes to the palm of the right hand—how this is so, 168, in the relevant note.

Our possessions are to be given away, although they are not ours but merely considered ours: how this is so, 123. Newly cleared fields are to be cleansed, 164. What the newness of life ought to be, 113. Let us serve the Lord in newness of spirit, 115.

Night. Why the Lord wishes us to disturb him from his bed at night, 39. How prayer made in the middle of the night may be beneficial. The evil of sleeping through the entire night. Night is changed into light when the Lord rises, and rejoices because it has been freed from the slavery of darkness, 77. It is called earth, 170. It darkens the day, 74.

Harmful things. Under the appearance of harmful things, salutary things are often given to children, 25. What a harmful tree does to the monuments of the ancestors, 162.

Clouds obscure the appearance of things, 74.

The father does not endure his son’s nakedness, 3. Not even on the foot. A person’s nakedness is covered by pardon; clothed in faith, it is warm, 99. The rich man was clothed in artfully contrived nakedness, 122. He will be naked in hell who refused to be rich in heaven, 125. Adam’s nakedness grows cold though covered by Christ, 106.

The numbers one hundred, eighty, fifty, forty, seven, ninety-nine, and twelve. See under their respective entries. Counting by the right and left hand, 168, in the relevant note.

The messenger of God’s betrothal gives a pledge and receives a dowry, 140. Through Christ’s two messengers the calling of the two peoples is shown, 170. John the Baptist, a fervent messenger, 91.

Weddings are friendly to torches, 22. Their chastity. How Christ’s wedding with the Church is adorned. Christians should be roused by the cry of these nuptials. Why Christ attended a wedding, in various respects, 157. Happy are those for whom Christ is present.

The child’s nurse is described most fully, 62. Completely reduced to a little child, he possesses the lie by virtue of its proper character, and so forth. Saint Paul became a nurse: how. The father does not mock the nurse who imitates the little child. Chrysologus, the spiritual nurse of little ones: how.

## O

**Obedient.** He keeps watch in fear at the command of the one giving orders, 109. Things that ought to be said should be said to the obedient, lest the teacher give offense, 137. He is gentle, but he who examines is harsh, 143. Obedience rendered to God causes the Lord to help us in our necessities, 39. It is to be rendered to God concerning fasts, 41. The obedience of creatures rendered to God. See **All things created**, **Command**. Obedience compels one to pray, 138. The obedience of the faithful is the grace of God, 58.

**Offering.** An offering made to God from another’s possessions is harmful, 54. A public offering is prepared for the king who is being born, 102. An offering to be made to God from riches, 66.

**Obscure.** What the obscurity of faith accomplishes, 102. Christ’s obscure deeds and sayings sharpen our understanding, 96. Obscure things are to be made clear, 112. Mortality is enveloped in obscurities, 160.

**Supplication.** Why Paul made a supplication through the mercy of God, 108.

**Service.** Reasonable service appeases God; unreasonable service provokes him, 109. At the service of a military king, the station trembles. Reasonable service is fervor; unreasonable service is madness. How service is to be rendered to God with virtues and humility.

**Demon-possessed.** What evils those possessed by a demon do to it, 17. They are tormented and they torment, 51. How they come to be attacked by a demon, 52. They are afflicted by the increase of the moon. Why they are freed by human beings, 170. See **Demon-possessed person**.

**Obstinacy.** It harshly cuts off reason, 131. It seeks to speak the falsehood of the Jews.

**Opportunity.** An opportunity is called “smoking,” and is kindled by heat and blood, 126. Unless it is removed, sins are not overcome. The opportunity for wrongdoing given to human beings through created things. What an opportunity accepted is. An opportunity for salvation sometimes becomes an instrument of destruction, 126. What is an occasion of error for a heretic should be an argument of faith for a Christian, 144. When an opportunity for destruction becomes the material of life, 156. Opportunity leads into sin, inferentially, 13. One who stubbornly proceeds toward occasions of sin is abandoned by God, 70. See **The Lord’s Prayer**. Occasions of sin cause charity to be abandoned, 162.

**Kill.** The demon usually kills rather than gives life, 131. The Jews took up stones to kill themselves, not God. That which gives birth to life does not deserve to be killed, 145. One killed for Christ will rise again in Christ, 173. No one could provide for the one who had been killed except Christ, who, having been killed, restored life, 116.

**Meet.** We ought to meet our Lord as he comes, 22. The father’s meeting his son shows mercy, 3. The Lord met the Gentile while he was still a sinner, 5. He meets him in the Son through the incarnation. God’s meeting is not delayed by flesh, 24.

**Hidden.** Some things appear hidden because of the depth of their mystery, 85. What is hidden in the grass is revealed in the ear of grain, 97. Through the Gospel Christ lays bare hidden things, 125.

**Eighty.** The number eighty prefigures the whole of faith and grace, 126.

**Eye.** The eyes of parents and relatives are lamps for their children, 1. The eyes of God see the sinner, although he has departed to a distant land, 2. They illuminate the sinner’s sight, 3. They lift the darkness from the eyes. Hypocrisy is caught by the eyes, 7. God’s eyes are closed lest they punish, and opened so that they may help, 21. The eyes were Eve’s occasion of stumbling, 27. God’s eyes deliver the sinner, 28. One seen by God is free from evils and endowed with goods, 34. Without God’s light, human eyes are deceived in God’s work, 51. An impious eye cannot see God, 55. Tender eyes are entrusted to a tender light, [Col. 1195] 64. They are to be raised upward in supplication, 65. Those stained by looking at the tree are cleansed by seeing the tomb, 77. The disciples’ eyes were blinded by the darkness of the Lord’s passion, 78. The eyes of love look more sharply. The eyes of the women were closed by the darkness of unbelief, 82. When eyes have been darkened, light must gradually be poured back into them, 87. The tree, by opening the eyes, closed them, 99. The mustard seed, by closing, opens the eyes. Salvation was denied to the eyes so that it might be wholly in faith, 110. A pure eye is troubled by smoke, 111. Eyes are not dulled by the greatness of light but by their own weakness, 112. The eye should not offend the foot’s ministry, 120. The eyes raised upward caused the rich man harm, 122. The roles of the eyes were changed in Lazarus and the rich man. Human eyes do not look upon how great God is, but that he is, 131. An eye is precious if it remains in the body, 132. Blind toward his own crimes, clear-sighted toward those of others, and other matters, 139. The eye is the author of transgression, and other evils of the eyes. It is God’s work that the eye is narrowed into the pupil, and why. It scarcely endures the radiance of the rising sun, 140. When poured out, it loses its light, 164. A narrow eye cannot contain many things, lofty things, or distant things. The eyes of three blind men were healed by Christ in different ways, 176. Why they are healed by the Lord’s spittle, 176. For the baptized sinner, there is a drop of holy dew for the eyes. Why, in imperfect eyes, forms grow large, appearances are confused, and things are mistaken. Forgiveness opens the eyes that guilt had closed, 176. See **Sight**, **Vision**.

**Hatred.** Hatred comes from the devil, 53. One incurs hatred who reproves the guilty, 127. A perverted human sense cannot hear what it has once decided to hate, 131.

**Office.** Earthly offices were mingled with heavenly ones when Christ and John were born, 89. Offices were exchanged by God so that he might change us for the better, 170. The offices of the members are not to be confused, 120.

**Oil.** Why the Jew needed oil, 126. When it is a figure of the Christian chrism. The olive tree dried up by the Jew comes back to life in the Christian. When oil was poured on Christ’s head, 160. What oil is to a lamp, piety is to fasting, 8. How it becomes chrism, 93.

**All things.** After God come all things, 131. See **Creation**. God bestowed all things upon us, 23.

**Burden.** One burden is lightened by another, 3. One weighed down cannot reach the work of the Lord’s harvest by the narrow way, 170. A burdened person advances more slowly to works.

**Works.** No one should boast of works in justification, 110. The works of the begetter: whoever does not act denies his lineage, 123. God gathers the quality of works from their meaning, not from their locations, 9. See **Deeds**. The diligent laborer, expecting to receive his wage, longs for the master’s arrival, 158. From the person who invites him he receives the necessities of sustenance—indeed, meals to overcome his labor, 170. How much more will he receive from God? See **Hired laborer**.

**Wealth.** See **Riches**.

**Craftsman.** The craftsman receives honor from restoring his work, 143.

**Mouth.** The mouth was infected by the taste of the poisonous tree, 99. It was healed by the taste of the saving tree. The poor man has as many mouths as wounds: when this occurs, 121.

**Prayer.** The prayer of the faithful is to be employed so that pastors may become capable of explaining Scripture, 5. The devil fears those who pray, 13. Perseverance in prayer, 39, throughout. God’s affection and desire toward those who pray, that he may bestow graces, extensively, 39. Good prayer, even when made from necessity. By enduring the delays of the giver, prayer knocks. It is especially good together with fasting and almsgiving, 42. These three must be joined together, throughout, 43. One must pray in the morning—or from human fear, if not from divine love—43. God is to be prayed to while he scourges, 45. He restores to us lost temporal goods, 46. How much the prayer of many united people accomplishes, 132. What harm neglect of communion brings. Prayer should burn at the festivals of the saints, 135. We must pray that we may be able to believe, see, and possess eternal goods, 139. Christ taught us to pray briefly because he wishes to give quickly, 67. Through prayer we were freed by Christ before we were redeemed through his passion, 24.

**The Lord’s Prayer.** It is explained at length, 67–72, including the matters below. It is the astonishment of heaven and the terror of earth, 67, 70, 72. It is not grasped by human beings, 68. It is the form of prayer given by God, 69, 70. Why God is called Father, 68–71. Why he is said to be in heaven, 67, 70. That God’s name may be sanctified, 67, 72. “Let the kingdom come”: what kingdom and in what manner, ibid. “Your will”: how it is to be done, ibid. What kind of bread we ask for, ibid. How we are to pray for sins to be forgiven, ibid. How we are to understand “Do not lead us into temptation,” ibid. That he may deliver us from evil, and from whom, ibid.

**Orators.** In praising great men, they recall grandfathers and great-grandfathers, 89. Their apology at the beginning of the speech, 186, throughout. 138. The end of the speech. See **Preacher**, **Teacher**, **Instructor**.

**World.** See **World**.

**Order.** Things that are not done in order cannot maintain order, 64. Human affairs recover strength through order, 109. Religious considerations often compel one to depart from the order of speaking, 114. The order of teaching must be regulated so that one thing is not obstructed by another.

**Original sin.** See **Sin of the world**.

**Origin.** Glory from origin precedes glory from labor, 89. It is sometimes unnecessary—and rash—to investigate the origins of causes, [Col. 1196] 166.

**Kisses.** Kisses redeem the sins of children, 3. Salvation comes from the kiss of confession, 60. They are a sign of reconciliation, 93. Judas’s bloody kisses, 137.

**Bones.** The bones were troubled by whom and how, 45. Christ’s bones establish the truth of his flesh, 81.

**Idleness.** Idleness of body and soul must be removed during Lent, 12, 13. What the idle person loses.

**Sheep.** The nations are sheep brought back by Christ the shepherd to the fold, and other matters concerning his sheep, 6. The sweetness of jubilation leads them to the fold. What kind of children of sheep are to be carried by God, and how, 10. The sheep’s offspring are led by the shepherd into the folds, 40. Whether the death of the shepherd was advantageous for Christ’s sheep, at length, 40. That they may rejoice for the shepherd, 46. That they may obey him, 53. The rabid sheep of the Jews tore apart their own shepherd, 100. They are the Shepherd’s life, salvation, and glory; therefore they must be taught what the shepherd knows, 147. When the Lord’s sheep are safe, the wolves rage, 149. Christ is the shepherd of the lost sheep, 168. One lost sheep had dispersed the entire hundred-number and reduced it from the right hand to the left: how this happened. In the one, all are found, and how, 2. This sheep was Adam. Against one sheep all the savagery of the beasts was directed, 171. It is good that it hear the shepherd’s voice, 173. The author addresses his sheep. If it wanders about according to its own desire, it does not reach the folds. Our house is God’s sheepfold, if God’s flock bleats there, 10.

**Egg.** The egg is the word of God: how this is so, 55.

## P
## P

**Palace.** The poor and unworthy man does not approach the palace doors, 141. See *House*.

**Palms** are the scourges of children, not of men, 38. Why they are to be endured by a Christian. Christ did not turn his face away from blows with the palm. The palm is won through patience, 151.

The **bread from heaven** is Christ, turned into a stone for the Jews, 55. How the Eucharistic bread is made, 71. Bread is given to dogs by human reasoning, 100. The Gentile hastened to lick the bread that the Hebrew trampled. The Gentile feasts on crumbs from the whole loaf. Bread does not hunger, 110. God seeks bread in the poor man, 121, 42. A crumb and a drop suffice to refresh the poor, 124. It must be given to the poor, 137. The five loaves were multiplied: how, 160. Having descended from heaven, he fed the Hebrews for forty years, 166. God will give bread to those who serve him, 170. Let Christ be our bread. The earthly bread prepared by Joseph, and the heavenly bread revealed by John: what each caused, 174. Christ is the bread descending from heaven, 13. Bread has no need of bread. See *Eucharist, Poor Man, Almsgiving*.

**New and rough cloth**, 31.

**Parables.** See *Figures*.

**Paradise.** If obstacles to sin had existed in paradise, death and injury to the Creator would not have occurred, 74. Before Christ’s ascension, a flaming sword was at paradise’s gate, so that access would not be open to man, 123. The fiery way to paradise was tempered by the water from Christ’s side. Its pleasant places were shut off by a flaming guardian, 172.

The **paralytic**, described in comparison with Matthew the tax collector, 30. A figure of the Jewish people. His body, not his soul, was directed toward healing, 50. Jesus is recognized as God in the healing of the paralytic. Why he is commanded to carry his bed. Man is commanded to spare himself, 23. We are bound to spare those who wrong us, 38, throughout. Whoever always spares others need not fear crimes, 72. Those who sin against us must be spared, so that we may be forgiven, 139. See *Forgive, Enemy, Lord’s Prayer, Forgiveness*.

**Sparing.** See *Abstinence, Sobriety*.

Those whom nature made unequal are made equal by virtue, 89.

**Births** are often painful, as in the case of a human being born in the seventh month, 56. Such is the birth of heavenly grace. So that the Virgin’s birth might shine upon the eyes of the faithless, God first sent the conception of an aged barren woman, 87. The Virgin’s birth is without childbirth. The Virgin’s birth is unknown to us, 87. A barren birth provides evidence of resurrection and salvation, 90. Why Elizabeth’s childbirth was delayed, 91. The Gospel concerning the barren woman’s childbirth leads us to the Virgin’s childbirth, 92. Why the virginal birth occurred on the way, 175.

The **Paschal solemnity** does not join the old things to the new; rather, it weans the infancy of the new regeneration, and other matters, 73. It weans us from milk so that we may take more solid food. The Paschal solemnity is not joined to Jewish antiquity. The children of the Church are nourished and weaned at Easter. How the Lord’s Passover is to be celebrated according to the Apostle, 172. How the Lamb of God is sacrificed in it. In it Christ was born and was transformed into complete joy and glory. At the Paschal season the sacraments of the symbol were explained, 56. It is the harbor, gain of life, and joy of resurrection, 8.

Earthly pastures have the bites of wolves, 170. The pastures of swine are muddy.

**Sufferings.** In severe illnesses, suffering finds its own medicine [Col. 1197], 35. Whoever shares in suffering will also share in glory, 40. The storm of suffering had shaken the women’s faith, 77. Paul endured as many sufferings while teaching as there are human characters, 101. They cast down the body, 109. How they dominate the human members through sins, 115. How they press upon people of every age, and how the law makes them more widely known. Once cut back by the law, they grow more vigorously. They make the law, an instrument of life, into an instrument of death. How we may triumph over sufferings which, though excluded outwardly, still make trial of us, 115. He cannot cut them off who does not suffer with them, 151. Christ bore ours in order to remove them. In his passion Christ is silent, 164. True love is tested by sufferings, 14. The centurion did not see sufferings in Christ, 15.

**Shepherd.** God assumed the role of shepherd for the varied benefit of the sheep, 6. Christ, shepherd of souls, seeks companions. He entrusts the sheep to Peter. Let the shepherd carry the tender lambs. He knows the fruitfulness of his flock, its sheep and its young, and commends them. He descended from heaven for the salvation of the sheep, 6. He has affection for the sheep, 23. He gathers the lambs and leads them to the folds, 40. Whether Christ the shepherd’s death was beneficial to his sheep, at length, 40. He prefers to die rather than see evil befall his sheep. By dying, Christ the shepherd opened for his sheep the way by which death might be conquered. How he feeds the flock, 46. His office among the people, 53. He hastens to the lost sheep, 54. God calls the sheep through the mouths of shepherds, 62. He is compelled by his office to preach, 77. He is a mystical dog, 100. Holy shepherds assist their flock in spirit even after death, 128. How the shepherd of souls should call his sheep, 147. Let him teach them what he himself knows. Blessed is the shepherd of souls who, while guarding himself, provides for another’s salvation, 155. The shepherds of Israel learn from the angels that the Lord has been born, 159. Prophets were sent to them repeatedly. The shepherd of the lost sheep is not earthly but heavenly, 168. Why he lost one from the hundred, and other matters. How Christ seeks us on the mountains and carries us on his shoulders to the heavenly folds, 170. How the good shepherd watches over the flock, 173. The shepherd of souls may preach from two places. The shepherd’s staff is taken up against the raging wolf. Why the shepherd keeps watch, 24.

**The heavenly and earthly father.** In the heavenly realm he is neither shut in nor released by death, 1. By the force of love and providence he holds the substance of his children. Living together with his son, he brings him good things. He needs no intercessor to grant forgiveness to his son, 2. He covers his son’s guilt. He wants his son to return, not to perish. The heavenly shepherd is the one against whom sin is committed in heaven, 2. He sees what is far away. Meeting his son, he bestows forgiveness, 3. The divine Father, sought in faith, is immediately present. He illuminates the sinful son. He is moved by mercy, though he does not move from his place. Out of mercy he falls upon us. Falling, he raises those who lie prostrate. He removes the burden of sins. He kisses the sinful son. He heals the wounds of his children, 3. What the father’s gaze does to the son. He cannot endure his son’s nakedness, although he endures his crimes. He rejoices more in forgiveness than in justice. He is swiftly merciful. He restores innocence and honor. His love for the returning son. He is disturbed by his children’s conduct, 4. The man who judges the father’s affection is foolish. Love covers the son’s shameful things. A son who envies his brother is not pleasing to his father. The son is the father’s substance. Though disobedient, the father recognizes his son. The father alone is to be sought. For the poor son he seeks new and future things.

The heavenly Father has two sons, the Gentile and the Hebrew, 5. He meets us in the incarnation of the Son and falls down, and so forth, 5. He kisses us. He gave the robe of the glory of immortality. What sort of ring was given at his command. He gave sandals in the preaching of the Gospel. He killed the calf—that is, the Son. The earthly father accomplishes nothing in generation without God, 6. Those placed in the house of the heavenly Father should take up the harmony. He keeps our goods in heaven, 7. Whoever does not believe the Father does not know what he is, nor does he know himself to be a son. From gifts the heavenly Father perceives love, 10. Sons of rams—that is, human beings—are to be brought to him. The heavenly father is to be preferred to the earthly, 19. He promises his servants a kingdom, 25. He wishes to enrich his servants, not strip them. The Father gives children what is salutary under the appearance of what is harmful. The sufferings of parents arise from affection and love for their children, 33. God repays the works of parents in their children. [The reading is uncertain:] the blessed [one] burdens the Father’s Son, 51. The son’s punishment overflows upon the father. When he wishes to show mercy to his son, he considers affection, not fault, 54. He loves his son and gives him good things, 55. He does not shrink from death for his children. God wished man to be a father so that he might recognize divine love, 55. Whatever came from God the Father, even if harsh, the ancients willingly received. The Father gives to the son who asks briefly, 71. He provides willingly. He does not see faults when he receives his son, 81. His praise overflows into the glory of his son, 89. He draws his son to discipline by love, not by power, 108. The Father wishes to be Lord. Let him draw the son away from sins, 155. He enriches his children while leaving them complete love, 162. He gives bread to his children, 163. He is God for us. Mystically, how he is divided into the Son and conversely, 164.

What a head of household ought to do, and what account he must render to God, 26. Let us beware lest news of our altered substance precede us to the Father, 125.

The Lord judged it worthy to suffer; therefore it is not unworthy for a servant to suffer, 38. By suffering, Christ forgave what he himself had imposed by commanding, 123. [Col. 1198] Christ suffers in his own people, 173. The tomb suffers him, 58.

Patience amid evils is brief; vengeance is slow for the good, 16. Christ’s patience toward sinners, 19. The rewards of patience, 38. Let there be patience in asking good things from God, 39. God’s patience toward us, 51. Through patience we await the things that belong to hope, 71. God’s patience comes to the aid of sinners, and what other good things arise from it, 97. It proves a young man suited to the virtues, 110. Patience itself heals the one who causes injury, 139. The palm comes from patience, 151.

**Homeland.** Why the prophet is without honor in it and in his own house, 48. It is restored to Adam, who had lost it, 49. Christ possessed it as a man. Our homeland is heaven, from which we were cast out through Adam and to which we were led back through Christ, 159.

**Patron.** What mercy, as patron, accomplishes in judgment, 8. See *Advocate*.

**Paul the Apostle** was Peter’s companion in tending the flock, 6. He spread knowledge of Christ throughout the world, 34. How he was both abortive and mature, 56, 58. His sudden conversion, 61. The spiritual nourisher of little ones, 62. He saw invisibly the mystery of God and disclosed it without betraying it, 72. Ananias wanted to uproot Paul, 97. Why he taught by being beaten, 101. What the physician and father did, 108. By escaping guilt he became an Apostle. How he shares himself with the unlearned, 113. What benefit his rigorous teaching brings us, 115. What his speech, commonly read, accomplishes, 120. Why he ascended to the third heaven. The martyrs, by fleeing Saul, made him Paul, 151. Having become a preacher from a persecutor through devotion, he attacked the law out of zeal for the law and sinned against God through love of God, 157. Why he scourged himself, 161. Sent out as a persecutor, he returned as a preacher, 168. The Jew fell so that the Christian might rise; blinded in the law, so that he might see in grace, 176.

**Terror.** See *Fear*.

**The poor man** carries our goods to heaven, having God as his guarantor in this matter, 7. He preserves for us what the belly would have squandered, 8. He is Abraham’s bosom, heaven’s treasure, Christ’s treasury, 16. The poor man’s mercy purchases divine mercy. What is given to the poor is ours; what is not given to him belongs to another, 16, 9, 23, 32. Modest poverty is in fear, 9. Help in the conflict comes from a poor man who has been fed, 12. What is the poor man’s shame is God’s glory, 14. God is fed by the poor man’s food. The poor man excuses sins. He willingly carries our goods to heaven, because he is not weighed down by their burden but lifted up, 25. For one thing given to the poor, God gives you a hundred, 25. What the poor man ought to do, 26. Let him give to one poorer; but if he has nothing, let him have the intention of giving. The poor man on earth is rich in heaven, 28. Whoever does not know how to lend to the poor does not know how to be healed, 32. Let our meal be the poor man’s supper. Whoever gives to the poor gathers a harvest in heaven, 42. God eats the bread given to the poor. What benefit comes from giving to the poor, 43. He who now rejoices in the misfortunes of the poor will wail in the other age, 47. The poor man must not be defrauded, nor may almsgiving be given from another’s fraud, 54. In the poor man’s lodging a likeness of the kingdom of God is found, 99. Let him give alms from what he possesses, 103. His burial, at length, 121. What good things result when he is received and lodged. In the poor man God seeks bread. When and how his flesh is arranged as a spectacle of piety. How the oppressors of the poor harm themselves, 121. His food and life consist in a drop and a crumb, 122, 24. A hand must be extended to the weak at table, 122. The conflict between the poor and the rich, 124. Let the poor man see the rich man, so that he may be seen, and let each in turn be cared for. A drop denied to the poor is sought in vain for refreshment. What is denied to the poor and scattered for display perishes. Our treasure must be given to them, so that we may think of heavenly things, 129. A rich man who lodges with the poor is first a debtor to humanity and only afterward a giver, 136. Clothing and food must be given to the poor, 137. The poor man is common to all, solitary yet open to everyone, 164. Whoever redeems the groans of the poor by almsgiving is not required by the Lord to answer for those groans, 166. A hand must be extended to him by man, 176. The needy poor man is described, 14. See *Almsgiving, Mercy, Piety*.

**Poverty** is akin to the virtues; its example is the athlete, sailor, soldier, and philosopher, 28. Temporal poverty is scarcely endured; how much more eternal poverty, 54. It is free from excuse in divine service, 93. Christ’s poverty is to be desired, since it possesses everlasting riches in heaven, 117. Its end, 121, throughout. It advances the poor man toward philosophy, 124. Toward the kingdom. It is not poverty but the disposition that leads the grateful to the reward or brings the ungrateful to punishment. Divine poverty is sufficient, 170. It is a spacious dwelling place for God, 14.

**Christian peace** makes us be called sons of God, 53. What peace is and what effects it has. It obtains everything from God. It must be preserved according to the commandment of our king. It is God’s work to plant it. It is the glory of the people and of the shepherd. Why it must be guarded, 53. It is to be loved. Peace exists wherever many are united in will, 68. When it was taken away from the earth, 81. Why it was repeated to the disciples, 84. Its internal and external benefits. It restored divine life to us, 110. How we may have peace through God. The peace of the world is sought for advantage or preserved through fear, 138. Christ’s peace is to be prayed for, and what it is. It is requested from God. The splendor of peace illuminates the Church, 149.

[Col. 1199] The desirable name of peace. It is the name of Christ himself. Christ’s peace embraces us all. We must meet God with gifts of peace. It is the exultation of angels and the lamentation of demons. It is praised by the saints. Heavenly and earthly beings send gifts of peace to one another. God is to be praised for the peace that follows.

Sins are conquered by fasting, 12. The poor man excuses sins, 14. Christ rebukes them: when, 21. The greater the sin, the more abundant the grace, 30. It is sin to deny that one is a sinner. In this life we cannot avoid sins of thought, negligence, and ignorance. People are ashamed to confess sins, 34. The first happiness is not to sin; the second is to find forgiveness for sins. What harm the illness of sins caused, 38. The merciful person will not be judged concerning sin, 42. Where sin is, God is not there, 44. God is recognized as God in the remission of sins, 50. No one is without sin, 54. Sins are forgiven through Christ, 57, 59. It is useful to forgive another’s sins, 68. One who always spares others need not fear sins, 72. That we may die to sin, 73. Sin is not contained in the broadest heavenly region, 83. We must not despair because of the magnitude of sins. Through human beings sins are forgiven to human beings, 84. The sin of the city is abolished by Christ alone, 93. Sins are conquered by love, 94. One must not sin merely so that greater love may be acquired, 94. When the forgiveness of sins will occur, 95. We must not remain in sin, so that grace may abound, 113. We are dead to sin, but sin is not altogether dead in us, 113. It is the sting of death. Who is the one who lives by sin. The body of sin must be destroyed. Sin must not reign but be trampled down. Sin will die in the other age. To attribute sins to nature is to live by sin. Sin is an accident, not created by God. It exercises a cruel dominion over sinners, 114. It falsely claims that man is free. Sin is known only through the law, which reveals it, 126. Sin brought death and made nature inclined to falls. Sin, the author of offenses, was removed by Christ. It was dead and buried in our ignorance, 116. Through the commandment it revived, when it made the sinner a transgressor. What the cruel tyrant did. The tyrant carries with him the instrument of his own punishment, 109. Through the union of sins the whole structure of the world is dissolved, 120. Public sin is punished, while God tolerates private sin, 125. The offense committed is punished by Christ through the Gospel. Sins must be forgiven to a brother, 139. God is the one who forgives sin, 145. To sell sins is to turn forgiveness into profit, 158. Sin becomes filthy, stinks, and darkens, 166. Whoever commits no sin carries God in his body, 168. Hell is the pit of sin, 170. War must be declared against sins during Lent, 13. Sin is paralysis, 15. God caresses the sinful man, 161. The crossroads of sins, 89.

The **sinner** departs from himself before departing from God, 2. The ungodly man gives, but does not receive, the price of his servitude, 1. He rises when he recognizes that he is lying prostrate, 2. He becomes a beast. Having gone abroad, he does not flee accusers or the eyes of God, 2. How the repentant sinner desires to be a hired servant. In despair of salvation, what evils he commits. He falls into the ruin of mind and body and into hell, 3. He is blind. He is illuminated by the eyes of God, 3. He is confused by darkness. Let him return to God. He is before God and without God, in himself and not with himself, 5. The sinner has many forms of servitude, 6. His return to God is to be celebrated, 6. His evil under the servitudes mentioned above. Christ flees from him for the sake of his salvation, 19. Although alive in body, he is dead in soul. When he turns to God, the scourges will cease, 20. The one who sins knowingly is punished more severely than the one who sins unknowingly, 26. Salvation comes to him through what Matthew did, 29. He deserves death when he denies that he is a sinner. He becomes a teacher of sinners, indeed sin itself, 30. Let the sinner recognize and confess his sin. The sinner accuses the virtues, 32. He arises from innate frailty, 34. He is ashamed not to do evil but to confess it. Where the first and second happiness lie. Why he receives punishment, 35. The sickness of sins was healed through the patience and death of Christians, 38. Let the sinner at least abandon his guilt when guilt has already abandoned him, 42. Everything is turned upside down for the sinner, 44. God despises sinners. When God seeks the sinner, he seeks the man, not the sins, 54. How Zacchaeus the sinner is converted, at length, 54. The sinner gives himself forgiveness, trusting that sins are forgiven through Christ, 57. Whoever does not believe that past sins have been forgiven him doubts that he will receive future goods, 59. He says that he will repent if someone should rise from the dead and tell him, but falsely, 66. Sinners flee judgment and grieve that the world is passing away, 66. Great is the man who does not sin in the flesh; greatest is he who does not sin even in the heart, 89. Sinners run toward destruction, and other evils, 165. Through love of God Paul sinned against God, 157. The greedy sinner is not corrected, 158. Overcome by enticements, he does not want Christ to come. Let him stop sinning, and that is sufficient: how, 125. How God caresses such a sinner, 161. What evils the sinner commits, for which he ought to repent, 167. John wanted sinners to be saved. Hope for sinners was advanced by the Lord, 168. God receives and sanctifies sinners. God rejoices at the sinner’s return. Sinners are healed by the gift of the one who calls, not by their own free choice, 176.

[Col. 1200] The **sin of the world** was washed away by Christ with his own blood, 164. Adam’s sin entered the world through guilt, through a human being, 111. It is neither nature nor substance but an accident, and it opposes us. Sin is to nature what smoke is to the eyes, fever to the body, and bitter saltiness to the sweetest springs, 5. It is the door of death, a cruel beast devouring with three mouths. It is the inheritance of our parent Adam. Through one person it passed into all. In Adam, or in his sin, all sinned, 111, 112. Sin was not changed into nature; rather, through death it exacts from nature the punishment owed to it, 111. The punishment of sin, death, was removed by Christ. We were all in Adam’s sin, as the whole tree is in the seed. Death, the punishment of the sin of the world, devoured the guilty and the innocent. Sin lives and rages toward our death. How sin arose from the devil and the woman as the sin of the world, 148. Through this, man, previously lord of all, was cast into servitude to all.

That breast is the tomb in which Christ is still held dead and buried, 75.

**Money.** Those possessed by money are freed in Matthew, 28. The Hebrews compensate for crimes with money, 76. Money denies faith in Christ’s resurrection. It is given for the purchase of those who are to be preserved, not destroyed, 80. It rules the world and worldly things, 126. It is a cruel burden. What evil it does to all human beings. It rules human bodies and minds unjustly. It closes the eyes of the person receiving it, 37. It corrupts hearts, redeems falsehood, and removes truth. See *Riches*.

**Payment.** What payment the Virgin’s womb demanded from God, 140.

The **scarcity of fruits** comes to us because we do not help the needy, 103.

Let our **bag** be our conscience, 170.

**To lose.** To lose something possessed is more grievous than never to have possessed it, 123. The occasion that becomes an instrument of destruction becomes an instrument of salvation, 126. To find what was lost is more pleasing to us than not to have lost what was preserved, 168.

Man is a **pilgrim** in this age, 89. He gladly returns to his own, 114. Whoever lodges him deserves to receive God with the angels, 121. The pilgrimage is hard, even among fellow citizens and brothers, 151. See *Traveler*.

Perfection is always square, 11. Our perfection comes from the grace of God, 91. Perfect is the person who gives alms from his whole substance, 54. A true companion of the virtues is the one who gives from half. The Eucharistic bread belongs to perfect blessedness, 72.

**Faithlessness** must be uprooted from hearts, 61. It is always hostile to contracts, 62. It lost life, 63. It wishes for someone to rise from the dead and tell of these things, and so forth, 66. It believes neither the dead nor Christ. It was taken from paradise, 74. It led Adam to hell, 77. It rolled the stone which faith rolled away from Christ’s tomb. In Christ’s resurrection it purchased falsehood, 80. Where it is, God is not seen. It is gradually removed by the brightness of faith, 87. It has its own leaven, 99. It makes us unworthy of grace, 100. It reduces sons to penal servitude, 102. When it received all the Hebrews, 131. Its weapons are taken from faith, 152. What its sickness causes, 94. The city of faithlessness described, 95. See *Infidelity, Unbelief*.

**Faithless.** Christ was formerly unknown to the faithless, 131. What is open to the faithful was darkened for them, 132. Through Christ’s flight the material for excuse was removed from the faithless, 150. He does not wish to be born as one who knows, 158. Faithless Bethsaida, 176. How the corpse of faithlessness was treated with funeral offices by the faithless, 19. See *Unfaithful*.

**Faith.** He who strives toward the kingdom despises danger, 22. The skill of a ship’s pilot is tested not in calm weather but in a storm, 20. See *Sailor*.

**Persecution.** During persecution it is better to flee than to deny, as is shown in Peter and John, 150. When the persecutor threatens, the comforter is not absent, 86. It ended with the death of Saint Apollinaris, 128. The one who provokes makes a persecutor; the one who withdraws corrects him, 151. We must pray for persecutors, so that they may be healed. Perseverance in prayer. See 39, throughout.

**Pestilence** is called “breathing,” that is, burning to devour us, 18. It occurred in the time of Chrysologus, 45. Dancers are a pestilence, 127. Remedies that create diseases must be avoided, 7. What the chair of pestilence is, 44, throughout. See *Contagion*.

What we ought to ask from God, so that it may be profitable, 39, throughout. Why at midnight. It is useful to ask out of necessity. Let the obedient person ask Christ for what is necessary. The suppliant petitioner waits for delays most patiently. God asks this of a person according to his strength, 41. Why a stone is set against the request for bread, and so forth, 55. To ask for what is one’s own is a matter of love, not necessity, 65. What things are to be asked from God, 132. To ask for more than is owed is to demand fraud, not tribute, 137.

**Rocks** accused the crime of Christ’s death by their sound, 78. See *Stone*.

**Peter the Apostle** received from Christ all the sheep, including the lambs, entrusted to him, 6. He was girded with God’s power so that he might go to martyrdom, 10. Why he asks Christ to depart from him, 15. He lets out the nets in the word of God [Col. 1201]. In Peter’s house not wine but tears were poured out, 18. Why and when Christ enters Peter’s house, 18. What he accomplished by following Christ, 29. Before victory he denied the Lord rather than the Lord himself; therefore afterward he follows him, 27. Together with Paul he makes Christ known, 34. He saw the Lord later because he readily heard the maidservant’s voice, 78. Why, naked because of his denial, he plunged clothed into the sea, 78. He girded himself because he was to be girded. Like a veteran soldier, he believes slowly, lest he rush forward like a child, 79. It does not prejudice him that the resurrection was first announced by women, 80. Unless he had received peace from Christ, he would have been considered inferior to the others, 84. Through repentance he returned and received the power to forgive the sins of others, 84. At sea he first begs concerning his fall before rejoicing over what was granted, 90. He dies more from necessity than from will, 90. His brother Andrew was like him, 133. Forgiveness made them equal. He ascended the cross. Out of fear he asked that the Lord depart, 147. Because he did not wish to flee, he denied him, 150. He is called from the rock, 154. What the prince of the Apostles does.
