When he is about to eat, kinds of the whole creation are set before him, 163. The servant still resists his decree, 175. He eagerly desired to have the fisherman Marcellinus as a colleague. He ascended the cross head downward, 14. He denied Christ during the passion, 171.

**Peter the bishop** received from heaven the apostolic name and the privilege of the high priest, 107. He is praised throughout.

The **Pharisee** reproves Christ for going to the meal of sinners, 30. He exhorts toward salvation. Their envy, 31. How he impiously accuses Christ, 32. Also because Christ heals on the Sabbath. Sitting in the chair of pestilence, he places human traditions before heavenly decrees, 44. He confesses and denies that Christ is God, 50. Why Christ went to his meal, 93. The Pharisee’s banquet. Christ’s piety is criticized because he eats with the Pharisee. The Pharisee is rebuked and instructed, 94. He does not believe that the Lord is a prophet. He does not recognize himself as sick. He is instructed. Why he is called the catholic of the Jews, 95. Belching forth his own righteousness, he is worse than the tax collector, 123. Their murmuring is silenced by the Lord, 168. How they were always made worse. They demanded the ritual washings of their superstition from the Lord’s disciples, 171. They did not know that the Lord has one baptism. He believes that he is cleansed by external water. He possessed the keys of knowledge of the law, but through envy preferred to remain outside himself rather than let another enter, 172. Hypocrisy swelled among the Pharisees through knowledge.

How the **philosopher** lost knowledge of God and the divinely given substance, 5. His labor. He sat in the chair of pestilence, 44. How he may deflate himself of his opinions, 110. He runs for a crown of glory through empty wisdom, 119. But he does not receive the prize. His labor concerning Christ’s birth is vain, 148. Why philosophy was invented by a demon, 16.

**Madness.** A person suffering from madness does not know that he is insane, 94. The source of the madness of vices, 41. What the madness of impiety did, 38. Of the synagogue, 18.

The Lord’s **piety** is shown in the figure of the prodigal son, 1. What evils the fugitive from piety encounters, 1. The heavenly Father restores innocence and honor, 3. Piety is the wing of fasting, 8. It contains no fraud, 55. Piety exists when someone entreats another to pray, 108. It must be taken up for the destruction of impiety. It is God’s work to erase offenses, not multiply them, 113. By divine piety we are commanded to give as much to holiness as we have given to iniquity, 114. The poor man is the furnace of piety, 121. Under the appearance of piety we are sometimes recalled to evil, 123. Christ’s piety veils human sins, 125. We flee to its protection at the end of life. Why it is said to offer an example of falsehood, 126. It bends toward the tears of little ones, 128. It is piety not to teach one who despises instruction, 137. There is no piety with God without justice, 145. The pious spirit, while suffering with another, is more fearful. Herod attacks the citadel of piety between the breasts, 152. He pursues it with utter impiety. Whoever obeys piety begins not to be subject to fear, 160. God will not deny pious children what he supplies to impious birds, 163. Christ’s piety seeks us out, 170. The one borne along by piety does not grow weary. Piety conquers anger, 38. It is hidden by God, 39. It is not seen by the ungodly, 55. We are sustained by piety, 81. The Father’s greatest grief arises from the son’s impiety, 73. Toward whom will the person who is impious to himself be pious? How it is violated, 16.

**Fishermen** are sent by Christ to the sea of this age, 47. Their nets. What the ecclesiastical fisherman does, 107. Bishop Marcellinus was first a fisherman, 176.

Fish are caught indiscriminately but chosen by discernment, 47, and quickly. Christ was a fish, 55. They are caught for human life, 175.

**Lamentation.** Where it is absent, hired singing is present, 19. Why the devil’s lamentation occurs, 52. It should be made to God for sins, not for the dead, 65. See *Weeping, Tears*.

**Plant.** Who gathers fruit from a plant before cultivation? 142. See *Tree*.

**Common people.** One must speak popularly to the people, 43. Whoever was about to hear God’s law washed his garments and body, 59. Christ joined the life and salvation of two peoples, 78. The people are invited to hear the Gospel, 106. Let each person among the people apply to himself the figure of the unjust steward, 125. The calling of the two peoples is represented in Christ’s two messengers, 170. Envy ravages peoples, 172. See *Sheep, People, Preacher*.

[Col. 1202] **Rain.** What rain is to seed, the Lord’s shower is to those who will rise again, 176.

**Cup.** By hypocrisy, burning is offered in a cold cup, 7. Herod drank up John’s blood in the cup of cruelty, 127. See *Thirst, Water*.

**Punishment.** Punishment rages where guilty liability had burned fiercely, 1. The order of punishments is changed at Christ’s nod, 17. It is incurred from guilt, 27. It is redeemed from the source from which the guilt was acquired, 28. In punishments a person is held against his will, 35. The physician undergoes punishment so that he may free the sick person from it, 38. To reckon another’s punishment as one’s own consolation is the act of a madman. The punishment of those who went into the counsel of ungodliness, 44. The devil’s punishment appears in the torment of the human body, 51. The son’s punishment rebounds upon the father. Punishment pierces the one whom repentance has not pierced, 66. The whole punishment of the Lord’s passion passed over to the disciples, 83. The punishment of one reciting letters, 101. What punishment an infant formerly paid, 111. Malice is not abandoned in it, 122. It is inflicted upon the member that sinned. How the punishment of hell is dissolved by Christ’s grace and the Church’s intercession, 123. Punishments are to be mourned. It led the poor man to reward, 124. Disposition, not riches, leads to punishment. He lives in it forever who once dies to life, 124. Let us seek to escape the eternal punishments of hell. Christ threatens punishment to one persisting in sins, 125. The time of punishments excludes the time of satisfaction. The time of punishments is at the Judgment. Where there is no punishment for sin, there is no penalty for one condemned, 135. It is escaped if, before committing the offense, one provides for oneself forgiveness, 139. Fearing it, the sinner would not want Christ to come to him, 158. He who did not wish to come into service is dragged to punishment.

**The repentant person** returns first to himself and then to the Father, 2. He recognizes that all things lie open before God. He acknowledges how evil it is to sin in God’s eyes. Having lost natural things, he does not judge that he deserves what belongs to grace. How he desires to become a hired servant, 2. He rises from the ruin of mind and body, and from hell, 3. He rises more through forgiveness than he fell through guilt. He is far away when he is merely crushed. The Father suffices for him, 4. He rejoices over innocence. New things are sought for the repentant person. He asks not for glory but for forgiveness, 5. He asks to be rebuked by God, but not in anger, 45. He approaches God as physician, 45, 94. Repentant persons are received by Peter and loosed from sins, 84. When the repentant person is regarded by Christ, the barking accuser is rebuked, 94. The repentant person triumphs over his tyrant, 113. Let him at least give God as much as he has granted to the flesh and vices, 114. He who has provided nothing for his own forgiveness presumptuously ventures to procure repentance for others, 123. Let repentant persons drink water, 137. Who ought to do penance, 167. Let the Christian do penance in proportion to the wound. The repentant person flies through the air to heaven on the wings of forgiveness. Let him bend his knees beneath the burdens of penance. How repentant persons triumph over the devil, 170. Let him return shod for the course of his former life, 3. Forgiveness is granted to the repentant person, 125. It suffices for him to stop squandering; Christ pays the rest.

**Repentance** in the sinner is to be described in joyful words, 2. It reveals the Father. It can be undertaken throughout life, 42, even in old age and when one can no longer sin. One must confess in the time of repentance, 46. Let it be done at once. The Church exhorts us to it, 73. So too Peter, casting himself into the sea, 78. John the Baptist was repentance, 88. The banquet of repentance offered to Christ by Magdalene, 93. Why our harvest is referred to the time of repentance, 97. Late repentance is useless in the rich man, 122. It must be done quickly, 125, and procured from the heart. At the Judgment there is no time for repentance but for punishments. Let us who are dying turn to repentance. Why the interest of repentance must be paid by the Jew, 126. John was its way, 127. Why it must be moderated, 166. Why it must be performed when the kingdom of heaven draws near, 167. Judgment must be forestalled by it. Repent quickly, because judgment is coming. If judgment has not yet come, it is because the Lord awaits us. It must be done even in straitened time. It helps the sick, not the healthy. How it must be done. It is the interest on innocence not preserved. Through John we are recalled to it. Its bitterness is tempered by sweet mercy. The repentance of the Christian people shone forth in one repentant sinner, 169. It was slain in the death of John, 174. How it must be carried out by satisfaction, from an example, 64.

**Worldly pomp** obscures the senses, 117. See *The Rich Man and Lazarus*.

**High priest.** His office must not be confined only within domestic concerns, 88. Aaron was the first high priest of the law, 89. Zacharias was one. See *Zacharias, Abel, Cain, Man, Priest, Bishop, Prelates*.

**People.** One must speak to peoples in a popular manner, 43. Those about to hear God’s law washed garments and bodies, 59. Christ joined the life and salvation of two peoples, 78. They are invited to hear the Gospel, 106. Let each one of the people adapt to himself the figure of the unjust steward, 125. The calling of the two peoples is figured in Christ’s two messengers, 170. Envy ravages peoples, 172.

A **pig** is a muddy animal, 1. An unruly herd has muddy pastures. Why the herd of demons asks to be sent into pigs, 16. The herd of pigs could not endure the demons. [Col. 1203] Why pigs are destroyed by demons, 16. Who is handed over to the slavery of pigs, 1. Who, mystically, are the devil’s pigs, 2. He feeds pigs who leads others into sin, ibid. A demon is called a pig, and how it is fed by a Gentile, 5.

We must carry God in our body with complete holiness, 168.

The same power that created us for life restores us to salvation, 80.

**To precede.** We can precede in two ways, 137.

**Teacher.** When he does what must be taught, he instructs by hearing and forms by example, 167. See *Doctor, Master, Preacher*.

The Lord’s **commandment** must be observed if we want what he has promised, 38. God’s commandments must be kept, 53. They are called remedies.
and the sword, 112. Christ confirmed by examples those whom he taught by precepts, 151. God insinuates his precepts through the labor of the teacher, 163. Institutions founded on precepts must be strengthened by example, 166. See Jussio, Mandata Dei.

**To gird oneself.** Virtue must be girded where the will must be restrained, 22. Peter girded himself. See Peter the Apostle.

**Spoils.** The true soldier does not seek the spoils of citizens but the king’s pay, 137. Innumerable raiders against one sheep or dove, 171.

**The predestined.** The predestined follow Christ, 49. While they do not yet belong to themselves, they belong to God, 70.

**Reward.** A reward is appointed for those who must contend; and it corresponds to the greatness of the contest, 22. A grateful spirit leads to the reward, 124. When it is received from the crown, from which guilt had already been taken away, 133. Who can confidently demand a reward from Christ? 170.

**Legal prescription.** A legal limitation dissolves contentious disputes within thirty years, 145.

**Present.** The one who slanders the past does not deserve to see the present, 96. A person is so occupied with present things that he leaves nothing within himself to serve the future life, 114.

**To preside.** To preside over others while he himself is idle is harmful to himself and to many, 106. See Bishop.

**Prelates.** The bishops of the churches should be faithful stewards of the divine word, 26. The angel is the prelate of the Synagogue, 106. See Bishop.

**Presumption.** There is no presumption in the one who speaks when there is the authority of the one who commands, 70. There is great presumption in aspiring to divine virtues before testing, 90. It is shameless presumption to wish to obtain penance for others while providing nothing for one’s own pardon, 123. Presumption is always the worst thing, 68, 152. The presumption of the scribe who said that he wished to follow Christ is rejected.

**Transgression.** The Law was established as a cause of transgression, 111. How the Law obliges one through the crime of transgression, 114. The sinner became a transgressor through the command—that is, rebellious and obstinate against the command, 116. See Obstinate.

**To forestall.** How we ought to forestall God in confession, 46.

**Meal.** Let our meal be before the face of the Creator, 127. To have a royal meal and seek out foul dishes is characteristic of a servile spirit, 163. May God, our provider, always be present at our meal. At the Creator’s meal all creation hastens together. See Supper, Banquet.

**Prayers.** If prayers are dictated by supplication, there is confidence in obtaining what is requested, 70. What benefit they bring to the sick and to the son, 108. Private prayers must not be preferred to the congregation, 132.

**Beginning.** When the beginnings of good things are tested by the devil, 11. If the beginning is evil, what will the end be? 44. If the beginning is good, what will the future end be? 91. The beginnings of things are hard, but harder still are the beginnings of the one who gives birth, 175. The one who is first is not so after another; the last leaves no other after himself, 57. The first is the one whom heavenly grace generates, not mortal nature, 73. Let the first prince return to Christ, 78.

**Prince.** The undefeated leadership of Christian warfare is fasting, 8. No stranger, impure, or unbelieving person approaches the prince’s bridal chamber, 141. And how one may approach it. See King, Ruler of the Synagogue.

**Profane.** The profane person does not wish God to be born, 158. What is the mourning of the profane? 19.

**To prohibit.** To prohibit something is to admonish concerning it, 115. Why the scribe was forbidden to follow Christ, 19.

**Projectus.** Consecrated bishop of Cornelia, 165. He is praised, ibid., with a note.

**Promises.** One must trust in divine promises, 163. And whoever does not believe is most deserving of complete misery. Promises cannot be denied by the one who fulfills what has been denied, 100. Nothing is rendered as a matter of right to an unworthy person. To deny promises is characteristic of a shameless debtor; to fulfill them immediately, of an honorable one, 123. While a promise is awaited, it kindles the spirit; when it is given, it awakens the senses, 130. The one who promises gives; he does not receive, 88.

**Prophets.** Their fear before the mystery that God should become human, 72. He knows only as much as God has given, 94. God is the author of prophecy. In the prophets the divine meaning is concealed, 99. They lamented the distinction between one people and one man, 111. John was the silence of the prophets, 127. They have died, but not forever, 131. What Christ promised through them, 150. Christ fled so that faith in prophecy might stand. Their truth must be fulfilled, 156. They were sent repeatedly to the shepherds of Israel, 159. How Christ prophesies, 14.

**To offer a drink.** Lazarus offered us a taste of the resurrection, 65. Christ offered pure draughts to drink from the vessel of his body, 160. With hypocrisy serving, what envy offers to its own, 172. Hypocrisy offers heat in a cold cup, 7.

**Relative.** If he owes honor to a relative, he counts it as servitude, 48. How he may honor badly, 49.

**Property.** When property is retained, if something is granted, the grantor requires little or nothing, 14. The one who preserves what must be abandoned does not guard his own property but another’s, 22.

**Prosperity.** Prosperities do not raise the idle, nor do adversities cast down the strong, 124. Prosperities are not preserved by one who has not experienced adversities, 131. As many human prosperities, so many torments of the envious, 172. Prosperity must not be mixed with adversities, 175. In prosperity and adversity Christ is the companion of the human being, 70. See Adversities.

**Providence.** Heavenly providence considers what the hearer can grasp, 39. Blessed are those who trust in divine providence, 163, throughout. Concerning it in relation to his servants, 170. The providence of God, 18. Divine providence concealed the fearfulness of the Godhead beneath the form of humanity, 6. Blessed is the one who provides for another’s salvation and guards his own life, 155. The one who flees from a merciful provider falls into the hands of a severe judge, 1.

**Neighbor.** One’s neighbor must be helped in spiritual matters, 10, 20. How sins must be forgiven to one’s neighbor, 139. He must not be judged on the basis of doubtful or merely apparent things, 145. Whoever frees his neighbor from sins gains a reward; whoever neglects him acquires an offense, 155.

**Prudence.** Who the wiser sons of this age are, and how this is to be understood, 126.

**Psalm.** David is the first prince of the psalms, 44. The key to the others. Why he says in it, “to depart in counsel” and “to stand in the way.” One must sing psalms for the advancement of salvation, 46.

**Tax collector.** The tax collector who was called caused scandal, 28. Zacchaeus, chief of the tax collectors. See Zacchaeus. The tax collector, pressed down by the devil, so that he would not raise his eyes to heaven, 105. He is guilty when he demands more than is owed, 137. A most cruel exactor, 54, throughout. See Exactor.

**Public.** How something done publicly is said to have been done secretly, 9. Why a public sin is punished by God, 125.

**Child.** A little child is nourished by nature, 39. He receives only good things from his father, 55. How we ought to act toward little children, or beginners in the service of God, 25. Children are given things beneficial under the appearance of harmful ones. He uses tears as weapons for breaking hearts, 128. Christ is described as a little and gentle child, 164. See Infancy. The childhood of Christians is animated by light commandments, so that youth may approach serious ones, 38.

**Beauty.** Bodily beauty is not lust, but it leads to the fall of lust, 116. The one who lusts after bodily beauty longs to be tall, 163. What does the Lord do so that a person may be beautiful?

**To knock.** We speak of the heavenly secret by repeating prayers and persevering through delays, 39.

**Dust.** Why is the human being, made from it, reduced to dust? At length, in detail, 101.

Things entrusted to divine ministries must be purified, 171.

Purple raised the rich man to arrogance, 124. Herod lost it, 174. Dyed with the blood of the martyrs. See Banqueter, Rich Man, Martyr.

A person small in body can be great in spirit, 54. He is accustomed to ask his father for an egg, 55. What is the little flock? 22.

## Q

**The number forty** is sacred and mystical, employed in the greatest affairs of God, 166.

**Lent.** What one entering its sea must do, 8. Let him carry grain. And let this be almsgiving and mercy. What mercy during the Lenten fast means. Divine songs are to be joined to the Lenten fast, 10. The divine institution contains the square discipline of faith, 11. It is a season of spiritual warfare, 12. What must be done during it. This fast is a campaign for the world. It reveals the devil’s ambushes, 20. In it virtues fight against vices, 113. It is the season for laying aside idleness, 18. What the idle person loses during it. In it victory is promised by Christ. In it angels are given for our defense. The Lenten fast conquers enemies. What the demons’ temptations are during it. During it the offspring of the Church are received by the pastors for baptism, 40. The Lenten fast repairs the vessels of our bodies, 60. Why it was handed down, 166. Through it we run to the font of baptism and salvation. We are also summoned to heaven. And many other things concerning it, 166. See **Fasting**, **Abstinence**. [Col. 1205]

**The four-horse chariot** is the Gospel, 92. Why we ascend into its seat. What its threefold character is and for what purpose, 170.

**To seek.** For what purpose Christ would be sought by a Jew, 37. What we ought to seek from God, 39. The soul had long sought God through stones and pieces of wood, 62. He who always seeks does not always possess, 104. To seek God and not know him is more a necessity than a fault, 157. We must not seek by art what cannot be found by art, 160.

**Question.** Why Matthew the tax collector was chosen by the Lord, 28. The malicious question put by the Jews about Christ, 49. The tax collector’s profit is not destroyed but changed, 54, 29. What kind of profit comes from sins, 158.

**Quality.** God gathers the quality of works not from places but from their meaning, 9.

**Complaint.** Blessed are those whom complaint has not touched, 91. Childhood, adolescence, and youth are wholly complaint. Who walks without complaint, 89.

There is no rest where gold is guarded, 22. Rest comes from labor, and conversely, 103.

**The number fifty** pertains to mercy, with an example from David and from the jubilee, 126.

How this is the speech of one who doubts, not of one who believes, 62.

## R

**The rabid man** does not eat bread, 174. Savage rage at Herod’s banquet.

**Root.** A root fixed deeply extends its shoot upward, 61. See **Tree**.

**Reason.** Reason gives rest to weary senses, 101. Things are to be done with both divine and human reason, 109. God quickly demands an account, so that he may release debts, 125. We must settle what concerns us, lest we return what belongs to another. The summons to render accounts is called bitter. Human reason does not comprehend the Creator of things, 131. God’s reason is one thing, man’s another, 141. Christ’s mystery must not be judged by earthly reason, 148. Who are bound to render an account to God, 26.

**The Church of Ravenna.** When it was to give birth for the first time, it felt the pains, and why, 175. See **Apollinaris**.

**Guilt.** Guilt always retreats beneath a covering, 78. It is guilt, not the guilty person, that perishes in Christ’s death and resurrection, 110. From the source from which guilt is taken, a reward can be taken, 133. Things lacking sense, because of their nature, do not know guilt, 171. It drove human beings from the sight of God, 6. We should at least abandon guilt when it itself abandons us, 42. See **Sin**, **Crime**.

**Rebellious.** When God turns away from the rebellious person, it is good for him, 131. He does not want a ruler to be born, 158.

A relapsed illness is more often fatal, 113.

**Ruler of the people.** What he is like and what his evils are, 152. What account he must render to God, 26. How the idle ruler harms both himself and the peoples, 106.

**To return.** To return a divine gift is not to lose it but to possess it, 59. If we have taken something belonging to another, it must be returned quickly, and why, 123. We must render an account of our stewardship, 125. The summons to render it is called bitter. Who are bound to render an account to God, 26.

**Redemption.** Redemption was accomplished through Christ’s body, 115. The redemption of man was accomplished by God, 161. See **Restoration**.

The prodigal son’s return to his father, 3.

The royal court is described, 42. Festivity and music honor royal births, 91. No one rushes into royal service unless summoned, 119. Royal garments leave us in hell, 122. When a ruler is present, what reverence and what service are due to royalty, 141. One who possesses royal equipment but searches out the filth of the kitchen has a degenerate spirit, 163. See **King**.

**The Queen of the South** against the Hebrews in judgment, 37. Death is queen of all evils, and why, 118.

**The kingdom of heaven** is promised to the faithful who contend, 22. Whoever is going to reign must abandon what belongs to him. What it means for a servant to wish to enter the kingdom without fear, 23. Whoever is going to reign must cast away worthless things. One summoned to the kingdom distributes his own private possessions among the needy. Fear is excluded by the promised kingdom, 25. Whoever is certain of the kingdom despises worldly things. What the heavenly Father promises. Those who are to reign should send their possessions ahead through the hands of the poor. God sells the kingdom for a fragment of bread, 41. It is compared with pearls, 47. It must be seized, 56. Those who once reigned in us, 67. When the kingdom of God exists, 67. The kingdom of God is always present, 69. It is within us in hope, 70. Death and sin reigned over us. How the devil distances the kingdom of God from us, 71. The kingdom is God the Father, and he contains all the power of the kingdom in himself, 72. Whoever does not long for the promised kingdom is idle. The kingdom of heaven is broadly compared with a mustard seed, 98. What the kingdom of heaven is like. How it comes into us. Its various and familiar likenesses, so that it may reach everyone, 99. Even those of different sex. The reign of sin must not be permitted in us, 113. How God gave himself a kingdom in Christ, 144. Human beings do not seek the kingdom, 144. For the sake of a temporal kingdom Herod seeks to extinguish the eternal one, 152. The kingdom of heaven is the reward of the righteous, the judgment of sinners, and the punishment of the impious, 167. John said that the kingdom of heaven was near when the world was still young; what, then, is its condition now? How Christians defer the kingdom to the Lord.

**Relation.** The truth of a relation is confirmed by indications of place, time, and person, 140.

**Religion.** The devil attempted to fashion something ridiculous from religion, 155. The fellowship of religion and care of the sacrament between John and the Virgin Mary, 49.

To abandon one’s possessions in order to serve God is to demand a secure reward from Christ, 170. To preserve what ought to be abandoned is to be the guardian not of one’s own things but of another’s, 22.

**Forgiveness of sins** must be believed, 58. The power to forgive sins was handed over to Peter and the priests, 84. The forgiveness of sins will occur when all material for sinning has been removed, 95. Its greatness is recognized from the greatness of guilt, 54.

**Renewal.** The renewal of creation will proceed from oldness into newness, 101.

**Restoration.** The restoration of human salvation follows the same lines by which it was lost, 77. It is greater to restore what has been lost than to preserve what is unharmed, 97. The restoration of humanity takes place through a woman, 99. From the restoration of created things it will be demonstrated that they are not gods, 101. How our restoration was accomplished by the whole Trinity, 157.

**The reprobate.** Their wickedness binds Christ’s hands, 100. They should not accuse Christ of having failed to offer them grace. From what they will be confounded at the judgment, 22.

Rest itself does not grow weary, 110. The rest of human labor comes from the Sabbath, 139. Rest comes from Jesus, 54. See **Rest**.

**Household property** must be left behind by one who is called to the kingdom, 22–23. It is called a narrow circumstance, 88.

To answer quickly is a mark of human readiness, 140. But to reflect is a mark of a mature judge.

**The resurrection of the dead** was Christ—how so, 13. God raises the dead more quickly than a human being awakens someone sleeping, 34. Its speed is explained by examples. The saints will rise through Christ’s resurrection, 40. And this certainly. Human resurrection takes place through God, 57. Why the resurrection of the flesh must be believed, 58. Of bodies, from Christ’s burial, 59. It must be believed because of many examples. The one who rises will live forever. The flesh will rise as we are, and why, 60. After it there will be neither an end of good things nor of evil things. Christ’s resurrection is also the resurrection of our body, 62. The decayed flesh will rise through God. A man rises from the tomb of a woman’s womb, and why, 64. There is a twofold resurrection: from the death of the body and from the faithlessness of the soul, 65. We receive a foretaste of the resurrection when Lazarus offers it, 65. In Christ the one killed for him will rise, 173. Who will rise in Christ. The flesh will rise through Christ, 62. The form of our resurrection is reported from the glory of the angel, 74. Also from his clothing and appearance, 77. It is madness not to believe it, 74. A human being will rise in his own flesh, 76. When the innocent rise, terror and death will possess the impious, 77. The human being will be restored in the very splendor of his body. Our resurrection has its form from the events of Christ’s resurrection, 89. Its day is eternal, 79. Its age is youthful, and it is at the right hand, 82. We should pray that we may rise to eternity. The garments of perpetual resurrection. In it all material for sinning will be removed, and other things, 95. It has its own leaven, 99. The resurrection of the widow’s son should not seem wondrous to those who believe in the universal resurrection, 103. The human being will be raised from dust. The resurrection is argued from times and seeds. In baptism we rise with Christ through newness of life, 113. A human being should acknowledge that it was accomplished through Christ. In the resurrection the flesh will be possessed by the Spirit; there corruption, guilt, and crime perish, 117. It must not be discussed cursorily. It is the whole hope of Christian faith, 118. The Apostle proves it. We must always speak of it, so that the terror of death may be driven away. It is demonstrated from the alternation of the rising and setting of the day, the sun, and the seasons; and from the seed of wheat, as described. It must be believed because it is promised without price. It is promised in Christ’s words, 131. The resurrection of the dead is a debt owed to the womb of Mary, 140. Herod’s statement about the resurrection of John the Baptist—how it is to be understood, 173. In it death succumbs to death. It is promised through the Law. Its credibility is shown by the illumination of the blind, 176. What rain is to seed, the Lord’s rain is to those who will rise. What has been buried in death will rise in life. The one who rises will see eternal and glorious things. See **Glory**.

**The guilty person.** The guilty soul stands behind the back, awaiting pardon, 93. The convicted guilty person is brought before Christ as an accused person is summoned to court, 125. Christ was made guilty on behalf of the guilty person. He does not want to be born as judge, 158. He cannot easily pronounce sentence against the innocent, 173. That the guilty person may fall, 75.

**King.** The king does not admit plebeian worship, 75. Why he ordered the man without a worthy garment to be bound. What account he will render to God concerning his administration, 26. When the King of heaven does not help, other defenses are useless, 46. He enters among enemies when he wishes to free a captive, 54. Kings are named by the titles of their triumphs, 57. At the king’s table one eats whatever his dominion and power possess, 95. One who has not been invited does not enter his presence, 102. A public offering is prepared for the newborn king, 103. At his service the military post trembles, 109. Noble and brave, he meets the enemy at a greater distance, 116. How the kings of Persia assume ridiculous forms, 120. To fall in battle on behalf of the king is a virtue; yet to complete the contests is perfection, 128. They cannot rule unless they are ruled by God, 131. The soldier runs to receive the king’s pay, 137. It is terrifying to them that Christ is born, 146. What a king does from the desire to reign, as shown by Herod’s example. What is owed to the king, perfect devotion owes to his image, 147. As the king proceeds, everything is cleansed and adorned, 149. He provides provisions for his devoted soldiers, 163. God is our king. He surpasses all in appearance and glory. Envy drives kings on, 172. What their painted image, together with concord, signifies, 149. The king keeps watch beforehand in the camp, 24. See **Royal**.

**Laughter.** Woe to those who laugh in the world, 46.

**Rome.** Its army was the avenger of Christ’s blood, 42. The doctrine of faith rests with the Romans, 102. The Romans, formerly persecutors, are now executors of the word of Christian faith, 20.

**Dew from heaven.** See **Manna**. The eyes of the sinner are baptized by a drop of holy dew, 176.

**Rose.** The rose is among thorns, 49. See **Flowers**.

**Rust.** Nourished by things kept in store, 7. An epithet of modesty, 22. An epithet of martyrdom, 98.

**Bush.** The bush carried, but did not contain, the divine fire, 164. A figure of the Jewish people. Why the fiery God shines forth, 170. In the bush the fiery God is gathered into a mass before Moses, 69.

The uneducated person is slow-witted, so as to weary his teacher, 106. The rustic hears from the Lord the commonplace parable about the fig tree, 106. See **Farmer**, **Steward**.

## S
## Sabbath

Why the priests watched Christ to see whether he would heal on the Sabbath, 32. Provision was made for salvation; therefore the sick person ought to be healed on it. Christ gave rest on the Sabbath to weary mortals. It is illumined through Christ, not abolished, so that it may shine in the Church on the Lord’s Day, 75. The primary Sabbath is the Lord’s Day; the secondary is the Jewish Sabbath, and what each was appointed for, 77. How it is wrongly observed by a Jew, 150. Blessed, appointed for the repose of human labor and divine work, 139. See Festivity.

## Moneybag

Why one is prepared in heaven, 25. Let the miser follow even moneybags. The moneybags of Matthew are not required by Christ, 28. To fast with a moneybag is vengeance, not devotion, 42. The miser reduces himself to a moneybag.

## Priest

How he may sin in heavenly things, 26. Appointed from among human beings in place of an angel. Why the priests Nadab and Abihu suffer punishment because of the sacrifice, 26. The drunkenness of priests is condemned. How the Hebrew priests watched Christ, 32. He receives the Lord’s body daily and is not healed because of a defect of faith, 33. The priest’s glory is the peace of the people, and the duty of both, 53. What he should say when he is about to proclaim grace, 60. God calls the people through the mouths of priests, 62. Christ entrusted to priests the power to forgive sins to human beings, 84. His speech is given when God wills, not when the priest wills, 86. The first was Aaron, 89. Why the priest of the ancient law had the right of marriage, 92. How he becomes a persecutor of the law, 96. Every person, through Paul, is both priest and victim, 108. He urges this. Saul, presumptuously undertaking the priesthood, loses his kingdom, 109. The priests profaned holy things and converted pardon into profit, 158. Why they were unwilling for Christ to be born. The holy one of the Jews until the time of Herod, 86. They are Christ’s feet, 95, 93. See Ecclesiastics; Preacher.

## Sacrament

The sacrament of piety is disclosed to us by Christ, lest it become an occasion of error, 160. Christ commands the sacraments. The care of the sacrament was entrusted between John and the Virgin Mary, 49.

## Sacrifice

A sacrifice to be offered to God, especially at Passover, and why, 73. The human being is wondrous, and why, 108. This derives from the form of Christ’s sacrifice. The best things are to be sacrificed to God, 109. When it is changed into punishment without reason, 109. What is to be offered to God from one’s wealth, 66. Adam, when created, did not render the sacrifice of praise, 101.

## Age

Its consummation. See Consummation; World. The Apostle reproves the form of the age—that is, its life, customs, institutions, vanities, luxury, and pomp, 120. The raging sea of the age, 20. Those who have avoided the contagion of the age, 23.

## Salt

The Apostles are the salt of the earth, 120. Grains of salt remain incorrupt when they descend into the marrow. Salt is a wholesome seasoning for food, provided moderation is not lacking, 125. Excess salt makes food bitter.

## Solomon

He demonstrates from where wisdom comes, 48. Among all kings he shone with singular glory and beauty of adornment, 163. He becomes king while still a little child and rules the people by virtue, not by arrogance, 48.

## Dancers

They are plagues, 127. The whole sermon concerns them. The dancing girl is described, [Col. 1208] 174. A serpent was hidden in her, and for what purpose. She was a beast, 127.

## Salutary Things

When a sick person rejects salutary things, it is a sign of illness, not of unwillingness, 108. They become a cause of danger if taken wrongly, 156. To avoid salutary things as though they were harmful is an affliction, 132.

## Salvation

To seek the salvation of souls is profitable, 10. Christ hungers for the salvation of human beings, 11. What is to be said when the salvation of many demands the death of one, 37. God is salvation for the despairing, 65. Human salvation is restored along the same lines by which it was lost, 77, 79. How it is hoped for when a barren woman gives birth, 90. Salvation was denied to the eyes of those who preceded and followed, so that it might be wholly grounded in faith, 110. There is no salvation without Christ, 111. Its occasion becomes an instrument of perdition, 126. The salvation of the lost comes from God; it is the fruit of Mary’s womb, 140. Our salvation would have been thwarted if Christ had been killed as a little child, 151. Blessed is the provider of another’s salvation, 155. From the material of error an occasion of salvation was made through Christ, 157. Salvation cannot perish, 158. Christ reproves those unwilling to recognize the time of salvation, 164. The salvation of one’s weak neighbor must be sought before everything else, 18. No one should presume to save himself, 68.

## Saints

Their deeds are mysterious, 37. They will be separated from the wicked at the judgment, 47. The saints’ fear that God became human, 72. In them age lived and advanced, 89. We are raised by their falls and strengthened by their trembling, 90. They know only as much as God has granted, 97. Their death becomes precious; why, 101. God reclaims their souls, 104. They rejoiced at Christ’s coming, 106. To be holy among sinners is difficult but glorious, 107. How they overcome three enemies, 120. They are greater than heaven and equal to the angels; brighter than the sun, more luminous than the moon and stars—how, 120. They shine with as many virtues as heaven has stars. They will remain in God’s glory and will not pass away with heaven, etc. In glory they will exercise the offices that they exercised here in holiness, 121. The virtues of the saints should be recalled soberly on their feast days, 122. Their own prerogative is sufficient for their glory. After Christ’s triumph they were released from the custody of hell, 123. After their labors they rest. Here they lose their soul in order to find it in everlasting life, 128. The dying precede the living for a time, 128. Why the dead assist their own flock. Their birthday is when they are born from earth into heaven, 129. On the birthday of the saints, their life is set forth for imitation, not indulgence in banquets. Their virtues should be requested from God. The congregation of the saints obtains everything here, 132. Their festivities are rightly celebrated through prayer and imitation, 135. Everything they had deserved they considered small if they did not see the Lord, 147. The names of the saints often indicate their merits and distinguishing marks, 154. When human resources fail, divine resources come to the aid of the saints, 156. At their death the infirmity perishes, not the person, 173. They feast at the heavenly table with the choirs of angels, 174. They always hear heavenly harmony. Whatever they do not attain, they fear, 175. The devil is always their enemy, 11. They stand and undergo evils for crowns, 15. See Confessor; Martyrs; Beatitude; Holiness.

## Holiness

It is wholly profaned by luxury, 27. It must be offered up so that folly may be brought to completion, 108. As much should be spent on holiness as on uncleanness, 114. Anxious, 116. The soul and body must be guarded, 117. The members of holiness should be content with the gifts of the generous giver, 120. Its model was John, 127. Hateful to sacrilegious people. Turned by the devil into sacrilege, 155. Always opposed to luxury, 174.

## Blood

When human blood made a sea upon the earth, 20. When it may be offered without blood, 108. Stephen’s blood was the first poured out in martyrdom, 154. The first blood shed upon the earth was that of righteous Abel, 172. See Martyrs.

## Health

The person who does not know how to lend to the poor does not know how to be healed, 32. It is poured forth more abundantly where the wound has been enlarged, 112. The person who does not desire it is ungrateful to the physician, 113. It returns at God’s command, 176.

## Wise

The wise person takes material for instruction from created things; the foolish person takes from them a cause of error, 89. Thus he learned the Creator from contemplation of creation. The demon makes the wise of the age foolish, 96. From what do the wise of the world consider themselves great? 118.

## Wisdom

Wisdom makes a man; folly does the opposite, 5. It did not know what the divine law taught, 11. Christ’s wisdom is unknown to the person who does not know God, 48. It is from God. Human wisdom is blindness to us, 76. The Lord’s wisdom is infinite, 90. Christ is the true wisdom of God, recognized by the faith of the heart, 119.

Sarah, barren and old, prepares three cakes baked under the ashes for the Lord’s hospitality—mystically, 99. Why her name was changed, 154. Why she calls her son Isaac.

## Satisfaction

Its period lasts until death, 125. See Penance.

Saul, arrogating the priesthood to himself, loses the kingdom, 109.

## Scandal

There are three kinds, 27. Scandal and the enemy: the same in active and passive form, and their effect. Judas the betrayer was the scandal of scandals. Why a millstone is fastened around the neck of the person who causes scandal—beautifully explained. Balaam’s scandal placed before the people, 27. Publicized so that it may be punished by God, 125.

## Stage

The scene of piety was the flesh of the poor man covered with sores, IX. Tragedy and comedy are found there, 173.

## Knowledge

What human knowledge has done, 5. What its hunger has done. It contains extensive matters in a narrow discourse, 5. It gives nourishment for salvation, 18. Through ourselves we are blinded by human knowledge, 76. Because of Christ’s merit it is admired by a Jew, 85. It has branches, 98. How great is the knowledge of the saints, 119. Divine knowledge is partial here and will be complete in heaven. Knowledge made the passions more widely known, 115. It is from God, 126. The person who fears knowing deserves to know, 143. Knowledge of the law should be sought through the law, 148. Sought through God, it should not be sought from human beings, 156. Knowledge of God was given to believers through the Magi, 158. It has the palm of faith rather than that of its simplicity, 166. True knowledge is that which is joined with virtue, 167. Why the Pharisee receives the keys of knowledge, 172. What was bad in the Pharisees’ knowledge. The disciple does not acquire it if he wishes to be taught according to his own will, 173. One should know what is asked as far as one can, 101.

What the scribes of Jerusalem did with heavenly teaching, 158. What the presumptuous scribe heard from Christ, 19. See Pharisee.

## Sacred Scripture

It benefits the learned and the unlearned, 20. Its mysteries would be innumerable if each word were recorded in a separate book, and even then they would not be fully revealed, 64. Sacred Scripture is often not expounded at length because of the hearers’ weariness, 101. It should be declared cautiously to rivals, securely to children, confidently to believers, and steadfastly to unbelievers, 112. While it is clear, one must rely upon it with complete simplicity. The whole sacred Gospel is full of mysteries, 146. Care must be taken lest, through the hearer’s ignorance, it bring harm to souls, 156. It is better explained through God, when the faithful pray for this, 5, so that it may be revealed, 96. See Gospel; Teacher; Preacher.

## Secret

How something may be called secret when it is before human beings, 9. A secret can be public, and the reverse. It cannot be known, 61. It would be revealed if a person paid closer attention, 101. Why it was disclosed to Christ, 160.

## Crops

Dry crops are consumed when fire is applied to them, 116. Seeds are described; they are raised from corruption in their proper form, 103. The whole tree is in the seed, and the defect of the seed is the defect of the whole tree, 111. The fruit serves the seed, 112. They teach our resurrection, 118. What belongs to the good struggle, 119. God gives them growth.

## Eternal Things

They are abandoned by those who covet temporal things, 22. One must labor for them, 124.

## Old Man / Old Age

An old man is said to be estranged from his wife, 88. Dead to himself and denied to offspring. Why the old man’s son does not know wine. Old age is cleansed of vices and free from youthful fires. Long old age loses hope of posterity, 90. The mystery of old age is to advance in virtues, 91. It has dry limbs marked with wrinkles, 92. Old age, when pregnant, is a source of laughter to everyone, 92. A person is called old by character and wisdom, not by time or age, 5. Old age is called the setting age, 87. See Old Woman.

## Senses

How our senses cause scandal for us, 27. They are given for life. Spiritual senses are found in the birds of heaven, 98. The divine sense is concealed in the law, the prophets, and the Gospel, 99. Our senses are aroused by the fearful proclamation of the Gospel, 115. They are held fast by apostolic vigor. They are deceived by cosmetics, 116. Why the senses of Sacred Scripture must keep to the proper measure, 125. The sense is honeyed when the mouth utters nothing bitter. Human senses are disturbed by John’s virtue and Herod’s savagery, 127. A perverse sense cannot hear what it has once decided to hate, 131. Why the meaning lies hidden in the letter, 132. The divine meaning is concealed in human words, 139. Human senses are carried away by countless vices, 171. A hostile meaning can nevertheless be truthful, 173.

## Sentence

The human sentence of condemnation ceased from Christ’s Advent into the world, 90. Christ does not wish to hasten it against the guilty person, 125. The person who flees the accuser flees it, 145. The person who refused to reach grace is dragged toward it, 158. The deceived judgment of the judge, which did not destroy the man who was killed but advanced him, 173.

## Separation

The bitterness of the world was removed through mercy, 6. The separation of the good and the wicked at the judgment consoles the saints, 47. Vices are overcome through separation, 116. In the separation of members there is foul destruction, 132. Separation produces evils; gathering produces life. Earthly separation is heavenly union, 164. See Discernment.

## Seven

The number seven is very rich in sacraments, and how, 139. Born in the seventh month, 56.

## Tomb

It has a door harder than hard death and is closed by an exceedingly hard stone, 65. Its sight raises the woman who had been cast down by the sight of a tree, 74. The house of death becomes a dwelling of life. Christ is born from the tomb of faith, 75. How its stone becomes a title of life and death. The tomb is the breast in which Christ is still held dead. It is the reproach of the woman’s transgression, 77. The title of her guilt, and other matters. The women enter the tomb so that, buried with the Lord, they might rise wholly into salvation by faith and rise together with Christ, 82. The one who cannot die does not know how to fear the tomb. The tomb was the house where the disciples reclined because of fear of the Jews, [Col. 1210] 83. The tomb is described as a prison of corpses, 118. A human being is the tomb of a human being, 120. In its natural clay the corpse does not know the bite of worms; it forestalls decay and stench, 121. Demons consign themselves to tombs so that they may reduce people, still alive, to tombs, 16. At Christ’s presence people come out of the tomb, 16. The banquet was the tomb of pomp, 121. See Demon; Angel.

## Calm

Calm is more welcome after the darkness of a storm, 84.

## Late

This adverb is explained in connection with the time when the Lord appeared to the disciples, 84. See Evening.

## Speech

Broad matters are not properly disclosed in a narrow discourse, 5. Ornate speech is to the ears as fragrance is to the nostrils, 18. It should be adapted to the occasion, 20, 21. What conceived speech does when it cannot evaporate, 57. Brief and sudden speech, before it enlightens the eyes, already retreats; it gives not light but fear, 64. Divine speech is not returned to the people without God, 77. Hasty speech both flees and passes over questions, 82. Worldly speech serves human minds; divine speech is in the power of the giver, not the speaker, 86. Divine speech rules; it does not serve. When it comes, it must be heard; when it does not come, one must endure. If the priest’s speech is delayed, it must not be taken away. It overflows when God gives it, 86. A brief discourse cannot include everything, 86. One must devote oneself wholly to what is more useful, 91. Human speech calls where there is angelic speech. The hearer grows weary of a long discourse, 101. Speech is uttered securely when commanded by the one giving the order, 107. Helpful speech is not to be refused, even if its eloquence is unskilled. Hasty speech does not reveal the secret of divine knowledge, 112. What the tripartite order of speech accomplishes, 115. What the Apostle’s commonly read speech accomplishes, 120. Frequent repetition produces weariness. It should be postponed when the time for speaking has passed, 121. It is better heard when the powers of the soul have been restored, 122. Why the angel’s speech troubled Mary, 140. Because of the greatness of the mystery it is postponed from day to day, 145. Great matters are sometimes concluded in a brief speech, 160. The Lord’s speech is contrary to the unlearned, and how, 164. It should be postponed rather than hastened, 173. Angelic speech speaks divine things, 156. See Gospel; Preacher; Teacher.

## Serpent

It has a head subjected to the human being, 173. It was the dancing girl. The shoots of the ancient serpent were extinguished by the shedding of John’s blood. A serpent was hidden in the dancer, 174. At that time it was reaching toward Christ’s death. See Devil; Herod.

## Preserve

The person who preserves what ought to be left behind is the guardian of another’s things, not his own, 22. Out of greed a person preserves many things, not for himself but for others—and for his own torment, 122.

## Serve

Those who serve money cannot serve God, 28. To serve God alone is freedom; to serve several masters is captivity, 61. How useful it is to serve the weak poor person, 122. We ought to serve the Lord, and how, 161. Him alone, not others, and why. Nevertheless, we devote the whole of our servitude to human beings and none to God. How one must serve the Lord out of duty.

## Servitude

Servitude is free in the presence of the Father, 3. Of the human being before Christ’s incarnation, 6. It should be ours toward God, not toward unjust powers, 20. The sons of God designated here remain in the condition of servitude, 71. Fear indicates servitude, 101. When the knowledge of the Lord existed throughout the servitude of the age, 102. The presumptuous woman is punished; the cautious one is rewarded, 119. The most disgraceful servitude is that of sin, 114. In the Gospel it has not been lost but changed. Devoted servitude is better than wandering and presumptuous freedom. The Gospel wipes away the stain of servitude. Servitude is driven out by servitude. The Gospel commands us to give God as much as we once gave the world, 114. The servitude of sin is removed, and the servitude of God succeeds it. The devil has the end of life and the beginning of punishment as his reward. The servitude of God is true dominion, 115. Every condition of servitude will be abolished in heaven, 139. All servitude to the world will be removed after Antichrist, 156.

## Servant

The service rendered to a master while he dines is described, 161. He makes the Lord magnificent, 170. Divine things must be preferred to human affections, 19. The servant of God stands; the servant of a human being lies down, 19. The servant of God suffers evils for a crown; the servant of a human being suffers them for punishment. A servant of the belly is called a beast, 22. He desires a kingdom with fear, 23. What he should do toward the Lord, 26. The servant of God spares those who injure him, 38. He will be with God in glory, 40. The merciful person has as many servants as coins, 54. When the master is killed at home through the crime of the servants, vengeance extends to the whole household, 78. There is no charity among the servants when they feast while the Lord’s corpse is still fresh, 83. The servants of the Lord go before him so that they may not incur guilt through silence, 97. How the servants of the Lord approach God, speak to him, and what they say, 97. They cannot bear to see the foulness of the Lord’s harvest. How much knowledge of God they possess. The servant snatches away grace rejected by the Lord, 100. A servant is one whose price is assessed, 102. When the soul rules, the body is a precious servant. The devoted person carries out commands; the defiant person does not. No one becomes a servant by himself, but only when called, 109. The human being was a servant and captive under the law—how, 116. But by God’s grace he is liberated. He does not wish the Lord to be born, 158. He prepares death for him so that he may be free of servitude, 158. The servant of God is the human being who has been created, redeemed, and purchased, 161. The servant assisting at the Lord’s supper is described, 161. Unless he keeps watch, he will breakfast on blows the next day. [Col. 1211] Whatever the Lord does around him is law for him. So that a person may know how to serve God. The person living at his own expense accuses the Lord, 163. He should inquire not why the Lord wishes something, but what the Lord wishes to be done, 166. The servant serving God should be free from earthly things, 170. What purse, bread, and money they ought to carry. A servant’s property belongs to the master, 15. Freed by the Lord while clothed in the condition of servitude, 96. Who is said to attend to himself, and how. See Attend.

## Signs

Signs indicate the thing that is to be found, 159. To whom signs, or miracles, should be granted, and for what purpose, 11. See Miracle. Signs harm the devil, 11.

## Silence

What kind of silence enables the sinner to reach pardon, 34. Why Chrysologus is silent during Christ’s Passion, 77. The Lord increases and repays the interest of devout silence. Chrysologus’s silence, 86. Silence and speech are from God. Let us not be ungrateful to God for them. The fault of the silent person does not exist if silence is commanded, 36. How voice arises from silence, 92. It proves guilt, 97. Silence is brought in from the barrenness of the soil, 107. To conceal virtues is the work of the right hand; to publicize them, of the left, 9.

## Simeon

Saint Simeon sees the Lord before he dies, 106.

## Comparisons

Why they are delivered in the vernacular, 39. Why they were given by Christ, 47. For teaching the ignorant, 106. See Example; Figures; Common Things.

## Simplicity

It possesses the grace of innocence, the fruit of faith rather than knowledge, and the reward of virtues, 166. It makes a good citizen but does not make a strong soldier. It is wholly ignorant of hypocrisy, 172. With simplicity and truth we sacrifice the Lamb of God, and why.

## Images

Those who make themselves images of idols lose the image of God, 155. These are not playthings but crimes.

## Mustard

The mustard seed is broadly likened to the kingdom of heaven, 98, and why. It must be sown in our minds. When the integrity of the seed is crushed, its hidden power appears. The mustard tree, while closing the eyes, opens them, 99.

## Singular

It is not referred to by example, 61. Singularity is not acceptable to God, but unity is, 132. It admits no example, 153. There is a bad kind of singularity, 170. Why it comes from the demon, 16.

## Left

In it we have a part of our vices, and what they are, 9. The evils of the left. Divinity admits nothing sinister. There is nothing left-handed in angels, 87. How the Lord’s sheep fell from the right to the left, 168. See Right.

## Thirst

How it is cured by a cold spring, 46, 79. A cup of cold water does not completely extinguish a traveler’s thirst, 112. It advances toward endurance, 124. In the burning person it is not extinguished but increased, 172. The dragon’s thirst toward the Lord, 174. See Cup.

## Sobriety

It must be observed with the greatest care in interpreting the Gospel’s meanings, and why, 125. Sobriety in food is useful, 41.

## Fellowship

Good fellowship, and why, 170. Those withdrawn from divine fellowship are possessed by the demon, 16. How love of fellowship removes fear of servitude, 166. See Union.

## Mother-in-law

How the mother-in-law is separated from bridegroom and bride, 164. The mother-in-law, the Synagogue, kills the son so that she may not see the companionship of the daughter-in-law. Peter’s mother-in-law is sick.

## Sun

The sun’s radiance makes the day brighter, 8. Its rays cannot be hidden, 9. It touches filth and is not defiled, 94, 35. The woman with the hemorrhage is not less than the sun, 36. It accuses fraudsters, 54. It gives darkness to bleary eyes, 60. It darkens an unwelcome sight, 61. When it flees, what of the moon’s and stars’ brightness can remain for the comfort of night? 78. At the Lord’s resurrection it arrives before its appointed time, 82. It traverses the boundaries of the seasons throughout the whole year, 87. It recalls birthday festivals. What is brighter than the sun? 101. It possesses doubled light, 103. It does not need light, 110. It is born and dies every day, 118. The saints are brighter than the sun, 120. When the sun’s rays burst forth, human sight is dulled, 146. Its splendor illumines heaven, 149.

## Consolation

There is consolation in punishments when they are general, 101.

## Solemnity

See Festivity.

## Solitary

The solitary person is always open to everyone, 164. How one can be alone while among a multitude, 36.

## Release

The hand that was bound by a command is released by a command, 32. How the slowness of release is compensated by God, 77. The person forced to pay what he does not owe is especially oppressed, 137. Release broke the security, 62. How the world will be dissolved, 101.

## Dreams

The dreams revealed by Joseph preserved his life, 174.

## Sleep

Why Christ slept in the endangered boat, 21. The sleep of the age is sleepless, 22. Why sleep should be indulged, 24. With God, death is sleep, 34. The Lord uses sleep in giving gifts, to veil piety, 39. It is also the sleep of grief, 81.

## Spectacle

There is a spectacle in heaven where on earth there is conflict between rich and poor, 124. Evil spectacles pollute the good, 155. See Stage.

## Watchtower

The heavenly watchtower shows mammon ruling the world, 126. From the watchtower of confession Zacchaeus saw the giver of pardon, 54. [Col. 1212]

## Cave

Why a cave is mentioned in the burial of Lazarus, 65.

## Hope

We hope for what we do not see, 62. Let us await what we hope for; when it arrives, hope ceases, 10. The human being is designated by hope, not by reality, and is not thereby advanced into heaven, 62, 71. Hope is not seen and is awaited through patience. Every class of human beings subsists by hope. We glory in hope, 110. Hope leads to the measure of Christ’s fullness. It is a mark of perfect virtue that, through the strength of hope, one possesses what one does not yet hold in reality. The whole hope of Christian faith lies in the resurrection of the dead, 118. It is a gift of God, 135. The hope of sinners is advanced by the Lord toward pardon, 168.

## Thorns

When thorns are cut down by a sickle, they increase even more, 115. The thorns of the fields are burned, 164.

## Holy Spirit

How he sometimes makes childbirth bitter, 56. Where he generates, the Virgin gives birth, 57. He is of one substance with the Father and the Son, 58. He is God, co-worker with the Father and the Son, 60. Whoever denies him denies the Father and the Son, 62. He is not in the drunkard, 88. Received within as victor over vices, he cuts down passions outwardly, 115. He makes Mary fruitful, 117. He descends upon the united Apostles, 132. At Pentecost he is signified by the number seven—how, 139. What is born from the Spirit is spirit, 142. Why he was present with the Father at Christ’s baptism, 157. Why he floats upon the waters in the form of a dove, 160. Why he appears as fire upon the Apostles, 164. His fire kindles the cold hearts of mortals, 169. Together with the Father and the Son he orders all ages through every span of time, 174. See Soul; Trinity; God. See Sermon 56–62.

## Splendor

Splendor leads to blindness, 124. Heavenly splendor is a veil, 142.

## Bride

The Church is Christ’s bride—how, 22. She is not separated from the bridegroom, 57. Christ receives his bride, the Virgin Mary, and does not seize another’s, 140. A wife is called a bride according to divine law, 145. His Church is both the shepherd’s mother and bride, 175.

## Betrothal

By whom and how betrothals should be properly handled, 140. The bridegroom seeking a bride lays aside fasts and gives himself wholly to joys, 31. The bride does what she wishes. Why Christ greets the Church as bride, 76. Who is admitted to the bridegroom’s chamber, 141. Why Joseph is called the bridegroom, 146.

## Spittle

The blind man is healed by the Lord’s spittle, 176.

## Stand

Everything stands by God’s will, 176. We stand when we are raised by good works toward progress, 54. See Servant.

## Star

What is more ornamented than the stars? 101. They mark the times during the nights and give guidance to travelers, 103. As many stars as heaven has, so many virtues illuminate the saints, 120. Christ began to have one, 156. It serves the Magi. The star appeared to the Magi not by human art but from God—descriptively, 156. The star leading the Magi belonged to Christ, not Christ to the star, and how, in various ways, 156, 157. And why the Magus was led by a star. The person whom the stars serve is not held by earthly power, 158. It is the language of the heavens, 159.

## Stephen

He was so called from a crown, and why, 154. The first of the martyrs. And other matters concerning him.

## Barrenness

The barrenness of nature—why, 87. The birth of a barren woman is called untimely, 88. The barrenness of Abraham, Sarah, Rebekah, and Hannah was made fruitful, 90. When it gives birth, it provides evidence of life for the dead and salvation for the despairing. It is a reproach, 92. Wretched in human eyes, but not in God’s, 92. Sarah’s, 99. The world made fruitful. The barrenness of speech imposes silence, 107. See Elizabeth.

## Drippings

Drippings water sprouts but do not destroy them, 143.

## Goad

To serve the goads of sin is to live in sin, 113.

## Straw

Cain’s straw served as fuel for the burning of his sacrifice, 109.

## Fool

He finds a cause of error in created things, 89. He considers creatures gods. The rich man who gathers, 104. The person who serves disgrace and vices, 114. Sublimity leads to ruin, 124.

## Support

The supports of life are not lacking for those who dwell before God and with God, 166.

## Substance

Substance given to a son makes him needy; when withheld, it preserves the rich man, 1. The whole substance of the Father is in the Son, 4. Human beings possess natural benefits, 5. And the books of the law. What is preserved generates moths, 7. It is exposed to plunder. What the substance of the Church was, 36. Heavenly substance cannot be confined in earthly prisons, 81. Let us beware lest the reputation of our altered substance precede us to the master of the household, 125. What substance the human being received and lost, 162. When the substance of food and drink should be carried, 8.

## Come to the Aid

Divine things come to the aid of the holy people when human resources fail, 156.

## Sweat

The person who sweats in interpreting Christ’s words receives fruit, 96. See Labor.

## Pride

Pride destroys what labor had acquired, 161. How it seeks to make evil from good, 168. The pride of the world is bowed by the meek victor, 170. Pride is suppressed by the Lord in those who murmur, 168. What pride lost, humility acquired, 23. What the flame of pride causes, 94. Why it comes from pomp, 16. [Col. 1213]

## Entreat

The form of entreaty is to raise one’s eyes upward, 65. Between God the Father and the Son there is no need for entreaty. Pure entreaty is incense pleasing to God, 87.

## Punishment

Through punishment the Lord completes the argument of faith, 90. There is no punishment of the condemned where there is no penalty for sin, 135.

## Superstition

The superstition of the pagans should be mocked for the evil things it has done, 5. One must beware every superstition, 18. The superstition of the pagans on the Kalends of January, 155. That of the Pharisees in washing their hands, 171.

## Rise

Through penance the sinner rises from ruin and from hell, and rises higher than he fell, 3. Likewise, 2. Martha rises in faith before Lazarus rises in the flesh, 63. The woman cast down by the sight of a tree rises at the sight of the tomb, 74.

## Above

What is above is above all, 137. See Entreat.

## Creed

The Creed is a pact of life and an agreement of salvation, 58. It must be placed in the heart. It must be heard and recited, 59. Through body and soul its hearers should be cleansed. It must be entrusted to the mind, not to writing tablets, 59, 60, 61. Its brevity gives the broadest passages to belief, 61. What it is according to human custom, 62. God asks it of us not for his own sake but for ours. Let everyone commit it to memory. Its explanation is partly from Christ’s death, 83. Chrysologus explains it, 56–62.

## Harmony

The harmony of various instruments that Magdalene presents to Christ’s ears, 93. David’s harps for soothing minds through understanding, 115. It arises from different kinds of instruments but with consonant sound, 116. The heavenly harmony is continually heard by the saints, 174. The heavenly harmony is sung at the sinner’s return, 6. When spiritual harmony should be taken up, 6. What the heavenly harmony accomplishes, 10. The harmony of piety drives away the envious person, 4.

## Synagogue

The Synagogue is represented by Peter’s feverish mother-in-law, 18. It has a withered hand, Sermon 32. It collapses before Christ, 33. It is represented by the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, 36. While Christ is going toward it, the Church of the Gentiles was shedding blood. It dies while Christ comes to the aid of the Church. Why it belongs to the Hebrews, not to Christ, 48. Christ reclined in it when he died, 95. How it lost Christ, who was found by the Church, 95. At the judgment it will be accused by Christ. It is always ruined and does not rise into heavenly construction unless a Christian has prepared it as the summit of the Church, 102. Its burdens are heavier than the burdens of idols, 105. It is most aptly compared to a fig tree, 106. Christ found no fruit of faith in it. It is manured by the mercy of the Gentiles. After receiving the law it was adulterous in many ways—descriptively, 115. It is despised by the law. Accused of adultery. The Apostle strives to recall it to Christ. It is dead, not the law. Its children are a brood of vipers, 137. It would have innocent children if Christ had not fled, 153. Mystically, it is separated from its husband, 164. The heir is separated from fellowship with the Church and Christ. The mother of the Church and the mother-in-law kills the son so that she may extinguish his love for the daughter-in-law. It had Christ and did not see him, 169. It had lost the one Word—that is, Christ—from the ten words of the law, and how. It rejected Christ after joining itself to the gods of the Gentiles. It stole the Lord’s resurrection and sought out false witnesses. See Law; Hebrew.

## T

**Talent.** A person dies before his time if he dissipates the talent entrusted to him by God, 125.

**Tartarus.** The Tartarean stench is not even endured by pigs, 17. Its case with Christ in the resurrection of Lazarus, discussed at length, 65. Ordered to seize the guilty, it held the innocent. He tells God that he keeps his commandments. He suddenly restores Lazarus, lest, while he delayed, all the dead should rise. Before the Lord’s coming it held both the just and the unjust, 66. At the Lord’s resurrection it is rebuked, 74. Its law is annulled, 82. Its ministers reclaim the souls of the wicked, 104. Its gates are shattered by the battering ram of the cross, 123. Since it is the prison of Tartarus, why do we not take care to escape from evils? 124. It receives the rich naked, 125. Herod received his reward there, 174.

**Roof.** Why Christ refuses to enter the centurion’s roof, 15. The body is a roof that repels divine approach, and how, 102. The Lord enters it.

**Temerity.** We incur blame through it, 151. It is: speaking silently; bringing forth things long kept in reserve; sometimes investigating the origins of causes, 166.

**Storm.** A violent storm, and the storm in Chrysologus’s time, 20, 21. While it is present, Christ is said to sleep in our boat. The great storm is changed into the greatest calm, and when, 21.

**Temple.** The Christian is the temple of God, 85. The Lord ascends into it, in order to provide the perfect festive day from heaven. And unless he ascends, no human being will ascend into heaven with Christ. It must be cleansed for God, 91. So that priests might serve the Solomonic temple, 92. Made into a mass of holiness, 99. A temple made for God from the clay of our flesh, 142. It is the human body, 143. Mary is the great temple of the Godhead, 144. Its holiness invites God to dwell there, 171. Our body belongs to God, 12. Human breasts through which they may rise into the temple of God, 43. The virgin’s womb is God’s, 59. [Col. 1214]

**Temporal things.** He who longs for them abandons eternal things, 22. If temporal evils cause grief, how much more eternal ones? Lost goods are recovered through prayer to God, 46.

**Time.** The demon, not observing time, complains about time, 16. Excluded from eternity, 34. Time brought temporality into being. Contempt for God makes our times evil, 43. One must confess during the time of indulgence, 46. Why one should repent of past things, rejoice in present things, and fear future things, 46. Time sometimes prevents the explanation of God’s mysteries, 56. One should speak at the proper time, 57. Grace is not denied at the decisive moment of time, 60, 61. The brevity of time is without lengthy preaching, 61. God is the author of times, 65. He does not allow one to linger over anything, 72. Zacharias offended, 88. He prescribes laws for human beings, not for the Creator, 90. How it is recalled, 92. The harvest is referred to the time of our repentance, 97. In miracles Christ served the proper time, 102. The times come as they pass, 103. He excluded the Law, 114. Once the time for speaking has passed, the discourse is postponed, 121. The time of satisfaction excludes punishments, 125. One must repent quickly, lest we lose the time of satisfaction. What excluded the time of stewardship should include the perpetuity of Christ’s gift. When the time for doing good has been taken away, a person desires to do good. The times are insufficient for labor. He who loses the time of stewardship dies quickly. The author of time does not know times; and Christ, for the sake of humanity, accepted day and time, 131. When he cannot allow everything to be said, let some things be said, 134. One should speak extemporaneously, 140. Time for repentance should be granted to the sinner, 151. Those who do not recognize salvation are accused by Christ, 164. There is never too little time for repentance, 167. There will be no time in glory, 82.

**Darkness.** Friendly to vices, 24. They drive away the light and return when the light departs, 44. They were driven away on the night of Christ’s resurrection, 77. They overwhelmed the disciples during the Lord’s passion, 78. The kinds associated with grief and fear, 84. The darkness of greed, 104.

**Temptation.** He enters into it who does not go to prayer, 43. It is human life, 67. What it is, 71. It is the devil’s preliminary servant, 72. Its weight bends one down, 77. It is useful when overcome, 113. When God is said to lead into temptation, 70, 71. See **Lord’s Prayer**.

**Earth.** Why David calls it to jubilation, 6. It trembled when the Ruler rose from the underworld, 74. At God’s command it floats upon the liquid element, not by nature, 101. What is more beneficial than it? It was made before the fruits, but the latter is more precious—why? 117. It raises one toward heaven, 124. When it accuses the sinner, then God investigates, 125. It blooms with its flowers, 130. Things produced by it grow wild when the Farmer’s diligence fails, 132. It does not produce fruit before labor, 142. On earth we prepare what we are to possess in heaven, 144. It was taken away by the Flood, 147. At God’s command it produces fruits in spontaneous servitude, 148. How heaven trembles when earth rages, 150. It is nourished by its own ashes, 164. It is purified by fire so that it may yield fruit. On earth everything germinates through heat and is nourished by moisture. It is the origin of our body, 166. It foreshadowed the form of our baptism. Formerly it brought human beings forth to death; now it brings the reborn forth to life. Envy burns the earth, 172. On earth the will of our enemies is often done, 70. It preserves our corpse from worms and decay, 121. An earthquake at Christ’s resurrection, 74. Would that it had been only a light whirlwind in Paradise. It will be greatest at the judgment, 77. If the earth does not endure the presence of a fellow servant, how will it endure the Judge? Earthly people are clothed in earthly garments, 82. The reborn should bear the image of God in heaven, 117. In earthly matters the human being is the Lord’s vicar, 148. Herod, longing for earthly things, rushed upon divine things, 152. Where there is no use of anything earthly, there everything belongs to the heavenly order, 153. Earthly things should be despised, 163. He who hesitates to possess earthly things, although he already feels heavenly things being given to him, is punished by fire, 163.

**Terror.** It throws down the guilty and soon returns to those who are conscious of guilt, 77.

**Bridal chamber.** Who may be admitted to the bridegroom’s chamber, 141. Within the chamber God admits the Virgin alone.

**Treasure.** Our treasure is kept stored up in heaven, 7. The bearers of our treasure into heaven are the poor. The poor person’s gift is treasure in heaven, 8. He who prefers a little coin to royal treasures has a plebeian spirit, 22. For security, place the treasure where Christ is. It raises and sinks the human heart; and how it must be sent beforehand into heaven, 11 and 25. Christ is the treasure of all good things, 129. Our treasure must be given to the poor. The treasure of God’s knowledge was given by the Magi to those who would believe, 158. That treasure cannot be exhausted, from which one coin is sufficient, 14. The Lord condemns temporal hoarding but commands eternal hoarding, 25.

**Thomas.** Why he desires to touch the wounds, at length, 84. What his curiosity might have produced. He took care of the uncertainty of all human beings. By prophetic spirit he knew that the Lord had retained the wounds. The others freely receive what he asks for more slowly. The showing of Christ’s wounds was necessary for him because Christ was thought to be a spirit. From the wounds he poured forth faith. [Col. 1215]

**Fear.** One must receive Communion with fear and humility, following the centurion, 15. It ceases where there is a desire for victory, 22. He who desires life comes to it, 62. Its darkness surpasses the darkness of night, 84. Fear is speaking with God, 86. Excessive fear drives the mind away from itself, 88. It indicates servitude, 101. Fear of a former fall should not delay our conversion, 115. When people fear human beings rather than God in legal matters, one easily deviates from justice, 127. No one fears willingly, 135. Sometimes he fears, while speaking, lest he harm his hearers, 137. He who finds grace has no fear, 142. There is no fear where the matter is divine, 144. What fear arising from the majesty of the invisible God has done to the whole creation, 147. He cannot love who fears sufficiently. Death itself is lighter than terror. Fear not tempered by love makes devoted service rebellious. He who obeys piety need not fear, 160. One born for the love of God cannot fear. How we are conceived by the Lord through salutary fear, 171. He fears who loses, not he who finds, 144. Who is there who does not fear? An infant does not know how to fear, 150. Fear is our teacher, 15. Fear of conscience, 36. Fearing to know what he deserves to know, 143. See **Terror**.

**Moth.** It is shut up in a prison but not excluded, 7.

**Inscriptions.** Inscriptions fixed at boundary markers announce the owner of estates, 154. The inscriptions of Saint Paul’s servitude, and what they are, 161. The inscriptions of the inhumanity of the banqueter, 66.

**Necklace.** Joseph’s was of gold, 174. John’s was of blood.

**Torturer.** The envious person always delights in having an intimate torturer within himself, 172. Hunger is the torturer of the throat, belly, and lust, 1. See **Executioner**.
