**Traditions.** The traditions of the Fathers, strengthened by the passage of time, are not debated by a Christian but venerated, 85.

**To draw.** We ought to draw our neighbor to God, even unwillingly, and how, 10. Demons are dragged by human beings into Christ’s presence to receive sentence, 16. How we are unwillingly drawn by Christ, 50.

**Calm.** The calm of the Christian sea comes from Christ, 20. When it arises from a storm, 21.

**To cross by sea.** What Christ’s mystical crossing of the sea means, 17. Why, when a crowd is around Christ, he himself crosses over, 19.

**Trepidation.** The fearfulness of others is our caution and protection, 175.

**Three.** The Lord offered three examples in praise of his piety, 55. The godly are encouraged and the ungodly refuted by three witnesses. Why Christ was dead for three days, 59. How the three measures are applied to the Trinity, 99. The three periods during which Christ sought fruit from the Synagogue, 106.

**Tribulation.** Permitted by God so that we may return to him, 5. Tribulation is the first thing that disturbs the infancy of a just man; but it teaches greater things to the one who endures, 110. See **Adversities**, **Evils**.

**Tributes.** They must not be exacted without justice, 137.

**Trinity.** What pleases the Son pleases it, 23. The three watches, and what they signify in expectation of it, 24. Who deserves to attain its blessedness, 44. How the divine generation of the Son takes place, 57. The grace of the Trinity was declared in the three days of Christ’s burial. It is equal in all things: one Godhead, power, and glory in the Trinity, 59. How it is openly expressed in “I believe in God,” and so forth, 60. The Trinity in persons, unity in divinity, distinct in persons but not divided in substances. The Godhead is neither divided by the Trinity nor confused by unity. The persons are of one majesty and glory. What the confession of the Trinity accomplishes is shown, 71. God the Father deigns to make human beings heirs; God the Son does not disdain to make servants coheirs; God the Holy Spirit assumes flesh to share in divinity, 71. God is one, with equal majesty in all things, 83. And other matters concerning the Trinity. The Father is another person but the same substance, and other matters concerning the Trinity, 88. It was represented figuratively in the three measures of flour, 99. John was the mediator through whom the whole Trinity is recognized, 127. It rewards those fervent in its love, 130. Why the whole Trinity was present at Christ’s baptism, 157. Why the Jordan did not flee from its presence as it did from the presence of the ark, 160. How it is carried throughout the whole world like a chariot or quadriga, and for what purpose, 170. It mounted a two-horse chariot to call the two peoples.

**Three-part.** The three-part order of discourse provides the salutary discipline of ecclesiastical teaching, 115.

**To dance for joy.** The innermost chambers of a house are said to dance in exultation, 175.

**Sad things.** They must not be mixed with joys, 175.

**Wheat.** From the Apostle he teaches our resurrection, descriptively, 118. He teaches not so much eating as understanding; he compels us not so much to labor as to believe. The grain of wheat is Christ, 126. The Jew gave darnel in place of wheat, 164.

**To triumph.** A person can triumph over his tyrant, that is, sin, 113. Through the grace of Christ we can triumph over passions, 115. He who wants to entrust triumph to the ages cannot undertake a hidden conflict, 150. What kind of trophy belongs to a singular triumph, 170.

**Trumpet.** It leads the soldier to war, 6. What the military trumpet does, 14. What the spiritual trumpet does. The heavenly trumpet raises minds bent down like sheep toward divine things, 23. The voice that will call the dead back to life will be divine, 103. Description of the material trumpet. The trumpet that at the beginning called the world forth from nothing will at the end call the world back from ruin. The trumpet of the divine voice created all things. See **Description**.

**Crowd.** The crowd is dismissed when the just renounce popular favor and devote themselves to the virtues, 21. The unteachable crowd, striving toward lofty things, is submerged in the depths, 19.

**Disturbance.** The soul standing between God’s commandments and the passions of the heart is disturbed, 45. The disturbance of the Virgin Mary when she was greeted, 140. See **Mary the Virgin**.

**Tyrant.** Once he is destroyed, his battle lines are broken, 11. Sin is cruel; it groans when it is placed beneath the feet of those who were once its captives, 113, 116. He is a tyrant who assumes the appearance of a tyrant, 155.

## U

**Vengeance.** It is slow for the good, 16. Vengeance and guilt were taking away everything that had entered the world; but mercy came to the rescue, 42. The Roman army is the avenger of Christ’s blood. Christ strengthens the wavering person through vengeance, 90. See **Retribution**.

**Shadow.** The heat of the body is unknown to the person whom the shadow of divine power protects, 142.

**Ointment.** When it is offered, it is an offering; when it runs down from the Lord’s footsteps, it is chrism, 93. It carried the rich man away into decay, 124.

**Union.** Fraternal union helps brothers in danger of body and soul, 20. All are one, and one is all, when one Spirit of God lives in everyone, 72. The union of married couples, what it is, 89. The value of the union of many in prayer, 132. In the Church union gives life, separation gives evils, and what these are. The unity of the Father and the Son shown, 23. And the unity of the Godhead. Unity, not singularity, is pleasing to God, 132. Christ came to restore the unity of the human race, 162. The unity of the world and the distinction of things, 103.

**City.** A city has delights, 13. See **Civitas**.

**Interest.** The world’s interest is one hundred to one; God receives one and gives back one hundred, 25. In Matthew it seemed to be taken up to heaven and to be pleasing to God, 28. It was healed in him. How the interest of time is repaid by God, 77. See **Usury**. The interest of honor, what it is, 88. The interest of sin, what it is, 94. The interest of time, to the detriment of offspring, arising from Adam’s sin, 123. Usurers are hard as flint, 95. The innocent person does not pay the interest of repentance, 167.

**Use.** It removes labor, 28. Long use of life gives instruction, 90. Matters should be undertaken according to their use, 99. It is useful to teach the obedient Law; otherwise the teacher gives offense, 137.

**Utility.** Christ is our utility, 161. Everything comes from him.

**Wineskins.** The old wineskins are the Jews, the new ones are Christians; how they are to be cleansed, and other matters, 31.

**Wife.** A wife is happy when she has one mind with her husband, 89. See **Union**, **Married Couples**.

## V

**Vain glory.** It must be avoided in the practice of justice, and why, 9.

**Fleece.** Since it comes from the body, it does not know the body’s sufferings, 113. What was done from the fleece of Christ the Lamb, 31, 22. The fleece of Christ’s sheep, 40.

**To wish and not be able.** This is human weakness, 100. To wish belongs to virtue; to acquiesce belongs to necessity, 110. Death is subject to the willing person and rules over the unwilling.

**To sell.** God sells the kingdom for a fragment of bread, 41. The sinner, not having received a price but having paid one, sells himself into wretched servitude. See **Purchase**.

**Pardon.** It is confidently sought by the sinner who readily forgives the one who sins, 68, 72. Otherwise, not at all, 71. He who has pardon in his heart does not fear crimes, 72. The pardon is as great as the offense against the Lord, 80. It is argued from the condescension Christ showed to other sinners, 93. It is granted to sinners solely from love of God, 94. It covers a person, 99. It is promised to the converted through the Gospel, 125. Christ longs for pardon to precede judgment. When pardon is bound, no place for pardon remains, 127. Pardon granted to a brother redounds to our reward, 139. It is always good, but sweetest when it is owed. It is useful to secure pardon for oneself before the offense. Why it is imposed by the Law. Pardon is left to the priest’s discretion and is to be given to the penitent, 139. The number seven is assigned to pardon. He does not hope for it who thinks nothing of correction, 158. It opened the eyes that guilt had closed, 176. See **Mercy**, **Piety**, **Indulgence**, **Remission**, **Repentance**.

**To come.** Why God came to us, at length, 30. He comes to fear who desires life, 62.

**Belly.** An overloaded belly brings the heart down toward vices and weighs upon the mind, so that it cannot perceive heavenly piety, 2. It must be emptied through fasting. See **Gluttony**. The belly is understood as the inner parts of the heart, 68. We are poured forth from the maternal womb into the present life, 133.

**Wind.** See **Elements**.

**Spring.** The breath of spring makes all the shoots of the fields bloom, [Col. 1217] 8. It is the season when the soldier advances onto the field. The Christian returns to God’s fasts, 13. The word of God is to be heard in Lent, 12.

**Word.** All things were made by God’s word, 15. One thing is speaking, another is doing, 15. All virtues are in it. Chrysologus dismissed it because of excessive heat, 51. It is called an egg, 55. See **Discourse**. It is in the power of the giver, not of the speaker, 86. It rules; it does not serve, 86. When uttered obscurely, it sharpens our understanding greatly, 96. Why divine meaning is concealed in the Word of God, 99. How it must be explained in various ways to different people, 112. The sick person is healed by the Word of God, 112. Those who corrupt it through their interpretation are rebuked by Paul, 113. From it, when wrongly interpreted, accusations of crimes are conceived. It is grasped through the proper hearing of it when the powers of minds have been restored, 122. Why it is “above,” not “to,” John, 137. Why it must be heeded, 139. It gives an infant its cry, 144. Divine words must not be weighed by human standards, 146. If it is heard beyond the doctrine of faith, it becomes an occasion of destruction, 156. It is contrary to the unskilled, and how, 164. How it should be heard, 173. God’s word lives in the Word of God, 13. See **Scripture**, **Gospel**, **Law**, **Trinity**, **Divine**, **Teacher**, **Preacher**.

An obscure word shines brightly through comparison of word and meaning, 96. The Word is above the voice, 137. The Word judges; the voice proclaims beforehand. God judges hearts, not words, 142.

**Truth.** Sometimes it is spoken by the worst person unwillingly because of God’s impulse, 49. It is violated by money, 126. Bitter truth increases hatred, 135. It is attacked only by falsehood, 169. It knows no swelling pride, 172. Why we eat Christ with truth. Something may be said in a truthful sense, though maliciously, 173.

**Truth of relation.** See **Relation**.

**The true.** The truth is not found by a judging mind amid reports of falsehoods, 131.

**Worms.** They are the executioners of the human body, 118. A corpse in the clay does not know worms, 121.

**Evening.** It is when the day of the age comes to an end, 18. When it becomes late, 21. The end of the age does not begin the day but changes its order when it recognizes its author, 74, 75. It grows light for the faithful and dark for unbelievers when Christ rises, 75. It grows light at what is usually the beginning of night, 77. The evening of Jewish teaching, 86.

**Garment.** The garment of the mortified body must be put on, 73. The angels’ garment foreshadows our form in the resurrection, 77. Earthly garments shine with newness and become dirty with age, 82. Heavenly garments are not defiled by age. Are they to be condemned in themselves? 121. A person is clothed in artificial nakedness, 122. The garments of Lazarus and the banqueter, 124. He who keeps tunics locked away is consumed by cold, to the poor person’s detriment, 137. The glory of the Lily’s garment, 163. What is less than a garment? God provides it for us. God will give clothing to those who serve him, 170. Roughness tramples the softness of the flesh, 13. The garment of flesh is assumed by the Word, 117. See **Cloth**.

**Old age.** There is no old age in created things that endure as they were born or made, 101. Old age perishes in time, not the creature before its Creator.

**Banner.** What the banner of faith, raised for salvation, accomplishes, 110. The banner of the cross. See **Cross**.

**Way.** A person chooses the way of sinners, not of life, even from the womb, 44. It is broad and spacious, leading to death. The way is the present life, into which a human being comes and through which he departs. We all come into the way of sinners; he stands in it who remains in sins. He crosses the way who conquers while suffering evils. Why the counsel of impiety is placed before the ways of sinners, 44. How a person falls more heavily on the way of sinners. The way of Paradise, set on fire, is cooled by the water from Christ’s side, 123. The way is always troublesome in itself and becomes more troublesome through fear, 150. How and why Christ is generated on the way, 175. The three-way crossroads of sinners, 89. The traveler grows weary because he believes he will reach his destinations, 71. He does not completely extinguish thirst with a cup of cold water, 112. The traveler, having found Christ, seeks heaven, 175.

**Provision for the journey.** Fasting is the provision for the journey of ecclesiastical life, 8. The traveler crosses steep paths singing, 10. Why he keeps watch, 24. See **Pilgrim**.

**Vicar.** In earthly matters the human being is the Lord’s vicar, 148.

**Victim.** See **Sacrifice**.

**Victory.** It is better often to report victory over enemies to one’s king than to die for him once, 128. It is glorious if the enemy is conquered openly, 150. A secret victory leaves no example for posterity. He who desires victory does not know fear, 22. The victory of many over the nations, who were conquered by vices, 41.

**To see.** He who seeks to see Christ should look toward heaven, 54. As much as one person sees another, so much will the other see in him, 139. Do not strive to see many things, so that you may see yourself. He sees nothing who thinks he sees everything, 164.

**Widow.** When the widow’s son was raised, 63. Everyone was astonished, 103. The son was raised in response to the widow’s tears, descriptively.

**To keep watch.** A person must keep watch for his own salvation, 21. At night, like a rooster; in the daytime, three times. He must awaken the Lord so that the storm may flee. One must keep watch for blessedness, 22. To keep watch more is to live more, 24. Watches are beneficial for everything. It is best to keep watch at midnight in order to pray to the Lord, 39. One must keep watch at dawn. He who keeps watch sees what has happened, 97. The good Shepherd keeps watch over his sheep, 173.

**Watches.** Expectation of the Trinity knows only three watches, and what they are, 24. Watches of soldiers, 27. What the watches of Christians are. They are always beneficial, 24. They are useful in prayer. Chrysologus’s watches, 74. We are commanded to keep watch at night in order to pray to the Lord, 31.

**Worthless things.** Why they should not be requested from God, 132.

**Farm.** What the devil’s farm is, 2.

**Steward.** A person appointed to cultivate the world is Christ’s steward, 125. The same person is called both steward and son because of the diversity of circumstances. He dissipated the property and goods. He must give an account of his stewardship. He is ashamed to beg. Let each person acknowledge himself to be a steward, not a master; a temporary servant, not an eternal possessor. He who loses the time of stewardship does not reach the appointed term of life. When called to give an account, what he ought to do, mystically. Why he is praised for his injustice, at length, 126. He urges the Jew not toward fraud but toward repentance. When he should wish the Lord to come for his own profit, 158.

**Bonds.** John had released the bonds of sins, and why he is bound by the bonds of the sinner, 127.

**Retribution.** The vengeance of the ancient Jews, 38. It extends to the whole house in which the Ruler was killed by the crime of servants, 78. It must not be taken against a brother who has harmed us; rather, he must be spared, 139. To delay vengeance is to escape guilt, 145. See **Vengeance**.

**Wine.** The new wine of the Gospel is put into new wineskins, which are Christians, 31. What evil it has done, 41. It weakens the strength of feverish people rather than restoring it, 60. It produces drunkenness and vices, 88. Wine is not drunkenness, but drunkenness is recognized through it, 116. The wine made from water by Christ was a manifestation of the Godhead, 157. Why wine was made from water, 160. Wines are changed at the banquets of the rich, 161. What the wine that is bought in moderation and drunk without moderation produces, 174. See **Drunkenness**. Wine placed before the dead. See **Food**.

**Viper.** How sinful human beings are offspring of vipers, 137. An offspring hostile to nature arises through the death of its parents. The conception of the viper and the death of the parents are described. The Synagogue was a viper toward Christ with its children.

**Man.** The man rises in Christ, 80. As much as the Lord surpasses the angel, so much does the man precede the woman in honor. He is at Christ’s head; the woman is at his feet, 80. The woman follows him. Through man and woman the cause of the world is brought to an end, 99. Labor awaits the man outside. How the woman restores the man, mystically, 142.

**Powers.** When the powers of minds have been restored, the discourse is heard in the proper way, 122. Wine weakens the powers of feverish people, 60.

**Rod.** Mary is the rod that will bear the fruit of the human race; the angel drives fear away from her so that she will not break, 142.

**Virginity.** It does not refuse childbirth to its Creator, 84. God causes a barren conception to precede, so that the Virgin’s childbirth may be believed, 87. The Virgin’s conception and childbirth are unknown. It is a grave thing to lack both virginity and children, 92. It is compared with the labors of self-restraint, 98. It is compared with lilies. It gives birth to the Son of God, 142. That the Virgin gives birth is a secret not to be investigated but believed, 143. Virginity is always akin to the angels and is greater than they are—why? Although it is in the flesh, it knows nothing of the vices of the flesh. It is like fleece. Unacquainted with corruption, it brought honor to Mary, 153. What John did through love of it, 174. See **Mary the Virgin**.

**Virtue.** Virtue is the punishment of the person who makes a vice out of virtue, 7. It is on the right-hand side, 9. It triumphs over the demon, 16. He who lays aside its belt does not know how to conquer bodily vices, 22. It shines with manifold light, 22. It is illuminated by freedom, 31. The sinner dreads it, 38. Necessity becomes virtue, 42. All virtues totter without mercy. Christian virtues flourish in peace, 53. Stern and courageous things are friendly to the virtues, 74. Things created for us by God stand midway between vices and virtues, 89. The wicked are oppressed by the virtues of the good. Virtue makes equal those whom nature made unequal. Its dwellings are rough. It tests freedom, 101. The innermost parts of the virtues must be sacrificed to God so that the arts of the vices may die, 108. How this is done. It is the mark of perfect virtue that you possess in reality, through the strength of hope, what you do not yet hold, 110. A person must embrace the difficult path of the virtues, 113. Virtues must drive out vices, and what they are. A person should give as much to virtue as he gave to vices, 114. A person began to desire virtues but did not attain them, 116. Virtue is difficult. Virtues fail while they are being cultivated. Through God they rule in the human mind and senses. We receive their reward in heavenly things, 119. The virtues of the saints. See **Saints**. The greatness of virtues is destroyed by the greatness of crimes, 127. Virtue is opposed to vices. It is virtuous to die in battle for a king; but more perfect to complete the contests, 138. Affliction consists in avoiding virtues as though they were vices, 132. When virtues are read, they raise minds toward progress, 150. Hidden virtue leaves no example for posterity. It is singular to trouble an enemy with his own sword, 157. True knowledge is knowledge mixed with virtue, 167. It must be acquired from necessity. Betrayed virtues will not remain, 7. The war of virtues and vices is the Lenten fast, 13. [Col. 1219] Where virtue heals, there sickness leaves no trace, 18. One must run in the virtues, 91. Where virtue is joined to virtue, no place remains for weakness, 57. The heavenly virtues rule the others, but they are ruled by Christ, 46. The virtues of the saints are to be imitated, 129.

**Force.** Force was done to Christ by the faith of the nations, 100. Not to see things that have been seen is a torment, 132. Chrysologus was shaken by the impiety of Herod toward John, 127. Human beings testify to what infancy can accomplish, 158. The visible makes the invisible known, 47.

**Vision.** The sight of the tree deceived the woman; the sight of the tomb restored her, 74. Its sincerity in recognizing Christ’s birth, 140. The vision of God in heaven. See **Glory**, **Appearance**, **Eyes**.

**Life.** Our life is called mortal, and why, 1. Wretched is the person living among pigs, since he cannot share a meal with them. One must live with parents and relatives. Human life is uncertain, 10. True life is free from suffering and eternal, 11. A person does not choose the way of life but the way of sinners, 44. The present life is a way. See **Way**. The present life was more desirable to the paralytic than the future one, 50. Eternal life succeeds dying death, 58. It must be sought through faith, 63. Eternal life does not have a second death, 83. Life is slippery, and in it there is falling, 89. It returned to everyone through Mary, 99. Temporal life becomes everlasting through death, 101. He cannot die who is killed by the life-giving sword, 108. Life cannot be made alive by anyone other than the one from whom it comes, 110. Life cannot die. It has been restored to us by God. He who lives by life owes himself to Christ, not to himself, 111. Human life is brief for understanding human and divine matters, 112. It has been restored through Christ. How one must walk in newness of life, 113. The life of the risen Christ must be imitated. The future is abandoned by a human being, 114. It is disturbed by human passions, 115. It is turned into a lethal sword by sin, 116. It is restored after being killed by Christ. The things that lead us to perpetual life should be treated in a lengthy discourse, 117. What is sufficient for life is little, 122. How the present life is a game, 124. He who loses the time of stewardship does not reach the appointed term of life, 125. In danger to life one must turn to repentance. To despise the present life for the Lord is the greatest gain, 128. Christ gives life again, and eternal life, 131. When life returns, there will be no death, 139. A person returns to life by the same courses by which he had slipped away toward death, 142. Heavenly life is to live in the flesh as beyond the flesh, 143. Blessed is he who guards his own life and provides for another’s salvation, 155. When the material of life becomes an occasion of destruction, 156. The cause of death has become the cause of life through Christ, 157. Life cannot perish, 158. The present life is like sleep, 159. The means of support for life are not lacking to those who dwell with God, 166. When life is dear, no care is hard, 167. Life arises at God’s command, 176.

The soul is the life of the body, but God is the life of the soul, 19. In this life we are pilgrims, and it is painful to be wretched; what will happen in the other life? 22.

**Vine.** Attached to the unfruitful tree, it receives a deadly shade, 106.

**Vice.** He who lives in vices dies to virtues, 1. The hungry commit more vices, 2. The portion of vices is on the left, 9. One must not obey vices as though they were created together with nature, 11. Weapons must be taken up against vices. Once the devil is defeated, vices have no power. They are conquered by fasting, 12. War must be declared against them in Lent, and how, 13. The noise of vices in the court of our heart, 15. Vices give demons power to harm, 16. The demon feeds on vices, 17. They are conquered by virtues, 22. The vice must be cut away, not the limb, 27. It is concealed by tricks, 31. Vices must be overcome by virtues, 38. Vices have captured the conquerors of nations, 41. The vices of the ages of human life, 42. It is difficult for sinners to pass by vices, 66. Flatteries serve them, 74. We must pray that we may die to vices, 82. Things created by God stand midway between vices and virtues, 89. Who walks undefiled through the whirlpools of vices? 89. The arts of vices die as often as the innermost parts of virtues are sacrificed to God, 108. Vices corrupt the body, 109. They must be changed into virtues, 113. To comply with vices is to live in sin. Not to know vices is blessedness; to know them is danger; to conquer them is virtue, 116. They are to the human body what fire is to dry grain. They are conquered more safely by separation. They produce a blazing fire in human strength. Once the Law was given, the human being began not to detest vices but to follow them, and so forth, 116. While vices are cut down, they grow. Let vices cease, so that the image of the Creator may be borne by us, 117. They have a pestilential itch. The members of vices, 120. Human frailty is corrupted by the foulness of vices, 167. How many vices seize the human senses, 171. Vices cannot return there where Christ dwells, 171. All vices aim at injuring their own kind, 172. The demon besieges us through the vine, 71. See **Crime**, **Error**, **Sin**, **Offense**.

**Calf.** The calf dies for the son and fattens the whole household, 3. It is Christ, killed for us and sacrificed daily, 5.

**To live.** One must live in the Word of God in order to live, 13. Those who died through sins live in Christ, 36. The almsgiver believes that he lives after death, 54. Those who had died through Adam in the underworld live for God through Christ, 65. Who are said to live for sin, 113. It is always delightful to live, 118. He lived without purpose who believed that he was born only to perish, 118. He always lives for God who does not know how to live for himself in the world, 124. He who dies once to life lives forever for punishment. Everyone who is reborn from a life-giving generation lives eternally, 131. One human being lives in many, and how from many, 132. It is one thing to live in idleness and in security for oneself; another to bear labors for everyone, 166. To live among women is not secure, 174. A person always lives by the heavenly word, but not always by bread, 11.

**Calling.** To be called belongs to grace; to exist belongs to nature, 2. The Christian calling gathers good and evil people, but divine election distinguishes them, 47. God calls the people through the mouths of priests, 62. The divine calling is for everyone without distinction of persons, 99. The Christian calling does not separate man from woman. We do not go to God unless called, 102. God calls Jews and nations, 105. God’s calling consists in our obeying his Gospel, 114. Our calling was made by Christ through the Gospel, 125. The calling to give an account is called bitter. What must be done when we are called to it. The calling of the two peoples was represented in Christ’s two messengers, 170. Sinners are healed by the gift of the one who calls, 176.

**Will.** The first will within us, whether good or evil, brings a return from God, 5. Will, not necessity, produces sin, 92. That which is not free and absolute succumbs to necessity, 100. God is appeased by will, not by necessity, 108. In adversities necessity cannot be compared with the will, 110. The will to sin is not removed by fear of human beings, 127. An ardent will is called charity, 135. He who did not seek merit from willing should acquire virtue at least from necessity, 167. We must pray that our will may be constrained by God, 67. How a single will is formed in a household. It is faithful peace, 68. The will of our enemies is often done on earth, 70. God’s will is done in heaven. What it means for God’s will to be done, 72. See **Lord’s Prayer**, **To Wish**, **Free Choice**.

**Pleasure.** It does not know how to be satisfied, 2. Pleasure and despair are companions, 5. A small pleasure in riches kindles a fire, 47. Cruelty arises from it, 127. When a person lived according to his pleasures, God did not deny him the necessities of food, 170. See **Riches**, **Lust**.

**Voice.** It is the bearer of faith, 62. The people should pray for the preacher so that they may be able to hear the discourse, 86. Zacharias loses it when he receives the voice, 88. It is born from silence, mystically, 92. The voice of only one person sometimes has no force, 121. How the voice precedes the Word but does not surpass it, 137. The Word judges; the voice proclaims beforehand. How the voice of the Lord is upon the waters, 160. It cannot be killed; rather, once freed from the constraints of the body, it cries out more loudly in distress, 174. The voice is temporarily lost, 90.

**Common things.** They are not unknown to one who teaches profound matters, 15. Why Christ’s parables are common, 99. The unteachable crowd, entering the shipwrecks of knowledge, is submerged, and Christ abandons it, 19. The breeze of popular favor is abandoned by the just who pursue the virtues, 21.

**Wound.** The Lord cures the one who is weakened by a wound, 90. The inner wound of the human being is opened by the Law and healed by Christ, 112. It is enlarged by the Law. Where it has been widened, health has overflowed. The medicine is applied according to the size of the wound, 113. One must not remain in it. The poor person has as many mouths as wounds, 121. Lazarus’s wound over his whole body was armor, 124.

**Fox.** The fox is described, 19. It is like Herod.

## Z
Zacchaeus. Through his humanity and faith we are advanced toward joy, 54. Chief of the publicans, and other matters concerning him.

Zechariah. While he was entreating, he became mute, although he had been the father of the one who would cry aloud, 86. By a sign he commands that no one inquire into the causes of his silence. A prophet to the peoples, he is silent for himself. He received the word from his son. While silent, he consoles Chrysologus. A saint among the impious. His merit and life surpassed the wickedness of the age. He entreats that the people be admitted into the temple. He is troubled and remains silent. His silence is the force of one commanding. He was the temple of God, 87. He offered the incense of supplication. He sees an angel on the right. He is troubled, 88. At the time of propitiation he gives offense, and how. The bishop prays for the common salvation, 88. He is praised, 89. He was not harmed by Herod in his priesthood. He lived in a holy marriage. He walked in all the commandments and ordinances, 89. In him the grounds for lamentation were cut off. He was chastised for unbelief, and why, 90. He prays to God for human salvation. Why God allows a son to be born from sterile old age, 90. From what things he doubted. Explanation of the words: “How shall I know this?” and so forth. He sinned venially by not believing. In himself and from himself he possessed the rule of believing. As he went out from the temple, he bore in his mouth the sign of barrenness and in his breast the figure of conception. In him the heavenly treasure lies hidden, 91. The words “They were both righteous” are explained. The punishment is silent, 92. From his silence a voice arises. Why, while he questions, he incurs punishment, whereas the Virgin Mary does not, 14. See Elizabeth.

Zeal. Accustomed to separate the Pharisees and the disciples of John, it united them, 31. See Envy.

Tares. Concerning the tares, throughout, 96, 97.

## INDEX OF SUBJECTS IN THE WORKS OF ST. NICETAS

The numbers in this index, indicating pagination, correspond to the numbers printed in bold type in the text, from col. 875 of this volume through 0000. [Note: [Col. 1225] In this index, Arabic numbers refer to column numbers printed in the text in bold type.]

### A
Formula of renunciation before baptism: in the early centuries of the Church it was not the same everywhere, 43. The word *pompa* (“pageantry”) was absent from the Aquileian formula in the time of St. Nicetas of Aquileia; nevertheless, he himself added it in his explanation of that same formula, 45. A single, double, triple, or quadruple renunciation was practiced, according to the division of the matters and words, and according to the custom of the Churches, 50. A double renunciation was practiced in the Milanese Church in the time of St. Ambrose and, apparently, also in Aquileia, 50, 51. In former times the renunciation was made by the candidates for baptism not only immediately before baptism, but also during the scrutinies, before the handing over of the Creed, 199, 200. See *Pageantry*. Frequent remembrance among the Fathers of the renunciations made at baptism, in order to keep Christian minds steadfast in their duty, etc., 233.

Acclamations, or good wishes, in funerary inscriptions, 78. Fontanini’s interpretation of the acclamation *In saecula* (“For ages”) in the funerary inscription of the holy virgin Columba is defended, 78, 79.

Adelphus, or Delphinus, bishop of Aquileia after Augustine, was celebrated with outstanding praises before the people of Ravenna, and in his own presence, by St. Peter Chrysologus; nevertheless, after his death he never received a cult of sanctity among the people of Aquileia, 217.

Adeodatus, a deacon of the Roman Church, probably brought St. Nicetas’ little work *On the Creed to the Candidates for Baptism* with him to Rome, 57. Perhaps from this fifth-century exemplar the Ghisian apograph of the fourteenth century was produced, 57, 58.

African Church. A very large number of bishops existed in the African Church in the fourth and fifth centuries, both on the Catholic side and on that of the Donatists, 104. Nevertheless, many of these are shown to have been merely auxiliary bishops of older sees, 105 ff. Abuses among them; measures taken against these abuses both by the African councils and by the Apostolic See, 107, 108.

Alexandrian see. The power of the Alexandrian bishops, according to canon 6 of Nicaea, over all the Churches of Egypt, Libya, and the Pentapolis, 103.

Allatius, Leo, had composed a treatise on Nicetas, which has perished, 177.

St. Ambrose. His admonitions concerning the renunciation made at baptism; from these the formula of renunciation then current in the Milanese Church is recovered, 50. He is said to have conferred episcopal ordination at Aquileia upon St. Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia, 128. St. Nicetas of Aquileia’s book *On the Faith*, which Gennadius mentions and which we lack, is found associated with St. Ambrose’s books *On the Faith* and *On the Holy Spirit* in the sixth and eleventh centuries, 192, 193. St. Ambrose is called by scholars the teacher of virginity, 255. His books on virginity were formed from sermons that he himself had delivered on this subject, 258. He did not admit any intermediate state between blessedness and damnation in the future life, 280, 283.

A certain Anastasius, a bishop, is called in the bull of Pope Stephen II, dated 753, “the first bishop of the diocesan bishops of the holy Apostolic See,” 98.

The Aquileian territory suffered much and frequently in the fourth and fifth centuries because of wars, 128–130. Above all, it suffered because of the arrival of the barbarians in Italy, to whom Aquileia was the first place in all Italy, or at least almost always the first, to lie open, ibid. The barbarians who under Odoacer possessed a third of the territory of Italy were undoubtedly given a third, and perhaps more than a third, of the Aquileian territory, 165.

Aquileian Church. The veneration of this Church for the letter of Pope St. Leo to Flavian, 28. Around the year 369, under Bishop St. Valerian, the Aquileian Church—the first of all the Italian Churches—was raised to metropolitan dignity, 60, 120. The renown of the Aquileian clergy in the fourth and fifth centuries, 74. Within the boundaries of the Aquileian Church lay Gennadius’ city of Romatiana, 89–91. The Churches of Concordia and Caprula remained parts of the very extensive Aquileian diocese until the end of the sixth century, 95, 96. Other episcopal Churches in coastal Venetia, some of which still survive and others of which have disappeared, were formerly parts of that same Aquileian Church, 96. The celebrated Council of Aquileia of the year 381, under St. Valerian as bishop, 111. How extensive the care of the bishops of Aquileia was in the early centuries of the Church, 118. Some discussion of the sacred building at Aquileia under the bishops Fortunatianus and St. Valerian, and whether it could be called a cathedral in the manner of our own churches, 127, 128. Whether the city of Aquileia was a fixed see of the Aquileian bishops and, as it were, the place of their residence, ibid. The Aquileian bishops had many reasons for withdrawing from the city of Aquileia after St. Valerian, 128 ff. In the eighth and ninth centuries the Aquileian bishops were called bishops of Forum Julii, and the Aquileian Church was called the Church of Forum Julii, from the long residence that the Aquileian bishops had in the city of Forum Julii, 133, 134. Within the boundaries of the Aquileian diocese in the fourth and fifth centuries there were not a few pagans who exercised the zeal of the Aquileian bishops, 137 ff. Indeed, they were present in the city of Aquileia itself, 146. There was scarcely any heresy against which the bishop of Aquileia could not, and indeed ought not, to fight, because of Aquileia’s situation: on account of commerce it was, as it were, the center of the union of the whole world, both Western and Eastern, 160. The renown of the Aquileian Church is not impaired by the fact that many people tainted by various heresies came to Aquileia and also lived within Aquileian territory, 161. The Aquileian bishops had particular methods and frequent opportunities for acting against the error of the Arians, 162 ff. In the fifth century, when Aquileia and other very famous cities had been destroyed, and when the Western Empire at last fell through the actions of the barbarians, among whom every kind of error prevailed, there was scarcely any heresy against which the Aquileian bishops ought not to have drawn up their battle line, 163 ff. The Pelagian heresy did gain access among men of the ecclesiastical order in the province of Aquileia, perhaps from the beginning of the fifth century, 167. A letter of Pope St. Leo exists to the bishop of Aquileia concerning priests, deacons, and clerics of various ranks suspected of the Pelagian heresy, ibid. and 168. According to St. Leo’s letter, these men were some individuals, not many, as Norisius maintained, 170. But in the time of St. Nicetas of Aquileia there was no stain of Pelagianism in the Aquileian Church, 170 ff. See *Pelagians* and *Pelagianism*. Who were the provincial bishops of the metropolitan Church of Aquileia in the age of St. Nicetas of Aquileia? 185. Muratorius unjustly censures the Aquileian Church, as though it had been excessively generous in conferring the cult of sanctity upon its bishops, 216. The distinctive Aquileian rite for the celebration of divine offices was abolished in 1596, 225. Three printed missals of the ancient Aquileian rite and a ritual book are listed, with their calendars placed at the beginning, ibid. The names of the holy Aquileian bishops Valerian, Chromatius, and Nicetas are absent from all these liturgical books of the Aquileian Church, ibid. The reasons for this omission are given; nevertheless, the cult of these three saints in the Aquileian Church is established, 225, 226. The use of sacred vigils was practiced in the Aquileian Church in the time of St. Nicetas, who also mentions the light of these vigils, 242. St. Nicetas likewise mentions the singing of hymns that was used in the sacred liturgy, and the heavenly readings that were given, ibid. and 243. Whether in the Aquileian Church, in the time of St. Nicetas, there was a book called the *Comes* for the sacred readings from Scripture, 243, 244.

The Creed of the Aquileian Church. See *Creed of the Aquileian Church*.

The formula of renunciation in the Aquileian Church in the time of St. Nicetas as bishop. See *Formula of Renunciation*.

The institution and discipline of holy virgins in the Aquileian Church. See *Holy Virgins* and *Virgin Monastery*.

The records of auxiliary bishops in the Aquileian Church. See *Auxiliary or Assistant Bishops*.

The suffragan Churches and suffragan bishops of the Aquileian Church. See *Suffragan Churches* and *Suffragan Bishops*.

City of Aquileia. Nicolaus Madrisius briefly collected the praises of this city from the testimonies of the ancients, 47. Many pieces of evidence show that it possessed a circus both before and after the disaster inflicted by Attila, 46 ff. It had possessed a famous temple of Jupiter and a Capitol; a college of Augustales; an order of Decurions called splendidissimus (“most splendid”); and consuls, ibid. Nor was it without theaters, and perhaps not without an amphitheater either, 48. Aquileia was not so utterly destroyed in the disaster inflicted by Attila that the larger and more solid buildings were leveled to the ground, as happened with the circus and the theaters, 49. Baronius wrote that Aquileia had at one time been called the city of Romatiana, or Romana, 85. De Rubeis and others, however, do not agree with him, 85. Nevertheless, even in the light of present scholarship, Baronius’ opinion could to some extent be clarified, though not defended, ibid. The city of Aquileia, in which the tyrant Maximus had taken refuge, endured a siege by the army of Theodosius the Great in 388, 128. It was besieged again and captured in 424 or 425 by the army of Theodosius the Younger, because it supported the tyrant John, 130. Finally, in 452, it was besieged, captured, and destroyed by Attila, king of the Huns, ibid.

The situation of Aquileia with respect to commerce, both in the time of St. Nicetas and earlier, 160, 176. The three-year siege of Aquileia by Attila’s army is commonly rejected by scholars, 182. The condition of Aquileia after the disaster inflicted by Attila is investigated anew, 211. The opinions of scholars on this matter, based on ancient testimonies, 212.

[Col. 1228A]

The title “archbishop” began to be used in the West for metropolitan prelates after the fifth century and appears to have become most common throughout the Western Church in the eighth century, 59. There is no example of this title in the West in genuine monuments of the fifth century, 60.

Arianism and the Arians. St. Nicetas attacks Arianism in his *Explanation of the Creed*, though without explicitly mentioning Arius or the Arians by name, 40. The Arians did not immediately, from the origin of the Arian heresy, establish a pseudo-church separated from the Catholic Church, 41. They did so only after the Council of Sardica and the assembly at Philippopolis, 42. The bishops of Aquileia very often had reason to draw up their battle line against Arianism, 162. Although not from the beginning, the Arians later admitted the abuse of rebaptizing those who came over to them, 164.

St. Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, was the guest of Fortunatianus, bishop of Aquileia, at Aquileia, and there took part in the sacred rites, 128. He was the one who either introduced monastic discipline for both sexes from the East into the West or at least made it more esteemed; and perhaps he advised the bishop of Aquileia to bring together in one place the holy virgins living there, etc., 246.

Attila, king of the Huns, besieged, captured, plundered, and burned Aquileia in 452, while Secundus occupied the episcopal see of Aquileia, 130. See *City of Aquileia*.

Augustine, bishop of Aquileia, successor of St. Chromatius, was probably, at least in part, the author of Sermon 242 in the appendix to the final Maurist edition of Augustine’s works, 64. That little work, a profession of faith infected by the taint of Pelagianism and published in the Augustinian appendices, was addressed to this Augustine of Aquileia, not to St. Augustine of Hippo, 65, 167. In the aforementioned sermon there is mention of pagans who may perhaps have been known to those listening, 145. This sermon is *On the Creed to the Candidates for Baptism*, that is, an exposition of the Creed according to the order of its articles, like so many other expositions by the holy Fathers, 153. During his life this Augustine was honored with the title “saint” and “holy,” but after his death he never received a cult, 216.

St. Augustine, bishop of Hippo. From one of his sermons to the candidates for baptism it is inferred what the subject matter may have been of St. Nicetas’ first little work, likewise addressed to the candidates for baptism, which is now lacking, 187. His eulogy of the holy virgin Demetrias, from the illustrious family of the Anicii, 236. His text in the sermon *On the Creed to Catechumens* was wrongly read by the illustrious Muratorius, 239, 240. His particular care for holy virgins, 258. His investigation of the final judgment of those who will be alive at the end: namely, whether they will be brought before the judgment without first dying or after death, 266–269. His opinion concerning the increase of blessedness among the righteous and of torments among the wicked after the resurrection and judgment, 278.

Gold miners (*aurilegi*, or *aurileguli*): who they are, 175. Their skill was commonly known, 176. Even the bishop of Aquileia could take an example from them in his sermon to the candidates for baptism, and for a particular reason, 176, 177.

Auxiliary or assistant bishops in the early centuries of the Church, in larger dioceses, 96 ff. They were of two kinds: some remained with the principal bishops; others were sent to the remote and more populous parts of the dioceses, 97. The auxiliary bishops of the Roman pontiffs who were present at Rome were called bishops of the city of Rome, or of Rome: three examples of this from the earlier centuries, 97, 98. In later centuries these auxiliary bishops of the Roman pontiffs were given another name, namely, “diocesan bishops of the holy Apostolic See,” 98. Other examples of auxiliary bishops of the first kind from the fifth century in the Church of Constantinople and in the Church of Antioch, 99. Another example from the same century in the Western Church, outside Rome and outside the boundaries of Italy, 99, 100. The discipline of auxiliary bishops of the second kind, from the canon of Sardica and the institution of the chorepiscopi, 100, 101. What was the situation in the Roman Church? 101. In the Alexandrian Church? 103. In the African Church? 104. The authority of auxiliary bishops in general was entirely nonexistent in themselves: for they were called bishops in name only and possessed no cities, 99. The authority of auxiliary bishops of the second kind belonging to the Roman pontiff was confined within very narrow limits, 103. The same was true of the bishops in the regions of Egypt, Libya, and the Pentapolis subject to the Alexandrian bishop, 103.

Records of auxiliary bishops in the Aquileian Church, 109. The first is from Photius’ *Bibliotheca*, where Marcellus and Alexander—both living at the same time and called bishops of Aquileia—are mentioned, ibid. The opinion of the illustrious De Rubeis on this matter is examined, ibid. ff. The second is from the Council of Aquileia of the year 381, where several bishops are found without sees, 111 ff. Of these, three seem undoubtedly to have belonged to the Aquileian Church, 113, 114. Others also probably belonged to it, because it is plausible that the Aquileian prelates established bishops in several places of their own very extensive diocese, especially in those places where the cathedral Churches of suffragan sees of this first see later arose, 116.

See *Suffragan Churches* and *Suffragan Bishops*.

The care of the bishops of Aquileia formerly extended very widely; for this they needed the assistance of auxiliary bishops, both those who remained with them and those who presided in remote regions in their place, with a permanent residence there, 118. This is also shown by the Acts that present the beginnings of the Aquileian Church; from them the opinion is strengthened that suffragan bishops originated from the auxiliary bishops of the earliest period, 119. It was not contrary to the discipline of the Church—indeed, it was consonant with it—that merely auxiliary bishops, both of Aquileia and of other Churches, should be advanced to the episcopate of the whole diocese when necessity required, 122, 123.

St. Avitus, bishop of Vienne. His views and works against the Eutychian error, 32 ff.

## B

Bachiarius, a monk. Our distinguished Francis Florius noted three errors of Gennadius in the single article on Bachiarius, 83.

Baptismal Churches, or parish Churches. From the manner in which new parish Churches arose, and continue daily to arise, from portions detached from a baptismal or parish Church, a method is inferred by which the suffragan episcopal Churches of the primitive period also formerly arose within the body of larger dioceses, from portions detached from their mother episcopal Churches, 121. See *Suffragan Churches*.

Sacrament of baptism. The catechumenate was formerly instituted for the sacrament of baptism; and why? 186. The rite of administering baptism introduced at a later period, and now in use, is a kind of abridgment of the ancient rite, when the discipline of the catechumenate flourished in its integrity, 200. St. Nicetas mentions exorcisms, lights, and white garments, 242.

Francis Barbarus, patriarch of Aquileia. The merits of this distinguished prelate toward the Aquileian Church and toward the cult of its ancient bishops are indicated, after the Roman rite had been introduced into the diocese and province, 227, 228.

Cardinal Baronius called Gennadius’ city of Romatiana Aquileia; and why? 85. Some scholars agreed with him, ibid. Far more, however, denied agreement with him; and who they were, 85, 86. Baronius’ opinion, or the foundation of his opinion, could, if one wished, be clarified and in some way supported even in the light of present scholarship, ibid. Baronius must nevertheless be wholly abandoned in his claim that Gennadius’ city of Romatiana was Aquileia itself; but he should be defended insofar as by the name “city of Romatiana” he understood the Aquileian episcopate of St. Nicetas, 87. Baronius is also defended against the charge of arbitrariness because he was the very first to insert the memory of St. Nicetas of Dacia on 7 January in his revision of the Roman Martyrology, 222, 223.

The designation “blessed” was a title of honor that in the fifth century was commonly given even to living bishops, and also to men distinguished for learning and piety who had died, whose works in particular stood out for the edification of the Church, 60. How the designation “blessed” and “saint” is to be understood in ancient Martyrologies, 219, 220.

Belenus, the celebrated divinity of the people of Aquileia; his temple still existed not far from Aquileia as the sixth century was drawing to a close, 147.

Pope Benedict XIV, in the latest revision of the Roman Martyrology, where he had proposed to remove superfluous material, left untouched the mention of St. Nicetas of Dacia on 7 January, which Cardinal Baronius had introduced, 222, 223. He himself was the first to enter the name of Pope St. Siricius into the Roman Martyrology and deliberately demonstrated his sanctity from his letters, 223.

The Bessi, a barbarian people: where were they situated in the time of St. Nicetas of Dacia? 14.

Brunius Bruno, editor and commentator on the works of St. Maximus of Turin, published at Rome in 1784, noted various errors of Gennadius, 82. He excellently defended St. Maximus concerning the omission of the procession of the Holy Spirit also from the Son; and on that occasion illuminated the entire matter, 270.

Thomas Burnet wrote a book *On the State of the Dead and of Those Who Rise Again*, published at London in 1726; Muratorius refuted it most thoroughly, 274, 275.

## C

White garments. St. Nicetas mentions the white garments of the neophytes, 242.

Canons. The native canons of the metropolitan Church of Aquileia are displayed in Aquileian monuments of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. Four suffragan bishops of that same Church—the bishops of Concordia, Justinopolis, Tergeste, and Emonia—are so presented, 117, 295 ff. Examples of other bishops in Gaul and England who were at the same time canons of other Churches, ibid. The canonry of the four Aquileian suffragans nevertheless seems to indicate the ancient Aquileian origin of these bishops, when they were merely auxiliary bishops, perhaps established in those very places where their cathedral Churches were later erected, ibid. and 118.

Singing. The use of singing in the Aquileian Church during the divine offices in the time of St. Nicetas, 243, 244.

The Church of Caprula, or Caprulana. This episcopal Church arose only as the sixth century was passing away; previously it had been part of the very extensive Aquileian diocese, 96.

Resurrection of the flesh. Why did the people of Aquileia add this expression in the Creed, in the article concerning the resurrection of the flesh? 161. See *Resurrection of the Dead*.

Cassiodorus. His testimony concerning St. Nicetas, and especially concerning his third little work *On the Faith*, which Gennadius mentions and which we lack, 191. Tillemont’s authority and opinion on this matter, ibid.

Catechumenate and catechumens. The catechumenate was formerly instituted for the sacrament of baptism; and why? 186. The catechumenate had various grades, the highest of which was that of the candidates for baptism, ibid. The discipline of the catechumenate, as it had been established in antiquity, fell into disuse throughout the Western Church after the ninth, or certainly after the tenth, century, 200. See *Sacrament of Baptism*.

Among other things, St. Nicetas of Aquileia prescribes the use of chains to bind the entrails for a fallen virgin who had violated her virginity, 263.

Cathedral Church. Cathedral Churches, in substance, arose only after the peace of the Church; in the use of the designation, however, they arose much later than the peace of the Church, 124, 125. Cathedral Churches and fixed episcopal sees in places where cathedrals had been established advanced everywhere at the same pace, 125, 126. The first mention perhaps of cathedral Churches, and of the law made for bishops requiring them to remain with those Churches, belongs to the end of the fourth century, 127.

Chorepiscopi were established in various places of the dioceses, like auxiliary bishops of the second kind; and, at least during the first five centuries, they held the rank of a true episcopate, 101.

Choirs of holy virgins, 255 ff.

St. Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia. In Treatise I on Matthew he mentions the *agonothetai* (“presidents of the games”), the *munerarii* (“sponsors of public spectacles”), and the stadium as well, as matters familiar to his hearers, 47, 48. He was at one time called a Roman bishop; but he ought rather to have been called Romatianus or Romatinus, from Pliny’s port of Romatinum, as De Rubeis conjectured, 93. He is said to have received episcopal ordination at Aquileia from St. Ambrose, bishop of Milan, 128. Probably he withdrew to Pliny’s port of Romatinum in the year 400, when the Aquileian territory—the first in all Italy—lay open to the barbarian forces under Alaric; and since he may also have stayed there for a longer period, he could have been called the bishop of Romatinus or Romatius, but not Romanus, 129. The successors of St. Chromatius in the Aquileian episcopate are counted down to St. Nicetas, 130. Not a few pagans still existed in the Aquileian diocese in the time of Chromatius, 142. The name of St. Chromatius is absent from the printed calendars and missals of the Aquileian rite; nevertheless, his cult in the Aquileian Church is established, 225, 226. No relics of the sacred ashes of this holy bishop are known, or were known, in the Aquileian Church, 229.

Circus. Much concerning the circus, the pageants, and the spectacles presented in the circus: see pp. 44–50. Circuses did not exist among barbarian peoples, 45. Many pieces of evidence show that Aquileia possessed a circus both before and after the disaster inflicted by Attila, 46 ff. What the Latins called a *circus*, the Greeks called a *stadium*, an *agon*, or also a *hippodrome*, 48. The madness of the peoples for circus games and theatrical spectacles, even amid the greatest calamities, 49.

Claudianus Mamertus, called by Sidonius Apollinaris a prelate “in the second rank,” that is, apparently, an auxiliary bishop of St. Mamertus, his brother and bishop of Vienne, 99, 100.

Pope St. Clement I. His two letters on virginity, or to virgins, which first came to light in the year 1752, etc., 250.

John Clericus, on the style of writers, 3.

The observations of Philip Cluverius on Pliny’s passage concerning the port and river of Romatinum, 90.

The Gennadian San-Germain codex cited by Lequien. See *Gennadius*.

The Ghisian codex of the *Explanation of the Creed* of Blessed Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia: what authority should be assigned to it? 56.

[Col. 1231]

The Vienna codex, from which we possess the remains of St. Nicetas’ little works that are missing, 173.

The two Forojulian Gennadian codices, which assert something unusual about Nicetas Romatianus. See *Gennadius*.

St. Columba, a virgin consecrated to God of the Aquileian Church, 76. Her funerary inscription was published by learned men and also illuminated by Fontanini in a commentary, 77. She died at the age of ninety during the consulship of Opilio, that is, in the year 453, according to Fontanini’s judgment, ibid. Fontanini’s opinion is defended, 78, 79. According to the same Fontanini’s conjecture, this holy virgin Columba was consecrated by St. Valerian, bishop of Aquileia, 246.

Candidates for baptism. Who in ancient times were the candidates for baptism in the Church? 186. Why were catechumens close to baptism called “candidates”? ibid. Six little works of St. Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, for the candidates for baptism are listed separately, 187 ff. Those who were called *competentes* by the Latins were called *illuminandi* (“those to be enlightened”) by the Greeks, 188. Most of the principal elements of Christian instruction were delivered to the candidates for baptism, but were not given to those occupying the lower grades of the catechumenate, 189, 190. The Creed was handed over by the bishop only to the candidates for baptism, together with a sermon, etc., 198. The candidates themselves recited the Creed; and the bishop’s sermon followed this recitation, ibid. See *Creed*. Complete and perfect instruction concerning the sacrament of the Eucharist was not given to the candidates for baptism; nevertheless, something was imparted to them so that, after the saving washing, they would not approach the sacred table entirely unprepared, 202, 203. Various discussions of this matter on the occasion of the sixth little work of St. Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, ibid., 204. See *Sacrament of the Eucharist*.

Communion. Learned men understand the absolution of sins by the term “communion” in canon XIII of Elvira, 285. The same is true in other passages where communion is denied to those guilty of certain crimes, even at the end of life, 286. In ancient times this same word was used in the same sense, even after the Council of Elvira, 288.

The Church of Concordia. Ughellus and De Rubeis begin the series of the bishops of Concordia, at the end of the sixth century, with a bishop named Clarissimus, 95. Before that time the diocese of Concordia was part of the very extensive Aquileian diocese, 95, 96. There is no basis for placing that bishop Laurentius, to whom Rufinus dedicated his commentary on the Creed, among the bishops of Concordia, 95. In ancient Aquileian monuments the bishops of Concordia are presented as native canons of the metropolitan Church of Aquileia, 117, 295. The bishop of Concordia, who is called “bishop of Concordia” in public records, is nevertheless commonly called the bishop of Portus Gruarius, from the fixed episcopal see that he has in the city of Portus Gruarius, 133.

The city of Concordia. Before the disaster inflicted by Attila, this city possessed a port: Pliny’s own Romatian port, situated at the estuary, 91. What is the present condition of Concordia? 95. Probably, as the sixth century was drawing to a close, the suffragan bishopric of Concordia, belonging to the Aquileian Church, took its name from this city because of its ancient renown, rather than from Pliny’s Romatian port, which no longer existed, or from the new Romatian port, which was recent, 123.

John Baptist Cotelerius was the first to attribute to Gennadian Nicetas the little work *To the Fallen Virgin*, 3.

Credulity and “credulous”: what do these words mean in the language of St. Nicetas? 264. Among the Fathers, both before St. Nicetas and in his own time, the word *credulitas* was frequently used to signify true faith, and especially the interior act of faith, ibid. and 265. The same is true in liturgical Acts, and specifically in those of the Aquileian Church, ibid.

That the hair of holy virgins remained uncut among the people of Aquileia in the fifth century is proved by the cutting of the hair that St. Nicetas prescribes, among other external signs of penance, for the fallen virgin of his monastery, 261. See *Virginity* and *Holy Virgins*.

The sign of the cross, in its two forms, major and minor. St. Nicetas complained of those Christians who covered their foreheads so completely with their hair that they left no free place for the sign of the cross to be rubbed upon it, 53.

St. Cyprian, bishop of Carthage. His particular care for holy virgins, 257, 258. His authority concerning the penance to be imposed upon fallen virgins is examined, 260.

St. Cyril of Jerusalem. From his *Pro-Catechesis* to those about to be enlightened, it is inferred what the subject matter may have been of St. Nicetas’ first little work to the candidates for baptism, which is missing and which Trithemius called *The Preparatory Work*, 188. From the same work we also learn what the arrangement of the Church was in giving instruction concerning the most sacred mystery of the Eucharist, whether to candidates for baptism or to neophytes, 202, 203.

## D

Dacia. There were two Dacias: one called Trajan’s Dacia, beyond the Danube, which was also called barbarian; the other, Aurelian’s Dacia, on this side of the Danube, which was also called Roman and New Dacia, 9. St. Nicetas of Dacia, the friend of St. Paulinus of Nola, exercised his episcopate not in this New Dacia but in the older one, called barbarian, 10 ff. Who are to be understood by the “northern Dacians” mentioned by Paulinus? 12. A Scythian people, 14. St. Paulinus calls that Dacia the silent region of the world, 15. The Dacians on this side of the Danube, subject to Roman rule and of Roman origin, cannot be called barbarian and savage peoples, 136. In this Dacia on this side of the Danube, where both Greek and Latin were in use in the time of St. Nicetas of Dacia, Latin speech could not be polished and elegant Latin, 155. In barbarian Dacia, however, where Nicetas of Dacia actually exercised his episcopate, the use of Latin could by that time no longer have existed at all, 155, 156.

Andrew Dandulus. His opinions concerning the epochs of St. Nicetas of Aquileia are examined, 181 ff.

Dardania was added by Aurelian to New Dacia, 10. St. Nicetas, bishop of the Dacians, was from Dardania, 12. The Greek language was formerly proper to Dardania; but in the time of St. Nicetas of Dacia both Greek and Latin were equally in use there, 155.

Demetrias, a celebrated holy virgin from the most illustrious family of the Anicii; what did the holy Fathers of the Church, Augustine and Jerome, say about her? 236. She had received the veiling of virginity from Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, 254.

Michael Denis, who made public fragments of the little works of Gennadian Nicetas that are missing, judged that this Nicetas was not a bishop of Aquileia but a bishop of Dacia, 173. He published six fragments of this Nicetas from a tenth-century Vienna codex, 173. To prove that this Nicetas was a Dacian, he drew an impressive argument from the third fragment, ibid. Nevertheless, a satisfactory answer is given to this argument, 175, 176.

Diphthong. The rule concerning diphthongs was very often disregarded in ancient stones, both pagan and Christian, 79.

Discipline. What must be noted when we examine and describe the discipline of one century or another, of one period or another? 127. The discipline of a Church cannot be inferred from one isolated and bare fact, especially if that discipline is foreign to the discipline of the other Churches situated around it, 150. From the discipline of earlier times, some practices still survive; others are traces of that discipline; while still others from that ancient discipline have become entirely obsolete, etc., 238. Rigorous discipline in penitential matters formerly prevailed, especially according to the canons of the Council of Elvira, 286. What did St. Augustine say about certain harsher aspects of discipline? ibid.

The doctrines of faith that are conveyed in a certain insufficiently investigated work of one of the holy Fathers often, though not always, provide the strongest evidence for judging who its author was, 21. The dogma of Christ’s true humanity, which Blessed Nicetas asserts, explains, and defends in his *Explanation of the Creed*, provides evidence for judging whether St. Nicetas of Dacia could be the author of that *Explanation*, 22.

## E
## E

**Church:** what it is; and how necessary communion with the one Catholic Church is, 232.

**Church of Emona.** The bishops of Emona are presented in ancient Aquileian documents as born canons of the metropolitan Church of Aquileia, 117, 297.

**Bishops.** In the West, metropolitan bishops too used the simple title “bishop” before the sixth century, 59, 60. See **Title of Archbishop**. In ancient times all, or nearly all, the priests of the episcopal presbyterate were distinguished by episcopal ordination, 97. During times of persecution, auxiliary bishops were appointed by the chief bishop even in the small towns and minor places of his own diocese, for the benefit and consolation of the faithful; later, once peace had been granted to the Church, this was forbidden, 110. It was especially prohibited by canon 6 of the Council of Sardica, 100. Saint Leo the Great likewise confirmed this prohibition with respect to the Churches of Africa, 107, 108. Examples of bishops of advanced age, 114. At what age could someone be consecrated bishop toward the end of the fourth century? 115. Numerous examples of those who received episcopal consecration in youth, ibid. Bishops of even the smallest places, and of merely titular designation, were never called sons by the greater bishops, or even by the Roman pontiffs, but always brothers, 122. Before the peace granted by Constantine, bishops had no cathedral church in the proper sense, nor any fixed place of residence, 124 ff. See **Cathedral Church**. Examples of bishops who, before and after the peace of the Church, were called not from a place of residence but from the region in which they exercised the episcopate, 126. It was the duty of bishops solemnly to hand over the Creed to the competentes and to give them explanations of the Creed, 151, 152. Sermons of holy bishops addressed to the competentes survive under the titles *At the Giving of the Creed* and also *At the Returning of the Creed*, [Col. 1233] 198. At the returning of the Creed, a little book, or sermon, was delivered to the competentes: the fifth sermon on the Creed by Saint Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, 199, 200. It was also always the duty of bishops to consecrate virgins, 254. **Auxiliary or assistant bishops.** See **Auxiliaries or assistant bishops**.

**Bishops of the nations**, 11. Saint Nicetas, bishop of the Dacians and friend of Saint Paulinus of Nola, seems to have been one of the bishops of the nations, and indeed of a particular Dacian people, ibid. Other bishops of the nations, but not of a particular people, were the auxiliary bishops of the supreme pontiff at Rome; they were called bishops of Rome, or bishops of the city of Rome, 97.

**Sacrament of the Eucharist.** The little book, or sixth sermon, of Saint Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, addressed to the competentes and entitled *On the Paschal Victim of the Lamb*, seems plainly to have concerned the sacrament of the Holy Eucharist, 201. The competentes, or rather the neophytes, became participants in this sacrament after receiving baptism, on that very night of Easter, ibid. Although a full and complete instruction concerning the sacrament of the Eucharist was not given to the competentes, something was nevertheless imparted to them, so that, after baptism, they would not approach the sacred table wholly unprepared, 202, 203. See **Competentes**.

The Eunomians, a branch of the Arians, rebaptized those who came over to them; later all the Arians adopted this abuse as their own, 164.

**Eutyches and the Eutychians.** In the fifth century, Eutyches, an archimandrite, revived the error of the ancient heretics against Christ’s true humanity, 23. Niceas, or Nicetas Gennadianus, expressly attacked Eutyches and the Eutychians in chapter 4 of his *Explanation of the Creed*, but not the predecessors of Eutyches, ibid. In the age of Saint Leo the Great and during the time of Saint Nicetas of Aquileia, the followers of Eutyches had not yet formed separate societies or established a kind of pseudo-Church distinct from the Catholic Church, 40.

The four Gospels were translated into the Gothic language by Ulfila, bishop of the Goths, in the fourth century, 159.

**Exorcisms.** Saint Nicetas mentions exorcisms before baptism; for what reason were they employed? 242.

**Explanation of the Creed of blessed Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, delivered to the competentes.** See **Saint Niceas or Nicetas**. See **Apostles’ Creed**.

## F

**Farlatus, Daniel**, author of *Illyricum Sacrum*, likewise discusses Dacia on both sides of the Danube, 9.

**Faustus of Riez.** His text against the error of Eutyches, inserted into a sermon under the name of Saint Augustine in the Augustinian appendices, agrees with the views of Saint Leo the Great in his letter to Flavian, 32.

**Fea, Carlo**, first brought to the attention of scholars in 1790 the work of the *Explanation of the Creed of Saint Nicetas* concealed in the Ghisian Library, 56.

A certain **Felix**, called bishop of the city of Rome during the pontificate of Saint Innocent I; and why? 98.

**Integrity of faith** in every article is necessary for salvation, 231. The confession of faith expressed by the mouth must continually be recalled, 231, 232.

**Filioque.** Where was this particle first added to the Creed? 271. Before it was commonly received, much effort was expended; and for what reason? 272. In whose writings is the word *Filioque* first recorded as having been introduced into Italy? 273.

**Flaminia**, that is, the wife of a *flamen*, continually wore the *flammeum*; and why? 249.

**Flammeum, or flammeus:** what is it? 249.

**Marital flammeum.** See **Marital veiling**.

**Virginal flammeum.** See **Virginal veiling**.

**Saint Flavia Domitilla, virgin**, consecrated by Pope Saint Clement with the sacred veil; and why? 250.

**Weeping of the eyes** in the Gospel text. See **Eyes’ weeping**.

**Florius, Franciscus**, noted three errors of Gennadius in a single article concerning Bachiarius, 83. In two monuments of the Church of Aquileia from the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, he found four suffragan bishops of the see of Aquileia described as born canons of that same metropolitan Church of Aquileia, 116, 117. In his dissertation on the Martyrs of Lyons, he clearly proved that those parishes of Gaul governed by Saint Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons, were not cared for by presbyters, but by bishops over whom Saint Irenaeus himself presided, 120. His sermons are mentioned which he delivered at the nuptial celebrations of sacred virgins, 255.

## G

**Gallican Church.** In its synodal letter to Saint Leo the Great, it testified that his letter to Flavian had been accepted by everyone and committed to memory as the Creed of faith, 27.

[Col. 1234]

**Saint Gaudentius of Brescia.** From his sermons we understand that pagans and pagan worship existed in his time in the diocese of Brescia, especially among the rural population, 142. His treatise, or sermon, *On the Order of the Sacraments*, which he delivered to neophytes who had come out from the font, 202, 204.

**Gennadius of Marseille**, in his book, or catalogue, *On Illustrious Men*, lists Niceas as bishop of the city of Romaciana, 2, 185. The Gennadian San-Germain codex cited by Lequien gives the reading *Remesianae*, 18, 19. We owe much to Gennadius’s book *On Illustrious Men*, 81. Nevertheless, in this work Gennadius showed excessive favor to the party of the Semi-Pelagians, to which he was attached, ibid. Scholars have also noted other errors in the same work, 82. This was noted especially by the recent editor and commentator on the works of Saint Maximus of Turin, the distinguished Bruno Brunius, ibid. Our distinguished Francis Florius noted not one but three errors in a single article concerning Bachiarius in his dissertations on the little works of the monk Bachiarius, 83. Did Gennadius therefore also err in the article on Niceas or Nicetas when he wrote that he was bishop of the city of Romaciana? ibid. See also **City of Romatiana**.

In the reading *Remesianae* found in the Gennadian San-Germain codex, that codex stands alone; nor does it seem preferable to all the other codices of Gennadius known to us, nor to all the editions made by comparison with manuscripts of the best quality, 88. Two other Gennadian codices—one from Civitate and the other from the town of San Daniele—display another variant in the reading *Romatianae*, 88, 89, 180. These two codices uniformly contain a singular addition, or rather critique, to Nicetas’s fourth little book against *Genethlialogy*, 193. This addition, or critique, is not a product of Gennadius, however, 196.

**Genethlialogy:** what it is; and who the genethliacs are, 193. Genethlialogy had great influence among the pagans, 194. Quite a few even among those who embraced the Christian religion lent an ear to genethliacs, ibid. Saint Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, wrote a little book addressed to the competentes against *Genethlialogy*, 195. The ancient Fathers also sharpened their pens against the foolishness of the genethliacs, as did the laws of Christian emperors, ibid. The excellent treatise of Saint Zeno addressed to neophytes, in which he turned the profanity of genethliacs into instruction for the neophytes, 195, 196.

**Paganism and pagans.** Saint Nicetas of Aquileia wrote a little book *On the Errors of Paganism*, because pagans still existed in his time and within the territory of Aquileia, against whom it was necessary to fight, 135 ff. The multitude of pagans throughout the Roman world in the fourth and fifth centuries, 137. What was the situation in the city of Rome itself? 138. What in the Church of Ravenna? 139. What in that of Turin? 140. What in that of Brescia? 142. And finally, what in that of Aquileia? ibid. Here the authority of Rufinus, cited by the distinguished Zabeus to prove that paganism in the Church of Aquileia did not require careful refutation in Nicetas’s time, is examined, 143 ff. Even at the beginning of the sixth century there were pagans in the city of Ravenna who followed the ancient worship of idols, 147. Likewise, at the end of that same century, paganism was present at Terracina, not far from Rome, and also in Sicily, Sardinia, and Corsica, 148.

**Georgius Dominicus**, editor of the *Martyrology of Ado*, does not correctly set against one another the letters of Saint Innocent, Pope I, in support of the episcopate of Saint Nicetas of Dacia in the city of Romatiana on the near side of the Danube, 20. In his historical dissertation *On the Episcopal See of Setia*, etc., he likewise incorrectly recognized genuine episcopal sees and bishops of a proper see and true jurisdiction in so many of the smallest places of Latium, Campania, and suburban Tuscia, etc., 101 ff. In his *Martyrology of Ado* he sides with those distinguished men who do not accept the addition of the mention of Saint Nicetas of Dacia to the Roman Martyrology on 7 January, 222.

**Getae**, a barbarian people, also called Goths: where were they located in the time of Nicetas of Dacia? 14.

**Goths, or part of the Goths**, brought to the Christian faith; and how? 17. Hence the Church of the Goths and the martyrs of the Gothic Church, ibid. Where was the Church of the Goths located? ibid. The Gothic bishop Theophilus, who attended the Council of Nicaea, ibid. Christian Goths admitted into the Roman lands on the near side of the Danube, while pagans remained beyond the Danube, 18. Gothic Arians, ibid. For the benefit of the Goths, the four Gospels were translated into the Gothic language in the fourth century, 159. Gothic military forces, corrupted by Arianism, repeatedly occupied both Aquileia and the Aquileian territory in the fourth and fifth centuries, 163.

**Grado**, an island in the Aquileian lagoon. While Augustine was bishop of Aquileia, the Aquileian nobles built a fortress on the shore of the island, 130. At the arrival of the Lombards, Paul, bishop of Aquileia, withdrew to the island of Grado with the treasures of his Church, 132.

**Gifts of divine grace through the Holy Spirit; and the necessity of grace for salvation**, 232.

**Saint Gregory Nazianzen.** Did he admit some intermediate state for adults in the next life, where there would be neither glory nor punishment? [Col. 1235] 279, 282.

## H

**Saint Helena**, mother of the emperor Constantine; what honor did she show to virgins consecrated to God? 236.

**Elias**, bishop of Aquileia, toward the end of the sixth century transformed a pagan temple into a monastery for girls, 74, 147.
