**Saint Hermagoras, proto-bishop of Aquileia and martyr.** His *Acts*, once treated more severely by critical scholars, were later judged genuine by others, apart from certain interpolations added in a later age, 119. In these *Acts*, Saint Hermagoras is said to have been made proto-bishop of the province of Italy by blessed Peter, ibid. He sent a presbyter and a deacon to the city of Tergeste, and did the same in other cities, ibid.

**Hieronymian Martyrologies.** See **Martyrologies**.

**Jerusalem** was what the Spaniards called any metropolitan church in ecclesiastical monuments, 87.

**Saint Hippolytus, bishop of Portus and martyr**, is found described as bishop of Rome; and why? 97.

**Honoratus a Sancta Maria:** his judgment on an argument drawn from style, 6.

**Honorius of Autun**, in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, speaks of Niceas, bishop of the city of Romaciana, 185.

**True humanity in Christ** was denied in the fifth century by the archimandrite Eutyches, but several other heretics had denied it before Eutyches, 22, 23.

**Huns.** The arrival of the Hunnic people in Transdanubian Dacia from Greater Scythia beyond the Tanais, 178.

**Hymn of virginity:** what is it according to Saint Nicetas? 216.

## I

**Canon 13 of the Council of Illiberis:** what does it decree concerning virgins who have lost their pledge of virginity? 261. From the discipline of this canon, Saint Nicetas probably sanctioned that a fallen virgin should expect a remedy for her sin from God alone, 285.

**The Western Empire** fell through the agency of the barbarians in the year 476, while Saint Nicetas was governing the Church of Aquileia, 164.

**The mark of the indiction** on inscriptions: in what different ways was it indicated? 78, 79.

**The Itala, the Latin version of the sacred Scriptures.** This prevailed in the West until the time of Saint Gregory the Great; afterward it became obsolete and even disappeared, 6. Peter Sabatier restored it for us, not without immense labor and with gaps remaining here and there, ibid. What is found in this old Latin version in the Gospel text, “There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth”? 7.

**Italy.** In the *Acts* of Saint Hermagoras, blessed Peter the Apostle is said to have made him proto-bishop of the province of Italy, 119. The barbarians under King Odoacer occupied a third part of the lands of Italy, 165.

**Januarius**, one of the bishops without a see who attended the Council of Aquileia in the year 381. He may also be the same person who later became bishop of Aquileia before Secundus, the immediate predecessor of Saint Nicetas, 114. Difficulties concerning chronology are resolved by examples and conjectures, ibid. and following pages. Saint Leo the Great commended the vigor of faith of this Januarius of Aquileia, ibid. and 171.

**Jovinus**, archdeacon of Aquileia; afterward perhaps one of the bishops without a see who attended the Council of Aquileia in 381, 113.

**The Last Judgment.** Did Saint Nicetas believe that those whom Christ’s coming would find alive would come to the Last Judgment without dying? 266. What was the opinion of the Greek Fathers on this matter? ibid. What did Saint Augustine say, who expressly undertook to clarify the question? ibid. up to p. 269. Other Latin Fathers, contemporaries of Saint Nicetas, likewise taught what Nicetas himself seems to have taught concerning the judgment of those living at the end, without a preceding death, 269. How long did this opinion continue after the time of Saint Nicetas? ibid. and 270. Did Saint Nicetas believe that the glory of the just and the punishment of the impious were to be deferred until the day of the Last Judgment? 274–277.

**Church of Justinopolis.** The bishops of Justinopolis are presented in ancient Aquileian documents as born canons of the metropolitan Church of Aquileia, 117, 297.

## K

**Calendars.** The calendars of the Church of Aquileia, published at the beginning of old Aquileian Missals, etc., are catalogued, 225. The thirteenth-century calendar of the Church of Aquileia was published by the distinguished Althanus in his work *On Calendars*, p. 227. The first calendar of the Church of Aquileia of the Roman rite to be printed is identified, 227, 228. Martyrologies in ancient times were formed principally from the calendars of particular Churches, [Col. 1236] 230. See **Missals**.

## L

**That Pope Laurence**—that is, bishop Laurence—to whom Rufinus dedicated his *Commentary on the Apostles’ Creed*: to which Church did he belong? 68. He was probably also one of the auxiliary bishops of the Church of Aquileia; perhaps he held the see of Concordia, or served as bishop of Aquileia at Portus Romatinus, 95. See **Rufinus**.

**Lebrunius, Petrus.** His singular opinion concerning the Apostles’ Creed, which Muratorius refutes, 240, 241.

**Proper lessons for the office of Saint Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia**, published by the Bollandist hagiologists, have no authority and were never used in the Church of Aquileia, 183.

**Saint Leo the Great** sent a letter to Saint Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, concerning various needs of his Church about which he had been consulted, 9. To Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, against the error of Eutyches, 24. To others also on the same matter, ibid. ff. The fame and authority of Saint Leo’s letter to Flavian: it was regarded as a rule of faith, 27. The text of the letter to Flavian compared with the text of Saint Nicetas’s *Explanation*, 18, 29. Saint Leo did not take from Saint Nicetas—who may have been a Dacian—the material contained in the cited text of his letter to Flavian against the error of Eutyches, 37. Saint Leo collected testimonies from Greek and Latin Fathers in support of the doctrine of Christ’s true humanity against the error of Eutyches; among them there is absolutely nothing from any Nicetas, 38. Gennadius’s very serious omission concerning Saint Leo the Great, 82. Saint Leo’s letter to the African bishops, concerning the abuse of multiplying bishops in small and obscure places, 107, 108. Saint Leo undoubtedly received from Saint Nicetas of Aquileia some written material concerning the needs of his Church, 157. There was, however, no reason for Saint Nicetas to reply to Saint Leo’s letter, 158. Saint Leo’s letter to the bishop of Aquileia concerning persons suspected of Pelagian heresy, 167, 168. Another of his letters to Januarius, bishop of Aquileia, 171. Learned disputes concerning two letters of Saint Leo—the second and the eighteenth according to the edition of the Ballerini—and what conclusion should be drawn after the matter has been debated, 170, 171. Saint Leo’s letter to Saint Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, is examined, 184. Saint Leo explicitly mentioned the procession of the Holy Spirit also from the Son, 272. What did he say concerning the Macedonians and sin against the Holy Spirit? 290.

**Lequien, Michel**, author of *Oriens Christianus*, presents the condition of Christianity in the regions on the near side of the Danube during the time of Saint Nicetas of Dacia, 16. He acknowledges that Saint Nicetas the Dacian preached the word of God to barbarian peoples dwelling beyond the Ister, yet nevertheless makes him bishop of Remesiana on the near side of the Danube, relying on a certain San-Germain codex that he cites, 18.

**Little book addressed to a fallen virgin**, by Saint Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia. See **Saint Niceas or Nicetas**.

**Pope Liberius**, of blessed memory, consecrated Saint Marcellina, the sister of Saint Ambrose, as a virgin at Rome; on that occasion he delivered an address, which the holy Doctor himself preserved for us, etc., 254, 255.

**Lirutus, Innocentius Maria**, author of the *Exercise on the Late Origin of Ecclesiastical Metropolitans in the West*, 60, and of the Italian dissertation *Sopra a primi vescovi Caprulensi*, etc., 96.

**Lirutus, Joannes Josephus**, wrote several things concerning the two Niceases, or Nicetases, of Aquileia; but he ventures many claims that distinguished scholars do not accept, 179, 182, 183.

**Special litanies of the Church of Aquileia**, in which Saint Nicetas is invoked, 180. Saint Valerian and Saint Chromatius are also invoked with Saint Nicetas, 226. Other, shorter litanies of the same Church of Aquileia—that is, less extensive litanies—from which these three holy bishops of Aquileia are absent, ibid.

**The place of light and the place of darkness**, where souls are kept until the day of judgment according to Saint Nicetas: what is it really? And did he himself believe that the glory of the just and the punishment of the impious were deferred until the day of the Last Judgment? 274–279.

**Church of Lyons**, already in the second century, was like a metropolitan Church, with its suffragans, under Saint Irenaeus the bishop, 120.

**Lights.** Saint Nicetas mentions the lights of the neophytes, 242. He also mentions the light of the sacred vigils, which could strike the eyes, 243.

## M

**Heresy of Macedonius.** Saint Nicetas attacks Macedonianism and the Macedonians in chapter 9 of his *Explanation of the Creed*, though without expressly naming Macedonius or the Macedonians, 40. He probably intended to indicate the Macedonians also in chapter 7 and to fortify his competentes against their error, 290.

A certain **Macedonius**, called bishop of the city of Rome during the pontificate of Saint Cornelius; and why? 97.

**Manichaeans and Manichaeism.** Manichaeans were present in Italy during the time of Saint Leo the Great, who wrote against them to all the bishops of Italy in the year 444, 165. How great was the impiety of the Manichaeans and Manichaeism? 166. How severely were the Manichaeans treated by the laws of the emperors themselves? ibid. There may also have been Manichaeans in the episcopate of Aquileia during the time of Saint Nicetas, owing to the unhappy condition of the times, ibid.

**Saint Marcellina**, sister of Saint Ambrose, made her profession of virginity in the basilica of Saint Peter at Rome on the birthday of our Savior, 253. At that time she received the veil from Pope Liberius, of blessed memory; he also delivered an address to her, 254, 255.

**Marcionites.** The distinguished Zabeus found one of the errors of the Marcionites in the words of chapter 4 of Saint Nicetas’s *Explanation*, but not the Eutychian error, 165.

**Martyrologies.** Testimonies drawn from martyrologies concerning Saint Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia. The holiness of Saint Nicetas and the reputation for holiness with which he died are confirmed by the inscription of his name in the martyrologies, Prologue. The oldest of all martyrologies is the one attributed to Saint Jerome, of which two or three copies of varying antiquity have appeared, 218. The Hieronymian martyrologies originated shortly after the death of Saint Jerome, 219. The very inclusion of someone’s name in the martyrologies, even without the title “blessed” or “saint,” sufficiently testifies to that individual’s holiness, ibid. Martyrologies were formed in ancient times principally from the calendars of particular Churches, 230.

**Noble matrons** are mentioned by Saint Nicetas in the little book addressed to a fallen virgin; they sought the kisses of sacred virgins in church, 73.

**Maximus**, one of the bishops without a see who attended the Council of Aquileia in 381, may be the same person who later became bishop of Aquileia between Adelphus and Januarius, 114. Difficulties arising from chronology are resolved by examples and conjectures, ibid. ff.

**Saint Maximus of Turin.** His views against the Eutychian error agree with the views of Pope Saint Leo in his letter to Flavian and with those of Saint Nicetas in the *Explanation of the Creed*, 30. Gennadius’s error concerning Saint Maximus of Turin, 82. From the sermons of Saint Maximus we understand that there were many pagans at that time in the region of the Subalpine peoples, especially among those living in rural districts and villages, 140, 141. In his homily *On the Giving of the Creed*, Saint Maximus did not explicitly mention the procession of the Holy Spirit also from the Son; and why? 270, 271.

**Mazochius, canon.** His observation concerning the languages of the two Moesias, 155. Concerning the discovery of the bodies of saints, from which the canonization of saints began in ancient times, 229.

**Church of Milan.** The veneration of this Church for the letter of Pope Saint Leo to Flavian, 28. Saint Eusebius, bishop of Milan, fled from Milan with the clergy and people at the approach of Attila in the fifth century, etc., 131, 132. Saint Honoratus did the same in the sixth century at the arrival of the Lombards; with the senior clergy of his Church he went to Genoa, where he established his see, etc., ibid.

**An intermediate state** between the glory of the blessed and the punishments of the damned: did Saint Nicetas admit one? See **Intermediate state**, etc.

Any metropolitan church in Spain was called **Jerusalem** in ecclesiastical monuments, 87.

**Metropolitan Churches**, in the true sense and with proper jurisdiction, arose late in the West, 60, 120. Nevertheless, even before the rise of metropolitan Churches, certain greater Churches existed in a metropolitan manner: their bishops appointed auxiliary bishops here and there within their own dioceses, as though they were suffragans, 120.

**Missals of the Church of Aquileia.** Three printed missals of the Church of Aquileia are catalogued, together with a ritual book, 225. The ancient missals and calendars of the Church of Aquileia preserve the Church’s old custom: namely, the worship of holy martyrs alone, with a feast day appointed together with a special office and Mass, and with only a few confessors introduced over the course of time, those of greater renown, 226, 227. See **Calendars**.

**Moesia.** The two Moesias, Upper and Lower. After parts had been taken away from both where they met one another, the emperor Aurelian established his new Dacia and added Dardania to it, 9, 10. The Romans called Moesia the granary of Ceres, 13. Latin speech was formerly used in Upper Moesia and Greek in Lower Moesia; but both Latin and Greek were used, during the time of Saint Nicetas of Dacia, in those parts of the two Moesias which, together with Dardania, constituted the new Dacia, [Col. 1238] 155.

**Virginal monastery.** A virginal monastery is mentioned in the little book *To a Fallen Virgin*, 73, 244. Saint Paulinus of Nola makes no mention there of virginal monasteries under the care of Saint Nicetas of Dacia, ibid. There are, however, several indications that a virginal monastery existed at Aquileia during the time of Saint Nicetas of Aquileia, 74 ff. Elias, bishop of Aquileia, toward the end of the sixth century transformed a pagan temple into a monastery for girls, ibid. The decrees of Saint Paulinus, patriarch of Aquileia, at the synod of 796 concerning monasteries for girls, especially their enclosure, 75. The virginal monastery of Aquileia, although perhaps destroyed in the catastrophe caused by Attila, was probably restored afterward through the efforts of Saint Nicetas, 80. Again concerning the Aquileian virginal monastery and its location, 244. What is to be said about the origin of virginal monasteries in the West? 244, 245. What about the antiquity of the Aquileian virginal monastery? 245, 246. How many sacred virgins constituted the Aquileian virginal monastery under Saint Nicetas? 246, 247. Examples of numerous virginal monasteries in the East, in Egypt, Africa, and Palestine, 247. But not so at the same time in the West, or in Italy itself, ibid. What about the virginal monastery at Bologna? ibid. What was the situation in the Roman Church, and even in the city of Rome itself? 248. In ancient times virginal monasteries did not have their own sacred buildings; hence the virgins’ need to go out in order to attend sacred services, 255. Nevertheless, these monasteries were generally near sacred buildings, as is demonstrated in the case of the monastery at Bethlehem and conjectured in the case of the one at Aquileia, 256. See **Virginity** and **Sacred virgins**.

**Monastery of men.** A monastery existed at Aquileia in the fourth century, in which Rufinus and Jerome, along with other highly distinguished men, flourished, 74.

**The error of the Montanists**, who denied that the Church had the power to forgive certain graver sins. See **Novatian**.

Saint Nicetas rebukes women’s vanity in the adornment of the body and describes it vividly, 54.

**Muratorius, Ludovicus Antonius.** He properly includes the Church of Aquileia among those which, in his judgment, were excessively liberal in honoring their bishops of earlier centuries with the title “saint,” 216. He excellently refutes Lebrunius’s opinion that no one at all wrote the Apostles’ Creed during the first four or five centuries; yet he too was somewhat mistaken, chiefly because he read a text of Augustine incorrectly, etc., 240. He also very solidly refuted Thomas Burnet’s book *On the State of the Dead and the Resurrected*, etc., 275.

## N
## Nestorianism

Nestorianism is also attacked by St. Nicetas in the *Explanation of the Creed*, but after Eutychianism and in only a few words, 61. In St. Nicetas’s time Nestorianism did not dare show itself openly, because it had both Catholics and Eutychians opposed to it, 62.

The Latin Church’s Martyrologies, the Greek Menologia, and the Calendars likewise present many forms: Niceas, Nicetas, Nicetos, Nicas, and Nicetios, 178. Niceas, the Aquileian subdeacon mentioned by St. Jerome, is not the Niceas or Nicetas who was bishop of Aquileia after Secundus and received a decretal letter from St. Leo the Great, 55, 178. The proper name of this Aquileian subdeacon was not Nicetas but Niceas, 179. This Niceas the subdeacon was by birth an Aquileian, 181.

St. Niceas, or Nicetas, bishop of the Dacians and friend of St. Paulinus of Nola, was not bishop of the city of Romatiana, established in Dacia on this side of the Danube; rather, he exercised his episcopate beyond the Danube, 8 ff. St. Paulinus of Nola never mentions the city of Romatiana in Dacia on this side of the Danube in the lengthy poem that he wrote to Nicetas on his return to Dacia, 10. This St. Nicetas was an apostolic bishop in Transdanubian Dacia, and belonged to the order of those who were called bishops of the nations; he was perhaps sent there by the Roman See, 11. He came from Dardania, 12.

St. Paulinus mentions the barbarian nations whom St. Nicetas the Dacian brought to the Christian religion; these peoples were situated not on this side, but beyond the Danube, 12 ff. St. Paulinus describes the region and peoples where his Nicetas exercised his episcopate in such a way that we must understand Transdanubian Dacia and the barbarian peoples settled there, and in no way the new Roman Dacia and its inhabitants, 14, 15.

The mention and eulogy of this Nicetas the Dacian occur in the Roman Martyrology on 7 January, 16. New Cisdanubian Dacia in St. Nicetas the Dacian’s time did not need the work of an apostolic bishop, both because pagan barbarians were either absent or few there and because it abounded in its own bishops and episcopal sees, 16. On the other hand [Col. 1239], in Transdanubian Dacia paganism dominated among those barbarian peoples, and there was no episcopal see; except for one Gothic Church, situated far away on the Tanais and not belonging to Dacia properly so called, 16, 17, 18.

Le Quien admits that St. Nicetas the Dacian preached to the peoples situated beyond the Ister; nevertheless, from a certain manuscript of Gennadius, he makes him bishop of Remesiana on this side of the Danube, 18. About what year did St. Nicetas begin his apostolate among the barbarian peoples beyond the Danube, and about what year did he die? 19.

St. Jerome also proclaimed the merits of this St. Nicetas when he testified to the progress in the Christian faith of the Bessi, Scythians, Huns, and Getae, ibid. Georgius Dominicus, in his Martyrology of Ado, wrongly sets against this the two letters of Pope St. Innocent I, in support of St. Nicetas the Dacian’s episcopate in the city of Romatiana on this side of the Danube, 20.

St. Niceas or Nicetas, bishop of the Dacians, could not have been the author of the *Explanation of the Creed for the Competentes*, which Gennadius attributes to Niceas or Nicetas, bishop of the city of Romatiana, because that work mentions the Eutychian heresy, which arose long after this holy Nicetas’s death, 34.

The period of St. Nicetas, bishop of the Dacians, is investigated, as well as the approximate year in which he departed to heaven; this is determined from a careful consideration of St. Paulinus of Nola’s age, his modes of expression, and St. Nicetas’s own many merits among the barbarian peoples, 35, 36. St. Nicetas the Dacian could not have mentioned spectacles and theatres among the barbarian peoples whom he was instructing, 45. Nor does he seem to have had occasion to say what appears in the third fragment of the Nicetan work transmitted by Gennadius, against excessive adornment of the flesh, and so forth, in men and women, 51.

The *Booklet to a Fallen Virgin*, which Gennadius attributes to Niceas or Nicetas, bishop of the city of Romatiana, could not have had St. Nicetas the Dacian, the friend of Paulinus of Nola, as its author, 73. St. Niceas or Nicetas, bishop of the Dacians and a native of Dardania, could not have possessed the polished, elegant Latin style that we admire in the *Explanation of the Creed*, 155. In barbarian Dacia, where he actually exercised his episcopate, there was no reason for him to use the Latin language, which those barbarians did not understand, 155, 156.

St. Nicetas the Dacian is not the author of the two treatises mentioned under his name in Labbe’s *New Library of Manuscripts*: *On the Vigils of the Servants of God* and *On the Good of Psalmody*, 214. The attack made by Baronius on St. Nicetas the Dacian in the Roman Martyrology on 7 January is defended, 222, 223.

St. Niceas or Nicetas, whom Gennadius mentions in his book *On Illustrious Men* and calls bishop of the city of Romatiana, is not that Niceas or Nicetas the Dacian who was a friend of St. Paulinus of Nola, etc., 21 ff. In chapter 4 of the *Explanation of the Creed*, this Niceas or Nicetas attacks the Eutychian error against true humanity in Christ; but Niceas or Nicetas, bishop of the Dacians, could not have spoken about this error, 23 ff.

Nicetas transmitted by Gennadius indicates this Eutychian error in the same modes of expression used by Pope St. Leo in several places, 24, 25, 26. In the *Explanation of the Creed*, Nicetas attacks the same error with the same ideas, arguments, and almost the same words with which St. Leo the Great attacks it in his letter to Flavian, 27, 28, 29. He does so also in exactly the same way in which the same error was attacked after St. Leo the Great, during that same fifth century, in several passages by St. Maximus of Turin and St. Peter Chrysologus in Italy, and by Faustus of Riez and St. Avitus of Vienne in Gaul, 30 ff.

The period of Nicetas the Dacian is investigated so that it may become clearer that this Dacian Nicetas could not be the author of that *Explanation* in which the Eutychian error is attacked, 34 ff. It was not St. Leo who borrowed from St. Nicetas, who preceded him and may have been a Dacian; rather, St. Nicetas borrowed from St. Leo what he wrote against the Eutychian error in the *Explanation of the Creed*, 37.

It was not necessary for Nicetas transmitted by Gennadius to name Eutyches expressly in the *Explanation of the Creed*, 40. Nor could he at that time name the pseudo-church of the Eutychians, 40, 41. Nicetas mentions spectacles and theatres, that is, the entertainments of the Roman world, which did not exist among barbarian peoples and which Nicetas the Dacian could not have mentioned, 45 ff. He rebukes excessive bodily adornment and superfluous decoration of the flesh—abuses, that is, which could not exist among barbarian peoples newly brought to the faith, 51.

St. Niceas or Nicetas, called by Gennadius bishop of the city of Romatiana, was unquestionably Niceas or Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, who flourished in the time of St. Leo the Great and to whom a letter of that same holy pontiff is extant, 55 ff. On the basis of what has been stated, it is shown that we must adhere to the authority of the Ghisianus manuscript, which makes St. Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, the author of the *Explanation of the Creed for the Competentes*—namely, the fifth booklet on the Creed, which Gennadius attributes to Niceas or Nicetas, bishop of the city of Romatiana, 55, 56.

The judgment of Carlo Fea, who first made learned men aware of the discovery of the *Explanation of the Creed* in the Ghisianus manuscript [Col. 1240], ibid. If there is an error either in Gennadius or in the Ghisianus manuscript, the Ghisianus manuscript should be believed rather than Gennadius, 57. Distinguished men who adopted the opposite opinion before the discovery of the *Explanation of the Creed* in the Ghisianus manuscript should be excused, ibid.

The title of the *Explanation of the Creed* was not falsified by the copyist, 58. The insertion of the word “Aquileian” in the title of the little work is not probable, ibid. The title of this little work displays its original and authentic integrity, 59. The little work, the *Explanation of the Creed*, contains features that identify the period of Nicetas of Aquileia, 61. Indeed, it also contains features showing that the work was a product of the Aquileian Church, 63.

The latter is proved by the quite evident traces of the particular Aquileian Creed that appear in St. Nicetas’s *Explanation*, although the use of that Creed—at least its public use—had by that time fallen into disuse in the Aquileian Church, ibid., through 67. It is likewise proved by many features in the *Explanation* that are entirely consistent with Rufinus of Aquileia’s *Commentary on the Creed*, 67–72.

The *Booklet to a Fallen Virgin*, which is genuinely related to the *Explanation of the Creed* and is cited by Gennadius among the works of Nicetas of Romatiana, contains both general and particular indications of Aquileian origin. These therefore increasingly confirm that the Nicetas of Gennadius is none other than St. Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, 74 ff.

In one of the Gennadian manuscripts this holy man is described not as bishop of the city of Romatiana but as bishop of the city of Romana, 93. This wording ought perhaps to have warned the distinguished De Rubeis of the fortunate interpretation he gave in favor of St. Chromatius of Aquileia, who had likewise been called a Roman bishop, 94.

St. Niceas or Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, was probably called bishop of the city of Romatiana because, before ascending the episcopal see of Aquileia, he may have been an auxiliary bishop of the Aquileian Church at the port called Romatium or Romatinum, 95 ff. This port of Romatium or Romatinum, where St. Nicetas may perhaps have sat as auxiliary bishop of the Aquileian Church before assuming the episcopate of Aquileia, was probably the very Romatium or Romatinum port of Pliny, situated at the mouth of the river of the same name, 123.

St. Niceas or Nicetas could also have been called bishop of the city of Romatiana because he probably resided frequently at the port of Romatium or Romatinum, even while he held the helm of the Aquileian Church, 124 ff. Nor is it contradictory to say both that he first sat at Pliny’s Romatinum port as an auxiliary bishop of the Aquileian Church and that, after being made bishop of Aquileia, he frequently stayed at the new port of Romatinum—or rather, in the city of that name, ibid., and 134.

In the year 454 St. Nicetas began his Aquileian episcopate; but, at least during the first years of his episcopate, he probably lived elsewhere rather than at Aquileia, perhaps at the new port of Romatinum, which already at that time may have had the appearance of a city. Hence he could easily have been called bishop of the city of Romatiana, 131.

The accusations of the distinguished Zabei against St. Nicetas of Aquileia are dispelled: namely, the charge that he was sparing in writing even in the urgent necessity of his Church, and that he neglected to reply to St. Leo, 157. Should this Aquileian bishop be called Niceas or rather Nicetas? 179. What should be thought concerning his homeland? 181. In what year did he assume the Aquileian episcopate? 182. In what year and on what day did he depart to heaven? 183. St. Leo’s letter to him is examined, 184.

St. Nicetas’s writings are catalogued from Gennadius, Honorius, and Trithemius, 185. What the first work of St. Nicetas, *To the Competentes*, which is lost, may have contained is investigated from Gennadius’s indication and from similar works of the holy Fathers, 187. Likewise the second, also lost, *On the Errors of Paganism*, 189. Likewise the third, *On the Faith of the One Majesty*, 190. Some notable points concerning this third work, 191, 192, 193.

What was the fourth work, likewise lost, *Against Genethlialogy*? 193. In all antiquity scarcely any other suitable work on this subject, addressed to the *competentes*, is found, 195. The judgment of two of our Forojulian manuscripts concerning this work of St. Nicetas is examined, and St. Nicetas is defended against the charge of Pelagianism or Semipelagianism, 196, 197.

What the fifth work of St. Nicetas, *On the Creed*, recently discovered, is, is explained, 198. Whether this work, or sermon on the Creed, was delivered by St. Nicetas to the *competentes* at the handing over of the Creed or rather at their recitation of it is investigated, 199, 200.

What the sixth work of St. Nicetas, which is lost, *On the Victim of the Paschal Lamb*, was, and whether it was delivered to the properly so-called *competentes* or rather to the neophytes or infants, 200, 204. The seventh book of St. Nicetas, long known, is reviewed: it is the work *To a Fallen Virgin*. Its vicissitudes are indicated, its epitome is given, its value is explained, and its use among students of ecclesiastical learning is described, 205 ff.

Fragments of St. Nicetas’s lost works are examined, and it is investigated to which work each should be assigned, 206 ff. What was St. Nicetas’s style? 209, 210. At what time and in what place did St. Nicetas write the works indicated? 210 ff. Did St. Nicetas produce anything else apart from the works indicated? 213.

The items mentioned elsewhere concerning St. Nicetas, or under the name of some Nicetas, are catalogued, as are also those that we conjecture to have been written by him, 214, 215, 216. The holiness of the life of St. Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, is demonstrated, as is the reputation for holiness with which he died, from the inscription of his name in the Martyrologies, 217.

When did St. Nicetas acquire a place in the Martyrologies? 218. Although the name of St. Nicetas does not belong to the genuine and original Hieronymian Martyrology, the addition of his name to those same Hieronymian Martyrologies is nevertheless extremely ancient, 219.

The objections of distinguished men are answered—those who, in the Martyrologies where St. Nicetas is mentioned under 10 Kalends of July, etc., wish to see Nicetas the Dacian rather than the Aquileian, and who say that the mention of St. Nicetas the Dacian on 7 January in the Roman Martyrology was an arbitrary later addition, 220, 223.

The holiness of St. Nicetas is also shown in another way, especially from the two works by him that survive, 223, 224. What should now be thought about the cult of St. Nicetas of Aquileia, especially in the Aquileian Church? 224, 230. The observations of learned men, and also of the distinguished Zabei, on this matter are answered, 225 ff.

No relics of the sacred remains of St. Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia—as also of the other Aquileian bishops, St. Valerian and St. Chromatius—exist among us; nor is there evidence that they ever existed in the Aquileian Church’s celebrated treasury of sacred relics, 229. What do we infer from this together with the distinguished Mazzochi? 230.

Certain statements by St. Nicetas that might appear to have been expressed either less exactly or too harshly are examined, 264 ff.

Cardinal Noris did not write with sufficient accuracy that very many members of the clergy in the Aquileian Church were suspected of the Pelagian heresy in the time of St. Leo the Great, 170. See *Pelagians* and *Pelagianism*.

Novatian, the false pope, was said to have been ordained bishop by two Aquileian bishops, Marcellus and Alexander, 109. But these are shown to have been none other than auxiliary bishops of the Aquileian Church, ibid. and following. Indeed, they were not Novatian’s ordainers, nor, probably, were they his followers in the schism, 111.

The error of the Novatians, who denied that the Church possessed the power to forgive certain more serious sins; and whether St. Nicetas at one point in the *Booklet to a Fallen Virgin* expressed the Novatian view, 284 ff. In a matter of this kind, doctrine must be distinguished from discipline, 285.

## O

The word *oculorum* in the Gospel text “There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” is found in both works of St. Nicetas, 6. This reading belonged to the very small number of manuscripts in the old Latin version called the Itala, 7. The use of this reading in both works confirms their authenticity, ibid. The Maurist editors of the works of St. Ambrose did not notice that St. Nicetas used this word *oculorum* twice in the *Booklet to a Fallen Virgin*, 8. In citing the same Gospel text, the holy Fathers of the Church—Ambrose, Jerome, and Augustine—never used this reading in the genuine works that we possess, ibid.

There were two consuls named Opilio: one in the year 453, the other in 524, 78. The first consulship in the funerary inscription of the holy Aquileian virgin Columba is defended, ibid.

The Lord’s Prayer. Along with the Creed of faith, the Lord’s Prayer was also handed over to those preparing for baptism; bishops also preached sermons on this prayer, 152.

The Osopian stone of St. Columba the virgin. See *St. Columba*.

## P

Paganism. See *Paganism* and *Pagans*.

Antonio Pagi, criticized by Wesseling for the word “Romatian” in Gennadius, which he would also have liked to see in the *Itinerary of Antoninus*, 84.

The apology of St. Pamphilus the martyr for Origen; and what St. Jerome thought of it, 4. Under the name of St. Pamphilus, in Rufinus’s translation, there exists a book *Against the Mathematicians*, etc., 195.

St. Paulinus of Nola, bishop, friend of St. Nicetas the Dacian. His poem to Nicetas on his return to Dacia, 10 ff., 35, 36. In what year of his age and of the common era did he depart to heaven? 35.

St. Paulinus, patriarch of Aquileia. His Council of Forum Julii [Col. 1242], and its two canons concerning virginal discipline, 75. The name of this St. Paulinus is not found in the thirteenth-century calendar of the Aquileian Church, 227. He first introduced the word *Filioque* into the Creed in Italy, 273.

Sins and sinners. St. Nicetas taught that sins lead to death, 234. The more serious sins are those that give scandal to the faithful and cause unbelievers to blaspheme the name of the Lord, 234. Sinners should not flatter themselves in their sins because of the multitude of their companions, 234.

It was the common practice of the Church in St. Nicetas of Aquileia’s time that a sin discovered through an investigation was considered greater and more serious than if the sinner had voluntarily confessed it, 258. According to the discipline of that period, some hidden sins also had to be disclosed publicly in confession, so that the public remedy of penance might be undertaken, 259. What investigation into sins and denunciation meant at that time, and what discipline from it now remains in force? ibid.

What should be thought of the particular sin of a holy virgin who had secretly permitted herself to be violated and was later discovered unwillingly? 259, 260. Of what crime was the violator of a holy virgin considered guilty? 263.

A common distinction among the Fathers between sins against God and sins against brothers, or human beings, 285. Among sins against God, indeed among the more serious sins of this kind, St. Nicetas rightly counted the sin of his fallen virgin, 285. What are sins against the Holy Spirit? And did St. Nicetas and the other Fathers declare sins of this kind against the Holy Spirit altogether unforgivable? 289, 290.

Pelagians and Pelagianism. The Pelagian heresy did indeed have followers in the province of Aquileia, including members of the ecclesiastical order, from the beginning of the fifth century, 167. A letter of St. Leo the Great to the bishop of Aquileia, approximately in the year 442, concerning those suspected of the Pelagian heresy, ibid. and 168.

The Pelagians never established a separate pseudo-church for themselves, ibid. and 169. They were few in number in the Aquileian Church under Pope St. Leo the Great and belonged only to the clerical order; nor were they Pelagians absolutely and openly, 170. What was the state of Pelagianism in the province of Aquileia after the cited letter of St. Leo from the year 442? ibid. What was its state when Januarius was bishop of Aquileia, to whom St. Leo sent another letter in 447? 171, 172. Finally, what was its state in the time of Bishop St. Nicetas, who held the Aquileian episcopate from 454 to 485? ibid.

St. Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, is vindicated from the charge of Pelagianism or Semipelagianism against the judgment of two Forojulian manuscripts of Gennadius, 196, 197.

St. Peter Chrysologus, bishop of Ravenna. His letter to Eutyches, and his position against the Eutychian error, corresponding to the positions of Pope St. Leo in his letter to Flavian and of St. Nicetas in the *Explanation of the Creed*, 31. From the sermons of this same St. Peter we infer that not a few pagans existed at that time in that part of Italy and in his own Ravennate diocese, 139.

He celebrated Adelphus or Delphinus, bishop of Aquileia, with outstanding praise in a sermon delivered to the people of Ravenna, with Adelphus himself present, 217. He arranged his degrees, as it were, excellently in the profession of faith; he assigned its place to belief and explained what belief is worth, 265. What did he think concerning the judgment of the last living? Were they to be brought before judgment after a preceding death, or without death? 269.

Phantasm. Eutyches and the Eutychians said that the Lord’s incarnation took place in a phantom, 22, 25. St. Leo the Great called the Eutychians “phantasmatic Christians,” 25. St. Avitus of Vienne called Eutyches a preacher of the Phantom, 32. St. Avitus wrote books against the Phantom itself, 33.

St. Pope Pius I, by birth an Aquileian, is displayed in a certain painting by Bosius and Aringhi as carrying out the initiation of a Christian virgin, etc., 251.

A passage of Pliny concerning the port and river of Romatinum, 89.

The eternity of punishment for the impious is clearly asserted by St. Nicetas, 232, 233.

Penance, understood as the disposition of the soul by which we detest sins and freely make satisfaction to God for our sins. St. Nicetas taught that penance was necessary for the fallen, 235. The magnitude of penance must correspond to the weight of the conscience, ibid.

Penance, understood as a part of the ancient ecclesiastical discipline. It was the common practice of the Church in St. Nicetas of Aquileia’s time that a sin discovered through an investigation was punished with more severe penance than if the sinner had voluntarily confessed it, 258.

For how long did St. Nicetas impose penance on his fallen virgin? 260. The authority of St. Cyprian and canon 13 of the Council of Elvira concerning public penance to be imposed on fallen virgins is examined, 260, 261. St. Nicetas calls the penitential course the “contest of penance”; and why? 261.

What external acts was the fallen virgin of his monastery required to perform in public penance, according to St. Nicetas’s prescription [Col. 1243], 261. What else was she required to do at the same time in order to conceive inwardly and nourish sorrow for the disgrace committed? 262. For how long did St. Nicetas impose public penance on the violator of the holy virgin? 263. What penitential acts were to constitute this violator’s public penance? 263. In imposing public penances in antiquity, consideration was given both to sex and to strength, ibid.

Penance, understood as the sacrament by which absolution is granted to sinners. According to the ancient sanction of certain canons, absolution was not granted even at the end of life to those guilty of certain crimes, 285, 286. From this ancient severity perhaps arose the present strictness of discipline by which absolution for certain sins is reserved either to the Supreme Pontiff or to the ordinaries of the places, ibid.

That ancient severity was not, however, the discipline of the whole Church; nevertheless, it prevailed in some places even in the fifth century and in St. Nicetas’s own time, 286, 287. During that same fifth century the Roman pontiffs placed a limit on this severity; finally, St. Leo the Great sanctioned that it should thereafter be observed only with regard to those who had sinned against God by abandoning the faith, 287, 288.

Alexander Politus. He accuses the opinion concerning the holiness of Bishop Nicetas among the Aquileians of novelty, and does not approve the cult rendered to him by them if they did so without some definite judgment of the Roman Church, 224.

The pomps of the devil, to which ancient Christians renounced before baptism prior to Constantine the Great: what were they? 44. What was understood by the term “pomps” after pomps in the proper sense had ceased with the granting of peace to the Church? 44 and 45.

The monastery of Pomposa. The library of this once-famous monastery, toward the end of the eleventh century, possessed St. Nicetas’s booklet *On the Faith of the One Majesty*, or *On the Reason of Faith*, which Gennadius mentions and which we lack, 191. Why, then, did this booklet of St. Nicetas, which existed in the monastery of Pomposa at the end of the eleventh century, later perish? 193.

The same library possessed two other works of St. Nicetas, bound in the same volume as the preceding booklet and not mentioned by the ancient writers, 214.

The modern Portus Gruarius is not the port of Romatinum indicated by Pliny, 91, 92. Portus Gruarius grew from the ruins of Concordia after the disaster inflicted by Attila, ibid. Portus Gruarius is probably that city of Romatiana about which Gennadius speaks, 92, 93. Portus Gruarius perhaps ought more properly to have been called the new port of Romatinum, or the city of Romatiana, ibid.

St. Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, probably sat for some time at this new port of Romatinum; hence he was called bishop of the city of Romatiana, 131. The bishop of Concordia now sits at this Portus Gruarius; for that reason he is also commonly called the bishop of Portus Gruarius, 133.

The port of Romatinum indicated by Pliny stood beyond Concordia, at the mouth of the river Romatinum, 91, 92. After the fate of Aquileia and Concordia, Pliny’s port of Romatinum vanished, as it were, from the world, 92. Before the destruction of Aquileia and Concordia, auxiliary bishops of the Aquileian Church probably sat at this port of Romatinum, situated in this part of Venetia, 123. Perhaps St. Nicetas did so as well, if he was an auxiliary bishop of the Aquileian Church at the port of Romatinum before taking the helm of that Church, 124, 134.

Presbyters and the presbyterate. In ancient times all, or nearly all, the priests of the episcopal presbyterate also possessed episcopal ordination, 97. Merely auxiliary bishops were generally not distinguished from presbyters and were also called presbyters, 100. The Council of Sardica decreed that a bishop should not be established in a village or small town where a presbyter was sufficient, ibid. St. Leo the Great recalled this same principle to the African bishops, 108.

At the Council of Aquileia in the year 381 no more than two presbyters attended; all the others were bishops, 112. Those presbyters who in the Acts of St. Hermagoras, the first bishop of Aquileia, are said to have been sent by him to the city of Tergeste and to other cities likewise may also have been endowed with episcopal rank, 119.

Prudentius. Whether he admitted in the next life some intermediate state for adults, where there is neither glory nor punishment, 280, 281.

Daily recitation of the fiftieth Psalm is imposed by St. Nicetas on the fallen virgin of his monastery, but only through verse 19, 262. Interrupted recitation of this same psalm, as also of other psalms in the same way, is prescribed in ancient penitential booklets, ibid.

Pseudo-churches. In the *Explanation of the Creed*, St. Nicetas names the pseudo-churches of the Manichaeans, Cataphrygians, and Marcionites, 39. Why not the pseudo-church of the Eutychians? 40. Heretics generally did not establish pseudo-churches for themselves immediately after the rise of their errors, but only after time had passed, 41. The example of the pseudo-churches of the Arians, ibid. and 42.

## R
Ravenna Church. This became an ecclesiastical metropolitan church at least from the time of St. Peter Chrysologus; nevertheless, its bishops were called by the simple title of bishops in documents before the year 553, 60.

Renunciation. See Abrenunciation.

Reservation of souls, whether in the place of light or in the place of darkness, until the day of the Lord’s coming: what is found in St. Nicetas? 275, 279.

Residence of bishops. Formerly it was permissible for bishops to remain anywhere they wished within their own diocese, 125ff. See also Cathedral Church.

Resurrection of the dead. What is meant by St. Nicetas’ words that, when all have been raised, there will be a just distinction between the good and the wicked, and that then the just will shine like the sun, etc., whereas the impious, etc.? 277, 278.

Divine revelations to private individuals concerning private matters were by no means rare in the age of St. Ambrose and St. Nicetas of Aquileia, 132.

Rhipaean Mountains, or Rhipaean regions, 13.

Roman Church, Roman See, Roman pontiff. From ancient times the Roman pontiffs ordained bishops for the peoples, for the conversion of the pagans, p. 11. St. Nicetas the Dacian was perhaps sent from the Roman See into barbarian Dacia, to be the apostle of those peoples there, 11, 15. Three examples of auxiliary bishops of the Roman pontiffs who resided at Rome with those pontiffs and were called bishops of Rome or of the city of Rome, 97, 98. In later centuries they were also called diocesan bishops of the holy apostolic see, 98. Other auxiliary bishops of a different kind belonging to the Roman pontiffs, whom the pontiffs appointed here and there in Latium, Campania, and suburban Tuscia, even in lowly little towns, 101, 102. How narrowly the authority of these bishops was circumscribed, 103. The providence of the apostolic See concerning the excessive multiplication of bishops in the churches of Africa, 107. Even in the fifth century the Roman pontiffs had to fight against pagan superstition raising itself up in the city of Rome itself, 138. Praises of the Roman Church, ibid. Synodal consultations of the East and West with the apostolic See, 184. Consultations of St. Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, with that same See, ibid.

The city of Romatiana—or rather Remesiana, Remisiana, or Romessiana—was situated in Cisdanubian Dacia, 10. St. Paulinus of Nola does not mention this city in his poem addressed to Nicetas as he returned to Dacia, ibid. Variations in the ancient records in naming this city of Cisdanubian Dacia, 84. The city of Romatiana mentioned by Gennadius in the article on Niceas or Nicetas is not to be sought in Dacia, but in the ancient diocese or province of Aquileia, 81ff. Gennadius perhaps was not mistaken when he described his Nicetas as bishop of the city of Romatiana; rather, those were mistaken who sought that same city not merely outside the diocese and province of Aquileia, but also so far away in Cisdanubian Dacia, 83. Yet that city of Dacia is never called Romatiana or Romaciana in the ancient records, 84.

Cardinal Baronius said that Gennadius’ city of Romatiana was Aquileia; and some scholars agreed with Cardinal Baronius, 85. Nevertheless, many more challenged his opinion and the basis of that opinion, in order to place Gennadius’ Romatiana unanimously in Cisdanubian Dacia, 86. Baronius’ opinion—or the basis of that opinion—could, if one wished, be elucidated and in some measure supported even in the present light of scholarship, ibid. But here Baronius must seem altogether to be abandoned in claiming that Gennadius’ city of Romatiana was Aquileia itself; he should instead be defended because, by the name of the city of Romatiana, he understood the Aquileian episcopate itself, 87. Variant readings of the word *Romatiana* in editions and manuscripts of Gennadius, ibid., and 88, 89.

What place in the extensive Aquileian diocese, in the time of St. Nicetas, corresponds to the names Romatiana and the like, which are found in the editions and manuscripts of Gennadius? 89. This place is the port of Romatinus; and our Lucretius Treus was the very first to identify this place in Nicetas, the holy bishop of Aquileia, ibid. The words of Pliny concerning the port of Romatinus are cited, together with variant readings in the Plinian editions for the word *Romatinum*, ibid. and 90. Observations on Pliny’s words by Philippus Cluverius; likewise the views of Hofmann and Baudrand concerning the city of Romatiana, the river Romatinus, and the port of Romatinus, ibid. and 91. Yet Pliny’s port of Romatinus disappeared, as it were, from the world after the disaster caused by Attila, 92. The present-day port of Gruarius, situated on the same river Romatinus, is probably the city of Romatiana mentioned by Gennadius, 92, 93. See Port of Romatinus and Port of Gruarius. See also De Rubeis.

St. Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia, probably withdrew to Pliny’s port of Romatinus, especially in the year 400, when the Aquileian territory lay open to the barbarian forces under the leadership of Alaric; and since he may also have stayed there for a considerable time, he could have been called Bishop Romatinus or Romatius rather than Romanus, 129. At the new port of Romatinus, or Gruarius, St. Nicetas probably began his Aquileian episcopate, and there too he either remained for a long time or returned there again; hence he could be called bishop of the city of Romatiana and be so designated by Gennadius as well, 131. Several examples relevant to this matter from the Church of Milan, then from the Church of Concordia, and finally from the Church of Aquileia itself, ibid. ff.

De Rubeis, Bernardus Maria, an elucidator of Aquileian affairs, attacked Baronius’ opinion concerning Gennadius’ city of Romatiana, 86. He suitably resolved the difficulty concerning the designation of the Roman bishop in the case of St. Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia, by calling him rather Romatinus by origin, from the port of Romatinus in Aquileian territory, 93. But why did he not devise at least something of this kind for St. Nicetas, whom Gennadius called bishop of the city of Romatiana, or even of Romana, as in one manuscript? 94. He rejected two Aquileian bishops named Marcellus and Alexander, but paid no attention to the discipline concerning auxiliary bishops, 109ff.

Rufinus of Aquileia. His Commentary on the Apostles’ Creed, and praise of this Commentary, 67. In what year and in what place he composed that Commentary is not known from the writers, 68. It cannot be doubted that this Commentary became known to the people of Aquileia from the beginning, 69. Venantius Fortunatus deliberately condensed Rufinus’ Commentary into an epitome in his exposition of the Creed, 68, 69. Much in St. Nicetas’ explanation conforms to Rufinus’ Commentary, 70, 71. Rufinus probably composed that Commentary while serving as a presbyter at Aquileia, 143. In his Commentary Rufinus deliberately and carefully attacked paganism, ibid. ff. Rufinus received baptism at Aquileia, not from St. Valerian, the bishop, but from St. Chromatius, then a presbyter at Aquileia, 150. In his Commentary he explains why the bishops of Aquileia inserted additions characteristic of the Aquileian formula into the Apostles’ Creed, 160, 161. He also expressly mentioned the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son, 273.

## S

Sabatier, Petrus, editor of the Latin Itala version, observed that the word *oculorum* (“of the eyes”) in the Gospel text “There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” was used only twice among the ancients, and therefore did not admit it into his text of the Itala, 7.

Salvianus. What is to be said about the madness of the people of Trier concerning circus and theatrical spectacles amid the very destruction of the ruined city? 49, 50. Did Salvianus admit some intermediate state for adults in the other life, where there is neither glory nor punishment? 282, 283.

Cult of the saints and of holy persons. In ancient times all bishops living under the title of saint and holiness were honored with that title, 216. Nevertheless, not all of them received the cult of holiness after death, except bishops crowned with the glory of martyrdom, ibid. Only three Aquileian bishops who were not martyrs, from the first five centuries, obtained the cult of holiness, ibid. Examples are given of fifth-century Aquileian bishops who, although honored during life both as holy men and with the title of holiness, did not at all receive the cult of holiness after death, 217. A testimony to someone’s holiness is the very inclusion of his name in the Martyrologies, ibid. This is so even when he is listed without any title of blessed or saint, 219. The designation “saint” and “blessed” in ancient Martyrologies must not be judged according to the Church’s current discipline, by which the blessed are considered inferior in rank to the saints with respect to cult, 220. The ancient rationale for venerating saints is investigated by eminent scholars, 225. In ancient times only holy martyrs were venerated in the Church, with a feast day appointed together with a special office and Mass; only later, and in small numbers—those who were more renowned—were confessors introduced, 226, 227. The canonization of saints who were not martyrs and belonged to somewhat earlier times began with the discovery of their bodies, 229. St. Nicetas asserts the merits and prayers of the saints on our behalf. He teaches the invocation of the saints, 233.

Canon 6 of the Council of Sardica, concerning the establishment of bishops not in villages or small towns but only in populous cities worthy of an episcopate, 101.

Scythians, a barbarian people: where were they situated? 14.

Sidonius Apollinaris, in the epitaph for Claudianus Mamertus, brother of St. Mamertus, bishop of Vienne, calls him a bishop “second in rank,” that is, apparently, an auxiliary bishop of St. Mamertus, his brother, 99. Sirmond’s opinion does not favor auxiliary bishops, 99.

Holy Spirit. The procession of the Holy Spirit, also from the Son. St. Nicetas of Aquileia did not expressly mention this procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son in his Explanation of the Creed; but in this he shared a common practice with other Fathers, both of his own age and of earlier times, 270. Why St. Nicetas and the other Fathers did not expressly mention the procession of the Holy Spirit also from the Son, ibid., 271. Nevertheless, St. Nicetas and the other Fathers cannot on that account be accused of denying the procession of the Holy Spirit also from the Son, 271, 272. Belief in the procession of the Holy Spirit also from the Son was a common profession in St. Nicetas’ time, even though it was not expressly set forth in the Creed, ibid., 273. Nevertheless, St. Nicetas appears to have made some mention of the procession of the Holy Spirit also from the Son, 273. See *Filioque*.

Intermediate state in the other life, where there is neither glory nor punishment. Did St. Nicetas admit this state in the other life? 279. Several similar expressions of the holy Fathers, both Greek and Latin, are examined, ibid. through 282. Following Jacobus Billius, the ambiguous or insufficiently clear passages of St. Nicetas and of other Fathers and writers on this subject are given a sound interpretation, 282, 283. Their ambiguous or insufficiently clear words are explained by other, clearer passages, especially in the case of St. Nicetas, 283, 284.

Style is the best rule for recognizing works, 4. From style we recognize the authenticity of St. Nicetas’ short works, *On the Creed* and *To the Fallen Virgin*, 5. Something beyond style is ordinarily required in judging writings, 6. The style of the *Explanation of the Creed* reveals Nicetas of Aquileia as its author rather than a Dacian, 154. The style of St. Nicetas’ short works is assessed, and its distinctive character is asserted, 209, 210.

Suffragan churches and suffragan bishops. Suffragan cathedral churches of the Aquileian metropolitan church were, in the course of time, for the most part erected where auxiliary bishops had originally been accustomed to sit for that same Aquileian Church, 116. Four bishops of the suffragan cathedral churches of the Aquileian Church are listed in twelfth- and thirteenth-century records as hereditary canons of the Aquileian Church, 117. Examples are found of bishops and archbishops in Gaul who were canons of the Church of St. Martin of Tours, as well as of bishops of the province of Canterbury in England who were canons of the metropolitan Church of Canterbury itself, ibid. But the canonry held in the Aquileian Church by the four suffragan bishops of that same Church seems to indicate their Aquileian origin: from the time when, as auxiliary bishops, they had perhaps been established there for the Aquileian bishop, they were regarded as belonging to the bosom of that Aquileian Church, ibid. and 118.

Suffragan churches existed in the West in a certain sense even before their mother churches enjoyed the name and dignity of metropolitan churches, 120. The manner is explained in which the primitive suffragan churches arose throughout the Christian world and in which the suffragan churches of the Aquileian metropolitan church were also formed, 121. By what marks of honor did suffragan churches, especially the suffragan churches of the Aquileian province, honor their metropolitan in ancient times? 121, 122. A certain Folcus, archbishop of Reims in the tenth century, called his suffragan bishops his sons, though this was an isolated example, ibid.

## Apostles’ Creed

What was the Apostles’ Creed of the Church of Aquileia, and in what did it differ from the old common Roman Apostles’ Creed? 63. In the time of St. Nicetas the use of the Aquileian Creed had already become obsolete in the Church of Aquileia itself, especially in public expositions of the Creed, 64. Probably long before St. Nicetas’ episcopate the Roman Creed had begun to prevail in the Church of Aquileia, ibid. Even though in St. Nicetas’ time the Roman Creed was publicly handed down in the Church of Aquileia, the old Aquileian formula had not become so obsolete that private individuals did not use it, or that the bishops of that Church did not sometimes employ its additions, for purposes of explanation, in expositions of the Roman Creed, 66. Wherever traces of the old Aquileian Creed are present in explanations of the Roman Creed, those explanations may rightly be regarded as offspring of the Aquileian Church, ibid. The bishops of Aquileia inserted additions into the Apostles’ Creed in order to counter certain heresies that could easily gain access among the people of Aquileia, and probably also for reasons connected with commercial intercourse, 160, 161.

Expositions of the Apostolic Creed were of two kinds: domestic and private, and public and solemn, 151. Inferior clergy, especially deacons, delivered the private expositions to the candidates for baptism; public expositions were always, or almost always, given by bishops, in the exercise of their proper office, 151, 152, 153. The Creed was delivered orally to the candidates; the candidates recited it orally, with every written page strictly forbidden as an aid, 238ff. This was likewise the discipline of the Church of Aquileia, 240. How long did this discipline continue in the Church, and especially in the Church of Aquileia? 241. St. Nicetas calls the creed of faith a pact made by the candidates with the Lord, 242. He also calls it a reminder of faith, 242.

## T

Church of Tergeste. The bishops of Tergeste are presented in ancient Aquileian records as hereditary canons of the metropolitan Church of Aquileia, 117, 295. In the apostolic age St. Hermagoras, proto-bishop of Aquileia, was the first to send a presbyter and a deacon to the city of Tergeste, 119.

Theater. The city of Aquileia had been equipped with theaters before the disaster caused by Attila, and perhaps afterward as well, 48, 49. Theaters were common even in smaller cities and municipalities, and sometimes existed in the villages themselves, 48.

Theophilus, bishop of the Goths. See Goths.

Treus, Lucretius, author of the work entitled *Sacred Monuments of the Province of Forum Julii*, was the very first to locate in the Church of Aquileia the city of Romatiana of Gennadius and the Roman Martyrology, 89.

Trithemius, Johannes. His testimony concerning St. Nicetas in his work *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, from Fabricius’ edition, 185. What, however, is peculiar in the Frankfurt edition of 1601, printed by Wechel? 182. Trithemius calls St. Nicetas’ first book for the candidates for baptism, which Gennadius describes, by the single word *Praeparatorium* (“Preparatory”), 187.

## U

In ancient times, in Spain, any principal cities were given the designations “city of Rome” and “Rome,” 86. In the early centuries the auxiliary bishops of the Roman pontiffs who resided at Rome with those pontiffs were called bishops of the city of Rome and of Rome, 97, 98.

## V

St. Valerian, bishop of Aquileia. During his episcopate, and while he presided together with St. Ambrose, bishop of Milan, the Council of Aquileia was celebrated in the year 381, 112. Some of the bishops without sees who attended this council probably belonged to Valerian, 113. He did not baptize Rufinus, because at that time he was absent from Aquileia for religious reasons, 150. The name of St. Valerian is absent from the printed calendars and missals of the Aquileian rite; nevertheless, his cult in the Church of Aquileia is asserted, 225, 226. No relics of the sacred ashes of this holy bishop are known, or were known in past centuries, in the Church of Aquileia, 229.

Married veiling: what was it among the pagan Romans, and what among Christians? 249, 250. Tertullian extended to virgins dedicated to God the Apostle’s command concerning women’s veiling in the Church; and why? 249.

Virgin’s veiling. See Virginity and Sacred Virgins.

Venantius Fortunatus, in his *Exposition of the Creed*, deliberately condensed Rufinus’ Commentary on the Apostles’ Creed into an epitome, 68.

Church of Vercelli. The virginal monastery at Vercelli, called that of St. Eusebius, is claimed in a certain book to have been the first in the West, etc., 245.

St. Nicetas reproved fine or delicate clothing among the faithful entrusted to him: what exactly is meant by this delicacy of clothing? 52. The abuse of such clothing does not seem to have prevailed among barbarian peoples, but it easily did so among the people of Aquileia, even after the disaster caused by Attila, 52, 53.

Sacred vigils. St. Nicetas mentions the practice of sacred vigils as prevailing in the Church of Aquileia, 242.

Virginity and sacred virgins. All scholars who have illuminated the subject of sacred virgins, their communities, and their institution have drawn from St. Nicetas’ little book *To the Fallen Virgin*, 72. Virginity was practiced by women at Aquileia, 74. What was decreed concerning virgins, whether consecrated or not consecrated, at the Council of Forum Julii in the year 796, under St. Paulinus, patriarch of Aquileia? 75. St. Columba, a sacred virgin of the Church of Aquileia, who died at the age of ninety in the year 453, and her funerary inscription, 76, 77.

What did the holy Fathers say about the resolve of virginity and about virgins? 235. What was a sacred virgin according to St. Nicetas? 235. What did a virginal body mean in his words and in those of the other Fathers? ibid. What did the glory of virginity and virgins dedicated to God signify in human opinion in the early centuries? 236. With what great care were girls examined before they were admitted to dedicate themselves to virginity for God? 236. What did the teaching of the Church in St. Nicetas’ time say concerning the solemnly expressed resolve of virginity? 237, 238.

What age was required of girls before they could be admitted to make the resolve of virginity? 246. The public and complete profession of the virginal resolve consisted in the solemn veiling, 248, 249. What did the veiling of virgins signify, and from where was this ceremony of veiling virgins derived? ibid. Records of the veiling of virgins in the first and second centuries in the Roman Church, 250, 251. Antiquity called the veil of virgins sacred and holy: where did its sanctity come from? 251. More is transmitted concerning this virginal veil, with respect to its form, material, quality, and use, chiefly from a certain passage of Tertullian, 251, 252.

The veiling of virgins was anciently called consecration, and was always so designated, 252. This was performed at the divine altar, especially on the holy day of the Lord’s Resurrection, 252, 253. This solemnity was also celebrated on the birthday of our Savior; eventually other feast days were appointed for it as well, ibid. What is to be said about the dress of sacred virgins? ibid. and 254. Who initiated the sacred virgins? ibid. The initiation of the virgins was accompanied by an address from the bishop to them, 255. See Hair of Sacred Virgins.

The procession of virgins into the church, in an arranged choir, for the singing of spiritual hymns, for heavenly readings, and also for the sacred night vigils, 255. Precautions inculcated by the Fathers and adopted by the virgins for their very entrance into the church, 256. The virgins of the Bethlehem monastery proceeded to the church only on Sunday, ibid. In the church all the sacred virgins were present together in one place; in the Church of Aquileia that place was also separated by screens and adorned with particular elegance, 257. Religious and noble married women came to this place to receive the kiss of peace from the sacred virgins, ibid. The special care of bishops for sacred virgins, and especially the care of St. Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, for the sacred virgins of his monastery, 257, 258.

The holy Fathers called a sacred virgin who had allowed herself to be violated an adulteress, 259, 260. St. Nicetas twice called his fallen virgin an adulteress; and why? ibid. To preserve the particular honor of intact virginity, no widow was admitted to receive the veil; and virgins themselves who had lost their virginity without personal fault were no longer counted among the community and number of virgins, ibid. Antiquity always punished more severely sacred virgins who through their own fault failed to keep their pact of virginity, ibid. See also Sins and Penance.

Eternal life cannot be attained outside the one Catholic Church, 232. Yet even within this Catholic Church eternal life is prepared only for the faithful who live chastely, ibid.

The living and the dead. How did Rufinus of Aquileia explain these words of the Creed in his Commentary on the Apostles’ Creed? 71. How did St. Nicetas explain them in his Explanation of the Creed? 266. How did St. Augustine and the other Fathers explain them? ibid., through 270. See Last Judgment.

## W

Wesseling, Petrus, editor and commentator on the *Itinerary of Antoninus*, criticized the opinion of Antonius Pagius, who wished to see in that *Itinerary*, in place of the word *Remisiana*, the word *Romatiana* of Gennadius, 84.

## Z

Zabeus, Joannes Prosdocimus, in a special dissertation published at Venice in 1803, proposed to prove that the *Explanation of the Creed* should more probably be attributed to St. Niceas, bishop of the Dacians, than to Blessed Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, 1. He joined the opinion of those who said that the Niceas or Nicetas called by Gennadius bishop of the city of Romatiana was different from the Aquileian Niceas or Nicetas, and defended him as bishop of that city in Dacia which is called Remesiana, or by another name little different from it; and therefore as the same man who was a friend of St. Paulinus of Nola, 1.

Zabeus acknowledged the authenticity of the two short works of Romatian Nicetas that survive: the *Explanation of the Creed* and the little book *To the Fallen Virgin*, 5. In St. Nicetas’ words in chapter 4 of the *Explanation*, Zabeus did not notice a refutation of the newly arisen Eutychian error, but only cursorily perceived a condemnation of those ancient heretics who denied true humanity in Christ and thus in a certain way anticipated Eutyches, 27. From the title in the Ghisi manuscript, “Of Blessed Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia,” Zabeus gratuitously asserts that it must be changed to “Of Blessed Nicetas or Niceas, bishop of Romatiana in Dacia,” 56. He thinks that the title of the *Explanation* was falsely altered by its copyist, who arbitrarily added the word *Aquileiensis*, 58.

Zabeus attempts to show that the *Explanation of the Creed* is not by St. Nicetas of Aquileia because it does not explain a distinctive creed of the Church of Aquileia, but the common ancient creed of the Roman Church; he does not notice that in St. Nicetas’ time the Aquileian Creed had already fallen into disuse with respect to public use and had yielded its place to the Roman Creed, 63. Zabeus did not observe the word *Impassibilis* (“impassible”), from the Aquileian Creed, used in St. Nicetas’ *Explanation*, 67. He considers the other words borrowed from the Aquileian Creed and used by St. Nicetas in the *Explanation*, which are indications of its Aquileian origin, to be entirely without weight in asserting that the same Nicetas held the Aquileian episcopate, ibid.

Variations in the ancient records for designating the Dacian city of which Gennadius’ Nicetas is said to have been bishop; among these, Gennadius’ own *Romatiana* or *Romaciana* has no place, 84. In chapter 7, Zabeus’ arguments against the Aquileian episcopate of Gennadius’ Niceas or Nicetas are deliberately answered, 134ff. Zabeus does not prove that a fifth-century Aquileian bishop would have had no reason to attack paganism in a book appended to his work or on a suitable occasion, just as Gennadius’ Nicetas attacked it, 135ff. See Paganism and Pagans.

The epithets “barbarian” and “savage” do not suit the Dacian people situated on this side of the Danube, where Zabeus places the episcopate of Gennadius’ Nicetas, 136. Zabeus does not establish that Aquileian bishops did not customarily deliver explanations of the Creed personally to catechumens, 150. Zabeus’ assertion is not based on truth: namely, that only those bishops customarily delivered an explanation of the Creed personally to catechumens who were accustomed to speak extemporaneously or whose habit of writing had made the pen readier for them, 153.

The style of the short works of Gennadius’ Nicetas does not support Zabeus in asserting that he was not an Aquileian but a Dacian; indeed, from the style itself we recognize that he was Aquileian rather than Dacian, 154. Zabeus does not prove a lack of practice in writing on the part of Nicetas of Aquileia from the accusations he brings against him—namely, his sparingness in writing even in the urgent need of his Church, and his neglect in replying to St. Leo’s letter, 157.

Zabeus does not resolve the objections drawn from the Latin language which he anticipates; indeed, the deed of the bishop Ulfilas, which Zabeus adduces against himself, is such that it entirely contradicts his position, 159. Once again he improperly calls the peoples of new Cisdanubian Dacia barbarian and savage nations, and confuses the barbarian Dacians with the Romans, 160. Nothing at all is proved against the Aquileian episcopate of Gennadius’ Nicetas by the mention in the *Explanation* of the Marcionites, Cataphrygians, Manichaeans, and even the error of the Arians, 160ff. Rather, Zabeus advances our case when he asserts that the errors of the Marcionites, Cataphrygians, and Manichaeans prevailed among the barbarian regions of Dacia, etc., 164, 165. For these barbarian peoples brought those errors with them into Italy and into Aquileian territory during their many invasions, etc., ibid. The Manichaeans, although not barbarians, could nevertheless have been present in the Aquileian episcopate in Nicetas’ time because of the unhappy condition of those times, 166.

There was no reason for St. Nicetas to mention the Pelagians or Pelagianism in chapter 10 of the *Explanation*, where he discusses the pseudo-churches of heretics and schismatics; and why? 167ff. Zabeus attempts to prove a recent cult of St. Nicetas of Aquileia within the Church of Aquileia itself from the absence of Nicetas’ name in all the surviving calendars and proper missals of the Church of Aquileia; but this observation is adequately answered, 224.

Zaccharias, Franciscus Antonius, wrongly accused Fontanini concerning his interpretation of the funerary inscription of Columba, the sacred virgin of Aquileia, 78.

St. Zeno, bishop of Verona. His excellent treatise, or sermon, *On the Twelve Signs*, addressed to the newly baptized after baptism, 195, 196.

St. Zosimus, Roman pontiff, published a *Tractoria* in the year 418 against the errors of Pelagius and Coelestius, 167.

**APOLOGY FOR ST. VALERIAN**, by Theophilus Raynaudus. 757

**PROLOGUE.**—The purpose and method of undertaking Valerian’s defense. 757

**CHAPTER I.**—Valerian’s see. On his age, nation, ancestry, private status, and conjectural circumstances. 759

**CHAPTER II.**—What seemed, or could have seemed, to tell against Valerian. 764

**CHAPTER III.**—Valerian’s first defense concerning Semi-Pelagianism, and its rejection. 771

**CHAPTER IV.**—After presenting a genuine exposition of Semi-Pelagianism, the way is prepared for Valerian’s legitimate exemption from that taint. 774

**CHAPTER V.**—It is directly demonstrated that Valerian rejected the Semi-Pelagianism just described. 789

**CHAPTER VI.**—What in earlier passages seemed to suggest Semi-Pelagianism in Valerian is shown to be entirely Catholic. 792

## ST. NICETAS

Preface by Peter Braida. 837

**ON THE RULE OF FAITH.** 847

**ON THE POWER OF THE HOLY SPIRIT.** 853

**ON THE VARIOUS TITLES APPROPRIATE TO OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST.** 863

**EXPLANATION OF THE CREED.** 865

Six fragments. 873

**BRAIDA’S DISSERTATION ON ST. NICETAS.** 875

**PROLOGUE.**—The aim and arrangement of the dissertation.

**CHAPTER I.**—Whether he was bishop of the Church of Aquileia or of another church in Dacia, the man whom Gennadius calls bishop of the city of Romatiana was beyond doubt the single author both of the *Explanation of the Creed for the Candidates for Baptism* and of the little book *To a Fallen Virgin*; these two works we now publish together for the first time under the name of St. Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia. 877

**CHAPTER II.**—Niceas or Nicetas, famous for his friendship with St. Paulinus, bishop of Nola, was not bishop of the city of Romatiana established in Dacia on this side of the Danube; rather, he held an episcopate beyond the Danube. 882

**CHAPTER III.**—Niceas, or Nicetas, bishop of the city of Romatiana mentioned by Gennadius, is not that Dacian Niceas or Nicetas who was a friend of St. Paulinus, bishop of Nola, and celebrated in his praises. 893

**CHAPTER IV.**—The Niceas, or Nicetas, bishop of the city of Romatiana mentioned by Gennadius, is beyond doubt Niceas, or Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, who flourished in the time of St. Leo the Great and to whom a letter of that holy pontiff survives. 924

**CHAPTER V.**—The city of Romatiana mentioned by Gennadius is not to be sought in Dacia, but in the old diocese or province of Aquileia; probably it is the place called Portus Romatianus, or Romatinus, or Romatius, not far from Concordia, which Pliny named from the river of the same name; or it is the place now called Portus-Gruarius, situated on the same river Romatium, or Romatinum, or Romatianum, which flows through it. 947

**CHAPTER VI.**—Niceas, or Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, was probably called bishop of the city of Romatiana either because, before ascending to the episcopal see of Aquileia, he had been an auxiliary bishop of the Church of Aquileia at the harbor situated on the Romatium or Romatinum, or because he frequently held his seat at the harbor or city of that name, even while he held the helm of the Church of Aquileia. 959

**CHAPTER VII.**—The arguments of the distinguished Zabeus against the Aquileian episcopate of Gennadius’s Niceas or Nicetas are answered. The authority and observations of the distinguished man Michael Denis are also addressed. 995

**CHAPTER VIII.**—On St. Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, and his works, both those now published and those either lost or still hidden; also on the fragments made known to us through the study and diligence of the most learned Michael Denis. Also on his sanctity and cult. 1033

**CHAPTER IX.**—Certain matters worthy of attention are presented, both concerning doctrine and morals and concerning discipline, from the works and fragments of St. Nicetas. 1080

**CHAPTER X.**—Certain statements are examined that might seem to have been expressed by St. Nicetas either less precisely or too harshly. 1110

**APPENDIX.**—TWO ANCIENT DOCUMENTS OF THE CHAPTER OF AQUILEIA. 1135

**END OF VOLUME FIFTY-TWO**
